context: An application for registration of copyright shall be in the prescribed form and shall contain particulars relating to the work, including its title, author, date of creation, and ownership details as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish a statement of ownership declaring whether they are the original creator or have acquired rights through assignment or other legal means. Where an application relates to a published work, evidence of publication, such as copies of newspapers or journals containing the work, may be required. Any subsequent alteration in ownership after the initial application must be notified under this Act and shall not invalidate the registration unless specifically determined otherwise by the Registrar.

An application for registration of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be made to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and shall contain particulars relating to the author of the work, the producer of the film, and the first publication, if any. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as may be required by the Receiving Officer to verify the statements made in the application. Where an application relates to a work which incorporates pre-existing copyright material, the applicant shall provide details regarding the ownership of those rights and demonstrate due diligence in securing necessary permissions or licenses. Any alteration to particulars submitted within the initial application requires notification to the Copyright Office and may necessitate additional verification procedures as provided herein.

An application for registration of copyright shall be made in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee, to the Copyright Office. The applicant must provide satisfactory evidence establishing their ownership or exclusive right to claim copyright in the work concerned; failure to do so may result in rejection of the application. Where an application is rejected, the Registrar shall issue a reasoned order detailing the grounds for such rejection and providing the applicant with an opportunity to submit further documentation or clarification within a specified period. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting their application may appeal to the relevant judicial authority as provided herein. The Copyright Office shall maintain records of all applications received and decisions rendered, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

An application for registration of copyright shall be made in the prescribed form and shall contain a statement of ownership, specifying whether the applicant is the author or an authorized assignee. The application must identify the work in sufficient detail to allow for its unambiguous identification; this includes providing particulars regarding title, authorship, date of first publication where applicable, and language of the work. Every such application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Where the work is a musical composition, the application shall also include details pertaining to lyrics or associated text. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. An incomplete application may be rejected, and notice of rejection shall be served upon the applicant, providing an opportunity for amendment within a stipulated period.

An application for registration of copyright shall be made in the prescribed form and shall contain a statement of ownership by the applicant, affirming that they are the exclusive owner of the claimed copyright or duly authorized to make the application on behalf of the owner. The application must specify the work to which the copyright relates, including its title and year of first publication where applicable. Provided that, if the work is an unpublished musical composition, the application may include a statement regarding such unpublished status. Further, the applicant shall furnish along with the application certified copies of any existing registrations relating to the same work in other countries. Any false or misleading information provided within the application renders it liable for rejection under this Act.

Any person claiming ownership of copyright in any work shall make an application to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. Such application must specify the particulars of ownership, nature of the work, and details of first publication, if applicable. Failure to disclose material facts in the application shall render the applicant liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Copyright Office may reject an application if it finds that the information provided is incomplete or misleading, and such rejection may be appealed before the Controller. Any wilful false statement made in an application constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and fine.

Where the owner of copyright in an artistic work desires to grant a license or assign their rights therein, they shall submit a formal application to the designated Copyright Office, detailing the scope and duration of the proposed arrangement. Such application must specify the territory covered by the license or assignment and identify all parties involved, including the licensor, licensee, or assignee. The owner may reserve certain exclusive rights under this Act, provided that such reservation is clearly stated within the application and does not unduly restrict the reasonable use of the work. Any subsequent modification to a granted license requires another application, subject to approval by the Copyright Office. An assignment shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the office, and failure to register will render the assignee unable to enforce their rights under this Act against third parties.

An application for registration of copyright shall be deemed invalid if the applicant fails to demonstrate exclusive ownership of the work in question at the time of its creation, subject to proof that the applicant was duly authorized by the original creator. Where a claim of joint authorship is asserted within an application, the Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the contributions of each claimant and their respective rights. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the validity of an application or the determination of ownership may appeal to the relevant judicial forum within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate authority shall consider whether the applicant has discharged the burden of proof as provided herein, and may affirm, reverse, or modify the original order.

An application for registration of copyright shall be made in the prescribed form and manner to the Copyright Office, specifying particulars of the work, the author, and the claimant. The applicant shall furnish proof of ownership or entitlement as may be required by the Registrar. Where the work is a derivative work, the application must clearly identify the original work from which it is derived and state the nature of the derivation. In cases where an international convention application has been filed in respect of the work within six months prior to the date of the Indian application, such fact shall be disclosed in the application, along with details of the receiving office and the reference number assigned thereto. The Registrar may require further documentation or information from the applicant to verify the correctness of the particulars furnished. Any alteration to the particulars stated in an application after its submission shall only be permissible with prior written consent of the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of copyright is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such rejection to the relevant High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Such appeal may be made on grounds that the Registrar’s decision was erroneous in law or fact, including but not limited to misinterpretation of originality criteria or improper consideration of evidence presented. The applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating such error; however, the Court may consider any reference use mark appearing on submitted materials as relevant context for assessing claimed authorship. It is provided that the High Court may require the Registrar to submit further documentation and reasoning supporting their decision prior to rendering judgment.

For the purposes of this Act, "trade mark" shall mean any sign, symbol, device, lettering, numerals, shapes, configurations, colours or any combination thereof adopted to distinguish goods or services of one enterprise from those of others and shall include any element that may constitute a trade mark as provided herein. A trade mark may be registered in respect of goods or services, or both, by way of use or intention to use. The registration of a trade mark does not confer upon the proprietor any right to prevent the use of the same sign or symbol by others unless such use is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin of the goods or services.

An applicant seeking registration of a trademark shall submit a request in the form specified by the Trade Marks Rules, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must clearly identify the mark proposed for registration and state the goods or services with which it is associated. Where the mark incorporates a geographical indication as defined under this Act, the applicant shall furnish an affidavit confirming their entitlement to use the said indication and detailing measures taken to prevent its misuse. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the distinctiveness of the trademark and its potential impact on existing registered marks. Any representation or statement made in the application is subject to verification during examination.

Any person claiming ownership of a registered trademark shall, upon discovery of infringement occurring within the territorial jurisdiction of a Trade Marks Registry, file a complaint with the Registrar. The complaint must specify the nature and extent of the alleged infringing use, including details regarding the mark infringed and the goods or services in relation to which such use occurs. Failure to provide these particulars may result in the rejection of the complaint under this Act. The Registrar shall, after providing notice to the respondent and affording them an opportunity for a hearing, determine whether infringement has indeed occurred. In cases where the Chairperson deems it necessary, expert testimony relating to reputation or dilution may be considered during proceedings. Any order issued by the Registrar is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

The term "Registrar" as used herein refers to the individual appointed by the Central Government to administer matters relating to copyright registration and related processes under this Act. The Registrar shall possess qualifications deemed appropriate by the government, typically including experience in law or intellectual property administration. Decisions of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of applications for copyright registration are subject to review as provided herein. Furthermore, the Registrar may delegate specific functions pertaining to examination of works and procedural aspects of registration to designated officers working under their direct supervision. The Registrar’s actions shall be guided by principles of fairness and transparency.

Applications for registration of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works may be made to the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain particulars relating to the work, the author, and the claimant, provided that where the applicant is not the author, they must furnish proof of assignment or other legal authorization under this Act. The Registrar shall scrutinize each application to ascertain compliance with the requirements herein stipulated; any deficiency shall be brought to the notice of the applicant for rectification within a period specified by the Registrar. Upon satisfactory verification and payment of prescribed fees, the work shall be admitted to registration, and an entry made in the Register of Copyrights.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of copyright, or refusal thereof, or concerning rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Tribunal may, after affording the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the order appealed against or substituting it with a new order. Any party to appeal proceedings before the Appellate Tribunal may apply to have a question of law arising in connection with the appeal referred for determination to a High Court. The Registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to any matter under consideration by the Appellate Tribunal.

Applications for registration of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works shall be made to the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. Every application so filed shall contain a statement of ownership by the applicant and particulars of the work, including its title, author, nationality, and first publication details, if any. The Registrar may require such further information from the applicant as he deems necessary for verification under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar is empowered to conduct searches and inquiries as deemed appropriate for ensuring compliance with the provisions herein.

The application for registration of literary or artistic works, as provided herein, shall be accompanied by three printed copies of the work, unless such work is in a form not susceptible to reproduction in physical copies, in which case the applicant may submit an equivalent digital representation conforming to standards prescribed by the Central Government. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding authorship, ownership, and first publication details, if deemed necessary for verification under this Act. Any alteration or addition made to a registered work subsequent to its initial registration shall be reported to the Registrar within thirty days of such modification; failure to comply will render the amended work subject to fresh examination and potential rejection. The Registrar’s decision on any matter relating to registration is final, subject to appeal before the relevant judicial authority as stipulated under this Act.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of copyright, examine whether the work is original and satisfies the requirements as provided herein. Failure to comply with prescribed formalities during submission will render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing, confirm, vary or reverse the order of the Registrar. Deliberate submission of false information during application processing shall attract penalties as determined under this Act and render the applicant liable for prosecution.

The assignment of copyright in any musical work registered under this Act, or subsequently registered following an alteration to such work, shall require prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignor, assignee, and the precise scope of rights transferred. Such notification must be accompanied by a sworn affidavit verifying the authenticity of the agreement and confirming that the assignor possesses full proprietary interest in the copyright being assigned. The Registrar may, after providing reasonable opportunity for objection from any interested party, record the assignment and issue a certificate thereof, which shall be prima facie evidence of the transfer. Any subsequent licensing of performing rights within the assigned work requires consent of the assignee, unless explicitly permitted under the recorded assignment agreement. Failure to notify the Registrar prior to assignment will render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor.

The application for registration of copyright, submitted in accordance with the prescribed form, may be rejected by the Registrar if he is satisfied that the work does not meet the originality threshold as defined under this Act or if the particulars furnished are demonstrably false. Any applicant aggrieved by such a rejection order shall have the right to appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said order. The grounds for appeal shall be limited to allegations of error apparent on the face of the record and misapplication of law, provided that the appellant must demonstrate prejudice arising directly from the Registrar's decision. Failure to comply with this procedural requirement will render the appeal inadmissible.

The term “Registrar” in relation to this Act means the individual appointed by the Central Government to perform the functions prescribed herein, including but not limited to receiving applications for copyright registration, examining works for compliance with statutory requirements, and maintaining records of registered copyrights. The Registrar shall be empowered to request information from applicants regarding the origin and derivation of any element within a work submitted for registration, particularly where such elements may relate to traditional knowledge or genetic resources. Any royalties derived from commercial exploitation of works incorporating material sourced from the national gene fund shall be subject to reporting requirements as determined by the Central Government under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “registration” shall mean the process whereby a society authorized under this Act receives and examines applications for the registration of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, and subsequently enters such works in its Register. An application for registration shall include particulars as prescribed, including but not limited to the name and address of the applicant, details regarding copyright ownership, and a statement affirming the originality of the work. The mere submission of an application does not confer any right under this Act; rights vest initially in the author or assignee thereof. Registration is prima facie evidence of the particulars entered in the Register, subject to appeal as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a literary work, musical work, dramatic work, cinematograph film or sound recording shall submit with the application prescribed forms containing particulars relating to the ownership of copyright in the work. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as he deems necessary for verifying the claim of ownership and authenticity of the work submitted for registration. Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in the work, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present his case under this Act. Registration confers no right of copyright but serves only as prima facie evidence of ownership, subject to the provisions regarding rectification of entries. Any alteration or correction to particulars entered in the Register may be made as provided herein upon application and verification.

Any individual claiming ownership of a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work shall be eligible for voluntary registration thereof as provided herein. Upon receipt of an application and requisite fee, the Copyright Office may register such work, subject to verification of originality and compliance with prescribed formalities. Failure to disclose material facts in the application renders the registration voidable at the discretion of the Controller. Where a work is registered, the claimant shall be presumed to be the first owner unless proven otherwise through clear evidence presented before an adjudicating officer. Any person infringing upon the exclusive rights conferred by a valid registration shall be liable for damages, including compensatory and punitive elements, as determined by civil courts. The right to seek injunctive relief against further infringement is expressly granted to registered owners.

An application for registration of a literary work, musical work, dramatic work, cinematograph film or sound recording shall be made to the Receiving Officer in such form and containing such information as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish with the application a certified copy of the work being registered, or where the work is not capable of being copied, such other evidence as the Registrar deems appropriate. Upon receipt of an application, the Receiving Officer shall assign it a serial number and intimate this to the applicant. Any person claiming to be affected by the registration may file objections within thirty days from the date of publication of the journal containing particulars of the work applied for registration. The Registrar shall consider any such objection and provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit their response, after which a decision regarding registration shall be made as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of an artistic work shall submit with the application three true copies of the work, unless the Registrar is satisfied that owing to the nature of the work, submission of copies is not feasible. The application must specify the full name and address of the owner of copyright in the work, and where applicable, details regarding any joint ownership or assignment of rights. Registration shall be refused if the applicant fails to comply with these requirements, or if the Registrar deems the submitted copies to be inadequate for proper examination under this Act. Any alteration made to the work after the date of application will render the registration voidable at the discretion of the Registrar. The Registrar may require further documentation verifying ownership where doubts arise concerning the accuracy of information provided in the application.

Any individual seeking to assert ownership claims regarding artistic works, including but not limited to musical compositions and cinematograph films, shall be required to obtain prior registration as provided herein. Failure to secure such registration before initiating legal proceedings alleging infringement will render the claimant ineligible for remedies relating to damages or injunctive relief under this Act. Any application for registration may be rejected if it contains false statements materially affecting the validity of the claim, in which case a subsequent application concerning the same work shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny and potential penalties. The Registrar may impose a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees upon any applicant found to have wilfully misrepresented facts during the registration process.

The right to grant non-exclusive licenses for reproduction and distribution of registered works shall vest solely with the registrant, subject to conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment of copyright in a work already registered requires prior notification to the Copyright Office and shall be deemed invalid unless such notification is received within thirty days of the execution of the assignment agreement. Furthermore, any subsequent licensing undertaken by an assignee must explicitly reference the original registration details maintained under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving representations from aggrieved parties, investigate instances where licenses are granted in contravention of these provisions and may issue directives to ensure compliance with the terms of the initial registration. An owner seeking to sub-license a registered work shall provide a detailed accounting of royalties distributed within six months of each fiscal year.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an applicant aggrieved by any decision relating to the refusal or acceptance of registration of a work shall have the right to appeal to the appellate authority constituted under this Act. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the order is challenged. The appellate authority, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the Controller, shall pass a reasoned order confirming, reversing or modifying the decision appealed against. Any further dispute arising from the order of the appellate authority may be subject to judicial review under principles of natural justice, provided that such review does not extend to questioning the merits of the original registration determination.

The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all applications for registration of works under this Act, including details pertaining to the claimant’s asserted ownership and the nature of the work. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate authority shall consider whether the Registrar acted reasonably in interpreting the criteria for eligibility under this Act, particularly concerning claims based on geographical indication respect relating to traditional artistic expressions. Provided that a claimant demonstrating prior customary usage and community consensus regarding an artwork’s origin may challenge a registration denial. Subject to due process, the Controller's order shall be final.

Where any person claims copyright in a layout design connected with a published book or other publication, he may apply for registration under this Act. Such application shall be accompanied by prescribed fees and particulars relating to the claimant and the work. The Registrar shall entertain an application only if the layout design is original and does not violate any existing right. Upon being satisfied that the applicant fulfills all requirements as provided herein, the Registrar shall register the layout design and issue a certificate of registration. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The remedies available under this Act for infringement of copyright in a registered layout design shall include damages and an injunction preventing further infringing acts.

For the purposes of this Act, a "geographical indication" means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. A geographical indication may include signs, symbols, shapes, pictures, letters, numerals, words, configurations, sounds or any combination thereof. The distinctive qualities associated with a geographical indication shall be inherent in the product and directly linked to its specified geographical location; provided that such link must be demonstrable through established production practices or historical usage. Any use of a geographical indication which does not conform to these requirements shall be deemed invalid under this Act.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication, the goods or services for which it is used, the area of its origin, and the history and characteristics of the product or service. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods or services originates from the specified geographical territory. Where an objection is raised against registration on grounds of likelihood of confusion with any prior mark registered under another Act, the application may proceed to hearing before the Registrar. Any person claiming rights in a prior mark shall be entitled to submit their response as provided herein. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant regarding the geographical indication’s distinctiveness.

Any person claiming damages for the use of a Geographical Indication in contravention of this Act may institute legal proceedings subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods. Such claim shall include compensation for loss of profits reasonably attributable to the infringement, and further, any dilution of the distinctiveness associated with the registered Geographical Indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an interested party or suo moto, issue a cease-and-desist order directing the infringing entity to immediately halt the unauthorized use. Failure to comply with such order shall render the infringer liable for penalties as provided herein and subject to further legal action by aggrieved proprietors of the Geographical Indication. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available at law or equity, ensuring adequate protection against unfair exploitation.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence, satisfactory to the Registrar, establishing the origin of the goods and their association with a particular geographical area. Where the name of the Geographical Indication includes an expression indicating quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods, the application shall specify the characteristics which give rise to that quality, reputation or other characteristic. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness and protectability of the proposed Geographical Indication. Any person claiming to be an interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of a notice under this Act, file objections relating to the registration of the Geographical Indication.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the Geographical Indication as proposed to be registered, a map indicating clearly the territorial limits of the area of origin, and a statement of the characteristics and qualities of the goods. The Registering Authority may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding these details, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the processing of the application. Goods claiming protection as a Geographical Indication must be essentially attributable to their geographical origin; any alteration which does not conform with this requirement shall render the product ineligible for registration under this Act. The Registering Authority shall consider evidence demonstrating continued adherence to established production methods.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which such indication is not authorized, shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Such use includes any representation that the goods originate from the place indicated by the geographical indication, or any practice likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, issue an injunction restraining such infringing activity and order seizure of the offending goods. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender liable for penalties as provided under this Act, including imprisonment up to three years and fines not exceeding ten lakh rupees.

The owner of a registered Geographical Indication may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in a written agreement, grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to make, use, offer for sale, expose for sale, sell, or import goods that are identifiable as originating from the territory specified within the registration. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and accompanied by a certified copy of the agreement governing the assignment. The Registrar may, after giving the owner of the Geographical Indication an opportunity for being heard, refuse registration of such assignment if it deems the terms unduly restrictive or contrary to the public interest. Further, any licensee or assignee shall be bound by the quality standards and production methods associated with the registered Geographical Indication as defined under this Act.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication may be refused if the Registrar, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, is satisfied that the proposed indication does not primarily identify goods as originating from a specific region in India, based on factors such as natural conditions and traditional practices. Any party aggrieved by such a refusal order shall have the right to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The Board may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision. Further appeals from orders of the Appellate Board are permissible to the High Court on grounds specified herein.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may, subject to the provisions herein, grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said indication in relation to goods for which it is registered. Such licenses shall specify the territory and duration of the authorization, and the terms governing quality control measures applicable to the licensed products. Any assignment of ownership or a license under this Act requires prior notification to the Registrar, who may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding consumer protection. Parliament recognizes that fostering innovation within traditional industries necessitates flexible arrangements; therefore, licensees shall be entitled to sub-license rights provided that such sub-licenses adhere strictly to the original terms and conditions. The Registrar may impose reasonable fees for registration of assignments or licenses, as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication relating to Alphonso mangoes, originating from Konkan region of Maharashtra, shall include particulars specifying the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods attributable to their origin. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information demonstrating the exclusive link between the specified geographical area and the unique qualities of the Alphonso mango. Upon successful registration, a notice shall be published in the Official Gazette detailing the registered Geographical Indication and its defined territory. Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register of Geographical Indications may apply for a Register Effect Order to rectify such errors as provided herein. The register effect order will be binding subject to appeal under this Act.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish particulars distinguishing the Geographical Indication, including its name as used on the goods or services, the area from which the goods originate, and details establishing the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics linked to that origin. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Geographical Indications Journal and may also publish it in such other manner as deemed appropriate for public awareness. Objections to the registration, if any, must be filed within the time specified under this Act. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond before making a determination regarding whether a registered geographical indication should be granted.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention” shall mean a new and useful art, process, manufacture, machine, apparatus, composition of matter, or improvement thereof; provided that the invention is patentable under section 3. An invention shall be deemed not obvious if, having regard to the state of knowledge in the prior art, it does not involve any element of novelty or an inventive step. The term "prior art" includes information which has been made available to the public anywhere in the world by means of written description, use, oral disclosure, or otherwise before the date of filing of the patent application for the invention to which it relates. A “patent” shall confer upon the patentee exclusive right as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent shall furnish, along with the application, a declaration specifying the class or classes to which the invention relates. The Controller may require the applicant to amend such declaration if it is deemed deficient in clarity or accuracy, provided that the amendment does not alter the scope of protection sought for the patent. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the classification under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all patents granted and applications filed, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees. Further, any alteration in the particulars relating to a patent registration must be notified to the Controller promptly.

Where the proprietor of a patent institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, the Court may grant such remedy or remedies as it deems fit, including but not limited to an injunction restraining the defendant from infringing the patent and an account of profits made by the defendant as a result of the infringement. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, the Court shall take into consideration any measure taken by the proprietor to prevent infringement and any contributory negligence on the part of the person against whom relief is sought. Further, where an injunction has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to claim reasonable compensation for loss or damage resulting from the infringement prior to the date of the judgment. The Court may also order delivery up or destruction of goods made without authority and embodying the invention claimed in the patent.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a declaration, made by the applicant or by any person authorized by him, stating that the invention disclosed is novel and involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary for the purpose of determining whether the claimed invention meets the criteria for patentability under this Act. Where an objection is taken on the ground that the invention lacks novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in support of his claim. The Board constituted under this Act may hear appeals arising from any decision made by the Controller regarding the grant or refusal of a patent. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions.

An applicant seeking a patent shall disclose the best method known to them for carrying out the invention, provided that such disclosure does not compromise the working of the claimed subject matter. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the manner of operation if the description is deemed ambiguous or insufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention without undue experimentation. Where an improvement to a prior patented process is sought as a patent, it must demonstrate non-obviousness relative to the existing patent and shall not involve the use of any prohibited substance under regulations framed by the Central Government. The grant of a patent is subject to the condition that the invention is novel and involves inventive step, as provided herein.

Any person who, having knowledge of the existence of a patent in force, makes, uses, sells, offers for sale, or imports into India any patented article or process without the authorization of the patentee shall be deemed guilty of an infringement of that patent. Such infringement shall render the infringing party liable to pay damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the patentee as determined by the High Court, and may also attract a penalty not exceeding five per cent of the infringer’s turnover for the preceding year. Further, where the infringement is proven to be willful, the Court may award exemplary damages in addition to compensatory damages. The Controller shall, upon receiving a complaint regarding such an act, issue notices and conduct inquiries as provided herein before initiating enforcement proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use the invention embodied in the patent, either wholly or partially, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, assignable, or revocable. The terms and conditions of any such license shall be determined solely by agreement between the patentee and the licensee, provided that no condition restricting the manufacture, use, or sale of the patented invention in India shall be deemed valid unless expressly approved by the Central Government. Further, a patentee may assign their entire interest in a patent, or any right to obtain a patent, including all rights to grant licenses as described herein, to another person upon execution of an instrument in writing and registration thereof under this Act. Such assignment shall vest in the assignee all rights and powers which the assignor had prior to the assignment, including the power to enforce the patent against infringement.

Where any question arises regarding the validity of a patent, whether relating to novelty, inventive step, sufficiency of disclosure, or otherwise as provided herein, such question shall be determined by the Appellate Board. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from any order made by the Controller under this Act concerning the grant, revocation, or infringement of a patent. The Board may, after giving all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, subject to such conditions and limitations as are prescribed under this Act regarding costs and time limits for filing appeals.

Where any question arises as to whether the subject matter of a patent application falls within the scope of section 3, and such determination involves consideration of prior publication or use, the Controller shall give due regard to evidence submitted by all interested parties. An appeal lies from an order made under this Act determining novelty or inventive step, but only if the appellant demonstrates that substantial injustice has resulted from the decision; provided that the appellate authority may dismiss appeals lacking merit or based on arguments already considered and rejected during the original examination process. The burden of proving prior use shall rest upon the party alleging it, subject to the Controller’s discretion in directing parties to produce relevant documentation.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent” shall mean an exclusive right granted by the Controller under this Act in respect of an invention and comprises such rights as are specified herein. An applicant for a patent may elect to seek international registration protection for their invention pursuant to the Patent Cooperation Treaty; provided that such election does not affect the validity or enforceability of the Indian patent grant. The term “invention” includes any new and useful art, process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, subject to exclusions as provided herein regarding inventions which are frivolous or obvious.

For the purposes of this Act, “educational institution” means any establishment registered under law and primarily engaged in providing instruction or training in any field of knowledge, including but not limited to schools, colleges, universities, vocational training centres, and research institutions; provided that such establishments are recognized by a governmental authority or accredited by an established body. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, add to or remove from the list of educational institutions as it deems fit, subject to guidelines framed under this Act. Any decision regarding recognition or accreditation shall be final and binding.

Applications for registration of literary works, including computer programs and databases, shall be made to the designated Copyright Office established under this Act, in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the work or such other evidence as may be deemed sufficient by the Copyright Office. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office shall assign a registration number and record particulars relating to the work, author, and claimant. The Central Government may, at its discretion, require further documentation or clarification from any applicant prior to processing the application. Registration is not conclusive evidence of ownership but serves as prima facie proof subject to challenge under this Act.

Where any person has been found, after due inquiry and subject to appeal under this Act, to have infringed copyright in any work, the Central Government may, upon application made by the owner of the copyright or any other aggrieved party, direct such infringing person to pay compensation commensurate with the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a consequence of the infringement. Such compensation shall be determined having regard to the extent of the damage sustained, the benefit accrued to the infringer, and factors relating to moral rights. The Central Government may also order the delivery or destruction of all copies, whether physical or digital, embodying the infringing work. Provided that any such direction for payment of compensation shall not preclude the aggrieved party from pursuing further remedies available under law.

The Central Government may, upon receiving a written representation from any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, direct that the case be referred to a High Court Judge for inquiry and report. Such reference shall specify the grounds of appeal and the new evidence, if any, which the appellant desires to submit. The High Court Judge so appointed shall afford all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, and shall record his findings on matters of fact and law. A copy of the report submitted by the High Court Judge shall be furnished to the Central Government, who shall consider the same before making a final determination. Any person dissatisfied with the decision of the Central Government following such a reference may approach the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. The expenses incurred in connection with any inquiry made pursuant to this provision shall be borne by the Central Government.

The Central Government may, upon receiving a written application from any person claiming to be aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the seizure or forfeiture of infringing copies or materials, direct that the matter be referred for review to a High Court Judge nominated by the judiciary. Such applications shall detail the grounds on which the applicant alleges the order is erroneous and demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting therefrom. The Central Government shall consider any such application within ninety days of its receipt, provided that all requisite documentation, including certified copies of the original order and supporting evidence, has been duly submitted. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in the rejection of the application without further consideration. The nominated High Court Judge’s decision shall be final and binding.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced or distributed any work in violation of the provisions of this Act shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, determined at the discretion of the civil court before which the suit is brought. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved copyright owner, direct law enforcement agencies to seize any infringing copies or materials found in possession of the offender. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed a contempt of the said court and subject the defaulting party to penalties as provided herein. Further, the Central Government reserves the right to impose additional pecuniary sanctions on repeat offenders determined through judicial review.

The Central Government may, upon application by any person claiming an interest in a copyrighted work, grant a non-exclusive license permitting reproduction and distribution of that work for purposes of educational research undertaken by institutions recognized under this Act. Such applications shall include detailed particulars of the proposed research, the scope of permitted use, and the number of copies to be made. The Central Government may impose conditions on such licenses, including limitations on commercial exploitation derived from the licensed material and requirements for acknowledgement of the copyright holder. Any assignment of copyright relating to a work subject to a license granted under this provision shall require prior notification and approval from the Central Government, ensuring continued compliance with the terms stipulated in the original licensing agreement. The fees payable for such licenses and assignments shall be determined by regulations framed by the Central Government.

The Central Government may, upon receiving a written representation from any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the grant or refusal of copyright protection, direct that the matter be referred for review to a panel constituted by it for the purpose. Such referral shall not be entertained if the aggrieved party has failed to exhaust all remedies available to them as provided herein; however, the Central Government may, in its discretion, waive this requirement where exceptional circumstances exist and demonstrable prejudice would result from adherence thereto. The decision of the review panel shall be final and binding, subject only to challenge through a writ petition before the High Court within ninety days of publication of said decision.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "Appellate Board" means a body established under notification by the Central Government, constituted as provided herein, and vested with exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals arising from orders passed by Copyright Adjudicating Officers. The Appellate Board shall be deemed to be a civil court for certain proceedings only as specified in this Act and subject to its own procedural rules. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final, but are subject to judicial review under law relating to writ petitions. The composition, powers, and functions of the Appellate Board are detailed elsewhere within this legislation.

Applications for registration of sound recordings shall be processed initially by the Copyright Office and, upon completion of examination as provided herein, may be referred to the Appellate Board if objections are raised regarding originality or ownership. The Registrar shall furnish all relevant documentation pertaining to such referrals, including claimant details, asserted rights, and grounds for dispute. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Copyright Office concerning registration, refusal, or amendment of a sound recording’s entry on the Register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Appellate Board shall consider all submitted evidence and arguments before rendering its decision, which shall be final subject to further appeals under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning copyright infringement or royalty disputes believes such order to be unjust or beyond the powers conferred upon the relevant authority, that person may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall entertain appeals only if the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Subject to provisions regarding costs as determined by the Board, an aggrieved party failing to pursue such an appeal within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed to have acquiesced in the original decision. The Appellate Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary or reverse any order appealed against. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, provided that remedies are available under this Act.

Appeals arising under this Act shall be made to the Appellate Board established for the purpose. The Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, being persons having experience in copyright law, intellectual property rights administration, or judicial matters. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to any matter specified under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said order. The Appellate Board shall follow such procedure as the Central Government prescribes, provided that it affords all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding subject to further appeals only to the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning copyright infringement or licensing conditions seeks redress, such person may file an appeal before the Appellate Board. The appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant, provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are submitted and found acceptable by the Board. Any appeal under this Act shall specify the grounds on which it is based and shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documents pertaining to the original proceeding. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned, affording them an opportunity to present their case and evidence before passing any order as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider appeals relating to decisions concerning infringement and the assessment of damages for copyright violation. An appeal lies only on a substantial question of law arising out of the decision appealed against, as provided herein. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated time shall be deemed a waiver of the right to challenge the original order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned, dismiss frivolous appeals with costs, and may award compensation for legal expenses incurred by the respondent party in defending such appeals.

The copyright owner shall be entitled to grant licenses for the reproduction and distribution of works under their control, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment of copyright, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall require registration with the designated authority and shall specify the duration and geographical scope of the rights transferred. Where a license is granted permitting adaptation of a work, the licensor may stipulate limitations on subsequent assignments of that adapted form, ensuring continued control over derivative works. Disputes concerning the validity or enforceability of such licenses or assignments shall be referred to the Appellate Board for determination, with due consideration given to principles of fair dealing and equitable compensation to all parties involved. The Appellate Board’s decision is final, provided it does not contravene any provision under this Act relating to moral rights.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights, or concerning disputes regarding ownership of copyright arising from assignments or transmissions, feels that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence submitted by both the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony pertaining to the originality and authorship of the work in question. Decisions made under this Act regarding infringement claims are also subject to review by the Appellate Board, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates a clear error of law or fact on the part of the Registrar. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal only to the High Court as provided herein.

The Appellate Board shall be constituted by a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court and two other Members to be appointed by the Central Government, one of whom shall be a person having special knowledge and experience in copyright law. The Board may, subject to the provisions under this Act, hear and decide appeals from any order passed by an Adjudicating Officer. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are recorded for such delay. For the purposes of determining whether an invention means new, the Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the parties and apply principles of established jurisprudence. The decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding.

Where a dispute arises concerning whether a photograph constitutes an ‘artistic work’ under this Act and is therefore subject to copyright protection, such determination shall be made by the Appellate Board. The Board may require the submission of expert testimony regarding the originality of the composition within the photograph, considering factors including but not limited to lighting, framing, and subject arrangement. Provided that the photographer demonstrates sufficient skill and judgment in creating the photograph beyond mere mechanical reproduction, the Board shall presume originality unless evidence is presented demonstrating substantial copying from a pre-existing work. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board may appeal further as provided herein, subject to compliance with prescribed timelines and procedural requirements.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider appeals relating to decisions concerning infringement and shall have power to determine whether an entitled assignment transmission of copyright was properly executed, particularly where disputes arise regarding the validity or scope of said assignment. Failure to demonstrate proper execution as provided herein will render any subsequent claim of ownership untenable. Penalties for non-compliance with orders issued by the Appellate Board shall be equivalent to those prescribed for offences under this Act and may include imprisonment and fines. The Board’s decision is final, subject to judicial review only on grounds limited to legal error.

For the purposes of this Act, a "registered user" is a person who has been duly recorded as such under this Act in respect of a registered trademark and who is entitled to use the trademark for any goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the conditions and limitations specified in the registration. A person shall only be considered a registered user if they have filed an application with the Registrar demonstrating their prior usage of the mark, or where such usage is not required under this Act. The rights of a registered user are governed by the terms of their recorded agreement and as provided herein, including restrictions on alteration or abandonment of that use.

A person shall be deemed a registered user where such person has been duly authorized by the proprietor of a trademark to use the trademark for specific goods or services and has applied for registration as a registered user under this Act, providing evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating continuous use consistent with the terms of authorization. The application for registration may include details regarding the geographical area of permitted use and the nature of the relationship between the applicant and the proprietor. Upon successful completion of the examination process and satisfaction of all prescribed requirements, including payment of requisite fees, the person shall be entered into the Register of Registered Users as provided herein. Any alteration to the scope of authorized use requires prior written consent from both the proprietor and subsequent notification to the Registrar.

A registered user shall be entitled to institute suits for infringement of the trademark under this Act as if they were the proprietor of the trademark. Such suits may be brought against any person infringing, or attempting to infringe, the rights granted to the proprietor and extending to the registered user. The remedies available to a registered user in an action for infringement shall include damages, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, and delivery up of the infringing goods or materials. Provided that, where the proprietor has knowledge of the use made by the registered user, they shall not be entitled to restrain such use unless it is established that the use is detrimental to the distinctiveness of the trademark or causes unfair prejudice to the reputation connecting with the trademark. The proprietor may, at any time, revoke the registration of a registered user if they fail to comply with conditions imposed under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, an application for registration as a registered user may be filed by any person who is using the trade mark under authorization from the proprietor of the trade mark. Such authorization shall be evidenced by a contract in writing, specifying the terms and conditions governing such use. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing the existence of such contractual relationship and the extent of their usage. A registered user shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of the trade mark relating to goods or services in connection with which the user is by registration authorized to use the mark. Any alteration in the terms of authorization affecting the scope of the registered user’s entitlement may require a fresh application, as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered users accessible for public inspection.

A registered user seeking to obtain relief under this Act shall first file an application with the relevant intellectual property office, detailing the extent and nature of the interference alleged. Such application must demonstrate that the proprietor of the trade mark has failed to duly control the use of the mark relating to specific goods or services for which the registered user is authorized. The applicant shall provide evidence substantiating their claim, including records of sales, advertising materials, and correspondence with the proprietor. Provided that the registered user’s activities do not amount to a misuse of the trade mark prejudicing the reputation thereof, and subject to compliance with any conditions stipulated in the registration certificate, the intellectual property office may grant such relief as it deems appropriate.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license to use such trademark under this Act, and subsequently fails to diligently protect the reputation of the trademark against misuse by said licensee, the registered user shall be deemed to have forfeited their right to continue as a registered user. Any person aggrieved by such failure may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for an order directing the proprietor to reinstate the registered user’s status or, alternatively, permitting the aggrieved party to directly enforce remedies available under this Act against the proprietor. Such enforcement actions shall be subject to a penalty of not less than five thousand rupees and may include injunctive relief preventing further unauthorized use. The proprietor shall also be liable for damages sustained by the registered user as a consequence of the proprietor’s inaction.

A registered user seeking to exploit the licensed rights associated with a trademark shall be entitled to grant sub-licenses thereof, subject to the prior approval of the proprietor of the trade mark. Such approval shall not be unreasonably withheld, and any conditions imposed upon such sublicense must be clearly documented and accessible to all parties involved. The registered user may also assign their right to use the trademark, including any associated goodwill, provided that such assignment is made with the written consent of the proprietor, which consent may be subject to a reasonable financial consideration as determined by mutual agreement or, in the absence thereof, arbitration. Further, any sublicense or assignment shall not prejudice the rights of other registered users under this Act and must expressly acknowledge their existing entitlements. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the reputation and character of the trademark, even when managed through a registered user’s sub-licensees.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is presented alleging that a registered user has acted outside the scope of the territory or conditions under which they were entered on the register, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor and the registered user. The registered user may then file with the Registrar a counter-statement refuting the allegations and presenting evidence in support of their use. Subject to any order made by the Appellate Board, if the Registrar finds that the registered user has indeed exceeded the scope of their registration or violated stipulated conditions, they shall be removed from the register; provided that such removal shall not prejudice any right of action which may have accrued to any party prior to the date of the Registrar’s determination.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is based on prior honest usage of a similar sign by a person other than the applicant, the Registrar may, upon hearing all parties involved, allow the registration if satisfied that the said person qualifies as a registered user. It shall be further considered whether the date filing specification of the trade mark in question predates the commencement of such prior usage. The burden of proving honest and continuous use rests with the claimant asserting registered user status. Provided that, any appeal against an order determining eligibility for registration as a registered user may only be made within sixty days from the date of communication of said order.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" shall mean the three-dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, accurately depicted through a mask, and which secures the original character of an integrated circuit. This definition includes both the spatial relationship between those elements and any other relevant data necessary for their faithful reproduction. A layout-design is deemed to be infringed if it is copied or has elements substantially similar to the protected layout-design without authorization from the owner. The term "element" encompasses active or passive electrical components, interconnections, insulating layers, and masks used in the fabrication of an integrated circuit, subject to any modifications that do not alter the overall topology as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original documentation pertaining to the design’s creation and detailing its technical specifications. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the layout-design's intended commercial exploitation, including anticipated manufacturing processes and distribution channels, as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. Any prior publication or disclosure of the layout-design before registration shall be disclosed in the application, along with a comprehensive explanation of the circumstances leading to such dissemination. The applicant shall also declare whether any person other than themselves possesses rights relating to the layout-design. Failure to provide complete and accurate information may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Where any person unlawfully makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell a layout-design infringing upon the exclusive right of the registered proprietor of a layout-design, such proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy which may be available in law or equity. Compensation for loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement shall be determined by the competent civil court, taking into consideration the profits made by the infringer and the damage sustained by the proprietor. Provided that, where the infringing layout-design is substantially similar to the registered layout-design, damages may be assessed on an enhanced basis. Subject to appeal to the High Court, any order for compensation shall be final. The proprietor may also recover costs incurred in pursuing such remedies as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including detailed schematics and a description of the functions performed by each element within the layout-design. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification deemed necessary for assessing the novelty and originality of the layout-design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller General shall publish a notice indicating the particulars of the application and inviting objections from any interested party within a period as provided herein. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit a written response addressing the concerns raised. The Controller General shall consider both the application and the submitted responses before proceeding with examination under this Act. Subject to compliance with all prescribed formalities, registration of the layout-design shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights against infringement as defined herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a layout-design shall be deemed infringed when any person without authorization makes, imports, sells, offers to sell, distributes, hires or displays for sale a semiconductor integrated circuit incorporating a substantially similar layout-design. Such infringement is actionable irrespective of whether the infringing layout-design was created independently or copied from the registered layout-design. Provided that minor variations not affecting the essential character and function of the layout-design shall not constitute infringement under this Act. The right to prevent infringement extends to acts performed for any commercial purpose, including but not limited to manufacture, reproduction, adaptation, and distribution as provided herein. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the relevant authority seeking redressal.

Any person who, having knowledge that an unauthorized copy has been made of a registered layout-design, and with intent to induce infringement thereof, commercially exploits such copy shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at the option of the owner of the layout-design, either as actual loss suffered or profits made by the infringing party, whichever is higher. Further, where an infringement occurs due to the wilful contravention of a provision under this Act relating to the protection of a layout-design, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe procedures for determining such damages and penalties.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a registered proprietor of a layout-design may grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the protected layout-design for specific purposes, including but not limited to manufacture, import, and sale. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of a layout-design right, whether partial or complete, also requires execution via a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignee and registered with the Controller General. The terms of any assignment shall clearly define the scope of rights transferred, including geographical limitations and duration. Further, where an assignment includes pre-existing contractual obligations relating to the layout-design, those obligations remain binding upon both assignor and assignee as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer of such assignment is subject to similar registration requirements.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon their registered layout-design, such allegation shall be made before the relevant High Court. The aggrieved party must demonstrate a clear and demonstrable reproduction of the protected elements within the claimed layout-design, subject to permissible minor variations arising from technological necessity. It is provided that mere similarity in functionality or overall appearance does not constitute infringement under this Act. Upon receiving notice of such an allegation, the High Court may issue interim injunctions restraining further acts of alleged infringement pending final determination. Any order issued by the High Court shall be appealable to the Supreme Court within a period of ninety days from the date of the judgment, as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, distributes, leases, or offers to lease a layout-design infringing upon a registered certify layout-design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the actual loss suffered by the proprietor nor exceeding fifty lakhs of rupees. Where the infringement is found to have been committed knowingly, the Court may enhance such penalty up to one crore rupees. Further, any goods manufactured or distributed in violation of this Act are deemed contraband and subject to seizure under procedures as provided herein. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical composition” means a combination of two or more active ingredients intended for use in the treatment, mitigation, or prevention of disease, or for improving health conditions; and where such pharmaceutical composition is claimed in an application for patent, it shall be examined with particular regard to novelty and inventive step. The term "objectionable matter" includes any information disclosed in the description or drawings which relates to a process for producing a substance but does not necessarily involve the use of that substance for a novel purpose. The Controller may, at any time during the examination of an application, require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to such objectionable matter.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish along with the application, certified copies of any prior published designs or other documents known to the applicant which relate to the claimed invention. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to such publications or documents and verify their authenticity through prescribed procedures. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning novelty or originality based on a cited publication, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity for reasoned rebuttal within a stipulated timeframe. Failure to respond adequately may result in rejection of the design application. The Controller’s decision regarding the validity of prior publications and their impact on registration shall be final, subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act, including orders relating to compulsory licensing or revocation of patents, desires to appeal against such order, he may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.
