The appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds of appeal and copies of all relevant documents. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the appeal inadmissible. The Board may, after giving notice to the Controller and opportunity for him to be heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, disposing of the appeal. Any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final subject to further appeal under the provisions of the Tribunals Act. Costs relating to the appeal shall be determined by the Board.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a request for extension of time under this Act from any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Patent Office, afford them an opportunity of being heard. Such hearing shall be conducted within sixty days of the date of receipt of the request and notice thereof shall be served on all parties concerned at least thirty days prior to the appointed date. The Controller may, after considering the representations made by the aggrieved party and any counter-representations filed by the Patent Office, pass such orders as he deems fit, subject to the provisions regarding natural justice. Any order passed by the Controller under this Act shall be final and binding, but appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Controller may require production of documents or attendance of witnesses as deemed necessary for the proper adjudication of such matters.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a request from the patentee seeking assignment of the patent, examine whether the proposed assignee fulfills all conditions precedent for eligibility under this Act. Such examination shall include verification that the proposed assignee is not an entity declared ineligible by governmental notification or subject to outstanding legal proceedings materially impacting their commercial capacity. Provided that the Controller may require further documentation demonstrating financial solvency and operational stability from the proposed assignee if deemed necessary, based on publicly available information or representations made during the assignment process. The patentee shall provide a sworn affidavit confirming due diligence in selecting the assignee; failure to do so renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Controller.

Any person aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by the Appellate Board and its decision shall be binding on all parties concerned. Failure to comply with the directions issued by the Controller regarding the rectification of any defect or omission in a patent application or registered patent shall render the applicant or patentee liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. The Controller may, at his discretion, grant a reasonable extension of time beyond the prescribed period provided that such extension is accompanied by a fee as determined by notification issued by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license under his patent shall file with the Controller a request specifying the terms and conditions of such license, including royalty rates, duration, and geographical area of application. The Controller may, after giving notice to the patentee and interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, approve or disapprove of the proposed license, provided that approval shall not be withheld solely on the grounds that the royalty rate is deemed inadequate. Assignment of a patent, or any interest therein, shall also require notification to the Controller, accompanied by prescribed fees. The Controller may record such assignments and provide certificates thereof, which shall be binding evidence of the transfer of rights as provided herein. Any subsequent dealing with the license or assignment requires similar notification.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of an objection under this Act from any person aggrieved by a patent granted, afford the patentee an opportunity of being heard, either in person or by advocate. Such hearing shall be conducted within a period not exceeding six months from the date of service of notice of the objection. The applicant for revocation may, at such hearing, present evidence and arguments to support their claim, subject to rules framed under this Act regarding admissibility. Provided that, if the Controller deems the objection to raise substantial questions of law, he may refer the matter to a High Court for determination. Any order passed by the Controller following such hearing is appealable before the Appellate Board, as provided herein, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, a registered trade mark shall be deemed to confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to the use of the said trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to prevent the use of any identical or similar marks or signs, subject to principles of fair dealing and honest practices in industrial competition. This exclusive right extends to all forms of representation including but not limited to written characters, graphical elements, and three-dimensional shapes, provided that such representations are used in a manner consistent with the distinctiveness of the registered trade mark as assessed under this Act. The proprietor may institute legal proceedings for infringement of this right.

An application for registration of a registered trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed mark is descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated. However, such refusal may be withdrawn under this Act if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application, supported by evidence of substantial sales and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall also refuse registration if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, provided that the earlier mark has a reputation in India. Any appeal against such refusal may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person using identical or confusingly similar marks in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those specified in the registration, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion among the public or to indicate that the goods or services originate from the proprietor. Where an injunction restraining the infringing activity has been granted, damages may be awarded to the proprietor, representing their loss by reason of the infringement; however, the Court shall not award exemplary damages unless it finds that the defendant acted with malice or fraudulent intent. Further, any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing use may be recovered by the registered trade mark owner as provided herein, subject to just and equitable considerations.

An application for registration of a registered trade mark shall be refused if the proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated. Where an objection is raised under this Act, the applicant may submit evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use in commerce prior to the date of the application. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider such evidence and may require a consumer survey to ascertain public perception of the mark. Further, any person claiming ownership of a similar registered trade mark may file a caveat opposing registration, provided that they demonstrate likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed mark’s use. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both parties to present arguments and documentary proof before rendering a decision as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the proprietor of a registered trade mark, record particulars of any place or premises at which goods bearing that registered trade mark are manufactured or produced. Such an application shall be accompanied by evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishing the applicant’s entitlement to use the trade mark and detailing the manufacturing process employed. The Registrar is not bound to register such particulars unless he is satisfied that the proprietor has complied with all relevant procedural requirements under this Act, including payment of prescribed fees. Any alteration or cessation in the manufacturing process at a place so recorded shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days; failure to do so may result in removal of those particulars from the Register. The registered trade mark remains valid notwithstanding any such recording.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, uses a registered trade mark identical or confusingly similar to that of another in connection with the offer for sale, supply or exhibition of goods or services shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees, or both. Where the use of a registered trade mark constitutes passing off, remedies available under this Act and at law shall be accessible to the proprietor of the registered trade mark. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe measures for preventing and detecting such infringements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the right to use is conferred, and the geographical area within which such use is permitted. Such licenses shall be assignable, subject to registration with the Registrar, provided that the assignment does not extend beyond the scope of the original registered trade mark. The proprietor may impose conditions relating to quality control or other standards concerning goods or services bearing the licensed trade mark. Further, a license granted under this Act may contain provisions restricting the licensee’s ability to challenge the validity of the registered trade mark itself. Any subsequent assignment of rights derived from such a license shall be deemed an endorsement by the original proprietor and subject to their consent.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration of a proposed trademark, the Appellate Board may, subject to any conditions specified therein, allow the appeal if it finds that the Registrar failed to properly consider material evidence presented by the applicant. The Board shall also entertain appeals arising from decisions concerning rectification proceedings initiated to expunge a registered trade mark based on use contrary to honest practices in an industrial or commercial field. It is provided that such appeals must be filed within sixty days of the date of notification of the Registry’s order, and failure to do so shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Board's decision shall be final, but may be challenged under judicial review as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure the proprietor of a registered trade mark, uses an identical or deceptively similar mark relating to goods or services for which the said registered trade mark is registered shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where such use also infringes patent rights relating to the manufacturing process of those goods or services, the aggregate penalty shall be doubled. The proprietor may further seek injunctions preventing future infringing acts as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of their mark, either exclusively or non-exclusively, subject to such terms and conditions as they may deem fit. Any license granted under this Act may specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to utilize the registered trade mark, as well as the specific goods or services in relation to which the mark can be employed. Provided that any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include all rights pertaining to existing licenses relating thereto. The owner shall retain the right to demand royalty from licensees for the use of the trademark, and the amount of such royalty shall be determined by agreement between the parties or, failing agreement, as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Further, a licensee’s unauthorized alteration of the registered trade mark constitutes a breach of license and renders them liable for damages.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the proprietor of a registered trade mark, grant a licence patent conferring specific rights relating to the use and exploitation of that trade mark within a defined geographical territory. Such licences shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks, maintaining a clear distinction between the proprietary rights vested in the original owner and those granted under the licence patent. An application for registration of a licence patent must specify the goods or services in relation to which the license is sought, as well as any restrictions placed upon its use. The Registrar shall consider whether the proposed licence unduly prejudices the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered trade mark. Any assignment or further licensing of such a licence patent requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar under this Act.

Subject to any directions issued under this Act, the proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person who, without his consent, applies a false or deceptive mark likely to be used as a zb trade mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in connection with goods or services for which the registered trade mark is registered. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by reason of the infringement and an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. The proprietor shall also have the right to demand account of profits made by the infringer, provided that such profits are attributable to the use of the infringing mark. Further remedies available under this Act include the recovery of costs incidental to the proceedings and orders for delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered proprietor" shall mean the person whose name is entered in the Register as the owner of a trademark and who is entitled to enforce the rights conferred under this Act relating thereto. The registered proprietor shall be deemed to possess exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any limitation specified in the registration. Where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall become the registered proprietor upon proper recording of the assignment as provided herein. Any person claiming rights as a registered proprietor must satisfy the requirements regarding proof of ownership under this Act.

The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in respect of the goods or services for which it is registered and to obtain reliefs under this Act. Where an application for registration has been refused, the applicant may appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of the registered trade mark without requiring proof of actual damage suffered by him, provided that the use complained of is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public as to the origin of goods or services. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered trade mark requires notification and approval from the Registrar.

Where any person infringes a registered trade mark, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the defendant from infringing the said trade mark, and may also claim damages for such infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, taking into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the use of the impugned mark. Provided that, in determining such damages, the Court shall consider whether the defendant was aware, or had reason to believe, that the trade mark was registered and belonged to the registered proprietor. Further, where a false representation is made concerning goods or services offered under a registered trade mark, remedies are available as provided herein for passing off. The registered proprietor may also seek account of profits derived from the infringing use.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act, the Hearing Officer may, after giving notice to all parties involved and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, direct that the evidence be taken on oath or affirmation. The applicant shall furnish such documents and information as the Hearing Officer deems necessary for proper adjudication of the opposition. Upon conclusion of the hearing, the Hearing Officer shall record findings of fact and reasons for the decision. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Hearing Officer may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The registered proprietor is entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of the trade mark in a suit filed under this Act, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures regarding service of notice and presentation of evidence.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is ultimately resolved in favour of the applicant, the Registrar shall record the particulars of the opposition and its resolution in the Register of Trade Marks. The successful applicant shall be deemed the registered proprietor of the trade mark as from the date of filing the application, subject to any rectification proceedings initiated subsequently. Any alteration to the register reflecting such registration shall be made only upon verification by a designated officer confirming compliance with prescribed procedural requirements. Further, the registered proprietor shall maintain accurate records pertaining to the use and exploitation of the trademarked goods or services, available for inspection as provided herein. Failure to do so may result in limitations on rights afforded under this Act.

Where any person knowingly makes, uses, imports, distributes, sells, offers to sell, or exposes for sale any goods bearing a false trademark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark, or where such acts are done with the consent or knowledge of the registered proprietor, such person shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. The registered proprietor may, subject to any conditions as provided herein, institute proceedings against any person infringing their trademark rights. Further, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, and prohibit the continuance of the infringing activity. Any false representation concerning the ownership of a trademark shall be deemed an offence under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of their trademark for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted activities and the duration of the license agreement. The registered proprietor retains ultimate control over the mark’s reputation and quality; any activity infringing upon these standards by a licensee may result in termination of the license as provided herein. Further, assignment of a trademark or any part thereof shall require prior written consent from the Registrar, confirming that such transfer does not prejudice existing rights granted under licenses previously executed. A registered proprietor is liable for damages arising from misuse of their mark by a licensee acting beyond the scope of their authorization.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing to accept an application for registration of a trade mark, the Appellate Board may, subject to any conditions it deems fit to impose, direct that the matter be remitted to the Registrar for reconsideration. Such direction shall specify the grounds upon which the original decision was deemed erroneous. The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the right to institute proceedings in the High Court against any person infringing their rights under this Act, notwithstanding any prior communication or warning given. Provided that, if the infringement is alleged to be unintentional, the Court may, as provided herein, order rectification of the error rather than award damages.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor desiring to grant a license for the use of their registered trademark shall do so in the prescribed manner, specifying therein the geographical area and the goods or services in respect of which such license is granted. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor. The registered proprietor retains full ownership of the trademark and may revoke any license if the licensee fails to use the mark in accordance with the terms stipulated, or engages in activities detrimental to the reputation of the trademark. Assignment of a registered trademark shall include any existing licenses attached thereto, unless expressly excluded within the assignment deed. Any subsequent registered proprietor is bound by the conditions of previously granted licenses as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a proposed trade mark alleging that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark already registered under this Act, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the registered proprietor with an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. The registered proprietor may demonstrate prior use of the conflicting mark in India, subject to providing satisfactory evidence establishing continuous and extensive commercial exploitation. Should the Registrar find that the proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to the earlier mark, despite any such demonstration by the registered proprietor, the applicant shall be entitled to appeal this decision to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Security India explanations regarding prior use may be considered during appellate proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, "exclusive right" with respect to a registered trade mark shall include, but not be limited to, the right to prevent the use of an identical or confusingly similar mark in connection with identical or closely related goods or services. The registered proprietor of a trade mark possesses such exclusive rights as are provided herein and is entitled to enforce them against any infringement. Subject to limitations prescribed under this Act regarding fair use and permitted uses, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to have standing to pursue remedies for acts that violate their registration. Any assignment or license of a registered trade mark shall not diminish the rights respect registration afforded to the original proprietor unless otherwise expressly agreed.

Where any person aggrieved by the revocation of registration of a trademark under this Act alleges that the revocation was effected without due consideration being given to the interests of a breeder who has legitimately utilized the mark in connection with plant varieties, such aggrieved party may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registered proprietor shall be deemed to have acted in bad faith if it is established that they were aware of the breeder’s prior use and failed to negotiate a reasonable license or assignment of rights. Further, any action taken by the registered proprietor which actively seeks to undermine the breeder's commercial viability following such notification will render them liable for damages as determined by the Board. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant factors including the duration and extent of the breeder’s use, and whether the mark has become generic within that specific agricultural context.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is granted, the registered proprietor shall be deemed the owner thereof and shall possess exclusive rights to apply the mark as provided herein. Any subsequent alteration to the description of goods or services associated with a registered trade mark may only occur through submission of an amendment specification document to the Trade Marks Registry. Such documents must conform precisely to the prescribed format outlined in the First Schedule, detailing the precise additions or deletions proposed. The Registrar shall review these amendment specification documents and may, after affording the registered proprietor an opportunity for representation, approve or reject them based on their compliance with this Act and any relevant rules framed thereunder. Objections raised by third parties concerning the validity of such amendments shall be addressed in accordance with established procedures regarding oppositions to registration.

For the purposes of this Act, “specification” shall mean a complete written description of an invention, disclosing the best method known to the applicant for performing it, and including all particulars necessary to enable any person skilled in the relevant field to make or use the invention. The specification shall be divided into two parts: one relating to the matter disclosed and the other detailing the claims defining the scope of protection sought. It is provided that the specification must clearly identify the technical problem which the invention seeks to solve, and demonstrate a sufficient enabling disclosure as required under this Act.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a request for registration of a biological material derived from an indigenous source, require submission of a detailed specification outlining the method of derivation, cultivation, and preservation. This specification must clearly identify the geographical origin of the biological material and demonstrate adherence to established protocols under this Act concerning bio-prospecting activities. The applicant shall further provide documentation confirming prior informed consent obtained from relevant community representatives, as provided herein. Failure to submit a complete and accurate specification, including details regarding any genetic modifications undertaken, will result in rejection of the registration request. Any subsequent alteration to the biological material’s characteristics after registration requires amendment of the original specification.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such proceedings shall be brought before the appropriate civil court having jurisdiction, and the aggrieved party must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Court that the alleged infringing act falls within the scope of the claims as defined in the specification of the patent. The defendant shall have the right to challenge the validity of the patent itself, presenting evidence demonstrating a lack of novelty or an absence of inventive step. Should the Court find infringement and invalidity concurrently, remedies may be limited to injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement, without entitlement to damages or account of profits. The specification constitutes the sole basis for determining the scope of protection afforded by the patent; any interpretation beyond its clear and unambiguous terms shall not be permitted.

The Controller may, at any time during the proceedings relating to an application for patent, require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars as he deems necessary for the determination of inventiveness. Such requirement shall be made in writing and specify the grounds upon which the request is based, referencing relevant prior art documents where applicable. The applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such communication within which to comply, subject to extensions granted under this Act. Failure to provide the requested information within the stipulated time may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The adequacy and clarity of the *specification* accompanying the patent application are paramount; any ambiguity or omission rendering the invention not readily reproducible by a person skilled in the art shall be grounds for rejection.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, clearly and accurately describe the nature of the alleged invention and how it is to be performed. Such description must disclose the best method known to the applicant at the time of filing for carrying out the invention. The specification shall also include, where applicable, particulars relating to any microorganism deposited under this Act. It is provided that the description need not extend to matters which are purely theoretical or speculative and which do not contribute to enabling a person skilled in the art to put the invention into practice. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding the specification may render the patent liable to revocation.

Where any person alleges that another has contravened any provision relating to the specification of a patent, such allegation shall be made within three years from the date of grant of the patent and shall specify with particularity the nature of the alleged non-compliance. Failure to adequately disclose the best method known to the inventor for carrying out the invention, as detailed in the specification, renders the patent liable to revocation under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the validity of a patent based on deficiencies within its specification may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Controller shall impose a penalty not exceeding one million rupees upon any applicant found to have knowingly misrepresented facts pertaining to their invention's specification.

The right to grant licenses relating to any patent granted under this Act shall vest solely with the patentee, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. A patentee may assign or license the benefit of the patent specification, either wholly or partially, to any person, firm, or company, provided that such assignment or license is recorded in the Patents Office within three months from the date of the agreement. Any subsequent transfer or further licensing shall also require registration as provided herein. The patentee shall disclose, in the registered document, the scope and duration of any licenses granted, including royalty rates and exclusivity provisions. Failure to register an assignment or license may render it unenforceable against third parties. Further, a licensee may not, without express written consent from the patentee, sub-license rights conferred under the specification.

The term “specification” when used herein shall mean the entire body of the patent application, comprising the title, abstract, claims, description, drawings if any, and such other particulars as are deemed necessary for conveying to any person skilled in the art the subject matter of the invention. It is provided that disputes regarding the clarity or sufficiency of the specification to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the claimed invention shall be resolved by considering the entire disclosure in light of the state of knowledge at the time of filing, and not solely based on isolated portions thereof. Further, any challenge asserting ambiguity within the claims due to lack of support within the specification may only succeed if such ambiguity renders it impossible for a skilled professional to ascertain the scope of protection sought, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where, in any proceeding under this Act concerning the validity of a patent, it is alleged that the specification does not describe the invention claimed with sufficient clarity and completeness as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the same, the Controller may require the patentee to furnish further particulars or explanations. Such requirement shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the specific deficiencies asserted within the allegation. The patentee shall have thirty days from the date of such requirement to respond, failing which the proceeding shall continue ex parte. Any party aggrieved by the Controller’s determination regarding clarity of specification may appeal under this Act, presenting arguments demonstrating either substantial compliance with the requirements or a misinterpretation of the technical field involved, including consideration of prior art disclosed through application patent cooperation treaties.

The Controller may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a biological material, require the applicant to submit a detailed specification outlining the method of isolation, cultivation, or generation of said material. This specification shall include comprehensive information regarding the genetic characteristics, phenotypic traits, and stability data demonstrating consistent performance over successive generations. Furthermore, the applicant must provide evidence confirming adherence to established bio-containment protocols during handling and storage procedures. A certificate from a recognized national repository verifying the authenticity and preservation status of the biological material may be submitted as supplementary documentation. The Controller shall consider this specification alongside other application details when determining eligibility for registration under this Act, provided that all requirements are met.

Where the specification of a patent application relating to a semiconductor device fails adequately to disclose the best method known to the applicant for working the claimed invention, the Controller may, under this Act, direct that the patent be revoked. Such revocation shall occur if it is demonstrated that a skilled professional in the relevant field would not have been able to practice the invention without undue experimentation based solely on the information contained within the specification. The applicant shall then be afforded an opportunity to amend the specification to remedy the deficiency, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the scope of protection initially sought. Any infringement action predicated upon a patent subsequently revoked under these provisions may be stayed pending determination of validity and any damages awarded prior to revocation are recoverable from the patentee.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall, subject to the provisions regarding claims, clearly and accurately describe the invention. Such description must enable any person skilled in the relevant field to make and use the invention without undue experimentation, disclosing the best method contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention at the date of filing. Where the invention relates to a registered layout, the specification shall further detail how the claimed features interact with or are embodied within said registered design. The description need not disclose anything which does not contribute to the enabling disclosure but may refer to prior art and state the objects of the invention. Provided that any matter disclosed in the specification is supported by the claims, the application will proceed for examination.

For the purposes of this Act, “design” means an exclusive pattern applied to any article of manufacture whether two-dimensional or three-dimensional, and shall include a layout or configuration of lines or colours applied to an article. A design may be registered under this Act if it is original, not primarily dictated by function, and does not contain scandalous or obscene matter. The aesthetic characteristics of the design are paramount in determining its registrability; however, designs that consist entirely of shape or configuration necessary to achieve a technical result shall not be considered eligible for registration as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a design shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive right to use and apply the design as applied to the article in accordance with the prescribed manner. An application for registration may be made by any person claiming to be the owner of the design, provided that such ownership is established through original creation or lawful assignment. The Controller General may require submission of detailed technical specifications relating to the manufacturing process employed in producing articles incorporating the design under consideration. Any alteration to the registered design subsequent to its initial registration shall necessitate a fresh application for registration as if no prior registration existed; however, subject to prescribed fees, such applications will be expedited.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, no person shall be entitled to sue for infringement of design unless such design is registered. An unregistered design may be enforced only by suit against a person who was at the time of the alleged infringement aware that the design had been copied from him. Where an injunction restraining the manufacture, sale or importation of any article has been granted in respect of a design, no damages shall be recoverable under this Act except for costs incurred in obtaining the injunction. Any proprietor of a registered design may serve a notice on a person infringing his exclusive right in the design, requiring him to cease manufacturing, selling or importing the infringing articles and to deliver up those articles for destruction. Failure to comply with such notice may render the infringer liable to damages.

For the purposes of this Act, a registered design shall confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to apply that design as or in connection with articles. Any person desiring to register a design may file an application for registration in the prescribed form and manner, specifying particulars of the design including its representation and description. The Controller General shall examine such applications and may require amendments or further information if deemed necessary. An objection to a design may be raised by any interested party within the stipulated period as provided herein. Where a design is registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to restrain any infringement under this Act, subject to procedural requirements established in the regulations. The term of protection for a registered design shall ordinarily extend for ten years from the date of registration, renewable once for a further five-year period, provided that an application for renewal is filed within the prescribed timeframe.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, no person shall register a design unless it is substantially new and possesses individual character. For the purposes of determining novelty, a design shall be considered not new if it is dictated by functional considerations alone, or if it is disclosed to the public whether by means of writing, word of mouth, use, exhibition or in any other way prior to the date of application for registration. An article shall be deemed to possess individual character if its overall impression differs from existing designs and creates a unique aesthetic effect on informed users. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with these criteria before proceeding with examination.

Any person who reproduces, for commercial purposes, any article in which the shape or configuration of all or part thereof embodies a registered design, without authorization from the proprietor of the design, shall be liable to prosecution. Such reproduction includes making copies, manufacturing, selling, importing, or offering for sale. The penalty for first-time offenders shall be imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to one hundred thousand rupees. Subsequent offences are subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein. Nothing in this Act shall prevent the use of information disclosed in respect of a design during its registration process, but such use must not constitute infringement.

The owner of copyright in a registered design shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights to grant licenses for the exploitation of that design, subject to the conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be granted on a sole, non-exclusive, or royalty-bearing basis, as determined by the copyright holder. Assignment of such copyright and associated license agreements requires registration with the designated Intellectual Property Office, providing details of both assignor and assignee. Any subsequent transfer of rights shall also necessitate similar registration to maintain validity under this Act. Provided that, a licensee may sub-license specific aspects of the design’s application only with prior written consent from the copyright owner, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. The terms governing any license agreement relating to a design are binding on all parties and enforceable as contracts within the jurisdiction.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of their registered design, such allegation shall be substantiated by evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the impugned article and the design as recorded in the register. The proprietor bears the onus of proving that the alleged infringing article creates confusion amongst purchasers regarding its origin or association with the proprietor’s enterprise. However, where the defendant demonstrates prior use of a similar aesthetic feature, subject to reasonable limitations on such use as may be prescribed by regulations, the Court may consider this factor in determining whether infringement has occurred. The proprietor shall have recourse to appeal any decision finding against them, provided that the appellate authority deems the original determination to be manifestly erroneous.

For the purposes of this Act, “design” means a purely aesthetic creation relating to the shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article. A design shall not include any trademark or service mark registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, nor shall it extend to features which are primarily functional in nature or dictated solely by factors such as mechanical utility, architectural requirements, or processes of manufacture. Designs may be two-dimensional or three-dimensional and shall be considered original if they were not previously disclosed anywhere in India or abroad. Subject to this definition, a design is eligible for protection under this Act provided that it is capable of being reproduced industrially.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, registration of a design shall confer upon the registered proprietor person exclusive rights relating to the use of the design. An application for registration may be made by any person claiming to be the creator of the design or who is the first to have lawfully commercialized the design. The Controller General shall, before registering a design, ascertain whether it contains any features that are substantially similar to those already registered under this Act, or which are dictated solely by the function or character of the article in connection with which the design is applied or proposed to be applied. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller General may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall receive applications for registration of designs and may entertain such applications subject to compliance with prescribed formalities. An application shall include a representation of the design, a statement of novelty, and particulars identifying the applicant. Where an objection is raised by the Designs Examiner regarding the registrability of a design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard. The Design Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar under this Act.

Registration of a design confers upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use or apply the design and to prevent others from using it in connection with articles as specified in the registration. Any person seeking to utilize a similar design may be required to demonstrate that their application for certification trade marks does not infringe upon existing registered designs, as provided herein.

Where registration of a design is sought under this Act, the application shall specify the article for which the design is intended and include a statement as to whether the design is two-dimensional, three-dimensional, or a combination thereof. The Registrar may require the applicant to classify the design according to an alphabetical index classification system maintained by the Office; failure to comply with such direction constitutes grounds for rejection of the application. An article shall be deemed to possess registered design protection only if the visual features of the article are novel and have industrial applicability, subject to the provisions regarding prior publication or use as determined under this Act. The design must not contain any elements that are solely functional or dictated by safety requirements.

Where infringement of design exists, and such infringement involves the reproduction for sale or hire, or the offering for sale or hire, of articles bearing a protected design, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings seeking an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. Damages shall be awarded to the plaintiff representing their actual losses, not less than five per centum of the infringer’s profits derived from the infringing activity, and costs incurred in pursuing the action. The Court may order the destruction or disposal of infringing articles subject to regulations prescribed by the Government. Furthermore, where a design is registered and subsequently exploited without authorization, the proprietor shall be entitled to share patent rights relating to any functional improvements arising directly from that exploitation.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patentee” shall be deemed to include any person to whom a patent has been granted or who is the proprietor of an invention for which a patent has been applied for. Where the inventor is not the first applicant for a patent, the term "patentee" shall refer to the individual or entity subsequently named as such in the patent grant. The rights and obligations conferred upon a patentee under this Act are subject to any conditions specified in the patent document itself. Further, a patentee may assign their interest in a patent, provided that such assignment is recorded as prescribed herein.

The Register of Patentees shall maintain a record for each patentee registered under this Act, detailing particulars including but not limited to their principal place of business, designated representatives where applicable, and any changes occurring therein. An application for registration as a patentee may be submitted electronically through the prescribed portal, accompanied by supporting documentation verifying identity and address as per rules framed hereunder. The Controller shall provide an acknowledgement receipt upon successful submission; however, this does not constitute acceptance of the application. Any alteration to information previously provided must be notified to the Register within thirty days, failing which penalties as provided herein may apply. Further, a patentee is obliged to update their contact details annually or face suspension of certain rights under this Act.

Where a patentee exercises their right to prevent another from making, using or importing the patented invention without consent, and such prevention is challenged by the alleged infringer, the patentee shall bear the burden of proving both ownership of the patent and validity of the claims asserted. Should the court find that the actions complained of do not constitute infringement under this Act, or that a claim lacks novelty or inventive step as provided herein, it may award compensation to the defendant for costs incurred in defending the action. Further, if the patentee has acted unreasonably or maliciously in pursuing an infringement suit, the court shall have discretion to order them to pay damages to the defendant reflecting such unreasonable conduct. The right of a patentee to enforce their patent is subject to any statutory limitations concerning compulsory licenses and government use.

Where an application for a patent is granted and the patentee fails to comply with the requirements of publication as provided herein, the Controller may issue a notice requiring the patentee to furnish within such time as specified in the notice, particulars regarding the working or non-working of the patented invention in India. Such particulars shall include details concerning the nature of the working, the quantity produced, and any impediments encountered. Failure by the patentee to respond adequately to this notice may result in an inquiry being initiated under this Act into the question of revocation of the patent. The Controller shall give a further opportunity for the patentee to be heard before making any determination regarding the validity or enforceability of the patent. Any person aggrieved by such a decision may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where a patentee elects to manufacture the patented invention within India following grant of the patent, such manufacturing shall be deemed an act of infringement only if it is carried out otherwise than in accordance with the terms and conditions stipulated under this Act or any rules made thereunder. Provided that, where the patentee has previously imported the patented article into India prior to commencement of manufacture within India, subsequent manufacture shall not constitute infringement unless it exceeds quantities reasonably required for demonstration, testing, or analysis purposes as determined by the Controller. Furthermore, a patentee seeking to enforce their rights under this Act must demonstrate continuous and active exploitation of the invention in India, failing which, such rights may be subject to limitation as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent or rectification of the register may appeal from such order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; and where such appeal is preferred, the Board shall hear the appeal expeditiously and make its decision as provided herein. Any party failing to comply with the provisions relating to payment of fees during appellate proceedings shall be deemed to have abandoned the appeal. Further, any act of manufacture, use or sale of the patented invention without authorization from the patentee shall constitute an infringement actionable at the suit of the patentee for damages and injunction as determined by the relevant court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee shall have the right to grant exclusive licences relating to the patented invention, either for the whole duration of the patent or for any limited period. Such licence may be granted to any person, firm, or company, Indian or foreign, and may include rights to make, use, sell, offer for sale, and import the patented article or substance. The patentee shall retain ownership of the patent unless expressly relinquished in the terms of the assignment or exclusive licence agreement. Any such assignment or exclusive licence must be executed in writing and registered with the Controller as provided herein. Further, where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensee shall be deemed to possess for the purposes of this Act those of the rights which were exclusively licensed.

Where a person claims to be aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to revocation or infringement proceedings, such person may appeal from that order to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The appellate board shall consider whether the patentee has demonstrated sufficient evidence to substantiate the grounds for the original decision and whether the findings of fact were based on a proper appreciation of the record. It shall be open to the aggrieved party to present counter-evidence challenging the claims made by the patentee, and the Board may direct further inquiry if necessary. The appellate board’s determination shall be final, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution on a question of law.

Where a patentee alleges that any entry in the rectification register is erroneous or prejudicial to his interests, he may apply to the rectification register court for an order directing amendment or deletion of such entry. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds upon which the claim is based and supported by all relevant documents. The rectification register court shall afford the person whose interest is affected by the proposed alteration a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and may direct any party to produce evidence in support of his case. Any order made under this Act by the rectification register court shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The patentee bears the burden of proving the error or prejudice as provided herein.

Where an infringement claim patent has been granted, the Controller may, upon receiving a written application from the patentee, direct any person found to be using, selling by way of trade or hire, importing, or offering for sale without authorization, any patented invention, to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified in the direction. Such directions shall include particulars of the alleged infringing activity and a copy of the patent relating to the invention in question. The person so directed shall be afforded an opportunity to make representations regarding the infringement claim patent and to present evidence rebutting the allegations made against them. Failure by any person to appear as directed, or to submit written representations within the stipulated time, may result in proceedings being instituted ex parte. The Controller shall record all such submissions and consider them while determining the validity of the infringement claim patent.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, grant registration if satisfied that the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. Such registration shall not confer upon the patentee any right to prevent others from using the said method or process unless it is shown that such use would involve exploitation of the patented invention directly or indirectly. Further, where a justified registration has been granted under this Act, the patentee shall be obliged to disclose all relevant information pertaining to the application and subsequent modifications thereof, as provided herein. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating adherence to ethical guidelines concerning genetically modified organisms if applicable to the registered process.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of a patent or rectification of entries in the Register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; and if the Board is satisfied that the order was manifestly unjust, erroneous in law, or based on evidence not duly considered, it may allow an appeal and pass such order as it deems fit. Further, any person who knowingly infringes a patent shall be liable to pay damages to the patentee, subject to such limitations as are provided herein regarding contributory infringement. Pharmaceutical products manufactured without authorization from the patentee shall be deemed an act of infringement attracting severe penalties as determined by the relevant authorities.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee may grant an exclusive licence relating to the patented invention, specifying the territory within which, and the goods or services in relation to which, such licence is granted. Any assignment or exclusive licence shall be recorded in the Register respect goods, and where such recording is not effected, the assignee or licensee shall only hold such rights as the assignor or patentee would have been entitled to exercise if the assignment or licence had not been made. The patentee shall provide a certified copy of the agreement for recording, detailing the consideration paid or promised, and any restrictions imposed on the use of the invention during the term of the exclusive licence. Further, under this Act, sub-licensing is permitted with the prior written consent of the patentee, such consent being recorded in the Register as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “licence” in relation to copyright shall mean an authorization granted by the owner of copyright, either expressly or impliedly, permitting specific acts which would otherwise constitute infringement. Such licence may be exclusive, restricting others from performing the authorized act, or non-exclusive, allowing multiple parties such permission. A licence is deemed to exist where a person performs an act with the knowledge and consent of the copyright owner, subject to any conditions stipulated therein. The terms of a licence shall govern the scope of permitted acts and any associated remuneration as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of licences granted under this Act for works comprising cinematograph films. An application for registration of a licence may be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by certified copies of the agreement creating such licence and details of the assignor and assignee. The applicant shall declare whether the licence is exclusive or non-exclusive and specify the territory within which it operates. Upon satisfactory verification of the particulars furnished and subject to payment of the requisite fee, the Registrar may register the licence and enter its particulars in the aforementioned register. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a licence may appeal to the Controller. The registered licences shall be open to public inspection as provided herein.

Where the owner of copyright in an artistic work grants a licence granting rights to reproduce that work in digital form, such licence shall be deemed to include the right to make available online versions of the reproduction, subject to any express limitations stated within the terms of the grant. Provided that where a licence is granted for commercial purposes and fails to specify the duration thereof, it shall be presumed to continue indefinitely until revoked by written notice from the copyright owner served upon the licensee at their last known address. Any unauthorized reproduction or distribution of the artistic work occurring after such revocation constitutes an infringement under this Act. The remedies available to the copyright owner in respect of such infringement include injunctive relief and damages as provided herein, without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available to them.

Where the copyright holder grants a licence to a third party enabling reproduction of works in an audio-visual format for broadcast purposes, such licence shall be deemed non-exclusive unless expressly stated otherwise within the terms of agreement. The application for registration of this licence, if contested by either party, may be referred to the relevant High Court for determination of its validity and scope. Any dispute concerning the remuneration payable under a licence granted as provided herein shall first be addressed through conciliation proceedings facilitated by an independent mediator appointed by mutual consent of both parties. Failure to reach a resolution via conciliation within ninety days shall permit either party to institute legal proceedings, subject to adherence to prescribed procedural timelines. The copyright holder retains the right to terminate any such licence upon written notice of sixty days if material breaches occur, as defined under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming exclusive right in copyright in an artistic work may grant a licence granting permission to reproduce such work in a book, provided that the terms of the licence clearly specify the geographical territory within which reproduction is permitted. Such licences shall be documented in writing and registered with the designated Copyright Office; failure to register a licence as provided herein renders it unenforceable against third parties. The grantor of the licence may stipulate conditions regarding the quality of reproduction, ensuring adherence to standards reasonably related to the original work’s aesthetic merit. Any subsequent assignment of copyright relating to the artistic work shall be deemed to include the rights and obligations pertaining to the existing licence, unless expressly excluded in writing by all relevant parties.

Any person granting a licence in respect of copyright in any work shall be liable to pay royalties as determined under this Act, provided that such royalties are remitted directly to the designated Copyright Society within thirty days of disbursement to the copyright owner. Failure to remit said royalties shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. The grant of a licence does not absolve the licensor from liability for acts of infringement committed by the licensee, subject to demonstrating due diligence in monitoring compliance with the terms of the licence agreement as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings seeking damages and injunctive relief against both the licensor and licensee.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an exclusive right under this Act may grant a licence granting permission to use copyrighted works. Such licences may be granted for specific acts, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, public performance, and distribution, as determined by the grantor. The terms and conditions of such a licence shall be governed by contract law principles, provided that any limitation on the scope of copyright conferred under this Act must be clearly defined within the agreement. A licence may be exclusive, granting only one party the right to exercise specified rights, or non-exclusive, permitting multiple parties to do so. Assignment of copyright remains distinct from a licence; however, an assignment may include provisions mirroring those found in a contractual licence concerning royalty payments and usage restrictions as provided herein.

Where a copyright owner grants a licence permitting reproduction of a cinematograph film for broadcast purposes, such licence shall be deemed to include the right to synchronization with music, provided that the licensee does not materially alter the original work. Any dispute arising concerning the scope or duration of this implied grant may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The copyright owner shall have the right to appeal any award made by the Arbitral Tribunal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of receipt of the said award. Further, it is provided that a licence granted under this Act does not extend to the creation of derivative works based on the original cinematograph film without express written consent.

Where the copyright holder grants a licence granting rights to reproduce or distribute works incorporated into tangible products, the licensee shall provide notification to the owner of the copyright within thirty days of commencing manufacture. This notification must specify the nature of the copyrighted work utilized, the quantity of goods manufactured incorporating such work, and the intended market for those goods. Failure to provide this notification as provided herein constitutes a breach of the licence agreement and renders the licensee liable for damages sustained by the copyright holder. The copyright holder may pursue remedies available under contract law in respect of any such breach. Further, where a licensee acts in violation of the terms of their licence, including failing to adhere to goods manufactured notification requirements, the copyright holder is entitled to injunctive relief preventing further manufacture and distribution.

Where the copyright holder desires to grant permission for acts restricted under this Act, such permission shall be formalized through a licence agreement executed in writing. The application for registration of a licence, detailing the scope of permitted acts, duration, geographical limitations, and royalty provisions, may be submitted to the Copyright Office by either the licensor or licensee. Such basic application must specify the work subject to the licence and identify all parties involved with due diligence regarding their legal standing. Any alteration to the terms of a registered licence requires submission of an amended application for approval, which shall be processed in accordance with procedures prescribed herein. The Registrar may reject any application if it contains provisions deemed contrary to public interest or unfairly restrictive of copyright owner’s rights as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming right in copyright in an artistic work may grant a licence conferring upon the licensee the specified exclusive right or rights to reproduce such work in a particular form. Such licence shall be deemed to be non-exclusive unless expressly stated otherwise within the terms and conditions agreed between the copyright owner and the prospective licensee. An authorised user, defined as one who has previously obtained permission for limited use of the copyrighted material under a separate agreement, may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence if the copyright owner fails to grant a reasonable licence on commercially justifiable terms. The application shall detail the intended scope of usage and demonstrate compliance with existing contractual obligations.

Any person granting a licence in respect of varieties registered under this Act shall be liable to prosecution if such licence contains terms that are demonstrably unconscionable or restrict the licensee’s ability to utilize the licensed material for legitimate research purposes. Failure to disclose all relevant information pertaining to the variety's genetic composition and propagation methods prior to granting a licence constitutes a violation, punishable with imprisonment extending to two years and a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any agreement purporting to assign copyright in respect of registered varieties shall be deemed void ab initio if it contravenes provisions relating to plant breeder’s rights as provided herein. Repeated infringements may result in the revocation of the licence and subsequent prohibition from granting further licences under this Act.

An assignment of copyright under this Act shall be deemed to include the exclusive right to reproduce the work in any material form, including but not limited to digital formats, unless the assignment expressly states otherwise. Such an assignment may relate to the whole or part of the copyright in the work, and shall clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred. Provided that where an assignment purports to transfer copyright relating to a cinematograph film, it shall also specify whether such assignment includes the right to make any sound recording of music composed for the film. An assignment shall not be effective unless it is signed by the assignor or their duly authorised representative.

An assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed to include the exclusive right to reproduce the film in any medium, including but not limited to digital formats accessible online, subject to any limitations expressly stated within the instrument of assignment. Such an assignment must clearly delineate whether it pertains to the entire copyright or only specific rights therein, and this delineation shall be recorded accurately on the Register of Copyrights maintained under this Act. Provided that, where a work is jointly authored, any assignment requires the consent of all co-owners unless otherwise agreed in writing prior to the creation of the work. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the assignor’s authority to effectuate such an assignment and shall record details of the assignee's contact information as provided herein.

An assignment of copyright under this Act shall be deemed to confer upon the assignee all the copyright therein comprised, subject to the terms and conditions specified within the instrument of assignment. Provided that an assignment purporting to transfer copyright shall clearly delineate the specific rights being assigned, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation. Where the assignor retains certain rights under the assignment, such retention must be explicitly stated in writing. Failure to adequately specify the scope or duration of the assignment may render it voidable at the assignee’s option. Any person acquiring copyright pursuant to a valid assignment shall have the same remedies against infringement as if they were the original copyright holder. The assignor shall remain liable for any breach of contract relating to the assignment, provided that such breach occurred prior to the transfer of ownership.

An assignment of copyright under this Act shall be effected only by way of a written instrument executed by or on behalf of the assignor, and attested by at least one witness competent to testify before a court. Such instrument shall clearly delineate the specific rights being assigned, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, and shall explicitly state the duration for which the assignment is granted, specifying a period not exceeding the term of copyright as provided herein. The written instrument must also identify the assignor and assignee by their full legal names and addresses, along with any relevant registration numbers pertaining to either party under this Act. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements shall render the purported assignment void. Any dispute concerning the validity or interpretation of an assignment may be referred for adjudication to a judicial forum as prescribed by law.

An assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed valid only if executed as a registered document under this Act, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities. Such assignment must clearly delineate the specific rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and exhibition rights, and shall specify the duration for which those rights are assigned; an assignment purporting to transfer copyright in perpetuity shall be deemed invalid. Provided that, where a film incorporates pre-existing works protected by copyright, the assignor warrants that they possess the requisite authority to effect such assignment concerning those incorporated elements. Failure to provide this warranty renders the assignment voidable at the assignee’s discretion and subject to remedies as provided herein.

Any assignment purporting to transfer the entire or partial copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed invalid if it fails to explicitly state whether the assignor retains any rights relating to exploitation of the film through broadcast, public performance, or digital transmission. Such failure constitutes conclusive evidence that the intention was not to effect an absolute and unrestricted transfer as provided herein. Any person knowingly utilizing an assignment obtained in contravention of this provision shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the potential royalty income had a valid assignment been executed. Furthermore, upon discovery of such unauthorized utilization, the copyright holder may seek injunctive relief preventing further exploitation without prejudice to claims for compensation and punitive penalties as determined by civil court jurisdiction.

The right to receive royalties accruing from any commercial exploitation of a copyrighted musical composition may be assigned by the composer or their legal heirs, subject to the terms stipulated within the instrument of assignment. Such an assignment shall clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and broadcasting rights. It is provided that any subsequent assignment relating to the same work must explicitly reference the prior assignment and its conditions, failing which it shall be deemed invalid under this Act. The assignor retains the right to audit royalty statements presented by the assignee for a period of three years from the date of publication of such statements. Further, an assignment may include provisions concerning reversion of copyright should specified performance criteria not be met within a defined timeframe, as agreed between parties.

An assignment purporting to transfer all or any part of the copyright in a musical composition shall be deemed invalid if it fails to expressly state whether the assignor retains the right to perform the work publicly. Where such an omission occurs, the assignee may institute proceedings seeking clarification from the relevant civil court regarding the scope of rights conveyed. The determination of the court on this matter shall be final and binding, subject to appeal only on grounds demonstrably showing a fundamental error of law or procedural irregularity. Further, any subsequent assignment by the assignor relating to the same work following an initial disputed assignment shall be voidable at the option of the original assignee, provided that action is taken within three years from the date of the second assignment.

An assignment of copyright subsisting in a registered certification mark representing a literary work shall be deemed valid only if executed by a person holding absolute title to both the copyright and the registration mark, as evidenced by certificates of ownership issued under this Act. Such assignment must explicitly state whether it pertains to the entire term of copyright or a specified period not exceeding twenty-five years from the date of first publication of the work. Further, any assignee acquiring rights through such an assignment shall be obligated to maintain the validity and integrity of the associated registration mark certification, adhering to all applicable regulations concerning its use and display. Provided that failure to do so may render the assignment voidable at the discretion of the copyright holder.

Any assignment purporting to transfer copyright in a literary or artistic work shall be deemed invalid if it fails to explicitly state the date patent shall commence for the benefit of the assignee, unless such omission is demonstrably inconsequential due to prior established practice. Where an assignment is procured by coercion or undue influence, any aggrieved party may petition the relevant High Court seeking declaration of its nullity and damages commensurate with losses suffered as a direct consequence thereof. Furthermore, wilful falsification of records pertaining to assignments, intended to mislead authorities regarding ownership rights, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than two years, and a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. Recovery of royalties due under an assignment is subject to the provisions relating to limitation periods as provided herein.

An assignment of copyright in a literary work, including source code embodied in computer programs, shall be deemed invalid if it purports to transfer ownership prior to the date of filing of a corresponding trade mark application relating to that work’s title or associated branding. Provided that, where such a trade mark application is subsequently found to have been filed without due diligence and bona fide intention to use the mark in commerce, the Court may, upon review of evidence presented by aggrieved parties, reinstate the assignment as originally executed. Any dispute arising from the validity of an assignment under this Act shall be subject to appeal to the appellate jurisdiction established for intellectual property matters, notwithstanding any provision to the contrary contained elsewhere within this legislation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an act of infringement occurs where a person, without authorization or license as provided herein, reproduces, adapts, distributes, publicly displays, or performs a copyrighted work. For the purposes of determining whether such acts constitute infringement, it shall be deemed that copies have been made if any storage medium contains information derived directly from the original work, irrespective of alterations.
