Nothing in this Act shall prevent fair dealing with a work for research, private study, criticism, or review, provided that such use is equitable and does not prejudice the rights holder’s ability to derive substantial benefit from their copyright.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, registration of literary works with the Office of Registrar of Copyrights is deemed prima facie evidence of ownership for the purposes of establishing infringement. An applicant seeking registration shall submit along with the application, a certified copy of the record of assignment, if the work has been assigned prior to the date of application; failure to do so may result in delayed processing and potential challenges to claimed ownership during any subsequent legal proceedings. Where an unregistered work is subject to unauthorized reproduction or distribution, the aggrieved party may still pursue remedies under this Act, but shall bear a heavier burden of proof regarding authorship and originality. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify authenticity as provided herein.

Where an act of reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of a copyrighted work is found to constitute infringement under this Act, the copyright owner shall be entitled to injunctive relief restraining further acts of the infringing conduct. Such injunction may extend to all forms of unauthorized use, including but not limited to public performance, broadcasting, and making available online. Provided that, in determining whether an act constitutes infringement, due consideration shall be given to fair dealing for purposes such as criticism, review, or reporting current events, subject to limitations regarding the extent and nature of the excerpt taken. The copyright owner may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the infringement, including any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized use, unless it can be demonstrated that the actual damage is ascertainable.

Where an act is alleged to constitute infringement of copyright under this Act, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings in the Original Court having jurisdiction over the cause of action. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date on which the alleged infringement was first committed; provided that the Appellate Tribunal may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, entertain a suit where the delay exceeds said period if it is satisfied that the delay was unintentional and did not prejudice the claimant. The Court shall have power to grant such remedies as are just and equitable, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages calculated according to principles established under this Act, and delivery up or destruction of infringing copies. Any party dissatisfied with the judgment or order of the Original Court may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such judgment or order.

Where an individual or entity utilizes a substantial portion of a copyrighted work without authorization, such action constitutes infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the reproduction is solely for private and non-commercial use, and does not prejudice the rights of the copyright owner as provided herein, it shall not be deemed to constitute infringement. Further, if the alleged infringing act involves fair dealing with a literary or artistic work for research, criticism, review, or reporting current events, such usage may be permissible subject to conditions relating to acknowledgement of the source and author. Any person found guilty of copyright infringement shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner, considering factors including the extent of unauthorized reproduction and commercial gain derived therefrom.

Where any person is found to have infringed copyright in respect of any work, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner of the copyright as a consequence thereof. The amount of compensation may be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the quantum of benefit derived by the infringer and the loss suffered by the copyright holder. Provided that, where the infringement is committed knowingly and with intent to deceive or cause damage, the Court shall award punitive damages not exceeding ten times the profit so made or the license fee which would have been payable had the infringing act been duly authorized. Any suit for recovery of damages relating to such infringement may be instituted in any District Court having jurisdiction.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the copyright in a musical work or dramatic work has been assigned by virtue of a license granting exclusive rights of reproduction and public performance, the assignor shall retain the right to grant non-exclusive licenses for the synchronization of the work with audio-visual media, provided that such synchronization does not constitute an act of infringement under this Act. Any subsequent assignment of copyright in the said musical or dramatic work shall be deemed to include these synchronization rights unless explicitly excluded by written agreement between the parties. Further, where a license has been granted for adaptation of a literary or artistic work, the licensor may grant further licenses relating to similar adaptations without prejudice to the original licensee’s exclusive right to exploit their adaptation as provided herein. The terms and conditions governing such sub-licensing shall be determined by contractual agreement.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of copyright under this Act, such party shall institute proceedings before the relevant High Court, demonstrating prima facie evidence of substantial similarity between the copyrighted work and the alleged infringing copy. The defendant may present counter-evidence asserting fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, provided that such use is accompanied by due acknowledgement of the author and source material. It shall be incumbent upon the plaintiff to establish both ownership of copyright and demonstrable copying of a substantial portion thereof. Any order restraining further distribution or reproduction requires reasoned justification documented within the court record; appeals against such orders may be filed within sixty days, subject to applicable procedural rules.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where an author’s work has been reproduced in a manner authorized under section fifty-two, and subsequently utilized for commercial purposes without due attribution or licensing agreement, such utilization shall constitute infringement. This determination is predicated upon demonstrable evidence establishing substantial similarity between the original work and the infringing reproduction, considering both qualitative and quantitative aspects of the adaptation. Provided that, where the manner applications clause permits transformative adaptations incorporating elements from multiple sources, a finding of infringement requires proof that the defendant’s actions exploited the unique creative expression embodied in the initial copyrighted work, rather than merely employing commonplace or generic components. The right to remedy such infringement shall be subject to equitable considerations as determined by the relevant judicial forum.

Where an act of reproduction, distribution, or public display of a copyrighted work is committed without license or authorization from the copyright owner, such act constitutes infringement under this Act. Any person found guilty of infringement shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright holder, and may also face imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. It is established that an invention means new; therefore, unauthorized adaptation or derivation of substantial portions of copyrighted material, even with minor alterations, will be deemed infringement if it lacks originality independent of the original work. The Court shall consider evidence of intent in determining the appropriate penalty and may order seizure and destruction of infringing copies.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the copyright in any work has been assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignor or licensor may, by instrument in writing, grant further licenses relating to the same rights in respect of the work. Such further license shall be valid only if the Chairperson of the Copyright Society is notified in writing and a copy of the assignment or initial license is provided for record. Any subsequent assignee or licensee shall hold the copyright subject to any prior assignments or licenses already existing, and may seek redress under this Act against any person committing infringement relating to those rights. Provided that, where an exclusive license has been granted, the licensee shall be deemed the owner of the copyright for all purposes as provided herein, except in cases involving moral rights.

For the purposes of this Act, an "authorised user" means a person who has been granted permission by the proprietor of the geographical indication to use such indication in relation to goods for which the indication is registered, subject to any conditions specified therein. An application for authorisation as an authorised user may be made to the Registrar, and shall include particulars regarding the nature and extent of the proposed use. The Registrar may grant or refuse such authorisation based on considerations including whether the use will prejudice the quality or reputation associated with the geographical indication, provided that the proprietor’s consent is obtained prior to any determination.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed by any person who is engaged in production, processing, packing, conditioning, handling, or marketing of goods conforming to the standard of quality and characteristics of the geographical indication. The Registrar shall consider applications from producers’ associations representing the interests of growers, processors, or other stakeholders involved in the production or distribution of goods originating from the defined geographical area. Where an application is filed by a producer's association, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the association has the support of at least fifty percent of the producers engaged in the relevant activity. Any person who obtains authorisation to use a registered geographical indication shall be deemed an *authorised user* and must adhere to the quality control measures as prescribed under this Act.

An application for rectification of a registration relating to a geographical indication may be made by any person claiming title or interest, including an *authorised user* who alleges that the registered geographical indication is being used in a manner contrary to the interests of the true and proper proprietors. Such an application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, demonstrating prejudice arising from the use of the indication, and may include evidence of dilution of distinctiveness or unfair competition. The Registrar may entertain such an application only if the applicant demonstrates a direct economic interest in the continued protection of the geographical indication’s reputation. Provided that any *authorised user* seeking rectification must first exhaust all remedies available under contractual agreements with the proprietor before pursuing action under this Act, and shall be subject to costs as determined by the Registrar.

An application for registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication may be made by any person who, at the time of application, is engaged in production or processing of goods conforming to the standard specified under this Act and whose use of the geographical indication is continuous for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of such application. The Registrar shall give notice of the application to the proprietor of the geographical indication and any other interested parties as provided herein, affording them an opportunity to submit objections within two months from the date of publication of the notice. Objections may be based on grounds that the applicant’s use does not conform to the prescribed standard or that their continued use is detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication. The Registrar shall consider any such objections and may require the applicant to provide further information or undertake modifications to their production process before determining whether registration as an authorised user should proceed.

An applicant seeking registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication shall demonstrate, through documented evidence, continuous and verifiable adherence to the quality standards prescribed by the consortium representing the collective interest in the indicated good. Such evidence must detail compliance with production methods, processing techniques, and any other relevant criteria outlined within the product specification document currently maintained by the consortium. The Registrar may require further verification from independent assessors appointed by the consortium to ascertain ongoing conformity. An authorised user’s rights are subject to revocation if they fail to maintain these standards or act in a manner detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication, as determined under this Act and following due process.

An application for registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication shall be rejected if the applicant’s use of the indication is found, upon investigation under this Act, to constitute unfair competition against producers genuinely entitled to utilise the same. Any person utilising a registered geographical indication without being recognised as an authorised user, or employing it in a manner that misrepresents the origin or quality of goods, shall be liable for damages assessed by the relevant High Court. Further, such unauthorised use may result in the seizure and forfeiture of goods bearing the infringing mark. Repeated contravention of these provisions will attract penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees per instance and may lead to prosecution under this Act.

An authorisation granted under this Act relating to the use of a registered geographical indication may, subject to the terms and conditions specified therein, be assigned by transfer in writing. Such assignment shall require registration with the Registrar, and the prescribed fee shall be paid upon submission. The assignee shall become vested with all rights and obligations of the assignor as an authorised user under this Act, including any pending applications for further authorisations relating to the same geographical indication. Any subsequent licensing or sub-licensing of such authorisation must also be registered, provided that the original authorisation agreement expressly permits such actions. An authorised user shall not undertake activities which are detrimental to the quality or reputation associated with the geographical indication, and may face revocation of their authorisation if they do so. The Registrar may issue directions regarding permissible uses consistent with maintaining the distinctiveness of the indicated goods.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be opposed by any person claiming an interest in the distinctive character of the goods concerned, or alleging that use of the proposed indication is contrary to law. Such opposition shall be heard by the Registrar, who shall give notice to the applicant and the opponent, affording them both opportunities to present evidence and arguments. The determination of whether a producer qualifies as an *authorised user* for purposes of this Act hinges upon demonstrating continuous and traditional connection with the geographical unit, subject to verification by the Registrar. Any decision made under this Act may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, provided that the appellant demonstrates prejudice resulting from any error apparent on the face of the record.

An authorisation granted under this Act relating to the use of a registered Geographical Indication may, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein, be assigned by transfer in writing to any person who is engaged in production or processing of goods conforming to the standards of quality and characteristics of the indication. Such assignment shall require prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to all existing contractual obligations pertaining to the Geographical Indication’s use. Any application for assignment must detail the proposed scope of usage by the assignee and demonstrate their capacity to maintain the reputation of the geographical indication. The Layout Design Registry may be consulted regarding design elements incorporated in packaging or labelling associated with the authorised user's products, ensuring consistency with established standards. An existing authorised user may sub-license rights under this Act, but only with the Registrar’s consent.

For the purposes of this Act, “High Court” means the High Court exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction in respect of any territory within India; and where a cause or matter arises outside the local limits of the High Court’s usual admirative jurisdiction, it shall be deemed to arise within those limits if the cause or matter relates to a copyright work first published or otherwise made available to the public within that territory. The expression “High Court” includes a permanent judge of the High Court and any other judge temporarily appointed to act in place of a permanent judge; provided that decisions regarding jurisdiction under this Act shall be subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Applications for registration of literary works, including computer programs and databases, shall be submitted to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form, accompanied by two certified copies of the work. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue a receipt and assign it an acknowledgement number. The applicant may subsequently request a status update regarding their application through the online portal maintained by the Copyright Office. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the work is original and eligible for registration under this Act, provisional registration shall be granted. Any party disputing the originality or ownership of a work undergoing registration may file an objection with the High Court within sixty days from the date of publication of notice of the application in the Official Gazette.

Where infringement of copyright subsists in respect of works situated beyond the local limits of a particular district, any aggrieved party shall be entitled to institute legal proceedings for redressal before a High Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the infringement occurred, or where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the defendant resides or carries on business within the territorial jurisdiction of two or more High Courts, suit may be instituted in any such court. The remedies available under this Act shall include, but not be limited to, an injunction restraining further acts of copyright infringement and a claim for damages sustained by the copyright owner as a consequence thereof. Subject to just compensation being paid, the Court may grant leave to use the copyrighted work where the infringement was unintentional or incidental.

Applications for rectification of entries relating to copyright ownership shall be filed with the office of the Registrar of Copyrights. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar shall serve notice thereof upon all parties whose interests are affected by the proposed rectification, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit objections under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar concerning the rectification of copyright entries may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The High Court shall have the same jurisdiction in respect of such appeals as it has in relation to appeals under other provisions of this Act. Provided that, where an objection is raised regarding the validity of a copyright itself, the High Court may determine the matter de novo.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any copyright owner seeking to enforce their rights relating to works published outside the territory of India shall file a suit exclusively in the High Court not subordinate to the jurisdiction where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the publication occurred through an authorized agent acting on behalf of the copyright owner, the suit may be filed in the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where such agent’s principal place of business is situated within India. Further, the High Court shall not entertain any such suit unless it is satisfied that all reasonable efforts have been made to obtain redress through alternative dispute resolution mechanisms as provided herein and a record of those attempts has been submitted to the court.

Any proprietor of copyright who discovers that any act restricted under this Act has been committed in relation to works for which he is entitled to copyright shall have the right to institute civil proceedings for damages and seek an injunction restraining further infringement. Provided that, where a work has been reproduced without authorization, the Court may award compensatory damages not exceeding ten times the actual damages proven or, if the actual damages cannot be reasonably ascertained, such sum as the Court deems just and reasonable. Further, any person found guilty of knowingly facilitating copyright infringement shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine such proceedings.

The owner of copyright in any musical work shall be entitled to grant licenses granting rights of reproduction and public performance, subject to the conditions specified herein. Such licenses may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively, and the terms thereof, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined as provided under this Act. Assignment of such copyright ownership, whether partial or complete, requires registration with the office designated for that purpose, and remains valid only if accompanied by a prescribed fee. Any person seeking to utilize a copyrighted musical work beyond the scope of a granted license may apply to the High Court for permission, demonstrating reasonable need and offering equitable compensation to the copyright owner. The High Court shall consider such applications in accordance with principles of fairness and public interest.

Where a dispute arises concerning the ownership of copyright in a musical work, and both parties claim exclusive rights based on conflicting assignments, the matter shall be referred to the High Court for determination. The court may, at its discretion, appoint an arbitrator with expertise in music industry practices to assist in evaluating evidence relating to the alleged assignment. Provided that any party disputing the findings of such arbitrator may appeal to a judge of the High Court within sixty days of the arbitration award. Further, it is provided that the determination of ownership made by the High Court shall be final, subject only to an appeal on grounds of law within ninety days from the date of the judgment.

Where a claim is made before a High Court alleging infringement of copyright in a literary work, and the defendant asserts that the said work constitutes fair dealing for the purpose of criticism or review, the plaintiff shall bear the burden of demonstrating to the satisfaction of the court that the extent of such use exceeds what is reasonably necessary for that purpose. Provided that, if the defendant has registered trade marks prominently featured within the allegedly infringing work, the court may consider the potential dilution of those marks as a factor in assessing whether the dealing was fair. The High Court shall have discretion to order discovery of documents relevant to determining the commercial impact of the alleged infringement, subject to just terms.

The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all works registered under this Act. Any party claiming to be adversely affected by an entry appearing in the Register relating to copyright ownership may submit an error amendment notice to the Registrar, setting forth particulars of the claimed error and supporting documentation. The Registrar shall consider such notices and provide an opportunity for both the claimant and the registered owner to present their arguments. Following due consideration, the Registrar may direct rectification of the register if satisfied that an error exists. Appeals against decisions made by the Registrar concerning entries in the Register are subject to appeal before a High Court.

Where infringement of copyright in any registered geographical indication associated with artistic work occurs, and the owner has suffered damage as a consequence thereof, such owner shall be entitled to seek remedies available under this Act. The High Court may, upon application by the copyright owner, grant an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to just terms for the alleged infringer. Compensation for damages sustained by the copyright owner due to the infringing act shall be determined by the High Court, taking into consideration factors including the extent of the damage and the profits derived from the infringing use. Provided that any dispute concerning the assessment of compensation may be referred to arbitration as agreed upon by both parties, with the award being enforceable in the High Court. The right to seek damages under this provision shall not preclude the owner from pursuing other remedies available under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “Official Gazette” means the publication notified by the Central Government as the official medium for public notices and announcements; where a document is published in more than one Official Gazette, such publication shall be deemed to be a single publication. Any notice required or permitted to be published under this Act shall be published in the Official Gazette in English and Hindi, or in such other languages as the Central Government may direct. The publication of any such notice shall be conclusive evidence of its due publication, subject to any appeal provided for elsewhere herein.

Registration of designs shall be deemed conclusive evidence of title to the design for all purposes under this Act, subject to any rights priorly acquired. An application for registration may be made jointly by two or more persons, and where a design has been previously registered in India, a subsequent applicant shall disclose such prior registration in their application. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct that it be published in the Official Gazette. Any person may, within three months from the date of publication in the Official Gazette, file any notice of opposition to the registration. The particulars of the design and the name and address of the applicant shall be prominently displayed in the Official Gazette.

Any person claiming infringement of copyright in any work published or otherwise made available to the public shall serve a notice upon the alleged infringer specifying the nature and extent of the alleged infringement and demanding that the infringing act be restrained. Such notice shall be served at least sixty days prior to instituting any legal proceedings relating to the matter, provided that this requirement does not apply where the infringement is flagrant or has caused substantial damage. Failure to serve such a notice shall deprive the complainant of injunctive relief under this Act. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the form and manner of serving such notices. Any aggrieved party may seek remedies for contributory copyright infringement as provided herein, subject to demonstrating knowledge of the infringing activity.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a literary work, examine whether the particulars furnished are complete and accurate, and if satisfied that the applicant is the first owner of copyright in the work, shall proceed to register the work under this Act. Notice of the proposed registration shall be published for public inspection in the Official Gazette, along with details of the work and the name and address of the claimant. Any person claiming to have rights adversely affected by such proposed registration may submit objections within a period specified therein; these objections shall be considered by the Registrar before making a determination. The Registrar’s decision on any objection shall be final and binding. Registration shall only confer the benefits provided herein, subject to compliance with all applicable provisions of this Act regarding ownership and duration of copyright.

Publication of notices relating to copyright registrations and renewals shall be effected only through publication in the Official Gazette. Any party seeking to challenge the validity of a copyright registration must provide written notice to the Registrar of Copyrights at least thirty days prior to submitting an application for review under this Act. Such notice shall clearly specify the grounds upon which the challenge is based, supported by documentary evidence as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Failure to comply with this notification requirement will render any subsequent application inadmissible. The Registrar may, subject to due process and after affording the copyright owner a reasonable opportunity to be heard, determine whether publication in the Official Gazette was appropriately undertaken.

Any person who reproduces any work in contravention of this Act, or causes to be reproduced, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees; provided that where the reproduction is made for commercial gain, the penalty shall be enhanced to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to seven years and with a fine which may extend to twenty-five thousand rupees. Notice of any such action taken under this Act shall be published in the Official Gazette as soon as reasonably practicable, detailing the nature of the infringement and the penalties imposed; failure to publish such notice accurately or completely shall render the initiating officer liable for damages recoverable by the aggrieved party.

Any copyright accruing by virtue of this Act in respect of any work published or otherwise made available to the public prior to the commencement of this section shall be assignable by the owner thereof, subject to any existing contractual obligations. Such assignment may be absolute or for a specific term, and shall include the right to grant exclusive licenses relating to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public performance of the work. Where an assignment is made, particulars thereof shall be registered in the prescribed manner and published in the Official Gazette for information of all parties concerned. Failure to register such assignments within three months from their execution shall render them voidable at the option of the assignor. The assignee may enforce the copyright as if originally vested in him or her, provided that any subsequent assignment requires similar registration and publication.

Publication in the Official Gazette shall constitute conclusive evidence for all purposes under this Act regarding the validity and authenticity of any copyright registration certificate or related document, subject to a challenge brought before the relevant judicial forum within ninety days from the date such publication is deemed to have taken effect. Provided that, where an aggrieved party alleges demonstrable error in the particulars published in the Official Gazette pertaining to ownership or authorship, they may petition for review; however, any such petition must be accompanied by verified affidavits and supporting documentation establishing reasonable grounds for doubt concerning the accuracy of the information disseminated. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the challenge non-maintainable, as provided herein.

Where any person claims that a work has been infringed under this Act, and the alleged infringer fails to appear or respond to notice served upon them as provided herein, the High Court may, subject to just cause shown, grant an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. Such notice shall be conspicuously published in the Official Gazette for a period of not less than seven days prior to the hearing date. The publication in the Official Gazette serves as prima facie evidence of due service, notwithstanding any claim by the defendant that they were unaware of the proceedings. Any party aggrieved by an ex parte order may apply to have it set aside, demonstrating satisfactory explanation for their failure to appear and presenting a meritorious defense against the allegations.

Publication in the Official Gazette shall constitute conclusive evidence for all purposes under this Act regarding the existence and validity of a registered design. Where an application for registration of a design is deemed to be incomplete or contains deficiencies, the Designs Office may require the applicant to submit further particulars or amendments within a period specified therein; failure to comply with such requirement shall render the application void. Any notification issued by the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding any other matter as provided herein, shall be published in the Official Gazette. Furthermore, where a design is amended after initial registration, the date of amendment shall priority date for determining rights under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “artistic work” includes any graphic, sculptural, or architectural work permanently or temporarily fixed in a tangible medium, irrespective of whether it possesses artistic quality as determined by expert opinion. An artistic work shall be deemed to be distinct from photographs and cinematograph films, unless such photographs or films incorporate elements that demonstrably qualify as original artistic works under this Act. The right of copyright subsists exclusively in the author of an artistic work; however, where the work is made for hire, the employer shall be considered the author for the purposes of ownership. Reproduction of any substantial part of an artistic work without authorization constitutes infringement.

Registration of musical works shall confer upon the owner of copyright a prima facie evidence of ownership for the purposes of any action alleging infringement under this Act. An application for registration of a compilation or arrangement of pre-existing musical works may be made jointly by all persons claiming to have co-authorship, provided that each such applicant consents in writing to the joint application and affirms their contribution to the originality of the work as a whole. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered works, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions regarding privacy and commercial sensitivity. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal to the Controller, whose decision shall be final. Copyright in such registered musical works remains protected for the full term prescribed under this Act.

Any person who infringes copyright in any work or contravenes any provisions of this Act shall be liable for damages comprising a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two lakh rupees. Such damages may be awarded to the owner of the copyright, or otherwise as determined by the competent court. Where an infringement has been committed wilfully and for commercial advantage or gain, the court may increase the amount of damages up to five times the actual loss suffered by the copyright owner. Further, a person found guilty of such infringement shall also be liable to pay costs incurred by the copyright owner in legal proceedings under this Act. The remedies available to the copyright owner are without prejudice to any other remedy or right which they may have under this Act or otherwise as provided herein.

Any person claiming an infringement of copyright under this Act may institute a suit for damages and seek injunctive relief against the alleged infringer, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods herein. The plaint shall specify with particularity the work in which copyright subsists, the manner in which such copyright has been infringed, and the reliefs sought. Where the defendant is found to have knowingly infringed the said copyright, the Court may, in addition to damages, award further compensation not exceeding five times the amount of damages awarded. The Central Government shall, upon receiving a complaint regarding an alleged infringement, undertake preliminary inquiries to ascertain prima facie evidence of such infringement and may issue directions for its cessation. Any appeal from an order made under this Act lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work only if it is original and has been fixed in a tangible form, whether by writing or otherwise. Where an author’s rights have been assigned under a written agreement, the assignee shall be entitled to exercise those rights as if they were the author's own, provided that such assignment expressly specifies the duration of the term for which copyright is transferred. Any person desiring to reproduce any work in which copyright subsists shall obtain prior authorization from the owner of the copyright, unless an exception applies under this Act. Failure to secure such authorization constitutes a violation and renders the infringing party liable to prosecution as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe conditions for granting exemptions from these requirements relating to fair dealing.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite license under this Act or without authorization from the owner of copyright, reproduces any work, or a substantial portion thereof, for commercial gain shall be deemed to have infringed the said copyright. Such infringement attracts penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Further, where the infringement is committed by an employee, the employer shall also be liable to prosecution and penalty, subject to demonstrating due diligence in preventing such acts. The Central Government may, upon receiving complaint of copyright violation, issue injunctions restraining further infringing activity.

The owner of copyright in any cinematograph film or sound recording shall be entitled to grant a license authorizing reproduction and distribution of the work in another country, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the copyright holder, and the consideration for such grants shall be agreed upon between the parties involved. Where an assignment of copyright has been made, the assignee shall possess all rights pertaining to licensing under this Act, including the power to sub-license the work within the territory specified in the assignment agreement. Provided that any license granted prior to an assignment shall remain valid and enforceable unless expressly revoked by the assignor, subject to applicable principles of equity. The terms of a license relating to copyright are deemed contractual obligations binding on all parties involved.

Where a work has been lawfully made available online without authorization by the copyright owner, and subsequent unauthorized reproduction or distribution thereof occurs, demonstrating substantial similarity to the original online version, any party claiming infringement shall be deemed to have established prima facie evidence of copyright violation. Provided that, such claim must specify the precise date and manner of initial availability and detail the elements constituting substantial similarity, subject to judicial assessment regarding originality and creative expression. The aggrieved owner may pursue remedies as provided herein, but it shall be open to the alleged infringer to demonstrate due diligence in ascertaining the lawful status of the work or a lack of knowledge concerning the copyright ownership.

For the purposes of this Act, “artistic work” includes any graphic, photographic or artistic creation whatsoever, irrespective of its reproduction method, and shall encompass designs incorporated within such works that are independently copyrightable. Where an artistic work incorporates a registered trade mark as an element thereof, the existence of such registration shall not affect the subsistence of copyright in the artistic work itself; provided that the use of the trade mark remains consistent with the rights afforded to the proprietor under the Trade Marks Act. Any adaptation of an existing artistic work, whether original or derivative, shall be deemed a new artistic work subject to the provisions relating to moral rights and ownership as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of copyright is filed, the Registrar shall examine whether the work in respect of which the application has been made is original and entitled to copyright under this Act. The applicant shall furnish such information and submit such documents as the Registrar may require to ascertain the originality of the work and establish the claim to copyright. If the Registrar is satisfied that the work fulfills the requirements for registration, he shall proceed with the examination of priority date. An objection regarding the originality or validity of the copyright may be raised by any person interested in the matter within sixty days from the date of publication of notice of the application under this Act. The applicant shall have an opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. Following due consideration, the Registrar shall determine whether the work shall priority date and proceed accordingly.

The reproduction of any artistic work, including designs incorporated within registered certify goods, shall be prohibited without a license obtained under this Act. Provided that, where such certified goods are manufactured or imported for trade or commerce, the owner of the copyright shall provide written notice to the certifying authority detailing the extent and nature of the copyrighted material utilized in their production. Failure to comply with this notification requirement may result in the revocation of certification. Any person infringing upon said copyright is liable to prosecution as provided herein, subject to the conditions relating to fair dealing and private use stipulated elsewhere under this Act. The right to issue licenses remains exclusively vested within the copyright holder unless otherwise determined by a competent court.

Where a patent has been granted, any interested person may institute proceedings before the Controller by way of opposition to the patent within six months from the date on which the patent was published as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, an “interested person” shall include any person who, at the time of grant of the patent, had a relevant interest in obtaining or maintaining protection for an invention. The grounds for opposition shall be limited to those specified under this Act, relating to novelty, inventive step, and sufficiency of disclosure. Any representation made during such proceedings shall be supported by evidence as deemed necessary by the Controller.

Any party aggrieved by a published application for registration of a design may, within six months from the date of publication, file a notice of opposition with the Designs Office. Such opposition shall be limited to grounds alleging that the registered design lacks novelty or originality as defined under this Act, or that it does not involve an aesthetic feature. The opponent must specify the particulars of their claim and provide supporting documentation demonstrating prior use or disclosure of a substantially similar design. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the opposition being deemed inadmissible. The Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition, after which proceedings will be conducted as provided herein.

Where any party believes that a granted patent has been obtained contrary to this Act, or that the grant thereof was wrongly made, such party may, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition with the Controller within six months from the date of publication of the patent. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to allegations of lack of novelty, inventive step, or that the invention was disclosed in a manner contrary to this Act. Upon receipt of such notice, the Controller shall serve a copy thereof on the patentee and provide an opportunity for both parties to submit written arguments and evidence. The Controller may, after considering all submissions, allow or dismiss the opposition, provided that any order allowing the opposition shall be subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a patent has been granted, any interested person may file a notice of opposition to the patent within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to novelty, inventive step, and undue anticipation. The Controller may require the opponent to furnish such further particulars as he deems necessary to enable the patentee to file a counterstatement. A counterstatement filed by the patentee shall address each ground of opposition raised in the notice. The Controller shall give both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence, either orally or in writing, subject to procedural guidelines issued by the Patents Office. Decisions regarding the validity of the patent following opposition proceedings are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted in accordance with the provisions of this Act, any interested person may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition to the patent. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to the claim that the invention was anticipated by prior existing public knowledge or involves an element obtained directly from another source during the period if eighteen months preceding the filing date of the application for the patent. The Controller may require the interested person to furnish security, as deemed appropriate, to ensure compliance with procedural requirements under this Act. Provided that any modification made to the claims after grant shall be subject to further opposition proceedings.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step as defined under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during the opposition proceedings may render the notice inadmissible and result in penalties for frivolous filings. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to present evidence and arguments; any attempt at obstruction or misleading testimony will be subject to fines and potential criminal prosecution. Decisions of the Controller regarding opposition are final, but appeal lies to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to assign or license the patented invention subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. Any assignment or license agreement shall clearly specify the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to geographical limitations and field of use. Furthermore, any party intending to oppose a patent under this Act may, prior to filing such opposition, seek a voluntary license from the patentee on reasonable terms. Should the patentee fail or refuse to grant such a license within a period of ninety days from receipt of a written request outlining the proposed terms, the potential opponent shall be free to proceed with their opposition. The Controller may, in determining whether the terms offered are reasonable, consider prevailing industry practices and the extent of research and development undertaken by the patentee.

Where a patent has been granted, any interested person may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such opposition shall be limited to the grounds specified in this Act and relating to the novelty, inventive step, or sufficiency of disclosure of the invention claimed in the patent. The Controller may, upon receiving such notice, serve a copy thereof on the patentee and afford both parties an opportunity for reasoned argument and presentation of evidence. Should the opposition be deemed frivolous or manifestly lacking merit, the Controller shall reject it summarily; otherwise, proceedings shall continue as provided herein, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period not exceeding three months from the date of order.

For the purposes of this Act, “breeder” means the person initially responsible for the development of a new plant variety, whether through selection, hybridization, genetic engineering, or any other technique, and includes—subject to provisions regarding farmers’ rights—the successor in title or assignee of such breeder; provided that where a variety has been developed by a public institution or agricultural university, the head of the institution or university shall be deemed the breeder. A person claiming to be a breeder shall furnish particulars relating to the origin and maintenance of the plant variety as may be prescribed, and shall be responsible for ensuring its genetic purity during propagation.

An application for registration as a breeder shall be made to the Authority in Form A, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The application must specify the name and address of the applicant, along with details regarding their claim to breeding rights over the plant variety concerned. Where the applicant is not the original breeder, they must demonstrate due authorization from the initial breeder, supported by relevant documentation as may be required under this Act. Information pertaining to the method of breeding, genetic composition, and distinctive characteristics of the variety shall also be included. The Authority may request further information or clarification at any stage during processing. A person claiming rights as a *breeder* must satisfy the Authority that they have exercised sufficient control over the entire development of the variety.

Where a plant variety is found to infringe the rights of a *breeder*, the Authority may, subject to appeal under this Act, direct the infringer to cease the infringing activity and provide compensation to the aggrieved breeder. Such compensation shall be determined based on the extent of commercial exploitation undertaken by the infringer without authorization, taking into account factors including sales revenue derived from the unauthorized propagation or distribution of the variety, and demonstrable damage to the market share of the original breeder’s protected plant variety. Further, the Authority may order the destruction of all propagating material of the infringing variety held by the infringer, provided that such action does not unduly prejudice the livelihoods of farmers who have legitimately acquired seeds prior to the infringement determination. The aggrieved *breeder* shall be entitled to recover costs incurred in pursuing remedies under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming to be a breeder may file an application for registration with the Authority in Form A. Such application shall contain particulars relating to the origin and maintenance of the variety, details regarding its expression of economically important traits, and evidence demonstrating that the applicant fulfills the criteria for recognition as a breeder under this Act. The application must also include a statement affirming compliance with relevant bio-safety guidelines where applicable. Upon receipt of an application, the Authority shall issue an acknowledgment and may request further information or clarification from the applicant. An advertisement regarding the application shall be published in the Official Gazette and in such other manner as the Authority deems appropriate to invite objections from any person interested in plant variety protection.

A person shall be deemed to be a breeder if that person has exercised rights as conferred under this Act and fulfills all conditions stipulated herein for recognition. Such recognition may be granted by the Authority upon submission of a detailed record demonstrating derivation, including parentage information where applicable, and confirmation that the variety’s essential characteristics remain stable through successive generations. The breeder shall maintain accurate records pertaining to propagation methods employed and any modifications introduced during development. Further, a breeder seeking protection must provide evidence confirming that the variety does not infringe upon existing plant varieties or farmers' rights as provided herein. Failure to comply with these record-keeping requirements may result in suspension of breeder privileges.

Any person claiming to be a breeder shall register their claim with the Authority within six months of first commercial cultivation. Failure to do so renders any subsequent enforcement action against infringers significantly diminished, subject to review by the Appellate Board. The Authority may impose a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and up to two hundred thousand rupees on any individual or entity found to have cultivated a protected variety without authorization from the registered breeder. Furthermore, any commercial exploitation of a plant variety for profit without proper licensing agreements shall be deemed an offence, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority is empowered to seize and destroy infringing material as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a breeder may grant licenses for the commercial use of their plant variety, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license. Such licenses shall clearly delineate the rights granted, including but not limited to propagation, sale, import, and export of seeds or planting material derived from the protected variety. The breeder retains ownership of the intellectual property rights unless a complete assignment is executed in writing, duly registered with the Authority. Any licensee may further sub-license these rights subject to prior written consent of the breeder, provided that such sub-licensee adheres to the terms and conditions originally stipulated within the primary license agreement. Furthermore, any transfer or assignment of a breeder’s right shall be notified to the Authority for record purposes.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon their rights as a breeder under this Act, such allegation shall be made before the designated Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. The Tribunal may, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, entertain claims relating to unauthorized exploitation of plant variety protection, including but not limited to commercialization without proper authorization or benefit sharing agreements. It shall be incumbent upon the claimant to demonstrate prima facie evidence of derivation from their protected material and subsequent unauthorized use. Further, the accused breeder may present counter-evidence demonstrating independent development or prior art predating the claimed protection; such evidence must be substantiated by expert testimony and documented records. The Tribunal’s decision regarding infringement shall be binding pending appellate review.

Where any person alleges that the rights of a *breeder* have been infringed under this Act, they may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred. Such proceedings shall be for damages sustained by the claimant as a direct result of the infringing activity, including but not limited to loss of profits and costs incurred in investigating the infringement. The court may also grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement, provided that such restraint is reasonably necessary to prevent continuing or irreparable harm. Further, any person found guilty of wilful infringement shall be liable to pay compensation to the *breeder* equivalent to three times the amount of damages proven. Services specified alphabetically relating to plant variety registration, including but not limited to seed certification and propagation, are subject to these remedies as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a plant variety, including disputes concerning whether an applicant qualifies as a *breeder* under this Act, may within sixty days from the date of such decision file an appeal before the Appellate Board. The appeal shall specify the grounds on which it is based and be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documents pertaining to the application for registration and the Registrar’s order. Subject to provisions regarding frivolous or vexatious appeals as provided herein, the Appellate Board may entertain any appeal arising from a decision concerning eligibility for breeder status, including challenges to claims of precedence against entries in the design register. The Board shall give notice to all parties affected by the appeal before issuing its determination.

For the purposes of this Act, a certification trade mark shall mean a mark which identifies agricultural products and foodstuffs as conforming to defined standards relating to their origin, method of manufacture or processing, quality, or other characteristics. Such standards shall be established by an institution approved under this Act and certified as competent to operate a system of inspection and certification. The proprietor of a certification trade mark may only use the mark in relation to goods which satisfy the prescribed standards and are produced under its supervision. Any person using a certification trade mark without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be deemed guilty of an offence, subject to penalties as provided herein.

An application for registration of a certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars relating to the applicant, the certified product or service, and the rules governing the use of the mark as are required by the regulations. The applicant must demonstrate that they possess control over the characteristics of the goods or services for which the certification trade mark is sought, including quality, origin, method of manufacture, or other relevant attributes. Such control shall be exercised through a system of inspection and supervision, details of which must be submitted with the application. Provided that the Registrar may require further documentation to verify compliance with these requirements, registration will only proceed if the applicant’s eligibility is established as provided herein.

The proprietor of a certification trade mark shall be entitled to enforce the provisions of this Act relating to infringement against any person using, without due authorization, a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered mark. Such enforcement may be pursued through remedies available under this Act for passing off, including an injunction restraining the infringing use and recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a consequence thereof. Where the unauthorized use constitutes a detriment to the integrity of the certification scheme underlying the trade mark, the Court may also order the deletion of offending matter from any labels, advertisements or other materials relating to the goods or services in question. The proprietor shall provide evidence demonstrating that the infringing sign creates a likelihood of confusion among consumers regarding the origin or quality of the certified products or services, as provided herein.

The Registrar may entertain an application for registration of a certification trade mark if the applicant demonstrates that it proposes to use the mark for purposes of guaranteeing the origin, quality, characteristics, or other specific attributes of goods or services. Such guarantee shall be certified by a defined body constituted under law or established custom, and possessing the requisite expertise in assessing conformity with predetermined standards. The application must specify the detailed procedures governing the certification process, including mechanisms for inspection, testing, and dispute resolution relating to adherence to those standards. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence of its legal standing to act as a certification body and demonstrate that it operates independently from the producers or providers of the certified goods or services. Any alteration to these procedures requires prior notification and approval by the Registrar.

A certification trade mark shall be registrable if its use by any party conforms strictly to the prescribed standards and regulations detailed within the relevant quality control guidelines, as notified under this Act. Application for registration must include a comprehensive specification outlining the characteristics of goods or services eligible to bear the mark, alongside a precise definition of the certification process. The applicant shall demonstrate to the Registrar that they possess the requisite authority to ensure compliance with these standards and have established an effective mechanism for monitoring adherence by certified users. Provided that such mechanism is independently verifiable, the Registrar may grant registration; however, this remains subject to periodic review to confirm continued suitability.

Any person who uses a certification trade mark in relation to goods or services without authorization from the proprietor shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which may extend to one million rupees. Where such use is made for the purpose of deceiving the public concerning the origin or quality of those goods or services, the penalty shall be doubled. The proprietor of a certification trade mark may apply to the relevant High Court for an injunction restraining any person from using the mark without authorization, subject to demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof. False or misleading representations relating to the certification process are also actionable under this Act.

The owner of a certification trade mark shall grant licenses for its use subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, provided that any such license agreement must specify the duration of the license and the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to apply the mark. Assignment of the right to use a certification trade mark requires prior written consent from the Registrar, who may impose reasonable royalties or other conditions deemed necessary to protect the integrity of the certification scheme. Further, any assignment shall include a detailed inventory of certified products or services currently benefiting from the mark’s protection. The Registrar may revoke such consent if it is determined that the assignee is not operating in accordance with the standards underlying the certification trade mark. Sub-licensing is permitted only with express authorization documented within the primary license agreement.

The Registrar may, upon application and subject to such terms and conditions as he deems fit, register a certification trade mark indicating that the certified products or services meet certain standards established by the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration, amendment, rectification, or cancellation of a certification trade mark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Board shall consider any evidence submitted by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony regarding adherence to prescribed quality benchmarks, and may affirm, reverse, or modify the Registrar's order. It is provided that a challenge to the validity of the standards themselves must be brought before a civil court.

An applicant seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner. The application shall specify the particulars of the association proposing to use the mark, including its constitution, objectives, and geographical area of operation. It shall also detail the standards which goods or services bearing the certification trade mark must meet to be eligible for such certification.

The applicant shall register proposed regulations governing the use of the certification trade mark, outlining procedures for inspection, verification, and enforcement of those standards. The Registrar may require amendments to these regulations before proceeding with registration. Further, the application shall include a declaration by an authorized representative of the association confirming adherence to all applicable laws and regulations as provided herein. Failure to comply with any of these requirements will render the application liable for rejection.

A certification trade mark shall be registrable if application demonstrates that it conforms to an approved standard relating to the characteristics, quality, origin, production methods, or other relevant attributes of the goods or services. The applicant must specify the institution responsible for administering such standard and ensuring compliance by those using certified goods or services. Registration is conditional upon ongoing adherence to the prescribed procedures for certification and periodic audits conducted by the Registrar. Any alteration to the approved standard requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, failing which registration may be revoked. Further, a trade mark shall not be registered as a certification trade mark if it conflicts with any well-known trade mark already established in India, as provided herein.

The use of a certification trade mark shall be permitted only by bodies duly recognized under this Act and possessing demonstrable expertise within their respective fields. Any entity utilizing a certification trade mark without such recognition, or employing it to falsely represent conformity to specified standards, shall be liable for damages proportionate to the misrepresentation caused and subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to a certification trade mark requires prior approval from the relevant recognizing authority; failure to obtain this approval renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Authority. The Registrar may, sua bonâ fide, initiate proceedings against any body found in violation of these provisions and impose fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees.

The owner of a certification trade mark shall grant licenses for its use subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, provided that any license granted under this Act shall clearly specify the scope of permitted activities relating to the certified products or services. Such licenses may be assigned, either wholly or partially, to third parties with the prior written consent of the Registrar, who may require demonstration of continued adherence to certification standards by the assignee. Where a licensee seeks to sub-license rights under this Act, such sub-licensing shall also be subject to approval from the Registrar and must not diminish the integrity of the certification mark. Further, any application for registration as a certification trade mark filed pursuant to a 73 convention application shall include details regarding existing licensing agreements and proposed assignment protocols relating to the mark’s use.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a proposed certification trade mark on the grounds that the standards of conformity prescribed for use of the mark are not clearly defined, or do not relate demonstrably to characteristics essential to the goods or services identified, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit documentary evidence and reasoned argument in support of said standards. Such submission shall be considered by the Registrar, who may require further clarification from any party affected by the proposed mark. Furthermore, where a certification trade mark application incorporates an international registration referred under this Act, the determination of distinctiveness shall take into account the assessment made during the original examination abroad, subject to review as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may appeal against such a decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, a certification trade mark shall mean a mark prescribed for exclusive use by an authorized body certifying conformity of goods or services to a particular standard, specification, characteristic, quality, or other attribute as provided herein. Such authorized body shall be a legal entity registered under applicable laws and may include consumer protection organizations or industry associations. The use of a certification trade mark shall be restricted to those goods or services meeting the criteria established by the authorized body. A patent filed designating a process relevant to the standard certified is not, in itself, grounds for refusal of registration as a certification trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a "trade mark registered" shall be deemed to include any mark that has been entered on the Register of Trade Marks under the provisions herein and certified as such. Such registration confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark registered in connection with the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any limitations specified in the certificate of registration. The term "trade mark registered" also extends to include any representation of the mark, whether exact or approximate, used in relation to those goods or services and adopted in good faith. Nothing in this Act shall prevent the use of a trade mark registered for descriptive purposes.

The Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the necessary fee, register any word, name, symbol, device, or combination thereof, as a trademark if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. An applicant shall disclose whether the mark is being used to distinguish goods or services, and if so, provide details of such use. Where a proposed trade mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trademark for identical or closely related goods or services, registration may be refused under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a trademark shall have the right to appeal as provided herein. The register of trademarks shall contain particulars of every trade mark registered and its proprietor.

The proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act shall be entitled to restrain the use of any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark if such use is made in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, and without due cause. Such restraint may include an injunction preventing further infringing acts and a remedy permitting the recovery of damages sustained by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement. Provided that, where the alleged infringer had been honestly and contemporaneously using the conflicting mark prior to the date of registration, and such use was not conducted with intent to deceive or trade upon the reputation of the registered trade mark, relief may be granted only under conditions determined by the relevant adjudicating authority. The proprietor shall also have recourse to account for profits made through the unauthorized application of a trade mark.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file a request for examination within one year from the date of receipt of the acknowledgment stipulated under this Act. Where an objection is taken against a proposed trademark during examination, the applicant may submit a reply addressing the grounds of the objection and supported by relevant documentation demonstrating distinctiveness or acquired reputation. The Registrar shall consider such replies and may either proceed with registration or direct further inquiry. A *trade mark registered* under this Act confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior conflicting rights as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A proprietor seeking renewal of a trade mark registered under this Act shall file an application for such renewal not less than six months before the date of its expiry and not more than twelve months after that date, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating continued use of the trademark in accordance with the regulations as provided herein during the five years preceding the expiration date. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of such continuous use may result in refusal of renewal. Where a trade mark is registered and subsequently assigned, the assignee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations applicable to the original registration. Any alteration to the goods or services listed in relation to a trade mark registered shall require prior approval from the relevant authority.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, uses a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a *trade mark registered* in respect of identical or closely related goods or services shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also be liable to a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees; and where the offence is committed by a company, every director, manager, secretary, or other officer in default shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence. Further, any goods bearing such infringing trademark are subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein, without prejudice to any damages recoverable under this Act. The Registrar may issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act may grant licences for the use of their registered trade mark, specifying the geographical area and the goods or services in relation to which such use is permitted. Such licences shall be in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Further, the proprietor may assign the entire interest in a registered trade mark, including all rights and privileges pertaining thereto, to any person, provided that such assignment is made in accordance with the prescribed formalities and duly recorded. Any subsequent licensee of a registered trade mark shall hold only those rights expressly conferred upon them within the terms of their licence agreement, and shall be bound by the conditions stipulated therein. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the use of their registered trade mark notwithstanding any licensing arrangement.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure the proprietor of a *trade mark registered* under this Act, uses an identical or confusingly similar mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the said *trade mark registered* is used, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Court. Such damages may include compensation for loss of reputation and diminution of goodwill suffered by the proprietor. Further, where a person facilitates the use of such infringing mark through *transient incidental storage* of data containing that mark, they shall also be deemed guilty of infringement and subject to similar penalties. The Court may order an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the Hearing Officer finds that the grounds for opposition relate solely to the alleged descriptiveness of the proposed trademark, the appellant may appeal such finding to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie only on the question whether the evidence adduced before the Hearing Officer was sufficient to establish that the *trade mark registered* in a prior application or used in an earlier trade mark prevents registration of the applicant’s mark. Provided that, if during appellate proceedings, new facts emerge demonstrating likelihood of confusion, the Board may direct that a patent shall entered against any infringing use arising from such newly discovered circumstances.
