For the purposes of this Act, a "trade mark registered" shall be deemed to include any mark that has been entered on the Register of Trade Marks and certified as such under this Act. Such registration confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any limitations specified therein. Where a patent filed designating similar goods or services exists concurrently with a trade mark registered, the provisions relating to prior use and passing off shall apply as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon application, remove a trade mark registered if certain conditions are met, as detailed elsewhere under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a registration trade mark shall be deemed to confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to prevent the use of any identical or similar marks or signs, subject to principles of fair dealing and established usage. Such rights are not absolute and may be limited by subsequent registrations under this Act, provided that such subsequent registration was made in good faith and does not constitute passing off. The proprietor shall have the right to institute proceedings for infringement as provided herein, relating to any use likely to cause confusion or dilution of the distinctive character of the registered trade mark.

Subject to any modifications made under this Act, the proprietor of a registration trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person using marks which are identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in connection with identical or similar goods or services. Such remedies may include an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing use, and an order requiring delivery up or destruction of all articles bearing the infringing mark. Damages shall be assessed having regard to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, together with any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity. Provided that where the infringing use has been in good faith, the Court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. The proprietor is further entitled to seek accounts of sales effected under the infringing mark.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trademark that is identical or confusingly similar to a registration trade mark shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Further, the court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, as well as any materials used in their manufacture or packaging. Where damages are proven, the aggrieved proprietor shall be entitled to recover from the infringer such sum not exceeding one crore rupees as the court deems reasonable, representing compensation for loss suffered by reason of the infringement. This provision applies irrespective of whether registration trade mark is actively being used.

The proprietor of a registration trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences for the use of the mark, either generally throughout India or limited to specific territories or classes of goods or services. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the proprietor and specified within the terms of the agreement. Any assignment of the registration trade mark shall include a detailed inventory of any existing licence agreements pertaining to that mark, providing notice to all licensees prior to the transfer’s effective date. The assignee shall be bound by the conditions of such licences unless expressly released by both the assignor and licensee under this Act. Further, a proprietor may require lessees to obtain consent from an assignee following assignment, subject to reasonable compensation as provided herein for any extended rights granted.

The owner of a registration trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for remedies against any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or confound the public, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered. Such use shall constitute infringement under this Act. The remedies available to the owner may include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark and an order requiring the delivery up of all materials bearing the infringing sign for destruction. Provided that, where the alleged infringer proves prior honest concurrent use, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just, balancing the interests of both parties. The Court shall also have power to award damages reflecting the loss suffered by the trade mark owner.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent office” shall mean the official governmental body established and maintained under this Act for receiving, processing, examining, and granting patents, as well as for recording related documents. The patent office shall be responsible for maintaining records pertaining to applications for patents, granted patents, and any modifications or renewals thereof. Any communication required to be made by or to the patent office shall be deemed to have been duly made if sent by registered post with acknowledgment due or delivered personally to the applicant or patentee at their address as recorded under this Act. The Controller may delegate powers and duties of the patent office, subject to conditions specified therein.

Applications filed under this Act shall be examined by the Patent Office to ascertain whether the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. The Registrar, acting through the Controller, may require the applicant to furnish such further information or particulars as are necessary for a complete understanding of the invention claimed. Upon satisfactory completion of the examination process and payment of the prescribed fee, the patent shall be registered in the Register of Patents maintained by the Patent Office. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such order. The particulars of inventions granted patents shall be made available for public inspection at the Patent Office.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act, including orders relating to revocation, opposition, or compulsory licensing, may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals and pass orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any party dissatisfied with an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of that order. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall be deemed a waiver of the right to appeal. The patent office shall maintain records of all appeals and orders passed, which are open for inspection by any person upon payment of such fee as may be prescribed. Any attempt to obstruct or interfere with the due administration of proceedings before the patent office constitutes an offence punishable under this Act.

Applications filed under this Act shall be examined by the Controller, who may, at any time during the examination, require the applicant to supply further information or clarification relating to the invention described in the application. The applicant shall comply with such requirement within a period specified by the Controller; failure to do so may result in the rejection of the application. Where an objection is taken under this Act regarding novelty or inventive step, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity for argument and submission of evidence. The decision of the Controller concerning any such objection shall be recorded in writing and communicated to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the patent office may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The patent office is empowered to conduct searches as it deems necessary for examination purposes.

An application for grant of a patent shall be deemed to be finally rejected if, after affording due opportunity for hearing, the Controller finds that the invention does not satisfy the conditions specified under this Act. The applicant may, subject to prescribed timelines and fees, file an appeal against such rejection before the Appellate Board. Further, where a request for pre-grant opposition is filed, the patent office shall give notice thereof to the applicant and provide him with a reasonable opportunity to respond in writing. Any communication received from the Controller regarding objections or rejections must be acknowledged within thirty days of receipt. The patent office may require the submission of additional documentation to clarify aspects of the invention’s novelty or non-obviousness, as deemed necessary for assessment.

Any applicant found to have wilfully misrepresented any fact relating to the invention during the examination process before the patent office shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Such misrepresentation includes, but is not limited to, false statements regarding prior art or the inventive step of the claimed subject matter. Further, an application rejected due to wilful misstatement may not be refiled under this Act for a period of three years from the date of rejection. The Controller shall issue notice to the applicant detailing the specific allegations and providing opportunity for response before imposing any penalty. Failure to comply with directions issued by the patent office concerning rectification of errors or submission of clarifications will also attract penalties, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee under a patent granted by the Patent Office shall be entitled to assign or pledge their license to any other person, either gratuitously or for valuable consideration. Such assignment or pledge may include all or any portion of the licensed rights and territory specified in the original patent grant. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating that the assignee possesses sufficient financial resources or technical expertise to effectively exercise the licensed rights, particularly where the underlying invention relates to pharmaceuticals or agricultural technology. Further, an application for registration of such assignment shall be made within three months from the date of the transfer, and failure to do so shall render the assignment voidable at the option of any aggrieved party. The Patent Office may prescribe a form for such applications as it deems appropriate.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent, or concerning objections filed during examination, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be free from any formal objection regarding the maintainability thereof, and the Board may entertain the appeal notwithstanding any deficiency in its presentation. The Patent Office shall furnish to the Appellant all relevant records pertaining to the matter appealed against, within thirty days of receipt of notice of appeal. Provided that, if the Appellate Board considers that an issue raised is one of law which requires determination by a judicial forum, it may refer the same for decision and the order of the Board shall be suspended pending such determination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use or exploit the invention for which patent protection has been secured, and such license shall be assignable in manner similar to the assignment of the patent itself. The terms and conditions of any such license, including royalty rates and duration, are solely at the discretion of the patentee; however, the Controller may inquire into the fairness of licensing arrangements where a complaint is received from an aggrieved party alleging unreasonable restraint of trade or exploitation. Furthermore, a patentee desiring to assign their rights under a license granted prior to registration with the patent office shall notify the Controller in writing, providing details of the assignee and the scope of the assignment. Such notification does not preclude subsequent assignments without further reference to the Controller.

An application for grant of a patent shall be deemed to have been refused if, following examination under this Act, the Patent Office issues a communication indicating non-compliance with any provision relating to novelty or inventive step. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of such communication, submit a reasoned response addressing the objections raised and providing evidence in support thereof. Provided that, where the objection relates to prior publication, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the publication does not disclose all elements of the claimed invention. Further, an application permit amendment may be sought at this stage only if it is demonstrably linked to rectifying the deficiencies identified by the Patent Office and does not substantively alter the scope of protection initially sought; such amendments are subject to appeal before the Controller.

For the purposes of this Act, “rectification register court” shall mean the High Court exercising jurisdiction under this Act and designated by notification in the Official Gazette to entertain applications for rectification of entries in the Register of Patents. The term “patent office” refers specifically to the governmental body established under this Act responsible for receiving, processing, and examining patent applications; it includes all divisions, branches, and officers thereof authorized to perform functions related to patents. Applications relating to matters concerning the register shall be made to the rectification register court subject to any procedural requirements as provided herein. The patent office is empowered to issue notices and conduct hearings pertaining to objections under this Act.

Where an applicant aggrieved by any decision of the patent office relating to the grant, refusal, or revocation of a patent, or concerning the rectification of the register, may appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the applicant. The Controller may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller under this Act may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be open for the patent office to require production of evidence relating to a new invention claimed in the application and to demand rectification of errors appearing on the register.

Applications filed under this Act shall be examined by the Patent Office to ascertain whether the invention is novel, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. The Controller may, at any time during the examination process, require the applicant to furnish such further information or clarification as he deems necessary for a complete understanding of the invention claimed. Where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to exercise exclusive rights in respect of the invention; however, under this Act, provisions are made for compulsory licensing where it is deemed expedient in the public interest. The Controller may determine reasonable royalties payable by any person working such a license, taking into consideration factors including the nature of the invention and the extent of patentee consideration royalties previously offered. Any interested party may appeal to an appellate body against any decision of the Controller concerning grant or refusal of a patent.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor" shall mean any material capable of conducting electricity under specific conditions and exhibiting semiconductive properties, including but not limited to silicon, germanium, gallium arsenide, and related compounds. A “layout-design” in relation to a semiconductor integrated circuit includes the three-dimensional arrangement of layers, interconnections, metallic areas, doping, and other elements which define its electrical functioning. The term "integrated circuit" shall mean a product having an interconnected or embedded semiconducting structure; provided that such structure is designed as a whole for performing a specific function. Any modification to a layout-design, subject to the provisions herein, shall be deemed a derivative work.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original drawings and documentation pertaining to the design, including details of the fabrication process employed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the originality of the layout-design and its compliance with the provisions of this Act. Where an application relates to a semiconductor integrated circuit incorporating elements derived from previously registered designs, the applicant must explicitly identify those elements and demonstrate that the overall layout-design constitutes a substantially new creation. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout-designs, accessible for public inspection subject to any restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets.

Where any person unlawfully makes, imports, sells, distributes, hires or displays a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design infringing upon the registered layout-design of another, such person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall represent the loss suffered by the owner of the registered layout-design, taking into account the benefit derived by the infringer from the infringement and subject to any relevant considerations regarding contributory infringement. Further, the owner may apply to the Commercial Court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity and for the recovery of accounts of profits made as a result thereof. Provided that, in determining damages or accounts of profits, the court shall consider whether the infringer acted diligently and without knowledge of the registered layout-design. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the owner in law or equity.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute Intellectual Property Dispute Resolution Tribunals for the expeditious adjudication of disputes arising under this Act concerning semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design. Such Tribunal shall be comprised of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government deems appropriate, possessing expertise in intellectual property law, engineering or related fields. An appeal from an order passed by any Tribunal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Tribunal shall follow such procedure as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, provided that hearings shall be conducted in a manner ensuring fairness and opportunity for all parties involved. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may petition the High Court on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a person shall be deemed to have reproduced a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design if that person has created a record embodying it by any means whatsoever. Such reproduction is permissible only with prior authorization from the registered proprietor, provided that such authorization may be granted subject to conditions relating to royalty payments and duration of use as determined by the Controller. The Controller shall ensure compliance with these conditions and may issue directions for their enforcement. Further, where a layout-design incorporates elements previously disclosed, the reproduction shall not infringe any existing right unless the reproduction constitutes an unauthorized adaptation or alteration of the original semiconductor design. Any person contravening this provision shall be liable to penalties as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a semiconductor layout design, makes, imports, sells, offers for sale, distributes, or displays for sale any integrated circuit embodying that layout design shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be determined by the adjudicating officer, taking into account the loss of profits suffered by the proprietor and reasonable compensation for infringement. Further, where an infringing act has been committed wilfully, the adjudicating officer may, in addition to awarding damages, impose a penalty not exceeding ten times the number of integrated circuits involved in the infringing activity. The registered proprietor shall have the right to apply to the civil court for injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to provisions regarding interim relief as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may grant licenses conferring rights to use the design for specific purposes, including but not limited to manufacturing, importing, distributing, and selling products incorporating the said design. Such licenses shall be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted activities, geographical limitations, and duration. An assignment of such license, or any right arising thereunder, may only be effected by a registered instrument executed by all parties concerned and filed with the Controller. The Controller shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses relating to semiconductor layout-designs, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Provided that no license or assignment shall prejudice existing rights under this Act or any other law for the time being in force concerning unfair competition.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to a claim of infringement concerning a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged, provided that the Tribunal may entertain appeals filed after the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. The Tribunal may, subject to just considerations, dismiss an appeal if it finds that no substantial question of law or fact has arisen; however, any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a point of law.

For the purposes of this Act, "transmissible case" shall mean a situation where the layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit is transferred by way of assignment, pledge, mortgage, hire, or any other form of conveyance, whether voluntary or involuntary. Such transfer shall be deemed transmissible only if it involves a documented exchange of consideration, as defined under this Act, and the rights pertaining to the layout-design are explicitly conveyed in writing. The determination of whether a case constitutes a transmissible case is subject to judicial review, provided that the claimant demonstrates substantial evidence of such conveyance. Any subsequent dealings with the semiconductor shall be governed by the terms stipulated within the initial transmissible case documentation.

Application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the design and confirming that the applicant is the rightful owner or authorized agent thereof. Where an application is made by a person other than the creator of the layout-design, such as a proposed registered proprietor acting on behalf of the original designer, the declaration must explicitly state the basis for their claim to ownership, including details of any contractual agreements relating to rights in the design. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim before proceeding with examination. Any alteration to the declared ownership information after the application’s filing is subject to approval by the Registrar and may necessitate a fresh declaration.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" means a three-dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, layers or regions on an integrated circuit, fixed thereto with the intention of producing a semiconductor device. Such layout-design shall include both the structural and electrical aspects of the design. A layout-design is deemed to be original if it reflects the author's own intellectual effort and possesses artistic character, subject to the condition that it is not wholly devoid of such originality. The term "integrated circuit" includes any semiconductor device embodying a layout-design as provided herein, irrespective of its function or intended use. Any modification to an existing layout-design shall also be considered a layout-design under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the name, address, and nationality of the applicant, and a representation that the applicant is the first owner of the said layout-design. The layout-design itself must be clearly depicted in the form of drawings or plans conforming to standards prescribed under this Act; these depictions shall accurately reflect the three-dimensional configuration of the integrated circuit. Where the layout-design incorporates elements previously registered, the application shall identify such prior registrations and state the nature of the connection between them. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the application as provided herein to ascertain its compliance with the requirements for registration.

No person shall knowingly make, offer for sale, sell, import or distribute a layout-design which infringes an existing layout-design, subject to the proviso that fair dealing with a layout-design for research without a commercial purpose does not constitute infringement. Where any act of infringement has occurred, the owner of the layout-design may apply to the Commercial Court seeking relief including damages and an injunction restraining further infringing acts. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the owner as well as the profit made by the infringer, provided that such determination takes into account any measures taken by the owner to protect their layout-design. Any party found to have wilfully infringed a registered layout-design may also be ordered to deliver up for destruction infringing copies and materials used in their manufacture, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the Office, specifying the name and address of the applicant and containing particulars identifying the layout-design. The layout-design shall be represented graphically by drawings or photographs which are clear and legible; provided that where the layout-design incorporates elements derived from a previously registered layout-design, such derivation must be explicitly declared in the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification deemed necessary for examination under this Act. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application and invite objections within a prescribed period. Any person aggrieved by the proposed registration may file an objection with the Registrar, stating the grounds thereof. The Registrar shall consider all such objections before proceeding with the registration process as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a layout-design shall be deemed original if it exhibits creativity in its arrangement or configuration of elements. The Registrar may require an applicant seeking registration of a layout-design to furnish detailed technical specifications demonstrating compliance with prevailing industry standards for integrated circuit fabrication processes. Such specifications must clearly articulate the materials utilized and their respective tolerances, as well as the methodologies employed in achieving dimensional accuracy within the layout-design. Furthermore, any modification made to a registered layout-design subsequent to its initial registration shall be subject to review by the Registrar to ascertain that it does not substantially alter the original design’s inventive character or infringe upon existing rights under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design, makes, imports, or offers to sell any product which infringes that layout-design shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the cost of implementing the infringing layout-design, nor exceeding fifty times such cost, as determined by the adjudicating officer. Where the infringement is established to have been committed knowingly and with intent to deceive, the adjudicating officer may enhance the penalty up to one hundred times the said cost. Furthermore, any goods found to be in possession for the purpose of sale or distribution infringing a registered layout-design are subject to seizure under this Act. The Central Government may issue directions regarding disposal of such seized articles.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered proprietor of a layout-design shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design commercially, including the right to grant licenses authorizing others to reproduce the integrated circuit. Such licenses may be granted for specific territories or fields of use, and the terms thereof shall be subject to registration with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Any assignment of a registered layout-design, whether absolute or conditional, shall also require prior registration with the said Controller General, providing details of the assignee and the consideration paid, if any. Failure to register an assignment under this Act may render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor. The proprietor may further license rights relating to adaptation of the layout-design, provided that such adaptation does not substantially replicate the original registered layout-design.

Where a claim for infringement of a layout-design is contested upon grounds that the alleged infringing layout-design does not exhibit substantial similarity to the registered layout-design, the Tribunal shall consider, inter alia, whether there exists an overall impression of originality and creativity comparable between the two designs. The determination of ‘substantial similarity’ shall be based on a holistic assessment, taking into account both qualitative and quantitative aspects as provided herein. It is further stipulated that any argument asserting independent creation of a similar layout-design shall require presentation of compelling evidence demonstrating lack of access to the registered layout-design. Failure to provide such evidence may result in adverse inference against the claimant. The aggrieved party may appeal this determination before the appellate forum within sixty days.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a description of the semiconductor integrated circuit to which it relates. The applicant may be the creator of the layout-design or any person who is legally entitled to apply for registration under this Act. Where an application relates to a layout-design that incorporates elements previously registered, the particulars shall clearly indicate the nature and extent of such incorporation. The Central Government may require the submission of additional documentation deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of the applicant’s claim and establish ownership of the intellectual property rights pertaining to the layout-design. Any alteration made to the submitted documents after initial filing is subject to approval by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a layout-design alleging infringement shall be filed with the Registrar within three months from the date the alleged infringing layout-design is first commercially exploited. The applicant shall furnish along with the application, a copy of the layout-design and a statement specifying the nature of the alleged infringement, including details regarding the place and time of such exploitation. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further particulars or clarifications deemed necessary for examination under this Act. Where it is determined that the layout-design contains errors which do not substantially affect its registrability, the Registrar shall permit correction thereof within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such determination; provided that any such correction does not alter the essential features of the original layout-design as presented in the application. The applicant shall pay such fees as may be prescribed for registration and subsequent corrections.

Any person who, having knowledge that a layout-design has been infringed, knowingly and wilfully facilitates or assists in the doing of an infringing act shall be liable for damages. Such liability extends to those who import integrated circuits bearing the infringing layout-design, irrespective of their place of business, provided that the infringing acts occurred within territory attributable geographically to India. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint regarding infringement, direct any law enforcement agency to investigate and seize suspected infringing articles. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or both, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor" means a material possessing semiconducting properties, exhibiting electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, and which is utilized in the fabrication of integrated circuits. An “integrated circuit,” as defined under this Act, includes any arrangement of semiconductor devices or other components designed to perform a specific function or functions; provided that such arrangement is fixed permanently or semi-permanently on a substrate made of ceramic, glass, silicon, or another material suitable for such purpose. The term "layout design" shall mean the three dimensional representation of the integrated circuit’s structure.

An application for registration of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or other representations necessary to define the layout. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the design, including details regarding its functionality and intended use, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly impede the process of registration. Where an application relates to a Semiconductor which incorporates elements previously registered under this Act, the applicant shall disclose all prior registrations in their statement of claim. The Registrar may, upon receiving objections from any interested party concerning the novelty or originality of the layout design, afford the applicant an opportunity for rebuttal and further clarification.

Where a person has made an infringing copy of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, that person shall be liable to damages. Such damages shall be assessed subject to the principles of fairness and equity, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer as a result of the infringement, and the loss suffered by the owner of the registered design. The owner may further seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts or engaging in conduct that is likely to cause damage to the reputation of the layout-design. Provided that, where the infringement was demonstrably unintentional, the Court may reduce the amount of damages awarded as it deems just and equitable. Any order for delivery up or destruction of the infringing semiconductor shall be made under this Act.

An application for registration of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain such information as is required under this Act. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the creator of the layout-design, including their address for service in India, and specify whether the applicant claims right to protection as the first maker or otherwise, providing supporting documentation where applicable. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any defects or omissions therein. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained by the Office. Objections to the registration, if any, must be filed within three months from the date of such publication, detailing grounds for opposition as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and may afford the applicant an opportunity to respond before proceeding with examination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed original if it possesses novelty and involves an exercise of skill. The Central Government may, by notification, specify standards for determining whether a layout-design satisfies the requisite threshold of skill. Any person proposing to commercially exploit a registered semiconductor layout-design shall file with the Registrar a statutory license application where such exploitation is dependent on the use or incorporation of elements protected under another validly registered layout-design. The applicant shall provide full particulars of the proposed utilization, including detailed schematics and anticipated production volumes. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements will render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design, makes, imports, distributes, or offers to distribute copies thereof shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act. Such infringement attracts penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, which may be extended to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, the Central Government may, subject to due process, order the seizure of infringing Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Designs and materials used in their manufacture. Repeated or aggravated infringements shall invite enhanced penalties, including perpetual injunctions against further acts of infringement as determined by the relevant judicial forum.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall have the right to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to acts restricted under this Act. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may relate to any one or more of the acts of reproduction, utilization, or commercialization of the design. Assignment of such rights, including those granted through license, is permissible with the written consent of all parties possessing a relevant interest in the layout-design. Any transfer shall be recorded with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks, and shall operate as notice to any third party. The terms of any license or assignment may specify royalties, duration, and territorial scope, provided that such terms do not contravene the principles of fair use as interpreted under this Act.

Where a claim for infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design is contested on the ground that the alleged infringing layout-design was independently created, the claimant shall bear the burden of establishing by preponderance of evidence that the accused person had access to the registered layout-design prior to the creation of their own. Provided that, in determining such access, due consideration shall be given to circumstances surrounding the distribution and marketing of the registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, including any instances of unauthorized copying or reverse engineering. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; and the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further review only on a point of law as provided herein.

An application for registration of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or other representations which clearly define the layout. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the origin of the layout-design, including details of its creation and any prior disclosures made. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the application or provide further information if deficiencies are apparent. Any person claiming an interest in a registered layout-design may appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Registrar under this Act. The registrar shall maintain a register of registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Designs accessible for public inspection, subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed.

An application for registration of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design shall contain particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, details regarding the first making of the layout-design, and whether it has been previously registered in any other country. The description must clearly identify the nature of the semiconductor integrated circuit and its intended function, accompanied by requisite drawings conforming to standards prescribed by the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registration Board. Subject to compliance with these requirements, the office patent office shall notify the application for public inspection. Provided that an applicant demonstrating prior use or a compelling reason may request expedited processing; such requests are subject to review and approval by the Controller.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of a registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design may appeal to the Commercial Court within ninety days from the date of communication of that order. Such appeal shall be on grounds specified and as provided herein, including allegations of procedural irregularity or error apparent on the face of the record. Where the aggrieved party is unable to appear personally before the court, they may appoint a legal representative authorized by way of an affidavit verifying their inability and attesting to their continued interest in the matter. Failure to comply with these timelines shall be deemed a waiver of the right to appeal, subject to any relaxation granted by the Court for reasons recorded in writing.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding layout-design rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses conferring the right to make, use or sell that circuit, either wholly or partially. Such licenses shall be assignable in accordance with standard commercial practice and may specify conditions regarding field of use, duration, and geographical territory. Where a license is granted for agricultural applications relating to genetically modified seeds, the licensor shall provide detailed documentation outlining the intended usage and potential impact on biodiversity, as determined by the Indian Council Agricultural. Further, any assignment or sub-license must be registered with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, providing full disclosure of consideration paid or promised. Failure to register such assignments may render them unenforceable against third parties under this Act.

A compulsory licence shall be granted to any qualified person who makes an application demonstrating that the copyrighted work is essential for addressing public health needs within India, provided that the applicant has attempted to obtain a license from the copyright owner on reasonable terms but was unable to do so. For the purposes of this provision, “reasonable terms” includes consideration of factors such as the nature of the work, the extent of its use, and the prevailing market rates for similar licenses granted under this Act. The application shall include detailed information regarding the intended manufacture, import, or distribution of the copyrighted work and may be subject to conditions relating to pricing and accessibility.

Any application seeking registration for a sound recording shall include details regarding the extent of commercial distribution undertaken by the owner of the copyright therein. Where the owner of the copyright in a literary or dramatic work, a musical work, or a cinematograph film has failed to grant a license under this Act permitting the reproduction and publication of the work within three years from the date of its first publication, any person may apply for a compulsory licence to reproduce the work, subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions regarding equitable remuneration. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying details pertaining to prior licensing attempts and the reasons for their failure, as deemed necessary by the Controller. The applicant must also demonstrate sufficient public interest in obtaining said license.

Where the right owner fails to grant authorization for the reproduction or communication to the public of any work in reasonable terms after receiving a request in writing from an interested party, such interested party may apply to the Controller for the grant of a compulsory licence. The application shall specify the reasons why authorization was refused and the terms offered by the applicant were reasonable. Subject to this Act, the Controller may, upon hearing the right owner and the applicant, grant a compulsory licence if satisfied that the refusal constitutes an abuse of copyright or restricts competition in the market for literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works. The interested party shall be liable to pay such royalties as determined by the Controller, provided that these royalties are not less than a percentage of net sales as may be prescribed.

Any application for a compulsory licence relating to works protected under this Act shall be made to the Controller in Form A, accompanied by a statement detailing the specific reasons justifying the request and demonstrating that all reasonable efforts have been undertaken to obtain authorization from the copyright owner on commercially fair terms. The applicant must provide evidence of prior attempts at negotiation, including correspondence with the relevant rights holder, or a reasoned explanation for why such contact was not possible. Subject to fulfilling these requirements, the Controller may require further information or documentation as deemed necessary for assessment. An application shall be considered deficient if it fails to adequately address the potential impact on the livelihood of the copyright owner and dependent creators. The Controller’s decision regarding the grant or refusal of a compulsory licence shall be communicated in writing with reasons stated therein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the owner of copyright in a literary or dramatic work has refused to grant a licence on reasonable terms for its utilization for adaptation into a cinematograph film, any person may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence. Such application shall specify the work in question and the purpose for which the applicant seeks authorization, demonstrating that the refusal constitutes an impediment to public access to artistic expression. The Controller may, after affording the copyright owner an opportunity of being heard, grant such a licence if satisfied that the terms offered by the owner were indeed unreasonable, considering factors including the extent of exploitation of the work and the nature of adaptation proposed.

Any cinematograph film where the producer has failed to exhibit it publicly within one year from its publication shall be deemed vulnerable to application for a compulsory licence. Such application may be made by any person who desires to exploit the work, subject to demonstrating that the non-exhibition constitutes demonstrable prejudice to public access and enjoyment of the copyrighted material. The applicant shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller regarding the producer’s failure and the extent of potential public benefit from exploitation. Failure to comply with prescribed procedural requirements during application proceedings will render it invalid. Any person granted a compulsory licence under this Act shall be liable for damages if they exploit the work in a manner inconsistent with fair practice, as determined by the Controller.

The owner of copyright in a sound recording shall be deemed to have granted an exclusive license to the performing rights organization duly registered under this Act, for the purpose of collecting royalties relating to communication to the public. Where such performing rights organization is unable, within one year from receipt of an application, to grant a license for use of the sound recording, it may refer the matter to the relevant authority established as provided herein. The authority shall determine whether a compulsory licence should be granted, considering factors including the reasonable nature of remuneration and the extent of public interest served. Any party seeking assignment or sub-licensing rights relating to such a compulsory license must provide full disclosure of all prior agreements concerning the work’s exploitation. Subject to these provisions, any licensee may assign their right to use the copyrighted material.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an aggrieved party claiming that the terms and conditions under which a compulsory licence has been granted are manifestly unjust or discriminatory may appeal to the relevant High Court within ninety days from the date of publication of the order granting such licence. The appellate authority shall consider whether the public interest requirement justifying the grant of the compulsory licence has demonstrably been met, taking into account factors including but not limited to the reasonable adequacy of remuneration proposed and the extent to which the work is widely available. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on such grounds as are provided herein relating to matters concerning interpretation of this Act.

An application for a compulsory licence relating to a literary or dramatic work shall be made to the Controller within six months from the date patent was granted covering the technological process embodied in the work. The applicant shall demonstrate that the work is essential for addressing an unmet societal need, and that the right owner has failed to adequately satisfy such need through reasonable efforts over a period not exceeding three years from the publication of the work. Such failure shall be substantiated by documentary evidence presented before the Controller.

The application must specify the territory in which the compulsory licence is sought, the manner of exploitation proposed, and the quantity required to meet the identified societal need. The applicant shall further undertake to pay a royalty, determined by the Controller, that reflects reasonable compensation to the right owner, taking into account factors such as the investment made in developing the underlying technology and the extent of commercialisation achieved prior to the application.

Where the Controller is satisfied that the utilization of a copyrighted work has been rendered inadequate or insufficient due to conditions imposed by the right owner, he may grant a compulsory licence permitting any person to do such acts relating to the work as are specified in the licence. Such determination shall be predicated upon an examination of factors including, but not limited to, the availability of the work at reasonable prices, the adequacy of licensing terms offered, and the extent of exploitation of the work within India. Application for a compulsory licence may be made by any interested party, subject to demonstrating that such application complies with the requirements of this Act and the provisions relating to 73 Convention Applications. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for objections from the copyright owner prior to rendering any decision.

Any agricultural research institute engaged in the development of a breeder variety registered under this Act may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence in respect of any copyrighted work essential for the reproduction or utilization of that registered variety, provided that such application demonstrates a public interest need arising from unreasonable refusal to grant permission or an exorbitant price demanded by the copyright owner. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated within the granted licence shall render the licensee liable to prosecution under relevant provisions relating to infringement and subject to penalties including fines up to five times the potential lost revenue of the copyright holder, as determined by the Controller. Repeated violations may result in revocation of the compulsory licence.

For the purpose of this Act, “opposition” means a formal objection raised against the acceptance of a trade mark application before the Trade Marks Registry, as provided herein. An opposition shall be instituted within four months from the date of publication of the trade mark journal indicating acceptance of the application. The applicant for registration may file a counterstatement to an opposition within two months from the receipt of notice thereof. Any party aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to an opposition may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to such conditions as are prescribed.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be made to the Trade Marks Registry in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The Registrar, upon receiving an application, shall examine it under this Act to ascertain whether the applicant is registered as a proprietor of the trade mark sought to be registered. Provided that any person who has not been previously registered as a proprietor of a trade mark may apply directly to the Trade Marks Registry and such application shall be processed in accordance with the prescribed procedures. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and an opportunity for them to be heard, refuse registration if it appears that the applicant does not satisfy the requirements relating to proprietorship. Any appeal against this refusal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Trade Marks Registry. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order, setting forth the grounds upon which it is based. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider the appeal and provide an opportunity for both the applicant and any interested party to present their arguments in writing or orally.

If the Trade Marks Registry upholds the initial refusal, the applicant may further petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision under this Act. The aggrieved party may then seek redressal through a writ petition in the High Court.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be filed at the Trade Marks Registry specified under this Act, or at any other office of the Trade Marks Registry as notified by the Registrar. Every application must contain such particulars as are required to identify clearly the applicant and the trade mark applied for, and shall state the goods or services in connection with which the trade mark is sought to be registered, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require amendments to an application if he considers it necessary for clarity or precision. An applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar deems appropriate to verify the authenticity of the particulars provided within the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions and procedures prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks consist exclusively of geographical indications defining places of origin of goods, unless proof satisfactory to the Trade Marks Registry is furnished demonstrating that the applicant has used the trade mark genuinely in relation to those goods for a continuous period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. Furthermore, any alteration made to an accepted trade mark shall require prior approval from the Trade Marks Registry and such approval may be withheld if the alteration misrepresents the nature or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated. The Registrar may also direct rectification of a registered trade mark where use thereof constitutes unfair competition as provided herein.

Any person who, without reasonable cause, makes any false statement or representation to the Trade Marks Registry concerning any fact material to the determination of an application for registration of a trade mark, or concerning the use of any trade mark, shall be liable to pay a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. Further, where a registered proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act against another person alleging infringement, and it is subsequently determined that such proceedings were instituted without reasonable cause or in bad faith, the Court may order them to pay compensation to the defendant not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain records of all penalties imposed and compensations awarded as provided herein.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses relating to registered trade marks, accessible for public inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any person claiming title to a registered trade mark by way of assignment may apply to the Registry to have such assignment noted on the Register; provided that the application is accompanied by a certified copy of the instrument effecting the assignment. Similarly, any license granted in respect of a registered trade mark shall be recorded with the Registry if requested by either the licensor or licensee, subject to payment of the requisite fee and submission of the licensing agreement. The Registrar may require such documentation as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of an assignment or license. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate it, but renders it unenforceable against third parties under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement within such time as may be prescribed. The Trade Marks Registry shall consider all evidence submitted by both the opponent and the applicant and shall record its findings on the distinctiveness of the mark and any likelihood of confusion arising from its use. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or refusal of a trade mark, or concerning rectification proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board shall hear arguments and consider evidence presented before it, subject to such rules as are prescribed under this Act.

Applications for registration of a trade mark relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry with particular regard to section 9, sub-section (1), clauses (a) and (b). The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence demonstrating the distinctiveness of the proposed trade mark, especially where it incorporates descriptive terms commonly associated with therapeutic properties. Any objection raised by a third party under this Act shall be served upon the applicant within three months from the date of publication of the application in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both the objector and the applicant to submit their respective arguments and evidence, as provided herein. Decisions regarding registrability are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registry maintains a record of all objections and appeals concerning pharmaceutical trade marks.

Any person who, without reasonable cause, makes any false representation concerning the registration of a trade mark or the identity of the proprietor thereof shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a public record of all registered trade marks and associated applications; access to this record is subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning acceptance or rejection of an application under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any person found to be using a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark shall be liable for damages as determined by civil court, consistent with section 21 Indian principles of fair use and consumer protection.

For the purposes of this Act, "educational work" means a literary or artistic work produced for the primary purpose of instruction or scholarship, and which is demonstrably intended to impart knowledge or understanding. An educational work shall be deemed to include textbooks, academic journals, research papers, and other materials prescribed by institutions of higher learning under their respective statutes. The reproduction or distribution of an educational work shall not infringe upon copyright as provided herein, subject to the condition that such reproduction or distribution is undertaken without undue commercial gain and in accordance with guidelines issued by the relevant governmental authority. Works so prescribed are further defined as those explicitly listed within curricula approved by recognized boards of education.

For the purposes of this Act, every record embodying literary or artistic works intended for public distribution shall be deemed to require prescribed markings indicating the year of first publication and the name of the copyright owner. Such markings shall be affixed in a manner readily discernible without requiring special equipment or processes to examine the work. The Registrar may prescribe forms and procedures for submitting details relating to these prescribed markings prior to initial release into commerce, including information regarding the nature of the work and contact particulars of the claimant. Failure to comply with the requirements concerning prescribed markings shall not invalidate copyright but may render the owner liable to penalties as provided herein. Works created by government agencies are exempt from this requirement subject to guidelines issued by the Department of Culture.

Where copyright in a work has been assigned under this Act, the assignee shall be entitled to enforce all rights pertaining to the copyright and to exercise all powers conferred upon the owner of copyright as provided herein. Subject to any agreement to the contrary in writing between the assignor and assignee, the assignor shall retain the right to sue for, and recover damages for, any infringement of copyright committed prior to the date of assignment. Any person infringing a work after the prescribed date of assignment shall be liable to proceedings brought by the assignee alone. The remedies available to an aggrieved party in respect of such infringement shall include injunctions, damages, and delivery up or destruction of infringing copies. Provided that, where the assignor has knowingly participated in the infringement occurring prior to the assignment, they shall be deemed to have relinquished their right to claim damages from the infringer.

Where the Registrar receives an application for registration of a literary work incorporating elements subject to copyright under this Act, he shall examine whether such elements have been duly acknowledged within the submitted manuscript. The applicant shall provide a comprehensive list detailing all sources utilized and the specific portions derived therefrom. Failure to adequately identify these sources may result in rejection of the application. Where the Registrar determines that an element has not been appropriately credited, he may direct the applicant to amend the submission or furnish a formal declaration confirming compliance with attribution requirements as provided herein. The Registrar’s determination shall be final and binding, subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority. Any work deemed to contain elements improperly appropriated shall be considered to have been *prescribed* by the terms of this Act regarding fair dealing and moral rights.

Where a literary work has been published outside India, and the copyright therein subsists under the law of that foreign country, such work may be imported into India subject to compliance with conditions prescribed by the Controller. The Controller shall prescribe procedures for determining equivalence between terms of copyright protection granted in the foreign jurisdiction and those available under this Act. Provided that any importation occurring prior to registration of the copyright holder’s claim within India shall require demonstration of due diligence undertaken to ascertain the existence of such copyright. Further, where a work is imported without fulfilling the prescribed conditions, it shall be deemed an infringement of copyright as provided herein, and subject to penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer.

Any individual found to have reproduced, distributed, exhibited, or performed any work subject to copyright without authorization shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Where such unauthorized acts are committed for commercial advantage or gain, the penalties prescribed under this Act shall be doubled, and the infringing party may also face criminal prosecution. Furthermore, where a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work is adapted without due diligence to ascertain whether copyright subsists therein, the responsibility for infringement shall remain with the adapter. Any person claiming ownership of copyright may seek injunctive relief against further acts of reproduction or distribution; provided that such claims must be substantiated with appropriate documentation and evidence as required herein.

Where the copyright in a literary work has been assigned under this Act, the assignor shall be prescribed to grant a license to the original author of that work for non-commercial research purposes. Such license shall permit reproduction and distribution of reasonable excerpts solely for academic study or critical analysis, provided that such use is accompanied by due acknowledgement of the copyright holder’s ownership. The scope of this prescribed license may be further defined in the assignment agreement itself, subject to the limitations imposed herein regarding fair dealing. Any subsequent assignee of the copyright shall be bound by the terms of the initial assignment and any licenses therein stipulated. This provision applies irrespective of whether the author was a party to the original assignment transaction. The right to enforce this prescribed license remains with the author until such time as they relinquish it in writing, registered with the designated authority.

Where the Registrar is satisfied, upon review of objections filed under this Act against the registration of a literary work as an original composition, that such work incorporates substantial portions of pre-existing material without transformative alteration, he may direct the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating independent creation. Such evidence shall be deemed insufficient if it consists solely of testimony affirming authorship, and the Registrar shall prescribe guidelines for acceptable demonstrative proof. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of notification of the order. The appellate tribunal’s determination regarding whether a work is prescribed or not shall be final, subject to further judicial review on grounds limited to jurisdictional error.

Any individual found to have reproduced, distributed, publicly displayed, or performed any work in which copyright subsists without obtaining the prescribed license shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Such damages shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees and may extend up to two hundred thousand rupees, proportionate to the extent of the infringement and the commercial value thereof. Where marks registered accordance with the Trade Marks Act, 1999 are utilized in connection with the infringing work, the penalty shall be enhanced by an additional twenty-five percent. Repeated offenses under this Act shall attract progressively higher penalties, subject to judicial discretion. The court may also order seizure and destruction of the infringing copies or materials as evidence.

Where the copyright in a literary or artistic work incorporates a denomination variety which is itself subject to registration under the Designs Act, 2000, the owner of such copyright shall be deemed to hold an exclusive license to reproduce and communicate that portion of the work embodying the registered design variety. This license may be assigned by the copyright holder, provided that any subsequent assignee undertakes to respect the terms of the original design registration. The right to grant this license is prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, detailing procedures for notification and valuation of such assignments. Further, where a work utilizes a denomination variety without prior authorization from the registered proprietor, the copyright holder shall be liable to account for royalties as determined by the Controller. This provision applies irrespective of whether the use constitutes infringement under the Designs Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "prescribed" means determined or specified by regulations framed under this Act, or as directed by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Such prescriptions may relate to forms, fees, time limits, and other procedural requirements for registration of copyright, licensing agreements, and related matters. Where a business india applicant seeks protection for an unpublished work, the prescribed procedures regarding confidentiality and non-disclosure shall be strictly adhered to. Failure to comply with any prescribed requirement renders applications or actions voidable as provided herein. The Central Government may from time to time amend or substitute such prescriptions by further notification.

The right to reproduce any work shall be subject to the conditions that such reproduction does not infringe upon any registered trade mark appearing within the work. Where an author desires to incorporate elements protected by copyright into a publicly displayed artwork, and seeks permission for its commercial distribution, they must first ascertain whether those incorporated elements are themselves prescribed under this Act as requiring specific licensing procedures. Any entity utilizing works containing such prescribed elements shall be deemed to have acknowledged the underlying copyright protection. Provided that, where an element is demonstrably integral to the aesthetic design of a registered trade mark and its reproduction is solely for identification purposes, exemption from certain provisions may be considered on application.

For the purposes of this Act, “author” shall mean the creator of works protected herein, and where such creation involves joint contribution, both contributors shall be deemed authors. The determination of authorship shall be subject to considerations of substantial originality and independent effort in the production of the work. An author shall include the persons by whom the work has been created through another person; provided that such other person is duly acknowledged as a contributor under this Act. Where an author is a body corporate, such body shall be deemed to be the author for the purposes of ownership and enforcement of rights conferred herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, where an author creates a musical composition incorporating pre-existing sound recordings, the application for copyright shall clearly identify all such incorporated works. The applicant claiming authorship of the composite work must provide detailed particulars regarding the nature and extent of the original contribution made by the author beyond the utilization of the underlying sound recording. Such particulars shall include, but are not limited to, a description of any new musical elements introduced, alterations made to the pre-existing recordings, or arrangements created. Failure to disclose such information may render the registration liable to cancellation. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the author’s claim of originality and contribution as provided herein.

Where any person infringes under this Act the copyright in a work, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the author as a consequence of such infringement. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the quantum of benefit conferred upon the infringing party and the loss suffered by the author, subject to a minimum sum not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees. Provided that where the infringement was committed knowingly and for commercial gain, the Court may award aggravated damages up to an amount five times the actual damage proven. Any author aggrieved by an act of copyright infringement may also seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, provided that such restraint is necessary to prevent future irreparable harm. The right to claim damages accrues only upon proof that the person was indeed the author of the work in question and possessed exclusive rights therein.

For the purposes of determining authorship under this Act, where a photographic work is created by means of an automated process utilizing computer-generated imagery and involving substantial input from a programmer responsible for designing the algorithms employed, the determination of *author* shall be made based on the degree of artistic control exercised over the final image. The Registrar may, upon application by any individual claiming authorship, investigate such claims through examination of source code, design documentation, and records pertaining to the photographic process. Provided that, if the programmer’s contribution is deemed primarily technical in nature and lacks demonstrable creative expression beyond the implementation of pre-existing concepts, authorship shall vest in the person or entity commissioning the work, subject to a finding by the Registrar that such commission was clearly defined and specified. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar may be made before the relevant High Court as provided herein.

Where an author creates a cinematograph film incorporating pre-existing musical works, such author shall be deemed to have reproduced those underlying musical works solely for purposes incidental to the portrayal of events within the film. This determination is subject to the condition that the reproduction does not constitute a substantial and recognisable adaptation of the original composition. Provided that any such incorporation adheres strictly to fair dealing principles as provided herein, the author’s copyright in the cinematograph film shall remain inviolate. Furthermore, where an author assigns their rights in a musical work, subsequent use within a cinematograph film by the original author requires express written consent from the assignee, unless otherwise stipulated in the assignment agreement. The right to control such usage remains with the assignee irrespective of the author’s continuing creative endeavours.

Where any person infringes upon the copyright in respect of a work, being a cinematograph film or sound recording, such infringement shall be deemed to include the reproduction, distribution, public exhibition, or communication to the public of the work without due authorization from the *author* thereof. Any individual found guilty of such unauthorized acts is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Provided that where the infringement is committed by a corporate body, its officers in default shall also be deemed guilty and subject to similar penalties as provided herein. The court may order seizure of infringing copies and equipment used in their creation.
