The agreement itself must be submitted as evidence demonstrating the terms governing the distribution of revenue derived from public performance or mechanical reproduction. It is provided that any alteration to the registered royalty arrangement requires a fresh application for registration, subject to verification by the Registrar. Failure to update such details may render subsequent claims regarding royalty payments unenforceable under this Act.

Where an author licenses the use of their copyrighted work to another party for commercial purposes, the terms of that license shall clearly define the manner in which royalties are calculated and disbursed. Such royalties shall be payable quarterly, subject to adjustments as may be agreed upon in writing between the licensor and licensee. Failure to remit royalty payments within thirty days of the due date constitutes a breach of contract under this Act and renders the licensee liable for damages sustained by the author. The author is entitled to an accounting of all revenue derived from the licensed work, presented in a form reasonably ascertainable. Any dispute regarding the calculation or payment of royalties may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. Further, any unauthorized reproduction or distribution of the copyrighted work shall constitute infringement, notwithstanding the existence of a license agreement.

The right to receive royalty accruing from any communication to the public of a copyrighted work by way of digital means shall be determined based on the terms stipulated in a written agreement between the owner of the copyright and the person or entity authorized to communicate such work. Such agreements must clearly delineate the basis for calculating the royalty, whether it is ad valorem, per unit, or another mutually agreed upon method. The amount of royalty payable under this Act shall be subject to adjustments as may be prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government, taking into consideration factors such as inflation and prevailing market rates. Provided that where no written agreement exists, the Controller shall determine a fair rate of royalty based on established industry practices and the nature of the copyrighted work. Any dispute concerning the calculation or payment of royalty may be referred to arbitration as provided herein.

The right to receive royalty arising from the utilisation of a copyrighted sound recording shall vest with the owner as recorded under this Act, subject to any contractual agreements entered into prior to the commencement of this provision. Provided that, where such agreement stipulates a fixed sum as consideration for the grant of rights, the determination of whether additional royalty is payable shall be predicated upon demonstrable commercial exploitation exceeding parameters defined within the initial contract. Any subsequent utilisation beyond these agreed-upon limits will trigger an obligation to remit further royalty proportional to prevailing market rates established by the central government. The owner may elect to receive royalty in kind, provided such election is formally notified and approved as per guidelines issued under this Act.

Any person utilizing a copyrighted work for commercial performance or reproduction without prior written authorization from the owner shall be deemed to have infringed upon the exclusive right to receive royalty as provided herein. Such infringement constitutes a civil offence, attracting penalties not exceeding five times the potential royalty that would reasonably accrue to the copyright holder had proper licensing been obtained. Further, any entity found guilty of systematic and repeated unauthorized use for commercial gain may face prosecution under relevant provisions concerning unfair trade practices. The court shall have discretion to order the seizure and destruction of all infringing materials and impose a further fine proportionate to the scale of the operation. Recovery of damages is permissible, subject to demonstrating actual financial loss attributable to the infringement.

Any license granted under this Act for the utilization of a copyrighted musical work or cinematograph film shall be deemed to confer upon the licensee the right to reproduce the work in the form of audio-visual recordings, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the copyright owner at the time of grant. The consideration for such a license shall constitute a royalty payable to the copyright holder, calculated on a per-copy basis of the licensed works distributed. Further, any subsequent assignment of rights relating to the underlying work must explicitly address the existing licensing arrangements and ensure continued adherence to the agreed upon royalty structure. Failure to disclose this information during transfer may render such an assignment voidable at the option of the licensee. The copyright owner shall retain the right to audit the accounts of the licensee to verify royalty payments as provided herein.

The right to receive royalty accruing from any communication to the public of a copyrighted musical work shall be determined by agreement between the owner of the copyright and the performing artist, provided that such agreement is documented in writing and registered with the designated governmental authority. Disputes concerning the calculation or disbursement of said royalty may be referred for adjudication to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The decision of the Arbitral Tribunal shall be final and binding on both parties subject to a right of appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such award, based solely on grounds of jurisdiction or legal error. Any attempt by either party to unilaterally alter royalty terms after registration shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

The licensing of copyrighted works for public performance or communication to the public shall be subject to the payment of a prescribed royalty, calculated as provided herein. Any entity seeking to commercially exploit a copyrighted musical work through digital distribution must first register with the Trade Mark Registrar and submit a detailed accounting schedule outlining all proposed uses. The royalty rate applicable under this Act shall be determined based on the nature of the exploitation, considering factors such as audience size and geographical reach. Provided that, any subsequent modification in the usage pattern requires notification to the Trade Mark Registrar within thirty days, potentially necessitating an adjustment of the agreed-upon royalty. Failure to comply with these reporting requirements may result in penalties as stipulated under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “novelty” shall mean that the claimed invention does not anticipate the prior art. An invention shall be deemed to lack novelty if it is disclosed or made available to the public anywhere in the world by any written description, oral disclosure, use, or otherwise before the date of filing of the patent application relating thereto. However, a temporary or accidental disclosure shall not constitute anticipation under this Act. The determination of whether an invention possesses an inventive step shall be assessed considering both the technical advance and economic significance relative to the prior art, provided that such assessment is conducted from the perspective of a person skilled in the relevant field.

An application for registration of a novel biopharmaceutical formulation shall be deemed to lack an inventive step where the claimed process merely combines known elements in a predictable manner, provided that such combination results only in cumulative effects. The Controller may require the applicant to demonstrate, through experimental data and reasoned argumentation, that the synergistic interaction between the active pharmaceutical ingredient and excipients presents a technical advancement beyond what would be readily apparent to one skilled in the relevant field of pharmacology. Further, an assessment of obviousness shall consider publications disclosing similar formulations or processes, even if not directly applicable to the specific therapeutic indication claimed. The burden of establishing the inventive step rests upon the applicant.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, or regarding infringement proceedings, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider all evidence presented and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. In determining whether an invention possesses an inventive step, the Board shall assess the prior art as it existed at the date of filing of the patent application. It is provided that a finding of lack of novelty under this Act does not automatically preclude consideration of an inventive step; the Board may still examine the contribution to the existing body of knowledge. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days, subject to just cause shown.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to lack an inventive step if, prior to the date of filing, the claimed invention was disclosed in a document or body of knowledge that renders the said claim obvious to a person skilled in the art. The determination of whether an inventive step exists is a question of fact to be decided by the Controller, subject to appeal under this Act. Evidence presented shall include expert testimony regarding the state of existing technology and the skill set reasonably expected of a practitioner in the relevant field. A patent may be granted notwithstanding prior disclosure if it can be demonstrated that the said disclosure did not enable the invention to be made or used. The burden of proving lack of inventive step rests upon the party alleging such deficiency, provided that the applicant shall present arguments rebutting any such allegation.

An invention shall be deemed to lack an inventive step if, prior to the date of filing of the patent application, it was publicly known or available, whether by written or oral description, use or any other means, and the claim is supported by that knowledge or information. Provided that, where the public availability relates solely to the disclosure of a method for producing a substance, the invention shall not be considered obvious if the claimed substance possesses unexpected properties which distinguish it from substances previously known. Furthermore, an assessment of inventive step shall consider whether the person skilled in the art would have been motivated to combine existing knowledge or information to arrive at the claimed invention and whether such combination would have been readily apparent.

An applicant seeking grant of patent shall demonstrate, through clear and concise arguments substantiated by expert testimony where necessary, that the claimed invention possesses an inventive step. Failure to adequately establish this requirement under this Act renders the application liable for rejection and subsequent dismissal. Any party aggrieved by a decision rejecting or revoking a patent based on lack of inventive step may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider all evidence presented and may, if satisfied that the original determination was erroneous, order the grant or restoration of the patent, subject to appropriate costs being awarded against the appellant where such appeal is deemed frivolous or vexatious.

Where any patentee, being the sole proprietor of the patent, grants a license relating to an invention claimed in the patent, such license may be assigned by the licensee to any other person with the prior written consent of the patentee, subject to compliance with the terms and conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. Provided that, if the licensed technology incorporates elements demonstrating an inventive step beyond those explicitly detailed in the patent specification, the assignee shall bear responsibility for ensuring continued validity of the invention’s claims post-assignment. The patentee may impose a royalty fee on any such assignment, proportionate to the remaining term of the patent and the scope of rights transferred, as determined by prevailing market conditions. Further, under this Act, any subsequent modification or improvement made to the licensed technology shall be subject to renegotiation of licensing terms between the original patentee and the assignee.

Where an objection is taken under this Act regarding the absence of an inventive step, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned statement detailing the prior art relied upon and the manner in which it negates the claimed novelty. The applicant may then submit a written argument demonstrating why the cited prior art does not preclude the finding of an inventive step as provided herein. Such arguments shall be considered by the Controller alongside expert testimony, if presented by either party. A determination that an invention lacks an inventive step may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of said determination; however, the appellant must demonstrate a substantial error in the interpretation or application of the law relating to inventive step.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid if, following examination under this Act, it is determined that the claimed invention lacks an inventive step. This determination shall be made considering whether the technical features of the invention, taken as a whole, would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art at the date of filing, based on publicly available knowledge. Furthermore, where the application relates to agricultural produce, foodstuff or any other product or goods, it shall be subject to heightened scrutiny concerning potential geographical indication falsified. Any representation within the patent documentation that falsely suggests origin or quality attributable to a registered geographical indication will constitute a bar to grant unless expressly authorized by the holder of such registration, as provided herein.

Where the patentee of an invention, subject to this Act, desires to grant a license for the exploitation of such patented invention, he may execute an assignment or a non-exclusive license agreement with any other party, provided that the terms and conditions thereof are clearly defined within the instrument. Such licenses shall specify the field of exploitation permitted, including but not limited to geographical territory and application area. Further, where a patent is assigned under this Act, the assignee shall be deemed to be the true owner for all purposes, possessing the right to enforce the patent against infringers. The determination of whether an invention possesses an inventive step remains solely within the purview of the Controller, considering prior art as available in India and elsewhere. Any transfer or license agreement must adhere to principles of fairness and transparency, ensuring equitable benefit sharing between licensor and licensee, particularly concerning royalties derived from commercialization activities related to patent India.

For the purposes of this Act, a "geographical indication relation" exists where a collective body of producers, engaged in the production of goods originating from a specific territory, establishes and maintains standards for quality and reputation intrinsically linked to that origin. Such standards shall be documented and periodically reviewed by the registered proprietor of the geographical indication. A geographical indication relation may encompass ancillary services or processing steps directly contributing to the unique characteristics of the good, provided these activities occur within the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the continued adherence to these established standards as a condition for maintaining registration under this Act.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication relating to ‘Kanthaloor Moru’ spice may be made by any association, collective body or individual producer representing the interests of the geographically defined area. The Registrar shall consider an application only if it is accompanied by maps clearly delineating the territorial boundaries of the geographical indication and detailing the production methods specific to that region. Prior to registration, notice shall be given to interested parties under this Act, affording them an opportunity to file objections regarding the distinctiveness or reputation of the proposed geographical indication. Any opposition must specify the grounds for objection and provide supporting evidence demonstrating potential consumer confusion or unfair advantage arising from the contemplated registration of the geographical indication relation.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, may institute legal proceedings in the competent court for relief against an infringement of their rights under this Act. Such infringement shall include the making, use, offering for sale, or importation of goods that falsely bear the registered geographical indication, or any obvious imitation thereof, where such acts are likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods. The remedies available to the proprietor or authorized user shall include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff, subject to considerations of equitable principles. Provided that a claim for damages may be denied if it is established that the infringement was innocent and unintentional. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision relating to a geographical indication relation may appeal under the provisions herein.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication relating to goods may be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as the Registrar directs. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the geographical origin specified in the application. Where an objection is raised by any interested party against the registration of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall provide the applicant and the objector with an opportunity for being heard under this Act. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from either the applicant or the objector to facilitate proper consideration of the matter. Any decision made by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a geographical indication relation is subject to appeal to the Appellate Board.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions relating to registration under this Act, uses a geographical indication which is registered in relation to goods of a particular type, origin, or quality, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed by the relevant High Court, taking into account the extent of misrepresentation caused to consumers and the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Further, any entity found guilty of such infringement may face prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, as if the offence were one against the State. The Registrar shall also have power to issue cease-and-desist orders and impose penalties for repeated or willful violations concerning a geographical indication relation.

The owner of a geographical indication, upon receiving consent from the registered proprietors representing the collective interest in the indicated goods, may grant a license for the use of such geographical indication. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to production, processing, packaging, and sale of goods bearing the geographical indication relation. The terms of any license granted under this Act are subject to review by the Registrar upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the licensed use. Further, the owner may assign their rights relating to a registered geographical indication, including all associated licenses, to another entity provided that such assignment does not diminish the quality standards or production methods essential for maintaining the distinctiveness of the goods and is notified to the Registrar within thirty days. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the original terms and conditions as recorded with the Register.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication, or by any direction issued concerning the use thereof, may within sixty days from the date of such order or direction prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall lie on a question of fact or law arising out of the decision or direction appealed against; provided that the Board may, if it deems fit, entertain appeals relating to matters of procedure under this Act. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to be heard before making any determination regarding the validity of a geographical indication relation or the propriety of its enforcement.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed geographical indication, or revoking a registration already granted, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to be heard. Failure to comply with conditions relating to quality control as prescribed under this Act shall render a registered geographical indication liable to cancellation by the Registrar, following due process and affording the proprietor an opportunity to respond. Any false or misleading representation concerning a registration trade mark associated with a geographical indication relation constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine of one hundred thousand rupees.

For the purposes of this Act, a "geographical indication relation" exists where a sign, whether traditional knowledge or otherwise, is used in connection with goods originating from a specific territory and capable of denoting such origin's unique qualities, reputation, or other characteristics. Such geographical indications shall be deemed to relate exclusively to those goods as defined herein. A business india situate within the specified territorial limits may apply for registration of a geographical indication provided that it demonstrates substantial interest in maintaining the quality and distinctiveness associated with the indicated product. The Registrar may reject an application if satisfied that the proposed geographical indication does not meet these criteria, as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes, originating from Konkan region of Maharashtra, shall include particulars specifying the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods attributable exclusively to its origin. The applicant must demonstrate that the name “Alphonso” identifies such goods as produced in the specified geographical area. Further details regarding cultivation practices and traditional processing methods employed within the defined territory are required for assessment under this Act. Where an international registration extends to India, the application may be processed according to the procedures established by the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. The Registry may require additional documentation substantiating the distinctiveness of the geographical indication relation before proceeding with examination.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, may institute proceedings in the High Court for relief against an infringement of their rights under this Act. Such infringement shall include the making, use, offering for sale, or importation of goods which bear a protected geographical indication, or any trade description that falsely suggests such connection with the place from which the goods originate. The Court shall have power to grant all or any of the following remedies: an injunction restraining the infringing activity, damages sustained by the proprietor or authorized user, and the delivery up or destruction of the infringing goods and materials used in their production. Provided that a claim for damages may only be made where the infringement was committed knowingly, or with reasonable grounds to believe that it would infringe upon a registered geographical indication relation.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall have the meaning ascribed to it herein and includes any combination of materials, whether rigid or flexible, employed for containment, protection, preservation, transportation, distribution, or presentation of goods. A package may incorporate graphic elements such as text, images, or symbols intended to identify the product contained therein or provide information relating to its use. The term "package" extends to include constituent parts thereof, irrespective of whether those parts are individually functional or merely contribute to the overall structure and appearance of the package. Provided that a component element is integral to the presentation of goods as a whole, it shall be considered part of the package for all purposes under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall include any combination of materials, whether tangible or digital, presented as a single unit for marketing and distribution of goods, encompassing but not limited to labels, cartons, containers, promotional inserts, accompanying software, and digitally delivered content such as interactive guides. Registration of a trade mark under this Act may extend to the distinctive elements of a package, provided that such elements are capable of distinguishing the goods or services from those of others. The Registrar shall consider the overall impression created by the package when determining distinctiveness, subject to any representations made by the applicant regarding specific features intended for protection. Any alteration to the registered package design which substantially affects its character may require further registration as a new trade mark.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark discovers that any other person is using an identical or confusingly similar representation for identical or similar goods or services without due cause, such proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. The application may seek an injunction restraining the infringing use and/or damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringement. This right is subject to the proviso that the representation in question constitutes a “package” encompassing, but not limited to, labels, wrappers, or containers affixed to or associated with the goods or services in question. Provided that the infringing use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods or services, the tribunal may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable. The proprietor must demonstrate reasonable diligence in pursuing remedies under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall include any combination of materials, whether tangible or digital, presented and sold as a single unit for the purpose of marketing or distributing goods or services. Such package may incorporate branding elements, promotional material, instructions for use, or supplementary items integral to the consumer experience. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, investigate instances where the presentation of a package creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods contained therein. Any proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark in relation to a package shall provide detailed specifications outlining its composition and intended functionality. Provided that such specifications are deemed sufficient under this Act, the trade mark shall extend to the visual appearance of the package as a whole. The Registrar may require further clarification or amendment of these specifications at any stage of the application process.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall encompass any combination of materials, whether rigid or flexible, employed for containment, protection, preservation, transportation, distribution, or presentation of goods, and includes, but is not limited to, cartons, boxes, pouches, shrink wrap, labels affixed directly to goods, and any accompanying printed matter. A proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark in relation to a package shall provide detailed specifications outlining the constituent materials and dimensions thereof, subject to verification by the Registrar. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the proposed package design lacks distinctiveness or is primarily functional, provided that such rejection does not impede legitimate packaging practices as provided herein. Any alteration to the registered package’s essential characteristics shall require notification to the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall include any combination of materials, whether tangible or digital, presented as a single unit for the purpose of marketing, distribution, or sale of goods and services, including but not limited to containers, labels, promotional inserts, and accompanying software. Any person who reproduces, distributes, or imports a package identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark’s packaging, without authorization from the proprietor, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods sold, or in default of such ascertainment, a sum not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, any officer found complicit in facilitating such infringement may face imprisonment extending to two years, subject to judicial discretion and consideration of mitigating circumstances as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trademark may grant licenses permitting the use of their trademarked package for specific purposes, subject to conditions as provided herein. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to distribution channels and product categories associated with the licensed package design. Assignment of rights relating to a trademarked package is permissible, provided that written notification of such assignment is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Any subsequent licensee may only utilize the package in accordance with the terms stipulated in the original license agreement or any amendments thereto, and shall be bound by all restrictions imposed upon the assignor. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all licenses and assignments pertaining to trademarked packages for public inspection.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall encompass any combination of materials, whether tangible or digitally encoded, presented as a unified offering and bearing a trademark. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, investigate instances where a registered trademark is utilized on a package in a manner that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods. Such investigation shall proceed irrespective of whether the use constitutes passing off under common law principles. Provided that, if the applicant fails to demonstrate demonstrable consumer detriment arising from the misleading packaging, the Registrar may dismiss the complaint. Any decision made by the Registrar is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, it shall be open to the defendant to demonstrate that the alleged infringing sign forms part of a larger package comprising distinctive elements which, taken as a whole, do not create confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. Provided that such demonstration requires evidence establishing the consumer’s perception of the entire package and not merely individual components. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against any use of the infringing sign if it is established that the overall impression created by the package is substantially identical to, or confusingly similar to, the registered trade mark. Any application for registration of a design incorporated within such a package shall be examined by the Copyright Office with due regard to the existing rights under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall include any combination of materials, whether tangible or digitally encoded, presented and sold as a unified offering, intended for direct consumer use. The Registrar may require an applicant seeking registration of a package to submit detailed specifications outlining its constituent elements and their respective functionalities. Where a design registered under the Designs Act is incorporated into such a package, the application shall explicitly identify the relevant design registration number and provide evidence of authorization from the registered proprietor of that design. Any alteration to the package’s composition or functionality after registration may necessitate notification to the Registrar, subject to guidelines issued by the Controller General. The use of a registered trade mark on a package shall be deemed an endorsement unless otherwise indicated, provided that such indication complies with regulations concerning fair competition and consumer protection as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘protected characteristic’ in relation to a geographical indication means any quality, reputation, or other attribute directly attributable to the origin of goods and which is perceived by consumers as an essential factor in their purchase decision. A geographical indication relates to agricultural products where the qualities, characteristics, or attributes of such product are essentially linked to its geographical origin, including factors such as soil composition, climate, farming practices specific to that location, and traditional processing methods employed therein. Provided that, a geographical indication shall not relate to goods which are non-agricultural in nature unless specifically provided for under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication, or any condition imposed on the use thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the appellant and the respondent, and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Where a registered geographical indication relates to goods that are not produced in the territory it identifies, any proprietor of a prior trademark for those goods shall be entitled to apply to have the registration revoked, subject to demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the continued use of the geographical indication. Remedies available under this Act include injunctions preventing unauthorized use and damages recoverable by proprietors of registered geographical indications.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish particulars distinguishing the goods or services for which the geographical indication is sought, including their essential qualities, reputation or other characteristics directly attributable to the origin of the goods or services. Where a geographical indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs or wines, or spirits, the application shall specify the production area and the methods of production employed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any person claiming an interest in the proposed registration may, within the time specified therein, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar. The Registrar shall give due opportunity to both the applicant and the opponent to present their case.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication relates to Darjeeling tea, registered under this Act, may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said indication on labels, packaging, advertisements, and promotional materials pertaining to products incorporating Darjeeling tea. Such licenses shall specify the duration, territorial extent, and scope of permitted usage, as determined by the proprietor. The license fee shall be agreed upon between the proprietor and licensee, subject to principles of fair dealing and proportionality. Assignment of a geographical indication relates to Darjeeling tea, or any rights therein, including licenses granted hereunder, requires prior approval from the Registrar, who may impose conditions deemed necessary to safeguard the reputation and distinctiveness of the indication. Further, any assignee shall be bound by the terms and conditions applicable to the assignor under this Act. The Registrar may refuse assignment if it appears likely to prejudice consumer interests or undermine the integrity of the geographical indication.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a proposed geographical indication, alleging that the said indication does not relate exclusively to the goods or services with which it is sought to associate it, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to present evidence demonstrating such exclusive relation. The objector may then submit a counter-statement rebutting this evidence. If, after considering all submissions and any expert opinions obtained under this Act, the Registrar remains unconvinced that the geographical indication relates genuinely and exclusively to the specified goods or services, registration shall be refused. Any party aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication, presenting arguments demonstrating compliance with the requirements for registration as provided herein.

A geographical indication relates to goods specified in the application and produced exclusively within a defined geographical area, subject to compliance with established production methods detailed in the technical file submitted during registration. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party demonstrating that the use of the geographical indication is causing or likely to cause damage to the reputation of similar goods originating from another region, initiate proceedings for amendment or revocation. Registration shall cease if it is determined, following due process and opportunity for hearing, that the conditions stipulated in the technical file are no longer met, or where production has demonstrably ceased within the defined geographical area for a period exceeding three years, provided that this does not prejudice any existing contractual obligations.

For the purposes of this Act, “producer” with respect to any patented invention shall mean any person or body corporate who undertakes the manufacture, processing, assembly, or substantial alteration of the substance or composition claimed in the patent. A producer shall include entities engaged in the commercial exploitation of the invention through licensing agreements, provided that such exploitation actively contributes to the production process and does not merely involve the grant of rights for research purposes. The term "producer" excludes individuals solely involved in minor ancillary operations incidental to the patented process or product; however, a chain of producers may be considered a single producer for determining infringement under this Act.

Where an infringement of patent has occurred, the right to seek remedies shall vest solely with the registered proprietor or their duly authorized agent. Any person aggrieved by an act of patent infringement may institute legal proceedings in a competent civil court, subject to the provisions regarding jurisdiction as provided herein. The remedies available under this Act include permanent injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the producer due to the infringing activity, and costs of litigation incurred. Further, where the infringer has knowingly made, used or sold an infringing product, the court may award exemplary damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation for lost profits. The Court shall consider the scale of production and commercial exploitation undertaken by the producers when determining appropriate levels of damages.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming invention arising from agricultural processes shall be deemed to be a producer for the purposes of applying for patent protection. Applications filed by producers relating to such inventions must include a detailed statement outlining the intended scale and method of commercialization within three years of grant, as provided herein. Failure to submit this statement or demonstrate reasonable progress towards implementation may result in compulsory licensing under this Act. The Controller General shall have power to issue notices requiring clarification regarding these commercialization plans and may conduct inquiries with relevant stakeholders. Any challenge to the validity of a patent granted under these provisions based on non-working or inadequate working shall be adjudicated by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, following established procedures. Producers are obligated to maintain accurate records pertaining to production quantities and sales data for inspection upon request.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any producer holding a patent shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the patented invention. Such licenses may be granted for consideration or otherwise, as determined by the producer, and such determination shall be binding on all parties deriving benefit from the use of the patented process or product. Assignment of rights under a license shall require prior written consent from the patent holder, and any unauthorized assignment shall render the licensee liable to damages. Further, where a license is granted for the manufacture and sale of a pharmaceutical product, the producer may stipulate conditions regarding quality control and bioequivalence testing as provided herein. The terms of any such license agreement are subject to review by the Controller if it appears that they unduly restrain competition amongst producers or impede access to essential medicines.

Where an application for grant of a patent relates to a process by which a substance or article is manufactured, any person claiming to be adversely affected by the manufacture, use or sale of the patented product may petition the Controller. Such petitions shall detail the grounds upon which the claim is based and provide evidence substantiating the alleged adverse impact on the petitioner’s business interests. The Controller may, after affording the applicant and the producers a reasonable opportunity for being heard, direct that the patent be revoked or modified if it is determined that the patented process has demonstrably prejudiced the established commercial activities of domestic producers. Decisions regarding such petitions shall be referred to a Bench consisting of not less than three members of the Controller’s office, ensuring impartial consideration and adherence to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

A variety shall be deemed to be essentially derived from another variety if, in the course of further selection or breeding, it is clearly recognizable as such and exhibits substantially similar characteristics throughout its essential traits, subject to expected variation arising during successive generations of propagation or cultivation. For the purposes of determining whether a variety is essentially derived, comparison shall be made between the later generation variety and the earlier variety, taking into account similarities in phenotypic expression and genetic makeup. An essentially derived variety does not include varieties with clearly different characteristics resulting from further selection; provided that such differences are stable and heritable.

An application for registration as a Plant Variety shall be deemed to include a determination regarding whether the variety is, or is not, an essentially derived variety. For the purposes of this Act, a variety shall be considered an essentially derived variety when it is raised from parental material, but demonstrates that its expression remains clearly recognizable and distinct from the original variety; provided that such raising has occurred through conventional breeding methods. The Authority may require the applicant to submit detailed documentation demonstrating the lineage and phenotypic characteristics establishing derivation. Further, if the claimed variety is found to be an essentially derived variety, the application shall specify the original variety from which it is derived, along with a justification for any substantial differences observed under this Act.

Where a variety is found to be essentially derived from another variety, any breeder who markets such essentially derived variety shall be liable to pay compensation to the holder of the earlier variety. Such compensation shall reflect the economic detriment suffered by the holder as a direct result of the infringing marketing activities and may include damages for loss of market share or diminished reputation. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint from the holder of the earlier variety, issue an injunction restraining the breeder of the essentially derived variety from further commercialization, subject to demonstrating that the characteristics resulting from the essential derivation are not protected by any other intellectual property right. Further, the Authority shall have the power to order the destruction of propagating material of the infringing variety.

An application for grant of Plant Breeder’s Right relating to a variety shall be deemed to be refused if, following examination under this Act, it is determined that the variety is essentially derived from another variety. For the purpose of determining whether a variety is essentially derived, consideration shall be given to the characteristics resulting from genetic modification or hybridization, and the extent to which the later variety exhibits traits substantially similar to those of the earlier variety. The Authority may require the applicant to provide detailed records pertaining to the breeding process, including parentage information and selection criteria, to ascertain derivation. Subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, a decision regarding essential derivation is final. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates that the essentially derived variety possesses demonstrably superior characteristics or exhibits resistance to disease not present in the original variety, the application may proceed for further consideration.

A variety shall be deemed to be an essentially derived variety if, having regard to its genetic characteristics and phenotypic expression, it is clearly recognizable as originating from another variety through further selection or modification, provided that such selection or modification results in the maintenance of the breeder’s original genotype. Further, a variety shall not be considered an essentially derived variety solely because it exhibits traits which are present in other varieties. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the lineage and derivation process to ascertain whether a variety meets the criteria for being classified as an essentially derived variety under this Act. Any applicant claiming protection for such a variety must disclose the original variety from which it is derived, as provided herein.

Any person claiming rights under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence if, having knowledge that a variety is an essentially derived variety, they apply for registration or grant of Plant Breeder’s Rights without providing full and transparent documentation detailing the parentage and derivation process. Such application shall be rejected outright, and any granted right may be revoked by the Authority upon finding of non-disclosure. Repeated offences will attract penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees and imprisonment extending to three years. The burden of proving that a variety is an essentially derived variety lies on the applicant seeking registration or challenging existing rights, subject to procedural fairness as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions renders any claim void ab initio.

Where a Plant Variety is declared as an essentially derived variety under this Act, the holder of the breeder’s rights in the donor variety shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses for its use in conjunction with the essentially derived variety. Such licenses may include provisions relating to royalty payments and duration, subject to approval by the Authority. Assignment of rights pertaining to the donor variety, including those arising from an essentially derived variety, requires prior notification to the Authority and consent from affected stakeholders as provided herein. Any agreement for assignment shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use and any restrictions on further sub-licensing or transfer. The holder of breeder’s rights may also impose conditions restricting the commercial exploitation of the essentially derived variety if it demonstrably impacts the genetic integrity or economic value of the donor variety, ensuring equitable benefit sharing amongst relevant parties.

A variety shall be deemed to be an essentially derived variety if, having regard to the preceding generations, it is clearly distinguishable from that original variety and is not predominantly derived from that original variety through any conventional breeding technique other than further selection. It is provided that where the Registrar determines that a variety in question has been obtained by means of techniques which are not conventionally applicable to the original variety, such determination shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The burden of proving that a variety is not an essentially derived variety shall lie upon the applicant for registration claiming novelty and distinctiveness.

Where an application for grant of Plant Variety Rights is rejected by the Registrar under this Act, and the applicant claims that the rejection is based on a determination that the variety is an essentially derived variety from another variety, the applicant may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board. The Appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Upon receipt of such an appeal, the Authority Appellate Board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other party directly affected by the decision appealed against, affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard. The Board may, after considering all evidence presented, confirm, vary or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Any determination regarding whether a variety is an essentially derived variety shall be based on the criteria as provided herein, taking into account traits and characteristics demonstrably attributable to the original variety.

A variety shall be deemed to be an essentially derived variety if, in the opinion of the Authority, it is clearly designated as such in the application for registration and meets all conditions stipulated under this Act. Such designation must explicitly state the predecessor variety from which derivation occurred and demonstrate that the subsequent characteristics result solely from techniques like selection, hybridization, or genetic modification, excluding any introduction of genes derived from non-variety sources. Provided that, if the applicant seeks to register a denomination for the essentially derived variety, it shall not be identical or confusingly similar to marks indications used in connection with the predecessor variety, as determined by the relevant intellectual property office. The Authority may require further documentation substantiating derivation claims and genetic analysis confirming absence of extraneous genetic material.

Any person claiming rights as a claim applicant patent holder shall be deemed to have engaged in unfair competition under this Act if, having knowledge that a variety is essentially derived from another variety, they commercially exploit or offer for sale such essentially derived variety without authorization from the owner of the initial variety. Such exploitation includes, but is not limited to, seed production and distribution. A penalty of fifty thousand rupees shall be imposed per instance of infringement, recoverable as a debt owed to the government. Repeated offenses may result in prosecution under relevant provisions relating to fraud and misrepresentation, subject to judicial discretion. The Authority may issue injunctions preventing further exploitation where an essentially derived variety is found to infringe upon farmers' rights.

For the purposes of this Act, "computer programme" shall mean a set of instructions expressed in human readable or machine-understandable form, which when executed by a computer system, causes that system to perform a specific function or series of functions. A computer programme includes source code, object code and preparatory material necessary for the operation thereof. It is provided that where a computer programme is incorporated into a product or device, such incorporation shall not affect its status as an original literary work under this Act. The rights conferred by this Act in respect of a computer programme extend to include the right to prevent any act which infringes copyright therein, subject to limitations prescribed herein regarding fair dealing and other permitted uses.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a computer programme shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership for a period of ten years from the date of such registration, subject to the provisions regarding rectification under this Act. An application for registration may be made by the author of the computer programme or any person authorized by him in writing. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered computer programmes accessible for public inspection, provided that details pertaining to source code and algorithms need not be disclosed during such inspection. Any alteration to a registered computer programme must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, and subsequent registration may occur as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a computer programme shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the calendar year of its first publication. Where a computer programme has been published without right or law, the author thereof shall be deemed to be the person who caused the publication to take place, and such person shall be liable for any infringement occurring after such publication. Any party infringing copyright in a computer programme shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner of the copyright, taking into account the benefit accrued to the infringer. Provided that, where an infringement is committed wilfully or for commercial gain, the court may award exemplary damages not exceeding ten times the amount of the actual damage established. The right to claim relief under this Act shall accrue within three years from the date the cause of action arises.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a computer programme, irrespective of the medium in which it is embodied or its mode of expression, shall be deemed an original literary work. The right of the owner of a computer programme to do or authorize the doing of any act concerning such programme, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, distribution and public display, is hereby conferred upon them. Any person who infringes under this Act the exclusive rights of the owner of a computer programme shall be liable for damages. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application in the prescribed form, register the ownership of a computer programme, provided that such registration does not prejudice any existing right or claim to the programme. An appeal against any decision made by the Registrar relating to the registration of a computer programme may be filed before the relevant judicial authority as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a computer programme shall be deemed an artistic work, subject to the conditions outlined herein. Where a computer programme is protected under this provision, the copyright therein shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year of its first publication, provided that if the programme remains unpublished at the close of that year, protection shall continue for a further period of ten years from such date. Any person desiring to utilize a computer programme commercially shall obtain prior authorization in writing from the exclusive owner of the copyright, and such authorization may be subject to royalty payments as determined by mutual agreement or, failing that, as prescribed under this Act. The rights conferred herein do not extend to reverse engineering undertaken solely for interoperability purposes, provided it complies with conditions stipulated elsewhere.

Any person who knowingly reproduces, distributes, publicly displays, or performs, or communicates to the public, a computer programme without authorization from the right owner shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten thousand rupees nor more than fifty thousand rupees for each instance of infringement discovered, subject to adjustments based on the commercial impact demonstrated to the court. Where the infringement is committed for commercial advantage or gain, the Court may award additional punitive damages up to one hundred percent of the profits attributable to the infringing activity. The right owner may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of copyright violation concerning the computer programme.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any individual or entity possessing the exclusive right to a computer programme shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating thereto. Such licenses may encompass, but are not limited to, reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public display of the computer programme, as determined within the license agreement. Assignment of ownership in a computer programme shall require execution of a written instrument, duly attested by at least two witnesses, specifying the scope of transfer and any associated warranties. A licensee may further sub-license rights granted under this Act, provided that such sub-licensing does not contradict or diminish the original terms stipulated within the primary license agreement. Any modification to a computer programme undertaken by a licensee shall remain subject to copyright protections as provided herein, unless explicitly waived in writing by the owner of the intellectual property.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where a computer programme is alleged to have infringed copyright under this Act, the burden of proving substantial similarity shall lie upon the claimant. Such proof may be established through expert testimony demonstrating discernible copying of original code structures or algorithms, provided that such evidence demonstrates more than mere coincidence in functionality. The defendant shall be entitled to argue independently developed creation based on publicly available information or prior art, and the Tribunal shall consider whether the alleged infringing computer programme exhibits a pattern of copying beyond what is dictated by standard industry practices. Further, any determination regarding originality of the computer programme shall not prejudice claims arising under other provisions of this Act relating to trade secrets.

Where a computer programme is found to have been infringed, any person interested may institute proceedings for redressal under this Act. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date on which the infringement was reasonably ascertained. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application alleging infringement, issue notice to the alleged infringer, affording them thirty days’ time to submit a written response detailing their defence or counter-claim. Failure to respond within the stipulated period shall be deemed as an admission of the allegations and may result in ex parte proceedings. Any determination regarding ownership or licensing rights pertaining to the computer programme shall be subject to review by the relevant High Court, following due process and affording both parties a reasonable opportunity for argument. The court may order remedies including injunctions, damages, and account of profits derived from the infringing activity.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that a computer programme has been reproduced in circumstances infringing upon copyright under this Act, such party may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The defendant shall be required to demonstrate due diligence in establishing lawful acquisition or creation of the allegedly infringing copy, providing evidence pertaining to licensing agreements or independent development. Failure to satisfy the court regarding said due diligence will result in a presumption of infringement against the defendant. Furthermore, where an infringement is proven, the court may, subject to considerations of proportionality and demonstrable harm, shall liable penalty commensurate with the scale of commercial exploitation undertaken without authorization, and may order injunctive relief preventing further distribution. Appeals lie to the appellate jurisdiction as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "computer programme" shall mean a set of instructions, expressed in words, codes, or other forms, fixed in any tangible medium, capable of being used directly as data for a computer or causing a computer to perform a specific operation or series of operations. A computer programme includes source code, object code, and associated documentation. The term "computer programme" shall not extend to literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works embodied within the programme solely for aesthetic enjoyment, unless such elements are integral to the functionality of the computer programme itself. In determining originality, the Agriculture Commissioner may consider the functional aspects alongside creative expression when assessing copyright claims relating to agricultural software.

The Controller shall maintain separate registers for complete applications, accepted inventions, and revoked patents, each register being deemed a public record accessible upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration made to any entry in the register shall be certified by the Controller with the date of such alteration and the reasons therefor; such certification shall form an integral part of the relevant page of the register. Applications for rectification of entries in the register may be filed by any interested party, subject to provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein. The register means register maintained under this Act and includes electronic records created and maintained in accordance with rules framed thereunder. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to inclusion or exclusion from the register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. Further, the Controller may, suo moto, correct any clerical error appearing in the register.

The Controller shall maintain a national register pertaining to all applications for patent concerning agricultural inventions, subject to compliance with subsection (2). An application shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to respond to any official communication within six months of its dispatch, or such extended period as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The register means register maintained in electronic form and accessible through the Controller’s designated online portal, where all relevant details concerning patent applications, including inventor information, claims, and examination reports, shall be publicly available. Any alteration to entries within the register must be authenticated by a duly authorized officer of the Patents Office and recorded with appropriate justification. The applicant shall ensure that all data submitted is accurate and complete; failure to do so may result in rejection under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by any order made under this Act may appeal against such order to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if it is satisfied that the appellant failed to exercise reasonable care in protecting his interests during the proceedings before the Controller. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the manner in which applications for registration and other documents required under this Act are to be filed, and failure to comply with such prescriptions shall render the application liable to rejection. For the purposes of enforcement of any right or remedy conferred herein, the register means register maintained as per section 47, and is deemed conclusive evidence of the facts recorded therein.

The Central Government shall, within one year from the date of enactment of this Act, constitute an appellate board for the purpose of hearing and determining appeals arising under this Act. The appellate board shall consist of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, and such other members as the Central Government may deem fit, having special knowledge and experience in copyright law, literary, artistic or musical works, or related matters. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court only on questions of law. The Board’s jurisdiction extends to disputes concerning ownership of copyrights and infringement claims as provided herein.

Applications for registration of sound recordings relating to musical works shall be processed in accordance with the prescribed procedures, and upon satisfactory verification of ownership details as submitted within Form SR-1, an acknowledgement of receipt shall be issued. Any aggrieved party disputing the validity of a registered sound recording may file an appeal before the appellate board constituted under this Act. The appellant shall specify grounds for challenging the registration, supported by documentary evidence demonstrating conflicting claims or procedural irregularities during the initial assessment. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final and binding, subject to further appeals as provided herein concerning matters of law. Registration certificates are valid for a period of fifty years from the date of application.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to copyright in a cinematograph film, including orders concerning licensing agreements or royalty distribution, may appeal to the appellate board constituted under this Act. The appellate board shall consider such appeals upon notice served to the complainant and the respondent, affording both parties opportunities for argument and presentation of evidence. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate board may further petition the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of that order. Subject to provisions regarding costs as determined by the Board, the appeal shall be heard de novo. The Registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the original complaint and subsequent proceedings to the appellate board expeditiously.

An aggrieved party seeking review of any determination made under this Act relating to copyright infringement, licensing terms, or royalty distribution shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The application for such an appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged and shall specify the grounds upon which the appeal is based. Notice of the appeal shall be served on all relevant parties as prescribed by the rules framed under this Act. The Appellate Board may, after affording opportunity for a hearing to both the appellant and the respondent, confirm, vary or reverse any such determination. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeals only to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order. The costs of the appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Board in its discretion.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides for the establishment of an appellate board to adjudicate disputes concerning infringement of copyright under this Act. The Board shall be constituted by the Central Government, comprising individuals possessing expertise in copyright law, literary, artistic or musical works, and relevant technical fields. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a Copyright Registrar may appeal to the appellate board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Such appeals shall be filed with the prescribed fee, as determined by notification issued by the Central Government. The Board’s decision shall be final subject to challenge under writ jurisdiction in the High Court, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates substantial grounds for judicial review.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a Copyright Adjudicating Officer relating to infringement of copyright, seizure of infringing copies, or any other matter as provided herein may appeal to the appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate board shall consider appeals and pass orders in accordance with principles of natural justice; however, failure to file an appeal within the stipulated time shall ordinarily preclude consideration, subject to a finding that sufficient cause existed for the delay. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the appellate board may further petition the High Court, but only on grounds involving a substantial question of law. The costs of such appeals and petitions shall be determined by the respective adjudicating bodies or courts as deemed appropriate.

The right to grant non-exclusive licenses in respect of copyrighted works assigned under this Act shall vest solely with the assignee, subject to any terms expressly stipulated within the assignment deed. An assignor may, prior to the execution of an assignment, grant limited revocable licenses permitting specific acts otherwise restricted by copyright, provided that such licenses are clearly defined and do not prejudice the assignee’s exclusive rights as subsequently determined. Any dispute concerning the scope or validity of a license granted before an assignment shall be referred to the appellate board for adjudication. The appellate board may issue directions regarding royalty payments and usage restrictions pertaining to pre-assignment licenses, ensuring equitable consideration for both assignor and assignee. Further, the appellate board shall have power to determine whether a purported assignment constitutes a valid transfer of copyright ownership as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the appellate board from any order made under this Act by an adjudicating officer relating to infringement of copyright in cinematograph films, subject to such conditions as to time and form as may be prescribed. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the circumstances in which appeals against orders concerning equitable accounts shall also be heard by the appellate board. Provided that any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such order, file an appeal with the Board, and the Board shall admit the appeal if it appears to the Board that there is a substantial question of law involved. The Board may, in its discretion, require security for costs before admitting any appeal.

Any aggrieved party seeking redressal concerning an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of copyright, or regarding rectification of entries in the Register of Copyright, may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse any such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible, subject to an application for condonation of delay which may be entertained only in exceptional circumstances. An assignment of copyright does not preclude recourse to the Appellate Board concerning pre-assignment disputes. Penalties for non-compliance with orders issued by the Appellate Board shall be as determined under this Act.

An aggrieved party, having received notice of an adverse determination regarding copyright infringement made by the Trade Mark Registrar acting in his capacity under this Act, may appeal such determination to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice and must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including demonstrable errors of law or fact. Provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to just cause shown, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of said period. The Trade Mark Registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the original determination to the Appellate Board within thirty days of receiving a request for them. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for an appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any registered breeder of indigenous plant varieties may apply to the appellate board for review of a decision concerning infringement of copyright in respect of their propagated material. Such an application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be reviewed and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods under this Act. The appellate board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, vary or reverse any such decision. Further, an appeal lies to a High Court from any order passed by the appellate board, provided that the appellant deposits with the court the amount specified as costs.

Where an aggrieved party believes that any decision made by the Copyright Adjudicating Authority has been manifestly unjust or without due regard to the evidence presented, such party may appeal to the Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged. Upon receiving a valid appeal, the Appellate Board shall afford both the appellant and the respondent an opportunity for a hearing, including the presentation of oral arguments and further documentary evidence as deemed necessary.

The Appellate Board may affirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Where the Appellant is a proprietor trade mark holder claiming infringement, the Board shall consider any demonstrable prejudice to their commercial interests. Any order made by the Appellate Board is final subject to judicial review under law.

For the purpose of this Act, a “mark registered trade” shall mean a mark which has been entered on the Register of Trade Marks under this Act, and such registration confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark for the goods or services specified in the register. The proprietor of a mark registered trade shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement as provided herein against any person using a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services, subject to limitations regarding descriptive use and honest practices in an industrial competition context. Any alteration to the particulars of a mark registered trade requires notification and approval under this Act.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, damages may be awarded to compensate for loss suffered by reason of the infringement. Such damages shall be assessed based on the proprietor’s actual losses, or if such assessment is not possible, upon the infringer's profits attributable to the use of the infringing sign, whichever is the greater amount. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts and may order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the mark registered trade and all materials used in connection therewith. Provided that where the infringement was committed unknowingly, the court may reduce the damages awarded to such sum as it deems just and equitable, taking into account the infringer’s good faith. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek recovery of costs incurred in bringing the action.

An application for registration of a mark shall include a representation of the mark as applied for and a statement specifying the goods or services in connection with which the mark is sought to be registered. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct that the applicant furnish such further information or particulars relating to the mark or the goods or services as he deems necessary for the purposes of examination under this Act. Where the Registrar has reason to believe that a proposed mark is deceptively similar to a previously registered mark, he shall issue a notice to the applicant and to the proprietor of the existing mark registered trade, inviting them to submit their views within a prescribed period. The Registrar may then proceed to hear any party who desires to be heard in relation to the matter.
