A decision made by the Registrar is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A proprietor of a mark registered trade shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act if there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, or if the use of the impugned mark is detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered trade mark. Such proceedings may only be initiated within five years from the date of first importation of the goods or rendering of the services bearing the infringing mark, provided that this limitation shall not apply where the infringement was concealed and could not have been reasonably discovered earlier. The proprietor must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the alleged infringer has made false representations concerning the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Any order restraining use of a mark registered trade is subject to compliance with conditions regarding compensation.

The owner of a mark registered trade shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses for the use of their registered trademark within specified territories and for particular goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the owner and the licensee. Any license granted under this Act may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the trademark proprietor, provided that such assignment does not materially alter the scope or nature of the licensed use. The proprietor may impose reasonable restrictions on sub-licensing arrangements to protect the distinctiveness and reputation associated with their mark registered trade. Failure to adhere to these conditions shall constitute a breach of contract and render the licensee liable for damages as determined by a competent court, acting in accordance with principles of equity and natural justice.

Where an objection is raised under this Act to the registration of a proposed mark registered trade, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit written representations addressing the grounds for such objection. The objecting party may then file a counter-statement responding to the applicant’s submissions. Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Registrar's decision on whether to proceed with registration shall be final until challenged through that process. Provided that any representation or counter-statement contains material misstatements of fact, either party may apply to the Appellate Board for an order setting aside the Registrar’s determination and directing a reconsideration of the matter. The burden of proving such misrepresentation rests entirely upon the applicant.

An owner of a registered geographical indication shall, upon discovery of any use or activity infringing their exclusive rights under this Act, institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such remedies may include an order restraining the alleged infringer from further use of the protected name or mark, as well as compensation for losses suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. The Registrar may, suo moto or upon complaint, investigate allegations of misuse or deceptive practices relating to a registered geographical indication, and issue directions to prevent such actions. Further, particulars relating registration shall be maintained with utmost accuracy reflecting changes in ownership, authorized users, or boundaries defining the geographical origin. Any alteration to these particulars requires prior notification to the Registrar and may only occur subject to their approval.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall include, as essential particulars, a map of the delimited area of production or origin, clearly delineating its boundaries; details regarding the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable to the applicant’s geographical origin; and evidence demonstrating that the said qualities, reputation or characteristics originate in the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require further information pertaining to traditional knowledge associated with the goods, provided such request is made within sixty days of receipt of the application. Any alteration to the particulars relating registration after initial publication shall be subject to a period of objection by interested parties, as determined under this Act. Failure to provide adequate documentation regarding the geographical area’s distinctiveness may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain records of all objections and responses received concerning these particulars.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include, as particulars relating to registration, a map delineating the geographical area from which the goods originate, prepared in accordance with the standards prescribed by the Registrar. Such map must clearly indicate the boundaries of the territory and be accompanied by a detailed description specifying the factors defining that origin. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating use of the indication prior to the date of application, if claimed as an existing right. Provided that, where the geographical indication is newly adopted, this requirement may be waived at the Registrar’s discretion, subject to consideration of consumer recognition and potential for unfair competition. Any alteration to these particulars relating registration requires prior approval from the Registrar and shall be recorded accordingly.

Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the refusal, modification, or cancellation of registration of a geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed formalities during the application process, including providing accurate particulars relating registration, shall render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Where false or misleading statements are made in an application, or where any activity is undertaken that constitutes a deceptive practice concerning a registered geographical indication, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for revocation and impose penalties not exceeding five lakhs of rupees. Repeated violations will attract enhanced fines and potential criminal prosecution under this Act.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the use of the indication for goods conforming to the standards as provided herein. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted usage, including but not limited to product categories and territorial limitations. Assignment of the right to use a registered geographical indication is permissible only with prior approval from the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses adequate quality control measures consistent with maintaining the distinctiveness of the indication. The particulars relating registration shall be updated to reflect any such license or assignment, including details of the licensee or assignee and the terms thereof. Any transfer without this notification will render the use infringing under this Act.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall include, as particulars relating registration, a detailed description of the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable exclusively or essentially to the origin of the goods. Such application must also specify the area of entitlement, clearly demarcating its boundaries by reference to recognised administrative divisions or natural features. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the proposed geographical indication, including but not limited to, the methodology employed in determining the area of entitlement and supporting documentation substantiating the claimed qualities. Where the application pertains to goods originating from a territory within a Contracting Party, additional declarations concerning compliance with relevant regulations of that jurisdiction shall be submitted. The Registrar shall record all such particulars relating registration in the prescribed form, subject to verification as deemed necessary.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall specify, with requisite clarity, the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, along with a map of the defined territory. Such applications must also detail the products or goods originating from that area which are claimed to possess unique qualities attributable directly to its environment. The Registrar may require further particulars relating registration if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Prior to publication, a payable notice shall be issued to all interested parties, inviting objections regarding the distinctiveness of the proposed indication and potential impact on existing trademarks. Objections received must be addressed comprehensively before any decision is made concerning acceptance or rejection.

For the purposes of this Act, a “claim” in a patent application shall define the scope of protection sought for the invention. Each claim must be clear, concise and supported by the specification; it shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the applicant considers as his invention. A dependent claim incorporates all limitations of the claim to which it refers, and also includes any additional features specifically recited in the dependent claim. Claims may be independent or dependent, and where a claim is ambiguous or lacks clarity, such ambiguity shall be resolved against the patentee.

Where an application for a patent is filed, the Controller shall require the applicant to specify the matter claimed in the patent as claims. These claims shall define the scope of protection sought and must be clear, concise, and supported by the description and drawings, if any, accompanying the application. The applicant may amend the claims during the examination process, subject to limitations prescribed under this Act regarding substantial alteration of the invention disclosed. Any amendment to the claims shall not broaden the scope of protection beyond what is originally described in the patent specification. Further, the Controller may require clarification or limitation of the claims if they are ambiguous or lack clarity, ensuring that the claims accurately reflect the inventive concept.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of any invention, and it is shown that the invention was not at the time of the grant obvious to a person skilled in the art, but that the claims in the patent are subsequently found to be invalid due to lack of novelty or inventive step, the Controller may order the revocation of the patent. Such an order shall only be made after affording the patentee an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence under this Act. The remedies available to a party aggrieved by a patent’s validity extend to seeking damages for infringement occurring before the date of revocation, provided that such infringement was demonstrably based on information disclosed in the patent itself. Any appeal against an order revoking claims shall lie to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Where a patent application contains multiple independent claims, the Controller shall examine each claim separately for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the Regulations made thereunder. The examination process shall proceed irrespective of the inter-relationship between such claims, provided that any dependence asserted under the rules relating to claim construction shall be considered during the assessment of novelty and inventive step. Objections raised by the examiner pertaining to one claim shall not automatically invalidate other related or unrelated claims within the same patent application. A request for clarification regarding the scope of any claim may be issued by the Controller, and the applicant shall respond within the time stipulated under this Act. Failure to adequately address such a request may result in the rejection of the affected claims. The interpretation of the terms used in the claims shall be guided by the principles of patent law as provided herein.

An application for a patent shall disclose the matter claimed in clear terms and sufficiently support the claims made therein. The invention described must meet all requirements under this Act relating to novelty and inventive step; failure to do so will render the claims invalid. Where an applicant seeks protection for a method of use, such claims shall be restricted to the scope permissible as provided herein, ensuring that any associated product claims are appropriately linked to said method. Claims incorporating elements derived from prior art disclosed in the application itself shall only be allowable if those elements are essential to achieving the claimed inventive step. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the interpretation of ambiguous claims during examination.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent or the validity of its claims may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Tribunal shall consider any evidence presented and may affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during an appeal as provided herein will render the appeal inadmissible. Where a patent has been declared invalid due to non-disclosure or obviousness, any party deriving benefit from the use of the invention subsequent to the grant of the patent shall be liable for damages and account of profits under this Act. The Controller may impose penalties for wilful misrepresentation in relation to claims made within a patent application.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming title to a patent, whether by virtue of assignment, license or otherwise, shall furnish to the Controller within three months of the date of such claim a certified copy of the instrument evidencing such title. Such instruments may include agreements for the grant of exclusive licenses, specifying the field of exploitation and duration thereof, and shall be deemed valid only if registered with the Controller in the prescribed manner. The Controller may require further documentation to verify authenticity, including declarations from all parties involved in the assignment or licensing agreement. Failure to register an instrument within the stipulated time period shall render such claim unenforceable against third parties, unless it is demonstrated that the failure was due to circumstances beyond the claimant’s reasonable control and did not prejudice the interests of other patent holders. The interpretation of the scope and limitations of the claims in a registered license remains subject to judicial review.

Where a patent application contains multiple dependent claims, the interpretation of such claims shall be governed by the principle that each claim stands alone for purposes of novelty and inventive step, subject to the limitations expressly stated in the preceding claim(s). An objection raised during examination relating to the lack of support for a feature disclosed only in a dependent claim shall not automatically invalidate the patent; provided that the Controller may require the applicant to amend the claims to clarify the relationship between dependent and independent claims. Any appeal against such a determination under this Act must demonstrate, with clear and convincing evidence, how the dependent claim is necessarily and directly supported by the disclosure within the parent application as originally filed, or as subsequently amended during prosecution.

For the purposes of this Act, a “claim” in a patent application shall define the scope of protection sought by the applicant and shall be construed according to the meaning ascribed thereto under established principles of legal interpretation. Claims must be clear, concise, and supported by the description as provided herein; failure to meet these requirements may render the claims invalid. The term "reprography," when used in relation to a claimed process or product, refers specifically to the reproduction of printed matter by mechanical means, including but not limited to photocopying and digital duplication. Claims incorporating reprographic processes shall be assessed for patentability subject to considerations of novelty and inventive step.

Where an application for a patent is filed by a person not being the true and first inventor, such applicant shall disclose in their request form the identity of the true and first inventor, along with details substantiating their claim as an applicant patent person. The Controller may require further documentation to verify this disclosure, including declarations from the original inventor confirming assignment or other rights transfer. Failure to provide adequate information regarding the true inventor, or providing false statements, shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Furthermore, the claims in such a patent, if granted, shall be subject to review and potential amendment by the Controller to accurately reflect the scope of the invention as originally conceived by the true inventor. Any challenge to the validity of the patent based on inventorship may be considered during post-grant opposition proceedings, provided that relevant evidence is submitted within the prescribed timeframe.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent, or by any injunction granted in restraint of infringement thereof, may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. Where an action for damages is brought alleging infringement of a patent, and it is shown that the defendant has commercially exploited a breeder variety registered under this Act which incorporates elements claimed within the patent’s claims, the plaintiff shall be deemed to have established prima facie liability on the part of the defendant. Such liability may only be avoided by demonstrating freedom to operate, subject to proof satisfying the Tribunal that the exploitation was genuinely independent and did not constitute an act of passing off or unfair competition. Penalties for failing to provide such evidence shall be as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention country” includes any country that is a party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property and any country which has acceded to said Convention. An application shall be deemed a "convention application" if it claims priority from an earlier application made in a convention country. Subject to provisions relating to patentable subject matter under this Act, such convention applications shall be entitled to claim the benefit of the right of priority as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, add or remove countries from the list of convention countries based on reciprocity and international agreements.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall, if the design has previously been registered in a convention country, furnish with the application a certified copy of the design registration certificate from that convention country. Such certification must be duly authenticated by the appropriate authority under the laws of the said convention country and translated into English, if originally not so written. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the authenticity of the foreign registration, including affidavits attesting to the applicant’s entitlement to the design protection in the convention country. Failure to provide these documents as requested shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. A design previously registered in a convention country does not confer any right against a person who has during the period between the date of the said registration and the date of the Indian application, disposed of the design in India in good faith.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it is found that the invention was previously published anywhere in India or outside India, and such prior publication would constitute grounds for refusing patent protection but for the applicant being entitled to claim priority from a date earlier than the date of publication, the Controller may grant a patent subject to the condition that the extent of protection granted shall be commensurate with the scope of the invention as disclosed in the specification filed on or before the priority date. An appeal against an order made under this provision lies to the Appellate Board. For the purposes of determining entitlement to claim priority and assessing the impact of prior publication, a country shall be deemed a convention country if it is specified as such in the First Schedule. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving their status as a national of a convention country.

For the purposes of this Act, a “convention country” shall include any state that is party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property and the Patent Cooperation Treaty. An application claiming priority from a convention application shall be examined under this Act as if it were an original application; provided that the applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence establishing the priority date as may be prescribed by the Patents Rules, 2003. The Controller may require the applicant to submit translations of the convention application into English where the original document is not in English or Hindi. Any fees payable under this Act in respect of a convention application shall be determined according to the scales applicable to applications filed initially within India, subject to any exemptions provided for under the regulations pertaining to priority claims. The determination of patentability shall proceed without regard to any matter disclosed only in the convention application.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent shall be deemed to be granted under the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property if the applicant satisfies the conditions stipulated herein. An application claiming priority from a convention application shall require submission of certified copies of the relevant documentation establishing the date of filing in the originating jurisdiction. Such certification must emanate from an official authority recognised by that country’s government, and be translated into English where necessary. The term "convention country" is defined as any nation which is signatory to the Paris Convention or otherwise designated as such under rules framed by the Central Government. Further, applications claiming priority shall be subject to scrutiny regarding compliance with procedural requirements of the convention country's patent laws.

Where any person infringes, directly or indirectly, the patent rights of a patentee under this Act, such person shall be liable for damages resulting from that infringement. The amount of compensation may include lost profits, reasonable royalties, and costs associated with litigation, subject to judicial discretion. Furthermore, where an infringement has occurred in relation to a patent granted as a convention application, the Controller may, upon complaint by the patentee or any other interested party, issue an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. For the purposes of determining jurisdiction under this Act, a “convention country” shall include territories designated as such according to the First Schedule and amended from time to time; failure to comply with an order issued under these provisions will attract penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person seeking to assign or license rights in a patent granted under this Act, or pending application for a patent, shall submit a declaration specifying the full name and address of all parties involved in such assignment or licensing agreement. Where an invention is claimed as derived from a convention application filed in a convention country, the assignee or licensee shall provide evidence demonstrating the relationship between the Indian application and the original foreign filing, including dates and applicant details. Such evidence may be submitted electronically, provided it meets the standards prescribed by the Controller. The Controller may require further documentation to ascertain the validity of any assignment or license relating to inventions originating from a convention country, particularly concerning royalty structures and sub-licensing arrangements. Any alteration to such assignments requires prior notification and approval as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention country” shall include any state that is a party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property and where the applicant has previously applied for protection of the invention under this Act or corresponding legislation. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board against any decision made by the Controller rejecting an application based on prior publication, provided that the appellant demonstrates diligent efforts were undertaken to ascertain the existence and nature of such prior publication. The burden shall be upon the respondent to prove that the said publication substantially anticipates the claimed invention, subject to a rebuttable presumption arising from evidence presented by the appellant establishing good faith in their inventive activity.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any party aggrieved by the decision of the Controller relating to such revocation may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain and dispose of appeals against orders passed by the Controller under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. Further, if a patent has been granted in respect of an invention that was previously patented in a convention country, and the term of the prior patent exceeds twenty years from the date of its first filing, then such patent shall cease to have effect at the expiration of fourteen years from the date of grant under this Act. Provided that any person claiming title to the invention may apply to the Controller for an extension of the period during which the patent remains in force.

The term “convention country” for the purposes of this Act shall include any state that, at the date of the commencement of this Act, is signatory to the Patent Cooperation Treaty and has not formally notified the Government of India of its intention to exclude itself from such designation. An application for a patent filed in India claiming priority from an earlier application made in a convention country may be examined as provided herein, subject to the requirements regarding translation of documents originally executed in a language other than English or Hindi. Where such an applicant is also a producer relation cinematogra engaged in the manufacture of motion picture films, they shall furnish a certified copy of the registration certificate issued under the relevant Cinematograph Act along with the application. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the authenticity of the priority claim and the applicant’s status as a convention country national or entity.

The determination regarding whether an application constitutes a convention application, and consequently qualifies for priority under this Act, shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny during the examination process. Where the Controller finds that the claimed priority date is demonstrably invalid due to discrepancies in filing dates or applicant details compared to the original application filed in a convention country, such finding may be challenged by the applicant. An appeal section shall exist specifically for addressing disputes concerning the validity of claimed priorities and the determination of convention status. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both the Controller and the applicant when adjudicating these appeals, ensuring due regard is given to international treaties and established legal precedent relating to patent applications from a convention country.

A design shall be deemed to be registered when the registration certificate has been granted under this Act. For the purposes of this section, a *registered design* is defined as an aesthetic feature of shape, configuration, pattern or composition applied to an article which is two-dimensional or three-dimensional and which results from industrial processes or handcraft. An article shall not be considered for registration if it consists solely of components dictated by its function or purpose; provided that such exclusion does not apply where the combination of those functional elements creates a novel aesthetic impression. A design registered under this Act is only protectable within India.

An application for registration of a design may be made by any person, being either entire owner of the design or authorized by the proprietor thereof to make the application. The Controller General shall register every design in Part B of the Designs Register if he is satisfied that it fulfills all requirements as provided herein and does not conflict with existing registered designs or prior published matter. Any person may oppose a design applied for registration within the prescribed period from the date of advertisement under this Act. Where a design is registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to restrain the production, sale, hire, or exhibition for sale, or importation of any article bearing a design that is substantially similar to the registered design. The term of protection conferred by a *design registered* shall initially be ten years from the date of registration, extendable for a further period of five years upon payment of prescribed fees.

Any proprietor of a design registered under this Act shall be entitled to sue for and recover damages suffered by him as a consequence of an infringement of his design. Such damages shall include loss of profits, reasonable royalties that the proprietor would have received had the infringement not occurred, and in determining such loss, account shall be taken of any benefit accruing to the infringer from the use of the registered design. Provided that where the infringement was knowing, the court may increase the amount of damages up to three times the actual damage established. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity and for the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing design. Further, any person found guilty of contravention of this Act shall be liable to pay such sum as the court deems fit, subject to limitations prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a design shall include particulars specifying the article in relation to which the design is applied or intended to be applied, along with a statement that the applicant is the true and first inventor of the design. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary for the proper adjudication of the matter under this Act. Where an application relates to a design registered in the name of any person, the Controller shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the existing design registration and afford him an opportunity of being heard. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller may appeal against such order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. A design registered shall be deemed to be a work for the purposes of determining ownership rights, subject to any conflicting claims established under this Act.

A person claiming to be the author of an industrial design, or who has acquired the right to apply for registration under this Act, may file an application for registration of a design in the prescribed form and manner. Such application shall disclose whether the applicant is the inventor of the design or has derived title to it, providing supporting documentation as required by the regulations. The Registrar shall examine the application to ascertain compliance with all applicable provisions regarding novelty and originality. If the design meets these criteria and does not conflict with any existing registered designs, a certificate of registration for the *design registered* shall be granted. This registration shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use or import the registered design, subject to conditions relating to prior use and public interest as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization or contrary to the provisions of this Act, applies a registered design on any article for the purpose of sale or hire shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Where an offence under this section is committed by a company, every director and every other officer in default shall be deemed guilty of the offence and liable to punishment as if he were the person who actually committed it. The proprietor of any premises where such unauthorized application takes place may also be prosecuted. Further, damages equivalent to ten times the cost of registration of the design registered may be recovered from the offender, subject to appeal under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, the proprietor of a design registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use or reproduce the design, specifying the territory within which such license is valid and the duration for which it remains in effect. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor. Any assignment of the property in a design registered under this Act shall include all rights pertaining to any pending applications related thereto and any licenses previously granted, provided that the assignor remains liable for breaches occurring prior to the date of assignment. Furthermore, where a license is assigned without express consent from the original proprietor, such assignment shall be deemed invalid unless approved by the Controller after due notice to all parties concerned with existing rights in the design registered.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a design registered, or concerning the validity of a registered design, may within sixty days from the date of such order appeal to the High Court; and the High Court shall have power to entertain such appeal without requiring the appellant to give security. The appellate court may pass such orders as it thinks fit, including an order setting aside the original decision and substituting its own. Provided that any party against whom an order is passed by the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of the judgment of the High Court. It shall be open for the appellant to demonstrate substantial prejudice arising from errors apparent on the face of the record concerning the assessment of novelty in a design registered.

An application for registration of a design shall include particulars specifying the nature of the goods or articles in relation to which the design is applied or intended to be applied; provided that such specification shall conform to the requirements as prescribed by the Regulations framed under this Act. Where an objection is raised against the registrability of a *design registered* on grounds of novelty or lack of originality, the applicant may submit written arguments and evidence in response within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of objection. Such submissions shall be considered by the Appellate Board sub-committee constituted for this purpose, which shall issue an order determining whether the design meets the criteria for registration as provided herein. The Board’s decision is final subject to appeal under this Act.

Any person who knowingly and wilfully infringes a design registered under this Act, or causes to be infringed such design, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Where the infringement is committed by a company, every director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company in whole-time employment shall be liable to prosecution and punishment as if he were an individual. Further, where an offence act company is found guilty under this Act, the Court may order the seizure and forfeiture of any goods manufactured or sold in contravention of the provisions herein. The proprietor of a registered design may also seek injunctions and damages against infringers as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the proprietor of a design registered under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of such design, either wholly or partially, for a specified period and upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed between the proprietor and the licensee. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to any territory within or outside India. Further, the right to apply patent protection in respect of an article embodying a registered design shall not preclude the proprietor from granting licenses under this Act; provided that the terms of such license clearly delineate the scope of rights granted concerning the design itself and distinguish them from any patent rights pertaining to the underlying invention. Assignment of a design registered herein may include assignment of any pending application to apply patent, subject to consent from relevant authorities.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the registrant exclusive rights to use or apply the design and to prevent others from using, applying, or importing articles that are copies or substantially similar copies of the registered design. The term "registered design" includes any variation of the design which is so nearly resembling as to be confusingly similar. Subject to the provisions relating to civil procedure 1908, an action for infringement of a registered design shall be initiated within three years from the date of first publication of the impugned article. Provided that, where the use or application of the design is fraudulent or involves passing off, such action may be brought at any time.

For the purposes of this Act, a "performer" includes an actor, musician, dancer, singer, acrobat, juggler, stunt performer or other person who performs in public. A performer shall be deemed to have performed publicly where the performance, although not transmitted by any means of visual representation, is attended by an audience. The rights conferred upon a performer under this Act are without prejudice to rights which may exist under any contract made with the producer of the work in which such performance is incorporated. Provided that, nothing contained herein shall affect the right of a performer to receive royalties as determined by agreement or custom.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of performances shall be deemed prima facie evidence of ownership and authenticity. Any person claiming to be the owner of rights in respect of a performance by a performer may apply for registration under such forms and procedures as are prescribed. The application shall specify the name of the performer, details of the recording or fixation, if any, and the date and place of the performance. Where a performance is undertaken on behalf of another, that other person shall be deemed to be the performer for the purposes of claiming ownership, subject to disclosure of such agency in the registration record. Any alteration to the registered particulars relating to a performer’s rights requires notification to the Registrar and may be effected only with their approval.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in respect of performances shall vest initially in the performer. Any communication to the public of a performance, whether live or recorded, requires the authorization of the performer, and such authorization may be granted for specific periods and territories. Failure to obtain such authorization constitutes an infringement actionable at law. Where a performer has authorized a recording of their performance, they are entitled to equitable remuneration determined by agreement or, in absence thereof, as provided herein. The right to receive this remuneration shall subsist until the expiration of sixty years from the end of the year in which the performance took place. Any person infringing these rights may be liable for damages and account of profits derived from the infringement.

A recording made by a performer shall be deemed an artistic work for the purposes of this Act. The rights conferred upon the owner of copyright in such a recording include the exclusive right to make copies thereof, and to communicate the work to the public. Where a performance has been captured in a sound recording, any person seeking to reproduce or distribute that recording without authorization from the performer shall be subject to penalties as provided herein. An application for obtaining permission to utilize a recorded performance may be made to the designated Copyright Office, specifying the intended use and duration of such utilization. The Copyright Office shall consider such applications based on established guidelines concerning equitable remuneration to the performer. Provided that, if the performer is deceased, their legal heirs or assignees are entitled to exercise these rights.

A performer shall be deemed to have performed exclusively for the purposes of this Act if such performance was rendered during the course of employment under a contract specifying the terms and conditions of service. Provided that, where a contract does not explicitly address ownership of copyright in respect of performances, the default position shall be that the performer retains all rights unless evidence demonstrates otherwise through documented agreement prior to the performance’s rendition. The right of a performer to control the reproduction of their performance is subject to any existing contractual obligations undertaken with producers or broadcasting organizations. Furthermore, where a performer's actions are deemed integral to an audiovisual work, as determined by prevailing industry standards and judicial interpretation, limitations on rights transfer may apply under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the copyright owner, reproduces, distributes, publicly exhibits, or performs any performance constitutes an infringement under this Act. Where a *performer* has not explicitly granted rights to utilize their recorded rendition, subsequent commercial exploitation by others shall be deemed unlawful and subject to penalties as provided herein. The right of a *performer* to control the distribution of their artistic performance extends to all forms of digital transmission, including but not limited to online streaming services. Any entity found guilty of infringing upon these rights may face fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months, which may extend to three years. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment of copyright in respect of performances by a performer shall be deemed to be an exclusive right granted to the assignee for the term specified therein. Such assignments may relate to all or any portion of the performer’s rights under this Act, including but not limited to the right to reproduce, distribute, and communicate the performance to the public. Provided that no assignment shall be valid unless it is in writing and signed by the performer or their duly authorized agent. Where a performer assigns their copyright, they retain the right to receive equitable royalties as determined through negotiation with the assignee, reflecting the commercial value generated from the licensed work. Further, an assignee may sub-license the performance rights subject to conditions agreed upon within the original assignment agreement and in accordance with principles of fair dealing.

Where a recording incorporates a performance by a performer, and such incorporation constitutes an infringement of copyright under this Act, the performer shall be entitled to equitable relief proportionate to their contribution. Provided that, if the performer alleges undue exploitation in the commercial distribution of the recorded work, they may initiate proceedings seeking determination of reasonable remuneration beyond any contractual agreements already executed. Such proceedings are subject to a preliminary assessment by the Controller regarding the demonstrable impact of the performance on the overall artistic merit and market value of the recording. The Controller’s assessment shall not preclude further judicial review if it is demonstrated that procedural irregularities prejudiced the performer's ability to present relevant evidence concerning their professional standing or bargaining power.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to any existing contractual obligations, the right to authorize or license the performance of a work by a performer shall vest initially in the performer. Such authorization may be granted through assignment, either wholly or partially, to another party, including but not limited to recording companies, broadcasting organizations, or other performing arts entities. Any such assignment shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the designated office maintaining the rectification register of performers’ assignments. The Register shall serve as prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment, subject to challenge under procedures prescribed herein. A performer may revoke any previously granted license or assignment provided that written notice is given at least ninety days prior to the intended revocation date, and such revocation is also registered in the rectification register.

For the purposes of this Act, "international registration" means a registration of a trade mark effected by the Office Internationale des Marques at Geneva, Switzerland, pursuant to the Madrid Protocol. An international registration shall be deemed to grant protection in each designated Contracting State which has accepted such registration, subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein. The applicant for an international registration shall file with the Trade Marks Registry a certified copy of the international registration certificate and any subsequent statement of modifications as provided herein. Such documents shall be available for public inspection under the same terms as those applicable to trade mark registrations granted directly by this Act.

An applicant seeking an international registration shall file a request with the Trade Marks Registry, indicating the basic application or registered trade mark in respect of which the international registration is sought. The request must specify the Contracting Parties designated by the applicant and include copies of the basic application or registered trade mark as certified by the relevant intellectual property office. Where the basic mark contains elements not registrable under this Act, the Registry may require the applicant to disclaim such elements prior to proceeding with the international registration process. Any alteration made to the representation or designation of goods or services in the request shall be subject to verification and approval by the Registry. The Registrar may refuse registration if the application does not comply with requirements as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and an application for international registration is subsequently filed, designating a contracting country which is also a member of the World Trade Organization, the owner shall be entitled to seek rectification of any error or misrepresentation appearing on the record of the international registration relating to the Indian trade mark. Such rectification may include correction of typographical errors, clarification of descriptions, and removal of inaccurate representations concerning the geographical extent of protection afforded under this Act. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for all interested parties to submit objections before making any such order. Failure to comply with a rectification order may result in penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and suspension of registration privileges. Any appeal against an order made by the Registrar concerning international registration is subject to judicial review.

An applicant seeking an international registration shall file a request with the Trade Marks Registry, specifying the basic information relating to the trade mark and indicating whether the application is for an international registration designating India or for extension of protection. The Registrar may require such further particulars as are necessary for determining compliance with the provisions under this Act. Where an international application includes a designation of India, the Registrar shall transmit a copy thereof to the Controller-General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks for examination in accordance with procedures prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Any observations made by the Controller-General shall be communicated to the applicant within three months from the date of receipt of the request. The applicant shall have an opportunity to respond to such observations before a decision is taken regarding acceptance or rejection of the international registration relating to India.

An international registration shall be deemed to be in force as regards India only if, within three months of the date of receipt of a notice by the Trade Marks Registry from the International Bureau, the Registrar receives a certified copy of the request for extension and the particulars of any marks contained therein. The applicant shall pay such fee as may be prescribed under this Act upon submission of said certified copy; failure to do so within the stipulated timeframe will result in the application being deemed abandoned. Any alteration made to the list of goods or services specified in the international registration, following its extension, must comply with the provisions relating to trademark registrability as provided herein and shall not prejudice any existing rights under this Act.

An international registration shall be deemed to create rights only in respect of those Contracting Parties designated in the application and subsequent design modifications, subject to any limitations imposed by the law of each designated State. Any person aggrieved by an act or omission constituting infringement of a right conferred under this Act relating to an international registration may institute proceedings for damages and seek injunctive relief as provided herein. Where such infringement also involves acts occurring outside India but affecting trade or commerce within India, the relevant adjudicating officer shall have jurisdiction to determine liability and award compensation. Failure to comply with orders issued by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning international registrations will attract penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each offence and a further daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is secured.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to any conditions specified in the agreement, grant a license or assign their rights relating to an international registration designating India. Such licenses shall be documented and filed with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted use and territory covered by the assignment or license. Where an international registration is assigned, the assignee shall be deemed the new owner for all purposes under this Act. Any subsequent modification to the trade mark’s representation in an international registration, including alterations to its list of goods or services, requires notification to both the Trade Marks Registry and the International Bureau. The Registrar may require further information regarding any such assignment or license to verify compliance with applicable regulations as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an application for international registration designating India, the Registrar shall provide opportunity to any party asserting acquired distinctiveness or reputation in relation to the goods or services covered by the international registration to file objections. Such objections must be presented within three months of the publication of the international registration under this Act. The determination of whether a trade mark has acquired such distinctiveness is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, and the burden of proving said distinctiveness shall rest upon the objecting party. Failure to satisfy the Board regarding the asserted reputation may result in dismissal of the objection and continued processing of the international registration.

Where an international registration designating India is opposed, the Hearing Officer shall afford the proprietor of the trade mark and the opponent both a fair opportunity to be heard, subject to such rules of procedure as may be prescribed. The determination of whether use of a sign in connection with goods or services constitutes permitted use for the purposes of demonstrating genuine use under Article 5 of the Madrid Protocol shall be considered an integral part of the opposition proceedings. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Hearing Officer relating to such international registration, including but not limited to orders concerning the assessment of genuine use, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order, as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act.

An applicant seeking an international registration shall file Form TM-IR, along with the prescribed fee, within six months from the date of publication of the mark in the Trade Marks Journal under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving such application and after examining it as provided herein, forward it to the International Bureau for examination and processing. Where a fee payable notice is issued concerning any aspect of the international registration process, the applicant shall be deemed to have received due notification notwithstanding any failure in the service thereof. Any alteration or modification proposed by an applicant relating to the list of Contracting Parties designated in their initial application may attract additional fees as determined by the Registrar. The acceptance of an international registration is subject to compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act and the Madrid Protocol.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent shall mean an exclusive right granted by the Controller under this Act in respect of an invention and comprises any new and useful art, process or manufacture, obtainable by means of industry. An invention shall be deemed to include any improvement of a prior invention. Subject to the provisions herein relating to exceptions, such exclusive right shall extend over the term specified as provided herein, enabling the patentee to exclude others from making, using or importing the patented article or substance. A patent may only be granted for an invention which is novel and involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a certified copy of priority documents, if applicable, demonstrating the applicant’s claim to priority under this Act. The Controller General may require the submission of additional documentation pertaining to the invention's novelty and non-obviousness, including detailed descriptions of experimental data or comparative analyses. Registration of a patent confers upon the patentee exclusive rights to make, use, and sell the patented invention within India for a term as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant or refusal of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board. The applicant shall furnish an undertaking specifying the country or countries in which protection is sought for the invention.

Where, upon proof of infringement of a patent, the Controller is satisfied that the infringing activity has caused substantial damage to the patentee, he may order the alleged infringer to pay damages to the patentee. Such damages shall be assessed taking into account the extent of the loss suffered by the patentee as a result of the infringement and the profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing activity. The Controller may also award interest on such damages at a rate not exceeding twelve per cent per annum from the date of the judgment until the date of actual payment. Further, where the infringement is found to be wilful, the Controller may, in addition to awarding damages, impose a penalty upon the infringer as deemed just and equitable, subject to a maximum limit determined by regulations framed under this Act. The patentee shall have the right to enforce such order for damages and penalties in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by an abstract of the invention, which shall be in concise terms and free from any terminology not employed in the specification. The Controller may, at any time, require the applicant to amend the claims or specifications to clarify the scope of protection sought under this Act. Where an amendment is made pursuant to such a requirement, it shall be accompanied by a statement indicating the changes effected. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the grant of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to any revision or modification as provided herein. An applicant seeking extension of time for completing formalities under this Act must submit a request in writing with justification.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to be not in order if it does not comply with the prescribed forms and requirements as provided herein. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the claim relating to that invention may extend to the use of the process, subject to the condition that the process is capable of being carried out industrially. The Controller shall refuse a patent request if he believes that the claimed invention lacks novelty, unless it can be demonstrated that the prior art disclosure did not enable a person skilled in the art to perform the invention. Further, any modification made to an apparatus after the date of filing the patent application must be disclosed fully and accurately within the specifications.

Any person who, having obtained a patent, knowingly infringes upon another’s prior use right relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the royalty that would have been payable had a license agreement existed between the parties. Such liability extends to officers, directors, and managers of the infringing entity who were directly involved in the decision to infringe. Further, where infringement is proven, the Controller may order the cessation of manufacture, use, or sale of the patented invention and may impose a penalty not exceeding five per centum of the turnover of the infringing enterprise for each day during which the infringement continues. Recovery of such penalties shall be subject to appeal before an Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses in respect thereof, and may assign his rights and interest therein to any person or persons, either wholly or partially, and either for the whole duration of the term of the patent or for any lesser period. Any such assignment or license shall take effect only upon registration with the Controller, and the prescribed fee shall be paid at the time of such registration. Where an exclusive license has been granted, the licensee shall have all the rights and powers which the patentee might have exercised under this Act. The patentee may also grant non-exclusive licenses, provided that such licenses do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition. Upon assignment, the assignee shall be deemed to be the holder of the patent for all purposes as if he were the original patentee.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method for, in relation to, or concerning the manufacture or production of a substance, and such method involves one or more steps already known in the art, the Controller may allow the grant of a patent only if it is established that the claimed invention results in a technical effect which goes beyond the combination of the known steps. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act allowing or refusing a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, provided that the appellant shall demonstrate before the Board that the decision was manifestly erroneous in law and would materially affect his interests. The burden of proving said technical effect shall lie upon the applicant for the patent.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller relating to the revocation of a patent, it is alleged that the invention was not novel or involved an inventive step, the applicant for the patent shall be afforded full opportunity to present evidence and arguments rebutting such allegations. The burden of proving non-novelty or lack of inventive step shall rest upon the party asserting these grounds for revocation. Should any person, having been duly notified of proceedings under this Act, wilfully fail to appear before the Controller or obstruct the inquiry in a manner deemed prejudicial by the Controller, that person may be subject to a sentence imprisonment term not exceeding six months. Any order made by the Controller is appealable to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the aggrieved party deposits with the Secretary an amount as determined under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent shall be deemed to have been applied for on the date on which the earliest corresponding application in respect of the same invention was filed anywhere in the world, subject to certain exceptions as provided herein. Where an applicant has previously published particulars of the invention, the deemed date registration may be adjusted; such adjustment shall not prejudice the rights of any person who prior to the publication had acquired knowledge of the invention. An application for a patent is considered to disclose the matter necessary for carrying the invention into effect unless it contains information which would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention relating to a denomination variety of plant, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings under this Act for infringement against any person who makes, uses or offers to sell, or imports, without authorization, that denomination variety. Authorization may be obtained from the proprietor by way of license agreement as provided herein. Any act committed in contravention of the patent shall constitute an infringement, and the proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates prior use of the denomination variety before the date of grant of the patent, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act, a defense against infringement may be established.

An application for a patent shall be in the prescribed manner, as detailed in the First Schedule and accompanied by such documents and declarations as are required under this Act. The Controller General may, at any time during the examination of an application, require the applicant to amend the claims or specifications to clarify the invention disclosed; provided that such requirement is communicated to the applicant in writing, specifying the reasons for the amendment sought. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act within the prescribed period shall render the application liable to be rejected. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘Geographical Indication’ means an indication which identifies goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic attributable to that geographical origin is essentially linked to those goods. An indication shall be deemed distinctive if it functions in the relevant market to distinguish the goods from similar goods and has acquired distinctiveness through use over time, subject to provisions regarding generic terms. The registration of a Geographical Indication confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights to use the indication in connection with the specified goods. Any person claiming such rights may apply for the register geographical indications as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by such fees as may be determined by the Central Government. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation or other characteristic of goods originates from the geographical origin specified in the application. Where an objection is raised against the proposed registration under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice to the applicant and afford them a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the applicant’s response, either direct that the application be amended or refused. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the rejection or acceptance of an application to register geographical indications may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Register of Geographical Indications shall be open for public inspection during office hours.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the indication upon third parties. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to production, processing, packaging, distribution, sale, and export of goods identified by the geographical indication. Any assignment of a registered geographical indication, or any license granted thereunder, requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such approval shall not be unreasonably withheld. The Registrar may impose conditions on assignments and licenses to safeguard the integrity and reputation associated with the register geographical indications. Further, the proprietor is obliged to ensure licensees adhere strictly to quality standards as defined under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an indication shall be deemed a geographical indication if it identifies goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic substantially attributable to its geographical origin is recognized. The term "included register geographical indication" refers to any geographical indication that has been formally entered into the Register of Geographical Indications maintained under this Act following due process and publication as provided herein. An application for inclusion in the included register geographical indication shall specify the name of the geographical location, the goods to which it relates, and details substantiating the link between the place of origin and the qualities or characteristics of those goods.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be accompanied by a map indicating clearly the territorial boundaries of the geographical area from which the goods originate, and any documents establishing the name and address of authorized users. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or evidence concerning the characteristics and qualities of the goods, as well as their connection with the geographical origin specified in the application. An indication shall be deemed to be “included register geographical” if it meets all requirements under this Act and is not refused registration under any provision herein. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and other interested parties, refuse registration if he considers that the proposed geographical indication is misleading or deceptive.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of an entry in the included register geographical indications shall file an application with the Registrar, setting forth the particulars of the error or omission and the relief sought. The Registrar may entertain such application only if it is made within three years from the date the indication was entered into the register, subject to a proviso allowing for extensions granted by order of the Appellate Board where exceptional circumstances are demonstrated. Where rectification is ordered, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the proposed amendment in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained under this Act. Any interested party may within sixty days from such publication file an objection to the rectification. The Registrar’s decision regarding objections shall be final, provided that remedies for challenging such decisions are available under the appropriate appellate provisions as provided herein.

Applications for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documents establishing, subject to verification by the Registrar, the origin and characteristics of the goods. The applicant shall specify the territorial extent of the geographical area from which the goods originate, clearly delineating its boundaries on an accompanying map. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further information or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any opposition to a proposed registration must be filed within three months from the date of publication in the Geographical Indications Journal. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and provide each party with an opportunity for hearing. If, after due consideration, the Registrar is satisfied that the geographical indication meets the criteria as provided herein, it shall be entered into the included register geographical.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall include particulars demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the specified geographical area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating this claim, including but not limited to affidavits from producers and trade organizations operating within the defined territory. Any opposition filed under this Act against inclusion in the register shall be adjudicated based on whether the impugned indication is primarily indicative of a quality or characteristic linked to that geographical origin. The Registrar shall maintain an included register geographical, accessible for public inspection, detailing registered indications and their respective areas of origin, subject to provisions regarding confidentiality where trade secrets are involved.

Any person aggrieved by an entry, or omission from entry, in the included register geographical indications shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the publication of the Register. Such appeal may be based on grounds that the indication is not distinctive of the goods for which it seeks registration, or that use of the indication would constitute unfair competition under this Act. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during application and subsequent proceedings shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Appellate Board may, after affording opportunity for hearing, direct rectification of the Register; non-compliance with such direction shall attract daily penalties until compliance is achieved.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the indication on goods matching the definition thereof. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may cover activities including, but not limited to, production, processing, packaging, distribution, and sale. Assignment of a geographical indication, or any license granted thereunder, requires prior approval from the Geographical Indications Registry, provided that such approval shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any person acquiring rights through assignment or license is deemed to be an authorized user and may enforce the provisions of this Act against infringers as if they were the original proprietor. The included register geographical indication remains subject to periodic review by the Registrar to ensure continued compliance with quality standards, and any alteration in these standards may impact existing licenses.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, direct that the said application be placed on the included register geographical pending determination of any opposition filed against it. Any party aggrieved by such direction or by the subsequent inclusion or exclusion of a geographical indication from the included register geographical may within sixty days of the publication of the Register in electronic form appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, determine whether the Registrar’s decision was justified under this Act and as provided herein. Further, the Board may direct the Registrar to revise the included register geographical accordingly, subject to principles of natural justice.

For the purposes of this Act, “association with goods” in relation to a trade mark means the use of a sign, whether registered or unregistered, in connection with goods or services in such a manner as to indicate, directly or indirectly, sponsorship or approval by the owner of the trade mark. A trade mark relation shall be deemed to exist where there is an intentional representation that the proprietor of the trade mark has approved of, or is connected with, the goods or services; provided that such representation may be inferred from the manner in which the sign is used and the impressions created in the mind of the public. Nothing herein shall prevent the use of a trade mark for descriptive purposes only, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the mark and may specify, where the mark comprises a device, the colours intended to be used therein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information relating to the mark as he deems necessary for the purposes of examination under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark that is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark in relation to identical goods or services, the application shall be refused, subject to any provisions regarding use and reputation. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, consider allowing registration notwithstanding such refusal. A trade mark relation exists between an applicant and the intellectual property rights conferred by successful registration.

Where any person infringes a registered trade mark, the proprietor shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the defendant from infringing the said trade mark, and may also claim damages for such infringement. Such damages shall be assessed by considering the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, taking into account the extent of the damage sustained and the profits made by the infringer as a result of using the impugned mark. The Court may award further compensation to the proprietor if it finds that the defendant has acted fraudulently or with malicious intent in relation to the trade mark relation. It is provided that any order for injunction or damages shall be subject to just considerations, including any bona fide use by another person prior to registration.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, upon examination under this Act, it is determined that the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier trade mark relating to identical or closely related goods or services. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application provided that the applicant demonstrates clear and substantial reason why there should not be a finding of conflict, including but not limited to evidence of acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to the date of prior registration. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider any submissions made by the applicant and the trade mark owner in relation to the trade mark relation, and pass such orders as it deems appropriate.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.
