Such appeal may only be pursued if the grounds for refusal are demonstrably based on a conflict with existing rights relating to similar goods or services. The appellant must provide evidence satisfying the tribunal that their proposed trade mark does not create confusion amongst consumers, and that any similarity is incidental or negligible. Further, the applicant shall demonstrate diligent efforts were undertaken to distinguish the mark from prior uses, as provided herein. A successful appeal requires compliance with prescribed timelines for filing documentation and payment of applicable fees; failure to adhere to these conditions will render the appeal invalidating the trade mark relation.

Where any person knowingly and wilfully infringes a registered trade mark, or causes to be infringed a registered trade mark, he shall be liable to pay damages to the proprietor of the trade mark. Such damages may include not only direct pecuniary loss resulting from the infringement but also consequential losses reasonably foreseeable as a result thereof. Further, under this Act, any person found guilty of falsely representing connection with a trade mark relation shall be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees. The court may, in determining the amount of damages, consider the flagrant nature of the infringement and its impact on consumer perception.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to any conditions specified in the agreement, grant licences relating to the use of the said trade mark upon application and payment of prescribed fees. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may extend to specific territories or classes of goods or services as determined by the proprietor. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include all rights pertaining to any existing licences connected with that trade mark relation unless explicitly excluded in writing by both the assignor and assignee. Further, where a licence is assigned alongside the trade mark itself, the terms of the original licensing agreement shall remain binding on the new licensee, provided that such terms do not conflict with the provisions of this Act or prejudice the rights of third parties. The proprietor may retain ownership of the trade mark while granting extensive usage rights under a commercial arrangement.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against any decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, the Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions herein, confirm, vary, or reverse such decision. The appellant shall be required to demonstrate before the Appellate Board that the grounds for rectification are substantiated by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising from the use of another sign in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court, but only on a question of law. The determination of whether a trade mark relation exists shall be final and binding unless overturned by the High Court.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark becomes aware that any person is making use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to his trade mark in contravention of this Act, he shall have the right to apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for an injunction restraining such use. Such application may seek damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing activity, and further request that the offending party be ordered to account for all profits derived from the unauthorized exploitation of the trade mark relation. The tribunal may also order the destruction of any goods or materials bearing the infringing sign. Notice of such orders shall be published in the Official Gazette for public information. Provided that, where an infringer has acted in good faith and without knowledge of the registered trade mark, the tribunal may grant relief proportionate to the harm suffered by the proprietor.

For the purposes of this Act, "passing off" means the representation, either directly or indirectly, that goods or services are those of another person, or are connected therewith, with the intention to deceive or likely to cause confusion. Such representation includes, but is not limited to, the use of a name, mark, device, sign, symbol, or other indicia of origin which falsely suggests an association with such other person. Nothing in this definition shall preclude a finding of passing off where goodwill has been established by the claimant through consistent reputation and consumer recognition associated with their goods or services, even absent direct misrepresentation.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall not be deemed to have established exclusive right to use a sign merely by virtue of such application pending examination. However, where an application for registration has been published and opposed, and the proceedings are ongoing, the Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating substantial confusion amongst consumers attributable to the contemporaneous use of an identical or deceptively similar mark by another party, issue an interim injunction restraining that other party from utilizing said sign in a manner constituting passing off. Such restraint shall remain in effect pending final determination of the opposition proceedings and subject to any orders made concerning the applicant’s trade mark application as provided herein.

Where a person misrepresents their goods or services as being those of another, or allows others so to do, resulting in confusion amongst consumers and damage to the reputation of the proprietor of the genuine goods or services, such actions constitute passing off. The proprietor aggrieved by such acts may institute proceedings seeking an injunction restraining the defendant from further engaging in the deceptive conduct. Damages shall be awarded to compensate for losses directly attributable to the passing off, including loss of profits, diminished value of goodwill, and costs incurred in mitigating the harm. Provided that, where the misrepresentation is unintentional, the Court may exercise its discretion to reduce or suspend the imposition of damages. Further, any party found guilty of passing off shall be liable to pay such sum as the Court deems fit by way of compensation to the aggrieved proprietor.

Where a proprietor of a trademark or get-up alleges that another person has engaged in conduct constituting an action of passing off, such allegation shall be investigated by the relevant Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. The Tribunal may, upon receiving a complaint, issue notices to all parties involved, requiring them to submit written statements outlining their respective positions and supporting documentation. Evidence presented before the Tribunal shall include, but not be limited to, evidence of reputation associated with the claimant’s mark or get-up, demonstrable misrepresentation by the respondent, and resultant damage suffered by the claimant. The Tribunal is empowered to order injunctive relief preventing further acts of passing off, as well as award compensation for losses incurred due to the misleading conduct. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Tribunal may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order.

Where a proprietor demonstrates that representations have been made in the course of trade likely to deceive the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, and that such misrepresentation has caused, or is likely to cause, damage to the goodwill associated with those goods or services, an action for passing off may be initiated under this Act. The proprietor shall provide evidence establishing a substantial connection between the misrepresented goods or services and those for which the claimant possesses reputation. Provided that, if the defendant proves that the public associates the sign used in the misrepresentation with the defendant’s goods or services rather than those of the claimant, relief may be refused. Such relief is subject to considerations of fair use and honest practices in industrial competition as provided herein.

Where a person misrepresents goods or services as being those of another, or allows others so to do, and thereby causes or is likely to cause damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the trademark or brand of that other person, such action constitutes passing off. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark or any person possessing goodwill in an unregistered trade mark may apply to the Commercial Court for relief against such misrepresentation. The court shall grant such injunctions, account for damages suffered and award costs as it deems just, subject to considerations of public interest and fair competition. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act shall be deemed a contempt of court and punishable accordingly.

Where the proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license permitting the use of their mark upon goods or services, such license may include provisions for assignment of the right to prevent acts of passing off. The licensee shall be entitled to assign the benefit of this protection against unauthorized use creating confusion amongst consumers, provided that such assignment is made in writing and duly executed. Further, where a trademark proprietor enters into an agreement with another party allowing them to utilize their mark under conditions restricting specific commercial activities, any subsequent attempt by a third party to engage in similar activities constituting passing off shall be actionable at the instance of both the original proprietor and the initially licensed party, subject to the terms outlined within the licensing arrangement. The rights granted or assigned hereunder are not transferable without prior written consent from the trademark proprietor.

Where an action is brought alleging acts of passing off relating to goods or services, the aggrieved party shall bear the burden of demonstrating a misrepresentation by the defendant which has caused, or is likely to cause, confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services. The defendant may raise as a defence that the use of the mark or get-up in question does not constitute a misrepresentation, or that any confusion arising is inconsequential and does not prejudice the plaintiff’s reputation or goodwill. Subject to appeal to the High Court, findings on issues of consumer perception and likelihood of confusion shall be final unless demonstrable error of law appears on the record of proceedings.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another has engaged in acts constituting passing off, and such allegation involves a comparison between goods or services offered by the defendant and those for which a trade mark is registered under this Act, the defendant may present evidence demonstrating due compliance with any registration notice published pursuant to the provisions herein. Such evidence shall be considered alongside all other submissions during proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. The aggrieved party shall bear the onus of proving that the defendant’s actions create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services in question, subject to the defendant's right to challenge this finding on appeal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, no person shall represent that goods or services are those of another person, or as being used by such other person, with the intention to deceive or likely to cause confusion; such misrepresentation constitutes an action for passing off. Where a trade mark has been assigned under this Act, the assignee shall be entitled to institute proceedings relating to passing off in respect of the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, as if he were the proprietor of the trade mark at the time of the alleged infringement or misrepresentation. The right to prevent and obtain relief from passing off remains irrespective of registration under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout design registered" shall mean a layout design that has been entered into the Register of Layout Designs and in respect of which a certificate of registration has been granted under this Act. A layout design registered is deemed to be original unless proven otherwise subject to the provisions regarding prior publication or disclosure. The right conferred by registration of a layout design registered extends only to the three-dimensional representation of that layout design, excluding any features solely for producing an integrated circuit carrying out a predetermined function. Any modification to a layout design registered shall not affect its validity as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit revised drawings deemed necessary for assessing novelty and originality under this Act. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical or substantially similar layout design, the Registrar shall reject the subsequent application without formal examination. A layout design registered in accordance with the provisions herein confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights relating to the reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation of that layout design within the territory of India. Any unauthorized act infringing these rights constitutes a violation subject to remedies as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an act of infringement of a layout design registered under this Act may institute civil proceedings in the District Court claiming damages. Such damages shall be assessed taking into account the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a consequence of the infringing activity, and also any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized use of the registered layout design. The Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing conduct, provided that it is satisfied that such infringement would cause further harm to the registered proprietor. Further remedies available under this Act include delivery up of all infringing articles, and orders for destruction of materials used in or capable of being used in connection with the infringing act. The Court shall also have power to award costs as deemed appropriate.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and representations as the Controller may prescribe, including detailed schematics illustrating the topological features of the integrated circuit. The applicant shall furnish an oath or affirmation verifying the correctness of the information provided in the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall issue an acknowledgment to the applicant. Where the Controller considers that any part of the layout design is not original, or does not fulfill the requirements under this Act, a notification specifying the grounds for objection shall be served on the applicant. The applicant may submit a response addressing the objections within the time specified in the notification. If the application meets all prescribed criteria and no valid objections remain, the Controller may proceed to register the layout design. A *layout design registered* is deemed to be protected as provided herein against unauthorized copying or reproduction.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be deemed complete only when all prescribed fees have been remitted and the required documentation, including detailed schematics and topographical representations conforming to standards specified by the Controller General, has been submitted. The Controller General may reject an application if it contains any material which is contrary to public order or decency, or if the layout design does not meet the originality criteria as provided herein. A layout design registered under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights relating to the reproduction and commercial use of that layout design within the territory of India. Subject to compliance with these provisions, a registered layout design remains valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration or for the term of copyright subsisting in any element incorporated therein, whichever is longer.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout design registered under this Act, makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any integrated circuit embodying a layout design that constitutes an infringement registered as such, shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be assessed by the relevant adjudicating officer and may include compensation for loss of profits, reasonable royalty, and other consequential losses suffered by the registered proprietor. Further, where the infringing activity is found to have been carried out with the intent to deceive or cause wrongful gain, a penalty not exceeding ten times the cost of the infringing layout design shall be imposed. The adjudicating officer may also order seizure and destruction of the infringing integrated circuits as provided herein.

The owner of a layout design registered under this Act may grant licenses conferring rights to use the registered layout design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, provided that any such assignment is documented by way of a memorandum of transfer filed with the Controller. The Controller shall maintain a record of all assignments and sub-licenses relating to a registered layout design. Further, where a licensee manufactures integrated circuits embodying the registered layout design, the owner may specify territorial limitations within which those manufacturing activities are permitted. Any variation in the registration variety of a layout design, such as alterations made during the manufacturing process, shall not affect the validity of the underlying registered layout design unless explicitly stated otherwise in the original registration documentation.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout design registered" shall mean a layout design that has been entered into the Register of Layout Designs and relates to an integrated circuit or semiconductor chip. A layout design registered under this Act is deemed original work subject to the provisions relating to prior publication. The right of the registered proprietor of a layout design registered hereunder includes the right to apply patent protection for related inventions, provided that such application does not directly claim the layout design itself. Any reproduction, import, or sale of a registered layout-design without authorization shall be deemed an infringement as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall include commodities, articles, and products manufactured, processed, or produced, whether for sale to the general public or for any specific purpose. Goods may encompass raw materials, intermediate goods used in production processes, and finished consumer items. The term "goods" also extends to services offered as merchandise, provided that such offerings are presented alongside tangible products. Subject to this definition, goods shall be classified according to their nature and intended use, as determined by the Registrar under this Act. Provided that, for clarity, unpackaged agricultural produce is deemed goods within the meaning of this legislation.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, “goods” shall be classified according to the International Nice Classification, as amended from time to time. An application for the registration of a trade mark shall specify in clear and precise terms the goods with which such trade mark is associated. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend or clarify the description of the goods if it appears vague or ambiguous. Goods specified in an application shall be understood to include identical or closely related articles, subject to any limitations expressly stated by the applicant during the registration process. Furthermore, where a trade mark is registered for particular goods, subsequent applications relating to similar goods may be refused if they are deemed likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled, subject to any conditions specified in the registration, to restrain the application of identical or deceptively similar marks to goods or services identical or closely related to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered. Where such restraint has been obtained, the proprietor may further seek damages from any person who, prior to the institution of the proceeding, had infringed under this Act and acted in good faith. It shall be a defence for the alleged infringer to demonstrate that their use of the mark did not create confusion among the relevant public concerning the origin of the goods. The remedies available to the proprietor are without prejudice to any other right or remedy available under this Act or otherwise by law relating to passing off or unfair competition involving these goods.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall include manufactured articles, raw materials, and any substance whether natural or processed, offered for sale or hire. The Registrar may, upon application by a registered proprietor seeking to extend the protection of their trade mark, investigate whether such goods fall within a class already designated in the registration. This investigation shall consider the essential character and intended use of the goods. An objection to the extension of protection may be filed by any person claiming a proprietary right or interest in similar goods under this Act. Such an objection must be supported by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers, provided that the Registrar shall give due weight to established trade channels and marketing practices. The applicant shall have opportunity to respond to such objections within the time prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall include any commodity offered for sale, whether tangible or capable of being embodied in a tangible form. Registration as a trade mark shall be refused if the application relates to goods which are primarily agricultural products and their production is exclusively carried out by persons engaged in agriculture. Provided that such refusal shall not apply where the applicant demonstrates sufficient association with processing or packaging of those goods, beyond mere primary production. Furthermore, registration may be opposed under this Act if it is shown that the proposed trade mark describes a characteristic concerning the quality, quantity, origin, or intended purpose of the goods. Any use of a registered trade mark on identical goods shall be deemed an infringement unless consent has been obtained from the proprietor.

No trade mark shall be registered if, in the opinion of the Registrar, it exclusively describes the characteristics of the goods. Any person aggrieved by a registration under this Act may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification, provided that such petition is filed within six months from the date of publication of the journal containing particulars of the registration. The Board shall have power to order the deletion of a trade mark from the register if it finds that the use of the registered goods has resulted in confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers. Failure to comply with an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may result in penalties, including fines and imprisonment, as determined by the Court.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark relating to specific goods shall be entitled to grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to manufacture, import, distribute, sell, or otherwise deal in those goods bearing a representation resembling the registered trade mark. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor within the terms of the agreement. Assignment of the entire undertaking relating to the said goods, including all rights and obligations pertaining thereto under this Act, shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry and publication in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that any license granted prior to such assignment shall remain valid unless expressly terminated by mutual consent or as otherwise stipulated within the original licensing agreement. The assignee shall be deemed the proprietor of the trade mark for those goods from the date of registration of the assignment.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a trade mark relating to any specified goods, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity for cross-examination and oral hearing. The grounds for such objection must be clearly stated in writing and supported by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates through documentary proof a period of continuous use of the mark on identical or similar goods prior to the date of the objection, the Registrar may consider this as a relevant factor. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar under this Act relating to the acceptance or rejection of any application for registration of goods may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods" shall include commodities, articles, and any product manufactured, processed, or altered for sale or distribution, whether tangible or having intangible characteristics. Goods may be classified under distinct categories as determined by the Registrar, considering their nature, use, and intended consumer base. The term “goods” extends to packaged products, containers used in the packaging of goods, and labels affixed thereto, provided such labels clearly identify the goods contained within. xii shall exempt certain agricultural produce from being considered "goods" for the purposes of infringement proceedings under this Act, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a *name* shall be deemed to include any word, letter, symbol, device, or combination thereof adopted for the purpose of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. A *name*, when used in relation to goods or services, shall not extend to geographical indications as defined under this Act, unless such use is expressly authorized by the proprietor of the relevant indication and does not indicate the origin, quality, or other characteristics thereof. The Registrar may require proof that a proposed *name* has been continuously used for a specified period prior to application, subject to conditions prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a name shall be deemed refused if the Registrar, upon examination, finds that the proposed name conflicts with an earlier registered name in respect of identical goods or services, or where the similarity between the names would likely cause confusion amongst consumers. The applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or lack of likelihood of confusion, which shall be considered by the Registrar. Provided that, a name descriptive of the characteristics or quality of the goods or services for which it is sought can only be registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application, as evidenced by verifiable market data. The Registrar may require further information regarding such usage.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act alleging that another person has, without due cause, infringed his right in the said trade mark, the Court may grant such remedy as it deems just and equitable. This includes an injunction restraining the defendant from using any *name* or mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration subsists. Further, the Court shall order the delivery up of all infringing materials, including labels, packaging, advertising matter, and any other articles bearing the unauthorized *name*. Provided that where the defendant proves prior honest concurrent use of the impugned *name*, the injunction may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Court considers appropriate to safeguard the interests of both parties. The proprietor shall also be entitled to damages sustained by reason of the infringement, or an account of profits made by the infringing party.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no trade mark shall be registered if it consists exclusively of a *name* which is indicative of the nature, quality, or characteristics of goods or services. Where an application for registration includes a *name*, the Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness in relation to the applied-for goods or services. Such evidence shall include documentary proof of the extent of use of the mark and its recognition by consumers. The Registrar shall consider any opposition filed under this Act against such an application, giving due weightage to arguments pertaining to consumer perception and potential confusion arising from the similarity between the proposed trade mark and existing marks. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A registered name shall continue to be deemed valid unless, following registration, the proprietor fails to file a renewal application within the prescribed period as provided herein. Such failure shall render the name liable for removal from the Register of Trade Marks upon application by any interested party demonstrating due diligence in attempting to ascertain the proprietor’s contact details. Provided that, if the Registrar is satisfied that the proprietor had reasonable grounds for failing to comply with the renewal requirements, and that there are extenuating circumstances justifying continued protection of the name, the Registrar may, at his discretion, permit a belated filing within a further period not exceeding six months from the original due date. Any challenge to this decision may be made under appeal as provided herein.

No trade mark shall be registered if, in the opinion of the Registrar, it consists exclusively of a *name* which is indicative of the kind, quality, or characteristic of goods or services. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that such a *name*, though descriptive, has acquired distinctiveness through use to warrant registration; failing sufficient demonstration, registration shall be refused. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Where a registered trade mark infringes upon an earlier right in a *name*, the proprietor of the earlier right may apply for rectification and seek its removal from the Register, subject to penalties as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered name shall be entitled to grant licences conferring rights to use the said name for specific commercial purposes, subject to conditions as may be stipulated in the licence agreement. Such agreements must clearly define the geographical territory covered by the granted usage and the classes of goods or services relating to which the name may be employed. Any assignment of a registered name shall require prior notification to the Registrar, accompanied by details of the assignee and the terms of transfer. The Registrar may, after providing an opportunity for objection under this Act, approve or reject such assignments based on considerations of public interest and fairness to existing licensees. Further, any subsequent use of the name following assignment must adhere strictly to the conditions originally registered, as modified by any approved licence agreements.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a proposed trade mark based upon its similarity to an earlier registered *name*, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant for registration and to the proprietor of the prior registration. The applicant may, within such time as prescribed, file a counter-statement rebutting the grounds of objection. Upon receiving the counter-statement, the Registrar shall afford the proprietor of the prior registration an opportunity to submit a reply. Subject to any directions issued by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Registrar shall consider all submissions and determine whether the proposed trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion as regards the identity of goods or services. The decision of the Registrar may be appealed against under this Act.

The registered owner of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the name embodied within that trade mark, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify geographical limitations on usage, permitted goods or services associated with the name, and duration of the license. Further, the registered proprietor may assign the entire interest in a trade mark, including any existing licenses relating to its use as a name, to another party, provided that all licensees consent to such assignment unless the license agreement expressly prohibits it. Any subsequent owner acquiring the trade marks registered shall be bound by the terms of any pre-existing license agreements concerning the use of the name, and may not unilaterally alter those conditions without obtaining licensee approval.

The Registrar may, upon receiving objection under this Act from any party claiming an interest in preventing the registration of a proposed trade mark, direct that the trademark application be refused. Such direction shall be accompanied by reasons in writing detailing the grounds for refusal, specifically addressing whether the proposed *name* conflicts with existing rights or is otherwise contrary to the provisions herein. Any applicant aggrieved by such a direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order. The Board shall hear the appeal and consider any counter-arguments presented by the objector, ensuring due process as provided herein. Further appeals from the Board’s decision are permissible under the appellate jurisdiction provisions relating to section 94 appeal.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar may prescribe, including a representation of the layout design and details regarding its origin. The applicant shall furnish an execution report confirming adherence to prescribed standards relating to data integrity during transmission to the office of the Registrar. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the submission of further documentation or clarifications deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Failure to comply with such requests within the stipulated timeframe will result in the application being considered withdrawn. The manner applying registrar shall be governed by regulations issued periodically and accessible on the official website.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be made to the Registrar in such form and containing such information as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish with the application, copies of the layout-design in accordance with the regulations issued by the Controller General. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further particulars or amendments deemed necessary for clarity and compliance with this Act. Any failure to comply with such a requirement within the time specified will result in rejection of the application. The manner applying registrar shall be governed by rules framed by the Central Government, detailing procedures for examination, advertisement, and opposition. Objections received during the advertisement period shall be considered by the Registrar, who may afford the applicant an opportunity to respond before proceeding further as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may prescribe, including but not limited to a technical description conforming to guidelines issued from time to time. The applicant shall furnish an address for service in India where communications relating to the application are to be sent; failure to maintain this address, or providing false information regarding it, renders the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation demonstrating compliance with prevailing standards of layout-design protection. Any alteration to the particulars initially provided shall be notified to the manner applying registrar within thirty days and subject to approval.

Any application filed with the Registrar shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and shall be deemed abandoned if not pursued within six months from the date of receipt, unless a request for extension is made prior to that deadline. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding the manner applying registrar, including but not limited to proper form submission and accurate representation of layout-design details, renders the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any person aggrieved by an order of rejection may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of thirty days from the date of communication of such order; however, appeals filed after this period shall be deemed time-barred and inadmissible. Deliberate misrepresentation or fraudulent conduct in connection with any application will attract penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, a proprietor of an integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license conferring specific rights pertaining to the use, reproduction, or adaptation of their design. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacturing processes and derivative works. The manner applying registrar for registration of assignments and licenses relating to registered layout designs shall be as prescribed by the Board. Provided that any assignment or license granted prior to the date of registration requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so renders such assignment voidable at the proprietor’s discretion. Furthermore, a licensee may further assign their rights under the license, subject to obtaining prior written consent from the original layout-design proprietor and subsequent registration with the registrar.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed improperly made if it fails to comply with the prescribed form and accompanying documentation, and the Registrar may, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, reject such application. Any party aggrieved by an order of rejection under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising out of the decision of the Registrar and may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. It is provided that the manner applying registrar in determining whether a layout-design is substantially similar to an earlier design shall be guided by principles of established jurisprudence concerning copyright infringement.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in relation to such decisions, and its determination shall be final. Further, an applicant who has been refused registration under this Act may apply for a review of the Registrar's initial assessment, provided that the application demonstrates newly discovered evidence not previously considered during the original examination process. The manner applying registrar to these reviews is governed by regulations framed by the Central Government. A record of all computer inspections undertaken relating to entries in the computer inspection register shall be maintained and made available for audit as per prescribed procedures.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may prescribe. The Registrar, upon receipt of an application, shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with all requirements under this Act and the regulations framed thereunder. If the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has complied with these stipulations, he or she may proceed to issue a certificate purporting to be a record of registration. This certificate shall only be issued after due consideration of any objections received within the prescribed period following publication of the application in the manner applying registrar as determined by the rules. The Registrar shall maintain a register containing details of registered layout-designs and all related documentation, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

A registered geographical indication is an indication which identifies goods originating in a territory and whose quality, reputation or other characteristic are essentially attributable to its geographical origin. For the purposes of this Act, "territory" includes any region, locality or place, whether within India or elsewhere, and shall be construed as encompassing both defined geographical areas and broader regions possessing distinctive qualities. An application for registration of a geographical indication shall specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, particulars of the territory to which the goods originate, and a statement of any characteristics, quality or reputation attributable to that origin. The Register of Geographical Indications shall record details relating to the proprietor of the registered geographical indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the quality and characteristics which are attributable to its origin, or by collectives or cooperatives. The Registrar shall register a geographical indication only if it is deemed distinctive enough to identify the goods as originating from a specific territory. Upon registration, the registered geographical indication shall be recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications, along with particulars relating to the applicant and the defined area of production. Any person claiming rights in a geographically linked product may object to the application under this Act within the prescribed time period, provided that such objection is based on demonstrable grounds preventing the grant of registration as a registered geographical indication.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suits for infringement and may seek remedies including injunctions, damages, and accounts of profits. Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes use of a registered geographical indication in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which it is registered shall be deemed to have infringed the said geographical indication. Provided that, where the use is made in good faith and does not constitute an unfair trade practice as determined under this Act, relief may be granted at the discretion of the court limiting the remedy available to the proprietor. The remedies available to a registered proprietor are subject to principles of equity and fairness; any order restraining the use of a geographical indication shall be proportionate to the harm suffered.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed, including details regarding the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory from which it originates, and the qualities, reputation or other characteristics attributable to its origin. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the said name is essentially linked to the geographical origin as claimed and that use of the indication by others is not likely to mislead consumers as to the true origin of the goods. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant. Where objections are raised against the registration of a registered geographical indication under this Act, the objector shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard. The Registrar shall consider all submissions and pass orders in writing.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the geographical area over which such goods are produced or manufactured, and a map of the alleged geographical territory. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further details demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to the origin of those goods within the defined geographical area. Any association representing producers of goods conforming to the standard specified in the application shall be deemed the exclusive proprietor of the registered geographical indication, subject to any conditions imposed by the Registrar. The use of a registered geographical indication shall be restricted to products genuinely originating from that location as determined under this Act.

Any person who without authorization uses as trademark, or in connection with trade, commerce, or business, a registered geographical indication relating to goods, or whose goods bear a label containing such indication, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed based on the loss suffered by the registered proprietor of the geographical indication and any other producers authorized to use it under this Act. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, institute appropriate proceedings in a District Court against the offender. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act regarding the cessation of unauthorized use shall render the offender liable to a penalty which may extend to three times the value of the infringing goods or rupees five lakhs, whichever is higher, and imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that indication on goods conforming to the standards established under this Act. Such licenses shall specify the duration, geographical area, and nature of the authorized use, including but not limited to packaging, labeling, and advertising. Assignment of the right to use a registered geographical indication is permissible with prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to maintain the quality and characteristics associated with the indication as defined in the registration certificate. Any subsequent license or assignment shall be subject to the terms of the original agreement and may require notification to the Registrar for record. The proprietor remains responsible for ensuring compliance with applicable laws concerning fair trade practices relating to goods bearing the registered geographical indication, even when licensed to third parties.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be opposed by any person claiming an interest in the prevention of the registered geographical indication being used in connection with goods not conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. Such opposition shall be made within the time specified in the notice of advertisement of the application, and must state the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to demonstrable consumer deception or unfair competition arising from use of a similar name or mark. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to the opposition, after which the Registrar shall consider all submissions and may, subject to due process, allow or dismiss the opposition. Any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication aggrieved by an act of unfair competition involving the use thereof, or by any other activity infringing upon their exclusive rights under this Act, may institute legal proceedings in the competent civil court. Such proceedings shall be available irrespective of whether the infringement is intentional or unintentional, and without prejudice to any criminal remedies provided elsewhere. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining the offending party from further acts of misuse, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such infringing activity. Further, where a geographical indication has been used in contravention of this Act, and such use constitutes deceptive trade practices under section 36e ixd, enhanced penalties may be imposed at the discretion of the court. The remedies available to proprietors are without prejudice to their right to pursue any other remedy available under law.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons, producer companies, cooperatives, or firms engaged in the production, processing, and/or packaging of goods originating from the territory specified in the application. The applicant shall furnish particulars regarding the history of the name, its character and essential qualities as they relate to the origin of the goods. Where an application is filed by an association or cooperative, it must demonstrate that it represents the interests of a significant proportion of producers concerned with the geographical indication. An application entitled breeder may be rejected if the Registrar determines that the claimed connection between the applicant and the specified territory is tenuous or lacks demonstrable historical basis. The registered geographical indication shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive right to use the said indication in relation to goods for which it is registered, subject to any conditions as provided herein.

An application for registration as a registered geographical indication may be filed by an association representing the producers of goods originating from the specified territory, or by individual producers subject to compliance with prescribed conditions. The applicant shall demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to their origin within the defined geographical area and that such origin is proven by records and historical data. Where the good in question is a pharmaceutical substance, additional documentation verifying adherence to Good Manufacturing Practices and relevant pharmacopoeial standards must be submitted. The Registering Authority may reject an application if it determines that use of the indication would likely mislead consumers or constitute unfair competition, provided that such determination considers existing trade practices within the territory.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which that indication is registered, or any identical or confusingly similar goods, shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be determined by the Appellate Board and may include compensation for loss of profits suffered by the registered proprietor, as well as punitive damages not exceeding ten times the value of the infringing goods sold. Furthermore, under this Act, a notice requiring payment of a filed registry fee is deemed sufficient service of process in relation to any enforcement proceedings. Failure to comply with such a notice may result in summary judgment against the defaulting party. The Register shall have power to issue injunctions restraining further infringement as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been rejected and such rejection is appealed against before the Controller, the appellant shall furnish within thirty days of admission of the appeal, a statement specifying the grounds on which the decision of the Controller is challenged; provided that the applicant may request an extension of this period not exceeding fifteen days, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Controller shall consider any arguments presented by the author of the invention relating to novelty or inventive step and may require further clarification or experimental data. Upon final determination of the appeal, if the patent is granted, it shall be deemed to have effect from the date of the original application; however, in cases where an appeal admitted expiry of the term has occurred, the term shall be adjusted accordingly as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a musical work shall be defined as a composition consisting of melody and harmony, irrespective of whether it is reduced to notation or embodied in phonograms. A musical work includes lyrics which form an integral part of the work, but does not extend to mere words or phrases forming part of such lyrics if they are common literary expressions. Where a musical work is accompanied by artistic elements, such as illustrations or cover art, copyright therein shall subsist separately under this Act in respect of those artistic works, subject to any agreement between the author of the music and the artist creating said accompanying elements.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a musical work shall be deemed to comprise not only the music notation but also lyrics, if such lyrics are integral to and inseparable from the composition. The Registrar may require submission of both the musical score and accompanying textual elements for complete assessment. Where a musical work incorporates pre-existing literary or dramatic material, the applicant must provide evidence demonstrating ownership of copyright in all constituent parts. Failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection. Any subsequent alterations made to a registered musical work, particularly concerning lyrics or arrangement, may necessitate notification to the Registrar and potentially require further documentation as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a musical work shall endure until the expiration of sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the death of the author. Where the composer and lyricist are different persons, copyright shall subsist independently in each such work, and for the purposes of determining the duration of copyright, the author shall be deemed to be the last surviving of them. Any person who infringes upon the exclusive rights conferred under this Act by reproducing a musical work without authorization may be liable for damages, including actual loss sustained or a sum not exceeding one million rupees, as determined by the competent court. Provided that, where such infringement is committed for commercial advantage or financial gain, enhanced penalties and imprisonment shall apply as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a musical work shall vest in the author of the work. Where the composer and lyricist are distinct persons, copyright shall subsist separately in respect of the music and the words. Any person claiming to be the owner of copyright in any musical work may, within thirty days from the date on which such claim is asserted, serve notice thereof upon the Registrar of Copyrights specifying particulars of the work and the grounds for the claim. The Registrar shall publish a notification regarding such claims in the Official Gazette. Upon receiving objections to the claimed ownership under this Act, the Registrar shall provide all parties with an opportunity for hearing before determining the matter. Decisions made by the Registrar are appealable to the relevant High Court as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a musical work shall be deemed to include not only melodies and harmonies but also orchestral arrangements thereof, provided that such arrangements demonstrably incorporate original compositional elements beyond mere transposition or alteration of tempo. The right of copyright in a musical work extends exclusively to the author unless assignment has been made in writing and registered as per the prescribed procedures. Any person reproducing, distributing, performing publicly, or broadcasting a musical work without due license from the owner of copyright shall be deemed to have infringed upon their exclusive rights. Further, where a musical work is jointly authored, all authors shall be considered joint owners unless an agreement specifying otherwise has been executed and notarized.

Any person who, without authorisation from the owner of copyright in a musical work, reproduces the work in any form, including but not limited to digital audio files for distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Such damages shall reflect the reasonable value of the infringed musical work and account for the commercial impact on the copyright holder’s potential earnings. Further, where a violation is established to have been committed with the intent to deceive or mislead the public regarding the authenticity of the copyrighted material, enhanced penalties may be imposed under this Act. The court may also order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies, provided that such action does not unduly prejudice other rights holders.

Where the copyright in a musical work has been assigned under this Act, the assignor shall retain the right to grant non-exclusive licenses for mechanical reproduction provided that such licenses are granted on terms consistent with the assignment and do not conflict with the exclusive rights transferred. Any subsequent assignee may, subject to existing licenses granted by the original assignor, further license or sub-license the musical work for performance in public places, including but not limited to radio broadcasts and digital streaming platforms. The right to authorize the distribution of copies of the musical work remains exclusively vested in the assignee unless explicitly excluded within the terms of the assignment agreement. Further, any adaptation of a musical work requires prior written consent from the copyright holder, which may be granted subject to royalty payments as determined by mutual agreement or, failing that, as provided herein.

Where a claim is made that a particular sound recording incorporates substantial elements of a pre-existing musical work, the claimant shall bear the onus of demonstrating both copyright subsistence in the asserted musical work and demonstrable copying by the defendant. This determination shall consider not only melodic and harmonic similarities but also rhythmic patterns and lyrical content, provided that such similarities are not attributable to common usage or public domain sources. The defendant may adduce evidence to establish independent creation, subject to a balancing exercise weighing the probative value of such evidence against the claimant’s proof of copyright infringement under this Act. Any appeal from an order determining originality of a musical work shall be made within ninety days of the date of that order.

Registration of a musical work shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the identity of the owner of copyright therein, subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. An application for registration may be filed by the author of the musical work, or in case of their death, by any person who was at the time of their death entitled to assign the copyright under this Act. The layout design registrar shall examine such an application to ascertain whether the particulars contained therein are correct and complete and whether the musical work is original. Provided that a request for inspection of the registered musical work may be made to the Registrar by any person, upon payment of prescribed fees. Any appeal against the decision of the layout design registrar regarding registration or rejection shall lie before the Controller.

A musical work shall be deemed to include not only compositions fixed permanently in a tangible medium but also improvisations performed live, provided that such improvisation is recorded and subsequently reproduced with the authorization of the practitioner person responsible for its creation. Such authorization shall be evidenced by a written agreement specifying the terms of reproduction, including royalty rates payable to the practitioner person. The right of copyright under this Act in respect of any musical work shall vest initially in the composer or arranger unless otherwise stipulated within a contractual arrangement executed prior to the first public performance. Any subsequent assignment of such rights must adhere to principles of transparency and fair dealing as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in a musical work, reproduces the work in any form, including but not limited to digital audio files for distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant civil court. The amount of such damages shall reflect the reasonable value that would have been paid for a license permitting such use, subject to adjustments based on factors including the extent of commercial exploitation and demonstrable financial loss suffered by the copyright owner. Further, an application for injunction may be made by the copyright owner against any party engaging in unauthorized reproduction or distribution; failure to comply with such an injunction shall constitute contempt of court and attract appropriate penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a musical work shall be entitled to grant licences granting rights to reproduce, distribute, perform, and communicate the work to the public, subject to the conditions specified therein. Such licences may be granted for exclusive or non-exclusive use, and the terms thereof, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined at the discretion of the copyright owner. Assignment of ownership of a musical work is permissible through written agreement, registered with the entry register maintained under this Act, detailing the scope of rights transferred. Where an assignment includes partial rights, the register shall clearly delineate those specific permissions conveyed. Any subsequent licensing or further assignment relating to the portion of the musical work assigned must also be recorded in the aforementioned entry register. Provided that, a copyright owner may revoke any licence granted, subject to reasonable notice and compensation as determined by prevailing legal precedent.

Where a claim is made regarding infringement of copyright in a musical work, and the claimant alleges that such infringement involves the unauthorized use of a registered certification trade mark associated with the said musical work, the Tribunal shall afford the defendant the opportunity to demonstrate that the alleged infringing activity constitutes fair dealing under this Act. The defendant may further present evidence demonstrating that the registered certification trade mark was improperly granted or lacks distinctiveness sufficient to warrant protection. Any order issued by the Tribunal regarding copyright infringement shall be subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days of its pronouncement, provided that the appellant establishes a prima facie case of substantial injustice arising from the Tribunal’s decision concerning the validity of the registered certification trade mark.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may specify conditions for use by authorised users, subject to approval by the Registrar. Such conditions shall relate exclusively to quality parameters and production methods directly attributable to the geographical origin. The Registrar shall publish notice of any proposed conditions in the Geographical Indications Journal, inviting objections from interested parties within two months of publication. Any objection received shall be considered during a hearing before the Registrar, where both the applicant and objector may present evidence. Unless the context otherwise requires,— (b) “authorised user” means a person or enterprise who has been granted permission by the registration proprietor to use the geographical indication in accordance with conditions approved under this Act. The Registrar may revoke authorisation if an authorised user fails to adhere to stipulated quality standards, as determined through periodic inspections and audits.

context: For the purposes of this Act, a "Darjeeling Tea Geographical Indication" shall considered geographical in relation to the defined territory comprising all areas within a radius of twenty kilometres from Darjeeling town, West Bengal. An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association, cooperative society, producer group, or individual interested in the collective protection and promotion of goods originating from a particular territory. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed geographical indication, or revoking a registered geographical indication, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact arising out of the decision under appeal and may direct the Registrar to revise the order in dispute. An appeal lies against an order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board to the High Court on a point of law, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Further, the proprietor of a geographical indicati registered under this Act shall be liable for damages arising from any use of the indication without consent.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a *geographical indicati registered*, including but not limited to orders concerning revocation, amendment, or opposition proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising from orders regarding the validity and scope of protection afforded to a geographical indication and may confirm, reverse, or modify any such order as it deems fit. Further, where infringement of a *geographical indicati registered* occurs, the owner thereof shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement and damages for losses sustained due to such infringement. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the aggrieved party in law or equity, provided that actions based on deceptive use of *marks indications* must be brought within three years from the date of first publication or display of the infringing mark.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association, cooperative society, producer group, or individual engaged in the production, processing, and/or supply of goods claiming such protection. The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application, issue a public notice inviting objections from interested parties within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit their response within one month thereafter. Following consideration of all submissions, if the Registrar is satisfied that the indication is distinctive and conforms to the requirements as provided herein, he or she shall proceed with registration. Upon registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall record particulars including the registered proprietor, which may be an assignee where ownership has been transferred in accordance with applicable law. The geographical indicati registered shall then be deemed protected under this Act.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, providing particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services for which it is used, and the area of its origin. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods or services originates from the specified geographical territory. Consideration will be given to whether the sign functions in the eyes of the public as a badge of originality. Any person claiming an interest may oppose the registration; such opposition must be filed within the time prescribed and shall state the grounds for objection. A geographical indication, once registered, is considered geographical indication and enjoys protection as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall lie on a question of law, and the Board may entertain appeals relating to facts only if they involve questions of public importance or affect the interests of a large number of persons. Where a geographical indication is considered geographical indication and its registration has been cancelled or revoked, any proprietor who was using the mark immediately prior to such cancellation or revocation shall be entitled to compensation as determined by the Central Government. The Central Government may, in prescribing the amount of compensation, consider factors including investments made in good faith and losses incurred due to reliance upon the registered geographical indication. Further, remedies for unfair competition involving a considered geographical indication are available under this Act.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, including particulars relating to the name of the applicant, the geographical area from which the goods originate, and the history and characteristics of the goods. The Registrar shall examine whether the proposed geographical indication is considered geographical indication under this Act, taking into account factors such as its distinctiveness and connection with the specified territory. Where an objection is raised by any person claiming to be adversely affected by the registration, the applicant shall have opportunity to file a reply within the time stipulated herein. The Registrar may, after affording both parties a hearing, either allow or reject the application. Any appeal against an order of the Registrar under this Act lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, handicraft, or any other good for which the protection is sought, and the geographical area from which it originates. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to the origin within the defined geographical area. Further, the application must detail the history and traditions associated with the production of the good, establishing a clear link between the product and the specified territory. A geographical indication shall not be considered geographical indication if it is generic in the relevant market, or if its use would mislead consumers regarding the true origin of the goods.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses a considered geographical indication relating to goods as defined under this Act, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the value of the infringing goods sold, or rupees five hundred thousand, whichever is greater, subject to judicial discretion considering the extent and duration of the infringement. Further, any proprietor seeking enforcement of their rights relating to a registered geographical indication may apply to the relevant High Court for an injunction restraining such use. The court shall grant interim relief pending final determination, provided that adequate security is furnished as deemed appropriate by the court.

Any proprietor of a considered geographical indication may, subject to the provisions herein, grant licences for use of the said indication in relation to goods belonging to the class for which the indication is registered. Such licence shall specify the territory within which and the duration for which the licensee is authorised to utilise the geographical indication. The proprietor shall retain the right to terminate any such licence if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with the considered geographical indication, as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered geographical indication, including licences granted thereunder, requires prior approval from the said Registry and is subject to payment of prescribed fees. Further, any assignment shall not prejudice existing contractual obligations relating to use of the geographical indication.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be refused if, following an examination under this Act and after providing the applicant with an opportunity of being heard, the Registrar is satisfied that use of the name in connection with goods or services is continuous and widespread, notwithstanding that such use does not constitute a deceptive practice. Any party aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or requiring amendment thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider whether the applicant has adequately demonstrated distinctiveness arising from qualities associated with the considered geographical indication and determine if the impugned use genuinely misleads consumers regarding origin.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as are prescribed, provided that the applicant shall demonstrate exclusive link between the goods and the territory of origin. The Registrar shall consider whether the name applied for is already considered geographical indication under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Further, the application must clearly define the quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods attributable to the specific geographical location. Any alteration to the form petition particulars after its initial presentation requires prior written consent from the Registrar and shall be subject to a prescribed fee. The applicant is obliged to provide documentary evidence substantiating the claim regarding origin and distinctiveness.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any submissions made by the appellant and, where a legal representative has been appointed on behalf of a minor or individual lacking capacity, shall also take into account their interests as presented through that representative. Failure to comply with an injunction issued pursuant to section 58, restraining use of a considered geographical indication without authorisation, shall attract penalties not exceeding five thousand rupees for each day the infringement continues. Further, any party found guilty of knowingly making false statements in support of an application for registration or in opposition thereto, as provided herein, is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine.

For the purposes of this Act, "attributable geographical origin" in relation to a good signifies that the quality, reputation or characteristics of the good are essentially attributable to its geographical location, and such location includes defined areas within territorial limits. This attribution shall consider factors including, but not limited to, traditional production methods, unique environmental conditions, and established agricultural practices prevalent in the specified region. A good may be considered to have an attributable geographical origin even if all stages of production or processing do not occur exclusively within that area, provided that a substantial part of its essential qualities are derived from the defined location as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may include particulars relating to the agricultural area, specified quality or other characteristic attributable geographical to the goods. Such an area shall be defined with precision and clarity, delineating its boundaries in terms readily ascertainable by reference to established physical features or administrative divisions. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further details concerning the production techniques employed within the identified geographical region, demonstrating a direct link between those methods and the unique qualities of the goods. Provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive use of the indication by authorized producers, as verified through supporting documentation, registration shall be granted subject to such conditions as the Registrar deems appropriate under this Act.
