The proprietor of a geographical indication, upon establishing infringement under this Act, shall be entitled to seek remedies including an injunction restraining the use of any sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication. Such remedy may extend to preventing the application of the infringing sign to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the geographical indication is registered. Further, where the infringement involves the false suggestion that goods originate from a place attributable geographical to the registered geographical indication, the proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages equivalent to the loss suffered by them as a direct result of such misrepresentation. The remedies available are without prejudice to any other rights or remedies which may be available under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are attributable geographical to the goods and which originate from the asserted geographical origin. The Registrar shall consider such statement in determining whether the applicant has established, to a reasonable degree of certainty, that the alleged connection between the goods and the geographical origin is inherent and not solely due to temporary factors. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the genuineness of the claimed geographical origin, the applicant shall be required to furnish documentary evidence substantiating the claim. The Registrar may, after affording the objector an opportunity of being heard, dismiss the application if satisfied that the asserted connection lacks a demonstrable basis. Any interested party may appeal against such a decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration as a collective bargain of goods indicating its attributable geographical origin shall include detailed particulars regarding the quality and characteristics of such goods, demonstrating their unique connection to the specified territory. The applicant must provide verifiable evidence establishing the historical production and reputation of the goods within that area, supported by documentation from at least twenty producers actively engaged in the cultivation or manufacture for a period exceeding five years prior to the application date. Further, the description shall explicitly delineate the boundaries of the attributable geographical area, conforming to established administrative divisions or recognized local customs. Any alteration to production methods which materially deviates from traditional practices may render the registration liable for review under this Act.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses a registered geographical indication, or any mark which is identical or confusingly similar thereto, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits suffered by the registered proprietor, as well as an amount not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees for each instance of infringement proven. Where the infringing use relates to goods attributable geographical origin different from that specified in the registration, the penalty may be increased up to double the aforementioned sum. Furthermore, any goods bearing the infringing mark are subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offender, as provided herein. The Central Government may institute civil proceedings for enforcement of these rights.

The owner of a registration for a geographical indication may, subject to the conditions specified herein, grant licences conferring rights to use the said indication in relation to goods belonging to the class for which the geographical indication is registered. Such licences shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to territory, duration, and quality control measures that must be adhered to by the licensee. Any assignment of a registration or a licence relating thereto shall require prior approval from the Registrar, who may impose conditions deemed necessary to protect the integrity of the geographical indication and ensure continued adherence to production standards as defined under this Act. The concept of an attributable geographical link shall remain paramount; any use that falsely suggests such a connection, even by a licensed user, is prohibited. Further, sub-licensing is permissible only with written consent from the owner of registration.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act concerning the registration of a proposed geographical indication, direct the applicant to provide further documentation substantiating the link between the goods and the territory sought to be protected. Such direction shall not preclude the original objector from subsequently raising arguments pertaining to the distinctiveness of the proposed indication or its potential impact on existing trade marks. Where an objection is based upon a claim that the geographical indication is not attributable geographically to the specified area, the applicant shall bear the onus of proving, through verifiable historical records and demonstrable production practices, that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from within the defined territory. Any appeal against such a determination by the Registrar shall be made before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include a proposed denomination, which shall not contain any word or words descriptive of the goods or product with which the geographical indication is associated, nor shall it incorporate any trademark registered under this Act or any other law. The Registry shall, prior to accepting an application, undertake a search to ascertain whether the proposed denomination constitutes an assignment denomination already in use for similar goods and services; if such usage is established, the applicant shall be directed to propose an alternative designation. Where the geographical indication sought to be registered relates to agricultural products or foodstuffs originating from a specific area, the Registry shall consider whether the characteristics of the product are attributable geographically, meaning they are essentially due to the unique environmental factors and traditional practices prevalent within that defined region.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses a registered geographical indication for goods which do not originate from the attributable geographical area specified in the registration certificate shall be liable for penalties. Such use includes, but is not limited to, affixing the indicator to labels, packaging, advertising materials, or offering such goods for sale as if they were products of the indicated locality. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint and after due inquiry, issue an order restraining such infringing activity and imposing fines commensurate with the scale of the violation. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment under this Act. Further, any profits derived from the deceptive use of a geographical indication are subject to confiscation as provided herein.

The owner of an attributable geographical indication relating to plant material, including but not limited to seeds, seedlings, and propagating material, may grant a license for the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted use, duration, and any royalty payments due to the proprietor. The Registrar General Plant may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating substantial investment in production adhering to the geographical indication’s code of conduct, facilitate negotiations for a non-exclusive license from the proprietor. Assignment of rights pertaining to an attributable geographical indication shall require prior approval of the Registrar General Plant and be subject to conditions ensuring continued adherence to established quality standards; failure to comply may render the assignment voidable. Any sub-licensing is permitted only with explicit written consent from the original proprietor, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "attributable geographical area" means a defined and limited geographic region on the territory of India from which goods originate, where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to its origin. This determination shall consider factors including natural conditions, traditional practices, and local expertise employed in production. Where such characteristics are widely advertised and accepted by consumers as indicative of origin, this advertised acceptance relates directly to the establishment of an attributable geographical area. Goods claiming protection under this Act must demonstrably derive these qualities from within the specified boundaries as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to include not only the representation of the mark itself, but also any associated colours, sounds, or other sensory elements as specified within the application. The Registrar may refuse registration if it appears that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association, subject to evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use. An applicant shall provide a clear statement of all goods and services for which registration is sought, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The process of application registration is considered complete upon issuance of the Registration Certificate.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file a statement of use after five years from the date of registration, provided that this requirement does not apply where the Registrar has granted a disclaimer under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the trade mark to conform with prescribed standards for clarity and distinctiveness. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or refusal of an application registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Further, where multiple applications are filed for identical marks in respect of similar goods, the Registrar shall prioritize the first filing date as per established practice.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed invalid if it contains any matter which, under this Act, is considered disclaimable. The Registrar may, at any time prior to registration, direct an applicant to amend their application to remove such objectionable matter, provided that the amendment does not substantially alter the identity of the goods or services for which the mark is sought. Further, where a trademark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trademark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the Registrar shall require the applicant to demonstrate clear and distinctiveness sufficient to avoid likelihood of confusion among consumers. Failure to comply with such direction within the prescribed period will result in rejection of the application registration.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to prosecute it diligently, as determined by the Controller, and within six months from the date on which any objection is raised under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal to the Appellate Board; provided that such appeal must be filed within sixty days of the order of refusal and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant for trademark registration to provide further documentation substantiating ownership or use, and non-compliance will result in penalties as provided herein. Misrepresentation during the application registration process is a cognizable offence subject to fines and imprisonment.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall be deemed to hold an irrevocable, non-exclusive license to use the mark for internal testing and demonstration purposes only, pending final determination of their application registration. This license is automatically terminated upon rejection of the application or withdrawal thereof by the applicant. Further, any subsequent assignment or licensing agreement entered into by the applicant concerning the proposed trade mark shall be subject to prior written notification to the Registrar, detailing the scope and beneficiaries of such transfer. The Registrar may require additional documentation substantiating the legitimacy of any such assignment. Provided that, where a license is granted under this provision, it does not confer upon the licensee any right to challenge the validity of the application or initiate proceedings against third parties infringing upon marks similar to the applied-for mark.

A geographical indication registered under this Act signifies that the collective characteristics, quality, and reputation of goods originate from a specific geographic area, being an agricultural product, natural product, manufactured product, or processed product. Such registration shall confer upon authorized users the exclusive right to use the registered geographical indication as a certification mark indicating conformity to defined standards. The Registrar may, at any time, require the registered proprietor to furnish evidence demonstrating continued adherence to those standards; failure to do so may result in cancellation of the registration. Goods not originating from the specified geographic area shall be prohibited from being designated with the registered geographical indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society, individual producer, or collective body engaged in production and processing of goods. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the geographical indication as are prescribed, including details regarding the history of its use, the quality and characteristics of the goods attributable to its origin, and the names of producers authorized to use the indicator. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant, provided that any deficiency in the particulars shall be communicated within two months of receipt. A geographical indication registered under this Act confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive right to prevent use of identical or deceptively similar indications with respect to the goods for which it is registered.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice stating that the proposed registered geographical indication relates to goods and specifying the class of goods. Objections to the registration, if any, must be received by the Registrar within three months from the date of publication. The Registrar shall give every objector an opportunity of being heard under this Act. If no objections are filed or all objections are dismissed, the Registrar may proceed with the examination of the application. A geographical indication registered under this Act shall be deemed to be a registrable intellectual property right for the purposes of enforcement against unfair competition and passing off. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall have the exclusive right to use the said indication in relation to goods as provided herein.

A registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall ensure that all goods sold under that registration conform to the quality and characteristics standards as defined in the product specification document filed during application. Any alteration to said product specification requires prior approval from the Geographical Indications Registry, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally deviate from the established production methods or origin linked to the registered name. Further, use of a geographical indication registered under this Act by any person other than an authorized user shall be deemed unfair competition and subject to penalties as prescribed herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaints regarding non-compliance with quality standards, initiate inquiries and impose sanctions including suspension of registration if violations are substantiated.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which that indication is registered, or any identical or confusingly similar goods, shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. The amount of such damages shall be determined taking into account the extent of the infringement and the profits made as a result thereof. Further, under this Act, enforcement officers may seize and detain goods bearing an unauthorized use of a geographical indication registered in accordance with these provisions. Any seized goods may be destroyed at the expense of the infringing party, provided that prior notice is given to such party. The Register shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all actions taken regarding infringements of a registered geographical indication.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee, provided that any such license shall not extend to dealings in counterfeit goods. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication registered under this Act shall require prior approval from the Registrar, who may demand evidence demonstrating the assignee’s commitment to upholding the quality standards associated with the indicated product. Further, where a geographical indication is jointly owned by multiple producers, any licensing or assignment agreement must be executed by all joint proprietors or their duly authorized representatives. The Registrar may impose conditions on licenses and assignments to ensure continued adherence to the code of conduct applicable to the registered geographical indication.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the Appellate Board may, after giving all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, allow the appeal and direct that the application proceed for further consideration, provided that such direction specifies the grounds upon which the opposition was based. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board in relation to a registered geographical indication may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar shall not be liable for any loss or damage arising from any act done or omitted to be done in good faith under the authority of this Act, including decisions made concerning a geographical indication registered and subsequently challenged.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against an order refusing registration of a geographical indication registered, the Appellate Board may entertain such appeal if it is satisfied that the Registrar has not acted in accordance with the principles of natural justice or that there has been a material error of law apparent on the face of the record. The appellant, being a geographical indication plaintiff, shall be required to demonstrate before the Board that the refusal was demonstrably prejudiced by an incorrect interpretation of the criteria for distinctiveness as provided herein. Further, the Board may, subject to just cause shown, dismiss any appeal if it finds that the grounds raised are frivolous or vexatious and intended solely to delay proceedings concerning a geographical indication registered.

A registered geographical indication confers upon the proprietor thereof exclusive right to use the said indication in connection with goods for which it is registered, subject to any conditions specified under this Act. The effect registered trade may have on existing commercial arrangements shall be determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, considering principles of equity and fair dealing. No person other than an authorized user shall be entitled to make use of a geographical indication registered under this Act in respect of goods belonging to the class for which the registration is granted. Any such unauthorized use shall constitute infringement as provided herein.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license to use the mark, whether exclusively or otherwise, subject to conditions as provided herein, such license may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the registered proprietor, unless the license agreement expressly prohibits assignment; provided that any such assignment shall not operate to discharge the licensee from any obligations undertaken under the original licensing agreement. Further, where a dispute arises concerning the validity or scope of an injunction interlocutory restraining the use of a trade mark pursuant to a licensing arrangement, the court may consider the terms and conditions of the license in determining whether the restraint is reasonable and equitable. The registered proprietor shall be deemed to retain ownership of the trade mark notwithstanding any such assignment of a license.

For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to a cinematographic work shall mean the individual or corporate body which has arranged for the making of the film and bears ultimate responsibility for its production. The producer shall be deemed the owner of all copyrights therein, subject to any agreements made with authors, composers, lyricists, photographers, or other individuals contributing to the creation of the work. Provided that where a work is produced jointly by two or more producers, they shall be deemed joint owners of copyright and shall hold such rights as tenants in common. The term "producer" does not include those engaged solely for technical assistance under contract.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a ‘producer’ shall be deemed to be the individual or legal entity responsible for the creation and initial fixation of an audio-visual work. This determination shall include, but not be limited to, those directly involved in directing, filming, editing, and sound recording processes. An applicant claiming status as producer must submit with their application a sworn affidavit detailing their specific contribution to the production’s genesis and outlining the chain of rights ownership pertaining to the work. Provided that where multiple individuals or entities contribute significantly to the creation process, the Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claimant's designation as producer, ensuring clarity regarding copyright ownership and protection afforded under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in any work shall vest initially in the producer thereof. For the purposes of this clause, "producer" means the person responsible for bringing out the publication of a cinematographic film, and where such film is produced jointly by two or more persons, each of them shall be deemed to be a producer. Any infringement of the copyright vested under this Act in a producer shall render the infringer liable to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the producer as a consequence of such infringement. Further, remedies available for copyright infringement, including injunctions and delivery of infringing copies, may be sought against any person who directly or indirectly assists or abets such infringement, provided that the producer demonstrates reasonable diligence in pursuing such action. The right to claim damages shall not extend to instances where the alleged infringement occurred prior to notice being given to the producer.

For the purposes of this Act, "producer" with respect to cinematographic works shall mean the individual or corporate body responsible for the arrangement and coordination of all elements necessary for the creation of such work, including but not limited to securing rights in musical compositions, literary works, and performances incorporated therein. The producer shall be deemed the owner of copyright in the cinematograph film except where ownership has been explicitly assigned by contract as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the determination of a "producer" under this Act may be referred to the Controller for adjudication. Where a work is produced jointly by two or more individuals or corporate bodies, they shall be considered joint producers and shall hold copyright in proportion to their respective contributions, subject to any agreement to the contrary registered with the designated authority. The producer shall be liable to ensure compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act relating to obtaining necessary consents and clearances.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘producer’ shall be deemed to be the individual or corporate body responsible for the initial fixation of audio-visual works and their subsequent distribution, provided that such responsibility is evidenced by verifiable records maintained in accordance with prescribed guidelines. A producer shall not include an entity solely engaged in post-production activities unless they demonstrably participated in decisions concerning artistic control during the work's creation. Where a work is produced jointly by multiple entities, each contributing significantly to its conception and execution, all such entities may be considered producers under this Act, subject to their respective contributions being clearly documented. Any claim of producer status shall require submission of supporting documentation for verification as provided herein.

Where any work is produced in which the copyright subsists and such production involves the substantial contribution of an individual claiming to be the producer, that individual shall be deemed the first owner of all rights pertaining to the commercial exploitation of the said work. Provided that, where a dispute arises concerning the identity of the producer, the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings seeking declaratory relief as provided herein. Any person found to have infringed upon the exclusive rights of the producer without due authorization shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than five per cent of the profits earned by the infringer, or one hundred thousand rupees, whichever is greater. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and may result in criminal prosecution under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a sound recording is produced by an individual or entity acting as a producer, that producer shall be deemed the first owner of all copyright therein. Such ownership extends to the right to authorize or prohibit the reproduction, distribution, public performance, and communication to the public of the sound recording. The producer may, by written agreement, assign or license any or all of these rights to another party, specifying the duration and geographical scope of such assignment or license. Provided that any subsequent assignee or licensee shall be bound by the terms initially stipulated in the producer’s authorization. Further, a producer may grant a royalty-free non-exclusive license for limited educational purposes, as determined under this Act. This right remains with the producer notwithstanding any contractual arrangements made with artists involved in the production of the sound recording.

For the purposes of determining ownership under this Act, where an audio-visual work is produced through collaborative effort involving multiple individuals contributing distinct elements, including but not limited to scriptwriting, musical composition, and cinematography, the determination of who shall be deemed the producer shall be a matter for adjudication. It is provided that in cases where such contributions are demonstrably inseparable and essential to the final form of the work, a joint ownership arrangement may be declared by the relevant adjudicating authority. Any party asserting sole proprietorship as the producer may be required to demonstrate their dominant creative control over the production process; failing which, an appeal lies to the appellate forum established under this Act against such determination.

For the purposes of this Act, "distinctiveness" with reference to a proposed trade mark shall be determined having regard to its inherent character and, where applicable, the practices of the relevant industry. The Registrar shall, when considering whether a mark is distinctive, take into account factors including the sound, appearance, meaning and overall impression conveyed by the mark. Further, the Registrar may consider evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use in commerce or promotion, provided that such evidence satisfies the requirements as provided herein for establishing reputation. Any decision of the Registrar regarding distinctiveness shall be subject to appeal under this Act.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. If the Registrar considers that the proposed trade mark is confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark or a pending application, he may direct the applicant to amend the application to avoid such conflict, provided that the amendment does not substantially alter the identity of the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar shall also consider whether the mark comprises solely geographical indications as defined under this Act and if so, refuse registration unless it is deemed deceptively misdescriptive. Further, the registrar may require submission of additional documentation to verify ownership claims.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity for presenting their response and evidence in support thereof. The Registrar shall consider such response and any counter-evidence filed by the objector, and may direct the publication of the trade mark for opposition purposes if satisfied that the objection merits further consideration. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application, or the direction for publication, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall have the power to remand the matter to the Registrar for fresh determination, subject to just terms and conditions as it deems fit. Further, the remedies available under this Act regarding passing off actions remain unaffected by any decision made herein.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others and whether it conflicts with any existing rights under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the nature of the goods or services in relation to which registration is sought, provided that such request is made within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of receipt of the application. If the Registrar finds that the proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark registered under this Act, or if it contains any matter which is likely to be deemed offensive, he shall issue a notice of objection to the applicant, specifying the grounds for such objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to file a reply addressing the objections raised by the Registrar. Following consideration of the applicant’s response, the Registrar shall proceed with further examination as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is received by the Registrar, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is distinctive in its class and conforms to all requirements as provided herein. If the Registrar finds that the proposed trademark conflicts with an earlier registered trademark or pending application under this Act, or if the applicant has failed to comply with prescribed forms and fees, the Registrar may issue a notice of examination report detailing the grounds for objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to respond to such objections within the time stipulated in the notice. Following consideration of the response, the Registrar shall determine whether the application meets the criteria for acceptance or rejection, subject to any appeal process as detailed elsewhere under this Act.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall serve notice thereof on the applicant and may require the applicant to submit within two months written representations addressing the grounds for objection. Failure by the applicant to respond as directed will be deemed abandonment of the application and the Registrar shall proceed to refuse registration without further notice. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration based upon such an objection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and penalties for late filing. The Registrar is empowered to impose a monetary penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees on any applicant found to have wilfully misrepresented facts in their application.

The registered proprietor of a trademark shall be permitted to grant licenses for the use of their trademark, both exclusive and non-exclusive, subject to conditions specified in writing and filed with the Registrar. Any such license agreement may include provisions relating to quality control measures that the licensee must adhere to, ensuring consistency with the reputation associated with the mark. Furthermore, a registered proprietor may assign their trademark rights, including any pending applications or granted licenses, to another party through a written instrument executed as per prescribed procedures and duly notified to the Registrar. The registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses affecting trademarks registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection upon request. Provided that such notifications are made within the stipulated timeframe, the assignment or license shall be deemed valid against third parties.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall provide written notice thereof to the applicant, detailing the grounds for such objection and affording the applicant an opportunity to file a reply within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice. The applicant’s reply, or lack thereof, shall be considered by the Registrar in determining whether to proceed with registration. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within three months of such decision; provided that the Appellant shall deposit before the Board a sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the prescribed fee for appeals. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the relevant provisions of the law relating to civil procedure.

For the purposes of this Act, "distinctiveness" with regard to a proposed trade mark shall be determined by considering its inherent capacity to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others, and where a trade mark is deemed descriptive under this Act, it may still acquire distinctiveness through acquired reputation. The Registrar shall, upon receiving evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness, conduct an inquiry as provided herein. Should the Registrar find insufficient grounds for registration based on inherent distinctiveness, but observes potential acquired distinctiveness, the plaintiff forthwith has the right to submit further documentation and arguments.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark, the applicant shall have the right to file a reply within the time specified by the Registrar. Should the Registrar consider the reply unsatisfactory or fail to adequately address all grounds of opposition, he may direct the applicant to amend the application or withdraw it entirely. Further, if an appeal is preferred against a decision declining registration, and the appellate authority remands the matter for reconsideration, the registrar shall afford the appellant another opportunity to submit evidence. Registration ought effected expeditiously where no substantial opposition exists; however, delays attributable to procedural irregularities by the applicant will not be grounds for automatic approval. The Registrar may, at any time, require further particulars or clarification from any party involved in proceedings before him.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a trademark, the Registrar shall examine whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. The examination shall include verification that the proposed mark does not conflict with existing registered trademarks or pending applications, considering phonetic and visual similarities as provided herein. Should any query arise regarding the clarity or accuracy of information furnished in the application, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation for clarification. In instances where an international trademark registration designates India under the Budapest Treaty, the Registrar shall consider such designation during this examination process. The Registrar is empowered to reject the application if it finds that the mark lacks distinctiveness or contravenes any provision of this Act. Any rejection order shall clearly state the reasons for refusal and provide the applicant with a right of appeal.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, and the applicant elects to pursue adjudication before the Registrar, the Registrar shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard. Any condition declared unlawful by the Registrar during such hearing, relating to use of the mark, permissible geographical areas, or goods/services covered, will render the application liable for immediate rejection. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Registrar concerning amendment of the application or submission of further documentation shall result in a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may also lead to the application being deemed abandoned. Repeated non-compliance as provided herein constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months.

For the purposes of this Act, “local jurisdiction” shall mean the territorial limits within which a district court exercises original civil and criminal jurisdiction. An application for rectification under this Act may be presented to a district court situated within the local jurisdiction where the patentee has their principal place of business or where the alleged infringer resides or carries on business. Subject to any appeal as provided herein, the decision of such district court shall be final and binding. The term “patentee” includes any person to whom a patent has been granted or assigned under this Act, or who is the nominee of the true inventor.

The Register of Designs shall maintain a record of all registered designs, including particulars relating to the proprietor, inventor, and any modifications made subsequent to initial registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of a design application may appeal to the appropriate district court within thirty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Register shall furnish certified copies of entries in the register upon payment of prescribed fees, subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets and confidential information disclosed during examination. Further, any alteration to the registered proprietor’s address must be notified to the office, and failure to do so may render subsequent communications invalid, as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act, including but not limited to orders relating to revocation, opposition, or infringement proceedings, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal from the said order to the district court. The appeal shall be filed within ninety days of the date of communication of the order to the appellant, subject to a provision for extension of time not exceeding thirty days where the appellant can demonstrate reasonable cause for delay. Upon hearing the parties and considering the record of proceedings before the relevant authority, the district court may confirm, reverse, or modify the original order. The decision of the district court shall be final, provided that an appeal lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. Costs incidental to the appeal shall be determined by the district court in its discretion.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person aggrieved by an order passed by a patent office relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent, or otherwise concerning matters which may be determined by the patent office, may appeal to the district court. The district court shall have the same powers as it would possess in relation to original suits brought before it under this Act and may entertain appeals from any order made by the Controller. An appeal lies within ninety days of the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. Provided that the district court may, if satisfied that there were sufficient grounds for delay, admit an appeal after the expiry of the said period. The decision of the district court shall be final, subject to further appeals as provided under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent may appeal to the district court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. Provided that such appeal shall only be admissible if the appellant has paid all fees prescribed in Schedule I and has complied with the requirements regarding service of notice on the respondent. The district court shall hear appeals expeditiously and may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both parties, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Further, the decision of the district court shall be final subject to appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Where any person contravenes the provisions of this Act, or fails to comply with any order made under it, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to institute proceedings for damages and injunction in a district court having jurisdiction over the matter. Such proceedings may include claims for recovery of profits derived from the infringing activity, subject to proof of reasonable royalties as determined by the court. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint regarding infringement, issue interim orders restraining further acts of infringement pending final adjudication under this Act. Failure to comply with an interim order shall be deemed contempt of the district court and punishable accordingly. Costs associated with such litigation shall be at the discretion of the court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the assignor of a patent shall be deemed to retain the right to grant non-exclusive licenses pertaining to the invention claimed therein until such time as written notification of the assignment has been registered with the office. Any subsequent assignee may, by instrument in writing duly executed and registered, further license or assign the patent rights subject to any conditions specified within that instrument. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of a license granted prior to registration of an assignment, the determination thereof shall be made by the appropriate district court, considering evidence presented regarding the assignor’s intent at the time of execution of the original agreement. The Controller may require proof of due diligence in any such licensing arrangement and may impose penalties for failure to comply with these provisions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, appeals arising from orders passed by the Controller relating to revocation of patents shall lie directly to the district court within whose territorial jurisdiction the patent was granted. Provided that where such an order relates to inventions falling under the category of pharmaceuticals or agricultural chemicals, the appeal may be filed before a High Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify alternative forums for appeals as it deems fit, provided that such specification shall not preclude recourse to judicial remedy. Any party aggrieved by an order of the district court may further appeal under the general principles of appellate law.

The Register of Plant Varieties shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all registered crop sciences innovations pertaining to genetically modified seeds and plant protection products. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the registration, rejection, or revocation of such varieties may appeal to the appropriate district court within whose jurisdiction the relevant field station or research facility is situated. The appellate authority in the district court shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and any objector, subject to procedural guidelines as provided herein. Further, the Register shall publish notices regarding pending applications and hearings concerning registration disputes, ensuring transparency under this Act. Such publications are deemed sufficient notification, provided that reasonable efforts are made to inform affected parties directly.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the district court under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a design registered under the Designs Act, may appeal from such order to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the district court originally exercised its authority. Such appeals shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate High Court may, after hearing all parties involved and considering the evidence presented, confirm, reverse, or modify the decision of the district court, as it deems just and equitable. Costs in such appeal shall be determined by the High Court. Further, any party dissatisfied with the judgment of the High Court may petition to the Supreme Court of India on a point of law, subject to the provisions regarding special leave petitions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, all applications for rectification of entries relating to registered patents shall be filed with the civil court registrar having jurisdiction over the district where the patentee’s principal place of business is situated. Where no such principal place of business exists within India, the application may be presented before the civil court registrar of a district specified by notification in the Official Gazette. The Registrar General may, after due notice to all interested parties, direct that any rectification proceedings be transferred from one civil court registrar to another for administrative convenience. Any order made under this provision shall be final and binding. Appeals against orders passed by the civil court registrar concerning rectification applications are cognizable only by a district court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction.

Where, upon receiving notification under this Act concerning the existence of sufficient grounds for revocation of a patent, the Controller determines that such determination warrants judicial review, he shall forward all relevant records and pleadings pertaining to the matter to the appropriate district court. The district court shall then proceed according to established civil procedure rules. An applicant patent person aggrieved by any order or decision made by the district court under this process may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of such order or decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to appellate jurisdictional requirements as provided herein. Further, the Controller may require submission of additional documentation if deemed necessary for proper adjudication by the district court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registration trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that trade mark. Such licenses shall clearly define the geographical area and the goods or services in respect of which the licensee is authorized to employ the registered trade mark. The license agreement may stipulate conditions restricting the quality control measures undertaken by the licensee, ensuring adherence to standards maintained by the proprietor. Further, a proprietor may assign the entire registration trade mark, or any part thereof, along with all associated rights and privileges, to another party through a written instrument duly executed. Any assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks as provided herein, and shall take effect from the date of such recording.

Subject to any direction from the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an appeal shall lie to the High Court within ninety days from the date of passing of the order sought to be appealed against under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion arising from the use of a similar mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, direct the cancellation of a registration trade mark. Provided that such direction shall only be issued after affording the registered proprietor an opportunity for hearing and submission of written arguments. Any party aggrieved by any order made under this Act may appeal against it as provided herein, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. The High Court may allow such appeals if satisfied there is error apparent on the face of the record.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the rectification of the register of trademarks, or refusing registration of a trademark, or revoking a registration, or otherwise concerning the validity of a registration trade mark, has no adequate remedy at law, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall have power to entertain and determine such appeals from its own order, and may grant any relief which it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to directing the Registrar to register or refuse registration of a trademark, or to amend the register accordingly. Provided that an appeal under this Act does not operate as a stay of the operation of the order appealed against unless the Board directs otherwise. Further, where a certification trade mark is involved in such proceedings, the interests of consumers shall be given due consideration by the Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registration trade may grant licenses for the use of their registered trademark, specifying the territory, duration, and scope of such license. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, by the proprietor, provided that notice of assignment is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days of the transfer. Where a patent consequence arises from the unauthorized use of a licensed trade mark, the licensee shall have standing to pursue remedies against infringers, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in their license agreement. Further, any subsequent registration trade granted by the proprietor relating to the same goods or services as those covered by an existing license shall not prejudice the rights of the original licensee unless expressly agreed upon in writing. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the continued validity of such licenses during periodic reviews under this Act.

An act constituting a commission offence under this Act occurs when any person, without authorization or lawful excuse, reproduces, distributes, exhibits, performs, or translates any work protected by copyright, knowing or having reason to believe that such action infringes the rights of the owner. Such knowledge shall be presumed where the infringing activity is conducted on a commercial scale or involves the use of specialized equipment designed for reproduction or distribution. The burden of proving lawful excuse rests upon the accused. Where an offence is committed in circumstances involving multiple actors, each person contributing to the infringement may be held accountable as per provisions herein relating to joint liability.

Where any work is knowingly registered under a false name or with fraudulent intent, such act constitutes a commission offence triable by a court of law. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information regarding the falsity of particulars furnished during registration, initiate inquiries and issue notices to the registrant concerned, affording them an opportunity for clarification. If, following such inquiry, it is determined that the registration was obtained through misrepresentation or suppression of material facts relating to ownership or authorship, the work shall be deemed unregistered ab initio. Any person involved in facilitating a fraudulent registration, including agents or intermediaries, shall also be considered guilty of a commission offence and subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any person, acting on behalf of another, infringes any copyright under this Act, or abets or induces such infringement, or participates in it, such person shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence. The High Court may, upon conviction, impose a fine not exceeding ten lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years. Any individual found guilty of a commission offence relating to the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of cinematograph films shall also be liable to pay compensation equivalent to fifty percent of the profits earned by the infringing party, as determined by the Court. Provided that if the infringement was committed due to negligence, the court may reduce both the fine and imprisonment term proportionally. Subject to appeal to a higher appellate forum, any order made under this provision shall be final.

Where any person residing outside India commits an act infringing copyright under this Act, or abets such an infringement, or participates in such contravention, he shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence within the meaning of this Act. Such offences may be investigated by officers authorized by the Central Government, and they shall possess all powers as are vested in police officers under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate such officers for the purposes of investigation. Provided that any evidence obtained during such investigation shall be admissible in accordance with the provisions relating to admissibility of electronic records under the Information Technology Act, 2000. Upon conclusion of the investigation, the officer shall submit a report to the nearest competent court as provided herein. The Court may issue warrants and summons as necessary for further proceedings.

Where any act or omission constituting an offence under this Act is committed by a person acting on behalf of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence if it is shown that the former was directed or abetted by him. Subject to the provisions herein, where an infringement of copyright occurs due to the actions of an employee in the course of their employment, the employer may also be held liable as a commission offence, provided that the infringing activity was undertaken with the knowledge and consent, express or implied, of the employer. Further, if it is established that the act was performed for the benefit of the directing person, they shall remain accountable notwithstanding any claim of ignorance regarding the specifics of the infringement.

Where any person, acting on behalf of or in connection with a commercial establishment engaged in the reproduction, distribution, or public display of copyrighted works, wilfully contravenes any provision under this Act, or abets such contravention, it shall constitute a commission offence. The court may, upon conviction, impose a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Where the offence is committed by a partnership firm, every partner shall be deemed guilty of the offence and liable to punishment. Further, any officer or employee directly involved in the commission of such an offence within the establishment shall also be subject to prosecution and penalties as provided herein.

Where a copyright owner desires to grant a license enabling the reproduction or distribution of works incorporated within an audiovisual recording, such license may be assigned to another party subject to conditions stipulated therein. The assignor retains the right to specify permitted uses, geographical limitations, and duration of the assignment. Any subsequent transfer of this assignment shall require written consent from the original copyright owner unless explicitly waived in the initial agreement. Failure to adhere to these stipulations constitutes a commission offence, punishable as provided herein. This provision applies equally where such reproduction or distribution is undertaken for commercial gain without proper authorization. The right to enforce these conditions remains with the copyright owner and any subsequent assignee acting within the scope of their granted license.

Where an act constituting an infringement of copyright is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence. This determination shall not preclude prosecution of the initial actor, who remains liable for their individual participation in the infringing activity. Any aggrieved party may appeal against a finding that a commission offence has occurred, presenting evidence demonstrating lack of direction or control; provided that the appellate authority shall consider whether the alleged directing person possessed the means and opportunity to influence the actions leading to copyright infringement. The burden of proving absence of such direction or control rests upon the appellant.

Where an act constituting a copyright infringement is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence. The Court may require any individual suspected of involvement in facilitating or abetting such infringement to submit documentation pertaining to their association with the infringing party, including records relating to trade mark applications filed on behalf of that party. Such submissions are subject to verification by the Registrar and may be scrutinized during proceedings. Any person failing to comply with a direction issued under this Act shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Court. The prosecution of an individual found guilty of a commission offence may proceed irrespective of whether the principal offender has been identified or prosecuted, provided that sufficient evidence exists establishing the directing or controlling influence.

For the purposes of determining deceptively similarity under this Act, marks shall be deemed deceptively similar if they are so nearly alike as to likely cause confusion in the minds of the public. This assessment shall consider not only the visual appearance of the trade marks but also their phonetic similarities and overall impression of identity. A mark shall also be considered deceptively similar where it incorporates a dominant element of another mark, even if other elements differ substantially. The Registrar may take into account the nature of the goods or services for which the marks are used in ascertaining whether such likelihood exists, provided that the relevant public is taken to include purchasers and potential customers.

The Registrar may refuse the registration of a proposed trade mark if he considers that it is deceptively similar to an earlier mark registered under this Act, even if the marks differ in some aspects. Such determination shall take into account not only the visual appearance of the respective signs but also their phonetic similarities and the ideas they evoke amongst the relevant consumer class. The Registrar may further refuse registration where the proposed trade mark includes a representation of the national flag or any emblem denoting governmental approval, subject to provisions regarding permissible use for describing goods or services. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within such time as provided herein.

Where any person considers that another person has infringed his right in a registered trademark, he may institute suit in the competent civil court for relief as provided herein. Such infringement shall be deemed to occur where the use by another person of any mark or sign is deceptively similar to the registered trade mark and causes, or is likely to cause, confusion among the public relating to the goods or services for which the trademark is registered. The Court may grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark, damages calculated on the basis of lost profits attributable to the infringement, and the delivery up or destruction of any goods bearing the infringing mark. Provided that a finding of deceptively similar marks shall not be invalidated by proof that the defendant’s trade has been carried on for a substantial period prior to registration.

Where an objection is taken against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior registered trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the applicant for registration and to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. The proprietor of the earlier trade mark may, within such time as prescribed under this Act, file with the Registry an affidavit verifying the existence of circumstances indicating that use of the impugned mark is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public or to damage the reputation of the prior registered trade mark. Such affidavit shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the claim of deceptive similarity and demonstrating actual or potential dilution of distinctiveness. The Registry may, after affording both parties an opportunity for hearing, determine whether the marks are indeed deceptively similar as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark proceeds upon a disclaimer of respect to any identical or similar mark already on the register, such disclaimer shall be deemed to be irrevocable and shall operate as a relinquishment of all rights pertaining to the disclaimed portion of the proposed trade mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish a reasoned explanation detailing the scope and limitations of the disclaimer, affirming that it does not prejudice existing proprietors’ entitlements under this Act. Furthermore, if any subsequent registered trade mark is found to be deceptively similar to a mark previously disclaimed in an application, the proprietor of the later registration shall be obligated to demonstrate clear distinction in use or inherent distinctiveness sufficient to avoid infringement claims.

Where any person, knowing that another has a registered trade mark, uses an identical or deceptively similar mark relating to goods or services identical or closely resembling those for which the registration is made, and such use is likely to cause confusion or deception among the public, such person shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, issue a notice requiring the offending party to show cause why they should not be restrained from further infringing use. Failure to comply with such notice, or subsequent refusal to cease the infringing activity, renders the offender liable to a penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees.

Where the owner of a registered trademark grants a license permitting the use of that trademark upon another party, such license may include provisions for the assignment of certain rights relating to associated trademarks. The licensee shall be entitled to assign these specified rights, including but not limited to those pertaining to colorable or deceptively similar marks used in connection with the licensed goods or services, subject to the prior consent of the licensor. Such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, provided that the proposed assignee meets criteria established by the licensor regarding financial stability and reputation. Any assignment made without such consent may be deemed a breach of the licensing agreement and render the licensee liable for damages as provided herein. The licensor retains the right to audit the records pertaining to any sub-licensing or further assignments undertaken by the original licensee.

Where an objection is raised alleging that a proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, the Registrar shall consider all relevant factors including the similarity of the marks, the identity or relatedness of the goods or services, and the likelyhood of confusion on the part of the public or damage to the proprietor of the earlier mark. The Appellate Board may, upon appeal, substitute its own assessment for that of the Registrar regarding whether the similarities between the trade marks warrant a finding of deceptive similarity, provided that such substitution is based on demonstrable errors in law or fact. Further, evidence presented by either party shall be weighed fairly and impartially, subject to admissibility under established principles of jurisprudence.

Where an appeal is filed before the Appellate Board alleging that a registration of a trademark constitutes deceptive similarity to any prior mark, the Board shall consider whether, having regard to the visual appearance, sound and phonetic similarities, as well as the ideas conveyed by both marks, consumers are likely to perceive a likelihood of association between them. The Board may require the appellant to demonstrate, through consumer surveys or other relevant evidence, that such deceptive similarity exists and is likely to cause confusion amongst the purchasing public. Provided that the prior mark was used in commerce before the date of application for registration of the allegedly deceptively similar mark, this assessment shall be conducted with due consideration given to the distinctiveness of both marks under this Act.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark desires to permit another party to utilize a visual recording embodying that trade mark for commercial purposes, such permission shall be granted through a license agreement executed in writing. This license may specify the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to geographical limitations and duration. The licensee shall be deemed to have knowledge of all prior assignments or licenses relating to the registered trade mark. Any assignment of this license must include an express acknowledgement of the original proprietor’s continuing rights under this Act. Further, a license granted hereunder does not constitute consent for use if such use is deceptively similar to any existing registered trade marks, as provided herein; and the licensee shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with all applicable provisions regarding distinctiveness and consumer confusion.

A trademark shall be considered deceptively similar to another if, in the course and circumstances of use, it is likely to create confusion or cause mistake among the public as to the identity of the origin of the goods or services. This assessment shall take into account the visual appearance, phonetic composition, ideational content, and overall impression of the marks involved. Where an application for registration includes a manner of application clause specifying particular goods or services, the comparison for deceptiveness shall be limited to those specified categories only. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates a substantial reputation in respect of goods or services not explicitly covered by the manner applications clause, the assessment may extend to consider potential dilution effects on such reputation.

A trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any individual, entity, or organization utilizes a sign, whether consisting exclusively of words, logos, numerals, figurative elements, or a combination thereof, that is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark. This infringement occurs when the use takes place in connection with goods or services for which the registration subsists and creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of those goods or services. Provided that such use does not constitute fair dealing under this Act, it shall be considered an act of trade mark infringed. The Registrar may issue directions to prevent any activity deemed likely to cause dilution of distinctiveness associated with a registered trade mark, subject to due process and opportunity for representation.

Where any person shall have infringed a trade mark, an action for damages may be brought in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The plaint filed under this Act shall specify the particulars of the trade mark infringed, including its registration number and date of registration, and state the manner in which such infringement has been committed. Evidence demonstrating the similarity between the infringing mark and the registered trade mark shall be presented before the Court. Provided that, where the defendant proves that use of the impugned mark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services, the claim for damages may be reduced accordingly. The remedies available to the proprietor of the infringed trade mark include injunctions restraining further infringing activity and compensation for losses sustained as a direct result of the infringement.

A trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any individual, firm, or company employs a sign, including words, logos, symbols, or combinations thereof, in connection with goods or services. This infringement occurs if said sign is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, and the use takes place within the class of goods or services for which registration subsists. Provided that, such use must create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of those goods or services. Further, this shall not apply where the defendant demonstrates honest concurrent usage established prior to the date of application for the registered trade mark, subject to conditions as provided herein concerning territorial scope and consumer perception. The burden of proving a trade mark infringed rests upon the claimant.

Where any person infringes a registered trade mark, that person shall be liable to pay damages to the registered proprietor. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a result of the infringement and also to the profit made by the infringing party. Provided that, in cases where the infringement is found to have been willful or malicious, the Court may award punitive damages not exceeding five times the sum it finds to represent the loss referred to above. Further, any goods manufactured or offered for sale bearing the infringed trade mark shall be liable for seizure and destruction by order of the Court. The registered proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark; a trade mark infringed constitutes actionable harm.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to grant licences conferring specific rights relating to the use of their trade mark, subject to conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licences may include provisions for territory limitation and permitted goods or services. Where a licence is assigned by the licensee to a third party, such assignment shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor, provided that the assignee becomes bound by all terms and conditions of the initial licence. Any use of an identical or deceptively similar mark without authorization constitutes a trade mark infringed, and the proprietor may pursue remedies as provided herein. Further, sub-licensing is permissible only with explicit endorsement documented in writing by the primary proprietor, ensuring continued protection against unauthorized exploitation of the registered mark.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical composition” includes any mixture or combination of two or more active ingredients intended for use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of disease, or for improving human health. A “patented article,” when used in relation to a pharmaceutical composition, shall mean an article embodying such composition and which is the subject matter of a patent granted under this Act. The manufacture, sale, offer for sale, import, or distribution of a patented article shall be deemed infringement unless it is undertaken with the authorization of the patentee, as provided herein. Subject to any conditions specified in the patent grant, the scope of protection conferred by a patent extends only to the patented article itself.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “patented article” shall be deemed to include any component part thereof, where such component is inextricably linked to the functionality of the patented invention and identified within the registered claims. The Controller may require submission of detailed technical specifications outlining the composition and manufacturing process of said components prior to acceptance of registration. Provided that, if an application for registration relates to a patented article incorporating improvements not claimed in the original patent, such improvement shall be subject to separate examination regarding its novelty and inventive step under this Act. Any alteration or modification to a patented article which substantially changes its nature or intended use may necessitate fresh registration as a distinct product.

Where any infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to claim damages shall accrue from the date of such infringement. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint regarding the manufacture, use, sale, offer for sale, or importation of a patented article, direct an inquiry into the matter and assess compensation payable by the infringing party. Such compensation shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the patentee as a result of the infringement, taking into account any profits earned by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized use of the invention. Provided that, in cases where the infringement was knowing and willful, the Controller may award enhanced damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation initially assessed. Further, the patentee shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts, subject to just terms being determined by the Controller.

Where any question arises regarding whether an article constitutes a patented article, the Controller may, at his discretion, direct that such question be determined by a Board of three persons constituted under this Act. The Board shall hear evidence from all interested parties and make findings of fact relevant to the determination. Any party aggrieved by the finding of the Board may appeal against it to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days of communication of the order. Subject to the provisions herein, the Controller’s decision on an appeal shall be final. The power to grant or refuse relief relating to infringement of a patent concerning a patented article remains vested in the High Court. Provided that any application for determination under this provision must specify the grounds upon which it is based and include all relevant documentation pertaining to the invention.

Where any patented article is imported into India, such importation shall be permissible only if the importer possesses a valid certificate of import issued by the Controller, certifying compliance with prescribed quality standards as provided herein. The application for said certificate must specify the intended use of the patented article and declare adherence to all relevant labeling requirements mandated under this Act. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating that adequate measures have been implemented to prevent reverse engineering or unauthorized reproduction of the patented invention embodied within the imported article. Failure to satisfy these conditions may result in seizure of the goods at the port of entry and imposition of penalties as determined by the Controller, subject to appeal before an appellate authority.
