Any person importing, manufacturing, selling, distributing, or offering to sell any patented article shall be deemed guilty of an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the importation occurs without actual knowledge that the imported goods are a patented article, and such lack of knowledge was exercised with due diligence, the penalty for infringement shall be reduced by fifty percent at the discretion of the Court. Further, any entity found to have wilfully infringed upon a patent relating to a patented article may be subject to enhanced damages, not exceeding three times the actual damages sustained by the patentee, as determined by the presiding officer. The Central Government may, through its designated authority, issue cease and desist orders against those engaged in such infringing activities.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted rights under a license relating to a patented article shall be entitled to assign such license, either wholly or partially, to any person or entity with the prior written consent of the patentee. Such assignment shall not prejudice the validity of the underlying patent nor affect the obligations of the original licensee pertaining to royalties and reporting requirements as provided herein. The patentee may, under this Act, demand full disclosure of all sub-licenses granted by a primary licensee, including details regarding royalty rates and territorial scope. Failure to provide such information within thirty days shall be deemed a breach of contract and subject to remedies available under the general law. Any assignment made without the requisite consent is void. The patentee retains the right to terminate any license agreement if it determines that the assignee is not fulfilling the terms agreed upon.

Where any question arises regarding whether goods offered for sale, or imported, constitute a patented article, the Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, determine such question based on evidence presented by interested parties. It shall be presumed that goods so offered or imported are manufactured using a patented process unless the importer demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that an alternative, non-infringing method was employed in their production. The burden of proving non-infringement rests entirely with the importer; provided that such proof must include detailed technical specifications and verifiable documentation pertaining to the manufacturing process. Decisions made by the Controller under this provision are subject to judicial review on grounds of perversity or demonstrable error of law.

Where the proprietor of a patent desires to grant a license relating to a patented article, such license may be granted either wholly or partly for consideration and may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as the proprietor deems fit. Any notice applicant intending to assign rights in respect of a patent shall, prior to effecting such assignment, provide written notification to the Controller detailing the proposed assignee and the scope of the intended transfer. The Controller may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, require further information from the notice applicant concerning the terms of the prospective assignment. Further, where a license is granted for a patented article, the proprietor shall ensure that the licensee adheres to all conditions stipulated within the patent specification and any subsequent amendments thereto. Failure to do so may render the license voidable as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patented article, seeks recourse under this Act, such party shall be entitled to appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. The determination of whether an invention constitutes a "new invention" for the purposes of maintaining patentability shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny by the Tribunal, considering all evidence presented and arguments advanced by both the appellant and the respondent. Provided that, in cases where the alleged lack of novelty arises from prior publication occurring outside India, the burden of proving such publication lies upon the appellant. The Tribunal may, at its discretion, require expert testimony to ascertain the technical merit of the invention and assess its impact on existing technologies.

For the purposes of this Act, “patented article” shall mean any tangible product embodying a patented invention as specified in the granted patent document. Such article includes, but is not limited to, goods manufactured using a patented process and those incorporating elements derived from a patented composition of matter. The supply or importation of a patented article shall be deemed an infringement under this Act unless expressly permitted by the patentee or authorized by a binding government order issued in accordance with provisions relating to national security or public health as provided herein. Any modification to a patented article does not alter its status as a patented article, subject to considerations regarding novelty and inventive step.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “patented article” shall be deemed to include any product wholly or partly manufactured using a patented process, irrespective of whether such process is itself subject to a separate patent. The Controller General may, upon application by an interested party and after due consideration of the public interest, grant a compulsory licence in respect of a patented article where it is satisfied that adequate provision has not been made for the manufacture and availability of the said article to the public at reasonable prices, provided that such application demonstrates non-infringement of any prior rights. The applicant shall furnish details regarding production capacity and intended distribution network as part of the registration documentation.

An application for registration of a patented invention shall be deemed to include a declaration by the applicant specifying the claims defining the scope of protection sought; such declaration being binding upon the applicant and forming an integral part of the registered patent. Where it is found that any process or article falls within the scope of a claim in a granted patent, then such act constitutes infringement patent under this Act. The Controller may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for hearing, issue directions regarding the interpretation of claims where ambiguity arises during proceedings relating to validity or infringement. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where any person without leave of the Controller makes, uses, sells, or offers to sell, or imports for sale, any patented article, or attempts to do so, such acts shall constitute infringement patent. The patentee may restrain by injunction such infringing activity and also recover damages from the infringer; provided that in determining the amount of damages, due account shall be taken of the flagrancy of the infringement and any benefit accruing to the infringer as a result thereof. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller may award costs against a party found to have acted in bad faith in pursuing an action for or defending against infringement. Further, where an injunction is granted, the Controller shall specify a reasonable period within which the infringer may dispose of the infringing stock held by him.

Where any person makes, uses, offers to sell, or imports into India any patented article, or attempts so to do, without the authority of the patentee, such person shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent. Any interested party may institute proceedings for redressal of alleged infringement before the relevant High Court, subject to compliance with prescribed rules regarding notice and service of process upon the accused. The court may grant temporary or permanent injunctions restraining the infringing activity, as well as award damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee, taking into account the profits made by the infringer. Provided that a person shall not be deemed to have committed an act of infringement if such making, using, offering for sale, or importing is solely for the purpose of research and experimentation, provided that no commercial exploitation ensues from such activity.

Where any person without leave of the Controller makes, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports into India any product in relation to which patent protection has been granted and which incorporates the subject matter of the claims as originally filed, such actions shall constitute infringement patent. This determination shall be made irrespective of whether the process by which the product is manufactured was described in the patent specification. However, where the invention claimed in the patent relates solely to a method or process, any person may use the patented method for their own purposes provided that such use does not involve the manufacture, sale, or offer for sale of the product resulting from the application of the method. Subject to this exception, any commercial exploitation shall be deemed an infringement patent and actionable under this Act.

Any person who without leave of the Controller makes, uses, exercises, sells or offers to sell any patented invention, or attempts to do so, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent. Where such infringement involves the reproduction of literary, artistic or musical works incorporated within the patented process or product, the infringing party shall also be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than five per cent and not exceeding ten per cent of the aggregate sales of the infringing goods. Further, upon conviction for infringement, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both, subject to review by the High Court. The Controller may issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a patent desires to permit another person or entity to exercise rights pertaining to the invention claimed in the patent, such permission may be conveyed through a license agreement executed as provided herein. Such license shall specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacture, use, sale, and importation, and the geographical territory within which these actions are authorized. The proprietor retains full ownership of the patent unless explicitly transferred by assignment in writing, duly registered under this Act. Any unauthorized making, using, or selling of the patented invention without a valid license agreement or assignment constitutes infringement patent, entitling the proprietor to seek remedies as prescribed. Further, any licensee may assign their rights and obligations under the license subject to the prior consent of the original patentee, which shall not be unreasonably withheld.

Where any person proposes to take action against another alleging infringement patent, such person shall first serve upon the alleged infringer a notice specifying the nature of the alleged infringement and demanding that the infringing activity be discontinued. The alleged infringer may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of such notice, submit their written response contesting the allegations contained therein, supported by evidence demonstrating non-infringement or prior use as provided herein. Failure to respond within the stipulated period shall constitute an admission of the infringement patent. Any subsequent legal proceedings concerning the validity or scope of the patent may be raised only after a reasoned order has been passed by the relevant intellectual property tribunal following consideration of the response submitted, subject to appeal under established procedures.

Where an act appears to constitute infringement patent of a registered invention, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings for redressal as provided herein. The Controller General may, upon receiving credible information indicating substantial and persistent misrepresentation concerning the novelty or inventive step of an invention during the registration process, initiate inquiries into the validity of the registration. If such inquiries establish that the initial application contained material falsehoods rendering the grant improper, the registration shall cease to have effect from the date of publication of the Controller General’s order. Further, any subsequent attempts to obtain a similar patent based on the same invention will be deemed inadmissible under this Act, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing.

Where any person without leave of the Controller makes, uses, sells, or offers to sell, or imports for sale, any patented article, or attempts so to do, knowing it to be an infringement patent, such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence. This determination is subject to the proviso that use solely for purposes directly related to research and development, conducted without commercial exploitation, does not constitute infringement. Further provided that a party demonstrating prior use of the patented invention in India before the date of application for the patent may petition the Controller for equitable relief, but shall remain liable for any subsequent infringing activity. Any individual convicted under this provision may be subject to a punishable imprisonment term extending up to three years and a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.

An applicant seeking registration of an invention shall furnish with the application a complete specification detailing the subject matter claimed. The complete specification must include a clear and concise description of the invention sufficient to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use it, along with drawings where necessary for understanding the invention. Claims defining the scope of protection sought shall be annexed to the complete specification and presented in a manner that is distinct from the descriptive matter. The Registrar may require amendments to claims if they are ambiguous or do not clearly define the subject matter of the invention as disclosed within the claim complete specification. Any alteration to the complete specification after its initial filing shall be permissible only with the consent of the Controller, provided that such alterations do not broaden the scope of protection initially sought.

Where an invention infringes upon a patent granted to another person, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing activity. Such injunction may be permanent or interlocutory, subject to considerations of balance of convenience and public interest as determined by the Controller. The determination of infringement shall hinge on whether the claimed invention, as defined in the claim complete specification, is substantially identical to the alleged infringing product or process. Provided that a party accused of infringement demonstrates prior use of the allegedly infringed technology before the date of publication of the patent application, they may be afforded a defense under this Act. Further, any damages awarded shall not exceed three times the proven loss suffered by the patentee, unless it is shown that the infringer acted with knowledge of the patent and willfully infringed the same.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant a license to use, or assign, the benefit of the invention claimed in a complete specification relating to such patent. Such license or assignment shall be deemed to include the right to make, use and sell the patented invention within India, unless the license agreement expressly restricts these rights. Where a complete specification contains multiple inventions, a licensee may elect to receive rights pertaining to only a subset of claims defining one or more of those inventions, provided that such election is clearly stated in the written instrument effecting the assignment or license. The patentee shall provide a certified copy of the claim complete specification to the assignee or licensee upon request and payment of the prescribed fee. Any subsequent modification to the invention as claimed shall require prior consent from the licensee, unless otherwise stipulated within the agreement.

The determination of whether a patent applicant has adequately defined the scope of protection sought shall be predicated upon a rigorous examination of the claim language within the complete specification. Where an ambiguity arises concerning the interpretation of a term employed in a claim, the Controller may direct that evidence be submitted by either party to elucidate the intended meaning, subject to principles of natural construction and considering the entire disclosure. An appeal against such direction lies to the Appellate Board, but only if it is demonstrated that the request for clarification unduly prejudices the appellant’s ability to present its case or infringes upon established protocols concerning claim complete specification interpretation under this Act. The burden of demonstrating prejudice rests entirely with the appealing party.

An applicant shall be deemed to have relinquished any right to enforce infringement proceedings relating to a patent if, within one year from the date of grant, they fail to provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating diligent pursuit of remedies against an alleged infringer. Provided that, where the infringement constitutes a substantial and repeated misappropriation of the invention as defined in the claim complete specification, the Controller may, upon application by the applicant patent claimant, extend this period for a further six months. Any party found guilty of such infringement shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the lost profits attributable to the infringing activity, or a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees, whichever is greater, and subject to recovery of legal costs incurred under this Act.

A “broadcasting organisation” with respect to this Act means any body corporate or society registered under the Companies Act, 1956, or any other law for the time being in force, which habitually communicates programmes through radio broadcasting or television broadcasting. For the purposes of determining whether an entity is a "broadcasting organisation," consideration shall be given to its regular transmission schedule and established infrastructure dedicated to such communication. A body corporate engaged primarily in telecommunications services but occasionally including broadcast content does not qualify as a “broadcasting organisation” under this definition, provided that it lacks a demonstrable commitment to programme creation or acquisition for broadcasting purposes.

A broadcasting organisation intending to make any communication to the public involving copyright works shall apply for registration with the Copyright Office in the form specified under this Act. Such application must detail the name and principal place of business of the broadcasting organisation, along with a comprehensive list of copyrighted works proposed for broadcast, including author details where ascertainable. The applicant shall also declare whether the work has been published elsewhere and provide evidence thereof, if applicable. Registration is subject to verification by the Copyright Office regarding the applicant’s status as a bona fide broadcasting organisation engaged in regular public broadcasts. Any alteration to the declared list of works requires subsequent notification to the Copyright Office for record.

A broadcasting organisation that makes use of any copyrighted work without authorization for transmission or retransmission by way of broadcast shall be liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner. Such liability extends to instances where the broadcasting organisation has acted through its employees or agents, and the actions were undertaken within the scope of their employment or agency. The right to claim damages is subject to a limitation period of three years from the date on which the infringement came to the knowledge of the copyright owner. Provided that, if the infringing broadcast was made for non-commercial purposes and without any intent to gain profit, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Any person aggrieved by such an action may institute civil proceedings as provided herein seeking injunctive relief and compensation.

A broadcasting organisation intending to include within any broadcast a cinematograph film or an adaptation thereof shall apply for and obtain permission from the Controller before undertaking such inclusion. Such application must specify the title of the film, the duration of the excerpt intended for broadcast, and the proposed date and time of transmission. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish copies of the script or scenario of the cinematograph film, as well as details regarding any musical works incorporated therein. Permission granted under this Act shall be valid for a period not exceeding one year, subject to renewal upon application demonstrating continued need. Any broadcasting organisation failing to secure prior permission as provided herein is liable to penalties determined by the Controller and may face restrictions on future broadcasts of copyrighted material. The Controller’s decision regarding applications may be appealed to the appellate authority established under this Act.

A broadcasting organisation intending to make any use of a copyrighted work under this Act shall first obtain a license from the owner or authorized agent thereof, provided that such organization demonstrates compliance with established industry standards for royalty distribution. The application for said license must include detailed particulars regarding the intended broadcast, including date, time, geographical area of transmission, and the specific works to be utilized. Further, where the copyrighted work incorporates elements subject to moral rights, the broadcasting organisation shall ensure adequate attribution is given as stipulated by law. Failure to secure prior authorization or demonstrable adherence to these conditions may render the broadcasting organization liable for infringement proceedings under this Act.

Any broadcasting organisation that reproduces any copyrighted work in a programme for public transmission without obtaining requisite permission from the owner of copyright shall be liable to pay remuneration determined by the Controller. This liability extends to instances where the reproduction is substantially similar to the original work, irrespective of whether it constitutes an exact copy. Failure to remit such remuneration within ninety days of demand notice served under this Act will attract a penalty equivalent to three times the amount due. The Controller may, upon receiving complaints regarding non-compliance by a broadcasting organisation, issue directions for rectification and impose further penalties as deemed appropriate. Any aggrieved copyright owner may appeal against orders issued by the Controller relating to remuneration or penalties.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any copyrighted work for transmission via radio or television signals shall obtain a license from the copyright holder or their designated agent. Such licenses shall specify the duration of usage, geographical territory covered, and the type of adaptation permitted, if any. The fees payable under these licenses may be determined through negotiation between the parties, provided that they are reasonable and reflect the value conferred by the broadcasting organisation’s transmission. Any assignment of copyright relating to a work previously licensed for broadcast shall require notification to the original licensor, enabling them to exercise rights of pre-emption as provided herein. Further, where a broadcasting organisation incorporates excerpts from multiple works into a single programme, it is deemed to hold a composite license encompassing all such materials, subject to limitations on subsequent commercial exploitation.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, a broadcasting organisation engaged primarily in the dissemination of news and current affairs programmes shall be deemed to have obtained sufficient consent for the inclusion of copyrighted works incidental to such broadcasts. Provided that, where such use is contested by the copyright holder, the broadcasting organisation bears the onus of demonstrating reasonable efforts were made to secure appropriate permissions prior to transmission. Any aggrieved party may appeal a determination regarding the sufficiency of these efforts to the relevant High Court, presenting evidence pertaining to the nature and extent of the copyrighted material utilized and the potential prejudice suffered as a consequence of its unauthorized use by the broadcasting organisation.

A broadcasting organisation intending to include within any broadcast a cinematograph film or a sound recording protected under this Act shall apply to the owner of copyright in that work for permission. Such application must specify the intended duration of inclusion and the geographical area covered by the proposed broadcast, and shall be accompanied by a detailed technical specification outlining transmission parameters relevant to signal integrity. The applicant may include within its application a preliminary assessment regarding potential impact on existing patent India claims related to broadcasting technology employed in the transmission. Failure to provide this assessment will not invalidate the application but may necessitate further inquiry under procedures as provided herein. The copyright owner shall respond within sixty days, indicating acceptance or rejection of the request, with reasons for any refusal.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise copyrighted works for transmission via radio or television signals shall obtain a license from the copyright owner unless an exception applies under this Act. Provided that, where the broadcasting organisation’s signal is primarily directed towards educational purposes and operates without commercial advertising, it may reproduce reasonable excerpts of such works without requiring prior express consent, subject to attribution requirements as prescribed by regulations. Any person found to have broadcast copyrighted material in violation of these provisions, or without securing the requisite license, shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for damages proportionate to the infringement. Furthermore, such offender may face punishable imprisonment extending up to three years, alongside a monetary penalty determined by the adjudicating officer.

Any broadcasting organisation that reproduces any work protected under this Act for transmission via radio or television signals shall be liable for damages proportionate to the extent of commercial detriment suffered by the copyright owner. An applicant patent person who, acting on behalf of a broadcasting organisation, knowingly facilitates such reproduction without obtaining the requisite license as provided herein, shall be deemed an agent of that organisation and subject to the same penalties. Failure to provide accurate records of copyrighted material used in broadcasts, upon demand from the Controller, will incur fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Repeated or wilful violations may result in revocation of broadcasting licenses and criminal prosecution under this Act.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any copyrighted work for transmission via radio or television signals shall obtain a license from the copyright holder or their designated agent. Such licenses may be granted on terms and conditions negotiated between the parties, including but not limited to royalty payments reflecting the extent of public exposure achieved through the broadcast. Where a work has been incorporated into a program initially transmitted before the date patent for that program expired, subsequent broadcasts require renewed licensing agreements reflective of evolving market values. Assignment of copyright in works used by a broadcasting organisation shall be recorded with the Copyright Office and deemed valid only upon such registration. The broadcasting organisation may sub-license rights to affiliated entities subject to conditions ensuring equitable distribution of royalties as determined under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, a broadcasting organisation engaged in the transmission of programmes incorporating copyrighted works shall be deemed to have fulfilled its obligations regarding licensing where it has demonstrably attempted to secure necessary permissions from copyright holders. However, failure to provide reasonable opportunity for negotiation and subsequent refusal by the copyright holder, duly documented through registered post with acknowledgment due, will not preclude the broadcasting organisation’s right to utilize the work subject to a royalty determination process as provided herein. The assessment of reasonableness shall be adjudicated considering prevailing industry standards and the nature of the services trade mark associated with the broadcast signal. Any aggrieved party may appeal such determination before the relevant appellate authority within ninety days from the date of notification.

The registration of a trademark, as provided herein, may be subject to cancellation upon application by any interested person demonstrating that, subsequent to the date of registration, the mark has not been genuinely used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. For the purposes of this Act, “interested person” shall include any party having a reasonable interest in the prevention of unfair competition or deception. The Registrar shall afford the proprietor of the trademark an opportunity to be heard and present evidence of genuine use before determining whether cancellation should proceed under this procedure cancelling registration.

Any person aggrieved by a registration, including but not limited to a current proprietor of a similar mark used in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, may file an application with the Registrar seeking cancellation of that registration. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, and must be supported by evidence demonstrating material prejudice resulting from the continued registration. The Registrar shall provide the registered trade mark proprietor with a copy of the application and opportunity to submit a counter-statement defending the validity of the registration. 

The Registrar may, after affording both parties an opportunity for hearing, order cancellation of the registration if satisfied that it was obtained fraudulently or through misrepresentation, or that its use is contrary to law or morality. The decision of the Registrar concerning procedure cancelling registration shall be subject to appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal.

An opposition to registration under this Act is deemed to exist when a registered proprietor or any other person interested in the reputation of a trade mark applied for, or of a similar mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, notifies the Registrar that they oppose the application. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use and acquired distinctiveness. The Registrar may require further particulars supporting the opposition within a prescribed timeframe. Failure to provide such particulars as provided herein may result in the rejection of the opposition. Any party affected by an opposition registration may appeal under this Act.

Any party possessing legitimate interest may institute proceedings under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, constituting an opposition registration. Such opposition shall be based upon grounds specified in Schedule I, including but not limited to prior use or registration of an identical or deceptively similar mark. The opponent must provide evidence substantiating their claim and demonstrating that the applicant’s proposed mark is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers or otherwise infringe upon existing rights. The Registrar may, after affording both parties a reasonable opportunity for hearing, determine whether the opposition is warranted and shall issue an order either accepting or rejecting the same, as provided herein.

Any registered trade mark owner aggrieved by an application for registration filed by another person may institute proceedings under this Act in the form of an opposition registration. Such opposition shall be based on grounds that the proposed trade mark is likely to be confused with a prior trade mark or is descriptive of the goods or services, and prejudices the distinctiveness or reputation of the earlier mark. The opponent must provide evidence substantiating these claims; failure to do so may result in dismissal of the opposition.

The applicant for registration shall have the right to file a counterstatement responding to the grounds raised by the opponent within a prescribed period. Further opportunities for submitting written arguments and documentary proof shall be afforded to both parties as provided herein. The Registrar, after considering all submissions, may allow or dismiss the opposition, subject to appeal to an appropriate forum.

Any party seeking to oppose an application for trade mark registration under this Act shall file a Notice of Opposition with the Registry within the prescribed time limit as determined by regulations framed hereunder. Such Notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or registration of a similar sign in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. The Registrar may require the party filing the opposition to furnish further particulars and evidence supporting their claim, subject to payment of additional fees as prescribed. Failure to comply with such requirements within the stipulated period shall render the Notice vulnerable to dismissal. An applicant facing an opposition registration may submit a counter-statement addressing the grounds raised by the opponent, also within a timeframe determined by the Registrar. The Registrar shall then proceed according to established procedures for resolving oppositions.

Any party possessing prior mercantile use of a sign or trade mark, or any registered user thereof, may institute an opposition registration against an application for registration under this Act, provided that such use occurred honestly and in the course of trade. The notice of opposition shall clearly specify the grounds upon which it is founded, including but not limited to similarity between the applied-for mark and a previously used sign, or likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed registration. Further, the opponent must demonstrate evidence substantiating their claim of prior use, failing which the Registrar may summarily dismiss the opposition. The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition within the prescribed timeframe as provided herein and present counter-evidence where applicable.

Any party possessing legitimate interest shall have the right to file an opposition registration against the acceptance of an application for trademark registration under this Act. Such opposition must be filed within three months from the date such acceptance is advertised in the Trade Marks Journal; failure to comply with this time limit shall render the opposition inadmissible. The Registrar may, upon receiving a duly supported notice of opposition, issue a hearing notice to both the applicant and the opponent, affording them an opportunity for argument. Any party failing to appear at the appointed hearing or submitting inadequate evidence as provided herein shall be subject to penalties prescribed by regulations. The decision of the Registrar regarding the merits of the opposition registration is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is subject to an opposition registration under this Act, the owner of any existing registered trade mark or any unregistered right in a similar mark may grant a limited license to another party allowing use of the applied-for mark solely for the purpose of presenting grounds of opposition. Such licenses shall be documented and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of their execution, detailing the scope and duration of permitted usage. The applicant whose registration is opposed may, subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar, assign the right to utilize the trade mark in question to a third party, provided that such assignment includes an undertaking to cease any activities which would constitute grounds for opposition if pursued by another. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by all prior obligations relating to the opposition proceedings.

Any party believing they would be prejudiced by the registration of a trade mark applied for under this Act may institute an opposition proceeding before the relevant Intellectual Property Office. Such opposition shall be grounded in evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation arising from the similarity between the applied-for mark and any existing prior right, including but not limited to registered trade marks or well-known marks. The applicant for registration shall have the opportunity to file a counterstatement responding to the grounds of opposition as provided herein. Further, the Intellectual Property Office may, subject to procedural guidelines, direct parties to mediation in an attempt to resolve the dispute amicably. Any order made by the Intellectual Property Office concerning such opposition registration is appealable to the appellate forum within a prescribed period.

Any party possessing legitimate interest shall have the right to file an opposition registration against an application for trademark registration under this Act. Such opposition must be filed within three months of the date the mark is advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, as provided herein. The grounds for opposition shall include, but not be limited to, similarity to prior marks and likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Where a court section rectifying errors in respect of an existing registration arises during proceedings before the Registrar, the Registrar may stay the opposition process until such rectification is finalized. Further, any evidence submitted must comply with prescribed formats; failure to do so shall render it inadmissible. The Registrar shall provide all parties with reasonable opportunity for argument and submission of counter-evidence.

Any registered trade mark proprietor aggrieved by an application for registration of a trade mark may institute proceedings under this Act in the form of an opposition registration. Such opposition shall be grounded in evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation arising from the proposed mark’s similarity to existing marks, including varieties registered under this Act and used in relation to identical or similar goods or services. Failure to provide verifiable documentary proof substantiating the grounds for opposition within the prescribed timeframe shall render the opposition inadmissible. The Registrar may, upon finding a prima facie case of infringement, issue an injunction restraining the applicant from proceeding with registration, subject to a hearing where both parties may present arguments and evidence. Penalties for frivolous or vexatious oppositions, as determined by the Registrar, shall be strictly enforced.

For the purposes of this Act, an *indication* is defined as a sign used to identify goods originating from a specific territory and whose quality, reputation, or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its geographical origin. An *indication* may consist of words, phrases in languages literary, artistic or symbolic character, and shall include any representation or distinguishing marks that conform to the requirements laid down herein. The use of an *indication* is deemed unfair if it exploits the reputation attached to a geographically identified product without due cause, or misleads consumers regarding the origin of such goods, as provided under this Act.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the Geographical Indication as it is proposed to be registered, a map of the territorial area comprising the locality from which the goods originate, and a statement indicating the characteristics and qualities of the goods attributable exclusively to its origin. The applicant shall also furnish proof establishing use of the indication within the specified territory for at least three years immediately preceding the date of application. Any association representing producers or users concerned with the quality and reputation of goods originating from that area may apply for registration as an authorized user, subject to fulfilling conditions prescribed herein. An existing Geographical Indication already recognized under traditional laws shall be eligible for registration provided that it meets all requirements stipulated in this Act.

The registration of a Geographical Indication does not confer any right to exclude any person from the use of any word or words which do not directly indicate, or are descriptive of, the characteristics of the goods. Provided that, an interested party may apply to the Registrar for rectification of a registered Geographical Indication if they demonstrate that its registration was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, or that it has become non-distinctive due to use by others. The remedies available under this Act include the amendment or cancellation of the register and orders restraining any person from making an infringing use of the Geographical Indication. Any infringement shall be actionable as a civil wrong, and the aggrieved party may seek damages proportionate to the loss suffered. Further, the Registrar may issue directions for the destruction of goods bearing the false or misleading indication.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, handicraft, or any other goods for which the indication is sought. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain whether the conditions precedent for registration are satisfied under this Act. Where an application relates to a geographical indication already registered, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the existing registration and afford him an opportunity of being heard in opposition to the proposed registration. Any person alleging that their interests would be prejudiced by the registration of a geographical indication may file an objection within such time as is prescribed. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and determine whether the proposed geographical indication qualifies as a distinctive indication of origin, free from descriptive or generic character.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall contain particulars specifying the name of the goods, the territory from which the goods originate, and the prior use, if any, of the name of the Geographical Indication. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin; failing this demonstration, registration shall be denied. Further, the proposed indication must not describe any ingredient or component of the goods but instead signify a specific locality. Any alteration to the registered Geographical Indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such alteration does not substantially affect the distinctiveness of the *indication*.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, uses a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which such indication is not defined, shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registration. Such use includes applying the indication as a trademark or trade name, or any mode of making available goods that falsely suggests an origin connected with the registered *indication*. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, issue an injunction restraining such infringing activity and order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the false geographical indication. Failure to comply with such orders shall attract penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication, duly registered under this Act, may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the use of their registered indication for goods conforming to the standards established in the registration certificate. Such licenses shall specify the territory and duration of the permitted usage, as well as any restrictions on quality or presentation of the licensed goods. The proprietor retains full authority to assign such licenses, subject to prior written consent from the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses sufficient resources to uphold the integrity of the geographical indication. Any sublicense granted by a licensee shall be void unless expressly authorized in writing by the original proprietor and registered with the Registrar. Further, any use of the geographical indication without authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act, regardless of whether such use is intended to deceive or mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods bearing that indication.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that use of the indication, even by the registered proprietor, is contrary to public interest or would mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Such refusal shall be subject to review under this Act; the applicant shall have the right to appeal within sixty days from the date of notification of the refusal. The appellate authority may, after hearing both parties and considering all relevant evidence, confirm, vary, or reverse the Registrar’s decision. It is further provided that a geographical indication once registered remains protected against use by any party not authorized under this Act, irrespective of whether such use constitutes an attempt to pass off goods as originating from the indicated locality.

The registration of a Geographical Indication shall not be refused solely on the grounds that goods produced or traded under an identical or similar name were previously subject to patent protection, provided that such patented article does not inherently misrepresent the origin or qualities associated with the agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, liquor, spice, medicinal plant, or pharmaceutical product in question. An appeal against a refusal of registration based on prior patent rights may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the Appellate Board, and such appeal shall be heard expeditiously. The Board may allow the appeal if it is satisfied that the use of the name does not constitute an attempt to unfairly exploit or misrepresent the established reputation of the Geographical Indication.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the Geographical Indication, the goods or services for which it is used, and the area comprising such territory from where the goods originate. The applicant shall furnish proof establishing the use of the indication within the specified geographical boundary for a period not less than three years preceding the date claim shall be made. Further, the application must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to the origin of the Geographical Indication. Any prior usage or registration affecting the distinctiveness of the proposed Geographical Indication may be considered during examination. The Registrar may require additional information as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention” means a new and useful art, process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, and includes any improvement thereof; provided that an invention shall not include a mere discovery, scientific principle, or formula discovered solely by observation of nature. An application for a patent india relating to such invention may be filed with the Controller, disclosing the manner in which the invention can be made or used. The term “patent” signifies exclusive right granted under this Act, subject to limitations as provided herein, and shall confer upon the patentee certain privileges concerning the patented article or process.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent india shall furnish particulars relating to any earlier applications for the same invention filed in any country outside India. Such particulars must include the date of filing, application number and the authority where the prior application was made. The Controller may require the applicant to provide certified copies of such prior applications as evidence. Failure to disclose relevant details regarding preceding patent applications shall render the subsequent registration liable to be revoked under this Act. An inventor claiming inventorship based on work performed during employment must declare the nature of their contractual relationship with their employer, and whether the invention falls within the scope of that agreement. The Controller may request further documentation to verify these claims as provided herein.

Where a patent india has been granted and the proprietor thereof becomes aware that any person other than himself or his licensee has infringed or is infringing the invention in respect of which the patent has been granted, he may institute suit for damages against such person. The measure of damages recoverable under this Act shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement and the profits made by the infringer attributable to the making, use or sale of the patented invention. Provided that in determining the said profits, due account shall be taken of any expenditure incurred by the infringer in making, using or selling the invention. Subject to this, damages may include reasonable royalties which the infringer would have been willing to pay. The proprietor shall also be entitled to an injunction restraining the infringing activity as provided herein.

An applicant seeking a patent india shall furnish a statement before the Controller detailing all applications made outside India in respect of the claimed invention. This statement must specify the country where each prior application was filed and its filing date, as provided herein. Failure to disclose such prior applications may render the subsequent Indian application liable for rejection under this Act. The Controller may require further clarification or documentation regarding these foreign filings at any stage during examination. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller concerning the disclosure requirements may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to revision by the High Court on grounds specified under this Act relating to law and jurisdiction.

An applicant seeking a patent india shall disclose to the Controller, at the time of filing the patent application, all prior publications, oral disclosures, exhibitions or uses relating to the invention existing anywhere in the world. Provided that such disclosure need not include information which was acquired by the applicant from any person otherwise than under a confidentiality agreement. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the extent and nature of these disclosures if deemed necessary for assessment of novelty and inventive step. Furthermore, where an application incorporates subject matter disclosed in a previously filed patent application, the applicant shall provide a copy of such prior application to the Controller. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the subsequent patent liable to revocation under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent india may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall only be entertained if the appellant demonstrates that they have suffered substantial loss or damage as a direct consequence of the impugned decision. Failure to demonstrate such prejudice will render the appeal inadmissible. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any costs relating to the appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Board as it deems just, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patent india holder may grant a license to use the patented invention to any person, firm, or company, either generally throughout India or in respect of specific territories. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the patentee, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contract law principles. Assignment of patent rights is permissible with the written consent of the Controller, who may require disclosure of consideration paid or to be paid for such assignment. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensee shall be entitled to use the invention solely within the scope of the agreement and shall not infringe upon any other intellectual property rights held by the patentee. Any dispute arising from a licensing agreement or assignment may be referred to arbitration as provided herein.

Where a determination under this Act regarding the validity of a patent india has been made and appeal therefrom has been filed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Board may, subject to any conditions it deems fit, direct that the proceedings relating to the suit pending before any civil court be stayed for such period as it considers necessary. Provided that if the appellant fails to prosecute the appeal diligently, or otherwise acts in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the patentee, the Board may dismiss the appeal and vacate the stay. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may prefer an appeal from such order to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order, and shall be bound by the decision of the court.

An applicant seeking registration of a design under this Act shall furnish a statement indicating whether any patent india has been applied for or granted in relation to the article comprising the design. Such statement must accurately reflect the status of prior applications and grants globally. Where the design incorporates elements previously disclosed, either directly or indirectly, which would otherwise invalidate a patent relating to the functional aspects of the article, the applicant shall provide a detailed explanation demonstrating how the claimed design remains distinct from any such prior disclosures. Failure to disclose relevant information regarding existing patents may result in objections during examination and potential invalidation proceedings later on, particularly if it is demonstrated that the undisclosed patent falsifies genuine trade practices.

For the purposes of this Act, “the Controller” shall mean the authority appointed by the Central Government under this Act to exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred upon it herein. The Controller may, subject to any directions given by the Central Government, determine all matters relating to the examination of patent applications and grant or refusal of patents. An officer designated by the Controller for specific functions shall act on behalf of the Controller in accordance with procedures prescribed under this Act. Decisions made by such an officer are deemed to be decisions of the Controller. The Controller’s powers extend to ensuring compliance with provisions as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars, documents and fees as may be prescribed, and shall be presented to the Controller in the form specified under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation deemed necessary for assessing compliance with the provisions herein relating to novelty and originality. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall assign a filing date and generate a unique acknowledgement number which shall be communicated to the applicant within thirty days. Any request for amendment or alteration to the layout design after the initial registration process has commenced shall be subject to approval by the Controller, provided that such alterations do not substantially affect the registered design’s aesthetic characteristics.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller under this Act, including orders relating to compulsory licensing or revocation of patents, has no other adequate remedy available, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall have power to entertain and dispose of appeals against orders of the Controller and may pass such orders as it deems fit, substituting or modifying any order passed by the Controller. Provided that an appeal under this provision shall be made within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with this time limit shall ordinarily preclude the Board from admitting the appeal, subject to just cause being shown. The Controller shall furnish all relevant records and documents pertaining to the matter to the Appellate Board upon request.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a request for extension of time under this Act, require the applicant to submit a duly verified statement setting forth the grounds justifying such extension and supported by documentary evidence demonstrating due diligence on the part of the applicant. Any application so filed may be rejected if the Controller is satisfied that the delay in processing has been occasioned by willful default or negligence attributable to the applicant. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for the applicant to be heard, either in person or through a duly authorized representative, before passing any order refusing such extension. Decisions of the Controller regarding extensions are subject to appeal under this Act. Further, the Controller may, at his discretion, require submission of additional information or clarification from any party involved in proceedings concerning patent applications or opposition matters.

The application for grant of a patent, once received by the Controller, shall be examined to ascertain compliance with all requirements under this Act and rules made thereunder. Provided that, if the applicant has failed to comply with the prescribed formalities relating to the making of the complete specification or claims, the Controller may direct the applicant to amend such deficiencies within a period not exceeding six months from the date of the direction. Further, where an objection is raised concerning the novelty or inventive step of the claimed invention, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for said objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to respond and present arguments rebutting the objection; such response must be filed within three months from the date of notification.

Any person aggrieved by any order passed by the Controller under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider only such grounds of appeal as are specifically pleaded and substantiated with relevant evidence; failure to do so will render the appeal inadmissible. Where a party fails to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal or any supporting documentation, the Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Furthermore, wilful suppression of material facts during appellate proceedings shall be deemed a cognizable offence and subject to prosecution under relevant penal laws as provided herein. The Controller’s decision on procedural matters relating to appeals is final.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license under his patent, or assign the benefit of his patent, shall make application to the Controller in the prescribed form. Such application shall specify the terms and conditions of the proposed license or assignment, including but not limited to royalty rates, duration, and geographical scope. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to the applicant and any other interested party, approve the proposed license or assignment as submitted, approve it with modifications, or reject it if he deems that the terms are unduly restrictive or prejudicial to public interest. Where a license is granted, the Controller shall record the details in the Register of Patents and make them available for public inspection. The patentee shall provide an annual report to the Controller detailing the exploitation of the patented invention under the license.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any decision or order made by the controller, the Appellate Board may, after giving notice to the appellant and the respondent, hear the appeal at such time and place as it thinks fit. The Board shall follow the procedure specified herein for hearing appeals, subject to such modifications as it deems necessary for ensuring fairness and expeditious disposal of the matter. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the grounds of appeal shall be limited to questions of law arising out of the decision or order of the Appellate Board. The controller shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the case to the Appellate Board and the High Court as required.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a complete application for registration of a patent, undertake a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the formal requirements under this Act. Where any deficiency is noted, the applicant shall be notified and afforded opportunity for rectification within a prescribed period; failure to comply may result in rejection of the application. The process of registration respects the priority date claimed by the applicant, provided that all necessary documentation substantiating such claim is filed concurrently with the application or within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the grant or refusal of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design, or concerning infringement proceedings, appeals to the Appellate Board, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, subject to provisions regarding natural justice, entertain and determine such appeal, and for that purpose shall have all powers of a civil court trying a suit under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final, provided that an appeal lies from such order to the High Court within ninety days from the date thereof on grounds specified in law relating to errors apparent on the face of the record. The composition and functioning of the *member appellate board* will adhere to guidelines prescribed by the Central Government.

The Appellate Board shall exercise its jurisdiction and discharge its functions subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the member appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Central Government may, if it considers necessary, extend this period by a further thirty days. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity of being heard before passing any order. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be binding on all parties involved in the appeal. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, at his discretion, require attendance of expert witnesses or technical advisors to assist the board in its deliberations concerning matters relating to layout-design protection.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the member appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate board shall be constituted as provided herein and shall hear appeals arising from orders relating to infringement of layout-design rights, including claims for damages and interim injunctions. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated period shall render the aggrieved party ineligible to pursue further remedies under this Act. Where a finding of wilful infringement is made by the appellate board, enhanced penalties, not exceeding three times the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, may be imposed. The member appellate board’s decision shall be final subject to revision by the High Court only on grounds of law.

Where the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design seeks to grant a license conferring rights relating to commercial exploitation, such license may be assigned by deed, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Any assignment shall include details regarding the duration of the license, geographical scope, and permitted field of use as determined within the original registration. Further, where an assignee subsequently desires to transfer their interest in a licensed right, they must obtain prior consent from the registered proprietor, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Disputes arising concerning the validity or enforceability of any assignment or license relating to a layout-design may be referred to the *member appellate board* for determination. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be binding on all parties involved, as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Member Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to a determination of infringement of layout-design rights. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order appealed against. The Member Appellate Board may, while hearing appeals, review any direction, decision or action taken by the Registrar and substitute such other directions, decisions or actions as it deems fit. Provided that where the appeal relates to a matter concerning rectification of the layout-design register, the Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard. The Member Appellate Board’s order shall be final subject to further appeals under the provisions relating to higher judicial review.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising from orders relating to infringement of layout-design rights and penalties imposed for contravention of provisions herein. Subject to any rules made by the Central Government, the Member Appellate Board may, while hearing an appeal, require the attendance of witnesses, examine them under oath, and order the discovery of documents relevant to the matter before it. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the appellant liable to a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. An appeal section shall be maintained by the board for public access, excluding sensitive personal data.

The term "Appellate Board" signifies the body constituted under this Act for adjudicating disputes relating to layout-design infringement and other matters as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall be presided over by a Chairperson appointed by the Central Government, possessing expertise in intellectual property law or technology. The Chairperson may delegate functions of the Appellate Board to Benches comprising not less than three members, each qualified under this Act. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to appeal to the relevant High Court. The term "Chairperson Appellate Board" refers specifically to the individual holding office as described above and exercising the powers vested in that position.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be deemed refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the design incorporates elements substantially derived from an earlier registered layout-design. Any applicant aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receiving notification of the refusal under this Act. The Appellate Board, consisting of the Chairperson Appellate Board and two other members nominated by the Central Government, shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the applicant and the Registrar. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeal to the High Court. The Chairperson Appellate Board may, at their discretion, require a hearing to be conducted in person or through video conferencing as deemed appropriate for efficient disposal of appeals.

The Appellate Board shall be presided over by the Chairperson appointed by the Central Government for a term not exceeding three years, and may be reappointed. The qualifications for appointment as Chairperson shall include being a person of eminence with substantial experience in intellectual property law or technology. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be made by a majority vote of the members present at any hearing, provided that where a Bench consists of three or more members, the Chairperson’s vote shall have a deciding weight in case of equality. The Central Government may, from time to time, issue regulations specifying procedures for hearings before the Appellate Board and regarding the filing of documents. Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Chairperson Appellate Board shall be responsible for ensuring adherence to these procedural guidelines as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a license granted under section 17 relating to a registered layout-design may be assigned by the licensee, either wholly or partially, provided that such assignment is in writing and duly executed. The assignee shall become vested with all rights and obligations of the original licensee as regards the licensed layout-design. Any transfer of interest in a layout-design, including through mortgage or pledge, requires prior notification to the Registrar of Layout-Designs. Furthermore, where an assignment involves a foreign entity, approval from the Appellate Board is mandatory before registration of such assignment with the Registrar. The Chairperson Appellate Board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, grant or refuse such approval based on considerations of national interest and reciprocity.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act is dissatisfied, such party may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, and it shall have the same powers as vested in a civil court while trying a suit originally before it. An appeal lies on a question of fact or law arising out of the Registrar’s decision regarding infringement of layout-design rights, including disputes concerning originality and substantial similarity. The Chairperson Appellate Board may, at any stage of the appellate proceedings, require the production of documents or other evidence relevant to the determination of the appeal.

The Appellate Board shall, for the purposes of hearing and determining appeals under this Act, be presided over by the Chairperson Appellate Board appointed as per the provisions outlined herein. Any communication required to be sent to the applicant concerning the registration process, including notices regarding objections to a layout-design application, may be served through advertised acceptance in a widely circulated national newspaper, provided that such advertisement clearly states the grounds of objection and the time limit for response. The Chairperson shall ensure that all appeals are disposed of expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice and affording each party an opportunity to present their case. Decisions rendered by the Appellate Board are final, save for further appeal as expressly permitted under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design, or concerning infringement proceedings, appeals to the Appellate Board, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. In determining whether infringement has occurred, the Board shall consider not only the literal similarity between the allegedly infringing layout-design and the registered design but also any substantial resemblance that creates confusion as to the origin of the goods or services. The Chairperson Appellate Board may issue directions for interim relief pending final adjudication. Further, where a denomination variety is involved in a claim of infringement, evidence establishing consumer perception shall be given significant weight.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any licensee desiring to assign a right under a license granted pursuant to an international registration make relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall provide prior notice in writing to the Chairperson Appellate Board. Such notice shall detail the proposed assignee, the scope of assignment, and consideration offered, if any. The Chairperson may, after affording an opportunity for objection to the registered proprietor, issue directions regarding the terms of the assignment deemed necessary to protect public interest or ensure equitable dealings. Failure to provide such prior notice shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the registered proprietor. Further, any transfer of a license by operation of law shall be reported to the Chairperson Appellate Board within thirty days.

The Appellate Board shall be presided over by an appellate board chairperson appointed by the Central Government. For the purposes of this Act, the appellate board chairperson is a person who holds office for a term not exceeding three years and may be removed from office under such conditions as are prescribed. The chairperson shall exercise all powers necessary for the proper discharge of functions vested in the Appellate Board, including the power to constitute Benches and direct proceedings. Subject to any rules made by the Central Government, the appellate board chairperson is entitled to remuneration as determined by the government. Provided that a person shall not be eligible for appointment as appellate board chairperson if they have previously been convicted of an offence involving dishonesty.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act by the Registrar is dissatisfied, such party may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall entertain appeals only if the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Subject to provisions regarding interim relief as provided herein, no relief shall be granted in any appeal unless it is shown that the order was manifestly unjust or perverse. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, at his discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Any decision made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, but such decisions are subject to judicial review under law. The appointment of the appellate board chairperson shall be made by notification in the Official Gazette.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall entertain appeals only if the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to file an appeal within that period shall be a bar against such appeal, subject to just cause shown. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, at his discretion, condone any delay in filing an appeal where sufficient reason for such delay is demonstrated. Any party failing to comply with directions issued by the Appellate Board during appellate proceedings shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and further penalties as determined by the Appellate Board chairperson.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, upon application by a registered proprietor of a layout-design, grant a non-exclusive license to utilize the design for research purposes only. Such licenses shall be granted where the applicant demonstrates a compelling need for access to facilitate innovation in related semiconductor technologies. The terms and conditions of any such license, including royalty rates and duration, will be determined by the Chairperson based on factors deemed relevant, provided that the registered proprietor retains full ownership rights.
