Assignment of these research-only licenses is permitted with prior written consent from the Appellate Board Chairperson, who may impose additional restrictions to safeguard the original layout-design’s integrity. Any disputes arising regarding license terms or assignment approvals shall be subject to appeal before a Bench of the Appellate Board.

The functions conferred upon the Appellate Board chairperson under this Act shall include the responsibility for constituting Benches to hear appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar. An appeal against an order of the Registrar relating to a determination of infringement may be presented before the Appellate Board within sixty days of communication of that order, subject to a further opportunity to file such appeal if the appellant demonstrates reasonable cause for delay. The chairperson may, at his discretion, extend this period by not more than thirty days where exceptional circumstances are demonstrated. Decisions regarding the allocation of appeals amongst Benches shall be made by the Appellate Board chairperson in consultation with senior members, and any dispute concerning such allocation is subject to review under provisions as provided herein.

The power to appoint the appellate board chairperson shall vest with the Central Government, subject to the provisions herein regarding qualifications and experience. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act; however, no such appeal may be admitted unless it is shown that the interests of justice require intervention. The Chairperson may, at his or her discretion, constitute Benches for hearing appeals, ensuring representation from amongst the Members possessing expertise in semiconductor technology and intellectual property law. Any party aggrieved by an order of a Bench may further appeal to the appellate board chairperson, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the Bench’s decision.

The Appellate Board Chairperson shall be a person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, appointed by the Central Government for a term as may be prescribed. The Chairperson shall preside over sittings of the Appellate Board and exercise such other powers as are conferred upon them under this Act. An individual seeking proprietor certification relating to a registered layout-design may petition the Appellate Board Chairperson for clarification regarding eligibility criteria or procedural requirements, provided that such petitions shall not constitute grounds for substantive appeal. The Central Government may remove the Appellate Board Chairperson from office if they are found guilty of misconduct as defined herein.

Where an appeal lies before the Appellate Board concerning infringement of layout-design rights, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, subject to due process, grant interim orders restraining the defendant from further acts of alleged infringement pending final determination of the appeal. Any exclusive licensee possessing a valid license agreement relating to the layout-design in question shall have standing to file such an appeal and pursue remedies on behalf of the original owner. The Chairperson’s decision regarding the award of damages shall take into account the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringement not occurred, as well as any demonstrable loss suffered by the appellant. Further, the Board may order the infringer to deliver up or destroy infringing copies, subject to conditions deemed just and equitable by the Appellate Board Chairperson.

For the purpose of this Act, a “trade marks registry” includes any office established under this Act for receiving applications for registration of trade marks, conducting hearings, and maintaining records pertaining to registered trade marks. The Registrar shall maintain at each trade marks registry a register of trade mark applications and registrations in that jurisdiction, accessible for public inspection subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any communication required or permitted to be made under this Act with the trade marks registry shall be deemed duly served when delivered at the appropriate office location, as notified by the Registrar. The term "jurisdiction" refers to the geographical area assigned to a particular trade marks registry.

Applications for registration of a trademark shall be made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a filing date. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as may be required under this Act to substantiate the claim of ownership or right to use the trademark. Objections to registration may be raised by any person claiming an interest in a similar mark already registered, or by the Registrar if there is reason to believe that the proposed mark would deceive or disparage the public. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations, accessible for inspection as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by the applicant and any opposing party. Failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein regarding the filing of appeals will render the appeal inadmissible.

The Trade Marks Registry shall, in determining whether a trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, take into account not only the visual appearance of the marks but also their phonetic similarities and conceptual meanings. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further petition the Supreme Court on a point of law.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be filed at the Trade Marks Registry specified under this Act, or at any other Registry as notified by the Registrar from time to time. Every application must contain such particulars as are required by the Regulations framed hereunder, including but not limited to, a representation of the mark and a list of goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the trade mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend any description or statement contained in the application if he considers it necessary for clarity or precision. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a serial number. Any objection to the acceptance of an application may be raised by any person within the time specified under this Act, providing reasons for such objection. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain records of all applications received and objections filed, accessible as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks include any representation or device likely to be mistaken for, or used as a deceptive imitation of, an existing registered trade mark under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving such an application, issue a notice to the proprietor of the prior registered trade mark, affording them an opportunity to file their objections within sixty days from the date of publication of the journal. Any objection filed shall be considered by the Registrar, who shall provide both applicants with a hearing if either party requests one. The Registrar’s decision regarding acceptance or refusal shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person who, without reasonable cause, makes any false representation concerning the registration of a trade mark under this Act, or the identity of the proprietor thereof, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. Further, where a registered trade mark is used in contravention of the provisions herein relating to passing off, the Registrar may, subject to due process, order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing that infringing mark. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain records of all such orders, and any person found to be dealing with goods so seized shall be liable for penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses for the use of their trade mark within India, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify geographical limitations, restrictions on goods or services covered, duration, and royalty payments. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether partial or complete, must be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein; failure to do so renders the assignee not vested with the rights of the assignor until registration is completed. The Registrar may require proof of consideration paid for any such assignment. A licensee may further sub-license their rights under this Act, but only with the prior written consent of the trade mark owner and notification to the Trade Marks Registry. Any alteration to a registered trademark requires approval from the registry before it can be implemented.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any person to the acceptance of a proposed trade mark under this Act, direct the applicant to file his reply within such time as may be specified. Such direction shall include notice that failure to comply will result in deemed abandonment of the application. The objector shall have the right to submit further evidence or arguments after the applicant’s reply is filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to an objection, acceptance, or refusal of a trade mark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented before it and issue such orders as it deems just and equitable.

The Registrar may, subject to any conditions specified in the agreement, grant a license to any person enabling them to use a registered trade mark belonging to another party, provided that such license is documented and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered trade mark shall be executed in the prescribed manner and notified to the Registrar for record; failure to do so renders the assignee’s claim to ownership unenforceable against third parties. Further, an owner may choose to register copyrights associated with designs incorporated within their trade marks, thereby securing protection under both regimes. The license agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, geographical limitations, and duration, as well as any royalties payable. Any alteration or sub-licensing requires prior written consent from the original proprietor and must also be recorded at the Trade Marks Registry.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the evidence submitted by both the applicant and the opponent shall be considered by the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may, after affording both parties an opportunity to be heard, either allow the opposition or dismiss it; provided that if the Registrar finds that the use of the impugned trade mark by the opponent constitutes a genuine and continuous trade mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services as those for which registration is sought, the opposition may be allowed subject to such conditions as the Registrar deems fit. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order.

For the purpose of this Act, “Security India Explanation” means a designation applied to trademarks registered under this Act pertaining exclusively to security-related products and services, including but not limited to surveillance equipment, cybersecurity solutions, and personnel protection devices. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a separate register for Security India Explanations, accessible upon request by authorized government agencies. Applications for registration bearing the Security India Explanation must demonstrate compliance with guidelines issued by the Controller under this Act concerning national security considerations. Such applications may be subject to additional scrutiny and verification procedures as provided herein.

Applications for registration of a trademark shall be made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the provisions of this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. If the application is found deficient or does not meet the formal requirements, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the defects within a specified period. Where the mark sought to be registered is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier trademark already registered in respect of goods or services, or to a well-known trademark, the application shall be refused under this Act. The registrar may also refuse registration if the proposed mark lacks distinctiveness and has no connection with any patent previously granted.

For the purposes of this Act, "artistic work" includes graphic works, photographic works, three-dimensional works of art, models for sculpture or caricature and any other works which are drawings or illustrations, subject to the provisions regarding architectural works as provided herein. An artistic work shall be considered fixed when it is in a form visible or capable of reproduction, and such fixation may occur through various means including but not limited to engraving, lithography, photography, digital rendering, or by moulding in clay, plaster, metal or any other material. The right of copyright under this Act in an artistic work subsists until sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death.

The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register for the recording of applications and certificates relating to copyright. Any person claiming ownership of copyright in any work shall be eligible to apply for registration under this Act, submitting prescribed forms detailing the nature of the work, date of creation, author’s particulars, and ownership details. The application may include certified copies of the work or excerpts thereof as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Registration is not a prerequisite for claiming copyright; however, it provides prima facie evidence of ownership in any legal proceeding relating to infringement. A certificate of registration shall be issued upon verification that the applicant fulfills all requirements as provided herein and that the work satisfies the criteria for copyright protection.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite license under this Act or without leaving due acknowledgement in the work from which the extract is taken, reproduces any substantial portion of a copyrighted work infringes the copyright in that work. Such infringement shall render the offender liable to prosecution and subject to penalties as provided herein. The remedies available to the owner of copyright include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, damages reflecting lost profits or reasonable royalties, and delivery up or destruction of infringing copies. Provided that fair dealing for research, private study, criticism, or review does not constitute infringement, subject to conditions regarding acknowledgement and limitation of use. Where the infringement is committed by a corporate body, its officers in default shall also be deemed liable.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author’s death. Where the author is not an individual, such period shall be reckoned from the beginning of the calendar year following the date on which the work is first published under circumstances indicating an intention to make it available to the public. Any person claiming infringement of copyright may file a suit in the district court having jurisdiction over the cause of action. The Court may, upon application made by any party to the proceedings, grant such temporary injunction as appears to the Court just and equitable. An appeal from the order of the District Court shall lie to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Any dispute concerning ownership of copyright arising under this Act may be referred for arbitration as agreed upon by the parties involved, provided that both parties consent in writing.

The reproduction of any cinematograph film, or part thereof, shall be deemed a violation of copyright unless the owner of the copyright in the work has granted a license permitting such reproduction; provided that where a cinematograph film incorporates pre-existing works, the copyright holder of the film is obligated to secure permissions for those incorporated elements prior to distribution. Any person utilizing a computer program, irrespective of its source code or intended purpose, shall be considered to infringe upon the copyright therein if such utilization exceeds fair dealing as defined under this Act and does not comply with conditions stipulated by the owner. The right to communicate a work to the public via digital means is exclusively vested in the copyright holder, subject to adherence to technological protection measures implemented by them.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite license under this Act or without authorization from the owner of copyright, reproduces any work, or a substantial portion thereof, and offers for sale or hires out or displays commercially, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. Provided that where the infringing copies are made during the subsistence of the copyright and the total value of such copies exceeds fifty thousand rupees, the court may also order forfeiture of equipment used in or for the purpose of making such copies. The owner of copyright shall be entitled to seek injunction restraining any person from doing anything which infringes his copyright as provided herein.

The assignment of copyright in works generated through artificial intelligence systems shall be permissible only with express written consent from the entity responsible for developing and maintaining that system, provided that such consent specifies the scope of permitted uses and reproduction rights. Any license granted under this Act relating to computer programs incorporating elements subject to copyright shall clearly delineate whether the licensee possesses the right to modify or distribute derivative works based on the original code. Further, where a work is jointly authored by a human creator and an artificial intelligence system, ownership of the resulting copyright shall be determined proportionally, as agreed upon in writing between the parties involved; failing such agreement, the courts may apportion rights considering the relative contribution of each author. This provision does not preclude assignment of copyright to third parties, subject to adherence with these stipulations.

Where a work has been communicated to the public under copyright, and subsequent use thereof without authorization results in demonstrable financial prejudice to the owner, such owner may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court seeking injunctive relief and damages. The determination of said prejudice shall be subject to an assessment of reasonable licensing fees which could have been negotiated had prior consent been obtained. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrates good faith belief in a lack of copyright infringement, or reliance upon advice from counsel asserting such lack, the court may reduce the quantum of damages awarded. Any order issued by the High Court under this Act shall be appealable to the Supreme Court within sixty days, as provided herein.

Any person who, without obtaining a license from the owner of copyright, reproduces any work protected under this Act for commercial gain shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty that would have been payable had such license been obtained. The amount of said royalty shall be determined by the relevant High Court, taking into consideration factors including the extent of reproduction, the potential impact on the market value of the original work, and any demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner as a direct consequence of the unauthorized act. Further, where an infringement has been committed wilfully and for the purpose of undue gain, the court may award punitive damages not exceeding ten times the amount of compensation determined under this provision. The right to claim such remedies is subject to limitations regarding time, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the author's death; provided that where the work is made under the direction or control of the trade mark proprietor, and the author is an employee, such copyright shall vest in the proprietor. Any person desiring to use a copyrighted work for commercial purposes other than private study, research, or criticism must obtain prior written permission from the owner of the copyright. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application by any aggrieved party demonstrating substantial reliance and demonstrable financial loss, issue an order restraining further unauthorized reproduction if it is established that the infringing act has caused undue prejudice.

For the purposes of this Act, "notify" with respect to a proposed trade mark shall mean the act of publishing particulars relating to the application for registration in the Trade Marks Journal. Such notification shall include, but not be limited to, the applicant’s name and address, a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services associated with the trade mark, and the date of filing. The Registrar may prescribe the form and manner of such notifications as provided herein. Any person may inspect the particulars so notified under this Act at the office of the Registrar during normal business hours.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, notify any persons by way of publication in the Trade Marks Journal who claim to have rights in relation to that trade mark. Such notification shall specify the grounds on which such right is claimed and provide a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such notification within which the claimant may file written opposition under this Act. The Registrar shall, prior to publishing any notice, verify the accuracy of the information contained therein with the applicant. Provided that, where the trade mark contains a geographical indication as defined herein, additional notifications may be issued to relevant producers’ associations or authorities concerned with protecting such indications.

Where any person believes that another person is using a trade mark in violation of his rights under this Act, he may notify the alleged infringer specifying the particulars of the infringement and demanding that such infringing use be ceased. The notification shall clearly state the grounds upon which the belief of infringement is based, including details of prior registration or established reputation where applicable. Failure to comply with a reasonable request made in the notification, requiring cessation of the infringing activity within thirty days from the date of receipt, shall constitute an actionable wrong. Any party aggrieved by such failure may institute proceedings for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. The Registrar may also issue directions concerning rectification of the register if satisfied that the use complained of constitutes a violation of rights.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application under this Act for registration of a trade mark, proceed to notify any persons whose interests in registered trademarks or pending applications may be affected by the proposed registration. Such notification shall be effected through publication in the Trade Marks Journal and by sending written communication to the registered proprietors of potentially conflicting marks as identified by the Registrar’s search protocols. The written communication shall clearly state the details of the applied-for mark, including representation thereof, and the grounds upon which any objection may be raised. Any interested person who wishes to oppose the application has a period of four months from the date of such notification within which to file their notice of opposition with the Registrar. Provided that the Registrar may, at his discretion, extend this period subject to just cause demonstrated in writing.

Where the Registrar deems it expedient for the public interest, or to facilitate informed decision-making by proprietors regarding their trade marks, he shall notify any proposed amendment to the Trade Marks Rules, 1999. Such notification shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal and on the official website of the Controller General, specifying the nature of the proposed changes and inviting objections from interested parties within a period not less than thirty days from the date of such publication. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar, who may require the objector to submit supporting documentation. The Registrar shall provide reasons in writing for any decision declining to incorporate an objection. This process is subject to compliance with principles of natural justice and does not preclude further modifications as provided herein.

Where any individual or entity believes that an unregistered trademark is being used in contravention of provisions under this Act, they may notify the Registrar in writing, specifying the infringing mark, the goods or services affected, and details of the alleged infringement. Such notification shall include evidence substantiating the claim, failing which it may be rejected without further consideration. The Registrar shall then issue a direction to the concerned party to cease the infringing activity within thirty days. Failure to comply with this direction will render the individual or entity liable for damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority and subject to penalties prescribed herein. Any appeal against such a decision is permitted, but will not suspend enforcement.

Where the Registrar deems it expedient for the promotion of fair trade practices, he may notify any proprietor of a registered trademark that they shall grant a non-exclusive license to utilize the mark upon specified goods or services. Such notification shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the terms and conditions proposed for the license agreement, including royalty rates and duration. The proprietor is obligated to respond within sixty days, either accepting the terms as presented or submitting a counterproposal. Failure to respond constitutes acceptance of the Registrar’s initial proposal. Any assignment of a trademark subject to such a license shall incorporate these conditions; subsequent licensees must adhere to the original stipulations as provided herein. This power may be exercised only after due consideration of any objections raised by affected parties and is without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act.

Where any person proposes to use a trade mark in contravention of the rights of the registered proprietor, that person shall be required to notify the Registrar of their intention at least sixty days prior to commencement of such use. The Registrar may, after affording opportunity of being heard to both the proposer and the registered proprietor, determine whether the proposed use constitutes an infringement under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the notification process may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within a period of ninety days from the date of such determination. Provided that, if the proposed use is demonstrably for fair dealing purposes, the Registrar may waive the requirement to notify, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

Where the Registrar considers it expedient, he may notify any interested party regarding a proposed design registration. Such notification shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal and displayed on the website maintained by the Office. The notice will specify the particulars of the design application, including but not limited to the applicant’s name, the class of goods or services associated with the design, and representations of the design itself. Any party intending to oppose the registration may submit their objections within a period as prescribed under this Act. Upon receipt of such objections, the Registrar shall give the applicant an opportunity to respond in writing. The design registry shall maintain records of all notifications issued and objections received pertaining to pending design applications. This process is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in relation registered trade marks may apply for rectification of the register under this Act if, upon such an application, it is demonstrated that a registered trade mark has become devoid of distinctive character due to use or non-use. An application for rectification based on non-use shall be made within five years from the date of registration, provided that the applicant demonstrates continued interest in maintaining the validity of the relation registered trade. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing such non-use and its impact on distinctiveness. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the rectification application as provided herein. Further, any opposition to a rectification application shall be considered according to established procedures.

Subject to any directions issued under this Act, no person shall institute any proceedings for the enforcement of any right granted herein against the proprietor of a registered trade mark unless he has previously given the proprietor notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that such infringement be stayed. Provided that where the infringement consists of the application of a false or deceptive indication relating to goods or services, the remedies available under this Act may be sought without prior demand. The proprietor shall have a right to apply to the relevant authority for an injunction restraining any act of infringement discovered after the notice has been served. Any damages recoverable in relation registered trade mark infringement shall be determined having regard to all relevant factors including loss suffered by the proprietor and profits made by the infringer.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in relation registered trade marks may file an application for rectification with the relevant Intellectual Property Office. Such applications shall be accompanied by a statement setting forth the grounds upon which the applicant relies and supported by all material documents considered necessary to substantiate the claim. The Intellectual Property Office shall serve notice of such application on the proprietor of the trade mark, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement within a prescribed period. Upon receipt of the counter-statement, or in default thereof, the office may proceed with examination of the matter. Any party aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to rectification proceedings may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Intellectual Property Office shall maintain records pertaining to all applications and decisions concerning relation registered trade marks, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in relation registered trade marks may apply to the Registrar for registration as a registered user. Such application shall specify the geographical extent within which the use is made and shall state the reasons why the applicant did not directly use the trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the continued and substantial use of the trade mark by the proprietor, or a licensed user, prior to the date of the application for registration as a registered user. Further, an application under this Act shall be refused if it is established that the proposed use is detrimental to the distinctive character and repute of the original trade mark. The Registrar may grant such registration provided that all conditions precedent are fulfilled.

Where any person seeks to institute proceedings under this Act relating to infringement of a registered trade mark, it shall be established that such person is the registered proprietor of the said trade mark. Any false representation concerning relation registered trade marks, including but not limited to the use of confusingly similar signs, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. Further, any individual found guilty of such deceptive practices shall be liable to pay damages to the aggrieved party as determined by the relevant court. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, issue interim injunctions restraining further acts of infringement pending final adjudication under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant licenses permitting the use of their registered trade mark upon such terms and conditions as they deem fit, including but not limited to limitations on geographical territory, field of use, or duration. Such licenses shall be in writing and may be assigned or sub-licensed by the grantor, provided that any assignment or sub-licence is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Where a registered trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights pertaining to the relation registered trade as if they were the original proprietor. Further, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the continued compliance with license terms and conditions during periodic reviews. Any alteration to the scope or duration of a previously granted license must be reported to the Registrar for record.

Where an application for registration is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be on grounds that the refusal was erroneous in law or fact and that the marks applied for are distinctive in their intended field of use. Further, a registered trade mark proprietor alleging dilution of distinctiveness due to subsequent use by another party may institute proceedings before the Board, provided that such use creates confusion among consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. The Board shall consider evidence presented by both parties and determine whether a relation registered trade mark has been unfairly exploited, subject to principles of fair dealing as established under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the proprietor of a registered trade mark, record particulars relating to any person claiming right to use the said registered trade mark under license or otherwise, and such record shall be deemed sufficient evidence of the extent of such claim. Any alteration to the recorded particulars concerning a relation registered trade mark requires notification to the Registrar at least ninety days prior to the intended change. A registered patent agent acting on behalf of an applicant may submit documentation and attestations in support of any application or modification under this Act, subject to fulfilling all requirements prescribed for agents. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing these recorded relations, available for inspection during office hours as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming through the proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act as if he were the proprietor. Where a registered trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall have the same rights and powers in relation thereto as the assignor would have had if that assignment had not been made. The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming such right, direct that the name of such person be entered in the Register of Registered Trade Marks as the proprietor of the trade mark, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities. Further, patentee includes exclusive rights granted under this Act relating to inventions and designs. Any alteration to the register affecting a relation registered trade mark shall be notified to all registered users thereof within thirty days of such alteration.

Where an application for registration is made in relation registered trade marks incorporating elements already appearing on existing trademarks, the Registrar shall consider whether such incorporation constitutes a modification that unfairly prejudices the rights of the prior trademark proprietor. Such prejudice will be presumed if the applicant’s use of the combined mark creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services. Provided that, where the application demonstrates bona fide intention to utilize the composite mark and includes substantial inventive effort beyond mere aggregation, the Registrar may grant the new registration subject to limitations on permissible usage as determined by the Registrar. Furthermore, any granted new patent relating to a process utilizing the registered trade mark shall not supersede these conditions of use.

For the purposes of this Act, "subject registration trade" shall mean the grant of exclusive rights pertaining to a trademark designating geographical origin, provided that such designation accurately identifies the place where the goods originate and possess characteristics attributable exclusively to their local geography, including natural factors and human craftsmanship. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating the link between the geographic indication and the unique qualities of the goods before registration is granted. Any use of a subject registration trade mark which misrepresents the origin or qualities of the goods shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

An application for subject registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks consist exclusively of geographical indications already indicating the origin of goods. Provided that, such refusal may be withdrawn where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to the date of first publication of the trade marks journal. The Registrar shall require evidence substantiating this acquired distinctiveness, including but not limited to market surveys and consumer perception studies. Further, a registered subject registration trade mark is deemed to confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to prevent the use of identical or confusingly similar marks in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. This protection extends to colour combinations associated with the registered trade mark as provided herein.

Any person employing a subject registration trade mark in connection with goods or services shall be liable for damages sustained by the proprietor of a prior and well-known trade mark as a result of such employment, provided that the use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services. The Registrar may, upon complaint from any aggrieved party, issue an injunction restraining further use of the infringing subject registration trade mark. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute a cognizable offence and render the offender liable for imprisonment extending to two years, or a fine, or both, as determined by a competent court under this Act. The proprietor may also seek recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered user trade" shall mean the right granted to a person, other than the proprietor of a trade mark and subject to any conditions specified therein, to use the trade mark for specific goods or services. Such registered user shall be entitled to institute proceedings relating to the infringement of the trade mark as if he were the proprietor, provided that such rights are conferred under this Act and do not prejudice the rights of the proprietor. The proprietor may, by agreement with a registered user, grant further privileges concerning the use of the trade mark, but any such agreement shall be consistent with the provisions herein relating to fair competition.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, an application for registration as a registered user may be filed by any person who is using the trade mark under authorization from the proprietor of the trade mark. Such application shall contain a statement specifying the territorial extent of such use, the goods or services in relation to which the use is made, and the period during which the use has continued. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing the validity of the authorization and the continuous use of the trade mark as claimed. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to notify the Registrar of any objection to the registration of a registered user, detailing grounds for such objection. The Registrar shall consider all submissions before making a determination regarding the application for registered user trade.

A registered user seeking to exploit their right to make use of a trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting the use of the trademarked goods or services under conditions specified therein. Such licenses may include restrictions on territory, duration, and scope of permitted activities relating to the trade mark. The owner of the trademark shall be notified in writing of any such licensing arrangement prior to its implementation, affording them an opportunity to object based solely on grounds that the licensed use is detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered trade mark. Assignment of a registered user’s rights under this Act relating to their registered user trade may occur with the consent of the trademark proprietor and subject to such terms as they deem fit. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by all prior obligations undertaken by the original registered user.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered user trade" shall mean the right granted to a person, other than the proprietor of the trade mark or a licensee under a registration, to make use of a registered trade mark under conditions specified in the register. Such conditions may relate to territorial extent, goods or services, and duration of the registered user’s entitlement. A registered user shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement relating to the trade mark as if they were the proprietor; provided that such right exists only during the period stipulated within the registration. The proprietor retains ultimate control over commercial exploitation of the trade mark, subject to the terms defined in the register regarding the registered user’s rights.

An ex parte injunction may be granted by a competent court under this Act where it appears to such court that there is an urgent need to restrain a party from continuing or commencing acts likely to infringe a registered trade mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates a reasonable apprehension of irreparable injury. Such an order shall remain in force for a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of its passing, during which time the defendant shall be required to appear and show cause why the injunction should not be made absolute. Failure to do so may result in the ex parte injunction becoming permanent, subject to further judicial review as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to grant the applicant exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register, subject to any prior conflicting rights as may be established under this Act. Where an infringement of these registered rights is reasonably apprehended, the Registrar may, ex parte, grant a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts pending determination by the relevant court. Such an order shall remain valid for a period not exceeding ninety days, or until the matter is heard and determined on its merits. The applicant seeking such an injunction must demonstrate a prima facie case of infringement and irreparable harm if the injunction were not granted, provided that any party aggrieved may apply to have the ex parte injunction set aside.

Where, in proceedings under this Act, a party institutes action against another without notice to that other party, the Court may, subject to due consideration of the balance of convenience and potential prejudice, grant an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from any act which would further infringe upon the plaintiff’s registered trade mark. Such an order shall be provisional in nature and remain valid for a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of its issuance. The Court shall direct that notice of the proceedings and the ex parte injunction be served on the defendant with utmost expedition, and the defendant shall be afforded an opportunity to demonstrate cause against the continuation of the injunction within the stipulated timeframe. Failure to do so may result in the order becoming permanent, provided that the plaintiff establishes a prima facie case for infringement.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to restrain by way of injunction any person from using any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered; provided that such restraint may be granted ex parte only where the applicant demonstrates a reasonable apprehension of further infringement and immediate irreparable injury. The court shall, prior to granting an ex parte injunction, consider whether notice has been given to the alleged infringer, specifying the grounds upon which the injunction is sought, and allowing them a reasonable opportunity to respond. Any order made ex parte shall be subject to modification or dissolution upon application by the respondent.

Where a trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, and such use causes actual damage to the reputation or goodwill of the proprietor, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from continuing such use. Such injunction may be granted without previous application for leave, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates a clear and imminent threat of further infringement and provides security satisfactory to the court for damages which the defendant may sustain by reason of the injunction. The court may order seizure of goods bearing the infringing mark as part of enforcing the injunction. Failure to comply with an ex parte injunction shall be deemed contempt of court, subject to penalties as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring rights to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to the conditions stipulated within the licence agreement; such agreements may include provisions relating to quality control and territory restrictions as determined by the grantor. Assignment of a trade mark, including any associated goodwill, requires registration with the Controller under this Act and shall be deemed effective only upon such registration. Where an application for assignment or license is opposed, the proprietor may seek an ex parte injunction restraining the opposing party from taking actions prejudicial to the pending proceedings, provided that reasonable notice is subsequently afforded. The Controller may, at any time, require disclosure of financial considerations relating to assignments and licences.

Where, in proceedings under this Act relating to a registered trade mark, the defendant fails to appear or contest the allegations made against them, the plaintiff shall be entitled to apply to the court for an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing activities. Such application may be granted if the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that infringement has occurred and that damages would not provide adequate relief. Provided that, before granting any such ex parte injunction, the court shall direct that notice of the proceedings and the proposed order be served upon the defendant within a specified period, allowing them an opportunity to challenge the application should they choose to do so. The plaintiff must demonstrate due diligence in attempting service; failure to do so may render the injunction vulnerable to appeal.

Where a registered trade mark proprietor establishes that another person is using a mark identical or confusingly similar to their registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, without leave of the court, the aggrieved party may apply for an ex parte injunction restraining such use. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the facts giving rise to the claim and demonstrating reasonable apprehension of irreparable injury. The respondent shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-affidavit disputing the allegations; however, the court may grant interim relief pending determination of the substantive issues, subject to conditions as it deems appropriate. It is provided that any mark uses registered by the defendant prior to the date of application shall be considered in assessing the balance of convenience.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and it appears to the Registrar that the opponent has established a prima facie case of likelihood of confusion arising from the use by the applicant of a sign identical or similar to a previously described trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the application, the Registrar may grant an ex parte injunction restraining the applicant from proceeding further with the registration application. Such injunction shall remain in force until the determination of the opposition proceedings, provided that the applicant shall be given reasonable opportunity to be heard and present evidence in rebuttal of the opponent’s claims. The Registrar may, at any time, modify or discharge such an order as deemed appropriate.

An applicant seeking interlocutory relief in a proceeding concerning the validity or infringement of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to an injunction subject terms as determined by the court, considering the balance between the applicant’s right to protection under this Act and any demonstrable prejudice to the respondent. Such terms may include limitations on the scope of goods or services covered by the injunction, restrictions on its territorial application, or requirements for the provision of security against potential damages suffered by the respondent as a consequence of the order. The court shall also consider whether the applicant has established a prima facie case and the likelihood of success at trial when determining the appropriateness of an injunction subject terms. Further, any such injunction may be granted pending determination of the registrability or distinctiveness of a mark.

Where a trade mark is registered in contravention of section 9 or otherwise than as provided herein, any person aggrieved may institute a suit for prohibition, and the court may grant an injunction subject terms designed to prevent further registration or use of the mark; such terms shall specify conditions relating to the alteration, abandonment, or limitation of the scope of the trade mark. The court may also order that costs be awarded against the applicant found to have acted in bad faith during the application process. Further, where a registered trade mark is used in a manner contrary to section 29, and such use constitutes an unfair trade practice as defined under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief; provided that any injunction granted shall not unduly restrain legitimate commercial activity.

Where a registered trade mark is assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignee or licensee shall be entitled to enforce all rights pertaining to the trade mark as if they were the registered proprietor, subject to the terms of the assignment or license agreement. Such agreements may stipulate conditions relating to quality control measures for goods bearing the licensed trade mark and require periodic audits by the licensor to ensure compliance with those standards. Further, an injunction subject terms concerning geographical limitations on use or specific product categories may be incorporated into a licensing arrangement without prejudice to the validity of the underlying agreement. Any attempt to circumvent these agreed restrictions through deceptive practices shall constitute infringement under this Act. The registered proprietor retains ultimate responsibility for maintaining the trade mark’s reputation and may terminate a license if such reputation is demonstrably harmed.

Where a suit is filed alleging dilution of a registered trade mark by use made in relation to goods or services not identical to those associated with the mark, the court may grant an injunction subject terms as it deems appropriate to prevent all such uses which create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public and damage the distinctiveness of the plaintiff’s trade mark. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrates bona fide use prior to the date of registration, the court shall consider the extent of said use and its impact on consumer perception in determining whether an injunction is warranted. The plaintiff may appeal any order refusing or limiting injunctive relief, subject to the provisions regarding costs as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “dramatic work” shall be construed as including works which, by their nature, are designed for presentation before an audience and embody performances involving live actors, dancers, musicians, or singers. A work shall be deemed a dramatic work whether it is wholly original or incorporates pre-existing material such as literary compositions or musical scores. Provided that, where a compilation comprises both literary and dramatic elements, the copyright therein shall extend only to the dramatic components of the work, subject to any rights existing in the underlying literary matter. Any adaptation of a literary work into a form suitable for theatrical performance shall also be considered a dramatic work as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a dramatic work shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership unless proven otherwise under due process. An applicant seeking such registration must submit a copy of the script, including all stage directions and dialogue, along with a declaration affirming originality and authorship. Where a dramatic work incorporates musical elements or adaptations of pre-existing literary works, separate consents from the copyright holders of those incorporated components shall be provided as part of the application. The Registrar may require further documentation to establish authenticity, particularly in cases involving collaborative authorship or anonymous submissions. Registration under this Act does not confer any rights beyond those already vested by law; it serves primarily as a record and facilitates enforcement against infringement of copyright in the dramatic work.

Where a person without authorization performs or causes to be performed publicly any substantial portion of a *dramatic work*, that person shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed based on a reasonable royalty rate applicable to similar performances under this Act, taking into account the commercial value of the infringed work and the extent of the unauthorized use. Provided that, if the performance is non-commercial in nature and undertaken without any intention to derive profit, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded, subject to considerations of fairness and equity. Further, a right holder *may* seek an injunction restraining future performances where such actions are demonstrably likely to cause further infringement. Any person aggrieved by an unauthorized performance has standing to bring suit for relief as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a *dramatic work* shall be deemed to include any musical work which is incorporated therein and forms an integral part thereof. Any person claiming copyright in such a *dramatic work* shall furnish to the Registrar of Copyrights a detailed synopsis outlining the plot, characters, and setting, along with a list of all musical works integrated within it. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary materials deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Where an adaptation of a dramatic work is registered, the copyright therein shall be subject to the prior rights of the original author as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of such registration must be filed with the relevant High Court within ninety days from the date of publication of the register and shall be adjudicated according to established procedures. The Registrar’s decision regarding the originality of a *dramatic work* is final, subject to judicial review.

A dramatic work shall be deemed to include stage performances, cinematograph films, and works intended for broadcast or other forms of public transmission. For purposes of determining originality under this Act, a dramatic work must demonstrate substantial creative authorship in the arrangement, selection, and presentation of characters, dialogue, music, and scenic elements. Provided that incidental musical compositions incorporated within a dramatic work shall not, by virtue of such incorporation, be considered copyright infringements unless separate permission is obtained from the composer or rights holder. Any adaptation of a dramatic work into another form, such as a novelization or screenplay, shall require prior written consent from the owner of the copyright in the original dramatic work, subject to conditions regarding royalty payments as provided herein.

Any person who performs or causes to be performed publicly any *dramatic work* without obtaining license from the owner of copyright therein shall be deemed to have infringed under this Act. Such infringement is actionable at the suit of the copyright owner and may result in damages proportionate to the loss suffered by such owner, but not less than fifty thousand rupees for a first offence. Repeated infringements shall attract penalties escalating up to two hundred thousand rupees per instance. Where an infringing performance includes music or other copyrighted material, liability shall extend to all copyright owners implicated in that portion of the *dramatic work*. The court may also order seizure and destruction of equipment used in facilitating such unauthorized performances, provided that due notice is given to the accused.

The owner of copyright in a dramatic work shall be entitled to grant licenses authorizing performances and adaptations thereof, subject to the conditions specified herein. Any such license may be granted for a specific term, geographic area, and class of audience, as determined by the licensor. Provided that, where a dramatic work incorporates substantial portions of pre-existing literary or musical works protected under this Act, the copyright owner’s ability to assign performance rights shall be subject to prior consent from the owners of those incorporated works. Further, any assignment of copyright in a dramatic work must clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including whether it encompasses adaptation rights and reproduction for broadcast purposes. The assignee shall be bound by all restrictions previously imposed on the original copyright owner regarding public domain elements or fair use considerations relating to underlying material.

Where a theatrical production incorporates elements substantially derived from pre-existing musical compositions and choreography, constituting an original arrangement thereof, such production shall be considered a dramatic work subject to the protections afforded under this Act. However, it is provided that the copyright in the incorporated musical works and choreographic sequences remains vested in their respective creators or assignees, and any reproduction or public performance of the entire dramatic work which infringes upon these existing copyrights shall constitute an actionable wrong. The determination of substantial derivation shall be a question of fact for the adjudicating authority, taking into account both qualitative and quantitative factors; appeals against such determinations may be made to the appellate forum as provided herein.

The copyright subsisting in a dramatic work shall vest initially in the author thereof, but may be assigned or licensed wholly or partially to any person. Where such assignment or license is granted prior to the first publication of the dramatic work, the terms and conditions relating to royalties and performance fees shall be clearly stipulated within the agreement, and copies of said agreements are required to be filed with the designated office as provided herein. Any subsequent assignee or licensee may further assign or sub-license their rights subject to adherence to the original contractual obligations. The author retains the right to terminate any assignment after a period of ten years from the date of execution, provided that written notice is given six months prior to termination. Publication of a dramatic work without authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the publisher liable for damages.

For the purposes of this Act, a “company” includes any body corporate or association registered under the Companies Act, 2013, or any other law for the time being in force relating to companies, and such company shall be considered a juristic person capable of owning copyright. Where copyright subsists in works created by an employee during the course of their employment, the assignment of that copyright to the employer, the company, shall be deemed valid provided that such assignment is evidenced in writing and signed by the employee. Further, any subsequent transfer or licensing of said copyright by the company shall remain subject to the provisions relating to fair dealing under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, where copyright subsists in an artistic work created by an employee during the course of their employment, such work shall be deemed to be owned by the employer, provided that if the services are rendered by a company, the term "employer" shall include the company and its subsidiaries as defined under the Companies Act. The Registrar may require any entity claiming ownership under this provision to submit documentation establishing the nature of the employment contract and demonstrating the employee’s status within the organizational structure of the company. Such documentation shall be verified against records maintained by relevant governmental authorities. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence, or providing information deemed demonstrably false, will result in a rejection of registration claims related to such works.

Where a copyright infringement occurs by an act of a company, liability shall extend to both the infringing entity and any director or manager thereof who was knowingly involved in the commission of the said infringement. The company shall be deemed guilty and subject to penalties as provided herein, without prejudice to individual culpability of those officers. Any person seeking redress for copyright violation against a company may pursue remedies directly against the company itself, or alternatively, against such directors or managers whose participation is established through clear evidence. Further, where an infringement is proven, the court may order disgorgement of profits attributable to the infringing activities undertaken by the company and its implicated officers. The right to claim damages shall not be diminished due to the involvement of a company.

Where a copyright infringement occurs attributable to the actions of a company, the Registrar shall serve notice upon the designated representative of the company, specifying the nature of the alleged infringement and providing an opportunity for written response within thirty days. The company shall, upon receipt of such notice, furnish to the Registrar details of all officers responsible for overseeing copyright compliance within its organizational structure. Failure to provide this information or a demonstrably inadequate response may be construed as evidence of willful disregard for copyright law under this Act. Any individual found, through inquiry initiated by the Registrar, to have been directly involved in the infringing activity shall be subject to penalties as provided herein, notwithstanding that the company itself is also liable. The liability of the company shall not preclude proceedings against such individuals.

Where a copyright subsists in a work created by an employee during the course of their employment, such copyright shall vest initially in the employer, provided that the terms of the employment contract explicitly stipulate this allocation of ownership. For purposes of determining ownership under this Act, “employer” includes any registered company or limited liability partnership engaged in commercial activity. Where a company has commissioned a work from an independent contractor, and the agreement does not assign copyright to the commissioning entity, copyright shall remain with the contractor; however, if the contract expressly transfers such rights, then the company shall be deemed the first owner. This provision is subject to any subsequent assignment or license granted by the original owner as provided herein.

Where a copyright infringement occurs attributable to the actions of a *company*, both the *company* itself and any director or manager thereof who knowingly authorized, permitted, or was negligent in preventing such infringement shall be held jointly and severally liable for damages. The amount recoverable under this Act shall not exceed an aggregate sum determined by the relevant High Court, considering factors including the scale of commercial exploitation and the demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner. Any person aggrieved may institute proceedings seeking injunctive relief and account of profits as provided herein. Failure to comply with a court order issued pursuant to these provisions will render the defaulting party subject to further penalties, including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and potential imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where a copyright subsists in any work created by a company, the right to grant licenses or assign ownership thereof shall vest initially with the Board of Directors. Such authorization may be delegated to a designated Copyright Officer appointed under this Act, acting on behalf of the company. Any license granted or assignment made pursuant to this provision shall clearly identify the copyright owner as the said company and specify the scope of rights transferred. The terms of any such license agreement are subject to review by the Controller of Copyrights for compliance with prevailing regulations regarding fair remuneration to authors and creators contributing to the work, provided that the Board may establish internal mechanisms for ensuring equitable distribution amongst its employees. Further, a company shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all copyright licenses and assignments, accessible upon request during inspection under this Act.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that copyright infringement has been committed by a company, such allegation shall be construed as asserting liability against the said company and any individual demonstrably involved in the management or control of its operations at the time of the alleged infringing act. The burden of establishing the identity of such individuals and their respective roles in directing or authorizing the infringing activity shall rest upon the claimant. Provided that, a company shall not be held vicariously liable for acts undertaken by employees acting outside the scope of their employment, unless it is demonstrated that the company’s policies or practices directly facilitated the infringement. Any appeal against an order determining liability under this Act may only be made within ninety days from the date of such order.

Where a copyright infringement occurs through acts performed by an employee or agent of a *company*, the liability of the *company* shall extend to encompass not only direct damages sustained by the copyright owner, but also consequential losses demonstrably attributable to such infringement. The *company* may present evidence demonstrating that reasonable care was taken to prevent the infringing activity; however, failure to implement adequate monitoring procedures or training programs for employees involved in the creation or distribution of works shall be considered a factor against mitigation of liability. Any individual submitting an *application entitled breeder* for registration of a copyrighted work on behalf of a *company* shall warrant that they possess full authority to act and bind the *company*. Remedies available to copyright owners, as provided herein, may include injunctive relief preventing further infringement and recovery of statutory damages, subject to judicial discretion.

Where a copyright subsists in any work created by a company, the assignment or licensing of such copyright shall require certification from an approved proprietor certification body prior to its registration with the Copyright Office. Such certification shall attest to the authorization of the transfer by the requisite corporate governance structures and demonstrate adherence to internal policies regarding intellectual property management. A company may grant exclusive licenses under this Act, but any such license shall clearly define the scope of rights transferred and the duration of exclusivity, subject to a royalty obligation payable to the company proportionate to net revenue derived from the licensed work. Further, where a proprietor certification is required, failure to obtain it prior to assignment will render the assignee liable for damages as determined by a civil court.

Where a copyright is sought in respect of works created by a *company*, and an opposition registration is filed alleging that the work infringes upon pre-existing rights, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to all parties claiming such rights. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of the opposition may appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The *company* asserting copyright shall bear the burden of demonstrating due diligence in ensuring originality, subject to the right of the opposing party to present evidence challenging such assertion. Further, if it is established that the alleged infringement arose from actions undertaken by an employee acting outside the scope of their employment, the *company* may seek indemnity under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “convention application” means an application for the grant of a patent made in India by a person who was the inventor, or is the assignee of the invention, and who is a citizen of, or has a domicile or place of business in, a convention country. Such an application shall be deemed to be one arising out of an earlier corresponding application filed in the convention country, provided that the application is filed within twelve months from the date of filing of such earlier application. The term “convention country” includes any country with which India has entered into an agreement providing for reciprocal treatment concerning patents, as may be notified under this Act.

An application constituting a convention application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent application initially filed in the convention country, duly authenticated by the authority specified therein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a complete translation of the said document into English, at the applicant’s expense, provided that such requirement shall not apply where the initial application was filed in a language recognised under this Act as being equivalent to English for official purposes. Upon receipt of the convention application and fulfilment of all prescribed formalities, including payment of requisite fees, the Controller shall record the date of filing of the corresponding earlier application made in the convention country. The applicant shall be deemed to have disclosed all information known to them at the time of filing the convention application.

Where an applicant, being a person who was not resident in India on the date of making of the application, claims priority from a convention application made outside India, he shall be required to furnish a certified copy of the convention application and any documents relating thereto filed in the foreign country. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified under this Act will render the application liable for rejection. The Controller may, however, grant an extension of time if satisfied that there was sufficient cause for the delay, provided that such cause was beyond the applicant’s control and did not prejudice the interests of any other party. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller rejecting a convention application or denying an extension of time may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An application constituting a convention application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which the corresponding application was first made in the Convention Country, subject to the provisions regarding priority under this Act. Where an applicant has filed more than one convention application relating to the same invention, he shall indicate in each such application the date of filing and particulars of any other convention application earlier filed in respect of the said invention. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the first application made in the Convention Country as evidence of the priority claim. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified by the Controller shall render the convention application liable to be deemed withdrawn. An official fee, as prescribed, shall be payable for the furnishing and examination of such certified copies.

An application constituting a convention application shall be deemed to comply with the requirements of novelty and inventive step only if it satisfies conditions prescribed under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates that the earlier application was filed in a designated convention country. The time period for determining compliance with these requirements shall run from the date of filing the earliest application made by the applicant or any person who was the true and first inventor. Further, where an international preliminary examination is requested under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the determination of inventive step may be deferred pending the outcome of such examination, subject to regulations framed for this purpose. The Controller may require submission of certified copies of prior applications as evidence supporting compliance with these stipulations.

An applicant seeking the grant of a patent under this Act shall, if the invention has been claimed protection for in a convention application made in a designated convention country, disclose such prior claiming in the prescribed manner within three months from the date of filing the patent application in India. Failure to make such disclosure, or making a false statement therein, renders the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may result in the rejection of the patent application. Further, any person aggrieved by an order relating to the acceptance or refusal of a patent based on non-disclosure or misrepresentation concerning a convention application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person seeking protection for an invention already claimed in a patent application filed in a convention country may file a convention application in India within twelve months from the date of first filing of the said patent application. Such applicant shall disclose in their Indian application the details of the earlier patent application and the convention country where it was initially filed, including the application number and filing date. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the claim of a convention application. Assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to an invention claimed under a convention application shall be governed by the same rules as apply to assignments and licenses relating to inventions arising from domestic applications, provided that any such assignment must explicitly reference the original convention application details.
