Where any question arises regarding the priority date for the purpose of claiming invention under this Act, and such question relates to a convention application filed outside India, the Controller shall determine the matter based on the documentation submitted by the applicant. The applicant shall be deemed to have established the date of filing as claimed in the convention application only if the supporting documents are complete and accurately reflect the details recorded in the foreign registry. Any party aggrieved by this determination may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, demonstrating a substantial error in law or fact affecting their interests; provided that the appellate board’s decision shall be final.

An application constituting a convention application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which the corresponding application was first made in the Convention Country, subject to the provisions regarding priority claims. Where an international application designating India is subsequently received, the filing date for the purposes of this Act shall be determined by reference to the international filing date and the applicable priority claim as per the rules framed under this Act. The applicant making a convention application shall furnish a certified copy of the first made application from the Convention Country within such time as may be prescribed. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the application being deemed not filed, provided that the Controller may grant an extension of time if satisfactory reasons are shown. Any fees paid in respect of the corresponding application in the Convention Country shall be taken into account under this Act when determining any fee payable upon the Indian convention application.

Where the subject matter of a patent application, filed as a convention application, incorporates a plant variety protection right granted under this Act or any other law for the time being in force, the assignor of such rights shall retain the power to grant licenses relating solely to the use of the protected plant variety within the scope of the patented invention. Provided that any such license agreement must explicitly state its connection to the underlying patent and the plant variety protection right. The Controller may require proof of assignment or licensing documentation as deemed necessary for verification purposes. Further, sub-licensing is permitted subject to conditions stipulated by the assignor in writing, ensuring continued adherence to the terms of the original grant. Any transfer of rights relating to both the patent and the plant variety shall be recorded with the appropriate authorities, maintaining transparency regarding ownership and usage permissions as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board from any order passed by the Layout Design Registrar under this Act, provided that the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the said order. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Where a convention application relating to a layout design has been filed in India, the Layout Design Registrar shall be satisfied that the appellant was the true and first inventor of the design as claimed in the said application; otherwise, the appeal may be dismissed summarily. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to just cause shown.

Registration of designs relating to integrated circuit layout topographies shall be governed by the provisions herein. Any person who, with intent to deceive, makes or uses a design substantially copying any registered design, or attempts to do so, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Such offence may include the unauthorized reproduction, adaptation, or distribution of the protected topography for commercial purposes. Where the infringing act is carried out by a corporate body, every director, manager, secretary, or other officer in default shall also be considered guilty and liable for penalties as provided herein. A commission offence shall attract a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment which may extend to three years.

Where any person makes a false statement or representation with intent to deceive, or suppresses material facts relating to the invention for which patent is sought, or otherwise acts contrary to honesty and good faith in relation to the grant of a patent, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such action may institute civil proceedings seeking damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct consequence of the false representation or suppression of facts. The Controller, upon receiving credible evidence of such deceptive conduct, may issue a notice requiring the individual or entity to rectify the misrepresentation within a specified period. Failure to comply with this notice shall render the party liable for further penalties and potential revocation of any patent granted based on the fraudulent information. A commission offence shall be cognizable under the relevant criminal procedure code.

Where any individual knowingly makes a false statement or conceals material information in an application for patent, or in furnishing particulars during prosecution proceedings under this Act, such individual shall be deemed to have committed an offence. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of such falsification or concealment, issue a notice to the applicant or patentee concerned, affording them an opportunity of being heard and presenting their rejoinder. Failure to respond adequately to the notice issued by the Controller within the stipulated period shall be construed as an admission of guilt. Further, where a person abets or induces another to commit such an offence, that person also shall be deemed guilty of the same offence. A commission offence shall be triable before a Tribunal constituted under this Act and is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

Where any individual, acting either alone or in concert with others, knowingly makes a false statement or representation in an application for a patent, or suppresses material information which would substantially influence the assessment of the invention’s novelty or inventive step, such act shall constitute a commission offence under this Act. Provided that where the false statement or suppressed information relates to prior art publications available outside India, the Controller may consider the circumstances surrounding the omission and determine whether it was made with intent to deceive. Further, any person abetting or conspiring to cause such a commission offence shall also be deemed guilty of an offence and subject to penalties as provided herein. The burden of proving that the false statement or suppressed information was not made with fraudulent intent shall lie upon the applicant.

Where a patentee grants a license or assigns the rights pertaining to an invention, and such license or assignment contains provisions restricting the use, sale, or importation of the patented article beyond the scope reasonably required for implementing the permitted activities, and it is subsequently determined that these restrictions unreasonably prejudice competition within India, then a commission offence shall be deemed to have occurred. This applies irrespective of whether the patentee acted with knowledge of such anti-competitive effect. Further, any party facilitating or inducing such a commission offence shall also be liable under this Act. The right to renew a patent remains unaffected by proceedings initiated concerning an alleged commission offence; however, evidence pertaining to the restrictive clauses may be considered during renewal examination.

An opposition, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to be a formal procedure whereby any person may, subject to prescribed timelines and conditions, object to the grant of a patent application or the maintenance of a granted patent. Such opposition must be filed with the Controller within the period specified under this Act following publication of the patent application or the date of advertisement of the grant. The grounds for opposition shall include but are not limited to matters relating to novelty, inventive step, and obviousness as provided herein. Any party initiating an opposition shall be required to furnish security, if deemed necessary by the Controller, to cover costs associated with the proceedings.

Any party aggrieved by the grant of a patent may, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty, obviousness, or insufficiency of disclosure. The Controller General shall, after giving due opportunity for hearing to both the patentee and the opponent, determine the merits of the opposition. Where an opposition is successful, the patent may be revoked, amended, or affirmed as originally granted; provided that any amendment shall not substantially alter the scope of protection claimed in the application. The costs of the opposition proceedings shall be determined by the Controller General as deemed appropriate under this Act.

Where any party believes that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of the patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by a statement setting out the facts relied upon to support those grounds. Opposition may be directed against the substance of the invention itself or against the manner in which it was patented. The Controller may, after giving notice to the patentee and other interested parties, afford them an opportunity of being heard. Subject to any directions issued by the Controller, the patentee shall have the right to file a counter-statement responding to the grounds of opposition. Any decision made under this Act regarding the validity of the patent is appealable to the Appellate Board.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by such documents or information as are necessary to substantiate the claims made therein. The Controller General, after giving due opportunity for hearing to both the patentee and the opponent, may determine the matter in issue. Where an opposition is preferred, the patent shall remain in force pending the final determination of the opposition unless the Controller General otherwise directs. The decision of the Controller General concerning any such opposition shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Further, a party who fails to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein may have their opposition dismissed.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant under this Act. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty, inventive step, or sufficiency of disclosure. The Controller General shall, after providing an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to present their respective arguments and evidence in a hearing conducted as provided herein, determine whether the grant should be maintained, modified, or revoked. Provided that if the opposition is not filed within the stipulated period, or if the grounds are manifestly frivolous or vexatious, the Controller General may summarily dismiss the opposition without further inquiry.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step under this Act, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed. The Controller shall serve a copy of the notice on the patentee, who may then file a counter-statement within two months defending the validity of the patent. Failure to file a timely counter-statement shall render the patent vulnerable to revocation. Where an opposition is filed, the Controller may direct the parties to submit written arguments and evidence; any wilful suppression of material facts will attract penalties as provided herein.

Where a licensee, granted rights to exploit a patented invention pursuant to a license agreement executed prior to the publication of a notice under this Act inviting opposition, subsequently seeks assignment of the entire patent, such assignment shall be deemed conditional. The condition being that the assignee expressly assumes all liabilities and obligations pertaining to any pending or future opposition proceedings against the patent. Further, where an opposition is filed by a third party claiming rights derived from prior use or publication, the patentee may offer a counter-assignment of specific territorial rights within the licensed area to the original licensee as part of settlement negotiations. This shall not prejudice the assignee’s right to defend the validity of the patent in other respects. The Controller may require both parties to demonstrate good faith during such negotiations and ensure equitable distribution of costs incurred in defending or prosecuting the opposition.

Where any party believes that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of the patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by a statement of facts relied upon to support the objection. Subject to any procedural direction issued by the Controller, the patentee shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition within a prescribed period. Any appeal against an order passed by the Controller in respect of such opposition lies to the Appellate Board, and is subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein.

Where, following grant of a patent, any interested party seeks to institute proceedings alleging that the invention claimed in the patent infringes upon rights arising from a prior assignment or license agreement, such party shall file a notice of opposition with the Controller. The notice must specify the grounds for the opposition and provide particulars of the relevant contractual arrangement which is asserted as conferring the alleged right. Subject to provisions regarding confidentiality under this Act, copies of the assignment or license agreement may be required to be submitted by the Controller for verification. Any licensee seeking to oppose a patent based on an alleged offence reason relating to breach of contract shall demonstrate that the terms of the license were material and directly relevant to the invention’s novelty or inventive step. The Controller may grant interim relief pending resolution of the opposition, as provided herein.

“'Opposition’ shall mean a proceeding instituted by any interested party, within the prescribed period from the date of publication of a patent under this Act, challenging the grant of such patent. An 'interested party' for the purpose of initiating an opposition includes any person considering that the patented invention is not novel or involves inventive step, or possesses obviousness due to prior use or knowledge; provided that such prior use or knowledge was available to the public before the date of filing of the patent application. The term ‘clause invention’ refers specifically to a claim within a patent specification defining the scope of protection sought for an innovation.”

Where any party aggrieved by the grant of a patent may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step, and the person opposing shall provide particulars supporting their claim. The Controller shall afford an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to be heard, and may direct the presentation of evidence as deemed necessary. If, following such hearing, the Controller finds merit in the opposition, a register effect order suspending the effects of the patent may be issued pending further inquiry or revocation proceedings. The patentee shall have the right to appeal any such register effect order under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "associated trade marks" shall mean two or more trade marks owned by different entities but relating to goods or services that are complementary, similar, or closely connected. Such trade marks may be registered jointly as associated trade marks subject to an application being made in that regard and fulfilling conditions prescribed herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the commercial relationship between the owners of such associated trade marks, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the entities are affiliated through common ownership. Registration as associated trade marks does not confer any right upon one owner affecting the rights of another under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a reference to any other trade mark owned by the applicant, and such other trade mark is not identical to the mark applied for, the Registrar may require the applicant to declare whether they desire those marks to be registered as associated trade marks. Such declaration shall specify the nature of the association between the trade marks, which may include common ownership, a parent-subsidiary relationship, or a contractual arrangement for joint marketing purposes. The registrar shall publish notice of such requirement and any subsequent registration of associated trade marks in the Trade Marks Journal. Any party may object to the registration of associated trade marks under this Act within the prescribed period, subject to conditions as provided herein.

The proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to enforce rights relating to any associated trade marks against any person using a sign identical or confusingly similar to such associated trade marks, subject to the provisions regarding fair use under this Act. Where an owner has registered multiple trade marks as associated trade marks, remedies for infringement affecting one mark shall extend to encompass the entirety of the association, provided that the infringing activity demonstrably impacts the distinctiveness or reputation of any member of said association. Any party seeking injunctive relief concerning associated trade marks must demonstrate a clear likelihood of confusion among consumers arising from the use of the infringing sign. Damages recoverable in respect of infringement of an associated trade mark shall be apportioned amongst the proprietors of the individual registered marks within the association, as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority.

Where two or more trade marks are registered as associated trade marks, the Registrar shall maintain a record indicating such association and specifying the principal trade mark. Any application for registration of a subsequent trade mark that seeks to claim benefit of an earlier registration under this Act relating to an associated trade mark shall be examined with particular regard to whether such use is consistent with the character and reputation of the principal trade mark, as determined by the Registrar. The proprietor of the principal trade mark may submit representations concerning any such application within a period prescribed herein. Subject to these representations and after due consideration thereof, the Registrar may direct that the subsequent trade mark be registered only if it does not create confusion or dilution of the distinctiveness of the associated marks. Any appeal against an order made under this provision shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where two or more trademarks are registered as associated trade marks, the proprietor shall ensure that the use of each such trademark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered under those marks. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party and after due consideration of all relevant factors including but not limited to the similarity of the marks and the relatedness of the goods or services, direct that a proprietor cease using one or more of the associated trade marks if such use is deemed likely to cause dilution of another mark within the association. Such direction shall be subject to appeal under this Act. The proprietor must provide evidence demonstrating compliance with any conditions imposed by the Registrar regarding the continued registration of associated trade marks.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark has, in relation to any goods or services, also registered one or more other trade marks as associated trade marks, no person shall, without the consent of the proprietor of the primary trade mark, use any representation that is identical or confusingly similar to such associated trade marks. Any infringement under this provision shall be deemed a willful violation and subject to damages assessed at not less than ten times the actual loss suffered by the registered proprietor, nor less than fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, upon finding of infringement, the Court may order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark, as well as any materials used in their manufacture or packaging, provided that such order is consistent with principles of natural justice.

The owner of an associated trade mark shall, upon written application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, be empowered to grant a license for the use of such mark. Such license may be granted for a term not exceeding five years, renewable by further application and fee. The licensee shall adhere strictly to quality control standards as stipulated in the licensing agreement, failing which the owner retains the right to revoke the license. Assignment of rights pertaining to an associated trade mark is permissible only with the prior written consent of the original proprietor, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld. Any subsequent assignee shall inherit all obligations and conditions attached to the initial license or assignment as provided herein. The Registrar may require a record of all licenses and assignments relating to associated trade marks to be maintained for public inspection.

Where two or more trademarks are registered as associated trade marks by the same proprietor, or by proprietors who have entered into an agreement for their joint use, any challenge to the validity of one such trademark shall be deemed a challenge to the validity of all other trademarks so registered or jointly used, subject to the presentation of evidence demonstrating that each mark serves a substantially similar function within the relevant market. The Registrar may, upon receiving such a challenge, direct the proprietor of the challenged trade mark to submit an affidavit affirming the continued existence and terms of any agreement underpinning their association. Failure to comply with this direction shall be considered conclusive evidence against the validity of all associated trade marks, provided that the respondent may appeal this determination before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license to use such trade mark, and that license expressly stipulates conditions regarding the use of associated trade marks, those conditions shall be binding on both licensor and licensee. Such stipulations may include limitations on geographic territory, scope of goods or services covered by the licensed use, and quality control measures pertaining to products bearing the associated trade marks. The proprietor may assign such a license, together with its attached conditions concerning associated trade marks, subject to prior written consent from the original licensor unless otherwise provided in the initial licensing agreement. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions of the original license relating to use registered trade marks and their association. Failure to adhere to these stipulations may render the licensee liable for damages as determined under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "associated trade marks" shall mean two or more trade marks owned by different persons but used in relation to goods or services that are essentially the same, closely related, or complementary. A trade mark may be designated as an associated trade mark through a formal declaration filed with the Registrar, provided that such designation is accompanied by evidence demonstrating the commercial relationship between the owners of the respective marks. Further, where any index registered trade mark is part of a series of identical signs used to identify goods or services, the Registrar may direct their registration as associated trade marks under this Act.

Where an owner of a trade mark, being a company, elects to register one or more other trade marks as associated trade marks, such registration shall be subject to the provisions regarding joint ownership and use stipulated under this Act. The proprietor of the primary trade mark shall have the right to control the quality and consistency of goods or services offered under any of the associated trade marks. Any unauthorized use of an associated trade mark by a third party, without express written consent from the proprietor of the primary trade mark, shall constitute infringement actionable at law. Remedies for such infringement may include injunctions preventing further use and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the company as a result of the infringing activity, provided that the association is clearly indicated on all relevant materials.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" means the three-dimensional representation of an integrated circuit, reduced to a physical form by any manufacturing technique and includes both the arrangement of elements on the semiconductor material and the interconnections between them. The term “element” shall include active and passive electronic components, semiconductors, interconnects, leads, pads, bonding wires, chips, or other functional units. An application for registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the registrar semiconductor integrated, who may require such particulars as are necessary to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public order or morality. The registrar semiconductor integrated shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations under this Act.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed and include a copy of the layout-design in a form specified by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design, its functionality, or any related documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign it a registration number and record the date of filing. Any modification to the layout-design after the initial filing must be disclosed to the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated prior to publication. Failure to do so may result in objections during examination. The applicant is responsible for ensuring accuracy of all submitted details; any discrepancies identified by the registrar shall necessitate correction as provided herein.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon their registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, such person may institute proceedings before the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design. The Registrar shall have the power to pass interim orders restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity pending final determination of the matter, provided that a cogent case for infringement is demonstrated. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court. Further, the aggrieved party may seek damages proportionate to the loss suffered due to the infringement, subject to limitations prescribed by regulations framed in accordance with this Act. The Registrar may also direct the infringing party to provide an account of sales and profits derived from the unauthorized use of the layout-design.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar deems necessary for identification of the layout-design and verification of compliance with the provisions of this Act. The applicant shall furnish a certified true copy of the layout-design, in a form specified by the Registrar, suitable for reproduction. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further documentation demonstrating ownership or right to apply under this Act. Any fees prescribed therefore shall be remitted as per rules made hereunder. The Registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs may, at any time, request a personal appearance of the applicant or their representative for clarification regarding the submitted details. Failure to comply with such a request may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications and correspondence relating thereto.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated may prescribe, including a technical description detailing the functionality and architecture of the design. The applicant must demonstrate that they are the rightful owner of the layout-design or have been duly authorized to apply for registration under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment and initiate examination procedures as provided herein. Any third party possessing a relevant interest may file a notification of objection within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance order. The Registrar Semiconductor Integrated is empowered to require further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with the technical disclosure requirements stipulated under this Act.

Any application filed with the registrar semiconductor integrated shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and may be rejected if found deficient under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to filing, including providing accurate representations of ownership or prior publication, renders the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any person who knowingly makes false statements in an application before the registrar semiconductor integrated is guilty of an offence and shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, as provided herein. The registrar may also issue cease-and-desist orders against infringing activities discovered during examination.

The owner of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use, reproduction, or adaptation of the design, subject to conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be registrable with the registrar semiconductor integrated, and upon registration, create an assignable interest in favour of the licensee. The registrar shall maintain a public record of all registered licenses, detailing the licensor, licensee, and scope of rights transferred. Assignment of a license requires notification to the registrar, who shall update the register accordingly. Provided that any subsequent assignment must include express consent from the original licensor unless otherwise agreed in writing. Failure to notify the registrar regarding an assignment will render such assignment void against third parties claiming under the registered license. The registrar may require supporting documentation demonstrating the validity of the licensing agreement or assignment.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be rejected by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the design incorporates an element substantially copied from an existing layout-design. Such rejection shall be accompanied by written reasons detailing the alleged infringement and specifying the prior layout-design in question. The applicant shall then have a period of sixty days from the date of notification of such rejection to submit a reasoned response, including counter-evidence, disputing the Registrar’s findings. Upon receipt of this response, the Registrar may either uphold the initial rejection or, if satisfied that the concerns are unfounded, proceed with registration as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and such documentary evidence as the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated deems necessary to establish ownership and validity. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design or its claimed originality, and failure to comply within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Upon receipt of a request from an interested party, the Registrar shall publish notice of the pending application in the Official Gazette, inviting objections under this Act. Any objection received shall be promptly communicated to the applicant, who may submit a written response. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall determine whether to proceed with registration or reject the application. The registered layout-design remains valid for a period as provided herein, subject to published expiry notifications issued by the Registrar periodically.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it is determined that an application patent india does not meet the requirements of novelty or inventive step, the examiner shall issue a communication to the applicant detailing the grounds for objection. The applicant may respond to such communication within six months from the date of its receipt, submitting arguments and evidence demonstrating compliance with the relevant provisions. Failure to adequately address the objections raised by the examiner within this timeframe shall be deemed an abandonment of the application. Furthermore, any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant or refusal of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstration of sufficient grounds for appeal. The Board’s determination shall be final, barring further recourse under the writ jurisdiction.

Where an objection is taken by the examiner under this Act against a patent application, and such objection relates to the novelty or inventive step of the invention claimed in the application patent india, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file written arguments rebutting said objection. The Controller may require the applicant to present evidence supporting their counter-arguments, including but not limited to experimental data or expert testimony. Failure by the applicant to adequately address the examiner’s concerns within the prescribed timeframe shall result in a recommendation for rejection being forwarded to the Controller. Any party aggrieved by such a recommendation may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein, subject to payment of the stipulated fee and adherence to procedural requirements outlined elsewhere under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “services trade mark” means a trade mark used solely or primarily for distinguishing between goods and services of different enterprises. The term "services" includes, but is not limited to, telecommunications, financial services, legal services, educational services, hotel accommodation, and entertainment. A services trade mark may incorporate words, letters, numerals, shapes, sounds, or any combination thereof. Registration of a services trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the specified services, subject to any rights prior existing under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a services trade mark shall furnish particulars relating to the goods and services for which the mark is proposed to be registered, classifying such services according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend or clarify any such particulars if they are not clear or specific enough to define the scope of the services. Provided that where the application relates to services falling within more than one class, a separate fee shall be payable for each class specified in the application. Further, an applicant shall declare whether the mark is being used to indicate the nature, quality, or geographical origin of the service, and if so, provide evidence of such use as provided herein. The Registrar may reject an application if he considers that the services are not bona fide.

A proprietor of a services trade mark shall be entitled to seek relief by way of an injunction restraining any person from using or continuing to use in connection with goods or services identical or confusingly similar representations which are used in such manner as to falsely suggest an association, connexion, or endorsement exists between their goods or services and those of the proprietor. Such injunction may include orders preventing the erasure or defacement of labels, marks, or packaging bearing the infringing representation. Where a false or misleading indication has been made regarding the quality of the goods or services offered under the infringing mark, damages shall be awarded to the proprietor as provided herein, taking into account the loss of reputation and goodwill suffered by them. The Court may also order the delivery up of all materials containing the infringing representation for destruction.

An application for the registration of a services trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for and a list specifying the particulars of the goods or services associated with that mark, categorized according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend any such specification if it appears deficient in clarity or precision, provided that the proposed amendment does not substantially alter the scope of the services claimed. Any party opposing the registration shall file a notice of opposition within the prescribed time limit as provided herein, detailing grounds for objection relating to distinctiveness or prior use. The Registrar shall afford both the applicant and the opponent an opportunity to present evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. Decisions regarding registrability are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A services trade mark shall be eligible for registration if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings and satisfies all conditions stipulated under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive use of the proposed mark within India, particularly where the mark lacks inherent distinctiveness. Provided that such evidence shall be deemed sufficient if it establishes consistent usage for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of the application. Further, registration shall be refused if the services trade mark is deceptive or contrary to law, or if its use would otherwise mislead consumers regarding the nature, quality, or geographical origin of the services rendered.

No services trade mark shall be registered if it is deemed deceptive under this Act, particularly when such deception relates directly to the nature, quality, or geographical origin of the services offered. Any proprietor registering a services trade mark in contravention of this provision shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and may face an order for its rectification. Furthermore, any person utilizing a registered services trade mark in a manner that misrepresents their affiliation with, or endorsement by, the trademark owner is guilty of an offence and subject to prosecution under relevant criminal law provisions. The Registrar shall have power to issue cease-and-desist orders where evidence of such deceptive use is presented.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a services trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark to another person, either for a fixed period or perpetually, and upon such terms as are agreed between the parties. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the grantor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a proprietor has assigned their services trade mark, any license granted prior to the assignment shall continue in force unless otherwise determined by agreement between the assignee and the original licensee. The assignee shall have the right to enforce the terms of such licenses as if they were the original grantor. Further, the proprietor may require the licensee to adhere to quality control standards relating to the services rendered under the licensed trade mark, as provided herein.

A services trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark if, considering the goods or services for which the marks are used or proposed to be used, and having regard to their overall impression on the mind of the average consumer, there exists a likelihood of confusion arising as to whether the origin of those goods or services is the same. However, this shall not preclude registration provided that the applicant demonstrates clear evidence of acquired distinctiveness through extensive use following the date of first use. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to deceptively similarity may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a services trade mark relating to financial advisory services may submit evidence demonstrating exclusive use through a licensing agreement, provided that such agreement clearly defines the scope and territory of permitted usage. The Registrar shall consider whether the licensed entity’s activities genuinely reflect the nature and quality of the services as initially proposed by the applicant. Where the licensed article incorporates patented technology essential for service delivery, the application must include details regarding patent ownership and any associated royalty obligations. Failure to disclose such information may render the registration vulnerable to challenge under this Act. The Registrar retains discretion to refuse registration if satisfied that the mark’s association with a patented article creates undue confusion within the relevant market segment.

A services trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to a prior registered trade mark if, considering the goods or services for which the marks are used or proposed to be used, and having regard to the nature of those goods or services, a relevant consumer is likely to believe that the services provided under the later mark are connected with the business of the proprietor of the earlier mark. Provided that, such likelihood shall not be presumed, but must be determined based on evidence adduced before the Registrar. Any person alleging that a proposed trade mark is deceptively similar may institute an opposition proceeding as provided herein, submitting documentary proof demonstrating the existence and reputation of their prior registered services trade mark and detailing the grounds for objection to registration. The Registrar shall consider all submitted evidence in determining the merits of such an opposition.

For the purposes of this Act, an “injunction subject” is defined as a mark which, at the time of application for registration, is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the applicant seeks registration. Such similarity shall be assessed considering not only the visual appearance of the marks but also their phonetic and conceptual elements, as provided herein. An injunction subject mark may still proceed towards registration if the applicant demonstrates honest concurrent use prior to the date of application, or that no confusion is likely to arise due to differences in the goods or services indicated.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark in respect of goods or services that are identical or closely related, provided that the proprietor of the earlier trade mark may apply to restrain the applicant from proceeding with such registration. Where an injunction is sought under this Act, the court shall consider whether the use of the impugned mark by the applicant would constitute a violation of the rights of the prior registered proprietor and cause damage to their reputation or goodwill. The court may grant an injunction subject to such terms as it deems just, including limitations on territory or duration of use.

Where a registered trade mark is infringed by the use of any identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services, the court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. This power shall extend to prohibiting activities that create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public regarding the origin or nature of the goods or services. The application for an injunction may be made at any time during the proceedings, subject to the court’s discretion considering the balance of convenience and potential prejudice to either party. Provided that the plaintiff demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that irreparable injury would result from continued infringement, a prohibitory *injunction subject* to such conditions as the Court deems appropriate shall be granted expeditiously. The defendant may apply to vary or discharge any injunction made under this Act.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may apply to the Court for an injunction. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating both the similarity between the registered trade mark and the impugned sign, and a reasonable prospect that consumer detriment will result from continued unauthorized use. The Court may grant such injunction subject to conditions regarding the scope of prohibited activities, provided that it is satisfied that the applicant has made sufficient effort to mitigate any potential harm to other interested parties. Further, the Court may require undertakings as to future conduct before granting an injunction.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring specific rights relating to the use of their mark, including but not limited to rights pertaining to particular goods or services, geographical territories, or periods of time; provided that such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, whether absolute or partial, shall include all associated licensing agreements then in force unless expressly excluded within the terms of the assignment deed. Where an infringement of a registered trade mark occurs through breach of a licence agreement, the owner may seek an injunction subject to such conditions as the court deems just and equitable, including limitations on scope and duration, to prevent further harm and ensure fairness between parties. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licences affecting registered trade marks.

An injunction subject to such conditions as the Court deems appropriate may be granted against any person who, having knowledge that another’s registered trade mark is used in relation to particular goods or services, uses a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the said registered trade mark, provided that the use of such sign does not constitute infringement under this Act. Further, where the defendant demonstrates bona fide belief that he possesses the right to use the impugned mark, the Court may grant an injunction only if it determines that the likelihood of confusion amongst the relevant public is substantial and prejudicial to the proprietor’s interests. This determination shall consider factors including, but not limited to, the similarity of goods or services and the distinctiveness of the mark as assessed under section 36e ixd.

Where a registered trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark used in relation to goods or services, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst the public, a court may grant an injunction subject to just terms and conditions as it deems appropriate, considering all relevant circumstances. An application for an interlocutory injunction under this Act shall be maintainable notwithstanding that the proprietor of the trade mark has not suffered, nor can demonstrate with reasonable certainty, actual damage; provided that the applicant establishes a strong prima facie case demonstrating likelihood of confusion. The respondent may apply to amend their defence at any stage of proceedings concerning such an application permit amendment only if they satisfy the court that the proposed amendments are material and do not prejudice the applicant’s right to a fair hearing.

For the purposes of this Act, "integrated circuit” shall mean any microchip whether or not containing discrete components and includes any set of connected wires, transistors, and other circuitry elements intended to perform a specific function; “layout-design" means the three dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, layers and all other relevant information necessary for the fabrication of an integrated circuit. The term "mask” refers to a template used in the manufacture of semiconductor devices. An application for registration shall be filed with the registrar semiconductor, who may require such particulars as are necessary for identification of the layout-design and verification of its originality, provided that any confidential information disclosed during examination remains protected under this Act.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a certified copy of the mask from which the layout-design is derived. The Registrar Semiconductor may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout-design and its derivation, provided that any such request must be communicated in writing and allow for reasonable time for compliance. Upon receipt of an application meeting the requirements under this Act, the Registrar shall assign it a registration number and record the date of filing. The applicant shall be notified of the assigned registration number within thirty days. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar Semiconductor relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Controller as provided herein.

Where any interested party alleges that a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design has been infringed, they may file a complaint with the Registrar Semiconductor. The Registrar shall serve notice upon the alleged infringer, providing them an opportunity to submit their response within sixty days of such service. If the infringer fails to respond or their response is deemed insufficient under this Act, the Registrar may proceed ex parte and issue an interlocutory order restraining the infringing activity pending a full hearing. Any party aggrieved by an interlocutory order may appeal to the relevant High Court within thirty days. Compensation for damages resulting from infringement shall be determined based on the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had a license been granted, or in absence thereof, net profits attributable to the infringing layout-design, as provided herein.

Applications for registration of semiconductor integrated circuit layout designs shall be filed with the Registrar Semiconductor in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application so filed must contain a full and accurate representation of the layout design, including all layers and interconnection patterns. The applicant shall also provide a statement specifying the nature of the semiconductor device to which the layout design relates, along with details regarding its intended function. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar Semiconductor may require the submission of additional information or clarification deemed necessary for proper examination. Any failure to comply with such requirements within the stipulated timeframe will render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications received and their respective status, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed conditions regarding confidentiality.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as the Registrar Semiconductor deems necessary for identification and verification of compliance with this Act. The applicant must provide certified copies of all relevant documentation pertaining to the design’s creation and ownership, including assignments or licenses granted prior to the application date. Where an application relates to a layout-design incorporating elements previously registered under this Act, the applicant shall explicitly identify those incorporated elements and demonstrate due diligence in ensuring compliance with any applicable conditions imposed upon such previous registrations. The Registrar Semiconductor may require further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for proper assessment of the application’s validity.

Any application filed with the registrar semiconductor that contains false representations or omits material facts shall be deemed void. Failure by any applicant or registered proprietor to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein regarding the filing of documents and payment of fees will render such actions subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The registrar may, at his discretion, issue a notice requiring rectification of deficiencies within thirty days; non-compliance after this period shall result in rejection or cancellation, respectively. Furthermore, any person found to be knowingly making use of a registered layout-design without authorization shall face prosecution under this Act and be liable for damages as determined by the relevant court.

The right to grant licenses relating to a registered integrated circuit layout design shall vest solely with the registered proprietor, and such licenses may be granted subject to the terms and conditions as provided herein. Any assignment of rights under this Act pertaining to a registered layout design requires prior written consent from the registrar semiconductor, who may demand proof satisfactory to them regarding the assignee’s technical competence in handling integrated circuit designs. Further, any license or assignment shall explicitly state the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to manufacturing, reproduction, and adaptation. The registrar semiconductor is empowered to review and approve proposed licensing agreements to ensure they do not unduly restrict competition within the semiconductor industry. Failure to disclose a material alteration to an existing license agreement to the registrar may render such alterations voidable.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be rejected by the Registrar Semiconductor if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the design incorporates an element copied from a previously registered layout-design. Such rejection shall be accompanied by written reasons specifying the alleged infringing element and the details of the prior registration. The applicant shall then have a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such notification within which to submit a reasoned response, disputing the Registrar’s findings and presenting any relevant evidence in support thereof. Provided that the Registrar may, after considering the applicant's response, either uphold the rejection or proceed with registration; this determination is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar Semiconductor relating to the registration or rejection of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence presented and may, subject to this Act, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during an appeal will render it inadmissible. Further, where the Registrar Semiconductor has issued an order cancellation subsequent to initial registration due to a finding of prior use, the aggrieved party shall be liable for damages as determined by the Appellate Board, reflecting loss of anticipated profits or demonstrable harm.

The Registrar Semiconductor may, upon application and subject to payment of prescribed fees, grant permission for the assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to a layout-design that has been justified registration under this Act. Such assignments or licenses shall be recorded in the Register, noting the assignor, assignee, licensor, and licensee respectively, along with the scope and duration of the granted rights. Where a license is granted permitting commercial exploitation, the Registrar may require disclosure of royalty rates and other financial considerations as deemed necessary to ensure transparency. Any subsequent assignment or further licensing of such rights shall also be recorded in like manner. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses for public inspection, provided that confidential business information may be redacted under guidelines prescribed by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design registration certificate" means a document issued by the registrar semiconductor confirming the registration of a layout-design under this Act. A layout-design registration certificate shall contain particulars specified as relevant by regulations framed hereunder, including but not limited to the name and address of the registered proprietor, the date of registration, and a reference number assigned for identification purposes. Any certificate purporting to be a layout-design registration certificate is admissible as evidence in any proceeding under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to presumption of genuineness. The registrar semiconductor may require production of such certificate for verification.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any mark proposed to be used as a proprietor use mark in connection with the layout-design. The Registrar Semiconductor may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to such mark, including details regarding its prior usage and intended scope of application. Where an objection is raised concerning the validity or appropriateness of the proposed proprietor use mark under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit written representations in response. Such representations must address the grounds for the objection and may include supporting documentation demonstrating compliance with relevant regulations. The Registrar Semiconductor’s decision on any such objection shall be final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

The registration of copyright shall not preclude its revocation under this Act. Revocation may occur if the copyright holder has demonstrably misrepresented material facts relating to ownership or authorship during the application process. Further, a copyright is liable for revocation where the holder, following registration, fails to adequately protect the work from unauthorized use and exploitation, resulting in substantial prejudice to any person claiming rights derived from the original author. Such failure must be proven to the satisfaction of the Controller and shall be subject to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of copyright in any work, record particulars relating to the claimant and the nature of the right claimed, subject to verification under this Act. Where a registered proprietor desires to relinquish all or any part of the copyright therein specified, he may file with the Registrar a request for such relinquishment, accompanied by an affidavit verifying the intention. The Registrar shall publish notice of the intended relinquishment in the Official Gazette and proceed as if it were an application for revocation of the registration. If no objection is received within the prescribed period, the Registrar may order the cancellation of the copyright registration pertaining to the relinquished portion.

Where the Registrar is satisfied, upon application made by any person aggrieved, that the holder of a copyright has failed demonstrably to exercise rights vested under this Act for a continuous period exceeding five years, and such failure constitutes abandonment of those rights, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for the revocation of the copyright. Such application shall specify the nature of the alleged dereliction and provide supporting evidence demonstrating the lack of commercial exploitation or other reasonable use of the work during the stipulated timeframe. The holder shall be afforded an opportunity to present a counter-statement refuting the claims. Provided that, if the Registrar finds that the failure was due to circumstances beyond the control of the copyright holder, revocation shall not be ordered. Any person acquiring rights following such revocation shall be subject to all prior encumbrances and conditions as they existed before the date of revocation.

Where the Registrar receives a petition seeking revocation of a copyright registration, the petitioner shall demonstrate cause for such revocation, supported by affidavits and documentary evidence establishing material misrepresentation or fraud in the original application. The Registrar may require further clarification or submissions from both the petitioner and the registered proprietor before proceeding. Upon finding reasonable grounds to believe that the conditions for revocation are met, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to submit a written response within sixty days of the date of such notice. Any decision regarding revocation shall be made after consideration of all submitted materials and may include a hearing before a designated officer. The Registrar's order concerning revocation is subject to appeal to the relevant High Court under this Act.

The registration of copyright shall remain valid for the term specified under this Act unless the Registrar, upon application by a person demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the continued validity of said registration, determines that grounds for revocation exist. Such determination requires evidence establishing that the copyright owner has demonstrably failed to exercise control over the work in a manner consistent with the exclusive rights granted, and that such failure has caused demonstrable financial loss or reputational harm to another party claiming an interest in the work. Provided that any application for revocation must be accompanied by an affidavit detailing the nature of the prejudice and supporting documentation; the Registrar may require further evidence before making a decision regarding revocation.

Where a copyright owner has demonstrably failed to adequately protect the integrity of their work against infringement for a continuous period exceeding two years, or has persistently engaged in conduct detrimental to the public interest relating to the distribution or accessibility of said work, aggrieved parties may petition the relevant High Court. The court shall consider evidence presented regarding such failures and detriments. Upon finding that the copyright owner’s actions warrant it, the High Court may order the revocation of the copyright registration. Such an order shall be subject to a right of appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days. Any person found to have knowingly exploited a revoked copyright shall be liable for damages as provided herein.

Where a copyright owner grants a license conferring exclusive rights in their work, and subsequently assigns the entirety of that copyright to another party, the assignee shall be deemed to possess all rights expressly or impliedly granted under the original license. Provided that, if the assignor demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the licensee has materially breached the terms of the license agreement, or persistently failed to exercise reasonable care in exploiting the licensed rights consistent with industry standards, the Controller may order the revocation of the assignment. Such revocation shall only occur after due notice is provided to both the assignee and the original licensee, affording them an opportunity for a hearing. The assignor’s claim must be substantiated by documentary evidence establishing the breach or failure, and demonstrating that such actions have prejudiced their interests as copyright owner.

Where a copyright owner alleges that a registered proprietor has demonstrably failed to exercise due diligence in protecting the integrity of the work for which copyright subsists, and presents prima facie evidence supporting this claim before the relevant adjudicating officer, the officer shall afford the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard. Following such hearing, if the officer finds that the registered proprietor’s negligence has materially prejudiced the original copyright owner's ability to exploit their rights, revocation of the registration may be ordered. Provided that any order for revocation is subject to appeal before a High Court within thirty days from the date of notification; and further provided that the appellate court shall consider whether the prejudice suffered by the copyright owner outweighs the public interest in maintaining the stability of registered copyrights.

Where a copyright owner grants an exclusive license conferring rights including reproduction and distribution, and subsequently seeks revocation of that license due to demonstrable breach by the licensee relating to territorial restrictions or permitted uses as defined in the license agreement, such revocation may be sought before the Copyright Office. The Registrar shall appear at any hearing convened under this provision, presenting evidence relevant to the validity of the license and the nature of the alleged breach. Provided that the copyright owner demonstrates a clear and substantial failure by the licensee to adhere to the terms of the exclusive license, the Copyright Office may order its revocation. This power is subject to the condition that the assignee was not demonstrably prejudiced by reliance on the license’s continued validity prior to notice of intended revocation.

Where a trade mark consists entirely or substantially of a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier trade mark lawfully used in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration is sought, and it is demonstrated that such use has resulted in demonstrable detriment to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, the Registrar may entertain a petition for revocation. Such petition shall be accompanied by evidence establishing the extent and nature of said detriment. The petitioner shall bear the burden of proving both similarity and harm. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days of such order, subject to any prescribed fee.

An international application shall mean an application for protection of an invention filed in one designated office and which contains an indication that it is desired to seek protection for the invention in other countries. Such an application may contain a statement claiming priority from any earlier application or applications. The term "designated office" refers to the office specified in the international application as receiving the request for examination, and shall include offices of Contracting States under this Act. An applicant seeking protection through an international application is subject to all applicable provisions relating to patentability as provided herein.

An applicant who has filed a patent application under this Act shall be entitled to file an international application claiming priority from such Indian application, subject to compliance with the prescribed formalities and regulations. The Controller General may, in writing, specify the forms and fees required for filing an international application. An international application so filed shall not prejudice the rights of any person who has acquired a legitimate interest under this Act prior to the date of publication of the international application. Further provisions relating to the examination and grant of patents based on such international applications are provided herein, ensuring alignment with the obligations undertaken by India as a contracting state to the Patent Cooperation Treaty. The applicant shall furnish true copies of all documents filed in connection with the Indian application.

Where an applicant has filed an international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty and subsequently seeks entry of the international patent into India, such entry shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to examination and grant. The Indian patent shall be treated as if it had been originally filed in India on the date specified in the international application. Any opposition proceedings may be initiated against the international patent as though it were a complete Indian application. Where an international search report or preliminary examination is available, the Controller may take such reports into consideration during the examination process. The applicant shall remain liable for any fees payable under this Act relating to the entry and subsequent prosecution of the international patent. Provided that the priority date of the original application remains unaffected by the filing of the international application.

An applicant who has filed a patent application under this Act may, within twelve months from the date of filing the said application, make an international application in respect thereof, subject to fulfilling all prescribed formalities. Such international application shall designate each country where protection is sought and shall be deemed to be an application for patents in those designated States. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the patent application filed in India along with the request for grant of patent under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an international application has been made, any subsequent amendment to the Indian patent application shall only be permissible if such amendment is also incorporated into the international application as provided herein. Failure to do so may result in the rejection of the later-filed application. The Controller General may issue directions regarding the procedure for filing and processing such applications.

An international application filed under this Act shall be deemed to comply with the requirements of novelty and inventive step only if it meets all conditions prescribed herein relating to disclosure. The Controller may require submission of translations of any documents not originally in English or Hindi, subject to payment of such fees as are determined by notification issued by the Central Government. Where an international application claims priority from an earlier application filed outside India, documentation establishing said priority shall be furnished within six months of the date of filing the international application. Failure to provide adequate documentary proof may result in rejection of the application under this Act, provided that the Controller considers any extenuating circumstances presented by the applicant.

Where an applicant has filed an international application claiming priority from an Indian patent application, and subsequently seeks to enforce rights derived therefrom within India, such enforcement shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to pre-grant opposition. Any party aggrieved by a patent granted on the basis of an international application may institute proceedings under this Act as if the patent were originally applied for in India. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing notices of objection or conducting revocation proceedings concerning patents arising from such applications shall render those actions void ab initio. The Controller General may, upon receiving evidence of improper translation or misrepresentation within an international application’s documentation, direct a re-examination as provided herein.

Where the patentee of an invention has filed an international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, and subsequently seeks to assign or license rights pertaining to the subject matter disclosed therein, such assignment or license shall be deemed valid only if it explicitly references the corresponding international application number. The assignee or licensee may exercise rights granted as provided herein relating to the patent, or patents derived from the aforementioned international application, but shall remain bound by any obligations undertaken by the original patentee concerning disclosure requirements and freedom-to-operate searches conducted prior to grant. Any transfer of ownership or licensing agreement must be registered with the Controller within three months of execution; failure to register shall render the assignment voidable at the option of a third party possessing superior rights.

Where any person claims priority from an international application under this Act, it shall be presumed, pending determination otherwise, that the claim is valid and that the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the said priority. However, the Controller may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant to furnish a certified true copy of the international application and relevant documentation establishing its authenticity and compliance with the Convention on Patent Cooperation Treaty. Failure to provide such documents within the time specified shall render the claim open to challenge regarding novelty and inventive step. Any appeal against an order rejecting priority based on an international application shall be subject to review by the Appellate Board, considering whether due process was followed in requesting the documentation.

Where an applicant has filed an international application designating India, the Registrar shall, upon receipt of notification from the International Bureau under this Act, proceed to examine the said application as if it were a domestic application. However, any objection raised during examination based on novelty or inventive step shall be considered without prejudice to the provisions relating to priority claims arising from earlier applications. The applicant may appeal against such objections before the Controller, and the Controller’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the appellate body as provided herein. It is clarified that the India Registrar require confirmation of compliance with prescribed formalities within six months of notification, failing which the application may be deemed withdrawn.

An international application shall mean an application for protection of an invention filed with a receiving office designated under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, and which designates at least one country other than India. Such application shall constitute a single request to carry out a search relating to the patentability of the invention claimed therein. The term “international application” includes any subsequent designation of India by the applicant within the time limits prescribed under this Act. An international application may be converted into an application to apply patent invention in India, subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein.
