An applicant seeking examination of a patent under this Act shall, if the invention is also claimed in an international application designating India, furnish to the Controller, within six months from the date of publication of the international search report relating to such international application, a certified copy of the said international application. The certification shall be provided by the International Bureau and attest to its authenticity. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the application being deemed withdrawn, subject to provisions for reinstatement as provided herein. Where an invention is also claimed under a certification trade mark registration, the applicant must additionally declare that the patent grant will not conflict with existing rights relating to the said trademark.

Where an applicant has filed an international application claiming priority from an Indian patent application, and a request for preliminary examination is received under this Act, the Controller shall proceed with the examination as if the international application were a domestic application. However, any communication relating to maintainability or novelty raised during the preliminary examination stage of the international application shall be deemed to be in response to the said application only, and not to the underlying Indian patent application. The applicant may appeal against such communications before a Bench constituted under sub-section (1) of section 105. Provided that any decision rendered by the Bench concerning an international application shall not prejudice the rights or remedies available to any party in relation to the corresponding Indian patent application, should it proceed independently.

An international application filed under this Act shall be processed in accordance with the Convention on Patents and the Paris Convention. The Controller General may, upon receipt of a certified copy of the priority document accompanying the international application, direct that the application be treated as if it were originally filed in India, subject to any modifications or clarifications deemed necessary by the Controller. Where an applicant has previously sought protection for an article through registration on the design registry, such prior action shall not prejudice the examination of the patent application relating thereto. The prescribed fees for processing an international application shall be remitted electronically, as provided herein. Any request for extension of time under this Act concerning an international application must be accompanied by a duly verified affidavit explaining the reasons for delay and supported by relevant documentation. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is advertised under this Act, any person claiming to be interested in preventing the registration by reason of prior use or other rights may file a notice of opposition with the Registrar within the time specified. Such notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by supporting documentation as required herein. The applicant for registration shall then have an opportunity to respond to the notice, submitting counter-statements and evidence in their defense. A notice opposition applicant may request a hearing before the Registrar to present arguments and examine witnesses relating to the validity of the application or the opposing rights asserted. The Registrar shall consider all submissions and determine whether the trade mark should be registered.

Where an application for trademark registration is opposed under this Act, any notice opposition applicant desiring to oppose such application may file with the Registrar a written statement of grounds of opposition specifying the goods or services in relation to which the mark is used or proposed to be used, and stating generally the nature of the case. The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice on the applicant for registration, who shall have the right to file a counterstatement within such time as may be prescribed. Failure by the applicant to respond with a duly filed counterstatement shall not preclude the Registrar from proceeding with the opposition hearing. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to an opposition may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and demonstrating standing to appeal as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, any person desiring to oppose such application may file a Notice of Opposition with the Registrar within the time period as prescribed. The Notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of a Notice of Opposition, the Registrar shall promptly serve a copy thereof on the applicant for registration.

The applicant for registration may, subject to any conditions specified by the Registrar, file a counterstatement in response to the Notice of Opposition within a period determined by regulations. The Registrar may, after giving both parties an opportunity of being heard, determine whether the grounds for opposition are sufficient to warrant the rejection or modification of the application. A notice opposition applicant shall be afforded due process as per rules framed under this Act.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act by a notice opposition applicant, such applicant shall specify in their notice the grounds upon which they rely for opposing the said application. The Registrar may require the notice opposition applicant to furnish security, as provided herein, to satisfy any costs or damages that the other party may incur should the opposition prove unsuccessful. Further, where the trade mark applied for is deemed deceptively similar to a previously used trade mark, the notice opposition applicant must provide evidence of such prior use and its reputation, subject to verification by the Registrar. The application owner shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the grounds raised in the notice opposition applicant's submission before any determination is made.

Any person aggrieved by an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar within the time period as prescribed. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use and reputation damage. Failure to adequately articulate these grounds in the notice shall render it liable for dismissal without further consideration. The applicant may then submit a counter-statement addressing the allegations made by the notice opposition applicant. Any wilful misrepresentation of facts within either the notice or the counter-statement is subject to penalties as provided herein, including fines and potential prohibition from filing future trade mark applications under this Act.

Where a trade mark is subject to a notice opposition applicant, the registered proprietor shall, upon request by such applicant, provide a written undertaking specifying the territorial extent of use of the trade mark. This undertaking may include details regarding licensed territories or assignments made subsequent to registration. Further, any assignment of the trade mark, including rights relating to usage and enforcement against a notice opposition applicant, shall be recorded with the Registrar within three months; failure to do so renders such assignment void against third parties. The registered proprietor is obligated to inform all licensees and assignees regarding existing notices of opposition and any related undertakings provided under this Act. A notice opposition applicant may seek an injunction preventing use inconsistent with a previously submitted undertaking, subject to procedural safeguards as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act by a notice opposition applicant, such applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of all facts relating to the trade mark and the business or goods or services connected therewith as are disclosed in the application. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence from either party demonstrating material prejudice due to non-disclosure or misrepresentation within the original application, direct that the proceedings be suspended until such time as a full investigation is concluded. Any order made under this provision shall be subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of its communication to the parties. The applicant for registration may file a counterstatement refuting the claims raised by the notice opposition applicant, supported by affidavit.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act by a notice opposition applicant, the applicant for registration shall have the right to file a counterstatement setting forth reasons why the trade mark should be registered. The Registrar shall consider all submissions made in the notice of opposition and the counterstatement, and may afford both parties an opportunity for oral hearing if deemed necessary. Should either party fail to comply with the timelines prescribed herein, the Registrar may proceed ex parte. Any decision rendered by the Registrar concerning such opposition is subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority. Further, any aggrieved party may institute proceedings in a decree civil court seeking redressal of grievances arising from the Registrar's order, provided that such action does not preclude an appeal under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed marks are descriptive of the goods or services with which they are associated. However, an applicant may overcome this refusal by demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, provided that such use occurred prior to the date of publication under this Act. The registration sub section dictates that any alteration to a registered trade mark shall be subject to similar scrutiny as the initial application, ensuring continued compliance with the provisions regarding deceptive similarity or generic character. Further, an appeal against refusal under this registration sub section lies before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed marks are identical with respect to goods or services identical with those for which the trademark is sought and confusion likely to arise under section 29. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice, submit a reply setting out grounds upon which the application should not be refused. Upon consideration of such reply, the Registrar shall either accept the application or maintain the refusal; provided that the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the proposed marks to distinguish them sufficiently from prior registrations. The Registrar’s decision on any objection raised under this Act is final subject to an appeal under Chapter VIII. Any person aggrieved by a direction issued by the Registrar relating to the registration sub section of a trade mark may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within such time as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, “disclosed justified registration” shall mean a registration granted under this Act where the applicant has, prior to the date of advertisement of the trademark for opposition, furnished evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating continuous use of the mark within India for at least three years immediately preceding the filing date. Such evidence must clearly establish the identity of goods or services with those specified in the application and shall be deemed sufficient justification only if it is accompanied by an affidavit verifying its authenticity. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding such disclosed justified registration, provided that any request shall not unduly delay the process.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, conduct a search to ascertain whether any identical or similar trade marks are already registered or applied for in relation to goods or services that are substantially alike. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the use of the proposed trade mark is disclosed and justified by reason of honest commercial practice and acquired reputation, and that such use does not create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, registration may proceed notwithstanding any prior conflicting rights. However, registration shall be refused if the applicant fails to adequately demonstrate the extent and duration of the use relied upon for establishing said disclosed justified registration, or if the Registrar deems the mark descriptive of the goods or services.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to submit evidence and arguments justifying the registrability of the mark. Such justification must demonstrate that the proposed mark does not conflict with any prior registered marks or pending applications, taking into consideration phonetic and visual similarities as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider such submissions diligently; however, a registration shall only be granted if the applicant satisfactorily demonstrates distinctiveness acquired through use, where applicable, and provides conclusive evidence supporting the claim of *disclosed justified registration*. Failure to adequately address objections raised during examination may result in continued refusal.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to this Act, have the right to grant licenses for the use of their trade mark upon such terms and conditions as they deem fit, including but not limited to territorial limitations, fields of use, and duration. Any assignment or license granted under this Act shall be in writing and may be recorded with the Registrar, who shall maintain a register of such assignments and licenses available for public inspection. Where a trade mark has been registered following a disclosure by an applicant that their use predates prior registration, and subsequent evidence demonstrates a lack of genuine commercial exploitation during that period, the Registrar may require justification for the continued validity of the registration; this is termed disclosed justified registration. Such justification shall be provided within a prescribed timeframe or risk cancellation proceedings.

Where a trade mark is registered, and objection was raised against such registration based on grounds not disclosed at the time of application, but subsequently revealed through evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion or deception, the aggrieved party may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification. Such an application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the material facts and supported by relevant documentation establishing a prima facie case for *disclosed justified registration*. The Board may direct the Registrar to investigate the matter further and consider whether the continued existence of the registry trade marks prejudices the interests of the aggrieved party. If, following such investigation, it is determined that the registration was improperly granted, the Board shall order rectification accordingly, providing remedies including damages where applicable.

Where an objection is taken to the registration of a proposed trade mark based on grounds of deceptively disclosing reputation, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and the interested party raising the objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to file its written response addressing the concerns raised. Following consideration of the applicant’s response and any further submissions from the interested party, the Registrar may proceed with registration only if satisfied that the mark does not unfairly trade upon the existing reputation or goodwill. This determination requires a finding of *disclosed justified registration*, demonstrating reasonable consumer understanding. Any registered trade mark may be subject to revocation proceedings initiated by an interested party alleging non-use for a continuous period exceeding five years, provided that such application is supported by evidence establishing material prejudice resulting from the continued registration.

The owner of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration certificate, be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of the geographical indication for goods conforming to the standards of quality and characteristics as disclosed justified registration. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may relate to specific territories or classes of producers. Any assignment of a registered geographical indication, whether absolute or partial, shall require prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such approval will not be withheld if it is demonstrated that the assignee possesses the technical ability and resources necessary to maintain the distinctiveness and reputation associated with the indication. The Registrar may impose conditions on any license or assignment to safeguard the integrity of the geographical indication and prevent dilution of its protected characteristics.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision concerning infringement or revocation of a patent, made by the Controller, may institute an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within ninety days from the date of such decision’s communication. The appellant shall deposit before the Tribunal such sum as is prescribed under this Act, representing costs incurred by the respondent in defending the appeal. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the appeal inadmissible. Where the Tribunal finds that a patent has been infringed or revoked improperly, it may order compensation to be paid by the infringing party, subject to limitations provided herein. The appeal shall disposed of expeditiously and without unnecessary delay, ensuring fairness to all parties involved.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, uses a trademark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade marks act, or to a mark which is substantially similar thereto, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, where the infringing activity continues after conviction, such person shall be punishable with additional fines equivalent to ten times the value of the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred, as determined by the court. The Central Government may, at any time, institute proceedings against an offender under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of their trade mark upon third parties, subject to the conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such agreements may include limitations on geographical territory, goods or services covered, and duration of usage. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether in whole or in part, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, as provided herein, and shall be deemed invalid unless such registration is completed within three months from the date of the agreement. Further, where a license or assignment includes provisions for royalties or other forms of consideration, these details must be clearly documented and accessible to relevant authorities upon request. The Registrar may require additional information regarding the terms of any trade marks act licensing arrangement if deemed necessary to protect public interest.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark shall be defined as a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is used or proposed to be used in connection with goods or services to distinguish those goods or services from goods or services of others. Such marks may include words, names, symbols, devices, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, or combinations thereof. A trade mark registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and within the territory of India, subject to any rights prior thereto. The Registrar may require proof of such use as provided herein.

An application for trade mark registration shall be deemed invalid if, at the time of filing, the applicant lacks demonstrable evidence of continuous use of the proposed mark in connection with the specified goods or services within the territory of India for a period exceeding six months immediately preceding the date of such application. The Registrar may require the submission of documentary proof substantiating this usage, including but not limited to invoices, advertising materials, and sales records. Provided that, where the applicant is unable to furnish such evidence due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, they may apply for an extension of time as provided herein. Any opposition to a trade mark registration based on lack of use shall be considered only if filed within five years from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application.

An application for trade mark registration shall be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee, to the Trade Marks Registry. The applicant must specify the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark that includes a geographical indication, they shall provide evidence demonstrating their connection with the territory named in the indication and ensuring its use complies with established practices. The Registry may require further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the application's validity. Any representation of a device used in relation to the trade mark must be filed as part of the application. Opposition to registration may be made by any person claiming prior rights under this Act, within the period specified herein.

An application for trade mark registration shall be refused if the proposed mark, when used in relation to the specified goods or services, conflicts with existing prior rights under this Act. Such conflict arises where a similar sign is used for identical or similar goods or services, creating a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that such likelihood does not exist, including consumer surveys and market analysis reports. Provided that an earlier trade mark registration covers descriptive terms relating to the qualities of the goods or services, use of a substantially identical term shall be permissible only if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive prior use exceeding five years.

Any individual or entity utilizing a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, without authorization from the proprietor, shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender is liable for damages equivalent to three times the licensee fee that would have been payable had the infringer been licensed to use the trade mark, or five hundred thousand rupees, whichever is greater. Further, any goods bearing a false or deceptive trade mark registration are subject to seizure and destruction at the discretion of the Registrar. Repeated contravention may result in imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and a fine exceeding one million rupees, as provided herein.

Where an application for trade mark registration is opposed under this Act, the evidence submitted by the applicant shall be confined to matters directly relevant to the grounds of opposition raised. Provided that, where the opponent alleges prior use of a sign identical or similar to the applied-for trade mark, the applicant may submit counter-evidence demonstrating lack of reputation acquired through the use of that sign. The Registrar may, at any stage of the opposition proceedings, direct either party to provide further clarification or documentation deemed necessary for a just determination. Any direction given by the Registrar shall be final and binding subject to an appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of such direction.

An application for trade mark registration shall be deemed to be refused if, upon examination, the Trade Mark Registrar finds that the proposed mark lacks distinctiveness by virtue of its composition consisting exclusively of non-figurative elements commonly used in relation to the goods or services. Provided that, such refusal may be withdrawn if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application, supported by evidence of substantial market penetration and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall consider documentary proof submitted by the applicant, including advertising expenditure, sales figures, and consumer surveys, in assessing whether acquired distinctiveness exists. Further, an appeal against a refusal under this Act lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to include any reproduction of a protected work without authorization from the owner of copyright therein. Such reproduction may take the form of printing, engraving, lithography, photography, mimeograph or any other process whatsoever. An infringing copy also includes works that substantially reproduce elements of the original work, even if alterations are made, provided that such alterations do not constitute a new work under this Act. The determination of substantial similarity shall be based on qualitative and quantitative assessment of the relevant features as provided herein. Copies made for private or domestic use are excluded from being considered an infringing copy unless they are distributed commercially.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to copyright under this Act, registration of a work shall be prima facie evidence of ownership. Where an application for registration has been duly filed and accepted, any subsequent reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of that work without authorization from the registered owner constitutes an infringing copy. Provided that, where multiple individuals claim joint authorship of a work, only one individual may apply for registration; such applicant shall declare the names and addresses of all co-authors as recorded in the application form. Further, any alteration to the submitted material after acceptance will invalidate the registration and render subsequent use thereof actionable as an infringing copy subject to appeal before the relevant adjudicating officer.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and sold without authorization from the owner of copyright, such owner shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by him as a consequence thereof. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the infringement, the flagrancy of the defendant’s conduct, and any profits earned by the infringer attributable to the infringing copy. Provided that, in cases where the infringing copy was made for private or domestic use without any commercial gain, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded, subject to considerations of fairness and equity. Further, the owner shall be entitled to an injunction restraining the defendant from further making, selling, importing, or distributing such infringing copies, as provided herein.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and offered for sale or distributed without authorization under this Act, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief. Such proceedings shall be brought before a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The court may, upon being satisfied that an infringing copy exists and has been made in violation of the provisions herein, grant temporary injunctions restraining the defendant from further acts of reproduction, distribution, or sale. It is provided that any party seeking such relief shall furnish security to compensate the other party for losses incurred as a result of the injunction. The court may also order the destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation, subject to due process considerations. Further, evidence presented demonstrating commercial exploitation of the infringing copy will be given significant weight during proceedings.

Where a work has been reproduced without authorization from the copyright holder, and such reproduction substantially replicates the original work’s protected elements, it shall be deemed an infringing copy. Provided that, where the alleged infringing copy incorporates only minor alterations to the original work's arrangement or presentation, and those alterations do not constitute transformative creativity as defined under this Act, a determination of infringement may require consideration of whether such alterations were undertaken in good faith for purposes of adaptation or improvement. Further, if the reproduction was made solely for private use and is not offered for commercial gain, it shall be subject to review regarding potential exemptions as provided herein. Any party claiming an infringing copy must demonstrate proof of copyright ownership and evidence of unauthorized reproduction.

Any person found to be wilfully making an infringing copy of a registered sound recording without authorization from the owner shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include not only direct pecuniary loss suffered by the owner but also any profits made by the infringer as a result of the infringement, provided that the Court may award exemplary damages in cases where the infringement is particularly egregious or malicious. Further, an infringing copy manufactured or distributed in violation of this Act may be seized and destroyed at the discretion of the authorized officer. The owner shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages and injunction against any person engaging in such unauthorized reproduction.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in an artistic work may grant a license permitting the reproduction and distribution of that work, specifying the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, either wholly or partially, and the assignee shall possess all rights granted under the original license agreement. Where a licensed copy is made without authorization, constituting an infringing copy of the original artistic work, the licensor may pursue remedies available under this Act against both the unauthorized reproducer and any distributor of such infringing copies. Provided that, where the reproduction is incidental to the lawful use of the original work as permitted by another license or exemption, it shall not be deemed an infringement unless explicitly prohibited within the terms of that other license. The terms of assignment shall govern the relationship between assignor and assignee regarding enforcement actions.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and distributed without due authorization from the owner of copyright therein, such distribution shall be deemed to constitute a violation under this Act. The aggrieved owner may institute proceedings in a court of competent jurisdiction seeking injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered as a result thereof. Provided that, where the defendant claims fair dealing for purposes of research or private study, the burden shall lie upon them to demonstrate such use falls within permissible limitations as provided herein. Any order restraining distribution may be appealed to an appellate forum established under this Act, subject to satisfaction of conditions regarding security and maintainability of appeal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where an infringing copy of a copyrighted work has been made by virtue of a license granted under section 33, the grantor of such license shall be deemed the owner for the purposes of assignment and transmission. Provided that any subsequent assignee of the copyright in the original work may apply to the relevant High Court seeking clarification regarding the scope and duration of the initial license agreement. The High Court may, after hearing all concerned parties, issue an order clarifying whether the infringing copies produced under the license constitute a permissible exercise of the granted rights or represent an unauthorized expansion beyond the terms stipulated therein. Further, any party aggrieved by such an order may seek review through an 112a order appellate process before a division bench of the High Court. This provision aims to ensure clarity and fairness in licensing arrangements concerning copyrighted material.

For the purposes of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to include any reproduction of a protected work without authorization from the copyright owner, except where such reproduction falls within the scope of fair dealing as provided herein. This definition extends to works subject to international registration sub-applications filed under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works, where the application designates India as a territory of protection. Any adaptation or translation of a work without due license constitutes an infringing copy. The reproduction need not be identical; it is sufficient if it substantially replicates the original work’s expression, subject to considerations of originality and transformative use.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and sold without authorization from the owner of copyright, such owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. The remedies available under this Act include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a consequence of the unauthorized reproduction or distribution. Further, where the infringing copy is a publish translation of an original work, the assessment of damages shall take into consideration the reasonable value that would have been obtained from such publication had it been authorized. The court may also order the destruction of all infringing copies and materials used in their creation, subject to any regulations prescribed by the Government. This provision applies irrespective of whether the infringement was committed knowingly or negligently.

Where any work is knowingly reproduced or distributed without authorization from the owner of copyright therein, and such reproduction or distribution constitutes a commercial use of the said work, then any person found guilty thereof shall be liable for damages as determined by the competent court. This liability extends to individuals directly involved in the unauthorized act, including those who procure, counsel, or aid in its commission. Further, if the infringement is committed by an employee acting within the scope of their employment, the employer may also be held accountable, subject to demonstrating that reasonable measures were not taken to prevent such infringing activity. An offence shall liable to a fine which may extend to rupees five lakhs and imprisonment for a term up to three years, or both, as provided herein.

Where any person is found to have knowingly reproduced or distributed a work in violation of the provisions relating to copyright infringement under this Act, such person shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees but not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Further, where the infringement involves commercial gain and demonstrates a pattern of disregard for the rights of the copyright owner, the court may also order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Any individual found guilty of abetting such an offence shall likewise be liable to similar penalties as provided herein. It is further stipulated that any entity employing individuals engaged in these unlawful activities shall also be deemed accountable and subject to prosecution; an offence shall liable for fines up to one million rupees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “derivative work” shall mean any work based upon or derived from the original copyrighted work, including but not limited to translations, adaptations, arrangements, and alterations thereof; provided that such derivative work shall retain sufficient originality to warrant copyright protection as an independent work. Where an infringement of copyright occurs through acts committed by multiple individuals in concert, each individual participating in said infringing activity shall be deemed guilty of a commission offence notwithstanding the fact that the ultimate product or benefit derived from the infringement is attributable to a single entity. This determination shall not preclude further action under any other law for aiding and abetting.

Where an application for registration of a literary work, musical work, or dramatic work is found to contain elements substantially copied from another registered work, and such copying constitutes an infringement under this Act, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring the applicant to demonstrate due diligence in securing necessary permissions. Failure to comply with such notice within the prescribed period shall render the application liable for rejection. Notwithstanding any action taken by the applicant following receipt of said notice, if it is subsequently determined that the work was registered through fraudulent misrepresentation or commission offence notwithstanding lawful attempts at rectification, the registration may be revoked as provided herein.

Where a copyright owner reasonably believes that any work has been infringed under this Act, they may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such proceedings shall include claims for damages sustained by the owner as a direct result of the infringement, calculated according to prevailing market rates or lost profits, whichever is higher. Further, injunctive relief may be granted restraining further acts of infringement, subject to just terms and conditions determined by the Court. It is provided that any person found guilty of an offence relating to copyright infringement, whether acting alone or in concert with others, shall remain liable for all associated damages irrespective of their corporate status or purported lack of direct involvement. This applies even where such actions were undertaken pursuant to instructions from a superior officer; a commission offence notwithstanding, individual responsibility remains paramount and enforceable under this Act.

Where an infringement of copyright has occurred outside India, but the infringer or authorising agent thereof had a place of business within India at the time of the infringement, proceedings for enforcing any right under this Act may be instituted in India as if the infringement had occurred within India. The Appellate Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar relating to requests for transborder rights enforcement. Any person found guilty of an offence involving copyright infringement, whether acting alone or jointly with others, shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. This liability extends to corporate entities where the act was committed with the knowledge or consent of its officers. A commission offence notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, a person assisting in the commission of such an offence shall be deemed as guilty and subject to penalties equivalent to those applicable for direct infringement.

Where an act constituting infringement of copyright is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, both such person and the one directing or controlling him shall be deemed guilty of said offence. This provision applies irrespective of whether the infringing material was created within India or imported into India; furthermore, it extends to acts performed in relation to works first published outside India. The liability stipulated herein shall not preclude prosecution of either party individually. A commission offence notwithstanding any contract, agreement, or understanding between parties, each individual participating in the infringement remains subject to penalties as provided herein. Any person assisting in the commission of such an act may also be deemed guilty and liable accordingly.

Where any person is found to have infringed copyright in a musical work or cinematograph film, or facilitated such infringement, whether by way of reproduction, distribution, public exhibition, or otherwise as provided herein, the Appellate Tribunal may, subject to appeal under this Act, impose a pecuniary penalty not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Further, where an offence relating to copyright infringement is committed outside India but has effects within India, any person found responsible for such actions shall be deemed guilty of a commission offence notwithstanding that such person was not present in India at the time of the act constituting the offence. The Tribunal may also order seizure and forfeiture of equipment used or intended to be used for the purpose of infringing copyright.

Where an act constituting infringement of copyright is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, such other person shall be deemed to be guilty of commission offence notwithstanding that they were not directly involved in the physical reproduction or dissemination of the copyrighted work. An appeal against any conviction or order made under this provision may be filed within sixty days from the date of such conviction or order before the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the offence was committed, and shall be governed by the provisions relating to appeals as provided herein. The appellate authority may, after hearing all parties involved, confirm, vary, or set aside any such order; however, the finding of guilt established at trial shall stand unless affirmatively challenged and substantiated on appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, a “derivative work” is defined as a work based upon one or more pre-existing works, subject to the condition that such derivative work incorporates sufficient originality to warrant copyright protection independently. The reproduction, adaptation, or translation of any work shall be deemed a derivative work unless it can be demonstrated that the resulting creation constitutes an independent artistic expression. Registration shall cease for any work found, through judicial determination, to be substantially infringing upon another copyrighted work; such finding is conclusive evidence against continued validity of registration. A commission offence notwithstanding any other provision under this Act, liability extends to all individuals knowingly participating in the infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, "prevent commission offence" with respect to copyright infringement shall mean any act or omission undertaken by a person with the primary intention of obstructing or hindering the enforcement of copyright as provided herein. Such acts may include, but are not limited to, the willful destruction or alteration of records pertaining to copyright ownership; the dissemination of false information concerning the availability or legality of works protected under this Act; and the deliberate misrepresentation of facts intended to mislead investigators engaged in ascertaining whether a prevent commission offence has occurred. Subject to any orders issued by an Adjudicating Officer, liability for such offences shall be determined according to established principles of vicarious responsibility.

The Registrar may, upon receipt of a complaint regarding an alleged infringement of copyright, initiate inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the creation and registration of the work. Such inquiries shall focus on determining whether the actions complained of constitute a prevent commission offence under this Act, particularly concerning unauthorized reproduction or distribution prior to formal registration. The complainant shall be required to submit evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that an infringing act has occurred or is likely to occur. Further, any person claiming ownership of copyright in the work subject to the complaint may present counter-evidence relating to the originality and validity of their claim, as provided herein. The Registrar’s findings are binding subject to appeal before the relevant judicial forum.

Where a person, acting either alone or in concert with others, undertakes an act infringing upon copyright in any work, and such act would constitute an offence under this Act but is prevented from full completion by intervention of law enforcement agencies or other lawful means, the individual so engaged shall be deemed to have attempted to commit that offence. The remedies available for a prevent commission offence are identical to those prescribed for completed offences, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further action and recovery of damages sustained by the copyright owner as a direct consequence of the thwarted infringement. It is provided that any evidence obtained during the prevention of such an act shall be admissible under this Act subject to standard rules of procedure. The court may also order compensation for loss of reputation suffered by the copyright holder due to publicity surrounding the attempted violation.

Where a person is found to have contravened any provision relating to copyright under this Act, an investigating officer duly authorized by the Controller may serve upon such person a notice requiring him or her to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified therein to show cause why he or she should not be deemed guilty of a prevent commission offence. The notice shall specify the particulars of the alleged infringement and the relevant provisions contravened. Failure to appear as directed, or failure to provide satisfactory explanation, may result in the Controller proceeding ex parte against the person concerned. Any evidence obtained during investigation, including digital records seized under warrant, shall be admissible before the Controller. The Controller shall record his findings and order appropriate remedies, which may include monetary penalties and directions for cessation of the infringing activity.

Where a work has been communicated to the public without authorization under this Act, any person who subsequently reproduces, distributes, exhibits or performs such work, knowing that it has been so unlawfully communicated, shall be deemed to have committed a prevent commission offence. This obligation applies irrespective of whether the initial unauthorized communication was undertaken for commercial gain or otherwise. Provided that, if the subsequent reproduction, distribution, exhibition or performance is done solely for private and non-commercial use by an individual, without any intention to profit therefrom, such person shall not be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. The burden of proving knowledge of the prior unlawful communication shall lie upon the prosecution.

Where any person is found to have reproduced a substantial portion of a cinematograph film without authorization, or has distributed copies thereof for commercial gain, such act constitutes a prevent commission offence under this Act. The offender shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. Further, any person abetting the aforementioned reproduction or distribution shall also be liable for prosecution and punishment as if they were the principal offender. It is provided that in determining whether reproduction constitutes a prevent commission offence, due consideration shall be given to the scale and nature of the unauthorized activity undertaken.

Where a copyright owner desires to grant a license or assignment of their exclusive rights in a work, they may execute a written instrument specifying the scope of such permission, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to any restrictions expressly stated within the licensing agreement itself. The owner retains the right to define permissible uses and geographical limitations for each granted license. Any party receiving an assignment of copyright is deemed a successor in title and inherits all rights and obligations pertaining to the work as provided herein. Failure to adhere to the terms stipulated in a validly executed license or assignment shall constitute a prevent commission offence, rendering the infringing party liable for damages and injunctive relief.

Where a work is found to have been reproduced without authorization, any person alleging such infringement may initiate proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The defendant shall bear the burden of demonstrating reasonable belief in the absence of copyright or other lawful justification for the reproduction. However, where the defendant claims that the alleged infringing act was undertaken unknowingly, it shall be presumed that they acted with due diligence unless proven otherwise by the plaintiff. This presumption is rebuttable and subject to challenge through presentation of counter-evidence. The determination of whether a *prevent commission offence* has occurred rests upon careful consideration of all presented facts and arguments, and any appeal against such determination may be made within sixty days.

Where a person, without authorization from the copyright owner, reproduces, distributes, or communicates any work protected under this Act, constituting a prevent commission offence, they shall be subject to civil remedies as provided herein. Such unauthorized acts may include the creation of derivative works substantially based on the original copyrighted material. The aggrieved copyright owner has the right to seek an injunction restraining further infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the infringing activity. Further, any person assisting or abetting such infringement shall also be liable for civil penalties. Cognizance offences relating to the falsification of records pertaining to copyright ownership may be taken by a judicial magistrate first class. The court may order the destruction of infringing copies and materials as part of its judgment.

Any individual or entity engaged in the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of works protected under this Act, including but not limited to literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, shall be deemed to have committed a prevent commission offence. Upon receiving a complaint from the owner of copyright or an authorized agent, any police officer may investigate such alleged infringement and seize infringing copies and materials found in connection therewith. The seized material shall be produced before a designated judicial magistrate within forty-eight hours of seizure. Where the work is associated with a registered geographical indication, indicating origin from a specific region of India, the severity of penalties for unauthorized use or reproduction will be enhanced as determined by the adjudicating officer. Further, any person found to have facilitated such an offence shall also be subject to prosecution and appropriate sanctions under this Act.

Where a person is found to have reproduced any work without authorization under this Act, constituting a prevent commission offence, the Copyright Enforcement Authority may issue a notice requiring the individual to demonstrate due diligence in preventing further infringement. Such demonstration shall include providing records of employee training on copyright awareness and implementation of technological measures designed to restrict unauthorized access or distribution. If the authority determines that reasonable precautions were not taken, it shall direct the person to submit an undertaking detailing remedial actions within thirty days. Failure to comply with this direction will result in a hearing wherein the Registrar shall appear as a witness to present evidence regarding the extent and nature of the infringing activity.

The Controller shall maintain separate registers for each class of inventions, detailing particulars relating to applications filed, patents granted, sealed patents, lapsed patents, and requests for restoration under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an entry in the register may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The register shall be open to public inspection during office hours, subject to such conditions as the Controller deems necessary to prevent abuse or interference with the due functioning of the office. Information pertaining to pending applications shall not be disclosed until the date of grant or refusal, whichever occurs first. Maintaining an accurate and comprehensive means register is paramount for ensuring transparency and facilitating informed decision-making by stakeholders within the patent ecosystem.

Any party aggrieved by an entry appearing in the public means register relating to a patent shall have the right to apply to the Controller for rectification of that entry. Such application may be made on grounds including but not limited to errors apparent on the face of the record, alterations arising from subsequent judicial decisions, or demonstrable inaccuracies impacting the legal validity of the patent’s registration. The Controller shall afford the applicant and any other interested party a reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. Failure by the Controller to determine such an application within six months from the date of its receipt will constitute deemed refusal, entitling the aggrieved party to seek redress under this Act through appropriate legal proceedings. The rectification shall not prejudice existing rights as provided herein.

Where any patentee desires to grant a license to use or exercise a patented invention, or assign the entire interest in such patent, it shall be his duty to enter particulars of such license or assignment in the means register maintained under this Act. The application for entry shall specify the licensee’s or assignee's name and address, the extent of the rights granted or assigned, and the consideration, if any, paid therefor. Subject to an appeal being filed within sixty days from the date of registration, such entries shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of the license or assignment as provided herein. Any person seeking to obtain a license or assign a patent may inspect the means register for details pertaining to existing licenses and assignments. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the terms of any proposed transaction affecting rights in registered patents.

Any party aggrieved by an entry made in the public means register relating to a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Controller within sixty days of such entry’s publication. The Controller may, after affording the patentee and the aggrieved party an opportunity for being heard, direct rectification of the register if satisfied that the entry is erroneous or contrary to the provisions of this Act. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this section by any person shall be deemed a contempt of the Controller and subject to a sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. Provided that an appeal under this provision does not operate as a stay of the operation of the entry in question, unless the Controller otherwise directs. The rectification process is without prejudice to other remedies available under law.

The Controller may, upon application by the patentee or assignee, grant a license to utilize the invention for which a patent has been registered, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit, provided that the applicant demonstrates compelling reasons justifying the need for such licensing. Any assignment of the patent, including the right to grant licenses under this Act, shall be recorded in the means register maintained by the Patent Office, and such recording shall vest validity upon the assignee’s entitlement to exercise all rights pertaining to the patented invention. Further, where a license is granted involving the use of a registered trade mark associated with the patented process or product, the Controller may stipulate conditions ensuring that the licensee adheres to quality standards equivalent to those maintained by the patentee. The fees for recording assignments and licenses shall be as prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered user layout” means a layout-design which has been duly registered under this Act and for which a person other than the initial registrant has been entered as a registered user. A registered user layout shall confer upon the registered user the right to exploit the layout-design commercially in accordance with the terms of registration, subject to any conditions specified therein. The rights conferred by a registered user layout are not exclusive against the prior owner or proprietor unless expressly stated otherwise during the registration process. Any assignment or transmission of a registered user layout shall be recorded as provided herein and shall be deemed valid only upon such recording.

An applicant seeking registration as a registered user layout shall furnish, along with the application, a detailed technical specification outlining the intended use and manufacturing processes relating to the layout-design. The Registering Authority may require further clarification or demonstration of these processes at any stage during examination. Where an existing registered proprietor grants permission for another party to become a registered user layout, such permission must be documented in a formal agreement filed with the Registrar, detailing the scope and duration of the permitted use. Any alteration to this agreement requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days. The rights conferred upon a registered user layout are subject to the terms stipulated by the proprietor’s original registration and as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions regarding fair use, a registered user layout shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating the said layout-design, and to exploit such layout-design commercially. Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, directly or indirectly makes, imports, sells, hires, or offers to sell or hire any integrated circuit embodying a registered user layout shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the court, taking into account the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a result of the infringement and considering any profits made by the infringer. Further, the registered proprietor may apply to the relevant judicial authority seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity, provided that such application is made within three years from the date of first exploitation of the layout-design.

An application for registration as a registered user layout shall be made to the Controller within six months from the date of first commercial exploitation of the layout-design, or where such exploitation has not occurred, within three years from the date of its initial publication. The application must specify the nature and extent of the use sought by the applicant, and provide evidence demonstrating a substantial investment in resources directly attributable to the utilization of the registered layout-design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may require further information or clarification regarding the proposed usage. Any objection to the registration of a registered user layout shall be filed within thirty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The Controller shall afford all parties an opportunity for hearing before making any determination concerning the validity of the registration.

A person shall be eligible to apply for registration as a registered user layout where such person has, prior to the date of application, lawfully manufactured integrated circuits incorporating the layout-design. The applicant must demonstrate continuous and uninterrupted use of the layout-design for commercial purposes for a period not less than three years preceding the application; provided that this requirement shall be waived in cases where the applicant can prove exceptional circumstances hindering such continued use. Registration as a registered user layout does not confer any right to exclude other persons from manufacturing integrated circuits incorporating the same layout-design, subject to compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act regarding reverse engineering and permitted acts. The Registrar may require submission of detailed production records to verify adherence to these conditions.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of a registered layout design, imports into India, manufactures for sale, distributes, hires or offers to hire, displays for sale, or otherwise deals with any integrated circuit embodying a registered user layout shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be determined by the Controller and may include compensation for loss of profits, reasonable costs incurred in enforcing rights under this Act, and an account of profits made as a result of the infringing activity. The owner may also apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating that irreparable harm would otherwise ensue. Repeated or flagrant violations shall attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

A registered user layout, having obtained a license to utilize a protected integrated circuit layout-design under this Act, shall be subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. Such agreements may include provisions regarding royalty payments, duration of use, and permitted geographical territories for exploitation of the layout-design. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered user layout is permissible, provided that prior written consent from the registered proprietor is obtained; this consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, any subsequent license granted by the registered user concerning the layout-design must accurately reflect the scope and limitations initially defined within the original agreement with the registered proprietor. The registered user’s obligations as provided herein are binding on all successors in title to their rights.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a registered user layout shall cease to confer rights under this Act upon the expiry of the term for which it was initially registered, or upon revocation thereof. Any person aggrieved by an order revoking a registered user layout may within sixty days from the date of such order prefer an appeal to the Tribunal. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. It is provided that the determination of whether a person qualifies as a registered user layout shall be subject to judicial review only on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record.

Any person who, having knowledge of a registered user layout, and without due authorization from the registered design owner, manufactures, imports, distributes, sells or offers to sell any product embodying the said layout shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the cost of reproduction of the integrated circuit, nor exceeding fifty times such cost, as determined by the Controller. Where a registered user layout has been extended through international registration under the provisions of the Paris Convention or any other treaty to which India is a party, infringement occurring within the territory of another contracting state shall be actionable in Indian courts subject to reciprocal arrangements. The remedies available to the registered design owner are without prejudice to any criminal prosecution that may be initiated.

Subject to the provisions relating to national security, a registered user layout shall not be assigned without prior written consent from the original proprietor of the semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. Such consent may be granted unconditionally or subject to terms and conditions as deemed appropriate by the proprietor, including but not limited to royalty payments and restrictions on field of use. Where an assignment is made with infringement patent granted against a third party, the registered user shall provide annual reports detailing utilization of the layout-design and any instances of suspected unauthorized reproduction. Further, under this Act, the proprietor may grant non-exclusive licenses for exploitation of the registered user layout to other entities, provided that such licenses do not conflict with existing assignments or impede the rights of the registered user as defined herein. Any sub-licensing shall require explicit authorization from both the proprietor and the registered user.

The right to seek redress under this Act concerning infringement relating to a registered user layout shall not preclude such registered user from pursuing remedies available under international treaties, provided that the claimant demonstrates standing as a beneficiary of protection afforded through accession to the Madrid Protocol. Any determination by the Registrar regarding the validity of a registered user layout may be appealed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the Appellate Board shall consider whether the registration was improperly granted considering the requirements for originality and freedom from prior publication. Further, any party aggrieved by an appellate board decision concerning a registered user layout may petition the Supreme Court on grounds limited to questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered user layout” means a layout-design which has been assigned to a person who is registered as a user under section 10, and such assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Layout-Designs. A registered user layout confers upon the assignee the right to exploit commercially the layout-design subject to the terms and conditions specified in the assignment agreement filed with the Registrar. The rights granted to a registered user layout holder are not absolute and may be limited by any prior registration or existing license agreements pertaining to the original layout-design, as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer of interest in a registered user layout shall also be recorded in the Register.

An applicant seeking registration as a registered user layout shall furnish, along with the application, detailed specifications pertaining to the intended use and reproduction of the layout-design. The Controller General may require submission of samples demonstrating adherence to established mark regulations concerning identification and differentiation from existing integrated circuits. Further, an individual already designated as a registered user layout may apply for modification of their registration under this Act, provided that such modifications do not substantially alter the original layout-design’s functionality or intended purpose. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all registered user layouts, including particulars of any subsequent amendments or changes to the initial application.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of this Act, means a distinct name assigned to a plant variety by its breeder or registrant, subject to the guidelines prescribed by the Authority. Such denomination shall be readily recognizable and serve as an identifier for that particular variety in commerce and records maintained under this Act. The denomination may incorporate elements reflecting characteristics of the variety, its origin, or the breeder’s identity, provided that it does not falsely suggest properties or qualities of the plant. No two registered varieties shall share a common denomination; applications proposing identical denominations shall be rejected as provided herein.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall include a statement affirming that the proposed denomination is not descriptive of the plant’s characteristics, essentially similar to other registered varieties, nor does it contain any element likely to cause confusion with existing denominations under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further details regarding the distinctiveness and stability of the denomination variety if there arises doubt concerning its compliance with these requirements. Provided that, an applicant seeking registration for a denomination variety derived from another registered variety shall disclose the parent variety’s name in the application. Further, any alteration or modification to the proposed denomination after submission requires prior written consent from the Registrar.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of a denomination variety registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in relation to the order and may, after affording the appellant and the respondent an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Subject to this, the Board’s decision shall be final. Further, where a denomination variety is found to infringe upon the rights of another person under this Act, the Authority may direct the registrant to cease using the infringing denomination and pay compensation as determined by the Authority. Provided that such determination shall not prejudice any right of action available to the aggrieved party in civil court.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a proposed denomination for that variety, accompanied by a reasoned statement justifying its distinctiveness and suitability as a *denomination variety*. The Authority may require an applicant to alter or reject a proposed denomination if it finds that it is descriptive of the variety’s characteristics, generic, deceptive, or contrary to public order. Further, any denomination already in use for another plant variety registered under this Act, or pending registration, shall be deemed unsuitable and rejected by the Authority. The Registrar shall maintain a register of denominations assigned to registered varieties, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein. An appeal against an order rejecting a proposed denomination may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order.

A person applying for registration of a plant variety shall propose a denomination that is not descriptive of the variety’s characteristics, nor suggestive of its origin or use. The proposed denomination must also be distinct from any existing denomination already registered under this Act or applied for with pending consideration. Further, it shall not comprise any trademark or geographical indication protected as provided herein. Where an application proposes a denomination deemed non-compliant by the Authority, the applicant may submit an alternative within sixty days of notification. The Authority reserves the right to reject multiple applications proposing identical or substantially similar denominations; priority shall be determined according to date of filing. Any alteration to a registered *denomination variety* requires prior approval from the Authority and publication in the Official Gazette.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the grant, refusal, revocation or amendment of registration of a denomination variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the application process for a denomination variety shall render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Any entity found to have used an unregistered denomination in bad faith, intending to deceive or cause confusion amongst farmers regarding the source of seeds, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may face prosecution under relevant provisions concerning unfair trade practices as provided herein. The Authority may issue directions for the recall of any seed sold using a misleading or deceptive denomination variety.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a registered denomination variety may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use, propagation, sale, export or import of planting material of that variety. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor. The terms of any such license shall clearly define the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to exercise the granted rights, along with a specification of the duration of the license agreement. Further, where a denomination variety has been assigned to another party, that assignee may, with the prior written consent of the assignor, grant sub-licenses under the terms originally stipulated or as otherwise mutually agreed upon. Any transfer or assignment of such licenses shall be recorded with the Authority and shall be subject to applicable fees.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a denomination variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum indicating the grounds of appeal and the relief sought, and failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal inadmissible. Provided that the Appellate Board may entertain appeals filed after the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar’s decision regarding distinctiveness or freedom from conflict in a proposed denomination variety is final; however, any party disputing such a determination may petition the Appellate Board seeking review based on demonstrable error of law or fact.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the holder of a registered denomination variety may grant licenses conferring rights to use such denomination for propagation or sale, either exclusively or non-exclusively, upon terms and conditions as they deem fit. Any such license shall be in writing and may specify geographical limitations, duration, and royalty rates payable to the denomination holder. Furthermore, the right to assign a registered denomination variety, including all associated licensing agreements, is transferable subject to prior approval from the Registrar. The registrar statement shall clearly indicate any encumbrances or assignments affecting the rights pertaining to the denomination variety upon request by any interested party. Provided that, any assignment or license granted subsequent to the initial registration must be notified to the Authority within thirty days of execution.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of this Act, means a distinct name assigned to a plant variety by its breeder or registrant, subject to approval by the Authority and published in the Official Gazette. The denomination shall be unique within the Register and shall not contain any reference to the characteristics of the plant, its biological nature, or its origin. Any application for registration which proposes a denomination already existing on the Register shall be rejected. Further, the breeder or registrant shall ensure that the denomination is used consistently in relation to the variety and as provided herein, may be subject to revocation if misused.

An application for registration of a denomination variety shall be accompanied by the prescribed filed registry fee, calculated as per the rates specified in Schedule A; provided that applicants who are small and marginal farmers, landless agricultural labourers, artisans engaged in traditional activities relating to plant varieties, or members of self-help groups may apply for exemption from all or part of the said fees, subject to verification by the Authority. The denomination proposed shall not be descriptive of the variety’s characteristics, nor resemble any existing trademark or geographical indication registered under this Act or any other law in force. Any alteration to a previously assigned denomination requires prior approval from the Authority and may incur an additional fee as determined by notification.

For the purposes of this Act, “transmission” with respect to a registered trademark shall mean the voluntary transfer of all rights and privileges pertaining to the said trademark from the proprietor thereof to another person. Such transmission may occur by way of assignment, license, pledge, or any other instrument recognized under law as conveying ownership or control. Provided that, where such transmission is effected through a license agreement, the terms and conditions governing the use of the mark shall be clearly stipulated within the agreement itself. The proprietor shall provide notice of any such transmission to the Registrar, who may require supporting documentation demonstrating due execution and validity thereof, as provided herein.
