The Registrar may require submission of additional technical documentation demonstrating compliance with prevailing industry standards relating to semiconductor performance and reliability. Regarding the manner applications clause, applicants shall adhere strictly to the prescribed forms and procedures outlined in the First Schedule; any deviation from these stipulations will render the application liable for rejection. Provided that, if an applicant demonstrates a compelling reason for non-compliance with aspects of the First Schedule, such variance may be considered by the Registrar subject to written justification and approval.

Any person seeking to register a layout-design shall comply strictly with the prescribed manner applications clause, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these stipulations regarding form and content will render the application void ab initio, precluding any subsequent registration. The Registrar may summarily reject an application demonstrably failing to meet requirements concerning supporting documentation or declarations of authorship. Repeated non-compliance, evidenced by three successive rejections under this Act, shall constitute a bar to future applications from the same individual or entity for a period not exceeding five years. Any attempt to circumvent these procedural safeguards through fraudulent misrepresentation will attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer and may result in criminal prosecution.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding a valid layout-design registration relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses conferring rights to use such registered layout-design. Such license shall specify the scope of permitted acts, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation, as agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. The manner applications clause concerning assignments of these licenses shall be governed by regulations prescribed for transfers of ownership under this Act; a written instrument executed in accordance with prevailing laws is required for validity. Further, any assignment or license granted subsequent to the initial registration must clearly identify the original registered layout-design and its owner. Failure to adhere to these stipulations may render such assignments voidable at the discretion of the Controller.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for registration of a layout-design shall be deemed improperly filed if it fails to comply with the prescribed format and particulars as detailed in Schedule A. The Registrar may reject such an application ab initio, but only after providing the applicant reasonable opportunity to rectify any deficiencies identified during examination. Disputes regarding whether an application has been submitted in the correct manner applications clause are cognizable by the Tribunal; however, a mere typographical error or inconsequential deviation from the prescribed format shall not be grounds for rejection if the substance of the application is clearly discernible and does not prejudice the interests of other layout-design holders. The applicant may petition the Tribunal seeking reconsideration of any such rejection order.

Applications for patents relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs shall be made in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The Controller General, upon receipt of an application, shall furnish a date accorded patent to the applicant, which date shall serve as the initial point for determining priority under this Act. Where an application incorporates by reference any other document, the manner applications clause dictates that such incorporation must clearly identify and describe the referenced material within the application itself. Failure to adhere to this requirement may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment at the Controller General’s discretion. The prescribed form shall include a detailed description of the layout design, including its functionality and intended use. Any alteration to the described features after the date accorded patent requires notification and approval from the Controller General.

An application for registration of a variety of integrated circuit layout design shall be deemed invalid if the applicant, in prescribing the manner applications clause within Form VL-3, fails to adequately demonstrate that said prescribed method ensures uniformity and clarity in the submission of requisite documentation. This deficiency may arise where the instructions provided are ambiguous regarding the precise dimensions of schematic diagrams or the acceptable file formats for mask data submissions. The Registrar shall entertain objections from third parties alleging non-compliance with this requirement within sixty days of publication of the acceptance of the application, subject to a reasoned rebuttal by the applicant demonstrating adherence to established industry standards. Any appeal against such an objection must specify precisely how the prescribed manner deviates from reasonable expectations and prejudices the integrity of the variety registered.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall mean any fixation in any medium—whether photographic, electronic, or otherwise—of one or more images that are capable of being reproduced. A visual recording includes, but is not limited to, cinematographic films, video recordings, and digital photographs. The term “visual recording” does not extend to works which are primarily literary or musical in character, even if they incorporate visual elements. Subject to the provisions herein relating to fair dealing, a visual recording shall be deemed an artistic work for the purposes of copyright protection under this Act. Any alteration made to a visual recording shall be considered a new work, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, a "visual recording" shall be deemed to include any fixation in any material medium of moving images or sounds, whether captured through photographic, electronic, or other technological processes. Any person claiming copyright in a visual recording may apply for registration thereof with the Copyright Office, submitting details including the title of the work, date of creation, name and address of the producer, and particulars of all persons involved in its production. Such application shall be accompanied by two certified copies of the visual recording. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the authenticity of the claim and ownership thereof. Registration under this Act does not prejudice any other rights which subsist in respect of elements incorporated within the visual recording.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a cinematograph film shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year in which the film is first published. Where a visual recording incorporates elements protected by separate copyrights, such as musical works or literary adaptations, the protection afforded under this Act extends only to the original authorship embodied within the film itself and does not encompass rights pertaining to those pre-existing works. Any person who reproduces, distributes, exhibits, or performs any substantial part of a cinematograph film without authorisation shall be liable for damages. Provided that such authorization may be granted by the owner of copyright in the film, and where infringement occurs, remedies including injunctions and account of profits are available as provided herein. The right to issue licenses is vested solely with the copyright holder.

For the purposes of this Act, "visual recording" shall include any fixation in any medium—whether photographic, electronic, or otherwise—of moving images, and such term encompasses cinematographic films, video recordings, and digital representations thereof. The right to reproduce a visual recording is vested in the producer who owns the copyright therein, subject to the provisions relating to joint ownership as provided herein. Any person desiring to make a reproduction of a protected visual recording shall first obtain written permission from the owner of the copyright, specifying the scope and duration of such permitted reproduction. Failure to secure such authorization constitutes an infringement under this Act. The Appellate Tribunal may, upon receiving a complaint regarding alleged infringement, issue notices to both the complainant and the accused, affording them opportunities for hearing. Any order made by the Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days.

For the purposes of this Act, a "visual recording" shall be deemed to include any fixation of images in a medium capable of reproduction, whether by photographic process or otherwise. Such recordings shall be subject to copyright under this Act if they demonstrate sufficient originality in their selection and arrangement, provided that incidental captures of events occurring naturally and spontaneously do not qualify as original works unless demonstrably shaped by creative intervention. The right to reproduce a visual recording is contingent upon obtaining prior authorization from the owner of copyright therein, except where such reproduction falls within the scope of fair dealing for research or private study. Any alteration of a visual recording without consent constitutes an infringement, subject to remedies available under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in a cinematograph film, reproduces or causes to be reproduced any part thereof by way of a visual recording, whether for private use or commercial distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the civil court. Such damages shall not be less than five times the cost of production of the original work and may extend up to ten times such cost, depending on the extent of infringement and the resultant loss suffered by the copyright owner. Further, any equipment used for making unauthorized visual recordings or distributing infringing copies is liable to seizure and forfeiture as provided herein. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

The right to reproduce a visual recording shall vest initially in the producer thereof, who may, by instrument in writing, assign or license such right to any other person, subject to the conditions specified therein. Such assignment or license may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may relate to all or any portion of the rights conferred under this Act. Where a visual recording incorporates pre-existing works protected by copyright, the producer shall ensure that appropriate licenses are obtained from the owners of those copyrights prior to any commercial exploitation of the visual recording. Any subsequent assignment or license relating to the visual recording must disclose the particulars of all previous assignments and licenses pertaining to underlying copyrighted material. The terms of such licenses may be registered with the designated authority as provided herein, and shall be binding on all parties involved.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, a "visual recording" shall be deemed to include any representation captured through electronic or digital means, irrespective of whether such representation is fixed in a tangible medium. The right of the producer of a cinematograph film incorporating such a visual recording shall extend to preventing the reproduction, adaptation, and public display of that portion of the work where the visual recording is prominently featured, subject to judicial review if any party claims fair use or incidental inclusion. Any aggrieved person disputing this restriction may appeal to the relevant High Court, demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the producer’s exclusive right; provided that such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of the contested action.

Where any person considers that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such person may, subject to fulfilling the conditions prescribed under this Act, institute proceedings for revocation of the means patent before the Controller. The Controller shall afford an opportunity to both the petitioner and the patentee to be heard, and may, after considering all evidence adduced, determine whether the patent should be revoked wholly or in part. If a patent is revoked, any person aggrieved by the order of revocation may appeal against such order to the Appellate Board within a period specified herein. The remedies available under this Act shall not extend to claims for damages arising from the infringement of a means patent prior to its revocation; however, equitable relief may be granted as provided herein.

The Controller may, upon receiving a request from any interested party alleging that a granted means patent does not satisfy the requirements of this Act, initiate proceedings for revocation. Such request shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds on which the revocation is sought and supported by such evidence as the requester deems appropriate. The Controller shall serve notice of the request upon the patentee, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement addressing the allegations made. Following consideration of both the request and the counter-statement, along with any further submissions from interested parties, the Controller may direct the Registrar to hold a hearing. At such hearing, all parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present oral arguments and additional evidence. The decision of the Controller regarding revocation shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “means patent” shall be interpreted to signify exclusive rights conferred upon the applicant following successful compliance with all stipulated requirements under this Act. A patent shall only be granted where the invention fulfills criteria regarding novelty and non-obviousness, as provided herein. The Controller may reject an application for a means patent if it is determined that the claimed subject matter lacks sufficient disclosure to enable the skilled person to practice the invention. Further, any request for extension of the term of a patent shall be considered only upon demonstration of delays attributable directly to governmental action and subject to prescribed fees. A compulsory license relating to a means patent may be granted under this Act in circumstances specified elsewhere.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted rights under a license relating to a patent may, with the prior written consent of the patentee, assign such license, either wholly or partially, to any person or entity. Such assignment shall be recorded in the prescribed manner and shall take effect only upon such recording. Where a patent has been assigned, any subsequent dealings concerning the exploitation of the invention for which the means patent is granted shall be deemed to relate to the assignee as if they were the original patentee. The patentee may grant further licenses relating to the same invention, provided that such grants do not conflict with existing assignments or licenses and are consistent with the terms previously agreed upon under this Act. Any person acquiring an interest in a means patent by way of assignment shall be subject to all covenants and conditions contained within the original license agreement.

For the purposes of this Act, “means patent” shall be interpreted to include not only the grant of exclusive rights as provided herein, but also any subsequent amendment or modification thereof duly registered with the Controller. An appeal against a decision relating to the scope of a means patent may be filed within three months from the date of communication of such decision, subject to the condition that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the contested interpretation. The Controller shall consider arguments pertaining to prior use and public interest when assessing validity, provided that evidence supporting such claims is presented with sufficient clarity and corroboration; failure to do so may result in dismissal of the appeal.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, “means patent” shall include any application for a patent filed with the Controller, irrespective of whether such application has been examined or granted. A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise material disclosed within a pending patent application, or a granted patent, for broadcast purposes may apply to the Controller for permission to do so, provided that such utilisation is incidental to the dissemination of news or current events. The Controller shall consider any objections raised by the patentee regarding the proposed use and may grant permission subject to conditions deemed appropriate to safeguard the interests of the patent holder. Any subsequent commercial exploitation beyond the scope of permitted broadcasting activities will be considered a violation under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "registered act" shall mean any action or proceeding undertaken by an individual or entity that directly relates to the maintenance, renewal, alteration, assignment, or revocation of a registered trademark. A registered act includes, but is not limited to, the filing of a notice of opposition under this Act, the submission of documentary evidence in support of a claim for rectification, and any application made seeking to vary the terms of registration as provided herein. The term "registered act" does not encompass actions taken prior to the initial registration of a trademark or those unrelated to its continued protection subject to such limitations as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that the mark, or any element thereof, is likely to cause confusion with an earlier registered act. The applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion; such submissions shall be considered by the Registrar in accordance with principles of natural justice. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered which includes a representation of a geographical indication as defined under another Act, the Registrar shall require proof that the applicant has authorization from the proprietor of the geographical indication or is otherwise entitled to use it. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order.

Where any goods or services are offered or provided by a person who has made use of a registered act without the consent of the registered proprietor, such person shall be liable to damages. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the damage sustained by the registered proprietor as a result of the infringing activity, including loss of reputation and dilution of goodwill associated with the trade mark.  Further, any goods bearing a representation which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark, made or sold without due cause or lawful authority, shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor, order the destruction of such infringing goods and materials used in their production.  Remedies are available irrespective of whether actual financial loss is proven, provided that the use constitutes a registered act as defined herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to include a statement of all goods or services with which the applicant proposes to associate the trademark. Upon receipt of an application, the Trademark Registry shall publish a notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal and upon the Trademark Journal’s publication, any person claiming rights in respect of an identical or similar mark may file a notification of opposition under this Act. The Registrar may entertain such opposition if it is filed within the prescribed period and contains grounds for objection as provided herein. Where an opposition is successfully maintained, the application shall be refused registration; however, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. A registered act confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the trademark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and must specify the grounds upon which the appellant considers the decision to be erroneous. The appellate board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other party who appeared in opposition proceedings, affording them an opportunity to present arguments against the appeal. A registered act relating to a trade mark shall remain valid subject to compliance with all relevant provisions concerning renewal fees and prescribed forms. Failure to adhere to these requirements may result in removal from the register as provided herein.

Any individual or entity utilizing a registered act relating to a trademark in a manner that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services shall be liable for damages. Such liability extends to instances where the unauthorized use dilutes the distinctiveness of the mark, irrespective of actual commercial competition. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint and after due inquiry, issue an injunction restraining further infringing activity. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender subject to penalties as provided herein, including fines up to five lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trademark for specific goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor, and the terms thereof shall be binding on both parties. Any assignment of the registered trademark, whether in whole or in part, including any associated goodwill, shall require prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry and registration of such assignment under this Act. A licensee operating under a registered act may enforce the rights granted to them against infringers, provided that the underlying trade mark remains validly registered and the license agreement is not terminated unlawfully. Further, sub-licensing is permitted with the express written consent of the registered proprietor, documented in writing and available for inspection by the Registry upon request.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark on the ground that it conflicts with a prior registered act, the Trade Marks Registry shall provide both the applicant and the claimant with an opportunity to submit written arguments and counter-arguments. Such submissions shall be considered by the Registrar, who may direct a hearing to be held if deemed necessary for clarification or further investigation into the merits of the dispute. The decision of the Registrar concerning the validity of the registered act and the propriety of registration shall be final, subject to an appeal being made within sixty days from the date of such decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by the appellate board’s order may further appeal to the High Court.

Where a registered act relating to a plant variety has been granted, the registered owner shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting the commercialization and propagation of that variety subject to conditions stipulated therein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and their terms shall be recorded in a supplementary register maintained by the Plant Varieties Registry. Any assignment of the registered act must include explicit provisions regarding continued enforcement against infringements occurring prior to the date of such assignment. The assignee shall inherit all rights and obligations pertaining to the registered act, including any pending litigation or regulatory proceedings. Provided that, the original owner may retain a reversionary interest in the plant variety’s commercial exploitation under conditions agreed upon during the initial registration process; this is subject to review by the Registrar of Plant Varieties.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be deemed complete upon receipt by the Trade Marks Registry of the prescribed fee and all requisite forms. The Registrar may, prior to acceptance, require the applicant to furnish further particulars or amendments relating to the representation of the mark or the specification of goods or services in connection with which it is sought to be registered. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning similarity to a previously registered act, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating distinctiveness. The Registrar’s decision on such objections shall be final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Registration applies goods which are clearly defined in the application's specification; any subsequent alteration requires consent from the Trade Marks Registry.

An application for registration as a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collectives, or by cooperatives, provided that such associations, collectives or cooperatives are involved in agriculture, handicrafts, natural resources or other rural industries. The Registrar shall examine the application to ascertain whether the indication is distinctive and capable of distinguishing goods originating from the specified geographical area. Where the Registrar considers that a proposed geographical indication is not sui generis or is deceptive, he may reject the application. Upon successful completion of examination and publication, if no opposition is received as provided herein, the Registrar shall register the geographical indication authorised and issue a certificate of registration.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication authorised under this Act shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement. Infringement occurs when any person, without due cause or consent, makes use of, or devises any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication, in relation to goods with which the indication is primarily associated. Such actions may include the sale, offering for sale, importation, or exposure for sale of goods bearing the infringing mark. The remedies available to the proprietor shall include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to considerations of equitable principles. Further, any goods found to be infringing the geographical indication are liable to be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

An application for registration as a geographical indication authorised may be filed with the Registrar by any association of persons or by producers whose interests are represented by an association of persons. Such application shall specify the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, and particulars of the territory in relation to which the goods originate. The applicant shall furnish evidence that the said conditions of origin are satisfied, including details regarding traditional production methods employed within the defined geographical area. Where an opposition is filed under this Act, the Appellate Board may direct the Registrar to consider whether the use of the geographical indication would be detrimental to the public interest or create confusion amongst consumers. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application and any subsequent oppositions as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall be deemed to be a *geographical indication authorised* under this Act if it relates to goods originating from a specific territory within India and whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to that origin. Application for registration as such may be made by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of the goods concerned, provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the use of the indication within the defined geographical area. The Registrar shall require evidence substantiating the link between the product’s characteristics and its geographical origin, including but not limited to traditional knowledge documentation and verifiable production processes. Any alteration to these established practices may invalidate the authorisation as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation or amendment of a registration of a geographical indication authorised may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during any proceedings concerning infringement of a registered geographical indication shall render the complainant ineligible for equitable remedies, including injunctions and damages. The Central Government may, subject to due process, impose penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees upon any entity found guilty of using an identical or deceptively similar indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards as provided herein. Repeated offences may attract further financial penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant laws.

The owner of a geographical indication authorised under this Act may grant licences to use the said indication subject to such terms and conditions as they deem fit, including limitations on territory, duration, and goods or services. Any such licence shall be in writing and may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the owner, provided that such assignment does not prejudice the rights of other licensees. The owner shall maintain a record of all licences granted and assignments made relating to their geographical indication, making it available for inspection under this Act. Further, any party seeking to utilize a registered geographical indication in commerce must obtain express authorization from the proprietor, failing which they are liable for damages as provided herein. The Registrar may require proof of such authorization upon request.

An aggrieved party alleging that a geographical indication is being used in contravention of this Act may file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order sought to be appealed. Such appeal shall lie on grounds demonstrating demonstrable misinterpretation or unjust application of the criteria for determining whether a name, sign, symbol, or presentation is a geographical indication authorised under this Act. The Tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against; provided that any decision regarding the validity of registration shall be subject to review by the Supreme Court on appeal from the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

A geographical indication shall be deemed to be a geographically defined area under this Act if the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of goods originates from that place. For the purposes of registration as a geographical indication authorised, the name of the geographical indication must accurately identify the originating area and not contain any descriptive terms which are misleading regarding such characteristics. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and the originating area; this evidence may include documentation relating to traditional production methods or integrated circuits layout designs employed in their manufacture. Goods bearing a registered geographical indication shall be identifiable as such, subject to provisions concerning fair use.

An application for registration as a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons or producers engaged in the production of goods conforming to the quality and characteristics attributed to that geographical indication. The particulars required in the application shall include details regarding the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the agricultural area or region constituting the territory from which the goods originate, and a map of the geographical area. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections under this Act. If no opposition is received within the prescribed period, or if any opposition is withdrawn or dismissed, the Registrar may proceed with registration. The registered *geographical indication authorised* will be entered in the register of *registration geographical* indications.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting a geographical indication authorised to a collective body or consortium may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds that the registration was obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or that the collective body or consortium does not meet the requirements for eligibility under this Act. The Board may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Further, where a geographical indication authorised infringes upon existing breeder's rights relating to plant varieties, remedies available under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act shall apply concurrently with those provided herein. Any infringement of a registered geographical indication shall be actionable as a civil wrong, entitling the proprietor to seek injunction and damages.

An application for registration as a geographical indication authorised to use an indication connecting it exclusively with the quality, reputation or other characteristic of goods originating from a specific territory may be filed with the Registrar. The application shall specify the name of the geographical indication and particulars of the territory which it purports to identify. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the Geographical Indications Journal inviting objections from interested parties within three months. Any objection received shall be forwarded to the applicant for comment, after which the Registrar may proceed with examination as provided herein. The Chairperson, acting upon recommendations from the Examination Board, will determine whether the geographical indication meets the criteria for registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a *registered layout* means a layout-design that has been registered under this Act in accordance with the provisions herein relating to registration. A registered layout shall include not only the three-dimensional representation of the integrated circuit but also any design or arrangement of elements incorporated therein which are original and possess aesthetic merit. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to fulfilling all prescribed conditions, grant a certificate of registration for a *registered layout*, conferring exclusive rights against infringement as provided herein. An unregistered layout shall not be afforded protection under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall contain particulars verifying ownership and detailing the nature of the design sought to be protected under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to rectify any deficiencies or ambiguities therein before proceeding with examination. Where the applicant demonstrates satisfactory compliance with prescribed formalities, the layout-design shall be deemed eligible for preliminary scrutiny. Upon successful completion of that process, a certificate of registration confirming the existence of a registered layout is issued, specifying the date of entry and other relevant details pertaining to the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may appeal as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered owner of a registered layout, makes any act prohibited under this Act shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than ten times the cost of taking out and maintaining the registration, nor less than a sum equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable if the infringing acts had been carried out under a license from the registered owner. The Court may also order the infringer to deliver up or destroy the infringing layouts, tools, equipment, and materials used in their manufacture. Further, where an infringement of a registered layout is established, the registered owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement, subject to just terms for the infringer. This remedy applies even if no actual damage has been proven, provided that the infringing activity constitutes a violation as provided herein.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as determined under this Act and submitted in the form specified by the Controller. The applicant shall furnish particulars including, but not limited to, a full name and address, details regarding the first manufacture of the integrated circuit relating to the layout-design, and a representation of the layout sufficient for enabling the Registrar to assess its originality. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant, provided that such requests shall be made within sixty days of the initial submission. Any opposition to registration must be filed within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application. The Controller shall determine any opposition as per procedures established herein and issue a certificate of registration if no valid objection is sustained.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall contain particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a representation of the layout in the form of a mask or other suitable medium, conforming to standards as may be prescribed. The Registrar may reject an application if he is satisfied that the layout-design does not substantially consist of a three-dimensional representation of any work protected under copyright law, or if it contains matter which is wholly devoid of originality. Provided that, where a registered layout incorporates elements derived from prior art, the applicant shall demonstrate sufficient inventive step to warrant registration under this Act. The Registrar shall notify the applicant and any other interested party before proceeding with examination.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered owner, makes, imports, sells, hires or displays a layout for an integrated circuit which infringes any registered layout shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees, or both. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the registered layout in whole or substantially as a whole. The owner of a registered layout design may apply to the Commercial Courts seeking an injunction restraining any person from continuing such infringing activity and for damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the owner. Provided that this shall not apply where the use is solely for private study, research or experimentation.

The owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the said registered layout design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such license agreements may encompass exclusive or non-exclusive rights relating to reproduction, adaptation, commercial exploitation, and import of integrated circuits incorporating the registered layout. Assignment of ownership of a registered layout is permissible with written consent from the Registrar, provided that such assignment includes a detailed description of the assignor’s and assignee's respective obligations concerning ongoing maintenance of quality control records as required under this Act. Any license or assignment shall be recorded in the Register within thirty days; failure to do so renders the agreement unenforceable against third parties except where fraud or misrepresentation is proven. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, investigate and determine the validity of any such license or assignment.

The determination of whether a layout design constitutes an infringement of a registered layout shall be undertaken by the Controller, who shall consider all evidence presented by both the complainant and the alleged infringer; provided that the burden of demonstrating substantial similarity lies upon the complainant. In instances where conflicting expert testimony is adduced regarding the aesthetic merit or overall impression created by the two layouts in question, the Controller may appoint an independent assessor with expertise in integrated circuit design to provide a reasoned opinion. Any party aggrieved by such appointment or by any finding made under this Act relating to infringement of a registered layout may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; subject to payment of prescribed fees and furnishing security for costs as deemed appropriate.

For the purposes of this Act, a registered layout is defined as the three-dimensional representation of the original works described in section 4, fixed on or incorporated into a semiconductor integrated circuit; and includes both the circuitry elements and the interconnections between such elements. A registered layout shall be deemed to include any specification amended during the pendency of an application for registration, provided that such amendment does not alter the essential features of the original design as initially presented. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical documentation demonstrating the originality of a claimed registered layout, subject to guidelines issued by the Controller General.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall include particulars identifying the applicant, including their address for service, and a representation in a form specified by the Registrar demonstrating the originality of the design. The application must also state whether the applicant claims right to the layout-design as proprietor or as an authorized person. Where the layout-design incorporates elements indicative of geographical indications relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs originating from a specific region within India, the applicant shall provide documentation substantiating their connection to that region and ensuring fair trade practices are maintained. The Registrar may require further information under this Act to ascertain compliance with these provisions prior to proceeding with examination.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall include a representation of the layout in the form of a mask or equivalent medium, accompanied by a statement verifying its originality and detailing any trade mark accordance employed within the design’s visual elements. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the layout lacks sufficient novelty under this Act, or if the claimed trade mark accordance is demonstrably misleading to consumers likely to associate the layout with a particular source. Further, registration shall be conditional upon compliance with prescribed standards regarding the clarity and reproducibility of the submitted mask representation; failure to maintain these standards may result in cancellation proceedings initiated by the Registrar. The proprietor of a registered layout shall provide annual declarations confirming continued adherence to these stipulations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of the mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which such use is permitted. Any such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may be granted for a fixed period or during the term of registration. Assignment of the registered trademark, including any associated goodwill, requires prior written consent from the Controller, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a license agreement includes provisions relating to quality control of goods or services bearing the mark, these provisions shall be deemed part of the terms under which the trademark is means registered and enforceable as if incorporated directly into the registration certificate. The registered proprietor may also assign the benefit of any security interest relating to the trademark.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a proposed trade mark, or the rectification of the Register, the Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the Registrar to hear the matter again. The Board shall allow all parties concerned the opportunity to present arguments and evidence afresh before the Registrar. It is provided that if the appeal concerns a claim that a trade mark is deceptively similar to a previously registered trade mark, the Appellate Board may require expert testimony on matters of consumer perception. For the purposes of this Act, “registered” means registered in the Trade Marks Register maintained under this Act and shall include any variation or amendment duly recorded therein.

Where an application for registration of a proposed trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall give notice to the Registrar of Trade Marks and afford him an opportunity to be heard in support of the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to just cause shown. For the purposes of this Act, “registered” means registered on the Trade Marks Register maintained by the Registrar and shall include registration under any prior enactment relating to trade marks. The chairperson shall ensure that all appeals are processed expeditiously and in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused, and the applicant appeals such refusal under this Act, the appellate authority shall consider whether the grounds presented demonstrate a likelihood of confusion arising amongst consumers. It is provided that if the appellant establishes, to the satisfaction of the appellate authority, that the mark sought to be registered possesses distinctive character acquired through use subsequent to its initial application, notwithstanding any prior conflicting registration, the trademark may be granted new patent protection subject to conditions as deemed appropriate. For purposes of this appeal, "registered" means registered under this Act and shall include trademarks previously considered but ultimately rejected due to similarity with existing marks. The decision of the appellate authority is final, subject to further appeal to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, "distinctiveness" with respect to a trade mark shall mean the quality of being capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. A trade mark shall be deemed not distinctive if it describes characteristics of the goods or services for which it is used, or indicates their geographical origin, mode or time of production, or qualities thereof. Registration ought effected only in respect of marks possessing such distinctiveness as will enable consumers to readily associate them with a particular undertaking and its goods or services; provided that acquired distinctiveness through use may be considered under this Act.

The Central Trademarks Registry shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trademark, conduct such searches as are deemed necessary to ascertain whether the mark is already registered or applied for under this Act. Any person claiming rights in respect of any existing trade name or trademark may, within four months from the date of advertisement of acceptance of the proposed trademark, file notice of opposition with the Registry. Such opposition shall be determined according to the procedures as provided herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further particulars relating to the use of the mark and the goods or services in connection therewith. It is a condition precedent that registration ought effected only after due consideration of any such opposition, and where applicable, subsequent hearings.

Where any proprietor, upon proof satisfactory to the Controller that use of a registered trade mark, without due cause, has resulted in damage to another person’s business interests, shall be entitled to apply for relief under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate reasonable grounds to believe that the continued registration is causing demonstrable harm and that alternative remedies are inadequate. Provided that such application shall specify the nature and extent of the damage sustained, and provide evidence supporting the claim. Further, where a trade mark has been registered in error or through fraudulent means, or where it conflicts with prior rights not brought to the Controller’s attention during examination, registration ought effected may be revoked by order of the Controller. The Controller shall consider all relevant factors before making any determination regarding revocation or relief.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall contain such particulars as are required to identify clearly the applicant and the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving an application, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark or the description of goods or services if it appears deficient or ambiguous. Where a proposed trade mark contains any element that is deemed capable of being confused with a prior registration, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the applicant to respond and demonstrate distinctiveness. Further, registration ought effected only after due consideration of any opposition filed by an interested party under this Act. The Registrar may require production of evidence demonstrating use of the trade mark in India as a condition precedent for proceeding with examination.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed admissible if it complies with all requirements as provided herein regarding form and representation, and further subject to the applicant demonstrating sufficient capacity to make use of the mark legitimately within the Indian territory. The Registrar may require submission of additional documentation substantiating such usage, including but not limited to sales figures and distribution agreements. Where an application relates to a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark, the applicant must provide a clear and reasoned explanation demonstrating absence of likelihood of confusion. It is further stipulated that registration ought effected only upon satisfaction that no prior conflicting rights exist which would prejudice another party’s interests.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered trade mark shall, subject to provisions regarding frivolous applications, file an application with the relevant intellectual property office. Such application must specify particulars of the alleged error, misrepresentation, or other ground for rectification as provided herein. Failure to demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the registration’s existence will render the application liable to dismissal without further hearing. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an application, direct a personal appearance and presentation of evidence by both proprietor and registered mark holder. It is established that registration ought effected only after due consideration of prior usage and existing rights; any contravention shall attract penalties as determined under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to any conditions specified in the registration, be entitled to grant exclusive licences relating to the use of the mark within the territory of India. Such licences may be granted for a term not exceeding twenty years from the date of the original registration, and may be assignable under this Act, provided that the terms of such assignment are notified to the Registrar within three months of execution. Any subsequent registered proprietor shall be bound by any prior conditions or restrictions imposed upon the use of the mark through licences granted before their acquisition. Further, where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall possess all rights and powers which the assignor possessed as regards the registration ought effected and its continued protection against infringement.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration, or the rectification of the Register under this Act, appeals to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Board shall hear such appeal and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein. It is provided that an appeal lies only if the appellant demonstrates a substantial prejudice resulting from the decision impugned; mere dissatisfaction with the Registry’s interpretation of existing law does not constitute sufficient grounds for appeal. Furthermore, where the Board determines that registration ought effected in error, it may direct the rectification of the Register and award costs to either party as deemed just, considering the merits of the dispute.

Application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed complete upon submission of the requisite fee and fulfillment of all procedural requirements as provided herein. The Controller, after due consideration of any objections received under this Act, may direct that registration ought effected only if it is established that the proposed mark is distinctive in its intended field of use and does not conflict with existing registered trademarks or pending applications. Further, where a trademark incorporates elements derived from an earlier patent act shall be considered to ensure no undue infringement arises; such consideration will involve assessment of novelty and inventive step. The applicant must demonstrate continuous use of the mark for at least five years prior to seeking renewal, subject to exceptions as determined by the Controller.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license conferring exclusive rights to use the mark within a defined territory, such license shall be deemed an assignment for all purposes under this Act unless the instrument creating the license expressly states otherwise. The register shall construed liberally to reflect the intent and scope of any such licensing agreement, particularly concerning sub-licensing arrangements permitted by the original proprietor. Any subsequent assignee or sublicensee may further assign their rights subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding notification to the Registrar and payment of applicable fees. Provided that registration ought effected promptly upon transfer of ownership through assignment or sub-license, failure to do so shall render the transferee vulnerable to claims of prior entitlement from third parties holding valid licenses. The proprietor retains the right to revoke a license if the licensee’s use is detrimental to the distinctiveness of the trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, “legal representative” shall mean the husband or wife of a deceased patent applicant or proprietor, if such husband or wife is capable of representing the estate of the deceased, or any other individual duly appointed by law to represent the estate of the deceased. Where a patent applicant or proprietor dies and has nominated a legal representative under this Act, that nominee shall be deemed to possess all rights and obligations which the deceased held in relation to the patent application or granted patent, subject to any restrictions imposed by applicable laws governing succession. The Controller may require proof of such appointment or capability as provided herein.

Where, in respect of any application for registration of a trademark, the applicant is found dead or insolvent, or has become subject to legal incapacity, the Controller may entertain an application filed by a legal representative duly authorized under this Act. Such authorization shall be evidenced by a certificate from a competent court or authority as prescribed. The legal representative shall possess all rights and obligations pertaining to the original applicant in relation to the trademark application and any subsequent proceedings. Provided that, where the legal representative is appointed after the expiration of the period for filing the response to an official action, the Controller may extend such period subject to a request made within thirty days from the date of appointment of the legal representative, accompanied by supporting documentation.

Where, in proceedings under this Act, any patent applicant or proprietor dies, the right to prosecute such proceedings shall vest in their legal representative as defined under the Representative of deceased persons Act. The Controller may require the legal representative to furnish satisfactory proof of appointment and authority to act on behalf of the estate, and until such proof is provided, no action shall be taken regarding the matter. Any notice required to be served upon a patent applicant or proprietor may be served upon their legal representative in like manner as if it were served directly upon the deceased party. The legal representative shall have all rights and obligations pertaining to the deceased individual concerning opposition proceedings, revocation applications, and infringement suits. Provided that any costs incurred by the Controller due to delays caused by establishing representation shall be borne by the estate.

Where, in proceedings under this Act, any patent applicant or proprietor dies, the Board shall be satisfied that such deceased individual has appointed a legal representative. The appointment of a legal representative may be evidenced by a duly attested will or other instrument recognized as valid under applicable law. Subject to the provisions herein, the legal representative shall possess all rights and obligations of the deceased in relation to the patent application or granted patent. Any communication required to be made to the applicant or proprietor shall be addressed to their legal representative until such time as the Board is notified otherwise by way of a formal declaration filed with the office. Provided that, where no legal representative has been appointed, any person claiming through inheritance or succession may apply to the Board for recognition as such, furnishing satisfactory evidence of their claim and entitlement.

Where, in proceedings under this Act, any patent applicant or proprietor dies, the Board shall be satisfied that such deceased individual had appointed a legal representative prior to their demise, and evidence of such appointment, duly attested, shall be filed with the Board. The Board may require further documentation demonstrating the legal representative’s capacity to act on behalf of the estate, including an inventory of assets pertaining to patent rights. Provided that if no legal representative is formally appointed, any individual claiming inheritance or ownership of the deceased's patent rights may petition the Board for recognition as such, subject to verification of familial relationship and due process. The Board shall not entertain claims from individuals failing to establish a clear nexus with the deceased applicant or proprietor.

Where any patentee, assignee or other person claiming under this Act fails to comply with the requirements of sub-section (1) of section eighty-two, the Controller may, after giving opportunity for hearing, issue an order directing such person to rectify the particulars relating to the invention within a specified time. Failure to do so shall render the patent liable to be revoked under this Act. In instances where the patentee is deceased or has become insolvent, action against the estate or insolvency representative shall proceed as if such individual were living and capable of acting. Any legal representative appointed by due process of law may, subject to any order made by a competent court, exercise all rights and powers vested in the deceased or bankrupt party concerning enforcement of patent validity and infringement remedies as provided herein.

Where any patentee, or their legal representative, desires to grant a license for exploiting the patented invention under this Act, such license shall be deemed an assignment of specified rights unless expressly stated otherwise within the terms of the agreement. The licensee may, subject to the conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement and as provided herein, sub-license the patent, including the right to manufacture, use, and sell the patented product or process. However, any transfer or assignment made by a legal representative shall be validated only upon notification to the Controller and registration with the Patents Office within three months of such transaction. Failure to register such assignments may render them voidable at the discretion of the Controller. The patentee’s legal representative is obligated to ensure compliance with all provisions relating to royalty payments as detailed in section 53, unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the parties.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act, the patent applicant or any other party is deceased or otherwise incapacitated from appearing personally, such party shall be deemed to be represented by their legal representative as defined under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Controller may, at any stage of the proceeding, require proof satisfactory to the Controller establishing the capacity of a person claiming to be a legal representative and may disallow participation if such proof is not furnished or if there are reasonable grounds for doubting the validity of that representation. Any order passed by the Controller based on the representations of a legal representative shall be valid against the estate or interests of the deceased or incapacitated party, subject to any appeal as provided herein.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act, any patent applicant or proprietor is found to be deceased or otherwise unable to appear personally, the Controller shall proceed with due diligence to ascertain whether such deceased or incapacitated individual has appointed a legal representative. The determination of who constitutes the appropriate legal representative for the purposes of challenging an objection regarding the validity of a patent, particularly concerning allegations of improper use certification trade practices employed by the proprietor, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. It is provided that any party aggrieved by the Controller’s decision identifying a legal representative may petition the Appellate Board within sixty days of such determination, demonstrating clear prejudice resulting from the appointment.

Where, in respect of any application for registration of a trademark, the applicant is declared dead by a competent court, or becomes incapable of managing his affairs, the right to proceed with the application shall vest in their legal representative. For the purposes of this Act, “legal representative” includes an executor, administrator, or anyone duly authorised under a will or succession certificate. The Controller may require such legal representative to furnish proof of their entitlement and authority to act on behalf of the deceased applicant or incapacitated individual. Provisions sub section (1) shall apply where the trademark was jointly owned; in such cases, all joint owners’ legal representatives are deemed to be acting together.

For the purposes of this Act, the priority date of an invention shall be determined according to the provisions outlined herein. A priority date establishes the point in time against which novelty and inventive step are assessed under this Act. Where an applicant claims a right of priority under a convention application filed in another country, such claim shall be supported by a certified copy of the earlier application as provided for under section 8. The invention must disclose the matter essential to the claimed subject matter; otherwise, the priority date claim is deemed invalid. Any alteration to the specification subsequent to establishing the priority date may impact the validity of claims referencing that date.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model shall be entitled to claim a priority date for an earlier application filed in respect of the same invention, subject to compliance with the provisions outlined herein. The said earlier application must have been made in a country or convention territory as recognized under this Act. To establish entitlement to such a priority date claim, the applicant must submit a certified copy of the prior application, duly authenticated by the appropriate authority within that jurisdiction. Further, it shall be demonstrated that the utility model sought for registration constitutes an improvement upon the invention disclosed in the earlier application, and that the disclosure is sufficiently clear and complete to enable persons skilled in the art to carry out the invention.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention, they shall furnish a declaration specifying the earliest preceding date on which any related invention was divulged. This declaration must identify the place and circumstances of such prior disclosure. The Controller may require further evidence substantiating the claimed priority date if reasonable doubts arise regarding its accuracy or validity. An applicant’s right to claim a priority date is contingent upon demonstrating that the complete specification fairly discloses the subject matter as described in the earlier application. Failure to satisfy this requirement, or providing false information within the declaration, renders the applicant liable for penalties under this Act and may result in the rejection of the patent application. The burden of proving the validity of the priority date claim rests entirely upon the applicant.

An applicant claiming a priority date shall file with the application a certified copy of the earlier patent application or published document relied upon to establish said priority. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish an English translation of such certified copy if it is not originally filed in English or Hindi. Where multiple documents are cited to support the priority date claim, the applicant must clearly indicate the specific portions of each document relevant to the invention as claimed. Failure to do so may result in the rejection of the application under this Act. The burden of proving the existence and contents of the earlier application rests solely upon the applicant. Any alteration made to the cited document after the priority date shall be brought to the attention of the Controller, along with a reasoned explanation for such alterations.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention described in a patent application, such date shall be deemed to be the filing date of the earliest related application, provided that the applicant demonstrates with reasonable certainty a continuous chain of derivation from said earlier application. The determination of this priority date claim is subject to verification by the Controller, who may require submission of certified copies of relevant documents pertaining to the prior application. Further, if the invention incorporates matter already disclosed in a previously published document, the applicant shall disclose such publication and demonstrate that the claimed invention constitutes an inventive step notwithstanding said disclosure. The burden of proving entitlement to a priority date rests entirely upon the applicant.

An applicant claiming a priority date shall furnish an English translation of the earlier application within thirty days from the date of filing the complete specification under this Act. Failure to comply with this requirement will render the claimed priority date invalid, subject to appeal before the Controller. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from reliance on a falsely asserted priority date may petition the High Court for injunctive relief and damages against the applicant or patentee. The burden of proving the validity of the priority date claim rests entirely upon the claimant, and any evidence presented must be clear, cogent, and contemporaneous with the alleged earlier application’s filing date; otherwise, it shall be deemed insufficient as provided herein.

Any patentee desiring to grant a license conferring rights to exploit an invention for which he has claimed a priority date shall execute a written assignment or licensing agreement specifying the scope of such rights. This agreement must clearly delineate the field of exploitation permitted, including geographical limitations and product categories. The patentee may assign this right to any person, firm, or company, subject to the condition that the assignee adheres to the terms initially stipulated in the original license or assignment. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses the patented invention, they shall provide the patentee with details of such sub-licensing arrangements within thirty days. Failure to do so may result in revocation of the initial license under this Act. The priority date claim remains vested solely with the patent holder unless explicitly transferred through documented legal means as provided herein.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention, it shall be incumbent upon them to demonstrate, through documentary evidence admissible under this Act, that the claimed subject matter was indeed disclosed in a prior application filed in another jurisdiction. The Controller may require such further particulars as are deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the priority date claim and may direct the applicant to furnish affidavits from individuals with personal knowledge of the invention’s genesis. Any challenge to the established priority date, brought by an interested party, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates a prima facie case of prejudice resulting from the acceptance of the disputed priority date.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted rights under a patent shall be entitled to assign or license such rights further, provided that such assignment or subsequent license does not prejudice the rights of the patentee. Where a patent has been assigned, any mark uses registered by the assignee shall be deemed to have been made with the consent of the original patent holder for the duration of the assignment. The determination of the priority date claim relating to an invention may be challenged by any party demonstrating that the application was not filed within twelve months from the earliest prior publication or disclosure, unless such delay is satisfactorily explained and does not substantially impact the novelty of the invention as assessed under this Act. Further, a patentee shall provide written notification to all licensees regarding any proceedings challenging the priority date claim.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention, it shall be incumbent upon them to demonstrate with reasonable certainty that the claimed subject matter was not previously disclosed under this Act or any other law. The Controller may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating the asserted priority claim, and failure to provide such satisfactory proof within the prescribed time period will render the application liable for rejection. It is provided that an appeal against such a decision of the Controller shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to the provisions regarding timelines and maintainability under this Act. A patent shall not be granted unless the priority date claim is definitively resolved and found to be valid.

Where an applicant seeks to establish a priority date for an invention, they shall present evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating the earliest date upon which a similar invention was first described. The burden of proof regarding the veracity of such claims rests entirely with the applicant. Should it be demonstrated that the applicant knowingly misrepresented facts pertaining to their claimed priority date, or acted fraudulently in obtaining patent protection based on an earlier disclosure, the Controller may order revocation of the patent. Furthermore, under this Act, where a plaintiff has asserted a claim of prior invention and subsequently, without further notice to the defendant, plaintiff forthwith ceased all actions demonstrating reliance upon that assertion, the court shall consider such cessation as evidence potentially undermining the credibility of the original priority date claim.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, an application for the registration of a plant variety shall be deemed invalid if the proposed denomination is demonstrably confusingly similar to a previously assigned denomination under this Act, or infringes upon any existing trademark or other intellectual property right. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating that the denomination does not constitute an unfair appropriation of another’s creative work, particularly where such work involves a dramatic work used in promotional material relating to the variety. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the governing assignment denomination may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Appellate Board shall consider whether the Registrar acted reasonably and fairly in reaching its determination.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of this Act, means a variety that exhibits stable and heritable characteristics differentiating it from other varieties, and to which a single designation has been assigned by the applicant seeking registration. Such designation shall not be descriptive of the variety’s substantial characteristics, nor shall it contain any geographical indication unless permitted under regulations framed as provided herein. The distinct denomination variety must also satisfy the criteria for novelty, uniformity, and stability established under this Act. Any alteration to a previously registered distinct denomination requires prior approval from the Authority and may necessitate further examination.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to grant registration for a distinct denomination variety may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals and may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the Registrar’s decision and directing him to proceed with the matter further or imposing terms and conditions for registration. Subject to this, no remedy shall be available to any person against an order passed by the Registrar relating to the grant of a distinct denomination variety other than through appeal under this Act. Provided that, in cases where infringement of farmers' rights is alleged due to unauthorized use of a registered distinct denomination variety, appropriate remedies including injunctions and damages may be sought before a competent civil court as provided herein.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed by the Examining Committee and demonstrating stability across three successive generations, subject to deviations permissible under established agricultural practices for that species. The Authority may reject an application if it determines that the proposed distinct denomination is confusingly similar to any existing denomination already registered or pending registration with respect to another plant variety. Further, a breeder shall provide evidence confirming freedom from restriction on saving and exchanging of farmer’s rights pertaining to the distinct denomination variety, as provided herein. Any alteration to the initially assigned denomination requires prior approval from the Authority and justification demonstrating no infringement upon established farmers' privileges.

Any person found to have knowingly and willfully used a distinct denomination variety without authorization from the registered plant breeder shall be liable for damages as determined by the Authority. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits, diminution in value of harvested produce, and costs incurred in rectifying misleading representations made to farmers regarding the origin or characteristics of the unauthorized variety. Further, any entity engaged in the commercialization, distribution, or sale of plants derived from an unregistered distinct denomination variety shall be subject to penalties not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each offense.
