Failure to comply with these requirements may result in cancellation of the relating registered design upon review by the relevant authority.

The owner of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use, reproduce, and commercially exploit the design. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and the terms thereof shall be subject to applicable competition laws. Assignment of relating registered layout-designs is permitted with prior written consent from the Controller General, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations previously held by the assignor under this Act. Any license granted or assignment made without such consent may be deemed voidable at the option of the Controller General. The royalty rates for licenses shall be determined through mutual agreement between the parties; however, disputes regarding these rates may be referred to an arbitrator appointed as provided herein.

Where an appeal is filed against a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, the Appellate Board shall admit such appeal if it appears that the decision was manifestly erroneous in law or fact. The appellant shall serve notice on the respondent, being the applicant for registration whose design is challenged, at least thirty days prior to the hearing date; failure to do so may result in the appeal’s dismissal. The respondent may file a counter-statement within fifteen days of receiving such notice. Any party aggrieved by an order relating registered layout-designs made under this Act may seek judicial review subject to just cause shown and limitation periods as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor trade mark shall be deemed to include any mark used or proposed to be used, whether descriptive or not, that distinguishes goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and is registered under this Act. A proprietor may assign his rights in a proprietor trade mark, including the right to sue for infringement, subject to any conditions specified during registration. The owner of a proprietor trade mark shall be entitled to prevent the use by any person of identical or confusingly similar marks in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the trade mark is registered, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for the registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming ownership or proposing to use the trade mark, and such applicant shall furnish all particulars required under this Act. Where an application relates to a proposed trade mark and the applicant is not the proprietor of the trade mark, the Registrar may require evidence that the applicant has obtained or will obtain the consent of the proprietor to register the trade mark. The registration of a trademark confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India relating to the goods or services specified in the register. Any person desiring to oppose an application for registration shall give notice of such opposition to the Registrar, as provided herein. The registrar may require further information from any applicant seeking to become a proprietor trade mark owner.

Subject to any other provision of this Act, a proprietor trade mark, once duly registered, confers upon its owner the exclusive right to employ the mark throughout India for the goods or services specified in the register and to prevent others from using identical or deceptively similar marks relating to such goods or services. Any person who, without due cause or consent, uses a trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered proprietor trade mark shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner of the trade mark. Further, the owner may apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining the infringing use and requiring delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. This right extends to preventing the application of the mark to packaging or advertising materials relating to the registered goods or services, provided that such application is likely to cause confusion among consumers.

Subject to appeal under Chapter VIII, a proprietor trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any unauthorized person, knowing that such use is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin of goods or services, uses a sign identical or deceptively similar to the registered trade mark in connection with such goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from the proprietor and after affording due opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, issue an injunction restraining the infringing activity. Further, any person seeking to challenge the validity of a registration shall file an application within five years from the date of publication of the acceptance thereof under this Act. Such applications are subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein and may be dismissed if found lacking in merit or failing to establish material prejudice.

Subject to compliance with prescribed formalities, a proprietor trade mark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, renewable indefinitely in intervals not exceeding fifteen years upon application and payment of the requisite fees as determined under this Act. An application for renewal may be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the use of the mark has been discontinued for a continuous period exceeding five years immediately preceding the date of such application; provided that evidence demonstrating continued bona fide intention to use the trade mark, submitted by the applicant, may persuade the Registrar otherwise. The proprietor shall file an account of the extent of the use of the trade mark every five years, as provided herein, and failure to do so may render the mark liable for revocation proceedings.

Subject to any other provision of this Act, a proprietor trade mark, once duly registered, confers upon the registrant the sole and exclusive right to employ the mark throughout India concerning the specified goods or services listed on the register. Any person who, without due cause or consent from the proprietor, uses a trade mark that is identical or deceptively similar to a registered proprietor trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority and may face imprisonment extending up to three years, provided that repeated infringements will attract enhanced penalties. The Registrar may issue injunctions against such infringing activities as he deems fit.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor trade mark may be assigned or licensed, either wholly or partially, in perpetuity or for a specific term, with or without royalty, and such assignment or license shall operate as if it were an absolute transfer unless otherwise specified within the agreement. Any subsequent proprietor following such an assignment shall be deemed to have acquired all rights and obligations pertaining to the trade mark under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence of any such assignment or license to be filed for public record, including details of consideration paid and duration of the grant. Provided that a license does not conflict with the fundamental character of the goods or services associated with the proprietor trade mark, it shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent change in ownership of the trade mark.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a proprietor trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any other person uses a sign identical or deceptively similar to the registered trade mark in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration is made, without the consent of the proprietor. Provided that, such use shall not constitute infringement if the defendant demonstrates clear and conspicuous over-riding user rights acquired prior to the date of application for registration of the said proprietor trade mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The Tribunal may, upon review, order cessation of such use or award damages, considering the extent of dilution caused to the distinctiveness of the proprietor’s mark.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences, both exclusive and non-exclusive, permitting the use of their proprietor trade mark for goods or services as defined under this Act. Such licences may include conditions relating to quality control and adherence to specified standards, particularly where the licensed use involves proprietor certification trade. Assignment of the right to use a registered trade mark, whether in whole or in part, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any assignment shall be recorded in the Register and shall take effect only upon such recording. Further, sub-licensing is permitted subject to the terms stipulated within the original licence agreement, as may be approved by the proprietor of the trade mark. The proprietor retains ultimate control over maintaining the distinctiveness and reputation associated with their registered mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor trade mark shall be deemed to include any mark used or proposed to be used, whether for goods or services, that is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and which, when registered, confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights as provided herein. Such exclusive rights extend to preventing the use by any person of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services, notwithstanding that such use may be accompanied by indications suggestive of the owner copyright case relating to associated literary works. The Registrar may require proof of continuous use as a condition for renewal of registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for registration of a m) “mark” shall be refused if it contains any matter which, under this Act or the rules made thereunder, is considered disingenuous or otherwise objectionable. Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry against an application, the applicant shall have the opportunity to file a written response addressing the grounds for such objection within the time specified in the notice of concern. The Registrar may require the submission of further documentation or evidence to substantiate claims made in the response. Upon review of the applicant’s reply and any additional materials presented, the Registrar shall determine whether the application meets the requirements as provided herein for registration as a proprietor trade mark. Failure to adequately address the objection may result in the refusal of the application.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes legal proceedings under this Act against any person for infringement, and subsequently obtains a decree establishing such infringement, the Court may, in addition to awarding damages as provided herein, order the infringer to account for all profits made by him from the sale of goods or services bearing the infringing trade mark. Furthermore, if the Court finds that the infringer acted with fraudulent intent in relation to the infringement, it shall impose sentence imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to five years, and also levy a fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The court may further order seizure and destruction of infringing goods and materials of manufacture.

Where an individual is convicted under this Act for knowingly and wilfully making false representations concerning the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services with the intent to deceive, such conviction shall be followed by a mandatory review of their professional licenses, if applicable. The Registrar may initiate proceedings against any person found guilty of contravening provisions relating to deceptive trade practices. Upon finding that an offence has been committed, the Adjudicating Officer shall issue a notice detailing the charges and providing opportunity for defence. Failure to appear before the Adjudicating Officer at the appointed time may result in ex parte findings. Where the offence involves commercial fraud or significant financial loss to consumers, the Court may impose sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, alongside a fine commensurate with the severity of the violation as provided herein.

Where an individual is found guilty under this Act of knowingly and wilfully employing a false trade description with intent to deceive, such individual shall be liable for a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Provided that, if the false trade description relates to goods or services affecting the public interest as determined by the Controller General, the court may also impose sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Further, where the offence is committed in relation to organic produce certification marks, the fine shall be doubled and sentence imprisonment may extend to five years. Any corporate body whose officer was knowingly involved in the commission of such an offence shall be deemed guilty of the offence and subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act against any person for alleged infringement, and such proceedings are ultimately determined in favour of the defendant, the plaintiff shall be liable to pay damages to the defendant equivalent to the costs incurred by the defendant in defending the action. Further, where it is established that the plaintiff acted maliciously or with reckless disregard for the rights of the defendant in initiating said proceedings, the Court may, subject to an appeal being filed within sixty days, impose sentence imprisonment upon the proprietor and any director or officer involved in authorizing such proceedings, for a term not exceeding two years. The imposition of this penalty shall be without prejudice to the plaintiff’s liability to pay costs as determined by the Court.

Where any person, being the registered proprietor of a trade mark, or having been previously refused registration thereof, institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and such proceedings are found to be frivolous or vexatious, the Court may impose sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year. For the purposes of determining whether proceedings are frivolous, the Court shall consider whether the specification claim in the plaint accurately reflects the scope of the registered trade mark and whether reasonable grounds existed for believing that infringement has occurred. This provision applies irrespective of any subsequent amendment or withdrawal of the said proceedings.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act for infringement of a registered trademark and obtains a decree establishing such infringement, the Court may, subject to any conditions it deems fit to impose, award damages to the proprietor equivalent to the loss suffered thereby. Further, where the defendant is found to have acted fraudulently in relation to the infringing activity, or has made use of a false representation concerning the trademark, the Court shall also impose sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and may order recovery from the defendant of any profits made by him as a result of the infringement. This provision applies even where the infringer attempts to circumvent existing patent India claims related to product design or functionality associated with the mark. The court retains discretion regarding the severity of penalties, considering mitigating factors such as good faith reliance on advice.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a map of the area from which the goods originate and such map shall clearly delineate the boundaries of the geographical territory. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the history, characteristics, and qualities associated with the goods in question, demonstrating their unique connection to the specified geographical origin. Provided that an application for a geographical indication relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs shall include details concerning traditional production methods employed within the defined area. Any prior registration of a trademark under the Trade Marks Act shall not preclude consideration of an application for a goods geographical indication as provided herein, subject to assessment of potential conflict and consumer confusion.

Any proprietor seeking remedies for use of a registered geographical indication shall file an application with the relevant High Court detailing the infringing activity and providing evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. The court may grant injunctions restraining further unauthorized use, subject to considerations of proportionality and public interest. Compensation for damages incurred by the proprietor due to such infringement shall be determined based on lost profits or demonstrable harm to the reputation associated with the goods geographical indication. Further, any person found guilty of infringing a registered geographical indication is liable to pay penalties as deemed appropriate by the court, taking into account the scale and duration of the unauthorized use. The Registrar may also issue cease-and-desist orders under this Act against those engaging in deceptive practices relating to protected indications.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying that the applicant is a producer organization representing the interests of producers of goods originating from the specified territory. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating exclusive control over production processes within the defined geographical area, provided that such control does not unduly restrict competition or innovation amongst producers. Any alteration to the boundaries defining the geographical indication shall be subject to prior approval by the Central Government and must demonstrate continued adherence to established quality standards as detailed in a prescribed code of conduct. The registered goods geographical indication may only be used by authorized users conforming to these standards, and any unauthorized use will constitute an infringement under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a goods geographical indication, or by any act of contravention of the rights conferred therein, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order or occurrence. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated during registration, including alterations in production methods that compromise the distinctive qualities associated with the geographical indication, shall constitute an offense punishable with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. Further, any entity found guilty of using a registered goods geographical indication without authorization will be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods sold.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products shall have the exclusive right to authorize the use of such geographical indication by others for putting those goods on the market. Any person desiring to utilize a protected geographical indication, subject to prior written consent from the proprietor, may apply for a license under this Act outlining the terms and conditions governing said usage. Such licenses may be granted non-exclusively or exclusively, and may specify limitations regarding quality control measures, packaging standards, or other relevant aspects of production as deemed necessary by the Registrar. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to assign their rights relating to licensing agreements pertaining to the geographical indication to any third party, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Geographical Indications Registry. Any unauthorized use of a protected goods geographical indication constitutes an infringement and may be subject to remedies available under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act and may seek remedies including an injunction restraining any person from using, or authorizing the use of, any sign that is identical or deceptively similar to the registered geographical indication. Such remedies are without prejudice to claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringing activity. The Registrar shall maintain an alphabetical index classification of all registered goods geographical indications, accessible for public inspection and used in determining likelihood of confusion under infringement proceedings. Provided that, where an alleged infringer demonstrates honest belief that the use does not constitute infringement, the remedies available may be limited at the discretion of the court. Any order granted by a court shall be enforceable as if it were a decree made under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

For the purposes of this Act, a “publish translation” shall mean a published version of a literary or dramatic work rendered into another language by means of interpretation and transcription. A publish translation is deemed to be an original work independently copyrightable, subject to the condition that such rendition demonstrates sufficient creativity and intellectual effort beyond mere literal conveyance of the source material’s meaning. Where a publish translation incorporates substantial portions of illustrations or other visual elements from the original work, those incorporated elements shall remain under the copyright control of the owner of the copyright in the original work, as provided herein.

Where a published translation of a copyrighted work is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall record particulars of the translator and the original author, alongside details pertaining to the copyright owner of the translated work. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence for the purposes of establishing ownership of the publish translation, subject to any demonstrable proof presented before an adjudicating officer. An application for registration of a published translation may include claims extending to derivative works based upon the translation itself. Provided that if the original author’s copyright has expired, the Registrar may require additional documentation substantiating the translator's claim to originality in adaptation. Any alteration to details recorded during registration shall be permissible only with prior written consent from all parties listed as owners or contributors.

Where a published translation of a copyrighted work is undertaken by an individual other than the copyright holder, such undertaking shall be deemed a communication to the public within the meaning of this Act. Provided that, where the original work was first published outside India, the publication of the translation must occur no earlier than thirty years from the date of its initial foreign publication; otherwise, it constitutes infringement. The right to undertake a publish translation is subject to compliance with prescribed formalities regarding attribution and acknowledgement of the copyright holder’s ownership under this Act. Any person desiring to produce or distribute such a published translation may apply for authorization, furnishing details of intended scope and language conversion.

Where the copyright holder of an original literary work grants a license permitting a publish translation into another language, such license shall be assignable by the licensee subject to the terms stipulated therein. Provided that any subsequent assignee of said license shall be bound by all covenants and conditions initially agreed upon between the copyright holder and the original licensee regarding royalties, distribution territories, and duration of exclusivity. Further, where a publish translation is made without authorization but subsequently licensed or assigned, the assignor warrants that they possess the right to effect such assignment and are not in breach of any existing contractual obligations concerning the work’s copyright. The copyright holder may, under this Act, seek injunctive relief and damages against any unauthorized assignment infringing upon their exclusive rights relating to the original work.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent shall furnish a detailed specification outlining the scope and boundaries of the claimed invention. The description must clearly articulate all elements encompassed within the claims, ensuring that any matter not explicitly described is understood to be excluded. Where an invention far claimed extends beyond the originally disclosed subject matter, the Controller may require further clarification demonstrating the inventive step relating to each additional element. Such requirements shall be considered met only upon submission of a revised specification and accompanying drawings, if applicable, accurately reflecting the broadened scope. The applicant’s compliance with these stipulations is essential for determining patentability under this Act and preventing subsequent challenges regarding claim interpretation.

Where an invention far claimed extends to a process for producing a substance intended for use or employed in the manufacture of a pharmaceutical product, and such product is subsequently marketed without due regard to established clinical trial protocols as prescribed under this Act, the patentee shall be liable for damages. Such damages may include compensation for losses suffered by consumers demonstrably harmed by the unauthorized marketing practices, and further encompass punitive measures proportionate to the scale of the deceptive conduct. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party or acting suo moto, order inspection of manufacturing facilities and clinical trial data relevant to the patented process. Failure to comply with such orders shall constitute contempt under this Act and render the patentee subject to penalties as provided herein.

An invention shall be deemed to be non-obvious if it does not involve any element which is susceptible of being anticipated or derived from knowledge available to a person skilled in the art prior to the priority date. The determination of obviousness shall take into account, inter alia, the totality of the circumstances, including relevant publications and public use, both before and after the priority date. Where an application claims an invention far claimed beyond the scope of the disclosure in the specification, the Controller may require the applicant to amend the claim to bring it within that scope. Such amendment shall be permissible only if the amended claim is supported by the original disclosure and does not introduce any new matter. The Board constituted under this Act may entertain appeals against orders passed by the Controller relating to the assessment of obviousness or the requirement for amendments, subject to prescribed procedures.

An invention shall be deemed non-patentable if the claims appended to the patent application extend beyond what is necessary to define the scope of the protected innovation, and such excess encompasses matter already disclosed in prior art publications or publicly utilized processes. The determination of whether an invention far claimed constitutes a violation of this provision will consider the technical effect achieved by the claimed subject matter and its relationship to the underlying inventive concept. Further, where the application incorporates material from previously filed applications, the Controller may require demonstration that such incorporation does not broaden the scope of protection beyond the original disclosure. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the earlier application resulted in a granted patent or remains pending, provided that the relevant information is accessible to the public.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of patent rights under this Act, and demonstrates through expert testimony and documentary evidence that the asserted invention far claimed exceeds the scope of the granted claims, the Controller may order the infringer to cease manufacture, use, or sale of the infringing product or process. Further, such infringer shall be liable for damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty reflecting the value of the unduly broad claim, calculated as provided herein. The Controller is empowered to impose additional penalties, including fines not exceeding five per centum of the infringer's turnover derived from the infringing activity, if it finds that the infringement was willful and demonstrably intended to undermine the patent holder’s commercial interests.

Where an invention far claimed extends to a process for producing a substance intended for use or employed in the manufacture, preparation, or processing of a pharmaceutical product, the patentee shall be obliged to grant licenses under this Act upon such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Such terms shall include provisions ensuring non-discriminatory access and pricing within India, subject to reasonable compensation being paid to the patentee reflecting their research and development expenditure. Assignment of rights relating to such processes requires prior notification to the Controller, detailing the assignee’s commitment to upholding these licensing obligations. Further, any subsequent assignment must also be notified. The Controller may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, impose conditions on licenses granted under this Act to safeguard public health and welfare, provided that such conditions do not unreasonably prejudice the patentee's commercial interests.

Where an objection is taken against a patent application on the ground that the claims are unduly broad or otherwise define an *invention far claimed*, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend the claims, subject to the condition that such amendment does not alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed in the specification. The Controller may allow such amendments if satisfied that they address the specific concerns raised in the objection and maintain compliance with the requirements under this Act regarding clarity and support within the description. Any party aggrieved by a decision permitting or rejecting claim amendments may appeal to the Appellate Board, presenting arguments demonstrating either undue breadth or lack of adequate support for the amended claims. The Board’s determination shall be final, provided that it is not contrary to principles of natural justice.

Where an invention far claimed in a patent application relates to a variety registered under the Varieties Registry Act, 1993, or any subsequent enactment amending or supplementing that Act, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, require the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating freedom to operate with respect to such registered varieties. Any license granted relating to an invention incorporating protected plant genetic material shall be deemed a transfer of rights under this Act and shall specify the royalty rate payable to the holder of the variety registration. The assignment of patent rights pertaining to inventions utilizing registered varieties requires consent from the Varieties Registry Authority, provided that such consent may only be withheld if the assignment would demonstrably prejudice the interests of plant breeders or impede further innovation in crop improvement.

Where an objection is taken against a patent grant on the ground that the claims are unduly broad or encompass subject matter beyond the scope of the asserted invention far claimed, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned opportunity to respond and amend the claims accordingly. Such amendment may be permitted only if it does not substantially alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed in the patent application. The determination of whether an amendment constitutes a substantial alteration shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the acceptance of the amended claim. This provision applies equally to applications filed under this Act and those claiming priority from an India patent.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed invalid if the mark contains any representation that is likely to offend religious susceptibilities. The Registrar may require an applicant seeking registration of a composite trademark comprising words and devices to indicate clearly which elements are intended to be distinctive, and specify whether the claim extends to the whole mark or only to particular features. Where an application includes a disclaimer of any right in respect of any part of the proposed trademark, such disclaimer shall be recorded and deemed part of the register. The acceptance of an application for registration is subject to publication in the Trade Marks Journal as provided herein. Any person may oppose such acceptance within the prescribed period.

A trademark shall be eligible for registration under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and is represented graphically. Provided that a mark may still be registered even though its elements are present in common usage, subject to demonstration by the applicant that, through their own efforts, the mark has acquired distinctiveness indicating recognition among the relevant public. Furthermore, an application for registration shall include a claim specifying the goods or services with which the trademark is associated and classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating use of the trade marks in commerce if there are doubts regarding its current validity as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from a proprietor of a registered trademark alleging that the application for registration of a similar mark is likely to cause confusion in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those associated with their existing trade marks, afford the applicant for new registration an opportunity to submit its written representations. Such representations shall be considered alongside evidence presented by the objector demonstrating demonstrable detriment resulting from prior use and reputation established through film sound recording associated with the earlier trademark. The Registrar may allow the application for registration if satisfied that no likelihood of confusion exists or that other conditions, as provided herein, are met; however, such a decision is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, "Bench" shall mean a constituted panel of judicial officers established under this Act for adjudicating disputes and exercising powers as provided herein. A Bench shall be comprised of such number of persons as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify; subject to the condition that at least one member of each Bench shall possess qualifications relevant to intellectual property law or a technical background related to semiconductor technology. The composition of a Bench may vary depending upon the nature and complexity of the matter before it, as determined by the presiding officer. Decisions of a Bench shall be made by a majority vote of the members present.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the initial examination report pertaining to the design. Where an applicant seeks to amend the layout-design described in their application following the publication thereof under this Act, such amendment must relate only to clerical errors or minor modifications not substantially altering the original design’s features. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional documentation demonstrating the originality of the layout-design and its compliance with prescribed standards. Disputes concerning the validity of a registration, or relating to the composition of a *Bench* convened to hear an appeal, shall be resolved as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision of such a *Bench* may further appeal under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to a Bench constituted for the purpose. The appellate authority shall, while admitting an appeal, stay further proceedings unless it is satisfied that such action would cause irreparable injury. An appeal lies within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Appellate Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are recorded for the delay. The Bench may, in its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Any party aggrieved by an order of a Bench may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Bench, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered layout-design, constitute a Bench to hear and determine the matter. Such Bench shall consist of not less than three members, appointed by notification in the Official Gazette, possessing expertise in intellectual property law and engineering disciplines relevant to semiconductor technology. The presiding member of the Bench shall be designated as its Chairperson. Parties seeking to present evidence or arguments before the Bench may do so through duly authorized representatives holding a certificate of practice under the Advocates Act. Decisions rendered by the Bench are subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, provided that appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar shall provide all necessary documentation and administrative support to facilitate the efficient functioning of the Bench as provided herein.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to a Bench constituted for the purpose. Such Bench shall be comprised of not less than three members, one of whom shall be a person having experience in intellectual property law and another a person possessing technical expertise relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Appellate Board may entertain an appeal filed after the expiry of said period if the appellant satisfies it that there was sufficient cause for such delay. Any member of a Bench may, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government, require production of documents or attendance of witnesses relevant to the proceedings.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to a Bench constituted for that purpose. The appellate Bench shall be presided over by a judicial member and two technical members, one of whom shall be experienced in semiconductor integrated circuit layout design. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to notice as provided herein before filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material facts in relation to any proceedings before a Bench, that person shall be liable to pay such penalty as may be determined by the Board, not exceeding five lakhs of rupees. The appellate Bench’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to revision by the High Court only on a point of law.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any registered proprietor of a layout-design may grant licenses relating to the use of their design, including rights to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating the design. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, and where an assignment is made, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all the rights which the assignor possessed under this Act immediately prior to the assignment. The terms of any license granted may specify royalties payable, duration of the license, and geographical limitations on use; provided that such terms are clearly stated within the licensing agreement. Any dispute concerning the validity or enforceability of a license shall be referred to a Bench for determination, and the decision of the Bench shall be final. Further, an application to transfer ownership of a layout-design may include assignment of any outstanding licenses attached thereto.

Appellate determination regarding infringement shall be made by a Bench constituted under this Act, comprising not less than three members, one of whom shall be a person having experience in semiconductor technology. An appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to rectification of the layout-design registration, and such appeal may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Bench may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of a Bench shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the High Court within ninety days of such decision, provided that the High Court may entertain appeals filed beyond this period if it is satisfied that the delay was unavoidable and caused no prejudice.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a competent authority under this Act may appeal to a Bench constituted for that purpose. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. Failure to comply with this time limit shall ordinarily preclude the appellate Bench from entertaining the appeal, subject to just cause being shown. The appellate Bench may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any decision made by a Bench regarding transmission operation law disputes is final and binding on all parties involved, and enforcement shall be pursued through civil courts as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "Bench" shall mean a judicial forum constituted under this Act for adjudicating disputes relating to infringement of layout-design rights and other matters as provided herein. A Bench shall be comprised of such number of persons as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify; subject to the condition that at least one member of each Bench shall possess qualifications or experience relevant to semiconductor integrated circuits technology or intellectual property law. The composition of a Bench and its procedures for hearing cases relating to board use layout shall be determined according to rules made under this Act.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, an applicant seeking protection for a layout-design relating to alphabetical index goods shall provide detailed schematics and descriptions sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the design. The Registrar may require submission of physical samples where deemed necessary to ascertain conformity with submitted documentation. Disputes concerning the validity of a registered layout-design or the scope of its protection shall be referred to a Bench constituted under this Act, comprising not less than three persons possessing expertise in semiconductor technology and intellectual property law. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to such Bench. The decision of the Bench shall be final and binding, subject to further appeals as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "commercial exploitation" with respect to a registered layout-design shall mean any act which directly infringes upon the exclusive rights granted to the registrant under this Act. Such acts include, but are not limited to, reproduction, imitation, modification, and adaptation of the layout-design for the manufacture of integrated circuits. Commercial exploitation also extends to the importation of infringing integrated circuits, or offering them for sale within India. Nothing in this definition shall be construed as permitting reverse engineering solely for the purpose of determining whether an integrated circuit infringes a registered layout-design, provided that such determination is not used for commercial exploitation.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include particulars verifying ownership and detailing the intended scope of commercial exploitation. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating lawful entitlement to the layout-design, including documentation pertaining to its creation and any prior assignments. Where an applicant seeks protection for a layout-design incorporating elements previously registered under this Act, the application must explicitly identify those incorporated features and provide justification demonstrating that the overall design constitutes a novel work deserving of independent registration. The Registrar shall refuse registration if it is determined that the claimed commercial exploitation infringes upon existing rights or lacks sufficient specificity to ascertain the extent of protection sought as provided herein.

Where any person without authorization makes an infringing copy of a registered layout-design, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner. The measure of damages shall reflect the loss of profits reasonably attributable to the infringement and shall also include compensation for unjust enrichment derived from the unauthorized commercial exploitation of the layout-design. Provided that, in determining reasonable royalties, regard may be had to the notional license fee which would have been payable had the infringing party obtained a license from the owner prior to the act of infringement. Further, subject to demonstrating actual harm, the owner shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of copying or commercial exploitation as provided herein. The court may also order delivery up or destruction of the infringing copies and layout-designs.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person who undertakes commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be liable for damages. The amount of such damages shall be determined by the Controller, taking into consideration the extent of the unauthorized use, the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a consequence thereof, and reasonable royalty which the infringer would have been willing to pay had he been licensed to exploit the layout-design. Any application seeking determination of damages under this Act shall be filed with the Controller within three years from the date of the first instance of infringement discovered by the registered proprietor. The Controller may require the parties to submit evidence and arguments in support of their respective claims, and may conduct hearings as deemed necessary. Further, the Controller shall provide both parties an opportunity to present oral submissions before rendering a decision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes for sale, hires, displays for sale, distributes, imports, or otherwise deals with a layout-design commercially exploited by the proprietor shall be deemed to have infringed upon the said layout-design. Provided that such dealing must directly relate to the commercial exploitation of the design and not merely incidental to another lawful activity. The registered proprietor may, under this Act, seek injunctive relief against any person engaging in acts restricted herein, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the infringement. Further, where the infringing act involves the reproduction of a substantial part of the layout-design, the court shall consider the qualitative and quantitative aspects of such reproduction when determining liability for commercial exploitation.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design, makes, imports, sells, hires or offers for sale or hire any product which infringes the design shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement is established when the overall impression created by the infringing product is substantially similar to that formed by viewing the registered layout-design. Where commercial exploitation of a protected layout-design occurs through intermediaries, liability extends to those who knowingly facilitate such acts. The Court may, upon conviction, impose a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and extendable to two hundred thousand rupees, alongside an order for damages reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringement. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a layout-design shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting commercial exploitation of the design. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor, and the terms thereof shall be binding on both licensor and licensee. An assignment of rights in a layout-design, whether absolute or subject to trusts, requires execution by all concerned parties and registration with the Controller General. Where a license is granted for a specified territory, the proprietor may subsequently grant further licenses covering overlapping territories, provided that such subsequent grants do not unreasonably prejudice existing licensees. The right to assign or license shall vest in the registered proprietor alone, unless otherwise stipulated in a will or succession plan filed with the designated authority.

Where any person alleges that another has engaged in an act restricted under this Act relating to a registered layout-design, such allegation shall be pursued through civil remedies as provided herein. The determination of whether commercial exploitation has occurred is subject to the understanding that incidental use during analysis for reverse engineering purposes, undertaken solely to determine functionality and not for reproduction or distribution, does not constitute infringement. However, any evidence demonstrating systematic replication of substantial portions of the layout-design beyond such permissible analytical activities shall be prima facie considered as indicative of unauthorized commercial exploitation. The aggrieved party may seek an injunction restraining further acts of alleged infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered, provided that a reasonable royalty determination is made by the relevant court.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, engages in any act restricted under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for damages. Such acts include, but are not limited to, reproduction, adaptation, or direct or indirect commercial exploitation of a protected layout-design. The registered patentee may pursue civil remedies including injunctions preventing further infringing activity and recovery of lost profits attributable to the unauthorized use. Further, where the infringement is proven to be willful, enhanced damages up to three times the actual loss suffered by the patentee may be awarded. Any employee or agent acting on behalf of an infringer shall also be held accountable for their contribution towards the violation, subject to mitigation based on demonstrable lack of knowledge.

Where an India patentee alleges unauthorized commercial exploitation of a registered layout design, the Tribunal shall first determine whether the alleged acts fall within the scope of protection as defined under this Act. It shall be presumed that such acts constitute infringement unless the respondent demonstrates, through clear and convincing evidence, that the layout design was independently created or derived from publicly available information prior to the date of registration. Further, any finding of infringement may be appealed to the High Court within ninety days from the date of order, subject to a stay application being filed concurrently with the appeal. The Tribunal’s decision shall not be binding on the High Court and all questions of law arising in connection with this Act are open to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, "commercial exploitation" with respect to a registered layout-design shall include any act that directly or indirectly utilizes the protected design for commercial advantage. Such acts encompass, but are not limited to, reproduction, imitation, and distribution of the layout-design. The right to commercial exploitation is contingent upon the validity of the registration and subject to any conditions imposed during the grant process. A person claiming entitlement to a layout-design may file a date application patent demonstrating prior rights, provided that such claim is substantiated with documentary evidence as prescribed herein. Any act constituting commercial exploitation without authorization shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include a statement specifying the intended duration of protection sought, which may not exceed ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the nature and extent of such commercial exploitation, including details of manufacturing processes, distribution channels, and licensing agreements entered into concerning the layout-design. Where the applicant seeks protection in a Contracting State that has reciprocity provisions differing from those under this Act, the application shall explicitly detail these differences. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation regarding commercial exploitation may result in rejection of the registration request. The Registrar’s decision on such matters is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

For the purposes of this Act, "Judicial Member" means a person who possesses experience in intellectual property law, commercial law, or technology and is appointed by the Central Government to exercise judicial functions under this Act. A Judicial Member shall be selected from amongst persons having qualifications as prescribed for appointment as a Judge of a High Court, subject to the condition that they have practiced law for not less than ten years. The duties of a Judicial Member include hearing and disposing of appeals against orders passed by the Registrar and providing reasoned judgments as provided herein. A Judicial Member shall be bound by the decisions of the appellate forums established under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the initial examination report and any subsequent clarifications received from the Controller. The applicant may request an opportunity for personal hearing before the Judicial Member in cases where objections are raised during the substantive examination process concerning originality or infringement potential. Such hearings shall be conducted according to principles of natural justice, with due regard afforded to representations made by all parties involved. Where a layout-design incorporates elements previously registered under this Act, the application must clearly delineate the novel contributions and demonstrate that they possess sufficient inventive step as determined by the Judicial Member. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating these claims prior to proceeding with registration.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consist of a Technical Member and a Judicial Member, appointed in accordance with the provisions outlined herein. Appeals shall be finally decided within six months from the date of their receipt by the Tribunal, subject to unavoidable delays. Any order passed by the Tribunal shall be binding on all parties involved and may direct remedies including injunctions preventing further infringing acts or orders for account of profits derived from unauthorized use of a layout-design. The aggrieved party may also seek compensation for damages suffered as a consequence of such infringement, provided that the amount is determined reasonably and fairly, considering the circumstances of the case.

The Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal shall be presided over by a Judicial Member and such other Members as the Central Government may deem appropriate. The Judicial Member shall possess expertise in intellectual property law and have at least ten years of experience as a practicing advocate or judge. Applications for review under this Act, pertaining to decisions rendered by the Registrar relating to layout-design validity or infringement, may be filed before the Tribunal within ninety days from the date of such decision. The Central Government shall establish procedures for the expeditious disposal of applications and appeals. Subject to appeal to the High Court, the Tribunal’s findings on questions of fact are final. Provided that any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may seek a stay of execution pending review before the Tribunal, upon demonstrating irreparable harm. The Tribunal shall conduct its proceedings in accordance with principles of natural justice and as provided herein.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act, the appeal shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine such appeals, subject to the provisions of the relevant rules framed for its governance. Appeals may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against; provided that the Tribunal may entertain an appeal lodged after the expiry of said period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal in a timely manner. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall, for purposes of hearing appeals under this Act, include a Judicial Member and a Technical Member appointed as per prescribed procedures.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall have the jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from orders of the Registrar relating to infringement proceedings and rectification applications. Appeals shall be admitted only if accompanied by a deposit of such sum as may be prescribed, refundable upon successful determination of the appeal. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall consist of a Technical Member and a Judicial Member, appointed in accordance with rules framed under this Act. Decisions of the Tribunal are final subject to further appeal before the Supreme Court on a point of law. Penalties for non-compliance with orders issued by the Tribunal may be imposed as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a proprietor of a registered layout-design may grant licenses conferring rights to utilize the design for commercial purposes, including but not limited to manufacture, import, sale, and distribution. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, and such assignment shall vest in the assignee all rights and privileges held by the assignor under that license. The proprietor shall disclose fully the terms of any such licensing agreement to the Registrar upon request, for record purposes only. Any dispute arising from a license or assignment may be referred to arbitration as agreed between the parties; failing which, it shall be adjudicated before the Judicial Member of the relevant Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Further, an assignee under this Act shall hold rights equivalent to those held by the original proprietor, subject to any limitations expressly stated within the written agreement.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such party may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear appeals arising from orders concerning infringement of layout-design rights and related matters, including disputes over validity of registration certificates. Subject to provisions regarding timelines for filing appeals, the Tribunal shall consider all evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent. It is provided that in cases involving technical complexities relating to semiconductor technology or integrated circuit design, the Tribunal may, at its discretion, include a Judicial Member possessing specialized expertise as part of the appellate bench. The decision of the Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant statute governing judicial review.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a layout-design or concerning the infringement thereof appeals to the High Court, such appeal shall lie within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The High Court may, in hearing such appeal, entertain all grounds arising out of substantial questions of law and fact pertaining to the interpretation and application of this Act. For the purpose of adjudicating disputes concerning layout-design rights respect registration, the High Court shall be assisted by a Judicial Member possessing expertise in intellectual property matters. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified under established appellate procedure as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "Judicial Member" means a person appointed as such by notification in the Official Gazette, possessing experience in intellectual property law and having adjudicated cases under any other enactment relating to intellectual property rights. A Judicial Member shall exercise judicial functions within the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal and may preside over hearings concerning disputes related to layout design consisting of three-dimensional features or topographical representations of integrated circuits. The qualifications for appointment as a Judicial Member are subject to such conditions as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, provided that preference shall be given to individuals with expertise in semiconductor technology.

For the purposes of this Act, "Member" shall mean a person who is registered as such under Chapter II and holds a valid certificate of registration issued by the Registrar. A Member may be an individual, partnership firm, company, or other body corporate engaged in the design, manufacture, import, or adaptation of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design. Every applicant seeking to be recognized as a Member shall submit an application in the prescribed form along with the requisite fee and supporting documentation demonstrating their compliance with the technical qualifications stipulated herein. The Registrar may reject any such application if it is found that the applicant does not meet the criteria for registration as a Member, subject to appeal under this Act.

An application for registration as a Member shall be submitted to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant must demonstrate that they are engaged in activities related to the design, fabrication, testing, or marketing of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs. A person shall not be registered as a Member unless they satisfy the Registrar that they possess the technical expertise and resources necessary for compliance with the provisions under this Act. Further, an application may be rejected if the applicant has previously been found guilty of infringing upon the rights of another layout-design owner. The Registrar may require such additional information from the applicant as is deemed necessary to verify their eligibility to become a Member.

A Member shall be liable for damages sustained by any person as a result of a contravention of this Act attributable to the Member’s actions or omissions. Such damages may include compensation for loss of profits, loss of market share, and impairment of goodwill. Where a contravention is committed by an employee acting within the scope of their employment, the employer shall also be liable, subject to the employer demonstrating reasonable care in preventing such acts. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a Member may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief to restrain further infringements. The right to seek damages or equitable remedies as provided herein is without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. A Member found guilty of wilful infringement shall be subject to enhanced penalties, as determined by a competent court.

An application for registration as a Member shall be submitted to the Controller in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall declare their place of business within India and provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller establishing their technical expertise relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may require further information or clarification from the applicant, and the applicant shall be obliged to furnish such details within the time stipulated by the Controller. A Member shall maintain accurate records pertaining to their activities under this Act, accessible for inspection by authorized officers upon reasonable notice. Any alteration in a Member’s declared place of business must be notified to the Controller within thirty days. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in suspension of membership privileges as provided herein.

A person shall be deemed a Member for the purposes of this Act if that person is registered as an entity engaged in the design, fabrication, testing, or marketing of semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs and has maintained continuous compliance with all applicable regulatory filings under this Act. A Member’s status may be suspended by the Controller if it is determined that the Member has failed to submit required annual reports detailing their activities related to semiconductor integrated circuits layout designs, or if a finding of substantial infringement of another party's registered layout design rights has been made against them following due process as provided herein. Any individual holding a significant managerial position within such an entity shall be considered responsible for ensuring adherence to these requirements and may be held liable under this Act in cases of non-compliance.

Any person who is registered as a Member under this Act shall be subject to penalties for acts constituting infringement. Such penalties may include imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, which may be extended to two hundred thousand rupees, where the infringement is proven to have been committed with the intent to deceive or cause loss to the registered owner. Further, any Member found guilty of repeated violations shall face enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the seizure and destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Compensation for damages suffered by the registered owner is recoverable from the defaulting Member under procedures outlined herein.

A Member desiring to grant a license relating to a registered layout-design shall provide written notification to the Controller specifying the terms and conditions proposed. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the Member, subject to ensuring that the royalty rates are just and equitable considering prevailing industry standards for similar integrated circuits. Any assignment of rights in a registered layout-design by a Member shall include a detailed inventory of the layout-design elements being transferred, along with a declaration confirming compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the accuracy of such declarations and to assess potential impacts on competition within the semiconductor industry. A licensee may sub-license rights granted under this Act, provided that prior consent is obtained from the Member and documented in writing.

A person shall be deemed a Member for the purposes of this Act if that person is registered as such under the prescribed manner and holds a valid certificate of registration issued by the Registrar. Any individual aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the eligibility criteria for becoming a Member, or concerning the revocation of their Membership, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. Provided that, where the decision relates to a matter of fact, the Tribunal shall confirm such decision unless it finds that there has been a material error or misapprehension. The Registrar may, notwithstanding anything contained herein, require further documentation from an applicant for Membership if reasonable doubt arises regarding their compliance with this Act.

Where any person claims to be a Member and such claim is disputed by the Registrar, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Intellectual Property Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consider evidence submitted by both parties, including documentation establishing continuous engagement in activities related to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, and shall determine whether the claimant meets the criteria for Membership as defined under this Act. Registration shall not be withheld solely on grounds of procedural irregularity but may be denied if the applicant demonstrably fails to satisfy the substantive requirements for qualification. The Tribunal’s decision is final, subject to a further appeal only on the limited ground that the Tribunal acted without jurisdiction or exceeded its powers, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days.

For the purposes of this Act, a "Member" shall mean any person who is registered as such under Chapter II and holds a valid certificate of registration issued by the Controller. A Member may include individuals, partnerships, companies, or other legal entities engaged in the design, manufacture, import, or distribution of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs. Every Member shall be subject to the provisions regarding confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements as provided herein. Further, any Member who discovers an error in their registered details is entitled to apply for direct notice rectification, following a prescribed procedure outlined by the Controller; such application must detail the specific inaccuracies requiring correction.

A person shall be deemed a Member for the purposes of this Act if such person is registered as the owner of a layout-design under this Act and maintains that registration current. Every application for registration as a Member must include a certified copy of the initial publication details pertaining to the layout-design, or provide evidence demonstrating that no such publication occurred. Failure to submit this documentation shall render the application liable for rejection. Upon successful registration, the Register shall issue a certificate confirming the applicant’s status as a Member and detailing the registered layout-design. Further, any Member desiring to transfer their rights in respect of a registered layout-design must notify the Register, who shall record such transfer subject to fulfilling prescribed formalities. A Member's right to challenge actions taken under this Act shall published expiry after six months from the date of notification.

An application for registration under this Act shall be in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required by the First Schedule, including but not limited to details relating to the applicant, the trade mark itself, and the goods or services with reference to which it is used or proposed to be used. An india application shall specify the date of first use of the trade mark in India, if such use has occurred; provided that failure to provide this information shall not, by itself, render the application inadmissible. The Registrar may require further information from an applicant to ascertain compliance with these provisions as provided herein.

Any individual or corporate body claiming exclusive right in a trademark used in connection with any goods or services, and seeking to secure the benefits of registration under this Act, shall file an application with the Registrar. The application must specify the mark sought to be registered, clearly identify the goods or services with which it is associated, and provide details of prior use, if applicable. An applicant shall also declare whether the trademark is being used by them currently. Further, any alteration made to a previously filed application may require payment of an additional fee as determined by the Registrar. Provided that where an application relates to geographically indicative information, the Registrar may request supplementary documentation substantiating such claim. Any misleading or fraudulent representation in an india application shall render it liable for rejection and potential penalties.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed service mark under this Act shall file an application with the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fees as determined by notification. The application must specify the particulars of the applicant, including their address for communication, and clearly state the representation of the mark sought to be registered. Where the applicant is not carrying on business or has no place of establishment in India, they shall appoint an agent resident in India to act on their behalf and file the application accordingly. The prescribed form must be completed accurately; any deficiency may result in rejection of the application. Further, india application shall include a list of goods or services with which the mark is associated, classified according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Any alteration to this information requires notification to the Registrar.

An application for registration under this Act shall be in the prescribed form and contain such particulars as are required by the regulations framed thereunder. The applicant shall specify the goods or services in relation to which he seeks to register the trade mark, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. An india application shall register respect goods falling within a single class only if the applicant demonstrates distinctiveness for those specific articles. Provided that where the goods are not ascertainable, the Registrar may require further clarification. The applicant shall also state the date from which he claims to have used the trade mark.

An application for registration of a trademark under this Act shall be in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required by the First Schedule. Where an india application is filed relating to a trademark that includes a geographical indication, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating due authorization to use the said geographical indication. The Registrar shall examine each india application in accordance with the provisions herein and may request further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for proper assessment. Any objection raised by any person against an india application shall be processed as provided under this Act, affording the applicant a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Decisions regarding the acceptance or rejection of applications are subject to review by a Bench constituted according to established procedures.

For the purposes of this Act, an “india application” is defined as an application filed with the Registrar by any person claiming to be proprietor of a trademark, seeking its registration under this Act. Such an india application must specify the mark sought to be registered, a description of the goods or services in relation to which it is used or proposed to be used, and the class or classes thereof as specified in Schedule I. An india application shall also include any representation of the trade mark, whether textual or graphical, faithfully reproduced. The Registrar may reject an india application if he considers that the applicant lacks the necessary standing to apply for registration.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed complete upon receipt by the Registrar of the requisite forms, fees, and representation of the mark as specified under this Act. Where an applicant seeks to register a device comprising words and figurative elements, clarity regarding the distinctiveness of each element is essential; any disclaimers required to ensure such distinctiveness must be clearly stated within the india application. The Registrar may require further clarification or amendment of the proposed representation if it lacks sufficient detail for proper examination.
