Provided that, during the pendency of such an appeal, the appellate tribunal may, subject to just cause shown, grant an interim injunction restraining the respondent from utilizing or adopting the trade mark in question. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate tribunal concerning a refusal of an erasure order injunction may further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified under this Act. The court shall consider whether the balance of convenience warrants such restraint pending final determination.

Where a trade mark proprietor seeks to enforce their rights under this Act, they may grant licenses permitting use of the registered trade mark subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable by the proprietor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days and published as per prescribed procedures. Further, where a court issues an erasure order injunction against a licensee acting beyond the scope of their granted rights, the proprietor retains ownership of the trade mark but may be obligated to compensate the licensee for losses reasonably incurred in reliance on the provisional specification claim outlining permitted usage. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all licenses and assignments relating to registered trade marks, accessible upon request by interested parties.

An erasure order injunction shall be granted by the Registrar or a designated authority where it is demonstrated that the use of a trade mark, registered under this Act, constitutes an unfair competition practice or otherwise violates principles of equity and good faith. Such an injunction may restrain any person from utilizing, displaying, or reproducing the impugned mark, subject to conditions as deemed necessary to mitigate undue hardship on bona fide users. An application for erasure order injunction shall be accompanied by a detailed assessment demonstrating the detrimental impact of the continued use of the trade mark. The Registrar may require submission of an India application detailing proposed alternative marks before proceeding with any such order.

An application for registration of a geographical indication, as provided herein, shall be in the prescribed form and contain particulars including the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, a map indicating the territorial limits of the geographical area for which the geographical indication is applicable, and details of the products or goods with which it is associated. The applicant shall also specify the history, qualities, and characteristics of the product attributable exclusively to its origin. Further, an application registration shall include a statement affirming that the applicant has the consent of producers representing the interests of the concerned agricultural area.

An application registration shall be filed with the Registrar by any association or individual claiming to represent the interests of producers of goods originating from a specified territory, provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the quality and reputation of those goods. The application must include detailed particulars regarding the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, a map delineating the geographical area constituting its origin, and a description of the product for which it is used. Further, the applicant shall furnish evidence establishing the existence of such geographical indication prior to the date of this application, including historical records or traditional knowledge documentation. The Registrar may require additional information or clarification as deemed necessary during processing of the registration.

An aggrieved party, including any registered proprietor or authorized user of a geographical indication, may institute legal proceedings in the competent civil court for relief against infringement of that geographical indication. Such infringement includes any use of the indication which is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods. An application registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the proprietorship of the geographical indication unless proven otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence before the court. The remedies available under this Act include an injunction restraining further infringing acts, damages sustained by the aggrieved party, and the disposal of infringing goods as per rules framed by the Central Government. Provided that any action taken by the Registrar or any officer acting under his direction shall not be challengeable in any civil court.

An application registration shall be filed with the Geographical Indications Registry by any society or association engaged in production, processing, or other activities relating to goods claiming origin from a specific geographical territory. The applicant must demonstrate that the indication is primarily associated with the quality, reputation, or characteristics of the goods as they are produced within the defined area. Such application shall include detailed particulars regarding the name of the geographical indication, the goods for which it is sought, the description of the geographical territory of origin, and a map delineating its boundaries. The Registrar may require further information to ascertain the distinctiveness of the indication and its connection to the specified region. Provided that an existing registration does not preclude such application, the Registry shall publish a notice inviting objections from interested parties within three months of receipt.

An application registration shall be deemed incomplete if it fails to include detailed specifications regarding cultivation, processing, or preparation methods unique to the goods claiming protection under this Act. Provided that, any applicant demonstrating prior use of the proposed geographical indication for commercial purposes within the defined territory, subject to verification by the Registrar, may submit supporting documentation in lieu of exhaustive procedural details. The Registrar shall notify the applicant and interested parties regarding the application registration and invite objections within a prescribed period. Any objection received must be substantiated with evidence establishing consumer confusion or misrepresentation. Further, the Registrar may require additional information from the applicant concerning the geographical boundaries defining the origin of the goods.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, upon discovery of any infringement occurring within the territory of India, file a complaint with the appropriate civil court or initiate proceedings before an adjudicating officer as provided herein. An application registration shall not preclude subsequent enforcement actions against parties engaging in deceptive practices utilizing similar indications that create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties including but not limited to fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Registrar may, subject to due process, issue cease and desist orders against any entity found to be misusing a protected geographical indication.

An application registration shall be deemed invalid if it is established, through evidence presented before the Registrar, that the applicant’s use of the indicated geographical name misrepresents the origin or characteristics of the goods in question. Provided that, an appeal against such determination lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification of the order. Further, the Board may, subject to just considerations and after affording the applicant a reasonable opportunity for being heard, direct the Registrar to reconsider the application registration or uphold the initial decision. Any party aggrieved by any order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within such time as may be prescribed.

An application registration shall be deemed invalid if the geographical indication sought to be registered does not exclusively identify goods originating from a specific territory or region within India, or a geographically defined area outside India. For the purposes of this Act, “originating” means produced, processed, and prepared within that territory, region, or area, respectively. An application may proceed only if the applicant demonstrates that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. Furthermore, the indication must be capable of industrial application in relation to those goods, as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication, seeking to enforce their exclusive rights under this Act, shall institute proceedings before a court having jurisdiction over the territory where the alleged infringement occurred. An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the quality, reputation or other characteristic of goods attributable to its origin and the area of production. Provided that any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application registration shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The remedies available to the proprietor upon establishing infringement include injunctions restraining further infringing activity, damages proportionate to the loss suffered, and the disposal of infringing goods. Further, the court may award costs to the prevailing party as deemed appropriate under this Act.

An application registration shall be filed with the Geographical Indications Registry by any society or association representing the interests of producers of goods originating from a defined geographical area, provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the quality and reputation of those goods. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the origin and characteristics unique to the indicated product. Any person intending to use a geographical indication identical or deceptively similar to a registered indication shall be deemed to be falsifying trade mark rights if such usage creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the source or nature of the goods. Such an application registration is subject to objection by any interested party within three months from the date of publication, detailing specific grounds for opposition under this Act. The Registrar shall provide opportunity for a hearing before making a determination on any objections received.

For the purposes of this Act, “tea” with reference to the geographical indication ‘Darjeeling’ shall mean tea produced exclusively in the defined geographical area comprising villages within Darjeeling district, excluding areas beyond its specified boundaries as delineated under notification issued by the Tea Board. Registration shall apply only to producers and processors who adhere strictly to cultivation and processing methods prescribed by the competent authority. Any alteration of such methods, or use of teas not originating from the defined geographical area, will render the registration liable for revocation. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating adherence to these standards as a condition for maintaining registration.

Application for registration of a geographical indication shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, containing particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, and the area of its origin. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin as provided herein. Where an application for registration includes a collective mark or certification trade mark relating to the geographical indication, the Registrar may require further information concerning the constitution and functioning of the association proposing to use such mark. Registration shall apply only to the applicant who meets all requirements under this Act and submits the necessary fees. Any alteration to the registered particulars must also be submitted for approval.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication, hereinafter referred to as the “right holder,” shall have the exclusive right to use the said indication in connection with goods for which it is registered. Any person who produces or deals with goods not conforming to the standards of quality, nature, production method, or other characteristics prescribed under this Act for the relevant geographical indication shall be deemed to be infringing the rights of the right holder. Such infringement may result in civil proceedings wherein the aggrieved party may seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the mark and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the right holder. Registration shall apply to all goods identical to those for which the geographical indication is registered, as well as similar goods. The Registrar may issue directions regarding corrective measures where infringement occurs.

An application for registration of a geographical indication, conforming to Form G as specified in the First Schedule, shall be filed with the Registrar, setting forth particulars of the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the region where it is produced, processed or prepared, and details of any trade association representing producers interested in the protection of the indication. The applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating a long-standing link between the geographical origin and the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of the goods. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar may serve notice to any persons likely to be affected by the registration. Objections received within the prescribed period shall be considered, and the applicant afforded an opportunity for rebuttal. Following due consideration, registration shall apply if the Registrar is satisfied that the conditions precedent are met.

Application for registration shall be made to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form, detailing the characteristics of the goods originating from the specified territory, including but not limited to agricultural practices employed, traditional processing methods utilized, and unique qualities attributable solely to that origin. The applicant must demonstrate exclusive control over the quality and reputation of the goods as they relate to the geographical indication sought. Provided that the proposed name does not conflict with any existing trademark or prior right under this Act, and subject to verification by the Registrar regarding the authenticity of the claimed territorial boundaries, registration shall apply upon satisfaction that the application meets all requirements stipulated herein. Further, the applicant must provide evidence of widespread recognition amongst consumers associating the goods with the indicated geographical origin.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, upon discovery of any infringement occurring within the territory of India, have recourse to civil remedies as provided herein, including an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. Any false or misleading representation that goods originate from a place associated with a geographically indicated product, regardless of actual origin, constitutes actionable misrepresentation subject to penalties prescribed under this Act. Registration shall apply to protect the distinctiveness and reputation of the geographical indication against dilution by unauthorized use. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in fines up to five hundred thousand rupees, and repeat offenders are liable for imprisonment extending to three years.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication relating to Darjeeling tea, desiring to grant a license conferring the right to use said indication on any other person for commercial purposes, shall submit an application to the Registrar detailing the scope and duration of such licence. The Registrar may, after due consideration and subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions regarding quality control and adherence to established production practices, approve the proposed licensing arrangement. Registration shall apply to all licences so approved, creating a publicly accessible record of permitted usage. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication license requires prior notification to the Registrar and their express consent, provided that such consent may be withheld if deemed detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of Darjeeling tea. The proprietor remains ultimately responsible for ensuring compliance with the terms of any licensed use under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication, aggrieved by any order made under this Act or by any act or omission constituting infringement thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order or discovery of the infringing act. Provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if the appellant satisfies it that there were sufficient reasons for not preferring the appeal within the time allowed and that the delay caused no prejudice to the other party. The Registrar shall, upon receiving notice of such an appeal, transmit all relevant records to the Appellate Board. It is further provided that registration shall apply even where a challenge to validity is pending before the Board.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication, aggrieved by any action taken or decision made under this Act relating to the registration or infringement thereof, may within sixty days from the date on which such action is taken or decision is communicated, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds specified in the appeal and shall be finally disposed of within a period of six months from the date it is filed; provided that the Board may, if reasonable cause is shown, extend this period by not more than three months. Where registration shall apply to a particular agricultural product or foodstuff originating from a defined geographical area, any use which constitutes infringement registered without consent will be deemed actionable under this Act.

An application for registration of a geographical indication, subject to the provisions regarding novelty requirements applicable to design register entries, shall include particulars specifying the agricultural area or region from which the goods originate, including maps where appropriate. The Registrar may require further clarification concerning the boundaries defining such area and may conduct site visits to ascertain these details. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the prescribed manner inviting objections from any interested party. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar, who shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond as provided herein. Ultimately, registration shall apply if the geographical indication is deemed distinctive within the relevant sector.

A geographical indication is deemed to indicate exclusive agricultural, natural or processed goods originating from a defined geographical territory where the quality, reputation or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to the origin of that place. For the purposes of this Act, ‘originating’ shall mean the entire production process, including cultivation, processing and preparation, takes place within the specified geographical boundaries. Registration shall be refused if the proposed indication comprises a deceptive indication as to the source or nature of the goods. An application for registration under this Act shall include particulars identifying the growers' association or other producers' collective proposing the registration.

Any person engaged in the production, processing, or packaging of Alphonso mangoes within the designated area of Konkan Taluka, Maharashtra, who desires to utilize the geographical indication “Konkani Alphonso” for commercial purposes, shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form. Such application shall detail the applicant’s connection to the defined geographical unit and demonstrate adherence to quality standards as determined by the Geographical Indications Council. Registration shall be granted only if the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant's activities contribute to maintaining the distinct characteristics of Konkani Alphonso mangoes. Provided that, any existing user of the indication prior to its registration may continue such use subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar and as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form, along with the requisite fee. Such application must specify the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods to which it relates, and particulars of the applicant claiming to represent the interests of the producers of such goods originating from the defined geographic area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the origin, qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods. Provided that, if the Registrar is satisfied that the geographical indication is not deceptively similar to an earlier trademark, and that use in accordance with this Act is customary in the defined geographic area, registration shall be granted. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating a connection between the goods and the specified geographic origin.

Application for registration shall be made by any association of persons or producer companies engaged in the production of goods conforming to the standard specified in the registered geographical indication, or by any other person who is lawfully engaged in producing such goods. Provided that an application under this Act may also be filed by a society as defined under the Societies Registration Act, 1960, if it represents the interests of producers and has their consent. The Registrar shall require evidence demonstrating adherence to quality control measures stipulated for the geographical indication; failure to provide satisfactory proof will result in rejection of the application. Further, any applicant seeking registration must demonstrate continuous production of goods within the defined geographical area as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, who discovers that any other person is making use of the said geographical indication in contravention of this Act, shall institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. Such proceedings may seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further such usage and recovery of damages sustained as a direct result of the infringement. Registration shall not confer upon the proprietor or authorized user the right to prevent the use of any description which constitutes a genuine prior trade mark in relation to goods or services. Any person found guilty of knowingly using a registered geographical indication without authorization, subject to appeal to the appellate authority, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees and subsequent offences may attract enhanced penalties as determined by the court.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication relating to Darjeeling tea, desiring to grant a license conferring the right to use said indication on any other person for commercial purposes, shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form. Such application shall detail the scope and duration of the proposed license, including specific restrictions on product quality and packaging as deemed necessary to maintain the distinctiveness of Darjeeling tea. The Registrar may approve or reject such application after affording the applicant and any interested party a reasonable opportunity for being heard. Upon registration, the license shall be recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications. Further, assignment of rights under a registered geographical indication requires prior consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent will not be unreasonably withheld. Registration shall confer upon the assignee all rights previously held by the assignor relating to the licensed use.

Any individual or association seeking to utilize a registered geographical indication for goods conforming to the standards of quality and reputation associated with that indication shall submit an application to the Registrar, detailing the proposed nature of use and demonstrating adherence to established production practices. Registration shall not be granted unless the applicant provides satisfactory evidence of their ongoing commitment to maintaining the distinct characteristics of the indicated good, as verified by a recognized trade association or consumer protection body. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding registration or refusal under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, presenting arguments and counter-evidence demonstrating material error or misinterpretation of relevant guidelines.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall, upon discovery of any infringement thereof, have the right to institute civil proceedings for damages and seek injunctive relief against the infringing party. Such remedies are without prejudice to any penal sanctions provided under this Act or any other law in force. The Registrar may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for hearing, issue orders restraining acts of unfair competition involving the registered geographical indication. Further, a basic registration shall not confer upon the proprietor exclusive right to use the name or emblem associated with the goods unless such usage constitutes an act of misrepresentation likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods. Any person aggrieved by an order issued under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as to the name of the applicant, the geographical area from which the goods originate, the class of goods to which the indication relates, and a map of the geographical area. Where it appears that the use of a registered geographical indication is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers or to be detrimental to the reputation of the collective interest in the indicated product, the Register may grant an order injunction restraining any person from using such indication in relation to goods not originating from the territory defined in the registration. This power shall extend to preventing the use of similar indications which create a likelihood of association with the registered geographical indication, provided that the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from such usage.

Where a proprietor establishes that use by another person is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication, the Board may grant an order injunction restraining such use. This restraint shall extend to acts which create a false association between the goods or services offered under the infringing mark and the genuine product originating from the geographically defined area. Provided that, in determining whether use constitutes dilution, the Board shall consider the extent to which the geographical indication has come to be recognized by the relevant public as identifying a particular quality, origin, or reputation of goods or services. Further, any person aggrieved by an order injunction may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to conditions regarding costs and interim relief pending disposal of the appeal.

Where an interested party alleges that a registered geographical indication is being used in contradiction to the provisions of this Act, or in a manner likely to cause dilution of its distinctiveness, such party may apply to the Geographical Indications Registry for directions. Upon receipt of such application, the Registry shall give notice thereof to the alleged infringer and any other interested parties as provided herein. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registry may direct that an order injunction be issued restraining the use of the geographical indication in the manner complained of. Such injunction may include provisions regarding costs and compensation for losses incurred by the proprietor of the registered geographical indication. The Registrar shall provide a reasoned order detailing the grounds upon which the injunction is based, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Court that use by another person is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication, or is misleading to consumers regarding the origin of goods, the Court may grant an order injunction restraining such use. This restraint shall be without prejudice to any right which the user may have under this Act relating to honest concurrent use established prior to the date of registration, provided that such use does not create a false association with the registered geographical indication in the minds of consumers. The proprietor seeking such injunctive relief shall further demonstrate reasonable efforts were undertaken to notify the infringing party of the potential violation and offer an opportunity for compliance.

Any person found to be using a registered geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the court, reflecting the loss suffered by the registered proprietor and detriment to the reputation of the indicated goods. Further, upon complaint made by the Registrar or any registered proprietor, the court may grant an order injunction restraining such use, subject to a hearing where the alleged infringer may present their defense. This power extends to preventing the sale, hire, or offering for sale of goods falsely bearing the geographical indication. Failure to comply with an order injunction shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender liable to further penalties as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act may grant non-exclusive licenses to use the indication in relation to goods that conform to the standards established for that indication, provided that such license agreements specify the duration, scope, and royalty payments due to the proprietor. Assignment of rights relating to a registered geographical indication shall require prior consent from the Registrar, who may impose conditions safeguarding the continued quality and reputation associated with the indication. Further, any person seeking to utilize a protected geographical indication without authorization from the rightful proprietor is liable for infringement, and the court may issue an order injunction restraining such unauthorized use, subject to considerations of fair dealing and public interest as determined by the presiding judge. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all licenses and assignments granted concerning registered geographical indications.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, and where during the pendency of such opposition proceedings, the applicant reasonably apprehends that any person is likely to use the distinctive signs or indications in relation to goods not conforming to the standards prescribed herein, the Appellate Board may, upon being satisfied that irreparable injury would otherwise result, grant an interim order injunction restraining such person from so doing. Such order shall be subject to review by the Board at its discretion and may include conditions regarding security and undertaking as it deems appropriate. Any party aggrieved by any order granted or refused under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the date of such order, provided that the appellate court shall not alter the substantive findings of fact made by the Appellate Board unless there is a clear error of law apparent on the record.

Where an authorized user demonstrates to the Registrar that a use of a registered geographical indication, notwithstanding its compliance with conditions prescribed under this Act, is causing dilution of the distinctiveness of the indication or is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods, the Registrar may direct such authorized user to cease such use. The Registrar shall, prior to issuing any such direction, provide the concerned party an opportunity for a hearing and shall consider submissions made in response to a form petition particulars submitted by that party. Further, upon application by the proprietor of the geographical indication, a court may grant an order injunction restraining any person from engaging in conduct detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication.

Any proprietor seeking to register said geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights in relation to its use for indicating origin in connection with such goods, subject to any prior registrations under this Act. Such registration confers upon the proprietor the right to grant licenses and assign these rights to other parties, provided that all subsequent licensees or assigns adhere strictly to quality control measures as prescribed by the Alphonso Mango Growers’ Association. Any unauthorized use of the registered geographical indication may be restrained by a court through an order injunction, preventing further misrepresentation of goods as originating from the designated region. The proprietor shall maintain a register detailing all licenses and assignments, accessible for inspection under conditions determined by the Registrar.

Where a proprietor establishes that use by another person is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the Geographical Indication, or is otherwise detrimental to the interests of the registered proprietors or authorized users, the Registrar may, subject to appeal under this Act, issue an order injunction restraining such use. This power shall extend to preventing the application of the Geographical Indication in relation to goods or services not conforming to the standards prescribed herein. It is provided that a trade description denotes origin within the defined geographical area only if it accurately reflects production methods and characteristics as registered; any misleading portrayal constitutes actionable infringement, justifying injunctive relief. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both parties regarding potential consumer confusion and economic impact when determining the scope of such an order injunction.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no court shall grant an injunction restraining a proprietor from using a geographical indication in relation to goods other than those for which the indication is registered, provided that such use is in accordance with honest practices in industrial and commercial matters and does not constitute an unfair trade practice. An order injunction may be granted against any person who, without authorization under this Act, makes any article or product identifying it with a registered geographical indication, or uses such indication in connection with the offering for sale of goods or services; further, the court may require erasure or alteration of any layout design providing visual representation of the protected indication.

An alteration certificate registration shall be deemed to occur when an application for modification of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design is submitted to the Registrar. Such applications must specify the original layout-design and detail the proposed alterations with precision, accompanied by a technical justification demonstrating that the changes do not constitute a new layout-design under this Act. The Registrar may require supporting documentation from a qualified engineer attesting to the nature and extent of the modifications. An alteration certificate registration shall be granted only if the Registrar is satisfied that the application complies with all requirements as provided herein, and does not prejudice existing rights.

An application for alteration certificate registration concerning a layout-design shall be made to the Registrar in Form Alpha, accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The applicant must demonstrate that the proposed alterations do not substantially affect the original layout-design’s functionality or intended purpose, and provide detailed documentation outlining the changes sought. Subject to verification of these details, the Registrar may require a technical expert appointed under this Act to assess the impact of the alteration. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding an application for alteration certificate registration may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Provided that such appeal shall not operate as a stay on the operation of the order appealed against.

Where an alteration has been made to a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, the registrant shall apply for and obtain an alteration certificate registration within six months from the date of such alteration. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original layout-design registration certificate and a detailed description of the modifications effected. Failure to secure this alteration certificate registration will render the altered layout-design vulnerable to infringement claims, as it is deemed not properly registered under this Act. Any person claiming damages for infringement relating to an unregistered alteration shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and compensation commensurate with the loss suffered. The Registrar may reject an application if the proposed alterations substantially depart from the original design or are demonstrably contrary to public interest, provided that such rejection is accompanied by a reasoned order.

An application for alteration certificate registration concerning a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be submitted to the Registrar in Form IC-A, accompanied by an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the proposed alterations and detailing the reasons necessitating such modification. The applicant must demonstrate that the changes sought do not substantially affect the original design’s inventive character or functionality as determined at the time of initial registration. Subject to verification of identity through prescribed documentation, the Registrar may direct a hearing if any objection is raised by an interested party within thirty days of the application's receipt. Any alteration certificate granted under this Act shall be published in the Official Gazette and deemed part of the original layout-design registration record. The applicant shall pay such fees as are prescribed for alteration certificate registration, which are non-refundable even if the application is rejected.

An application for alteration certificate registration shall be made to the Registrar in Form Alpha, accompanied by an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the proposed alterations and detailing the reasons necessitating such modification. The applicant must demonstrate that the original layout-design remains substantially similar following the changes, and that no new element has been introduced which would independently qualify for protection under this Act. Provided that the alteration does not extend to the essential features of the registered layout-design, the Registrar may grant the certificate upon satisfaction that the proposed modifications comply with the provisions herein regarding permissible alterations. The applicant shall also pay such fees as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may file a complaint with the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Authority shall issue notice to the accused party, affording them an opportunity for response within thirty days. Failure to respond or a demonstrably false denial will be deemed conclusive evidence against the accused. Where alteration of the registered layout-design is claimed by the proprietor, they must submit an alteration certificate registration application with supporting documentation. The Registrar may reject such an application if it determines that the alterations substantially depart from the original design. Any unauthorized reproduction based on a rejected alteration certificate shall constitute infringement subject to penalties as provided herein.

The registered owner of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights relating to reproduction and use, subject to the terms specified therein. Such licenses may be assigned to any person or entity with the prior written consent of the original registrant, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Registrar within thirty days. Where a license agreement involves alterations to the registered layout-design which substantially affect its functionality or appearance, the assignee shall apply for an alteration certificate registration demonstrating the nature and extent of those changes. The Registrar may require submission of technical documentation substantiating these modifications before processing the application. Failure to obtain such certification prior to commercial exploitation of the altered design renders the assignee liable for infringement proceedings under this Act.

An application for alteration certificate registration shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the proposed alterations and demonstrating that such changes do not substantially affect the original layout-design’s technical solution. The Registrar may, after providing notice to all interested parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, reject the application if satisfied that the proposed alterations constitute a new layout-design or infringe upon any existing registered right. Any party aggrieved by an order of rejection under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order; provided that the appellate tribunal shall consider only questions of law arising out of the Registrar’s decision and not matters of fact already determined.

An application for alteration certificate registration shall be made to the Registrar in Form D and accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The applicant must demonstrate that the proposed alterations do not substantially affect the original layout-design’s character or functionality, providing detailed schematics and a comparative analysis where applicable. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall consider whether the proposed modifications are minor corrections or represent a new layout-design altogether. If satisfied that the changes qualify for alteration certificate registration as provided herein, the registrar may proceed with examination. The applicant is required to submit an affidavit confirming the veracity of the information furnished and attesting to the originality of the altered design.

For the purposes of this Act, Right Management Information signifies information attached to or associated with works in electronic form, including but not limited to authorial identifiers, copyright notices, terms and conditions governing use, and data relating to rights ownership. Such information shall be deemed integral to the work itself and its protection under this Act. The reproduction, distribution, import, or communication of a work knowing that such actions involve alteration or removal of Right Management Information without authorization constitutes an infringement. Provided that, where Right Management Information is inadvertently altered or removed during legitimate use, liability shall not attach unless demonstrable negligence is proven.

For the purposes of this Act, every owner of copyright in an artistic work or musical work shall be entitled to control the incorporation and communication of Right Management Information. Such information may include, but is not limited to, the name of the author, the title of the work, the copyright owner’s identification, and terms and conditions for use. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register of declared Right Management Information, upon application by the copyright owner accompanied by prescribed fees and supporting documentation establishing ownership. Any person who knowingly alters or removes such information without authorization is liable to prosecution under this Act. Provided that, registration of Right Management Information does not confer any additional rights beyond those already vested in the copyright holder as provided herein.

Any person who, without the authority of the owner of copyright, knowingly and willfully removes or alters any Right Management Information, distributes, imports for distribution, communicates to the public, or exhibits in public any work knowing that such Right Management Information has been removed or altered, shall be liable to prosecution. Such actions are deemed infringements under this Act. The right holder may pursue civil remedies including damages equivalent to actual loss suffered or a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, whichever is greater. Provided that, where the infringement is committed for commercial advantage or financial gain, the court may award aggravated damages at its discretion. Further, any intermediary facilitating such acts shall be deemed liable unless they demonstrate reasonable efforts to prevent the infringing conduct as provided herein.

The owner of copyright in any work shall be entitled to control the inclusion of Right Management Information pertaining to that work and any copies thereof. Such Right Management Information includes, but is not limited to, the name of the author, the title of the work, and information regarding terms and conditions for use. Any person who knowingly removes or alters such Right Management Information without authorization from the owner shall be deemed to have infringed under this Act. The Central Government may prescribe procedures for verifying claims concerning ownership of Right Management Information and resolving disputes arising therefrom. Provided that, where Right Management Information is embedded within a digital work, the removal or alteration thereof shall be considered an act of circumvention of technological protection measures as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may file a complaint with the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Authority established under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where works are made available digitally, any information attached to such works, including but not limited to author details, copyright notices, terms of use and licensing conditions, shall be deemed Right Management Information. The reproduction or distribution of a work in digital form is prohibited if it is accompanied by Right Management Information that has been altered without authorization from the rights owner. Any person who knowingly removes or modifies such information with the intent to mislead concerning the ownership or status of copyright under this Act shall be liable for damages. Furthermore, providing false Right Management Information constitutes an offence and may result in penalties as provided herein. The responsibility for ensuring compliance rests with distributors and platforms facilitating access to copyrighted material.

Any person who, without the authority of the owner of copyright, knowingly and willfully removes or alters any Right Management Information, or distributes, imports for distribution, or communicates to the public any work knowing that such Right Management Information has been removed or altered, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Court may, in determining the amount of compensation payable under this Act, take into consideration the commercial gain attributable to the infringement and the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a direct result thereof. Provided that, where the infringing act is committed for trade or financial gain, the minimum penalty shall be two lakh rupees. Any such contravention shall also constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

The owner of copyright in any work shall have the exclusive right to control the incorporation and communication of Right Management Information, including but not limited to identifying information pertaining to the author, creator, and initial proprietor. Such Right Management Information may be embedded within digital works or attached thereto as metadata. Assignment of copyright under this Act shall include assignment of all rights relating to the management and protection of such information; provided that any subsequent licensee acquiring rights through transfer shall be bound by conditions precedent concerning the maintenance and accurate representation of said Right Management Information. Failure to adhere to these requirements may render a party liable for damages, subject to judicial determination as to reasonable compensation. The owner is empowered to license third parties to manage this information on their behalf, with terms agreed upon in writing.

Where copyright in a work is infringed by the alteration, modification, or adaptation of such work, and where such alteration incorporates Right Management Information, being information which identifies the author or right holder, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further dissemination of the infringing material. Provided that, if the alleged infringer demonstrates, subject to verification by an expert appointed by the High Court, that the Right Management Information was inadvertently altered during a legitimate process of data migration or archival storage, and without any commercial gain, such injunction may be withheld or modified as the court deems just. Any appeal against an order granting or refusing such relief shall lie to the appellate jurisdiction established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, Right Management Information means integrated data which identifies the work, author, copyright owner, terms and conditions governing the use of the work, and any trade marks proprietor associated with it, and which is disseminated alongside or in relation to a copy of the work. Such information shall include, but not be limited to, embedded metadata, electronic watermarks, digital signatures, and access control protocols. The dissemination of Right Management Information shall be deemed part of the distribution process. Any alteration or removal of such information without authorization from the copyright owner or trade marks proprietor shall constitute an infringement under this Act, subject to any exemptions provided herein.

Where copyright subsists in any work, the author or owner of copyright shall be entitled to control the inclusion of Right Management Information pertaining to that work. Such information includes, but is not limited to, the title of the work, the name of its author, and details regarding the terms and conditions under which it may be used. Any person who knowingly distributes a copy of a work containing altered or removed Right Management Information shall be deemed to have infringed upon the copyright therein. The Registrar of the Patent Office may, at the request of any aggrieved party, investigate allegations of such infringement and issue directives for compliance with this provision. Further, failure to comply with these directives may result in penalties as provided herein. This right is subject to reasonable limitations necessary to enable lawful research or analysis undertaken by accredited institutions.

For the purposes of this Act, infringement registered shall occur when a sign used in commerce becomes likely to cause confusion amongst the public regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services. Such likelihood shall be determined considering all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the similarity of the signs, the relatedness of the goods or services, and the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark. Nothing in this Act shall prevent a proprietor from taking action against any person using a sign similar to their registered trade mark where such use takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the said mark as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark has been refused under this Act, and the applicant appeals against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark is registrable, direct that the trade mark be registered as if the appeal had been made from a decision of the Registrar. Any use of an identical or deceptively similar mark following registration shall constitute infringement registered under this Act, irrespective of any prior usage by another party. The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to exercise all rights and remedies available to them against such infringement. Provided that, nothing in this section shall prevent the rectification of the register on grounds other than those relating to use or non-use.

Where an act constitutes infringement registered of a trademark as provided herein, the aggrieved proprietor may institute suit for damages sustained by reason of such infringement. The measure of damages shall be not less than a sum equivalent to the lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringement and not more than three times the amount of such losses where the infringement was found to have been committed wilfully. Further, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from any further act of infringement registered, subject to just terms. It is provided that in determining damages, the Court shall consider any measures taken by the proprietor to make known the trademark in India and the extent to which the infringing use has damaged the reputation or goodwill associated with the mark. Costs of the suit shall be awarded at the discretion of the Court.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is opposed under this Act, and the Hearing Officer finds that the grounds for opposition relate solely to matters of fact ascertainable outside the record of proceedings, the officer may direct either party to produce such evidence as the officer deems necessary. Any determination made by the Hearing Officer regarding the admissibility or relevance of such evidence shall be final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, where a registered trademark is being used in relation to goods or services not identical with those specified in the registration, and another party seeks to use an apparently similar mark, the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate whether such use constitutes infringement registered. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to submit written objections within sixty days of notification of the investigation.

Where an owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another person is engaging in activities constituting infringement registered under this Act, such owner may serve upon the alleged infringer a notice specifying the nature of the infringing activity and demanding cessation thereof within thirty days from the date of service. Provided that, if the infringing activity involves the importation or attempted importation into India of goods bearing the impugned mark, the notice shall also specify the quantity of such goods involved. Failure to comply with this notice within the stipulated period shall constitute prima facie evidence of continued infringement registered and may be presented as evidence in subsequent legal proceedings. The owner shall further provide documentation substantiating their claim of ownership and demonstrating likelihood of consumer confusion arising from the alleged infringing use, as provided herein.

Where an act constitutes infringement registered of a trademark as provided herein, and such infringement causes demonstrable damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trademark, the aggrieved proprietor may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages. The amount recoverable shall include compensation for loss of profits suffered by the proprietor, together with any royalties that the infringer would have reasonably paid had they been licensed to use the mark. Further, the Court may award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of actual damages proven, where the infringement is found to be willful and deliberate. The proprietor shall also be entitled to an injunction restraining further acts of infringement registered, subject to just terms.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license conferring an exclusive right to use the trade mark within a defined geographical territory, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Any assignment shall require prior written consent from the original proprietor unless expressly waived under the licensing agreement. Further, where a registered trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed to possess all rights and privileges of the assignor, including the right to pursue remedies for infringement registered against any unauthorized user. The proprietor may impose reasonable conditions on any assignment to protect the reputation and distinctiveness associated with the registered trade mark; provided that such conditions do not unduly restrict the licensee’s ability to exploit the licensed territory. Any attempt to circumvent these provisions shall be considered a breach of contract and subject to appropriate legal action.

Where an action alleging infringement registered of a trademark is brought before a High Court, the defendant may appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of the judgment or order appealed against. Such appeals shall be on points of law only, provided that an appeal based solely on findings of fact may be entertained if those findings are shown to be perverse or manifestly unsupported by the record. The High Court may, in its discretion, stay proceedings pending such an appeal under this Act, subject to just terms and conditions. Further, any party aggrieved by an order made during appellate proceedings may seek a review thereof before the same High Court, as provided herein.

Use of a registered trade mark, or an essential simulated reproduction thereof, in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registration is granted, without the consent of the proprietor, shall constitute infringement registered. For the purposes of this Act, “infringement registered” includes any use of such trade mark that is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers as to the origin, sponsorship, or approval of the goods or services. Where a trade mark has been extended through an international registration sub, the provisions relating to territorial scope and remedies for infringement shall apply with reference to the designated contracting state concerned, as provided herein.

An action alleging infringement registered may be commenced only within the jurisdiction specified under this Act. Where an applicant registration has been refused on grounds pertaining to distinctiveness, subsequent use of a sign identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for mark by another party shall not constitute evidence against the earlier refusal. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person claiming entitlement to relief in respect of infringement registered, direct the alleged infringer to appear before the Registrar and submit its defence within a period as determined by the Registrar. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed an admission of the allegations contained in the complaint. Any order made under this Act is appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to any fees prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application made under the Patent Cooperation Treaty for protection of an invention, and such application shall be deemed to be filed on the date it is received by the International Bureau. An international application may designate India as one of the designated States; provided that where an international application so designates India, the application shall be treated as if it were a national phase application filed in India on the earliest priority date claimed in the international application. The provisions relating to examination and grant of patents under this Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to applications arising from international applications.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to the provisions of international treaties and conventions, be treated as applications for the purposes of claiming priority from an application made in a contracting state. Where an applicant has filed a provisional or complete application relating to an invention in India, and subsequently files a Patent Cooperation Treaty application designating India, the date of filing the earlier Indian application shall be taken into account in determining the right to claim priority. The Controller General may, as provided herein, require applicants seeking benefits under the Patent Cooperation Treaty to furnish certified copies of relevant documents pertaining to the international stage. Such documents shall be deemed part of the record for examination purposes and are subject to scrutiny under this Act.

Where an application for a patent has been filed under this Act and subsequently enters the stage of international phase under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller shall be deemed to possess jurisdiction over any proceedings relating to revocation or infringement arising from such international application. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning the examination of the patent application in its international phase may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The right to initiate rectification proceedings against a patent granted following an international application remains subject to the same limitations and conditions applicable to patents granted solely under this Act. Further, any claim for damages arising from infringement shall be assessed according to prevailing principles of equity and fairness, considering the extent to which the infringing activity was predicated on information obtained during the international search phase.

Applications filed under this Act may be claimed as priority from an application filed in a Convention country, or from an international application filed pursuant to the Patent Cooperation Treaty. The Controller General shall have power to require the applicant to furnish such particulars concerning the international application as he deems necessary for determining the claim of priority, including certified copies of relevant sections of the request and any documents relating to the designation of countries. Where an international application is claimed as prior art, the applicant shall be responsible for providing a duly authenticated translation of any portions thereof not originally in English or Hindi. The Controller may, at his discretion, require such translations to be verified by a person approved by him. Any delay caused by the provision of these documents shall not prejudice the processing of the application provided that the applicant complies with all reasonable requests made under this Act.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to compliance with the regulations prescribed by the Controller, be treated as international applications for the purposes of the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an applicant elects to pursue examination and grant in India following a stage under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the application shall be deemed to have been filed on the date it was initially received by the International Bureau. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating adherence to timelines stipulated within the Patent Cooperation Treaty for processing international applications. Further, any fees paid to the International Bureau relating to search or preliminary examination shall be taken into account when determining applicable Indian patent application fees, provided that a certificate of payment is submitted with the request for such consideration.

Any applicant seeking to benefit from the provisions relating to international applications under this Act shall, subject to the regulations framed by the Controller, file a certified copy of the relevant documentation pertaining to their Patent Cooperation Treaty application within six months of the date on which the request for grant of a patent is received. Failure to comply with this requirement will render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may result in the rejection of the patent application. Furthermore, any person found to have knowingly submitted false or misleading information concerning their international filing status shall be deemed guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in an invention for which a patent has been applied under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to such pending application. Such license may include the right to make, use or sell the subject matter of the invention within India. The Controller may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence of assignment of said rights, register the assignee as having an interest in the patent application and any subsequent granted patent. Further, a licensee under this provision shall be obligated to provide annual reports detailing exploitation of the licensed technology, as prescribed by regulations. Provided that such reporting requirements shall not apply where the license is granted to a research institution for non-commercial purposes. Any transfer or assignment of rights under this Act relating to inventions filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty requires prior notification to the Controller.

Where an application for a patent is filed in India claiming priority from an application made outside India, and such foreign application has been published under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the publication as provided herein. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable to be deemed abandoned, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. The appellate determination concerning abandonment shall be final, unless it is shown that the failure arose from circumstances beyond the reasonable control of the applicant and prejudiced their ability to secure the certified copy; in such cases, the Controller may, at his discretion, allow a further period for compliance.

Where an application for a patent is filed under this Act claiming priority from an application made outside India, and that earlier application has been published internationally under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as he deems necessary to establish the authenticity of the claimed priority. Failure to comply with such requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, any infringement action predicated on a patent arising from an international application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall be subject to a preliminary assessment by the Controller regarding the validity of the priority claim. This assessment is without prejudice to any other remedies available to aggrieved parties concerning trade marks established prior to the filing date of the patent application.

An application filed under this Act claiming priority from an earlier application made outside India shall, to be entertained, demonstrate compliance with Article 6 of the Patent Cooperation Treaty. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the prior application and a translation thereof into English, provided that such requirement shall not apply if the said prior application was published in English. Furthermore, where the form petition submitted alongside the priority claim contains discrepancies regarding the date of filing or inventor details as compared with the original foreign application, the Controller may direct rectification before proceeding further. Any failure to rectify these inconsistencies within the timeframe specified by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

Where an application for a patent has been filed under this Act and subsequently enters the stage of international phase under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, any request or communication received from an International Bureau shall be treated as a document officially served upon the applicant. Failure to respond to such communications within the prescribed time period, as determined by the International Bureau and notified in manner informing international, shall constitute abandonment of the application for all purposes. Any person aggrieved by an action taken by the Controller relating to the processing of an application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Controller shall impose a penalty not exceeding one thousand rupees for each day of delay in complying with any requirement under this Act pertaining to the international phase, recoverable from the defaulting party.

For the purposes of this Act, “security india relates” shall mean information pertaining to designs registered or applied for registration concerning articles essential for national defence, strategic infrastructure, or critical technological advancement as determined by the Central Government. Such determination shall be published in the Official Gazette and may be amended or revoked at any time. An officer of the Designs Office, or any person assisting him, shall not disclose any details regarding a design falling under this definition to any unauthorized individual. This restriction applies irrespective of whether the disclosure is made directly or indirectly, and provided that such information could reasonably compromise national security interests.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, the proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to grant licenses for the exploitation of their design rights. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and shall clearly define the geographical territory and field of use permitted to the licensee. Assignment of design rights is permissible with prior written consent from the Controller, provided that such assignment includes a detailed inventory of all associated security india relates documentation pertaining to the registered design. Any sub-license granted under a license agreement requires notification to the Controller within thirty days of its execution. The Controller may impose conditions on licenses and assignments deemed necessary to protect public interest or prevent anti-competitive practices, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these stipulations shall render the license or assignment voidable at the discretion of the Controller.

For the purposes of this Act, "specify security india" means information pertaining to designs relating to military equipment, critical infrastructure, or technologies essential for national defence, as determined by notification in the Official Gazette by the Controller. Such determination shall consider factors including, but not limited to, vulnerability assessments conducted by designated government agencies and potential impact on strategic assets. The registration of a design falling under the definition of "specify security india" may be withheld or revoked if it is deemed detrimental to the interests of national security, subject to due process as provided herein. Any applicant seeking registration shall warrant that their design does not constitute “specify security india”.

For the purposes of this Act, “prior use” with respect to an invention shall mean utilization of an article or substance embodying features of the invention within the territory of India, prior to the date of filing of the patent application relating thereto; provided that such prior use was open and public. An act reference provision regarding prior use shall be conclusive evidence only if it is established that the person claiming prior use had knowledge of the existence of the invention as claimed in the patent application. The burden of proving prior use lies upon the party asserting it, subject to any regulations prescribed by the Controller.

Registration of Designs relating to Integrated Circuits shall be governed by procedures substantially similar to those prescribed under this Act for registration of designs. An application for registration of an integrated circuit layout design may be filed jointly by two or more persons, and where such joint application is made, the rights conferred by the registration shall be enjoyed by the applicants jointly. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish such particulars concerning the ownership of the design as he deems necessary to ascertain compliance with provisions relating to inventorship. Any act reference provision pertaining to the examination or sealing of designs shall apply mutatis mutandis to integrated circuit layout designs, subject to any modifications deemed appropriate by the Central Government through regulations.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of patent rights under this Act, they shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of infringement. Such injunctions may be granted by the relevant High Court, subject to just terms and conditions determined at its discretion, considering the balance between protecting the patentee’s exclusive privileges and ensuring reasonable access for others. The court may also order compensation for past infringements, calculated based on the loss suffered by the patent holder or a reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. Further, any act of inducement to infringe shall be deemed an infringement under this Act, rendering those who actively encourage such acts liable for remedies as provided herein. This includes providing technical assistance with knowledge that it will facilitate infringement; however, a mere suggestion does not constitute an act reference provision triggering liability.

An application for compulsory license under this Act shall be made to the Controller in Form X. The applicant shall specify the public interest considerations which warrant the grant of the license, including but not limited to, non-availability of the patented invention at a reasonable price or in sufficient quantities. Notice of such application shall be served upon the patentee within thirty days of its receipt by the Controller and the patentee shall have an opportunity to file its response within sixty days thereafter. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the proposed working conditions, including details regarding manufacturing facilities and intended market reach. Any act reference provision concerning royalty payments shall be determined by the Controller based on prevailing industry standards and the nature of the invention as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relates to an invention which includes matter already disclosed as public knowledge prior to the date of filing, the Controller may, acting upon his own motion or at the request of any interested party, require the applicant to demonstrate that such prior disclosure does not anticipate the claimed invention. Such demonstration shall involve submission of a reasoned affidavit detailing the inventive step distinguishing the claim from the aforementioned matter; failure to provide this satisfactory explanation within the time stipulated under this Act will render the application liable for rejection. The Controller may also direct an amendment to the claims if they are deemed to be improperly supported by the description, subject to the condition that such amendment does not alter the act reference provision of the original claim.

Any person who knowingly makes or causes to be made any false statement or suppresses any material fact in relation to the grant or maintenance of a patent shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine extending to one hundred thousand rupees. Further, where an infringement action is brought under this Act based on information provided by an agent acting without due diligence, the aggrieved party shall have recourse to recover all costs incurred in pursuing such action from that agent. The Central Government may, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, issue directives regarding penalties for non-compliance with provisions relating to post-grant opposition procedures as provided herein. This act reference provision ensures transparency and accountability within the patent system.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an interest in a patent, or who is desirous of obtaining a license under this Act, may apply to the Controller for registration of an assignment or a license relating to the patent.
