Such application shall specify the terms and conditions of the proposed assignment or license, including royalty rates and duration, as deemed appropriate by the Controller. The Controller may require further information regarding the intended use of the patented invention if the application involves a compulsory license or an act reference provision impacting public health. An assignment shall vest in the assignee all rights and powers which the assignor had under this Act. A license shall grant to the licensee the right to exploit the patent for the period specified, provided that the terms are fair and reasonable.

Where an application for patent is rejected under this Act on the ground that the invention lacks novelty or involves an inventive step being obvious in view of prior publications or practices, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the rejection order and shall specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged. The Board may, after affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against; however, any determination regarding patentability remains subject to judicial review under Article 226 of the Constitution. An act reference provision within this appeal process requires meticulous adherence to procedural timelines and evidentiary standards.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, grant a patent only if he is satisfied that the invention does not involve the use of biological material other than micro-organisms. This determination shall be made in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time. Further, any act reference provision pertaining to the examination of such applications requires specific documentation demonstrating adherence to bio-containment protocols as detailed in Schedule K. The amendment specification for inventions falling under this category must explicitly state the nature and quantity of micro-organisms utilized, provided that such disclosure does not compromise trade secrets.

For the purposes of this Act, “agricultural producer” means any person or cooperative society engaged in agricultural activities including cultivation, harvesting, processing, grading, packaging, storage, transportation, marketing, sale, and export of agricultural produce; provided that such activity is undertaken primarily for livelihood. An act reference provision relating to compulsory licensing under this Act shall be interpreted as applying specifically to applications made by agricultural producers seeking to utilize patented processes or technologies directly related to the enhancement or preservation of indigenous crop varieties. Such applications shall be considered in light of their potential impact on food security and rural employment, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

An international registration shall have effect only in relation to each Contracting Party designated in the declaration made at the time of application for international registration, and such designation shall constitute a separate registration under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence that the international registration is current and maintained in force as per the International Bureau’s regulations. Any alteration to the list of goods or services comprising an international registration shall be treated as a new application requiring examination and publication subject to any exemptions provided herein. Further, where an international registration includes designations for multiple Contracting Parties, cancellation or limitation affecting one designation does not automatically affect others, as determined by the International Bureau’s procedures.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the marks are registered in India under this Act. Where an international registration extends to India, the International Bureau shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a certified copy of the relevant parts of the international registration record. The Registrar may, upon receiving such certified copy and after due examination as provided herein, enter the marks on the Register subject to any modifications necessary to conform with Indian law. Any application for rectification relating to an internationally registered mark shall be entertained only if the said mark is already reflected in the Register of Trade Marks. Further, a notice of opposition may be filed against an international registration extending to India as though it were an original application under this Act.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that it designates India and subject to any modifications required by this Act. Where an international registration designating India is opposed under this Act, the opposition proceedings shall be conducted as if the application for registration were made under section 9 and the International Bureau shall furnish such information as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar may require the deposit of security with any applicant or registered proprietor in connection with an international registration, provided that such requirement is proportionate to the potential damages arising from infringement. Further, remedies for passing off shall be available notwithstanding any registration under this Act relating to a mark included in an international registration.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the marks are registered in one or more countries specified in the declaration under Regulation 3 of the Madrid Protocol. The Registrar may, upon receipt of a request from the International Bureau, require the applicant for an international registration designating India to furnish such information and documentation as the Registrar deems necessary to verify compliance with the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder. Provided that any opposition proceedings arising in relation to an international registration shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures applicable to applications for registration under this Act, subject to any modifications prescribed by the rules. The registrar may require security from the applicant as deemed appropriate to cover costs incurred in processing the request. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall render the application liable to rejection.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registrable under this Act and subject to any modifications required to ensure compliance with provisions relating to deceptive similarity. Where an international registration extends to territory comprising India, the Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of the international registration, examine such registration in accordance with the procedures prescribed herein. Provided that, if the examination reveals a conflict with any prior right existing in India, the Registrar shall issue directions for rectification as deemed necessary. Further, the applicant shall furnish a certified true copy of the international mark and designation details, duly authenticated by the International Bureau, before proceeding under this Act.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that the mark is registered in India under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, and the Board may order rectification of the register or grant damages as it deems just. Where an international registration includes goods or services for which the mark is registered in India prior to the date of designation, any subsequent infringement shall be actionable under this Act irrespective of whether the earlier Indian registration was obtained before or after the initial filing date of the international application. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the infringer liable to a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs rupees.

Where an international registration is made under this Act, the proprietor shall have the option to extend the protection conferred thereby to any country designated in such registration where India maintains reciprocal trade relations with that designated state. Such extension may be effected by way of a license granted to another party, provided that the terms of said license are filed with the Registrar within three months of the grant thereof and specify the scope of permitted use relating to the registered trademark. Further, any assignment of rights pertaining to an international registration shall require prior notification to the Controller, detailing the assignor and assignee, along with a declaration confirming adherence to all conditions stipulated under this Act regarding fair competition and consumer protection. The Registrar may request further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance.

Where an international registration is extended to India under this Act, any subsequent application for registration of the same mark shall be deemed to be opposed by the proprietor of the earlier international registration. Provided that such opposition may only be raised within a period of ninety days from the date of publication of the application for registration in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar shall afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence, including expert testimony relating to reputation acquired prior to the extended international registration’s Indian extension. Any appeal against the Registrar's decision under this provision shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to such fees as may be prescribed. It is further provided that the proprietor of an international registration shall be entitled to challenge any conflicting mark already registered in India through a similar process.

An international registration shall have effect only to the extent that it designates India and any application for extension of such registration under this Act shall be made within a period of six months from the date of expiration of the initial term of the international registration. Where an international registration designating India is opposed, the Registrar may require the deposit of a sum not exceeding fifty thousand rupees as security for costs; failure to comply with such requirement within thirty days shall render the international registration liable to be refused. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to services trade mark protection afforded through an international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to a penalty of ten thousand rupees for each day of delay.

Where an international registration extends to territory comprising India, and a conflict arises between that registration and an earlier Indian trade mark lawfully used in relation to identical or similar goods, the Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, direct rectification of the register of trade marks. Such direction shall be subject to the condition that the international registration was not applied for within three months of its initial registration under this Act. The applicant seeking rectification bears the onus of proving prior use and likelihood of confusion. Any party aggrieved by such a decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. International registration shall not confer rights beyond those specified in the international application and applies goods as defined therein.

The Controller shall prescribe a detailed procedure for maintaining the register of patents and related documents, including but not limited to applications, granted patents, sealed patents, and requests for rectification. The register shall kept in such form as the Controller deems appropriate, facilitating efficient search and retrieval of information by the public and authorized personnel. Every entry made in the register shall be signed by an officer duly authorized by the Controller, and a record of all signatures shall be maintained securely. Applications for inspection of the register may be submitted to the Controller’s office, subject to applicable fees as determined under this Act. The Controller may, at any time, revise the format and content of the register to improve its usability and accuracy, provided that prior notice is given through publication in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by an error or omission in the register may apply for amendment, following a prescribed procedure.

The Controller shall maintain a comprehensive register pertaining to all patent applications filed under this Act, detailing the particulars of each applicant, inventor, and subject matter claimed. This register shall kept in such form as the Central Government may prescribe, ensuring accessibility for public inspection subject to any restrictions deemed necessary by the Controller to protect confidential information relating to ongoing proceedings. The record of priority claims, if any, shall be meticulously noted within this register. Any alteration or addition made to a patent application after its initial filing must also be recorded in the register, provided that such alterations do not substantively affect the original claim’s scope as determined by the Controller. Failure to accurately maintain this register constitutes an offense punishable under this Act.

The Register of Registered Designs maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person found to wilfully alter or deface entries within the register shall be liable to prosecution and may face imprisonment extending to two years, or a fine, or both, as determined by the relevant court. The Controller shall ensure that the register is maintained with meticulous accuracy; any demonstrable negligence in maintaining this record will render the Controller subject to disciplinary action and potential civil penalties. A comprehensive index shall accompany the register, regularly updated to facilitate efficient searches. Furthermore, the register shall kept secure from unauthorized access or tampering at all times.

Where a patentee elects to grant a license or assign their patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical product, a detailed record of such transaction shall be entered into the register maintained under this Act. The register shall kept accurately and comprehensively, including particulars of the licensee’s identity, the scope of the licensed territory, any royalty rates stipulated, and the duration of the agreement. Assignment records will similarly detail the assignee's information and the extent of rights transferred.

Provided that, where a license or assignment is made to an entity incorporated outside India, the Controller may require submission of authenticated documentation verifying the legitimacy of such entity under its governing laws. Further, any modification or termination of a licensed patent right must also be recorded promptly in the register, subject to verification by the Controller. The information contained within the register shall be deemed public record and accessible for inspection as provided herein.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license or assign their patent rights, an application for registration of such license or assignment shall be made to the Registrar within thirty days of the execution of the agreement. The register shall kept accurately reflecting all licenses and assignments pertaining to registered patents, including details of the licensor, licensee, assignee, and assigned rights. Any alteration to a licensed right, whether through sub-licensing or further assignment, must also be recorded in the register promptly. Should any dispute arise regarding the validity or scope of a license or assignment, the court directs registrar to provide all relevant documentation from the register as evidence. Provided that, the Registrar may require additional information or security deposits as deemed necessary to ensure proper recording and prevent fraudulent claims concerning patent rights under this Act.

An appeal lies to the Order Appellate Authority against any decision or direction made by a Controller under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or seal of a patent, or concerning opposition proceedings. The Order Appellate Authority shall consist of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, possessing expertise in patents, designs, trademarks or related fields. Decisions of the Order Appellate Authority shall be final subject to appeal under the relevant provisions relating to appeals from orders of civil courts. The authority may, at any stage of the proceedings, require parties to furnish further information or documentation deemed necessary for a just determination.

Any person dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar regarding the registration of a layout plan for an industrial estate or area, including objections raised during the public notice period, may file an application before the order appellate authority. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged and accompanied by copies of relevant documents submitted during the initial registration process. Subject to provisions concerning frivolous or vexatious applications, the order appellate authority shall consider such appeals within a prescribed timeframe, as determined by the Central Government. Further, the applicant shall be entitled to present oral arguments before the authority. The authority’s decision is final and binding, provided that it does not contravene principles of urban planning under this Act.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by a Controller under this Act is dissatisfied, that party shall have the right to appeal to the Order Appellate Authority. The appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of service of the order appealed against and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be annulled or modified. Subject to provisions regarding time extensions granted by the appellate authority, failure to comply with this timeframe will render the appeal inadmissible.

The Order Appellate Authority may, after affording an opportunity for a hearing to all parties concerned, confirm as it stands, vary, or reverse any order appealed against. Any party demonstrating prejudice due to non-compliance with procedural requirements during proceedings before the Controller may petition the appellate authority for appropriate remedies. The decision of the Order Appellate Authority shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal under the provisions outlined herein.

An application for review of an order passed by a Controller relating to the revocation of a patent shall be made to the Order Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of service of the said order. The applicant shall serve a copy of the application on the patentee and any other party directly affected by the order under review, as notified by the Central Government. Upon receipt of such an application, the Order Appellate Authority may require the applicant to furnish security for costs, subject to regulations prescribed by the government. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Order Appellate Authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellate authority shall record its reasons for any decision made and such reasoning shall be deemed part of the record.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision regarding compulsory licensing issued by a Controller shall have recourse to an appeal before the Order Appellate Authority. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the appellate authority may entertain appeals filed after the stipulated period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal within the prescribed time. The Order Appellate Authority shall consider all relevant factors including the nature and extent of the invention, the working of the patent in India, and the reasonable availability of the patented product or process to the public. Any party may be directed to furnish further information as deemed necessary by the appellate authority for a just determination of the matter.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to revocation of a patent or rectification of the register, and failing satisfaction with the decision, seeks redressal before the Order Appellate Authority, such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellate authority may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure by any party to comply with a direction issued by the appellate authority regarding production of documents or attendance at hearings shall render them liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Any willful disregard of an order made under this Act may be deemed contempt of the Order Appellate Authority.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license for an invention in respect of which a compulsory license has been granted under this Act, they shall notify the Controller and all licensees previously identified. The terms of any subsequent license agreement must not conflict with the conditions stipulated in the original compulsory license, provided that the patentee may apply to the order appellate authority for modification or revocation of such conflicting clauses. Any assignment of a patent, whether partial or complete, including rights pertaining to a compulsory license, shall require prior notification and approval from the Controller. The order appellate authority may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review any decision made by the Controller concerning the validity or terms of such assignments. Further, the authority shall consider representations regarding equitable compensation to the patentee for licenses granted post-compulsory licensing.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the revocation of a patent based on grounds of non-obviousness or lack of inventive step shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Order Appellate Authority. Such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said decision, and shall specify the orders sought for reversal or modification, along with concise reasons supporting the appeal. The Order Appellate Authority may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or set aside the order appealed against. Provided that if any party demonstrates to the satisfaction of the appellate authority that they were unable to file within the stipulated time due to circumstances beyond their control, an extension of time may be granted at the discretion of the Authority.

Where an appeal is preferred before the Order Appellate Authority against any decision made by a Controller relating to the revocation of a patent, the Authority shall consider all evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent. The appellant shall provide detailed reasoning for challenging the Controller’s determination, supported by documentary proof demonstrating substantial grounds for reconsideration. Provided that, if the respondent raises objections concerning the timeliness of the appeal, the Order Appellate Authority may require the appellant to demonstrate that the appeal was filed within the prescribed period; such demonstration shall date filing and be conclusive for purposes of jurisdiction. Any order passed by the appellate authority shall be final subject to further appeal under this Act.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision regarding the rectification of registered trade marks made by the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Order Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Order Appellate Authority shall, while hearing appeals, have the same powers as the Registrar relating to the calling of evidence and examination of witnesses. An applicant seeking rectification shall be required to furnish a security deposit, determined according to regulations prescribed by the Central Government, ensuring compliance with procedural requirements under this Act. Further, any appeal concerning matters of fact or law pertaining to the distinctiveness of a mark shall be subject to review by the Order Appellate Authority based on evidence presented and arguments advanced.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for patent, or any condition imposed therein, may prefer an appeal to the Order Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Order Appellate Authority shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint. Appeals under this Act shall be disposed of expeditiously, subject to the provisions regarding hearings and opportunities for all parties concerned to present their case. Where an appeal involves questions relating to whether a trade description denotes any particular goods or services, the Order Appellate Authority shall consider expert testimony as it deems appropriate. The Central Government may prescribe the procedure for appeals before the Order Appellate Authority, provided that such procedure ensures fairness and adherence to principles of natural justice.

Where an application for registration of a mark is accepted by the Registrar, either absolutely or subject to conditions, the applicant shall be entitled to proceed with payment of the requisite fees as determined under this Act. Failure to remit such fees within the period specified in the acceptance notice shall render the acceptance liable to revocation. Any party aggrieved by a condition imposed upon an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of notification of the acceptance, and the Board’s decision shall be final. The Registrar may, at any time prior to registration, modify or remove such conditions if satisfied that they are no longer necessary or appropriate, provided that due notice is given to all interested parties. Any person claiming damages resulting from reliance upon an application accepted conditions may pursue remedies under the general law relating to torts and contract.

Where an application for registration of a mark is accepted by the Registrar, such acceptance shall not preclude subsequent challenge under this Act. The acceptance of an application, whether absolute or conditional, does not constitute conclusive evidence of registrability and remains subject to review pending opposition proceedings. Any party aggrieved by the decision to accept an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of publication of such acceptance in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar shall provide reasons for any conditions imposed as part of the accepted application, which reasons are open to scrutiny during appellate review. It is provided that failure to comply with stipulated conditions following an application accepted conditions may render registration liable to cancellation.

Any party desiring to oppose the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark under this Act shall file a Notice of Opposition with the Registrar within the period specified herein. Such Notice shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by regulations framed thereunder. The opposition must state the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to prior use or registration of an identical or deceptively similar mark. Upon receipt of a valid Notice of Opposition, the Registrar shall promptly notify the applicant for registration, affording them an opportunity to file a counterstatement addressing the allegations made. The Registrar may, at their discretion and as provided herein, require both parties to submit further documentation or attend hearings to clarify the issues in dispute relating to the registrar opposition registration process.

Where an application for registration is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement within such time as may be prescribed, addressing the grounds of opposition raised in the notice. Failure by the applicant to file a timely counter-statement shall be deemed an abandonment of the application and preclude any subsequent challenge to the Registrar’s decision. The Registrar may, after affording both parties an opportunity for hearing, dismiss the opposition or direct registration subject to such conditions as he deems fit. Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to a notice applicant registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate board’s decision shall be final and binding.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish to the Registrar, along with the application, a clear representation of the marks as applied for, conforming to prescribed guidelines regarding colouration or stylization. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, issue a notice to any persons claiming rights in relation to similar trademarks already registered under this Act. Such notice applicant registration must specify the grounds on which objection is raised and shall be accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating prior use or established reputation. Failure of the applicant to respond adequately within the stipulated period, as provided herein, may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Registrar shall consider any representations made by interested parties before proceeding with examination.

Any person aggrieved by an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to this Act, file a written notice of opposition with the Registrar within the period specified herein. Such notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use and likelihood of confusion. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice, as provided herein, and may submit counter-arguments and evidence in support of their application. Failure by the Registrar to promptly address a valid notice of opposition shall render them liable for penalties under this Act. Any wilful misrepresentation made within a notice applicant registration is punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Where an applicant for registration of a trade mark has entered into an agreement granting a license or assignment of the right to apply for, or use, the trade mark, such agreement shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the execution thereof. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating the scope and duration of any such license or assignment. Any subsequent transfer or modification of rights under this Act relating to a notice applicant registration must also be reported to the Registrar in like manner. Failure to do so will render the assignee liable to penalties as provided herein, and may affect their ability to enforce the trade mark. The original applicant retains responsibility for ensuring compliance with all provisions of this Act until formally released by the Registrar following due process.

For the purposes of this Act, "security india action" with respect to a design shall mean any measure undertaken or proposed to be undertaken by an officer authorized under this Act, including but not limited to inspection, seizure, or destruction of articles embodying a registered design, where such measure is deemed necessary to safeguard national security interests. An officer taking security india action shall provide written notice to the proprietor of the design, detailing the reasons for the action and affording them an opportunity to be heard as provided herein. Such actions are subject to review by the Controller, who may confirm, vary or revoke the order relating to security india action upon consideration of representations submitted by any party concerned.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish an affidavit verifying that the design does not incorporate elements derived from or substantially similar to existing designs already in public use, and confirming diligent searches have been conducted. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating originality, including sketches, technical drawings, and evidence of prior conception. Where it is determined that a registered design infringes upon national security interests, particularly concerning critical infrastructure protection or defense technologies, the Central Government shall have power to direct its revocation. Any action taken under this Act relating to designs deemed detrimental to the security india action will be subject to judicial review only after exhaustion of administrative remedies as provided herein.

Any person found to be engaging in activities detrimental to the aesthetic integrity of registered designs shall be subject to penalties as provided herein. Such actions include, but are not limited to, unauthorized reproduction, importation for sale, or distribution of articles infringing upon a design’s unique visual features. Where such infringement demonstrably compromises the security india action relating to national industrial heritage, the Central Government may order seizure of offending goods and impose fines up to five times the cost of production. Furthermore, any individual convicted under this Act of deliberately undermining registered designs for malicious purposes faces imprisonment extending to three years. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all enforcement actions taken, accessible to designated government agencies.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to grant licenses for the exploitation of their design rights, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license. Any assignment of a design or any interest therein shall include all rights pertaining to security india action relating to that design, as determined by the Controller. A licensee may sub-license their rights under this Act with the prior written consent of the proprietor, provided that such sub-licensing does not contravene the terms and conditions stipulated in the original license agreement. The Central Government may, upon application by any interested party, investigate instances where a design license appears to be unreasonably restrictive or discriminatory, impacting national economic interests. Such investigations shall be conducted with due regard for confidentiality and intellectual property rights as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "security india action" shall be deemed to include any measure undertaken by or on behalf of the Central Government reasonably believed to be necessary to protect the sovereignty, integrity, defence, strategic interests, and friendly relations of India. The power to undertake such security india action may extend to suspending design apply registration processes, preventing the publication of designs, and restricting access to registered designs where a reasonable apprehension exists that disclosure or availability would compromise national security. Provided that any restriction imposed under this definition shall be proportionate to the risk identified and subject to periodic review as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “security india explanation” means that information concerning a design, its application for registration, or related processes shall be deemed confidential where disclosure thereof would reasonably prejudice the national security of India. This determination shall be made solely at the discretion of the Controller and is subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board upon request from an aggrieved party. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding the assessment of potential harm to the security of India, but such guidelines are advisory only and do not bind the Controller’s decision as provided herein.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed to involve considerations relating to the security of India if it incorporates elements that could facilitate counterfeiting or unauthorized reproduction of articles essential for national defense or public safety. The Registrar may require an applicant whose design raises such concerns to submit detailed technical specifications and production processes, subject to confidentiality agreements binding on all parties involved. Information provided under this requirement shall be treated as confidential and not disclosed to any person except with the prior written consent of the applicant and authorization from the Central Government. Provided that, if the Registrar believes a design poses an imminent threat to security india explanation, they may provisionally suspend registration pending further investigation by designated government agencies.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed to be refused if the Controller considers that the design is likely to offend religious susceptibilities or prejudices public morality, or if its publication would be contrary to accepted principles of decency. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars concerning the design as he deems necessary for the purposes of examination under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the rejection of a design application or the revocation of registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. However, no such appeal shall be entertained if it is made after the expiration of sixty days from the date on which notice of the order was received by the appellant. The Central Government may, in consultation with the Controller, specify designs that relate directly or indirectly to articles associated with the security india explanation and require enhanced scrutiny during examination.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed invalid if the proposed design incorporates elements that compromise the security india explanation, particularly where such elements relate to military hardware or infrastructure. The Controller General may require an applicant to submit detailed specifications and technical drawings demonstrating the absence of any such compromising features prior to proceeding with examination. Provided that, the Central Government may, at any time, direct the Controller General to withhold registration pending a review by a designated security agency. Any design found to contravene this provision shall be subject to immediate cancellation, and the applicant may face penalties as determined under this Act. Further, information regarding such designs shall not be disclosed publicly without explicit authorization from the Central Government.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed invalid if the proposed design incorporates elements that compromise the security india explanation as determined by the Controller, acting on information received from designated national agencies. The Registrar may require an applicant to submit detailed technical specifications and manufacturing processes relating to the design, particularly where it pertains to articles intended for use in critical infrastructure or defense applications. Such submissions are subject to confidentiality agreements binding upon the applicant and their representatives. Furthermore, designs referencing plant varieties registered under the Plant Varieties Registry shall include a declaration confirming compliance with relevant biosafety regulations and acknowledging any intellectual property rights held by the variety’s breeder. Failure to provide this declaration will result in rejection of the application.

The Registrar shall not be obligated to register a design if it incorporates elements that, in the opinion of the Controller, relate directly or indirectly to matters affecting the security india explanation. This determination shall consider whether the creation provided layout, including its aesthetic features and functional aspects, possesses characteristics demonstrably linked to national defense, strategic infrastructure, or critical technological assets. Any applicant aggrieved by such a decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receiving notification of the refusal. The Board’s finding on this matter shall be final, subject to further judicial review under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution, concerning demonstrable errors of law apparent on the face of the record.

For the purposes of this Act, “necessary security india” shall be deemed to include protection of critical infrastructure relating to national power grids, transportation networks, and communication systems. Any design incorporating representations or configurations directly replicating elements essential for the functionality or identification of such infrastructure shall be ineligible for registration under this Act. The Registrar may refuse registration if satisfied that a proposed design’s similarity to existing designs poses a threat to necessary security india, provided that such determination is based on objective criteria and documented reasoning. Information pertaining to applications and registrations deemed relevant to necessary security india shall be treated as confidential.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish such particulars as are prescribed, including detailed representations demonstrating novelty and industrial applicability. The Controller General may require further documentation substantiating the claimed originality and distinguishing features of the design from prior published matter. Where a design incorporates elements essential for necessary security india, the application must explicitly state this dependence and provide a reasoned justification to the Registrar. Such designs are subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act and may be granted registration with restricted rights relating to reproduction or commercial exploitation deemed vital for national interests. The Controller General shall have the power to impose conditions on such registrations as he deems fit, provided that these conditions do not unduly impede legitimate industrial activity.

Where an infringement of a registered design is established, the appropriate court shall grant all remedies available under this Act and at law. The aggrieved party may seek injunction relief restraining the defendant from making, importing, selling, hiring or offering for sale any article which is a copy of the registered design or so nearly resembling it as to deceive the eye; provided that such injunction may be granted subject to just terms. Further, damages shall be awarded to compensate the proprietor for loss sustained by reason of the infringement, calculated in accordance with principles of fairness and equity. The court may also order the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods, materials used in their manufacture, and equipment employed in making them. Nothing herein shall prevent a party from claiming relief based on *necessary security india* if such infringement demonstrably jeopardizes national interests.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the design incorporates or comprises any coat of arms, public seal, flag, emblem, name or initials of any sovereign nation or foreign state; provided that the Registrar may entertain an application containing such elements if the applicant demonstrates to his satisfaction that use is authorized by the appropriate government authority. The Controller General shall furnish a certified copy of the design registration to any person applying for it, upon payment of the prescribed fee and subject to verification of identity as per rules framed under this Act. Any individual found to be infringing a registered design may be required to submit detailed documentation pertaining to their manufacturing processes. Designs deemed essential for national security, particularly those relating to defense or critical infrastructure, are considered necessary security india and shall receive heightened protection.

The proprietor of a registered design shall furnish such reports and documentation as may be prescribed by the Controller relating to the manufacturing process employed in the production of articles incorporating said design. Such information need not be disclosed if it pertains directly to techniques deemed essential for maintaining necessary security india, or where compliance would compromise national strategic interests as determined by the Central Government. Provided that, any request for disclosure shall include a detailed justification outlining the specific governmental concern necessitating access and specifying the measures taken to safeguard confidential commercial data during review. The Controller may, after consultation with relevant government agencies, issue directives regarding the level of detail required in these reports, subject to ensuring fairness and proportionality between national security concerns and proprietary rights.

Any person who knowingly makes, offers for sale, or imports into India any article embodying a design that is substantially similar to a registered design shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where the infringement involves the reproduction or imitation of a design registered as a necessary security india, the penalty shall be doubled. The Central Government may, subject to due process, order the seizure and destruction of infringing articles and materials used in their manufacture. Any proprietor aggrieved by such an action may appeal under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, a proprietor of a registered design shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the design for commercial purposes. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, provided that any license agreement includes a clear statement regarding the duration and geographical scope of the granted rights. Furthermore, where a licensed product incorporates elements deemed essential for national security, the licensee shall undertake to adhere strictly to quality control measures prescribed by the Controller. Assignment of design ownership or licenses requires registration with the Designs Office, detailing all parties involved and the extent of transferred rights. The Central Government may, in circumstances affecting necessary security India, direct the revocation of any license deemed detrimental to public interest.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of a design relating to articles intended for use in connection with defence or national security, the Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard and may require the applicant to submit such evidence as he deems necessary to demonstrate that the design does not compromise necessary security india. The Controller’s decision on whether a design poses a threat to national security is final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. An appeal under this Act shall lie only if it can be demonstrated that the Controller acted without due consideration of relevant material or exercised his discretion in an arbitrary manner, and such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against.

For the purposes of this Act, "necessary security india" shall be deemed to include protection against unauthorized replication or adaptation of designs employed in agricultural implements, irrigation systems, and other infrastructure vital for food production and rural development. Any design incorporating elements derived from traditional knowledge relating to plant varieties shall be subject to review under guidelines established by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. The Registrar may refuse registration if it is determined that a proposed design unfairly restricts access to essential technologies or impedes the exercise of breeder's right concerning improved crop cultivars, provided that such determination is based on publicly available information and scientific assessment.

An application for registration of a design shall include a statement verifying that the design does not infringe upon any prior registered design or any confidential information relating to industrial processes. The Controller General may require an applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the origin and evolution of the design, particularly where it appears to incorporate elements derived from traditional artistic practices. Any person utilizing a design in connection with trade or business shall be deemed an authorised user only if they have obtained prior written consent from the registered proprietor. Designs employed for purposes directly impacting national security, including those related to defence equipment or critical infrastructure, are subject to heightened scrutiny and may require clearance under provisions concerning necessary security india.

Any proprietor of a registered design shall be entitled to sue for relief in respect of an infringement of their design rights. Such relief may include damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringing activity, and an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. Where a person falsely applies goods with a design that is substantially similar to a registered design, or incorporates such a design into labels, packaging, or advertisements relating to those goods, they shall be deemed guilty of infringement under this Act. The Court may order the destruction of infringing goods, labels, and materials used in their production, provided that such orders are consistent with ensuring necessary security india. Any proprietor seeking remedies for infringement must demonstrate reasonable diligence in pursuing their rights.

For the purposes of this Act, “security india” with reference to a design shall mean information pertaining to the aesthetic or functional characteristics of a design that, if disclosed, would compromise national security interests as determined by the Central Government. Any officer or employee of the Office may withhold from public disclosure any document or record containing such "security india" relating to an application for registration or registered design under this Act. Provided that, the Central Government may, in its discretion, permit access to restricted information deemed vital for academic research or journalistic inquiry, subject to stringent confidentiality agreements and oversight mechanisms as provided herein.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the design incorporates elements that compromise the security of India, or are deemed to do so by the Controller. The Registrar may require an applicant to submit additional documentation demonstrating that the proposed design does not pose a threat to national interests, particularly concerning critical infrastructure and strategic assets. Such documentation shall include detailed technical specifications and manufacturing processes, subject to review by designated government agencies. Any information submitted in compliance with this requirement shall be treated as confidential and protected from unauthorized disclosure under this Act. The Controller may, at any time during the registration process or subsequent to registration, initiate an inquiry if concerns arise regarding a design’s potential impact on security india.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish an affidavit verifying that the design does not incorporate elements derived from or substantially similar to any existing work protected under copyright law. The Controller General may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence in ascertaining originality, particularly where the design incorporates figurative representations. Registration shall be refused if it is determined that the design’s aesthetic features are dictated solely by function or technical necessity. Furthermore, a registered design relating to articles intended for use within critical infrastructure, including those pertaining to security india, may be subject to periodic review under this Act and may be revoked if deemed detrimental to national interests as assessed by an empowered committee.

Any person who, without authorization, reproduces, distributes, or commercially exploits a design registered as relating to an article connected with the security of India shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than three years but which may extend to seven years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, any property used or obtained in connection with the commission of this offence relating to security india is liable to confiscation by order of the Controller. The Central Government may, subject to due process, issue warrants for arrest and search concerning suspected violations as provided herein. Any appeal against an order under this Act shall lie before the High Court.

The proprietor of a registered design relating to an article embodying elements essential for national infrastructure shall be deemed to hold a special license concerning its commercial exploitation. This license may grant rights to third parties subject to prior approval from the Controller and adherence to prescribed conditions safeguarding security india. Any assignment of such design, or any sub-license granted thereunder, must explicitly detail the intended use and duration of the rights transferred, ensuring continued compliance with national interest considerations. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, stipulate limitations on the scope of these licenses, particularly concerning designs utilized in sectors deemed critical for public safety or economic stability. Further, any licensee shall undertake to maintain records pertaining to production, distribution and sales, accessible for inspection upon request from authorized government officials.

For the purposes of this Act, “security india” shall mean any information, including but not limited to technical specifications, manufacturing processes, or design schematics, the unauthorized disclosure of which would materially compromise the strategic interests of India relating to national security, defence, or critical infrastructure. Any user party proceeding with an application for registration of a design incorporating elements falling under this definition shall be required to submit a declaration confirming that the design does not contain any such information. The Controller may request further clarification from the applicant regarding the nature and extent of any potential impact on security india, as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish with the application such particulars as are prescribed, including detailed representations demonstrating the novelty and industrial applicability of the proposed design. The Controller may require the applicant to submit additional documentation or specimens to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and freedom from prior publication. Where the design incorporates elements indicative of national security, particularly those pertaining to infrastructure protection or critical systems, the application shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act. Such designs may necessitate a security india clearance certificate issued by the designated authority before proceeding towards registration. The grant of registration mark certification will only follow verification that the design does not compromise national interests as determined by the Central Government.

The Controller shall maintain an omission register, being a record distinct from the official gazette and patent registers, wherein particulars of inventions for which applications have been refused, deemed to be withdrawn, or otherwise not proceeded with under this Act are documented. An entry in the omission register shall include the application number, the title of the invention as initially claimed, the date on which the action leading to its inclusion was taken, and a brief statement indicating the grounds for non-prosecution. The omission register is open to public inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Controller; however, details revealing confidential aspects of an invention may be redacted as provided herein.

The Controller shall maintain an Omission Register, separate from the main Register of Patents, for recording particulars of inventions which were eligible for registration under this Act but were not registered due to procedural deficiencies or failures in application. Any person aggrieved by an omission recorded in the Omission Register may file a representation before the Controller within six months of such entry, detailing the grounds upon which registration should have been granted and providing any supporting documentation as deemed necessary. The Controller shall consider such representations and may direct that the invention be treated as if it had been originally applied for, subject to payment of prescribed fees and compliance with all applicable requirements under this Act. This process does not prejudice any right or remedy available to a person otherwise aggrieved by the grant of a patent.

Any applicant whose invention is not entered into the omission register shall have the right to appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision regarding the non-inclusion. Such an appeal may be made on grounds demonstrating a clear error in the assessment of patentability, novelty, or inventive step as provided herein. The Controller shall consider such appeals expeditiously and issue reasoned orders, which shall be final subject to further appeal under the relevant provisions relating to judicial review. Failure by the Controller to adjudicate upon an appeal within ninety days from its receipt will constitute deemed refusal, entitling the applicant to seek remedies for undue delay. Any person demonstrating prejudice due to inaccuracies in the omission register may petition the Controller for rectification and claim compensation for losses incurred.

The Controller shall maintain an omission register, separate from the main register of patents, for recording particulars of inventions which have been refused, rejected, deemed to be not patentable, or otherwise removed from consideration under this Act. Entries in the omission register shall include the application number, the applicant’s name and address, a concise description of the invention as claimed in the original application, and the date on which the decision leading to the omission was recorded. Any person aggrieved by an entry made in the omission register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such entry, following procedures prescribed herein for appeals against decisions of the Controller. The Controller shall provide a certified copy of any entry in the omission register upon application and payment of the prescribed fee. Information contained therein is subject to confidentiality restrictions as provided under this Act, particularly concerning trade secrets disclosed during examination.

Any applicant for a patent shall maintain an omission register, recording particulars of inventions which are not reflected within the main register due to refusal, abandonment, or lapsing under this Act. The omission register must be kept separate from other records pertaining to patent applications and shall be accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed by the Controller General. An entry in the omission register shall include the application number, inventor’s name, title of invention, date of refusal or abandonment, and reasons therefore. Any person aggrieved by an incorrect or misleading entry within the omission register may apply to the Controller for rectification, provided that such application is accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating the error. The Controller may direct correction of the omission register as deemed appropriate.

Any applicant for a patent who fails to diligently prosecute an application, as determined under this Act and based upon repeated non-compliance with prescribed timelines, shall be subject to penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, where such failure results in the abandonment of a patent application, the Controller shall record the details pertaining thereto within the omission register, clearly indicating the reasons for abandonment and identifying the applicant responsible. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice due to the delayed or omitted entry in the omission register may petition the relevant High Court for redressal, subject to payment of prescribed court fees and demonstration of direct financial loss. Repeated instances of such negligence by an applicant may result in disqualification from applying for patents for a period not less than two years.

Where a patentee desires to grant an exclusive license, or assign their patent rights, relating to any invention for which they are recorded in the omission register, such license or assignment shall be subject to registration under this Act. The Controller may require submission of a detailed memorandum outlining the scope and duration of the proposed license, including provisions for royalty payments and sub-licensing opportunities. Provided that, where the patentee has previously granted a non-exclusive license, the subsequent exclusive license shall not prejudice the rights of existing licensees unless expressly agreed to in writing by all parties involved. Any assignment or license agreement failing to adequately address ongoing obligations relating to maintenance fees as provided herein may be deemed invalid. The omission register shall reflect any such registered licenses and assignments, noting the licensee’s or assignee's name and contact details for public record.

Any applicant whose invention is recorded as an omission in the omission register may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the omission register, file a notice of objection with the Controller. Such objection shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and provide supporting documentation demonstrating reasonable grounds to believe that the claimed invention was not properly considered during the initial examination process. The Controller shall afford the original applicant an opportunity to respond to the objection within thirty days, after which the Controller may either direct the removal of the entry from the omission register or require further investigation into the matter. Any party aggrieved by such a determination may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An appeal lies to the Appellate Board under this Act if a Controller, acting upon an application for inclusion of an invention in the omission register, determines that such invention was not disclosed as prior art during examination proceedings. The applicant may challenge this determination, demonstrating with reasonable certainty that the cited document did not reasonably inform the skilled person regarding the claimed subject matter. Provided that, where the omitted information relates to a design registered under the Design Act 2000 and concerns ornamental features, the Board shall consider whether such omission prejudiced the patentability assessment of the invention. The Controller’s decision is final unless it appears to the Appellate Board that there was an error apparent on the face of the record or that the Controller acted without due consideration of relevant evidence presented during opposition proceedings.

The Controller shall maintain an omission register, recording particulars of inventions for which a request for registration has been refused under this Act, or where registration has been revoked, and such register shall be open to public inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Government. Any person claiming right to an invention that is recorded in the omission register may, within six months from the date of publication of the refusal or revocation notice, file a request for reconsideration before the Controller. Where an inventor subsequently seeks registration of an invention substantially identical to one previously refused and noted in the omission register, they shall be required to demonstrate significant advancements beyond the originally rejected matter; this may include specification patent additions that clarify ambiguities or overcome prior objections.

Any applicant whose invention is recorded as an omission in the omission register may, within sixty days from the date of such recording, file a notice rectify register with the Controller seeking rectification of the record. The Controller shall consider such notice and afford the patentee against whom the omission was made an opportunity to be heard, subject to just procedures under this Act. If, after due consideration and hearing, the Controller finds that the omission was unwarranted or resulted from an error, the Controller may direct the rectification of the register. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Controller shall render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein. The patentee against whom such rectification is ordered may appeal under this Act within sixty days of the order’s communication.

The Controller shall maintain an omission register, separate from the main register of patents, for recording details of applications that are refused, deemed to be withdrawn, or otherwise do not proceed to grant. Entries in the omission register shall include the application number, the date of the decision leading to its exclusion from consideration for patentability, and a concise statement of the reasons therefor, as determined by the Controller under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an entry made in the omission register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of such entry. The Controller shall provide copies of entries in the omission register upon request, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Further, where a registered breeder variety is involved and the application for patent relates to that variety, the reasons for exclusion from consideration shall explicitly address any conflict with provisions relating to plant varieties protection.

For the purposes of this Act, two signs shall be considered identical for the purpose of determining trade mark identity if they directly correspond to each other. This correspondence need not extend to every detail; however, any differences must be immaterial in the overall impression created upon the mind of the average consumer. Where a sign incorporates elements derived from a prior trade mark, such incorporation shall be assessed with particular regard to the distinctiveness of the earlier mark. The assessment of trade mark identity is subject to consideration of all relevant surrounding circumstances and may include examination of the mode of presentation and intended purpose of the signs in question.

A trademark shall be deemed distinctive if it possesses inherent characteristics that differentiate it from existing marks in the relevant class of goods or services. The Registrar may refuse registration where an application seeks to register a mark identical to a prior registered trade mark relating to identical or closely related goods or services, unless the applicant can demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through extensive use subsequent to the earlier registration. This determination of trade mark identity shall consider not only the visual appearance but also phonetic and conceptual similarities between the marks. Further, where a proposed mark is similar to an existing mark and the goods or services are identical, a finding of likelihood of confusion will generally preclude registration, provided that such similarity creates unfair advantage or is detrimental to consumers.

Where any person seeks to restrain the use of a trade mark under this Act, it shall be established that the defendant has used such sign in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the plaintiff’s trade mark is registered. The determination of *trade mark identity* requires consideration of the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the signs involved, taking into account the overall impression created upon the mind of the relevant consumer. Provided that a finding of similarity does not automatically establish infringement, it must further be demonstrated that such use creates a likelihood of confusion or causes damage to the reputation of the plaintiff’s trade mark. The court may grant an injunction and award damages as provided herein, subject to equitable considerations and any demonstrable lack of bad faith on the part of the defendant.

A trademark shall be deemed to infringe if, subject to the provisions regarding use in describing the character or quality of certain goods, it is identical to the registered trademark or so nearly resembling it as to likely cause confusion among the public. The determination of such likelihood shall consider all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to the nature of the goods or services, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark, and any prior use by the defendant. Where an application for registration is refused on the ground of similarity to a previously registered trademark, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider whether the marks in question possess trade mark identity sufficient to warrant protection under this Act. Evidence presented before the Board shall be admissible as provided herein and subject to established rules of evidence.

A trademark shall be deemed to infringe if it is used in relation to goods or services identical with those for which the prior registered trademark is established, or so nearly as to cause confusion. Such infringement may also occur where the use relates to goods or services similar to those for which the earlier mark is registered, provided that the similarity between the marks and the relatedness of the goods or services are such as to create a likelihood of association in the minds of consumers. For the purposes of determining trade mark identity, consideration shall be given to the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the signs involved. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating actual confusion amongst members of the public where similarity exists but the connection is not immediately apparent.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed to infringe upon the prior rights of another proprietor under this Act. Such infringement arises where there is demonstrable trade mark identity between the applied-for mark and an existing registered mark, considering the goods or services for which each mark is used. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating a lack of confusion among consumers before registration proceeds. Any party aggrieved by the registration of a trademark infringing upon their prior rights shall be entitled to apply to the relevant court for relief, including injunctions preventing use and damages proportionate to the losses sustained as a direct result of such infringement, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the right to use shall extend. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding thirty years from the date of the license agreement and are assignable subject to prior registration of the assignment under this Act. Where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall be entitled to exercise all rights pertaining to the trade mark as if they were the original proprietor, including the right to grant further licenses or assignments. The determination of trade mark identity for the purposes of assessing validity of a license agreement shall be based on an assessment of the visual, phonetic and conceptual similarities between the licensed mark and any conflicting prior marks.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the alleged absence of distinctiveness in a proposed trade mark based upon its resemblance to signs commonly designating the kind, quality, quantity, or other characteristics of goods or services, the Registrar shall consider whether the essential features of the marks are sufficiently dissimilar to preclude a finding of likelihood of confusion. The determination of trade mark identity for this purpose requires careful assessment of both visual and phonetic similarities, taking into account the overall impression created on the mind of the average consumer. An appeal against such a decision by the Registrar may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Registrar's findings.

For the purposes of this Act, “trade mark identity” shall be determined considering the visual appearance, phonetic representation, descriptive content, and conceptual meaning conveyed by the sign. A sign possessing substantial trade mark identity with an earlier registered trade mark shall preclude registration unless it is demonstrated that the conflicting use will not cause confusion among consumers. The Registrar may consider entries in the design register when assessing trade mark identity, particularly where a design incorporates elements of a proposed trade mark; however, such consideration does not automatically establish or negate trade mark identity as provided herein. Any proprietor seeking to challenge registration based on lack of distinctiveness shall bear the onus of proving absence of trade mark identity.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the Registrar finds that the proposed mark lacks distinctiveness solely due to its descriptive nature relating to the specified goods or services. However, such refusal may be overcome where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition, as evidenced by market surveys and sales figures submitted with the application. The specification of goods or services in a trade marks application shall be precise and accurate; any ambiguity therein may render the registration vulnerable to challenge under this Act. Further, an applicant seeking to register a trade mark incorporating elements of a specification patent addition relating to a novel process must provide detailed technical documentation supporting the inventive step. Trade mark identity is paramount in assessing registrability.

A trademark shall be deemed to lack novelty if it is identical to a prior registered trademark in respect of identical goods or services, or if such identity creates an unreasonable likelihood of association with said prior registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that use of the mark following registration will not cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Where an objection is raised under this Act based on a claim of lack of novelty, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit counter-arguments and relevant documentation establishing distinctiveness. The burden of proving said distinctiveness rests upon the applicant. Further, where the prior trademark incorporates descriptive terms commonly associated with the goods or services, the assessment of trade mark identity shall consider whether the use of the applied-for mark constitutes a deceptive practice.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed identical to a previously registered mark in respect of identical or similar goods or services, subject to the proviso that demonstrable evidence of consumer recognition and established goodwill associated with the earlier mark must be presented. Furthermore, any entity found to have employed a deceptively similar mark, knowing that such use infringes upon the existing trade mark identity, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the infringing sales achieved during the period of infringement. A specification patent shall be required for any trademark incorporating novel technological elements beyond common design features, and failure to provide this will render registration voidable.

For the purposes of this Act, "forfeiture directed conviction" shall mean a judicial order issued following a finding of guilt for an offence involving unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication, wherein the Court may, subject to due process and principles of natural justice, direct the confiscation and transfer to the Registering Proprietor of all goods bearing the false or misleading indication, as well as any instruments of manufacture or packaging utilized in their production. Such forfeiture shall be deemed compensatory relief intended to mitigate harm to the reputation and commercial interests associated with the protected geographical indication, provided that the value of forfeited assets is demonstrably linked to the infringing activity.
