The Registrar shall provide an opportunity to be heard to any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a map indicating clearly the territorial boundaries of the geographical area comprising the territory from which the goods originate. The Registrar may, after giving an opportunity to be heard to the applicant, reject the application if he is satisfied that the proposed geographical indication does not meet the criteria specified under this Act or that its registration would likely mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods. Any person claiming to be a *geographical indication plaintiff* aggrieved by any order passed by the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The trade proprietor registered in relation to a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement as provided herein, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures regarding notice and service.

An application for registration as a geographical indication plaintiff shall be deemed admissible only if it is accompanied by an affidavit, duly sworn before a Magistrate First Class or equivalent authority, confirming that the applicant represents the collective interests of producers whose goods originate from the defined geographical area. The affidavit must specify the criteria used to determine ‘producer’ and demonstrate adherence to quality standards as prescribed under this Act. Further, where the geographical indication is utilized in connection with a certification trade mark, the application shall include detailed specifications outlining the procedures for inspection and enforcement of those standards. Any deviation from these established protocols will render the application liable to rejection, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" means the three dimensional representation of an integrated circuit used in the manufacture of a semiconductor integrated circuit. A registered layout-design shall be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights in respect of the layout-design within India. Such rights include the right to apply for, or be granted, patents relating to the functional elements represented by the layout-design, subject to any conflicting claims under other intellectual property laws. The term "registered layout-design" includes any modifications of the original layout-design that do not alter its essential character as provided herein and are duly registered as such.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed, including detailed schematics illustrating the topological features of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the formal requirements stipulated herein. If satisfied that the layout-design is original and not contrary to public interest, the Registrar shall proceed with registration, entering the particulars in the Register of Layout-Designs. A registered layout-design confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights as provided herein, subject to any subsequent revocation proceedings initiated under this Act.

Where any person infringes a registered layout-design, such person shall be liable to pay damages to the registered proprietor. The amount of damages shall be determined by considering factors including the notional loss of profits which the registered proprietor would reasonably be expected to have obtained but for the infringement, and any benefit or advantage accruing to the infringing party from the use of the layout-design. Provided that in determining such damages, due account shall be taken of any measures adopted by the registered proprietor to protect the confidentiality of the layout-design prior to its registration. Further, subject to an appeal under this Act, a court may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further infringing acts and order delivery up or destruction of infringing materials. The remedies available as provided herein are without prejudice to any other remedy which may be available to the registered proprietor in law or equity.

An application for registration of a registered layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Office may prescribe, including certified copies of drawings illustrating the salient features of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation deemed necessary for assessing the novelty and originality of the layout-design under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing, which shall be conclusive evidence as to such date subject to any appeal filed within the prescribed time limit. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The layout-design must not contain elements dictated solely by technical function and should demonstrate inventive step beyond what is obvious to a person skilled in the art.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this Act if it contains a clear and accurate representation of the integrated circuit layout, accompanied by a written description detailing its functionality and intended use. The Registrar may reject an application if he is satisfied that the layout-design in question does not constitute an original work, or if it incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout-design without due acknowledgement under this Act. A registered layout-design confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to exploit the design for commercial purposes, subject to any conditions specified during registration relating to fair use and non-infringement of existing intellectual property. The Registrar shall maintain a public record detailing all registered layout-designs, including dates of registration and any associated licensing agreements.

Any person who reproduces a registered layout-design without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant court, taking into account the loss of profits suffered by the registered proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized reproduction and any other incidental harm. Further, where an infringement is proven to have been committed with the intent to deceive or cause confusion regarding the source or ownership of the layout-design, enhanced penalties may be imposed under this Act. The court shall also order the infringer to cease all infringing activities and account for profits made through such actions. This provision applies irrespective of whether the reproduction was for commercial gain or private use, provided that it constitutes an infringement as defined herein.

The registered layout-design may be assigned by transfer or license to any other person with the prior written consent of the Controller, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit. Such assignment shall not operate as a mortgage unless expressly stated in the instrument effecting the assignment. Where a license is granted, it shall specify the field of exploitation permitted under this Act, including but not limited to manufacture, sale, hire, or use of integrated circuits incorporating the registered layout-design. Any subsequent assignee or licensee shall be bound by the terms and conditions originally stipulated in the initial assignment or license agreement. The Controller may require disclosure of consideration paid for any such transfer or license before registering the change in ownership or licensing details as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions will render the assignment voidable at the option of the registered proprietor.

Where any question arises as to whether an alleged infringement involves a copy of a registered layout-design, the Tribunal shall determine such question based upon an examination of the relevant features and characteristics of both the registered layout-design and the impugned layout-design. It is provided that the mere existence of similarities between the two designs does not, by itself, constitute proof of copying; rather, it must be demonstrated that said similarities result from deliberate reproduction or substantial similarity in overall impression. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may appeal to the High Court any order passed by the Tribunal under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as the High Court deems fit. Any party aggrieved by an appellate order may further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor integrated circuit" means a set of elements and interconnections of those elements fixed within a single rigid material or combination of materials embodying a spatially fixed pattern, whether or not active devices are present therein; provided that such elements and interconnections are described by a layout-design. The term “element” includes but is not limited to transistors, diodes, resistors, conductors, and insulators. A semiconductor integrated circuit shall be deemed to include any three-dimensional arrangement of elements which functions as an electronic device. This definition extends to microchips and microfabricated structures incorporated within such circuits, subject to the conditions outlined herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed, including a certified copy of the first published version of the layout-design, if any. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the nature and extent of the layout-design claimed in the application, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the processing of the registration. Any person claiming an interest in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, subject to conditions as provided herein, file objections to the proposed registration within the time specified under this Act. The applicant shall be given an opportunity to respond to any objection raised. Registration confers upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights relating to the layout-design.

Where any person imports or deals with a semiconductor integrated circuit knowing, or having reasonable grounds to believe, that such act constitutes an infringement of registered design rights under this Act, such person shall be liable to pay damages to the registered proprietor. The amount of damages shall be determined by considering the loss suffered by the registered proprietor as a consequence of the infringing act, taking into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringement. Provided that, in determining damages, the Court may consider factors including but not limited to the extent of use of the semiconductor integrated circuit, the reasonableness of the infringer’s actions, and whether the infringer acted with knowledge of the registered design. Further, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts, subject to just terms.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a full and accurate representation of the layout-design. The Controller General shall examine each application in accordance with the provisions herein relating to examination and shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard if any objection is taken to the registration. Any person interested may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application for registration, file a notice of opposition under this Act. The Controller General may require such further information or clarification as he deems necessary from the applicant or the opponent. Upon hearing all parties and considering any evidence submitted, the Controller General shall pass an order either allowing or refusing the registration, providing reasons for the decision. Appeals against such orders are subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A semiconductor integrated circuit shall be deemed to infringe upon the rights of the registered proprietor where a layout design that incorporates substantial similarity to the protected layout is manufactured, imported, or sold within India. Such infringement exists if the overall impression created by the infringing layout design is substantially similar to that of the original, considering factors including component placement and interconnection patterns. Provided that, this shall not apply where the similarity arises from features dictated solely by technical necessity or functionality inherent in semiconductor integrated circuits. The registered proprietor may pursue remedies under this Act only after demonstrating due diligence in attempting amicable resolution with the alleged infringer; failure to do so will be considered when assessing damages.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, distributes, sells, or offers to sell any semiconductor integrated circuit incorporating a protected layout-design shall be liable to pay damages of not less than ten times the cost of implementing the design. Such damages may include compensation for loss of profits reasonably foreseeable as a result of the infringement. Further, where an infringing act is committed with the intention to deceive, the offender shall also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudication officer may order seizure and destruction of the infringing semiconductor integrated circuits under this Act, provided that the registered proprietor files a complaint within one year of discovering the infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring rights to use the design. Such license shall specify the field of use, geographical territory, and duration of the granted right. Assignment of ownership or a security interest in a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design is permissible, provided that such assignment or security interest is recorded with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks. Any subsequent licensee may further sublicense rights as provided herein, subject to maintaining confidentiality obligations stipulated within the original license agreement. The Controller may require disclosure of licensing terms in certain circumstances deemed necessary for promoting fair competition under this Act.

Where any question arises as to whether an alleged infringement involves a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, the Tribunal shall determine such question based upon a comparative assessment of the overall impression created by the allegedly infringing layout-design and that which is protected under this Act. It shall be presumed, subject to proof to the contrary, that the similarity between two layout-designs is substantial if an expert, possessing specialized knowledge in the field of integrated circuit design, testifies that the essential features of one layout-design are clearly discernible in the other. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the Tribunal’s findings concerning originality or technical merit.

An applicant intending to file a later publication application relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall furnish with the application a detailed technical description of the layout-design, including its functionality and intended use. Such description must be accompanied by certified copies of all prior publications or disclosures concerning the same design, as may be required under this Act. The Controller General shall examine the application to ascertain whether the later publication application contains any elements that are substantially similar to a previously published semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. If the Controller General is satisfied that the applicant has complied with these requirements and that the application meets all procedural stipulations provided herein, the application may proceed for registration. Any interested party may file objections within the prescribed time limit, challenging the novelty or originality of the design as presented in the later publication application.

An opposition to the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be filed within ninety days from the date of publication of the application under this Act. Such opposition must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to prior use or existence of an identical layout-design elsewhere. The opponent shall provide verifiable evidence substantiating their claim and demonstrating that registration would constitute infringement of existing rights. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing the opposition is frivolous or vexatious, they may apply to the relevant authority for a stay on proceedings pending assessment. Any decision regarding such a stay shall be subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit or any other matter under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged, failing which the appeal shall be deemed void ab initio. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Decisions of the Appellate Tribunal are final subject to further appeals under the relevant provisions concerning copyrights appellate jurisdiction. Any infringement of layout-design rights shall attract penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses granting rights to use, reproduce, or commercially exploit the said layout-design. Such license shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, by instrument in writing duly executed and registered with the Controller General. Where the terms of a license are not clearly defined, any dispute arising therefrom shall be resolved as per principles of equity and good faith. Further, cancellation of registration under this Act shall automatically render all existing licenses relating to that semiconductor integrated circuit null and void; however, rights accrued prior to such cancelling registration shall remain enforceable against those who have legitimately obtained them through the registered proprietor’s actions. The Controller General may issue guidelines regarding the form and content of assignment documents as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor integrated circuit" means a three-dimensional arrangement of active and passive electronic components and interconnections embodied upon a semiconductor material or insulative material, wherein the arrangement is defined by a layout-design. A notice applicant shall be deemed to have fulfilled the requirements of due diligence under this Act if such applicant provides an affidavit verifying that reasonable efforts were made to ascertain whether any identical or substantially similar layout-design has been previously registered. Subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, a determination regarding substantial similarity shall be binding on all parties involved in proceedings concerning infringement as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “breeder complied provisions” shall mean the conditions stipulated within a Plant Variety Registration Certificate pertaining to the sharing of breeder’s material and derived varieties. These stipulations are binding upon any person conducting activities involving the registered variety, including but not limited to commercialization, propagation, or research. Failure to adhere to these breeder complied provisions, as determined by the Board under this Act, constitutes an infringement of the rights granted to the plant breeder. Such infringements may result in penalties and injunctive relief, provided that farmers’ rights relating to saved seed are unaffected.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed declaration affirming compliance with breeder complied provisions as stipulated under this Act. Such declaration must explicitly state whether the applicant is the original breeder or has derived the variety through genetic engineering, hybridization, or other methods. The Authority may require submission of supporting documentation demonstrating adherence to established breeding protocols and traceability records pertaining to parental lines. Failure to provide accurate information regarding compliance with breeder complied provisions shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, any subsequent discovery of non-compliance after registration may lead to revocation of protection as provided herein, subject to due process and opportunity for a hearing.

Where a plant variety is registered under this Act and subsequent evidence demonstrates non-compliance with breeder complied provisions relating to farmers’ rights, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for modification or revocation of the registration. Any farmer alleging such non-compliance shall have the right to file a written complaint before the Authority, detailing the specific instances where the registered breeder has failed to adhere to obligations concerning seed sharing, access to propagating material, and compensation for any adverse effects arising from the variety’s use. The Authority shall provide an opportunity for both the farmer complainant and the registered breeder to present their respective cases, with due consideration given to expert testimony regarding agronomic practices and genetic purity. Failure by the breeder to satisfy the Authority that they have fulfilled their obligations as stipulated herein may result in a reduction of protection duration or complete revocation.

Where a plant variety is registered under this Act, the Registering Authority shall maintain a record indicating whether the breeder complied provisions relating to farmers’ rights and benefit-sharing arrangements. An application for registration may be refused if the Registrar determines that the proposed breeder has failed to adequately address requirements concerning on-farm conservation and seed saving practices as detailed in the prescribed guidelines. Further, any registered variety is subject to compulsory licensing under this Act if it is demonstrated that the breeder has not made the variety available to small and marginal farmers at a reasonable price, or has otherwise acted contrary to the principles of equity and access enshrined within this legislation. The Authority may issue directions regarding adherence to these stipulations; non-compliance shall be deemed a material breach of registration conditions.

Where a plant variety is registered under this Act, the breeder shall provide for the deposit of propagating material in an approved gene bank or national collection centre as specified by the Register. Such deposit must be made within six months from the date of publication of registration and maintained for a period not less than twenty-four years thereafter. The Register may require periodic verification to ensure viability and accessibility of said deposited materials, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. Failure to maintain such deposits as required shall constitute non-compliance with breeder complied provisions and render the registered variety liable for review under this Act. Any person claiming rights in the variety may petition the Authority if these conditions are not met, provided that due notice is given to the registered breeder.

Any breeder seeking protection for a plant variety shall demonstrate full compliance with the provisions relating to farmers’ rights as provided herein. Failure to provide evidence, satisfactory to the Authority, demonstrating adherence to these obligations, including but not limited to ensuring access to propagating material and providing compensation mechanisms where applicable, will render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, existing protection may be suspended or terminated if subsequent investigation reveals non-compliance with breeder complied provisions; such determination shall be made after due opportunity is afforded to the concerned breeder for a hearing. Penalties for wilful violation of these requirements include fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees and potential revocation of granted rights, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where a plant variety is protected under this Act and the breeder elects to provide for farmer’s rights including saving and exchange of seed, such election shall be recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties. The breeder may, through an assignment or license agreement, stipulate conditions relating to the use of such saved seed by farmers, provided that any such condition restricts only activities directly impacting the distinctiveness of the variety and does not impede legitimate research efforts. Further, where a breeder complied provisions regarding farmer’s rights are found to be non-compliant with the principles of equitable access to plant genetic resources, the Plant Variety Authority may direct modification or renegotiation of the relevant agreement. Any assignment of rights relating to saved seed shall clearly delineate the scope and duration of such assignment as provided herein.

Where a complaint is filed alleging non-compliance with breeder complied provisions relating to farmers’ rights concerning access to propagating material, the Biodiversity Board shall initiate an inquiry. The complainant shall bear the burden of demonstrating, through documentary evidence and witness testimony, that the registered plant variety has been reproduced or distributed in violation of conditions stipulated under this Act regarding benefit sharing with local communities. Should the Board find merit in the complaint, it may direct the breeder to provide compensation as determined by a Disputes Resolution Panel constituted for this purpose. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Authority within sixty days, presenting arguments demonstrating substantial compliance or procedural irregularity.

A breeder shall be deemed to have complied with the ‘breeder complied provisions’ where, prior to the filing of an application for a Plant Variety Registration, the breeder has demonstrably provided evidence of conducting field trials in accordance with guidelines issued by the Central Government and published in the Official Gazette. Such evidence must include detailed records pertaining to planting density, pest management strategies, irrigation schedules, and yield assessments across diverse agro-climatic zones. Failure to furnish such documentation shall render the application liable for rejection. Further, where a claim of prior compliance is disputed, an aggrieved party may seek an ex parte injunction restraining registration pending resolution of the dispute by the Authority.

For the purposes of this Act, “literary work” shall include any creation in the form of words, irrespective of its medium of expression, and such works may encompass computer programs, tables, compilations, and dramatic works. A literary work is deemed original if it originates from the author and possesses minimal independent creative labour. The right of a cinematograph film producer, as provided herein, shall extend to include the reproduction of any literary work incorporated therein. This protection shall not apply to works already in the public domain under this Act or where such incorporation constitutes fair dealing for research or private use, subject to conditions prescribed elsewhere. Provisions sub section (1) applies equally to derivative works.

Application for registration of a literary work shall be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by copies of the work as may be required under this Act. The Registrar shall register such work upon being satisfied that the applicant is the author or rightful assignee thereof and that the work fulfills all requirements for originality as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a work may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The provisions sub section (1) shall not apply where the work has been previously registered in another country under an agreement to which India is a party. Further, registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership for the purposes of civil proceedings.

Where an author demonstrates that a substantial portion of their copyrighted work has been reproduced without authorization, and such reproduction constitutes infringement under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of copying or distribution. Provided that, where the alleged infringing act involves fair dealing for purposes of research, private study, criticism, or review, the court may consider whether the use was reasonable and did not unduly prejudice the author’s ability to derive benefit from their work. The remedies available under this Act shall include damages equivalent to any actual losses suffered by the author as a result of the infringement, or in cases where actual damage is difficult to ascertain, a sum determined by the court that is just and equitable. Subject to appeal to the appellate jurisdiction established herein, decisions regarding these provisions sub section (1) are final.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, an aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright in a cinematograph film shall file a written complaint with the designated Copyright Enforcement Officer at such place as may be specified by the Central Government. The complaint must detail the alleged infringing activity, including dates, locations, and descriptions of the infringing works or devices. Upon receipt of the complaint, the Copyright Enforcement Officer shall record reasons for non-acceptance or acceptance of the same. Further, the officer shall serve a notice upon the person against whom the complaint is made, affording them an opportunity to be heard under this Act. The provisions sub section (2) empowers the Copyright Enforcement Officer to issue interim orders restraining further infringement pending final determination of the matter. Any order issued pursuant to these provisions may be challenged before the Appellate Tribunal within thirty days.

Subject to the provisions of this Act relating to fair dealing, any person desiring to reproduce a cinematograph film shall first obtain a written license from the owner of copyright therein. Such license shall specify the manner and duration of reproduction, as well as the territory within which such reproduction is permitted. Provided that where the proposed reproduction is solely for private use and non-commercial purposes, the owner may grant permission without requiring payment of any royalty. Further, under this Act, a licensee shall be deemed to have complied with the conditions of the license if they provide the copyright owner with an undertaking in writing confirming adherence to stipulated terms. The provisions sub section (1) shall not apply where reproduction is incidental to the lawful exhibition of the film.

Any person who knowingly reproduces or distributes a work in violation of the provisions sub section relating to copyright infringement shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender is liable for imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both. Further, where such reproduction or distribution has been made for commercial gain, the court may enhance the aforementioned penalty by a multiple of five. The owner of copyright shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings against any person infringing their rights as provided herein, seeking damages and an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. Repeated offences shall attract progressively higher penalties at the discretion of the Court.

Subject to the conditions outlined herein, a copyright owner desiring to grant a license in respect of their work shall execute a written instrument specifying the scope of such license, including but not limited to the geographical territory, duration, and permitted acts. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive at the discretion of the copyright owner, provided that any assignment of copyright under this Act must also be evidenced by a written instrument. Further, where a work is jointly authored, the provisions sub section (1) relating to licensing shall apply with modification to reflect the rights and obligations of each co-owner. Any party receiving a license or assignment shall be bound by the terms stipulated therein, and any unauthorized use beyond the scope of such agreement constitutes infringement. The copyright owner retains the right to terminate a license upon written notice if material breaches occur.

For the purposes of this Act, a “geographical indication applied” shall mean the use of a registered geographical indication by any person in relation to goods with the intention to indicate that such goods originate from the place named in the geographical indication and possess qualities, reputation or other characteristics which are essentially attributable to its origin. This application may be through labels, marks, names or images directly associated with the product. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent a registered proprietor of a trademark from using their trademark on goods as permitted under the Trade Marks Act. The use of a geographical indication applied is subject to conditions prescribed by the Registrar.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant document establishing the collective interest in the good and its connection to the territory. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods which are attributable to the origin within the defined geographical area. Where an application relates to a *geographical indication applied* for agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirit distillates, cereals, or spices, evidence demonstrating traditional production methods shall be submitted. The applicant must also specify the producers, dealers, and other stakeholders who will benefit from the registration under this Act. Any alteration to the proposed name or geographical boundaries may necessitate a fresh application as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication applied shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act. Infringement occurs when an unauthorized person makes use of the said indication likely to cause confusion among the public as to the origin or nature of the goods. Remedies available to the proprietor include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to a minimum amount as determined by the relevant court. Further, any goods found to be in respect of which infringement has occurred shall be liable for seizure and destruction at the infringer’s expense. The Registrar may also issue directions regarding the disposal of such seized goods. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent a proprietor from seeking remedies under other laws relating to unfair competition or passing off.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the resolution passed by the producers’ consortium or other organization representing the interests of the geographically defined area. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the production techniques employed and the quality characteristics that define the goods associated with the proposed geographical indication, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly burden the application process. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the distinctiveness or reputation of a *geographical indication applied*, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with a written statement detailing the grounds for the objection. The applicant may then submit a written response addressing these concerns, along with any supporting documentation deemed relevant to demonstrate the validity of their claim. A hearing may be convened at the discretion of the Registrar to allow both parties to present oral arguments.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be deemed inadmissible if the applicant fails to demonstrate continuous and exclusive use of the name by producers within the defined territory for a minimum period of three years preceding the date of the application. The Registrar may require submission of documented evidence, including but not limited to sales records, harvest reports, and affidavits from local communities, substantiating this usage. Further, any geographical indication applied must be linked directly to qualities, reputation or other characteristics attributable essentially to its origin. Provided that a prior use by another party does not constitute grounds for rejection if such use is demonstrably incidental and non-competitive with the proposed registration. The applicant shall also disclose any existing contractual agreements pertaining to the use of the name within the territory.

Any proprietor utilizing a geographical indication applied to goods shall be liable for damages sustained by an authorized user as a direct result of such utilization, provided that the unauthorized use constitutes a misrepresentation likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any authorized user, issue a cease and desist order against the proprietor engaging in the infringing activity. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the proprietor liable for a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, repeated or willful infringement may result in the revocation of the registration under this Act, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication applied to goods may grant exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said indication on specific products within the defined territory and for a stipulated period, subject to such terms and conditions as agreed upon between the proprietor and licensee, which shall be documented in writing. Such licenses may be assigned to any person or entity with the prior written consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all obligations imposed under this Act pertaining to the protection of the geographical indication. Further, a proprietor intending to assign their rights in respect of a geographical indication applied must notify the Registrar at least thirty days prior to the assignment taking effect, detailing the proposed assignee and the scope of the assigned rights. The Registrar may object to such an assignment if it deems it detrimental to the interests of producers associated with the geographical indication.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication applied by an applicant, provided that the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a point of law arising out of the said decision. Subject to such appeals, orders made under this Act shall be final. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules prescribing the manner in which applications for registration and subsequent appeals are processed.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act refusing registration of a geographical indication applied for, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the decision. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Where the application relates to a geographical indication signifying a musical work intrinsically linked to the agricultural practices of a particular territory, the Registrar shall consider evidence pertaining to the continuity of that association. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law.

Any proprietor of a registered certification mark incorporating a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings in the High Court for redressal of infringement. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use of the geographical indication applied, taking into account any benefit accruing to the infringing party. The Court shall have power to grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and an order requiring the infringer to recall goods bearing the mark from all points of sale. Provided that a claim for damages may be denied if the proprietor failed to exercise due diligence in monitoring use of the geographical indication applied. The Court shall also consider any registered certification marks impacted by the infringing activity when determining appropriate remedies.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant document establishing collective ownership or control over the quality and reputation of the goods associated with the indicated geographical origin. Where an objection is raised concerning the distinctiveness of the proposed geographical indication, the applicant may submit counter-evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall consider such evidence in accordance with established principles of trademark law. Furthermore, any person claiming rights adversely affected by the registration of a geographical indication applied to goods may petition for invalidation under this Act within six months from the date of publication of the registered geographical indication. Such petitions must specify grounds relating to lack of distinctiveness or misrepresentation. The validity of such registration shall be subject to periodic review, and an addition validity patent may be sought after ten years.

The Copyright Office shall, subject to the provisions herein, serve as the central repository for all applications relating to copyright registration and related matters. Any person claiming copyright in an original work shall file an application with the Copyright Office in the prescribed form, providing details of ownership, creation date, and nature of the work. The Registrar of Copyrights, exercising powers delegated under this Act, may require further documentation deemed necessary for verification. Decisions regarding acceptance or rejection of applications are final, appealable only to the relevant judicial authority as provided herein. The Copyright Office maintains records accessible according to regulations framed by the Central Government.

Applications for registration of copyright in literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works may be made to the Copyright Office in such form and manner as prescribed by rules framed under this Act. Every application shall contain particulars relating to the owner of the copyright and the nature of the work claimed to be original. The Registrar of Copyrights, acting through officers authorized by him, shall examine each application and any documents submitted therewith, determining whether the requirements for registration are satisfied. Where an applicant fails to provide requisite information or documentation as demanded by the Copyright Office, the application may be rejected. Registered copyright provides conclusive evidence of ownership subject to fraud or error apparent on the face of the record.

Any person claiming infringement of copyright in any work shall, subject to provisions regarding limitation periods, institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the cause of action. Upon receiving complaint of alleged copyright infringement, the court may issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, provided that such restraint is necessary to prevent irreparable injury. The remedies available under this Act include damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a result of the infringement, and in cases of flagrant or wilful infringement, punitive damages not exceeding ten times the actual damages. Furthermore, any works seized during investigation of alleged infringements shall be held in custody of the Copyright Office until determination of the case by the court.

Applications for registration of copyright shall be submitted in the prescribed form to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by notification issued from time to time. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the work and its author as may be required under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar of Copyrights may require the applicant to submit certified copies of any document relevant to the claim of copyright. Information submitted to the Copyright Office shall be treated as confidential, subject to disclosure for the purposes of processing applications and conducting inquiries.

Applications received by the Copyright Office requesting registration of cinematograph films shall include, as an essential component, three certified copies of the film itself, each on separate reels conforming to standard industry specifications. These copies must demonstrate visual and auditory integrity, free from defects rendering reproduction impaired. Furthermore, applicants intending to claim copyright in musical works incorporated within the film are obliged to submit a complete score or sheet music transcription alongside their application. Any alteration to submitted materials after initial receipt by the Copyright Office will necessitate resubmission of all relevant documentation and may attract additional processing fees as determined by regulations issued under this Act. The Registrar of Copyrights may reject applications failing to comply with these stipulations.

Any person aggrieved by any order passed by the Copyright Office relating to registration, renewal or rectification of copyright may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during application submission renders the application liable for rejection without further notice and forfeits any fees paid. The Registrar of Copyrights shall have the power to issue summons and administer oaths, and any person failing to appear or answer truthfully when duly summoned shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with a fine, or both, as provided herein. Any fraudulent representation made in connection with copyright registration is subject to penalties under this Act.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a public register detailing all assignments and licenses relating to copyright in works, including but not limited to literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works, as well as cinematograph films and sound recordings. Any individual or entity seeking to assign their copyright or grant a license, exclusive or otherwise, shall file the relevant documentation with the Copyright Office within thirty days of execution. Such filings must include full particulars of the assignor, assignee, licensor, and licensee, alongside a clear description of the work subject to the assignment or license and the scope of rights transferred. The Registrar of Copyrights may require further clarification or supporting evidence as deemed necessary. Assignments and licenses filed under this Act shall be binding upon all parties involved, subject to any terms explicitly stated therein. Any subsequent transfer of rights must also be registered with the Copyright Office to remain valid against third parties.

The Registrar of Copyrights may, upon receiving an appeal against a decision made by an Examining Officer within the Copyright Office regarding the originality or ownership of a literary work, direct that the matter be reheard. Such direction shall be accompanied by written reasons specifying the grounds upon which the appeal is entertained. Any party aggrieved by the outcome of the rehearing may further appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision of the Examining Officer following the rehearing. The Copyright Office shall maintain a record of all appeals and rehearings conducted under this Act, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as determined by the Central Government.

Applications for registration of copyright, once received by the Copyright Office, shall be examined in accordance with procedures as provided herein; however, any applicant aggrieved by a decision refusing registration or registering a work subject to conditions may within sixty days from the date of such decision file an appeal before the Controller. Such appeals shall be accompanied by a fee prescribed under this Act and supported by a reasoned statement outlining grounds for challenge. The Controller may, after affording the Copyright Office and any other party affected an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the original decision. A legal practitioner duly enrolled under the Advocates Act shall be permitted to represent applicants in such appeal proceedings.

Applications for registration of copyright, as provided herein, shall be submitted in the prescribed form to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the work and its author as the Copyright Office may require. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office shall issue a preliminary acknowledgement slip indicating the date of receipt. A statement of originality, signed by the applicant or their authorized representative, must be included with each submission. The Registrar of Copyrights may request further documentation or clarification from the applicant to verify authenticity and ownership claims. Any form issuing relating to copyright registration is subject to review under this Act.

Applications for registration of copyright, as provided herein, shall be submitted in the prescribed form to the Copyright Office. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the work and the author as the Central Government deems necessary; failure to do so may result in rejection of the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant by post or electronic means. During any house parliament session, the Registrar of Copyrights is obligated to provide regular updates on pending applications to the relevant standing committee. The examination of works for originality and compliance with this Act rests solely within the purview of the Copyright Office staff. Objections to registration must be filed within a stipulated period as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Applications for registration of copyright in artistic works, including architectural designs, shall be submitted to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form accompanied by three copies of the work or design. The applicant must declare that they are the sole author and owner of the copyright claimed, subject to any assignments registered under this Act. Where the work incorporates a new variety of plant material, the application shall include a detailed botanical description conforming to standards set by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. Registration may be refused if the submitted materials do not comply with these requirements or if the applicant fails to provide satisfactory evidence of ownership as provided herein. The Copyright Office may request further documentation at any stage during processing.

For the purposes of this Act, “person interested” includes any individual who, prior to the date of filing of the patent application, has acquired an interest in the invention through assignment, license or other agreement, and such person shall be deemed to have derived title to the invention from the original inventor. A person shall not be considered a "person interested" solely by virtue of having been involved in discussions regarding the potential exploitation of the inventive concept. Further, where an employee has made an invention during his employment, and the terms of his contract of service provide for remuneration or other benefits contingent upon patent grant, such employee shall also be deemed a “person interested” subject to the provisions relating to inventorship as provided herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly funded research and development leading to the claimed invention, provided that such funding was material to the conception or reduction to practice thereof. Further, a person interested includes an assignee of the right to apply for a patent, where assignment is duly registered with the Controller. Any entity claiming status as a “person interested” shall file a declaration along with the application for registration, specifying the nature and extent of their interest in the invention. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating such claim under this Act. This determination rests solely within the discretion of the Controller, subject to appeal before an appellate tribunal.

Where an application for patents has been refused under this Act, any person interested may appeal against such refusal to the Controller. The term “person interested” includes, but is not limited to, the applicant’s assignees, legal representatives, and those who have derived a right to make an application from the true inventor or their assignees. Such an appeal shall be filed within three months of the date of communication of the refusal order. Upon receiving such an appeal, the Controller may require the appellant to furnish security for costs, as provided herein. The Controller shall afford the applicant and any other person interested an opportunity to present their views in writing or orally regarding the merits of the application. Failure to comply with procedural requirements under this Act may render the appeal inadmissible.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly or indirectly derived benefit from the patent application prior to its grant, subject to verification by the Controller. Such benefit may encompass financial support provided for research leading to the invention, collaborative development efforts documented through written agreements, or assignment of rights pertaining to the inventive concept. The Controller shall issue a notice to any such person interested upon receipt of an objection under this Act and afford them an opportunity to present their views in writing within sixty days from the date of such notice. Failure to respond within that period shall be construed as acquiescence to the objections raised. Any representation made by a person interested shall be considered during examination, provided it is substantiated with relevant documentation.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly or indirectly acquired rights pertaining to the patent, or who is engaged in the manufacture, use, or sale of an article embodying the invention claimed in the patent application. Such person shall also encompass any legal entity that has provided substantial financial support towards the research and development leading to the invention, provided that such contribution is documented through a formal agreement executed prior to the filing date of the patent application. A person interested may file applications for rectification under this Act concerning the validity or scope of the patent, subject to demonstrating a material interest adversely affected by the patent’s existence or interpretation. The Controller shall consider any objections raised by a person interested with due regard to the principles of natural justice.

Where an infringement of patent has occurred, any person interested may institute suit for relief as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, a “person interested” shall include, but not be limited to, the registered proprietor of the patent, their licensees, assignees, and those who have acquired an undivided interest in the patent rights through succession or otherwise. Any such action brought under this Act shall specify the nature of the infringement and the damages sustained as a direct consequence thereof. Failure to accurately quantify demonstrable losses may result in dismissal of the claim without prejudice to costs. The Controller may, upon application by any party aggrieved, issue summons requiring attendance and production of relevant documents pertaining to the alleged infringement.

Where an invention has been assigned or licensed under this Act, and the assignor or licensee desires to exploit such invention beyond the scope of the assignment or license agreement respectively, they shall apply to the Controller for permission to do so. Such application must specify the nature of the exploitation sought and demonstrate that it does not unduly prejudice the interests of the assignee or licensee. The Controller may grant or refuse such permission at his discretion, subject to a hearing where both parties are afforded an opportunity to be heard. For the purposes of this section, a “person interested” includes any individual or entity holding a valid assignment or license relating to the patent in question. Provided that, if the exploitation sought involves manufacturing for domestic use, the Controller shall consider factors including affordability and accessibility as relevant considerations.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly or indirectly derived benefit from the patent application prior to its grant, provided that such derivation is established through documented evidence presented before the Controller. The determination of whether a person qualifies as a "person interested" for the purposes of challenging validity under this Act may be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board if it is contested by the applicant or any other party claiming an interest in the patent. Further, where a claim arises regarding benefit derived through assignment or licensing agreements, the Controller shall consider whether such arrangements were entered into with the primary intent to circumvent provisions relating to novelty and inventive step as provided herein.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “person interested” shall include any individual or body corporate holding a beneficial interest in an invention claimed in an application, whether arising from assignment, license, or other contractual arrangement. Such person shall be deemed to have sufficient cause for seeking rectification of the register if it is demonstrated that their rights, as derived under this Act, are adversely affected by an entry made therein. Provided that, where a condition declared unlawful by a competent authority relates directly to the subject matter of the invention and impacts the validity of registration, any person interested may petition the Controller for review of the application’s status. The Controller shall consider such petitions in accordance with procedures as provided herein.

Where an application for patents contains deficiencies rendering it not in compliance with the requirements of this Act, the Controller may, subject to conditions specified herein, allow the applicant a period not exceeding six months from the date of communication of such deficiencies to rectify the same. Such rectification shall be effected by way of amendment and must adhere strictly to prescribed forms and procedures as provided under this Act. An application corrected in accordance with these provisions shall be deemed to be an original application for all purposes, except where the correction substantially alters the claimed invention. A “person interested,” including but not limited to assignees or legal representatives, may file a notice of objection against any such amended claim within thirty days of its publication.

For the purposes of this Act, “official form” means any form prescribed by the Controller for use in connection with applications, requests, notices, and other documents required under this Act; "prescribed manner" includes compliance with all instructions issued by the Controller regarding the completion and submission of such forms, including but not limited to requirements relating to electronic filing where available. Any document submitted not in the official form or otherwise than in the prescribed manner shall be deemed invalid unless specifically ratified by the Controller. The Controller may issue general directions as provided herein concerning the use of official forms and the acceptance of documents.

The Register of Designs shall maintain records pertaining to registered designs in the prescribed manner, including details of the proprietor, design number, class, and date of registration. Any alteration to these particulars, such as a change in ownership or address of the proprietor, must be notified to the Office within thirty days of such change and recorded accordingly. The Office may, at its discretion, require supporting documentation for any alterations submitted. Failure to update information in the prescribed manner will not invalidate the design registration but may result in penalties under this Act. Further, a request for rectification of entries concerning a registered design shall be made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein.

Where any patentee institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, the court shall require such patentee to furnish, as evidence of validity, a certificate issued by the Controller confirming that the prescribed manner for notification of grant has been duly observed. Failure to provide this certificate within the time specified by the court will render the patent unenforceable in those proceedings and preclude the patentee from seeking injunctive relief or damages relating to the alleged infringement. Provided that, if the defendant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the court that the failure to notify was not attributable to the patentee’s negligence, the court may, at its discretion, permit the continuation of the suit subject to such terms as it deems just, including requiring the payment of costs. The Controller shall prescribe the form and procedure for obtaining this certificate in a manner consistent with principles of natural justice.

The Controller shall require every application for registration of a layout design under this Act to be accompanied by such particulars as are prescribed, including detailed representations illustrating the aesthetic characteristics of the design and a statement specifying any functional elements incorporated therein. Such applications must be filed in the prescribed manner, utilizing the forms designated on the Controller’s website or obtained from the Patent Office. The applicant shall also furnish an inventor's declaration, duly executed by all claimed inventors, attesting to their contribution towards the creation of the design and confirming its novelty as against prior publications. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application. Any alteration made to the submitted documentation after filing is permissible only with written consent from the Controller and shall be recorded in the prescribed manner.

The Controller shall require that all applications for registration of plant varieties under this Act be accompanied by a detailed report, prepared in the prescribed manner, documenting the method of propagation employed and demonstrating genetic stability across at least three successive generations. Such reports must include photographic evidence illustrating key morphological characteristics, as determined by established botanical criteria. The applicant shall further provide an assurance that the variety has been cultivated exclusively under conditions conforming to Good Agricultural Practices, subject to verification through inspection conducted by officers authorized herein. Provided that, if the plant variety is genetically modified, a comprehensive risk assessment report, approved by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee, must also be submitted in the prescribed manner alongside the aforementioned documentation.

Any application for registration as a plant variety shall be accompanied by documentation demonstrating compliance with the prescribed manner relating to seed multiplication and propagation techniques, as detailed in the First Schedule. Failure to submit such documentation, or demonstrable deviation from these protocols during inspection under this Act, renders the application liable for rejection without further notice. Furthermore, any person found to have reproduced or marketed plant propagating material derived from a registered variety in contravention of the conditions stipulated within the registration certificate, or otherwise than in the prescribed manner, shall be subject to penalties as provided herein and may face civil action for damages recoverable by the registered proprietor.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license for exploiting any patented invention under this Act, such license shall be documented in a form prescribed by the Controller and executed in the prescribed manner. The terms of the license, including but not limited to royalty rates, territorial scope, and duration, must be clearly articulated within said document. Assignment of patent rights, whether partial or complete, similarly requires adherence to the prescribed manner, ensuring proper recording with the Patent Office. Provided that any licensee may, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement, assign their right to use the patented invention, but such assignment shall not prejudice the original patentee’s rights as provided herein. Failure to execute a license or assignment in the prescribed manner renders it void and unenforceable against third parties.

The Controller may, upon receiving written objection from any interested party regarding the acceptance of a patent application under this Act, direct the applicant to submit further particulars relating to the claimed invention within a period not exceeding ninety days. Such direction shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement outlining the specific deficiencies identified in the application and the information required for rectification. Failure by the applicant to comply with such direction within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection, subject to an opportunity being afforded to the objector to present arguments against the proposed course of action. The Controller’s decision regarding compliance shall be deemed final unless appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board in the prescribed manner.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all breeder variety registrations, including particulars relating to the applicant, the denomination of the variety, its essential derivation and any relevant documentation pertaining to its genetic stability. Such records shall be updated periodically as provided herein and made accessible for public inspection in the prescribed manner, subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential information submitted during the registration process. Any alteration or addition to a breeder variety registered shall be recorded with due acknowledgement of the changes and their effective date. The Registrar may require applicants to submit additional data demonstrating adherence to established protocols for maintaining genetic purity, as deemed necessary to uphold the integrity of the register.

The Controller shall maintain an entry register for all applications filed under this Act, detailing each stage of processing including examination, hearing, and determination of patentability. Such entries shall be made in the prescribed manner, utilizing forms as notified by the Patents Office from time to time. The entry register shall record the date upon which any communication is dispatched to the applicant or any other person interested in the application, along with a concise summary of the contents thereof. Any modification to an existing entry must also be recorded, clearly indicating the original and revised information. Failure to adhere to the prescribed manner during registration may render such entries voidable at the discretion of the Controller. The register shall be open for public inspection subject to any restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets or confidential commercial information.

Where a patentee elects to grant a license relating to any patented invention under this Act, such license shall be assignable in the prescribed manner, subject to the terms and conditions agreed upon between the parties, and recorded with the Controller as per rules framed for that purpose. Provided that where the licensed party subsequently seeks to assign the said license to a third party, prior written consent of the original patentee shall be obtained and documented. The assignment shall not affect any existing trade mark exists associated with the invention unless explicitly stated otherwise in the agreement between the parties. Any attempt to transfer or pledge such a license without adhering to this prescribed manner will render the transaction voidable at the option of the patentee, who may seek injunctive relief as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “invention” includes any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof; "patentable subject matter" shall be restricted to inventions relating to a product or process that can be produced by means of an industrial application. An invention shall not include a scientific theory, or discovery concerning a natural principle or law. The term “register patents” signifies the formal entry of a patent into the official record maintained under this Act, signifying its legal recognition and conferring upon the patentee exclusive rights as provided herein, subject to any limitations imposed by other laws.

An application for registration of a patent shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the true inventor or inventors of the invention claimed in the application, and such declaration shall be signed by the applicant. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the derivation of the invention, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the invention is solely based on publicly available information. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application to register patents may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Register of Patents maintained under this Act shall be open for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the grant or refusal to register patents, or by any condition imposed in connection therewith, appeals under this Act, the Appellate Board may allow such appeal if it is satisfied that the decision was erroneous in law or fact. The Board shall have power to substitute the decision with its own, and may order a fresh examination of the patent application. Further, where an infringement action is brought before a court, evidence demonstrating prior publication or use undermining novelty shall be admissible, subject to provisions regarding reasonable access and due process. Any party dissatisfied with a judgment rendered by such court relating to validity or enforceability of patents may appeal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the suit was instituted, provided that the appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the judgment.

An application for the grant of a patent shall be made to the Controller in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required under this Act. The applicant shall specify whether the application relates to an invention or to the design thereof, and shall state clearly the claims supported by proper description. Where the applicant is not the true and first inventor, he shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the Controller establishing his right to make the application. Upon receipt of such application, the Controller may direct that the application be accompanied by such additional information as he deems necessary for examination. The Controller shall register patents in accordance with the provisions herein, subject to a search being conducted and an examination undertaken to ascertain novelty and inventive step. Any person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

An application for the grant of a patent shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a statement declaring whether the invention relates to a process involving microorganisms or genetic elements. The Controller General shall examine each application in accordance with the provisions herein and may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the claimed subject matter if deemed necessary for assessing novelty and inventive step. Where an applicant has previously published particulars of the invention, the application to register patents shall disclose such publication and its date. Any prior use or knowledge of the invention before the filing date shall be taken into account during examination; provided that evidence demonstrating commercial exploitation under a confidentiality agreement may be considered mitigating circumstances subject to prescribed conditions.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, refusal, or revocation of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision; provided that the Tribunal shall not entertain any appeal if it finds that no substantial question of law is involved. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller may, upon receiving information regarding patent infringement, initiate inquiries and issue notices requiring parties to show cause why a penalty should not be imposed; such penalties may extend up to three times the profit made by the infringer. It is incumbent on the Registrar to diligently register patents in accordance with the provisions of this Act.

Where any question arises as to whether an application has been filed with priority under this Act, the Controller may require such evidence as he deems necessary to establish the date of filing and the claim of priority; and if the applicant fails to produce satisfactory evidence within the time specified by the Controller, the application shall be deemed not to have been filed with that priority. An appeal lies against any order made by the Controller under this provision, subject to the provisions regarding appeals as provided herein. The appellate authority may direct the Controller to reconsider the matter or substitute its own decision; and a further appeal from such appellate authority shall lie to the High Court within ninety days of the date of the order appealed from, provided that the grounds for such further appeal are limited to matters of law. It is open to any party aggrieved by an order relating to the register patents to challenge it in court.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” with reference to a registered trade mark includes, but is not limited to, the application of the mark to goods, or packaging thereof, offering or exposing goods for sale under the mark, the use of the mark in connection with the provision of services, and any other act whereby the proprietor puts forth the mark as an indication of origin or quality.
