Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the potential for consumer confusion arising from a proposed geographical indication, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit counter-arguments and evidence. The Register may, after considering all submissions, direct that the application proceed with modifications or reject it entirely. Any party aggrieved by such a direction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication. A geographical indication falsified through deceptive packaging or labelling shall be treated as an infringement under this Act, subject to provisions regarding rectification proceedings.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall institute proceedings for relief under this Act if it is established that another party has engaged in conduct constituting a geographical indication falsified. Such falsification occurs when any sign, whether identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication “Kashmir Apples”, is used in connection with goods not conforming to the standards and quality characteristics defined in the registration certificate for "Kashmir Apples". This applies even if the use incorporates additional descriptive matter, such as “Kashmir Apples – Premium Blend”. Provided that, a sign shall not be considered deceptively similar unless it creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or qualities of the goods. The Registrar may issue cease and desist orders against any party found to have falsified a geographical indication.

Any enterprise found to have knowingly used a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act shall be liable for penalties commensurate with the scale of misrepresentation and resultant economic harm. Such enterprises may face fines up to five times the value of the infringing goods sold, and imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years. Further, any packaging or labelling bearing a geographical indication falsified in contravention of this Act shall be subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offender. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders against those engaged in such deceptive practices, and recovery of costs incurred by the registered proprietor is also provided for herein.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in the High Court alleging that another party has engaged in acts constituting a geographical indication falsified. Such an action shall require demonstration, through clear and convincing evidence, that the defendant’s use of signs or indications creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services offered. The court may consider factors including, but not limited to, the similarity of the signs, the nature of the goods or services, the degree of consumer recognition of the registered geographical indication, and any deliberate attempt by the defendant to trade upon the reputation associated with the genuine article. An appeal from an order made under this Act lies to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court within sixty days of such order.

Any individual who produces, markets, distributes, or exports goods bearing a geographical indication which is demonstrably false, misleading, or constitutes a geographical indication falsified, shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. Such an alleged offence carries a minimum fine of fifty thousand rupees and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees, alongside imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. Where the goods are exported, additional punitive measures including seizure of the consignment and revocation of export licenses shall apply. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify further conditions relating to the assessment of damages and enforcement procedures under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant a license conferring the right to use such indication in relation to goods or services specified in the license agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall be documented in writing, clearly defining the scope of permitted usage and duration. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered geographical indication is permissible with prior written consent from the Registrar, and such assignment shall include provisions safeguarding against any subsequent geographical indication falsified use by the assignee. Further, Security India Action protocols may be invoked where unauthorized application or deceptive imitation threatens the distinctiveness and reputation of the protected geographical indication, allowing for expedited remedies and seizure of infringing goods. The proprietor retains ultimate control over maintaining the integrity of the registered mark.

A suit alleging a geographical indication falsified may be instituted in the High Court having jurisdiction over the area within which the goods constituting the geographical indication are produced, subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving that their use of a sign similar to a registered goods geographical indication does not indicate an intention to deceive or cause confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Further, where the plaintiff claims damages arising from such falsification, they must demonstrate actual financial loss attributable directly to the deceptive practices employed by the defendant. The appellate forum may order costs against either party based on the merits of the appeal.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be rejected if the Examining Officer has reason to believe that the use of the proposed indication is likely to mislead consumers as to the true origin of the goods. The Registrar, after giving notice to the applicant and an opportunity to be heard, shall determine whether such misleading is probable. Further, any alteration or addition to a registered geographical indication which results in a *geographical indication falsified*, creating confusion amongst purchasers regarding the source of the goods, constitutes an offence under this Act. This determination shall take into account manner informing international trade practices and conventions relating to intellectual property rights. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating consumer understanding concerning the geographical origin of the goods.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to “Kashmir Apples” shall include detailed particulars regarding the agricultural practices employed in cultivation, harvesting, and processing unique to the specified geographical area. The Registrar may require submission of maps delineating the boundaries of the region, along with affidavits from growers’ cooperatives attesting to adherence to traditional methods. Any use of the indication "Kashmir Apples" or any confusingly similar designation on products not originating within that defined territory shall be deemed a *geographical indication falsifies* the registered right. Provided that, this restriction does not apply where such use is incidental and does not suggest an origin in Kashmir. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaints, initiate inquiries into alleged instances of geographical indication falsification.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods claiming origin from a registered geographical indication shall be liable for damages if it is established that such enterprise has knowingly used a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said geographical indication. Such use constitutes a *geographical indication falsifies* and prejudices the interests of the registered proprietor and consumers alike. The authorised user may, subject to due process, seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further misrepresentation and demand compensation for losses incurred as a direct consequence of the deceptive practice. Further, goods bearing the false or misleading geographical indication shall be liable for seizure and destruction at the expense of the offending enterprise, provided that such action is proportionate to the infringement.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that use of the indication is likely to mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods concerned. The applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the distinctiveness and reputation of the proposed geographical indication, including documentation relating to traditional knowledge and production methods. Where a registered geographical indication is falsified through the application of a mark or sign that creates an identical or confusingly similar impression, the aggrieved party may file a complaint with the Registrar detailing the nature of the infringement. The Registrar shall investigate such complaints and may issue directions for rectification of the register or impose penalties as provided herein. Any person found to be engaging in activities constituting geographical indication falsifies is liable to prosecution under this Act.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods claiming origin from a registered geographical indication shall ensure that all packaging and labelling clearly indicate the protected designation. Failure to comply with this requirement constitutes prima facie evidence of intent to mislead consumers regarding the provenance of said goods. Further, any use of a geographical indication, or any mark which is identical or confusingly similar thereto, in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as defined under this Act shall be deemed an act of geographical indication falsifies. Such acts are subject to penalties as provided herein and may result in revocation of any associated registrations. The Central Registry may issue directions regarding corrective measures where a violation is detected.

Any enterprise found to employ a protected geographical indication in connection with goods not originating from the registered area, or which are not produced according to the prescribed method of production as defined under this Act, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Such enterprises may face fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and potential injunctions preventing further use of the misleading mark. Furthermore, any individual or entity knowingly facilitating the geographical indication falsifies through deceptive packaging or advertising will be subject to similar sanctions and may be ordered to pay compensation to registered proprietors for damages incurred. The Registrar shall have power to issue cease-and-desist orders and initiate prosecution proceedings as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant a license conferring the right to use such indication in relation to goods or services specified in the license agreement, subject to conditions as prescribed therein and recorded with the Registrar. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and shall clearly define the scope of permitted usage, including territorial limitations and quality control measures. Assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication is permissible only with prior written consent from the Registrar, ensuring that the assignee undertakes to uphold the standards associated with the indication. Furthermore, any person who knowingly uses a geographical indication in contravention of these provisions, or engages in conduct amounting to geographical indication falsifies, shall be liable for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods claiming origin from a registered geographical indication shall be liable for prosecution under this Act if it is established that such enterprise has knowingly utilized a sign identical or confusingly similar to the protected indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an authorized user or any interested party, initiate inquiries into alleged instances where a geographical indication falsifies the reputation of genuine products originating from the designated area. Such inquiries shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, affording the accused enterprise an opportunity to present its defence and counter-evidence. Appeals against decisions made by the Registrar concerning allegations of geographical indication falsification may be filed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

A producer seeking registration of a geographical indication for ‘Kesar Mangoes of Nashik’ shall be liable for prosecution if it is established that the applicant has knowingly utilized a sign identical or deceptively similar to an existing, unregistered identifier associated with mango cultivation in the Jalgaon district. Such utilization constitutes a *geographical indication falsifies* the distinctiveness and reputation of the latter. The aggrieved party, being a cooperative society representing growers in Jalgaon, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the registration notice. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence pertaining to prior customary use and consumer perception when determining whether deceptive similarity exists under this Act.

Any enterprise found to have employed a deceptive mark resembling a registered geographical indication shall be liable for damages as determined by the High Court, taking into account the extent of misrepresentation and resultant loss suffered by producers entitled to use the indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an authorized user or any affected producer, issue a cease-and-desist order against any party engaging in such deceptive practices. Further, goods bearing a geographical indication falsifies through misleading packaging or labeling are subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the infringing party. Convention application shall extend to protect similar indications registered under treaties to which India is a signatory. The right to apply for rectification of entries on the register remains available to any interested party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from inaccurate registration.

Where a copyright owner seeks to enforce their rights under this Act, civil courts shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine such actions, subject to the provisions herein. The aggrieved party may institute proceedings for infringement, seeking remedies including but not limited to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner or any reasonable compensation which the court deems just. Provided that in determining the amount of damages, the court shall consider the flagrancy of the infringing conduct and any benefit accruing to the infringer as a direct result thereof. Further, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, provided that such restraint is necessary to prevent irreparable harm to the copyright owner. The powers civil court shall extend to ordering the destruction of infringing copies or materials.

Any copyright owner desiring to grant a license for reproduction or adaptation of their work may execute an assignment, irrevocable during the term of copyright, transferring such rights to another party. Such assignments shall be in writing and registered with the Copyright Office, specifying the scope of permitted acts and any royalty obligations payable to the original copyright owner. Where an assignment is made, the assignee shall hold exclusive powers civil court for enforcing the terms of that assignment against infringers, subject to a right of action by the assignor for breach of contract should the assignee fail to diligently pursue such enforcement. Further, where a license is granted under this Act, the licensor retains the power to terminate said license upon written notice if the licensee engages in activities demonstrably detrimental to the commercial exploitation of the work.

For the purposes of this Act, “priority date” means the date on which an application for protection of the invention was filed in a convention country, subject to the provisions regarding claims and amendments under this Act. Where an applicant elects to claim priority from a previously filed application, the statement of inventorship shall be construed as referencing that earlier filing. The Controller may require evidence substantiating the claimed priority date, including certified copies of records from the relevant intellectual property office. An invention shall be deemed novel notwithstanding the disclosure arising from such prior application, provided that the disclosure did not compromise the inventive step.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed to relate back to an earlier date, being the priority date, in respect of any matter disclosed in the specification and claimed as new, provided that the applicant demonstrates, through documentary evidence submitted with the initial application, that the same or substantially similar design was previously registered or applied for in another country. Such evidence must clearly establish the filing date of the foreign application or registration. The Controller may require further verification of this documentation under this Act. For the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step, as provided herein, the priority date shall be taken into account irrespective of any subsequent publication or disclosure relating to the design.

Where an application for a patent relates to subject matter in respect of which any earlier publication exists, under this Act, the determination of the priority date shall be undertaken with due regard to whether such publication would have influenced the skilled user in the art at the time of filing. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the claimed invention possesses sufficient inventive step over prior publications, and failure to do so may result in a rejection of the application. Further, where an applicant seeks to claim priority from a foreign application, it shall be incumbent upon them to satisfy the Controller that they were indeed entitled to claim such priority; otherwise, the application will be deemed to have been filed on the date of its actual filing under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the priority date may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relating to an invention made jointly by two or more persons contains a statement that one or more of them are assignees of the right to make and exploit the invention, the Controller may require such joint applicants to furnish evidence demonstrating the extent of their respective contributions towards the invention. In determining the priority date under this Act, the Controller shall consider any documentation submitted by the applicant establishing an earlier disclosure of the invention, provided that such documentation is accompanied by a certified copy of the record of the first publication or filing in the foreign country concerned. The applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of matters disclosed in any prior application for which he claims priority, and failure to disclose such information may prejudice his claim to the priority date. Further, an appeal against an order determining the priority date lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order.

Where an application for a patent relating to an invention made jointly by two or more persons contains a statement that one or more of them are claiming priority under this Act, the Controller may require such joint applicants to furnish evidence demonstrating their respective contributions towards the claimed invention; failing which, the application shall be deemed abandoned. For the purposes of determining the priority date, the applicant shall submit an affidavit verifying the accuracy of the information pertaining to earlier applications filed outside India, and affirming that no material modification or improvement has been made to the subject matter since the initial filing. The Controller may, at his discretion, request further documentation substantiating this affirmation before proceeding with examination.

Where any patent application claims priority from a previously filed application under this Act or any other law for the time being in force, the Controller shall, upon receiving notice of opposition under section 25, be obligated to ascertain and record the said earlier filing date as the priority date for the purposes of novelty assessment. Failure to do so shall render the patent grant vulnerable to revocation proceedings initiated by aggrieved parties. Any person demonstrating that a substantially similar invention was publicly known or used prior to the recorded priority date may petition the Controller for review, subject to payment of prescribed fees and furnishing adequate evidence. The Controller’s determination regarding the validity of the priority date is final, barring appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for a patent relating to an invention has been filed in a convention country, the applicant may elect to avail of the benefit of the earlier filing date as its priority date under this Act; such election shall be made within twelve months from the date of the Indian application and evidenced by a certified copy of the first-filed application. The Controller General may, upon satisfactory demonstration that the assignment or licensing agreement relating to the invention was executed before the priority date, permit the transfer of rights in respect of the patent application even if the assignor or licensee was not originally named as an applicant on record. Provided that such demonstration shall include a duly authenticated copy of the relevant contractual document and an affidavit verifying its authenticity; failure to comply with this provision will render the assignment void.

Where any question arises as to the priority date of an application for patent revocation, the Controller shall determine such date based on evidence presented by both the petitioner and the patentee, subject to the provisions relating to grace periods under this Act. The burden of proving a prior publication or disclosure affecting the priority date shall lie upon the party asserting it; provided that the Controller may, at his discretion, direct either party to produce further documentation relevant to establishing the veracity of claims concerning an earlier invention. Any order made by the Controller determining the priority date may be appealed before the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, and the appeal shall be finally determined as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the “priority date” in relation to an application for patent shall mean the date on which an earlier identical application relating to the same invention was filed in any convention country, provided that such earlier application claimed priority from a still earlier date. Where multiple applications claiming priority are involved, the earliest such date shall be deemed the priority date. Determination of the priority date may become a matter for adjudication under this Act and the court having jurisdiction shall consider all relevant documentation submitted by the applicant and any interested party to establish said date accurately.

An application for patent registration shall disclose the priority date of the invention, if any, claimed therein. Where the applicant seeks to claim priority under this Act, they must furnish a certified copy of the earlier application made in a convention country, duly authenticated by the authority competent to authenticate documents under the law of that country. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the authenticity and completeness of such certified copy. Failure to provide adequate proof of the claimed priority date may result in the rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of the patent granted. It is provided that the applicant shall be deemed to have knowledge of the contents of any earlier application for the same invention filed in a convention country.

Where an application for patent is founded on one or more earlier applications made in respect of the same invention in any convention country, the applicant shall disclose particulars of such earlier applications in Form 1 and furnish copies thereof as prescribed. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further documentation substantiating the claim to a priority date, including certified true copies of relevant records from the receiving office concerned. Failure to provide such documentation within the time specified by the Controller shall not, however, automatically invalidate the application; instead, the Controller may direct that the application be treated as if it were filed on the date of the later of the filing dates of the earlier applications. The applicant shall register sufficient cause for any delay in providing requested documents and the Controller will consider such reasons when determining whether to proceed with examination.

Where an applicant seeks to claim a priority date under this Act, such claim shall be substantiated by submission of certified copies of the application as originally filed in the country of origin, duly authenticated by that nation’s competent authority. The Controller may require the petitioner to furnish petition particulars detailing the precise nature of the invention disclosed in the foreign application and demonstrating its correspondence with the subject matter of the Indian patent application. Provided that, if the applicant fails to submit these particulars within thirty days from the date of request, or provides information deemed insufficient by the Controller, the claim of priority date shall be rejected without further notice. The burden of proving the validity of the claimed priority date rests solely upon the applicant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, ‘patent rights’ shall extend to the acts of manufacturing, applying, dealing with, and distributing an invention. For the purpose of determining infringement under this Act, 'dealing' includes offering a patented article for sale or hire, exposing it for sale or hire, or by means of any act enabling another person to use or enjoy the invention. Provided that such ‘patent rights’ shall not extend to acts done independently by others in their own right and not derived from the patentee. The term 'invention' as used herein includes any new and useful article, substance, process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter.

Subject to the provisions contained herein and the regulations framed thereunder, an application for registration of a patent shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the claim of priority, if any, under this Act. The Controller General may require such further particulars as he deems necessary to ascertain whether the invention is novel and involves inventive step. Upon satisfactory verification of the prescribed forms and payment of requisite fees, provisional registration of the patent rights shall be granted for a period not exceeding twelve months. This provisional registration shall confer limited protection against exploitation pending examination of the complete specification. The applicant may, during this period, file the complete specification as provided herein. Failure to do so will result in lapse of the provisional registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain appeals against orders relating to revocation of patent rights, infringement proceedings, or compulsory licenses. An appeal lies only if the appellant demonstrates a substantial injustice has occurred due to an error apparent on the face of the record. Where the Appellate Board finds that a patentee has acted in bad faith regarding the exercise of their patent rights, it may award costs against them. Further, any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may petition the Supreme Court under this Act, provided that such petition is filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed from.

Subject to the provisions contained herein and the regulations framed by the Controller General, an application for the grant of patent rights shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the invention for which protection is sought. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to priority, if any claim is made based on a prior application filed in another convention country. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Patent Office may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be deemed to be a civil suit and will be adjudicated according to established legal procedures. The Controller, acting under this Act, may require further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage during examination. Failure to comply with such requirements may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Subject to compliance with regulations pertaining to pharmaceutical manufacturing practices as provided herein, and notwithstanding any provision to the contrary under this Act, a patent rights holder shall be entitled to exercise exclusive privileges concerning an invention relating to a novel process for producing a chemical substance. Such entitlement is conditional upon demonstrating to the Controller that the patented process achieves at least twenty percent improvement in yield compared to existing methodologies documented within publicly accessible scientific literature prior to the date of application. Further, the patent rights holder shall provide evidence satisfying the Controller regarding adequate measures undertaken to prevent bio-piracy and ensure equitable benefit sharing with indigenous communities if the invention is derived from traditional knowledge.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal against such order within sixty days from the date of receipt thereof to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Where a patent rights has been infringed, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedy through civil proceedings before a Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The court may grant injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and award damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff, taking into account the profits made by the defendant as a result of the infringing activity. Failure to comply with an order of the Commercial Court relating to patent rights shall render the defaulter liable to a fine which may extend to two thousand rupees for every day during which such default continues and also subject the offender to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.

Subject to the provisions contained within this Act and the regulations prescribed herein, any licensee granted rights under a patent shall be entitled to assign such license, either wholly or partially, to another party with the prior written consent of the patentee. Such assignment shall not prejudice the original patentee’s underlying patent rights nor diminish their ability to enforce those rights against any assignee who fails to adhere to the terms and conditions stipulated in the initial licensing agreement. Where a patent has been assigned, subsequent licenses granted by the assignee shall be subject to review under this Act to ensure they do not unduly restrict competition or unfairly prejudice the public interest. The patentee may revoke an assignment only upon demonstrating substantial breach of contract by the assignee, as determined by the Controller.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall lie on a substantial question of law arising out of the decision or determination of the Controller. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. It is provided that the exercise of any power conferred under this Act relating to revocation of patent rights shall be subject to judicial review by the High Court on a limited ground of error apparent on the record.

An application for grant of patent rights shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed, including a specification detailing the invention claimed, its utility, and any prior art known to the applicant. The Controller General may require further information regarding the India application if deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the application shall clearly describe how to verify such production. A provisional specification may be filed initially, followed by a complete specification within twelve months; failure to do so will render the provisional application lapsed. The applicant shall furnish certified copies of drawings where necessary to illustrate the invention as claimed in the patent rights sought.

An appeal shall be instituted in the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The Board may, if satisfied that there were sufficient grounds for such delay, entertain an appeal lodged after the expiry of the said period, provided that the applicant satisfies the Board regarding the reasons for the delay and that the delay has not prejudiced the other party. Subject to this provision, any person aggrieved by any decision or order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the High Court as provided herein. The High Court shall dispose of such appeals expeditiously.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or other goods may be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner. Subject to the provisions under this Act, an aggrieved party may file an appeal against any decision refusing registration, or revoking registration, within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The appeal shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that, where a decision relates to a matter of fact, the Board may confirm, vary, or reverse such decision. Further, an appeal shall also lie against any order passed by the Registrar concerning rectification proceedings relating to registered geographical indications.

Where a Board constituted under this Act has made an order relating to revocation of a patent, or concerning rectification of the register, any person aggrieved by such order may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate court shall have power to confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against, and may also direct that the matter be remitted to the Board for further consideration. An appeal shall lie notwithstanding any error apparent on the face of the record in the order sought to be challenged. Provided that an appeal does not suspend the operation of the order unless the High Court otherwise directs. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the procedure for filing and dealing with appeals under this Act.

Where a Board of Appeal finds that an invention does not fulfil the requirements of novelty or inventive step under this Act, the applicant may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Board of Appeal. The Appellate Tribunal may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Board of Appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. An appeal shall only be on grounds of law and not on matters of fact already decided by the Appellate Tribunal unless those facts have been determined in accordance with principles of natural justice. The High Court may, while hearing an appeal, dismiss it or entertain it subject to just conditions.

Where a person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning opposition proceedings, desires to challenge the validity thereof, such person shall be entitled to file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that the appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Further, any party to the appeal may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, apply for a reasoned speaking order detailing the grounds upon which the decision was based; it is provided that such application shall not delay the final disposal of the appeal. An appeal shall only be maintainable if the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the impugned order.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent, or concerning rectification of entries in the Register of Patents and Designs, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of service of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to the filing of such appeals may result in dismissal under this Act. Costs associated with the appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Board, subject to regulations prescribed for recovery thereof.

Where a patentee grants an exclusive license under this Act, conferring upon the licensee full rights to exploit the invention commercially within the territory of India, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to prior written consent of the patentee. Provided that any assignment made without such consent shall be deemed invalid and unenforceable against third parties unless the patentee subsequently ratifies it in writing. Further, where a dispute arises concerning the validity or scope of an exclusive license, either party shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The patentee may also appeal from any order made by the Appellate Board relating to the terms and conditions of such licenses, including matters pertaining to royalty payments or sub-licensing arrangements. An appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where a Hearing Officer, acting under this Act, determines that an invention does not satisfy the criteria for patentability as provided herein, and such determination is accompanied by reasoned findings, the applicant may prefer an appeal. Such appeal shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board may, after affording opportunity to both the appellant and the Controller, confirm, vary or reverse the decision of the Hearing Officer. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court, subject to satisfaction of the conditions prescribed under this Act regarding deposit with the appellate body.

Where a patent has been granted and registration relating registered inventions is challenged before an intellectual property tribunal, an aggrieved party shall have the right to file an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal may be directed against any decision concerning revocation or modification of claims in the patent. The appellate body shall consider all evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent, affording each a fair opportunity to be heard under this Act. 

Provided that, if the tribunal’s determination involves questions of fact only, the appellate body shall not entertain an appeal unless it is satisfied that the decision was manifestly erroneous. Further, any appeal shall be accompanied by a security deposit as determined by regulations framed for this purpose. The appellant shall bear costs incurred in the appeal process, subject to orders made otherwise by the appellate authority.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a claim in a patent, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The form petition for appeal shall contain a concise statement of the grounds on which the appeal is founded and must be verified by the appellant or their authorized representative. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in dismissal of the appeal. Further, where an appeal concerns infringement proceedings, any party dissatisfied with the outcome may pursue remedies under this Act, subject to penalties for frivolous claims as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person aggrieved by an order relating to the grant, revocation or sealing up of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of service of the order. Where the appellant is seeking assignment or licensing of rights pertaining to the *article patented*, the grounds for appeal must specifically address the fairness and reasonableness of any conditions imposed by the Controller concerning royalty rates, field of use, or duration of such license. The Appellate Board may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to all concerned parties, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Further appeals from orders of the Appellate Board shall lie to the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.

Where a Board of Appeal finds that an objection raised by the Comptroller is not supported by the evidence presented and relates to the patentability of the invention under this Act, the appellant may, subject to prescribed conditions, appeal shall lie to the High Court within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Provided that where the appellant fails to comply with the requirements for filing an appeal in the authorised prescribed manner, the Board of Appeal may entertain the appeal if it is satisfied that the failure was due to a clerical error or some other unintentional oversight and that the delay caused by such failure has not prejudiced the respondent. The High Court shall hear such appeals expeditiously and dispose of them as early as reasonably practicable.

For the purposes of this Act, a “mark relation goods” is defined as any sign, whether consisting exclusively of words, letters, symbols, figures, or a combination thereof, capable of distinguishing the goods of one undertaking from those of other undertakings and used, or proposed to be used, in connection with such goods. This definition shall include three-dimensional shapes, configurations, colours, sounds, tastes, textures, and any other marks which can serve to identify particular goods. A mark relation goods may incorporate descriptive elements but is not registrable if it directly describes the characteristics of the goods or their intended purpose, provided that such description does not acquire distinctiveness through use under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if, prior to the date of filing of the application, an identical or similar mark is registered under this Act in respect of identical or similar goods, and the applicant can reasonably be precluded from adopting such mark under the principles followed in determining the likelihood of confusion as provided herein. However, registration may proceed subject to a condition limiting the scope of protection afforded to the earlier trade mark where the marks relate to different classes of goods or services, and there is no demonstrable risk of dilution or unfair appropriation. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented by either party demonstrating the *mark relation goods* in question and its impact on consumer perception.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and it is demonstrated that the impugned mark is used in relation to goods identical or similar to those for which the plaintiff’s mark is registered, the defendant shall be liable for damages. Such damages may include loss of profits sustained by the plaintiff as a result of the infringement, together with any profits made by the defendant through the infringing use. The court may also grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further using the impugned mark in relation to such goods or other similar goods. This right shall be subject to the condition that the plaintiff has not unduly delayed in bringing the action and that such delay has prejudiced the defendant’s ability to defend the case. A finding of a *mark relation goods* infringement does not preclude claims for passing off, provided that those claims are based on matters distinct from the registered trademark itself.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall provide written reasons for such refusal. Any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the applicant has demonstrated clear distinction between the applied-for mark and the earlier trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified therein, taking into account all relevant factors including visual similarity, phonetic similarity, and conceptual similarity. A finding of deceptiveness requires consideration of consumer perception and potential confusion arising from a *mark relation goods*. The Registry may require further evidence as it deems necessary during proceedings.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar or identical to a prior existing mark, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating that use of the applied-for mark in relation to the specified goods does not create confusion among consumers. This obligation applies irrespective of whether the earlier mark is registered or unregistered. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit an affidavit verifying the accuracy and completeness of such evidence. Further, if a prior existing mark relates to different classes of goods than those for which registration is sought, the applicant shall demonstrate that there exists a substantial and relevant similarity between the two categories of goods sufficient to cause likelihood of association. The determination of a *mark relation goods* will be based on prevailing market conditions and consumer perception as provided herein.

Where any registered trade mark is used in contravention of this Act, and such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods, the proprietor of an earlier registered trade mark relating to identical or similar goods shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. Such injunction may extend to prohibiting the display, offering for sale, or importation of the infringing goods. The Court may, in determining whether infringement has occurred, consider the inherent similarity between the marks and the nature of the goods involved; a finding of deceptive mark relation goods is conclusive evidence of such contravention. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall be deemed a contempt of court and subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark relating to goods desires to grant a license for its use, he may do so by entering into an agreement with another party, specifying the scope and duration of such usage. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to the terms stipulated within the licensing agreement itself, provided that any assignment requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days of execution. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments relating to trade mark licenses concerning goods. Further, where a registered proprietor assigns his entire undertaking including the ownership of a trade mark relation goods, the assignee shall be deemed to have acquired all rights and obligations pertaining to any existing license granted under that trade mark. Any subsequent modification or termination of such a license will require written consent from both licensor and licensee.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark already registered under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. The appellate board shall consider whether the use of the applied-for mark in relation to the goods for which registration is sought would likely cause confusion among consumers due to a similarity between the marks, taking into account not only the visual appearance but also phonetic and conceptual similarities. A prior mark’s distinctiveness relating to its registered goods shall be given significant weight when determining any mark relation goods issue.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar to any existing mark, and the Registrar is satisfied that such existing mark is used in relation to identical or closely related goods, the applicant shall be entitled to apply for a compulsory licence subject to compliance with prescribed conditions. Such application must demonstrate demonstrable efforts made to negotiate a voluntary agreement with the proprietor of the prior mark within a period not exceeding six months from the date of refusal. The Registrar may grant such a licence if satisfied that the continued non-registration would substantially restrain trade or prevent the introduction of new goods, provided that adequate compensation is paid to the existing mark relation goods proprietor as determined by an arbitration panel established under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark relating to identical or closely related goods, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be entertained only if the applicant demonstrates, with reasonable certainty, that the public perception of the marks in question does not create confusion as to origin or sponsorship. It is provided that this demonstration must account for any deliberate attempts by the prior mark proprietor to expand their *mark relation goods* portfolio. For the purposes of determining similarity, it shall be relevant whether either mark incorporates an *invention means new* element which significantly alters consumer understanding. The Board may require further evidence as deemed necessary to resolve disputes concerning deceptive similarity.

For the purposes of this Act, a “reference use mark” means a mark employed by an owner of a registered trademark solely for the purpose of indicating that the goods or services are used with, or are compatible with, another product bearing a different trademark. Such reference use shall not be construed as constituting use of the reference use mark in relation to those goods or services for the purposes of assessing likelihood of confusion under this Act. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent an action being taken against any person who uses a reference use mark in a manner which falsely suggests affiliation with, or endorsement by, the owner of the other trademark.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a reference use mark, signifying an association with another registered trade mark owned by the applicant or affiliated entity. Such inclusion shall not constitute grounds for absolute refusal under this Act but is subject to scrutiny regarding potential consumer confusion. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the nature and extent of the reference use, ensuring it does not falsely suggest endorsement or affiliation where none exists. Further, the representation of the reference use mark on the register shall be clearly distinguished from the principal trade mark, using a prescribed notation indicating its status as a reference. Any alteration to the registered marks affecting the relationship implied by the reference use mark requires prior approval from the Registrar.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of a “reference use mark” where such use creates confusion amongst the public regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services. A reference use mark is defined as a mark used in relation to goods or services to indicate that those goods or services are offered by an entity associated with the proprietor of the registered trade mark. This right shall extend to preventing dilution of distinctiveness where the reference use mark exploits the reputation connected with the registered trade mark, even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services. Provided that, such restraint shall not apply where the reference use mark is used honestly and fairly for purposes of comparison, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding clarity and prominence of indication of lack of affiliation.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a trade mark, register a “reference use mark” if it is demonstrated that the mark has been used exclusively for the purpose of clearly identifying and referencing another registered trade mark without offering goods or services under that referenced mark. Such an application shall include detailed documentation substantiating the exclusive reference use, including but not limited to advertising materials, product packaging, and internal records demonstrating lack of commercial exploitation. The Registrar may require a declaration from the applicant affirming their intention to maintain this restricted usage. Any alteration in the nature or scope of the reference use mark’s application without prior approval from the Registrar shall constitute an abandonment of rights under this Act. Further, any goods or services offered using the reference use mark will be deemed a violation and subject to remedies as provided herein.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark desires to make reference use of another identifiable trade mark, belonging to a person other than the owner, in association with their own trade mark for the purpose of honestly advertising goods or services, such reference use shall be permissible subject to compliance with conditions as provided herein. The advertisement containing the reference use mark must clearly and unambiguously indicate that the referenced trade mark belongs to another entity; failing this, it shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Prior written consent from the owner of the referenced trade mark is not a prerequisite for such reference use, provided that the comparison made does not denigrate or disparage the goods or services associated with the other trade mark and is limited solely to objective comparisons of features.

The use of a reference use mark, being a mark used only for referencing another trademark and not for advertising purposes, shall not constitute infringement under this Act unless it is employed in a manner that creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services. Any proprietor seeking to assert rights relating to a reference use mark must demonstrate, through clear and convincing evidence presented before an adjudicating officer, that such use has resulted in demonstrable financial loss or dilution of the distinctive character of the referenced trademark. Failure to provide such evidence shall render any claim for damages untenable, subject to penalties as provided herein for frivolous litigation. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders against unauthorized reference use marks deemed prejudicial to consumer interests.

The owner of a registered trademark shall, subject to any conditions specified in the agreement, grant a license permitting the use of their trademark as a reference use mark by another party for the purpose of demonstrating compatibility with specific technological standards. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and shall define the scope of permitted usage, including geographical limitations and product categories. The licensee under this arrangement shall not, without express written consent from the licensor, alter or modify the trademark in any manner that detracts from its distinctiveness. Assignment of such reference use mark license is permissible, provided that prior approval is obtained from the original licensor, ensuring continued adherence to the terms and conditions initially established. The licensor retains the right to terminate the license if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trademark.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a trade mark, direct the removal of a reference use mark from any material where it is displayed. Such direction shall be issued only after due consideration of an objection filed by the proprietor of the trade mark to which the reference pertains, and provided that the Registrar finds that the continued display of the reference use mark creates confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of goods or services offered under the reference use mark. An appeal against such direction lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; however, the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if it is shown that the applicant failed to provide adequate notice to the proprietor prior to the initial application.

The registration of a reference use mark shall not preclude any party from using a similar mark legitimately engaged in trade prior to the date of application for said reference use mark, provided that such prior use does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Any proprietor seeking protection under this Act for a reference use mark must demonstrate demonstrable and continuous commercial activity utilizing the mark within India; failure to do so shall render the registration vulnerable to expungement proceedings initiated by any aggrieved party. Further, applications for international registration designating India are subject to examination as if they were domestic applications, adhering to principles outlined in the Protocol Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. Penalties for deceptive use or misrepresentation relating to a reference use mark shall be commensurate with those prescribed under this Act for trade mark infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trademark may grant a license to use their trademark, including a reference use mark, for specific purposes and within defined geographical territories. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, along with all rights pertaining thereto, provided that prior written consent from the trademark proprietor is obtained. Any patent shall entered into the Register of Patents and Designs upon application by the inventor, and any assignment of such patent may also be recorded as a license under this Act, subject to prescribed fees. The terms of any reference use mark license agreement must clearly delineate permitted uses and restrictions, failing which it will be deemed an unrestricted transfer and subject to remedies available under this Act for infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, a “reference use mark” is defined as a mark employed solely for the purpose of indicating that goods or services conform to a particular standard, specification, or characteristic, and which does not function as a trademark in relation to any specific enterprise’s goods or services. Such marks may be used to denote compliance with industry benchmarks relating to semiconductor integrated circuits, provided that the use is accompanied by clear and conspicuous indication of the body establishing such standards. The Registrar shall have the power to direct against the use of a mark deemed to be a reference use mark if it creates confusion amongst consumers regarding its source or quality.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and the applicant seeks to indicate by way of reference use that the mark is used in relation to goods or services not covered by the refusal, such indication shall constitute a reference use mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence demonstrating continued use of the mark in the specified manner, permit the registry shall place a notation on the trade marks register indicating the scope and duration of this reference use. Provided that the goods or services to which the reference use mark relates are clearly defined and do not create confusion with registered marks. Further, any challenge to the validity of the registration based on the reference use mark may be made within the period prescribed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “services use mark” means a mark used exclusively in designating or distinguishing the offering of any service, whether for profit or not, and shall include marks used solely to indicate the geographical origin of such services. A services use mark may consist of words, letters, symbols, designs, or a combination thereof. The right to apply for registration of a services use mark shall accrue only to persons who propose to provide the specified service under that mark. Provided that, where a person has previously used a mark as a services use mark, they may also apply for its registration irrespective of whether they are currently providing the service.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if, prior to the date of filing of the application, an identical mark is registered under this Act in respect of services use marks relating to financial advisory services. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such evidence as he deems necessary to establish that the proposed mark does not conflict with any existing rights or create confusion among consumers. Provided that, if the applicant can demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through extensive use subsequent to an earlier registration, the application may proceed subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar regarding limitations on the scope of protection afforded. The Registrar shall consider all relevant factors including reputation and consumer perception when determining whether a conflict exists.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark seeks to extend its protection to cover services use, it shall be open to any party claiming proprietary rights in an identical or similar mark used in relation to such services to apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for revocation of the registration. Such application may only be made if the applicant demonstrates that the services use mark has been employed continuously and without interruption for a period exceeding five years, and that the proprietor’s claim to exclusive rights is causing demonstrable confusion or dilution amongst consumers. The Board shall afford the trade mark proprietor an opportunity to defend its position, presenting evidence of genuine commercial activity relating to the registered goods or services. Failure to do so may result in the revocation order being upheld, subject to a determination regarding appropriate remedies and damages.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if, prior to the date of filing thereof, an identical mark is being used by another person in India in relation to services and such use constitutes a “services use mark” under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the proposed mark does not create confusion among consumers regarding the origin or nature of the services. Where the Registrar deems it necessary, an inquiry shall be conducted wherein both the applicant and the existing user of the services use mark shall be afforded an opportunity to present their respective arguments and documentary proof. The decision of the Registrar following such inquiry shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by a decision may file an application for revision with the High Court.

A person shall be entitled to register a trademark under this Act if it is used, or proposed to be used, in relation to specified services. The application for registration must clearly state the particulars of such services use mark and demonstrate bona fide intention to utilize the mark commercially within India. Where the applicant has previously refused registration based on an earlier conflicting mark, subsequent registration shall only be permitted provided that evidence is furnished demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through consistent and substantial use of the services use mark in the relevant market segment. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating such usage before granting registration, as provided herein. Any alteration to the specified services after registration will necessitate a fresh application under this Act.

Where any person makes use of a mark, identical or confusingly similar to a registered services use mark, in relation to goods or services, without the consent of the proprietor, such use shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Provided that where the infringing use is made by a party authorized to do so under a contractual agreement with the proprietor, and subsequently breaches the terms thereof relating to permitted scope of services, remedies may be pursued both contractually and as provided herein for trade mark infringement. Any person found guilty of such infringement shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to five times the value of the infringing goods or services sold, or in default of satisfactory proof of sales, an assessment based on prevailing market rates; further penalties may be imposed at the discretion of the adjudicating officer.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark, being a “services use mark”, grants a license for the use of their mark relating to specified services, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the grantor. Provided that any assignment made without such consent shall be deemed void and unenforceable under this Act. The grantor retains the right to impose reasonable conditions within the licensing agreement regarding quality control measures applicable to the licensed services. Furthermore, where a trade mark portfolio including a “services use mark” is transferred by way of assignment, all rights pertaining to that mark, including any existing licenses, shall automatically vest in the assignee. Any sub-license granted by an assignee shall be subject to similar conditions as originally stipulated within the primary license agreement and may require notification to the grantor.

For the purposes of this Act, a “business india applicant” is defined as an individual or body corporate ordinarily resident in India who demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that their primary business operations are conducted within India and involve the publication, distribution, or dissemination of news, current affairs, or general interest content through any medium, including but not limited to print, electronic, or digital platforms. An applicant qualifying as a “business india applicant” shall be entitled to priority rights under this Act in respect of marks used primarily in connection with their journalistic activities, provided that such use is bona fide and consistent with the nature of their business.

Where any person has obtained registration of a trade mark, and another party subsequently institutes proceedings alleging that such registration was procured by misrepresentation or fraud, the Registrar shall entertain such proceedings. If, after due inquiry, it is established that the registration was indeed secured through fraudulent means, the Registrar may order its cancellation. This power extends to cases where a *business india applicant* knowingly presented false information concerning the use of the mark prior to registration, intending to deceive the public or gain an unfair advantage over competitors. Any party aggrieved by such an order of cancellation shall have the right to appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal. The appellant must demonstrate substantial prejudice resulting from the Registrar’s decision.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, who is conducting business in India, shall file the application electronically through the Trade Marks Registry portal. The application must include a clear representation of the mark, a list specifying all goods or services with which the mark is associated, and details regarding the period of use of the mark, if any, prior to the date of filing. Where an applicant has previously filed an identical trade mark for dissimilar goods or services, they shall disclose such previous application in their current submission. The Registrar may require the business india applicant to furnish further documentation verifying identity and address as provided herein. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application. Any alteration to the particulars submitted must be made through a formal amendment request, subject to approval by the Registrar.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall, upon submission of an application, furnish evidence demonstrating continuous use of the mark in India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of such application. This requirement is waived where the applicant qualifies as a “business india applicant,” defined herein as an entity incorporated and conducting substantial business operations within India for a period exceeding three years prior to the filing date. Provided that, if the trade mark includes a geographical indication, additional documentation substantiating exclusive rights over said indication shall be submitted alongside the application. The Registrar may request further clarification or supplementary materials at any stage of the examination process to ascertain compliance with these provisions and ensure proper assessment of distinctiveness.

Where any applicant, being a business india applicant, files an application for the registration of a trade mark that includes a geographical indication associated with agricultural products exclusively originating from India, the Registrar may require such applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive use and control over the quality characteristics defining said geographical indication. Failure to provide satisfactory proof within the time stipulated under this Act shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any person employing a registered trade mark in a manner that falsely suggests association with or approval by the business india applicant shall be guilty of an offence, punishable with imprisonment and a fine as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark grants a license to any person, such license may be assignable subject to the terms thereof and as provided herein. Any business india applicant seeking assignment of a trade mark license shall provide to the Registrar a certified copy of the licensing agreement and details of both licensor and licensee. The Registrar may require further documentation demonstrating due diligence in assessing the assignee’s capacity to utilize the licensed mark appropriately, particularly where the goods or services relate to regulated industries such as pharmaceuticals or financial services. Assignment is deemed complete upon registration by the Registrar, which shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to disclose material terms of the license agreement may render the assignment voidable at the option of the original licensor.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the Registrar’s decision. The business india applicant shall be deemed to have been duly served with notice if the objection is published in the Trade Marks Journal and on the website maintained by the Registrar. Provided that, where the objector demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the Tribunal may entertain an appeal filed after the expiry of sixty days but before ninety days from such date. The business india applicant retains the right to present counter-arguments and evidence rebutting the grounds of objection during the appellate proceedings as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration filed by a business india applicant, such applicant shall have the right to submit written representations rebutting the grounds of said objection. These representations must be accompanied by evidence demonstrating that the mark does not conflict with existing rights or designations as provided herein. Failure to adequately address the Registry’s concerns within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being refused registration. Further, any decision of the Registrar refusing registration is subject to appeal; a business india applicant aggrieved by such refusal may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of receipt of the order, as per the procedure outlined for section 94 appeals.

For the purposes of this Act, a “business india applicant” is defined as an individual or entity habitually engaged in commercial activities within India, demonstrating substantial business operations directly related to the goods or services for which registration is sought. Such applicants must provide documentary evidence substantiating their ongoing trade and investment in relevant sectors. An application filed by a business india applicant shall be considered with due regard to whether it demonstrates genuine use of the mark in connection with those goods or services, subject to provisions regarding respect registered trade already established under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, who is conducting business in India, shall file an application with the Registrar specifying the trade mark sought to be registered, the class or classes of goods or services associated therewith, and the address for service in India. The application must include a clear representation of the trade mark and a list of names and addresses of all persons interested in the applicant’s business. Where the applicant utilizes a descriptive term as part of the trade mark, they shall provide an affidavit demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and advertising, establishing that the public associates the term with the applicant's goods or services. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify the accuracy of information provided concerning the business india applicant’s activities and the proposed trade description.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, being a business india entity, must satisfy the Registrar that it possesses the requisite legal standing to conduct commercial operations within India. The application shall include detailed particulars regarding the constitution of the business india entity, including certified copies of its incorporation documents and relevant resolutions. Further, where an applicant is represented by a designated chairperson, such chairperson shall be duly authorized to act on behalf of the applicant in all matters pertaining to the trade mark registration process. Any alteration in the composition or leadership of the business india applicant after the initial application must be promptly notified to the Registrar, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a proposed trade mark, register said mark in the prescribed class of goods or services. Such registration shall confer on the applicant exclusive right to use the mark throughout India in relation to the specified goods or services, subject to limitations imposed under this Act. The manner of displaying the registered mark shall adhere strictly to the representation as accepted during the application process; any alteration thereof without prior consent from the Registrar may constitute a violation and render the user liable for penalties.
