Any person found guilty of using a registered geographical indication without authorization shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the value of the goods or services in respect of which such infringement has been proven, and may also face imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards as defined in the registration certificate. Such license may specify the territory within which and the duration for which the licensee is authorized to utilize the geographical indication, subject to conditions ensuring continued compliance with those standards. The proprietor may also assign the right to use a registered geographical indication to any person, provided that such assignment does not prejudice the rights of other proprietors or licensees. Any transfer or license granted shall be recorded in the Register and shall be binding on all subsequent dealings concerning the geographical indication. Further, under this Act, the proprietor retains the power to revoke licenses for breach of conditions or misuse detrimental to the reputation of the registered geographical indication.

An application for registration as a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be deemed invalid if it is shown that use of the proposed indication, prior to the date of application, by any producer or trader in relation to identical or similar goods, has resulted in a substantial and established association between the indication and such goods within the territory of India. The Registrar may entertain objections from interested parties alleging such pre-existing usage, provided that the objection is filed within three months of publication of the application under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of an application based on prior use may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to further appeals as provided herein.

An application for registration as a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall not be entertained if it pertains to a pharmaceutical substance unless the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the production process adheres strictly to Good Manufacturing Practices and incorporates traditional knowledge documented within verifiable community records. The burden of proof regarding adherence to such practices rests entirely upon the applicant. Any aggrieved party may appeal against the Registrar’s decision concerning this demonstration before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, any challenge to the authenticity of community records shall be adjudicated solely by a civil court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include a detailed statement specifying the relevant agricultural area or the area within which the goods originate. This statement must clearly delineate the boundaries of the territory from which the goods derive their qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to that origin. The applicant shall further provide evidence demonstrating the link between the distinctive qualities of the goods and the specific geographical environment as provided herein. A geographical indication is deemed a *statement geographical indication* if it identifies a product’s unique attributes directly linked to its place of production. Any alteration to this defined territory after registration may be subject to review under this Act, pending approval by the Registrar.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication shall institute suit in the competent civil court, subject to appeal under this Act. The court shall grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including injunction restraining further infringing activity, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registrant, and disposal of infringing goods or destruction thereof at the infringer’s expense. Where an infringement involves the use of a deceptive statement geographical indication, the court may also order the publication of a corrective notice in such manner as it considers appropriate to rectify the misleading impression created amongst consumers. The right to sue for infringement accrues only upon registration and remains valid for the duration specified under this Act, renewable as provided herein. Any false or fraudulent representation concerning goods indicated by a geographical indication shall be deemed an offence punishable with monetary penalties.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include a detailed statement specifying the relevant qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to the goods and directly linked to their origin within the defined geographical area. This statement must demonstrate that these attributes are not commonly found in similar products from elsewhere and contribute significantly to the distinctiveness of the goods. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this connection, including but not limited to historical records, scientific analyses, or producer testimonials. Any alteration to the proposed geographical boundary shall be accompanied by a revised statement justifying the change and its impact on the defining characteristics. A false or misleading statement within the application renders it liable for rejection under this Act. The Registrar is empowered to seek expert opinions to verify the accuracy of the *statement geographical indication* presented.

Any person utilizing a statement geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of financial loss suffered by registered proprietors and bona fide users. Such damages may include lost profits, diminution in value of goods, and costs incurred in rectifying misleading representations to consumers. Further, any entity found guilty of unauthorized use or misrepresentation concerning a protected geographical indication is subject to penalties not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees for the first offence, escalating to one million rupees for subsequent violations. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders compelling immediate cessation of infringing activities and confiscation of goods bearing the false designation, as provided herein.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of the statement geographical indication under this Act. Such licenses may be granted for specified goods or services and for a defined period, subject to conditions as determined by the Registrar. Any license granted shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted usage, including restrictions on alterations or misrepresentation of the registered indication. The proprietor may assign their rights relating to such licenses to another party with prior notification to the Registrar, provided that any subsequent assignee assumes all obligations and liabilities associated with the original license agreement. Further, a licensee may, subject to the terms of the granted license, sub-license the right to use the geographical indication for specific purposes as agreed upon, without requiring further approval from the proprietor or the Registrar.

A registered statement geographical indication shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the indication for the goods specified in the register. Any person desiring to make, sell, offer for sale, expose for sale, or import any goods bearing the registered geographical indication may apply to the Registrar for a license under this Act. Such application shall include details of the proposed use and quantity required, along with a prescribed fee. The Registrar may grant such licenses subject to conditions as deemed fit, including limitations on territory and duration. Assignment of rights relating to a licensed geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, recorded in an entry register maintained for this purpose. Provided that existing licensees shall retain their entitlements until the expiration of their license period, unless otherwise agreed upon with the registered proprietor.

A ‘Good’ for the purposes of this Act shall include any agricultural product, foodstuff, wine, spirit, liquor, spice, cereal, handicraft, manufactured article, or natural resource capable of differentiation based on its origin. For the avoidance of doubt, a Good shall not be considered to have an indication of geographical origin unless such indication is primarily attributable to factors relating to the geography of the territory, including climate, soil quality, and traditional production methods. The term ‘territory’ as used herein shall apply geographical areas which are either wholly or partly within the boundaries of India; provided that a collective mark may be registered in respect of goods originating from such territory.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars relating to the growers’ associations or producers' collectives involved in the production of goods claiming protection under this Act. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive use of the proposed name by such associations or collectives, and that they represent the interests of all significant producers within the defined geographical area. Further, the application must specify the quality control measures implemented to maintain the distinctiveness of the goods and ensure adherence to established production standards. Any alteration to these standards following registration shall be subject to approval by the Registrar. The term "shall apply geographical" is understood to mean that the protection afforded herein extends only to products originating from within the specified territory.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered Geographical Indication shall apply to the Registrar within five years from the date of registration, alleging inter alia that any right has been infringed by use by another person without appropriate cause. The Registrar may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, grant such rectification as appears equitable under this Act. Provided that a registered Geographical Indication shall apply geographical indications which are deemed deceptive if used in relation to goods or services not conforming to the standards established therefor. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order. The remedies available under this Act include injunctions and damages, as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the goods originate from the territory specified in the application, and that the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of those goods are essentially attributable to the particular geographical origin. Where an objection is raised by any interested party under this Act, the Registrar shall provide the applicant with a reasonable opportunity to submit its response in writing, along with supporting documentation. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning production techniques or traditional knowledge relevant to the claimed geographical indication. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar shall apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for review, subject to such fees as are prescribed herein and within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The term "shall apply geographical" is central to determining eligibility under this Act.

An application for registration as a Geographical Indication shall include detailed particulars regarding the production methods employed within the defined territory. The applicant must demonstrate that the name proposed as a Geographical Indication is not descriptive of the goods in relation to their kind, quality or other characteristic and does not conform to established trade practices. Furthermore, evidence establishing consumer recognition of the connection between the goods and the geographical origin shall be submitted. Any alteration to production techniques which materially affects the distinctive qualities of the goods shall apply geographical indications only if approved by a committee constituted under this Act. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed Geographical Indication would likely deceive or cause confusion among consumers.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a geographical indication shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed quality standards, as defined by the Register and notified in the Official Gazette, shall constitute a violation, rendering the user liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by registered proprietors. Any unauthorized use or imitation of a registered geographical indication shall be deemed an offence under this Act and subject to penalties including imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and fines ranging from fifty thousand rupees to two hundred thousand rupees; such penalties may be imposed cumulately. The Register shall apply geographical indications as they relate to goods.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of that indication on goods conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. Such licenses may be granted for consideration or otherwise, as determined by the proprietor, and are subject to revocation upon written notice if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with the geographical indication. Assignment of a registered geographical indication, including any existing license rights, requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such assignment shall not prejudice the right of subsequent holders to enforce the provisions herein against infringing parties. The Registrar may impose conditions on assignments to ensure continued adherence to established production norms and protect the integrity of goods which shall apply geographical origin designations.

An appeal under this Act shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order sought to be appealed against. Provided that where an objection is raised regarding the distinctiveness of a proposed indication, the appellant may, with leave of the Board, present evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through use subsequent to the initial application. The Board shall consider such evidence and determine whether the geographical indications shall apply geographically as claimed, or if modification or rejection is warranted due to consumer confusion arising from similarity to existing marks registered under the Trade Marks Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall apply geographical names that conform to the prescribed format and contain an exhaustive index of all registered names pertaining to similar goods or services. Where any objection is raised by a prior registrant alleging likelihood of confusion with existing index names registered under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments rebutting such objections within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice. The Registrar may, after considering the submissions and representations made by both parties, either reject the application or direct modification of the proposed geographical indication to mitigate any potential conflict. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such order.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the collective body proposing to make the application, along with its address and details of its members engaged in production or processing related to the goods. The Registrar may require such further information as is deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar refusing registration, conditionally registering, or revoking a geographical indication shall have the right to appeal specified within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Such appeals shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and are subject to such fees as may be prescribed. The Registrar shall provide reasons in writing for any decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, and this reasoning shall apply geographical considerations relevant to the claimed origin.

A suit concerning the validity of registration of a geographical indication, or seeking rectification of the register under this Act, shall lie only in the jurisdiction try suit of the High Court specified for the State within which the alleged geographical territory is situated. Provided that where the geographical indication relates to goods produced or rendered in more than one State, suits may be instituted in the jurisdiction try suit of any such High Court. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify alternative forums for entertaining such suits, subject to conditions as provided herein and ensuring equitable access to justice.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the territorial limits of the geographical area from which the goods originate, and such limits shall be defined by reference to well-established administrative or natural boundaries. Where disputes arise concerning the correctness of these stated limits, or regarding the eligibility of producers within the claimed territory, jurisdiction try suit relating to those matters shall lie exclusively with the High Court having territorial jurisdiction over the area in question. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant or registered proprietor to furnish further information or clarification pertaining to the geographical boundaries and production practices associated with the indication. Failure to comply with such a request may result in rejection of the application or revocation of registration, as provided herein.

Any suit seeking damages or injunctive relief concerning the misuse of a registered Geographical Indication shall be entertained only by courts within whose local jurisdiction the cause of action arose. This determination shall consider the place where the infringing activity occurred, the location of the defendant’s principal place of business, and the territory to which the goods or services incorporating the misused indication were directed. Provided that, in cases involving widespread infringement affecting multiple regions, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate additional courts with concurrent jurisdiction for hearing such suits. Further, a suit under this Act shall not be entertained if it is barred by res judicata or otherwise precluded by law. The determination of jurisdiction try suit shall be decided at the threshold and without prejudice to any other proceedings that may be initiated against the defendant.

Any suit seeking damages or injunctive relief concerning the misuse of a registered geographical indication, or challenging the validity of registration thereof, shall be filed exclusively before the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the alleged infringement occurs. Provided that, where the cause of action arises in more than one such territory, the plaintiff may institute the suit in any of those jurisdictions. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate a specific District or Commercial Court to exercise subordinate civil jurisdiction relating to matters concerning registered geographical indications, subject to appeal to the High Court. Further provided that no court other than as specified herein shall entertain such suits; however, appeals from orders of designated courts shall lie before the appropriate appellate forum under this Act. The determination of jurisdiction try suit shall be decided expeditiously and without reference to technicalities of pleading.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a suit concerning the validity of a registration, or for alleged infringement of a registered Geographical Indication, may only be instituted in the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the defendant’s business is situated, or where the cause of action arose. Provided that, if the defendant has places of business in more than one such territory, suit may be brought in any of them. Further provided that, a suit relating to rectification of entries in the Register shall lie only in the High Court specified under this Act as having local jurisdiction over the place where the alleged erroneous entry was made. The determination of jurisdiction try suit shall be subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any suit seeking damages or injunctive relief for acts contrary to this Act concerning a registered geographical indication shall be entertained only by courts exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction within the local limits of either the place where the alleged infringement occurred or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Provided that, in cases involving widespread distribution or marketing activities impacting multiple regions, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, designate additional jurisdictions for entertaining such suits. Further, no suit shall be entertained if it is shown to have been instituted without first giving notice of claim to damages under this Act to the registered proprietor, unless exceptional circumstances warrant otherwise as determined by the court. The determination of jurisdiction try suit shall be subject to judicial review.

Any person seeking to commercialize goods bearing a registered Geographical Indication may apply to the proprietor for a license granting them the right to use the Indication in connection with those goods. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted usage, including but not limited to product categories and geographical territories. The proprietor retains full authority to assign such licensing rights to another party, provided that any assignee assumes all obligations and liabilities associated with the original license agreement. Further, under this Act, jurisdiction try suit for breach of a license or assignment shall vest solely in the jurisdictional High Court specified within the registration certificate pertaining to the Geographical Indication. Any sub-license granted by a licensee must be approved by the proprietor and documented as per regulations outlined herein.

Any suit concerning the validity of a registration of a geographical indication, or seeking rectification of the register in relation to such registration, shall lie only before the Geographical Indications Registry and may be entertained by the High Court only upon appeal from an order made under this Act by the said Registry. Provided that where a suit is pending before any civil court at the time this Act comes into force, such suit may continue as if this Act had not been enacted. The Geographical Indications Registry shall have exclusive jurisdiction try suit relating to matters of fact arising in connection with applications for registration and proceedings for revocation or amendment thereof, subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any suit concerning the validity of a registration of a geographical indication, or seeking relief pertaining to alleged misuse thereof, shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction try suit of the High Court within whose territorial limits the authorized user’s production area is situated. Provided that, where the defendant resides or carries on business outside such territory, any High Court exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction may entertain the suit. Further provided that a suit relating to trade mark accordance with registered geographical indications shall not preclude the aggrieved party from seeking remedies under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct otherwise for specific cases involving inter-state disputes concerning protected goods.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout design, makes, imports, or offers for sale any integrated circuit embodying that layout design shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Such damages may include compensation for loss of profits reasonably foreseeable as a result of the infringement and also an account of profits made by the infringer. Further, where the infringing activity is proven to have been undertaken with the intent to deceive or mislead, the Court may impose punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of the actual damages awarded. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint under this Act, direct investigation into alleged violations and issue notices for rectification of the layout design act.

The National Gene Fund shall comprise funds contributed by breeders registering plant varieties under this Act, and any sums received from grants, donations, or investments made in accordance with regulations framed by the Central Government. Contributions towards the Fund shall be determined based on a percentage of the sale proceeds derived from propagating material of registered varieties, as notified periodically. The accrued interest and other income generated by the National Gene Fund may be utilized to support research relating to plant genetic resources, provide financial assistance to farmers for conservation of traditional crop varieties, and fund programs promoting sustainable agricultural practices, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the source germplasm utilized in the development of the variety, including its geographical origin and any relevant access agreements. Where a plant variety incorporates genetic material originating from sources within India that are not readily available or accessible to the public, the applicant shall contribute a percentage of the benefit sharing amount towards the National Gene Fund. This contribution is calculated as specified by the Registering Authority, taking into account the extent of reliance on such germplasm and the potential for future research and development. The funds received into the National Gene Fund may be utilized for supporting conservation efforts, promoting access to genetic resources, and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in traditional plant breeding practices, subject to guidelines framed by the Central Government.

Any person who, in contravention of any condition imposed by the Authority regarding the use of plant material obtained from an approved source, commercially exploits a variety shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the forum established under this Act. Such compensation shall be not less than five times the value of the infringing commercial exploitation and may extend up to ten times such value, depending on the severity and duration of the infringement. Funds recovered through such compensation proceedings shall be credited to the National Gene Fund. The Authority may, subject to due process, issue an injunction restraining any person from further exploiting the variety in question pending resolution of the dispute. Further, a right holder aggrieved by an order of the forum may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Authority shall maintain a detailed register of all contributions made to the National Gene Fund, specifying the source of the funds, the amount deposited, and the date of receipt. Any person seeking access to information pertaining to specific deposits within the National Gene Fund may apply in writing to the Authority, providing justification for such access based on legitimate research or public interest considerations. The Authority shall review each application and determine whether disclosure is permissible, subject to provisions safeguarding confidential commercial information as provided herein. Funds allocated from the National Gene Fund shall be utilized exclusively for supporting activities related to plant genetic resource conservation, including in-situ and ex-situ gene banking programs, and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in traditional seed saving practices. The Comptroller and Auditor General of India shall conduct audits of the National Gene Fund annually, submitting reports to both Houses of Parliament.

Contributions to the National Gene Fund shall be made by any person seeking to obtain benefit-sharing agreements concerning plant varieties for commercial use, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Authority. The amount contributed shall be determined based on a formula considering the anticipated market value of propagating material derived from the variety and the extent of farmer participation in its development, as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Provided that, any research institution engaged in publicly funded plant breeding programs may apply for exemption from contribution requirements, contingent upon demonstrating adherence to guidelines regarding open-source seed distribution and royalty-free licensing. Further, the Fund shall be utilized exclusively for supporting ex situ conservation efforts, providing grants to farmers’ collectives promoting biodiversity, and compensating indigenous communities for traditional knowledge related to crop genetic resources, as provided herein.

Any person who, having benefited directly or indirectly from the use of plant genetic resources for the development of a new variety, fails to contribute an equitable share of the profits derived therefrom to the National Gene Fund shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Contributions to the National Gene Fund are deemed public money and any willful default in making such contributions constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority may, subject to due process, seize assets derived from the infringing activity to recover unpaid sums owed to the Fund. Further, repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety contributing to the National Gene Fund shall be eligible to license those rights for research purposes relating to traits deemed beneficial for food security or rural livelihoods. Such licenses may be granted on non-exclusive terms, provided that the licensee undertakes to share resultant data and findings with the Central Government within a stipulated timeframe. Assignment of rights related to varieties contributing to the National Gene Fund shall require prior approval from the Authority, ensuring equitable distribution of benefits derived from commercialization. The Authority may stipulate conditions regarding royalty rates and geographical limitations in such assignments. Further, any transfer of technology involving plant genetic resources linked to contributions made to the National Gene Fund must include provisions for benefit-sharing with local communities involved in conservation efforts.

The Authority shall maintain a National Gene Fund for the purpose of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing assistance to farmers engaged in conserving biodiversity. Any dispute arising concerning the determination of benefit-sharing obligations under this Act, or regarding the eligibility of a farmer for compensation from the said Fund, may be referred to an Appellate Tribunal constituted as provided herein. The Tribunal’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the order's communication, on grounds limited to questions of law only. Further, any claim against the National Gene Fund must be substantiated by documentary evidence and verified by a recognized agricultural institution.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the source and lineage of the germplasm utilized in the development of the variety. Where a breeder utilizes genetic resources accessed from India’s gene bank or obtained through benefit-sharing arrangements, a prescribed percentage of the proceeds derived from commercialization of the resultant variety shall be remitted to the National Gene Fund. The amount so remitted will contribute towards sustaining and expanding access to these vital resources for future research and development activities. Any dispute concerning the calculation or remittance to the National Gene Fund may be referred to the member appellate board for determination, as provided herein. Breeders are required to maintain meticulous records of all transactions related to genetic resource utilization.

Any person utilizing data derived from plant varieties protected under this Act for commercial research purposes shall be obligated to contribute a portion of their profits, as determined by the Central Government, to the national gene fund. This contribution is intended to ensure equitable benefit sharing and support further agricultural innovation. Provided that, where such utilization involves transient incidental storage of genetic information during data processing, solely for facilitating analysis and not for reproduction or distribution, this obligation shall be waived subject to audit verification by a designated authority. Failure to remit the prescribed amount within the stipulated timeframe will constitute an offense, rendering the offender liable to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to fines and potential revocation of research permits. The Central Government may issue guidelines detailing acceptable methods for profit calculation and auditing procedures.

The Central Government shall establish and maintain a National Gene Fund for the purposes of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing benefit-sharing compensation to traditional farming communities. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from registered plant variety breeders, as determined by regulations framed under this Act, and any grants received from international organizations or philanthropic entities. The Central Government may also direct that a portion of royalties derived from licensed propagating material be credited into the National Gene Fund. An advisory committee shall be constituted to oversee the management and disbursement of funds; it shall prescribed chairperson appointed by the Central Government from amongst eminent scientists and agricultural economists. All accounts pertaining to the Fund shall be audited annually, and reports submitted to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as provided herein.

Any person utilizing plant genetic resources for commercial purposes shall be obligated to contribute an amount determined by the Central Government to the National Gene Fund, as provided herein. The rate of contribution shall be subject to periodic review and may vary based on the scale of operation and potential benefit derived from such utilization. Failure to remit contributions within thirty days of the date claim shall be made for commercial exploitation will attract a penalty equivalent to ten percent of the assessed amount. Repeated or willful non-compliance, including providing false information regarding genetic resource usage, is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months and may extend to three years, alongside a fine which may exceed five hundred thousand rupees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety shall be permitted to grant licenses for the commercial use of propagating material derived from that variety. Such license agreements may include stipulations regarding geographical limitations, specific end-uses, or restrictions on sub-licensing, as mutually agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. Further, assignment of such rights, including licenses, requires registration with the Plant Varieties Registry, detailing all relevant terms and conditions pertaining to royalty payments and benefit sharing arrangements. Any sums received by the assignee through exploitation of the assigned variety shall be subject to contribution into the National Gene Fund, proportionate to the commercial gains derived, as determined by the Authority. This provision applies equally whether the assignment arises from section 21 Indian or any other legal basis for transfer.

For the purposes of this Act, an “issued breeder” shall mean a person to whom a certificate of protection for a plant variety has been granted under this Act and who is registered as such with the Authority. An issued breeder shall be entitled to exercise rights relating to the commercial exploitation of the protected variety, subject to any conditions specified in the certificate of registration. The term “issued breeder” includes where the right to seek protection was derived from a previous breeder or developer, provided that such derivation is clearly documented within the application for protection and acknowledged as part of the record maintained by the Authority. An issued breeder may assign their rights under this Act subject to prior approval from the Central Government.

An application for registration as an issued breeder shall include a detailed statement specifying the derivation of the plant variety, including parentage and any innovative selection or hybridization techniques employed. The application must further identify the geographical location where the initial experimentation and evaluation were conducted, along with evidence demonstrating the novelty and distinctiveness of the variety relative to existing cultivars. Where the applicant claims rights based on traditional breeding methods, documentation substantiating continuous cultivation and propagation by farmers within a defined community may be required as provided herein. The Authority shall consider any objections raised concerning the veracity of these claims before proceeding with assessment; failure to adequately substantiate derivation may result in rejection of the application.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an issued breeder shall retain exclusive rights over the commercial exploitation of the registered plant variety for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of grant of protection. Any person infringing upon these rights may be served with a notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding cessation thereof within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice renders the infringer liable to damages, calculated at the discretion of the court, but not less than five times the value of the infringing activity. Further, where an issued breeder demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from unauthorized propagation or sale of the protected variety, injunctive relief may be sought and granted by a competent civil court as provided herein.

An application for recognition as an issued breeder shall be made to the Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal in Form-D, accompanied by documentary evidence establishing a demonstrable contribution towards the development and maintenance of plant genetic resources. The Tribunal may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim, including records pertaining to seed multiplication, distribution networks, and collaborative research undertaken. Recognition as an issued breeder confers specific rights under this Act, enabling the holder to apply for protection certificates for novel varieties derived from their work. However, such recognition is subject to periodic review by the Tribunal, not less than once every five years, to ensure continued adherence to standards of professional conduct and contribution to plant breeding innovation. The applicant shall disclose any prior assignments or licenses relating to relevant genetic material.

An issued breeder shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to the commercial exploitation of the protected plant variety for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of publication of the registration. Provided that, such rights are contingent upon the continued adherence to best practices in seed production and distribution as prescribed by the Plant Variety Authority. Further, any alteration to the genetic composition of the registered variety undertaken by the issued breeder without prior authorization from the Authority shall render the protection liable for suspension. The issued breeder is obligated to provide reasonable access to propagating material for research purposes, subject to a non-disclosure agreement executed in the manner as provided herein and ensuring equitable benefit sharing with relevant farmer collectives.

Any person aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of protection granted to an issued breeder may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such action. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the appeal process shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized propagation or sale of protected plant varieties by any person other than the issued breeder or their registered agents, issue a notice requiring them to cease such activities within thirty days. Non-compliance with this notice is subject to penalties as provided herein, including fines up to one million rupees and imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an issued breeder shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization and propagation of the protected plant variety. However, such rights may be licensed or assigned to other entities with the prior written consent of the issued breeder, provided that a royalty fee is stipulated within the licensing agreement. The form and terms of any assignment shall be registered with the Plant Varieties Registry, and failure to do so renders the assignment void. Further, an issued breeder may grant non-exclusive licenses allowing for research and development activities related to the protected variety, subject to conditions ensuring the preservation of the breeder’s rights and preventing unauthorized commercial exploitation. Any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee shall require explicit authorization from the original issued breeder.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an application for revocation of protection granted to an issued breeder may be presented to the Authority within three years from the date of such grant, alleging non-satisfaction of conditions relating to geographical indication. The Authority shall entertain only those applications which demonstrate a prima facie case of misleading the public regarding the origin or qualities of the plant variety. Where the application is admitted, the issued breeder shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in their defense. Any order made by the Authority under this Act may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, as provided herein.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, an issued breeder shall be liable for damages in a civil suit if it is proven that the commercial exploitation of their protected plant variety infringes upon the layout-design rights of another party. Such infringement occurs when the visual appearance of packaging or labeling associated with the unauthorized propagation of the registered variety substantially copies elements of a previously registered layout-design, creating confusion amongst farmers and consumers. The amount of damages shall be determined by the court, taking into consideration the extent of the infringement, the profits derived from the infringing activity, and the losses suffered by the holder of the layout-design right. Provided that, any claim for damages must be brought within three years from the date the infringement was first discovered, as provided herein.

An issued breeder shall retain exclusive rights over a registered plant variety subject to compliance with prescribed conditions regarding benefit sharing with traditional agricultural communities. Any application for revocation of such protection, alleging non-compliance with these obligations, must be filed within three years from the date of issuance and accompanied by evidence demonstrating demonstrable harm resulting from the breeder’s actions. The Authority may require the applicant to provide detailed documentation substantiating claims concerning the utilization of farmers' rights and customary knowledge in the development or commercialization process. Provided that the issued breeder demonstrates adherence to guidelines regarding varietal release and traceability, as provided herein, the application shall be deemed without merit.

Any person alleging infringement of a plant variety protection right vested in an issued breeder shall institute proceedings before the designated Intellectual Property Enforcement Tribunal. Failure to comply with prescribed notification procedures prior to commercial exploitation of a protected variety constitutes prima facie evidence of wilful infringement, attracting enhanced penalties as determined under this Act. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized use of a registered plant variety’s design, direct the design registry shall maintain records pertaining to such alleged infringements and provide them to the Tribunal for evidentiary purposes. Repeated or systematic violations will result in fines not exceeding five crore rupees and potential imprisonment for a term up to seven years, subject to judicial discretion.

Subject to the provisions contained herein, an issued breeder shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization and propagation of a registered plant variety for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of grant. Such rights may be licensed to other parties, both domestic and international, under terms and conditions as agreed upon in writing between the issued breeder and the licensee. Any assignment of these rights, including but not limited to those relating to seeds or planting material classified under International Classification Goods pertaining to agricultural products, requires prior notification to the Plant Varieties Authority and shall be registered with them. Provided that such assignments do not unduly restrict farmers’ rights to save, use, exchange, and share farm-saved seed of the protected variety, as guaranteed under this Act. The issued breeder may stipulate royalty payments or other considerations for the utilization of their intellectual property.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board under this Act, a certificate of protection granted to an issued breeder shall be deemed invalid if it is established through due process that the variety in question was not distinct at the time of application. The Authority may initiate such proceedings based on a complaint filed by any interested party demonstrating a lack of novelty or unexpected similarity to an extant variety. Provided that, where the rights under the certificate have been assigned to another person, the assignee shall be substituted as the respondent in such revocation proceedings. Further, the issued breeder retains the right to present counter-evidence and challenge the veracity of claims made against them, demonstrating the distinctiveness of their protected plant variety as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an *assignee* shall be deemed to include not only a party to whom rights have been expressly transferred under a written instrument, but also any person receiving such rights by operation of law or through a duly authorized agent. Where a patent has been assigned, subsequent dealings with the patent, including licenses granted and royalties paid, shall be governed as if the assignee were originally the inventor for all intents and purposes under this Act. An *assignee* may further assign their interest in the patent subject to any restrictions contained within the original assignment agreement. The rights of an *assignee* are not diminished by prior dealings between the inventor and another party.

An assignment under this Act shall be in writing and executed by the assignor, and may be evidenced by a registered instrument. Where an invention has been assigned, any reference to the assignor shall include references to the assignee. The Controller may require proof of the execution of such assignments as he deems necessary for the purposes of maintaining the register. Any person claiming assignment of a patent or application under this Act shall furnish such documentation substantiating their claim as the Controller prescribes; failure to do so may result in the rejection of any subsequent request made by that person relating to the patent or application. An assignee acquires all rights and powers which the assignor had prior to the assignment, subject to any terms and conditions specified therein.

Where, upon assignment of a patent under this Act, the assignor fails to provide written notice of such assignment to the Controller within thirty days from the date of execution of the agreement, the assignee shall be deemed not to be the absolute owner for the purposes of exercising remedies against infringers. However, provided that the Controller is satisfied that the assignor had no knowledge of the invention or its patentable subject matter at the time of assignment, such remedy may be granted to the original patentee. Any person claiming through an assignee shall be bound by the terms and conditions stipulated in the assignment agreement relating to the scope and duration of rights transferred. The Controller may require proof of the assignment agreement and supporting documentation before recognizing the assignee’s entitlement to enforcement actions as provided herein.

Where, upon application made by the patentee or their duly authorized agent, the Controller is satisfied that a right in the invention has been validly assigned to any person, the Controller may record such assignment in the Register. Such recording shall be conclusive evidence of the title of the assignee as against all persons except where such assignment is void or has been procured by fraud. Notice of any such recorded assignment shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any person claiming under an unregistered assignment may petition to the Controller for registration, subject to fulfilling prescribed conditions and payment of requisite fees. The Controller may require production of documentation substantiating the transfer of right before proceeding with registration. An assignee may, by instrument in writing, further assign their rights under this Act.

An assignment of a patent, as provided herein, shall be in writing and executed by the assignor, or by a duly authorized representative acting under written power of attorney. Such assignment must specify the patent to which it relates, including the application number where applicable, and contain a statement affirming the transfer of all rights and title pertaining thereto. Where an invention has been jointly made, any assignment shall require the consent of each inventor unless such consent is waived in writing by the inventor. An assignee acquiring interest under this Act may exercise the powers and privileges which would accrue to the patentee. Further, notice of any assignment shall be registered with the Controller within three months from the date of execution; failure to register shall render the assignment void against subsequent assignees.

An assignment under this Act shall be in writing and executed by the assignor, and may be registered at the Patent Office. Failure to register an assignment within six months from the date thereof shall render the assignee liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable by way of suit. Any person claiming rights as an assignee shall be deemed to have acquired such rights only upon registration under this Act; provided that, where the assignor fails to notify the Controller of Patents of the assignment within thirty days of its execution, any subsequent party dealing with the patent may deem the assignor to retain ownership and not be bound by the unregistered assignment. The Controller shall publish particulars of registered assignments for public information.

Where a patentee, prior to the grant of a patent or during its term, enters into an agreement for the working, use, or exploitation of the patented invention with any other party, such agreement shall be deemed to create an interest in favour of that party. This interest may be conveyed by way of assignment under this Act, provided that the terms of the original agreement expressly authorize such transfer and specify the scope of rights being assigned. The patentee shall notify the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks within thirty days of any such assignment to an assignee, detailing the nature of the initial working agreement and the extent of the transferred rights. Failure to provide this notification will render the assignee liable for penalties as provided herein. An assignee deriving title through a chain of assignments shall be subject to the same obligations regarding notification as the original patentee.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, it is alleged that the patent has been assigned, the party asserting the assignment shall bear the burden of establishing, by documentary evidence or otherwise as provided herein, the validity and extent of such assignment. The Controller may require production of original documents pertaining to the transfer and may consider testimony from relevant parties involved in the purported assignment. Should the Controller find that the alleged assignee has not demonstrated a clear chain of title, or that the terms of the assignment are ambiguous concerning the scope of rights transferred, the revocation proceedings shall continue as if no assignment had occurred. Any decision regarding the validity of an assignment is appealable to the Appellate Board.

Where, in respect of any patent, the right to make an application for the patent or to obtain a grant of the patent has been assigned under this Act, the Controller may require the assignor to furnish such information as he deems necessary relating to the transmission operation undertaken by him. Such information shall include details pertaining to the consideration provided, the date of execution of the assignment deed, and the manner in which notice of the assignment was given to the Controller. Failure on the part of the assignor to comply with this requirement within the time specified by the Controller shall render the assignee liable to administrative penalties as determined under this Act. The Controller may, at his discretion, permit an extension of time for compliance, provided that a reasoned request is submitted and supported by relevant documentation. An assignee claiming right through another assignee shall be deemed to have derived their title from the original assignor in relation to any proceedings before the Controller.

Where, upon revocation or expiry of a patent under this Act, it is determined that the rights were previously assigned without proper disclosure as required herein, any such assignment shall be deemed voidable at the instance of the Controller. The Controller may, subject to due process and after providing an opportunity for hearing, order the cancellation of the assignment and restore the patent to the original inventor or their legal representatives. Furthermore, any person acquiring rights under a voidable assignment shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the benefit derived from such acquisition, as determined by the Controller. An assignee who knowingly participates in proceedings that misrepresent material facts relating to an India patent may face penalties including fines and imprisonment.

Where, under this Act, an application for patent is assigned by the applicant, the assignment shall be in writing and executed by the assignor and the assignee. Such assignment may include a power of attorney authorizing the assignee to act as the applicant for all purposes under this Act. The Controller General shall publish a notice of such assignment in the Patent Journal, specifying the date of assignment and the extent of rights transferred. Any person aggrieved by an assignment may, within three months from the date of publication of the application notice opposition, file a written objection with the Controller, detailing grounds for challenging the validity or scope of the assignment. The assignee shall be deemed to hold all rights and privileges which the applicant would have had but subject to any pending objections filed as provided herein.

Where, upon registration of a patent, the inventor transfers their rights under this Act by way of assignment, and such assignment is not duly recorded in the Register of Patents and Designs, an objection may be raised by any person claiming to have a superior right to the invention. The Controller shall provide the assignee with an opportunity to demonstrate the validity of the assignment and its compliance with the provisions herein relating to notification and registration. Failure to satisfy the Controller that the assignment was executed properly, or that reasonable steps were taken for timely registration, may result in the rejection of the application for recording the assignment within the Marks Registry established under this Act. An appeal against such a decision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, an “assignee” shall mean a person to whom the rights and interest in a patent have been transferred by way of assignment under this Act or otherwise as provided herein. Such assignee shall be deemed to step into the shoes of the assignor for all purposes relating to the patent, including but not limited to proceedings before any authority established under this Act. Where an assignment is made subject to certain conditions, such conditions shall be binding on the assignee. An assignee may also hold rights derived from a previous assignee and shall be bound by any prior agreements concerning the patent, particularly those related to the use of a reference trade mark associated with the invention.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “patent controller” shall mean the officer appointed by the Central Government and designated as such, who is responsible for exercising powers and performing duties relating to the examination of patent applications, determining whether an invention meets the criteria for patentability under this Act, and granting or refusing patents in accordance with prescribed procedures. The patent controller may delegate any of their functions to other officers working under their direction, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. Decisions made by the patent controller are appealable as provided herein, and such decisions shall be binding until modified or reversed by an appellate authority.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model shall file Form U-1 along with the prescribed fee. The form shall contain particulars relating to the invention, including its title, technical field, statement of the problem addressed, and details of novelty and inventive step. Upon receipt of the application, the Patent Controller shall issue an acknowledgment indicating the date of filing. Subsequently, a request for written opinion regarding patentability may be made by any interested party or by the Controller himself. The Controller is empowered to examine such requests and provide reasoned opinions on whether the utility model fulfills the criteria as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Patent Controller may prefer an appeal under this Act.

Where a patent is granted and subsequently challenged under this Act, the aggrieved party shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Patent Controller may, upon receiving such an appeal, direct that the appellant furnish security, as provided herein, to safeguard against any loss or damage caused to the patentee by reason of the challenge. Failure to provide the requisite security within the time specified by the Controller shall render the appeal deemed abandoned and the proceedings closed accordingly. The Patent Controller is empowered to order interim relief, including injunctions, pending the final determination of an appeal, if it appears that irreparable injury may result without such intervention. Any party dissatisfied with an order made by the Patent Controller relating to security or interim relief may further appeal to the Appellate Board.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Patent Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for patents, or the institution of proceedings for revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The appeal must specify the grounds upon which it is based and state the relief sought. Where the Patent Controller has directed the amendment of any claim in a patent application, the appeal may also challenge the propriety of such direction. The Board shall give notice to the Patent Controller and afford him an opportunity to be heard under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order.

An applicant seeking registration of a chemical process patent shall furnish detailed specifications including all parameters relating to reaction conditions, catalysts employed and purification methods utilized. The Patent Controller may require the submission of additional data demonstrating the novelty and non-obviousness of the claimed invention, particularly where prior art discloses similar processes or compounds. Furthermore, any request for amendment to the claims during examination must be accompanied by a declaration confirming that such amendments do not substantially alter the originally disclosed matter. Subject to compliance with these requirements, the Controller shall proceed with assessment according to established procedures under this Act. The applicant is obliged to respond within sixty days of notification regarding any objections raised; failure to do so may result in abandonment of the application.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Patent Controller relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and accompanied by a fee as prescribed. Failure to pay the requisite fee shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Patent Controller may, at any time, require the appellant to furnish security for costs, which if not furnished within thirty days, will result in dismissal of the appeal. Any wilful suppression of material facts during proceedings before the Appellate Board is a cognizable offence and subject to penalties as provided herein, including fines up to five lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term extending to three years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses relating to the invention for which patent protection is granted. Such license may be granted either wholly within India or extending to territories outside India, provided that the terms and conditions of any such license are filed with the Patent Controller within thirty days of execution. The Patent Controller may require modification of the licensing agreement if it deems the terms unduly restrictive of competition under this Act. Assignment of a patent, or any interest therein, including licenses, shall be made by instrument in writing signed by the assignor and assignee, and such assignment shall be registered with the office. Failure to register an assignment within six months renders it voidable at the Controller’s discretion.

Where an objection is raised by the Patent Controller against a request for extension of term of a patent, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit its response and supporting documentation demonstrating continued industrial application within India. The Controller may then consider such response alongside the original grounds for objection, and issue an order either upholding or rejecting the requested extension. Any party aggrieved by the Patent Controller’s decision under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the said order. Provided that, the Appellate Board shall not be bound by any observations made by the Controller in arriving at its own conclusion and may direct further inquiry as it deems fit.

An applicant seeking examination of a patent application shall furnish to the Patent Controller a petition containing particulars conforming precisely to Form 1. The petition must specify the title of the invention, the applicant’s address for communication, and the claims as originally filed. Provided that if any alteration is made to the claims after the first statement of inventorship, a supplementary statement detailing such alterations shall be appended to the petition. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding form petition particulars will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Patent Controller may permit rectification of errors in the petition subject to ensuring that no substantive rights are prejudiced thereby and that the correction does not alter the essence of the invention claimed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the holder of a patent shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses relating to the patented invention, including assignments of the entire undertaking. Any such license agreement may specify territorial limitations and fields of use; provided that any assignment shall vest complete title in the assignee. The Patent Controller may require disclosure of details concerning royalty rates and other financial considerations within licensing agreements exceeding a specified duration or involving parties domiciled outside India. Furthermore, where a patent is assigned or licensed for the manufacture of goods incorporating a services use mark, the assignor or licensor shall retain responsibility to ensure continued compliance with relevant trademark legislation. The Controller may inquire into any agreement deemed restrictive of trade or contrary to public interest.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "Patent Controller" shall mean the officer appointed by the Central Government and designated as such, who is responsible for exercising all powers and performing all duties conferred or imposed upon him under this Act relating to the examination of patent applications, the determination of inventions’ patentability, and the granting or refusal of patents. The Patent Controller may, subject to any directions issued by the Central Government, request information from any governmental agency if such information is deemed necessary for assessing whether a claimed invention poses a threat to the security of India. Decisions made by the Patent Controller are appealable as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a utility model shall furnish to the Patent Controller, along with the prescribed fee, a detailed description of the invention, including its technical field and intended use. The application must also include at least one drawing illustrating the construction and operation of the utility model. Any alteration or addition made to the drawings after the date of filing shall be accompanied by an affidavit provided by the applicant, duly sworn before a Magistrate or Notary Public, attesting to the veracity of such changes and confirming that they do not substantially alter the claimed invention as originally disclosed. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Patent Controller may require further clarification from the applicant regarding any aspect of the utility model's description or drawings.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to be patented if it is a new and non-obvious technical solution to a problem. An invention shall not include discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, schemes or processes for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business, or artistic creations; however, these may be patentable if they are embodied in an apparatus for putting them into effect. Subject to the provisions regarding exceptions under this Act, a patented invention shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use and sell the invention within India for the term specified herein, provided that such rights are enforceable against all other persons.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a public record, accessible electronically, detailing all applications for patents and subsequent registrations under this Act. An applicant seeking registration of a design incorporated within an invention shall provide detailed schematics demonstrating its novelty and distinctiveness from prior art. Where an application discloses matter already patented or claimed in a pending application, the Registrar may issue a communication requiring clarification or amendment. The record shall indicate the date of filing, the name of the inventor(s), the applicant’s designation, and any subsequent modifications to the patent specifications. Any challenge to the validity of a registered patent must be accompanied by evidence demonstrating prior publication or lack of inventive step as provided herein.

Where an infringement of a patent has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to seek relief under this Act including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the patented invention. Damages adequate to compensate for the loss caused thereby shall also be recoverable, calculated subject to principles of fairness and equity. The measure of damages may include lost profits attributable to the infringement, a reasonable royalty for the use of the patented invention, or in cases where actual damages are difficult to ascertain, such other sum as the Court deems just and appropriate. Provided that, any counterclaim alleging invalidity of the patent shall be adjudicated concurrently with the primary claim of infringement. The defendant may also seek an order requiring the patentee to account for profits made from the sale of products manufactured under license granted in contravention of this Act.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to an article during or after its manufacture, and such method or process is patented, the Controller may require the applicant to disclose the best method known to him at the time of making the application for carrying out the invention. Such disclosure shall include particulars relating to any apparatus necessary for the operation of the method or process. The requirement under this Act shall be deemed satisfied if the disclosure enables a person skilled in the art to practice the patented method without undue experimentation. Failure to comply with such a requirement may result in an objection being raised against the grant of the patent, which the applicant shall have opportunity to address through written submissions and hearings before the Controller. The decision of the Controller regarding compliance is final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process for producing a substance, such patent shall only be grantable if the process is or includes a step involving an inventive concept over what would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art; provided that this requirement shall not apply where the substance itself is novel and non-obvious. Any party demonstrating that a patented invention infringes upon existing prior use rights, established before the date of application for the patent, may petition the Controller for rectification of the patent’s scope. The Controller shall consider such petitions in accordance with principles of natural justice and may order modifications to the claims if infringement is substantiated. Further, any challenge to the validity of a patented invention must be brought within six years from its grant date.

Any person who knowingly manufactures, uses, imports, or sells goods made using a process that infringes upon a patent shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing party licensed the patented invention from the patentee. Further, where infringement is proven, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from continuing such acts, subject to considerations of public interest and equitable principles. The patentee shall also be entitled to recover costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies under this Act, provided that the infringement was substantial and deliberate. Any appeal against a finding of infringement may only be made after deposit of twenty-five percent of the awarded damages.

Subject to the conditions outlined herein, the holder of a patented invention shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses and assign rights pertaining thereto. Any license granted under this Act may be either sole, partial, or non-exclusive, as determined by the patentee’s discretion, provided that the terms and conditions of such license are clearly documented and accessible for public record. Furthermore, assignment of a patented invention shall require registration with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, and shall only be valid upon confirmation of compliance with prescribed formalities. The assignee acquires all rights and privileges previously held by the assignor relating to the patented invention. Any subsequent transfer or sub-license must also adhere to these stipulations as provided herein, ensuring transparency and accountability in intellectual property transactions.

Where an application for a patent is deemed to be refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such decision before the Appellate Board. The Board shall hear arguments from both the Controller and the appellant, considering whether the grounds for refusal are substantiated by evidence demonstrating novelty or inventive step. It shall be open to the respondent, being the Controller, to argue that the invention was previously known or obvious, thereby negating the claim of patentability. Further, a party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court on any question of law arising out of the decision; provided that such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and shall not operate as a stay of the original order. The determination of whether something is patented remains subject to judicial review.

Where an invention has been patented under this Act, the patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licences relating thereto, and such licence may extend to any territory within or outside India. Any assignment of the patent, whether absolute or partial, shall include all rights granted by virtue of the patent, including but not limited to the right to exploit the invention commercially through manufacture, use, sale, offer for sale, or importation. The patentee may also grant licences under this Act subject to the conditions that such licences do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition, as provided herein. Further, any licensee shall be bound by the terms and conditions of the licence agreement; a breach thereof may render the license voidable at the discretion of the patentee, notwithstanding anything contained in section 53 zn.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed to be patented if it is a new and non-obvious process or article, and its subject matter satisfies the requirements as provided herein. The determination of novelty and inventive step shall consider any information disclosed to the public anywhere in the world prior to the date of filing of the patent application. Any reference made under this Act to entries in the Register of Patents shall be construed as referring to details recorded accurately within the official records maintained by the Controller General, including particulars relating to applicants, inventors, and dates of priority claims. Such register references are conclusive evidence for all purposes unless proven otherwise through due process.

An order adjudicating officer made under this Act shall be deemed final subject to an application for revision filed before the Controller. For the purpose of this provision, an “adjudicating officer” means a person appointed by the Central Government to exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred upon such officers relating to matters concerning revocation or infringement proceedings as provided herein.
