The grant of such registration confers upon the registrant exclusive rights relating to the production, sale, distribution, and importation of propagating material of the registration variety. Any person who, knowingly or fraudulently, uses a false trade description in relation to any plant material offered or exposed for sale as being a registration variety shall be liable to penalty, as provided herein. This prohibition extends to misrepresenting the origin or characteristics of such material.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical composition” shall mean a combination of two or more active ingredients, or an active ingredient and an excipient, formulated for therapeutic use in human beings or animals. A pharmaceutical composition shall be deemed to possess inventive step if it exhibits unexpected efficacy, safety, or a synergistic effect not predictable from the properties of its individual components as understood by a person skilled in the art. The term “active ingredient” includes any substance intended to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, relieve, or prevent disease; provided that salts, esters, ethers, and other derivatives of an active ingredient shall be considered such ingredient unless they possess substantially different properties.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “pharmaceutical composition” shall be deemed to include any novel combination of active pharmaceutical ingredients intended for therapeutic or prophylactic use, provided that such combination results in a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual properties of the constituents. The Controller General may require applicants seeking registration of a pharmaceutical composition to submit detailed data demonstrating said synergistic effect and its clinical relevance. Further, an application relating to a process for producing a pharmaceutical substance shall include particulars regarding all critical parameters affecting product quality and stability. Any alteration in these parameters without prior notification to the Controller General may render the registration liable to revocation.

Where an infringement of patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical product has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to seek relief under this Act. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringer from making, using, or importing the patented invention, as well as damages adequate to compensate for the loss suffered by the patentee as a result of the infringement. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the injury to the patentee and the profits which the infringer made from the sale of the infringing product. Provided that, in cases where the alleged infringement involves a process patent for a pharmaceutical substance, the burden of proving that the patented process is essential to the manufacture of the product shall lie upon the defendant. Further, any order granted under this Act may be subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems just and equitable.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical product is filed, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates the working of the invention in India within the time specified under this Act. Such evidence shall include details regarding manufacturing processes, quality control measures employed, and clinical trial data, if applicable, pertaining to the efficacy and safety of the pharmaceutical substance. Failure to comply with a requirement issued by the Controller may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to make representations against any adverse findings arising from the examination of submitted documentation. Any objection raised concerning the patentability of the invention on grounds of prior publication or lack of novelty must be addressed comprehensively within the response filed before the Controller.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall be considered only if it discloses the method of manufacture or production in sufficient detail as to enable any person skilled in the art to make or use the invention without undue experimentation. The applicant must demonstrate that the claimed process yields a product meeting established pharmacopoeial standards, unless such deviation is explicitly justified and supported by data demonstrating equivalent efficacy and safety. Furthermore, where the application incorporates information derived from prior publications, the applicant shall provide an exhaustive list of all such references, confirming their accuracy and relevance to the invention as claimed. Any alteration to the disclosed process post-application filing requires notification and may necessitate re-examination under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to compulsory licensing of a pharmaceutical product may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the conditions specified for grant of compulsory license have been duly satisfied, including but not limited to the inadequacy of working and the reasonable availability of the patented invention to the public at affordable prices. Failure to demonstrate compliance with these requirements shall render the compulsory license invalid. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days, subject to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees for delay beyond that time.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any patentee of a pharmaceutical product may grant an exclusive license to manufacture such product for sale within India. Such license shall be documented in writing and registered with the Controller, specifying the duration, geographical limitations, and royalty rates applicable. The patentee shall provide reasonable notice to the licensee prior to assigning or transferring the said license to any other party; failing which, the assignee may claim damages under this Act. Further provision is made for compulsory licensing of pharmaceutical inventions where such licenses are deemed necessary to address public health emergencies or ensure affordability, as provided herein. The Controller may determine the terms and conditions of such compulsory licenses, including royalty payments to the patentee.

Where an application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition is rejected under this Act on the grounds that the claimed invention lacks novelty or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating the inventive step. Such presentation may include expert testimony substantiating unexpected therapeutic effects or improved efficacy compared to prior art disclosures. The Controller may, after considering such arguments and evidence, uphold the rejection or direct that the application proceed for examination; however, any such direction shall be subject to appeal before an appellate authority as provided herein. Further, a party aggrieved by a decision of the appellate authority concerning novelty in pharmaceutical inventions may petition the Supreme Court on grounds of law alone.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any patentee holding a patent for a pharmaceutical substance may grant exclusive licenses relating thereto. Such license shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to exploit the patented invention, as well as the field of use pertaining to such exploitation. The patentee shall retain ownership of the index registered trade mark associated with the pharmaceutical product and may stipulate conditions regarding its utilization by the licensee. Further provision is made for assignment of rights under this Act; a licensee may assign their interest in the license to another party, provided that prior written consent of the original patentee is obtained. The assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions of the initial license agreement.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical composition” shall mean a novel combination of active and inactive ingredients intended for use in human or animal therapeutics, diagnostics, or prophylaxis. Such composition shall be deemed non-obvious if it exhibits a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual properties of its components, as demonstrated by established scientific methods. The term "active ingredient" includes substances derived from plant variety sources, provided that such derivation does not render the resulting pharmaceutical composition obvious to a person skilled in the art. A process for producing a pharmaceutical composition shall be patentable subject to compliance with the provisions relating to inventive step and non-disclosure under this Act.

An application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition shall be deemed incomplete if it does not include a detailed description of the manufacturing process, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to reproduce the invention. Business India applicant entities seeking protection under this Act must provide documentary evidence demonstrating their commercial interest and ongoing investment in the development of the claimed innovation. The Controller General may require further clarification regarding the scope of claims or the novelty assessment if ambiguities arise during examination. Provided that, any prior publication by the applicant, whether intentional or unintentional, shall not invalidate the patent application subject to a grace period as provided herein. Further, the applicant must disclose all known uses of the pharmaceutical substance relevant to the claimed invention.

Where an infringement of patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical product is established under this Act, the Controller may grant such remedies as are just and equitable. Such remedies shall include, but not be limited to, an injunction restraining the infringer from making, using, or selling the infringing product; damages equivalent to the lost profits suffered by the patentee, or where that cannot be accurately determined, a reasonable royalty; and the disposal of any infringing stock held by the infringer. The Controller may also order the delivery up of all materials and records relevant to the infringement. Where a pharmaceutical formulation is found to be deceptively similar to an existing patented product, prejudicing public interest or creating confusion amongst consumers, the Controller shall consider enhanced damages.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application patent invention” shall mean a new and non-obvious process or product, relating to an article manufactured or produced in India, for which an application for grant of patent has been filed. An invention shall be deemed not obvious if, having regard to the state of knowledge existing as the date of filing of the patent application, it does not involve any element of surprise and is not simply a combination of known elements. The term "invention" includes improvements relating to the subject matter in respect of which an application patent invention has been granted under this Act, provided that such improvement results in material advancement.

Where a patent is granted under this Act, the exclusive right conferred thereby shall extend only to the acts specified in section 47, and for the duration as provided herein. Any person infringing such exclusive right may be restrained by injunction pending determination of the suit, subject to just compensation being awarded to the patentee for any loss or damage suffered due to such restraint. Further, a party aggrieved by an order relating to a patent, including orders concerning revocation or opposition proceedings against an application patent invention, may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Board shall have power to grant directions and issue orders as it deems fit, ensuring fairness and equity in resolving disputes pertaining to intellectual property rights. Costs of such appeals shall be determined according to established legal principles.

Any party aggrieved by a decision refusing registration of an application patent invention may, within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision, appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall only be entertained if the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the refusal and provides evidence substantiating the claim. Failure to comply with this evidentiary requirement will render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller may, after affording the patent examiner an opportunity to be heard, dismiss the appeal or direct registration subject to such modifications as he deems fit. Any person found to have filed a false statement in relation to an application patent invention shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Where a patent has been granted as an application patent invention, the patentee shall retain exclusive rights subject to any license agreements entered into prior to the grant. Any subsequent assignment of the patent shall be deemed to include all rights and obligations arising under existing licenses pertaining to the patented invention. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from a licensee alleging breach of contract by the assignee, initiate inquiries as provided herein; however, such inquiries shall not extend to questioning the validity of the application patent invention itself. A license granted prior to assignment continues in force unless expressly terminated by written agreement between the original parties, and any transferor’s rights relating to royalties or other considerations stipulated within that license remain enforceable against the assignee.

Where a patent has been granted as an application patent invention, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights pertaining thereto, subject to any licenses previously granted under this Act. Such licenses may be assigned or transferred wholly or in part, provided that prior written consent of the Controller is obtained for assignments affecting the scope of exclusivity originally defined within the license agreement. Further, where a licensee seeks to sublicense the patented technology, they shall notify the registered proprietor and provide details of the proposed sublicensing arrangement. The registered proprietor may, within sixty days from receipt of such notification, raise objections which, if not addressed satisfactorily by the licensee, may be grounds for cancelling registration under this Act. Any assignment or sublicense must be executed in the prescribed manner and duly recorded with the Controller.

Where a patent is granted for an application patent invention relating to a process, the rights conferred shall extend only to the manufacture, use or sale of goods produced in India using that process, unless the specification expressly provides otherwise. Any person importing into India any goods made by means of a patented process without the authorization of the patentee shall be deemed to have infringed the patent and is liable for damages as provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party, issue directions requiring disclosure of information relating to the origin or production methods of imported India produced articles if reasonable suspicion arises that such goods are manufactured using a patented process without due license. Such disclosures shall be subject to confidentiality safeguards under this Act and applicable regulations.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed authority” means an authority specified by notification in the Official Gazette, and such authority shall exercise all powers and discharge all duties conferred or imposed upon it under this Act. The Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, designate any officer to be the prescribed authority for a local area or for specific purposes. Any decision taken by the Central Government under this section shall be final, subject to appeal to such appellate body as the Central Government may specify. The Central Government shall establish guidelines regarding the qualifications and experience of officers designated as prescribed authorities.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be submitted to the Central Government in the prescribed form and accompanied by such documents and materials as may be specified therein. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the genetic composition of the variety, its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, along with details regarding its expression potential and resistance to pests or diseases. Upon receipt of an application, the Central Government shall publish a notice indicating the nature of the plant variety sought to be registered and inviting objections from any person having knowledge of the matter. Objections received shall be considered by the Central Government, which may require further information from the applicant or objector as deemed necessary for proper evaluation.

Where a patent is granted in contravention of or prejudice to any right subsisting under this Act, the central government may, subject to such inquiry as it deems fit, direct that the patent be declared invalid, wholly or in part. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The High Court shall admit the appeal only if it is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for interfering with the decision of the central government. Costs of the appeal shall be determined by the High Court. Further, where a patent has been declared invalid under this provision, any person who was prevented from exploiting the invention by the existence of the patent may apply to the central government for relief, including compensation proportionate to the loss suffered.

Applications for registration of designs shall be filed with the Designs Office specified by the central government, and each such application must contain a full representation of the design. The applicant shall furnish particulars as to whether the design is new or not, and any statement relating thereto shall be deemed part of the application. Upon receipt of an application, the Designs Registry may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the design’s novelty or distinctiveness.

The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the form for applications and other documents required under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision made by the Designs Office relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to such authority as the central government may specify. The appellate authority shall consider all relevant evidence and pass orders which shall be binding on the Designs Registry.

Where an application for patents relating to agricultural processes is filed, the central government may, after giving notice to the applicant and affording him an opportunity of being heard, direct that such application be examined by a designated authority possessing specialized knowledge in agronomy or plant pathology. Such direction shall only be issued if the central government deems it necessary to ascertain whether the process described in the patent application is likely to prejudice public interest, particularly concerning food security or biodiversity conservation. The applicant shall provide all relevant data pertaining to field trials and efficacy assessments as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Failure to comply with such requirements will render the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before an appellate body constituted as provided herein.

Any person found guilty of making or publishing false statements concerning the subsistence of a patent, or the extent of its claims, shall be liable for damages to the patentee, recoverable by suit in a District Court. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party alleging infringement of patent rights, direct the Registrar to initiate inquiries into the matter and issue notices to all concerned parties. Failure to comply with such directions issued by the Central Government shall constitute contempt of court and render the defaulting party liable for penalties as determined by the Court. Further, any entity found to be wilfully violating provisions relating to post-grant opposition may face suspension of its registration under this Act, subject to judicial review.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention relating to pharmaceuticals or agricultural chemicals, the central government may, acting through designated officers, require the patentee to grant a non-exclusive license to manufacture and sell the patented product within India. Such requirement shall only be made if the central government is satisfied that adequate supplies of the drug or chemical are not reasonably available to the public at affordable prices. The terms of such licenses, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by the central government in consultation with an expert committee established for this purpose. Assignment of patent rights relating to these licensed products requires prior notification and approval from the central government, ensuring equitable access and preventing undue exploitation.

Where an application for patents relating to agricultural inventions is filed, and objections are raised concerning the novelty or inventive step under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond in writing within ninety days. The Central Government may, after considering the written response and any further evidence submitted, direct that the proceedings against the patent application continue, be dismissed, or be referred for oral hearing before a designated authority. Any party aggrieved by such direction of the Central Government may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds involving questions of law.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed authority” means an authority notified by the central government for performing specific functions relating to the examination of patent applications and determining whether inventions are obvious or not. The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, delegate its powers under this Act to any other officer or authority as it deems fit. Any decision taken by the prescribed authority shall be binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal to such appellate body as may be specified therein. The central government shall establish guidelines for the conduct of hearings before the prescribed authority and ensure transparency in their operations concerning patents.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention relating to a work published outside India, and such publication contains a translation of the invention’s description, the central government may, upon application by any person aggrieved, direct that the patent be deemed to have been applied for on a date not earlier than the date of first publication of the translated work. Such direction shall only be issued if it is demonstrated that the applicant did not know of the prior publication and that the translation substantially discloses the invention claimed in the patent. Any party adversely affected by such a direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, and the Board’s decision shall be final. The central government shall consider any evidence submitted regarding undue delay or prejudice caused by the granting of the patent, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable commercial harm resulting from the publication work translation.

Where an act constituting an offence under this Act is committed by a department or unit within a public sector enterprise, every officer of the enterprise who was responsible for the management or control of the department or unit at the time when the act was so committed shall be deemed to be guilty of such offence. For the purposes of determining liability, a commission offence attributable to an employee acting on behalf of their employer shall be considered as having been committed by both the employee and the employer, subject to due process considerations as provided herein. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines for apportioning responsibility in cases involving multiple parties.

Where an application for registration of a layout design is found, upon investigation, to incorporate elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout design without due acknowledgement or authorization, the Controller may issue a notice requiring the applicant to demonstrate originality. Failure to satisfy the Controller regarding such derivation shall render the application liable for rejection. Any person who knowingly makes false statements in an application for registration, or conceals material facts relevant to the determination of novelty or distinctiveness, commits a commission offence attributable to their intent to deceive the Controller and obtain an unwarranted advantage under this Act. Such offences are cognizable and may attract penalties as determined by the appropriate authority.

Where any act or omission constituting an offence under this Act is committed by a department or unit within a public corporation, every officer of the said corporation who was responsible for the management, control, or supervision of the department or unit at the time when the act or omission was so committed shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence attributable to such department or unit. Such officers shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Controller, proportionate to their degree of responsibility in failing to prevent the infringing activity. The Controller may, upon receiving complaints regarding inadequate oversight, issue directives for improved internal controls within the corporation. Further, any person abetting or conspiring to commit an offence under this Act shall also be subject to penalties as provided herein, and such liability extends to those who knowingly benefit from the illegal activities.

Where an individual, acting as an agent or representative of a patent applicant or patentee, knowingly makes a false statement or conceals material information relating to the invention described in a patent application or during post-grant opposition proceedings, such act shall constitute a commission offence attributable to both the individual and the applicant or patentee. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of such an offence, issue a notice requiring the accused to appear before a designated officer for examination. Failure to attend as directed without reasonable cause, or providing evasive responses, shall be deemed conclusive proof of guilt regarding the false statement or concealment. Further, any person assisting in the commission of this offence may also be held liable under this Act. The penalty for such offences shall be determined based on the severity and impact of the misleading information provided.

Where a patent is granted in contravention of any provision under this Act, or where information disclosed in the application for patents contains matter which does not meet the requirements of novelty or inventive step as provided herein, the Controller may, subject to due process and affording an opportunity for hearing, declare the patent invalid. Any person who knowingly makes, uses, sells, or imports a patented invention without authorization from the patentee shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence attributable to the act of infringement. Provided that such acts are undertaken with the intent to derive commercial benefit from the unauthorized exploitation of the intellectual property rights vested in the patent holder. The Controller may also issue directions for rectification of the patent, if necessary.

Where any act or omission constituting an offence under this Act is committed by a department or unit within a public sector undertaking, every officer of such department or unit who, at the time the offence was committed, was responsible for the direction, control, or supervision thereof, shall be deemed to be guilty of that offence. The liability of such officers shall be joint and several with the public sector undertaking. A commission offence attributable to an employee acting within the scope of their employment shall also render the employer liable to prosecution under this Act. Further, where a false representation is made in relation to any matter relevant to the grant or validity of a patent, any person knowingly making such representation shall be punishable as provided herein.

Where a patentee grants a license conferring rights to make, use or sell an invention, any subsequent assignment of such patent shall be subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. The assignor retains responsibility for ensuring compliance with these pre-existing obligations during the period of the assignment. Further, where a licensee sublicenses the patented technology, they are bound by the limitations imposed in both their license and any subsequent sublicense agreements. A commission offence attributable to a breach of licensing terms shall be deemed to have been committed not only by the direct violator but also by any party knowingly participating in or facilitating such a violation, including those involved in distribution chains. The Controller may issue directions for rectifying non-compliance with licensing conditions as provided herein.

Where an individual, acting as an agent or representative of a patent applicant or assignee, knowingly makes a false statement material to the determination of patentability or enforceability under this Act, such act shall constitute a commission offence attributable to both the individual and the principal for whom the act was performed. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence suggesting such a falsification, issue a notice requiring the principal to demonstrate due diligence in preventing the misleading representation. Failure by the principal to satisfactorily rebut the allegation of negligence within the stipulated period shall render them jointly liable with the agent for any penalties prescribed herein. An appeal against this determination lies to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification.

Where an applicant knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses any material fact in relation to the particulars disclosed in a filing application for patent, or in any document filed under this Act, such act constitutes a commission offence attributable to the applicant. The Controller may, upon discovery of such falsity or suppression, direct that the filing application be deemed not to have been made and shall proceed accordingly. Further, where an agent acting on behalf of the applicant is found to have facilitated such false statement or suppression, the applicant shall remain liable for any penalties as provided herein. Any person assisting in the preparation or prosecution of a patent application may also be subject to investigation under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “commission alleged offence” shall mean an act or omission constituting an offence under this Act committed by any person, whether within or outside India. Such commission may occur directly or through another’s agency, and includes acts performed with the intent to deceive or mislead the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services. Where a trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without due cause, such use shall be deemed a commission alleged offence if it creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the relevant consumer base, as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and it is alleged that the applicant has committed an offence involving the use of another’s registered trade mark without due cause, the Registrar shall record particulars of the commission alleged offence in a register maintained for that purpose. Such record shall include details pertaining to the nature of the infringement, the date upon which the alleged infringing activity commenced, and the geographical area where such activity is said to have occurred. The proprietor of the registered trade mark may provide evidence substantiating the claim, subject to procedural safeguards as provided herein. Further, any party aggrieved by a record made under this provision may apply for its rectification, following procedures established elsewhere within this Act.

Where a proprietor alleges an offence has been committed against their registered trademark, they may institute civil proceedings seeking remedies as provided herein. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them due to the infringing activity, taking into consideration factors such as the extent of reproduction, distribution, and sales of the counterfeit goods or services. Further, an injunction may be granted restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, subject to just terms being determined by the court. In instances where a commission alleged offence has occurred through the actions of an agent or employee, the proprietor may pursue both the principal and the individual responsible for the infringement. The court shall consider evidence pertaining to knowledge and intent in determining liability.

Where an investigation into a suspected violation of this Act is initiated based on information received by the Registrar or any officer authorized by him, such officer shall record the particulars of the informant and the nature of the alleged offence. The investigating officer may serve a notice upon the person against whom the commission alleged offence has been reported, requiring them to appear before him at a specified time and place to answer questions relating to the matter under investigation. Failure to comply with such a notice without reasonable cause shall be deemed as obstruction of an investigation and subject to penalties as provided herein. The investigating officer is empowered to seize any documents or materials relevant to the inquiry. A report, detailing findings and recommendations, must be submitted to the Registrar within ninety days from the commencement of the investigation, unless extended by order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an investigation into a suspected infringement of registered trademarks is initiated under this Act, any individual appearing before an adjudicating officer shall be deemed to have been served with notice of the commencement of such proceedings. The investigating officer may require production of books and documents relevant to the alleged offence, subject to appropriate safeguards regarding confidentiality as provided herein. Failure to produce such documentation without reasonable cause shall constitute a ground for further inquiry into potential obstruction of justice. Where a commission alleged offence involves the use of counterfeit goods bearing a deceptively similar trademark, the investigating officer shall assess the scale of production and distribution involved. Any person making a complaint must provide verifiable evidence substantiating the claim of infringement.

Where any individual is alleged to have committed an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark, such individual shall be deemed to have engaged in unfair trade practices and may be subjected to civil penalties as provided herein. The investigating officer, upon receiving a complaint regarding a commission alleged offence, shall immediately record statements from all relevant parties including the complainant, the accused, and any witnesses. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act concerning the cessation of infringing activities will result in enhanced fines and potential imprisonment for those found responsible. Further, damages may be awarded to the registered proprietor to compensate for losses incurred due to the infringement.

Any proprietor desiring to grant a license relating to the use of their registered trademark shall execute an assignment agreement specifying the scope of permitted activities, geographical limitations, and duration of such license. Such agreements may be assigned by the licensor or licensee, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the other party, unless otherwise stipulated within the original licensing terms. Where a commission alleged offence arises concerning unauthorized use of a trademark following an assignment, the assignee shall be deemed liable for any damages resulting from actions preceding their acquisition of the license, subject to demonstrating due diligence in verifying the assignor’s right to grant such permissions. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the form and content of these assignments to ensure clarity and prevent ambiguity concerning rights and obligations under this Act.

Where a complaint alleging an offence under this Act is filed before the Registrar, such complaint shall specify the particulars of the alleged offence, including the date, place, and manner in which it is claimed to have been committed. The respondent may, within thirty days from the date of service of notice of the complaint, file with the Registrar a written statement denying or explaining the commission alleged offence, supported by affidavits where necessary. Provided that the Registrar shall afford the complainant an opportunity to rebut such defence. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final.

Where an investigation is initiated concerning a commission alleged offence relating to the use of a trademark without due cause, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the applicant seeking registration. This notice will detail the particulars of the alleged infringement and invite the applicant to submit evidence pertaining to their claim of prior rights or honest concurrent usage. Evidence submitted may include documentation establishing a priority date for the mark's adoption or first use in commerce, subject to verification by the Registrar. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond within a prescribed timeframe; failure to do so may result in the investigation proceeding ex parte. Any response received will be considered alongside other relevant information before a determination is made as provided herein.

Where a registered proprietor alleges an offence relating to the use of their trademark without due authorization, they may institute civil proceedings against the alleged infringer. Such proceedings shall be initiated within three years from the date the infringement came to the knowledge of the proprietor, provided that this limitation does not apply where the infringement involves fraud. The court, upon finding a commission alleged offence has occurred, may grant an injunction restraining further infringing activity and order damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, taking into account the infringer's profits derived from the unauthorized use. Further, in cases of persistent or willful infringement demonstrating bad faith, the court may direct that the patent shall cease to have effect for a period determined at its discretion, impacting future trademark protection.

Where an investigation is initiated pursuant to a complaint alleging an offence under this Act, the Investigating Officer shall record the particulars of the complainant, the alleged offender, and the nature of the commission alleged offence. The Registrar may, upon receiving such a complaint, issue notice to the person against whom the allegation is made, directing them to appear before the designated authority at a specified time and place to present their defence. Such notice shall clearly state the grounds for the complaint and provide copies of all supporting documentation submitted by the complainant.

The Investigating Officer shall ensure that any application registered proprieto the trade mark in question is duly considered during the investigation process, taking into account the rights and interests of all parties involved. The authority may require further evidence or clarification from either party as deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the allegations. Failure to appear before the designated authority without reasonable cause shall be deemed a contravention under this Act and subject to appropriate penalties.

Where an investigation into a suspected infringement of registered trademarks is initiated by the Registrar, any person alleging a commission alleged offence relating to such infringement shall furnish a written complaint detailing the specific acts constituting the violation. The complaint must specify the trademark purportedly infringed, the goods or services in relation to which the infringement occurred, and identify the individual or entity believed responsible for the infringing activity. Provided that the Registrar deems the complaint prima facie credible, he may direct the alleged offender to appear before a designated officer for questioning. Parliament retains the power to amend procedures relating to such investigations as deemed necessary to ensure fairness and efficiency in adjudicating trademark disputes under this Act.

Where a registered proprietor of a trademark grants a license allowing use of their mark for specific goods or services, and subsequently alleges an offence relating to unauthorized exploitation of that trademark by the licensee, such allegation shall be deemed substantiated if it is established that the terms of the license agreement were demonstrably breached. This determination is subject to the proviso that the registered proprietor provided clear and unambiguous stipulations regarding permitted usage within the licensing arrangement. Furthermore, a reasonable period shall be afforded to the accused party to rectify any deviations from the agreed-upon scope of use before formal proceedings are initiated under this Act. The right to assign or sub-license trademarks remains with the original proprietor unless expressly permitted as provided herein; any unauthorized assignment constitutes a commission alleged offence and is actionable accordingly.

Where an appeal lies under this Act from any order made by a Registrar, the register court shall have power to entertain and determine the said appeal. The register court shall not be bound by any decision previously rendered in relation to the matter appealed from but may take into consideration such decisions as it thinks relevant. Subject to any rules made under section 65, the register court shall observe such procedure as it deems appropriate for the disposal of the appeals brought before it. Provided that the register court may, at its discretion, require parties to submit written arguments or documents in support of their case.

Application for registration of a proposed service mark shall be refused if the marks are identical or confusingly similar to any existing registered trade mark used in relation to services identical or closely related to those for which the application is made. Where an objection is raised under this Act, the applicant may submit counter-statements and evidence rebutting the grounds for refusal. The register court shall consider all such submissions and evidence before determining whether the proposed service mark should be accepted for registration. Provided that if the register court finds that a registered trade mark has been used as per conditions stipulated therein, it may allow registration notwithstanding any similarity. Further, the register court shall provide reasons in writing for its decision.

Where an appeal lies from any order made by the Registrar under this Act, and the aggrieved party alleges that the decision was manifestly unjust due to error in fact finding, the register court shall consider whether a material factual determination was demonstrably flawed. The register court may, subject to principles of natural justice, examine evidence not presented before the Registrar if it appears such evidence would have materially altered the outcome. Provided that any such examination shall be conducted with due regard for fairness and procedural propriety. Further, where damages are claimed in relation to trade mark infringement, the register court shall assess whether the defendant acted with knowledge of the registered trade mark and intended to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers. The register court shall also consider mitigating factors when determining the appropriate level of compensation.

Where an appeal lies from an order passed by the Registrar under this Act, and the appellant seeks to challenge the validity of a registered trade mark on grounds not previously raised in opposition proceedings, the register court shall require the appellant to file with the appeal a concise statement outlining the basis of the challenge. Such statement must specify each alleged ground of invalidity with particularity and identify any documentary evidence intended to be relied upon at the hearing. The register court may, subject to just cause shown, direct the respondent to provide written submissions addressing the grounds raised in the appellant’s statement within a prescribed timeframe. Failure by either party to comply with such directions shall not, of itself, render the appeal incompetent but may affect the admissibility of evidence presented before the register court. The register court shall proceed to hear and determine the appeal expeditiously, considering all relevant submissions and evidence adduced.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is filed under this Act, and the Registrar deems it necessary to ascertain facts beyond those presented in the record, the register court shall be empowered to conduct such inquiries as are deemed appropriate. Provided that any party aggrieved by a decision of the Register Court may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The register court shall provide each party with written notice at least thirty days prior to any hearing and shall allow for the presentation of evidence, subject to rules framed under this Act concerning procedural fairness. Further, the register court shall record reasons in writing for every decision rendered, ensuring transparency and accountability as provided herein.

Where any person institutes proceedings alleging an infringement of a registered trade mark before a register court, and the respondent claims that the trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark used in relation to identical or similar goods, the register court shall direct the claimant to provide evidence establishing distinctiveness acquired by use subsequent to registration. Failure to comply with such direction may result in the proceedings being dismissed without further hearing. The register court shall also have power to award costs against the claimant if it finds that the allegation of infringement was frivolous or vexatious and intended solely to harass the respondent, subject to a finding of actual damage caused by any alleged infringing activity.

Where a registered trademark owner desires to grant a license conferring rights in relation to any goods or services specified in the register, they shall execute an assignment agreement detailing the scope and duration of said license. Such agreements must explicitly state whether the license is exclusive or non-exclusive, and the geographical territory covered by the same. Further, where disputes arise concerning the terms of such a licensing arrangement, the register court shall have jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the matter, provided that any decision made by the court regarding the validity of the underlying trademark registration remains subject to appeal under this Act. The owner may also assign the entire registered trademark or any part thereof to another party, with notification filed as prescribed.

Where an appeal arises under this Act from any decision or order of a Registrar, and the appellant alleges demonstrable prejudice resulting from an error apparent on the face of the record pertaining to the acceptance or refusal of registration of a trade mark, the Register Court shall give priority consideration to such appeal. Provided that, if the respondent disputes the existence of said prejudice, the Register Court may direct the production of further evidence by either party. The Register Court shall not be bound by any prior determination made by the Registrar regarding the similarity of marks or the descriptiveness thereof, subject to a finding that the Registrar’s decision was manifestly unjust. Any order issued by the Register Court concerning such appeals is final, save for an appeal to the Supreme Court under established procedures.

Where an appeal lies under this Act from any decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration, or regarding the removal of a trade mark from the Register, the register court shall give notice to all parties who are affected by such decision. The register court may require the Registrar to submit to it such information as it deems necessary for the proper determination of the appeal. Provided that any party aggrieved by an order made by the register court under this Act may further appeal to the Supreme Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to the provisions of the Supreme Court’s Rules regarding appeals. The Registrar shall furnish copies of all documents filed in connection with the appeal to the register court upon request and at its own expense. Any application for an extension of time under this section must be made in writing and supported by affidavit.

Where an application for registration of a design is opposed under this Act, and the grounds of opposition relate specifically to alleged prior use of a substantially identical design in commerce, the Design Registry shall provide the applicant and the opponent with a joint opportunity to present documentary evidence substantiating their respective claims. The Registrar may, at his discretion, appoint an expert to assess the similarity between the designs in question. Should either party fail to comply with the timelines prescribed for submission of documents, as determined by the Registrar, the Design Registry shall proceed to consider the opposition based solely on the available record. Further, if a dispute arises regarding the interpretation of documentary evidence, the register court shall be empowered to make findings of fact and determine the outcome of the opposition proceeding.

Where an article patented under this Act has been assigned or licensed, and the assignor or licensor seeks to enforce any right relating to the trade mark registered in connection with that article, the register court shall consider whether the assignment or license agreement contains provisions governing such enforcement. Provided that where the agreement is silent on the matter of enforcement, the register court may determine the extent of the assignor’s or licensor's rights based upon principles of equity and fairness, taking into account the nature of the licensed use and any representations made during registration. Further, subject to any contractual limitations, an assignee or licensee shall be deemed to possess all the rights which the registered proprietor had at the time of assignment or license, including the right to initiate proceedings before the register court for infringement.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused by the Registrar, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals and make orders as it deems fit, which may include setting aside the refusal and directing the Registrar to proceed with examination or ordering the application be deemed abandoned. Further, where a trade mark is registered in contravention of this Act, any person aggrieved may apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register. The registrar shall powers to entertain such applications and make orders rectifying the register, including expunging the registration, subject to just consideration of all relevant factors presented by parties involved. Any order made under this Act is appealable to the Appellate Board.

Any proprietor seeking remedies under this Act relating to the use of a registered geographical indication shall file a complaint before the relevant High Court. The complaint must specify the unauthorized use and its impact on the distinctiveness and reputation associated with the geographical indication. Where such use causes dilution of the said association, or creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods, the court may grant an injunction restraining further infringing activity. It is provided that a proprietor shall be liable to compensate any party demonstrably harmed by the pursuit of remedies under this Act. Furthermore, where a registered geographical indication has become generic through common usage, its protection as an indication used geographically may be revoked following due process and public notice.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a map conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act, clearly delineating the territory from which the goods originate and demonstrating that such territory is linked to the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributed to those goods. The applicant must provide detailed documentation substantiating the unique production methods employed within the defined geographical area, including but not limited to traditional practices and local expertise. Any alteration of these documented methods following registration shall require prior approval from the Registrar, subject to a public notice period allowing for objections from interested parties claiming rights related to the indication used geographically.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, uses a geographical indication as an indication used geographically to identify goods with intent to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of such goods shall be liable to pay damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the relevant High Court, taking into consideration the extent of misrepresentation and the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Further, any importer found to have knowingly brought into India goods bearing an unauthorized geographical indication shall face seizure of those goods and a penalty equivalent to three times the value of the imported goods, as provided herein. Repeated offences may result in prosecution under relevant penal codes.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement under this Act and may seek injunctive relief restraining any person from making use of the geographical indication or any confusingly similar indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed. Provided that, where an alleged infringer has honestly used the geographical indication prior to the date of registration, but without intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin of the goods uses geographical indications, a court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including a direction for the payment of damages. Any person found to have infringed a registered geographical indication shall be liable to pay compensation equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor or a sum not exceeding five per cent of the turnover attributable to the infringing activity, whichever is higher.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence that the quality, reputation or other characteristic, primarily attributable to the geographical origin of the goods, is capable of distinguishing them from other similar goods. Where an objection is taken by any person against the registration of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar may afford the objector and the applicant opportunities of being heard. The Registrar shall consider all such objections and representations as provided herein before making a decision regarding registration. Goods uses geographical origin must be clearly defined in the application, including detailed maps delineating the area of production. Any alteration to this definition requires prior approval from the Registrar and may necessitate public notice.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed admissible only if the applicant demonstrates exclusive use of the indication by the producers and other interested parties within the defined geographical area. The specified geographical area must correspond precisely with the territory where the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to its origin; any deviation from this requirement will render the application liable for rejection. Further, the applicant shall provide documented evidence confirming adherence to established production practices and standards unique to the identified goods uses geographical indication. Provided that such standards are demonstrably linked to the qualities associated with the place of origin, as verified by a recognized agricultural or industrial authority.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act relating to a registered geographical indication shall be liable to pay such fees as may be prescribed. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated during registration, including limitations on permissible uses of the geographical indication and restrictions concerning authorized users, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or both. Furthermore, any person found using a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as provided herein shall be subject to damages assessed by the relevant court, considering lost profits and reputational harm. The Registrar may issue injunctions against infringing activities affecting the distinctiveness of goods uses geographical indications.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication relating to goods may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the indication on specific categories of goods consistent with the registered characteristics. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted usage, duration, and any restrictions imposed by the proprietor. Assignment of a geographical indication, including rights pertaining to existing licenses, requires prior consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued protection of the collective interests associated with the goods uses geographical origin. Any subsequent transfer or assignment shall be subject to conditions safeguarding the reputation and quality standards defining the registered indication, as provided herein. The Registrar may issue directions regarding royalty payments arising from licensed usage, aimed at equitable distribution among producers within the defined geographical area.

Any proprietor seeking to restrain the use of a geographical indication under this Act shall furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive rights and prior continuous use within the defined territory. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the link between the goods and their origin, including historical records and production methods. An aggrieved party alleging misuse or deceptive application of a geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if satisfied that the Registrar’s determination was manifestly erroneous. Such appeals shall be heard expeditiously, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the initial decision concerning goods uses geographical indications. The burden of proof regarding authenticity and distinctiveness rests upon the claimant.

An application to apply geographical indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence of continuous use of the proposed name or sign by a group of producers over a defined area, demonstrating its association with quality, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to that origin. Where an application relates to agricultural products or foodstuffs, the applicant must submit a detailed description of the production method and geographical boundaries defining the territory from which the goods originate. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding the proposed indication’s distinctiveness and connection to its geographic origin. Any objection received under this Act shall be served on the applicant, who may file a written response within the time specified. The Registrar shall consider all submissions before proceeding with examination of the application.

An application to apply geographical indication shall be deemed invalid if the applicant is not a producer class authorized under this Act and registered with the competent authority. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish proof of such authorization, including documentation demonstrating adherence to established production standards and conformity assessments performed by recognized bodies. Provided that, an association representing producers may also apply for registration, subject to fulfilling all requirements pertaining to representation of a substantial majority of producers within the defined geographical area. Furthermore, any use of the indication which creates confusion or misleads consumers regarding the origin of the goods shall be deemed a violation and is prohibited as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “used geographical indication” means an indication that relates to goods and refers to a place or region with such characteristics as are essentially attributable to its geographical origin, and is used in commerce in relation to those goods. An indication shall be deemed a "used geographical indication" if it is presented in any manner whatsoever, including by way of marks, labels, notices, advertisements, brochures or other forms of publicity, and where the use thereof may indicate that the goods originate from the place or region named in such indication. Provided that an indication used to describe the characteristics of agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines or spirits shall not be considered a "used geographical indication" if it does not conform with standards as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the agricultural product or good indicating its origin, the area of geographical territory from which the goods originate, and a map of the area. The applicant must demonstrate that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to the geographical origin as defined in the application. Where an indication has been previously used in relation to identical products or services, the Registrar may require further evidence establishing consumer recognition of the *used geographical indication* and its association with the specified territory. The applicant shall also provide a statement outlining measures proposed for collective management and control of the registered geographical indication.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suit in the competent court for redress against any person who, without authorization, makes use of such used geographical indication indicating that the goods originate from a different territory than the one defined under this Act. Such unauthorized use shall constitute unfair competition and passing off, and the remedies available under general law relating to infringement shall apply mutatis mutandis. The court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the geographical indication, as well as award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor due to the deceptive practice. Provided that, a genuine user who prior to the date of registration had lawfully used the indicator is not prohibited from continuing such use, subject to conditions determined by the court.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be refused if the applicant is unable to demonstrate exclusive rights to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods specified in the application. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning distinctiveness, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence establishing that the proposed geographical indication has become qualitatively associated with the goods over a period of at least three years prior to the date of application. The Registrar shall consider any submissions made by interested parties regarding the potential impact on existing trade marks or other intellectual property rights. Any person claiming proprietary rights in a used geographical indication may, within sixty days from the publication of an acceptance under this Act, file notice of opposition with the Registrar. Such opposition must specify the grounds upon which it is based and provide supporting documentation as provided herein.

An indication shall be deemed to be a used geographical indication if it is affixed to goods conforming to the standard as prescribed under this Act and relating to such goods, and that affixation occurs with the consent of the registered proprietor. Provided that, where an application for registration of a geographical indication relates to agricultural products or foodstuffs, the applicant must demonstrate through documented evidence that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the product is essentially attributable to its origin as defined in the application. Further, any use of a used geographical indication shall be subject to conditions regarding traceability and verification procedures established by the Geographical Indications Registry, ensuring compliance with the prescribed specifications for authenticity.

Any person utilizing a used geographical indication in connection with goods not originating from the area specified by that indication shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. Such utilization is deemed an infringement and carries a penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing such unauthorized use are subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders against offenders, and failure to comply with these orders will result in additional penalties, including daily fines until compliance is achieved. Recovery of damages for losses incurred by registered proprietors due to the used geographical indication’s misuse is also permissible.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses to use the used geographical indication relating to goods for specific purposes, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication, including any existing or future licenses, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, provided that such consent may only be withheld on grounds demonstrably prejudicial to the interests of consumers or the reputation of the indicated goods. Further, a licensee using a used geographical indication shall adhere strictly to quality standards prescribed by the relevant sectoral authority and as notified under this Act. The registered proprietor retains ultimate responsibility for ensuring compliance with these standards by all licensees.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act concerning the registration of a geographical indication, direct the party seeking registration to submit documentary evidence demonstrating exclusive use and control over the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics associated with the goods specified. Should the objector contend that the proposed geographical indication constitutes a *used geographical indication* in relation to identical or similar goods, the applicant shall be obligated to provide verifiable data establishing prior usage predating the objection’s filing date. Failure to satisfy this evidentiary burden may result in rejection of the application. Any party aggrieved by such a direction or subsequent decision may appeal under the provisions herein, presenting arguments and counter-evidence before the relevant appellate authority.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be refused if the proposed used geographical indication is deemed descriptive of the characteristics of the goods for which it seeks to be registered, and such description would unfairly indicate that the goods originate from a different geographical location. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through prolonged or substantial use, provided that such use has not misled consumers regarding the origin of the goods. Further, an application shall be rejected if the proposed indication conflicts with existing rights under trade mark regulations, including but not limited to registered trademarks and pending trademark applications. The Registrar shall publish a notice of any opposition filed against the registration and provide the applicant an opportunity to respond as provided herein.

The use of a geographical indication, as defined under this Act, shall be permitted only by authorized users who have complied with the prescribed quality and production standards detailed in the registered GI specification. Any entity utilizing a used geographical indication in relation to goods not originating from the territory specified in the registration certificate shall be deemed to be engaging in unfair trade practices and subject to penalties as provided herein. Furthermore, reproduction of the distinctive signs or indications associated with a protected geographical indication, even for promotional purposes, may constitute infringement copyright if such reproduction creates an identical or confusingly similar impression regarding the origin of the goods. Such actions are prohibited unless expressly authorized by the registered proprietor following written consent.

Any person proposing to use a sign likely to be confused with a registered geographical indication shall, under this Act, provide notice to the Register within three months of such proposed use. The Register may, after giving an opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the proposer, issue directions restricting or prohibiting the use of the mark if it determines that continued use would constitute infringement registered geographical indications. Such directions shall specify the nature and extent of the restriction or prohibition. An appeal against any order made under this provision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Register may also require evidence demonstrating consumer understanding regarding the distinctiveness of a sign, particularly where similarity exists with an existing registration.

Any person who uses, without due cause and after notice from the Register of Geographical Indications, a sign that is identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication for goods of the same class shall be deemed to have committed an infringement. Such use includes, but is not limited to, applying the sign to goods, offering or exposing them for sale, using them in advertising, and importing or exporting them. Provided that, where the alleged infringing activity constitutes fair use under established principles of trade practice, as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority, no action shall be taken under this Act. The Register may, upon receiving a complaint regarding potential infringement registered geographical indications, issue directions to cease such activities subject to compliance with due process.

Any person holding a license granted under this Act pertaining to a registered geographical indication may, subject to the terms and conditions of that license, assign or transfer such license to any other person, provided that such assignment or transfer is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The Registrar shall record such assignment or transfer in the Register of Geographical Indications and publish notice thereof. Further, where a registered geographical indication has been assigned or transferred, the assignee or transferee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the geographical indication for the purposes of enforcing rights relating to infringement registered geographical indications. No license granted under this Act shall be assignable if the original registration agreement expressly prohibits such assignment; however, consent from the owner of the registered geographical indication may override this restriction as provided herein.

Where a dispute arises concerning alleged infringement registered geographical indication of Darjeeling tea, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Such proceedings shall be deemed civil suits for the purposes of limitation and applicable procedure. Provided that, if the defendant contends that the use by him does not constitute an act of infringement under this Act, or that the registered proprietor was not duly authorized to make the application for registration, such contention may be raised as a defence and determined as part of the principal cause of action. The authority shall afford both parties an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence, subject to appeal to the High Court on any question of law arising during the proceedings.

Where a claim is made alleging infringement registered geographical indication of Darjeeling tea, the aggrieved proprietor may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Such proceedings shall be subject to an amendment claim specification being filed within sixty days from the date of the initial complaint, detailing the specific goods or services purported to infringe and outlining the manner in which such use creates confusion amongst consumers. Provided that, if the defendant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from said amendment, the authority may, notwithstanding, permit the amended claim specification to proceed under conditions it deems just. Any order made by the authority is appealable to the High Court within a period of ninety days, and the appellate court shall consider whether the infringement caused genuine commercial detriment to the registered proprietor.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctive quality” with reference to any goods shall mean characteristics, including but not limited to taste, aroma, texture, appearance, or other qualities attributable solely to the unique natural conditions prevalent within a defined geographical area. A plaintiff right geographical indication shall be deemed to exist where such distinctive quality is essentially linked to that origin and reputation of the goods originates from, or is associated with, that geographical location. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating this link before registration is granted, provided that prior use of similar names or indications by producers outside the defined area shall not invalidate a claim under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person or entity utilizing, displaying, or otherwise representing goods as originating from the territory associated with the said indication without due authorization. Such action may be brought before an appropriate judicial forum to prevent such unauthorized use and seek remedies available under this Act. Provided that where the infringing activity is demonstrably unintentional and ceases promptly upon notification of the infringement, the court may, at its discretion, limit any injunctive relief granted to the registered proprietor. The plaintiff right geographical shall extend to preventing dilution of the distinctiveness of the indication through misleading association or false representation. Further, damages recoverable in such suits shall be determined considering the extent of the infringing activity and the resultant harm to the reputation and commercial interests of the registered proprietor.

An application for registration as a plaintiff right geographical indication shall be deemed admissible if it demonstrates, through documented historical records spanning not less than one hundred years, continuous use of the specified good within the defined territory. The applicant must further provide evidence confirming that the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to its origin within said territory and that such connection is perceived by consumers as a significant factor in their purchasing decisions. Provided that any prior registration or established usage of an identical or deceptively similar indication shall be considered during examination, and the Registrar may reject the application if it contravenes provisions relating to unfair competition under this Act.

Any person claiming to be the registered proprietor of a plaintiff right geographical indication, or authorized user thereof, shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act.
