The Controller General Patents may, at any time, issue registered draft regulations pertaining to procedural aspects of hearings before the Board, including timelines for submission of written arguments and modalities for video conferencing. These draft regulations are subject to public consultation prior to finalization and shall be binding on all parties involved in proceedings under this Act.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears erroneous by reason of a clerical error, inadvertence, or misapprehension of fact, the Controller may, subject to provisions regarding notice and opportunity for all interested parties to be heard, direct rectification of the register. For the purposes of this Act, *rectifying register shall* involve correcting any such errors relating to the identity of the inventor, the scope of the claim, or the date of filing, provided that the rectification does not substantially alter the rights granted by the patent. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears to be erroneous by reason of a clerical error, inadvertence, or misapprehension of fact, any person aggrieved may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application shall specify the particulars of the alleged error and state the relief sought. The Controller shall give notice to all interested parties as provided herein, affording them an opportunity to be heard in opposition to the proposed rectification. Upon consideration of the evidence presented, and subject to compliance with principles of natural justice, the Controller may direct that the register shall be rectified accordingly. Rectifying register shall not extend to matters involving questions of patentability or validity unless specifically raised during the initial examination process.

Where an entry in the Register of Patents appears erroneous by reason of a clerical error, inadvertence, or misapprehension of fact, the Controller may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for all interested parties to be heard, direct rectification of the register. For purposes of clarity, “rectifying register shall” encompass correction of errors relating to the applicant’s name, inventor details, claims defining the invention, or any other particulars recorded therein. Such rectification will not extend to altering the substance of the patent itself; genera species specified in the original claim construction remain inviolate. The Controller may also order rectification where a subsequent discovery demonstrates an initial misinterpretation of prior art.

For the purposes of this Act, “use patented” with reference to a patent shall mean the making, selling, offering for sale, distributing, importing, or hiring out of any process or article claimed in the patent, or the use of such process or article. Such use includes not only direct exploitation but also indirect utilization where the activity contributes substantially to the working of the patented invention. Provided that activities undertaken solely for experimental purposes relating to the patented invention shall not be considered as “use patented” under this Act. Further, the term "use patented" extends to acts performed by a licensee in accordance with the terms of their license agreement, subject to any restrictions stipulated therein.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a process for producing a substance, and such process involves the use patented by another person, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that consent has been obtained from the patentee for the use patented. This requirement shall apply irrespective of whether the patented invention is directly employed in the production process or contributes substantially thereto. The application for registration may be rejected if the applicant fails to provide satisfactory proof of such consent within a period specified by the Controller, provided that the rejection can only occur after affording the applicant an opportunity to present their case and defend against the allegations. Further, any subsequent use patented without prior authorization shall constitute an infringement under this Act.

Where any person, without authorization from the patentee, shall use a patented invention for the purpose of import into India, or manufacture, production, offering for sale, or exhibition for sale, or knowingly disposing of such patented article, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant authority. Such proceedings shall be directed towards seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity and recovery of damages sustained by the patentee as a direct consequence thereof. The amount of damages recoverable shall be determined having regard to the extent of the use patented, the prevailing market rate for the invention, and any profits derived from the unauthorized exploitation. Provided that where the infringement was demonstrably innocent, such as arising from reliance on representations made by the alleged infringer concerning validity or scope of the patent, a reduction in damages may be awarded.

Where, following the grant of a patent, an interested party alleges that the patentee has failed to work the patented invention within the time limit as provided herein, such party may apply to the Controller for revocation of the patent on the ground of non-use. The application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents substantiating the claim of non-working. Upon receipt of such an application, the Controller shall serve notice on the patentee, affording them a reasonable opportunity to present their case and rebut the allegations. If, after due inquiry and consideration of evidence presented by both parties, the Controller finds that the patentee has not adequately demonstrated use patented within India or elsewhere, they may order revocation of the patent. The Controller shall record the reasons for such decision in writing.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, nothing shall prevent any person from using a patented invention for purposes solely incidental to the use of another patented invention, provided that such use does not constitute an infringement of the claim of the primary patent. Where a patented invention is used in combination with one or more other inventions, and where the combined operation results in a synergistic effect exceeding the sum of the individual effects, the determination of whether such use infringes the claims of the main patent shall be made considering the totality of the process employed. Any entity seeking to commercially use patented technology must demonstrate that their activities do not unduly impede the patentee’s rights under this Act and have obtained any necessary licenses or permissions where applicable.

Any person who, without authorization from the patentee, shall commercially use patented inventions within the territory of India, including but not limited to manufacturing, offering for sale, distributing, importing, or hiring out, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the High Court, taking into account the extent of infringement and the loss suffered by the patentee as a direct consequence thereof. Further, where such use is found to have been willful, the court may award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation assessed. The patentee may also seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing the unauthorized use, subject to demonstrating irreparable harm.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an interest in a patent may grant a license under this Act to use patented inventions, either wholly or partially, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as they deem fit. Any assignment of the patent shall include all licenses granted prior to the date of assignment unless otherwise specified in the instrument of assignment. Where a licensee is permitted to manufacture for sale, the patentee shall have the right to terminate the license if the licensee fails to market the patented product within a reasonable period, as determined by the Controller. Further, any sub-licensee under this Act shall be bound by the terms and conditions stipulated in the original license agreement. The power to grant licenses and assignments remains with the patentee or their legal representatives, provided that such actions do not contravene the public interest.

Where, following an objection raised under this Act concerning the non-working of a patented invention within India, the patentee disputes that such non-working constitutes a failure to use patented and asserts that circumstances beyond reasonable control prevented said use, the Controller shall require the patentee to furnish documentary evidence substantiating the claim. The burden of proving these exceptional circumstances rests solely upon the patentee. Provided that if the Controller finds the submitted documentation insufficient or unreliable, he may direct an inquiry into the matter, affording the objector an opportunity to present counter-evidence. Any order made by the Controller following such inquiry shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under provisions as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “use patented” with respect to a patented invention shall mean making, using, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention into India, or any process involving the patented invention. This definition includes the use of the patented invention in combination with other goods or services. Where the patented invention relates to a new variety of plant, “use patented” shall extend to propagation and marketing of plants derived from that new variety, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act regarding farmers’ rights and seed saving practices, provided that such activities do not infringe upon any process claims associated with the invention.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, examine whether the proposed marks are distinctive and not descriptive of the goods or services with which they seek association. Rules carry provisions concerning the form of applications, including requirements for representation of marks and specification of goods or services. An applicant may be required to submit further information or clarification regarding the nature of their business if deemed necessary by the Registrar. The examination process shall include a search of existing registered trade marks and pending applications to ascertain similarity. Any objection raised during this scrutiny must be addressed by the applicant within the time prescribed, failing which the application may be refused. Consideration will be given to any prior use or reputation associated with the mark.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. The remedies available shall include an injunction restraining the infringing user from continuing such use, as well as damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Rules carry provisions detailing the procedures for calculating said damages, taking into account factors such as the infringer’s profits and the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the registered trade mark been validly licensed. Provided that a finding of likelihood of confusion is established, the Court may also order delivery up or destruction of the infringing goods or materials bearing the impugned mark.

Applications filed under this Act shall be examined by the Registrar, and where an application is found to contain a description of marks which are deemed to be merely descriptive of the goods or services with which they are associated, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark. Such direction shall be accompanied by written reasons for the decision. The applicant shall then have the right to appeal against such direction before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of the communication. Rules carry provisions prescribing the form and manner in which appeals are to be filed, heard, and disposed of, as provided herein. Further, the Registrar may require any applicant to furnish security for costs subject to guidelines established by the Central Government.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a mark, examine whether the proposed mark is distinctive in its class and conflicts with any existing registered marks. Rules carry provisions regarding the procedure for such examination, stipulating that the applicant must furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where the mark lacks inherent distinctiveness at the time of filing. Further, if the Registrar finds that use of the mark would be likely to cause confusion amongst consumers or is descriptive of the goods or services, a notice of objection shall be issued. The applicant may then submit a reply addressing these objections; however, failure to comply with stipulated timelines will result in abandonment of the application as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a complaint alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, serve notice on the complainant and the alleged infringer, providing each party with a period of thirty days to submit written representations. Any representation received shall be considered by the Registrar before proceeding further under this Act. Rules carry provisions prescribing penalties for failing to comply with such notices, including fines not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and potential seizure of infringing goods. The Registrar may order interim relief pending resolution of the complaint, provided that a prima facie case of infringement is established. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences conferring rights to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the consideration for granting a licence shall be determined by contract. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include any existing licences attached thereto unless explicitly excluded in writing by both parties involved. The rules carry provisions regarding the recording of such assignments and licences with the Trade Marks Registry, ensuring transparency and priority among claimants. Further, where a licensee defaults on the terms of their licence agreement, the proprietor may seek redress through appropriate legal channels as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from a person claiming proprietary interest in relation to a registered trade mark, afford the applicant and objector each a reasonable opportunity to present their respective arguments in writing. Rules carry provisions for the conduct of such hearings, which may be either oral or documentary as determined by the Registrar. An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal against any order passed by the Registrar under this section, provided that the appellant shall deposit before the Tribunal such fees as are prescribed. The Tribunal’s decision is final subject only to further appeal to the High Court on a limited ground of law relating to jurisdiction or violation of principles of natural justice.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from a person claiming that a proposed trade mark is confusingly similar to an earlier mark, afford the applicant and the objector each a reasonable opportunity to present their respective arguments in writing. Rules carry provisions for the determination of such similarity, which shall consider not only the visual appearance and phonetic resemblance of the marks but also the goods or services with which they are associated. The decision of the Registrar regarding confusing similarity is subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It is further provided that where an objection relates to a claim of prior use, the objector must demonstrate such use with sufficient evidence as determined by the Registrar; otherwise, the applicant’s registration shall proceed unimpeded. A patentee includes exclusive rights over the territorial application of the mark.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, examine whether the proposed marks are distinctive and not descriptive of the goods or services with which they are associated. Rules carry provisions regarding the form of applications, including requirements for representation of the mark and specification of goods or services. An applicant seeking to utilize a previously registered trade mark under license shall file an application for registration as an authorised use mark, providing evidence of consent from the proprietor of the original trade mark. Such authorisation must clearly define the scope of permitted usage and geographical territory. The Registrar may reject any application if it appears that the proposed mark is confusingly similar to an existing mark, subject to consideration of the goods or services involved.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is likely to cause confusion among the public, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. The Registrar shall, upon receiving evidence of such misuse, issue directions prescribing the manner issuing cease and desist orders against the infringing party, provided that the trade mark owner demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the unauthorized application. Rules carry provisions detailing the procedures for filing complaints regarding deceptive use, including requirements for submitting documentary proof and affidavits substantiating the claim of consumer confusion. Further, any order issued under this provision may include an assessment of damages to compensate the registered proprietor for losses incurred as a direct consequence of the infringing activity.

For the purposes of this Act, "cinematograph film" shall include works captured and recorded using any apparatus which produces moving images, whether such images are accompanied by sound or not. The term "producer relation cinematogra" signifies the individual or corporate body exercising ultimate creative control over a cinematograph film’s production, encompassing decisions regarding script selection, casting, location scouting, and overall artistic direction. This designation shall vest in the entity registered as producer under the rules framed thereunder. Provided that where such registration is absent, determination of the "producer relation cinematogra" may be made by the Controller based on demonstrable evidence of creative authority.

For the purposes of this Act, where a cinematographic work has been produced and registered with the competent authority, the producer relation cinematogra shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein. This ownership extends to all rights comprised within the work, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, public exhibition, and distribution. Provided that, if the production was undertaken under a contract between the producer and any other party, such as a director or composer, the terms of that contract shall govern the allocation of copyright ownership subject to the provisions regarding fair remuneration for creative contributions. Any assignment of copyright in respect of a registered cinematographic work must be executed in writing and attested by at least two witnesses, and duly recorded with the Registrar.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the producer relation cinematograph shall be deemed the owner of copyright in the film for all purposes. This ownership extends to include the right to reproduce the work in any form, including but not limited to digital formats and adaptations; to sell or lease copies of the film; to communicate the film publicly through broadcast, streaming, or other means; and to adapt the film into a different medium. Provided that, where a cinematograph film incorporates pre-existing works such as literary compositions or musical pieces, the copyright in those incorporated elements remains with the original creators unless otherwise expressly assigned. Any infringement of these rights may be subject to civil suit for damages and injunctive relief, as provided herein. The producer shall have the right to pursue remedies against any party engaging in unauthorized exploitation of the film’s copyright.

The producer relation cinematograph shall be deemed the first owner of copyright in respect of all cinematographic works produced by them, subject to the rights of performers and music composers as provided herein. Where a work is jointly produced, the ownership shall vest jointly in the producers, and their respective shares shall be determined according to an agreement in writing executed between them prior to the completion of the film. Any assignment of copyright under this Act relating to a cinematograph film must be evidenced by a registered document, specifying the extent and duration of such assignment. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments filed for registration, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Further, any person seeking to utilize excerpts from a cinematographic work requires prior written consent from the producer relation cinematograph, detailing the scope and purpose of such utilization.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and where a cinematographic work incorporates elements produced by multiple parties, the producer relation cinematogra shall be deemed the owner of copyright therein. Provided that, if such work is jointly produced by two or more individuals or entities, they shall be considered joint owners with equal rights unless otherwise agreed in writing. The right to control reproduction, distribution, and communication to the public of the entire work remains vested solely within the producer relation cinematogra, irrespective of contributions made by other creative personnel involved in its creation. Any assignment of copyright relating to a cinematographic film must clearly delineate the scope of such assignment with respect to elements contributed by performers or musicians under this Act.

Any individual claiming to be the producer relation cinematogra of a film shall be deemed guilty of copyright infringement if such individual reproduces, distributes, communicates to the public, adapts, or translates the copyrighted work without due authorization from the owner of the copyright in that film. Where an unauthorized reproduction is made for commercial gain, the infringing party shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the reasonable licensing fee which would have been payable had the infringer obtained a license as provided herein. Furthermore, any person found guilty of such infringement may face imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. The court may also order the destruction of all infringing copies.

The producer relation cinematograph shall be deemed the first owner of all copyright subsisting in the film, subject to any agreement entered into prior to its creation assigning such rights. Any license granted by the producer relating to reproduction or public exhibition of the film shall be valid only if it specifies the duration and geographical extent of such permission. Further, a performer appearing in a cinematograph film may grant exclusive licenses for their performance independently of the producer’s copyright, provided that such assignment explicitly acknowledges the producer's ownership of the underlying work. The remuneration payable to the performer under this arrangement shall be determined as per guidelines issued by the Central Government from time to time. Any subsequent transfer or assignment of rights in the film must clearly delineate which aspects of copyright are being conveyed, distinguishing between those held by the producer and any individual performer’s rights.

Where a cinematograph film incorporates works protected under this Act, the producer relation cinematogra shall be deemed the first owner of the copyright therein, subject to the rights of the authors and performers whose works are so incorporated. Provided that, in cases where such incorporation is undertaken without due authorization or contractual agreement, any aggrieved author or performer may appeal to the relevant High Court seeking a declaration regarding ownership and entitlement to royalties proportionate to the utilization of their work within the film. The determination of ‘due authorization’ shall be based on evidence presented demonstrating consent, licensing agreements, or other legally binding arrangements. Further, disputes concerning the apportionment of profits derived from such films may be adjudicated by the High Court, considering prevailing industry standards and equitable principles.

The producer relation cinematograph film shall be deemed the owner of copyright therein, subject to any agreement entered into prior to the commencement of principal photography. Any license granted by the producer relating to reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of the work may specify a limited duration and geographical territory as determined within the terms of such license. Further, assignment of copyright in the cinematograph film, whether partial or complete, requires execution of a written agreement specifying the scope of rights transferred and the consideration paid. The exclusive rights conferred upon the producer under this Act include the right to authorize or prohibit the making of copies, communication to the public, and any other acts restricted by law. Provided that, where a performer’s contribution is demonstrably integral to the film's artistic merit, they may negotiate for a share in royalties derived from exploitation of those rights as provided herein.

Where any patentee, or their assignee, desires to grant a license for exploiting an invention, such license shall be documented in writing and registered with the Controller. The terms of the license agreement may specify the field of exploitation, including but not limited to geographical territory and application area. Assignment of rights under this Act relating to an *invention means new* and any subsequent licenses granted thereafter, must also be recorded as per prescribed procedures. Provided that, where a licensee sub-licenses the patented invention, such sub-licensee shall adhere to the terms stipulated in the original license agreement or obtain consent from both the patentee and the initial licensee. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party, investigate instances of non-compliance with licensing conditions as provided herein and issue directives for rectification. Any transfer of rights must include a declaration affirming the validity of the underlying patent.

Where any person considers that another has infringed his patent, or designs registered under this Act, he may institute suit for relief in a District Court having jurisdiction. Such suit shall be actionable upon proof of prior registration and demonstration that the alleged infringing activity constitutes exploitation of the patented invention or unauthorized reproduction of the design. The remedies available to the aggrieved party include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee or registered proprietor, and compensation for costs incurred in pursuing legal action. Provided that a finding of prior art negating novelty shall preclude recovery of damages. An invention means new and any act replicating a protected design with intent to deceive constitutes actionable infringement subject to equitable considerations as determined by the Court.

Where any person considers himself aggrieved by any order made under this Act, he may appeal against such order within sixty days from the date of communication thereof to an appellate authority as provided herein. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds specified and demonstrated with reasonable evidence pertaining to errors apparent on the face of the record or substantial misinterpretations of law impacting the validity of a patent. The appellate authority may, after affording the appellant and respondent an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order of the appellate authority may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days, subject to satisfaction of conditions regarding pecuniary jurisdiction. For purposes of this Act, a *means invention* if it is patentable under the provisions relating to novelty and inventive step.

For the purposes of this Act, “means invention technology” shall include any novel and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, whether existing previously or newly devised. An invention technology is deemed to be new if it does not contain any element disclosed in the prior art; provided that a disclosure made at an exhibition or demonstration under this Act shall not constitute prior art. The term "prior art" includes any information which was made available to the public anywhere in the world, by means of written description, use, knowledge or otherwise, before the date of filing of the patent application. An invention technology must also be capable of being manufactured or used in an industry.

An application for registration of a technology relating to an invention shall contain a full and clear description of the invention, disclosing the manner in which it may be carried into effect and providing sufficient detail to enable any person skilled in the relevant field to make or use the invention. The description shall identify the specific means by which the invention is achieved, including all essential components and their interaction. Where the technology incorporates a process, the application must specify the materials required and the conditions necessary for its operation. It is provided that the applicant may submit drawings illustrating the invention, but these are supplementary to the written description. The Controller General shall require verification of the technical accuracy of the described means invention technology.

For the purposes of this Act, “means invention technology” shall be construed to encompass any novel process or apparatus demonstrating utility within an industrial setting. An application for a patent relating to such invention technology shall disclose the manner and conditions under which it is produced, and its best mode of operation as known to the applicant at the date of filing. Provided that, where the invention technology involves biological material, the disclosure requirements may be relaxed subject to regulations framed by the Controller General; however, failure to adequately describe the source or derivation of such biological material shall constitute grounds for revocation under this Act. The application must also satisfy the criteria pertaining to non-obviousness and industrial applicability as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “means patent granted” shall include any patent which has been sealed and published under the prescribed rules, signifying its validity and conferring exclusive rights as provided herein. A means patent granted may be amended only in accordance with procedures established under this Act, subject to limitations regarding scope and claims. Further, a means patent granted remains in force for a term of twenty years from the date of filing of the application unless otherwise specified or revoked by judicial order. The right conferred by a means patent granted is assignable, whether absolutely or conditionally, as may be permitted under this Act.

The Register of Patents shall be maintained by the Controller, and shall contain particulars relating to every patent granted, including the name and address of the patentee, the title of the invention, the date of application for registration, the date of grant of the patent, and the prescribed fees paid. An entry in the Register of Patents shall create a presumption that the person entered therein is the true proprietor of the means patent granted. Any modification to the particulars relating to a patent, such as a change in ownership or address, may be recorded upon application by the concerned party and subject to verification under this Act. The Controller shall provide certified copies of entries in the Register of Patents to any person requiring them for lawful purposes, provided that a fee is paid as prescribed.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to have been refused if, after affording opportunity for such hearing as is provided herein, the Controller finds that the invention does not involve an inventive step. The term “means patent granted” refers exclusively to a patent conferred under this Act and subsequent amendments thereto, and excludes any provisional protection or similar arrangements. Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the decision of the Controller regarding such refusal shall be final. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may prefer an appeal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the claims in the patent application to define more clearly the subject matter for which protection is sought, provided that such amendment does not alter the inventive concept disclosed in the specification. A patent granted shall remain in force for a term of twenty years from the date of filing the patent application.

A means patent granted shall be deemed invalid under this Act if, at the time of application for such patent, the invention was not novel or did not involve an inventive step over prior art as determined by the Controller. Provided that, where a person has derived from the aforementioned prior art, and filed an application within twelve months of publication, the means patent granted may be considered valid subject to compliance with prescribed procedures regarding disclosure of such derivation. Furthermore, any alteration made to the invention subsequent to the date of filing the application shall render the means patent granted liable for revocation if such alteration goes beyond what is described in the claims and does not contribute significantly to the inventive concept as provided herein. The burden of proving non-compliance rests upon the petitioner seeking invalidation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses under the means patent granted, either for the whole duration of the patent or for such period as may be specified in the license agreement. Such license agreements may include conditions relating to royalty payments and sub-licensing rights, provided that these conditions do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition. Where a patentee desires to assign their interest in a means patent granted, including any pending application therefor, they shall execute an instrument of assignment in the prescribed form. This assignment shall be registrable under this Act and shall vest in the assignee all rights and privileges which the assignor possessed as patentee. The Controller may require such further information or undertakings from the assignee as are deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions relating to working conditions.

An applicant seeking to obtain a patent under this Act shall furnish with the filed application india a declaration specifying the invention and its class or classes. The Controller may require, within such time as he deems appropriate, further particulars relating to the claimed subject matter, provided that any request for additional information shall be accompanied by an opportunity for the applicant to respond in writing. Where an application relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture, horticulture, or animal husbandry, the declaration must explicitly state the intended scope of use and potential impact on biodiversity. Failure to provide such clarification may result in rejection of the application under this Act. The applicant shall be deemed to have complied with these requirements upon submission of the requisite documentation.

Where an applicant has made a request for amendment to a patent application under this Act and such request incorporates subject matter not disclosed in the original complete specification, the Patent Office may require the applicant to submit a declaration stating whether the amended application is based on any prior published document. If the applicant fails to provide such a declaration within the time specified by the Controller, or if it is determined that the amendment introduces new inventive concept beyond what was originally sought, the application shall be deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by an order abandoning a filed application india may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review under law.

An applicant who has made a public disclosure of an invention prior to the date of filing an application for patent shall nevertheless be entitled to proceed with his application provided that he satisfies the Controller that such disclosure was unavoidable and did not prejudice the interests of any person. The time elapsed between the date of first publication and the date of filing the application may, at the discretion of the Controller, be taken into account when determining whether the invention is novel or involves an inventive step. Where a patent has been granted based on a previously rejected application, the grounds for rejection shall be recorded in the order granting the patent. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to a filed application india may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Controller shall give notice of such appeals to all parties concerned.

An applicant seeking to obtain a patent under this Act shall ensure that all drawings accompanying a filed application india are clear and complete, accurately depicting the invention as claimed. The Controller may require the applicant to amend or provide additional drawings if they fail to meet these standards, provided that such requirement does not substantially alter the scope of the claims. Further, an applicant whose filed application india includes matter derived from prior publications shall disclose all such sources in a declaration accompanying the application. Failure to do so may render the patent liable to revocation under this Act. The examination process will proceed only after compliance with these requirements and verification by the prescribed authority that the invention is novel and non-obvious.

Any person who, having made an application for a patent in India, knowingly presents false or misleading information relating to the prior art or the inventiveness of the invention claimed, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of such misrepresentation, issue notice requiring the applicant to appear and demonstrate the veracity of their claims. Failure to satisfy the Controller regarding the accuracy of the information presented will result in the rejection of the filed application india and potential prohibition from filing subsequent patent applications for a period as determined by the Controller. Repeated or egregious violations may attract further penalties including criminal prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code.

Where an invention for which a patent has been granted or a filed application india exists, and the rights to such invention have been assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignee or licensee may, subject to the terms of the assignment or license agreement, grant further licenses relating to the same invention. Provided that any such further license shall not be exclusive unless expressly authorized by the assignor or original licensor, and such authorization shall be evidenced in writing. The Controller may require the production of a copy of the assignment or license agreement for inspection purposes if he deems it necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions herein relating to licensing terms and conditions. Any alteration to the scope of rights granted under an initial license requires prior notification to the Controller, detailing the proposed changes and their justification.

Applications for registration of plant varieties may include a statement regarding anticipated propagation methods and their impact on genetic stability, as provided herein. The Controller General shall maintain a register detailing all registered plant varieties, including dates of initial registration and subsequent amendments relating to variety denomination or essential characteristics. Subject to appeal under this Act, the term of patent protection for such registered plant varieties shall extend for twenty-one years from the date of first filing, unless the invention incorporates a novel biotechnological process which significantly enhances the inherent traits of the original species. The register shall be open to public inspection, subject to reasonable restrictions as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance controlled under any other law in force, and the patent includes claims relating to that substance in its final form, the patent shall be subject to compulsory licensing as provided herein, notwithstanding anything contained in sections 107 or 108. The term of patent granted under this Act for such an invention shall be twelve years from the date of grant, and not twenty years from the date of filing the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a compulsory license may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with this provision shall render such an appeal void ab initio. The Controller may, subject to just compensation, grant licenses under this Act if the conditions stipulated are not met.

Any person infringing a patent in respect of an invention, or inducing infringement thereof, shall be liable to pay damages which are commensurate with the loss suffered by the patentee as a consequence of such infringement; provided that where the infringer was cognizant of the existence of the patent and continued the infringing activity thereafter, enhanced damages may be awarded not exceeding six times the amount of damage assessed. The term of patent granted under this Act shall extend for twenty years from the date of filing of the application unless the invention relates to a process for producing a substance applied as or contained in an article, in which case the term shall be five years from the date of grant. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the offender liable for prosecution and penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted rights under a patent, whether through assignment or otherwise, shall hold those rights subject to the original term of the patent as provided herein. Where an invention is jointly owned and patented, the right to grant licenses relating to the entire scope of the patent may be reserved by one inventor, but such reservation shall not prejudice the other joint inventors’ ability to license specific aspects of the claimed invention, provided that a royalty proportionate to their contribution is paid. The term of patent granted under this Act shall extend for twenty years from the date of filing of the application; however, any assignment or licensing agreement may stipulate conditions regarding sub-licensing rights and termination clauses relating to such licenses, subject to approval by the Controller. Further, a licensee’s right to continue exploiting the patented invention beyond the patent's term shall be expressly prohibited unless explicitly granted within the initial license agreement.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an appeal lies to the Appellate Board under this Act if any person aggrieved by an order determining the term of a patent alleges that the Controller has failed to adequately consider evidence pertaining to the date of first working of the patented invention. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order and may seek review of whether the claimed date demonstrably establishes commercial exploitation as required under this Act. The Appellate Board, in entertaining such an appeal, shall give due regard to any expert testimony submitted by either party regarding industry practices relevant to establishing first working. It is provided that the term of patent remains twenty years from the filing date unless altered by a finding of the Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking a patent shall furnish an international application form in accordance with the Patents Rules, detailing the priority claim and specifying the countries where protection is sought; provided that such form must be accompanied by a certified true copy of the original priority document. The determination of the term of patent shall commence from the date the initial application was filed, irrespective of subsequent amendments or additions to the claims. Where an international application claiming priority arises, the expiry date for the patent will remain consistent with the twenty-year period as provided herein, calculated from the earliest priority date claimed in the original Indian application. Any discrepancies found during examination may necessitate further clarification under this Act.

An aggrieved party seeking review of any decision made by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent may file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of that order. The period for filing such an appeal may be extended by the Board for a further period not exceeding thirty days, provided that the appellant shall satisfy the Board that there were sufficient reasons which prevented them from filing the appeal within the initial time frame. Any application for extension of the *appeal period* must state the grounds for delay and provide supporting documentation as required by regulations framed under this Act.

An applicant whose application for registration of a geographical indication is rejected by the Registrar, or who is otherwise dissatisfied with any decision rendered by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or refusal of registration, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall deposit before the Board such fees as may be prescribed under this Act. Provided that the Board may, if it considers it necessary, extend this period by a further period not exceeding two months for reasons to be recorded in writing. An appeal is deemed to have been filed when the memorandum of appeal and the fee are received by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board; the *appeal period* shall run from the date of receipt of such documents.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent, or any matter arising during prosecution, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall deposit such fees as may be prescribed under this Act; failure to do so will render the appeal inadmissible. Provided that where the decision relates to a compulsory license, the *appeal period* shall extend to six months from the date of communication. An appeal lies only on grounds specified in writing and supported by relevant evidence presented during the original proceedings or demonstrably unavailable at that time. The Board may dismiss an appeal if it finds the appellant has acted vexatiously or with malicious intent.

An aggrieved party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent, or concerning any matter arising during patent examination, may institute an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal must be filed within three months from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and include relevant documents supporting the claim. Where the appellant resides outside India, the appeal period shall extend to six months from the date of communication of the decision. Provided that a request for an extension of time may be made to the Appellate Board, accompanied by an affidavit explaining the reasons for delay; such requests may be granted at the discretion of the Board. The Board shall consider all submissions and evidence presented before rendering its determination.

An applicant whose patent application has been rejected or deemed to be invalid under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order. Provided that, if the rejection relates to a matter of fact which could have been ascertained by the Controller before the institution of the appeal, the applicant shall furnish such evidence as is necessary for proper determination thereof. The Board may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and timelines, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the stipulated period only where it is satisfied that the delay was caused due to sufficient reason, recorded in writing. Such reasons must pertain directly to impediments preventing timely filing during the appeal period.

Any assignment or license granted relating to a patent, or any right conferred thereunder, shall remain valid notwithstanding that an appeal has been filed against a decision concerning the validity of the patent itself; provided that such assignment or license was executed prior to the expiry of the sixty-day period for preferring an appeal under this Act. Where a patent holder assigns their interest in a patent, and subsequently receives notice of an order questioning the patent’s validity, the assignee shall be deemed to have inherited the right to exercise the appeal period as if they were the original patentee. Further, any sub-licensee deriving rights from such assignment may also pursue this appeal within the prescribed timeframe, subject to fulfilling conditions stipulated by the Controller. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding procedural aspects of these appeals relating to assignments and licenses.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision rendered by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of patent rights, or concerning any matter provided for under this Act where an opportunity for being heard has been afforded, may institute an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal must be filed within three months from the date on which the decision was communicated to the appellant. The Board shall admit appeals only if the appellant demonstrates a substantial question of law arising out of the Controller’s order; otherwise, the appeal stands dismissed. An extension of time for filing an appeal may be granted by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for cause shown, but such extension shall not exceed thirty days beyond the prescribed *appeal period*.

An aggrieved party seeking redressal against any decision made by the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent, or concerning objections raised during examination, may file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be submitted within ninety days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant. The tribunal shall consider all relevant evidence presented and provide reasoned findings. Provided that, in cases where the decision relates to a compulsory license or revocation based on non-working, the *appeal period* shall extend to one hundred twenty days. Further, any society registered under this Act as a registration copyright society may, with the permission of the Tribunal, intervene in such appeals presenting arguments relevant to the broader public interest concerning patentability and innovation. The appellant is responsible for ensuring timely filing and adherence to procedural requirements as provided herein.

An applicant whose patent application has been rejected or deemed to be invalid, subject to compliance with regulations pertaining to registered draft regulations issued by the Controller General, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appeal period shall commence from the date of communication of the order concerned and shall extend to sixty days; however, this period may be extended for a further thirty days if the applicant demonstrates reasonable cause for delay in filing, as determined by the Board. Failure to comply with the prescribed format and content requirements stipulated under this Act will render the appeal inadmissible. The Board shall consider any relevant evidence submitted by the applicant and the Controller within the appeal period before issuing its determination.

A basic application, for the purposes of this Act, means an application for protection of an invention made in a country executing the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property or the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights. Such application shall be deemed to specify the date of the earlier application as its priority date, subject to the provisions regarding grace periods as provided herein. An applicant claiming priority under a basic application shall furnish a certified copy of the said basic application along with the translation thereof into English, if it was originally filed in another language. The Controller may require further documentation relating to the basic application to verify its authenticity.

An applicant desiring to file a patent application relating to an invention for which a prior publication or disclosure has already occurred shall, in the prescribed form and manner, disclose all particulars of such prior publication or disclosure. Where an applicant claims priority from a basic application made in another country, he shall furnish with his Indian application a certified true copy of the basic application, along with a translation thereof into English if it was originally filed in any other language. The Controller may require further documentation to verify the authenticity and completeness of such copies and translations. Failure to comply with these requirements as provided herein may render the patent application liable for rejection under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Controller regarding a basic application may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention, and subsequently files a further application under this Act, such subsequent application shall be deemed to relate back to the date of the initial basic application for the purposes of determining priority. Provided that if the applicant or their assignee fails to disclose all information known to them which could reasonably affect the patentability of the invention at the time of filing the subsequent application, the Controller may refuse the grant of a patent or impose such conditions as they deem fit. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this provision relating to priority or patentability may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The applicant shall be liable for costs incurred in any proceedings challenging the validity of the patent based on non-disclosure, subject to considerations of fairness and good faith.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention outside India, and subsequently seeks protection for that same invention under this Act, such subsequent application shall be deemed to be one arising out of the aforementioned basic application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the basic application, including all documents filed therewith, as evidence of prior claiming. Provided that failure to submit said documentation within the time stipulated by the Controller shall render the Indian application liable for rejection on grounds of lack of novelty or obviousness. Further, any amendment proposed in the subsequent application must be demonstrably supported by disclosures contained within the basic application; otherwise, it will not be entertained. The applicant shall also declare the date of the basic application and the country where it was filed.

Where a person has made a basic application relating to an invention outside India, and subsequently files a corresponding application under this Act, such subsequent application shall be deemed to relate back to the date of the initial basic application. Provided that the applicant demonstrates satisfactory evidence of the filing date of the basic application, authenticated as provided herein, within six months from the date of the Indian application. Furthermore, if the invention disclosed in the Indian application differs substantially from the subject matter described in the basic application, the Controller may require amendments to ensure consistency and compliance with the novelty requirements under this Act. The applicant shall also provide a certified copy of the basic application as part of their submission.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention, and subsequently files a corresponding application under this Act, failure to disclose all information known to the applicant at the time of filing the basic application shall render the Indian application liable for rejection. Any party demonstrating that such non-disclosure materially impacted the assessment of patentability may petition the Controller for review and revocation. The Controller shall issue notice to the applicant affording an opportunity to be heard, and may impose a monetary penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees where non-disclosure is proven. Further, wilful suppression of material facts constitutes a cognizable offence under this Act, punishable with imprisonment and fines as determined by the appropriate court.

Where a basic application relating to an invention has been made outside India, any person may file in India an application for a patent constituting a continuation thereof, provided that such application is filed within twelve months from the date of the first filing of the basic application. Subject to this, the applicant shall disclose all information known to him as to the state of progress of the invention and shall furnish particulars of the basic application. Any assignment or license granted prior to the institution of proceedings in India relating to the subject matter of the patent under this Act shall be recorded with the Controller, along with an affidavit verifying its authenticity. Failure to do so may render such assignment void. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating the transferor’s entitlement as per the basic application.

Where any applicant, having made a basic application relating to an inventive step, subsequently files a further application under this Act, the Controller shall be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the earlier basic application did not disclose the invention in its entirety. Failure to provide adequate documentation substantiating the novelty of the later application relative to the basic application may result in rejection. An appeal against such a determination lies to the Appellate Board, subject to the condition that the appellant demonstrates prejudice arising directly from the Controller’s assessment regarding the disclosure contained within the earlier basic application. The burden of proving said prejudice shall rest entirely upon the appellant.

An applicant making a basic application shall furnish, along with the application, certified copies of all drawings relating to the invention. The Controller may require the applicant to amend any claim in the basic application if it is unclear or ambiguous. Where an applicant has previously filed a patent application disclosing subject matter identical or substantially similar to that claimed in the basic application, the Controller shall notify the applicant and provide an opportunity for response before proceeding with examination. Further, the applicant must declare whether the invention relates to any process known prior to the date of filing of the basic application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application under this Act.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention outside India, and subsequently seeks to obtain a patent in India, such applicant shall file a request disclosing the particulars of the aforementioned basic application. The request must specify the country where the basic application was filed, the filing date thereof, and a copy of such basic application certified by the Controller or other designated authority in that foreign jurisdiction. Upon receipt of this request, the Controller may require further documentation to verify its authenticity. An entry relating to the design registered in connection with the invention shall be recorded in the Design Register, noting the details of both the Indian and corresponding foreign applications. The applicant is responsible for ensuring the accuracy of all information provided; any discrepancies discovered during examination may result in rejection of the application or other remedial action as deemed appropriate under this Act.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention outside India, and subsequently files a corresponding application under this Act, such applicant shall be deemed to be the first inventor only if the application date shall not exceed thirty-six months from the date of the aforementioned basic application. Failure to adhere to this time limit will render the Indian application liable for rejection on grounds of novelty and inventive step. Any attempt to circumvent this provision through fraudulent misrepresentation regarding the application date is a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment extending to three years and a fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The Controller shall have the power to order the destruction of any infringing material produced in reliance upon such a false declaration.

For the purposes of this Act, "service" includes the offering for sale, supply, or performance of activities relating to banking, insurance, telecommunications, health care, education, transportation, entertainment, and any other activity which the Registrar may deem appropriate. A service shall be considered distinct from goods even where such services are ancillary to the distribution or sale of goods. The description of a service in an application for registration under this Act must clearly identify the nature of the service being offered. Such descriptions shall not include mere indications of geographical origin, unless directly associated with the provision of the service as provided herein.

An application for registration of a service shall be refused if the proposed marks are deemed descriptive of the nature or quality of the services. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such information and documentary evidence as is necessary to ascertain whether the applicant provides, or intends to provide, the specified service. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the genuineness of user of the mark in relation to the claimed service, the applicant shall be called upon to substantiate such use through affidavits and supporting documentation. The Registrar may, after giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity for being heard, direct that the application proceed or not, subject to any appeal as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to registration of a service may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

A proprietor of a service mark shall be entitled to restrain the use in India of any trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to his registered service mark if such use is made in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registration is granted. Provided that where the alleged infringing use occurs in relation to goods or services not identical, the proprietor shall establish a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, and that such use would be detrimental to the distinctiveness of the mark or the reputation connecting with it. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered service mark may institute suit for damages sustained thereby, or for injunction relief as provided herein. The remedy of account shall also be available where the defendant has made profits attributable to the infringement.

Where an application for registration of a service is opposed by any person claiming such right or interest as is specified under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and to the opponent. Both parties shall be afforded opportunities to present their respective arguments in writing and to submit documentary evidence supporting their claims. The Registrar may, after considering the submissions made, direct a hearing to be held wherein both parties may appear and adduce oral testimony. Decisions regarding the validity of an opposition shall be recorded in writing and communicated to the applicant and opponent. Any party aggrieved by such decision may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within the time prescribed. The Registrar is empowered to examine any documents produced during proceedings, and may request further clarification from either party as deemed necessary for a just determination of the matter concerning the service mark application.

A service shall be deemed registrable under this Act if it is specified as such by the applicant and relates solely to activities offered to members of the public for direct or indirect remuneration. The applicant must demonstrate, through documentary evidence, that the service has been used continuously by the applicant in India or elsewhere for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of application. Provided that, where the service involves intellectual creations originating from within India, such use shall be considered with particular regard to its impact on domestic innovation. Any representation employed in connection with the service must clearly and unambiguously identify the nature of the service being offered and shall not contravene any provisions relating to misleading advertisements as provided herein.

Where any person offers or provides a service relating to telecommunications infrastructure, and uses a sign, whether descriptive or not, which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark used by another person for services identical or akin to their own, that first-mentioned person shall be deemed to have engaged in an act of detrimental imitation. Such acts are actionable under this Act as passing off, irrespective of any prior use or registration relating to the imitated mark. Any proprietor of a registered trademark may apply to the relevant adjudicating authority for relief, including injunctions preventing further infringing conduct and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such infringement. The adjudicating authority shall have power to impose penalties not exceeding ten lakhs rupees for each instance of proven violation.

A licensee granted permission to provide a service under this Act shall be subject to the conditions stipulated within the assignment agreement executed with the registered proprietor. Such agreements may include provisions regarding territorial limitations, duration of license, and permitted scope of services offered bearing reference to the trademark. The registered proprietor retains the right to assign or otherwise transfer their interest in the trademark, provided that any such assignment is recorded as prescribed herein and includes a clear delineation of the licensee’s existing rights and obligations. Further, where a service mark has been licensed for use on goods, subsequent licensing of the same service mark for use relating to services shall require explicit consent from the registered proprietor, documented in writing and filed with the relevant authority. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the initial license was exclusive or non-exclusive as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a service by the Trade Marks Registry alleging that the proposed marks are descriptive of the characteristics or quality of the service, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness. Such evidence may include representations from consumers, market surveys, and advertising expenditure incurred in promoting the service under the impugned marks. The Registrar may, after considering the objection and the applicant’s response, direct that the registration proceed subject to limitations on the scope of goods or services covered, provided that such limitation does not unduly restrict the applicant's ability to utilize the mark effectively. Any party aggrieved by this decision may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

An application for registration of a service shall be deemed complete upon submission of the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee and representation of the proposed service marks. The applicant shall specify, with clarity, the nature of the services to be rendered under the mark, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. Where an objection is raised by the examiner relating to distinctiveness or other grounds as provided herein, the applicant may submit a reply within the time stipulated, supported by relevant documentary evidence. The court registrar shall consider such objections and replies before proceeding with examination. Failure to respond adequately may result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the court registrar concerning registration may appeal under this Act.

Where a broadcasting organisation provides a service incorporating distinctive signs or images used to identify its programmes or broadcasts, such signs and images shall be deemed capable of constituting a registrable trademark under this Act. The right to use and exclusively represent such a trademark shall extend to preventing the unauthorized use thereof in connection with identical or similar services offered by another entity, provided that the broadcasting organisation demonstrates genuine use of the mark within the territory for which registration is sought. Any person infringing upon these rights may be subject to remedies including injunctions restraining further infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the broadcasting organisation. A broadcasting organisation shall also have standing to pursue actions against those who falsely represent their services as affiliated with or endorsed by the organization, utilizing similar marks in a misleading manner.

An application for registration of a service shall be refused if the proposed marks are deemed descriptive of the nature of the service. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish such further information or documentary evidence as is necessary to ascertain the character, conditions, and extent of use of the services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Where a geographical indication is included within the description of the service, the application shall specify the territory from which the goods or services originate, and the Registrar may direct that such geographical limitation be incorporated into the register. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The register said geographical indication shall be open for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any conditions prescribed in regulations made under this Act.

The owner of a registered service mark relating to financial advisory services may grant a license permitting another party to provide those services under the mark, subject to conditions specified in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, along with any associated goodwill, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the Registrar. Where the provision of the service incorporates a patented process, the license may explicitly include rights relating to the use of said patent for the duration of the licensed term. Any assignment made without such consent shall be deemed void and unenforceable against the Registrar or any third party relying upon the public register of trade marks. The licensee shall remain bound by all obligations imposed under this Act pertaining to quality standards and consumer protection, as if they were the registered proprietor.

For the purposes of this Act, a "trade description" includes any statement or indication, whether by words, figures, symbols, marks, labels, or otherwise, which is used to describe goods or services and relates to their origin, quality, characteristics, quantity, size, shape, fitness for purpose, mode of manufacture or use, or other relevant attributes. A trade description shall be deemed false if it is likely to mislead a person as to any of the matters aforesaid. Nothing in this Act shall prevent a trade description from being used provided that it does not contain information which is untrue, inaccurate, or deceptive and complies with regulations made under this Act concerning fair trading practices.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a clear and accurate description of the goods or services with which the trade mark is associated. The Registrar may require the applicant to specify further, by way of classes according to the International Classification of Goods and Services, the precise nature of those goods or services. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark incorporating a geographical indication as part of its visual representation, they must provide evidence demonstrating that such use does not constitute a false trade description intended to mislead consumers regarding the origin of the goods. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the geographical indication is protected under any other law. The Registrar shall reject an application if satisfied that the proposed trade description is deceptive or likely to cause confusion.

Where any person applies goods or services with a false or misleading *trade description*, that person shall be guilty of an offence and liable to prosecution. A *trade description* includes statements regarding the quantity, quality, characteristics, origin, mode of manufacture, or suitability for a particular purpose of those goods or services. Any consumer who suffers damage by reason of reliance upon a false *trade description* may bring an action against the person making such representation for damages under this Act. The Court shall have discretion to award exemplary damages where the misleading statement was made knowingly and with intent to deceive. Further, any trade mark proprietor whose reputation is damaged as a consequence of a false *trade description* relating to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the proprietor’s trade mark is registered may also pursue remedies provided herein.

Where any goods are knowingly offered or exposed for sale, or deceptively represented as possessing particular qualities, characteristics, or properties, by the use of any false trade description, the offender shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. A trade description is deemed false if it misleads, or is likely to mislead, the public regarding the nature, quality, quantity, origin, or suitability for a given purpose of such goods. The Central Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving a complaint duly verified by affidavit, initiate inquiries into alleged violations concerning misleading trade descriptions. Any person aggrieved by the findings of such inquiry may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification of the order. Provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal if the complainant has failed to demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the false trade description.

Where any goods are offered or exposed for sale, or are dispatched or delivered for hire or reward, it shall be an offence to make use of any false trade description. For the purposes of this Act, a ‘trade description’ includes any statement or indication which is likely to deceive the public concerning the nature, quality, quantity, origin, characteristics, suitability or other attribute of such goods. This prohibition applies irrespective of whether the false representation is made in relation to the price at which the goods are offered for sale. Provided that, nothing herein shall apply where the false trade description relates solely to a matter which does not affect the commercial assessment of the goods by consumers and is disclosed clearly and conspicuously. Any person found guilty of such an offence may be subject to penalties as provided herein.
