Provided that any authorized reference use must include a clear and conspicuous statement indicating that the geographical indication is used solely for descriptive purposes and does not represent origin. The Registering Authority shall consider objections from registered proprietors regarding potential consumer confusion arising from such reference use geographical indications, and may deny or revoke permission if misleading impressions are likely to occur.

The Registrar may entertain an application for registration of a geographical indication only if the applicant demonstrates exclusive linkage between the goods and the territory specified in the application, provided that such linkage is established through documented evidence of traditional knowledge, agricultural practices, or manufacturing processes. An objection raised by any interested party alleging insufficient reference use geographical connection shall be considered by the Registrar after affording the applicant an opportunity for a hearing. The burden of proving adequate geographical association lies with the applicant; however, where historical records are presented contradicting the applicant’s claim, the Registrar may require further substantiating evidence from both parties. Any appeal against the Registrar's decision on this matter shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

An application for registration of a Geographical Indication may include particulars relating to the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of goods which are attributable to the geographical origin of such goods, and any applicant seeking registration shall furnish evidence substantiating these claims. Where the use of a geographical indication is deemed by the Registrar to be solely indicative of reference use geographical origin as opposed to descriptive qualities, the application may proceed under conditions specified herein. The proprietor of a registered Geographical Indication shall have the right to prevent the use of any identical or confusingly similar indications relating to goods not conforming to the standards established for that indication. Any company seeking registration must demonstrate its connection with the defined geographical area and adherence to prescribed production practices, provided that such adherence is verifiable through documented processes.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include particulars regarding the history and evolution of the name, including traditional practices relating to its production. The Registrar shall consider whether the proposed geographical indication is being used in relation to goods with which it is essentially linked, as provided herein. Any person claiming an interest in opposition to the registration of a geographical indication shall be required to demonstrate that the use of the geographical indication by the applicant would constitute unfair competition or detrimentally affect the quality and reputation associated with similar goods. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claimed link between the geographical indication use and the characteristics of the goods, ensuring authenticity and traceability.

No proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall permit its use in relation to goods not conforming to the standards established under this Act for that indication, and any such use shall constitute an infringement. Where a person makes available for sale goods bearing a false or misleading indication of the origin of those goods, intending to cause confusion among consumers regarding the true origin, they shall be liable for damages as determined by the competent civil court. The registered proprietor may institute legal proceedings against any party engaging in unauthorized geographical indication use within one year from the date such infringement comes to their notice. Provided that, a suit relating to infringement of a geographical indication may be filed in the district where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose.

The Registering Authority may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, direct the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding the quality and characteristics of the goods or products for which the indication is sought, provided that such direction shall be accompanied by reasons in writing. Any person claiming proprietary rights in relation to the geographical indication may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Registering Authority. The Registering Authority shall consider any opposition received and provide an opportunity for both the applicant and the opponent to be heard. Unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication by any person other than an authorized user is prohibited, subject to exceptions as provided herein relating to prior uses. The definition of *geographical indication use* includes employing the indication in a manner that falsely suggests the origin of the goods or services.

The authorized user of a registered geographical indication shall ensure that all goods sold under that indication conform to the standards of quality and characteristics as defined in the product specification for the relevant geographical indication. Any alteration to the established production methods, packaging, or presentation of such goods which deviates from the approved norms may be subject to review by the Registrar. The use of a geographical indication on goods not originating within the specified geographical area is strictly prohibited, provided that evidence demonstrating origin can be furnished upon request. Furthermore, any entity engaging in deceptive practices regarding the geographical indication use, including falsely claiming adherence to product specifications, shall be liable for penalties as determined under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses under this Act permitting the use of the indication in relation to goods conforming to the standards established for that indication, provided that such license specifies the terms and conditions governing its exercise. Any licensee shall be bound by these conditions and subject to inspection by the Registrar to ensure compliance. Assignment of a geographical indication or any associated rights, including licenses, requires prior approval from the Registrar, who may impose reasonable royalty obligations on subsequent transferees. Further, where a registered proprietor seeks to assign a license, they must provide detailed information regarding the consideration received and the intended use by the assignee. The Registrar shall have the power to refuse assignment if it deems such transfer detrimental to the reputation or quality associated with the geographical indication use.

The authorized user of a registered geographical indication shall not permit its use in relation to goods not conforming to the standards of quality, reputation, and other characteristics directly attributable to that geographical origin, provided that any person alleging such non-conformity may initiate proceedings before the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by both the complainant and the alleged infringer, including expert testimony regarding agricultural practices or traditional production methods. An appeal against an order of the Registrar determining a dispute concerning geographical indication use lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order; however, the Board’s decision shall be final subject to further judicial review under this Act on grounds limited to errors apparent on the face of the record.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act concerning the alleged improper geographical indication use relating to ‘Kashmir Apples’, direct the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating exclusive linkage between the goods and the specified territory. Such evidence shall include verifiable data on agricultural practices, unique environmental factors, and historical production records. The objector shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rebut such evidence through expert testimony; for this purpose, the Registrar may appoint independent scientific bodies possessing expertise in pomology and soil science. Any dispute arising from the assessment of said evidence may be referred to an appellate authority constituted as provided herein, whose decision shall be final subject to judicial review on limited grounds.

For the purposes of this Act, a “geographical indication” means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. An *indication use geographical* shall be deemed to qualify as a geographical indication only if such indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirits, beverages, herbs, spices, cereals, or manufactured articles having a distinctive name corresponding to a specific region or locality. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and their origin, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the connection is apparent from the geographical indication itself.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief in respect of any use calculated to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the said indication, even if such use does not constitute passing off. Any person who makes use of an identical or confusingly similar geographical indication relating to goods for which the indication is registered, or uses a geographical indication in contravention of conditions as provided herein, shall be liable to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Further, the Appellate Board may order such person to cease such use and destroy any infringing materials found in their possession. The right to prevent use of a geographical indication extends also to preventing misrepresentation that goods originate from the area associated with the said *indication use geographical*, subject to procedural safeguards ensuring fairness to accused parties.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses authorizing specific uses of the indication in relation to goods matching the description defined within the registration. Such licenses shall specify the duration, territorial extent, and permitted activities relating to production, processing, packing, conditioning, or marketing. Any assignment of rights under this Act pertaining to a geographical indication requires prior consent from the Registrar, who may impose conditions safeguarding the continued protection of the geographical indication’s reputation. The Registrar shall consider whether the proposed assignee possesses the requisite expertise and commitment to uphold quality standards associated with the indication use geographically. Further, any licensee or assignee is bound by the code of conduct established under this Act for goods bearing the registered geographical indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collective bodies representing such producers. The Registrar shall consider an application only if it is accompanied by evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the specified geographical area and that the applicant has the interest of the registered proprietor to protect the indication use geographical. Where multiple applications are received for the same geographical indication, the Registrar shall give preference to the applicant who can demonstrate a longer history of continuous use within the defined territory. Any company seeking registration must provide its certificate of incorporation and details of its governing body as part of the application process. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made in the application before proceeding with examination.

A good faith use of a name indicating the origin of goods does not constitute a falsification under this Act if such use is in accordance with equitable principles and established trade practices. For the purposes of this legislation, "falsifies genuine geographical indication" means any act which misrepresents or creates an erroneous impression regarding the true geographical origin of goods. This includes, but is not limited to, the application of a sign liable to be confused with a registered geographical indication, or the use of a mark that suggests such origin where it does not exist. Such acts shall prejudice the interests of the producers of the genuine product and mislead consumers as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused if the proposed name contains matter which is likely to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods indicated therein. Where an applicant seeks to register a geographical indication that, through its use in commerce, has come to identify goods not originating from the specified geographical area, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the applicant to demonstrate distinctive character and acquired reputation within the defined territory. The application may proceed only if such demonstration is satisfactory. Furthermore, any use of a geographical indication which falsifies genuine geographical indications relating to other products or services shall be considered an impediment to registration, subject to provisions regarding fair competition and consumer protection as provided herein.

Any individual or enterprise who knowingly uses a protected geographical indication in relation to goods not originating from the registered geographical territory, or employs such an indication in a manner that misrepresents the true origin of those goods, shall be liable for damages as provided herein. This includes instances where packaging, advertising, or labelling falsely suggests a connection to the registered area. Furthermore, any act which falsifies genuine geographical indications by way of imitation, colourable representation, or misleading association with the registered indication constitutes an infringement under this Act. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may issue cease and desist orders, direct destruction of infringing materials, and impose penalties not exceeding ten times the value of the infringing goods sold.

Any enterprise seeking registration of a geographical indication for agricultural produce relating to Alphonso mangoes shall demonstrate exclusive cultivation within the designated region of Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg districts in Maharashtra State. Such demonstration must include verifiable records maintained by registered farmer cooperatives, detailing planting material provenance and adherence to prescribed harvesting protocols as outlined under this Act. Further, any use of the geographical indication "Alphonso" on mangoes not meeting these criteria, or which otherwise falsifies genuine geographical indications relating to Alphonso mangoes through misleading packaging or promotional materials, shall be deemed an infringement. The Registrar may require submission of independent expert reports confirming compliance with cultivation and processing standards prior to granting registration, provided that such reports are submitted within sixty days of the application date.

Any enterprise found to utilize a registered geographical indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards established under this Act shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Geographical Indications Registry. Such enterprises may face fines up to five times the value of the infringing goods or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both, at the discretion of the court. Furthermore, any packaging, labeling, advertising, or promotional material employing a falsely applied geographical indication shall be subject to seizure and destruction. The authorized user of a geographical indication may initiate civil proceedings against those who falsifies genuine geographical indications, seeking injunctive relief and damages for loss of reputation and market share.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute an action in the High Court alleging that another party has engaged in deceptive practices undermining the distinctiveness and reputation associated with their protected designation. Such an action arises when it is demonstrated, through clear and convincing evidence, that goods or services offered by the respondent are presented as originating from the geographically defined area, thereby falsifies genuine geographical indications recognized under this Act. The respondent shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present counter-evidence establishing either lack of deceptive intent or demonstrating that their products possess characteristics substantially similar to those traditionally produced within the indicated region. Decisions regarding similarity and consumer confusion remain subject to judicial review on appeal.

A product shall be considered to bear a protected geographical indication where the name of the geographical origin is indicated in such a manner as to suggest that the goods originate from that place, subject to conditions prescribed under this Act. For the purposes of this provision, "falsify geographical indication" means any act which misrepresents the true and accurate geographical origin of goods, including but not limited to, using a name or mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered geographical indication without authorization. Such falsification extends to alterations, additions, or omissions that create an erroneous impression regarding the place of manufacture or production, provided that the intent is to deceive consumers as to the product’s origin.

Any goods or produce a mark which is likely to be mistaken for a registered geographical indication, or falsely suggest an association with such indication, shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant High Court. The authorised user of a geographical indication may institute proceedings against any person who falsifies that geographical indication and seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, due consideration shall be given to the extent of the loss suffered by the authorised user, including but not limited to lost profits and damage to reputation. Further, where an act of falsification is committed with fraudulent intent, the court may award punitive damages up to three times the actual damages proven. Nothing in this Act prevents a person from using their own trade name or trademark, subject to it not constituting a falsify geographical indication under this Act.

Any goods produced or traded in a manner which misrepresents their origin and utilizes a protected geographical indication shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an authorized user or any interested party demonstrating actual damage due to the deceptive use of a geographical indication, issue a notice requiring the alleged infringer to cease such activity within thirty days. Failure to comply with this notice will result in prosecution under this Act and subject the offender to fines not exceeding five lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. It is specifically prohibited to falsify geographical indications through packaging or advertising, creating an impression that goods originate from the registered area.

Any goods or services a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered geographical indication shall be guilty of an offence and liable to prosecution under this Act. It shall be a defence for the accused to prove that he had used the said mark in good faith prior to the registration of the geographical indication, provided that such use did not constitute an attempt to deceive consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. An appeal against any order made by the Registrar determining whether a particular act constitutes falsify geographical indication may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. The Appellate Board shall hear and dispose of such appeals expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice.

Any enterprise found to have knowingly used a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards established under this Act shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of reputation suffered by the registered proprietor, and any profits made as a result of the infringing use. Furthermore, where an infringer has employed a distinctive board use layout incorporating the protected geographical indication, the court may order its destruction or alteration to remove the deceptive element. The authorised user may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of falsify geographical indication, including the display or distribution of goods bearing the misleading mark. Provided that, nothing in this section shall prevent the fair and accurate reporting of facts relating to such infringing use.

For the purposes of this Act, a "registered geographical indication" includes any representation, mark, or sign which, when used in relation to goods for which the geographical indication is registered, refers directly or indirectly to the registration thereof. Such reference shall be considered a “registration referred fact.” The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that consumers associate the characteristics of the goods with their origin within the defined geographical area during the consideration of an application for registration. Further, any alteration or modification of a registered geographical indication which misleads consumers as to the true geographical origin of the goods is prohibited under this Act and shall be deemed detrimental to the reputation of the indication.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall include particulars demonstrating the qualitative and reputational characteristics attributable exclusively to the origin of the goods. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further evidence substantiating these claims, including historical records pertaining to cultivation practices and market presence. Where an objection is raised against the application based on a challenge to the asserted geographical boundaries, the applicant must submit documentation establishing the factual basis for those boundaries as a registration referred fact. This documentation shall be deemed sufficient if it comprises verifiable data from meteorological reports, soil surveys, or trade association records. The Registrar may conduct site visits to verify these details and consider expert opinions in assessing the validity of the application.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall include detailed documentation substantiating the unique qualities and characteristics attributable solely to the specified geographical area. Such documentation must be verified by an authorized consortium representing growers within the defined region; failure to provide such verification will render the application ineligible for consideration under this Act. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating continued adherence to traditional production methods, provided that any alterations to these methods are disclosed and assessed for their impact on the geographical indication's distinctiveness. A ‘registration referred fact’ concerning a prior use of the name shall be considered only if it is accompanied by affidavits from at least three producers actively engaged in cultivation within the relevant territory.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising out of orders concerning rectification proceedings and disputes relating to consumer legal metrology marks. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act, or any condition imposed during registration, shall constitute an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the Appellate Board finds that a registered geographical indication has been used in contravention of provisions relating to unfair competition, it may order cessation of such use and impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees. The existence of a registration referred fact shall be conclusive evidence for all purposes as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include a statement affirming the historical production and characteristics of the goods associated with the indicated territory. Such affirmation shall be accompanied by documentary evidence establishing the continuous use of the geographical indication in connection with those goods over a period not less than five years preceding the date of the application. The Registrar, upon receiving an application containing a registration referred fact, may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or submit additional documentation substantiating the claims made therein. Failure to comply with such requirements within the prescribed time shall render the application liable for rejection. Where the geographical indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuff or wine, patent shall not be granted in respect of that product if it conflicts with the registered geographical indication. The Registrar may, at any stage, seek expert opinion on the veracity of the registration referred fact presented.

The Register shall, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party alleging misrepresentation made by a registered user during the registration process, initiate inquiries as provided herein. Such complaints must specify the nature of the alleged misrepresentation and demonstrate its material impact on the validity of the layout-design registration. If, following due inquiry, it is established that a registered user misrepresented facts concerning prior publication or existing similar designs to obtain registration under this Act, the Register may issue a notice requiring rectification within ninety days. Failure to rectify the record as directed shall render the registration liable for cancellation. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to submit evidence and arguments during these proceedings, subject to procedural fairness.

Where a registered user, having obtained registration under this Act, makes a representation to a third party concerning the availability and suitability for use of a protected integrated circuit layout design, such representation shall constitute a material fact. If it is subsequently determined that the registered user misrepresented the nature or extent of protection afforded by the registration, or falsely asserted rights not vested in them as per the register, the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party and after affording the registered user an opportunity for hearing, issue a direction to rectify the public record. Such rectification shall include a notation indicating the specific misrepresentation made. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek redressal under general principles of law regarding damages arising from such misrepresentation; provided that any action taken by the Registrar does not preclude recourse to civil courts.

Where a registered user, having obtained registration under this Act for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, subsequently engages in commercial activities utilizing said design, they shall not represent to any person that their use is authorized by the original registrant unless such authorization has been expressly granted and documented. Any misrepresentation made by a registered user concerning the legitimacy of their usage, whether through advertising, product labeling, or other promotional materials, constitutes a violation under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from the original registrant demonstrating such a registered user misrepresented the scope of their permitted use, initiate an inquiry and, if found to be substantiated, impose penalties as provided herein.

Where a registered user alleges that the original registrant has, subsequent to registration and without consent, engaged in acts restricted under this Act, the registered user shall file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within ninety days of becoming aware of such acts. The Tribunal may, after affording both parties an opportunity for being heard, direct the respondent registrant to cease the infringing activity and award compensation for demonstrable losses suffered by the appellant. However, if it is established that the registered user misrepresented material facts during their application for registration as a registered user, rendering their claim untenable, the appeal shall be dismissed summarily, subject to a reasoned order detailing the specific misrepresentation.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to rectification or invalidation of a registered layout-design is dissatisfied, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall have the power to entertain appeals from orders concerning infringement proceedings as well, provided that the appeal is made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Subject to just cause shown, delays in filing an appeal beyond this period shall not be entertained. The Tribunal may, while hearing an appeal, require the appellant to furnish security for costs and damages. Further, a *functions judicial member* of the Tribunal shall possess such qualifications as prescribed by the Central Government regulations concerning expertise in intellectual property law or related fields.

The Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal shall exercise original jurisdiction in matters concerning alleged infringement of layout-designs registered under this Act. The Tribunal shall comprise a Chairperson appointed by notification of the Central Government, and such number of Technical Members and a *functions judicial member* as the Central Government considers necessary for efficient disposal of cases. Proceedings before the Tribunal shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, and parties are entitled to representation by advocates authorized under the Advocates Act. The Chairperson may, at their discretion, permit expert witnesses to provide testimony relevant to technical aspects of layout-design functionality. Decisions of the Tribunal shall be appealable to the High Court within a period specified herein, subject to prescribed limitations on grounds for appeal. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding case management and procedural timelines to ensure expeditious resolution of disputes as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or concerning rectification proceedings may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal shall be duly constituted with a Chairperson and at least two other members, including a *functions judicial member* possessing expertise in intellectual property law. Appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to file an appeal within this period shall ordinarily preclude further recourse under this Act. Where the aggrieved party is located in a *Contracting Party*, as defined under Article 1(1) of the Paris Convention, the Appellate Tribunal may consider relevant jurisprudence and administrative practices of that Contracting Party when determining the merits of the appeal. Penalties for non-compliance with orders of the Appellate Tribunal shall be determined as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall accompany a detailed technical specification outlining the architecture and functionality of the design, prepared by a qualified engineer or technologist. The Registrar may require submission of additional documentation demonstrating originality and inventive step, particularly where the layout incorporates elements derived from previously registered designs. Consideration will be given to whether the applicant possesses sufficient expertise in integrated circuit technology to warrant registration under this Act; accordingly, the presence of a designated *judicial member technical* within the applicant’s team shall be viewed favorably during assessment. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the layout-design lacks substantial novelty or infringes upon existing intellectual property rights as provided herein.

Where infringement of layout-design rights has occurred, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. Such remedies include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further manufacture, import, sale, offer for sale, or hire of the infringing integrated circuit layout-design. Damages recoverable shall be assessed at a rate not exceeding three times the actual cost incurred by the proprietor in establishing and protecting their rights under this Act, or where such costs cannot be ascertained, an amount determined to be just and reasonable considering factors such as lost profits and the infringer’s gain. The Central Government may, upon application of any party, appoint a judicial member technical to assist the relevant court in determining complex issues relating to semiconductor technology involved in infringement proceedings.

Where an investigation is initiated under this Act concerning alleged infringement of a registered layout-design, the Intellectual Property Office shall provide all relevant documentation pertaining to the registration, including technical specifications and design schematics, to the appointed judicial member technical. The judicial member technical may request further clarification or supplementary information from either the complainant or the respondent, provided that such requests are limited to matters directly impacting the determination of infringement. Any expert testimony presented must be accompanied by a written report detailing the methodology employed and the basis for conclusions reached; this shall be accessible to both parties under this Act. The Intellectual Property Office shall ensure compliance with procedural timelines as prescribed herein.

Where the registered owner of a layout-design for a semiconductor integrated circuit desires to grant a license or assign their rights under this Act, such license agreement or assignment deed shall clearly specify the scope of permitted acts, including but not limited to reproduction, modification, and commercial use. The consideration provided in any such transaction is subject to fair market value as determined by an independent valuation expert appointed jointly by the licensor and licensee, or assignor and assignee. Any transfer of rights must be registered with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, providing details of the judicial member technical expertise consulted during the assessment of the layout-design’s commercial potential. Failure to register such a transaction within six months shall render it voidable at the option of the non-transferring party, provided that due notice is given.

The Authority Appellate Board is constituted for adjudicating disputes arising under this Act concerning layout-design registrations or related matters. The Chairperson of the Board shall be a retired Judge of a High Court, appointed by notification in the Official Gazette. Members of the Board shall include individuals possessing specialized knowledge and experience in semiconductor technology, intellectual property law, or industrial design, as determined by the Central Government. Decisions of the Authority Appellate Board shall be binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal to such higher judicial forum as may be prescribed under this Act. The Board’s proceedings shall adhere to principles of natural justice.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout-design under this Act. Any applicant aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appeal shall be disposed of as expeditiously as possible, and the Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeals only on a point of law to the High Court. The Board may, while hearing an appeal, require the production of relevant documents or call upon any person to furnish information deemed necessary for the purpose of the inquiry.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or rectification proceedings, including orders concerning interim injunctions or damages awards, desires to appeal, such person may file an application for appeal before the Authority Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of service of the order. The Board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising out of any decision or direction made by the Registrar or Controller under this Act. Subject to just and equitable considerations, the Board may allow a further opportunity to be heard where it finds that a party was substantially prejudiced due to non-compliance with principles of natural justice. Any order passed by the Authority Appellate Board shall be final subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order, provided that no appeal shall lie against any interlocutory order.

An appeal lies to the Authority Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to revocation of registration or rectification of layout-design registrations. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order appealed against, and the appellant may file such appeals in the prescribed form along with a copy of the order sought to be appealed. The Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Subject to this, the Board shall hear parties and evidence adduced before it, and may pass such orders as it deems just and equitable. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Authority Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall record its reasons for decision in writing, provided that any confidential information disclosed during proceedings shall be treated accordingly.

An appeal against any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design shall lie to the Authority Appellate Board. The appellant shall, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an application for appeal with the Board, accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that sufficient cause existed, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period. The Board may, while hearing appeals, require the appellant and respondent to furnish further information or documents relevant to the determination of the dispute. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Authority Appellate Board may apply to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act by the Registrar or any other officer authorized in that behalf may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appeal shall be admitted only if the Appellant deposits with the Appeal, a sum equivalent to twenty-five percent of the penalty imposed, provided that the Board may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, waive or reduce this deposit. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Authority Appellate Board shall have the power to pass such orders as it deems fit, including affirming, modifying, or reversing the order appealed from and may impose a further penalty not exceeding the amount originally prescribed under this Act for non-compliance.

The right to grant licenses relating to integrated circuit layout-designs registered under this Act may be assigned or transferred subject to approval from the relevant Registering Authority, provided that such assignment or transfer is documented in writing and submitted for registration. Any person claiming to be aggrieved by a decision of the Registering Authority concerning the validity of an assignment or license shall have recourse to appeal before the authority appellate board. The authority appellate board may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Further, any licensee seeking sub-licensing rights must obtain prior consent from the layout-design owner and notify the Registering Authority accordingly; failure to do so shall render such sub-license void under this Act.

An appeal lies to the Authority Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design, or concerning allegations of infringement where preliminary relief has been granted. The aggrieved party may prefer such an appeal within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of said period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal in a timely manner. Decisions of the Authority Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to further review only upon demonstration of perversity or demonstrable error of law. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned before any hearing takes place.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or concerning the validity of a registered layout-design may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appeal shall be admitted only if the Appellant deposits with the Board, as per rules framed thereunder, such sum as determined by the Central Government; failure to do so will render the appeal inadmissible. Where an infringement involves a distinct denomination variety of a layout-design, the Board may, in addition to any other penalty prescribed under this Act, impose a further pecuniary sanction not exceeding five times the cost of reproduction and distribution of the infringing layout-design. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal only to the High Court within ninety days.

The registered layout-design owner shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses for the use or exploitation of their protected integrated circuit layout design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Any assignment of such rights, including licensing agreements, must be executed in writing and attested by a notary public, and a certified copy thereof submitted to the Registrar within thirty days of execution. Where a license is granted permitting reproduction or adaptation of the registered layout-design, the licensee shall remain bound by any restrictions expressly stated therein. Should the Registrar determine that a cancelled registrar layout has been improperly assigned or licensed in contravention of this Act, they may initiate proceedings before the Authority Appellate Board for review and rectification. The Board’s decision on matters concerning licensing validity is final.

An appeal lies to the Authority Appellate Board from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to the registration of a layout-design or concerning rectification proceedings initiated against a proprietor registered trade mark incorporated within a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order appealed against, and the Board may, if it considers expedient so to do, entertain appeals received after the expiry of that period if satisfactory reasons are shown for the delay. The Authority Appellate Board may call for such records or evidence as it deems necessary for the purpose of hearing an appeal, and shall have the same powers as a civil court trying cases under code of civil procedure, 1908.

For the purposes of adjudicating disputes under this Act relating to infringement or validity of registered layout-designs, there shall be constituted a member appointed bench known as the Layout-Design Adjudication Tribunal. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish such number of Benches as it deems necessary for expeditious disposal of cases. Each Bench shall comprise at least one Judicial Member and two Technical Members, all possessing expertise in semiconductor technology or intellectual property law, as provided herein. Decisions of a member appointed bench shall be final subject to appeal under the provisions relating to appeals against orders of the Controller.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall accompany a certified copy of the appointment notification pertaining to any member appointed bench constituted under this Act to hear appeals against decisions concerning the validity of the layout-design. Provided that, where such notification is not readily available, an affidavit from the applicant confirming the existence and composition of the relevant member appointed bench may be submitted in lieu thereof. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity of the submission. Any alteration or modification to a registered layout-design shall necessitate a fresh application subject to the same requirements concerning notification verification as provided herein, ensuring continued compliance with the provisions relating to registration and protection under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or rectification proceedings seeks redressal, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall constitute a member appointed bench for hearing appeals concerning semiconductor integrated circuit layout designs, ensuring specialized expertise in technological and legal matters relevant to these disputes. Provided that, where the appeal involves questions of fact requiring extensive technical evaluation, the Tribunal may appoint expert assessors to assist the bench. Any order passed by the Tribunal affirming or reversing a decision of the Controller shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The aggrieved party shall have the right to present evidence and arguments before the member appointed bench as provided herein.

The Intellectual Property Disputes Resolution Tribunal shall exercise original jurisdiction in matters concerning infringement of layout-design rights under this Act. The Central Government shall, from time to time, constitute a member appointed bench for hearing appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar or any other authority empowered to adjudicate upon such matters. Such a bench shall be comprised of one Judicial Member and two Technical Members, each possessing expertise in semiconductor technology or intellectual property law as determined by the government notification. The Chairperson of the Tribunal may constitute benches as deemed necessary for efficient disposal of cases, provided that no bench shall sit without at least three members present. Decisions of the member appointed bench shall be made by a majority vote and recorded in writing, including reasons for the decision. Parties aggrieved by any order of the Tribunal may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order as provided herein.

Where any question arises concerning the validity of a registered layout-design or relating to infringement proceedings under this Act, such question shall be referred for determination to a member appointed bench constituted by the Controller. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the composition of such benches, provided that at least one member shall possess demonstrable experience in semiconductor technology or integrated circuit design. Any appeal from an order passed by the Controller concerning the rectification of a registered layout-design shall be heard and determined by a member appointed bench. The Registrar shall furnish all relevant records to the designated bench within thirty days of notification regarding the reference, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement or suspected infringement of a registered layout-design may appeal to a member appointed bench constituted for that purpose. The Central Government shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish such benches as it deems necessary for expeditious disposal of appeals. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during investigation and adjudication of claims concerning layout-design rights shall render any order susceptible to challenge under this Act. Any party found to have wilfully violated provisions relating to layout-design protection shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, and repeat offenders may face further penalties as determined by the member appointed bench.

Where a layout-design owner grants a license conferring rights to utilize a protected integrated circuit layout design for commercial purposes, such license agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and distribution. Assignment of ownership or any portion thereof under this Act requires registration with the Controller General, provided that prior consent from all registered licensees must be obtained unless expressly waived in writing by each licensee. Failure to secure such consent may render the assignment voidable at the option of an aggrieved licensee. Disputes concerning the validity or interpretation of license agreements and assignments shall be referred to a member appointed bench constituted under this Act for resolution, ensuring equitable consideration of both the layout-design owner’s rights and the licensees' legitimate expectations.

Where an appeal is filed under this Act against any order passed by the Registrar relating to the validity of a registered layout-design or concerning infringement proceedings, the appeal shall be heard and disposed of by a member appointed bench constituted by the Appellate Tribunal. Provided that, where the matter involves intricate questions of fact pertaining to the originality of a layout-design, the Chairperson of the Appellate Tribunal may, at his discretion, constitute a Bench comprising two Judicial Members and one Technical Member. The decision of such a member appointed bench shall be final, subject to appeal before the High Court only on grounds of legal error apparent on the face of the record. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Tribunal may seek review within sixty days as provided herein.

For the purposes of adjudicating disputes concerning infringement or violation of layout-design rights under this Act, there shall be constituted a ‘Member Appointed Bench’. A Member Appointed Bench shall comprise such number of Members as the Central Government considers appropriate, appointed from amongst individuals possessing expertise in semiconductor technology, intellectual property law, or related fields. The constitution and functioning of each Member Appointed Bench may be determined by rules made under this Act. Decisions of a Member Appointed Bench shall be binding subject to appeal before the relevant judicial forum. Consideration will always be given to matters affecting the security of India when interpreting provisions relating to layout-design protection.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or rectification proceedings seeks redressal, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall be duly constituted for each hearing with at least one chairperson and a single judicial member appointed in accordance with established procedures as provided herein. Any party dissatisfied with the findings of the Tribunal concerning damages awarded for wilful infringement is further entitled to petition the Supreme Court on grounds of law alone, subject to payment of prescribed costs. The tribunal shall ensure that interim orders regarding injunctions or preservation of evidence are promptly addressed and enforced, safeguarding the layout-design right holder’s interests pending final adjudication. Decisions made by a Tribunal bench, including those involving a chairperson judicial member, are binding unless overturned on appeal.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars relating to its denomination, geographical area where it is cultivated, and details concerning its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information or documentation deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall initiate proceedings for examination, including verification of claimed characteristics and evaluation against established criteria. A key component of registration is varieties compulsory cataloguing; all registered varieties must be included in the National Plant Variety Catalogue maintained by the Authority. This catalogue will serve as a public record accessible to breeders, researchers, and farmers, facilitating transparency and promoting informed decision-making regarding plant variety selection.

An application for inclusion of a farmer’s variety in the Register of Farmers' Varieties shall be made to the Authority in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The application must specify the name, address, and occupation of the farmer claiming rights over the variety, along with a detailed description encompassing its morphological characteristics, cultivation practices employed, and geographical area where it is predominantly grown. Documentation substantiating traditional knowledge relating to the variety’s origin and propagation shall also accompany the submission. Subject to verification by the Authority through field evaluation and documentation as provided herein, successful applicants shall be entered into the Register, granting them recognition for their stewardship of cataloguing farmers varieties and associated rights under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the recognition or rejection of a farmers’ variety, or concerning any infringement of rights pertaining thereto, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and conduct a judicial proceeding affording them reasonable opportunity for being heard. Failure to comply with the provisions regarding farmers varieties compulsory cultivation as stipulated by the Authority shall render the cultivator liable to pay compensation, determined at the discretion of the Board, not exceeding five thousand rupees per instance of non-compliance. Repeated violations may attract further penalties, including revocation of registration privileges and prohibition from participating in subsequent variety recognition processes.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its genetic composition, lineage tracing back at least three generations, and demonstrated stability across multiple growing seasons. The application must also specify the geographical area within which the applicant intends to commercialize the registered variety. Subject to verification by the Examining Authority, applicants demonstrating adherence to established protocols for maintaining breeder’s records may be granted provisional registration pending full phenotypic evaluation. Registration shall confer upon the registrant exclusive rights relating to the production, sale, and distribution of propagating material of the protected varieties plants ensuring their integrity and preventing unauthorized exploitation. Provided that farmers' rights, including privilege in saving, exchanging, and cultivating seed, are not prejudiced by such registration.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a plant variety protection, or concerning the infringement of farmers’ rights pertaining to the saving and exchange of seed, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising in relation to the impugned order, subject to the provisions regarding evidence as provided herein. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the registration process concerning varieties plants ensuring their distinctiveness and stability may render a protection vulnerable to challenge under this Act. Remedies for infringement include injunctions preventing further unauthorized use and compensation determined by the Board, considering factors such as loss of profits and damage to reputation.

A plant breeder shall be eligible for grant of protection under this Act if the variety possesses a distinctive novelty, uniformity and stability, and satisfies conditions as provided herein. The application for such protection must specify the denomination of the variety and include detailed information regarding its genetic composition, method of production, and any relevant phenotypic characteristics demonstrating adherence to established standards. Protection shall not be granted where the variety is demonstrably identical to an extant variety, or where it has been obtained through means prohibited under this Act. Farmers’ rights concerning varieties plants ensuring seed saving, exchange and cultivation are guaranteed subject to compliance with bio-security protocols outlined by the National Gene Bank.

Any person who knowingly makes or deals with any plant material derived from a registered variety, infringing the breeder’s rights under this Act, shall be liable to pay compensation equivalent to three times the total value of such infringing plant material. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized multiplication and sale of propagating material involving protected varieties plants ensuring genetic purity, issue an order directing the cessation of such activities and impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of violation. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender subject to further penalties, including imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. The Authority is empowered to recover costs incurred in investigations related to these infringements.

The proprietor of a registered variety shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring rights to exploit the breeding material derived from such variety, subject to conditions as provided herein. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to a plant variety shall include all rights pertaining to derivative materials and subsequent generations thereof, unless specifically excluded in the instrument of assignment. Where a license is granted for research purposes concerning the creation of new varieties plants ensuring genetic improvement, the licensee may utilize propagating material without royalty payments during the term of the research activity. Provided that, commercial exploitation of resultant varieties derived from such licensed research shall be subject to royalty obligations as negotiated between the proprietor and the licensee. The terms of any license or assignment are binding on all successors and assigns, and may be enforced through appropriate legal proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a plant variety shall mean that the variety exhibits characteristics which differentiate it from other known varieties and are readily reproducible. A plant variety shall be deemed not to possess distinctiveness if its phenotypic expression is solely due to growing conditions or environmental factors. The term "essentially derived variety" means a plant variety that is not distinctly different from a donor variety but retains the genetic traits of the donor variety, subject to permitted variations arising during propagation or cultivation. Any variety exhibiting such characteristics shall be considered to regard plant varieties as essentially derived under this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed under this Act, including morphological characteristics and essential derivation data. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding the expression of traits relevant to distinguishing the plant variety from existing ones. Any applicant demonstrating that their plant variety is essentially derived from an extant variety through conventional breeding techniques shall provide evidence substantiating such derivation, detailing parentage and selection processes. Registration of a plant variety does not grant exclusive rights over any traditional knowledge associated with it; such knowledge remains freely accessible to farming communities as provided herein. The Registrar may refuse registration if the claimed novelty is deemed insufficient or if the application fails to adequately regard plant varieties already documented in the National Register.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of a plant variety protection, or concerning any infringement of farmers’ rights regarding regard plant varieties, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony pertaining to genetic stability and distinctiveness. Subject to just considerations, the Board may affirm, reverse, or modify the original order. Failure to comply with a cease-and-desist order issued by the Board concerning unauthorized propagation of protected plant varieties shall render the offender liable to pay damages as determined by the Board, provided that such damages shall not exceed five times the value of the infringing material.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming rights in a plant variety shall file an application with the Authority specifying details including the denomination proposed for the plant variety, its genetic composition as ascertained through analysis, and the source material from which it was derived. The application must also include particulars regarding the stability of the characteristics of the plant variety across successive generations, demonstrated by data collected over at least three growing seasons. Further, where the plant variety is a result of genetic modification, such information shall be disclosed with full documentation pertaining to the introduced genes and their expression. Registration of regard plant varieties will only proceed upon verification that the applicant fulfills all prescribed conditions concerning prior disclosure and novelty.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a person claiming rights in a plant variety shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the commercial exploitation of that variety. Such licenses may include, but are not limited to, rights pertaining to seed production, distribution, or sale, and shall specify the geographical area within which such rights are exercisable. Assignment of rights in a plant variety, including all associated licensing entitlements, may be effected by way of a registered instrument, provided that prior consent of the Registrar is obtained. Any transfer or assignment shall include details regarding any restrictions imposed on subsequent dealings with the plant variety and its derived varieties. The Registrar may impose conditions relating to royalty payments and benefit-sharing arrangements as deemed necessary to protect farmers’ rights in regard plant varieties.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the grant or refusal of protection in regard plant varieties, or concerning conditions attached thereto, appeals to the Appellate Board, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days, subject to just cause shown. Decisions of the High Court shall be final. The Authority shall provide reasons for any decision taken concerning eligibility criteria for protection.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming rights in a plant variety shall file an application with the Authority specifying details regarding its genetic composition, expression potential, and stability across diverse agro-climatic conditions. Such applications must include documentation demonstrating compliance with established protocols for novelty assessment and freedom from restriction concerning prior dissemination. The Authority may, after due inquiry and providing opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, grant protection in regard plant varieties meeting the prescribed criteria. Further, where a compelling need arises to address situations of public interest, including food security or access to essential medicines derived from protected plant material, the central government may grant a compulsory licence under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a person claiming rights in a plant variety shall be entitled to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the multiplication, sale, distribution, or export of propagating material of that regard plant varieties. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding five years, renewable by mutual agreement between the licensor and licensee. Any assignment of rights under this Act concerning a registered variety shall require prior notification to the Authority, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the assigned rights. Further, any judicial proceeding relating to infringement of plant variety protection shall be subject to mediation as an initial step, with failure to reach amicable resolution leading to adjudication by the designated court. The terms of such licenses and assignments are governed by principles of fairness and transparency as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an entitled produce variety shall mean a plant variety that has been formally recorded in the Register as fulfilling the conditions specified under this Act and which demonstrates stability and uniformity across generations. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Committee, grant entitlement to a produce variety if it is demonstrably distinct from all other varieties registered prior to the date of such application. Further, an entitled produce variety shall be eligible for benefit under provisions relating to farmers’ rights concerning saved seed, provided that the applicant provides evidence of cultivation and propagation practices consistent with good agricultural practice.

An application for registration as an entitled produce variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, lineage where ascertainable, and distinctive characteristics observable under normal growing conditions. The application must also specify the geographical area within which the applicant exercises effective control over the production and marketing of the entitled produce variety. Further particulars regarding the method of propagation employed shall be submitted to facilitate assessment of genetic stability. Provided that an applicant demonstrating substantial investment in research and development relating to the variety may request confidential treatment of certain technical data, subject to review by the Examining Officer. The Registrar may require additional information or clarification as deemed necessary for a complete evaluation under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing protection for an entitled produce variety, or by any condition attached thereto, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed against and may confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed from, subject to just considerations of fairness and equity. Where a farmer alleges infringement of his right to save, reuse, exchange or share farm saved seed of an entitled produce variety, he may institute civil proceedings for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. The burden of proving such infringement shall lie upon the claimant, and any award of damages shall be proportionate to the loss suffered by the farmer.

The application for grant of protection relating to an entitled produce variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its botanical name, parentage, method of propagation and any distinctive characteristics which clearly identify it. The applicant shall also furnish documentation demonstrating that the variety has been duly tested and evaluated in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Plant Variety Protection Board. Upon receipt of an application, the Board may direct the applicant to submit further information or clarification concerning the entitled produce variety’s stability, uniformity and distinctiveness. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Board relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Board shall maintain a register of applications and granted protections, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

A plant variety shall be deemed an entitled produce variety if it has been cultivated by a farmer for less than twenty years from its first cultivation and demonstrates consistent expression of essential characteristics conforming to established descriptors as approved by the Central Government. Provided that, where the farmer cultivates the variety through propagation or division of parental plants, the period of twenty years shall be calculated from the date of initial propagation. Further, eligibility as an entitled produce variety is contingent upon a declaration confirming absence of intentional alteration of genetic material under this Act and adherence to prescribed bio-containment protocols if genetically modified techniques were employed during its development. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines for verification of such declarations.

Any person who knowingly markets seeds or other propagating material of an entitled produce variety which he knows or has reason to believe to be infringing under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees, and such amount may be recovered as if it were a decree of a civil court. Further, any officer in charge of a seed production unit found to have facilitated the unlawful marketing of an entitled produce variety shall face suspension from service for a period determined by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board. Repeated contravention of these provisions may result in revocation of registration and imposition of additional penalties as provided herein, taking into account the extent of damage caused to registered breeders and farmers’ rights.

The proprietor of an entitled produce variety shall be deemed to hold exclusive rights pertaining to its propagation, subject to any conditions stipulated within the grant certificate. Such rights extend to the production and sale of seeds or planting material derived from the entitled produce variety, provided that a written license agreement is executed with any entity seeking to undertake such activities. Any assignment of these rights must be registered with the Plant Varieties Registry, detailing the scope of transfer and associated royalties payable to the original proprietor. Further, under this Act, the Registrar may grant compulsory licenses for the production and sale of seeds of an entitled produce variety in circumstances where the proprietor has failed to adequately serve the needs of farmers within a designated geographical area, as determined by the relevant Agricultural Committee.

The term "entitled produce variety" shall mean a plant variety which has been formally registered under this Act and whose rights are vested in a breeder or other eligible person, subject to any conditions stipulated during registration. Any person claiming entitlement to an entitled produce variety may institute proceedings before the Appellate Board alleging infringement of their rights by another party cultivating, selling, or distributing propagating material derived from that variety without authorization. Provided that such claim must be substantiated with documentary evidence demonstrating prior registration and continued adherence to the terms outlined therein. The Board shall consider any counter-claims presented by the alleged infringer asserting bona fide use or customary cultivation practices predating the registration of the entitled produce variety, as provided herein.

An entitled produce variety shall be deemed eligible for protection under this Act if it demonstrates stability, uniformity and predictability of inheritance as certified by an appropriate examining authority. The application for entitlement must include a detailed specification claim outlining distinctive characteristics, including but not limited to morphological traits, disease resistance profiles, and yield data obtained from replicated field trials conducted over at least three successive seasons in diverse agro-climatic zones. Provided that the applicant shall furnish evidence of adherence to Good Agricultural Practices throughout the trial period. Further, any prior disclosure or publication concerning the entitled produce variety before the date of application will be considered as a bar to entitlement unless such disclosure was made under conditions of confidentiality and with the express written consent of the prospective applicant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title to an entitled produce variety shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the variety. Such license may include the right to sell, import, or otherwise commercially utilize seeds or other propagating material derived from the entitled produce variety. The grantor of such a license may impose reasonable conditions relating to royalty payments and reporting requirements as provided herein. Further, an exclusive licensee shall be afforded the same protections against infringement under this Act as would accrue to the holder of title itself, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the licensing agreement. Assignment of rights pertaining to an entitled produce variety is permissible, but must be registered with the designated authority prior to becoming effective against third parties. Any transfer or assignment shall not prejudice existing farmers’ rights relating to saved seed.

For the purposes of this Act, an “entitled produce variety” shall mean a plant variety that has been formally registered under this Act and which is demonstrably derived from a protected variety through subsequent generations, subject to meeting established criteria regarding genetic stability as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating such derivation, including but not limited to molecular marker data and pedigree records. Further, the rights holder of an entitled produce variety shall be deemed to possess certain exclusive privileges concerning its propagation and distribution, notwithstanding any existing copyrights appellate decisions pertaining to similar subject matter.

An application for registration of an entitled produce variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant material, including its morphological characteristics and any distinctive features differentiating it from other known varieties. The applicant must also submit data demonstrating genetic stability and uniformity across generations. Upon receipt of an application, the Plant Varieties Registrar may direct that particulars relating to the entitled produce variety be entered into the computer inspection register for public access. Any person aggrieved by an entry in the register may appeal to the Authority within sixty days from the date of such entry. The registrar shall maintain a record of all appeals and their resolutions as part of the computer inspection register, accessible subject to reasonable restrictions.

A breeder's right shall confer upon the breeder exclusive rights to produce, sell, import, and export the plant variety, subject to conditions as provided herein. For the purpose of this Act, a “breeder” includes any person who has exercised his skill and ingenuity in developing a new variety or for whom such skill and ingenuity has been exercised. The right shall extend to the harvested material of the variety, unless otherwise specified by notification under this Act.
