Any party aggrieved by a decision under this provision relating to registration common regulations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "registration common regulations" are established to ensure uniformity in procedures relating to the acceptance and processing of applications for registration of trade marks. An application shall be deemed improperly filed if it does not comply with prescribed forms or contains information manifestly incomplete or inaccurate. Further, under this Act, any applicant seeking registration may elect to designate goods or services according to specified classes as defined by the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register geographical indications, distinct from the principal trade marks registry, for recording such designations.

A registered trade mark may be assigned or transmitted by any means whatsoever, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties. For the purposes of this Act, a “transmissible case” shall mean an instance where the assignor or transferor has not actively used the trade mark for a continuous period exceeding five years immediately preceding the assignment or transmission, and there exists demonstrable evidence indicating a likelihood of consumer confusion arising from such inactivity. Provided that, any assignment or transmission in a transmissible case may be opposed by interested parties under this Act within ninety days of its public notice.

The registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any rights prior existing. An application for registration may be assigned or transmitted by way of mortgage, pledge or otherwise, provided that such assignment or transmission does not affect the validity of the registration itself. Where a trade mark has been used continuously by the previous proprietor and the subsequent assignee or transferee ceases such use within the period specified under this Act, the right to use the trade mark may revert to the original registered proprietor. A transmissible case arises when an application for registration is assigned before its acceptance, and the assignor retains a continuing interest in the outcome of that application.

The right to utilize a registered trade mark is subject to the limitations prescribed herein and may be transferred by way of absolute or conditional assignment, license, or other means consistent with established commercial practice. Provided that any such transfer shall only vest upon registration of the instrument effecting the transfer with the Trade Marks Registry, and failure to register will render the transfer void. Where a trade mark has been used in connection with goods or services without consent, and subsequent ownership is transferred, the incoming proprietor shall be liable for all acts committed by the previous owner prior to the date of registration of the transfer. This includes actions constituting infringement under this Act. A transmissible case arises when a registered trade mark’s rights are assigned while ongoing disputes regarding its validity or use remain unresolved; such cases require judicial determination before full ownership transfers.

The right to utilize a registered trademark is subject to transfer by way of assignment or transmission, provided that such transfer does not prejudice existing rights under this Act. An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed a transmissible case upon notification to the Registrar, specifying the proposed assignee or transferee and detailing the extent of the rights being conveyed. The Registrar may require verification of consent from any registered proprietor whose interests might be affected by such transmission. Any objection to the transfer must be filed within thirty days of publication of the notice in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to file an objection within this period shall preclude further challenge to the validity of the assignment or transmission. The Registrar, after considering all objections and relevant documentation, may approve or reject the proposed transfer.

A registered trademark may be transmitted by operation of law or otherwise, subject to compliance with the provisions herein relating to registration. Transmission shall only occur where the assignee undertakes all obligations and liabilities associated with the mark’s prior use and maintenance under this Act. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating such acceptance before registering the transmission. A transmissible case arises when a trademark owner seeks to transfer rights to another party, provided that the proposed assignee possesses the legal capacity to utilize the mark in conformity with existing regulations concerning fair trade practices and consumer protection. Further, any alteration of goods or services associated with the trademark following transmission shall require prior approval from the Registrar.

The registration of a trademark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trademark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and any use of an identical or confusingly similar mark relating to those goods or services without due cause shall constitute infringement. Where a trademark has been assigned or transmitted, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities under this Act, the assignee or transferee shall be deemed a successor in title to the original proprietor and possess all rights and remedies pertaining thereto. A transmissible case arising from an alleged infringement may be pursued by either the registered proprietor or their duly authorized assignee for recovery of damages and equitable relief as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions will render any subsequent enforcement action voidable.

The right to use a registered trade mark may be assigned or transmitted by the proprietor subject to the provisions herein. Where such an assignment or transmission involves a transfer of the entire business undertaking, including all assets and liabilities associated with the use of the trade mark, it shall constitute a transmissible case and is deemed to include goodwill. Provided that, any subsequent assignee or transferee may only exercise those rights explicitly conveyed in the instrument of assignment or transmission. The Registrar may require evidence satisfactory to him demonstrating the continuity of business operations following such transfer, particularly where the registered proprietor’s activities have ceased. Further, an assignment or transmission shall not be effective against third parties until its details are duly registered with the Registrar within three months from the date of execution, as provided herein.

The right to institute proceedings under this Act relating to any registered trade mark shall vest with the assignee or transferee where such assignment or transmission has been duly recorded. Provided that, in cases involving conflicting claims regarding the ownership of a transmissible case arising from an alleged fraudulent transfer, the Registrar may require both claimants to submit evidence substantiating their respective rights. Further, if it appears to the Registrar that the purported transfer was intended to circumvent any order made under this Act or to prejudice the interests of any other party, he shall notify all concerned and reserve the right to adjudicate on the validity of the transfer before determining the rightful claimant. Any decision taken by the Registrar concerning such a transmissible case is subject to appeal to the relevant appellate authority.

The right accruing to the proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be subject to transmissibility under this Act, whether by way of absolute transfer, license, pledge or any other means. Where an artistic work incorporates a registrable trade mark and such work is assigned or transmitted alongside the trade mark, the assignee or transferee shall acquire rights pertaining solely to the trade mark, provided that the assignment or transmission does not prejudice existing rights in the underlying artistic work held by another party. A transmissible case arises when a registered trade mark, used in connection with goods or services, is transferred and the subsequent proprietor continues use of said mark without demonstrable dilution of reputation. Any person aggrieved by an unauthorized transfer may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The Registrar may require proof of consent from prior proprietors before registering any such transmission.

A registered trade mark, whether used in relation to goods or services, may be assigned or transmitted, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions and procedures as provided herein. Where such an assignment or transmission involves a change in ownership affecting the use of the mark, the assignor shall provide written notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the transaction’s completion. Failure to do so constitutes a commission offence notwithstanding good faith on the part of the assignee. A transmissible case arises where the proposed assignee lacks demonstrable experience in the relevant goods or services class; such cases require prior approval from the Registrar, who may impose conditions safeguarding consumer interests and preventing dilution of the mark's distinctiveness.

The right to use a registered trademark, including any associated process respect patent relating to its manufacture or application, may be assigned or transmitted subject to the provisions herein. An agreement for such assignment or transmission shall specify whether it includes the goodwill connected with the trade mark. Where a trade mark constitutes a transmissible case involving multiple exclusive rights, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the proposed assignee possesses sufficient resources and expertise to adequately protect the distinctiveness of each right involved. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall render the assignment voidable at the Registrar’s discretion. Any person acquiring an interest in a trademark by way of transmission or assignment shall be deemed a successor in title, with all rights and obligations attaching thereto as if they were the original registered proprietor.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and the Registrar determines that there exists sufficient cause for refusing the registration, he shall provide both the applicant and the opponent with written reasons for such determination. The Registrar may, upon review of any evidence submitted by either party following notification of the initial decision, reconsider whether register sufficient cause has been demonstrated to warrant refusal. Further, if a registered trade mark is subsequently used in a manner contrary to accepted principles of fair trading practices, or if the proprietor fails to renew the registration within the prescribed time limit, an application may be made for removal from the register and the Registrar shall consider such applications accordingly.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is presented alleging non-use, the Registrar shall direct the proprietor of the trade mark to show cause why the registration should not be expunged. Such direction shall specify the period during which the trade mark has not been used and require the proprietor to provide evidence demonstrating continued honest intent to use the mark. The Registrar may consider factors including advertising expenditure, sales figures, and licensing agreements in assessing such intent. If, after considering all submissions, the Registrar finds that the trademark has not been genuinely used, or there was no intention to use it, then register sufficient cause exists for expungement under this Act; provided that a period of six months may be allowed for remedial action as determined by the Registrar.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is filed alleging use contrary to honest practices in industrial competition, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall consider whether such use has resulted in damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the mark. If it appears that the respondent has engaged in activities detrimental to fair trade and that the applicant has suffered demonstrable harm as a direct consequence, the Board may order cessation of the impugned activity and award compensation not exceeding five times the value of the infringing goods or services. The Registrar shall be satisfied that there is register sufficient cause for rectification before any such order is made, provided that costs incidental to the proceedings shall be determined by the Appellate Board.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license conferring exclusive rights to use the trade mark within a defined geographical territory, and subsequently seeks to assign the ownership of that trade mark, such assignment shall be conditional upon obtaining the written consent of the licensee. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the license is freely granted or arises from an agreement. The Registrar may, under this Act, require evidence demonstrating the continued validity of the licensing arrangement at the time of application for registration of the assignment. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence will constitute register sufficient cause for refusing the proposed transfer. Provided that, if the licensee defaults in their obligations as stipulated within the license agreement, the registered proprietor shall be relieved from the obligation to obtain consent for assignment purposes.

The Registering Officer shall maintain an inspection register at each place where applications for registration of trademarks are received and examined. This inspection register shall record particulars relating to trademark applications filed, including the date of filing, applicant’s name and address, description of goods or services, representation of the mark, and any official actions taken on the application. Access to the inspection register shall be available to any person for inspection during specified office hours, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. The Registrar may prescribe conditions governing access and use of information contained within the inspection register, provided that confidential commercial information is protected as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain an inspection register at each Trade Marks Registry office, containing particulars of applications for registration of trademarks, including the applicant’s name and address, the goods or services in relation to which the trademark is used or proposed to be used, and the date of filing. Any person may, upon payment of a prescribed fee, inspect entries in the inspection register during specified hours as provided herein. The Registrar may restrict access to certain information within the inspection register if deemed necessary for protecting confidential business data submitted by applicants. An entry shall be presumed correct until proven otherwise under this Act. Requests for copies of entries from the inspection register shall be processed according to established procedures, subject to applicable privacy regulations.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the inspection register relating to a registered trademark shall have the right to apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification of that entry. Such application must be made within sixty days from the date on which the cause of grievance became known to the applicant, provided that this time limit may be extended by the Board for reasons to be recorded in writing. The Board shall afford the trademark proprietor an opportunity to make representations against the application and shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both parties. If, after due consideration, the Board finds merit in the aggrieved person’s claim, it may direct rectification of the inspection register accordingly. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act is actionable as civil contempt.

Any person aggrieved by an entry made in the inspection register relating to a registered trademark may, within sixty days from the date of such entry, file with the Trade Marks Registry a written request for amendment or deletion of that entry. Such request shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by any supporting documentation deemed relevant by the Registrar. The Registrar shall, after giving notice to the party whose interests are affected by the inspection register entry, afford them an opportunity of being heard in the matter. 

The Registrar may, following such hearing and considering all material placed before him or her, direct amendment or deletion of the entry as he or she deems fit. Any order made under this provision shall be communicated to the applicant for inspection and the aggrieved party by registered post. The Registrar’s decision is final subject to appeal under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to requests filed against entries in the inspection register may result in rejection of such request.

Any person aggrieved by an entry made in the inspection register relating to a registered trademark shall, within thirty days from the date of such entry, serve upon the Registrar a notice specifying the particulars of the entry and the grounds on which he claims to be aggrieved. The Registrar may, after giving the trade mark proprietor concerned an opportunity of being heard, direct amendment or deletion of any entry in the inspection register if satisfied that the entry is erroneous or has been made without due cause. Such direction shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Provided that a notice served under this provision shall not preclude the aggrieved person from pursuing other remedies available to him as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such notices and directions issued.

Any person who, without reasonable excuse, inspects entries in the inspection register maintained under this Act, and subsequently reproduces, transmits, or disseminates information obtained therefrom that relates to pending applications or oppositions, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender is liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may also be subject to further penalties as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized access or dissemination of confidential register details, initiate inquiries and impose additional fines up to one hundred thousand rupees where wilful misconduct is established. Provided that authorized representatives of the Trade Marks Registry are exempt from these restrictions when performing duties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting inspection of the inspection register pertaining to their mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed. Such licenses may include stipulations regarding the purpose for which the information contained within the register is utilized and restrictions on its reproduction or dissemination. Any assignment of a trademark under this Act shall automatically transfer any existing licenses granted for inspection register access related to that trademark to the assignee, provided that the assignor retains the right to grant further such licenses in respect of future assignments. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party, investigate whether licensed inspection is being conducted in violation of the terms stipulated within the license agreement and may impose penalties as deemed appropriate. Further, any person obtaining access through a valid license shall be bound by confidentiality agreements protecting sensitive business information revealed therein.

The Registrar shall maintain an inspection register at each Trade Marks Registry office, containing particulars of applications filed, marks registered, and renewals granted, as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to grant access to the inspection register, or by information contained therein which appears to be inaccurate or misleading, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such refusal or discovery. The Registrar may require the appellant to furnish security for costs before entertaining any such appeal. Provided that, where the aggrieved party demonstrates a reasonable apprehension of prejudice due to restricted access, the Appellate Board may waive the requirement of furnishing security. Any entry in the inspection register shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the matters recorded therein, subject to an order altering or reversing it by the Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain an inspection register at each Trade Marks Registry office, accessible during prescribed business hours to any person interested in trade mark matters. Any party seeking access to the inspection register may request a certified copy of entries relating to a specific trade mark application or registered trade mark, subject to payment of applicable fees as determined by notification issued under this Act. The Registrar is empowered to refuse access to the inspection register if satisfied that such access would likely prejudice ongoing proceedings or compromise confidential information pertaining to an applicant or proprietor. Upon registration, details regarding the expiry date of a trade mark shall be prominently recorded in the inspection register and publicly available. Notice of published expiry will be disseminated through the Trade Marks Registry website for a period not less than thirty days prior to the effective date of cessation.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the inspection register relating to a registered trademark shall, within sixty days from the date of such entry, file a notice of objection with the Registrar. Such notice must specify the particulars of the entry challenged and state the grounds upon which the objection is founded. The Registrar may, after giving due opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, direct amendment or deletion of any entry in the inspection register if it finds that the entry was made erroneously or without sufficient cause. This power shall be exercised subject to the provisions relating to rectification proceedings under this Act and without prejudice to any right to apply to a court for relief. The Registrar’s decision regarding entries in the inspection register is analogous to decisions concerning patent office registers, ensuring transparency and fairness.

The proprietor proposed registered may, subject to entering into a written licensing agreement with another party, grant such other party the right to access and extract data from the inspection register pertaining to their trade mark. Such agreements shall specify the purpose for which the extracted information is utilized, ensuring it remains solely for internal business analysis and does not infringe upon the proprietor’s exclusive rights under this Act. The Registrar may require a copy of any such licensing agreement to be filed prior to granting access, provided that confidential commercial details are redacted as per guidelines issued by the Trade Marks Office. Further, assignment of trade mark ownership shall not automatically transfer the right to access the inspection register; explicit consent from the original proprietor is required for continued access under previously granted licenses. Any unauthorized extraction or dissemination of data constitutes a violation and may be subject to penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the “computer inspection register” shall mean an electronic record maintained by the Registrar containing particulars of registered trade marks, pending applications for registration, and related documentation. Access to the computer inspection register shall be available to the public subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, including payment of a specified fee. Information displayed in the computer inspection register is deemed to be a true copy of the official record under this Act. Any person authorized by the Registrar may request copies of entries from the computer inspection register. The Registrar may provide access remotely or at designated locations, provided that security protocols are adhered to as prescribed herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to inspect the computer inspection register maintained under this Act relating to their application. Such inspection may be conducted during normal business hours at a location designated by the Registrar, and access shall be provided subject to reasonable restrictions necessary to prevent disruption or damage to the system. The Registrar may prescribe fees for such inspections, which shall be remitted to the Consolidated Fund of India. Any person found tampering with the register or extracting data in violation of these provisions is liable to prosecution under the Information Technology Act. Further, any unauthorized reproduction or dissemination of information obtained through inspection will constitute an offense and render the offender subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the computer inspection register relating to a registered trade mark may file a written complaint with the Trade Marks Registry within sixty days of such entry’s publication. The complaint shall specify the grounds upon which the aggrieved party challenges the accuracy or propriety of the information recorded, and must be accompanied by supporting documentation as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Upon receiving such a complaint, the Registrar shall afford the applicant whose details are subject to challenge an opportunity to submit a written response within thirty days. Failure to respond may be treated as acquiescence. The Registrar shall then issue an order either confirming, modifying, or deleting the entry in question. Any party dissatisfied with this order may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a computer inspection register containing particulars of applications for registration of service marks, including details of the applicant, the services for which the mark is sought, and the date of filing. Any person may inspect this computer inspection register during office hours as provided herein, subject to payment of such fees as the Registrar may prescribe. The Registrar shall provide access to digital records within the computer inspection register in a manner that facilitates searching and retrieval. Information pertaining to pending oppositions or rectification proceedings relating to any service mark application shall be clearly indicated within the register. Any person desiring copies of entries from the computer inspection register shall apply in writing, specifying the particulars required, and shall pay such copying charges as may be determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may refuse access to information if it contains confidential business data, provided that a reasoned order is issued explaining the refusal.

Access to the computer inspection register shall be permitted to any person who provides satisfactory proof of identity as determined by the Registrar. Such access is conditional upon compliance with the rules governing electronic record retrieval, and any attempt to circumvent these protocols will render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, at their discretion, restrict access to specific portions of the computer inspection register pertaining to sensitive trade mark applications, particularly those involving ongoing litigation or confidential business information. Further, a person seeking to obtain copies of entries from the computer inspection register shall pay such fees as are prescribed by regulations issued under this Act; provided that journalists accredited by the Press Council of India may be granted exemptions subject to verification and approval by the Registrar.

Any person found to have gained unauthorized access to, or extracted data from, the computer inspection register maintained under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender is liable for a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year. The Registrar shall report any suspected instances of unauthorized access to the relevant law enforcement agencies without delay. Further, any information obtained through such unlawful means and used for commercial gain or to prejudice the interests of registered proprietors is subject to enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. Provided that this restriction does not impede legitimate research conducted with prior authorization from the Registrar.

The right to access and inspect the computer inspection register pertaining to registered trademarks shall be granted subject to payment of prescribed fees as determined under this Act. Any person holding a license to utilize a trademark, whether through assignment or otherwise, may apply for such access, provided that they demonstrate a legitimate commercial interest directly related to the assessment of potential infringement or validity challenges concerning the mark listed in the register. The Registrar may, at their discretion and after due consideration of the application, grant limited inspection rights allowing access only to specific data fields within the computer inspection register. Such licenses are transferable subject to prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued compliance with the conditions stipulated herein. Further, any assignment of a trademark shall include an automatic transfer of associated inspection register access privileges unless explicitly excluded in writing.

Access to the computer inspection register shall be permitted to any person upon payment of such fee as may be prescribed, provided that access is subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential commercial information. Any party aggrieved by a denial of access or by conditions placed on such access may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order denying or restricting access. The Tribunal shall consider any submissions made by the applicant and the Registrar, and may direct the Registrar to grant access subject to reasonable safeguards designed to protect legitimate business interests. Further, the Registrar may require a bond to be executed by an applicant seeking access if there is reason to believe that information obtained will be misused.

The Registrar may, subject to regulations made under this Act, grant licenses to qualified third-party data processors enabling them to provide remote access services for inspection of the computer inspection register pertaining to registered trade marks. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permissible activities and restrict any actions that could compromise the integrity or confidentiality of information contained therein. A licensee may sub-license these rights, provided that such sub-licenses are approved by the Registrar and adhere strictly to the terms initially granted. Any assignment of a license, whether through sale, merger, or other transfer, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, who shall consider potential impacts on trade mark regulations and public access. The Registrar may impose conditions relating to data security protocols and audit trails as part of any licensing agreement.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a statement indicating whether the applicant seeks international registration of the trade mark under the Madrid Protocol. Where an applicant elects to pursue such international registration, the Trade Marks Registry shall record this election on the register and may require the provision of additional information as deemed necessary for facilitating the informing international process. The Registrar is empowered to request translations or transliterations of the trade mark and its representation where required by the International Bureau’s regulations. Such requests are subject to a prescribed fee, payable by the applicant. Failure to comply with these requirements within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned, as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered in India, and an identical or confusingly similar trade mark is subsequently applied for registration in a foreign country, the Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receiving due notice from the proprietor of the Indian trade mark, provide such information as may be necessary to the relevant intellectual property office in that jurisdiction. This informing international process aims to safeguard the rights of proprietors against potentially conflicting registrations abroad. The Registrar may require verification of the similarity and distinctiveness of the marks involved, and shall consider any evidence submitted by either party regarding prior use or reputation enjoyed by the Indian trade mark. Any proprietor failing to comply with a direction from the Registrar in relation to informing international proceedings is liable to a penalty as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of notified international trade mark registrations. Upon receipt of an official notification from an International Bureau concerning an extension of protection relating to India, the Registrar may record such extension in the Register and publish particulars thereof as provided herein. Any party claiming interest in relation to a trade mark subject to an informing international notification may, within sixty days from the date of publication, file with the Registrar an objection under this Act. The Registrar shall give notice of any such objection to the International Bureau. The International Bureau shall be afforded opportunity to submit its response to the Registrar within thirty days of receipt of said notice. Decisions regarding objections relating to informing international notifications are appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to procedural requirements as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is filed containing a representation that the trade mark is used internationally, the applicant shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within thirty days of the request made by the Registrar, documentary evidence demonstrating such international use. Such evidence must clearly indicate the territories where the trade mark is being employed in commerce and the dates upon which such use commenced. The Registrar may require further clarification or additional documentation if the initial submission is deemed insufficient to satisfy the requirements as provided herein. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the application liable for rejection, subject to an opportunity granted to the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a stipulated period. Informing international usage does not, however, constitute a right of exclusive ownership in any jurisdiction.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently subject to an opposition based on prior use outside of India, the Registrar shall require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued and substantial commercial activity relating to the goods or services indicated in the application within Indian territory. Failure to provide such satisfactory evidence, as determined by the Registrar, will result in the mark being deemed liable for expungement under this Act. The Registrar may also direct the applicant to undertake measures of informing international trade communities regarding the scope and validity of their registered trade marks. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning informing international may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement between the proprietor and licensee. Any assignment of a trade mark, or any license granted thereunder, requires notification to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of execution, accompanied by prescribed fees. Failure to provide such informing international notice shall render the assignment or license revocable at the discretion of the Registrar. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application from any interested party demonstrating prejudice due to lack of timely notification, initiate proceedings for revocation. This provision applies equally to licenses granted outside India relating to goods or services intended for consumption within Indian territory.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark registered in a country other than India, the Trade Marks Registry shall give notice thereof to the applicant. Such notice shall clearly state the particulars of the conflicting mark and the grounds upon which the objection is founded, as provided herein. The applicant may then file its response within the time specified, demonstrating why the marks do not create likelihood of confusion or deception among consumers. Failure to respond adequately shall be deemed an admission of conflict. The Registry may, after considering all submissions, direct registration subject to limitations or refuse it entirely; any such direction is appealable under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Informing international authorities regarding these proceedings is mandatory.

An international registration made in respect of a trade mark shall have effect as to constitute a further registration of that trade mark in India subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder. The Registrar may require the applicant for an advertising international registration to furnish such information, documents, or declarations as are necessary to establish the extent of protection sought within Indian territory. Such protection shall be limited to the goods or services specified in the Statement of Registering Goods and Services included with the application for international registration. Any opposition under this Act may be filed against the proposed extension of an advertising international registration as if it were a new trade mark application, provided that the deadline for such opposition is extended as determined by the Registrar.

An international registration made in respect of a trade mark shall have effect as to grant rights only in relation to the territory of India where an application for corresponding goods or services has been filed within three months from the date of such international registration, provided that the Registrar may extend this period if satisfied that circumstances exist which prevent timely filing. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark identical or similar to the trade mark subject to advertising international registration may, under this Act, apply to the High Court for relief in cases of dilution or unfair competition arising from the said international registration. The remedies available shall include an injunction restraining further use of the mark and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the aggrieved party. Such application must be made within one year of the publication of the international registration.

An international registration made in respect of a trade mark shall have effect subject to compliance with the provisions relating to territorial extent and priority as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the applicant is duly authorized to make an advertising international registration on behalf of the proprietor, including but not limited to a certified copy of board resolution or power of attorney. Where an application for advertising international registration includes goods or services not previously covered by the mark’s initial registration, the Registrar shall notify the International Bureau and any interested parties under this Act. Such notification shall detail the extent of alteration proposed and provide opportunity for opposition as if it were a new trade mark application.

An international registration made in respect of a trade mark shall have effect as a basic registration only if the application for advertising an international registration is filed within six months from the date of publication of the international registration under this Act. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the international registration void, and any use of the mark subsequent to such failure shall be deemed infringement actionable under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating a material error in the published details of an international registration, permit a belated filing for advertising, provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar that the delay was not attributable to wilful neglect or fraudulent intent. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the validity of an advertising international registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Following an application for registration of a trade mark, the Registrar shall direct that notice be given to the public. Such notice shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal and at least one widely circulated newspaper published or printed in the vernacular language of the region where the applicant’s principal place of business is situated. The form and manner of such advertisement shall be as prescribed by the rules made under this Act. Provided that, if the Registrar considers it necessary for ensuring adequate publicity, he may direct advertising to be carried out in additional newspapers or journals beyond those initially specified by the applicant. Registration shall advertised even where the trade mark consists exclusively of a geographical indication. The costs associated with such advertisement shall be borne by the applicant, subject to reimbursement as determined by the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is accepted, the Registrar shall direct that notice of such acceptance be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal and in such other publications as the Registrar deems appropriate. Any person may, within sixty days from the date of first publication of the advertisement, file with the Registrar a written objection to the proposed registration, stating clearly the grounds upon which such objection is founded; provided that any such objection shall not be entertained if it relates to matters which could have been raised in an earlier proceeding under this Act. The Registrar may, after giving all parties interested an opportunity of being heard, either dismiss the objection or direct further inquiry into the matter. Registration shall advertised notwithstanding any pending objection unless otherwise directed by the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration” shall mean a registrable trade mark that has been extended to India in accordance with the provisions of the Treaty on Intellectual Property. An international registration shall be deemed to be an application for registration only insofar as it relates to the territory of India and subject to any limitations specified therein. The Registrar may require such evidence, documentation, or declarations as are necessary to verify the validity of an international registration under this Act. Information concerning the acceptance of an international registration, including details regarding any refusals or objections, shall be communicated to the International Bureau in the manner informing international practice and as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for and a statement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. Where the applicant seeks to register a composite mark consisting of words, devices, or three dimensional features, the application shall clearly delineate each element comprising the mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the representation if it is deemed insufficiently clear. Further, an applicant intending to claim priority under this Act shall furnish a certified copy of the earlier trade mark registration. This information regarding prior applications and registrations shall be communicated to the International Bureau in the manner informing international practice as provided herein.

Applications for registration shall be examined by the Registry in accordance with the prescribed procedure. Where an application includes a representation of goods or services which incorporates a design registered under the Designs Act, 2000, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence of their right to use such design. The determination of similarity between marks shall take into account not only the visual appearance but also phonetic and conceptual similarities. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications, registrations, and oppositions, accessible for public inspection as provided herein. Information concerning pending applications shall be made available on the Registry’s website in the manner informing international trade organizations.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is made relating to goods or services, including those which are considered agricultural products, the applicant shall furnish a declaration verifying that such goods or services originate from India. This verification must specify the location within India where the goods were manufactured or the service was rendered. Provided that, if the applicant’s business has operations in multiple locations, the declaration may list all relevant places of origin. Furthermore, any subsequent alteration to the place of origin shall be reported to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days, accompanied by an updated declaration. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the declared origin, and failure to comply with these requirements will impact registration in a manner informing international trade relations.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration is effective, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also to a fine. The Court may, in determining the appropriate penalty, consider the extent of the deception caused and any financial loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Further, where such deceptive use occurs through advertising or other promotional material, the offender shall be liable for additional penalties as provided herein. This provision applies irrespective of whether the infringing mark is used in a manner informing international trade.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms of the agreement between the proprietor and the licensee. Assignment of a trade mark, or any license granted thereunder, requires registration with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Where an assignment or license involves a party located outside India, the manner informing international authorities shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures outlined by the International Bureau. The Registrar may require submission of documentation verifying the legal standing and address of foreign assignees or licensees. Any alteration to the terms of a registered license must also be notified to the Registry for record.

Where an objection is raised by a party against the acceptance of a trade mark application on grounds specified in this Act, the Trade Marks Registry shall afford that party an opportunity to present its case and be heard. The Registrar may, after considering the evidence submitted, either uphold the objection or direct acceptance of the application, providing reasons for the decision recorded in writing. Any party aggrieved by such order of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. Further, the Appellate Board’s determination shall be final and binding, subject only to an appeal under the provisions relating to appeals from orders of appellate tribunals. The manner informing international authorities concerning any rectification proceedings shall adhere strictly to regulations prescribed herein.

Applications for registration of a trade mark incorporating or comprising a representation of a semiconductor device shall be examined in accordance with the provisions relating to descriptive trade marks, subject to the additional requirements specified herein. The Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish a technical explanation detailing the function and characteristics of the represented semiconductor device, verifying its non-distinctive nature if such representation is deemed potentially deceptive or misleading. Failure to provide this explanation within the time stipulated by the Registrar shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any alteration to the trade mark following acceptance but prior to registration, particularly concerning the depiction of the semiconductor element, must be reported to the International Bureau in the manner informing international notification as prescribed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "significant similarity" in relation to marks shall be determined having regard to the visual, phonetic and conceptual similarities between the signs; a mark shall be deemed significantly similar to another if, considering the impressions created on the mind of the average consumer encountering such marks in the course of trade, there exists a likelihood of confusion as to whether the goods or services are sourced from the same enterprise, subject to section 36e ixd. This assessment shall take into account all relevant surrounding circumstances, including but not limited to the nature of the goods or services, the channels through which they are marketed and the degree of awareness of the prior mark among consumers.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks, when considered in relation to not only identical goods or services but also those which are similar or related thereto, conflict with any prior registered trade mark or pending application as determined under section 36e ixd. This determination shall take into account the overall impression created by the marks and the field of activity covered by the earlier registration or application. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further evidence demonstrating that a likelihood of confusion or deception is unlikely, provided that such evidence addresses all relevant aspects of the comparison under this Act. Any such requirement shall be communicated in writing to the applicant.

Where a registered trade mark is deceptively similar or identical to an earlier mark used in relation to goods or services, and such use has resulted in demonstrable misrepresentation to the public leading to damages, the proprietor of the earlier mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. This right exists irrespective of whether the earlier mark was registered prior to the date of first use or registration of the infringing trade mark. The remedies available under this Act may include an order requiring the infringer to account for profits derived from the infringing activities and a direction to recall goods bearing the infringing mark from the market, provided that such recall is deemed reasonably practicable by the adjudicating authority. For the purposes of determining similarity as per section 36e ixd, consideration shall be given to all relevant factors including visual appearance, phonetic resemblance, and conceptual meaning.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if it contains any element which is liable to be considered deceptive as per this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this provision, issue a notice to the applicant requiring them to submit arguments and evidence demonstrating why the proposed trade mark should not be construed as misleading consumers. Such submissions must be filed within sixty days of the date of the notice. Failure to comply with this requirement shall result in automatic refusal of the application. The Registrar shall then consider all materials presented, including any counter-submissions from interested parties who may file objections within thirty days of the applicant’s response. Decisions regarding deceptive elements are appealable under section 36e ixd before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is demonstrably calculated to create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, an interested party may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such petitions shall be entertained only if the petitioner establishes, through documentary evidence including but not limited to market surveys and consumer perception studies, that the infringing use has resulted in demonstrable financial detriment. The Board shall consider whether the continued registration is consistent with the public interest under this Act. Further, any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning section 36e ixd shall be subject to appeal before the relevant High Court.

Any person who, having knowledge of a registered trade mark used in relation to goods or services, makes use of an identical or confusingly similar marks in such manner as to create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public shall be guilty of an offence and liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of reputation suffered by the proprietor of the registered trade mark, and any profits made by the infringing party attributable to the infringement. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint under section 36e ixd, issue an injunction restraining the infringing activities, subject to due process and opportunity being afforded to the alleged infringer to be heard. Failure to comply with such an order shall render the offender liable for further penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding twenty years from the date of the grant, and may be assignable subject to registration of the assignment with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license is assigned under this Act, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights and privileges which were vested in the licensor immediately prior to the assignment. The Registrar may, upon application by any party claiming interest, investigate whether a license has been granted in contravention of section 36e ixd, particularly where the terms restrict competition unreasonably or impose undue burdens on licensees. Any such investigation shall be conducted as provided herein and findings made are binding.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against a decision refusing registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deemed to be generic, the Appellate Board shall consider whether, at the date of application for registration, use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified had become so prevalent as to have resulted in the mark losing its distinctive character and acquiring a common descriptive meaning within the relevant geographical area. The Board may, subject to just considerations, allow such appeal if it finds that the evidence presented does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that section 36e ixd has been contravened. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court on any question of law arising out of the decision.

Where a registered trade mark is deceptively similar to a prior registered layout, and the owner of the earlier layout demonstrates that use as a trade mark would likely cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings in the Commercial Court. Such proceedings shall be limited to claims for damages sustained directly by reason of the infringing use, excluding any claim for injunctive relief against continued manufacture or sale of products bearing the infringing mark unless such infringement also constitutes a violation under section 36e ixd. The court shall consider evidence pertaining to consumer perception and market conditions in determining the extent of said damages. A distinguishable registered layout does not, however, automatically preclude registration; it merely establishes a potential cause for action as provided herein.

An application for registration as a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, upon examination, it is found that the proposed marks are substantially identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical to those for which the application is filed. Where such refusal is based on grounds relating to section 36e ixd of this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a further opportunity to amend the application to distinguish it from the prior mark. This amendment may include alterations to the representation of the trade mark or limitations upon the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar shall provide written reasons for any such refusal and the applicant may submit counter-arguments within sixty days of receipt of the notice of refusal. Furthermore, an application patent relating to a similar invention may be considered in determining similarity under this provision.

No proprietor shall be entitled to restrain the use of a trade mark by any person otherwise than in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, provided that such use would result in a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, or where such use constitutes taking unfair advantage of the reputation of the trade mark under section 36e ixd. Where a proprietor seeks to enforce this provision, it shall be presumed that there is an intention to derive benefit from the reference use mark unless the contrary is proved. Any person found in violation of this restriction shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor and may also face prosecution under relevant penal provisions as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, a proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences relating to the use of that trade mark in accordance with the terms specified therein. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may extend to specific goods or services as defined within the scope of registration. Where a licence is granted, the licensee shall be deemed an authorized user for the duration of the agreement, subject to compliance with all conditions stipulated by the proprietor. Assignment of rights under section 36e ixd requires prior written consent from the Controller and must clearly delineate the extent of such assignment, including any limitations on subsequent licensing activities. The Registrar may require a declaration confirming adherence to these provisions as part of the assignment documentation.

For the purposes of this Act, “work” shall include literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, cinematograph films, and sound recordings, subject to such exceptions as are provided herein relating to fair dealing. The Copyrights Appellate Board established under this Act is a body constituted for adjudicating disputes concerning copyright arising from decisions made by the Registrar of Copyrights or other authorities empowered to enforce copyrights. Appeals may be filed before the Board within sixty days of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by such fees as prescribed. The Board’s orders are final, subject to appeal to a High Court under conditions specified herein.

Applications for registration of copyright shall be made to the Copyrights Appellate Board in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish with the application a certified true copy of the work or, where the work is not capable of being copied, a still or other visual representation of the work. Upon receipt of an application, the Board shall issue an acknowledgement containing the date of its receipt. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar of Copyrights relating to the registration of copyright may appeal to the Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Board may entertain appeals filed after the said period only if the appellant satisfies it that there was a sufficient reason for the delay.

Any aggrieved party seeking redress against an order passed by a Copyrights Appellate Board concerning infringement of copyright in a cinematograph film, or relating to equitable accounting between authors, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate court shall consider whether the Board acted without due regard to the principles of natural justice, or if there was an error apparent on the face of the record. Subject to this, the decision of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final. Provided that, where the appeal relates to a claim for damages exceeding ten lakh rupees, the appellant shall deposit twenty percent of the claimed amount with the appellate court as security before the appeal is entertained. The High Court may, in its discretion, allow an extension of time for filing the appeal if satisfactory reasons are shown.

Applications for review of decisions rendered by Copyright Adjudicating Officers shall be made to the Copyrights Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The application must specify the order sought for review and state the grounds upon which it is based, including any errors apparent on the face of the record. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Copyrights Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the appellate court shall admit the appeal only if it involves a substantial question of law. The Board shall conduct its proceedings in accordance with principles of natural justice and may, subject to this Act, regulate its own procedure.

Any aggrieved party seeking review of a decision made by the Copyrights Appellate Board concerning infringement proceedings shall, within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, file an application for revision with the Intellectual Property Tribunal. The application must specify the grounds upon which the decision is challenged and include certified copies of all relevant documents pertaining to the original proceeding before the Board. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the Tribunal may condone the delay in filing the application. Further, the Tribunal shall not entertain any application where the aggrieved party has failed to exhaust remedies available under this Act or rules made thereunder. The Copyrights Appellate Board’s decision is binding unless revised by the Intellectual Property Tribunal as provided herein.

Any individual found to have reproduced a copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than ten times the reasonable licensing fee that would have been payable had such license been granted, or in default thereof, an amount determined by the Copyrights Appellate Board based on factors including the commercial value of the infringing copy and the resultant loss suffered by the copyright owner. Furthermore, where the infringement is committed for gain or reward, the Board may impose a further penalty not exceeding twenty-five times the reasonable licensing fee. The Board shall issue notices to both parties prior to determining any monetary penalties, providing an opportunity for representation as provided herein.

Any copyright owner desiring to grant a license for reproduction or adaptation of their work may execute an assignment, irrevocably transferring such rights to another party, subject to the terms stipulated within the agreement. Such assignments shall be registered with the Copyrights Appellate Board, and failure to register will render the assignee unable to enforce the assigned rights in any legal proceeding under this Act. The Board may, upon application by a third party demonstrating substantial reliance on an unregistered assignment, grant temporary relief pending registration, provided that such application includes evidence of good faith and demonstrable prejudice resulting from the lack of registration. Further, where a license is granted through a collective management organization, the terms governing royalty distribution shall be subject to review and approval by the Copyrights Appellate Board.

Where a determination has been made by the Copyrights Appellate Board concerning infringement of copyright in a musical work, an aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such determination. Such appeal shall lie only on grounds specified in the memorandum of appeal, clearly articulating errors of law or fact apparent on the record. The Board shall furnish to the High Court all relevant records pertaining to the original proceeding, including transcripts and any expert testimony presented. Provided that, if the appellant fails to demonstrate a prima facie case of substantial injustice arising from the Board’s decision, the High Court may summarily dismiss the appeal without requiring further argument. Further, the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be deemed a tribunal for the purposes of natural justice.

Appeals relating to decisions of the Copyright Board concerning the registration of copyrights in literary works, musical compositions, cinematograph films, and sound recordings shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. The Copyrights Appellate Board may, at its discretion, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the aforementioned period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are furnished. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Board concerning royalties payable to copyright owners, particularly in circumstances involving export concerned pharmaceutical product packaging designs, may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein. The appellant shall serve a copy of the memorandum of appeal on the respondent at least thirty days before the date fixed for hearing. Evidence may be adduced before the Copyrights Appellate Board both orally and documentary, subject to rules framed by the Central Government.

Any aggrieved party seeking review of a decision made by the Registrar concerning copyright registration or renewal shall, within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, file an appeal with the Copyrights Appellate Board. The appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds and relevant documents substantiating the claim that the Registrar’s order was erroneous in law or fact. Provided that the appellate board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs. Further, the board shall give notice to the Registrar and any other interested party, affording them an opportunity to submit written arguments within thirty days of receiving the appeal papers. The Board’s decision is final subject to further appeals as provided herein.

Any aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright under this Act may appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board against an order passed by the Registrar of Copyrights. The appellant shall deposit with the Board such sum as may be prescribed, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. Where a dispute arises concerning the determination of who is the true and first inventor of a work subject to copyright, the Board may conduct inquiries and hear evidence from all relevant parties before rendering its decision. Any person found guilty of wilful infringement by the Board shall be liable to pay damages not exceeding ten times the actual pecuniary loss suffered by the copyright owner or rupees one million, whichever is greater, and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

For the purposes of this Act, a “work” shall include literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works fixed in any medium of expression, as well as cinematograph films and sound recordings. The term "author" with reference to a computer-generated work shall be deemed to be the person who caused the work to be generated; provided that where such work has been created by employing an algorithm or artificial intelligence, the determination of authorship shall be subject to review under this Act. Any dispute concerning the validity of copyright, or any question relating to infringement thereof, may be referred for decision to a Copyrights Appellate body constituted as provided herein. Decisions of the appellate body shall be binding and final.

Applications for registration of copyrights shall be made to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office may request further information or clarification from the applicant concerning the nature of the work, its authorship, and any prior assignments or licenses relating thereto. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements under this Act. Where a decision regarding registration is contested, an appeal lies to the copyrights appellate tribunal constituted for this purpose. Such appeals shall be heard expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice, and the tribunal’s determination shall be final, provided that it does not contravene any provision of the Constitution.

Any aggrieved party claiming to have suffered damages as a result of an infringement of copyright under this Act may institute proceedings before the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall, upon hearing all parties involved, determine the extent and nature of such damages, taking into consideration factors including the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing acts occurred with the owner’s consent, any profits realized by the infringer as a consequence of the infringement, and the flagrancy of the violation. Provided that, in assessing damages, the Tribunal shall not award sums exceeding an amount equivalent to three times the actual damage sustained or, where such damage cannot be readily ascertained, an amount deemed just and equitable under the circumstances. The decision of the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to appeal to a High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the infringement occurred.

Appeals against orders passed by the Copyright Registrar shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, and may be made within sixty days from the date of such order. The Tribunal shall admit an appeal if it is satisfied that there are sufficient grounds for interference with the decision of the Registrar. An aggrieved party seeking review under this Act must demonstrate a clear error of law or fact in the original determination. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall, while hearing appeals, be guided by principles of natural justice and may grant any interim relief as it deems appropriate to ensure fairness during proceedings. Decisions of the Tribunal are final subject to further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of the order, provided that such appeal is limited to questions of law only. The Copyrights Appellate process shall be conducted in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Central Government.

Any aggrieved party seeking redressal concerning a determination made under this Act relating to copyright may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such determination, file an appeal with the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a concise statement outlining the grounds upon which the appellant challenges the original decision and demonstrating how it contravenes established principles of fairness or legal precedent. The Tribunal shall provide the respondent with a copy of the appeal and all supporting documentation, allowing for a written response within thirty days thereafter. Provided that the Tribunal may, subject to just cause shown, extend these timelines. Decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal shall be binding on all parties involved, pending judicial review under appropriate legal procedures.

Any aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright under this Act may appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of order, provided that the appellate tribunal shall not be bound by the decisions or findings of any lower authority. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during such an appeal shall render it inadmissible. The Tribunal may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Any person found guilty of wilful infringement shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding ten times the actual damages suffered by the copyright owner, or in default of payment, imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

The right to assign copyright in a musical work shall extend to the granting of exclusive licenses, provided that such license explicitly defines the scope of reproduction, distribution, or public performance rights conveyed. Any assignment made under this Act must be in writing and signed by the assignor or their duly authorized representative; failure to comply with this requirement renders the assignment voidable at the assignee’s option. Where a copyright owner has granted an exclusive license, subsequent assignments of any conflicting right shall be deemed invalid unless consent is obtained from the licensee. The Copyrights Appellate body may entertain appeals arising from decisions concerning the validity or enforceability of such assignments and licenses, including disputes regarding the interpretation of their terms. Further, sub-licensing rights may be stipulated within an initial assignment agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Where a determination has been made under this Act regarding copyright infringement or the originality of works, any aggrieved party may appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against, and shall state specifically the grounds on which the appeal is based. The appellate tribunal may, after affording opportunity for a hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, vary or reverse any such determination, subject to principles of natural justice. Provided that if the appellant fails to demonstrate prejudice arising from the original determination, the appeal shall be dismissed. Decisions of the Tribunal are final and binding, but remain open to judicial review under appropriate articles of the Constitution.

An appeal against an order passed by the Registrar under this Act shall lie to the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal. The aggrieved party may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, file an application for appeal in the prescribed form and manner. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order sought to be appealed against, as well as any relevant entry register pertaining to the copyright concerned. The Copyrights Appellate Tribunal shall give notice to all parties affected by the appeal and provide them with an opportunity to present their case. Decisions regarding the admissibility of evidence are at the discretion of the Tribunal, subject to principles of natural justice. The Tribunal may, after hearing both sides, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against, and may also direct such other action as it deems fit.

Where a copyright owner believes that an order passed by the Copyrights Appellate Tribunal is erroneous in law or fact, such owner may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appeal shall be admitted only if the appellant deposits with the High Court such sum as determined by the Central Government, representing costs incurred by other parties involved in the original proceeding. Provided that, where the appellate tribunal finds a substantial question of law arising for its determination, it may direct the copyright owner to deposit an enhanced amount. The High Court shall hear and dispose of appeals expeditiously, considering all relevant evidence presented by both the appellant, acting as the aggrieved owner copyright case, and any respondent parties.

For the purposes of this Act, an “article patented process” is defined as a method or series of acts involving one or more steps which are novel, inventive, and applicable in producing a particular article or substance. Such a process shall be considered to encompass not only the precise sequence of operations described in the patent specification but also any equivalent variations thereof that achieve substantially the same result.
