The determination of equivalence shall take into account the prior art as it existed at the date of filing of the patent application. An article produced wholly from an article patented process shall, subject to provisions regarding essential features, be deemed to infringe upon the rights conferred by the patent.

The Register of Patented Processes shall maintain a publicly accessible record detailing each process for which registration has been granted under this Act, including particulars of the applicant, inventor, and the nature of the invention as claimed in the application. Any person intending to utilize a patented process commercially shall be required to file a declaration with the Register prior to commencement of such use, specifying the intended scale of operation and anticipated output. The Register may, upon receiving credible information suggesting infringement or unauthorized adaptation of a registered article patented process, initiate an inquiry and issue directives for compliance as provided herein. Failure to comply with these directives shall render the user liable for penalties determined by the Controller. This requirement does not apply to research activities conducted solely for non-commercial purposes.

Where infringement of a patent relating to an article patented process has occurred, the right to restrain such infringement shall be vested in the registered proprietor or their duly authorized agent. Any person aggrieved by an act of infringement may institute suit in the competent civil court for remedy, seeking either damages or an injunction, or both, as deemed appropriate by the Court. The measure of damages awarded under this Act shall reflect the loss suffered by the patentee due to the infringing activity, taking into consideration reasonable royalty rates and profits derived from the unauthorized use of the patented process. Provided that, in cases where the infringement was committed unknowingly or without intent to deceive, the court may reduce the amount of damages accordingly. Further, a party found guilty of infringement shall be liable for costs incurred by the patentee in pursuing legal action as provided herein.

Where an application relates to a process for producing a substance or article, it shall be permissible to claim the invention as a *process* notwithstanding that the substance or article so produced is also claimed, provided that the claims clearly define the scope of protection sought and distinguish the inventive concept from prior art disclosures. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish detailed particulars regarding the process parameters, including but not limited to temperature ranges, pressure conditions, catalyst specifications, and reaction times, if such information is deemed necessary for determining novelty or inventiveness under this Act. Furthermore, any modification of the claimed *article patented process* which results in a marked improvement in efficacy or safety shall be subject to re-examination to ascertain compliance with provisions relating to public interest.

Any person who, without authorization from the patentee or their duly appointed agent, utilizes a patented process for the manufacture, use, or sale of any substance or article shall be deemed to have infringed upon the rights conferred under this Act. Such infringement will attract penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods produced in contravention of the patented process are subject to seizure and forfeiture. The patentee is entitled to seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such unauthorized exploitation of the article patented process.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Controller refusing to grant patent protection for an invention relating to an article patented process, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the claimed subject matter falls within the scope of section 3; and if it finds that the refusal was based on an erroneous interpretation of said section, may direct the Controller to reconsider the application. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating a clear error in the Controller’s assessment regarding novelty or inventive step. Provided that, where the invention involves a process for producing a known article, the Board may allow the appeal if it is satisfied that the claimed process yields demonstrably superior results compared to existing methods, subject to considerations of public interest and freedom to practice.

Where an infringement of a patent relating to an article patented process is established under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing activity, subject to such terms as the Court deems just. Damages recoverable in respect of such infringement shall be determined by assessing the reasonable royalty that the infringer would have paid had they lawfully obtained a license for the use of the patented process. Furthermore, where the infringing article bears a trade mark falsely suggesting association with the patentee or any prior user, the Court may also order the destruction of goods bearing said falsifying trade mark and impose additional penalties not exceeding five times the value of the infringing goods. The Controller shall have power to issue interim orders pending final determination.

An application for rectification of entries relating to registered trademarks, including claims of dilution or unfair competition, shall be heard and determined by an Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act. The term "Adjudicating Officer Period" refers to the duration during which an Adjudicating Officer holds office, which shall not exceed five years from the date on which they assume charge, subject to earlier termination upon resignation or removal as provided herein. Any order passed by the Adjudicating Officer may be appealed against before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such order. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines for the conduct of proceedings and the assessment of costs.

An application for registration of a biotechnological invention relating to a genetically modified microorganism shall include particulars specifying the source organism and the nature of the genetic modification effected, along with details of any vector utilized. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning such aspects as are deemed necessary for proper evaluation under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall assign it to an adjudicating officer period, who will conduct a preliminary examination regarding compliance with formal requirements and novelty assessment. Any objection raised by any person during the publication process may be addressed by the applicant within two months from the date of such objection; failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection by the adjudicating officer.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an adjudicating officer concerning infringement proceedings or revocation requests relating to pharmaceutical patents shall have the right to file an application for review before the Intellectual Property Tribunal. Such application must be submitted within ninety days from the date of communication of the order, and it shall specify the grounds upon which the challenge is based, including demonstrable errors of law or fact. The adjudicating officer period for issuing interim orders relating to interlocutory applications concerning discovery or preservation of evidence shall not exceed thirty days from the date of application. Provided that, if the Tribunal finds the decision to be manifestly erroneous, it may remit the matter back to the adjudicating officer for reconsideration with specific directions.

Where any party is dissatisfied with a decision made by an adjudicating officer relating to rectification of entries in the Register of Patents, that party may prefer an appeal to the Controller within three months from the date of communication of the order. The Controller shall give notice to all other interested parties and opportunity for them to be heard. An application for review of any order passed by the adjudicating officer concerning the determination of patent validity under this Act may also be made before the Controller, subject to a limitation period of ninety days from the date of such order’s communication. The Controller shall record reasons in writing for any decision taken on an appeal or review. An adjudicating officer period is defined as the duration during which an individual holds office as an adjudicating officer, and this period may be extended by the Central Government.

An application for rectification of entries relating to registered trademarks, if filed with the Controller, shall be processed only if the applicant demonstrates compliance with all applicable procedural requirements as provided herein. The Controller may direct any party concerned to submit further documentation or attend a hearing at a time and place specified by the Controller. Any order passed by an adjudicating officer concerning infringement proceedings is subject to review upon demonstration that the affected party was not afforded reasonable opportunity for representation during the initial adjudication process. A person aggrieved by such an order of the adjudicating officer period may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order, provided that the grounds of appeal are clearly articulated and supported by relevant evidence.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an adjudicating officer concerning infringement proceedings relating to a registered trademark shall have recourse to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within ninety days of communication of that decision. Failure to file such an appeal within the prescribed period will render the aggrieved party estopped from further challenging the adjudicating officer’s determination, subject to just cause demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Tribunal. The adjudicating officer period for rendering a reasoned order following a hearing shall not exceed one hundred and twenty days from the date of service of notice; exceeding this timeframe may invite penalties as determined by the Tribunal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any licensee granted rights under an assignment of patent, or otherwise permitted to exploit a patented invention during the adjudicating officer period, shall be entitled to sub-license such rights with the prior written consent of the assignee. Such consent may be withheld only if it demonstrably prejudices the interests of the patentee in maintaining the validity and scope of the patent. The terms and conditions of any sub-licence granted shall be filed with the Controller within thirty days, detailing royalty rates and territorial limitations. Failure to comply with this provision renders the sub-license void. An adjudicating officer may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unfair or discriminatory licensing practices, initiate an inquiry and issue directions for rectification, subject to appeal before the appellate authority.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an Adjudicating Officer concerning infringement proceedings relating to registered trademarks or designs may, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal must be lodged within ninety days from the date of communication of the order; failure to adhere to this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. Further, the appellant is obligated to deposit a sum determined by the Central Government, which may vary based on the nature and value of the dispute. An Adjudicating Officer period for considering counter-claims or objections raised during proceedings shall not exceed six months, extendable only with reasoned justification recorded in writing.

Any patent holder desiring to grant a license for exploitation of the patented invention relating to a process or composition for producing a substance defined by the claims shall file with the Trade Marks Registrar a notice specifying the terms and conditions of such licensing arrangement, including royalty rates and duration. This filing is mandatory prior to the commencement of any commercial activity under the granted license. The adjudicating officer period for determining disputes arising from alleged infringement of rights pertaining to these licensed processes or compositions shall be ninety days from the date of receipt of the complaint. Provided that, where a licensee sub-licenses the patented technology, such sublicensee must also notify the Trade Marks Registrar within thirty days of entering into the sublicensing agreement under this Act. Failure to comply with these notification requirements may render the license unenforceable and subject the patent holder to penalties as provided herein.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision rendered by an Adjudicating Officer concerning the revocation of a patent or the determination of validity following a post-grant opposition proceeding may, within ninety days from the date of such decision, file an appeal to the Controller. The appeal shall state specifically the orders against which it is taken and the grounds on which it is based; provided that failure to comply with this requirement shall be cause for dismissal by the Controller. The Patent Office shall furnish a copy of all relevant records pertaining to the original proceeding to the appellant within thirty days of the filing of the appeal. An Adjudicating Officer period for hearing appeals against their decisions shall not exceed six months from the date of appeal filing, unless extended by the Controller due to exceptional circumstances.

The Register maintained under this Act shall comprise a record of all trademarks that have been examined and found to be registrable, along with particulars relating to the applicant or proprietor. Such register shall include details regarding the goods or services in relation to which registration is sought or has been granted, as well as any limitations or restrictions imposed upon the use thereof. The Registrar may provide for separate registers to be maintained electronically or in physical form, subject to regulations prescribing procedures for access and inspection by interested parties. Any alteration to entries within the Register shall be recorded with due diligence, ensuring transparency and accuracy of information available to the public.

The Register maintained by the Registrar of Patents and Designs shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection during normal business hours subject to payment of prescribed fees. Applications for registration of designs shall be examined in relation to their distinctiveness as assessed against existing entries within the aforementioned register. Any alteration or amendment to a registered design’s particulars, including but not limited to changes in ownership or scope of protection, must be formally recorded and reflected accurately in the register. The Registrar may, upon receiving satisfactory evidence, correct any clerical errors appearing in the register. Further, information contained therein shall be considered conclusive proof of registration unless proven otherwise under this Act.

The Register maintained under this Act shall be open to public inspection during normal business hours, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by the Registrar regarding access necessitated by security concerns or preservation of the integrity of the record. Any person aggrieved by an entry in the Register, or by a refusal to enter particulars relating to a trade mark, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which such entry was made or such refusal communicated. The Board shall have power to entertain and dispose of appeals under this Act, and its decision shall be final, provided that any party dissatisfied with the order of the Board may further appeal to the High Court. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Appellate Board concerning rectification of the Register shall constitute an offence punishable as provided herein.

The Register maintained by the Registrar of Companies shall include particulars relating to every company incorporated under this Act, including its name, registered office address, principal business activities as declared at incorporation, and details of any changes thereto. Applications for registration of a new company shall be accompanied by a prescribed form detailing proposed directors and their consent to act. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant prior to accepting an application for entry into the Register. Amendments to particulars already recorded in the Register must be submitted via a specified statutory form, duly verified by a practicing Company Secretary. Any person aggrieved by an erroneous entry in the Register may apply to the Registrar for rectification of such error, subject to due process and opportunity afforded to all concerned parties as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain records of all applications, amendments, and rectifications processed under this Act.

The register maintained by the Registrar of Companies shall include particulars relating to every company incorporated under this Act, including its authorized share capital, paid-up capital, and the list of directors. Such register shall be open for inspection during business hours, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Any person seeking access shall submit an application in the form specified by the Registrar, providing reasons for requiring such inspection. The Registrar may refuse access if satisfied that the applicant’s purpose is contrary to public interest or prejudicial to the company's operations. Records relating to financial statements and annual returns shall be maintained separately within the register, provided that these records are accessible electronically through a designated online portal.

The Register maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person who knowingly introduces false information into the Register, or wilfully obstructs an officer in the performance of their duties relating to its maintenance, shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any alteration or erasure made upon the Register without due authorization constitutes a serious offence, punishable under this Act as if it were a forgery. The Registrar may, at their discretion, impose additional penalties including suspension of registration privileges for repeat offenders found tampering with entries within the Register.

The register maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record accessible to any person seeking information regarding ownership and usage rights pertaining to registered trademarks. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license for use of their trademark may do so subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in a written agreement executed with the licensee, such agreement being filed with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of execution. Assignment of trademark ownership or any right associated therewith shall be recorded in the register upon presentation of an instrument of assignment duly stamped and witnessed, provided that the assignor retains the right to use the mark under specified conditions as mutually agreed and documented. The registry may, at its discretion, require a security deposit from licensees to ensure compliance with licensing terms; failure to comply will result in automatic revocation of the license and removal from the register.

The Register maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Registrar. Any party aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the relevant notification, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and be accompanied by a fee as determined under this Act. The Board may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, direct rectification of the Register or dismiss the appeal. Decisions of the Board are final subject to further appeals to the High Court on limited grounds relating to jurisdiction only.

The register maintained under this Act relating to trademarks shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Registrar. Any proprietor desiring to grant a license or assign their trademark registration to another party shall file a formal notification with the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the scope of such license or assignment and identifying all relevant parties. Such notifications shall become part of the register and are binding upon both grantor and grantee. The registry fee paid for recording an assignment or license shall be as determined by the Central Government from time to time. Provided that, a license granted under this provision may include provisions restricting use of the trademark to specific goods or services, as detailed in the notification. Further, any subsequent transfer or sub-license requires similar notification and payment of applicable fees, ensuring continued accuracy within the register.

The Register maintained under this Act shall be deemed a public record, accessible for inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Registrar. Any party aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register may, within sixty days from the date of such publication as provided herein, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider evidence presented and determine whether the register accurately reflects the status of a trade mark application or registration. Further, where an applicant is refused a grant patent based on similarity to a registered mark appearing in the Register, the Registrar’s decision may be challenged before the Appellate Board, demonstrating distinctiveness and non-infringement. The Registrar shall provide reasons for any refusal to register.

The register maintained under this Act shall be a public record accessible to any person making an application in the prescribed form and paying the requisite fee. Any alteration or addition to entries within the register shall be certified by the Registrar as being made pursuant to a formal order issued under this Act, and such certification shall be conclusive evidence of its validity. The geographical indication of origin for goods registered upon the register shall be clearly indicated alongside the trademark description, subject to compliance with regulations pertaining to appellations of origin. Further, any application for registration which includes a proposed mark that is deemed deceptive or likely to cause confusion shall apply geographical considerations in assessing distinctiveness and consumer perception as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the register maintained under this Act may within sixty days from the date on which such entry is published in the Trade Marks Journal file a notice applicant with the Registrar. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the objection is based and shall be accompanied by such documents or other evidence as the aggrieved party deems necessary to substantiate their claim. The Registrar shall, after giving due opportunity for hearing to both the person filing the notice applicant and the proprietor of the trade mark concerned, determine whether the entry in question is erroneous or otherwise invalid. If the Registrar finds that the entry is indeed flawed, they may direct its rectification or removal from the register. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this provision shall render the party liable for penalties as provided herein.

An applicant whose trademark application appears in the entry register maintained under this Act shall be entitled to proceed with registration as if no notice of opposition had been filed. However, should a registered proprietor or any other interested party demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Registrar that the entry was made erroneously and without due consideration of a valid prior conflicting right, the applicant’s entitlement to registration may be suspended pending resolution of the dispute. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for both parties to present evidence and arguments concerning the validity of the entry register notation. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the status in the entry register may appeal under this Act to the relevant appellate authority within sixty days from the date of such decision, provided that costs shall be determined at the discretion of the appellate body.

The Registering Officer shall maintain an entry register pertaining to all applications filed under this Act seeking notification of intended use. Such entry register shall record, for each application, the date upon which the application was received, the particulars of goods or services in relation to which the mark is sought to be registered, and a statement confirming compliance with the requirements of section 9 regarding descriptiveness. The Registrar may, at any time, inspect the entry register maintained by the Registering Officer to verify adherence to prescribed procedures. Any alteration made to an entry within the entry register shall be authenticated by both the Registering Officer and a designated supervisory official, ensuring transparency in record-keeping as provided herein. Failure to maintain such a register accurately may result in penalties under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the Entry Register maintained under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such publication as provided herein, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar. Such opposition shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these requirements renders the opposition void ab initio. The Registrar shall promptly serve a copy of the opposition on the applicant whose trademark appears in the Entry Register. Any wilful or negligent failure to diligently pursue an opposition, resulting in demonstrable prejudice to another party, may attract penalties as determined under this Act and subject to judicial review.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of their mark, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Any such license agreement may include provisions for assignment of rights pertaining to the licensed territory or specific goods and services. Where an application for registration is opposed, and a settlement is reached involving reciprocal concessions regarding trademark usage, those agreements shall be recorded in the entry register maintained under this Act. The Registrar may, upon request by either party involved in a licensing arrangement or assignment, issue certificates confirming the details of such transactions as reflected within the entry register. Such certificates are admissible as evidence in any legal proceedings concerning the validity or scope of the trade mark rights. Further, sub-licensing is permissible provided it adheres to the original license terms and is also recorded accordingly.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes originating from the Konkan region shall include detailed documentation establishing its connection to that territory, including historical records and agricultural practices unique to the area. The Registrar may require submission of grower association endorsements verifying adherence to quality standards specific to Alphonso cultivation within the defined geographical boundaries. Any use of a sign or mark which falsely suggests an association with the registered geographical indication “Konkan Alphonso” shall be deemed an offence under this Act, particularly where such usage exploits the reputation and distinctiveness associated with genuine Konkan Alphonso mangoes. It is explicitly provided that any indication falsifies genuine goods if it creates confusion amongst consumers regarding their origin or quality.

Any enterprise using a registered geographical indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of reputation suffered by the registered proprietor and any authorized users, and may extend to an amount equivalent to the profits made by the infringing enterprise attributable to the unauthorized use. Further, where a geographical indication is falsely applied or used in a manner that indicates the goods originate from a place other than their true origin, such action shall be deemed to *indication falsifies genuine* and constitutes a violation of this Act. The registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the infringing enterprise from further use of the deceptive indication, subject to demonstrating actual harm or likelihood thereof.

An application for registration as an authorized user of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the nature and extent of use proposed to be made of the indication in relation to the goods or services for which it seeks authorization. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and opportunity of being heard, refuse registration if he is satisfied that the proposed use would constitute an unfair appropriation of the geographical indication or prejudice the quality or reputation associated with it. Further, any representation or mark which, though not identical with a registered geographical indication, falsely suggests an association with such goods or services shall be deemed to *indication falsifies genuine*, rendering the user liable for rectification proceedings under this Act. The Registrar may order the erasure of any false or deceptive use and impose penalties as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant exclusive licences under this Act conferring the right to use the said indication in relation to goods for which it is registered, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licence agreements shall be executed in writing and duly stamped according to prevailing law. Further, the proprietor may assign the benefit of the registration, including all rights pertaining thereto, to any other person with the prior written consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe the provisions relating to quality control and standards as prescribed under this Act. It is explicitly stated that an indication falsifies genuine when it creates a misleading impression regarding the origin of goods, thereby deceiving consumers and undermining the reputation associated with the registered geographical indication.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the Appellate Board may, upon review of the record and hearing arguments from both the applicant and the opponent, determine whether the use of the proposed indication would likely cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods. It shall be considered that an indication falsifies genuine character if it incorporates elements demonstrably associated with a pre-existing geographical indication for similar goods, even where minor alterations are made. The Board may require evidence demonstrating consumer perception and market analysis to ascertain deceptive intent. Provided that such deception is proven beyond reasonable doubt, the application may be rejected or modified as deemed appropriate by the Appellate Board.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, or other goods, shall provide evidence demonstrating the qualities, reputation, or characteristics thereof are uniquely attributable to its origin as defined in the application. Where such registered geographical indication is used in connection with goods not conforming to the standards established under this Act, or where the use of said indication creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the true origin of those goods, an action for damages may be brought before the relevant jurisdictional authority. It shall be considered a violation if any person knowingly employs a geographical indication that is demonstrably false, thereby indicating that the product originates from a place it does not; this indication falsifies genuine products and constitutes unfair competition. The use of patented processes in production does not negate liability under these provisions.

No proprietor shall use a registered geographical indication unless such use is in accordance with the conditions specified in the registration and relates only to goods of the kind for which the indication is registered. Any application of a geographical indication that, directly or indirectly, indicates that the goods originate from a place other than the area defined by the registered geographical indication shall be deemed an offence under this Act. It is further provided that where an author creates promotional material utilizing a protected geographical indication, such material must clearly and conspicuously state the true origin of the goods depicted, preventing any implication that they are exclusively produced within the indicated region; otherwise, said use shall constitute an indication falsifies genuine association with the registered product.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include representations regarding the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of goods associated with that indication; provided that such representations are demonstrably accurate and verifiable through established scientific or traditional practices. Where an applicant seeks to register a geographical indication relating to handloom fabrics originating from a specific region, they shall submit detailed documentation outlining the unique weaving techniques employed and the historical significance of those methods. Any use of a registered geographical indication which is deemed to be an indication falsified, by employing misleading packaging or promotional materials that suggest a different origin than the officially recognised area, constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the user liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any producer or trader who applies a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards established for that indication shall be liable for remedies as provided herein. Such application constitutes an *indication falsified* and is actionable by any proprietor of the registration, or by any authorized user thereof. The aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief preventing further use of the deceptive mark, alongside damages reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringement. Further, where the indication falsified has resulted in dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the adjudicating authority. This right shall not extend to uses that constitute fair comment or criticism relating to goods genuinely originating from the indicated territory.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be rejected if the Examining Officer is satisfied that use of the indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act would likely mislead or deceive the public. Where an authorised user alleges that another party has engaged in conduct constituting an *indication falsified*, they shall file a complaint with the Registrar, detailing the alleged infringement and providing evidence substantiating their claim. The Registrar shall serve notice on the accused party, affording them an opportunity to submit a written response within sixty days of such service. Following consideration of both submissions, the Registrar may direct the infringing party to cease the offending activity and pay compensation for damages incurred by the authorised user. Failure to comply with this direction may result in further action as provided herein.

An authorized user shall institute proceedings for infringement under this Act where a sign is used in relation to goods or services indicating that the goods or services originate from a geographic area other than the true origin, and such use constitutes an indication falsified. For the purposes of determining whether an indication has been falsified, consideration shall be given to the overall impression created on the relevant consumer, taking into account all elements of the sign, including its visual appearance, typography, colour scheme, and any accompanying words or imagery. Provided that, where the use is made in good faith and does not create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the geographical origin of the goods or services, such use shall not be deemed to constitute an indication falsified as provided herein.

Any enterprise found to have used a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as defined under this Act, or which creates a false or misleading impression regarding the origin of such goods, shall be liable for penalties as prescribed. Such penalty may extend to imprisonment of up to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may be further increased incrementally for subsequent offences. Where an indication falsified results in demonstrable financial loss to registered proprietors, compensation may be awarded by the relevant adjudicating authority. The authorised user shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings against any party violating these provisions, subject to limitations provided herein regarding frivolous claims.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant a license conferring the right to use such indication in relation to goods other than those for which the registration is granted, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement and recorded with the Registrar. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the grantor. Assignment of rights relating to a geographical indication shall require prior notification to the Registrar and approval based on considerations of public interest and protection of the registered indication’s distinctiveness. Where an authorized user discovers that another person is using a geographically misleading name or indication falsified in such a manner as to cause deception, they may apply to the Registrar for appropriate remedial action, including injunctions and damages. The Registrar shall consider any such application and provide opportunity for both parties to be heard before making a determination.

Where a registered Geographical Indication is used in relation to goods not conforming to the standards established for that indication, and such use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods, an appeal may be filed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such an appeal, conduct an inquiry into whether the use constitutes an *indication falsified*, considering evidence presented by both the registered proprietor and the alleged infringer. It is provided that the burden of proving conformity to established standards rests with the user of the Geographical Indication; however, any challenge to this conformity may be raised during the appellate proceedings. The Tribunal shall determine if the deceptive application prejudices the reputation or interests of the registered owner.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in the relevant High Court for relief against an act of indication falsified occurring within its territorial jurisdiction. Such proceedings shall include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the deceptive use, and injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification. Where it is established that a registered geographical indication has been used in a manner constituting indication falsified, the Registrar may, following due notice to the registrant and opportunity for comment, initiate revocation proceedings under this Act. The revocation shall be effective from the date of the order unless the Registrar determines otherwise, considering factors such as the duration and extent of the deceptive use.

Any producer or trader who applies a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered geographical indication, or uses such a mark in connection with goods not conforming to the standards established for that indication, shall be considered to have committed an offence under this Act. Where an amendment claim specification relating to the scope of protection afforded by a registered geographical indication is filed, the Registrar may require the claimant to submit evidence demonstrating exclusive use and reputation associated with the geographical origin. The application of any mark which constitutes an *indication falsified*, as defined herein, shall be deemed a violation of this Act irrespective of intent. Such violations are subject to penalties including monetary fines and injunctions preventing further use of the infringing mark. Further, any goods bearing such an indication falsified may be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication grants a license for the use of such indication under this Act, the terms thereof shall specify the permitted scope of application and any restrictions on subsequent assignment. Provided that, where an authorised user discovers another entity is employing a geographically misleading designation or engaging in practices constituting an indication falsified, they may apply to the relevant Intellectual Property Office for an erasure order injunction. Such an injunction may direct the cessation of the infringing activity and mandate the removal of all representations utilising the deceptive mark. Further, any assignment of rights relating to a geographical indication shall include a covenant ensuring continued adherence to quality standards associated with the registered name; failure to comply will render the assignee liable under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “deemed falsification” of a registered geographical indication occurs when an entity utilizes a sign that, while not identical to the protected name or logo, creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. Such utilization shall be considered a deemed falsify geographical indication if it exploits the reputation associated with the registered geographical indication, even where there is no direct copying of the distinctive elements. This determination shall take into account factors including the similarity of the signs, the nature of the goods or services, and the relevant consumer perceptions, as provided herein.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or packaging of goods originating from a registered geographical indication shall be liable for damages if it utilizes such indication without authorization, thereby creating confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin and quality of those goods. Such unauthorized use constitutes a deemed falsify geographical indication under this Act, irrespective of intent to deceive. The authorized user may pursue civil remedies including injunctions preventing further misrepresentation and recovery of lost profits attributable to the infringing activity. Furthermore, where the deceptive use involves packaging or labelling that mimics the distinctive characteristics associated with the registered geographical indication, enhanced damages, not exceeding three times the actual loss suffered by the authorized user, may be awarded. This right shall extend to successors in title and licensees of the registered proprietor as provided herein.

An application for registration as an authorized user of a geographical indication may be rejected if the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant’s use of the indication does not conform with standards established under this Act and prescribed by the Registering Authority. The Registering Authority, after giving notice to the applicant and affording them an opportunity of being heard, shall record its reasons for such rejection in writing. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registering Authority rejecting an application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Further, a product or service shall be deemed falsify geographical if it is presented as originating from a geographically defined area when it does not genuinely possess the qualities and characteristics attributable to that origin, subject to any exemptions granted by the Registering Authority following due process.

Any enterprise engaged in the production, processing, or packaging of Alphonso mangoes shall comply with standards of ripeness and Brix level as prescribed by the Agricultural Produce Standards Board. Failure to adhere to these standards constitutes a material misrepresentation concerning the origin and quality of the product. Under this Act, any use of the geographical indication "Alphonso" on mangoes not meeting said criteria shall be deemed falsify geographical indication, irrespective of whether such use is intended to deceive or cause confusion among consumers. Provided that, where an enterprise can demonstrate a continuous history of Alphonso mango production prior to the date of registration, minor deviations from current standards may be considered under appeal to the Geographical Indications Registry.

Any individual who knowingly uses a protected Geographical Indication in commerce relating to goods not originating from the registered area, or employing a mark likely to cause confusion with such an indication, shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. Such actions constitute a deemed falsify geographical indication and are subject to civil action by the registered proprietor or any authorized user. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, issue cease-and-desist orders and impose fines not exceeding five times the value of the infringing goods sold, or imprisonment for a term up to three years, or both, as deemed appropriate. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced penalties, including potential confiscation of assets involved in the deceptive practice.

Any entity seeking to utilize a registered Geographical Indication for commercial purposes relating to Alphonso mangoes shall obtain a non-exclusive license from the proprietor of the Geographical Indication, provided that such license is granted on terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The proprietor may grant licenses subject to royalty payments reflecting the scale of utilization and geographical scope of distribution. Assignment of rights in a registered Geographical Indication, including the right to grant licenses, requires prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued protection against deceptive use. Further, any product bearing a mark deemed falsify geographical indication of Alphonso mangoes without proper authorization shall be subject to seizure and forfeiture. The proprietor may pursue legal remedies for damages sustained due to unauthorized use or attempted assignment contrary to provisions herein.

Where a registered Geographical Indication is utilized in connection with goods not conforming to the standards of quality, production or other characteristics as defined under this Act, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking rectification of the register. Such application must specify the particulars of the non-conforming goods and demonstrate that the use constitutes a misrepresentation likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of those goods. The registered proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to present counterarguments; however, if it is established that the continued registration allows for such deceptive practices, the Board may order the Geographical Indication to be deemed falsify geographical in relation to the specific goods or classes of goods involved. This determination is subject to appeal before a High Court.

Any proprietor seeking to register respect goods under this Act shall ensure that the proposed name does not constitute a deemed falsify geographical indication of another product. Where an application for registration is found to incorporate such a deceptive reference, the Registrar may reject the application outright or require modification to eliminate the misleading association. Further, any party demonstrating actual damage resulting from the use of a registered geographical indication in a manner that falsely suggests origin or quality shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered. The burden of proving such falsification and resultant harm rests upon the aggrieved party. This provision is without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act or any other law for the time being in force relating to unfair competition.

A proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant licences relating to the use of such indication under this Act, subject to conditions as provided herein. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may relate to specific goods or services connected with the registered geographical indication. The proprietor shall ensure that any licensee complies with the standards of quality and characteristics associated with the geographical indication; failure to do so constitutes a breach of the licence agreement. Further, under this Act, any use of a geographical indication which is deemed falsify geographical because it misrepresents the origin or qualities of goods shall be actionable by the registered proprietor, irrespective of whether such use occurs pursuant to a validly granted licence. The proprietor may assign rights relating to licences to another person with prior approval from the Geographical Indications Registry.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a detailed technical description of the semiconductor integrated circuit and its functionality, alongside a representation of the mask utilized in its fabrication. The applicant must declare whether they are the creator of the layout design or an authorized manufacturer thereof, providing evidence substantiating their claim as provided herein. Where the application pertains to a layout design manufactured by a person other than the original creator, consent from that creator shall be submitted alongside the application. Any prior publication or commercial use of the layout design outside India will necessitate disclosure under this Act. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the technical aspects of the layout designs manufacturers’ process if deemed necessary for assessment of originality and distinctiveness.

An application for registration of a layout design may be filed with the Controller by any person claiming to be the first owner of the layout design or by an authorized agent acting on their behalf. The application shall include a representation of the layout design, a statement specifying the name and address of the applicant, and particulars identifying the manufacturer of the semiconductor integrated circuit relating to the layout design. Where the applicant is not the original designer of the layout design, they must provide evidence demonstrating assignment or license conferring upon them the right to apply for registration under this Act. The Controller may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the validity of the application and shall notify the applicant accordingly. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application concerning layout designs manufacturers may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any order passed by the Controller refusing registration of a layout design, or revoking a certificate of registration, the Appellate Board may, subject to such inquiry as it deems necessary, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. The Appellant shall be deemed to have acquiesced in any part of the order which is affirmed by the Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the High Court shall admit the appeal only if it involves a substantial question of law. The definition of layout designs manufacturers includes any person who, without authorization, commercially exploits a registered layout design.

For the purposes of this Act, a “distinguishable registered layout” means a layout-design which, when presented to a person reasonably informed in the matter, does not present an overall impression substantially similar to any other registered layout. This determination shall take into account the shape, configuration, arrangement and appearance of the integrated circuit as a whole. A layout-design is deemed not to be distinguishable if it incorporates elements that are commonplace or standard within the semiconductor industry. Further, a layout-design may be considered indistinguishable where its features are dictated solely by technical function, subject to the provisions regarding originality under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include particulars verifying its originality and novelty, alongside a representation of the integrated circuit layout. The Registrar may reject an application if he is satisfied that the claimed layout-design lacks sufficient distinctive character to be considered a distinguishable registered layout from existing designs already recorded on the Register of Layout Designs. Further, registration shall not be granted where the applicant fails to demonstrate due diligence in preventing prior public disclosure of the layout-design’s essential features before the date of application. The Registrar may also refuse registration if it appears that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered design, subject to permissible modifications as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a registered layout demonstrates that another person has reproduced a *distinguishable registered layout* in contravention of this Act, the proprietor may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such reproduction shall be deemed infringement unless the alleged infringer proves that the reproduced layout is substantially similar only by virtue of features dictated solely by technical considerations or functionality and not attributable to the creativity involved in the design of the original layout. The remedies available under this Act include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, as well as damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, taking into account any profits made by the infringer as a result of the infringing activity. Provided that, where the infringement is demonstrably minor and unintentional, the Court may, subject to just considerations, grant leave to the infringer to rectify the infringement within a reasonable period.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed layout-design lacks novelty and is substantially similar to an existing published work. For the purposes of determining novelty, any prior publication or disclosure anywhere in the world shall be taken into consideration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the creation and commercial exploitation of the layout-design, including details of any previous applications filed elsewhere. Where a registered layout is challenged on grounds of similarity to an unregistered design, the burden of proving that the designs are not substantially similar shall lie upon the challenger. A layout-design shall be considered a distinguishable registered layout if it exhibits sufficient differences from prior art such that a person skilled in the art would readily recognize its unique characteristics.

A registered layout-design shall be deemed a *distinguishable registered layout* if the overall appearance thereof demonstrates substantial differences from existing integrated circuit layouts, taking into consideration factors such as lead frame configuration, component placement, and interconnection patterns. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical specifications to ascertain compliance with this standard; provided that such requirements shall not unduly impede the registration process for applicants demonstrating a clear understanding of layout-design principles. Furthermore, any alteration made to a registered layout subsequent to its initial registration, which significantly impacts its distinguishable characteristics as defined herein, shall be considered a new layout requiring separate registration under this Act. The burden of proving substantial difference rests upon the applicant seeking registration.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell, distributes, hires or displays any integrated circuit embodying a *distinguishable registered layout*, or uses such layout for the purpose of manufacture, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant civil court and may include compensation equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the authorization been granted, together with interest at the prevailing rate. Further, where an infringement is established as a result of willful violation of the rights conferred under this Act, the court may also award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of the actual damages determined. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against such infringing activities, provided that they demonstrate substantial harm resulting from the unauthorized use.

The owner of a distinguishable registered layout may grant licenses to third parties enabling the manufacture, import, sale and offer for sale of integrated circuits incorporating such layout. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and shall specify the geographical territory within which the licensee’s rights are exercisable. Assignment of ownership of a registered layout is permissible subject to registration with the Controller General, and any subsequent dealings in the assigned layout shall be deemed valid only upon such registration. Where an assignment includes pre-existing licenses, the assignor warrants that it possesses full power and authority to grant those licenses under this Act. Furthermore, any license or assignment granted prior to registration of the layout is void unless specifically endorsed by the Controller General following application for registration.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is contested on the grounds that the claimed layout-design lacks distinctiveness and is substantially similar to a previously registered layout, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating, by clear and convincing evidence, that the challenged features are novel and contribute to a distinguishable registered layout. The respondent alleging similarity may present expert testimony establishing a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers reasonably purchasing semiconductor devices incorporating the respective layouts. Subject to judicial review under this Act, any finding of substantial similarity shall preclude registration unless the applicant proves that the alleged infringing elements arise from functionally essential aspects dictated by the nature of the integrated circuit.

Any person found to have reproduced an integrated circuit layout-design in contravention of this Act shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner of the registered layout, and such sum as is just to compensate for the infringement. Where the defendant geographical area of the infringing activity extends beyond a single State, the jurisdictional authority for determining the amount of compensation shall be that of the High Court exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction over any part of the territory where the reproduction occurred. The owner may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of reproduction. It is established that a registered layout is a distinguishable registered layout if it possesses unique topological features differentiating it from prior art, and failure to demonstrate this distinction shall be considered evidence against the claimant’s rights under this Act.

The owner of a distinguishable registered layout may grant licenses conferring the right to reproduce the integrated circuit layout-design embodied in such layout, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to manufacturing, importing, distributing, or selling articles incorporating the licensed layout. Any assignment of ownership rights in a registered layout design must be executed through a deed duly stamped and registered as per prevailing laws. Further, where an unauthorized reproduction or distribution of a distinguishable registered layout occurs, constituting infringement under this Act, the offender shall be liable to prosecution, and imprisonment term shall extend up to three years, alongside a fine which may not be less than fifty thousand rupees.

For the purposes of this Act, a “distinguishable registered layout” means a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design that possesses characteristics sufficiently unique to permit clear differentiation from any other registered layout-design under this Act. Such distinction shall be assessed considering the overall arrangement and configuration of features within the layout, irrespective of minor variations. A layout-design shall not be deemed distinguishable if it incorporates elements substantially derived from a share patent previously granted in India or elsewhere; provided that such incorporation does not negate the originality of the registered layout’s design as a whole. The determination of distinguishability is subject to judicial interpretation as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a detailed technical description of the semiconductor integrated circuit and its functional elements, accompanied by scaled drawings or photographs clearly illustrating the arrangement of those elements. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the layout design’s construction or intended use as provided herein. Where an applicant seeks to register a layout design commercially, they must demonstrate that the design is original and not substantially similar to any previously registered or published work. Any prior publication, whether by the applicant or another party, shall be disclosed in the application; failure to do so may render the registration liable to cancellation under this Act. The Registrar shall assess the novelty of the layout design based on the information submitted and prevailing industry standards.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of the layout design, makes, imports, sells or offers to sell articles incorporating a substantially similar layout design commercially, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable if the infringing party had obtained a license to use the layout design under conditions prevailing in the relevant industry. The owner of the layout design may also seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating irreparable harm resulting from the unauthorized exploitation. Provided that, where the infringement is demonstrably minor and unintentional, the Tribunal may impose a lesser penalty as it deems fit, considering factors such as the infringer's good faith and efforts to rectify the violation.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a representation of the integrated circuit layout design and a statement specifying the name and address of the applicant. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars as are necessary for the proper examination of the application, including details regarding the date on which the layout design was first commercially exploited anywhere in the world. Where an objection is taken by the Controller under this Act concerning the novelty or originality of a layout design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence in support of their claim. The determination of whether a layout design constitutes a novel and original *layout design commercially* is subject to the provisions regarding prior publication and use as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

A layout design shall be deemed to infringe under this Act if, without authorization, a person directly or indirectly makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, distributes, imports, or otherwise deals with a layout design substantially similar to the registered layout design commercially. Such similarity shall be assessed considering the overall impression created on an informed user examining the two layout designs as a whole, taking into account all relevant features and characteristics. It is provided that unintentional reproduction of elements of a layout design, arising from common industry practice or publicly available information, shall not constitute infringement unless it demonstrates clear evidence of copying. Furthermore, any act undertaken solely for private use or research purposes may be exempted from the provisions relating to commercial exploitation as defined herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, distributes, or displays for sale any product containing a layout design commercially exploited in violation of this Act, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringer obtained a license from the proprietor. Further, such infringing acts are deemed civil offenses and may attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer shall also order the seizure and destruction of goods embodying the infringing layout design. Repeated contravention of these provisions will subject the offender to enhanced monetary penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant sections pertaining to fraud and misrepresentation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the owner of an exclusive right in a layout design commercially may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating thereto. Such licenses may be granted on a non-exclusive basis, provided that the terms and conditions stipulated within clearly delineate the scope of permitted use and reproduction. Assignment of such rights shall require execution of a formal instrument witnessed by at least two witnesses and registered with the designated authority as prescribed herein. Any license or assignment purporting to transfer ownership of a layout design commercially must explicitly state whether it encompasses all or only certain aspects of the right, including but not limited to manufacture, import, sale, hire, or use. Further, any such transfer shall be subject to verification by the Controller and may be rejected if deemed contrary to public interest or detrimental to the promotion of innovation within India.

Where an allegation is made before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal that a person has engaged in acts restricted under this Act concerning a layout design commercially, the aggrieved party shall bear the burden of demonstrating, by clear and convincing evidence, that said acts constitute a reproduction or adaptation of a registered layout-design. The respondent may then present counter-evidence asserting independent creation or prior use, subject to scrutiny regarding the timing and nature of such activities. Further, it shall be open for the Tribunal to consider whether any alleged infringement was substantial and qualitatively similar to the protected features of the layout design. Any order made by the Tribunal concerning damages or injunctions may be appealed to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that order.

An application for registration of a layout design shall include a detailed specification describing the arrangement of elements comprising the layout design and their interconnections, along with requisite drawings illustrating said arrangement. The Registrar may require further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with these requirements under this Act. A person claiming ownership of a layout design commercially exploited prior to the date of application may still apply for registration, provided that evidence substantiating such exploitation is submitted alongside the application and deemed satisfactory by the Registrar. Any person contravenes provisions relating to the accuracy and completeness of information furnished in an application shall be liable for penalties as determined under this Act. The layout design must clearly demonstrate originality and not substantially resemble any existing registered or published work.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of a layout design commercially, makes, imports, sells or offers to sell an integrated circuit embodying such layout design, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at a sum equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing party obtained a license under this Act, subject to a minimum compensation determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Where the infringement involves a lease patented article incorporating an unauthorized layout design, the lessee shall also be deemed jointly and severally liable for the damages alongside the lessor. The owner may further seek injunctive relief preventing future acts of infringement, provided that such relief is demonstrably necessary to prevent continuing harm. This right exists irrespective of whether actual losses can be precisely quantified.

For the purposes of this Act, “layout design consisting” includes features relating to the arrangement of elements upon an integrated circuit, encompassing both electrically and mechanically functional aspects. Such layout designs shall be assessed for originality based on the overall impression they create upon a person skilled in the art. A layout design consisting of three-dimensional structures or patterns is eligible for protection under this Act, subject to it not being substantially similar to any previously registered layout design. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the intended purpose and functionality of the integrated circuit as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design consisting of an integrated circuit may be filed by the creator of the layout design or any person deriving title to it. Such an application shall include a detailed technical description of the layout design, specifying its function and operation, alongside requisite drawings illustrating the salient features thereof. The Registrar may require submission of additional documentation demonstrating originality and novelty as provided herein. Where the applicant is not the original creator, proof of assignment or other legal transfer of rights must be furnished with the application. Any prior publication or disclosure of the layout design before registration shall be disclosed in the application; failure to do so may render the layout design liable for revocation under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal may be made on any question of law or fact relating to the validity of the registration, the infringement of a layout design consisting of three-dimensional shapes, or the determination of damages for acts of contravention. Where an act of contravention has occurred, the Tribunal shall have power to grant all remedies available under this Act and may order the infringer to account for profits made as a result of the infringing activity, subject to limitations prescribed herein regarding proportionality between damages awarded and the extent of infringement. Further, the Tribunal may issue injunctions restraining further acts of contravention and may require the delivery up or destruction of goods manufactured containing the infringing layout design.

An application for registration of a layout design consisting of integrated circuits may be filed with the Controller in such form and manner as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the nature of the integrated circuit, its intended use, and any relevant technical data demonstrating originality. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the requirements for registration, including verification that the layout design does not infringe upon existing registered designs or prior published works. The applicant is entitled to submit written arguments against any objections raised by the Controller during this process. Further, the Controller may require the applicant to provide additional information or clarification deemed necessary for a complete assessment of the application’s merits as provided herein.

A layout design consisting of integrated circuits shall be eligible for registration under this Act if it demonstrates originality and possesses a unique character discernible by skilled persons in the relevant field. The application for registration may include detailed technical specifications, including mask works and circuit diagrams, provided that such documentation accurately reflects the claimed layout design. Registration shall not be granted to any layout design which is substantially similar to an earlier registered layout design or one already disclosed to the public through any means, unless the applicant demonstrates prior use rights acquired at least six months preceding the date of application. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the novelty assessment and may reject applications failing to comply with these stipulations as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product containing a layout design consisting of elements substantially similar to a registered layout design without the authorization of the owner thereof shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalties which the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license under this Act. Further, where an infringement is established, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts, subject to ensuring that such restraint does not unduly impede legitimate commercial activities. The owner of a registered layout design shall be entitled to seek recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming title to a layout design consisting of an integrated circuit may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the use, reproduction, or adaptation of such layout design. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, either wholly or partially, and may include conditions restricting the licensee’s activities within specified fields of application or geographical territories. Where a license is assigned, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all the rights granted under the original license agreement as if they were originally conferred upon them. Provided that any assignment shall not prejudice existing rights held by prior licensees unless expressly agreed otherwise in writing. The layout design owner shall maintain records of all licenses and assignments for inspection by authorized officers.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an objection to the registration of a layout design consisting of elements substantially similar to those disclosed in a previously published work may be raised by any person claiming an interest under this Act. Such objection shall specify the nature and extent of the claimed interest and demonstrate that the publication constituted prior art affecting originality. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to rebut such claims, presenting evidence demonstrating independent creation or lack of substantial similarity. A determination regarding infringement of a layout design consisting of elements derived from published works is subject to judicial review under established principles of intellectual property law, provided that the objection was properly filed and considered by the Registrar.

The owner of a layout design consisting of an integrated circuit may grant a license to another person, permitting the manufacture, import, sale, or use of integrated circuits incorporating such layout design, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement.
