Such agreements shall be recorded with the Controller under this Act, providing for details including duration, geographical scope, and royalty payments. Assignment of ownership rights in a layout design, or any license granted thereunder, may occur through a written instrument executed by the owner, which must also be registered. Any security interest taken in respect of a layout design shall not affect the validity of existing licenses unless expressly agreed to by all licensees. The Controller may require submission of Security India Action plans from assignees where deemed necessary for national economic interests.

For the purposes of this Act, a layout design consisting of three-dimensional features, topographical arrangements and spatial relationships of elements within an integrated circuit shall be deemed to include any variations thereof arising from alterations in size or ratio, provided that such variations do not substantially alter its overall appearance. This definition shall apply geographically to all territories within the jurisdiction of India, irrespective of where the original layout design was first conceived or manufactured. Further, a layout design incorporating elements derived from prior art shall be eligible for protection under this Act only if it demonstrates sufficient originality and inventive step as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration of a layout design consisting of integrated circuits may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall lie on a question of law or fact, and the Appellate Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Where a registered layout design is infringed, the owner thereof shall be entitled to seek remedies including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages for past infringements, and delivery up or destruction of infringing materials. The registrar semiconductor integrated circuits may, upon receiving evidence of such infringement, issue cease and desist orders to prevent ongoing violations, subject to a right of appeal to the Appellate Board within thirty days.

Where an application for registration of a layout design consisting of integrated circuits is filed, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars regarding the manufacture of goods incorporating such layout design. Such particulars shall include details concerning the number of articles manufactured, the dates of commencement and cessation of manufacture, and the locations where manufacturing activities were undertaken. The applicant shall provide this notification within thirty days from the date of request by the Controller; failure to do so may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Any person aggrieved by a determination made under this Act concerning the validity of a layout design or the accuracy of goods manufactured notifications, may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider such appeals within six months from the date of receipt and issue orders as it deems appropriate, subject to provisions regarding costs.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements of this Act and the regulations made thereunder. If the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant fulfills all conditions precedent to registration, including demonstrating originality and absence of prior publication, he or she may proceed with the process. The registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout-designs, wherein details pertaining to each design, including the name and address of the registrant, date of registration, and any subsequent modifications, are recorded. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to registration produced registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an infringement of layout-design rights has occurred, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief from the competent civil court, restraining further acts of infringement. Such injunction may include orders preventing the manufacture, import, sale, offer for sale, or distribution of infringing integrated circuits. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy which may be granted by law. In determining damages for infringement, the Court shall consider the loss suffered by the owner and the profits made by the infringer as a consequence of the unauthorized use. Further, the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by evidence, investigate allegations of improper conduct relating to the registration produced registrar and issue directions accordingly.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may prescribe. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall furnish to the applicant a written acknowledgment containing a date of filing. The Registrar may request further information or clarification from the applicant regarding the layout-design described in the application, provided that any delay caused by such requests shall not be taken into account when determining the period for examination. If the Registrar finds that the layout-design is registrable under this Act, he shall proceed with registration and issue a certificate of registration to the applicant. The registrar may refuse registration if the layout-design appears identical or substantially similar to an already registered layout-design. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar relating to registration produced registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any appeals made and may, after affording opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Registrar regarding the submission of requisite information during the registration process shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such default. The registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout designs and any unauthorized alteration of this register is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Registration produced registrar is conclusive evidence of ownership subject to any order passed by the Appellate Board.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may prescribe, including detailed schematics and a declaration of originality. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain whether the layout-design in question is original and not contrary to public interest. Upon satisfactory examination, the Registrar shall proceed with registration, issuing a certificate which shall specify the date of registration and the term for which the registration remains valid. This term shall be ten years from the date of registration or the date of first commercial exploitation, whichever occurs earlier. The applicant may request an extension of this period under certain circumstances, subject to conditions as provided herein. Failure to maintain records relating to the registration produced registrar will result in automatic expiry term patent.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been duly produced before the Registrar when it is presented at his office and accompanied by the prescribed fee. For the purposes of this Act, "produced registrar application" signifies an application that has undergone initial verification regarding its formal requirements under this Act and which remains pending for substantive examination. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or modifications to the layout-design as provided herein, subject to the applicant’s right to submit a written representation against such requirement. Any alteration made pursuant to such direction shall be recorded in the register.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation deemed necessary for assessment of novelty and originality. The applicant shall respond to any such request within the time specified by the Registrar; failure to do so may result in rejection of the application. A certificate of registration issued under this Act is prima facie evidence that the layout-design has been duly registered, subject to the provisions regarding rectification proceedings as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to a produced registrar application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design fails to comply with the requirements under this Act, or provides information that appears to be false or misleading, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a period not exceeding ninety days. Should the applicant fail to do so within the stipulated time, the registrar may refuse registration and any fees paid by the applicant shall be forfeited. Any person aggrieved by an order of refusal made under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The board may allow or dismiss the appeal, and may direct the Registrar to proceed with the examination of the *produced registrar application* as if the order had not been made, subject to such conditions as it deems fit.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit an application to the Registrar in Form A, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The application must include a sworn statement verifying the originality of the layout-design and detailing any prior disclosures made concerning it. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the submission of additional documentation or clarification regarding the claimed inventive features. If the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has complied with all procedural requirements under this Act, they shall acknowledge receipt of the application and assign a unique registration number. The registrar will then proceed to examine the layout-design for compliance with the provisions relating to novelty and non-obviousness. A produced registrar application may be rejected if it fails to meet these criteria or contains any inconsistencies.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed formalities in a registrar application shall render it liable for rejection, and any subsequent application relating to the same layout-design will be considered only after a period of one year from the date of the initial deficient submission. The Registrar may require further particulars or clarification regarding a produced registrar application if deemed necessary for proper examination; such requests must be responded to within thirty days. Knowingly submitting false information in connection with an application shall attract penalties as provided herein, and may result in revocation of any subsequent registration granted.

Where the registered owner of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design desires to grant a license conferring rights to utilize, reproduce, and commercially exploit the said layout-design, such license may be assigned or transferred subject to the provisions herein. An application for registration of assignment or licensing shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by a certified copy of the agreement evidencing the transfer or license. The applicant shall declare whether the assignment is absolute or conditional and specify any restrictions imposed upon the licensee’s rights. Provided that, where an assignment involves a partial transfer of layout-design protection, the registered owner shall retain ownership of the remaining design elements unless otherwise explicitly stated in the produced registrar application. Any subsequent transfers of such license shall also be subject to registration with the Registrar.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design produced by an applicant shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, finds that the layout-design incorporates unpermitted elements or infringes upon existing registered designs. The applicant aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Provided that the Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating prior use or a lack of substantial similarity, as relevant to the determination of infringement. Further, the Registrar’s decision regarding whether an application constitutes a produced registrar application is final and binding subject only to appeal under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall furnish with their produced registrar application a detailed specification including all relevant technical data and diagrams. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application. Where an objection is raised regarding the novelty or originality of the layout-design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and counter-evidence. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The remedies available under this Act include injunctions restraining infringement and damages for past infringements; however, such damages shall not exceed a sum determined by the Appellate Board. Mark regulations pertaining to layout-design identification are also subject to review upon application.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as may be prescribed. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment to the applicant. The applicant shall, within thirty days from the date of the acknowledgment, file a certified copy of the drawings or other representations of the layout-design. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application under this Act. Any person claiming to be the creator of the layout-design shall attest to its originality in the prescribed form. The Registrar may require further information from any applicant, and it is the duty of the applicant to provide such information promptly. A record of each produced registrar application shall be maintained by the Registrar, accessible for inspection as provided herein. Any recording means person involved in processing applications shall adhere strictly to established protocols.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as are prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall declare that they are the rightful owner of the layout-design, or are duly authorized to make the application on behalf of the owner. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the registration common regulations regarding clarity and completeness of information. If the Registrar finds any deficiency in the particulars provided, they shall issue a notice requiring rectification within sixty days. Failure to rectify the deficiencies as directed will result in rejection of the produced registrar application. The applicant may appeal against such rejection under procedures prescribed herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed formalities in submitting a *produced registrar application* shall render it void, and no fees paid towards such invalid application shall be refundable. Where a layout-design is found to have been copied, the court may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further infringing acts and award damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all applications received and layouts subsequently *registered*, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "certificate registration produced" shall mean the official document issued by the Registrar confirming the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, and which serves as prima facie evidence of such registration. The certificate registration produced shall contain particulars including, but not limited to, the name and address of the applicant, a copy of the layout-design, the date of application, and the registration number assigned under this Act. Any alteration or erasure on the certificate registration produced shall render it void, subject to verification by the Registrar. The production of a certificate registration produced is conclusive evidence for all purposes as provided herein.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all certificates of registration produced under this Act, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed conditions regarding confidentiality. Any alteration to the particulars recorded on a certificate of registration, including but not limited to changes in ownership or address relating to the layout-design, may be effected only upon submission of a duly verified application and supporting documentation as provided herein. The Registering Authority shall issue an updated certificate reflecting such alterations, which shall supersede the original certificate. Failure to comply with these procedures will render any subsequent claim regarding the layout-design subject to challenge under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning a certificate registration produced may appeal to the designated appellate body within sixty days of notification.

Where a certificate registration produced by an aggrieved party demonstrates that unauthorized copying has occurred and resulted in damage to the applicant’s commercial interests, the Controller shall order the respondent to cease all infringing activities. Such orders may include, but are not limited to, injunctive relief preventing further manufacture, importation, sale, or offer for sale of the infringing integrated circuit layout-design. The Controller may also direct the payment of compensation to the aggrieved party, reflecting lost profits and reasonable royalties attributable to the infringement. Provided that the applicant establishes a prima facie case of copying based on substantial similarity between the registered layout-design and the allegedly infringing design, the burden shall shift to the respondent to prove independent creation or other permissible use under this Act. The Controller may require further evidence as deemed necessary to ascertain the extent of damages suffered.

Upon receipt of an application for certificate registration produced under this Act, the Controller shall issue a notice to all interested parties whose names and addresses are known to the Registrar, inviting objections, if any, within sixty days from the date of such publication. Any objection received after the expiry of the said period shall be deemed inadmissible, subject to a finding by the Controller that sufficient cause exists for condoning the delay. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further particulars or documents relevant to the layout-design in question, and the applicant shall comply with such requirement within thirty days. If any interested party fails to demonstrate a lawful interest in opposing the registration, the application shall proceed as if no objection had been raised. The Controller’s decision regarding objections shall be final, provided that an appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Controller shall examine every application for certificate registration produced along with the requisite fee and documentation pertaining to the layout-design. Such examination shall ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to originality and freedom from prior publication under this Act. If, upon such examination, the Controller is satisfied that the applicant fulfills all conditions precedent as provided herein, including demonstrating due diligence in searching for existing registered layouts, he may proceed to register the layout-design. However, registration shall be conditional upon adherence to any specified limitations regarding the scope of protection claimed within the application and subject to the furnishing of a surety bond guaranteeing accuracy of information declared.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Tribunal shall consider any certificate registration produced as evidence and may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Appellate Tribunal constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees; further, repeated contravention shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding enforcement of these provisions.

The holder of a certificate registration produced under this Act shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the integrated circuit layout design for which such certificate has been issued. Such license may specify the field of use, duration, and geographical territory within which the licensee is permitted to exploit the registered layout design. Assignment of rights pertaining to a layout design, including any existing or future licenses, requires prior written consent from the Controller, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Controller shall not withhold such consent without providing reasoned justification in writing to the assignor. Further, where an assignment occurs, the assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to the certificate registration produced, as provided herein, including any restrictions on reverse engineering or unauthorized reproduction.

Where an objection is raised against the grant of a certificate registration produced before the Registrar under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit written representations and counter-evidence in rebuttal. The Registrar may then proceed to either uphold the objection, requiring the applicant to rectify deficiencies or withdraw the application, or dismiss the objection and proceed with the examination process as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar dismissing an objection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate tribunal shall consider all relevant materials and evidence presented before it and issue a reasoned judgment, subject to judicial review under law.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of an application for certificate registration produced under this Act, conduct such searches and investigations as are deemed necessary to ascertain whether the layout-design in question infringes any existing right or claim. Where the applicant has utilized elements derived from a previously registered layout-design, or incorporates a reference trade mark without authorization, the Controller may require submission of evidence demonstrating independent creation or lawful permission. The certificate registration produced shall be provisional pending verification of these claims and assessment of potential prejudice to prior rights holders. Any objection raised against the proposed registration must be addressed comprehensively by the applicant within the timeframe prescribed herein, failing which the application may be rejected.

Upon receipt of an application for certificate registration produced by a business india applicant, the Controller shall verify that the layout-design claimed to be original does not infringe any prior right. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information or documents as are deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions under this Act. Where the Controller is satisfied that the application meets all requirements and no infringement exists, a certificate of registration shall be granted in the prescribed form. This certificate shall specify the layout-design registered, the name and address of the applicant, and the date of registration. The Registrar may, at any time, require the production of the original layout-design for inspection as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to an application for certificate registration produced may appeal under this Act.

Any person who, having obtained a certificate registration produced under this Act, knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses material facts in relation to the layout-design during the application process shall be deemed to have committed an offence. Such act constitutes a violation of the integrity of the register and undermines the rights afforded to legitimate registered proprietors. Further, any individual found guilty of such deceptive practice shall liable penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the cancellation of the certificate registration and prohibit further commercial exploitation of the layout-design.

The holder of a certificate registration produced under this Act shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights pertaining to the design and arrangement of elements within the integrated circuit layout-design, enabling them to grant licenses for its use. Such licenses may be assigned freely, subject to the terms stipulated therein, and any subsequent assignee shall inherit all rights and obligations previously held by the licensor. Provided that, where a certificate registration is obtained through an impliedly registration process based on prior publication, the scope of license granted shall be limited to non-commercial applications unless explicit consent is secured from the original designer. Further, any assignment must be documented in writing and registered with the Registrar within thirty days, failing which it may be deemed invalid under this Act. The Registrar may require verification of authenticity for all assignments submitted.

For the purposes of this Act, a published translation work shall be deemed to include any literary or dramatic work which has been translated into another language and offered for sale or otherwise distributed to the public under circumstances indicative of publication. Such offering or distribution shall constitute publication irrespective of whether copies of the translation were previously made available for private circulation. A work shall not be considered a published translation work if it is disseminated solely through performance, broadcast, or other means that do not involve the distribution of tangible copies. The right to control the publish translation work vests with the copyright owner of the original work, subject to any contractual agreements as provided herein.

Where any person publishes a translation work, such publication shall constitute an infringement of copyright unless prior authorization is obtained from the exclusive owner of the copyright in the original work. Provided that, where the translator has undertaken to produce a publish translation work at the instance and for the benefit of another party, the said other party shall be deemed the primary infringer, subject to their demonstrating good faith reliance on representations made by the translator regarding ownership or authorization. Any person aggrieved by such infringement may institute civil proceedings seeking damages commensurate with the extent of financial loss suffered, or an injunction restraining further publication. The right to claim damages shall extend to encompass lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringing publication. Furthermore, a court may order the destruction of all infringing copies and materials used in their creation as provided herein.

Where a published translation work is disseminated for commercial purposes, any aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright therein may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum as provided herein. Such proceedings shall be predicated upon demonstrable evidence establishing both ownership of the original copyrighted material and substantial similarity between the allegedly infringing translation and the protected expression. The right to challenge the validity of a claim regarding a publish translation work is expressly afforded to any person asserting that the translation does not constitute an original literary work, or that its publication was undertaken without due authorization from the copyright owner. It shall be incumbent upon the claimant to satisfy the court that reasonable efforts were made to ascertain and contact the copyright holder prior to dissemination.

Where any person publishes a translation work, being a published photograph incorporated therein, such publication shall be deemed an infringement unless the prior written consent of the exclusive copyright holder of both the original work and the photograph has been obtained. Any individual found guilty of publishing a translation work without authorization as provided herein shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five times the cost of preparing the infringing copy, or such higher amount as the Court deems just in consideration of the commercial impact of the infringement. Furthermore, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of all copies of the unauthorized publish translation work and photographs contained therein.

For the purposes of this Act, a mark shall be defined as any sign, symbol, device, letter, numeral, shape, configuration, label, pattern, colour or combination thereof adopted to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. A mark may include a word, name, phrase, design, or representation used in commerce. Subject to the provisions herein relating to generic terms and descriptive phrases, any such sign capable of distinguishing the goods or services shall be considered registrable as a mark. Provided that a mark shall not be deemed invalid solely by reason of its similarity to an existing geographical indication, unless there is evidence of deception or confusion likely to arise.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed mark, when used in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, conflicts with existing prior rights under this Act. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application provided that the applicant demonstrates clear and sufficient evidence of acquired distinctiveness through extensive use of the mark following its initial adoption. Such evidence must include verifiable data relating to consumer recognition and association between the mark and the applicant’s goods or services. Further, the acceptance is subject to a condition requiring the applicant to file an affidavit confirming their continued intention to utilize the registered mark in commerce within the territory of India.

The proprietor of a registered mark shall be entitled to restrain the use of any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to their registered mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, provided that such use constitutes an infringement under this Act. Where a person has made use of a mark infringing the rights of the proprietor without reasonable grounds to believe that they were entitled so to do, the court may award damages against them equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement. Further, in cases where the infringing mark is applied in an unauthorized manner to goods or affixed to packaging, the court shall order its destruction or other disposal as it deems fit. The proprietor may also seek injunctions preventing further acts of infringement and account for profits derived from the infringing use of the mark.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be the proprietor of a mark shall file an application for registration in the prescribed form with the Registrar. The application shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the mark proposes to be registered and shall include a representation of the mark. Where the mark incorporates a geographical indication, the applicant shall furnish a declaration confirming that they are entitled to use the indication under this Act. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the application, including evidence of prior usage if the mark has been used before the date of filing. An adverse report from any person objecting to the registration of the mark shall be considered by the Registrar during examination and may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

A mark shall be eligible for registration under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Provided that a mark may still be registered even if it describes them, subject to compliance with conditions as provided herein regarding acceptable disclaimers and permissible additions. The Registrar may refuse registration if he considers that the proposed mark is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public or indicate that the goods or services originate from a different source than they actually do. Further, any mark which is primarily geographically distinctive shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny concerning its potential for misleading consumers regarding origin.

Where any proprietor of a registered mark becomes aware that any other person, without his consent, is using an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration is effective, he shall be entitled to apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. Such application may seek an injunction restraining the infringing use and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement. The tribunal shall consider whether the defendant’s mark causes confusion amongst consumers or dilutes the distinctiveness of the registered mark, and if so, shall grant appropriate remedies. Failure to comply with any order made under this Act may result in penalties including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

The owner of a registered mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that mark, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may permit the licensee to apply the mark to goods or provide services as defined within the scope of the original registration, provided that the terms and duration are clearly articulated. Assignment of a registered mark, including any associated goodwill, requires execution of a formal instrument witnessed as per prescribed procedures under this Act. Any subsequent transfer shall be notified to the Registrar for recordal, ensuring transparency in ownership. Further, where a license agreement contains provisions restricting the licensee’s ability to challenge the validity of the mark, such restrictions are enforceable, provided they do not contravene public policy or impede fair competition concerning the use of the mark.

Subject to any rules made under this Act, no mark shall be registered if it contains any matter which, when used in relation to goods or services, is likely to deceive or cause confusion as to the nature, quality, or geographical origin of such goods or services. An appeal lies from an order refusing registration on the ground that a proposed mark is deceptive under this provision, and the Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties, substitute its own decision for that of the Registrar. The burden of proving deception shall lie upon the applicant alleging it, provided that evidence demonstrating actual confusion amongst consumers may be admitted as prima facie proof. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board under this section may further appeal to the High Court.

Any individual, firm, company, or association employing any mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark in connection with goods or services for which the registration is subsisting shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Where such use includes reproduction of a literary work incorporated within the mark without due authorization from the owner of that copyright, the offender shall also be liable for damages as determined by the relevant civil court. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, issue a cease and desist order requiring immediate cessation of the infringing activity. Failure to comply with such an order renders the defaulter subject to penalties including fines not exceeding one million rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

For the purposes of this Act, "pharmaceutical product" means any substance intended for use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of disease, or for the modification of physiological processes in humans or animals, and includes a “drug” as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (23 of 1940). Such pharmaceutical product shall be deemed to include any combination thereof, presented in dosage form suitable for administration to humans or animals. The term "pharmaceutical product" does not extend to devices intended solely for use in human or animal health, unless such device incorporates a drug as an integral component. Any alteration of a registered trademark relating to a pharmaceutical product shall be subject to approval by the Controller.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively the name or depiction of any drug, unless such use is authorized by or under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the proposed trade mark distinguishes the goods from those of other persons in relation to the said drug. Where a trade mark includes a representation of a medicinal plant, the application shall include a botanical description sufficient for identification purposes as provided herein. Further, any alteration made to a registered trade mark relating to a drug after registration shall be subject to approval by the Registrar and may only occur with demonstrable justification related to packaging or presentation.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to a drug in a manner likely to mislead the public regarding its nature, quality, or origin, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such misleading use shall include the representation that the drug possesses particular properties or characteristics which it does not possess, or that it is manufactured by, or is connected with, a different manufacturer than is actually the case. The remedies available to an aggrieved party shall include an injunction restraining the continued use of the trade mark in the deceptive manner and damages proportionate to the loss suffered thereby. Provided that where the misleading representation relates to a drug’s efficacy, the Court may also order the publication of a corrective notice at the defendant's expense. Nothing herein shall prevent a suit for passing off being brought under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark including a representation of a drug, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the proposed trade mark does not falsely suggest any connection with any existing medicinal product or therapeutic benefit. Such evidence shall include, but is not limited to, comparative analyses of chemical composition and pharmacological activity where applicable. The Registrar shall consider objections raised by any person claiming an interest in a similar registered trade mark within three months from the date of publication under this Act. Any such objection must be supported by a duly verified affidavit detailing the grounds for opposition and demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall register a trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark relating to any drug unless such use has been continuous for at least five years immediately preceding the date of application and demonstrably indicates consumer recognition of the applicant’s goods as distinct from those of the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. Where an application for registration includes a representation of a drug, it shall be accompanied by a certificate from a recognized pharmacopoeia confirming compliance with established standards regarding efficacy and safety. The Registrar may require further evidence to ascertain whether the proposed use of the trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion among consumers concerning the origin or quality of the drug.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to a drug in a manner likely to mislead the public regarding its nature, quality or origin, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings for relief under this Act. Such misleading use shall be deemed an infringement, irrespective of intent. The proprietor of the registered trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctions restraining such infringing use and recovering damages proportionate to the loss suffered by him as a consequence thereof. Further, where the misleading use involves false or deceptive representations concerning the efficacy or safety of the drug, the offender shall also be liable for penalties prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, without prejudice to any other action that may be taken against them as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a registered trade mark for a drug shall be permitted to grant licences conferring the right to use such trade mark relating to that drug. Such licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover all or part of the territory of India. The owner of the trade mark shall retain ownership of the trade mark and may specify conditions within the licence regarding quality control measures for the manufactured drug. Assignment of a registered trade mark relating to a drug is permissible with the prior written consent of the Controller General, provided that such assignment includes all rights and obligations pertaining to any existing licences associated with the trade mark. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the terms of those licences as if they were an original party thereto.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a trade mark for a drug on the ground that it is deceptively similar to any other trade mark already registered, or applied for registration, relating to another drug, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. The parties shall be afforded an opportunity to submit their views in writing and may request a hearing before the Registrar. Subject to such hearing, the Registrar’s decision on whether the impugned trade mark is deceptively similar shall be final, provided that any party aggrieved by this decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The burden of proving deceptive similarity shall lie upon the party alleging it.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark for a drug, such application shall be accompanied by a certificate from a recognized analytical laboratory confirming compliance with prescribed pharmacopoeial standards. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating bioequivalence where the drug is intended as a generic substitute for an already marketed product. Any applicant intending to apply patent protection concurrently with trade mark registration must disclose details of pending or granted patents relating to the manufacturing process or composition of the drug in their application. Failure to provide such disclosure, if required by the Registrar, shall render the trade mark liable for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may also reject an application where the proposed trade mark is deemed deceptive concerning the nature or quality of the drug.

For the purposes of this Act, "food" includes all articles intended for human consumption and their ingredients, whether processed, manufactured, cultivated, gathered or caught. This definition shall extend to beverages, condiments, seasonings, spices, flavourings, nutritional supplements, and any substance which is ordinarily used, or represented as being suitable, for food. “Food” excludes medicinal products as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, but includes infant formula and dietetic substances as provided herein. Any product sold or offered for sale as "food" shall conform to standards of purity and composition prescribed by regulations made under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to food shall be refused if the representation includes any element which, by its very nature, directly indicates a particular ingredient or quality of that food. However, this restriction shall not apply where such indication is demonstrably and truthfully reflective of the actual composition and characteristics of the food product as certified by an accredited laboratory under established standards. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence substantiating any claim regarding ingredients or qualities before proceeding with examination. Further, a trade mark for food shall be deemed descriptive if it merely signifies the type, class, quality, or intended purpose of the goods. Such registration is subject to opposition by interested parties as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark used in relation to food alleges that another person is using any identical or confusingly similar mark in relation to food, and such use constitutes an infringement under this Act, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including but not limited to an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark. Such injunction may extend to all goods or services which are substantially identical or confusingly similar to those for which the registered trade mark is used. Provided that where the alleged infringer has demonstrably altered their packaging or marketing materials following a warning notice from the proprietor, and such alterations mitigate any likelihood of consumer confusion, the court may consider this as a relevant factor in determining the scope of any injunction granted. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any right of action for damages sustained by the proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no trade mark shall be registered if it consists exclusively of a sign which indicates the quality of the food offered under that trade mark. Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of food, the Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with applicable standards prescribed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration or directing deletion of a trade mark relating to food may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider any submissions made by the appellant and the respondent, and pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to principles of natural justice. This provision applies irrespective of whether the food is processed or unprocessed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no trade mark shall be registered for food unless it is clearly distinguishable from those used for similar goods. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the proposed trade mark does not indicate the nutritional composition, qualities, or properties of the food beyond what is generally known about such foods. Furthermore, any representation employed as a trade mark relating to food must comply with standards prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act concerning permitted colours, additives, and labelling requirements. Provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar regarding adherence to these regulations, registration may proceed. Any alteration to the formulation or processing of the food after registration shall necessitate notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

No proprietor shall be entitled to prohibit the use of a mark by any person solely on the ground that such mark has been used previously by another, provided that such subsequent user demonstrates clear and unambiguous differentiation in relation to the goods or services offered. Where a registered trade mark is employed in connection with food products, any representation likely to deceive or cause confusion regarding the origin, quality, or suitability of the food shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Such infringements are subject to penalties including monetary fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and potential imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Further, damages may be awarded to the proprietor as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority.

The owner of a registered trade mark consisting exclusively of or predominantly comprising a representation of food, whether actual or imitated, shall be entitled to grant licences for the use of such trade mark relating to similar classes of goods or services. Such licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may specify conditions regarding quality control measures implemented by the licensee to ensure consistency with the registered trade mark’s representation of the food product. Assignment of a trade mark, including any associated licensing agreements, shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry and notification to all existing licensees. Provided that, where the assignment involves a change in the nature of the goods or services for which the trade mark is used, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continued consumer association between the original food product and the assignee’s offering. Any subsequent transfer of rights under such an assignment shall be subject to similar registration requirements as provided herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an appeal shall lie to the Appellate Tribunal under this Act if a consumer alleges that the use of a trade mark by any person in relation to food products constitutes unfair competition, provided that such allegation is based on demonstrable misrepresentation regarding the origin, quality or ingredients of the food. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating actual confusion amongst consumers due to the similarity between competing trademarks applied to similar classes of food items, issue an injunction restraining further use of the impugned mark. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to a stay order granted by the court below.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to food in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality or characteristics of such food, the proprietor of an earlier trade mark may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear and determine the matter expeditiously, affording both parties opportunity for full argument and presentation of evidence. It is provided that if, subsequent to the filing of a suit under this Act, the defendant demonstrates unequivocally that the plaintiff forthwith ceased all use of the impugned trade mark in relation to food, the Tribunal may dismiss the claim on grounds of lack of ongoing harm. The decision of the Tribunal shall be appealable to the High Court within stipulated timelines as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "goods providing services" means tangible products offered alongside an activity performed for a consumer, where such activity is integral to the functionality or intended use of the product. This definition shall include, but not be limited to, pre-packaged meals accompanied by table service, software bundled with hardware requiring activation, and diagnostic equipment provided with accompanying technical support. The offering of goods providing services must clearly indicate that the service element is a component of the overall transaction; otherwise, it will be considered solely as the provision of goods. This determination shall not preclude the registration of marks relating to either the good or the associated service independently.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively such descriptive characters relating to the goods providing services which are commonly used by traders in that field, provided that such refusal may be withheld if subsequent use has acquired distinctiveness through consumer recognition. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating established usage and widespread familiarity with the proposed mark within the relevant trade sector. Further, a mark shall not be registered if it is deemed likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the identity of the provider of goods or services, considering the inherent similarity between the applied-for mark and existing registrations for identical or similar goods providing services.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to restrain the use in India of any trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to the distinctive elements of their registered trade mark, where such use is made in connection with goods providing services identical or closely resembling those for which the trade mark is registered. This right extends to preventing the application of a similar mark to goods or services that would otherwise create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. Provided that nothing in this section shall prevent the use of a trade mark describing the characteristics of the goods or services, or indicating their geographical origin; however, such use must not be deceptive and shall not constitute an unfair appropriation of the registered proprietor’s reputation. Any infringement may be subject to damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating authority under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively such indications as are capable of distinguishing the goods providing services from those of other persons. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the trade mark or the specification of goods providing services in respect of which registration is sought, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the identity of the trade mark. Any person aggrieved by any direction issued by the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider the appeal and pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to principles of natural justice. Further, a registered trade mark shall be deemed to be infringed if an identical or confusingly similar sign is used in relation to goods providing services which are identical or closely related to those for which the registration is made.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act in relation to particular goods providing services, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the exclusive right to use the trade mark in respect of those goods providing services. However, such entitlement is subject to compliance with prescribed advertising standards relating to the representation of said goods or services. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by evidence, direct the proprietor to cease any advertisement deemed misleading concerning the nature, quality or suitability of the goods providing services for which the trade mark is registered. Provided that, such direction shall not preclude the proprietor from continuing to use the trade mark in accordance with established commercial practices and as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods providing services without the consent of the proprietor, any person claiming an interest may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. Such relief shall include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark and an order requiring delivery up or destruction of all materials bearing the infringing mark. The tribunal may also award damages reflecting the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, taking into account the extent to which the infringing use has damaged the reputation associated with the trade mark. Provided that, where the infringement is demonstrably malicious, punitive damages may be awarded subject to principles of fairness and proportionality as determined by the tribunal.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to goods providing services may grant a license permitting the use of that trade mark by another person, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, along with the underlying right of representation afforded by registration under this Act. Provided that any assignment of a license shall not prejudice existing rights accrued by the licensee prior to notification thereof to the registered proprietor. The registered proprietor may, further, grant exclusive licenses, conferring upon the licensee the sole right to use the trade mark within a defined territory or for specific goods providing services. Any such exclusive license shall be deemed an assignment for the purposes of revocation proceedings under this Act if the conditions stipulated in the license are not diligently observed by the licensee.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark used in relation to goods providing services, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. The proprietor may then file written submissions rebutting the objection, supported by evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or acquired reputation. Such evidence shall be considered by the Registrar alongside the applicant’s response, if any. If, after considering all submissions and evidence presented, the Registrar remains satisfied that a likelihood of confusion exists, registration shall be refused. However, an appeal against such refusal may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Where an objection is taken under this Act to the acceptance of a proposed trade mark relating to goods providing services, the Controller may, after giving notice thereof to the applicant and any other interested party, direct a hearing to be held before him or such officer as he deems fit. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Controller in respect of such objection shall have the right to appeal from that order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against, and may substitute any order which it deems just and equitable.

Where an application is filed by a registered trade mark proprietor for extension of registration of a trade mark relating to goods providing services, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued use of the trade mark during the five years immediately preceding the date of the application. Such evidence shall include affidavits from distributors, retailers, or end-users confirming the availability and consumption of products bearing the trade mark. In cases where the proprietor is a cooperative society representing farmers engaged in agricultural activities, documentary proof substantiating collective marketing efforts and farmer participation may be accepted as supplementary evidence. The Registrar shall afford any interested party an opportunity to file objections to the application for extension, based on grounds that the use has not been continuous or substantial. Decisions regarding such objections are appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The registration of a trademark, as provided herein, may be subject to cancellation upon application by any interested person demonstrating that the acquired distinctiveness of the mark has ceased to exist. For the purposes of this Act, “interested person” includes, but is not limited to, competitors, consumers, and proprietors of similar trademarks. The Registrar shall consider evidence pertaining to changes in consumer perception or market conditions impacting recognition of the trademark. Further, a registration may be cancelled if it appears that the mark was registered fraudulently; however, establishing fraudulent intent requires clear and convincing proof. Any order for cancelling registration shall be subject to appeal under this Act.

The registration of a trademark, once granted, remains valid subject to compliance with the provisions outlined herein; however, an application for rectification may be filed by any person claiming interest, alleging that the continued use or maintenance of such registration is contrary to law. The Registrar shall consider all evidence presented and may direct the cancellation of the registration if it is established that the mark has become non-distinctive through common usage, or that the registered proprietor was guilty of bad faith during the application process. Furthermore, cancelling registration shall also occur where the trademark is deemed deceptively similar to an earlier mark already in use, causing confusion amongst consumers and prejudicing their interests; provided that due consideration will be given to any demonstrable goodwill accrued by the registrant.

Where an objection has been made against a trade mark registration, and that objection remains unresolved following consideration by the relevant authority, any interested party may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal for review. The Tribunal shall afford both the registrant and the objector a full opportunity to present evidence and argument relating to the validity of the registration. Upon such hearing, if it is determined that the trade mark was registered in contravention of this Act or that its use has become deceptive or confusing, cancelling registration shall be ordered by the Tribunal. The order for cancellation may specify a period within which the registrant must cease using the trade mark and remove all infringing materials from commerce. Further, damages may be awarded to the objector as determined appropriate under principles of equity and fairness.

An application for the cancellation of registration may be made by any person claiming interest, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, alleging that the trade mark is being used contrary to law or public interest. The Registrar shall give notice of the application in the prescribed manner to the registered proprietor and all other persons appearing on the register as proprietors of similar marks. Upon receiving an objection from the registered proprietor, the Registrar shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either in person or by counsel. If, after considering the evidence presented, the Registrar is satisfied that grounds for cancellation exist, cancelling registration shall be effected, and the mark shall be removed from the register. The Registrar may require security to be furnished as deemed appropriate before proceeding with any inquiry under this Act.

The registration of a trademark, having been duly granted under this Act, shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of such registration; however, provided that the owner fails to file renewal documentation within the prescribed timeframe prior to the expiration of said initial term, or demonstrates demonstrable non-use of the mark continuously for a period exceeding five years immediately preceding an application for cancellation, then the Registrar may initiate proceedings. Upon receiving evidence satisfying the requirements as provided herein, demonstrating likelihood of confusion with existing trademarks or misleading the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services, cancelling registration shall be permissible. Such action requires prior notification to the trademark proprietor and opportunity for response.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry, including but not limited to decisions relating to rectification or opposition proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Board shall have power to entertain appeals arising under this Act and shall pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to just consideration of the interests involved. Further, where a trade mark is registered in contravention of section 9 or has become unserviceable through non-use for a continuous period of five years, cancelling registration shall be permissible upon application by any interested party. Any person found guilty of knowingly making false statements under this Act shall be liable to a fine extending to rupees two lakhs.

The owner of a registered trademark may, by instrument in writing executed as per the requirements for transferring title to immovable property, grant an exclusive license to use the mark relating to specified goods or services. Such license shall be assignable subject to the prior consent of the Registrar, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a registration is assigned and the assignee continues to use the trademark in accordance with the terms of assignment, the benefit of any pending application for revocation under this Act shall accrue to the assignee. Further, cancelling registration shall occur if the registered proprietor fails to obtain such consent within six months from the date of written request by the prospective licensee or assignee; the Registrar may then initiate proceedings as provided herein. The license agreement must be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution.

Where an objection is raised against a registered trademark alleging that it has become deceptive, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the registered proprietor an opportunity for being heard. Such hearing may be conducted by video conferencing as provided herein. If, after considering the evidence presented and any counter-arguments submitted, the Registrar finds merit in the objection, cancelling registration shall be permissible. However, before proceeding to such cancellation, the Registrar must record reasons in writing demonstrating that the mark’s continued existence is likely to mislead or deceive the public concerning the nature, quality, or origin of goods or services. An appeal lies from any order made under this provision to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The registration of a trademark, including those representing sound recordings, shall be deemed invalid if it has been obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation or by taking unfair advantage of another’s goodwill. Cancelling registration shall occur where the use of the mark, following its initial registration, is demonstrably contrary to honest practices in industrial competition and causes confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Further, a trademark representing a sound recording may be expunged if it has become incapable of distinguishing the goods or services of the registered proprietor from those of others, subject to provisions concerning bona fide users.

The registration of a trademark, as provided herein, may be subject to review and subsequent modification if it transpires that the use thereof has been discontinued for a continuous period exceeding five years. Furthermore, any person demonstrating substantial prejudice arising from the continued registration shall have standing to petition the Registrar for its cancellation. Such petitions must specify with particularity the grounds upon which they are founded and provide verifiable evidence supporting the claim of prejudice. The Registrar shall consider limitations on remedies where the trademark owner can demonstrate a reasonable explanation for cessation of use, such as temporary export restrictions or unavoidable operational disruptions. Cancelling registration shall not be ordered unless the Registrar is satisfied that the conditions precedent have been fully met.

Where an application is filed seeking to amend a registered trade mark, such application shall specify with particularity the alterations proposed to be made to the representation of the trade mark, including but not limited to changes in colour, device, or wordings. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of the proposed amendments. An application to *amend register* shall be refused if the alteration sought would substantially affect the distinctive character of the registered trade mark as it was originally accepted for registration, subject to any prior use established under this Act. Any such refusal shall state the reasons therefor.

Where a registered trade mark owner desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights relating to specific goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, such license agreement shall be recorded with the Registrar upon application and payment of the prescribed fee. The Registrar may require an affidavit verifying the terms of the license, including the duration and geographical scope thereof. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark, or of rights pertaining to a licensed use as defined in the license agreement, shall also be recorded similarly. Upon receiving such applications, the Registrar shall *amend register* accordingly, noting the licensee or assignee as having standing under this Act concerning the specified goods and services. The recordation does not prejudice any other right which the registered proprietor may have to enforce his trade mark.

Where an application is made to amend a registered trade mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such evidence as demonstrates likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed alteration, particularly where the amended mark incorporates elements similar to existing marks in related classes. Such determination shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar shall provide notice of any intended amendment and opportunity for objection by interested parties; objections may be challenged under this Act. Failure to satisfy the Registrar regarding likelihood of confusion or non-compliance with procedural requirements will result in rejection of the application to amend register, and such rejection is also subject to appeal.

An aggrieved party, including any registered proprietor dissatisfied with a decision concerning renewal or alteration of their trade mark registration, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. This right to appeal shall extend to decisions relating to rectification proceedings initiated against a registered trade mark, and also encompasses disputes arising from objections raised during the examination process under this Act. Provided that, if the aggrieved party fails to file the appeal within the specified period, the order or decision in question shall be deemed final and binding. The Board may, subject to just considerations and reasons recorded in writing, entertain an appeal filed after the expiry of the appeal specified period only if adequate cause is demonstrated for the delay.

An aggrieved party seeking review of a determination made by the Registrar concerning the rectification of a trade mark, subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal must be lodged within sixty days from the date notification of the decision is served upon the appellant, or where service is deemed to have occurred under this Act, from the date it would reasonably have been received. Provided that, if the Registrar has failed to communicate the order within thirty days of its passing, the specified period for filing an appeal shall be extended by a number of days equivalent to the duration of such delay. Further, any application for condonation of delay in preferring an appeal must demonstrate exceptional circumstances justifying deviation from the prescribed appeal specified period.

Where a registered trade mark has been assigned or licensed, and any dispute arises concerning the validity of that assignment or license, or relating to infringement claims predicated upon the use of the mark, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum. Such proceedings shall be deemed to include appeals against decisions made by the Registrar regarding revocation or rectification applications affecting the registered trade mark. The appeal specified period for challenging a decision under this Act concerning such assignments or licenses is sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that an extension of time may be granted in circumstances where demonstrable hardship would result from strict adherence to the prescribed timeframe. Any party seeking such an extension must file a written application justifying the delay within thirty days of the expiry of the initial appeal specified period.

A plant variety shall be deemed a new variety for the purposes of this Act when it is not explicitly included in any established catalogue or record maintained under this Act, or by any recognized authority prior to the date of application for registration. For the avoidance of doubt, an essentially derived variety shall not qualify as a new variety unless it demonstrates substantial and unexpected phenotypic differences from the original variety, rendering it clearly distinguishable. The determination of such substantial difference shall be subject to scientific evaluation and consideration of traits relevant to agricultural performance and consumer preference, as provided herein.

An application for registration as a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation establishing distinctiveness and stability across successive generations. The Registrar may require submission of data pertaining to morphological characteristics, genetic uniformity, and disease resistance relevant to assessing the traits of the applied-for new variety. Such data must demonstrate that the variety maintains its essential features under specified environmental conditions as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Further, an applicant shall provide a comprehensive pedigree chart tracing lineage and demonstrating derivation from known parentage where applicable. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the claimed new variety does not meet the criteria for novelty, or if the documentation submitted fails to adequately substantiate its stability.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in a new variety shall be entitled to seek remedies for infringement before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Infringement shall include unauthorized exploitation of the registered variety through means such as commercial propagation, sale, or distribution, without prior consent from the right holder. Where an infringement is established, the authority may grant injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the claimant, taking into consideration factors like the extent of reproduction and profits derived therefrom. The right holder shall be responsible for ensuring the genetic purity and identity of the new variety throughout its lifecycle; failure to do so may render them liable to rectification proceedings under this Act.

An application for registration of a new variety may be filed with the Authority, accompanied by detailed documentation pertaining to its lineage, breeding history, and morphological characteristics, as prescribed in the First Schedule.
