The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the claimed new variety possesses distinctiveness when compared to commonly known varieties of the same species, through rigorous field trials conducted under conditions approved by the Authority. Provided that, if the application relates to a variety derived from an extant variety, the documentation must explicitly detail the derivation process and demonstrate substantial genetic differentiation. The Authority may require further testing or analysis at the applicant's expense to verify these claims. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding registration or rejection of a new variety may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision.

A new variety shall be eligible for registration as a plant variety under this Act if it is demonstrably distinct, uniform and stable, meeting the criteria established in the First Schedule. The Registrar may require further testing to confirm these characteristics, particularly concerning stability across successive generations. Provided that, any variety derived from an existing variety through conventional breeding techniques shall not be considered novel unless such derivation results in a significant change in one or more of its essential characteristics, as determined by the Board. Further, if the applicant can demonstrate that the new variety possesses substantially similar traits to another registered variety, the application may be rejected subject to appeal before the Appellate Authority. The breeder shall provide detailed documentation regarding propagation methods and phenotypic expression for assessment.

Any person who, having obtained registration of a new variety, makes or causes to be made any false statement in his application for registration, or in any document filed therewith, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. Further, where an infringer of the rights associated with a registered new variety acts in contravention of conditions stipulated under this Act regarding farmers’ privilege, such infringement shall be deemed a cognizable offence and reported immediately to the nearest police station; officers authorized by the competent authority may seize infringing material. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the Authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding rights in a new variety may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the commercial exploitation thereof, including but not limited to rights for propagation, sale, distribution, or research purposes. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area and duration for which they are valid, and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of rights in a new variety is permissible with prior notification to the Authority, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the protected material. The Authority may impose conditions on such assignments to ensure continued benefit to farmers and preservation of genetic resources. Further, any license granted or assignment made shall be recorded within one month with the designated registering authority, as provided herein.

A person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act relating to the grant or refusal of registration of a new variety may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall lie on a question of fact or law and the Board may, after giving all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. The determination of the Appellate Board shall be final subject only to further appeals as provided herein. Where any doubt arises regarding whether a variety qualifies as a new variety due to its similarity with existing varieties, the Examining Authority may request expert opinion and the burden of proving distinctiveness shall rest upon the applicant for registration.

Where a person alleges that their right to a new variety has been infringed, they may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred. Such infringement shall include any act passing off goods or produce as being derived from the protected new variety without authorization from the registered breeder. The remedies available under this Act for infringement include an injunction restraining further infringing acts and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the right holder, taking into account the infringer’s profits, if any. Provided that, in determining damages, the Court shall consider whether the alleged infringer acted in good faith and was unaware of the existence of the registered new variety. The provisions relating to provisional application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall apply mutatis mutandis for facilitating access to foreign courts seeking redressal.

Where an application for registration of a new variety is approved by the Authority, the applicant shall furnish to the Registrar, within thirty days from the date of notification of approval, a detailed report specifying the geographical location where seeds or planting material of the registered variety are being cultivated and maintained. Such report may be amended by the applicant with the prior written consent of the Registrar at any time during the term of protection. The right to exploit the new variety shall vest in the registrant; provided that an entitled assignment transmission of such rights, executed before a Notary Public and duly registered under this Act, shall be deemed valid only if it specifies the scope and duration of the assigned rights. Failure to submit the required report may result in suspension of protection as provided herein.

A new variety shall be deemed eligible for registration where evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishes that its essential characteristics are stable and predictable across successive generations, subject to variations inherent in the plant’s propagation method. Provided that, if a claim of novelty is challenged by any interested party based on prior disclosure or public use, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating continued compliance with the requirements for registration as provided herein. Further, where an infringement action concerning the registered new variety is initiated, and it is determined by a competent authority that the defendant’s activities constitute such infringement, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all actions contributing to the alleged violation pending resolution of the matter through due process.

Where a person makes a false statement in an application for registration of a new variety, intending to deceive the Registrar, that person shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and the registered variety may be subject to revocation. The Registrar considers all evidence presented regarding distinctness, uniformity, and stability when assessing applications; however, any attempt to subvert this assessment through fraudulent data or misrepresentation constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, alongside a fine not less than one hundred thousand rupees but which may extend to two million rupees. Furthermore, any individual found guilty of knowingly assisting in such deception shall be subject to similar penalties as the applicant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any user party proceeding with commercialization activities involving a registered new variety may enter into licensing agreements with the registered breeder or their authorized agents. Such licenses shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to seed production, distribution, and cultivation for sale. The royalty rates payable under these agreements shall be determined through mutual consent, provided that they are equitable and do not unduly restrict access to the new variety by farmers. Assignment of rights in a registered new variety is permissible with prior written approval from the Authority, ensuring continued adherence to benefit-sharing principles as outlined herein. Any transfer or assignment shall include provisions for traceability and reporting requirements concerning subsequent commercial exploitation.

For the purposes of this Act, "artistic work" includes any graphic, sculptural, architectural work, otherwise than purely architectural, existing in a tangible form; provided that photographs and cinematographic films shall be deemed to be artistic works. An “architectural work” is defined as any building or structure, or any part thereof, fixed to the earth, including bridges, tunnels, dams, viaducts and other constructions which are primarily intended for public use. The reproduction of an architectural work under this Copyright Act requires authorization from the owner unless such reproduction is deemed fair dealing for educational purposes, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Registration of literary works is deemed prima facie evidence of ownership under this Act, subject to the provisions herein relating to proof of creation and first publication. An applicant seeking registration of a musical work shall furnish particulars regarding the composer, lyricist, and publisher, along with certified copies of assignments or licenses granted in respect thereof. Where an application for copyright act registration is accompanied by a statement claiming joint authorship, each author shall be deemed to hold equal shares unless otherwise specified within the accompanying documentation. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the authenticity of the claim and the validity of any assignment presented. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment under this Act.

Any person who, without obtaining license from the owner of copyright, does anything which is exclusively reserved for the owner under this Act, or otherwise infringes any right conferred upon him by this Copyright Act, shall be liable to pay such compensation as the court may determine, having regard to the loss suffered by the copyright owner and the benefit accrued to the infringer. Provided that in determining the amount of compensation, the Court shall take into account factors including but not limited to the flagrancy of the infringement, any remedial steps taken by the infringer to cease the infringing activity, and whether the infringement was committed for commercial gain. Further, where an infringement has resulted in damage to reputation or goodwill, additional damages may be awarded subject to principles of fairness and equity as determined by the Court.

Any person claiming an infringement of copyright under this Act may institute a suit for damages and seek interlocutory relief subject to the provisions herein. The plaint shall specify the work in which copyright is claimed, the manner in which such claim of copyright has been infringed, and state the relief sought. Where the alleged infringer admits the acts complained of but contends that such acts do not constitute an infringement of copyright, the Court may determine the question whether or not the acts amount to infringement. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, direct any person found infringing copyright to cease from the infringing activity and pay compensation to the owner of the copyright. Any appeal arising out of a decision under this Copyright Act shall lie to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the suit was originally filed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright shall subsist in a literary work only if it is original and has been fixed in a tangible form, whether written or otherwise recorded. Provided that works produced for certain purposes specified under this Act, namely, those undertaken by government departments or public institutions for official use, may be exempted from the requirement of originality as defined herein. The author of the copyright in such work shall be deemed to be the department or institution concerned. Any person desiring to reproduce, distribute, or communicate a copyrighted work commercially must obtain prior written permission from the owner of the copyright, demonstrating compliance with prescribed royalty rates and usage guidelines as provided herein. Failure to secure such authorization constitutes an infringement under this Copyright Act.

Any person who, without obtaining leave from the owner of copyright, causes to be published any work in which copyright subsists, or any adaptation thereof, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. Further, where such publication is made for commercial gain, the court may, subject to appeal, order the confiscation of all copies of the work and any equipment used in their production. The owner of copyright shall be entitled to claim damages from any person infringing under this Act, calculated as provided herein, taking into consideration the extent of the infringement and the loss suffered by the copyright holder. Repeated offences relating to violations of the *copyright act* will attract enhanced penalties.

The assignment of copyright under this Act shall be in writing and signed by the assignor or his authorized representative. Such assignment shall specify the work to which it relates, the duration of the term of assignment, and the geographical area for which such assignment is valid. Any license granted under this Copyright Act granting rights typically reserved exclusively to the owner of copyright shall require prior registration with the designated government authority, provided that such registration shall not be a prerequisite for the validity of the license itself. The assignor may retain certain rights relating to the work, as expressly stipulated in the assignment agreement; however, any subsequent assignments or licenses granted by the assignee shall supersede the terms of the original assignment unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. Further, an author may grant exclusive distribution rights separate from copyright ownership, subject to transparency requirements regarding authorship attribution.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any order passed by the Controller, the Appellate Tribunal shall hear such appeal and may pass such orders as it thinks fit, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The aggrieved party may further appeal from any decision of the Appellate Tribunal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Any order passed by the High Court shall be final. It is clarified that determination of originality for purposes of copyright act protection remains solely at the discretion of the Controller unless demonstrably arbitrary or perverse.

The copyright act grants exclusive rights to the owner of a work, but these rights are subject to certain limitations regarding licensing and assignment. Any person claiming ownership of copyright in an artistic work or musical composition may enter into agreements for the reproduction, distribution, or public performance of that work, provided such agreement is documented in writing and registered with the designated authority. Assignment of copyright shall be deemed valid only upon registration, transferring all rights as specified within the application section 35. Further, a license granted under this Act may be exclusive or non-exclusive, at the discretion of the copyright owner, but any conditions attached to such licenses must be clearly articulated in the registered agreement. The Central Government may, by order, permit certain uses of copyrighted works that would otherwise constitute infringement, provided it is deemed beneficial for public interest.

Where, upon examination of an application for patent, or at any time during the pendency thereof, it appears that there is a discrepancy between the claimed invention and the description contained in the specification, or where any person has acquired rights by virtue of prior use or publication, notice rectification shall be initiated. The Controller may, after giving all interested parties reasonable opportunity to make their representations, direct the amendment of the patent application to reflect the true scope of the invention as originally disclosed, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the nature of the claimed invention. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Where, subsequent to registration of a patent under this Act, particulars relating thereto are found to be incorrect, ambiguous or omitted, any person aggrieved may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application shall specify the errors sought to be corrected and state the relief claimed. The Controller shall serve notice upon the patentee and other interested parties as provided herein, affording them a reasonable opportunity to file their objections or counter-claims. Upon consideration of all materials presented, including any expert testimony deemed relevant, the Controller may order such rectification as appears just and equitable. It is further provided that notice rectification shall be effected within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt of the application, unless circumstances warrant an extension granted by the Controller.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears that an entry in the Register of Patents contains errors whether arising from clerical mistakes, inadvertent omissions, or misinterpretations of facts presented during examination, the Controller may initiate proceedings for rectification. Such proceedings shall be commenced by way of application filed by any interested party, including but not limited to the patentee, a person claiming through the patentee, or an aggrieved third party demonstrably prejudiced by the erroneous entry. Notice rectification shall be afforded to all parties having a substantial interest in the matter, and opportunity for argument given before making any order altering the register. The Controller may, subject to principles of natural justice, direct amendment, variation, or deletion of entries as deemed necessary to accurately reflect the status of the patent. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears that there is an error apparent from the record relating to the identity of the inventor or the extent of protection afforded by the patent, the Controller may initiate proceedings for rectification. Such proceedings shall be commenced by way of application filed in the prescribed form and accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating the nature of the error. Notice rectification shall be undertaken following a formal notification served upon the patentee and any interested party as determined under this Act. The Controller shall provide all parties with an opportunity to present arguments and evidence pertaining to the proposed rectification. Decisions regarding rectification are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeals must be filed within the stipulated time frame as prescribed herein.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears that an entry on the Register of Patents contains particulars which do not accurately reflect the subject matter or conditions of the patent, or where there is evidence of clerical error affecting the rights conferred thereby, the Controller may entertain an application for rectification. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds upon which the rectification is sought and supported by relevant documentation. Notice rectification shall be effected only after due opportunity has been afforded to the patentee and any other interested party to present their objections or counter-claims. The Controller, acting reasonably and fairly, may order such variations or deletions as are necessary to ensure accuracy, provided that the rectification does not substantively alter the scope of protection originally granted.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears that an entry in the Register of Patents contains errors affecting the validity or enforceability of the patent, the Controller may initiate proceedings for rectification. Such proceedings shall be conducted with due regard to natural justice, affording all interested parties opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines during these proceedings will render a party liable to penalties as determined by the Controller. Notice rectification shall be served upon the patentee and any other person claiming an interest in the matter, ensuring adequate time for response. Any order made under this Act concerning rectification is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a patentee, by assignment or otherwise, has transferred rights pertaining to a registered invention, and the assignee subsequently desires to grant a license for exploitation of such patented invention, notice rectification shall be initiated if the register fails accurately to reflect the details of said licensing agreement. The Controller may, upon receiving an application supported by requisite documentation demonstrating the terms and scope of the license granted, direct that the register be amended to include particulars of the licensee’s name and the extent of their rights under this Act. Provided that any existing patent holder or other interested party may submit objections to such rectification within a period as prescribed herein. The Controller shall consider all submissions before issuing an order regarding notice rectification. Such orders are subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, an interested party alleges material errors affecting the validity or scope of such patent, and presents prima facie evidence supporting said allegations, the Controller shall issue a notice rectification shall be initiated. Such notice shall be served upon the patentee and all other parties appearing to have a substantial interest in the matter, affording them reasonable opportunity to file objections or counter-statements. The Controller may, after considering the representations of all parties and any relevant evidence adduced before it, determine whether rectification is warranted. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, subject to its jurisdiction and as provided herein.

Where, following a notice rectification shall be sought concerning an importation patented pharmaceutical product, and it is established before the Controller that such importation occurred without due regard for the patentee’s exclusive rights as provided herein, the Controller may order the importer to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods imported. Such determination shall take into account any demonstrable efforts made by the importer to ascertain the validity or scope of the relevant patent. Failure to comply with an order issued under this provision renders the importer liable for prosecution and subject to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. The Controller may also direct seizure of goods where evidence suggests ongoing infringement.

Where, following a decision by the Controller concerning the validity of a patent and subsequent appeal to the High Court, demonstrable errors exist within the Register of Patents pertaining to the claimed invention’s priority date or ownership details, notice rectification shall be initiated by any aggrieved party. Such application for rectification must specify the nature of the error and provide supporting evidence as determined under this Act. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for response to the patentee or other interested parties, direct rectification if satisfied that the Register is inaccurate. Any order made by the Controller concerning notice rectification is subject to appeal before the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, and any challenge must be brought within a period of ninety days from the date of such order.

Where, subsequent to the grant of a patent and prior to its expiration, it is demonstrated that an entry in the Register of Patents relating to the right to priority or the particulars of invention contains an error apparent from the record, notice rectification shall be sought by application to the Controller. Such application must specify the erroneous entry and clearly state the correct information as evidenced by documentary proof filed therewith. The provisions act shall govern the procedure for such applications, including timelines for response and hearing. The Controller may, after affording a party an opportunity of being heard, direct amendment of the Register accordingly, subject to ensuring that any alteration does not prejudice existing rights or create undue hardship.

Where, following registration of a mark under this Act, it appears that there is an error or omission affecting the particulars of goods providing services in relation to which the trademark is registered, or concerning the proprietor thereof, notice rectification shall be applied for by any person claiming interest. Such application may be made to the Controller, who shall afford all interested parties an opportunity of being heard. The Controller may, after considering the evidence presented and subject to principles of natural justice, direct that the register be amended to reflect the correct particulars. Any order made under this provision shall be recorded in the register and a certified copy thereof furnished to the applicant. Further, any party aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where, following publication of a patent document under this Act, any person claiming title or interest in the invention is aggrieved by an error appearing in the patent grant, such person may apply to the Controller for rectification. The application shall specify the particulars of the error and the relief sought. Direct notice rectification proceedings are initiated when the applicant demonstrates that they possessed knowledge of the erroneous entry prior to its publication, either through actual communication or circumstances rendering such knowledge reasonably inferable. The Controller may grant such reliefs as are necessary to correct the record, subject to ensuring fairness to all interested parties.

Where, upon examination of a patent granted under this Act, it appears to the Controller that the patent was granted without proper consideration of prior published documents which would have prevented its grant, or where there is evidence demonstrating an error in the assessment of novelty or inventive step, any person may apply for direct notice rectification. Such application shall be accompanied by all relevant documentation substantiating the grounds for rectification and clearly identifying the specific errors requiring correction. The Controller shall serve notice upon the patentee detailing the nature of the alleged error and providing a reasonable opportunity to respond under this Act. If, after considering the response, the Controller is satisfied that rectification is warranted, an order may be made amending or revoking the patent. This process is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where, following the publication of a patent grant, any person claiming title or interest in the invention aggrieved by an error appearing on the Register shall be entitled to apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification of such error. Such application shall specify the particulars of the error and the rectification sought, accompanied by supporting documentation as deemed necessary by the Controller. The Controller may require the patentee to file a counter-statement responding to the claims made in the application. Upon receipt of the counter-statement, if any, the Controller shall afford both parties an opportunity for hearing, subject to principles of natural justice. Any order rectifying the Register passed under this Act shall be final, provided that the aggrieved party may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. The rectification shall take effect as if it had been originally recorded in the Register.

Where a patentee, or any other person aggrieved by an entry in the Register of Patents, has reason to believe that the said entry contains errors not apparent upon the face of the document, they may apply to the Controller for rectification. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for seeking rectification and specifying the particulars of the error sought to be corrected. The Controller shall serve notice of such application on the patent holder or other interested party whose rights are affected, providing a period of not less than sixty days for response. Direct notice rectification may be ordered only if the applicant demonstrates that the erroneous entry resulted from an inadvertent oversight and did not prejudice any other person’s interests under this Act.

Where a patentee, or any other person aggrieved by an entry in the Register of Patents, has reason to believe that such entry is erroneous and prejudicial to their interests, they may apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds upon which the rectification is sought and specifying the relief claimed. The Controller shall serve notice of the application on the patent holder whose right is affected, affording them a period of sixty days to file a counter-statement. Failure by the Controller to provide adequate opportunity for response shall render any subsequent order vulnerable to challenge under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order made under these provisions may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months, subject to penalty for delay.

Where a patentee, or any person claiming through him by assignment or license, becomes aware of particulars appearing on the Register which are erroneous and prejudicial to their interests, they may apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification of those particulars. Such an application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating the error and its detrimental effect upon the assignor or licensee’s rights under this Act. The Controller may, after affording the patent holder and any other interested party a reasonable opportunity to be heard, order such alterations to the Register as are necessary to correct the erroneous particulars. Provided that, where the rectification involves modification of details relating to ownership by assignment, the application must include an authenticated copy of the relevant assignment deed or license agreement. The Controller shall record the reasons for any order made under this provision and may grant costs as deemed appropriate.

Where a patentee, or any other person interested in a granted patent, alleges that particulars of the invention are not disclosed in the specification as required by law, and that such deficiency materially affects the patentability of the invention, an application for direct notice rectification may be made to the Controller. The Controller shall issue notice to the patent holder and any other party with a demonstrable interest, affording them opportunity to file objections within sixty days. Any objection received shall be considered in conjunction with the applicant’s response, and a hearing conducted if deemed necessary. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller's order regarding rectification shall be binding, provided that it does not extend beyond the scope of the originally claimed invention.

Where, following the publication of a patent document under this Act, any person claiming title or interest in respect of the invention is aggrieved by an error appearing therein, such person may apply to the Controller for rectification of that error. The application shall specify the particulars of the error and the rectification sought. A form issuing from the office of the Controller shall be used for making such applications, as prescribed. Direct notice rectification shall be effected only after due consideration of all relevant documents and representations submitted by parties concerned, subject to ensuring fairness and adherence to principles of natural justice.

Where, upon examination of a registered patent, it appears that the entry on the Register of Patents contains an error which arose from want of due diligence by the Controller or relates to particulars made known to the Controller prior to the sealing of the register, any person claiming title as author or inventor may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification. Such application shall specify the nature of the error and the rectification sought. The Controller shall be served with a copy of such application not less than thirty days before the hearing. The High Court may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to all interested parties, make such order as it deems fit regarding the correction or amendment of the register, provided that no alteration is made which prejudices the rights of any party without their consent.

Where a patentee, or any other person interested in a granted patent, becomes aware of particulars which indicate that an entry in the Register of Patents is incorrect, prejudicial to their interests and obtained without due notice to them, they may apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification. Such application shall state the nature of the error and the relief sought, and shall be accompanied by such evidence as reasonably supports the claim. The Controller may, after giving notice to all parties appearing on the Register who would be affected by the proposed rectification, hold a hearing and appoint an adjudicating officer to assist in evaluating the merits of the application. An order adjudicating officer shall consider any submissions made by interested parties and report findings to the Controller. The Controller shall then determine whether the entry should be rectified, varied or deleted, as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the validity of a patent granted, the aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be accompanied by a duly executed affidavit verifying the factual basis of the claims made and the supporting documentation submitted. The Controller may, at his discretion, require any appellant to provide oral testimony in lieu of or supplementary to the affidavit, particularly where discrepancies arise or the veracity of the statements is called into question. Failure to comply with this requirement regarding the shall given affidavit may result in the appeal being deemed frivolous and dismissed summarily, subject to a hearing opportunity afforded to the appellant.

A proceeding before an adjudicating officer under this Act shall be deemed a case proceeding for the purposes of sub-section (1) of section 90 and shall be conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, provided that any party may present evidence and arguments relevant to the determination of the matter. The adjudicating officer shall record reasons in writing for every decision rendered, and such reasons shall form part of the case proceeding. Any order passed by an adjudicating officer may be appealed against as provided herein, subject to the satisfaction of prescribed conditions relating to deposit of costs.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to initiate a case proceeding under this Act if an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry regarding similarity to existing marks or any other impediment to registration as provided herein. The applicant may, within the prescribed time limit, submit a written response addressing the grounds of objection and providing supporting arguments demonstrating distinctiveness and non-infringement. Failure to respond adequately may result in the rejection of the application. Any third party possessing a prior right in relation to an identical or similar mark may also initiate a case proceeding seeking revocation of registration if it is subsequently granted, subject to due process and opportunity for both parties to present their evidence before the relevant authority.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act from any decision or order made by the Registrar, the Appellate Board shall have power to entertain the case proceeding and may, subject to any provisions of the law for the time being in force, determine the said decision or order. The Board shall not be bound by the decisions or findings of the Registrar but may take such evidence as it thinks necessary for the purpose of its determination. Any party to a case proceeding before the Appellate Board aggrieved by an order made by the Board may appeal from that order to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of the order. The High Court shall have similar powers as the Appellate Board in dealing with such appeals and may make any necessary orders regarding costs.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act from any decision or order made by the Registrar, the Appellate Board shall give notice thereof to all parties concerned and may direct that the hearing be conducted before it at such time and place as it may appoint. The Board shall proceed with the case proceeding in a summary manner, affording all parties reasonable opportunity for being heard and presenting their evidence. Any party intending to call witnesses or produce documents during the hearing shall give notice thereof to the other parties not less than thirty days prior to the appointed date. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision, provided that the High Court may entertain an appeal only on a question of law. The Registrar shall maintain records pertaining to all case proceedings and make them available for inspection as prescribed.

Where an appeal is filed under this Act against any decision rendered by the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or concerning rectification of the Register, the appellate authority shall give notice thereof to all parties concerned as provided herein. The appellant shall serve copies of the grounds of appeal on each respondent at least thirty days prior to the date fixed for hearing. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the appeal being dismissed. Any party desiring to be heard in a case proceeding arising from such an appeal must file their written submissions within fifteen days of service of the appellant’s grounds. The appellate authority shall consider all submitted evidence and arguments before issuing its final order.

Where an infringement of a registered trademark is alleged, any proprietor seeking redress shall institute a case proceeding before the appropriate jurisdictional civil court, subject to provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein. The court may, upon finding infringement, grant injunctions restraining further acts of violation and order damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, or such sum not exceeding rupees five lakhs as it deems just. Further, in cases involving wilful infringement demonstrated through deceptive packaging or advertising, the Court shall impose punitive damages up to ten times the value of the infringing goods sold. Costs associated with the case proceeding shall be determined at the discretion of the court, considering the conduct of both parties.

Where a registered trade mark is involved in a case proceeding concerning infringement, and where such proceedings are settled through an agreement between the parties involving the assignment of rights relating to the mark, the assignor shall provide a formal notification to the Registrar within thirty days of the settlement. This notification must detail the scope of the assigned rights, including any geographical limitations or product categories covered by the assignment. The assignee shall be deemed substituted for the assignor in respect of those specific rights as provided herein. Further, where a license is granted during such a case proceeding to utilize the registered trade mark, the terms and conditions of that license are subject to review under this Act upon request from either licensor or licensee. Any subsequent assignment of the entire undertaking shall automatically transfer all associated licenses and assignments.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark under this Act, and such objection is not resolved through compromise as provided herein, the aggrieved party shall have the right to institute a case proceeding before the relevant Intellectual Property Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear evidence from both the applicant and the objector, affording each opportunity to present arguments and counter-arguments pertaining to the distinctiveness of the mark and any likelihood of confusion with existing trademarks. Decisions of the Tribunal may be appealed to the High Court within ninety days of notification, subject to a stay order granted by the Tribunal in exceptional circumstances demonstrating irreparable harm. The appellate court shall review findings of fact and law made by the Tribunal.

A case proceeding relating to rectification of a registered trademark shall be instituted only by way of an application made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such applications must specify the grounds for seeking rectification and comply with all requirements as provided herein regarding form and content. The Board may, upon receiving an application, issue a fee payable notice to the applicant requiring payment of the prescribed fees within a specified period. Failure to pay such fees within that period shall result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Further, any party to a case proceeding may appeal to the High Court under this Act.

Where a proprietor institutes a case proceeding against an alleged infringer under this Act, and demonstrates reasonable grounds to believe that the infringing activity involves the unauthorized use of their trade mark for proprietor certification purposes, the Court shall grant such relief as is equitable and just. This includes, but is not limited to, injunctions restraining further infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and costs incurred in bringing the case proceeding. Provided that, if the alleged infringer demonstrates good faith reliance on an honest belief that their use of the trade mark did not constitute infringement, the Court may reduce or deny the award of damages as it deems appropriate. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such proceedings and make them available for public inspection subject to confidentiality restrictions imposed by the Court.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of a proposed trademark during the examination stage, and the applicant fails to submit a satisfactory response within the time stipulated under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice inviting representations from interested parties. Such notice shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal and on the website maintained by the Office. Following publication, any party possessing a substantial interest may file a representation supporting or opposing the acceptance of the mark. The Registrar shall consider all submissions received before making a determination regarding registration. A decision rendered by the Registrar concerning such an objection constitutes a *case proceeding* for the purposes of appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, should the Registrar deem it necessary to establish a precedent relating to trademark classification, a portion of any funds allocated to the gene fund shall be utilized towards documenting and disseminating the rationale behind this decision.

Any proprietor instituting a case proceeding against an infringer shall file with the relevant jurisdictional authority a sworn affidavit detailing the initial date claim for use of the impugned mark within India. Failure to provide such documentation, or providing information demonstrably false under oath, renders the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may prejudice their right to seek injunctive relief as provided herein. The Registrar shall have the power to issue summons requiring further clarification regarding the veracity of any date claim presented. Further, where an infringer demonstrates prior honest concurrent use predating the proprietor’s asserted date claim, the Court may dismiss the case proceeding with costs against the plaintiff.

For the purposes of this Act, "registration mentioned clause" means a statement appearing on a certificate of registration issued under this Act which explicitly references another registered trade mark owned by the applicant or registrant. Such reference shall indicate that the mark in question benefits from, or is related to, the earlier registration. The inclusion of a registration mentioned clause does not, however, confer any right upon the proprietor of the later mark beyond those expressly granted as provided herein. Further, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the connection between marks bearing a registration mentioned clause during examination and opposition proceedings.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed marks, when used in relation to the goods or services for which registration is sought, are likely to be confused with any registered trade mark appearing on the register. This determination shall take into account not only the visual similarity of the marks but also their phonetic and conceptual similarities. The applicant may submit counter-arguments demonstrating that confusion is unlikely, provided that such arguments address all relevant factors considered by the Registrar. Further, where a registration exists for goods or services identical or closely related to those specified in the application, the existence of a registration mentioned clause shall be given significant weight in assessing the likelihood of confusion.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark proceeds according to the provisions of this Act, and such registration is opposed by any person claiming rights in respect thereof, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the opponent an opportunity of being heard, both orally and in writing. Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the decision of the Registrar on any question arising during opposition proceedings shall be final. Any party aggrieved by a determination made under this Act relating to the registration of a trade mark may seek redressal through appropriate legal channels. The right to oppose an application for registration is contingent upon demonstrating a pre-existing and protectable interest; otherwise, such opposition shall be deemed frivolous and dismissed summarily. This provision safeguards existing rights holders and ensures fairness in the process of registration mentioned clause.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that any registered trade mark or trade mark applied for by another person in respect of identical or similar goods or services creates an unreasonable likelihood of confusion, subject to the provisions regarding honest concurrent use. The applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating that no such likelihood exists; this submission must be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice. Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, any subsequent application for registration containing a similar representation shall be examined with particular regard to the existing registration’s *registration mentioned clause*, ensuring that the public interest in maintaining distinctiveness and preventing unfair competition is adequately protected. The Registrar may require further clarification from either party during these proceedings.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed marks include any official emblem adopted by the Government, subject to an exception where such use is demonstrably pursuant to explicit authorization granted in writing by the appropriate governmental authority. Furthermore, where an applicant seeks registration based on acquired distinctiveness, they must provide documentary evidence substantiating continuous use of the mark for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the mark was initially refused under this Act due to descriptiveness or similarity to prior marks. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding such usage if deemed insufficient, and registration is contingent upon satisfactory compliance with these conditions relating to acquired distinctiveness and registration mentioned clause.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have knowledge of all prior applications and registrations appearing on the public register. Failure to conduct a diligent search prior to filing, or subsequent discovery of conflicting marks, will not absolve the applicant from liability for infringement. Where an application proceeds to registration despite such conflict, the Registrar may, upon complaint by any aggrieved party, order rectification of the register removing the mark from the registry. Such orders shall be enforceable as if they were original judgments and wilful disobedience may attract penalties including fines up to one million rupees and imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. The provisions relating to registration mentioned clause apply with particular force in cases involving well-known marks.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights pertaining to the use of the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior usage or registrations. Any party desiring to utilize a registered trade mark for commercial purposes beyond the scope of a permitted activity as defined under this Act may apply to the proprietor for a license. Such application shall specify the intended use and duration of the proposed utilization. The proprietor may grant such license on terms and conditions, including royalty payments, as they deem fit, provided that any assignment or sub-licensing of rights granted under this clause requires prior written consent from the registered proprietor. This provision concerning registration mentioned clause applies equally to assignments made before or after the date of registration.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any person claiming rights in relation to a proposed trade mark, direct the applicant to amend the representation of the mark contained in the application. Such direction shall be accompanied by a statement outlining the grounds for the objection and specifying the particular features of the mark that are deemed problematic under this Act. The applicant shall then have an opportunity to respond to the objection within a period as prescribed; failing which, the Registrar may proceed as if the applicant had not responded. Any party aggrieved by such direction or subsequent decision relating to amendment or refusal based on registration mentioned clause may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

For the purposes of this Act, an "alleged offence reason" shall be deemed to exist where a registered proprietor initiates proceedings against a defendant claiming infringement of their trademark. Such proceedings must demonstrate a reasonable belief, based on available evidence, that the defendant’s activities constitute use of an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration subsists. The alleged offence reason shall include any claim of dilution, unfair competition, or passing off arising from the defendant's actions as provided herein. Nothing in this definition shall preclude a finding that no genuine infringement has occurred.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed refused if, following an examination under this Act, it is determined that the mark conflicts with any prior registered trademark or pending application. The Registrar may, however, direct registration if the applicant demonstrates clear and distinguishable use of the mark in relation to goods or services not identical to those covered by the conflicting right. In instances where such a direction is issued, the alleged offence reason for the initial refusal shall be recorded and made publicly available on the Trade Marks Registry website. This record will include details regarding the prior right holder’s objection and the applicant's demonstration of distinctiveness, provided that this does not compromise any confidential business information as defined herein.

Where a registered proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence relating to the use of their trademark without just cause, the Court shall consider the extent to which such allegation impedes legitimate commercial activity by the alleged infringer. The proprietor must demonstrate a reasonable belief that the actions in question constitute infringement under this Act and are likely to cause demonstrable harm to the distinctiveness or reputation of the mark. Failure to establish this reasonable belief will render the proceedings frivolous, entitling the respondent to costs incurred. Furthermore, if the Court finds that the alleged offence reason is based on a misinterpretation of fair use principles or constitutes an attempt to stifle competition, it may order the proprietor to pay damages to the respondent. The remedies available are subject to proportionality and shall not unduly restrict freedom of expression.

Where a complaint alleging an offence relating to the use of a trademark is filed before the Registrar, such Registrar shall serve notice upon the respondent named in the complaint specifying the particulars of the alleged offence and requiring him to appear or send his authorised representative before the Registrar at a time and place specified in the notice. The respondent may, within thirty days from the date of service of the notice, file with the Registrar a written statement setting forth any defence or explanation he wishes to offer against the complaint. Upon receipt of the written statement, if any, the Registrar shall afford both the complainant and the respondent an opportunity for hearing. The *alleged offence reason* will be considered in light of all evidence presented at such hearing. Decisions regarding infringement shall be made based on a preponderance of the evidence as provided herein.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an offence relating to the use of a trademark under this Act, the court shall require the proprietor to demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the alleged offence has occurred. Such demonstration must include evidence establishing both the identity of the infringing party and a clear indication of the manner in which the mark is being used without due authorization. The court may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements, dismiss the proceedings if it finds that the proprietor has failed to provide sufficient evidence supporting the alleged offence reason. Provided that, where the infringement involves counterfeit goods, the proprietor shall also submit a declaration confirming efforts undertaken to mitigate consumer deception and prevent further distribution of such goods.

Where any proprietor alleges an offence relating to the use of a trademark as identical or confusingly similar to their own registered mark, the investigating officer shall record detailed statements from both parties. The alleged offence reason must be clearly articulated and supported by documentary evidence demonstrating actual consumer confusion or likelihood thereof. Failure to provide such substantiating material will render the complaint unsustainable. Any proprietor seeking injunctive relief under this Act shall further demonstrate quantifiable damages suffered as a direct consequence of the infringing use, subject to provisions regarding fair usage and parody. The adjudicating authority may impose penalties including monetary fines and orders for destruction of infringing goods, provided that due process is observed throughout the proceedings.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to assignment and licensing agreements concerning said mark, provided that any licensee granted permission under such an agreement may further sub-license those rights with the prior written consent of the proprietor. Where a third party alleges an offence relating to the use of a licensed trade mark without authorization, the alleged offence reason will be assessed considering the terms stipulated within the original licensing contract and any subsequent sub-licensing agreements. The proprietor shall provide documentation detailing the chain of licenses where such an allegation arises. Failure to obtain consent for sub-licensing as provided herein constitutes a breach of contract and does not diminish the registered proprietor’s underlying rights under this Act. Any transfer or assignment of a trade mark license must be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to prescribed fees.

Where a complaint alleging an infringement of a registered trademark is filed before the relevant intellectual property forum, the complainant shall bear the onus of demonstrating prima facie evidence of use ascribing the alleged offence reason to the respondent. The respondent may then present counter-evidence refuting such use or asserting fair dealing under this Act. Provided that, if the respondent claims prior honest concurrent use, they must demonstrate continuous and contemporaneous usage predating the complainant’s registration, subject to conditions prescribed herein regarding geographical limitations and potential consumer confusion. Any appeal against a finding of infringement shall be limited to arguments pertaining directly to the assessment of evidence concerning the alleged offence reason and its impact on the likelihood of deception among consumers.

The registered proprietor of a trademark shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses pertaining to the use of the mark within specified territories and for defined goods or services, provided that such license agreements are executed in writing and duly filed with the Registrar. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to a trademark, including but not limited to licensing arrangements, requires prior consent from the Controller, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The alleged offence reason for refusal of consent may include concerns regarding anticompetitive practices or detrimental impact on consumer interests. Further, notice rectification shall be afforded to any party claiming rights in relation to the mark following a license termination or assignment, allowing them an opportunity to present evidence and arguments concerning the validity of such claims as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark proceeds to final hearing, and objection has been raised alleging use contrary to section 9, the Registrar shall consider whether the alleged offence reason arises from a failure to conduct due diligence prior to the initial advertisement of the mark. It is provided that if the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that registration ought effected despite such an allegation, based on evidence of diligent searching and monitoring practices, the Registrar may proceed with examination as if the objection had not been raised. Further, the burden shall rest upon the objector to prove, by affirmative evidence, the continued existence of the circumstances giving rise to the alleged offence reason at the time of hearing.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a proposed geographical indication means that the indication is capable of distinguishing goods as originating from the specified territory, and further signifies that, prior to registration, such indication does not primarily denote characteristics of the goods other than those attributable to the origin. An owner of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to restrain any person who, without authorization, uses or attempts to use such indication in connection with goods not conforming to the standards as provided herein. Where an infringement is established under this Act, the plaintiff forthwith ceased to utilize the infringing mark and account for profits derived from said usage.

An application for registration of a Geographical Indication relating to “Kanthaloor Pepper” shall be considered complete upon submission of documentation demonstrating exclusive use by authorized producers within the defined geographical area, as detailed in Schedule A. The Registrar may require further evidence substantiating this exclusivity and adherence to established production standards, including but not limited to traditional farming practices and quality control measures. Should a challenge arise from an interested party alleging improper or misleading association with the Geographical Indication, the applicant shall be afforded opportunity for rebuttal. However, if the Registrar finds that the use of the mark is detrimental to the reputation of “Kanthaloor Pepper” or creates confusion amongst consumers, the plaintiff forthwith ceased any activities contributing to such detriment and the registration may be refused or revoked.

Where an authorized user institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief from acts likely to constitute a violation of registered Geographical Indication rights, the Court may grant such remedies as are just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further infringing activity and orders for delivery up or destruction of goods bearing false indications. Should the defendant in such proceedings demonstrate that they acted in good faith and without intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services involved, the Court may exercise its discretion to grant a period of time for compliance with any order issued. However, where it is established that the infringing activity has caused demonstrable harm to the reputation or distinctiveness of the Geographical Indication, the plaintiff forthwith ceased such activity and further orders may be made requiring compensation for losses incurred by registered proprietors.

Where an authorized user applies for registration as a collective bargain, and any other person claims a proprietary right or interest in respect of such application, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to that claimant. The claimant may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the notice under this Act, file objections relating to the distinctiveness of the indication or its association with a particular geographical area. Should the Registrar consider any objection to be meritorious and relevant to the registration process, he shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity for hearing, both parties being entitled to present evidence and arguments. In instances where infringement is established following a determination by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, pending further orders from the Board.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, and the Appellate Board finds, after due inquiry and affording all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, that the use of the proposed indication, as specified in the application, is likely to cause confusion amongst the consumers or is detrimental to the public interest, it may direct the applicant to modify the description of goods or services associated with the geographical indication. Further, if the Appellate Board determines that a registered proprietor’s use of a protected geographical indication infringes upon the rights of other producers within the defined territory, the plaintiff forthwith ceased such infringing use and shall undertake remedial measures as directed by the Board to mitigate any resulting harm to those producers.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce rights conferred under this Act shall be entitled to an injunction restraining any person from making, using, or applying for registration of a geographical indication which is identical or deceptively similar to the registered geographical indication. Provided that where a use of a geographical indication is found to constitute infringement, the court may order the defendant plaintiff forthwith ceased such use and destroy all infringing materials including labels, packaging, and advertising matter. Further, failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall render the defaulter liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each day during which the default continues, without prejudice to any other remedy available as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication relating to Alphonso mangoes may, subject to the provisions herein, grant exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said Indication on any person engaged in processing, packaging, or exporting Alphonso mangoes. Such license shall be documented by a written agreement specifying the duration, geographical area of application, and royalty payable. The registered proprietor shall retain the power to terminate any such license if the licensee fails to adhere to quality control standards as prescribed under this Act. Furthermore, assignment of the Geographical Indication or any rights therein requires prior approval from the Registrar, who may impose conditions safeguarding the continued authenticity and reputation associated with Alphonso mangoes. Where a breach of licensing terms occurs, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to require the licensee plaintiff forthwith ceased all use of the Geographical Indication.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, and the Appellate Board determines that the applicant’s use of the indication is likely to cause confusion or deception among consumers regarding the origin of the goods, it may direct the applicant to modify their production methods or cease using the indication altogether. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present arguments against such a direction. However, if the Appellate Board's order remains unsatisfied after a period specified therein, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring the plaintiff forthwith ceased all use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods for which registration was sought. Failure to comply with this notice will render the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a Geographical Indication is opposed, and the Appellate Board finds merit in the grounds of opposition relating to deceptively similar goods or services, the Registrar may direct the applicant to modify the proposed indication. Such direction shall be accompanied by a reasoned order detailing the specific aspects requiring alteration. Further, where it is established that the use of the Geographical Indication infringes upon an existing right, including a patent shall granted for a related process, the plaintiff forthwith ceased such infringing activity under this Act. The aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of receipt of the Appellate Board’s order, provided that interim relief is not precluded pending determination of the appeal.

Where an authorized user applies for registration as a collective bargain or a guarantee mark indicating a particular good conforming to a specification, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish detailed documentation substantiating the traditional knowledge associated with that geographical indication. Such documentation shall include verifiable records of agricultural practices, processing methods, and quality control measures employed by producers within the defined geographical area. Upon finding evidence of misuse or unfair competition affecting the reputation of the registered geographical indication, the Registrar shall issue a cease-and-desist order to the infringing party. Further, where such infringement continues despite the issuance of said order, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all activities constituting the violation and may be subject to penalties as provided herein. A specification patent addition relating to novel processing techniques can be included in subsequent amendments.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods attributable to its origin. Where any person believes that the acceptance of an application for registration is erroneous, or that any registered geographical indication is being used in contravention of this Act, such person may, relating plaintiff forthwith to the Geographical Indications Registry, file a representation against the proposed registration or the existing registration. The Registry shall consider such representations and provide an opportunity for all interested parties to be heard under this Act. Any decision made by the Registry regarding a representation is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such notice, file with the Registrar a reply addressing each ground of opposition raised by the opponent. Upon review of the application, supporting documents, and any reply submitted by the applicant, the Registrar shall determine whether to proceed with registration or reject the application entirely. Should the Registrar find merit in an objection, the opponent shall be *relating plaintiff forthwith* to the Registrar a reasoned statement detailing the basis for their claim. The Registrar may then afford the applicant a further opportunity to respond to this statement. Decisions made under this Act are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards as prescribed. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may specify territory, time period, and type of goods covered by the authorization. Where an assignment of a registered Geographical Indication is made, the assignee shall forthwith notify the Registrar in writing of such assignment, including details of the assignor and the date of transfer. Failure to do so will render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor. The Registrar may require further documentation as deemed necessary to verify the validity of any license or assignment granted under this Act. Any person claiming rights through a license or assignment shall be bound by the terms thereof, provided that such claims are made promptly and relating plaintiff forthwith to the registered proprietor.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed, and the Registrar determines that the opposition raises substantial questions regarding the distinctiveness or reputation associated with the proposed indication, the applicant shall be notified forthwith of the grounds of objection. The applicant may then submit a written response addressing each point raised in the notice, supported by relevant evidence demonstrating the acquired characteristics of the goods originating from the geographical area. Should the Registrar remain unconvinced following consideration of the applicant’s reply, and believes that prejudice to any proprietary rights exists, the matter shall be referred for determination before an adjudicating officer. The aggrieved party may appeal against such a decision relating plaintiff forthwith to the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “distinctiveness” with respect to a proposed geographical indication shall mean that the indication is capable of distinguishing goods as originating from a specific territory or region, and that such origin conveys to the consumer qualities, reputation or other characteristics attributable thereto. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where the initial assessment indicates a lack thereof. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the distinctiveness of a proposed indication, the plaintiff forthwith shall be required to submit documentary proof substantiating their claim and rebutting the grounds for objection; failure to do so within the prescribed timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding the quality and characteristics of the goods attributable exclusively to the origin within the defined geographical area. Where any person believes that another has acquired a right to use the geographical indication applied for, or claims an interest in the proposed registration, such person may file notice of opposition under this Act within the time specified. If an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall give both parties concerned opportunity to present their case and evidence. Should either party fail to appear at any hearing, the Registrar may proceed as if that party had attended. The plaintiff forthwith shall be deemed to have abandoned their claim should they repeatedly disregard procedural directives issued by the Registrar.

Where an interested party alleges unfair competition arising from the use of a registered Geographical Indication, they shall institute proceedings before the appropriate forum as provided herein. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements, the plaintiff forthwith may seek interim relief including injunctions restraining the infringing activity pending final determination of the matter. Such interim orders shall be granted only upon demonstration of likelihood of irreparable harm and subject to conditions deemed just by the court. The defendant in such proceedings shall bear the burden of proving that their use of the Geographical Indication does not constitute unfair competition, or that any confusion caused is minimal and inconsequential. Failure to comply with a final order issued under this Act may result in penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority, including but not limited to fines and orders for destruction of infringing goods.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall provide notice thereof to the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. Both parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their respective arguments in writing and submit documentary evidence as they deem fit. The Registrar may, at his discretion, direct either party to appear before him for oral submissions. Following consideration of all materials presented, the Registrar’s order shall be communicated to both applicant and opponent. Should an aggrieved party contend that the Registrar's decision is manifestly unjust or erroneous, such party may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. In any instance where a geographical indication has been registered and its exclusivity is challenged, the plaintiff forthwith shall initiate proceedings before the appropriate judicial forum as provided herein.

Where an authorized user of a registered geographical indication alleges unfair competition or any act likely to cause confusion as to the origin of goods, such authorized user shall be entitled to institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority. Provided that, prior to initiating such legal action, the authorized user must furnish written notice to the registered proprietor detailing the specific alleged infringement and outlining remedial measures proposed. Failure to comply with this notification requirement will render the subsequent claim untenable under this Act. Further, if the registered proprietor acknowledges receipt of said notice and undertakes corrective actions within a period of ninety days, the plaintiff forthwith shall be precluded from pursuing legal remedies unless the infringing activity persists or escalates beyond an acceptable threshold as determined by the authority.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief against any contravention of this Act, or any rule made thereunder. Where such contravention has occurred, the plaintiff forthwith shall apply to the appropriate civil court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity and for recovery of damages sustained by reason thereof.
