The court may award costs in favour of the prevailing party. Provided that where the infringement is found to be wilful and intentional, the court may also impose a penalty not exceeding ten times the value of the goods or services affected by the infringement. Further, any officer authorised under this Act shall have the power to seize and detain goods suspected of infringing upon a registered geographical indication.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of their protected indication for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the Geographical Indication and the duration of the license agreement. Further, the registered proprietor may assign the benefit of the registration, including all rights pertaining thereto, to any other person with the prior approval of the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not prejudice existing licensees. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or scope of a license or assignment, the plaintiff forthwith shall institute proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the terms and conditions governing assignments to ensure fair trade practices within the relevant sector.

Where an appeal is preferred under this Act against any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration, or directing removal of a registered Geographical Indication from the Register, the aggrieved party shall be deemed to be a plaintiff forthwith entitled to challenge the validity of such order. Provided that, in cases where the refusal or direction relates to non-distinctiveness or adaptation of a geographical indication, the appellant must demonstrate demonstrable and substantial misdirection of law by the Registrar. Further, any counter-claim asserting prior use or right to employ a similar indication shall be adjudicated concurrently with the appeal itself. The appellate authority may, subject to just considerations, grant interim relief pending determination of the appeal, including suspension of operation of the order appealed against.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars relating to the name, address, and nationality of the applicant, whether individual or association, and a map of the territory constituting the geographical indication. The Registrar may require such further information as is necessary for proper examination of the application. Where an objection is raised by any interested party against the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the plaintiff forthwith shall be notified of the grounds of objection and afforded an opportunity to submit its response within a period specified by the Registrar. A registered practitioner may represent the applicant in proceedings before the Registrar or any other authority constituted under this Act. The Registrar’s decision on such objections shall be final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where an authorized user, being one of the producers registered under this Act as entitled to use a particular Geographical Indication, alleges infringement by another party, such authorized user shall be obliged to provide detailed documentation substantiating their claim, including records of production volume, quality control measures, and adherence to established standards for that indication. The Registrar may require further clarification or additional data to assess the validity of the allegation. Provided that the alleged infringer fails to demonstrate a legitimate right to use the Geographical Indication, the authorized user shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief; in such circumstances, the plaintiff forthwith shall apply to the appropriate jurisdictional authority for an order restraining the infringing activity and preventing further dilution of the protected indication’s distinctiveness.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person or entity engaged in activities infringing upon their exclusive right, including but not limited to the unauthorized use thereof in connection with goods or services. Where such infringement is discovered, the plaintiff forthwith shall apply to the appropriate civil court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity and seeking damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor. The court may also order the seizure and destruction of any goods bearing the false or misleading indication. Further, where a registered certification trade mark is associated with the geographical indication, remedies available under that legislation shall be applicable in conjunction with this Act.

An *indication plaintiff* shall be defined as an association or collective body, duly incorporated under the Companies Act, representing the interests of producers of goods originating from a registered geographical indication. Such an association must demonstrate that its members are engaged exclusively in production within the specified geographical area and adhere to standards prescribed by relevant authorities. The registration of an *indication plaintiff* shall be subject to verification of their representation of genuine producers and their commitment to upholding the quality and reputation associated with the geographical indication. An application for registration as an *indication plaintiff* may be rejected if it appears that the applicant does not meet these requirements, as provided herein.

An application for registration as an indication plaintiff shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the geographical area from which the goods originate, a map of such area, and a statement detailing the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of the goods attributable to their origin. The Registrar may require further information deemed necessary to ascertain the distinctiveness of the indication and its association with the specified territory. Provided that an application relating to an agricultural product, foodstuff, wine or spirit shall also include evidence demonstrating ongoing production within the defined geographical area. Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff must demonstrate a connection with the goods in question, as provided herein, and may be required to submit affidavits verifying such claims.

An indication plaintiff shall be entitled to seek remedies against any party using, or proposing to use, an identical or deceptively similar indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards applicable under this Act. Such remedies may include injunctions restraining the infringing use, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor, and delivery up or destruction of the goods bearing the infringing indication. Provided that, where the infringement is found to be negligent, the court may award punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of compensation determined under this Act. The right to seek remedies as an indication plaintiff shall accrue from the date of registration of the geographical indication and continue for its duration. Nothing in this provision shall prevent a registered proprietor from pursuing any other remedy available under law against such infringement.

An application for registration as a Geographical Indication shall be accompanied by such particulars, including maps and statistical data, as the Registrar may require. The applicant shall furnish proof of control over the quality or other characteristics of goods attributable to the geographical origin, demonstrating adherence to established standards and practices within the defined territory. Where an objection is raised against the registration of a Geographical Indication under this Act, the objector shall be deemed an indication plaintiff for the purposes of presenting their case before the Registrar. The Registrar may afford the applicant and the indication plaintiff opportunities for oral hearings, subject to procedural guidelines as prescribed by regulations framed hereunder. Any order passed by the Registrar concerning objections or revocation is appealable to the Appellate Board within a period specified herein.

An application for registration as an indication plaintiff shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating continuous and exclusive use of the good or service associated with the proposed indication, extending back a minimum period of five years immediately preceding the date of the application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claim, including but not limited to sales records, export data, and affidavits from producers and distributors. Provided that an applicant demonstrates adherence to established quality standards and production methods specific to the geographical origin, as certified by a recognized consortium or authority representing the interests of producers within the defined area, registration may be granted. Any alteration in these standards after registration shall require prior approval from the Registrar, following consultation with relevant stakeholders.

Any person claiming to be an *indication plaintiff* aggrieved by the use of a protected Geographical Indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as provided herein, may institute legal proceedings against any party engaging in such unauthorized use. Such action shall be subject to the condition that the indication plaintiff demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the infringing activity, including but not limited to loss of market share or dilution of reputation. The court may order an injunction restraining further infringement and direct the infringer to recall goods bearing the misleading Geographical Indication from all points of sale. Failure to comply with such orders shall render the offender liable to a penalty which may extend to ten times the value of the infringing goods, as determined by the court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of such indication, specifying the goods or services to which such use pertains. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may be assigned to any person, firm, or company, with the prior consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all conditions stipulated in the original license agreement. An indication plaintiff seeking assignment of a Geographical Indication shall provide evidence demonstrating legitimate commercial interest and adherence to quality control standards as defined by the relevant sectoral authority. Further, any transfer or sub-license granted without such consent shall be deemed void. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review assignments where it is demonstrated that they prejudice the distinctiveness of the Geographical Indication or its association with the originating area.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the opponent with an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence. Should either party feel aggrieved by any decision rendered by the Registrar under this Act, they may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The burden of proof regarding the distinctiveness or reputation associated with a geographical indication shall lie upon the applicant or, in cases of opposition, upon the opponent. An *indication plaintiff* seeking injunctive relief must demonstrate actual damage resulting from unauthorized use, subject to provisions allowing for equitable considerations where misuse is unintentional and limited in scope.

An application for registration as an indication plaintiff shall be entertained only if it demonstrates continuous, uninterrupted production or processing of goods within a defined geographical area for a period exceeding three generations of producers. The applicant must further provide documented evidence establishing a direct link between the quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods and that specific geographic origin. Any use of the registered indication by any person other than an authorized user, or in a manner which is likely to falsely suggest such connection where it does not exist, shall constitute falsifying trade and be actionable under this Act. Provided that, the Central Registry may permit limited exceptions for scientific research or educational purposes, subject to conditions as prescribed by regulations.

Any person claiming to be an *indication plaintiff* aggrieved by the improper use or likelihood of use of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the territory where the infringement occurs. Such proceedings shall be directed towards seeking injunctive relief, including but not limited to restraining orders and permanent injunctions, as provided herein. The court may also order the apprehension and seizure of goods bearing the infringing mark. Compensation for damages suffered by the indication plaintiff due to such improper use shall be determined at the discretion of the court, subject to a maximum penalty equivalent to ten times the value of the infringing goods or services. An alphabetical index classification of registered geographical indications shall be maintained for ease of reference during enforcement actions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of their indication for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that prior written consent from the registration office is obtained and filed within thirty days of the assignment. An indication plaintiff seeking to enforce the terms of any such license agreement may file a suit in the appropriate jurisdiction, notwithstanding that the original proprietor has not itself taken action against the infringer. India filed months ago a request for protection of the ‘Kesar Mango’ Geographical Indication, and subsequent licensees are bound by all conditions stipulated during the initial registration process. Any transfer or sub-license shall be deemed to create an interest in favor of the assignee, subject to any limitations expressly stated within the original license agreement.

Where an action is brought before a competent authority alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, the defendant shall be required to demonstrate, as provided herein, compliance with all applicable conditions precedent. Specifically, the defendant must satisfy the court that their use of the indication does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services in question and that such use is consistent with established trade practices within the relevant sector. Further, if the defendant contends good faith reliance on a prior registration or usage, they shall submit documentary evidence substantiating this claim, including but not limited to marketing materials and sales records. The authority may require further submissions as deemed necessary for assessment of the infringement defendant satisfies these conditions.

For the purposes of this Act, “fee paid fee” means any sum remitted or waived under section 14, and shall be treated as a reduction from the original prescribed fee for that particular service. The Registrar may, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government, accept payment of fees in installments, provided that each installment is accompanied by an administrative charge as determined by notification. Any amount paid towards a registration or application which remains outstanding due to subsequent cancellation or rejection shall be deemed a fee paid fee and refunded to the applicant, less any charges incurred under this Act for processing the application.

Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be accompanied by a non-refundable application fee as determined under this Act, and any subsequent request for amendment to particulars furnished with such application will incur an additional processing fee. The Registrar may require payment of a further examination fee if, during scrutiny, deficiencies are identified that necessitate extensive investigation into the distinctiveness or reputation associated with the indicated goods. Failure to remit the prescribed fee paid fee within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection without further notice. Renewal of registration requires timely remittance of renewal fees; default in payment will result in provisional lapse and a subsequent reinstatement fee.

The Register may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, issue a provisional certificate of registration pending examination under this Act. Any objection raised against the proposed registration shall be communicated to the applicant within three months from the date of receipt of the application and the applicant shall have opportunity to file its response within two months thereafter. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence supporting the claim of distinctiveness of the geographical indication, and any costs incurred by the Register in obtaining such information shall be recoverable as a fee paid fee from the applicant. Failure to comply with this requirement within the stipulated time will render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar may also require proof of prior customary use or established reputation associated with the geographical indication.

Any proprietor seeking to maintain registration of a geographical indication shall remit an annual maintenance fee as prescribed; failure to pay this fee on or before the due date will render the registration liable for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence of non-payment, issue a notice affording thirty days for compliance and payment of any applicable surcharge. Repeated default in the timely remittance of the fee paid fee shall constitute conclusive proof of abandonment of interest in the geographical indication by the proprietor. Furthermore, any person utilizing a registered geographical indication without authorization following such revocation will be subject to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to compensatory damages and injunctive relief.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may grant licenses to third parties for the use of their indication, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement and approved by the Registrar. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to production, processing, packaging, sale, and export of goods claiming origin from the registered geographical area. Any assignment or transfer of a Geographical Indication, or any right pertaining thereto, requires prior consent of the Central Government and involves payment of a prescribed fee paid fee as determined by regulations framed under this Act. The Registrar may impose conditions relating to quality control and traceability for licensees, ensuring adherence to standards associated with the geographical indication’s reputation. Failure to comply with these conditions may result in revocation of the license or other penalties as provided herein.

The Register may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication and after due consideration of the particulars furnished therein, demand payment of the prescribed registration fee. Failure to remit the full amount of the fee within thirty days from the date of such demand shall render the application liable to rejection, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by an order rejecting an application on grounds of non-payment of a fee paid fee may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted regarding timely payment or extenuating circumstances preventing remittance, and may reinstate the application if satisfied that injustice would otherwise result.

The Register may, upon receipt of a duly completed application for registration of a geographical indication and after verification of all particulars as provided herein, issue an acknowledgement to the applicant specifying the provisional date of filing. Any subsequent alteration to the proposed name or emblem of the geographical indication shall be deemed a fresh application subject to payment of the prescribed fee paid fee. The Registrar may, at any time, require the proprietor of a registered geographical indication to furnish such further information as the Registrar deems necessary for verification of authenticity and continued protection under this Act. A transmissible use layout depicting the territorial boundaries associated with the geographical indication shall be submitted alongside the application, and any subsequent modifications must be approved by the Registrar. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in suspension or revocation of registration.

Registration of a geographical indication for ‘Kashmir Apples’ requires annual maintenance fees to be remitted within thirty days of the anniversary of its registration, as provided herein. Failure to remit said fee shall render the geographical indication liable to removal from the Register of Geographical Indications. Any application for restoration following such removal must include payment of all outstanding fees and a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the original prescribed fee. The Registrar may, subject to due process, waive or reduce these fees in cases where demonstrable hardship is presented by the registered proprietor. Furthermore, any layout design vested in the consortium managing the ‘Kashmir Apples’ geographical indication shall be protected from unauthorized use unless accompanied by timely payment of the requisite fee paid fee.

For the purposes of this Act, “fee paid fee” means any sum remitted or waived under section 14, and which shall be treated as having been fully discharged towards the original liability for that fee. Any subsequent amendment claim specification relating to an indication already registered, where such amendment necessitates a recalculation of fees due, shall not be processed until confirmation is received from the Registrar verifying that the fee paid fee has been appropriately accounted for in the revised assessment. This provision applies irrespective of whether the initial fee was tendered electronically or through traditional means, provided that adequate records exist substantiating its payment and subsequent remission as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “genetically modified organism” with respect to crop sciences means an organism whose genetic material has been altered through techniques of gene technology, including but not limited to recombinant DNA technology, and which exhibits a novel characteristic; provided that such alteration is demonstrable and reproducible. An organism shall be deemed genetically modified if the modification results in phenotypic expression or inheritance of traits not previously observed within its species under normal conditions. The Central Government may, by notification, specify further categories of organisms considered genetically modified for the purposes of this Act, subject to scientific consensus.

An application for registration of a novel plant variety shall include detailed documentation pertaining to its genetic composition and expression, including but not limited to data derived from molecular marker analysis and quantitative trait locus mapping. The applicant must demonstrate that the variety possesses distinct, uniform, and stable characteristics as determined through rigorous field trials conducted over at least three successive growing seasons in diverse agro-climatic zones. Such trials shall adhere to guidelines prescribed by the Central Government relating to statistical significance and reproducibility of observations concerning crop sciences. Further, the application shall specify the geographical location where the variety was initially developed and demonstrate its potential contribution to enhanced agricultural productivity or nutritional value.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a Plant Variety Protection granted in respect of a novel variety developed through crop sciences may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider any question of fact or law arising out of the order appealed against and may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the order. Subject to this, the Board’s decision shall be final. Further appeals lie only to the High Court on a point of law. Provided that any claim for damages resulting from infringement of Plant Variety Protection rights shall be adjudicated by a competent civil court, as provided herein.

Applications for registration of a Plant Variety shall include particulars relating to its denomination, origin, method of production, and any available information concerning its genetic characteristics. Where an application relates to a variety derived from another variety, the applicant shall furnish details regarding the parentage and the extent of derivation. The Authority may require the submission of additional data pertaining to crop sciences, including but not limited to field trials demonstrating stability and uniformity across generations and geographical locations. Such trials shall be conducted in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Central Government, and reports thereof submitted for evaluation. An applicant who fails to provide the requisite information or conduct trials as directed may have their application rejected under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications and related documentation accessible for public inspection, subject to provisions regarding confidential data.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration of a novel plant variety, require the applicant to submit detailed documentation pertaining to its derivation and stability. Such documentation shall include comprehensive data demonstrating adherence to established crop sciences principles regarding genetic modification or conventional breeding techniques employed in the creation of the variety. The applicant must further provide evidence confirming that field trials have been conducted under diverse agro-climatic conditions, as specified by the Central Government’s guidelines. Any deviation from these prescribed protocols requires prior written approval obtained from the Plant Variety Protection Committee and shall be explicitly stated within the application. Registration is conditional upon compliance with these requirements and verification of the variety's distinctiveness and uniformity.

Any person who, having knowledge of the registration of a Plant Variety, commercially markets seeds or other propagating material derived from such variety, and falsely represents that it possesses characteristics not demonstrably present in the registered variety, shall be liable to pay compensation determined by the Authority. This compensation may include damages suffered by affected farmers and breeders, as well as punitive measures proportionate to the scale of the misrepresentation. Furthermore, any entity found guilty of such deceptive practices concerning crop sciences is subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and repeat offenses shall attract enhanced penalties up to one million rupees. The Authority may also issue orders restraining further marketing activities as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a Plant Breeder who has obtained registration of a plant variety may grant licenses for propagation or other exploitation of such registered variety. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may be granted for specific territories or uses, as determined by the grantor. Any assignment of rights in respect of a registered plant variety shall require prior notification to the Authority, detailing the terms and conditions of transfer. The assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights and obligations of the assignor under this Act. Consideration for licenses or assignments relating to crop sciences may include royalty payments, lump sum fees, or a combination thereof, as agreed upon by the parties involved. Provided that any license granted must clearly state its duration and scope.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Appeal Tribunal determines, upon review of evidence presented under this Act, that a claim of novelty in a plant variety is demonstrably undermined by prior public knowledge or usage within India, the appellant may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for further consideration. Such petitions shall be accompanied by an expert report from a qualified crop sciences professional detailing the extent and nature of the pre-existing disclosure. The Board may, subject to established principles of natural justice, direct the Tribunal to rehear the matter or substitute its decision with one it deems more appropriate, provided that the appellant establishes prejudice resulting from any error apparent on the record. Decisions of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final, save for appeals under the relevant appellate provisions.

For the purposes of determining novelty and distinctiveness under this Act, a Plant Variety shall be deemed to exhibit substantial similarity with an existing variety if, based on readily observable characteristics determined through established crop sciences methodologies, it demonstrates phenotypic traits that are not significantly different from those consistently expressed in the reference variety. Such assessment shall consider factors including yield potential, disease resistance, and morphological features as defined by relevant national guidelines. The Registrar may require further analysis, including molecular marker data, to resolve ambiguities when assessing claims purposes related to distinctiveness, provided that such requests adhere to principles of fairness and transparency.

An application for registration of a Plant Variety shall include particulars relating to its denomination, including any proposed trade marks deemed suitable for identification purposes, and a detailed description encompassing its essential characteristics relevant to crop sciences. Such description shall specify traits pertaining to morphology, physiology, disease resistance, and yield potential, as determined through rigorous field trials conducted over at least three successive growing seasons in diverse agro-climatic zones. The application must also state the source variety or method of derivation, provided that if the variety is derived from an existing one, a statement regarding the contribution of the breeder shall be included. Further particulars concerning seed multiplication and distribution practices may be submitted as deemed necessary by the Registrar.

The Registering Authority shall, upon receiving an application for compulsory licensing relating to a registered plant variety, undertake a thorough assessment of the applicant’s demonstrated need and the potential impact on agricultural practices. Such applications must detail the specific geographical area where the compulsory license is sought, along with justification based on reasonable non-infringement by the variety's holder. The Authority may grant a compulsory license if it determines that the registered plant variety is not being made available to farmers in sufficient quantities or at affordable prices, subject to provisions safeguarding the legitimate interests of the breeder and ensuring equitable compensation reflecting research investments. Further, any such license shall be granted for a limited period as provided herein.

Where a plant variety is deemed essential for food security or public health needs, and the registered breeder has failed to grant licenses on reasonable terms, the Central Government may, subject to conditions as provided herein, issue a compulsory license. Such a license shall permit any person to make, sell, import, or distribute the protected plant variety for non-commercial research purposes only, without authorization from the right holder. Applications for compulsory licensing may be made to the Controller, who shall consider factors including the inadequacy of measures taken by the breeder to ensure availability and affordability of the variety. The registered breeder shall have the right to be heard in any proceedings concerning a compulsory license application. Compensation commensurate with the use of the protected variety shall be determined by the Controller and paid to the breeder.

Any person claiming an invention relating to a plant variety registered under this Act may apply to the Controller for authorization to use the registered variety for purposes other than those specified in the granted Plant Variety Protection. Such application shall include detailed justification demonstrating that the refusal of the right holder to grant permission constitutes an impediment to agricultural development or access to essential medicines derived from the plant variety. The Controller, after giving notice to the concerned right holder and providing them a reasonable opportunity to be heard, may determine whether a compulsory licensing is warranted, considering factors such as public interest, freedom to operate for research institutions, and the adequacy of remuneration proposed. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the terms and conditions, including duration and royalty rates, as provided herein.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority has refused an application for compulsory licensing under this Act, or has imposed conditions which the applicant alleges are unreasonable, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Authority. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days, subject to just cause shown.

Where a plant variety is registered and its commercial exploitation demonstrably impacts food security or farmer livelihoods within India, the Registering Authority shall consider applications for compulsory licensing. Such an application must demonstrate that the registered breeder has failed to adequately address the identified need through reasonable efforts, as determined by the relevant governmental body. The form issuing a compulsory license will specify the terms and conditions, including royalty rates not exceeding ten percent of the sales revenue derived from the licensed variety. Provided that the applicant demonstrates financial hardship or lack of resources, the Authority may prescribe reduced royalty obligations. Any aggrieved party may appeal the decision regarding the grant or terms of a compulsory license to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days.

The Authority shall maintain a Register of Plant Varieties for each class of varieties and upon receipt of an application for registration, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish details regarding the source material utilized in the development of the variety. Any sums received by the Authority as registration fees, benefit-sharing amounts from commercialized varieties, or penalties imposed under this Act shall be credited into a dedicated account maintained with the Reserve Bank of India. This account shall constitute fund for the purposes of supporting research and development activities related to plant breeding, conservation of genetic resources, and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in seed production. The Authority may also invest portions of this fund as deemed prudent by its governing board, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to revocation of registration, imposition of penalties, or any other action affecting their rights concerning plant varieties shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be binding and final, subject to further review only upon a petition made to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order. Any funds received by the Registrar as fees for registration, benefit-sharing payments, or penalties imposed under this Act shall constitute fund to be utilized exclusively for promoting plant breeding research, safeguarding farmers’ rights, and administering the provisions herein. Provided that any shortfall in these activities may be met through grants from the Central Government. The Registrar shall maintain detailed accounts of all receipts and disbursements related to this fund and submit annual reports to the Central Government.

Any person found to have knowingly and willfully exploited plant genetic resources for commercial purposes without prior authorization from the Central Government shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding five times the value of the infringing material or propagation units involved, whichever is higher. Further, any entity convicted under this Act relating to unauthorized exploitation may face suspension of its registration as a Plant Breeder Rights holder for a period determined by the Board. The sums recovered from such penalties and any costs incurred in enforcement proceedings shall constitute fund, which will be utilized exclusively for supporting research into indigenous varieties and providing assistance to farmers affected by biopiracy. Repeated offenses shall attract progressively enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution as provided herein.

The Authority may, subject to conditions specified therein, grant non-exclusive licenses in respect of rights granted under this Act relating to a plant variety, provided that any such license shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities including but not limited to propagation, sale, and export. Assignment of such licenses is permissible with prior approval from the Authority, and the assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to the original licensee. Further, where an assignment or a license involves benefit-sharing obligations as determined under this Act, the assignor or licensor shall remain jointly and severally liable for ensuring compliance until the expiry of the relevant period. The proceeds derived from such licenses and assignments shall constitute fund which will be utilized exclusively for supporting research relating to indigenous plant varieties and promoting farmers’ rights, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order restricting access to propagating material of a plant variety, including restrictions imposed on reference use geographical indications associated with that variety, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum stating the grounds of appeal and the relief sought. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated under this Act relating to benefit sharing shall constitute fund misappropriation, rendering the offender liable to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of the infringing propagating material. Further, any party demonstrating demonstrable financial loss due to such infringement may seek compensatory damages as provided herein.

For the purpose of facilitating research and development relating to plant genetic resources, and promoting sustainable agricultural practices, there shall be established a Sources Gene Fund. Contributions to the Sources Gene Fund shall include any sums received from institutions engaged in research concerning traditional crop varieties, as determined by the Board under this Act. The Board may also direct that royalties derived from commercial applications of germplasm originating from community conserved lands be credited into the Fund. Further, benefit-sharing amounts received from researchers utilizing access to plant genetic resources, subject to prescribed guidelines, shall be deposited therein. These funds are intended to support initiatives aimed at conserving and sustainably utilizing indigenous plant varieties.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed information regarding contributions anticipated towards the sources gene fund. The Registrar may require applicants demonstrating substantial reliance on traditional knowledge in the development of a novel variety to provide evidence of community consent and benefit-sharing agreements, as applicable under this Act. Contributions to the sources gene fund are deemed essential where genetic material sourced from indigenous varieties or landraces has been utilized, subject to verification by the Plant Varieties Committee. The amount contributed shall be determined based on the extent of utilization and potential commercial gain derived therefrom, provided that a minimum contribution is prescribed for all registered varieties utilizing such resources. Failure to remit contributions as stipulated may result in suspension of propagation rights.

Any person who utilizes plant genetic resources obtained from India’s germplasm centers or research institutions without fulfilling the prescribed benefit-sharing obligations shall be liable for damages. Such damages will be determined by a competent authority appointed under this Act, considering factors including the extent of commercial exploitation and the potential impact on farmer livelihoods. The Central Government may, through notification, establish guidelines regarding the assessment of these damages, ensuring fairness and proportionality. All funds recovered as damages shall be credited to the sources gene fund, administered by the Protection of Plant Varieties Authority. Further, any entity found in violation of this provision is prohibited from seeking registration of a new plant variety under this Act for a period not exceeding five years, subject to appeal before an appellate tribunal.

Applications for access to the sources gene fund shall be made to the Authority in Form G, accompanied by a detailed research proposal outlining the intended use and anticipated outcomes. The application must specify the quantity of genetic material required, the duration of access, and any proposed modifications or analyses planned. Access will only be granted subject to a determination that the applicant possesses adequate facilities and expertise for responsible handling and utilization of the germplasm.

The Authority may require applicants to furnish security deposits, as determined by regulations framed under this Act, to ensure compliance with stipulated conditions regarding data sharing and benefit-sharing arrangements. Any commercial exploitation derived from accessing the sources gene fund shall be subject to prior approval from the Authority and a proportionate contribution remitted into the Fund, as prescribed. The applicant shall provide regular progress reports detailing research findings and adherence to agreed protocols.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Plant Variety Sources Gene Fund for the purpose of supporting research relating to the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from registered plant breeders upon commercialization of varieties derived, wholly or partly, from accessions obtained from public germplasm banks under this Act, provided that such accessions were not subject to prior benefit-sharing agreements. The Authority may also accept voluntary contributions from governmental and non-governmental organizations engaged in agricultural research and development. Funds disbursed from the Sources Gene Fund shall be allocated solely for projects approved by a committee constituted by the Central Government, ensuring equitable distribution amongst institutions promoting biodiversity conservation and farmer participation.

Any person who utilizes plant genetic resources obtained from India’s germplasm centers without contributing appropriately to the sources gene fund shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Authority. The Authority may impose a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees per instance of non-compliance, and may order the seizure of propagating material derived from such unauthorized utilization. Further, any entity found repeatedly failing to remit contributions to the sources gene fund, despite written notice and opportunity for redressal, shall be deemed to be acting in contravention of this Act. Such entities are subject to suspension of registration privileges and potential civil suits initiated by the Central Government seeking recovery of unpaid sums with applicable interest.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety shall be permitted to license those rights, including access to germplasm resources contributing to the registered variety’s genetic makeup, for research purposes or commercial exploitation. Such licenses may grant exclusive or non-exclusive rights, and the terms thereof shall be determined by mutual agreement between the licensor and licensee. Where a license involves utilization of material derived from sources gene fund contributions, the licensee shall provide periodic reports detailing such usage to the Authority, as prescribed. Assignment of plant variety rights, including associated germplasm access privileges, may occur with the consent of the Registrar, provided that the assignee adheres to all obligations previously undertaken by the assignor under this Act. The Central Government may, after due inquiry, direct a transfer of rights if it is deemed necessary for public benefit.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Sources Gene Fund for the purpose of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in conservation efforts. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from entities commercializing registered varieties derived from protected germplasm, as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Any dispute concerning the calculation or allocation of funds within the Sources Gene Fund may be referred to an appellate tribunal constituted for that purpose. The decision of such tribunal shall be final, subject to appeal only on grounds of legal error demonstrable through documented evidence presented during the original hearing. Further, any claim against the Fund’s assets must be substantiated by a certificate from the Comptroller and Auditor General.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the proposed contribution to the sources gene fund. Such contributions are mandatory and reflect a commitment to preserving genetic diversity within registered varieties. The amount contributed shall be determined based on factors including, but not limited to, the commercial viability projections submitted by the applicant during the registration process, as assessed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Further, applicants demonstrating significant investment in conservation efforts may petition the authority for adjustments to their contribution schedule. During each house parliament session, a review of the fund’s operational efficiency and allocation procedures shall be undertaken to ensure equitable distribution amongst deserving research institutions.

The Authority shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all contributions made to the sources gene fund. Contributions shall include, but are not limited to, benefit-sharing amounts received from registered plant varieties and their essentially derived varieties, as determined under this Act. The Register shall be accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Authority concerning commercial confidentiality. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding the assessment or collection of contributions may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. Further, any funds accrued from royalties derived from the exploitation of film sound recordings incorporated into promotional material for registered plant varieties shall be deposited directly into the sources gene fund. The Authority is empowered to prescribe procedures for auditing and verifying transactions related to the fund as provided herein.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Plant Variety Sources Gene Fund for the purpose of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing financial assistance to farmers engaged in conserving traditional varieties. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from registration fees paid by breeders seeking protection under this Act, as well as any benefit-sharing amounts received pursuant to agreements entered into concerning registered plant varieties. The Authority may also accept grants or donations from governmental agencies or private entities for deposit into the Sources Gene Fund. Registration shall apply only where the applicant demonstrates compliance with the prescribed guidelines regarding access and utilization of genetic resources. Any expenditure from the Fund requires prior approval by a committee constituted under this Act.

For the purpose of facilitating research and development relating to plant genetic resources, and ensuring equitable access to benefits arising from the commercial utilization thereof, there shall be established a Gene Fund Sub-Account. Contributions to this sub-account shall consist of levies collected under this Act from entities engaged in the import or export of propagating material derived from registered plant varieties, as determined by regulations framed by the Central Government. The funds held within the Gene Fund Sub-Account may be utilized exclusively for supporting research grants focused on conserving indigenous crop diversity and promoting sustainable agricultural practices, subject to guidelines issued by the Authority. Any surplus arising shall be reinvested into the National Gene Fund.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding contributions anticipated towards the Gene Fund sub. This contribution is calculated based on the projected commercial exploitation of the registered variety and assessed by the Plant Variety Authority. Applicants demonstrating a history of providing access to germplasm resources or actively participating in farmer-led breeding initiatives may, subject to verification, be eligible for reduced assessment rates under this Act. The authority shall maintain records detailing all contributions received and their allocation towards supporting research on indigenous plant genetic resources and promoting sustainable agricultural practices. Further, any modification to the projected commercial exploitation post-registration requires notification and potential reassessment of the Gene Fund sub liability.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the imposition of penalties, revocation of registration, or any other action taken against them concerning plant varieties, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence and arguments presented by both parties and shall pass a reasoned order affirming, reversing, or modifying the original decision. Failure to deposit the prescribed fee for maintaining a registered variety shall render the registration liable for cancellation, subject to an opportunity being afforded to the registrant to demonstrate sufficient cause for the delay. Further, any breeder who fails to contribute their share of benefit-sharing amounts to the gene fund sub as determined by the Central Government shall be deemed guilty of an offense and liable to penalties as provided herein.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the proposed contribution to the gene fund sub. The Authority may require applicants demonstrating a history of traditional farming practices or possessing indigenous knowledge relevant to the germplasm utilized in developing the variety, to submit supplementary documentation verifying such claims. Contributions to the gene fund sub shall be determined based on factors including, but not limited to, the extent of genetic modification involved, commercialization projections, and reliance upon publicly funded research. The Authority shall maintain a register detailing all contributions received and disbursements made from the gene fund sub. Any disputes concerning the assessment or collection of contributions may be referred to an appellate body constituted under this Act for resolution. Provided that, the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding the utilization of funds derived from the gene fund sub.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Gene Fund sub-account specifically designated for supporting research into traditional crop varieties and their wild relatives. Contributions to this sub-account shall comprise ten percent of all benefit sharing amounts received by the Central Government under this Act from entities commercializing plant varieties derived, wholly or partly, from germplasm accessions sourced from India’s public sector agricultural institutions. Provided that, any such contribution exceeding one crore rupees in a financial year may be adjusted against outstanding liabilities owed to farmers for compensation related to unintended consequences arising from genetically modified organisms. The Authority shall publish an annual report detailing the disbursement of funds from this Gene Fund sub-account and ensuring transparency regarding compliance with prescribed guidelines.

Any person who contravenes any provision of this Act relating to the proper utilization and management of the gene fund sub shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to five hundred thousand rupees, and in the case of a continuing offence, an additional penalty of ten thousand rupees for every day during which the default continues. The Authority may issue directions to any person failing to comply with these provisions, and failure to adhere to such directions will constitute an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year or a fine, or both. Further, any entity found to be misappropriating funds from the gene fund sub shall face prosecution under relevant sections of the Indian Penal Code, as determined by the adjudicating officer.

Any person holding rights pertaining to a plant variety shall, upon request by the Central Government or any State Government, grant a non-exclusive license for research and development purposes relating to the utilization of germplasm resources. Such licenses shall specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to genetic modification and analysis for traits relevant to crop improvement. The terms of such licenses may include stipulations regarding benefit sharing with the gene fund sub, proportionate to the commercial success derived from the licensed research. Further, assignment of rights relating to plant varieties incorporating germplasm accessed under license shall be subject to a royalty payment to the original holder, calculated as a percentage of net sales and remitted into the aforementioned gene fund sub. The Central Government may prescribe guidelines for determining reasonable royalty rates and dispute resolution mechanisms concerning these assignments.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Gene Fund sub-account specifically designated for supporting research into traditional crop varieties and farmer-led breeding initiatives. Contributions to this sub-account shall include a portion of benefit-sharing fees received from commercial breeders, as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Any dispute concerning the allocation or disbursement of funds from the Gene Fund sub-account may be referred to an appellate forum constituted for that purpose. The Authority’s decision regarding such allocations is final, subject to review on grounds of legal error demonstrable through documentary evidence presented within sixty days of notification. Further, any farmer aggrieved by a determination impacting their eligibility for accessing resources derived from this sub-account may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding rights in a plant variety shall be permitted to grant licenses for the commercial use thereof, including but not limited to propagation, sale, distribution, or import. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms and conditions thereof shall be determined by the licensor, provided that such terms do not contravene any provisions of this Act relating to farmers’ rights or benefit sharing. Further, assignment of plant variety rights is permissible with the prior approval of the Authority, and a record of all licenses and assignments shall be maintained in the Register of Plant Varieties. Where a license agreement involves access to a gene fund sub derived from an essentially derived variety, the licensee shall be bound by any patent amended conditions relating to research exemptions as stipulated within that original grant.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Gene Fund sub-account specifically designated for the disbursement of compensation awarded in appeals concerning contested registration decisions. Any applicant aggrieved by an order denying registration, or imposing conditions deemed unduly restrictive under this Act, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of notification. The amount remitted as registry fee upon initial application shall be credited towards this Gene Fund sub-account and is non-refundable even if the appeal is successful. Provided that, where a finding of mala fide intent on the part of an Authority member is established during appellate proceedings, the applicant may petition for reimbursement from the said sub-account, subject to verification by a designated committee appointed by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, “compensation deposited gene” means any genetic material extracted from a plant variety and placed in secure storage by an authority designated under this Act, following a determination that the breeder or registered owner has failed to provide adequate compensation for the use of such genetic resources as required under this Act. The designation of authorities shall be notified in the Official Gazette. Any application for registration of a new plant variety shall disclose whether it incorporates any material derived from a compensation deposited gene and, if so, specify the source and circumstances of its deposition. Access to a compensation deposited gene may only be granted subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include details regarding any compensation deposited gene utilized in its development, specifying the donor source and the terms governing access and benefit sharing related thereto. The Authority may require submission of documentation substantiating compliance with relevant agreements concerning such genetic material, including proof of royalty payments or other forms of remuneration to rights holders. Where a compensation deposited gene is incorporated, the applicant shall declare whether any restrictions apply to subsequent use or commercialization of the registered variety, as provided herein. Failure to disclose this information accurately may render the registration liable for cancellation under this Act and subject the applicant to penalties.

Where a plant variety is found to have been developed using a compensation deposited gene without authorization from the depositor, and commercial exploitation thereof has occurred, the breeder shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include not only direct financial losses suffered by the depositor but also reasonable costs incurred in monitoring and enforcing their rights under this Act. The amount of compensation recoverable may be adjusted to account for any intervening use or development undertaken by a third party acting in good faith, subject to due process as provided herein. Further, the Authority may order the breeder to provide an accounting of profits derived from the infringing variety. Any funds recovered through litigation or settlement shall first be applied towards reimbursing the depositor’s enforcement costs and then deposited into the National Gene Fund for distribution according to regulations framed by the Central Government.

Where a plant variety is deemed to infringe upon the rights of another person under this Act, and where the infringing act involves the unauthorized utilization of a compensation deposited gene, the Registering Authority shall issue a notice to both the alleged infringer and the claimant. Such notice shall detail the nature of the infringement, including specific genetic markers demonstrating derivation from the protected material. The alleged infringer shall be afforded an opportunity for hearing within sixty days of receipt of the notice, during which they may present evidence refuting the claim or mitigating damages. Following the hearing, the Registering Authority may order the infringing party to pay compensation directly into the National Gene Fund, proportionate to the extent of unauthorized use and demonstrable harm caused. This sum shall be disbursed as per guidelines established by the Central Government for supporting research related to plant breeding and farmer welfare.

Where a plant variety is deemed eligible for registration subject to conditions relating to farmers’ rights and benefit sharing, the Authority shall establish a dedicated account within the National Gene Fund. Any compensation deposited into this account, hereinafter referred to as a ‘compensation deposited gene’, shall be held in trust for the exclusive benefit of affected farmer communities demonstrably impacted by the commercial exploitation of the registered variety. Such funds may only be disbursed upon verification by an independent committee constituted under these rules and regulations, confirming adherence to pre-determined criteria regarding equitable distribution amongst eligible beneficiaries. Provided that any disbursement from a compensation deposited gene shall not exceed the initially assessed impact value as determined during registration proceedings, and subject to annual auditing procedures as provided herein.

Any person found to have utilized a compensation deposited gene without authorization from the Registering Authority shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Such unauthorized utilization includes, but is not limited to, commercial propagation and sale of plant material derived therefrom. The Controller may impose fines ranging from fifty thousand rupees to five hundred thousand rupees per instance of infringement, subject to aggravating factors such as intent to deceive or substantial economic harm to the registered breeder. Further, any propagating material produced in violation of this Act shall be deemed contraband and seized by enforcement officers. Repeated offenses may result in criminal prosecution under relevant provisions relating to fraud and intellectual property violations, as provided herein.

Any person holding rights pertaining to a plant variety shall be permitted to license those rights, including the right to utilize a compensation deposited gene contained therein, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in a written agreement. Such agreements may grant exclusive or non-exclusive licenses for specific acts, including but not limited to propagation, sale, distribution, import, and export of propagating material derived from the variety. Assignment of rights under this Act, encompassing those related to compensation deposited genes, requires registration with the Plant Varieties Registry and shall be deemed valid only upon such registration. The assignee shall succeed to all rights and obligations of the assignor as provided herein. Any license or assignment agreement must clearly define the scope of permitted use and any royalty payments due to the right holder, failing which it may be declared invalid by an adjudicating officer.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a farmer has suffered demonstrable economic loss due to the failure of a protected plant variety to perform as represented, and where such failure is attributable to the actions or omissions of the registered breeder, the Authority may order the breeder to contribute to a compensation deposited gene pool. This contribution shall be equivalent to a sum determined by the Authority, taking into account the extent of the farmer’s loss and the breeder's annual turnover as provided herein. Any dispute arising from such determination or the calculation of the contribution may be appealed to the Appellate Board within sixty days. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further judicial review under this Act on grounds limited to jurisdiction only.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Authority determines that a farmer has suffered loss due to the exercise of rights conferred by a plant breeder, including but not limited to losses arising from infringement of intellectual property rights relating to registered varieties, the Authority shall direct the relevant breeder or entity holding propagation rights to deposit an amount as compensation into the National Gene Fund. This compensation, designated as a ‘compensation deposited gene’, shall be held in trust and utilized solely for providing relief and support to affected farmers, prioritizing those engaged in traditional farming practices. An application filed patent relating to the variety need not preclude such determination of loss or subsequent direction for deposit; however, the Authority will consider any contractual agreements between farmer and breeder when assessing damages. The amount deposited shall accrue interest as prescribed by the Central Government and may be disbursed according to guidelines formulated by a committee comprising representatives from farmers’ organizations and relevant government departments, subject to due process.

Any person found to have commercially exploited a plant variety without authorization, and who has thereby benefited from the use of a compensation deposited gene established for safeguarding farmers’ rights, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing propagation material sold or distributed. Furthermore, where such exploitation involves the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of propagating material, the Authority may direct the infringer relating plaintiff forthwith to provide full disclosure of all records pertaining to sales, distribution channels, and financial transactions associated with the infringing activity. Failure to comply with this direction shall attract a further penalty not exceeding one million rupees. The Central Government may also issue recovery certificates for outstanding dues under this Act.

Where a Plant Variety Protection Committee determines that a farmer has suffered loss due to the failure of a protected plant variety, attributable to factors including but not limited to unforeseen pest infestation or climatic conditions, and such determination is upheld on appeal before the Appellate Board, the Committee shall order the deposit of compensation into a designated “compensation deposited gene” account. This sum shall be equivalent to the demonstrable financial detriment incurred by the farmer, subject to a maximum limit as may be prescribed by notification under this Act. The breeder or registered owner shall have the right to challenge the assessment of loss and the amount ordered for deposit before the Appellate Board, providing evidence supporting their contention. Provisions relating to the disbursement of funds from such account shall be governed by regulations framed by the Central Government.

The Authority shall establish a comprehensive scheme under this Act relating to the grant of compulsory licenses for plant varieties, subject to the provisions herein. This scheme shall define the categories of applicants eligible to apply for such licenses, prioritizing those engaged in research and development aimed at improving nutritional value or disease resistance in locally adapted cultivars. The criteria for determining reasonable remuneration to the variety holder shall be clearly outlined within the scheme, considering factors like sales volume and research investment. Further, the scheme may specify procedures for addressing disputes arising from applications under this Act concerning the section 41 scheme.

An application for registration under this Act shall include a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and expression potential. The Registrar may require submission of documentation verifying the distinctiveness of the variety, such as data from field trials or molecular marker analysis. Further, an applicant seeking protection through the section 41 scheme must demonstrate that the variety has been developed using methods permissible under this Act, including traditional breeding techniques and genetic engineering approved by the designated authority. The Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections to the proposed registration, allowing interested parties to raise concerns regarding novelty or compliance with provisions relating to farmers’ rights as provided herein.

Where a plant variety is deemed an essentially derived variety under this Act, and a dispute arises concerning whether it fulfills the conditions outlined in the section 41 scheme relating to prior art disclosure, the Authority shall conduct an inquiry. The claimant asserting derivation shall bear the onus of demonstrating that the variety does not infringe upon any existing rights or previously disclosed information as per the established protocols within the said scheme. Any party aggrieved by the findings of the Authority may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, submitting detailed grounds for challenge and supporting documentation. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further judicial review on a limited ground.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed statement specifying the essential derived characteristics relevant to distinguishing it from other varieties and demonstrating novelty as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish documentation substantiating the stability of these characteristics across successive generations, particularly concerning traits impacting yield or disease resistance. For claims purposes relating to farmers' rights, the application must clearly delineate any contributions made by traditional agricultural practices or indigenous knowledge in the development of the variety. Further, the application shall identify all locations where propagation material has been cultivated for assessment and verification. The Authority may require additional data regarding genetic composition if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board relating to the revocation of protection, or the imposition of conditions on the grant of protection, may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellate court shall have the same jurisdiction as it would have in respect of original suits under this Act and may entertain appeals against orders concerning claims purposes, including but not limited to disputes regarding essential derivation or farmer’s rights. Provided that, where an appeal is preferred, the Board's order shall remain suspended unless the High Court directs otherwise. The appellant shall be liable to compensate any respondent for costs incurred in defending the appeal if the appeal is found to be frivolous or vexatious. Further, a party may apply to the appellate court for interim relief pending disposal of the appeal, subject to such terms and conditions as the court deems fit.

Applications filed under this Act for compulsory licensing shall be examined by the Authority constituted as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish with the application a statement detailing the reasons which compel the grant of such license, including particulars regarding non-availability of the plant variety and its essential characteristics. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that the proposed use is primarily for domestic consumption and addresses unmet needs within India.

The Authority may require the applicant to provide additional information or clarification concerning the claims purposes articulated in the application. Any interested party, including the registered holder of the plant variety concerned, shall be afforded an opportunity to present their objections or counter-arguments during the inquiry process. The decision of the Authority regarding the grant or refusal of a compulsory license shall be final and binding, subject to appeal under this Act.

An application for compulsory licensing under this Act shall be deemed admissible only if it demonstrates that the plant variety in question has been marketed in India for a period exceeding three years from the date of grant of protection. Provided that, where the holder of the rights has failed to satisfy the requirements of clause (b) of section 29 concerning accessibility and affordability of seeds or planting material, the application may be considered even if the marketing period is less than three years. The Authority shall, while determining eligibility for claims purposes, take into account whether reasonable steps have been taken by the rights holder to ensure widespread cultivation of the variety across diverse agro-climatic zones within India. Further, any applicant seeking a compulsory license must satisfy the conditions as provided herein regarding financial capacity and technical expertise.

Any person found to have made a false claim regarding the novelty or distinctiveness of a plant variety during the process of seeking protection under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Such penalties may be imposed by the Authority, after due inquiry and affording the accused an opportunity for being heard. Further, any individual who obstructs or attempts to obstruct the proper functioning of the Authority in assessing claims purposes relating to plant variety registration is deemed guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or both. The Authority shall have the power to issue warrants and summon witnesses as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a Plant Breeder who has obtained protection under this Act shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the protected plant variety. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover all or any of the rights conferred by the registration, including rights pertaining to seed production, propagation material sales, and importation. The terms and conditions of any license granted shall be recorded in writing and filed with the Plant Variety Registration Office. Assignment of protected plant variety rights is permissible, provided that such assignment includes a detailed description of the licensed activities and territorial scope. For claims purposes relating to infringement actions, the licensee shall be deemed to act on behalf of the assignor unless otherwise notified in writing. Any transfer or sub-license granted without prior consent from the Plant Variety Registration Office shall be void.

Where an application for compulsory licensing is filed under this Act, the Examining Authority shall determine whether the claimed use of the plant variety constitutes a substantial and necessary purpose. The applicant bears the burden of demonstrating that the asserted need aligns with the criteria as provided herein, particularly concerning public interest and equitable access to seeds. Any dispute regarding the validity of such claims purposes may be referred to an Appellate Board constituted under this Act. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to a further appeal to the High Court on grounds limited to questions of law pertaining to the interpretation of this Act or any rules made thereunder. The Authority may require additional evidence to substantiate the applicant's assertions and assess potential impacts on registered breeders.

Where a plant variety is subject to an infringement action under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedies including, but not limited to, injunctive relief and damages. Claims purposes relating to the unauthorized exploitation of registered varieties are governed by principles of equity and fairness as provided herein. The Authority may, upon application by any person demonstrating substantial dependence on the variety in question for their livelihood, grant a compulsory licence permitting production or sale of the protected plant variety subject to terms determined by the Authority. Such determination shall consider factors including the reasonable compensation payable to the registered holder and the extent of dependency demonstrated by the applicant.
