The term "invention" includes any process, product or substance comprising one or more steps, and may relate to an existing invention where improvements are made.

Where a patent granted new has been duly and legally assigned under this Act, the assignee shall be entitled to exercise all powers and privileges that were vested in the assignor immediately prior to the assignment. Any infringement of such patent shall constitute an infringement against the assignee with the same force and effect as if the patent had originally been granted in their name. The aggrieved party may institute proceedings for remedy under this Act, seeking either damages or an injunction, or both, subject to the provisions relating to limitation periods. Further, where a counterclaim is filed alleging invalidity of the patent, the assignee shall have the right to defend such claim and present evidence rebutting the allegations. It is provided that any agreement related to assignment must be in writing and duly registered with the Controller.

An application for a patent granted new may be made to the Controller by any person claiming to be the inventor of the invention. Such an application shall contain particulars specifying the subject matter of the invention, including details regarding its utility and novelty, accompanied by full disclosure sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art or technology to fabricate or reproduce the said invention without undue experimentation. The applicant shall also furnish a declaration as to inventorship, confirming that they are the true and first inventor. Where an application relates to more than one invention, each such invention must be clearly defined; however, the Controller may allow the inclusion of inventions dependent upon or arising from those already claimed, provided that such additions do not substantially alter the scope of the original subject matter as originally disclosed under this Act.

Where an application for a patent granted new has been filed and examined, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed formalities, grant letters patent if he is satisfied that the invention relates to a process for the manufacture of a substance intended for use as or in a pharmaceutical product. Such grant shall be conditional upon the applicant furnishing within six months a working document detailing the scale of production and demonstrating commercial viability, as determined by the Controller. Provided that, where the invention concerns a method of medical treatment, the applicant must also submit clinical trial data conforming to guidelines issued under this Act. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the patent liable for revocation following due process.

Any patent granted new and relating to a process for manufacturing an active pharmaceutical ingredient shall be subject to compulsory licensing under this Act if, following its grant, it is determined that the invention is not available to the public at a reasonable price. The Controller may initiate such determination upon receiving a complaint from any person demonstrating substantial impediment to access. Failure by the patentee to comply with directions issued concerning pricing or availability, as provided herein, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees, which may be extended to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any infringing activity arising from such non-compliance is actionable under the relevant provisions.

Where a patent granted new for an invention relates to a process for producing a substance applied in or used for manufacturing a pharmaceutical product, the patent holder shall be obligated to grant a non-exclusive license to manufacture and sell such product within India. This obligation applies provided that no domestic manufacturer has previously engaged in commercial production of that substance or similar substances. The terms of such licenses may be determined by agreement between the parties; however, where an agreement cannot be reached, the Controller shall determine a royalty rate deemed reasonable under this Act. Any assignment of the patent shall include provisions ensuring continued compliance with these licensing obligations. Further, sub-licensees are bound to adhere to the same conditions as the primary licensee and may not impose terms unduly restrictive on downstream users.

Where an application for a patent granted new has been rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Such appeal shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall hear parties de novo and may allow the appeal if it is satisfied that the rejection was unwarranted or based on an erroneous interpretation of the law, provided that the applicant demonstrates a substantial merit in their claim. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Appellate Board under this Act may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to the provisions regarding costs as determined by the Board.

Where an application for a patent granted new has been examined and found to be in order, the Controller may direct that the invention be advertised in the Patent Journal. Such advertisement shall include particulars specified by the Controller, including but not limited to the applicant’s name, title of the invention, and claims as filed. Any person considering themselves aggrieved by the grant of a patent under this Act may within sixty days from the date of such advertisement file grounds of opposition with the Controller. The Controller shall, upon receiving an objection, constitute an adjudicating officer who will hear evidence and arguments presented by all parties concerned. An order adjudicating officer’s decision is final subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where a patent granted new for an invention relates to a process for producing a substance controlled under narcotics legislation, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, issue directions regarding the conditions under which such patent holder may exercise their rights. Such conditions shall include mandatory reporting of production quantities and destinations of the produced substance to designated government agencies, as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Failure to comply with these conditions constitutes a violation, rendering the patent holder liable for penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall decide, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating substantial prejudice due to non-compliance, whether further remedial action is warranted, including suspension of patent rights until compliance is achieved.

Where an application for a patent granted new has been examined and found to be in order, the Controller shall publish a notification indicating the acceptance of the patent. Such notification shall specify the invention claimed, the applicant’s name and address, and the date on which the patent is deemed to have been applied for. Any person aggrieved by such acceptance may, within sixty days from the date of publication, file notice of objection with the Controller, setting forth the grounds upon which they rely. The Controller shall consider any objections received and provide an opportunity for the applicant to respond in writing. Registered user shall be entitled to submit their views regarding the patent’s impact on their existing practices. Following due consideration, the Controller may proceed to grant the patent or reject the application entirely, as provided herein.

Where a patent granted new has been duly advertised in accordance with the prescribed procedures and the requisite fees have been remitted, the Controller shall proceed to consider the application for grant. Subject to compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act, including but not limited to those pertaining to novelty and inventive step, the patent shall be granted upon satisfaction that the invention meets the stipulated criteria. The registered proprietor of such a patent shall be entitled to exercise exclusive rights relating to the invention as defined in the claims appended to the patent document. Provided that any objection raised by a third party during the post-grant opposition period, demonstrating invalidity or non-compliance with this Act, may result in revocation of the patent after due consideration and hearing.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without due cause, and another person, having no connection with the proprietor, applies for registration thereof, the Registrar shall consider whether such application is likely to deceive or cause confusion as to the origin of the goods or services. In determining this likelihood, regard shall be had to all relevant circumstances including, but not limited to, the similarity of the marks and the corresponding wares. The register shall construed liberally in favour of protecting the distinctiveness of registered trade marks against unauthorized use by others. Any proprietor demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from such deceptive use may apply to a court for an injunction restraining the infringing application or subsequent registration. Further, damages may be awarded as provided herein to compensate for losses incurred due to the misleading nature of the competing mark.

Where an application for registration of a mark is refused under this Act, and the applicant appeals against such refusal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the appeal shall be deemed to have been filed within the prescribed time if it is received by post marked with the official postal stamp indicating dispatch on or before the expiry of the period specified in the relevant rules. Further, where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those for which it is registered, such use shall not be deemed to infringe the rights of the proprietor unless the said use is calculated to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. The register shall construed strictly according to the provisions outlined herein and any deviation from these stipulations will render the registration voidable at the discretion of the Trade Marks Registry.

Where a register shall construed to include any document or record maintained electronically by the Trade Marks Registry, any reference therein to a ‘signature’ shall be deemed to include an electronic signature as defined under the Information Technology Act. Any person who knowingly makes a false statement in any application for registration or in any other document submitted under this Act is liable to prosecution and may face imprisonment of up to three years, alongside a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Furthermore, wilful infringement of a registered trade mark, proven through substantial evidence demonstrating consumer confusion, shall attract damages equivalent to five times the loss suffered by the proprietor, or one crore rupees, whichever is higher, subject to judicial discretion.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark desires to grant a license for use of the mark, or assign the entire interest in the registration, an application detailing the proposed terms shall be made to the Trade Marks Registry. Such applications may include provisions relating to quality control measures required during licensed usage, and any geographical limitations on permitted sales. The Registrar shall review such applications and may require further clarification regarding the scope of the license or assignment. A registered trademark, as provided herein, shall not be deemed abandoned solely due to a licensing arrangement, provided that the proprietor continues to exercise control over the mark's use consistent with maintaining its distinctiveness. This register shall construed liberally to ensure fair dealings in trademarks and facilitate commercial innovation.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Trade Marks Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The registrar shall consider any submissions made by the applicant in support of the appeal and may require further information or clarification regarding the distinctiveness of the proposed mark or its potential conflict with existing registrations. Should the registrar, after due consideration and adherence to established principles, find that the trade mark possesses sufficient inherent distinctiveness and does not contravene provisions relating to deceptively similar marks, the application shall be processed accordingly. The register shall construed in a manner consistent with promoting fair competition and protecting consumer interests, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a safeguards prescribed register shall be maintained by the Registrar of Trade Marks, detailing specific measures implemented to protect entries recorded therein. This register shall include particulars relating to any rectification proceedings initiated under this Act, including details of applications for removal of entries based on non-use or other grounds as provided herein. The information contained within the safeguards prescribed register is deemed confidential and access thereto shall be restricted to authorized personnel only. Any alteration or addition to an entry in the main Register shall necessitate a corresponding notation within the safeguards prescribed register, ensuring transparency and accountability.

The Register of Registered Trade Marks maintained by the Registrar shall contain particulars of each mark as specified in the application for registration, including representations of the mark and any accompanying claim. Any alteration to a registered trade marks details, whether relating to ownership, goods or services, or the representation itself, must be recorded within the safeguards prescribed register. The Registrar may, upon receipt of a duly verified request from an interested party, correct errors or omissions in the Register; however, such corrections shall not affect existing rights under this Act. Further, any notation concerning rectification proceedings or opposition to registration will also be maintained as part of the public record. This ensures transparency and facilitates verification of ownership and usage details for all registered marks.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to restrain the use in India of any mark identical or deceptively similar to the registered trademark in connection with goods or services for which the registration is effective, provided that such use constitutes infringement under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the safeguards prescribed register relating to a trade mark may, subject to conditions as provided herein, apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification of that entry. The Board shall have power to entertain and determine appeals against orders made by the Registrar concerning entries on the safeguards prescribed register. Further, any order of the Appellate Board may be appealed to the High Court within a time limit specified under this Act. Failure to comply with an injunction granted pursuant to these provisions shall render the defaulter liable for damages.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for rectification of a trademark appearing on the safeguards prescribed register, direct that the matter be referred to an intellectual property specialist for investigation. Such specialist shall submit a report within sixty days detailing findings regarding the alleged infringement or deceptive use claimed in the application. The Registrar shall consider this report alongside any counter-submissions filed by the registered proprietor. If, after due consideration, the Registrar finds merit in the rectification sought, notice of intention to remove the trademark from the safeguards prescribed register shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal and on the Registry’s website. Objections received within thirty days of such publication may be considered before a final determination is made under this Act. The Registrar's decision regarding any application for rectification shall be final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

The Register of Registered Trade Marks maintained by the Registrar shall contain particulars as prescribed under this Act relating to each trademark’s registration date, proprietor details, goods or services for which it is registered, and any licensed users. Any alteration to a registered trade mark's specifications, including changes in ownership or the description of associated goods, shall be recorded promptly upon verification by the Registrar. The safeguards prescribed register shall be open to public inspection during specified hours, subject to applicable regulations regarding confidentiality of sensitive commercial information. Applications for rectification of entries on the Register may be filed with the Registrar, and such applications shall be processed according to procedures as provided herein. Any appeal against a decision concerning an entry on the safeguards prescribed register lies before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the safeguards prescribed register relating to a trademark may, within sixty days from the date of such entry’s publication in the Trade Marks Journal, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be on grounds that the entry is manifestly unjust or has been procured through fraud or misrepresentation. Failure to comply with this time limit shall permanently preclude any challenge under this Act. The Tribunal may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, order rectification of the register, including removal of entries or modification of conditions. Any party failing to adhere to orders issued by the Tribunal shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and further subject to costs as determined by the Tribunal.

The proprietor of a registered trademark may grant a license to use the mark subject to terms and conditions recorded in the safeguards prescribed register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The Registrar shall record such notification as part of the safeguards prescribed register, creating a publicly accessible record of ownership transfer. Further, where a trademark has been assigned, the assignee may subsequently grant further licenses consistent with the original terms and conditions registered under this Act. Any alteration to the licensed scope or permitted geographical area requires prior approval from the Registrar and subsequent recording in the safeguards prescribed register. Failure to notify assignments or alterations shall render the license unenforceable against third parties.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person aggrieved by the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, direct the hearing of the matter before an intellectual property officer. Such officer shall record evidence both oral and documentary, and determine whether the grounds for opposition are substantiated to the requisite legal standard. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the intellectual property officer may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days from the date of that decision. The safeguards prescribed register shall be maintained accurately reflecting all such decisions and appeals, ensuring transparency in the registration process and providing a clear record for future disputes concerning ownership or use of trade marks as provided herein.

The safeguards prescribed register maintained under this Act shall denote a publicly accessible record documenting entries relating to trademarks, including but not limited to applications for registration, acceptance thereof, opposition proceedings, and any subsequent amendments or modifications. The date patent, as it pertains to the determination of prior use and entitlement in cases of conflicting marks, is deemed the date on which documentary evidence establishing such use is formally submitted to the Trade Marks Registry. Any alteration to entries within the safeguards prescribed register shall be made only by authorized officers and accompanied by a clear indication of the amendment and the date upon which it took effect, as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a representation from any person aggrieved by an entry in the safeguards prescribed register, direct that the matter be investigated. Such investigation shall include notice to the proprietor of the trade mark concerned and opportunity for both parties to submit evidence. If, following such investigation, the Registrar finds that the entry is erroneous or prejudicial to the interests of other registered users, including those providing services under a related trade mark, the Registrar may rectify the register. Any person whose rights have been adversely affected by an incorrect entry in the safeguards prescribed register shall be entitled to seek redress through appropriate legal proceedings, subject to any limitations provided herein regarding timelines for filing such claims. The Registrar’s decision on rectification is final and binding, but appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days.

The Registrar shall maintain a Register of Registered Designs, electronically or in physical form as he deems appropriate, detailing particulars of each design registered under this Act. The register shall include the name and address of the proprietor, the class to which the design relates, the date of registration, and any modifications made subsequent thereto. Any person may inspect the Register upon payment of such fees as may be prescribed. Applications for rectification of entries in the Register concerning validity or ownership may be filed with the Registrar, subject to provisions regarding timelines and supporting documentation. The Registrar shall consider all applications received and record his decisions on the Register, providing reasons for any refusal or modification. Further, the registrar register shall be open to public search during specified hours.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all designs recorded under this Act. This register shall be deemed a public document and accessible for inspection during office hours, subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by the Registry to prevent undue interference with its operations. Applications for registration of designs shall be examined in accordance with prescribed procedures, and particulars relating to each application, including representations, claims, and correspondence, shall be meticulously recorded within the register. The Registrar may require applicants to furnish further information or clarification as deemed necessary for a thorough assessment. Any alteration to the status of a registered design, whether through amendment, renewal, or cancellation, must be accurately reflected in the register. Furthermore, the registrar register shall include details pertaining to any licensed users and the terms governing such licenses, ensuring transparency and facilitating informed decision-making by interested parties.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all designs recorded under this Act. The register shall include particulars relating to each design, namely, the name and address of the proprietor claiming priority, the date of application for registration, the class of goods or services associated with the design, and any modifications made during examination. Any alteration to these particulars must be notified to the Registrar in writing, subject to verification by the examining officer. The registrar register shall be open to public inspection during office hours, provided that a fee as prescribed may be levied for copies thereof. Further, information pertaining to pending applications shall not be accessible unless specifically authorized under this Act or with the consent of the applicant.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all designs recorded under this Act. Any application for design registration that is found to be substantially identical or deceptively similar to an existing registered design, or one applied for with prior claim, shall be rejected outright; the applicant shall not receive notification of such rejection beyond a single communication outlining grounds for refusal. Failure by the Registrar to promptly update the register following any alteration in ownership or status of a registered design will render them liable to penalties as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The registrar register shall be open to public inspection during specified hours, subject to reasonable regulations promulgated by the Controller.

The Registrar shall maintain a register detailing assignments and licenses granted in relation to registered trademarks under this Act. Any proprietor desiring to assign their exclusive right to use a trademark or grant a license, whether absolute or subject to certain conditions, shall file with the Registrar a formal instrument specifying the details of the assignment or license agreement. Such instruments must clearly identify the assigned mark, the assignor and assignee, or the licensor and licensee, respectively, along with the territorial extent of the transfer. The registrar register shall be updated accordingly within thirty days of receipt of the properly executed document, provided that the Registrar may request further clarification if deemed necessary. Any subsequent assignment of a trademark already subject to an earlier assignment or license shall also be recorded in like manner.

A trademark shall be eligible for registration under this Act if it is used in relation to the specified goods or services. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating such use prior to acceptance of the application, particularly where the mark has not been previously registered. Where a proposed mark is deemed descriptive of the character or quality of the *mark registered goods*, registration shall be refused unless the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use over a significant period. This requirement applies irrespective of any prior publication or advertising undertaken by the applicant. Further, an application may be opposed by interested parties claiming rights in earlier marks, provided that such opposition is filed within the prescribed timeframe as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be refused if the marks applied for are identical to marks already registered under this Act in relation to identical goods or services. Where an objection is taken on the ground that the proposed mark is confusingly similar to an earlier mark registered in respect of dissimilar goods, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion. The Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier mark before making a determination. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this Act relating to the refusal or acceptance of registration of a mark registered goods may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The appellate board’s decision shall be final and binding.

The proprietor of a mark registered for goods may grant licenses permitting the use of the mark in relation to those registered goods, subject to conditions specified in the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any partial assignment is accompanied by an undertaking from the assignee regarding continued adherence to the original licensing terms. Where a proprietor seeks to assign the entire registration relating to marks registered for goods, consent of the Registrar may be required if the proposed assignee does not possess experience in manufacturing, trading, or providing services related to the goods specified within the mark registration. The license agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use and geographical limitations applicable to the mark registered goods. Any alteration to the licensed activities requires prior written approval from the original proprietor.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed mark for particular goods, or by the acceptance of a registered mark as identical or similar to an earlier mark used in relation to those goods, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. It is provided that registration of a mark for goods shall not be refused solely upon the basis of prior use unless such use demonstrably affects the distinctiveness of the mark registered goods.

A trademark shall be deemed to be a *mark registered different* from another trademark if, upon examination under this Act, it does not contain identical elements to the earlier mark, and the goods or services for which registration is sought are not so closely related as to create an impression of connection between the two. For the purposes of determining similarity, consideration shall be given to the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the marks. The Registrar may require proof that consumers recognize the trademarks as originating from different sources, even if some degree of resemblance exists. Provided that this determination is made without regard to any subsequent alteration or addition to either mark.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no trademark shall be registered if it is identical to a mark already registered under this Act in relation to identical goods or services. Where a mark applied for is similar to a mark already registered and the goods or services are identical or closely related, the Registrar may refuse registration unless he considers that the subsequent user of the trade mark is unlikely to cause confusion among the public. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The remedies available in such an appeal shall include seeking registration, subject to compliance with all applicable requirements as provided herein. Further, damages for infringement of a mark registered different from another are recoverable as determined by the relevant court.

Where an application for registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal by the applicant. The Board shall give notice to all parties who appeared in the proceedings before the Registrar and afford them an opportunity of being heard. If the mark applied for is a *mark registered different* from a previously registered trade mark, the Appellate Board shall consider whether use of the applied-for mark would constitute passing off or otherwise infringe any right conferred by registration under this Act. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within a further period of sixty days.

No trade mark shall be registered if it is deemed identical or confusingly similar to a *mark registered different* from the applicant’s in relation to goods or services. Where an objection is raised under this Act based upon such similarity, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate clear distinction between the marks and provide evidence of consumer understanding that prevents any likelihood of confusion. Failure to satisfy the Registrar shall result in rejection of the application. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark aggrieved by the registration of a *mark registered different* may institute proceedings for damages and an injunction, subject to demonstrating actual or potential damage arising from the infringing use as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered mark may be licensed under a written agreement specifying the scope of use permitted. Such license shall not extend beyond the geographical territory in which the proprietor exercises rights relating to the mark, unless expressly agreed otherwise. The licensee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations applicable to the registered mark as held by the proprietor. Assignment of a registered mark, or any part thereof, including associated goodwill, requires registration with the Registrar, accompanied by prescribed fees. Where a mark registered different from another is assigned, the assignee’s rights shall be subject to any existing licenses granted prior to such assignment; these pre-existing licensees retain their entitlements as provided herein. The proprietor may reserve specific rights relating to quality control and enforcement against unauthorized use, even within licensed territories.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the rectification of a registered trademark believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal from that order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellate board shall consider whether the Registrar’s decision adequately addressed evidence presented concerning the distinctiveness of the mark registered differently and its potential impact on consumers familiar with prior usage. It shall be open to the appellant to demonstrate a material error in the assessment of likelihood of confusion, or that relevant considerations were improperly weighed. Subject to just cause shown, appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed identical or confusingly similar to a mark already registered under this Act, subject to provisions regarding honest descriptive use. Where a proprietor demonstrates that a patented process is intrinsically linked to the distinctive character and reputation of their registered mark, any unauthorized use thereof by another party shall constitute infringement. Such infringement carries a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as damages for loss suffered by the trademark owner. Further, repeat offenders may face imprisonment extending up to three years, without prejudice to criminal proceedings under other applicable laws. The Registrar may order seizure of infringing goods and materials of any kind used in connection with the mark registered different.

A registered trade mark may be licensed under this Act subject to the terms and conditions agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such license shall clearly define the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to use the mark, as well as the specific goods or services relating to that mark. The proprietor retains ultimate ownership of the mark and may revoke the license if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation of the trade mark. Assignment of a registered trade mark, including any associated licenses, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, who shall consider whether such assignment prejudices existing licensees. Where a mark registered different from another is involved, careful consideration will be given to ensuring continued protection for all parties concerned, maintaining trade mark identity and preventing unfair competition.

A trademark shall be deemed similar if it gives rise to a general impression of resemblance between two marks, irrespective of any minor differences in appearance, sound, or connotation. Similarity is assessed considering the overall visual, phonetic, and conceptual impact on the relevant consumer base. The assessment of trade mark similarity under this Act shall take into account factors such as the distinctiveness of the earlier mark, the degree of overlap in goods or services specified, and any established channels of trade. Provided that a mark consisting exclusively of descriptive terms relating to the characteristics of the goods or services shall not be considered similar unless it has acquired secondary meaning through extensive use.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, or refusing or revoking registration, may appeal from such order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall allow such appeal only if it is satisfied that the original decision was erroneous in law or fact. In determining whether there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, regard shall be had to the similarity between the marks, taking into account not merely the appearance thereof but also their phonetic and conceptual components. The assessment of trade mark similarity shall consider all relevant surrounding circumstances, including the nature of the goods or services and the state of mind of the average consumer purchasing those goods or services. Any proprietor demonstrating such confusion has arisen may seek an injunction under this Act.

Where any application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act upon the ground of similarity with a previously registered trade mark, the Hearing Officer shall direct both the applicant and the opponent to submit their respective pleadings and evidence within such time as may be specified in the directions. The determination of trade mark similarity shall involve an assessment considering not only the visual appearance and phonetic resemblance of the signs but also the conceptual meaning conveyed by them. Any comparison undertaken shall take into account the goods or services for which each trade mark is used or proposed to be used, as well as the conditions of use in the market. The Hearing Officer may require expert testimony regarding consumer perception and recognition. Provided that, if the opponent fails to appear at the hearing, the application may proceed ex parte.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed deceptively similar to a prior existing mark. The determination of trade mark similarity shall consider not only the visual appearance and phonetic rendition of the marks but also their conceptual meaning and overall impression upon the relevant consuming public. Where such deceptive similarity exists, and the goods or services associated with both marks are identical or closely related, an injunction may be issued preventing the applicant from using the infringing mark. Any party aggrieved by the registration of a deceptively similar trademark shall have standing to apply for redress under this Act, subject to demonstrating actual damage resulting from the infringement. Penalties for wilful violation shall include substantial monetary fines and potential imprisonment.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person owning a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark, including the right to assign the benefit of that registration, provided that the terms and conditions of such license or assignment are documented in writing. Where a license is granted permitting the use of a trade mark, the licensee shall be bound by all obligations imposed upon the proprietor under this Act. Furthermore, any subsequent assignee of a registered trade mark shall inherit all existing licenses attached to said registration, subject to their original terms and conditions. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of such assignments or licenses before acknowledging them in the Register of Trade Marks. Consideration must be given to trade mark similarity when evaluating potential conflicts arising from licensed usage or assignment.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the similarity of a proposed trade mark to an existing one, the Registrar shall consider all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the signs. The determination of trade mark similarity shall be undertaken with due regard for the nature of the goods or services intended to be covered by each trade mark, as well as the likely behaviour of the average consumer purchasing such goods or services. An appeal against a decision of the Registrar regarding this matter may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the appellant shall demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the Registrar’s finding.

A trademark shall be deemed similar if it gives rise to a deceptive or confusing effect upon the mind of the public, considering the overall impression left by the marks in relation to the goods or services for which they are used. The assessment of trade mark similarity shall take into account, but not be limited to, the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the signs. Where an application for renewal of a registered trademark is filed after the expiration of the registration period, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating continued use of the mark in India during the preceding five years, provided that such non-use does not preclude assessment of similarity with subsequently applied marks. Any objection based on trade mark similarity must be substantiated by documentary proof and expert testimony as deemed appropriate by the Registrar.

No trademark shall be registered if it is deemed deceptively similar to a prior registered trademark under this Act. The determination of such similarity shall consider not only the visual appearance and phonetic rendition of the marks but also their overall impression of novelty and distinctiveness. Where an infringement action arises from use of a mark found to possess trade mark similarity, the proprietor of the earlier mark may seek injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct consequence of the infringing activity. Further, any assignment of rights in a trademark shall be deemed invalid if it facilitates or perpetuates such deceptive similarity and constitutes an attempt to circumvent this provision.

Where an objection is taken under this Act regarding the similarity of a proposed trade mark to any existing mark, the Registrar shall consider not only the visual appearance and phonetic resemblance of the signs but also their conceptual meaning as perceived by the relevant consumer base. This assessment shall account for the nature of the goods or services associated with both marks; specifically, in cases involving semiconductor devices or related technologies, a higher degree of distinctiveness may be required to avoid findings of trade mark similarity. The applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that any such conceptual difference negates the likelihood of confusion. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be recognised as distinctive if it is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. An application for registration may be refused if the proposed trade mark is deemed descriptive of the characteristics of the goods or services for which it seeks registration, but such refusal may be overridden where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall consider evidence submitted by the applicant relating to advertising expenditure, sales figures, market surveys, and length of consistent use in establishing this acquired distinctiveness. Further, a trade mark recognised as distinctive is entitled to protection against unfair competition and passing off.

A proprietor of a trade mark recognised under this Act may grant a license to use the trade mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which such use is permitted and the geographical area covered by the license. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to any conditions stipulated therein. Where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee shall be entitled to exercise all rights and powers of the assignor relating to the licensed use of the trade mark, including the right to grant further sub-licenses as provided herein. Any alteration to the scope or duration of a license requires prior written consent from both the proprietor and the licensee, unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. The proprietor shall retain ultimate control over the quality standards associated with goods or services bearing the licensed trade mark, and may revoke any license if those standards are not maintained.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark registered under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating distinctive character acquired through use subsequent to the date of first use. Such evidence shall be assessed in relation to the goods or services for which registration is sought and those specified in the earlier trade mark. The Appellate Board may allow an appeal against a decision declining to accept such evidence, provided that the appellant demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the Registrar's assessment regarding acquired distinctiveness. A trade mark recognised as having reputation prior to any use by the applicant shall be afforded due consideration during this process.

Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier trade mark recognised under this Act, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier trade mark with an opportunity for written submissions. Such submissions may include evidence demonstrating use or reputation acquired by either trade mark. The Registrar may, after considering these submissions and any counter-submissions filed, direct that the inspection register be made available to both parties for a period not exceeding thirty days, enabling them to ascertain relevant entries. Any party aggrieved by such direction or subsequent decision of the Registrar concerning the conflicting marks may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

A proprietor shall be entitled to relief against any person infringing a trade mark recognised under this Act, including an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and an account of profits made as a result of the infringement. Where damages have been awarded under this Act, the amount so awarded shall not exceed five times the actual damages or loss suffered by the proprietor, whichever is greater. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person alleging that another has engaged in unfair competition involving the use of a trade mark without due cause, issue an order directing the cessation of such practices and requiring restitution for losses incurred. Commercial exploitation of a registered trade mark shall not be permitted where it creates confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of goods or services.

For the purposes of this Act, a “mark” includes any sign, symbol, device, lettering, numerals, shape, configuration, colour or combination thereof adopted for distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and used or proposed to be used under this *mark registration act* in relation to such goods or services. A mark shall be capable of being registered even if it has not prior use in trade; provided that the Registrar may require evidence of distinctiveness by way of acquired reputation before registration is granted, particularly where the mark describes those goods or services, or gives a quality indication thereof. Any representation of a mark which is disclaimed from protection under this Act shall be noted accordingly on the register.

An applicant seeking a mark registration act shall furnish particulars of such marks as are being used by him and shall state the goods or services in relation to which he proposes to use the mark. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information concerning the period during which the mark has been in use, and the geographical areas where such use occurs. Where an application for a mark registration act relates to a composite mark consisting of words and figurative elements, the representation of each element shall be clearly delineated within the application form. Any alteration made to the proposed mark after its initial submission is subject to approval by the Registrar, who may request additional documentation substantiating the continued distinctiveness of the mark as presented.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no mark shall be registered if it is identical or confusingly similar to a prior existing mark used by another person in relation to goods or services. The owner of a prior existing mark may apply to the relevant intellectual property authority for an injunction restraining the registration of such mark and preventing its use in commerce. Compensation for damages suffered due to the infringing mark’s use shall be determined based on the lost profits attributable to the infringement, as well as any costs incurred by the plaintiff in bringing the action. The Registrar may order the erasure of a mark registration act if it has not been genuinely used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered within five years from its first registration and no adequate reason exists for non-use. Further remedies are available under this Act, including rectification proceedings to correct errors on the register.

An applicant seeking a mark registration act shall furnish with the application a verified statement affirming exclusive right ownership over the proposed mark. This verification must detail the basis for claim, whether derived from creation, assignment, or inheritance, and be supported by documentary evidence as deemed necessary by the Registrar. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the asserted rights if inconsistencies arise during examination. Furthermore, an applicant shall disclose any prior use of the mark, even if unregistered, specifying dates, geographical locations, and goods/services connected with such use. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements renders the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, as determined by the Court. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction without compensation. The owner of a registered mark may apply to restrain the use of any mark contrary to the provisions herein relating to mark registration act. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall attract penalties as prescribed by law, including daily fines until compliance is achieved.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any registered proprietor of a mark may grant a license to use such mark, specifying the goods or services in relation to which the right to use is granted, and the geographical area covered by such license. Such license shall be assignable along with the registration of the mark, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all conditions and limitations stipulated within the original mark registration act. Further, a licensee may, with prior written consent of the registered proprietor, sub-license the right to use the mark for any of the goods or services specified in the license agreement. Any assignment or sub-licensing shall be recorded in the Register, and such recording shall confer validity upon the assignee’s or sub-licensee's rights as provided herein. The registered proprietor retains ultimate control over the reputation and goodwill associated with the mark.

Where an objection is raised against a proposed mark registration act on the grounds of likelihood of confusion with any existing mark registered under this Act, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier mark with an opportunity for written submissions and oral hearing. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions and hearings, direct that the marks be accepted or refused, or impose limitations on the scope of either registration, provided that such limitations are demonstrably necessary to avoid a likelihood of confusion as assessed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any direction issued by the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

For the purposes of this Act, “carry business india” means engaging in commercial activities within India under any name or style, whether as a sole proprietor, partnership firm, limited liability entity, or otherwise, where such activities are regularly undertaken and represent an identifiable business presence. A person shall be deemed to carry business india if they habitually offer goods or services for sale, advertise those goods or services, or maintain a physical place of business within the territory of India. This definition applies irrespective of whether the principal place of business is located outside of India, provided that such activities are demonstrably linked to and conducted in furtherance of operations within India.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act shall, in the application, clearly indicate whether the trade mark is being used in relation to any goods or services. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark indicating that they *carry business india* in connection with specified goods, they must provide documentary evidence demonstrating continuous use of the mark within India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature and extent of such usage if deemed necessary. Failure to adequately substantiate this claim shall render the application liable for rejection. Any alteration to the goods or services associated with a registered trade mark requires notification to the Registrar, subject to prescribed fees.

An applicant seeking to register a trade mark under this Act shall, in the application, specify whether the trade mark is being used by him or proposed to be used by him. Where an applicant seeks registration indicating that he *carry business india* in relation to goods or services, he must provide documentary evidence demonstrating continuous and substantial use of the trade mark within India for a period not less than six months immediately preceding the date of application, as provided herein. The Registrar may require further clarification or additional documentation regarding such use if deemed necessary. Failure to adequately substantiate this usage shall render the application liable for rejection. Any opposition filed against registration based on non-use must be supported by verifiable evidence demonstrating lack of genuine commercial activity under the trade mark. The applicant shall have the opportunity to respond to any such challenge within the prescribed timeframe.

Where any entity elects to utilize the phrase "carry business india" as a trademark, such use is subject to compliance with all applicable regulations under this Act pertaining to domain name registration and internet protocol address allocation. The Registrar may require submission of documented proof demonstrating continuous and verifiable operational presence within India for a period not less than three years prior to application for trademark registration. Furthermore, any entity employing "carry business india" must maintain publicly accessible contact information, including a registered office address and designated local representative, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these stipulations shall render the applicant ineligible for trademark protection, irrespective of demonstrated commercial intent or investment in promotional materials.

Any individual or corporate entity utilizing the phrase "carry business india" as a trademark, or any confusingly similar variation thereof, to promote commercial activities within the territory of India shall be deemed to be engaging in an act of trade mark infringement under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from a registered proprietor possessing prior rights to an identical or deceptively similar mark, issue a notice requiring the infringing party to cease such usage and submit evidence of compliance with these provisions within thirty days. Failure to comply shall render the infringer liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of profits derived from the unauthorized use, alongside costs incurred by the complainant in pursuing legal remedies as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark desires to grant a license or assign the right to use such trade mark, including the phrase “carry business india”, he shall execute an instrument in writing specifying the scope and duration of the license or assignment. Such instrument may include provisions relating to quality control, permitted geographical areas for operation, and restrictions on the licensed user’s activities. The proprietor shall file a certified copy of the license agreement or assignment deed with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution, as provided herein. Failure to do so will render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the Registrar. Any subsequent transfer of such license or assignment requires prior written consent from the original proprietor and notification to the Registrar, subject to applicable fees.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trademark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice of the Registrar’s decision. The appellant shall state the grounds of appeal and serve a copy thereof on the applicant. Provided that if the objection relates solely to the absolute ground under section 9 concerning deceptiveness, the applicant may, within thirty days of service of the copy of the grounds of appeal, file its written response. It is established that ‘carry business india’ constitutes a descriptive phrase used by the respondent, and any claim to exclusive right therein shall be subject to challenge based on demonstrable lack of acquired distinctiveness.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon their registered trade mark by using, in connection with the sale or advertising of goods or services, a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said trade mark, and such use incorporates the phrase “Carry Business India” prominently within its branding, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. It shall be a defence for the alleged infringer to demonstrate that their use of "Carry Business India" is solely descriptive of the goods or services offered and does not indicate any trade connection with the proprietor. Further, if the geographical indications associated with the goods or services are demonstrably different, the Board may consider this factor in determining likelihood of confusion as provided herein.

No proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act unless he has registered such trade mark, or is the registered user of the trade mark, and any person proposing to carry business india using a name or mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark may be restrained by injunction. Where reprography of works incorporating a registered trade mark occurs without authorization from the proprietor, constituting infringement, the court shall order the cessation of such activity and award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor. Further, any party found guilty of contributory infringement, knowingly supplying goods or services for use in relation to the infringing act, shall be subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may also issue cease and desist orders against entities engaging in deceptive trade practices utilizing similar marks.

An applicant seeking to register a trade mark relating to goods or services used, or proposed to be used, under the name “Carry Business India” shall submit an invention application concurrently with their initial trade mark registration request. This concurrent submission is mandatory where the applicant claims novelty based on a technical process integral to the branding of said goods or services. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this claimed novelty and its direct relevance to the proposed use of “Carry Business India”. Failure to provide such documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the invention application being deemed withdrawn, without prejudice to the trade mark registration proceeding independently. Any alteration to the invention application after initial submission is subject to approval by the Registrar and may impact the overall timeline for both processes as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a mark is advertised under this Act and subsequently accepted by the Registrar, such acceptance shall constitute conclusive evidence against all persons claiming through the applicant until the expiry of the opposition period. Any party aggrieved by an acceptance may institute proceedings to challenge the validity of the acceptance before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines for filing objections following application advertised acceptance will render any subsequent claim invalid and subject the claimant to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall be empowered to impose a monetary fine not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees upon any party found to have wilfully obstructed or hindered the advertisement process.

For the purposes of this Act, “circumstances application advertised” means the period commencing from the date on which notice of acceptance of an application for registration is first published under this Act and concluding thirty days thereafter. During such circumstances application advertised, any person claiming by use as a prior right shall be entitled to file a notice of opposition. The Registrar may, subject to prescribed conditions, extend the duration of the circumstances application advertised where satisfied that representations concerning the trade mark have been made to the public before the date of publication of acceptance. Such extensions shall not exceed sixty days in aggregate.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trade mark under this Act and submits representations demonstrating prior use of the mark within India, the Registrar shall consider such evidence when determining distinctiveness. The Registrar may direct an advertisement of the application for registration to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, particularly where the applied-for mark bears similarity to existing registered marks or pending applications. Such advertisements shall clearly state the trade mark sought to be registered and any relevant disclaimers filed by the applicant. The Registrar shall consider any objections raised during the period specified in the advertisement concerning the circumstances application advertised and its potential impact on consumer confusion, provided that such objections are substantiated with credible evidence of prior use or reputation.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, and subsequent circumstances arise wherein an advertisement relating to the goods or services for which registration subsists is employed by the proprietor in a manner calculated to mislead consumers regarding the nature, quality, or geographical origin of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be predicated on demonstrable evidence that the advertised representation creates confusion amongst potential purchasers. The proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to present counter-evidence demonstrating a lack of such misleading effect. If the tribunal finds that the circumstances application advertised has indeed caused or is likely to cause deception, it may order injunctive relief restricting the continued use of the advertisement and award damages commensurate with the harm suffered by the aggrieved party.

Where an application for registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal such refusal. The Appellate Board may, after affording the applicant and the objector an opportunity of being heard, allow the appeal if it finds that the circumstances surrounding the use or proposed use of the mark demonstrate a likelihood of confusion arising with respect to any registered trade mark or other prior rights. Further, where the Registrar deems it necessary to ascertain such circumstances application advertised in publications, he may direct an inquiry into the matter. The Board shall consider evidence presented regarding consumer perception and market conditions when determining whether grounds for refusal are substantiated.

Where a registered trade mark is held by an individual or body corporate engaged primarily in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, and where such registration was obtained subsequent to the advertisement of prior applications concerning similar marks, the proprietor shall have the power to grant non-exclusive licenses for use of the mark within specific therapeutic areas. Such licenses may be assigned freely subject to conditions stipulated therein regarding quality control and adherence to prevailing regulatory standards. The Registrar may, upon application by a third party demonstrating substantial investment in advertising campaigns utilizing a confusingly similar mark, require disclosure of all licensing agreements related to the registered trade mark. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render such licenses voidable at the discretion of the Registrar, considering the circumstances application advertised and potential consumer confusion.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trade mark under this Act and submits evidence demonstrating prior use or intended use thereof, the Registrar shall consider such circumstances during examination. If the application is deemed acceptable, the Registrar may direct its advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal, subject to any limitations imposed by the provisions herein. Such advertising shall clearly indicate the date from which the applicant claims priority, if applicable. Further, where a trade mark is registered pursuant to a licence means licence granted under this Act, the particulars of such license and the licensee’s rights shall be recorded in the Register. The Registrar may, at any time, require the applicant or registered proprietor to furnish further information relating to the circumstances application advertised.

Where a trade mark is advertised under this Act, and an interested person objects to the registration of such trade mark, the Registrar shall consider the objection and any counter-objections filed by the applicant. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to advertisement shall render the registration liable for cancellation at the instance of any aggrieved party. Any person making a false representation concerning the circumstances application advertised or otherwise misleading the public regarding the availability or registration of a trade mark shall be guilty of an offence and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence of such misrepresentation, initiate proceedings for recovery of damages and costs incurred in connection with the law registration referred.

For the purposes of this Act, "advertised acceptance" means the publication of a notice by the Registrar indicating that an application for registration of a trade mark has been accepted, either absolutely or conditionally. Such advertisement shall include particulars identifying the trade mark and specifying any conditions to which the acceptance is subject. Where an advertised acceptance relates to a proposed trade mark identical or similar to a previously registered trade mark, the notice shall also indicate the earlier trade mark and its proprietor. The Registrar may prescribe the form and manner of such advertisements as provided herein. Any challenge to the acceptance under this Act must be made within the period specified in the advertisement.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and demonstrates that an alleged infringing advertisement contains an express or implied acceptance of offer relating to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, such acceptance shall be deemed material for establishing passing off. The court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the offending advertisement if it finds that the advertised acceptance relates directly to the distinctive character of the registered trade mark and creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Damages, including loss of profits and account of profits, shall be awarded subject to principles of fairness and equity, considering the extent to which the defendant’s conduct has exploited the reputation associated with the registered trade mark.

Where an objection is raised against a trade mark application under this Act and such objection is withdrawn or overruled, the applicant shall file within thirty days of the withdrawal or overruling, a declaration confirming acceptance of the decision. Failure to do so will render the application deemed abandoned. The Registrar shall then proceed as if the original objection had not been raised. Where an advertised acceptance relates to a trade mark that incorporates a geographical indication as defined under another Act, the applicant must provide an affidavit verifying non-use of the term in relation to goods or services not originating from that geographical area. This affidavit is subject to verification by the Registrar and may be challenged by any interested party through submission of evidence. The Registrar shall maintain records of all such affidavits and related correspondence for a period of seven years from the date of registration, if granted.

Where a license is granted under this Act relating to a registered trade mark, the terms of such license shall expressly define the scope of permitted use and geographical territory. Any subsequent assignment or further licensing of the rights conferred by the initial license shall be subject to prior written consent from the original proprietor of the trade mark, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Furthermore, where an advertised acceptance of a trade mark application is made conditional upon specific usage stipulations, any subsequent transfer of ownership or licensing agreement must ensure continued adherence to those conditions. It is clarified that an advertised acceptance relates directly to the obligations undertaken by the applicant and their successors in title concerning the use of the mark. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the license voidable at the proprietor’s discretion.

Where a registered trade mark is held by an individual or body corporate, and such holder desires to grant a license for use of the mark, they shall execute a written instrument specifying the goods or services in relation to which the license extends, the territory within which it operates, and the duration thereof. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. The licensee shall be bound by all conditions limitations registered with respect to the trade mark, and any breach of these conditions shall constitute a material infringement under this Act. Assignment of such licenses requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days; failure to do so renders the assignment void. Further, sub-licensing is permitted only with express written consent from the original licensor, subject to terms agreed between them. The Regis trar may require production of these instruments for inspection as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, following publication under this Act, an objection is raised by any person claiming such right or interest as is specified herein. Such objection must be communicated to the Registrar in writing within the prescribed period, and shall clearly state the grounds upon which it is based. The Registrar shall then serve notice of the objection on the applicant for registration, affording them an opportunity to file a counterstatement. A notice served under this Act shall include the date of service and details of the objecting party. Further, any subsequent communication relating to the application registration notice will be deemed valid if delivered electronically as per regulations.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar receives an objection under this Act within the prescribed period following publication of the acceptance thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, any person intending to oppose may file such notice electronically or in physical form at the designated office, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by regulations. The applicant for registration shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to respond to the objection and submit counterarguments or evidence in support of their application. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to the filing of an application registration notice may render it invalid. Further, any alteration to the proposed trade mark after acceptance requires notification to the Registrar and may necessitate re-examination.

Any proprietor seeking to challenge the acceptance of an application for trade mark registration shall file a written notice of opposition with the Registry within three months of the date such acceptance is advertised under this Act. The notice must specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use or registration of a similar mark in respect of identical or closely related goods or services. Failure to adequately articulate these grounds may result in the Registrar dismissing the opposition as frivolous.

The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice and submit counter-arguments within one month from receipt thereof. Provided that the Registrar deems the opposition to have merit, a hearing shall be convened wherein both parties may present evidence and arguments. The Registrar’s decision on the validity of the application registration notice shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act.

Any proprietor desiring to register a trade mark shall publish a public notice detailing the application and inviting objections under this Act. Such notice must clearly state the goods or services associated with the proposed trade mark and specify the date upon which the application was filed. Failure to comply with prescribed notification procedures regarding an application registration notice will render the registration voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party. Any person demonstrating demonstrable financial loss due to reliance on a deceptively similar unregistered mark, following publication of such a notice, may pursue remedies under civil law and shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the harm suffered. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of fraudulent intent in an application, issue a cautionary notice.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered trade mark owner desiring to grant a license or assign their rights in relation to a registered trade mark may publish a public application registration notice detailing the terms and conditions of such proposed transaction. Such notice shall specify the geographical extent of the license or assignment, the goods or services for which it applies, and the duration thereof. The Registrar shall maintain a register of these notices, accessible for public inspection upon payment of a prescribed fee. Any party intending to challenge the validity of an assignment made pursuant to such a notice may do so within three months from the date of its publication by submitting a written objection to the Registrar. Provided that the registered proprietor ensures compliance with all applicable regulations concerning fair trade practices during any licensing arrangement, as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to provisions regarding frivolous applications, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of publication of the decision in the Trade Marks Journal. The appellant shall specify the grounds upon which the appeal is based and provide all relevant documentation supporting their claim. Failure to comply with these requirements will render the appeal inadmissible. Further, where a notice of opposition has been served on an applicant, and that applicant subsequently seeks registration, the party who initially issued the notice may challenge the validity of any subsequent application registration notice through a counter-statement filed within three months of its publication.
