The Registrar may issue directions for recovery of unpaid sums as arrears of land revenue.

A permitted register trade mark, once assigned under this Act, shall remain subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the assignment deed. Such deeds may specify limitations regarding subsequent licensing or sub-licensing of the registered name associated with the trade mark, provided that any such limitation does not contravene the fundamental principles of fair competition as defined herein. The assignor retains no right to further exploitation of the permitted register trade mark unless explicitly released by the assignee through a written instrument duly executed and filed with the Registrar. Further, an assignee may grant non-exclusive licenses relating to specific geographical territories or product categories, subject to prior notification to the Registrar and approval where such license materially alters the scope of protection afforded under this Act.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of an application for a permitted register trade mark, or directing its removal from the register. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Where the refusal relates to a similarity assessment with a prior patent process application, the Tribunal shall consider evidence pertaining to inventive step and non-obviousness as relevant to the distinctiveness argument. The decision of the Tribunal is final subject to further appeal under this Act.

Where an application has been opposed under this Act, and the Hearing Officer has rendered a decision, any party affected by that decision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall lie on a question of law or fact arising out of the decision of the Hearing Officer. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Further, the Board may direct the Registrar to undertake such actions as it deems necessary to ensure compliance with this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board relating to an application section 71 may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order.

Any person aggrieved by a decision made under this Act relating to an application section 71 may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall only be entertained if the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the impugned order; frivolous or vexatious appeals are strictly prohibited and will incur a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Board may, after affording the respondent an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against. Failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the appeal inadmissible. Any party found to be deliberately obstructing the appellate process faces prosecution under relevant provisions concerning contempt of court.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered draft regulations” means a document submitted by a trade association or consumer protection body proposing standards for goods or services relating to a registered trademark, and which has been formally acknowledged by the Registrar as being under consideration. Such acknowledgement shall constitute registration of the draft regulations, subject to their subsequent approval following public consultation as provided herein. A registered draft regulation binds all producers and providers of relevant goods or services only upon formal notification in the Trade Marks Journal. Any amendment to a registered draft regulation requires re-submission and fresh acknowledgment by the Registrar.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a public record of all registered draft regulations submitted pursuant to applications for trademark certification. An applicant seeking registration of a mark relating to geographical indications may submit, along with their application, proposed draft regulations governing the use and quality control of goods bearing that mark. These registered draft regulations shall be binding on all users of the certified trade mark, subject to any modifications approved by the Registrar. Any alteration to a registered draft regulation requires prior notification to the Registry and subsequent approval following public consultation as provided herein. The applicant shall ensure that the proposed draft regulations are consistent with existing laws relating to consumer protection and fair trade practices. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or revocation of registration.

Where a trade mark is registered subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar, and those conditions are subsequently formalized as registered draft regulations concerning permissible usage or quality standards, any person aggrieved by such registered draft regulations may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of publication of the registered draft regulations in the Trade Marks Journal. Such an appeal may be based on grounds that the conditions are unreasonable, discriminatory, or impose a burden disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon the trade mark proprietor. Failure to comply with any provision contained within the registered draft regulations shall constitute a violation under this Act and render the infringing party liable for damages as determined by the Tribunal. The Registrar may, sua sponte or upon complaint, investigate alleged violations of these registered draft regulations.

The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receipt of a proposed amendment to a registered trade mark, publish notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the amendment and invite objections from any interested person within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be forwarded to the applicant for comment, provided that the Registry may summarily dismiss frivolous or vexatious objections as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar shall consider all submissions made before determining whether to approve the amendment. Where the proposed amendment constitutes a substantial alteration affecting the distinctive character of the registered trade mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to file a fresh application under this Act. Furthermore, any *registered draft regulations* pertaining to trademark usage guidelines are binding on all applicants and registrants.

The Board shall, upon receipt of a proposed amendment to a registered trade mark, verify compliance with the provisions relating to permissible alterations as provided herein. Any such proposed alteration, including changes to colour schemes or stylistic elements, must adhere strictly to guidelines issued by the Controller from time to time and be accompanied by a reasoned justification demonstrating that the amended mark continues to identify the goods or services for which registration is sought. Furthermore, where the amendment incorporates a registered draft regulations pertaining to product specifications, the Board shall require certification from an accredited standards body confirming adherence to those regulations. Failure to provide such certification will result in rejection of the proposed alteration. The Registrar may request further clarification if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the rejection, modification, or acceptance of registered draft regulations published under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Appellate Tribunal shall hear appeals and may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside or modifying any order made by the Registrar. Failure to comply with the provisions regarding public notice prior to implementation of these draft regulations shall render the implementing authority liable for penalties not exceeding ten thousand rupees per day until compliance is achieved. Any false statement made in connection with a registered draft regulation constitutes an offence and is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or both, as provided herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of their registered trade mark. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover all or part of the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall include, unless otherwise specified in the instrument of assignment, any pending applications for registration related thereto. The Registrar may require proof of consent from the grantor of a license prior to recording such license on the register, provided that this requirement does not apply to licenses granted before the commencement of these regulations. Registered draft regulations pertaining to trade mark usage guidelines shall be accessible for public inspection and may be cited in licensing agreements as evidence of permissible practices.

The Trade Marks Act, 1999, provides that any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the approval or rejection of registered draft regulations submitted under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Such an appeal shall be in respect of matters of law and fact pertaining to the compliance with prescribed procedures during the formulation and submission of the draft regulations, as well as concerning the interpretation of any provision relating to their content. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against; provided that any order made by the Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions governing appeals to the Supreme Court.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, be entitled to grant licenses allowing use of the mark upon goods or services as specified in the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof relating to royalties, duration, and territory shall be governed by contractual arrangement between the proprietor and licensee. Where a registered draft regulations pertaining to trade mark usage are proposed, the Registrar may require submission of a detailed plan outlining intended implementation and impact on existing licensees. Any party adversely affected by such draft regulations may file an opposition within the prescribed time limit, detailing grounds for objection based upon undue restriction or prejudice to their contractual rights under previously granted licenses. The Registrar shall consider all oppositions before finalizing the registered draft regulations.

The Trade Marks Act, 1999, provides that any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the acceptance or rejection of a registered draft regulations pertaining to a trade mark shall have recourse to appeal under this Act. Such appeals may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order and must specify the grounds upon which the challenge is based. The appellate authority, while considering such an appeal, shall afford all parties concerned an opportunity for being heard, subject to the proviso that any amendment to the registered draft regulations sought during the appeal process may only be permitted if it does not fundamentally alter the scope of the specification patent addition initially claimed.

For the purposes of this Act, “registered draft regulations” shall mean a set of rules pertaining to the application, acceptance, or maintenance of a trade mark registration, formally submitted to the Registrar and acknowledged as being under consideration by him. Such registered draft regulations shall not alter existing provisions relating to distinctiveness, but may clarify procedural aspects concerning the examination process. Where these regulations propose modifications impacting the assessment of design elements incorporated within a proposed mark, the Registrar shall provide an opportunity for public comment before final determination. Any such regulation remains provisional until formally adopted and published as provided herein.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a public record of all registered draft regulations pertaining to genetically modified organisms, accessible through the official online portal. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark incorporating elements derived from or referencing a gene fund established under national biodiversity legislation shall submit alongside their application a detailed report outlining the source and permissible usage of such genetic material. This report must be certified by an accredited bioethics committee and will form part of the public record. The Registrar may, at any time, require further clarification regarding the applicant’s compliance with relevant regulations concerning intellectual property rights in biological resources, as provided herein. Registration shall be conditional upon adherence to these stipulations.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall include a representation of the mark, which may be in the form of words only, or accompanied by a device or depiction. The Registrar shall examine each such application and, if satisfied that the mark is distinctive in its class and does not conflict with any existing registered trade marks or pending applications, unconditionally registrar shall proceed to accept the same for publication in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, where the applicant seeks registration of a colour as a trademark, they must furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. Any opposition filed under this Act against an accepted mark shall be heard by the relevant intellectual property tribunal, and the Registrar’s decision is subject to appeal.

Upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered trade mark, the Registrar shall promptly acknowledge its receipt to the applicant by post or electronic means. The Registrar may, at his discretion, direct any interested party wishing to oppose the rectification sought to file their response within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such direction. Failure to comply with this directive will render the opposition inadmissible. Where an objection is raised concerning alleged descriptiveness of the trade mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the registered proprietor and unconditionally registrar shall afford both parties an opportunity for written submissions and oral hearings as deemed necessary. The decision regarding rectification shall be communicated in writing to all interested parties, detailing the reasoning behind the determination, and may include orders pertaining to costs incurred during proceedings.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to an application and payment of prescribed fees, unconditionally registrar shall grant a license permitting the use of their trademark by another party where such license specifies the geographical area and range of goods or services covered. This authorization may include provisions for royalty payments to be remitted directly to the proprietor, as determined within the licensing agreement. Provided that any assignment of rights under this license must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by evidence of consent from the original trade mark owner. Further, the Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such licenses and assignments, accessible for inspection upon request. Any alteration to the scope or duration of a granted license requires prior approval from both the proprietor and the licensee, and subsequent notification to the Registrar.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark, or by the Trade Marks Registry, against the acceptance of an application for registration on grounds specified under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file written submissions rebutting such objections. The Registrar shall consider these submissions and the original grounds of objection, and unconditionally registrar shall determine whether the trade mark is distinctive in relation to the goods or services indicated in the application, taking into account any relevant prior use or reputation established under this Act. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision, provided that the appellant deposits with the Board such sum as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, a “distinctive trade mark” means a sign capable of distinguishing goods of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, and shall include any word, name, symbol, device, or combination thereof. The Registrar shall decide whether a proposed trade mark is distinctive, taking into consideration all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the inherent nature of the sign, its established usage in commerce, and consumer perception as provided herein. An application for registration may be refused if the Registrar determines that the mark lacks distinctiveness by reason of being descriptive of the goods or services with which it is associated, subject to any acquired distinctiveness demonstrated through extensive use.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark, accompanied by the requisite fee and containing all particulars as provided herein, shall be examined by the Registrar. The examination shall include verification that the mark does not conflict with any existing registered trade marks or pending applications, and whether it is deceptive or contrary to law. Should any objection arise during this process, the Registrar shall issue a notice of concern to the applicant, affording them an opportunity for response and argument within the prescribed time. Following consideration of such response, the *Registrar shall decide* whether to proceed with registration, refuse the application entirely, or direct amendment of the mark as deemed appropriate. The decision of the Registrar is subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an objection is raised by any person against a proposed trade mark application under this Act, such objector shall have the right to submit written arguments and evidence substantiating their opposition. The applicant may then file a reply addressing the points of objection raised. Following consideration of both the initial objection and the subsequent response from the applicant, the Registrar shall decide whether the grounds for opposition are sufficient to warrant refusal of registration.

Provided that if the Registrar finds merit in the objector’s claims but believes complete refusal would be unduly harsh, they may impose conditions on registration as a remedy. Such conditions might limit the scope of protection afforded by the trade mark or require specific disclaimers. The decision of the Registrar shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property tribunal.

Where an objection is raised by any person against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and opportunity of being heard. Such hearing may be conducted either in writing or orally, as the Registrar deems appropriate, provided that the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable time to submit their response to the objection. The Registrar shall consider all submissions made by the objector and the applicant before proceeding with any decision. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The registrar shall decide on objections relating to similarity between marks, or whether a mark is deceptive or contrary to law, based solely upon the evidence presented and arguments advanced during the hearing process.

An application for rectification of a registered trade mark, presented under this Act, shall contain particulars specifying the alleged error or misrepresentation relied upon. The Registrar shall examine such application and may direct that any document relevant to the determination of the matter be filed within a specified period. Provided that if the applicant fails to comply with such direction, the Registrar may summarily reject the rectification application. Further, where an objection is raised by the registered proprietor in response to the application, the Registrar shall decide whether the grounds for rectification are established and whether any relief should be granted. The decision of the Registrar shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a complaint is received alleging deceptive use of a trade mark, the Registrar shall decide upon examination of the evidence presented by both complainant and respondent, whether such use constitutes a violation under this Act. The Registrar may order the cessation of the infringing activity and direct the erasure or modification of any marks, labels, signs, or advertisements found to be in breach. Failure to comply with an order issued by the Registrar shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Further, repeat offenders may face prosecution under relevant penal codes, subject to judicial discretion and considerations of public interest.

The assignment of a trade mark, or any right accruing thereunder, shall require execution of a formal instrument witnessed as per prevailing practice and registered with the Registrar within thirty days of such assignment. Where an application for registration is assigned prior to its acceptance by the Registrar, the assignee may, subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, apply to have the benefit of the said application transferred to them, providing evidence of the assignment. The Registrar shall decide upon applications for transfer of assignments based on the validity and completeness of the documentation presented. Any license granted in respect of a registered trade mark shall be recorded with the Registrar, detailing the scope and duration of such rights conferred upon the licensee. Provided that any subsequent assignment or further licensing agreement relating to the same trade mark must also be duly recorded as per these provisions.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark, or by the Trade Marks Registry, against the acceptance of an application for registration, such objection shall be referred to the Registrar for determination. The Registrar shall give notice of the hearing to all parties interested and afford them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, both orally and in writing, presenting evidence and arguments as they deem fit. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal against such decision to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; provided that the Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision of the Registrar. The registrar shall decide objections based on principles of natural justice and fairness.

Where an objection is raised by any person, other than the applicant, against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall decide such objection within a period not exceeding six months from the date of receipt thereof. The decision of the Registrar shall be based solely on the evidence submitted and arguments presented by both the applicant and the objector, provided that any evidence pertaining to prior use or reputation of a sign shall be carefully scrutinized. Further, should the Registrar find that the transmission operation of data relating to the objection has been compromised, rendering the integrity of the record uncertain, he may direct a fresh hearing. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal under this Act.

Where an objection is raised by any person, including a consumer group representing interests related to food products, against the acceptance of a proposed trade mark application based on grounds of deceptiveness or misrepresentation concerning the nature, quality, or origin of goods, the Registrar shall decide whether such objection warrants rejection of the application. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence in response to the objection, and any interested party may present counter-arguments as provided herein. A hearing before the Registrar may be convened at the request of either the applicant or the objector, subject to the provisions regarding procedural fairness under this Act. The decision of the Registrar shall be recorded in writing and reasons for the same shall be stated therein. Appeals against such decisions are permissible only to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as per the prescribed procedure.

Where an objection is raised by any person claiming an interest in a trade mark relation against the acceptance of an application for registration, such interested party may file with the Registrar within sixty days of the publication of the said acceptance a notice of opposition specifying the grounds upon which it is founded. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such notice, serve a copy thereof on the applicant and provide them both with an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence in support of their respective positions. Following consideration of all submissions received, the Registrar shall decide whether the trade mark should be registered as applied for or if any modifications are necessary to ensure compliance with this Act. The decision of the Registrar shall be final, subject to appeal under provisions detailed elsewhere herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a petition from any interested party demonstrating substantial and demonstrable prejudice arising directly from a registered trade mark’s use, undertake an assessment of the mark's current configuration. Such assessment shall consider whether the modification unconditionally registrar is warranted in order to safeguard consumer interests and prevent unfair competition. Provided that the petitioner establishes prima facie evidence of misleading similarity with prior marks or generic usage impacting distinctiveness, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring the trade mark proprietor to submit representations within sixty days. Any proposed modification must adhere to guidelines published by the Trade Marks Registry and shall not diminish the inherent protectability of the mark as determined under this Act.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, be permitted to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark unconditionally to another party, provided that such license is recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Any modification unconditionally registrar of a trade mark license agreement, whether relating to territory, duration, or scope of use, shall also require recording in like manner. Failure to record any such license or modification thereof shall render the licensee liable to prosecution for infringement as if they were not authorized to use the mark. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, direct the rectification of the register to reflect accurately the terms and conditions of a recorded trade mark license agreement. Such agreements are assignable alongside the underlying ownership of the registered trade mark, subject to any restrictions specified within the license itself.

Any party dissatisfied with a determination made by the Registrar regarding the rectification of a registered trade mark, or concerning the validity of a user affidavit filed in support of an application for registration, may institute an *appeal high court* within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The High Court shall consider such appeal upon examination of the record and evidence presented before the Registrar. Provided that, if the aggrieved party demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the High Court may condone the delay in preferring the appeal. Further, where an *appeal high court* challenges a finding of likelihood of confusion between trade marks, the appellant must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the decision under challenge. The respondent shall be afforded full opportunity to rebut any arguments presented during the appellate proceedings as provided herein.

Any party dissatisfied with a determination made by the Registrar regarding the rectification of a registered trade mark, or concerning an objection raised during trademark application proceedings, may institute an *appeal high court* within sixty days from the date of communication of that determination. The appeal shall be filed in the High Court exercising jurisdiction over the place where the aggrieved party carries on business, or resides, or has their principal place of establishment. Provided that, if the determination relates to a matter of fact ascertainable by the Registrar, the High Court may dismiss the appeal at the threshold if it finds no material irregularity affecting substantial justice. Further, an appellant shall be required to deposit such fees as are prescribed under this Act before the *appeal high court* will be entertained. The High Court shall hear appeals expeditiously and may pass such orders as it deems just and equitable in the circumstances.

Any party dissatisfied with a determination made by the Registrar concerning the rectification of a registered trade mark, subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements, may institute an *appeal high court* within sixty days from the date of communication of said determination. Provided that, if the aggrieved party demonstrates reasonable cause for delay, the High Court may condone such delay in its discretion. Further, any appeal under this Act shall be filed in the jurisdictional High Court as defined by the relevant geographical boundaries of the trade mark registration. The appellant shall deposit such fees as are prescribed to facilitate processing of the appeal. Failure to comply with these procedural stipulations will render the appeal inadmissible and deemed without merit.

Any proprietor dissatisfied with a determination made by the Registrar regarding rectification proceedings, including claims of dilution or passing off, may institute an *appeal high court* within sixty days from the date of communication of such determination. Provided that, where the determination concerns a refusal to register a trade mark based on acquired distinctiveness, the period for appeal shall be extended to ninety days. Failure to file the appeal within the prescribed timeframe shall render the aggrieved party estopped from challenging the Registrar’s decision further under this Act. The High Court may, subject to just considerations and after affording all parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against; any costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined at the discretion of the court.

An appeal specified under this Act may be filed by any party who, prior to the date of the hearing, has given notice to all other parties concerned, as provided herein. Such an appeal shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which the order is received. The Board may, subject to just considerations and natural justice, entertain appeals arising from orders concerning the rectification of trade marks registers or decisions relating to acquired distinctiveness. An appeal will not be admitted if it does not state the grounds of appeal clearly and concisely. Further, any delay in filing an appeal shall require explanation satisfactory to the Appellate Board.

Any party dissatisfied with a determination made by the Registrar regarding the distinctiveness of a proposed trade mark, or concerning rectification proceedings initiated under this Act, may institute an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the relevant order. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision appealed against. Provided that, if the appellant fails to demonstrate a prima facie case establishing prejudice resulting from the Registrar's determination, the appeal shall be deemed frivolous and dismissed summarily. Further, any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may itself be subject to appeal specified under this Act to the High Court.

An appeal under this Act may be presented to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which the order or decision sought appealed against is communicated to the appellant. The Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal and any party aggrieved by an order of the Board may further appeal to the High Court. Provided that where a question of law arises in relation to any matter dealt with under this Act, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may refer the same to the High Court for determination. The decision of the High Court shall be final.

Where any party considers that a direction issued by the Registrar concerning the rectification of a registered trade mark has been made erroneously, or in excess of jurisdiction, such party may institute an appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. The appeal shall be accompanied by a concise statement of grounds and a certified copy of the order sought appealed against. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the appeal inadmissible.

The Tribunal shall afford all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, including the presentation of evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. Decisions of the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal are subject to further appeal to the High Court under such terms as may be prescribed. The Registrar shall publish notice of any appeal filed and the decision rendered by the Tribunal, as provided herein.

Where a trademark proprietor seeks to appeal an adverse determination regarding the distinctiveness of their mark, they must file a notice of appeal with the relevant Intellectual Property Office within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds upon which the decision is sought appealed and supported by an affidavit verifying the material facts asserted therein. The Intellectual Property Office may, subject to compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein, entertain such appeal. Provided that if the appellant fails to deposit the prescribed fee within fifteen days of filing the notice, the appeal shall be deemed withdrawn. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision on appeal may petition the High Court under this Act.

Any proprietor whose trade mark registration has been revoked, or who believes that another party’s use of a similar mark constitutes detrimental passing off, may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such action shall be predicated upon demonstrable evidence of consumer confusion and resultant financial loss to the proprietor. Where a decision is rendered against the proprietor, they shall have recourse to appeal to the appellate forum established under this Act within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The appellant must demonstrate reasonable grounds for seeking reversal; failure to do so will result in dismissal of the appeal, and imposition of costs reflective of the frivolous nature of the sought appealed action.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark, desiring to facilitate its wider commercial exploitation, grants a license conferring specific rights relating to use and adaptation of the mark, such license may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to conditions prescribed herein. The assignee shall be bound by all terms and limitations initially stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Any attempt to alter the scope of permitted uses without express written consent from the registered proprietor will constitute a breach of contract and render the assignee liable for damages as determined under applicable principles of equity, potentially including penalties as may be prescribed under the Indian Penal Code relating to fraud or misrepresentation. Further, any appeal against a decision concerning the validity of such assignment shall be entertained only if it demonstrates prejudice arising directly from non-compliance with these provisions; otherwise, the sought appealed will be dismissed.

An application for registration of a trade mark, once examined and refused by the Registry, may be subject to an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant shall, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal order, file a written petition particulars contained therein detailing the grounds upon which the sought appealed is based. Such petition must clearly articulate how the trade mark satisfies the requirements for registration as provided herein and addresses any objections raised by the examining officer. Failure to adequately address these objections in the appeal may result in its dismissal. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented, including prior use of the mark, consumer perception, and potential confusion with existing marks.

Where a person supplies or offers to supply goods under a false trade description, that person shall be liable to prosecution and may be subject to civil action by aggrieved parties. Such a false trade description includes the representation that the nature, quality, quantity, origin, or characteristics of those goods correspond to facts which are not so. The remedies available to a consumer demonstrably misled by such a false trade description include damages proportionate to the loss suffered, and an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the deceptive practice. Further, any profits made as a result of employing the misleading trade description goods may be recoverable by the wronged party. This liability shall extend to those who knowingly participate in or facilitate the use of such a false representation, even if they are not directly involved in the supply of the goods themselves.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark has developed a unique and recognizable trade description relating to specific goods, such proprietor may grant a license permitting another party to utilize said trade description in connection with the sale or distribution of those identical goods. Such licenses shall be assignable subject to prior written consent from the original proprietor, provided that any assignee assumes all rights and obligations pertaining to the licensed use as if originally granted. Further, where a registered trade mark has been assigned, the assignee may, under this Act, grant sub-licenses concerning the permitted trade description goods within the scope of the assignment, subject to conditions stipulated in the primary license agreement. The proprietor retains the right to terminate any such license or sub-license should the licensee fail to adhere to the terms and conditions agreed upon, as provided herein.

Where a person supplies or offers to supply goods with a false trade description goods, or uses such a false trade description in connection with the supply or offer thereof, that person shall be guilty of an offence and liable to prosecution under this Act. Such offences may include the representation that goods are of a different quality, origin, quantity, characteristic or grade than they actually possess. Any individual found guilty of employing a deceptive trade description goods is subject to fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Further, any such false descriptions shall be deemed actionable at the instance of any person suffering damage by reason thereof, conferring exclusive rights to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

Where a person offers or exposes for sale, or knowingly permits to be offered or exposed for sale, any goods under a false trade description, or where the trade description is likely to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality or geographical origin of those goods, such person shall be liable to prosecution. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify categories of goods with respect to which particular descriptions shall be deemed to be false trade descriptions for the purposes of this Act. Any consumer who suffers loss or injury as a consequence of an action taken contrary to these provisions may institute civil proceedings to claim damages. Further, any proprietor of a registered trademark may bring an action against a person violating these provisions, seeking injunctive relief and compensation for losses incurred due to the misleading trade description goods.

An application for registration of a trademark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier mark registered under this Act in relation to identical or closely related goods or services. However, where the applicant demonstrates that use of the mark has been made honestly and continuously for a period exceeding three years prior to the date of such application, and that there is no evidence of intent to deceive or take unfair advantage of the reputation of the proprietor of the earlier trademark, registration may be granted subject to limitations as provided herein. Any person convicted of knowingly making a false statement in an application under this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, and it is considered innocently punishable imprisonment where such falsity was made without malicious intent or knowledge of its impact on the registration process.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act against a person alleged to have infringed a registered trademark, and it is subsequently determined that such infringement did not occur, the Court may, subject to an assessment of the circumstances surrounding the initiation of the action, order the proprietor to pay compensation to the defendant. Such compensation shall be commensurate with the losses suffered by the defendant as a direct consequence of the unwarranted proceedings, including but not limited to costs incurred in defending the claim and loss of business opportunities. Furthermore, where the proprietor acted maliciously or recklessly in initiating such proceedings, they may also be subject to innocently punishable imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. This provision is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act, provided that the defendant demonstrates demonstrable harm resulting from the frivolous litigation.

Where a person is convicted under this Act for an offence involving the use of a trademark without authorization from the registered proprietor, and it is established during the inquiry proceedings that such use was undertaken due to demonstrable reliance upon representations made by a third party reasonably appearing to be authorized to grant permission, the Court may, subject to considerations of proportionality and public interest, impose a sentence of imprisonment which shall not exceed three months. This provision applies irrespective of whether the offender has been compensated for any losses incurred as a consequence of their actions. The Court shall record its reasons for imposing such an innocently punishable imprisonment, detailing the nature of the representations relied upon and the steps taken by the accused to verify their authenticity. Further, the court may order restitution to the registered proprietor commensurate with demonstrable financial harm suffered.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act and obtains a decree against a defendant, it shall be permissible to request the Court to impose a sentence of imprisonment as part of its judgment. Such imprisonment may not exceed two years, provided that the Court finds that the defendant’s actions demonstrate a reckless disregard for the intellectual property rights of others and that the infringement has caused demonstrable financial harm to the proprietor. Where the defendant proves, by clear and convincing evidence, that they acted under a genuine and reasonable belief in the validity of their conduct, and took all reasonable steps to ascertain its legality, the Court may, at its discretion, impose a sentence of innocently punishable imprisonment not exceeding six months.

Any person found guilty of knowingly using a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, without due cause and for fraudulent purposes, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to pay a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. Where such use is committed by an individual who demonstrates, upon investigation, that they were acting under the direction or control of another person and had no direct intent to deceive consumers, the court may, subject to prevailing sentencing guidelines, impose imprisonment for a term which shall not exceed one year; this constitutes an innocently punishable imprisonment. Further, any goods bearing the infringing trademark are liable to be seized and destroyed as provided herein.

Where a registered proprietor of a trademark grants a license to use such trademark, and subsequently assigns the entire undertaking to another party without explicitly transferring the said license, the assignee shall be deemed to have acquired only those rights pertaining to the trade mark as were expressly conveyed in the assignment deed. The licensee may continue to utilize the trademark under the terms initially stipulated in the licensing agreement, subject to adherence with all applicable provisions of this Act regarding quality control and permitted goods or services. Any breach of these conditions by the licensee shall constitute a civil infraction, but where such breach arises from demonstrable reliance on representations made by the assignor concerning the scope of their rights, the offender may be considered for innocently punishable imprisonment, not exceeding three months.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act and obtains a decree against a defendant who demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the court, that such infringement occurred without knowledge or intent to infringe, and further proves reasonable reliance upon representations made by an agent acting within their apparent authority, the court may, as part of its judgment, direct the imposition of a term of innocently punishable imprisonment not exceeding three months for any individual found guilty of contributory infringement. This provision is subject to appeal to the appellate forum established under this Act, and the defendant shall bear the burden of proving both lack of knowledge and reasonable reliance. Provided that such an appeal may be filed within sixty days from the date of the decree.

For the purposes of this Act, "infringement" shall include the use of a registered trademark in relation to goods or services identical or metamerically similar to those for which the mark is registered, without authorization from the proprietor. Such use shall be deemed an act of infringement irrespective of any demonstrable intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers, provided that where such use occurs due to honest and reasonable belief in a right to do so, the offender may be subject to innocently punishable imprisonment not exceeding three months. Nothing herein shall prevent a court from considering whether a patent shall be granted for an invention incorporating elements of a registered trademark.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act and obtains a decree against a defendant who proves, to the satisfaction of the court, that such infringement occurred due to an honest belief in the proprietorship of the trade mark, the court may, subject to certain conditions, direct that the defendant shall not be liable to pay damages or account for profits. Provided that, where the infringing use involves replication of a distinctive creator layout design registered under this Act, and the defendant’s actions were undertaken without reasonable inquiry into the validity of the registration, they may still be deemed wilfully infringing. In such cases, notwithstanding the demonstration of honest belief, the court retains discretion to impose an innocently punishable imprisonment term not exceeding three months, alongside a direction for compensation to the proprietor for demonstrable losses incurred.

Where a person is convicted under this Act for an offence involving the use of a registered trade mark without authorization from the proprietor, and it is established beyond reasonable doubt that such use was undertaken in complete good faith and without any intention to deceive or infringe upon the rights of the proprietor, the Court may, subject to considerations of public interest and the severity of the infringement, impose a sentence of imprisonment which shall not exceed three months. This provision regarding innocently punishable imprisonment applies irrespective of whether the infringing goods were offered for sale or otherwise made available for use. The date accorded patent protection to a similar mark by any competent authority shall be considered as relevant background information during sentencing deliberations, particularly in determining the potential for consumer confusion and subsequent damages. Further, such individuals may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for rectification of their understanding regarding permissible trade mark usage.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed on the ground that the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark, the Hearing Officer may direct that the matter be referred to settlement between the parties. Should settlement fail, the Hearing Officer shall proceed with the hearing and determine whether use of the applied-for mark would likely cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to infringement registered trade marks may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal as provided herein.

Where an action is brought before a court alleging infringement registered trade marks, the claimant shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining the respondent from any further acts constituting such infringement. Provided that, where the alleged infringing use occurs in relation to goods or services distinct from those for which the trade mark is registered, the court may consider the likelihood of confusion arising amongst consumers and may grant a more limited remedy tailored to prevent such confusion. Further, under this Act, damages shall be awarded to the claimant representing their loss by reason of the infringement, calculated on the basis of lost profits or, in the absence thereof, a reasonable royalty. The respondent may offer evidence demonstrating lack of intent to deceive or cause damage; however, this shall not preclude liability for infringement registered trade marks.

Where an action is brought before the relevant jurisdictional authority alleging infringement registered trade marks, the claimant shall be required to furnish evidence demonstrating a likelihood of confusion arising from the use of the impugned sign. Such evidence must clearly establish that consumers are likely to associate the defendant’s goods or services with those for which the plaintiff's mark is registered, or with the proprietor thereof. The authority may, at its discretion, direct a party to submit further documentation or attend an evidentiary hearing to clarify any ambiguities in the presented case. Provided that the defendant demonstrates prior use of a similar sign under conditions not constituting infringement as provided herein, the claimant’s claim may be dismissed. Further, where the defendant asserts a challenge to the validity of the registered trade mark itself, such challenge shall be adjudicated concurrently with the matter of alleged infringement.

Where an action is brought before a competent court alleging infringement registered trade marks, it shall be incumbent upon the claimant to demonstrate that use of the impugned sign creates likelihood of confusion amongst the relevant consuming public concerning the origin of goods or services. Provided that, such demonstration need not be conclusive if the defendant establishes prior honest concurrent use of a similar sign for identical or similar goods or services, and where such use has been continuous for a period exceeding five years from the date of first registration of the claimant’s trade mark. Furthermore, the court may consider evidence pertaining to the reputation enjoyed by the registered trade mark at the time of the alleged infringing activity, subject to principles of fairness and proportionality as provided herein.

Where an action is brought before a court alleging infringement registered trade marks, and the defendant asserts that the use of the impugned sign does not give rise to likelihood of confusion under this Act, the plaintiff shall be required to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, the distinctiveness acquired by the mark through use. Failure to provide such evidence will result in dismissal of the claim for infringement registered trade marks with no order as to costs. The court may, upon application by either party, issue interim injunctions restraining acts of alleged infringement pending final determination of the suit, provided that a substantial pecuniary penalty shall be imposed on any party found to have acted frivolously or vexatiously in seeking such relief. Any finding of infringement registered trade marks carries with it an entitlement for the plaintiff to seek damages and account of profits derived from the infringing activity.

Where an action is brought before a court alleging infringement registered trade marks, and the defendant asserts that the said trade mark was used as a generic descriptor prior to the date of application for registration by the claimant, the court shall determine whether such use constitutes fair dealing under this Act. Provided that, if the defendant demonstrates through documentary evidence, including but not limited to advertising materials and sales records, that widespread adoption of the term occurred without any commercial exploitation attributable to the claimant, the claim for infringement registered trade may be dismissed. Further, should the court find merit in the defendant’s argument regarding prior use, it may order a re-examination of the registration by the relevant intellectual property authority, subject to appeal under provisions as provided herein.

Where an action is brought before a court alleging infringement registered trade marks, and it is demonstrated that the defendant has used a sign identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the trade mark is registered, the court shall grant such remedy as it deems appropriate. This may include an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing sign and ordering the delivery up or destruction of all materials bearing that sign. Provided that evidence establishes a likelihood of consumer confusion arising from the defendant’s actions, damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered by the registered proprietor. Furthermore, if the infringing use incorporates a photograph depicting the goods or services in connection with the trade mark, the court may consider this an aggravating factor when determining the appropriate level of damages.

Where an action is brought before a competent court alleging infringement registered trade marks, the claimant shall furnish evidence establishing both ownership of the said trade mark and demonstrable use thereof in commerce prior to the date patent asserted by the respondent. The defendant may present counterclaims demonstrating prior honest concurrent usage, provided that such usage predates the registration date and does not constitute passing off under this Act. Further, if the defendant claims a right to use a similar sign based on an earlier trade mark registration for dissimilar goods, the court shall consider whether there exists a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. The claimant may apply to the court for interim relief pending determination of the suit, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding security and undertakings. Any order granted under this provision is reviewable by appeal before the appellate authority.

Where a registered trade mark is infringed, the Court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. This injunction sub section applies irrespective of whether damages have been claimed by the plaintiff or an account of profits has been rendered. The scope of any interlocutory injunction shall be determined having regard to the balance between protecting the registered trade mark owner’s rights and preventing undue prejudice to the defendant, provided that such prejudice is demonstrably substantial. Any order for delivery up may also be granted under this Act.

Where a registered trade mark owner grants a license to use their trade mark, subject to conditions specified in the licensing agreement, such license may be assigned by the licensee to another party provided that the original licensor’s consent is obtained prior to the assignment. Failure to secure this consent shall render the assignee jointly and severally liable for any breach of contract arising from the licensed usage. Furthermore, where a trade mark owner seeks to prevent unauthorized use or dilution of their registered mark, they may apply to the court for an injunction sub section restricting such activities, even if no direct contractual relationship exists between the proprietor and the infringing party. The court shall consider the terms of any prior licensing agreements when determining the scope and validity of such injunctive relief.

Where a proprietor demonstrates that use by another person is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public as to the origin of goods or services, or if such use dilutes the distinctiveness of the trade mark, the court may grant an injunction sub section restraining that other person from engaging in conduct constituting infringement under this Act. This power shall extend to preventing acts which are deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, even where the marks relate to different classes of goods or services, provided that there is evidence of actual or likely deception. The proprietor must satisfy the court that the infringing use has caused, or is reasonably likely to cause, damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with their separate trade marks.

For the purposes of this Act, "regulations deposited section" means a designated portion within the public register maintained under this Act, specifically allocated to record detailed stipulations pertaining to the use of registered trade marks. Such regulations shall be submitted by the proprietor of a mark following registration and may address matters including permitted colour schemes, specific product categories for application, or geographical limitations on sale. The Registrar shall verify that any regulation deposited is consistent with the provisions herein and does not unduly restrict competition. Any third party may inspect a regulations deposited section upon payment of prescribed fees.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trademark incorporating a geographical indication as per this Act, they shall submit to the Registrar, along with the application, detailed regulations deposited section outlining procedures for ensuring continued authenticity and exclusivity of that geographical indication. These regulations must specify mechanisms for monitoring production standards, preventing adulteration, and maintaining consumer confidence in goods bearing the mark. The Registrar may, after consultation with relevant stakeholders including producers' associations representing the geographical indication, approve or reject the proposed regulations based on their adequacy to safeguard the distinctiveness of the trademark and protect the interests of those engaged in producing goods under that indication. Any alteration to these deposited regulations shall require prior approval from the Registrar and notification through public advertisement.

For the purposes of this Act, “regulations deposited section” means a portion of an official record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry containing particulars relating to conditions, limitations, or restrictions imposed upon the registration of a trade mark, and which are expressly recorded as part of the registered instrument. Such regulations shall be deemed to form an integral component of the registered trade mark. An assignment denomination pertaining to a trade mark subject to a regulations deposited section shall clearly indicate the applicability of those specific conditions in any subsequent transfer or licensing agreement. The Registrar may require such indication under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, the “relevant entry register” shall mean the official record maintained by the Registrar pertaining to a trade mark application or registered trade mark, including but not limited to details concerning prior usage, opposed applications, and assignments. The relevant entry register is deemed conclusive evidence of particulars entered therein, subject to any order made under appeal. Any party seeking to challenge information contained within the relevant entry register must do so through appropriate rectification proceedings as provided herein. Information pertaining to consumer perception of a mark, while potentially relevant in certain disputes, shall not be considered part of the relevant entry register itself.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register pertaining to each class of goods or services appearing in the Fourth Schedule, wherein particulars of applications for registration, pending oppositions, and entries made upon the Register of Trade Marks shall be recorded. Any alteration or addition to an existing trade mark, including changes to the description of goods or services associated therewith, shall also be noted within this register. The relevant entry register is deemed a public record and may be inspected by any person subject to payment of such fees as prescribed under this Act. Information contained therein relating to confidential business strategies shall not be disclosed without prior authorization from the applicant or registered proprietor. Further, entries made in the relevant entry register are prima facie evidence of the matters recorded therein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the relevant entry register may file a representation with the Registrar within sixty days from the date of such publication. The representation shall state the grounds upon which the objection is based and shall be supported by such evidence as the aggrieved party deems appropriate to substantiate their claim. Upon receiving a representation, the Registrar shall afford the applicant for registration or the proprietor of the trade mark concerned an opportunity to file a reply within thirty days. 

The Registrar may, after considering the representation and any reply filed, direct that the entry be amended, removed, or affirmed as originally recorded. Such direction shall be final subject to appeal under this Act. Failure to comply with the directions of the Registrar may render the aggrieved party liable for costs incurred by the other party in defending the proceedings. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all representations filed and decisions rendered concerning entries in the relevant entry register.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register for each class of goods or services appearing in the Trade Marks Register. This register shall record particulars relating to entries made concerning trade marks, including but not limited to applications filed, advertisements published under this Act, and any alterations or amendments effected to existing registrations. The Registrar may prescribe the form and manner in which such relevant entry registers are maintained, provided that they allow for efficient retrieval of information pertaining to individual trade mark records. Any party seeking access to a relevant entry register shall submit a written request specifying the particulars required, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Registrar shall process requests promptly; however, confidential commercial information contained within the register may be redacted as deemed appropriate by the Registrar.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register pertaining to each class of goods or services for which an application for registration has been filed under this Act. This register shall accurately reflect the status of applications, including those opposed, accepted with modifications, and finally registered trade marks. The information recorded within the relevant entry register is deemed public record and may be inspected by any person subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Any alteration or addition to an entry in the relevant entry register must be certified by the Registrar as correct and shall include the date and reason for such modification. Furthermore, copies extracted from the relevant entry register are admissible as evidence under this Act without proof of the original, provided they are duly authenticated.

Any person aggrieved by an entry in the relevant entry register shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such entry’s publication. Failure to comply with this timeframe shall render the appeal inadmissible, subject to exemptions granted solely at the discretion of the Tribunal. The appellant must demonstrate a direct and substantial prejudice arising directly from the erroneous inclusion or omission in the relevant entry register; mere dissatisfaction is insufficient grounds for redressal. Any party seeking injunctive relief against infringement predicated on an inaccurate representation within the relevant entry register shall be liable to pay compensatory damages to the affected party, as determined by the Tribunal, reflecting loss of reputation and commercial detriment.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licences relating to the use of their mark as recorded in the relevant entry register, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the owner and the licensee. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover specific goods or services delineated within the scope of the registration. Assignment of a trade mark, including any associated licences granted under this Act, requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days of execution, accompanied by prescribed fees. Further, where a licence is assigned alongside the trade mark itself, the assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights and obligations pertaining to that licence as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the validity of any assignment or sub-licence agreement for verification purposes.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register pertaining to each trademark application examined under this Act, recording particulars of objections received from third parties and the applicant’s response thereto. Any party aggrieved by an entry made or omitted to be made in the relevant entry register may, within sixty days from the date such entry is published as provided herein, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant entry register extract. The Board may, after affording both parties an opportunity to be heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision regarding entries in the register; provided that any order modifying or reversing a decision shall not prejudice the rights of other trademark proprietors.

The relevant entry register shall be maintained electronically and shall include particulars of each denomination variety sub-classification applied for alongside the principal trade mark. Any alteration to a registered trade mark’s classification, including the addition or removal of a denomination variety sub-, must be recorded within fourteen days of notification to the Registrar. The Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating the basis for any such classification amendment, particularly where it pertains to a geographical indication or relates to goods identical to those already registered under another trade mark. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the amended registration provisional until full compliance is demonstrated. Further, an applicant seeking inclusion of a denomination variety sub- must provide evidence demonstrating distinctiveness in relation to the specified goods and services as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the relevant entry register relating to a layout-design shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of publication of the entry, and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Tribunal shall afford all parties an opportunity of being heard, and may order discovery of documents as deemed necessary for a just determination. Any party failing to appear before the Tribunal at the appointed date shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Decisions of the Tribunal are final subject to further appeals under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, the “relevant entry register” shall mean the official record maintained by the Registrar containing particulars relating to registered trade marks, pending applications for registration, and entries concerning opposed trademarks. This register includes, but is not limited to, information regarding ownership, dates of application and registration, goods or services associated with a mark, and any modifications made thereto under this Act. The Registrar shall ensure that the relevant entry register is accessible for public inspection, subject to regulations as may be prescribed. Any party aggrieved by an error or omission in the relevant entry register may seek redress through appropriate proceedings before the High Court.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register pertaining to international marks designating India under this Act, recording particulars of such designations and subsequent alterations thereof. An application for registration of an international mark shall be deemed to have been made on the date specified in the statement of designation filed with the International Bureau under the Protocol Madrid Agreement. The Registrar may require the deposit of a certified true copy of the international registration certificate as evidence of entitlement. Any modification to the list of goods or services indicated in the international registration, if not already reflected in the relevant entry register, shall be recorded separately and made available for public inspection. Further, any limitation of protection afforded by an international mark within India will also be documented as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, and the Registrar, after affording both the applicant and the opponent opportunities for being heard, is satisfied that the opposition lacks merit or is frivolous, the Registrar shall direct the disposal of the opposition. Any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this Act shall render the defaulting party liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and further penalties may be imposed for continued non-compliance as provided herein. The Registrar’s satisfaction in respect of a registrar satisfied application is final, subject to appeal.

Where an owner of a geographical indication seeks to grant a license conferring rights relating to the use of the registered geographical indication for goods other than those for which it is registered, such application shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the proposed licensee possesses the requisite expertise and resources to maintain the quality standards associated with the protected indication, approve the license agreement. Any assignment of a geographical indication or any interest therein, including licenses granted under this Act, requires prior notification to the Registrar. Provided that such notification includes details of the assignee and the terms of the transfer, the Registrar may raise objections if he deems it detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the geographical indication. The registrar satisfied application shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of the assignment unless challenged under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a "defendant geographical indication" means an indication that identifies goods as originating from a specific territory or region where a given quality, reputation, or other characteristic substantially attributable to its origin is claimed; and such indication shall include signs which, even if not registered under this Act, are essentially similar to a registered geographical indication. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating the use of an unregistered sign in relation to goods originating from outside the territory associated with a protected geographical indication, determine whether said use constitutes deceptive practices or unfair competition as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society, producer company, or other body of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collectives, but no such application shall be entertained unless it is accompanied by an affidavit verifying that the applicant has the consent of all producers concerned with the manufacture of the good and that the geographical indication sought to be registered truly identifies the product originating from the specified area. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating exclusive use and reputation within the defined territory, particularly where a defendant geographical seeks to challenge existing claims. Any alteration to the boundaries defining the geographical origin shall necessitate re-examination under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in a suit before the District Court within whose local jurisdiction the cause of action arises for relief against a defendant geographical entity engaging in activities infringing upon their exclusive rights. Such infringement includes, but is not limited to, the use of the geographical indication or any confusingly similar indicator in connection with goods or services not authorized under this Act. The court shall have power to grant such remedies as it deems just and equitable, including injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, and the disposal of infringing goods or materials. Provided that a defendant geographical entity may demonstrate prior honest usage before the date of registration, subject to conditions determined by the court regarding continued use and consumer association with the genuine product.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be opposed by any person who believes that the applicant is not entitled to registration under this Act. Such opposition must be filed within the prescribed period from the date of publication of the application in the Geographical Indications Journal and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to demonstrable evidence that the claimed geographical origin lacks distinctiveness or that the use by the defendant would constitute unfair competition. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to the opposition within a stipulated timeframe. Following consideration of both submissions, the Registrar may either allow the registration as applied for, reject the application entirely, or grant registration subject to such limitations or conditions as deemed appropriate. A successful defendant geographical may appeal the Registrar’s decision to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for registration as a geographical indication may be refused if the applicant fails to demonstrate exclusive rights over the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to the goods specified in the application.
