Furthermore, any person seeking to challenge the validity of a registered geographical indication must provide evidence that use by a defendant geographical entity does not conform with the standards of production and quality as defined in the registration certificate. Such challenges shall be considered only if the defendant demonstrates prior established usage predating the date of application for registration, provided that such usage did not constitute deceptive or misleading practices under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify compliance with these conditions.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses a protected geographical indication in relation to goods for which that indication is registered, or uses any indicator likely to deceive consumers into believing that the goods originate from the geographically defined area specified in the registration, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant civil court and may include compensation for loss of profits suffered by authorized users and costs incurred in combating the infringing use. Further, a defendant geographical indication user found guilty of such infringement is subject to penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and fines ranging from fifty thousand rupees to two hundred thousand rupees.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses conferring upon the licensee the right to use the said geographical indication in relation to goods for which it is registered. Such license shall be assignable subject to the prior consent of the registering authority, provided that any such assignment does not prejudice the distinctiveness or reputation of the geographical indication itself. The defendant geographical proprietor may impose conditions within a license relating to quality control and continued adherence to standards as prescribed under this Act for goods bearing the indication. Further, where a license is granted, the licensee shall be deemed an authorized user with standing to enforce the rights conveyed by such license against infringers. Any transfer of ownership of the defendant geographical registration itself requires notification to the registering authority at least ninety days prior to its effective date.

An action may be instituted against a defendant geographical indication proprietor alleging improper use of a protected name where such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. Provided that, the aggrieved party must demonstrate demonstrable misrepresentation and resultant damage attributable directly to the defendant’s activities under this Act. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving that their use does not constitute an infringement or unfair competition as provided herein. Further, any appeal arising from a finding of infringement may be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order being communicated; however, such appeals are subject to review for frivolousness and vexatiousness at the discretion of the Board.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant licences in respect of the application of that indication to goods. Such licence shall specify the exclusive rights granted and the duration thereof, subject to conditions as provided herein regarding quality control and continued adherence to standards prescribed under this Act. A defendant geographical indication proprietor seeking to assign their rights or any portion thereof relating to a registered geographical indication shall publish notice of such intention in the Official Gazette, detailing the proposed assignee and scope of assignment. Objections to the assignment may be raised within three months from the date of publication; failing resolution through amicable agreement, the Registrar may determine whether the assignment is prejudicial to the interests of consumers or producers associated with the geographical indication.

A ‘defendant geographical indication’ means an indication that relates to goods originating from a specific geographic area in India and which has been applied for registration under this Act. For the purposes of determining similarity under this Act, the ‘trade description meaning’ of a defendant geographical indication shall be construed broadly to encompass not only the literal words used but also any associated imagery, symbols or phrases commonly understood by consumers to represent that geographical origin. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating consumer perception regarding such trade descriptions before making a determination concerning deceptive use. Provided that, an indication shall not be considered a ‘defendant geographical indication’ if it is demonstrably generic within the relevant geographic area.

Any proprietor seeking remedies against a defendant geographical indication user found to have engaged in activities constituting unfair competition or misrepresentation under this Act may institute proceedings in the High Court. Such action shall be predicated upon demonstrable evidence of consumer confusion reasonably attributable to the defendant’s use of a sign identical or deceptively similar to the registered Geographical Indication. The court, upon finding infringement, may grant such relief as it deems appropriate, including but not limited to injunctions preventing further infringing acts and orders for accounts of profits derived from the unauthorized use. Where an international application has been filed in respect of a geographical indication, the provisions relating to remedies shall apply with due regard to any conflicting rights or obligations arising under treaties or conventions ratified by India. The court may also order the defendant to undertake corrective advertising to mitigate consumer deception.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication has been filed, and the Registrar deems it necessary to ascertain the views of interested parties regarding the distinctiveness of the goods or services associated with the proposed indication, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the Official Gazette. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the application, including the name of the notice applicant and a description of the geographical area sought to be protected. Any person having a lawful interest may, within the period specified in the notice, submit objections or representations to the Registrar. The defendant geographical indication holder shall be deemed to have a lawful interest for the purposes of this provision. Objections received shall be considered by the Registrar and an opportunity afforded to both the applicant and objector to present their case under this Act.

A defendant geographical indication, for the purposes of this Act, means a person who, without authorization from the proprietor of the registered geographical indication, directly or indirectly makes, uses, offers for sale, sells, or distributes goods that are identified by such indication as indicating the origin of those goods. Such use shall be deemed to constitute an infringement under this Act if it is likely to cause confusion in the minds of the public regarding the origin of the goods. The proprietor may institute proceedings against a defendant geographical indication seeking remedies including injunction and damages, subject to the provisions relating to fair use as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons or producers, organisations or businesses engaged in the production of goods originating from that territory. The Registrar shall examine such an application and if satisfied that the applicant meets the criteria as provided herein, including demonstrating control over the quality and other characteristics of the goods, shall proceed to publication for opposition. Any person alleging a proprietory or otherwise protectable right in relation to the geographical indication sought to be registered may file a notice of opposition under this Act. Where an opposition is filed against a proposed registration, the defendant geographical indication must demonstrate its legitimate interest in maintaining that objection.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute a suit in the competent court against a defendant geographical indication for relief from acts of manufacture, processing, packaging, sale, hire, exhibition, or use which constitute an infringement of their exclusive right under this Act. Such infringement includes any representation, mark, label, notice, sign, or symbol falsely suggesting association with the registered geographical indication, or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. The court shall grant such remedies as it deems appropriate, including injunctions restraining further infringing acts and an order for the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. Damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered by the proprietor, provided that wilful infringement is established. Costs of litigation shall be determined according to prevailing rules.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be opposed by any person under this Act within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance thereof in the Geographical Indications Journal. Such opposition must be made in writing and shall state the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations that the proposed geographical indication conflicts with existing rights or is deceptively similar to a prior mark. The Registrar may require the opponent to furnish security as deemed appropriate to protect the interests of the applicant. If an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and afford both parties an opportunity for hearing in accordance with the prescribed procedure. In determining whether a defendant geographical indication constitutes infringement, due regard shall be had to the distinctiveness of the registered mark and the likelihood of confusion amongst consumers.

An action may be instituted against a defendant geographical indication where it is demonstrated that such defendant has engaged in production, processing, packing, distribution, sale or offering for sale of goods which are identified as originating from the geographically indicated area specified in the registration, and where said goods do not conform to the standards of quality, reputation or other characteristics prescribed under this Act. Provided that, a producer demonstrating exclusive rights to a particular method of production within the defined geographical boundary shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against any party utilizing a substantially similar process. Further, such action is permissible only if the defendant’s activities cause demonstrable dilution of the distinctiveness and reputation associated with the registered indication, as determined by the relevant intellectual property tribunal.

Any person found to be using a protected geographical indication in contravention of this Act shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant High Court, taking into account the extent of the defendant’s infringing activities and the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Further, where a defendant geographical indication is used in connection with goods not conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act, enhanced penalties may be imposed, up to twice the amount of damages awarded. The Central Government shall have the power to issue cease-and-desist orders against any entity engaging in unauthorized use, and failure to comply therewith shall constitute a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment or fine, as provided herein.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the said geographical indication in connection with goods matching the definition and characteristics as specified under this Act. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to product categories, geographic territories, and duration. Assignment of rights relating to a defendant geographical indication is permissible subject to prior written consent from the Registrar, and such assignment must be registered within three months of execution to be valid against third parties. Any person acquiring a license or assignment shall be bound by the conditions applicable to the original owner as provided herein. The Registrar may require additional security deposits for licenses granted involving export activities relating to the protected goods. Further, any use of the defendant geographical indication without authorization constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act.

An action may be instituted against a defendant geographical indication alleging unfair competition where the defendant’s use of a sign suggests an association with the registered geographical indication, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods. Provided that, the Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating substantial alteration in the production process or characteristics of goods associated with a registered geographical indication, entertain petitions seeking modification of the registration’s scope. Any order modifying a registration shall be subject to appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of publication of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the defendant geographical indication has genuinely exploited the reputation and distinctiveness of the registered mark.

Where an appeal lies from a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed geographical indication, or revoking a certificate of registration, the Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the defendant geographical indication proprietor to produce before it all books and documents relating to the use of the said indication in commerce. The Board shall consider whether the continued use by the defendant constitutes an abuse of distinctiveness or unfair advantage, particularly where the registration term approaches its expiry term patent period, and may order interim relief pending final determination. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a prescribed time, as provided herein.

A ‘defendant geographical indication’ is defined as a geographical indication that has been entered in the Register of Geographical Indications and against which an opposition was filed under this Act, but where such opposition was not upheld by the Registrar. For the purposes of determining infringement proceedings, the defendant geographical indication retains its status as registered until such time as it is removed from the Register following a successful appeal or other order made under this Act. An entry register maintained in relation to each registered geographical indication shall record details pertaining to any oppositions filed and their subsequent resolution, including the designation of any defendant geographical indications arising therefrom.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society, producer company or other body of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collectives, but no person shall represent themselves as a legal practitioner person unless they are duly enrolled under the Advocates Act. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar shall issue a public notice inviting objections to the proposed registration, and any interested party may file such objections within the time specified therein. If, after considering all objections, the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant meets the criteria for eligibility as defined under this Act, and that the geographical indication qualifies as a defendant geographical indication signifying unique qualities attributable to its origin, then provisional registration shall be granted pending examination of distinctiveness.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute a suit for relief against a defendant geographical indication engaging in activities likely to cause dilution of distinctiveness or confusion amongst consumers. Such actions include, but are not limited to, use of the protected name or any colourable imitation thereof on goods or services not originating from the territory defined by the registration. The remedies available under this Act shall encompass injunctions preventing further infringing activity and an order for accounts detailing profits derived from such misuse. Provided that, where the defendant’s actions are proven to be undertaken with fraudulent intent to deceive or mislead, they may also be liable to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code relating to cheating and dishonesty. The court shall have discretion to award damages reflecting the harm caused to the reputation and goodwill associated with the geographical indication.

Where an action is brought alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, service of notice of such action upon the defendant geographical indication society shall be effected in accordance with the rules of civil procedure as modified by this Act. Provided that where the defendant geographical indication society fails to appear and defend within thirty days from the date of such service, the Registrar may, ex parte, proceed with the hearing of the matter. In cases where the defendant geographical indication society is a body corporate, service shall be upon its registered office or any other address as notified by it to the Registrar for that purpose. If the defendant geographical indication society defaults in appearing, any legal representative duly authorized to act on its behalf may appear and contest the proceedings. The Registrar shall record reasons for any ex parte order passed under this Act.

A person claiming to be a defendant geographical indication shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating continuous and exclusive use of the relevant goods within the defined geographical territory for a minimum period of five years preceding the date of application. Such evidence must include verifiable documentation pertaining to production techniques, local traditions, and established commercial practices directly linked to the quality and reputation of the goods. The registered proprietor trade mark shall be entitled to initiate proceedings under this Act if it can demonstrate that the defendant’s use creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods. Further, any alteration in production methods following registration may require prior approval from the Registrar, provided that such alterations do not adversely affect the distinctive character of the geographical indication.

Any person proposing to make use of a geographical indication as authorized under this Act shall file an application for registration with the Geographical Indications Registry. The application shall specify the goods or services to which the geographical indication relates and provide particulars demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods or services is essentially attributable to their origin within the defined geographical area. Upon receiving such an application, the Registry may require the applicant to submit further documentation substantiating the claim regarding origin and distinctiveness. Objections to the proposed registration may be filed by any interested party within the prescribed period, demonstrating a legitimate interest in preventing the use defendant geographical indication. The Registrar shall consider all objections and provide the applicant with an opportunity for rebuttal before making a determination on the application’s merits as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking remedies against an unauthorized use defendant geographical indication shall file a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs or where the defendant conducts business. The plaint shall specify the particulars of the registered geographical indication and detail the infringing activity, including dates, locations, and quantities involved. Damages recoverable under this Act shall be determined by considering the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the unauthorized use, alongside any profits made by the infringer attributable to that use. A court may also grant an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. It is provided that where a patentee includes exclusive rights relating to a process or product associated with a geographical indication, such exclusivity shall not preclude claims under this Act concerning deceptive use of the geographical indication itself.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall mean an original layout design fixed on a semiconductor integrated circuit or embodied in a mask used for the fabrication of a semiconductor integrated circuit. Such proprietor layout design includes any alteration or adaptation thereof which is not substantially similar to any prior published work under this Act. The right of a proprietor layout design extends to the reproduction of the layout design, including its duplication and modification, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding reverse engineering for lawful purposes. A layout design shall be deemed original if it possesses an element of creativity and is not merely a literal copy of any existing design.

An application for registration as a proprietor layout design shall include a certified copy of the integrated circuit, detailed specifications outlining its functionality and architecture, and a complete list of elements comprising the layout-design. The applicant must demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Registrar that they are indeed the rightful proprietor, possessing exclusive rights over the layout-design in question. Where an application relates to a layout-design incorporating features derived from previously registered designs, the applicant shall provide a clear statement identifying such incorporated elements and confirming compliance with existing intellectual property protections under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation or clarification as deemed necessary for assessment of originality and proprietorship.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall enjoy protection for a period of ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation. Any person who, without authorisation from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, hires or offers to sell or hire any integrated circuit embodying a proprietor layout design, shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Such damages may include compensation for infringement and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing legal remedies. Further, where an infringing copy is manufactured or imported with intent for commercial gain, the court may order its destruction as provided herein. The proprietor may also seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success. This protection extends to all forms of reproduction and adaptation of the layout design.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to exploit commercially the layout-design for the term specified herein. Application for registration as a proprietor layout design may be made by any person claiming to be the first inventor of the layout-design, or by their legal representative duly authorised in writing. The Controller General shall entertain such application only if it is accompanied by an affidavit verifying the originality and novelty of the claimed layout design. Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the validity of a proprietor layout design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and evidence within the time prescribed. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller General may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to exploit commercially the layout-design and to prevent others from doing any act prohibited under this Act. Such exploitation includes, but is not limited to, reproduction, modification, sale, hire or import of integrated circuits incorporating the proprietor layout design. Provided that, where an integrated circuit containing a proprietor layout design is manufactured for export out of India, the registered proprietor shall be deemed not to have contravened any provision relating to unauthorized exploitation. The right conferred under this Act shall be enforceable against any person who, without authorization, does anything which constitutes infringement as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the proprietor layout design, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or displays a layout-design that infringes any copyright therein shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees, or both. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the layout design in whole or substantially as a whole. Where the infringing act is committed for commercial gain, the court may enhance the penalty up to twice the amount specified above. The proprietor layout design shall have the right to apply to the Commercial Court seeking an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. This provision applies irrespective of whether the infringer was aware that their actions constituted an offence under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design may be licensed by the registered proprietor for specific uses, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, geographical limitations, and duration, as agreed upon between the proprietor and licensee. Assignment of a proprietor layout design is permissible only through a written instrument executed in accordance with prescribed procedures, transferring all rights and privileges associated therewith. Provided that any assignment shall require registration with the designated authority to be deemed valid against third parties. The registered proprietor retains the right to grant non-exclusive licenses without requiring consent from previous licensees, subject to ensuring such grants do not unreasonably prejudice existing contractual obligations. Further, sublicensing is permitted where explicitly authorized within the terms of a primary license agreement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall be deemed infringed where a person without authorisation reproduces the layout-design for any commercial purpose. The right of action under this provision may be exercised only by the registered proprietor and not by any other individual claiming an interest therein unless expressly authorised by the proprietor. Disputes concerning the scope of permissible reproduction or the validity of a registration as a proprietor layout design shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. It is provided that evidence demonstrating substantial similarity, even absent verbatim copying, may suffice to establish infringement, considering the overall impression created upon an informed user. The burden of proving lack of authorisation rests upon the alleged infringer.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall be eligible for registration upon application made by the first owner thereof. An applicant seeking registration as the proprietor must demonstrate exclusive right and title over the layout-design, supported by documentary evidence establishing creation or lawful assignment. Where an alleged infringement involves a deemed falsify geographical indication associated with the integrated circuit’s intended function, the Registrar may require additional declarations confirming non-misleading use. Registration shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, hire, and import layout designs corresponding substantially to the registered design, provided that such reproduction does not unduly prejudice existing rights under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a proprietor layout design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce the layout design in any form, including but not limited to manufacturing integrated circuits. Any person who without authorization from the registered proprietor makes, imports, or offers for sale an integrated circuit incorporating the proprietor layout design shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the relevant court, taking into account factors such as the extent of infringement and lost profits. An application for registration, constituting an india application, must disclose full details regarding the applicant’s claim to being the first inventor of the layout design. Provided that rectification proceedings may be initiated under this Act if it is demonstrated that a proprietor layout design has been registered in error or through misrepresentation.

For the purposes of this Act, a "layout design file" means any data representing a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design recorded in a machine-readable form and submitted to the Registrar for registration; provided that such file must conform to the prescribed format as notified by the Registrar. The registrar prescribed requirement for submission of a layout design file includes, but is not limited to, an affirmation by the applicant attesting to the originality of the design and a declaration confirming compliance with all relevant export control regulations. Further, any modification or alteration to the submitted layout design file after initial registration shall be subject to approval from the Registrar as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall include a detailed schematic representation conforming to the standards specified by the registrar and accompanied by a technical description elucidating the functionality and architecture of the design. The applicant must also furnish three certified copies of the layout-design, suitable for reproduction and examination under this Act. Further, the registrar prescribed requirement mandates submission of a declaration affirming that the applicant is the rightful owner of the intellectual property rights pertaining to the integrated circuit layout-design, free from any encumbrances or conflicting claims. Provided that, in cases where the design incorporates elements derived from prior art, a comprehensive list of such elements must be appended, detailing their source and nature of adaptation.

Where a proprietor alleges infringement of layout-design rights under this Act, and seeks injunctive relief, the Registrar may require submission of specific documentation demonstrating reasonable efforts to ascertain the identity of the alleged infringer. This requirement is intended to prevent frivolous claims and ensure due diligence in pursuing remedies. Such documentation shall include, but not be limited to, records of online searches, inquiries with distributors, and any correspondence undertaken to identify the responsible party. The Registrar’s determination regarding whether sufficient effort has been demonstrated shall be final and binding on all parties subject to appeal before a designated appellate tribunal. Failure to comply with the registrar prescribed requirement may result in the rejection of the infringement claim or imposition of costs against the claimant.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall include particulars in Form A, as may be prescribed by the registrar, detailing the applicant’s entitlement to protection under this Act and specifying the geographical extent of such protection sought. The registrar may require submission of certified copies of relevant prior agreements or assignments pertaining to the right to apply for registration, provided that such requirement shall not unduly delay the processing of applications from small-scale enterprises as defined by the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises. Further, an applicant intending to claim priority under Article 1(3) of the Berne Convention must submit a certified copy of the original application within ninety days of its filing date. The registrar prescribed requirement for verification of these documents shall be strictly adhered to, and failure to comply may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment proceedings.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall include a detailed schematic diagram conforming to standards as may be prescribed by the registrar and accompanied by a technical specification outlining the functionality and architecture of the design. Provided that, where an applicant seeks to register a layout-design incorporating elements previously registered under this Act, the application must explicitly identify such prior registrations and demonstrate substantial modification justifying independent registration. The registrar prescribed requirement for verification of originality shall involve examination by a designated expert panel appointed by the Controller. Any deficiency in compliance with these stipulations may result in rejection of the application or request for further clarification, as deemed necessary by the registrar.

Any applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design under this Act shall furnish to the Registrar, in such form and manner as the registrar prescribed requirement dictates, a detailed declaration specifying all prior publications or disclosures concerning the layout-design, whether within India or abroad. Failure to disclose any such prior publication constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further affidavits from the applicant confirming the veracity of this declaration. Any person found guilty of making a false statement shall be liable to pay compensation to any aggrieved party as determined by the relevant court, subject to appeal under established procedures.

Where a layout design owner desires to grant a license for the exploitation of their protected integrated circuit layout design, such license may be assigned or transferred subject to the provisions herein. Any assignment or transfer shall be in writing and executed by all parties concerned, including the original layout-design owner and the assignee or transferee. The Registrar prescribed requirement stipulates that prior to any such assignment or transfer being recorded with the office, a declaration must be filed detailing the scope of the license granted, specifying whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive, and outlining the permitted field of use. This declaration shall also include information regarding royalty rates, if applicable, and the duration of the license agreement. Failure to comply with this Registrar prescribed requirement will render the assignment voidable at the option of any affected party.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations against such rejection and may also request a hearing before the Registrar. The Registrar, after considering any submissions made by the applicant and any evidence presented, shall issue an order either upholding the original rejection or setting aside the same and directing that the application proceed for registration. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The registrar prescribed requirement regarding documentary proof of prior publication, if disputed, shall be subject to review during any such appellate proceedings.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an article patented process shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the nature and extent of the protection sought, including detailed schematics illustrating the integration of the patented process within the semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. The registrar prescribed requirement concerning such applications mandates submission of a declaration from the applicant affirming that they possess the exclusive right to apply for registration under this Act, or are duly authorized by the owner thereof. Furthermore, applicants must provide an affidavit verifying the accuracy and completeness of all information furnished in support of their application. Failure to comply with these procedural stipulations may result in rejection of the application. The registrar may, at any time, require submission of additional documentation deemed necessary for a thorough assessment of the merits of the application as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall include a detailed schematic representation conforming to the standards prescribed by the registrar and accompanied by a technical specification outlining the functionality and intended use of the design. Such applications must also demonstrate compliance with all relevant safety regulations as may be notified from time to time under this Act. The registrar, in assessing an application, may require submission of additional data pertaining to manufacturing processes or security protocols employed. Failure to satisfy a registrar prescribed requirement regarding these submissions will render the application liable for rejection. Further, any subsequent grant of registration based on incomplete information could potentially impact claims arising from patent consequences related to similar inventions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person holding layout-design registration relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant a license conferring rights to use such design, either wholly or partially, for specific purposes or fields of use. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including manufacture, import, sale, hire, or display of integrated circuits incorporating the registered layout-design. The registrar prescribed requirement for assignment of such rights includes a declaration affirming that all prior assignees have consented to the transfer. Any dispute arising from the terms of a license or assignment may be referred to the member appellate board for resolution, whose decision shall be binding on all parties involved, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days of the date of notification of the disputed action.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a description of the functions performed by the integrated circuit. Where a layout-design has been *entered register disclosed* prior to the date of filing the application, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating the nature and extent of such disclosure. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information or documentation deemed necessary for assessing novelty and originality under this Act. Further, any modification made to the layout-design subsequent to its initial *entered register disclosed* status must be reported to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by a justification for said alterations as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a description sufficient to enable the Registrar to ascertain its nature and scope. Where a layout-design has been previously *entered register disclosed* to the public through any means, the application must explicitly state such disclosure, including details of the date, place, and manner of dissemination. The applicant shall further provide an affirmation verifying the accuracy of the information furnished and confirming that they are the rightful owner or authorized representative of the layout-design’s creator. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar may, at any time, require the applicant to submit further documentation as deemed necessary for verification under this Act.

Where a layout design has entered the register and subsequently been disclosed to the public under this Act, the registered proprietor shall retain exclusive rights relating to commercial exploitation, subject to any licenses granted or assignments made prior to such disclosure. Any license agreement pertaining to a layout design previously entered register disclosed may be assigned in whole or in part, provided that written notification of such assignment is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days. Further, an assignee under this Act shall hold rights equivalent to those possessed by the original licensee, and shall be bound by any restrictions contained within the initial license agreement. The registered proprietor may grant non-exclusive licenses for specific applications or territories, as deemed appropriate, but must ensure that such grants do not prejudice existing exclusive rights.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be on any ground alleging that the refusal was erroneous in law or fact, including but not limited to challenges regarding novelty and originality. It is provided that where a layout-design has been entered register disclosed prior to the filing of the application, the appellant must demonstrate that such disclosure did not prejudice the applicant’s right to registration. The Tribunal shall give notice to all interested parties and may direct any party to produce documents or other evidence relevant to the appeal. Any order made by the Tribunal under this Act shall be final subject to further appeal as provided herein.

Where an applicant has filed an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design and such application meets all requirements as provided herein, including payment of prescribed fees and submission of requisite documentation demonstrating originality and inventive step, the registrar shall register the layout-design in the Register of Integrated Circuits. The applicant shall provide an exhaustive list of all prior disclosures made concerning the layout-design before its entry into the register disclosed. Further, where a layout-design has been entered register disclosed to any person by the applicant for the purpose of evaluation or manufacture, the registrar may require additional verification confirming such disclosure and its extent. Any challenge to registration based on prior publication must be submitted within ninety days from the date of public notice of acceptance.

For the purposes of this Act, a layout design is deemed to have been “entered register disclosed” when particulars relating to such layout design, including but not limited to its title, name and address of the claimant, and a copy of the relevant documentation as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, are published in the Official Gazette. The chairperson shall ensure that such publication occurs within thirty days of the registration being completed. Further, any person may inspect the register entry so disclosed at the office of the Registrar. This disclosure does not prejudice any right to confidentiality otherwise enjoyed by the claimant as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “layout-design” means a three-dimensional representation of the integrated circuit; provided that such representation is defined by the arrangement, or interconnection, or any combination thereof, of active and passive components and interconnections, or representing such arrangement or interconnection. An application to register a layout-design shall register proposed original work, and it shall include a description of the layout-design sufficient for enabling an assessment of its novelty and inventive step under this Act. The applicant shall also submit details regarding the date of first commercial exploitation, if any, of the layout-design; subject to such particulars being duly verified by affidavit.

An applicant who seeks to obtain protection for a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall register proposed layout designs in accordance with the provisions herein. Such registration shall be refused if the layout design incorporates elements which are substantially similar to any other layout design already registered under this Act, or for which application has been filed and is pending. The applicant shall furnish along with the application a detailed description of the integrated circuit functionality and its intended use, including diagrams illustrating the interconnection of various components. Provided that an applicant may submit supplementary documentation demonstrating prior publication or disclosure if deemed relevant by the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register proposed layout designs may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.

Where a person alleges that any act constitutes infringement of layout-design rights under this Act, such person shall institute proceedings before the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act occurred or where the cause of action arose. Upon receiving complaint, the court may issue an injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity, provided that it is satisfied that the plaintiff has a reasonable apprehension of further infringement. The court shall also be empowered to order the delivery up or destruction of goods manufactured containing the infringing layout-design, and any materials used in their manufacture. Any person seeking to register a layout-design shall register proposed modifications to existing registered designs with the Registrar within three months of such modification. Failure to do so will render the modified design vulnerable to challenge under this Act.

An application to register a layout-design shall contain particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the integrated circuit layout-design, and the date of first publication, if any, of the layout-design outside India. The application shall also include drawings or photographic reproductions conforming to standards prescribed by the Registrar, clearly depicting the salient features of the layout-design. Any person claiming an interest in a layout-design may file with the Registrar within two months from the date of receipt of notice under this Act, objections to the registration of the proposed layout-design. The Registrar shall register proposed registered designs only if satisfied that the design is original and not contrary to established principles of morality or public order. The applicant shall furnish such undertakings as the Registrar may require regarding the authenticity of the information provided in the application.

An applicant desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall register proposed design documentation with the Controller, detailing all aspects of the circuit’s architecture and functionality as provided herein. Such documentation must include precise geometrical representations conforming to established industry standards and be accompanied by a declaration affirming originality and freedom from prior publication. The applicant shall further submit proof of diligent search undertaken to ascertain absence of identical layout-designs already registered under this Act, or pending registration. Registration may be refused if the Controller determines that the proposed design lacks sufficient novelty or is substantially similar to an existing layout-design. Subject to compliance with these requirements and payment of prescribed fees, the Controller shall register proposed designs within a period not exceeding ninety days.

Any person desiring to obtain protection under this Act shall register proposed layout designs relating to semiconductor integrated circuits in accordance with the provisions herein. Failure to disclose all relevant prior art during the registration process may result in a subsequent revocation of the registered design, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations, and any unauthorized reproduction or importation for commercial purposes without consent constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act. Penalties for such infringements include fines not exceeding five million rupees and imprisonment extending up to three years, as determined by competent courts. Any party aggrieved may file a complaint with the appropriate authority seeking redressal of damages.

Where a layout design owner desires to grant a license conferring rights to utilize a protected integrated circuit layout design, such license may be assigned or transferred subject to approval by the Controller. Any assignment or transfer of a license shall require notification to the Controller within thirty days of execution and shall include details of the assignor, assignee, and the scope of the licensed rights being conveyed. The Registrar shall register proposed assignments of licenses only upon verification that the terms do not contravene any provisions under this Act relating to fair competition or anti-trust measures. Further, a license granted prior to registration of the layout design itself may be registered as an assignment if the original owner provides satisfactory evidence of their entitlement and the assignee consents in writing. The Controller may require additional documentation demonstrating due diligence regarding potential infringement risks associated with the licensed use.

Where an application to register a layout-design is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of rejection, have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal may be made on any ground including but not limited to allegations that the Registrar has erred in interpreting the provisions relating to originality or that the claimed layout-design does not infringe upon any prior registered design. The appellant shall demonstrate a prima facie case of error, and failure to do so will render the appeal frivolous. It is provided that the Tribunal may require the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating their claim before considering the merits of the appeal; otherwise, the application shall register proposed designs as deemed inadmissible.

An applicant seeking to secure protection for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall register proposed designs in accordance with the procedures outlined herein. Such registration shall be denied if the design incorporates elements substantially identical to a previously registered trade mark, unless it is demonstrated that such incorporation does not create confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical specifications and flowcharts illustrating the functionality of the integrated circuit layout-design as part of the registration process. Furthermore, an applicant shall provide a declaration affirming that they are the rightful owner of the intellectual property rights pertaining to the design, subject to any existing licensing agreements.

Any person who knowingly and wilfully infringes a registered layout-design shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the registrant, or an amount not exceeding five per cent of the aggregate worldwide sales of the infringing integrated circuit, whichever is higher. Furthermore, under this Act, any application for registration that contains false representations concerning prior use or publication shall be deemed invalid and subject to immediate revocation. The Registrar shall register proposed layout-designs only if they meet all stipulated criteria as provided herein; failure to disclose relevant information during the registration trade process will result in penalties. Repeated offences may attract criminal prosecution and imprisonment, as determined by a competent court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a person claiming right in an integrated circuit layout-design may enter into agreements for the grant of licenses relating to such design, including exclusive licenses, provided that such agreement specifies the field of exploitation permitted under the license. Any assignment or mortgage of a registered layout-design shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and shall include details regarding the assignor, assignee, and consideration paid. The Registrar shall register proposed assignments upon satisfaction that the transfer is lawful and does not prejudice existing rights granted under this Act. Furthermore, where an application for registration includes a specification patent addition relating to a novel feature of the layout-design, such addition shall be treated as part of the registered design for licensing purposes.

The proceeding appellate board established under this Act shall consist of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, and such other members as the Central Government may appoint, not being less than three in number, possessing expertise in intellectual property law, semiconductor technology, or related fields. The Board shall exercise jurisdiction to hear and dispose of appeals arising from orders passed by the Controller under this Act relating to layout-design registration, infringement proceedings, and civil remedies. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final subject to appeal to the High Court within a period specified herein, provided that such appeal is limited to questions of law only.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be refused under this Act if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout-design incorporates any protected design already registered, or for which an application has been filed, provided that such incorporation does not constitute independent creation. Any applicant aggrieved by an order of refusal made by the Registrar shall have the right to appeal to the proceeding appellate board. The Board shall hear appeals from the orders of the Registrar and may confirm, vary, or reverse any such order as it deems fit. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject only to judicial review under law.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Central Government may, if it is satisfied that sufficient cause existed, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period. The Appellate Board shall follow the procedure as nearly as may be, in accordance with the principles of natural justice and shall have power to determine the appeal de novo or on the evidence already brought before it. Subject to this Act, the board shall possess all such powers as may be necessary for the discharge of its functions; including the power to summon witnesses, examine them under oath, and require production of documents relevant to the inquiry. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding.

An appeal under this Act lies to the proceeding appellate board constituted under subsection (1) of section 37 from any order passed by the Registrar or the Controller. Such an appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the appellate board may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if it is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal in time and that the delay has not been undue or unwarranted. The Board shall follow such procedure as it deems fit, subject to the principles of natural justice, and shall have power to direct any party to produce documents or other evidence relevant to the inquiry. Decisions of the appellate board are final, but subject to further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of the order.

An appeal under this Act lies to the proceeding appellate board from any order passed by an adjudicating officer requiring the cessation of manufacture, sale or import of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit; provided that the appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall give notice to all concerned parties and opportunity for them to present their case in writing or orally, subject to such timelines as the Board may prescribe. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the proceeding appellate board may seek redressal under the provisions relating to writ jurisdiction in the High Court; however, no further appeal lies from the order of the Appellate Board except as provided herein regarding enforcement of its orders.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend such period for a further period not exceeding thirty days. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall be deemed sufficient ground for its rejection. The Board shall have power to impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each day of delay in filing the appeal. Decisions of the proceeding appellate board are final and binding, subject only to challenge under Article 226 of the Constitution; however, costs may be awarded at the discretion of the Board against any party found to have acted vexatiously or frivolously in bringing an appeal.

Where a layout-design owner grants a license conferring rights to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating their protected design, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to prior written consent from the licensor, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all terms and conditions of the original license agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or scope of an assignment under this Act shall be referred to the proceeding appellate board for determination. The board’s decision on such matters relating to assignments is final, subject to appeal only on grounds of legal error demonstrable in the record of proceedings before it. Further, a layout-design owner may assign their entire design rights, including all pending license agreements, with notification provided to all existing licensees as stipulated under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be filed in a form prescribed as provided herein and accompanied by a fee as determined by the Central Government. The Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear the appeal de novo and may pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. An order passed by the proceeding appellate board shall be final, but the aggrieved party may challenge the same under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the revocation of a grant patent for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board within sixty days from the date of such order. The board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to just cause and reasonable explanation. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing appeals may render the appeal inadmissible, at the discretion of the appellate board. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the proceeding appellate board may petition the Supreme Court under Article 136 of the Constitution.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit may be opposed by any person claiming an interest in a related earlier registered layout-design, or who alleges that the applicant has not complied with the requirements under this Act. Such opposition shall be made within three months from the date of publication of the application as notified in the Official Gazette. Upon receipt of such opposition, the matter shall be referred to a proceeding appellate board constituted for the purpose, and the Board shall give notice to both the applicant and the opponent. A member appellate board shall conduct hearings and consider evidence submitted by all parties involved before rendering its determination regarding the validity of the registration application.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be refused if the Controller is satisfied that the design incorporates unprotectable elements, or that it lacks sufficient originality as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order of refusal made under this Act may within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority. The appellate authority shall give notice to the applicant and the Controller, affording them opportunities for being heard. Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the appellate authority’s decision shall be final. An appeal under this Act shall not suspend the operation of the order appealed from unless the appellate authority directs otherwise.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or validity of a registered layout-design may prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such appeals shall be admitted only if the appellant deposits with the appellate authority such sum as may be determined by regulations framed by the Central Government, representing costs incurred by the respondent in defending the original order. The appellate authority shall hear the appeal de novo and pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the prescribed proceeding appellate authority may further appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of that order.

An appeal from any order passed under this Act may be presented to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Tribunal shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hold a prescribed proceeding appellate inquiry wherein both sides shall be afforded an opportunity for being heard and presenting relevant evidence. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the said order, subject to such fees as may be prescribed. The High Court shall hear appeals only on questions of law arising out of the interpretation or application of the provisions of this Act. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine its own procedure for conducting hearings and issuing directions related to the appeal process, provided that it adheres to principles of natural justice and fairness as mandated under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by that authority as provided herein, subject to further appeal to the High Court only on a question of law. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated period shall ordinarily preclude any subsequent challenge to the original order. The Appellate Authority may impose a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each day of delay in compliance with its orders, recoverable from the defaulting party as civil debt. Costs of the appeal shall be determined by the Appellate Authority and awarded as it deems just, considering the conduct of the parties involved.

Where a layout-design owner grants a license conferring rights to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating their protected design, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to prior written consent from the licensor, provided that the assignee becomes bound by all terms and conditions of the original licensing agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or scope of such assignment shall be referred to a prescribed proceeding appellate authority established under this Act for resolution. The authority shall consider representations from both the licensor and assignee and may order specific performance, damages, or injunctive relief as deemed appropriate. Further, an assignment made without the requisite consent is void; however, any good faith purchaser for value of such an invalid assignment shall retain rights proportionate to the consideration paid, subject to a claim against the assignor for recovery of that sum.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or concerning rectification proceedings believes that such order is manifestly erroneous in law or fact, he may prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate authority shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to be heard. Subject to this Act, the appellate authority may confirm, vary, or reverse the original order, or remand the matter for reconsideration. Provided that an appeal under this Act does not operate as a stay of execution of the order appealed against unless the appellate authority directs otherwise. The decision of the prescribed proceeding appellate authority shall be final and binding.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be opposed by any person claiming such right or interest as is provided herein. Such opposition shall be made within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application under this Act. Where an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall forthwith direct the applicant and the opponent to submit their pleadings in a prescribed proceeding appellate before the designated authority. The form petition for opposition shall contain particulars as specified by the rules framed thereunder, including details regarding the claimed right or interest and grounds for objection. The authority shall afford both parties an opportunity of being heard and may order discovery of documents relevant to the dispute.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the prescribed proceeding appellate authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate authority shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for them to be heard. Any party intending to support or oppose the appeal shall file a written submission along with relevant documents; it shall given affidavit verifying the truthfulness of contents thereof. Subject to this, the appellate authority may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final and binding. Provided that an appeal from the order of the appellate authority lies to the High Court within a further period of sixty days, on any ground of law.

A proceeding appellate under this Act is defined as a formal process initiated by an aggrieved party seeking review of an order passed by the Registrar or any other authority empowered to adjudicate disputes concerning layout-design rights. For the purposes of such a proceeding, “aggrieved party” includes but is not limited to the registered proprietor, a person claiming ownership through assignment or license, and any individual demonstrably prejudiced by the decision under review. The appellate body shall be constituted as provided herein and may entertain appeals only against orders relating to registration refusal, revocation, or infringement determinations. Subject to regulations prescribed, oral arguments may be permitted at the discretion of the appellate authority.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be refused if the Controller is satisfied that the design incorporates elements substantially copied from a previously registered layout-design, provided that such copying does not constitute a permissible adaptation as defined under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing registration or imposing any condition thereon shall have the right to prefer a proceeding appellate before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The tribunal shall follow the prescribed procedure for entertaining and disposing of appeals, including providing notice to all parties concerned and affording them opportunities for argument. Decisions rendered in such a proceeding appellate are subject to review by the relevant High Court as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, such person may prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. An appeal under this Act shall lie only on a question of fact or law arising out of the said order and not otherwise. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall admit appeals only if it is satisfied that the appellant has made out a sufficient case for the appeal to be admitted. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, the Tribunal may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the order appealed against or substituting it with an appropriate order. Any party aggrieved by any order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further prefer a proceeding appellate to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

An appeal from any order passed under this Act may be presented to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. Every appeal shall be in writing, stating the grounds on which it is based and accompanied by certified copies of the orders appealed against and all relevant documents relied upon. The Tribunal shall give notice to the respondent and opportunity for them to file their written submissions in response to the appeal, within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of service of such notice. Subject to this Act, the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may hear parties or any party appearing before it, and may pass such orders as it deems fit. The proceeding appellate shall be conducted fairly and impartially, with due regard to the principles of natural justice. Any order made by the Tribunal may be appealed to the High Court within a further period of sixty days.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or concerning rectification proceedings may prefer an appeal to the designated appellate authority, such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellant shall deposit with the registry a sum as determined by notification issued by the Controller, failing which the appeal shall not be entertained. Provided that the appellate authority may, upon application made in this behalf and after hearing the respondent, condone any delay in filing the appeal if satisfied with reasonable cause. Further, the appellate authority shall record reasons for its decision in writing, and such reasons shall be communicated to all parties involved in the proceeding appellate.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement or damages may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority within sixty days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum indicating the orders against which the appeal is brought and the grounds on which it is based, and shall be presented in six copies. The appellate authority may, after giving notice to all parties concerned, dismiss the appeal or pass any order modifying or reversing the original order as it deems fit. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to the filing of an appeal shall not preclude the appellate authority from considering the merits of the case, provided that sufficient cause is shown. The decision of a proceeding appellate authority shall be final and binding.

Where a layout-design owner grants a license conferring rights to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating their protected design, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the terms stipulated therein and provided that prior written consent of the licensor is obtained unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. Any assignment made without such consent shall be deemed void. Further, where an assignment includes the right to sublicense, the assignee shall notify the original layout-design owner within thirty days of the assignment’s execution detailing the scope and duration of the sublicensing rights granted. Disputes arising from assignments or attempted assignments may be referred for a proceeding appellate before a designated authority as provided herein. The authority shall have the power to determine the validity of such assignments and enforce the terms of any existing license agreements.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act is dissatisfied with such order, that party may prefer an appeal from the said order to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to that party and shall state specifically the grounds of appeal. The Tribunal may, in a proceeding appellate, entertain appeals relating to any matter arising out of decisions or directions made by an adjudicating officer under this Act concerning infringement of layout-design rights. Provided that the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may dismiss an appeal if it is satisfied that no substantial question of law has arisen and that the order appealed against does not suffer from any material irregularity.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement or validity of a registered layout-design, or concerning interlocutory matters arising in such proceedings, desires to appeal, he may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; however, the appellate authority may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of that period if it is satisfied that the delay was unavoidable and caused no prejudice to the respondent. The appellant shall deposit such fees as may be prescribed. Decisions regarding patentability considerations, particularly where layout-design features overlap with subject matter eligible for protection under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, are reviewable through this proceeding appellate process.

An appeal under this Act is deemed a proceeding appellate and shall be instituted within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged. For the purposes of such an appeal, the aggrieved party may submit written arguments and supporting documentation as prescribed by regulations framed hereunder. The manner applying appellate jurisdiction shall require that all appeals are first heard by a single member of the relevant tribunal, unless otherwise directed by the Chairperson. Decisions on interlocutory matters during the proceeding appellate shall be subject to review by the same tribunal. Further appeals from such decisions may only be entertained with leave granted by the tribunal.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be refused by the Registrar if it is determined that the design incorporates unprotectable elements or lacks sufficient originality, subject to the right of the applicant to initiate a proceeding appellate before the relevant authority. In such a proceeding appellate, the manner applying registrar’s previous assessment shall be carefully scrutinized for adherence to established guidelines and principles of fairness. The applicant shall furnish all pertinent documentation substantiating the claim of originality and demonstrating that the design is not substantially derived from prior art. Decisions regarding registration are final unless challenged through this process. The Registrar may require further clarification or amendments during the proceeding appellate, as deemed necessary.
