Any proprietor utilizing a certification trade mark shall be deemed strictly liable for ensuring adherence to the standards prescribed under this Act by all entities authorized to use said mark. Failure to maintain such compliance, or demonstrable evidence of deliberate misrepresentation regarding conformity with established criteria, constitutes an actionable offense. Upon conviction, the court may order immediate suspension of the proprietor’s rights in the certification trade mark and shall apply certification measures as a punitive remedy. Further, where wilful infringement is proven, the court directed forfeiture of all goods bearing the offending mark to the State Government for disposal, with proceeds remitted to the Trade Marks Registry.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused under this Act if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark in respect of goods or services identical to those for which the registration is sought, provided that such refusal may be overridden where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of application. The Registrar shall consider evidence submitted by the applicant regarding advertising expenditure, sales figures, and market surveys as relevant factors in assessing this acquired distinctiveness. Further, any representation made in the application concerning the nature or quality of the goods or services covered by the trade mark shall be deemed material for determining similarity under sections 28 and may form grounds for objection.

Where the proprietor of a trade mark has granted a license to use the trade mark under this Act, such license may be assigned by the licensee subject to the prior written consent of the grantor, provided that any assignment shall not operate to release the assignee from its obligations as defined in the original licensing agreement. Further, where an exclusive license is granted, the licensee shall have the right to assign the benefit of such exclusivity without requiring the proprietor’s consent, but must notify the proprietor in writing of their intention to do so at least thirty days prior to the assignment taking effect. The proprietor may, within that period, offer conditions relating to the continued use and protection of the trade mark. This provision regarding assignments shall not apply where the license is granted for a term less than one year; however, sections 28 concerning deceptively similar marks remain applicable in all circumstances.

Where an objection is taken to the acceptance of a proposed trade mark under this Act on the ground that it is deceptively similar or identical to an earlier trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry shall afford the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier trade mark an opportunity for cross-examination of witnesses and presentation of evidence. The Registrar may, after hearing both parties and considering any written submissions filed, determine whether the use of the proposed trade mark would likely deceive or cause confusion as provided herein under sections 28. Any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to further appeal to the appellate forum as prescribed.

Where a registered trade mark is infringed, the owner shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein, including an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts and damages for loss or injury suffered by the plaintiff. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the infringement and the profits derived by the defendant therefrom, subject to a ceiling not exceeding five times the value of the benefit accruing to the defendant from the infringement. It is provided that in cases involving wilful infringement, the Court may award exemplary damages at its discretion. The remedies available under this Act shall be without prejudice to any other right or remedy which the owner may have under clauses sub section of any other law for the time being in force.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark for specific goods or services, provided that the terms and conditions of such license are clearly defined in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, subject to prior written consent from the licensee, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a trade mark has been assigned, any existing license relating thereto shall continue in force as if the assignee were the original licensor, unless such license expressly provides otherwise. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party, inquire into the reasonableness of any clauses sub section within a licensing agreement and issue directions accordingly. Further, the proprietor shall be liable to account for royalties received from licensees under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "used falsifying trade" with respect to a registered trademark shall mean the application to any goods or services of a sign that is identical or confusingly similar to the said mark, and which creates a false or misleading impression as to the nature, quality, origin, or characteristics of those goods or services. Such use shall be deemed deceptive if it is likely to cause confusion among the public regarding the trade source of the goods or services. Nothing in this definition shall prevent the use of a sign that describes the applicant's goods or services, provided that such use does not constitute used falsifying trade as defined herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains elements likely to cause confusion with respect to earlier marks, and further, where the proposed mark incorporates a representation or device that is substantially similar to a registered trade mark used in relation to dissimilar goods, such use shall constitute used falsifying trade. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating clear distinction between the applied-for mark and any existing registrations, particularly if the similarity raises concerns regarding consumer deception. Provided that the applicant demonstrates a genuine and non-deliberate intention not to deceive or cause confusion, the application may proceed subject to limitations on the scope of protection granted.

Where a person, knowing that another’s registered trademark is connected in the minds of the public with particular goods or services, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar thereto in relation to dissimilar goods or services with the intention to mislead consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, such use shall constitute used falsifying trade. The owner of the registered trademark may institute legal proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of the said used falsifying trade, including loss of profits and any damage to reputation caused thereby. Further, a court may grant an injunction restraining the person from continuing such infringing conduct. It is provided that the right to claim damages shall not arise unless the owner proves actual financial detriment attributable to the misleading use.

Where a person, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark in relation to goods or services not authorized by the proprietor of the mark, such use shall be deemed to constitute used falsifying trade. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party, issue notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to submit representations within thirty days. Failure to respond adequately to the notice, or where the response is unsatisfactory, the Registrar may proceed ex parte. Evidence pertaining to the similarity of the signs and likelihood of confusion shall be considered by the Registrar. Any goods bearing a mark constituting used falsifying trade are liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark has established a reputation in relation to specified goods or services, no person shall use any sign or mark, or any mode of presentation thereof, that is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark and which, when used in relation to goods or services not authorized by the proprietor, creates a false impression regarding the nature, quality, origin, or suitability for purpose of those goods or services. This prohibition extends where such use constitutes used falsifying trade, being an imitation intended to deceive consumers into believing that the goods or services originate from, or are approved by, the registered proprietor. Provided that this restriction shall not apply if the defendant demonstrates clear and conspicuous differentiation sufficient to preclude consumer confusion, as determined under this Act.

Where a person, with intent to deceive and for fraudulent gain, uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark in relation to goods or services, constituting used falsifying trade, such person shall be guilty of an offence. The offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods the subject of the offence are deemed contraband and shall be seized by enforcement officers. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including mandatory confiscation of assets derived from the infringing activity, as provided herein. The Registrar may issue an injunction restraining further use of the mark upon application by the registered proprietor.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark grants a license permitting the use of the mark upon specified goods or services, such license may include provisions relating to the assignment of rights arising from instances of used falsifying trade. The licensee shall be deemed to hold assignable rights in respect of any action brought under this Act against a third party for infringement predicated on the licensee’s unauthorized application of the registered trade mark, provided that such application constitutes used falsifying trade and directly results from a breach of the licensing agreement. Further, the registered proprietor may, by written consent, authorize the licensee to assign these rights to another entity, subject to conditions stipulated within the assignment deed. Any such assignment shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry for evidentiary purposes and shall not prejudice the original proprietor’s right to pursue remedies against infringers independent of the license or subsequent assignment.

Where a proprietor establishes that another has employed deceptive practices in connection with registered trademarks, and such practices involve the use of a sign substantially identical to the trademark in relation to dissimilar goods, creating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods, the aggrieved party may petition the relevant intellectual property tribunal for injunctive relief. This right shall be subject to the respondent demonstrating that their use constitutes fair dealing under this Act and does not amount to used falsifying trade. Provided that any finding of used falsifying trade requires clear and convincing evidence establishing intent to deceive or capitalize on the reputation associated with the registered trademark, appeals may be made to the appellate forum within sixty days of such a determination.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark licenses another party to use such trade mark, and that licensee subsequently assigns their rights under the license agreement to a third party, the assignment shall be deemed valid only if the assignee provides written notification of said assignment to the Trade Marks Registry. Such notification must include details of both the original licensor, the initial licensee, and the subsequent assignee, as recorded in the computer inspection register maintained by the office. Failure to provide such notification will render the assignee’s use of the trade mark vulnerable to claims of used falsifying trade, particularly where the assignment materially alters the scope or nature of the licensed activities. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify authenticity and prevent fraudulent assignments, provided that this does not unduly delay the processing of legitimate transfers.

For the purposes of this Act, "used falsifying trade" with respect to a registered trade mark shall mean the application to goods or their packaging of a sign identical or confusingly similar to that trade mark, where such use is made in a manner calculated to mislead the public as to the origin or nature of those goods. This includes instances where the infringing sign incorporates elements of an international registration sub designating India, even if the primary indication originates elsewhere. Nothing herein shall prevent genuine and reasonable use of the sign by another person for describing those goods, provided that such use is not used in a deceptive manner or to take unfair advantage of the reputation connected with the registered trade mark.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a trade mark in respect of goods, and the proposed trade mark incorporates or comprises a representation that is identical or confusingly similar to a protected geographical indication as defined under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating due cause for such inclusion. Furthermore, any person who falsely applies goods with a sign likely to be mistaken for a registered trade mark, or where such application creates a false and misleading impression regarding the nature, quality, or origin of those goods, shall be deemed to have contravened this Act. This prohibition extends to instances where the use is intended to take unfair advantage of, or prejudice, the distinctive character or reputation of the earlier trade mark.

Where a person falsely applies goods with a sign identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark, and such application is made without the consent of the proprietor of the trademark, that person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the extent of the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the deceptive use, including but not limited to lost profits and damage to reputation. Further, any goods bearing such false application are deemed infringing goods under this Act. The proprietor may apply to the Court for an injunction restraining the person from further falsely applying goods or disposing of them. Provided that, where the false application is made in good faith and without knowledge of the existence of the registered trademark, the Court may reduce the amount of damages awarded.

Where a person falsely applies goods with a sign identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark, such application shall constitute an offence under this Act. The proprietor of the trademark may institute proceedings for infringement and seek remedies as provided herein, including but not limited to damages and injunctive relief. Any officer of a company, or any director, manager, secretary, or other similar official thereof, who is shown to be privy to, or knowingly concerned in, such false application shall also be deemed guilty of the offence and subject to penalties. The Tribunal may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating consumer confusion arising from the deceptive use, order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. Further, any person found guilty of falsely applying goods is liable to a fine which may extend to rupees five lakhs, and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark has established that another person falsely applies goods with a sign identical or confusingly similar to the said registered trademark, and such application is made without consent, the aggrieved proprietor may petition the relevant intellectual property tribunal. The tribunal shall consider whether the use of the mark creates a likelihood of confusion among consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods. It must also be demonstrated that the falsely applied sign exploits the reputation connected with the registered trademark to gain an unfair commercial advantage, or is detrimental to its distinctiveness. Provided that the proprietor can satisfy these conditions, relief may include an injunction restraining further false application and damages proportionate to the loss suffered.

Where any person falsely applies goods with a sign identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark, and such application is made without the consent of the proprietor of the trademark, that person shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also to a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees; or both. Further, any goods so falsely applied are subject to seizure and destruction by order of the Controller General. The proprietor of the trademark may also apply to the Commercial Court seeking an injunction restraining further acts of false application, alongside damages for losses incurred as a direct result thereof, provided that evidence of such loss is presented.

For the purposes of this Act, “falsification” with respect to a registered trademark shall mean the reproduction, imitation, or adoption of such trademark in connection with goods or services that are identical or confusingly similar to those associated with the registered mark, without authorization from the owner. A person falsifies trade where they create a representation intended to deceive consumers into believing there is a commercial association between their goods or services and the proprietor of the registered trademark. This shall include alterations or modifications which retain substantial deceptive similarity. Provided that, nothing in this definition shall apply to uses that constitute fair use under established legal principles.

Where the Registrar has reason to believe that any person is engaged in the manufacture, importation, sale or offer for sale of goods bearing a mark used in relation to goods or services for which a trade mark is registered under this Act, and that such use constitutes a falsifies trade mark, he may direct such person to appear before him at a time and place specified in the direction. The direction shall specify the grounds upon which the belief is based and provide the party concerned with an opportunity of being heard. If, after affording such opportunity, the Registrar finds that the mark does indeed falsify the registered trade mark, he may issue an order prohibiting further use of the infringing mark, subject to any conditions he deems fit to protect the interests of the proprietor of the registered trade mark and ensure fair competition.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark becomes aware that another person is using a sign in the course of trade in relation to goods or services, and such use constitutes a falsifies trade mark, the proprietor may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts. Such proceedings shall be directed towards seeking an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing the deceptive practice, as well as claiming damages for losses suffered by the proprietor attributable to the infringement. The amount of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the injury caused and the profits derived by the infringer, subject to a minimum award as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Provided that, where the falsifies trade mark is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or characteristics of the goods or services, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the Court.

Where a person, with intent to deceive, reproduces marks identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark and offers for sale, distributes, or advertises goods or services in relation to which the said trade mark is registered, such action shall constitute falsifies trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by evidence of such reproduction and deceptive intent, issue a notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to appear before the relevant adjudicating officer at a time and place specified therein. Failure to appear or provide satisfactory explanation as provided herein may result in an ex parte order being passed against the infringer. Any goods bearing the falsified trade mark shall be liable for seizure and destruction under this Act, subject to due process of law and affording the alleged infringer opportunity to be heard.

Where a registered trade mark is affixed to goods in such a manner as to create a likelihood of confusion amongst the public regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods, and it is established that such affixation constitutes a falsifies trade mark, the proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. This entitlement subsists provided that the defendant has acted with knowledge, or ought reasonably to have had knowledge, that the registered trade mark was being so affixed. Further, where the falsification involves the use of a colour scheme substantially similar to that associated with the registered trade mark, demonstrating intent to deceive, damages may be awarded to compensate for loss of reputation and goodwill suffered by the proprietor. The Registrar may also order the destruction of goods bearing the falsified mark.

Where any person knowingly and willfully falsifies a registered trade mark with the intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services, such person shall be guilty of an offence. This offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, any goods the subject of the falsified trade mark are liable to seizure and forfeiture. The owner of the registered trade mark may also institute civil proceedings for damages sustained as a direct result of the act that constitutes the falsifies trade mark.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark becomes aware that another person is using a sign in the course of trade in relation to goods or services, and such use constitutes a falsifies trade mark, the proprietor may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be directed towards seeking an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing said deceptive practice, alongside claims for damages sustained as a direct consequence of the infringement. It is provided that the respondent in these proceedings may present evidence demonstrating honest and contemporaneous intent to adopt a similar sign, lacking knowledge of the prior registration; however, this defense shall not be entertained if the proprietor can demonstrate demonstrable consumer confusion arising from the use. The tribunal’s decision regarding such matters shall be subject to appeal under this Act.

Where a person, with intent to deceive, falsely represents that goods or services are connected with any registered trade mark, and such representation is of a nature likely to injure the reputation of the owner of the trade mark, that person shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into account the extent of the deception caused, the loss suffered by the trade mark proprietor, and any profits made by the offending party as a result of the falsifies trade mark. Further, under this Act, an injunction may be granted restraining the person from continuing such deceptive practices. It shall binding on the defendant to cease all use of the falsely represented trade mark immediately upon service of the order. Any goods bearing the false representation are subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein.

Goods seized under this Act by Customs Officers shall be deemed to be in the custody of the Central Government and subject to verification as potentially infringing registered trade marks. Upon suspicion that imported goods bear a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, the Customs Officer may detain the consignment pending determination of validity. The owner of the registered trade mark shall be notified immediately by the Customs Authority detailing the particulars of the suspected infringement, including photographs and relevant documentation. Such notification shall provide an opportunity for the trademark proprietor to submit evidence supporting their claim within thirty days. Following this period, a decision regarding seizure or release will be made by the designated Customs Appellate Tribunal, considering all submitted materials and applicable precedents under this Act and the 112 customs act.

Goods infringing a registered trade mark, as determined under this Act, are deemed counterfeit goods. The owner of the registered trade mark may apply to the appropriate authority for an order directing the confiscation of such counterfeit goods and any materials used in their production or packaging. Confiscation goods clause shall be interpreted to mean that where goods are seized pursuant to a search warrant obtained under provisions relating to inspection, seizure and detention, these goods are subject to immediate provisional confiscation pending final adjudication. Provided that, the authority may, after giving notice to the concerned parties, order their destruction or disposal as deemed fit, in accordance with rules framed for this purpose.

Where any goods are seized pursuant to a warrant issued under this Act in respect of alleged infringement of a registered trademark, such goods shall be deemed to be in the custody of the enforcement officer executing the warrant. The owner of the trademark may apply to the High Court for an order directing the disposal of the seized goods, provided that such application is made within ninety days from the date of seizure. Upon receiving such application, the High Court shall give notice to the person from whose possession the goods were seized and afford him a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The confiscation goods clause provides that any goods determined by the High Court to be infringing copies shall be liable for destruction, sale or other disposal as the court may direct, with due regard to the nature of the goods and their potential for further infringement.

Where goods bearing a registered trade mark are found to be in the possession of any person under circumstances which suggest that those goods are intended for use or sale otherwise than as permitted by the proprietor of the trade mark, the Adjudicating Officer may order the confiscation of such goods. The proprietor shall provide evidence demonstrating both the infringing nature of the goods and the suspect’s intent to engage in unauthorized commercial activity. Any person whose goods are subject to a confiscation order may appeal that order before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of notification of the order. Such an appeal shall be heard expeditiously, and the Tribunal's decision shall be final. The confiscation goods clause applies irrespective of whether any civil proceedings for infringement have been initiated under this Act.

Goods bearing counterfeit or otherwise infringing trademarks, whether found at the place where the offence was committed or elsewhere, are deemed contraband and subject to confiscation under this Act. Any person involved in the production, importation, distribution, sale, or exposure for sale of such goods shall be liable to prosecution and penalties as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify categories of goods particularly vulnerable to trademark infringement and prescribe enhanced seizure procedures for these items. Upon conviction, courts shall order the destruction or disposal of confiscated infringing goods, ensuring that their subsequent re-entry into commerce is prevented. This confiscation goods clause applies irrespective of whether a civil suit for damages has been initiated.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark reasonably believes that goods bearing an infringing mark have been imported and are held in possession by any person with intent for sale or distribution within the territory of India, such proprietor may apply to the Customs Authority for orders relating to the confiscation of those goods. The Customs Authority shall, upon receiving such application and after due consideration of evidence presented, determine whether the goods are indeed subject to the confiscation goods clause as provided herein. Any party possessing a license or assignment related to the trademark in question shall be deemed an interested party and entitled to participate fully in any proceedings concerning the determination of confiscation. The proprietor may further grant sub-licenses for the disposal of confiscated goods, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where any goods are seized at a customs port pursuant to information received regarding infringement of a registered trademark, the Customs Officer effecting such seizure shall immediately notify the Registrar of Trade Marks. The Registrar shall then provide written intimation to the proprietor of the trade mark in question, detailing the nature and quantity of the infringing goods seized, along with particulars of the seizing officer and the port involved. Any person aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to goods detained at a customs port may file an appeal before the Appellate Authority as provided herein. The Appellate Authority shall consider any submissions made by the proprietor of the trade mark, the importer, and the Customs Department. Decisions of the Appellate Authority are subject to review by the High Court. Further, seizure proceedings under this Act relating to goods imported in violation of section 112 customs may be initiated based on reasonable suspicion.

Where any goods are seized by customs officers pursuant to a suspicion of infringement of a registered trade mark, such seizure shall be subject to verification as provided herein. The Customs Officer effecting the seizure shall immediately notify the owner of the registered trade mark and provide them with particulars relating to the detained goods, including quantity, description, and port of entry. Upon receipt of this notification, the trade mark owner may submit evidence demonstrating either the infringing nature or the non-infringing nature of the imported goods. If, following such submission and further investigation, the Customs Officer determines infringement has occurred, the goods shall be dealt with under section 112 customs, subject to any orders issued by the relevant adjudicating authority.

The owner of a registered trade mark may grant a license to any person enabling them to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to conditions agreed upon in writing and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Such licenses shall be assignable along with the underlying trade mark ownership, provided that notice of assignment is duly recorded as prescribed herein. Where infringement of the registered trade mark occurs through importation of goods bearing an unauthorized use of the mark, customs officers are empowered to detain such goods pending verification under this Act and in accordance with procedures established by the Central Government. Any party holding a valid license shall be entitled to pursue remedies for infringement against any person utilizing the mark without authorization, including actions relating to seizure of infringing imported goods as per section 112 customs.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all assignments and licenses relating to registered trademarks, including notations regarding any sub-licenses granted subsequent to the initial assignment. Any party seeking to assign or license a registered trademark shall file with the Registrar a certified copy of the agreement, which shall be indexed alongside the original registration details. The registrar index registered trademarks according to the terms specified in such agreements and may require additional information deemed necessary for clarity regarding royalty structures or territorial limitations. Provided that the assignment or license does not conflict with any existing rights under this Act, the Registrar shall decide upon its validity and record it accordingly. Failure to properly register an assignment will render it unenforceable against third parties claiming prior good faith reliance on the registrar index.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all patents granted under this Act. This registrar index shall include, for each patent, its registration number, the title of the invention, the name and address of the patentee, the date of grant, and a concise abstract summarizing the subject matter claimed. Further, the registrar index shall indicate any subsequent modifications to the patent, such as assignments or licenses, as recorded under this Act. Any person may inspect the registrar index and obtain certified copies thereof, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, electronically searchable, detailing all patents granted under this Act. This index shall include particulars relating to the patentee’s name and address, the title of the invention, the filing date of the application, the grant date, and the claims as initially registered. Any subsequent amendments or modifications to the registered claims shall also be recorded within the registrar index, clearly indicating the nature and date of such alterations. The public may access this registrar index for a prescribed fee, subject to restrictions imposed to protect confidential information relating to pending applications. Further, the Registrar may, at their discretion, provide certified copies of entries in the registrar index upon payment of an additional fee.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, alongside corresponding information regarding their classes of goods or services. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from inaccuracies or omissions within the registrar index may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification; such petitions must specify the nature of the error and its detrimental impact on the petitioner’s legal interests. The Board shall have the power to direct the Registrar to amend the registrar index accordingly, provided that any amendment does not adversely affect existing rights holders without due process. Further, a person aggrieved by a refusal to grant access to information contained within the registrar index may appeal such decision to the Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstration of legitimate need for said information.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, digitally accessible to all applicants and members of the public, detailing particulars of every design registered under this Act. This index shall include, but not be limited to, the registration number, the title of the design, the name and address of the proprietor, the class specification according to the international classification scheme, and the date of registration. Applications for inspection of entries in the registrar index may be made to the Registrar, who shall provide access subject to payment of a prescribed fee. The Registrar may, at any time, correct or amend any entry in the registrar index if it appears to contain an error or omission, provided that such correction does not prejudice the rights of any proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a correction or amendment made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, electronically searchable, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act and those applications currently undergoing examination. This index shall include, for each entry, the trademark itself, the applicant’s name and address as filed, the goods or services specification associated with the mark, and the date of registration or filing, respectively. Any alteration to these particulars following initial submission requires notification to the Registrar, who may update the registrar index accordingly, provided that such alterations do not fundamentally alter the nature of the trademark or its designated scope. The public shall have access to this registrar index during normal office hours, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by the Registrar to prevent disruption and ensure data security.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, alongside corresponding details of applicants whose registrations remain pending. Any party demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from inaccuracies or omissions within the registrar index may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for rectification; such petitions must specify the nature and extent of the alleged harm. Failure to rectify demonstrably erroneous entries within a period of ninety days following receipt of a valid petition shall render the Registrar liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable from the Government’s contingency fund. Furthermore, wilful suppression of information pertinent to the registrar index constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, including particulars of ownership and associated licensing agreements. Any proprietor seeking to assign or license rights in a registered trademark shall file with the Registrar a notice specifying the scope of such assignment or license, including details of the assignee or licensee’s identity and permitted use. Such notices shall be recorded within the registrar index as an addendum to the original registration record, publicly accessible subject to reasonable restrictions regarding confidential business information. Further, any subsequent modification or termination of a licensing agreement must also be notified to the Registrar for recording in the index. Failure to properly update the registrar index concerning assignments and licenses may render such agreements unenforceable against third parties acting in good faith upon the public record.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, alongside those applications currently undergoing examination or opposition. This index shall be publicly accessible for inspection during normal office hours, subject to regulations prescribed by the Trade Marks Rules Committee. Any party aggrieved by an entry, or omission thereof, in the registrar index may within sixty days of such publication file a notice of objection with the Registrar, specifying the grounds for challenge. The Registrar shall then provide the applicant or registered proprietor concerned an opportunity to be heard before determining whether amendment or rectification is warranted; decisions made under this process are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, detailing all trademarks registered under this Act, including particulars of ownership and goods or services associated with each mark. Any party aggrieved by an entry, or omission thereof, in the registrar index may, within sixty days from the date such index is made publicly available, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appellate tribunal shall consider any evidence submitted by the appellant demonstrating material error or demonstrable prejudice arising from the inaccuracy of the registrar index. Provided that, a decision regarding the accuracy of entries in the registrar clause section relating to geographical indications shall be subject to further review under provisions concerning specialized designations as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, electronically searchable, detailing all plant breeder’s rights granted under this Act. This index shall include particulars relating to the denomination of the variety, the name and address of the issued breeder, the class of plants concerned, and the date of registration. Applications for rectification of entries in the registrar index may be made by any person aggrieved, subject to a prescribed fee and demonstrating sufficient cause for alteration. The Registrar may, upon receiving such an application, direct that the relevant entry be amended or expunged, provided that due notice is given to the issued breeder concerned. Information contained within the registrar index shall be accessible to the public during normal office hours as provided herein.

An *index registered* is deemed to include, but not be limited to, particulars relating to the applicant’s name and address as filed under this Act, the goods or services for which registration is sought or has been granted, the date of application and any subsequent amendments thereto, and a representation of the mark itself. The Registrar shall maintain such *index registered* in an electronic form accessible to the public subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by regulations framed under this Act. Information contained within the *index registered* may be used for statistical analysis and enforcement purposes as provided herein; however, personal data shall be handled in accordance with applicable privacy legislation.

An application for registration of a mark shall be refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to an existing *index registered* trademark, subject to provisions regarding permissible modifications as provided herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use after the date of prior registration where similarity exists but does not preclude registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to refusal under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, an application for rectification challenging the validity of a registered trademark shall be deemed vexatious if it is based solely on grounds discoverable through examination of the *index registered* and publicly accessible records maintained by the Registrar.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings alleging infringement under this Act, they shall provide to the defendant within thirty days of service of the writ or summons, a certified copy of the register entry showing their *index registered* in respect of the impugned mark. Failure to comply with this provision shall not preclude the proprietor from pursuing such remedies but may render them liable for costs incurred by the defendant as a consequence of the delay. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party and after due notice to the proprietor, direct the rectification of the register if it appears that an entry is falsely represented or contains incorrect particulars relating to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the relevant High Court as provided herein.

An application for rectification of a registered trade mark may be made to the Registrar by any person claiming interest, subject to provisions regarding frivolous or vexatious applications as provided herein. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such an application, serve a copy thereof on the proprietor of the trademark and afford both parties an opportunity of being heard in respect of the grounds alleged in the rectification proceedings. Where the rectification sought involves challenging the validity of the registration itself, the applicant shall be required to furnish security for costs as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct that evidence be submitted in writing or require oral hearings to be conducted. A record of all such rectification applications and their disposition shall be maintained within the *index registered*, accessible for public inspection under prescribed conditions.

An application for rectification of a registered trade mark may be made by any person claiming interest, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees, alleging that the registration has been obtained fraudulently or contrary to law, or that the use of the trade mark is likely to cause confusion in relation to goods or services. Where such an application relates to an entry appearing in the index registered, the Registrar shall serve a copy thereof upon the proprietor of the trade mark. The proprietor may then file a counter-statement within the time specified under this Act. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines shall render the application void, provided that the Registrar considers the delay has prejudiced the opposing party’s ability to respond adequately.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, knowingly makes use of a mark identical or confusingly similar to an *index registered* trademark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act and liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the trademark. Such offender may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, or both, as determined by the relevant court. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and shall be seized and destroyed at the expense of the infringer, without compensation. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all enforcement actions taken under this provision.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to grant licenses relating to the use of their mark, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee, provided that any such license agreement expressly identifies the specific goods or services for which the right to use is granted. Where an index registered trademark has been assigned, the assignee shall possess all rights pertaining to licensing previously held by the assignor, including but not limited to existing license agreements and the ability to grant further licenses consistent with the terms of assignment. The Registrar may require a copy of any material license agreement relating to an index registered mark to be filed for public record, ensuring transparency in commercial dealings concerning protected trademarks. Any party seeking to enforce the terms of such a license shall have standing under this Act.

Where any person alleges that a registered trade mark is being used contrary to the provisions of this Act, or that the use thereof is likely to be detrimental to the interests of the proprietor, such person may file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consider whether the alleged infringing activity constitutes a genuine and reasonable challenge to the validity of the index registered trade mark, taking into account factors including but not limited to the duration of the use, the extent of consumer confusion likely caused thereby, and any evidence presented demonstrating demonstrable harm to goodwill. It is provided that the proprietor of the index registered trade mark shall be afforded an opportunity to present counter-evidence under this process.

An *index registered* in relation to integrated circuits shall comprise particulars of each circuit design registered under this Act, including but not limited to the name and address of the claimant, the date of registration, a representation of the circuit layout, and any associated marks or symbols affixed thereto. The Registrar may require that such representations be presented in both physical and digital formats as deemed necessary for efficient record-keeping. This *index registered* shall be maintained with due diligence and made accessible to the public subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential information relating to national security or trade secrets, provided that access may be granted upon application and payment of a prescribed fee.

An applicant seeking registration of a plant variety shall submit, along with the application, a proposed index registered designation comprising a unique alphanumeric code reflecting the species, lineage, and distinctive characteristics as determined by the Agriculture Commissioner. This index registered designation shall be subject to approval by the Registrar, who may reject it if deemed confusingly similar to existing designations or failing to adequately differentiate the plant variety. The applicant’s right to use the approved index registered designation is contingent upon successful registration under this Act and shall be renewable every ten years, provided that continued compliance with varietal purity standards is demonstrated through periodic inspection reports submitted to the Registrar. Any alteration of the approved designation requires prior consent from the Registrar.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act against any person using, without due cause or consent, a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to their index registered trademark. Such use may constitute infringement, and the proprietor may apply for an injunction restraining the infringing activity, as provided herein. Where the alleged infringer has, in the course of trade, employed language or designs that are descriptive but do not directly incorporate the index registered trademark, a court shall consider whether such usage creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services. An invention far claimed within an advertising campaign utilizing the infringing mark may be considered as aggravating circumstances when determining damages. The Registrar may also order the erasure of any registration obtained through fraudulent means related to this infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, "index names registered" shall mean a publicly accessible record maintained by the Registrar containing the alphabetical listing of all entities formally recognized as owners or licensees of intellectual property rights pertaining to plant varieties. Such index names registered shall include both individual proprietors and corporate bodies, alongside their associated registration numbers and geographical areas of protection granted under this Act. The information contained within the index names registered may be inspected by any person during office hours, subject to regulations prescribed by the Registrar regarding access and reproduction. Any alteration or addition to an index name registered requires prior notification and approval from the Controller General.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours subject to any restrictions deemed necessary by the Registrar to protect confidential commercial information. Applications for registration of index names shall be examined in accordance with established procedures and may be refused if they are deemed deceptive or likely to cause confusion with existing trademarks. The register shall clearly indicate the goods or services associated with each registered index name, along with the date of registration and any subsequent modifications or renewals as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration or rejection of an index name may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection during normal office hours subject to payment of prescribed fees. Applications for registration of index names shall be examined in accordance with procedures analogous to those applicable to trade mark applications, including assessment of distinctiveness and potential for confusion with existing marks. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of an index name may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar shall publish notices concerning accepted and rejected applications in the Trade Marks Journal, as provided herein. Furthermore, any alteration or deletion of entries relating to registered index names requires prior notification to the affected parties and adherence to prescribed protocols for rectification proceedings.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours subject to applicable fees as prescribed by regulations. Any person seeking to ascertain whether a particular index name is registered may request a certified copy of the relevant entry from the registrar, upon payment of the stipulated fee. The registration of an index name shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of its initial registration and may be renewed for successive periods of ten years each, provided that renewal applications are filed within the prescribed timeframe and accompanied by the requisite fees. Furthermore, any alteration to a registered index name requires prior approval from the Registrar and adherence to guidelines concerning phonetic or visual similarity to existing marks.

The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any person aggrieved by the inclusion or omission of a name within an index of registered trade marks, initiate inquiries to ascertain the veracity of such grievance. Such inquiries shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, affording all parties concerned an opportunity for hearing and representation. Where it is determined that an entry in the index names registered is erroneous or misleading due to misrepresentation by the applicant during registration proceedings, the Registrar may direct its rectification or removal from the index. An appeal against any such direction shall lie to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication, subject to a stay on operation of the order pending disposal of the appeal unless otherwise directed by the Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing all index names registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection subject to any reasonable restrictions deemed necessary by the Registrar to protect sensitive commercial information. Applications for registration of index names shall be examined in accordance with established procedures and principles applicable to other trade mark registrations. A basic registration of an index name confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the index name in connection with the goods or services specified in the register, preventing unauthorized adoption by competitors. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the registration or refusal of an index name may appeal under this Act to the relevant intellectual property appellate body. The Registrar may require applicants to provide further documentation substantiating their claim of distinctiveness for registered index names.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive index names registered as proprietary identifiers for goods and services, accessible to the public upon payment of prescribed fees. Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in this index may file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of publication of the relevant notice under this Act. The Tribunal’s decision shall be final subject to further appeal to the High Court. Where a registered trade mark is involved in legal proceedings concerning ownership, the Registrar shall provide certified copies of entries in the index names registered as evidence upon request by either party and payment of applicable charges. This provision does not preclude reliance on other documentary or testimonial evidence; however, such index entries carry significant evidentiary weight. The owner copyright case relating to derivative works incorporating these identifiers may seek clarification from the Tribunal regarding permissible usage.

For the purposes of this Act, an *index registered trade* shall be deemed to include any mark that has been entered on the Register of Trade Marks in accordance with the provisions herein relating to registration. Such entry shall constitute conclusive evidence of the proprietorship of the said mark, subject to any rectification proceedings initiated under this Act. The Registrar may, at his discretion and from time to time, publish extracts from the index registered trade for public information. Any person seeking to ascertain the status of a particular trade mark shall be entitled to inspect the relevant portion of the Register maintained by the Registrar as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include particulars sufficient to identify clearly the goods or services with which the index registered trade is associated, and such identification must conform to classes as prescribed by the Regulations. The Registrar may require any applicant to furnish further details concerning the nature and extent of use of the proposed trade mark prior to acceptance, particularly where there exists a likelihood of confusion with an earlier registration. Where an application relates to multiple goods or services, the fees payable shall be determined according to the number of classes involved. Any alteration to the representation of a registered trade mark must be notified to the Registrar and approved as provided herein before it takes effect.

Where a proprietor of an *index registered trade* institutes proceedings alleging infringement under this Act, the Court may grant such remedy or remedies as it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of representation, damages for loss sustained by the proprietor, and delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the extent of the injury suffered and the benefit thereby accruing to the infringer, provided that in cases where the infringement was committed wilfully or with knowledge of the prior registration, enhanced damages may be awarded. Further, any person found to have made false representations concerning the goods or services of another through use of a similar mark shall be liable for compensation to the injured party.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive index registered trade mark database, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing particulars relating to each registered trade mark including but not limited to the applicant’s name, address for service in India, goods or services for which registration is sought, and the date of registration. Any person may inspect this index registered trade mark database upon payment of a prescribed fee. The Registrar shall provide certified copies of entries from the index registered trade mark database to any party requesting them, subject to payment of an additional certification fee as determined by notification issued under this Act. Applications for amendment or rectification relating to particulars recorded in the index may be filed with the Registrar and shall be processed according to procedures prescribed herein. The Registrar may, at his discretion, publish extracts from the index registered trade mark database in such manner as he deems appropriate to facilitate public awareness of registered trademarks.

An application for rectification of a registered trade mark may be made by any person claiming interest, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees, alleging that the index registered trade is deemed unentitled to protection under this Act. Such applications shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to instances of generic usage or deceptive similarity to prior marks. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence supporting the allegations made in the application; failure to do so within a stipulated period will result in its rejection. Further, any proprietor of a trade mark appearing on the index shall be entitled to file a counter-statement responding to the rectification proceedings. The Registrar shall provide both parties with an opportunity for hearing as provided herein.

Any person who, knowing that a particular mark is an *index registered trade* or deceptively similar to such a mark, uses any trademark in contravention of this Act shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to fine. Further, where the use of a trademark constitutes a violation as provided herein, the proprietor of the *index registered trade* may apply to the relevant court for an injunction restraining such use, together with damages sustained by reason of that infringement. The court shall have power to order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the infringing mark, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing being afforded to the defendant.

The proprietor of an index registered trade mark shall be deemed to hold a valuable right, assignable in whole or in part, subject to any conditions stipulated within the original registration certificate. Any assignment under this Act requires notification to the Registrar within three months of execution and shall be recorded by him as evidence of transfer. Furthermore, a license granted concerning an index registered trade mark may include provisions restricting territorial scope or specific goods and services covered, provided that such restrictions are clearly defined in the licensing agreement and filed with the Registrar for public record. The Registrar may refuse to register any assignment or license if it appears to prejudice the interests of consumers or unfairly limits competition within the relevant market segment. Any subsequent transfer of a licensed index registered trade mark shall be subject to the original terms unless otherwise agreed upon by all parties involved, as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark, including but not limited to decisions concerning the invalidity or revocation of such registration. The Tribunal may entertain an appeal only if the appellant demonstrates that they have suffered material prejudice as a result of the decision appealed against; provided that this shall not preclude appeals regarding entries in the index registered trade marks, where the accuracy of said entry directly impacts the enforceability of rights under this Act. The Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall give notice to all parties affected by the appeal and may direct any party to produce documents or other evidence relevant to the determination of the appeal.

An index registered trade mark, once certified as eligible for renewal under this Act, shall remain listed within the public register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry until such time as the proprietor formally requests its removal or the expiry period is reached. The Registrar may, upon receiving a written application from a proprietor seeking to maintain an index registered trade mark beyond its initial term, require submission of evidence demonstrating continued use and distinctiveness in accordance with established guidelines. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence within the stipulated timeframe shall result in automatic delisting. Furthermore, any published expiry period pertaining to an index registered trade mark is deemed conclusive for all purposes under this Act unless successfully challenged through appropriate legal proceedings.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure, uses a mark identical or confusingly similar to an *index registered trade* in connection with goods or services for which that trade mark is registered shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The effect registered trade enjoys protection against dilution even where there is no direct competition between the proprietor of the registered trade mark and the alleged infringer.

The proprietor of an index registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee; provided that any such license agreement must explicitly state the geographical territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the index registered trade mark. Further, a proprietor intending to assign their entire interest in an index registered trade mark shall provide prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the proposed assignee and the scope of assignment. Such assignments may be facilitated through adherence to procedures consistent with those outlined under the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks, allowing for streamlined international extensions of protection where applicable. The Registrar may require undertakings from assignees regarding continued compliance with this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “matters included register” shall mean particulars relating to a trade mark as are required to be entered into the Register of Trade Marks under this Act. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the name and address of the applicant, a representation of the trade mark, a statement of limitation of goods or services in relation to which it is registered, and the date of application for registration. Further, matters included register shall also encompass any modifications or amendments made to these particulars as permitted under this Act, provided that such modifications do not alter the essential character of the original trade mark.

Applications for registration shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain whether the mark is distinctive and not deceptive. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark or any other relevant matter. Where an application relates to a composite mark consisting of words, devices, or three-dimensional features, the representation of each element shall be clearly delineated in the application. Matters included register are subject to periodic review by the Registrar and may be amended or removed if they no longer comply with the provisions of this Act or any rules made thereunder. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to matters included register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person infringing his right under this Act and recover damages sustained by him as a consequence of such infringement. Where an application for registration is refused, or a registered trade mark is subsequently cancelled, any person who, prior to the date of refusal or cancellation, had used the trade mark in India without reasonable cause shall be liable to pay compensation to the applicant or former proprietor, as the case may be. The amount of such compensation shall be determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, taking into account factors including the extent of use and any resulting goodwill damage. Matters included register are subject to periodic review; the Registrar may direct removal if use has ceased for a continuous period exceeding five years.

Applications for registration of marks shall be examined by the Registrar to determine whether they are opposed under this Act. Any person who believes that a mark applied for is identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark, or to any prior use having reputation, may file a notice of opposition with the Registrar within four months from the date of advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar shall serve a copy of such notice on the applicant and provide them an opportunity to submit their response as provided herein. Upon consideration of the opposition and the applicant’s reply, the Registrar may direct the hearing of the matter before an appointed officer. Decisions regarding matters included register are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all oppositions filed and their respective outcomes.

Applications for registration of marks shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain whether the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others and complies with the provisions relating to registrability. The Registrar may, prior to acceptance of an application, require the applicant to amend the representation of the mark or the designation of goods or services if such amendment would bring the application into compliance with this Act. Any proposed amendments shall be communicated to the applicant for their consent. Matters included register are subject to periodic review by the Registrar and may be removed if they fail to meet continued requirements regarding distinctiveness, use in commerce, or other criteria as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an entry relating to a trademark in the register, or by any matter affecting the registrability thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which such entry was made or became known to him, whichever is earlier. The Board shall have power to entertain and determine appeals against orders of the Registrar refusing registration, directing deletion from the *matters included register*, or concerning rectification of entries. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during appeal proceedings may result in dismissal. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days, subject to a penalty of five thousand rupees for delay beyond that period. The Registrar shall enforce these provisions diligently.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively within specified territories or for particular goods or services. Such licenses may be granted freely, but any assignment of the registration itself requires prior consent from the Registrar, obtained through submission of an affidavit provided by both the assignor and assignee confirming their agreement to the transfer. The Registrar may, after due consideration, refuse such consent if it deems the proposed assignment detrimental to consumers or unfairly restricts competition within the relevant market segment. Matters included register shall be updated accordingly upon notification of any such assignments. Further, sub-licensing is permissible provided that the primary license terms are adhered to and a record of all sub-licenses is maintained for inspection by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be deemed an *application corrected* where the Registrar, following examination under this Act, identifies deficiencies or omissions within the originally submitted documentation. Such deficiencies shall include, but are not limited to, inaccuracies in the description of goods, inadequate representation of producers’ consent, or failure to comply with prescribed formatting requirements as provided herein. The applicant shall be afforded a period of ninety days from the date of notification to rectify these identified issues and resubmit the application accordingly. An *application corrected* shall be treated as a fresh submission for the purposes of further examination.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar rejecting an application for registration, or requiring amendments thereto, may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider any documents submitted in support of the appeal and may direct the Registrar to reconsider the matter. If, following reconsideration, the Registrar maintains the original decision, the Appellate Board shall determine the appeal according to principles of natural justice. Where an application for registration is deemed deficient under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a single opportunity to submit a corrected application addressing the deficiencies identified by the Registrar. Such *application corrected* must be received within sixty days from the date of notification of the deficiency and shall constitute the final version for consideration.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar rejecting an application for registration of a geographical indication, or requiring amendments thereto, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any documents filed in support of or opposing the appeal and may direct the Registrar to reconsider any aspect of the decision under appeal. Where an application has been rejected due to deficiencies identified by the Registrar, the applicant may submit a revised application addressing those deficiencies; this is deemed an *application corrected* for the purposes of further consideration. The Registrar shall then examine the corrected application as if it were originally filed and may proceed with examination or registration subject to any other requirements under this Act. Any appeal against a decision relating to an application corrected shall be made within the same time limits applicable to appeals from initial rejection orders.

An application for registration of a geographical indication submitted under this Act shall be deemed an *application corrected* where the Registrar, following examination and prior notice served upon the applicant detailing deficiencies or non-compliance with the provisions herein, receives a response from the applicant within the stipulated period. Such response must address all points raised by the Registrar and demonstrate adherence to prescribed standards for distinctiveness and traceability of goods originating from the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation if the submitted correction remains ambiguous or incomplete. Provided that the corrected application satisfies all requirements as provided herein, it shall proceed towards consideration for registration; otherwise, rejection proceedings will be initiated.

Where an applicant submits a corrected application following notification under this Act regarding deficiencies, the Registrar shall review said correction solely for compliance with the formal requirements of Form GI-1 and related documentation. Any alteration to the description of goods or the geographical area claimed beyond what is strictly necessary to rectify identified errors shall render the corrected application deemed abandoned, and the prescribed fee forfeited to the Government. Furthermore, any person aggrieved by a decision regarding an *application corrected* may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, subject to payment of the stipulated appellate fee; failure to comply with this timeframe shall preclude all avenues for redressal under this Act.

An owner of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant exclusive licences relating to the use of the said indication for goods conforming to the standards specified under this Act; provided that any such licence granted shall not extend to uses which are detrimental to the quality or reputation of the geographical indication. Further, an application corrected following objections raised by the Registrar concerning the scope of permissible uses may be assigned in whole or in part, subject to prior approval from the Geographical Indications Registry and upon notification to all interested parties as determined by the Registry. Such assignment shall not prejudice existing rights under any licence granted before the date of assignment; however, subsequent licensees shall be bound by any conditions imposed on the original owner relating to quality control measures for goods bearing the geographical indication.

Where an applicant submits a corrected application following notice under this Act regarding deficiencies identified by the Registrar, such correction shall not constitute a new application but shall be treated as a continuation of the original submission; however, if the alterations introduced render the initial claim substantially different from that originally presented, the Registrar may deem it to represent a fresh application and require payment of the prescribed fee anew. Any party aggrieved by this determination concerning an *application corrected* may within sixty days of publication of the Registrar’s order file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.
