The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted by both the applicant and any interested parties, provided that such evidence relates directly to the scope of the alteration and its impact on distinctiveness as defined herein.

An applicant whose geographical indication is initially rejected under this Act may submit a corrected application addressing the reasons for rejection communicated by the Registrar. Such an application corrected shall be treated as a fresh application and subject to all requirements applicable at the time of its filing, including payment of prescribed fees. The Registrar shall then consider the corrected application de novo. Any party possessing a legitimate interest in opposition to the geographical indication may file an opposition within the period specified under this Act from the date of advertisement of the corrected application as if it were an original application. The Registrar shall give due notice and opportunity of being heard to all interested parties before making any decision on the validity of the corrected application.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Geographical Indication” shall mean an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. The civil court registrar appointed under this Act shall exercise jurisdiction relating to applications for registration and subsequent proceedings concerning Geographical Indications, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Such registrar may require applicants to furnish such documentation substantiating the connection between the goods and their specified origin as he deems necessary. Further, the registrar shall maintain a register of all registered Geographical Indications accessible for public inspection.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the civil court registrar designated by the State Government for that purpose. The applicant shall provide detailed particulars regarding the history and characteristics of the goods or products associated with the proposed indication, including maps delineating the geographical area of origin. Any interested party may file an objection to the application within three months from the date of publication under this Act; such objections will be adjudicated by the civil court registrar after providing due opportunity for hearing to both the applicant and the objector. The registrar shall record his findings and reasons for decision, which shall be final subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication shall file an application with the civil court registrar having jurisdiction over the area where the alleged erroneous registration occurred. Such application must specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and state clearly the grounds upon which it is based, including any evidence demonstrating misleading use or unfair competition arising from the registration. The civil court registrar may direct any party seeking to oppose such rectification to file their response within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of notice. Failure to respond shall be deemed as acquiescence to the application. Any order made by the civil court registrar under this Act is subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the order.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the civil court registrar designated by the State Government for that purpose. The registrar is empowered to require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documents relating to the application and may direct amendments to be made where necessary, provided such directions are communicated in writing to the applicant within thirty days of receipt of the application. Any party aggrieved by a direction issued under this Act may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The civil court registrar shall maintain a register of applications and registrations, accessible for public inspection during normal business hours. Decisions of the Controller on appeals are final subject to further appeal to the High Court. The Registrar is obligated to provide copies of any documents in the register upon payment of prescribed fees.

Applications for registration of a geographical indication shall be submitted to the civil court registrar designated by the State Government for that purpose. The applicant must provide detailed documentation substantiating the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of the goods linked to the indicated geographical origin; this includes verifiable historical records and demonstrable production methods unique to the specified territory. Provided that any challenge to the distinctiveness of a proposed indication may be raised before the civil court registrar by any interested party within sixty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The civil court registrar shall afford all parties an opportunity for hearing, subject to procedural rules as prescribed herein and may require further evidence or clarification at any stage.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication shall file an application with the civil court registrar having jurisdiction over the area where the alleged infringement occurred. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar shall serve notice upon all parties affected by the proposed rectification, affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard under this Act. Failure to comply with any order issued by the Registrar regarding production of evidence or attendance of witnesses may result in penalties as determined by the civil court registrar, including fines not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term up to six months. The Registrar’s decisions concerning enforcement are subject to judicial review only on grounds of legal error.

The owner of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of that indication on goods conforming to the standards established under this Act. Such licenses may include authorization for manufacture, processing, packaging, distribution, or sale, provided that the terms and conditions are clearly defined in writing and filed with the civil court registrar within thirty days of execution. Any assignment of a geographical indication or any license granted thereunder shall also be registered with the said registrar, accompanied by prescribed fees. The registrar may refuse registration of an assignment or license if it appears to contravene the public interest or prejudices the quality and reputation associated with the geographical indication. Further, sub-licensing is permitted only with prior written consent from the owner, recorded with the civil court registrar.

Appeals against decisions of the civil court registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a geographical indication shall lie to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Provided that where any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the rectification of the Register, including amendments to descriptions of goods or alterations to boundaries of a defined geographical area, believes such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may prefer an appeal directly to the High Court. The civil court registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the dispute to the Appellate Board or the High Court upon request. Any interlocutory orders made by the appellate authority or the High Court shall be binding on the civil court registrar.

Any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the register disclosed shall have the right to appeal to the civil court registrar within sixty days from the date on which such entry was entered register disclosed. The appellate authority, being the civil court registrar, may entertain appeals only if they are accompanied by a fee as prescribed under this Act. Failure to pay said fee will render the appeal inadmissible. Any order made by the civil court registrar in disposing of an appeal shall be final, subject to further appeal to the High Court within ninety days thereafter. Knowingly making false statements or representations in connection with any appeal before the civil court registrar shall attract penalties as provided herein, including fines and imprisonment.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication for goods conforming to the standards of quality and characteristics prescribed under this Act. Such licenses may include provisions regarding royalty payments and duration, subject to approval by the civil court registrar prior to their enforcement. An application permit amendment concerning the scope or terms of a previously granted license shall be submitted to the registrar in writing, detailing the proposed changes and justification for such modification. The registrar may require further documentation demonstrating continued adherence to established quality standards before approving any amendment. Assignment of rights pertaining to geographical indications, including licensed usage, requires registration with the registrar and is valid only upon confirmation of compliance with conditions stipulated herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Geographical Indication” shall mean an indication identifying goods originating from a place where a quality, reputation or other characteristic is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. The civil court registrar appointed under this Act shall be deemed to be a local authority for the exercise of all powers necessary for facilitating hearings and managing evidence presented before them. During any house parliament session, the Registrar may request additional support staff from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry to expedite proceedings related to applications for registration or oppositions thereto, provided that such requests are approved by the Secretary.

Any proprietor seeking remedies against an action proceeding infringement of a registered geographical indication shall file a suit directly with the civil court registrar having jurisdiction over the territory where the alleged infringement takes place. The registrar shall be empowered to order interim injunctions and other conservatory measures, provided that such orders are reported immediately to the High Court for confirmation within thirty days. Failure to obtain such confirmation will render the order unenforceable. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the civil court registrar may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of the order. The High Court shall consider all evidence presented and determine whether the alleged use constitutes a misuse likely to cause dilution or misrepresentation of the registered geographical indication as provided herein.

The Register may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, serve notice to the applicant requiring payment of any prescribed fees or surcharge due under this Act. Such notice shall specify the amount outstanding and provide a period not exceeding thirty days within which the deficiency must be remitted. Failure to comply with the notice will render the application liable to rejection, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Central Government may, from time to time, revise the fees surcharge prescribed for various processes under this Act through notification in the Official Gazette.

Any proprietor seeking to maintain registration of a geographical indication may apply for renewal under this Act, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent as provided herein. Failure to submit the prescribed application and accompanying documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall render the geographical indication liable for removal from the Register of Geographical Indications. In instances where an application for renewal is filed after the expiry date but prior to the lapse of six months thereafter, a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the original registration fee shall be payable. This fees surcharge prescribed under this Act aims to discourage undue delay in renewal processes and ensure timely maintenance of registered geographical indications. Any person aggrieved by an order removing a geographical indication from the Register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such order.

The Register may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, issue a provisional acceptance notice subject to verification of compliance with the provisions herein. Any applicant failing to submit all prescribed documents within thirty days from the date of the provisional acceptance notice shall be deemed to have withdrawn their application and no further action will be taken without fresh application and payment of requisite fees. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a surcharge on any fee payable under this Act where an application or document is filed after the due date. This surcharge shall not exceed twenty-five percent of the original fee amount. Any appeal against an order passed by the Registrar regarding the assessment of such fees surcharge prescribed must be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, accompanied by the appellate fee as determined by the Central Government.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is filed after the expiry of the prescribed time limit under this Act, or where any documentation submitted with such application is found to be incomplete or deficient, the Registrar may, subject to conditions as provided herein, accept the application upon payment of a surcharge. This surcharge shall be equivalent to fifty percent of the registration fee initially stipulated and payable at the time of filing. Further, if the applicant fails to rectify deficiencies within thirty days from the date of notification by the Registrar, the application shall stand rejected. Any appeal against an order rejecting an application due to non-compliance with these provisions is subject to a further fees surcharge prescribed by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed fee” means any sum specified as a *paid fee payable* under regulations framed by the Central Government and published in the Official Gazette; such fees shall be applicable to all applications for registration of geographical indications, renewals thereof, and proceedings before the Geographical Indications Registry. The amount of the prescribed fee may vary based on factors including, but not limited to, the class of goods or services associated with the indication, the applicant’s status as a smallholder producer group, and whether an application is filed electronically. Any fees due shall be remitted in accordance with rules made under this Act.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee, and no application will be entertained unless such fee has been duly remitted. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentation relevant to establishing distinctiveness and origin as provided herein, and any additional requests will necessitate payment of an ancillary processing fee. Failure to submit all required information alongside the initial paid fee payable shall result in rejection of the application without further notice. Any alteration or amendment proposed by the registrant after registration is subject to a separate assessment and requires remittance of a revised fee before consideration. The Registrar may, at his discretion, waive fees for applications from recognized producers' cooperatives operating within the claimed geographical area.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act may institute legal proceedings for relief against acts constituting infringement or any use likely to be confused with, or detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of, the registered geographical indication. Such remedies shall include an injunction restraining further infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to limitations prescribed regarding contributory infringement. Where a notice of demand is served upon an infringer failing to comply with such a notice, the proprietor may recover from the infringer reasonable compensation representing the unpaid fee payable for the use of the geographical indication. The Central Government may, on application by any aggrieved party, order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing false indications or marks.

The Register may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, issue a notice to interested parties inviting objections, provided that such notice shall specify the particulars of the proposed geographical indication and the class under which it falls. Any objection received shall be forwarded to the applicant along with a copy thereof, and the applicant shall have opportunity to file its response within the time specified therein. Following consideration of any objections and responses filed, the Register may proceed with examination as provided herein. The fee payable for publication of such notice in the Official Gazette shall be determined by notification issued by the Central Government from time to time. Failure to remit the paid fee payable at the prescribed rate will result in suspension of proceedings until full payment is received. Any appeal against an order passed under this Act requires the remittance of a further fee, as detailed in the First Schedule.

An application for registration of a geographical indication under this Act shall be accompanied by a non-refundable initial fee as prescribed; provided that an applicant demonstrating financial hardship, certified by a recognized authority, may apply for a waiver of such initial fee, subject to review and approval by the Registrar. The continued processing of an application is contingent upon timely payment of subsequent examination fees, due within thirty days of notification under this Act. Failure to remit these fees shall result in suspension of proceedings until all outstanding amounts are cleared. Any appeal against a decision concerning registration requires payment of a prescribed appellate fee payable before the appeal will be entertained. The Registrar may require proof of remittance for any paid fee payable prior to proceeding with further action.

Any proprietor seeking to institute proceedings under this Act for alleged infringement of a registered geographical indication shall first deposit with the designated authority, an amount equivalent to twenty-five percent of the assessed damages suffered, as a prerequisite for the acceptance of such proceedings. Failure to comply with this provision will render the application inadmissible. The said sum is deemed a paid fee payable towards administrative costs and serves as security against frivolous claims. Provided that, if the court finds in favour of the proprietor, the deposited amount shall be refunded without interest. Any person found to have acted in bad faith or maliciously in initiating such proceedings may face penalties under the relevant criminal code.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may grant exclusive licenses to third parties for specific uses relating to goods or services authorized under this Act, provided that such license agreements are documented and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. Any assignment of rights in a registered Geographical Indication shall require prior consent from the Central Government, obtainable upon submission of a detailed proposal outlining the proposed assignee’s capabilities and intended use. The fee payable for registration of an assignment is determined according to the prescribed scale, as amended from time to time. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee must be explicitly stated in the original license agreement and shall attract a further paid fee payable to the Registrar, calculated as a percentage of the sub-licensee’s turnover derived from the licensed goods or services.

The Register may, upon receiving an application for registration of a geographical indication, issue a notice to interested parties inviting objections to the proposed registration, provided that such notice shall clearly state the amount of the paid fee payable for lodging an objection. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Register regarding the acceptance or rejection of an objection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted by either the applicant, the objector, or any other interested party and may direct the Register to reconsider its determination concerning the paid fee payable for processing the appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, “prescribed fee” means any sum specified as a *paid fee payable* under regulations framed by the Central Government, and such fees shall be subject to adjustments determined periodically based on prevailing economic conditions. The amount of prescribed fee applicable for registration of a geographical indication shall include an initial application fee and subsequent renewal fees, both payable at intervals as notified. Failure to remit any prescribed fee within the stipulated timeframe will render the application or registration liable for cancellation. Any dispute regarding the assessment or collection of such fees may be referred to the Appellate Board, whose decision the *chairperson appellate board* is empowered to make binding.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee payable to the Geographical Indications Registry. The applicant shall furnish particulars demonstrating exclusive use of the name or sign, and evidence establishing its link to the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of goods originating from the defined geographical area. Where an application relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, liquors, spices, cereals, or processed horticultural products, it shall apply geographical boundaries with precision. The Registry may require further documentation substantiating these claims and a paid fee payable for each additional document submitted. Any alteration of the proposed name or boundary requires a fresh application and associated fees as determined by regulations under this Act.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act against any infringement shall be entitled to seek remedy for damages sustained by reason of such infringement, provided that the amount of damages shall not exceed three times the value of the goods or services sold bearing the geographical indication. Further, where a notice of opposition is filed and subsequently withdrawn, the applicant shall be entitled to recover from the opponent a paid fee payable representing costs incurred in defending the application during the period of opposition. The Registrar may, upon receiving proof of such costs, issue an order directing the opponent to pay the sum so determined. Any variety registered as a geographical indication shall enjoy protection against use by any person who is not authorized to do so, and unauthorized use will be deemed unfair competition.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the defined geographical area comprising all lands with an elevation not less than one thousand feet above mean sea level and within a specified boundary delineated under regulations framed by the Central Government; such production shall include plucking, processing, sorting, grading, presenting, and packaging. The term “defined geographical area” includes any subsequent modifications to said boundaries as may be notified in the Official Gazette. Any use of the indication "Darjeeling Tea" or any deceptive use thereof shall act as an infringement under this Act. This Act shall binding on all persons involved in the production, processing, distribution, and sale of tea within the defined geographical area.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society or other organization engaged in production and processing of goods, or by collectives representing such producers. Such an application shall contain particulars as prescribed, including but not limited to, the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, a map of the area indicating its boundaries, and a statement of the characteristics and qualities of the goods attributable exclusively to their origin. The Registrar may require further information or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any person claiming an interest in relation to the proposed registration shall have the right to file representations against the application, subject to such fees as are determined. This Act shall binding on all persons involved in the production, processing and trade of goods originating from a registered geographical indication.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act against any alleged infringer shall file a suit in the High Court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the infringement has occurred or is likely to occur. The remedies available to the proprietor, subject to such terms as the court may deem just, include an injunction restraining the infringing activity, damages sustained by the proprietor due to the infringement, and the delivery up of any goods bearing the registered Geographical Indication for destruction. Further, where the infringer has made a false representation that the goods or services originate from a place other than the registered geographical indication area, the court may order the erasure of such false representation. This Act shall binding on all persons, both Indian and foreign, engaged in trade or commerce relating to goods or services affected by a registered Geographical Indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed, including but not limited to details regarding the name of the collective body or organization proposing registration, the area of production of the goods, and a map indicating the boundaries of that area. The Registrar shall issue an examination report within three months from the date of receipt of the application, detailing any objections raised under this Act. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the examination report, file representations against the registration. These representations shall be considered by the Registrar and a hearing shall be afforded to all parties concerned. The decision of the Registrar following such consideration shall be final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This Act shall binding on all persons seeking to utilize or apply a geographical indication in commerce without due authorization.

Any collective body seeking registration of an indication as a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes must demonstrate, through verifiable documentation, that such indication identifies goods originating in the specified region of Konkan Maharashtra and possesses qualities, reputation or other characteristics attributable exclusively to the said origin; provided that the application shall include a detailed map delineating the geographical boundaries of the area from which the goods originate. Further, any use of the registered geographical indication by persons not authorized under this Act shall be deemed an infringement, and such act shall binding on all courts exercising jurisdiction in matters relating to intellectual property rights. The Registrar may require submission of additional data substantiating these claims prior to granting registration, as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice under this Act, uses any indication falsely purporting to be the Geographical Indication of Kanchipuram Silk sarees, or applies such mark to the packaging or labelling of goods not conforming to the standards prescribed herein, shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to a penalty of one lakh rupees for the first instance and two lakhs rupees for each subsequent instance. The Registrar may, ex parte, issue an injunction restraining any person from making use of or applying the Geographical Indication in contravention of this Act. This act shall binding on all producers, traders, and retailers involved in the production, distribution, and sale of Kanchipuram Silk sarees; failure to comply will result in prosecution under relevant provisions.

Any proprietor seeking to grant a license in respect of an indication registered under this Act shall, prior to such grant, furnish a detailed memorandum to the Registrar outlining the scope and duration of the proposed license, including any restrictions imposed upon the use of the geographical indication by the licensee. Such licenses may be granted for specific goods or classes of goods, as determined by the proprietor, provided that the terms and conditions are clearly defined within the licensing agreement. The act shall binding on all licensees to adhere strictly to these stipulated conditions; failure to do so will render the license liable for revocation. Assignment of rights relating to a registered geographical indication requires prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignee and assignor, and is subject to approval as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer must also be reported in like manner.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs may be filed with the Registrar, specifying the name of the indication and the geographical area comprising the territory where such goods are produced. The application shall include particulars regarding the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which identify the goods as originating from that area, along with a map of the defined geographical boundary. Any person claiming to represent the interests of the producers of the indicated good may apply for registration, provided that they demonstrate adequate representation under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections. The gene fund shall be utilized for supporting research and development activities related to the preservation and promotion of registered geographical indications. This act shall binding on all persons involved in the production, processing, or trade of goods bearing a registered geographical indication.

Any proprietor seeking to prevent use of a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards set out in the registration certificate, shall file an application with the Registrar detailing the infringing activity and providing evidence thereof. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such application, issue notice to the alleged infringer in the manner issuing notice under this Act, affording them a period of sixty days within which to submit their response. Failure by the alleged infringer to respond within that timeframe, or if their response is deemed unsatisfactory by the Registrar, shall be considered conclusive evidence of infringement. The proprietor shall then be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. This act shall binding on all persons engaged in production, processing, packaging, sale, import, export or use of goods bearing a registered geographical indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society or other organization engaged in production and processing of goods emanating from the territory to which the geographical indication relates, or by collectives representing such producers. Such an application shall be accompanied by certified true copies of documents establishing the conditions under which the good is produced, processed, and prepared within the defined geographical area, including details regarding traditional knowledge relating to that process. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claim of origin and distinctiveness of the goods. An applicant shall furnish such additional information as the Registrar deems necessary for examination of the application. This Act shall binding on all persons seeking to utilize a protected geographical indication without authorization, and any attempt to do so will be deemed an infringement under this Act. The Registrar’s decision regarding acceptance or rejection of an application is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, “plant variety” means a class of plants which possess a common characteristic, distinguishable from other classes of plants, and includes any group deriving from such class through propagation. A plant variety shall be deemed distinct if, when propagated under substantially uniform conditions, it is clearly differentiated from all other known varieties based on its expression of heritable characteristics. The determination of distinctness shall consider the stability of these characteristics over successive generations. Subject to this, a plant variety may also include transgenic plants where the genetic modification does not alter the fundamental nature of the plant variety as defined herein.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars as to its denomination, title, and repository number, along with details regarding the breeder or registrant. The application must also specify the source variety, if applicable, and provide a comprehensive description of the plant variety’s characteristics, conforming to the guidelines prescribed by the Authority. Any technical data substantiating the distinctiveness of the plant variety shall be submitted as an annexure to the application. Provided that, where the applicant is a farmer claiming rights over a landrace or locally adapted plant variety, documentation establishing lineage and cultivation history may suffice in lieu of extensive technical data, subject to verification by the Authority. The Registrar may require further information deemed necessary for assessment under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of protection granted for a plant variety, or concerning the imposition of conditions restricting farmer’s rights pertaining to the saving and exchange of propagating material, has grounds to believe that such order was manifestly unjust or based on an erroneous interpretation of the law, he may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall admit appeals only if it is satisfied that a prima facie case exists warranting consideration; provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the original decision. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal to the High Court within ninety days of its communication. Failure to comply with conditions imposed on farmer’s rights concerning plant variety propagation may render the infringing party liable for damages as determined by a civil court.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed by the Register, including particulars relating to its origin, method of reproduction, and any known uses. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the proposed plant variety is distinct, uniform, and stable. Where an objection is raised against the novelty or stability of a plant variety under this Act, the applicant may submit counter-evidence within the time specified by the Register. The Register shall consider all submitted evidence and issue a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the application. Any person aggrieved by such an order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Register may require further trials or observations concerning the plant variety’s characteristics before making a determination regarding its registration, provided that these are conducted in accordance with established protocols.

A plant variety shall be deemed eligible for registration under this Act only if it is demonstrated to possess stability exhibiting uniformity across successive generations, subject to naturally occurring variations. The application for registration must include detailed documentation pertaining to the method of propagation employed and a comprehensive description of its distinctiveness relative to commonly known varieties. Provided that any applicant demonstrating prior use of the plant variety by farming communities for at least three years preceding the date of application may be granted an exemption from certain novelty requirements, as provided herein. Further, evidence substantiating the absence of adverse effects on the environment resulting from cultivation of the plant variety shall accompany the submission and be subject to review by the relevant authority.

Any person who knowingly markets a plant variety infringing upon the rights of the registered breeder shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing sales, recoverable by way of suit in a District Court. Furthermore, where an unregistered entity is found to have engaged in activities constituting biopiracy concerning a protected plant variety, such as unauthorized collection and commercial exploitation of germplasm without prior informed consent, they shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees. The Authority may issue orders restraining the manufacture, sale, or importation of any infringing material. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act will attract daily penalties until compliance is achieved, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered holder of rights in a plant variety may grant licenses for the commercial exploitation of that plant variety. Such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and may cover specific geographical areas or particular uses relating to the propagation or sale of seeds or other planting material derived from the plant variety. The terms of any such license shall be recorded in writing and registered with the Plant Varieties Registration and Farmers’ Rights Authority, providing details regarding royalty rates and duration. Assignment of rights in a plant variety is permissible, but requires prior notification to the Authority, who may inquire into the fairness and transparency of the transaction. Any subsequent licensee or assignee shall be bound by any restrictions previously imposed under this Act concerning farmer's privilege relating to saved seed.

Where any person alleges that a plant variety has been obtained through means otherwise than by breeding or hybridization, or where the distinctiveness of a plant variety is challenged based on its genetic composition, such allegation or challenge may be referred to the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Authority. The Authority shall provide both parties with an opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence pertaining to the method of derivation and phenotypic stability over successive generations. Decisions regarding essential characteristics and whether a plant variety is essentially derived from another are subject to review under this Act, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from any error apparent on the record. The Authority’s determination shall be final, barring appeals solely concerning questions of fact to the High Court.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has failed to disclose all information relevant to the assessment of novelty and distinctiveness, as provided herein. Further, an application may be rejected where it is demonstrated that the claimed plant variety does not conform to the prescribed criteria regarding stability of its characteristics across successive generations, or if evidence suggests that the variety’s genetic composition deviates significantly from previously published descriptions. The Registrar shall also refuse register assignment if it appears that the applicant has misrepresented any fact concerning the origin or breeding history of the plant variety, and such misrepresentation materially affects the assessment of eligibility under this Act.

A “variety registered” shall mean a plant variety which has been formally recognized and recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties maintained under this Act. For the purposes of this Act, a "variety registered" is deemed to possess distinct characteristics conforming to the description as specified in the registration certificate; such conformity shall be assessed by reference to the essential derivation criteria established herein. The holder of rights pertaining to a “variety registered” may exercise those rights subject to any conditions stipulated during the registration process and provided that any subsequent modifications affecting the distinctive features do not invalidate the original registration.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming rights over a registered variety may apply for registration of plant propagating material derived from such *variety registered* as a distinct variety. The application shall specify the characteristics of the derived material and demonstrate its traceability back to the original registered variety. Such registration is subject to an examination confirming that the derived material maintains essential traits consistent with the parent *variety registered*, without introducing substantial alterations affecting its identity or stability. An applicant seeking registration of propagating material may be required to submit samples for testing at a designated authority, as provided herein. The Central Government shall maintain a record of all registrations pertaining to derived plant propagating material.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of registration of a *variety registered* under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant materials and hear arguments from both the appellant and the Authority whose decision is being appealed. Any infringement upon the rights associated with a registered variety, including unauthorized commercialization or offering for sale without due authorization, shall be actionable as a civil wrong. Compensation for damages resulting from such infringement may include monetary relief commensurate with lost profits and reasonable attorney's fees, as determined by the Board. Further, the Authority may issue injunction orders to restrain continuing acts of infringement, provided that evidence of substantial harm is presented.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, an application for registration as a *variety registered* shall be accompanied by such particulars relating to its denomination, origin, method of breeding, stability, distinctness, uniformity and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses as the Authority may prescribe. The applicant shall furnish true copies of relevant documentation pertaining to the variety’s development, including details of any prior disclosures or publications concerning the same genetic material. Upon receipt of an application, the Authority shall publish a notification inviting objections from the public within a period specified herein. Any objection received shall be considered by the Registrar who may afford the applicant an opportunity for rebuttal. The decision of the Registrar regarding such objections is final and binding subject to appeal under this Act.

Subject to the provisions regarding farmers’ rights, any application for registration of a plant variety shall include detailed documentation demonstrating distinctness and stability across three generations or equivalent periods as determined by the Authority. The applicant must provide evidence confirming that the proposed denomination conforms to guidelines established under this Act and does not mislead concerning the variety's characteristics or origin. Furthermore, prior public use of the plant material constituting the *variety registered* shall be disclosed in the application, with supporting documentation establishing the date and geographic location of such use. The Central Government may require additional testing at designated institutions to verify these claims before proceeding with examination. Any challenge to the registration based on non-compliance with these requirements may be raised within a prescribed timeframe as provided herein.

Any person who produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports or exports any propagating material of a *variety registered* without authorization from the holder of the rights conferred by registration shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Authority. Such damages shall not be less than five times the value of the infringing material and may extend up to ten times such value, subject to considerations of the extent of harm caused to the registrant. Further, any person found guilty of contravention under this Act relating to a *variety registered* shall also be liable for prosecution before a court competent to try offences, where they may face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not exceeding one million rupees. The Authority may issue injunctions as provided herein to restrain further infringement.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, any person holding a certificate of registration for a variety registered under this Act may grant licenses conferring rights to use propagating material derived from such variety. Such license shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to conduct activities relating to production, sale, or distribution. The grantor retains full ownership of the variety registered and may impose conditions restricting the scope of the licensed rights, including limitations on subsequent assignments by the licensee. Any assignment of a license granted under this Act shall be recorded with the Authority and shall be binding upon all successors in title. Provided that no license shall grant rights inconsistent with the breeder’s right to retain control over essential derivation data pertaining to the variety registered. The Central Government may, as provided herein, intervene where licensing terms unduly restrict farmer's access to propagating material.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration of a plant variety, or revoking a certificate of registration for a *variety registered* under this Act, may within sixty days from the date of such order file an application seeking review. Such application shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board may entertain any such application if it is satisfied that no sufficient opportunity was given to the applicant for presenting his case, or that the findings of fact in the original decision are not supported by substantial evidence. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction act.

Subject to appeal under this Act, any person seeking to obtain rights relating to a *variety registered* shall file an application with the Authority in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must specify the denomination of the variety and details regarding its essential derivation or modification. Upon receipt of such an application, the Authority may direct the publication of notice thereof, including particulars of the applicant licence publish, for a period not exceeding three months from the date of the direction. Objections to the grant of rights, if any, shall be considered by the Authority after affording the applicant and the objector an opportunity of being heard. The Authority’s decision on such objections shall be final. Further, the Registrar may require submission of additional data or information deemed necessary for assessing the novelty and distinctiveness of the variety.

Any person who, without due cause and after reasonable notice from the Registrar, continues to propagate, sell, or offer for sale any plant material derived from a *variety registered* under this Act shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Authority. Such compensation shall not exceed five times the value of the infringing material and may include damages sustained by the registrant due to loss of market share. Further, an applicant intending to file an *international application form* for protection of a variety shall provide a certified copy of the Indian registration certificate along with the prescribed fee. Failure to disclose this information or providing false particulars relating thereto constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine as provided herein.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, where a variety registered under this Act is developed by an institution funded wholly or substantially by public funds, the rights pertaining to such variety shall vest initially with that institution. However, the registering authority may, upon application from said institution, specify rights assigned by the institution to any third party, including but not limited to commercial entities engaged in agricultural research and development. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and Registrants, detailing the scope and duration of the licensee’s privileges concerning production, sale, and distribution of propagating material derived from the registered variety. The institution retains the right to revoke such assignments under conditions of non-compliance with agreed upon terms, as provided herein. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by a third party shall require prior written consent from both the registering institution and the Central Government.

A *variety registered* under this Act shall be deemed to possess a distinctive character attributable to its genetic composition and phenotypic expression. For the purposes of determining entitlement to Farmers’ Rights, a *variety registered* shall be considered distinct from any other variety unless it is demonstrably derived from that registered variety through conventional plant breeding techniques. The Registrar may, upon application by an interested party, investigate claims regarding the origin or lineage of a variety and determine whether it constitutes a derivative thereof, taking into consideration established practices relating to geographical indications associated with agricultural produce. Such determination shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Controller rejecting an application patent act shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and must specify the grounds upon which the rejection is challenged. The Board, after affording the appellant and the Controller reasonable opportunity for being heard, may allow the appeal and direct the Controller to proceed with examination or may dismiss the appeal. Where an appeal is allowed, the applicant shall be entitled to costs as determined by the Appellate Board. Further, any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may petition the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of that order, subject to satisfying the conditions for granting special leave to appeal.

Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent granted under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by the Board, subject to review by the High Court only on a point of law. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during an application patent act proceeding renders any subsequent enforcement action vulnerable to challenge and dismissal. The Controller may, upon receiving evidence of wilful infringement, initiate proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by the patentee, including lost profits demonstrably attributable to the infringing activity. Penalties for false statements made in support of a patent application shall be imposed as provided herein.

An applicant seeking protection under this Act for an invention shall submit a request for grant of patent as per the prescribed form. The request must be accompanied by the requisite fee and a certified copy of any document claiming priority. Where the invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the application shall clearly define the scope of the claim relating to that substance. An application patent act is deemed to have been filed on the date the first inventor or their legal representative submits the prescribed documentation to the Controller General. Provided that if an applicant has previously filed an identical application in another jurisdiction, the application date shall be governed by the principles outlined under this Act regarding prior disclosures.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice applicant” means an individual or body corporate who has duly filed an application for registration of a trade mark under this Act and who subsequently receives notification from the Trade Marks Registry indicating that another person seeks to oppose such registration. A notice applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement in response to the notice of opposition, as provided herein. The counter-statement must address each ground of objection raised by the opponent and may include evidence supporting the distinctiveness or acquired reputation of the trade mark. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing a counter-statement shall be deemed abandonment of the right to oppose the proceedings.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if, after publication under this Act, the applicant fails to proceed with the matter within six months, unless such failure is satisfactorily explained. Where an objection is raised by any person against the acceptance of an application, or where the Registrar directs amendment or alteration of the proposed trade marks, the notice applicant shall have a period of three months from the date of receipt of such direction or objection to file his response and take necessary steps as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving a satisfactory explanation for the delay, extend this time limit by a further period not exceeding three months. Failure to comply with these timelines will result in automatic abandonment without further notice.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, every other person proposing to oppose shall serve a notice of opposition on the applicant within the time specified in the regulations. Such notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by such documentary evidence as may reasonably support those grounds. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding the content or timing of the notice shall render the opposition vulnerable to challenge and potential dismissal. The applicant, upon receiving a notice from a notice applicant, shall have the right to file a counterstatement within a prescribed period, responding to the allegations made in the notice. Any delay in filing either the notice or the counterstatement may be condoned by the Trade Marks Registry, subject to just cause being demonstrated.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant. Such notice shall be in writing and shall state the grounds upon which the refusal is based, specifying each relevant provision of this Act or the Rules made thereunder that has been invoked. The notice applicant shall have a period of sixty days from the date of receipt of such notice within which to file a reply addressing the reasons for refusal. Failure by the notice applicant to respond within the stipulated time shall be deemed as acceptance of the Registrar’s decision, and the application shall stand rejected. The Registrar may extend this period upon a written request from the notice applicant demonstrating reasonable cause for delay. Any extension granted shall not exceed thirty days.

Where a trade mark application is filed by a notice applicant, that applicant shall be deemed to hold a provisional license granting limited rights to use the proposed trade mark solely for demonstrative purposes during pendency of the application. This license may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to prior written consent from the Trade Marks Registry and payment of an assignment fee as prescribed. Any subsequent proprietor acquiring title to the trade mark shall automatically inherit this provisional license, but is obligated to notify the registry of such acquisition within thirty days. The registry may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unauthorized commercial use during pendency, issue a cautionary notice to both the applicant and any assignee. Further, the applicant shall be liable for damages arising from misuse of the provisional mark, provided that such misuse occurs without express authorization under the terms of the license as defined herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant. Such notice shall specify the grounds of opposition as detailed in the Notice of Opposition filed by the opponent. The applicant may, within such time as prescribed, file a counter-statement addressing each ground raised and presenting any relevant evidence in rebuttal. Failure to respond to the Notice of Opposition within the stipulated period shall be deemed an admission of the allegations contained therein, subject to the Registrar’s discretion to entertain late submissions upon demonstration of sufficient cause. The opponent may then submit a rejoinder to the applicant's counter-statement. Any party aggrieved by any decision made concerning the Notice Applicant or related proceedings may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice applicant of the hearing appointed to consider the said opposition. Such notice shall be served upon the applicant in the prescribed manner, affording them not less than thirty days’ time from the date of such service to file their written submissions and evidence. Failure to receive such notice shall not, however, invalidate the proceedings unless it is demonstrated that the Registrar acted with demonstrable negligence in effecting service. Should the applicant fail to appear or submit a response at the appointed hearing after due notice, the opposition may proceed ex parte; and if, following such ex parte consideration, the trade mark registration is refused, the aforesaid committed forfeiture of any fees paid by the applicant towards the application.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice applicant” is defined as an individual or body corporate who has duly filed a request with the Trade Marks Registry to be informed of the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark. Such notice shall be provided in the prescribed form and manner, as detailed in the First Schedule. A notice applicant may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, receive information regarding any subsequent proceedings relating to that trade mark application. The Registrar shall not be obliged to provide notice where the applicant has elected to waive such notification. Further, a notice applicant retains no rights to use registered trade marks.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent specification shall include a precise and exhaustive description of the invention, enabling persons skilled in the art to perform or utilize it. The specification must disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the invention at the date of filing; provided that such disclosure does not prejudice the rights of the applicant under this Act. It shall also contain claims defining the scope of protection sought, and these claims shall be clear, concise, and supported by the description. The patent specification may include drawings where necessary to aid understanding.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a comprehensive record of all patent specifications submitted for registration under this Act. Each patent specification presented must include detailed descriptions of the invention’s composition, method of manufacture, and intended use, accompanied by requisite drawings where applicable. The applicant shall provide an exhaustive list of prior art documents known to them at the time of filing, failing which a notice may be issued requiring disclosure within a stipulated period. Furthermore, the patent specification must clearly delineate the scope of protection sought, defining the claims with precision to avoid ambiguity during subsequent enforcement proceedings. Any alteration to the submitted patent specification requires prior approval from the Controller and shall be documented as an addendum to the original registration record.

Where infringement of a patent has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act including an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee. The assessment of such damages shall take into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringement and may include reasonable royalty where the patentee has not been able to ascertain their actual losses. It is provided that a claim for damages may be brought only within five years from the date of first ascertained infringement, subject to just exceptions as determined by the relevant court. The clarity and completeness of the patent specification are paramount; any ambiguity arising therein shall be resolved in favour of the public domain unless such resolution demonstrably prejudices the rights conferred under this Act.

The Controller shall examine whether the patent specification fully and clearly describes the invention and enables a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. Where the applicant seeks to introduce new matter into the patent specification during examination, such introduction shall be permissible only if it is supported by prior submissions or by amendments previously considered and found acceptable under this Act. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding any aspect of the invention disclosed in the patent specification, including details concerning working examples and experimental data. Any request for additional particulars shall be accompanied by a reasoned explanation outlining the deficiencies perceived within the existing disclosure. Failure to respond adequately to such requests may result in rejection of the application. The applicant shall have the right to appeal against any decision made under this provision.

The patent specification accompanying an application for a granted patent shall fully and clearly describe the invention in a manner enabling any person skilled in the art to make and use it. Such description must disclose the best method contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention at the date of filing, provided that where alternative methods are known, all such methods shall be adequately disclosed within the specification. The patent specification is deemed insufficient if it fails to specify the class of compounds or matter to which the invention relates, or if it contains any statement which would mislead a person skilled in the art regarding the scope of protection sought under this Act. Any alteration to the patent specification after its publication shall be permissible only with prior approval from the Controller and subject to compliance with prescribed regulations.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding the sufficiency of a patent specification may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall only be entertained if the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from deficiencies identified in the specification, and establishes that these deficiencies materially impacted the assessability of claim novelty or inventive step under this Act. Failure to adequately disclose the best method known to the inventor for carrying out the invention, as detailed within the patent specification, constitutes a ground for revocation upon application by an interested party. The Board may impose a penalty of up to one hundred thousand rupees for frivolous appeals filed without reasonable cause.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and notwithstanding anything contained in the patent specification, a patentee may grant exclusive licences under the granted patent, or assign the entire interest therein, relating to specific fields of use disclosed within the said specification. Such licence or assignment shall be deemed to include the right to make, sell, hire, import and offer for sale the patented invention only within the defined field of use as explicitly detailed in the patent specification. The Controller may require a declaration from the patentee specifying the precise boundaries of such licensed field or assigned interest before registration under this Act. Further, any subsequent amendment to the patent specification shall automatically invalidate any existing licences or assignments predicated on the original wording unless expressly agreed upon in writing by all parties involved.

The completeness of a patent specification shall be determined with reference to its enabling disclosure and best mode provisions, and where an objection is raised regarding inadequacy of description or lack of clarity in relation to the claimed invention, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating compliance under this Act. The Controller may, upon review of such objections and considering expert testimony presented by either party, direct a revision of the patent specification; however, any alteration made pursuant to such direction shall not substantively broaden the scope of protection initially sought, subject to appeal before an appellate authority. It is provided that the determination of whether a specification discloses the best mode remains within the exclusive purview of the Controller and is amenable to judicial review only on grounds of perversity.

Where a patentee desires to assign or license rights pertaining to an invention disclosed in the patent specification, and such assignment or license involves claims extending beyond the scope explicitly defined within the specification itself, the assignee or licensee shall provide a written declaration to the Controller detailing the basis for said extension. This declaration must specifically identify any modifications to the originally claimed subject matter and justify their inclusion under principles of inventive step as provided herein. Failure to submit such a declaration, or submission of a declaration containing materially false statements, constitutes a commission offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. The patentee retains responsibility for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of this declaration, irrespective of whether the assignment or license was negotiated at arm's length.

The completeness of a patent specification shall be determined with reference to the disclosure required under this Act, and where an objection is raised during examination regarding the sufficiency of the description or claims within said specification, the applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating compliance. The Controller may entertain amendments proposed by the applicant to address such objections; however, any amendment introduced after the first instance of publication in the Patent Journal shall be permissible only if it clarifies the originally filed patent specification and does not substantially alter the scope of protection sought. Disputes arising from decisions regarding completeness or amendability are appealable to the Appellate Board, with hearings scheduled during a designated house parliament session for efficient resolution.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "patent specification" means the entire body of written description and claims accompanying a patent application, detailing the invention for which protection is sought. It shall include, but not be limited to, the title, abstract, summary of the invention, detailed description, drawings where applicable, and the set of claims defining the scope of protection. The patent specification must disclose the invention in a manner as would enable a person skilled in the art to make and use it. Any ambiguity or vagueness within the patent specification may be subject to interpretation during a proceeding appellate relating to validity or infringement.

Where a patent specification contains matter which does not disclose the invention claimed therein clearly and completely, and it is shown that the applicant or patentee has failed to comply with the requirements of this Act regarding the disclosure of information as mandated under this Act, the Controller may direct the rectification of such deficiency. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Furthermore, where a patentee fails to pay the prescribed fees surcharge relating to maintenance of the patent within the stipulated time, and despite notice served as provided herein, remains in default, the Controller shall issue a notification declaring the patent liable for revocation. The aggrieved party may then petition the Controller seeking reinstatement, subject to payment of all outstanding dues and applicable penalties.

The assignment of a registered trade mark shall be permitted subject to the provisions outlined herein regarding prior consent. Any licensee operating under a contractual agreement relating to a registered trade mark may, with the written approval of the proprietor and the india registrar, assign their rights and obligations arising from such license. Such assignments must be executed in the prescribed form and submitted to the Registrar for registration, accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar shall verify that the proposed assignee is not an employee of the proprietor unless specifically authorized under a documented policy approved prior to assignment. Failure to obtain the india registrar’s approval will render any such assignment void. Further, any transfer of ownership involving a trade mark licensed for specific goods or services requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counter-statement within two months from the date of service of notice of the objection. Provided that, if the Registrar deems the grounds of opposition to be manifestly frivolous or vexatious, he may direct the opponent to pay costs to the applicant. Further, any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application, or concerning rectification proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall consider evidence submitted and determine whether the decision of the india registrar was legally sound and in accordance with established principles.

A Mark Certification Trade, as provided herein, signifies a mark used to guarantee that goods or services conform to a specified standard, quality, characteristic, or production method. Such standards must be defined with precision in the regulations submitted alongside the application for registration. The applicant seeking certification trade mark registration shall demonstrate control over the conformity assessment process and possess the requisite authority to use the proposed mark. Further, the Registrar may require evidence of ongoing compliance with the prescribed standards throughout the duration of the registration. Any alteration to these standards requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar.

An application for registration as a mark certification trade may be filed with the Registrar, detailing the characteristics of goods or services eligible for certification. The applicant must demonstrate control over the certified product’s quality and adherence to specified standards, providing evidence of operational procedures and supervisory mechanisms. Regulations governing the use of the certification trade mark shall be submitted alongside the application, outlining eligibility criteria, inspection protocols, and dispute resolution processes. Further, the Registrar may require submission of a bond guaranteeing compliance with these regulations and ensuring continued maintenance of product integrity. The applicant’s identity and legal standing must be clearly established under this Act to facilitate due diligence during examination.

The owner of a registered mark certification trade may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts for recovery of damages sustained by any person through the use by another party of a false or fraudulent certification mark. Such damages shall include not only direct pecuniary loss but also consequential losses reasonably foreseeable as a result of the infringement, provided that the infringing activity was undertaken with knowledge or reasonable grounds to believe that it would cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods certified. Further, any person aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the registration or revocation of a mark certification trade may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such action. The Board shall have power to grant remedies including injunctions and orders for account of profits derived from the infringing use.

Any entity seeking registration as a proprietor of a mark certification trade must submit an application to the Registrar, detailing the specific standards governing eligibility for certification. Such standards shall be demonstrably objective and verifiable, ensuring consistent assessment across all certified products or services. The applicant shall also furnish evidence confirming their capacity to administer these standards impartially and effectively. Further, the proposed regulations concerning use of the mark certification trade must be deposited with the Registrar, outlining procedures for monitoring compliance and addressing instances of misuse or deviation from established criteria. Approval is conditional upon demonstrating a robust mechanism for resolving disputes related to certification eligibility and maintaining consumer confidence in the integrity of the mark.

Any person seeking registration as a proprietor of a mark certification trade relating to agricultural produce, handicrafts or goods manufactured in India shall submit detailed specifications outlining quality control procedures. Failure to adhere to these prescribed standards, as verified by the Registrar through independent audits, constitutes grounds for revocation of the certificate under this Act. Any entity utilizing a registered mark certification trade deceptively, or representing products as conforming to certified standards when they do not, shall be liable to prosecution and subject to penalties including fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment extending to three years. The Registrar may issue cease-and-desist orders and direct the seizure of misbranded goods as provided herein.

The holder of a mark certification trade may grant licenses conferring specific rights to use the certified mark, subject to conditions approved by the Registrar. Such licenses shall specify the goods or services for which the mark is authorized to be used, along with limitations on quality standards maintained by the licensee. Assignment of the right to utilize a mark certification trade requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued adherence to prescribed norms. Any transfer of such rights must include a detailed undertaking guaranteeing that licensees will continue to comply with all regulations governing the certified mark. Further, the proprietor shall provide annual reports detailing licensed usage and quality control measures implemented by each licensee as provided herein. Failure to do so may result in revocation of licensing privileges under this Act.

An appeal against the refusal of registration of a mark certification trade may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, and the appellant shall file with the Board a certified copy of the order appealed from. The Board may, after giving notice to the applicant and any other party who appeared in the original proceedings, hear any evidence offered by either side relevant to the determination of the dispute. Provided that the Board’s decision on such appeal shall be final, subject only to further review under this Act if it appears that a substantial question of law has arisen which was not previously decided. The Registrar may require security from an appellant as provided herein.
