Applications for registration as proprietors of mark certification trade marks shall be filed with the Registrar, detailing the specifications for goods or services eligible for certification. The application must include a copy of the proposed regulations governing the use of the certification mark, outlining eligibility criteria, inspection procedures, and dispute resolution mechanisms. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of a mark certification trade mark for registration may institute proceedings before the Opposition Board within sixty days from the date of advertisement under this Act. Such opposition shall be based on grounds demonstrating that the proposed mark is deceptive or contrary to public interest. The Registrar may require further information or clarification regarding the regulations submitted, and any amendment thereto must be notified to the Opposition Board for consideration. Decisions of the Opposition Board are appealable to the Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

A registered certification mark signifies that the goods or services certified thereunder conform to a defined standard, specification, or characteristic established by the registrant. For the purposes of this Act, “certification” means a representation that goods or services have been produced, processed, handled, packaged, distributed, or sold in conformity with such standards as are prescribed under this Act. The proprietor of a registered certification mark shall maintain records detailing all entities authorised to use the mark and their adherence to the specified standard. Any alteration to the certifying standard requires prior notification to the Registrar and may be subject to review.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed certification trade mark shall furnish detailed specifications outlining the characteristics, quality, or other attributes that certified products must possess. The application shall also identify the standards employed for assessing conformity to these requirements, including testing methodologies and inspection protocols. Upon acceptance of the application, the Registrar may require the deposit of a security commensurate with the potential damages arising from misuse of the certification trade mark. Such security shall be refunded upon cancellation or surrender of registration, less any amounts disbursed under this Act in respect of infringement proceedings. The proprietor of the registered certification shall maintain records detailing all certified products and authorized users, available for inspection by the Registrar.

The owner of a registered certification mark shall be liable to prosecution for damages if they fail to ensure that persons using the mark in accordance with the regulations filed under this Act comply with those regulations. Any proprietor who, without due cause, neglects or fails to provide information requested by the Registrar relating to the continued compliance with said regulations may have their registration subject to cancellation proceedings. Further, a person aggrieved by any act or omission of the proprietor of a registered certification mark concerning the quality or characteristics of goods certified under the mark may institute legal action seeking injunctive relief and compensation for losses sustained. The Registrar shall have power to conduct inquiries into complaints regarding the administration of a registered certification mark and may issue directions as deemed necessary to ensure adherence to prescribed standards, provided that such directions are consistent with the regulations filed.

The Registering Authority shall prescribe detailed procedures for applications relating to registered certification marks, requiring applicants to demonstrate adherence to a defined quality standard applicable to the certified products or services. Such standards must be documented and readily accessible for public inspection at the Trade Marks Registry. An application for registration as a registered certification mark shall include a comprehensive description of the goods or services eligible for certification, alongside a detailed operational manual outlining the certification process. The Registrar may require amendments to these documents if they are deemed deficient in clarity or fail to adequately define the scope of certification. Further, under this Act, proprietors of registered certification marks shall maintain accurate records of all certified products and authorized users, subject to periodic audits by the Registrar. Any alteration to the quality standard requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar.

A person seeking registration of a registered certification mark shall submit an application detailing the specifications for goods or services eligible for certification under the proposed mark. The applicant must demonstrate that they possess the requisite control over the certified characteristics, including but not limited to quality, origin, process, or other features as specified in the application. Such control shall be evidenced by legally binding agreements with producers and certifiers, ensuring adherence to prescribed standards. Certification marks may only be used on goods or services meeting these established criteria, and any deviation from those criteria constitutes a violation under this Act. The Registrar may require periodic audits of certification processes to verify ongoing compliance as provided herein.

Any person employing a registered certification trade mark in contravention of the regulations filed under this Act shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall ensure that all goods certified as conforming to the standards specified in the regulations are accompanied by documentation verifying compliance, failing which they shall be subject to penalties as determined by the Registrar. Further, any false representation concerning conformity to the standard for which the certification is granted constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, initiate inquiries and impose sanctions under this Act against those found violating these provisions.

The owner of a registered certification trade mark shall grant licenses for the use of the mark only upon written agreement specifying the certified characteristics of the goods or services. Such agreements may be assigned subject to the prior consent of the proprietor, provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any licensee utilizing the certification trade mark is obligated to maintain records demonstrating adherence to the standards defined within the regulations filed with the Trade Marks Registry under this Act. Further, the proprietor retains the right to audit these records at reasonable intervals and may terminate any license agreement if non-compliance is established. Assignment of a license without proprietor consent shall render the assignee jointly and severally liable for any infringement occurring prior to notification of assignment to the Registrar. The proprietor’s authority to enforce quality control measures as provided herein remains paramount.

The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence if they fail to ensure that all goods certified under the mark conform to the standards specified in the regulations filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the validity of such regulations, or alleging non-compliance with those standards by a certifier authorised by the proprietor, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall hear appeals under this Act and may direct rectification of the register, award damages, or issue injunctions as it deems appropriate. Provided that any appeal must be filed within three months from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order, subject to just cause shown for delay.

The owner of a registered certification mark shall maintain detailed records pertaining to all persons utilising the mark under authorisation. Applications for authorisation as an authorised user shall be submitted to the proprietor of the certification mark in such form and manner as they prescribe, including particulars regarding the goods or services intended to be certified. The proprietor is obligated to verify each application’s compliance with established standards and regulations governing the certification process. Subject to these requirements, the proprietor may grant authorisation for a specified period, renewable upon satisfactory demonstration of continued adherence to quality benchmarks. Any alteration in production processes or materials used by an authorised user necessitates prior notification and approval from the mark's owner. Failure to comply with conditions stipulated under this Act regarding registered certification may result in revocation of authorisation and potential penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered certification trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the application of the certification mark to goods or services meeting prescribed standards. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding five years, renewable subject to review and compliance with ongoing quality assurance protocols as provided herein. Any assignment of the registration itself shall include an inventory of all existing license agreements pertaining to the certification mark, along with details of licensees’ rights and obligations. Further, any layout design connected with the certification mark, used in promotional materials or product packaging certified under the mark, may be licensed separately, subject to a royalty rate determined by the Registrar based on prevailing market conditions and the scope of usage permitted. The proprietor shall ensure that all sub-licensees adhere strictly to the standards underpinning the registered certification.

The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence if they fail to ensure that all parties using the mark do so in the authorised prescribed manner. Any consumer demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation arising from such non-compliance may institute proceedings before the relevant jurisdictional authority, seeking injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the harm suffered. The proprietor bears the onus of proving adherence to stipulated guidelines; failure to provide satisfactory evidence shall be construed as a violation under this Act. An appeal against any order made by the jurisdictional authority concerning alleged misuse or improper application of the certification trade mark lies to the appellate forum, subject to such conditions and timelines as are prescribed herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent procedure Budapest” shall mean the process established under the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposited Sequences of Biological Material for the Purposes of Patent Law. This includes, but is not limited to, requirements relating to the filing of sequences, their accessibility and availability during examination and opposition proceedings, and the determination of novelty and inventive step where such sequences are incorporated into a claimed invention. The Controller may require applicants to provide evidence demonstrating compliance with the Budapest Treaty’s provisions regarding sequence listings, provided that such requirement does not unduly impede innovation.

Where, upon examination, it is determined that an invention lacks novelty or involves an obvious modification of existing technology, the Controller shall issue a written communication detailing the grounds for rejection to the applicant. The applicant may then file a response addressing these objections within six months from the date of such communication, supported by arguments and evidence demonstrating the inventive step. Failure to adequately respond, or failure to demonstrate compliance with the requirements under this Act, will result in the application being deemed abandoned. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision relating to patent procedure Budapest may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of the order. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal to the High Court on grounds specified therein.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a request for international search under this Act, and such request may be filed in accordance with the procedures established by the Patents Act, 1970, as amended. The Controller General shall determine whether an applicant has complied with all requirements pertaining to the Budapest Treaty concerning the appointment of receiving offices and the designation of examination. Provided that if the prescribed fees for international search have not been remitted at the time of filing, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. Further, any alteration made to the priority claims after the initial filing must adhere strictly to guidelines issued by the Controller, subject to a penalty as determined under this Act. The applicant is responsible for ensuring accurate translation where necessary, and failure to do so may invalidate subsequent patent procedure Budapest proceedings.

Any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act may, subject to provisions regarding time limits, file an appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. Such appeals shall be based solely upon demonstrable errors of law or fact appearing in the record of the original proceeding. Failure to comply with prescribed procedural requirements during examination or opposition proceedings will constitute grounds for penalty and dismissal. The Controller may, at any stage, issue a notice requiring production of documents relevant to the patent procedure Budapest process, and non-compliance shall attract penalties as provided herein. Infringement of a patent, including acts preparatory to infringement, is actionable with damages recoverable under this Act; willful infringement will be subject to enhanced penalties.

Where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the patented invention under this Act. Such license may be granted for consideration or otherwise, as determined by the patentee; provided that any such license agreement must clearly specify the scope and duration of the rights being assigned. Further, a patentee may assign their entire interest in a patent, or any part thereof, to another party through a written instrument duly executed and registered with the Controller. Assignment shall include the right to exploit the patented invention commercially within India. The assignment process shall be governed by rules made under this Act concerning patent procedure Budapest, ensuring transparency and proper notification of all parties involved. Any subsequent transfer of rights relating to such an assigned patent requires similar registration.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to a request for grant of patent, an objection is raised concerning the novelty or inventive step of the invention, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to furnish written arguments and evidence rebutting said objection. The Controller may, at his discretion, require the appearance of the applicant or their representative to clarify any points arising from such submissions. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller concerning patent procedure Budapest may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. Such appeals shall be disposed of expeditiously, and the decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the Supreme Court Act.

Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed procedural requirements during the examination process shall render an application vulnerable to challenge and potential invalidation. The Controller may, upon receiving information indicating irregularities in the matters included register pertaining to patent applications, initiate inquiries and impose penalties for false statements or fraudulent practices. Any person found guilty of wilfully violating provisions relating to patent procedure Budapest, including unauthorized disclosure of confidential information, shall be liable to a fine extending to ten lakh rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years.

Where, in proceedings before the Controller under this Act relating to a request for grant of patent procedure budapest, an objection is raised by any interested party alleging lack of novelty or inventive step based upon prior publication, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rebut such objection with documentary evidence. The Controller may, after hearing both parties and considering all submitted materials, direct that the said objection be deemed withdrawn if satisfied that the publication does not anticipate the claimed invention or render it obvious. Any party aggrieved by this determination of the Controller may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that a Government undertaking claiming sovereign immunity shall have ninety days for such an appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, “patent procedure Budapest” shall mean the process undertaken in accordance with the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposits of Microorganisms, as applied within India. Any microorganism deposited under the patent procedure Budapest shall be deemed to remain subject to the depositor’s control and may be accessed by the Controller for verification purposes only. The term “deposit” when used in relation to such microorganisms shall not affect the validity of a patent granted or sought under this Act, provided that the conditions stipulated within the Treaty are adhered to throughout the duration of the patent consequence.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, an applicant for restoration demonstrates that the decision was based solely on a misinterpretation of international obligations arising from the *Aba Budapest Treaty*, the Controller may, subject to just terms and conditions as determined by him, restore the patent in force. Such terms shall include compensation to any party demonstrably prejudiced by the revocation, including but not limited to those who exploited the invention during the period of invalidity. The applicant shall bear the burden of proving both the misinterpretation and the prejudice suffered. Further, where a patent has been granted incorporating details filed under the Budapest Treaty, any challenge to its validity shall be deemed inadmissible if it relates solely to matters already considered by an International Searching Authority. This provision is without prejudice to remedies available under general principles of equity.

An application for registration as an international design shall be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by such fees as may be determined under this Act. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the statement of priority, if claiming priority under the Paris Convention or the Budapest Treaty International system relating to the grant of patents. Where the design is already registered in any convention country, particulars regarding such registration including the date and registry shall be disclosed within the application. Any alteration made to the design after the initial filing shall require notification to the Controller, who may request further documentation demonstrating compliance with provisions concerning novelty and industrial applicability as provided herein. The applicant shall also declare whether the design incorporates any protected elements subject to copyright.

For the purposes of this Act, “international application” shall mean an application for a patent filed in accordance with the Budapest Treaty International system and designating India as one of the designated States. An international application shall be deemed to be laid before the Controller under this Act upon receipt of a copy thereof by the Receiving Office, transmitted to the Indian Patent Office pursuant to arrangements made between the Government of India and the International Bureau. The filing date of an international application shall be relevant for determining novelty and inventive step, subject to provisions relating to priority claims and trade mark registration already in force.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any party other than the registered proprietor person demonstrates to the Controller that they were diligently pursuing the development of the invention prior to the date of filing of the patent application, and that the grant of the patent has prejudiced their reasonable expectations, the Controller may order the patentee to provide compensation. Such compensation shall be determined considering the extent of prejudice suffered, the investment made by the claimant in developing the invention, and any licensing agreements entered into. The Budapest Treaty international system for designating states shall not preclude a party from seeking remedies under this provision; however, designation under the Budapest Treaty does not automatically confer standing to claim prejudice. Any appeal against an order issued under these provisions shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking to obtain a grant patent shall file with the Controller a detailed register specifying all prior registrations or applications relating to the invention claimed in the patent application. This register must include particulars regarding the registration number, filing date, inventor’s name as recorded therein, and the scope of protection afforded under those previous filings. The Controller may require further clarification or supplementary documentation concerning any entry within this register if deemed necessary for a complete assessment. Failure to provide such information promptly shall be considered an abandonment of the application. Any person aggrieved by the contents of the register may petition the Controller for rectification, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

An applicant seeking to obtain a grant patent shall file an examination request within thirty-six months from the date of filing the patent application or priority date, as applicable, subject to any extension granted under this Act. The Patent Office may require the applicant to provide further information relating to the invention described in the specification and claims, including details regarding experimental data substantiating novelty and non-obviousness. Any third party possessing a relevant prior publication art shall be afforded an opportunity to file a post-grant opposition within one month of the grant’s advertisement. The Controller may, after giving notice to all interested parties, determine whether the invention is patentable based on the evidence presented. Provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient compliance with prescribed formalities and satisfies the criteria for inventive step, the grant patent shall be deemed valid for a term extending from the date of filing.

An applicant seeking to obtain a grant patent shall submit a complete specification detailing the invention, including its utility and mode of manufacture, accompanied by requisite drawings where applicable. The Controller may require further clarification or experimental data demonstrating non-obviousness over existing prior art, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay processing. An invention shall be deemed obvious if it is readily deducible by a person skilled in the relevant field from knowledge available before the date of filing. Furthermore, any claim within the patent application must clearly define the scope of protection sought; ambiguous or overly broad claims may be rejected under this Act. The applicant’s entitlement to the grant shall also be verified against records maintained by the government.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant patent or revocation thereof under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear appeals arising under this Act and may pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside the original decision and substituting its own. Failure to comply with any order made by the Appellate Board shall render the defaulting party liable for a penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, wilful infringement of an order of the Appellate Board constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a licensee under a patent granted pursuant to this Act shall have the right to assign or pledge their license to any person, firm, or company, provided that such assignment or pledge is recorded with the Controller. The grant patent itself may be assigned by the patentee in like manner and subject to similar recording requirements as are applicable to licenses. Any subsequent assignee of a license shall hold only those rights expressly granted within the original licensing agreement; no implied rights beyond the scope of the initial contract shall accrue. Further, where an assignment or pledge is made, notice thereof shall be served upon the patentee within thirty days of registration. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignor liable for damages as determined by a competent court.

Where an application for a grant patent is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such rejection to the Appellate Board constituted as provided herein. The Board may, after affording the applicant and the Controller an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by any order passed by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of the said order. It shall be open for the Controller to require production of evidence in support of claims made by either party during appellate proceedings; failure to comply with such requisition may result in dismissal of the appeal, subject to just cause shown.

For the purposes of this Act, a “grant patent” shall mean the formal issuance by the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks conferring upon the applicant exclusive rights in respect of an invention as described in the complete specification accompanying the application. The grant patent is conditional upon compliance with all requirements under this Act, including but not limited to novelty, non-obviousness, and industrial applicability. An amendment complete specification may be made prior to the sealing of the patent, subject to the provisions relating to permissible alterations and the Controller General’s satisfaction that such alteration does not substantially alter the nature of the invention claimed.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a grant patent for an invention relating to a process for manufacturing a pharmaceutical substance, the Controller shall assess whether the claimed subject matter is novel and involves an inventive step, as provided herein. The application shall include detailed descriptions of the process parameters, including but not limited to temperature, pressure, reaction time, and catalyst concentrations. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that commercial exploitation of the patented process would not unduly prejudice existing pharmaceutical manufacturers. Any party demonstrating a reasonable apprehension of threatened infringement trade arising from the grant of such patent may petition the Controller for an advisory opinion regarding the validity and scope of the claim.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant patent for an invention under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal within sixty days of communication of that decision. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the application process, including but not limited to inadequate disclosure or failure to pay requisite fees, shall render the applicant liable to penalties as determined by the Controller. Further, any entity found to be engaging in activities infringing upon a patent granted under this Act, without authorization from the patent holder, is subject to damages and injunctive relief. The registration copyright society may, with consent of the aggrieved party, initiate legal proceedings on behalf of its members against such infringers to recover losses incurred.

Where an application for registration as a plant variety protection has been examined and found to satisfy the requirements under this Act, and a provisional certificate of registration has been issued, any person manufacturing, selling, importing or exporting any propagating material of the registered variety shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent granted if such activities are undertaken without the prior written consent of the holder of the plant variety protection. This determination shall not apply where the infringing activity was unknowingly conducted before the publication of the grant of registration in the Official Gazette. Further, any commercial use of the registered variety for research purposes is permitted subject to conditions as provided herein and may be challenged by the registrant.

Where any person without leave of the Controller makes, uses, sells, or offers to sell, or imports into India, any patented article, or attempts to do so, or does any act which if done after the grant of a patent would constitute an infringement thereof, such person shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent granted. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller may restrain any person from engaging in such acts pending determination of whether they amount to infringement. The right to claim damages for infringement shall accrue only after the patent is granted and shall be limited to losses directly attributable to the infringing activity. Provided that a party alleging infringement may apply for interim relief including an injunction prior to final judgment, demonstrating likelihood of substantial loss or irreparable injury. Further, any proceedings relating to revocation of the patent shall not affect the right of the patentee to sue for damages for infringement committed before such revocation.

Where any person makes, uses, exercises, sells or offers to sell, or imports any patented article without the authority of the patentee, such act constitutes infringement patent granted under this Act. Any party claiming relief from an alleged instance of infringement shall file a suit within three years from the date on which the acts complained of first became known to him. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint regarding potential infringement, issue directions to any person believed to be engaged in infringing activities, requiring them to appear before the Controller and submit evidence pertaining to their actions. Subject to appeal under this Act, the decision of the Controller shall be binding on all parties involved. Provided that where an injunction is sought against infringement, the suit may proceed irrespective of whether damages are claimed.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention, the patentee shall be entitled to exclusive rights as provided herein, subject to any compulsory license issued under this Act. The patentee may, by written agreement, grant licenses conferring specific rights to use or exploit the patented invention; such licenses shall be assignable in accordance with the provisions relating to assignment of patents. Any party utilizing a patented invention without the express and documented consent of the patent holder constitutes infringement patent granted, rendering them liable for damages and injunctive relief. Further, any assignment of a patent, whether partial or complete, must be executed in the prescribed manner and registered as per regulations established under this Act to be deemed valid against third parties. The patentee shall provide clear documentation regarding the scope of licensed rights upon request from relevant authorities.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or surrender of a patent, or concerning the validity of a patent, or alleging infringement patent granted, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; and where such appeal relates to an order made in exercise of disciplinary jurisdiction, the appeal shall lie with the High Court. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against, subject to any technical provisions under this Act relating to procedure; provided that a decision on the validity of a patent made by the Appellate Board shall be final, but may be challenged in appeal before the Supreme Court.

Where any person makes, uses or imports an article, or offers to make, use or import an article, which embodies or contains the invention claimed in a patent granted under this Act without the authorization of the patentee, such person shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent granted. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from any interested party alleging infringement, issue notices to both the complainant and the alleged infringer requiring them to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified in the notice. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Controller shall determine whether or not an act of infringement has occurred. Where it is established that falsifying trade marks was employed as part of the infringing activity, the Controller may consider such conduct when assessing remedies and penalties. The patentee shall be entitled to seek relief including injunctions and damages as provided herein.

Any person who without leave of the Controller makes, uses, exercises, offers to sell, or imports for sale any patented invention shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement patent granted. Where such infringement occurs by means of an article manufactured before the date of grant of the patent, the penalty shall be a fine not exceeding two thousand rupees and in the case of a second or subsequent offence, a further fine may be imposed. The Controller may require any person alleged to have committed infringement to pay a fee payable notice prior to any proceedings being instituted against them; failure to do so will render such proceedings voidable. Subject to appeal under this Act, damages shall be awarded to the patentee for loss and detriment suffered thereby.

Where a person considers himself aggrieved by an act or omission relating to the grant, revocation, or validity of a patent, or by infringement claim patent asserted against him, such person may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The court shall have jurisdiction to determine all questions concerning the construction of this Act and the interpretation of any patent granted under it. Any party found to have wilfully infringed a patent shall be liable to pay damages amounting to three times the actual loss or harm suffered by the patentee, whichever is higher. Further, the court may issue an injunction restraining the infringing activity, subject to considerations of public interest as provided herein. Costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined at the discretion of the court.

Where a person alleges that their patented invention has suffered infringement, they may institute proceedings before the High Court claiming relief against acts deemed unlawful under this Act. The defendant in such an infringement claim patent action may challenge the validity of the patent itself, presenting evidence demonstrating prior use or lack of novelty as provided herein. Subject to due process and natural justice, the court shall afford both parties a full opportunity to present their case and cross-examine witnesses. Further, any order made by the High Court concerning the infringement claim patent is subject to appeal before the Supreme Court within a period prescribed under this Act, ensuring fairness and judicial review of decisions impacting intellectual property rights.

Where a person alleging infringement of a patent institutes proceedings claiming relief against another party for such infringement, the defendant may raise as a defence that the acts complained of do not amount to infringement under this Act. Provided that, if the defendant asserts such a defence and further alleges that the patent is threatened with infringement by the plaintiff’s actions, the court shall determine whether the plaintiff's conduct constitutes a threat of infringement. The court may grant an injunction restraining the plaintiff from engaging in acts likely to cause such threatened infringement, subject to considerations of public interest and proportionality. Any order made under this provision shall be without prejudice to the defendant’s right to pursue a counterclaim for damages arising from the alleged infringement claim patent.

For the purposes of this Act, an india patent shall denote a grant made under this Act conferring upon the patentee exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented article or substance within India. An application for an india patent may be filed jointly by two or more applicants; provided that where there are joint applicants, their rights and liabilities shall be governed as provided herein. The term "invention" with reference to an india patent includes any process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter which is new and involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. Further, the grant of an india patent does not preclude further innovation based on the patented subject matter.

An application for a india patent may be made by any person unless he is less than eighteen years of age, and may be signed by himself or by his agent; provided that where the applicant is not residing in India, the application shall be presented through an attorney practicing in India. The prescribed form shall include particulars relating to the inventor, assignees, and priority claims, if any, as determined under this Act. Every complete application shall contain a specification describing the invention clearly and fully for enabling any person skilled in the art to make or use it, accompanied by such drawings as are necessary to understand the invention. The Controller General may require amendments to ensure compliance with these requirements before proceeding with examination.

Where an interested party alleges infringement of a india patent, they may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court, subject to the provisions regarding jurisdiction as provided herein. The court shall have power to grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the patentee, and costs incurred in bringing the action. It is provided that a defendant claiming prior use may demonstrate continuous use of the invention prior to the date of application for the india patent, establishing thereby lack of novelty or inventive step sufficient to invalidate the claim. The court shall consider evidence presented by both parties and may order expert testimony to determine validity and scope of the patent in question.

An application for a india patent may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed manner, electronically or otherwise as determined by the Controller’s instructions. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the invention as are required under this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it an official number. Any request for amendment to claims after the first examination shall be processed only with the consent of the Controller, and subject to a prescribed fee. The applicant is obliged to provide translations of the specification and claims into English if the original language differs. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or other action as deemed appropriate by the Controller. An appeal against any decision made under this Act lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An application for an india patent may be filed with the Controller, subject to compliance with the prescribed fee and form requirements as provided herein. The applicant shall disclose the matter known to them which relates to the claimed invention at the time of filing, failing which the patent may be deemed invalid under this Act. Where a previously published specification contains information relevant to assessing novelty or inventive step, the Controller shall consider such publication in determining whether the claimed invention is new and involves an inventive step. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the grant or revocation of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Board may, if it considers it necessary, entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are shown for the delay. Where a patent is granted in contravention of any provision of this Act or the Rules made thereunder, an interested person may prefer a suit for revocation against the patentee in the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The grant of a india patent shall not affect previously existing rights; however, infringement proceedings relating to a patented invention are actionable with penalties and damages as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to any right otherwise vested in any person, the absolute owner of an india patent may grant exclusive licences under the patent, either for the whole or part of India, or for a term not exceeding the remaining period of the patent; and such licence may be granted unconditionally or subject to any terms and conditions. Any assignment of an india patent shall include, unless otherwise agreed in writing, all rights and powers which the assignor had under this Act relating to the patent. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensee shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement of the patent as if he were the absolute owner thereof; provided that such right shall not extend beyond the scope of the exclusive licence. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating due diligence in any assignment or licensing agreement submitted under this Act.

Where an application for a india patent relates to a process for producing a substance, and the invention is such that the claimed substance can be produced by a known process, the Controller may require the applicant to disclose the nature of the said process; and if the applicant fails to comply with such requirement, or if it appears that the invention does not involve an inventive step beyond the obviousness arising from the disclosure of the process, the application shall stand rejected. Any party aggrieved by such a rejection may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of communication of the order, subject to demonstrating prejudice resulting directly from the Controller’s failure to adequately consider prior art submissions.

An application for a india patent may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined under this Act. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to priority if claiming right of priority under any international convention or treaty. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall examine it for compliance with the formal requirements and shall publish a notice of the filing thereof. Any person may, within such time as is prescribed, file a representation with the Controller objecting to the grant of the patent. The Controller shall consider all representations received and afford the applicant an opportunity to reply thereto. Subject to fulfilling the conditions specified herein, and after due consideration of any objections raised, the Controller may proceed with examination for purposes section 41 relating to novelty and inventive step.

Where an application for a india patent relates to an invention that is, at the date of filing, already commercially exploited in India, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, grant the patent only if the applicant demonstrates sufficient novelty and inventive step beyond what has been disclosed in relation to such commercial exploitation. Further, where infringement of a granted india patent is reasonably apprehended, the patentee shall be entitled to apply for an order injunction sub against any person or entity engaged in activities that would constitute infringement, provided that the patentee establishes demonstrable prejudice resulting from the threatened actions and furnishes security as determined by the Controller.

Any party aggrieved by an order relating to a india patent, including but not limited to orders of revocation, opposition, or compulsory licensing, shall have the right to appeal under this Act. Notice of such appeal must be served upon all other parties involved in the original proceeding within sixty days of the date of the order; failure to adhere to this timeframe shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Controller General may, at his discretion, require proof of service of notice and may impose a penalty for non-compliance with the manner issuing notice as prescribed herein. Further, any deliberate misrepresentation made during proceedings concerning a patent, intended to mislead the Controller or influence the outcome, will be deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment and a substantial fine.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent process” shall mean any method or sequence of operations employed in the manufacture of a substance or article, and includes processes involving biotechnological techniques where such techniques are used to produce an invention. The term "process" also encompasses methods for improving existing industrial procedures, provided that such improvements result in a technical effect which is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. An application relating to a patent process shall specify clearly the scope of the process and any essential parameters required for its implementation as described herein. Further, where a patent process involves multiple steps, each step shall be disclosed with sufficient clarity.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all patent process applications filed under this Act, detailing the applicant’s name and address, the title of the invention, and the date of filing. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may issue a provisional registration number which shall be valid for a period not exceeding six months, during which time the novelty search will be conducted. Any third party possessing knowledge relevant to the patent process claim must file a written objection within three months from the publication of the application in the Patent Journal. The applicant shall have an opportunity to respond to such objections and present counter-arguments as provided herein. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application.

Where a patent is granted under this Act and subsequently revoked by order of the Controller, any person aggrieved by that revocation may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board shall hear such appeals expeditiously and may allow the appeal, substituting its own order for that of the Controller, or dismiss the appeal. If a patent is revoked and the appellant fails to demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing they would have obtained a patent but for an error apparent on the face of the record, they shall be liable to pay costs incurred by the respondent in defending the revocation proceeding. Further, any party who has knowingly made false statements or withheld material information during the patent process is subject to penalties as provided herein and may be ordered to account for profits derived from the infringing activity.

An application for a patent relating to a process may be filed with the Controller in the prescribed form and shall include particulars specifying the nature of the invention, the prior art knowledge, and the manner in which the process is carried out. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate the claims made within the application, including detailed schematics and experimental data demonstrating reproducibility. Where an objection is raised by the Examiner concerning the novelty or inventive step of the patent process, the applicant may submit a written response addressing the concerns articulated. Such response must be supported by reasoned arguments and additional evidence as appropriate. The Controller shall consider both the original application and the subsequent response before proceeding with examination under this Act. Any third party possessing relevant information pertaining to the patent process may file a pre-grant opposition within the stipulated timeframe, subject to procedural requirements.

An applicant seeking a patent under this Act relating to a process shall furnish particulars regarding any prior publication, oral or written, anywhere in the world concerning the invention claimed, including details of the date, author, and place of such disclosure. The Controller may require the applicant to submit an affidavit verifying the accuracy of these disclosures and confirming that no material information has been withheld. Further, if the process involves a combination of known methods, the application shall clearly articulate the inventive step contributing to the overall novelty of the patent process. Any alteration or modification made to the claimed process after the initial filing date must be disclosed in subsequent amendments and may impact the grant of the patent, subject to satisfying all requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order, provided that the delay in filing the appeal shall not be grounds for dismissal unless the Appellate Board considers that sufficient reason does not exist. The Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, grant a certificate to any person authorized by it to act as an agent for the purposes of representing parties before it. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during a patent process shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding one lakh rupees and further proceedings may be stayed until compliance is demonstrated. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days.

Where a patent relating to a pharmaceutical process is granted under this Act, the Controller may, upon application by any person demonstrating substantial investment in research and development related to the patented invention, authorize the compulsory licensing of that process. Such authorization shall be subject to conditions ensuring fair remuneration to the patentee, determined based on prevailing market rates and accounting for the costs incurred in establishing and maintaining the patent process. The license may be granted for a period not exceeding five years, renewable only upon demonstration of continued need and adherence to stipulated royalty payments. Assignment of such compulsory licenses shall require prior approval from the Controller, who will consider the licensee’s capacity to manufacture and distribute the pharmaceutical product effectively and equitably across India.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the patent process described in a patent specification, the Controller may, at any time before the date of sealing the patent, require the applicant to submit further particulars or amend the claims to clarify the scope and manner of execution of the invention. Such requirement shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement outlining the deficiencies perceived. The applicant shall have thirty days from the date of receipt of such requirement to comply, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned. Any party aggrieved by the Controller’s decision regarding amendment or rejection of claims may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to demonstrating prejudice resulting directly from the action taken.

A person shall be deemed a *person entitled patent* if such person is the inventor of the invention, or is the assignee of the entire right to the invention from the inventor, or is the legal representative of a deceased inventor. For the purposes of this Act, an inventor includes any person who, for the purpose of carrying out an invention, makes and records discoveries necessary for the solution of the problem. Where an invention is made jointly by two or more persons, each such person shall be deemed to be an inventor in relation to that invention; provided that the right to a patent may be granted to one inventor only if all inventors consent thereto under conditions as prescribed herein.

Where an inventor assigns their rights in respect of an invention to another party, such assignment shall be recorded with the Patents Office within a period not exceeding six months from the date of execution thereof; provided that the Controller may, subject to conditions as prescribed, extend this time limit where satisfactory cause is demonstrated. Any person claiming title through such assignment, or by way of transmission under intestacy or other operation of law, shall be deemed a *person entitled patent* for the purposes of this Act and may apply for registration of their interest in the register maintained under this Act. The application shall specify the details of the original inventor, the date and terms of the assignment, and provide supporting documentation as required by the Controller. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignee’s claim vulnerable to challenge.

Where an invention is claimed by multiple applicants jointly, the determination of who is considered a person entitled patent shall be made according to the provisions outlined herein regarding joint applications and subsequent assignments. The Controller may require such applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the nature and extent of each party’s contribution towards the inventive concept underlying the claim. Further, where an application for a patent has been filed by one individual and subsequently assigned to another, or transmitted through testamentary succession, the assignee or successor shall provide documentation satisfactory to the Controller substantiating the transfer. This includes, but is not limited to, executed assignment deeds registered with the appropriate authorities, or certified copies of probate orders. The Controller may conduct hearings as deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of claims regarding entitlement and may issue interim orders restricting exploitation pending resolution of disputes concerning a person entitled patent.

A person entitled patent under this Act shall, upon filing an application with the Patents Office, disclose all information pertaining to the derivation of their right, including details of any prior assignments, transmissions, or testamentary distributions affecting the invention’s ownership. Such disclosure must be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documentation substantiating the transfer, provided that the Controller may require further evidence if deemed necessary for verification. The application shall specify the nature and extent of the claimant's interest in the patent, whether as sole proprietor, co-owner, or otherwise. Failure to provide complete and accurate information regarding entitlement may render the applicant’s claim vulnerable to challenge by third parties asserting conflicting rights, subject to due process considerations as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be a *person entitled patent* under this Act and alleging infringement of such patent shall institute proceedings before the relevant High Court within six months from the date on which the Controller issues notification regarding the grant of the patent, provided that the delay is condoned by the court if sufficient cause is demonstrated. Failure to adhere to this timeframe shall render any subsequent action for damages or injunctions unsustainable and deemed barred as a matter of right. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of fraudulent claims relating to entitlement, initiate an inquiry and issue warrants for seizure of infringing goods. Any individual found guilty of knowingly making false statements regarding their claim as a *person entitled patent* shall be liable to imprisonment extending to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees.

A person entitled to a patent by way of assignment or transmission shall, upon becoming aware of such entitlement, provide written notification to the Controller within ninety days of the date of acquisition. Such notification shall detail the originating patentee and the terms of transfer as agreed between parties. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the claim of ownership or interest, including but not limited to deeds of assignment and testamentary records. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensee may assign such license subject to the consent of the patentee unless the original agreement expressly prohibits it. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the terms of the initial license agreement. A person entitled patent arising from an operation of law shall also adhere to these notification requirements and provide supporting legal documentation.

Where an application for a patent has been filed and subsequently amended under this Act, determining who is the person entitled patent presents a complex inquiry requiring careful consideration of all relevant documentation pertaining to prior ownership or assignment. The Controller shall, upon receiving objections regarding the identity of the applicant as the person entitled, conduct a thorough investigation into the claimed transfer of rights, examining evidence such as deeds of assignment and transmission records. Provided that any party aggrieved by the Controller’s determination may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; however, the burden of proving rightful entitlement shall remain on the appellant. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further judicial review under law.

Where an invention is patented and subsequently misappropriated by another party through unauthorized manufacture, use, or sale, any person entitled patent to that invention shall have recourse to remedies available under this Act. Such a person may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum seeking injunctive relief to restrain further acts of infringement. Provided that, in determining entitlement, due consideration shall be given to any prior use mark relation established by another party, demonstrating legitimate commercial activity predating the patent grant; however, such prior use does not constitute grounds for invalidation unless it demonstrably undermines the novelty or inventive step of the patented invention. The Controller may also issue directions regarding compensation and damages payable by the infringing party, subject to principles of fairness and equity as provided herein.

An invention application shall be deemed to include, but not be limited to, the prescribed forms and accompanying documents submitted to the Controller General for examination. Such an application must contain a clear and concise specification describing the invention in sufficient detail to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use it; claims defining the scope of protection sought; and such drawings as are necessary to understand the invention. The term "specification" as used herein, shall encompass both the abstract of the technical field and the detailed description of the inventive step. An applicant may request a provisional filing date under this Act, subject to fulfilling all prescribed requirements.

An application for an invention shall be in the prescribed form and shall contain particulars as to the inventor, the title of the invention, and the matter claimed to be new and inventive. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence establishing ownership or right to make the application as may be required by the Controller. Where an invention is not obvious to a person skilled in the art, it shall be deemed to be inventive. Any person claiming to be interested may file notice of opposition to the grant of patent within a period specified under this Act from the date of publication of the application. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the invention application to clarify any ambiguity or inconsistency therein.

Where an invention application is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal such rejection to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a point of law. Subject to payment of such fees as may be prescribed, failure to comply with procedural requirements during proceedings before the Appellate Board shall not be grounds for dismissal provided that the omission is curable and does not substantially prejudice another party’s rights. The Controller shall provide reasons in writing for any decision relating to an invention application, and these reasons shall be made available to the applicant.

An application for an invention shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by such documents, drawings, and information as are necessary to enable the Controller to determine whether the claimed invention is novel and involves inventive step. The applicant shall specify the priority claim, if any, asserted in the application, furnishing certified copies of earlier applications relating to the same invention. Where an invention application relates to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the claims shall clearly define the scope of protection sought. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the application to clarify the description or drawings, provided that such amendments do not alter the essence of the claimed invention. Any person may file a request for pre-grant opposition under this Act within six months from the date of publication of the patent application.

An invention application shall be deemed invalid if, prior to the date of filing, an identical invention was publicly known or used in India, unless such knowledge or use was concealed from the applicant and could not reasonably have been discovered by any person skilled in the art. Further, where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance defined as per this Act, the application shall disclose how to manufacture said substance; failure to do so constitutes non-compliance. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish additional information or clarification regarding the working of the invention, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the examination process. Any alteration made to the original invention application after its publication shall be subject to approval by the Controller.

An application for an invention shall be deemed invalid if, within six months from the date of publication under this Act, a written representation is received by the Controller alleging lack of novelty or inventive step and supported by prior documentary evidence. The applicant shall then have three months to submit a counter-statement refuting said allegations, failing which the application will stand rejected. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding an invention application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Repeated failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the applicant liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and potential costs awarded against them in any subsequent proceedings.

Where an invention application relates to technology essential for the operation of a telecommunications network, and where the applicant has entered into agreements granting licenses or assignments of rights pertaining to such invention, the Controller may, upon application by any person demonstrating substantial non-infringing use affected by the patent, direct the applicant to grant a further license under this Act. Such direction shall be subject to the condition that the proposed licensee offers reasonable compensation reflecting the value of the patented technology and taking into account prior licensing arrangements. The applicant shall provide full disclosure of all assignments and licenses relating to the invention application within thirty days of receiving notice from the Controller, failing which penalties as provided herein may apply. Any such license granted pursuant to this provision shall be recorded with the Patents Office.

Where an invention application is deemed, upon examination, to lack clarity as provided herein, the Controller shall issue a communication specifying the deficiencies and affording the applicant an opportunity for amendment. Such amendment shall be permissible only where the originally filed specification could reasonably have been construed to encompass the altered matter; otherwise, the application shall stand rejected. An appeal against this determination may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of such communication. The Board’s decision on any question arising from the interpretation of “reasonable construal” shall be final and binding, subject to a further petition for special leave to the Supreme Court arguing manifest error of law.

Where an invention application is filed claiming priority from a previously filed application in another country, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the earlier application. Such certification shall be obtained from the appropriate authority designated by that foreign jurisdiction and submitted within three months of the date of filing the Indian invention application. Failure to comply with this requirement will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The procedure investigation undertaken by the Controller in relation to such applications shall include verification of the authenticity of the certified copy and confirmation of the priority claim’s validity. Any discrepancies observed during this process may necessitate further inquiry and submission of additional documentation as deemed necessary by the Controller, subject to guidelines issued from time to time.

For the purposes of determining patent enforceability under this Act, a “reasonable period” relating to any delay in seeking redressal for infringement shall be assessed considering factors including, but not limited to, the complexity of the infringing activity, the availability and cost of evidence pertaining thereto, and demonstrable efforts undertaken by the claimant to mitigate prejudice arising from such delay. Subject to provisions regarding laches, a reasonable period shall not preclude an action where the patentee has actively concealed the infringing use or misrepresented facts relevant to its detection. The Controller may, in determining what constitutes a reasonable period, consider analogous cases decided under this Act and principles of equity.

The Registering Authority, upon receiving an application for registration of a utility model, shall assess whether the proposed design incorporates elements previously registered under this Act or any corresponding legislation. Such assessment will consider novelty and inventive step, taking into account prior disclosures made publicly before the date of filing. The applicant shall be deemed to have satisfied the requirement of originality if the design demonstrably differs from existing precedents. Furthermore, where a utility model relates to an improvement upon an existing patented invention, the application must demonstrate that the enhancement is substantial enough to warrant independent registration. A reasonable period for demonstrating such substantiation will be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Where an interested party alleges infringement of a patent, and seeks remedies under this Act, the patentee shall bear the burden of demonstrating continued validity of the patent for the claimed invention. Should it be established that the patentee has failed to diligently exploit the patented invention within India during any portion of the period since grant, or has otherwise acted in a manner inconsistent with the purposes of promoting innovation and technological advancement, the Controller may, subject to due process, reduce the scope of protection afforded by the patent. The determination of what constitutes a reasonable period for exploitation shall be based on factors including but not limited to the nature of the invention, prevailing market conditions, and any demonstrable impediments encountered by the patentee. Further, remedies available to an aggrieved party may be curtailed if the patentee demonstrates that the alleged infringement occurred outside of a reasonable period following notification of the infringing activity.

The Board, while determining whether an invention has been exploited commercially under this Act, shall consider all relevant factors pertaining to the nature and extent of commercial activity undertaken by the patentee or their licensee. Such factors include, but are not limited to, the volume of production, sales realized, territory covered by exploitation, and any demonstrable efforts towards market penetration. Where a party alleges non-exploitation, the Board may require the patentee to furnish documentary evidence substantiating the extent of commercialization. The determination of what constitutes a reasonable period for exploitation is fact-specific and shall be assessed considering prevailing industry practices, technological advancements relevant to the invention, and any impediments encountered by the patentee in establishing commercial operations. A reasonable period does not imply an inflexible timeframe; it acknowledges that circumstances vary across industries and inventions.

Where an application for compulsory license is filed under this Act, the Controller shall determine whether the patentee has conducted business at a reasonable period and in a manner commensurate with the demand arising from the patented invention within the territory to which the grant relates. The Controller may consider factors including, but not limited to, the extent of local manufacture, availability of the patented invention to the public, and efforts made by the patentee to make the invention available at affordable rates. Subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, if it is found that the patentee has failed to satisfy these conditions during a reasonable period, the Controller may grant a compulsory license on such terms as he deems fit, provided that the applicant demonstrates an intent to use the patented invention primarily for domestic production.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting, revoking or modifying a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Where an appeal relates to a claim for damages or other monetary relief, the appellate authority shall determine the amount of compensation due and payable, subject to the provisions regarding limitation under this Act. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during infringement proceedings will render any subsequent claims untenable. The Controller may, upon receiving credible evidence of persistent and willful infringement following a cease-and-desist notice, impose penalties proportionate to the loss suffered by the patent holder due to such actions. A reasonable period for responding to notices shall be deemed as thirty days unless otherwise specified in regulations framed under this Act.

Where a patent has been granted, the patentee shall retain exclusive rights subject to any license agreements entered into prior to or subsequent to the grant. Any assignment or licensing agreement relating to a patent may stipulate conditions regarding field of use, duration, and royalty payments, provided that such conditions do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition under this Act. The Controller may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating prejudice due to restrictive terms in a license, direct the patentee to grant a non-exclusive license on reasonable terms. A “reasonable period” for negotiations regarding licensing shall be determined considering prevailing industry practices and the complexity of the technology involved; generally, not exceeding three years from the date of initial communication. The patentee is obliged to provide full disclosure of relevant documentation pertaining to licensing offers made during this reasonable period.

Where an application for compulsory license is filed under this Act, the Controller shall determine whether the patentee has failed to exploit the patented invention adequately within India. Such determination shall consider, without limitation, the extent of local manufacture, the availability of the patented product at affordable prices to the public, and any efforts made by the patentee to seek production or importation from other sources. The period considered for assessing adequate exploitation shall be a reasonable period, taking into account the nature of the invention and the time required for its commercial development. Any party aggrieved by the Controller’s determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the finding regarding the reasonable period.

Where an application for registration of a utility model is granted and subsequently challenged under this Act, the validity of such registration shall be determined by the Controller based upon evidence presented by both the registrant and the challenger. The determination shall specifically address whether the invention in question was novel and non-obvious at the time of filing the application, taking into consideration any prior publications or use. Further, it shall be considered whether the period claimed for exploitation of the utility model exceeded a reasonable period, as determined by the Controller considering prevailing market conditions and technological advancements. Should the challenger successfully demonstrate that registration was improperly granted or has become untenable due to expiry of a reasonable period, registration shall cease immediately upon order of the Controller.

For the purposes of determining patent validity under this Act, a “reasonable period” shall mean the time necessary to establish commercial viability and recoup reasonable investment costs incurred in research, development, and initial marketing of goods incorporating the patented invention. The Controller may consider prevailing industry practices relating to product lifecycles when assessing what constitutes a reasonable period; provided that such consideration does not override the obligation to ensure patent claims are clearly defined and do not unduly restrain innovation. This assessment shall take into account factors including, but not limited to, market demand for the goods and the extent of technological advancements impacting their production or use.

The Registering Authority, while examining an application for registration of a utility model, shall consider whether the invention relates to a method of manufacture already disclosed and practiced prior to the date of filing. Where such prior practice is established, the applicant may demonstrate that the inventive step introduced constitutes a significant advancement over existing methods, rendering it worthy of protection under this Act. The duration of patentability for registered utility models shall be twenty years from the date of application, subject to renewal fees paid as provided herein. This period represents a reasonable period considering the nature of technological innovation and the need to balance incentivizing invention with ensuring public access; however, extensions may be granted in exceptional circumstances determined by the Controller. The mark registered manner of displaying the utility model’s designation shall adhere strictly to prescribed guidelines.

Where an application for compulsory license is filed against a trade proprietor registered under this Act, the Controller shall determine whether the patentee has failed to grant licenses on terms and conditions that are reasonable. Such determination shall consider, amongst other factors, the extent to which the invention has been worked in India, the nature of the invention, and the time elapsed since the date of grant. The Controller may allow a compulsory license if it finds that the patentee has not satisfied the requirements for working the patented invention within a reasonable period, or if the terms offered by the trade proprietor are demonstrably unjust or discriminatory. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.
