An application for patent, once filed, shall remain pending until such time as the Controller determines whether the invention is novel and involves an inventive step, subject to any objections raised under this Act. The period during which an application remains outstanding may be extended by the Controller where a request for extension is made within six months of the date application claim publication, provided that satisfactory evidence demonstrating special circumstances justifying such extension is submitted. Further, if the applicant fails to respond adequately to examination reports issued by the Controller within the prescribed timelines, or otherwise defaults in complying with procedural requirements as provided herein, the application may be deemed abandoned after a reasonable period. This reasonable period shall not exceed thirty-six months from the date of the last communication sent to the applicant.

Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material information during proceedings before the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or maintenance of a patent, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated by the Controller. Such inquiry may be conducted by the Controller personally or through an officer duly authorised under this Act. The amount of the penalty shall not exceed one million rupees and is subject to adjustments as determined by the Central Government based on prevailing economic conditions. Any appeal against an order made during such inquiry imposing penalty shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where any registered proprietor or other person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of entries in the Register of Designs believes that such decision was made without due consideration of all relevant evidence presented during the registration inquiry, they may apply to the Design Appellate Board for review. The Board shall conduct a fresh inquiry imposing penalty where it finds that the Registrar’s order resulted from demonstrable bias or procedural unfairness. Such an inquiry shall be deemed a quasi-judicial proceeding and the applicant shall have the right to cross-examine witnesses presented by the Registrar. The Board may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity to present their case, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision of the Registrar.

Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material information during proceedings before the Controller relating to the grant, revocation or maintenance of a patent, or otherwise acted fraudulently under this Act, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty. Such inquiry may be conducted by the Controller personally or delegated to an officer authorised for that purpose. The person against whom the inquiry is initiated shall be served with notice specifying the nature of the allegation and given a reasonable opportunity to present their defence, including the right to cross-examine witnesses presented by the Controller. If, after due consideration of all evidence, the Controller finds the allegations substantiated, they may impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each such false statement or act of fraud. The amount so recovered shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Where the Controller deems it necessary to ascertain whether any person has contravened any provision of this Act or rules made thereunder, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty for such contravention. The inquiry shall be conducted by the Controller or by an officer authorised by the Controller in writing for that purpose. Notice of the inquiry shall be served upon the alleged contravener at least thirty days prior to the commencement of proceedings, specifying the nature of the alleged contravention and the provisions applicable thereto. The person against whom the inquiry is initiated shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case, including cross-examination of witnesses presented by the Controller. Evidence may be adduced both orally and in writing, subject to rules of procedure prescribed by the Central Government. Following conclusion of the inquiry, the Controller shall issue an order detailing findings and any penalty imposed, providing reasons for the decision. Appeals against such orders are permitted under this Act.

Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material facts in relation to the grant of a patent, or during proceedings before the Controller concerning validity or revocation, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated by the Controller. Such inquiry may be conducted by an officer authorised under this Act for that purpose. The Controller shall provide written notice to the individual concerned detailing the allegations and affording them a reasonable opportunity to present their defence and submit relevant evidence. Provided that if the false statement or suppressed fact relates to matters affecting public health or safety, the inquiry imposing penalty may commence without prior notice where deemed necessary by the Controller. Any penalty imposed under this Act shall be recoverable as an arrears of land revenue.

Where any individual or entity is found to have contravened any provision relating to patent infringement, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty commensurate with the scale and duration of the infringing activity. Such inquiry will proceed expeditiously, affording the accused party a chance to present its defence and offer relevant evidence. The Controller may direct seizure and destruction of goods made, used or sold in violation of the patent, as deemed necessary to mitigate further harm. Failure to comply with orders issued during this process shall attract additional penalties, including daily fines until compliance is achieved. The Controller’s decision regarding penalty is final, subject to appeal under this Act within a prescribed timeframe.

Where any patentee or licensee fails to comply with the conditions of a license granted under this Act, or otherwise acts in contravention of the provisions relating to assignment or transmission of patents, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty. Such inquiry may be conducted by the Controller or by an officer duly authorised for that purpose. The person against whom the inquiry is initiated shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case and adduce evidence in mitigation. Any agreement restricting the exploitation of the patented invention, entered into without complying with the requirements as provided herein, shall be deemed void and subject to such penalties as may be determined during the inquiry. Further, any assignment made contrary to the provisions regarding royalty payments shall be liable for rectification or revocation at the Controller’s discretion.

Where, following a complaint received under this Act alleging non-compliance with conditions stipulated in a patent grant or engaging in practices prejudicial to the interests of invention, the Controller deems it necessary, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated. The Controller may appoint any officer competent to investigate such matters as an inquiring authority. The person against whom the inquiry is directed shall be served with notice detailing the allegations and provided a reasonable opportunity to submit evidence and arguments in their defense. Any order made by the inquiring authority shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, within sixty days of its communication. Provided that the Appellate Board may entertain appeals even if such delay has occurred, if satisfactory reasons for the same are demonstrated.

Where any person is found to have contravened any provision of this Act or the regulations framed thereunder, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty, and for that purpose, may constitute a Committee consisting of such persons as he deems appropriate, possessing expertise in intellectual property law and related fields. The Committee shall afford the alleged offender a fair opportunity to present their case and submit evidence in mitigation. An authorised user of a patented invention, acting within the scope of their authorisation, shall not be subject to penalty unless it is established that they acted with knowledge of the contravention and failed to promptly report it to the patentee.

Where any person is found to have contravened any provision of this Act relating to the registration of patent applications or the maintenance of the register, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated by the Controller. The Controller may direct the court registrar to serve notice upon such person detailing the alleged infraction and specifying the maximum amount of penalty that may be levied under this Act. Such inquiry shall proceed expeditiously, affording the concerned party a reasonable opportunity to present their defence and any relevant evidence. The Controller is empowered to determine whether a contravention has occurred and, if so, to impose a penalty as deemed appropriate, subject to principles of natural justice and proportionality. Appeals against such determinations may be made under the prescribed procedure.

Where any proprietor or registered licensee contravenes any provision of this Act or the regulations made thereunder, or fails to comply with any direction issued by the Controller, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated against such proprietor or registered licensee. The Controller may, subject to due process and affording a reasonable opportunity for representation, direct that such inquiry be conducted by an officer designated by him. Upon conclusion of the inquiry, if it is established that a contravention has occurred, the Controller may impose a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, where a mark separately registered under this Act is involved in the contravention, the penalty shall be doubled. The Controller’s order imposing penalty shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of its communication.

Where any proprietor fails to comply with a direction issued by the Controller relating to the alteration or removal of features incorporated into a registered design, or where such failure persists for a period exceeding thirty days from the date of the said direction, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated under this Act. The Controller may, prior to initiating such an inquiry, issue a notice requiring the proprietor to demonstrate compliance within fifteen days, detailing the corrective actions undertaken. Should the proprietor fail to adequately respond or rectify the non-compliance as directed, the Controller shall proceed with the inquiry. Evidence pertaining to the design registry exercise and any associated documentation will be considered during this process. The penalty imposed may extend up to one thousand rupees for each day of continued default, subject to a maximum aggregate amount as determined by the Controller.

A person shall be deemed to be a registered patent agent if such person has applied for registration under this Act and been admitted by the Controller after satisfying the prescribed requirements relating to qualifications, experience and good character. A registered patent agent may appear before the Controller on behalf of any applicant or party in proceedings concerning the grant, revocation or infringement of patents. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered patent agent shall be entitled to perform all acts which an attorney representing a client is permitted to do under this Act. Provided that no registered patent agent shall represent more than fifty clients at any given time.

An application for registration as a registered patent agent shall include particulars of educational qualifications, professional experience relating to inventions and intellectual property law, and details of any disciplinary proceedings initiated against the applicant. The Controller may require such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain the suitability of an applicant under this Act. Every individual seeking registration must furnish proof of having undergone training prescribed by the Patents Office, demonstrating competence in patent drafting and prosecution procedures. A registered patent agent shall maintain a record of all matters handled on behalf of clients, accessible for inspection upon request by the Controller. Any change in address or partnership details shall be promptly notified to the office, as provided herein.

Any person acting on behalf of an applicant or proprietor in connection with the preparation, filing, prosecution, or maintenance of a patent application under this Act shall be deemed to be practising as a registered patent agent. Such agents shall be subject to disciplinary proceedings and penalties as provided herein for acts of professional misconduct including, but not limited to, wilful misrepresentation before the Controller or any other authority constituted under this Act. An aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings seeking damages arising from negligence or fraudulent conduct by a registered patent agent in the performance of their duties; however, such actions shall be barred after three years from the date the cause of action arose. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint, investigate allegations against a registered patent agent and issue orders restricting their practice or revoking their registration if misconduct is established.

An application for registration as a registered patent agent shall include particulars of educational qualifications, professional experience relating to inventions and technology transfer, and details of any disciplinary proceedings initiated against the applicant under this Act or any other law. The Controller General may require such further information from an applicant as he deems necessary for assessing their suitability to act as a registered patent agent. An applicant who has been convicted of an offence involving dishonesty or fraud is not eligible for registration, subject to review by an Appellate Board. Registration shall be provisional until the applicant satisfies the Controller General that they possess the requisite knowledge and skills relating to patent law and practice. A registered patent agent may represent clients before the Intellectual Property Office in matters concerning patents and related proceedings.

A person seeking registration as a registered patent agent shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by evidence demonstrating academic qualifications equivalent to at least a bachelor’s degree in science or engineering. The applicant must also provide proof of having completed practical training under the supervision of a practicing registered patent agent for a minimum period of twelve months, as certified by that supervising agent. Further, the application shall include an affidavit confirming good character and professional integrity. Subject to verification of these credentials and successful completion of an examination administered by the Controller, the applicant may be admitted to the Register of Patent Agents. Provided that any individual previously convicted of a criminal offence involving fraud or dishonesty shall not be eligible for registration under this Act.

Any person acting as an agent for the purposes of procuring, protecting, or enforcing patents shall be deemed a registered patent agent subject to fulfilling requirements prescribed under this Act. Failure to maintain adequate professional indemnity insurance, as specified in the regulations, will render such registration liable for immediate revocation. Any individual falsely representing themselves as a registered patent agent and engaging in activities related to patent filings or litigation shall face penalties including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Controller is empowered to initiate suo moto proceedings against any person suspected of violating these provisions, without prejudice to civil remedies available to aggrieved parties.

Any assignment of a patent, or any right or interest therein, whether complete or partial, voluntary or involuntary, shall be in writing and executed by the patentee or their duly authorized representative, including a registered patent agent acting on their behalf. Such assignments may include the power to sue for infringement and the benefit of all causes of action accrued prior to the assignment. Where an assignment is made subject to any royalty or other consideration, such terms shall be clearly stated within the instrument of assignment. Further, the Controller may require proof of registration of a registered patent agent executing on behalf of a patentee, satisfactory to the Controller, before acknowledging validity of the assignment for official record. The patentee shall provide notification of any such assignments to the Controller within thirty days of execution, as provided herein.

A person aggrieved by the refusal of registration as a registered patent agent may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. Such an appeal shall be on grounds that the decision was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of the requirements for eligibility under this Act, including but not limited to demonstrating sufficient technical qualifications and good standing in the legal profession. The Board may, after affording the appellant and the Controller an opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against; provided that any finding by the Board shall be final subject to further appeal to the High Court only on a question of law.

An application for registration as a registered patent agent shall include particulars of educational qualifications, professional experience, and such other details as prescribed by the regulations framed under this Act. The Controller may require an applicant to undergo such examinations or training as deemed necessary to assess their competence in matters relating to patents and intellectual property law. Subject to fulfilling these requirements, and providing satisfactory proof of good character and integrity, the applicant shall be eligible for registration. Further, any individual engaged in subject registration trade related activities involving patent filings must disclose all relevant affiliations within the application. A registered patent agent is deemed to possess the requisite knowledge to advise clients appropriately on matters pertaining to patentability and infringement.

An application for registration as a registered patent agent shall contain such information as the Controller requires to ascertain that the applicant possesses the requisite qualifications and experience under this Act. The prescribed fee shall be remitted with the application, and failure to do so will render the application void. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may direct the applicant to submit further particulars or documents deemed necessary for verification. Any individual found to have misrepresented their credentials during the registration process is liable to have their registration revoked. Further, a registered patent agent shall be subject to disciplinary proceedings as provided herein if they fail to maintain professional standards. The number of registered patent agents at any given time shall not exceed such figure as the Central Government may determine from time to time, taking into account section 15 countable factors.

Where the proprietor of a patent has granted a license conferring rights to exploit the patented invention, such license agreement shall specify the terms governing assignment of those rights. Any transfer of ownership in respect of a registered patent agent’s authority to act on behalf of a licensee shall be subject to prior written consent from both the patent proprietor and the Controller. Further, where a cessation patent is declared due to non-payment of renewal fees, any pending license agreements relating to that invention shall remain valid for a period not exceeding six months from the date of such declaration, provided that the licensee continues to exploit the patented invention during this interim period. The Controller may, upon application by an aggrieved party, extend this validity period in circumstances deemed equitable under this Act.

A certificate purporting to be issued by an authorized officer under this Act, and bearing the official seal of that office, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding before a court or tribunal. Such certificate shall be deemed prima facie proof of the facts stated therein, relating to the grant, modification, or revocation of patents, subject to the provisions allowing for rebuttal by presentation of contrary evidence. The validity of such a certificate may only be challenged upon establishing demonstrable fraud or fabrication affecting its issuance. Any person relying on a certificate purporting to contain information regarding patent specifications shall do so without prejudice to any other rights under this Act.

The Register of Registered Designs maintained under this Act shall, at all times during office hours, be open to inspection by any person interested in obtaining copies thereof. Any person may obtain a certified true copy of any design registered, or any particulars relating thereto, upon payment of the prescribed fee. A certificate purporting to be signed by an officer authorised by the Designs Office and certifying that such copy is a true copy shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding. The Controller may, at his discretion, issue certificates pertaining to modifications made to registered designs, reflecting changes in class or other relevant details, provided that such modifications adhere to the requirements of this Act.

Where an objection is raised against a patent grant alleging non-compliance with the provisions relating to inventiveness, the Controller may require the applicant to submit documentary evidence substantiating the inventive step claimed. Failure by the applicant to provide such documentation within the time specified shall be deemed conclusive proof of absence of novelty or inventive step, and the application may proceed for rejection. Any certificate purporting to have been issued by a duly constituted expert appointed under this Act, verifying the technical soundness of the invention or confirming its compliance with prescribed standards, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding relating to the patent’s validity. Such certificates are subject to challenge based on demonstrable bias or lack of expertise, provided that such challenges are brought within six months of the certificate's issuance.

Where an application for a patent is rejected under this Act, and the applicant appeals against such rejection to the Appellate Board, the Board may, after affording the appellant an opportunity of being heard, direct that the certificate purporting to be issued by the Controller relating to the examination of the invention shall be submitted for its consideration. The Controller shall furnish such certificate within thirty days of receiving a requisition from the Appellate Board. Provided that if the Controller deems it necessary, due to the complexity or volume of information contained in the certificate, he may extend this period by a further fifteen days, notifying the Appellate Board of the reasons for such extension. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to the provisions regarding costs as provided herein.

A certificate purporting to have been issued by an authorized officer under this Act, relating to the validity of a patent application, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding before a court or tribunal. Such certificate shall be deemed prima facie correct and binding on all parties unless proven otherwise through clear and convincing evidence demonstrating material errors in the process followed by the said officer. The burden of disproving the correctness of such certificate shall lie solely upon the party challenging its validity, provided that the challenge is brought within a period of ninety days from the date of publication of the certificate. Further, any alteration or erasure made on a certificate purporting to be issued under this Act shall render it inadmissible unless authenticated by the signature of both the issuing officer and an independent witness.

Any certificate purporting to be issued under this Act by an officer duly authorised for that purpose shall, upon its face appearing regular on its form and execution, be admissible as evidence in any proceeding before a court or tribunal. Such proceedings may concern revocation actions, infringement claims, or challenges to patent validity. The burden of proving the certificate’s invalidity or fabrication shall rest entirely with the party contesting its authenticity. Failure to demonstrate such falsification will result in costs being awarded against that party, as determined by the presiding authority. Further, any person knowingly presenting a fraudulent certificate purporting to be an official record may face penalties including imprisonment and fines, subject to judicial discretion.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license conferring rights to use, manufacture, or sell an invention for which they hold a patent under this Act, such license may be assigned or otherwise transferred subject to the provisions herein. Any instrument purporting to transfer such licensing rights shall be executed by both the assignor and assignee, and duly stamped as required by law. The Controller may, upon application by any party claiming interest in a patented invention, investigate whether a certificate purporting to be evidence of assignment of a license has been properly executed and registered. Failure to comply with these requirements renders the purported transfer voidable at the discretion of the Controller. Further, where an exclusive license is granted, the patentee shall notify the Controller within thirty days of such grant, providing details as prescribed by regulations made under this Act.

Where an objection is raised against a patent grant alleging non-compliance with the provisions relating to inventiveness, the Controller shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. Any certificate purporting to be signed by the Controller affirming the validity of such inventive step, following due consideration of these submissions, shall be admissible as evidence in any subsequent proceedings under this Act concerning the patent’s revocation or infringement. Provided that, if either party disputes the authenticity of the certificate purporting to be the Controller's signature, the burden of proving its genuineness shall lie upon the party producing it. The Controller may, at his discretion, require further expert testimony regarding the technical aspects of the invention in question.

Where an application for registration of a patent is opposed, the Controller may require the applicant and the opponent both to submit written arguments and such evidence as they deem relevant to the merits of the opposition. Should either party present a certificate purporting to be a record of proceedings before a lower authority concerning prior use or publication relating to the invention, that certificate shall be admissible as evidence subject to challenge regarding its authenticity and proper execution. The Controller may, at his discretion, order an inspection of the original records upon which such certificate is based. Any party aggrieved by a decision made following opposition registration may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This right of appeal shall not prejudice any other rights or remedies available to that party as provided herein.

A certificate purporting to be issued by the Controller-General under this Act, declaring a patent granted and specifying its term, shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding relating to that patent. Such certificate is prima facie conclusive proof of the grant and validity of the patent for the period indicated therein, subject to challenge based on demonstrable fraud or misrepresentation during the application process. Any party disputing the contents of a certificate purporting to have been issued by the Controller-General may apply to the court registrar for an examination of the records pertaining to its issuance. The court registrar shall, upon receiving such an application and after providing notice to all interested parties, conduct an inquiry into the matter and submit a report to the relevant judicial forum. This process is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act or as provided herein.

Any person knowingly making, selling, offering for sale, or importing into India any product bearing a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, or utilizing an invention without just cause and after obtaining a certificate purporting to be issued by the Controller General under this Act, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. Where such infringement involves international registration required as per the provisions concerning Madrid Protocol, the penalty of imprisonment shall be increased by a further period of one year, and the fine enhanced to fifteen lakhs rupees.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license, assign, or otherwise transfer rights relating to a patent granted under this Act, such intention shall be formally recorded by filing a form prescribed for that purpose with the Patents Office. The form filed patent shall contain particulars including but not limited to the full name and address of both the transferring party and the recipient of the rights, a detailed description of the patented invention subject to the transfer, and the scope and duration of any license granted. A certificate purporting to be signed by an authorised officer of the Patents Office confirming the registration of such form shall serve as conclusive evidence of the transfer or licensing agreement for all purposes, subject to challenge based solely on demonstrable fraud in the execution of said certificate. Any subsequent dealings with the patent are deemed governed by this recorded transfer until a further formal notification is filed and registered.

A certificate purporting to have been issued by a duly appointed Examiner of Patents, affirming compliance with the requirements under this Act concerning novelty and inventive step, shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding relating to the validity of a patent. Such certificate may be challenged if it is demonstrated that the issuance was procured through fraud or misrepresentation; however, the burden of proof regarding such fraudulent procurement shall rest entirely upon the party contesting the certificate’s veracity. Provided that, where an appeal against a decision based on said certificate is filed, the appellate authority may require production of all records and correspondence leading to its formulation. The patent consequence arising from reliance on this certificate remains subject to judicial review as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to have priority from the date of its first filing under this Act, provided that where an earlier identical or deceptively similar mark exists registered in another country, the applicant may submit evidence substantiating such prior use and foreign registration. The Registrar shall record the details of any such submitted documentation pertaining to the claimed priority. For determining entitlement to remedies for infringement, the *shall registered date* is conclusive proof of the applicant’s initial claim to exclusive rights in relation to the goods or services specified in the register. Any subsequent alteration to the description of goods or services will not affect the original registration date as recorded by the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, the “court rectification register” means a publicly accessible record maintained by the Registrar, detailing all applications filed before a competent court seeking rectification of entries in the Trade Marks Register. Such an application may concern claims of invalidity, revocation, or any other error appearing on the register. The court rectification register shall include particulars such as the trade mark involved, the names and addresses of the parties to the proceedings, and the date upon which the application was filed. Information contained within this register is subject to confidentiality provisions under this Act relating to sensitive commercial information.

Applications for entry in the court rectification register relating to registered trademarks shall be made to the appropriate jurisdictional authority, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods under this Act. Such applications must specify with particularity the grounds upon which the applicant contends that the trademark registration is erroneous or otherwise invalid, including but not limited to instances of improper acceptance, misleading representation, or conflict with prior rights. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating these claims and shall provide a reasonable opportunity for the registered proprietor to respond in writing. Provided that any decision regarding rectification made by the court shall be final and binding, barring appeal only on grounds of law as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an entry on the court rectification register concerning a registered trade mark believes that such entry is erroneous or has been obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or any other improper means, he shall have the right to appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein. The appellate authority may, after affording the respondent an opportunity of being heard, direct the removal of the erroneous entry from the court rectification register and restore the original registration details. Further, if the appellant demonstrates that the registered trade mark has not been used honestly in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered during a continuous period of five years following its registration, the appellate authority may order cancellation of the registration. The respondent shall be entitled to counter such claims with evidence demonstrating genuine use and good faith.

An application for rectification of the register may be made to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal by any person aggrieved by an entry in the register relating to a trade mark. Such application shall specify the grounds on which the applicant relies and shall be accompanied by such documents or other evidence as the applicant deems necessary to substantiate their claim. The Tribunal shall serve notice of the application upon the Registrar and the proprietor of the trade mark concerned, affording them reasonable opportunity to file counter-statements. Upon consideration of the pleadings and any oral arguments presented, the Tribunal may order rectification of the register by deletion of an entry, amendment of an entry, or otherwise as it deems just and equitable. Decisions regarding rectification shall be final subject to appeal under this Act to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such decision. The Registrar shall promptly give effect to any order made by the Tribunal concerning the court rectification register.

Where an entry in the court rectification register has been made pursuant to an order under this Act, and any person aggrieved by that entry seeks to challenge its validity, they shall institute proceedings directly in the relevant High Court within six months of the date of such registration. Failure to do so will be deemed conclusive evidence against their right to contest the rectification. The court may, subject to just cause shown, grant an extension of this period not exceeding three months. Any party failing to comply with these timelines shall be liable for a penalty of fifty thousand rupees and costs incurred by the opposing party in defending the proceedings; provided that wilful default attracts a further penalty as determined by the Court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any proprietor of a registered trade mark who has entered into an assignment or license agreement relating to the use of their trade mark shall, upon request from the assignee or licensee respectively, provide them with a certified copy of the entry in the court rectification register pertaining to any application for correction or deletion filed by the proprietor. Such copies shall be deemed sufficient evidence of the existence and details of the rectification proceedings. Further, where an assignment includes the right to apply for rectification, the assignee may, with written consent from the assignor, pursue such applications independently. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding failure to provide this information, issue directions compelling compliance, subject to appeal under this Act.

An application for rectification of the Trade Marks Register may be made by any person claiming title or interest in a trade mark registered under this Act, provided that such applicant demonstrates a clear and demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the continued registration. Where an application is filed concerning a Business India application previously accepted, the Registrar shall serve notice upon the proprietor of the said Business India application, affording them thirty days to submit a counter-statement. The court rectification register shall be maintained electronically by the Registrar, detailing all applications received and their respective statuses, including dates of filing, hearings scheduled, and orders passed. Any order altering the Register is subject to appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date thereof.

Where an entry in the court rectification register has been made pursuant to an order rectifying a registered trade mark, and any party aggrieved by that entry appeals under this Act, the appellate authority shall consider whether the original decision leading to the rectification was demonstrably erroneous in law or fact. The appeal may be predicated on grounds including, but not limited to, procedural irregularities during the initial rectification proceedings, newly discovered evidence materially affecting the outcome, or a misinterpretation of established legal precedent relating to trade mark distinctiveness. Provided that a broadcasting organisation shall continue to utilise the registered trade mark until the appellate authority’s determination is conclusive, and subject to any interim orders issued by the court.

Where a trade mark is registered in respect of goods manufactured exclusively outside India, the Registrar may, upon application by any interested person, direct that the registration be accompanied by a notification specifying the country or countries where such goods are manufactured. Such notification shall remain part of the register and shall be subject to amendment under this Act if the manufacturing location changes. The applicant for such direction must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that consumers are likely to be misled regarding the origin of the goods. Failure to comply with a direction issued under this provision may result in rectification proceedings initiated by any interested party, as provided herein. Any alteration to the goods manufactured notification requires prior approval from the Registrar.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods manufactured outside India, the proprietor shall provide written notice to the Registrar specifying the country or countries where those goods are manufactured. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the trade mark was originally registered for use in connection with goods manufactured within India. Failure to comply with this provision may result in the Registrar issuing a warning and, subsequently, restricting the scope of protection afforded by the registration to exclude use relating to goods manufactured outside India. Any party aggrieved by such restriction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act. The Registrar shall publish details of any such notice and subsequent restrictions in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, the proprietor may apply to the Registrar for a waiver from the requirement of providing a goods manufactured notification if compelling circumstances exist.

Where a trade mark is registered in respect of goods manufactured exclusively outside India, the Registrar shall, upon application made by the proprietor and accompanied by an affidavit verifying the truthfulness of the statements contained therein, direct that notice be given to any person or persons claiming to manufacture such goods in India. Such notice shall specify the class of goods in relation to which the trade mark is registered and invite objections from those claiming a right to manufacture them. The Registrar may entertain objections relating solely to the question whether the goods are manufactured outside India, as provided herein. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence regarding manufacturing location may result in cancellation proceedings. Further, where the proprietor subsequently commences manufacturing of the said goods within India, they shall be obligated to furnish a notification to the Registrar detailing such commencement and specifying the place of manufacture; this requirement constitutes a goods manufactured notification.

Where a trade mark is registered in respect of goods manufactured exclusively outside the territory of India, the Registrar shall require the proprietor to furnish, within thirty days of the request, details pertaining to the manufacturing process and location. Such information must be verified by an affidavit confirming adherence to established quality control standards as prescribed under this Act. Failure to provide such particulars or demonstrable non-compliance with said standards may result in a direction for suspension of registration. Furthermore, where goods manufactured outside India are subsequently also produced within India, the proprietor shall notify the Registrar within ninety days, detailing the commencement date and location of domestic manufacture; this constitutes a requirement for goods manufactured notification.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods manufactured outside India, the proprietor shall, subject to any conditions specified therein, provide a written notification to the Trade Marks Registry within ninety days of the commencement of such manufacture. This notification must detail the country of origin and the manufacturing process employed. Failure to comply with this requirement does not, however, render the registration void but may be raised as a ground for revocation under this Act by any interested party. An appeal against an order requiring such goods manufactured notification lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order; provided that the Board shall consider whether the non-compliance constitutes substantial deception or misrepresentation to consumers.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods manufactured outside India, the proprietor shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within thirty days of commencement of manufacture for export, a notification specifying the class of goods under the relevant alphabetical index classification. Failure to provide such notification, or providing it with material inaccuracies, constitutes an offence and renders the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Any person aggrieved by the omission or inaccuracy in a goods manufactured notification may file a complaint before the Registrar, who shall afford opportunity for hearing and issue directions as provided herein. Repeat offenders are subject to enhanced penalties and potential suspension of registration rights.

Where a trade mark is registered for goods manufactured in India, the Registrar may, upon application by any interested person and after due inquiry, direct the registration proprietor to furnish, within a prescribed period, particulars relating to the geographical location of the manufacturing premises where such goods are produced. Failure to comply with this direction shall render the registration liable to be amended to reflect that the trade mark is registered for goods manufactured in India generally, rather than from a specific defendant geographical area. The Registrar may also issue a notification requiring all proprietors of trade marks registered for goods manufactured notification to provide updated details regarding their manufacturing locations annually, as provided herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods manufactured outside India, the proprietor shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within thirty days of the commencement of manufacture or production beyond the limits of India, a notification specifying the country where such goods are manufactured. Failure to provide this goods manufactured notification may result in the Registrar issuing a direction for suspension of rights under this Act. The date claim associated with the initial registration shall be deemed relevant when assessing whether the proprietor has acted diligently in fulfilling their obligations as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order suspending rights may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating prejudice resulting directly from the suspension.

A person shall be deemed a “person threatened infringement” where such person reasonably believes that another has engaged, or intends to engage, in conduct infringing upon their registered trade mark, and has made a written representation to the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the perceived infringement and requesting cessation thereof. For the purposes of this Act, "reasonable belief" shall mean a good faith conviction based on objective facts available at the time, subject to judicial review. A person threatened infringement may pursue remedies as provided herein, notwithstanding that no actual damage has yet been suffered by the trade mark proprietor; however, any injunction granted shall be proportionate to the potential harm reasonably anticipated.

Any individual, firm, or company seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish an affidavit verifying that, to their knowledge, no proceedings for infringement have been initiated against them concerning any marks identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for trade mark. Where a person is threatened with infringement action relating to a registered trade mark, and reasonably believes such threat constitutes undue interference with their own legitimate commercial activities, they may petition the relevant intellectual property authority for interim relief. Such petitions shall detail the nature of the threatened infringement and demonstrate that the applicant is a person threatened infringement under this Act. The authority may grant temporary measures pending resolution of the matter, provided that adequate security is furnished as deemed appropriate.

Where any individual or entity reasonably believes that their trade mark rights are likely to be infringed, and such belief is based on representations made by another party concerning intended use or sale of goods or services, they may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. The aggrieved person shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining the threatening party from continuing those actions. This remedy is available even if no actual infringement has yet occurred, provided that the threatened infringement would, if carried out, constitute a violation under this Act. Further, damages may be awarded to compensate for losses incurred as a result of the unwarranted threat, including costs associated with defending against baseless claims. A person threatened infringement shall not be precluded from pursuing other remedies available at law or equity.

Where any individual, firm, or company believes that their trade mark rights are being infringed or threatened by the actions of another party, they may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such a proceeding shall be initiated within ninety days from the date on which the person threatened infringement first becomes aware of the infringing activity or threat. The application must specify the trade mark in question, detail the nature of the alleged infringement, and provide evidence supporting the claim that the respondent’s conduct constitutes a threat to the validity or reputation of the registered trade mark. The tribunal may, upon review of the submitted documentation and after affording the respondent an opportunity for response, issue interim orders restraining further infringing activity pending final determination. Costs associated with such proceedings shall be determined as provided herein, considering the complexity of the matter and the conduct of both parties.

Any individual anticipating threatened infringement of a registered trademark shall possess the right to grant a non-exclusive license pertaining specifically to the use of said mark within defined geographical territories. Such licenses may be assigned freely, subject to adherence with conditions stipulated herein regarding fair market value and reasonable royalty payments to the grantor. Where an assignment of such a license occurs, the assignee shall inherit all rights and obligations associated with that specific usage permitted under the original licensing agreement. A person threatened infringement may also enter into reciprocal agreements for cross-licensing of trademarks, provided both parties consent in writing and acknowledge mutual benefit. Further, any transfer or encumbrance of trademark ownership must explicitly detail the scope of licensed use retained by the individual initially facing a threat of infringement.

Where any individual, firm, or company reasonably believes that their trade mark registration is likely to be infringed by another party’s activities, and such belief arises from demonstrable actions indicating an intention to utilize a similar sign in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the trade mark is registered, they may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Provided that the aggrieved party can demonstrate a clear nexus between the alleged infringing activity and potential damage to their commercial interests, they shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The determination of whether a person constitutes a “person threatened infringement” shall be subject to review on appeal by the appellate forum, considering all relevant factors including the proportionality of the remedy sought.

For the purposes of this Act, "threatened infringement" shall mean an instance where a party communicates, either directly or indirectly, to another party that they intend to pursue legal action alleging trade mark infringement, dilution, or passing off. Such communication must reasonably appear to convey an intention to enforce rights claimed under this Act against the recipient’s use of a sign, whether identical or similar to a registered trade mark. The threat may be explicit or implied and need not specify the precise nature of the alleged violation. Provided that such communication is made in bad faith or with the primary purpose of intimidation, it shall constitute threatened infringement as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another party intends to use a mark identical or confusingly similar to their registered trade mark in connection with goods or services for which it is registered, they may serve upon such other party a notice specifying the acts constituting the threatened infringement. Such notice shall detail the grounds upon which the alleged infringement is based and clearly articulate the remedies sought by the proprietor. The recipient of such a notice shall be afforded a period of sixty days from the date of service to respond with their position, providing evidence supporting their use or intended use. Failure to adequately address the concerns raised in the notice may result in proceedings initiated under this Act seeking injunctive relief and damages for threatened infringement.

Where any individual or entity engages in conduct reasonably appearing to constitute threatened infringement of a registered trade mark, and such conduct includes representations, either express or implied, that they will initiate legal proceedings against another party for utilizing similar indicia, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief from the relevant jurisdictional authority. This right is subject to the condition that the threatened use genuinely creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services. Provided that the trade mark owner demonstrates a credible and substantial risk of damage resulting from the threatened action, interim measures may be granted pending final determination. The respondent shall bear the burden of demonstrating that their actions do not constitute threatened infringement as defined under this Act, nor create an unreasonable apprehension of litigation.

Where any individual or entity engages in conduct reasonably appearing to constitute threatened infringement of a registered trade mark, and such conduct includes communication, either written or oral, to another party indicating an intention to pursue legal remedies for alleged unauthorized use, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such proceedings shall be initiated within ninety days from the date of receipt of the initial communication constituting the threatened infringement. The Board may, upon review of evidence presented by both parties, issue orders restraining further communications or actions indicative of threatened infringement. Provided that, a finding of threatened infringement does not automatically establish actual infringement; it solely addresses the nature and scope of the intimidating conduct. Any order issued under this Act shall be subject to appeal before the High Court within sixty days thereafter.

Where any entity engages in conduct reasonably appearing to constitute threatened infringement of a registered trade mark, and such conduct includes communication, either written or oral, to another party indicating an intention to pursue legal remedies for alleged use of the mark, that other party shall be deemed aggrieved. Provided that, the communication must specifically detail the nature of the alleged infringing activity and the remedial measures demanded; otherwise, it does not constitute threatened infringement as provided herein. Further, a notice may be served upon the entity engaging in such conduct requiring cessation of the threatening behaviour within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the entity liable for damages sustained by the aggrieved party, subject to assessment by the relevant adjudicating authority.

Where any entity engages in conduct reasonably likely to induce confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services associated with a registered trade mark, and such conduct constitutes threatened infringement, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief from the relevant jurisdictional authority. Such injunction may restrain the offending entity from continuing said conduct, subject to demonstrating actual or imminent loss as a consequence thereof. Furthermore, where an undertaking is found to have made false representations concerning the existence or nature of a registered trade mark in order to gain an unfair commercial advantage, it shall be liable for damages proportionate to the detriment suffered by the trade mark proprietor. Penalties may also be imposed under this Act.

Where the owner of a registered trademark reasonably believes that another party’s activities constitute threatened infringement, they may grant a non-exclusive license to utilize the mark for specific purposes, provided that such license is documented in writing and includes provisions safeguarding the integrity of the trademark. The licensee shall be bound by conditions stipulated within the agreement, including limitations on geographical scope and product categories. Further, any assignment of rights relating to this licensed use must receive prior written consent from the original owner, subject to a fee determined according to regulations framed under this Act. This requirement ensures continued oversight and prevents unauthorized exploitation beyond the initially agreed terms. The owner retains the right to revoke the license if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the trademark.

Where any entity engages in conduct reasonably appearing to constitute threatened infringement of a registered trade mark, and such conduct includes the issuance of notices demanding cessation of use or sale of goods bearing a similar sign, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. The tribunal shall consider whether the notice was issued with the intent to unlawfully restrain competition or create undue hardship for the recipient. Provided that the threatened infringement is demonstrably based on a misrepresentation of fact regarding the similarity of signs or the absence of consumer confusion, the tribunal may issue an injunction restraining further communication of such notices. Any order made under this Act shall be subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark possesses reasonable apprehension that another party intends to use a sign in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, and such intended use would constitute threatened infringement under this Act, the proprietor may serve upon the potential infringer a notice specifying the acts likely to amount to such infringement. The notice shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the apprehension of infringement is based, including particulars relating to any confusing similarity between the potentially infringing sign and the registered trade mark, especially concerning the appearance or arrangement of lettering on a plate bearing the sign.

Where any proprietor of a trade mark reasonably believes that another person intends to use a sign in relation to goods or services for which the trade mark is registered, and such intended use constitutes threatened infringement under this Act, the proprietor may serve upon the potential infringer a formal notice detailing the specific aspects of the proposed use giving rise to concern. This notice shall include particulars of the relevant trade mark registration and a clear explanation of how the intended use would likely cause confusion amongst consumers or otherwise infringe the distinctiveness of the registered mark. The notice may also specify remedial measures, such as modification of packaging or alteration of marketing materials, which would mitigate the risk of infringement. A package of information regarding prior similar uses shall be included with the notice.

Where any individual or entity engages in conduct reasonably appearing to constitute threatened infringement of a registered trade mark, an affected party may institute proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such proceedings shall be initiated within ninety days from the date on which the threat became known to the aggrieved party. The respondent shall be required to demonstrate that their actions do not, and are not likely to, cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services. Where the respondent utilizes a distinctive board use layout incorporating elements similar to the registered trade mark, this factor shall be considered in assessing the likelihood of consumer deception. The Tribunal may issue an injunction restraining further conduct deemed to constitute threatened infringement, subject to principles of proportionality and freedom of expression as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "proceeding infringement" shall mean an action undertaken by any party which creates a reasonable apprehension in the mind of another that their trade mark rights are being, or are likely to be, infringed. Such actions include, but are not limited to, the publication of false or misleading statements concerning the quality or origin of goods or services; the use of signs identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services not authorized by the proprietor; and any other conduct calculated to deceive or confuse consumers regarding the source or affiliation of products. Provided that mere advertising, devoid of such deceptive intent, shall not constitute proceeding infringement as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trademark has been granted and the certificate of registration issued, any party claiming ownership rights in a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use of the trade mark. The Registrar shall have the power to issue interim injunctions restraining acts of proceeding infringement pending final determination of the matter before an appropriate judicial forum, provided that such action is demonstrably causing irreparable harm to the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered trademark. Further, any representation or false designation made in connection with goods or services utilizing a similar mark shall be considered actionable under this Act.

Where any party institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, such proceedings shall be commenced within the jurisdiction of the High Court designated to entertain suits relating to intellectual property rights in the State where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose. Notice of institution of these proceedings must be served upon the defendant by registered post with acknowledgment due, and a copy simultaneously furnished to the Registrar. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such commenced infringement actions, including details of parties involved and the trade mark in question. Failure to adhere to prescribed service protocols may render the proceeding vulnerable to challenge under this Act. Provided that, where an interlocutory application is filed concerning discovery or inspection of documents, the High Court may direct any party to produce relevant materials as deemed necessary for a just determination of the matter relating to proceeding infringement.

Where any party institutes a proceeding infringement action against another in respect of a registered trade mark, such action shall only be maintainable if the claimant demonstrates demonstrable and ongoing commercial harm directly attributable to the alleged infringing activity. The claimant must provide evidence, satisfactory to the relevant adjudicating authority, establishing that the defendant’s use of the impugned sign creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of goods or services. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrably acted in good faith and without knowledge of the registered trade mark's existence at the time of initial adoption, the claimant shall be entitled to seek only injunctive relief and proportionate damages, as determined under this Act. Further, any counter-claim alleging misuse of the registered trade mark by the claimant shall be considered only if supported by verifiable documentary evidence.

Where any party institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, and such proceedings are found by the relevant adjudicating authority to be manifestly frivolous or vexatious, or brought with the primary intent to harass or delay the defendant, the court may order that party to pay compensatory damages to the defendant. Such damages shall include, but not be limited to, reimbursement for reasonable legal costs incurred in defending against the unfounded claim, and any demonstrable loss of business opportunity directly attributable to the unwarranted proceeding infringement. Further, the adjudicating authority may impose a punitive element on such damages, subject to judicial review, to deter similar abusive litigation tactics. The court shall also have the power to award costs against the claimant in respect of such frivolous proceedings.

Subject to any agreement entered into under this Act, the owner of a registered trade mark shall have the right to grant licenses permitting the use of their trademark for specific goods or services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and the terms thereof, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by mutual consent between the licensor and licensee. Where a license is assigned, such assignment shall not affect any existing rights accrued under the license prior to its transfer. Any party utilizing a trademark pursuant to a valid license agreement shall be deemed an authorized user for the purposes of determining proceeding infringement. Further, the owner may assign their right to proceed against infringers to another entity, provided that such assignment is recorded with the relevant Trade Marks Registry and does not prejudice any existing licensee’s rights as defined within the licensing contract.

Where any party institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, and such proceedings are subsequently stayed by order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board on grounds of lack of territorial jurisdiction, the aggrieved party may appeal directly to the High Court within ninety days from the date of receipt of the said order. The appellate court shall consider whether the initial jurisdictional assessment was demonstrably flawed based on a misinterpretation of the facts presented and relevant case law. Provided that, if the appellant fails to demonstrate such demonstrable flaw, the stay shall remain in effect. Further, any counter-claim alleging misuse of process or frivolous proceeding infringement filed during these appeal proceedings shall be adjudicated concurrently with the primary appeal, subject to the Court’s discretion.

Any applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish an affidavit verifying the distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness of the proposed mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Failure to do so may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before the relevant intellectual property authority. Where it is established that a registered trade mark has been used in connection with goods or services without consent, and such use constitutes proceeding infringement, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages. In cases involving wilful trading of counterfeit goods bearing a protected mark, an imprisonment term shall not be less than six months and may extend to three years.

Where any individual knowingly and wilfully utilizes a trademark identical or deceptively similar to a registered mark in connection with goods or services for which such registration subsists, constituting a proceeding infringement, they shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such damages may include compensation for lost profits, diminution in value of goodwill, and any other financial detriment suffered by the trademark proprietor. Further, where the infringing activity is demonstrated to have been undertaken with intent to deceive or mislead consumers, the offender shall also be subject to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. In egregious cases involving persistent and widespread infringement, the court may impose sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

Any party claiming relief against an act of proceeding infringement shall furnish evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the impugned mark and the registered trade mark, considering both visual appearance and phonetic representation. Where such a claim arises concerning a mark’s registration mentioned clause, the aggrieved party must further demonstrate that the infringing use creates likelihood of confusion amongst relevant consumers regarding origin or sponsorship. Failure to provide satisfactory proof as provided herein shall render the proceeding untenable and subject the claimant to costs incurred by the defendant in defending the action. The Tribunal may, upon finding an unwarranted threat of legal proceedings, impose a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for each instance of such conduct.

Any person desiring to register a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit shall established registry with the Controller. Applications for registration shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, failure to remit which shall render the application void ab initio. The Controller may reject any application if it contains false particulars or is otherwise not in conformity with the provisions of this Act; such rejection shall be communicated to the applicant with reasons and opportunity for a hearing as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Controller rejecting an application, or refusing registration, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe penalties for making false statements in any application or document submitted under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “Geographical Indication” means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin; and includes signs that signify such geographical origin and are used to define the same. The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act defines "place" to mean any defined geographic area. An application for registration shall be examined by the Geographical Indication Registrar, who may request further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. The Registrar’s decision on such requests is final subject to appeal as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “design registry registration” shall mean the entry of a layout-design into the Register of Layout-Designs maintained by the Registrar, signifying that the layout-design has been examined and found to be eligible for protection under this Act. An application for design registry registration shall include particulars relating to the applicant, the layout-design itself, and any claims regarding originality and industrial applicability as provided herein. The Registrar may require such further information or modifications to the layout-design as are necessary to ensure compliance with the requirements of this Act. A registered layout-design confers upon the registrant exclusive rights subject to any subsequent conflicting registrations.

An application for design registry registration may be made by any person claiming to be the first inventor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design or who is authorized by the first inventor to make such an application. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, its intended use, and specify the relevant technical data pertaining to its fabrication process. Provided that the applicant demonstrates originality and lack of prior publication under this Act, the Registrar may proceed with examination. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration or refusal thereof may appeal to the designated Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The register maintained by the Registrar shall be open for public inspection during normal business hours, subject to prescribed regulations.

Upon registration of a design within the design registry, the registered proprietor shall possess exclusive rights to exploit commercially the protected layout-design throughout India. Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, offers to sell, or distributes any article embodying the registered layout-design, or any substantially similar design, shall be deemed to have infringed upon the registered right. The remedies available to the registered proprietor in cases of infringement include an injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to considerations of equitable principles. Provided that, a claim for damages may only be pursued if the proprietor had given notice of the design registry registration prior to the commencement of the infringing activity.

An application for design registry registration may be made to the Controller in such form and containing such particulars as the Controller specifies by notification in the Official Gazette. The application shall include a representation of the layout-design, accompanied by a statement indicating whether the applicant is the first maker or subsequent owner of the design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall furnish the applicant with a deemed date of filing for the purpose of priority assessment, provided that the applicant submits all requisite documentation as prescribed herein within the stipulated timeframe. The Controller may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the layout-design and its ownership. If satisfied that the design is registrable under this Act, the Controller shall proceed with registration, subject to payment of applicable fees.

An application for design registry registration may be filed by any person claiming to be the first inventor of the layout-design, or by a registered proprietor of the rights pertaining thereto. Such an application shall contain a full and accurate representation of the integrated circuit layout-design, accompanied by a statement specifying the date on which the claim of invention arose. The Registrar shall examine each application to ascertain compliance with prescribed formalities; provided that any deficiency in form may be rectified under this Act if notified within the stipulated period. Registration shall only be granted where the layout-design is original and not substantially similar to any prior published matter, as determined by the Registrar’s assessment of its aesthetic or functional characteristics.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to grant design registry registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be finally disposed of within six months from the date it is filed before the Tribunal, subject to just and equitable considerations. Failure to comply with prescribed formalities during the application process or subsequent proceedings relating to design registry registration renders the applicant liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any act of knowingly making, importing, selling, hiring, or displaying an article infringing a registered layout-design is deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein.

The holder of a design registry registration relating to an integrated circuit layout-design may grant a license conferring specific rights pertaining to the manufacture, import, or sale of products incorporating the registered layout-design. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor and detailed within the licensing agreement. Assignment of such design registry registrations, or any portion thereof, shall require prior written consent from the Registrar, provided that evidence demonstrating a legitimate commercial interest is submitted alongside the assignment documentation. Any subsequent transfer of rights under a license granted pursuant to this Act must be disclosed to the Registrar within thirty days. The licensor retains full authority to terminate licenses upon material breach by the licensee, subject to contractual stipulations and remedies available under general principles of contract law as provided herein.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal if any party is aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the refusal of registration of a design or the revocation of a design registry registration. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date on which the order is communicated to the appellant, provided that the Tribunal may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay. The Appellate Tribunal shall hear arguments and consider evidence relevant to the dispute, subject to such procedures as it deems fit; its decision shall be final, though further appeal lies to the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of an order passed by the Tribunal.

Any person aggrieved by a decision to refuse registration of a design under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order.
