Failure to comply with prescribed formalities during the application process for design registry registration shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, any unauthorized reproduction or importation for sale of an article incorporating a registered layout-design, irrespective of whether it infringes associated trade marks, constitutes infringement and is subject to damages equivalent to three times the value of goods produced or imported, or a sum not less than ten thousand rupees per infringing item, as determined by the Tribunal.

An applicant seeking registration of a design register layout shall furnish to the Registrar a detailed specification including all views necessary for understanding the layout-design. The specification must clearly identify any mask works incorporated within the layout-design and their respective owners, provided that such identification does not compromise trade secrets. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may request further clarification or modifications to ensure compliance with these requirements. If the applicant fails to provide the requested information within the stipulated time, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. The design register layout, once registered, will be recorded in the Register of Layout-Designs and open for public inspection as provided herein.

Where a registered design register layout is infringed, the proprietor may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such infringement occurs when any person without authorisation makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell articles embodying the registered design, or does anything that would otherwise constitute an infringement under this Act. The remedies available to the proprietor shall include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and damages reflecting lost profits attributable to the infringing activity. Provided that in determining damages, the court may consider any benefit accruing to the infringer as a result of the infringement. Further, the proprietor is entitled to account for all gains derived from the infringement, even if such gains are not directly quantifiable. Subject to principles of fairness, an injunction may be granted prior to judgment pending determination of the merits of the claim.

An application for registration of a design register layout may be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such information as the Registrar deems necessary to ascertain whether the layout-design is original. The Registrar shall examine each application and may require the applicant to submit further particulars or modifications, provided that the applicant shall have a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of such requirement to comply. If the Registrar finds that the design register layout does not satisfy the requirements under this Act, the Registrar shall reject the application and intimate the reasons for rejection to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar rejecting an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Registrar maintains a public record of registered design register layouts accessible upon payment of prescribed fees.

An application for registration of a design register layout may be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout-design does not involve a degree of skill and ingenuity sufficient to constitute an original work. Provided that, such refusal shall only be made after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard under this Act. The Registrar shall require the applicant to furnish detailed specifications including all layers comprising the integrated circuit layout-design, along with a technical explanation demonstrating the novelty and inventive step involved. Further, any modification or alteration to a registered design register layout subsequent to registration requires prior approval from the Registrar, subject to compliance with prescribed procedural requirements as provided herein. The applicant shall also declare whether the layout-design incorporates elements derived from previously published works.

Any person who, having knowledge of a registered design register layout, reproduces, copies, or imitates any substantial part thereof for commercial purposes without the authorization of the owner shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. Such damages shall not be less than five per centum of the cost of production and may extend up to ten times the value of infringing goods or services. Further, under this Act, any entity found guilty of such infringement is subject to seizure of the infringing layout-design and related materials. The owner of a design register layout may also apply for an injunction restraining further acts of reproduction or imitation, provided that they demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the unauthorized use.

The holder of a design register relating to a layout-design may grant a license conferring rights to use the registered layout-design, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacture, import, sale, hire, and exhibition of integrated circuits incorporating the design register layout. Assignment of rights pertaining to a registered layout-design is permissible, provided that such assignment is executed in writing and duly stamped as required under relevant laws. Any subsequent licensee or assignee shall be bound by the original terms of registration and any conditions imposed during the initial grant. The Registrar may require submission of details regarding assignments and licenses for record purposes, as provided herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an aggrieved party alleging infringement of a registered design register layout may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such proceedings shall be deemed civil suits subject to the pecuniary jurisdiction as determined under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate prima facie evidence of registration and substantial similarity between the impugned layout-design and the registered layout-design, providing detailed technical specifications for comparison. Failure to present such evidence may result in dismissal of the suit without further consideration. The High Court shall afford the respondent an opportunity to rebut the claims and submit counter-evidence as provided herein, ensuring a fair hearing before rendering any judgment concerning validity or infringement.

The registered design register layout may be assigned by the registrant to any person, either wholly or partially, and subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register within thirty days of its execution, provided that the Registrar may require submission of a certified copy of the instrument effecting the assignment. Where an assignment is made, the assignee shall become the absolute owner of the design register layout for the duration of the term of protection as specified under this Act. Furthermore, the right to grant licenses relating to the use or exploitation of the registered design register layout may be exercised by the registrant and such licenses shall be subject to copyright design considerations where applicable, ensuring that any reproduction or adaptation respects existing intellectual property rights.

An application for registration of a design register layout may be made to the Registrar by any person claiming to be the first inventor of the layout-design or who is authorized by the first inventor to make the application. The layout design consisting of three dimensional features, if deemed original and not infringing existing registered designs under this Act, shall be eligible for registration upon fulfillment of prescribed formalities. Any modification to the submitted layout design prior to registration will render the application liable for rejection. Upon satisfactory examination and verification that the layout-design is capable of protection as provided herein, the Registrar may proceed with its registration in the register maintained for such purpose. The applicant shall furnish a copy of the layout-design for inclusion in the public record.

For the purposes of this Act, a “layout-design” means the three-dimensional representation of an integrated circuit used to produce a semiconductor integrated circuit. The term "integrated circuit" includes any set of interconnections and arrangements of active and passive electrical components embodied on or within a single semiconducting material. An application for registration of a layout-design shall include particulars as prescribed, including but not limited to the name and address of the applicant and a representation of the layout-design. The Registrar may require such further information as is necessary for examination under this Act. To register said layout, the applicant must demonstrate originality in the arrangement of elements within the design.

An applicant seeking to register a layout-design shall submit an application electronically through the designated portal, accompanied by requisite fees as determined under this Act. The application must include detailed technical specifications and representations of the integrated circuit layout-design sought to be registered, conforming to standards prescribed by the Registrar. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may undertake preliminary scrutiny to ascertain compliance with formal requirements. If satisfied that the layout-design is original and not contrary to public interest, the Registrar shall proceed to register said layout. The registration shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights relating to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation of the registered layout-design, subject to any subsequent modifications or amendments as provided herein.

Subject to appeal under this Act, any person who, without authorization from the registered owner, directly or indirectly makes, uses, imports, or offers for sale a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying a registered layout, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at a minimum of five times the reasonable royalty that the infringer would have paid had they obtained a license to use the said layout. The registered owner may also seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, provided that such injunction is necessary to prevent irreparable harm. Further, where the infringement involves commercial exploitation of the registered layout, the Court may order the destruction or disposal of the infringing articles and materials as it deems fit. A person shall not be deemed to have infringed a right under this Act if they can prove prior use of the layout in India. It is imperative that any party seeking to register said layout provides full disclosure of all relevant prior art.

An applicant seeking to register a layout-design under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form along with the requisite fee. The application must contain a full and accurate representation of the layout-design, including any ancillary information deemed necessary by the Registrar for proper identification. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar may conduct such searches as are considered appropriate to ascertain whether the layout-design is substantially similar to any previously registered design or pending application. If, after due consideration, the Registrar finds no impediment to registration, notice thereof shall be published in the Official Gazette. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of an application for registration may, within a specified period, file a timely opposition with the Registrar, setting forth grounds for objection as provided herein. The Registrar shall then proceed to evaluate the merits of the opposition before making a determination regarding whether to register said layout.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, reproduces a registered layout-design for commercial purposes shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Such reproduction includes any act that exploits or copies substantial elements of the design, irrespective of minor alterations. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding infringement, issue an order directing the alleged infringer to cease such activity and submit accounts detailing profits derived from the unauthorized use. Failure to comply with this order shall constitute contempt of court and render the offender subject to penalties as provided herein. A registered layout-design confers exclusive rights; therefore, any attempt to register a substantially similar design will be rejected under this Act. It is imperative that one diligently checks the public register before proceeding to register said layout.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout may be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout without due authorization. The applicant aggrieved by such refusal shall have thirty days from the date of receipt of notice thereof to file an appeal under this Act. Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may, upon examination of evidence presented by both parties, direct the Registrar to reconsider the application and register said layout if it finds that the elements in question do not constitute a substantial derivation or that due authorization was indeed obtained. The decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified herein.

An applicant desiring to obtain protection under this Act may file an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout. Such an application shall be accompanied by requisite fees as prescribed and shall specify particulars relating to the layout design, including its title and date of first commercial exploitation, if any. The Registrar shall examine the application to ascertain compliance with the provisions herein and may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification. Following examination, if satisfied that the layout-design is eligible for registration, the Registrar shall register said layout in the Register of Layout Designs. India filed months after the initial filing date are permissible under certain conditions as detailed elsewhere within this Act, provided that the design remains novel and original.

An application to register a layout design may be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by such fees as are determined under this Act. The application shall specify the name and address of the applicant, a description of the layout design, and particulars of any geographical indication associated with its creation or intended use. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice thereof in the Official Gazette. Any person may, within three months from the date of such publication, file written representations objecting to the registration on grounds specified herein. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and provide the applicant an opportunity for response. If, after due consideration, the Registrar is satisfied that the layout design is original and eligible for registration, he or she shall register said layout and issue a certificate of registration.

For the purposes of this Act, “layout design” means the three dimensional representation of an integrated circuit upon a semiconductor chip resulting from the arrangement or combination of active and passive components and interconnections; provided that such representation is defined by reference to a pattern. The term "integrated circuit" has the meaning assigned to it under the Patents Act. An application for registration shall be deemed to include a claim extending to layout designs that are substantially similar to the design claimed, as determined by the Layout Design Registrar considering the overall impression created upon an informed user. The Layout Design Registrar may require further clarification of any aspect of a layout design during examination.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design under this Act shall furnish to the Layout Design Registrar such particulars relating to the layout design as are prescribed, including but not limited to, a complete description of the circuitry and its intended function. The registrar may require the submission of additional documentation deemed necessary for verification of originality and novelty, provided that any request for further information must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation. Upon receipt of an application, the Layout Design Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Any alteration to the layout design after the initial filing requires notification to the registrar prior to proceeding with registration.

Where a registered layout design is infringed, the copyright owner may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such action shall be brought before a competent court exercising ordinary original jurisdiction, notwithstanding any prior communication with the Layout Design Registrar regarding the alleged infringement. The remedies available to the copyright owner include damages equivalent to the loss suffered by him or her as a consequence of the infringement, and in determining such damages, the court may consider the profits made by the infringer attributable to the infringing layout design. Furthermore, an injunction may be granted restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement, provided that the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that irreparable harm will result without such relief. The Layout Design Registrar shall provide all relevant documentation pertaining to registration and prior communications upon request from a court hearing such proceedings.

An appeal against any decision made by the Layout Design Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or relating to rectification of the Register, may be filed with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The appellant shall serve a copy of the memorandum of appeal on the Layout Design Registrar not less than thirty days before the date of filing the same. Provided that the Board may, if it considers it necessary, require the appellant to satisfy itself as to the merits of the appeal before admitting it for hearing. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The Layout Design Registrar shall maintain a record of all appeals and orders made therein, accessible for public inspection as provided herein.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be deemed to have been refused if the prescribed fee has not been remitted within thirty days from the date of issue of the notice under this Act. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates satisfactory cause for the delay in payment, the Registrar may, at his discretion and after affording an opportunity for hearing, extend the time limit by a period not exceeding fifteen days. The layout design registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout designs accessible for public inspection, subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning trade secrets. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the layout design registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a registered layout design may grant a license conferring rights to use such layout design, either wholly or partially, for specific purposes and within defined territories. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and shall clearly specify the duration and scope of permitted activities. Assignment of ownership of a registered layout design is permissible, provided that prior consent from the Layout Design Registrar is obtained, confirming due diligence regarding any existing encumbrances on the design. The assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights and obligations of the assignor under this Act. Any transfer or license granted without such notification will be considered void and subject to penalties as prescribed herein. Further, a licensee may sub-license their rights with the express written permission of the layout design owner.

Where an aggrieved party disputes a decision made by the Layout Design Registrar concerning the validity of a registered layout design, such dispute may be referred to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall lie within ninety days from the date of communication of the order under challenge. Provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates reasonable grounds for delay, the Tribunal may entertain an appeal filed after the expiry of the said period. Further, the Registrar shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the registration and any subsequent opposition proceedings to the Tribunal upon request. The Tribunal’s decision on such appeals shall be final, subject to further review under provisions relating to writ petitions in the High Courts.

For the purposes of this Act, “acquiring restrict” means a legally binding agreement, whether express or implied, whereby a person undertakes to refrain from utilizing, commercially exploiting, or disclosing information pertaining to a registered layout design, and such undertaking is granted by the owner of the layout design to another person. The Layout Design Registrar shall maintain a register of acquiring restricts, detailing the parties involved, the scope of restriction, and the duration thereof. Any application for registration of an acquiring restrict must specify the layout design concerned and demonstrate that the applicant possesses a legitimate interest in obtaining such restrictions as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout design may be made by any person claiming to be the first owner thereof, or by an authorized agent acting on their behalf. Such applications shall be submitted to the Layout Design Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the registrar deems necessary to establish ownership, including details of the company responsible for the design’s creation where applicable. Registration shall confer upon the registrant exclusive rights relating to the layout design, subject to any conditions imposed during registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Layout Design Registrar may appeal to the relevant appellate authority within sixty days from the date of such decision, as provided herein.

Where a registered layout design is infringed by any act constituting certification trade, the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such proceedings shall be before the relevant jurisdictional court, subject to its discretion regarding interim injunctions and other equitable remedies as provided herein. The court may grant relief including damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the copyright holder, or a reasonable royalty, whichever is greater. Furthermore, the infringing party shall be liable to pay costs of the litigation. Any application for rectification of registration alleging infringement under this Act must first be made before the Layout Design Registrar, who shall entertain such applications and conduct hearings as deemed appropriate. The registrar’s decision may then be appealed to the jurisdictional court.

An application for rectification of a registered layout design may be made to the Layout Design Registrar by any person aggrieved by a decision or order relating to the registration, or by the existence of any right or interest in relation to such registration. The applicant shall state the grounds upon which the rectification is sought and shall furnish all relevant documents and information as required by the registrar. Upon receipt of an application for rectification, the Layout Design Registrar shall serve notice thereof on the registered proprietor, affording them a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-statement. Subject to this Act, the registrar may proceed with the inquiry ex parte if the registered proprietor fails to respond within the stipulated period. A permitted use of a layout design shall not constitute grounds for rectification unless it demonstrably prejudices the interests of the original registrant. The Layout Design Registrar’s decision in such matters is final and binding.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the business india application filed with respect to the same integrated circuit, demonstrating commercial intent and prior public disclosure considerations. The Layout Design Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the originality of the layout design, including detailed schematics and manufacturing process descriptions, provided that such requests are limited to ensuring compliance with the Act’s novelty requirements. Any applicant failing to submit the requisite business india application within thirty days of the initial registration request shall have their application deemed withdrawn unless a written extension is granted by the Registrar upon demonstration of exceptional circumstances. The registrar's decision regarding extensions may be appealed under this Act.

Any person found to have reproduced a registered integrated circuit layout design without authorization from the owner shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five per cent of the plaintiff’s net profits attributable to the infringing acts. The Layout Design Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly supported by an affidavit alleging infringement and accompanied by a detailed application patent specification outlining the claimed novelty and inventive step of the layout design, issue summons to the alleged infringer requiring them to appear before the Registrar for a hearing. Failure to comply with such summons shall be deemed conclusive evidence of admission of guilt, rendering the offender liable to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar’s decision in matters concerning infringement is final and binding, subject to appeal to the relevant High Court.

Any farmer aggrieved by any action taken by a plant variety registration authority or the farmers rights authority may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which such action is communicated to the appellant, and the Board shall have the power to entertain appeals against orders relating to revocation of registration, imposition of penalties, or any other matter where the farmer’s rights are concerned. The Authority may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, provide for alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to address grievances concerning benefit sharing agreements between farmers and breeders. Provided that decisions of the Appellate Board shall be binding on all parties involved, and remedies including compensation for losses sustained due to wrongful actions may be awarded as deemed appropriate by the Board.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copy translation work” shall mean a work which is an adaptation of another work, being a literary or dramatic work, wherein the original work has been translated into another language by way of expression. Such copy translation work shall be deemed an original work for the purposes of copyright protection, provided that the translator introduces sufficient alterations and additions to the original text so as to constitute new matter and creative labour. The right to reproduce a copy translation work shall vest in the author of such adaptation unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the translator and the owner of the underlying work, subject to any terms stipulated under this Act regarding fair dealing.

For the purposes of this Act, a copy translation work shall be deemed an original literary work if it exhibits sufficient originality in its adaptation and rendering of the source text. An application for registration of such a copy translation work may be made by the translator, or by the copyright owner of the source material with the consent of the translator, subject to verification of authorship as provided herein. The application shall include a certified true copy of the original work from which the translation was derived and a statement affirming the extent of alterations undertaken during the translation process. Registration of a copy translation work does not confer any rights in respect of the copyright subsisting in the original literary work, but protects the originality inherent in the translator’s rendition.

The right to reproduce a copy translation work shall vest initially with the translator, subject to the provisions regarding authorial contributions as provided herein. Where a literary or dramatic work has been translated into another language, and such translation incorporates substantial original authorship beyond the mere rendering of the source text, the copyright in the resulting copy translation work shall be jointly owned by the translator and the owner of the copyright in the original work, with each party possessing exclusive rights to exploit their respective contributions. Any unauthorized reproduction or distribution of a copy translation work infringing upon these joint ownership rights constitutes an act of piracy, entitling the aggrieved party to seek injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. Furthermore, any person found guilty of such infringement may be liable for imprisonment under this Act.

Where a copy translation work is undertaken by an individual acting as an employee, the copyright therein shall vest initially in the employer. The employer shall be deemed the author of such copy translation work for the purposes of this Act, subject to any agreement entered into between the employer and the employee specifying otherwise. Any dispute arising concerning the ownership of a copy translation work under this provision may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted as provided herein. Such tribunal’s decision shall be final and binding on all parties involved. The application for arbitration must be made within three years from the date of completion of the copy translation work. Further, where permission is sought to reproduce or distribute a copy translation work, such permission may only be granted by the copyright owner after due consideration of any contractual obligations existing between the employee and employer.

Where a copy translation work is created based upon an existing literary or dramatic work, the translator shall be entitled to recognition as the author of that copy translation work subject to the conditions outlined herein. Such recognition shall not prejudice or diminish the copyright subsisting in the original work under this Act. A person seeking to commercially exploit a copy translation work must provide evidence demonstrating due diligence was exercised to ascertain and comply with any existing rights holders’ permissions regarding the underlying work, including payment of equitable remuneration where applicable. Provided that, if the terms of such permission are not explicitly documented, the copyright holder of the original work may challenge the validity of the commercial exploitation under this Act within three years from the date of first publication of the copy translation work.

Where a copy translation work is produced without authorization from the copyright owner, such act shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Any individual found guilty of producing or distributing infringing copies of a copy translation work may be liable to pay damages equivalent to a sum not less than ten times the cost of production of the said work and not exceeding one million rupees. Furthermore, where the infringement is committed for commercial gain, the court may order seizure and destruction of the infringing copies as well as impose imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The copyright owner shall have the right to apply to the civil court for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement.

The owner of copyright in an original literary work shall be deemed the exclusive proprietor of any copy translation work derived therefrom, subject to the provisions herein relating to compulsory licences. Where a translator is engaged under contract to create such a copy translation work, the assignment of copyright therein shall be governed by the terms stipulated within that agreement; provided that if no such explicit terms are present, ownership shall vest initially in the commissioning party, but may be assigned subsequently with the consent of the translator. Any subsequent commercial exploitation of the copy translation work beyond the scope of the initial contractual arrangement requires further authorization from the original copyright owner and the translator, where applicable. The right to grant licences for reproduction or distribution of a copy translation work remains solely with the copyright holder unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Where a copy translation work is produced without authorization from the owner of copyright in the original work, such production shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the translator demonstrates good faith belief that the said copy translation work was undertaken for purposes of fair dealing, including criticism, review, or reporting of current events, and the extent of reproduction is limited to what is necessary for those purposes, a claim of infringement may be contested before the relevant judicial authority. The owner of copyright in the original work shall bear the burden of proving that the translator did not possess such good faith belief, subject to appeal to a higher court on grounds of misapplication of law or error apparent on the record.

Where a copy translation work is published without due authorisation by the owner of copyright in the original work, such owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further publication. The remedies available under this Act regarding infringement extend equally to unauthorized copy translations; however, provided that any person claiming damages must demonstrate reasonable diligence in pursuing the alleged infringer and quantifying the losses suffered as a direct result of the infringing publication. Further, where an individual has knowingly facilitated the creation or distribution of a copy translation work without proper copyright clearance, they shall be deemed jointly liable with the primary infringer for any resulting pecuniary loss to the original copyright holder. The right to claim damages arising from such infringement remains valid for a period of six years from the date of first publication of the infringing copy translation work.

Where a copy translation work is created based upon an existing copyrighted work, the translator shall be deemed the author of that copy translation work subject to the provisions regarding underlying works. An application for registration of such a copy translation work may be made before the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must specify the original work from which the copy translation work is derived, including details of publication where available. A practitioner person registered under this Act as a translator shall attest to the accuracy and fidelity of the copy translation work to the underlying copyrighted material. Any objection raised against registration may be addressed through written submissions within sixty days of the date of receipt by the Copyright Office. The Registrar may require further clarification or submission of additional documentation as deemed necessary for assessment.

The right to exploit a copy translation work shall vest initially with the copyright owner of the original work, subject to the provisions herein relating to prior publication. A practitioner engaged in the creation of such a copy translation work may, by written agreement executed before the completion of the work, assign the entire copyright therein to another party; provided that such assignment explicitly details the scope and duration of rights transferred. Further, where an author’s consent is required under this Act for the publication of a copy translation work, any subsequent licensing of reproduction or distribution rights shall be deemed invalid unless expressly authorized by both the original copyright owner and the translator-author. The copyright owner may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the adaptation or performance of the copy translation work, retaining all underlying rights in the original text.

Where a copy translation work is produced without authorization from the copyright owner, and such work incorporates substantial portions of the original literary or dramatic work, an aggrieved party shall have the right to appeal to the relevant High Court. The determination of what constitutes a “substantial portion” for the purposes of this provision shall be subject to interpretation based on qualitative and quantitative assessments, considering the nature of the original work and the extent of translation involved. Further, it shall be deemed insufficient defense that the translator acted under the direction or employment of a patent agent who believed, reasonably but erroneously, that authorization had been obtained. The High Court may award damages reflecting lost profits or unjust enrichment, as determined appropriate after consideration of evidence presented by both parties.

For the purposes of this Act, “derivative work” means a work based upon one or more pre-existing works, subject to the condition that such derivative work does not infringe any existing copyright under this Act. The term "derivative work" includes translations, adaptations, and arrangements of musical works, dramatic works, cinematograph films, and sound recordings, provided that the author of such derivative work acknowledges the original source material in a manner consistent with fair practice. Any person creating or distributing a derivative work shall be deemed to have taken an assignment of india rights pertaining solely to the elements derived from the pre-existing work, as agreed upon by the copyright holder of said original work.

Subject to the provisions herein, registration of works under this Act shall confer upon the applicant a presumption of ownership of india rights in respect of the work claimed. An application for registration may be made by the author or any person claiming through him, and shall include particulars as prescribed regarding the nature of the work, date of its creation, and details of first publication, if any. Where an application is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Controller within a period specified; such appeal shall be finally determined by the Controller after affording the applicant an opportunity for being heard. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify claims made in the application concerning ownership or prior assignment of india rights.

Where a person has infringed upon any copyright under this Act, such person shall be liable for damages sustained by the owner of the copyright as a consequence of the infringement. The amount of compensation may include lost profits attributable to the infringing acts and reasonable expenses incurred in protecting the india rights concerned. Provided that, where the infringement was knowing and willful, the court may increase the amount of damages up to three times the actual damages proven. Further, any person found guilty of contributory copyright infringement shall also be subject to liability for damages as determined by the court. The owner of the copyright may also seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, subject to equitable considerations. Remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedies available under general law.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a literary work, examine whether the work is original and constitutes an *india rights* accruing under this Act. Where the applicant fails to provide satisfactory evidence establishing ownership or authorship, as provided herein, the Registrar may require submission of further documentation within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of notification of such deficiency. Any appeal against an order passed by the Registrar refusing registration shall be made to the Controller within three months from the date of communication of the order. The Controller’s decision on any such appeal shall be final and binding, subject to revision by the High Court under writ jurisdiction. Registration is not conclusive proof of originality but serves as prima facie evidence in legal proceedings concerning copyright infringement.

Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines, a person claiming ownership of copyright in any cinematograph film shall furnish a statutory declaration, in the form specified by the Registrar, detailing the extent of their *india rights* and identifying all persons entitled to share in those rights. This declaration must be submitted within thirty days of the first publication of the work. Provided that, where such publication occurs outside India, the declaration may be filed within ninety days thereafter. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the copyright holder liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may preclude enforcement of certain exclusive rights under this Act against any person demonstrably unaware of the claimant’s entitlement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made in such declarations.

Any person who, knowing that a work has been infringed by the doing of another, induces, directly or indirectly, any act infringing that work shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such inducement includes the publication of works containing substantial copies of copyrighted material without authorization from the owner of india rights. Where infringement is established, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of all infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Further, a penalty not exceeding ten lakhs rupees shall be imposed upon conviction for such offences; repeat offenders are liable to double that sum and imprisonment extending up to three years. The right to seek injunctive relief against further infringement remains with the copyright owner as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions herein, a proprietor of copyright in an artistic work may grant a non-exclusive license permitting reproduction for educational purposes, provided that such license specifies the duration and geographical scope of the permitted use. Any assignment of india rights relating to cinematograph films shall be deemed to include all available rights pertaining to the soundtrack component thereof unless explicitly stated otherwise within the instrument of assignment. Furthermore, where an author has assigned copyright in a musical work, the assignee may sub-license the right to perform the work publicly electronically, subject to the condition that royalties are distributed according to a scheme approved by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. The assignor retains the right to audit the accounts relating to such licenses for a period of five years from the date of assignment.

Where a dispute arises concerning the subsistence of india rights in respect of a cinematograph film, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal constituted under this Act. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based. The Tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, reverse or modify the order appealed against, or remand the case to the original authority with directions as to how the matter should be dealt with. Provided that any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law. The decision of the Supreme Court shall be final.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered owner of india rights in a literary or artistic work, reproduces the work in any material form, including but not limited to digital formats for distribution, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the relevant civil court. Such damages shall account for lost profits and reasonable compensation to the right holder. Where infringement is committed with the intent to deceive or mislead the public regarding the ownership of such rights, a penalty may also be imposed, up to five times the amount of damages awarded. The breeder of any plant variety protected under the Plant Varieties Protection Act who utilizes copyrighted material without permission shall face similar penalties and enforcement actions as provided herein.

Where a dispute arises concerning the subsistence of india rights in respect of a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of notification of the Registrar's decision under this Act and shall state specifically the grounds upon which it is based. The Controller shall afford both parties an opportunity for being heard, and may require the production of such evidence as he deems necessary to determine the validity of the india rights claimed. The Registrar shall be deemed a witness in any proceedings before the Controller and shall be subject to examination on oath regarding the records under his control. Any order made by the Controller may be appealed against to the appellate body, as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant or refusal of registration of copyright, or by any condition imposed in connection therewith, desires to appeal against such decision, he shall file an appeal with the designated authority within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate authority may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the original decision. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the appellate authority may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such order, subject to the satisfaction of the court that there is substantial question of law involved. The applicant shall be entitled to seek remedies for any loss or damage suffered as a direct result of an erroneous refusal of registration copyright.

An applicant seeking registration of copyright shall submit a prescribed form, duly completed and accompanied by certified copies of the work in question or where such is not feasible, a detailed description thereof. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars regarding ownership and authorship as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. Upon receipt of the application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Any objection to the registration, based on grounds including lack of originality or prior conflicting claims, may be filed within a period specified herein. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to such objections in writing. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar shall either approve the application and proceed with granting registration copyright or reject it, providing reasons for the rejection.

An applicant seeking registration of copyright shall submit Form CG along with the prescribed fee, payable electronically or by demand draft. The application must clearly identify the work in question and specify the nature of the copyright claimed, whether it pertains to an original literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, or cinematograph film work. Provided that if the work incorporates pre-existing material protected under this Act, a detailed list of such incorporated elements shall be appended as Schedule A to the application. The Registrar may require further documentation establishing ownership and authenticity, including but not limited to assignments or licenses. Any alteration made to the submitted application after its initial filing will invalidate the registration copyright unless expressly approved by the Registrar in writing.

Any person claiming ownership of any work in respect of which registration of copyright has been obtained, and who discovers that another is infringing such copyright, shall be entitled to institute proceedings for redressal of grievances before the appropriate judicial forum. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence substantiating the validity of the copyright registration at the commencement of legal action may result in summary dismissal of the claim. Where an infringement occurs subsequent to a challenge to the validity of the copyright registration and prior to its determination, any judgment rendered shall be binding on all parties involved. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all copyright registrations and related challenges, subject to restrictions as provided herein regarding personal data. Penalties for wilful misrepresentation during the application process for registration copyright extend to monetary fines and potential imprisonment.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant or refusal of registration of copyright, or by any condition imposed in connection therewith, appeals to the High Court under this Act, the appellate court shall admit the appeal and may entertain such appeal notwithstanding any technical objection. The appellant shall be required to demonstrate that the decision complained of is manifestly arbitrary or perverse, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. Provided that an appeal against a refusal of registration copyright does not lie merely on grounds of differing interpretation of the law regarding originality. Any order made by the High Court may be challenged further through a special leave petition before the Supreme Court, subject to its discretion.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright, or by any act or omission constituting infringement of copyright, seeks redressal, such person shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings in the competent court. The court shall, upon receiving evidence pertaining to the alleged infringement and considering arguments presented by all parties involved, undertake a thorough *cc inquiry* into the validity and extent of the claimed copyright. This inquiry shall encompass examination of the work’s originality, authorship, and compliance with the provisions regarding subsistence of copyright as provided herein. Further, the court may order the production of relevant documents or materials to facilitate this determination. Any finding of infringement shall permit the aggrieved party to seek remedies including damages, injunctions, and delivery up of infringing copies, subject to principles of fairness and proportionality.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the subsistence of copyright, or the extent of any right conferred thereby, desires to challenge such order, he may institute an inquiry. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of notice of intention to seek review, serve a copy thereof on all parties involved in the original proceeding and afford them a period of thirty days for response as provided herein. Following this period, the Registrar shall convene a hearing at which both sides may present evidence and arguments relevant to the propriety of the order under challenge. The inquiry shall be conducted according to principles of natural justice, ensuring fair opportunity for all parties to be heard. Decisions regarding admissibility of documentary or testimonial evidence are subject to review by the Adjudicating Officer. This cc inquiry is governed by procedural rules established by notification in the Official Gazette and may involve expert testimony as deemed necessary.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed upon his copyright in respect of any work, such person may institute proceedings seeking remedy and damages. The Court shall, prior to adjudicating on the merits of the claim, undertake a preliminary *cc inquiry* into the validity of the asserted copyright. This inquiry shall encompass examination of evidence pertaining to originality, ownership, and compliance with all requirements for registration as provided herein. Failure to adequately demonstrate these elements will result in dismissal of the infringement action without further hearing. The Court may impose costs upon any party found to have initiated frivolous or vexatious proceedings designed solely to harass or delay resolution of a copyright dispute; such costs shall be recoverable under this Act.

Where any person claims that a work has been reproduced, distributed, or communicated to the public in violation of their copyright, and seeks an injunction or other remedy under this Act, the Tribunal shall undertake a preliminary *cc inquiry* into the validity of the claim. This inquiry shall encompass assessment of ownership, originality, and substantial similarity between the alleged infringing work and the copyrighted work. The defendant may present evidence challenging these aspects, subject to rules of procedure as determined by the Tribunal. Provided that the plaintiff demonstrates prima facie infringement, they shall be entitled to a temporary injunction pending the completion of the full inquiry. However, upon demonstration by the defendant that the claimed copyright is demonstrably invalid or that the use falls under an exception provided herein, the plaintiff forthwith ceased all actions related to the claim and bears responsibility for costs incurred by the defendant.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copyright society” shall mean a society registered under this Act and functioning as provided herein to protect and promote the interests of authors or owners in respect of any works. The amount payable by a copyright society as a copyright society fee shall be determined annually by the Central Government, taking into consideration the income and expenditure of the society during the preceding financial year. Such fees are subject to adjustments based on the number of registered members and the collective licensing activities undertaken. Any shortfall in the remittance of the copyright society fee may result in penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Every copyright society established under this Act shall, within thirty days from the close of each financial year, submit to the designated authority a statement detailing all receipts and disbursements pertaining to its operations during that year. The statement shall include a comprehensive breakdown of collections remitted by collecting societies and affiliated entities, alongside expenditures incurred for distribution of royalties and administrative purposes. Further, every copyright society is required to maintain a separate account for the collection and disbursement of copyright society fee levied on behalf of authors and owners of copyrights. Such accounts are subject to audit as may be prescribed, with findings reported annually. The designated authority shall have power to call for further clarification or documentation related to these financial transactions.

Any collecting society operating under this Act shall, within three months from the close of each financial year, remit to the Government such percentage of its total receipts as may be prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government. Failure to remit the said amount constitutes an offence and renders the defaulting society liable to a penalty not exceeding ten times the sum due, recoverable from the responsible officers thereof. The Government shall have the power to issue directions regarding the calculation of total receipts for the purposes of this provision, subject to appeal before the designated authority. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the assessment or recovery of copyright society fee may apply for redressal to the Registrar of Copyrights, who shall entertain such applications and pass orders as deemed appropriate, providing reasons for the order passed.

The collected sums received by a society registered under this Act, including all royalties and other remuneration distributed pursuant to licensing agreements, shall be held in trust and managed according to prescribed guidelines. Every such society is obligated to remit annually to the Office of the Registrar a sum equivalent to ten percentum of its gross receipts for the preceding financial year; this remittance constitutes the copyright society fee. The amount due may be adjusted periodically based on prevailing economic indicators as determined by the Central Government, notification of which shall be published in the Official Gazette. Failure to remit the full copyright society fee within the stipulated timeframe will attract a penalty equivalent to fifteen percentum of the outstanding sum and further proceedings under this Act relating to revocation of registration may be initiated. The Registrar may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, recover any unpaid fees as arrears of land revenue.

The Copyright Act provides that any society formed under this Act shall, within three months of its establishment and subsequently on or before the thirty-first day of March in each year, remit to the Office a sum calculated as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. This remittance constitutes the annual copyright society fee, determined based upon the total royalties collected during the preceding calendar year, adjusted for any approved deductions relating to administrative expenses incurred in collecting and distributing those royalties. Provided that, where a society fails to submit its accounts within the stipulated timeframe, the Office may assess the fee based on available data and issue a notice of demand. Further, any appeal against such assessment shall be made within sixty days from the date of the notice, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures as provided herein.

Any society collecting or receiving sums on behalf of authors and owners of copyrights shall, within three months of the close of each financial year, render to the designated Government authority a detailed account of all collections made and disbursements effected. Failure to submit such an account as provided herein will attract a penalty equivalent to ten percent of the total sum collected during that financial year, recoverable by way of attachment and sale of society assets. Further, any unauthorized utilization of funds received for distribution amongst copyright holders shall be deemed a violation under this Act and subject to prosecution, with potential imprisonment extending up to two years and fines not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Government authority may also direct the recovery of all sums improperly disbursed as a copyright society fee from responsible officers of the society.

The collection society established under this Act shall, upon receiving authorization from its constituent authors and rightsholders, execute assignment agreements transferring exclusive rights in respect of musical works to designated licensees. Such assignments shall specify the territorial scope and duration of the license granted, subject to review and renegotiation every five years as determined by a majority vote of the society’s general body. Any licensee receiving authorization through such an assignment may sub-license performing rights within their defined territory, provided that all sub-licensing fees are remitted directly to the collection society for equitable distribution amongst rightsholders. The society shall maintain detailed records of all assignments and licenses executed, readily accessible for inspection by authorized government officials. Further, a portion of all copyright society fee collected from licensees shall be allocated towards funding initiatives promoting musical literacy and supporting emerging artists within India.

The Copyright Act provides that any society registered under this Act shall, within three months of the close of each financial year, remit to the Office prescribed fees as determined by the Central Government. Failure to remit such fees in full and on time constitutes a breach of the terms of registration and renders the society liable for penalties as may be specified through notification. Any aggrieved party, including but not limited to authors or beneficiaries entitled to royalties, may file an appeal against any assessment of copyright society fee deemed excessive or improperly levied. Such appeals shall be heard by a designated officer appointed by the Central Government, whose decision is final subject to judicial review under established principles of law.

The Copyright Act provides that every copyright society shall, within thirty days of its establishment and subsequently on or before the thirtieth day of April each year, submit to the designated Government authority a detailed statement of its receipts and disbursements. This statement must include particulars regarding collections made pursuant to the copyright society fee levied under this Act, specifying the works covered by such levies and the rates applicable thereto. Further, any copyright society intending to undertake a design registry exercise for the purpose of identifying derivative works or facilitating licensing shall obtain prior approval from the Government authority. The application for such approval must include comprehensive details regarding the scope of the proposed exercise and its potential impact on existing rights holders.

Applications for registration as a Copyright Society shall be submitted to the Copyright Societies Registrar in the prescribed Form VII, accompanied by certified copies of the society’s memorandum and articles of association, detailing its objectives relating to the collection and distribution of royalties. The applicant shall furnish proof of representation of not less than seven copyright owners or authors, demonstrating their consent to the society's formation and activities as provided herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may call for such further information as he deems necessary to ascertain compliance with the requirements under this Act. Registration shall be granted if the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed society fulfills all stipulated conditions and operates in the public interest; otherwise, rejection notices will be issued detailing reasons for non-compliance.

Any copyright society desiring to collect royalties on behalf of right owners shall, upon receiving written complaint from any person alleging infringement of copyright, be obligated to investigate such allegation expeditiously and report its findings within ninety days. Failure to do so may result in the Copyright Societies Registrar issuing a notice requiring rectification of procedures or imposing a monetary penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. The right owner affected by an alleged infringement is entitled to file a petition before the Copyright Societies Registrar seeking redressal, provided that such petition must specify the nature of the infringement and the relief sought. Any decision rendered by the Copyright Societies Registrar concerning royalty distribution or licensing terms shall be final subject to appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that every copyright society shall, within three months from the date of its registration, submit to the Copyright Societies Registrar a detailed statement of its constitution, including names and addresses of its governing body members. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary for verification purposes, and the Society shall comply with any such request within thirty days. Any alteration in the composition of the governing body must be notified to the Registrar promptly, not exceeding fourteen days from the date of change. Failure to provide the required documentation or respond to inquiries as provided herein may result in suspension of the society’s operational privileges. The Copyright Societies Registrar shall maintain a public register containing particulars of all registered societies and any amendments thereto, accessible for inspection during office hours. Any aggrieved party may appeal against decisions made by the Registrar within sixty days of notification.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any society seeking initial registration or subsequent renewal thereof shall submit detailed accounts audited by a qualified chartered accountant, demonstrating adherence to prescribed financial guidelines as determined by the central government. The Registrar of Copyright Societies may, after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, reject an application if it finds that the proposed rules of the society are inconsistent with the objectives of this Act or fail to adequately protect the interests of copyright owners. Furthermore, a registered society shall maintain records accessible for inspection by the Registrar upon written request and subject to appropriate confidentiality safeguards. Any alteration to the society's constitution must be notified to the Copyright Societies Registrar at least ninety days prior to implementation, allowing for review and potential objection under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Copyright Societies Registrar relating to the suspension or revocation of a copyright society’s license, or concerning disputes over distribution royalties as provided herein, may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures for submitting appeals shall render them inadmissible. The Registrar shall furnish detailed reasons for any adverse action taken against a copyright society, and these reasons must be made available to the aggrieved party. Any unauthorized distribution or collection of royalties by a copyright society, subject to regulations under this Act, will attract penalties as determined by the High Court, including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and potential revocation of its registration.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any collective management organisation seeking to operate as a copyright society shall submit to the Copyright Societies Registrar a comprehensive schedule detailing all works proposed for administration and the terms governing their exploitation. This schedule must specify the percentage share allocated to right holders and users under each licensing scheme. Assignment of rights to a copyright society, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, requires formal registration with the Registrar, accompanied by irrevocable consent from the assignor. The Copyright Societies Registrar may, after due notice and opportunity for hearing, reject any proposed assignment deemed detrimental to the public interest or inconsistent with principles of fair dealing as provided herein. Further, any modification to existing licensing terms must be pre-approved by the Registrar before implementation, ensuring transparency and equitable distribution of royalties among stakeholders.

The Copyright Act, 1957 provides that any aggrieved party seeking review of a decision made by the Copyright Societies Registrar concerning the assessment of royalties or the allocation of distribution proceeds may file an appeal with the relevant High Court. Such appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against to the appellant, subject to extensions granted under conditions prescribed herein. The Registrar may, at any time, entertain objections regarding the validity of a copyright society's operational procedures or its adherence to equitable distribution practices. Any objection raised shall be considered by the Registrar and his decision is appealable as provided herein, notwithstanding that such objection relates to matters deemed administrative in nature.

Any person aggrieved by any decision or order made by the Copyright Societies Registrar relating to the suspension, revocation, or modification of a copyright society’s license shall have the right to appeal to the relevant High Court. Such an appeal may be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant, subject to provisions regarding condonation of delay. The Registrar shall provide reasoned orders and make them available for public inspection as provided herein. Further, a copyright society seeking to apply patent protection for works incorporated into its distribution mechanisms must notify the Registrar in writing, detailing the scope of such application and any potential impact on user access. Failure to do so may result in penalties as determined by the Registrar, without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act.

The Copyright Societies Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a society under this Act, serve notice thereof on all known interested parties, including but not limited to owners of integrated circuits incorporated within works proposed to be administered by the applicant. Any party claiming a right to object may file their objections with the Registrar within sixty days from the date of such service. The Registrar shall provide a reasonable opportunity for hearing to both the applicant society and any objecting parties before making a determination regarding registration, subject to principles of natural justice. An application for registration may be rejected if the Registrar finds that the proposed activities of the society would constitute an unreasonable restraint of trade or unfairly prejudice the rights of copyright holders not members of the society. The Registrar’s decision is appealable to the relevant judicial authority as provided herein.

Any copyright society seeking continued recognition as such shall, prior to each quinquennial period, submit to the Copyright Societies Registrar a detailed report outlining its operational activities during the preceding five years. This report must include audited financial statements demonstrating proper accounting and distribution of royalties collected under this Act. The Registrar may, after affording the society an opportunity for being heard, reject the application if it finds that the society has failed to adequately protect the interests of right owners or has engaged in practices inconsistent with the principles of fair dealing. Furthermore, any member found to have knowingly authorized or participated in acts constituting infringement of copyright shall be deemed ineligible for continued membership within a recognized copyright society.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright, or by the refusal of the Registrar to register a work, or by any other decision affecting their rights as conferred herein, may apply to the relevant judicial authority for redress. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order or decision in question, and must specify the grounds upon which it is based. The judicial authority shall afford all parties an opportunity of being heard, and may direct any inquiry deemed necessary to determine the validity of the challenged action. A finding that a copyright has been infringed does not preclude subsequent proceedings for *cc inquiry cancellation* of registration if substantial questions arise regarding the originality or ownership of the work in question. The judicial authority shall provide reasons for its decision, which is final subject to appeal under the relevant appellate provisions.

The owner of any copyright, intending to assign or license exclusive rights in their work, shall provide a clear and unambiguous statement within the assignment deed or licensing agreement detailing the scope of such exclusivity. This provision applies equally to assignments made prior to or subsequent to the initial registration of the copyright under this Act. Where an objection is raised concerning the validity of a registered copyright, triggering a cc inquiry cancellation process, the assignor or licensee shall be deemed to have implicitly warranted that they possessed the full and unrestricted rights necessary for such assignment or license at the time it was executed. Failure to provide adequate clarity regarding exclusivity may render the assignment or license revocable by the original copyright owner, subject to equitable considerations. Any subsequent transfer of rights derived from a flawed initial assignment is also affected as provided herein.

A restoration patent shall be granted only if an application for its grant is made within six months from the date on which the patent ceased to have effect; provided that the applicant demonstrates satisfactory cause for the failure to pay the requisite renewal fee under this Act. For the purposes of determining such “satisfactory cause”, the Controller may consider factors including, but not limited to, documented administrative delays or unforeseen circumstances preventing timely payment. The application shall include a copy of the original patent specification and claims as they existed prior to its lapse; subject to any amendments permissible under the rules framed hereunder. A restoration patent, if granted, shall have effect only from the date of its grant.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within three years from the date on which the said lapse occurred. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to comply was accidental or arose from circumstances beyond their reasonable control and shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating these assertions. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, grant a restoration patent for the unexpired term of the original patent, provided that the application demonstrates sufficient cause justifying reinstatement. A fee equivalent to fifty percent of the renewal fee applicable at the time of the original grant shall be payable upon such restoration.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, or for any other reason whatsoever resulting in its termination, the former patentee shall be eligible to apply for a restoration patent. Such application may be made within three years from the date of lapse, provided that the applicant demonstrates continued commercial interest in the invention and satisfies the Controller that the grounds for the original lapse have been adequately addressed. The Controller may require submission of supplementary documentation or hearings as deemed necessary to ascertain these facts. Upon successful determination, a restoration patent shall confer rights equivalent to those initially granted, subject to any intervening patents or prior use established under this Act. Any fees payable for such restoration shall be determined according to the prevailing schedule prescribed by the Central Government.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within six months from the date on which the said lapse occurred. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the applicant seeks restoration and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documents relevant to the assessment of the merits of the application. Restoration patent, if granted, shall revive the patent as if it had not lapsed, subject to any modifications deemed necessary by the Controller to ensure fairness and equity. Any third party who was a party to the opposition proceedings may be heard before a decision is made regarding restoration. The applicant must demonstrate diligent efforts were undertaken to address the reasons for the original lapse.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within six months from the date the patent ceased to have effect. Such application shall state the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to comply was unintentional and attributable to circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating diligent efforts undertaken to remedy the non-compliance prior to the lapse of the patent, including but not limited to documented attempts at communication with relevant authorities. A restoration patent, if granted, shall have effect only from the date of its grant and shall be subject to any pending proceedings relating to the original patent.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-compliance with any provision relating to post-grant opposition under this Act, an application for restoration may be made to the Controller within six months from the date on which the said lapsing occurred. Such application shall include a statement setting out the grounds upon which the applicant seeks restoration and demonstrating reasonable cause for the failure to comply with the relevant statutory requirements.
