The grant of a patent confers upon the patentee exclusive rights to make, use and sell the invention for a term specified as provided herein. A compulsory license relating to an act patent may be granted in accordance with the procedures outlined under this Act.

An act patent shall be deemed invalid if it is established before the Controller, subject to appeal under this Act, that the invention was not novel at the date of filing the application for the patent. The burden of proving lack of novelty rests upon the person alleging non-novelty, and such proof must consist of prior public knowledge or use anywhere in the world. Provided that, if the applicant can demonstrate diligent inquiry into relevant publications and publicly available information, the Controller may consider this a mitigating factor when assessing the validity of the act patent. Further, an invention shall not be considered novel if it was disclosed in a document published or used in India, unless such disclosure resulted from improper means.

Any party aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or validity of a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals and pass orders as it deems fit, subject to just cause shown for delay in filing the appeal. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where infringement of a patent is established, the Court may grant damages equivalent to the licensee’s reasonable royalty or three times the profits made by the infringer, whichever is higher. The Central Government may institute proceedings against any person found guilty of falsely representing themselves as holding an act patent.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an act patent may be assigned or licensed absolutely or conditionally, either during its term or before it is granted. Such assignment or license shall require registration with the Controller and shall take effect only upon such registration. Where a patent has been assigned, any person claiming under the assignee shall be deemed to be the true owner of the patent for all purposes. A licensee may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, enforce the act patent against any infringement thereof. The Controller may require particulars relating to the consideration paid for an assignment or license to be disclosed in the register, provided that such disclosure is not mandatory if the parties agree otherwise in writing. Any subsequent assignee shall hold the patent subject to any rights existing in favour of prior assignees or licensees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, an act patent shall be deemed invalid if it is proven before the Controller that the subject matter was previously published or described in a publicly accessible document anywhere in the world. Such determination may be challenged by way of appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of order. The burden of proving prior publication rests upon the petitioner, and such proof must demonstrate clear and unambiguous disclosure sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention. Provided that, if the patentee establishes that the publication was made without their consent or knowledge, the appellate board may consider mitigating circumstances when assessing the validity of the act patent.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patent shall be deemed invalid if it is established before the Controller that the applicant did not fulfill all requirements pertaining to novelty and inventive step at the date of filing the application. Further, where an application for a patent relates to a method of using a substance in agriculture or horticulture, the grant of such act patent shall require demonstration, satisfactory to the Central Government, that the use does not pose unreasonable risk of harm to the environment or human health. Provided that, if it is shown that the conditions stipulated under this section were not met at the time of grant, the patent shall cease to have effect as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person aggrieved by an act patent may institute a suit for damages or seek injunctive relief against any party infringing upon the rights conferred thereby. Such infringement shall include, but not be limited to, unauthorized making, use, sale, offer for sale, or importation of the patented invention. The registered proprietor person shall be liable to pay compensation for all losses sustained by the aggrieved party as a consequence of the infringement. Failure to comply with an order restraining such acts may result in penalties including fines and imprisonment, as determined by the court. Further, wilful infringement shall attract enhanced penalties under this Act.

Where infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to restrain such infringement shall be vested in the registered proprietor or their duly authorized agent. Any person aggrieved by an act of patent infringement may institute legal proceedings seeking equitable remedies, including damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the plaintiff as a direct result of the infringing activity. The measure of damages shall take into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized use of the invention. Further, the Court may grant an injunction preventing further acts of infringement, subject to considerations of public interest and balance of convenience. For the purposes of this Act, “includes article patented” means any product or substance embodying the claimed invention, regardless of alterations or modifications made thereto, provided that such alterations do not substantially change the nature of the original invention as described in the patent specification.

Where proceedings are instituted under this Act relating to infringement of a patent, the Controller may, upon application by the patentee or any interested party, direct the Registrar to issue notice to any person who is shown to be in possession or control of an article patented and alleged to have been infringed. Such notice shall specify the particulars of the patent, the nature of the alleged infringement, and require such person to appear before the Controller at a time and place specified in the notice to show cause why they should not be restrained from dealing with the said article. The Controller may, after hearing all parties concerned, make such order as it deems fit, including an order for the destruction or disposal of the includes article patented found in possession or control of the person failing to satisfy the Controller. This power shall extend to articles manufactured outside India and imported into India.

Where in proceedings under this Act relating to infringement of a patent, it is alleged that an article offered for sale or used constitutes an includes article patented, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, determine whether such article falls within the scope of the claims as originally granted or subsequently amended. The burden shall lie upon the claimant alleging infringement to demonstrate, with reasonable certainty, that the alleged infringing article embodies all limitations specified in the patent’s claims. Provided that, where the patented invention relates to a process for producing an article, the Controller may consider evidence pertaining to the method of manufacture employed in relation to the allegedly infringing product. Any order made by the Controller under this provision is subject to review on grounds of legal error.

Where infringement of a patent has occurred, the right to damages shall accrue to the patentee or, where applicable, the author of the invention as recognized under this Act. Such damages shall be calculated based on the loss suffered by the patentee as a result of the infringing activity, taking into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the use of the patented article. The Controller may order an infringer found guilty of infringement to cease the manufacture, sale, or importation of the includes article patented and to provide accounts of sales for assessment of damages. Further, the Controller may impose a penalty not exceeding three times the amount of damages awarded, provided that the infringing activity was undertaken knowingly and with intent to deceive. The patentee shall be entitled to recover costs incurred in establishing infringement, subject to limitations as determined by the Controller.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical product” means any substance intended for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, or prevention of disease in humans or animals, or for the modification of physiological processes, and shall include vaccines, sera, antibodies, antigens, and diagnostic reagents; provided that such substances are manufactured using a process which is either patented under this Act or otherwise protected by intellectual property rights. A “requires patented article” means any pharmaceutical product whose manufacture necessitates the use of at least one ingredient produced through a method claimed in an active patent, as determined by the Controller based on evidence presented regarding manufacturing processes and relevant patent specifications.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is granted under this Act, the Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible Register of Registered Plant Varieties, detailing particulars including the name and address of the registrant, the denomination of the variety, its botanical classification, and any distinctive characteristics as determined during examination. The Register shall also specify whether the registered variety is protected as a “requires patented article” for commercial exploitation, subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government regarding licensing and compulsory acquisition for research purposes. Any person seeking to utilize or reproduce a requires patented article must provide evidence of authorization from the registrant, unless an exception applies under this Act concerning farmers’ rights or bona fide academic investigation.

Where infringement of a patent has been established under this Act, the remedies available to the patentee shall include injunctive relief preventing further acts of manufacture, use, sale or importation of the infringing product. The Court may also order the defendant to account for profits derived from the unauthorized exploitation of the patented invention, provided that the patentee demonstrates that such profits were obtained as a direct result of the infringement. Furthermore, damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty on sales of the patented article may be awarded where the infringer was aware, or had reason to believe, that the product constituted a requires patented article. The Court shall consider factors including the extent of the infringement and any willful misconduct by the defendant in determining the appropriate amount of damages.

Where an application for compulsory license is filed under this Act relating to a pharmaceutical product, the Controller shall require the applicant to demonstrate that the patented invention fulfills all conditions precedent as provided herein. The applicant must provide evidence establishing that the article in question constitutes a requires patented article, meaning it is directly produced by or derived from the process claimed in the patent. Further, the application shall include a detailed analysis confirming that importation of the pharmaceutical product would not be reasonably avoidable without infringing the patent. Subject to compliance with these requirements and provided that adequate remuneration, as determined under this Act, is offered to the patentee, the Controller may grant the compulsory license.

Where a patentee elects to license the manufacture or use of a patented article, such license shall be assignable in accordance with the provisions under this Act relating to assignment of patents, subject to the conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. Any subsequent assignee of such a license shall be deemed to hold the rights and obligations as if they were the initial licensor, provided that the patentee retains the right to revoke the license upon demonstrating substantial breach of contract by either the licensee or any assignee. The patentee may grant multiple licenses relating to the same patented article, but where such licenses are non-exclusive, priority shall be determined according to the date of execution of each respective agreement. A requirement exists that all assignments and sub-licenses concerning a requires patented article must be registered with the Controller within three months of their creation.

Where a claim for infringement of patent is brought before a competent court, it shall be incumbent upon the claimant to demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged infringing product constitutes a requires patented article as defined under this Act. The defendant may, subject to procedural fairness and without prejudice to any other available defence, contend that the process employed in manufacturing the impugned item does not fall within the scope of the patent claims or that the article itself was produced utilizing methods demonstrably outside the parameters established by the patent specification. Such a contention shall be supported by expert testimony and verifiable evidence presented before the court. The burden of rebuttal rests with the claimant, who may seek to adduce counter-evidence establishing the required connection between the patented process and the final product.

Where proceedings are instituted under this Act challenging the validity of a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition, the burden shall lie upon the petitioner alleging non-infringement to demonstrate that the claimed invention does not satisfy the requirements for a requires patented article as defined herein. It is provided that such demonstration may be achieved by establishing through expert testimony and comparative analysis that the marketed product contains substantially similar active ingredients and dosages to those disclosed in the patent specification, notwithstanding minor variations in excipients or manufacturing processes. Furthermore, any argument asserting that a trade mark consists of a distinctive packaging configuration shall not preclude consideration of the underlying chemical composition’s novelty and inventive step; such arguments are subject to review by the relevant authority.

For the purposes of this Act, a “requires patented article” shall be deemed to exist where the functionality or intended use of a product is inextricably linked to the application of a process protected by a valid patent, such that the absence of said patented process renders the product non-viable for its prescribed purpose. This determination shall consider not only the direct manufacturing steps but also any essential ancillary processes. Furthermore, in instances involving specialized machinery incorporating elements derived from a patented invention, the layout registered under this Act as a “registered user layout” may be relevant to establishing such dependency.

For the purposes of this Act, an “article patented” shall be construed as encompassing not only the specific substance or composition detailed within the patent specification but also any variant thereof exhibiting substantially identical properties for the intended use disclosed therein. An article patented may include a product incorporating the invention, provided that such incorporation is clearly and explicitly described in the patent. The determination of substantial identity shall consider established scientific principles and industry standards as applied to the relevant field of technology. Further, an article patented shall be deemed to extend to any process or method employed for its manufacture if such process is integral to achieving the claimed properties, subject to limitations imposed by other provisions under this Act.

An application for registration of a design relating to an *article patented* under this Act shall be accompanied by particulars specifying the class or classes in which the invention falls, as determined according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further details concerning the manufacturing process employed in producing said *article patented*, particularly where such manufacture involves novel techniques or materials. Registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to make, sell, import, offer for sale, or otherwise dispose of the design, subject to any prior use or publication as provided herein. Any alteration to the design after registration may render it liable for cancellation under this Act; however, minor modifications not affecting the essential character thereof shall be permissible with prior notification to the Controller.

An application for grant of a patent relating to an *article patented* shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including detailed specifications outlining the construction, composition, and intended use of the claimed invention. The Controller General, upon receiving an application, shall publish it in the Patent Journal under this Act, inviting representations from any person interested or claiming entitlement to the invention. Any objection raised against the grant of a patent must be filed within three months from the date of such publication, specifying clearly the grounds for opposition and supported by relevant documentation. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the *article patented* if deemed necessary for proper examination. Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, the decision of the Controller on any objection shall be final.

An article patented under this Act shall be deemed to include not only the precise form of the invention as claimed in the patent specification, but also any novel variant thereof which incorporates all essential features disclosed therein and achieves substantially the same result or effect. Subject to compliance with prescribed standards for quality control, an authorized manufacturer may produce a generic version of such article patented, provided that the manufacturing process does not directly infringe upon any claim specifically delineated within the patent document. Any alteration to the original formulation, however minor, which demonstrably deviates from the disclosed method and yields a materially different outcome, shall be considered outside the scope of the patented article. Furthermore, importation of an article patented is permissible only if it satisfies all relevant regulatory requirements as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly imports or offers for sale within India any article patented under this Act, without the authorization of the patentee or a registered licensee, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees. The Controller, upon receiving a complaint from the patentee, may issue a warrant authorizing entry and seizure of such infringing article. Further, damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringer been licensed by the patentee shall be recoverable under this Act. Provided that where the infringement is established as being wilful, the Court may award enhanced damages not exceeding twice the amount of the actual damages determined.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant licenses relating to the use or exploitation of their patented article, either wholly or partially, for specific territories or fields of application. Such licenses shall be assignable in whole or in part, and may include conditions restricting the scope of such license, provided that these restrictions are reasonable and do not unduly prejudice the interests of the licensee. Where a patentee assigns their interest in a patent, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights and privileges which were vested in the patentee immediately before the assignment. The power to grant licenses relating to an article patented under this Act includes the right to demand royalties or other consideration as determined by contract between the parties. Any agreement concerning such licensing or assignment shall be admissible as evidence, subject to verification by the Controller.

Where an objection is taken before the Controller regarding the patentability of an *article patented* under this Act on the grounds that it lacks novelty or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge, the applicant shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to rebut such objection with documentary evidence and expert testimony. The Controller may, after considering the submissions of both the applicant and the objector, issue a reasoned order either upholding the objection and refusing registration, or dismissing the same and proceeding with examination. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order; provided that the Appellate Board shall not be bound by any conclusion recorded by the Controller but may substitute its own findings based on a fresh assessment of the evidence presented.

Any person who knowingly manufactures, imports, or offers for sale within India any article patented in contravention of the provisions of this Act shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the value of goods so manufactured, imported, or offered for sale, as determined by a civil court. Such determination shall consider the extent of infringement and the resultant loss suffered by the patentee. Further, where an infringing article is found in possession without lawful excuse, it shall be subject to seizure and forfeiture. The sums recovered under this provision shall constitute fund to be utilized exclusively for compensating aggrieved parties and promoting awareness regarding intellectual property rights among small-scale industries, as may be prescribed by the Central Government. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and criminal prosecution.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the patentee of a patented article desires to grant a license for its manufacture, use or sale, such license may be assigned or otherwise transferred to any person, firm or company, provided that the terms and conditions of such assignment or transfer are clearly documented and registered with the Controller. Any registered breeder intending to utilize an article patented under this Act shall obtain prior written consent from the patentee, specifying the scope of use and associated royalty payments as determined by mutual agreement or, failing that, as prescribed by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any subsequent assignment of such a license relating to the patented article requires notification to both the assignor and assignee within thirty days; failure to do so renders the assignee liable for damages incurred by either party.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the patentability of an *article patented*, specifically relating to novelty or inventive step, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars demonstrating compliance with the provisions herein. Such a requirement shall not be deemed to invalidate the application unless the applicant fails to respond within the time stipulated by the Controller and such failure is substantiated before a High Court on appeal. Further, if it is alleged that the claimed invention infringes upon existing rights or utilizes a gene fund shall be considered as prior art, the burden of proof lies with the party making such allegation; provided that the Controller may, at his discretion, order an inquiry into the veracity of said claim.

For the purposes of this Act, an “article patented” is defined as any tangible object or substance which embodies or incorporates within its physical structure elements derived directly from the subject matter claimed in a patent granted under this Act. This definition extends to composite articles where one or more components are themselves articles patented. Where the invention relates to a process for producing an article, the resulting article shall be considered an article patented if it is produced by means of that patented process. Further, registrar case shall be deemed to include any proceedings relating to objections filed against such an article patented, irrespective of the stage of examination.

The Register of Patents shall maintain a comprehensive record pertaining to each registered *article patented*, detailing its technical specifications, claimed novelty, and the name and address of the patent holder. Upon initial registration, and subsequently at intervals as determined by the Controller General, every patent holder shall furnish detailed declarations affirming continued compliance with stipulations under this Act regarding manufacturing processes and commercial exploitation. Failure to submit such declarations within the prescribed timeframe will render the *article patented* liable for review and potential revocation. Furthermore, a nominal fee, constituting a portion of the copyright society fee collected by the government, may be levied annually from patent holders engaged in the mass production or importation of their registered articles, allocated towards supporting innovation initiatives as provided herein.

For the purpose of this Act, “new chemical entity” with reference to pharmaceutical products means a compound not previously known in India or elsewhere, subject to the proviso that salts, esters, ethers, and other derivatives of a new chemical entity shall be considered as such only if they possess substantially enhanced therapeutic efficacy compared to the parent compound. A pharmaceutical product incorporating a new chemical entity shall be deemed non-obvious where it demonstrates unexpected technical effect relative to existing knowledge in the field of medicinal chemistry, provided that such effect is clearly and consistently demonstrated through clinical trials conducted under established protocols.

The Registering Authority shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing all applications for registration of pharmaceutical products claiming novelty under this Act. Each application must include comprehensive documentation pertaining to the composition, manufacturing process, intended therapeutic use, and proposed brand name of the product. The applicant shall furnish three certified samples of the pharmaceutical product for analysis by the Controller, who may require further testing as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with prescribed quality standards. Registration shall be granted only upon successful completion of these analyses and verification that the claimed novelty meets the criteria outlined herein. Any challenge to a registration may be brought before the relevant appellate body within six months of publication in the register.

Where an infringement of patent rights relating to a pharmaceutical product has occurred, the patentee shall be entitled to injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from further acts of such infringement, subject to just terms being determined by the Controller. Compensation for loss or damage resulting from the infringement may be awarded to the patentee, taking into account the extent of the use made of the patented invention and the flagrant nature of the infringement. The Controller may, upon application by the alleged infringer, determine whether the terms offered by the patentee are just and equitable; provided that such determination shall not prejudice the right of the patentee to enforce their patent rights. Any party aggrieved by an order or decision made under this Act relating to pharmaceutical products may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order or decision.

Applications for patents relating to pharmaceutical products shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding patentability as provided herein. An application concerning a pharmaceutical product may be rejected if it is determined that the invention was not novel or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge. The Controller General may, upon receiving representations from interested parties, including generic drug manufacturers and consumer protection groups, direct the examination branch to undertake a supplementary assessment regarding the inventive step involved in such inventions. Evidence pertaining to clinical trial data and bioequivalence studies shall be considered relevant during this process. Any decision made by the examining officer concerning the patentability of a pharmaceutical product is subject to review by an appellate authority as provided under this Act, ensuring due consideration for public interest concerns.

Where an application relates to a pharmaceutical product, it shall disclose the particular territory in which the invention is proposed to be manufactured or used commercially; provided that such disclosure does not preclude the applicant from subsequently seeking patent protection in other territories. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating sufficient clinical trial data supporting the safety and efficacy of the claimed pharmaceutical product, particularly where the application claims a new chemical entity or a significant modification to an existing therapeutic agent. Further, any claim directed towards a method of treatment shall be supported by documentation establishing adherence to Good Clinical Practice guidelines as provided herein. The applicant shall also confirm compliance with all applicable regulatory requirements pertaining to manufacturing and marketing of such pharmaceutical products.

Any person who manufactures, imports, distributes, sells, or offers for sale any pharmaceutical products in contravention of this Act, or the rules made thereunder, shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to ten times the cost of the patented product manufactured, imported, distributed, sold, or offered for sale. Such penalty shall be imposed by the Controller after affording the accused an opportunity of being heard under this Act. Further, any infringing activity discovered during inspection or investigation shall result in seizure of the goods and materials used in such infringement. Repeated offences may attract imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, alongside a continuing penalty assessed as provided herein.

Where an appeal is made under this Act against a decision of the Controller refusing patent rights in respect of a pharmaceutical products invention, the Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the Controller to reconsider any question of fact or law arising out of the order appealed from. Such reconsideration shall be undertaken expeditiously and without prejudice to the original merits of the case. The Controller’s subsequent decision following such direction shall be final, provided that the appellant demonstrates a substantial injustice would result otherwise. Any party aggrieved by the Appellate Board's determination may further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds limited to questions of law arising out of this Act and respect patent granted.

Where an interested party alleges that a compulsory license has been granted in violation of this Act, or that the terms and conditions attached to such license are manifestly unfair or unreasonable, they may institute proceedings before the Controller. The Controller shall afford all parties concerned an opportunity of being heard and shall determine whether the grant of the compulsory license was justified under this Act and whether the royalty rate stipulated is adequate compensation for the patentee’s rights. Any party aggrieved by the order of the Controller may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Appellate Board's decision shall be final and binding. Security India explanation regarding equitable access to pharmaceutical products shall be considered during these proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, "well known trade mark" with respect to particular goods or services means a trademark which has attained considerable recognition amongst the relevant section of the public, irrespective of whether that recognition is direct or indirect. A mark shall be deemed to be well known if, through association and use over time, it signifies a specific source or quality of those goods or services. The determination of whether a trade mark is well known shall take into account factors including duration of usage, geographical extent of the trade, reputation and get-up of the mark, and advertising expenditure incurred in relation to the mark as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall not be opposed on the ground alone that it is similar or identical with a well known trade mark, unless it is demonstrated that such use or intended use is likely to cause confusion or deception among the public as to the origin of the goods or services. The Registrar may require the applicant seeking registration to furnish evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through the rendering of services or sale of goods. Where an objection is raised under this Act based on a claim of similarity to a well known trade mark, the opponent shall be required to provide verifiable data substantiating the extent and nature of public recognition. The Registrar may, at his discretion, conduct hearings to assess such evidence.

Where the Registrar is satisfied, following an application under this Act, that a particular trade mark has acquired substantial recognition of the public and enjoys a reputation which extends beyond a specific geographical area, such trade mark shall be deemed a well known trade mark. The applicant must demonstrate through evidence, including market surveys and consumer perception data, the extent of such recognition and reputation. Any person infringing upon the rights associated with a well known trade mark shall be liable to damages, even where there is no direct competition between the goods or services offered under the infringed mark and those using a confusingly similar sign. Further, the Registrar may order the seizure and destruction of any goods bearing an infringing mark as provided herein. The remedies available are without prejudice to any other rights or remedies which a proprietor may have under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a trade mark, investigate whether a particular trade mark is a well known trade mark in India. Such investigation shall proceed according to principles of natural justice, affording all interested parties an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. The applicant shall furnish such documentation as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the claim, including but not limited to market share data, consumer surveys, and advertising expenditure records relating to the use of the trade mark. Evidence demonstrating widespread recognition and association of the mark with its proprietor is essential for establishing well known status under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision.

A trademark shall be deemed a well known trade mark if, through its continued use and reputation over a considerable period, it has come to possess distinctive recognition amongst a significant portion of the relevant public for the goods or services with which it is associated. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party, declare a trademark to be a well known trade mark, provided that such declaration is based on evidence demonstrating widespread recognition and consumer association across multiple regions within India. This determination shall consider factors including duration of use, advertising expenditure, market share, sales figures, and unsolicited media coverage. Any subsequent use of an identical or confusingly similar mark relating to goods or services not identical to those for which the well known trade mark is registered will be prohibited if it creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers.

Where any person seeks to register a trade mark, the Registrar shall refuse registration if it includes identical or confusingly similar elements to a well known trade mark, even if used for dissimilar goods or services. Such refusal may be appealed before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Any proprietor of a well known trade mark is entitled to apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the use in commerce of any marks which are likely to cause confusion or dilution of the distinctiveness of the said well known trade mark, subject to demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof. The penalty for infringing upon rights relating to a well known trade mark shall be imprisonment and a fine as determined by the court.

Where the proprietor of a well known trade mark desires to permit another person to use the mark, subject to conditions reasonably designed to protect the distinctiveness and reputation of the well known trade mark, they may grant a license for such use. Such license shall be documented in writing and specify the goods or services in relation to which the use is permitted, the geographical area covered by the license, and any restrictions on the manner of use. The proprietor retains the right to terminate the license if the licensee’s activities are detrimental to the well known trade mark's reputation or otherwise violate the terms stipulated within the agreement. Assignment of a license granted under this Act shall be permissible with the prior written consent of both the grantor and assignee, provided that such assignment does not diminish the protections afforded to the well known trade mark as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised before the Registrar alleging that a proposed trade mark is deceptively similar to a well known trade mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor of the said well known trade mark and afford him an opportunity of being heard. Such proprietor may, within the time specified in the notice, file with the Registrar an affidavit verifying the extent to which the alleged well known trade mark is recognized by substantial portions of the public and demonstrating that use on non-identical goods would likely cause confusion. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented and may require further clarification or additional documentation from either party. Any order made by the Registrar under this Act concerning a determination of deceptiveness may be appealed to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

Where any person alleges that an earlier mark is a well known trade mark in respect of particular goods or services, they may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal seeking relief. Such proceedings shall require the claimant to demonstrate, through evidence such as market surveys and sales figures, that the alleged well known trade mark has acquired distinctiveness sufficient to cause confusion among consumers. The tribunal may grant an injunction restraining the use of a sign identical or similar to the well known trade mark where it is used in relation to goods or services not identical with those for which the well known trade mark enjoys reputation, provided that such use creates a likelihood of confusion. Failure to pay the requisite filing application fees associated with initiating these proceedings may result in their dismissal as being frivolous or vexatious.

For the purposes of this Act, an “establishment” shall be deemed a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment if it possesses demonstrable physical infrastructure suitable for conducting business operations, including but not limited to office space, warehousing facilities, or manufacturing plants. Such infrastructure must be actively utilized in the promotion, sale, or distribution of goods or services under the trade mark in question. An entity maintaining only a registered address or a postal box shall not be considered to possess an establishment as provided herein. This determination is subject to review by the Registrar who may require further documentation substantiating the operational nature and extent of such activities.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of registration under this Act, an applicant claiming to possess a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment shall furnish documentary evidence substantiating such claim. This evidence must demonstrate continuous operation within India for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of application, and may include audited financial statements, utility bills reflecting consistent usage at a designated business address, and employment records indicating active personnel engaged in trade or manufacture related to the mark. Provided that, where the applicant is a partnership firm, such evidence shall pertain to the partnership’s operations. The Registrar may require further clarification or additional documentation if deemed necessary to verify the existence and operational status of the establishment as provided herein.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Where any proprietor institutes legal proceedings alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, the Court shall determine whether the defendant maintains a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment utilizing the impugned sign. It shall be presumed, subject to rebuttal by evidence adduced by the defendant, that use in advertising materials alone does not constitute such an establishment under this Act. Further, where the proprietor demonstrates demonstrable goodwill and reputation associated with the trade mark within India, the Court may grant interim relief pending final determination of the matter, provided that a bond is furnished as deemed appropriate by the Court to compensate any party found to have acted without sufficient cause. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving the absence of such an establishment if the proprietor establishes a prima facie case of infringement.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief under this Act relating to passing off, an applicant shall demonstrate possession of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India. The existence of such an establishment shall be evidenced by verifiable documentation including, but not limited to, registered agreements for leasehold property, utility bills demonstrating consistent consumption at a specific location, and records of employee payroll and taxation compliance pertaining to operations conducted within the territory of India. Where an applicant’s activities are primarily directed towards export markets, evidence establishing a dedicated warehousing or distribution facility operated under their direct control within India shall be considered sufficient for satisfying this requirement. Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates substantial engagement in marketing and promotional activities targeted at Indian consumers, the Trade Marks Registry may consider such activity as indicative of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment even absent physical infrastructure.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of determining entitlement to registration under this Act, an applicant claiming a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment” in India shall furnish documentation demonstrating continuous operation at a specific physical location for a minimum period of twelve months preceding the date of application. Such documentation must include utility bills bearing the applicant’s name and address, lease agreements or property ownership records, and evidence of ongoing business activity as determined by relevant governmental authorities. Provided that, where an applicant operates through a franchise agreement, proof of such agreement and authorization from the franchisor shall be submitted. The Registrar may require further verification to ascertain the genuineness of the establishment, and failure to comply with these requirements will render the application liable for rejection.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement, the Tribunal shall determine whether the defendant possesses a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in relation to the goods or services for which the alleged infringing use occurs. Provided that, if the defendant demonstrates such an establishment, but fails to adequately substantiate its prior honest belief in the availability of the mark, the Tribunal may impose a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Further, any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the existence or absence of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order; failure to do so shall preclude further recourse.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to use such trade mark for goods or services relating to their field of activity. Such licenses may be granted exclusively or non-exclusively and may specify geographical limitations or other restrictions as deemed appropriate by the grantor. Where a license is assigned without the consent of the proprietor, such assignment shall be void unless the assignee demonstrates that they possess a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment engaged in activities related to the licensed goods or services. Further, any agreement for the use of a trade mark under this Act must clearly define the scope of permitted usage and specify remedies available to the grantor in case of breach. The proprietor retains ultimate control over quality assurance relating to products bearing their registered trademark, even when operating through licensees.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief under this Act concerning passing off actions, it shall be conclusively presumed that a defendant possesses a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment within India if evidence demonstrates consistent supply chain operations originating from premises located therein, even where ultimate product distribution occurs outside Indian territory. This presumption may be rebutted only by affirmative proof establishing the absence of substantial managerial control exercised over said operations from within India, provided that such rebuttal necessitates demonstrating that decisions concerning pricing, marketing, and quality assurance were demonstrably dictated by entities situated wholly outside the nation’s jurisdiction. The burden of proving this lack of control rests entirely upon the defendant.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: For the purposes of determining entitlement to registration under this Act, an applicant claiming a priority date for a trade mark shall furnish evidence demonstrating the existence of a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India at the time of the earliest use or application thereof, wherever such use or application occurred. The Registrar may require submission of documents including, but not limited to, audited financial statements, utility bills registered under the name of the applicant or its designated agent, and declarations from relevant government authorities confirming operational presence. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence as provided herein shall render the priority date claim invalid, and registration shall proceed based on the filing date alone. An appeal against such a determination may be made before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of the Registrar’s decision.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: Where any proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, it shall be conclusively presumed that the alleged infringing mark is used in connection with an enterprise lacking a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India unless the defendant demonstrates, by way of admissible evidence, the existence of such an establishment. Such demonstration must include verifiable documentation establishing continuous operation and substantial investment within Indian territory for a period exceeding two years prior to the date of the infringement notice. Failure to provide this evidence shall result in summary judgment against the defendant, accompanied by penalties as provided herein. Copy translation work undertaken solely for promotional purposes does not constitute sufficient proof of such an establishment.
primary_entity: real and effective industrial or commercial establishment

context: An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the mark and a statement indicating the goods or services with which it is associated. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating prior use of the mark in India, provided that such use was continuous and not abandoned. Where the applicant seeks to register a word mark, the description thereof shall be clear and unambiguous, specifying the font style and colour if applicable. A trade mark registration may be refused if it conflicts with an earlier registered trade mark or one pending application, particularly where the goods or services are identical or closely related. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the applicant’s entitlement to use the trade mark, especially concerning instances where uses trade mark in a deceptive manner.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without the consent of the proprietor, and such use creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public as to the origin, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services, an action may be brought under this Act. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating that the continued uses trade mark in question are detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered mark. Provided that, if the defendant can demonstrate prior honest and contemporaneous use of a similar sign before the date of registration, such use may not constitute infringement subject to conditions as provided herein regarding validity registration trade. The proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages in respect of any such unauthorized use.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark already uses trade mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations and counter-statements. The Registrar shall unconditionally registrar shall consider all such submissions, including evidence presented by both the objector and the applicant, and may direct the holding of hearings where necessary for clarification. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees and compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act alleging that another person has infringed their rights, the Court shall determine whether the defendant’s use of a sign creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public to the detriment of the proprietor. Such infringement shall be actionable by way of remedy, including an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of unfair competition and requiring delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. The Court may also award damages reflecting the loss suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringement. It is provided that where the defendant proves prior honest concurrent use, the remedies available to the proprietor shall be limited in accordance with principles of equity and fairness. A person shall not apply trade mark without authorization from the registered proprietor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered trade mark owner desiring to grant a license or assign their rights in respect of a trade mark shall file an application with the Registrar. Such application must specify the full terms and conditions of the proposed license agreement or assignment deed, including details regarding royalties, territory, duration, and permitted uses. The Registrar may, after providing notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity for objection, approve the license or assignment as applied for. Any subsequent modification to the approved license or assignment requires a fresh application filed under this Act. Failure to disclose material terms in the initial application shall render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the Registrar. The proceedings act registrar may also require security deposits from licensees where deemed necessary, safeguarding against misuse of the trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a “legal practitioner person” means an individual who is admitted to practice law before any High Court or Supreme Court in India; provided that such legal practitioner person shall be deemed to possess the requisite qualifications for representing clients under this Act only if they hold a valid license issued by the Bar Council of India and maintain continuous professional development as prescribed. A legal practitioner person may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, represent any individual or entity seeking redressal or enforcement of rights relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design; further, such representation shall be limited to matters directly pertaining to intellectual property law.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or by a legal practitioner duly authorized to act on their behalf. Where the applicant is an organization, the verification shall be signed by a person holding a position of authority within that organization and authorised to verify the contents of the application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made in the application concerning prior publication or use of the layout-design outside India. Any person making a false statement in the verification is liable for prosecution under this Act. Furthermore, an applicant who is not a legal practitioner person must appoint a registered agent to represent them during proceedings relating to registration.

Where an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design is presented to the Registrar, it shall be accompanied by a verification made before a legal practitioner person practicing within the jurisdiction of the High Court claiming to be duly authorized by the applicant to make such verification. Such verification must explicitly state that the applicant is the rightful owner of the layout design and that all information provided in the application is true and correct to the best of their knowledge. The Registrar may, subject to satisfaction regarding the validity of the verification, proceed with examination of the application under this Act. Provided that if the Registrar has reasonable grounds to believe that the legal practitioner person was not duly authorized or acted improperly during the verification process, they shall notify both the applicant and the said practitioner for an opportunity to be heard before any further action is taken.

Any individual acting as a legal practitioner person found to have knowingly presented false evidence relating to the ownership or infringement of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may also face proceedings for professional misconduct before the Bar Council of India. Further, any such individual who obstructs an investigation undertaken by an authorized officer under this Act is deemed guilty of an offence and subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or until the completion of the investigation, whichever is less. The Central Government may, through notification, prescribe guidelines regarding the conduct of legal practitioners in matters pertaining to layout-design rights as provided herein.

The right to grant licenses pertaining to a protected semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall vest initially with the proprietor, but may be assigned or otherwise transferred subject to the provisions herein relating to fair dealing. Any legal practitioner person acting on behalf of a proprietor intending to assign such rights must file a declaration with the Controller specifying the scope and duration of the proposed license agreement, including details regarding royalty rates and any restrictions on use. Provided that, where an assignment is made to a related entity as defined under this Act, the Controller may require additional information demonstrating that the transaction was conducted at arm's length and does not unduly prejudice the interests of third parties. Further, sub-licensing rights may be granted by the licensee with prior written consent from the proprietor, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or an authorized signatory thereof, including a legal practitioner person acting on behalf of the applicant where the applicant is a body corporate or association of individuals. The verification shall attest to the truth and accuracy of the particulars furnished in the application and confirm that no prior registration exists for the layout-design sought to be registered under this Act. Further, an applicant claiming inventive step relating to the layout-design may submit details pertaining to any corresponding patent application filed, including its filing date and jurisdictional scope, provided that such disclosure does not prejudice the confidentiality of either proceeding.

Any infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall render the infringing party liable to damages, calculated at the option of the owner either on the basis of lost profits resulting from the infringement or reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. The owner may also seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement and requiring delivery up of all infringing layouts. Where a legal practitioner person acting as an agent for the layout-design owner has knowingly participated in the infringement, such practitioner shall be jointly and severally liable with the principal for any damages awarded under this Act. Further, where an infringement is committed by a body corporate, the liability shall extend to its officers in default, provided that they were directly involved in the infringing activity. The court may order seizure of materials used in or resulting from the infringement, as deemed necessary in the prescribed manner.

For the purposes of this Act, a “legal practitioner” means an individual who is a holder of a degree in law from an institution recognized by the Bar Council of India and is enrolled with the State Bar Council under which he proposes to practice; provided that such legal practitioner shall be deemed to possess the requisite qualifications for representing clients or providing expert opinions concerning matters pertaining to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, subject to any specific conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. A person not meeting these criteria but regularly employed by a law firm engaged in intellectual property litigation may assist a legal practitioner as defined herein, but shall not independently represent parties before tribunals.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or an authorized signatory, including a legal practitioner representing the applicant. The Registrar may require further documentation to ascertain the identity and authority of any such legal practitioner, particularly where the applicant is a body corporate or a partnership firm. Provided that, if the application relates to a layout-design generated in the course of employment, the verification shall also state the terms under which the layout-design was created and assign ownership rights as provided herein. Any alteration made to the verified document after its initial submission will invalidate the registration process unless approved by the Registrar following notification from the applicant or their legal practitioner.

Where infringement of layout-design rights has occurred, the owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of such infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts having been made to mitigate actual damages suffered as a direct consequence thereof. Compensation for loss or damage sustained by reason of the infringement may include not only the profits earned by the infringing party attributable to the unauthorized use of the layout-design, but also any losses incurred by the owner in respect of goodwill and reputation. A legal practitioner representing the aggrieved party shall be deemed an officer of this court for purposes of discovery and examination under this Act. The Court may order the infringer to account for profits made, provided that such accounting is conducted with due regard to principles of fairness and proportionality.

Where an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design is presented to the Registrar, it shall be accompanied by a verification in the prescribed form signed by the applicant or by a legal practitioner duly authorized by the applicant. Such verification shall attest to the truthfulness of the statements made in the accompanying documents and affirm that the applicant is the first owner of the layout design as claimed in the application. The Registrar may, at any time, require further information from the applicant or the legal practitioner concerning the ownership details or technical specifications contained within the application. Failure to provide such information within the stipulated period shall render the application liable for rejection. Any communication relating to the application shall be deemed valid if addressed to the legal practitioner, provided that the practitioner has formally notified the Registrar of their representation. The Registrar is empowered to issue notices and serve documents upon a legal practitioner in this manner.

Where an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the designated Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the rejection order. The appellant shall, along with the memorandum of appeal, pay such fee as may be prescribed. Further, a legal practitioner representing the appellant must provide an affidavit verifying the accuracy and completeness of the information contained therein. Subject to compliance with regulations regarding professional conduct, any registered patent agent or advocate duly enrolled in India may act as a legal practitioner for these purposes. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to engage such representation, they may submit a self-verification affirming due diligence.

Any individual seeking to initiate proceedings under this Act relating to infringement of layout-designs shall be represented by a legal practitioner duly enrolled with a State Bar Council. Provided that, where an aggrieved party elects to represent themselves personally, they shall nonetheless furnish an affidavit verifying their understanding of the procedural requirements as provided herein. Failure to comply with these representation stipulations may result in the rejection of pleadings and delay in adjudication. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines for ensuring equitable access to legal practitioners for individuals unable to afford professional fees. Any person found to be falsely representing themselves as a legal practitioner for purposes of this Act shall be liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees.

Where a proprietor elects to license rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design under this Act, such license shall be documented in writing and executed by both the proprietor and the licensee, specifying the scope of permitted acts including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and sale. The license may grant exclusive or non-exclusive rights as agreed upon between the parties; however, any assignment of ownership resulting from a license requires prior written consent from the registered proprietor. A legal practitioner representing either party in such transactions shall be bound by confidentiality agreements pertaining to the layout design’s technical specifications and commercial value. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses rights, they must provide full disclosure of the original licensing agreement to any subsequent assignee, as provided herein. The proprietor retains the right to terminate any license if the licensee materially breaches its terms, subject to due process considerations.

Where any aggrieved party alleges that an act constituting infringement of layout-design rights has been committed, such party shall be entitled to file a complaint before the designated Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal established under this Act. The tribunal may, subject to regulations framed by the Central Government, entertain complaints relating to acts performed beyond the territorial jurisdiction where the cause of action arose, provided that the respondent maintains a place of business or has a presence within India. Any legal practitioner duly enrolled with a State Bar Council shall be permitted to represent parties before the Tribunal; however, representation by an unregistered individual will render the complaint liable for summary dismissal. The decision of the Tribunal may be appealed to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such decision, subject to just and equitable grounds being demonstrated.

Where an applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design has previously published the design, whether directly or indirectly, under this Act, the Board may entertain a later publication application only if the applicant demonstrates to its satisfaction that such prior publication was undertaken without the applicant’s consent and constituted a prejudicial act. The burden of proving said lack of consent shall rest entirely upon the applicant. Any decision by the Board regarding the admissibility of evidence pertaining to the circumstances surrounding the earlier publication is final, subject to appeal before the High Court. A legal practitioner representing an aggrieved party may petition for judicial review if they believe that the Board’s determination was manifestly arbitrary or based on a misinterpretation of the provisions relating to prejudicial acts.

Where infringement of any right conferred by an application patent shall be established before the Controller, the aggrieved party may apply for relief including damages, injunctions, and account of profits derived from the infringing activity. The assessment of damages shall take into consideration the loss suffered by the applicant or patentee as a result of the infringement, together with the profit made by the infringer. An injunction may be granted to restrain further acts of infringement, subject to just terms being determined under this Act. Any legal practitioner representing a party in proceedings before the Controller shall be deemed an officer of the court and is bound by professional ethics. The Controller may order the infringing party to deliver up for destruction the infringing goods or materials used in their manufacture.

Where any application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design is presented to the Registrar, it shall be accompanied by a verification in the form specified in Schedule A, signed by the applicant or an authorized signatory thereof, including a legal practitioner acting on behalf of the applicant. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the identity and authority of any such legal practitioner. An application filed without proper verification, or with a verification containing material misstatements, is liable to be rejected under this Act.

The Registrar shall serve notice of the receipt of an application upon all persons appearing from the records maintained by the office to be interested in the layout design, providing them opportunity for objection as provided herein. Any objections received must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying their factual basis and signed by a legal practitioner representing the objector. Furthermore, where an applicant seeks protection under the Patent Cooperation Treaty concerning a layout design, they shall submit a certificate of compliance confirming adherence to treaty requirements.

Where an allegation of threatened infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design is made against any individual or entity, such individual or entity shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to present its case before the relevant adjudicating authority. The adjudicating authority may require production of documentation demonstrating compliance with prescribed standards relating to manufacturing processes and quality control measures. Any legal practitioner representing a party in proceedings under this Act shall provide written confirmation to the adjudicating authority detailing their qualifications and experience in intellectual property law, as stipulated by professional regulatory bodies. Provided that, if the threatened infringement is based on allegations of reverse engineering, the accused may submit evidence demonstrating independent creation or prior art.

For the purposes of this Act, a “proprietor registered layout” means a person who is entered in the Register of Layout-Designs as the owner of the exclusive right to exploit a layout-design and who has fulfilled all requirements for registration as provided herein. Such proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings under this Act relating to infringement of the registered layout-design, subject to any conditions imposed during the registration process. A person claiming to be a proprietor registered layout may demonstrate such claim by producing the certificate of registration issued under this Act and satisfying the relevant authority that they possess the requisite right as defined in section 4.

An application for registration as a proprietor registered layout shall include a certified copy of the integrated circuit, a description of the functions performed by the integrated circuit, and details regarding any mask works incorporated therein. The Registrar may require further information deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to originality and distinctiveness under this Act. Where an applicant demonstrates prior use of the layout-design in trade or commerce within India, such evidence shall be considered during examination. Any person claiming entitlement to registration as a proprietor registered layout must satisfy the Registrar that they possess the exclusive right to apply for registration, subject to any assignments or licenses previously granted. The application shall also specify the address for service of processes and notices.

Where any person infringes a registered layout design, such person shall be liable to pay damages to the proprietor registered layout equivalent to a reasonable royalty that could have been granted by way of license had the infringement not occurred, subject to adjustments as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer may also order the infringer to account for profits made from the infringing activity, provided that such profits are demonstrably attributable to the unauthorized use of the layout-design. Further, any person found guilty of wilful infringement shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees; however, in cases where the infringement is committed by a company, its officers who were responsible for the conduct of business at the time of the offence shall be deemed guilty.

An application for the registration of a layout-design shall be made to the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, containing particulars verifying ownership and detailing the nature of the integrated circuit. Where an applicant seeks recognition as a proprietor registered layout, they must demonstrate exclusive right over the design under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed technical specifications and schematics supporting the application, and shall provide the applicant an opportunity to rectify any deficiencies identified during examination. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to registration or rejection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout-designs, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees and conditions.

A proprietor registered layout shall remain valid for a period not exceeding fourteen years from the date of its first registration, subject to renewal as provided herein. Renewal may be applied for within one year preceding the expiry of the term and shall extend the protection for a further period not exceeding ten years. An application for renewal must demonstrate continued commercial exploitation of the registered layout or provide evidence of ongoing research and development directly related thereto. Failure to satisfy these conditions will render the renewal request ineligible, and the proprietor registered layout shall lapse accordingly. Any alteration made to a registered layout design after its initial registration without prior approval from the Controller shall constitute an infringement under this Act.

Any person who knowingly and wilfully reproduces, copies, distributes, imports, or offers to sell any integrated circuit layout which is protected by the right of a proprietor registered layout shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor. Such damages may include compensation for lost profits, reasonable expenses incurred in bringing an action under this Act, and punitive damages not exceeding three times the amount of actual damages awarded. Further, where infringement occurs through unauthorized use or adaptation of a registered layout, the Court may order the destruction of infringing articles and materials used in their manufacture. The proprietor shall have the right to apply to the Commercial Courts for interim injunctions restraining such acts pending final determination of the matter as provided herein.

A proprietor registered layout may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to acts restricted under this Act, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation of the registered layout-design. The proprietor retains full ownership of the intellectual property unless explicitly transferred through a written assignment executed as per prescribed procedures. Any assignment of a proprietor registered layout must disclose all prior licenses granted and their material terms. Further, any licensee may sub-license rights within the scope permitted by the original license agreement, provided that such sub-licensing is expressly authorized therein. The proprietor shall maintain records of all licenses and assignments and make them available for inspection upon request by the Controller.

Where any person alleges that an action taken by the Registrar, including but not limited to the refusal of registration or the revocation of a certificate of registration relating to a proprietor registered layout, is unlawful, unjust, or beyond the powers conferred upon the Registrar under this Act, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order appealed against and shall state specifically the grounds on which the action is challenged. Provided that the Tribunal may admit an appeal delayed by reason of circumstances deemed sufficient by it.
