Any decision of the Tribunal affirming, reversing or modifying the Registrar’s action shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “proprietor registered layout” means the person whose name is entered in the Register of Layout-Designs as the proprietor of a registered layout-design and who possesses exclusive rights therein, subject to any licenses granted or agreements made prior to registration. The right of a proprietor registered layout shall extend to the reproduction of the layout-design, its sale, hire, import, and offer for sale or hire. Where a person claims originality in a layout-design, the date claim shall be deemed conclusive evidence of such originality unless proven otherwise by another party under this Act.

An application for registration as a proprietor registered layout shall include a certified copy of the layout-design, a statement of the rights claimed by the applicant, and details regarding any prior publication of the design anywhere in the world. The Registrar may require such further particulars or documents as are necessary to ascertain whether the requirements of this Act have been fulfilled. Where an application relates to a layout-design which incorporates elements protected under other intellectual property laws, the applicant shall disclose these incorporated elements within the application. Furthermore, if the applicant intends to rely on convention application rights from a designated country, evidence substantiating such priority must be submitted alongside the initial registration documents. The Registrar shall record all details pertaining to convention applications in the Register of Layout-Designs.

Where any person infringes the right of a proprietor registered layout, such proprietor shall be entitled to seek relief by way of injunction restraining the infringing activity and damages commensurate with the loss suffered. The amount of damages awarded may take into account the notional profits made by the infringer, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding proportionality to the actual harm caused to the proprietor. Further, in determining the quantum of damages, the Tribunal shall consider whether the infringement involved the use of a mark registered respect for similar goods or services, and if so, enhance the award accordingly to reflect the potential consumer confusion arising from such combined violation. Any interlocutory order granted under this Act shall be subject to appeal before the appellate authority.

An application for the registration of a layout-design may be made by any person claiming to be the first inventor of the layout-design, or by any registered proprietor thereof, or by an exclusive licensee authorized to manufacture integrated circuits incorporating the layout-design. Such application shall contain particulars verifying ownership and detailing the nature of the claimed invention as prescribed in the First Schedule. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require submission of further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim as a proprietor registered layout, including evidence of prior publication or use. Where the applicant is acting on behalf of another, such as an exclusive licensee, they must provide written authorization from the original proprietor confirming their right to apply for registration under this Act. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application and any objections received will be considered in accordance with procedures established herein.

Any person who, having knowledge of a registered layout being protected under this Act, reproduces, copies, or otherwise utilizes such layout for the manufacture of integrated circuits, or causes such reproduction, copying, or utilization to occur, shall be deemed guilty of an offence and is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees, or both. Further, where the infringement involves the use of an indication certification trade mark associated with the proprietor registered layout, the penalty shall be doubled. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe measures for the seizure and forfeiture of goods infringing upon registered layouts as provided herein.

The Registrar General Plant shall exercise all powers conferred upon him or her by this Act and is responsible for maintaining records pertaining to applications for registration, granted registrations, and related documentation. For the purposes of fulfilling these duties, the Registrar General Plant may delegate authority to subordinate officers as deemed necessary, subject to guidelines issued by the Authority. The term "Registrar General Plant" includes any officer authorized by him or her to perform specific functions under this Act. Any communication required to be made under this Act shall be deemed served when delivered to the Registrar General Plant or sent by registered post with acknowledgment due.

An application for registration of a novel plant variety shall be accompanied by a detailed description conforming to the format specified in Schedule B, including particulars regarding its origin, method of breeding, and distinctive characteristics. The Registrar General Plant Varieties may require the applicant to furnish additional information or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar General shall issue an acknowledgment and assign it a registration number. A notice of the application, containing prescribed details, shall be published in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained by the Authority. Objections, if any, may be filed within the period stipulated therein, subject to procedural requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Board of Protection relating to the revocation of plant variety protection, or by any action taken by the Registrar General Plant in respect of registration procedures, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed from. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines under this Act regarding appeals will render the appeal inadmissible. Further, any party seeking injunctive relief relating to infringement of plant variety rights shall apply directly to the relevant High Court, subject to demonstrating irreparable harm and providing security as determined by the court.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be submitted to the Registrar General Plant in the prescribed form, accompanied by requisite documentation including detailed morphological data, genetic purity assessment reports, and evidence demonstrating stability across generations. The Registrar General Plant may require applicants to furnish additional information or clarification deemed necessary for a comprehensive evaluation under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar General Plant shall issue an acknowledgment and assign it a unique registration number. Processing fees, as determined by notification published in the Official Gazette, are payable at the time of submission. Any alteration to the particulars furnished in the initial application must be notified to the Registrar General Plant in writing, along with justification for the change. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of registration as provided herein.

An application for registration of a novel plant variety shall include detailed particulars regarding its lineage, including parentage information where ascertainable, and must demonstrate stability through at least three generations of propagation. The Registrar General Plant Varieties may require submission of additional data pertaining to morphological characteristics and genetic uniformity, as deemed necessary to satisfy the requirements under this Act concerning distinctiveness. Any applicant failing to provide complete documentation or demonstrating non-compliance with established protocols shall have their application rejected, subject to a right of appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any alteration in the declared lineage after initial registration requires prior approval from the Registrar General Plant Varieties and may necessitate reevaluation of the variety’s compliance.

The right to commercially exploit a registered plant variety, including through seed production and distribution, may be assigned or licensed subject to conditions as provided herein. Any such assignment or license shall require prior written consent from the Registrar General Plant Variety, who shall review the proposed terms for fairness and impact on farmers’ rights. The assignee or licensee shall be deemed to hold title to the right granted only insofar as it relates to the specific activities covered by the assignment or license agreement. Further, any sub-licensing of a plant variety requires notification to the Registrar General Plant Variety at least thirty days prior to such action. Failure to obtain consent or notify as required may result in penalties and revocation of the relevant rights under this Act. The Registrar General Plant Variety shall maintain a public record of all assignments and licenses relating to registered plant varieties.

The Registrar General Plant shall determine, at his discretion, whether an application for compulsory licensing relating to a registered variety satisfies the conditions stipulated under this Act concerning reasonable remuneration and public interest. Any aggrieved party disputing the Registrar General’s determination may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of notification of the order. The appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds and relevant evidence, subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Provided that, where the appellant is unable to pay the prescribed fee due to financial hardship, the Board may waive or reduce the same upon satisfactory demonstration of indigency. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final, barring further appeal only to the High Court on grounds limited to jurisdiction and violation of natural justice.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar General plant relating to the registration, revocation, or amendment of a plant variety protection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed and stating specifically the grounds on which the appeal is based. Provided that, where an order has been passed by the Registrar General plant imposing a penalty under this Act, the aggrieved party may also seek remedies available to them under the Customs Act 1962 concerning seizure of goods related to the infringing variety. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and afford them an opportunity of being heard. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding rights in a plant variety shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the commercial exploitation of that variety. Such licenses may include, but are not limited to, rights pertaining to seed production, propagation material distribution, and sales within defined geographical territories. The terms of any such license agreement shall be recorded with the Authority and made publicly accessible, provided that confidential business information may be redacted as deemed appropriate by the Registrar. Assignment of plant variety rights, including all associated licensing agreements, requires prior notification to the Authority and is only valid upon confirmation of receipt by the Registrar. Proceedings act authority concerning disputes arising from license terms or assignments shall be adjudicated according to established procedures under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall admit appeals only if the appellant demonstrates, through a duly completed ZM form petition, that they have suffered substantial prejudice due to the error apparent on the face of the record. Subject to this requirement and provided that the appeal relates to a decision concerning the grant or refusal of Plant Variety Registration, the Authority shall furnish all relevant records pertaining to the original proceedings to the Appellate Board within thirty days. The Authority’s determination regarding procedural irregularities during initial proceedings act authority is final unless demonstrably impacting fairness as determined by the Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder registered variety” shall mean a variety that has been formally protected under this Act and whose details are recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties. Such registration confers upon the breeder exclusive rights to produce, sell, export, or import propagating material of the breeder registered variety, subject to any conditions specified during the grant of protection. The Registrar may, after due inquiry and providing an opportunity for hearing, refuse to register a variety if it is deemed to be essentially derived from another variety, provided that such derivation does not involve an exclusive characteristic differentiating the new variety. Any person infringing these rights shall be liable for damages as determined under this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, details regarding the method and duration of its derivation, and a comprehensive description conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. The application must also clearly identify whether the variety is a *breeder registered variety* and, if so, provide evidence demonstrating that the breeder has fulfilled all obligations pertaining to the maintenance of genetic purity as mandated by regulations. Further, the applicant shall furnish documentation substantiating the distinctiveness and stability of the plant variety over successive generations. The Registrar may require additional information or clarification deemed necessary for assessing the validity of the application, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation or modification of protection granted to a breeder registered variety may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall only be admitted if the appellant demonstrates that they have suffered substantial prejudice due to the decision under challenge, and has paid such fees as may be prescribed. The Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary or annul the order appealed against. Further, any act of commercial exploitation undertaken without authorization from the registered breeder, including the unauthorized sale of propagating material derived from a breeder registered variety, shall constitute an infringement actionable under this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety as a breeder registered variety shall include particulars relating to the title under which the variety is known, the seed distributor, and the geographical area where the variety is intended to be sold. The Authority may require the applicant to furnish such further information or documentation as it deems necessary for assessing compliance with the provisions concerning distinctness, uniformity, and stability. Where an application relates to a variety derived from another variety, the applicant shall disclose the parentage of the variety and provide evidence demonstrating that the derivation does not prejudice the rights of the breeder of the original variety. The Registrar may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, refuse registration if it is satisfied that the application lacks sufficient merit or contravenes any provision under this Act.

A breeder shall not be entitled to claim protection under this Act for a plant variety unless the variety is demonstrably stable and uniform, exhibiting characteristics consistent with its genetic composition as evidenced through successive generations. Further, any application seeking registration of a *breeder registered variety* must include detailed documentation pertaining to the lineage and propagation methods employed, along with evidence confirming that the variety has been cultivated under conditions substantially similar to those prevalent in India for at least three growing seasons prior to submission. The Registrar may require additional data concerning disease resistance or yield performance if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these requirements. Provided that any challenge to the stability of a registered variety must be substantiated by scientific evidence and presented within two years of its registration.

Any person who knowingly markets a plant variety infringing the rights of a breeder registered variety shall be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of commercial exploitation and loss suffered by the aggrieved party. Such damages shall include, but not be limited to, lost profits, reasonable royalty fees, and costs incurred in bringing an action under this Act. Furthermore, any entity found guilty of such infringement may face penalties as provided herein, including fines up to five times the value of the infringing goods or services. The Registrar shall have the power to issue injunctions restraining further marketing activities where a breach of rights relating to a breeder registered variety is established.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a breeder registered variety shall be freely assignable, licenseable, and transferable, either in whole or in part, to any person, firm, or company, provided that such assignment, license, or transfer is recorded with the Registrar within thirty days. Any licensee utilizing a breeder registered variety for commercial purposes shall adhere strictly to the terms stipulated in the licensing agreement, including but not limited to royalty payments and restrictions on further sub-licensing without prior written consent from the registered breeder. The registered breeder may grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of the breeder registered variety for research or experimental purposes without requiring royalty payments, as provided herein. Any assignment or transfer shall include a detailed description of the rights being conveyed and specify the geographical territory covered by such transaction.

Where a person aggrieved by any decision made under this Act relating to the registration, revocation or amendment concerning a breeder registered variety, or by any condition attached thereto, may within sixty days from the date of publication of such decision in the Official Gazette, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall consider appeals upon statements of objections and replies submitted by all parties concerned, and may affirm, reverse or modify the order appealed from, subject to just considerations and natural justice. Any party dissatisfied with the order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the order, provided that the grounds for such appeal are limited to questions of law arising out of this Act.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, whether the applicant is the breeder or not, and if not, the relationship of the applicant to the breeder. Where an application relates to a *breeder registered variety*, the application must further state the details of the original registration under this Act, including the registering authority and date of such prior registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing their right to make the application, particularly where the applicant is not the initial breeder or a successor company deriving rights through assignment. Any challenge to the validity of the claimed relationship shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein. The Registrar shall publish notice of the application and any objections received will be considered before proceeding with examination.

A breeder shall not commercialize a breeder registered variety unless the requisite documentation confirming registration is submitted and acknowledged by the Plant Varieties Authority. Subject to compliance with the provisions regarding essential derivation, any farmer intending to sell seeds of a breeder registered variety must obtain prior authorization from the registered breeder, detailing the quantity permitted for sale and specifying royalty payments due. The Plant Varieties Authority may, upon receiving complaints concerning unauthorized seed sales or non-compliance with royalty stipulations, conduct inspections and issue notices requiring demonstration of adherence to these conditions. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of compliance shall render the farmer liable to penalties as provided herein. Further, any registered breeder is obligated to maintain records pertaining to licensing agreements and royalty distribution for a period not less than seven years from the date of commercialization.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a breeder shall retain exclusive rights over a breeder registered variety for a period commencing from the date filing application, unless such rights are expressly assigned or licensed. Any assignment or license of rights in a breeder registered variety shall be recorded with the Authority within thirty days of execution, and shall specify the scope of such assignment or license, including geographical limitations and permitted uses. The assignee or licensee may, subject to conditions prescribed by the Authority, exercise the rights granted under the assignment or license as if they were the original breeder. Further, a registered breeder may grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the commercialization of the breeder registered variety; however, such licenses shall not impair the breeder’s right to continue propagating and selling the variety.

For the purposes of this Act, a “breeder registered variety” shall mean a variety that has been formally protected under this Act and for which a certificate of protection has been granted to a person fulfilling the conditions as provided herein. Such registration confers upon the breeder exclusive rights in relation to the production, sale, distribution, and importation of propagating material of the breeder registered variety. Further, nothing in this Act shall prevent a breeder from simultaneously seeking an international application patent for their variety under applicable international treaties, subject to compliance with all relevant regulations pertaining to such applications. The Registrar may specify conditions relating to benefit-sharing arrangements concerning any breeder registered variety.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent invention shall mean a new and non-obvious technical solution to a problem in any field, including but not limited to industrial processes, machines, manufactured articles, compositions of matter, or improvements thereof. An invention shall be considered obvious if it is within the scope of existing knowledge, whether such knowledge exists as prior art under this Act or is otherwise readily available and accessible. The term "technical solution" implies that the invention must possess utility and be capable of being applied in an industry; provided that discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, aesthetic creations, and schemes are excluded from consideration as a patent invention.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent invention shall furnish, along with the prescribed fee, a detailed specification including claims defining the scope of protection sought. The Controller General may require the submission of additional documentation pertaining to the derivation and development history of the claimed invention, particularly where novelty or inventive step is challenged. Such documentation must clearly establish the applicant’s diligent efforts in pursuing the patent invention and demonstrate adherence to established research protocols. Further, a declaration confirming the veracity of the information provided shall be executed by the applicant or their authorized representative. The Controller General may, subject to due process, reject an application if it determines that the submitted materials are insufficient to satisfy the requirements as provided herein.

Where a patent invention is, after grant, found to infringe upon prior usage or knowledge existing within India, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. Such proceedings shall be commenced within three years from the date of sealing of the patent and require demonstrable proof of continuous use or public acknowledgement predating the patent application’s filing date. The court may, after affording the patentee an opportunity to be heard, determine whether the alleged prior usage constitutes a valid defense against infringement claims. If infringement is established based on such prior usage, the court shall have the power to grant relief including, but not limited to, an injunction restraining the patentee from enforcing their rights and awarding damages proportionate to the losses suffered by the aggrieved party as provided herein.

An application for a patent invention shall be accompanied by a declaration, made under this Act, setting forth the subject matter which the applicant considers to be his invention. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish any further information or documentary proof considered necessary for examination of the application and determination of novelty and inventive step. Where an amendment is proposed to the claims in the patent invention application, such amendment shall not alter the nature of the invention as disclosed in the original specification; provided that it does not broaden the scope of protection sought. The applicant shall be entitled to prosecute the application by filing responses to objections raised by the Controller within a prescribed time limit. Failure to respond may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to provisions regarding revival under this Act.

An application for a patent invention shall disclose the matter which the applicant considers to be new and for which protection is sought, accompanied by requisite drawings where necessary to understand the invention. The description must specify the nature of the alleged invention and how it may be performed or used, provided that such disclosure renders the invention obvious to a person skilled in the art. Where the invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the application shall also disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the process on an industrial scale. Any prior publication or use of the invention before the date of filing this application shall be disclosed under this Act and may affect the grant of patentability as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent invention may, within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision, file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be admitted only if it is established that the decision was manifestly unjust or perverse. Failure to demonstrate this shall render the appeal inadmissible and subject the appellant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any person found to have instituted frivolous proceedings relating to patent invention revocation with intent to harass or delay may be ordered by the Board to pay compensatory costs to the respondent, as determined appropriate under this Act. The Board’s order on such costs shall be final and binding.

Where a patent invention has been assigned or licensed, subject to the terms of the assignment or license agreement, the assignor or licensor shall retain the right to grant further licenses relating to the same patent invention provided that such subsequent licensing does not conflict with the existing rights granted under the initial assignment or license. Any licensee may, with the prior written consent of the patentee and the assignee, sub-license the patented process or product within the scope of the original license agreement as provided herein. The patentee shall be obliged to provide a certified copy of the assignment or license details to any prospective sublicensee upon reasonable request and payment of prescribed fees. Failure to disclose such information may render the subsequent license voidable under this Act. Further, an assignee may apply for revocation of a patent if the patentee acts in contradiction with the terms of the assignment agreement relating to exploitation of the patent invention.

Where a patent invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the Controller may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party alleging that the claimed subject matter lacks utility or involves undue experimentation, direct the applicant to furnish within a period not exceeding six months further information demonstrating the practical application of the process and the reproducibility of results. Such direction shall be accompanied by a reasoned order outlining the specific deficiencies identified. The applicant may appeal against such an order under this Act within thirty days from the date of communication thereof. Any party aggrieved by the appellate determination may, further, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal, subject to satisfying the requirements for maintainability as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent invention, or by any order made under this Act concerning the validity or enforceability thereof, shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. Such appeal may be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the relevant order, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Failure to comply with these timelines will render the appeal inadmissible. Further, any person found to have knowingly made a false statement or suppressed material facts in connection with case registration valid for patent protection shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees and may also face criminal prosecution under relevant provisions of law as provided herein.

Where a patent invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the Controller may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating substantial duplication of the inventive steps and resultant product characteristics, issue a notice inviting representations from any person alleging prior use or publication. Such allegations shall be considered only if they predate the date of filing of the patent application under this Act. If, following due consideration of these representations, the Controller finds that the alleged prior use or publication has materially impacted the novelty of the invention, he may direct a re-examination of the claims. Further, any party aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board, demonstrating how the findings constitute a trade mark falsified and unfairly prejudice their commercial interests.

For the purposes of this Act, a patent invention shall mean a new and non-obvious technical solution to a problem in any field, including but not limited to industrial processes, machines, manufactured articles, compositions of matter, or improvements thereof. An invention shall be considered non-obvious if it does not appear to a person skilled in the art, considering the state of knowledge as provided herein. The determination of obviousness may take into account prior publications relating to marks registry trade and other relevant factors. Subject to certain exceptions detailed elsewhere under this Act, an application for a patent invention must disclose the manner and method of performing it.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent invention shall, in the application, clearly define the scope of protection sought for the invention. The particulars required under this Act regarding the subject matter of the claimed invention must be explicitly stated and supported by detailed descriptions within the technical portion of the application. Where an application relates to more than one invention, each invention must be separately claimed; provided that inventions described in the specification may be linked if they relate to a single inventive concept. The Controller may require further clarification regarding any aspect of the patent invention or its claims during examination. Any amendment to the application sub section relating to the description of the invention shall not alter the nature of the originally filed claim.

Where a patent invention has been granted, the proprietor shall be entitled to take action against any party infringing upon the exclusive rights conferred under this Act. Such infringement includes, but is not limited to, making, using or importing the patented article without authorization from the proprietor. The remedies available to the proprietor include seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity and claiming damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of such infringement. Provided that, a party alleging infringement shall demonstrate clear evidence establishing both validity of the patent and substantial similarity between the alleged infringing product and the claimed invention. Further, register patents shall be subject to periodic review as provided herein, ensuring continued compliance with statutory requirements.

An appeal shall lie to the Appellate Board under this Act against any order passed by the Controller refusing the grant of patent or revoking a patent, and the Board may entertain an appeal only if the appellant deposits with the Registry such sum as may be prescribed. The Board shall consider whether the invention in question is indeed novel and inventive, subject to demonstrating that the prior publication or use does not invalidate the claim for protection invention convention. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the grounds of appeal are limited to questions of law arising out of this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any patentee or person duly authorized by the patentee may grant a license to use the patented invention under conditions specified therein. Such licenses shall be assignable, whether in whole or in part, and may include rights relating to manufacture, sale, and importation. Where a license is granted through a collective management organization functioning as a copyright society fee collector for related technological applications, the terms of such grant shall be subject to review by the relevant governmental authority to ensure equitable distribution amongst licensees. The patentee shall provide notice of any assignment or license to the Controller within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope and duration of rights transferred. Failure to comply with this provision may render the assignment or license voidable as provided herein. Any subsequent protection invention convention relating to the patented subject matter requires prior consent from the original assignee.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent” shall mean an exclusive right granted by the Controller under this Act in respect of an invention and conferred upon the patentee for a limited period. A patent may be granted only for inventions relating to a process or apparatus, an article or substance that is new and involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application as provided herein. The term “patentee” shall mean the person who is registered as the owner of a patent under this Act; where such ownership arises from assignment or succession, it includes the assignee or successor in title. Patents granted prior to the commencement of this Act shall be deemed to be patents for all purposes under this Act.

Applications for patents granted under this Act shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any grant or publication relating to the invention made elsewhere, detailing the date of such earlier disclosure. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the aforementioned disclosures, including translations where necessary, to facilitate examination. Where an application incorporates subject matter already disclosed prior to the filing date, the applicant shall provide a comprehensive explanation demonstrating how the claimed invention represents a substantial and inventive step over said prior art. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the patent application or limitation of the claims as provided herein. The record of all such disclosures and explanations shall be maintained by the office for public inspection.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or the rectification of entries in the Register of Patents, or otherwise affecting his rights as secured by patents granted, desires to appeal against such order, he may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the order, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall give notice to all parties concerned and hold a hearing wherein both sides may present arguments and evidence relevant to the matter under consideration. Any party failing to appear before the Board at the appointed time may be declared absent, and the appeal heard ex parte. Decisions of the Board are final subject to further appeal to the High Court within three months from the date of the order.

Where an application for patents granted relates to a process for producing a substance identified by its chemical formula, the Controller may require the applicant to disclose, with sufficient particularity, the precise method of utilizing such process industrially. Such disclosure shall include details concerning reaction conditions, catalysts employed, and purification techniques utilized to achieve the desired product purity as specified in the claims. Failure to provide this information, or providing information deemed inadequate by the Controller, shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The applicant may subsequently amend the application to comply with these requirements, provided that such amendments do not substantially alter the claimed invention’s scope and are supported by the original disclosure.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the patentee shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the patented invention. Such license may be granted for consideration or otherwise, as determined by the patentee, and the terms thereof shall be governed by contract law principles. Assignment of patents granted under this Act requires registration with the Controller, and such assignment shall only operate from the date of that registration. Where a patent has been assigned, the assignee shall possess all rights and powers which the assignor possessed as patentee, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the instrument of assignment. The patentee may also enter into agreements for the exploitation of the patented invention through manufacturing or otherwise, provided that such agreements do not unduly restrain trade or competition. Any license granted under this Act shall be revocable only under circumstances prescribed herein.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against the decision of the Controller refusing the grant of patents, the Appellate Board may, subject to such inquiry as it deems necessary, confirm, vary or reverse the said decision. The appellant shall be deemed to have acquiesced in any ground on which the Controller’s decision was based if that ground was not specifically challenged in the memorandum of appeal. Provided that where the Controller has failed to give reasons for his decision, the Appellate Board may direct him to do so before determining whether or not to entertain the appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may prefer further appeals to the Supreme Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, and shall be bound by the final determination therein regarding patents granted.

Where an application for patents granted has been examined and found eligible for grant, and the Controller has published a notice of readiness for grant under this Act, any person aggrieved by such decision may within sixty days from the date of publication file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of grounds of appeal and the prescribed fee. The Board may, after affording opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, vary or set aside the order appealed against. Provided that if the applicant has effected international registration of the patent under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the time limit for filing an appeal shall be extended by ninety days from the date of notification of such registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent” shall mean an exclusive right granted by the Controller under this Act in respect of an invention and conferred upon the patentee for a limited period. A patent shall only be granted where the invention relates to a process or apparatus, is novel, involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. The Registrar shall decide all applications relating to patents subject to appeals being made before the Controller as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar may appeal to the Controller within such time and manner as prescribed. Patents granted under this Act are assignable or transmissible in the same manner as any movable property.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or the rectification of the register, or otherwise affecting his rights as secured by patents granted, appeals to the Appellate Board, the Board may entertain such appeal if it is satisfied that the order was manifestly erroneous in law or fact. The Board shall have the power to affirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from and may substitute any other order which it considers just and equitable. Further, where a patent has been extended under provisions relating to pharmaceutical products, challenges to validity based on non-obviousness shall be subject to heightened scrutiny. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may appeal further to the Supreme Court within sixty days, provided that such appeals are only on questions of law. The application of the Madrid Protocol International system for designating India as a receiving office does not preclude remedies available under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for a patent may be filed by any person claiming to be the inventor of the invention. Where an invention relates to or comprises a plant variety or seed, the applicant shall disclose details regarding the method and means employed in its development, including information pertaining to breeder's right considerations where applicable. The Controller General shall, upon receiving such an application, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the claimed invention is novel, involves inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. Patents granted under this Act are subject to opposition proceedings within a period specified herein, during which any interested person may file notice of objection. Such objections must be supported by evidence demonstrating that the patent does not satisfy the requirements for grant as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent has been refused under this Act, and such refusal contains findings of fact which demonstrate a clear error apparent on the face of the record, any person aggrieved by the order of rejection may apply for rectification. Such application shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the applicant. The Controller, upon receiving an application for direct notice rectification, shall afford the patent office opportunity to file its response within thirty days. If, after considering all submissions and evidence presented, the Controller finds that the refusal was indeed based on demonstrable error, patents granted may be amended or revoked as provided herein, subject to compliance with procedural requirements outlined elsewhere under this Act.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of layout-design rights, and such proceedings result in a judgment finding the defendant guilty of said infringement, the court may order the recovery of damages as determined by prevailing schedules. Further, where the defendant has been found to have acted with intent to deceive or wilfully disregard the proprietary rights vested in the registered layout-design, the court shall be empowered to direct the forfeiture to the Government of any equipment, materials, and intermediate products utilized directly in the infringing activity. This order for forfeiture is without prejudice to any other penalties prescribed under this Act. The proprietor may petition for restoration of such forfeited assets subject to a demonstration that they are not readily identifiable as having been used in the commission of the offence. A convicted order forfeited shall be deemed final and binding, barring appeal solely on grounds of procedural irregularity.

Where an integrated circuit layout-design has been subject to a search warrant under this Act and subsequently seized, such seizure shall remain valid notwithstanding any subsequent challenge to the validity of the warrant itself. Any person convicted of infringing upon a registered layout-design shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer; furthermore, assets derived directly from the infringing activity, including but not limited to profits generated and equipment utilized in the unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of the layout-design, may be subject to a court order forfeiting such assets. Provided that limitations on liability relating to contributory infringement shall apply as provided herein. The adjudicating officer shall consider all relevant factors when assessing damages and determining whether a convicted order forfeited applies.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to include all accompanying documentation submitted by the applicant, including but not limited to maps delineating the geographical area, descriptions of production methods, and lists of authorized users. The court registrar, upon receipt of an application under this Act, shall verify that the prescribed fees have been remitted and that the application complies with the formal requirements as provided herein. Any deficiency in these respects may be notified to the applicant for rectification, subject to a time limit specified by the Registrar. Failure to rectify such deficiencies within the stipulated period will result in rejection of the court registrar application.

Any farmer submitting an application to the court registrar seeking registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to have declared that they possess exclusive right over the use of the said name for goods originating from the specified territory. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and procedures during this process will render the application liable for rejection, without prejudice to subsequent attempts under this Act. The Registrar may impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees on any farmer found to have made a false statement in their court registrar application concerning the geographical origin or production methods of the goods. Repeated violations shall attract penalties up to one hundred thousand rupees and potential revocation of any granted registration.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments executed under this Act, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Any person claiming an interest in a copyrighted work may apply to the Registrar for registration of an assignment, providing certified copies of the instrument effecting such assignment and details of the assignor and assignee. The application shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by notification issued by the Copyright Office. Upon verification that the proposed assignment complies with the provisions herein regarding formalities and subject matter, the Registrar may register the same. Registration of an assignment does not prejudice any rights previously vested in another person; however, it serves as prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment rights specified therein.

An assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed to include only those rights which are specifically enumerated therein; any right not so specified shall remain vested in the owner of copyright under this Act. Where an assignment is executed relating to a work already published, the assignee shall be liable to pay to the assignor such sum as may be determined by the Controller, representing royalties accruing from such publication prior to the date of the assignment, provided that the assignor provides full and accurate accounting records pertaining to those sales. Any dispute regarding the calculation of said royalty shall be subject to resolution through arbitration conducted in accordance with procedures prescribed by the Central Government. The Registrar may require production of supporting documentation substantiating any claims made under this provision relating to an assignment copyright work.

Any assignment of copyright in a musical composition or dramatic work shall be deemed to include, subject to any specific exclusions expressly stated therein, the exclusive right to author adaptations thereof, provided that such adaptation is not already in existence at the time of the assignment. Where an assignment purports to transfer all rights in a cinematograph film, it shall be construed as including the copyright in associated literary or musical works incorporated within the film unless explicitly limited by the terms of the agreement. An assignor may retain the right to receive a share of any sums received by the assignee from exploitation of the work beyond a specified amount, as agreed upon in writing. Further, an assignment shall not be deemed to transfer title to any preliminary materials used in the creation of the work unless such transfer is explicitly provided for within the document effecting the assignment copyright work.

Where an author executes an instrument purporting to be an assignment of copyright in a musical work, the validity thereof shall be determined solely upon examination of its terms and conditions; provided that such instrument does not explicitly transfer all rights subsisting under this Act, it shall be presumed, subject to proof to the contrary, that only limited rights have been assigned. Any dispute concerning the scope or duration of an assignment copyright work may be referred for adjudication to a court exercising civil jurisdiction. The author shall bear the burden of proving any modification to the terms as prescribed in the instrument; failing which, the interpretation most favourable to the assignee shall prevail. An appeal from such determination lies to the appellate forum established under law.

For the purposes of this Act, “literary work” with respect to computer programs includes source code and object code, and any preparatory material required for their production; provided that such materials are not independently copyrightable as literary works under this Act. The term "derivative work" shall mean a work based upon one or more pre-existing works, but excluding works which merely reproduce the original in whole or in part. Any adaptation of a computer program to ensure its compatibility with other programs shall be considered a derivative work subject to the restrictions herein. It is clarified that decisions regarding copyright infringement relating to such works are ultimately reviewable by the courts acting under authority delegated by parliament.

Applications for registration of musical works, including sound recordings and cinematograph films incorporating such works, shall be made in the prescribed form to the Copyright Office. Every application must contain a certified copy of the work itself, along with details regarding the author’s identity and ownership. Where the applicant is not the original author, proof of assignment or legal right to register the work shall accompany the submission. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims of authorship or ownership as deemed necessary for verification under this Act. Decisions concerning registration are subject to review by an appellate body constituted by parliament. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office may appeal within three months from the date of such determination.

Where any person infringes upon the copyright in a work, the owner of the copyright shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining that infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success and irreparable harm resulting from the continued violation. Furthermore, such owner may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the infringement, taking into consideration the benefit accruing to the infringer, provided that the amount claimed does not exceed an aggregate sum as determined by the court. The right to seek remedies under this Act is without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available to the copyright owner in law or equity. It shall be the duty of every judicial officer exercising jurisdiction in a matter relating to infringement to ensure fair representation for all parties involved, recognizing the significant role of parliament in safeguarding artistic expression and intellectual creation.

Where any question arises as to whether an adaptation of a work infringes the copyright in the original work, the matter shall be determined by reference to the substantial similarity between the two works, considering not only quantitative aspects but also qualitative elements and the overall impression left upon the mind of the ordinary observer. The determination of such infringement is subject to judicial review under established principles of law. For purposes of this assessment, evidence presented before a court may include expert testimony regarding technical processes employed in creation or reproduction. Any person aggrieved by an order made concerning copyright infringement may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The power to grant interim injunctions relating to alleged infringements remains vested with the civil courts as provided herein, and any application for such relief shall be adjudicated according to established procedures. This determination is without prejudice to the powers of parliament to amend or repeal this Act.

Where any work, including but not limited to literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works, is created in the course of employment, the author shall for the purposes of this Act be deemed to be the employer unless and until it is established that the said work was produced independently by an employee acting outside the scope of their contractual obligations. Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines issued by the Central Government, any person claiming entitlement to copyright under this provision may submit evidence demonstrating the nature of the employment relationship and the degree of creative input provided by the employee. The determination of such claims shall be made in accordance with principles of fairness and equity as determined by a tribunal appointed by parliament. Provided that, where the work is commissioned, the terms of commission shall be considered when assessing authorship.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced, distributed, exhibited, or performed any work subject to copyright without authorization from the owner thereof shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Where such infringement involves commercial gain, the court may further impose a fine equivalent to three times the value of the infringed work or ten million rupees, whichever is greater. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding assessment of damages under this Act. It shall be the duty of every law enforcement agency to assist aggrieved copyright owners in securing remedies as provided herein. Parliament believes that robust protection necessitates stringent measures against unauthorized use.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding copyright in a musical work may grant an exclusive license authorizing the reproduction and distribution of sound recordings incorporating such work, provided that the terms of such license are clearly defined within a written agreement executed prior to the commencement of commercial exploitation. The licensee shall be entitled to sub-license rights under this Act with the consent of the copyright holder, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, where a musical work is jointly authored, the parliament recognizes that each co-author possesses an independent right to assign or license their share of the copyright, and any such assignment shall bind all other co-authors unless explicitly agreed otherwise in writing. The remuneration payable to authors for licenses granted under this Act shall be determined by principles of fairness and equity as may be prescribed.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the determination of copyright infringement, or concerning the rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, he may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate court shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed from and may confirm, reverse, or modify the order under appeal. Provided that an appeal lies notwithstanding any technical objection, and the Parliament may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe conditions for granting leave to appeal. Any party dissatisfied with the judgment of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on such grounds as are provided herein.

Where any person claims copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work, and such claim is predicated upon original contributions made subsequent to a prior publication of substantially similar material, the Registrar shall require submission of documentary evidence demonstrating due diligence undertaken to ascertain the initial date filing application for said prior publication. Such evidence must include certified copies of registration records from relevant national libraries and copyright offices. Failure to provide satisfactory documentation within ninety days of the request shall render the application deemed abandoned. The Parliament may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the form of such documentary evidence. This provision applies irrespective of whether the work is registered under this Act or claimed as an unpublished creation.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding copyright in works relating to plant varieties registered with the Plant Varieties Registry may grant licenses conferring exclusive rights for reproduction, distribution, and commercial use within specified territories. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, and the assignment must be executed by the copyright holder or their duly authorized agent. The terms of a license, including royalty rates and duration, are subject to approval by the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks, ensuring equitable compensation for the original creator. Further, any transfer of rights relating to registered plant varieties shall require notification to both the Plant Varieties Registry and the Controller General. Parliament recognizes that fostering innovation in agricultural technology necessitates clear guidelines regarding intellectual property licensing, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “audiovisual work” means a compilation comprising cinematographic films and literary works, including musical scores, lyrics, and dramatic elements, fixed in any medium; provided that such compilation shall be considered an audiovisual work only if it constitutes an original work of authorship. The right to reproduce an audiovisual work under this Act extends only to the entire work as presented, and not to individual components unless expressly authorized by the copyright owner of each component element. Any determination regarding whether a work qualifies as an audiovisual work shall be subject to review by Parliament, acting through a committee appointed for that purpose, particularly in relation to works originating from a Contracting Party.

Where a cinematograph film has been commercially exhibited without due authorization under this Act, any person involved in the unauthorized exhibition, including but not limited to the exhibitor and those facilitating the distribution of copies for such exhibition, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. This applies irrespective of whether the infringing copy was generated directly from the original or derived through subsequent reproduction. Provided that if the infringement was committed by a minor, the liability of any adult supervising or guiding the minor’s actions relating to the film's unauthorized use shall be assessed considering their degree of knowledge and control over the situation. This offence notwithstanding contained in any other law for the time being in force, remains actionable under this Act with penalties as prescribed herein.

Where a copyright owner desires to grant a license for the reproduction or adaptation of any work, such license may be assigned by way of endorsement upon the original copy or copies of the work, specifying the scope of permissible use, duration, and royalty rates applicable. This assignment shall be deemed valid notwithstanding any subsequent alteration in ownership of the copyright itself, provided that the assignee adheres to the terms stipulated within the endorsed document. Further, a license granted under this Act may include provisions for sub-licensing rights, enabling the initial licensee to grant further permissions subject to conditions approved by the Controller. An offence notwithstanding contained in any agreement relating to such licenses shall be actionable as a civil wrong, and remedies available under contract law shall apply.

Applications for patents filed in India, claiming priority from a prior application made in a convention country shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the earlier application within such time as may be specified by the patent office, failing which the application shall be deemed to have been withdrawn. Where an application is filed as a convention application, the date of filing of the prior application shall be taken into account for determining the period of grace allowed under this Act for claiming priority. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documents relating to the earlier application if he deems it necessary for the purposes of examination. Any appeal arising from an order passed by the Controller concerning a convention country section shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for the grant of a patent has been filed in a convention country, and such application is subsequently deemed to be a convention application under this Act, any person aggrieved by the granting of a patent based on that convention application may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. Such proceedings shall be limited to challenging the validity of the registered patent, and not its subsistence. Failure to demonstrate reasonable grounds for challenging novelty or inventive step, as defined herein, will render the petitioner liable for costs incurred by the patentee in defending the action. The Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, impose a penalty of up to one hundred thousand rupees upon any party found to have filed frivolous challenges against a registered invention originating from a convention country section.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it appears that the invention claimed in a patent application relates to subject matter disclosed in a prior publication or where such disclosure would have rendered the claim obvious to a person skilled in the art, the Controller may require the applicant to demonstrate that the invention was not anticipated by said prior publication. Failure to satisfy the Controller’s requirements shall result in rejection of the claims concerned. In cases involving a 73 convention application, the date of priority for determining novelty and inventive step shall be as provided herein, notwithstanding any conflicting information presented regarding earlier disclosures. The applicant may appeal such a decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act concerning the validity or infringement of a patent may institute proceedings to challenge said order in the High Court.

An application constituting a 73 convention application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent application initially filed in the Convention Country, duly authenticated by the appropriate authority therein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a complete translation of the said patent application into English, along with the certified copy. Provided that, if the translation is not furnished within the time specified by the Controller, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. Further, under this Act, the date of filing for priority purposes shall be determined in accordance with the provisions relating to convention applications as provided herein. The applicant shall also file a statement indicating the Convention Country where the initial patent application was filed and the date on which it was so filed. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the 73 convention application, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

An application constituting a 73 convention application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent grant or published application, whichever occurred earlier, and such certification must be obtained from the competent authority designated under the laws of the originating country. The prescribed fee for filing a 73 convention application shall be double that payable for an ordinary first application as provided herein. Subject to compliance with regulations regarding translation requirements, where the specification is not in English or Hindi, the applicant may submit a translated version within six months from the date of the initial application. Provided that any delay beyond this stipulated period will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Controller shall notify the applicant if deficiencies are observed during examination.

Where any person has made a patentable invention abroad, he may apply for patents for the same in India by filing a convention application within twelve months from the date of the first filing. Any false representation made in a convention application shall be deemed to be an offence under this Act and subject to penalties as prescribed herein. Furthermore, where it is determined that a patent has been granted based on a fraudulent or deceptive convention application, the Controller may order revocation of the patent, notwithstanding any other provision. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify guidelines regarding the verification of documents submitted with a 73 convention application to prevent abuse and ensure compliance.

Where the right to make, use and sell a patented invention has been assigned or licensed under this Act, any subsequent 73 convention application filed by the assignee or licensee shall be subject to the terms and conditions of such assignment or license. Provided that where an assignment is made prior to the grant of a patent, the assignor may, with the written consent of the assignee, file a further convention application relating to the same invention, but only if the original application had not been abandoned or refused. The Controller shall have power to require production of documentation evidencing such assignments and licenses as provided herein, and may inquire into their validity for the purpose of determining entitlement under this Act. Any dispute regarding the scope or enforceability of an assignment or license relating to a patentable invention shall be resolved in accordance with general principles of contract law.

Where any person claiming right to a patent, or alleging that the invention claimed in a patent does not satisfy the requirements of this Act, appeals against an order passed by the Controller under this Act, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the appellant has demonstrated, with reasonable certainty and supported by documentary evidence, that the invention was previously published or described in a manner which makes it available to the public, thereby rendering the application ineligible for grant. Further, where such appeal concerns a 73 convention application, the Board shall also examine if the claimed invention was disclosed within the prescribed time limit from the date of first filing in the relevant convention country, and whether any subsequent modifications or additions materially alter the original disclosure to the detriment of public interest.

An application claiming priority under a 73 convention application shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the patent application initially filed in the convention country, duly authenticated. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish such further particulars or documents relating to the invention and its exploitation as he deems necessary for the purposes of examination. Where the invention relates to plant varieties or novel hybrids, the applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating that adequate measures are in place to protect breeder's rights consistent with international obligations. Such evidence may include details regarding licensing agreements or mechanisms for benefit-sharing amongst relevant stakeholders involved in the development and propagation of the variety. The application is subject to all provisions relating to novelty and inventive step as provided herein.

An application constituting a 73 convention application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent grant or published application, as applicable, from the first filed country. The prescribed fee for the institution of such proceedings under this Act shall be remitted along with the application and any deficiency thereof may be remedied within thirty days from the date of notification issued by the Patent Office. Where an objection is raised regarding the compliance with the requirements pertaining to a convention application, the applicant shall have opportunity to address the same in writing within two months. Any dispute arising concerning the validity of such certified copy or the determination of priority under this Act may be referred to a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the Patent Office is situated for adjudication. The Controller may require further documentation as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions, provided that the applicant shall be given reasonable time to furnish the same.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent under this Act shall, if the invention is also claimed by a patent granted or applied for in a convention country, be required to disclose within the application particulars of such prior applications. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the patent liable for revocation by the Controller upon petition from any interested party demonstrating prejudice arising directly from the non-disclosure. Where an applicant has filed a 73 convention application relating to an invention already patented in India, the subsequent patent shall be deemed invalid if it does not substantially differ from the earlier granted patent and incorporates elements disclosed therein without proper acknowledgement or justification. Penalties for wilful misrepresentation regarding prior applications extend to fines exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and potential imprisonment of up to three years.

Where the right to make and sell a patented invention has been assigned or licensed under this Act, any subsequent 73 convention application filed by the assignee or licensee shall be subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the original assignment or license agreement. Provided that such agreement expressly permits the filing of a convention application, and further provided that the Controller is satisfied that the interests of the true inventor have been adequately protected, impliedly registration shall proceed as if the assignee or licensee were the original applicant. The patentee may grant multiple licenses relating to the same invention, but any subsequent assignment made by a licensee without prior written consent from the patentee shall be deemed void and unenforceable under this Act. Any transfer of rights arising from a 73 convention application requires notification to the Controller within thirty days.

An exclusive licensee under this Act shall register with the Controller within thirty days from the date on which the license agreement comes into effect, providing a certified copy of the said agreement and details of the licensed territory. Such registration is subject to verification by the Controller regarding the terms granting rights as an invention exclusive licensee. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating the validity of the license and its compliance with provisions relating to patentability. Failure to register shall render the exclusive licensee unable to enforce certain remedies under this Act pertaining to infringement, provided that a grace period of fifteen days is allowed for rectifying any clerical errors in the submitted documents. Any alteration to the terms of the license agreement must also be reported to and re-registered with the Controller.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee may grant an exclusive licence relating to the patented invention, either for the whole or part of the term of the patent, and either for the whole or any specified territory. Such exclusive licence shall confer on the licensee the right to exercise the rights which are exclusively vested in the patentee under this Act. The patentee shall notify the Controller within thirty days of granting any such exclusive licence, specifying the identity of the licensee and the scope of the licensed rights. Further, assignment of a patent or an invention exclusive licensee requires registration with the Controller, and failure to register shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee. The patentee may retain certain rights even under an exclusive license, as agreed in writing between the parties.

For the purposes of this Act, “compulsory license” means a license granted by the Controller under this Act authorizing manufacture, use or sale of a patented invention without the consent of the patentee; and where a compulsory license is granted, any person holding such license shall be deemed to be an exclusive licensee with respect only to the acts specifically authorized therein. An exclusive licensee shall have standing to enforce the rights conferred by the patent against infringers not parties to the licensing agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein relating to reasonable terms and conditions of use. The Controller may specify these conditions in the grant of a compulsory license.

Where a patent has been granted and an exclusive licence agreement is executed, registration thereof shall be mandatory under this Act. The application for such registration must specify the patented invention, the names and addresses of both the patentee and the exclusive licensee, and the duration of the exclusivity conferred. Any modification to the terms of the exclusive license agreement subsequent to initial registration may also be registered, subject to a fee as prescribed by the regulations. An exclusive licensee shall have standing to pursue enforcement actions relating to infringement of the patent during the term of the registered licence, provided that such actions are undertaken in conjunction with the patentee or with their written consent. Failure to register an exclusive license agreement will render the licensee unable to assert rights under this Act.

Where an exclusive licensee exercises a right granted under this Act to make, use or sell a patented invention, any person infringing that right shall be deemed to have also infringed the patent itself. The patentee shall not, without reasonable justification and subject to due process, restrain an exclusive licensee from exercising such rights unless it is demonstrated that the actions of the licensee are inconsistent with the terms of the licence agreement.
