Where any question arises as to whether an invention constitutes an india patented invention, the Controller may, at his discretion and subject to appeal under this Act, direct the presentation of evidence on oath relating to such invention. Such direction shall be given if it appears to the Controller that there exists a reasonable doubt regarding novelty or inventive step, particularly concerning prior use or publication within India. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating, by clear and convincing evidence, that the challenged determination was erroneous in law or fact. Further, any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may seek judicial review only after exhausting all available remedies as provided herein, failing which such a petition shall be deemed premature.

For the purposes of this Act, an india patented invention shall mean an invention which has been granted protection under this Act and relates to a product or process concerning pharmaceuticals, agricultural chemicals, or biotechnology applications. The determination of whether an invention qualifies as an india patented invention shall be subject to scrutiny regarding its novelty and non-obviousness compared to existing prior art. Further, where a patentee licenses the use of their india patented invention, the terms governing such license, including any royalty payable by the licensee, are subject to review under this Act to ensure fairness and prevent anti-competitive practices as provided herein.

For the purposes of administering proceedings relating to revocation or infringement of patents, the Central Government shall, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint officers to be Adjudicating Officers. An Adjudicating Officer so appointed shall exercise such powers and perform such duties as may be prescribed under this Act, including but not limited to hearing evidence, examining witnesses, and recording findings of fact and law. Subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, any order passed by an Adjudicating Officer shall be binding on all parties concerned. The Central Government may remove an Adjudicating Officer from their office for cause, as provided herein.

Applications for registration of designs shall be examined by the Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act, who shall verify that the design complies with all requirements pertaining to novelty and originality as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence and specimens as the Adjudicating Officer may deem necessary to ascertain these qualities. Where an objection is raised concerning prior publication or a similar registered design, the Adjudicating Officer shall provide the applicant an opportunity for written response and presentation of counter-evidence. Decisions regarding registrability are subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Adjudicating Officer’s determination on matters of fact relating to design features shall be final, barring appeals based solely on legal errors.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the revocation or infringement of a patent believes such order to be manifestly unjust or without due regard to the evidence presented, that party may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all other parties interested in the matter and afford them an opportunity to present their views. Upon hearing arguments and considering the record of proceedings before the Controller, the Appellate Board may confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any amount directed to be paid as damages or costs under this Act shall be recoverable from the defaulting party as if it were a decree of a civil court. The adjudicating officer appointed by the Controller for conducting inquiries relating to patent infringement shall act in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Where any question arises regarding the determination of whether an invention is obvious or involves an inventive step, the Controller shall refer the matter to an adjudicating officer appointed by notification in the Official Gazette. The adjudicating officer shall possess qualifications and experience as may be prescribed under this Act and shall conduct proceedings in a manner consistent with principles of natural justice. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the adjudicating officer may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Controller may, after affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Decisions made by the adjudicating officer shall be recorded in writing and accompanied by reasons for the decision.

Where an application for grant of patent is rejected by the Patent Office, any interested party shall have the right to appeal to the Adjudicating Officer. The Adjudicating Officer shall provide notice to all parties involved, including the applicant and any third parties who submitted objections, specifying the grounds upon which the rejection was based. Subject to compliance with prescribed timelines, submissions from each party may be filed in writing, supported by relevant documentation demonstrating adherence to conditions stipulated under this Act concerning patentable subject matter. A trade mark shall be deemed established where the applicant demonstrates continuous use of the mark in commerce within India for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application, subject to compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act. Provided that, if the trade mark is intended for export purposes only, the aforementioned usage requirement may be satisfied through demonstrable marketing and promotional activities directed towards foreign markets, as certified by an authorized Export Promotion Council. Furthermore, evidence of widespread recognition of the trade marks established shall be presented to the Registrar, including but not limited to consumer surveys and market research data, confirming that a substantial portion of relevant consumers associate the mark with the applicant’s goods or services. The Registrar may require additional documentation as deemed necessary to verify these claims.

For the purposes of this Act, a "mark" includes any sign or indication used or proposed to be used in commerce, whether capable of being represented graphically or otherwise, including a word, name, symbol, device, signature, or shape of goods, containers, or packaging. A “marks registry act” is defined as the process by which applications for registration of marks are received, examined, and adjudicated upon, subject to the provisions herein regarding distinctiveness and prior use. Any mark shall be registrable if it is not descriptive of the goods or services with which it is associated, provided that acquired distinctiveness through extensive use may be considered under this Act. The Registrar may reject an application if the proposed mark conflicts with existing registered marks.

Applications for registration of a mark shall be made to the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain a clear representation of the mark sought to be registered and a statement specifying the goods or services with which the mark is associated, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend any description or illustration contained in the application if he considers it necessary for clarity or precision. An appeal against such requirement shall lie to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Where an application includes a device likely to be mistaken for a geographical indication, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the applicant and any interested party as provided herein. The marks registry act governs procedures regarding conflicting applications and prior use claims.

An application for registration of a mark shall include a representation of the mark in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by a statement clearly identifying all goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the description of goods or services to align with the International Classification of Goods and Services; failure to comply within the stipulated timeframe will result in rejection of the application. Any proposed mark that contains any emblem, symbol, or name exclusively used for the purpose of denoting government activities shall not be registered under this Act unless prior authorization is obtained from the relevant governmental authority. The marks registry act mandates a search of existing registrations before filing and allows for opposition by interested parties within four months of publication in the Trade Marks Journal.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions relating to distinctiveness under this Act, applies for or attempts to register a mark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trademark shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both, as determined by the court. Further, any goods sold bearing such infringing mark are deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offending party. The Registrar may, ex officio, initiate proceedings against any applicant found to be engaging in deceptive practices concerning the marks registry act, without prejudice to civil remedies available to aggrieved trademark owners.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses relating to trademarks registered under this Act, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees. Any person claiming title to a trademark by way of assignment or license may apply to the Registrar to have such assignment or license noted in the marks registry act. The application shall specify the mark assigned or licensed, the assignor or licensor, and the assignee or licensee, along with supporting documentation demonstrating due execution. Provided that an assignment is not effective against a third party unless it is so noted. Further, any license granted may contain conditions relating to quality control of goods or services bearing the trademark, as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may require such undertakings from licensees to safeguard consumer interests and prevent dilution of the registered mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a “marks registry” means the official record maintained by the Registrar of Trade Marks, containing particulars relating to registered trademarks and applications pending examination. The marks registry established under this Act shall be deemed a public document, accessible for inspection subject to any regulations prescribed by the Central Government regarding fees and access protocols. Any alteration or addition to entries within the marks registry must be authenticated by the Registrar’s official seal and signature. Information contained therein shall be considered prima facie evidence of registration, provided that such evidence is not contradicted by admissible legal argument as provided herein.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of all trademarks applied for and registered under this Act, distinguishing between marks classified according to international classes. Any person claiming entitlement to a trademark may apply for its registration, submitting such particulars as are prescribed, including a representation of the mark and a list of goods or services with which it is associated. The Trade Marks Registry established herein shall be deemed a public office, accessible during specified hours for inspection by interested parties subject to reasonable regulations framed by the Registrar. Applications received shall be examined for compliance with statutory requirements; objections may be raised by any person claiming a proprietary right in a similar mark. Decisions regarding acceptance or rejection of applications are appealable as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to be refused if it is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier mark registered under this Act in relation to identical goods or services, provided that the applicant demonstrates honest concurrent use of the mark immediately prior to the date of such earlier registration. Any proprietor aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application for registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Trade Marks Registry established under this Act shall maintain a record of all registered trade marks, accessible for public inspection subject to prescribed fees. Further, any person infringing a registered trade mark shall be liable to damages and an injunction as provided herein, without prejudice to any other remedies available under law.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive record of all applications for registration of marks, including particulars of the applicant, the mark itself, the goods or services in relation to which it is used or proposed to be used, and the class or classes to which those goods or services belong. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The marks registry established under this Act shall be open to inspection during specified hours, subject to such conditions as the Central Government may prescribe to protect confidentiality and prevent disruption of official work. Applications for rectification of registered trade marks may be made to the Registrar, detailing grounds for challenging the validity or registration of a mark, provided that all supporting documentation is submitted with the application. The Registrar shall consider any opposition filed against an application within the prescribed timeframe as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed to have been refused if the proposed mark is identical or confusingly similar to any existing registered trademark under this Act, or to any mark pending registration. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application provided that the applicant demonstrates distinctiveness acquired through use subsequent to another’s prior registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to acceptance or refusal of an application shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Trade Marks Registry established under this Act shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all applications, registrations and oppositions, subject to any restrictions imposed for commercial confidentiality as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or the entry of a mark on the Register of Trade Marks, shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against and failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar may, at any time, require the surrender of a certificate of registration if it is found that the mark was registered in contravention of provisions under this Act or through fraudulent means. Penalties for wilful violation of these provisions include fines up to one million rupees and imprisonment extending to three years. The marks registry established herein shall maintain records accessible only upon due process.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses relating to trademarks registered under this Act; any person claiming title to a trademark by way of assignment or license may apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner for entry of such assignment or license in the said register. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the particulars of the transaction, including the consideration paid or promised and the duration of the license, if applicable. The Registrar may, subject to any terms and conditions specified therein, enter such assignments and licenses in the register, provided that a copy of the instrument creating the assignment or license is filed with the application. Any entry made under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment or license and shall be binding on all parties claiming under the trademark. The marks registry established herein serves as public record for these transactions.

Applications for registration of marks shall be examined by the Registrar in accordance with the provisions herein, and where an application is refused, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The decision of the Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act. Any person aggrieved by a notice issued by the Registrar relating to acceptance or registration of a mark may also file an appeal within the prescribed time limit. Disputes concerning distinctiveness, as determined during examination or subsequent opposition proceedings, are amenable to appeal and review before the Appellate Board. The marks registry established shall maintain records accessible for public inspection, subject to regulations regarding confidentiality.

An appeal lies to the High Court within sixty days from the date of order made by the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration under this Act, or relating to the removal of a mark from the Register. Provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend the period specified above by a further period not exceeding thirty days where it considers such extension necessary due to circumstances beyond the control of the appellant. The marks registry established as per section 9 shall be subject to judicial review by the High Court on any question of law arising during proceedings before the Registrar. Any order made by the High Court may be enforced by it in like manner as if it were an order of that Court.

For the purposes of this Act, the marks registry established shall be deemed a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. It shall have power to make regulations not inconsistent with this Act regarding the procedure for filing applications for registration of trademarks and the examination thereof. Any specification patent shall clearly define the goods or services in relation to which the trademark is sought to be registered, adhering to prescribed classifications as provided herein. The marks registry may require amendments to such specifications if they are deemed ambiguous or otherwise deficient under this Act. Applications received by the marks registry shall be processed sequentially according to established protocols.

Applications for the registration of registry trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain such particulars as are required by the regulations. The applicant shall indicate whether he is claiming priority from a prior application made in a country outside India, and if so, shall furnish proof of the date of the earlier application. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct that any amendments be made thereto to ensure clarity or compliance with the provisions under this Act. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The registrar shall record all details pertaining to each trade mark registration and maintain them in an accessible manner for public inspection, subject to any restrictions as provided herein.

Applications for the registration of registry trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. Every application shall state an address for service in India, and if the applicant is not residing or carrying on business in India, he shall appoint a person resident in India as his agent for the purpose of receiving communications under this Act. The Registrar may require any further information to ascertain whether the proposed trade mark is distinctive in its class and refuse registration if the application does not comply with these requirements. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall furnish a copy thereof to the applicant and publish it in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may, within the time specified therein, file a notice of opposition under this Act. The registrar shall consider any such opposition and determine whether registration should proceed as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for a registry trade mark, direct that the hearing be conducted before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if any interested person makes a timely objection to the proposed mark under this Act. Such objections shall relate specifically to matters of distinctiveness or deceptive similarity as provided herein. The applicant shall have the right to submit written arguments in response to such objections and may request an opportunity for oral presentation before the Board. Decisions rendered by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning registry trade marks shall be appealable to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, subject to the provisions regarding costs as determined under this Act.

Applications for the registration of registry trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Such applications must clearly indicate the goods or services with which the mark is associated, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services. The applicant shall provide proof of use of the trademark in relation to those goods or services if required by the registrar. Where an application contains more than one representation of the mark, each representation shall date filing separately for the purposes of determining priority under this Act. Any alteration made to an application after it is filed shall be noted and shall not affect the original filing date, provided that such alterations do not substantially change the nature of the mark as described herein.

Applications for the registration of offices trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. An application relating to an office trademark shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the mark is proposed to be used, classifying such goods or services according to the International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as may be required by the Registrar to establish entitlement to use the trade mark and to demonstrate that the mark is distinctive in relation to the specified goods or services. Where an application includes a representation of the office trademark, it must comply with the requirements set out under this Act regarding clarity and accuracy. The registrar may request further information from the applicant as deemed necessary for assessment.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall be entitled to institute proceedings against any person infringing their rights conferred by registration, seeking an injunction restraining the infringing activity, damages proportionate to the loss sustained by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, and the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. Where an infringement involves the use of identical or deceptively similar offices trade marks in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including account of profits made by the infringer. Provided that a proprietor seeking remedies under this Act shall demonstrate reasonable diligence in the exercise of their trademark rights. Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the appellate body as provided herein.

Applications for the registration of offices trade marks shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Every application shall contain a clear representation of the mark distinguishing it from any other mark registered under this Act or applied for, and shall state the goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the mark. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to determine whether an application is complete and complies with the provisions herein. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall acknowledge its receipt and assign it a filing date. Objections to the acceptance of any trade mark for registration may be raised by any person claiming an interest in a similar mark already registered or applied for under this Act within the time specified. The Registrar shall consider such objections and issue a decision as provided herein.

Any person who, having knowledge of registered offices trade marks used in relation to any goods or services, uses a mark which is identical or deceptively similar to that registered office trademark in connection with goods or services identical or closely resembling those in respect of which the trade mark is registered, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at such amount as may be determined by the court, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor of the registered offices trade marks and any benefit gained by the infringing party. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint, issue an injunction restraining the use of the infringing mark, provided that it is satisfied that the infringement causes or is likely to cause damage to the reputation or goodwill of the registered trademark.

The proprietor of a registered trademark relating to offices may grant a license conferring the right to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to terms and conditions agreed upon in writing. Such licenses shall be assignable alongside the underlying trademark ownership, provided that notice of assignment is furnished to the Registrar within thirty days. Where a force cessation patent pertaining to a process integral to the manufacture of goods bearing the licensed trademark occurs, the licensee may negotiate with the proprietor for adjustments to royalty payments reflecting such disruption, as determined by an independent valuation. The proprietor shall retain ultimate control over quality standards associated with the use of their offices trade marks under any license agreement. Any sub-licensing activity requires prior written consent from the original proprietor and must adhere to conditions mirroring those stipulated in the primary license.

Applications for the registration of offices trade marks relating to goods or services connected with banking, insurance, financial services, or any other form of investment shall be examined by an officer specifically designated for that purpose under this Act. The Registrar may, at any stage of the examination process, refer the matter to a Bench constituted in accordance with the provisions herein for further consideration and determination of complex issues arising concerning distinctiveness or deceptive similarity. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by such a Bench may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that order. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all proceedings before the designated officer and any constituted Bench, including reasons for decisions and dissenting opinions, accessible for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as provided herein.

A trademark shall be deemed deceptively similar to another if, considering the impressions created in the minds of the average consumer, it is likely to cause mistaken identity. This assessment shall take into account the visual appearance, phonetic composition, and ideational significance of the marks, as well as the nature of the goods or services with which they are associated. The determination of similarity is a question of fact dependent on the overall impression created without undue emphasis on any single element. Crucially, there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, which may arise even where the marks possess some distinguishing features.

Further, where wilful infringement is established, the Court may impose punitive damages not exceeding ten times the amount of damage actually suffered by the proprietor. Costs associated with these proceedings shall be determined at the discretion of the Court, taking into consideration the conduct of both parties.

Where a trademark has been assigned, the assignee shall become entitled to exercise all rights and powers which the assignor might have had under this Act. However, any use of a registered trade mark by a licensee or assignee without authorization from the proprietor shall constitute an infringement. context: A trade mark exists where it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. For the purposes of this Act, a sign shall be deemed to be distinctive if, because of its inherent character, the informed user recognizes that sign as indicating the origin of particular goods or services and differentiating them from those of others. A trade mark may include a word, name, symbol, device, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, sounds or any combination thereof. Provided that signs which contain only generic terms describing the characteristics of the goods are not registrable as trade marks under this Act unless they have acquired distinctiveness through use.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act. Such rights are subject to the limitations prescribed herein relating to fair dealing and permitted uses by others, provided that any use of a similar sign which creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services shall constitute an actionable infringement. The proprietor may seek remedies including injunctions restraining further infringing acts, damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a result of the infringement, and delivery up or destruction of materials bearing the infringing trade mark. Further, where an infringement has resulted in dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered trade mark, enhanced damages may be awarded at the discretion of the Court. A trade mark exists for ten years from the date of registration, renewable indefinitely upon payment of prescribed fees.

A trade mark shall exist in relation to goods or services offered under that trade mark. An application for registration of a trade mark may be made by any person claiming ownership, subject to fulfilling all prescribed conditions as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry shall examine each such application and determine whether the proposed trade mark is distinctive and not deceptive, considering prior usage and existing registrations. Where an objection arises concerning similarity to an earlier registered trade mark, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit a written response and attend a hearing before the Registrar. The Registrar may require further evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or clarifying the scope of goods or services. If the Registrar finds that a trade mark exists which is identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for mark, registration shall be refused.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and may be licensed to any person subject to such terms and conditions as the proprietor deems fit. The proprietor of a trade mark may grant an assignment of the entire trade mark, or of any part of the rights conferred thereby, including the right to use the trade mark in relation to specific goods or services; provided that such assignment shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry within three months from the date of execution. Any license granted under this Act shall be revocable by the proprietor if the licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions stipulated therein. A trade mark exists as a valuable commercial asset, and its transfer is governed by principles ensuring transparency and protection for all parties involved in such transactions.

A trade mark exists in respect of goods or services associated with the name displayed thereon, but this shall not preclude rectification proceedings initiated under this Act if it is demonstrated that subsequent use by another party has resulted in a change in the character or reputation of the said trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence establishing such alteration and considering representations from all interested parties, direct amendment to the register reflecting the modified association. An appeal lies against any order made by the Registrar under this provision, subject to the condition that the appellant shall demonstrate prejudice resulting directly from the decision appealed. Further, a party aggrieved by an interlocutory order may seek redress through appropriate proceedings as provided herein.

An application for the registration of a trade mark may include a designation indicating that it is intended to be registered primarily as a promotion trade mark, provided that such designation clearly specifies the goods or services with reference to which the promotion is conducted. The Registrar shall consider an application containing such a designation in accordance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness under this Act and may require further clarification regarding the nature and duration of the promotional activities if deemed necessary. Where a trade mark is registered as a promotion trade mark, it shall be subject to renewal requirements similar to those applicable to ordinary trade marks, but the Registrar may prescribe different fees reflecting the limited scope of protection afforded. Any challenge to the validity of such registration must specifically address the promotional use aspect.

A registered trade mark owner shall be entitled to restrain the use of any trademark which is identical or confusingly similar to their registered trade mark where such use constitutes a promotion trade mark, and is employed in connection with goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registered trade mark is used. Provided that, nothing in this provision shall prevent the use of an otherwise infringing mark if such use falls within the fair use doctrine as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, a proprietor may apply to the relevant court for relief including damages and injunctions against any person who has made false representations concerning the origin or characteristics of goods or services through the unauthorized application of a promotion trade mark. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy available to the registered proprietor.

An application for the registration of a trade mark may include a designation indicating that the applicant seeks registration as a promoter of goods or services relating to the trade mark. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice in the Trade Marks Journal specifying the trade mark and the nature of the goods or services in relation to which promotion is claimed. Any person alleging that the use of the trade mark for promotional purposes would constitute an unfair practice or be detrimental to consumers may file written objections with the Registrar within three months from the date of such publication, stating the grounds upon which they rely. The Registrar shall consider any objections received and provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond in writing. A decision regarding the validity of a promotion trade mark registration shall be appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this Act.

A trade mark may be registered as a promotion trade mark subject to compliance with the conditions hereinafter prescribed. An application for registration as a promotion trade mark shall specify the goods or services in relation to which the promotion is conducted and the period during which such promotion is intended to operate, provided that this period shall not exceed one year from the date of registration. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the genuineness of the promotional activity and its connection with the underlying trade mark. Further, the applicant must satisfy the Registrar that the use of the trade mark as a promotion trade mark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Any alteration to the promotional scheme requires prior approval from the Registrar.

A registered trade mark owner shall be liable for damages sustained by any person who has been deceived or misled, directly or indirectly, by the use of a promotion trade mark in contravention of this Act. Any proprietor utilizing a promotion trade mark without express written consent from the registered proprietor may face prosecution under this Act and shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees for each instance of infringement. Further, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of all goods bearing the infringing promotion trade mark. The Registrar may, upon complaint, issue an injunction restraining any person from continuing such deceptive practices, provided that evidence of actual damage or likelihood thereof is presented.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant a license to use such trade mark for goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, geographical territory, and duration of the license. Where a promotion trade mark is involved, as defined under this Act, the proprietor shall ensure that any licensed party adheres strictly to quality control standards maintained by the grantor, failing which revocation proceedings may be initiated. The assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right pertaining thereto including licenses, requires execution of a formal instrument and registration with the Trade Marks Registry. Any transfer of rights under a promotion trade mark license shall not prejudice existing contractual obligations between the original proprietor and licensee.

A registered trade mark shall continue to enjoy protection notwithstanding its use being discontinued for a period exceeding three years, provided that such discontinuation did not result from an act of deliberate abandonment undertaken with the intention of prejudicing another person’s rights under this Act. Where a proprietor seeks to revive a registration following such cessation of use, they must demonstrate to the Registrar, through documentary evidence and testimony, that there has been no alteration in the nature of the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. The Registrar may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party asserting prior rights relating to a similar promotion trade mark, direct further inquiry into the matter, leading to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking registration of a promotion trade mark shall furnish with the application a detailed statement outlining the promotional activity for which the mark is intended, including but not limited to proposed duration, geographical scope and specific goods or services involved. Such statement must demonstrate that the promotional use genuinely promotes the sale or advertising of the underlying goods or services and does not constitute an attempt to unfairly exploit the reputation of any existing trade mark. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating these claims, including copies of marketing materials and distribution agreements. An international application form filed under this Act shall include a declaration confirming adherence to these promotional stipulations; failure to do so will render the application liable for rejection.

For the purposes of this Act, “registration respect” means the legal entitlement afforded to a registered trade mark holder by virtue of its registration and shall include the exclusive right to use, license, and otherwise exploit the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. This right extends to preventing the use by any person of an identical or confusingly similar sign in relation to identical or similar goods or services without due cause, subject to principles of fair dealing as provided herein. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to grant registration respect beyond the scope of the specific goods and services listed in the trade mark register.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark institutes proceedings alleging infringement under this Act, and it is established that another person has used a mark identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark, the Court may grant such remedy as it deems fit, including an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing mark. The measure of damages recoverable shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, and also taking into account any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized use. It is provided that in determining such damages, the Court shall consider the extent to which the registered trade mark enjoys *registration respect* within the relevant market segment. The defendant may offer evidence demonstrating honest belief in the availability of the mark prior to the registration date; however, this shall not preclude a finding of infringement if confusion likely exists.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall furnish such particulars as may be prescribed, including a representation of the mark and a clear statement of the goods or services with which it is proposed to be associated. Upon receipt of an application, the Trade Marks Registry shall publish a notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person claiming rights or interests in relation to any trade mark appearing in such notice may, within the period specified therein, file a representation objecting to registration on grounds as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider all representations received and afford the applicant and objector an opportunity of being heard. Registration respect for existing prior marks is paramount; consequently, where objections are substantiated, the application may be refused or amended subject to conditions deemed appropriate by the Registrar. The decision of the Registrar shall be final, save for appeal under this Act.

Where a proprietor seeks to register a trade mark under this Act, and such trade mark incorporates elements already present within a previously registered trade mark belonging to another party, the Registrar shall conduct an assessment regarding potential dilution. This assessment will consider whether use of the proposed trade mark is likely to cause confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers concerning the origin or affiliation of goods or services. The proprietor seeking registration shall provide evidence demonstrating that their intended use will not infringe upon the existing registered trade mark’s *registration respect*. Provided that, if the Registrar determines a likelihood of such confusion exists, registration may be refused unless the applicant demonstrates clear and conspicuous differentiation in marketing channels or consumer perception.

Any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice from the Registrar that a trade mark has been registered, uses a registered trade mark in such a manner as to be likely to create confusion or to damage the reputation of the proprietor shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and where the offence is a continuing one, a further penalty may be imposed for each day during which the use continues. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding such unauthorized use, issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. This provision applies irrespective of whether the infringer had knowledge of the registered trade mark and aims to protect the registration respect afforded to proprietors under this Act.

Where the proprietor of a registered trademark desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the mark exclusively within a defined geographical territory, such license shall be deemed an assignment for the purposes of this Act, subject to any conditions expressly stated in the licensing agreement. The licensee may, with the prior written consent of the registered proprietor, further assign or sub-license the rights granted under the original license, provided that such subsequent assignments do not diminish the respect afforded to the trademark by its initial registration. Any assignment or sub-license shall be recorded at the Trade Marks Registry within three months of execution; failure to comply with this provision renders the assignment voidable. The registered proprietor retains ultimate control over quality assurance relating to goods and services offered under any license, and may revoke a license if standards are not maintained, thereby safeguarding the continued registration respect of the mark.

Where a proprietor claims infringement of a registered trade mark under this Act, and the defendant asserts that use of the impugned sign does not create confusion amongst the relevant public, the Tribunal shall consider all surrounding circumstances including, but not limited to, the similarity of the goods or services, the degree of recognition enjoyed by the plaintiff’s trade mark, and any evidence demonstrating dilution of distinctiveness. The proprietor seeking relief for registration respect shall bear the onus of proving such infringement. However, if the defendant demonstrates that the alleged infringing use is in honest descriptive employment relating to the characteristics of their own goods, or constitutes permissible comparative advertising, the Tribunal may allow such use subject to conditions designed to mitigate any potential confusion. Appeals against decisions of the Tribunal under this provision lie to the High Court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any proprietor holding a registered trademark shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring the right to use such trademark in relation to specific goods providing services. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the terms stipulated within the license agreement. The assignment of registration respect relating to a trademark is permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to maintain the validity and integrity of the registered mark. Any subsequent licensee or assignee shall adhere to the conditions precedent established under this Act regarding quality control and consumer protection associated with the goods providing services bearing the licensed or assigned trademark. Failure to comply with these obligations may result in revocation of the license or assignment, as deemed appropriate by the relevant authorities.

A trade mark shall be deemed to enjoy registration respect from the date of publication of acceptance under this Act. Such respect extends to any identical or confusingly similar signs used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, provided that such use is undertaken by a person who had knowledge of the prior registration. Where a proprietor utilizes a reference use mark—that is, a sign adopted solely for the purpose of indicating the source or intended purpose of goods—such utilization shall not constitute an infringement of the registered trade mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed and without prejudice to the rights of the registered proprietor to seek remedies under this Act.

Upon receipt of an application for the registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as demonstrates distinctiveness and acquired reputation, particularly where the mark incorporates descriptive terms or alludes to goods or services. The Registrar shall examine whether the applied-for mark conflicts with any existing proprietor trade marks already registered under this Act, considering similarity of signs and identity or likelihood of confusion regarding related goods or services. If the applicant fails to satisfy the Registrar concerning these requirements, registration may be refused. Any person aggrieved by a refusal order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a prescribed period, as provided herein. The registrar shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations.

The Registrar may, upon application made by the proprietor of a trade mark, direct that any alteration to such trade mark shall be noted in the Register. Such application shall specify the nature of the proposed alteration and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the trade mark as altered. The Registrar shall give notice of the proposed notation under this Act and may require the applicant to furnish security for costs incidental to any opposition that may be filed against the proposed alteration. Any person aggrieved by such direction or by the failure of the Registrar to grant it, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The proprietor shall remain accountable for maintaining the distinctiveness and reputation associated with their proprietor trade marks throughout the duration of registration.

Any person who, without due cause or consent from the proprietor of a registered trademark, uses any mark which is identical or deceptively similar to such proprietor’s trademark, shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages recoverable shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringing use and the profits made by the infringer. Further, where an infringement has occurred, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark or packaging thereof. It is provided that any registered proprietor trade marks shall be afforded protection against dilution even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services associated with those marks.

The proprietor of any proprietor trade mark may grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensee, provided that prior written consent of the proprietor is obtained, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Further, a proprietor may enter into agreements whereby another party undertakes to use the trade mark under defined circumstances, including but not limited to distribution or manufacturing arrangements; these undertakings are also considered assignable with the proprietor’s approval. Any assignment or license granted in contravention of this provision shall be void and unenforceable against third parties claiming rights under this Act. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the reputation and goodwill associated with their proprietor trade marks, even when licensed to others.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade marks proprietor” is defined as any person, whether Indian or foreign, who owns the right to use and register a trade mark under this Act. Such ownership may be derived from initial registration, assignment, operation of law, or other means recognized herein. A trade marks proprietor shall have the exclusive right to institute proceedings relating to their registered trade mark, including actions for infringement and rectification. The rights of a trade marks proprietor are subject to limitations imposed by prior use or registration under this Act, provided that such prior use or registration was lawfully established. Any entity claiming to be a trade marks proprietor must demonstrate valid title as provided herein.

Upon receipt of an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence establishing their identity as a *trade marks proprietor* and demonstrating their entitlement to use the mark as is deemed necessary. Where the applicant seeks to register a trade mark encompassing a geographical indication, they shall provide an affidavit verifying that they possess sufficient control over the relevant quality aspects of goods or services associated with that indication. Further, any person claiming rights in opposition to a pending application may submit evidence substantiating their claim, provided that such evidence is directly related to the distinctiveness or reputation of the mark as it exists under this Act. The Registrar shall consider all submitted documentation when determining whether to accept the application for examination.

Subject to any conditions specified in the certificate of registration, a trade marks proprietor shall have exclusive right to use the trademark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered and to prevent the use of an identical mark or a mark likely to be confused with it in connection with such goods or services. Any person desiring to challenge the validity of a registered trademark may institute proceedings under this Act within five years from the date of its registration, alleging that the trade marks proprietor was not the true owner of the right sought to be protected at the time of application for registration. Where infringement is established, the court may grant such relief as it deems appropriate, including an injunction restraining the infringing party and ordering the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark. The trade marks proprietor shall also be entitled to claim damages sustained by reason of the infringement.

The Registrar may, upon application made by a trade marks proprietor seeking rectification of the register, entertain and determine an objection to the continued registration of a mark based on acquired distinctiveness. Such applications shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating use of the mark subsequent to its initial registration, and detailing the geographical extent and duration of such use. The Registrar is empowered to request further information from the applicant or any interested party under this Act, including but not limited to consumer surveys and market analysis reports. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of that decision. The trade marks proprietor bears the onus of proving acquired distinctiveness on a balance of probabilities. Provided that, where an objection relates to non-use, the applicant must demonstrate satisfactory reason for such non-use.

A trade marks proprietor seeking to assign rights in a registered trade mark shall provide written notice of such assignment to the Registrar within thirty days of execution. The notice must specify the trade mark, the assignor, and the assignee, along with a copy of the instrument effecting the assignment duly executed. Provided that, where the assignment is made pursuant to a contractual agreement, a certified copy of said contract may be submitted in lieu of the full instrument. Further, any subsequent alteration to the details provided within the notice shall require a fresh submission under this Act. The Registrar may request further documentation substantiating the validity of the assignment and the identity of the trade marks proprietor if deemed necessary for verification purposes.

Any person who, without due cause or consent from the trade marks proprietor, uses a deceptively similar mark to that which is registered, or any confusingly similar packaging or label associated therewith, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits sustained by the proprietor and an amount not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees as penalty. Further, where infringement is established, the Court may order seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, as well as any materials used in their manufacture or packaging. The trade marks proprietor has the right to apply to the District Court for interim injunctions restraining such use pending final determination of the matter, subject to providing security satisfactory to the Court.

A trade marks proprietor may grant licences relating to the use of their registered trade mark, subject to the conditions specified therein and provided that such conditions do not contravene any provision under this Act. Any licence granted shall be in writing and clearly define the geographical area and the goods or services for which the licensee is authorised to use the trade mark. The proprietor retains ownership of the trade mark and may revoke a licence if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation of the trade mark, as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, a trade marks proprietor shall be entitled to assign their registered trade mark or the benefit of any registration to another party, with the written consent of the Registrar being obtained prior to such assignment taking effect.

Where any person alleges that another has infringed a registered trade mark, such allegation may be made only by filing a complaint before the appropriate intellectual property forum, provided that the complainant is demonstrably recognized as the trade marks proprietor for the mark in question. The defendant shall have the right to challenge the complainant’s standing as a trade marks proprietor by presenting evidence demonstrating lack of continuous use or abandonment of the mark. Further, any determination regarding ownership of the trade mark shall be subject to appeal to the appellate body within ninety days from the date of the original order. This process is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act relating to passing off or unfair competition.

Any person who, without due cause or reasonable excuse, represents that goods or services are affiliated with or endorsed by a trade marks proprietor shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or both. Provisions act shall ensure that such representations are deemed false if they create a likelihood of confusion amongst the public regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services. Further, any trade marks proprietor aggrieved by such misrepresentation may institute civil proceedings seeking damages and an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing the deceptive practice. The Court may also order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing representation as it deems fit.

Where any person alleges that the use of a sign or mark by another constitutes infringement under this Act, and such alleged infringer claims to be a bona fide user having adopted the sign or mark prior to the date of application for registration by the trade marks proprietor, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property forum. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, both their prior use and that said use was genuinely continuous and not solely for the purpose of establishing rights against the proprietor. Further, if the alleged infringer is also a patentee holding valid patent protection relating to goods or services identical or closely related to those associated with the trade mark in question, this shall not automatically preclude them from claiming bona fide user status; however, such claim will be subject to heightened scrutiny as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade marks proprietor is defined as any person, firm, company or association who owns the right to use and register a trademark under this Act, including but not limited to the registered owner of the mark. Such ownership shall vest upon successful application and registration, subject to any subsequent challenges. An appeal against an order cancellation may be made to the relevant intellectual property appellate tribunal as provided herein. The trade marks proprietor retains exclusive rights pertaining to the use of the trademark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, but such rights are not absolute and may be limited by other provisions under this Act.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark contains any representation of goods or services, the Registrar may require the applicant to amend such representation to conform to the prescribed forms and classifications. Upon receipt of such a requirement, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to comply therewith; failure to do so within the stipulated period shall render the application liable for rejection. The trade marks proprietor is deemed to have knowledge of all particulars relating to the registration, including any limitations or conditions imposed upon the registered mark. Any person alleging proceeding infringement of a registered trade mark may file a complaint with the Registrar detailing the nature and extent of such alleged infringement, subject to provisions regarding evidence and remedies as provided herein.

Where any person seeks revocation of a trade mark registration under this Act, alleging that the trade marks proprietor has not used the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered during a continuous period of five years immediately preceding the date of application for revocation, the registrar shall consider whether such non-use was involuntary. Provided that, if the applicant for revocation can demonstrate that the non-use occurred as a result of any act or omission by the trade marks proprietor intentionally creating confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods or services, the registrar may proceed with the assessment of revocation without further inquiry into involuntariness. Further, where such an application is made, the trade marks proprietor shall be afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence rebutting the allegation of non-use and demonstrating continued use, even if limited in scope.

Where an application for the registration of a mark includes a reference to any other mark already registered under this Act, or which is pending registration, and such marks are owned by the applicant, the Registrar may direct that the two marks shall be treated as *marks registered associated* for the purposes of examination and subsequent enforcement. Such direction shall be recorded in the register of trade marks. The proprietor of any mark so directed to be treated as associated shall be entitled to use both marks jointly or separately, subject to compliance with all relevant provisions regarding permissible usage. Further, any opposition filed against one of such *marks registered associated* shall be deemed to extend to the other mark, provided that notice is given to the proprietor accordingly and the grounds for opposition are applicable to both.

Where a mark is registered under this Act, any other mark which identifies goods or services connected to those for which the first-mentioned mark is registered, and which is used or proposed to be used by the proprietor of the first-mentioned mark, may be deemed marks registered associated with the original registration. The Registrar shall, upon application made in the prescribed form and subject to payment of the requisite fee, record such association within the register of trade marks. Any person seeking to assert rights relating to a mark registered associated shall demonstrate that the connection between the marks is clearly established and not misleading to consumers. Failure to do so may result in an action for passing off being dismissed. The proprietor of a mark registered associated retains all rights pertaining to their individual mark, as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, direct that the reasons for such refusal be recorded in writing and made available to the applicant. Further, if any marks registered are subsequently found to be deceptively similar to other existing marks, or where confusion likely arises due to similarity between marks registered associated with different proprietors, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the proprietor of the potentially infringing mark to submit representations within a prescribed period. Failure to respond adequately may result in an order directing the amendment of the register, including the removal of the offending mark from the register and consequential adjustments to any related classifications. The Registrar’s decision on such matters is final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act on the ground that it conflicts with a mark already registered, or applied for by another person, and the Registrar considers that the conflicting mark has been used to create confusion among the public regarding the origin of goods or services, he may allow the applicant’s application if the applicant demonstrates a clear and demonstrable association between their proposed mark and the marks registered associated. Such demonstration shall include evidence of prior dealings, advertising campaigns, or other activities undertaken by the applicant that explicitly link the two marks in the consumer's perception. The Registrar shall provide reasons for any such allowance, which reasons must be recorded in the register. This power is subject to ensuring no undue prejudice results to the proprietor of the earlier mark.

Where a proprietor seeks to grant a license relating to a mark registered under this Act, or to assign such mark, it shall be permissible to include within the terms of that license or assignment provision for the use of marks registered associated with the principal mark. Such provisions may specify permitted territories, goods and services in relation to which the licensee or assignee may utilize the associated marks, subject to conditions ensuring no confusion arises amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods or services. The Registrar shall have the power to require modification of any such license or assignment terms if they deem them unduly restrictive or contrary to the public interest. Further, a proprietor transferring ownership of a mark is deemed to transfer all rights pertaining to marks registered associated therewith unless expressly excluded in the instrument of transfer.

For the purposes of this Act, where two or more signs, whether identical or not, are used to distinguish goods of different enterprises, they shall be considered separate trade marks if their visual appearance, phonetic similarity, or conceptual meaning do not create a likelihood of confusion on the part of the relevant public. This determination shall take into account all surrounding circumstances, including the channels of trade and the classes of goods or services. A mark consisting exclusively of signs or indications which are common to the trade shall not be considered a separate trade mark unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use following the date of registration.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark identical or nearly identical with a mark already registered in connection with goods or services, or goods or services similar to those in relation to which the earlier mark is registered, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired by use after the date of the earlier registration. This requirement shall apply irrespective of whether the marks are for identical goods and services; however, consideration will be given to any demonstrable consumer confusion arising from the similarity. The existence of separate trade marks does not preclude an assessment of potential unfair advantage gained through such application. Any representation made by the applicant regarding acquired distinctiveness is subject to verification under this Act.

Where two or more signs are applied for by an applicant for registration as trade marks, and it is established that such signs, though distinct, function to identify goods or services offered under a common enterprise or brand identity, the Registrar may, subject to due consideration of consumer perception and potential confusion, register them as separate trade marks. This power shall not be exercised if such registration would unfairly prejudice existing proprietors of similar marks. Any proprietor aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar registering signs as separate trade marks may appeal under this Act within sixty days from the date of that decision. The Appellate Board shall consider whether the distinctiveness of each mark is adequately protected and whether consumer confusion is reasonably likely to arise, taking into account all relevant circumstances presented during the appeal proceedings.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark that includes or contains identical or similar elements to a previously registered trade mark, and such elements are capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, the Registrar may direct that the later mark be registered as a separate trade mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient dissimilarity in overall impression. This direction shall only be given after affording the proprietor of the earlier trade mark an opportunity to make representations under this Act. The Registrar’s decision regarding registration as separate trade marks is final subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any subsequent application incorporating elements from either registered mark must adhere to established principles concerning likelihood of confusion and honest practices in industrial property.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark that includes any other mark already registered under this Act, or which is identical to such a registered mark, the Registrar may require the applicant to specify whether they claim separate trade marks. If the applicant elects to register the marks as separate trade marks, provided that the distinctiveness of each mark can be established independently and without reliance on the reputation associated with any other mark, registration shall proceed for each mark individually. The Registrar shall consider evidence demonstrating such independent distinctiveness before granting registration. Further, where a proprietor owns multiple registered marks, the use of one mark shall not prejudice the rights pertaining to another registered as a separate trade mark unless explicitly authorized in writing by all relevant proprietors.

Where two or more signs are applied for registration under this Act as separate trade marks, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating distinctiveness between each mark. Failure to provide such satisfactory evidence within the time prescribed shall render the application liable for rejection. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark aggrieved by the registration of another’s mark as a *separate* trade mark may institute rectification proceedings before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, seeking its removal from the Register. Such proceedings must demonstrate likelihood of confusion or detrimental impact on the reputation of the earlier mark. The Board shall impose penalties, including monetary fines and injunction orders, for wilful infringement arising from such registration.

Where any two or more trade marks are registered as separate trade marks by the same proprietor, or where such proprietor subsequently acquires ownership of additional trade marks that bear similarity to previously registered marks, the proprietor may grant licences for the use of any one or more of those separate trade marks subject to conditions specified in a written agreement. Such agreements shall clearly delineate the geographical territory and scope of permitted usage as defined within the licensed activities. Further, assignment of rights pertaining to these separate trade marks is permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to all existing restrictions and limitations previously imposed upon the assignor’s use or licensing thereof. The Registrar may require a declaration confirming compliance with such conditions prior to registration of any assignment. This provision does not preclude the proprietor from retaining control over the overall quality standards associated with goods or services bearing these trade marks.

Where two or more signs are applied for by an applicant under this Act, and the Registrar is satisfied that such signs, though distinct, relate to the same goods or services, he may register them as separate trade marks, provided that the applicant demonstrates a clear intention to utilize each sign independently in commerce. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar registering signs as separate trade marks may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The Board shall consider whether the Registrar’s determination was demonstrably flawed and if so, may direct the rectification of the register or dismiss the appeal, with reasons recorded in writing.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark identical or nearly identical with a mark already registered in respect of goods or services, or those which are similar to the goods or services for which the earlier mark is registered, and the applicant demonstrates that the earlier mark has been used exclusively under conditions likely to create confusion amongst the public, the Registrar may refuse the registration of the later mark unless the proprietor of the earlier mark consents. This refusal shall not preclude the registration of separate trade marks where the goods or services are clearly distinguishable and there is no likelihood of dilution occurring. A permitted register trade may be granted if the applicant satisfies the Registrar that use has been made in good faith, and that such use does not unfairly prejudice the distinctiveness of the earlier mark as provided herein.

Where an application is filed for the registration of a mark identical or nearly identical with a mark already registered in respect of goods or services, and such existing mark constitutes a separate trade marks under this Act, the Trade Marks Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant. The notice shall specify the particulars of the earlier registration and invite the applicant to either amend their application to distinguish their proposed mark or submit evidence demonstrating that no likelihood of confusion exists between the two marks. Provided that if the applicant fails to respond within the time specified in the notice, or if the Registrar is satisfied that a likelihood of confusion would indeed result from registration, the application shall be rejected. The registrar may require further documentation to assess this likelihood as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "trade marks registrar" means the officer appointed by the Central Government to perform the functions specified herein and includes any officer authorized by the trade marks registrar to exercise all or any of those functions. The trade marks registrar shall be responsible for receiving applications for registration of trade marks, examining such applications in accordance with prescribed procedures, and determining their registrability subject to appeals under this Act. Any decision made by the trade marks registrar concerning acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding rectification proceedings, is appealable as provided herein before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Central Government may prescribe the qualifications and conditions of service for the trade marks registrar.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by such particulars relating to the goods or services and the applicant as the Trade Marks Registrar may require. The Registrar, upon receiving an application, shall furnish a copy thereof to the territorial authorities within India, requesting them to ascertain whether the proposed marks are in use in their respective jurisdictions. Any person claiming to be interested in opposing the registration of a trade mark under this Act may, subject to prescribed timelines and procedures, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registrar. The Registrar shall then provide the applicant with an opportunity to submit its response to such opposition. Decisions regarding oppositions shall be made by the Registrar based on evidence presented and as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a trade mark, or by any condition imposed or alteration made in respect thereof, alleges that such decision is erroneous in law or fact, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which the aggrieved party receives notice of the decision. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, reverse, or modify the decision appealed against, and may substitute such decision with one of its own. Any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction as provided herein.
