Where an application for the registration of a trade mark includes a designation indicating India as a territory for which protection is sought under an international registration, the acceptance or rejection thereof shall be subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board upon appeal from any party aggrieved. Provided that such appeal must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order. The Board may, after affording all parties a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse the decision of the Registrar concerning the registration india designated. Further, if the designation relates to a mark identical or confusingly similar to an earlier trade mark registered in India, the appeal shall specifically address the likelihood of confusion as per established principles under this Act.

An application for the registration india designated under this Act shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed and shall state clearly the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receiving an application, issue a receipt acknowledging its date of presentation and assign it an official number. Any alteration made to the representation or specification of marks after the initial filing requires prior approval from the Registrar, obtained through a formal request submitted in the prescribed form. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the mark liable for removal from the register. The trade mark proprietor shall be responsible for ensuring continued compliance with all relevant provisions as provided herein and may be required to furnish periodic declarations confirming such adherence.

An application for registration india designated under this Act shall be refused if the proposed trade mark, or any element thereof, comprises solely a representation of a plate used primarily for culinary purposes and depicting generic foodstuffs. Provided that such refusal may be waived where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the date of this application, evidenced by verifiable sales figures and consumer surveys confirming recognition of the mark as indicating origin. Furthermore, if the Registrar deems the depiction on the plate to be deceptive or contrary to public interest, registration shall also be denied. The Registrar may require submission of detailed manufacturing processes relating to the creation of such plates in instances where ambiguity exists regarding their primary function.

Any proprietor seeking registration india designated under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence if, at the time of application, the mark is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical to those for which registration is sought. Such proprietors are liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may face prosecution under relevant criminal statutes. Further, any registration granted in contravention of this provision shall be deemed invalid and subject to cancellation by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating demonstrable confusion amongst consumers. The validity registration trade mark is contingent on adherence to these stipulations; failure to comply will result in swift legal action.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark contains a reference to prior rights enjoyed by a person outside India, the Trade Marks Registry shall consider such evidence as is presented demonstrating the extent and nature of those rights. Protection inform international jurisdictions shall be afforded due regard during examination, subject to compliance with requirements under this Act concerning distinctiveness and non-infringement. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation regarding foreign trade mark registrations if deemed necessary for a proper assessment. Furthermore, where such prior rights are demonstrably essential to the continued operation of an industry in another country, and where the use of the trade mark within India would cause demonstrable prejudice, the Central Government may, after due inquiry, grant a compulsory licence permitting specified uses under conditions it deems equitable.

An application for an international registration referred to under this Act shall be deemed to be an application for the registration of a trade mark in India relating only to the goods or services specified in the list of countries designated in the international registration. Such an application may contain such particulars as the Registrar deems necessary for the purposes of examination and processing, subject to any prescribed requirements regarding translation or adaptation of the mark. The applicant shall furnish all information required by the Registrar concerning the status of the international registration. Any alteration to the goods or services covered by the international registration shall be notified to the Registrar in accordance with regulations framed under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark under this Act may be made by a proprietor of an international registration designating India, provided that such designation was effected within five years from the date of the international registration. The Registrar shall examine any such application as if it were an application for original registration, subject to the provisions regarding priority claims arising from the earlier international registration. Where an international registration referred includes a mark identical to one already registered in India, or which is deemed to be registered under this Act, the Registrar may refuse registration unless satisfied that use of the trade mark in India would not create confusion with such existing registration. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to establish entitlement and validity.

An application for rectification of a trade mark shall be entertained against an internationally registered trade mark where India has been designated only if the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the existence of such registration within Indian territory. The proprietor of the internationally registered trade mark shall, upon receipt of notice of any such application, have thirty days to file a counter-statement denying the allegations and presenting relevant evidence in support of their rights. Failure to do so may result in the Registrar proceeding ex parte. Subject to this, rectification proceedings concerning an international registration referred shall be conducted according to procedures applicable to domestic trade mark applications, provided that any claim of prior use must be substantiated with documentary proof admissible under Indian law. The Registrar may order the cancellation or limitation of rights in respect of the internationally registered mark if satisfied that it is contrary to public interest or infringes upon existing Indian trade mark rights.

An application for an international registration referred to under Article 2 of the Madrid Protocol may be filed with the Trade Marks Registry by a registered proprietor of a trade mark. Such an application shall contain particulars as prescribed, including a copy of the statement of the International Bureau and any designation of India contained therein. The Registrar may require such further information or declarations as are necessary for determining compliance with this Act and the Regulations made thereunder. Upon receipt of the application and after satisfying himself that all requirements have been met, the Registrar shall publish a notice of the proposed registration in the Trade Marks Journal. Any opposition to the international registration shall be dealt with according to procedures established under this Act, as if it were an original application for registration. The applicant shall be entitled to submit evidence and arguments in response to any such opposition.

An application for an international registration referred to under this Act shall be examined as if it were an application for the registration of a trade mark in India. Such examination shall proceed subject to compliance with all relevant provisions relating to distinctiveness and deceptively similarity, as though the mark were being initially considered for Indian registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification concerning the goods or services listed in relation to the international registration, provided that such request is made within a period of six months from the date of receipt of the International Bureau’s advice. Any opposition proceedings arising from an international registration shall be conducted according to procedures prescribed for domestic trade mark oppositions.

An application for rectification of a trade mark shall be entertained against an internationally registered trade mark only if the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising from the continued protection afforded by such international registration within India. The Registrar may, subject to due process and affording the proprietor of the internationally registered trade mark an opportunity of being heard, grant relief as provided herein if satisfied that the use or non-use of the trade mark in any designated country has rendered the said registration liable to cancellation under the law of that country. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to an international registration referred may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, and penalties for frivolous applications shall apply as if the application were made concerning a domestic trade mark.

The owner of an internationally registered trade mark designating India may grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark within Indian territory, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. Further, where an international registration referred to under this Act has been assigned, the assignee shall be deemed to be the proprietor for the purposes of using and enforcing rights relating to the trade mark in India. The Registrar may require production of a certified copy of such assignments or licenses as evidence of title. Any subsequent dealings concerning the licensed use or ownership shall also be subject to notification requirements as provided herein.

An application for rectification of a trade mark shall be heard by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if it relates to an international registration referred to under this Act and concerns a designation of India. The Board may, subject to any procedural requirements as provided herein, entertain such applications notwithstanding any apparent inconsistency between the designated goods or services and those already registered in India. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board under this provision may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate court shall hear arguments pertaining to whether the designation of India was properly executed, and may remit the matter for further consideration if necessary.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is made under this Act based on an earlier foreign registration, and such foreign registration constitutes an international registration referred to in Schedule I, the applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating use of the trade mark in India. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in refusal of registration. The Registrar may require further documentation or information as deemed necessary to ascertain genuine use.

Furthermore, where a proprietor of a registered trade mark reasonably believes that any other person is using a sign identical or confusingly similar to their trade mark, creating likelihood of confusion amongst the public and causing damage, they shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act. Such actions may include an injunction preventing further infringing use, as well as damages for losses sustained due to the passing off. The proprietor must demonstrate that their reputation has been unfairly exploited.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark as an international registration referred is opposed under this Act, the evidence presented by the applicant shall be considered alongside any counterstatement filed by the opponent. The Appellate Board may, upon review of such evidence and counterstatement, determine whether the grounds for opposition are substantiated to the extent that they affect only the designation of India within the international registration. It is provided that if the proprietor registered layout of the mark incorporates elements previously used in commerce without authorization, this shall be a material consideration in assessing the distinctiveness of the mark as against the opponent’s claim. The Board may order rectification of the register accordingly, subject to principles of natural justice.

An application for an international registration prescribed under Article 2 of the Madrid Protocol may be filed with the Trade Marks Registry by a registered proprietor of a trade mark in India. Such an application shall contain particulars as specified in Form TM-M, including details of the designated contracting countries and any limitations or amendments sought to the protection afforded by the basic trade mark registration. The Registrar may require such further information as is necessary for determining compliance with the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder. An international registration shall be deemed to extend to India only in respect of those goods or services for which registration is secured, subject to any limitations indicated in the application.

An application for an international registration designating India shall be examined as if it were an application for the registration of a trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to priority. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish such further information or documents as are necessary for the purposes of examination. Where an international registration designates India and contains representation of goods or services for which there is no corresponding class under the prescribed classification, the Registrar shall determine the appropriate class or classes in accordance with established practice. Any opposition filed against a trade mark arising from an international registration prescribed shall be dealt with as if it were an opposition against a registered trade mark. The applicant shall provide proof of payment of the requisite fees as provided herein.

An application for an international registration shall be made by any person who is registered as a trade mark owner under this Act or is entitled to apply for registration of a trade mark under this Act. Such applications may be filed with the prescribed fee, and shall include all information required by the Regulations concerning the International Registration of Marks adopted under the Madrid Protocol. The Registrar shall examine such application in accordance with procedures consistent with those applicable to domestic trademark applications, provided that any conflict arising from an international registration’s designation of India shall be resolved according to principles of priority as established herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or subsequent cancellation of rights conferred. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration prescribed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision.

An application for an international registration prescribed under Article 2 of the Madrid Protocol may be filed with the Trade Marks Registry by any person who is eligible to file a trade mark application under this Act and who possesses a base trade mark registration. Such an application shall include a certified copy of the international registration, together with a declaration specifying the goods or services in respect of which protection is sought in India, provided that such specification does not extend beyond those covered by the base registration. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify compliance with this Act and the Regulations framed thereunder. Upon examination and satisfaction that the requirements are met, the application shall be recorded, and a certified copy thereof published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any opposition to the extension of protection under the international registration must be filed within four months from the date of such publication as provided herein.

An application for an international registration prescribed under this Act shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within a period of six months from the date on which the mark is registered as an international trademark. The applicant must provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating compliance with all applicable provisions relating to priority claims, subject to any exemptions granted by notification in the Official Gazette. Provided that if the application includes designations for multiple countries, including India, the applicant shall pay a separate prescribed fee for each designation. Furthermore, the Registrar may require the submission of translated materials where the mark or description contains elements not readily understandable within the Indian context. Any alteration to the international registration after its initial recording requires prior approval from the Registry and adherence to stipulated procedural guidelines.

An application for an international registration shall be filed with the Prescribed Office within thirty days of the date of publication of the International Bureau’s advice regarding designation of India. Failure to comply with this time limit will render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Registrar may require such further particulars or documentary evidence as are necessary for verification purposes; refusal to provide these shall constitute an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or a fine, or both. Any person aggrieved by the rejection of an international registration prescribed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days.

An applicant seeking an international registration under this Act may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use the trade mark within the territory of India, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall be executed prior to the filing of the request for extension of protection or recording of the international registration with the International Bureau. The applicant retains ownership of the underlying trade mark rights unless expressly relinquished through a written assignment registered with the Registrar. Any subsequent assignee of the trade mark, whether arising from an assignment or transfer under this Act, shall be deemed to have inherited any existing licenses and their associated obligations. Further, the Registrar may require disclosure of all such licensing arrangements as part of the application process for international registration prescribed herein.

An application for an international registration prescribed under this Act shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar, upon examination, finds that the mark includes a design or device which, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, conflicts with emblems denoting public order, decency or morality, or is otherwise deceptive. The applicant may appeal such refusal within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision, presenting arguments demonstrating compliance with relevant legal standards and providing evidence mitigating concerns raised by the Registrar’s assessment. Such an appeal shall be heard by the Appellate Board, whose determination shall be final, subject to judicial review on limited grounds as provided herein concerning procedural fairness.

The right to use a registered trademark is, subject to any conditions specified in the registration, freely transferable. For the purposes of this Act, “transferable” includes, without limitation, assignment, pledge, license, and any other method by which ownership or rights pertaining to the trademark may be conveyed. A trademark shall be deemed transmissible even where such transfer involves a change in the goods or services for which it is registered, provided that the assignee undertakes to use the mark in accordance with the terms of registration and applicable law. Any agreement relating to the transmission of a trademark shall be void if it restricts the free assignability of the trademark under this Act.

The right to use a registered trade mark is subject to being freely transmissible, whether by way of absolute transfer, license agreement, or operation of law. Provided that such transmission does not contravene any provision under this Act relating to permissible uses or geographical limitations previously stipulated during registration, the Registrar shall maintain an updated record reflecting the change in ownership. Any application for registration of a subsequent trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a mark already registered shall be considered with due regard to the extent and nature of such transmission. Further, any party claiming title through assignment or transmission must satisfy the Registrar as to the validity of that claim, submitting relevant documentation demonstrating clear chain of ownership.

The right to use a registered trade mark is subject to the provisions relating to revocation under this Act and may be transferred by way of absolute assignment or through operation of law. Any such assignment shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry, failing which it shall be void. The assignee shall become entitled to all rights and privileges that were vested in the assignor as at the date of the assignment, provided that the assignor continues to use the trade mark until the expiry of the registration period unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the parties. This right is expressly transmissible, including by will or succession, subject to any conditions stipulated within the original registration certificate and applicable regulations concerning foreign nationals. The remedies available for breach of assignment include an action for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein.

The right to use a registered trademark is subject to the provisions relating to registration and opposition under this Act and may be transferred by way of absolute assignment or license. Such assignments, whether absolute or conditional, shall require prior written consent from the Trade Marks Registry, provided that such consent shall not be withheld without due cause and after affording the applicant for assignment an opportunity of being heard. The Registrar may, in writing, specify conditions relating to any such assignment or license, including provisions regarding quality control and fair trade practices. Further, a trademark’s ownership is demonstrably transmissible, even where the underlying business has undergone structural changes, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures for updating records maintained by the Registry. Any alteration of beneficial interest in a registered trademark must be reported within thirty days to facilitate accurate record-keeping.

The right to use a registered service mark is deemed personal to the registrant unless such right has been formally assigned or transmitted under this Act. Such assignment or transmission shall only be valid if executed by a duly authorized representative of the registrant, and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry within ninety days of its execution; failure to record will render the transfer void against third parties claiming under the original registration. The consent of the Controller may be required for assignments involving foreign entities, as provided herein, particularly where such entities lack substantial commercial presence in India. Any transmission of a service mark shall include all associated rights and obligations pertaining to the mark’s maintenance and enforcement; furthermore, the transmissible right is subject to any existing encumbrances or limitations registered against the trade mark.

The right to use a registered trade mark is subject to the provisions relating to transmission and may be transferred by way of absolute assignment or by operation of law. Any such transfer shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry, failing which it shall be void. The Registrar may refuse registration of any assignment or transmission if he has reason to believe that the proposed assignee or transferee lacks the financial capacity or technical expertise necessary for proper use of the mark in accordance with accepted industrial practice. Further, an agreement purporting to effect a transmissible right is liable to be deemed invalid where it contains provisions restricting competition within India without just cause and to the detriment of consumers. Penalties for unauthorized transfer are prescribed under this Act.

The right to use a registered trade mark, including any associated designs or slogans, may be assigned by the proprietor subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and payment of requisite fees. Such assignments shall create in the assignee all rights and privileges that were vested in the assignor as at the date of assignment, provided that the Registrar confirms the validity of the assignment under this Act. Further, a registered trade mark is deemed *transmissible* by operation of law, including through inheritance or devolution of property, without requiring formal registration of such transmission; however, notification of any such transmission to the Registrar shall be mandatory within three months thereafter. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to them regarding the legal basis for claiming ownership following a transmission and may refuse recognition until such proof is provided.

The right to use a registered service mark is, subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, freely *transmissible* by way of license agreement, pledge, or absolute assignment, whether with or without the benefit of the goodwill associated therewith. However, any such transmission shall be void if it purports to transfer the exclusive right to use the service mark in relation to goods other than those specified in the registration certificate, and a party claiming validity of such an assignment shall bear the burden of proving that the assignee’s activities do not infringe upon existing rights under this Act. Further, any dispute arising from the terms or effect of a transmission may be referred to arbitration as provided herein, with both parties consenting to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal.

The right to use a registered trade mark is, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, deemed to be transmissible by way of operation of law or by agreement in writing. Provided that any such transmission shall only be effective upon registration thereof with the Trade Marks Registry, and such registration may be refused if the proposed assignee does not meet the eligibility criteria as determined under this Act. Further, where a trade mark is registered jointly, the consent of all co-owners shall be required for its transmission unless otherwise stipulated in the agreement establishing joint ownership. The High Court may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review any registration of transmission deemed to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation.

The right to use a registered trademark is intrinsically transmissible, subject to the conditions outlined herein. Any assignment or transmission of a trademark shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry, and such registration may be refused if it appears that the proposed manner registered proprietor intends to use the mark in a way detrimental to consumer interests or contrary to accepted principles of fair trade. Failure to register an assignment within six months of its execution renders the assignee liable for penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, any person using a trademark without authorization following such unregistered transfer shall be deemed guilty of infringement and subject to damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the rightful owner.

The right to use a registered trade mark is deemed personal to the proprietor unless explicitly provided otherwise under this Act. Such rights are, however, freely *transmissible* by way of absolute assignment, pledge, or operation of law, subject to registration of such transfer with the Trade Marks Registry. Any governing assignment denomination shall be clearly stated in the instrument of transfer and must specify the exact trade mark(s) being assigned, along with any associated goods or services as defined in the original registration. The assignee becomes vested with all rights, privileges, and obligations that were held by the assignor immediately prior to the assignment. Provided that, where a pledge is made, the pledgor retains ultimate ownership until default occurs under the terms of the pledge agreement. Further, any subsequent dealing with the pledged trade mark shall require consent from both pledgor and pledgee.

The right to utilize a registered trade mark is deemed transmissible, whether by way of absolute transfer, license agreement, or other instrument, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. Any party claiming such transmissibility shall provide documented evidence satisfactory to the Trade Marks Registry establishing the validity and completeness of the transfer process. Failure to adequately demonstrate this compliance may result in a refusal to register the transmission. Where an alleged offence relating to the use of the trade mark arises subsequent to its purported transmission, liability for said offence shall vest with the original proprietor unless demonstrable proof exists that the transferee was acting under express direction and control of the former proprietor at the time of the infraction. Appeals against decisions concerning transmissibility are permitted before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The right to a registered trademark may be transferred by way of assignment or transmission, whether absolute or conditional. Any person claiming title to a registered trademark through such an entitled assignment transmission shall file with the Registrar within three months of the date of the instrument effecting that transfer, a request for registration of their title in the prescribed form and accompanied by certified copies of the relevant documentation establishing the transfer. The Registrar may require further evidence as deemed necessary to verify the authenticity and validity of the assignment or transmission. Upon satisfactory examination of the submitted documents and subject to any objections received within thirty days from the date of publication of notice thereof, the Registrar shall register the assignee or transferee as the proprietor of the trademark for the relevant goods and services. The registration shall take effect from the date of recording in the Register of Trade Marks.

Where a registered trademark is subject to an entitled assignment transmission, the assignee shall, within ninety days from the date of such assignment, provide written notice thereof to the Registrar, failing which, the assignor retains all enforcement rights pertaining to the mark. Any subsequent infringement occurring prior to registration of the assignee's title under this Act may be pursued by either the assignor or the assignee as determined by a civil court. The Registrar shall publish notification of the assignment in the Trade Marks Journal and any party claiming damages arising from use of the trademark before such publication may bring proceedings against the assignor. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the assignee liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

An application for registration of a trademark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any matter which, subject to the provisions of this Act, is likely to deceive or confuse the public relating to the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Where an applicant seeks to refuse register assignment of a trademark already registered, they must provide evidence demonstrating that the proposed assignee lacks the capacity to use the mark in accordance with honest practices in industrial commerce and without undue restriction. Such refusal shall be deemed invalid if it is shown that the assignor had full knowledge of the assignee’s capabilities at the time of assignment.

Where an applicant for registration of a trade mark is refused registration under this Act, and subsequently seeks to assign the right to apply for registration to another party, the Registrar may require both the original applicant and the assignee to furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to establish the grounds for refusal. The assignment shall not be effective until the Registrar has acknowledged receipt of the required documentation and deemed it satisfactory. Further, if the initial application was refused due to a conflict with an earlier trade mark, the assignee’s right to proceed is subject to the existing rights holder's consent or a determination by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board that the refusal was unwarranted. The Registrar shall refuse register assignment where the grounds for original refusal remain unresolved.

Where an applicant’s application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and such refusal is based on grounds relating to acquired distinctiveness, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. However, where the applicant subsequently seeks to refuse register assignment of the said trade mark to another party, acknowledging that the grounds for initial refusal remain valid, they shall be deemed to have abandoned any right to challenge those grounds further under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving notice of such a proposed assignment and acknowledgement, issue a certificate confirming the acceptance of the assignment subject to the original conditions of refusal. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board concerning such an appeal may file an application for revision before the High Court.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, and such refusal is based upon grounds relating to acquired distinctiveness, the applicant may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the refusal, file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant shall serve a copy of the memorandum of appeal on the Registrar not less than thirty days before the date appointed for hearing the appeal. The Registrar may, at any time during the pendency of the appeal, submit observations or arguments in writing to the Board. Furthermore, where an applicant seeks to refuse register assignment of a trademark due to concerns regarding prior use by another party, they must provide documentary evidence substantiating such prior use and demonstrating consumer confusion. The Board shall consider all submissions and render its decision as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and such refusal is based solely upon grounds relating to acquired distinctiveness, the applicant may, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, apply to the Registrar for review of that decision. The application for review shall specify the reasons why the initial determination was erroneous and provide evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use or promotion within the relevant territory. Furthermore, where a registered trade mark is the subject of an assignment, any subsequent attempt to refuse registration based on prior conflicting rights shall be considered only if the assignor had previously failed to disclose such conflicting rights during their own application process. The Registrar may refuse register assignment in cases of non-disclosure.

Where an applicant for registration of a trademark is refused registration under this Act, and subsequently assigns the right to apply to another party, that other party may, subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein, petition the Registrar for acceptance. The Registrar shall refuse register assignment where it is established that the assignor did not possess the requisite legal standing to effect such transfer, or if the proposed assignee has been previously refused registration for an identical mark in relation to similar goods and services. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing register assignment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days; failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible, and the applicant liable for costs incurred.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, and such refusal is based upon grounds relating to deceptiveness arising from prior use by another party, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear any counter-claim presented by the party alleging prior use, and may require both parties to submit evidence substantiating their respective assertions concerning consumer perception and likelihood of confusion. Furthermore, where a registered trademark proprietor seeks to refuse register assignment of their mark due to concerns regarding the assignee’s reputation or conduct detrimental to the distinctiveness of the trade mark, such refusal shall be subject to review by the Tribunal upon application by the prospective assignee, provided that the proprietor demonstrates reasonable grounds for apprehension.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be refused by the Registrar if the applicant seeks to secure registration for a term exceeding ten years, subject to renewal as provided herein. Furthermore, an applicant’s request to refuse register assignment shall not be entertained where the proposed assignee is demonstrably engaged in practices detrimental to the quality or reputation of the geographical indication comprised within the application. Such detriment includes, but is not limited to, dilution through unauthorized use or alteration of production methods inconsistent with established traditions. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating such detrimental practices before rendering a decision on refusal.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused by the Registrar under this Act, and such refusal is based on grounds relating to deceptiveness or conflict with prior rights, the applicant may, subject to prescribed timelines, file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, where a registered proprietor seeks to refuse register assignment of their trade mark due to concerns regarding the assignee’s reputation or conduct that could damage the distinctiveness of the mark, they shall provide written justification to the Registrar. The Registrar shall consider such justification and may require the proposed assignee to submit representations. Any party aggrieved by a decision concerning refusal of registration or an attempted refusal register assignment may initiate procedure cancelling registration through appropriate legal channels as provided herein.

Where a registered trademark is assigned or transmitted, the assignee or transferee shall be entitled to exercise all rights and privileges that were vested in the assignor or transferor immediately prior to the assignment or transmission. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to the Registrar of such assignment or transmission before registering the new proprietor. Any person claiming right to the said trademark by way of subsequent assignment or transmission shall, subject to any agreement to the contrary, be deemed constructively noticee of all earlier assignments and transmissions. Failure to provide adequate documentation demonstrating a clear chain of title relating to an assignment transmission rights may result in the Registrar’s refusal to register the claim. The assignor shall remain liable for any infringement committed prior to the date of assignment or transmission unless expressly released by agreement.

Where a registered trademark is assigned or transmitted, the assignee or transferee may, subject to any terms specified in the instrument effecting such assignment or transmission, grant further licenses relating to the use of the mark within the territory covered by the registration. Such sub-licenses shall be deemed assignments for the purposes of this Act and are subject to the same requirements regarding notification to the Registrar as an initial assignment. The proprietor of a registered trademark shall retain the right to revoke any license or sub-license granted, provided that adequate compensation is offered to the licensee in accordance with principles of fairness and equity. Further, any subsequent assignment transmission rights relating to the mark are contingent upon adherence to these licensing conditions unless expressly waived by the original proprietor through a written agreement filed with the Registrar.

Where the right to a registered trademark is transferred by way of assignment or transmission, such transfer shall be deemed operative only upon registration of the assignee’s title with the Registrar, provided that the assignor remains liable for any infringement committed prior to this registration. An objection may be raised to the proposed registration of an assignee's title if it is demonstrated that the original assignment was procured by fraud or misrepresentation. The aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal such a determination under this Act within sixty days from the date of notification, and the Appellate Board shall consider whether the circumstances surrounding the initial transfer warrant invalidation of the subsequent registration. Further, any claim contesting the validity of an assignment transmission rights must be substantiated with documentary evidence.

For the purposes of this Act, a respect registered application shall mean an application filed under this Act seeking rectification of a registered trademark. Such application may seek to have a registered trademark expunged from the register or amended concerning its description of goods or services. A respect registered application is deemed to be without merit if it alleges solely that the mark has become non-distinctive due to use by another party, provided that such other party’s use was undertaken with consent from the registered proprietor. The Registrar may reject a respect registered application if it appears frivolous or vexatious as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark, once filed, shall proceed to examination unless the Registrar directs otherwise under this Act. Where an objection is raised during examination concerning distinctiveness or deceptiveness, the applicant may submit arguments and evidence to overcome said objections; such submissions shall be considered by the Registrar in determining whether to accept or reject the respect registered application. If the Registrar rejects the application, notice of rejection shall be served on the applicant, providing reasons for the decision and affording a period for response. Further, any party claiming an interest in opposing registration may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed timeframe following publication under this Act.

An owner of a registered trade mark shall, upon becoming aware of a pending respect registered application which incorporates an identical or deceptively similar mark relating to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registered trade mark is protected, have the right to file written objections with the Registrar. Such objections must specify the grounds on which the registration should be refused, including but not limited to likelihood of confusion and dilution of distinctiveness. The Registrar shall provide the applicant for the respect registered application an opportunity to respond to these objections within a prescribed timeframe. Failure by the applicant to adequately address the concerns raised may result in the rejection of the respect registered application or conditions being imposed on its registration, as deemed appropriate by the Registrar. Remedies available to the owner of the existing mark include injunctive relief against any use of the conflicting mark pending determination of the objection.

An application for registration of a trade mark, hereinafter referred to as a respect registered application, may be opposed by any person claiming rights or interest in relation to an earlier trade mark or other similar sign under this Act. Such opposition shall be filed within the period prescribed and shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to prior use of a confusingly similar mark. The Registrar shall serve notice of the opposition on the applicant for registration and provide them with an opportunity to file their counterstatement in accordance with the procedures as provided herein. Failure by the applicant to submit a timely counterstatement may result in deemed abandonment of the respect registered application, subject to any directions issued by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar shall then proceed to hear the opposition and determine the matter based on evidence submitted by both parties.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to comply with the requirements prescribed under this Act relating to the filing of the statement of goods or services. Provided that, where an examiner identifies deficiencies in the said statement and communicates these to the applicant, the applicant shall have a period of ninety days from the date of such communication to rectify those deficiencies; failure to do so will result in abandonment. Further, any person aggrieved by a decision regarding a respect registered application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receiving notice of the order. The Board’s determination shall be final, subject to revision only on grounds specified under this Act pertaining to legal error apparent on the face of the record.

Any person seeking to challenge the acceptance of a respect registered application shall file an objection with the Registrar within three months from the date of advertisement under this Act. Such objection must specify, with particularity, the grounds upon which the challenge is based and demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from registration proceeding. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements will render the objection inadmissible. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further evidence substantiating the claims made in the objection. Where an objection is upheld, any fees paid towards the respect registered application shall be forfeited to the government. Deliberate submission of false information within an objection constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a trade mark may grant a license or assign the entire interest in a respect registered application to any person, whether already engaged in trade or not. Such license shall be documented in writing and specify the goods or services for which the right to use the trade mark is granted, as well as the duration of such license. Where an assignment occurs, the assignee shall become the new proprietor with all rights and obligations pertaining thereto. The Registrar may require evidence satisfactory to him demonstrating that any such license agreement has been entered into freely and without coercion. Further, a registered application may be licensed or assigned jointly by multiple applicants, provided that the terms of the arrangement are clearly defined in writing and submitted for recordation.

An objection may be raised to a respect registered application under this Act by any interested party within two months from the date of advertisement of such application in the Trade Marks Journal. Such objection shall specify the grounds upon which it is founded, and may include allegations of deceptive similarity to an earlier mark or that the proposed mark would disparage goods or services connected with another’s trade. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-statement addressing the objections raised. Upon consideration of both the objection and the counter-statement, as well as any further submissions made by either party, the Registrar may allow the respect registered application, reject it entirely, or direct amendment of the proposed marks, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

An objection may be raised against a respect registered application upon proof, satisfactory to the Registrar, that the proposed mark is deceptive and likely to cause confusion amongst the public, or that such use would constitute an unfair trade practice. The Registrar shall give notice of the objection to the applicant for registration and opportunity of being heard, either in person or by advocate. Where the Registrar determines that the objection is well-founded, he may direct rejection of the respect registered application. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order; provided that where an order has been passed directing rejection of a respect registered application, shall compelled court review the decision if it is demonstrated that material irregularities occurred in the proceedings before the Appellate Board.

Any party dissatisfied with a decision regarding a respect registered application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed forms and fees during an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Registrar, upon receiving credible evidence suggesting fraudulent misrepresentation or material omissions in a respect registered application, may initiate inquiries and impound documents. Any person found guilty of knowingly submitting false information or engaging in deceptive practices concerning a respect registered application is liable to a fine which may extend to two hundred thousand rupees, and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. This provision shall be interpreted consistently with the principles outlined within the Budapest Treaty regarding international registration procedures.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be a mark registered proprietor may apply for registration of a service mark used in relation to goods, provided that such application is made within six months from the date of initial trade mark registration. The Registrar shall consider applications relating to colour marks only if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. Where an opposition is filed against an application by a mark registered proprietor, the evidence presented must clearly establish likelihood of confusion with existing registrations or prior use. Further, any alteration to the representation of a registered mark requires consent from all registered proprietors sharing identical rights under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to rectification of a trade mark register has exhausted all remedies available under this Act, such person may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal shall admit appeals only if it is satisfied that no substantial question of law remains unresolved and that the order in question would operate so as to cause prejudice to the appellant. Upon hearing the appeal, the Tribunal may confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. A *mark registered proprietor* shall be liable for damages sustained by any person due to a false or misleading representation concerning the trade mark, made without reasonable grounds and with intent to deceive. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other remedy available to the aggrieved party in law.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to file a counterstatement within two months from the date of service of the notice of opposition. Such counterstatement shall address each ground of opposition raised and may include evidence in support of the claim that the trade mark should be registered. The Registrar may, after giving both parties an opportunity for hearing, direct the withdrawal of the opposition or proceed with the examination of the merits thereof. In cases where a trade mark is registered, the *mark registered proprietor* shall maintain records detailing the use of the trade mark in commerce and shall provide such information to the Registrar upon request. Failure to comply with this provision may result in action as provided herein against the proprietor.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider any objections raised by interested parties, provided that such objections are filed within thirty days of the publication of notice of the appeal. Further, a mark registered proprietor is obligated to maintain records pertaining to the use and exploitation of the registered trade mark, detailing geographical areas and goods or services in relation to which it is used. Failure to provide these records upon request by the Registrar shall render the mark liable for removal from the Register under provisions as provided herein.

Any person who, without due cause and after notice served under this Act, uses a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a mark for which another has registration, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to five times the value of the infringing goods or services provided. The amount so determined may be further augmented by an additional penalty not exceeding twenty-five percent where the infringement is found to have been willful and calculated to undermine the goodwill associated with the registered trade mark. A *mark registered proprietor* shall, upon discovery of such infringement, immediately lodge a complaint before the appropriate civil court detailing the extent of the damage suffered. Failure to cease infringing activity within thirty days of judgment may result in summary arrest and confiscation of all related inventory.

A mark registered proprietor shall have the exclusive right to grant licenses relating to the use of the trade mark for specific goods or services as defined within the license agreement. Such licenses may be granted on a sole, exclusive basis or in a non-exclusive manner, subject to conditions stipulated by the proprietor and recorded with the Registrar. Any assignment of the registered trademark, whether partial or complete, shall include provisions regarding any existing licenses; these provisions must ensure that the rights of licensees are not prejudiced without their express written consent. Further, where a mark registered proprietor intends to sub-license usage rights, they must provide prior notification to all current licensees, detailing the scope and terms of the proposed sub-licensing arrangement. This requirement is provided that it does not unduly restrict the proprietary’s ability to commercialize its intellectual property.

Notwithstanding any direction issued under this Act, an appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal against any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed trade mark based on alleged similarity to a mark already registered by another party. The appellant, being the unsuccessful applicant, shall demonstrate that the Registrar’s assessment failed adequately to consider evidence presented regarding consumer perception and distinctiveness. Further, where the refusal is predicated upon a finding that use in relation to goods or services would likely cause confusion, the *mark registered proprietor* may challenge this determination by presenting evidence demonstrating clear differentiation of channels of trade or intended consumers. The Tribunal shall allow for cross-examination of witnesses presented by both parties and may order further inquiry as it deems fit.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be a mark registered proprietor may apply for registration of a trade mark relating to a pharmaceutical substance if such application is made within six months from the date on which the said pharmaceutical substance was first advertised or offered for sale in India. The Registrar shall consider an application only if it contains a clear representation of the proposed mark and a list specifying all goods or services in relation to which registration is sought, provided that where the mark includes a word or words descriptive of the qualities or characteristics of the pharmaceutical substance, such use shall not be permitted unless prior consent has been obtained from the Controller-General. The registered proprietor shall furnish such documents as may be required by the Registrar.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trade mark is filed under this Act, the applicant shall serve a copy of such application on the mark registered proprietor within thirty days from the date of filing. The Registrar may, upon receipt of the application and after service thereof as required, issue notice to the registered proprietor inviting them to file their counter-statement within sixty days. Failure by the registered proprietor to file a counter-statement within the stipulated period shall not preclude the Registrar from proceeding with the rectification proceedings ex parte. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the order. The mark registered proprietor retains all rights and remedies available under this Act pending determination of any rectification application or appeal. It is further provided that uses trade mark without consent are actionable as infringement.

Any person who, without due cause and after receiving notice from the Registrar, uses a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to a mark for which registration has been granted under this Act, shall be guilty of an offence. Such offender is liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where the infringing use relates to goods or services connected with international registration shall have been sought by the mark registered proprietor, the penalties prescribed herein shall be doubled. The Registrar may, ex officio, initiate prosecution for such offences without prejudice to any right of action available under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered proprietor person” is defined as the individual or entity whose name appears on the Register of Trade Marks as the owner of a registered trade mark, and who holds exclusive rights pertaining to that mark subject to any limitations or conditions recorded therein. A registered proprietor person shall be deemed to possess all such powers and privileges as are conferred upon them under this Act relating to the use, licensing, assignment, and enforcement of their registered trade mark. The term “registered proprietor person” includes successors in title and assignees of a registered trade mark, provided that such succession or assignment is duly recorded as required herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, and such opposition is determined against the applicant, the Registrar may, subject to any conditions specified in the order determining the opposition, allow the applicant to proceed with the registration process provided that the applicant furnishes within thirty days from the date of the order, a security deposit as prescribed. The amount of said security shall be proportionate to the anticipated costs incurred by the registered proprietor in defending any subsequent action for infringement arising directly from the mark’s registration. Further, where a change occurs in the particulars relating to the registered proprietor person, including but not limited to a merger or acquisition affecting ownership, notification thereof must be submitted to the Registrar within fourteen days of such alteration as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an objection from any party regarding the acceptance of a proposed trademark application, provide notice thereof to the applicant and afford them an opportunity to submit written representations within sixty days. Such representations may include arguments demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use or challenging the validity of prior conflicting marks. The court registrar register shall record all objections and responses in a manner accessible for public inspection. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar regarding such objection may appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Provided that the Appellate Board’s determination is final, barring further recourse under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, an earlier use of a trade mark shall be deemed to include prior public display of goods bearing that trade mark, irrespective of whether such display constituted registration under any other law. Where a person has used a trade mark in relation to specified goods or services and subsequently seeks registration thereof, the date of such use shall be relevant for determining priority; however, if an application for registration was filed by another party prior to such use, but that application was abandoned before grant, the principle of amendment antedating registration shall apply. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating any claim of earlier use as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending, and prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark has been established by another party, the Registrar may, upon review of documentary evidence demonstrating such prior use, entertain objections notwithstanding that the earlier use predates the filing date of the applicant’s trade mark. This power shall be exercised cautiously, balancing the interests of both parties and considering any demonstrable goodwill accrued by the later applicant through honest commercial dealing. However, where it is demonstrated to the Registrar's satisfaction that the prior user had knowledge of the pending application and continued use despite such knowledge, an amendment antedating registration may be refused in order to prevent unjust enrichment.

Where a trade mark is registered, and subsequently an earlier right arises that would, but for the registration, preclude the use of the sign by the proprietor of the registered trade mark, the proprietor may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking relief. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating the prior honest usage of the sign in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which registration is sought, and establishing that the public would be unduly confused if both marks were permitted to continue concurrently. The Board may grant such remedies as it deems fit, including but not limited to a declaration regarding the validity of the registration. Notably, an amendment antedating registration, arising from this prior right, shall take precedence over the registered mark’s exclusive rights, subject to equitable considerations and due regard for bona fide users.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and subsequently amended prior to the passing of an order allowing appeal against such refusal, the provisions relating to priority of earlier rights shall apply as if the amended application were filed on the date of such amendment. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or representations in relation to the amended trade mark, irrespective of any previous examination undertaken with respect to the original application. Such requirement shall be served upon the applicant by registered post and deemed received seven days from the date of posting. An appeal against an order relating to an amendment antedating registration may only be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of that order to the appellant, subject to any extension granted by the Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is pending, and prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark exists, demonstrating continuous use in India before the date of such pending application, the applicant’s entitlement to registration shall be assessed with due consideration given to that pre-existing use. Provided that if the proprietor of the earlier mark subsequently applies for registration under this Act, and their application is accepted and registered, any amendment antedating registration by the later applicant shall not prejudice the rights established through such prior continuous use. Further, the Registrar may require evidence substantiating the extent and nature of said pre-existing use before making a determination as provided herein. The burden of proving such prior use rests upon the proprietor of the earlier mark.

Where a trade mark is registered, and subsequently an application for registration of an identical or deceptively similar mark is filed, and that subsequent application demonstrates use of the mark antedating the earlier registration date, the proprietor of the earlier registered trade mark shall be afforded opportunity to submit evidence refuting such prior usage. Failure to adequately rebut this claim of prior use may result in a finding that the earlier registration lacks distinctiveness under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order relating to amendment antedating registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting from the decision.

Where a proprietor seeks to amend a registered trade mark by way of alteration, addition, or deletion of elements, and such proposed amendment incorporates features identical or substantially similar to those appearing in an earlier application for registration that remains pending, the Registrar may grant leave for the amendment only if the applicant demonstrates that they have obtained express written consent from the proprietor of the pending application. Such consent shall be deemed a license granting rights equivalent to assignment insofar as it relates solely to the elements incorporated into the amended mark. The Registrar shall record this licensing arrangement on the register, noting its duration and scope. Provided that any such amendment antedating registration is subject to a royalty payment calculated according to regulations framed under this Act, payable by the proprietor of the amended trade mark to the proprietor of the earlier application until the pending application either proceeds to registration or is abandoned.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, and subsequently amended prior to the filing of an appeal against such refusal, the Registrar may, subject to due process, consider the impact of said amendments upon the distinctiveness of the mark. It shall be presumed that any amendment antedating registration, which materially alters the visual representation or phonetic composition of the trade mark as originally applied for, constitutes a departure from the initial intention underlying the application. This presumption is rebuttable by evidence presented by the applicant demonstrating continued use and consumer recognition of the mark in its amended form prior to the date of refusal. The appellate authority may order restoration of the original mark if it finds such use insufficient to overcome the aforementioned presumption.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where a mark has been used by another person prior to the date of application for registration under this Act, and such use constitutes an honest concurrent use demonstrating bona fide intention to maintain or recapture market share, the Registrar may permit registration subject to limitations as prescribed. Such permission shall not prejudice any rights acquired by that other person before the amendment antedating registration occurred. The design register shall be consulted in determining whether prior use has resulted in a mark confusingly similar to a registered design. This provision applies only where the subsequent applicant can demonstrate continuous and substantial use of the mark.

A collective mark shall be deemed to exclusively identify goods or services offered by members of an association of producers, manufacturers, merchants, service providers, or users, and shall represent a common characteristic attributable to the collectivity. Such characteristic may relate to the quality, origin, mode of production, or other distinguishing features of those goods or services. The registration of a collective mark shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified therein, subject to any conditions as provided herein relating to authorized users and their adherence to standards maintained by the association.

An application for registration as a collective mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the mark. The applicant must demonstrate that it represents an identifiable association of persons engaged in producing goods or rendering services of a particular quality or reputation, or offering a guarantee thereof. Further, the regulations governing eligibility for membership within the association shall be clearly articulated within the application. Such regulations will detail criteria for maintaining membership and procedures for disciplinary action against members found to violate these standards. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the applicant’s operational structure before proceeding with examination under this Act.

A collective mark shall be registered only upon an application by a society or association formed under law, representing persons engaged in trade or commerce, and having regard to the objects of the society or association as stated in its memorandum. The Registrar may require such proof as he deems necessary to establish that the applicant qualifies as a society or association within the meaning of this Act. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a collective mark may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, demonstrating prejudice arising from the mark’s use and asserting a right to relief including an injunction preventing its unauthorized application. Further, any proprietor of a registered trade mark who demonstrates that the use of a collective mark is creating unfair competition or dilution of their distinctive character may apply for rectification under this Act.

A collective mark shall be registered by the Registrar only upon satisfying him that an association of persons has been formed with a common purpose and that the marks applied for genuinely represents such association. The applicant shall furnish, along with the application, a detailed memorandum outlining the composition of the association, its governing rules, and the geographical area within which members are entitled to use the collective mark. Further, the Registrar may require the submission of audited accounts demonstrating the equitable distribution of profits derived from the use of the collective mark amongst the members. Any member found to be utilizing the mark in a manner inconsistent with the registered regulations shall be subject to disciplinary action by the association and may have their right to use the mark suspended under this Act. The Registrar, acting upon complaint or suo moto investigation, may inquire into such actions.

A collective mark shall be registrable only if application demonstrates that it is proposed to be used by an association of users who are engaged in producing goods of similar kind or providing services of similar kind. The applicant must satisfy the Registrar that the regulations governing use of the mark prescribe detailed procedures for ensuring uniformity in the quality of goods or characteristics of services indicated thereby, and further, that such regulations provide mechanisms for monitoring compliance amongst all authorised users. Provided that any alteration to these regulations shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days of adoption by the association. The Registrar may require submission of audited accounts demonstrating adherence to these prescribed standards before granting registration.

A collective mark shall be registered only where the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the adaptation and usage standards governing its display and application. Any member utilizing a registered collective mark who contravenes these prescribed standards, or engages in conduct detrimental to the reputation of the mark, shall be liable for damages as determined by the appropriate civil court. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party or acting suo moto, initiate proceedings against such offending member and, following due process, may order suspension or revocation of their membership privileges within the collective body. Furthermore, wilful infringement resulting in substantial financial loss to other members shall attract penalties as provided herein, including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term up to three years.

A collective mark shall be assignable only with the consent of the Registrar, and such consent shall not be granted unless the assignee undertakes to maintain the quality standards associated with membership in the group promoting or protecting the interests of its members. Any license granted under this Act relating to a collective mark shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is authorized to use the mark, as well as the goods or services for which such use is permitted. The Registrar may require proof that all licensees are bound by contractual obligations ensuring adherence to these standards and proper usage guidelines. Further, any transfer of rights in a collective mark, whether through assignment or license, shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days; failure to do so renders the transfer void. Provided that existing licenses valid immediately prior to the amendment of this provision remain operative until their natural expiration.

A collective mark shall be deemed distinctive irrespective of prior use or registration under this Act if it signifies affiliation with a recognized producers’ cooperative society engaged in the cultivation and processing of Alphonso mangoes. Any proprietor utilizing a similar indicia without express authorization from the registered proprietors, and demonstrably causing confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the mangoes, shall be liable for an injunction. An appeal against such an order may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the appellant must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice arising from any error apparent on the face of the record. The Registrar may, suo moto, initiate inquiries into alleged misuse and impose penalties as deemed appropriate.

An application for registration of a collective mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the mark and a statement of all goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the said mark. The applicant must demonstrate that it represents an association of users, and that such users are engaged in the production, manufacture, processing, or supply of goods or services as specified in the application. Further, the regulations governing use of the collective mark shall be submitted alongside, detailing procedures for ensuring uniformity of quality and adherence to standards. Where a publication translation of promotional material relating to the goods or services is included, it must be certified accurate by an authorised translator.

A collective mark shall be registered only where the applicant demonstrates exclusive control over the quality and authenticity of goods or services signified by the mark, and provides satisfactory evidence of a not-for-profit association of users operating under a common law or regulatory framework. The Registrar may require further documentation establishing this operational structure before registration is granted. Any proprietor of a collective mark shall be liable to prosecution if they permit use of the mark in a manner that diminishes its distinctiveness, or by any person who is not authorized to use it under the rules of the association. An alleged offence reason relating to unauthorized usage may trigger an investigation and subsequent enforcement action as provided herein.
