For the purposes of this Act, an “independent scientific adviser” means a person possessing demonstrable expertise in a field relevant to the invention claimed in a patent application or relating to the alleged infringement thereof, who is not employed by, nor has any significant financial interest in, either the applicant or the accused infringer. Such an adviser shall be appointed under this Act where the Controller deems that technical complexities necessitate external assistance for informed decision-making. Recognition trade marks, if presented as evidence concerning prior use or public familiarity with a technology, may be considered by the Controller during proceedings involving an independent scientific adviser’s assessment.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use, or produced in connection with the manufacture of a pharmaceutical product, the Controller may, subject to appeal under this Act, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the efficacy and safety of such process. In determining whether sufficient evidence has been provided, the Controller shall have regard to established scientific principles and prevailing regulatory standards. Further, where complex technical issues arise during examination or in subsequent proceedings concerning patent validity or infringement, the Controller may appoint an independent scientific adviser to provide expert opinion. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to such advice may institute a court suit infringement action against another party involved in the process.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use, or produced in the course of, food or drink production, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the said process was applied on a commercial scale prior to the date of filing of the patent application. Such evidence shall include documented records of manufacturing processes and sales data, as deemed necessary by the Controller. Further, where an inventor seeks assistance from an independent scientific adviser in formulating or assessing aspects of their invention, the identity and qualifications of such advisor must be disclosed within the patent application. The Controller may request further clarification regarding the role and involvement of any such independent scientific adviser. All applications meeting these criteria shall register patents thereof as provided herein.

An error amendment notice is defined as a written communication served by a registered proprietor upon another party claiming rights relating to a layout design, wherein the proprietor seeks rectification of inaccuracies contained within previously issued documents pertaining to the registration or subsequent dealings concerning that layout design. Such notices shall specify with particularity the erroneous information and propose the corresponding correction. The recipient of an error amendment notice may, subject to conditions as provided herein, file objections within sixty days from the date of service; failing such objection, the proposed rectification shall be deemed accepted and effectuated by the Controller.

An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, at any time during the pendency of the application and prior to the grant of certification, submit an error amendment notice to the Registrar detailing any inadvertent errors or omissions contained within the submitted documentation relating to the layout-design. Such notice shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the original document and the proposed corrected version. The Registrar shall consider the error amendment notice and may allow the correction if satisfied that it does not substantially alter the claimed layout-design or prejudice the rights of any third party. Any such allowance will be recorded in the register, noting the date of the amendment and a brief description thereof, subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees as provided herein.

Where an integrated circuit layout design registration is found to contain an inadvertent error affecting the accuracy of the description of the layout design, or relating to the identity of the registered proprietor, the proprietor may serve upon the Controller an error amendment notice specifying the nature of the error and proposing a correction thereto. Such notice shall be served within three years from the date of registration. The Controller shall consider any such error amendment notice and may, after affording opportunity for objection to any interested party, direct that the register be amended accordingly. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The rectification directed by the Controller shall take effect as if it had been originally recorded in the Register; provided that no alteration shall prejudice existing rights or remedies available to any other person.

An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, at any time during the pendency of the application and prior to the publication thereof under this Act, submit to the Registrar an error amendment notice detailing any inadvertent errors or omissions contained within the submitted documentation pertaining to the layout-design. Such notice shall be accompanied by a duly affirmed affidavit verifying the accuracy of the corrections proposed therein. The Registrar shall consider each error amendment notice received and may, subject to satisfaction that the proposed correction does not substantially alter the original claimed design or prejudice the rights of any other party, grant permission for the amendment. Any decision regarding an error amendment notice shall be communicated in writing to the applicant within sixty days from the date of receipt. Failure to comply with procedural requirements as provided herein may render the error amendment notice invalid and without effect.

An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may submit to the Controller an error amendment notice concerning particulars specified in their initial application, provided that such notice is submitted within ninety days from the date of publication of the advertisement referred to under this Act. The Controller shall consider any error amendment notice and may allow it if satisfied that the correction or amendment does not substantially alter the layout-design claimed or affect the rights of third parties. Any objection raised by an interested party regarding the proposed amendment must be addressed by the applicant within thirty days, failing which the application shall stand rejected. The Controller’s decision on whether to accept or reject an error amendment notice shall be final and binding.

Where an error is discovered within an approved layout design registration, or where rectification of information is deemed necessary to ensure accuracy and public clarity, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to serve an error amendment notice upon the Controller. Such notice must specify the erroneous particulars and propose the correct details for substitution. The Controller may, after affording a reasonable opportunity for objection by any interested party, direct the rectification as proposed or with modifications he deems appropriate. Failure to comply with such direction within the stipulated period shall render the proprietor liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as an arrears of land revenue. This power is without prejudice to other remedies available under this Act.

Where a licensee under a layout-design registration has discovered an inadvertent discrepancy between the recorded design specification and the actual integrated circuit layout, they may serve upon the registered proprietor an error amendment notice detailing the nature of said discrepancy. Such notice shall be accompanied by supporting documentation reasonably demonstrating the existence and extent of the error. The registered proprietor shall then have thirty days to either accept or reject the proposed amendment as detailed within the error amendment notice. Acceptance constitutes a deemed license modification, binding upon both parties subject to any existing contractual limitations regarding further sub-licensing rights. Provided that rejection does not prejudice the licensee’s right to pursue remedies under this Act for misrepresentation relating to the registered layout design.

An aggrieved party alleging material inaccuracy within a registered layout design may serve upon the proprietor an error amendment notice specifying the particulars of the alleged error and proposing a corresponding rectification. Such notice shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any document substantiating the claim, as provided herein. The proprietor is then afforded thirty days to either accept the proposed amendment or formally dispute its validity. Disputed notices may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted under this Act for determination; the Tribunal’s decision shall be binding subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of notification. Failure to respond to an error amendment notice within the stipulated timeframe shall constitute acceptance thereof, unless a formal dispute is subsequently raised.

An error amendment notice, as provided herein, shall be issued by the Registrar where rectification of inaccuracies within a registered layout design is sought following initial registration. Such notices may concern errors pertaining to technical specifications, geographical designations, or ownership details declared in the original application. The manner applications clause dictates that an error amendment notice must clearly articulate the erroneous information and the proposed correction, accompanied by supporting documentation deemed necessary by the Registrar. Further, any such notice shall be served upon all registered proprietors claiming rights under the layout design, affording them opportunity for objection as per established procedures under this Act.

Where a registered layout design incorporates elements demonstrably attributable to prior art not constituting infringement under this Act, the proprietor may serve upon any person claiming right to those elements an error amendment notice specifying the nature and extent of the perceived inaccuracy in the register. Such notice shall be served through the International Bureau or another designated channel as prescribed by regulations framed thereunder. The recipient of such a notice has thirty days from the date of service within which to respond, either acknowledging the validity of the claimed error and consenting to amendment, or disputing it with reasoned justification. Failure to respond within this period shall constitute an admission of the error’s existence, obligating the Registering Authority to initiate amendment proceedings as provided herein. The proprietor shall be liable for any costs incurred by the recipient in defending a spurious error amendment notice.

Where a registered layout design incorporates elements identical or substantially similar to a previously registered trade mark, and such incorporation constitutes infringement as provided herein, the registrant shall be deemed liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the trade mark proprietor. Upon discovery of such unauthorized inclusion, the registrant may serve an error amendment notice upon the alleged infringer within ninety days of registration. This notice must specify the infringing element and propose a corrective modification to the layout design. Failure to comply with the requirements of the error amendment notice within sixty days shall render the registrant subject to penalties as determined by the Controller, including but not limited to monetary fines and compulsory redesignation.

An error in a registered layout design shall be deemed to exist where there is demonstrable inaccuracy in the depiction of elements within the documented mask work, arising from unintentional deviation during the fabrication process or transcription errors during documentation. Such an error does not constitute infringement under this Act provided that the rectification thereof constitutes an error amendment and is undertaken with the written consent of the Controller. The Controller may, subject to regulations as prescribed, grant such error amendment if it is satisfied that the correction does not substantially alter the original layout design or prejudice the interests of any third party holding rights in a similar design.

Where an integrated circuit layout design registration is granted containing an inadvertent clerical error, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to apply to the Controller for rectification within six months of the date of publication of the register. Such application must specify the nature of the error and the correct particulars intended to be recorded. The Controller may entertain such applications subject to ensuring that the proposed correction does not adversely affect the rights or interests of any other person claiming under this Act, including but not limited to those who have entered into agreements based on the published register. An application for rectification based on an error amendment shall be adjudicated expeditiously and a reasoned order shall be issued within ninety days. The Controller may require supporting documentation as deemed necessary to verify the accuracy of the proposed correction.

Where, subsequent to the grant of registration for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, it is determined that an error occurred during the examination process or the recording of particulars relating to the registered design, the Controller may entertain an application for amendment. Such application shall be accompanied by a duly affirmed affidavit detailing the nature of the error and demonstrating its material impact on the accuracy of the register. The applicant shall further provide such documentary evidence as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate the claim. Notice of the application for error amendment shall be served upon the registered proprietor, who may file objections within sixty days from the date of service. Any objection received shall be considered by the Controller and a reasoned order issued, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Where a registered layout design contains demonstrable errors attributable to clerical mistakes or inadvertent omissions during the registration process, the Controller may, upon written application by the registrant and after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, authorize appropriate rectification. Such authorization shall be subject to the condition that the error amendment does not substantively alter the original layout design as it was described in the initial registration documents; any alteration affecting the functional or aesthetic characteristics of the integrated circuit layout design will be considered a material change requiring fresh application under this Act. The Controller may require supporting documentation, including expert testimony, to verify the nature and extent of the error amendment sought, ensuring compliance with established standards for accuracy and integrity of registered designs.

Where an error is discovered in a registered layout design relating to technical specifications, geometrical representations, or ownership details, the owner shall be entitled to apply for an error amendment within six months of the date of registration. Such application must specify the nature of the error and provide supporting documentation demonstrating its factual inaccuracy. The Controller may, after affording opportunity for hearing to any interested party who objects to the proposed amendment, grant or refuse the error amendment as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing an error amendment may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order; failure to comply with procedural requirements shall render the application liable for rejection and potential penalties.

Where a registered layout design incorporates elements derived from a prior layout design held by another party, and such incorporation was unintentional due to demonstrable error during the creation process, the owner of the later registered layout design shall be obligated to grant a non-exclusive license for use of the erroneous element to the original holder. This obligation exists subject to the provision that the license fee shall not exceed two percent of the annual turnover attributable to the sale of integrated circuits incorporating the registered layout design. The Registrar may, upon application by either party and after due consideration of all relevant circumstances, order an error amendment to the register reflecting the corrected layout design, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the original inventive concept. Assignment of rights under this license shall be permissible with the prior written consent of the owner of the registered layout design.

Where, following registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Controller that an inadvertent clerical error occurred during the process of publication or recordation, such as in the description of features or the designation of assignees, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, permit its correction. Provided that any amendment sought under this Act shall not substantially alter the registered layout-design and must be demonstrably attributable to an error; otherwise, it will be deemed a request for re-examination with attendant costs as determined by the Controller. Any party aggrieved by such decision regarding an error amendment may appeal within sixty days of notification thereof.

Where a registered layout design incorporates elements derived from a well-known trade mark, and such incorporation constitutes infringement as provided herein, the proprietor of the layout design shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner of the trade mark. Any party aggrieved by an erroneous determination regarding infringement may apply to the Controller for review; this application must be made within ninety days from the date of the order sought to be reviewed. The Controller may, subject to just considerations and after affording opportunity of being heard, allow an error amendment to rectify factual inaccuracies or misinterpretations of law that materially affect the outcome of the infringement assessment. Such amendments shall not introduce new evidence or arguments beyond those originally presented during the initial proceedings.

Where an integrated circuit layout design registration is granted based upon information presented in the application, and subsequent to such grant it becomes apparent that an error occurred during the examination process leading to a misrepresentation of material facts concerning the originality of the layout design, the Register shall have the power to initiate proceedings for an *error amendment*. Such proceedings may be commenced by either the registered proprietor or any interested party demonstrating prejudice resulting from the erroneous registration. Notice of such intended action must be served upon all parties appearing on the register as having an interest in the layout design. The Register shall provide a period of thirty days for objections to the proposed error amendment, after which a hearing will be conducted. If the Register finds that the indication falsified during examination was material and affected the validity of the registration, the correction may be implemented subject to conditions deemed just by the Register.

Where a registered layout design contains an inadvertent technical inaccuracy discovered subsequent to registration, the Register may, upon application by the registrant and subject to verification that such inaccuracy does not substantially alter the character of the layout design, permit an error amendment. Such amendment shall be recorded in the register with effect from the date of the original registration, provided that any party demonstrably prejudiced by reliance on the erroneous record prior to the error amendment may pursue remedies under civil law. The Register shall provide notice of such amendment and its effective date. Transient incidental storage of data during processing related to an error amendment does not constitute infringement under this Act. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures for seeking an error amendment will render any subsequent claim void.

For the purposes of this Act, a “protected geographical indication” means an indication that is registered under this Act and relates to goods originating from a specific territory within India, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. The term "territory" shall include any region, locality or appellation as defined by established usage in relation to the production of those goods. A registered proprietor geographical indication has the right to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act and may seek remedies including injunctions and damages against any person using a sign falsely indicating that the goods originate from the territory associated with the protected geographical indication.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to include a statement of the prior usage of the sign in relation to the goods or services for which protection is sought, and where such prior usage has been continuous for a period exceeding three years immediately preceding the date of the application, the applicant shall provide documentary evidence substantiating said usage. Upon successful registration, the registered proprietor geographical indication enjoys exclusive rights to use the indication as specified in the register, preventing unauthorized exploitation thereof by any person. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar and may be subject to objections from interested parties under this Act.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, makes use of that indication in connection with goods or services specified in the registration, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed based on the extent of dilution caused to the distinctiveness and reputation of the protected geographical indication. The registered proprietor geographical may institute civil proceedings against any such infringer seeking an injunction restraining further infringing activity and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing said action. Further, where infringement is proven, goods bearing the unauthorized indication are liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein. Any false or misleading representation concerning the origin of goods shall be deemed a violation subject to penalties under this Act.

Where a dispute arises concerning the exclusive right of the registered proprietor geographical indication, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order sought to be challenged. Such appeal shall lie on grounds alleging improper registration or use contrary to the provisions relating to distinctiveness and agricultural origin. The Board may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both the registered proprietor geographical indication and the appellant, affirm, reverse, or modify the decision appealed from. Further appeals against orders of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board are permissible to the Supreme Court on a question of law, subject to satisfaction of conditions as provided herein regarding maintainability.

For the purposes of this Act, "performance" shall mean any recitation, delivery, declamation, address, presentation, enactment, or musical rendering given live before an audience. Such performance may include dramatic works, literary works, and musical compositions as incorporated therein. A performance is deemed to be a derivative work only if it substantially alters the original work’s character or expression; provided that incidental elements necessary for the delivery of the performance itself shall not constitute such alteration. The right of a performer in respect of their performance shall subsist independently of, and subject to any rights existing under this Act relating to copyright in the underlying work.

For the purposes of this Act, "performance" shall mean any recitation, delivery, declamation, theatrical presentation, musical rendition, dance, acrobatic display, or similar artistic expression presented live before an audience. A recording made of such a performance shall be deemed derivative work subject to copyright ownership by the entity securing registration under this Act, provided that the original performer’s rights are not prejudiced. Any individual or legal person intending to commercially exploit a recorded performance must first apply for and obtain a certificate of registration detailing the nature of the performance, date, venue, and names of all participating performers. Failure to secure such registration prior to commercial distribution shall render the distributor liable to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may require submission of video or audio evidence substantiating the claimed performance.

Where a performer alleges infringement of their right under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of such infringement. Such injunction may include an order preventing the communication to the public, by any means, of a performance or an adaptation thereof, without due authorization. The remedies available to a performer whose rights have been infringed shall also extend to damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct result of the infringing act. Provided that, in determining such damages, consideration shall be given to any benefit accruing to the infringer from the unauthorized use of the performance. Any person found to have wilfully and knowingly contributed to the infringement of a performer’s right may be held jointly liable for the remedies awarded under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "performance" with respect to performers’ rights shall mean any presentation by one or more individuals before an audience, whether vocal or instrumental, dramatic or non-dramatic, literary or otherwise. A recorded performance, including but not limited to audio and video recordings, shall be considered a derivative work requiring consent from the performer(s) involved, subject to provisions regarding fair dealing as provided herein. Any person desiring to utilize a recorded performance for commercial purposes must first obtain written authorization from the owner of the copyright in such recording or, where applicable, from the performers themselves. Failure to secure such authorization shall render the user liable for damages and injunctive relief. The right to grant or withhold such consent remains vested solely with the performer unless explicitly assigned through a legally binding agreement registered under this Act. Any dispute concerning the ownership or validity of such an assignment may be referred to the relevant judicial authority.

A public exhibition of dramatic work shall be deemed a performance for the purposes of this Act if it incorporates substantial elements of original choreography and musical composition. Such performance may be recorded by means of cinematography, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the authors of all incorporated works, including but not limited to the choreographer and composer. The right of a performer in their performance shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year of the first public presentation; however, this period shall extend to seventy-five years where the performance constitutes an adaptation of another copyrighted work. Any subsequent commercial exploitation of such recorded performance requires adherence to stipulations regarding equitable remuneration for all participating performers as provided herein.

Any unauthorized recording of a live musical performance shall be deemed a violation under this Act, attracting penalties as prescribed herein. Where such recording is for commercial gain, the offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than two years and with fine which may extend to ten lakhs of rupees. The right of a performer to control the first public showing or broadcast of their performance extends to prevent any subsequent reproduction without express written consent. Any person found guilty of infringing upon this exclusive right is subject to civil action, including claims for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the performer. Provided that, an exception may be made where the recording serves solely as a personal memento and is not distributed publicly.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any copyright subsisting in a performance shall be assignable by the performer either wholly or partially and either for the duration of copyright or for any period thereof. Such assignment may be made by way of present disposition or as a security interest, provided that the terms of such assignment are clearly documented and registered with the designated authority. Where a performance is undertaken in collaboration between two or more performers, the assignment provisions herein shall apply jointly to all participating individuals unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. Any subsequent transfer of rights under an assignment requires prior written consent from the original assigning party, as stipulated within the initial agreement. The right to receive royalties attributable to such performance remains with the performer unless explicitly relinquished through a documented and registered assignment.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, where a public exhibition of a dramatic work incorporates a substantial performance by one or more performers, and such performance is recorded without their express written consent, the copyright subsisting in that recording shall be deemed jointly owned by the owner of the copyright in the dramatic work and each performer whose performance was so recorded. Any dispute arising regarding the determination of ‘substantiality’ under this provision may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted as per the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The decision of such tribunal shall be final and binding, subject to appeal only on grounds limited to procedural irregularities during arbitration proceedings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to section 51, where a copyright in a dramatic work or musical work has been assigned to an exclusive licensee, that licensee shall be entitled to communicate to the public any portion of such work by way of performance. The right to grant licenses for performances under this provision is deemed to be part of the assignment unless expressly excluded. Any person proposing to give a public performance of a work in which copyright subsists shall, at least thirty days prior to the date appointed for such performance, provide written notice to the owner of the copyright or, if the copyright has been assigned, to the assignee. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the organizer liable for damages as determined by a civil court. The scope of permissible performances granted under an exclusive license shall be defined in the assignment agreement; any ambiguity shall be resolved against the assignor.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and without prejudice to section 51, any copyright subsisting in a recorded performance shall be assignable by way of license or otherwise. Such assignment may relate to the entire term of copyright or for such period as the assigning party deems fit, and shall be valid only if executed in writing and duly attested. Where a performer has granted an exclusive license concerning their performance, subsequent assignments relating to the same rights are void unless consented to by the original licensee. Further, any cessation patent related to the underlying musical composition performed shall not affect the assignability of the performance copyright itself; however, such cessation will be noted in all assignment documentation. The assigning party retains the right to terminate an assignment under this Act if material breach occurs, as provided herein.

Where a public performance of a dramatic work or musical work is recorded without the authorization of the performer and such recording purports to indicate that it was made under official patronage or with the consent of the copyright owner, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum. This right subsists notwithstanding any contractual agreement between the performer and another party concerning the exploitation of their performance. It is provided that an indication falsified through misrepresentation regarding the authenticity or origin of the recording may constitute a violation under this Act, attracting remedies as determined by the court. The burden of proving such falsification shall lie upon the claimant.

For the purposes of this Act, "photograph" means a fixation of an image on light-sensitive material produced through a process involving optics and chemical or electronic means. A photograph shall be deemed to include any positive or negative representation derived therefrom, whether such derivation involves alteration or manipulation of the original image. The term “photograph” does not extend to representations that are primarily artistic in nature, even if created using photographic techniques; however, where a photograph incorporates substantial elements of originality beyond mere mechanical reproduction, it may be considered an artistic work subject to protection under this Act. As provided herein, ownership of copyright in a photograph shall vest initially in the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the photograph’s creation have been undertaken.

For the purposes of this Act, a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work and is subject to copyright protection. The right in a photograph subsists with the photographer, being the person responsible for capturing the image through photographic means. Where a photograph is taken during the course of employment, under this Act, the employer shall be considered the first owner of the copyright unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the employer and the employee. Any application for registration of a photograph must include details regarding the photographer’s name and address, along with a statement affirming originality and confirming that no prior rights exist concerning the work. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify ownership claims as provided herein.

Where a photograph is made in the course of and for the purposes of commercial photography, the author shall be deemed to be the photographer. Provided that, where such photograph is commissioned by another party, the copyright therein shall vest initially in the commissioning party unless otherwise agreed in writing between the parties. Any person who reproduces, distributes, exhibits or communicates a photograph in which copyright subsists without authorization from the owner of the copyright shall be liable for damages. Such damages may include compensation to the copyright owner for loss of license fees and any consequential losses reasonably foreseeable as a result of the infringement. Further, subject to this Act, remedies available under the general law relating to tortious interference with contract shall also apply in cases involving unauthorized use of commissioned photographs.

A photograph shall be deemed to be an artistic work for the purposes of this Act and is subject to copyright under this Act in the manner and to the extent provided herein. The author of a photograph shall, where the photograph is taken with the intention of recording a scenic view or architectural work, be determined as the person operating the camera equipment. Where such photographs are commissioned by another party, the contract governing their creation shall specify whether copyright vests in the photographer or the commissioning entity; failing such specification, copyright shall vest jointly in both parties. Any dispute concerning ownership of copyright in a photograph may be referred to an Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act for resolution. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all registered photographs and related copyright claims as provided herein.

A photograph shall be deemed to be an artistic work under this Act and is subject to the protections afforded herein. Provided that, where a photograph is taken solely for commercial purposes, and the principal purpose of its creation was not aesthetic or artistic expression, the copyright therein shall vest initially in the person commissioning the photograph, unless otherwise agreed in writing. Such agreement may specify terms regarding subsequent reproduction or distribution rights. Further, if the photographer’s contribution to the photograph is deemed minimal, consisting only of operating photographic equipment under direct instructions, ownership may reside with the instructing party. The right to use a photograph for news reporting purposes shall not be affected by this provision, provided that due acknowledgement is given where reasonably practicable.

A photograph shall be deemed to be an artistic work for the purposes of this Act and is subject to protection as provided herein. Any person who reproduces, distributes, communicates to the public, adapts, or displays a photograph without authorization from the owner of copyright therein shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. Where a photograph has been published prior to the commencement of this provision, such publication shall not prejudice the rights of the copyright holder unless it was undertaken with due license. The right to issue licenses in respect of a photograph remains solely vested with the copyright owner, and any unauthorized issuance constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment and fine as determined by the relevant court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the copyright in a photograph shall vest initially in the photographer. Any agreement for the creation of a photograph may stipulate that the right to assign the copyright subsists with another party, provided that such assignment is executed in writing and duly registered under procedures prescribed by the Central Government. Where a photograph is commissioned by an individual or entity other than the photographer, the contract of commission shall expressly define the ownership of copyright therein; absent such clarity, copyright shall remain with the photographer. Further, where a photograph incorporates elements subject to pre-existing copyright, such as architectural designs or artistic works visible within the frame, the assignment of copyright in the photograph does not extend to those underlying rights unless explicitly agreed upon by all relevant right holders. The transfer of copyright relating to a photograph is deemed complete upon registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work and its copyright shall vest in the photographer unless such photographer is an employee and the photograph is created during and as part of their employment, in which case the copyright vests in the employer. Where ownership of the photograph is disputed, it shall be presumed that the person holding the camera at the time of capture is the photographer, subject to evidence demonstrating otherwise. Any aggrieved party may appeal a determination regarding authorship or ownership to the relevant High Court within ninety days of notification of such determination. Provided that, in cases involving photographs taken for journalistic purposes, fair dealing considerations as provided herein shall be paramount when assessing infringement claims.

For the purposes of this Act, a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work and is subject to copyright under the provisions herein. The right in a photograph subsists until sixty years from the end of the year of its creation. Where a photograph is created as part of a permitted register trade, relating specifically to portraiture or commercial photography undertaken for remuneration, the assignment of copyright may be facilitated through standardized contractual agreements approved by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Such agreements shall clearly delineate ownership rights and usage permissions. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all photographs registered under this Act, accessible upon application and payment of prescribed fees. Any alteration to a photograph that substantially changes its character may be considered a new artistic work, subject to separate copyright protection.

For the purposes of this Act, "plate" means any lithographic, photogravure, etching, or similar artistic work produced by mechanical means and intended for reproduction, whether singly or in combination with other works. A plate shall be deemed to include stereoscopic plates and electrotypes derived therefrom. The right of copyright subsists in a plate as if it were an engraving under this Act, subject to the condition that such plate is original in its creation. Reproduction of any substantial part of a plate without authorization from the owner of the copyright therein shall constitute infringement, provided that fair dealing for research or private study is permitted as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "plate" shall mean any lithographic, photographic, or digital reproduction of artistic work, including but not limited to engravings, etchings, and digitally generated images intended for commercial dissemination. Registration of a plate under this Act confers upon the copyright holder exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, and display copies thereof. An application for registration of a plate shall include three clear prints demonstrating the originality of the work and detailing the method of production employed. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the plate constitutes a mere copy of existing copyrighted material or lacks sufficient artistic merit as provided herein. Subject to any directions issued by the Controller, registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership for all purposes under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a plate shall subsist until fifty years from the end of the year in which it was first published. Any person infringing the exclusive rights conferred under this Act by reproducing a plate in any manner without authorization shall be liable for damages assessed at such amount as may be determined by the court. Where an infringement has occurred, the owner of the copyright in the plate may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of reproduction or distribution. The right to claim damages and injunctive relief shall accrue irrespective of whether the infringing copy is identical or substantially similar to the original plate. Provided that, a fair dealing with a plate for research purposes does not constitute infringement, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "plate" shall mean any lithographic, photographic, or stereoscopic impression, whether coloured or uncoloured, and includes any such impression incorporated in or affixed to a card, label, poster, or similar article. The reproduction of any work by way of a plate is deemed an infringement under this Act unless the owner of copyright has granted permission for such reproduction. Any person desiring to reproduce a copyrighted work through means involving a plate shall first apply to the Controller for authorization, submitting details of the proposed reproduction including quantity and intended distribution. The Controller may grant or refuse such authorization after considering representations from the copyright holder, provided that any fee prescribed under this Act shall be paid prior to consideration. An appeal against an order of the Controller refusing authorization may be made to the relevant High Court within a period specified herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a plate shall be deemed an artistic work and is subject to copyright protection. The right to reproduce a plate shall vest in the creator thereof, provided that such creation demonstrates originality as determined under this Act. Where a plate incorporates elements derived from pre-existing works, permission for their inclusion must have been obtained prior to its registration. Any commercial exploitation of a plate without authorization from the copyright holder shall constitute infringement. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to due process, grant licenses permitting reproduction where such reproduction is demonstrably in the public interest or serves educational purposes, provided that equitable remuneration is paid to the copyright owner. This protection extends to all forms of plates, including but not limited to lithographic stones and electrotypes.

Any person found to have reproduced, distributed, exhibited, or communicated to the public any artistic work in the form of a plate without due authority shall be liable for damages as determined by the civil court. Such damages shall account for lost licensing fees and demonstrable harm to the copyright holder’s commercial interests. Where infringement is proven through evidence including but not limited to seized copies and witness testimony, the infringing party may also face an order restraining further acts of reproduction or distribution. The right to seek injunctive relief against continued unauthorized use of a plate remains with the copyright owner as provided herein. Penalties for repeat offenders shall be significantly increased, subject to judicial discretion considering the scale of the infringement.

The owner of copyright in a plate shall be deemed the creator thereof unless such creation is demonstrably attributable to another individual acting under express instruction and contractual agreement. Such agreement must specify the scope of rights granted concerning reproduction, distribution, and public display of the plate. Assignment of copyright in a plate may be effected by instrument in writing signed by the assignor or their duly authorized agent. A license granting limited usage rights pertaining to a plate shall not preclude further assignment or licensing by the original copyright holder, provided that any subsequent licensee is notified in writing of prior encumbrances. Where a plate incorporates elements subject to pre-existing copyright, the owner’s exclusive right extends only to the novel contribution embodied within the plate itself, as determined under this Act. Any alteration to a licensed plate requires consent from the original copyright holder.

Where the reproduction of a plate constitutes a substantial copying of an underlying work protected under this Act, and such plate is used for commercial purposes without due authorization from the owner of the copyright in said underlying work, any aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum seeking injunctive relief and damages. The determination of ‘substantial copying’ shall be based on qualitative and quantitative assessment of the similarities between the original work and the reproduced plate, considering inter alia the originality of the elements copied. Provided that, where the defendant demonstrates a reasonable belief in a lack of copyright ownership or validity, the burden shall shift to the claimant to substantiate their claim. Appeals against such determinations may be made as provided herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the reproduction of a plate, whether in its original form or as an adaptation derived from an article patented process, shall not constitute copyright infringement if such reproduction is demonstrably incidental to the lawful manufacture, use, or sale of that article. An aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum asserting that the said reproduction exceeds the scope of incidental utility and constitutes a substantial taking of the original plate’s artistic merit. The burden of proving such excess shall lie upon the claimant, subject to the right for the defendant to adduce evidence demonstrating adherence to established industrial practices. Any order made under this provision may be appealed before the appellate forum as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "reprography" means the reproduction of works in literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic form by photographic, xerographic, mimeographic, electronic, or similar processes. Such reproduction shall be deemed a copy within the meaning of under this Act. The term reprography includes, but is not limited to, the creation of copies for private use and research, provided that such use does not constitute commercial exploitation of the copyrighted work. Any person engaged in the systematic production of reprographic copies may be subject to limitations as provided herein regarding fair dealing and equitable compensation to copyright holders.

For the purposes of this Act, every application for registration of works involving reprography shall include a detailed inventory listing all source materials from which copies have been derived. This inventory must specify the title, author, and publication details of each original work utilized in the creation of the reprographic compilation. The Registrar may require submission of samples demonstrating the fidelity of the reproduction to the original, particularly where digital manipulation or alteration has occurred. Registration shall not be granted if the application fails to adequately disclose the provenance of the copied material or if it is determined that the reprography constitutes an infringement of copyright under this Act. Applicants seeking registration must provide a sworn affidavit attesting to due diligence in ascertaining the copyright status of all included works.

Where any person, without authorization from the copyright owner, undertakes reprography of works protected under this Act for commercial purposes, such person shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the extent of infringement. The amount of damages shall take into account not only the reasonable royalties that would have been paid had proper licenses been obtained but also any demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright holder as a direct consequence of the unauthorized reprography.  Further, where an infringing act is committed repeatedly or on a substantial scale, the court may award exemplary damages to deter future violations. Any individual found guilty of such infringement shall be subject to criminal proceedings and penalties as provided herein. The right to seek injunctive relief against further acts of reprography remains explicitly reserved to copyright owners.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, reprography of works protected under this Act shall be permitted only with prior authorization from the owner of copyright in such work. Such authorization may be granted on non-exclusive terms, provided that the applicant demonstrates a reasonable need for the reprographic facility and undertakes to adhere to conditions stipulated by the Controller. The Controller may require submission of detailed plans regarding equipment, distribution channels, and measures taken to prevent unauthorized copying. Any person engaging in reprography without obtaining requisite authorization shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act. Further, any entity found to be facilitating or profiting from such unauthorized reprography is liable for civil penalties as provided herein. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint, initiate inquiries and issue directions concerning the operation of reprographic establishments.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, reproduction by means of reprography shall be permissible only where such reproduction is undertaken for private and non-commercial use. Provided that, where the work reproduced comprises literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, a reasonable number of copies may be made for educational purposes within institutions recognized by the Central Government, provided further that prior written permission from the copyright holder is not required in such instances. However, any commercial distribution or public display of materials obtained through reprography shall constitute an infringement under this Act and render the distributor liable to prosecution. The right to control reprography extends to all forms of works fixed in a tangible medium, as provided herein.

Any individual engaged in the unauthorized reprography of literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works for commercial gain shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Such activity is strictly prohibited without obtaining prior written permission from the exclusive owner of the copyright in question, and any person found guilty thereof shall be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The right to initiate legal proceedings against infringers rests solely with the copyright holder, who may seek injunctive relief to restrain further acts of reprography and claim damages commensurate with the loss suffered as a direct result of the infringement. Repeated violations shall attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, and notwithstanding anything contained in any agreement relating to copyright, the owner of copyright in a literary or dramatic work shall be entitled to grant licences permitting reprography for private use. Such licences may be granted non-exclusively and may specify the type of works covered, the number of copies permitted per licensee, and the duration of the licence. The terms of any such licence shall be determined by the owner, provided that the owner must make reasonable efforts to ensure equitable remuneration is distributed amongst rightsholders whose works are subject to reprography under these licences. Any assignment of copyright shall include the power to grant or revoke such reprography licences unless expressly excluded in writing. Further, a licensee granted permission for reprography may assign their rights under that licence to another party with the prior written consent of the copyright owner.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, the making of copies by reprography for private and non-commercial use shall not be deemed to infringe copyright, provided that such copying is undertaken solely for personal study or research and does not involve a substantial portion of the work. An aggrieved owner may institute proceedings challenging the assertion that a particular act constitutes fair dealing under this provision, demonstrating demonstrable commercial harm resulting from the reprography in question. Such challenges shall be adjudicated by the relevant judicial forum, considering factors including the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount and substantiality of the portion copied, and the effect of the copying on the potential market for the original work. The burden of proof regarding both fair dealing and resultant harm shall rest upon the parties as determined by the court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and as provided herein, the right to control reprography of works protected under this Copyright Act shall vest in the copyright owner. Where such work incorporates elements indicative of a geographical indication registered under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the consent of the holder of that registration shall be obtained prior to any commercial reproduction or distribution via reprography. A license granting permission for limited reprographic use may be assigned by the copyright owner to collecting societies duly authorized under this Act; such assignment shall specify the scope and duration of permitted reproductions. Any subsequent assignment of rights relating to reprography, including licenses granted by collecting societies, must be registered with the designated office as per rules framed thereunder. The copyright owner retains ultimate control over granting or revoking these permissions.

For the purposes of this Act, "reprography" means the reproduction of works in tangible form by means not involving any printed medium, including but not limited to photocopying, digital scanning, and photographic copying. Such reproductions shall be deemed acts of reprography irrespective of whether they are undertaken for commercial gain or private use. The term “meaning act goods” when used in relation to reprographic material refers to the creation of physical items displaying copyrighted works, intended for distribution or sale, which directly infringe upon the exclusive rights vested under this Act in the owner of such copyright. Provided that, fair dealing as defined herein shall not be considered an act of reprography.

For the purposes of facilitating registration under this Act, "reprography" shall be deemed to include the creation of copies of literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works by means of photographic, xerographic, or similar processes. Any person intending to undertake large-scale reprography for commercial distribution shall file a detailed declaration with the civil court registrar in whose jurisdiction their principal place of business is located. This declaration must specify the nature of the works intended for reproduction, the estimated number of copies to be made, and the proposed methods of dissemination. The civil court registrar may require further information as deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with provisions relating to fair dealing and equitable remuneration. Provided that such registration shall not preclude subsequent legal challenges concerning copyright infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photograph is taken by an employee during the course of their employment and such photograph constitutes an artistic work, shall owner copyright therein vest initially with the employer. Provided that, if the terms of the contract of service explicitly stipulate otherwise, then ownership may be assigned to the employee as agreed between the parties. For the purposes of this section, ‘photograph’ includes any digital image captured by a camera or similar device and fixed in a tangible medium. The right to reproduce such photograph shall remain with the owner unless expressly transferred under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where any sound recording is created during the course of employment, the employer shall be the owner of copyright therein. Provided that, if such creation is a work of joint authorship, the employees involved shall jointly own copyright with the employer, and their respective shares shall be determined as agreed upon in writing at the time of creation or subsequently ratified by them. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation pertaining to the terms of employment contracts and ownership agreements for verification purposes. Any party claiming that they shall owner copyright in a sound recording must submit proof of registration with the designated authority, detailing the circumstances surrounding its production and outlining the allocation of rights amongst all contributors.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photograph is taken or an engraving produced in pursuance of a commission, shall owner copyright therein the person by whom the commission was issued; provided that if such photograph or engraving has been commissioned jointly by two or more persons, they shall be deemed joint owners of the copyright. Any infringement of such copyright may give rise to a remedy of damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a consequence thereof. Further, where an infringing copy is made and sold, the court may order its destruction without compensation. The right to sue for infringement shall accrue to the copyright owner or their duly authorized assignee, subject to any limitations prescribed under this Act concerning fair dealing with copyrighted works.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photographic work is created by an artist acting as an agent for another person, that other person shall owner copyright therein. Provided that, if such agreement between the artist and the principal is recorded in writing and deposited with the Registrar of Copyrights, it shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the terms of the agency. The Registrar may, at the request of any party aggrieved by such an agreement or its deposit, inquire into the circumstances surrounding the creation of the work and determine whether the conditions for establishing ownership as provided herein have been met. Any person claiming to be the rightful owner of copyright under this section shall file a petition with the Registrar within ninety days from the date of publication of the photographic work. The Registrar shall provide an opportunity for all interested parties to present their case before making any determination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photograph is taken by an employee during the course of their employment and solely for purposes connected with the business of the employer, shall owner copyright therein vests in that employer; provided that such employment contract explicitly stipulates assignment of copyright ownership. Further, if the photographic work incorporates pre-existing artistic elements, including but not limited to illustrations or designs, then copyright in those incorporated elements shall remain with their respective owners unless a separate and written agreement expressly transfers such rights. The employer’s entitlement under this Act is conditional upon demonstrable evidence that the photograph was created within the scope of employment and contributed directly to the employer's commercial activities as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a sound recording is created through commission by an entity engaged in commercial broadcasting, shall owner copyright therein vest initially with that commissioning entity. Provided that, if such agreement between the broadcaster and the creator explicitly assigns all or any portion of said copyright to the creator, then the creator shall become the sole owner as provided herein, notwithstanding the initial vesting. Further, where a film is produced under an assignment of copyright from multiple contributors, including cinematograph film producers and music composers, the terms of such assignments shall be binding on all parties involved. Any subsequent licensing or transfer of copyright relating to the sound recording component shall require written consent from both the commissioning entity and the original creator, if ownership has been transferred as per this provision.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where an audio-visual recording is created through the collaborative efforts of multiple parties, including but not limited to cinematograph film producers and sound recording owners, determining who shall owner copyright therein presents unique challenges. The ownership shall vest jointly in those parties whose contributions are demonstrably essential to the creation of the work; provided that a dispute arises regarding the extent of such contribution or the relative importance thereof, the aggrieved party may appeal to the relevant High Court for declaratory relief. Such an appeal must be accompanied by expert testimony substantiating the claimant’s assertion and detailing the nature of their involvement in the recording's creation. The court shall consider all evidence presented before rendering its judgment.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, shall owner copyright in any cinematograph film be vested initially in the producer thereof; provided that where such producer is a corporate body, the appointment of a member appointed bench by the High Court may be sought if disputes arise concerning the determination of ownership arising from contractual arrangements made prior to the commencement of production. Further, where an agreement exists assigning copyright to another party, and the validity of said assignment is challenged on grounds of misrepresentation or undue influence, the aggrieved party shall have recourse to appeal under this Act to a judicial authority designated by the Central Government. The burden of proving such misrepresentation or undue influence shall rest upon the claimant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where any photographic work is created by an artist acting as agent for another person, such other person shall owner copyright therein; provided that if the terms of engagement between the artist and the principal specify that the copyright belongs to the artist, then the artist shall be deemed the first owner. Further, it shall be the duty of any person claiming ownership under this Act to display a notice indicating such claim on all copies of the work available for sale or distribution. Failure to provide such registration notice shall not invalidate the copyright but may affect remedies available against infringement. Any wilful and knowing reproduction or communication to the public of a copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages, including actual loss and profits derived from the infringing activities, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a photographic work is created by a person acting as an agent of another and the circumstances surrounding its creation indicate that the principal intended the photograph to be used primarily for advertising purposes or promotional material relating to a trade mark, then shall owner copyright in such work vest solely in the principal. Provided that, if the contract between the photographer and the principal expressly stipulates otherwise regarding ownership of copyright, the terms of that agreement shall prevail. Furthermore, where the photographic work incorporates elements protected by trade mark regulations, any reproduction or distribution infringing upon those registered marks shall be deemed a violation under this Act and may be subject to remedies as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "publication translation" means a work being a translation of another work published outside India, where such publication was authorized by the owner of the copyright in the original work. A publication translation shall be deemed to be published on the date it first becomes available to the public, irrespective of whether copies are offered for sale or otherwise distributed. The right to reproduce a publication translation is subject to the condition that the original work has not been published in India with the authorization of the copyright owner. Provided that, where such authorization was obtained prior to the publication translation, this restriction shall not apply.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of translations registered under this Act. Any person claiming to be the author of a publication translation shall make application in the prescribed form and manner, accompanied by certified copies of the original work and the proposed translation, for registration of such translation. The application shall specify the language of the original work and the language into which it is translated. Registration of a publication translation shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, and adapt the said translation within India, subject to any prior copyright subsisting in the original work. An appeal against refusal of registration may be made to the relevant judicial authority as provided herein.

The right to undertake a publication translation of a copyrighted work shall vest initially with the exclusive benefit of the copyright holder. Provided that, where a publication translation is made without authorization from the rights owner, and subsequently published, the copyright holder may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by reason of such infringement. Such damages shall be assessed considering the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had due license been obtained prior to the unauthorized publication translation. Further, any person found guilty of publishing a publication translation without requisite authorization is liable to pay compensation equivalent to twice the cost of production of the infringing copies. Subject to this, the copyright holder may also seek an injunction restraining further distribution or display of the offending publication translation.

Where a published work has been translated into another language and that translation is subsequently published without authorization from the copyright holder of either the original work or the translation, such publication shall constitute an infringement under this Act. The right to control publication translation extends to ensuring accuracy and faithfulness to the original work; any alteration deemed substantial by the Controller may also be considered infringing. An application for permission to undertake a publication translation may be made to the Controller, detailing the intended scope of distribution and demonstrating due diligence in attempting to ascertain the copyright holders’ consent. The Controller shall consider such applications based on factors including the potential impact on the marketability of both the original work and existing translations. Provided that, where the translation is deemed a fair use under principles established elsewhere herein, permission may be granted subject to conditions as determined by the Controller.

Where a literary or dramatic work has been published abroad and subsequently translated into Indian languages by a translator, that publication translation shall be deemed to be a new work subject to the provisions of this Act. The copyright subsisting in such publication translation shall vest initially in the translator unless otherwise agreed upon in writing between the translator and the author or owner of the original work. Provided that, if the translation faithfully reproduces the original work and does not contain substantial alterations or additions, the term of copyright protection for the publication translation shall be limited to the remainder of the term for which copyright subsists in the original work under this Act. The right to control distribution of such translations may also be assigned by the translator as provided herein.

Where a copyrighted work has been published abroad and subsequently translated into Indian languages without authorization from the copyright holder, such unauthorized publication shall constitute a violation of this Act. Any individual engaging in the reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation of a publication translation lacking requisite permission is liable to prosecution under this Act. The penalty for first-time offenders shall be imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine ranging from fifty thousand rupees to two hundred thousand rupees. Repeat offences will attract enhanced penalties, including forfeiture of assets derived from the infringing publication translation and potential prohibition from engaging in similar activities for a period as determined by the court.

The right to authorize or control the publication translation of a copyrighted work shall vest solely with the copyright holder unless otherwise expressly stipulated in a written agreement. Any party desiring to undertake a publication translation must obtain prior, express consent from the copyright holder, and such consent may be granted subject to terms and conditions as determined by the grantor. Where an assignment of copyright has occurred, the assignee’s rights extend to include the authorization of publication translations, provided that the assignor retains no continuing interest in this specific right unless explicitly stated within the assignment document. Further, a license granting permission for reproduction may not be construed as encompassing the right to create and distribute a publication translation without separate, explicit authorization. The copyright holder may impose reasonable royalties and other conditions on such licenses, taking into consideration the scope of distribution and intended audience.

Where a publication undertakes a translation of a copyrighted work, and subsequently disputes the validity of the copyright subsisting in the original work, the aggrieved copyright owner shall be entitled to institute proceedings before the relevant judicial forum. Such proceedings may seek declaratory relief affirming the existence of copyright, as well as damages for infringement. It is provided that the burden of proving non-infringement rests upon the publication asserting a lack of valid copyright under this Act. Further, any challenge to the originality of the work shall be considered only if it is raised within three years of the initial publication translation and accompanied by evidence demonstrating reasonable grounds for doubt regarding the author’s creative contribution.

For the purposes of this Act, “publication translation” means a work being a translation of another work published outside India, where such publication was undertaken without authorization from the owner of the copyright in the original work. A publication translation shall be deemed to infringe under this Act if it reproduces or adapts any substantial part of the original work, irrespective of whether patents related to processes described within that original work have been granted elsewhere. Provided that, a publication translation may not be considered an infringement if it falls within the scope of fair dealing as provided herein and is accompanied by appropriate acknowledgement of the original author and source.

Where a copyrighted work has undergone publication translation into another language, and the translator is duly registered as the author of that translation under this Act, the copyright subsisting in the original work shall not prejudice the copyright accruing to the translator. Provided that, if the publication translation incorporates substantial additions or modifications which constitute an inventive step beyond the mere rendering of the original text, such additions may be subject to considerations analogous to those governing patent addition regard, and the translator’s copyright shall extend only to these added elements unless otherwise agreed in writing with the owner of the original work. Further, any subsequent publication translation derived from a prior published translation shall require consent from the author of the initial translation, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "translation" with reference to a published work shall mean reproduction thereof in another language by means of literary, musical, or artistic arrangement; provided that such reproduction does not constitute an original work as defined under this Act. A person seeking authorization for a translation shall be deemed to request a license and is subject to the conditions prescribed herein regarding remuneration and duration. The right to undertake a publication work translation shall vest with the owner of copyright in the original work, unless otherwise agreed upon through contract or permitted by specific exemptions provided within this legislation.

The right to undertake a publication work translation shall vest initially with the copyright owner of the original work, subject to the provisions herein relating to prior publication. An applicant seeking registration of a translation work must submit alongside the prescribed application form, a certified copy of the copyright registration pertaining to the underlying original work, demonstrating ownership or authorization as provided under this Act. Where the original work has been published outside India, the applicant shall furnish an affidavit confirming that such publication did not prejudice the rights of the copyright owner in India. Registration of a translation work does not confer any right beyond those explicitly granted by law and is subject to revocation if conditions precedent are not met.

Where a published work has been translated into another language, the right to reproduce the translation shall vest solely with the translator, subject to the conditions stipulated by contract between the translator and the original author. Provided that, if such contract is silent on the matter of commercial exploitation beyond initial publication, the translator shall be deemed to have retained full rights regarding subsequent translations or adaptations into further languages. Any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, display or sale of a translation work constitutes infringement under this Act, entitling the aggrieved translator to seek injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. Further, where an author has assigned their copyright in the original work, any claim arising from the publication work translation shall be pursued against the assignee.

Where a published work is translated into another language, the translator shall be deemed the author of the translation so far as regards the translations themselves. The copyright in such translation shall extend throughout the lifetime of the translator and for sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the translator’s death. An application for permission to make or publish a translation may be made to the Controller, who shall consider such applications according to prescribed procedures and guidelines. Provided that any person seeking authorization under this Act to undertake a publication work translation must submit a detailed statement outlining the intended scope, methodology, and potential impact of the translated version on existing works in the original language.
