Such an application must specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and state the grounds upon which it is based, providing supporting documentation as prescribed by regulations. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish a security deposit, the amount determined according to prevailing guidelines, ensuring compliance with procedural requirements under this Act. Provided that, if the rectification register appellate board finds merit in the application, any costs incurred shall be borne by the respondent party; otherwise, the applicant is liable for all associated expenses.

An application for registration as a farmer shall include a declaration verifying that the applicant is indeed a cultivator engaged in seed saving and exchange, or possesses traditional knowledge relating to plant genetic resources, and has been conserving such varieties for at least one generation. The application must detail the geographical area where the variety has been cultivated by the farmer’s family or community, along with an affirmation confirming adherence to customary practices regarding seed usage and distribution. Further, the applicant shall provide documentation substantiating their claim as a holder of farmers rights, which may include village records, testimonials from fellow cultivators, or evidence of participation in local agricultural fairs showcasing indigenous varieties. The Authority may request additional information deemed necessary for verification under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any farmer aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the recognition of their farmers rights, including but not limited to orders concerning entitlement to saved seed or propagation material, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Authority within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Authority shall give notice to all parties concerned and opportunity for being heard before passing any order in appeal. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Appellate Authority may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the said order, provided that the appellate authority’s decision is demonstrably contrary to established principles of equity or involves a substantial question of law pertaining to farmers rights.

Applications received for registration of plant varieties shall be examined by a Registration Committee constituted by the Authority, and the composition of this Committee will reflect expertise in relevant fields including botany, agronomy, and intellectual property law. The Authority may establish specialized sub-committees within the Registration Committee to address specific technical aspects of applications concerning genetically modified organisms or varieties exhibiting novel traits. Any person aggrieved by an order of a sub-committee under this Act may appeal to the Registration Committee itself. Committees necessary for evaluating breeder’s rights claims and farmers' participatory plant breeding efforts shall be constituted as per guidelines issued by the Central Government, ensuring representation from relevant stakeholders including seed companies and agricultural universities.

For the purposes of this Act, a "plant variety" means a plant resulting from breeding or selection process originating from one or more plants, which exhibits a unique and uniform character distinguishable from other known varieties; provided that mutations and selections arising directly from cultivated varieties shall be regarded as distinct varieties. The Plant Varieties Registry shall maintain separate registers for extant varieties, new varieties, and farmers’ rights-protected varieties, each containing particulars of the variety's denomination, geographical area of cultivation, breeder or right holder details, and any relevant technical data demonstrating its conformity to established criteria under this Act. Applications for registration shall be processed as provided herein.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars relating to the denomination of the variety, its origin, method of reproduction, cycle of life, proposed area of cultivation, and any distinctive characteristics which clearly identify it. The applicant shall furnish such documentation as is required under this Act to substantiate the claims made in the application, including details regarding genetic stability and purity maintained through successive generations. Upon receipt of an application, the Plant Varieties Registry may request further information or clarification from the applicant to ensure completeness and accuracy. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registry relating to acceptance or rejection of an application may prefer an appeal to the Authority within sixty days of such decision, as provided herein.

Applications for entry into the Plant Varieties Registry shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall specify the denomination of the variety, its source, method of derivation, any distinguishing characteristics, and a description sufficient for identification purposes. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or clarification regarding the variety’s stability and uniformity. An advertisement inviting objections to the proposed registration shall be published in the Official Gazette and such other manner as the Authority deems appropriate. Objections received within the stipulated period shall be forwarded to the Applicant for a response, which will then be considered by the Registrar before making a recommendation to the Authority. The Authority may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to both parties, either allow or reject the registration request.

An application for inclusion of a plant variety in the Plant Varieties Registry shall contain particulars regarding its denomination, method of reproduction, distinctiveness, uniformity, stability, and any traits relevant to agricultural practices. The applicant must provide documentation demonstrating that the variety has been cultivated or exploited for at least three years prior to the date of application, subject to exemptions granted by the Authority under this Act. Further, a declaration confirming freedom from restrictions on propagation material shall accompany each submission. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of notification, provided that such appeal must specify grounds for challenging the initial determination as provided herein.

Any person who knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses material facts in an application filed under this Act relating to the registration of a plant variety shall be liable to a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months. Furthermore, any breeder or researcher found to have acted fraudulently in obtaining registration on the Plant Varieties Registry, including through misrepresentation of data concerning distinctiveness or stability, shall have their registration revoked and may face additional penalties as determined by the Authority. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced fines and potential prohibition from applying for future registrations under this Act. The Authority may also issue cease and desist orders to those violating these provisions.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a registered plant variety shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the commercial advantages arising from that variety. Such licenses may include, but are not limited to, rights relating to seed production, distribution, and marketing. The terms and conditions of such licenses shall be determined by mutual agreement between the licensor and licensee, recorded in writing and submitted for registration with the Plant Varieties Registry. Assignment of registered plant varieties is permissible, provided that prior consent of the Plant Varieties Registry is obtained, confirming adherence to stipulations regarding farmers' rights and benefit-sharing arrangements as detailed herein. Any transfer or assignment shall be deemed invalid unless duly registered within ninety days; furthermore, any sub-license granted must also be recorded with the registry.

An application for entry of a plant variety into the Plant Varieties Registry shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the variety does not possess novelty, uniformity, or stability. Any person aggrieved by such refusal may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall consider any documents submitted in support of the application and may direct the Registrar to register the plant variety if it is satisfied that the initial determination was erroneous. Provided that, where a claim of prior disclosure arises, the burden of proving such disclosure shall lie upon the appellant. Subject to this, the decision of the Appellate Board shall be final.

A plant variety shall be deemed to be registered under this Act if it is shown to possess a denomination which satisfies the Registrar that it meets the criteria for distinctness, uniformity and stability. The Plant Varieties Registry maintains records of all registered varieties, including details pertaining to the breeder, geographical location of initial development, and any modifications made during evaluation. Any person claiming rights in a variety may apply to the Registrar for registration, providing evidence substantiating its characteristics as provided herein. Subject to appeal under this Act, the Registrar’s decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application shall be final.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall contain particulars specified by the Registrar, including details regarding its denomination, origin, method of production, and any unique characteristics distinguishing it from other known varieties. The applicant shall furnish documentation substantiating claims made in the application, including data on genetic stability and expression potential across diverse agro-climatic zones. Upon receiving an application, the Plant Varieties Registry may direct the applicant to submit further information or clarification if deficiencies are identified. An alleged offence reason relating to misrepresentation of variety characteristics within the registration dossier shall be considered a material non-compliance under this Act, potentially leading to rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of granted rights.

Applications for entry into the plant varieties registry shall be submitted to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by requisite documentation detailing lineage, morphological characteristics, and geographical distribution of the variety. The Registrar may require applicants to provide additional data or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue a provisional acknowledgement and assign it a unique identification number. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The court provided registrar shall maintain records pertaining to all applications, registrations, and appeals, accessible for inspection subject to regulations prescribed by the Authority. Further, the Registrar is empowered to request expert opinions from designated scientists as deemed necessary during examination procedures.

A plant variety holder desiring to relinquish rights vested under this Act may apply for a formal surrender of their Plant Variety Rights Certificate to the Authority. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the reasons for seeking surrender and any consequential impact on existing licensing agreements, if applicable. The Authority shall review the application and may require further information or clarification from the applicant before proceeding. Upon satisfaction that the surrender is voluntary and does not prejudice the interests of farmers or other stakeholders, the Authority shall issue an order declaring the Plant Variety Rights Certificate surrendered, effective from a date specified therein.

An applicant for registration of a plant variety who has obtained a granted certificate under this Act may, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent as provided herein, elect to surrender said certificate at any point during its term of protection. Such election shall be made by submitting a formal declaration in the prescribed form to the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee specified in Schedule B. The Registrar shall acknowledge receipt of the declaration and publish notice thereof in the Plant Varieties Journal within thirty days. Upon verification that all procedural requirements have been satisfied, including confirmation of any outstanding obligations relating to benefit-sharing agreements entered into under this Act, the certificate shall be deemed surrendered and removed from the Register of Registered Plant Varieties.

Any plant breeder who has obtained a Plant Variety Registration may elect to relinquish their rights conferred by that registration through a formal process of surrender, provided that this decision is demonstrably not motivated by an intent to circumvent obligations under agreements related to benefit-sharing arising from the initial application for registration. Upon notification of such intention to surrender, submitted in the form prescribed herein, the Registrar shall publish notice thereof prominently on the Register and provide opportunity for any registered agents or licensees currently operating under that variety’s protection to submit objections within sixty days. Should no valid objection be received, or where objections are overruled by the Authority, the Registrar may proceed with the cancellation of registration and declare the variety freely available for use, subject to existing farmers' rights as provided herein.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Registration may apply for the voluntary termination of that registration through a written application submitted to the Authority, detailing the reasons for seeking such termination and accompanied by all relevant documentation as specified under this Act. Upon receipt of an application requesting surrender, the Authority shall publish a public notice in at least two widely circulated national newspapers, inviting objections from any interested party within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of publication. If no valid objection is received within that timeframe, or if any objection is deemed frivolous by the Appellate Board, the Authority may proceed to record the surrender. The Plant Variety Registration shall be deemed terminated upon the date specified in the order issued by the Authority following the completion of this process; provided that such termination does not prejudice any existing rights accrued prior to the effective date of surrender.

A plant variety breeder who has obtained a certificate of registration under this Act may elect to surrender said certificate subject to compliance with stipulated conditions. Such election shall be communicated to the Authority in writing, detailing reasons for the proposed surrender and accompanied by an affidavit verifying adherence to all reporting obligations as provided herein during the period of registration. The Authority may, after due consideration and consultation with relevant stakeholders, accept or reject the offer of surrender. Acceptance is contingent upon confirmation that no pending applications exist relating to the same variety and that any accrued royalties remain fully disbursed according to contractual agreements. Upon acceptance, the certificate shall be deemed revoked and its details removed from the Register.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Registration may elect to surrender their rights under this Act by submitting a formal declaration to the Authority, accompanied by a detailed justification for said action. Upon receipt of such declaration, the Authority shall publish notice thereof in at least two widely circulated national newspapers and on its official website. Failure to provide a satisfactory explanation within thirty days of publication, as determined by the Authority, will result in imposition of a monetary penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Further, any attempt to circumvent obligations under this Act through an unwarranted surrender, intended to avoid enforcement actions or licensing requirements, shall be deemed a violation and subject to prosecution under relevant provisions concerning biopiracy.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Rights license granted under this Act may, subject to fulfilling all obligations stipulated within the terms of that license, assign or otherwise transfer their rights pertaining to the propagation material and seeds of the protected variety to another party, provided that such assignment is recorded with the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by a fee as determined. The assignee shall be deemed to succeed to all rights, privileges, and obligations of the original licensee. Furthermore, a Plant Variety Rights holder may elect to surrender their license entirely, thereby relinquishing all associated propagation and commercialization entitlements concerning the protected variety; such surrender shall become effective upon notification to the Registrar and publication in the prescribed manner. Any subsequent use of the variety without express authorization following surrender constitutes an infringement under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Authority regarding the acceptance or rejection of a request for surrender of a plant variety protection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which may include directing the Authority to reconsider its decision or substituting the same with a new decision. Provided that where the surrender is sought due to non-compliance with conditions stipulated under this Act concerning farmers’ rights, the Board shall consider evidence pertaining to such non-compliance before entertaining an appeal and may dismiss the appeal ab initio if it finds merit in the Authority's findings.

An applicant seeking registration of a denomination variety sub may, subject to fulfilling all conditions precedent under this Act, elect to surrender their application for registration at any stage prior to grant of protection. Such election shall be made by submitting a written declaration in the prescribed form to the Registrar, stating unequivocally the intention to relinquish all rights pertaining to the application and any provisional protection previously afforded. The Registrar may, upon receipt of such declaration, proceed to record the surrender and shall notify the same through publication in the official gazette. Further, an applicant who has once surrendered their application shall be precluded from submitting a subsequent application for registration relating to the identical denomination variety sub unless a period of five years has elapsed since the date of the recorded surrender.

Any holder of a Plant Variety Registration, seeking to relinquish their rights conferred under this Act, may effect a surrender by submitting a written application to the Authority, detailing the reasons for such relinquishment and accompanied by any documentation deemed necessary by the Authority. Upon receipt of such an application, the Authority shall publish notice of the proposed surrender in the Official Gazette and on its website, affording interested parties a period of ninety days within which to submit objections. Should objections be received, the Authority may initiate inquiries and hearings as it deems appropriate. The Authority is empowered to refuse the surrender if it finds that the holder has acted contrary to the provisions herein or where revocation proceedings are pending against them; otherwise, registration shall cease upon notification in the Gazette.

A plant variety breeder who has previously obtained a Granted Certificate of Protection under this Act may elect to surrender said certificate, provided that such election is made through a written application submitted to the Plant Varieties Authority at least ninety days prior to the intended effective date of surrender. The authority shall verify that all outstanding obligations pertaining to the protected variety, including but not limited to royalty payments and reporting requirements as stipulated herein, have been fully satisfied before processing the surrender request. Failure to comply with these financial and reporting stipulations may result in a period of innocently punishable imprisonment not exceeding six months, alongside forfeiture of any accrued benefits under this Act. The Registrar shall publish notice of the surrender in the Official Gazette upon its finalization.

Any person holding a Plant Variety Registration who elects to surrender their rights under this Act shall be liable for outstanding fees and penalties accrued prior to the effective date of surrender. Such surrender shall not absolve the registrant from responsibility regarding any infringement committed during the period of registration, and civil proceedings may be initiated by aggrieved parties as provided herein. The Registrar shall publish notice of the surrender in the Official Gazette, detailing the variety’s designation and the date of relinquishment. Further, a sum equivalent to three years' worth of copyright society fees, calculated based on projected royalty income from the surrendered variety, must be deposited with the Authority before the surrender becomes effective, ensuring continued support for research initiatives. Failure to comply shall render the surrender invalid.

Where an individual residing outside of India directly and materially contributes to the creation of a copyrighted work within India, and that work is subsequently reproduced or distributed without authorization, constituting an infringement under this Act, such individual shall be deemed to have acted in concert with any party facilitating said infringement. The rights holder may pursue legal remedies against both the infringing entity and the foreign contributor, subject to demonstrating substantial involvement by the latter in the unauthorized reproduction. Provided that, where the contribution is demonstrably minimal or incidental, a court may consider this as a mitigating factor when assessing liability. Any judgment concerning damages awarded for such india infringing activity shall be enforceable under reciprocal arrangements between India and the jurisdiction of the foreign contributor, as per existing international treaties.

Where an individual residing outside of India has reason to believe that their copyrighted work is being infringed within the territory of India, they may file a complaint with the designated Copyright Enforcement Officer in the district where the infringement is alleged to have occurred. Such complaints shall detail the nature of the copyright, the specific acts constituting the infringing activity, and provide evidence reasonably demonstrating ownership and validity of the copyright under this Act. The Copyright Enforcement Officer shall serve notice upon the alleged infringer, affording them an opportunity for a hearing within thirty days from the date of such service. If, after due consideration of all submitted materials, it is determined that infringement has occurred, the Copyright Enforcement Officer may issue orders restraining further acts of india infringing and directing compensation to be paid to the copyright owner.

Where an individual residing outside of India reproduces, distributes, communicates to the public, adapts, or performs any copyrighted work originating within India without due authorization from the copyright owner, such actions shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the reproduction occurs for private and non-commercial use, and does not substantially impact the marketability of the original work in India, it may be considered a fair dealing subject to review by the relevant adjudicating officer. Furthermore, any entity demonstrating willful blindness regarding the infringing nature of their activities shall be deemed liable for damages proportionate to the commercial value derived from such india infringing conduct. The copyright owner retains the right to pursue legal remedies as provided herein against both direct and contributory infringers.

Any person found to be engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of copyrighted works originating within India shall be deemed guilty of an offense under this Act. Such infringement, particularly where it involves commercial exploitation without due license or authorization, carries a penalty not exceeding three years imprisonment and a fine commensurate with the extent of damages caused to the copyright owner. Repeated acts of infringing upon intellectual property rights may result in enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The right to seek injunctive relief against further acts of india infringing is explicitly vested in the copyright holder. Compensation for loss of revenue and damage to reputation shall be recoverable through civil proceedings, subject to limitations prescribed herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any copyright owner desiring to grant a license for the reproduction and distribution of their copyrighted works within India may execute an assignment agreement in writing specifying the scope, duration, and royalty terms applicable to such license. Such agreements shall be registrable with the Office of the Registrar of Copyrights, and registration thereof shall create a public record of the licensed rights. Where it is determined that unauthorized reproduction or distribution has occurred, constituting india infringing upon a registered copyright, the aggrieved owner may pursue remedies as provided herein against both the direct infringer and any party who knowingly facilitated such infringement through an assignment agreement lacking proper authorization. The Registrar may issue directives regarding standard royalty rates for certain categories of works to ensure equitable compensation to copyright owners.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another has engaged in acts constituting infringement under this Act, such party shall institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The plaint must specify with particularity the copyrighted work claimed to be infringed and the nature of the infringing activity. It shall further detail the measures taken to mitigate damages resulting from said infringement. Provided that, a defendant may counter-claim asserting fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, subject to demonstrating such use was limited to the amount necessary for that purpose. The Court may, upon application by either party, appoint an arbitrator with expertise in intellectual property law to assess technical aspects of the alleged india infringing activity and its impact on the market value of the copyrighted work.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that another person has engaged in acts constituting infringement under this Act, such party shall file a complaint with the designated Copyright Enforcement Officer. The complaint must specify the nature of the alleged infringing activity and provide particulars of the copyrighted work claimed to be infringed. Supporting documentation, including but not limited to copies of copyright registrations, licenses, and relevant correspondence, shall accompany the complaint. Furthermore, an affidavit provided by the complainant attesting to the veracity of the information contained within the complaint is mandatory for its consideration. The Copyright Enforcement Officer may require further clarification or additional evidence as deemed necessary. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in the rejection of the complaint. Any person found to be india infringing shall be liable to prosecution under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “broadcast shall pay” means that any entity engaged in the broadcasting of programmes containing works protected under this Act shall remit a sum determined by the designated authority to the right owners or their nominated collecting societies. Such remuneration is payable irrespective of whether the broadcaster has obtained prior permission from the right owner for the inclusion of the work within the broadcast programme, provided that the work was published before its broadcast. The amount remitted shall be commensurate with the frequency and duration of the work’s appearance in the broadcast, as determined by guidelines issued under this Act.

Any entity engaged in the commercial broadcast of copyrighted works shall pay royalties to the copyright holders or their designated collecting societies, as provided herein. Failure to remit these royalties within ninety days of the due date will incur a penalty equivalent to twenty percent of the outstanding amount. The Copyright Organisation may initiate recovery proceedings against defaulting broadcasters through civil courts for amounts not remitted. Any person found guilty of willful non-compliance with this provision shall be liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or both, subject to judicial discretion. Broadcast shall pay obligations are deemed paramount and supersede any contractual agreements that diminish the rights afforded to copyright owners under this Act.

Any entity receiving remuneration for the right to communicate a copyrighted work through broadcast shall pay royalties directly into the designated Government account within thirty days of each calendar quarter’s close. Failure to remit said royalties constitutes a violation under this Act and renders the defaulting broadcaster liable to penalties as determined by the relevant adjudicating officer, not exceeding five times the amount due. The registered proprietor person of the copyright in question shall be entitled to initiate legal proceedings for recovery of unpaid royalties, including interest at such rate as may be prescribed. Provided that any dispute regarding the quantum of royalties payable shall be resolved through arbitration under rules framed by the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, a “broadcast work stating” means any work, whether literary, dramatic, musical or artistic, which is included in a broadcast signal and which contains an explicit declaration or assertion concerning a fact, opinion, belief, or circumstance. Such declaration shall be considered part of the work for copyright protection if it forms an integral element of the creative expression embodied within the broadcast. The right to include a broadcast work stating shall vest in the owner of the copyright in the underlying work, subject to any contractual agreements regarding broadcasting rights as provided herein. This definition applies irrespective of whether the declaration is presented as commentary or incorporated into narrative content.

A person claiming copyright in any broadcast work stating that it is an original work shall, upon making a formal application to the Copyright Office, furnish particulars including the date and time of the first broadcast, the name of the broadcasting station or stations involved, and a synopsis of the work. The application may include details regarding ownership transfer if applicable. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the claimant’s entitlement under this Act, subject to challenge by any aggrieved party within three months from the date of publication of the Copyright Register. Any alteration to the broadcast work subsequent to its initial transmission will require a fresh application and registration process as provided herein.

Where any person reproduces the entirety or a substantial portion of a *broadcast work*, being a work which has been communicated to the public by way of a broadcast, without obtaining requisite permission from the owner of copyright therein, such person shall be deemed to have infringed copyright under this Act. Provided that, where the reproduction is undertaken for private and non-commercial use, it shall not constitute an infringement if such reproduction does not exceed reasonable limits and does not cause undue prejudice to the rights holder. The owner of copyright in a *broadcast work stating* may pursue civil remedies including damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a consequence of the unauthorized reproduction. Further, any intermediary facilitating or enabling such infringing activity shall be liable to assist in preventing further infringements and providing information relating thereto.

A person making a broadcast work stating any copyrighted work shall, within thirty days from the date of the first broadcast, deposit with the Copyright Office two copies of the recorded programme embodying that work. These copies shall be deposited in a format specified by the Registrar and maintained as part of the public record under this Act. Failure to comply with this provision renders the broadcaster liable for damages as determined by a civil court. The Registrar may, at any time, require the person making the broadcast to substitute such copies as are deemed necessary to ensure accurate preservation. Any application for rectification or amendment concerning a deposited copy shall be processed according to established procedures and subject to verification of authenticity by an expert appointed by the Copyright Office.

A person shall be deemed to have communicated to the public any work by way of a broadcast work stating if that work has been transmitted over radio frequencies accessible within the territory of India. Provided that, where a cinematograph film has been exclusively exhibited in a cinema hall for a period exceeding six months from its first exhibition, subsequent communication thereof by way of a broadcast work stating shall not be deemed to infringe any right under this Act. Further, such transmission requires prior authorization from the owner of copyright in the underlying work, unless that owner has expressly waived such requirement through a written agreement registered with the designated authority. Any unauthorized broadcast work stating is subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the owner of copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, broadcasts that work by means of a *broadcast work stating* the source of the work and ownership details shall be deemed to have committed an infringement. Such infringement is subject to penalties as provided herein, including but not limited to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Where the infringement is committed for commercial gain, the court may enhance such penalty up to double the amount specified above. The owner of copyright shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining further acts of broadcasting, provided that they demonstrate reasonable efforts were made to ascertain ownership details.

Any person holding copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work intended for broadcast, and subsequently incorporated into a broadcast work stating, may grant a license conferring the right to reproduce the work in any medium. Such licenses shall specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses of the reproduction rights granted. The grantor retains full ownership of copyright under this Act unless explicitly transferred by written assignment registered with the Copyright Office. Any assignee acquiring such rights shall be bound by the terms stipulated within the original license agreement. Further, a broadcaster may elect to secure exclusive performance rights for a broadcast work stating, provided that equitable remuneration is paid to the copyright holder as determined through negotiation or, failing that, arbitration under procedures established herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where a copyright owner alleges that a broadcaster has infringed their rights relating to a *broadcast work stating* a literary or dramatic work, the broadcaster shall be deemed to have satisfied the requirements of due diligence if they demonstrate having taken reasonable steps to ascertain and clear any potential copyright subsisting in such stated work. However, this presumption of due diligence may be rebutted by the copyright owner through production of evidence establishing that the broadcaster failed to take those reasonable steps or acted with knowledge of infringement. Any appeal against a finding that a broadcaster has not discharged their burden under this provision shall lie to the appellate forum as provided herein within sixty days from the date of such finding, subject to further appeals as may be prescribed by law.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where a broadcast work stating that copyright subsists in any work is transmitted by a broadcasting organization, and objection is raised by any person claiming ownership of said copyright alleging misrepresentation or lack of due diligence on the part of the broadcaster, such objection may be presented to the relevant High Court. The court shall consider whether reasonable inquiry was undertaken prior to the broadcast. Provided that, the burden of proving the veracity of the claim regarding copyright ownership and the broadcaster’s negligence shall rest upon the objector. Further, a notice registered breeder claiming exclusive rights related to any underlying genetic material incorporated within the work may also challenge the broadcast under similar procedures, subject to demonstrating prejudice arising from the unauthorized dissemination.

For the purposes of this Act, a "broadcast work stating" means any work comprised primarily of matter or materials originally communicated to the public by means of a broadcast signal. Such communication includes, but is not limited to, television broadcasts, radio transmissions, and online streaming services as may be defined under regulations framed in accordance with this Act. A broadcast work stating shall retain its status as such even if subsequently reproduced in any other medium. The Registrar of Copyright within the offices patent office shall maintain a record of all registered broadcast works stating, accessible to the public subject to reasonable restrictions.

A person claiming copyright in any broadcast work stating a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work shall make an application for registration within thirty days from the date of first publication of that broadcast. Such application shall include particulars relating to the title of the work as broadcast, the name and address of the broadcasting organisation, and the duration of the broadcast. The application may also contain a visual recording embodying scenes from the broadcast, submitted solely for identification purposes; such recording shall not be considered part of the registered copyright itself. Provided that where the broadcast incorporates works by multiple authors, each author’s consent to inclusion in the broadcast work stating must be documented and filed with the Registrar.

Any person who reproduces any portion of a *broadcast work stating* without authorization from the owner of copyright therein shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, determined by the court considering the extent of infringement and resultant loss to the copyright owner. Where such unauthorized reproduction is undertaken for commercial gain, the court may also order the seizure and destruction of all infringing copies and materials used in their creation. A *business india application* seeking permission to reproduce a broadcast work stating may be filed with the Controller, who shall consider it based on prevailing licensing rates and equitable compensation principles as provided herein. The copyright owner is entitled to injunctive relief against any threatened or continuing infringement under this Act.

A person making a broadcast work stating any copyrighted work shall, within thirty days from the date of the first broadcast, furnish a payable notice to the Copyright Office. Such notice shall contain particulars including, but not limited to, the title and author of the original work, the name and address of the copyright owner as ascertained with due diligence, and the duration of the broadcast rights claimed. The Copyright Office may require further documentation substantiating the claims made in the payable notice. Failure to furnish a timely and complete payable notice shall render the broadcaster liable to penalties as provided herein. Any objection to the accuracy or completeness of information contained within a payable notice may be submitted to the Copyright Office within sixty days from its public display, subject to verification procedures established under this Act.

A broadcasting organisation shall include any body corporate, firm, or individual engaged in the transmission by radio means of visual images, sounds, or both, intended for reception by the public. For the purposes of this Act, a broadcasting organisation is deemed to have made a public display of works included in its broadcasts. Any such organisation intending to reproduce excerpts from copyrighted literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic works shall obtain prior permission from the owner of copyright therein, provided that fair dealing under this Act may be permitted without such consent. The right to grant or withhold such permission remains solely with the copyright holder as defined herein.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any cinematograph film, literary work, or musical composition for transmission via radio waves or other electronic means shall register a declaration with the Copyright Office detailing the particulars of the intended broadcast. Such registration must include the title and duration of the work, the name and address of the right owner, and the proposed dates of broadcast. The broadcasting organisation shall further provide an undertaking to compensate the right owner in accordance with rates determined as per guidelines issued by the Central Government. Provided that a broadcasting organisation may utilise works for ephemeral broadcasts without prior registration if it provides a written notification to the right owners at least thirty days before transmission, detailing the same information required under this provision.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any cinematograph film for public exhibition through broadcast shall obtain a license from the Controller under this Act. Such license shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates that adequate measures have been implemented to prevent unauthorised reproduction or distribution of the said cinematograph film, including but not limited to technological protection measures and contractual safeguards with all involved parties. The broadcasting organisation shall furthermore ensure that any accompanying commentary or adaptation does not distort the original artistic intent as embodied within the cinematograph film. Provided that a written agreement exists between the broadcasting organisation and the copyright owner of the cinematograph film, outlining royalty payments and usage terms, the Controller may waive certain procedural requirements as provided herein.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any copyrighted cinematograph film or literary work for transmission via radio waves shall first secure a license from the owner of copyright therein, provided that such owner is ascertainable. The licensing fee payable under this section shall be determined based on factors including but not limited to the frequency of broadcast, geographical reach and duration of usage as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Where the broadcasting organisation proposes to incorporate excerpts of multiple copyrighted works within a single programme, it shall obtain separate licenses for each work concerned. Any assignment of copyright relating to broadcasts made by a broadcasting organisation shall be deemed to include the right to make subsequent broadcasts of recordings of those original transmissions, subject to conditions agreed upon with the assignor.

A broadcasting organisation shall, upon commencing the transmission of any copyrighted work, provide a detailed attribution statement identifying the author and copyright holder, prominently displayed during the initial five minutes of said transmission. Failure to adhere to this requirement constitutes a prima facie violation, subject to review by an adjudicating officer appointed under this Act. Any aggrieved party claiming damages due to inadequate or absent attribution may file a complaint with such officer, who shall afford both the complainant and the broadcasting organisation an opportunity for argument and presentation of evidence. The adjudicating officer’s decision is appealable before the appellate authority established as provided herein, whose determination shall be final subject to judicial review on grounds limited to errors apparent on the record.

A broadcasting organisation shall, upon intending to utilise any copyrighted work for transmission via radio or television signals, obtain a license from the owner of copyright therein, provided that such licensing fees are determined according to guidelines established by the Central Government. Where a member of staff within the broadcasting organisation undertakes the adaptation of a literary work prior to broadcast, ensuring compliance with fair dealing principles as provided herein, the broadcasting organisation shall remain ultimately responsible for any infringement claims arising from said adaptation. Any member found to have acted in contravention of these stipulations may be subject to disciplinary action by their employer and potential civil liability under this Act. The Central Government may issue further directives regarding permissible uses and limitations concerning copyrighted material broadcasted by such organisations.

Any person intending to commercially exploit audio-visual works through broadcasting shall first register a Declaration of Intent with the designated Copyright Office. Such declaration must specify the title of the work, the name and address of the copyright owner, and the intended method of broadcasting, differentiating clearly whether it is via terrestrial radio, satellite transmission, or internet streaming platforms. The registration shall be deemed incomplete until all requisite fees are remitted and supporting documentation verifying ownership is submitted. Broadcasting shall different from mere public performance; a separate license is required for each distinct broadcast event involving copyrighted material. Provided that, works falling under the domain of fair dealing as provided herein are exempt from this requirement.

Any person proposing to make a communication to the public by way of broadcasting of any cinematograph film or sound recording shall first obtain from the owner of copyright in that work a written license for such purpose. Such license shall specify the duration and geographical extent of the permitted broadcast, as well as any restrictions on subsequent uses of the copyrighted material. The applicant shall furnish to the Copyright Office a certified copy of the proposed broadcasting agreement, including details of remuneration paid or to be paid to the copyright owner. Failure to submit this documentation within thirty days prior to the intended broadcast will render the broadcaster liable for penalties under this Act. It is provided that where the work has been previously published, broadcasting shall different from other forms of publication and require a distinct assessment of fair dealing considerations.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments of copyright relating to musical works, wherein particulars of any agreement transferring rights concerning royalties manner shall be recorded. Any person claiming an assignment under this Act must apply for registration within three months from the date of execution of such agreement. The application shall specify the work assigned, the assignor and assignee, the duration of the assignment, and the specific rights transferred, including details pertaining to royalty distribution and collection. Provided that, if the assignment relates to a work jointly authored, each author’s consent must be evidenced in the registration documents. Failure to register an assignment concerning royalties manner shall render such assignment unenforceable against any third party claiming prior interest under this Act.

The right to receive royalties arising from the public performance of a copyrighted musical work shall vest initially with the copyright owner, but may be assigned by express written agreement. Such assignment shall not extend beyond the term for which the original copyright was granted, and any attempt to assign rights exceeding this period shall be deemed void ab initio. Disputes concerning the proper calculation or distribution of royalties manner are subject to resolution through arbitration conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice. An aggrieved party may appeal an arbitral award to a High Court only on grounds limited to jurisdiction, fraud, or violation of fundamental fairness as provided herein. The appellate authority shall not re-examine the merits of the underlying dispute but shall determine solely whether procedural irregularities prejudiced the outcome.

Where an article patented process incorporates elements protected by copyright under this Act, and a license is granted permitting utilization of said patented process, the terms governing royalties manner shall be explicitly defined within the licensing agreement. Such agreements must detail the calculation methodology for royalty payments, specifying whether these are based on net sales revenue derived from products manufactured using the licensed process or another agreed-upon metric. Provided that the copyright owner retains all rights not expressly assigned under the license, any assignment of such rights relating to the patented process shall require a written instrument duly executed and registered as provided herein. Furthermore, sublicensing is permitted subject to conditions stipulated in the primary license agreement, ensuring continued adherence to the agreed royalties manner and safeguarding the integrity of copyright protection.

For the purposes of this Act, a “translated printed copy” shall mean a reproduction of a literary or dramatic work presented in printed form which embodies a translation of the original work into another language. Such translated printed copies are deemed to be an adaptation of the original work and are subject to copyright under this Act, provided that the translator is duly acknowledged as such on every published copy of the translated printed copy. The owner of the copyright in the original work shall initially possess exclusive rights over any subsequent translations unless otherwise agreed upon by contract or assignment. Any person infringing these rights may be liable for damages as provided herein.

Application for registration of translated printed copies shall be made to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant must furnish a certified copy of the original work, along with a complete version of the translation submitted for registration. Where the translation is from a work first published outside India, proof of copyright ownership in that foreign work must also be provided. Registration of a translated printed copy does not confer any rights to the copyright in the underlying original work; such rights remain vested as per provisions under this Act. The application shall specify the language of the original work and the language into which it has been translated. Any alterations made to the translation after its submission will invalidate the registration, subject to approval by the Copyright Office.

Where a translated printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is published without authorization from the copyright owner, such publication shall constitute an infringement actionable by either the owner or their duly authorized representative. The remedies available to the copyright owner under this Act include injunctive relief preventing further distribution and sale of the infringing copies, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the unauthorized publication. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, consideration shall be given to any reasonable fees paid by the infringer for services rendered in connection with the translation or printing process. Any person found guilty of contributory infringement relating to these translated printed copies may also be held liable under this Act. The copyright owner shall have the right to demand an account of profits derived from such infringing publication, subject to equitable considerations.

Where a translated printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration specifying the particulars of the original work, the language into which it has been translated, and the name and address of the translator. Such certificate shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein and conclusive as to the validity of the translation for all purposes under this Act. An application for registration of a translated printed copy may be made by the translator or any person duly authorised by him in writing. Provided that, if the copyright in the original work is vested in any other person than the applicant, consent from such owner shall be obtained and submitted as evidence with the application. The Registrar may require such further information to be furnished as he deems necessary for verification of the claim. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar relating to registration of translated printed copies shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Where the copyright subsists in a published literary or dramatic work, and where a person desires to create translated printed copies thereof, such person shall apply for registration of translation as a separate work. The applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating due diligence in ascertaining the current copyright status of the original work, including verification with recognised publishers and rights societies. Subject to the provisions regarding fair dealing under this Act, permission to undertake the creation and distribution of translated printed copies may be granted by the owner of copyright in the original work or their duly authorised agent. Any assignment of such right to create translated printed copies shall be recorded as per the prescribed procedures and remain valid only for the specific languages indicated within the assignment document. Provided that any subsequent translation into another language requires a fresh application and consent.

Where the copyright subsists in a published printed copy of a work, and a person desires to create translated printed copies thereof in a language other than that in which the original work was initially published, such person shall apply for registration of translation as an original work under this Act. The application shall specify the details of the original work, including its title, author, and publication particulars. Subject to the provisions regarding fair dealing, permission to create and distribute translated printed copies may be granted by the copyright owner or their duly authorized agent through a licensing agreement. Any assignment of rights relating to such translations must be executed in writing and registered as provided herein. A commission offence shall arise if a person creates and distributes translated printed copies without obtaining the requisite license or authorization, thereby infringing upon the existing copyright.

Where an application is made for registration of a translation, the Registrar shall require particulars to be furnished regarding the original work, including its title, author, and country of origin. The applicant shall also provide evidence demonstrating ownership or authorization to create the copies translation ii. Provided that if the original work has been published outside India, the applicant must submit an official certificate confirming such publication and detailing its date. Furthermore, the application shall specify whether the translation is intended for public distribution or private use only. Any subsequent alterations made to the registered translation after registration require notification to the Registrar and may necessitate a fresh assessment of copyright ownership under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "printed copies translation" means a work which is an adaptation of another work and consists entirely or substantially of the rendering into English or any other language of a literary or dramatic work fixed in the form of printed copies. Such translation shall be deemed an original work only if it involves sufficient intellectual effort and judgment to create new expression, subject to the condition that the copyright in the original work remains with its owner. A printed copies translation shall not be considered infringing under this Act unless it reproduces substantial portions of the original work without due acknowledgement or authorization from the copyright holder.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a printed copies translation of a work, such application shall include a certified copy of the original work and a complete transcript of the translated version. The Registrar may require the submission of additional materials demonstrating the fidelity of the translation to the underlying work, particularly where the original work is technical or literary in nature. Registration of a printed copies translation does not confer upon the applicant any rights with respect to the copyright in the original work; such rights remain vested as provided under this Act. The application shall state whether the translated version has been previously published anywhere in the world and, if so, provide full details including dates and locations. Failure to disclose prior publication may render the registration voidable.

Where the translation of a literary or dramatic work is published without authorisation from the copyright owner, and such publication constitutes an infringement under this Act, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further distribution or display of the infringing printed copies. Provided that where the translator claims originality in their rendition, demonstrating substantial creative adaptation beyond mere linguistic conversion, they may also assert a claim for damages reflecting the commercial detriment suffered by the copyright owner due to the unauthorised printed copies translation. The right to claim damages shall be subject to proof of actual financial loss or demonstrable harm to reputation resulting directly from the infringing publication. Any person found guilty of such infringement shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the appropriate judicial forum, considering factors including the extent of reproduction and commercial exploitation.

Where a printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is translated into another language, and copyright subsists in such translation under this Act, an application for registration of that translation may be filed with the Copyright Office. Such application shall contain particulars as prescribed, including a statement affirming that the applicant is the exclusive owner of the copyright in the said printed copy and its translation. The application must further specify the language into which the work has been translated and provide a certified true copy of the original work alongside the translated version for examination by the Registrar. Provided that if the translator is not the author of the translation, the application shall also name the author and state the basis of the applicant’s claim to ownership. The Registrar may require such further information as he deems necessary to verify the correctness of the statements made in the application concerning printed copies translation.

Where a printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is translated into another language, and such translation is subsequently reproduced without authorization from the copyright owner, that act shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Provided that, if the copyright owner has not published the original work within two years from the date of first publication in India, any person may reproduce the printed copies translation without infringing copyright, subject to conditions as provided herein. Any individual found guilty of such unauthorized reproduction shall be liable to a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years. Further, damages equivalent to fifty percent of the anticipated profits from the infringing act may be claimed by the copyright owner.

The right to authorize or prohibit the creation of printed copies through translation shall vest solely with the copyright holder. Any person desiring to undertake a printed copies translation of an original work, be it literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic, must first obtain written consent from the owner of copyright in that work. Such consent may be granted subject to terms and conditions regarding royalties, duration of exclusivity, and territorial limitations as agreed upon between the parties. Provided that, where a printed copies translation is licensed under this Act, the original copyright holder shall retain the right to assign or transfer their underlying copyright without prejudice to the licensee’s rights concerning the translated work. Further, any assignment of such translation rights must be registered with the designated Copyright Office and shall be deemed invalid unless so recorded within three months of its execution.

Where a printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is translated into another language, and such translation is published without authorization from the copyright owner, an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief against further publication and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to the unauthorized printed copies translation. Provided that, if the defendant demonstrates, by reasonable evidence, that they reasonably believed the work was already in the public domain or had been lawfully published elsewhere, the appellate tribunal may reduce the amount of damages awarded. The copyright owner bears the burden of proving ownership and authorization under this Act; any dispute regarding the authenticity of such proof shall be resolved at the discretion of the Tribunal.

Where a printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is translated into an Indian language, and copyright subsists in such translation by virtue of this Act, the translator shall be entitled to all rights comprised therein, subject to any agreement to the contrary made with the owner of the copyright in the original work. Provided that where the original work relates to food products, including recipes or nutritional information pertaining thereto, the prior consent of the owner of the copyright in such original work must be obtained before registration of the translation for copyright protection. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the refusal of registration of a printed copies translation may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Controller shall consider any appeals made and issue orders as provided herein, affording all parties an opportunity for being heard.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark application” shall mean an application filed with the registrar trade marks for registration of a mark under Chapter II. The term "applicant" refers to the person making such an application and may be either the proprietor of the proposed trade mark or any agent duly authorized by him. An application is deemed to be deficient if it does not comply with the prescribed formalities as provided herein, including but not limited to the accurate representation of the mark and the clear designation of goods or services. The registrar shall notify the applicant of such deficiencies, allowing a period for rectification before proceeding further.

Applications for registration of a trade mark shall be made to the registrar trade marks in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Where an application relates to more than one class of goods or services, separate fees shall be paid for each such class. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as may be required by the registrar demonstrating entitlement to use the proposed trade mark and establishing its distinctiveness. Any person interested in the opposed trade marks may within the time specified under this Act file a notice of opposition with the registrar. Upon receipt of an opposition, the registrar shall give due intimation thereof to the applicant and proceed according to the prescribed procedure as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar trade marks relating to the acceptance, refusal, or advertisement of a trademark application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. The appellant shall serve notice on the respondent, namely, the Registrar, along with a copy of the grounds of appeal. Failure to comply with this provision will render the appeal inadmissible. Where the appeal concerns a matter of fact, the Tribunal may require the appellant to produce evidence supporting their claim. Under this Act, the registrar trade marks is obligated to provide reasons in writing for any decision that adversely affects the interests of an applicant or registered proprietor. The tribunal’s determination shall be final, subject to further appeal under the provisions governing judicial review.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be made to the registrar trade marks in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. Every applicant shall furnish such documents and pay such fees as are required under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, direct that any deficiencies apparent on the face thereof be remedied within a specified time; failure to comply with such direction will result in the rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications, registrations, and oppositions received, accessible for public inspection subject to any restrictions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar trade marks relating to the acceptance, refusal, or modification of a trademark application, or concerning rectification proceedings, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during registration shall render the applicant liable for penalties as determined under this Act. The tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against and may also award costs. Any wilful violation of these provisions regarding trademark examination processes will attract a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and subsequent offences shall be subject to double penalties.

The owner of any registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as may be stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall be executed in writing and notarized, with copies submitted to the registrar trade marks for record purposes within thirty days of execution. The registrar may refuse registration if the agreement contains provisions that are manifestly contrary to public interest or restrain competition unreasonably. Assignment of a registered trade mark, including any associated licenses, requires prior written consent from the registrar, provided that such consent shall not be withheld arbitrarily. Any subsequent transfer of rights under an existing license must also be reported to the registrar within fifteen days.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused by the registrar trade marks, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal. Such appeal shall be made to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal constituted under this Act. The tribunal may, after affording opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the respondent, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed from. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to satisfaction of the court that the case involves a substantial question of law. The tribunal shall record its reasons for any decision made and provide copies as provided herein.

The registrar trade marks shall maintain a register of proposed trademarks, distinct from the principal Register, wherein applications pending examination or opposed proceedings are recorded. Any party aggrieved by an entry in this register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal as provided herein. The registrar shall, upon receipt of a request accompanied by the prescribed fee, furnish certified copies of entries and documents relating to trademarks registered or pending registration. Further, the registrar may, at any time, require the rectification of any error or omission appearing in the proposed trademark register. Applications for registration under this Act are subject to scrutiny regarding distinctiveness and compliance with established guidelines; the registrar shall issue directions accordingly.

For the purposes of this Act, “infringement copyright work” with respect to a computer program shall occur where any person, without authorization from the owner of the copyright, does reproduce the program in whole or in part, or creates derivative works based upon it. Such reproduction includes, but is not limited to, making copies for distribution, adaptation into another form, and importing such unauthorized copies. The term "authorization" shall be interpreted as encompassing express permission granted by the copyright owner, or implied consent demonstrated through licensing agreements as provided herein. Nothing in this definition shall prevent fair dealing with computer programs under conditions prescribed elsewhere under this Act.

Where any person reproduces, distributes, exhibits, performs, or communicates to the public any work in contravention of the provisions of this Act, such act shall constitute an infringement copyright work. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all registered works, including details pertaining to the claimant’s ownership and the date of initial registration. Any aggrieved party claiming infringement may file a complaint with the designated authority, submitting evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the original work and the alleged infringing copy. It is provided that an application for rectification of entry in the Register concerning copyright shall be entertained only if it demonstrates demonstrable error or fraud impacting the validity of the registered claim. The remedies available to the copyright owner are subject to considerations of fair dealing as defined under this Act.

Where an act constitutes infringement copyright work, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedy in a court of appropriate jurisdiction. Such remedy may include an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, and recovery of damages sustained by reason of such infringement. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the loss suffered by the copyright owner as a result of the infringing act, taking into account any profit made by the infringer attributable to the infringement. Provided that in assessing damages, the court may consider factors including but not limited to the reasonable royalty which the infringer would have been willing to pay for the right to use the work. Further, where the infringement is proven to be a continuing one, interlocutory injunctions may be granted as provided herein to prevent further dissemination of the infringing material.

Where an aggrieved party alleges infringement copyright work, such party shall institute proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The plaint shall specify with particularity the nature of the copyrighted work, the manner in which it is claimed to have been infringed, and the relief sought. Upon receipt of the plaint, the court may direct the plaintiff to furnish security for costs as deemed appropriate. Notice of such proceedings shall be served upon the defendant at least thirty days prior to the first hearing, detailing the particulars of the claim and providing an opportunity for response. The court shall afford both parties a reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments relating to the alleged infringement copyright work and any defenses raised. Decisions regarding substantial similarity will be made based on established principles under this Act.

Where any person reproduces, distributes, exhibits, performs, or communicates to the public any substantial portion of a copyrighted work without authorization from the owner of copyright in such work, or their duly authorized agent, such act shall constitute an infringement copyright work. This determination is subject to the condition that the reproduction, distribution, exhibition, performance, or communication does not fall within the scope of fair dealing as provided herein. Further, where the infringing activity involves the making available of the copyrighted work online, the person responsible for operating the website or platform facilitating such availability shall be deemed liable unless they demonstrate having taken reasonable steps to prevent the infringement. Any claim of contributory infringement must establish a direct causal link between the actions and the subsequent unauthorized use.

Any reproduction of a substantial portion of a copyrighted work, whether published or unpublished, without authorization from the copyright holder constitutes infringement copyright work. Such unauthorized acts include, but are not limited to, photocopying, digital scanning, and distribution in any medium. Where an infringing copy is made for commercial gain, the offender shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a percentage of the potential lost revenue reasonably attributable to the infringement, as determined by the relevant civil court. Further, where the infringement is proven to have been willful, aggravated damages may be awarded up to three times the amount of actual damages. The owner of copyright may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement under this Act.

The assignment of copyright in a musical composition shall be valid only if executed in writing and attested by at least two witnesses, one of whom must be a practicing advocate or a notary public. Where an agreement purports to grant a license for reproduction of a cinematograph film, such agreement shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to exercise the rights granted; failure to do so renders the license void ab initio. Any subsequent assignment of that limited right shall further restrict the scope of transfer to the original territorial limitation. Subject to this, an owner may assign all or any part of their copyright in a work, including the exclusive right to communicate the work to the public, provided that such assignment is registered with the designated authority. Infringement copyright work occurs when a person reproduces a substantial portion of a literary work without authorization, and where such reproduction is for commercial gain.

Where any person without due authorization makes use of copyright in a work, constituting an act of infringement copyright work, such person shall be liable to action by the owner of the copyright. The aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings seeking equitable relief, including but not limited to permanent injunctions restraining further acts of reproduction or distribution. Provided that where the alleged infringing activity involves fair dealing for research or private study, the defendant may adduce evidence demonstrating such use was undertaken in good faith and without any commercial advantage accruing thereby. The court shall consider whether the extent and nature of the copying were reasonable under the circumstances; a finding against this consideration shall be subject to appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

Copyright in artistic works shall be deemed to be infringed where a person reproduces such work without authorization from the copyright holder. This prohibition extends to instances of distribution, adaptation, or public display undertaken without due consent. Where an international registration prescribed under this Act designates India as a beneficiary territory, the rights afforded to the registrant are considered valid and enforceable within Indian jurisdiction for the duration specified in the relevant treaty provisions.
