Furthermore, the Central Government may consult with an independent scientific adviser possessing expertise in relevant fields of plant breeding and genetics prior to rendering a decision on the application. Final approval central government is contingent upon satisfactory completion of these assessments and adherence to all procedural requirements as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to a decree civil court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. For the purpose of exercising jurisdiction in such appeals, a decree civil court shall be deemed to be a civil court as defined under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The appellate authority shall furnish to the decree civil court all relevant materials and records pertaining to the original order. Any decision made by the decree civil court shall not impede or delay the exercise of powers vested in the Board for safeguarding farmers’ rights as provided herein.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application, or relating to any other matter under this Act, desires to appeal, he may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant materials and evidence presented before it and pass appropriate orders. Any question concerning the validity of an order made by the Appellate Board shall be subject to adjudication in a decree civil court having jurisdiction, notwithstanding anything contained otherwise under this Act.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning the revocation or modification of plant breeder’s rights, or relating to infringement proceedings, feels that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, they may appeal to a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the matter. The appellate court shall be entitled to review all findings of fact and conclusions of law made by the relevant forum under this Act. Provided that the aggrieved party must demonstrate a clear error in the original decision and satisfy the court that no substantial justice has been done. Subject to limitations prescribed for appeals in other civil matters, the decree civil court may grant such remedies as it deems fit, including but not limited to injunctions, damages, and declarations. The forum’s decisions are subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Where any question arises concerning the validity of a Plant Variety Registration or the enforceability of any right conferred under this Act, such question shall be determined by a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the cause of action arose. The Authority may, at its discretion, refer any dispute relating to infringement of Farmers’ Rights to a decree civil court for adjudication, provided that the Authority has first attempted conciliation between the parties as per the procedures outlined herein. Any order made by a decree civil court in relation to matters falling under this Act shall be final and binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days of such order. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the jurisdiction of particular courts for certain types of disputes as provided herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning the revocation or modification of plant variety protection, or relating to farmers’ rights in saved seed, may prefer an appeal to a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the matter. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall comply with the procedural requirements applicable to appeals before such courts. The decree civil court shall not entertain any suit or other proceeding relating to any matter which is required to be determined under this Act, unless it has been shown that no remedy is available under this Act. Provided that the appellate authority’s findings on scientific evidence shall bind the decree civil court.

Any person found to have made any false statement or suppressed material fact in an application for registration of a plant variety shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, where infringement of farmers’ rights occurs due to unauthorized use of registered varieties, aggrieved parties may institute proceedings in a decree civil court seeking injunctions and damages. The Authority shall provide assistance to such courts upon request regarding technical aspects relating to plant breeding and genetic resources. Any order passed by the decree civil court concerning enforcement of these provisions is final, subject to appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Repeated or willful violations may result in revocation of registration and further penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the holder of Plant Variety Rights may grant a license conferring specific rights relating to the commercial use, propagation, or sale of the protected variety. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor. Assignment of Plant Variety Rights, including all associated licensing agreements, requires prior approval from the Controller General and must adhere to prescribed forms and fees. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or enforceability of a license agreement, or regarding an alleged infringement of rights granted under this Act, shall be subject to adjudication in a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the matter. The Controller General may issue guidelines for standard licensing terms, but these are advisory and do not bind either the licensor or licensee.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of protection or concerning infringement proceedings may appeal to the appellate authority. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the appellate authority shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent. Provided that if the appellate authority finds that the delay in filing the appeal was caused by sufficient reason, it may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay. Any decision of the appellate authority regarding claims of farmer’s rights or compensation for damages arising from alleged infringement shall be subject to review by a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the matter.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed particulars pertaining to its denomination, origin, method of reproduction, and any distinctive characteristics as may be prescribed. Where an applicant alleges infringement of farmers’ rights relating to a registered plant variety, such allegation shall be adjudicated solely within the jurisdiction of a decree civil court having appropriate pecuniary limits. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence demonstrating substantial conformity between a claimed farmer's right and the registered variety, direct the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating their claim. This direction shall not prejudice the rights of any party pending determination by the decree civil court. Decisions regarding manner applying registrar for appeals are subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to a decree civil court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the Court shall hear the appeal de novo. The Court shall have all powers vested in a civil court for determining questions arising under this Act, including the power to grant injunctions restraining any act infringing upon farmers' rights or hindering the lawful exercise of privileges conferred herein. Any party failing to comply with an order issued by the decree civil court may be subject to a punishable imprisonment term which may extend to one year and shall also be liable to pay a fine. This remedy is without prejudice to any other remedies available under law.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to compulsory licensing or revocation of registration may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority. The appellate authority shall consider such appeals expeditiously, affording all parties concerned a reasonable opportunity of being heard. An application sub section regarding the filing of appeals shall prescribe a time limit not exceeding ninety days from the date of communication of the order appealed against. Provided that the appellate authority may entertain appeals filed after the expiry of the said period if satisfactory reasons for the delay are adduced. Further, any question concerning the subsistence of a plant variety right or the validity of a registration shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of a decree civil court not subordinate to the High Court. The decision of the appellate authority shall be final and binding, subject to appeal under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

For the purpose of maintaining accurate records pertaining to registration applications and granted Plant Variety Rights, every State Government shall establish and maintain a civil court registry. This registry shall serve as the central repository for all documentation submitted under this Act relating to plant variety registrations, including but not limited to breeder’s declarations, technical data reports, and evidence of distinctness, uniformity, and stability. Access to information held within the civil court registry shall be governed by regulations framed by the State Government, provided that such access does not compromise confidentiality as defined herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding access may appeal under this Act.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be accompanied by detailed particulars pertaining to the denomination, lineage, method of reproduction, and any distinctive characteristics observed during field trials. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign a unique identification number and record the same in the civil court registry maintained at the designated office. The applicant shall furnish three certified true copies of all documentation submitted for inspection by authorized officials. Any alteration or addition to information provided post-application requires prior written consent from the Registrar, recorded within the civil court registry alongside the original submission. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements may render the application liable for rejection as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration or revocation of plant variety rights may appeal to a civil court registry having jurisdiction over the matter. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, and the civil court registry shall admit the appeal subject to payment of prescribed fees. The appellate authority shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony regarding distinctiveness and stability of traits. Decisions of the appellate authority are final, but may be challenged further under the provisions relating to judicial review. Provided that any party failing to appear before the civil court registry at a hearing after due notice shall have their appeal deemed abandoned, as provided herein.

Applications relating to registration of plant varieties shall be presented in triplicate to the Registrar at the designated office. The applicant shall furnish with the application a concise description of the variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, distinguishing characteristics, and any available data on its stability and uniformity. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant, provided that such requests are made within sixty days of the initial submission. All applications and accompanying documents shall be entered into the civil court registry maintained by the Registrar’s office, indexed according to a system prescribed by notification. Access to this registry shall be subject to regulations issued by the Controller General under this Act, ensuring confidentiality where appropriate. Any party aggrieved by an action taken concerning the civil court registry may appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of such action.

Applications concerning the registration of plant varieties shall be deemed to be matters requiring meticulous record-keeping. Every application submitted under this Act must include three certified copies of all relevant documentation pertaining to the variety’s distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity. These documents shall be filed with the appropriate civil court registry designated by the Central Government for maintaining records related to plant variety registrations. The Registrar may, at any time, require applicants to furnish further information or clarification regarding their submissions, provided that such requests are accompanied by a reasonable timeframe for compliance. Failure to comply with these requirements within the stipulated period shall render the application liable for rejection, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the registration or revocation of plant variety protection may appeal to the appellate authority. Failure to comply with a summons issued by the civil court registry, acting on behalf of the Authority, shall render the defaulter liable for penalties as determined by the Authority and recoverable through civil courts. The Authority may direct the civil court registry to seize any infringing material or records pertaining to unauthorized propagation or sale of protected plant varieties. Further, any individual found guilty of wilful misrepresentation regarding the origin or characteristics of a registered variety shall be subject to fines not exceeding five lakhs rupees, and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, as deemed appropriate by the civil court.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming title or an interest in a registered plant variety may assign such title or interest, including rights pertaining to breeder’s entitlement and farmers' privilege, by way of a license agreement. Such assignment or license shall be recorded in the civil court registry maintained under this Act, along with details of the assignee or licensee, duration of the right granted, and any royalty stipulations agreed upon. The Registrar may prescribe forms for such registrations and demand fees as deemed appropriate. Further, where an assignment is made to a body corporate, the registration shall specify the authorized representative executing the document. Any subsequent transfer or modification of rights under this Act must also be registered in the civil court registry to remain valid against third parties.

Any application seeking registration of a plant variety, or any subsequent challenge to such registration, shall be deemed a civil proceeding. The aggrieved party may appeal an order passed by the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding revocation proceedings, to the Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Where evidence is presented before the civil court registry pertaining to the distinctness and stability of a plant variety, that evidence shall be admissible subject to verification by the Registrar as provided herein. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final, but remains open to judicial review under Article 226 of the Constitution on grounds limited to jurisdiction or other errors apparent on the record.

For the purpose of maintaining records pertaining to Plant Varieties registered under this Act, each State Government shall establish a civil court registry at such locations as it deems appropriate. The registry shall maintain an index of all registrations, including details of the breeder, variety denomination, and date the patent shall dated, alongside relevant documentation submitted during the registration process. Access to information held within the civil court registry shall be subject to regulations prescribed by the State Government, provided that such access does not compromise confidentiality or impede enforcement actions under this Act. The records maintained in the civil court registry are deemed official for all purposes as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “variety” means a plant grouping exhibiting a consistent combination of desirable characteristics which are genetically stable and distinct, sexually or asexually reproduced. The Plant Varieties Registry shall maintain registers containing particulars relating to registered varieties, including denomination, geographical location of first cultivation, breeder details, and any indication of farmers’ rights involved in the development thereof. An application for registration under this Act shall specify the essential characteristics defining the variety and include documentation substantiating its distinctness. Subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, decisions regarding acceptance or rejection of applications by the Plant Varieties Registry are final.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be made to the Plant Varieties Registry in the prescribed form accompanied by such particulars as are required under this Act. The Registrar shall upon receipt of an application, issue an acknowledgment and assign it a serial number. Any person claiming right to the variety may apply for registration, provided that the applicant possesses evidence demonstrating distinctness, uniformity, and stability of the variety. The Plant Varieties Registry maintains records pertaining to all applications received and registrations granted, which are open to public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions as determined by the Registrar. Objections to an application under consideration may be filed with the Registry within a period specified herein, detailing grounds for rejection.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Varieties Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration, or by any condition imposed during registration, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. The Appellate Board shall consider such appeals and pass orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding natural justice. Further, if a registered variety is found to be infringing upon the rights of a traditional farmer or indigenous community, demonstrated through documented evidence of prior use and cultivation, the Authority may order revocation of registration and award compensation for damages suffered. The remedies available under this Act shall include injunctions preventing unauthorized exploitation of protected varieties, as provided herein.

Applications for entry into the Plant Varieties Registry shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall specify the denomination of the variety, its source, method of derivation, distinguishing characteristics, stability over successive generations, and any other information as may be required under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further particulars or clarification concerning the variety’s essential traits.

The Registrar shall publish a notification indicating the acceptance of the application for registration, inviting objections from any person claiming right or interest in the variety. Objections received shall be forwarded to the applicant and the applicant shall have an opportunity to file a reply. The Plant Varieties Registry shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all registered varieties, including details pertaining to their breeders and geographical origin, as provided herein.

An application for entry of a variety into the Plant Varieties Registry shall contain particulars specifying the denomination of the variety, its hybridity status, details regarding its initial source and lineage, and a comprehensive description conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate that the variety exhibits stability through repeated propagation or multiplication, ensuring consistent expression of its essential characteristics. Further, an application may be rejected if it is determined that the denomination falsely indicates the variety’s traits or origin, or if the applicant fails to provide evidence confirming freedom from any existing third-party rights relating to the variety's name as provided herein. The Registrar shall notify all applications publicly and allow for objections within a stipulated period.

Any person who knowingly makes a false statement or suppresses material facts in an application for registration of a variety before the Plant Varieties Registry shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. The Registrar, acting under this Act, may, at any time, require the applicant to furnish further information or submit additional documentation relevant to the distinctness and stability of the claimed variety; failure to comply within thirty days shall render the application void. Furthermore, where an infringing party utilizes a registered variety without authorization, as provided herein, they are subject to damages equivalent to three times the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had a license been granted. Repeated offenses may result in imprisonment for a term not less than six months and may extend to two years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a right to intellectual property in a registered variety shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights to use propagating material derived from that variety. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may specify conditions relating to royalty payments, geographical limitations, and duration. Assignment of such rights, including the entire registered variety or specific aspects thereof, is also permissible by way of written agreement, duly executed and recorded with the Plant Varieties Registry. Any licensee seeking to sub-license rights under this Act shall obtain prior consent from the original right holder, as provided herein. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation pertaining to any proposed assignment or license for review and approval to ensure compliance with the objectives of promoting farmer’s rights and preventing anti-competitive practices.

Subject to appeal under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 58, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Varieties Registry relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application for registration of a variety shall have the right to challenge such decision before the Appellate Board. The Registrar may, upon receiving written objection from any interested party regarding the distinctiveness of a variety proposed for inclusion in the varieties registry, require the applicant to submit further evidence substantiating its claim. Provided that such requirement shall be accompanied by an opportunity for the objector to present their grounds in writing. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on the Plant Varieties Registry, subject to revision by the High Court as provided herein.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be made to the Plant Varieties Registrar in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall specify the denomination of the variety, its source, method of derivation, any distinguishing characteristics, and other relevant information as determined by the Authority. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may publish a notification thereof in the Official Gazette, inviting objections from the public within a period not exceeding two months from the date of publication. Any person having sufficient cause may file an objection under this Act. The Plant Varieties Registry shall maintain a register containing particulars of registered varieties and any amendments thereto, which shall be open to inspection by the public subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Applications for entry into the National Register of Plant Varieties shall be submitted to the Plant Varieties Registry in the prescribed form accompanied by requisite documentation detailing lineage, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application, issue an acknowledgement and assign it a serial number. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Authority within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Where imported plant material is utilized in the development of a variety for registration purposes, documentation verifying compliance with the provisions of the Customs Act 1962 relating to import permits and phytosanitary certificates shall be provided as evidence. The Plant Varieties Registry may request further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage during processing.

Any person found to have knowingly registered a plant variety in the Plant Varieties Registry which infringes upon the rights of another shall be liable to pay compensation determined by the Controller, not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Furthermore, any unauthorized assignment or transfer of registration relating to a protected variety, undertaken without prior written consent from the original registrant, constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and a fine as the Court deems fit. The Controller shall have power to issue orders restraining further propagation or sale of infringing material under this Act. Failure to comply with such orders will attract additional penalties, including daily fines until compliance is achieved, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application entitled breeder” shall mean a person who has exercised his right to perfect a new plant variety through selection, hybridization, mutation, or genetic engineering. Such a person shall possess demonstrable evidence substantiating their contribution to the creation and identification of the distinct characteristics of the plant variety in question. An application entitled breeder may be an individual, a firm, an association, or a company. Provided that, where the applicant is a body corporate, the term "breeder" shall refer to the person duly authorized by such body corporate to represent its interests concerning the plant variety. Subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, an application entitled breeder is eligible for registration of their new plant variety.

An application entitled breeder shall be deemed to have failed to disclose a substantial and novel characteristic where the applicant has demonstrably misrepresented data submitted regarding field trials, subject to an appeal to the Appellate Board. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority refusing registration based on novelty grounds may institute proceedings in the District Court, provided that such proceedings are commenced within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Further, where an infringement of plant variety rights is established, the remedies available under this Act include injunctions preventing further propagation and sale, as well as compensation for loss suffered by the breeder due to the unauthorized exploitation of their protected variety. The Authority may, upon receiving a complaint regarding such infringement, issue interim orders restraining the infringing activities pending final adjudication.

An application entitled breeder shall contain a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and expression as influenced by environmental factors. The application must also specify the geographical area within which the applicant exercises control over the reproduction of the variety. Further particulars regarding the method of propagation employed shall be included, along with evidence demonstrating genetic uniformity and stability across successive generations. Any technical data substantiating the novelty and distinctiveness of the plant variety relative to existing varieties must be submitted in a format prescribed by the Authority. The applicant is required to provide documentation confirming ownership or right to make the application under this Act. Provided that an applicant may amend their initial submission, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding substantial alterations affecting registrability.

An application entitled breeder shall contain a detailed description of the plant variety, including its botanical name, parentage where known, and any distinguishing characteristics observed across multiple generations. The applicant must provide evidence demonstrating freedom from rights to the variety under this Act, as well as confirmation that the variety has been reproduced or produced through means permissible under extant regulations concerning genetically modified organisms. Further, the application shall include a declaration affirming adherence to bio-containment protocols during multiplication and distribution of propagating material. Provided that any prior disclosure of the plant variety, whether published or otherwise, does not preclude registration if it can be demonstrated that such disclosure did not compromise the applicant’s rights as provided herein.

An application entitled breeder shall be deemed to have misrepresented facts if, at any time after the publication of an advertisement under this Act, it is established through verifiable documentation that the claimed novelty of the plant variety was not maintained during the entire period preceding the date of filing. Such misrepresentation shall render the applicant liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may result in the revocation of the certificate of registration granted, as provided herein. Further, any person demonstrating demonstrable financial loss due to reliance on false information presented by an application entitled breeder may pursue civil remedies against that individual or entity. Repeated instances of such misrepresentation shall attract enhanced penalties and potential prohibition from future applications under this Act.

An application entitled breeder shall, upon successful registration of a plant variety, possess exclusive rights pertaining to propagation material thereof. Such rights may be assigned or licensed subject to conditions as provided herein. Any license granted by a breeder shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to cultivation, distribution, and sale of propagating material derived from the registered variety. Further, any assignment of breeder’s rights must be executed in writing and notarized, with notification filed with the Plant Varieties Registry within thirty days of execution. The Registrar may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating undue restriction or exploitation under a license agreement, impose conditions to ensure equitable access and benefit-sharing. Any transfer of rights shall not prejudice existing farmers' rights as guaranteed under this Act.

An application entitled breeder shall be deemed to have failed to disclose all material information where it is established, through evidence presented before the Authority, that the applicant was previously engaged in activities directly contravening principles of bio-diversity conservation as defined under this Act. Such determination shall not preclude a subsequent application by the same individual provided that they submit an affidavit detailing corrective measures undertaken and demonstrating adherence to ethical research practices. Any party aggrieved by such a finding may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days, submitting arguments substantiating why the assessment of material non-disclosure was erroneous or disproportionate to the alleged transgression. The Authority shall consider any submitted evidence before upholding or reversing its initial determination.

An application entitled breeder shall be accompanied by a detailed report, authenticated by an authorized officer, specifying the essential derivation and expression of characteristics of the plant variety. The report must include data pertaining to field trials conducted under conditions substantially similar to those prevailing in India, demonstrating stability and uniformity across generations. Further, the applicant shall furnish evidence establishing freedom from any existing rights or claims relating to the variety, subject to provisions regarding prior disclosure. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority concerning registration may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of such decision. The grant of registered certification is contingent upon compliance with all prescribed procedures and adherence to guidelines issued by the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the rejection, revocation, or amendment of a plant variety registration, or concerning any penalty imposed, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during the transmission operation law governing the handling and storage of propagating material shall be deemed a violation, attracting penalties as determined by the Authority. An application entitled breeder who makes false statements or suppresses material facts in their application for registration is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also to a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Repeated offences shall result in enhanced penalties and potential disqualification from applying for further registrations under this Act.

An application for a plant variety shall be deemed an *applicant variety registrable* where the applicant demonstrates, through documented field trials conducted over at least three successive seasons, substantial and uniform expression of characteristics conforming to the description furnished with the application. Provided that, if the variety is essentially derived from another variety, the applicant must satisfy the Authority that the repeated use of the parental variety has not resulted in a change in its essential characteristics. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence confirming freedom from viral or other pathogens as determined by testing protocols prescribed under this Act. Any prior disclosure of the plant variety’s characteristics before the date of application will be considered only if the applicant provides an exhaustive list and supporting documentation thereof.

An application for a certificate of registration shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements for an *applicant variety registrable* where the applicant provides documentary evidence demonstrating stability and uniformity consistent with established agricultural practices. However, any person aggrieved by a decision granting such a certificate may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the notification under this Act. The appellate board shall consider whether the grounds for registration were adequately substantiated, particularly concerning distinctiveness relative to existing varieties. Provided that an opposition is filed demonstrating prior use or knowledge of the variety by another party, the Board may direct a fresh examination of the application and its compliance with the provisions herein.

An opposition to the registration of a plant variety, as provided herein, shall be instituted within one year from the date of publication of the advertisement under this Act. Such opposition may be founded on the grounds that the variety does not conform to the description in the application, or that the applicant has not satisfied the requirements for obtaining protection. Further, an opposition registration sub-committee established by the Authority shall hear and determine such oppositions, affording both the applicant and the opponent a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The committee's decision shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

An opposition to the registration of a plant variety shall be filed with the Registrar within one year from the date of publication of the advertisement referred to under this Act. The application for opposition must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to assertions that the claimed novelty lacks substantial distinction from existing varieties or that the applicant has failed to satisfy requirements regarding geographical isolation during multiplication. Provided that any prior public disclosure by the applicant shall be considered in assessing distinctiveness. Further, an opponent may seek interim relief pending resolution of the opposition registration sub, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations framed under this Act, ensuring due consideration for the interests of all parties involved.

Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding opposition registration, including but not limited to decisions concerning the acceptance or rejection of grounds for opposition, shall have the right to appeal under this Act. The Appellate Authority shall consider all evidence presented by both the applicant and the opponent, ensuring due process and natural justice are observed throughout the proceedings. Where an objection is raised alleging that a variety has been previously sold commercially under an earlier designation, the burden of proof regarding such prior sale rests upon the person raising the objection. Decisions concerning revocation of registration following successful opposition may be reviewed by the Appellate Authority if new evidence emerges demonstrating material errors in the original assessment. The authority shall provide reasons for its decision, which must be made available to all parties involved in the opposition registration sub proceedings.

An opposition registration sub-committee shall be constituted by the Registrar for each Plant Variety Registration and Farmers’ Rights Authority regional centre, comprising a Chairperson who is a retired judge of a District Court and two other members possessing expertise in plant breeding, agricultural science, or intellectual property law. The committee shall hear and determine all oppositions filed under this Act against applications for registration of plant varieties. Notice of the hearing shall be served upon both the applicant and the opponent at least thirty days prior to the scheduled date, specifying the grounds of opposition and providing copies of relevant documents submitted. Either party may present evidence and arguments in support of their respective positions. The committee’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

An opposition registration sub-committee shall be constituted by the Registrar for hearing and disposing of oppositions filed under this Act. The committee shall comprise a Chairperson, who shall be a retired Judge of a District Court or a person having experience in intellectual property matters, and such other members as the Central Government may specify, ensuring representation from relevant scientific disciplines. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the opposition registration sub-committee may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s communication. The committee shall provide each party with an opportunity for presenting evidence and arguments, subject to procedural rules prescribed by the Registrar. Decisions made by the committee are binding, provided that they adhere to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision granting registration of a plant variety, or by any condition attached thereto, shall be entitled to file an opposition within sixty days from the date of publication of such decision under this Act. The Board shall entertain only those oppositions demonstrating demonstrable prejudice resulting directly from the registered variety’s characteristics or conditions. Failure to demonstrate such prejudice will result in immediate dismissal of the opposition. Any frivolous or vexatious opposition filed with intent to harass the registrant shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Board may order costs against an unsuccessful opponent. Further, any false statements made within an opposition registration sub-process are actionable under relevant provisions concerning perjury and defamation.

The registered plant variety holder shall, subject to any conditions stipulated during registration, retain exclusive rights pertaining to propagation and sale. However, a licensee granted under this Act may assign such license, including all associated rights of sub-licensing, provided that prior written consent is obtained from the original registered holder. Any assignment shall be recorded with the Plant Varieties Registry within thirty days thereof. Further, any person intending to challenge the validity of a registration through an opposition registration sub process must demonstrate a substantial and demonstrable economic interest directly affected by the continued protection afforded to the variety. The Registrar may, upon application, grant temporary licenses for research purposes without prejudice to the registered holder’s rights, but such licenses shall be subject to royalty payments as determined by the Authority.

An opposition to the registration of a plant variety, as provided herein, shall be filed within one year from the date of publication of the advertisement under this Act. Such opposition must specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to assertions that the claimed novelty lacks demonstrable distinction from existing varieties or that the applicant has failed to adequately disclose essential derivation data. The Authority may, subject to due process and opportunity for both parties to be heard, dismiss an opposition if it finds the ground raised is frivolous or vexatious. Furthermore, where a condition declared unlawful by a competent authority relates directly to traits exhibited by the plant variety in question, this shall constitute valid grounds for opposition registration sub proceedings.

A variety shall be deemed a *registration public variety* if, upon application and subject to examination as provided herein, it is determined to possess characteristics substantially uniform and stable, and exhibits distinctness from extant varieties. For the purposes of this Act, an applicant seeking registration of a public variety shall disclose all available information concerning its origin, method of breeding, and genetic composition. The Authority may require further documentation demonstrating that the variety’s propagation material will be made reasonably accessible to farmers, consistent with principles of equitable benefit-sharing. Further, any person claiming rights in relation to an extant variety may oppose registration on grounds of prior disclosure or similarity.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed description conforming to the format prescribed by the Register, encompassing morphological characteristics, genetic purity data, and any distinctive features relevant to assessing novelty. The Registrar may require submission of additional documentation substantiating claims regarding stability and uniformity across generations. Where an applicant seeks recognition as a farmer’s right holder for a *registration public variety*, they must demonstrate propagation solely from seed or planting material acquired legitimately under this Act. Any prior disclosure of the plant variety, whether intentional or unintentional, shall be disclosed in the application; however, such disclosure does not automatically disqualify registration provided that it meets criteria as provided herein regarding novelty and distinctiveness.

An aggrieved party, including but not limited to a farmer demonstrating substantial reliance on a plant variety, shall be entitled to seek redressal before the Authority if they believe the registration of a *registration public variety* has been obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation concerning its origin or characteristics. Such an application for redressal must specify the nature of the alleged fraud and provide supporting evidence substantiating the claim. The Authority may, after affording the registrant a reasonable opportunity to be heard, order the cancellation of the registration certificate if it finds that the fraud materially influenced the decision-making process under this Act. Further, any person suffering loss or damage as a direct consequence of reliance on false information presented during the registration process may pursue civil remedies against the registrant for compensation, subject to limitations prescribed by law regarding contributory negligence.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a breeder’s right for a registered plant variety may, by written agreement, license the rights pertaining to such variety to another party. Such licensing agreements shall clearly specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to propagation, distribution, and sale, and the royalty rates applicable. Assignment of breeder's rights in a registration public variety is permissible only with prior approval from the Authority, and any such assignment must be registered as per prescribed procedures. The Authority may stipulate conditions relating to benefit-sharing arrangements where indigenous knowledge has contributed to the development of the plant variety. Further, any licensee shall not undertake activities that compromise the integrity or distinctiveness of the registered public variety, nor shall they claim ownership rights exceeding those granted under the licensing agreement.

For the purposes of this Act, a “notice registered breeder” means a person who has formally notified the Authority, in the prescribed form and manner, of their intention to exercise breeder’s rights relating to a plant variety that is already registered under this Act. Such notification shall include details regarding the geographical area where the breeder intends to commercialize the variety, and may specify conditions for subsequent generations of farmers utilizing propagating material of the notified variety. A notice registered breeder shall be entitled to benefit from provisions concerning infringement of breeders’ rights as provided herein, subject to any limitations stipulated in the notification.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars identifying the notice registered breeder and specifying the geographical area within which the applicant exercises rights derived from that registration. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim as a notice registered breeder, including evidence of prior breeding efforts and lineage tracing. Where an application is found to be deficient in these details, the Registrar shall provide an opportunity for amendment under this Act. Any subsequent transfer or assignment of rights relating to the plant variety shall be recorded by the Registrar with the consent of both the transferring and receiving parties, as provided herein. The registrar may also require a declaration from the notice registered breeder confirming freedom from encumbrances.

Where a notice registered breeder institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of plant variety rights, the burden shall lie upon the defendant to demonstrate that the alleged infringing material was not derived directly or indirectly from the protected variety. Should the defendant fail to satisfy this evidentiary requirement, judgment may be entered in favor of the notice registered breeder and damages assessed according to prevailing market rates for similar varieties, subject to a deduction for any demonstrable cost savings achieved by the defendant through unauthorized use. Further, the Court may order the destruction or non-commercialization of propagating material derived from the infringing variety. The remedies available as provided herein are without prejudice to any other rights or reliefs that the notice registered breeder may be entitled to under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

A notice registered breeder shall be entitled to maintain legal proceedings against any person who is found to have made use of propagating material of a protected plant variety without due authorization, subject to compliance with the prescribed procedures for serving notice under this Act. Provided that, such proceedings may only commence after the expiry of thirty days from the date of dispatch of the notice to the alleged infringer, and provided further that the notice shall clearly specify the nature of the infringement and the remedies sought by the registered breeder. The Registrar may require the registered breeder to furnish evidence demonstrating reasonable efforts were made to resolve the matter through negotiation prior to initiating legal action, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the proceedings untenable.

Any person who sells, distributes, exports, offers for sale, or imports seeds or planting material of a plant variety without authorization from the registered breeder shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Authority. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits and infringement of rights under this Act. Where an infringing act is committed knowingly, the offender may also face imprisonment extending to two years, in addition to the aforementioned penalties. Failure to provide proper documentation identifying the variety and confirming authorization from the registered breeder at the time of sale constitutes a violation subject to these provisions. The Authority shall issue notices to suspected infringers before initiating enforcement proceedings against a notice registered breeder.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a notice registered breeder shall be entitled to grant licenses for the commercial use of their plant variety, specifying the geographical area and duration of such license. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the breeder. Any assignment of rights in a plant variety, including but not limited to the right to grant licenses, shall require prior registration with the Registrar and publication in the Plant Varieties Journal. The consideration for any such assignment or license agreement must be clearly stated within the registered document. Provided that, where a farmer utilizes propagating material of a protected variety under this Act, the notice registered breeder may impose reasonable terms relating to subsequent sales, ensuring equitable benefit-sharing arrangements are maintained.

A notice registered breeder is a person who has applied for registration of a plant variety and whose application has been accepted by the Authority but not yet granted registration. Such a breeder shall be entitled to certain rights as provided herein, including the right to use the designation "notice registered" in conjunction with the name of the variety. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a notice registered breeder may initiate a procedure cancelling registration under this Act, subject to demonstrating that the applicant does not fulfill the requirements for registration or has acted fraudulently. The Authority shall consider such petitions and render a decision as per prescribed guidelines.

An application for registration as a notice registered breeder shall be accompanied by a detailed declaration specifying the denomination proposed for the plant variety and confirming that the applicant fulfills all eligibility criteria under this Act. The Registrar, upon receiving an application, may require submission of additional documentation pertaining to the lineage and stability characteristics of the variety concerned. Any alteration to the particulars recorded in the entry register document relating to a registered breeder’s rights, including changes in ownership or address, must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days. Failure to do so shall render such alterations invalid until formally acknowledged by the Registrar through an amendment process as provided herein. The Register maintained by the Authority is deemed conclusive evidence of registration for all purposes.

Where a notice registered breeder intends to commercialize a plant variety for which protection has been granted under this Act, they shall furnish to the Authority, prior to the first commercial sale, detailed documentation confirming compliance with all applicable design registry registration requirements pertaining to any novel ornamental characteristics incorporated within the variety. Such documentation must include certified copies of relevant registrations and affirmations that the designs do not infringe upon existing intellectual property rights. The Authority may request further clarification or supplementary information if deemed necessary for verification purposes. Provided that a registered breeder fails to submit the requisite documentation, commercialization shall be suspended until compliance is demonstrated; however, the breeder may appeal this suspension under procedures as provided herein.

An entry register variety is deemed to be established when an application for registration, accompanied by requisite documentation as provided herein, has been received and acknowledged by the Registrar. Such acknowledgement shall constitute provisional acceptance pending examination under this Act. The entry register variety shall include details pertaining to the denomination assigned to the variety, its characteristics as determined through rigorous testing, and the geographical location where it was initially developed. Further, the entry register variety is subject to periodic review; any alterations in these particulars must be reported to the Registrar within a stipulated timeframe, failing which may result in removal from the Register.

Any person aggrieved by an entry register variety recorded in the Register may within sixty days from the date on which particulars of the entry are published in the Official Gazette file an appeal to the Registrar. Such appeal shall be finally determined by the Appellate Board constituted under this Act, and the Board’s decision shall be binding. The appellant shall bear the burden of proving that the entry is erroneous or contrary to the provisions herein. Failure to demonstrate such error may result in dismissal of the appeal with costs awarded against the appellant. Further, any person who knowingly makes a false statement in connection with an application for inclusion in the entry register variety, or in support of an appeal under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty as determined by the Board.

An application for inclusion of a variety in the entry register shall be made by the applicant in the prescribed form and accompanied by evidence demonstrating that the variety possesses distinct characteristics conforming to established standards under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the stability of these characteristics across successive generations, particularly where the variety is propagated through methods other than seed. Provided that the applicant demonstrates compliance with all relevant guidelines regarding genetic modification or gene editing, as applicable, and subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Committee, the entry register variety shall be considered for inclusion. Any objection received concerning the accuracy of information provided in the application must be addressed satisfactorily before a decision is made.

Any person who knowingly makes a false statement material to the inclusion of a variety in the entry register variety shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of such misstatement. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information regarding fraudulent entries or deliberate concealment of relevant data pertaining to a candidate variety’s distinctiveness or stability, initiate suo moto proceedings to review and potentially expunge said entry from the entry register variety. Failure to comply with directions issued by the Registrar during such review proceedings shall attract further penalties up to ten thousand rupees per day until compliance is achieved. Repeated offenses may result in disqualification of the applicant from applying for registration under this Act, as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the holder of a registration for a plant variety shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights pertaining to the commercialization thereof. Any person desiring to utilize propagating material of an entry register variety for purposes other than research or development may apply to the Registrar for a license, specifying the intended scope and duration of such utilization. The Registrar may grant such licenses on terms and conditions as it deems fit, including royalty payments to the registration holder proportionate to sales generated from the licensed activity. Assignment of rights in an entry register variety shall require prior notification to the Registrar and be subject to approval based on considerations of public interest and equitable access for farmers. Further, any sub-licensing of such rights is permissible only with express written consent from the original registration holder.

The Registrar shall maintain an entry register variety for each plant variety recorded under this Act, detailing essential characteristics and geographical provenance as declared by the applicant. Any person aggrieved by an entry made, or omitted to be made, in the entry register variety may within sixty days from the date such entry is published, file an appeal before the Appellate Board. The appellate board shall consider any evidence submitted by both the appellant and the Registrar, including expert testimony regarding varietal stability and distinctiveness. Provided that, the burden of demonstrating error or material misrepresentation in the entry register variety shall lie with the appellant. Decisions of the Appellate Board are final subject to further appeal under the appropriate provisions relating to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, “breeder entry relating” means an alteration, addition, or deletion made to a record pertaining to a registered plant variety concerning information about the breeder, including but not limited to changes in address, legal representatives, ownership details, and rights assignments. Such entries shall be made only upon application by the breeder or their authorized agent, subject to verification of identity and authenticity of documents as provided herein. Any person making a false statement under this Act relating to a breeder entry relating is liable for penalty. The Registrar may require such supporting documentation as deemed necessary to validate any proposed alteration to a registered variety's breeder information.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars regarding its genetic composition and lineage. Where a plant variety is found to be essentially derived from another variety, and where the applicant demonstrates that the new variety possesses one or more traits substantially and demonstrably different from the original variety, an examination may proceed as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider any evidence presented by the registered breeder of the earlier variety concerning whether the application constitutes a *breeder entry relating* to their protected rights. Such consideration will include assessment of whether the new variety infringes upon the expression of the essential character of the older variety. The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present arguments against such claims.

Where a plant variety has been registered under this Act and subsequently developed through genetic engineering techniques utilizing protected germplasm, the original breeder shall be entitled to seek redress for unauthorized exploitation of their intellectual property rights. Any person infringing upon such rights may be required to account for profits derived from the commercialization of the modified variety. Further, where a new variety is found to be a ‘breeder entry relating’ to an extant registered variety, demonstrating substantial similarity in essential characteristics and genetic makeup, the later registration shall not prejudice the prior breeder's claim to recognition as the originator. The Authority may order compensation for damages sustained, including but not limited to lost profits and reasonable legal costs, subject to due process and opportunity for a hearing.

Where a plant variety has been developed from an existing variety and the resultant variety possesses at least one essential characteristic demonstrably derived from the initial variety, the developer shall be deemed to have created a ‘breeder entry relating’ to the original variety. Such breeder entry relating shall not confer any right upon the developer in respect of the traits inherent within the predecessor plant variety. Provided that, if the developed variety exhibits substantially similar characteristics to the original variety and the development process involved repeated crossing with the initial variety, the Registrar may require demonstration of significant contribution beyond mere replication. Further, the breeder making a breeder entry relating shall disclose details pertaining to the parentage and derivation process as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning a plant variety registration, including but not limited to orders relating to revocation or modification, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by all parties and may impose costs on any party found to have acted frivolously or vexatiously. Where a plant variety is determined to be a breeder entry relating to an extant registered variety, the original breeder shall be afforded priority in subsequent claims, subject to penalties for wilful infringement as provided herein. The Board’s decision is final and binding, enforceable through civil courts.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered plant breeder may grant a license conferring rights relating to the commercialization of their protected variety. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to conduct activities such as propagation, sale, or distribution. The terms of any license granted under this Act may include royalty payments payable by the licensee to the grantor, and the frequency with which such payments are made. Furthermore, a breeder entry relating to an assignment of rights in a protected variety shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of the execution of the assignment agreement. Any subsequent transfer of rights by the assignee shall also require notification to the Registrar as provided herein.

Where a plant variety is registered and subsequently found to be essentially derived from another variety previously cultivated by a farmer, and the registration was obtained without due acknowledgement of that prior cultivation, an aggrieved party may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be predicated on demonstrable evidence establishing derivation and lack of consent for breeder entry relating to the contested variety. The Board shall consider whether the registered breeder has substantially deprived the farmer of recognition or benefit arising from their contribution to the genetic lineage. Provided that, the burden of proof regarding essential derivation rests upon the appellant; failure to meet this standard will preclude further consideration under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Subject to provisions regarding costs, no fee shall be payable in relation to any application for revision under this Act, nor shall any fees in any proceeding before the Appellate Board or the High Court be recoverable from a public servant acting in his official capacity. Provided that, where an appeal is frivolous or vexatious, the appellate authority may order the appellant to pay such costs as it deems fit, including reasonable expenses incurred by the respondent.

Any application filed by an eligible breeder seeking registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, as determined by notification issued by the Registrar. The amount of such fee shall vary depending on the applicant’s status, with reduced fees applicable to small and marginal farmers, tribal communities, and research institutions engaged in public interest activities. Failure to remit the requisite fee at the time of filing shall render the application void ab initio. Further, any appeal against a decision of the Registrar regarding registration or revocation may be pursued by any party aggrieved, but such appeals shall necessitate payment of an appellate fee, as specified under this Act. Fees in any proceeding are subject to periodic review and adjustment by the Central Government.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellant shall be liable to pay such fees in any proceeding before the High Court as determined by the rules framed under this Act, provided that a default in payment of such fees shall not automatically preclude the appellate authority from considering the merits of the case if the appellant demonstrates sufficient financial hardship and satisfies the court that payment would cause undue burden. The Board may, at its discretion, waive or reduce any applicable fees for applicants who are smallholder farmers or belong to scheduled castes or tribes, as a measure to promote equitable access to justice. Further, costs incidental to the appeal shall be determined by the High Court in its discretion, taking into account the complexity of the matter and the conduct of the parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to compulsory licensing may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum indicating the orders appealed against and the grounds of appeal, and a copy thereof shall be served on the Registrar. Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the Appellate Board may entertain an appeal only if the appellant has deposited with it the fees in any proceeding as determined by the Central Government, which fees shall be non-refundable even if the appeal is dismissed. Provided that, where the aggrieved person is a farmer or a public institution engaged in research relating to plant varieties, they may apply for waiver of such fees under prescribed conditions. The Appellate Board shall follow such procedure as it deems fit for hearing appeals and may pass such orders as it considers appropriate.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the grant or refusal of registration of a plant variety shall be required to remit a non-refundable fee, calculated as per the prevailing schedule annexed to this Act, prior to filing an appeal before the Appellate Board. Provided that, in cases where the appellant is demonstrably unable to pay such fees due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, duly substantiated by certified documentation from a recognized authority, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, waive or reduce the applicable fee. Further, any application for review of an order concerning revocation of registration shall also necessitate payment of prescribed fees in any proceeding; failure to remit said fees will render the application ineligible for consideration as provided herein.

Any person initiating proceedings against an authorized breeder or research institution alleging infringement of plant variety rights shall be required to remit a non-refundable application fee as determined by the Central Government, such amount subject to periodic revision. Failure to pay this initial fee within thirty days of filing the complaint will result in automatic dismissal of the claim without further notice. Further, should any party found to have acted vexatiously or maliciously in pursuing a legal action under this Act shall be liable to pay compensatory costs, including fees in any proceeding incurred by the respondent. The Registrar may, at his discretion, order recovery of such costs through attachment of assets.

Any entity seeking to commercialize a protected plant variety shall be required to execute a licensing agreement with the Registrar prior to engaging in propagation activities beyond the scope permitted under this Act. Such agreements may stipulate royalty rates, duration of license, and geographical limitations on exploitation. The Registrar shall have the power to assign licenses to third parties where the initial licensee fails to diligently pursue commercialization within a prescribed timeframe, subject to due process considerations for the original holder. Furthermore, any transfer or assignment of rights pertaining to a protected plant variety requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, accompanied by evidence of consent from all relevant stakeholders as determined under this Act. Fees in any proceeding relating to license modifications, assignments, or disputes shall be prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Tribunal may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellant shall be liable to pay such fees in any proceeding before the High Court as determined by the rules framed under this Act, provided that a party demonstrating financial hardship, duly verified by a recognized social welfare organization, may apply for a waiver or reduction of these fees. Failure to demonstrate sufficient grounds for fee exemption shall result in the appeal being deemed withdrawn. The Tribunal’s decision on whether such hardship exists shall be final and binding, subject to review under judicial oversight as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. Subject to the provisions of this Act, all appeals shall be finally determinable by the High Court. The Registrar may require any appellant to furnish security for costs and, provided that the appellant fails to do so within the time specified, the appeal shall stand dismissed. Further, where an application is made under this Act or in connection with any proceeding, a party may submit an affidavit provided it is duly sworn before a Magistrate or Notary Public verifying the material facts stated therein. Any fees in any proceeding relating to appeals, including those for filing and representation, shall be as prescribed by the Central Government notification from time to time.

Any application filed by an issued breeder seeking revocation of registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee as determined by the Central Government, published in the Official Gazette. The Registrar may entertain such applications only if the prescribed fee has been remitted and the application is otherwise complete under this Act. Provided that any appeal against an order passed by the Authority concerning fees in any proceeding relating to revocation shall be subject to a further appellate fee, payable at the time of filing the memorandum of appeal. Failure to remit said appellate fee within thirty days from the date of the order appealed against will render the appeal void ab initio. The Registrar may require additional documentation substantiating the grounds for revocation and may impose penalties for frivolous or vexatious applications as provided herein.

Any application filed by an eligible person seeking registration of a plant variety shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee, as determined under this Act. Provided that, where such application relates to a plant variety exhibiting novel and distinctive characteristics derived from indigenous knowledge or traditional farming practices, the Authority may waive all applicable fees in any proceeding pertaining to the examination and grant of registration. Furthermore, if an appeal is lodged against a decision of the Registrar concerning the validity of a registered design incorporated into the presentation of the plant material, the appellant shall be required to remit a non-refundable appellate fee prior to the hearing. Failure to comply with this requirement will render the appeal inadmissible, as provided herein.

Any person seeking to assign rights pertaining to a Plant Variety Protection granted under this Act shall execute a formal assignment deed before a registered notary public, detailing the specific rights being transferred and the consideration paid. Such deeds must be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution for record purposes. The assignee may subsequently license these assigned rights subject to conditions approved by the Controller, ensuring continued benefit accrues to the original registrant or their nominated successors. Where an appeal is made concerning a decision related to infringement of Plant Variety Protection, all fees in any proceeding shall be borne by the appellant unless otherwise determined by the Appellate Board. Patents granted for derived varieties remain distinct from protection under this Act and are governed separately; however, assignment deeds must explicitly acknowledge such existing patent rights.

Any broadcasting organisation transmitting programmes incorporating plant varieties shall be deemed to have acted as an agent of the breeder, and accordingly, liability for infringement of farmers’ rights relating to saved seed or propagating material shall accrue against the broadcaster. Provided that, where a dispute arises concerning such alleged infringement, the broadcasting organisation may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of notification of the order in question. The amount of fees in any proceeding before the Appellate Board, including those pertaining to appeals by broadcasters contesting findings of infringement or seeking clarification on the scope of farmers’ rights, shall be determined as per the scales prescribed under this Act and may be subject to review based on demonstrated financial hardship.

A person who holds title to a patent jointly with another individual or entity shall be deemed to possess a share patent. For the purposes of this Act, a share patent confers upon the holder rights proportionate to their designated share, as recorded in the Register of Patents. The extent of such rights may include, but is not limited to, the privilege of exploiting the invention commercially and enforcing the patent against infringement, subject to any contractual agreements between co-patent holders. Assignment or licensing of a share patent shall require consent from all registered co-holders unless otherwise stipulated under this Act; provided that a court may determine equitable distribution in cases of dispute.

Where a patent relating to any invention has been jointly assigned or licensed to multiple entities, such assignment or license shall be deemed to create a share patent amongst those assignees or licensees. The Register may, upon application by any assignee or licensee holding a share patent, record the extent of their respective rights and interests in the public register maintained under this Act. Any transfer or disposal of a share patent shall require prior notification to the Register, detailing the proportion transferred and the identity of the transferee. Further, where disputes arise concerning the valuation or distribution of proceeds generated from an invention subject to a share patent, the Controller may intervene to facilitate resolution, provided that all parties consent to such intervention as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted jointly to multiple applicants, each applicant shall be deemed to hold a share patent proportionate to their contribution towards the invention, as determined by a resolution passed at a general meeting of the patentees and recorded with the Controller. Subject to this Act, any patentee holding a share patent may assign or license their interest without requiring consent from other co-patentees, provided that such assignment or license does not prejudice the rights of others in respect of the invention as a whole. Any action taken by a patentee concerning their share patent shall be subject to judicial review if another patentee demonstrates demonstrable harm resulting from said action. Further, where a dispute arises regarding the valuation of contributions towards an invention, the Intellectual Property Disputes Tribunal may be approached for resolution and determination of appropriate compensation.
