Where a patent relating to an invention has been jointly assigned or licensed to multiple entities, such assignment or license shall be deemed to create a share patent amongst those assignees or licensees. The Controller may, upon application by any assignee or licensee holding a share patent, investigate the terms of the original assignment or license agreement concerning the allocation of rights and responsibilities pertaining to that share. Such investigation is subject to the applicant demonstrating a dispute regarding the exercise of said rights under this Act. Further, where an agreement relating to the share patent is silent on matters of exploitation or enforcement, the Controller shall determine reasonable terms based on industry practice and the nature of the invention. Any party aggrieved by the Controller’s determination may appeal as provided herein. The Controller's decision regarding a share patent shall be final, subject to judicial review only on grounds of legal error.

Where a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition has been jointly applied for by multiple applicants, and a share patent is subsequently declared under this Act, the Controller may, upon application by any one applicant demonstrating undue hardship, permit the transfer of a portion or all of that applicant’s interest in the patent. Such transfer shall be subject to prior written consent from each remaining co-patentee unless it can be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Controller that such consent is unobtainable after reasonable attempts. The application for permission to transfer must detail the financial circumstances justifying the request and provide evidence of diligent efforts made to secure agreement amongst all parties. Any share patent so transferred shall remain subject to the terms and conditions applicable under this Act, as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted jointly to multiple applicants, constituting a share patent, the rights pertaining thereto shall be held by those patentees subject to any contractual agreements executed prior to grant. Any infringement of the patent shall constitute an infringement by all co-patentees and may be pursued through legal action initiated by any one or more of them. The Controller may, upon application from a co-patentee alleging unfair prejudice arising from another’s actions relating to the share patent, issue directions restricting such conduct as provided herein. Failure to comply with these directions shall render the offending party liable for penalties and damages proportionate to their contribution towards the invention's development, as determined by the Controller.

Where a patent is jointly owned by multiple applicants, each owner shall hold an equal share patent in the invention, subject to any contractual agreements executed prior to the grant. Such agreements may specify varying percentages of ownership and define rights pertaining to exploitation of the patented invention. The Controller may, upon application from one or more joint owners, facilitate the transfer or assignment of a share patent to another party, provided that all other co-owners consent in writing or demonstrate an inability to participate in the commercialization efforts. Any license granted by one joint owner shall be deemed to bind all other joint owners unless explicitly excluded within the original agreement establishing the share patent arrangement. Further, any action taken concerning the patent’s enforcement requires the collective authorization of the holders of a majority share patent interest.

Where a patent relating to any invention is jointly owned by multiple patentees, they shall hold such ownership as share patents, subject to a written agreement specifying the respective rights and obligations of each co-owner. Disputes concerning the interpretation or enforcement of such agreements may be referred to arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, provided that either party furnishes evidence demonstrating good faith efforts toward amicable resolution prior to initiating legal proceedings. The Controller shall entertain applications for revocation challenging the validity of a share patent only if it is demonstrated that the agreement governing the co-ownership was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, and that such deception materially impacted the inventive step claimed in the patent.

Where a patent relating to an invention is held jointly by multiple patentees, constituting a share patent, any party claiming entitlement to such a share may institute proceedings under this Act seeking determination of their rightful proportion. The Controller General shall, upon receiving such claim, issue notice to all registered co-owners and interested parties, affording them opportunity for objection. Failure to disclose the true name of a claimant during these proceedings will render that claim inadmissible. Any person found to have misrepresented their interest or attempted to fraudulently acquire a share patent through false declarations shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs of rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Enforcement of rights pertaining to a share patent is subject to the provisions regarding limitation and jurisdiction as provided herein.

Where a patent relating to a pharmaceutical composition is held as a share patent by multiple entities, the holder may grant non-exclusive licenses under the patent, provided that such licenses do not diminish the rights of co-patent holders without their express written consent. Any assignment of the entire or substantial portion of the share patent shall require unanimous agreement amongst all registered proprietors and be recorded with the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks. Failure to obtain such consent or record the assignment as provided herein shall render the assignor liable for a commission offence attributable to unauthorized disposition of intellectual property rights. Further, any licensee may sub-license the patented technology subject to terms approved by all share patent holders, ensuring equitable distribution of benefits derived from commercial exploitation.

Where a patent relating to a process or composition for producing a substance has been granted jointly to multiple applicants, the rights conferred by such patent shall be deemed to constitute a share patent, divisible amongst the co-patentees. Subject to any contractual agreements between them, no co-patentee may grant a licence patent covering the entire subject matter of the invention without the consent of all other co-patentees; however, a partial license may be granted with written notification to the others. Any dispute arising regarding the validity or enforcement of such share patent, including disagreements concerning the granting of licences, shall be resolved by arbitration as provided herein, and any award made therein may be challenged in the High Court on grounds specified under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person may grant a holder licence patent relating to an invention for a term specified therein, provided that such grant shall be documented in writing and registered with the Controller. The terms of the holder licence patent, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by mutual agreement between the patentee and the licensee, subject to principles of fairness and equity as may be prescribed. Further, where the invention is required for national security or public health purposes, the Central Government may, after due inquiry and affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, modify the terms of such a holder licence patent. The Controller shall not register any agreement that appears discriminatory or contrary to the interests of promoting innovation within India.

Any party aggrieved by an infringement of a patent, or by any act likely to constitute an infringement, may institute suit in the competent civil court. Where a person has obtained a holder licence patent and subsequently engages in activities infringing upon the rights granted under the primary patent, such actions shall be deemed actionable as direct infringement. The Controller may, subject to due process, issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement or mandating reasonable licensing terms where exploitation is demonstrably restricted. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act shall render the defaulter liable for a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees and continuing violations may attract daily penalties up to ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved.

Where any licensee challenges the validity of a patent, or seeks revocation thereof, under this Act, such challenge shall be predicated upon grounds specified herein and supported by evidence demonstrating substantial prejudice arising directly from the actions or omissions of the patentee. The Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, permit an intervention by any third party claiming interest in the patent, provided that such intervening party demonstrates a clear and demonstrable economic detriment attributable to the continued enforcement of the patent. It is further provided that the holder licence patent shall be deemed to have waived their right to contest the validity if they fail to respond within sixty days to a notice served under this provision, unless exceptional circumstances are established before the Appellate Board.

An applicant seeking rectification of a registered trade mark shall file an application in the registrar prescribed manner, supported by all relevant documents establishing grounds for relief. Such application must specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the nature of the alleged error or misrepresentation. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the registered proprietor and any other interested parties as he deems appropriate, conduct such inquiries as are necessary to determine the merits of the application. Failure by an applicant to comply with the requirements for filing under this Act shall render the application void. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning rectification proceedings may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of that decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed trade mark shall submit all required documentation in the registrar prescribed manner, including but not limited to, a clear representation of the mark, a list of goods or services with which it is intended to be associated, and details of prior use, if any. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant at any stage of the examination process, and failure to provide such information within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable for rejection. Any representation submitted electronically must conform precisely to the technical specifications published by the registrar periodically on the official website. Where a trade mark is deemed descriptive of the goods or services, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through evidence of extensive use and consumer recognition, as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a proposed trade mark shall furnish particulars of the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought, classifying them according to the International Classification of Goods and Services as prescribed by the Regulations. Such classification must adhere strictly to the terms defined therein; any deviation will render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the nature of the goods or services if deemed necessary to ascertain their proper categorization. Applications submitted in a manner not conforming to the registrar prescribed manner, including deficiencies in the specified forms and accompanying documentation, shall be deemed invalid and subject to immediate dismissal without further notice to the applicant.

Any person seeking to file a document with the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark shall do so in the registrar prescribed manner, utilizing forms specified on the Trade Marks Registry website and accompanied by all requisite fees as detailed in Schedule I. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render the application void ab initio, precluding any subsequent consideration thereof. Where an applicant knowingly or wilfully submits a false statement within such a document, they shall be liable for penalties not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees and may face prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar is empowered to reject applications demonstrably lacking in clarity or completeness, without providing opportunity for amendment.

The registered proprietor of a trademark shall have the right to assign the entire interest in the mark, including any associated goodwill, to another party, provided that such assignment is executed in the prescribed manner and duly recorded with the Registrar. Further, a license granting rights to use the trademark may be granted subject to conditions stipulated therein, which conditions are binding on both the grantor and licensee. Any sub-license of such rights shall also adhere to the registrar prescribed manner for recording and notification. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to him that the assignee or licensee has sufficient resources and expertise to protect the reputation and distinctiveness of the trademark. Failure to comply with these requirements may render any assignment or license voidable at the instance of a third party claiming rights under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered trade mark” includes any mark which has been duly registered under this Act in the name of a person and is currently reflected on the Register of Trade Marks. The proprietor registered trade mark shall be deemed to possess exclusive rights to use the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any prior usage or registration as provided herein. Any alteration to a registered trade mark, whether in respect of representation, meaning or legal effect, shall require notification and approval from the Trade Marks Registry. The proprietor registered trade mark may enforce these rights against infringement by any person using an identical or confusingly similar mark.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be made in good faith where the applicant has conducted a diligent search of existing registrations under this Act and prior usage records, and demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing that the proposed mark is distinctive. The Registrar may require an applicant claiming priority from a foreign application to furnish such evidence as he deems necessary to establish the existence and validity of the earlier registration. A proprietor registered trade mark confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register, subject to any rights previously acquired under this Act. Any alteration to the list of goods or services associated with a registered trade mark shall require notification to the Registrar and may be refused if deemed confusingly similar to existing marks.

Where a proprietor registered trade mark is infringed by the use of an identical or confusingly similar sign, such infringement shall constitute a cause of action and the proprietor may seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from further use of the offending sign. Damages adequate to compensate for the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement shall be recoverable under this Act, subject to limitations prescribed herein regarding calculation of reasonable royalties in cases of demonstrably unavoidable similarity. Further, where such infringement is found to have resulted in dilution of distinctiveness of the proprietor registered trade mark, enhanced damages may be awarded not exceeding three times the amount of actual damages sustained. The proprietor shall also be entitled to an account of profits made by the infringer as a result of the infringing use, provided that the infringer knew or had reason to believe that the use was infringing.

Where a proprietor registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without the consent of the registered proprietor, and such use creates confusion or misrepresentation among the public concerning the origin, nature, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may file an application for rectification of the register with the relevant intellectual property office. The application shall specify the particulars of the infringing use and state the grounds upon which the rectification is sought. Upon receiving such an application, the office shall serve notice on the registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to respond and present counter-evidence. Subject to this Act, the office may order the removal of the offending entry from the register if it finds that the use complained of constitutes a violation of rights associated with the proprietor registered trade mark. The office shall provide reasons for its decision in writing.

The proprietor registered trade mark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of application, subject to renewal as provided herein. Renewal may be effected by tendering the prescribed fee within one hundred and eighty days preceding the expiration of the registration. Where the applicant has failed to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered continuously for a period of five years, any person claiming an interest shall be entitled to apply to the relevant authority requesting cancellation of the said proprietor registered trade mark. Such application must demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the non-use. The Registrar may require evidence substantiating such claim before proceeding with consideration under this Act.

Any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark is a proprietor registered trade, uses such trade mark in connection with goods or services without the consent of the proprietor shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Where any infringing use occurs after the proprietor has given notice specifying the nature of the infringement, the offender shall also be liable to pay damages to the proprietor. Further, where goods are knowingly offered for sale or exposed for hire or otherwise made available for use bearing a false trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a proprietor registered trade, such goods shall be deemed forfeited and may be destroyed under this Act.

The proprietor registered trade mark may grant a license to use the trade mark for goods or services, subject to any limitations specified in the license agreement and consistent with the protection afforded under this Act. Such licenses shall be assignable along with the underlying proprietorship of the trade mark, provided that notice of assignment is filed with the Registrar within three months of the transfer. Any person acquiring a license through assignment shall hold such rights as were granted to the original licensee, subject to any conditions imposed by the proprietor at the time of initial licensing or subsequent amendment. The proprietor may impose reasonable royalties and other considerations for the grant of licenses, and failure to comply with these terms constitutes a breach of contract actionable under general principles of law. Further, sub-licensing shall be permissible only with express written consent from the original proprietor.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark by the Trade Marks Registry, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to file their written submissions in response to said objection. Such submissions must address each material point raised and may include evidence supporting the distinctiveness of the proposed trade mark or demonstrating acquired reputation thereof. The Registrar shall consider these submissions alongside the original grounds for objection and may, after providing notice to both objector and applicant, uphold, modify, or dismiss the objection. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, provided that the appeal shall be on grounds specified in the Act. The proprietor registered trade mark holder retains all rights as conferred herein.

Where an appeal is filed under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed trade mark, the Appellate Board may, upon hearing the appellant and the respondent, allow the appeal and direct the Registrar to proceed with the examination of the application for registration, or may dismiss the appeal. It shall be open to the Respondent to demonstrate that the proprietor registered trade in question is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers due to a similarity with an earlier mark used in connection with export patented pharmaceutical products. The Board shall consider evidence presented regarding actual consumer perception and market conditions. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court, subject to such terms as the High Court deems fit.

For the purposes of this Act, a proprietor registered trade mark includes any person who is entered on the Register of Trade Marks as the registered owner of the mark and holds exclusive rights therein, subject to any limitation or restriction specified in the register. Where an amendment specification relating to a registered trade mark is filed with the Registrar, it shall be deemed to constitute a request for alteration of the particulars of registration; provided that such amendment does not extend the description of goods or services associated with the proprietor registered trade mark beyond those already covered under this Act. The Registrar may require further information regarding any proposed amendment specification before proceeding with its consideration.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the examiner finds that the proposed trade mark is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark. However, where the applicant can demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through extensive use prior to the filing date of the examination application patent relating to the earlier registered trade mark, the Registrar may direct acceptance of the new application. The proprietor registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement under this Act against any person using a sign identical or similar in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registration is sought. Such use shall constitute an unfair advantage and dilution of the distinctive character of the earlier mark.

Where a proprietor registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services not identical with those specified in the registration, an application for the removal of the mark from the Register may be made to the Registrar by any person claiming interest. Such application shall state the grounds upon which it is based and shall include evidence demonstrating non-use of the proprietor registered trade mark for a continuous period of five years immediately preceding the date of the application. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant for removal and affording him an opportunity of being heard, direct that the mark be removed from the Register if satisfied that the grounds for removal have been established. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The mark registered goods shall remain subject to these provisions regarding potential removal from the register.

For the purposes of this Act, a “design” shall include any composition or arrangement of lines or colours or shapes or forms applied to any article in two-dimensional or three-dimensional form, whether or not aesthetic. The Controller may refuse registration if he deems that the design is primarily functional and lacks originality, provided that such refusal does not apply where the design incorporates elements essential for its utility. Further, a design shall be deemed invalid if it contains matter which is scandalous or obscene, or which is likely to offend the religious susceptibilities of any class of persons in India, or if its registration would be prejudicial to the interest of the security of India.

An application for registration of a design shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant, being a foreign national, fails to provide documentary evidence satisfactory to the Registrar establishing continuous commercial presence within India or demonstrating substantial investment in manufacturing infrastructure supporting the proposed design’s production. The Registrar may require further declarations under oath regarding the origin and intended use of the design. Provided that, where a design is deemed essential for maintaining the security of India, as determined by the Central Government acting on advice from the Ministry of Home Affairs, such procedural requirements relating to commercial presence or investment may be waived at the discretion of the Registrar. The applicant shall remain liable to provide any information requested by the Controller in relation to this determination.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered design shall furnish an affidavit verifying the grounds for such application, detailing all relevant circumstances pertaining to alleged infringement or misrepresentation. Provided that, if the Controller reasonably believes that the rectification sought could compromise the interest of the security of India, he may direct the proprietor to submit further documentation and appear before him in person, at his own expense. Failure to comply with such a direction shall render the application void ab initio. The Central Government may, acting upon intelligence received from designated national agencies, issue an order temporarily suspending the enforcement of design rights where it is deemed necessary for safeguarding critical infrastructure or essential services. Such orders shall be subject to judicial review under this Act.

The Controller shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a design, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the design is capable of being registered under this Act. Where it appears to the Controller that the registration of a design would be prejudicial to the interest of the security of India, or likely to affect public order, he may direct the Registrar to refuse the registration and shall provide reasons for such refusal in writing to the applicant. Any party aggrieved by an order refusing registration under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe guidelines regarding the assessment of potential threats to national security arising from registered designs. Information submitted during examination shall be treated as confidential and not disclosed unless required for proceedings before the Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the Controller may refuse registration of a design if he deems that its use or importation would be detrimental to the interests of the security of India. Such determination shall be based on an assessment of whether the design incorporates elements directly related to military insignia, national emblems, or confidential technological processes essential for defense preparedness. Provided that, any objection raised under this provision must be accompanied by a written justification detailing the specific threat posed and supported by evidence from relevant governmental agencies. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with an opportunity to respond to such objections before a final decision is rendered. Furthermore, appeals against decisions made on grounds of security of India are subject to review only by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person found to be engaging in activities related to the reproduction, adaptation, or commercial exploitation of registered designs that are deemed detrimental to the security of India shall be liable for prosecution under this Act and relevant penal codes. The Controller, acting upon information received from designated intelligence agencies, may issue directives restricting access to design registration records and imposing limitations on the import and export of goods bearing protected designs if such actions are necessary to safeguard national interests. Failure to comply with these directives will constitute a punishable offense, subject to fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years. The Central Government shall have the power to seize any infringing articles found in violation as provided herein.

The Controller shall grant licenses for the exploitation of registered designs where an application is made by a foreign national or entity demonstrating substantial investment in manufacturing infrastructure within India, provided that such license explicitly stipulates adherence to quality standards as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards. Any assignment of design rights undertaken pursuant to a license granted under this Act requires prior approval from the Central Government, particularly when the assignee holds interests in sectors deemed critical for the security of India, including but not limited to aerospace and defense technologies. The government may impose conditions on such assignments, restricting sub-licensing or further transfers without explicit authorization. Failure to comply with these stipulations renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Central Government.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, where an objection is raised against the registration of a design on the ground that its use or reproduction would be detrimental to the interests of the security of India, the Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard. The applicant may present evidence and arguments demonstrating why such concerns are unfounded or disproportionate to the potential benefit derived from the registered design. Subject to this, if, after considering all submissions, the Controller remains satisfied that a reasonable apprehension exists regarding a threat to national security arising directly from the design’s application, registration shall be refused. Any party aggrieved by an order of refusal may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "entitled produce variety" means a plant variety that has been officially recognized by the National Plant Variety Registry as possessing unique characteristics demonstrably linked to traditional agricultural practices within a geographically defined region of India. The Registrar shall have the power to refuse registration of any design relating to an entitled produce variety if such registration would reasonably be deemed detrimental to the interest of the security of India, considering factors including but not limited to national food security and preservation of indigenous knowledge systems. Any appeal against such refusal may be made as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall be entitled to sue for infringement of a registered design unless he has complied with all procedural requirements relating to the application for and grant of registration. Provided that, where an act constituting infringement occurs prior to the publication of the acceptance of the design for registration under this Act, but after the date of filing of the application, remedies shall be available as if the design had been registered on the date of filing the application. Furthermore, the Central Government may, in instances deemed prejudicial to the security of India, issue directives restricting or suspending the enforcement of design rights, and such directives shall have the force of law. The layout design government agencies are obligated to report any suspected infringement impacting national interests directly to the relevant authorities for investigation and appropriate action.

Any person found to be engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or application of registered designs relating to military equipment, critical infrastructure components, or systems vital to national defense shall be deemed guilty of an offense against this Act. Such offenses are particularly egregious when undertaken with the intent to compromise the security of India or undermine its strategic interests. Where it is established that a design infringement constitutes a threat to public order or involves a condition declared unlawful by the Central Government, the infringing party shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than five years and a fine exceeding fifty lakhs of rupees. Further, any assets derived from such illicit activities are subject to seizure under procedures as provided herein.

For the purpose of determining copyright infringement under this Act, "publication" shall mean the reproduction and dissemination of a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work in a form accessible to the understanding of the public through sale, lease, loan, gratuitous distribution, or otherwise. A work shall be deemed published when copies are offered for sale or distributed without authorization from the owner of copyright therein. Provided that, making available electronically on a digital network, irrespective of whether such availability is restricted by password or other means, shall also constitute publication. This definition applies equally to works initially disseminated within India and those originating elsewhere.

For the purposes of this Act, where an applicant seeks registration of copyright in respect of a literary or artistic work, it shall be deemed that such work has been published if copies thereof have been offered for sale or distributed to the public within India. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating the extent and nature of said distribution, including details regarding venues of exhibition or points of sale where the work was made available. Provided that, a private display of the work to a limited audience, not intended for wider dissemination, shall not be considered publication under this Act. Furthermore, an electronic offering accessible via a secure password system does not constitute publication unless expressly authorized by the applicant in writing during the registration process.

Where any copyrighted work has been made available to the public without authorization through unauthorized publication, the copyright owner shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining further acts of such publication. Provided that, where the infringing publication constitutes a fair dealing with the work for purposes of criticism or review, or for reporting current events, such relief may be refused if it is demonstrated that the use has been undertaken in good faith and without undue prejudice to the rights of the copyright owner under this Act. The remedies available to the copyright owner shall include damages equivalent to any actual losses suffered by reason of the infringement, or where ascertainment of such losses is not reasonably possible, a sum as the Court deems just and equitable. Any person found guilty of contributory infringement relating to unauthorized publication shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Where any literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work has been published outside India, it shall be deemed to have been first published in India if such publication was made prior to the date on which copyright subsists under this Act and if a copy of the work was simultaneously offered for sale or distributed within India. The Registrar may require evidence satisfactory to him demonstrating the circumstances surrounding such overseas publication, including dates and locations where copies were disseminated. Provided that, where the initial publication outside India was undertaken without any commercial gain accruing to the author or publisher, and subsequent distribution in India is initiated by a party other than the original author or publisher, the Registrar may, after due inquiry and notice to all interested parties, determine whether such overseas act constitutes valid publication under this Act. Any appeal against an order of the Registrar concerning the determination of publication shall lie before the relevant High Court.

For the purposes of determining whether a work has been brought into the public domain, publication shall be deemed to have occurred when copies of the work are offered for sale or distributed free of charge to the public within India, or when the work is otherwise made available to the public through any medium whatsoever. Provided that, where a work is initially published outside of India and subsequently imported into India without authorization from the copyright owner, such importation shall not constitute publication under this Act unless accompanied by an offer for sale or distribution within Indian territory. Furthermore, any unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a work displayed publicly via digital means, accessible to the general public, may be considered equivalent to publication, subject to verification by the Controller.

Where any person publishes an infringing copy of a copyrighted work without authorization from the copyright owner, such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable for damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable through civil suit in addition to any criminal penalties as may be prescribed under this Act. Provided that, where the publication is undertaken by a commercial entity with demonstrable intent to profit from the infringing activity, the court may award punitive damages up to ten times the actual damages proven. Any individual or organization facilitating such unauthorized publication shall also be subject to prosecution and liability for contributory infringement, as provided herein. The copyright owner shall have standing to seek injunctive relief preventing further publication of the infringing work.

Where any copyright in a literary or artistic work has been assigned or licensed under this Act, the assignor or licensor shall retain the right to grant non-exclusive licenses for reproduction and distribution only if such assignment or license expressly provides for it; provided that where the original author’s consent was not obtained prior to publication of the work, any subsequent licensing arrangement relating to public performance rights shall be deemed exclusive. Further, a person claiming an interest in copyright by virtue of a previous publication may grant a further assignment or licence subject to the terms and conditions stipulated therein. Any such subsequent assignment or license shall not prejudice existing rights held by prior assignees or licensees unless explicitly waived within the documentation governing those earlier interests. The right to control adaptation of the work remains with the original copyright holder, irrespective of any licensing agreements concerning its initial publication.

Where the copyright subsists in a work published anonymously or pseudonymously, any person claiming to be the first publisher thereof shall be deemed the owner of the copyright therein unless he proves that he was not aware of the identity of the author and had no reasonable grounds for believing himself to be the first publisher. An appeal against such determination may be made to the relevant High Court within ninety days from the date of the order, provided that the appellant demonstrates prejudice arising directly from the decision under challenge. The burden of proof regarding lack of awareness shall rest entirely upon the claimant seeking recognition as first publisher; and this provision shall not preclude a subsequent author from establishing prior publication elsewhere.

Where any person claiming to be the copyright proprietor of a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work alleges that such work has been reproduced without authorization, it shall be presumed, pending proof to the contrary, that the said work was published with the intention of gaining profit and in violation of the rights vested in the claimant. The claimant may pursue remedies available under this Act for infringement, including an injunction restraining further reproduction or distribution, and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the unauthorized publication. Provided that, where the infringing act involves the use of a trade mark registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, in connection with the copyrighted work, the claimant shall be entitled to claim additional damages reflecting the dilution of goodwill associated with their proprietor trade mark. The burden of proving authorization rests upon the person alleged to have reproduced and published without consent.

The term "publication," for the purposes of this Act, shall mean the reproduction of a work in tangible form and its dissemination to the public, whether through sale, distribution, rental, lending, or any other means that makes it accessible to members of the public beyond a limited circle of individuals present at the time of communication. A work shall be deemed published when such copies have been made available for use or enjoyment by the public. Any person claiming copyright in a work prior to its publication may register their claim with the designated office, submitting prescribed particulars and supporting documentation as provided herein. Such registration shall not, however, confer any additional rights beyond those already vested under this Act. The Registrar of Copyrights may require further evidence to substantiate the claim and may reject the application if it finds that the work has already been published or that the claimant lacks sufficient title.

Where any person publishes any work infringing upon the copyright therein subsisting, such person shall be deemed to have committed a civil offence under this Act. The penalty for first-time offenders shall be imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Subsequent offences will attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer, subject to judicial review. Further, any entity engaged in the commercial exploitation of works obtained through unauthorized publication is liable to pay damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty that would have been payable had due diligence regarding patent rights and copyright clearances been exercised. The court may also order seizure and destruction of infringing copies.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to request permission from the Registrar to amend particulars contained within their application. Such amendment may include alterations to the representation of the mark, the list of goods or services associated with it, or any other detail specified in the prescribed forms. The Registrar shall consider such requests and may grant an application permit amendment if satisfied that the proposed change does not substantially alter the character of the trade mark sought to be registered nor prejudice the interests of prior registrants. Any amendment permitted under this Act must adhere to relevant statutory requirements regarding clarity and distinctiveness.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to request the Registrar to allow an amendment to their application at any stage of the proceedings, subject to compliance with the provisions herein relating to distinctiveness and acceptable representation of the mark. Such requests may include alterations to the identification of goods or services associated with the trade mark, clarification of the description of the trade mark itself, or adjustments to the claimed geographical extent of protection. The Registrar shall consider such amendment requests in light of whether they are merely clerical corrections or constitute substantive changes impacting the registrability criteria as defined under this Act. An application permit amendment only if it does not prejudice any prior rights or existing registrations.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to request the Registrar for permission to amend their application, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the character of the goods or services specified therein. The Registrar may grant or refuse such an application permit amendment at his discretion, considering whether the proposed alteration is merely clerical or affects the distinctiveness of the mark as claimed. Where a refusal is made, the reasons for such decision shall be recorded in writing and communicated to the applicant without delay. Any party opposing the trade mark registration may submit objections to any proposed amendment within thirty days of notification under this Act. The Registrar shall consider these submissions before making a final determination regarding the requested alteration.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to submit a request for amendment of their application, provided such request is made within six months from the date of publication under this Act. The Registrar may entertain an application permit amendment if satisfied that the proposed alteration does not substantially affect the identity of goods or services for which the trade mark is sought and does not mislead consumers as to the nature, quality or origin of those goods or services. Any such request shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a clear statement detailing the existing representation and the intended modification. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant before determining whether to grant the application permit amendment. Decisions regarding amendments are subject to appeal under procedures as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to assign, license, or otherwise transfer their interest in the pending application subject to the provisions herein relating to conflicting marks. Such assignment or license agreement must be filed with the Trade Marks Registry and shall become publicly accessible. The Registrar may, upon review of such documentation, require further clarification regarding the scope and duration of any licensed rights granted. Further, an application permit amendment if it is demonstrated that the proposed alteration does not substantially depart from the original intention as reflected in the initial application form or subsequent correspondence with the Registry. Any third party possessing a beneficial interest in the trade mark application may be heard under this Act regarding such amendments and assignments.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have constructively consented to the introduction of alterations to their submitted representation, provided that such alteration does not fundamentally alter the distinctive character claimed for the mark and is consistent with the goods or services specified in the application. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, refuse an amendment if it determines that the proposed change introduces a new trade mark or substantially departs from the original specification. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar permitting or refusing an application permit amendment may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of such determination, subject to payment of prescribed fees and demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the Registry’s action.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark may, at any time during the pendency of the application and subject to compliance with prescribed forms and fees, apply to the Registrar for permission to amend the representation of goods or services specified in the application. Such amendment shall not alter the character of the trade mark itself nor extend the scope of protection sought beyond that which was reasonably contemplated at the time of filing. The Registrar may allow an application permit amendment if satisfied that the proposed alteration does not prejudice any prior right or create confusion amongst consumers, and provided that the amended list is consistent with the International Classification of Goods and Services under this Act. Any party adversely affected by such permission may within sixty days file a representation before the Registrar contesting the allowance. The register sub section pertaining to pending applications shall be updated accordingly upon approval of the amendment.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have acted in bad faith if, following the filing of their initial application, they subsequently seek permission to amend said application in a manner that substantially alters the goods or services for which protection is claimed. Such amendment requests will be scrutinized with particular diligence where the original application was filed with insufficient specificity regarding these particulars. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision granting or denying an application permit amendment may appeal under this Act, and shall be liable to pay a penalty of fifty thousand rupees if found to have misrepresented facts in support of their appeal. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to amendment requests will render the application vulnerable to cancellation.

An applicant for registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions herein and upon payment of such fees as may be prescribed, apply to have an application permit amendment relating to the goods or services specified in the application, or any class thereof. Such amendment shall not alter the fundamental character of the trade mark or extend its scope beyond that which would be permissible under this Act without further consent. Where a license has been granted permitting such amendment, and the amended trade mark is subsequently assigned to another party, the assignee shall hold the benefit of said permission as if they were the original applicant. Any dispute concerning the validity of an application permit amendment may be referred to the High Court for determination, whose decision shall be final.

For the purposes of this Act, “case registration valid” means that a trade mark application, once registered following examination and opposition proceedings, shall be deemed conclusively valid against all persons except in cases where fraud has been proven before an intellectual property tribunal. Such validity is subject to any order made under this Act concerning rectification or revocation. An appeal from an order determining case registration valid may only be brought within ninety days of the date of such order. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding the apparent invalidity of a registered trade mark, initiate inquiries as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall include a statement of disclaimer of any right or interest in respect of any element of the mark, and where such disclaimer is made, it shall be recorded on the register. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend their application to clarify the scope of goods or services associated with the proposed mark, ensuring distinctiveness under this Act. Upon satisfactory completion of examination and publication, and subject to no opposition being filed within the prescribed period, a certificate of registration shall be issued. This certificate confirms the case registration valid for the trademark as described in the schedule annexed thereto, granting exclusive rights to the applicant concerning use and application thereof. Any alteration to the registered mark requires prior approval from the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of a proposed trade mark has been filed and subsequently entered upon the register, any person aggrieved by reason of that *case registration valid* may institute proceedings in the Commercial Courts seeking a declaration that such registration is invalid. Such proceedings shall be deemed to be civil suits governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The applicant for the declaration must demonstrate a special damage directly attributable to the registered trade mark’s use or threatened use; mere inconvenience or indirect competition shall not suffice as grounds for challenge. Provided that the aggrieved person demonstrates standing and provides sufficient evidence substantiating their claim, the Court may order rectification of the register removing the challenged entry. The costs of such proceedings shall be determined by the court based on the merits of the case and the conduct of the parties involved.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a request for case registration valid in respect of goods or services to which the trade mark relates. Upon receipt of such an application, the Trade Marks Registry shall publish a notice indicating the acceptance of the application and inviting objections under this Act. Any party considering the requested case registration invalid may file a written opposition within the prescribed period, stating the grounds for objection and supported by relevant evidence. The Registrar shall provide the applicant with a copy of any such opposition.

The applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the opposition in writing, submitting counter-statements and supporting documentation as deemed necessary. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar may direct a hearing to be held before an officer duly authorized for this purpose. The decision regarding the validity of the case registration shall be recorded by the Registrar and communicated to all parties involved, subject to appeal under provisions outlined herein.

The owner of a registered trade mark may grant licences conferring specific rights to use the trade mark in relation to particular goods or services, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licence agreement. Such licences shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that prior written consent from the Registrar is obtained, detailing the scope of assignment and any associated modifications to existing user agreements. Where a case registration valid has been established for a trade mark, subsequent assignments affecting rights relating to colour marks require notification to the Registrar within thirty days, outlining the transferee’s intention regarding continued use and maintenance of the registered colours. Any alteration to the licensed territory or scope of goods/services necessitates further approval from the Registrar before becoming effective against third parties. The owner retains ultimate control over quality assurance pertaining to products sold under a licensed trade mark.

Where a proprietor seeks to license or assign rights in a registered trademark under this Act, and the proposed licensee or assignee is engaged in the manufacture or sale of goods or services that utilize the distinctive shape associated with the mark, such licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the permitted scope of use. The Registrar may require submission of detailed plans illustrating how the trade marks shape will be replicated or adapted by the licensee, ensuring consistency with the registered design and preventing dilution of brand identity. Further, any case registration valid for assignment must include a declaration from both proprietor and assignee confirming adherence to these stipulations. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed use does not mislead consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods or services, consent shall be deemed granted. The proprietor retains ultimate control over permissible alterations to the trade marks shape during the term of the license.

For the purposes of this Act, a “distinctive mark” means a sign or combination of signs that is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, and shall include, but not be limited to, words, names, symbols, devices, numerals, letters, shapes, configurations, patterns, or any combination thereof. A court may, in determining whether a mark is distinctive, consider the inherent distinctiveness of the mark, as well as its acquired distinctiveness through use in commerce. Nothing herein shall prevent a court from considering evidence relating to consumer perception and recognition when assessing distinctiveness; however, such considerations shall be secondary to established principles regarding genericness and descriptive terms. A compelled court say concerning market surveys is permissible only upon written application and judicial review.

The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark and after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, direct that certain marks appearing on the register be removed if it is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Registrar that such marks are deceptive or contrary to law. This direction shall only be issued following a compelled court say confirming the veracity of the evidence presented regarding the misleading nature of the mark and its potential impact upon consumers. The applicant seeking removal need not demonstrate actual consumer confusion, but must establish a reasonable likelihood thereof. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services without due cause, and such use constitutes an unfair appropriation of reputation or goodwill associated with the said trade mark, the aggrieved proprietor shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief under this Act. Such injunction may restrain not only the infringing party but also any person deriving benefit from the infringement, provided that the court is satisfied that the continued use would likely cause further damage to the registered trade mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. The court shall consider all relevant circumstances when determining whether a compelled court say by an expert witness regarding consumer perception is necessary for just adjudication of the matter; however, such compulsion will be limited to clarifying technical aspects directly impacting assessment of likelihood of confusion.

Any proprietor seeking enforcement of a trade mark under this Act, and who subsequently institutes proceedings alleging infringement or passing off, shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Court demonstrating reasonable grounds for believing that the defendant’s activities constitute an undue dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered mark. Failure to do so will render the proprietor liable to pay compensatory costs reflective of the defendant's legal expenses incurred in defending the action. The Court may, upon application by the defendant and after considering all relevant factors, issue a mandatory injunction compelling the plaintiff to disclose specific commercial data underpinning their claim; this compelled court say is permissible only where such disclosure is demonstrably necessary for a fair assessment of the case’s merits.

Where a registered trade mark proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act seeking relief from an alleged infringement, and the defendant asserts a defence founded upon prior honest concurrent use, the Court may, subject to the provisions herein relating to territoriality and reputation, require the proprietor to demonstrate that the continued use of the impugned mark by the defendant constitutes a substantial misrepresentation likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers. This compelled court say shall be undertaken in good faith and without prejudice to any subsequent appeal. Provided that, if the Court finds insufficient evidence supporting the proprietor’s claim of deception, it may order the defendant to undertake specific measures to mitigate potential consumer confusion, as deemed appropriate by the presiding officer.

Where a registered trade mark is alleged to be infringed, and the defendant asserts that the use of the impugned sign does not create confusion amongst the relevant consuming public, the Court shall require the plaintiff to demonstrate, through clear and convincing evidence, the extent of actual damage suffered as a direct consequence of such alleged infringement. This requirement applies irrespective of any prior declarations made in an application patent specification relating to similar goods or services. Failure by the plaintiff to satisfy this burden shall result in dismissal of the claim with costs awarded against them. The Court may, at its discretion, order inspection of sales records and consumer surveys to ascertain the veracity of the plaintiff’s claims; however, no officer shall be compelled court say regarding privileged commercial strategies employed during market analysis.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark, desiring to grant a license for use of their mark under conditions that extend beyond mere representation or sale, may execute an assignment agreement transferring such rights subject to the limitations prescribed herein. Such agreements shall clearly delineate the geographical scope and permitted goods or services covered by the license or assignment. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or extent of these permissions, a compelled court say regarding the proprietary interest in the trade mark shall be binding on all parties involved, irrespective of any prior representations made during registration proceedings. Furthermore, any unauthorized use of the registered trade mark, constituting a breach of the licensing agreement and demonstrably impacting the distinctiveness of the mark, may result in convicting direct forfeiture of the license granted, without prejudice to claims for damages under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark and after affording due opportunity to all interested parties to submit objections under this Act, direct that certain descriptive matter appearing within the proposed marks be expunged if such matter directly relates to the characteristics or qualities of the goods or services with which the applicant seeks association. Such direction shall not prejudice the registrability of the remaining elements of the mark, provided that the resultant mark possesses distinctiveness and is not deceptive. Where a party aggrieved by this compelled court say challenges the Registrar’s order before a judicial forum, the burden of proving the distinctiveness of the modified trade mark rests solely upon the applicant. This provision shall apply irrespective of whether the application relates to an ii India document or any other form of representation.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars specifying the name of the geographical indication as it is known to the applicant, a map of the area from which the goods originate, and a statement of the land, terroirs or other natural factors that contribute to the qualities or characteristics of the goods. The Registering Authority may require further information demonstrating the conformity of the goods with established standards, including production methods and quality control measures, as provided herein. Any person claiming rights in respect of a geographical indication may file an objection under this Act within three months from the date of publication of the application for registration. Such objections shall be considered by the Authority, ensuring due regard to the principles of geographical indication respect and fair trade practices.

An application for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a detailed report, prepared by an expert approved under sub-regulation (1), specifying the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of goods originating from the specified territory. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the territorial extent claimed and the production methods employed in relation to the goods. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, stating the grounds upon which such opposition is based. Where an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall provide all parties concerned with an opportunity for hearing. The grant of registration as a geographical indication respects the collective interests of producers within the defined territory and safeguards their traditional knowledge concerning those goods.

The owner of a registered geographical indication relating to Darjeeling tea may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the use of the indication on products other than Darjeeling tea, provided that such license explicitly restricts the licensed product’s marketing as originating from Darjeeling. Any assignment of rights in respect of a geographical indication shall require prior notification to the Registrar and registration of the transfer with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registrar may refuse registration of an assignment if it appears that the proposed assignee lacks the capacity or intention to protect the geographical indication's distinctiveness and reputation, upholding its inherent geographical indication respect. Further, any licensee granted rights under this Act shall be bound by conditions ensuring continued adherence to quality standards associated with the Darjeeling tea geographical indication.

The use of a geographical indication by any person other than an authorized user shall be permissible only if such use is consistent with the quality and reputation associated with that indication, and does not create confusion among consumers regarding the origin of the goods. An aggrieved party may file an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order under this Act, demonstrating demonstrable misrepresentation or unfair advantage derived from the unauthorized use. The Board shall consider evidence pertaining to consumer perception and market analysis in determining whether a violation of geographical indication respect has occurred; provided that the burden of proving such violation rests upon the appellant.

For the purposes of this Act, “geographical indication” means an indication which identifies goods as originating from a place where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of those goods is essentially attributable to their geographical origin. A geographical indication may consist exclusively of, or contain, as a predominant feature, words having geographical significance, including services specified alphabetically. The protection afforded by this Act shall extend to prevent the use of any such indication or false indications likely to deceive consumers regarding the true origin of goods. Provided that nothing in this definition shall apply to generic terms or expressions commonly used to describe those goods. Any alteration which misleads as to the geographical origin constitutes a violation of geographical indication respect.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the Darjeeling district and cultivated at an altitude not less than two thousand feet above mean sea level, conforming to established agricultural practices and possessing a characteristic flavour profile as determined by the Registration Authority; provided that any person or entity engaged in the production, processing, packaging, sale, or export of goods falsely claiming to be "Darjeeling Tea" shall be deemed to have committed an offence cognizable under the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), and subject to prosecution as if such act were a violation of this Act. The Registration Authority may specify further parameters for authenticity.

An application for registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes cultivated in the Konkan region of Maharashtra shall include detailed particulars regarding the agricultural practices employed, including irrigation methods and harvesting techniques, as certified by the Mango Growers’ Association of Konkan. The Registrar may require submission of maps delineating the precise geographical boundaries claimed under this Act, along with a declaration affirming adherence to traditional production standards. Any person found to be using a registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions herein shall be liable for prosecution under section 483 of the Indian Penal Code, and further subject to civil penalties as determined by the High Court. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence, initiate inquiries into alleged misuse.

Any proprietor registered as having exclusive right to use a geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, may institute civil proceedings for infringement under this Act and shall be entitled to seek remedies including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor or authorized user, and disposal of infringing goods. Provided that where an act constituting infringement also constitutes an offence under the Indian Penal Code, the offender shall be liable to prosecution under both this Act and the said penal code. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from any registered proprietor, direct law enforcement agencies to investigate suspected infringements and initiate appropriate action as deemed necessary. Further, costs of litigation relating to infringement proceedings shall be determined by the court considering the nature and extent of the infringement.

Any individual seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or beverages shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar, detailing the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services to which it relates, and the area of its origin. The applicant must also furnish particulars regarding the history, traditions, and characteristics of the indicated product, demonstrating a clear link between the product’s qualities and its specified geographical origin. Further, the application shall include a map of the relevant territory as determined by the Registrar. Any false or misleading statement in the application renders the applicant liable for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify authenticity and prevent fraudulent claims, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs shall provide detailed documentation substantiating the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable exclusively to the origin of the goods within the defined geographical area. Such documentation must include verifiable data regarding traditional farming practices and processing methods employed over a continuous period not less than twenty years prior to the date of application. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any act of use or imitation of a registered geographical indication by an unauthorized party, intended to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers, constitutes an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code and may attract civil penalties as provided herein.

Any individual or entity found to have made, used, sold, offered for sale, distributed, or imported goods falsely bearing a Geographical Indication registered under this Act shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing goods. Such actions constitute an offence cognizable by a Magistrate and are subject to prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, specifically provisions relating to fraud and cheating. Further, where the infringement is committed with the intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. The Registrar may also issue an injunction restraining further infringing activity as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication relating to Alphonso mangoes may, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, grant non-exclusive licenses in respect of the use of the said indication. Such license shall specify the territory within which the licensee is authorized to utilize the geographical indication and the goods or services to which such utilization pertains. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication, including assignments arising from the transfer of ownership of a licensed right, requires prior approval from the Registrar, provided that the assignee undertakes to observe all terms and conditions previously stipulated in any existing license agreement. Further, where an infringement of the geographical indication occurs through unauthorized use, the registered proprietor may pursue remedies available under this Act and also initiate proceedings under the Indian Penal Code for offences involving fraud or forgery related to the false representation of origin.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication alleging that such registration was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation, may file an application with the Geographical Indications Registry. Such application shall specify the particulars of the alleged fraudulent conduct and provide supporting evidence demonstrating material deception influencing the initial grant. The Registry shall serve notice upon the applicant whose registration is challenged, affording them opportunity to respond under this Act. Should the Registrar find merit in the allegations, rectification may be ordered; however, any party aggrieved by such order or refusal thereof, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days. Such appeal shall be subject to the provisions of the Indian Penal Code relating to false evidence and conspiracy where relevant.

For the purposes of this Act, “authorised user” means any person who has been granted a license or otherwise permitted by the registered proprietor of a geographical indication to use such indication in connection with goods belonging to the class specified in the registration; provided that an authorised user shall not be deemed to infringe under this Act if the use is consistent with the terms and conditions of the authorisation, and subject to compliance with all applicable laws. Any act involving the application or use of a registered geographical indication in a manner prejudicial to the public interest, or constituting an offence under the Indian Penal Code, shall be actionable as per provisions herein. Registration respect for authorised users is paramount.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or other goods as provided herein shall furnish with the application particulars detailing the quality and characteristics directly attributable to the origin of such goods within the defined geographical area. The Registrar may require submission of documentary evidence substantiating these claims, including historical records, traditional knowledge documentation, and scientific analyses. Further, any act of use of a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards prescribed under this Act or otherwise infringing upon the rights of the registered proprietor shall be deemed an offence cognizable under the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may also initiate proceedings for revocation of registration if it is established that the registered geographical indication has been misrepresented or obtained through fraudulent means, impacting its authenticity and consumer perception.

Any individual engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or dissemination of visual recordings depicting goods bearing a registered geographical indication, with the intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin of such goods, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act and may also face penalties as prescribed under the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register documenting all instances of suspected infringement involving visual recording evidence, available for inspection by authorized law enforcement agencies and aggrieved proprietors. Upon receiving a complaint substantiated by documented visual recordings demonstrating misleading use of a geographical indication, the Registrar shall promptly notify the relevant police authorities to initiate investigations. Further, any proprietor seeking recourse against such deceptive practices may submit authenticated copies of the visual recordings as prima facie evidence during proceedings before adjudicating officers.

For the purposes of this Act, an “affidavit provided registrar” means a statement made under oath before a person authorized to administer oaths, and submitted to the Registrar as prima facie proof of facts relevant to any application for registration, opposition thereto, or revocation proceedings. Such affidavit shall be in the prescribed form, clearly stating the identity of the deponent and the particulars of the facts affirmed. The Registrar may require production of original documents referred to in an affidavit provided registrar. Any false statement made within an affidavit provided registrar shall render the deponent liable for penalties as provided herein.
