The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall have the exclusive right to authorize the use of the indication upon any goods conforming to the standards as defined in the registration certificate. Any person seeking to utilize the geographical indication for commercial purposes must obtain prior written consent from the proprietor, and such authorization may be granted subject to royalty payments and other conditions stipulated within a licensing agreement. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and licenses relating to registered Geographical Indications. An affidavit provided registrar confirming the terms of any assignment or license is required before registration thereof, attesting to the veracity of the details furnished. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the authorization and potential legal action under this Act.

Subject to the provisions herein, the Register shall have the power, at his discretion, to permit correction of errors appearing in a registered layout design, provided that such correction does not alter the original character or essential features of the layout design as initially registered. For the purposes of this Act, “correction” means rectification of clerical mistakes, typographical errors, or minor inconsistencies arising during the registration process or subsequent administrative actions. Any application for permit correction shall be accompanied by a reasoned justification demonstrating that the proposed alteration does not substantively impact the protectable subject matter and is merely corrective in nature.

Where rectification of a registered layout-design is sought due to inadvertent errors introduced during registration, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and upon receiving written application from the registrant or any interested party, entertain such request. The applicant shall demonstrate that the proposed correction does not substantially alter the original design features as recorded in the register and does not prejudice the rights of third parties who have legitimately relied upon the registered layout-design. Any objection received under this Act regarding a permitted correction shall be adjudicated according to principles of natural justice, affording all concerned an opportunity for hearing. The Controller may allow or reject the application for permit correction after considering all relevant factors, provided that such decision is reasoned and recorded in writing.

An aggrieved party seeking rectification of a registered layout-design shall file an application before the Controller, setting forth the grounds for such rectification and supported by all relevant documentation demonstrating manifest errors or omissions impacting the validity or scope of protection afforded to the registered design. The application must specify the particulars of the error sought to be corrected or the amendment proposed, along with a clear articulation of how the rectification will align the register with the true intention of the original layout-design and consistent with principles of fairness and equity as provided herein. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties including the registered proprietor, permit correction of such errors or grant amendments if satisfied that they are necessitated by demonstrable inaccuracies or ambiguities. Any order permitting correction shall be published in the Official Gazette.

Subject to compliance with prescribed forms and procedures as provided herein, the Controller may, upon receiving a written request from the registered proprietor of a layout design, permit correction of errors appearing on the register relating to such layout design. Such correction shall be limited to typographical errors or inaccuracies in respect of details pertaining solely to identification of the layout design or the proprietor’s address; it shall not extend to alterations affecting the scope or validity of the registration itself. The Controller may require supporting documentation, including affidavits verifying the accuracy of the proposed correction, prior to granting permission. Any request for permit correction must be accompanied by the requisite fee as determined under this Act and will be considered only if all pending appeals relating to the layout design have been resolved.

Where rectification of a registered layout-design is sought by any interested party alleging inadvertent errors or omissions during registration proceedings, such request shall be submitted to the Controller within six months from the date of publication of the design in the Design Journal. The Controller may, after affording the registrant an opportunity for hearing and subject to satisfaction that the proposed correction does not substantially alter the registered layout-design or prejudice the rights of third parties, permit correction of the register. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to permit correction may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such decision. Failure to comply with these procedures shall render the rectification request inadmissible and subject the applicant to penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, the registered owner of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall be entitled to grant licenses permitting correction of the said layout-design. Such license may be granted for specific purposes, including but not limited to, error rectification during manufacturing processes or adaptation for compatibility with evolving technological standards. The terms and conditions of any such license, including royalty rates and duration, shall be determined by mutual agreement between the registered owner and the licensee; provided that a copy of the license agreement is filed with the Controller within thirty days of execution. Assignment of rights to permit correction may also occur as part of a broader transfer of ownership or intellectual property portfolio, subject to notification requirements as prescribed herein.

Where a registered layout design is found to contain inadvertent discrepancies attributable to clerical errors during registration proceedings, the Controller may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, permit correction of such errors without requiring fresh application and payment of prescribed fees. Provided that any proposed correction shall not substantively alter the original layout design as recorded in the Register of Layout Designs, nor introduce new matter not disclosed therein; and further provided that a notice of objection regarding the proposed correction may be filed by any interested party within thirty days from the date of publication of such proposal under this Act. The Tribunal’s decision on an appeal against an order permitting or refusing correction shall be final.

For the purposes of this Act, “critical infrastructure” with regard to semiconductor integrated circuits shall mean systems and assets, whether tangible or intangible, essential for the uninterrupted provision of services vital to national security, economic stability, public health or safety, or any other function deemed crucial by the Central Government. Information pertaining to layout-designs incorporated within critical infrastructure, including but not limited to design specifications, manufacturing processes, and testing protocols, shall be considered confidential. Disclosure of such information, whether intentional or negligent, is prohibited if it is determined that such disclosure would prejudice the interest of the security of India, subject to review by a designated appellate authority.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall furnish such documents and information as may be prescribed, including details pertaining to the origin of the design and its intended use. The Registrar may require an applicant to provide further clarification or documentation if deemed necessary for assessing compliance with the provisions herein. Registration shall not be granted if the Central Government, after due consideration, determines that the layout-design’s disclosure or registration would be prejudicial to the interest of the security of India. This determination shall be final and binding on the Registrar. The applicant shall have a right to appeal such a decision before an Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, subject to any conditions stipulated under this Act.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of a registered integrated circuit layout design may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Tribunal shall hear appeals expeditiously and may pass such orders as it deems fit, including directing compensation for any loss suffered due to the erroneous decision appealed against. Provided that, where an investigation is initiated by or on behalf of the Central Government concerning a suspected infringement impacting the interest of the security of India, no appeal under this Act shall be entertained until the conclusion of such investigation and subsequent report submitted. Further, the Central Government may, acting upon information received, issue directions to any person involved in the manufacture, import, or distribution of integrated circuits relating to measures necessary for safeguarding national interests.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Any person engaged in the examination or assessment of an integrated circuit layout-design for purposes of registration shall be deemed a public servant within the meaning of section 2(5)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. Such persons are prohibited from accepting any gratification, whether pecuniary or otherwise, and any violation thereof shall render them liable to prosecution under that Act. The Director-General may, subject to due process, issue directives concerning access to layout-design documentation submitted for registration, provided that such access is restricted where the information relates directly to technologies deemed critical infrastructure. Furthermore, the Central Government may, acting upon a report from the National Security Council Secretariat, direct the suspension of any registration proceedings or revoke an existing registration if it reasonably believes that continued processing or maintenance thereof would be detrimental to the interest of the security of India.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Any person engaged in the reverse engineering of an integrated circuit layout-design shall be subject to compliance verification by the Controller, at such intervals as may be prescribed. Such verification shall encompass assessment of all documentation pertaining to the design process, including but not limited to source code repositories and fabrication records. The Controller may require submission of a detailed report outlining the methodology employed for reverse engineering, along with justifications demonstrating adherence to fair practices. Failure to provide this information or demonstrable non-compliance with established protocols will trigger an inquiry into whether such actions are detrimental to the interest of the security of India. Any determination that reverse engineering poses a threat shall be reported immediately to the Central Government.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Any person found to be in possession of unauthorized copies or reproductions of a protected semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be subject to penalties as provided herein. Such reproduction is deemed unlawful where it reasonably appears that the act was undertaken with intent to manufacture integrated circuits for distribution within India, or for export, and such activity poses a demonstrable threat to the interest of the security of India. The Central Government may, upon receiving credible intelligence regarding potential infringement impacting national security, order the seizure of suspected infringing materials and equipment. Any individual failing to comply with an order issued under this Act shall be liable to further penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any licensee granted rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be obligated to provide reasonable access to relevant documentation pertaining to the design’s architecture and functionality to designated officers of the government. This provision is without prejudice to the security requirements stipulated herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe conditions for such licenses, including limitations on sub-licensing or assignment, particularly where the layout-design incorporates technology deemed critical to the interest of the security of India. Assignment of rights under a license shall require prior approval from the Controller General and will be subject to a royalty payment determined by the Central Government, proportionate to the original license fee. Any attempt to circumvent these provisions may result in revocation of the license and penalties as provided herein.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the Controller may, acting upon information received from an authorized intelligence agency of the Union, issue an order temporarily suspending the grant or continuation of protection to any integrated circuit layout design if such action is deemed necessary in the interest of the security of India. Such suspension shall remain valid for a period not exceeding six months, during which time the Controller shall conduct an inquiry and provide the applicant with a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Any party aggrieved by an order under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Tribunal shall consider any evidence presented demonstrating potential prejudice to national security before dismissing such an appeal.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, serve notice on the applicant and all other persons claiming interest in the design as provided herein. Such notice shall specify the grounds of rectification alleged and invite objections within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of publication of the notice in the Official Gazette. The Registrar may, after considering any objections received and affording an opportunity for hearing to all interested parties, proceed with the inquiry under this Act. Where the rectification sought involves allegations affecting the interest of the security of India, the Central Government shall be notified immediately, and the proceedings may be stayed pending further direction. Furthermore, in instances where a dispute arises concerning the validity of a layout-design registration, the Registrar shall appear before any adjudicating authority as a witness to testify regarding procedural compliance.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: An applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall furnish such documentation as is prescribed, demonstrating compliance with all applicable technical standards established by the Controller General. Provided that, where an international application patent corresponding to the claimed layout-design has been filed in a foreign country, the applicant must submit a certified copy of said international application patent alongside the required drawings and specifications. Further, registration may be refused or subsequent revocation ordered if it is determined that the layout-design’s disclosure, or its exploitation within India, would be detrimental to the interest of the security of India, as assessed by the Central Government acting upon advice from the Ministry of Defence.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: Any person found to have reproduced or exploited a protected integrated circuit layout design without authorization shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not exceeding five per cent of the plaintiff’s reasonable royalty losses, or one million rupees, whichever is greater. Furthermore, where such reproduction or exploitation demonstrably jeopardizes the interest of the security of India, as determined by the Central Government, the infringing party may also face prosecution under relevant penal provisions. The government shall have the power to grant patent protection for innovations incorporated within layout designs deemed critical to national technological advancement, provided that such grants do not conflict with existing obligations under this Act and are subject to rigorous review.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: The Controller may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating substantial investment in the development or adaptation of a protected integrated circuit layout design, grant a non-exclusive license to utilize such design for purposes directly related to national defense or critical infrastructure security. Such licenses shall be subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government, including limitations on sub-licensing and requirements for periodic reporting regarding usage patterns. The Controller may permit correction of minor technical errors in the licensed layout design, provided that such corrections do not substantially alter the original inventive concept and are approved prior to implementation. Any assignment or transfer of rights under a license granted as provided herein shall require prior notification to and approval from the Central Government, considering the interest of the security of India and ensuring continued compliance with stipulated conditions.
primary_entity: interest of the security of India

context: An application for registration of a plant variety shall include, inter alia, a detailed botanical description conforming to the guidelines issued by the Authority, including precise identification of the genera species specified in Schedule D and any deviations observed during evaluation trials. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the variety possesses distinctiveness relative to commonly known varieties, supported by data from field observations and comparative analyses. Further, an undertaking affirming compliance with extant regulations regarding genetic modification or utilization of gene technology must be submitted. Provided that if the application relates to a transgenic variety, additional documentation pertaining to the insertion event and expression levels shall be required as provided herein. The Registrar may request supplementary information at any stage during examination.

Any breeder, being a person or entity engaged in the research, development, or commercialization of plant varieties, shall be entitled to seek protection for a new variety under this Act, provided that such variety demonstrates novelty and stability as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The authority may grant protection only if the applicant establishes, through verifiable documentation, that the claimed variety does not fall within any exclusion specified in Schedule B. Further, where an application pertains to a variety derived from another protected variety, the breeder shall disclose the parentage and provide evidence of compliance with conditions imposed during the original registration. The authority shall refuse protection for varieties falling under genera species specified as excluded by government notification, acting on recommendations from the National Biodiversity Authority. Infringement remedies are available as provided herein to registered breeders.

Applications for recognition as a Plant Variety, whether novel or essentially derived, shall be accompanied by a detailed botanical description conforming to the format prescribed in Schedule B, including precise identification of the genera species specified within the application. The Authority may require submission of additional data pertaining to reproductive characteristics, disease resistance, and yield performance, particularly where the claimed novelty is marginal. An applicant demonstrating prior public knowledge or use of the variety shall be deemed ineligible for recognition unless such disclosure occurred inadvertently and without the applicant’s consent. Further, any technical information submitted as part of the application remains confidential subject to a right of inspection by the Examining Officer during examination proceedings. The Registrar may issue notices requiring clarification or amendment of particulars at any stage prior to publication for objections.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any application for registration of a plant variety shall include a detailed botanical description conforming to internationally recognized taxonomic standards and specifying the genera species specified in Schedule D. Such description must accurately reflect the essential characteristics distinguishing the variety from other known varieties within its kind, including data relating to morphological traits, disease resistance, and yield potential. The Authority may require submission of additional documentation, including propagation protocols and genetic purity assessments, if deemed necessary for evaluation. Provided that any applicant demonstrating adherence to established customary practices in relation to traditional knowledge concerning the plant variety shall be afforded due consideration during examination.

Any breeder, hereinafter defined, who registers a plant variety shall be liable to pay annual fees proportionate to the extent of commercial exploitation undertaken, as determined by the Board established under this Act. Failure to remit such fees within the prescribed period will result in suspension of registration and forfeiture of rights accrued under this Act. Any person found infringing upon the registered rights of another, including unauthorized propagation or sale of a variety belonging to a protected genera species specified during registration, shall be deemed guilty of an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Repeated offenses may attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any breeder who has obtained registration of a plant variety shall be entitled to grant licenses for the commercial exploitation thereof, including rights pertaining to seed production, sale, and distribution, specifying therein the genera species specified in the registration certificate. Such license agreements may stipulate royalty payments, duration, and geographical limitations, as determined by mutual consent between the breeder and the licensee. Further provided that any assignment of such registered variety’s rights, whether partial or complete, shall require prior notification to the Plant Variety Authority and be recorded with them for validity under this Act. The authority may impose conditions on assignments ensuring continued access for farmers to propagating material, particularly concerning varieties derived from traditional cultivars.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application for compulsory licensing relating to a plant variety shall be deemed admissible if it is demonstrated that the registered breeder has failed to adequately address the reasonable requirements of the Indian farming community concerning access to propagating material. The Authority may entertain such applications only where the genera species specified in the registration documentation demonstrably differ from those traditionally cultivated by farmers within the affected region, and where a substantial body of evidence substantiates claims of economic hardship or food insecurity attributable to restricted availability. Any order granting compulsory licensing shall be subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant establishes prejudice resulting directly from the Authority’s findings regarding the aforementioned differences in genera species.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding rights in a protected plant variety may grant a license for the commercial exploitation thereof, specifying the genera species specified within the scope of such license. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment requires prior notification and approval from the Plant Variety Authority, detailing the terms and conditions transferred. The licensee shall adhere to all stipulations outlined in the original protection order concerning geographical limitations or end-use restrictions. Any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or sale of propagating material derived from a protected variety, without proper licensing as provided herein, shall cognizance offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. Further, any alteration of license terms post-approval requires written consent from both licensor and licensee, recorded with the Authority.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the determination of whether a plant variety qualifies for protection shall be predicated upon a rigorous assessment of its novelty and distinctiveness, considering established taxonomic classifications. Where disputes arise concerning the accurate identification of genera species specified in the application, particularly relating to varieties exhibiting traits consistent with multiple classifications or demonstrating potential pharmaceutical substance utility, the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Authority may appoint an independent panel of botanists and pharmacognosists. The decision of such a panel shall be binding, subject to judicial review only on grounds of procedural irregularity or demonstrable error of law. Any appeal against this determination must be filed within ninety days from the date of notification of the appellate authority’s order.

For the purposes of this Act, a copyright case shall be deemed to exist where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of rights vested under this Act and seeks redress through legal proceedings. Such a case may involve claims relating to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or public performance of copyrighted works. The determination of whether a copyright case has arisen is subject to considerations of originality as defined herein; a work lacking sufficient originality shall not be eligible for copyright protection, thereby precluding the possibility of an actionable infringement claim. Further, any assertion of fair dealing under this Act shall constitute a defense in a copyright case.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming ownership of copyright in an artistic work registered with the Copyright Office shall be deemed the owner thereof until such time as a determination is made by the relevant adjudicating authority. Applications for registration of copyright shall include particulars relating to the claimant’s identity and address, along with certified copies of agreements pertaining to the creation or assignment of rights under this Act. Where a copyright case arises concerning an unregistered work, the applicant must demonstrate that they were in possession of the original manuscript or recording prior to the date of publication or alleged infringement. The Copyright Office may require further documentation to substantiate claims of ownership and originality as provided herein.

Where copyright infringement has occurred, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. The remedy of injunction may be granted by the High Court to restrain acts that are reasonably certain to occur, infringing upon the exclusive rights vested under this Act. Damages shall be assessed at the option of the plaintiff, either based on the actual loss suffered or a reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. Subject to appeal to the Supreme Court, findings made by the High Court in any copyright case shall be final. The court may also order delivery up or destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation. Provided that, where an infringement is committed unknowingly and without malice, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the subsistence of copyright, or to any question of fact arising under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Tribunal shall follow such procedure as the Central Government may prescribe in this behalf and shall have the same powers as it possesses in relation to appeals under other provisions of this Act. Any order passed by the Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The determination of ownership in a copyright case shall be governed by principles of natural justice and fair hearing, ensuring all parties are afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where a copyright case arises concerning a cinematograph film incorporating musical works, the determination of infringement shall be predicated upon whether the reproduction, adaptation, or communication to the public of such film constitutes a substantial taking of both the underlying film and the incorporated music. Provided that, if it is demonstrated that the owner of the musical work did not grant permission for its inclusion in the cinematograph film, and the use was not reasonable or fair dealing under this Act, then liability shall attach to the producer of the film as well as any party involved in distributing the infringing copy. Further, evidence presented regarding licensing agreements pertaining to both the film and the music shall be considered by the adjudicating authority when assessing damages.

Where any person infringes copyright in respect of a work, such person shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the Court; provided that, where the infringement is committed knowingly and with intent to gain an undue advantage, the Court may award exemplary damages not exceeding ten times the amount of the actual damage sustained. Any aggrieved party seeking redress for a copyright case may institute civil proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The Court shall have power to grant injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, and to order the delivery up or destruction of infringing copies or materials as it deems just. Failure to comply with an order of the Court may result in a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any copyright case arising from the assignment of musical works shall be governed as follows: Where an author assigns their copyright in a composition to a performing rights society, such assignment may include the exclusive right to grant or withhold licenses for public performance and mechanical reproduction. Provided that, where the assignment is silent on the issue of synchronization rights—that is, the right to use the musical work in conjunction with visual images—the assignor retains ownership thereof unless explicitly transferred by written agreement. Further, a performing rights society may sub-license its assigned copyright to other entities engaged in related activities such as music publishing or collection agencies, subject to conditions ensuring equitable distribution of royalties among the original authors and composers. Any subsequent assignment of these sub-licenses shall require consent from both the assigning entity and the original author.

Where an appeal lies from a decision of the High Court determining the validity of a copyright case, such appeal shall be made to the Supreme Court within ninety days from the date of that order. The Appellate Bench may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for costs; provided that failure to provide such security shall not automatically preclude the appeal but may be considered by the Court in determining the final award of costs. It is further stipulated that any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to infringement or non-infringement of copyright may, subject to just cause shown, apply for a review of the decision before the High Court within thirty days of such order.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any assignment of copyright in a musical composition shall be deemed an exclusive license unless the instrument explicitly states otherwise. Such assignments may cover all or part of the rights specified under this Act, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and public performance. Where a patent addition relating to a copyrighted software program is granted, the assignor’s obligations regarding royalties and attribution shall extend to encompass any derivative works created as a consequence of said patent addition. A copyright case arising from an unauthorized adaptation of such a work will be adjudicated considering both the original copyright assignment and the implications of the related patent addition. Further, sub-licensing rights may be granted by the assignee subject to prior written consent from the assignor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.

Subject to this Act, a copyright case shall be deemed to arise where any person alleges infringement of rights vested under this Act. The determination of such a case requires examination of the work’s originality and substantial similarity to the claimed copyrighted material. Further, the aggrieved party may apply to the relevant High Court for rectification of entries in the court rectification register pertaining to copyright ownership or duration. Such applications shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for rectification and supporting documentation as provided herein. The Court may order correction if it finds the existing entry erroneous or misleading.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where copyright is claimed in respect of an audio-visual work incorporating elements such as musical compositions and literary text, the applicant shall furnish with the application for registration a comprehensive inventory detailing all underlying works. This inventory must clearly identify the owner copyright case pertaining to each element incorporated, including names and addresses of respective owners or their duly authorized representatives. Failure to provide this detailed inventory may render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating ownership claims as provided herein. Any subsequent transfer or assignment of rights in respect of such underlying works shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by relevant execution documents.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to copyright case may prefer an appeal from such order to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant, and the High Court may entertain the appeal if it is satisfied that there is sufficient reason for believing that the order has been passed without due regard to the provisions of this Act or in exercise of any power which such authority does not possess. The High Court shall have the same powers as it would exercise in relation to appeals from civil court decrees, and may allow a party to be heard and adduce further evidence. Further, section appeal shall only be permissible if the aggrieved party has first exhausted all remedies available under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where copyright subsists in an unpublished musical work, the owner copyright case shall be deemed to vest initially in the composer unless such work has been assigned to another party by way of written agreement. Such assignment may specify the duration and scope of rights transferred, including reproduction, distribution, public performance, and broadcasting. Provided that, if the composer is a minor or otherwise legally incapacitated, the owner copyright case shall be held by their legal guardian or representative, acting in their best interests. Further, any subsequent transfer of ownership must also be evidenced in writing to be valid under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where copyright is claimed in any musical work, sound recording, cinematograph film, or compilation thereof, the applicant shall furnish with the application for registration a sworn declaration verifying the authenticity of the particulars furnished regarding ownership and authorship. Such declaration must explicitly state whether the applicant asserts sole owner copyright case or joint ownership, detailing the respective contributions of each claimant. Where the work is derived from pre-existing material, the application shall identify such source material and confirm due diligence in securing necessary permissions or licenses as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the registration liable for cancellation by an adjudicating officer. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims of ownership at any stage during processing.

Where any person claims to be the owner of copyright in respect of a work, and such claim is disputed, an action may be brought in a court of competent jurisdiction to determine the question of ownership. The plaintiff shall demonstrate, by admissible evidence, their entitlement to said copyright, including but not limited to proof of authorship or assignment as provided herein. Should the defendant dispute the plaintiff’s claim, they must present counter-evidence substantiating their own right to the copyright. 

The court may order discovery and inspection of relevant documents pertaining to the creation, ownership transfer, or licensing of the work in question. A finding that a person is the owner copyright case shall be conclusive for all purposes under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such a judgment may appeal to the appellate forum as prescribed.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where an audio-visual recording is created through the collaborative efforts of multiple parties, including but not limited to cinematograph film producers and music composers, determining the owner copyright case shall be predicated upon demonstrable contribution to the underlying work. The producer who secured requisite permissions and financed the initial creation of the recording shall be presumed to be the primary owner, provided that such presumption is rebuttable by evidence establishing significant creative input from other parties. Any party claiming ownership must satisfy the Controller with documentary proof of their involvement in the conceptualization, scripting, or musical composition integral to the final audio-visual product. Further, assignment of copyright under this Act shall require registration as provided herein.

Where any person institutes an action claiming to be the owner copyright case of a copyrighted work and fails to establish such ownership to the satisfaction of the Court, that person shall be liable to pay costs including reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the defendant. Any infringement of copyright under this Act may be subject to damages not less than five per cent nor more than ten per cent of the actual loss or damage proved to have been caused to the owner by the infringing act. Further, where an infringer is found to have acted with knowledge of the copyright existing in the work, enhanced penalties as determined by the Court shall apply. The Court may also issue injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and order the destruction of infringing copies.

Where any person claims ownership of copyright in respect of an original cinematograph film, and such claim is disputed by another alleging prior contribution to its creation as a scriptwriter, composer, or performer, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court. The court shall consider evidence pertaining to the extent of creative input furnished by each claimant, subject to the understanding that mere incidental participation does not confer ownership rights under this Act. It shall be presumed, in cases where an author’s contribution is asserted, that such contribution was essential for the film's artistic merit unless proven otherwise. The determination of owner copyright case rests entirely upon a careful evaluation of submitted documentation and testimony.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where copyright subsists in an audiovisual work created during the course of employment, the owner copyright case shall vest initially with the employer, provided that such creation is directly related to the terms and conditions of the employment contract. The employer may, by a written agreement executed prior to the publication or communication to the public of the work, assign all or any part of their copyright to another party, specifying the scope and duration of the assignment. Any international application form filed under the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works shall be deemed conclusive evidence of such assignment, subject to verification by the Controller. Further, a subsequent owner may license rights in the work, including reproduction and distribution, without requiring consent from any prior assignee, provided that royalties are distributed according to the terms stipulated in the original assignment agreement.

Where any person claims ownership of copyright in respect of an original musical composition, and such claim is disputed by another asserting prior authorship, the aggrieved party may apply to the Controller seeking determination of owner copyright case. The application shall specify the grounds upon which the claim is contested, including particulars relating to the creation and first publication or dissemination of the work. The Controller may require both claimants to furnish evidence substantiating their respective assertions, including but not limited to testimonies, correspondence, and records pertaining to the manner applying registrar for copyright registration. Decisions made by the Controller are subject to appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, provided that such appeals must be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order.

Subject to this Act, where copyright subsists in an audio-visual work embodying musical elements, the owner copyright case shall be determined with reference to the contributions made by each creator. The author of the literary work comprising the scenario and dialogue shall be deemed the primary owner unless otherwise stipulated through a written agreement executed prior to the creation of such work. Any dispute concerning ownership may be referred for adjudication under procedures as provided herein, and any party aggrieved by an order in such proceeding appellate may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order.

Any agreement whereby the entire copyright or exclusive rights pertaining thereto in respect of any cinematograph film are assigned to another party shall be deemed an assignment copyright under this Act, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. Such assignments may encompass the right to reproduce the work, include its adaptation, distribute prints, and exhibit publicly, as mutually agreed upon by the assignor and assignee through a written contract. Provided that, where the assignment relates to a work jointly authored, all co-owners of the copyright shall execute the agreement or their duly authorised representatives do so on their behalf. The duration of any such assignment shall not exceed seventy years from the year following the date of creation of the cinematograph film, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the written instrument. Further, an assignee may sub-license rights as provided herein.

Any assignment purporting to transfer copyright in cinematograph films or sound recordings shall be deemed invalid if it fails to explicitly state whether the assignor retains any rights relating to performance, broadcast, or public exhibition of the work. Such assignments are subject to review by the Controller, who may, upon application by an aggrieved party demonstrating a lack of clarity regarding the extent assignment rights granted, issue an order declaring portions of the agreement unenforceable. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the assignor liable for damages and costs incurred by the assignee in defending against any claim arising from ambiguity within the purported assignment. Repeated or willful violations may attract penalties as provided herein.

The transfer of copyright ownership in cinematograph films shall be documented through a formal registration process administered by the Office of the Registrar of Copyrights. Any individual or entity seeking to effect an assignment rights relating to such film must submit Form CG-F, accompanied by requisite fees as prescribed under this Act. The form shall detail the work assigned, including its title and year of creation, alongside a comprehensive list of rights transferred, whether exclusive or partial. Such assignments may cover reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or any other protected right as defined herein. Provided that, where an assignment is made to a body corporate, it must be countersigned by at least two officers of the corporation duly authorised in writing.

An assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed to include the exclusive right to reproduce the film in any medium, subject to compliance with conditions stipulated therein. Such an assignment shall not be effective unless it is executed by a person duly authorised to act on behalf of the owner of the copyright, and such authorisation must be evidenced by a registered power of attorney or equivalent document as prescribed under this Act. Provided that where the cinematograph film incorporates pre-existing works protected by copyright, the assignment shall explicitly address the rights pertaining to those incorporated elements. The assignor shall retain the obligation to provide necessary documentation verifying ownership for the duration of the assigned rights. Any subsequent transfer of such assignment rights requires prior written consent from the original assignee.

The right to assign copyright in an artistic work, including but not limited to cinematograph films and sound recordings, may be exercised by the owner subject to the conditions hereinafter prescribed. Any agreement transferring ownership of copyright shall be evidenced in writing and executed by both the transferor and transferee, clearly delineating the scope of rights conveyed. Such assignment shall specify whether it pertains to the entire copyright or a portion thereof, including reproduction, distribution, adaptation, and public performance rights. The duration of the assignment shall also be explicitly stated, not exceeding the term permitted under this Act. Provided that, where an assignment is made without specifying a duration, it shall be deemed to continue in perpetuity unless revoked by notice in writing served on the assignee. Further, any subsequent licensing agreements relating to the assigned work are subject to the terms of the initial assignment rights.

The transfer of ownership interest in a literary or artistic work under this Act shall be deemed an assignment only if executed as a registered instrument before the Registrar of Copyrights, subject to exceptions for assignments made prior to the amendment of 1999. Provided that, any dispute concerning the validity of such assignment may be referred to arbitration by mutual consent of the assignor and assignee, with the arbitral award being final and binding. An appeal from an arbitral award under this provision lies only to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of the award, predicated on demonstrable irregularities in the arbitral process or manifest error of law. The assignment rights conferred herein are irrevocable except by written agreement between the parties, which must also be registered.

An assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be deemed invalid if it purports to transfer ownership of elements constituting the underlying literary, dramatic or musical work without explicit consent obtained from the owners thereof prior to the registration of said film with the Copyright Office. Any party claiming validity of such an assignment may petition the relevant High Court demonstrating that due diligence was exercised in ascertaining and securing requisite permissions. The burden of proof regarding the existence and scope of these consents shall rest upon the claimant asserting the validity of the assignment rights. Provided that, where the assignor acted without authority to grant such broad copyright transfer, the assignee’s claim may be challenged under principles of estoppel as provided herein.

The registration of an assignment of copyright under this Act shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of such assignment, subject to judicial review on grounds of fraud or misrepresentation. Where a copyright owner desires to assign specific rights relating to a literary or dramatic work, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and adaptation, the instrument effecting such assignment shall clearly delineate the precise rights assigned. Such specification shall detail whether the assignment is exclusive or non-exclusive, and for what period it remains in effect. Any subsequent transfer of copyright, or any further assignments relating to the same work, must be registered separately as provided herein. Failure to accurately specify rights assigned may render the registration voidable at the discretion of the Registrar.

Where an author assigns their copyright in a musical composition to a publisher, that assignment shall be deemed valid only if it explicitly details the specific performance rights transferred, including but not limited to mechanical, public, and synchronization licenses. Such assignments may include provisions for reversion of rights should specified sales thresholds not be met within a period of five years from the date of assignment. The assignor retains the right to terminate the assignment under this Act upon providing six months’ written notice to the assignee, provided that such termination does not prejudice any existing license agreements executed by the publisher prior to the notice. Failure to clearly specify rights assigned in the initial documentation renders the assignment unenforceable against third parties claiming interest based on the purported transfer.

Where an author assigns their copyright under this Act to another party, such assignment shall be executed as a deed, attested by two witnesses, one of whom must be a practicing advocate or a Notary Public. The instrument of assignment shall clearly delineate the specific works subject to the transfer, detailing each work with precision and referencing any identifying metadata available at the time of execution. Furthermore, it shall explicitly specify rights assigned, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation, alongside the duration for which these rights are conveyed. The territorial scope of the assignment must also be clearly stated within the deed. Any subsequent modification or revocation of such an assignment requires a similar written instrument executed with the same formalities as the original assignment, provided that all parties consent in writing to the alteration.

An applicant seeking a licence to publish any literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work shall submit a detailed application to the Copyright Office outlining the intended publication and its scope. The application must specify the work’s title, author, date of first publication, if applicable, and the reasons necessitating the applicant's desire to publish it. Provided that the applicant demonstrates reasonable efforts have been made to ascertain the copyright owner’s identity and consent, and such attempts are documented within the application, the Copyright Office may proceed with an assessment of the request. The applicant licence publish shall further provide a statement affirming compliance with all relevant provisions under this Act pertaining to moral rights and attribution requirements.

An applicant seeking a licence to publish under this Act shall submit a detailed proposal to the Copyright Office outlining the intended publication, including the title, author (if ascertainable), and proposed format. The application must be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the due diligence undertaken to identify and contact the copyright owner or their heirs. Provided that the Registrar is satisfied that reasonable efforts have been made to locate the copyright owner, the applicant may proceed with a public notice inviting objections within sixty days from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be considered by the Copyright Office, which may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification. The applicant licence publish shall demonstrate an understanding of fair dealing principles as they pertain to derivative works and ensure compliance with all relevant provisions regarding moral rights.

Any individual seeking to obtain a license to publish copyrighted works under this Act shall submit a detailed application specifying the intended publication, including the number of copies and proposed distribution channels. Failure to accurately represent these details constitutes a material misrepresentation, rendering the applicant liable for penalties as provided herein. Where the copyright owner has granted an exclusive licence, any subsequent applicant licence publish without consent from the exclusive licensee is deemed a violation. Such violations are subject to damages equivalent to three times the potential royalties that would have been payable had the publication occurred with authorization, and may also attract criminal prosecution under this Act for infringement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an action alleging copyright infringement relating to a cinematograph film shall not be directly actionable before a civil court unless such claim arises from a demonstrable violation of the exclusive rights granted under this Act. For the purposes of determining jurisdiction, any suit or proceeding brought concerning alleged unauthorized reproduction, distribution, public exhibition, or adaptation of a cinematograph film shall be deemed exclusively cognizable by an instituted district court situated within the local limits of which the cause of action arose, provided that such determination is not affected by subsequent relocation of either party.

Where an application for registration of a literary work, musical work, dramatic work, cinematograph film, or sound recording has been refused under this Act, the applicant may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal, appeal to an *instituted district court*. Such appeal shall be made in accordance with the procedure as provided herein and shall not suspend the operation of the order unless the district court directs otherwise. The appellate authority may, after affording the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm the order of refusal, modify it, or direct registration subject to such conditions as it deems fit. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the *instituted district court* may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of that decision.

Where an aggrieved party alleges violation of their copyright under this Act, they may institute district court proceedings seeking redress for such infringement. Subject to provisions regarding territorial jurisdiction as prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, any suit concerning the reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of a copyrighted work shall be brought before the district court within whose local limits the cause of action arose, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Provided that, in cases involving multiple defendants situated in different jurisdictions, an action may be commenced in any district court convenient to the plaintiff. The remedies available under this Act, including injunctions and damages, shall be pursued through these instituted district court proceedings; furthermore, costs of litigation shall be determined as deemed appropriate by the presiding judge.

Where an appeal under this Act concerning a determination made by the Registrar regarding the originality of a literary work or musical composition has been filed and remains unresolved, such matter may be directly instituted district court. The institution of proceedings before the District Court shall operate as a bar to further appeals against the Registrar’s initial decision, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates diligent pursuit of remedies available under this Act prior to seeking recourse in the judicial forum. Subject to the provisions relating to limitation periods applicable generally within the jurisdiction, suits instituted district court concerning copyright infringement or related matters shall be governed by the procedural rules pertaining to civil actions. The District Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to determine questions of fact and law arising from such appeals. Any order made by the District Court shall be final and binding on all parties involved.

The assignment of copyright in cinematograph films produced under this Act shall be valid only if executed by an individual holding at least fifty percent equity shareholding in the production company and registered with the designated Copyright Office within thirty days of execution. Such assignments may include, but are not limited to, rights pertaining to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or public performance. Where a copyright owner desires to license any right under this Act, the terms of such licensing agreement shall be clearly defined, specifying duration, geographical scope, and royalty rates payable to the assignor. Any dispute arising from an assignment or license agreement may be referred for resolution to an instituted district court, whose decision shall be final and binding on all parties involved. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and licenses registered under this provision.

Where an appeal arises from an order passed by a civil court exercising original jurisdiction under this Act concerning allegations of unauthorized reproduction or distribution of cinematograph films, such appeal may be made to the High Court within one year from the date of the said order. Provided that, if the appellant is able to satisfy the appellate court that they were prevented by accident or some other exceptional circumstance from preferring the appeal within the aforementioned period, the High Court may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision of an instituted district court concerning the quantum of damages awarded for copyright infringement shall have the right to petition the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of that decision.

For the purposes of this Act, "invention" means a new and useful art, process, manufacture or composition of matter; provided that an invention shall not include a mere discovery, scientific principle, or formula discovered solely by observation of nature. An invention is deemed to be obvious if, prior to the date of filing of the patent application, it was known or used in India, or if it could have been readily deduced from knowledge and practice within the art at that time. The term "application" includes an amended application filed under this Act; and where such amendment relates to a matter not disclosed in the original application, the act 1970 extends only to the extent of the disclosure made therein.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance intended for use or employed in therapeutic applications, the patent shall extend only to the process itself, and not to the substance produced by that process. Provided that if the substance so produced is novel and non-obvious, a subsequent application for a patent may be filed relating solely to that substance. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Central Government may, acting through officers duly authorized by it, institute proceedings against any party found to have infringed upon a patent right as provided herein. This act 1970 extends its jurisdiction to cover instances where infringement occurs outside India but has an effect within Indian territory.

An application for a patent shall not be entertained if the invention relates to a process for obtaining an article by means essentially utilizing seeds or propagating material. Provided that such exclusion does not apply where the processed article results directly from such process and is new and involves inventive step. The Central Government may, acting through officers duly authorized in this behalf, require the applicant to furnish such further information as it deems necessary for determining whether the invention claimed meets the requirements of novelty and inventiveness under this Act. Where an application extends to a method or process, it shall be subject to examination regarding its compliance with stipulations concerning public interest and potential impact on agricultural practices, as provided herein. This act 1970 extends to include provisions relating to compulsory licensing where such conditions are met.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming an interest in a patent, or who is desirous of obtaining a license to exercise a right conferred by a patent, may apply to the Controller for registration of an assignment or a license. Such application shall specify the details of the assignor and assignee, or licensor and licensee, as the case may be, including their addresses for communication. The Act 1970 extends to cover situations where such assignments or licenses are granted outside India, provided that the patent itself relates to an invention applicable in India. Further, any assignment shall include a description of the right assigned, whether it is sole or partial and for specific territories. Consideration paid for the grant of a license shall be disclosed in the application, and may be subject to review by the Controller to ensure fairness and transparency under this Act.

An application for a patent under this Act shall disclose the matter which the invention is said to relate to, and it shall describe the invention in sufficient detail to enable the person skilled in the art to put the same into practice; provided that where an invention relates to a method or process, the specification must particularly describe the method or process. The Controller may require the applicant to disclose any further information concerning or relating to the invention which the Controller considers necessary for the purposes of assessing patentability. Where the claims in a patent application are not clear and precise, or do not define the subject matter claimed, the act 1970 extends to allow the Controller to direct the applicant to amend the claims accordingly. An invention far claimed shall be construed according to the meaning intended by the inventor at the time of filing the application, as determined by reference to the entire specification.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent amended” is defined as a patent that has undergone modification to its claims or description following the initial filing date, subject to the conditions prescribed herein. Such amendment shall only be permissible if it does not substantially alter the nature of the invention originally disclosed and meets the requirements for clarity and support within the original specification. An application for an amended patent may be rejected if the proposed changes introduce matter which was not reasonably foreseeable by a person skilled in the art at the time of the initial filing, provided that such rejection is accompanied by reasoned justification.

Where an application for a patent has been granted and subsequently amended, the Controller may, upon receiving written objection from any person aggrieved by the amendment, direct that the amended specification be re-examined. Such direction shall be accompanied by a statement outlining the grounds of the objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to respond in writing to the objections raised. Following consideration of both the objection and the applicant’s response, the Controller may determine whether the patent, as amended, satisfies the requirements for patentability under this Act. If the Controller finds that the amendment introduces subject matter not disclosed in the original application, or otherwise renders the invention unpatentable, the patent shall be deemed to have been *patent amended* and may be revoked accordingly. The aggrieved person shall be entitled to seek remedies available under this Act arising from such revocation.

Where an application for a patent has been granted and subsequently amended pursuant to a request made under this Act, such amendment shall only be permissible if it does not alter the nature of the invention claimed. The Controller may require further particulars or modifications to ensure compliance with the provisions relating to clarity and support in the specification as originally filed. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting an application for patent amended in accordance with these procedures may appeal under this Act within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Provided that, if the amendment relates solely to the claims, the Controller shall consider whether the amended claims are clear and distinct.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to a patent amended subsequent to its grant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed against; however, it may direct the Controller to investigate any fact pertaining to the validity of the patent if such fact was not previously considered during examination. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where a finding of non-infringement is made, damages and compensation for losses suffered due to allegations of infringement shall be assessed at the discretion of the Board, subject to a maximum penalty as determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Where the proprietor of a patent amended pursuant to a license granted under this Act desires to assign or otherwise transfer his interest in the patent, including the right to exploit the invention as defined within the scope of such license, he shall provide prior written notification to the licensee. Such notification must detail the proposed assignment and the consideration offered. The licensee may, subject to the terms of the original license agreement, consent to the assignment or propose alternative licensing arrangements acceptable to both parties. Failure by the proprietor to obtain the licensee’s consent within a period of ninety days from the date of notification shall render the assignment void ab initio, except where the assignee is an affiliated entity as defined under this Act. The Controller may intervene only if disputes arise concerning the validity or scope of such license and its impact on the patent rights conferred herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to a patent amended subsequent to the initial grant may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall hear appeals arising under this Act concerning allegations of infringement related to processes involving a pharmaceutical substance, and may award compensation for losses sustained due to wrongful restraint of trade or unlawful exploitation of intellectual property rights. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during amendment proceedings will render any subsequent patent vulnerable to revocation by the Controller. Such revocation may be enforced through civil suits seeking injunctions and damages, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding contributory infringement and wilful blindness.

Where an application for a patent has been granted and subsequently lapses due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may file a request for revival of the lapsed patent subject to conditions prescribed under this Act. Such request shall be accompanied by the necessary fee calculated on the basis of the number of years for which the renewal fees remained unpaid, plus an additional surcharge not exceeding fifty percent of the said unpaid fees. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating continued novelty and industrial applicability of the invention as at the date of the request. Further, where a patent has been revived under this provision, it shall be subject to all limitations and conditions that would have applied had the renewal fee been paid on time.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the said failure occurred and shall state the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the lapse was accidental or arose from circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may, subject to satisfaction regarding the genuineness of the claim and after affording an opportunity for hearing to any interested party, restore the patent as if it had not lapsed, provided that the renewal fees outstanding at the time of lapse, along with a prescribed late fee, are paid within such period as determined by the Controller. The restoration shall revive the patent from the date it lapsed, but shall not prejudice rights acquired by third parties under this Act prior to the date of restoration.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for institution of proceedings requesting restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date of such lapse and shall state fully the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to pay the renewal fee was accidental or arose from circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may, after affording an opportunity of being heard to the applicant and any other interested party, direct restoration of the patent if satisfied that the grounds alleged are substantiated. Restoration shall revive the patent as if it had not lapsed, subject to payment of all overdue renewal fees together with a surcharge calculated at such rate as may be prescribed by the Central Government. The Controller shall record the order of restoration and publish it in the Patent Journal.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date the patent ceased to have effect and shall state the grounds upon which the applicant claims that the failure to pay was unintentional or attributable to circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating these claimed circumstances, including but not limited to documentation relating to financial hardship or administrative error. Restoration of a patent under this provision shall revive the patent as if it had not lapsed, subject to any applicable fees and penalties determined by the Controller.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may apply to the Controller for restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable ground for the omission to pay the fee. The Controller may, subject to satisfaction that the applicant has diligently pursued the invention and that no prejudice accrues to other parties, grant a certificate restoring the patent as if it had not lapsed. However, any claim in respect of an invention disclosed in the restored patent shall be deemed invalid if such claims were previously challenged under this Act during the original term of the patent. The Controller may require payment of all overdue renewal fees and a penalty for late payment before granting restoration.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any licensee operating under a license granted prior to such lapse shall be entitled to continue exercising the rights licensed to them for a period not exceeding six months from the date of the lapse. This entitlement is subject to the condition that the licensee files an application with the Controller seeking recognition of their continued right to practice the invention and provides evidence demonstrating substantial reliance on the license during its active term, including documented investments made in manufacturing or commercialization activities. The Controller may grant a temporary extension beyond this six-month period if satisfied that the licensee’s interests would suffer undue hardship due to the abrupt cessation of operations; provided that such extension shall not prejudice any subsequent application for patent restoration by the original patentee.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal seeking restoration of the patent. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating diligent efforts made to secure payment within a reasonable timeframe following notification of default and a compelling justification for the delay. The Tribunal may entertain such applications only if satisfied that the failure pay renewal was attributable to circumstances beyond the control of the patentee, including but not limited to natural disasters or documented administrative errors on the part of the Patent Office. Subject to this, the Tribunal shall consider all relevant factors before determining whether to grant leave for restoration and any conditions attached thereto.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, an application for revival may be made within six months from the date on which the said fee became payable. Such application shall be accompanied by the requisite fee and a statement setting forth the reasons for the delay in payment of the renewal fee. The Controller may, subject to just cause shown, allow the application if satisfied that the failure was unintentional and due to circumstances beyond the control of the patentee or their authorized representative. Further, where a revival is granted under this provision, a patent addition shall be permissible at the time of such revival, provided it relates to the same invention as originally claimed in the lapsed patent. The Controller may require supporting documentation demonstrating the validity of the reasons for non-payment and the continued novelty of the subject matter.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as prescribed under this Act, an application for restoration may be filed within six months from the date such lapse occurred. Such application shall include a statement detailing the reasons for the omission and demonstrating reasonable grounds for excusing the default. The Controller may require submission of supporting documentation substantiating these grounds. Provided that if it is established that the failure to pay renewal fees resulted from demonstrable circumstances beyond the control of the patentee, including but not limited to natural disaster or documented administrative error, cancellation justified registration may be considered. Subject to payment of all overdue renewal fees together with any applicable late fee as determined by the Controller, restoration shall only be granted if it does not prejudice existing third-party rights.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any person may institute proceedings before the Controller seeking restoration of the patent. Such application for restoration shall be made within six months from the date filing application for the patent and must demonstrate diligent efforts were undertaken to secure payment of the outstanding renewal fee. The Controller may require evidence substantiating these efforts and may impose a penalty not exceeding one thousand rupees for each year the renewal fee remained unpaid. Restoration shall only occur if the applicant satisfies the Controller that there are reasonable grounds for believing the failure pay was unintentional, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit.

Where a patent has lapsed due to failure pay renewal fees as provided herein, any licensee operating under a valid assignment agreement may continue exploitation of the patented invention for a period not exceeding three years from the date of such lapse. This provision shall apply irrespective of whether the original patentee subsequently restores the patent or attempts to secure a fresh grant. The Controller may, subject to just cause demonstrated by the assignee, extend this period beyond three years, provided that compensation is paid to the former patentee at a rate determined according to prevailing market conditions and as agreed upon between the parties; failing agreement, as per guidelines issued by the Government.
