Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an accused offence relating to the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, the Court shall afford the defendant an opportunity to demonstrate due cause for their continued application. Such demonstration may include evidence establishing honest concurrent usage, bona fide adoption prior to any demonstrable consumer confusion, or reliance upon a registered trade mark held by another party under license. The proprietor is entitled to injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct result of the infringing activity; provided that such damages shall not exceed an amount determined by the Court based on prevailing market rates and the extent of commercial harm. Further, the defendant shall be liable for costs incurred by the proprietor in bringing the action, subject to considerations of equitable fairness as assessed by the presiding judge.

Where any individual is charged with an accused offence relating to the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark, such individual shall be served with a notice detailing the particulars of the accusation. The notice must specify the registered proprietor’s rights and the alleged infringing activity. Failure to provide this notice prior to commencement of proceedings will render any subsequent judgment void ab initio. An accused offence may include, but is not limited to, the manufacture, sale, or importation of goods bearing the infringing mark. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such notices served, accessible for inspection by interested parties subject to applicable privacy regulations. Any party aggrieved by an action taken under this Act relating to an accused offence may appeal to the relevant judicial authority within sixty days of notification.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging an accused offence relating to the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to their registered mark, such proceedings shall be deemed civil in nature. The defendant may present evidence demonstrating honest, contemporaneous belief regarding the validity and ownership of the alleged infringing mark, provided that such belief was formed prior to any public communication concerning the proprietor’s rights. Further, if the defendant establishes a lack of commercial intent to deceive or confuse consumers through the use of the impugned mark, the court shall consider this factor in assessing damages. The proprietor bears the onus of proving both infringement and resultant damage, subject to procedural safeguards as provided herein for ensuring fairness to the accused offence.

Any proprietor who discovers that another person has contravened any provision of this Act relating to registered trademarks shall be entitled to institute appropriate proceedings before a District Forum. Where such violation involves the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark for goods or services identical to those in respect of which the trademark is registered, the accused offence will attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. Such penalties may include monetary compensation to the proprietor reflecting lost profits and damage to reputation. Further, the offender shall be ordered to cease the infringing activity immediately and destroy all offending materials subject to a verification process conducted under this Act.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark grants a license allowing use of the mark under conditions including territorial restriction, such license may be assigned to another party with the prior written consent of the original proprietor. This assignment shall not affect any rights accrued by the licensee prior to notification of the transfer, provided that the assignee undertakes all obligations previously held by the initial licensee regarding quality control and permitted goods or services as defined in the original licensing agreement. Any subsequent unauthorized use of the trademark following such an assignment may constitute an accused offence under this Act, subject to due process and investigation. The proprietor retains the right to audit records pertaining to sales and usage data relating to the licensed mark for a period of three years after any assignment is completed.

Where any individual is charged with an accused offence involving the use of a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark, such individual shall be entitled to present evidence demonstrating honest, contemporaneous belief regarding the absence of infringement. This evidentiary burden extends to establishing that the alleged infringing use occurred within a reasonable understanding of fair dealing principles as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon review of submitted documentation and hearing arguments from both parties, determine whether this belief negates the elements constituting the accused offence. Any such determination shall be subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority, with provisions for costs awarded at its discretion based on the merits of the dispute.

Where any individual is charged with an accused offence relating to the use of a trademark without due cause, the Investigating Officer shall serve upon such individual a notice specifying the particulars of the alleged infringement and detailing the trade mark recognised as belonging to the registered proprietor. The notice shall afford the accused a reasonable opportunity to submit their written defence, including any evidence demonstrating fair dealing or lack of intent to deceive. Failure by the Investigating Officer to adhere to this procedural requirement may render subsequent proceedings vulnerable to challenge under principles of natural justice.

The prosecution bears the onus of proving beyond reasonable doubt that the alleged actions constitute an infringement and that the accused was aware, or ought reasonably to have been aware, of the existence of the trade mark recognised in favour of another party. Any submission made by the accused shall be considered by the adjudicating authority before a determination is reached regarding culpability.

Any person found to have employed a false trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods or services sold under the infringing mark, as determined by the Commercial Court. Further, where the accused offence involves the intentional passing off of goods or services, the court may order the destruction of all remaining stock bearing the false trade mark. A person entitled patent shall not be shielded from liability under this Act if their patented process is used to manufacture counterfeit goods infringing upon registered trademarks. The Registrar may initiate proceedings against any such offender without prejudice to civil remedies available under this Act.

Where a person accused of an offence relating to the use of a trademark without due cause shall have reasonable grounds to believe that the trademark is not registered under this Act, such person may apply to the Registrar for a certificate stating whether or not the trademark in question is indeed registered. The Registrar shall consider the application and provide a determination within sixty days, subject to any procedural requirements as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar's determination may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. It shall be the duty of the Tribunal to hear appeals expeditiously and render its decision within ninety days of the appeal’s filing. The person accused offence is entitled to legal representation throughout these proceedings, and all records pertaining to the application and subsequent appeal shall be maintained in accordance with established archival protocols.

For the purposes of this Act, "material information" relating to a trade mark application shall include any oral or written communication provided by an applicant or their authorized representative to an examiner during examination proceedings. Such material information encompasses, but is not limited to, clarifications regarding the meaning of the goods or services listed in respect of which the trade mark is sought, and details concerning distinctive character. Where a prosecutor gave information that directly influenced the acceptance or rejection of a trade mark application, such information shall be considered material for purposes of any subsequent challenge under this Act, provided that it was not previously disclosed publicly.

In determining whether a proposed trade mark is distinctive, the Registrar shall consider any information furnished by the applicant relating to prior use of the mark or a mark confusingly similar thereto. Where an applicant, during examination proceedings, provides information indicating that a competing mark has been used in connection with identical or similar goods or services, and such information includes details regarding the extent and duration of said use, the Registrar may afford weight to this evidence in assessing distinctiveness. However, it shall be open to any interested party to challenge the veracity of the information provided by the applicant; a finding that the prosecutor gave information which is demonstrably false renders the applicant liable for costs incurred as a consequence of such misrepresentation.

In any proceeding under this Act concerning rectification of a registered trademark, where the Registrar considers it necessary to ascertain whether the applicant or proprietor has acted fraudulently or deceptively, the Registrar may require such person to disclose all information relating to the acquisition, use, and maintenance of the trademark. Such disclosure shall be made in writing, verified by affidavit, and submitted within the time specified by the Registrar. Failure to comply with this requirement without reasonable cause constitutes a ground for adverse inference against the defaulting party. It is provided that if, during such proceedings, it comes to the attention of the Registrar that the prosecutor gave information which was false or misleading, the Registrar shall record the fact and may consider its impact on the credibility of the evidence presented. The Registrar shall maintain a confidential record of all disclosed information for a period of five years from the conclusion of the rectification proceeding.

Where an applicant for registration of a trade mark furnishes information relating to prior use of the proposed mark, such information shall be deemed relevant for consideration under this Act. Provided that, if it is subsequently demonstrated that the applicant or any person acting on their behalf knowingly provided false or misleading information regarding said prior use, the Trade Marks Registry may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register and impose a monetary penalty not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees. Further, where such information is furnished by an agent acting on behalf of the applicant, the responsibility for ensuring accuracy rests with both the applicant and the agent; however, the prosecutor gave information that was later determined to be inaccurate due to reliance on outdated public records.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the right to grant a license conferring the exclusive privilege to use the mark in relation to specific goods or services, provided that such license agreement explicitly details the scope of permitted usage and any territorial limitations. Further, where the registered proprietor, during the course of an application for registration under this Act, furnished information pertaining to prior use or knowledge of similar marks to a designated authority, such information shall be deemed confidential and may not be disclosed without express written consent from the proprietor unless required by law. Any assignment of the trade mark, including any associated licenses, must include a declaration confirming that the assignor has fully transferred all rights and interests, acknowledging the prosecutor gave information as part of the registration process.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark proceeds to final hearing, and the Registrar determines that the applicant has failed to adequately substantiate claims made during prosecution, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to present further evidence. This right shall not extend to introducing information wholly novel to the proceedings, except where such information directly addresses concerns raised by the opposing party or the Registrar regarding the distinctiveness of the mark. It is provided that if, in demonstrating said substantiation, the applicant discloses information previously withheld and which was known to them at the time of filing, but not communicated to the Registrar, the opposing party may appeal this decision before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, arguing prejudice arising from the prosecutor gave information belatedly.

Any individual who knowingly provides false or misleading information to an investigating officer during any inquiry under this Act relating to infringement of a registered trademark shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees. Such penalties may be recovered as if they were debts due to the Government. Where it is established that such false information was provided with the intent to obstruct investigation or prejudice the rights of the trademark proprietor, further enforcement action including criminal prosecution under the Indian Penal Code shall be initiated. It is a material factor in determining culpability that the prosecutor gave information which directly influenced the direction of the inquiry and subsequently proved inaccurate, impacting investigations concerning citizens India.

For the purposes of this Act, “material information” shall mean any fact, circumstance, or representation communicated by a trademark applicant, their agent, or legal representative to an officer of the Trade Marks Registry during the examination process. This includes, but is not limited to, disclosures regarding prior use, similarity searches undertaken, and arguments presented in opposition to objections raised. Where a prosecutor gave information concerning distinctive character, such information shall be deemed material unless demonstrated otherwise by the applicant. The Patent Office shall maintain records of all material information received and considered during examination. This record shall be accessible for internal review under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "distinctiveness" with regard to a trade mark shall mean the capability of a sign to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. A trade mark shall be deemed distinctive if, prior to its use, it possesses a reputation which enables consumers to associate it exclusively with a particular enterprise and its products or services. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, no court shall cognizance of any suit alleging infringement of a registered trade mark unless the plaintiff demonstrates demonstrable evidence of actual confusion amongst a material segment of the relevant consuming public. This provision is subject to the right of rectification as provided under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a representation of the marks applied for and may specify any colour or other features claimed as distinctive. Where the applicant seeks to register a three-dimensional shape, packaging or other non-traditional trade mark, the description accompanying the application must clearly define the essential characteristics that contribute to its distinctiveness. The Trade Marks Registry shall examine such applications according to established procedures, considering whether the marks are capable of distinguishing goods or services and not descriptive of their nature. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board. However, no court shall cognizance of any matter arising from an order passed by the Appellate Board except in accordance with the provisions relating to writ petitions under the Constitution.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for the recovery of damages for the infringement of a trade mark under this Act, the court shall cognizance of such suit subject to the provisions regarding limitation as provided herein. The measure of damages recoverable shall be proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor and may include compensation for injury to reputation or goodwill arising from the use of the infringing mark. Further, where the infringement is established, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and may order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark, as it deems fit. Provided that any counterclaim alleging validity challenges to the registered trade mark shall be adjudicated concurrently with the main suit.

Subject to appeal under this Act, any suit for infringement of a trade mark or for passing off relating to goods or services shall be tried in accordance with the procedure prescribed under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The District Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose shall have original jurisdiction; however, the High Court may entertain such suits if it is satisfied that there is a substantial question of law involved. Where an interlocutory application is made concerning discovery or inspection of documents relevant to the suit, the court shall determine the matter expeditiously and in accordance with principles of natural justice. It is provided that any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may seek redressal through appeal as prescribed herein. The court shall cognizance only of matters pertaining directly to the infringement alleged or the passing off claimed, excluding extraneous issues not essential for adjudication on the merits of the claim.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and such proceedings are stayed pending determination of a counterclaim alleging prior use or registration, the court shall cognizance of the said counterclaim only if the claimant has furnished security satisfactory to the court, as determined by rules made in consultation with the Trade Marks Registry. This furnishing is subject to the condition that the counterclaimant demonstrates, through documentary evidence and testimony, continuous and bona fide usage of the mark prior to the date of first use by the proprietor, or the filing date of the proprietor’s trademark application, whichever is earlier. Provided further that if the claimant fails to furnish such security within thirty days from the date of service of notice requiring it, the counterclaim shall be deemed abandoned, and the court may proceed with the original claim for infringement.

Any proprietor seeking relief under this Act concerning infringement of their trade mark shall institute proceedings before a District Court within whose local jurisdiction any part of the infringing activity takes place. The court shall cognizance only of complaints filed with sufficient evidence demonstrating likelihood of consumer confusion and demonstrable damage to reputation or goodwill attributable to the alleged infringement. Further, where damages are claimed, such claims must be substantiated by documented financial records; failure to provide adequate proof may result in dismissal of the claim for recovery of losses. Any order issued under this Act regarding injunctions or account adjustments shall remain enforceable until modified or vacated by a higher appellate authority.

Where the proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license for use of the mark, or assign the entire interest in the trade mark, such agreement shall be documented in writing and executed before a notary public. The licensee or assignee, as applicable, shall be bound by all conditions and limitations stipulated within the licensing or assignment agreement, subject to any modifications approved by the Registrar. Further, where an assignment is made, notice thereof shall be provided to the Registrar within thirty days of execution, accompanied by prescribed fees. Any dispute arising from a license or assignment agreement relating to a trade mark shall be resolved through arbitration as agreed upon by the parties involved; failing such agreement, any court shall cognizance of the matter and adjudicate accordingly.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings alleging the infringement of a trade mark under this Act, and the defendant raises a defence asserting prior honest concurrent use of the impugned sign, the Court shall cognizance of such defence subject to the provisions regarding territorial extent as provided herein. The proprietor bears the onus of establishing, by clear and convincing evidence, that the defendant’s use is not genuinely concurrent or has ceased to be honest. Should the defendant further contend that the mark lacks distinctiveness, the Court may direct a hearing to determine this issue independently of the infringement claim. Any order made concerning prior use shall remain valid notwithstanding subsequent amendments under this Act, provided that such amendments do not fundamentally alter the nature of the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, no civil court shall exercise jurisdiction in relation to any matter concerning rectification of the Register based solely upon claims of passing off or unfair competition unless such claim is substantiated by evidence demonstrating prior and consistent use establishing an *unregistered trade mark* right. Provided that a consumer survey report submitted as evidence may be challenged on grounds of methodological flaw, and the court shall consider such challenge before determining its probative value. Further, where a party alleges dilution of distinctiveness due to subsequent use, it shall be incumbent upon them to demonstrate demonstrable prejudice to their goodwill; failing which, the claim shall stand dismissed. The court shall cognizance only of complaints filed within three years from the date of the alleged infringing act, as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a trade mark containing a representation of an invention which is patented under this Act or otherwise protected as an India patented invention shall be examined with particular regard to the provisions relating to deceptive similarity. The Trade Marks Registry may, prior to acceptance of such an application, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the use of the trade mark in relation to goods or services does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of the patented invention. Further, a court shall cognizance only of complaints alleging infringement arising from the misuse of such registered trade marks where it is established that the registration was obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation concerning the patent status.

An international registration sub shall be deemed to extend to each designated Contracting Party unless a limitation of geographical extent is indicated in the application for registration. Such indication shall specify either the entire territory of a designated Contracting Party or, where permitted by the Regulations under the Madrid Protocol, a part thereof. The Registrar may require further particulars regarding any such limitation and shall record them accordingly on the register. An international registration sub designating India shall be subject to examination as if it were an application for registration filed directly under this Act, provided that priority shall be accorded in accordance with established practice.

An international registration sub shall be deemed to be infringed if there exists a use of an identical mark in relation to identical goods or services, or related goods or services, within the territory of India without the authorization of the proprietor of the international registration. The owner of the registered trade mark may institute suit for relief against any person infringing such sub, and shall be entitled to all remedies available under this Act as if the international registration had been applied for directly in India. Provided that, where an opposition is filed against an application for registration arising from an international registration sub, the Registrar may require the proprietor of the mark to furnish evidence establishing reputation and distinctiveness of the mark in relation to the goods or services concerned within the Indian territory.

An application for international registration shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry by an applicant who is a national of India or domiciled in India, or has a place of business in India. The application must contain particulars identifying the trade mark, a list of the Contracting Parties in respect of which protection is sought, and any priority claimed under this Act. Where the international registration sub divides the goods or services for which protection is requested, the Registrar may require the applicant to specify with greater precision the classes of goods or services to which the application relates. The Registry shall examine the application to ensure compliance with the requirements of the Madrid Protocol and as provided herein. Any deficiency in the application may be brought to the attention of the applicant who shall have an opportunity to rectify it within a prescribed time.

An international registration sub shall be deemed to have been filed in India where an application for such registration is based on an earlier trademark registration made in a country which is party to the Madrid Protocol concerning the International Registration of Marks, and the applicant provides a certified copy of the said earlier registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating compliance with all applicable provisions under this Act relating to distinctiveness and permissible disclaimers as if the international registration sub were an initial application filed directly within India. Further, any mark contained in such an international registration sub shall be subject to examination for conflict with existing Indian trademarks prior to acceptance, provided that the applicant undertakes to satisfy any objections raised by the Registrar concerning registrability.

An international registration sub shall be deemed an infringement if, at the time of application for extension of protection, the mark is being used in India in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those specified in the original international registration. Any proprietor seeking relief from such infringement may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal and shall furnish evidence demonstrating ongoing use within Indian territory. Failure to provide satisfactory proof of continued usage will result in dismissal of the application, and the applicant shall be liable for costs incurred by the opposing party. Furthermore, wilful disregard of this provision constitutes a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment and a substantial monetary penalty as determined by the court.

An international registration sub shall be deemed an assignment of the right to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services as specified in the application for such registration, subject to the terms and conditions agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee. Such agreement may include provisions regarding royalty payments, territory limitations, and duration of the license. The proprietor retains ownership of the underlying trade mark but grants the licensee a limited right to exploit it within the designated international jurisdiction. Further, any subsequent assignment or transfer of the proprietary interest in the trade mark shall be subject to existing licensing agreements pertaining to the international registration sub, provided that the assignee assumes all obligations and benefits arising under those agreements. The Registrar may require disclosure of such licensing arrangements as part of the application process.

An application for international registration shall be deemed to be refused if the marks specified in the multiple-class indication are not registrable under this Act in India; however, such refusal may be appealed before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the refusal. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentary evidence demonstrating distinctiveness where a mark is challenged on grounds of descriptiveness relating to goods or services identical or similar to those for which registration is sought. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding an international registration sub, whether concerning acceptance, refusal, or limitation of protection, shall have the right to appeal as provided herein, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with procedural requirements.

An international registration sub shall be deemed to extend to the territory of India only in respect of goods or services as are specified therein and which correspond to the International Registration. For the purposes of determining whether an earlier trade mark exists under this Act, any application for registration or registered trade mark shall be taken into account irrespective of whether it was filed or registered before or after the date of entry of the international registration sub in the Register of International Marks. A person aggrieved by a notice rectify register relating to an international registration sub may file representations with the Registrar as provided herein.

An international registration sub shall be examined in accordance with the provisions relating to examination of applications for registration under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receiving an international registration application designating India, conduct such searches as it deems necessary to ascertain whether there exists any identical mark or a mark likely to be confused with the mark sought to be registered. Where the Registrar finds that the designation relates to goods or services not registrable in India, the applicant may be called upon to amend the list of goods and services. The manner issuing certificates relating to international registrations shall conform to forms prescribed by the Registry, indicating the extent of protection granted within Indian territory. Any objection raised during examination shall be communicated to the International Bureau as provided herein.

A fee payable notice, as provided herein, shall be issued by the Registrar to the applicant in respect of any application for registration of a trade mark under this Act where the prescribed fee has not been duly paid. Such a notice shall specify the amount due, the date on which payment was originally due, and provide a period, not exceeding sixty days from the date of issue of the notice, within which the deficiency can be made good. Failure to comply with the requirements of a fee payable notice may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to any appeal filed under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, upon filing the application, remit a prescribed fee as detailed in Schedule I. Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act concerning distinctiveness or any other ground, the applicant may respond within the time specified, accompanied by arguments and evidence addressing the concerns articulated. Following such response, if the Registrar remains unconvinced of the registrability of the trade mark, a fee payable notice shall be issued to the applicant, informing them of the continued objection and providing an opportunity for further representation or withdrawal of the application. Failure to comply with the requirements outlined in the fee payable notice within the stipulated period will result in the abandonment of the application.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant specifying the grounds of refusal and the amount of the prescribed fee. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of service of such notice, elect either to withdraw the application or to pay the specified fee and submit observations addressing each ground for refusal stated in the notice. Failure to comply with this provision within the stipulated time shall render the application deemed abandoned. Any fees paid under this process are non-refundable should the Registrar subsequently reject the trade mark application following consideration of any submitted observations, provided that such rejection is based on grounds consistent with those initially specified. The Registrar may extend the period for payment of the fee payable notice upon a written request demonstrating sufficient cause.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a *fee payable notice* to the applicant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the refusal is based and state the amount of the prescribed fee that may be paid within the time specified therein, being not less than thirty days from the date of publication of the trade mark journal containing the notice. The applicant shall, if desiring to pursue the application notwithstanding the refusal, remit the stated fee within the stipulated period. Failure to do so will render the application deemed abandoned. Any person may, subject to any conditions prescribed herein, file a representation against the acceptance of the trade mark following payment of the fee and publication of such acceptance. The Registrar shall consider all representations received before determining whether or not to proceed with registration.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall serve upon the applicant a written notification specifying the grounds of refusal. Such notification shall clearly state the reasons for the rejection and detail any conditions precedent to reconsideration of the application. The applicant shall, within sixty days from the date of service of the fee payable notice, be afforded an opportunity to submit their response or make representations against the findings contained therein. Failure to respond within this stipulated timeframe will render the application deemed abandoned. Any representation submitted must address each ground of refusal specifically and may include supporting documentation demonstrating compliance with relevant provisions as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant specifying the grounds of refusal and the amount of the prescribed fee. Failure to remit said fee within the period stipulated in the fee payable notice constitutes abandonment of the application and renders it liable for immediate rejection without further consideration. Any person aggrieved by such rejection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, but only upon payment of a further penalty equal to twice the original registration fee, provided that this penalty shall be forfeited if the appeal is deemed frivolous or vexatious. The Registrar may, at any time, require an explanation from any party regarding compliance with these provisions and impose additional penalties for non-compliance as determined appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to any person claiming rights in respect of an earlier trade mark, provided that such claim arises from use prior to the date of application for registration or from a pending application filed before the relevant priority date. The notice shall specify the details of the registration and the grounds upon which the challenge is based. Any assignment or transmission of the registered trade mark shall be deemed invalid if the fee payable notice was not served on the claimant within ninety days of the publication of the acceptance of the trademark for registration, unless consent to such assignment has been explicitly provided in writing by the claimant. Failure to pay the prescribed fee within the stipulated time period will result in the claim being considered abandoned and the original registration remaining valid.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant specifying the grounds of refusal and the amount of the prescribed fee which may be paid within sixty days from the date of receipt of the notice. Failure to remit said fee within the stipulated period shall render the application deemed abandoned, notwithstanding any subsequent attempt at revival. Any party aggrieved by such abandonment may, within a further period of thirty days from the date of publication of the abandonment in the Trade Marks Journal, file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, demonstrating sufficient cause for failing to comply with the fee payable notice requirements as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the refusal is based, and clearly state the amount of the prescribed fee that must be remitted within the stipulated period as provided herein. The manner issuing such notices shall be electronically, through a secure online portal accessible to applicants, with acknowledgement of receipt automatically generated. Failure to remit the fee payable notice within the specified timeframe will render the application deemed abandoned, subject to any subsequent revival under this Act. Any appeal against the refusal and the issuance of a fee payable notice must be filed within sixty days from the date of such notice.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a fee payable notice to the applicant specifying the grounds of refusal and the amount of the prescribed fee. The applicant may, within sixty days from the date of service of such notice, elect to pursue the application by paying the specified fee. Failure to pay the fee within the stipulated period shall render the trade mark application deemed abandoned, and the Registrar shall record accordingly in the Register of Trade Marks. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the fee payable notice may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of three months from the date of such decision, subject to payment of the prescribed appellate fee. The Board’s order shall be final and binding.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed renewed upon payment of the prescribed renewal fee within the time limit specified under this Act. For the purposes of this section, “renewal” means the continuation of protection conferred by the registered trade mark for a further period of ten years from the expiry of the initial or previous term of registration. The Registrar may entertain an application for renewal even if it is filed after the due date, provided that any additional fee prescribed in this behalf is remitted along with the renewal application. Any alteration to the representation of the trade mark shall be treated as a new application and not as part of the forms application renewal process.

For the purposes of this Act, “payable notice” means a notice served under this Act which satisfies the requirements of being delivered in a form specified by regulations made by the Registrar, containing all information prescribed therein, and dispatched to the intended recipient at the address registered with the Registrar or otherwise notified as their principal place of business. A payable notice shall be deemed to have been duly served when it is received by the addressee, or if sent by post, upon proof of dispatch in accordance with postal regulations. Failure to comply with these requirements renders a notice not a payable notice and may preclude reliance on its contents under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have been duly served on the applicant where it is sent by registered post with acknowledgement due to the address specified in the application form. Where such acknowledgement is not received within thirty days from the date of dispatch, the Registrar may presume that the applicant has received the notice. This presumption shall be conclusive unless the applicant proves, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the failure to receive the acknowledgement was due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control. The Registrar shall record any such proof and may direct a fresh notice to be sent. Failure to provide a valid address in the application form will preclude the applicant from claiming they received payable notice under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, the applicant shall be entitled to file a counterstatement within the time specified in the notice of the opposition. Failure to file such counterstatement within the prescribed period shall render the applicant liable to have their application deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, upon receiving a request from the applicant demonstrating exceptional circumstances preventing timely filing, extend the deadline for submission; however, this extension shall not exceed thirty days and requires prior written approval from the Registrar. Any notice served on the applicant relating to the opposition or counterstatement shall be considered payable notice, irrespective of whether it is received at the address specified in their application. The rights afforded under this Act to both parties are subject to principles of natural justice and fairness.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, service of the notice of opposition shall be effected upon the applicant in the prescribed manner. Such service shall constitute payable notice only when it is acknowledged by the applicant or their authorized representative, or when proof of delivery is obtained from the postal authority confirming receipt of the document at the address specified in the application for registration. Failure to obtain such acknowledgement or proof of delivery shall not invalidate the opposition proceedings provided that reasonable efforts were demonstrably undertaken to effect service as per the regulations outlined herein. The Registrar may, upon application by either party, direct a substituted mode of service if difficulties arise in complying with the prescribed methods. Any dispute concerning the validity of payable notice shall be resolved solely through an interlocutory application before the Registrar.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, service of that opposition shall constitute payable notice to the applicant. Such service must be effected by way of registered post with acknowledgement due or through electronic means as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The applicant shall be deemed to have received such payable notice within seven days of the date of posting or transmission, whichever is earlier. Provided that, if the address for service specified in the application changes after its filing, it shall be the responsibility of the applicant to promptly notify the Registrar of the updated details; failure to do so will not invalidate the operation of payable notice. The opposition period shall run from the date of such service and remain subject to any extensions granted as provided herein.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings under this Act against any person for infringement, and fails to obtain a decree establishing such infringement, the Court may order that the costs of the defendant shall be paid by the plaintiff. This applies particularly where the plaintiff’s claim was manifestly unfounded or vexatious, or based on information which ought reasonably to have been ascertained prior to the commencement of proceedings. Furthermore, if a trade mark owner fails to provide payable notice of an intended action against a potential infringer for a period exceeding ninety days from the date such intention is formed, they shall be liable to pay damages to the infringed party equivalent to twice the reasonable royalties that would have accrued had a licensing agreement existed.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the trade mark in relation to specified goods or services. Such licenses may be granted for a term not exceeding twenty years from the date of the license agreement, renewable by mutual consent. Any assignment of a trade mark, or any interest therein, including a license, shall require registration with the Trade Marks Registry and shall only take effect upon such registration. Where a licensee uses a registered trade mark without complying with the terms of their license, the proprietor may serve a payable notice requiring rectification of the breach within sixty days. Failure to rectify the breach as detailed in the payable notice will constitute grounds for termination of the license agreement under this Act and forfeiture of any rights granted therein.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity to be heard. The objector shall serve upon the applicant, by registered post or article delivered personally, a copy of the notice of opposition not less than thirty days prior to the date fixed for hearing; such service constituting payable notice. Failure to provide this payable notice shall render the objection unenforceable in proceedings before the Appellate Board. Provided that, if the objector demonstrates reasonable cause for failing to comply with the prescribed timeframe, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, entertain the appeal notwithstanding the deficiency in notice, subject to just terms and conditions.

For the purposes of this Act, "payable notice" shall mean a notice served in accordance with the prescribed procedures, including but not limited to registered post or electronic means as detailed in the First Schedule, and which has been duly acknowledged by the recipient. A payable notice is deemed to be conclusively received on the date of such acknowledgement, or where no acknowledgement is received, seven days from the date of dispatch. Where a provisional specification relating to a trade mark application contains details that are subsequently altered under this Act, any subsequent payable notice concerning amendments shall reference both the original and revised specifications. Failure to adhere to these requirements renders the notice invalid as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have been duly served on the applicant where such application has been published in the Trade Marks Journal under this Act. Provided that, where the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant has failed to maintain an accurate record of their postal address for service purposes, notice may be served by way of registered post addressed to the last known place of business of the applicant as recorded in the Register. Such service shall constitute payable notice notwithstanding any subsequent change of address not notified to the Registrar. The limitations on liability arising from such substituted service shall be as provided herein and subject to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, a “house parliament session” shall mean any period during which either House of Parliament assembles for the transaction of legislative business and includes sittings both public and private. A house parliament session commences with the issuance of a summons by the President under article 86 of the Constitution and concludes upon prorogation or adjournment sine die, as determined by each respective House. Any official record pertaining to proceedings during a house parliament session shall be deemed prima facie evidence thereof, subject to challenge based on demonstrable error. The Registrar may require production of such records in matters relating to trade mark oppositions.

An application for registration of a trade mark representing a visual depiction of the proceedings within a house parliament session shall be examined to ascertain distinctiveness. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness if the mark, though descriptive when applied to goods or services, has, through extensive use and advertising, become widely recognized as identifying only those goods or services with the applicant. Such evidence must include verifiable data relating to sales figures, market share, consumer surveys, and media coverage during a period not less than three years preceding the date of application. The Registrar shall consider any opposition filed under this Act based on likelihood of confusion with prior marks.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to goods or services shall be entitled to restrain the use of marks which are identical or confusingly similar, and also to seek damages for any loss suffered by reason of such infringing use. Where an infringement involves the unauthorized application of a trade mark to goods or services, the court may order the destruction or disposal of the infringing materials, subject to regulations framed under this Act. Any person seeking relief from an injunction restraining the conduct of a legitimate *house parliament session* relating to matters of public interest shall be required to demonstrate that the use of the impugned trade mark is essential for fair reporting and commentary on such proceedings. Provided that, nothing in this provision shall prevent the registered proprietor from pursuing remedies against any activity which constitutes unfair competition or detrimental imitation.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark relating to services connected with proceedings within a house parliament session, conduct such examination as is provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration on the grounds that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the said parliamentary services may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear appeals under this Act and may allow or dismiss the appeal, or make such other order as it deems fit. Further, where an objection is raised alleging likelihood of confusion with a prior registered trade mark used in connection with similar services, the Registrar shall provide both parties with an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. The Registrar’s decision on any such matter shall be final subject to appeal as provided herein.

The registration of a trade mark representing a parliamentary proceeding shall require prior approval from the Central Government, provided that such proceedings relate directly to matters of national security or public order. An application for registration under this Act concerning a “house parliament session” must explicitly detail the nature and scope of the proceeding being represented, including dates, locations, and key participants. The Registrar may reject an application if he deems the representation misleading or likely to cause confusion amongst the consuming public regarding the authenticity or official status of the house parliament session. Further, any registered trade mark depicting a house parliament session is subject to revocation if it is used in a manner inconsistent with the dignity and solemnity expected of such proceedings as provided herein.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, uses a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark in relation to goods or services for which the trademark is registered, or has applied for registration, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and also liable to a fine. Where such use occurs during a house parliament session, the penalty shall be doubled. The owner of the trademark may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity, subject to demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof. Any goods manufactured or offered for sale in contravention of this Act are deemed forfeited and may be destroyed as provided herein.

The registered trade mark ‘Lok Sabha Debates’, representing a compilation of transcripts and proceedings from a house parliament session, shall be assignable in accordance with the provisions herein. Any assignment shall include not only the right to use the trade mark but also the associated database containing indexed records of parliamentary debates, subject to the condition that the assignee maintains the accuracy and integrity of said database. Furthermore, licenses granted for the reproduction or dissemination of materials encompassed within ‘Lok Sabha Debates’ may be transferred with the consent of the registered proprietor, provided that such transfer does not diminish the quality or scope of the original license agreement. The registered proprietor shall provide a certificate of assignment or sub-license to the Registrar of Trade Marks, detailing the parties involved and the extent of rights conveyed, as required under this Act.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving a communication alleging that a registered trade mark has been used in relation to goods or services in contravention of conditions specified during registration, issue a notice to the proprietor of the trade mark. Such notice shall provide a period not exceeding sixty days for the proprietor to demonstrate satisfactory use of the mark as per those conditions, submitting evidence verifiable under this Act. Failure to adequately respond may result in an inquiry initiated by the Registrar concerning the continued validity of the registration, affording the proprietor opportunity for appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This process shall be suspended if a dispute arises regarding whether the alleged infringing activity occurred during a specific house parliament session.

For the purposes of this Act, a “house parliament session” shall mean any period during which either House of Parliament is duly assembled for legislative business. The determination of whether a house parliament session has occurred shall be conclusive based on official records maintained by the Lok Sabha Secretariat and the Rajya Sabha Secretariat. Any indication or suggestion that a mark relates to goods or services originating from a registered geographical indication, as provided herein, shall not constitute grounds for objection under this Act if such origin is demonstrably linked to activities undertaken during a house parliament session concerning legislative review of agricultural policy.

An application for registration of a trade mark depicting or referring to proceedings within a house parliament session shall be examined in accordance with the provisions herein. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the specific dates and nature of such parliamentary sessions depicted, provided that this requirement shall only apply where the representation is deemed likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of goods or services. Any prescribed forms for submission of these particulars shall be readily available on the Trade Marks Registry website. The applicant shall also declare whether the depiction constitutes a fair and accurate portrayal, subject to verification by the Registrar.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services connected with parliamentary proceedings, specifically during a house parliament session, and another person uses an identical or confusingly similar mark relating to dissimilar goods or services, the owner of the registered trade mark shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief. Such relief may include an order restraining the infringing party from further use of the impugned mark, and may also encompass damages for losses suffered by the proprietor as a direct result of the infringement. The register shall brought before the relevant court as prima facie evidence of ownership and validity of the trade mark. Provided that, any defence based on honest concurrent use shall be considered only if the infringing party can demonstrate continuous and bona fide usage prior to the date of registration, subject to conditions prescribed herein.

The term "Geographical Indication" with reference to goods originates from a place or region where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic is essentially attributable to its geographical origin; such indication may consist of either any name or word geographically indicative of the goods. Where an objection is raised against the acceptance of an application for registration under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice to both the applicant and the objector, specifying the grounds of objection. The registrar shall hearing both parties in person or through duly authorized representatives at a time and place specified in the notice; such hearings may be conducted via video conferencing as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may contain particulars relating to the quality, reputation or other characteristic of goods which are attributable to the geographical origin of such goods. Where an opposition is filed against an application under this Act, the Registrar shall serve notice on the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. The Registrar shall then direct both parties to submit their pleadings within a prescribed timeframe. Following submission of pleadings, the registrar shall hearing be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice, allowing each party to present evidence and arguments relevant to the matter. Decisions regarding registration or rejection will be recorded by the Registrar and communicated to all involved parties as provided herein.

Where any application for registration of a geographical indication is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall serve a copy of notice of the opposition on the applicant and the opponent. The applicant and the opponent shall each be given an opportunity to submit their comments and evidence in support of their respective positions. The Registrar shall provide both parties with a reasonable period, not exceeding sixty days from the date of service of the notice, for compliance as provided herein. Following the expiry of this period, the *Registrar shall hearing* all interested parties, including the applicant and the opponent, at a time and place fixed by him, giving them reasonable notice of such hearing. The decision of the Registrar after such hearing shall be final subject to appeal under Chapter VI. Any party failing to appear at the hearing may be deemed to have withdrawn their submissions.

Where any interested party opposes the registration of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall serve notice upon both the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. The Registrar may require the submission of further documentation from either party to clarify the nature of the claim or objection. Following such service, the registrar shall hearing be convened within ninety days, unless circumstances demonstrably preclude adherence to this timeline; a reasoned order detailing any deviation must then be recorded. During the hearing, both parties shall present arguments and evidence relevant to the opposition. The Registrar’s decision, provided that it is in writing and accompanied by reasons, shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Where any interested party opposes the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a notice to both the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds for opposition. The registrar shall hearing be convened within ninety days from the date of such notice, affording each party a reasonable opportunity to present their case and submit documentary evidence in support thereof. Failure by either party to appear at the appointed time may result in the Registrar proceeding ex parte. Any order made by the Registrar following such hearing is final subject to appeal under this Act. Knowingly submitting false or misleading information during the hearing shall be deemed a cognizable offence, punishable with imprisonment and a fine as determined by the appropriate authority.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the indication in connection with goods matching the definition thereof. Such licenses may be assigned freely, subject to the terms stipulated within the license agreement itself, provided that any assignment does not alter the essential quality or characteristics associated with the protected good. Where disputes arise concerning the validity or scope of such a license, or regarding the conditions under which it was granted, the registrar shall hearing all parties involved and consider relevant evidence presented before rendering a decision. The registrar may also require the licensee to provide security for the due performance of their obligations as defined within the licensing agreement. Further, any sub-license granted without prior consent from the owner is deemed void ab initio, as provided herein.

Where any objection is taken against the registration of a geographical indication under this Act, the Registrar shall issue notice to the applicant and the objector, specifying the grounds of objection. Both parties shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit written arguments and counter-arguments as provided herein. The registrar shall hearing both the applicant and the objector, or their authorized representatives, in person or through video conferencing, at such time and place as may be determined by him. Decisions made following this hearing are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Any party aggrieved by an interlocutory order of the Registrar may also seek redressal through an appeal under this Act.

Where any objection is taken against the registration of a proposed geographical indication relating to a pharmaceutical substance, the applicant and the objector shall be given an opportunity to present their case before the Registrar. The registrar shall hearing both parties and any witnesses they may call, affording each a reasonable chance to rebut evidence presented by the other. Decisions regarding the distinctiveness or reputation of the indicated goods are subject to judicial review under this Act if either party files an appeal within sixty days from the date of the order. Provided that the Registrar’s decision is final pending such appeal and shall be binding on both parties unless modified by a higher court.

For the purposes of this Act, "Geographical Indication" means a sign used to identify goods originating from a specific geographical area, where such use is capable of distinguishing the goods by their qualities, reputation, or other characteristics which are essentially attributable to that origin; and for clarity, includes signs signifying agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, handicrafts, and manufactured goods. The Registrar shall provide notice of any application for registration of a Geographical Indication to interested parties, and such parties may file opposition under this Act. Following the filing of an opposition, the Registrar shall hearing all parties involved, considering arguments regarding permissible geographical indication use and distinctive character.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the registration of a geographical indication, or the revocation or amendment thereof, desires to appeal, he may, within sixty days from the date of such decision, file an appeal with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds of appeal and any documents relied upon. Upon receipt of such appeal, the Registrar shall transmit all relevant records pertaining to the matter to the Board. Should the geographical indication in question relate to goods or services produced in an area where there exists an unregistered geographical name already in common usage, the registrar shall hearing both the applicant and those claiming rights under that existing name before any determination is made concerning validity.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be refused if the Registrar has reason to believe that the applicant is likely to engage in practices which are contrary to honest practice and/or cause confusion among consumers. The use of any words, phrases or symbols descriptive of goods or services originating from a territory other than the registered geographical indication, where such use implies that the goods or services originate in the indicated territory, shall be deemed an offence under this Act. Any person who, without authorization, applies a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication, or otherwise engages in activities constituting falsifying geographical indications, is liable for damages as determined by the relevant intellectual property tribunal.

Any goods or services a geographical indication where such goods or services are not the products of the area specified in relation to that geographical indication; provided that nothing in this sub-section shall prevent the use of any geographical indication which is merely descriptive of those goods or services, or which is used as a generic term. Applications for registration of geographical indications shall be examined by the Registrar and may be opposed by any interested party within the prescribed time period. The Registrar shall give notice of such opposition to the applicant and both parties shall have an opportunity to present their case under this Act. Where it is established that a person has engaged in acts constituting falsifying geographical indication, the Registrar may issue directions for rectification or other appropriate action as deemed fit.

Any person who, without authorization from the Register, uses a protected geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards established under this Act for that indication shall be deemed to have engaged in an act of falsifying geographical indications. Such use includes, but is not limited to, affixing labels or marks bearing the geographical indication, advertising goods as originating from the indicated territory, and employing packaging which creates a false impression regarding the origin of the product. Provided that, where the use of a geographical indication is incidental to describing the characteristics of the goods, and does not mislead consumers regarding their true origin, it shall not be considered falsifying under this Act. The Register may issue directions for preventing such deceptive practices as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization as provided herein, makes, uses, offers for sale, sells, or otherwise deals with goods that bear a registered geographical indication in a manner which is likely to cause confusion or mislead consumers regarding the origin of such goods, shall be deemed to have falsified the geographical indication. Such an act constitutes a civil offence and the proprietor of the geographical indication may apply to the relevant High Court for an injunction restraining the infringing activity, as well as damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. Further, any goods found to be bearing a falsely applied or falsifying geographical indication are liable to seizure and destruction at the expense of the offender. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including fines up to five times the value of the infringing goods.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may grant licences conferring rights to use the said indication in relation to goods for which it is protected, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the parties and recorded with the Registrar. Such licences may be assigned or transferred wholly or partially, provided that any assignment or transfer shall require prior notification to and registration with the Registrar, failing which it shall be deemed invalid. Where a person falsely applies a geographical indication in contravention of this Act, or uses such indication in a manner likely to mislead consumers regarding the origin of goods, they shall be liable for damages recoverable by the registered proprietor or any authorised user. The right to prevent falsifying geographical indications extends to preventing the use of any mark which is identical or confusingly similar thereto, even if applied to dissimilar goods.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Trade Mark Registrar relating to the registration of a geographical indication may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order. An appeal shall lie if it is alleged that the Registrar has acted without due regard to natural justice, or exceeded his powers as provided herein, or committed an error apparent on the face of the record. Specifically, a ground for appeal exists where the appellant demonstrates that goods are being offered or sold under circumstances indicating use of a protected geographical indication in a manner constituting falsifying geographical indication, despite lacking the requisite authorization from the registered proprietor. The Board may, after affording opportunity to both parties, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against.

A limitation entered register shall be construed as defining the exclusive right of use relating to the notified geographical indication for goods belonging to the class specified therein. Such limitation, when applied, prevents any party from adopting or using a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the registered geographical indication, but only in relation to those goods explicitly listed within the register’s entry. Provided that, where the application for registration includes an element of ornamentation not integral to the inherent qualities of the good, such ornamentation shall be considered separately when assessing likelihood of confusion under this Act. The extent of protection afforded by a limitation entered register is subject to subsequent amendments as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to have a limitation entered register if, following publication under this Act, no opposition is filed within the prescribed period, provided that any interested party may subsequently challenge the validity of such registration on grounds specified herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence demonstrating that due diligence was not exercised in considering an application or that a material fact was concealed during the examination process, entertain objections to a geographical indication already having a limitation entered register. Such objections shall be processed as if the application were still under consideration, subject to the applicant’s right to submit counter-arguments and relevant documentation demonstrating compliance with all applicable provisions.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a register entry concerning a geographical indication shall, within three months from the date such limitation entered register, serve notice upon the Registrar detailing the grounds for objection and specifying the relief sought. Failure to comply with this provision will render the application inadmissible. The Registrar may, after affording opportunity of hearing to all interested parties, order rectification if satisfied that the limitation is erroneous or contrary to law. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to a geographical indication’s registration or limitation entered register may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Penalties for non-compliance with orders issued under this Act shall be as provided herein, including fines and potential injunctions against infringing activities.

A limitation entered register shall be construed as defining the exclusive right of use relating to the notified geographical indication for goods conforming to the technical specifications and production methods detailed within the registered draft regulations pertaining thereto. Such limitations, when applied, do not preclude the use of similar names or indications referring to geographically distinct regions unless such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of the goods. The Registrar may, upon application by any interested party, review a limitation entered register if it appears that the limitation unduly restricts trade or innovation relating to analogous products.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may, subject to such terms and conditions as they deem fit, grant licenses relating to the use of the said geographical indication for specific goods or services. Such license shall be assignable by the proprietor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications. The assignee shall hold the rights granted under the license as if they were the original licensor, but may not further sub-license the right unless expressly authorized in writing by the original proprietor. Further, an inventive step incorporated into a process used in producing goods associated with a registered geographical indication shall not preclude registration of that process, provided it does not directly mislead consumers regarding the origin of the product and is consistent with maintaining the distinctiveness of the register registration.

A person shall be deemed to contravene provisions under this Act if, without authorization from the Register, he uses, in relation to goods or services, an indication likely to cause confusion as to the origin of such goods or services. Such use includes, but is not limited to, affixing a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication, employing packaging that mimics established characteristics of the indicated good, or making false claims regarding its provenance. For the purposes of this section, "origin" shall mean the place where the agricultural product or foodstuff has been produced, processed and prepared. A person contravenes provisions if he knowingly participates in such an act.

Any individual seeking to register a collective bargain relating to Alphonso mangoes shall submit detailed documentation outlining the historical cultivation practices, including irrigation techniques and harvesting methods, unique to the Konkan region. The application must also specify the geographical boundaries defining the area of origin for these mangoes, delineated with precision using established surveying coordinates. Failure to provide such comprehensive details may result in rejection of the registration request. Furthermore, any person contravenes provisions relating to the exclusive use of the registered geographical indication “Konkani Alphonso” by falsely representing their product as originating from that region shall be liable for penalties as provided herein and subject to civil action by the registered proprietor.

Any person who uses a protected geographical indication, identical or confusingly similar to the registered name or logo, without authorization from the proprietor shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall include compensation for loss of profits sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the unauthorized use, and further, an amount not exceeding five per centum of the turnover attributable to the infringing activity during the period of contravention. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from any registered proprietor, issue an injunction restraining any person from continuing such use. A person contravenes provisions under this Act if they falsely represent goods as originating from the geographical unit for which the indication is registered, with intent to mislead consumers regarding their origin or quality. This right of action shall not prejudice any other rights available to the proprietor under any other law for the time being in force.

Any individual or body corporate engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of goods originating from a registered geographical indication area shall maintain meticulous records pertaining to their activities. These records must detail sourcing practices, manufacturing processes, and quality control measures implemented to ensure adherence to established standards as prescribed by the Register. Failure to do so may result in an inspection by an authorized officer appointed under this Act. If, upon such inspection, it is determined that a person contravenes provisions relating to the use of the geographical indication or otherwise acts in a manner detrimental to its reputation, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring rectification within sixty days. Persistent non-compliance following the notice may lead to suspension of registration privileges and imposition of penalties as provided herein. The Register shall maintain a public register of all such notices and subsequent actions taken.

Any individual engaged in the production, processing, or distribution of Alphonso mangoes shall comply with the quality standards as prescribed by the Registration Authority. Failure to adhere to these specifications, including but not limited to fruit size, Brix value, and absence of prohibited pesticides, constitutes a violation under this Act. A person contravenes provisions if they utilize the term "Alphonso" or any confusingly similar designation in connection with mangoes that do not originate from the geographically defined area of Konkan Taluka, Maharashtra.
