Such a certificate may relate to the registration of a trade mark, the renewal thereof, or any alteration made to the register concerning a registered trade mark. The Registrar may issue certificates relating to assignments and licenses affecting registered trade marks, and these shall be deemed conclusive evidence of such transactions unless proven otherwise before an intellectual property tribunal. Any challenge to the validity of a certificate must be brought within the time limits prescribed under this Act.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include a representation of the trade mark, and where such representation is in colour, the applicant shall specify the colours used in the representation. Upon satisfactory examination under this Act, and subject to any opposition filed as provided herein, the Registrar may proceed with the grant of a certificate of registration. Such certificate shall be conclusive evidence of proprietorship of the trade mark, unless proven otherwise by legal process. The Registrar is empowered to issue certificates electronically, and such electronic certificates shall hold the same evidentiary value as those issued in paper form. Any alteration or cancellation of a registered trade mark requires notification via a revised certificate published under this Act.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark who has suffered damage by reason of any use of another’s trade mark without due cause or in breach of rights under this Act may institute suit for damages. Such damages shall be assessed taking into account the loss of profits sustained by the proprietor, and any expenditure reasonably incurred by him to mitigate the damage. Further, where a certificate has been issued by the Registrar confirming that a registered trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier mark, the proprietor of the earlier mark may apply for interlocutory orders restraining the use of the infringing mark pending determination of the suit. The Registrar shall provide such information as is available relating to the application and registration process in support of any proceedings concerning the certificate. Any appeal from a decision regarding the issuance or refusal of a certificate lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar may, upon application made by any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act, issue a certificate specifying the goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is registered and indicating the date of registration. Such application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and shall state the grounds for requesting the issuance of the certificate. The Registrar shall consider the application and may require further information from the applicant if deemed necessary for verification. Upon satisfactory examination, the Registrar shall issue the certificate in the form as provided herein, which certificate shall be prima facie evidence of the proprietor’s rights subject to any rectification proceedings under this Act. Any challenge to the validity of a trade mark registered shall not invalidate the certificate issued by the Registrar unless proven otherwise before an appropriate forum. The certificate remains valid until amended or revoked according to procedures established within this legislation.

The Registrar may, upon application made by a registered proprietor seeking alteration of their trade mark, investigate whether such proposed alteration complies with the provisions relating to registrability under this Act and does not conflict with any existing rights. Any applicant requesting a certificate confirming compliance with these conditions shall submit detailed specifications of the intended alterations alongside an affirmation that the amended mark will continue to function as an identifier for the goods or services originally specified in the registration. The Registrar shall, after due consideration of all submitted documentation and any objections received under this Act, issue a certificate only if satisfied that the proposed alteration meets all stipulated requirements and does not mislead consumers regarding the nature or origin of the goods or services.

Any proprietor seeking to alter particulars of a registered trade mark shall apply in writing to the Registrar for a certificate confirming the proposed modifications. Such application must detail the changes sought and provide justification demonstrating that they do not affect the distinctive character or identity of the trade mark. Failure to adequately substantiate the request may result in rejection, and any subsequent appeal will be subject to stringent review. The Registrar shall publish notice of the application and any opposition received under this Act may lead to a hearing before an adjudicating officer. Deliberate misrepresentation within an application for a certificate is a punishable offence, attracting fines and potential invalidation of the trade mark registration.

The holder of a Trade Mark Certificate, upon application to the Controller, may grant a limited license for the use of their registered trade mark within a specified geographical territory, subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems appropriate. Such licenses shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, provided that prior written consent from the Controller is obtained before any assignment takes effect. Any party receiving an assignment of a Trade Mark Certificate’s usage rights under this Act shall be deemed a licensee for the remainder of the assigned term. Further, the original certificate holder retains the right to terminate any license granted if the licensee engages in activities detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the trade mark. A certificate issued by the Registrar confirming the terms and conditions of such licenses and assignments shall be binding on all parties involved, and its validity is incontestable under this Act.

The Registrar may, upon application made by any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to the registration of a trade mark, issue a certificate verifying particulars concerning the examination process followed, including but not limited to dates of advertisement, objections raised, and hearings conducted. Such certificate shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, subject to proof to the contrary being adduced before an adjudicating officer. Any party disputing the accuracy or completeness of information contained within a certificate may file an appeal against the Registrar’s decision to issue it, provided that such appeal must be accompanied by an affidavit detailing the grounds for challenge and supporting documentation. The appellate authority shall consider all evidence presented and determine whether the issuance of the certificate was justified as provided herein.

Application for a certificate of registration may be made by any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark under this Act, or by any registered company claiming to be the proprietor thereof, subject to compliance with the prescribed formalities and payment of requisite fees as provided herein. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar shall examine whether the trade mark is registrable under this Act and whether the applicant fulfills all conditions precedent for registration. If satisfied that the trade mark qualifies for registration and the company or individual meets the requirements, the Registrar may proceed to register the trade mark in the Register of Trade Marks. A certificate of registration issued by the Registrar shall be prima facie evidence of the proprietor’s right to use the registered trade mark. Any appeal against a decision regarding the issuance of a certificate lies with the Intellectual Property Appellate Board as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be considered to be outside India contravention if it relates to a process by which a substance is produced, manufactured, used or imported into India, and such process has been applied for as a patent in a country other than India, where the application was made without prior authorization from the Controller. Provided that this restriction shall not apply where the applicant demonstrates that the foreign application was filed solely to secure priority rights under international treaties and subsequently abandoned within twelve months of its initial filing date. The burden of proving such abandonment rests upon the patent applicant.

Where an applicant for a patent has filed a corresponding application for a patent outside India in contravention of the provisions relating to publication, the Controller may, subject to due process, issue a notice requiring the applicant to demonstrate that the interests of national security or public order have not been prejudiced by the premature disclosure. Failure to satisfy the Controller within the prescribed time shall render the Indian patent application liable for revocation. Further, any party aggrieved by such revocation may appeal to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal. The remedies available under this Act relating to damages and injunctions shall be applicable where an act of infringement arises directly from the unauthorized publication facilitated by the applicant’s actions outside India contravention.

Where an applicant seeks rectification of a granted patent relating to an invention first described outside India, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the claimed subject matter does not infringe any right vested in any person within India. Such evidence must include, but is not limited to, declarations from relevant parties and expert opinions pertaining to prior use or publication. The application for rectification shall be processed as provided herein, with due consideration given to any submissions made by interested parties. Any act of applying for a patent outside India contravention of the provisions relating to compulsory licensing under this Act shall render the applicant liable to administrative penalties determined by the Central Government. Further, the Controller may issue directions regarding the disclosure of information pertaining to such applications.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent relating to a process by which a substance is manufactured, such patent shall not be granted if the process has already been used outside India. This restriction applies notwithstanding that the substance so manufactured in India possesses characteristics or properties different from those possessed by substances previously produced elsewhere. Provided that, where the use of the process outside India was undertaken solely for experimental purposes and did not involve commercial exploitation, the Controller may, after due inquiry and subject to conditions as he deems fit, allow a patent to be granted. Any application filed in contravention of this provision shall be deemed to be an attempt to circumvent the intent of this Act and is considered an outside india contravention.

Any person who, being engaged in the manufacture, use or sale of any patented invention, knowingly and wilfully imports into India any article embodying such invention from outside India, where the making, using or selling of that invention is prohibited or restricted by law as provided herein, shall be liable to pay a penalty equivalent to ten times the value of goods so imported. This liability extends even if the importation was undertaken without direct knowledge of the patent’s existence in India; however, due diligence exercised to ascertain compliance with Indian patent laws shall be considered during determination of the penalty amount. Further, any such import constitutes an outside india contravention and renders the importer subject to civil proceedings for damages recoverable from both the importer and the foreign entity facilitating the importation.

Where a registered layout-design right is infringed by any act committed outside India, constituting an infringement had such act been committed within India, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings for damages and seek injunctive relief as provided herein. This remedy shall extend where the infringing activity directly impacts or is reasonably calculated to impact the commercial exploitation of the design within India, irrespective of whether the infringer has a place of business or permanent establishment here. However, such action shall not be maintainable if the act outside India was undertaken by a person who had obtained authorization from the registered proprietor for that specific use. Any determination regarding an ‘outside India contravention’ will consider the nature and extent of the infringing activity, alongside its demonstrable effect on the Indian market.

An applicant seeking a patent under this Act shall furnish a declaration as to the true inventor, specifying their names and addresses. Where the invention relates to a process utilizing a microorganism, the Controller may require the applicant to submit the microorganism in an acceptable form for deposit with an internationally recognized depository authority. Failure to comply with such a requirement within the time specified by the Controller shall render the application liable to be rejected. Any person who makes or causes to be made an application for grant of a patent outside India contravention of the provisions relating to disclosure under this Act, particularly concerning prior publication or use, is subject to penalties as determined by the relevant authority in that jurisdiction and may also face administrative action within India. A form issuing from the Controller detailing these potential consequences shall be provided to all applicants at the time of filing.

Where a patent has been granted following proceedings prosecution shall be initiated against any party found to have engaged in activities infringing upon the rights conferred by that patent, irrespective of whether such activities occur within India or outside India contravention. Such infringement includes, but is not limited to, unauthorized manufacture, use, sale, offer for sale, and importation. Penalties for infringement as provided herein shall apply equally to acts committed abroad, subject to principles of comity between nations. Further, any person found guilty of inducing infringement outside India, with the intent to facilitate or enable infringing activities within India, shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. The Controller may issue injunctions and orders restraining such actions deemed detrimental to the interests of patent holders.

Subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licenses as provided herein, any licensee granted a license under this Act pertaining to a patented invention may, with the prior written consent of the patentee, assign such license, in whole or in part, to another party engaged in the manufacture, use, or sale of goods embodying the invention. Such assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Patents and shall take effect only upon such recording. Further, where a registered certification trade mark is associated with an invention covered by a patent, any transfer of rights relating to both the trademark and the patented process must include explicit provisions ensuring continued adherence to quality standards stipulated under the Certification Trade Marks Act. This requirement applies particularly when the assignment involves activities outside India contravention of existing agreements regarding technology transfer or manufacturing protocols.

For the purpose of determining patent validity and enforceability under this Act, “use invention” means employing an invention in a process, manufacture, or production of goods, whether directly or indirectly, and includes offering for sale, selling, hiring, or otherwise disposing of products incorporating the invention. Such use shall be deemed to occur when the invention is applied in any activity relating to commercial exploitation, irrespective of whether such exploitation results in immediate profit. The application of an invention within a research laboratory, undertaken solely for experimental purposes and not intended for commercial gain, shall not constitute “use invention” as provided herein.

An application for registration of an invention under this Act shall disclose, with particularity, the manner in which the invention is used and all relevant conditions pertaining to its commercial exploitation. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further details regarding the use invention, including but not limited to, specific industrial processes wherein it finds utility, anticipated market penetration strategies, and any limitations imposed on its application due to safety or environmental considerations. Such information shall be deemed part of the public record upon registration. Provided that, if the applicant fails to adequately demonstrate the practical applicability of the invention’s use, the Controller may issue a notice requiring clarification within three months; failure to respond satisfactorily may result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Where an invention has been patented under this Act, and the patentee institutes proceedings for infringement relating to the use invention, the court may grant such remedies as are just and equitable. This includes, but is not limited to, injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss sustained by the patentee as a result of the infringing activity, and costs incurred in bringing the action. Provided that, where the alleged infringer demonstrates prior unawareness of the existence of the patent and has acted in good faith, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Further, any party claiming entitlement to the invention shall be permitted to challenge the validity of the patent during such infringement proceedings, subject to applicable rules regarding limitation periods and standing. The patentee shall bear the burden of proving both infringement and the validity of their patent.

Where an application for patent is granted and published under this Act, the Controller may, upon receiving a written request from the Central Government or a prescribed authority, direct the patentee to disclose information relating to the manner in which the invention may be used. Such direction shall specify the particular aspects of the use of the invention deemed relevant to public interest, including but not limited to its application in sectors vital for national security or public health. The patentee shall comply with such direction within a period as determined by the Controller and failing compliance, the Controller may impose a monetary penalty. Any information disclosed pursuant to this provision shall be treated as confidential and access restricted subject to approval from the Controller. It is provided that the right of the patentee to use invention remains unaffected except to the extent explicitly directed by the Controller.

Where an invention has been patented under this Act, and the patentee demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the invention is being commercially used within India, a right of action shall accrue to the patentee for infringement. Any person who, without authorisation from the patentee, makes, constructs, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports into India any patented article, or attempts so to do, shall be deemed to have infringed the patent and is liable for damages. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint of infringement, issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, provided that such actions demonstrably impede the use invention by others. Penalties for wilful infringement as determined under this Act will apply.

Where an invention has been granted patent protection under this Act, the patentee shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of the invention, specifying the field of application, territory, and duration of such license. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the patentee. Assignment of rights pertaining to the use invention is permissible, subject to registration with the Controller, and such assignment shall include all rights and obligations arising under this Act related to the patented process or product. The Controller may require disclosure of royalty rates in any license agreement presented for registration, ensuring equitable access to technology. Furthermore, a patentee intending to assign or license an invention relating to pharmaceuticals must provide notification to the government detailing proposed terms, provided that such terms do not unduly restrict competition within the pharmaceutical sector.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall specify the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory which it denotes as its origin, and particulars of the prior use of the name by producers. The period during which an application may be opposed is deemed the *application registration period*, and this period commences from the date on which notice of acceptance of the application is published in the Official Gazette under this Act. Provided that, if any changes are made to the geographical indication as described in the application after its initial publication, a fresh application registration period shall begin anew following notification of these alterations.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars relating to the name of the agricultural product or good concerned, the territory from which it originates, the qualities, reputation or other characteristics that are attributable to its origin, and the producers, dealers, processors or distributors engaged in making such products or goods. The Registrar may entertain an application only if it is accompanied by the prescribed fee and meets all requirements as provided herein. Following publication of an application, a period of three months shall constitute the registration period during which any interested party may file notice of opposition. This application registration period may be extended by the Registrar for a further two months upon request from either the applicant or the opponent, subject to demonstration of sufficient cause.

An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication shall diligently adhere to the stipulated *application registration period* as determined by the Registrar. Failure to file all required documentation within this timeframe, which commences from the date of publication of the application under this Act, will render the application liable for rejection without further notice. However, the Registrar may, subject to just cause and upon a reasoned request submitted in writing, extend the *application registration period* by a duration not exceeding six months. Any extension granted shall be recorded as part of the official proceedings. Furthermore, any interested party aggrieved by a decision regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application during this period may seek redressal through appropriate legal channels, provided that such action is initiated within ninety days from the date of communication of the relevant order.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to have been filed with the requisite particulars when it is received by the Registrar. The period for filing an application constitutes the *application registration period*, and this period commences from the date the prospective registrant first publicly utilizes the indication in relation to the goods or products defining the geographical origin, whichever is earlier. Provided that, if the applicant can demonstrate exceptional circumstances preventing timely submission, the Registrar may, after affording opportunity of hearing, extend the application registration period by a duration not exceeding six months. Any extension granted shall be recorded and published on the Register. The Registrar shall notify applicants regarding any deficiencies in their applications within thirty days of receipt; failure to rectify these deficiencies within the stipulated timeframe will result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed complete only upon submission of all requisite documentation, including but not limited to proof of use by producers conforming to established production practices and a map delineating the geographical area. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary information from the applicant at any stage prior to acceptance. During the application registration period, which commences upon acknowledgement of a complete application and continues for a duration not exceeding twelve months, interested parties are entitled to file notices of opposition under this Act. Provided that an opposition is filed within this timeframe, the Registrar shall afford both the applicant and the opponent opportunities for argument and evidence submission. Failure to adhere to prescribed timelines may result in rejection of the application or dismissal of any opposition.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to have lapsed if the applicant fails to comply with all requirements under this Act within the stipulated application registration period. The Registrar may, upon receiving a written request from an interested party demonstrating exceptional circumstances and supported by verifiable evidence, extend the application registration period, but such extension shall not exceed six months in aggregate. Any entity utilizing a registered geographical indication without authorization during the pendency of an application or after registration shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to ten times the value of goods sold under that misrepresentation, recoverable through civil court proceedings as provided herein. Repeated violations may result in prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment and fines.

An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall, upon successful completion of the application registration period, be deemed to hold a provisional right to license the use of the said indication. This provisional right may be assigned or sub-licensed subject to prior written consent from the Registrar and payment of an assignment fee as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Any subsequent registered proprietor of the geographical indication shall inherit all existing licenses and assignments, provided that the terms and conditions of such licenses remain unaltered unless mutually agreed upon in writing between the original licensee and the new proprietor. Further, any entity wishing to utilize the geographical indication for commercial purposes after the expiry of an initial license period must apply for a fresh license directly from the registered proprietor, adhering to prescribed guidelines regarding quality control and authenticity verification as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be deemed to have been filed within the stipulated application registration period if it is received by the Registry before the expiry of that period, subject to the proviso that any delay caused solely due to demonstrable technical malfunction on the online portal maintained by the Registrar shall not automatically disqualify an applicant. However, where such a claim of technical malfunction is raised, the applicant bears the onus of providing verifiable evidence substantiating the disruption and its direct impact on timely submission. The Registrar may, after affording the opposing party an opportunity for hearing, determine whether the delay was justifiable; any determination made by the Registrar shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any individual or association seeking registration of a geographical indication shall file an application with the Registrar within the stipulated application registration period, which is initially set at twelve months from the date the relevant good or product becomes eligible for consideration. Failure to submit the application within this timeframe may result in automatic rejection and forfeiture of any prior claims. Upon receipt of a complete application, the Registrar shall publish particulars of the application for public inspection. Any party believing that the geographical indication sought is contrary to law or would cause undue prejudice may lodge an opposition within three months from such publication. Successful registration confers exclusive rights; infringement will be actionable under this Act and subject to substantial penalties including damages and injunctions.

An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to “Kashmir Apples” shall, upon successful completion of the application registration period and prior to final entry onto the Register, provide evidence demonstrating assignment or licensing agreements pertaining to the use of the registered geographical indication. Such agreements must clearly delineate the rights granted to licensees regarding production, processing, packaging, distribution, and sale of goods conforming to the definition of “Kashmir Apples.” The Registrar may require submission of security deposits from assignees and licensees to ensure compliance with stipulated quality control measures and prevent dilution of the geographical indication’s distinctiveness. Further, any subsequent assignment or licensing of rights relating to registered geographical indications shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by requisite documentation for record purposes; failure to do so may render such assignments voidable. The applicant retains the right to register patents thereof related to processing techniques unique to Kashmir Apples, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Use of a Geographical Indication without authorization shall constitute infringement under this Act if, at the time of use, the indication is being sought to be registered and the use is likely to cause confusion amongst the public regarding the origin of the goods. For the purposes of determining likelihood of confusion, relevant factors include but are not limited to the similarity of names, marks, or other indications; the nature of the goods; and the conditions under which the indication has been used. Infringement unregistered may be pursued by any registered proprietor or authorized user of a similar geographical indication, subject to demonstrating demonstrable prejudice arising from such unauthorized use.

Any individual seeking to establish a claim regarding unfair use of a geographical indication not formally registered under this Act faces significant procedural hurdles, requiring demonstration that such use causes demonstrable confusion amongst consumers concerning the origin of the relevant goods. The burden of proof shall rest entirely upon the claimant to substantiate both the reputation and distinctiveness associated with the purported geographical indication prior to its attempted registration. Further, any action alleging infringement unregistered must clearly articulate the specific commercial detriment suffered as a direct consequence of the unauthorized application of the indicator. This provision is without prejudice to existing remedies available under other statutes relating to unfair competition or deceptive trade practices, provided that such actions do not directly challenge the validity of an intended geographical indication registration.

Any individual or enterprise claiming exclusive right to a name, sign, symbol, or other representation signifying geographical origin may petition the Registrar for registration under this Act; however, such claim shall not preclude liability for acts constituting infringement unregistered. Where an indication is used in relation to goods without being registered, and such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the true origin of those goods, the owner of a prior similar indication, whether registered or unregistered, may institute proceedings before a competent court seeking equitable remedies. Such remedies may include injunctions restraining further infringing use, as well as compensation for losses sustained by the claimant due to the misrepresentation and dilution of their reputation. The Registrar shall not be bound to entertain petitions from parties whose claims are demonstrably frivolous or vexatious, provided that such determination is made after affording a reasonable opportunity for hearing.

Any individual aggrieved by the use of a geographical indication which is not registered may file a complaint with the Registrar, setting forth particulars of the alleged infringement and the relief sought. The Registrar shall serve notice upon the party accused of infringing the geographical indication, affording them an opportunity to submit their response within sixty days from the date of such service. Upon consideration of the complaint and the respondent’s reply, if any, the Registrar may direct the cessation of the impugned use or impose such other measures as are deemed appropriate under this Act to prevent further infringement. The aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek interim relief pending final determination by the Registrar. This process is without prejudice to any civil action that may be initiated by the aggrieved party in a court of competent jurisdiction for damages or equitable remedies relating to the alleged infringement unregistered.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirit distillates, cereals, spices, or other such goods may, subject to conditions prescribed by the Register, grant non-exclusive licenses allowing use of the said indication on goods conforming to the standards as defined under this Act. Such licenses shall be assignable, and any assignment must be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry for it to be valid against third parties. Where a geographical indication is being used in relation to goods without registration, constituting infringement unregistered, the proprietor may pursue remedies available under general principles of equity and fairness, but such remedies shall not extend to preventing the use of similar names or indications that do not falsely suggest origin. The Register may, upon application by any interested party, impose conditions on licenses granted, including limitations on territory and duration, provided that such conditions are reasonable and proportionate.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a proprietor of an existing geographical indication, not registered under this Act but otherwise eligible for registration, may grant exclusive licenses relating to specific industrial applications of that indication. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry, detailing the scope of permitted use, including product categories and territorial limitations. Any assignment of such a license requires prior notification to the Registry. Infringement unregistered of a geographical indication, even where no registration exists, is actionable under this Act, provided that the proprietor has granted licenses as described above; subsequent licensees shall be bound by the terms of their respective agreements. The Registrar may issue directions regarding the enforcement of these licenses and may require periodic reporting on compliance with agreed-upon usage parameters.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a suit alleging infringement of an unregistered geographical indication may be instituted by the registered proprietor of a similar mark, provided that such proprietor demonstrates demonstrable and substantial misrepresentation to the consuming public resulting directly from the use of the impugned indicator. The Central Registry shall entertain applications for amendment of pending registrations relating to geographical indications, subject to the condition that any proposed alteration does not broaden the scope of protection beyond the originally claimed territory or product characteristics. An appeal lies to the Appellate Board against any order refusing an application permitted amended, or affirming a finding of infringement unregistered, and such appeal may be based on any error apparent on the record.

For the purposes of this Act, an integrated circuits layout shall mean a three-dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, layers and interconnections on a semiconductor chip. Such representation includes both mask works used for the manufacture of semiconductors and the top surface of a semiconductor chip. An integrated circuit layout does not include features which are solely functional or operational in nature, nor does it encompass any data representing electrical characteristics. The term "element" shall mean an active or passive component, conductive structure, insulating layer or interconnections within the layout. Subject to this definition, any modification that alters the original layout design shall be considered a derivative work under this Act.

An application for registration of an integrated circuits layout design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the drawings or photolithographic masks representing the layout. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the creation of the integrated circuits layout, including details regarding the date of first manufacture and the place where such manufacture occurred. Provided that, if the applicant is unable to provide all requested information, an affidavit explaining the reasons for omission may be submitted under this Act. Any person claiming rights in a registered integrated circuits layout design shall notify the Registrar of any change in ownership or control affecting those rights, within thirty days of such alteration as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of an integrated circuits layout, makes, imports, distributes, or offers to distribute a product containing a substantially similar integrated circuits layout shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed by considering the lost profits attributable to the infringement and a reasonable royalty that the infringer would have been willing to pay for the right to use the registered integrated circuits layout. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining the infringing activities, subject to demonstrating irreparable harm resulting from the continued unauthorized exploitation of their intellectual property rights. Further, any imported product found to contain an infringing integrated circuits layout shall be liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein. This remedy is without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act or at law.

An application for registration of an integrated circuits layout shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain a full and accurate representation of the layout. The applicant shall furnish particulars as to the origin of the layout design and, where the applicant is not the creator of the layout, evidence of the assignment or contract under which the application is made. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may require such further information or clarification as he deems necessary for determining whether the requirements of this Act have been met. The Registrar shall publish a notification of the application in the Official Gazette and afford every interested person an opportunity to file objections within two months from the date of publication. Objections received shall be determined by the Registrar after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, subject to principles of natural justice as provided herein.

An integrated circuits layout shall be deemed original if it exhibits creativity and possesses characteristics that distinguish it from existing layouts. Subject to compliance with prevailing technical standards prescribed by the Controller General, an applicant seeking registration of an integrated circuits layout must demonstrate exclusive right over the layout design for a period not exceeding ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation or from the date of application, whichever is earlier. Provided that, if the layout incorporates elements derived from prior art which are not original, such incorporation shall not invalidate the registration unless it constitutes substantial copying. The applicant must also furnish a detailed technical description outlining the functionality and architecture of the integrated circuits layout, along with supporting documentation verifying its authenticity as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of an integrated circuits layout, commercially exploits or attempts to exploit a protected integrated circuits layout shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall be determined by the adjudicating officer, taking into account the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement and any profits made by the infringer attributable to the unauthorized exploitation. Further, where an infringing act involves the manufacture, import, or offer for sale of articles incorporating the protected integrated circuits layout, the adjudicating officer may order the seizure and destruction of such articles. Repeated contravention of this provision shall attract enhanced penalties, as determined under this Act, including imprisonment up to three years and a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person claiming right in an integrated circuits layout design may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to make, use or sell products incorporating the said layout design. Such license shall specify the scope of the rights granted and the duration for which they are exercisable, and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of such rights in an integrated circuits layout design is permissible, provided that the assignment is in writing and executed with the same formality as a deed. Further, any subsequent transfer of such assigned right shall also be documented in writing. The assignee under this Act shall possess all the rights which the assignor possessed prior to the assignment, including the power to further license or assign the integrated circuits layout design.

Where a claim alleging infringement of an integrated circuits layout design is brought before a Tribunal, the claimant shall bear the burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent has copied substantial elements of the said layout. However, where the respondent demonstrates that the allegedly infringing layout was independently developed, or derived from publicly available information, the onus shall shift to the claimant to prove that the respondent acted with knowledge or reasonable grounds for knowing that the integrated circuits layout design had been taken without authorization. Any appeal against a finding under this Act may only be made on the ground of substantial misdirection of law or fact, and subject to such conditions as the Appellate Tribunal deems fit to ensure fairness and expeditious resolution of disputes.

The registered proprietor of an integrated circuits layout design shall have the exclusive right to make, import, sell, hire or offer to sell or hire the said layout-design, subject to a license granted under this Act. Any person desiring to utilize a protected integrated circuits layout design commercially may apply for a non-exclusive license from the proprietor, specifying the intended scope and duration of such utilization. The proprietor shall consider all applications in good faith and may grant licenses on terms and conditions as they deem fit, including royalty payments reflecting fair market value. Provided that, where the application involves a publish translation work derived from the layout design’s documentation, the proprietor must acknowledge the translator's contribution in any publicly disseminated license agreement. Assignment of rights in an integrated circuits layout design shall require registration with the Controller and be deemed invalid without such registration.

For the purposes of this Act, "digital reproduction" with reference to any work shall mean its conversion into a directly readable or executable form through electronic means, including but not limited to photocopying, scanning, digitizing, or otherwise reproducing the work in a manner enabling access and use thereof by computer systems or digital devices. The Copyright Amendment Act introduced provisions specifically addressing such reproductions, recognizing them as acts of copyright infringement unless expressly authorized under an exception provided herein or a license granted subject to conditions prescribed by the government. Any person engaging in unauthorized digital reproduction shall be deemed to have violated the exclusive rights of the copyright owner.

Any entity seeking to commercially exploit audio-visual works, including cinematograph films incorporating literary or dramatic elements, shall be required to register such works with the designated Copyright Office prior to offering them for public display or distribution. This requirement applies irrespective of whether copyright subsists in the underlying work or solely in the film itself. The application for registration shall include a detailed synopsis, list of contributors and rights holders, and proof of ownership as determined by the Copyright Amendment Act. Failure to register under this Act will render any subsequent commercial exploitation liable to penalties, including but not limited to fines and injunctions preventing further distribution. Registration may be refused if the work is deemed contrary to established principles of morality or public order, as provided herein.

Where an act of copyright infringement is committed by a person acting under the direction or control of another, both such person and that other person shall be liable in tort for damages resulting from the infringement. The Court may, subject to appeal before the relevant appellate authority, award compensatory damages as provided herein, taking into account the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had the copyright owner licensed the work in question. Further, where the infringing act involves the reproduction or distribution of works in a manner that is commercial and substantially imitative of the original copyrighted material, punitive damages may be awarded up to an amount not exceeding ten times the actual damage suffered by the copyright owner. This provision shall apply irrespective of whether the infringement constitutes a violation under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. The Copyright Amendment Act aims to strengthen remedies available to rightsholders against digital piracy.

The Copyright Amendment Act has introduced provisions concerning the accessibility of works for persons with disabilities. Subject to compliance with prescribed technical standards and guidelines issued by the Department of Information Technology, a person may make available any copyrighted work in an accessible format, including braille, large print, audio, or electronic text, solely for individuals who are blind, visually impaired, deafblind, or otherwise disabled. Such making available shall not be deemed a violation of copyright under this Act, provided that the accessibility is achieved through means authorized by regulations framed as per section 52. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register detailing formats considered accessible and any modifications permitted. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal with the relevant High Court against decisions concerning format accessibility or technical compliance.

Where a cinematograph film incorporates works protected by copyright, and such incorporation is undertaken without due authorization from the respective copyright holders, the producer shall be deemed to have committed an infringement. This determination applies irrespective of whether the inclusion constitutes a substantial portion or merely a recognizable excerpt of the original work. Further, provided that the infringing use occurs subsequent to the coming into force of the Copyright Amendment Act, 2012, any statutory licenses previously granted under this Act shall be deemed superseded with respect to such incorporated works. The right to seek injunctive relief and damages remains available to copyright owners as provided herein. Any distributor found complicit in disseminating a film containing unauthorized copyrighted material shall also be liable for contributory infringement.

Any individual found to be knowingly reproducing, distributing, or communicating a protected work without authorization shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than five times the reasonable cost of licensing such use, as determined by the relevant High Court. Where the infringement is committed for commercial advantage or financial gain, and involves multiple acts of reproduction, the penalty may extend up to ten times said amount. Furthermore, under this Act, any entity facilitating copyright infringement through digital means shall be deemed an accessory and subject to similar penalties. This provision applies with particular force following the Copyright Amendment Act, ensuring robust protection against online piracy and unauthorized dissemination of copyrighted material.

The Copyright Amendment Act has introduced significant modifications concerning the assignment and licensing of cinematograph films. Any individual or entity seeking to grant exclusive licenses for the reproduction, distribution, or public exhibition of a film shall provide a detailed accounting statement to the copyright holder every six months, outlining all royalties received and expenses incurred in connection with the licensed rights. This provision applies irrespective of whether the license was granted prior to or subsequent to the commencement of this Act. Further, any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film must be registered with the designated office as provided herein, and shall only become valid upon such registration. The copyright holder retains the right to audit these accounts at reasonable intervals, subject to due process.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where a literary or dramatic work has been published digitally without authorization by the author, and subsequent commercial exploitation occurs through unauthorized reproduction or distribution, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court seeking injunctive relief and damages. Such proceedings shall be subject to the condition that the claimant demonstrates reasonable efforts were made to ascertain the identity of the infringing party prior to initiating legal action. The Copyright Amendment Act provides for a rebuttable presumption that commercial exploitation without authorization constitutes infringement, which presumption may be challenged by the respondent through evidence demonstrating legitimate access or fair dealing under this Act. Any order issued shall be appealable to an appellate tribunal as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any copyright owner desiring to grant a non-exclusive license for the reproduction and distribution of works in which copyright subsists may execute an assignment or licensing agreement specifying the scope, duration, and territorial extent of such rights. Such agreements shall clearly delineate royalty rates payable to the assignor or licensor, calculated as a percentage of net sales revenue derived from the licensed work. Where the assigned work incorporates elements demonstrating novelty over existing prior art, the assignee shall be obligated to provide a written declaration affirming this originality to the copyright owner within ninety days of the assignment’s execution. Failure to comply with this provision may render the assignment voidable at the copyright owner's discretion. The Copyright Amendment Act recognizes and facilitates these commercial arrangements to promote wider dissemination of creative works while safeguarding the rights of creators.

For the purposes of this Act, “storage” with reference to any work includes any material record of the work in any physical form, and shall be deemed to include transient incidental storage. Transient incidental storage is defined as the temporary recording of a work or performance on a computer system or other electronic device solely for the purpose of enabling communication between that device and another device, or facilitating access to such work or performance through an online service, provided that such storage does not constitute reproduction under this Act. Such storage shall be considered incidental where it is neither intended nor reasonably foreseeable by the user as a primary function of the device or service.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of digital repositories claiming exclusive rights pertaining to works accessed through online distribution platforms. Any entity seeking registration as a repository under this Act must submit a detailed declaration outlining its data management practices, including protocols for handling user-generated content and ensuring compliance with copyright restrictions. The declaration shall specifically address the procedures employed regarding transient incidental storage arising from network transmission during access by end users. Such temporary storage, solely necessitated by the technical functionality of the platform and not intended for commercial exploitation or distribution, is deemed permissible provided that appropriate measures are in place to prevent unauthorized copying or dissemination. This provision applies irrespective of whether the work is otherwise protected under this Act.

Where any individual or entity engages in the reproduction of a copyrighted work solely for the purpose of facilitating its communication to the public through a digital network, such reproduction shall be deemed a transient incidental storage if it is wholly necessary for that transmission and does not prejudice the rights of the copyright owner. Provided that, where such transient incidental storage results in the distribution of the work beyond the intended recipient or geographic area, or enables access otherwise restricted by the copyright holder, it shall be considered an infringement under this Act. The right to prevent unauthorized reproduction is subject to the condition that the storage does not involve commercial gain derived from the underlying copyrighted material itself. Any person aggrieved by such unauthorized transient incidental storage may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

Where an intermediary provides services involving the making available to the public of works protected under this Act, the mere transient incidental storage of such works, solely for the purpose of onward transmission to a user requesting it, shall not be deemed to constitute copyright infringement. Provided that, such storage must be undertaken in accordance with established technical protocols and without any alteration or modification of the work itself. The intermediary shall maintain records detailing the nature and duration of such transient incidental storage, accessible for inspection by authorized officers upon due notice. Any person aggrieved by a determination regarding whether storage constitutes mere transient incidental storage may appeal to the relevant judicial forum as provided herein. Further, intermediaries are obligated to implement reasonable measures to prevent unauthorized access or distribution facilitated through their services, subject to guidelines issued by the competent authority.

Where an online service provider facilitates access to works protected under this Act, the temporary reproduction of those works on a user’s device during transmission shall not be deemed copyright infringement, provided that such reproduction is solely for the purpose of enabling the user to view or listen to the work. This exemption applies only where the storage is transient incidental storage and does not prejudice the right holder's ability to derive reasonable benefit from their copyrighted material. The online service provider shall ensure that users are made aware of any restrictions imposed by the copyright owner regarding subsequent use or distribution of the accessed content, as displayed on the platform. Further, such providers must implement measures reasonably designed to prevent unauthorized retention of works beyond the period necessary for transmission.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the making of any copies of copyrighted works solely for the purpose of enabling their transmission over a network shall not be considered an infringement of copyright, provided that such copying involves only transient incidental storage. This exception applies exclusively to automated processes integral to the digital communication and does not extend to the deliberate retention or distribution of protected material. Any individual or entity found to have exploited this provision for commercial gain beyond facilitating legitimate transmission shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable by way of suit in a District Court. Repeated offences may attract further penalties as determined under this Act.

The assignment of copyright in any digital work accessed through an interactive online platform shall be deemed valid notwithstanding the absence of a formal written agreement, provided that demonstrable evidence exists establishing the intention of the licensor to grant such rights. Where a user utilizes an online service for accessing copyrighted material, the temporary and automatic creation of copies on servers or devices incidental to the provision of that service constitutes transient incidental storage, and does not, in itself, constitute copyright infringement under this Act. However, any subsequent distribution or reproduction of data resulting from such transient incidental storage requires express authorization from the copyright owner, subject to limitations as provided herein regarding fair dealing for research or private study. The right to license such access may be assigned freely, but sub-licensing shall require prior notification to and approval by the original licensor.

Notwithstanding anything contained under this Act, the making of copies of works in digital form solely for the purpose of their transmission over a communication network shall not be deemed to infringe copyright, provided that such copying is undertaken as part of a technical process and does not prejudice the rights of the owner of the copyright. This exception applies specifically to transient incidental storage occurring during the lawful distribution of copyrighted material via electronic means, where the storage is solely necessary for enabling said transmission and lacks independent utility beyond facilitating the transfer. Any party claiming infringement based on such storage shall bear the burden of proving that the storage was not genuinely transient or incidental, or that it resulted in demonstrable economic harm to the copyright holder.

Where any person, in the course of operating an online platform facilitating the digital distribution of copyrighted works, makes use of transient incidental storage to enable the functionality of that platform, such storage shall not be considered a violation of copyright under this Act, provided that such storage is solely for the purpose of rendering the work accessible to individual users and does not involve copying or reproduction beyond what is strictly necessary. This exception shall not apply where the online platform knowingly facilitates or encourages acts infringing upon copyright. Furthermore, if a trade mark identical or deceptively similar to an existing registered trade mark is used in connection with such transient incidental storage, remedies available under the Trade Marks Act may be pursued notwithstanding this provision. The right holder may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copy thereof court” shall mean a judicial forum established specifically to adjudicate disputes relating to copyright infringement involving works digitally reproduced or distributed. Such courts shall be constituted by notification under this Act and shall exercise jurisdiction as provided herein over matters pertaining to claims of unauthorized reproduction, adaptation, distribution, or public performance of copyrighted material. The determination of substantial similarity between the original work and the alleged infringing copy shall be a primary consideration before a copy thereof court. Decisions rendered by a copy thereof court shall be appealable to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose.

Any individual or legal entity claiming ownership of a literary or artistic work shall be required to submit an application for registration with the Copyright Office, detailing the nature of the work, its date of creation, and particulars of authorship. The application must include two certified copies thereof, one retained by the office and the other returned to the applicant upon payment of the prescribed fee. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of copyright in any registered work, the aggrieved party may petition the appropriate court for determination. Such a copy thereof court shall consider evidence pertaining to originality and ownership as provided herein. The Copyright Office may reject an application if it finds that the submitted copies are not faithful reproductions of the original work.

Where a copy thereof court finds that the reproduction of a work infringes under this Act, it shall order the infringer to deliver to the copyright owner, or to any person nominated by the copyright owner, all copies of the infringing material in its possession or control. Such delivery shall include not only physical copies but also digital reproductions and derivative works derived from the original copyrighted material. The court may further direct the destruction or obliteration of such infringing copies, subject to reasonable considerations regarding their commercial value and potential for reuse. Provided that, where the infringement is established through contributory means, the court may apportion liability amongst those contributing to the act of infringement. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to a higher judicial forum as provided herein.

Where a work is alleged to be a copy thereof, subject to the provisions regarding fair dealing under this Act, the aggrieved party shall institute proceedings before a competent court. Such court shall, upon receipt of a complaint detailing the substantial similarity between the original work and the purported copy, issue notice to both parties, affording them reasonable opportunity for presenting evidence pertaining to ownership and originality. The court may appoint an expert, possessing demonstrable proficiency in the relevant field of artistic or literary endeavour, to furnish a technical assessment regarding the alleged infringement. Provided that such assessment is advisory only and does not bind the court’s determination; the final decision rests with the court as copy thereof court, exercising its judicial discretion based on established legal principles.

Any individual found to have reproduced a substantial portion of a copyrighted work without authorization shall be liable for damages, calculated at the option of the copyright owner as either the reasonable royalty license fee that would have been payable had such reproduction been undertaken with due permission or the actual loss suffered by the copyright owner attributable directly to the infringing act. Furthermore, where an infringement is established through the presentation of a demonstrably accurate copy thereof court determination, the Court may order the destruction of all copies and materials derived from those copies held by the infringer, subject to such conditions as it deems fit to ensure minimal disruption to legitimate commercial activities. Repeated or flagrant violations shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a copyright owner may grant licenses authorizing reproduction or adaptation of their work, specifying the territory, duration, and scope of such rights. Any assignment of copyright shall be in writing and signed by the assignor or his authorized representative, clearly identifying the work assigned and the assignee’s name and address. Where a license or assignment includes a right to create a copy thereof court for judicial proceedings, the terms governing such use shall be explicitly stated within the agreement; failure to do so will render the grant unenforceable regarding that specific application. The copyright owner retains the power to revoke any license granted under this Act, provided that written notice is given to the licensee at least ninety days prior to the intended revocation date and compensation, if deemed appropriate by a civil court, is offered.

Where a determination regarding ownership of copyright subsists in relation to a copy thereof court proceedings, an aggrieved party may appeal such determination to the High Court within one hundred and eighty days from the date of the order appealed against. The appeal shall be deemed a suit pending in that High Court and subject to all procedures applicable thereto under this Act. Provided that, if the appellate authority finds that the original copyright was infringed prior to the purported transfer or assignment, the determination may be revised accordingly. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law arising out of the judgment.

For the purposes of this Act, a “copy thereof court” shall be deemed to exist where an infringement of copyright subsists in respect of works comprising literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, and such infringement is alleged to have occurred within the territorial jurisdiction of a civil court. The determination of whether a work constitutes a substantial copy for the purposes of establishing infringement shall be undertaken by said copy thereof court, applying principles of originality and access as provided herein. Any person found guilty of copyright infringement before a copy thereof court may, subject to appeal under this Act, be liable to impose sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Any application for registration of a literary work or musical work shall be accompanied by a certified copy thereof, duly authenticated as prescribed under this Act. The Copyright Office may require the applicant to furnish further copies for verification purposes and to ensure accurate recordation against potential claims of infringement. Upon satisfactory examination of the submitted materials and payment of the requisite fees, the Registrar shall proceed with the registration process. A register patents thereof relating to registered works shall be maintained electronically and made accessible to the public subject to restrictions as provided herein regarding personal data. Any aggrieved party may challenge the validity of a copy thereof court determination through an appeal to the relevant judicial forum.

Where a copy thereof court determines that an act of copyright infringement has occurred, it shall order the infringer to provide full accountings of profits derived from the infringing work. Such accounting shall be presented in a manner informing international standards of financial reporting, as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The court may also direct the infringer to deliver to the owner of the copyright all copies or material embodying the copyrighted work within a reasonable time. Failure to comply with such an order constitutes contempt of the copy thereof court and is subject to penalties as provided herein. Further, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of infringement, notwithstanding any prior determination of damages.

Where a claim is made before a copy thereof court alleging infringement of copyright in respect of works transmitted electronically, the court shall first determine whether such transmission constitutes a substantial copying of the work. The claimant shall be required to demonstrate prima facie evidence of ownership and originality under this Act. The defendant may present counter-evidence demonstrating fair dealing for purposes of research, private study, criticism or review, provided that such use is not for commercial advantage or gain. Any party aggrieved by an order issued by the court relating to the seizure of equipment used in the alleged infringement may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The court shall have the power to issue interim injunctions restraining further acts of copying, subject to just terms and conditions as it deems fit.

Where a work has been reproduced in circumstances involving substantial similarity to another copyrighted work, and a dispute arises regarding infringement, an aggrieved party may petition the Copyright Office for preliminary assessment. The Copyright Office shall, upon receipt of such a petition and after providing notice to the alleged infringer, conduct a prima facie examination of the works involved. If, following this examination, the Copyright Office determines that there exists reasonable cause to believe that a copy thereof court is warranted, it shall issue an order directing both parties to submit written arguments and evidence pertaining specifically to the originality and authorship of each work. The Copyright Office’s determination is subject to judicial review under this Act.

Any individual discovering an unauthorized copy thereof court proceeding to reproduce or distribute a work protected under this Act shall be liable for damages, calculated at the discretion of the adjudicating officer. Such damages may include compensation equivalent to reasonable royalties that would have been payable had the authorization been obtained. Further, where the infringement involves the replication of a distinctive design register layout incorporated within the copyrighted material, an enhanced penalty, not exceeding five times the assessed value of the infringing copies, shall be imposed. The adjudicating officer may also order the seizure and destruction of all infringing materials, subject to due process as provided herein. Failure to comply with such orders shall attract further penalties and render the offender liable for contempt proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, an invention shall be deemed capable of industrial application if its production or use can be achieved in any kind of industry, including agriculture. This determination is not limited to existing industries but extends to those which may develop through continued innovation. An invention that demonstrates a practical utility and can be reproduced or utilized by others possessing ordinary skill in the relevant field shall satisfy this requirement. Provided that, an invention solely theoretical in nature, lacking demonstrable functionality or tangible result, shall not be considered capable of industrial application as provided herein.

An application for registration of a utility model shall be deemed admissible if it discloses an invention relating to an article or substance, and such invention is novel, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the working of the utility model, including details regarding its manufacture and use, provided that the information sought does not relate to trade secrets already disclosed in the application. Where a utility model registration has been granted based on an invention derived from prior art which was not readily accessible, the Controller shall issue a notice inviting representations from interested parties concerning the validity of such registration. Any challenge to the registration may be made within six months of publication.

Where an invention is deemed not capable of industrial application under this Act, the Controller may, upon receiving a written representation from the applicant demonstrating reasonable grounds for reconsideration, afford the applicant an opportunity to present evidence and argument in support of the invention's applicability. Such representation shall detail the specific circumstances justifying reassessment and provide supporting documentation. The Controller shall consider such material and may direct that further inquiry be made into the matter. If, following this process, the Controller remains satisfied that the invention lacks industrial utility, the application shall stand rejected. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller under these provisions may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to prescribed procedures and fees.

An invention shall be deemed capable of industrial application if its production can be reproduced or economically worked within the territory of India. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from any party regarding the industrial applicability of a claimed invention, direct the applicant to furnish, within a period not exceeding six months, such documentary evidence and technical information as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate the claim. Failure to comply with this direction shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. The burden of proving that an invention is capable of industrial application rests upon the applicant. Where the claimed invention relates to a process for producing a substance, the demonstration of industrial applicability may involve proof of feasibility and economic viability of such production on a commercial scale. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the invention is novel or non-obvious as provided herein.

An invention shall be deemed capable of industrial application if its production can be reproduced by a person skilled in the art, utilizing readily available materials and processes, without undue experimentation. Provided that, where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance, it shall also demonstrate utility in relation to at least one specific product or article. The determination of whether an invention satisfies this requirement is subject to scrutiny regarding its practical implementation and commercial viability; mere theoretical possibility does not suffice. Further, the applicant must provide documented evidence demonstrating adherence to established industry standards relevant to the claimed process or substance. Any deviation from such standards requires explicit justification within the patent application.

Where an invention is deemed not capable of industrial application under this Act, any party aggrieved by such determination may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision. The Controller shall consider all evidence presented and may, after affording a reasonable opportunity for hearing to both the appellant and the original authority, confirm, vary or reverse the said determination. Any person found to have knowingly made a false representation in connection with an appeal under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. Further, repeated or systematic misrepresentation may result in prosecution for offences cognizable by a criminal court.

Where a patentee, subject to the provisions of this Act, grants a license for making, using or selling an invention in India, such license may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the patentee. Such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. An assignment under this Act shall include the right to sue for infringement of the patent relating to which the assignment is made, provided that the assignee undertakes to exercise such rights diligently and in a manner consistent with the terms of the license agreement. The patentee may retain the right to make, use or sell the invention during the term of the license, unless otherwise agreed upon in writing. For an invention to be considered capable of industrial application as required for patentability, it must demonstrate utility within a manufacturing process or provide a tangible benefit applicable to commercial production.

Where an invention is deemed not capable of industrial application solely by reason of its potential for use in a process involving biological materials, the Controller may, upon review and after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, determine whether such exclusion constitutes a reasonable restriction on the scope of patentability. This determination shall consider evidence presented demonstrating that the inventive step contributes significantly to the advancement of industrial practice beyond mere utilization of existing biological processes. Further, any party aggrieved by this decision may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice arising directly from the Controller’s assessment concerning capability of industrial application and its impact on the patent's validity.

An invention shall be considered patentable under this Act if it is novel, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. For the purposes of determining capability of industrial application, a demonstration that the claimed process or product operates as described in the specification, consistently and reliably, may be required by the Controller. Business India applicants seeking to secure patents relating to pharmaceutical compositions must provide detailed documentation outlining manufacturing processes and quality control measures, conforming to Good Manufacturing Practices guidelines established under relevant regulatory authorities.
