Further, any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the original terms of license granted under this provision. The applicant retains full authority over the trade mark’s core identity but must ensure compliance with conditions imposed during licensing and assignment processes as provided herein.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall file a registrar application prescribed under this Act in Form TM-A, accompanied by the requisite fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of an application, or regarding any condition imposed thereon, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider such appeals and may allow, dismiss, or modify the order appealed against; provided that the applicant bears the burden of demonstrating prima facie validity of the mark in relation to all goods or services specified in the registrar application. Any appeal against an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board lies to the High Court.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have acted in bad faith if it is shown that the registrar application prescribed was filed with intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the source or nature of goods or services. Such an intention may be inferred from evidence demonstrating a deliberate attempt to imitate a registered trade mark, or a trade mark already widely used within India. Where a business india application presents substantial similarity to an existing mark, and the applicant has prior knowledge of such use, the Registrar may refuse registration. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this Act relating to bad faith may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Board shall consider all relevant factors and may award costs against any party found to have acted unreasonably or in vexatiously pursuing an appeal.

Where a trade mark owner possesses rights over a distinctive sign used extensively in connection with software applications, that owner may grant a non-exclusive license permitting another party to utilize said sign within specified digital platforms. Such licenses shall be documented through an assignment agreement filed with the Registrar, detailing the scope of permitted use and duration of validity. The Registrar shall review such agreements to ensure they do not conflict with existing registered trade marks or create undue consumer confusion. Provided that the licensing arrangement does not dilute the distinctiveness of the original mark, the complied registrar shall issue a certificate confirming the assignment’s registration. Any subsequent transfer of these rights requires similar notification and compliance under this Act, maintaining transparency regarding ownership and usage permissions related to the licensed software applications.

Where a trade mark license agreement includes provisions for assignment of registered rights, the complied registrar shall scrutinize such agreements to ascertain whether the terms are consistent with the public interest and do not unduly restrict competition. The Registrar may require further declarations from both the licensor and licensee regarding the scope and duration of the assigned rights, particularly concerning geographical limitations or product categories. Provided that the license agreement explicitly outlines mechanisms for sub-licensing, the assignee shall be deemed to possess all rights conveyed by the original registration, subject to any conditions stipulated within the initial trade mark application. Any attempt to utilize a registered trademark in a manner constituting passing off, despite assignment of certain usage rights, will remain actionable under this Act and may result in injunctive relief.

A registered user shall, upon registration under this Act, be entitled to institute suits for infringement of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in connection with which he is so registered, and may also recover damages from any person infringing such registered user’s right. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered user shall have the same rights and remedies as the proprietor of the trade mark in respect of the use of the trade mark for the purposes specified in his registration. Provided that, where the proprietor has entered into an express agreement prohibiting the registered user from initiating such suits, this provision shall not apply; furthermore, any assignment of a registered user’s right shall be subject to prior consent from the proprietor.

A registered user seeking to extend the area of exclusive use granted under this Act shall provide notice to the Registrar within three months prior to undertaking such extension. The application for extension must specify the geographical limits and classes of goods or services to which the extended use relates, along with a detailed justification demonstrating legitimate interests acquired subsequent to initial registration. Where the proprietor of the trade mark has consented to the proposed extension, the Registrar may grant permission as provided herein, subject to no registered user objecting within sixty days of publication of the application. A registered user shall not be permitted to extend their area of exclusive use if such extension would prejudice the interests of other registered users or dilute the distinctiveness of the trade mark.

Where a trade mark is registered, a registered user shall possess the right to institute proceedings relating to infringement of that trade mark as if they were the proprietor thereof. Such proceedings may be brought in the name of the registered user, and judgment for damages or other relief shall be enforceable against the defendant as though the registered user were the registered proprietor. However, it is provided that a registered user’s right to sue for infringement shall be subject to any conditions or limitations expressly stated in the agreement under which they are registered. Further, where an action has been commenced by the registered proprietor prior to the registration of the user, the registered user may participate as a party but shall not be substituted as plaintiff unless the proprietor consents. The registered user’s remedies shall include injunctive relief and recovery of costs incurred in pursuing such actions.

Where an application for registration as a registered user is filed under this Act, the trade mark proprietor shall provide written consent to the Registrar within sixty days from the date of receipt of such application. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant and the trade mark proprietor, afford them an opportunity to be heard, direct that the application proceed or reject it if he deems the proposed registered user does not fulfill the requirements as provided herein. A registered user shall, upon registration, be entitled to use the trademark in relation to the goods or services for which they are registered, subject to any limitations stipulated in their consent and subsequent modifications approved by the Registrar. Any alteration to the scope of a registered user’s entitlement requires prior notification and approval from both the trade mark proprietor and the Registrar.

A registered user shall not undertake activities that directly contravene the quality control standards established by the trade mark proprietor, as provided herein. Subject to compliance with these standards, a registered user may utilize the registered trade mark in relation to the licensed goods or services, and shall maintain detailed records of production, sales, and distribution for inspection by the proprietor upon reasonable notice. Provided that any alteration to the product packaging bearing the trade mark requires prior written consent from the proprietor, demonstrating adherence to approved designs and specifications. Furthermore, a registered user shall promptly notify the proprietor of any adverse feedback received concerning the quality or characteristics of goods offered under the trade mark, enabling timely corrective action.

Where a registered user seeks to challenge an order restricting their use of a trade mark under this Act, such challenge must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall be accompanied by a security deposit equivalent to ten percentum of the claimed damages. Failure to comply with this time limit or provide the requisite security shall render the challenge inadmissible. Any person who knowingly makes a false statement in any application or representation relating to the rights of a registered user shall be liable for penalties as provided herein, including imprisonment and fines. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such falsity, initiate suo moto proceedings against the offending party. A registered user shall not engage in activities that are detrimental to the reputation of the trade mark.

A registered user may grant a license to use the trade mark for which he is registered, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in such license being consistent with the protection afforded under this Act. Such licenses shall be assignable by the registered user, provided that any assignment requires prior notification to the proprietor of the trade mark and consent obtained where the license expressly stipulates it. The proprietor may object to an assignment on reasonable grounds relating to the potential dilution or impairment of the distinctive character of the trade mark; such objections must be communicated within thirty days of the notice. A registered user shall not, without express written authorization from the proprietor, use the trade mark in a manner that is deceptive or contrary to honest practices in industrial competition. Any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee shall remain subject to the original license terms and conditions as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark by a registered user under this Act, the applicant for such registration shall have the right to submit written arguments and counter-evidence within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the objection. The Registrar may, after considering the objections and the applicant’s response, either allow or reject the application, providing reasons in writing for the decision. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this provision relating to a registered user shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against, subject to principles of natural justice and as provided herein.

Any person claiming authorization to use a registered trade mark as a registered user shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating continuous and substantial use in accordance with the terms of registration. Failure to do so within three years from the date of registration of the registered user, or upon any material alteration to the goods or services for which the mark is registered, renders such authorization liable to revocation by order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Registrar may, at any time, require a registered user to submit further documentation substantiating their continued compliance with conditions imposed under this Act; non-compliance shall be deemed an infringement and subject to penalties as provided herein. Marks indications used without consent constitute actionable misrepresentation.

A registered user shall, upon application made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, be entitled to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services for which it is registered, subject to compliance with the terms and conditions stipulated in its registration. Such a registered user’s right to use the trade mark as provided herein shall not extend beyond the scope of the geographical area specified during the application process, unless expressly authorized by the proprietor of the trade mark. The rights respect registration conferred upon a registered user are further subject to any limitations or qualifications imposed under this Act concerning fair competition and consumer protection.

For the purposes of this Act, a “colourable imitation” of a trade mark means a mark which, without directly adopting the identical form or arrangement of elements of the original trade mark, bears a striking similarity thereto, and is used in relation to goods or services that are identical or closely related to those for which the original trade mark is registered. Such colourable imitation shall be deemed to create confusion in the minds of the public, irrespective of any differences in overall impression. The Registrar may refuse registration of a proposed trade mark if it constitutes a colourable imitation, as provided herein, and subject to the provisions relating to honest descriptive use. Mark regulations concerning permissible variations are detailed elsewhere under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration of a service mark shall furnish detailed particulars regarding the nature of services rendered under the proposed mark. Such application must include representations of the mark, specifying whether it is word-based, figurative, or a combination thereof, along with a clear statement of the goods or services with which the mark is associated. The Registrar may require further clarification concerning any aspect of the application and shall provide an opportunity for the applicant to respond in writing. Regulations governing the use of the mark by authorized users must be submitted alongside the application; these regulations are crucial for ensuring consistent brand representation and preventing dilution under this Act. Any alteration to these mark regulations requires prior notification to, and approval from, the Registrar.

Where a registered trade mark is used in contravention of an agreement relating to the use of that mark, or where such use otherwise constitutes unfair competition under this Act, any person aggrieved may institute legal proceedings for recovery of damages. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant factors including, but not limited to, the extent of the infringement and the loss sustained by the claimant. Further, a proprietor of a registered trade mark may apply to the appropriate forum seeking an injunction restraining such infringing use or unfair competition. Such application shall specify the particulars of the infringing activity and the relief sought. The forum may grant such remedy as it deems just, provided that any order restricting the use of a mark must be narrowly tailored to prevent further infringement of the registered mark regulations.

Applications for registration of service marks shall be examined by the Registrar with particular regard to whether the proposed mark is descriptive of the services it purports to represent. The Registrar may require an applicant to furnish further particulars relating to the nature or condition of use of the mark, or to provide evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where a refusal has been issued under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that decision. The Registrar shall publish notice of such appeals in the Trade Marks Journal. Regulations governing the use of service marks, as provided herein, must clearly define permissible variations and adaptations for authorized users. Any alteration to these mark regulations requires prior approval from the Registrar.

Any proprietor utilizing a trade mark in contravention of prescribed mark regulations shall be liable for damages sustained by the registered proprietor. Such damages shall include loss of profits attributable to the infringement, and reasonable compensation for dilution of distinctiveness. Further, where an unauthorized person applies a deceptive mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark upon goods or services, the offender may face prosecution under this Act. The Registrar shall have power to issue cease and desist orders against such infringers, mandating immediate cessation of the infringing activity. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order shall attract penalties as provided herein, including substantial monetary fines and potential imprisonment for repeat offenders.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may grant a license to use the mark subject to terms and conditions recorded in writing. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The licensee under a granted license shall hold only such rights as are expressly conferred upon them by the written agreement; no implied right to challenge the validity of the mark or claim ownership thereof shall arise from the licensing arrangement. Further, where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee may, with the consent of the assignor and subject to any restrictions contained in the assignment deed, grant sub-licenses relating to the mark’s use within the scope of the original license agreement. These mark regulations are intended to facilitate commercial exploitation while safeguarding the integrity of registered trademarks.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, a registered trade mark shall be deemed to confer on the proprietor the exclusive right to the use of the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. However, this right shall not extend to prevent the use of an identical or confusingly similar mark by any person legitimately using it before the date of registration, provided that such prior use was honest and without intention to deceive or trade upon the reputation of the proprietor. Any dispute concerning whether a subsequent user’s activities constitute deceptive trading practices under this Act may be referred to arbitration as agreed between the parties, but the arbitrator's award shall be subject to judicial review. The Registrar may, on application by an aggrieved party, investigate and determine any alleged infringement of mark regulations.

Where a trade mark is alleged to be used in a manner contrary to the regulations governing its registration, or where it is asserted that the registered proprietor has failed to prevent the use of their mark by an unauthorized user, any person claiming interest may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be deemed to constitute an alleged offence under this Act, and the tribunal shall have jurisdiction to determine whether the trade mark regulations have been violated or if there is demonstrable prejudice to the distinctiveness or reputation of the registered mark. The proprietor shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence rebutting the allegations; however, any order made by the tribunal remains subject to appeal before the appellate authority.

For the purposes of this Act, an “authorised use mark” means a trade mark registered under this Act wherein the proprietor has expressly granted permission to another person, hereinafter referred to as the "permitted user," to utilise the mark in connection with specific goods or services. Such permission shall be documented in a written agreement filed with the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the scope and limitations of the permitted use. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the mark’s reputation and quality; any alteration or misuse by the permitted user is subject to remedies available under this Act and general principles of contract law. Further, the permitted user shall be bound by conditions stipulated in the agreement as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may include an indication signifying that it is an authorised use mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates entitlement to authorise use under this Act. Such authorisation shall be evidenced by a written agreement between the proprietor of the trade mark and the proposed user, detailing the scope and limitations of permitted usage. The Registrar may require further documentation establishing the relationship between the parties and ensuring quality control measures are in place for goods or services bearing the authorised use mark. Any alteration to the terms of such authorisation shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, and a revised agreement submitted for record. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the authorised use designation liable to cancellation.

The proprietor of a trade mark may grant authorisation for specific parties to utilise their registered trade mark under defined circumstances, creating what is hereinafter referred to as an authorised use mark. Such authorisation shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so renders the utilisation void. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the trade mark’s reputation and may revoke any authorisation granted if the authorised user engages in activities detrimental to the distinctiveness or goodwill associated with the mark, subject to due process as provided herein. Any person utilising a trade mark without proper authorisation from the proprietor shall be liable for damages, including but not limited to lost profits and injunctive relief, and may face prosecution under this Act for infringement.

The Registrar may register an “authorised use mark” where the application demonstrates that a trade mark is used by or on behalf of another person with their express consent. Such consent shall be evidenced by a written agreement filed with the Registrar alongside the initial application, detailing the scope and duration of the permitted usage. The applicant for registration as proprietor of an authorised use mark must provide evidence demonstrating their capacity to control the quality and consistency of goods or services bearing the mark. Any alteration in the terms of the consent agreement shall be notified to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by a revised schedule outlining the continued authorisation. Failure to do so may result in cancellation proceedings initiated under this Act. The proprietor of the underlying trade mark retains ultimate ownership rights, subject to any limitations stipulated in the filed consent agreement as provided herein.

The Registrar may register an authorised use mark where an application is made by a proprietor who has granted permission for the use of their registered trade mark to another party. Such authorisation shall be evidenced by a written agreement specifying the goods or services in relation to which the use is permitted, and the geographical area covered by such permission. The applicant seeking registration as an authorised user must demonstrate that they possess sufficient control over the quality of the goods or services rendered under the mark. Further, the Registrar may require submission of periodic reports detailing compliance with the terms of the authorisation agreement; failure to submit these reports shall render the registered authorised use mark liable for cancellation.

Any person utilising a trade mark under an agreement authorising such utilisation shall be deemed to be using an *authorised use mark* for the purposes of this Act. Such authorisation must be in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of commencement of the authorised use, along with a fee prescribed by regulations. Failure to file this documentation constitutes a violation punishable with a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and subsequent offences shall attract fines escalating incrementally up to one hundred thousand rupees. The proprietor of the trade mark may pursue civil remedies against any party utilising an unauthorised use mark, including injunctive relief and damages for loss of reputation or goodwill. Misrepresentation regarding the scope of such authorisation is subject to penalties as provided herein.

The proprietor of a trade mark may grant licences for the use of their registered trade mark, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licence agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities relating to the goods or services associated with the trade mark. Where a licensee is granted permission to apply a trade mark, or a representation substantially identical thereto, to goods other than those for which it is registered, they shall be deemed to hold an authorised use mark for such additional goods. The proprietor retains ultimate control over the quality of goods bearing this authorised use mark and may specify standards in the licence agreement. Any assignment of rights under this Act relating to a trade mark shall include provisions regarding continuing obligations concerning the maintenance of goodwill associated with any existing authorised use marks.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark grants authorisation for another person’s use of that trade mark under this Act, such authorisation shall constitute an authorised use mark, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the agreement governing said use. Any dispute arising regarding the scope or validity of such authorisation, including claims of exceeding the permitted geographical area or alteration of the goods or services covered, may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. The proprietor shall provide a written statement detailing the extent of authorised use upon request from any interested party demonstrating a legitimate concern about potential consumer confusion. An appeal against an arbitral award concerning an authorised use mark lies to the relevant High Court within sixty days of the award’s pronouncement, subject to just cause shown.

For the purposes of this Act, an “authorised use mark” means a trade mark registered under this Act wherein the register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry specifies particular goods or services in relation to which use of the mark is restricted to specific entities designated within the application for registration. Such designation shall be clearly defined and subject to conditions as outlined therein. The proprietor of a trade mark bearing an authorised use mark may, through contractual agreement, grant permission for others to utilise the mark; however, such utilisation remains strictly conditional upon adherence to the limitations and stipulations recorded in the register. Any deviation constitutes infringement under this Act.

Where a proprietor permits another person to use a trade mark under an express or implied licence, or by virtue of any agreement or practice, that other person shall be deemed to be using an authorised use mark in relation to the goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. The proprietor may institute proceedings against any person who uses an authorised use mark in a manner contrary to the terms of the permission granted, including seeking injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. Further, where such misuse causes dilution of distinctiveness of the original trade mark, the Controller may order the infringing user to undertake corrective advertising measures at their own expense. Any agreement relating to the permitted use shall be admissible as evidence in any proceedings under this Act concerning infringement or authorisation.

Where a proprietor of a trade mark has granted authorisation for another person’s use of that trade mark, constituting an authorised use mark, the Registrar may, upon application by the authorised user and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, register such authorised user in relation to the said trade mark. Such registration shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the proprietor's consent to the continued use of the mark by the registered authorised user within the terms specified in the application. An applicant seeking registration as an authorised user shall provide a detailed statement outlining the nature and extent of their intended use, including any geographical limitations. Further, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate that they possess the technical expertise necessary to apply patent invention related to goods or services bearing the trade mark, if such application is relevant to the mark’s character.

The Registrar may register an “authorised use mark” where a trade mark is proposed for registration indicating that its use is restricted to specific goods or services and to particular persons authorised by the owner. Any person utilising an authorised use mark in a manner inconsistent with the conditions stipulated under this Act, or exceeding the scope of authorisation granted by the owner, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such infringement attracts penalties including fines up to two hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term not less than six months. Furthermore, any digital Right Management Information embedded within the mark’s promotional materials, altered or removed during such unauthorised use, will be considered evidence in establishing liability under this Act.

An applicant seeking registration mark certification relating to goods must demonstrate adherence to a prescribed quality standard as determined by a recognized standards body. Such determination shall be evidenced by a certificate issued prior to application submission. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish detailed documentation outlining the processes employed for ensuring conformity with said standard, including audit trails and testing protocols. Further, the regulations governing the use of the certification trade mark must explicitly define the scope of goods eligible for bearing the mark and specify penalties for non-compliance. Any alteration to the quality standards or operational procedures requires prior notification to and approval by the Registrar, provided that such changes do not fundamentally alter the nature of the certification.

Any person utilizing a registration mark certification without authorization from the registered proprietor shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act and liable for damages. Such unauthorized use constitutes a violation of the exclusive rights granted by the registration and may include display, distribution, or advertising employing confusingly similar representations. The Registrar shall, upon receiving complaint, issue notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to cease such activity within thirty days. Failure to comply with said notice will result in summary judgment against the offender, entailing a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and potential injunctions restricting further infringing conduct as provided herein. Repeated offences may attract enhanced penalties and criminal prosecution.

The owner of a registration mark certified under this Act may grant licenses conferring the right to use such certification mark upon goods or services meeting specified standards. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted usage, duration, and any associated royalties payable to the registration mark proprietor. Assignment of a registration mark certification, whether partial or complete, requires prior written consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued adherence to the quality control protocols outlined during initial application. Any alteration to these protocols following assignment shall be subject to review and approval by the Registrar before the revised standards may be applied to goods bearing the certification mark. Further, sub-licensing of a registration mark certification is permitted only with express authorization from the original licensor, as provided herein.

The Registrar may, upon receiving an application for registration mark certification relating to goods or services conforming to a prescribed standard, direct that a hearing be convened if any interested party objects to the proposed registration on grounds of likelihood of confusion with existing marks or deceptive similarity. Such objections must specifically detail the alleged infringing characteristics and demonstrate demonstrable consumer detriment. The applicant shall have the opportunity to rebut these claims at the appointed hearing, presenting evidence substantiating adherence to the prescribed standard and demonstrating a lack of misleading association. Decisions rendered following such hearings are appealable to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days, subject to payment of the stipulated fee, provided that the Board’s determination is final.

The holder of a registration mark certification may grant licenses conferring the right to use such certification mark upon goods or services meeting specified standards as provided herein. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, detailing the scope of permitted usage, duration, and any associated royalties. Assignment of the right to license the registration mark certification is permissible subject to prior approval from the Registrar, who may require demonstration that the assignee possesses adequate resources and expertise to uphold the integrity of the certification standards. Any alteration to the terms of a license granted under this Act shall also be filed with the Registrar for record. Further, the proprietor of the registration mark certification shall ensure that any entity utilizing the mark adheres strictly to the regulations governing its use, maintaining the validity of the certification trade and preventing dilution of its distinctiveness.

An application for registration of a mark may be made by any person claiming ownership or use thereof, subject to the requirements as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, an “application registration mark” is defined as a representation of a sign, whether well-known or not, proposed for registration under this Act and which includes, but is not limited to, words, symbols, letters, numerals, shapes, configurations, patterns, or any combination thereof. The Registrar shall examine each application registration mark to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness, as applicable. Any alteration made to an application registration mark after its initial filing shall be subject to approval by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a mark may be made by any person claiming ownership or use thereof, provided that such applicant satisfies the Registrar as to their entitlement under this Act. Where an application includes a device, the applicant shall furnish sufficient copies of the proposed mark for inspection and comparison purposes. The Registrar may require the applicant to specify the goods or services in relation to which the registration is sought, classifying them according to the prescribed schedule. Upon satisfying that the requirements of this Act have been met, the Registrar shall accept the application and proceed with examination, recording the acceptance date alongside the proposed application registration mark in the register. Any person may oppose an accepted application within the period specified herein.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register an application for a mark, or by the acceptance of another’s application, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be finally determined under this Act, and the Board's decision is binding on all parties involved. Where a registration has been improperly granted, any person claiming an interest in the mark may petition the High Court for relief, including but not limited to seeking rectification of the register. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such a petition, provide copies to all interested parties as provided herein. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during proceedings relating to an application registration mark may render submissions inadmissible. Remedies available include injunctions and damages against those infringing on registered marks.

An application for registration of a proposed application registration mark may be filed with the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence substantiating their claim to use the mark as required under this Act. Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry regarding distinctiveness or similarity to existing marks, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit a written response and supporting arguments within the timeframe specified. Failure to respond adequately may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, after considering all submissions, direct that certain aspects of the mark be altered or amended to ensure compliance with the provisions herein. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The registration shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the application registration mark in relation to the goods or services specified.

An application for registration of a mark may be filed by any person claiming ownership or use thereof, provided that such applicant demonstrates continuous usage of the proposed application registration mark within the territory of India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of filing. The Registrar shall examine whether the mark is distinctive in its class and not deceptive, and further ascertains if it conflicts with existing registered marks or pending applications under this Act. Any opposition to the acceptance of the application must be filed within four months from the date of publication thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in rejection of the application registration mark by the Registrar.

Any person employing a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered application registration mark without leave from the Registrar shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender is liable for damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the said mark, and may also face prosecution for passing off, subject to judicial determination of wilful intent. Further, any goods bearing such infringing mark are subject to seizure and destruction at the expense of the infringer. The Registrar shall have power to issue injunctions restraining the use of a mark that creates likelihood of confusion with a pending application registration mark, even prior to its formal registration. Repeated or systematic infringement will attract enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating authority.

The owner of a registered application registration mark may grant a license conferring upon the licensee the right to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to such terms and conditions as are stipulated in the licensing agreement. Such agreements shall be executed in writing and notarized, providing evidence of the authorized usage. Further, the proprietor may assign the entire interest in the application registration mark, including all rights and privileges accruing thereunder, to another party through a deed of assignment registered with the Registrar. Any subsequent licensee or assignee shall be bound by any prior conditions imposed on the use of the mark as recorded within the Register of Trade Marks. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses pertaining to application registration marks, accessible for public inspection upon request.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of an application for registration of a mark, or by the entry of any particulars into the Register of Trade Marks, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order appealed against, and the Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned, hear arguments and consider evidence presented before it. The Board’s decision on any such appeal shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act. It is provided that an appeal lies only where the dispute directly concerns the validity or registrability of a proposed application registration mark, or its similarity to existing marks already registered.

An application for registration of a proposed application registration mark may be filed with the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall furnish details including but not limited to the representation of the mark, goods or services associated therewith, and the period of exclusivity sought. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish it in the Trade Marks Journal for public inspection and opposition. Any person possessing a relevant interest may file a notice of opposition within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. If an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence. The applicant’s right to the mark may be assigned subject to compliance with regulations governing such assignments under this Act; however, patent shall assigned only upon written consent from the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks.

Any person making an application for registration of a mark claiming priority under Article 15 of the Paris Convention shall be deemed to have made such claim from the date appearing on the prior application, provided that the applicant furnishes satisfactory evidence thereof within three months from the date of filing the application in India. Failure to submit this documentary proof as required herein will render the claimed priority invalid and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any misleading or fraudulent representation regarding the date claim made in an application registration mark shall be deemed a cognizable offence under this Act, punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with a fine.

The owner of a registered application registration mark may grant licenses conferring rights to use the mark for specific goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Further, where a license agreement includes provisions restricting the licensed party’s ability to advertise or promote the goods or services bearing the mark, as contemplated under section 41 clause (a), these restrictions shall be deemed part of the terms governing permissible use of the application registration mark. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the registered mark shall not affect existing license agreements unless expressly modified by mutual consent of all parties involved, and such modifications must also be recorded with the Registrar.

For the purposes of this Act, an "indication certification trade mark" means a mark which exclusively indicates that any goods or services conform to a given standard, specification, particular quality, original guarantee or characteristic, or production method, as determined by a person other than the producer of those goods or provider of those services. Such marks shall be capable of distinguishing goods or services and may include geographical indications, provided that the standards are verifiable and applied in a transparent manner. The proprietor of an indication certification trade mark must ensure adherence to the prescribed regulations concerning the use thereof and maintain records demonstrating compliance with the specified criteria as provided herein.

The use of any indication purporting to certify that goods or services conform to a particular standard, specification, quality, characteristic, or origin, which is not authorized by the Registrar, shall be deemed an offence under this Act. Any person employing such unauthorized indication shall be liable to pay compensation to affected parties for losses demonstrably arising from the misleading nature of said indication. Further, the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint regarding the deceptive use of an indication certification trade mark, issue an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing such usage and ordering the destruction of any materials bearing the unauthorized mark. The proprietor of a registered indication certification trade mark shall be entitled to seek damages for infringement, subject to demonstrating that the infringing use creates confusion amongst consumers concerning the origin or quality of the goods or services in question.

An application for registration as an indication certification trade mark may be filed with the Registrar, conforming to Form T-CS prescribed under this Act. The applicant must demonstrate control over the characteristics defining the goods or services certified, ensuring adherence to a detailed specification document submitted alongside the application. This specification shall outline the standards, methods of assessment, and procedures for maintaining quality consistent with the proposed certification mark. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence of a constitution establishing an independent body responsible for administering the certification scheme and resolving disputes arising under it. The Registrar may require additional documentation to verify compliance with these requirements; failure to submit such information within the stipulated timeframe will result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Any entity seeking registration as a proprietor of an indication certification trade mark must demonstrate exclusive control over the characteristics defining the goods or services it certifies. Such demonstration requires submission of detailed operational protocols outlining quality assurance measures and adherence standards applicable to all certified producers. The Registrar may, after due consideration, require further clarification regarding these protocols if they are deemed insufficiently specific to ensure consumer confidence. Certification marks shall not be used in relation to goods or services that do not conform to the prescribed regulations as provided herein; any deviation from those regulations constitutes a violation under this Act and is subject to penalties. The Registrar may revoke registration where it appears that the entity no longer maintains such control.

Where a trade mark is registered as an indication of certification, the proprietor shall ensure that goods or services certified under the regulations governing such registration conform strictly to the prescribed standards. Failure to maintain these standards, evidenced by documented complaints received by the Registrar, shall constitute grounds for revocation of the registration. Any person aggrieved by the use of a registered indication certification trade mark in a manner contrary to its regulations may institute proceedings before the relevant civil court, seeking injunctive relief and damages proportionate to the loss suffered. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of non-compliance, issue a warning notice; persistent disregard for this notice shall render the proprietor liable to penalties as provided herein.

The owner of a registered indication certification trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Further, where a proprietor seeks to transfer ownership of their registered indication certification trade mark, including all associated licensing agreements, they must provide detailed documentation outlining the terms and conditions applicable to each existing license. The assignee shall be bound by any restrictions or limitations previously imposed on licensees under this Act. Any alteration to these conditions requires prior consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued adherence to standards of quality and origin as originally defined for the certification mark.

Where any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to the revocation or amendment of a registration for an indication certification trade mark, or by a refusal to register such a mark, appeals to the Appellate Board, the Board may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. The appeal shall be instituted within sixty days from the date of service of notice of the order; provided that the Board may, if it considers reasonable to do so, entertain an appeal lodged after the expiration of that period where satisfactory explanation for the delay is furnished. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision, subject to just cause shown.

An application for registration as an indication certification trade mark may be filed with the Registrar, accompanied by a detailed memorandum outlining the characteristics, quality, or other attributes that goods or services must possess to qualify for use of the proposed mark. The applicant shall demonstrate control over the production or processing of the certified goods or services and provide evidence of adherence to established standards. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further information or clarification concerning the proposed regulations governing certification. Any interested party may, within sixty days from the date of advertisement under this Act, file a notice of opposition. The Registrar shall consider any such opposition in accordance with prescribed procedures and afford both the applicant and opponent opportunities for argument. A registered indication certification trade mark confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark as provided herein.

An indication certification trade mark application shall specify the characteristics or qualities, production method, or origin of goods or services which it purports to certify. Such specification must be precise and verifiable under this Act. The applicant seeking registration as a proprietor of an indication certification trade mark must demonstrate control over the conformity assessment process for certified goods or services, ensuring adherence to the prescribed standards. The Trade Marks Registry may require submission of detailed operational manuals outlining these procedures prior to acceptance of the application. Provided that the applicant demonstrates adequate resources and expertise, the Registrar shall consider the suitability of the proposed certification scheme. Any alteration to the specified characteristics requires notification to the Trade Marks Registry for approval.

Where any person seeks registration as proprietor of an indication certification trade mark relating to goods or services produced by members of a particular society, such application shall specify with precision the conditions under which those goods or services may be certified as originating from that society. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the specification claim in the application if he deems it insufficiently detailed to adequately define the scope and limitations of certification. An appeal against any decision of the Registrar refusing registration on grounds of inadequate specificity, or requiring amendment of a specification, lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision; provided that the appellant shall demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Registrar’s determination.

For the purposes of this Act, an indication certification trade mark means a mark distinguishing goods or services of one or more producers of such goods or services as conforming to certain standards relating to origin, quality, mode of production, characteristic, or other particular attribute. Such marks may be used only by persons who are registered in accordance with regulations prescribed under this Act and who comply with the said regulations. An application for registration as a proprietor of an indication certification trade mark shall be subject to opposition from any interested party demonstrating that use of the proposed mark would constitute a misrepresentation or otherwise violate equitable principles, as provided herein.

A trademark, for the purposes of this Act, shall be defined as a mark capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others and shall include a printed design, symbol, letter, numeral, shape, colour, or container. The registration of a trade mark regulations confers upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any rights prior to the date of such registration. A proposed trade mark shall be refused registration if it is deemed deceptive, contrary to law, or offensive to religious susceptibilities, as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a proposed trade mark relating to pharmaceutical products shall submit with the application a detailed composition analysis conforming to Schedule II, specifying all active ingredients and excipients present in quantities exceeding 0.5 percent by weight. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the claimed therapeutic efficacy and safety profile as provided herein. Use of a registered trade mark on goods other than those specified in the registration certificate is prohibited unless prior written consent has been obtained from the proprietor, subject to conditions regarding fair competition and consumer protection. Any alteration to the product formulation after registration necessitates notification to the Registrar within thirty days, accompanied by updated composition data for review and approval. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in cancellation of the trade mark regulations.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive, uses a trademark identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where the infringing use relates to goods or services identical or confusingly similar to those in respect of which the trademark is registered, the court may order the infringer to pay damages equivalent to five times the profits derived from such infringement. Furthermore, any proprietor demonstrating a loss of goodwill as a direct result of the deceptive trade mark regulations shall be entitled to claim further compensatory damages.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark regulations on the ground that it conflicts with matter already protected, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity for hearing. The Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal may, upon review of such objections and after considering evidence presented by both the Registrar and the applicant, direct the acceptance or rejection of the application. Provided that, if the Tribunal finds that the conflict is only partial or relates to a specific aspect of use, it may impose conditions limiting the scope of registration to mitigate said conflict. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order, subject to satisfying the appellate court that they have a substantial ground for appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, a “trade mark accordance” exists where a proposed trade mark, when used in relation to specified goods or services, does not directly signify an association with another enterprise engaged in similar activities unless such association is demonstrably authorized through a written agreement. This determination shall consider the overall impression created upon the relevant consumer base and whether the use of the mark creates confusion regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Further, trade mark accordance shall be assessed irrespective of any superficial differences between the marks, focusing instead on their conceptual similarity as perceived by an average consumer exercising reasonable care in purchasing decisions.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains only such signs as do not indicate a connection in the course of trade between the goods or services and the applicant or some other party entitled to use the mark under this Act. However, an exception exists where the applied-for mark is demonstrably established as possessing distinctiveness acquired through the exclusive and continuous use of that mark relating to those goods or services for a substantial period, as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness. Further, any representation made in the application concerning trade mark accordance with existing registrations shall be subject to verification and may require submission of supporting documentation.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings alleging that another person has used a sign identical or confusingly similar to their trade mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services, the Court shall determine whether such use constitutes a violation under this Act. The Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from any further acts of infringement, and may order the delivery up or destruction of all goods bearing the infringing sign. Further, where it is established that the defendant’s actions have resulted in damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark, the owner shall be entitled to claim damages commensurate with such harm. The determination of trade mark accordance requires consideration of consumer perception and the likelihood of confusion arising from the use of the allegedly infringing sign.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to lack accordance where it contains an identical representation to a previously registered trade mark used in relation to identical goods or services, unless the Registrar is satisfied that there exists no likelihood of confusion on the part of the public. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating such absence of likelihood, including consumer surveys and expert testimony. Further, if the application includes a device substantially similar to an earlier trade mark, the applicant shall provide a reasoned explanation for the similarities and demonstrate distinctive character acquired through use subsequent to the prior registration. Any objection raised by any person under this Act regarding lack of trade mark accordance must be filed within four months from the date of advertisement of the trademark. The Registrar’s decision on such objections is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a representation of another’s trade mark, subject to compliance with subsection (2), such inclusion shall not preclude registration if it is demonstrably necessary to clearly convey the nature or scope of the goods or services proposed to be covered. The Registrar may require evidence establishing that the depiction of the existing trade mark does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the source or quality of the applicant’s wares, and that due regard has been given to the rights holder's reputation. Registration shall only proceed if there is demonstrable trade mark accordance between the proposed use and the established identity of the referenced mark. The Registrar may impose conditions restricting usage as provided herein to safeguard against dilution or unfair competition.

Any person employing a sign identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark without due cause shall be liable for damages as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such liability extends to instances where the use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods or services. The proprietor of the registered trade mark may apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining such infringing activity, provided that evidence demonstrating actual damage or likelihood thereof is presented. Further, any party found in violation shall be subject to a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and repeat offenders may face enhanced penalties as determined by the court. The principle of trade mark accordance dictates that all users must respect existing registrations.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses for the use of their trade mark, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may include restrictions on geographical territory, scope of goods or services covered, and quality control measures relating to those goods or services. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, shall be made in writing and executed by the assignor and assignee. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all such assignments and licenses as provided herein. Where a license agreement stipulates a right of revocation upon breach of contract by the licensee, that provision shall be enforceable under this Act. Further, the proprietor may require periodic audits to ensure continued trade mark accordance with the terms of any licensing arrangement, failing which the license may be subject to termination.

Where an objection is raised under this Act concerning the similarity of a proposed trade mark to a previously registered mark, the Appellate Board shall consider whether there exists a demonstrable likelihood of confusion on the part of the relevant public. It shall be presumed that such likelihood exists if the marks are identical and relate to identical or closely related goods or services. However, this presumption may be rebutted by evidence demonstrating clear distinction in connotation or mode of application. The determination of trade mark accordance requires careful assessment of visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar concerning such similarity may appeal under the provisions herein to the Appellate Board, whose decision shall be final.

An application for registration of a layout-design under this Act shall be deemed to involve an assessment of trade mark accordance where the design incorporates elements functioning as a trade mark. The Registrar shall consider whether such incorporation creates confusion likely to deceive or cause dilution of existing registered marks, subject to demonstrating clear distinction in overall impression. An applicant may submit evidence establishing that the layout-design’s distinctive character does not infringe upon any prior rights under this Act. Provided that, if the design's visual representation substantially replicates a pre-existing trade mark, registration shall be refused unless the applicant demonstrates secondary meaning acquired through extensive use and consumer recognition. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the intended commercial application of the layout-design to ascertain its compliance with these provisions.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to have been refused if the applicant fails to comply with the requirements as provided herein relating to the statement of goods or services. For the purposes of this Act, "application registered proprieto" refers to an application that has successfully navigated the examination process and is formally entered into the Register of Trade Marks, conferring upon the applicant a provisional right to use and exclude others from using the mark in relation to the specified goods or services. This registration remains subject to opposition proceedings under this Act and may be revoked if certain conditions are met as detailed elsewhere herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that the proposed marks are substantially identical with respect to goods or services identical to those in relation to which an earlier registered trade mark exists. The applicant, upon receiving notification of such refusal under this Act, may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or likelihood of confusion is minimal. Where a trade mark has been registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any party using a sign identical or confusingly similar to their registered trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party, investigate allegations of improper use and order remedies as provided herein relating to the application registered proprieto.

Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the rectification of a registered trademark may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. The proprietor of an application registered proprieto shall be deemed guilty of an offence if, without reasonable justification, they fail to comply with any direction issued under this Act regarding the quality control or standards for goods or services associated with the mark. Such failure constitutes a violation and renders the proprietor liable to prosecution before a criminal court. Further, where a trademark is used in a manner contrary to honest practices in industrial property, the aggrieved party may apply to restrain such use through an injunction granted by a competent civil court. The remedies available under this Act are without prejudice to any other right or remedy which may be available to the aggrieved person under any other law for the time being in force.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file the requisite form TM-A within six months from the date of receipt of the examination report under this Act. Where an objection is raised during examination, the applicant may submit their response and evidence as provided herein, subject to limitations on subsequent amendments. The Registrar shall consider such response and may direct further inquiry or proceed with evaluation. Upon successful completion of examination and acceptance of the trade mark, it shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person aggrieved by the advertisement may file a notice of opposition within four months thereafter. Following resolution of any oppositions, the Registrar shall determine whether to grant registration, establishing an application registered proprieto for the applicant.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to comply with all prescribed requirements relating to the submission of documentary evidence substantiating the claimed user date. Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates reasonable cause for non-compliance, such as unforeseen technical difficulties in procuring requisite records, the Registrar may, at his discretion and after due consideration of representations made by the applicant, reinstate the application. The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain accurate and readily accessible records detailing all instances of use of the mark within India. Failure to do so may render the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of an application registered proprieto must be brought before the relevant intellectual property tribunal within six months of publication in the Trade Marks Journal.

Any person seeking to enforce an application registered proprieto a trademark shall first serve upon the alleged infringer a notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that such infringing activities cease within thirty days. Failure to comply with this demand shall constitute prima facie evidence of wilful disregard for the rights vested under this Act, rendering the defendant liable to aggravated damages as determined by the Court. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, subject to demonstrating substantial loss or damage resulting from the unauthorized use of the mark. Any false representation that goods or services are certified under a registered trademark shall be deemed a criminal offence and punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

An application registered proprieto a trademark relating to software applications may grant licenses for its use subject to conditions specified within the license agreement. Such agreements shall not diminish the proprietor’s exclusive right to use the trademark as provided herein; however, limitations on permitted uses must be clearly defined and accessible to licensees. The proprietor is empowered to assign the entire registered trademark, including all associated licensing rights, to another party through a written instrument duly executed. Any subsequent assignee shall inherit all existing license agreements and obligations pertaining to the mark. Further, the Registrar may require submission of details regarding significant modifications to standard licensing terms affecting a substantial portion of users. Failure to comply with such requests may result in penalties as determined under this Act.

An application registered proprieto a trademark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to file a renewal within the prescribed time, subject to the provision that an extension of time for filing such renewal may be granted by the Registrar upon demonstration of reasonable cause. Any party aggrieved by an order granting or refusing such extension may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Board shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant, the trademark registrar, and any other interested parties before rendering its decision. Further, a challenge to the validity of a registered trademark based on prior use may be initiated only after proper notice is served upon the proprietor.

An application registered proprieto a trade mark relating to photographic lenses shall be deemed to extend to visual recordings produced using such lenses, provided that the applicant demonstrates, through documentary evidence submitted during opposition proceedings or subsequent rectification actions, that the use of the mark in relation to said recordings does not create confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods. The Registrar may, upon review of this evidence and consideration of arguments presented by interested parties, determine whether such an extension is permissible; a determination made under this Act shall be final subject only to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Further, any party aggrieved by a decision concerning the scope of protection afforded to a registered trade mark relating to visual recordings may institute proceedings as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to semiconductor integrated circuits shall be examined to ascertain whether the proposed marks are distinctive in their class and as between such circuits. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness where the initial assessment indicates a lack thereof, provided that such evidence satisfies the criteria established under this Act concerning reputation and consumer recognition. An application registered proprieto shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register, subject to any limitations imposed during registration relating to specific functionalities of the integrated circuit. Any challenge to the validity of such a registration must be brought within the prescribed timeframe and adhere to procedural requirements as provided herein.

An application for registration as a proprietor of a use certification trade mark relating to agricultural produce, foodstuffs, or other products of agriculture may be made by any association engaged in promoting and protecting the interests of producers of such goods. The applicant must demonstrate that it operates exclusively for the benefit of its members, who are registered proprietors of trademarks concerning those goods, and that the certification scheme is administered impartially and without profit motive. Such application shall include detailed regulations governing eligibility for certification, inspection procedures, and dispute resolution mechanisms. Registration under this Act confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to authorize the use of the mark on goods meeting specified standards, provided that the association maintains a record of certified products available for public scrutiny.

The proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person who uses a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the certified mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, provided that such use is made without the proprietor’s consent. Any false or misleading indication concerning the quality, origin, characteristics, or suitability of goods or services shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Where infringement has occurred, the proprietor may seek damages equivalent to the loss suffered by them as a consequence of the infringing activity, or in default thereof, such sum not exceeding rupees five lakhs as the Court deems just. Further, any goods manufactured, imported, or sold bearing the infringing mark shall be liable for seizure and destruction as provided herein.

An application for registration as a proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be accompanied by a detailed scheme outlining the standards and procedures governing the certification process, including provisions for inspection, testing, and ongoing compliance verification. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further documentation demonstrating adherence to these prescribed standards and establishing the impartiality of the certifying body. Such a scheme must specify the categories of goods or services eligible for certification under the mark.

The application shall also include evidence confirming that the proposed certification trade mark is distinctive in its character and capable of distinguishing certified products from those not so certified, as provided herein. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the certifying body lacks sufficient expertise or resources to effectively administer the scheme or if the standards are deemed arbitrary or discriminatory. Any alteration to the approved scheme requires prior notification and approval by the Registrar.

Any entity seeking registration as a proprietor of a use certification trade mark relating to agricultural produce, geographical indications of origin, or processes shall demonstrate adherence to prescribed quality standards and operational guidelines. Such entity must submit detailed documentation outlining the methodology for assessing conformity with these standards, including sampling procedures and testing protocols. The Registrar may require verification of these methodologies through independent audits conducted by accredited bodies. Further, the applicant shall provide evidence of a robust system for handling consumer complaints regarding the certified goods or services. Continued registration is conditional upon periodic review of compliance, as provided herein, and any failure to maintain prescribed standards will render the proprietor liable for revocation under this Act.

Any proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall diligently monitor the market for unauthorized use of their registered mark and may, upon discovery of such infringement, institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief and damages. Failure to actively enforce the exclusive rights granted under this Act constitutes an abandonment of said rights, permitting the Registrar to initiate revocation proceedings. Any party employing a deceptive or misleading representation falsely suggesting association with or endorsement by the proprietor shall be liable for penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, ex officio, investigate complaints regarding misuse and impose fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees upon finding violation. Such fines shall be remitted to the Government of India.

The proprietor of a use certification trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the application of the mark, provided that such license expressly defines the scope and limitations of permitted usage. Any assignment of the registration of a use certification trade mark shall include all associated licensing agreements then in force unless otherwise stipulated within the instrument of transfer. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses the certified goods or services, the proprietor retains the right to audit records pertaining to such sub-licensing activities and ensure adherence to quality standards as defined under this Act. The proprietor may revoke any license agreement if the licensee engages in practices detrimental to the reputation or integrity of the certification trade mark. Such revocation shall not affect existing assignments made by the licensee, subject to their continued compliance with the original terms.

Where an appeal is brought before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal alleging that a proprietor of a use certification trade mark has acted contrary to the terms and conditions under which the registration was granted, the Tribunal shall consider whether the alleged conduct demonstrably misrepresents the quality or characteristics of goods certified.
