An assignment of a registration for a geographical indication may be executed only by an instrument in writing duly stamped and attested, specifying clearly the geographical area covered, the goods comprised within the geographical indication, and the consideration paid or to be paid for such assignment. The register maintained under this Act shall reflect any transfer of ownership upon submission of certified copies of the relevant instruments and payment of the prescribed fee. A licensee of a registered geographical indication may sub-license their rights only with the express permission of the owner, subject to conditions ensuring quality control consistent with the established standards for that geographical indication. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render any such transfer void *ab initio*. Any dispute regarding the validity or scope of an assignment shall be adjudicated by the designated authority as provided herein.

A person desiring to register a geographical indication in respect of goods originating from a specific region shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, identifying such region and detailing the characteristics unique to those goods attributable to their place of origin. The applicant must demonstrate that the proposed geographical indication serves to identify the goods as originating from that region and possesses qualities or reputation linked to its geographical origin. An existing permitted register trade mark relating to similar goods shall not be considered an absolute ground for refusal, provided that such trade mark was registered before the application for registration of the geographical indication and the applicant demonstrates coexistence is possible without causing consumer confusion. The Registry may require further evidence regarding the link between the specified region, the qualities of the goods, and their reputation as a condition to proceeding with examination. Any false or misleading representation concerning the origin shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person claiming infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions herein, have the right to institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing goods are sold or manufactured. The proprietor of a geographical indication may seek an injunction restraining the manufacture or sale of goods bearing a deceptively similar description that misleads consumers as to the origin or quality of the genuine article. Where infringement is established, the court may also order delivery up and destruction of the offending goods. 

Consistent with Common Regulations pertaining to border measures adopted by relevant international bodies, customs authorities shall have powers to seize suspected counterfeit goods bearing a falsely applied geographical indication. Any aggrieved party may apply for an ex parte interim injunction pending final disposal of the suit, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated. The court shall consider all evidence presented and determine appropriate damages, including lost profits and costs associated with remediation.

A producer seeking registration of a geographical indication shall submit an application to the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, demonstrating a clear link between the goods, their qualities or reputation, and the specified geographical area. The application must include a statement detailing the rules for determining the origin of the goods, including inspection procedures and certification mechanisms. Where an applicant relies upon an international registration basic as a priority claim under any treaty ratified by India, such claim shall be submitted with the application and verified according to established protocols. 

The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification regarding the geographical indication’s characteristics or origin. Any association of producers seeking collective rights in relation to a geographical indication must demonstrate that it is duly constituted and authorized to act on behalf of its members, subject to verification by the Registrar as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

A “patent” shall be construed as the exclusive right granted for an invention, and includes inventions relating to processes, machines, manufactures, compositions of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, subject to the provisions contained herein. For the purposes of this Act, ‘invention’ extends to a novel product produced by biotechnological or microbiological means, provided that such product is capable of industrial application. Any combination of features presented as an invention shall not be considered inventive if it lacks inherent novelty or involves obvious steps to a person skilled in the art. A patentee may exercise these exclusive rights for a period specified as provided herein, subject to payment of prescribed renewal fees and compliance with all applicable conditions.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification and the necessary fee as provided herein. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and manner in which it is to be performed; and where diagrams or drawings are referred to in the specification, they shall be so prepared as to admit of being easily understood. A patent application claiming priority from a corresponding foreign application must identify that application with details including country of origin and filing date. Subject to verification by the Controller, an applicant may amend the claims of their patent application during examination provided such amendment does not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. The grant of a patent shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights for twenty years from the date of filing, subject to payment of renewal fees and compliance with all statutory requirements under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing to grant a patent, revoking a patent, or dismissing an application for amendment of a patent may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to questions of law and not facts, unless the Controller’s decision is demonstrably based on no evidence whatsoever. Where a patent is revoked due to non-payment of renewal fees as provided herein, the former proprietor may apply for restoration within one year from the date of expiry of the last paid renewal fee, subject to payment of additional prescribed fees and proof of reasonable cause for delay. A licensee of a patented invention shall have standing to seek redressal for infringement by any party other than the patent holder, provided that the terms of the license agreement do not preclude such action. Any assignment of a patent must be in writing and registered with the Patent Office to be effective against third parties.

A person desiring to obtain a patent shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification and the necessary fee as provided herein. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and manner in which it is to be performed; and where diagrams or drawings are referred to in the specification, they shall conform to the requirements of the rules made under this Act. Any amendment to the specification may be permitted by the Controller, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, provided that no amendment shall introduce matter extending beyond the content of the original application. 

Where an applicant claims a patent for a process, he shall disclose the best method known to him for carrying out the invention; and failure to do so may be grounds for rejection of the application. A patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights in relation to the invention, subject to limitations as are prescribed. The term of every patent granted under this Act shall be twenty years from the date of filing the application.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall submit an application in the prescribed manner, demonstrating novel features and inventive steps as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish detailed specifications including a complete description of the invention, its operation, and the best method contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. A claim defining the scope of the patent sought shall be included, subject to the condition that it clearly corresponds with the described invention. 

Where an application relates to a process for producing a new article or substance, the applicant may also include a declaration regarding its industrial applicability and non-obviousness to a person skilled in the art. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the patent application, unless rectified within a period stipulated by the Controller. Any subsequent amendment to the specification shall not extend beyond the scope originally disclosed.

Any person who publishes information relating to any invention, whether patentable or not, with intent to deceive the public or induce the belief that such publication constitutes a valid patent shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a patent is obtained through fraudulent means, including misrepresentation of prior art or concealment of material facts as provided herein, it shall be void ab initio and subject to revocation by the Controller. Any individual who knowingly infringes a valid patent, whether by making, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention, shall be liable to pay damages assessed on reasonable royalty terms, not exceeding Rupees five crore. Furthermore, repeated offences under this Act may result in enhanced penalties and disqualification from applying for future patents. The Controller may issue cease-and-desist orders against continuing infringement.

Any assignment of a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be made in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions governing such assignment, including but not limited to territorial scope and duration. Where a patent is assigned with goodwill, notice thereof shall be given to the Controller within thirty days from the date of assignment, failing which any subsequent transfer may be subject to challenge. A licensee of a patent may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, further assign their interest in the licensed rights; provided that such sub-assignment does not exceed the scope of the original license granted by the patent holder. The proprietor of a patent may grant licenses, either exclusive or non-exclusive, as provided herein, and any dispute arising from licensing agreements shall be subject to arbitration under the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding assignment or licensing may render such transactions voidable at the discretion of a court of competent jurisdiction.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent shall, prior to the institution of any suit for such infringement, provide the alleged infringer with written notice of such claim and a copy of the patent in question. Should the alleged infringer, within one month from receipt of said notice, submit a declaration asserting that the process or article complained of does not infringe the patent, or that the patent is invalid, then no suit may be instituted without first presenting evidence of such assertion to the High Court having jurisdiction. The court shall, subject to rules made under this Act, determine whether sufficient grounds exist for proceeding with the infringement claim, and may direct a preliminary inquiry into the validity of the patent itself. An appeal from any order relating to said preliminary inquiry shall lie before the Division Bench of the same High Court, provided that such an appeal is filed within sixty days of the impugned order. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the suit unsustainable.

A patent granted under this Act shall be subject to revocation on proof that it lacks novelty, involving an obvious step to a person skilled in the art, or failing to adequately describe the invention. Any aggrieved party may petition the High Court for such revocation, provided that such petition is filed within three years from the date of publication of the grant of the patent. The applicant opposing the validity of a patent shall furnish detailed evidence demonstrating prior public knowledge or use relevant to the claimed invention. Furthermore, where a description trade mark has been incorporated into the patented article as an integral part thereof and is essential for its identification, the Controller may direct amendment of the claims to exclude said trade mark if it unduly restricts competition. Decisions of the High Court regarding revocation are subject to appeal before the Supreme Court. The burden of proof concerning inventive step shall lie with the patentee.

A patent, as provided herein, shall be granted for an invention that is new, useful, and non-obvious, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning inventiveness and industrial applicability. The term “invention” includes any novel process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter or improvement thereof. Where an invention relates to a performance—that is to say, a dramatic, musical or artistic work—the patent shall extend only to the inventive step embodied within the technical application or apparatus enabling such performance and not to the performance itself. A performer’s rights in relation to their performance are governed by separate legislation; however, any patented invention utilized in the rendition of said performance may be subject to licensing terms as determined under this Act. Any patent granted shall subsist for a period specified herein, contingent upon payment of renewal fees.

Any person aggrieved by the revocation of a patent, or by the refusal of an application for a patent, shall have a right to appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such extension as the Appellate Board may allow. Where a patent relates to a gene fund established for the preservation and sustainable utilization of genetic resources, the aggrieved party may also seek remedies pertaining to benefit-sharing arrangements, provided that evidence of prior informed consent obtained in accordance with relevant international agreements is furnished. The patent holder shall maintain accurate records relating to the origin of any biological material utilized in the patented invention. Failure to do so may be considered grounds for invalidation of the patent as provided herein. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises which requires consideration by the High Court.

A patent granted under this Act shall be subject to post-grant opposition proceedings, initiated by any person interested, within one year from the date of publication of the grant. Any petition for revocation based on lack of novelty, inventive step or industrial application, must clearly demonstrate prior art and a reasoned argument establishing grounds for invalidity. The Controller, upon receiving such petition, shall notify the patentee and invite their response within a period not exceeding three months. Should the Controller deem the opposition substantiated, a hearing will be conducted affording both parties an opportunity to present evidence. A request for cancellation of a compulsory license granted under this Act may also be initiated through similar proceedings, subject to demonstrating sufficient cause and altered circumstances justifying its revocation. Failure by the patentee to respond within the stipulated timeframe may result in ex parte determination. All decisions regarding opposition or cc inquiry cancellation shall be communicated in writing with detailed reasoning.

The Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, designate any officer or class of officers to exercise any power conferred by this Act, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit. Where a work is made available online without the authorization of the copyright owner, the designated officer shall, upon receipt of a duly substantiated complaint, issue a notice requiring the intermediary to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing content. The Central Government shall maintain a register of all such designations and modifications thereto, accessible to public inspection during office hours. Any decision of the designated officer may be appealed to an appellate authority constituted by the Central Government for this purpose, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the order.

The Central Government may establish and maintain a national register of cinematograph films conforming to the provisions of this Act, wherein particulars relating to authorship, ownership, and all relevant production details shall be recorded. Any person intending to claim copyright in a cinematograph film shall submit an application for registration to the designated authority within thirty days of the making of such film, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the film’s script or scenario. The Central Government reserves the right to inspect any premises where cinematograph films are produced or stored, subject to reasonable notice being given to the owner or occupier thereof. Provided that, in cases of urgent necessity, no prior notice shall be required. All registrations granted under this Act shall be valid for a period of five years and may be renewed upon re-application and payment of renewal fees as determined by the Central Government. The register maintained shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of a prescribed fee.

The Central Government may, if satisfied that a class of persons is unduly prejudiced by any provision of this Act, issue directions modifying the application of such provisions to that class. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the licensing authority under this Act shall have the right to appeal to an Appellate Authority constituted for the purpose and designated by the Central Government; provided that no such appeal shall be entertained unless it is made within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The Central Government reserves the right to inspect records maintained pursuant to licenses granted as provided herein, subject to reasonable notice being given to the licensee. Where a work has been imported into India in contravention of this Act, the Central Government may issue an order for its seizure and disposal, with due consideration afforded to the rights of any lawful owner who can demonstrate legitimate entitlement. Failure to comply with directives issued by the Central Government shall attract penalties as prescribed under Schedule VI.

The Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, establish a National Committee for Copyright Awareness with the object of promoting and ensuring respect for copyright amongst members of the public and stakeholders. The composition of said Committee shall include representatives from relevant Ministries, industry associations representing creators and users of copyrighted works, and legal experts nominated by the Central Government. Subject to availability of funds as may be allocated in this regard, the National Committee shall undertake activities including conducting seminars, workshops, and awareness campaigns; developing educational materials for dissemination through various channels; and collaborating with academic institutions and civil society organizations. 

Any person aggrieved by any decision or action taken by the National Committee may submit a representation to the Central Government, which shall consider such representation and convey its decision to the complainant within sixty days. The Central Government’s decision on such representations shall be final and binding; provided that this process does not prejudice any other remedies available under this Act.

The Central Government may, having regard to the interests of authors, publishers, and the public generally, formulate policies for the promotion of creative works and their dissemination both domestically and internationally. Any scheme established under this Act for financial assistance to creators or performing rights societies shall be subject to conditions prescribed by notification issued by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. All applications for such assistance must demonstrate compliance with existing regulatory frameworks pertaining to intellectual property rights, including but not limited to accurate record-keeping of ownership and licensing agreements. The Central Government reserves the right to conduct audits of any entity receiving funds as provided herein, ensuring proper utilization and adherence to stipulated guidelines. Provided that, in cases where a scheme involves international collaboration, prior consultation with relevant ministries is mandatory before final approval and disbursement of funds. Any deviation from these conditions shall render the applicant ineligible for continued support.

The Central Government may, if satisfied that any class of works has not been adequately protected under this Act, declare such class of works to be a specially protected work and issue directions for enhanced enforcement measures. Any person who contravenes any direction issued by the Central Government relating to specially protected works shall be liable to a fine which may extend to five lakh rupees. Where an offence involves continuing contravention, a further daily penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees may be imposed until such contravention ceases. The Central Government is empowered to appoint investigating officers with powers equivalent to those of a police officer for the purpose of ascertaining any violation of directions issued as provided herein. All costs and expenses incurred in connection with investigations shall be recoverable from the offender, subject to appeal before a designated court. Any evidence obtained during investigation shall be admissible in proceedings under this Act.

The Central Government may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant licenses for the use of copyrighted works in cases where a work is required for purposes of public interest, including but not limited to educational or research institutions lacking commercial viability. Any assignment of copyright relating to cinematograph films intended for public exhibition shall require prior intimation to the Central Government, detailing the scope of rights transferred and the duration of such transfer. Where the assignee fails to adhere to stipulated conditions regarding royalty payments or quality control as determined by the licensor and communicated to the Central Government, the latter may initiate proceedings for revocation of the assignment. Further, the Central Government retains the right to direct compulsory licensing where a copyright holder unreasonably refuses to permit reproduction of a work for national emergency or public health purposes, provided that adequate remuneration is offered and deposited with a designated escrow account maintained by the Reserve Bank of India. All such licenses and assignments shall be registered with the appropriate authority as prescribed under this Act.

The Central Government may, upon receipt of a reasoned representation from any registered copyright society alleging widespread unauthorized reproduction of cinematograph films impacting revenue collection, direct an investigation to be conducted by an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary. Should such investigation reveal prima facie evidence substantiating the allegations, the Central Government shall issue a notice to all internet service providers operating within Indian territory requiring them to block access to websites demonstrably facilitating said unauthorized reproduction. Any aggrieved party—including website operators or copyright owners disputing the findings—may file an appeal before the High Court having territorial jurisdiction within thirty days of receiving notification of the blocking order, subject to furnishing a bank guarantee equivalent to the estimated revenue loss claimed by the society. The High Court’s decision shall be final and binding, though further appeals may lie to the Supreme Court as provided herein. Failure to comply with a valid blocking order constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine of up to five lakh rupees, or both.

The Central Government may, for purposes deemed conducive to the promotion of creative works and subject to conditions it may prescribe, establish a national register of cinematograph films intended for public exhibition. All producers shall register their cinematograph films with the designated authority within thirty days of obtaining certification from the Board of Film Certification. Registration shall be effected upon submission of requisite documentation including details of authorship, ownership, and a synopsis of the work. The Central Government may grant licences to entities facilitating digital preservation of registered works, ensuring accessibility and preventing unauthorized reproduction. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration or licensing may appeal to an officer appointed by the Central Government, provided that such appeal is lodged within sixty days of the impugned order. Failure to register a cinematograph film as required under this Act shall not invalidate copyright but may be considered during legal proceedings concerning infringement.

The Central Government may, upon sufficient cause being shown and subject to the provisions hereinafter contained, direct any person claiming copyright in a work to furnish certified copies of the register entry relating to that work, along with proof establishing the date of such registration. Any failure to comply with such direction within thirty days shall be deemed an obstruction of lawful authority and may attract penalties as provided herein. Where the Central Government reasonably believes a copyright holder is engaging in practices detrimental to public interest concerning access to copyrighted material essential for education or research, it may issue a notice requiring justification for said practices. Should satisfactory explanation not be furnished within sixty days from the date of such notice, the Central Government shall have the right to initiate proceedings for compulsory licensing under this Act. All applications pertaining to these matters shall registered date and be maintained in a secure digital repository accessible only with appropriate authorization. Any aggrieved party may seek redressal through established judicial channels.

The Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, designate competent authorities to administer this Act and exercise the powers conferred herein. Such designation shall be subject to review at intervals not exceeding five years, ensuring continued efficacy and alignment with evolving international standards for copyright administration. Where an application claiming convention priority under Article 8 of the Berne Convention, or relating to a 73 convention application as per relevant treaties, is filed before a designated authority, that authority shall expeditiously examine its formal requirements and forward it to the appropriate division within fourteen days. The Central Government reserves the right to issue directives regarding procedural uniformity across all designated authorities, promoting consistency in copyright enforcement. Any decision of an authority may be appealed to a higher judicial forum as provided under existing laws relating to civil procedure; however, administrative review by the Central Government shall not be available prior to such appeal. All registers maintained by these authorities shall be open for public inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

The Central Government may, upon reasonable cause being shown and subject to the provisions contained herein, direct any agency or officer authorized under this Act to undertake a comprehensive review of copyrighted works suspected of infringing existing rights. Such direction shall be issued following an investigation indicating substantial grounds for belief that the work in question is deceptively similar to a previously registered copyright, potentially causing confusion amongst consumers. Any such directive must specify the scope of the review and the timeline for its completion, not exceeding ninety days from the date of issuance. The agency or officer so directed shall submit a detailed report of findings to the Central Government, including evidence supporting any determination of infringement or lack thereof. Failure to comply with this provision may result in administrative penalties as prescribed under these rules. Provided that, all reviews conducted pursuant to this clause shall adhere strictly to principles of natural justice and due process.

The Central Government may, if satisfied that a class of works possesses sufficient novelty and merits special protection under this Act, declare such class to be eligible for enhanced copyright terms. Any person contravening the provisions relating to such declared classes shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per work infringed. Where an infringement involves commercial exploitation without due authorization, the Central Government may additionally impose a custodial sentence not exceeding three years, subject to evidence of deliberate and widespread dissemination. All penalties collected under this Act shall accrue to the Consolidated Fund of India. Any appeal against orders issued by officers authorized to enforce these provisions shall lie with such appellate authority as the Central Government designates through public notification; provided that no appeal shall be entertained without deposit of a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with directions issued during investigation may attract daily penalties.

The Appellate Board shall be constituted for the purpose of hearing appeals from orders passed by licensing bodies and other authorities under this Act. The Board may consist of such number of members as the Central Government deems necessary, possessing expertise in law, copyright matters, and relevant creative fields. Any person aggrieved by an order relating to rates or terms of compulsory licenses, or any decision concerning infringement or fair dealing, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of such order. Subject to rules made under this Act, the Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, reverse, or remand the matter with directions for fresh consideration by the originating authority. Provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless accompanied by the prescribed fee. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties concerned.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such extensions as the Appellate Board may allow for sufficient cause. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint; all appointments being made from persons possessing expertise in law relating to copyright or extensive knowledge of the creative industries. An application for appeal must be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, alongside prescribed fees. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of proceedings, require additional evidence or documentation as it deems necessary to adjudicate upon the matter fairly and justly. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for rights of review under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend this period subject to sufficient cause being shown. All appeals preferred to the Appellate Board shall be heard in open court unless exceptional circumstances warrant a closed-door hearing, as determined by the Board itself. 

The Appellate Board possesses all powers of a civil court regarding the summoning of witnesses and documents, subject to such limitations as may be prescribed. Any decision rendered by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties concerned, provided that recourse to writ jurisdiction before the High Court remains open in cases involving substantial questions of law. The Board may also direct specific performance or grant injunctions where appropriate to remedy a violation of copyright.

The Appellate Board shall be comprised of persons possessing such legal knowledge and experience as the Central Government deems fit, and appointments thereto shall be for a term not exceeding five years. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright infringement, royalty rates, or licensing terms may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of said order. Such appeals shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed statement of grounds for objection. The Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it thinks fit, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the royalty or fees in dispute, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the appellant demonstrates undue financial hardship. All decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where an appeal lies before the Supreme Court on questions of law. The Board may regulate its own procedure for conducting hearings and disposing of appeals expeditiously; it shall maintain records of all proceedings and orders issued.

The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may appoint. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright licensing, rate fixation, or infringement, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the said order. Such appeal shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend the period for filing an appeal but not beyond a further thirty days. All decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding subject to any remedy available under the Code of Civil Procedure where fraud or manifest error is alleged. Evidence presented before the Appellate Board must conform to rules established by notification in the Gazette. The board may request expert opinions relating to technical matters relevant to the appeal, provided that such experts are duly qualified professionals.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by a Licensing Officer as provided herein may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the said order and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of such appeal, may require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount in dispute, as security for the payment of costs. Failure to comply with this requirement within thirty days shall result in dismissal of the appeal. Any false representation made before the Appellate Board concerning the grounds of appeal will be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject only to writ jurisdiction by the High Court. All orders issued by the Appellate Board shall be enforceable as decrees of a civil court.

Any assignment of copyright in respect of works intended for educational purposes shall be subject to prior approval of the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. An applicant seeking such approval shall submit an application detailing the nature of the copyrighted work, the proposed assignee, and evidence demonstrating that the assignment will not unduly restrict access to educational materials or prejudice the interests of students. The Appellate Board may, after considering the application and any relevant objections received within thirty days from publication of notice, grant or refuse approval; provided that refusal shall be accompanied by a reasoned order. Where copyright is assigned as security for a loan, the lender may exercise rights of recovery only through a process overseen by the Appellate Board to ensure equitable treatment of all stakeholders. Any dispute arising concerning an assignment governed by this provision may be referred to the Appellate Board for final and binding adjudication, subject to the provisions regarding appeals contained herein. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Licensing Competent Authority relating to compulsory licenses, revocation of licenses, or determination of royalty rates, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order and shall be accompanied by a certified copy thereof, alongside prescribed fees. The Appellate Board, constituted with legal experts possessing knowledge in copyright law and industry practices, will hear the appellant and the Licensing Competent Authority and may call for relevant records to substantiate claims. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the time for filing an appeal but not beyond a further period of thirty days. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where grounds exist for judicial review as provided herein, and any aggrieved party seeking such review must approach the High Court having jurisdiction.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights regarding the rectification of the register of copyright may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board, upon receiving an appeal, may require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount in dispute before it, as security for the payment of costs which may be awarded against him. Where an application for registration includes a reference trade mark claiming prior rights, the Appellate Board shall consider evidence relating to continuous use and goodwill associated with that trade mark when determining whether confusion is likely to arise. The Board may confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed from, or remit the case back to the Registrar with such directions as it thinks fit; provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for questioning the correctness of the original decision and has exhausted all available remedies under this Act.

The Appellate Board shall consist of such number of members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify. All applications for appeal under this Act shall be made to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay not exceeding thirty days if sufficient cause is shown. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all appeals filed and disposed of by the Appellate Board, including details of parties, grounds of appeal, and final orders. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may apply for review before the same Board within thirty days of such order, provided that no application for review shall be entertained unless it demonstrates substantial error apparent on the face of the record. The Registrar shall forward all applications for review to the Appellate Board without delay and ensure their prompt consideration as provided herein.

The Appellate Board established under this Act shall exercise jurisdiction over appeals arising from decisions concerning the registration of copyright and disputes relating to infringement. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of prescribed fees and furnishing satisfactory proof that reasonable grounds exist for questioning the decision. Where a claim for justified registration is made based on prior artistic creation demonstrably predating the alleged infringement, the burden of disproving said creation shall lie with the opposing party. Failure to comply with procedural requirements regarding appeal submission or fee payment shall render the appeal inadmissible and may attract a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees. The Appellate Board’s decisions are final and binding except where gross error of law is established before a court of competent jurisdiction, subject to applicable limitations periods. Any attempt to obstruct the functioning of the Appellate Board constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment up to two years or fine, or both.

Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be subject to the prior approval of the Appellate Board constituted under this Act, and such approval may be granted or refused at the discretion of the said Board. An applicant seeking approval for an assignment shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the Appellate Board demonstrating that the proposed assignee is capable of adequately exploiting the assigned copyright and ensuring continued production and dissemination of cinematographic works. Where a person reasonably believes that an assignment of copyright is likely to result in threatened infringement of existing rights, such person may lodge a formal objection with the Appellate Board prior to the completion of said assignment. The Appellate Board shall consider all objections received and may require the applicant to provide further clarification or undertake specific conditions as it deems necessary for protecting legitimate interests. All decisions of the Appellate Board regarding assignments shall be final and binding, subject only to judicial review on grounds of natural justice. Licensing agreements relating to copyright in sound recordings shall also adhere to these provisions concerning assignment approval.

A person shall be deemed to be a registered user of a trademark when they have been duly recorded as such in the register maintained under this Act, subject to the conditions specified herein. Such registration confers upon the registered user the right to use the trademark for those goods and services specifically enumerated in the entry recording their usage, and no further or other rights. The proprietor of the trade mark may, at any time, revoke the registration of a registered user if sufficient cause exists, including but not limited to failure to adhere to quality control standards as agreed upon by both parties. Provided that, such revocation shall be subject to a notice period of thirty days and an opportunity for hearing afforded to the registered user. A co-owner of a trademark may also act as a registered user.

A person shall be considered a registered user in respect of specified goods within Class 32, provided that such registration is effected in accordance with the procedure as laid down herein and subject to the proprietor’s consent duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. The application for registration as a registered user shall include details regarding the extent of usage, geographical territory, and duration for which exclusive rights are sought. Upon satisfactory verification and payment of the prescribed fee, the Registrar may record the applicant as a registered user in the Register of Registered Users maintained alongside the principal register. A registered user’s rights are however strictly limited to those goods specified in their registration and shall not extend beyond the terms agreed with the trade mark proprietor. Any association or corporate body seeking such registration must furnish proof of its legal existence and authorized signatory details as per prevailing company law. Failure to adhere to these provisions may result in cancellation of registered user status.

A registered user of a trademark shall possess the right to utilize the said trademark in respect of those goods specified in the registration, subject to the terms and conditions of their agreement with the proprietor. Should a dispute arise concerning the scope of such permitted use, either party may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register or seek appropriate injunctive relief as provided herein. The proprietor shall not be liable for any infringement committed by a registered user acting within the defined parameters of their usage rights; however, this protection does not extend to acts constituting passing off or unfair competition beyond those expressly authorized. Where a registered user persistently exceeds the scope of permitted use and fails to rectify such breach upon reasonable notice from the proprietor, the registration as a user may be revoked. Any aggrieved party alleging misuse by a registered user may initiate proceedings for damages, provided that prior notification has been served on both the proprietor and the alleged infringing user.

A person shall be deemed to be a registered user in respect of specified goods within Class 33 of the Fourth Schedule, if such person is duly recorded as such in the Register maintained under this Act and has furnished an undertaking acceptable to the Trade Marks Registry affirming adherence to quality control standards stipulated by the proprietor. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted documentation and a finding that the applicant exercises bona fide use of the mark, record such user in the register. Any assignment or transfer of rights as a registered user shall require prior written consent from the trade mark proprietor, and notification thereof must be filed with the Registry within thirty days of such transaction. Failure to obtain requisite consent may render the continued usage unlawful. Provided that, where the registered user defaults in maintaining quality control standards, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for removal of their name from the Register as provided herein, after affording a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The proprietor retains full ownership and rights over the trade mark itself.

A person shall be considered a registered user in respect of one or more goods included in a class of goods in relation to which a trademark is registered, if such person has been duly authorized by the proprietor of the trade mark to use it. Such authorization must be evidenced by a written agreement containing all material terms and conditions governing the permitted scope of usage, including but not limited to geographical territory, duration, quality control standards, and royalty payments, as agreed upon between the parties. Any assignment or transfer of rights under such an agreement shall require prior written consent from the trade mark proprietor. A registered user may, subject to the terms of their agreement, exercise all rights associated with the use of the trademark as if they were the owner, provided that they adhere strictly to quality standards stipulated by the proprietor and cooperate fully in preventing any infringement or misuse of the said trade mark. Failure to comply with these conditions shall render the registration of such user liable for revocation under this Act.

Any person becoming a registered user of a trademark as provided herein shall be bound by such conditions as may be specified in the register and any variation thereof duly recorded. Failure to comply with said conditions, or use of the trademark beyond the scope of permitted usage, shall constitute an infringement actionable under this Act. A registered user may apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register if circumstances so warrant, subject to notice being served upon the proprietor of the trade mark. The proprietor retains the right to supervise the quality of goods and services offered by a registered user, and any deficiency therein impacting reputation shall be grounds for revocation of registration as a user. Any false representation regarding association with or endorsement by the trademark holder committed by a registered user will attract penalties including fines not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment up to two years, or both.

A registered user of a trademark shall be entitled to utilize the said mark in accordance with the terms and conditions specified in the registration certificate and any subsequent agreements executed between the proprietor and such user. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered user, whether whole or partial, requires prior written consent from the trade mark proprietor, subject to provisions concerning bona fide business transfers. The proprietor may revoke the license granted to a registered user upon reasonable cause being shown and after providing not less than sixty days’ notice outlining specific breaches of agreement or detrimental impact on the reputation of the trademark. Notwithstanding such revocation, any goods already in circulation bearing the trademark prior to the effective date of revocation shall remain lawful for sale until existing stocks are depleted. A transfer of ownership of the registered user's business as a going concern does not require fresh consent from the proprietor but notification must be provided within thirty days of completion of the transfer. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the continued use unlawful under this Act.

A person duly recorded as a registered user of a trademark shall be entitled to utilize said mark for those goods specified in the register and subject to the conditions, if any, endorsed therein. However, such entitlement does not preclude the rights of the proprietor to independently employ the trade mark or authorize other users, unless expressly restricted by agreement. Any dispute concerning the scope of usage permitted to a registered user, or alleging infringement of the proprietor’s rights through exceeding those bounds, may be submitted for adjudication to the High Court having jurisdiction. An appeal from any decision rendered by such court shall lie before the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained as per established procedure. The registrar may, upon sufficient cause shown and after notice to both parties, direct a registered user to amend their register entry if it inaccurately reflects agreed usage limitations or causes confusion in the market. Failure to comply with this direction constitutes grounds for cancellation of registration as a user under this Act.

A registered user of a trademark shall be entitled to continue using such trademark in respect of those goods and services for which they were originally registered, subject to adherence to conditions specified within their registration as a user. Any act constituting an infringement of the principal proprietor’s rights by a third party shall also extend to prejudice the interests of a registered user, entitling them to seek remedies as provided herein. However, such entitlement is conditional upon the continued validity of both the trademark itself and the agreement establishing the registered user status. The principal proprietor may not unilaterally terminate the registration respect afforded to a registered user without reasonable cause and due notice, failing which they shall be liable for damages. A registered user may petition the court for independent relief against infringement where their commercial interests are demonstrably distinct from those of the principal proprietor, provided that such action does not prejudice the latter’s own enforcement rights under this Act. Any assignment or transfer of a registered user's rights requires prior written consent from the trademark owner.

A person shall be considered a registered user in respect of one or more goods included in the classes of goods in which the trade mark is registered, subject to the conditions set forth herein. An application for registration as a registered user must be made to the Trade Marks Registry in writing and shall identify the specific goods for which usage is sought. The proprietor of the trade mark may, at their discretion, enter into an agreement with any person specifying the terms of use, including duration, territory, and quality control standards. Where the register disclosed details of a registered user’s limitations regarding scope or duration of permitted use, such disclosures shall be binding on both the proprietor and the registered user. Failure to adhere to agreed-upon conditions may result in revocation of registration as a user, as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry maintains discretion to require updated information concerning continued usage and compliance with any stipulated terms. Any dispute regarding the rights or obligations of a registered user shall be subject to adjudication under this Act.

A person duly recorded as a registered user of a trademark shall be entitled to obtain redress under this Act for any infringement of such trademark, subject to the terms and conditions of registration and any limitations specified therein. However, nothing herein shall prejudice the rights of the proprietor to initiate independent legal proceedings in respect of said infringement. An authorised user, though not formally recorded as a registered user, may, with the express written consent of the registered user, pursue remedies for acts constituting an unlawful use of the mark, provided that such authorisation is demonstrably valid and subsisting at the time of the alleged infringement. Any fraudulent misrepresentation regarding the status of being a registered or authorised user shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Failure to provide accurate records relating to usage as required under this Act will attract penalties up to fifty thousand rupees.

A registered user of a trademark shall enjoy the rights as conferred under this Act subject to the terms and conditions specified in the registration certificate and any subsequent agreement with the proprietor. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may, at their discretion, grant licenses permitting use of the mark by another party, defining therein the scope of permitted usage including geographical territory, class of goods, and duration. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a registered user shall require prior written consent from the trademark proprietor unless otherwise stipulated in the original agreement establishing the registered user status. Failure to obtain such consent may render the assignment voidable at the option of the proprietor. The registrar maintains a public register of registered users linked to corresponding registration trade marks, detailing the extent of authorized usage and any limitations imposed by the owner. A transfer of ownership affecting a registered user does not automatically affect the validity of their registration; however, it triggers a requirement for notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

A registered user of a trademark shall be entitled to oppose any application for registration of a similar mark likely to cause confusion, notwithstanding any prior association between the applicant and the proprietor. However, such opposition may be waived if the registered user fails to demonstrate actual damage resulting from the potential conflict within one year of notification of the application. The rights conferred upon a registered user are transmissible, subject to conditions mutually agreed upon with the trademark proprietor, and any transfer without prior consent shall constitute grounds for revocation of the registration of the transferee. Any dispute regarding the validity of such transmission or the extent of permissible use under this Act may be referred to the High Court having jurisdiction; provided that a party aggrieved by the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days. The proprietor retains the right to supervise the quality of goods and services offered by the registered user, ensuring adherence to established standards.

A layout-design is defined as the finalized topographical arrangement of the elements and interconnections of an integrated circuit, including channel substrates, but excluding any features solely for testing, assembly or packaging. Such a layout-design shall be original if it has been independently created and possesses no substantial similarity to any existing layout-design, subject to verification by the appropriate authority as provided herein. The term ‘integrated circuit’ refers to those circuits intended for use in electronic devices, performing functions such as amplification, switching, or data processing. Any person deriving a semiconductor integrated circuit from an earlier layout-design shall be deemed to have commercially exploited said layout-design unless otherwise permitted under this Act. A registered layout-design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit and import the same.

Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form accompanied by the appropriate fee as provided herein. The application shall disclose and define the scope of the layout-design for which protection is sought, including a detailed description of each layer constituting the layout-design and its intended function within the semiconductor device. A representation or drawing of the layout-design, clearly demonstrating all layers, must also be furnished with the application. 

Where an applicant claims priority from an earlier application filed in another country party to any treaty or convention for the protection of intellectual property rights, such claim shall be made at the time of filing and accompanied by relevant documents establishing the date of the prior application. Subject to verification and confirmation that the layout-design is novel and intrinsically capable of being distinguished from other registered layout-designs, the Controller may register the layout-design in the Register of Layout-Designs. Registration confers exclusive rights on the applicant for a period of ten years from the date of filing.

Any person who has created an original layout-design shall be entitled to register the same under this Act, subject to fulfilling such conditions as may be prescribed. Registration of a layout-design confers upon the registered owner the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit commercially, distribute and import articles embodying such layout-design. Where a person makes any act contrary to these rights without the license or authorization of the registered owner, an action for infringement may be instituted in the appropriate District Court. The proprietor of a registered layout-design shall have the right to seek interlocutory injunctions restraining further acts of infringement and also claim damages for loss suffered due to such unauthorized use. A person alleging infringement may, as provided herein, apply for search and seizure of infringing articles. Any information relating to the creation or exploitation of a layout-design which is confidential in nature shall be protected against disclosure unless required by law or with the consent of the owner. The rights conferred under this Act are subject to such limitations as may be necessary to prevent abuse or unfair competition.

Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller in such form and manner as may be prescribed. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, indicating its topological features and dimensions, and shall be accompanied by necessary drawings or representations sufficient for complete disclosure thereof. A statement of ownership asserting the applicant’s right to the layout-design is also mandatory; provided that where the layout-design was made during employment, the employer shall be deemed to be the owner unless otherwise agreed in writing. 

The Controller may require the applicant to amend the application or submit further information as considered necessary for proper examination. Subject to verification and satisfaction of all requirements as provided herein, the Controller shall register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration. Registration confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, distribute, import, or otherwise commercially exploit the layout-design for a period of ten years from the date of filing; however, such rights are subject to limitations regarding independent development or prior art.

Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Intellectual Property Office as provided herein, accompanied by the prescribed fee and all necessary documentation demonstrating originality. The application shall clearly delineate the three-dimensional arrangement of the elements constituting the layout-design, specifying each layer and its function within the semiconductor integrated circuit. A registered layout-design shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or commercially exploit the said layout-design for a period of ten years from the date of registration, subject to continued payment of annual renewal fees. However, such rights shall not extend to ideas, procedures, systems, methods of operation, computer programs, or data; protection is strictly limited to the specific layout-design itself. Any unauthorized reproduction or commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design constitutes an infringement under this Act and may be subject to legal remedies including injunctions and damages. A person claiming prior art must submit evidence substantiating its existence before the filing date of the application.

Any person who reproduces, distributes, imports, exports, sells, or otherwise commercially exploits a registered layout-design without the authorization of the proprietor shall be liable to a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees and may extend to ten lakh rupees per such act. Where the infringement involves multiple integrated circuits embodying the same layout-design, each such circuit shall constitute a separate offence for purposes of determining the aggregate penalty. A court, upon establishing infringement under this Act and considering aggravating factors such as willful intent or repeated violations, may also grant an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. Any material used in the manufacture of infringing integrated circuits, including but not limited to masking works and photomasks, shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure by duly authorized officers. The proprietor of a layout-design may pursue civil remedies for damages sustained as a result of such unauthorized exploitation, independent of any penalties imposed under this Act.

Any person possessing a layout-design right shall have the right to assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of such right by any instrument in writing, subject to the terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties concerned. An assignment of a layout-design right must clearly identify the specific layout-design being transferred and specify whether the assignment is for the whole of India or for a limited geographical area. Where a layout-design is jointly owned, no owner shall grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other owners, provided that any dispute regarding such consent may be resolved through arbitration as per the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The assignee of a registered layout-design shall have the same rights and remedies as the original proprietor, subject to any limitations expressly stated in the assignment agreement. A license granted under this Act shall not preclude the licensor from granting further licenses unless otherwise agreed. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a layout-design, or imposing conditions on such registration, may prefer an appeal to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction within ninety days from the date of the said order; provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and a statement of facts giving rise to the dispute. The appellant shall demonstrate substantial question of law arising from the refusal or condition imposed, relating to novelty or inventive step in the layout-design as assessed under this Act. Where an appeal is dismissed, the High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct the appellant to pay costs incurred by the respondent; however, no appeal shall lie from any order made by the High Court concerning costs. Any claim of prior art asserted during registration proceedings must be supported by dated documentary evidence admissible under the rules established herein.

Any person who fabricates a layout-design in violation of the provisions contained herein shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such fabrication. Where a layout-design is commercially exploited without the authorization of the proprietor, a civil court may, subject to the conditions as prescribed, grant an injunction restraining such exploitation and award damages to the proprietor. Any funds generated from penalties levied under this Act relating to unauthorized use of registered layout-designs shall be credited to a Sources Gene Fund dedicated to supporting research and development in semiconductor technology. A person falsely representing a layout-design as their own, or using another’s layout-design on any article for sale, may face imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. The Registrar may initiate investigations into suspected violations of rights pertaining to a registered layout-design and shall submit reports to the Central Government.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design registered under this Act may institute proceedings for recovery of damages before the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing activity has occurred. However, an invention exclusive licensee shall, subject to the terms of their license agreement, have the right to sue for such infringement independently and recover damages proportionate to their licensed interest; provided that the registered owner of the layout-design may join as a party in any such proceedings initiated by the invention exclusive licensee. Any order granting relief or awarding damages may be appealed to the High Court, subject to established appellate procedures. The court shall consider evidence presented regarding actual losses suffered and reasonable royalty rates when determining damage amounts. A finding of wilful infringement will result in enhanced damages as provided herein, not exceeding three times the proven loss.

The Controller shall exercise all powers and perform all functions conferred by this Act, subject to such rules as may be prescribed. The Controller may, for the purposes of conducting any examination or hearing under this Act, require attendance of any person acquainted with the subject-matter of the application or opposition. Any failure to attend such requirement, without sufficient cause, shall be deemed an obstruction of official duty and punishable accordingly. Where a request for information is made by the Controller as provided herein, the applicant or opponent shall respond within thirty days from the date of receipt of said request; provided that an extension may be granted at the discretion of the Controller upon demonstration of reasonable grounds. The decision of the Controller on matters relating to patent examination shall be final and binding.

The Controller shall maintain a public Register of Patents wherein all patents granted and applications for patents pending examination are recorded, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person may inspect the said Register upon payment of the prescribed fee and obtain certified copies of any entry therein. The Controller may, at their discretion, require an applicant seeking registration of a patent to submit a declaration confirming sole inventorship and detailing prior art known to the inventor. Should a request for rectification of the register be filed with the Controller alleging incorrect particulars, notice shall be served upon the proprietor of the patent or applicant as the case may be. The Controller’s decision on such rectification requests is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board, provided that any such appeal must be lodged within ninety days from the date of the Controller's order. All records maintained by the Controller are deemed public documents until otherwise restricted by an order of a competent court.

The Controller shall, upon receipt of a petition alleging improper revocation of a patent by the High Court, conduct a review of the record of such proceedings and may, subject to sufficient cause being shown and payment of prescribed fees, restore the patent to the register if satisfied that the revocation was based on grounds not permissible under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing restoration may appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of said order. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all restored patents, detailing the reasons for initial revocation and subsequent reinstatement. Provided that, if the High Court’s decision was based on prior art not previously considered during examination, the Controller may require submission of an amended specification addressing such art before restoration is granted. Failure to comply with this requirement within sixty days shall render the petition ineligible, and the Controller's decision final. The Controller possesses the authority to impose costs upon frivolous or vexatious petitions.

The Controller shall, subject to the provisions contained herein and upon receipt of a request accompanied by the prescribed fee, grant a hearing to any person interested in opposing the grant of a patent. Any such request must clearly articulate the grounds for opposition, referencing specific claims within the application which are alleged to lack novelty or involve inventive step as determined under this Act. The Controller may, if satisfied that prima facie case exists, direct the applicant to furnish evidence addressing the objections raised by the opponent within a period not exceeding three months from the date of such direction. Failure to comply with this directive shall be deemed an abandonment of the application, unless otherwise provided for in these rules. Where conflicting claims are presented, the Controller’s decision shall be final and binding, subject only to appeal to the appellate board established under this Act. The Controller retains discretion to modify procedures as necessary to ensure a fair and efficient examination process.

The Controller shall, subject to the provisions contained herein, exercise all powers and perform all functions relating to the administration of this Act. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Controller may, within one month from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided for under this Act. The Controller may require any applicant or patentee to furnish a declaration verifying the truthfulness of statements made in any application or document filed before them. Provided that failure to comply with such requirement shall not *ipso jure* invalidate the application but may be considered during examination. All registers maintained by the Controller shall be open for inspection by any member of the public, subject to payment of a prescribed fee and adherence to conditions stipulated by the Controller regarding access to confidential information. The Controller reserves the right to revoke any patent granted in contravention of this Act.

The Controller, acting as the administrative head for matters pertaining to patents under this Act, shall possess the authority to impose penalties on any person who knowingly provides false information in connection with an application for a patent. Any such misrepresentation, subject to verification by investigation initiated at the direction of the Controller, may result in a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, if the Controller determines that a patented invention has been exploited contrary to public interest or national security, they may, after providing reasonable opportunity for hearing, revoke the patent and order appropriate remedial action. Failure to comply with an order issued by the Controller shall be punishable by imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. All decisions of the Controller are subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Controller shall maintain a register of registered patent licensees, and any assignment or transfer of the license shall be subject to notification to, and recording by, the Controller within thirty days of such transaction. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of the Controller to record an assignment may appeal to the High Court. A licensee, with the prior written consent of the patentee, may further assign their interest in the licensed technology, provided that such sub-assignment does not contravene any terms stipulated in the original license agreement. Where a license is granted for more than one undertaking, the Controller may require separate accounting records to be maintained for each undertaking subject to the license. The Controller reserves the right to inspect these records as provided herein, ensuring compliance with royalty payments and other obligations outlined within the licensing contract. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the licensee liable to penalties under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Controller relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, amendment of a patent, or any other matter concerning a patent shall have grounds to prefer an appeal. Such appeal shall lie before the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to the provisions herein and within a period not exceeding three months from the date of the Controller’s order communicated to the appellant. The Appellant must demonstrate substantial question of law involved in the decision for the appeal to be admissible. Where the Controller determines that grounds for an application are frivolous or vexatious, they may dismiss it with costs; however, such dismissal is itself subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. The Controller shall furnish all relevant documents and records pertaining to the case to the Appellate Board within thirty days of receiving a request from said body. Failure to do so may be considered adverse inference against the Controller’s original decision.

The Controller, upon receipt of a request accompanied by the prescribed fee and satisfying themselves that reasonable cause exists, may order an examination of any patent application even if such application is not prioritized according to the provisions herein. Any party opposing a grant shall submit their evidence within a period not exceeding one month from the date of notification issued by the Controller; failure to do so will render such opposition inadmissible. Where the Controller deems further clarification necessary, they may request additional information from either the applicant or the opponent, allowing a maximum of thirty days for response. All records and documents pertaining to an examination conducted under this Act shall be admissible as evidence before any civil court purposes relating to patent validity or infringement, subject to verification by the presiding officer. Provided that, the Controller’s decision regarding admissibility of evidence remains final unless successfully appealed through due process established within these rules.

The Controller, upon receiving credible information indicating unauthorized propagation or commercial exploitation of any breeder variety registered under this Act, shall initiate an inquiry without undue delay. Any person found guilty of such infringement, including but not limited to the sale, distribution, or exchange of propagating material derived from a protected variety without license from the breeder, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per incident. Provided that, if the infringement is continuing in nature, an additional daily penalty of ten thousand rupees may be imposed for each day the infringement persists. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as deemed appropriate, order the destruction or disposal of all infringing material at the expense of the offender. Failure to comply with any direction issued by the Controller under this Act shall constitute a separate offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both.

The Controller shall exercise all powers and perform all functions conferred by this Act, subject to such rules as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Controller may, within one month from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the grounds for such appeal are clearly stated in writing. If any person knowingly makes a false representation to the Controller or withholds material information relevant to proceedings before them, they shall be punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
