The Controller may require any applicant to furnish a declaration verifying the truth of statements made in their application and supporting documents. Failure to comply with such requirement may render the application liable to rejection as provided herein.

A registered trade mark shall be a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another; and may consist of words, numerals, letters, devices, symbols, shapes, colours or combinations thereof. For the purposes of this Act, a well-known mark, even if not registered, shall be entitled to protection as a trade mark under certain conditions specified herein. The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. Subject to provisions contained elsewhere in this Act, no person other than the registered proprietor shall use such trade mark.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to renewal upon expiry of the initial registration period of ten years from the date of application, provided that an application for such renewal is presented to the Trade Marks Registry not earlier than six months and not later than one month before the expiration of the said period. The Registrar may, however, allow an extension of time for filing the application subject to payment of a late fee as prescribed under the rules made herein. Where a registered trade mark has been assigned or transmitted, notice of such assignment or transmission shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within six months of the date of assignment or transmission; failure to do so may render the transfer unenforceable against any subsequent purchaser for value without notice. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to renewal or transfer of a registered trade mark may appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

A person who adopts a registered trade mark with intent to deceive or cause confusion shall be liable to account for all profits made by him which may be attributable to the use of the said trade mark. The owner of the registered trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, may institute suit for recovery of damages for loss suffered due to such user and obtain an injunction restraining further unlawful use. Where a defendant proves that the goods or services are identical with those for which the plaintiff’s registered trade mark is used, and that the use of the mark by the defendant is likely to cause confusion, the court may order delivery up or destruction of the infringing goods. Provided that no such order shall be made unless the owner of the registered trade mark first establishes a prima facie case of passing off. Any contract containing an obligation not to challenge the validity of a registered trade mark may be declared void as against public policy if it unduly restricts legitimate competition.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to rectification proceedings before the Trade Marks Registry upon application made in the prescribed manner alleging that the trade mark has ceased to be distinctive, or is deceptively similar to another trade mark used by any other person. Any aggrieved person may initiate such proceedings, provided that a period of not less than five years has elapsed since the registration of the contested registered trade mark. The Registrar shall, following due notice to the proprietor of the registered trade mark and consideration of all evidence submitted, determine whether sufficient grounds exist for rectification. 

Where non-use is alleged as a ground for rectification, proof of continuous use, or reasonable cause for lack thereof, shall be borne by the owner of the registered trade mark. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in removal of the mark from the Register. The decision of the Registrar regarding rectification is subject to appeal to the High Court, conforming to procedures as provided herein.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to continuous use for the purpose of maintaining its validity as provided herein. Any proprietor of a registered trade mark who fails to demonstrate bona fide use within a period of five years from the date of registration may, upon application by an aggrieved party and satisfaction of the Registrar, have their registration revoked. However, non-use shall not be deemed established if such failure is attributable to circumstances beyond the control of the proprietor, including but not limited to government restrictions or natural disasters duly evidenced before the Registrar. A licensee utilizing a registered trade mark under a valid license agreement shall be considered as demonstrating use on behalf of the proprietor for purposes of maintaining registration, provided that the terms of said license are consistent with this Act and do not otherwise invalidate the mark’s standing. Any assignment of a registered trade mark must be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry to ensure proper transfer of ownership and continued validity.

Any person who uses in the course of trade, a deceptive variant of a registered trade mark, or any deceptively similar indication likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, shall be liable to penalties as provided herein. A registered trade mark confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered and to obtain relief against infringement. However, continuous non-use of a registered trade mark for a period exceeding five years may render the registration revocable, subject to justifiable cause being shown. Any transfer of ownership of a registered trade mark shall be subject to assignment procedures outlined under this Act, failing which such transfer will be deemed invalid. False application for registration or fraudulent alteration of the register shall attract imprisonment and monetary fines as determined by the adjudicating authority. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may pursue civil remedies including injunctions and damages against any infringer.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding transmission and assignment of property. A license may be granted to a person for the use of a registered trade mark, either generally or subject to limitations as to time, place, or the manner of use; such licenses must be in writing signed by the owner of the trade mark, or duly authorised agent. Where a registered trade mark is assigned with goodwill, the assignee shall acquire the right to maintain and renew the registration. However, assignment without goodwill does not confer any entitlement to renewal unless expressly agreed upon between parties as provided herein. The registrar may record assignments and licenses in the register of Trade Marks upon application made by or on behalf of either party; failure to do so will not invalidate the transaction but affects its enforceability against third parties. Any dispute regarding validity of such assignment or license shall be adjudicated according to established principles of equity and law.

Any person claiming infringement of a registered trade mark shall file a written complaint with the High Court having jurisdiction, detailing the nature of the alleged violation and providing evidence sufficient to establish a prima facie case. The defendant may respond within thirty days, submitting a counter-statement denying the allegations or asserting any valid defense, including but not limited to proof of prior use or lack of deceptive similarity. Should the plaintiff fail to adequately demonstrate likelihood of confusion under this Act, the complaint shall be dismissed with costs. An appeal from any order of the High Court relating to such infringement may be made to the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is first obtained from the High Court itself. The court may, subject to due process and evidence presented, grant an injunction restraining further use of the registered trade mark by the defendant pending final determination of the matter. Any rectification petition concerning the registerability of a registered trade mark shall be heard separately.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive right to the use of the said trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and shall include the right to sue for infringement. However, such right shall be subject to the provisions contained herein and any other applicable law for the time being in force. Where a patent shall relate to an article capable of being sold under different trade marks, the proprietor of the registered trade mark may, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, obtain an injunction restraining the sale of such articles by any person other than a licensee authorized by him. Provided that nothing herein contained shall prejudice the rights and remedies available to the patentee under the Patents Act, 1970. Any assignment or transmission of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules as prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, the term ‘registered proprietor’ shall mean the person or entity entered in the Register as the holder of the registration for a trademark, and includes any assignee of that registration who has duly recorded their title with the Trade Marks Registry. A registered proprietor is entitled to exercise all rights conferred by virtue of such registration, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a trade mark is jointly owned, each joint owner shall be deemed a registered proprietor, and may act independently in relation to the trademark unless otherwise agreed between them in writing. Any transfer of ownership or interest in a registered trade mark requires formal assignment as provided within this Act, failing which such transfer shall not confer rights equivalent to those of a registered proprietor.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registration, or any interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and require written instrument duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the goods or services in respect of which the transfer applies. A co-ownership of a registered trade mark may be permissible, provided that all co-owners are jointly responsible for ensuring lawful use and preventing infringement. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise reasonable diligence to maintain control over the quality of certified goods associated with a collective trade mark, the Registrar may initiate proceedings as deemed appropriate. The rights conferred by registration shall not extend to goods or services unrelated to those specified in the register, nor shall it prejudice the lawful use of prior marks.

The registered proprietor of a trademark shall have the exclusive right to use the said trademark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any person who uses a deceptive or confusingly similar mark, without the consent of the registered proprietor, as provided herein, commits an act of infringement and shall be liable to remedies under this Act. A court may grant an injunction restraining such infringer from further use of the mark, along with damages for loss suffered by the registered proprietor due to the infringement. 

However, a registered proprietor’s rights are subject to any lawful use of descriptive terms or geographical indications that predate registration and are bona fide. Furthermore, a non-use of the trademark for a continuous period of five years may be grounds for revocation of registration, unless justifiable cause is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the court. The remedies available shall also extend to include an account of profits made by the infringer.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registration, or any interest therein, shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. A transfer of goodwill of the business including the trade mark does not automatically confer ownership of the trade mark itself; separate application for its transfer under this Act must be made and approved by the Registrar. 

Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise their rights, or permits widespread unauthorized use without due legal recourse, the Trade Marks Registry may entertain an application seeking revocation based on non-use as provided herein. However, legitimate reasons for such non-use, duly substantiated with evidence acceptable to the Registry, shall be considered favorably. The continued registration of a trade mark is contingent upon diligent and bona fide use by the registered proprietor, demonstrating genuine commercial activity.

The registered proprietor shall ensure diligent pursuit of all necessary remedies against any person dealing in counterfeit goods bearing a deceptively similar mark to their own registered trade mark, as provided herein. Failure to exercise such diligence may be considered grounds for non-use and potential revocation of the registration, subject to established procedures under this Act. Any license granted by the registered proprietor shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry, and compliance with licensing terms is a continuing obligation. A co-owner of a trade mark must demonstrate mutual agreement regarding enforcement actions; however, any one co-owner may initiate proceedings for passing off independently. The rights conferred upon the registered proprietor are subject to prior legitimate use by another party, which shall be determined through evidence presented before the appropriate authority and in accordance with established principles of equity. Any assignment of the trade mark must adhere to specified formalities.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a trade mark or an authorized user thereof, uses in the course of trade, or for the purpose of any business, any colourable variation of the registered trade mark shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein. Where such use is with intent to deceive or cause confusion, the penalty shall not be less than five thousand rupees but may extend to two lakh rupees. The court, upon application by the registered proprietor and subject to verification of damages suffered, may also grant an injunction restraining further unlawful use and order delivery up for destruction of goods bearing such infringing mark. Any false representation as to being a licensed user or agent of the registered proprietor shall constitute grounds for enhanced penalty and immediate injunctive relief. Provided that no prosecution is initiated without prior notice served upon the alleged infringer.

Any assignment of the rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be agreed upon between the parties and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. The registered proprietor may, at their discretion, grant licenses to use the trade mark concerning specific goods or services, delineating territorial scope and duration within the license agreement. Such licensing arrangements shall not prejudice the rights of the registered proprietor to further assign or license the mark independently. Where a license is granted for a limited period, renewal shall require mutual consent between the licensor and licensee, failing which the license lapses as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership, whether by assignment or operation of law, does not invalidate existing licenses unless expressly stipulated in the instrument of transfer; however, prospective licensees must be informed of the change in registered proprietorship. The Trade Marks Registry maintains a public record of all assignments and licensed user details to ensure transparency and facilitate enforcement actions.

The rights conferred upon a registered proprietor shall be subject to rectification proceedings initiated before the Trade Marks Registry where it is alleged that the registration was obtained unlawfully, or that circumstances exist which would have entitled another party to register the mark. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order; provided that the High Court may extend this period for sufficient cause shown. A registered proprietor who assigns their rights, or otherwise transfers ownership, shall promptly notify the Registry and provide details of the assignee, failing which any subsequent actions taken by the unregistered party will be considered void ab initio. Where a claim of prior use is asserted against the registered proprietor, evidence must demonstrate continuous and uninterrupted usage preceding the date of registration as provided herein. The onus of proving such prior use rests solely with the claimant.

For the purposes of this Act, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to include a person who, although not formally recorded as such in the register, possesses and exercises dominion over the trade mark, subject to proof of ownership satisfactory to the Controller. A finding of register sufficient cause for non-registration despite actual use may be made where the applicant fails to demonstrate bona fide adoption or continuous user prior to opposition. However, assignment or transmission of rights shall not be valid without appropriate notation in the register, and any subsequent claim by a transferee will be assessed from the date of such registration. The registered proprietor retains exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered as provided herein.

The specification shall constitute a full and particular description of the invention, including the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. It must be clear and complete enough for a person skilled in the relevant art to carry the invention into effect without undue experimentation. Where the invention involves a biological material, a deposit of such material with a recognised depository institution shall be included as part of the specification, subject to the provisions relating to access thereto. Any subsequent alteration to the deposited material must also be fully disclosed within an amended specification filed under this Act. The specification may contain drawings where necessary for better understanding of the invention and these drawings shall form part thereof.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with utmost clarity and precision, fully describing the invention and enabling a person skilled in the relevant field to carry it into effect. The specification must disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention at the time of filing. Any omission or inaccurate statement within the specification relating to prior art known to the applicant shall render the patent liable to be revoked as provided herein. Where an invention involves a biological material, the specification shall include a detailed description of its characteristics and deposit information with a recognized depository institution. Claims defining the scope of the invention must be supported by matter disclosed in the specification; any claim extending beyond such disclosure will not be allowed. The applicant may amend the specification subject to conditions prescribed, but no amendment altering the substance of the invention shall be permitted after publication.

The specification accompanying any patent application shall be construed as defining the scope of the claimed invention, and no allegation of inventive merit outside of what is particularly delineated therein will be considered. Any amendment to the specification, subject to the Controller’s approval, may only clarify or limit the claims presented; expansion beyond the original disclosure is strictly prohibited. Should a dispute arise concerning the interpretation of the specification, evidence relating to the prosecution history—including objections raised by the Patent Office and responses thereto—may be admitted as relevant to ascertain the inventor's intended meaning. A patentee aggrieved by an incorrect construction of their specification may seek rectification before the High Court, provided that such application is made within three years from the grant of the patent. Failure to adequately describe the invention in the specification shall render the patent void *ab initio*, and any resulting damages will be assessed based on actual losses demonstrably caused by the deficient disclosure.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with utmost clarity and precision, detailing the invention in a manner reasonably comprehensible to a person skilled in the relevant art. It shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention, ensuring full enablement thereof. Where the invention involves biological material, a deposit of such material in a recognized depository authority, as prescribed under rules made by the Controller, shall be deemed essential and referenced within the specification. 

Any amendment to the specification, subject to verification by the Controller that it does not introduce matter extending beyond the content originally disclosed, may be permitted provided that such amendment is made before acceptance of the application. A complete specification must fully and particularly describe the invention and conclude with a statement defining the scope of the claim or claims; failure to do so shall render the patent vulnerable to revocation under this Act. The Controller may require translation of any part of the specification if it is not in an official language.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with utmost clarity and precision, fully describing the invention and enabling a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect. It shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention at the time of filing. Any amendment to the specification relating to matter extending beyond the content of the original application is prohibited unless it is necessary to correct an obvious mistake or to clarify ambiguity, subject to a reasoned justification being submitted to and accepted by the Controller. Where the specification refers to biological material, a deposit of such material in a recognized depository shall be considered sufficient disclosure provided that details of the deposit are clearly stated within the specification itself. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding the specification may render the patent invalid or subject it to revocation as provided herein.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with absolute clarity and precision, detailing the invention in a manner sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Failure to adequately disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention within the specification shall render the patent voidable at the suit of any person aggrieved. Any deliberate omission or misrepresentation concerning prior art known to the applicant, and not disclosed within the specification as required under this Act, will be deemed an act of fraud. Such fraudulent behaviour shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may further result in forfeiture of all rights pertaining to the patent. The Controller may, subject to due process, order rectification of the specification if it is found deficient or misleading, and any costs associated with such rectification shall be borne by the applicant.

Any assignment of the patent, or any right therein arising from the specification, shall be made by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and attested by at least two witnesses. The assignee may, subject to the provisions contained herein, apply for registration of the assignment with the Controller of Patents; provided that failure to register such assignment shall not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against third parties. A licensee acquiring a right under this Act through an assignment of the patent or any part thereof, shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if they were directly granted by the patentee. Where the specification details multiple distinct inventions, separate assignments pertaining to individual inventions within that single specification are permissible; however, such partial assignments must clearly delineate the scope of each assigned invention. The Controller may require evidence of title before registering any assignment or license, and shall maintain a register of all registered assignments. Any instrument creating an interest in the patent shall be deemed to include a reference to these provisions regarding assignment.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with utmost clarity and precision, detailing the invention in a manner reasonably comprehensible to a person ordinarily skilled in the relevant field. Any ambiguity or lack of sufficient detail within the specification may render the patent vulnerable to revocation proceedings initiated under this Act. Should an objection arise concerning the adequacy of the specification during examination, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to amend it subject to conditions prescribed by the Controller. However, such amendment shall not extend beyond the scope originally disclosed; any addition introducing a new invention will be deemed unsupported by the initial disclosure and rejected. A clear and concise description of the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention is also mandatory within said specification, failing which, an appeal may lie before the Appellate Board alleging insufficient enablement. The Controller’s decision regarding sufficiency shall be final unless successfully appealed.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with sufficient clarity and completeness so as to enable a person skilled in the relevant field to carry out the invention. The description therein must disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention at the time of filing, and fully explain how to make and use it. Any amendments to the specification subsequent to examination shall be strictly limited to what was originally disclosed; expansion beyond this is prohibited as provided herein. 

The Controller may require a translation of any part of the specification if it is not in an official language. All specifications accepted for registration will be duly entered into the registrar index, maintained electronically and open for public inspection subject to prescribed fees. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding the specification may result in refusal of the patent or its subsequent revocation.

The specification forming part of any patent application shall be construed with such breadth as will avoid anticipating what is not disclosed therein, but not so broadly as to cover matter extending beyond the scope fairly indicated by the description. Any registered user layout demonstrably incorporated within the complete specification and materially contributing to the inventive step described shall be considered an integral component of the claimed invention for purposes of determining novelty and non-obviousness. Should a patentee fail to adequately disclose all essential features of such a layout within the specification, any subsequent claim relying upon it may be subject to revocation. A person aggrieved by a grant of patent based on insufficient or misleading disclosure in the specification may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register, and the court shall have power to order amendment or revoke the patent as provided herein. The burden of proving sufficient description rests with the patentee, subject to evidence presented by any opposing party demonstrating prior art.

In this Act, “design” means the visual features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament, or composition of lines or colours, applied to any article whether in two dimensional or three dimensional nature, or both; and includes in its definition ornamentation and colour. A design shall not be registrable under this Act if it does not meet the requirements of novelty and originality. The aesthetic feature of an article is considered a design only when it is capable of being separated from the article itself, or where such features are integral to the article but visually distinct. Subject to provisions herein, a registered design confers upon the proprietor exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or import the designed article. Any fraudulent imitation of a registered design shall be actionable as provided in this Act.

Any person desiring to register a design under this Act shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed form along with the necessary fee. The application shall include a representation of the design by means of drawings or photographs and a statement of novelty and originality. A design, as provided herein, relates to the features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to any article capable of being made by industrial process and which is visually appealing. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, registration of a design shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class of articles for which it is registered. Provided that no design registration shall subsist for a period exceeding fifteen years from the date of registration. Any subsequent modification of a registered design, if substantial, shall require a separate application and assessment as a new design.

Any person who creates a design shall be entitled to register the same under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding novelty and originality. A registered design confers upon the owner the exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class of articles for which it is registered. Such right extends to any article capable of bearing the design, irrespective of whether such article is made by hand or mechanically. Where a design incorporates a trade mark, registration of the design shall not confer any right to the use of the trade mark unless independently protected under the Trade Marks Act, 1999. Any person dealing with an article incorporating an infringing design without the consent of the registered owner may be subject to injunction and damages as determined by the Court. Provided that, if a design is found to be substantially similar to a prior art design, registration may be revoked upon application made in accordance with established procedure. The duration of protection for a registered design shall be ten years from the date of registration.

A design, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be novel and original. A design is deemed novel if it has not been previously published, or known to the public, or registered under this Act prior to the date of application for registration. Originality in relation to a design signifies that the design must originate from the creator’s own independent intellectual effort; mere imitation or slavish copying shall not constitute originality. 

The aesthetic features of an article are considered integral to the definition of a design, and such features may relate to shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines and colours applied to any article whether in two dimensional or three dimensional nature. Subject to provisions regarding articles capable of being separately made, a design shall not be registrable if it does not substantially differ from any known design; provided that minor variations are permissible where they do not affect the overall aesthetic impression. An application for registration must include a representation of the design as prescribed herein.

Any person intending to register a design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and such evidence as may be required. A design, as provided herein, means a feature of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament, or composition of lines or colours applied to any article whether in two dimensional or three dimensional nature, or combination thereof, which is visible to the eye but does not include any principle or mode which serves a functional purpose. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, an application for registration shall contain a representation of the design by means of drawings or photographs. The Controller may, after examination, refuse to register a design if it is found identical with or closely resembles another registered design; provided that designs not originally registered in India but registrable under this Act may also be considered. Any false entry made in an application shall render it void.

Any person who unlawfully reproduces, imports, sells, or distributes a design registered as provided herein shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such infringement. Where a design incorporates an artistic work protected under this Act, proof of copyright in that artistic work shall constitute prima facie evidence of the unlawful reproduction of the design itself. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information and reasonable suspicion of an impending infringement involving a registered design, initiate a search of premises or seize infringing articles subject to procedural safeguards as prescribed by rules made under this Act. Any person aggrieved by such seizure may apply to a District Court for restoration of seized items; provided that no application shall be entertained after sixty days from the date of seizure. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court and attract further penalties, including imprisonment not exceeding one year.

Any person who is the author of a design, being a novel and original visual appearance applied to an article, shall be entitled to register the same under this Act subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The registration of a design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or import the article in which the design is incorporated for a period not exceeding ten years from the date of registration. An assignment of any right in a registered design shall be in writing and duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the scope of rights transferred and any associated consideration. A license to use a registered design may also be granted under terms agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee; such licenses must be recorded with the appropriate authority as provided herein. Where a design incorporates elements of an existing artistic work protected by copyright, the assignment or licensing of the design right shall not affect the rights subsisting in that artistic work unless expressly stated within the agreement.

A registered design, as provided herein, shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to apply that design to articles belonging to the class specified in the registration certificate. However, this exclusivity is subject to the provisions relating to licensing and assignments under this Act. Any person alleging infringement of a registered design may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing article is manufactured or sold. The defendant may rebut such claims by demonstrating that the alleged infringing article does not substantially resemble the registered design, or that it constitutes a functional feature necessary for the operation of the article itself; proof of artistic merit alone shall not be sufficient to establish infringement. Appeals from original decrees in respect of designs shall lie before the High Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained where the value of the subject matter does not exceed a sum prescribed by notification. A design registration may be revoked if it can be proven that prior art existed which anticipated the claimed design.

Any person who creates a design, being an aesthetic feature of an article, shall be entitled to register such design under this Act, subject to novelty and originality requirements as may be prescribed. The right conferred by registration shall subsist for ten years from the date of registration. Where a semiconductor integrated circuit is embodied in an article, the layout-design thereof shall also constitute a registrable design provided it satisfies the criteria outlined herein. The exclusive right of the registered proprietor extends to reproduction or substantial imitation of the design, and any unauthorized act infringing such right shall be actionable. Remedies for infringement include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages accounting for lost profits, and delivery up of infringing articles for destruction as determined by a competent court. A person aggrieved by an incorrect refusal of registration may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such refusal, subject to prescribed procedures and fees.

A patentee shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean a person or entity to whom a valid patent has been granted and vested with all rights appertaining thereto, subject to any security interest duly registered as provided herein. The term includes an assignee of a patent, where such assignment is complete and legally enforceable, and extends to jointly held patents wherein each holder possesses equivalent rights unless otherwise stipulated in the patent documentation. A prospective patentee applying for a patent shall be deemed a patentee only upon grant of the patent by the Controller. Any act infringing the patented invention requires prior authorization from the patentee or their duly appointed agent; failure to obtain such authorization constitutes grounds for legal remedy.

A patentee may assign the patent or any share therein to any other person, and such assignment shall be subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Any transfer of ownership of a patent, whether by way of assignment, mortgage or otherwise, shall be registered with the Controller of Patents within thirty days from the date of execution of the instrument effecting such transfer; provided that failure to register does not invalidate the transfer itself but affects enforceability against third parties without notice. The register maintained for this purpose shall be open to inspection subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Where a patentee is a legal person, any authorized representative acting under a duly recorded power of attorney may effect such registration on behalf of the patentee. A registered user, granted rights as provided herein, shall also maintain records relating to the scope and duration of their usage license.

A patentee aggrieved by any infringement of his patent may institute a suit for recovery of damages sustained as a result of such infringement and shall not be limited to actual damages but may also include reasonable royalty or profit attributable to the infringement. Where a defendant proves that he was unaware, and had no reasonable means of becoming aware, of the existence of the patent at the time of the infringement, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded accordingly; provided that such reduction shall not extend below fifty percent of the assessed damages. Any relief granted by way of injunction or damages under this Act shall be subject to principles of equity and good faith. A co-patentee, in cases of joint patent ownership, may independently bring a suit for infringement unless otherwise agreed upon in writing amongst all patentees. The court may also award costs as it deems just, considering the conduct of both parties throughout the proceedings.

A patentee aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to questions of law and not those of fact, unless the Controller’s determination demonstrably lacks reasoned basis. Any person claiming to be a patentee, or the assignee of a patentee, must demonstrate clear title and locus standi before initiating proceedings under this Act; failure to do so may result in dismissal of their claim with costs. Where a co-patentee seeks to exercise rights independently of other co- patentees, they shall provide written notice detailing the scope of such independent action, and any dispute arising therefrom will be subject to mediation as provided herein. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require security for costs from an appellant patentee before proceeding with a hearing, particularly if the appeal appears frivolous or vexatious. All submissions made by a patentee shall adhere strictly to the prescribed format and timelines.

A patentee may assign the patent or any share therein to any other person, and every such assignment shall be in writing and signed by the patentee or his duly authorised agent. Subject to the provisions contained herein, an assignee shall possess the same rights as the original patentee in respect of the assigned patent, including the right to apply for further patents relating to the invention. However, any subsequent assignment by the assignee shall require prior written consent from the original patentee unless otherwise agreed upon in the initial assignment deed. Where a licensee is granted an exclusive license, such licensee shall be entitled to exercise all rights of the patentee concerning the subject matter of that license, provided they diligently pursue commercialization and pay royalties as stipulated in the licensing agreement. Failure by the assignee or exclusive licensee to comply with these conditions may result in revocation of their respective rights under this Act. The patentee remains responsible for maintaining accurate records relating to all assignments and licenses granted.

Any person who publishes or causes to be published any information relating to a patented invention, knowing that such publication is likely to induce infringement of a valid patent granted under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where a patentee proves actual inducement of infringement resulting in demonstrable loss, the court may award damages commensurate with said loss, in addition to any penalties imposed herein. However, no action shall lie against a person who publishes information obtained directly from examination of the patented article itself, provided that such examination was lawfully conducted and does not reveal confidential manufacturing processes. Any assignee of the patentee’s rights retains equivalent recourse under this Act, subject to demonstrating valid chain of title. Failure to report known instances of wilful infringement by any party shall render the patentee liable for a reduction in renewal fees, as determined by the Controller.

Any assignment of a patent made under this Act shall be subject to the terms and conditions that may be mutually agreed upon between the assignor and assignee, and such agreement shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the Patent Office within six months from the date of execution. The patentee, notwithstanding any assignment, retains the right to receive royalties or other consideration as stipulated in the assignment deed, unless explicitly waived by a subsequent written agreement. Where an exclusive license is granted by the patentee, the licensee may further assign their interest subject to the original terms governing the exclusivity and with prior notification to the patentee, who shall have thirty days to object if such sub-assignment materially alters the scope of the initial grant. A non-exclusive license does not confer assignment rights upon the licensee; however, it may be transferred along with the goodwill of a business. Failure to register an assignment renders it unenforceable against third parties. The patentee’s successor in title shall inherit all rights and obligations pertaining to any registered assignments.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or injunction, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The patentee, however, shall not be entitled to recover damages in respect of any act committed before the date of publication of the particulars of grant of the patent, unless it is proved that the defendant had knowledge of the invention prior to said publication. Where a counter-claim for revocation of the patent is filed by the alleged infringer, the court may direct stay of civil proceedings pending final determination of the counterclaim; provided that such stay shall not exceed one year from the date of filing of the counterclaim. Any appeal under this Act concerning the rights of a patentee shall be heard by a Division Bench of the High Court and must be filed within ninety days of the impugned order, unless extended by the court for sufficient cause. A licensee may also pursue remedies where the patentee fails to diligently exploit the patented invention as provided herein.

A patentee desiring registration of a process for the production of novel food items utilising genetically modified organisms shall submit an application to the Controller as provided herein. The application shall include a detailed description of the biological material employed and demonstrate substantial differentiation from previously known varieties, alongside evidence of nutritional value or improved shelf life. Any claim relating to traditional Indian foods or processes must be accompanied by documented proof of indigenous knowledge and benefit-sharing arrangements with relevant communities. Failure to disclose such information may invalidate the patent. The Controller may require a sample of the food item for independent verification. A patentee shall maintain accurate records concerning the origin, modification, and production scale of any patented food product subject to inspection under this Act. Provided that, registration does not confer immunity from regulations governing food safety and standards established by other competent authorities.

A patentee aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents relating to revocation of a patent or amendment thereof, may apply to the court registrar application for an order setting aside such decision. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the said decision and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the Controller’s order appealed against. The court, upon receipt of any such application, may direct the Controller to transmit thereto all papers relating to the patent in question. Any person intending to oppose the grant of a patent or to institute proceedings for infringement thereof, must first satisfy the court that the patentee is duly authorized to receive notices and pleadings on behalf of the applicant. Provided that, where a patentee is a corporation, service shall be effected upon its registered agent. Failure by the patentee to comply with directions issued under this Act regarding disclosure or amendment may result in limitations on remedies available for infringement. The court retains discretion to award costs as it deems just.

A licence shall be construed as a right granted to another to perform, reproduce, distribute, or otherwise exploit a work, subject to such conditions as may be mutually agreed upon by the licensor and licensee. Such licence may be exclusive, conferring sole rights on the licensee for a defined scope and duration, or non-exclusive, permitting multiple licensees concurrent operation within specified parameters. Where a transfer of copyright is effected, any subsisting licence shall remain valid unless expressly terminated by the parties or as provided herein. A voluntary licence requires consideration, though royalty rates are not fixed under this Act but determined through negotiation; however, statutory licensing provisions may apply in specific instances concerning broadcasting organisations and educational purposes. Any dispute regarding the terms of a licence shall be subject to judicial determination.

Any person desiring to obtain a licence to reproduce a substantial portion of a published literary work for educational purposes shall submit an application in Form L-Edu to the Registrar of Copyrights. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant pages of the work proposed to be reproduced, along with a detailed syllabus indicating the extent of use and the number of copies required. A non-refundable processing fee, as prescribed under the rules made herein, must also accompany the application. 

The Registrar may, subject to verification that the reproduction falls within the permissible limits for educational dealing, grant a licence specifying the duration, scope, and royalty payable to the copyright holder. Should the applicant fail to comply with the terms of the granted licence, or reproduce beyond the permitted extent, the copyright owner may seek remedies as provided under this Act relating to infringement. Any dispute regarding royalty rates shall be determined by an arbitral tribunal appointed jointly by both parties.

Any person desiring to obtain a licence to reproduce, distribute, perform, or adapt a copyrighted work shall apply in writing to the owner of the copyright, specifying the nature of the intended use, the duration for which the licence is sought, and the territory within which it will be effective. The copyright owner may grant such licence subject to mutually agreed terms and conditions regarding royalty payments and other considerations. Should the copyright owner fail to respond to the application within sixty days, or unreasonably refuse a reasonable request, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for an order compelling the granting of a licence on equitable terms. Any licence granted under this Act shall be non-exclusive unless expressly stated otherwise in the agreement. The licensor retains the right to seek legal remedies for any breach of the licensing terms as provided herein, including but not limited to injunctive relief and damages commensurate with the extent of the infringement. A transfer of copyright does not invalidate a pre-existing valid licence.

Any person desiring to obtain a licence to reproduce, perform, or communicate a copyrighted work shall submit an application in writing to the owner of the copyright, setting forth the nature of the use sought, the duration for which such licence is required, and the remuneration proposed. The copyright owner may, within sixty days from the date of receipt of such application, either grant or refuse the licence, stating reasons for any refusal; provided that failure to respond within said period shall be deemed a provisional acceptance of the terms offered in the application, subject to subsequent negotiation regarding specific conditions. Where the applicant and copyright owner are unable to agree on reasonable terms, either party may request adjudication by a designated officer appointed under this Act. Any licence granted shall specify the scope of permitted use, including any territorial limitations or restrictions on further sub-licensing; it shall also delineate the rights reserved by the copyright owner. A transfer of ownership does not affect validly existing licences unless expressly stated in the instrument of transfer.

Any person desiring to obtain a licence to reproduce, distribute, perform, or adapt a copyrighted work shall submit an application in writing to the owner of the copyright, detailing the specific nature of the proposed use and the duration for which such licence is sought. The owner may grant a licence subject to mutually agreed terms and conditions regarding royalty payments, territorial scope, and exclusivity. Provided that, if the applicant intends to utilise the work for educational purposes, a reduced royalty rate shall be considered. Any licence granted under this Act shall explicitly state the permitted extent of exploitation, and any deviation from these terms constitutes a breach entitling the copyright owner to seek remedies as provided herein. The copyright owner may refuse a licence without stating cause, except where such refusal is deemed anti-competitive by a competent authority. All licences exceeding five years duration require registration with the relevant registry.

Any person desiring to grant a licence in respect of a copyright under this Act shall furnish particulars of such licence to the Central Government within thirty days from the date on which such licence is granted. Failure to comply with this provision shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. Where a licence is granted for a term, any purported assignment or further licensing of rights beyond that term shall be void ab initio and subject to immediate revocation by the copyright owner. Any person aggrieved by an unlawful grant of a licence, or violation of the terms thereof, may apply to the District Court having jurisdiction. The court, upon being satisfied with prima facie evidence of such irregularity, may issue an injunction restraining further acts in breach, and impose damages not exceeding twice the value of the copyrighted work. Repeated violations shall be cognizable offences punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Any person possessing copyright in a cinematograph film may grant a licence to exhibit such film in any place, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the owner and the licensee. Such licence shall specify the territorial extent, duration, and scope of permitted exhibition, including but not limited to the number of screenings and permissible venues. Where a copyright owner assigns their rights to another person, all existing licences continue in full force and effect unless otherwise stipulated within the instrument of assignment or agreed upon by the assignee and the licensee. A licence may further provide for royalty payments calculated as a percentage of gross receipts derived from exhibition, or a fixed sum payable periodically. Should any dispute arise regarding interpretation of the licensing terms, parties may seek resolution through arbitration conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The copyright owner retains the right to revoke a licence upon material breach of its conditions, following reasonable notice to the licensee.

Any person desiring to obtain a licence under this Act shall submit an application in writing to the appropriate authority, detailing the nature of the work for which such licence is sought, the duration requested, and the geographical territory covered by the proposed use. The applicant shall demonstrate that all reasonable efforts have been made to secure a voluntary licence from the copyright holder, failing which sufficient cause must be established justifying intervention under this Act. Should the application be refused, an appeal may be filed with the High Court within sixty days of the refusal order, provided that such appeal is accompanied by a detailed statement outlining grounds for review and any new evidence supporting the claim. A grant of licence shall not prejudice existing rights or remedies available to the copyright holder in cases of misuse or breach of conditions as stipulated herein; furthermore, royalty rates determined under this Act are subject to periodic revision based on prevailing market standards and equitable considerations.

Any person intending to grant a licence relating to copyright in a cinematograph film shall submit a statement detailing the scope of permitted acts, duration of the licence, and geographical territory covered, to the Registrar of Copyright. Failure to furnish such a statement prior to execution of the licensing agreement will render the licence unenforceable against third parties claiming interest through legitimate assignment or further licensing. Registration of the licence itself is not compulsory; however, registered licences shall be *prima facie* evidence of valid grant and terms as stated therein. A licensee may seek judicial redressal for breach of a licenced right only if they can demonstrate due diligence in ascertaining the licensor’s authority to grant said licence. Subject to the provisions contained herein, any royalty payments stipulated within the licensing agreement shall be considered contractual obligations enforceable through civil proceedings. Any dispute regarding interpretation of the licence terms will be subject to arbitration as mutually agreed upon by both parties.

An assignment of copyright is a transfer of all or part of the bundle of rights comprised in the copyright subsisting in a work, subject to provisions contained herein. Such an assignment may be complete, transferring all rights indefinitely, or partial, limited to specific rights such as reproduction, distribution, or adaptation. Any instrument purporting to effect an assignment shall be construed as a transfer of interest and not as a grant of license, unless it expressly states otherwise. An assignment is effective upon execution of the instrument, provided that reasonable notice thereof is given to the Registry of Copyrights. Where copyright is assigned by way of security for a debt, the assignee’s rights are subject to redemption upon discharge of the underlying obligation and shall not constitute an outright transfer absent further agreement.

Any person desiring to effect an assignment of copyright in a work, whether wholly or partially, shall furnish to the Registrar of Copyrights a statement containing particulars of the assignment. Such statement shall be accompanied by a copy of the instrument of assignment duly executed by both parties, and shall identify the work subject to assignment with sufficient precision to avoid reasonable doubt as to its identity. The statement must also clearly delineate the specific rights being assigned, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or public performance, and specify whether the assignment is for a fixed term or in perpetuity. Provided that an assignment extending beyond the duration of copyright as provided herein shall be treated as void *ab initio*. Subject to verification by the Registrar, registration of such assignment confers evidentiary weight upon its validity; however, failure to register does not invalidate the assignment itself but may affect remedies available under this Act.

Any person being the owner of copyright, or having an exclusive license to do so, may assign the copyright or any part thereof by writing under his hand, or that of his duly authorized agent. Such assignment shall be subject to the provisions contained herein regarding duration, scope, and territorial extent, and must clearly identify the work assigned. An assignee acquiring rights as provided herein shall be entitled to all remedies available to the original owner against infringement of copyright in the assigned portion, save where expressly restricted by the terms of the assignment itself. Where an assignment is made for a defined period, any failure to exercise rights within that period does not constitute abandonment unless explicitly stated in the instrument of assignment. The assignor retains the right to seek accounting of royalties paid, and may petition a competent court for redressal should discrepancies arise concerning amounts due as per the terms of the assignment. An assignment lacking these specifications shall be voidable at the option of either party.

Any person possessing copyright in a work may assign all or any of the rights comprised therein to another by an instrument in writing, subject to the provisions contained herein. Such assignment shall vest in the assignee the exclusive right to exercise the assigned rights to the exclusion of the assignor, unless otherwise expressly agreed upon within the terms of the assignment itself. Where an assignment is made for a term of years only, any subsequent assignment without the consent of the original assignor shall be voidable at the option of such assignor. 

An assignment creating or purporting to create an interest in copyright must be registered with the Registrar of Copyrights to provide constructive notice of the ownership and rights therein; however, failure to register does not invalidate the assignment itself. The instrument of assignment shall clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, performance, and translation, and any limitations placed upon their exercise. A partial assignment affecting only specific rights is permissible, provided that it doesn’t unduly prejudice the enjoyment of other retained rights by the original copyright holder.

Any transfer of ownership of copyright by way of assignment shall be effected only through an instrument in writing, executed by or on behalf of the owner of the copyright, demonstrating unequivocal intent to relinquish rights. Such instrument shall clearly delineate the specific work subject to assignment, encompassing all constituent elements protected under this Act and any subsequent revisions thereto. The scope of rights assigned must be expressly stated, detailing whether it concerns the whole copyright or only a portion thereof, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, distribution, and public performance. 

Provided that an assignment creating a beneficial interest in another person may be recorded with the Registrar of Copyrights to provide constructive notice of such transfer. The duration for which the rights are assigned shall also be specified; failing which it will be deemed a perpetual transfer subject to the limitations prescribed herein. Any consideration exchanged for the assignment, whether monetary or otherwise, must be accurately reflected in the instrument.

Any person desiring to transfer by way of assignment all or part of their copyright in a work, whether literary, dramatic, musical or artistic, shall execute an instrument of assignment complying with the provisions hereinafter set forth. Failure to do so renders such purported assignment null and void ab initio, and subject to penalties as provided herein. An assignment must clearly delineate the specific rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, performance, and translation; ambiguity in this regard shall be construed against the assignee. Should an assignment fail to specify a duration, it shall be deemed perpetual, though revocable upon demonstration of undue hardship to the assignor. Any false representation regarding the validity of such assignment constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or with fine, or with both. All instruments of assignment must be registered with the designated authority within thirty days of execution; non-registration shall attract a daily penalty until rectified.

Any person possessing copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work may assign all or part of their copyright by instrument in writing. Such an assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding duration, termination, and permissible scope. Where the owner of copyright assigns the right to receive royalties, such assignment must clearly delineate the basis for calculating said royalties, including but not limited to a percentage of gross sales or a fixed sum per unit sold. 

Provided that an assignment intended to be effective only in relation to specific modes of exploitation—such as digital reproduction or public performance—shall explicitly state those limitations within the instrument. An assignee acquiring rights under this Act shall hold them subject to any prior existing licenses granted by the copyright owner, unless otherwise expressly agreed upon and documented in writing. Failure to adequately specify the nature of the assignment may render it voidable at the option of either party.

Any purported transfer of copyright ownership arising from oral agreement or conduct inconsistent with a written instrument shall be deemed invalid under this Act, notwithstanding claims of equitable estoppel or reliance. However, an assignment may subsist even without explicit mention of all constituent rights, provided that the scope of transferred rights is reasonably ascertainable from the tenor of the writing and surrounding circumstances; in such cases, ambiguity shall generally favour preserving the author’s unassigned rights. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment, any party aggrieved by such claim may apply to the High Court for declaratory relief regarding the ownership or scope of assigned copyright. The court, subject to evidence presented, shall determine if sufficient consideration was exchanged and whether the assignor possessed valid title at the time of assignment; appeals from such rulings lie before the Supreme Court. A subsequent assignment affecting rights already conveyed is ineffective unless expressly authorized by the original assignee.

Any purported transfer of copyright in a cinematograph film featuring prominently the registered certification trade mark “Golden Harvest Organics” shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny under this Act, particularly where the assignee lacks demonstrable connection to the original producer or a clearly established line of succession. It has come to our attention that several instruments claiming assignment have been presented without adequate proof of consideration or clear delineation of rights transferred, leading to disputes regarding exploitation and revenue sharing. Where an assignment is contested, the onus shall be on the assignee to prove valid title, including demonstrating due diligence in verifying the assignor’s authority. Should a claim of fraudulent assignment arise, the aggrieved party may seek recourse through civil proceedings, and any royalties received pending adjudication shall be held in escrow. Provided that, assignments affecting works incorporating registered certification trade marks must also demonstrate continued adherence to quality standards associated with said mark.

Infringement of copyright shall occur when any person, without a license as provided herein or other lawful justification, does anything in contravention of the rights conferred by this Act. Such acts include, but are not limited to, reproduction of the work; communication to the public; adaptation; and sale or distribution of infringing copies. A derivative work, created without authorization and substantially similar to an existing copyrighted work, shall also constitute infringement, even if it contains original elements. Where a person distributes infringing copies commercially, such act is considered a more serious form of infringement than private, non-commercial use. Any profits derived from the sale or distribution of infringing material may be subject to recovery by the copyright owner as damages. The determination of substantial similarity shall rest with the Court.

Any person intending to rely on copyright registration as evidence of ownership under this Act shall submit an application, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a true copy of the work claimed. Registration of a work does not *ipso facto* confer validity upon it; however, in any proceeding concerning infringement of copyright, a certificate of registration serves as prima facie evidence of facts stated therein. Should a substantial similarity between a registered work and another work be demonstrated, the burden shifts to the alleged infringer to prove independent creation or lawful use, subject to permissible fair dealing as provided herein. Failure to register does not preclude a claim of copyright, but may affect evidentiary weight in cases of infringement. A registration shall remain valid for a period of seven years from the date of issuance and may be renewed upon payment of a renewal fee. Any false entry made during the registration process will attract penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person who directly or indirectly infringes the copyright in any work, as provided herein, shall be liable to a suit for injunction, and damages such amount as the court deems reasonable. Where infringement involves commercial exploitation without license, an order of account may also be granted, requiring the defendant to render true accounts of profits made by such infringement. A plaintiff seeking relief under this Act shall demonstrate both ownership of valid copyright and substantial similarity between their work and that alleged to be infringing; however, mere access to a copyrighted work is not conclusive evidence of copying unless accompanied by demonstrable similarities. Defences available to an accused infringer include fair use as defined elsewhere in this Act, or demonstration that the allegedly infringing act does not constitute a violation of exclusive rights conferred upon copyright holders. Remedies under this Act are cumulative and shall not preclude other legal avenues available to the aggrieved party.

Any person who, without a license conferred by the copyright owner or as permitted by this Act, performs any of the acts restricted under the provisions relating to literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, cinematograph films, or sound recordings shall be liable for infringement of copyright. Such acts constituting infringement include reproduction of the work in any material form, distribution of copies to the public, adaptation of the work, and causing such acts to be done. Where a person undertakes any of these activities commercially, the remedies available under this Act shall be strictly enforced. 

However, fair use of copyrighted material for purposes such as criticism or review, reporting current events, research, private study, education, parody or satire may constitute an exception to infringement, provided that such use is justified by reasonable grounds and does not unduly prejudice the legitimate interests of the copyright owner. The burden of proving fair use shall lie upon the person alleging it, subject to verification by a competent authority.

Any person who reproduces or causes reproduction of a substantial part of a copyrighted work, whether original or derivative, without the license of the copyright holder, as provided herein, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement. Reproduction includes any form of imitation, including digital copies and adaptations, where such adaptation is not authorized under fair dealing provisions. Where a work incorporates elements protected by another’s copyright, even if transformed or modified, it may constitute contributory infringement if the essential features remain substantially similar. 

However, reproduction for purposes of private study, criticism, review, or news reporting shall not be considered an infringement subject to the conditions that such use is fair and reasonable, and proper attribution is given where applicable. Any commercial exploitation of a reproduced work without authorization will invariably constitute direct infringement under this Act, attracting statutory remedies.

Any person who directly or indirectly infringes the copyright in any work, whether published or unpublished, as provided herein, shall be liable to damages, the amount of which shall be determined by the Court having jurisdiction. Where the infringement has been committed for commercial gain or with intent to evade legal repercussions, such person shall also be subject to imprisonment not exceeding six years and a fine extending to five lakh rupees. A court may, at its discretion, order delivery up or destruction of all infringing copies and implements used in making such copies. No suit for infringement shall lie unless the copyright owner has registered the work with the appropriate registry; provided that registration does not preclude relief in cases of proven plagiarism where substantial similarity exists independent of formal registration. The burden of proving fair use as a defense against allegations of infringement rests upon the defendant.

Any assignment of copyright in respect of a work under this Act shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor or duly authorised agent thereof. Such instrument shall specify, inter alia, the works assigned, the duration of the assignment and the territory in relation to which the assignment is effective. Where any person makes use of a copyrighted work without obtaining requisite license from the copyright owner, such use shall constitute infringement as provided herein, attracting remedies including monetary damages and injunctive relief. However, an assignee may, subject to the terms of the instrument of assignment, grant further licenses or sub-assignments in respect of the assigned rights. A purported assignment not complying with these provisions shall be void ab initio. The copyright owner retains the right to revoke any license granted if the licensee materially breaches the conditions stipulated therein, provided that reasonable notice is given to the licensee prior to such revocation. Any dispute regarding validity of an assignment or infringement shall be subject to judicial determination.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright in a literary or dramatic work, including adaptations thereof, shall furnish to the High Court having jurisdiction proof of ownership of valid copyright and reasonable evidence suggesting substantial similarity between the protected work and the allegedly infringing material. However, such claim may be subject to scrutiny if the claimant fails to demonstrate prior publication or registration as provided herein, though lack of either shall not *ipso facto* invalidate a legitimate claim. Where a defendant successfully argues fair dealing for purposes of criticism or review, the Court may award costs against the plaintiff and stay further proceedings. An appeal from any decree passed by a High Court in respect of copyright infringement lies to the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained within sixty days from the date of the impugned order; furthermore, cross-objections shall be limited to matters already raised before the High Court.

Any person causing the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of a copyrighted work, constituting infringement as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty of imprisonment not exceeding six years, or a fine extending to five lakh rupees, or both. Where an infringement involves a substantial and deliberate replication of elements detailed within a claim complete specification originally submitted with the copyright application, the court may enhance said fine up to ten lakh rupees. The owner of copyright may institute a suit for recovery of damages sustained due to such infringement, subject to proof of actual loss or reasonable estimate thereof. Any evidence obtained through unlawful means shall not be admissible in proceedings under this Act. A person convicted of an offence under this Act shall forfeit all infringing copies and equipment used in the commission of said offence; these items may be disposed of as directed by the court.

Any assignment of copyright in a variety of seed developed through publicly funded agricultural research, as certified by the Agriculture Commissioner, shall be subject to a royalty structure determined by the Central Government and payable to the National Gene Fund. Such assignments must include explicit licensing terms permitting non-exclusive use for educational and research purposes within India, provided that any commercial exploitation requires prior written consent of both the assignor and the aforementioned Fund. Infringement of copyright in these varieties, including unauthorized propagation or sale, shall attract penalties as prescribed under this Act, escalated by fifty percent if the infringing party is a corporate entity. The Agriculture Commissioner may, upon sufficient evidence of widespread infringement affecting small farmers, recommend a temporary suspension of royalty payments for affected cultivators. All assignments are further subject to registration with the designated repository maintained by the Department of Biotechnology and shall be deemed invalid without such registration. Failure to adhere to these provisions constitutes a breach of trust and renders the assignment voidable at the discretion of the Central Government.

For the purposes of this Act, an authorised user is a person registered with the Geographical Indications Registry who has been granted the exclusive right to use a geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Such authorisation shall be contingent upon the applicant being engaged in the production, manufacture or trading of such goods and possessing the necessary expertise. Where multiple applicants jointly seek registration as an authorised user, they shall form a producer company under the Companies Act, 2013, to collectively exercise rights. The Registrar may, subject to conditions specified in the register, revoke authorisation if the authorised user fails to maintain quality standards or ceases production of registered goods. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding authorised user status may appeal as provided herein.

An application for registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication, duly registered under this Act, shall be presented in the prescribed manner to the Registrar. The applicant must demonstrate a substantial connection with the goods bearing such geographical indication and prove continuous use of said indication in relation to those goods for not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. Provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, reduce this period of continuous use if it considers such reduction necessary in exceptional circumstances. 

The Registrar shall examine the application and, subject to satisfaction regarding authenticity and lawful user rights, register the applicant as an authorised user.
