Registration confers upon the authorised user the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the specified goods, within the defined geographical area, and remedies for infringement are available as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board.

An authorised user, possessing the requisite standing under this Act, shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings for infringement of a registered geographical indication against any person engaged in unlawful use thereof. Such proceedings may include seeking injunctions restraining the defendant from manufacturing or selling goods bearing the protected geographical indication, or any deceptively similar representation likely to cause confusion. A proprietor who is not an authorised user may also pursue remedies subject to demonstrating prior consent from the authorised user or establishing exceptional circumstances warranting direct action. Any act of material alteration of a registered geographical indication by an unauthorised party shall be deemed a violation and actionable as such. The court, upon finding infringement, may award damages commensurate with the harm suffered by the authorised user, including lost profits and costs associated with corrective advertising. Provided that, the court may also order delivery up or destruction of infringing goods.

An application for registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication, duly registered under this Act, shall be presented in the prescribed manner to the Registrar. The applicant shall demonstrate possessory use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods concerned and provide evidence establishing a prima facie link between the goods and the specified geographical area. Where multiple applicants claim rights as an authorised user concerning identical goods originating from the same geographical indication, the Registrar may require them to jointly apply or establish priority based on continuous and demonstrable usage for a period not less than five years prior to the date of application. 

Subject to verification by the Registrar, and provided that no objection is received within the prescribed time limit, an individual or legal entity fulfilling the criteria shall be registered as an authorised user. The register of authorised users maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection subject to payment of a fee as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration as an authorised user may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

An applicant seeking registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication registered under this Act shall submit evidence demonstrating lawful production of goods conforming to the standards prescribed in relation to such geographical indication, and a no-objection certificate from the producers’ association, where one exists. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, register such applicant as an authorised user for a period not exceeding ten years, renewable upon reapplication and satisfactory compliance with ongoing quality control measures. An authorised user shall conspicuously display the registered geographical indication on all packaged goods, and maintain accurate records relating to production volume and origin, available for inspection by officers duly appointed under this Act. Failure to adhere to prescribed standards or misrepresentation regarding geographical origin may result in suspension or revocation of authorisation, provided that a reasonable opportunity for rectification is afforded. Any person aggrieved by the actions of an authorised user may lodge a complaint with the Registrar as provided herein.

Any person falsely representing themselves as an authorised user of a registered geographical indication, or using such representation in the course of trade, business, or commerce, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. An ‘authorised user’ is defined as one who has been formally recorded as such in the Register maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry, and whose application for registration as authorised user has satisfied all criteria as provided herein. Any individual found guilty of unlawfully using a registered geographical indication, or falsely claiming to be an authorised user without valid registration, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. Furthermore, any goods bearing such false representation shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure by the appropriate authority, with no compensation payable to the offender. The Registrar may initiate investigations ex officio upon reasonable suspicion of such offences.

An application for the assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication, or any interest therein, shall be made to the Registrar in such form and accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed. Any transfer by operation of law, including through inheritance, succession, amalgamation, or otherwise, affecting title to a registered geographical indication, shall require notification to the Registrar within six months of such transfer. The Registrar shall maintain a register of assignments and transfers reflecting current ownership. 

An ‘authorised user’ of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions contained herein, grant licenses or assign rights in respect of specific goods falling within the scope of that geographical indication to other persons or entities. Any license granted shall be recorded with the Registrar and shall specify the territory, duration, and conditions governing its use. The original proprietor retains the right to revoke a license upon demonstrating material breach of its terms; provided that any such revocation is subject to dispute resolution mechanisms as established under this Act.

Any person claiming to be an authorised user of a registered geographical indication may apply to the Registrar for recognition as such, submitting evidence of their association with the goods bearing that indication and demonstrating continuous use in the area specified within the register. The application shall be subject to public notice inviting objections from interested parties who may dispute the veracity of the claim or demonstrate prior legitimate usage. Should an objection be sustained following a hearing conducted by the Registrar, the applicant’s status as an authorised user shall not be granted; however, such decision may be appealed before the Appellate Board established under this Act. A registered proprietor failing to exercise reasonable diligence in maintaining quality control associated with the geographical indication risks revocation of authorisation for any user found deficient in adherence to prescribed standards, notwithstanding prior recognition. The Registrar may, at their discretion, initiate *suo motu* inquiry into allegations of misuse or substandard production by an alleged authorised user.

An application for the amendment of the Register of Geographical Indications concerning ‘Kashmir Saffron’ was recently dismissed by the Registrar, prompting an appeal before this Authority. The appellant, Himalayan Agro Industries, asserts its status as an authorised user following a purported assignment from the original registered proprietor, Kashmir Valley Farmers Collective. However, evidence submitted indicates that the assigned rights did not extend to the specific pharmaceutical substance derived from saffron—namely, crocin—which constitutes a significant portion of Himalayan Agro’s commercial activity. 

The Registrar held that mere registration as an authorised user for ‘Kashmir Saffron’ does not automatically confer rights over derivative products or distinct chemical compounds extracted therefrom; such rights require separate demonstration of origin and quality standards as provided herein. The appellant contends this interpretation is overly restrictive, arguing a broad reading of “authorised use” should encompass all commercially viable applications. This Authority shall determine whether the Registrar erred in limiting the scope of authorisation, particularly concerning the manufacture and sale of crocin-based medicinal preparations bearing the ‘Kashmir Saffron’ geographical indication.

The High Court shall have exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and determine all matters concerning copyright disputes not specifically assigned to any other court or tribunal as provided herein. Subject to the provisions contained in this Act, an aggrieved party may institute a suit before the appropriate High Court for redressal of any violation of their copyright. The High Court may grant such reliefs as are permissible under civil law, including injunctions, damages, and rendition of accounts. Provided that no suit shall be instituted in any High Court unless reasonable notice has been served upon the alleged infringer outlining the nature of the grievance. Appeals from original decrees of the High Court relating to copyright matters lie before the Supreme Court of India as per established legal procedure.

Any copyright owner desiring registration of a work shall submit an application to the Registrar of Copyrights in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee and a copy of the work claimed. The Registrar, upon examination, may require further information or clarification from the applicant subject to the provisions herein. Should the Registrar deem the application deficient or lacking necessary documentation, it shall communicate such deficiencies within thirty days of receipt; failure to respond adequately within ninety days thereafter will result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding registration may appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of the Registrar’s communication. The High Court shall consider evidence presented and may affirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar's decision as it deems just and equitable; its orders are final and binding unless appealed further to the Supreme Court.

Any author or publisher alleging infringement of copyright as provided herein shall be entitled to apply to the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred for an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. The High Court, upon being satisfied by prima facie evidence of ownership and infringement, may grant such injunction pending final determination of the matter; however, no such injunction shall continue for a period exceeding fifteen days unless extended by subsequent order based on demonstrable progress in the proceedings. A defendant seeking to prove fair dealing as an exception to copyright restrictions shall bear the onus of establishing that their use falls within the permissible parameters outlined under this Act. Should the High Court find against the plaintiff, it may award costs and damages commensurate with the proven loss suffered due to the infringement, or alternatively, account for any profits unjustly gained by the defendant through such unlawful reproduction or distribution. Any order made by the High Court is subject to appeal as per established civil procedure rules.

Any party desiring interim relief in respect of infringement of copyright, prior to the institution of a suit before a competent District Court, may apply ex parte to a High Court not ordinarily exercising jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated for seeking recourse outside normal jurisdictional boundaries. The High Court shall, upon such application and subject to verification of the prima facie case presented by the applicant, have the power to grant a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. Such injunction may be modified or vacated pending final adjudication of the matter in the District Court having jurisdiction. Where the High Court deems it necessary for effective relief, it may direct the seizure and custody of all infringing copies or plates used in the making of such copies. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may prefer an appeal to a Division Bench of the same High Court as provided herein.

Any party claiming infringement of copyright shall, prior to initiating proceedings before a competent court, furnish a statutory notice to the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the infringed work and the specific acts constituting the infringement. Such notice shall be served by registered post with acknowledgement due, or through electronic means where expressly permitted under the Information Technology Act, 2000, and proof of service maintained for production as required. Where the aggrieved party seeks interim relief pending resolution of the dispute, application therefor may be made directly to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The High Court shall, subject to verification of prima facie evidence of copyright ownership and infringement, consider such applications expeditiously. Provided that no ex parte order restraining publication or circulation shall remain in force for a period exceeding fourteen days without affording a reasonable opportunity for hearing to the respondent. Any appeal against an order of the High Court relating to interim relief shall lie before the designated appellate authority as provided herein.

Any infringement of copyright established before a competent High Court shall be actionable by the owner of copyright, and remedies available as provided herein include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement. Where a plaintiff demonstrates actual damages sustained due to said infringement, recovery of such damages, not exceeding a sum equivalent to the retail price of legitimately produced copies reasonably estimated, may be awarded. However, should the defendant prove that the infringement was unintentional and they exercised due diligence in preventing its occurrence, the court may reduce the recoverable amount. Any person found knowingly facilitating or aiding an act of copyright infringement shall also be liable for damages as determined by the High Court. Furthermore, repeated violations despite injunctive relief will constitute aggravated circumstances subject to enhanced penalties, including imprisonment not exceeding three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. All appeals concerning orders relating to interim injunctions issued under this Act lie before the designated bench of the relevant High Court.

Any assignment of copyright relating to cinematograph films shall be subject to prior approval of the Central Government where the assignee is not a citizen of India or a body corporate incorporated in India. Provided that the High Court, upon application made by any party claiming interest in such copyright and after giving notice to the proposed assignee and the Central Government, may dispense with such requirement if it deems fit, subject to appropriate safeguards being undertaken to protect the interests of the owner of copyright and ensure compliance with this Act. All assignments recorded under this provision shall be open for inspection during office hours by any person paying the prescribed fee. Furthermore, a register of such assignments maintained by the Central Government shall be conclusive evidence of the validity of the assignment unless successfully challenged before the High Court through established legal procedures as provided herein. Any transfer without requisite approval or judicial dispensation shall render the assignment void ab initio.

Any party claiming infringement of copyright, and dissatisfied with the decree of the District Court having original jurisdiction, shall have the right to prefer an appeal before the High Court. Provided that such appeal lies only where a substantial question of law is involved, as determined by the single judge assigned to hear preliminary objections. The High Court may, subject to its discretion and in cases involving complex technical issues relating to digital rights management or derivative works, appoint a technical assessor to provide expert opinion on matters of fact. An application for such assessment shall be made within thirty days of the filing of the appeal. Furthermore, any order passed by the High Court regarding interim injunctions restraining reproduction or distribution may be modified upon review if circumstances materially change prior to final adjudication, and notice thereof shall be served on all affected parties. The aggrieved party may seek a stay of execution pending disposal of the appeal before the appropriate bench of the High Court.

Any assignment of copyright in a design register layout, whether partial or complete, shall be subject to the prior written consent of the High Court, unless otherwise provided herein. An applicant seeking such consent shall demonstrate sufficient cause and provide full particulars of the proposed assignee, including their legal standing and intended use of the copyrighted material. The High Court may, at its discretion, impose conditions on any assignment so approved, ensuring continued protection of the original creator’s moral rights as established under this Act. Where an assignment is made without requisite consent, it shall be deemed void ab initio; however, a party acting in good faith and relying upon such assignment may seek redress from the assignor. Provided that, the High Court retains jurisdiction to review any dispute arising from the interpretation or enforcement of these provisions, and its decisions shall be final and binding on all parties concerned. Any appeal against an order of the High Court relating to copyright assignments shall lie only before the Supreme Court.

The High Court shall be the first appellate court for all matters pertaining to copyright disputes arising under this Act, save where express provision is made for appeals to another forum. Any aggrieved party desiring a review of an order passed by the Copyrights Appellate Board may prefer an appeal to the appropriate High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, provided that such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said order. The High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, stay the execution of any decision or order appealed from pending disposal of the appeal. No second appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a High Court in copyright matters; however, special leave petitions may be entertained by the Supreme Court under established legal principles.

Any party alleging infringement of copyright, and dissatisfied with a decree passed by a District Court regarding such infringement, may prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction over the said District Court. Such appeals shall be subject to the provisions contained in this Act and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as applicable. The High Court, upon consideration of any appeal relating to copyright, may confirm, modify or reverse the decree appealed from; provided that no appeal shall lie before the High Court unless a substantial question of law is involved. Further, where the High Court finds that a copyright license was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation, it may, subject to due process and hearing of all parties concerned, order revocation of such license with effect from a date as deemed appropriate. Any decision of the High Court in respect of copyright matters shall be final and binding on all parties, save for any recourse permissible under the law relating to appeals to the Supreme Court.

The register of copyrights maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection subject to payment of such fee as may be prescribed and during office hours. Any person desiring to inspect any entry in the said register shall apply therefor in writing to the Principal Registrar of Copyrights. Notice of every application for registration, and of every alteration made therein subsequent to registration, shall be published in the Official Gazette. The publication in the Official Gazette shall be conclusive evidence as to the date of such registration or alteration. Any document required to be filed with the Principal Registrar may, subject to rules made by the Central Government, be filed electronically through a system maintained for that purpose and notification of such filing shall also appear in the Official Gazette.

Any person intending to register a copyright under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar of Copyrights, accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in Schedule I. The application shall include details regarding the work’s authorship, publication status and any prior existing rights claimed therein. Upon receipt of a complete application, the Registrar may examine the particulars furnished and, if satisfied that the work is eligible for copyright protection as provided herein, shall enter the details in the Register of Copyrights. Notice of such registration shall be published in the Official Gazette to provide public notice of the claimant’s rights. Any person aggrieved by such entry may file a written objection with the Registrar within thirty days from the date of publication in the Official Gazette, subject to fulfilling requirements for standing as determined by the Registrar. The Register maintained shall be prima facie evidence of facts stated therein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar of Copyrights relating to registration of copyright or any matter connected therewith, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within which the cause of action arises. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the High Court may entertain an appeal even after the expiry of the said period if sufficient cause is shown. Notice of such appeal shall be served on the Registrar and all other parties concerned as directed by the court. All notifications regarding appeals, including any modifications to procedures established under this Act, shall be published in the Official Gazette for public awareness. The Central Government may, through notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe forms and fees applicable to proceedings before the High Court relating to copyright disputes; such prescription shall not unduly burden applicants seeking legitimate redress. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines or fee structures may render an appeal inadmissible as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a copyright under this Act shall be made in writing and submitted to the Registrar of Copyrights in the prescribed form. The Registrar, upon receipt of any such application and subject to verification of accompanying documentation establishing prima facie ownership and originality, may cause an examination of the work to be undertaken. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the work meets the requirements for registration as provided herein, notice of such registration shall be published in the Official Gazette. Such publication shall constitute conclusive evidence of the validity of the copyright subject to any subsequent challenge initiated through due process of law. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration may, within sixty days from the date of notification of such refusal, file an appeal with the High Court having jurisdiction. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all copyrights registered and published in the Official Gazette, accessible for inspection during office hours upon payment of the prescribed fee.

All applications for registration of copyright, and all notices relating to alterations affecting any entry recorded in the Register of Copyrights, shall be published in the Official Gazette in a manner prescribed. Any person aggrieved by an act specified under this Act involving infringement of their exclusive right may lodge a complaint with the designated authority, subject to providing documented evidence of ownership as detailed within these rules. The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all such complaints received and actions taken, also published periodically in the Official Gazette for transparency. Failure to comply with the prescribed format for applications or notices submitted for publication may result in their rejection, provided that applicants are afforded one opportunity to rectify deficiencies. All statutory fees associated with registration and related processes shall be remitted as per the schedule appended to these regulations, and proof of payment must accompany each submission intended for inclusion in the Official Gazette.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar of Copyrights relating to registration of copyright or any matter incidental thereto, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within which the cause of action arises. Such appeal shall be filed subject to the provisions contained herein and within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of the order appealed against; provided that the High Court may entertain such appeal even after the expiry of said period if sufficient cause is shown. All notifications, orders, and rules pertaining to appeals under this Act shall be published in the Official Gazette, ensuring public access to procedural details. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines for filing an appeal or any deliberate misrepresentation made before the High Court shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. The Registrar may, where appropriate, initiate proceedings for contempt of court against those obstructing due process.

Any person desiring to assign or otherwise transfer copyright in a work, or any right therein, whether wholly or partially, and whether exclusively or non-exclusively, shall submit an application for registration of such assignment or transfer to the designated Copyright Office. Such application shall be accompanied by an instrument of assignment duly executed by both parties, clearly specifying the scope of rights transferred and any limitations thereto. The Copyright Office, upon verification of the submitted documents and satisfaction that the transaction conforms with provisions under this Act, shall register the assignment and issue a certificate of registration. Notice of such registration shall be published in the Official Gazette to provide constructive notice to all interested parties. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against subsequent purchasers or licensees acting in good faith. The Copyright Office maintains a public registry accessible for inspection, subject to prescribed fees, allowing verification of ownership and transfer history as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity of such assignment shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights refusing registration or revoking a copyright, or varying the terms of any license granted under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within which the principal place of business of the complainant lies. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause demonstrated to the satisfaction of the court. Notice of such appeal shall be served on the Registrar and all parties concerned as directed by the High Court. The Registrar’s detailed reasons for any refusal or revocation must be published in the Official Gazette within thirty days of communication to the appellant, failing which a rebuttable presumption arises against the validity of said order. Any further appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court, as provided herein. All applications and supporting documentation relating to appeals must conform strictly to the prescribed format.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding an application for registration of copyright, or any refusal or revocation thereof, shall have recourse to appeal as provided herein. Such appeal shall be presented to the High Court within which the office of the Registrar lies, subject to payment of prescribed fees and fulfillment of all procedural requirements stipulated by that court. Notice of such appeal shall be served upon the Registrar, with a copy of the impugned decision duly authenticated from records maintained for publication in the Official Gazette. The High Court may, at its discretion, require further evidence or submissions from either party before rendering judgment. A failure to comply with timelines established by the court registrar application process will render the appeal inadmissible; however, extensions may be granted under exceptional circumstances determined solely by the presiding judge. Decisions of the High Court in such matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition as per constitutional provisions.

Any person claiming copyright in a work shall submit an application for registration as provided herein, and upon satisfactory verification, their name shall be entered in the Register of Copyrights maintained in accordance with established procedures. The Controller of Copyrights may, at any time prior to acceptance of such application or during its processing, require further information or clarification from the applicant. An application permitted amended, subject to reasonable justification and within prescribed timelines, shall not be deemed a new application for purposes of establishing priority date; however, amendments materially altering the scope of the claimed work may necessitate re-examination. Notice of any refusal of registration, or of any amendment proposed by the Controller, shall be published in the Official Gazette, affording the applicant an opportunity to submit representations. Failure to respond within the stipulated period may result in closure of the application and loss of associated rights as determined under this Act. Any aggrieved party may seek redressal through established judicial channels.

Any person intending to claim copyright in a work consisting of a film sound recording, or asserting rights therein, shall submit a notice of such claim to the Registrar of Copyrights. Such notice shall be accompanied by a specimen copy of the sound recording and a statement detailing the particulars of its creation, including the names and addresses of all persons involved in its production. The Registrar shall, upon examination of the submitted materials and satisfaction that the requirements as provided herein have been met, cause the particulars to be entered into the Register of Copyrights. 

Publication of such entry in the Official Gazette shall constitute prima facie evidence of the validity of the claim, subject to any objections filed within a period of thirty days from the date of publication. Any objection shall be adjudicated upon by the Registrar following principles of natural justice and affording opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned. Failure to publish particulars in the Official Gazette does not invalidate copyright but may affect the evidentiary value of the registration.

Copyright subsists, as provided herein, upon the creation of original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Such copyright vests initially with the author of the work, subject to provisions relating to works made for consideration or employment under a contract of service. A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be an artistic work. The term of copyright in any such work shall generally extend for the life of the author plus sixty years; however, this duration may vary depending on the nature of the work and its first publication date. Assignment of copyright must be by instrument in writing signed by the assignor or their duly authorised agent. Moral rights are also recognised, allowing authors to claim authorship and object to distortion of their works even after assignment. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of copyright may apply to the appropriate court for redressal.

Any person claiming copyright in a work shall apply for registration with the Registrar of Copyrights in the prescribed form and shall pay the applicable fee. The application shall include particulars of the applicant, details relating to the creation of the work, and a clear statement of the extent of copyright claimed. Where the work includes contributions by multiple authors, each author or their authorized representative may jointly apply for registration, specifying the nature and scope of each contribution. Registration is not compulsory but serves as prima facie evidence of ownership under this Act. Provided that failure to register shall not prejudice the right of a person to claim copyright in a work; however, such a claimant may face evidentiary challenges regarding the date of creation or authorship. A certificate of registration, once issued, may be subject to rectification if substantial errors are discovered and brought to the attention of the Registrar as provided herein. The registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered copyrights.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of copyright, or alleging unfair practice relating to copyright, may institute a suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, subject to limitations prescribed herein. The plaintiff shall demonstrate substantial similarity between their work and that alleged to be infringing, establishing both ownership of copyright and actual copying. Defences available to the defendant include fair dealing for purposes such as criticism or review, provided that sufficient acknowledgement is made and the use does not unreasonably prejudice the rights of the copyright owner. Where a work incorporates elements protected by design registration under the Designs Act, 2000, remedies shall be pursued in accordance with that Act concerning the design element; however, copyright protection remains valid for aspects not covered by design law. Damages awarded may include actual losses suffered and reasonable royalties due, or an account of profits made by the infringer, at the discretion of the Court. An injunction restraining further infringement may also be granted.

Any work involving authorship, whether published or unpublished, shall be eligible for copyright protection under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding originality and expression. The author of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work shall, as provided herein, be the first owner of the copyright therein; however, in the case of a work created during the course of employment by an individual, the employer shall ordinarily possess such copyright unless otherwise agreed in writing. A person claiming to be the rightful owner of copyright may apply to the appropriate authority for registration of their claim, and such registration shall constitute *prima facie* evidence of ownership but shall not be conclusive proof. Transfer of copyright must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the transferor; any oral agreement relating to such transfer shall be inadmissible as evidence. The duration of copyright shall vary depending upon the nature of the work, with provisions made for both limited terms and perpetual rights concerning certain categories of works. Infringement of copyright gives rise to civil remedies including injunctions and damages, and may also constitute a cognizable offence under criminal law.

Any work which is original—meaning it originates from the author and demonstrates a minimum degree of creativity—shall be eligible for copyright protection under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained. Such works include literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, as well as cinematograph films and sound recordings. A person claiming copyright must demonstrate sufficient connection with the work’s creation; mere possession of a physical copy shall not constitute ownership. The author's economic rights encompass reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation, provided that fair dealing for purposes such as criticism or private study does not infringe these rights. Moral rights, including the right to be identified as the author and to prevent distortion of the work, are also vested in the creator, even after transfer of copyright. Assignment of copyright must be in writing and signed by the assignor, and any subsequent dispute regarding validity shall be subject to judicial determination.

Any person who infringes the copyright in a work shall be liable to damages, assessed in accordance with the provisions of this Act and having regard to the nature and extent of the infringement. Where an infringement has occurred due to the propagation of illicit recordings, the proprietor of copyright may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, apply ex-officio to a Magistrate for an order directing the seizure of infringing copies and all equipment used in making such copies. Any magistrate empowered under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, may grant such order. Failure to comply with any order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court and be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or with fine, or with both. The rights conferred by copyright are subject to limitations as provided herein, including fair dealing for purposes such as criticism or private study.

Any person being the owner of copyright in a work, whether published or unpublished, may grant licenses for the use of that work under terms and conditions mutually agreed upon with any prospective licensee, subject to the provisions contained herein. Such license may be exclusive, limited to specific territories or media, or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Assignment of copyright shall require a written instrument signed by the assignor or duly authorized agent, clearly identifying the work and specifying the rights assigned. Where an assignment is made for a term of years, any rights not expressly granted to the assignee shall remain with the assignor. 

A license may also be coupled with a right of reversion, allowing the licensor to reclaim exclusive rights upon fulfillment of certain conditions or after a specified period. The licensee shall have no power to further sub-license the copyright without express written consent from the original owner, unless otherwise stipulated in the initial licensing agreement as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these provisions may render the license voidable at the discretion of the copyright holder.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright under this Act shall furnish to the High Court a declaration stating substantially whether the matter complained of has been previously published or exhibited in public, and if so, where and when; provided that such requirement shall not apply where the plaintiff demonstrates irreparable harm pending full discovery. An appeal from any decree passed by a District Court concerning rights in copyright shall lie to the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. However, no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant satisfies the court that substantial grounds exist for an appeal and that the matter involves a question of law requiring determination. Furthermore, where a claim of fair dealing is asserted as a defense against alleged infringement, the burden of proving such dealing lies with the defendant; this remains so even if ownership of copyright is not in dispute. Any order made on appeal may be subject to further review by the Supreme Court.

Copyright subsists, as provided herein, in original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Such copyright vests initially with the author of the work, subject to provisions relating to works created during employment or under commission. A person claiming ownership of copyright may enter their particulars in the entry register maintained by the competent authority for purposes of record, though such registration shall not be conclusive evidence of title but is admissible as *prima facie* evidence. The rights conferred by copyright include the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, perform and adapt the work. Any infringement of copyright shall be actionable under this Act, attracting remedies including injunctions and damages. Transfer of copyright may occur through assignment or licensing, both of which require written instrument for validity.

Any person interested in opposing the grant of a patent shall file a notice of opposition with the Controller within four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent. Such notice shall contain a detailed statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by supporting evidence where available. The applicant whose patent is subject to opposition may, within three months of receiving a copy of the notice of opposition, file a statement addressing the grounds raised therein; provided that such statement does not exceed fifty pages. A hearing may be conducted by the Controller to determine the validity of the opposition and shall consider all evidence submitted by both parties, subject to rules prescribed herein. Failure to comply with these timelines may result in dismissal of the opposition or rejection of supporting materials.

Any person intending to oppose a patent application shall submit a notice of opposition to the Controller in the prescribed form and manner, together with the grounds on which the opposition is based. Such notice shall be filed within a period of four months from the date of publication of the complete specification as provided herein. The applicant whose patent is subject to opposition may, within three months of receiving the copy of the opposition, file a statement setting out the reasons for disagreeing with the grounds on which the opposition is based. Evidence in support of the grounds of opposition or the applicant’s statement shall be filed by both parties within such time as may be specified by the Controller. The Controller shall consider all evidence and hear both sides before issuing a decision regarding the validity of the patent, subject to any provisions concerning revocation petitions under this Act. Failure to adhere to these timelines may result in dismissal of the opposition or forfeiture of rights.

Any person may file a written opposition to the grant of a patent at any time within four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent, as provided herein. Such opposition shall be based only on grounds specified under this Act and shall clearly state the applicant’s case with full particulars thereof. The Controller, upon receiving an opposition, shall cause a copy of it to be served on the applicant, who may, within three months from the date of such service, file a statement setting forth his arguments against the opposition. Should the Controller deem a hearing necessary, notice thereof shall be given to both parties and conducted in accordance with established procedures. A decision regarding the opposition shall be made after considering all evidence presented and submissions made by either party; however, an opportunity for amendment of claims may be granted subject to conditions deemed appropriate. Failure to respond within stipulated timeframes may result in dismissal of the opposition or acceptance of the application without further consideration. The aggrieved party retains a right to appeal any decision rendered under this Act.

Any person interested may file an opposition to a granted patent as provided herein, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and within a period not exceeding four months from the date of advertisement of the grant of the patent. The opposition shall be in writing and shall clearly state the grounds upon which it is based, including any relevant prior art relied upon to demonstrate lack of novelty or inventive step. Upon receipt of an opposition, the Controller shall furnish a copy thereof to the patentee, who may file a statement setting forth his views within three months. Should the Controller deem the opposition well-founded and supported by sufficient evidence, he may initiate an inquiry, allowing both parties opportunity to present arguments and submit further documentation. The Controller’s decision on the opposition shall be final and binding, except where appeal is provided under this Act; however, a mere allegation of non-compliance with statutory requirements without supporting evidence will not constitute valid grounds for opposition.

Any person interested may file an opposition to a granted patent as provided herein, subject to compliance with the prescribed fees and within a period not exceeding four months from the date of advertisement of the grant of the patent. The opposition shall be in writing and shall clearly state the grounds on which it is based, including any anticipation by prior art or obviousness under this Act. A complete specification of the opposing party’s asserted prior art must accompany the representation. 

The Controller shall, upon receipt of an opposition, furnish a copy to the patentee, who may, within three months, file a statement setting forth his views. Should the Controller deem it necessary, a hearing shall be conducted wherein both parties may present evidence and arguments; however, personal appearance is not mandatory unless specifically requested by the Controller. Failure to comply with timelines prescribed under this Act may result in dismissal of the opposition or rejection of submitted evidence.

Any person may file a written opposition to the grant of a patent at any time within four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent, as provided herein. Such opposition shall be based on grounds specified under this Act and shall clearly articulate the alleged deficiencies in the claimed invention. Failure to submit a complete and reasoned opposition may render it inadmissible. The Controller, upon receiving an opposition, shall furnish a copy thereof to the applicant, who shall have three months to file a counter-statement. Evidence supporting both the opposition and the counter-statement shall be filed within a further period stipulated by the Controller. Any false or misleading representation made in connection with an opposition shall attract a penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The decision of the Controller on the opposition is subject to appeal before the High Court.

Any assignment of a pending application for a patent shall be subject to verification by the Controller as to its validity and enforceability, and no such assignment shall take effect until so verified. A prospective assignee may file notice of an intended assignment with the Controller, accompanied by a statement outlining the terms and conditions governing the transfer of rights. Should any person wish to lodge an opposition to the proposed assignment, they may do so within one month from the date of publication of the notice in the Official Journal; such opposition shall clearly state the grounds upon which the validity of the assignment is contested. The Controller shall provide all parties with a reasonable opportunity to be heard before rendering a decision regarding the assignment’s approval or rejection. Provided that, an assignee who demonstrates sufficient interest and due diligence may continue prosecution of the application even pending resolution of any opposition relating to the transfer itself, subject to such conditions as the Controller deems appropriate. Any rights accrued prior to the effective date of the assignment remain unaffected by this process.

Any person interested may file an opposition to a granted patent as provided herein within a period of twelve months from the date of publication of the grant in the Official Journal, subject to extension of time not exceeding three months for sufficient cause. Such opposition shall be filed with the Controller and shall set forth the grounds upon which it is based, alleging facts constituting invalidity under this Act. The patentee shall be served with a copy of the notice of opposition and may file a counter-statement within three months, detailing reasons why the opposition should not succeed. Evidence may then be submitted by both parties, and a hearing shall be conducted where each party has the right to present arguments and cross-examine witnesses. If, after considering all evidence and submissions, the Controller is satisfied that grounds for revocation exist, he may revoke the patent; otherwise, the opposition shall be dismissed, and the patent remains in force. An appeal from any decision of the Controller regarding an opposition may lie before the Appellate Board.

Any natural person or legal entity may file a pre-grant opposition against an application for a patent relating to biological material sourced from India, subject to the provisions herein. Such opposition shall be filed with the Controller of Patents within twelve months from the date of publication of the said application and must clearly articulate grounds relevant under this Act concerning novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability. Where the claimed invention pertains to genetic sequences or utilizes indigenous biodiversity, the applicant shall demonstrate evidence of benefit-sharing arrangements established with the National Gene Fund as per prevailing guidelines issued by the competent authority. The Controller may require the opponent to furnish security for costs and shall provide a reasonable opportunity for both the applicant and the opponent to present their case in writing. Failure to comply with timelines prescribed herein may render the opposition inadmissible, provided that extensions may be granted at the discretion of the Controller under exceptional circumstances.

Any person intending to oppose the grant of a patent shall submit a notice of opposition to the Controller within four months from the date of publication of the application. Such notice shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the relevant facts and evidence supporting those grounds. The applicant whose patent is subject to opposition may, within three months of receiving a copy of the opposition filed, file a counter-statement addressing each ground raised. Should credible evidence of prior art demonstrating infringement registered against a similar invention already exist, such evidence shall be given due consideration by the Controller during adjudication of the opposition. Failure to submit a notice or counter-statement within the prescribed timeframes may result in its rejection, unless sufficient cause is shown. The Controller, after examining all submissions and conducting any necessary hearings, shall issue a reasoned order either upholding or dismissing the opposition, as provided herein.

Any assignment or licensing of a patented invention relating to pharmaceutical formulations shall be subject to scrutiny by the Controller as provided herein, particularly where the assignee or licensee is not a registered user trade entity duly authorized for manufacture and sale within India. An opposition may be filed with the Controller against such transfer if it appears that the terms of assignment or license do not adequately secure public health interests, or unduly restrict access to essential medicines. The Controller shall consider evidence demonstrating whether the assignee possesses the requisite manufacturing capabilities and distribution networks to ensure widespread availability of the patented product at a reasonable price. Provided that, an opposition based on commercial considerations alone shall not be entertained unless accompanied by demonstrable proof of anti-competitive practices. All oppositions must be filed within four months from the date of publication of the assignment or license agreement in the Official Gazette and shall adhere to prescribed procedural requirements. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the transfer invalid.

In this Act, a “breeder” shall mean any person being a natural or juridical person who has bred, developed or commercially exploited a new variety; provided that a farmer who is engaged in propagation, multiplication and conservation of plant genetic resources for varieties locally adapted to their agro-climatic zones may also be considered a breeder subject to the conditions as prescribed. The term “essentially derived variety” means a variety obtained through the modification of a parent variety which retains the characteristics of the latter while exhibiting distinct, identifiable traits; such derivation must be demonstrably based on the protected variety and conform to criteria established under this Act. Any person claiming status as a breeder shall maintain records demonstrating their contribution to the development of the plant variety.

A person shall be considered a breeder under this Act if they have developed or discovered and propagated any new, distinct, uniform and stable plant variety. The application for registration of such variety must demonstrate that the applicant is indeed the breeder, evidenced by documented proof of creation or discovery including field trials and records maintained thereof. Where a plant variety is jointly bred, all breeders shall be named in the application; however, one breeder may be designated as the lead applicant subject to written consent from all other participating breeders. A breeder who has commercially exploited any protected variety without registration, as provided herein, may be liable for penalties commensurate with the duration of such exploitation and calculated on a pro-rata basis. The register of plant varieties shall maintain details regarding each registered breeder including their address for service and nominated agent where applicable. Any transfer of breeding rights must be duly recorded with the Authority to ensure transparency and enforceability.

A breeder whose plant variety is registered under this Act shall have the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export and stock propagative material of that variety. However, farmers’ rights to save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange and share seeds or propagating material in any farm are not prejudiced by such exclusivity, provided that commercial marketing of harvested material shall be subject to the provisions herein. Any person who contravenes the exclusive right of a breeder as established under this Act may be subjected to an injunction restraining further acts of infringement. A registered breeder aggrieved by any act constituting an infringement of their rights may apply to the Central Government for appropriate remedial action, including assessment of damages and recovery thereof. The determination of damages shall consider the loss suffered by the breeder due to the unlawful activity, as well as any undue profits made by the infringer; a reasonable royalty rate may be considered in such calculation. A breeder demonstrating substantial investment in developing a new variety will have recourse to these remedies.

A person shall be deemed to be a breeder in respect of any variety if he has been instrumental in discovering and developing or in commercially exploiting that variety. Provided that, where any trait or characteristic of a variety is derived from a traditional knowledge base associated with plants and accessed through indigenous communities, the breeder shall acknowledge the contribution of such community in his application for registration. The Authority may, subject to conditions as it deems fit, require the breeder to share benefits equitably with those indigenous communities who contributed to the development of said variety. Any person claiming to be a breeder must furnish proof of having substantially derived a new variety, demonstrating distinctness, uniformity and stability as per established protocols. A registered breeder shall have exclusive rights in respect of the protected variety subject to limitations as provided herein, including the right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import or export the propagating material of such variety. However, farmers’ rights to save, use, sow, re-sow and exchange seeds shall not be prejudiced by these provisions.

A person shall be considered a breeder under this Act if they have developed or discovered a new, distinct, uniform and stable plant variety. The discovery of essentially derived varieties, however, does not confer independent status as a breeder; such persons are subject to the rights of the original breeder whose parental line was used in developing the essentially derived variety. Any person claiming to be a breeder shall maintain detailed records demonstrating the derivation and characteristics of the claimed variety, including evidence of its novelty. Provided that, where a plant variety is developed through public funds or by a publicly funded institution, the provisions relating to ownership and benefit sharing as provided herein shall apply with necessary modifications. A breeder may seek registration of their variety in accordance with the procedures established under this Act, subject to fulfilling all prescribed criteria regarding genetic purity and stability. Failure to comply with record-keeping requirements may result in revocation of any granted breeder’s rights.

Any person claiming to be a breeder shall furnish proof of having engaged in the breeding of a new, distinct, uniform and stable plant variety as provided herein. Failure to adequately demonstrate such engagement, including maintaining detailed records of lineage tracing and selection processes, shall constitute grounds for rejection of their claim under this Act. A registered breeder who knowingly markets seed derived from an essentially derived variety without due authorization or fails to remit royalties payable to the original breeder, may be subject to a penalty not exceeding five times the value of the illegally marketed seed. Provided that, if such offense is repeated within three years of a prior conviction, the penalties shall include imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. The Authority reserves the right to conduct unannounced inspections of breeding facilities and records to ensure compliance with these provisions. Any false representation made by a breeder in relation to their variety will be treated as an offence punishable under this Act.

A breeder desiring to commercially exploit a new plant variety developed by them shall apply for registration under this Act and may, subject to the provisions herein, assign all or any rights in the registered variety to another person. Any assignment of breeders’ rights must be in writing and duly attested, specifying clearly the scope of the assigned rights including territorial limitations and duration of the assignment. Where a breeder is a legal entity, such as a company or research institution, the assignment shall require authorization from its governing body as evidenced by board resolution. The assignee becomes entitled to all benefits accruing from the exploitation of the variety, subject to any pre-existing contractual obligations of the original breeder. A licensee of the breeders’ rights may not further sub-license without express written consent from both the breeder and the primary licensor; provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. The register maintained under this Act shall reflect all valid assignments and licenses pertaining to a registered variety, ensuring transparency in ownership and exploitation.

A person claiming to be a breeder shall furnish proof of having engaged in breeding activities resulting in the development of a new plant variety, and such proof may include records maintained during the breeding process, testimonials from experts familiar with the developmental history, and evidence demonstrating distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability as per established protocols. However, any challenge to the veracity of said claim shall be adjudicated by the Tribunal, subject to an application filed within ninety days of notification of registration of the variety. The Tribunal may require additional evidence or expert testimony in such proceedings, and its decision shall be final except for appeals to the High Court on grounds of legal error. A breeder whose variety is found not substantially derived from a prior variety, despite claims to the contrary, may seek damages as provided herein, but only if it can demonstrate actual economic loss directly attributable to the erroneous determination.

A breeder desiring to commercially exploit a registered plant variety shall apply to the Registrar for a license, specifying the scope of permitted acts including propagation, sale and other forms of exploitation as provided herein. Any assignment of rights relating to such licensed variety requires prior written consent of the original breeder unless otherwise stipulated in the licensing agreement. Where a trade mark consists of or comprises a distinctive sign capable of identifying a plant variety, its use in connection with another variety shall be deemed an infringement of the breeder’s exclusive right, subject to principles of fair competition and consumer protection. The Registrar may refuse assignment if it prejudices the interests of farmers or hinders access to essential planting material. A breeder failing to adhere to licensing terms will be liable for revocation of license and associated penalties as determined by the Tribunal. Provided that, a farmer exercising rights under this Act shall not require any such consent for seed saving and exchange within established community practices.

A breeder aggrieved by the refusal of the Authority to register a plant variety based on novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days of the date of such refusal, providing detailed grounds for contesting the decision. Such appeal shall be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documentation submitted during the initial application process, including evidence demonstrating substantial derivation from a registered layout design if the variety incorporates features protected under any other applicable law relating to integrated circuits. The Appellate Board may, subject to reasonable notice to the Authority and any third parties who filed objections, request additional expert testimony or conduct independent verification of claimed characteristics. Provided that, failure by the breeder to demonstrate prima facie evidence supporting the grounds of appeal shall render the petition inadmissible, and a decision of the Appellate Board on such matter is final and binding. Any person claiming rights in opposition to the breeder’s claim may also submit representations to the Appellate Board during this process.

A certification trade mark shall denote a mark indicating that the goods or services in connection with which it is used possess qualities, characteristics or standards determined by the proprietor of the mark. The proprietor may be an individual, a body corporate, or any other entity capable of undertaking legal obligations and must ensure consistent assessment and verification of those qualities. No certification trade mark shall be refused registration if it is otherwise registrable under this Act and conforms to all applicable requirements regarding distinctiveness and lawful use. Subject to the provisions herein, the registrar may require evidence demonstrating the existence of a viable scheme for ensuring quality control relating to certified goods or services before granting registration. Any alteration to such a scheme must be promptly notified to the Trade Marks Registry.

A person seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, demonstrating that the applicant is authorized by the owner of the certification trade mark. The application shall include a statement detailing the standards and procedures governing the use of the mark, ensuring consistent quality or characteristics of goods or services certified thereby. Where a collective trade mark has been registered, any association of applicants may apply for registration of a corresponding certification trade mark to certify that goods or services originate from members who meet certain criteria. The Registrar shall examine the application and, subject to satisfaction of all requirements as provided herein, register the certification trade mark. Registration shall confer upon the owner the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to certified goods or services, preventing unauthorized usage by any other entity; however, such right is limited to ensuring adherence to the stated standards and does not constitute ownership over the underlying goods themselves.

A person claiming ownership of a certification trade mark shall submit an affidavit verifying their adherence to prescribed standards for certifying goods or services, and demonstrating control over the use of said mark by others. The Registrar may require further evidence establishing such control, including details of licensing agreements and quality assurance mechanisms. Any aggrieved party alleging misrepresentation concerning certified characteristics of goods or services bearing a registered certification trade mark may seek an injunction restraining such misrepresentation as provided herein. A collective trade mark association duly authorized to administer the certification trade mark shall be jointly liable with any licensee for damages resulting from false certification, unless it proves reasonable care was exercised to prevent such occurrence. The owner of a certification trade mark must publish annually a list of all registered users and details regarding quality control procedures. Failure to do so may result in suspension of registration subject to review by the Registrar. Remedies under this Act shall be available irrespective of any contract relating to the sale or distribution of certified goods.

A certification trade mark denoting conformity to specific standards may be registered under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained. An application for such registration shall clearly state the nature of the certification and the persons or classes of persons authorized to use the mark upon compliance with specified requirements. The Registrar shall, before accepting any application for a certification trade mark, satisfy himself as to the existence of an institution or body capable of effectively performing the functions of ensuring that goods or services conform to the certified standards. 

Where the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant meets all criteria and the proposed use will not be deceptive, registration may proceed. The owner of a registered certification trade mark shall maintain records demonstrating compliance by licensees with established quality control measures. Any aggrieved person may apply to the Appellate Board for redressal if they believe the standards are not being consistently upheld or that misuse is occurring; such application shall be made within ninety days of becoming aware of the alleged violation, and subject to payment of prescribed fees.

A certification trade mark applied for registration shall not resemble an existing trade mark and shall be distinctive, subject to the provisions contained herein. The applicant seeking registration of such mark shall demonstrate to the Registrar that they are competent to examine the goods or services certified and possess the necessary infrastructure for conducting said examination. Any body corporate applying as a certifier may be required to furnish proof of its legal standing and financial solvency. Where a certification trade mark is used in relation to agricultural produce, compliance with standards prescribed by relevant authorities shall be mandatory. The Registrar may, at any time, conduct an audit of the certifying entity to ensure adherence to established quality control procedures. Failure to maintain these procedures or repeated instances of inaccurate certification may result in revocation of the registered certification trade mark as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may file a complaint regarding misuse or improper application of such marks.

Any person claiming ownership of a certification trade mark shall submit an affidavit detailing the standards and procedures employed in certifying goods or services, failing which the application for registration may be rejected as provided herein. Where a registered proprietor of a certification trade mark fails to exercise reasonable diligence in maintaining those standards, any aggrieved party may apply to the Registrar for revocation of such registration. The Registrar, upon being satisfied that said standards are no longer consistently met, shall issue an order revoking the trade mark and publish it in the Journal. Any false representation regarding certification, including use of a deceptively similar mark, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or fine not exceeding two lakh rupees, or both. A court may also order seizure of incorrectly marked goods as directed under this Act.

A certification trade mark vested in an entity shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by the registering authority and consistent with ensuring continued public trust in the certified characteristics. Any transfer of rights relating to such a mark, whether absolute assignment or partial assignment of interests, requires prior written consent from said authority, demonstrating that the assignee possesses equivalent capacity to maintain certification standards. The register of trade marks shall reflect any approved assignments or licensed usage agreements. A licensee operating under an authorized arrangement may pursue remedies against infringers as if they were the owner, subject to limitations defined in the licensing contract and as provided herein. Failure to adhere to stipulated quality control measures by either assignor or assignee constitutes grounds for revocation of the certification trade mark. The registering authority shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all valid licenses granted concerning each registered certification trade mark, including duration and scope of permitted use.

A certification trade mark applied for shall not be refused registration if the applicant demonstrates to the Registrar that they are competent to examine the goods or services bearing the mark and ensure their standards conform to those certified. However, any objection under this Act relating to deceptive description of goods or services, or lack of distinctiveness, may still be raised and considered on its merits. Should a dispute arise regarding the veracity of certification claimed by the owner of such a trade mark, any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the Registrar for investigation; provided that such complaint is accompanied by prima facie evidence of misrepresentation. The decision of the Registrar shall be subject to appeal before the High Court having jurisdiction, and the appellant shall bear the onus of proving material error in the Registrar’s findings concerning quality control or standards verification as required herein.

Any person claiming ownership of a certification trade mark shall submit an affidavit detailing the standards and procedures applied for certifying goods or services, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to rejection as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any stage, require further clarification regarding said standards, and non-compliance with such request within thirty days shall constitute sufficient grounds for suspension of the certification trade mark’s registration. Any false representation concerning certification, or use of a substantially similar mark intending to deceive consumers about certified characteristics, shall attract a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees per violation. The manner applying registrar in cases of contested applications relating to standards will be determined by the Central Government through notification and such determination is final subject to judicial review. Repeated offences under this Act may result in cancellation of the certification trade mark registration.

A certification trade mark applied for registration shall not be refused solely on the grounds that it is not distinctive of any particular manufacturer, merchant, or trader. However, the Registrar may require evidence demonstrating legitimate use of such a mark to establish its distinctiveness as a symbol of quality, origin, or other characteristics. An appeal against refusal under this provision lies before the Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and filing within ninety days of the order. Furthermore, where a certification trade mark is used in relation to goods incorporating an integrated circuit demonstrating advanced technological features, proof of due diligence in preventing counterfeiting shall be considered during examination. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding such evidence may petition for review based on newly discovered facts or errors apparent on the face of the record. The Appellate Board’s decisions are final except where grounds for writ jurisdiction exist.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be taken as conclusive evidence of the proprietorship thereof and of the exclusive right to use the said trade mark subject to the provisions contained herein. However, such registration may be challenged on grounds including but not limited to a prior existing identical or deceptively similar trade mark, or where the registered trade mark is devoid of any distinctive character at the time of application. A collective trade mark, being a mark distinguishing goods or services of members of an association, shall confer rights only upon those authorized by the association and subject to its regulations as filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Any assignment of a registered trade mark requires written consent from the Registrar and adherence to prescribed procedures.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to renewal upon expiry of the initial registration period of ten years from the date of application, provided that an application for such renewal is presented to the Trade Marks Registry not earlier than one year and not later than six months before the expiration of the said period. The Registrar may, however, allow an extension of time for filing the application subject to payment of a late fee as prescribed in the Schedule. Where a trade mark has been registered in respect of particular goods or services, renewal shall extend to those goods or services only unless specifically amended during the renewal process. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of renewal may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such refusal. A falsely applied for trade mark registration is subject to rectification as provided herein. The register of trade marks shall be open to inspection, subject to payment of a prescribed fee.

A person who adopts a deceptive trade name or falsely represents a trade mark as being registered under this Act shall be liable to penalties as prescribed. Any aggrieved party may institute a suit for infringement of their trade mark, subject to providing proof of ownership and prior use relating to the goods or services specified in the registration certificate. Where a trade mark registered is used by a person not duly authorized, the owner thereof may seek an injunction restraining such unauthorized use, along with damages sustained due to said infringement. Provided that, no suit for rectification of the register shall be entertained unless filed within three years from the date of registration of the trade mark in question. The Court may, at its discretion, order delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark and award costs as deemed appropriate. A registered proprietor may assign their trade mark rights subject to any conditions specified in the instrument of assignment.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be deemed to be personal property and the proprietor thereof shall have the right to sue for its infringement. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to an instrument in writing, duly executed by both parties, and capable of being produced before a competent authority as evidence of transfer of ownership. Where a trade mark has been registered in the name of a person who is not the actual user, a caveat may be filed with the Trade Marks Registry outlining the circumstances and legitimate interests of the true proprietor. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all such caveats and shall notify the assignee or transferee of the registered trade mark of their existence prior to any transfer proceedings being completed. Provided that, failure to file a caveat shall not preclude a claim for rectification of the Register based on non-user or misrepresentation as provided herein. Any dispute regarding ownership of a trade mark registered under this Act may be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall vest in the proprietor thereof, subject to the provisions contained herein and any conditions specified in the register of trade marks. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules prescribed, requiring written instrument and intimation to the Trade Marks Registry within the stipulated timeframe. A person aggrieved by an incorrect association or disclaimer relating to a trade mark may apply to the Registrar for rectification; provided that such application is made within one year from the date of registration or other relevant act. The registrar may, after due inquiry and subject to payment of prescribed fees, direct amendment of the register accordingly. Use of a registered trade mark by a licensee shall be permissible only under terms consistent with quality control as stipulated in the licensing agreement; failure to maintain such control may constitute grounds for revocation of registration, as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership without proper intimation will render the subsequent assignee ineligible to claim rights associated with the trade mark.
