Any person who contravenes the provisions relating to assignment of a trade mark registered under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where any fraudulent act is committed with intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin or quality of goods bearing a trade mark registered as provided herein, such person shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Any application made knowingly containing false particulars relating to a trade mark registration shall render it void ab initio and subject the applicant to prosecution. The Registrar may, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, require additional evidence if satisfied that a registered trade mark is likely to cause confusion. Provided that any decision of the Registrar may be appealed before the High Court as prescribed. Any goods found bearing an illegally applied trade mark shall be seized and destroyed at the discretion of the appropriate authority.

Any assignment of a trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be specified in the instrument of assignment and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. A license granting rights in a registered trade mark may be granted for all or any of the goods for which the trade mark is registered, or for a specific region within India, provided that the terms of such license are consistent with maintaining control over the quality of goods bearing the trade mark. The assignee or licensee shall furnish to the Registry a copy of the assignment or licensing agreement within thirty days of its execution. Failure to do so may result in revocation of the registered trade mark, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing. Where an assignment involves transfer of goodwill, it shall be conclusive evidence of the validity of the trade mark registration unless successfully challenged on grounds existing prior to the assignment. Any dispute concerning royalty payments arising from a license agreement shall be resolved through arbitration as provided herein.

Any person claiming that a trade mark registered under this Act is likely to deceive or cause confusion, or is descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services concerned, may apply to the Appellate Board for revocation of such registration. Such application shall be made in writing and shall state the grounds upon which it is based, accompanied by supporting evidence as provided herein. The registered proprietor of the trade mark shall have an opportunity to file a counter-statement contesting the claim, and both parties may present evidence before the Appellate Board. Should the Appellate Board determine that the registration does not meet the requirements for validity, it may order its revocation, either in whole or in part. Any decision of the Appellate Board is subject to appeal to the High Court, provided such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the order. A trade mark registered deceptively shall be considered an infringement under this Act.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to renewal upon expiry of the initial registration period of ten years, and such renewal may be effected by application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The applicant shall demonstrate continued bona fide use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, failing which the renewal request may be disallowed. Safeguards prescribed register relating to associated rights, including but not limited to licensing agreements and assignments, must accompany any application for renewal where such arrangements are extant. Provided that, if a valid objection is raised concerning potential conflict with prior rights, the Registry may suspend processing of the renewal until resolution of said dispute as provided herein. Any alteration to the registered trade mark during renewal shall be treated as a separate registration process and subject to examination anew. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in cancellation of the trade mark.

Any assignment of a trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the assignor and the assignee, and evidenced in writing. Where an assignment includes a registered layout design subsisting in a semi-conductor integrated circuit, separate consideration for the layout design rights must be explicitly stated within the instrument of assignment; failing which, it shall be presumed that the transfer is inclusive of all associated intellectual property. The Registrar shall maintain a record of assignments and licenses pertaining to trade marks as provided herein. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, further license its rights to sub-licensees with the prior written consent of the owner of the trade mark. Any assignment or license not recorded within the prescribed period shall be deemed invalid against subsequent purchasers or licensees in good faith and without notice. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may grant security interests over their trademark rights.

A registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the owner exclusive rights to use the trade mark in respect of the goods or services for which it is registered and to prevent others from using identical or deceptively similar marks likely to cause confusion. The register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of ownership, subject to proof of due process having been followed during application and examination. A collective trade mark may be registered wherein the applicant identifies its members as being entitled to use the mark. Any assignment of a registration trade mark must be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective against third parties; provided that such assignment does not conflict with any existing legal restrictions or prior agreements. The Registrar may, where appropriate, require evidence of genuine use of the registered trade mark.

A person aggrieved by any infringement of a registration trade mark may institute a suit for recovery of damages. Such damages shall not exceed the amount suffered by the plaintiff as a result of the infringement, and may include loss of profits, or an account of profits made by the defendant due to the unlawful use. Where counterfeiting is proven, statutory damages up to a sum determined by the Court, but not less than five thousand rupees per counterfeit article, shall be awarded. 

Any order granting relief in such suit may also include an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement and an order for delivery up or destruction of infringing labels and packaging. A proprietor of a registered trade mark who suffers loss as a result of any act constituting passing off by another person, notwithstanding that no deception or cause of action for trade mark infringement exists, shall be entitled to damages subject to the limitations provided herein. The Court may, at its discretion, award costs in favour of the successful party.

Any person who falsely applies a registered trade mark, or any deceptively similar variation thereof, to goods intended for sale, shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such application includes affixing the registration trade mark to packaging, whether direct or indirect, and extends to digital representations offered for commercial purposes. Where a complaint is made alleging such falsification, the Registrar may, subject to verification of prima facie evidence, issue a cease and desist notice to the offender. Non-compliance with said notice within thirty days shall render the offender liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Furthermore, all goods bearing the falsely applied registration trade mark may be seized and destroyed as provided herein, and the costs of seizure and destruction borne by the offender. Any person abetting such offence shall also be deemed guilty under this Act.

Any assignment of a registration of a trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be agreed upon between the parties and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. A license, whether sole or otherwise, for the use of a registered trade mark may be granted by the proprietor thereof to another person, subject to provisions regarding quality control as the Central Government may prescribe. The instrument granting such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the license including duration, territory, and goods or services in respect of which the license is granted. Where a registered trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, notice of the assignment shall be sent to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days from the date of the assignment. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignment unenforceable as provided herein. Any dispute arising out of an assignment or licensing agreement relating to a registration trade mark shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person claiming ownership of a registration trade mark shall submit an affidavit detailing the first date of use and a representation of how the mark is used in commerce. An application for rectification of the register, alleging that such a trade mark was not in legitimate use prior to the opposition period, may be filed with the Registrar within one year from the publication of the advertisement accepting the registration. The Registrar shall, following due process including notice to the registered proprietor and opportunity for rebuttal, determine whether continuous user has been established as provided herein. Should the Registrar uphold the rectification application, the trade mark’s registration shall stand revoked prospectively, though any rights accrued prior to revocation remain unaffected subject to principles of equity. An appeal from the decision of the Registrar lies before the High Court, and such appeal must be lodged within sixty days of the order being communicated.

Any person claiming ownership of a registration trade mark shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement before a District Court having jurisdiction over the alleged offence. The proprietor of such a registration trade mark may, subject to the provisions contained herein, seek an injunction restraining any defendant from using the trade mark, or any deceptively similar variation thereof. Where an act constitutes both an infringement and an alleged offence under this Act, remedies available shall not be mutually exclusive; a court may grant relief in respect of either or both such claims. Any order for damages awarded to the proprietor shall account for actual loss suffered as well as potential profits lost due to the unauthorized use. Provided that, if the defendant proves they used the mark prior to the claimant’s registration and with honest intent, the Court may modify its decree accordingly. The Registrar may, upon application, direct rectification of the register where fraudulent or erroneous particulars are discovered concerning a registered trade mark.

The patent office shall be constituted as a department of the central government responsible for the administration of this Act and the grant of patents. It may establish branches and sub-offices at such places, as it deems necessary to facilitate access by applicants and the public. All applications for patents, along with any accompanying documents or fees, shall be filed with the patent office or its designated branch. The Controller of Patents, appointed under this Act, shall act as the head of the patent office and exercise all powers conferred upon him by virtue of this legislation. Any communication regarding a patent application or granted patent shall be addressed to and received at the official address of the patent office. Records maintained by the patent office shall be open for inspection subject to such rules as may be prescribed.

The application for registration of a design shall be made to the patent office in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain a statement of novelty, indicating how the features of the design are new or original compared to designs previously known. The applicant shall submit clear representations of the design from multiple perspectives, demonstrating its ornamental aspects. Upon receipt, the patent office will conduct a formal examination to ensure compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein. If satisfied, the controller may register the design and issue a certificate of registration. Subject to payment of the prescribed fee, such registration confers exclusive rights on the applicant for a period of ten years from the date of registration. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the patent office regarding refusal of registration may file an appeal before the designated appellate authority within the time frame stipulated.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, lodge a complaint with the patent office regarding any act constituting an infringement of a valid patent. The patent office shall, upon receipt of such complaint and after providing reasonable notice to the alleged infringer, conduct an inquiry into the matter. Where the patent office finds sufficient evidence of infringement, it may issue a cease and desist order directing the alleged infringer to immediately halt the infringing activity. Any person disaffected by an order of the patent office may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The patent office is further empowered to impose monetary penalties on infringers, commensurate with the extent of damage suffered by the patentee and calculated as provided in Schedule V. Provided that, no penalty shall exceed five lakh rupees. All fees collected pursuant to this provision shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. A register of complaints received and orders issued by the patent office shall be maintained and made available for public inspection.

The patent office shall maintain a public Register of Patents in which all patents granted under this Act, and applications for patents that have been published, are recorded. Any person may inspect such Register subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with conditions as may be determined by regulations. The Controller of Patents, acting as head of the patent office, shall ensure the accuracy and integrity of said Register, and is empowered to rectify any errors or omissions discovered therein. All communications with the patent office regarding applications, oppositions, or other matters pertaining to patents must be submitted in a prescribed format and accompanied by the appropriate fees. The Controller may require further information or documentation from an applicant or opponent as deemed necessary for proper examination of the case. Subject to provisions concerning confidentiality, records relating to proceedings before the patent office are open to inspection by interested parties. Any appeal against a decision of the Controller shall lie with the Appellate Board established under this Act.

The patent office shall maintain a public Register wherein all patents granted and applications for patents pending, are recorded accurately and contemporaneously. Any person desiring to inspect any document available at the patent office may do so subject to payment of such fee as may be prescribed by regulations. All communications directed to the patent office regarding an application must clearly indicate the application number assigned upon initial filing; failure to do so may result in processing delays. The Controller of Patents, acting on behalf of the patent office, may require applicants to amend their claims to ensure clarity and compliance with this Act. Provided that any such amendment does not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. All records maintained by the patent office shall be deemed official evidence for all purposes related to intellectual property rights under this Act, unless proven otherwise. The Controller may also establish a system for electronic filing and management of applications, subject to security protocols ensuring data integrity.

Any officer of the patent office who, having authority to examine an application for a patent, wilfully and with intent to cause delay rejects such application without reasonable grounds shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine, or with both. Should any person present to the patent office forged documents as part of a claim for inventorship, that person shall forfeit all rights relating to said invention and be liable to prosecution under the Indian Penal Code. The Controller of Patents, subject to directions issued by the Central Government, may establish regional offices of the patent office to facilitate access for applicants residing in remote areas. Any false representation made to obtain an expedited hearing before the patent office will attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. All records maintained by the patent office shall be deemed public documents and open to inspection as provided herein.

Any assignment of a patent application pending before the patent office shall be subject to the provisions contained herein, and no such assignment shall be valid unless it is in writing and duly executed by both the assignor and the assignee. The patent office may require submission of an instrument of transfer verifying the complete vesting of rights in the assignee, failing which processing of the application may be suspended. Where a license is granted to practice or use a patented invention, the terms of such license, including royalty rates and duration, shall be clearly stipulated in a written agreement filed with the patent office within thirty days of its execution. Any dispute arising from an assignment or licensing arrangement concerning a patent shall be subject to arbitration as provided herein, unless parties mutually agree upon another mode of resolution. The patentee remains responsible for ensuring continued payment of renewal fees even after valid assignment of the patent.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, file an appeal before the Appellate Board against any decision of the patent office refusing to grant a patent or revoking a patent. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to those specifically enumerated in the notice of refusal or revocation issued by the patent office and must demonstrate substantial question of law involved. Should the Appellate Board determine that no such substantial question exists, it may dismiss the appeal summarily with costs as deemed appropriate. Further, any party disputing an order of the patent office relating to amendment of a claim shall first seek rectification from the patent office itself; only upon failure of this recourse may they then petition the High Court having jurisdiction. The patent office shall maintain a detailed record of all appeals and rectifications received, alongside supporting documentation, for a period not less than ten years.

Any assignment of a patent application pending before the patent office shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, and shall not prejudice any rights accruing to the original applicant prior to the date of assignment. Where a person asserts that an act is about to be done which would constitute infringement of their valid patent, they may apply to the patent office for an interim injunction restraining such threatened infringement, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated and security as determined by the patent office is furnished. The assignee shall, within thirty days of the assignment’s execution, notify the patent office in writing, detailing the particulars of both assignor and assignee, along with a certified copy of the instrument of assignment. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the assignment unenforceable as provided herein. Licensing agreements relating to assigned patents remain valid subject to the terms of the original grant and any subsequent modifications agreed upon by all parties concerned.

Any aggrieved party may, within one month from the date of receipt of an application registration notice issued by the patent office relating to an invention which is alleged not to satisfy the requirements for grant of a patent as provided herein, file a petition contesting said registration with the Controller. Such petition shall clearly delineate the grounds upon which the applicant fails to meet the criteria established under this Act and must be accompanied by supporting evidence admissible in legal proceedings. The Controller shall, following due process including affording the applicant an opportunity to respond, issue a reasoned order either upholding or rejecting the challenge. An appeal from any decision of the Controller regarding such contestation may be preferred before the Appellate Board constituted for the purpose, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to timelines stipulated by rules made under this Act; provided that no appeal shall lie in cases where the grounds are frivolous or vexatious as determined by the Appellate Board.

The Patent Office shall be constituted as a statutory body responsible for the administration and enforcement of this Act, functioning under the central government. It may establish regional offices at such places as it deems necessary to facilitate access for applicants across the country. All applications for patents, including those relating to amendments or revocations, shall be filed with and processed by the Patent Office. The Controller of Patents, appointed by the central government, will head the office and exercise all powers conferred by this Act. Registration trade marks, while governed by a separate statute, may be considered as prior art during patent examination proceedings conducted by the Patent Office, subject to established legal principles regarding novelty and inventive step. Any fees prescribed under this Act shall be payable to the Patent Office.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to such conditions and payment of prescribed fees as may be determined by regulations, lodge a complaint with the Patent Office regarding improper refusal of an application for a pharmaceutical formulation where prior art cited by the Controller lacks sufficient public disclosure to render the claimed invention obvious. The Patent Office shall, upon receipt of such complaint and after affording opportunity of being heard to both parties, conduct a review of the decision within ninety days. If the Patent Office determines that the refusal was unwarranted, it may direct the Controller to reconsider the application. Provided that any direction issued under this Act shall not prejudice the right of the complainant to pursue other remedies available under law. The patent office’s determination is final and binding except in cases where an appeal lies before a designated appellate authority as provided herein. Any false representation made within a complaint submitted to the Patent Office will be subject to penalties, including fines up to five lakh rupees.

A semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to include a three-dimensional depiction of any layer of an active or passive device used in the manufacture of a semiconductor. The term ‘semiconductor’ as employed throughout this Act refers to materials having electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, typically silicon or germanium, and capable of exhibiting properties useful in electronic devices. Any combination of such materials forming a functional electronic circuit is also considered a semiconductor for the purposes of registration under this Act. A layout-design shall not be considered distinct if it represents only the regular repetition of a basic element necessary to achieve the functionality of the semiconductor, subject to demonstrable novelty as provided herein. The Registrar may request further clarification regarding material composition during examination.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein. The application shall disclose the fullest details of the layout-design including its topological features and dimensions, and demonstrate novelty and originality. A representation or drawing showing the layout-design shall be a necessary component of every such application. Where an applicant claims priority from an earlier application filed in a convention country, this must be stated within the prescribed period. Subject to verification by the Controller, registration will confer exclusive rights on the proprietor for a term of ten years from the date of filing. Any information submitted as part of the registration process shall be treated as confidential unless otherwise required under law or for purposes of examination. The controller may require an applicant to amend their application if it does not meet requirements.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an infringing semiconductor layout-design shall be liable to pay actual damages and any lost profits attributable to the infringement, subject to proof of such amounts by the registered proprietor. Where a defendant proves that they were unaware and had no reasonable grounds for believing that their actions constituted an infringement of a validly registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, the court may reduce the damages awarded accordingly, but shall not extinguish liability entirely. A registered proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement as provided herein. 

Notwithstanding any other provision, if the infringement is found to be willful, the court may increase the damages up to three times the actual damages and lost profits. Any person importing a semiconductor article embodying an infringing layout-design shall be deemed a party to the infringement and subject to these remedies. The burden of proving fair use or legitimate reverse engineering relating to a semiconductor shall rest upon the defendant.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the appropriate Office as provided herein, accompanied by the prescribed fee and all necessary documentation demonstrating originality. The applicant shall clearly delineate the scope of the layout-design, specifying its intended use within a finished article embodying the semiconductor. Subject to verification confirming that the layout-design is novel and involves inventive step, registration shall be granted. A registered proprietor may, during the period of validity of the registration, exercise exclusive rights in respect of the layout-design including the right to prevent any act of reproduction, communication or commercial exploitation without prior authorization. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning refusal of registration or revocation thereof may file an appeal with the designated authority within ninety days from the date of such order. The Office shall maintain a public register of all registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs accessible for inspection during office hours and subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as stipulated under this Act.

Any person exploiting a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall maintain accurate records as to the production and actual sales quantities of any article embodying such layout-design. Such records shall be open for inspection by an officer duly authorized under this Act, upon reasonable notice being given to the registrant. Provided that, access to confidential information relating to manufacturing processes or cost data may be restricted subject to a determination made by the said officer in consultation with the Controller of Patents and Designs. Failure to comply with record-keeping requirements as provided herein shall constitute grounds for revocation of registration, unless satisfactory cause is demonstrated within ninety days of notification of non-compliance. Any registered proprietor intending to assign rights relating to a semiconductor layout-design must furnish written notice thereof to the Controller, detailing the terms of assignment and particulars of the assignee. The controller may maintain a public register of such assignments.

Any person who fabricates a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design in violation of the exclusive right conferred under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such fabrication. Where any act is committed by a company, every person who at the time of the commission of the act was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the contravention and shall be liable for action accordingly unless they prove that the act was done without their knowledge or consent. Any semiconductor layout-design registered as provided herein, if commercially exploited without due authorization, constitutes an infringement actionable before a competent court. The court may, at its discretion, grant interim injunctions to prevent further exploitation and award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the registrant; however, such damages shall not be less than one lakh rupees. Any evidence obtained through reverse engineering of a registered semiconductor layout-design is inadmissible as proof of independent creation.

Any person being the proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall have the right to assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of all or any of the rights vested in such layout-design as provided herein. Such assignment or transfer shall be subject to a written instrument duly executed by both parties and registered with the appropriate authority designated for this purpose. Where a license is granted to another party for commercial exploitation of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, the terms and conditions governing royalty payments, duration, territory, and scope of use must be clearly stipulated in the licensing agreement. A licensee may not sub-license rights without express written consent from the proprietor; provided that such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Any dispute arising out of an assignment or license concerning a semiconductor layout-design shall be subject to arbitration as per the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. The registered owner remains entitled to pursue remedies for any infringement occurring despite a valid licensing arrangement.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor layout-design may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from the acts constituting such infringement, and the Court shall, subject to verification of the registry of the layout-design, grant such injunction if prima facie case is made out. However, any order granting an interim injunction shall not be valid for a period exceeding thirty days unless extended by further orders of the court following notice to the defendant. An appeal from any decision regarding such injunction shall lie before the Division Bench of the same High Court, provided that the appellant satisfies the court concerning substantial grounds for appealing. Where a registered semiconductor layout-design is used in the manufacture of an integrated circuit and commercial exploitation thereof occurs without authorization as provided herein, the aggrieved party may also claim damages not exceeding Rupees one crore. The burden of proving fair use or legitimate research shall rest upon the defendant.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a semiconductor layout-design may file an appeal with the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order. Such appeals shall be heard by a bench comprised of not less than two judges experienced in matters of technology and intellectual property, and the appellant shall demonstrate substantial grounds for disputing the finding that the proposed layout-design lacks novelty or is common knowledge. Provided that, where multiple applications relate to denominations of semiconductor layouts exhibiting only variety – differing solely in minor aesthetic features – the High Court may consolidate proceedings to determine a representative claim, subject to payment of additional fees as prescribed. The Registrar’s decision regarding denomination variety shall be considered prima facie evidence but not conclusive; furthermore, any finding of non-novelty based on prior art must be supported by clear and convincing evidence presented under this Act.

A semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to include all layers of the integrated circuit, irrespective of their order of creation and shall extend to features, patterns, masks, and any combination thereof intended for use in manufacturing a semiconductor product. Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter. Should the plaintiff forthwith fail to demonstrate reasonable grounds for their claim, the court may dismiss the application with costs. A layout-design is considered original if it has been generated through independent skill and ingenuity; however, mere aesthetic variations of existing designs do not qualify as originality as provided herein. The registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs.

Any person exploiting a registered semiconductor layout-design without the authorization of the proprietor shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. However, such liability shall not extend to acts done solely for private and non-commercial research, including experimentation relating to pharmaceutical substances where the integrated circuit is utilized in analytical equipment or process control systems integral to drug discovery. A registered proprietor may, subject to conditions prescribed by regulations, grant licenses authorizing others to exploit their layout-design. Any dispute regarding the validity of registration or infringement shall be adjudicated by the designated Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal following a summary procedure established for expeditious resolution. The Tribunal may issue injunctions restraining further exploitation and award damages commensurate with actual loss suffered or reasonable royalty, whichever is higher. Evidence presented before the Tribunal relating to manufacturing costs must include detailed breakdowns of semiconductor fabrication expenses. Any appeal from decisions of the Tribunal shall lie directly to the Supreme Court.

A Layout-Design is defined as the final three-dimensional arrangement of the electronic circuits wherein all layers of a semiconductor integrated circuit are included. Such a Layout-Design shall be eligible for registration under this Act provided it is original, and not previously published or exploited in any manner anywhere in India or elsewhere. The term ‘integrated circuit’ refers to those structures which are intended to perform an electronic function, capable of being mass produced, and having elements and interconnections essential for that function. Any Layout-Design substantially similar to a registered Layout-Design shall be considered infringing, subject to the provisions regarding permitted use as outlined herein. Registration confers upon the applicant exclusive rights in respect of the Layout-Design. The right extends to acts such as reproduction, communication to the public, sale and import.

Any person desiring registration of a Layout-Design shall submit an application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the appropriate fee as specified in Schedule I. The application shall include detailed drawings or representations of the Layout-Design, clearly indicating its constituent elements and dimensions, alongside a statement of originality. An applicant may also submit a description of the intended use of the Layout-Design, though this is not mandatory for registration purposes. 

Registration of a Layout-Design confers upon the applicant exclusive rights to reproduce, exploit, or commercially utilize said Layout-Design; however, such rights are subject to prior art and do not extend to the underlying semiconductor integrated circuit itself. A registered proprietor shall maintain a record of all licenses granted relating to the Layout-Design and may assign their registration as provided herein, with proper notification to the Registry. Failure to comply with these requirements may invalidate the registration or render it liable for revocation.

A person shall be entitled to register a Layout-Design if it is an original layout-design created by them. The right to a registered Layout-Design shall vest with the creator, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding assignment, transmission and licensing. Any act constituting infringement of such a right, including replication, distribution, or commercial exploitation of the Layout-Design without due authorization, shall be actionable under this Act. Where an unregistered Layout-Design is commercially exploited, remedies may be pursued based on principles of equity and good faith, provided that prompt action is taken upon discovery of such exploitation. 

The registered owner of a Layout-Design may grant licenses to others for its use, subject to mutually agreed terms and conditions. Any dispute arising from licensing agreements or alleged infringement shall be adjudicated by the designated authority as prescribed in this Act; however, interim relief, including injunctions, may be sought from any competent court. A ‘Layout-Design’ does not confer rights equivalent to a patent but provides exclusive rights specific to its topography.

A layout-design, being a final three-dimensional handling of elements and interconnections of integrated circuits, shall be distinct from the circuit’s functionality. Any person deriving a layout-design shall register it with the Intellectual Property Office as provided herein, subject to verification of novelty and originality; however, registration is not compulsory for claiming protection under this Act. The application for registration shall include detailed drawings or representations demonstrating the scale and interconnections within the layout-design. 

Where a registered layout-design is substantially similar to an earlier layout-design, irrespective of whether such earlier design is registered or unregistered, it may be deemed an infringement unless proven otherwise by the applicant. A person aggrieved by any act constituting an infringement of their registered layout-design may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for redressal, and the Board shall have the power to grant injunctions and award damages commensurate with the extent of the injury suffered. The term of protection for a registered layout-design is ten years from the date of filing, or until the circuit is commercially exploited, whichever occurs first.

A layout-design, being a three dimensional configuration of electronic circuits, shall be considered original if it demonstrates sufficient skill and judgment in its creation. Any person deriving commercial benefit from a registered layout-design must ensure strict compliance with licensing terms as stipulated by the owner, subject to provisions for fair use as determined by the appropriate authority. The registration of a layout-design does not confer any right independent of intellectual property rights existing under other applicable laws; however, it establishes a presumption of validity in cases of infringement. A person alleging infringement may seek interim injunctions pending final determination of the matter. Any confidential information disclosed during the process of licensing or transfer of a layout-design shall be protected and maintained as proprietary, provided that such confidentiality does not impede legitimate investigation by duly authorized officers under this Act. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties including monetary fines and revocation of registration.

Any person who, without the permission of the proprietor, commercially exploits a layout-design registered under this Act shall be liable to pay damages. Such damages shall not be less than five thousand rupees per layout-design infringed upon, or twice the amount of actual losses suffered by the proprietor due to such infringement, whichever is greater. Where commercial exploitation involves integrated circuits intended for mass production, the court may impose enhanced penalties up to ten lakh rupees per infringing unit. A person claiming ownership of a layout-design shall maintain accurate records demonstrating independent creation and first commercial exploitation within India, subject to verification as provided herein. Failure to demonstrate such provenance may be considered evidence of invalidity of the registered layout-design. Any act of aiding or abetting infringement is also punishable with similar penalties, and all infringing articles and materials used in the process are liable for confiscation.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a Layout-Design registered under this Act shall apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for a license if such commercial exploitation would constitute an infringement as provided herein. The application for license shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the proposed use, duration and geographical scope of the intended commercial exploitation, alongside reasonable royalty payments offered to the proprietor of the Layout-Design. Assignment of rights in a registered Layout-Design shall be subject to written agreement between the assignor and assignee, specifying all terms including but not limited to territorial limitations and exclusive or non-exclusive nature of the assignment. Where a Layout-Design incorporates a trade secret, such trade secret remains protected independently of the registration under this Act, and any disclosure thereof during license negotiation or exploitation shall be governed by applicable confidentiality agreements. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, subject to justifiable cause, reject an application for license if it deems the proposed royalty inadequate or the terms unfavorable to the Layout-Design proprietor.

Any person alleging infringement of a Layout-Design registered under this Act shall furnish to the High Court having jurisdiction, a statement detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and specific particulars of the registered Layout-Design relied upon as being infringed. The defendant may file a counter-statement denying such infringement or asserting invalidity of the registration of the Layout-Design, subject to providing evidence supporting said assertion within ninety days from service of the plaintiff’s statement. Where a claim of prior art is raised in the counter-statement, the burden shall lie on the defendant to demonstrate substantial similarity between the alleged infringing Layout-Design and existing publicly available information; however, mere functional necessity shall not constitute such prior art as provided herein. An appeal from any decision of the High Court regarding registration or infringement may be made to the Supreme Court within sixty days of the judgment. The court may also award costs in favour of the prevailing party.

A Layout-Design means an original design embodying all layers of a semiconductor integrated circuit, including channel stops, diffusion regions, oxide layers, metal interconnects and other features. Such a Layout-Design shall be distinct from the underlying functionality or performance characteristics of the integrated circuit itself; however, it may incorporate elements protectable as trade marks registered with the Trade Marks Registrar. Any person deriving commercial benefit from a Layout-Design must possess either ownership thereof or a license granted by the owner, subject to provisions concerning exhaustion of intellectual property rights as provided herein. Registration of a Layout-Design confers exclusive rights on the registrant for a period of ten years from the date of registration, renewable for subsequent terms. Any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation of a registered Layout-Design constitutes an infringement under this Act.

Any person desiring registration of a Layout-Design under this Act shall submit an application to the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated Circuits, in the prescribed form, together with the applicable fee. The application shall include detailed drawings or representations illustrating the Layout-Design for which protection is sought and a statement of its functionality. Subject to verification by the Registrar, and confirmation that the Layout-Design is novel and intrinsically capable of being distinguished from any other registered Layout-Design, registration shall be granted. Provided that, if an objection is raised regarding novelty, the applicant may submit evidence addressing such concerns within thirty days of notification. The register maintained by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated Circuits shall contain particulars of every registered Layout-Design, including the name and address of the proprietor, the date of registration, and a clear depiction of the Layout-Design itself. Any modification to a registered Layout-Design requires prior approval as provided herein, failing which protection may be revoked.

A layout-design, registered under this Act, shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially utilize the said layout-design. Such rights are subject to a term of ten years from the date of filing, or until expiry of a patent relating to any article embodying that layout-design, whichever is less. Any person desiring to use a registered layout-design for purposes not authorized by the proprietor may apply to the appropriate authority seeking a license under this Act; such application shall detail the intended use and proposed remuneration. Where a layout-design incorporates elements already protected by an existing patent, its registration herein does not prejudice the rights of the patent holder, provided that due consideration is given to principles of fair competition. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the offender liable for statutory damages as determined by the authority. The proprietor shall maintain accurate records relating to the layout-design and make them available for inspection upon reasonable request.

A semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design means an original creation pertaining to the three-dimensional disposition of electronic circuits on a semiconductor substrate or within it. The term ‘semiconductor’ shall include silicon, gallium arsenide, and other materials with electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, used in the manufacture of such circuits. A registered layout-design proprietor shall have exclusive rights in the making, selling, distributing, importing, or otherwise exploiting the layout-design as provided herein. Subject to provisions relating to licensing, no person may commercially exploit a registered layout-design without authorization from the registrant. Any act infringing these rights will be actionable under this Act and may attract both injunctive relief and monetary damages, assessed according to the loss suffered by the proprietor due to such infringement. The term of protection for any layout-design is ten years from the date of filing.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein. The application shall disclose the fullest details known to the applicant regarding the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its creation and essential characteristics. A representation or drawing of the semiconductor layout-design must also accompany the application, clearly illustrating all layers constituting the design. 

Registration shall vest in the applicant unless it is established that another person has a prior claim, subject to verification by the Controller. The controller may require an affidavit confirming originality and first creation within India. A registered layout-design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially utilize the semiconductor integrated circuit embodying such design for a period of ten years from the date of filing the application, unless otherwise determined under this Act.

Any person making an application for registration of a semiconductor layout-design shall furnish with it such information and statement as may be prescribed. The registered proprietor of a semiconductor layout-design shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, or import articles embodying such layout-design; provided that such rights are subject to limitations regarding national emergency or public interest as determined by the appropriate authority. Any person who infringes this right shall be liable for actual damages and may also be subject to injunctive relief restraining further infringement. 

Where a semiconductor integrated circuit is manufactured using an illegally copied layout-design, customs officials may seize such articles at any port of entry. The owner of a registered semiconductor layout-design may apply to the court for an order directing the destruction or disposal of infringing articles. Any appeal under this Act shall lie before the High Court and must be filed within ninety days from the date of the decision appealed against, unless otherwise provided herein.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein. The application shall disclose all essential features of the layout-design including its topological arrangement and dimensions, and must clearly identify the semiconductor material utilized in its fabrication. A representation, being a graphical depiction of the layout-design, shall also be furnished with such application; said representation may be in black and white or colour as deemed appropriate by the applicant. 

Where an applicant claims priority from an earlier application filed in a convention country, details thereof including the filing date and country must be stated within the prescribed period. The Controller, upon examination of the application and finding it to be complete and compliant with the provisions of this Act, shall register the layout-design subject to verification of novelty and originality; however, registration may be refused if the layout-design is found to be plagiarized or lacking in distinctive character. Any registered semiconductor layout-design shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights as stipulated herein.

Any person exploiting a semiconductor layout-design commercially without due authorization shall be liable to legal proceedings as provided herein. A registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall have exclusive rights in respect of that layout-design insofar as it is embodied in a semiconductor article or an article incorporating such a semiconductor. Subject to the provisions relating to licensing, no person shall manufacture, sell, distribute, import or otherwise commercially exploit any semiconductor embodying a registered layout-design without obtaining a license from the registered proprietor. Provided that reverse engineering solely for experimental purposes and not for commercial gain is permissible, but all derived designs must be demonstrably distinct. Any dispute regarding alleged infringement of rights in a semiconductor layout-design shall be subject to adjudication by the designated authority established under this Act, and evidence of substantial similarity will be considered prima facie proof of infringement unless rebutted. Compliance with registration requirements is mandatory for asserting these rights.

Any person who, without the permission of the registered proprietor or duly authorized licensee, manufactures, imports, sells, hires, distributes, or otherwise exploits a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. The term “semiconductor” includes any material with electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, commonly used in the fabrication of integrated circuits. Where such exploitation is undertaken commercially, the penalty shall not be less than ten lakh rupees, and may extend to five crore rupees, or three times the amount of actual damages suffered by the proprietor, whichever is greater. Any goods infringing this Act, along with all materials and instruments used in the manufacture thereof, shall be deemed forfeited to the Government. Subject to an application made to the appropriate court, a decree of prohibitory injunction may also be issued restraining further infringement, and any person dealing with such infringing goods knowing them to be so manufactured or imported shall be liable for contributory infringement.

Any registered proprietor of a semiconductor layout-design shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit commercially, distribute, or import articles embodying such layout-design, subject to the provisions contained herein. Assignment of all rights relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be made by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties and filed with the appropriate authority as prescribed. A license granted under this Act shall be construed as a contract between the licensor and licensee, specifying the scope of use, duration, territory, and royalty payable; provided that such licenses must not contravene any mandatory provisions of this Act concerning national policy or public interest. Where a semiconductor layout-design is created jointly, ownership shall vest equally in all creators unless otherwise agreed in writing prior to creation. Any transfer of rights relating to a registered semiconductor layout-design without due execution and filing of the instrument as provided herein shall be considered null and void. The appropriate authority may maintain a public register of assignments and licenses for transparency.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor layout-design shall first serve a notice of intention to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing with reasonable specificity the nature of the asserted claim and identifying the specific integrated circuit wherein the protected layout-design is embodied. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of service, submit a counter-notice demonstrating either invalidity of the registration or non-infringement through prior art or independent development, the aggrieved party may then initiate proceedings before the High Court having jurisdiction. However, provided that such counter-notice contains a reasonable offer of license, the court may direct mediation as an initial step toward amicable resolution. A registered proprietor failing to diligently pursue litigation following receipt of a valid infringement notice shall be estopped from seeking injunctive relief after six months, subject to demonstrable excusable delay. Appeals from any order of the High Court concerning registration or infringement shall lie before the Supreme Court.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from a semiconductor layout-design registered under this Act shall be entitled to an exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, or import articles embodying that layout-design. Subject to the provisions herein, where a person makes, sells, offers for sale, distributes, imports or otherwise commercially exploits a semiconductor integrated circuit in respect of which a validly subsisting registration exists, such act shall constitute infringement. The registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings in a competent court for relief against any infringer, including an injunction restraining further acts of infringement and recovery of damages. A grant patent relating to the fabrication process used in creating the semiconductor does not negate rights established under this Act; however, exploitation of the layout-design must remain within the scope of the registered right. Provided that, if a person proves legitimate prior use of the layout-design before registration, such use shall not be considered infringement, subject to verification by the appropriate authority as provided herein. Any assignment or transfer of rights relating to a semiconductor layout-design shall be in writing and duly recorded.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. The application must disclose the fullest details of the layout-design, including its topological characteristics, and demonstrate sufficient novelty and inventive step relative to existing semiconductor technologies. Where a layout-design is substantially similar to one previously registered or publicly known, registration may be refused under this Act. 

However, where an applicant seeks protection for a layout-design incorporating elements protected by a valid patent, evidence of such patent ownership must accompany the application; failure to do so shall not invalidate the layout-design registration itself but may affect its enforceability against the patent holder. The Controller shall examine each application and, subject to satisfying all requirements as provided herein, grant a certificate of registration. Registered layout-designs shall be valid for ten years from the date of filing or until expiration of any applicable patent term covering incorporated elements, whichever is shorter.

Any person exploiting a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design commercially shall ensure strict adherence to the conditions stipulated herein regarding registration and permissible duration. A registered proprietor of a layout-design may assign, transfer or license all or any of their rights under this Act, subject to notification to the appropriate authority and compliance with prescribed fees. Where a copy translation work is undertaken involving said layout-design for purposes beyond private study or research, explicit authorization from the registered proprietor shall be mandatory; failure to obtain such authorization constitutes infringement as provided herein. The scope of protection afforded to a semiconductor integrated circuit extends only to the original layout-design itself and does not confer any right in respect of the underlying circuitry or functionality. Any reverse engineering undertaken must conform strictly with the limitations detailed within these regulations, and shall be subject to inspection upon reasonable request by authorized officers. A person aggrieved by any act contravening this Act may seek redressal through established judicial processes.

A compulsory licence shall be granted to a person who intends to make or sell copies of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, subject to the provisions contained herein. Such application for a compulsory license may be made to the designated authority where the owner of the copyright has refused to grant a reasonable licence on mutually agreed terms. Provided that such refusal is not based on legitimate grounds including but not limited to non-exploitation of the work. The applicant shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the authority, an adequate need for making copies and that such use will not be prejudicial to the interests of the copyright owner or unduly diminish the market for their work. Any royalty fixed by the authority shall be payable as a condition precedent to the exercise of rights under this compulsory licence.

Any person intending to reproduce a substantial portion of a published literary or dramatic work for creating accessible formats for persons with visual impairment shall register their intention with the designated National Registry maintained by the Controller of Copyrights. Such registration shall be subject to verification of the applicant’s status as an organisation dedicated to serving persons with disability, and confirmation that commercial exploitation is not the primary objective. Where a copyright owner unreasonably refuses permission for such reproduction despite reasonable notice and offer of remuneration, or fails to respond within sixty days of receiving said notice, a compulsory licence shall be deemed to have been granted under this Act. The Registry may, following due process as provided herein, determine fair and equitable terms for the royalty payable by the applicant to the copyright owner, considering prevailing market rates and the non-commercial nature of the undertaking. Failure to register prior to reproduction will render such act a violation of copyright.

Any author or publisher aggrieved by an unauthorized reproduction of their work, notwithstanding any other remedy available under this Act, may petition the High Court for relief against such infringement. Where a determination is made that a significant portion of the copyrighted material has been reproduced without authorization and causes demonstrable harm to the rights holder’s commercial interests, the court may grant injunctive relief restraining further reproduction or distribution. However, subject to certain conditions being met, including proof of diligent efforts to obtain a voluntary license from the copyright owner, the Court shall have power to impose a compulsory licence upon terms it deems just and equitable. The royalty rate fixed under such compulsory licence shall reflect comparable market rates for similar works, and payment shall be made into an escrow account pending final determination of amounts due. Provided that this remedy is not available where the infringement relates solely to fair dealing as provided herein or criticism and review.

A person desiring to make use of a copyrighted work in circumstances where obtaining voluntary consent from the owner is unreasonably withheld or unavailable shall have recourse to an application for compulsory licence as provided herein. Such application, addressed to the designated authority within the Central Government, shall clearly demonstrate both diligent effort made to secure a license on mutually agreeable terms and the nature of the intended use, specifying whether it be reproduction, communication to the public, or adaptation. The applicant shall further furnish a statement detailing the proposed remuneration commensurate with the exploitation of the work, subject to review by the authority. Where the application concerns a musical work or literary work, consideration will also be given to any existing statutory licence provisions relating to broadcasting and such like. A compulsory licence granted under this Act shall not prejudice the right of the copyright owner to receive fair compensation, determined in accordance with established principles of valuation. Provided that, if the applicant fails to utilise the license within a period of two years from the date of grant, the authority may revoke said license.

A compulsory license shall be granted to any entity intending to reproduce a cinematograph film, sound recording or literary work where such reproduction is for purposes of education or research, provided that the applicant demonstrates a reasonable effort to obtain a voluntary licence from the copyright holder on mutually agreeable terms but has been unsuccessful. The application for such compulsory licence shall include detailed particulars of the intended use, including the estimated number of copies and the proposed distribution method. Any royalty payable under this provision shall be determined by the High Court, subject to considerations of prevailing market rates and the nature of the utilization. Where a work is translated into an Indian language, a further compulsory license may be issued for reproduction in that language, provided it serves a demonstrable public benefit and does not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the copyright owner as provided herein.

Any person demonstrating substantial public need and inability to obtain a voluntary license from the copyright holder shall be eligible to petition the High Court for a compulsory licence pertaining to any published literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, excluding cinematograph films. The petitioner shall demonstrate diligent efforts made to secure a license on reasonable terms, evidenced by written correspondence maintained for no less than six months prior to filing such petition. Should the court determine that a compelling case exists, it may grant a compulsory licence subject to payment of adequate remuneration as fixed by the Court and periodically reviewed. Failure to remit said remuneration within ninety days of its due date shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. Any work reproduced under this provision must clearly indicate the source and copyright owner; contravention thereof invites penalties as provided herein.

A person desiring to utilise a copyrighted literary or dramatic work, musical composition, or sound recording—not being an adaptation by way of translation—shall submit a petition to the designated authority seeking a compulsory licence where such work has been fixed in any tangible medium other than a cinematograph film. The application shall detail the intended use and demonstrate that reasonable efforts have been made to obtain a voluntary license from the copyright holder on mutually agreeable terms, which attempts must be documented and submitted with the petition. Should the designated authority determine that sufficient grounds exist and that the proposed utilisation does not prejudice the legitimate interests of the owner, it may grant a compulsory licence subject to payment of an equitable royalty as determined by the authority. Any dispute regarding such royalty shall be adjudicated through established civil procedures. Assignment of rights conferred under this compulsory license is permissible only with prior written consent from the copyright holder and the designated authority; however, sublicensing remains strictly prohibited.

Any aggrieved party alleging infringement of their copyrighted work shall first serve a notice of intent to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing the nature of the infringement and demanding immediate cessation thereof, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, where such notice fails to elicit a satisfactory response within sixty days, or where the alleged infringer demonstrates undue delay in negotiating a voluntary license, the aggrieved party may petition the High Court for an order directing the grant of a compulsory licence. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating reasonable efforts made to secure a voluntary license and proof that the work is not readily available to the public. Provided that, if the copyright holder establishes legitimate grounds for withholding permission—including but not limited to ongoing negotiations for a fair licensing agreement—the Court may dismiss the petition or impose conditions on the compulsory licence granted, ensuring equitable remuneration to the owner. Any order issued under this Act shall be appealable to the Supreme Court.

A compulsory license shall be granted where an application is made to the High Court demonstrating reasonable grounds for belief that works protected under this Act are unavailable to the public at large despite diligent efforts. Any such application relating to a sound recording, cinematograph film or literary work subject to an India application must demonstrate prior negotiation with the copyright holder in good faith and a clear indication of proposed remuneration consistent with prevailing market rates. The Court may, if satisfied that the conditions for grant are met, direct the Registrar of Copyrights to issue a license upon such terms as it deems fit, including royalty payments and duration. Provided that no compulsory licence shall be granted unless the applicant undertakes to make the work available to persons with disabilities at no additional cost beyond standard access fees. The copyright holder may appeal any decision regarding the grant of a compulsory license before the designated appellate authority within sixty days of the order’s issuance, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

A compulsory license shall be granted for the production or sale of copyrighted works embodying a geographical indication registered under the Geographical Indications Act, 1999, provided that such work is primarily directed at making the indicated goods available to persons residing within the geographically demarcated region associated with said indication. Any application for a compulsory licence as provided herein must demonstrate reasonable efforts made by the applicant to obtain a voluntary license from the copyright holder on comparable terms and conditions. The Central Government may, subject to payment of adequate remuneration determined in accordance with rules prescribed under this Act, grant such license if it is satisfied that the copyright owner has unreasonably refused or failed to negotiate a voluntary licence. Any licensee granted permission under these provisions shall ensure strict adherence to quality control standards established for the relevant geographical indication and shall submit periodic reports verifying compliance. Failure to do so may result in revocation of the compulsory licence.

Any owner of copyright in a literary or musical work shall be liable to grant a compulsory license to any person desiring to make copies thereof for purposes authorized under this Act, provided that such person demonstrates a genuine need and offers remuneration as determined by the District Court having jurisdiction. Failure to comply with an order issued by said court regarding terms of access or royalty payments shall constitute contempt, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine extending to five lakh rupees, or both. Subject to the provisions herein, any aggrieved party may initiate proceedings before the District Court seeking enforcement of rights relating to compulsory licenses and associated remuneration. The court may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party and direct specific performance of obligations arising from such license. Any false claim made in support of an application for a compulsory licence shall render the applicant liable to prosecution under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright in a sound recording shall, prior to initiating proceedings before a competent court, furnish proof of registration with the Central Government as evidence of ownership; however, failure to provide such proof shall not *ipso facto* bar consideration of their claim but may be considered by the Court when assessing credibility. Where a request for a compulsory licence pertaining to a musical work or sound recording is made under this Act, and the copyright owner fails to respond within sixty days from receipt of said request with reasonable terms, an application may be filed with the designated authority seeking adjudication on appropriate royalty rates. Any determination rendered by that authority shall be binding on all parties subject to appeal before the High Court; provided that such appeal must commence within ninety days of the order’s issuance and demonstrate substantial grounds for review regarding either procedural fairness or quantum of remuneration. The aggrieved party may seek interim relief pending final adjudication, but only upon demonstrating irreparable harm.

The Trade Marks Registry established under this Act shall function as a central authority for the administration of trade marks throughout India. The registry may, subject to rules made thereunder, maintain a register of all registered trade marks, including details relating to ownership, renewal dates, and any recorded assignments or transmissions. Any person desiring to apply for registration of a trade mark shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as stipulated in Schedule I. The registry is empowered to examine such applications and determine their acceptability based on criteria outlined herein, including distinctiveness and potential conflict with existing marks. All official communications regarding any matter pertaining to a registered trade mark shall be addressed to and processed through the Trade Marks Registry.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, categorized according to the Nice Classification as adopted from time to time. Any person claiming ownership of a trade mark may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for its registration, furnishing details regarding use, proposed goods or services, and a clear representation of the mark. Upon receipt of an application, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine it for compliance with provisions herein and conduct a search for prior conflicting marks. Where an objection is raised, the applicant may file a response within the stipulated period; otherwise, the application shall be deemed abandoned. Subject to satisfactory examination and acceptance, notice of the proposed registration will be advertised in the Journal. Any person desiring to oppose the registration may file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry within four months from such advertisement.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks lawfully used in India, and any person aggrieved by an incorrect entry therein may apply to the Registry for rectification. Any application for registration filed with the Trade Marks Registry must adhere strictly to the prescribed forms and fees as detailed in the relevant rules. The Registrar of Trade Marks, acting on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry, possesses the authority to examine each application and determine its acceptability based on established criteria regarding distinctiveness and potential conflict with existing marks. Should an objection be raised by the Examiner, the applicant shall have a defined period to submit evidence or arguments in support of their claim. A proprietor whose trade mark is registered may initiate legal proceedings for infringement before any competent court, subject to fulfilling all procedural requirements as provided herein. The Registry reserves the right to suspend or revoke registration under certain circumstances, including non-renewal of fees or proven fraudulent application. Any appeal against a decision of the Trade Marks Registry shall lie with the High Court having jurisdiction.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect the register may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in writing specifying the class or classes of trade marks they wish to examine. The Trade Marks Registry may, if satisfied as to the bona fide nature of the application, permit access to the register and copies of entries therein. All applications for registration shall be examined by an officer of the Trade Marks Registry who shall ascertain whether the mark meets the requirements of this Act and is not likely to cause confusion with existing marks. Where a mark is found registrable, notice of acceptance shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed time limit, which shall then be adjudicated upon by the Registry according to established procedure, ensuring due process for all parties concerned. The Controller of Trade Marks possesses ultimate authority regarding registration decisions.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, ensuring accuracy and accessibility to interested parties subject to prescribed fees. Any person intending to apply for registration of a trade mark shall conduct a search within the records of the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain whether any identical or deceptively similar mark already exists; failure to do so does not, however, automatically invalidate an application but may be considered during examination. All correspondence with the Trade Marks Registry must include a valid postal address and contact details for service of notices. The Registrar of Trade Marks may require additional evidence or clarification from applicants regarding the use and distinctiveness of their marks as provided herein. Any amendment to an application after acceptance, affecting its substance, shall be subject to re-examination by the Trade Marks Registry. All records maintained by the Trade Marks Registry are deemed public documents, available for inspection during office hours upon payment of a specified fee.

Any person who falsifies any entry in a register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, or knowingly makes a false representation to an officer of the said registry, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct rectification of any incorrect entry discovered upon inspection of its records. Any application for registration found to contain deliberately misleading information, and submitted despite knowledge of its falsity, shall be deemed void ab initio, and the applicant barred from submitting further applications for a period of two years. Provided that, an honest mistake regarding a material fact may be rectified by amendment within one month of discovery, subject to payment of a prescribed fee.
