All records maintained by the Trade Marks Registry are open to inspection during office hours by any person paying the specified fees, but sensitive information relating to applicant addresses shall remain confidential.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to an application being made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The applicant for registration of such assignment shall furnish proof of title demonstrating lawful ownership of the mark prior to the date of assignment, and any transfer instrument must clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to geographical limitations or restrictions on use within specific classes of goods or services. Where an assignment is made subject to a condition requiring future consideration, such condition shall be disclosed to the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar may require evidence satisfactory to it regarding fulfillment of any outstanding conditions prior to effecting complete transfer in its records. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, with the consent of the proprietor and compliance with procedures as provided herein, apply for registration of assignment of the license itself; however, such registration does not confer ownership but merely establishes a record of the licensed rights. Failure to register an assignment or license shall not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of an Assistant Controller of Trade Marks may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all appeals filed and their respective statuses, accessible for public inspection during office hours. Provided that any application for extension of time for filing an appeal shall be considered only upon demonstration of sufficient cause and payment of applicable fees as determined by the Appellate Board. Furthermore, should the Appellate Board deem the initial decision manifestly erroneous or based on a misinterpretation of established principles under this Act, it may direct the Trade Marks Registry to rectify its records accordingly and award costs against the party found to have acted improperly. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding except where review is permissible under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect the register may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in writing specifying the particulars of the trade mark or class of trade marks sought to be inspected. Upon receipt of a valid application and requisite fees, the Trade Marks Registry shall permit inspection at such time and place as it deems fit. Should any applicant allege infringement of a registered trade mark, that plaintiff forthwith furnish to the Trade Marks Registry documentary evidence substantiating the claim of ownership and prior use. The Registrar may, subject to rules made under this Act, require additional information or clarification from either party before proceeding with an investigation into such allegations. All decisions of the Trade Marks Registry regarding applications for registration or objections thereto shall be communicated in writing to the applicant or objector, as the case may be.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, ensuring accurate record-keeping and public accessibility as provided herein. Any person seeking registration must submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry accompanied by the prescribed fee and a clear representation of the mark. Examination by the registry will determine if the proposed mark meets requirements regarding distinctiveness and conflicts with existing marks. Where an applicant demonstrates prior art establishing use of a similar mark, or holds a patent granted used relating to goods or services covered by the application, the Trade Marks Registry may require further evidence substantiating claims of legitimate differentiation. Subject to satisfactory examination and acceptance, the registry shall publish notice of allowance, after which opposition proceedings may be initiated. Failure to comply with timelines set forth by the Trade Marks Registry will result in abandonment of the application.

In this Act, "digital preservation copy" shall mean a complete and unaltered reproduction of a copyrighted work in a digital format, created solely for the purpose of archival storage as prescribed by the National Archives. Such copies may be made from any lawfully acquired original or authorized derivative work. Provided that, the creation of a digital preservation copy does not confer any ownership rights to the copy’s creator beyond those already vested under this Act. The format and technical specifications for these copies shall be determined and periodically updated by regulations published by the Ministry of Culture, ensuring long-term accessibility and integrity subject to reasonable technological advancements. Any access to such preserved works shall adhere to existing copyright restrictions as provided herein.

Any work capable of being copyrighted under this Act shall be subject to registration with the Registrar of Copyrights in order to establish a conclusive presumption of ownership and date of creation. The application for such registration shall be made in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. Where a work is jointly authored, all authors must execute or authorize the execution of the application. Provided that, if any author refuses or fails to do so, the remaining author(s) may proceed with the application subject to furnishing an affidavit explaining such refusal or failure and undertaking responsibility for ensuring compliance with rights pertaining to all contributors. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of copyrighted works as prescribed, accessible for inspection during office hours, and issue a certificate of registration upon successful completion of the process. Failure to register does not invalidate copyright but affects evidentiary weight.

Any person aggrieved by the unauthorized reproduction of a work in which copyright subsists, as provided herein, may institute a suit for injunction restraining such infringement. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all suits arising under this Act relating to copyright. Where a plaintiff proves that an act constitutes an infringement of copyright, the court may grant relief including damages or account of profits, at the option of the plaintiff. The amount of damages awarded shall be determined having regard to the nature and extent of the infringement, and any benefit accruing to the defendant by reason of such infringement. 

The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a register of copyrights, and all entries therein shall be *prescribed* in accordance with rules made under this Act. Any person desiring to obtain copyright in a work shall submit an application to the Registrar in the form so *prescribed*, accompanied by the necessary fee. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the registration invalid or subject to revocation, and no rights shall accrue until proper registration is effected as per the rules.

The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a Register of Works in which particulars of all published works and artistic works shall be entered subject to the provisions herein. Any person claiming copyright in a work, or intending to become the owner thereof by virtue of any assignment or license, may apply for registration of such work in the manner prescribed. The application shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed and must include a true copy of the work being registered. Where a work is jointly authored, the application shall identify all authors and their respective shares in the copyright subject to proof satisfactory to the Registrar. A certificate of registration shall be issued upon successful completion of verification procedures and confirmation that the work satisfies the criteria as provided herein; however, such registration shall not be construed as evidence of validity of copyright. The Register maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection by any person on payment of a fee prescribed.

Any application for registration of a copyright in a cinematograph film shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the particulars of all musical works and sound recordings incorporated therein, as prescribed. The applicant shall furnish a certificate from each composer, lyricist, and owner of sound recording confirming their no-objection to the inclusion of such work within the cinematograph film and authorizing its use for the purposes described in the application. Where any such certificate is absent or incomplete, the Registrar may require further evidence or reject the application subject to providing a reasoned order. All fees associated with registration shall be paid as prescribed through designated payment gateways only. Any failure to comply with these requirements within thirty days of notification from the Registrar will render the application liable for rejection and no rights shall accrue under this Act until full compliance is demonstrated. The Registrar may, however, extend this period at their discretion if sufficient cause is shown.

Any person dealing in cinematographic films as prescribed by the Central Government shall maintain accurate records of all transactions relating to such films, including details of licensing and distribution agreements. Failure to comply with this requirement shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. Where an offence involves continuing contravention, a further daily fine of two thousand rupees may be imposed until the default is rectified. Any evidence obtained through inspection conducted under the authority of this Act shall be admissible in any legal proceedings as conclusive proof, subject to verification by a designated officer. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe additional procedures for record-keeping and auditing to ensure effective enforcement of these provisions. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. Any person aggrieved by an order imposing a penalty may appeal to the High Court within thirty days.

Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor or duly authorized agent. Where the owner of copyright is a legal person, such instrument shall be executed by a person authorised to bind that entity and shall bear its official seal or equivalent authentication. The terms of any license granted under this Act concerning exclusive rights relating to adaptation, reproduction, distribution, or public performance may, subject to provisions herein, prescribe royalty rates, duration, territorial scope, and permissible uses. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of such prescribed terms shall be resolved through arbitration as mutually agreed upon by the parties; provided that failure to agree on an arbitral forum will vest jurisdiction in the District Court having local jurisdiction. A licensee may assign their rights under a license only with prior written consent of the copyright owner, unless otherwise specifically permitted within the licensing agreement itself. All assignments and licenses shall be registered with the Registrar of Copyrights to be effective against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Competent Authority refusing grant of a compulsory license under this Act may file an appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial injury resulting directly from the refusal and deposits with the High Court a sum equivalent to the royalty as prescribed for such work. The High Court shall, after examining evidence submitted by both parties and considering any objections raised regarding the valuation of the work or the appropriateness of the prescribed royalty rate, issue its decision within one hundred and eighty days. Should the appellant succeed in their appeal, the Licensing Competent Authority shall reconsider the application subject to the directions issued by the High Court; however, failure to deposit the aforementioned sum shall render the appeal inadmissible. Any further appeals from the decisions of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court as provided herein.

Any assignment of copyright in respect of works created under a government contract shall be subject to the prior written consent of the commissioning authority, and such consent may be granted upon terms as prescribed. Where an inventor seeks to assign their rights in a patentable invention arising from said work to a third party, they shall furnish a statement detailing the nature of the government contract and the extent of any retained interest therein. A registered patent agent acting on behalf of either the inventor or assignee shall ensure full disclosure of this contractual obligation prior to completing the assignment. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment voidable at the option of the commissioning authority, provided that such authority demonstrates a material prejudice resulting from the non-disclosure. Licensing agreements relating to such works shall similarly be subject to review and approval as prescribed, ensuring equitable access and preventing exploitation contrary to public policy. The terms of any such license or assignment must clearly delineate the scope of permitted use and duration.

Any person claiming copyright in a work embodying a new invention, whether wholly or partially created within the territory of India, shall register such work with the Copyright Office as prescribed. The application for registration shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the inventive concept and supporting documentation demonstrating originality. Where an applicant asserts that the work represents a significant advancement over prior art, they shall furnish evidence establishing the novelty and non-obviousness thereof. Registration is not mandatory for copyright to subsist but serves as prima facie evidence of ownership and date of creation. The Copyright Office may, subject to verification of submitted materials and compliance with these regulations, grant a certificate of registration. Failure to adhere to the prescribed format or provide accurate information may result in rejection of the application; however, such rejection shall not affect any rights already accrued under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “author” shall denote the person who creates the work, and includes, in relation to a cinematograph film, the producer. Where a work is created by multiple persons jointly, those persons shall be considered co-authors, and ownership vests equally amongst them subject to any agreement to the contrary evidenced in writing. An author need not necessarily be a natural person; where a legal entity creates a work as part of its business operations, that entity may be deemed the author under this Act. However, authorship is contingent upon originality, and works derived substantially from pre-existing material without sufficient independent skill or judgment shall not qualify for protection as provided herein. The determination of authorship remains subject to proof of creation and intent.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, and subject to the provisions herein contained regarding ownership of copyright, the term “author” shall denote the natural person who creates the work. Where a work is created by multiple persons jointly, those persons shall be considered co-authors, and the register of copyrights shall reflect all such authorship proportionately as determined by their respective contributions to the final creation. In cases where a work is generated through computer means, or is an automated process resulting in original expression, the person causing the work to be created shall be deemed the author, provided that such person exercises creative control over the generation of said work. Any claim regarding authorship must be substantiated with evidence demonstrating originality and intent at the time of creation, as determined by the registering authority. The register may require a declaration from all claiming authors affirming their contribution.

The author of a work shall be deemed to include the person undertaking the arrangements necessary for the creation of a cinematograph film, subject to provisions relating to producers as defined herein. Where a sound recording is made, the producer thereof shall be considered an author with respect to such recording, provided that any pre-existing work incorporated within the sound recording retains its original authorship. Any person who commissions a photograph or portrait under a contract of service shall not be deemed the author, unless expressly agreed upon in writing and subject to proof of substantial creative contribution beyond mere direction. An author aggrieved by an infringement of their copyright may apply to the District Court for injunctive relief and damages, as provided herein, demonstrating both ownership and the nature of the infringing act. Rights conferred on an author are personal property rights and shall be transferable by assignment or testamentary disposition; however, any transfer must be in writing and signed by the author or their duly authorized agent.

For the purposes of this Act, the determination of authorship shall vest with the individual recognized as the creator of the original work, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a work is created by multiple individuals jointly, such individuals shall be considered co-authors and their respective contributions may be documented for clarity regarding rights assignment, as provided in regulations established by the Central Government. In cases where a work is generated through employment, the employer shall, unless otherwise agreed in writing, be deemed to be the first owner of copyright therein; however, the actual author remains the originator of the intellectual creation. 

Provided that, if an individual creates a work during the course of their employment but utilizing resources wholly independent of the employer, authorship and subsequent rights may vest with said individual following due process established by competent authority. Any dispute regarding authorship shall be subject to investigation and resolution through prescribed mechanisms ensuring fairness and transparency. The author retains moral rights in relation to the work even after assignment of economic rights.

The determination of authorship shall vest with the individual recognized as the creator of the original work, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a work is created by multiple individuals collaboratively, such individuals shall be considered joint authors and their respective contributions must be demonstrably distinct; failing which, proof of equal creative control will suffice for establishing co-authorship. An author may assign their copyright through a written instrument duly executed before two or more witnesses. However, any assignment made without full disclosure of material facts relating to the work’s creation shall be voidable at the option of the assignee. Where authorship is claimed on behalf of a corporation, the individual demonstrably responsible for its creative direction shall be deemed the author for purposes of this Act. Provided that, moral rights remain vested in the original author irrespective of any assignment or transfer of copyright. Any dispute regarding attribution of authorship may be adjudicated by a competent court.

Any person claiming to be the author of a work shall furnish to the Registrar of Copyrights a declaration affirming such authorship and detailing the nature of their contribution. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence establishing authorship, as determined by the Registrar, may result in rejection of the copyright application. Where multiple individuals contribute to a work, jointly authored under this Act, each contributor shall be considered an author with proportionate rights subject to any agreement amongst them defining respective shares. Any false declaration regarding authorship constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, provided that reasonable cause is shown, initiate investigations into claims of disputed authorship and impose penalties on those found to have misrepresented their status as author. All records pertaining to such determinations shall be maintained confidentially.

The author of a copyrightable work shall be deemed the first owner of all rights therein, subject to provisions concerning works made under contract of service or apprenticeship as provided herein. Where an individual creates a work pursuant to a contract for services with another person, and consideration is paid for such creation, the ownership of copyright may vest in that other person unless otherwise agreed in writing; however, such agreement shall not prejudice the author’s right to be identified with the work. Any assignment of copyright interest must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, specifying clearly the rights assigned and the duration of the assignment. A license granted under this Act may be exclusive, limited to specific territories or media, or non-exclusive, as determined by mutual agreement between the author and licensee. The author retains the right to revoke a non-exclusive license upon providing reasonable notice to the licensee, subject to any ongoing obligations stipulated in the licensing agreement.

The determination of authorship shall, in cases where a work is computer-generated, vest with the person who causes the work to be generated, subject to proof of substantial direction and control over the creation process. However, an appeal has been lodged contesting this provision wherein it is alleged that mere initiation of a generative artificial intelligence system does not constitute sufficient ‘direction’ as envisioned by this Act; rather, demonstrable creative input influencing the final output must be established. It is further provided herein that where multiple persons contribute to such direction and control, authorship shall be jointly held proportionate to their respective contributions, assessed through evidence presented before the adjudicating authority. Any dispute regarding the quantum of contribution shall be subject to review, and the burden of proof lies with the claimant asserting a greater share in the authorial rights. The aggrieved party may petition for re-evaluation if new evidence emerges demonstrating altered levels of creative input.

The author of a work shall be deemed to include the person who creates the work. Where a work is created by multiple persons collaboratively, such persons shall jointly be considered the authors, subject to an agreement amongst them determining respective shares in copyright ownership as provided herein. If any contribution attributable geographically originates from outside India, but results in a unique and original work first published within Indian territory, the author or authors of that contributing element retain rights under international conventions adopted by India, while the publisher within India acquires rights pertaining to publication and distribution subject to remittance agreements. Any person claiming authorship must demonstrate sufficient creative input; mere mechanical assistance shall not constitute authorship. An employer commissioning a work from an employee may acquire copyright ownership through contract, provided that such transfer does not prejudice the author’s moral rights as defined under this Act. Failure to properly attribute authorship where required constitutes infringement and renders the infringing party liable for statutory damages.

A copyright society may be formed by authors, or other right holders, including their assignees, for the collective administration of their rights, and such society shall operate on a non-profit basis. The central government may, upon application made to it in this behalf, register a copyright society if it is satisfied that the objects of the society are likely to be beneficial to the interests of authors and right holders. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a registered copyright society may grant licenses consistent with the provisions of this Act, collect royalties, distribute such royalties amongst its members as per agreed terms or determined by an independent auditor, and take necessary steps to prevent infringement of copyright. Any person aggrieved by any decision of a copyright society may apply for redressal to the High Court.

Any person intending to establish a copyright society for the collective administration of rights in literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works may apply to the Central Government in the prescribed form for registration as a copyright society. Such application shall be accompanied by detailed information regarding the aims and objectives of the proposed society, its membership structure, and the categories of works it intends to administer. The applicant shall also submit audited financial statements demonstrating sufficient capital and resources to effectively manage rights and distribute royalties. Registration shall be granted only if the Central Government is satisfied that the copyright society will operate in the interests of authors and owners of copyright, subject to such conditions as may be specified. A registered copyright society may enter into agreements with users of copyrighted works for licensing and collection of fees, provided that these agreements are consistent with the provisions of this Act and do not unduly restrict access to creative content. The register of copyright societies shall be maintained by the Central Government and open for public inspection.

Any author, composer or other person having an interest in any right comprised in the copyright of a work may become a member of a copyright society established under this Act, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. A copyright society shall grant licenses consistent with the provisions of this Act, enabling multiple users to access copyrighted works upon remittance of appropriate royalties. Should a copyright owner object to the inclusion of their work within the repertoire of a copyright society, they shall have the right to withdraw said work, providing not less than sixty days’ written notice to the society. Any dispute concerning royalty rates determined by a copyright society may be subject to judicial review; provided that such application for review is made within ninety days from the date of notification of the rate. The society shall maintain accurate records of all licenses granted and royalties collected, which records shall be open to inspection as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the society liable to penalties, including revocation of its registration.

Any person intending to establish a copyright society for the collective administration of rights in literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works may apply to the Central Government in the prescribed manner setting forth particulars as to its aims and objects, composition, area of operation and financial resources. The application shall be accompanied by a draft memorandum of association and rules and regulations governing the functioning of the proposed copyright society. Upon receipt of such application, the Central Government may, after making such inquiry as it deems fit, register the copyright society if it is satisfied that the applicant fulfils all requirements as provided herein. A registered copyright society shall act on behalf of its members in licensing their rights and collecting royalties for the use of their works, subject to terms and conditions determined by the society itself but consistent with this Act. The funds collected by a copyright society shall be distributed amongst its members after deducting administrative expenses, according to predetermined rules ensuring equitable distribution based on usage data. Any dispute regarding such distribution may be resolved through internal grievance redressal mechanisms established within the society.

Any group of authors or other right holders intending to administer copyright and related rights collectively may form a copyright society subject to the conditions as provided herein. Application for registration as a copyright society shall be made to the Central Government, demonstrating sufficient membership representing significant interests in the relevant class or classes of works. The application must detail the proposed rules governing royalty distribution among members, ensuring transparency and equitable remuneration proportionate to usage. A registered copyright society may grant licenses authorising the public performance, reproduction, communication to the public, or any other act restricted by this Act. Such licensing shall be non-discriminatory and based on mutually agreed terms, but subject to oversight to prevent abuse of dominant position. The society’s accounts shall be audited annually by a qualified accountant and open for inspection as directed by the Central Government, ensuring compliance with financial regulations. Failure to adhere to these provisions may result in suspension or revocation of registration.

Any copyright society established under this Act failing to comply with the regulations framed as provided herein regarding transparent accounting of royalties collected from licensees, or failing to distribute such royalties to right holders within ninety days of receipt, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Should a copyright society repeatedly fail to furnish audited accounts for inspection by authorized officers, it may be subject to suspension of its registration for a period not exceeding one year. Furthermore, any officer of the copyright society found complicit in fraudulent manipulation of royalty payments or misrepresentation of collected amounts shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Central Government may, after due inquiry and opportunity afforded to the concerned copyright society, direct its dissolution if it is determined that the society has persistently acted against the interests of right holders or in violation of this Act.

Any author, composer or other person having exclusive right of control over a work may assign all or any of his rights under this Act to a copyright society duly registered as per the regulations established herein. Such an assignment shall be effected through a written instrument specifying clearly the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, communication to the public and adaptation. A copyright society receiving such assignments may grant licenses to users subject to terms and conditions determined by it, ensuring equitable remuneration to right holders as stipulated in the regulations. Provided that any license granted shall be non-exclusive unless expressly stated otherwise in the assignment or agreement between the author and the society. The copyright society shall maintain a register of all works assigned to it and furnish copies thereof upon request to interested parties subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any dispute regarding royalty payments or licensing terms may be resolved through arbitration as provided for within the regulations governing such societies.

Any author, composer or other person having an interest in any right comprised in the copyright of a work may become a member of a copyright society established under this Act, provided that such membership is subject to the rules and regulations of said society. Should a dispute arise concerning the refusal of membership by a copyright society, the aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court, setting forth grounds demonstrating compliance with all applicable criteria and lack of arbitrary exclusion. The High Court shall consider evidence presented by both parties and may direct the copyright society to admit the applicant as a member if satisfied that such direction is warranted under the provisions herein. Furthermore, any royalty collected by a copyright society shall be disbursed transparently amongst right holders according to pre-determined distribution rules, and failure to do so constitutes grounds for legal action before the appropriate court. Any appeal against High Court orders lies with the Supreme Court.

Any author, composer or other person having exclusive right of control over a work may become a member of a copyright society duly registered under this Act, subject to adherence to its bylaws regarding licensing and collection of royalties. A copyright owner desiring to assign rights in their work to such a society shall execute an assignment agreement detailing the scope of permitted uses, including but not limited to reproduction, communication to the public, and adaptation. Such agreements may provide for cross-border exploitation consistent with principles established under international treaties like the Patent Cooperation Treaty concerning reciprocal recognition of intellectual property rights. Where an author assigns exclusive rights, the copyright society shall maintain a publicly accessible register of such assignments, specifying duration and territorial limitations. Any dispute regarding royalty rates or assignment validity shall be subject to arbitration as provided herein, and societies may establish internal mechanisms for expeditious resolution; however, members retain the right to seek judicial review. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor.

A copyright society established under this Act may collect royalties and distribute them to right holders for the public performance or communication to the public of works protected by copyright, subject to regulations prescribed by the Central Government. Such societies shall operate on a non-profit basis and maintain transparent accounting practices regarding collected funds. Where a patented article is incorporated into a copyrighted work—for example, a machine embodying a patented invention used in creating a cinematograph film—the rights holder of the copyright shall not be prejudiced by the patentee’s right to prevent the making or use of said patented article independently of the copyrighted work; however, licensing terms for both may be negotiated separately. Any dispute regarding royalty distribution or membership within a copyright society shall be resolved through established grievance redressal mechanisms as provided herein.

Any person intending to establish a copyright society for the collective administration of rights in literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works shall apply to the Central Government in the prescribed manner, furnishing proof of its constitution and rules relating to membership, management, and financial operations. The application shall also detail the categories of works the society proposes to administer and the scale of fees proposed for licenses issued by it. A copyright society seeking registration must demonstrate a clear use mark relation between itself and the rights holders whose work it intends to represent, establishing that such representation is authorized through written agreements. Subject to verification of these details and satisfaction that the society operates in the public interest, the Central Government may register the copyright society. Registration shall be valid for five years unless revoked due to non-compliance with regulations as provided herein or upon application for voluntary dissolution.

A trade mark shall be considered a well-known trade mark as provided herein if, through promotional activity and widespread recognition amongst the relevant public, it has achieved a significant reputation in India. The determination of whether a mark qualifies as well-known shall include consideration of factors such as the extent of use of the mark, the duration of its use, the extent of any publicity relating to the trade mark, and the claims made by the proprietor concerning the goods or services associated with it. A registered trade mark is not a prerequisite for recognition as a well-known trade mark; however, registration may be persuasive evidence in establishing such status. Subject to provisions regarding dilution, the owner of a well-known trade mark shall have rights in rem and may seek remedies even against identical marks used on non-competing goods or services if such use is likely to cause confusion or diminish its distinctive character.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be a well-known trade mark if, through extensive use and promotion, it has become recognizable to the relevant public as identifying goods or services connected with the applicant. Determination of such recognition may consider factors including the extent of geographical reach of publicity, consumer awareness surveys conducted by recognized organizations, and evidence of unsolicited media coverage. A mark registered for a limited class of goods or services may still be considered well-known in relation to other non-similar goods or services if it possesses inherent distinctive character and substantial reputation. However, such extended recognition shall not automatically confer rights beyond the scope of registration unless dilution is proven as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to established procedures, maintain a register of well-known marks for enhanced protection against infringement and unfair competition. Any person alleging well-known status bears the burden of proof.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall not be infringed by the use of an identical or similar sign for dissimilar goods or services where no likelihood of confusion exists, provided that such use takes place in different classes of goods or services as classified according to the Nice Classification. However, where a trade mark is a well-known trade mark, and another entity uses an identical or similar sign even for dissimilar goods or services, the owner of the well-known trade mark may seek remedies under this Act irrespective of the absence of likelihood of confusion. Such remedies shall include injunctions restraining further use and damages for loss suffered due to dilution of its distinctive character. The court, in determining whether a mark is well-known, may consider factors including the extent of recognition amongst the relevant public and any instances of unauthorized use having resulted in damage to reputation. A proprietor failing to reasonably enforce rights against infringing use shall not be entitled to remedies as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be well-known within the meaning of this Act if, through extensive use and promotion, it has become recognizable to a substantial segment of the relevant public as identifying particular goods or services. Determination of whether a mark qualifies as well-known may consider factors including the extent of any unsolicited media coverage relating to the trade mark, actual sales figures demonstrated by evidence filed with the Trade Marks Registry, investment in advertising and promotional activities, and duration of use. However, mere registration of a trade mark, even if longstanding, shall not *per se* constitute proof of well-known status; such recognition must be established through demonstrable public awareness. 

A proprietor of a well-known trade mark is entitled to restraining orders against the unauthorized use of identical or similar marks, irrespective of whether those goods or services are directly competitive, provided that such use would likely cause confusion or dilution of the distinctive character of the well-known mark. Any aggrieved party may apply for relief as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be considered a well-known trade mark under this Act if it has become recognised by the relevant public as identifying goods or services connected with a particular person. Determination of such recognition may consider the extent of use of the mark, duration of use, and the extent to which others have taken unfair advantage of, or are likely to take unfair advantage of, its reputation. A trade mark registered in one jurisdiction may also be recognised as well-known within India, subject to proof of reputation here. Notwithstanding registration of another party’s similar mark, a proprietor of a well-known trade mark is entitled to restraining orders against use of the later mark that is likely to cause confusion or dilution. However, such remedies shall not apply where the subsequent user demonstrates legitimate and continuous use prior to the date on which the earlier mark became well-known in relation to those goods or services. Any action taken under this provision must be proportionate to the potential harm caused.

Any person who uses a trade mark that is likely to cause confusion, or is deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be liable to an action for infringement under this Act. However, where a trade mark has been established as a well-known trade mark, even use in relation to dissimilar goods or services may constitute infringement, provided that such use takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to the distinctive character or repute of the well-known trade mark. A proprietor of a registered trade mark may seek an injunction restraining any such unauthorized use and also claim damages for loss suffered as a result thereof. Any person contravening this provision shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both; and all goods infringing upon the rights conferred herein shall be deemed forfeited property. The Court may, subject to applicable rules, order destruction of such counterfeit goods.

Any assignment or licensing of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties concerned, provided that any license granted must not diminish the inherent reputation of the trade mark itself. Where a trade mark is recognised as a well-known trade mark under this Act, the proprietor thereof shall have recourse to remedies against any use by another party which is likely to cause confusion or dilution of distinctiveness, even in respect of dissimilar goods or services. Assignment of rights relating to a well-known trade mark requires prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry and may be subject to conditions ensuring continued quality control. Furthermore, licenses pertaining to such marks shall explicitly define the scope of permitted use, geographical limitations, and duration, with provisions for revocation upon breach of these terms. The reputation of a well-known trade mark extends beyond its specific class of goods or services and is protectable as an asset in itself. Any assignment failing to meet these requirements may be deemed void at the discretion of the adjudicating officer.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall not be deemed to be infringed merely by reason of its use in connection with goods identical with those for which it is registered, if such use is necessary to describe the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of those goods. However, an allegation of dilution may arise where a later mark, even for dissimilar goods, erodes the distinctive character of a well-known trade mark, irrespective of any likelihood of confusion. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing protection to their mark as a well-known trade mark may appeal to the High Court; such appeals shall be heard expeditiously and subject to established rules of evidence. The Registrar may, prior to registration of a conflicting mark, require an undertaking from the applicant that they will not use it in a manner likely to cause dilution or misrepresentation concerning the reputation associated with any existing well-known trade mark as determined under this Act.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be well-known within the meaning of this Act if, through extensive use and promotion, it has become recognizable by a significant portion of the relevant public as identifying the goods or services of one undertaking. The Registrar may, upon application supported by evidence demonstrating such recognition, declare a mark to be well-known, even absent registration under this Act. However, any declaration shall be subject to proof that use of the mark does not likely cause confusion amongst consumers. Where a registered user exists with consent from the proprietor of a well-known trade mark, and allegations of infringement are made by a third party, the Registrar may direct proceedings against both the proprietor and such registered user jointly. Any appeal arising from a decision regarding ‘well-known’ status or registered user liability shall lie before the Appellate Board as provided herein, with timelines for filing set forth in the rules.

A geographical indication shall identify goods originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. Such identification may extend to qualities relating to the climate, soil, flora, fauna and traditional practices associated with that region, provided that these factors demonstrably contribute to the unique attributes of the good. Where a product possesses characteristics fundamentally linked to its geographical provenance, it shall be considered eligible for registration as a geographical indication under this Act. The reputation enjoyed by goods bearing such an indication must be genuine and not misleadingly created or promoted; any claim regarding origin shall be verifiable through established documentation and practices. A registered geographical indication confers upon the producers within that area exclusive rights to utilize the indication in relation to their products, subject to adherence to specified standards of quality and production methods as prescribed by the Board.

A geographical indication shall, for the purposes of registration under this Act, denote an indication which identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. An application for registration as a geographical indication may be filed by any association of producers, artisans or persons engaged in the production of goods corresponding to the geographical indication. The applicant shall demonstrate proof of continuous use of the geographical indication for at least five years preceding the date of application and provide a detailed description of the characteristics linking the good to its geographical origin. Provided that where such a geographical indication is protected in the country of origin through legislation, evidence of such protection shall be sufficient proof of reputation. Registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered.

A registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to institute civil proceedings for infringement before a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing act has occurred. Any person dealing in goods with a false representation of a geographical indication, or employing deceptive packaging indicating a connection with a registered geographical indication, may be subject to an injunction restraining such acts and damages not exceeding Rupees Five Lakhs as determined by the court. Provided that, if the infringement is shown to be wilful, the Court may also award enhanced damages up to Rupees Ten Lakhs. 

A collective body representing producers of goods associated with a geographical indication shall, subject to rules made under this Act, have standing to represent the interests of its members in any legal proceedings relating to that geographical indication. The court may, as provided herein, order the destruction or forfeiture of infringing goods and materials used in the commission of the offence. A geographical indication shall be infringed when material possession, display for sale, or offering for sale constitutes a false application of said indication.

A geographical indication shall, for the purposes of this Act, denote an indication which identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application and subject to verification of prescribed criteria relating to specificity and traditional knowledge associated with the goods, register a geographical indication in respect of such goods. Provided that no registration shall be granted if the indicated quality or reputation is generic or customary in the trade concerned. Any association of producers, artisans or individuals engaged in the production of goods identified by a geographical indication may apply for its registration. The application shall include details regarding the area of origin, methods of production and standards maintained to ensure consistent quality. A registered geographical indication shall be protected against unfair competition including acts likely to mislead consumers as to the true origin of the goods, as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication may apply to the appropriate court for redressal.

A geographical indication shall be subject to registration under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates a clear link between the goods and the geographical area of origin. Such linkage must be evidenced by reputation or quality attributable to said place. Where a collective body seeks registration on behalf of producers, it shall furnish proof of its legal authority to represent those producers and their adherence to established rules concerning production methods and quality control. Any alteration to these methods, impacting the characteristics uniquely associated with the geographical indication, requires prior notification to the Registry and may be subject to review. The Register of Geographical Indications maintained under this Act shall contain details of authorized users, specifications for the goods, and the defined geographical area. Failure to comply with conditions regarding use or quality standards as stipulated in the register may result in revocation of registration, subject to due process outlined herein.

A geographical indication shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and any person who uses a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not originating from the territory associated with such indication commits an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that where the use is made bona fide and for the purpose of identifying the origin of the goods, no such offence shall be deemed to have been committed. Any false application for registration of a geographical indication, including misrepresentation of origin, shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, subject to an inquiry conducted as provided herein, direct rectification of the register in cases of fraudulent or erroneous entries concerning a geographical indication and impose costs on the offending party. Any appeal against such direction shall lie before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of order.

A geographical indication, being an indication referring to a place and the goods which originate from that place, may be licensed by the registered proprietor to applicants fulfilling such conditions as may be prescribed. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the scope of permitted use, including territorial limitations and quality standards pertaining to the goods bearing the geographical indication. The registrar may maintain a public register of all licenses recorded, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Assignment of any right in a registered geographical indication shall be effected only through a written instrument duly executed by both parties and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry. Provided that no assignment shall prejudice the rights of existing licensees unless their consent is obtained or alternative arrangements are agreed upon as provided herein. The proprietor may revoke a license for cause, following due process and affording reasonable opportunity to be heard; however, such revocation shall not affect contracts entered into prior to notice of termination.

A geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be registered for goods originating from a specific region within India and possessing qualities or reputation attributable to that origin. Any person claiming ownership of a geographical indication may apply for registration with the Registrar, furnishing detailed evidence establishing the link between the goods, their characteristics, and the specified geographical area. An application shall not be accepted if it is proven, through demonstrable evidence presented by an opposing party, that the claimed geographical indication lacks distinctiveness or is generic in nature. Where a dispute arises concerning the authenticity of origin or the quality standards associated with a registered geographical indication, any aggrieved party may file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for errors apparent on the face of the record, and may include directions regarding corrective action or revocation of registration. Provided that, failure to adhere to prescribed standards of quality may render a registrant liable to penalties as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall signify an indication referring to a place in India, a specific region or locality in India, from which goods originate and whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in accordance with the provisions of this Act, the registrar shall register such geographical indications subject to fulfilling the criteria as laid down herein. Provided that a geographical indication shall not be registered if it includes scandalous or deceptive matter, or is contrary to public order or morality. The application for registration shall include a statement detailing the characteristics linked to place and how those characteristics are essential to the goods’ identity. Any person claiming rights over a geographical indication may apply for its registration as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall, for the purposes of registration under this Act, identify goods originating from a specific geographical area where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. An application for registration seeking protection as a geographical indication must include a clear and concise definition of the geographical area with demarcated boundaries, alongside a detailed specification outlining the qualities or characteristics linked to that origin. Where an applicant seeks international registration prescribed by the Madrid Protocol, compliance with all requirements of this Act is mandatory prior to filing such request through the International Bureau. The Register shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and associated specifications, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration affecting the defined geographical area or good specification requires formal amendment duly recorded in the Register.

A geographical indication shall, for the purposes of this Act, denote an indication which identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and in accordance with existing law concerning unfair competition. An application for registration claiming a geographical indication as defined herein may be converted into an international application under the 73 convention application procedure if filed within six months from the date of filing the initial Indian application, subject to payment of requisite fees and compliance with regulations prescribed by the Registrar. The Registrar shall examine such conversion requests and determine their validity based on adherence to established timelines and procedural requirements as provided herein. Where a geographical indication is registered, no person other than an authorised user shall use it in relation to goods for which it is registered or any deceptively similar depiction thereof. Any contravention of this provision shall be actionable under the remedies specified within this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a sound recording shall mean the recording of sounds, irrespective of the medium on which such sounds are embodied or the method by which they are recorded. A ‘performer’ in relation to a sound recording means the primary vocalist or musician whose performance is fixed in the sound recording; provided that where a sound recording includes the performances of more than one performer, all such performers shall be deemed to be performers in relation to that sound recording. The rights conferred by this Act in respect of a sound recording are subject to any existing contractual obligations between the owner of copyright in the sound recording and the performer or performers featured therein. Any broadcast of a sound recording requires prior authorization from the copyright holder, as provided herein.

A sound recording shall be deemed to include any method of storing sounds, whether fixed on tangible medium such as tape, disc, or other physical format, or embodied electronically or otherwise. Registration of copyright in a sound recording under this Act is permissible for the producer thereof, being the person who causes the sound recording to be made; provided that where a work has been produced by virtue of employment under a contract of service, the employer shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein subject to the terms of such contract. The application for registration must include particulars relating to the publisher and composer of any musical or literary work incorporated within the sound recording, as provided herein. Any transfer of rights in a sound recording shall be documented and submitted with an amended registration statement. Failure to accurately disclose relevant information may invalidate the registration.

The owner of copyright in a sound recording shall have the exclusive right to make any other sound recording that incorporates it. Any person who, without obtaining a license from the copyright owner, performs the sound recording in public, or communicates the sound recording to the public by any means including digital transmission, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. However, such performance or communication may be permitted subject to terms and conditions determined by the licensing body established under this Act. 

Where a sound recording is made of a published literary or dramatic work, the owner of copyright in that work shall be entitled to receive royalties as prescribed. The rights conferred by virtue of ownership in a sound recording are distinct from those subsisting in any underlying musical or literary work; accordingly, separate licenses may be required for each. A producer of a sound recording shall be deemed to have sufficient interest to bring an infringement action relating to the sound recording itself.

A sound recording shall be defined as any disc, tape, perforated roll, or other device in which sounds are embodied so as to be capable of being reproduced therefrom. The owner of such a sound recording is deemed to be the producer thereof, and shall have all rights conferred by this Act, subject to contractual obligations existing at the time of production. Any person who performs the musical work incorporated within a sound recording may request royalty payments from the producer, as provided herein, and disputes regarding equitable remuneration shall be adjudicated by a competent court. 

Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, the first owner of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be the producer; and in relation to a sound recording, such ownership vests until assignment or expiry of term. A performer’s right in respect of their performance featured in a sound recording is distinct from the copyright in the work itself, but both are protectable under this Act. Any unauthorized duplication or distribution of a sound recording constitutes an infringement.

Any person who undertakes the making of a sound recording shall ensure that all necessary permissions have been obtained from the owners of copyright in the underlying musical work or works and the literary work, if any, incorporated therein, prior to such undertaking. A producer of a sound recording may, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise rights independent of the owner of copyright in the underlying work, including the right to equitable remuneration for broadcasting and public performance. However, where a sound recording is made without such permissions, it shall be deemed an infringing copy and liable to seizure as provided herein. The term ‘sound recording’ includes any method by which sounds are captured or reproduced, whether directly or indirectly, and encompasses both analogue and digital formats. Compliance with royalty rates fixed by the licensing body for mechanical rights relating to musical works is mandatory for continued lawful production and distribution of such sound recordings.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite licenses as provided herein, engages in the commercial exploitation of a sound recording shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The unauthorized duplication of any sound recording for purposes of sale or distribution constitutes prima facie evidence of such commercial exploitation and shifts the burden of proof onto the accused to demonstrate lawful authorization. Furthermore, any instrumentality used in the making of an infringing sound recording, including but not limited to mixing consoles and digital audio workstations, shall be liable to seizure by a Magistrate First Class. A copyright owner may initiate proceedings for recovery of damages sustained due to such infringement, which shall include actual losses suffered as well as statutory damages not less than five thousand rupees per infringing unit. Provided that, legitimate licensees operating under compulsory license provisions are excluded from the ambit of this prohibition.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a sound recording shall obtain a license from the owner of both the copyright in the musical work incorporated therein and the copyright in the sound recording itself. An assignment of rights in a sound recording may be effected only through an instrument in writing, duly executed by or on behalf of the owner, specifying clearly the scope of such assignment including territorial limits and duration. Where a sound recording is made for purposes of broadcasting, a separate license shall be required from the performer whose performance is embodied in that sound recording, subject to terms negotiated between the parties concerned. The licensing authority may, upon application, determine reasonable royalty rates where agreement cannot be reached. A licensee operating under this Act shall maintain accurate records of all royalties paid and received, available for inspection as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding licenses or assignments will render such commercial exploitation unlawful and subject to penalties.

A sound recording shall be deemed to have been made if it embodies sounds fixed by any method whatsoever, irrespective of whether such fixation is temporary or permanent. However, a mere transcription of a live performance, absent demonstrable creative input beyond the act of capture, does not automatically confer copyright as provided herein. Any dispute regarding originality in relation to a sound recording shall be subject to evidence demonstrating sufficient skill and judgment exercised in its creation; simple mechanical reproduction will not suffice. An appeal from any decision concerning such disputes may be made to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the initial ruling. Where a claim arises regarding ownership of rights in a sound recording incorporating pre-existing musical or literary works, determination shall first address the underlying copyright status of those incorporated elements before considering the sound recording itself.

Any person intending to avail benefits under this Act relating to a sound recording shall ensure that all requisite particulars regarding the producer, principal performer, and duration are furnished to the Register maintained for such purposes. Compliance with these requirements is a condition precedent to the registration of copyright in a sound recording, and failure to accurately declare such details may render the application liable to rejection. The Register shall, upon verification of submitted information, issue a certificate of registration if satisfied that the sound recording meets the criteria as provided herein. A registered proprietor of a sound recording may assign or transfer their rights subject to notification to the Register, and any subsequent dealings without proper recordation will not be binding on prospective purchasers. Any dispute regarding ownership of copyright in a sound recording shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court having jurisdiction.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a sound recording wholly or partially shall obtain a license from the owner of copyright in such sound recording, subject to the provisions contained herein. A registered user maintaining a digital music platform may, however, operate under a blanket license arrangement with collective management organizations duly recognized by the Central Government for royalty distribution pertaining to public performance and communication to the public of such sound recordings. Assignment of rights relating to a sound recording shall be evidenced in writing and filed with the Copyright Office within thirty days of execution; failure to do so may render the assignment unenforceable against subsequent purchasers or licensees acting in good faith. The owner of copyright in a sound recording retains the right to authorize adaptations, reproductions, and distribution, even after assigning rights for specific uses as outlined in any agreement. Any dispute regarding royalty rates shall be subject to arbitration under the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

An application patent shall be deemed to have been duly made when it satisfies all requirements as provided herein regarding provisional or complete specifications and is accompanied by the prescribed fee. The applicant may submit a request for examination of such application, subject to fulfilling conditions relating to utility, novelty, and non-obviousness. A divisional application may arise from an initial application patent where the specification relates to more than one invention, provided that each division maintains sufficient independent inventive step. Any subsequent amendment to the complete specification shall not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure; however, clarification for better understanding is permissible. The controller may require evidence of diligent steps taken towards development if a request for examination remains pending for a period exceeding five years from the date of filing the application patent.

Every application patent filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a complete specification describing the invention and enabling a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. The applicant must also furnish drawings where necessary for understanding the invention, subject to such requirements as may be prescribed. An incomplete specification or absence of required drawings may render the application liable to be refused. Where an application patent claims priority from one or more prior applications filed in a convention country, details thereof including dates and serial numbers shall be submitted within the stipulated timeframe. The Controller of Patents may require translation of any documents not in an official language as provided herein. Any amendment to the specification after filing is permissible, provided that it does not introduce matter extending beyond the content of the original disclosure; such amendments shall be subject to examination by the Patent Office and may attract additional fees.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing an application patent, or requiring it to be amended, shall have a right to appeal to the Appellate Board within a period not exceeding three months from the date of such decision. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to questions of law and may include allegations that the invention claimed in the application patent satisfies the requirements for patentability as provided herein. Where an applicant demonstrates reasonable efforts to work the patented invention commercially within a prescribed timeframe, failure by any third party to do so shall not constitute sufficient grounds for revocation of the application patent under this Act. However, such demonstration must be supported by documented evidence submitted to the Controller and subject to verification. A licensee of the application patent may seek remedies for infringement independently of the patentee, provided that the terms of the license permit such action. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties concerned.

Every application patent filed under this Act shall be examined by an officer duly appointed by the Controller of Patents, who shall ascertain whether the claimed invention satisfies the requirements of novelty and inventive step as provided herein. The applicant may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, request a hearing before such officer should substantive objections arise during examination. Where the officer is satisfied that the application meets all statutory criteria, a notification of acceptance shall be issued to the applicant, after which the patent shall be sealed upon final payment of fees. 

An incomplete application patent may be completed within a period not exceeding fifteen months from the date of initial filing, provided that any deficiency is remedied as directed by the Controller. Failure to comply with such directions will result in the abandonment of the application. The Controller may, however, extend this period in exceptional circumstances and for reasons to be recorded in writing. Any provisional specification submitted shall be followed by a complete specification within twelve months from the date of filing of the provisional application.

Every application patent filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a complete specification detailing the invention and enabling a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. The applicant shall furnish information relating to any other patents or publications known to them which are relevant to their application, failing which the patent may be subject to revocation. An incomplete specification, or one not meeting the requirements as provided herein, shall render the application liable to be refused. Subject to verification by the Controller of Patents, an application claiming priority from a prior application filed in another country must demonstrate compliance with international conventions regarding timelines and documentation. Where a provisional specification is initially submitted, a complete specification fulfilling all criteria shall follow within twelve months from the date of filing the provisional; otherwise, the provisional application will be deemed abandoned. Any false representation made during the process may attract penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent resulting from a falsely marked application patent shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where any person, by way of fraud or misrepresentation, obtains registration of an application patent for an invention which is not new, or does not involve an inventive step, or does not relate to a patentable subject matter as provided herein, such registration shall be void ab initio and the Controller may revoke the patent forthwith. The aggrieved party may initiate proceedings before the High Court seeking damages commensurate with actual loss suffered due to the fraudulent application. Provided that no action for recovery of damages shall lie against any person who proves reasonable diligence in ascertaining the novelty and inventive step prior to filing the application patent. Any false representation concerning the scope of a granted patent, including claims not supported by the specification, will attract similar penalties.

Any person making an application patent for an invention shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, have the exclusive rights conferred thereby for a period of twenty years from the date of filing such application. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, where an applicant is a small entity as defined by notification issued by the Central Government, the prescribed fees for maintaining the pending application patent shall be reduced by seventy-five percent. Assignment of the right to an application patent may be made either wholly or partially and shall be in writing registered with the Controller of Patents; such registration being conclusive evidence of title subject to proof of fraud. A license granted under an application patent, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be recorded with the Controller and any subsequent transfer of such license requires similar recording as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding assignment or licensing may render the transaction unenforceable against third parties.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent resulting from a complete specification filed as an application patent shall furnish to the Controller a statement detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and particulars of the patented invention purportedly infringed. The Controller, upon receipt of such statement and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, may direct the parties concerned to appear before him for preliminary hearing to ascertain the veracity of the claims made therein. Should the Controller deem the allegation frivolous or unsubstantiated, he may dismiss it with costs; provided that an aggrieved party may appeal such dismissal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of order. Where a counter-claim of invalidity of the application patent is raised during said hearing, evidence supporting such claim shall be submitted and considered alongside the infringement allegation, subject to timelines determined by the Controller. Any amendment to the complete specification following filing of the application patent requires prior approval as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal of an application patent, or by any condition imposed in respect thereof, may file a writ petition before a High Court alleging violation of principles of natural justice or demonstrating manifest error apparent on the record. Such a judicial proceeding shall be initiated within ninety days from the date of communication of the order refusing the application or imposing such conditions, and failure to do so will preclude any subsequent challenge based on those grounds. The applicant, subject to payment of prescribed fees, may request reconsideration of the refusal by submitting further evidence or arguments demonstrating inventive step and industrial applicability as provided herein. Where a patent is revoked through judicial proceeding, the Controller shall maintain a public register detailing the reasons for revocation and the effective date thereof. A subsequent application relating to the same invention will be considered subject to an assessment of prior art including details from the earlier, unsuccessful application patent.

An application patent filed under this Act shall be examined by the Controller of Patents in accordance with the prescribed procedure to ascertain its conformity with the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The proprietor proposed registered design, if any, accompanying such application shall be duly verified as to its novelty and inventive step. Where an applicant seeks a priority date based on a corresponding foreign application, sufficient documentary evidence establishing said filing and specification must accompany the initial submission. Any omission or deficiency in the application patent may render it liable to rejection; however, the Controller may, subject to such terms as he deems fit, allow rectification of formal errors within a specified period. Provided that any amendment affecting the substance of the invention requires prior written permission and shall not unduly prejudice other applicants. The controller may require an applicant to furnish further information or documents relevant to the examination process, and failure to comply with such requests may result in abandonment of the application patent.

Every application patent filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a complete specification detailing the invention and enabling any person skilled in the art to carry it into effect.
