The applicant shall furnish evidence of diligent steps taken in relation to the development of the invention, subject to verification by the Controller of Patents. Where an objection is raised regarding the completeness or clarity of the specification, the applicant may be required to amend it within a prescribed period. Any appeal against the decision of the Controller concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application patent shall lie before the Appellate Board established for this purpose, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board’s decisions are final and binding except where review may be sought as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in abandonment of the application.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent resulting from a falsely marked application patent shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller General of Patents may, after due inquiry and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct the rectification of any false marking on goods or services pertaining to an alleged patented invention. Failure to comply with a direction issued by the Controller General patents under this Act shall attract further penalties, up to twice the initial amount. Any application patent found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation will be void ab initio and subject to immediate revocation. A person aggrieved by such revocation may appeal to the appropriate authority as provided herein, but only within ninety days of the Controller General’s decision. Repeated offenses relating to falsely marked applications shall incur escalating penalties and potential imprisonment not exceeding one year.

A person may be registered as a patent agent subject to fulfilling such conditions as may be prescribed. The Controller shall maintain a register of patent agents, and all entries therein shall be open to inspection at reasonable times by any person paying the prescribed fee. A registered patent agent shall be entitled to act on behalf of applicants for patents, or proprietors of patents, before the Controller, and shall possess such qualifications and experience as are determined by regulations made under this Act. Any person who holds a degree in engineering or science may apply for registration as a patent agent, provided that they have passed an examination conducted by the Controller demonstrating competence in patent law and practice. The register of patent agents may be amended or updated from time to time.

Any person desiring to act as a patent agent shall make an application in such form as may be prescribed, to the Controller of Patents. The application shall be accompanied by proof of passing the examination conducted by the Controller, demonstrating requisite knowledge of patent law and practice. A register of patent agents shall be maintained by the Controller, wherein the names and addresses of all registered patent agents will be recorded. Subject to payment of the prescribed fee, renewal of registration as a patent agent may be undertaken every five years; provided that failure to renew shall result in removal from the register. The Controller may, after notice and opportunity for hearing, remove a person’s name from the register if they have been convicted of an offence involving professional misconduct or are found to have engaged in fraudulent practices related to patents as provided herein. A person whose name has been removed may apply for reinstatement following a period of two years.

A patent agent, if found to have acted with reasonable care and skill but nonetheless provided incorrect advice resulting in the rejection of a valid patent application, shall not be liable for any loss suffered by the applicant unless such loss arises from demonstrable fraud or wilful misrepresentation on the part of the agent. However, nothing contained herein shall preclude an action for professional negligence against a patent agent where it is established that the agent failed to conduct reasonable searches as provided within the prescribed rules, and this failure directly contributed to the invalidation of a subsequently granted patent. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a patent agent may lodge a complaint with the Controller of Patents, who shall investigate such complaints and may impose penalties including suspension or revocation of registration, subject to principles of natural justice. The Controller’s decision in any matter relating to disciplinary proceedings against a patent agent shall be final and binding, save for appeal to the High Court.

A person desiring to act as a patent agent shall make an application in such form, and accompanied by such fee, as may be prescribed. The Controller shall, upon receipt of the application and after satisfying himself as to the applicant’s qualifications—including possession of a degree in engineering or technology, or holding a master's degree in science, or being a registered attorney—register the applicant as a patent agent if he is found fit for such registration. Registration as a patent agent shall be subject to payment of an annual fee and renewal thereof as prescribed. The Controller may, after notice to the patent agent concerned, remove his name from the register if he fails to pay the prescribed fees or is found guilty of professional misconduct. Any person aggrieved by any order of the Controller relating to registration or removal of a patent agent may prefer an appeal to the High Court within such period and in such manner as may be provided for herein. A registered patent agent shall, subject to the rules made under this Act, be entitled to practice before the Patent Office.

A person desiring to act as a patent agent shall possess a Bachelor’s degree in Science, Engineering or Technology from a recognized university as prescribed by the Controller. An applicant for registration as a patent agent may be required to undergo and successfully complete an examination conducted by the Controller to demonstrate competency in patent law and practice. Subject to successful completion of said examination, and fulfillment of all other requirements stipulated under this Act, the Controller shall register such person as a patent agent and issue a certificate of registration. Registration as a patent agent is valid for a period of five years from the date of issuance, subject to renewal upon payment of the prescribed fee and demonstration of continuing professional development. A registered patent agent may represent applicants before the Patent Office in matters relating to patents, provided that such representation does not extend to appearing before any court or tribunal unless specifically authorized by law. Any person practicing as a patent agent without valid registration shall be liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any person practicing as a patent agent shall possess a Bachelor’s degree in Engineering, Science, or Technology from a recognized university, subject to such exceptions as the Controller may determine. A registered patent agent who knowingly and wilfully provides false information in any representation made to the Controller, or assists another unqualified person in preparing or prosecuting an application for a patent, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, continued practice as a patent agent following revocation of registration, or suspension under this Act, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, after due inquiry and affording the alleged offender a reasonable opportunity to be heard, impose such penalties as are provided herein. Any fees collected pursuant to these penalties shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any assignment of rights deriving from a patent application, whether pending, granted, or refused, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing duly executed by the assignor and assignee. Such instruments relating to assignments of patent agent engagements are subject to registration with the Controller of Patents within thirty days of execution, failing which such assignment shall have no effect against any subsequent equitable interest therein. A registered patent agent may, with the express written consent of both parties, facilitate the negotiation and documentation of these assignments, acting as an intermediary solely for procedural compliance. Provided that, a transfer of rights without due registration may be subject to rectification under provisions relating to fraudulent transfers. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all recorded assignments and engagements of patent agents, accessible for inspection during office hours. Any dispute concerning the validity or scope of such assignment shall be adjudicated as provided herein, with standing granted to registered patent agents to represent either party.

Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller refusing to register them as a patent agent may, within sixty days from the date of such order, file an appeal before the High Court. Such appeal shall be filed subject to conditions prescribed and accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documents including the application for registration and the order appealed against. The Controller’s refusal to register a candidate who has demonstrably met the qualifications as provided herein, particularly regarding passing the requisite examination and possessing the necessary experience in patent law, will be considered with utmost scrutiny on appeal. Furthermore, any allegation of bias or improper conduct by the examining authority during the assessment process shall constitute valid grounds for review by the appellate court. The High Court may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller, and its order shall be final and binding; provided that a further intra-court appeal is permissible on questions of law only.

Any person desiring to act as a patent agent shall possess a Bachelor’s degree in Science, Engineering, or Technology from a recognized university, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. A qualified patent agent must register with the Controller of Patents and maintain valid professional indemnity insurance throughout the period of practice, details of which shall be filed annually. The Controller may refuse registration if satisfied that the applicant lacks requisite qualifications or has been convicted of an offence involving professional misconduct. Where a patentee includes exclusive licensees of a patented invention, such licensee may, with the express written consent of the patentee, authorize a patent agent to act on their behalf in proceedings under this Act. Failure by a registered patent agent to comply with continuing professional development requirements shall render them liable to suspension or revocation of registration as provided herein. All agents must adhere strictly to the code of conduct prescribed by the Controller.

Any person claiming to be a patent agent shall, prior to acting on behalf of any applicant for a patent, furnish proof of requisite qualifications as may be prescribed by the Controller. Failure to do so shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees and may result in temporary suspension from practicing as a patent agent under this Act. Any patent agent found aiding or abetting the filing of frivolous applications, or knowingly misrepresenting the novelty of an invention subject to a protection invention convention agreement, shall be liable for imprisonment up to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, following due inquiry and subject to established procedure, revoke the registration of any patent agent convicted of professional misconduct as provided herein. All fees collected from penalties under this provision shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

A patent agent shall be a person duly qualified by examination and registered as such under this Act, possessing the requisite knowledge and experience to act on behalf of applicants for patents and proprietors thereof. The Controller may refuse registration if the applicant does not meet prescribed qualifications or lacks good character. A registered breeder, while distinct from a patent agent, may engage a patent agent to secure protection for any new variety of plant developed by them, subject to fulfilling the criteria as provided herein regarding novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability. Any person falsely claiming to be a registered patent agent shall be punishable with imprisonment and a fine. The Controller maintains a register of all active patent agents, open for public inspection.

A collective mark shall signify a mark designating members of an association—whether incorporated or unincorporated—who apply for registration and use such mark to identify their respective goods or services, indicating membership in that association. The application for registration of a collective mark may be made by the association itself as proprietor, subject to demonstrating its existence and lawful operation under applicable law. Any regulations governing the use of a collective mark, including conditions relating to quality, geographical origin, or other characteristics, shall be filed with the Registrar at the time of application and are binding on all members entitled to use the mark as provided herein. Failure to adhere to such regulations may result in revocation of registration under this Act.

A collective mark denoting membership in an association, cooperative, or other organization shall be registrable under this Act if the applicant demonstrates that its members use the mark to identify themselves as such and to distinguish their goods or services from those of others. An application for registration of a collective mark must include a statement detailing the rules governing the use of the mark by members, including provisions relating to quality control and licensing. The Registrar may require evidence of actual use of the mark by multiple members before proceeding with registration. Subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, the Registrar shall maintain a register of authorized users of each collective mark. Any alteration to the rules governing usage must be promptly notified to the Trade Marks Registry and may necessitate an amendment to the registered collective mark. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein.

A collective mark denoting membership in an association, cooperative, or other group shall be registrable under this Act if the applicant demonstrates that its members use the mark to identify their respective goods or services and to distinguish them from those of others. The registrar may require evidence establishing legitimate control by the collective association over the quality and characteristics of the goods bearing such a mark. Any member of the association, subject to reasonable regulations established by the governing body, shall have the right to use the registered collective mark in connection with their authorized activities. Where an infringement of a collective mark occurs, any member of the associated group may maintain an action for remedies including injunctions and damages, provided that such action is brought with the consent or under the direction of the association itself. The registrar retains authority to revoke registration if the association fails to exercise adequate control over the standard of goods offered under the mark, or upon demonstrated dissolution of the collective body.

A collective mark may be registered under this Act when application is made by an association, including those incorporated or unincorporated, representing the members who use such mark to identify their respective goods or services. The applicant shall demonstrate that the mark indicates membership in a group and that the quality of the goods or services is consistent due to the efforts of all members. Registration as a collective mark confers no right to any member individually to exclude others; rather, it establishes a common right for those authorized by the association to use the mark subject to rules governing such usage. Any alteration to these rules shall be promptly notified to the Trade Marks Registry. A register of current members authorised to use the collective mark shall be maintained and accessible for inspection during usual business hours. The Registrar may require, as a condition of registration or continued registration, evidence of ongoing association activity and adherence to established standards. Failure to comply with requirements outlined herein may result in removal of the mark from the Register.

A collective mark denoting membership in an association shall be registrable under this Act if the applicant demonstrates that the association exercising control over the use of such mark is legitimate and has been established for lawful purposes. The application for registration of a collective mark shall include a statement detailing the rules governing the use of the mark by members, including conditions relating to quality control and standards applicable to goods or services offered under the mark. Any alteration to these rules subsequent to registration must be notified to the Trade Marks Registry in writing and may be subject to further scrutiny as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence of compliance with said rules before allowing continued use of the collective mark, and failure to demonstrate such compliance shall constitute grounds for revocation of registration. A member utilizing the collective mark shall do so in a manner consistent with the established standards and any misrepresentation regarding membership or quality will be actionable under this Act.

Any person claiming ownership of a collective mark shall furnish to the Registrar a statement of membership rules governing the use of such mark, and any subsequent amendment thereto shall be duly notified. Failure to maintain accurate records of members authorized to use the collective mark, or misuse by an unauthorized party despite reasonable efforts to prevent it, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a dispute arises regarding membership or the right to use the collective mark, any aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for redressal, subject to exhaustion of internal grievance mechanisms as outlined in the stated rules. The Registrar may initiate *suo motu* inquiry into allegations of fraudulent registration or improper usage and impose penalties including suspension of rights under this Act. Any profits derived from unlawful use shall be recoverable by way of damages.

A collective mark denoting membership in an association may be registered by that association, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning registration of trademarks generally. The application for such mark shall include a statement identifying the members of the association and outlining the conditions of membership, as determined by its governing body. Any transfer of rights in a collective mark requires prior written consent from not less than two-thirds of the members present at a duly convened general meeting of the association; provided that assignment to a successor entity resulting from amalgamation or reorganization shall be exempt from this requirement upon demonstration of continuity of control and purpose. Licensing of a collective mark may be permitted by the association, subject to stipulations ensuring quality control consistent with the standards established for membership and use of the mark. The register shall note any restrictions on assignment or licensing as conditions attached to the registration of the collective mark, and such conditions are binding upon all subsequent proprietors. Failure to adhere to these provisions may result in revocation of the registered collective mark under this Act.

A collective mark signifying membership in an association of spice farmers in Wayanad district was refused registration by the Registrar of Trade Marks on grounds that the applicant, the Kerala Spice Growers Cooperative Society Limited, had not demonstrated sufficient control over the quality and standards of spices sold under the proposed mark. An appeal to the Appellate Board resulted in a remand order directing the Registrar to reconsider evidence pertaining to the society’s internal mechanisms for ensuring consistent product characteristics, specifically referencing the documented grading protocols established as per Agricultural Produce Grading and Standardization Act. The Society subsequently submitted revised documentation detailing mandatory quality checks at harvest and processing stages; however, a competing claim asserting prior use of a similar mark in local markets was filed by individual farmers alleging misrepresentation and potential consumer confusion. This matter is now subject to further examination under this Act regarding the permissible scope of collective ownership and the burden of proof for establishing distinctiveness against unregistered usage.

A collective mark signifying membership in an association, cooperative, or other group shall be registrable under this Act if the applicant demonstrates that its members use the mark to identify and distinguish their goods or services. The application for such a mark shall include the rules governing the use of the mark by members, which rules must ensure quality control consistent with the standards associated with the collective mark. Any alteration to these rules requires notification to the Registrar and may be subject to further examination as provided herein. Registration of a collective mark does not confer exclusive rights on individual members but rather on the association itself, which shall exercise reasonable diligence in preventing improper use by non-members. Provisions act shall apply equally to applications for certification marks where an applicant demonstrates control over quality standards. Failure to maintain adequate records of membership and usage may result in revocation of registration.

A collective mark signifying membership in an association of spice farmers shall be registrable under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates lawful establishment and operation of said association. Any license granted for use of such a collective mark shall be subject to terms ensuring adherence to quality standards established by the association, and any breach thereof may result in revocation of the license as determined by the Registrar. Assignment of rights in a registered collective mark requires prior written consent from a majority of members of the originating association, and notice of said assignment must be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days. Where the collective mark incorporates a unique layout design for spice packaging, registration details pertaining to that layout design register shall be cross-referenced in the trade mark registry as a matter of record. Failure to maintain active membership in the association shall automatically terminate any licensing rights granted under this provision. The Registrar may, subject to due process, impose reasonable royalty fees on licensed use.

A collective mark signifying membership in the All-India Spice Growers Association was refused registration by the Registrar on grounds that the application failed to demonstrate sufficient common interest amongst its purported members, and lacked evidence of adherence to rules governing use consistent with an invention convention held annually wherein standards for spice quality were ostensibly established. This decision was appealed before the Appellate Board, which remanded the case noting a procedural irregularity – namely, failure to provide details regarding the association’s dispute resolution mechanism as provided herein. The appellant subsequently submitted amended bylaws detailing arbitration procedures; however, objections were raised by rival associations alleging that these procedures unduly favored members originating from a single state. Further appeal is now pending before the High Court concerning whether such localized bias invalidates the collective mark's claim to represent a nationwide interest and thus its eligibility for registration under this Act.

A collective mark shall signify a sign capable of identifying the goods or services of members of an association and distinguishing them from those of other undertakings. Such associations may be constituted by producers, manufacturers, traders, or any other persons involved in promoting their interests. Registration of a collective mark vests ownership not in a single entity but in the association itself, which shall exercise control over the quality and characteristics of goods or services bearing the mark. The rights conferred by registration are subject to regulations established by the association’s members. A treaty means patent relating to any process for manufacture may be considered as evidence of distinctiveness when applying for collective mark registration, provided that such a patent is publicly available and relevant to the goods or services in question, as determined under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a register of authorized users of the collective mark.

A collective mark denoting membership in an association, cooperative, or other group may be registered under this Act, subject to verification of lawful establishment and operational status of the applicant entity. The application for such mark shall include a clear statement of the rules governing the use of the mark by members, including provisions relating to quality control and permissible scope of activities. Where the goods or services associated with the collective mark incorporate patented technology licensed from third parties, full details of such licenses, including territorial limitations and royalty arrangements, must accompany the application. Registration of a collective mark shall not confer exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to goods or services outside the defined membership or scope as determined by the association; however, unauthorized use constituting misrepresentation may be actionable. The Registrar may require periodic evidence of continued compliance with these provisions for maintaining registration.

The Controller shall maintain a register of designs, wherein all registered designs shall be recorded subject to the provisions herein contained. Any application for registration must demonstrate novelty and originality as determined by examination under this Act. The register shall include particulars relating to the proprietor of each design, including name, address, and where applicable, details of any assignment or transmission of ownership rights. A certified copy of any entry in the register shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein. Any person may inspect the register upon payment of a fee as prescribed, provided that confidential information relating to licensing agreements shall not be disclosed without consent. The Controller may rectify the register where errors appear and maintain its accuracy.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall submit an application for registration to the Controller of Patents in accordance with the regulations established under this Act. The particulars required for such registration shall include a complete specification of the invention, any drawings necessary for its understanding, and a declaration of inventorship as provided herein. A request for registration must be accompanied by the prescribed fee, failing which it shall not be processed. 

The Controller may require an applicant to amend their application or provide further information before proceeding with the examination for registration. Upon satisfactory completion of the examination and subject to fulfilling all statutory requirements, the invention shall be entered in the register, and a patent will be granted. The register maintained by the Controller is open to public inspection during office hours. Any alteration to details recorded in the register requires notification to, and subsequent registration with, the Controller.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Controller to register a patent, or by any rectification of the register which affects their rights, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of order of the Controller. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Controller an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order appealed against; provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant has deposited with the Registrar such fees as may be prescribed. Where a patent is registered in contravention of any provision of this Act, any person may apply to the High Court for revocation of the patent on grounds specified herein. The register maintained by the Controller shall at all times be open to inspection subject to payment of a fee and compliance with conditions as determined by public notice. Any entry made falsely or improperly in the register may be rectified upon due process established under this Act, offering redress to any party demonstrably harmed thereby.

Any person desiring to be registered as a patent agent shall submit an application to the Controller of Patents in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule IV. The Controller may require such further evidence regarding qualifications and experience as deemed necessary for assessing suitability. Upon satisfactory verification of credentials and payment of fees, the applicant’s name shall be entered into the register of patent agents maintained by the office. A separate register shall also be kept containing details of all registered patent agents including their addresses for service and any disciplinary actions taken against them. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, remove a name from the register if the agent is found guilty of professional misconduct or has failed to comply with provisions under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order of removal may appeal to the High Court within sixty days. All entries in the register shall be conclusive evidence of facts stated therein unless proven otherwise.

Any person desiring to become a registered agent shall submit an application to the Controller of Patents in the prescribed form, accompanied by proof of possessing the requisite qualifications as determined by regulations made under this Act. The register of patent agents maintained by the Controller shall be open for inspection subject to payment of a fee specified in Schedule I. An applicant who fails to disclose any material particular in their application or provides false information shall be liable for removal from the register and may be disqualified from future applications for a period not exceeding five years. A person whose name is entered on the register as a registered agent may, subject to compliance with continuing professional development requirements, renew their registration every three years. The Controller may require any registered agent to furnish such information regarding their practice as deemed necessary to ensure adherence to ethical standards and proper conduct under these rules.

Any person failing to maintain the accuracy of any entry in the register shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each such failure, and the Controller may, after giving reasonable opportunity for explanation, direct rectification of the register accordingly. Where a false entry is knowingly made or permitted to remain in the register, the person responsible therefor shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Any application for registration found to contain materially false information, subject to verification as provided herein, shall be deemed void ab initio and no rights shall accrue therefrom. The Controller may, in cases of demonstrable hardship, waive the penalty where non-compliance arises from circumstances beyond the applicant’s reasonable control; however, such waiver shall not extend to instances of deliberate misrepresentation concerning prior art or inventorship. All amendments to the register must be duly certified by a qualified patent agent.

Any assignment of rights relating to a registered patent shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and require written consent from both the assignor and assignee, detailing the scope of transferred interests. A register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall record all assignments, licenses—both exclusive and non-exclusive—and any subsequent modifications thereto; failure to register such transactions does not invalidate them but may affect their enforceability against third parties who acquire an interest in good faith. The Controller may, upon application and subject to payment of a prescribed fee, restore an assignment to the register if it was inadvertently omitted or incorrectly recorded. Any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the register may appeal to the High Court as provided herein. A license granted without adequate consideration shall be voidable at the option of the licensor; however, licenses of right under this Act remain unaffected. The Controller reserves the right to inspect records pertaining to registered assignments and licenses during routine audits.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Controller to register a patent, or any amendment to a patent following examination, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellant shall furnish security for costs as determined by the Appellate Board and failure to do so will render the appeal non-maintainable. Where a request for registration is refused on grounds relating to novelty or inventive step, the Controller’s decision shall include detailed reasoning referencing prior art considered during examination. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Controller's refusal to register, no further appeal under this Act shall be permissible; however, a petition may lie before the High Court on points of law only. The register maintained by the Controller shall be prima facie evidence of all matters entered therein and is open for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Any person making an application for registration of a patent shall submit a detailed declaration as to inventive step and ownership, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to rejection under this Act. The Controller may require such further evidence as may be necessary to satisfy themselves regarding the veracity of said declaration. Where a pharmaceutical formulation is presented within a distinctive package intended to deceive or cause confusion with a legitimately patented product, the applicant’s right to register shall be forfeited, and the improperly packaged goods are subject to seizure. Any false entry made in the register constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that any rectification of the register necessitated by such falsity shall be at the expense of the offender. All fees associated with maintaining the register shall be determined and collected as provided herein.

Any aggrieved party may file an appeal with the Appellate Board concerning the refusal of the Controller to register a patent application, provided that such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Contracting Party asserting grounds for invalidation of a registration must demonstrate prior art sufficient to establish lack of novelty or inventive step as determined under this Act. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Controller’s decision, the applicant may seek rectification of the register through an application for review based on newly discovered evidence relevant to patentability; however, such review shall be limited to matters pertaining to the original grounds for refusal and not a re-argument of previously considered issues. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements will render any appeal or application inadmissible. The Controller’s discretion in maintaining the register is subject to judicial oversight only on questions of law.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection by any member of the public subject to such reasonable conditions as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by any entry in the register, or omission therefrom, may apply to the Controller for rectification thereof and such application shall constitute a proceeding appellate before the High Court if the decision of the Controller is not satisfactory. The Controller shall, following due process and consideration of evidence presented, amend the register accordingly. Provided that no amendment affecting priority shall be made without the consent of the applicant or patentee, unless it is established that the original entry was manifestly erroneous. Any rectification undertaken shall be recorded in the register as a matter of public record.

Any application for a patent shall be subject to registration with the Controller of Patents in accordance with the procedures as provided herein. The register maintained by the Controller shall contain particulars of each patent granted, including the name and address of the patentee, the date of filing, and details relating to any international registration protection claimed under treaties to which India is a party. A complete search of the register may be undertaken prior to application to ascertain novelty and avoid duplication of effort. Provided that, failure to properly maintain the annual renewal fees associated with a registration shall result in its lapse as if it were never granted. The Controller reserves the right to amend any entry within the register upon demonstration of manifest error or fraud. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to registration may appeal to the appropriate authority.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Controller to register a patent application, or by any decision concerning amendment or revocation of a registration, may submit a reasoned statement of objection to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such decision. The High Court shall, subject to such rules as it deems fit and after affording an opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, review the Controller’s decision and either confirm, modify, or reverse the same. Where a registration is revoked due to non-payment of renewal fees, the former proprietor may apply for reinstatement of the register within one year from the date of revocation, provided that all outstanding fees and a surcharge are paid as prescribed herein. Any dispute relating to the application registration trade concerning rights arising from a jointly held patent shall be determined by arbitration in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein.

An integrated circuit shall mean a three dimensional microelectronic structure consisting of semiconductor materials and passive and active elements including interconnections, intended for use in an electronic device. For the purposes of this Act, a ‘layout-design’ is defined as the topographical map or plan embodying the arrangement of the elements and interconnections of an integrated circuit, irrespective of whether it is expressed in two or three dimensions. Subject to provisions concerning originality, any layout-design which is capable of being distinctly identified shall be considered unique. A semiconductor material includes but is not limited to silicon, germanium, and gallium arsenide as provided herein. Any person exploiting a registered layout-design without authorization shall be liable for infringement under this Act.

Any layout-design, wholly or partially embodied in a semiconductor integrated circuit, shall be eligible for registration under this Act provided that it is original and has not been previously disclosed to the public by any means. An applicant seeking registration of an integrated circuit layout-design must submit detailed technical drawings demonstrating the arrangement of transistors and other elements within the circuit, along with a statement of novelty. The application shall also include particulars identifying the semiconductor material used in fabrication. Registration confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or commercially exploit the registered layout-design for a period of ten years from the date of registration, subject to payment of prescribed fees and renewal requirements as provided herein. A derivative integrated circuit based on a registered layout-design requires prior authorization from the registered owner; however, independent development resulting in an identical layout is not precluded.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an integrated circuit which incorporates a layout-design registered under this Act shall be liable for such derivation unless duly licensed by the proprietor of said layout-design. A registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings in a competent court having jurisdiction over the matter to restrain any act constituting infringement of their rights, and may also claim damages sustained due to such infringement; however, no injunction shall be granted if the defendant proves they were unaware of the registration and exercised reasonable diligence in ascertaining whether a valid layout-design existed. Subject to provisions concerning national emergency or non-commercial research, compulsory licensing of a registered layout-design may be granted by the court upon application demonstrating sufficient cause and payment of adequate remuneration to the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by an order pertaining to such licensing shall have recourse to appeal as provided herein, and any falsification of information presented in support of either infringement claims or applications for compulsory license constitutes grounds for prosecution under relevant penal laws.

An integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be construed as a three dimensional microelectronic structure including all layers and interconnections therein, which is designed for the performance of electronic functions. Any person exploiting such an integrated circuit commercially without due authorization from the proprietor of the layout-design registered under this Act, shall be liable to legal proceedings. The Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs and associated proprietors. A layout-design is considered distinct if it demonstrates novelty and originality in its configuration; however, mere aesthetic variations are insufficient for establishing such distinction as provided herein. Where a dispute arises concerning ownership of a particular integrated circuit’s layout-design, the appropriate authority shall conduct an inquiry to determine rightful proprietorship based on evidence presented by all parties concerned. Any application for registration must include detailed technical drawings and specifications of the said layout-design. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

Any person desiring registration of an integrated circuit layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller as provided herein, accompanied by the prescribed fee and relevant documentation demonstrating originality. The layout-design must relate to a finished semiconductor product intended for commercial exploitation; however, layouts solely for research purposes are subject to expedited review but limited protection duration. A three-dimensional representation illustrating the topology of each layer constituting the integrated circuit shall be included with the application. Any modification to a registered layout-design requires notification to the Controller and may necessitate a new registration dependent on the extent of alteration. Failure to comply with these requirements, or submission of false information, shall render the application liable for rejection and may attract penalties under this Act. Provided that, rights in an integrated circuit do not confer any right concerning the underlying semiconductor device itself.

Any person who fabricates an integrated circuit in violation of the exclusive right conferred by this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where such fabrication is undertaken for commercial gain, the court may, at its discretion, also order seizure and destruction of all infringing articles and equipment used in the process. Any person who imports an integrated circuit knowing it to be fabricated in contravention of this Act shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act and shall be liable for prosecution as herein provided. A registered proprietor may initiate civil proceedings for injunction, damages or rendition of accounts against any infringer; however, such action must commence within three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement. Failure to comply with a court order issued under this Act will constitute contempt of court, attracting further penalties.

Any person possessing rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be entitled to assign such rights by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the scope of assignment whether partial or absolute. Such assignment shall vest ownership of the layout-design, subject to any existing licensing agreements and conditions as may be stipulated within the instrument of assignment. A registered proprietor may grant licenses, either exclusive or non-exclusive, for the commercial exploitation of their integrated circuit layout-design, specifying royalty rates and territorial limitations. Any transfer of rights relating to a three-dimensional feature embodied in the layout-design shall require explicit mention thereof in the assignment deed; otherwise such features will remain with the assignor. Where an assignment is made as security for a loan or other financial obligation, the assignee’s rights are limited to recovery of the debt and do not confer ownership unless foreclosure proceedings are completed as provided herein. The registrar may maintain a public register of all assignments and licenses recorded under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from such acts as are prejudicial to the rights conferred by this Act. The applicant shall furnish proof of registration and demonstrate substantial similarity between the registered layout-design and that which is alleged to be infringing, subject to considerations regarding permissible variations inherent in integrated circuit manufacturing processes. Should the respondent dispute the validity of the registration or assert a prior art defense establishing independent development of an identical or substantially similar integrated circuit, the Court may appoint a technical expert for assessment. Any decision rendered by the High Court shall be appealable to the Supreme Court on questions of law only, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of judgment and accompanied by certified copies of all pleadings. The aggrieved party may also seek damages commensurate with actual loss or reasonable royalty.

Any person possessing an integrated circuit layout-design registered under this Act shall have exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, commercially exploit and import the same, subject to the provisions contained herein. An assignment of such exclusive rights may be effected by a written instrument duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the scope of the transfer including territorial limitations if any, and detailing any retained rights by the assignor. Licenses concerning these rights shall also be in writing and specify royalty payments or other consideration, as mutually agreed upon between the licensor and licensee. Any assignment or license not complying with these requirements shall be void ab initio. Where an integrated circuit is embodied in an article, the exclusive right extends to such article; provided that this does not extend to acts done solely for private personal use. The registered owner may grant compulsory licenses under certain conditions as determined by the Central Government and communicated through official gazette notification.

Any person claiming to be interested in preventing the fraudulent use of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Registrar for an order restraining such user. The application shall contain a statement of facts substantiating the claim and shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating prior use or legitimate interest in the relevant goods bearing that registration geographical indication. Failure to provide sufficient evidence may result in dismissal of the application with costs payable to the alleged infringer. Any person found guilty of applying for registration of a geographical indication knowing it to be false, or assisting another in such an act, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, as provided herein, initiate *suo motu* inquiries into potential infringements and impose penalties accordingly. All orders issued under this Act shall be final and binding, subject to appeal before the High Court.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be specified in the instrument of assignment and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license is granted permitting a party other than the registered proprietor to use the trade mark, the licensor shall maintain control over the quality of goods or services associated with the application registration trade, failing which the rights conferred by such license may be revoked as provided herein. An exclusive licensee shall have the right to sue for infringement of the trade mark subject to the terms of the licensing agreement and notification to the registered proprietor. Assignment or transmission of a trade mark shall not affect the validity of any existing registrations unless expressly stated in the instrument, but all subsequent dealings with the trade mark must reflect the updated ownership as recorded with the Registry. Any assignment without proper recording is voidable at the option of the assignor.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— "associated trade" means a trade which is similar to a registered trade and is used in such manner as to cause confusion or deception; provided that association shall not be deemed to exist where the use of the later trade is fair and honest. A trade mark shall be considered ‘registered’ when particulars thereof have been entered in the Register maintained under this Act, and the entry satisfies all requirements as provided herein. The proprietor of a registered trade mark acquires exclusive rights to use the said trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, subject to limitations outlined within these provisions. Any assignment or transmission of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules prescribed and notified by the Trade Marks Registry.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be registered only upon entry in the Register and subject to the provisions contained herein. Any application for registration must demonstrate distinctive character capable of distinguishing goods or services, and shall not describe the characteristics of those goods or services, nor consist exclusively of a descriptive term commonly used in the relevant trade. Provided that a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registered notwithstanding its initial lack of inherent distinction. The Controller may require evidence of such acquired distinctiveness as deemed necessary for registration. A falsely applied for or improperly registered trade mark shall be vulnerable to rectification proceedings, and any person aggrieved by such registration may initiate appropriate action under this Act. Registration confers exclusive rights in respect of the goods or services specified in the register, subject to limitations as provided herein.

Any person who obtains a registration for a trade mark shall be entitled to use such registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any conditions or limitations specified in the certificate of registration. Where a registered trade mark has been used by an unauthorised party, the registered proprietor may institute legal proceedings for infringement as provided herein, seeking remedies including but not limited to injunctions restraining further use and damages for loss suffered. A court considering such claims shall have full power to grant relief on equitable grounds. Provided that, if the defendant proves legitimate prior use of a similar mark, or establishes that their use is descriptive only, then no infringement shall be deemed to have occurred. The register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of ownership and validity of registration; however, such evidence may be rebutted by proof of fraud or other vitiating factors. Any assignment of a registered trade mark must be recorded in the Register to be effective against third parties.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be registered only upon entry in the Register and issuance of a certificate of registration as provided herein. The Controller may, subject to such conditions and after such examination as may be prescribed, refuse to register a trade mark that is devoid of any distinctive character or deceptively similar to an existing trade mark. An application for registration shall not be proceeded with if it appears from the records that there exists a prior pending application for identical marks in respect of identical goods or description of goods. Where a mark has been registered, the proprietor thereof acquires the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to an instrument in writing and notice thereof filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Provided that such registration may be revoked on grounds specified within this Act, including non-use for a continuous period of five years and proven likelihood of confusion. A person aggrieved by any decision of the Controller relating to a registered trade mark may file an appeal before the High Court.

Any goods which are offered for sale or sold with a trade mark not duly registered shall be deemed counterfeit goods under this Act and subject to seizure. A party claiming ownership of a registered trade mark may, upon reasonable cause being shown to the satisfaction of a Magistrate, request an ex parte order directing any person possessing such counterfeit goods to submit them for inspection. Provided that no action shall proceed unless the claimant demonstrates prior registration of the mark in question with the Trade Marks Registry and furnishes evidence of potential damage suffered due to the infringement. The Registrar may, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures, maintain a public database of all registered trade marks accessible for search purposes. Any alteration or falsification of details pertaining to a registered proprietor recorded within said registry shall constitute an offence punishable as provided herein. Failure to renew a registered trade mark within the stipulated timeframe may result in its removal from the register.

Any person who contravenes the provisions relating to the rectification of the register of trade marks, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each such contravention. Where a trade mark is registered through misrepresentation or by providing false particulars, the Registrar may, upon application made in writing and supported by evidence, revoke the registration after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard. Any assignment of a registered trade mark without prior written consent of the Registrar shall be void ab initio and subject to a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Furthermore, any goods bearing an unlawfully applied or falsely represented registered trade mark offered for sale shall be deemed counterfeit goods and are liable to seizure and destruction under the orders of a competent court. The burden of proving lawful registration shall lie with the proprietor claiming such right.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be agreed upon between the parties and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a registered trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, notice of the assignment shall be given to the Registry in writing by the assignee within thirty days from the date of assignment; failure to do so may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties acquiring rights after such date. A license granted concerning a registered trade mark must be recorded for it to be effective against any subsequent assignee or licensee, and the proprietor of the trade mark shall furnish particulars as prescribed. Subject to provisions contained herein, the assignee of a registered trade mark shall possess the same rights and remedies as the original proprietor in respect of infringement thereof; provided that such assignment does not contravene any existing statutory restrictions or judicial orders. Any dispute regarding validity of an assignment or license shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration of a trade mark, or varying the conditions subject to which a trade mark is registered, may file an appeal with the High Court within ninety days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be filed in the form prescribed under the relevant rules and accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by the court. The appellant shall demonstrate sufficient cause why the Registrar’s decision regarding distinctiveness was erroneous or failed to consider all material facts presented during examination. Provided that, where the dispute concerns a mark already registered, the onus shall be on the challenging party to prove invalidity based on prior use or descriptive character as provided herein. A counter-affidavit may be filed by the Registrar within sixty days of service of appeal notice and the court may direct either party to produce further evidence relevant to determining whether the trade mark is legitimately registered.

A trade mark shall be considered registered only upon entry in the Register and issuance of a certificate of registration in accordance with the prescribed procedure. Any application permitted amended under this Act must adhere to the conditions specified regarding permissible alterations, namely that such amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark as originally applied for. Where an applicant seeks to amend an application after acceptance but prior to registration, notice of said amendment shall be served upon any party who has filed a notice of opposition. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the subsequent registration vulnerable to revocation proceedings. A registered trade mark confers exclusive rights in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding limitations and exceptions. The Registrar may require evidence of continued use as a condition of maintaining a registered trade mark on the Register.

Any person who counterfeits or falsely applies to goods any trade mark that is registered under this Act, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with fine not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where an application is made ex parte seeking an injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, advertising or importing counterfeit goods bearing a registered trade mark, and sufficient cause is shown, the court may grant such injunction pending disposal of the suit. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of such an ex parte injunction may appeal to the High Court within thirty days. Failure to comply with any order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court, attracting further penalties as deemed fit. The registered proprietor may also seek damages for loss suffered due to the infringement.

Any application for registration filed with the Marks Registry established under this Act and subsequently refused shall be subject to review by an officer duly appointed for such purpose. An aggrieved party may file a statement of grounds for appeal within sixty days from the date of refusal, supported by evidence demonstrating prior use or distinctiveness not initially considered. The Registrar, upon receiving such appeal, shall conduct a de novo examination, and may require additional evidence or submissions from either party. A trade mark registered in error, or found to be deceptively similar to an existing registered mark following this process, shall be subject to rectification or cancellation as provided herein. Decisions of the Registrar are final unless appealed to the High Court having jurisdiction; however, a request for reconsideration by the same officer may be permitted at their discretion, subject to payment of prescribed fees and within thirty days of the initial decision.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any person desiring to inspect the said register shall apply to the registrar in writing and may, upon payment of the prescribed fee, inspect the same subject to such conditions as the registrar may deem fit. The registrar may require any applicant for registration to furnish a statement of use showing how the trade mark has been used within the period specified herein. Provided that the registrar may, if satisfied with sufficient cause, extend the time for furnishing such a statement. All decisions made by the registrar shall be communicated in writing and are subject to appeal as provided under this Act. The registrar’s functions include the examination of applications and the determination of registrability.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. Any application for registration must be filed with the registrar in the prescribed manner, accompanied by all necessary documents and fees as stipulated. The registrar may examine such applications and require amendments or further information if deemed necessary to determine registrability under this Act. Where an application is accepted, the registrar shall advertise it in the Trade Marks Journal as provided herein. Any person may file a notice of opposition with the registrar within the prescribed time limit, contesting the registration. Upon consideration of any opposition filed, and subject to due process being followed, the registrar shall either register the trade mark or reject the application, recording reasons for such decision. The registrar’s decisions are appealable to the appellate board established under this Act.

The registrar, upon receiving an application for rectification of the register alleging wrongful removal or inclusion of a trade mark, shall cause notice to be served on the parties concerned, including the applicant and the proprietor of the trade mark in question. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar relating to such rectification may, subject to the provisions herein, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of communication of the said decision. Provided that the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause existed for not preferring the appeal within the stipulated period, extend the time for doing so but not exceeding a further thirty days. The registrar shall maintain a record of all rectifications and appeals, accessible to public inspection during office hours upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure by the proprietor to respond to notices issued by the registrar may result in ex parte proceedings being conducted as provided herein, potentially leading to adverse findings.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any person desiring to inspect the register or any part thereof, may apply to the registrar for that purpose, submitting a fee as prescribed. The registrar may, subject to such conditions as deemed appropriate, permit inspection of the register. Where an application is made for registration of a trade mark, the registrar shall examine it and determine whether it meets all requirements under this Act. If the registrar objects to the application, notice of such objection shall be sent to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to respond within thirty days from the date of said notice. The registrar may, after considering any response received, either withdraw the objection or proceed with the refusal of the application. Any decision of the registrar regarding acceptance or refusal of a trade mark is subject to appeal before the appellate board as provided herein. All records maintained by the registrar shall be deemed public documents until otherwise ordered by a court of competent jurisdiction.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, ensuring its accessibility to public inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person desiring to inspect the register or obtain certified copies thereof may apply to the registrar in writing, specifying the class and mark details for which inspection is sought. The registrar may require such applicant to furnish reasonable proof of identity before granting access. Where an application for registration is deemed defective by the registrar, notice of such deficiency shall be served upon the applicant, affording a period not less than thirty days for rectification; provided that failure to rectify within said timeframe may result in abandonment of the application. All decisions of the registrar relating to examination, advertisement or refusal of trade marks shall be reasoned and communicated in writing to the concerned party. The registrar’s functions are subject to appeal before the appropriate appellate authority as provided herein.

The registrar, upon reasonable cause being shown and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, may initiate an inquiry into any matter relating to a registered trade mark where it appears that the trade mark is being used in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion. Any person aggrieved by an act of the registrar under this provision shall have the right to appeal to such authority as provided herein, within a period not exceeding one month from the date of communication of the order. Failure to comply with any lawful direction issued by the registrar during such inquiry shall constitute an obstruction of due process and may attract a penalty up to five thousand rupees. Moreover, deliberate provision of false evidence or misrepresentation to the registrar will be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. All records pertaining to inquiries conducted by the registrar are deemed public documents subject to confidentiality provisions relating to commercial sensitivity.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as the registrar may deem fit to impose, ensuring adequate protection of consumer interests and preventing dilution of the distinctive character of the mark. Where an application for registration of an assignment is made, the registrar shall examine it to verify compliance with the provisions of this Act and ascertain that the assignee possesses the legal capacity to hold and utilize the trade mark. The registrar may require evidence of consideration paid or to be paid for the assignment, though a nominal consideration shall not *per se* invalidate the transfer, provided there is no intent to defraud creditors or circumvent other legal obligations. Should the registrar find grounds to believe that the assignment is fraudulent or contrary to public policy, it may refuse registration and initiate appropriate proceedings. A licensee of a trade mark, with the consent of the registered proprietor and subject to such terms as the registrar approves, may also apply for assignment where the proprietary rights are being transferred alongside the license.

The registrar, upon receiving an application for rectification alleging that a registered trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion, shall issue notice to the proprietor of said trade mark requiring them to state grounds for opposing the rectification within a period not exceeding two months from service of such notice. Should the proprietor fail to respond adequately, or if their response is deemed insufficient by the registrar after examination of supporting evidence submitted by both parties, an ex parte decision may be rendered ordering rectification or dismissing the application. Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the registrar’s decision shall have a right to appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of said order; provided that such appeal shall not operate as a stay of the registrar's decision unless specifically ordered by the Appellate Board upon demonstrating prima facie grounds for substantial merit. The registrar may, subject to just terms, direct either party to provide copies of evidence to the other.

The registrar, exercising functions conferred by this Act, shall maintain a register of trade marks comprising all particulars of registered trade marks and applications currently pending before him. Any proprietor trade mark desiring to inspect said register may do so at the Trade Marks Office during office hours, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with such conditions as the registrar deems necessary for ensuring proper access and preservation of records. The registrar may require a statutory declaration from any person seeking inspection, confirming that the purpose is legitimate and not intended for unlawful gain or harassment. Where an application for registration includes a trade mark identical with one already registered by another proprietor, the registrar shall notify the applicant accordingly, providing details of the existing registration and opportunity to respond. Provided that such notification does not preclude examination on merits as provided herein. Any decision of the registrar may be subject to appeal before the appropriate appellate authority within the time frame stipulated under these rules.

The registrar, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, shall examine it as provided herein and ensure compliance with all procedural requirements under this Act. Any deficiency in the application, including but not limited to incomplete details regarding industrial application or inaccurate classification of goods or services, shall be communicated to the applicant within one month from the date of such receipt, affording them an opportunity to rectify the same. Failure to respond to such communication within a period of thirty days may result in rejection of the application. The registrar may, subject to justifiable cause and upon payment of prescribed fees, extend this timeframe at their discretion. All decisions of the registrar regarding acceptance or refusal shall be recorded in writing and reasoned grounds communicated to the applicant; furthermore, any appeal against such decision lies with the Appellate Board as per established procedure.

The registrar, upon receiving an application alleging infringement involving a resulting international registration, shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the grounds for such allegation are prima facie established. Should the registrar deem sufficient cause exists, notice of the complaint shall be served upon the alleged infringer within thirty days of determination; failure to serve said notice will render the registrar liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar relating to the acceptance or rejection of evidence presented in support of an allegation may appeal to the High Court, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to timelines as provided herein. Knowingly providing false information to the registrar shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or a fine, or both. All records maintained by the registrar are deemed public documents unless otherwise restricted by rules framed under this Act.

The registrar, upon receipt of a valid instrument of transfer relating to a registered trade mark, shall examine said instrument to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act concerning lawful assignment. Any application for registration of an assignment recorded in a Contracting State, where reciprocal arrangements exist as determined by the Central Government, may be accepted subject to verification of authenticity through established diplomatic channels. Where the registrar deems the instrument incomplete or defective, notice shall be issued to the applicant requiring rectification within thirty days; failure to comply may result in rejection of the application for recordal. An assignment not duly recorded shall not bind any subsequent proprietor acquiring interest in the mark. The registrar retains discretion to require further evidence regarding beneficial ownership, particularly where nominee assignments are suspected, and may initiate inquiries as provided herein to ascertain true control over the trade mark. All records pertaining to such transfers shall be maintained securely and accessible for public inspection.

The registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder. Any person claiming to be the owner of an invention relating to a novel process capable of being applied industrially, or alleging prior rights in a mark, may apply to the registrar for inspection of the register subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The registrar may require such applicant to furnish evidence establishing legitimate interest before granting access. Where a trade mark application is refused, the registrar shall communicate the reasons for refusal to the applicant within thirty days. Provided that, the decision of the registrar may be appealed to the appellate board as provided herein. All records maintained by the registrar shall be deemed public documents unless otherwise restricted by rules relating to confidential information concerning inventions.

A design, for the purposes of this Act, signifies the three-dimensional arrangement of the electronic circuits within a semiconductor integrated circuit, irrespective of whether it is expressed or embodied in any article. Such a design shall be considered original if it is generated through independent intellectual effort and possesses no substantial similarity to any existing registered design or layout-design. The creator of a design may register it with the appropriate authority as provided herein, thereby establishing a right to prevent unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation. A registered design confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights in respect of that design for a period of ten years from the date of registration, subject to payment of prescribed fees and compliance with renewal requirements. Any act infringing such a registered design shall be actionable under this Act.

A layout-design, being a three dimensional configuration of layers of semiconductor material containing active and passive elements, shall be registerable under this Act if it is original and capable of being distinctly identified. An applicant seeking registration of a design must submit an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, demonstrating sufficient detail regarding the topology depicted therein. The layout-design shall not be considered identical if differences relate only to ornamentation or minor modifications that do not materially affect its essential characteristics. Subject to verification and confirmation of novelty by the Controller, a certificate of registration will be issued, conferring exclusive rights on the applicant for a period of ten years from the date of filing. Any commercial exploitation of such registered design without authorization shall constitute an infringement, attracting remedies as provided herein, including injunctions and damages. A person may file a petition to revoke a registration if it is proven that the layout-design lacked originality at the time of its initial registration.

A registered layout-design shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit commercially, distribute, or import articles embodying that layout-design. Subject to the provisions herein, no person shall, without the prior written consent of the proprietor, perform any of the aforementioned acts in relation to a registered design. Where a commercial exploitation involves an act not contemplated by the original registration, the proprietor may seek appropriate relief as provided under this Act. Any person dealing in goods incorporating a layout-design believing reasonably that such use is lawful shall not be liable for infringement; however, this defense does not extend to instances of willful or negligent disregard of registered rights. The registrar may, upon application and sufficient cause shown, revoke the registration of a design if it is proven substantially similar to an earlier layout-design or lacks novelty as defined herein.
