Remedies for infringement include injunctions, damages, and account of profits, determined by the designated authority following due process.

A layout-design, being a three dimensional configuration of layers of semiconductor material containing active and passive elements, shall be considered original if it demonstrates sufficient skill and judgment in its creation. The Controller may, upon application made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, register any such original layout-design which has not been previously published or otherwise publicly disclosed. Subject to the provisions contained herein, registration of a layout-design confers upon the applicant the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, sell, or import articles embodying that design. 

However, this exclusivity shall not extend to acts done privately and for non-commercial purposes. Any person aggrieved by an act constituting infringement of a registered layout-design may apply to the Controller for redressal; provided that such application is made within three years from the date of knowledge of the infringing act. The applicant must demonstrate substantial similarity between the registered design and the alleged infringing article, establishing a clear nexus of derivation or copying.

A layout-design, qualifying as a design under this Act, shall be original if it is generated by the creator’s own skill, labour and judgment and has not been previously made available to the public. Subject to the provisions herein, a person deriving commercial benefit from such a design must register it with the appropriate authority within two years of its first use or disclosure. Registration confers exclusive rights on the proprietor for ten years from the date of registration, or until expiry of any applicable term under international treaties. Any act infringing upon these registered layout-designs, including reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation without authorization, shall be actionable as provided herein. However, reverse engineering solely for limited experimentation and analysis is permitted, provided that such activity does not amount to commercial duplication or derivation of a substantially similar design. The proprietor may seek injunctions and damages in respect of any proven infringement.

Any person who commercially exploits a layout-design which is identical to, or derived from, a registered design without the authorization of the proprietor shall be liable to damages. Such damages shall not be less than ten thousand rupees per integrated circuit embodying the infringing layout-design and may extend to one lakh rupees per such integrated circuit, as determined by the Court having jurisdiction over the matter. Where an act constitutes an offence under this Act and also gives rise to a civil claim for infringement of a registered design, the proprietor may pursue either remedy independently or simultaneously. A court, when adjudicating claims relating to layout-design rights, shall consider evidence regarding reasonable licensing fees that would have been charged had a license been negotiated. Any person assisting in the manufacture or commercial exploitation of an infringing layout-design shall be deemed complicit and subject to similar penalties as provided herein. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining further infringement.

Any registered design right in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall vest initially in the creator of that design, subject to contractual obligations or assignments as provided herein. A person who is an employee or consultant undertaking the creation of a design pursuant to a contract of service or apprenticeship shall assign all rights in such design to their employer or principal, unless otherwise agreed in writing. Any assignment of a registered design right must be in writing and duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the scope of the transferred interest, whether it is a complete transfer or a license. 

A licensee may sub-license the assigned design only with prior written consent from the original owner, and such sub-licensing shall be subject to royalty payments as determined mutually or, failing that, by an arbitral tribunal constituted under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The registered proprietor of a design may grant exclusive licenses, but any such license must define the territorial scope and duration clearly; non-exclusive licenses are permissible without such limitations. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment or licensing shall render the transaction voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

A registered layout-design, being a function of its constituent elements and their interconnections, shall vest with the applicant as provided herein, notwithstanding any prior art or existing technical knowledge unless demonstrably proven otherwise before the appellate authority. Any person alleging infringement of a design right must first submit a detailed representation to the Registrar outlining the specific similarities between the allegedly infringing layout-design and the registered design, accompanied by expert testimony where necessary. Should the Registrar deem the representation sufficient grounds for investigation, notice shall be served upon the respondent, allowing thirty days to file a counter-statement. Appeals from decisions of the Registrar regarding validity or infringement may be made to the High Court having jurisdiction; however, such appeals must demonstrate substantial question of law and not merely factual disagreement with the initial finding. A design right is subject to lapse fifteen years from the date of filing, unless renewed in accordance with prescribed fees.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a layout-design, being a design registered under this Act, shall obtain a license from the proprietor of such design, subject to terms mutually agreed upon between both parties; provided that where a breeder, meaning a person who has systematically modified an existing layout-design to create a new one, seeks such a license, the royalty payable shall reflect the incremental innovation embodied in the derivative work. Assignment of rights relating to any registered design shall be effected through a written instrument duly executed by both assignor and assignee, and such assignment must specify the scope of transferred rights, including territorial limitations if any. The proprietor may grant exclusive licenses concerning the layout-design or portions thereof, but all such grants shall be recorded with the appropriate authority as provided herein to ensure enforceability against third parties. Failure to obtain necessary licensing prior to commercial exploitation will constitute infringement under this Act and render the offender liable to legal remedies.

For the purposes of this Act, a cinematograph film shall mean any moving picture recorded on any medium, including magnetic tape, video cassette, optical disc or any other device capable of storing visual images, whether accompanied by sound or not. A cinematograph film is deemed to be a literary work as provided herein, and shall enjoy copyright protection accordingly. The term includes any still taken from such a film; however, such a still shall not be considered part of the original cinematograph film itself unless explicitly incorporated as a substantive element thereof. Any alteration or dubbing of a cinematograph film constitutes a derivative work subject to the rights of the owner, provided that fair dealing exceptions apply as elsewhere stipulated in this Act.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a “work” for the purposes of this Act and includes the various elements constituting such film. Registration of a cinematograph film with the Registrar of Copyrights shall vest in the producer ownership of copyright therein, subject to any contractual agreements to the contrary entered into prior to registration. The application for registration must include a still from the film, a synopsis of the story depicted, and details regarding all individuals possessing significant creative control over the production, including but not limited to the director and music composer. Provided that, where a cinematograph film is produced by a company or other corporate body, the applicant shall identify the officer authorized to act on behalf of such entity. Any alteration to a registered cinematograph film which substantially affects its original character may necessitate fresh registration as provided herein. Failure to register does not invalidate copyright but limits remedies available under this Act.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a “work” under this Act and enjoy copyright protection as such, subject to the provisions herein contained. The producer of a cinematograph film shall be considered the author thereof, notwithstanding any existing rights in underlying works incorporated within the film, including literary or musical works. Where a work is adapted for inclusion in a cinematograph film, the right to make further adaptations from the film itself remains with the film’s producer unless expressly assigned otherwise in writing. Any person who infringes the copyright in a cinematograph film by causing it to be exhibited in public without the consent of the copyright owner may be subject to statutory damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. A distributor or exhibitor acting in good faith and unaware of any infringement shall not be held liable, but must cease exhibition upon receiving notice from the rights holder. The term of protection for a cinematograph film shall be sixty years from the beginning of the calendar year following the year in which the film was first published.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a ‘work’ for the purposes of this Act and shall include any visual recording made on film or otherwise. The author of a cinematograph film is the producer, and in cases where the film is produced by a body corporate, that body corporate shall be deemed to be the author. Ownership of copyright in a cinematograph film subsists from the date on which the work is first fixed in its final form, subject to any contract to the contrary executed between the producer and another party concerning rights therein. 

Any person intending to make a copy of a cinematograph film for private use or for purposes as provided herein shall apply to the appropriate authority with full particulars of the intended copying. The competent authority may grant permission subject to such terms and conditions, including payment of royalty, as it deems fit. Failure to comply with these provisions constitutes an infringement under this Act and renders the offender liable to legal proceedings. Rights in a cinematograph film are distinct from rights in any underlying literary or dramatic work used in its production.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a ‘work’ for the purposes of this Act and enjoy copyright protection as such, subject to compliance with the provisions herein. The producer of a cinematograph film shall be considered the author thereof, provided that in cases where the film is produced under a contract of service or apprenticeship, the person directing the making of the film, if different from the producer, may also be deemed an author jointly with the producer. Any synchronization of a musical work or sound recording within a cinematograph film requires prior authorization from the copyright holder of such work or recording, unless expressly exempted as fair dealing for purposes permitted under this Act. Distribution of copies of a cinematograph film shall not infringe copyright if undertaken with the explicit consent of the owner, and any subsequent digital transmission must adhere to technological protection measures implemented by said owner. A person aggrieved by unauthorized reproduction or distribution may seek remedies as provided herein.

Any person who makes for sale or hire or distributes copies of a cinematograph film in contravention of the provisions of this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six years, and with fine. The making of an unauthorized copy of a cinematograph film, including digital reproduction, constitutes infringement as provided herein, and is subject to seizure by any officer duly authorized by the Central Government. Where a cinematograph film incorporates sound recordings, the rights in such sound recording shall be deemed to be co-extensive with those pertaining to the visual elements of the film, unless otherwise agreed between the copyright holder of the film and the owner of the sound recording. Any appeal against an order of confiscation may be made to the District Court having jurisdiction. Proof of direct knowledge of infringement need not be established if reasonable grounds exist to believe that such activity is occurring; however, good faith shall be considered a mitigating factor in determining penalties.

Any person desiring to make available for public viewing a cinematograph film, whether through theatrical exhibition, television broadcast, digital streaming, or other means, shall obtain a license from the copyright holder, unless expressly exempted as provided herein. The licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, including territorial restrictions and duration of rights granted. Assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film, or any portion thereof, requires written instrument duly executed by both parties and registered with the appropriate authority to be legally valid. A producer may grant exclusive licenses for specific formats or territories, reserving all other rights. Subject to the terms of the license or assignment, the copyright holder retains the right to control derivative works based upon the cinematograph film, including adaptations and sequels. Any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or public exhibition of a licensed or assigned cinematograph film constitutes an infringement under this Act and shall be subject to legal remedies. The rights in a sound recording incorporated within a cinematograph film are distinct from, but related to, the copyright in the film itself.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a ‘work’ for the purposes of this Act and enjoy copyright protection as such, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding ownership and duration. Any person claiming an interest in a cinematograph film, whether as producer, director, or principal photographer, may apply to the High Court alleging infringement of rights therein. Where a dispute arises concerning the authorship of a musical work incorporated within a cinematograph film, the court shall determine such authorship based on evidence presented regarding original composition and demonstrable creative contribution; provided that synchronization licenses obtained prior to production do not automatically confer ownership of copyright in the underlying musical work. Appeals from decisions of the High Court relating to claims of infringement concerning a cinematograph film may be made to the Supreme Court within sixty days of the judgment, subject to fulfilling requirements as prescribed by law for such appeals. The rights conferred by this Act shall extend to all modes of reproduction and communication to the public of the cinematograph film.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to include any visual recording on celluloid or other medium, and the rights therein vest initially with the producer. However, where a cinematograph film is produced based upon a pre-existing literary or artistic work, the owner of copyright in such work retains their respective rights, subject to the terms of contract between them and the producer. Any dispute regarding ownership of copyright in a cinematograph film, or concerning infringement thereof, may be brought before the High Court having jurisdiction. Should any party feel aggrieved by an order of the High Court, they shall have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order and demonstrating substantial questions of law requiring consideration on appeal; the manner applying appellate procedure will be as prescribed by the rules of said court. The producer’s rights are not absolute and remain subject to provisions relating to fair dealing as provided herein.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a ‘work’ for the purposes of this Act and is subject to copyright as provided herein. Registration of such films with the Registrar of Copyrights is compulsory prior to commercial exploitation, including public exhibition and distribution. An applicant seeking registration of a cinematograph film must submit a complete transcript of the visual and audio components alongside details of all underlying works incorporated therein, including literary or musical compositions. Where an application for registration claims priority based on a 73 convention application filed in a signatory country, such claim shall be accompanied by certified copies demonstrating the original filing date and scope of protection sought abroad. The Registrar may require clarification regarding ownership or originality before granting a certificate of registration; failure to respond within thirty days may result in rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal as prescribed.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to be a ‘work’ for the purposes of this Act and enjoy copyright protection as such, subject to the provisions herein contained. The author of a cinematograph film shall be the producer thereof, and in the case of a film where the producer is a body corporate, that body shall be deemed to be the author. Any person intending to make a copy of an existing cinematograph film for purposes permitted under this Act, including educational or research use, may apply to the copyright owner for a license; failing agreement on reasonable terms, recourse lies with the High Court as provided herein. 

Where a ‘reference use mark’ is affixed to a cinematograph film indicating its availability for specific non-commercial uses, such display shall not be construed as an express or implied waiver of any rights otherwise available under this Act, but may be considered by a court in determining fair dealing. The copyright owner retains the right to control derivative works and adaptations of the cinematograph film, notwithstanding any permitted use.

An exclusive licence granted under this Act shall confer upon the licensee, subject to the terms of the contract between the licensor and the licensee, all rights in the copyright that were by this Act vested in the licensor. Such a licence shall extinguish any right of the owner to grant further licences in respect of the same work or class of works, unless expressly reserved within the instrument creating the exclusive licence. A non-exclusive licence however permits the copyright owner to license the same work to multiple parties concurrently. Where an exclusive licence is granted for a defined period, upon expiry of that period, all rights revert to the licensor, subject to any accrued contractual obligations. Any assignment of an exclusive licence shall be governed by provisions relating to copyright assignments as provided herein.

Any person intending to grant an exclusive licence in respect of a copyright work shall register such assignment with the Registrar of Copyrights according to procedure established under this Act. The application for registration of an exclusive licence shall be accompanied by certified copies of the instrument granting such licence, and shall clearly delineate the scope of rights exclusively licensed, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, performance, and adaptation. Registration of an exclusive licence creates a presumption of validity against third parties, subject to proof of fraud or misrepresentation. The Registrar may require further evidence as deemed necessary to ascertain the genuineness and completeness of the application. An exclusive licensee shall be entitled to all rights and remedies available to the copyright owner in respect of the exclusively licensed rights, provided that such entitlement is not otherwise restricted by the terms of the assignment agreement. Failure to register an exclusive licence does not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against certain parties.

Any person possessing copyright in a work may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an exclusive licence for the exercise of any right comprised in the copyright. Such exclusive licence shall be enforceable as if it were an assignment of the copyright, but only insofar as the rights specifically granted are concerned and shall not prejudice the licensor’s right to exploit those rights not expressly transferred. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensor may nevertheless authorize other persons to exercise such rights subject to terms that do not materially diminish the value of the licensed rights. Any breach of condition in an exclusive licence agreement shall entitle the licensee to seek specific performance or claim damages as provided herein. The grant of an exclusive license does not divest the copyright owner of their right to take legal action against any infringement committed by a third party, and such actions may be pursued independently of the licensee’s own remedies. Provided that, the licensor shall promptly inform the licensee of any intended legal proceedings.

Any person possessing copyright in a work may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an exclusive licence for the doing of any act which would otherwise constitute an infringement of that copyright. Such exclusive licence shall be construed as transferring to the licensee all rights necessary for exercising the licensed acts, save where expressly reserved by the licensor. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the licensor may not itself exploit the copyrighted work in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the license, provided that such inconsistency does not prejudice the licensee’s exercise of their rights. 

Any dispute concerning the scope or validity of an exclusive licence shall be determined by the appropriate High Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The grant of an exclusive licence may specify territorial limitations and duration; absent any such specification, it shall be deemed to extend throughout India for the remaining term of copyright subsisting in the work. A non-exclusive license does not confer these rights.

Any person intending to grant an exclusive licence relating to copyright in a work shall furnish a statement in writing specifying the nature of the interest granted, the duration for which such licence is given, the territory within which it operates, and the terms subject to which said licence may be exercised. The licensor shall ensure that any limitations on the exercise of rights under the exclusive licence are clearly delineated in the written instrument constituting the grant. Provided that, an exclusive licence granted without a defined duration or territorial scope will be construed as perpetual and worldwide respectively, unless successfully challenged before a competent court demonstrating justifiable cause for such omission. Any transfer of an exclusive licence shall require prior notification to all known assignees of the copyright itself, subject to confidentiality obligations as agreed upon between parties. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the exclusive licence voidable at the option of the copyright owner or any affected assignee.

Any person desiring to grant an exclusive licence in respect of a work shall furnish particulars thereof in writing to the Registrar of Copyrights, who shall maintain a Register of such licences open for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with this requirement renders the purported exclusive licence void *ab initio*, and any infringement committed by a third party relying on such invalid license shall not be actionable under this Act. However, an exclusive licensee may initiate proceedings for infringement independently of the copyright owner, provided that they demonstrate substantial investment in exploiting the licensed rights. Any false declaration made in relation to particulars furnished under this provision shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause shown, revoke any registration found to be based on fraudulent information or non-compliance with these provisions.

Any person possessing copyright in a cinematograph film may grant an exclusive licence to another party for the communication to the public of such film through digital platforms, subject to the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon between the parties. Such exclusive licence shall specify the territorial extent, duration, and scope of permitted exploitation, including but not limited to streaming, downloading, and any other forms of online distribution. Where an exclusive licence is granted, the copyright owner shall retain the right to enforce the provisions of this Act against any unauthorized infringement occurring outside the terms of said license. Any assignment of such exclusive licence shall be in writing and registered with the relevant registry as provided herein, failing which it will not be valid against third parties claiming interest in the cinematograph film. The licensee may further sub-license their rights only with prior written consent from the copyright owner; however, any royalty sharing arrangement arising from such sub-licensing remains subject to the original agreement between the copyright owner and the initial licensee.

Any person claiming an interest in copyright may apply to the High Court for a determination as to whether an exclusive licence granted under this Act is validly subsisting. Such application shall be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant documentation evidencing the alleged grant and consideration, failing which it shall not be entertained. Where the court determines that a valid exclusive licence exists, any infringement committed thereafter shall be actionable solely by the licensor or the licensee, as mutually agreed upon in writing; provided that if no such agreement is present, recourse shall lie with the copyright owner of record. Any aggrieved party may appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of the High Court’s judgment, subject to satisfying all procedural requirements for appeals before that court. The burden of proof regarding the scope and limitations of any exclusive licence shall rest upon the party asserting its validity.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, where a breeder, through diligent effort and skill, has developed a new variety of plant capable of commercial exploitation, an exclusive licence pertaining to the propagation and sale of said variety may be granted by the Central Government. Such grant shall be subject to the condition that the breeder demonstrates substantial novelty and distinctiveness as per established botanical protocols, and further, proves genuine economic benefit accruing to Indian agriculture. Any dispute regarding the validity of such demonstration or the scope of the exclusive licence shall first be adjudicated by a specially constituted committee of horticultural experts appointed by the Government. An appeal from any decision of said committee lies before the High Court having territorial jurisdiction, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the committee’s order and accompanied by a non-refundable fee as prescribed. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the licence voidable at the discretion of the Central Government.

Any person claiming ownership over a registered geographical indication shall maintain a register detailing authorized users, subject to verification by the Geographical Indications Registry at intervals not exceeding five years. Failure to update this register or providing materially false information therein constitutes an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, upon reasonable suspicion of misuse or fraudulent application relating to a registration geographical indication, initiate an inquiry and demand production of relevant records from any applicant or registered proprietor. Any obstruction of such inquiry, or refusal to provide requested documentation, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per instance. A false claim to the exclusive right to use a geographical indication, even if unregistered, is also actionable under this Act, with remedies including injunction and damages.

An artistic work shall include paintings, sculptures, drawings, engravings, photographs, works of architecture and other works of artistic craftsmanship. For the purposes of this Act, an artistic work need not be itself copyright subject matter but must demonstrate some degree of creative skill and judgment in its creation. A work produced by a purely mechanical process, however, is generally excluded from protection as an artistic work unless substantial human intervention occurs during production. Subject to the provisions herein, the creator of an artistic work shall be considered the first owner of the copyright therein; provided that where any such work is commissioned, ownership may vest with the commissioning party as mutually agreed upon in writing. Any modification or alteration to a registered artistic work requires notification to the Registrar of Copyrights.

An artistic work, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall include paintings, sculptures, drawings, engravings, photographs and works of architecture. A work of applied art, whether it is functional in nature or not, may also qualify as an artistic work provided that aesthetic considerations are demonstrably paramount in its creation. Registration of an artistic work requires full particulars of the author and claimant, along with a clear representation of the work itself; such representation shall be accompanied by a statement confirming originality. Where an artistic work is created during employment pursuant to a contract of service, the employer shall be deemed the first owner of copyright subject to any agreement to the contrary. Any person claiming ownership of rights in an unregistered artistic work may apply for registration as provided herein, and upon satisfactory verification, a certificate of registration shall be issued. The register maintained under this Act is prima facie evidence of facts stated therein.

An artistic work shall be protected under this Act irrespective of its aesthetic merit and includes paintings, sculptures, drawings, engravings, photographs, works of architecture and other similar creations. The author of an artistic work is generally the artist who creates it; however, in cases where a photograph is taken on commission or through employment, the person commissioning or employing the photographer shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein, subject to contractual provisions otherwise agreed upon. Any person alleging infringement of rights in an artistic work may apply to the District Court for injunctive relief and damages. Damages assessed shall consider actual loss suffered by the right holder, as well as any profits unjustly gained by the infringer. Fair dealing with an artistic work for purposes such as criticism or review is permitted, provided that sufficient acknowledgement is made and it does not substantially prejudice the legitimate rights of the copyright owner. The reproduction of an artistic work for private use shall not constitute infringement unless done commercially.

An artistic work shall be deemed to include paintings, sculptures, drawings, engravings, photographs, works of architecture and other works of artistic craftsmanship, whether two-dimensional or three-dimensional. For the purposes of this Act, a photograph includes pictorial representations produced by any means whatsoever, including digital imaging techniques; provided that such photograph is original in character. The originality requirement shall not extend to mere mechanical reproduction of an existing work but must demonstrate some degree of creative skill and judgment exercised in capturing the image or selecting its elements. 

Any individual claiming ownership of an artistic work may register it with the Registrar of Copyrights, subject to verification of authorship and compliance with prescribed formalities as provided herein. Registration shall constitute *prima facie* evidence of copyright; however, absence thereof does not prejudice the right of the author to enforce their rights under this Act. A work that is purely mechanical or lacking in artistic merit will not qualify as an artistic work for the purposes of protection.

An artistic work shall be deemed to include paintings, sculptures, and drawings, regardless of medium, and encompasses works of architecture insofar as they are artistic. Any model or design, whether two-dimensional or three-dimensional, registered under this Act shall also constitute an artistic work, provided that such registration is valid and subsisting at the time of assertion of right. The creator of an artistic work shall be considered the author, subject to any contractual agreement assigning rights as provided herein. Where an artistic work is commissioned, ownership of copyright may vest with the commissioner, unless otherwise agreed in writing between the parties. Any reproduction or adaptation of a registered artistic work without lawful authorization constitutes infringement and is actionable under this Act. A photograph shall be considered an artistic work insofar as it possesses aesthetic merit and creative skill beyond mere mechanical capture.

Any person who, without lawful justification and with intent to deceive, publishes, exhibits, distributes, or causes to be published, exhibited, or distributed an artistic work—being a painting, sculpture, drawing, engraving, photograph, architectural work, or other work of artistic craftsmanship—that is substantially similar to a registered artistic work as provided herein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and a fine. Where the offence involves commercial exploitation of the infringing artistic work, the court may also order seizure of all infringing copies and materials used in the commission of the offense. Any person assisting in such infringement, including those involved in the manufacture or sale of counterfeit works, shall be deemed an abettor and subject to equivalent penalties. A second or subsequent offence under this Act shall carry a minimum imprisonment term of one year.

Any person desiring to assign the copyright in an artistic work shall execute an instrument in writing under his hand signifying such assignment and specifying clearly the scope of rights assigned. Such assignment may be for all rights or some only, and shall be subject to the provisions contained herein regarding voluntary licensing. Where an artistic work is created pursuant to a contract of service or apprenticeship, it shall be deemed that the copyright therein vests initially with the employer or master, unless otherwise agreed in writing. However, the author of such artistic work retains the right to claim authorship even after assignment, subject to any contractual stipulations to the contrary. Any subsequent assignment by the assignee shall require prior written notice to the original creator of the artistic work and a reasonable opportunity for them to match the terms offered. A license granted under this Act may be exclusive or non-exclusive, territorial or worldwide, and is freely transferable unless expressly restricted in the licensing agreement.

An artistic work, including a painting, sculpture, photograph, engraving, or architectural work, shall be protected under this Act, provided that such work possesses sufficient originality in its conception and execution. However, mere tracing of an existing work, even with minor modifications, does not constitute original artistic creation and is expressly excluded from protection as provided herein. A claim of authorship regarding an artistic work may be disputed if evidence demonstrates substantial derivation from a pre-existing source, notwithstanding any assertion of independent skill and labour. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the assessing officer concerning originality shall have recourse to appeal before the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to timelines stipulated in rules framed under this Act. The burden of proving sufficient originality rests with the claimant. Architectural works include both artistic designs and functional blueprints; however, purely utilitarian aspects are not protectable as artistic works.

An artistic work shall be deemed to include paintings, sculptures, and works of artistic craftsmanship, but does not encompass photographs unless meeting the criteria of originality as established under this Act. Where an artistic work incorporates a design registered layout—specifically concerning integrated circuits—compliance with the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000 is mandatory for asserting exclusive rights therein. Any reproduction or adaptation of such a combined work shall be subject to the provisions relating to both copyright and layout-design registration, as applicable. It is clarified that mere mechanical application of a design registered layout to an artistic work does not constitute sufficient originality in itself; substantial modification or creative input must be demonstrated. The rights conferred by this Act are conditional upon proper notice being affixed to copies of the artistic work where reasonably practicable, and failure to do so may affect remedies available under this Act. Any person claiming copyright in an artistic work shall maintain adequate records proving authorship and date of creation.

Any person desiring to assign or license the copyright in an artistic work, being a painting depicting a recognizable name or logo used for commercial purposes, shall submit a detailed statement of assignment or licensing terms to the Registrar of Copyrights. Such statement shall clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and derivative works. Assignment of copyright in such an artistic work requires the explicit consent of the entity associated with the name or logo portrayed therein, unless it is demonstrated that said portrayal falls under fair dealing as provided herein. A license granted may be exclusive or non-exclusive, territorial or worldwide, subject to a defined duration and royalty structure. Failure to fully disclose all material terms relating to commercial exploitation of both the artistic work and the associated name shall render the assignment or license voidable at the option of any aggrieved party. The Registrar may require further clarification or documentation as deemed necessary to ensure compliance with this Act.

Royalties arising from the licensing of copyrights are governed by agreements negotiated between parties, subject to the provisions contained herein. A licensee utilising copyrighted material as provided under this Act shall remit to the owner of copyright a royalty determined by mutual consent or, in the absence thereof, fixed by an appropriate authority following established principles of equitable remuneration. The rate of royalty may be expressed as a percentage of gross sales, net profits, or any other mutually agreed metric, and shall be payable at intervals specified within the licensing agreement. Provided that, where a license is granted for translation, adaptation, or reproduction in another form, the royalty structure may account for differing production costs and market values. Failure to remit earned royalties constitutes grounds for legal recourse as outlined elsewhere under this Act.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a copyrighted work through licensing or other means, shall register the terms of such exploitation with the Registrar of Copyrights to ensure proper accounting of remuneration due to the owner. Registration of royalty rates is mandatory for all licenses exceeding a period of one year, and shall include details regarding the basis of calculation, frequency of payment, and any deductions permissible as provided herein. The copyright owner may, subject to mutual agreement, specify different royalty structures for various modes of exploitation including reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation. Provided that where a license is terminated prematurely by either party, final accounting of all accrued royalties shall be completed within ninety days from the date of termination and any dispute regarding such accounting shall be resolved through arbitration. Failure to register the terms may result in penalties as determined by the Registrar.

Every licensee under this Act shall be entitled to receive royalty payments for the use of copyrighted works as agreed upon with the owner, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Where such an agreement fails to explicitly define the rate or method of calculating royalty, a reasonable royalty shall be determined having regard to prevailing industry standards and comparable licenses. The copyright owner may withhold payment of royalty only upon demonstration of insufficient sales figures or legitimate deductions as permitted under this Act; any undue delay in remittance shall attract interest at a rate not exceeding twelve percent per annum from the date on which payment became due. Should a dispute arise regarding the amount of royalty payable, either party may apply to the High Court for adjudication and such court’s decision shall be final and binding. Failure to remit rightfully determined royalties constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act, entitling the licensee to damages and injunctive relief.

The owner of a copyright may license another to exercise any or all of the rights conferred by this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as mutually agreed upon between the parties; however, every such license shall be construed as granting a right to receive reasonable royalty commensurate with the nature and extent of use authorized. Where a license is granted for a defined period, the determination of royalty shall account for the remaining useful life of the copyright, and may provide for periodic review thereof based on prevailing market conditions or demonstrable increases in commercial exploitation. 

Provided that, if the licensee substantially fails to exploit the licensed rights within a reasonable timeframe as determined by mutual agreement or, failing such agreement, by an arbitral tribunal appointed under the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the licensor may terminate the license subject to providing adequate notice. Any dispute regarding the appropriate amount of royalty or the interpretation of licensing terms shall be resolved through negotiation; if unresolved, recourse may be had to mediation as a prerequisite for judicial intervention.

The owner of a copyrighted work licensed for commercial exploitation shall be entitled to receive equitable remuneration determined as provided herein. Any agreement relating to licensing, including those concerning cinematograph films or sound recordings, must clearly articulate the method of calculating royalty payments, specifying whether such calculation is based on gross sales, net profits, or any other mutually agreed metric. Subject to the terms of the license, a statement of accounts detailing all revenues derived from the exploitation of the copyrighted work shall be furnished by the licensee to the copyright owner within sixty days of the close of each accounting period. Should discrepancies arise regarding royalty calculations or account statements, either party may seek resolution through arbitration conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Failure to provide a clear and accurate statement of accounts shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license, provided that reasonable opportunity for rectification is first afforded.

Any person making or importing an article incorporating a copyrighted work, subject to licensing terms as provided herein, shall remit all due royalties to the owner of the copyright within thirty days of sale or import, whichever is earlier. Failure to do so shall constitute a breach of contract and render the defaulting party liable to pay a late fee equivalent to two percent per month on the outstanding royalty amount. Should the accumulated overdue royalty exceed ten thousand rupees, the aggrieved copyright owner may apply directly to the District Court for an order directing immediate payment, accompanied by costs not exceeding five thousand rupees. Any falsification of sales records intended to reduce calculated royalty payments shall be deemed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year or a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees, or both. The determination of reasonable royalty rates may consider prevailing industry standards and the nature of the copyrighted work itself.

Any transfer of ownership concerning cinematograph films as provided herein shall be subject to a written agreement detailing the scope of rights conveyed, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation. Such agreements must explicitly state whether the transfer is absolute or limited in duration or territory. Where the transfer constitutes a license rather than an assignment, the licensor shall be entitled to receive royalty payments calculated as a percentage of gross revenues derived from the exploitation of said cinematograph film. The rate of such royalty shall not be less than that prescribed by rules made under this Act and may be adjusted subject to mutual agreement between parties. Provided that, in cases where the license is exclusive, the licensor retains the right to audit the licensee’s accounts for verification of reported revenues and accurate calculation of royalty due. Failure to provide access for such audit shall constitute a breach of contract. Any dispute regarding the determination of appropriate royalty rates or payment schedules may be resolved through arbitration as mutually agreed upon by both parties.

Any licensee under this Act, aggrieved by an inadequate or unfairly determined rate of royalty payable for use of copyrighted material, may submit a representation to the appropriate District Court outlining grounds for revision of said rates. Such representations shall be accompanied by full particulars of the licensing agreement, including evidence demonstrating commercial viability and prevailing industry standards for comparable licenses. The Court, subject to verification of submitted documentation and consideration of arguments from both parties, may direct recalculation of royalty payments based on principles of equitable remuneration. Provided that, any determination made under this provision shall not be retrospective beyond a period of twelve months preceding the date of representation. An appeal against such order lies before the High Court, provided it is filed within sixty days of the District Court’s decision and concerns a substantial question of law relating to the assessment of royalty or interpretation of licensing terms.

Any person engaging in the commercial exploitation of seeds or varieties registered under the Seeds Act, 1966, where such seed propagation relies upon copyrighted genetic material, shall be liable to pay royalty to the copyright holder as determined by an agreement freely negotiated between parties. Provided that, if no such agreement exists, and a dispute arises concerning reasonable royalty rates, application may be made to the Agriculture Commissioner for determination of said rates, subject to evidence demonstrating both the commercial value derived from the copyrighted material and the costs incurred in its development. Failure to remit assessed royalty within ninety days of notification by the Agriculture Commissioner shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. Any person knowingly providing false information to the Agriculture Commissioner as provided herein shall be similarly penalized, and all royalties unpaid at the time of conviction become immediately due and payable with interest accrued at twelve percent per annum.

Any licensee under this Act shall pay to the owner of the copyright, or to his legal representative where transmission has occurred by operation of law or testamentary disposition, a royalty determined as mutually agreed upon between the parties at the time of granting the license. Provided that in the absence of such mutual agreement, the royalty shall be ascertainable based on prevailing industry standards for comparable licenses and usages, taking into account the nature of the copyrighted work and the extent of permitted exploitation. The copyright owner may demand an accounting of receipts related to the licensed work at reasonable intervals, not exceeding once per calendar year, subject to providing a minimum of thirty days’ prior notice. Should any dispute arise regarding the calculation or payment of royalty, either party may seek resolution through arbitration conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Failure to remit earned royalties within sixty days of accounting shall constitute a breach of the licensing agreement as provided herein.

Royalties payable for the exploitation of copyrighted works shall be determined by mutual agreement between the owner of the copyright and the user, subject to provisions contained within licensing agreements or as otherwise provided herein. Where such agreement cannot be reached, the Copyright Societies Registrar may, upon application by either party and after due inquiry, determine a fair and equitable royalty rate considering prevailing industry standards and the nature of the exploitation. Any collective administration organization authorized to administer rights in works shall distribute royalties collected amongst copyright owners according to pre-established rules transparently communicated to members. Provided that, disputes regarding distribution of royalties may be addressed through established grievance redressal mechanisms within such organizations, failing which recourse lies with appropriate legal forums. The rate so determined shall remain valid for a period not exceeding three years unless renegotiated.

An invention shall be deemed to involve an inventive step, as provided herein, if it is not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field, having regard to the existing knowledge. Existing knowledge shall encompass both public knowledge and any matter disclosed in oral presentations or through use prior to the date of filing. However, mere aggregation of previously known elements shall not constitute an inventive step unless such combination produces synergistic effects resulting in unexpected advantages. A finding of non-obviousness may consider objective indicators of technical advance, including but not limited to long-felt but unsolved needs, commercial success, or failure of others. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a trivial modification of a known process or product shall not be considered an inventive step.

An application for a patent shall disclose, in a manner clear and complete enough for a person skilled in the relevant art to carry out the invention, the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. An invention must possess an inventive step to be eligible for registration under this Act; however, mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance, even if novel, shall not constitute an inventive step. The assessment of whether an invention involves an inventive step requires consideration of existing knowledge common to a person skilled in the art and determination that the invention is not obvious given such knowledge. Evidence of commercial success may be considered as corroborating evidence of non-obviousness, subject to satisfying other requirements as provided herein. A combination of previously known elements shall not constitute an inventive step unless it produces synergistic effects beyond the sum of its parts or solves a long-felt but unresolved need in the art.

A patent application shall be deemed to lack an inventive step if the subject matter claimed is obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field, considering existing prior art. However, such assessment shall not diminish from the rights of the applicant where combinations of previously known elements produce unexpected results or synergistic effects, provided that evidence demonstrating said effect is submitted with the application and accepted by the Controller. Any party alleging lack of inventive step may submit evidence of prior art to the Controller during examination as provided herein. Should a patent be granted despite subsequent proof establishing obviousness, any aggrieved person may apply for revocation before the High Court, subject to limitations periods prescribed under this Act. The burden of proving non-obviousness rests with the applicant or patentee and failure to discharge such burden shall constitute grounds for rejection or revocation. A mere discovery lacking technical advancement does not qualify as an invention deserving protection.

An application for a patent shall be examined by the Controller, with due regard to the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where an applicant claims an invention, it shall be demonstrated that said invention possesses an inventive step, being a feature which constitutes technical advance as compared to existing knowledge. Such existing knowledge includes anything publicly known anywhere in the world before the date of the application, whether by written or oral disclosure, by use or otherwise. A combination of previously known elements may constitute an inventive step if such combination produces a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual components. However, mere substitution of one equivalent for another shall not be considered to involve an inventive step. The burden of proving the existence of said inventive step rests upon the applicant and must be substantiated with evidence acceptable under these rules; failure to do so may result in rejection of the application as provided herein. Any objection raised by the Controller regarding lack of inventive step shall be communicated to the applicant, affording them opportunity for response.

An application for a patent shall be examined, inter alia, with respect to whether the claimed subject matter involves an inventive step. An invention shall be deemed to involve an inventive step if it exhibits any technical advance over existing knowledge and does not render the invention obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art. Consideration shall be given to all matters made available to the public before the priority date of the claim, including oral disclosures and use. However, mere aggregation of known elements, even if resulting in a new combination, shall not constitute an inventive step unless such combination produces unexpected or enhanced effects. 

Provided that, evidence demonstrating commercial success, long-felt but unmet need, or failure of others may be considered as corroborating evidence supporting the existence of an inventive step, subject to satisfying other requirements as provided herein. A technical effect must be clearly demonstrable and not merely speculative for a finding of non-obviousness.

Any person claiming entitlement to a patent shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Controller, an inventive step possessed by the claimed invention. Failure to adequately establish this inventive step, assessed against existing prior art and common knowledge within the relevant technical field, shall constitute grounds for rejection of the application as provided herein. A mere combination of known elements, without demonstrable synergistic effect or unexpected result, will not satisfy the requirement of an inventive step. Furthermore, any modification deemed obvious to a person skilled in the art—considering available resources and standard practices—shall negate a claim to novelty based on said modification. Any false representation made regarding the existence of such inventive step shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated offences under this Act may result in revocation of existing patents held by the offender, subject to judicial review.

Any assignment of the right, title, and interest in a patent application or a patent shall be made by an instrument in writing duly executed by the assignor and assignee. Such instrument shall clearly identify the invention subject to assignment, including detailed technical specifications as originally filed, and any subsequent amendments accepted under this Act. Where an inventor assigns their rights to another person or entity, it shall be deemed that such assignment includes the right to pursue all claims embodying an inventive step relating to said invention. However, a further assignment of these specifically claimed inventive steps may only occur with express written consent from the original inventor, subject to reasonable royalties as determined by arbitration. Any licensing agreement concerning rights derived from this assigned inventive step shall be consistent with the terms of the initial assignment and must not diminish the scope of protection afforded under this Act. Failure to adhere to these provisions renders any subsequent transfer voidable at the option of the original inventor or their legal representatives.

A claim for patentability shall be subject to examination regarding novelty and, critically, an inventive step. Where an application alleges a combination of previously known elements, the onus lies on the applicant to demonstrate that such a combination results in synergy—that is, an effect greater than the sum of its parts—and constitutes an inventive step as provided herein. An objection raised by the Controller regarding lack of inventive step may be rebutted by evidence establishing non-obviousness to a person skilled in the art, considering common general knowledge and publicly available information. However, mere substitution of one known element for another without demonstrable advantage shall not suffice to establish inventiveness. Any appeal against a decision refusing patentability on grounds of lacking an inventive step shall be heard by the Appellate Board, which may request further evidence or expert opinion to ascertain whether the claimed invention possesses sufficient distinguishing features and is non-obvious.

Any patent application claiming an invention lacking a demonstrable inventive step shall be deemed invalid, and the applicant may be subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, if the claimed invention is substantially similar to a prior artistic composition protected by copyright, and where applicable, relevant royalty or copyright society fee remains unpaid as determined by the appropriate authority, the penalty may be doubled. Furthermore, any person knowingly submitting such an application with intent to defraud shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. All penalties levied under this Act shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue. The Controller of Patents may, subject to established procedure, initiate investigations into suspected violations and impose provisional penalties pending full adjudication.

Any assignment of rights relating to a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing registered with the Trade Marks Registrar as provided herein. Such registration shall be subject to the condition that the assignee undertakes to prosecute the application, if any, diligently and to exercise all reasonable skill and dispatch in securing a patent. Where a license is granted under this Act permitting another person to work a patented invention, the terms of such license including royalty payments and duration, must clearly define the scope of permitted use and shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registrar within six months of its execution. A determination of whether an invention possesses an inventive step shall consider not only prior art but also any publicly known practice or combination thereof; a mere alteration to existing technology will not suffice unless it demonstrates a non-obvious advancement. Failure to comply with these registration requirements may render the assignment or license unenforceable.

A claim for patentability shall be assessed considering whether it embodies an inventive step, meaning a feature which demonstrates technical advance over known art, possesses economic significance, or exhibits both qualities and is non-obvious to a person ordinarily skilled in the relevant field. An application seeking to extend the scope of a previously patented invention through a patent addition, as provided herein, shall be subject to the same requirements regarding inventive step as an original claim. However, such addition must relate directly to the main invention and not independently stand as a separate invention itself. The Controller may require proof demonstrating that the claimed patent addition satisfies this requirement and possesses sufficient novelty and an inventive step distinct from the parent patent. Failure to demonstrate either shall render the application for the patent addition ineligible for grant under this Act, irrespective of the validity of the primary patent.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘geographical indication relation’ shall exist where goods originate from a specific geographical area and possess qualities, reputation, or characteristics essentially attributable to that place. Such a connection need not be exclusively causal; it is sufficient if there exists a strong link between the goods and their origin in terms of natural factors, human skills developed over generations, or traditional practices. Where a product derives its essential qualities from both geographical origin and specific processing techniques, the latter shall be considered integral to establishing this relation. However, mere packaging or marketing referencing a place does not, by itself, constitute a geographical indication relation as provided herein; demonstrable characteristics linked to the territory are required. Any claim of such relation must be substantiated with evidence acceptable under established procedures.

A producer seeking registration of a geographical indication shall demonstrate a demonstrable connection between the goods and the specified geographical area, establishing that qualities or reputation of the goods are intrinsically linked to their origin. Such connection may be evidenced by historical documentation proving traditional production methods unique to that region, or expert testimony detailing how local environmental factors contribute to characteristics not replicable elsewhere. The applicant must further prove consistent quality maintained through practices reflecting this geographical indication relation and shall submit a detailed register of producers within the defined territory. Registration is subject to verification by the Registrar confirming genuine origin and adherence to established standards. Provided that where goods are processed, a substantial part of processing must occur within the identified geographical area to maintain the integrity of the claimed link; otherwise, registration may be refused or revoked as provided herein.

Any person claiming an injury resulting from the unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication, or any act in contravention of the provisions relating to geographical indication relation, shall have the right to institute civil proceedings for injunction, damages, and account of profits. The quantum of damages awarded shall not be less than such amount as may be specified in the rules made under this Act, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the claimant due to the infringement. Where proof of actual damage or profit is difficult to establish, the court may determine damages based on a reasonable royalty rate applicable to goods bearing the impugned geographical indication relation. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an authorized user may seek relief against any person who offers for sale, sells, or otherwise deals in goods with a false or deceptively similar geographical indication. Such proceedings shall be subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and evidence admitted therein shall be governed by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The court may also order delivery for destruction of infringing goods.

A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions contained herein, apply to the Registrar for an order restraining any person from dealing in goods bearing a false or deceptive indication of origin. Any application under this Act shall be accompanied by such evidence as is necessary to establish a clear geographical indication relation between the goods and the specified region. The applicant shall demonstrate that the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to their geographical origin and that said origin contributes to uniqueness. 

Provided that where a claim of geographical indication relation is based on traditional knowledge, evidence thereof must be submitted in a manner acceptable to the Registrar, including but not limited to documented practices and expert testimony. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant as deemed necessary for proper adjudication. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to such appellate authority as is prescribed.

A geographical indication, for the purposes of registration and protection under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear connection to the goods’ origin in a specific territory or locality within India. This connection must be established through reputation, quality, or any other characteristic that is essentially attributable to said place of origin. Where a proposed geographical indication relates to agricultural goods, demonstrable evidence of traditional knowledge connected to production and processing practices prevalent in the specified region shall strengthen the claim of geographical indication relation. Any applicant seeking registration shall submit proof substantiating this link, including historical records or expert testimony as provided herein. Provided that, if the geographical indication incorporates a pre-existing registered trademark, consent of the trademark holder is mandatory for successful registration. Failure to adequately demonstrate geographical indication relation will render the application liable for rejection and may preclude future applications concerning similar goods originating from the same territory.

Any person who falsely represents goods as originating from a specific geographical area, thereby creating a false geographical indication relation, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act. Such misrepresentation includes the use of any name, sign, or symbol which indicates a false provenance in connection with the sale or distribution of goods. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication proves that another party has engaged in such deceptive practices intending to mislead consumers regarding the true origin of the goods, the adjudicating officer may impose a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any goods found to bear such falsely applied geographical indications shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, subject to investigation and proof of intent.

Any assignment of the right to use a registered geographical indication, or any license to deal with such right, shall be subject to provisions ensuring continued quality control in accordance with the standards established for goods originating from the specified geographical area. The proprietor of a geographical indication may grant licenses to producers within that region who adhere to these prescribed standards, and such licensing agreements shall specify the duration, territorial scope, and royalty payable. Where a license is granted exclusively to one or more producers, the remaining producers within the geographical area retain the right to apply for non-exclusive licenses under equitable terms. Any transfer of rights relating to a registered geographical indication must be recorded with the Registry; failure to do so shall render such assignment or license unenforceable. A demonstrable geographical indication relation between the goods and their origin is fundamental to any valid licensing arrangement, and the licensor remains responsible for verifying ongoing compliance by licensees. The Registrar may revoke licenses found in violation of these provisions as provided herein.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, relating to goods originating from a defined area and possessing qualities or reputation attributable to that origin, may apply to the Registrar for an order restraining the infringing conduct. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a clear geographical indication relation between the specified goods and their place of origin, including historical documentation establishing traditional production methods unique to that region. The Registrar, upon review, may issue an interim injunction pending a full hearing; however, such injunction may be discharged if the applicant fails to demonstrate prima facie case or causes undue delay in proceedings. Any aggrieved party against an order of the Registrar may prefer an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of said order, subject to deposit of prescribed fees and fulfillment of other conditions as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person claiming an injury resulting from the unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication relation, whether by way of direct infringement or colourable variation thereof, may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the offending goods are sold or manufactured. The Central Government shall, upon receiving credible evidence of widespread and serious infringements affecting multiple registered geographical indications, have the power to issue cease and desist orders directly to entities engaged in such unlawful activity, irrespective of any pending private litigation. Any profits accruing from the sale of counterfeit goods bearing a falsely applied geographical indication shall be recoverable by way of damages, subject to verification through account books and other relevant documentation. Provided that, the claimant demonstrates a direct nexus between the unauthorized use and quantifiable economic loss. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining further infringement and order the destruction or forfeiture of infringing goods.

For the purposes of this Act, "package" shall mean any enclosure, wrapping, container or covering used for containing, protecting, promoting or delivering goods, whether such enclosure is composed of paperboard, plastic, metal, glass or any other material and includes all labels, tags, bands, seals and markings affixed to or printed on such enclosure. A package may incorporate a trade mark as an integral part of its design or presentation, subject to the provisions relating to artistic works under this Act. Where a package is identical in form and material to that customarily used for similar goods, it shall not be considered distinctive unless additional elements confer distinctiveness. Any alteration to a registered package requiring re-registration shall follow procedures as provided herein.

A package bearing a representation of a trade mark, even if not itself a trade mark, may be registered as a trade mark under this Act provided that such representation is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services associated with it. An application for registration of a package shall include a clear depiction of its form and materials alongside details of the trade mark represented thereon. The Registrar may require evidence establishing genuine use of the package in relation to the goods or services specified, subject to fulfilling requirements as provided herein regarding user declarations. Registration of a package does not confer exclusive rights over the underlying goods contained within unless those goods themselves are also protected by separate registrations or other legal means. Any alteration to the registered package affecting the trade mark representation shall necessitate an application for amendment under these rules.

Any person who applies a deceptive package likely to cause confusion as to the nature, origin, quality or characteristics of goods shall be liable to proceedings for infringement under this Act. A “package” for the purposes of this Act includes all forms of encasement, wrapping, and presentation of goods, whether natural or artificial, and extends to any marking or labelling affixed thereto. Where a registered trade mark owner demonstrates that another party has applied their mark—or a deceptively similar mark—to packaging intended for sale, distribution, or export, an injunction may be granted restraining such acts. The proprietor shall also have the right to claim damages sustained as a consequence of such infringement and seek recovery of costs associated with investigating and remedying the deceptive practice. Provided that, if the defendant proves they acted without knowledge of the registered trade mark and exercised due diligence in ascertaining its validity, the court may reduce or waive damages accordingly. Any goods found bearing infringing packaging may be ordered for destruction by a competent authority as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to institute legal proceedings for infringement where any other person uses a deceptive or confusingly similar mark on goods or services concerning which the trade mark is registered. Such rights extend to use of the mark not only on the goods themselves, but also upon their packaging and in connection with any business carried out under that mark. For the purposes of this Act, “package” shall mean any enclosure, wrapping, container, or covering used to contain, protect, or present goods for sale, including without limitation cardboard boxes, plastic blister packs, glass bottles, metal tins, and any accompanying labels affixed thereto. Any application of a deceptively similar mark to a package intended to be offered for sale shall constitute an infringement actionable under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding comparative advertising as provided herein. A defendant may demonstrate lack of intent to deceive; however, such demonstration does not absolve liability where actual confusion has occurred among consumers. The court may grant injunctions and award damages commensurate with the harm suffered by the trade mark proprietor.

Any application for registration of a trade mark which incorporates a distinctive feature of the packaging of goods shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry may require evidence demonstrating that such package feature has acquired distinctiveness and functions solely to distinguish the applicant’s goods from those of others, and is not merely descriptive or functional. Where a three-dimensional mark constitutes the package itself, proof of inherent or acquired distinctiveness shall be mandatory for acceptance of the application. A refusal under this Act relating to packaging may be appealed as per established procedures. Provided that, if the package feature is commonplace in the relevant industry, registration will not be granted unless exceptional circumstances are demonstrated. The applicant shall submit clear depictions of the package and its use in commerce with the application. Any alteration to the registered package following grant of a trade mark requires notification to the Registry.

Any person who applies a deceptive package resembling that used by another with intent to cause confusion or deception shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The term “package” for the purposes herein extends to all forms of encasement, including but not limited to boxes, wrappers, and labels affixed directly to goods. Any such application of a similar package, even without direct imitation of a registered trade mark, is actionable if it demonstrates intent to mislead consumers as to the source or quality of the goods. A manufacturer found in violation shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or both. Furthermore, all goods bearing such deceptive package shall be deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The burden of proving lawful use rests with the accused.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark extending to the get-up or packaging of goods shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and require prior written consent from the Trade Marks Registry, unless such assignment is between entities under common control as determined by the Central Government. The term “package” for the purposes of this provision shall include all forms of encasement, wrapping, containers, labels, bands, and any other means used to present goods for sale or distribution, irrespective of material composition. An assignee seeking consent shall submit a detailed description of the package, including visual representations, along with evidence demonstrating no likelihood of confusion in the marketplace. The Registrar may require an amended package design if deemed necessary to protect existing trade mark rights.
