Failure to obtain requisite approval prior to assignment will render such transfer voidable at the option of the original proprietor, subject to a period of one year from the date of assignment. Any license granted relating to packaging shall be similarly documented and registered as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a trade mark which presents a deceptive similarity with the package of another registered trade mark shall be refused as provided herein. However, such refusal may not apply where the applicant demonstrates that the distinguishing features of their package are substantial enough to avoid consumer confusion and that any similarities are merely incidental to functional requirements or common industry practice. An appeal against this refusal shall lie before the Appellate Board within ninety days of the Registrar’s order, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Appellate Board may, after examining evidence submitted by both parties including expert testimony on packaging design and market research data, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Should the Appellate Board uphold the refusal, the applicant may seek judicial review under the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Any misleading representation regarding the nature or characteristics of a package shall also constitute grounds for rectification of the register.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark relating to the get-up or packaging of goods shall be subject to such conditions as may be specified in the instrument of assignment and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where an assignment includes rights pertaining to different defendant geographical areas, the assignor may reserve specific territorial limitations, provided that such reservations are clearly delineated within the assignment deed. A licensee of a trade mark applied to package goods shall not transfer their interest without prior written consent from the registered proprietor, except where expressly permitted under the terms of the licensing agreement. The register of assignments maintained by the Registry shall be open for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any dispute regarding the validity or scope of an assignment concerning a package trade mark shall be adjudicated as provided herein, and may involve evidence relating to the material form and presentation of the goods concerned. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

The distinctive appearance of a package associated with goods shall be registrable as a trade mark under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods from those of other persons. A package, for the purposes of registration, includes all forms of encasement and presentation necessary for containment, transport, and display of goods to consumers. Where the appearance of a package incorporates an artistic work, such as a unique design or sculptural element, that work shall be considered integral to the overall distinctiveness assessment. The rights conferred by registration of a package mark extend to preventing others from using identical or deceptively similar packaging likely to cause confusion among substantial numbers of consumers. Any person aggrieved by unauthorized use of a registered package trade mark may apply for an injunction restraining such use, and may also claim damages sustained as a result thereof. Subject to the provisions herein, remedies available shall include account of profits and delivery up of infringing goods or materials used in the manufacture of such goods.

A geographical indication relates to goods the quality, reputation or other characteristics of which are essentially attributable to their geographical origin and in case of natural goods, growth, production, processing, preparation, packaging and marketing take place in such geographical area. For the purposes of this Act, ‘producer’ shall mean a person who produces agricultural goods, handicrafts, foodstuff, wine and spirits or any other goods in a specified geographical area and possesses traditional knowledge relating to such goods. A registered geographical indication confers upon the authorized users exclusive rights to use it in relation to those goods, subject to conditions as may be prescribed. Any act of infringement shall attract remedies provided herein, including injunctions, damages and delivery up of infringing goods.

A geographical indication relates to goods originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be presented in triplicate to the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks in the prescribed form along with the prescribed fee. The applicant must demonstrate that the goods possess qualities or characteristics unique to that region and are traditionally produced there. Provided that where such a geographical indication is already protected under any other law for the time being in force, an application for registration under this Act shall not be entertained unless a no-objection certificate is obtained from the competent authority administering such prior protection. The Controller may, subject to verification of these claims and compliance with all procedural requirements as provided herein, register the geographical indication. Registration confers upon the applicant exclusive rights to use the geographical indication in relation to those goods.

A geographical indication relates to goods the quality, reputation or other characteristics of which are essentially attributable to their geographical origin and in consequence serves to distinguish the goods from those originating elsewhere. For the purposes of registration under this Act, a producer shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified product and its place of origin; such demonstration may include historical documentation evidencing traditional production methods unique to that region. Where a collective or association of producers applies for registration, it shall submit evidence of membership criteria and internal control mechanisms ensuring consistent quality standards aligned with the geographical indication’s specifications. The Register of Geographical Indications maintained by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks shall be open for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller may file an appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein, within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of such decision. Provided that the Appellate Board may extend this time for sufficient cause shown.

A geographical indication relates to goods originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. Any person claiming a geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified product and that geography, substantiated by traditional knowledge documented in a register maintained as provided herein. Registration of a geographical indication confers upon the applicant the exclusive right to use it in relation to those goods originating from that territory. However, such protection shall not preclude the continued use of common names or local terms customary in commerce prior to registration, provided that such usage does not mislead consumers regarding origin. The Registrar may require evidence of quality control mechanisms ensuring consistent standards for goods bearing the registered geographical indication and compliance with these standards is mandatory for continued validity of registration. Failure to adhere to prescribed standards shall render the registrant liable to penalties as detailed within this Act.

Any assignment of the right to use a registered geographical indication relating to goods shall be subject to such conditions, and may be limited in scope and duration, as the Registrar deems fit, having regard to the maintenance of the quality and reputation of the said goods. An assignee shall, prior to exercising any rights derived from such assignment, notify the Registrar of the transfer of ownership and furnish evidence satisfactory to the Registrar confirming the transaction. Where a geographical indication relates to agricultural produce, the assignment may be subject to provisions ensuring continued access for producers within the defined geographical region. The registered proprietor may grant licenses to use the geographical indication under terms that secure adequate quality control and prevent misuse; such licensing agreements shall be filed with the Registrar. Failure to comply with these requirements as provided herein may render the assignment or license invalid, and expose the parties involved to penalties outlined elsewhere in this Act. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be adjudicated by the designated appellate authority.

A dispute concerning the registration of ‘Darjeeling’ tea arising from West Bengal has been brought before the Geographical Indications Registry, alleging improper attribution and dilution of the geographical indication. The applicant, a consortium of tea estates, asserts that certain teas marketed as originating from ‘Himalayan Foothills’ constitute a violation, given their close proximity and potential for consumer confusion; however, the opposing party contends this is permissible descriptive usage relating to terrain, not a claim to the protected geographical indication itself. Should the Registrar determine a prima facie case of misrepresentation exists under this Act, an inquiry shall be conducted involving expert testimony regarding tea varietals and regional growing conditions. Any aggrieved party may appeal such a decision to the Appellate Board, subject to prescribed fees and timelines as provided herein. The central question remains whether the term ‘Himalayan Foothills’ functions as a geographical indication relates to a specific origin or merely describes a general location, impacting its potential for creating deceptive similarity with established registered indications.

For the purposes of this Act, a “producer” shall mean any person who undertakes or participates in the creation of a patented invention through manufacturing, processing, or other substantial modification resulting in a commercially viable product. Where such production involves reliance upon technical information disclosed within a patent specification, the producer shall be deemed to have exercised due diligence subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts to independently verify the accuracy and completeness of said information. Any person claiming status as a producer may submit evidence of their manufacturing process for inspection as provided herein. Acknowledged producers are entitled to certain benefits relating to royalty payments, contingent upon adherence to quality control standards established by the Controller. Failure to maintain such standards may result in revocation of producer status.

All persons claiming to be producers of cinematographic films intended for commercial exhibition shall register with the Film Producers’ Welfare Fund established under this Act, within thirty days of completing principal photography. Registration shall involve submission of a detailed synopsis of the film, including cast and crew credits, along with evidence of completion of such photography. The registering authority may require additional information to verify the claim of production. A producer failing to register as provided herein shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, any producer demonstrating justifiable cause for delay, subject to the discretion of the registering authority, may be granted an extension of time for registration. Records maintained regarding registered producers and their films shall be open for inspection by authorized officers during regular business hours, and such records constitute public domain information relating to film production activity within India.

Any person who engages in the production of patented articles or uses a patented process shall be deemed a producer for the purposes of this Act, and their rights and liabilities shall accrue accordingly. A producer aggrieved by any infringement of a patent relating to an article or process they produce may apply to the High Court for a decree of injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of production or use. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the patented invention and the alleged infringing activity, as well as proof of actual damage suffered or likely to be suffered. Where wilful infringement is established, the court may also award enhanced damages not exceeding three times the proven loss. Provided that a producer importing articles for personal use only shall not be subject to these provisions unless such import constitutes commercial dealing. The burden of proving non-infringement shall lie upon the defendant. Any order made under this Act relating to producers may include reasonable conditions regarding ongoing royalties or licensing terms.

Any person engaged in the production of patented goods shall maintain accurate records relating to the quantity produced, materials used, and costs incurred in such production. These records shall be open for inspection by a duly authorized officer under this Act, upon presentation of valid identification and reasonable notice, subject to maintaining confidentiality as provided herein regarding trade secrets legitimately possessed by the producer. A producer may apply to the Controller for exemption from specific record-keeping requirements if compliance would cause undue hardship, demonstrating such hardship with supporting documentation. The Controller shall consider any such application within sixty days, and a refusal of exemption may be appealed before the Appellate Board. Failure to maintain accurate records or obstructing lawful inspection constitutes an offence punishable by imprisonment not exceeding two years, or a fine, or both. All producers are responsible for ensuring compliance with licensing terms related to patented inventions utilized in their production processes.

Any person engaged in the production of patented goods shall maintain accurate records detailing the quantity produced, raw materials utilized, and costs incurred in such production. Such records shall be open for inspection by a duly authorized officer under this Act, upon presentation of valid identification and reasonable notice, subject to maintaining confidentiality regarding commercially sensitive information not directly related to determining compliance with royalty obligations or alleged infringement. Producers failing to maintain adequate records, or obstructing lawful inspection, may be liable to penalties as prescribed herein. Provided that, producers operating on a small scale, defined as those with annual production value not exceeding twenty lakh rupees, shall submit simplified reports instead of detailed accounts, subject to verification by the Controller. The controller may require additional information from any producer if deemed necessary for proper assessment.

Any person being a producer of a patented invention, or deriving title from such a producer, may assign the patent to any other person, subject to the terms and conditions as may be prescribed. An assignment shall not be operative unless it is in writing and duly attested by at least two witnesses; provided that an assignment of a patentable invention made prior to its acceptance under this Act shall be void. Where a producer assigns a patent, they shall furnish notice thereof to the appropriate office within thirty days from the date of such assignment. 

The assignee may, subject to any existing contractual obligations between the original producer and any other party, exercise all rights conferred by the patent as if they were the original holder; however, failure to comply with notification requirements as provided herein shall render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or the rights of producers shall be subject to judicial determination.

Any person claiming to be a producer of goods incorporating a patented invention shall register with the designated authority as provided herein, submitting details of production capacity, volume, and geographical location of manufacture. Registration shall be renewed annually, subject to verification of continued compliance with manufacturing standards established by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. A producer failing to maintain valid registration may be restricted from asserting rights relating to the patented invention in any legal proceeding under this Act. Business India situate entities are encouraged to prioritize domestic production and may receive expedited processing of their registration applications. The register of producers shall be open for inspection by interested parties upon payment of a prescribed fee, provided that confidential business information is appropriately redacted. Any false declaration made during the registration process shall attract penalties as specified in Schedule VI.

An essentially derived variety shall be deemed to be a variety obtained by expression of the characteristics resulting from one or more traits, genes or combinations thereof, which are traceable to the initial variety, whether directly or through hybridization with other varieties, and for which no substantially different new variety has been commercialized. Provided that such derivation must be clearly demonstrable and based on objective evidence as determined under this Act. A variety shall not be considered essentially derived if the initial variety’s breeder had reasonable grounds to believe it would lead to such a derivative, or where the process of deriving the new variety involved independent discovery. Subject to the provisions herein, rights pertaining to an essentially derived variety are limited in scope compared to those afforded to the initial variety.

A variety shall be considered an essentially derived variety if it is not distinguishable from the initial variety in terms of characteristics relevant to its identification, while retaining the essential characteristics of that initial variety. The applicant seeking registration of such a variety shall submit evidence demonstrating a clear lineage tracing back to the parent or initial variety, and proof establishing that the essentially derived variety has been produced from the initial variety through successive propagation or hybridization. Provided that, if the production of the essentially derived variety requires repeated use of the initial variety, then consent of the breeder of such initial variety shall be mandatory for registration as provided herein. Any person alleging a variety to be an essentially derived variety may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority with supporting documentation and evidence of propagation history. The authority may require expert testimony or field inspections to verify the claim.

Any person alleging that a new variety is an essentially derived variety from his registered variety may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, furnishing such evidence as may be prescribed. The authority shall, following verification and subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, register the applicant as the breeder of the essentially derived variety if satisfied that said variety is indeed so derived. However, no such registration shall prejudice the rights accruing to the original breeder of the parent variety, and the breeder of an essentially derived variety shall require explicit authorization from the breeder of the original variety for any commercial exploitation. A farmer who has, in good faith and without knowledge, saved seed of a protected variety for replanting may continue to do so subject to notification requirements as provided herein, but such seeds shall not be sold or otherwise commercially exploited. Any dispute regarding derivation shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority following principles of natural justice.

A variety shall be considered an essentially derived variety if it is predominantly derived from, and retains the essential characteristics of, the mother variety as defined under this Act. The determination of ‘essentially derived’ shall be subject to reasonable limitations arising from the act of breeding itself, notwithstanding that such breeding does not result in a substantially new or distinct variety. Evidence demonstrating the maintenance of genetic purity and phenotypic conformity with the mother variety, over a period demonstrably sufficient for stable propagation, may be presented as corroborating evidence before the Plant Variety Protection Authority. However, mere morphological similarity alone shall not suffice to establish essential derivation; proof of genealogical relationship through authorized propagation or breeding schemes is also required. A farmer who has cultivated a protected variety and whose harvest constitutes an essentially derived variety, shall have no right to commercially exploit said harvest without the breeder’s authorization, provided that reasonable recourse for seed saving for personal cultivation remains unaffected as per provisions herein.

A variety shall be considered an essentially derived variety if it is not distinguishable from the initial variety in terms of characteristics relevant to its identification, whilst retaining the essential characteristics of that initial variety. Subject to the provisions herein, determination of ‘essentially derived’ status requires demonstration of derivation from the initial variety through propagation or crossing and a clear resemblance throughout successive generations. However, any variety resulting solely from generally known properties of plants shall not be deemed essentially derived, even if it exhibits substantial similarity. Where a farmer conserves and propagates an extant variety, and subsequently develops a demonstrably similar variety through traditional practices, such development does not automatically confer ‘essentially derived’ status unless the conditions outlined herein are met. Compliance with these criteria is mandatory for registration as an essentially derived variety under this Act, and failure to demonstrate substantial derivation will result in rejection of the application.

Any person who commercially exploits a new plant variety that is proven to be an essentially derived variety from an existing registered variety, without the explicit authorization of the breeder holding rights to said registered variety, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement as provided herein. The determination of whether a variety is an essentially derived variety shall consider its derivation from the mother variety and retention of its essential characteristics. However, subject to proof that the essentially derived variety was produced from a variety which is itself no longer protected or from a farmer’s saved seed, such commercial exploitation may be permissible. Any profits accrued through unauthorized propagation or sale of an essentially derived variety shall be recoverable by the breeder, along with statutory damages not exceeding twenty-five lakh rupees per variety and any associated costs incurred in pursuing legal remedy under this Act. Failure to comply will result in a civil penalty as determined by the designated authority.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, if such variety is found to be substantially similar to any existing commercially exploited variety registered under this Act, demonstrate that the claimed variety possesses distinct characteristics justifying its separate recognition. Where a variety is determined to be an essentially derived variety from an initial variety, the breeder of the initial variety shall have the right to receive equitable remuneration from the holder of the registration for the essentially derived variety; such remuneration may be negotiated between parties or, failing agreement, determined by the Central Government based on reasonable commercial terms. Assignment of rights relating to an essentially derived variety requires written consent from both the breeder of the initial variety and the holder of the registration for the derivative variety, subject to any pre-existing contractual obligations. The scope of licensing for commercially exploiting an essentially derived variety shall be proportionate to the degree of derivation and must not prejudice the legitimate interests of the original breeder as provided herein.

A registered breeder may initiate proceedings before the Plant Variety Protection Tribunal alleging that another variety, commercially exploited without authorization, is an essentially derived variety. Such a claim shall be substantiated with evidence demonstrating the new variety’s derivation from the protected variety through modification in characteristics which are not substantially different from the parent line, and where the production of the new variety requires repeated asexual or sexual reproduction of the registered variety. However, if the alleged infringer demonstrates that the essentially derived variety was independently developed—that is, without utilizing any propagating material of the registered variety—the claim shall be dismissed. Any appeal arising from a decision regarding independent development may be made to the High Court having jurisdiction; provided that such an appeal must commence within ninety days of the Tribunal’s order and shall be subject to established appellate procedures as provided herein. The burden of proof concerning essential derivation rests with the claimant breeder.

Any person who commercially exploits a new plant variety that is proven to be an essentially derived variety from an existing registered variety, without the explicit authorization of the breeder holding rights to the parent variety, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act. Evidence of commercial exploitation may include sales records, propagation activities, or distribution patterns presented as part of a formal complaint. The Registrar shall maintain an entry register document detailing all claims of essentially derived varieties and associated authorizations. Failure to produce such authorization, when requested by the authorized officer during investigation, will attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated offenses may result in imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, subject to provisions regarding prior conviction as determined by a competent court. Any profits generated from unauthorized exploitation shall be recoverable by the breeder, along with legal costs incurred in pursuing redressal.

For the purposes of this Act, a computer programme shall be considered literary work. Such a computer programme includes expressions in machine-readable form, whether or not such expression is fixed in any tangible medium. This definition encompasses source code as well as object code and shall extend to include design and preparation of the said programme. However, the underlying principles or ideas of a computer programme are not protected as copyright under this Act; protection extends only to the expressions thereof. A compilation of data, even if expressed in machine-readable form, may be considered a work provided that it constitutes an original selection or arrangement of such data and is subject to the provisions herein relating to originality. Any modification or adaptation of an existing computer programme shall be treated as a derivative work, requiring authorization from the owner of the copyright in the original work unless otherwise permitted under this Act.

A computer programme, whether original or derivative, shall be deemed to be a literary work for the purposes of this Act and is eligible for copyright subject to the provisions herein. Registration of copyright in a computer programme may be undertaken by submitting an application to the Registrar of Copyrights along with the prescribed fee and requisite documentation demonstrating authorship and ownership. The application shall include source code, object code or sufficient material to adequately identify the programme. Where a computer programme incorporates elements of design, such as graphical user interfaces, protection for those elements may be sought separately under relevant legislation governing industrial designs, provided that such design is separable from the underlying code. Any person intending to commercially exploit a registered computer programme shall maintain accurate records of licensing and distribution agreements as evidence of compliance with this Act. Failure to do so may result in penalties as prescribed herein.

A person who develops a computer programme shall be considered its author under this Act, notwithstanding any contractual stipulations to the contrary, and shall possess all rights as conferred by virtue of authorship. Where a computer programme is generated through artificial intelligence or automated means, the individual undertaking reasonable effort in creating the conditions for such generation, including selecting data sets and defining parameters, may be deemed the author, subject to proof of substantial intellectual contribution. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of copyright in a computer programme may institute a suit before a competent court for injunction, damages, or both; however, no such suit shall abate by reason of any subsequent license granted by the defendant. The owner of a copyright in a computer programme may grant licenses to others, and such licenses shall be enforceable as provided herein, with royalty rates determined through mutual agreement or, failing that, by reference to prevailing industry standards. Any person dealing in counterfeit computer programmes shall be liable for criminal prosecution under relevant penal laws.

A computer programme, including its source code and object code, shall be considered a literary work for the purposes of this Act. The protection extended to a computer programme under this Act is subject to the condition that it must possess sufficient originality in its expression; mere functionality or the underlying idea will not qualify for copyright. Where a computer programme is generated by artificial intelligence without significant human intervention, determination of authorship shall vest with the person who undertakes the arrangements necessary for the creation of such work, provided that such person is identifiable and possesses legal capacity. Any adaptation or modification of an existing computer programme resulting in a derivative work shall be subject to the rights of the original author as provided herein, unless expressly permitted through licensing or assignment. The reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation of a computer programme without authorization from the copyright holder may constitute infringement under this Act and render the offender liable to legal remedies including injunctions and damages. Any dispute regarding ownership or infringement shall be subject to judicial determination.

A computer programme, including its source code and object code, shall be considered a literary work under this Act and is accordingly protected by copyright subject to the provisions herein. Any person intending to commercially exploit a computer programme through reproduction, adaptation, distribution or other forms of exploitation may obtain a license from the owner of the copyright in such programme. However, making backup copies of a lawfully acquired computer programme for personal use shall not constitute an infringement of copyright as provided herein. Where a computer programme is embedded within a larger system or device, the rights holder’s authorization is required for any modification or alteration to that programme, even if such modification does not directly affect the functionality of the overall system. Any reverse engineering undertaken must be solely for interoperability purposes and shall be subject to demonstrable necessity; otherwise it will be considered an infringement. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for all stakeholders involved in the creation, distribution and use of computer programmes.

Any person causing a computer programme to be infringed shall be liable to damages as determined by a Civil Court, and such damages shall not be less than five thousand rupees per infringing copy. Where the infringement involves commercial use or distribution of the computer programme without due license, the aggregate damages may extend up to ten lakh rupees. Any attempt to circumvent technological protection measures incorporated into a computer programme, with knowledge that such circumvention will facilitate an act constituting infringement as provided herein, shall be deemed an independent act of infringement. A person found guilty of distributing pirated copies of a computer programme, or abetting the same, may face imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, in addition to any pecuniary penalty imposed by the Court. The owner of copyright in a computer programme may initiate legal proceedings irrespective of whether the infringing acts occur within or outside India, subject to principles of comity.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a computer programme, whether original or derivative, shall be required to register such programme with the designated authority as provided herein. Registration shall confer no right to copyright but serves as *prima facie* evidence of ownership and facilitates licensing arrangements. Assignment of all rights in a computer programme, including source code and object code, requires written instrument duly executed by both parties, specifying the scope of assignment and any retained rights. A licensee may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, grant sub-licenses but only with prior written consent from the original copyright holder. Where a computer programme incorporates elements of design as defined under the Designs Act, 2000, such design shall be protectable independently unless expressly waived by the designer in writing. Failure to comply with registration requirements does not invalidate copyright itself, however may affect remedies available under this Act. All disputes regarding assignment or licensing shall be subject to judicial determination.

A computer programme, whether original or derivative, shall be considered a literary work under this Act and is accordingly subject to copyright protection as such. However, the reproduction of a computer programme for the sole purpose of backing up, or adapting it for use with another machine, shall not constitute an infringement provided that such copy is used only by the lawful owner and no further copies are made. Any person aggrieved by a claim of infringement relating to a computer programme may apply to the High Court for redressal, submitting evidence of both ownership and the alleged infringing act. The defendant may rebut this claim by demonstrating independent creation or fair dealing as permitted herein. Appeals from decisions of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court subject to established appellate procedures; furthermore, any determination regarding the scope of permissible adaptation must consider the functional elements inherent in the computer programme’s design.

A computer programme, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to be a literary work. The author of such a computer programme is the person who causes the programme to be created, irrespective of whether that person possesses technical skill in its creation. Where a computer programme has been generated by artificial intelligence without significant human intervention determining the final form of the code, the Controller of Patents may, upon application and subject to prescribed fees, register the applicant as possessing *de facto* authorship for a period not exceeding five years from the date of registration. 

Any request for such registration shall include detailed documentation outlining the degree of artificial intelligence involvement. The Geographical Indications Registry may, where a computer programme is demonstrably linked to a specific geographical indication and used in its promotion or preservation, maintain a register of programmes associated with that indication. Such listing does not confer any additional copyright protection beyond what is provided herein but serves as public notice of association. Any person aggrieved by the registration of authorship under this provision may submit representations to the Controller within sixty days of notification.

A computer programme, whether original or derivative, shall be deemed to be a literary work for the purposes of this Act and is accordingly protected by copyright as such. However, where a computer programme is specifically designed and utilized for agricultural practices by a farmer, including but not limited to irrigation control, yield monitoring, or pest management, compliance with certain conditions is mandatory. The farmer utilizing such a programme shall maintain records demonstrating its exclusive use within their farming operations and may be required to submit these records to the appropriate authority upon request. Provided that any modification of the computer programme by the farmer for purposes specific to their landholding does not constitute an infringement, subject to acknowledgement of the original author’s copyright. Any commercial distribution or licensing of such modified programmes is prohibited without prior written consent from the copyright holder as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of protection afforded under this Act.

Any computer programme created for the purpose of assisting in pharmaceutical research, specifically relating to the identification of novel drug candidates or optimisation of existing formulations, shall be deemed a literary work under this Act and is subject to copyright protection from the moment of its creation. Assignment of all rights in such a computer programme, including but not limited to source code, object code, and accompanying documentation, may be effected by written instrument duly executed by the author or their authorised agent. Where a pharmaceutical company commissions the development of a bespoke computer programme for drug discovery, it shall have the right to negotiate an exclusive license to utilise said programme for a defined period, subject to equitable remuneration being agreed upon with the programmer. Provided that, any modifications or derivative works created utilising the original computer programme remain subject to the terms of the initial assignment or licensing agreement unless otherwise stipulated in writing. The rights conferred herein are not diminished by the incidental use of publicly available algorithms within the said computer programme.

A computer programme licensed for use shall be deemed to have conferred upon the licensee a right to exercise all necessary privileges incidental to its lawful operation, subject to the terms and conditions expressly stipulated in the licensing agreement. However, where such agreement provides for a recurring paid fee payable for continued access or updates to said computer programme, any interruption of service exceeding fourteen days without demonstrable cause attributable to force majeure shall constitute grounds for a claim of breach of contract. Any dispute regarding the quantum of damages arising from such breach may be referred to an arbitrator appointed jointly by both parties, provided that the aggrieved party initiates proceedings within ninety days of the date of service interruption. Should arbitration fail to yield resolution, appeal shall lie before the High Court having territorial jurisdiction over the registered office of the licensor, but only on grounds of procedural irregularity or manifest error in law.

In this Act, a computer programme shall be considered literary work. For the purposes herein, ‘computer programme’ includes expressions, instructions, data and other information that result in or may result in a performance by a computer. A computer programme may consist of one or more modules, subroutines or routines. Where a trade mark consists of elements incorporated within a computer programme's user interface, such trade mark shall not be construed as affecting the copyright in the underlying code, subject to established principles of intellectual property law and licensing agreements. Any modification or adaptation of an existing computer programme resulting in a derivative work is also protected as provided herein, unless otherwise stipulated by contractual agreement between parties. The author of a computer programme is deemed to be the person who creates it.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish an appellate board to hear appeals from orders passed by the Copyright Office concerning registration, infringement or other matters arising under this Act. The composition of such an appellate board shall consist of persons possessing expertise in law relating to copyright and preferably with knowledge of relevant industries. Any person aggrieved by any order made by the Copyright Office may prefer an appeal to the appellate board within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of prescribed fees and fulfillment of such conditions as may be determined. The appellate board shall have the power to confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Copyright Office and its orders shall be final and binding, except where an appeal lies before the High Court.

The Appellate Board established under this Act shall entertain appeals from orders passed by the licensing officer or any other designated authority concerning copyright compliance and royalty payments as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order relating to rates fixed for equitable remuneration may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of receiving notice of said order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee. The Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse such orders, ensuring fairness and adherence to principles of copyright law. Provided that the Appellate Board may require submission of expert evidence relating to market value or comparable licensing arrangements to aid in its determination. All proceedings before the Appellate Board shall be conducted in a manner consistent with natural justice, affording reasonable opportunity for all parties to present their case. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject only to judicial review by the High Court on grounds of error apparent on the face of the record.

The Appellate Board constituted for the resolution of disputes pertaining to copyright shall have exclusive original jurisdiction over all matters concerning infringement of rights, save as otherwise provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the licensing body regarding royalty rates or terms of license may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such decision. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period not exceeding thirty days. All appeals shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and supporting documentation demonstrating substantial grounds for review. Where the Appellate Board finds that the licensing body acted without due diligence or in excess of its powers, it may direct rectification of records and award such damages as it deems fit to compensate the aggrieved party. Provided that no appeal shall lie before the Appellate Board unless all alternative dispute resolution mechanisms have been exhausted or are demonstrably inapplicable to the nature of the grievance. The decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties, subject only to writ jurisdiction by the High Court.

The Appellate Board established under this Act shall exercise jurisdiction over appeals from orders passed by the Copyright Office concerning registration, rectification, or any other matter arising under this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Office may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee and furnishing of security for costs as determined by the Board. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the production of evidence or call upon witnesses to substantiate claims made in any appeal. 

Provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain an appeal unless it is satisfied that substantial questions of law are involved and that the appellant has exhausted all other remedies available under this Act. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be communicated to all parties concerned, and a reasoned order reflecting its findings and conclusions shall form part of the record. The Board’s decisions may be challenged before the High Court on grounds of legal error or jurisdictional excess.

The Appellate Board established under this Act shall exercise exclusive jurisdiction over all appeals arising from decisions of the Licensing Competent Authority concerning compulsory licenses as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Competent Authority may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee and furnishing of security for costs, if so directed. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require additional evidence or submissions from any party before it. All proceedings before the Appellate Board shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice and adherence to timelines stipulated by rules made under this Act. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition filed before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of fundamental rights. The composition of the Appellate Board will consist of at least one legally qualified member and one expert in copyright matters.

The Appellate Board constituted for the resolution of disputes pertaining to copyright as provided herein, shall possess the exclusive authority to adjudicate matters concerning alleged infringements exceeding a value of five lakh rupees. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Assessing Officer may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order; however, a deposit of twenty-five percent of the disputed amount shall be mandatory as a condition for entertaining said appeal. Failure to comply with this requirement will result in automatic dismissal of the application. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period by an additional thirty days and shall issue reasoned orders within one hundred and eighty days of receiving the complete appeal dossier. Any wilful misrepresentation before the Appellate Board shall attract a penalty not exceeding two lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or both.

Any person desiring to assign copyright in any work, or any part thereof, whether present or future, shall execute an instrument of assignment in writing identifying the work and specifying the rights assigned. Such instrument may provide for consideration, but failure to state consideration shall not invalidate the assignment; provided that such assignment relating to future copyrights shall be subject to conditions reasonably necessary to ensure the creation of the work. Where a copyright is assigned absolutely, the assignee shall possess all the rights subsisting in the copyright as if they were originally vested in them. 

Any dispute arising from an assignment or licensing agreement concerning copyright may be referred to the Appellate Board for resolution, and the decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties subject to appeal to the High Court. The Appellate Board may require full disclosure of relevant records pertaining to the terms of such agreements before rendering its determination. An assignee failing to exercise rights within a period of five years from the date of assignment may have their claim extinguished, unless otherwise agreed upon in writing.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to copyright ownership, licensing, or infringement, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established for the purposes of this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order, subject to condonation of delay upon sufficient cause being shown to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall have the power to call for the records pertaining to any case before it and may, if deemed necessary, direct a fresh examination of evidence or require additional submissions from the parties concerned. Provided that no appeal shall lie against an order relating to interim injunctions unless such injunction continues for a period exceeding six months. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for rights of review as provided herein, and may be enforced in the same manner as decrees of a civil court. The Appellate Board may also impose costs on parties appearing before it, subject to principles of fairness and equity.

The Appellate Board established under this Act shall have exclusive jurisdiction over all appeals arising from decisions of the Registrar of Copyrights, including refusals of registration india applications and disputes concerning ownership as determined through examination of records maintained by said office. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days of receiving notice of such decision, provided that sufficient cause for delay is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Board. Failure to lodge an appeal within the stipulated timeframe shall preclude any further recourse under this Act. The Appellate Board may, subject to rules made herein, impose costs on frivolous or vexatious appeals and any person found to have knowingly misrepresented facts before it shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or both. All orders of the Appellate Board are final and binding except as otherwise provided by law.

The Appellate Board constituted for matters arising under this Act shall have exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes pertaining to licensing of copyrights, including but not limited to royalty rates, duration of licenses, and scope of permitted exploitation. Any party seeking redress regarding a copyright license agreement, or alleging breach thereof, may initiate a user party proceeding before the Appellate Board by filing a statement outlining the grounds for their claim and supporting documentation. The Board shall, subject to rules prescribed, facilitate mediation between parties prior to formal adjudication; however, such mediation shall not be compulsory. Where assignment of copyright is contested, the Appellate Board’s determination regarding valid transfer of ownership shall be final and binding, provided that due process as outlined in this Act has been followed. Decisions of the Appellate Board may be appealed only before the Supreme Court. The Board may also issue interim injunctions to prevent irreparable harm pending resolution of disputes.

A mark registered trade shall mean a mark duly entered in the Register maintained under this Act, signifying ownership and exclusive rights to use said mark concerning specified goods or services. Such registration confers upon the proprietor, subject to provisions herein, the right to prevent others from using identical or deceptively similar marks for analogous goods or services, thereby safeguarding consumer interests and preventing unfair competition. A collective mark, denoting membership in a particular association, is also considered a registered trade under this Act, provided that its use adheres to established rules governing such collectives. The proprietor may license the registered trade to another party, subject to quality control mechanisms ensuring continued standards. Any assignment of rights shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry as prescribed.

A mark registered trade shall vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any assignment, transfer, or licensing of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules prescribed and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark has been used continuously for five years and is likely to cause confusion in the minds of consumers, an application may be made for its rectification or removal from the register. However, honest concurrent use of a similar mark by another trader shall not constitute infringement unless it leads to deception or unfair competition. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may maintain a suit for infringement before a competent court and seek remedies including injunctions, damages, and an account of profits. A collective mark signifying membership in an association is also registrable under this Act, provided that the rules governing its use are submitted with the application.

A mark registered trade shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the said mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment or transmission of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules prescribed and notification thereof filed with the Trade Marks Registry within the stipulated timeframe. Where a registered trade mark has been used continuously for a period exceeding five years, and there is no legitimate reason why such use should not continue, it shall be deemed to be well known within the relevant section of the public. 

Provided that, a proprietor may seek rectification of the register where a mark resembling their registered trade mark appears on the registry, potentially causing confusion or deception amongst consumers; however, such application must demonstrate genuine and continuous user of the earlier mark. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by both parties before issuing an order regarding such rectification as provided herein. Failure to comply with these procedures may result in loss of rights.

A registered trade mark shall vest perpetually in the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment of a registered trade mark must be executed in writing and shall not prejudice the rights of any existing licensee unless expressly provided for within the instrument of assignment or with prior written consent from such licensees. Where a mark registered trade is used by a person other than the registered proprietor under a license, such use shall be deemed to be lawful use as long as it conforms to the terms and conditions stipulated in the licensing agreement and remains current. The Registrar may, upon application made in writing and accompanied by the prescribed fee, record details of all licenses pertaining to a registered trade mark in the Register of Trade Marks. Failure to comply with these recording requirements shall not invalidate the license but may be considered during dispute resolution proceedings as provided herein. A proprietor failing to exercise reasonable diligence to prevent infringement of their registered trade mark may forfeit certain remedies available under this Act.

Any person who applies for registration of a mark registered trade deceptively similar to an existing registered trademark shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a fraudulent application is made, intending to deceive or mislead, such applicant shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act and upon sufficient cause being shown, direct rectification of the register in cases where a mark has been registered improperly. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or directing rectification, may appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order; provided that any delay exceeding said period may be condoned if reasonable cause is demonstrated. Failure to comply with directions issued under this Act shall attract daily penalties as determined by the Registrar.

A registered trade mark shall vest in the proprietor subject to the provisions contained herein, and may be assigned with or without goodwill. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly executed by both parties, and notice thereof is transmitted to the Trade Marks Registry as provided under this Act. The registrar may require further evidence regarding such assignment before recording it in the register. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, enforce rights against an infringing party where the proprietor fails to do so within a reasonable period after being requested by the licensee in writing. However, no exclusive licence shall confer upon the licensee any right to assign or further license the registered trade mark without the express written consent of the proprietor; such consent may be subject to conditions regarding quality control and royalty payments as mutually agreed. Any transfer of ownership of a mark registered trade must adhere strictly to these provisions for validity.

A registered trade mark shall vest in the proprietor thereof subject to the provisions contained herein and any assignment or transmission thereof must be duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a complaint is made alleging non-use of a registered trade mark for a continuous period of five years, an application for revocation may be presented to the Appellate Board by any person aggrieved; provided that such application shall not be entertained unless prior notice has been served upon the registered proprietor and they have failed to demonstrate sufficient cause. The Appellate Board, after hearing both parties and considering evidence as to bona fide intention to use or continued use of the mark, may either dismiss the application or order cancellation of the registration. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be subject to appeal before the High Court having jurisdiction; however, such appeals must be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. A mark registered trade is presumed valid unless proven otherwise.

A claim shall be construed in a manner consistent with the specification and drawings, if any, accompanying the complete application, and with the prosecution history thereof. The claims defining the invention shall clearly and concisely particularize the matter which the applicant regards as his invention; provided that a single claim may combine alternatives or optional features. Where an independent claim refers to a prior art document for any purpose, such reference shall not be construed as an admission that the prior art anticipates or renders obvious the claimed invention. Subject to the provisions contained herein, dependent claims shall specifically incorporate by reference all limitations of the independent claim to which they refer, and shall further define particular features thereof. Any ambiguity in a claim shall be resolved against the applicant.

A claim shall be construed in a manner consistent with the specification and drawings, and reasonable equivalents thereof, and limitations appearing in a claim shall not be interpreted as dedicated to the public. Where a claim contains an ‘a’ or ‘an’ before a noun, it extends to any number of such nouns unless otherwise specified within that claim itself. Any dependent claim shall refer to all features recited in the independent claim upon which it depends, and additionally only those features specifically enumerated therein. Subject to provisions relating to added matter, amendments to claims may be permitted during prosecution provided they do not introduce subject matter extending beyond the content of the original disclosure as appearing in the complete specification. A claim defining a process shall be construed to include all steps necessary for its performance, even if such steps are not explicitly recited within the claim language itself. Provided that, any ambiguity arising from claim construction shall favour the patentee.

A patentee aggrieved by a revocation of their patent under this Act may apply to the High Court for a review of such revocation, subject to payment of prescribed fees and fulfillment of conditions as may be determined by rules. Any person alleging infringement of valid claims arising from a patented invention shall have recourse to civil remedies including injunctions and damages, assessed in accordance with principles of equity and proportionality. Where a court finds that a claim was improperly broadened during prosecution, it may amend the specification to reflect the originally disclosed invention, provided that such amendment does not introduce matter beyond the scope of the initial disclosure. A finding of essential use under licensing provisions as provided herein shall be binding on all parties concerned, and failure to comply with terms relating to essential use may constitute grounds for revocation of the license. The burden of proving invalidity of claims rests upon the party alleging such invalidity.

A patent application shall be examined with particularity regarding the claims presented therein, and such examination shall ascertain whether said claims define a manner of new manufacture. Claims so drafted must clearly and concisely delineate the scope of the invention, avoiding ambiguity and encompassing only matter which is fully supported by the description provided within the complete specification. Where a claim depends upon or refers to an earlier claim, that dependency shall be explicitly stated and such dependent claim shall further limit the subject-matter defined in the prior claim. 

Any attempt to broaden the scope of the invention beyond what is disclosed in the specification, through expansive claims, shall render those claims invalid as lacking sufficient basis. Provided that, where a claim includes an alternative or disjunctive feature, each distinct element of said alternative shall be separately assessed for novelty and inventive step. The Controller of Patents may require amendment of claims to ensure clarity and compliance with provisions under this Act; however, such amendments shall not introduce new matter beyond the scope originally disclosed.

A claim shall be construed in a manner consistent with the specification and drawings, where applicable, and with the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Where a claim contains an alternative or disjunctive term, the scope of the claim shall extend to each alternative or disjunctive term individually, unless expressly limited by the description. Any dependent claim shall refer specifically to one or more claims preceding it, and shall be interpreted as narrowing those claims; however, such dependence does not invalidate the claim if it otherwise satisfies the requirements as provided herein. A claim defining a process shall be construed to include all steps necessary for its performance, subject to demonstration of feasibility and non-obviousness. Where an inventor seeks protection for a mark associated with goods or services, compliance with the Trade Marks Act, 1999 is mandatory before asserting rights under this Act relating to such marks. Failure to adequately define the claims may result in rejection of the patent application.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act shall, prior to initiating proceedings before any court, furnish security to the Controller in such amount as may be prescribed. Failure to provide adequate security shall render the allegation of infringement unsustainable and subject the claimant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The scope of claims in a patent application shall be strictly construed; broadening interpretations for purposes of establishing infringement are prohibited. Any claim found to be excessively broad, lacking clarity, or unsupported by the disclosure within the complete specification may be amended only upon demonstration that such amendment does not introduce matter beyond the content originally filed and is essential to rectify deficiencies identified during examination. Knowingly asserting a patent against another with malicious intent, despite clear evidence of non-infringement, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine, or with both.

Any assignment of patent rights arising from a licensing agreement shall vest in the assignee subject to the terms and conditions stipulated within such agreement, provided that any royalty payments due to the original patentee remain enforceable against both parties. Where claims relating to improvements on an already patented invention are assigned independently of the primary patent, the assignee of the improvement claims may exercise those rights only insofar as they do not infringe upon the existing patent held by another party, and shall be liable for any such infringement. A licensee acquiring exclusive rights to specific claims within a patent portfolio must demonstrate sufficient consideration has been exchanged, and evidence thereof maintained for a period of five years from the date of assignment. Failure to adequately document such consideration may render the assignment voidable under this Act. The scope of assigned claims shall be determined by their literal meaning as interpreted in light of the specification accompanying the original patent application.

A patent applicant shall formulate their claims with specificity and clarity, ensuring each claim defines a single inventive concept. Any claim lacking such precision may be subject to objection by the Controller of Patents during examination, and the applicant afforded an opportunity to amend said claim within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of notification of the objection. Should the amended claim still fail to meet the requirements as provided herein regarding clarity or specificity, it shall be deemed withdrawn without further recourse, unless appeal is lodged with the Appellate Board. The scope of claims must be supported by disclosure in the complete specification; an extension beyond that disclosed constitutes added matter and renders the claim invalid. Furthermore, any dispute concerning the allowable breadth of a claim, following rejection by the Controller and unsuccessful amendment, may be escalated to the Appellate Board for review, subject to prescribed fees and timelines.

A claim in a complete application shall clearly and concisely define the matter for which protection is sought, and shall be supported by one or more examples illustrating its practical applicability. The scope of any claim shall be determined according to the principles of patent law applicable under this Act, and no claim shall extend beyond the disclosure contained within the specification. A producer intending to commercially exploit a patented invention must demonstrate sufficient working of the invention on Indian territory as may be required by the Controller. Claims relating to a process shall not be construed as extending to an apparatus for carrying out that process unless such apparatus is specifically recited in the claim itself. Provided that, claims dependent upon another claim shall particularly point out the features distinguishing it from said other claim. Any ambiguity within the claims will be resolved against the applicant.

A patent application shall not be deemed valid unless the claims defining the scope of the invention are clear and supported by the description provided herein. Claims so drafted must particularly define the matter for which protection is sought, distinguishing it from prior art and establishing a definite boundary for the exclusive right conferred upon grant of a patent. Where a mark use is asserted as integral to the functioning or identification of an invention claimed, such use shall be explicitly detailed within the specification and correspondingly reflected in the claims themselves. Any claim lacking sufficient clarity or support may be subject to objection during examination and require amendment before proceeding further. Provided that, amendments made to claims must not extend beyond the disclosure originally presented in the complete specification. The Controller of Patents may, notwithstanding any other provision, reject a claim deemed ambiguous or unsupported by adequate description, thereby affecting its validity under this Act. Failure to adhere to these requirements shall render the application liable for refusal.

A patent for addition may be obtained for any improvement or modification of an existing patented invention, subject to the provisions of this Act and provided that such improvement or modification is itself new and involves a substantial inventive step. The claims in a patent of addition shall define the scope of the improvement or modification only, and not extend to the original invention; however, where the improvement or modification is of such nature that it could independently constitute an invention, the claims may be drafted accordingly but must clearly delineate the novel contribution. An applicant seeking a patent of addition shall file a declaration stating the basis for claiming priority from the earlier patented invention and demonstrating how the claimed subject matter differs sufficiently to warrant separate protection. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable to be refused, or the patent invalid upon challenge. The controller may require amendment of claims to ensure compliance as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “convention country” shall mean any country or state which is party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, and includes any member state of the World Trade Organization that affords reciprocal treatment to applicants from India. A country may be designated as a convention country by the Central Government through official notification if it possesses a legal system substantially similar to that of India, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Where an applicant seeks priority under this Act based on an application first filed in a convention country, they shall submit a certified copy of the said prior application along with their Indian application within the period stipulated herein. The determination of whether a nation qualifies as a convention country rests solely with the Central Government.

A person seeking protection under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, shall file such application within twelve months from the date of the first filing in that convention country. For the purposes of determining priority, a ‘convention country’ shall mean any country to which India adheres for the purpose of reciprocal protection of patents as notified by the Central Government in the Gazette. The applicant may be required to furnish a certified copy of the first application filed in the convention country and its complete specification, duly translated into English if necessary, subject to verification by the Controller. Provided that failure to submit such documents within the prescribed period may render the application liable to be deemed withdrawn as provided herein. An international search report and written opinion are not mandatory for applications claiming priority from a convention country but may expedite examination.

Any person making an application for a patent under this Act, claiming priority from an earlier application made in a convention country, shall file a declaration stating the details of said prior application within the prescribed period. Failure to furnish such a declaration, or submission of a materially false declaration, shall render the application liable to be refused, subject to provisions regarding rectification as provided herein. Where a complete application is filed without claiming priority from a convention country, but subsequently seeks to rely on an earlier foreign filing for purposes of establishing novelty, the applicant may submit a request for association with such prior art within twelve months from the international filing date, provided that sufficient justification demonstrating due diligence in pursuing the initial application is furnished. A “convention country” shall be deemed to include any nation party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property or any treaty or agreement affording reciprocal rights as determined by the Central Government through notification in the Gazette. Any dispute regarding whether a particular state qualifies as a convention country shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

A person seeking protection under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, shall file such application within twelve months from the date of the first filing in that convention country. The applicant may be required to furnish, at the time of filing his complete specification, a certified copy of the application, together with an English translation if it is not in English, filed in each convention country from which priority is claimed. Where the applicant claims priority based on multiple applications filed in different convention countries, the period of twelve months shall be calculated separately for each such application, reckoning from the date of filing of the earliest application. Failure to comply with these requirements relating to a convention application may render the application liable to be treated as withdrawn, subject to provisions for restoration under this Act and any associated rules. The Controller may require evidence establishing that the applicant is entitled to claim priority based on the filings in the designated convention country or countries.

A person claiming the benefit of an earlier application filed in a convention country shall, at the time of filing an application under this Act, furnish a declaration stating that the application is based on any prior application and identifying such prior application with its filing date, number, and country. The applicant must also submit a certified copy of the documents relating to the said prior application within the prescribed period, subject to payment of the requisite fee as provided herein. For the purposes of this provision, a convention country shall mean any country or state which is party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, or to any treaty or arrangement recognised by the Central Government as fulfilling similar objectives. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application ineligible for the priority date claimed from the earlier filing in that convention country and will be subject to examination under this Act.

Any person claiming priority from a convention country, for the purpose of obtaining a patent under this Act, shall file a declaration stating that the application was filed in their home country within twelve months preceding the date of filing in India. Failure to submit such a declaration, or submission of a materially false declaration, shall render the application liable to be deemed withdrawn as provided herein. Where an applicant purports to claim priority from a convention country but fails to demonstrate sufficient connection to that nation—that is, proof of domicile, nationality, or effective establishment—the Controller may reject the claimed priority date and proceed with examination based on the actual filing date in India. Any person knowingly providing false information regarding their status as resident of a convention country shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

Any person deriving benefit from a patented invention, whether through license granted under this Act or assignment of the patent rights, shall maintain accurate records of royalties paid and received relating to such exploitation. Where an applicant seeks protection for an invention based on a prior application filed in a convention country, they shall furnish a certified copy of that earlier application together with a declaration verifying its filing date and authenticity, as provided herein. The Controller may require translation of any document not in an official language of India. A failure to comply with these requirements relating to convention applications may render the application subject to revocation. Should a licensee fail to remit royalties due to the patentee within ninety days of their becoming payable, the patentee may seek recourse through established legal channels for breach of contract or infringement, subject to the terms of the licensing agreement. Any dispute regarding royalty rates shall be determined by arbitration in accordance with prevailing law.

A person claiming the priority date of an earlier application filed in a convention country shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the document containing the earlier application and its translation if not in English, failing which the priority claim shall be deemed to have been abandoned. However, any objection regarding the validity of such a claim, or the genuineness of the documents submitted, may be raised by an opposing party during examination, and shall be subject to review by the Controller as provided herein. Should the Controller determine that the application was not filed within twelve months from the date of the first filing in the convention country, or if discrepancies exist between the claims presented and those disclosed in the priority document, the claim may be disallowed. An appeal against any such decision shall lie before the Appellate Board, subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to timelines stipulated under this Act.
