The Controller’s determination regarding a ‘convention country’ is final unless successfully challenged on grounds of demonstrable error or misinterpretation of international agreements.

A person seeking protection under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, shall file such application within the period prescribed, subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein. For the purposes of determining priority dates arising from applications originating outside India, the Trade Marks Registry may maintain records pertaining to corresponding applications filed in other jurisdictions, facilitating verification of claims under this Act. A “convention country” shall be deemed to include any nation party to a treaty or agreement with India concerning reciprocal patent protection, as notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. Provided that where an applicant fails to demonstrate satisfactory evidence of prior filing in a convention country, the application may be treated as a new application for all purposes. Any dispute regarding the status of a particular nation as a convention country shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction over matters relating to intellectual property. The Controller may request information from the Trade Marks Registry concerning related trademark applications when assessing novelty or inventive step.

A person seeking protection under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, shall submit a declaration verifying the priority claim within the prescribed period. The declaration must identify the first filing date and the name of the convention country where such initial application was made. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in forfeiture of the claimed priority date. Where the subject matter of the invention includes a cinematograph film, the applicant shall furnish details regarding its production, including dates and locations of principal photography, as part of the complete specification. Provided that an applicant claiming convention priority based on an application disclosing a cinematograph film must also submit certified copies of any official documentation relating to said film from the competent authority in the convention country. Any misrepresentation or omission concerning these details shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

A person seeking protection for an invention under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, may apply for a patent in India within the prescribed period, claiming priority from such earlier application. The applicant shall furnish details of the original filing date and number of the corresponding application in the convention country at the time of making the Indian application. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the requirements relating to priority have been duly met, including evidence of deposit of necessary documents as per registrar regulations deposited with the International Bureau of World Intellectual Property Organisation, such application shall be treated as a complete application for the purposes of this Act. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the claim of priority invalid and subject the applicant to appropriate remedies available under law. Any assignment or licensing agreement relating to a patent originating from a convention country shall clearly specify the territory covered by said rights.

Any person claiming priority from a convention country, seeking grant of a patent under this Act, shall file a petition with the Controller demonstrating sufficient grounds for establishing entitlement to such priority. The petition particulars contained therein must clearly delineate the date of the first application made in the convention country, and provide certified copies of that initial filing along with translated versions where necessary, as determined by the Controller. Should the Controller find deficiencies in these particulars or reasonable doubt regarding the authenticity of the claim, a hearing shall be scheduled wherein the applicant bears the burden of proof to substantiate their assertion. A failure to adequately demonstrate entitlement to convention priority may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board as provided herein; however, such an appeal does not automatically stay proceedings related to examination on merits. The Controller’s decision regarding a claim based on convention country status is final unless successfully overturned on appeal.

A design registered under this Act confers upon the proprietor an exclusive right to make, get made or import any article embodying such design. This exclusive right shall subsist for a period of ten years from the date of registration, subject to possible extensions as provided herein. A ‘design’ means features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament, or composition of lines or colours applied to any article whether in two dimensional or three dimensional nature, and includes such features when they are integral to an article. Where a design is not novel, or does not relate to the features specified above, it shall not be eligible for registration; however, features which serve solely a functional purpose are expressly excluded from consideration as ‘design’ under this Act. Any contravention of the exclusive right conferred by a registered design constitutes infringement.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class specified in the registration certificate, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person who knowingly applies a design which is identical with or deceptively similar to a design registered under this Act to any article for sale without the license of the registered proprietor shall be liable to an accounting of profits and also to damages not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a design, though not itself new, receives substantial novelty through its application to an article, such application may constitute grounds for registration provided that the resulting ensemble is aesthetically pleasing. The Controller may require evidence of diligent efforts made to exploit the registered design commercially; failure to demonstrate such effort may be considered during renewal proceedings as provided herein. Any dispute regarding ownership of a design shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the District Court.

A person who has registered a design under this Act shall, subject to the provisions herein, have the exclusive right to apply that design to articles of the class specified in the registration certificate. Any act of imitation of a design registered as provided herein, whether for commercial gain or otherwise, and without the consent of the proprietor of such design, constitutes an infringement of the exclusive right. Where a design is registered, any person dealing with articles incorporating an infringing design may be liable to account for profits made from such dealings. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all designs duly registered, which shall be open for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. A design registration confers a right in rem and is enforceable against anyone who violates it, provided that this right does not extend to articles lawfully manufactured before the date of registration or those made bona fide for export purposes. Any person aggrieved by an infringement may apply to the High Court for relief.

A design registration shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles belonging to the class in which it is registered. Any person who knowingly infringes this exclusive right by applying a design identical or substantially similar to a design registered under this Act to any article, with intent to sell, offer for sale, or distribute such article in India, shall be liable to an accounting of profits and damages not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per infringing article. However, no registration shall subsist if it is proven that the design was already publicly known before the date of application. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered design proprietor may institute infringement proceedings in any District Court competent to hear such matters. Where a design incorporates both aesthetic and functional features, the aesthetic features alone will be considered for purposes of determining novelty and originality as required by this Act. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all designs registered under this Act, accessible for inspection during office hours.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to make, sell and import the article in which the design is embodied, subject to the provisions herein contained. Any person who knowingly infringes such a registered design by making, selling or importing an article similar in form or configuration shall be liable to account for profits to the proprietor of the design. However, no infringement proceedings may be initiated unless the article incorporating the infringing design has been commercially exploited within India. The right conferred by registration of a design shall subsist for ten years from the date of registration and may be extended for a further period of five years upon application and payment of the prescribed fee, provided that such extension does not exceed a total term of fifteen years from the original date of registration. Any alteration to a registered design must also be notified as provided herein.

Any person who contravenes the provisions of this Act relating to registration of a design, or falsely applies a design registered under this Act to articles not authorized thereby, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a design is registered and any other person manufactures, sells, or imports an article embodying a fraudulent or obvious imitation of such design, knowing it to be so imitated, they shall be liable to damages not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each infringing article. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as he deems fit, grant a license to work a registered design where the design is not being commercially exploited. Any appeal against an order of the Controller refusing or revoking registration of a design shall lie before the High Court and must be filed within sixty days from the date of the said order.

Any person possessing a design registered under this Act may grant licenses to others for the exploitation of that design, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties involved. Such license shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to geographical territory, duration, and exclusivity, if any. The registered proprietor of a design may assign the right, title, and interest therein to another person by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties; notice of such assignment shall be given to the Controller within thirty days of its execution. Where a license or assignment is made without the explicit consent of the registered owner, it shall be voidable at their option. A design registration remains valid for ten years from the date of registration and may be renewed subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with all requirements as provided herein. Failure to renew will result in cancellation of the design registered.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class specified in the registration certificate, subject to such limitations as may be prescribed. Any person alleging infringement of a design registered herein may institute civil proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing article is manufactured or sold, and seek injunctions restraining further manufacture or sale. However, no such suit shall lie unless the alleged infringer has been served with a notice of complaint at least thirty days prior to the institution of legal proceedings. The Controller may, upon application by any person, rectify the register if it appears that a design was not new or did not possess requisite features when it was registered; provided that no rectification shall be made after three years from the date of registration without sufficient cause shown. Any decision of the Controller regarding such rectification is subject to appeal before the High Court.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to apply that design to articles of the class in which it is registered. Such registration, however, shall be subject to the condition that the article must be new or original at the time of application. Where a design for an article is already registered and the applicant seeks to register a modification thereof, a patent of addition may be applied for, provided that such modification is itself novel and does not substantially alter the character of the original design. The proprietor’s right shall extend to articles resulting from industrial application of the design, but any act done before the date of registration shall not constitute an infringement. Any person who knowingly infringes this exclusive right as provided herein shall be liable to damages and other remedies available under civil law. Compliance with all procedural requirements for maintaining annual renewal fees is essential for continued validity of a registered design.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class specified in the certificate of registration, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person who knowingly infringes the rights conferred by a design registration shall be liable to damages not exceeding rupees fifty thousand for each article or part thereof which constitutes an infringement. Where an issued breeder, being a person who has bred or developed a new variety of plant using a registered design as a key characteristic, commercially exploits said variety without the license of the proprietor, such exploitation shall constitute grounds for injunctive relief and account of profits. The Controller may, upon sufficient cause shown and payment of prescribed fees, extend the period of registration of a design beyond fifteen years from the date of registration, provided that an application for extension is filed within six months prior to expiry. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the offender liable to prosecution as per relevant criminal law.

A design registered under this Act shall confer upon the proprietor an exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class specified in the certificate of registration, subject to such limitations as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to obtain a license to use a design registered herein, or to acquire assignment of rights therein, shall make application in writing to the Controller, setting forth the terms and conditions proposed for such license or assignment. The proprietor of the design may, if dissatisfied with the terms offered, apply to the High Court for directions regarding the grant of a reasonable license. Should any person manufacture, import, sell, or otherwise deal in articles embodying an infringing design without lawful authority, the registered proprietor may seek an ex parte injunction from a competent court restraining such acts and claiming damages for infringement as provided herein. Failure to comply with the terms of any licensed agreement shall be actionable by either party according to the principles governing contract law.

In this Act, a performer includes an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. The term ‘performance’ encompasses any act whatsoever, whether it involves recitation, delivery, singing, playing an instrument or otherwise, presented before a public audience. A performer shall be deemed to have made a performance even if such performance is fixed in any medium of recording, including but not limited to audio and video recordings. Rights granted under this Act to performers are subject to the provisions relating to moral rights as provided herein, and do not extend to performances that fall within the scope of fair dealing for purposes such as criticism or review. Any adaptation or alteration of a recorded performance requires authorization from the performer unless otherwise expressly permitted.

In this Act, a performer shall mean an individual who makes a performance, and includes a singer, musician, dancer, actor and any other person engaged in a like act. Registration of such performances with the designated Registry as provided herein shall be compulsory for all commercially exploited works. The application for registration shall include details regarding the nature of the performance, its duration, the venue where it was first performed, and particulars identifying the performer. Subject to verification by the Registrar, a certificate of registration will be issued confirming the date of such registration and establishing a prima facie record of ownership. Any person intending to utilize a registered performance for commercial purposes may do so only upon obtaining requisite permissions from the performer or their duly authorized agent, failing which remedies under this Act shall be available. The Registry may maintain a public database of registered performances accessible for search and verification.

A performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. The exclusive right of a performer exists in relation to their performance, and includes the right to authorize its communication to the public, whether directly or indirectly, by any means including broadcasting and digital transmission. Subject to the provisions herein, such rights shall subsist for a period of fifty years from the date of the first fixation of the performance. Any person who, without the consent of the performer, communicates their performance to the public in contravention of this Act shall be liable to damages as determined by a competent court. A registered performers’ society may, with the permission of the court, collect and distribute royalties arising from such communication on behalf of its members. Provided that, where a performance is made for purposes of bona fide reporting of current events, no authorization need be sought. The performer retains the right to restrain infringement of their rights through injunctive relief.

A performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. Where a cinematograph film is made, the principal photographer shall be considered the author of such film as provided herein, but nothing contained in this Act shall prejudice the rights conferred upon a performer by virtue of their individual performance captured within said cinematograph film. Any adaptation or alteration of a recorded performance requiring significant creative input beyond mere reproduction may constitute an independent work subject to copyright, however, the original performer’s right to attribution and integrity remains unaffected. A performer who has consented to the recording of a live performance shall be entitled to a share in any royalties earned from the subsequent communication to the public of such recording, subject to agreements made between the performer and the producer or broadcasting entity. The duration of moral rights granted to a performer under this Act shall extend for a period of fifty years from the date of their last performance.

In this Act, a performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. Subject to the provisions herein, the exclusive right to authorize any act in relation to the reproduction, communication to the public, or adaptation of a performance vests with the performer. However, such rights are subject to limitations as may be prescribed for private use only. Where a sound recording is made embodying a performance, the performer shall have the right to receive royalties in respect of commercial exploitation of said recording, provided that the terms governing royalty distribution are mutually agreed upon or determined by a designated authority. Any assignment of these rights must be in writing and clearly specify the scope and duration of such transfer. A performer may seek legal recourse for any infringement of their exclusive rights as established under this Act. Compliance with registration requirements does not create an independent right but serves as evidence of ownership.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite permissions as provided herein, directly or indirectly communicates to the public, performs, or causes to be performed any substantial part of the work of a performer shall be deemed to have infringed the exclusive right granted to such performer under this Act. A performer, for the purposes of this Act, includes an actor, singer, musician, dancer, or any other person engaged in performing artistic works. Where a performance is recorded, the producer of such recording shall, subject to contractual agreements with the performer, be responsible for securing necessary authorizations for further communication to the public. Any violation of these provisions shall attract a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but may extend to two lakh rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. Repeated offences shall result in enhanced penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer.

In this Act, a performer includes an actor, singer, musician, dancer, or any other person who makes a performance. Any assignment of the rights conferred by this Act relating to the commercial exploitation of such performances shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the performer. Subject to the provisions herein, a performer may grant licenses for the communication to the public of their performances through any means including broadcast, digital transmission, and streaming services. Where a performance is made jointly with another, assignment or licensing requires the consent of all performers involved unless otherwise agreed in writing amongst them. A collective bargaining organization duly recognized by the Central Government may act on behalf of performers for negotiating terms of such licenses and assignments. Provided that any agreement concerning royalty rates shall be transparent and non-discriminatory, and subject to review upon application made to the appropriate High Court. The duration of exclusive licensing rights granted under this Act shall not exceed five years from the date of assignment or license.

A performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. However, such recognition as a performer, as provided herein, is subject to the establishment that the individual exercises creative control over the rendition itself, distinct from mere mechanical reproduction of a pre-existing work. A recent appeal before the High Court concerned the status of a voice actor providing narration for an audiobook; the court held that absent demonstrable improvisation or unique interpretation, the individual was not considered a performer under this Act but rather a service provider to the copyright holder of the underlying literary work. Notwithstanding any other provision, where a performance is captured in a phonogram or cinematograph film, the rights pertaining thereto shall vest jointly with the performer and the producer, subject to contractual agreements outlining revenue sharing. Any dispute regarding the determination of creative control shall be adjudicated by a designated officer appointed by the Central Government.

A performer shall be deemed to include an actor, singer, musician, dancer, lecturer, and any other person who makes a performance. The rights conferred by this Act in relation to performances are subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any broadcast or communication to the public of a previously unrecorded performance requires prior authorization from the performer, unless expressly permitted under provisions relating to incidental inclusion within news reporting or educational broadcasts. Provided that any use for purposes of criticism, review, or bona fide teaching shall not require such authorisation, subject to acknowledgement of the performer and the source of the recording. A performer may assign their rights in a performance, but such assignment must be in writing and specify the scope and duration of the transfer. Failure to comply with these provisions constitutes an infringement under this Act and attracts associated penalties. Any dispute regarding permitted use shall be adjudicated by a designated officer.

A performer, for the purposes of assignment and licensing under this Act, shall be deemed to include an artist, singer, musician, dancer, actor, lecturer, or any other individual who makes a performance. Any rights in a performance may be assigned either wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to specific conditions as to territory, duration, medium, or otherwise; provided that such assignment is evidenced by a writing signed by the performer or their duly authorized agent. Where a performer engages with Specify Security India for security services relating to live performances, any subsequent licensing of recordings made during those secured events shall require prior written consent from both the performer and Specify Security India, acknowledging their respective interests in maintaining event integrity and data protection. The assignee shall be entitled to all rights vested in the assignor, subject to the terms of the assignment and as provided herein regarding co-ownership with security providers where applicable. A performer may also grant licenses directly to entities for use of their performances, retaining ownership of copyright.

In this Act, a performer includes an actor, singer, musician, dancer, or any other person who makes a performance. Registration of such performances with the duly designated Registry shall be compulsory for all commercially exploited works and confers evidentiary weight on matters relating to ownership and duration of rights as provided herein. A performer’s right extends to the audio-visual representation of their performance, irrespective of the medium through which it is disseminated. Any unauthorized reproduction, adaptation, distribution or communication to the public of a registered performance constitutes infringement, attracting remedies including injunction and damages. However, fair dealing for purposes such as criticism, review, reporting current events, or research shall not be considered an infringement, subject to acknowledgment of the performer’s contribution. The Registry may prescribe forms and fees for registration, ensuring accessibility and transparency in the process. Failure to register does not invalidate the performance itself but limits access to certain legal protections under this Act.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, "international registration" means a registration of a trade mark with the designating authority of each designated country, effected through the Madrid Protocol or other international treaties to which India is a party. An applicant seeking an international registration shall first file a basic application for registration in India, and such application shall serve as the basis for extension of protection to other countries. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may refuse an international registration if it conflicts with existing Indian trade marks or violates public order. The scope of goods and services covered by the international registration shall be subject to examination as provided under this Act, and any limitation requested by the applicant will be recorded accordingly. A designated country may notify objections regarding the international registration within a prescribed period.

An applicant desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark in India, who has already secured an international registration designating India, shall make an application as provided herein within six months from the date of notification by the Trade Marks Registry of acceptance of their international registration. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement verifying that the international registration is still subsisting and a certified copy of the said registration. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as deemed fit, require additional evidence regarding the use of the trade mark in the country of origin or elsewhere. Where an applicant fails to comply with these requirements within the stipulated timeframe, the application for registration based on international registration shall be deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to an international registration may file a review petition before the Registrar, provided that such petition is filed within one month from the date of the order appealed against.

Any person who has legitimately acquired rights in a trade mark through use, and who subsequently files an application for international registration designating India as one of the designated countries, shall be entitled to claim priority based on their Indian application or earlier filing date, subject to the provisions of the Madrid Protocol. Where an applicant seeks to rely upon prior domestic applications for purposes of establishing seniority in relation to a corresponding international registration, they must furnish certified copies thereof with their request. The Registrar may, at any time and following reasonable notice to the applicant, require additional evidence substantiating such claims of priority or earlier filings. Should a conflict arise between rights derived from an international registration and prior national registrations, the matter shall be adjudicated in accordance with established principles of comparative date and legitimate use as provided herein. An owner of a registered trade mark may oppose an application for international registration within a prescribed period, following procedures analogous to those governing opposition to domestic applications.

An applicant desiring to secure an international registration for a trade mark, in addition to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein relating to domestic applications, shall file with the Trade Marks Registry a statement indicating the countries or territories beyond India where protection is sought. The application for international registration shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any basic application or registration relied upon and shall conform to the provisions of the Madrid Protocol on International Registration of Marks. Where an applicant seeks to designate a country which is not a member of the said Protocol, such designation shall have no effect unless reciprocal arrangements exist between India and that country as determined by notification in the Official Gazette. The Registry may require translation of any document submitted which is not in English or Hindi, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any opposition to an international registration extending to India shall be governed by the provisions relating to domestic oppositions, with such modifications as the Central Government may deem necessary. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in refusal of the application for international registration or limitation of its effect.

An applicant seeking international registration of a trade mark shall, prior to filing such application with the Trade Marks Registry, ensure full compliance with the provisions of the Madrid Protocol relating to international registration of marks and its associated Regulations. The application for international registration, as provided herein, must be accompanied by a clear indication of the basic application or registration upon which it is founded, specifying the Contracting Party where such basic mark finds origin. Where the applicant designates India as a designated country within their international registration, they shall furnish a statement confirming that any required translation of the trade mark has been submitted in accordance with established procedures. Failure to provide accurate details regarding the basic application or designate countries correctly may render the international registration ineffective concerning India. The Registrar may require further information or documentation from the applicant or the International Bureau to verify compliance and ensure proper processing of the international registration request, subject to timelines prescribed by relevant treaties.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark through an international registration shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within six months of notification by the International Bureau of completion of such registration designating India, a statement of use demonstrating bona fide adoption and continued use of the mark in relation to goods or services specified in the application as provided herein. Failure to submit such a statement shall render the international registration vulnerable to revocation upon petition filed with the Registry, subject to established procedures for notice and opportunity to be heard. Any false representation made within said statement concerning use constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, notwithstanding any prior approval of the mark, initiate *suo motu* proceedings where credible evidence suggests fraudulent intent in securing or maintaining an international registration. All fees associated with examination and processing of statements related to international registrations shall be governed by rules prescribed under this Act.

Any person who is the owner of a registered trade mark under this Act may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply for international registration of that trade mark through the Trade Marks Registry. The application shall be in the manner specified by the Madrid Protocol and accompanied by a statement identifying the goods or services for which protection is sought in each designated country. Where an applicant seeks to limit the scope of protection in any designated country, such limitation must be clearly stated within the application itself. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, with the express written consent of the owner, apply for international registration as if they were the owner, provided that evidence of this licensing agreement is submitted alongside the application. Any assignment of an international registration or application for international registration shall be subject to the same requirements and procedures governing domestic assignments under this Act; failure to comply may render such transfer invalid. The Trade Marks Registry retains discretion to refuse processing where inconsistencies arise between the national registration and the details provided in the international application.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered in a Convention country may, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules prescribed therein, apply for international registration through the Trade Marks Registry. The application shall be examined as if it were an application for registration under this Act, with due regard to any relevant opposition filed or pending before the applicant’s home authority. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the mark meets the requirements of both domestic law and the Madrid Protocol, a statement of grant of international registration shall be issued. However, such registration may be revoked if it appears, upon appeal to the Appellate Board, that the initial examination was flawed or failed to adequately consider prior rights established under this Act. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal within ninety days from the date of publication of the international registration in the Trade Marks Journal, and the decision of the Appellate Board shall be final subject to writ jurisdiction by the High Court.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark through international registration, and alleging infringement involving a dramatic work performed publicly without license or authorization as provided herein, shall furnish to the Registrar a certified copy of the basic application or registration relied upon within thirty days of receiving notice of such alleged infringement. Failure to do so shall render the claimant ineligible for statutory relief under this Act. Where an international registration is challenged on grounds of prior use of a similar mark in India relating to a dramatic work, the onus of proving lawful use lies with the opposing party and must be substantiated by evidence predating the filing date of the basic application. Any false representation made regarding the authenticity of such international registration or supporting documentation shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, subject to due process, order seizure of infringing materials and impose costs on the offending party.

Any person who has lawfully used a trade mark in India and seeks international registration of such trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, demonstrating sufficient grounds for its distinctiveness as recognised under this Act. An application for international registration may be refused if the applicant fails to provide evidence of genuine use within a period specified by the Registrar. Where an assignee of rights in a registered trade mark seeks such international registration, they shall submit documentation establishing valid assignment and chain of title, including any relevant licensing agreements pertaining to the mark’s exploitation outside India. The Trade Marks Registry may require verification from the International Bureau regarding the status of corresponding applications or registrations in other countries. Subject to satisfactory completion of all procedural requirements as provided herein, a certificate of international registration shall be issued, facilitating protection in designated contracting states. Any alteration to ownership following initial registration requires notification and amendment of records with the registry.

An application for international registration, seeking protection in India, shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Such an application must designate India as a country to which the protection is sought and comply with all requirements pertaining to translation of documents where applicable under relevant international agreements. The applicant may, subject to fulfilling prescribed fees and formalities, claim priority from an earlier national or regional trademark application, if such claim is made within the stipulated period. Where an international registration has been granted, any subsequent India application shall be examined in accordance with this Act, considering the effects of the international registration as if it were a direct filing under these rules. The Registrar may require verification of details furnished in support of the international registration to ensure compliance and prevent fraudulent practices. Any opposition to such registration shall proceed according to procedures established for national trademark oppositions.

A person who has legitimately acquired rights in a trade mark through use, and subsequently files an application for international registration designating India, shall be entitled to claim seniority over any conflicting earlier trade mark not yet registered in India, provided that such conflicting mark was subject to honest concurrent use prior to the applicant’s earliest good faith adoption of their mark. However, this right is contingent upon a demonstration that the invention far claimed by the earlier mark's proprietor does not invalidate the distinctiveness or lawful basis for registration of the international trade mark as applied in India. Any opposition filed under this Act relating to such an international registration shall consider evidence of both use and the scope of any alleged inventive step, with the burden lying on the opposing party to prove detrimental similarity. The Registrar may, subject to due process, direct amendment of the international application to address concerns regarding invention far claimed or descriptive character. Failure to comply with a direction for amendment may result in refusal of protection in India.

A patent, as provided herein, shall be an exclusive right granted for an invention which is new, useful and non-obvious, relating to a process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter or an improvement thereof. Such right extends to preventing others from making, using, selling, importing or distributing the patented invention. A ‘process’ includes a method or system; however, a mathematical method or business method shall not be patentable subject to provisions elsewhere in this Act. An applicant seeking a patent must demonstrate sufficient inventive step and industrial applicability. The term of every patent granted under this Act shall be twenty years from the date of filing the application, unless otherwise provided for in specific circumstances relating to pharmaceutical products as detailed herein. Any person aggrieved by the grant or refusal of a patent may file an appeal.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller of Patents, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification and the necessary fee as provided herein. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and manner in which it is to be performed, and shall disclose the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the invention. A patent may be granted only for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application. Subject to provisions relating to plant varieties, a patentable subject matter includes any composition of matter resulting from a biotechnological process, provided it meets the novelty and inventiveness criteria. The applicant shall furnish a declaration stating they are the true inventor or derive title from the inventor; failure to do so may invalidate the patent. Any communication regarding the application shall be addressed to the Controller in writing.

Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing a patent, or revoking a patent, or imposing limitations upon its scope, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of order appealed against, subject to such extension as the Appellate Board may allow for sufficient cause. The applicant or patentee, as the case may be, shall deposit with the Registrar a fee prescribed for filing an appeal. A patent once granted shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, sell and distribute the invention throughout India for a period of twenty years from the date of filing the complete specification. However, such exclusivity is subject to provisions relating to compulsory licensing as provided herein, where reasonable requirements of the public are not met. Any infringement of a valid patent shall be actionable under civil law with remedies including injunctions and damages. The determination of essentiality for compulsory licenses may consider national emergency or public interest needs.

A patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee, for a period expiring at the expiration of twenty years from the date of filing the complete specification, the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, importing or distributing the invention in India. Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller of Patents, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification and the necessary fee as provided herein. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and manner in which it is to be performed. 

Where a foreign applicant seeks a patent for an invention previously made public outside India, priority may be claimed based on an application filed in a convention country within twelve months from such earlier filing date, subject to fulfilling all requirements. A patentee may assign or license the patent rights to another person; however, any assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Controller as per established procedure. Failure to pay renewal fees will result in lapsing of the patent.

A patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee, subject to the provisions herein contained, the exclusive right to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention in India. Any person desiring to obtain a patent must demonstrate novelty and an inventive step as assessed against prior public knowledge; however, mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance shall not constitute patentable subject matter. Where a process is claimed, sufficient disclosure regarding its operation must be provided to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it out. A licensee of a patented invention may exercise rights only within the scope permitted by the license agreement and compliance with royalty obligations as stipulated therein is mandatory. Failure to diligently work the patent, or demonstrate reasonable efforts towards commercialization within a period of three years from the date of grant, may render the patent liable for revocation upon application made under this Act.

Any person who publishes information concerning an invention, whether patented or unpatented, with intent to mislead the public as to its novelty or inventive step shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where a patent has been obtained through misrepresentation of material facts relating to prior art, such patent may be revoked by the Controller and the patentee shall forfeit all costs incurred in obtaining and maintaining said patent. Any person found to have abetted the infringement of a valid patent shall be jointly and severally liable with the primary infringer for damages as determined by a competent court. The Controller may, subject to conditions prescribed, grant licenses compulsorily if reasonable requirements of the public are not met. Failure to comply with an order issued under this Act constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment up to three years or fine, or both.

Any patent granted under this Act shall be subject to licensing terms determined by the Central Government in cases where a relevant patent is deemed essential for national emergency, public health, or industrial development. Assignment of any such patent requires prior written consent from the Controller of Patents, and failure to obtain said consent renders the assignment void ab initio. A registered assignee shall possess all rights pertaining to the patent, subject to the original terms of grant and any subsequent modifications approved by the Controller. Where a patent owner seeks to assign a patent as security for a loan, they must register such an arrangement with the designated authority within thirty days of the transaction. The licensee may sub-license the patented invention only with express permission from the patentee or as otherwise provided herein. Any dispute regarding assignment or licensing shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. A transfer of ownership does not affect any pending applications related to the patent.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent, as provided herein, shall furnish proof of due diligence in preventing unauthorized manufacture, use, sale or importation of the patented invention. Where a defendant demonstrates prior art constituting an anticipation of the claimed subject matter, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to establish inventive step and non-obviousness. An appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding revocation of a patent shall lie before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such decision; provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause shown, extend this period not exceeding thirty days. The grant of a compulsory license may be considered where reasonable requirements of the public have not been met and the patented invention relates to a field essential for socio-economic development. Any dispute concerning entitlement to a patent shall be subject to rectification proceedings initiated before the High Court having jurisdiction. Failure to comply with these provisions constitutes grounds for dismissal of the infringement claim or invalidation of the patent.

A patent for an invention shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer upon the patentee exclusive rights in relation to the invention. Any assignment of a patent shall be made in writing and registered with the Controller as provided herein; failure to register such assignment may render it unenforceable against subsequent assignees or purchasers acting in good faith. Where an essentially derived variety of a plant has been commercially exploited without the authorization of the breeder holding a valid patent for that plant, the patentee may seek injunctive relief and damages. A license granted under this Act shall be personal to the licensee and not transferable except with the prior written consent of the patentee or as otherwise expressly provided in the licensing agreement. The Controller may, upon application by either party, determine the reasonableness of royalties stipulated in any such assignment or license, considering comparable licenses within the relevant industry. Any dispute concerning the validity of an assignment shall be subject to appeal before the designated appellate authority.

A patent, as provided herein, shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, sell and import the invention throughout India for a period specified under this Act. Such exclusivity is subject to diligent working of the patented invention within a reasonable time after sealing of the patent, failing which revocation proceedings may be initiated. A registered user trade, established through licensing agreements approved by the Controller, permits another party to utilize the patented invention in exchange for adequate remuneration determined as per regulations. The scope of any such license shall not extend beyond the terms and conditions explicitly outlined within the agreement and recorded with the Patent Office; provided that, the patentee retains ultimate authority over the quality of articles made under said license.

A patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee, subject to the provisions contained herein, the exclusive right to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention in India. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a patented invention without being the patentee may apply to the Controller for a license under reasonable terms and conditions. Where an exclusive license is granted to a single entity, that exclusive licensee shall possess all rights of the patentee in respect of the licensed subject matter, save as otherwise agreed between the patentee and the exclusive licensee. The patentee retains the right to enforce infringement against any unauthorized exploitation by third parties, even where an exclusive license exists; provided that the terms of such enforcement are consistent with the exclusivity granted. Any assignment or further licensing of rights by the exclusive licensee shall be subject to the prior written consent of the patentee unless otherwise stipulated in the original agreement.

Any person claiming a geographical indication for goods shall apply for registration thereof in writing to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement as to the extent of area in India in which such goods are produced. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he thinks fit, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence to satisfy himself as to the accuracy of the particulars furnished. Where an application for registration is found to be incomplete or deficient in any respect, the Registrar shall communicate the same to the applicant and fix a period not exceeding thirty days for rectifying the deficiency. Failure to rectify such deficiencies within the stipulated time shall render the application liable to be rejected. Any person contravening the provisions relating to register geographical indications as provided herein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may initiate *suo motu* inquiries into possible infringements of registered geographical indications and impose penalties accordingly.

Any person claiming a geographical indication for goods originating from a specific region shall submit a petition to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, detailing particulars including the name of the concerned goods, description of the territory of origin, and standards applicable to those goods. The petition shall further specify how such geographical indication distinguishes the goods as being inherently connected with that place of origin, and demonstrate a reputation or quality attributable to its geographical origin. An application seeking to register geographical indications must be accompanied by a statement outlining the rules governing the use of the said indication by producers within the defined territory. Provided that, where multiple producers are involved, evidence of consensus amongst them regarding these rules shall also form part of the petition particulars. The Registry may require further information or clarification as deemed necessary for examination under this Act.

Any person registered as the proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of their registration, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment or transfer of such registration shall be effected by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties and submitted to the Geographical Indications Registry for recordation. The Registrar may, upon satisfaction that the transaction is bona fide and does not prejudice the interests of producers associated with the geographical indication, effectuate said recordation. A register of assignments and transfers shall be maintained by the Registry and open for inspection as provided herein. Where a registered proprietor seeks to license another party to use the included register geographical indication, such licensing agreement must specify the area of operation, quality control mechanisms, and duration of the license. Failure to adhere to these stipulations may render the license voidable at the discretion of the Registrar or any aggrieved producer association.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or varying the conditions of registration, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of such decision. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to errors apparent on the record and demonstrable misinterpretation of provisions contained herein concerning the included register geographical indication’s specifications or boundaries. Provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period by a further thirty days. Any application for registration which is refused due to non-compliance with prescribed formats shall not be admissible for appeal unless rectified and resubmitted within sixty days of the refusal notice. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where an error of law is alleged and supported by documented evidence demonstrating substantial prejudice to the applicant's rights as established under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a trade mark relation shall exist when a subsequent trade mark is so similar to an earlier trade mark as to create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Such likelihood may arise from similarities in the marks themselves, including appearance, sound, and meaning, or through associated conceptual characteristics. A finding of trade mark relation does not require proof of actual deception, but rather a real possibility thereof; however, evidence of instances where such confusion has occurred shall be strong corroborative proof. Where a mark is registered as a series, the overall impression created by the series shall be considered in determining any trade mark relation with another mark. The proprietor of the earlier trade mark may seek remedies as provided herein against infringement arising from this relationship.

A registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the said trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Where two or more trade marks are identical or nearly resembling and relate to similar descriptions of goods or services, there shall be considered a trade mark relation, and the later registration shall not be permitted unless sufficient grounds are demonstrated establishing no likelihood of confusion. However, an application for registration may proceed if the proprietor of the earlier trade mark consents in writing to such registration, or where the marks are used by different persons in different localities, provided that there is no evidence of deceptive practices. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing registration on the grounds of existing trade mark relation may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered trade marks and any associated correspondence relating to claims of trade mark relation.

Any person who avails themselves of a trade mark relation, whether registered or unregistered, and thereby causes loss or damage to another party holding rights under this Act, shall be liable for such loss or damage. A claimant seeking redress may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing the unlawful use, subject to demonstrating a prima facie case of likelihood of confusion or misrepresentation amongst consumers. Where a defendant proves that their use was bona fide and intended solely to indicate geographical origin, or other characteristics which do not relate to trade mark identity, relief may be refused or modified as the Court deems just. However, no injunction shall issue if the claimant has acquiesced in the defendant’s use for an unreasonable period, thereby creating a legitimate expectation of continued usage. The Court may also award damages calculated on the basis of lost profits, costs associated with corrective advertising and reasonable attorney fees, as provided herein.

A registered trade mark shall not be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark merely by reason of resemblance in the get-up, packaging, or colour scheme if such elements do not constitute an essential part of the trade mark itself and are customary in the relevant trade. However, where a plaintiff seeks relief based on a claim of trade mark relation, evidence establishing that consumers associate the defendant’s goods with those of the plaintiff due to similarities extending beyond mere visual resemblance shall be admissible. Such association may arise from extended use or promotional activities creating an impression of a business connection. 

Provided that, in determining whether such trade mark relation exists, the Tribunal shall consider all relevant factors including the nature of the goods or services, the channels of trade and the class of persons who are likely to purchase those goods or services. A finding of deceptive similarity requires proof of actual deception or a strong likelihood thereof, subject to evidence presented by either party regarding consumer perception and market conditions as provided herein.

A registered trade mark shall not be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark solely on account of any minor differences in visual representation, provided that such differences do not affect the overall impression created by the marks. Where a determination of deceptive similarity is required under this Act, due regard shall be given to all relevant factors including the nature of the goods or services, the class of persons likely to deal with them and the manner in which the trade mark relation arises between the competing marks. Any finding of deceptive similarity must demonstrate a likelihood of confusion on the part of an average consumer exercising reasonable care. However, if a mark is demonstrably well-known within India, a lower threshold for establishing such likelihood shall apply, subject to proof of actual or potential economic harm resulting from the use of the similar mark. The Registrar may request evidence relating to actual trade usage and consumer perception when assessing deceptive similarity as provided herein.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark, knowing it to be identical with or deceptively similar to an existing trade mark registered under this Act and used by another party, shall be deemed to have committed an act of unfair competition. Where a finding is made that a trade mark relation exists between the applied-for mark and a prior registered mark, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require the applicant to submit evidence demonstrating legitimate use or intent to use within a specified period. Failure to comply with such requirement shall result in rejection of the application and forfeiture of any associated fees. Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting their trade mark application under this provision may appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the Registrar’s decision; non-compliance will bar further recourse. A deliberate misrepresentation regarding prior rights shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to an obligation on the assignee to continue using the trade mark in respect of those goods or services for which it was originally registered, failing which the registration may be revoked under this Act. Where a licensing agreement concerning a registered trade mark is entered into, the licensor shall exercise reasonable quality control over the goods or services produced by the licensee, ensuring they conform to standards equivalent to those met by the goods or services sold under the trade mark by the licensor themselves. A demonstrable trade mark relation must exist between the licensor and the licensee, signifying a genuine connection in the course of trade beyond mere permission for use. Should such a relationship cease, the licensing agreement shall automatically terminate unless otherwise expressly provided therein. Any transfer of ownership or assignment without due recording with the Trade Marks Registry will be considered null and void as provided herein. The assignee assumes all rights and liabilities pertaining to the assigned mark.

Any person alleging a non-infringing similarity between their registered trade mark and another mark, shall submit evidence demonstrating a lack of deceptive resemblance, subject to the principles established under this Act concerning comparative advertising. Where a dispute arises regarding whether marks possess a sufficient trade mark relation to cause confusion amongst consumers, the Registrar may appoint an independent expert to assess the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between said marks. An appeal from any decision of the Registrar relating to such assessment shall lie before the High Court having jurisdiction. Provided that, if the aggrieved party demonstrates prior use establishing goodwill exceeding a period of five years, the burden of proof shifts to the respondent to prove distinctiveness. The expert’s report shall not be conclusive but may be given significant weight in determining whether a likelihood of confusion exists as provided herein. Any finding of trade mark relation must consider all relevant factors including class of goods and channels of trade.

Any person who owns a registered trade mark and desires to alter it, whether by changing its essential particulars, rectifying errors, or limiting the goods or services covered thereby, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry for an alteration certificate registration. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he deems fit, register the altered trade mark, provided that the alteration does not affect the distinctive character of the original trade mark and is not likely to deceive the public. A finding of a trade mark relation exists where a later mark is identical with or deceptively similar to an earlier registered trade mark, and is used in respect of goods or services identical with those for which the earlier mark is registered. However, no such relation shall be deemed to exist if the use of the later mark is permitted by law or under a license granted by the owner of the earlier mark. Any aggrieved person may apply to the court for an injunction restraining the infringement of their trade mark rights as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed to have a relation with another, where, notwithstanding any difference in the marks themselves, a substantial number of consumers are likely to perceive a connection between the goods or services offered under those marks. Such perception may arise from similarities in visual appearance, phonetic resemblance, conceptual association, or other relevant factors as determined by prudent trade practices and consumer behaviour. Where an invention means invention—including any novel process satisfying the requirements for patentability but not yet patented—and is represented visually on goods bearing a trade mark, the existence of such relation shall be considered alongside evidence of actual confusion in the marketplace. However, this provision shall not apply where the marks are used by different entities in entirely unrelated fields and there is no likelihood of consumer deception; provided that legitimate competitive activity is not unduly restricted as provided herein. Any party alleging a trade mark relation must demonstrate sufficient evidence to establish such connection to the satisfaction of the adjudicating authority.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark deceptively similar to an existing registered trade mark, establishing a clear trade mark relation with said existing mark, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The Registrar shall register a trade mark only upon satisfactory verification that no such deceptive similarity exists and that the applicant has not previously engaged in fraudulent practices concerning trade marks. Any person found guilty of applying for such deceptively similar marks, or abetting such application, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. Provided that, if the offence involves repeated violations, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees and imprisonment up to five years. All evidence presented before the Registrar is subject to verification as provided herein, and false statements shall incur additional penalties.

Any person claiming a trade mark relation between their unregistered mark and a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions herein, submit an application to the High Court having jurisdiction. The registered proprietor proposed to defend the registration may file a counter-affidavit within thirty days of service of such application, detailing grounds for opposing the claim of similarity likely to cause confusion. Where the court finds that a demonstrable and continuous use exists establishing a clear trade mark relation, it may direct an inquiry as provided herein. Such inquiry shall consider factors including but not limited to the degree of visual or conceptual similarity, the nature of goods/services, and evidence of actual confusion amongst consumers. A finding adverse to the registered proprietor does not automatically invalidate the registration; rather, it establishes a qualified co-existence subject to terms determined by the court. Any appeal from such order shall lie before the Division Bench of the same High Court.

A person shall not be entitled to relief in a suit for passing off unless they demonstrate goodwill existing in the jurisdiction where the cause of action arises. Such goodwill must relate to goods or services connected with the marks sought to be protected and shall subsist at the time of the alleged act of passing off. A likelihood of deception, or causing confusion amongst consumers as to the source or connection between the defendant’s goods or services and those of the plaintiff, is a necessary element for establishing passing off. Where a mark is well known in India, even absent registration under this Act, relief may be granted against deceptive imitation or use likely to cause confusion. However, such relief shall be subject to principles of equity and fairness.

Any person claiming that another is engaged in acts amounting to passing off, and seeking redress under this Act, shall demonstrate a sufficient reputation attached to their distinctive signs, marks, or names as are likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers. Such a claim may also extend to goodwill associated with services offered under said signs, marks, or names, provided that the plaintiff can establish prior use in relation to those services. A court considering an action for passing off shall have regard to all relevant factors including the extent of similarity between the sign, mark, or name used by the defendant and that of the claimant, as well as the class of goods or services offered under each. Misrepresentation intended to mislead the public, or damage to established reputation, shall be considered strong evidence supporting a finding of passing off; however, mere resemblance is insufficient without demonstration of deceptive intent or actual confusion.

Any person who suffers loss or damage as a consequence of another party's deceptive trading practices, constituting passing off, shall have recourse to remedies as provided herein. A claimant must demonstrate goodwill existing in the jurisdiction and misrepresentation likely to deceive a substantial number of consumers, leading to potential damage. Where a defendant attempts to pass off their goods or services as those of the plaintiff, by employing a name, sign, symbol, or other distinguishing feature deceptively similar to a trade mark owned by the claimant—whether registered or unregistered—an injunction may be granted restraining such acts. Monetary damages shall be assessed based on actual losses suffered by the claimant, including loss of profits and damage to reputation; an account of profits earned by the defendant through the wrongful conduct may also be ordered. Relief under this Act is not exclusive, and a claimant may pursue other remedies available at law, subject to principles of equity and fairness. The court may consider factors such as the extent of confusion created and any attempts made by the defendant to mitigate harm.

Any person aggrieved by instances of passing off and desiring relief may apply to the High Court, or where no High Court has jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, to a District Court. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating that substantial damage will be caused if an injunction is not granted without delay. The court, upon receiving such application and being satisfied of the likelihood of passing off and potential for irreparable harm, may grant a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from using the deceptive mark or engaging in activities likely to cause confusion amongst consumers. A plaintiff seeking relief based on alleged passing off shall demonstrate goodwill attached to their unregistered trade mark, and that the defendant’s actions are calculated to deceive purchasers into believing goods or services originate from, or are connected with, the plaintiff. The court may, subject to due process, order an account of profits made by the defendant through such deceptive practices, as provided herein. Any person defending against a claim of passing off may demonstrate legitimate competitive activity and absence of intent to mislead.

Any person aggrieved by any wrongful act likely to cause damage to their goodwill and reputation through the deceptive resemblance of goods or services offered by another, may seek redressal under this Act. A claim for passing off shall subsist where the plaintiff demonstrates a sufficient degree of public recognition of its distinguishing features associated with the goods or services in question. The defendant’s conduct must be such that it is likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers, leading them to believe that the offered goods or services originate from, or are connected with, the plaintiff. 

However, no action for passing off shall lie where the resemblance is incidental and does not create a likelihood of deception, or where the plaintiff has acquiesced in the use of similar marks by others. A defendant may establish a valid defense by proving legitimate competitive activity and demonstrating that their actions are consistent with honest trade practices, subject to evidentiary requirements as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by instances of passing off, and alleging that another party has engaged in conduct likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers as to the source or sponsorship of goods or services, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining such acts. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed affidavit outlining the grounds upon which the claim of passing off is based, including evidence establishing goodwill and reputation associated with the claimant’s mark or trade presentation. The court, if satisfied that prima facie case exists, may grant an interim injunction pending final determination of the matter. Failure to comply with any order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. Any goods found in violation of such orders may be seized and disposed of as directed by the Court.

Any assignment of goodwill relating to a trade mark used for goods or services concerning which a finding of passing off has been established under this Act, shall be subject to prior written consent of the Registrar. Such consent may be granted only upon satisfaction that the assignee possesses demonstrable capacity and intention to maintain the quality and reputation associated with the original goodwill. Where an assignment occurs without such consent, any subsequent claim for relief based on said goodwill arising from acts constituting passing off, shall be deemed unsustainable before any competent authority. A license of such goodwill is permissible, provided that the terms thereof include provisions ensuring ongoing quality control equivalent to that exercised by the original owner and subject to a requirement for periodic reporting to the Registrar regarding adherence to those standards. Failure to comply with these reporting requirements may result in revocation of the licensing agreement as provided herein. The assignee or licensee shall be liable for any damages arising from misrepresentation caused through use of said goodwill.

Any person aggrieved by conduct likely to cause deception or confusion amongst consumers, and alleging that such conduct constitutes passing off, may apply to a Court competent to hear disputes under this Act for an injunction restraining the defendant from such conduct. Such application shall demonstrate that the claimant possesses goodwill or reputation in relation to goods or services to which the alleged deceptive practice relates, and that the defendant’s actions are likely to misrepresent association with the claimant. Where evidence of actual deception or confusion is presented, it shall strengthen but not be conclusive for a finding of passing off. A preliminary injunction may be granted pending full adjudication, subject to such terms as the Court deems fit, including security for damages. Any order made under this provision may be appealed before the appellate authority established by law, provided that leave to appeal is obtained from the originating court. The burden of proving misrepresentation lies with the claimant.

Any assignment of rights relating to a patented process used in the manufacture of goods bearing a distinctive trade mark shall be subject to the provisions concerning passing off as detailed herein. A licensee of such patented process may, provided that reasonable royalties are paid and the terms of the license agreement are adhered to, continue use of said process even after assignment of the trade mark itself, unless it can be demonstrated that such continued use is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. However, where an assignee of a trade mark also acquires rights in the associated patented process, they shall not engage in any activity calculated to mislead the public into believing that goods manufactured using a different process are equivalent to those previously produced under the assigned mark and process combination. Any claim of passing off arising from such circumstances may be adjudicated upon by the appropriate court as provided herein, considering both trade mark rights and patent entitlements. The burden of proving lack of deceptive intent shall lie with the assignee.

Any person who contravenes the provisions relating to confidential information as provided herein, and discloses, uses or reproduces a registered layout design without the authorization of the registered proprietor, shall be liable to damages. Such damages shall not be less than five lakh rupees, and may extend to ten lakh rupees per instance of infringement, assessed with reference to the actual loss suffered by the registered proprietor due to such contravention. Where the disclosure is proven malicious or intended to cause undue commercial gain, a court may enhance said damages up to twenty-five lakh rupees.
