Any act constituting an indirect infringement through aiding, inducing, or procuring another person’s unlawful activity relating to a layout design registered under this Act shall be treated as equivalent to direct infringement and subject to the same penalties. The burden of proving reasonable care taken to prevent such infringement lies with the defendant.

Any assignment of rights in a layout design registered under this Act shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. Such an instrument of assignment shall identify the layout design with reasonable particularity and specify clearly the rights being assigned, whether those rights are exclusive or non-exclusive, territorial scope of such assignment, and any conditions attached thereto. A licensee of a registered layout-design may further license its interest to one or more third parties, subject to the terms of the original licensing agreement and as provided herein. The registered proprietor may grant licenses, either exclusive or non-exclusive, in respect of the layout design for specific fields of use or limited territories. Where a layout design is jointly held, any assignment or licensing must be undertaken with the consent of all registered proprietors unless otherwise agreed in writing amongst them. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment and licensing shall render such transactions voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The transfer of ownership of a semiconductor product embodying a layout-design does not constitute an assignment of rights in the layout design itself.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing registration of a layout design or revoking a registration may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to errors apparent on the record and relating to the interpretation or application of provisions under this Act concerning the validity of the layout design registered, including claims of prior art not duly considered. Provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the time for filing an appeal but not beyond a further period of thirty days. The Controller shall transmit all relevant documents and records pertaining to the disputed layout design registered to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receiving notice of the appeal. Any party opposing the appeal may file its submissions before the Appellate Board within forty-five days from the date of receipt of notice, failing which no further representation on that matter shall be accepted.

Any person who fabricates a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying a layout design registered as provided herein, or causes another to do so, without the authorization of the registered proprietor, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act. Such infringement extends to circuits commercially exploited, or made available for commercial exploitation, irrespective of whether such fabrication occurs within the territory of India. A layout-design must demonstrate industrial application to qualify for protection; a design lacking demonstrable utility in semiconductor fabrication is ineligible for registration and therefore not subject to remedies herein. Any person dealing in infringing integrated circuits, including offering for sale, selling or distributing them, shall be liable to pay damages as determined by the appropriate court. Repeated infringement, despite due notice from the registered proprietor, may attract enhanced penalties up to a sum equivalent to three times the actual damages suffered.

Any assignment of rights in a layout design registered under this Act shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the assignor and assignee, and evidenced in writing duly notarized. The registered proprietor may grant licenses, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, relating to the commercial exploitation of any layout design vested in them, specifying the duration, scope, and territorial extent of such license. Where a layout design is derived from sources gene fund contributions as defined by regulations established for promoting research and development in semiconductor technologies, assignment or licensing shall require prior intimation to the designated authority ensuring equitable benefit sharing with contributing entities. Failure to provide said intimation may render the assignment or license voidable at the option of such entities. A transfer of ownership of a registered layout-design does not affect any existing licensed rights unless expressly stipulated in the instrument of transfer, and all assignments shall be recorded with the appropriate registry as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall mean any kind of movable property including stock and animals, but excluding money and immovable property. Where goods are offered for sale or provided by way of service, they shall be classified in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may notify. A collective mark denoting membership in an association, or a certification mark guaranteeing certain qualities relating to goods, is also considered within the definition of “goods” as provided herein. The proprietor of a registered trade mark pertaining to specific goods shall have exclusive right to use said mark in relation to those goods. Any unauthorized use constituting a passing off shall be actionable under this Act.

Goods proposed for registration shall be classified according to the Nice Classification, as adopted by this Act, and an applicant seeking registration must clearly specify the class or classes to which the goods relate. An application failing to accurately delineate the goods, or claiming goods falling outside of permissible classifications, may be subject to objection under these rules. Where a mark is registered in respect of specific goods, protection shall extend only to those goods and reasonably foreseeable extensions thereof; however, no extension shall encompass dissimilar goods unless demonstrated use establishes a clear connection. The Registrar may require an applicant to limit the specification of goods if it is unduly broad or lacks clarity, provided that such limitation does not fundamentally alter the nature of the application as originally presented. Goods deemed scandalous or contrary to morality will not be registered under any circumstances and applications relating thereto shall be refused outright.

Any person dealing in goods bearing an unauthorized trade mark, where such trade mark is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark relating to those goods, shall be liable for abatement as provided herein. A registered proprietor of a trade mark may apply to the Court for an order restraining any person from manufacturing, selling, importing, exporting, or advertising goods bearing said unauthorized mark. Such application shall include proof of special damages suffered by reason of such dealing, or where special damages are difficult to ascertain, an account of profits made by the defendant through the unlawful use of the trade mark on the goods. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a registered proprietor may elect to pursue remedies for conversion instead of abatement, provided that they demonstrate clear evidence of mistaken belief by the dealer regarding the legitimacy of the goods. The Court, subject to due process and consideration of all relevant factors, shall determine appropriate relief including damages, injunctions, and delivery up of infringing goods.

Goods offered, or purported to be offered, for sale shall be classified according to the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe. A proprietor of a trade mark used in connection with specified goods may, where it appears to him that similar goods are being sold bearing an identical or deceptively similar mark, apply to the Registrar for a direction restraining the offending party. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating actual confusion amongst consumers and potential damage to goodwill. The Registrar may, after hearing both parties and considering all relevant factors as provided herein, issue an injunction prohibiting further sale of the infringing goods. Any person aggrieved by such order may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order. Goods seized under this Act shall be subject to disposal in accordance with procedures established by law, prioritizing return to the rightful owner where possible or destruction if deemed unfit for commerce.

Goods offered for sale, or made available for sale, shall be classified according to the Nice Classification, subject to the provisions contained herein. A registered proprietor may apply to the Registrar to amend the specification of goods in respect of a registered trade mark, provided that such amendment does not extend beyond the scope of the class in which the trade mark is registered. Any application for amendment relating to goods shall be advertised in accordance with established procedure as prescribed under this Act, allowing opportunity for opposition by aggrieved parties. Where goods are imported into India bearing an unauthorized trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark used on like goods, customs authorities may seize such goods and notify the rights holder. The determination of ‘like’ goods shall be based upon similarity in nature, purpose and channels of trade; however, consideration may also be given to consumer perception. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding goods may result in penalties as stipulated herein.

Any person dealing in goods which bear a false trade mark, or falsely representing such goods as being those of another person, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The provisions relating to seizure of offending goods, as provided herein, extend to any consignment of goods reasonably suspected of bearing such false marks, irrespective of ownership at the time of seizure. Where a court finds that any goods seized are indeed counterfeit or falsely marked, it may order their destruction or otherwise dispose of them in a manner deemed fit, subject to due notice being given to the owner, if known. Failure to comply with an order for disposal shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per item. Any person abetting such offence, or knowingly assisting in the sale of these goods, also incurs similar liabilities and penalties as provided herein.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions relating to licensing, mutatis mutandis, as provided herein. A license granted under this Act may be exclusive, limited to specific goods, geographical area, or duration, and such limitations shall be clearly defined within the instrument of assignment or license. The proprietor of a trade mark used in connection with specified goods may assign their rights entirely, or partially, restricting use to certain classes of those goods only; however, any subsequent transfer of restricted rights must reflect that limitation. Where an assignment concerns goods falling under multiple class headings as per the Nice Classification, each class shall be individually delineated within the agreement. Failure to accurately specify the goods in relation to which rights are assigned may render the instrument voidable at the discretion of the Registrar. The assignee shall possess all rights and remedies available to the assignor concerning those designated goods, subject to the terms stipulated in the assignment deed.

Goods offered for sale under a registered trade mark shall be of merchantable quality, conforming to industry standards as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Any aggrieved person alleging defective goods, resulting in demonstrable harm, may lodge a complaint with the Registrar who shall initiate an inquiry and may require submission of samples for verification by a designated laboratory. Should the inquiry reveal non-conformity or defects attributable to the trade mark holder’s negligence, the Registrar may order rectification of the defect or award compensation to the complainant, subject to limitations as provided herein. An appeal against any such order shall lie before the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the said order; however, a counter-appeal by the trade mark holder is permissible if they demonstrate prior attempts at good faith resolution were rejected without due consideration. The determination of ‘merchantable quality’ shall consider prevailing market conditions and reasonable consumer expectations regarding such goods.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a false trade mark, or falsely representing such goods as being genuine articles of a class of goods to which that trade mark applies, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Where any food product is offered for sale with a counterfeit mark identical to a registered trademark relating to similar foodstuffs, the burden of proving authenticity shall lie upon the seller. Any person convicted of such an offence involving adulterated or spurious food items shall be liable to imprisonment not exceeding three years, or to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, or both. The court may also order confiscation of all goods found in violation and direct their destruction as provided herein. Repeated offences relating to the same goods shall attract enhanced penalties. All seizures made under this Act shall be subject to verification by an officer duly appointed for that purpose.

Goods offered for sale under a registered trade mark shall be of merchantable quality, conforming to established standards as may be prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Any representation made regarding the goods, whether explicit or implicit through packaging or advertising, constitutes an integral part of the description of said goods and is subject to verification upon complaint filed with the Registrar. Where a proprietor knowingly offers substandard goods bearing their registered trade mark, it shall constitute a commission offence attributable to wilful misrepresentation. An aggrieved party may appeal such a finding before the appellate authority established for this purpose, providing evidence of non-conformity or deliberate deception. The burden of proof regarding merchantability and accurate representation rests with the proprietor; however, subject to demonstrating due diligence in quality control, they may rebut claims of intentional wrongdoing. Any order issued by the appellate authority shall be binding on all parties concerned.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall mean any kind of movable property including stock and all manufactures. The classification of goods for the registration of trade marks shall be in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as may be prescribed. An application claiming priority under Article 8 of the Paris Convention, or a 73 convention application asserting earlier filing dates in a contracting state, shall specify the country and date of the prior application within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. Where goods fall into more than one class, separate fees shall be payable for each such class. The Registrar may require an applicant to indicate specifically the goods for which registration is sought, clarifying broad descriptions where necessary.

In this Act, a ‘name’ shall mean any word, designation, sign, symbol, numeral or combination thereof legally adopted and used by a person as a trade mark to distinguish their goods or services from those of others. A name forming part of a collective mark or certification mark is also included within the definition as provided herein. Where a registered proprietor of a trade mark consisting wholly or substantially of a descriptive name seeks to prevent another from using that name in connection with dissimilar goods or services, such prevention may be subject to proof of likelihood of confusion and bad faith on the part of the subsequent user. However, nothing contained within this Act shall prejudice the right to use one’s own personal name for identification purposes.

A name, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be registrable as a trade mark if it satisfies all criteria outlined herein and does not fall within the prohibitions specified elsewhere in this Act. However, a name consisting exclusively of descriptive terms relating to the goods or services sought to be represented by the trade mark is not registrable unless sufficient distinctiveness has been acquired through continuous use for a period of not less than five years prior to the date of application. Subject to due diligence and verification procedures as prescribed in the relevant rules, a name which is commonly known in the trade may still proceed to examination if it possesses inherent or acquired distinctive character. Provided that any name deemed scandalous or contrary to morality shall be absolutely prohibited from registration under this Act, irrespective of use or distinctiveness. The Registrar may require evidence of lawful user of the name prior to acceptance of an application.

Any person aggrieved by an unauthorized use of their registered trade mark, including any variation thereof which is deceptively similar, shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining such use. A proprietor of a trade mark incorporating a distinctive name may also pursue remedies for passing off, subject to demonstrating goodwill and the likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Where a defendant proves that the allegedly infringing use constitutes fair comparative advertising, as provided herein, no injunction shall issue in respect of such specific usage. However, nothing contained within this Act shall prejudice the rights of any person trading under their own name, provided that such trade is bona fide and does not intend to deceive or cause confusion with a registered trade mark. The court may, at its discretion, award damages based on lost profits or an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unauthorized use of the name or mark.

A name, when used as a trade mark or part thereof, shall be registrable subject to the provisions of this Act concerning distinctiveness and descriptiveness. However, a name which is customary in the current language of the relevant trade or is descriptive of the goods or services concerned may not be registered except where it has acquired secondary meaning through continuous use for a period not less than five years. Where an application for registration includes a name identical with or resembling the name of another person carrying on similar business, the Registrar shall require evidence demonstrating lack of intention to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates prior lawful use of the name before the date of application by another party, such evidence may be considered sufficient grounds for registration. The Registrar may, at their discretion and subject to due process as provided herein, request an affidavit attesting to the bona fide nature of the trade mark application concerning the claimed name. Any false representation in said affidavit shall render the applicant liable for prosecution under this Act.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to restrain any other person from using, in the course of trade, a deceptively similar name as their business identifier. However, this entitlement is subject to proof of likelihood of confusion on the part of consumers and demonstrable damage arising therefrom. Where a subsequent applicant for registration demonstrates continuous use of a name prior to the application date of the registered mark, and such use was bona fide and in good faith, the Registrar may allow coexistence under conditions deemed appropriate. Any person aggrieved by the use of a deceptively similar name may apply to the court for an injunction restraining such use, provided that they can establish their ownership of a previously used distinctive name relevant to the same class of goods or services. The court shall consider all material circumstances including the duration and extent of prior usage when determining whether to grant relief as provided herein.

Any person using, in the course of trade, any deceptive name or representation likely to cause confusion, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. A registered proprietor of a trade mark, aggrieved by such use of a deceptively similar name, may apply to the appropriate court for an injunction restraining the offender from further unlawful activity and seeking damages sustained as a result thereof. Provided that no injunction shall be granted unless it appears to the Court that the continued use of said name would cause irreparable harm to the trade mark owner’s goodwill or reputation. Any goods found bearing such deceptive name, subject to verification by an officer duly appointed under this Act, may be seized and destroyed. A person convicted of an offence herein shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The court may also order the defendant to pay costs incurred during the proceedings.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark incorporating a corporate name, or any license to utilize said mark, shall be subject to prior written consent from all partners in the firm whose name forms part of the trade mark, unless it can be demonstrated that such partnership has been dissolved and appropriate public notice thereof given as provided herein. Where the trade mark consists solely of a personal name, assignment requires proof of due cause demonstrating legitimate transfer of goodwill associated with said name; mere cessation of active business shall not constitute sufficient cause. A licensee acquiring rights under this Act may seek independent registration of a modified version of the assigned name, provided that such modification is substantial and does not create confusion in the marketplace. Failure to obtain requisite consent where stipulated herein renders any assignment or license voidable at the option of the aggrieved partner or original proprietor of the name. Any dispute regarding validity shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark incorporating a distinctive name, or objecting to an application on grounds relating to deceptive similarity with a registered name, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such refusal or objection. The Appellant shall submit a statement outlining the basis for their claim that the proposed name does not cause confusion amongst consumers and demonstrates sufficient distinctiveness as provided herein. Should the Appellate Board determine that the Registrar’s decision was justified, it may impose costs on the appellant, subject to consideration of any mitigating circumstances presented. Furthermore, if an appeal is frivolous or vexatious, the Board may dismiss it summarily and direct the Appellant to cease further pursuit of registration under this Act. Any party opposing the appeal shall be given reasonable opportunity to present evidence supporting their position regarding the contested name.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a trade mark consisting of, or comprising, a name may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such an appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to extension granted by the Appellate Board for sufficient cause shown. Where the application relates to a permitted register trade and the Registrar has refused registration on grounds that the name is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, the aggrieved party must demonstrate distinctiveness acquired through continuous use exceeding five years prior to the date of application. The Appellate Board may require evidence of such use, including sales figures and advertising materials, and shall consider any objections filed by opposing parties regarding potential confusion with existing registered names. A decision of the Appellate Board is final except on grounds of legal error apparent on the face of the record.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark shall apply to the Trade Mark Registrar in writing in the prescribed form, indicating the name under which goods or services are to be identified. The application shall include a clear representation of the mark as it will appear on the goods or their packaging and details regarding its use. Should the proposed name closely resemble an existing registered trade mark, or a pending application for registration, the Trade Mark Registrar may require evidence demonstrating distinctiveness or consent from the proprietor of the earlier mark. An applicant may seek to register a series of names provided that they demonstrate a consistent and unified branding strategy. The registrar shall examine each application meticulously as provided herein, ensuring compliance with all provisions of this Act relating to registrability and potential conflicts. Failure to provide accurate information may result in rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of registration.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, as provided herein, furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a clear representation of the name proposed to be registered, along with details regarding its user in relation to specific goods or services. Where an application discloses a name which is identical or deceptively similar to a previously registered trade mark, or to a name that has been lawfully used by another prior to the date of application, the Registry may require evidence substantiating distinctiveness and bona fide intent to use. Should any officer of the Trade Marks Registry discover reasonable grounds to believe that an applicant knowingly submitted false information regarding the ownership or user of said name, constituting a commission offence attributable to fraudulent misrepresentation, they shall immediately report such matter to the appropriate authority for investigation and potential prosecution. The Registrar may, subject to due process, reject applications lacking sufficient clarity or containing demonstrably misleading particulars concerning the proposed trade mark’s name and associated goods or services.

The Registrar shall maintain a public register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs as provided herein. Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and supporting documentation demonstrating originality. The Registrar may require such further information or evidence as deemed necessary for examination of the application. A request for expedited processing of an application shall be considered subject to payment of an additional fee determined by regulations. Regarding the manner applying registrar, a refusal to register must include reasoned grounds; furthermore, any decision made by the Registrar is appealable before the designated appellate authority within sixty days of notification. The register shall be open for inspection during office hours upon payment of a prescribed fee and subject to such conditions as may be specified.

The Registrar shall maintain a Register of Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Designs and shall ensure its accessibility to the public subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall present an application in the manner applying registrar, along with all necessary documentation including detailed drawings and a statement of novelty. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application or provide further information if deemed necessary for proper examination. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the layout-design meets the requirements as provided herein, registration shall be granted and an official certificate issued. However, should any objection arise concerning prior art or lack of originality, a hearing will be conducted affording opportunity to all interested parties to present their case before a decision is rendered regarding the manner applying registrar. The Register shall be conclusive evidence of ownership unless proven otherwise.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design shall have the right to institute civil proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing activity has occurred, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The registrar, acting in manner applying registrar, shall maintain a record of all complaints received regarding alleged infringements and shall transmit copies thereof to the appropriate court upon request or as provided herein. Where a defendant proves that the layout-design was not originally generated by the plaintiff but rather derived from publicly available information, such proof may constitute a valid defense against claims of infringement. A proprietor may seek an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, along with damages for loss suffered due to such infringement, calculated in accordance with established principles of law. Provided that no action shall be brought before the expiration of thirty days after notice has been served upon the alleged infringer requesting cessation of the infringing act and stating the grounds on which relief is claimed.

The Registrar shall maintain a public register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs as provided herein and may prescribe such forms and procedures for registration as are necessary to ensure accurate record keeping. Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall submit an application in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee, to the Registrar, demonstrating originality and applicability to manufacture. The manner applying registrar includes verification of the applicant’s claim of ownership and a technical examination to ascertain whether the submitted layout-design satisfies the criteria for registrability under this Act. Should the Registrar deem further clarification necessary, they may issue a notice requiring the applicant to provide additional information or evidence within a specified timeframe. Subject to satisfactory completion of these procedures, the Registrar shall register the layout-design and assign a registration number; however, refusal of registration will be communicated in writing with reasons stated. The Register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee, facilitating transparency and promoting innovation within the semiconductor industry.

The Registrar shall maintain a public register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs and shall ensure its accessibility to interested persons subject to payment of such fee as may be prescribed. Any person intending to apply for registration of a layout-design shall submit an application, in the manner applying registrar, together with all necessary documentation demonstrating originality and technical feasibility, to the Registrar within the timeframes stipulated under this Act. The application must clearly delineate the scope of the claimed layout-design and identify any prior art known to the applicant. Provided that, if a layout-design is part of a larger integrated circuit, only the novel aspects thereof need be disclosed in detail. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or limitation of the rights conferred upon registration; however, the Registrar may request clarification from an applicant before final determination. The Registrar shall conduct a preliminary examination for completeness and conformity with this Act.

Any person who contravenes the provisions regarding exclusive rights, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such infringement. Where an application to the Registrar concerning the manner applying registrar is found to be deliberately misleading or contains false representations, the applicant shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The imposition of any penalty or sentence under this Act shall be subject to a reasonable opportunity being given to the alleged offender for presenting their case and evidence before a designated officer. Any fees collected as penalties pursuant to adjudications conducted under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. Provided that, if the infringement is continuing in nature, an additional daily penalty may be imposed until such time as the infringing activity ceases.

Any person being the proprietor of a layout-design shall have the right to assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of the same, whether wholly or partially, and such assignment or transfer shall be subject to the provisions contained herein. Where an application for registration of a layout-design is made jointly by two or more persons, it shall be presumed that each person is entitled to an equal share in the rights accruing under this Act unless otherwise agreed between them in writing and recorded with the registrar. The manner applying registrar to disputes concerning co-ownership of registered layout-designs shall prioritize amicable resolution through mediation facilitated by a mutually appointed expert; provided that if such mediation fails within ninety days, any party may apply to the appropriate court for adjudication. Licensing agreements relating to layout-design rights must be in writing and clearly define the scope of permitted use, duration, and territorial limits, subject to review by the registrar upon reasonable cause shown. Any assignment or license not complying with these provisions shall be deemed invalid as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to grant a certificate of registration, or varying the terms of registration, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order and a statement setting forth clearly the grounds on which it is based. The manner applying registrar, in cases where the Registrar deems further clarification necessary regarding the novelty or originality of the layout-design, may request the applicant to submit additional technical data within thirty days; failure to do so shall be considered an abandonment of the application as provided herein. However, any decision relating to the substantive merits of a claim concerning commercial exploitation rights remains exclusively within the purview of the Appellate Board subject to principles of natural justice and fair hearing. The Appellate Board’s decisions are final except where review is permissible under general law.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration claiming a priority date based on a prior filing elsewhere, conduct a manner applying registrar assessment to verify the veracity of such claim and its compliance with international treaty obligations. This assessment shall include examination of supporting documentation establishing the earlier filing, including certified copies of the initial application and any subsequent communications relating thereto. Provided that, if the applicant fails to submit satisfactory evidence within ninety days from a request by the Registrar, the priority date claim will be deemed abandoned and registration will proceed based solely on the Indian filing date. The Registrar may require translation of documents not in an official language as provided herein. Any layout-design found to have been improperly assigned a priority date shall be subject to revocation under this Act. All decisions regarding manner applying registrar are final, save for appeal to the appellate board.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application seeking registration and accompanying documentation as provided herein, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain that the application meets the procedural requirements stipulated within these rules. Should the application satisfy said requirements, the Registrar may proceed to examine the layout-design for novelty and originality, considering prior art in the field of semiconductor technology both nationally and internationally. The manner applying registrar shall include verification of the applicant’s right to make the application, ensuring proper assignment or licensing agreements are extant where applicable. Any deficiencies identified during examination will be communicated to the applicant, allowing a period not exceeding thirty days for rectification; failure to adequately address such deficiencies may result in rejection of the application. Provided that, if the layout-design incorporates a standard cell or a mask common to multiple integrated circuits, this shall not *per se* disqualify it from registration, subject to demonstrating sufficient original contribution beyond said standard elements. The Registrar’s decision regarding registrability is final and binding unless appealed to the appropriate appellate authority as prescribed under this Act.

A registered geographical indication identifies goods originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. Such registration confers upon producers within that defined territory exclusive rights to utilize the geographical indication in relation to those goods, subject to adherence to established standards for production and quality control as prescribed by the Board constituted under this Act. A ‘producer’ shall mean a natural or legal person who produces, processes, packages, markets, or sells goods bearing such registered geographical indication. Any use of a registered geographical indication by a non-authorized party constitutes an infringement, actionable as provided herein, unless expressly permitted by the owner of the registration or through established licensing arrangements. The register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of ownership.

Any association of producers seeking registration of a registered geographical indication shall jointly establish a code of practice for production, processing, packaging, labelling, storage and marketing, and such code may provide for quality control and standards proportionate to the nature of the goods. The application for registration shall include a statement detailing how the specified goods are linked to the geographical area concerned, including details of traditional knowledge connected with the goods. A register of authorized users maintaining production within the defined geographical indication territory shall be maintained by the association and submitted annually to the Registrar. Provided that, where no such association exists, individual producers may jointly submit a common code of practice acceptable to the Board. The Registrar may require modifications to any proposed code before accepting it as fulfilling requirements under this Act, subject to providing reasonable opportunity for clarification from applicants. Failure to adhere to the established code may result in suspension or revocation of registration as provided herein.

Any person who is a producer of goods originating from a registered geographical indication may apply to the Registrar for registration as a registered proprietor, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. A registered geographical indication shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the said geographical indication in relation to those goods in the manner specified in the register and to seek legal recourse against any unauthorized use of that indication by another person. Where an act constitutes an infringement of a registered geographical indication, the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings for injunction, damages or an account of profits. The court shall, while granting relief, consider the customs and usages reasonably applicable to trade practices concerning the goods in question. Any association of producers or artisans concerned with the promotion of a registered geographical indication may, subject to rules, represent the interests of those producers before any relevant authority. A false representation regarding the origin of goods bearing a protected geographical indication shall be actionable under this Act.

A registered geographical indication conferred by this Act shall vest in the producers associated with such goods, subject to provisions relating to assignment and transmission. Any association of producers or artisans, or a cooperative society representing those producers, may apply for registration of a geographical indication as provided herein. The application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement specifying the items constituting the goods, defining the area of origin, and outlining the manner in which the produce is traditionally produced. Where a registered geographical indication is associated with a traditional craft, evidence demonstrating continuity of practice for not less than fifty years may strengthen the claim to its unique characteristics. The Registrar shall examine the application and, where satisfied that it meets all requirements, proceed to advertise it in the Journal. Any person claiming an interest may oppose the registration within three months from the date of advertisement; such opposition shall be adjudicated upon according to established procedure. A false representation or unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication constitutes infringement under this Act.

Any producer seeking registration of a geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the goods and the specified geographical area, establishing that qualities or reputation originate from that place. A registered geographical indication confers upon producers within the defined territory the exclusive right to use the indication in relation to those goods, subject to compliance with quality standards as prescribed by the Board established under this Act. The application for registration shall include a detailed specification of items constituting the goods, their characteristics, and the methods of production traditionally practiced in that geographical area. Where a collective or association of producers applies, it must demonstrate authorization to act on behalf of all relevant producers. Failure to maintain consistent quality standards, as determined through periodic inspections, may result in suspension or revocation of the registered geographical indication. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal against decisions relating to registration or cancellation, following procedures outlined herein.

Any person who falsely represents goods as possessing a registered geographical indication shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such false representation includes, but is not limited to, the direct application of the registered geographical indication to goods not originating from the specified geographical area, or any colourable variation thereof likely to deceive consumers. Where a collective body representing producers of the registered geographical indication brings evidence before a court of competent jurisdiction demonstrating material loss due to such misrepresentation, the offender shall be liable to pay damages assessed by the Court, not exceeding twice the value of goods falsely represented as originating from that area. Furthermore, any consignment of goods bearing the false or misleading geographical indication may be seized and destroyed, subject to confirmation by a designated officer. A second offence committed by the same person shall attract imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to any financial penalties imposed as provided herein.

Any assignment of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to such conditions and restrictions as may be prescribed. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may, with the prior written consent of the Geographical Indications Registry, assign the right to use the said geographical indication to one or more licensees, specifying the territory, duration, and scope of permitted usage. Such assignment agreements shall be in writing and filed with the Registry within thirty days of their execution. Failure to file such agreement will render the assignment invalid as provided herein. 

A licensee may further sub-license the assigned rights only if expressly authorized by the original proprietor and subject to the same conditions applicable to the primary license. The registered geographical indication, even when licensed or sub-licensed, remains subject to the quality control mechanisms established under this Act; any breach of those standards shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license. Transfer of ownership of a registered geographical indication requires formal application to the Registry and is contingent upon satisfactory demonstration that the transferee meets all eligibility criteria for registration.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a geographical indication, or varying the register in respect of a registered geographical indication, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of such decision. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to errors apparent on the record and shall not extend to questions of fact unless demonstrably erroneous. A counter-claim relating to the same or connected matter may be filed by any opposing party before the Appellate Board, subject to conditions prescribed in regulations. Where a registered geographical indication is alleged to have been falsely applied to goods, an application for rectification may be made to the Registrar, and notice thereof shall be served on the proprietor of the said geographical indication. The Registrar, after hearing both parties and considering evidence as provided herein, shall determine whether such false application constitutes grounds for revocation or amendment of the register concerning that registered geographical indication.

Any person claiming infringement of a registered geographical indication shall have the right to institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing act occurred, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing or selling goods bearing an unregistered geographical indication deceptively similar to the registered one, or which otherwise constitutes passing off. Where a registered geographical indication is subject to international registration protection under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, remedies available shall extend to acts committed outside of Indian territory that have a demonstrable effect within India. The Court may also order delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark and award damages not exceeding twice the amount of actual loss suffered by the proprietor, or statutory damages where actual loss cannot be proven. A finding of infringement shall create a rebuttable presumption of damage.

A registered geographical indication, once entered into the Register maintained under this Act, shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to use such geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any person who, without authorization from the proprietor of a registered geographical indication, uses such indication or any deceptively similar indication for goods covered by the registration, shall be liable to legal proceedings. The Registrar may, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate, require an applicant seeking registration to submit a visual recording demonstrating the traditional method of production associated with the geographical indication. Such visual recording shall form part of the official record and may be considered during any dispute regarding authenticity or quality. Provided that, failure to provide such visual recording shall not *per se* invalidate an otherwise valid application for registration; however, it may affect the evidentiary weight assigned to claims concerning traditional production methods. Any alteration to a registered geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar as provided herein.

Any registered geographical indication denoting the origin of goods shall vest in the producers associated with that geographical area and shall be subject to the provisions of this Act concerning assignment, transmission, and licensing. A producer seeking registration must demonstrate a substantial connection to the defined geographical region and consistently produce goods conforming to the standards established for the relevant registered geographical indication. The Register shall maintain a record of authorized producers, updated annually based on verification reports submitted by designated enforcement officers. Failure by a producer to adhere to these quality standards or to accurately represent the origin of their goods may result in suspension from the register and revocation of rights pertaining to the use of the registered geographical indication, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding producer eligibility shall be adjudicated through established grievance redressal mechanisms.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents relating to an application for patent or revocation thereof, may present a petition of appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The petition shall clearly state the grounds on which the appellant relies and shall be accompanied by all relevant documents pertaining to the decision appealed against. An appeal admitted under these provisions shall not operate as a stay of execution of the Controller’s order unless specifically directed by the Appellate Board. Where an appeal remains pending for a period exceeding one year from the date of its admission, and no further evidence or submissions are forthcoming from the appellant, the Appellate Board may, after giving reasonable notice to the appellant, deem the appeal admitted expiry and proceed accordingly. The Controller shall transmit all relevant records relating to the case without delay upon receipt of intimation regarding an appeal being lodged.

Any person aggrieved by an order rejecting their application for patent grant, or imposing conditions deemed unduly onerous, may initiate proceedings before the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to fulfilling the requirements of pre-deposit as provided herein. The amount of such pre-deposit shall not exceed twenty percent of the assessed value of the invention, determined by a committee constituted by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Should an appeal admitted remain unresolved for a period exceeding two years from the date of its filing, the High Court shall provide reasoned justification in writing; failure to do so will incur a penalty of five thousand rupees per day of continued delay, payable to the aggrieved applicant. An appeal admitted expiry due to non-prosecution by the appellant shall forfeit all rights previously claimed and render any pre-deposit non-refundable, unless extenuating circumstances are proven before the Court. Any false representation made during the appellate process will be considered an offence punishable under this Act.

Any person desiring to challenge the grant of a patent following an examination report objecting to its registrability, and having filed a response thereto which has been duly considered, may initiate proceedings for appeal admitted expiry within ninety days from the date of notification of the final order rejecting the application. Provided that such appeal shall be admissible only upon satisfying the Controller of Patents that reasonable grounds exist demonstrating potential prejudice arising from the initial rejection. The register proposed registered design, if any, associated with the patent application must also be concurrently submitted for review as part of the appellate process to ascertain its validity and distinctiveness. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in automatic dismissal of the appeal, subject to a single opportunity for rectification within fifteen days of such notification. All submissions shall adhere strictly to the prescribed format outlined herein.

A musical work shall be deemed to include any musical composition, with or without words, intended to be sung, played or otherwise produced by any means. For the purposes of this Act, a musical work extends to arrangements of a musical work, and such arrangements shall be protected as original works subject to the provisions herein. Where a musical work is adapted or altered, the author of the original work shall remain the author of the adapted work, unless it is demonstrated that the adaptation constitutes a substantial transformation creating a new and original work. The rights in a musical work shall subsist from the date on which the work is first fixed in a tangible medium, and shall endure for a period as provided herein. Any person intending to reproduce, distribute, or perform a musical work shall obtain the prior consent of the copyright owner, or be subject to the remedies available under this Act. A performer’s right in respect of a musical work may be exercised independently of the copyright in the work itself, provided that the performance is authorized by, or with the license of, the copyright owner.

A musical work shall be deemed to include any musical composition, with or without words, intended to be sung or otherwise performed, and a record thereof, but excludes any arrangement or adaptation of a musical work not constituting an original work. Any person desiring to reproduce a musical work, whether by mechanical means or otherwise, shall obtain a license from the owner of the copyright therein, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding compulsory licensing. Where a musical work is performed publicly, the owner of the copyright may, as provided herein, claim royalties for such performance, provided that reasonable notice of such performance has been given. The duration of copyright in a musical work shall be for the life of the author plus sixty years from the date of their death. Any dispute regarding ownership of copyright in a musical work shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

Any person who, without a license of the owner of the copyright, or in contravention of the conditions of a license granted under this Act, performs or causes to be performed any musical work in public, or distributes copies of such work, shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to two lakh rupees for each such performance or distribution. Where the infringement relates to a musical work incorporated in a cinematograph film, the penalty shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Any apparatus used in the commission of an offence relating to a musical work, and any copies or transcriptions of such work, shall be liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein. A court, upon conviction for an offence involving a musical work, may also order the offender to pay compensatory damages to the copyright owner, subject to proof of actual loss or harm suffered. Repeated offences concerning a musical work shall attract enhanced penalties and may constitute grounds for imprisonment not exceeding three years.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a musical work, whether by reproduction, distribution, public performance, or digital transmission, shall obtain a license from the owner of the copyright therein, subject to the provisions of this Act. An assignment of copyright in a musical work shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, signed by the assignor or duly authorized agent, and shall specify the nature of the assignment, including the duration and territorial scope. Where a musical work incorporates a sound recording, the rights in the musical work and the sound recording may be assigned separately, or jointly, provided that any such joint assignment clearly delineates the respective rights assigned to each party. The owner of a musical work may grant exclusive licenses to different entities for different rights, or for different territories, and such licenses shall be binding on all parties concerned. Any transfer of ownership of a musical work, whether by assignment or testamentary succession, shall be registered with the appropriate registry as provided herein to establish clear title.

A musical work shall be deemed to include any combination of melody and lyrics, or instrumental music, irrespective of whether such work is recorded or not. However, mere arrangements of pre-existing musical works, without substantial alteration or originality, shall not constitute an independently copyrightable musical work as provided herein. An appeal was recently lodged concerning the composition ‘Raga Megh Mallhar’, wherein the appellant claimed authorship based on a novel rhythmic interpretation of a traditional melody; the High Court, however, ruled against the appellant, finding the rhythmic variation insufficient to establish originality. Should a dispute arise regarding the authorship of a jointly created musical work, the contributions of each author shall be assessed, and copyright shall be apportioned accordingly, subject to a written agreement amongst the authors. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding apportionment may apply for review before the appropriate court. The determination of substantial similarity in cases of alleged infringement shall consider both melodic and harmonic elements.

Any person who, in contravention of the provisions of this Act, infringes the copyright in a musical work shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to three lakh rupees. Where the infringement involves a commercial undertaking, the term of imprisonment may extend to six years and the fine may extend to six lakh rupees. Any appeal from an order of a court of first instance concerning such infringement, being a proceeding appellate, shall be heard by the High Court, and the High Court may, in addition to confirming, modifying, or reversing the order, enhance the fine imposed, provided that such enhancement shall not exceed the maximum fine prescribed herein. A second or subsequent infringement shall be punishable with a minimum imprisonment of one year.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (b) “authorised user” means a person, firm, society, trust, or company registered as such under this Act in respect of a geographical indication, and who exercises rights to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered, or is reasonably likely to exercise such rights. An authorised user shall be subject to the conditions as may be prescribed, and may include, but is not limited to, producers, artisans, or a consortium of producers associated with the geographical area. Provided that, no person shall be deemed to be an authorised user if their use of the geographical indication is inconsistent with the established standards for the goods as defined under this Act.

context: A geographical indication registered under this Act shall vest in the producers of the goods concerned, collectively or through an association representing them, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any association of producers seeking registration of a geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear nexus between the goods and the geographical area of origin, substantiated by traditional knowledge or practices documented for at least fifty years. The Registrar may, upon application, record the name and address of the association as the registered proprietor. Where no such association exists, individual producers jointly may apply for registration, and the Registrar shall nominate a lead applicant responsible for coordinating the registration process and subsequent enforcement. A registered geographical indication shall be valid for ten years and may be renewed indefinitely, provided that the renewal fee is paid and the conditions pertaining to quality and origin continue to be met. Any alteration to the specification of a geographical indicati registered shall require prior approval of the Registrar.

A “considered geographical indication” shall mean a name or a combination of names which identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area and which possesses qualities or a reputation that are linked to that origin, and which distinguishes it from goods of similar character originating from other places. Such qualities may relate to the natural factors of the geographical area, or to traditional practices associated with the production of the good, or a combination of both. A geographical indication shall be considered to be linked to the origin if a substantial proportion of the goods are produced or processed within that geographical area. Provided that the reputation of the good need not be universal, but shall be established within the relevant sector of the public. Any determination as to whether a geographical indication is ‘considered’ shall be subject to the provisions of this Act.

A product originating from a defined geographical area shall be considered a geographical indication if its qualities, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, possess a special quality, reputation or other characteristics which distinguish it from other goods of the same category. The applicant seeking registration of a considered geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified geographical area, the qualities of the goods, and the reputation enjoyed by those goods. Evidence of traditional production methods consistently practiced within the geographical area, and contributing to the unique characteristics, may be submitted as supporting documentation. Provided that the geographical area is not a country, but a region, locality, or even an identifiable sub-region within a country. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, accept the application and proceed with the registration process as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the link shall be resolved through established procedures.

A geographical indication, when considered as such under this Act, shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any person who, without authorization, uses a considered geographical indication, or a deceptively similar indication, in the course of trade, shall be liable to legal proceedings for infringement. The proprietor may seek an injunction restraining such unauthorized use, as well as damages for loss suffered due to the infringement. A collective body representing producers of goods associated with a considered geographical indication may, subject to the provisions herein, be registered as the proprietor. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of goods bearing a considered geographical indication shall be adjudicated by the Geographical Indications Registry, and its decision shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal may lie to the High Court. The Registry may, at the request of the proprietor, order the destruction of goods bearing an infringing indication.

A geographical indication shall be considered a geographical indication if the goods originate from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, the perception of consumers associates the goods with that geographical area. The applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified goods and the geographical area of origin, substantiated by traditional knowledge or evidence of consistent production within that area. Any natural or legal person, including an association of producers, may apply for registration, provided that such person or association is competent to represent the interests of the producers in the relevant geographical area. Where a product is manufactured using a process developed within the geographical area and contributes to the good’s qualities, it may be considered part of the essential characteristics. The Register shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications, accessible for inspection subject to prescribed fees. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of a considered geographical indication shall be subject to the remedies provided herein.

A geographical indication shall be considered a geographical indication under this Act if the goods originate from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and is in conformity with traditional production methods. Provided that such geographical area is within the territory of India. An applicant seeking registration of a considered geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified goods and the geographical area of origin, supported by verifiable evidence of traditional knowledge or practices. The applicant shall also furnish a detailed description of the methods of production, quality control, and inspection undertaken to ensure consistency with the established standards. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may, after examination, accept or reject the application based on its compliance with the criteria outlined in this Act. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the geographical origin or the adherence to traditional methods shall be subject to the procedures for rectification as provided herein.

Any article of goods offered for sale, which does not genuinely originate from a geographical area representing a quality, reputation or other characteristic associated with that place, shall be deemed to falsely represent a considered geographical indication and be subject to the penalties prescribed herein. A person dealing in goods falsely representing a considered geographical indication may, upon conviction, be subject to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, or both. The Registrar, acting upon a duly filed complaint and subject to verification of evidence, may issue an order of injunction restraining the sale or distribution of such falsely represented goods. Any such order shall be enforceable by a Magistrate of first class and non-compliance therewith shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment. Provided that, the Registrar may, prior to any enforcement action, offer a period of thirty days for voluntary compliance.

A geographical indication, when considered as such under this Act, shall vest in the producers of the goods to which it refers, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment, transfer, or licensing of rights in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to prior notification to the Registrar, and such notification shall include the terms and conditions of the proposed assignment, transfer, or license. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the proposed arrangement does not prejudice the interests of the producers or the reputation of the geographical indication, register the assignment, transfer, or license. A collective rights management organization, duly constituted and recognized by the Central Government, may, with the consent of a majority of the producers, act as the assignee or licensee on behalf of all producers associated with a considered geographical indication. Any license granted shall specify the area of operation and the duration for which it is valid, and may be revoked by the licensor if the licensee fails to adhere to the quality standards associated with the geographical indication.

A geographical indication shall be considered a considered geographical indication where the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of goods are essentially attributable to the geographical origin of those goods, and such origin is understood by the relevant public as arising from a place, region or locality in India. However, this attribution shall not apply where such qualities, reputation or characteristics are non-distinctive, or are commonly inherent in the goods originating from that place, region or locality. Any application for registration claiming a considered geographical indication shall be subject to a rigorous examination as provided herein, including scrutiny of historical evidence demonstrating a clear and established link between the goods and their geographical origin. An aggrieved party may file a representation against the acceptance of such application, and the Registrar, after due consideration of the representation and any evidence submitted, may either dismiss the application or require the applicant to amend their claim to accurately reflect the true geographical origin and characteristics of the goods. Any decision of the Registrar may be appealed to the Appellate Board.

A geographical indication shall be considered a ‘considered geographical indication’ where the rules of the concerned association of producers, or board established under this Act, specify a detailed standard for the goods, including quality control and inspection processes, and such standards are publicly available. Any person aggrieved by the use of a considered geographical indication not in conformity with the specified standards, may apply to the Registrar for an order directing the infringing party to cease such use. Where an application for registration of a geographical indication is pending, and the applicant seeks international registration referred under the Madrid Protocol, the Registrar shall, subject to the applicant fulfilling all requirements as provided herein, transmit the application to the International Bureau within one month of receiving a formal request. Failure to comply with the standards of a considered geographical indication shall constitute an act of unfair competition, attracting remedies including injunction and damages. The Registrar may, in exceptional circumstances, impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for repeated violations.

For the purposes of this Act, a “linked indicator” shall be deemed to be attributable geographical if the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of a good are essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, accordingly, perceived as originating in that region by consumers. Such attribution shall be established through demonstrable evidence of a causal nexus between the goods’ characteristics and the place of production, processing, or preparation. Provided that, where a good undergoes substantial transformation outside the defined geographical area, the indicator may still be considered attributable geographical if a significant activity in the production process, crucial to the good’s qualities, remains confined to the region. The Board, as provided herein, shall assess the degree of such linkage based on expert testimony and relevant documentation.

Any goods bearing a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be deemed to originate from a geographical area where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin, and which is understood as arising from that place. The applicant for registration shall submit evidence demonstrating a clear link between the specified goods and the geographical area, including traditional knowledge connected to the production and processing of said goods. Provided that, where the quality or reputation is attributable to a wider geographical area encompassing multiple administrative units, the application may define a composite geographical indication reflecting such broader origin. The Registrar may, subject to verification of such evidence, register the geographical indication if satisfied that the goods genuinely possess qualities, reputation or characteristics linked to the attributable geographical area and that the application meets all requirements as provided herein. Any claim of origin must be verifiable and not misleading to the consumer.

A geographical indication shall be considered attributable to a specific geographical area if the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of a good are essentially linked to that place’s natural, human, or historical factors. The linkage shall be demonstrable through evidence accepted as provided herein, including but not limited to traditional practices, documented history, and expert testimony. Where a good possesses qualities arising from a combination of natural and human factors, both must contribute significantly to the good’s distinctiveness and be demonstrably connected to the geographical origin. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the Registrar may, subject to a reasoned application and sufficient evidence, determine that a geographical indication is not attributable if the evidence fails to establish a clear and direct connection between the good and its claimed geographical origin. Any determination regarding attributable geographical status shall be subject to review as per the established appellate procedures under this Act, and shall be binding on all parties concerned. The burden of proof regarding such attribution rests with the applicant.

Any person who falsely applies a geographical indication to goods not attributable to that geographical area, or who trades, describes or offers for sale goods so falsely labelled, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such misrepresentation, initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied, direct the cessation of the offending activity. Any goods found to bear a false geographical indication shall be liable to seizure and destruction, subject to the discretion of a designated officer. A person convicted of an offence under this provision shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. Furthermore, any profits derived from the sale of goods with falsely attributable geographical indications shall be forfeited to the Central Government. Provided that, a first-time offender may be issued a warning in lieu of prosecution, at the discretion of the Registrar.

Any claim of a geographical indication being attributable to a specific geographical area shall be substantiated by a prima facie case demonstrating a consistent, historical, and demonstrable connection between the goods and that area. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, require evidence of such connection, including but not limited to traditional knowledge documentation, production records spanning a minimum of twenty-five years, and expert testimony regarding unique qualities derived from the geographical origin. An appeal against the Registrar’s requirement for further evidence shall lie before the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Registrar’s communication. Where a dispute arises concerning whether a good is truly attributable geographical, the burden of proof rests upon the applicant to establish that the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the good are essentially linked to that geographical area. Failure to adequately demonstrate this link shall render the application liable to be rejected.

Any goods offered for sale or exposed for sale with a false indication of their geographical origin, or which are otherwise calculated to mislead the public as to the goods’ attributable geographical origin, shall be deemed to be an infringement under this Act. Where a registered geographical indication has been lawfully assigned to a person or entity, such assignee shall have the right to maintain an action for infringement, and any relief granted shall be enforceable as if the assignee were the original proprietor. Any person dealing in goods bearing such false indications, knowing or having reason to believe them to be so falsely indicated, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The court may, subject to the circumstances, also order the destruction of the infringing goods. Failure to comply with an order for destruction shall constitute a further offence, punishable with a daily fine.

Any claim of geographical indication registration shall be subject to rigorous examination to ascertain the attributable geographical origin of the goods in question, and the reputation or qualities thereof are essentially linked to that place. Where a dispute arises concerning the precise geographical boundaries defining the region of origin, the Registrar may appoint an expert committee to submit a report, which shall be binding unless successfully appealed to the Appellate Board. Evidence presented in support of such attributable connection may include, but is not limited to, historical records, traditional knowledge, and detailed descriptions analogous to those found within a patent specification outlining the manufacturing process or cultivation techniques unique to the claimed geographical area. An applicant failing to demonstrate this essential link shall have their application rejected, and such rejection may be challenged before the Appellate Board on grounds of factual error or misinterpretation of evidence as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a geographical indication shall be considered attributable geographical if a specific quality, reputation, or other characteristic of a good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and consequently influences its quality or reputation.
