Such attribution shall be demonstrated through objective evidence, including traditional knowledge documented in mark trade description or other publicly available records, consistently maintained and verifiable. Provided that the link between the specified quality and the geographical origin is not merely a general connection, but a causal relationship demonstrably impacting the goods. Subject to the provisions herein, the competent authority may, upon application, determine whether a geographical indication meets the criteria of attributable geographical origin and register it accordingly. Any claim of attributable geographical origin must be substantiated with evidence acceptable to the Registrar.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be misdescribed in the register if it incorrectly states the claimant’s address or description of goods or services. The Registrar may, at any time before acceptance of an application, require the applicant to amend the application to accurately reflect the particulars of the trade mark, subject to the condition that such amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark. Where an application is filed claiming priority under any convention or agreement, proof of such priority shall be furnished to the Registrar within the prescribed period. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of priority may result in the application being treated as if no priority claim was made. The complete application registration process, as provided herein, is subject to the payment of the requisite fees.

Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing application registration may, within a period of ninety days from the date of such refusal, file a statement of grounds and documents with the Appellate Board, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Trade Marks Registry an opportunity of being heard, pass such order as it deems fit, confirming, modifying, or setting aside the decision of the Registry. An application for registration shall not be deemed to be abandoned merely by reason of the applicant’s failure to respond to an examination report within the stipulated time, provided that the applicant, within one month of the expiry of such time, submits a request for restoration along with a statement explaining the cause of delay. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the delay was due to unavoidable circumstances, the application may be restored to the register. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person making an application for registration of a trade mark shall furnish a clear and concise statement of the use of the mark, and the goods or services in relation to which such use exists, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned after a period of six months from the date of notice requiring such statement. Provided that, where the application concerns a proposed use of the trade mark, a declaration of intent to use, accompanied by a detailed plan for such use within a specified timeframe, shall be accepted subject to verification by the Registrar. Any false representation in an application regarding the extent or nature of use, or the intent to use, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, persistent failure to comply with requests for information relating to the application registration, despite reasonable notice, may result in the Registrar refusing the application outright and barring the applicant from submitting a similar application for a period of two years.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein, and the Registry may require the applicant to amend or modify the application to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. Where the Registry determines that a mark applied for is identical or deceptively similar to a previously registered trade mark, the application shall be subject to objection, and the applicant shall be given an opportunity to respond. However, if the Registry is satisfied that a mark applied for is likely to cause confusion, or is descriptive, or is devoid of distinctive character, it may refuse the application. Provided that, where a mark is a well known trade mark, the Registry shall refuse the application irrespective of whether the prior mark is registered in the same or different class of goods or services, unless the applicant demonstrates a legitimate interest in the mark. Any decision of the Registry regarding the application registration may be appealed to the appellate board.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall denote an indication which identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area, where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, serves to distinguish the goods of that region from those originating elsewhere. For the purposes of registration, a geographical indication must be descriptive of the goods’ origin and not merely generic or laudatory; it shall not be likely to mislead the public as to the true place of origin. The Registrar may, subject to conditions, register a geographical indication even if it includes terms which, though descriptive, have acquired distinctiveness through use. Any association of producers or artisans concerned with the goods may apply for registration.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall vest in the registered proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. The registrar shall maintain a register of all geographical indications, detailing the particulars of the goods, the geographical area of origin, and the name of the registered proprietor. Any association of producers or artisans, or a body representing producers, may apply for registration of a geographical indication, provided that such association demonstrates a clear link between the goods and the specified geographical area. The application shall include a statement of user requirements, outlining the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to the geographical origin. A registered geographical indication shall be valid for ten years and may be renewed upon payment of the prescribed fee. Where a registered geographical indication is found to be falsely applied to goods not originating from the designated area, the proprietor may pursue legal remedies as provided herein, including injunction and damages.

Any person who, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication registered under this Act, finds that any other person is using a deceptively similar geographical indication for identical or similar goods, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, and an account of profits. The court, upon establishing such infringement, shall grant relief as it deems appropriate, considering the extent of the deceptive similarity and the potential damage to the reputation of the registered geographical indication. Where a registered geographical indication is used in relation to goods which are not in fact originating from the geographical area indicated, the court may also order the destruction or obliteration of the offending goods, subject to just compensation to the owner. A collective body representing producers of goods bearing a geographical indication registered under this Act may, with the leave of the court, represent the interests of all such producers in any proceedings relating to infringement. Provided that, no such action shall be brought without prior notice to the alleged infringer.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall vest in the registered proprietor and be subject to the provisions contained herein regarding assignment, transmission and licensing. The registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to such conditions as may be specified in the application, record the assignment, transmission or licensing of a registered geographical indication in the Register. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the registrar to record such assignment, transmission or licensing may, within a period of thirty days from the date of such refusal, appeal to the Appellate Board. Where a registered geographical indication is not actively being used by the registered proprietor for a period of five years, any person claiming an interest in the geographical indication may apply to the registrar for its removal from the Register, subject to such notice and opportunity of being heard as the registrar may deem fit. The registrar shall, after considering the application and evidence presented, determine whether the geographical indication may be removed.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall be subject to renewal upon the expiration of ten years from the date of registration, and such renewal may be granted for a further period of ten years, contingent upon the continued adherence to the standards and specifications outlined in the register of geographical indications. The registered proprietor shall, not less than one month prior to the expiry of the initial or any renewal period, apply for renewal in the prescribed manner and remit the applicable fee. Failure to comply with these requirements shall result in the removal of the geographical indication from the register. Where a collective body maintains and enforces the standards of a geographical indication, it shall submit an annual report detailing quality control measures and any instances of unauthorized use. Any dispute regarding the authenticity or standards of a geographical indication registered as provided herein shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the designated appellate authority.

Any person causing false application of a geographical indication registered under this Act, or falsely representing goods as originating from a geographical area in respect of which a registered geographical indication exists, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. The court, upon conviction, may also order the destruction or forfeiture of the falsely marked goods. Where a registered geographical indication has been falsely applied to goods intended for export, the penalties prescribed herein shall be doubled. Any evidence of intent to deceive, or of prior conviction for an offence involving intellectual property, shall be considered an aggravating factor in determining the severity of the penalty. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for injunction and damages.

Any assignment of a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be subject to such conditions, limitations, and restrictions as may be prescribed, and shall be effected in writing and registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to other persons to use the said geographical indication in respect of goods in relation to which it is registered. Such licenses may be exclusive, limited in territorial extent, or limited in the form and manner of use of the geographical indication, as agreed upon between the parties. Where a license is granted, the licensor shall have the right to revoke the license upon the occurrence of any condition specified in the license agreement or in case of non-compliance with the terms and conditions of the license. A transfer of ownership of a geographical indication, whether by assignment, inheritance, or operation of law, shall not prejudice the rights and obligations of existing licensees, provided that such rights and obligations are consistent with the terms of the original license agreement.

The Registrar, following a petition filed by the All India Cashew Manufacturers Association contesting the registration of ‘Kerala Cashews’ as a geographical indication, has issued a preliminary order suspending the registration pending further inquiry into claims of genericness. This suspension shall remain in effect for a period not exceeding ninety days, subject to extension by the Registrar if substantial evidence of prior, widespread use outside the defined geographical region is presented. The petitioner alleges that the term ‘cashew’ has become fully generic for the nut irrespective of its origin, and therefore, cannot legitimately function as a geographical indication registered under this Act. The respondent, the Kerala State Agricultural Board, maintains that specific cultivation and processing techniques unique to the Kerala region justify protection. Any party aggrieved by this preliminary order may file a statement of grounds for appeal with the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of this notification, demonstrating sufficient cause and providing supporting documentation as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or by any order made by the Registrar regarding the amendment or revocation of a registration of a geographical indication registered under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of the decision or order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to appear before him or her in person or through authorized representatives. Provided that, no appeal shall lie against an order dismissing an application for registration on the grounds that the geographical indication does not satisfy the criteria for registration as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, and any further recourse to judicial review shall be limited to grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any person who, without the consent of the registered proprietor, uses a geographical indication that is identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication, shall be liable to legal proceedings for infringement. However, such right shall not preclude the use of generic terms descriptive of the goods, even if those terms form part of the registered geographical indication, provided that such use is in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters. Where a patented invention is integral to the production of goods bearing a registered geographical indication, the proprietor of the patent shall have no right to prevent the use of the geographical indication by the registered proprietor, subject to the payment of royalties as may be determined by the appropriate authority. Any aggrieved party may apply to the court for an injunction and damages.

In this Act, a “producer” shall mean a person who undertakes the responsibility for the making of a work, including, but not limited to, cinematograph films and sound recordings, and exercises primary control over the resultant work. The producer may be an individual, a firm, a company, or any other legal entity capable of bearing such responsibility. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the producer of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein. However, where the producer is not the author of the work, ownership shall be subject to any agreement existing between the producer and the author, provided that such agreement does not contravene the public policy as established under the laws of India. A sound recording producer similarly holds initial copyright subject to contractual stipulations with contributing artists.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, any person claiming to be a producer of a cinematograph film shall submit a duly completed Form-V, accompanied by the prescribed fee, to the designated Registrar of Copyrights. The application shall clearly identify the film, including its title, duration, and language, and shall state the name and address of the producer. A producer, for the purposes of this registration, includes any person who owns the rights to produce or has undertaken the responsibility for the making of the film. Should the application be incomplete or contain inaccuracies, the Registrar may require the applicant to provide further information or clarification within a period of thirty days. Registration shall be conclusive evidence of ownership, subject to any existing rights or valid claims. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered cinematograph films, accessible for inspection as provided herein. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered film shall necessitate a fresh application for amendment.

A person who causes a work to be produced shall be deemed the producer of that work, and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, possess the rights accruing to a producer in respect of such work. Where a cinematograph film is produced by a person acting under the direction of another, the latter shall be deemed the producer. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of the rights of a producer may, subject to the limitations as provided herein, institute a suit in a court of competent jurisdiction for injunction, damages, or both. The quantum of damages shall be determined with regard to the actual loss suffered by the producer, or, if such loss cannot be ascertained, a sum of not less than five thousand rupees. A producer may assign their rights, or any part thereof, by writing under their hand. Such assignment shall be subject to the terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties, and shall be enforceable as if it were a contract. No assignment shall be effective without prior written notice to the Registrar of Copyrights.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘producer’ shall be deemed to include the person who undertakes the risks and manages the financial aspects of making a work available to the public, irrespective of whether such person is directly involved in the creative process. The determination of a producer, where multiple entities contribute to the creation of a work, shall be subject to a consideration of the degree of control exercised over the final form of the work and the assumption of financial responsibility. Any person claiming to be a producer as provided herein may, upon reasonable cause, apply to the appropriate authority for a declaration confirming their status. 

Provided that, where a work is created under a contract of service, the employer shall, unless otherwise agreed, be considered the producer. The rights of a producer shall extend to all technological formats in which the work is embodied or reproduced, and any unauthorized exploitation of such rights may be subject to the remedies available under this Act. A producer’s rights are, however, subordinate to the rights of the author, as established elsewhere in this Act.

A person undertaking the production of a work shall be deemed the producer, irrespective of whether such production involves substantial creative contribution or merely technical execution. However, where a work is produced under a contract for service, the terms of such contract shall govern the determination of the producer, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person claiming to be a producer must maintain a register of all works produced, detailing the nature of production and the extent of creative input. Failure to maintain such a register, or providing false information therein, shall attract a penalty as prescribed. The rights of a producer shall extend to all reproductions and adaptations of the work, provided that such reproductions or adaptations do not violate any existing copyright. A producer may assign their rights to another party, but such assignment must be in writing and duly registered. The producer’s liability for any infringement arising from the work remains, even after assignment, unless explicitly discharged by the assignee.

Any person who, without lawful authority, makes for sale or hire, or distributes, exhibits, or causes to be exhibited, any work in which copyright subsists, shall be liable to a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees for each such infringement. Where the infringement is committed in respect of a cinematograph film or a sound recording, the fine may extend to one lakh rupees for each such infringement. A person shall be considered a producer of a work if they have assumed responsibility for the financing and arrangement of its creation, and such producer shall be jointly and severally liable with any other infringer. Any evidence of commercial scale operation shall be admissible as proof of intent to profit from the infringement, and may result in enhanced penalties. All works seized under this Act shall be subject to confiscation, and the offender shall bear the costs of such seizure and storage.

A person who causes a work to be produced shall be deemed the producer of that work, and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, possess the exclusive right to license the reproduction, adaptation, distribution, and public performance of such work. Any assignment of the producer’s rights in a work shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, and shall specify the nature of the rights assigned and the duration of the assignment. Where a work is produced jointly by two or more persons, the rights as producer shall vest in those persons jointly, and each producer may license the work independently, subject to an agreement to the contrary. A prospective licensee may apply to the producer for a license, and the producer shall not unreasonably withhold such license, provided that the terms offered are commercially reasonable and consistent with prevailing industry practices. The producer may, however, refuse a license if the proposed use would be detrimental to the integrity of the work or would infringe the rights of others.

A person who causes a work to be produced shall be deemed the producer of that work, notwithstanding any contractual arrangement to the contrary, provided that such causation directly results in the creation of the work and is not merely incidental to another undertaking. Any dispute regarding the determination of a producer, where multiple parties claim such status, shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the work was first embodied in a tangible form. An appeal from any decision of the High Court on such matter may be made to the Supreme Court, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules framed thereunder. Where a work is produced collaboratively, the parties involved may, by mutual agreement, designate a lead producer, and such designation shall be binding unless challenged on grounds of fraud or coercion. Failure to designate a lead producer shall not invalidate the claim of any party to producer status, but may complicate proceedings.

A person claiming to be a producer of a cinematograph film shall furnish to the India Registrar a declaration outlining the scope of their production rights, including details of all creative contributions and financial investments made towards the film’s creation. Any dispute regarding the veracity of such a declaration, or the rightful identification of the producer, may be raised by any interested party before the Registrar within sixty days of the declaration’s filing. The Registrar shall, following a reasoned inquiry and opportunity for all parties to present evidence, issue a determination as to the valid producer. An appeal from any determination of the Registrar shall lie before the High Court having jurisdiction, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act regarding producer declarations may render the film ineligible for copyright protection as provided herein.

A person claiming to be a producer of a work shall register particulars of the work with the Registrar of Copyrights in the manner as provided herein. The application for registration shall be accompanied by the requisite fee and a copy of the work, or a sufficient portion thereof, to enable the Registrar to satisfy themselves as to the work’s originality. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant is the producer and that the work is eligible for copyright, a certificate of registration shall be issued. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a work, or by any other decision concerning registration, may submit an appeal specified to the High Court within thirty days of the date of the decision. Such appeal shall be heard by a single judge and the decision of the High Court shall be final, subject to further recourse as permitted by law. The register maintained by the Registrar shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein.

A person who causes a work to be made shall be deemed to be the producer of that work, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a work is commissioned, the commissioning party shall, unless otherwise agreed in writing, be the first owner of the copyright therein. However, in the case of a semiconductor integrated circuit as defined under the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000, the producer shall be the person who undertakes the layout-design. Any dispute regarding the determination of the producer, where multiple parties claim involvement in causing the work, may be referred to a designated officer for investigation and report. The officer shall consider all relevant evidence, including contracts, correspondence, and witness statements, and submit a reasoned report within ninety days. The decision of the officer shall be final and binding on all parties, provided that an appeal may lie before the High Court on a point of law. A producer, in exercising rights under this Act, shall ensure compliance with all applicable licensing requirements.

A person qualifying as a producer of a cinematograph film shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be deemed the first owner of the copyright therein. However, where the producer is not the author of the film, the copyright shall vest in the producer subject to any contract existing between the producer and the author. Any dispute regarding the determination of the first owner of copyright, or the validity of any contract relating thereto, may be brought before an order adjudicating officer appointed for the purpose. The application to the officer shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant contract, if any, and all supporting documentation. The decision of the order adjudicating officer shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal may lie to the High Court on a point of law. A producer failing to comply with the requirements of registration as provided herein shall forfeit certain rights relating to statutory damages.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. The registrar may, if satisfied that the mark meets the requirements of this Act, proceed to advertise the application in the prescribed manner. However, the registrar shall refuse the application if the mark is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, or if it is prohibited under the provisions relating to scandalous or offensive marks. Subject to the payment of the prescribed fees, the registrar may, at any time before the completion of the registration process, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. Any decision of the registrar regarding refusal may be appealed as per the established procedure.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Trade Marks Register as provided herein, to ascertain whether any trade mark identical with, or deceptively similar to, the mark applied for is already registered or pending. The registrar may, if satisfied that the mark applied for is distinctive and not prohibited under this Act, accept the application subject to any conditions deemed necessary for clarity or to avoid confusion. Provided that, if the registrar objects to the application, a notice of such objection, specifying the grounds therefor, shall be sent to the applicant, who shall be afforded an opportunity to respond within a period of thirty days. The registrar shall, after considering the applicant’s response, either withdraw the objection or proceed with the examination of the application. Any decision of the registrar regarding acceptance or refusal may be appealed to the appellate board.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of a notice of proposed assignment of a registered trade mark, enter such notice in the Register of Trade Marks within the prescribed period, subject to payment of the applicable fee as provided herein. Where the registrar is satisfied that the assignment is in accordance with this Act and does not contravene any existing legal restrictions, they shall record the transfer of ownership in the Register. However, the registrar may, if reasonable cause exists to believe a fraudulent transfer is intended, require the parties to furnish evidence of legitimate consideration and good faith. Provided that, failure to provide such evidence within thirty days shall render the proposed assignment liable to be refused. Any aggrieved party may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the High Court for rectification of the Register where they believe the registrar has acted unfairly or without due consideration. The registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and transfers.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark meets the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The Registrar may, at any stage of the examination, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information or documents, subject to such conditions as may be deemed appropriate. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the trade mark is not registrable, the Registrar shall record the reasons for such refusal in writing and communicate the same to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, within the prescribed time, file a petition for review before the Registrar, supported by a statement of grounds. The Registrar shall consider such petition and may, after giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the original decision. Provided that no review petition shall be entertained unless it is accompanied by a prescribed fee.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark meets the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The registrar may require the applicant to amend the application, or to furnish further information or documents, within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. Subject to compliance with the provisions of this Act, the registrar shall, if satisfied that the trade mark is registrable, proceed to advertise it in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, where an objection is raised by the registrar, the applicant shall have the opportunity to submit a response, supported by evidence, within sixty days of the notice of objection. The registrar shall consider such response and may, if satisfied, allow the application to proceed or, if not satisfied, reject the same, recording the reasons for such rejection. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the registrar may file an appeal as prescribed.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging the application of a deceptive or scandalous mark, conduct a preliminary inquiry to ascertain the veracity of the allegations and may require the complainant to furnish documentary evidence supporting their claims, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. If, following such inquiry, the registrar is satisfied that a prima facie case exists, they shall notify the applicant and direct them to submit a written response within thirty days. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an admission of the allegations and the registrar may, without further notice, reject the application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar under this Act may file an appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the registrar’s order and accompanied by a certified copy thereof. The registrar shall maintain a register of all complaints received and actions taken, which shall be open for inspection by any person upon payment of a reasonable fee.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of a duly completed instrument of transfer, record the assignment of a registered trade mark, subject to verification of the instrument’s authenticity and the applicant’s entitlement to assign. Any assignment not recorded with the registrar shall be ineffective against a subsequent assignee unless the subsequent assignee had actual knowledge of the prior unrecorded assignment. Where an assignment involves a series of trade marks owned by a single proprietor, the registrar may require a consolidated instrument covering all marks to facilitate efficient record-keeping. Provided that, the registrar may, at their discretion, waive the requirement for a consolidated instrument if sufficient justification is provided. The registrar shall maintain a public register of all recorded assignments, accessible for inspection as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar regarding the recording of an assignment may, within sixty days, file a statement of reasons for review.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of the register alleging wrongful inclusion of a mark, cause a notice to be issued to the proprietor of the mark, requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not less than thirty days. Provided that, where the application for rectification is based on a claim of prior use of a similar mark, the Registrar may, subject to the applicant demonstrating prima facie evidence of such use, direct the parties to submit evidence for adjudication. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision on the admissibility of evidence, or by any interlocutory order made during the rectification proceedings, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after considering the records and hearing the parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and its decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided herein.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a request for rectification of the register alleging wrongful inclusion of a mark, cause an inquiry to be conducted, and may require the applicant to furnish evidence in support of the allegation, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Marks Registry established under this Act shall maintain a record of all such requests and the evidence submitted therein, ensuring confidentiality to the extent provided herein. If the Registrar is satisfied that the mark was wrongly included, they shall order its removal from the register and notify the owner of the mark accordingly. Provided that, any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, and the Registrar shall implement the Board’s order without delay. Any costs associated with the rectification process, including those incurred by the Registrar, may be recovered from the requesting party if the allegation is found to be frivolous or vexatious.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark accompanied by the prescribed fee and all necessary documents, examine the application as provided herein. If the Registrar is satisfied that the application meets all requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder, the Registrar shall proceed to advertise the trade mark in the prescribed manner. However, if the application relates to a trade mark incorporating a depiction or reference to a patented invention for which the patent is still in force, the Registrar shall require the applicant to submit a no-objection certificate from the patent holder. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence as deemed necessary. Provided that any such requirement shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, specifying a reasonable timeframe for compliance. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all applications received and shall record the status of each application therein.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration claiming priority under this Act, conduct a search for identical or similar trade marks already registered or applied for, and shall examine the application in accordance with the provisions herein. Provided that, if the application claims priority based on a trade mark recognized as a well known trade mark in India, the registrar shall expedite such examination and afford the applicant an opportunity to be heard within thirty days of acknowledging receipt of a satisfactory demonstration of such recognition. Subject to the provisions relating to conflict, the registrar may require the applicant to amend the application to remove any ambiguity or to clarify the scope of goods or services. Any refusal to amend, where reasonably required, shall be communicated to the applicant with a statement of reasons, and the applicant may appeal such decision as provided herein. The registrar shall maintain a register of all applications and registered trade marks.

The term “district court” shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean the Principal District Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the principal place of business of the patentee or the applicant, as the case may be, is situated, or where there is no such place of business in India, the Principal District Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the cause of action arises. Provided that, if the cause of action arises in more than one district, the district court having jurisdiction over the district where the patentee or applicant first received notice of the infringement or alleged infringement shall be the appropriate district court. Any appeal from the decision of a district court shall lie to the High Court. A nominated officer may, subject to the rules, assist the district court in technical matters.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, or by any decision concerning the rectification of the register of patents, may present an appeal to the appropriate district court. Such appeal shall be presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the district court may, for sufficient cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. The district court exercising jurisdiction under this Act shall maintain a register of all appeals received and the status thereof, updated monthly. All evidence submitted before the district court shall be certified as true copies of the original documents. Subject to the provisions herein, the district court shall follow the principles of natural justice and may, at its discretion, require further evidence or expert testimony to arrive at a just determination. The decision of the district court shall be final and binding, except where an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent, as provided herein, may institute a suit in the appropriate district court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The plaintiff shall, within thirty days of commencing the suit, submit to the defendant a detailed statement of the alleged infringement, including specific claims and particulars of the patent in question. The district court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing act, pending the final determination of the suit. Any person defending against a claim of infringement may, in addition to other defenses, demonstrate non-infringement or the invalidity of the patent. Costs associated with such litigation shall be borne by the losing party, unless the court determines otherwise, and may include reasonable attorney’s fees. A decree for damages, including an accounting of profits, may be issued in favour of the successful party.

Any suit for infringement of a patent, under this Act, shall be instituted in the district court within the local limits of which the cause of action arises, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Where multiple defendants reside or carry on business in different districts, the plaintiff may institute a suit in any one of those districts, provided that such plaintiff satisfies the Court that it is necessary for the ends of justice to do so. The district court, upon receiving a plaint alleging infringement, shall issue a summons to the defendant requiring them to appear and defend the claim. Any evidence submitted in support of a claim of infringement shall be subject to the rules of evidence as applicable in civil proceedings. The Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to produce any document or thing necessary for the purpose of the suit, and may impose reasonable costs for non-compliance. A temporary injunction may be granted pending the final determination of the suit, subject to such terms and conditions as the Court deems fit.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of a Licensing Officer, or by an order of the Controller relating to the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the appropriate district court. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding limitation contained in the Limitation Act, 1963. The district court, upon receipt of an appeal, may require the appellant to deposit with the court, such sum as it deems reasonable, to cover the costs of the respondent. Provided that, if the appellant satisfies the court that he is unable to bear such costs, the court may waive the requirement. The district court shall, after examining the records and hearing both parties, deliver a reasoned judgment within one hundred and eighty days. Any further appeal shall lie to the High Court, subject to the conditions as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of a Licensing Officer, or by any order made by the Controller relating to the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the appropriate district court. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be in such form and be accompanied by such documents as may be prescribed. The district court, upon receipt of an appeal, may, if satisfied that there is a substantial question of law involved, admit the appeal and shall issue notice to the respondent. Failure to comply with the prescribed time limits for presenting an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible, subject to the discretion of the court to extend the time for sufficient cause. Any person found to have knowingly made a false statement in an appeal under this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both.

Any assignment of a patent application or a patent, whether wholly or partially, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, and such instrument shall be registered with the appropriate district court having jurisdiction over the matter. The district court, upon registration of the assignment, shall issue a certificate of registration to the assignee, confirming the transfer of rights, title, and interest in the patent or patent application. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a licensee of a patent may, with the consent of the patent holder, further assign their rights to a third party, and such subsequent assignment shall also require registration with the district court. Where a patent is jointly held, any assignment requires the written consent of all co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a prior agreement filed with the district court. Failure to register an assignment shall not invalidate the assignment itself, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer. The district court may prescribe fees for registration and maintain a public register of all assignments.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller rejecting an application for a patent, or revoking a patent, or dismissing an opposition, may prefer an appeal to the appropriate district court. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to an extension of a further thirty days, if the appellant satisfactorily demonstrates cause for delay. The district court, upon receipt of a memorandum of appeal and the prescribed fee, may direct the Controller to transmit the relevant records to the court. Provided that, the district court may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit with the court such sum as it deems reasonable to cover the costs of the Controller in preparing and transmitting said records. Any decision of the district court shall be final and binding, save for a further appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein. The powers of the district court in such appeals shall be equivalent to those of a civil court trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act, relating to an article patented, may institute a suit in the district court within whose jurisdiction the offence arises. The suit shall be filed within three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement, provided that the court may grant an extension of time for sufficient cause. Upon receiving a complaint of infringement, the district court may, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, grant a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement pending final determination of the suit. Any person defending against such a suit may, subject to such terms as the court deems fit, seek a counter-claim for revocation of the patent, alleging it to be invalid. The court shall, as expeditiously as possible, hear the matter and may award damages to the plaintiff, or grant an account of profits, or both, as provided herein. Costs shall be awarded to the prevailing party.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the district court relating to the infringement of a patent, or the revocation of a patent, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Where a registration copyright society, duly registered under the relevant legislation, alleges infringement of copyright on behalf of its members, the district court shall expedite proceedings and may, at its discretion, impose enhanced damages not exceeding three times the actual damages proven, if it finds the infringement to be willful and calculated. Any officer of the district court failing to comply with this provision shall be liable to disciplinary action, including potential removal from service. Furthermore, any false claim submitted to the district court by a registration copyright society shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. All appeals under this Act shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order.

In this Act, “registration trade” shall mean the process by which a mark, capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, is entered in the Register maintained under this Act, conferring upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to those goods or services. A “well-known trade mark”, for the purposes of enhanced protection as provided herein, shall be a mark which has become recognizable to the relevant public by reason of its use, and may be registered even if not currently in use. Subject to the provisions relating to prior rights and honest concurrent use, a registered trade mark shall be evidence of ownership, and the right to sue for infringement. Any assignment of a registration trade shall be subject to the conditions prescribed.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration of a trade mark, or requiring an amendment of an application for registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order of the Registry. Such appeal shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the prescribed fee, and shall state the grounds upon which the appellant relies for setting aside or modifying the decision appealed against. The Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum sufficient to cover the costs of notice to any person likely to be affected by the appeal. Where a trade mark is refused registration on the grounds that it is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, the Appellate Board shall consider evidence of actual confusion, if any, and the extent to which the existing trade mark has acquired goodwill. Provided that the Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct the parties to attempt mediation before proceeding with the hearing of the appeal, to facilitate an amicable resolution of the dispute concerning the registration trade.

A person shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence under this Act where such person, with knowledge of an infringement of copyright in a work, procures or knowingly facilitates the infringement. Such facilitation shall include, but not be limited to, providing the means for infringing reproduction, distribution, or public performance of the copyrighted work. Where the commission offence is proven, the offender shall be liable to the same penalties as if they had directly committed the primary act of infringement, subject to the provisions relating to abetment as contained within the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Provided that, a mere intermediary service provider shall not be held liable for a commission offence unless they fail to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing material upon receiving due notice from the copyright holder.

Any person who, with knowledge of a work being in copyright, undertakes for profit any commercial dealing with such work, including sale, hire, distribution, or import, without the authorization of the copyright owner, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence as provided herein. The commission offence shall be cognizable by a Judicial First Class Magistrate or any higher court. Where the offence involves the reproduction or circulation of a substantial number of copies, or a significant commercial gain is demonstrably derived from the unauthorized dealing, the court may, in addition to any fine imposed, order the seizure and destruction of all infringing copies and the means by which such copies were made. Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by such an offence may apply to the appropriate court for an injunction restraining further infringement. Provided that no such application shall be entertained without prior notice to the alleged infringer.

Any person who, with knowledge of an infringement of copyright as provided herein, induces, enables, procures, or authorizes such infringement, shall be liable for a commission offence and shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the commission offence involves a work that is commercially rented or lent, the court may, at its discretion, also order the forfeiture of any equipment used in the commission of the offence. 

Notwithstanding any other provision, a person who distributes infringing copies of a work, knowing that such copies are likely to be used for commercial gain, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence. The owner of the copyright may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining the offender from further acts of infringement and for recovery of damages. Any damages awarded shall be proportionate to the extent of the infringement and the commercial benefit derived therefrom.

Any person who, with knowledge of an infringement of copyright in a work, procures, publishes, distributes, or causes to be exhibited or performed any such work, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence as provided herein, and shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six years, or with fine, or with both. Where the commission offence involves a cinematograph film, the provisions of this Act relating to literary, dramatic or musical works shall apply mutatis mutandis. 

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a person abetting the commission of an offence shall be liable as if they had actually committed the offence. The court, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, may, in addition to any imprisonment or fine imposed, order the seizure of all infringing copies and the apparatus used in the making of such copies. Any order made under this provision shall be final and not appealable, provided that an application for review may be made to the court within thirty days of the order.

Any person who, without lawful excuse, assists in the doing of any act which constitutes a commission offence under this Act, or abets the doing of such an act, or attempts to do such an act, shall be liable for the commission offence as if he were the principal offender. Where a commission offence is committed by a person who, by reason of his official position, has access to any work in which copyright subsists, and he commits the offence in the course of his employment, the employer shall also be deemed to have committed a commission offence unless he proves that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. However, no prosecution for a commission offence shall be instituted without the prior written consent of the Central Government, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding the time limitation for initiating legal proceedings. Any evidence obtained through unlawful means shall not be admissible in proceedings related to a commission offence.

Any person who, with knowledge of an infringement of copyright as provided herein, distributes, sells, or exhibits infringing works, or causes any other person to do so, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence under this Act. Where the commission offence involves commercial scale reproduction for gain, the penalty shall be imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to three lakh rupees. However, if the offence does not involve commercial gain, the penalty shall be imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or a fine not exceeding one lakh rupees, or both. Any evidence obtained by an investigating officer, including digital records, shall be admissible in court, subject to the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of all infringing copies and implements used in the commission of the offence.

Any person who, without lawful excuse, undertakes for profit any commercial exploitation of a work in which copyright subsists, in contravention of the rights of the copyright owner, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence under this Act, and shall be liable to the penalties prescribed herein. Such exploitation shall include, but not be limited to, reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation of the work, whether in whole or in part. Where the commission offence involves an assignment or licensing of copyright, any agreement purporting to effect such assignment or license without the express written consent of the copyright owner shall be null and void. However, a bona fide assignee or licensee, acting in good faith and without knowledge of the unlawful nature of the exploitation, may seek recourse through civil remedies as provided herein. The copyright owner may, subject to the provisions of this Act, pursue both civil and criminal remedies in respect of any such commission offence.

Any person who, with knowledge of a work being in copyright, undertakes any act restricted by this Act, and thereby commits an infringement, shall be liable for a commission offence, attracting the penalties as provided herein. However, a finding of commission offence shall not be made unless it is established that the alleged infringer acted with a deliberate intent to deceive or to gain an unfair commercial advantage. Where a claim of innocent infringement is raised, the onus of proving knowledge or intent shall lie upon the complainant, subject to the provisions relating to fair dealing as permissible under this Act. An appeal against a finding of a commission offence may be made to the High Court, provided such appeal is filed within ninety days of the decision of the adjudicating authority. The High Court shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision, and may direct further investigation if deemed necessary.

Any person who, with knowledge of a work being protected by copyright and without the authorization of the copyright owner, engages in the reproduction, distribution, or public exhibition of said work, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence under this Act and shall be liable for statutory damages as provided herein. Where the commission offence relates to a business basic application, such as software distributed as part of a larger system or a template used in the creation of derivative works, the liability extends to all instances of unauthorized use facilitated by the initial infringement. Provided that, if the person committing the offence proves that such reproduction, distribution, or exhibition was incidental to a legitimate technical process and did not materially contribute to economic prejudice to the copyright owner, the court may reduce the statutory damages. The copyright owner may, subject to the rules of evidence, demonstrate the extent of actual damages suffered as a result of the commission offence, and the court shall consider such evidence in determining the appropriate penalty.

Any person who, subject to the provisions of this Act, undertakes any act constituting a commission offence relating to copyright shall be liable for such offence, and the liability shall extend to all works affected by such act. Where such an offence involves the making of claims inconsistent with the rights of the copyright owner, the claimant shall furnish evidence substantiating the basis of such claims to the investigating officer within thirty days of being requested to do so. Failure to provide adequate substantiation may be considered an aggravating factor in determining the penalty. Provided that, if the act is committed due to a demonstrable lack of reasonable diligence in preventing the infringement, a lesser penalty may be imposed at the discretion of the adjudicating authority. Any proceeds derived from the commission offence shall be forfeited to the Government.

Any person who undertakes any act in violation of the exclusive rights conferred by this Act, with knowledge or reasonable grounds for believing that such act will result in an infringement of copyright, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence, and shall be punishable as provided herein. However, a finding of commission offence shall not preclude a separate action for civil remedies available to the copyright holder. Where an application for interim injunction is made, and the court finds credible evidence suggesting a commission offence, it may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct the applicant to deposit security with the Registrar for the purposes of application section 71, to cover potential damages. Provided that such security shall not exceed an amount commensurate with the estimated scale of infringement. Any appeal against an order relating to such security shall lie before the designated appellate authority within thirty days of the order’s issuance.

A person shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence under this Act where such person procures or permits any infringement of copyright, or abets such infringement. Where the commission offence is committed by an offence act company, every director, manager, secretary, or other officer of the company who is responsible for the conduct of the business of the company shall also be deemed to be guilty of the commission offence, unless they prove that the infringement occurred without their knowledge or that they exercised all due diligence to prevent such infringement. Any finding of guilt against a company shall not preclude the prosecution of any individual liable for the commission offence. Subject to the provisions herein, all penalties shall be determined as per the schedule.

For the purposes of determining deceptively similar trade marks under this Act, regard shall be given to all relevant circumstances including, but not limited to, the class of goods or services to which the trade marks relate, the manner of use of the marks, and the channels of trade through which the goods or services are likely to be offered to the public. A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar if it is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin, character or quality of the goods or services, even if the marks are not identical. However, a mere visual resemblance shall not, by itself, be sufficient to establish deceptive similarity; phonetic similarity and conceptual similarity, considered in their totality, must also be demonstrated. Provided that, in cases involving well-known marks, a lesser degree of similarity may be sufficient to establish deception.

A trade mark shall not be registered if it is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, and the Registrar, having regard to all relevant circumstances, including the nature of the goods or services, the channel of trade, and the class of persons likely to be deceived, determines that such similarity is likely to cause confusion among consumers. However, a registration may proceed if the proprietor of the earlier trade mark consents in writing to the registration of the later mark, or if the marks are used in different classes of goods or services, provided that no likelihood of confusion exists. Where a mark incorporates elements of a well-known trade mark not registered in India, but possessing a reputation therein, registration shall be refused if use of the mark would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the earlier mark, as provided herein. The Registrar may require evidence of concurrent use to determine deceptive similarity.

Any person aggrieved by a registration of a trade mark which is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, and who satisfies the conditions set forth herein, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for rectification of the register. Such application shall be made in writing and shall clearly demonstrate the prior use of the aggrieved party’s trade mark and the likelihood of confusion resulting from the subsequent registration. The Registry, upon receiving such application, shall notify the registered proprietor and afford them an opportunity to be heard. Where the Registry finds that the marks are indeed deceptively similar, and that the registration was made without due diligence regarding the existence of the prior mark, it may order the rectification of the register, removing or amending the offending entry. A finding of deceptive similarity shall consider the overall impression created by the marks, including visual, aural, and conceptual aspects, and shall be subject to the principles of honest trade practice. The aggrieved party may also seek an injunction restraining the use of the deceptively similar mark, as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining whether trade marks are deceptively similar, regard shall be given to all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to the nature of the goods or services, the channels of trade, and the class of persons likely to be affected thereby. A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar if it is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers, even if it does not precisely replicate the earlier trade mark. Consideration shall also be given to the overall impression created by the marks, and not merely to individual elements thereof. Where a mark incorporates elements of an earlier mark, but with variations in colour, font, or minor design features, such variations shall not preclude a finding of deceptive similarity, provided that the overall effect is likely to mislead. The onus of proving deceptive similarity rests with the complainant, subject to the provisions herein relating to evidence. A mark shall not be considered deceptively similar if the earlier mark lacks inherent distinctiveness or has acquired no goodwill.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the goods or services in relation to which the marks are used. In determining whether marks are deceptively similar, due regard shall be given to the overall impression created by the marks, including the visual, aural, and conceptual characteristics. Where a mark incorporates elements identical to a previously registered mark, but with minor variations, such variations shall not be considered sufficient to negate a finding of deceptive similarity, unless those variations are substantial and demonstrably alter the overall character of the mark. A mark shall not be considered deceptively similar if the prior mark is well-known and the subsequent mark is used on entirely dissimilar goods or services, provided that such use does not take unfair advantage of, or injure the reputation of, the prior mark as provided herein. Any party alleging deceptive similarity bears the onus of proving such similarity.

Any person who applies for the registration of a trade mark which is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, and wherein such existing trade mark relates to identical or similar goods or services, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, if the applicant proves prior bona fide use of the mark prior to the application of the existing trade mark, the penalty may be reduced at the discretion of the adjudicating officer. Furthermore, any goods bearing a deceptively similar mark, knowingly sold or offered for sale, shall be deemed counterfeit goods as provided herein, and subject to seizure and destruction. The owner of the registered trade mark, upon establishing deceptive similarity and resulting damage, may seek an injunction restraining further use and claim damages for loss of goodwill. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the assignment of goods and goodwill. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under that trade mark, the assignee shall, subject to conditions as may be prescribed, be entitled to use the trade mark as if it were registered in their name. However, an assignment of a trade mark without goodwill, or an assignment of part only of the goodwill, shall not confer any right to use the trade mark. Where a mark is deceptively similar to a registered trade mark and is assigned, the assignee’s rights to use the assigned mark shall be conditional upon a clear disclaimer demonstrating no intent to mislead the public or cause confusion with the existing registered mark. Any transfer of rights must be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry to be legally effective, and failure to do so may invalidate subsequent claims.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion among consumers, and such confusion may arise from the similarity in the marks’ visual appearance, phonetic pronunciation, or conceptual meaning, or a combination thereof. However, mere resemblance shall not, on its own, constitute deceptive similarity; the Tribunal shall consider the overall impression created by the marks, including the nature of the goods or services to which they relate, and the class of persons likely to purchase those goods or services. An appeal may be filed with the High Court concerning a decision of the Tribunal regarding deceptive similarity, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Tribunal’s order. Where a finding of deceptive similarity is successfully challenged on appeal, the registration of the later trade mark may be revoked, subject to the rights of any bona fide adopter.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the use of marks and the potential for confusion arising therefrom. Where a mark, though not identical to an existing registered trade mark, is deceptively similar, the assignment shall require a clear demonstration that the continued use of the assigned mark will not likely cause confusion amongst consumers. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, require evidence of actual use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the assignment, to ascertain the extent of potential overlap and the likelihood of deception. Consideration shall also be given to the nature of the goods or services and the channels of trade, determining the use mark relation. An assignment failing to adequately address these concerns may be refused or subject to conditions designed to mitigate the risk of consumer confusion, as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion among consumers, considering the overall impression created and the class of persons likely to deal with the goods or services concerned. However, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct that two trade marks, though deceptively similar, may be registered in respect of different descriptions of goods or services, provided that such goods or services are not ordinarily likely to be confused as being the same or of the same kind. Where a trade mark incorporates a geographical indication prescribed under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the assessment of deceptive similarity shall also consider the reputation and distinctiveness of the geographical indication itself, and whether its use in relation to the disputed mark would mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods. Any decision of the Registrar regarding deceptive similarity shall be subject to appeal to the High Court.

For the purposes of determining deceptively similar trade marks under this Act, regard shall be given to the totality of the marks, including the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities, and the class of goods or services to which they relate. A trade mark shall not be considered deceptively similar merely because it incorporates elements common to the trade or industry in question, provided that such elements do not create a likelihood of confusion. Where a trade mark incorporates a registered geographical indication, the assessment of deceptive similarity shall also consider the reputation and distinctiveness of the geographical indication itself, and whether the use of the mark would likely mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods or services. Any mark determined to be deceptively similar shall be liable to be refused registration or revoked, as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion among the public, or a substantial section thereof, as to the goods or services in relation to which the marks are used. The assessment of deceptive similarity shall consider all relevant factors, including the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the marks, as well as the overall impression created by each. The India Registrar, when examining applications for registration, shall apply a comparative analysis, considering the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark and the likelihood of association in the minds of consumers. Provided that, mere resemblance shall not, by itself, constitute deceptive similarity; the likelihood of confusion must be demonstrated. Any party opposing a trade mark application on grounds of deceptive similarity shall bear the burden of proving such likelihood to the satisfaction of the India Registrar.

A registered trade mark shall be infringed by any person who uses in the course of trade a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, concerning goods or services for which the mark is registered, where such use is likely to cause confusion amongst the public, or is likely to be taken as being connected with the proprietor of the registered trade mark. However, a use of a mark shall not be considered an infringement as provided herein if it constitutes a fair use under this Act, or is demonstrably descriptive of the goods or services themselves. Furthermore, a registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the mark and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to the trade mark infringed. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning infringement may appeal to the appropriate authority.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be infringed where a person, not being the registered proprietor or a licensee, uses a mark in the course of trade, which is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, and such use occurs in relation to goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. However, a use of a mark shall not be considered an infringement if it is demonstrably different in the overall impression created, considering all relevant factors including sight, sound, and meaning. Where a registered trade mark consists of a well-known mark, infringement shall be determined irrespective of whether the allegedly infringing mark is used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion or is likely to diminish the distinctive character or repute of the registered trade mark. Any person aggrieved by such trade mark infringed may apply to the Court for appropriate relief, including injunction and damages, as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be infringed if any person, not being the registered proprietor or a licensee authorized by such proprietor, uses a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and such use is likely to cause confusion or deception among the public, or is likely to injure the character or reputation of the trade mark. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall be entitled to use the trade mark as if they were the registered proprietor, subject to any limitations specified in the instrument of assignment. However, a bare license does not confer ownership, and any unauthorized use beyond the scope of the license constitutes trade mark infringed. The registered proprietor may seek injunctive relief and damages for any proven infringement.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be infringed if a person, not being the registered proprietor or a licensee, uses a mark in the course of trade, which is identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, and such use is in relation to goods or services for which the trade mark is registered. However, a mere similarity of marks is insufficient to establish infringement, and the court shall consider the overall impression created by the marks, including their visual, aural, and conceptual characteristics, and the class of persons likely to be deceived. Where a defendant demonstrates legitimate use of a descriptive term within the trade mark, such use shall not, in itself, constitute trade mark infringed, provided that such use is fair and honest and does not create confusion. Any aggrieved party may apply to the court for an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringement, and the court may, subject to the equities of the case, grant such injunction. An appeal from any order of the court shall lie to the High Court.

A patented article shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean any article, substance, or combination thereof, in respect of which a valid and currently enforceable patent has been granted. Such a patented article need not be newly manufactured, but its manufacture, use, sale, import, or export shall be subject to the rights conferred upon the patent holder as provided herein. Where an article embodies a patented invention, but also incorporates elements not claimed in the patent, it shall not be considered wholly a patented article unless the patented elements contribute substantially to the article’s essential character.
