A process resulting in a patented article is considered integral to the protection afforded to that article, and any unauthorized replication of said process, even if yielding a non-identical article, may constitute infringement.

Any article in respect of which a valid and unrevoked patent has been granted under this Act shall be deemed a patented article for the purposes of this Act, and shall be subject to the rights conferred upon the patentee. The patentee of a patented article may, subject to the provisions contained herein, grant licenses to others for the manufacture, use, or sale of said article, and shall maintain a register of all such licenses granted. Any person dealing with a patented article without the license of the patentee, or in contravention of the terms of any such license, shall be liable to the remedies provided for infringement under this Act. However, a patented article, if imported into India, shall be subject to the inspection and examination by the Customs authorities as provided herein, to verify compliance with the terms of the patent and prevent the entry of counterfeit goods. The register of licenses shall be open for inspection during office hours.

Any person who makes, sells, offers for sale, or distributes a patented article without the license of the patent holder, or uses a patented process without authorization, shall be liable for patent infringement as provided herein. A patent holder, upon establishing infringement, may seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. Damages shall be ascertainable on the basis of reasonable royalty or actual losses, whichever is higher. 

However, a bona fide licensee of the patent, or a person utilizing the patented article for research purposes, shall not be held liable for infringement, subject to the terms of any existing license agreement. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the High Court for redressal, and the Court may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party. The patent holder’s right to remedies is cumulative with any other remedies available under law.

A patented article, when manufactured or imported, shall be deemed to be an infringement of a patent unless it is proven to be for the purposes of research or private, non-commercial experimentation, and subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person dealing in a patented article, or importing it into India, may be required by the Controller to furnish information as to the origin of such article, including details of manufacture and importation, and the quantity thereof. Failure to comply with such requirement shall attract penalties as prescribed under this Act. Where a patented article is essential for public health and safety, the Central Government may, after due consideration and notification in the Official Gazette, authorize its use by any person or entity, subject to payment of reasonable royalties to the patent holder. Provided that, such authorization shall not be granted if the patent holder demonstrates adequate domestic manufacture and supply of the patented article. Any dispute regarding the determination of reasonable royalties shall be adjudicated by a designated court.

Any patented article manufactured or imported into India shall be subject to marking requirements as provided herein. The patentee, or person having a right to manufacture or import the patented article, shall clearly and legibly mark the article with the patent number and the name of the patentee. Failure to comply with this marking requirement shall not invalidate the patent, provided that such failure is remedied within a period of three months from the date of notification by the Controller. Where a patented article is comprised in a larger article, marking shall be performed on a part of the larger article that is readily visible and identifiable. Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person dealing with an unmarked patented article shall not be liable for infringement. The Controller may, by notification, prescribe additional requirements relating to the marking of patented articles to ensure effective public notice.

Any person who, without the license of the patentee or his duly authorized agent, makes, sells, offers for sale, distributes, imports or exports a patented article shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to three times the value of the patented article subject to a minimum fine of fifty thousand rupees. Where the patented article is a component part of a larger article, the penalty shall be calculated on the value added by the patented article to the larger article. Provided that, if the infringement is proven to be unintentional, the adjudicating officer may reduce the penalty, but not below ten thousand rupees. Any evidence of intent to deceive or conceal the infringement shall negate the possibility of a reduced penalty. All seized patented articles shall be subject to destruction or disposal as directed by the court, and the costs of such destruction or disposal shall be borne by the infringer. A patentee may seek injunctive relief to prevent further infringement as provided herein.

Any assignment of right, title and interest in a patented article shall be in writing and executed by or on behalf of the assignor and shall specify the patent to which it relates, including the application number and date. Where a patented article is subject to a license, the terms and conditions of such license, including the scope of permitted use, royalty payments, and duration, shall be clearly delineated in a written agreement between the patentee and the licensee. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a licensee may, with the express written consent of the patentee, further assign their rights under the license to a third party. However, any such further assignment shall not prejudice the original terms of the license agreement as approved by the patentee. The patentee retains the right to seek equitable relief in the event of unauthorized assignment or exploitation of the patented article, and may pursue remedies as available under this Act. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent relating to a patented article shall, prior to the institution of any suit, provide the alleged infringer with a clear and detailed statement of the grounds for such allegation, including a demonstration of how the alleged infringer’s article embodies or derives from the claims of the patent. Should the alleged infringer, within a period of thirty days from receipt of said statement, submit a reasoned argument disputing the validity of the patent or the assertion of infringement, the complainant may apply to the High Court for a preliminary assessment of the patent’s validity. Provided that, such application shall be subject to the payment of a prescribed fee and may be dismissed if the Court deems the dispute frivolous or lacking in sufficient merit. A finding of non-infringement, even preliminary, shall not preclude a subsequent finding of infringement based on newly presented evidence, but shall be considered by the Court in any final determination. Any appeal from a decision of the High Court regarding patent validity shall lie with the Supreme Court.

Any person alleging infringement of a patented article shall, prior to the institution of any suit, notify the patent holder of such alleged infringement, providing detailed particulars thereof, including but not limited to the manner of infringement and the quantity of articles alleged to be so infringed. Should the patent holder, within a period of sixty days from receipt of such notification, fail to demonstrate a prima facie case of infringement, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for a declaration of non-infringement. The Registrar shall register all notices of alleged infringement received, maintaining a public record subject to redaction of commercially sensitive information. Any appeal from a decision of the High Court regarding such a declaration shall lie before the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained. A finding of non-infringement shall not preclude subsequent claims based on newly discovered evidence, subject to the limitations period as provided herein.

A patented article shall mean any article, substance, or combination thereof, in respect of which a valid and currently enforceable patent has been granted under this Act. The determination of whether an article falls within this definition shall be subject to proof of a direct correspondence between the claims of the patent and the physical characteristics of the article in question. Any dispute regarding the scope of a patented article, or the validity of the patent itself, may be submitted to the India Registrar for preliminary examination. Provided that such examination by the India Registrar shall not be construed as a final adjudication of the matter, and any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s findings may pursue further legal remedies as provided herein. The existence of a patent does not, by itself, establish that an article *is* a patented article; demonstrable equivalence is required.

Any assignment of a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the assignment, including whether it covers the right to apply for patents in any territory outside of India. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, granted under this Act, shall be construed as a contractual agreement between the patentee and the licensee, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a patent is assigned, the assignee shall, subject to the terms of the assignment, possess the same rights as the original patentee to pursue remedies for infringement of the patent. However, any act constituting an infringement patent committed before the date of assignment shall remain the responsibility of the original patentee unless otherwise agreed in writing between the parties. Should a licensee seek to further assign or license the rights granted to them, prior written consent of the patentee shall be required, unless the original license agreement explicitly permits such sub-licensing. Failure to obtain such consent may render the subsequent assignment or license voidable at the discretion of the patentee.

A complete specification, submitted under this Act, shall fully and particularly describe the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. The specification must disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Every claim shall be supported by matter in the complete specification as filed; any claim not so supported shall be deemed invalid. A claim complete specification, for the purposes of determining inventive step, shall be construed in light of the common knowledge in the relevant field. Provided that, where an invention involves a process, the specification shall clearly define the process and its essential features, subject to the provisions relating to secrecy where applicable. The specification may contain diagrams or drawings to illustrate the invention.

A complete specification, for the purposes of this Act, shall fully and particularly describe the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. The specification shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Every claim shall define clearly the scope of the invention and the matter for which protection is sought. A claim complete specification, failing to satisfy these requirements, may be subject to objection during examination. Where an invention comprises a combination of known elements, the specification shall demonstrate how the combination produces a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual elements. Any amendment to the complete specification, after filing, shall be subject to the provisions regarding allowable amendments as provided herein, and must not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. The applicant may, subject to prescribed fees, request re-examination of the specification if objections remain unresolved.

A complete specification, submitted under this Act for the purpose of a patent grant, shall fully and particularly describe the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. The specification shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Every claim shall define the scope of the invention for which protection is sought, and shall be clear and concise. A claim complete specification, failing to satisfy these requirements, may be subject to objection by the Controller of Patents. Where an inventor seeks amendment to a claim, such amendment shall not extend beyond the matter originally disclosed in the specification; provided that, the amendment does not introduce new matter. Any specification not adhering to the prescribed form, or lacking the necessary drawings where applicable, shall be deemed incomplete and may be returned to the applicant for rectification, subject to a prescribed timeframe for compliance. Failure to comply within said timeframe may result in abandonment of the application.

A complete specification, conforming to the requirements as provided herein, shall be filed in respect of every invention for which a patent is sought. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed, enabling a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Every claim shall define the scope of the invention for which protection is sought, and shall be clear and concise. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a claim complete specification must disclose the best method known to the applicant for performing the invention at the time of filing. Where an invention involves a process, the specification shall disclose the process in sufficient detail to enable a person skilled in the art to conduct it. Any amendment to a claim complete specification shall not extend beyond the content of the original specification. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the patent application liable to be refused.

A broadcasting organisation shall be deemed to be the author of the broadcast, and shall possess copyright in respect of that broadcast, subject to the provisions of this Act. For the purposes of this definition, ‘broadcast’ includes any communication to the public by any means, whether wired or wireless, of visual or aural works. A broadcasting organisation may, subject to the terms of any agreement with the owner of a work, broadcast a work that is already protected by copyright. Provided that, where a broadcasting organisation re-broadcasts a program received from another broadcasting organisation, the copyright shall vest in the organisation undertaking the re-broadcast, unless otherwise agreed. The rights conferred on a broadcasting organisation shall be independent of any rights in the underlying work.

Any broadcasting organisation intending to communicate to the public a sound recording, whether previously published or otherwise, shall register its details with the Registrar of Copyrights, maintaining a publicly accessible register as provided herein. Such registration shall include the name and address of the broadcasting organisation, the duration for which broadcasting rights are sought, and a clear identification of the sound recording intended for broadcast. A broadcasting organisation may, subject to the terms of any existing license or agreement with the owner of the copyright in the sound recording, apply for a statutory license for such broadcast. Provided that, where a broadcasting organisation broadcasts a work for public service purposes, including news and current affairs, it shall be exempt from the requirement of prior registration, but must notify the Registrar within fourteen days of the initial broadcast. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the broadcasting organisation liable to a penalty, as determined by the Registrar.

A broadcasting organisation shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright in the broadcast, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning assignments and licences. Notwithstanding such ownership, a broadcasting organisation’s right to broadcast a work shall not prejudice the copyright already subsisting in that work, and the owner of the underlying copyright retains all rights therein. However, any person who, without the consent of the broadcasting organisation, re-broadcasts a program shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. Where a broadcasting organisation broadcasts a work in which copyright subsists, and such broadcast constitutes an adaptation, the adaptation shall be considered a separate work subject to copyright. The rights conferred upon a broadcasting organisation extend to all forms of simultaneous and subsequent transmission, including digital and satellite broadcasting, provided that reasonable measures are taken to prevent unauthorized recording or reproduction. Any aggrieved party may seek remedies, including injunctions and damages, for infringements of these rights.

A broadcasting organisation intending to communicate to the public a work, whether literary, musical or dramatic, or a sound recording, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding statutory licensing where such work has already been published. Provided that, no broadcasting organisation shall undertake such communication without first ascertaining the identity of the copyright owner, or making reasonable efforts to do so, and offering remuneration as determined by the licensing authority. The licensing authority, upon receipt of an application from a broadcasting organisation and after considering representations from copyright owners, may grant a license subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, including but not limited to the duration, territory, and mode of communication. Any dispute concerning the amount of remuneration shall be adjudicated by the designated appellate tribunal. A broadcasting organisation failing to comply with these provisions shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and may have its license suspended or revoked. The rights of the author or composer remain unaffected by any license granted to a broadcasting organisation as provided herein.

A broadcasting organisation intending to communicate to the public a work, whether literary, musical, or dramatic, shall secure the requisite authorization from the copyright owner, except as otherwise provided herein. However, a broadcasting organisation may, subject to the conditions stipulated, simultaneously record and broadcast any performance in which copyright subsists, provided that reasonable royalties are paid to the copyright holder as determined by the Central Government. Any communication of a broadcast, including re-broadcast, shall be deemed a distinct communication requiring separate authorization unless expressly exempted under this Act. The broadcasting organisation shall maintain accurate records of all broadcasts made and royalties paid, and these records shall be open to inspection upon demand by a duly authorized officer. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties, including revocation of broadcasting rights and imposition of fines. A broadcasting organisation shall not alter the character or integrity of the work during broadcast without explicit consent.

Any broadcasting organisation undertaking the simultaneous transmission or reception of sounds or images, whether by radio, television, or any other means, shall be deemed to have exercised exclusive rights in respect of such broadcast, subject to the provisions contained herein. A broadcasting organisation failing to secure appropriate licenses for the communication to the public of any work protected under this Act shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such instance of unlicensed broadcast. Provided that, if the broadcast is determined to be of a wilful and repeated nature, the court may, in addition to the fine, impose imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. Any person assisting a broadcasting organisation in the unlawful broadcast, including those providing technical support, may be held jointly and severally liable. The determination of fair compensation for broadcasts shall be adjudicated by the designated authority, and any appeal shall lie before the High Court.

A broadcasting organisation intending to utilise any existing copyrighted work for the purpose of communication to the public through a broadcast, shall secure a license from the copyright owner, unless otherwise provided herein. Such license may be granted on terms mutually agreed upon between the parties, including but not limited to royalty rates and the territorial scope of the broadcast. Where a broadcasting organisation desires to broadcast a dramatic work, a separate license shall be required from both the author and the owner of the performance rights. Assignment of broadcasting rights, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be in writing and shall clearly define the duration, territory, and permitted modes of communication. Should the copyright owner unreasonably withhold license or demand exorbitant royalties, any aggrieved broadcasting organisation may apply to the High Court for redress. A failure to comply with these provisions, subject to the defences available under this Act, shall constitute an infringement of copyright.

A broadcasting organisation, intending to communicate a work to the public through broadcast, shall secure a license from the copyright holder, unless expressly exempted as provided herein. However, any dispute regarding the scope of such license, or the reasonable royalty payable, may be submitted to the High Court having jurisdiction. Should the copyright holder allege unauthorized broadcast, they shall furnish proof of ownership and demonstrate substantial similarity between the broadcast content and the copyrighted work. The broadcasting organisation may rebut such claims by demonstrating fair dealing or a valid statutory exception. Provided that, if the broadcast is for non-commercial, educational purposes, the royalty payable shall be determined by the Court considering the public benefit accrued. Appeals from the decision of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court, subject to the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction rules. Any wilful disregard of a Court order shall constitute contempt.

A broadcasting organisation intending to communicate to the public a work, whether literary, musical or dramatic, or a sound recording, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding rights in such works. Any such communication, if undertaken without requisite authorization from the copyright holder, may be subject to opposition proceedings initiated by the owner of the copyright or their duly authorized agent. Such opposition shall be filed within thirty days of the initial broadcast or performance, and shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the communication is alleged to infringe copyright. The broadcasting organisation, upon receipt of notice of opposition, shall furnish a detailed account of the scope and duration of the broadcast, and any licensing arrangements, if any, pertaining to the work in question. Failure to provide such an account may result in a presumption of infringement. The adjudicating authority may, subject to verification of facts, direct the cessation of the broadcast pending a final determination. Any broadcasting organisation found to have wilfully infringed copyright shall be liable to damages as determined by the authority.

A broadcasting organisation intending to communicate to the public a work in which copyright subsists, whether literary, dramatic, musical or cinematographic, shall secure requisite permissions from the copyright holder, unless exempted under this Act. However, a broadcasting organisation may, subject to the payment of royalty fixed by the licensing body, simultaneously broadcast news relating to current events, including sports, provided that such broadcast does not impede the legitimate rights of the copyright owner. Where a broadcasting organisation seeks to exploit an invention disclosed in a published patent application, particularly one filed under the application patent cooperation treaty, it shall ensure compliance with the provisions relating to patent licensing as stipulated by the relevant authority. Failure to adhere to these provisions, or to remit royalties as determined, shall render the broadcasting organisation liable to statutory damages and injunctive relief, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding royalty rates shall be subject to arbitration.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by a proposed registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, similarity to existing marks, lack of distinctiveness, or deceptive character. The applicant for registration, upon receipt of the notice of opposition, shall be entitled to file a counter-statement, addressing each ground raised by the opponent, within a period stipulated by the Registrar. Failure to file a counter-statement within the prescribed time may result in the abandonment of the application. Evidence may be submitted by both parties, and the Registrar shall consider such evidence before rendering a decision on the opposition registration.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall file a notice of opposition in the prescribed form with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and the relevant evidence in support thereof. The Registrar, upon receipt of such notice, shall serve a copy thereof upon the applicant, requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding two months. Should the applicant fail to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, proceed to decide the matter ex parte. Evidence may be filed by both parties, and the Registrar shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, record a reasoned decision regarding the opposition registration. An appeal from any decision of the Registrar relating to opposition proceedings shall lie to the Appellate Board, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by, or having legitimate grounds to oppose, an application for registration of a trade mark, may file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and adherence to the procedural requirements as provided herein. Such notice shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, lack of distinctiveness, or potential to deceive the public. The applicant for registration shall be entitled to file a counter-statement, addressing the allegations raised in the notice of opposition, within a period stipulated by the Registrar. Evidence may be submitted by both parties to substantiate their respective claims, and the Registrar, after considering such evidence and conducting an examination of the matter, shall issue a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the opposition registration. Where an opposition is successful, the application for registration shall be deemed to have failed. A party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision may seek redressal through an appeal to the appropriate appellate authority.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall file a notice of opposition in the prescribed form with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and a fee as specified in the Schedule. Failure to submit the prescribed fee shall render the opposition invalid and subject the filer to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. The Registrar, upon receiving such notice, shall notify the applicant, affording them one month to deliver a counter-statement. Should the applicant fail to file a counter-statement within the stipulated period, the Registrar may deem the opposition admitted and proceed accordingly. Evidence may be submitted by both parties, subject to timelines determined by the Registrar, and any false or misleading evidence presented shall be punishable with imprisonment up to two years or a fine, or both, as provided herein. All proceedings relating to opposition registration shall be conducted in accordance with the rules framed under this Act.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding opposition registration, and no such assignment shall be valid unless the Registrar is satisfied that the assignee is a person qualified to claim ownership of the mark. Where an opposition registration is pending concerning a trade mark, the rights therein may be assigned, provided that the assignee agrees to be bound by the outcome of the pending opposition proceedings. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require the assignee to demonstrate sufficient interest in the mark to continue the opposition. An applicant seeking to assign an application for registration must furnish a statement detailing the nature of the assignment and the consideration paid, subject to verification by the Registrar. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment voidable, and the application liable to be abandoned as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership without due regard to pending oppositions shall be considered a contravention of these regulations.

Any person intending to acquire rights in a registered trade mark, or a pending application for registration, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, demonstrate a clear and lawful basis for such acquisition. An assignment or licensing of a trade mark shall be void if it contravenes any existing statutory prohibition or judicial order. Where an opposition registration is filed contesting the validity of a mark based on prior rights, the transferor of those prior rights must furnish evidence of due diligence in maintaining those rights, including proof of continuous and legitimate use in commerce. Consideration shall be given to the denomination variety of the mark in question, assessing whether the proposed assignment or license would create an unconscionable likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require a full audit of all licensing agreements pertaining to the mark before approving any further transfer of ownership. Any assignment not in conformity with these provisions may be subject to rectification or annulment.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall file a notice of opposition in the prescribed form with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and the relevant particulars supporting such grounds. The statement shall clearly demonstrate how the mark sought to be registered conflicts with existing rights, and may include evidence relating to prior use or the distinctive character of the opposing party’s mark. Where the opposition relies on a literary work as establishing prior rights, a certified copy of the published work, or evidence of diligent efforts to publish it, shall be submitted. The Registrar may, subject to such terms as it deems fit, require further evidence or clarification from either party. Failure to comply with the requirements as provided herein may render the opposition vulnerable to dismissal. The Registrar shall, following due consideration of all submissions, issue a reasoned order regarding the opposition registration.

For the purposes of this Act, an indication shall be deemed to be a geographical indication if it identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, consequently, affects its quality or reputation. Such geographical area may be a town, village, or region, and the indication must be distinctive of those goods. A producer shall be considered to have a legitimate connection to the geographical area if they cultivate, process, or prepare the goods within that area. Provided that the reputation of the geographical indication is not misleading as to the origin, quality, or characteristics of the goods, it shall be registrable as provided herein.

A geographical indication identifying agricultural goods shall be considered distinct, provided that such indication, by virtue of its origin, possesses qualities or a reputation that are attributable to that place. The applicant seeking registration of an indication shall submit evidence establishing a clear link between the goods and the geographical area of origin, demonstrating that the qualities, characteristics, or reputation of the goods are essentially due to that geographical origin. Any indication which, although not a geographical indication in itself, incorporates a geographical name and suggests a connection to a particular place, may also be subject to registration as provided herein. The Registrar shall, prior to registration, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the proposed indication meets the criteria for distinctiveness and is not generic or misleading. A register of geographical indications shall be maintained, open for inspection by the public, and shall contain details of the indication, the goods it identifies, and the region of origin.

Any person claiming an interest in a registered geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to institute civil proceedings for infringement of such indication. Where a geographical indication is used by a person other than an authorised user in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered, and such use results in likelihood of confusion or deception, it shall constitute an infringement. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, as provided herein, apply to the court for an injunction restraining the infringing conduct, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. A false indication of origin, or the false representation of goods as originating from a geographical area when they do not, shall be actionable under this Act. Any evidence demonstrating the distinctiveness of the indication and its connection to the goods’ origin may be presented to substantiate a claim. Remedies available shall be proportionate to the extent of the infringement and the harm caused.

A geographical indication identifying agricultural goods shall be considered distinct from a geographical indication identifying goods of a different category, even if the names share common elements, provided that such shared elements do not mislead consumers as to the true origin or quality of the goods. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act and upon application, determine whether a proposed indication constitutes a geographical indication as defined herein. Any association of producers, or any enterprise acting as the collective owner, may apply for registration of a geographical indication, demonstrating a clear link between the goods and the geographical area of origin. A specification detailing the qualities, characteristics, or reputation of the goods attributable to their geographical origin shall accompany any such application. The specification shall be open to public inspection, and objections may be filed within a period stipulated by the Registrar. Where a dispute arises regarding the authenticity of a claimed indication, the Registrar shall conduct an inquiry and may require supporting evidence from relevant stakeholders.

A geographical indication shall be considered valid for registration under this Act, provided that the goods originate from a defined geographical area and possess qualities or a reputation attributable to that origin. The applicant seeking registration of an indication must demonstrate a clear link between the goods and the geographical area, substantiated by verifiable evidence of traditional production methods or unique characteristics. Any indication presented as a geographical indication must be distinctive and not generic, and shall not be contrary to public order or morality. Where a collective or group of producers seeks registration, evidence of established rules governing the use of the indication and quality control mechanisms shall be submitted. Failure to maintain the established standards of quality or origin may result in the revocation of registration, subject to due process as provided herein. The Register shall maintain a public register of all registered indications.

Any person who falsely applies a geographical indication to goods not originating in the territory associated with that indication, or who trades, sells, or otherwise deals in goods bearing such falsely applied indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where a collective body or association is deemed to be the proprietor of a geographical indication, any act constituting a contravention of this Act committed by a member shall also be deemed to be an offence committed by the collective body, subject to their demonstrating reasonable efforts to prevent such act. Any evidence of intent to mislead the public regarding the true origin of goods, or to unfairly exploit the reputation of a registered geographical indication, may be considered an aggravating factor in determining the penalty. A court may, as provided herein, order the seizure and destruction of goods found to be in violation.

Any assignment of the right to exercise any right in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to such conditions, and may be subject to such fees, as may be prescribed. The proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of the indication, or any right in respect of it, to any person or class of persons. Any assignment of a geographical indication shall not be operative until it is registered with the Registry. The Registry shall maintain a register of all assignments and transfers of geographical indications, and shall publish such register in such manner as it deems fit. A licensee of a geographical indication may, with the consent of the proprietor, assign its license to another person, provided that such assignment does not contravene any terms or conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Failure to register an assignment as provided herein shall render the assignment void. The indication remains protected even after assignment, subject to continued adherence to the standards specified in the register.

Any person claiming to be adversely affected by the registration of a geographical indication, or by any act in purported exercise of right to such indication, may file a petition with the Appellate Board. Such petition shall be filed within ninety days from the date of order sought to be challenged, and shall clearly demonstrate a prima facie case of damage or potential damage resulting from the continued registration or use of the contested indication. The Appellate Board, upon receiving such petition, shall issue notice to the registered proprietor and may direct them to submit evidence substantiating the validity of the geographical indication and its continued adherence to the established standards of quality and origin. Provided that, the Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the period for submission of evidence. A finding that the registered indication does not accurately reflect the geographical origin or qualities associated with the goods shall be grounds for revocation of registration, and the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court.

An indication, for the purposes of this Act, shall denote a name or a sign used on products that, as a link to the geographical area of origin, confer a specific quality, reputation or other characteristic to such products. Such indication shall be capable of identifying products as originating from a particular geographical area, even if the inherent qualities of the product are not solely attributable to that place of origin. A registration notice, detailing the particulars of the geographical indication and the goods to which it applies, shall be published in the Journal as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the applicant to amend the indication to avoid confusion with existing registered indications. Any alteration to a registered indication shall also be subject to a similar notice and opportunity for opposition.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent in India shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller of Patents, demonstrating sufficient disclosure of the invention for which a patent is sought. The application shall include a complete specification, clearly and concisely describing the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. A claim or claims defining the scope of the invention for which protection is sought, adhering to the principles of patent india, must accompany the specification. 

Provided that, if the invention relates to a microorganism, a deposit of the microorganism with any internationally recognized depositary authority shall be a prerequisite for filing a complete specification. The applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, request for examination of the application, and such examination shall be conducted as per the established procedure. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the application being deemed abandoned.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, relating to a patent application or a patent granted under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, reverse or set aside the decision of the Controller, and may also direct fresh consideration of the matter by the Controller. A patent, even if validly obtained, may be revoked by the Appellate Board if it is proved to the satisfaction of the Board that the patent was obtained unlawfully, or that the patentee is not the true and first inventor of the patent india. Any person alleging infringement of a patent shall be entitled to bring a suit for injunction and damages, and the court shall have jurisdiction to grant relief as it deems fit, including an account of profits.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent in India shall submit an application to the Controller of Patents in the manner as prescribed. The application shall disclose the invention in a clear and complete manner sufficient to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect, and shall include a claim or claims defining the scope of the patent sought. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a patent may be granted for any invention, whether a product or a process, involving a novel step and capable of industrial application. 

However, a patent for an invention shall not be granted if it falls within the exclusions specified, including inventions whose primary or intended use is contrary to public order or morality. Where a complete specification does not fully and particularly describe the invention, and the manner in which it is to be performed, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish the same within a period not exceeding fifteen months from the date of the initial requirement. The grant of a patent india confers upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, exercise, and sell the invention throughout India for a period of twenty years from the date of filing the application.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent in India shall submit an application demonstrating novelty and non-obviousness, as provided herein, and fulfilling all requirements relating to patent india as stipulated within this Act. The application shall disclose the invention in a clear and complete manner sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Subject to the provisions concerning priority dates, an applicant claiming convention priority under the Paris Convention shall file the necessary documents within the prescribed timeframe. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application. Furthermore, any subsequent amendment to the application shall not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. A patent granted under this Act shall be subject to revocation on grounds of lack of novelty, obviousness, or insufficient disclosure, as determined by due process.

Any person who infringes a valid patent in India shall be liable to an action for damages, the quantum of which shall be determined by the Court having jurisdiction, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where infringement is proven to be willful, the Court may enhance the damages awarded to an amount not exceeding three times the actual damages, or a sum of twenty crore rupees, whichever is less. Any person making a false representation in relation to a patent india, including falsely claiming to be the inventor or providing misleading information to the Patent Office, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, after due inquiry, revoke a patent obtained through such false representation. Any appeal against the decision of the Controller shall lie before the High Court, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and within the stipulated time period as provided herein.

Any person possessing a patent in India may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses or assignments of the patent and the rights therein, either generally or subject to limitations as to field of use, duration, or geographical area. Any assignment of a patent shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions governing the assignment, including the consideration paid or to be paid for the assignment. Where a patent is assigned without consideration, such assignment shall be voidable at the option of the assignor, provided that notice of intention to avoid the assignment is given to the assignee within two years from the date of assignment. 

A licensee, with the consent of the patent holder, may further assign or license their interest in the patent, subject to the same conditions as apply to the original patent holder. Failure to register any assignment or license as provided herein shall not invalidate the assignment or license, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer. The Controller shall maintain a register of all assignments and licenses of patent india.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents may, within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed in the manner and subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Controller of Patents a reasonable opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the Controller. 

Where an appeal relates to the validity of a patent, the Appellate Board may, subject to such terms as it thinks fit, direct that the patent be amended in accordance with the appeal. Any dispute regarding the novelty or inventive step of a patent india shall be determined by the Appellate Board based on evidence presented by both parties, and its decision shall be final and binding. Provided that, the Appellate Board may refer the matter to a technical expert for opinion.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent in India shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller of Patents, establishing the novelty of the invention and its potential for industrial application, thereby fulfilling the criteria for a patent india as provided herein. The application shall include a complete and clear description of the invention, and shall be accompanied by claims defining the scope of the invention for which protection is sought. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller shall enter it in the Register of Patent Applications, initiating the application registration process and assigning an application number. Should the applicant fail to comply with any requirement relating to form or content within the stipulated timeframe, the Controller may require rectification, and failure to rectify may result in abandonment of the application. A request for examination shall be filed, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, after which the Controller shall examine the application. Provided that, the Controller may, at any stage, require evidence of the applicant’s right to make the application.

The Controller shall exercise the powers and perform the functions assigned to him under this Act and the rules made thereunder, and shall be the final authority in matters relating to the grant of patents, designs and trade marks. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, delegate any of his powers to an officer subordinate to him, provided that such delegation shall not absolve the Controller of ultimate responsibility. Any decision of the Controller may be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein, and the Controller shall furnish all necessary information and documents to the said Board upon request. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all patents, designs and trade marks granted or pending, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee.

The controller shall maintain a public register of all applications for patents, recording the date of filing, the applicant’s name and address, and a short summary of the invention. Any person may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, inspect the register and obtain certified copies of entries therein. The controller may, where an application is found to be incomplete or does not meet the formal requirements as provided herein, require the applicant to amend it within a specified period. Failure to comply with such requirement shall be deemed a withdrawal of the application. Should a patent be granted, the controller shall issue a patent certificate, noting the patent number and the date of grant. The controller’s decision regarding the registration of a patent, or any matter pertaining to it, shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the appropriate appellate authority. All records maintained by the controller shall be deemed official evidence for all purposes under this Act.

The controller, exercising powers as provided herein, shall maintain a public register of all patents granted and applications undergoing examination, subject to reasonable restrictions necessary for confidentiality concerning sensitive technological details as determined by the central government. Any person aggrieved by an order of the controller refusing an application, revoking a patent, or imposing conditions may, within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of such appeal and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, shall afford the appellant a reasonable opportunity to be heard and may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the controller. Should the controller fail to dispose of an application within a period of three years from the date of filing, any interested party may petition the High Court for a writ of mandamus compelling timely adjudication, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated. The controller may, with the approval of the central government, delegate certain administrative powers to designated officers.

The Controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise all powers and perform all duties conferred or imposed by this Act, or by the rules made thereunder. Any decision of the Controller regarding the grant or refusal of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, shall be communicated to the applicant or other interested party in writing, and shall state the reasons for such decision. Where an application for a patent is amended, the Controller may, if satisfied that the amendment does not extend beyond the matter originally disclosed in the specification, direct the application to be amended accordingly. Provided that, the Controller may require the applicant to submit an undertaking as to the validity of the patent based on the amended specification. The Controller may, at any stage of the proceedings, require evidence or information from any person, and such person shall be bound to provide the same within a reasonable time as specified by the Controller. Any failure to comply with such requirement shall be deemed a contempt of the Controller’s authority. The Controller shall maintain a register of patents and shall cause it to be open to inspection by the public, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

The controller, exercising functions under this Act, shall maintain a register of patents, ensuring its accuracy and accessibility to the public subject to prescribed fees. Any person seeking inspection of the register shall submit a written request detailing the specific patent or information desired, and the controller may require a statutory declaration regarding the purpose of such inspection. Where an application for a patent is rejected, the controller shall communicate the grounds for rejection to the applicant within ninety days from the date of such rejection, affording an opportunity for amendment or appeal as provided herein. The controller may, with reasonable cause, direct a patentee to furnish specimens of the patented invention for official examination, provided that such specimens are handled with due confidentiality. Failure to comply with a lawful direction of the controller shall constitute grounds for revocation of the patent, subject to a hearing.

The Controller shall, upon receiving a petition alleging improper revocation of a patent, conduct a thorough inquiry, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing such inquiry may, within sixty days, appeal to the High Court. Failure to comply with the prescribed fee structure, as detailed in Schedule IV, shall render the petition inadmissible and may attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. The Controller, while examining evidence submitted under this Act, may require an affidavit verifying the authenticity of any technical document. Provided that, deliberate submission of falsified evidence to the Controller constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. All decisions of the Controller shall be reasoned and communicated in writing to the parties concerned.

The controller shall, upon receipt of a duly filed instrument of assignment of a patent, record the assignment in the register of patents and shall notify the assignor and assignee of such recordal. Any assignment not so recorded shall be void as against any assignee subsequent to the assignor, subject to proof of equitable title. Where a license is granted, the controller may, on application made by either the licensor or the licensee and after giving reasonable opportunity to the other party to be heard, determine the scope and terms of such license, particularly regarding royalty payments and duration. A licensee, with the consent of the controller, may further assign or license their interest in the licensed patent. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of an assignment or license, the controller’s decision shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the appropriate court as provided herein. The controller reserves the right to require evidence of valid consideration for any assignment or license.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the controller relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The controller, upon receipt of a notice of intention to appeal, shall furnish to the appellant all documents relating to the case, subject to any confidentiality restrictions applicable. Should the controller fail to provide such documents within thirty days, the Appellate Board may, upon application, direct the controller to do so and impose costs. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court. The controller’s discretion in granting or refusing a stay of proceedings pending appeal shall be exercised judiciously.

The Controller, upon receiving a petition alleging improper revocation of a patent, shall first examine the grounds for such revocation as detailed in the petition and any accompanying evidence. Should the Controller deem the petition substantiated, a notice shall be issued to the patentee, affording them a period of sixty days to submit a reasoned response. Provided that, if the patentee fails to respond within the stipulated timeframe, or if the response is deemed insufficient by the Controller, the revocation shall be confirmed. Any aggrieved party may, subject to the provisions of this Act, appeal the Controller’s decision to the High Court, demonstrating substantial grounds for review. The Controller’s determination regarding the novelty of a clause invention, and its distinction from prior art, shall be a key consideration in any such appeal. The High Court’s decision shall be final, except in cases involving questions of law of general public importance, which may be subject to further review.

The Controller, upon receiving an application for registration of a resulting international registration under this Act, shall examine the application for compliance with the requirements as prescribed. Should the Controller deem the application deficient, a notice specifying the defects shall be issued to the applicant, allowing a period not exceeding thirty days for rectification. Provided that, failure to rectify the defects within the stipulated period may lead to the rejection of the application. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may, subject to the provisions herein, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Controller may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, prescribe fees for all processes related to the registration of international registrations, including examination, rectification, and the issuance of certificates. All registers maintained by the Controller shall be open for inspection by the public, subject to reasonable restrictions.

The Controller shall, upon a reasoned request by an applicant for a patent, and subject to the payment of a prescribed fee, conduct an examination of the completeness of an application patent to determine if it satisfies the requirements of this Act regarding form and content. Should the Controller determine that the application is deficient, a notice specifying the deficiencies shall be issued to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days to remedy the same. Failure to adequately address the deficiencies within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to the completeness of an application may, within sixty days of the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Controller may, in exceptional circumstances and with prior approval of the Central Government, extend the time for remedy, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated. The Controller’s discretion in such matters shall be exercised judiciously and in accordance with principles of natural justice.

The Controller, exercising the powers vested under this Act, shall maintain a public register of all patents granted and applications pending, ensuring accessibility subject to reasonable fees as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect such register shall submit a written request to the Controller, detailing the scope of inspection and identifying the patent or application of interest. The India Registrar requires that all entries in the register be accurately maintained and indexed, facilitating efficient search and retrieval of information. Where an application is amended, the Controller shall ensure that the register reflects the most current version of the specification and claims. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, require a certified copy of any document to be furnished by the applicant before granting access to the register. Any objection to a decision of the Controller regarding access may be made to the designated appellate authority as provided herein, and the India Registrar shall forward such objection without delay.

The Controller, exercising the powers vested under this Act, shall maintain a register of all patents granted and applications pending, ensuring its accessibility to the public subject to reasonable fees as may be prescribed. Any person seeking inspection of the register shall submit a written request outlining the specific details required, and the Controller may, if deemed necessary, require a justification for such request to prevent frivolous or vexatious inquiries. Where an application for a patent involves a trade mark, the Controller shall, prior to grant, consult with the Trade Marks Registrar to ascertain any potential conflict or infringement of existing registered trade marks. Failure of the applicant to disclose relevant prior art known to them shall be considered grounds for revocation of the patent, subject to a due process of hearing before the Controller. The Controller’s decision regarding the validity of a patent may be appealed to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Member Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such number of other members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe. A person shall be qualified to be appointed as a member if they possess a degree in engineering or technology, or are a legally qualified advocate with at least ten years of experience in intellectual property matters. The term of office for each member shall be five years from the date of their appointment, or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. Vacancies arising on the Member Appellate Board shall be filled in the manner prescribed by the Central Government, and any member may be removed for cause, subject to an inquiry as provided herein. The Board shall have the power to regulate its own procedure.

The applicant seeking registration of a layout-design, aggrieved by the decision of the Controller of Designs, may prefer an appeal to the member appellate board within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The appellate board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may deem necessary, possessing expertise in semiconductor technology or law. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or imposing conditions on registration, shall furnish a statement of grounds for appeal, accompanied by a certified copy of the Controller’s order and the prescribed fee. The member appellate board may, at its discretion, require additional evidence or documentation from the appellant or the Controller, and shall provide a reasoned order within ninety days of the appeal’s receipt. Provided that, the appellate board may extend this period for justifiable cause, duly recorded in writing.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the registration of a layout-design, or the refusal to register, or the rectification or revocation of such registration, may prefer an appeal to the member appellate board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions for condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The member appellate board shall, upon receipt of an appeal and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order of the Registrar. The Board may, while considering an appeal, require the appellant to furnish evidence or documents as it deems necessary. Decisions of the member appellate board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court. The Board shall be assisted by technical experts as required for proper adjudication of the matters before it.

The Member Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two other members, to be appointed by the Central Government. A person shall be eligible for appointment as Chairperson if they are, or have been, a Judge of a High Court. Other members shall be persons possessing technical expertise in the field of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, or holding a degree in engineering, science, or law with demonstrated knowledge of the subject. The term of office for each member shall be five years from the date of appointment, or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. 

Vacancies arising on the Member Appellate Board, whether due to resignation, death, or otherwise, shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment. The Board may regulate its own procedure and shall have the power to require evidence, issue summons, and examine witnesses under oath, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any decision of the Member Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of law.

The Member Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such number of other members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe. A person shall be qualified to be appointed as a member if they possess a degree in engineering or technology, or are a legally qualified advocate with at least ten years of experience in intellectual property matters. All members shall be appointed by the Central Government and shall hold office for a term of five years or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. Vacancies arising on the Member Appellate Board shall be filled in the manner prescribed herein, and any decision of the Board shall require the concurrence of a majority of its members present and voting. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Member Appellate Board may regulate its own procedure and shall have the power to summon witnesses and compel the production of documents. Any appeal against an order of the Registrar shall be filed with the Member Appellate Board within ninety days of the date of such order.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar, or by any refusal or revocation of registration, may prefer an appeal to the member appellate board within a period of ninety days from the date of such decision or order. The member appellate board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the Registrar. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated period shall not be a ground for dismissal unless sufficient cause is shown. Any deliberate misrepresentation made before the member appellate board, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. The member appellate board may, subject to rules made under this Act, require the appellant to deposit costs as a condition for entertaining the appeal. All orders of the member appellate board shall be final and binding.

Any registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or otherwise transfer the rights therein, either wholly or in part, to any person. All assignments shall be in writing and shall specify the rights assigned, and a copy of every such instrument of assignment shall be furnished to the Controller within such period as may be prescribed. Where a layout-design is jointly held, no joint proprietor shall assign their rights without the consent of the other joint proprietor or proprietors, unless otherwise agreed in writing. 

The Member Appellate Board shall have the jurisdiction to hear and decide any dispute arising out of or relating to the assignment or transfer of rights in a registered layout-design, including disputes concerning the validity of the assignment or the scope of rights transferred. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller regarding assignment may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. The Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar regarding the validity of a layout-design right, or the refusal to register such a right, may prefer an appeal to the member appellate board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions for condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The appellate board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal concerns a claim of prior art, the appellant shall furnish detailed particulars thereof at the time of filing the appeal, and failure to do so may be considered by the member appellate board as sufficient grounds for dismissal. Decisions of the member appellate board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises for consideration by a court of competent jurisdiction. The Board may, at its discretion, require security for costs from the appellant.

The Member Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint. A person qualified to be appointed as a member shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design or possess technical expertise in related areas. The Board shall have the power to hear and decide appeals arising from the decisions of the Layout-Design Registry, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any copy translation work submitted as evidence before the Member Appellate Board shall be certified as a true and accurate translation by a translator duly authorized by the Registry. The Board may, if deemed necessary, request further clarification or evidence from the parties concerned to ensure a just determination of the appeal.

The Member Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of a petition seeking rectification of a registered layout-design, conduct a hearing wherein both the petitioner and the registered proprietor are afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case. Any legal practitioner person, duly qualified and authorized to practice before the Board, may represent a party before the Member Appellate Board, subject to the payment of prescribed fees. The Board may, at its discretion, request further evidence or clarification from either party to ensure a comprehensive assessment of the matter. Decisions of the Member Appellate Board regarding rectification shall be based solely on the merits of the case and in accordance with the provisions of this Act. A registrar shall maintain a complete record of all petitions, evidence, and decisions related to rectification proceedings. The Board’s decision shall be communicated to both parties in writing and shall be final, subject to any appeal as provided herein.

The Member Appellate Board constituted under this Act shall, upon receipt of a notice of appeal from any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller of Designs, examine the grounds of such appeal and may, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the respondent, confirm, modify, reverse or vary the said decision. Where the appeal concerns a claim of ownership by a registered proprietor proposed as such, the Board shall require satisfactory evidence of registration and the locus standi of the appellant to pursue the matter. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Member Appellate Board may, if it deems necessary, direct the Controller to undertake further investigation or examination of the relevant layout-design. Any order made by the Member Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Board shall dispose of all appeals within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the date of receipt of the appeal.

The Member Appellate Board constituted under this Act shall exercise jurisdiction over appeals arising from the decisions of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. Any person aggrieved by an order pertaining to the registration of a layout-design, or the rejection of an application for registration, may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Registry shall notify the Member Appellate Board of any such appeal filed, along with all relevant documents and evidence. The Board may, at its discretion, require further information or clarification from the appellant or the Registry. Provided that, no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates prima facie grounds for challenging the decision. The Member Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to any remedies available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Designs, relating to a layout-design, may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee. The Member Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller. Where an applicant seeks to rely upon an international registration filed under the relevant treaty, the Board may require certified copies of such registration and related documents, failing which the appeal may not be entertained. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein, or any attempt to willfully delay proceedings, shall attract a penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees. Any false statement made before the Member Appellate Board constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

The Chairperson Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence from the field of semiconductor technology, or law, or possessing a combination of both, appointed by the Central Government. The Chairperson shall hold office for a term of five years from the date of assumption of office, or until attaining the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier. A retired Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court may also be appointed as the Chairperson, subject to the conditions prescribed. The Chairperson shall exercise such powers as are necessary to ensure the effective functioning of the Appellate Board, including the constitution of Benches and the regulation of proceedings. Any vacancy arising in the office of the Chairperson shall be filled by the Central Government in a manner consistent with the provisions herein. The decisions of the Chairperson on administrative matters shall be final.

The Chairperson Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence from the field of semiconductor technology, appointed by the Central Government, and shall hold office for a term of five years or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. A retired Judge of a High Court may also be appointed as Chairperson, subject to the aforementioned age limit. Any person appointed as Chairperson shall, before entering upon their duties, make and subscribe to an oath or affirmation as may be prescribed. The Central Government may, in the event of an absence or inability of the Chairperson to act, designate a Bench member to perform the duties of the Chairperson. All applications for registration, and any subsequent rectification requests, shall be initially scrutinized by the Registrar, and thereafter forwarded to the Chairperson Appellate Board for consideration and final determination as provided herein. The Registrar may request further information from the applicant to facilitate the Chairperson’s review.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of a Registrar may, within a period of sixty days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Chairperson Appellate Board. The Chairperson Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, pass such orders as the Chairperson deems fit, confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Registrar. Failure to prefer an appeal within the stipulated period shall not be a bar to seeking redressal before a court of competent jurisdiction, subject to the limitations as provided herein. Any frivolous or vexatious appeal preferred before the Chairperson Appellate Board may attract a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of public revenue. The Chairperson Appellate Board may, if satisfied that an appeal is wholly without merit, impose costs on the appellant, not exceeding five thousand rupees. All orders of the Chairperson Appellate Board shall be final and binding.
