The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise exclusive jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to the licensing and assignment of registered layout-designs. Any person intending to assign a registered layout-design, or a right to use such layout-design, shall submit a detailed statement of the proposed terms and conditions to the Chairperson for review, ensuring compliance with the regulatory framework established herein. The Chairperson may, if satisfied that the proposed assignment does not contravene any provisions of this Act or prejudice the interests of the original creator, grant approval, and such approval shall be recorded as a matter of public record. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment or the scope of a license, the aggrieved party may petition the Chairperson Appellate Board, providing full particulars of the grievance and supporting documentation. The Chairperson shall endeavor to resolve such disputes expeditiously, and any decision rendered shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review as provided under the relevant laws.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the registration of a layout-design, or the rectification thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Chairperson Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of such fees as may be prescribed. The Chairperson Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of such appeal and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Provided that the Chairperson may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs. A request for extension of time for filing an appeal may be considered by the Chairperson, provided sufficient cause is demonstrated. The decision of the Chairperson Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a question of law of general public importance arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise final authority in matters relating to the grant or refusal of registrations and the validity thereof. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning an application for registration, or the refusal to extend a registration, may appeal to the Chairperson Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. Where an applicant seeks registration based upon an international registration basic, demonstrating priority claim under a reciprocal agreement, the Chairperson shall expedite review of such applications, provided that all requisite documentation and translations are submitted as per established procedures. Assignment of rights in a registered layout-design shall be evidenced in writing and filed with the office, and the Chairperson may, upon sufficient cause shown, direct rectification of the register to reflect such assignment. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the assignment unenforceable. The Chairperson may also issue licenses under such terms and conditions as deemed appropriate.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence from the field of semiconductor technology, law, or intellectual property rights, possessing not less than fifteen years of experience in any of these domains. The Central Government shall appoint the Chairperson, and such appointment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding qualifications and the process of selection. A retired Judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court may also be considered eligible for appointment as the Chairperson, provided that they meet the aforementioned criteria regarding technical or intellectual property expertise. The Appellate Board Chairperson shall exercise administrative control over the Board and be responsible for ensuring the efficient and timely disposal of appeals as provided herein. Any vacancy arising in the office of the Chairperson shall be filled in accordance with the procedure outlined in this Act.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor technology or law, possessing at least ten years of experience in either domain. A search-cum-selection committee, constituted by the Central Government, shall recommend candidates for appointment to the position, and the appointment shall be made by notification in the Official Gazette. The Appellate Board Chairperson may delegate administrative powers to a Registrar, appointed as provided herein, but all judicial decisions shall remain the sole responsibility of the Chairperson or a designated Bench. Any vacancy arising in the office of the Appellate Board Chairperson shall be filled within ninety days from the date of such vacancy. The remuneration and other terms of service of the Appellate Board Chairperson shall be as prescribed by the Central Government. Appeals concerning the validity of registered layout-designs shall be adjudicated by the Appellate Board under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to limitation.

The Appellate Board chairperson shall exercise final authority in all matters pertaining to appeals under this Act, and may, subject to the provisions herein, constitute special Benches as deemed necessary for the expeditious disposal of cases. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within ninety days of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board, providing reasonable grounds for such appeal and demonstrating potential prejudice suffered. The Appellate Board chairperson possesses the power to review any interim order issued by the Board and may, after notice to the concerned parties, modify or set aside such order if considered unjust or inequitable. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be binding, save for any recourse available through writ jurisdiction before the High Court. The chairperson shall ensure that all proceedings are conducted in a transparent and impartial manner, and shall maintain detailed records of all decisions and orders issued by the Board. Failure to comply with the directions of the Appellate Board may attract penalties as prescribed.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor technology or law, possessing not less than ten years of experience in either domain. The Central Government shall appoint the Chairperson, and any vacancy arising shall be filled in like manner. The Appellate Board Chairperson shall exercise administrative control over the Board and be responsible for ensuring the efficient and timely disposal of appeals. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Chairperson may constitute Benches of the Appellate Board as deemed necessary to hear and decide on pending matters. All decisions of a Bench shall be made by majority vote, with the Chairperson having a casting vote in the event of a tie. The Chairperson shall also oversee the maintenance of records and the implementation of procedures established under this Act, and may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate rules for the smooth functioning of the Appellate Board. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may seek review before the Chairperson, provided that such application is made within thirty days of the order’s issuance.

The Appellate Board chairperson shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor technology or law, possessing at least ten years of experience in either discipline. A search-cum-selection committee, constituted by the Central Government and comprising representatives from the Department of Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Patent Office, and a nominee from a recognised institute of technology, shall recommend a panel of three candidates for consideration. The Central Government may, from the panel, appoint the chairperson, and shall communicate the appointment through official notification. 

The chairperson shall exercise administrative control over the Appellate Board and be responsible for ensuring the efficient disposal of appeals. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the chairperson may constitute Benches of the Appellate Board as needed to address pending matters. Any vacancy arising in the office of the chairperson shall be filled in accordance with this procedure, and the newly appointed chairperson shall assume office immediately upon appointment.

The registered proprietor of a layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the rights therein, or any interest therein, to any person, and such assignment shall be in writing and signed by the assignor. Any assignment of a layout-design, or any interest therein, shall be subject to any existing license granted by the registered proprietor, unless the assignment agreement provides otherwise and all licensees have consented to the transfer. The Appellate Board Chairperson shall, upon application by either party to an assignment dispute, have the power to issue interim orders restraining the assignee from exploiting the layout-design pending resolution of the dispute. Where a layout-design is jointly held, no joint proprietor shall assign their rights without the consent of all other joint proprietors, and any such assignment made without consent shall be void *ab initio*. The Appellate Board Chairperson may, if satisfied that reasonable efforts have been made to obtain consent but it has been unreasonably withheld, direct the assignment to proceed subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with an order of the Registrar regarding the rectification of the register of layout-designs, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fee as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board chairperson shall, upon receipt of such appeal and after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the Registrar, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Provided that, the Appellate Board chairperson may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs. Further, any application for leave to appeal to the Appellate Board, where the Registrar’s order does not involve a question of law, shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the grounds for challenging the decision and demonstrating substantial grounds for appeal, as determined by the chairperson. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding.

The Trade Marks Registry established under this Act shall maintain a register of trade marks, divided into Parts A and B, relating to goods and services as specified in the Fourth Schedule. Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark used or proposed to be used in relation to particular goods or services may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for the registration of the trade mark in the appropriate Part of the Register. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to the provisions of this Act, accept or refuse any application for registration. All fees payable to the Trade Marks Registry shall be in accordance with the Schedule annexed to these rules, and shall be non-refundable except as otherwise provided herein. Any rectification of the register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry shall be governed by the procedures outlined in this Act.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of trade marks, divided into parts relating to goods and services, and shall be open for inspection by the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The Trade Marks Registry may, if satisfied that the applicant has a genuine interest, permit inspection of the register and copies of entries therein. All applications for registration shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain whether the trade mark is registrable under the provisions of this Act and whether it conflicts with any existing trade mark on the register. Where the Trade Marks Registry deems an application to be defective, it shall issue an objection notice to the applicant, requiring rectification within a specified period. Failure to comply with such notice may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon satisfaction of all requirements, register the trade mark and issue a certificate of registration.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Trade Marks Registry relating to an application for registration, or the rectification or removal of a trade mark, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend this period, provided that sufficient cause is shown. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receipt of an appeal, transmit the relevant records to the Appellate Board. Where an appeal is dismissed, the aggrieved party may, subject to such terms and conditions as the Appellate Board deems fit, apply for a review of the decision. Any person who, having obtained registration of a trade mark, fails to use it for a continuous period of five years, may have their registration revoked, unless they can demonstrate legitimate reasons for non-use as provided herein.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of trade marks, comprising both registered and pending applications, and such register shall be open for inspection by the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in writing, specifying the class or classes of trade marks to be inspected and the period of inspection. The Trade Marks Registry may, if it deems necessary, require a reasonable security deposit to ensure proper handling of the register and prevent damage or loss. All applications for registration, notices of opposition, and other documents filed with the Trade Marks Registry shall be deemed to be public documents and may be accessed by any person, except where restricted by order of a competent court. The Controller of Trade Marks, acting on behalf of the Trade Marks Registry, shall have the power to require evidence of user of a registered trade mark, and failure to provide such evidence may be considered grounds for rectification of the register. Any rectification proceedings initiated by or against the Trade Marks Registry shall be conducted in accordance with the procedures as provided herein.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any application for registration, to be considered complete, shall be accompanied by a clear representation of the trade mark and a statement as to the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registry may, where an application is found to be deficient in any respect, require the applicant to amend it within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. All correspondence with the Trade Marks Registry shall be addressed to the appropriate branch office, and any notice served upon the Registry shall be deemed to have been duly served upon actual delivery. Provided that, the Registry reserves the right to reject any application not complying with the provisions as provided herein, and such rejection shall be communicated to the applicant in writing with reasons.

Any person who falsifies or fraudulently alters any document kept by the Trade Marks Registry shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Any application to the Trade Marks Registry made with intent to deceive shall be deemed a fraudulent application and the applicant shall forfeit all fees paid. The Controller of Trade Marks may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require any person to attend before him or to produce documents relating to a trade mark application or registration. Failure to comply with such requirement shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees per day of default. Provided that, any rectification of the register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, if found to be erroneous, may be undertaken by the Controller, but any aggrieved party may appeal such rectification to the High Court. All records of the Trade Marks Registry shall be open to inspection by any member of the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, executed by the assignor and authenticated in a manner prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument of assignment shall clearly identify the trade mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and state the consideration for the assignment, if any. An application for the registration of the assignment shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within a period of six months from the date of execution of the instrument. 

Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, notice of such assignment shall be furnished to the Trade Marks Registry. Failure to register an assignment, or to furnish the required notice, may render the assignment unenforceable as against subsequent purchasers for value. The Trade Marks Registry maintains a register of assignments and licenses, open to inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any licensee, with the consent of the registered proprietor, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for registration as the proprietor of the trade mark.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration, or requiring amendment of an application, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the date of such decision, providing sufficient cause for the delay if exceeding this period. The Appellate Board, upon review, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Trade Marks Registry, and its decision shall be final and binding, subject to further recourse to the High Court on questions of law. Where a conflict arises regarding the ownership of a trade mark, the Registry may, as provided herein, direct the parties to seek resolution through mediation before proceeding with adjudication.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark for a pharmaceutical substance, or rejecting evidence submitted in support of such application, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order of the Registry. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order and a statement of the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit a sum equivalent to the prescribed fee for registration of the trade mark as security for payment of costs. Provided that, if the Appellate Board is satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, it may dismiss the appeal with costs and direct the Trade Marks Registry to restore the application to its original status, or to proceed with examination as if no appeal had been filed. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

The Trade Marks Registry established under this Act shall maintain a register of trade marks, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any application for the registration of a trade mark shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. An indication of the class of goods or services to which the trade mark relates shall be clearly stated in the application. The Trade Marks Registry may, prior to acceptance of an application, require the applicant to amend the specification of goods or services to ensure proper classification. Provided that, the Trade Marks Registry shall not reject an application solely on the basis of a minor discrepancy in the indication, if the overall intention is clear and unambiguous. All records maintained by the Trade Marks Registry shall be deemed public documents.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all registered trade marks, and all applications for registration shall be examined in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration, or requiring an amendment to an application, may, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, seek appeal to the Appellate Board within the time specified herein. The Appellate Board shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant and may, after due consideration, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Trade Marks Registry. Provided that, a second appeal from the decision of the Appellate Board shall not be permissible except where a substantial question of law is involved. All records pertaining to applications sought appealed shall be maintained securely by the Trade Marks Registry for a period of not less than ten years. The Registrar may, at their discretion, grant an extension of time for filing any document, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit.

Copyright, as established under this Act, shall subsist in original literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works. Originality in the context of copyright shall denote that the work originates from the author and is not merely a copy of another work; however, the degree of originality required is not one of novelty, but rather that the work demonstrates a minimal level of skill and labour. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the author of a work shall be the first owner of the copyright therein, and such copyright shall endure for the life of the author plus sixty years from the year of their death. Where a work is made by an employee during the course of their employment, the employer shall, subject to any contract to the contrary, be the first owner of the copyright. Any assignment of copyright shall be in writing and signed by the assignor.

Any person claiming copyright in a work shall apply to the Copyright Office for registration of such copyright, submitting a completed Form-I together with the prescribed fee. The application shall include a clear statement of the applicant’s claim of ownership, details regarding the author and the work itself, and a copy of the work, or a reasonable portion thereof, sufficient to demonstrate its originality. Registration is not compulsory for the existence of copyright, but it serves as prima facie evidence of ownership and shall be admissible in any legal proceeding concerning the copyright in question. A certificate of registration, once issued, may be subject to rectification if substantial errors are discovered, provided that any such application for rectification is made within one year of the date of registration. The Registrar may, subject to due process, refuse registration if the work does not meet the requirements for copyright protection as provided herein, or if a conflicting claim is already registered and substantiated.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of copyright, or alleging an apprehension of such infringement, may institute a suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The plaintiff shall, prior to the institution of such suit, provide the defendant with a notice of claim, specifying the nature of the copyright and the particulars of the alleged infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the remedies available to the copyright holder shall include an injunction restraining the infringement, damages for the loss suffered, and an account of profits derived by the defendant from the infringing act. Where the infringement is committed for commercial gain, statutory damages, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per work infringed, may be awarded. A copyright owner may, as provided herein, also seek delivery up or destruction of infringing copies. The court may, at its discretion, grant costs of the suit to the successful party. Any person dealing in good faith with a published work shall not be liable for infringement if unaware of the copyright status.

Any work shall be considered original if it originates from the author and contains a minimum degree of creativity. A work involving adaptation or translation shall be considered an original work, provided that the adaptation or translation demonstrates sufficient skill and judgment. The author of a literary or dramatic work shall be the person who creates the work. In the case of a cinematograph film, the author shall be the producer. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the first owner of copyright shall be the author of the work. Assignment of the copyright must be in writing and signed by the assignor or their duly authorized agent. 

Where a work is commissioned, the copyright shall vest in the commissioning party, unless otherwise agreed in writing. However, the author shall be entitled to claim authorship of the work and to receive recognition accordingly. Infringement of copyright shall be a civil wrong and shall be subject to remedies as provided herein, including injunction and damages. The duration of copyright shall be for the life of the author plus sixty years.

Any work shall be considered original subject to the requirement that it must originate from the author and not be copied from any other source, and sufficient skill and labour must have been exercised in its creation. Where a person undertakes the creation of a cinematograph film, the producer shall be deemed to be the author of the film, provided that such producer has exercised control over the final form of the work. The rights conferred by copyright shall subsist in literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, and cinematograph films, and shall include the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, perform, and adapt the work. Assignment of copyright must be in writing and signed by the assignor, specifying clearly the rights assigned and the duration of the assignment. Infringement of copyright shall be a civil wrong, subject to the remedies available under this Act and other applicable laws. Any person aggrieved by such infringement may seek redressal through a competent court.

Any person who infringes the copyright in a work shall be liable to a penalty, the amount of which may extend to two lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. Where the infringement is committed for commercial gain or involves a substantial number of copies, the penalty shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees and may extend to five lakh rupees, along with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years. Any profits made by the infringing party through the unauthorized reproduction or distribution of copyrighted material shall be recoverable by the owner of the copyright as damages. Subject to the provisions herein, a civil suit may be instituted for the recovery of damages and an injunction restraining further infringement. The court may, at its discretion, grant an ex parte injunction in cases of prima facie evidence of copyright violation. A police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector may, if satisfied, seize all infringing copies.

Any person being the author of a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work shall be the first owner of the copyright therein, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding assignment and licensing. An assignment of copyright must be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, specifying the rights assigned and the duration of the assignment. Where a work is made for valuable consideration, the recipient of the work may, subject to any agreement to the contrary, be deemed the author for the purposes of copyright, and shall possess all rights as such. Licensing of copyright may be granted to any person, and such license shall be subject to terms and conditions mutually agreed upon between the owner and the licensee. The owner of the copyright may, at any time, revoke a license granted under this Act, provided that reasonable notice is given to the licensee and any outstanding consideration is duly settled. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment or licensing shall render the act void and unenforceable.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright in a cinematograph film shall, prior to the institution of any suit for such infringement, provide to the alleged infringer a notice of claim detailing the nature of the copyright, the specific acts constituting the infringement, and a demand for rectification or cessation of the infringing activity. Provided that, such notice shall be served at least thirty days prior to the filing of the plaint, and failure to comply with this requirement may render the suit unsustainable, subject to the discretion of the Court. An appeal from any decree refusing relief in such a case may be preferred to the High Court, and the High Court shall consider whether due diligence was exercised in ascertaining the validity of the claimed copyright and the extent of the alleged infringement. Where a claim of copyright is successfully defended on grounds of fair dealing as provided herein, the defendant may be awarded costs commensurate with the frivolous nature of the initial claim.

Any person claiming copyright in a work shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration of copyright in the prescribed form to the Registrar of Copyrights. The application shall be accompanied by the requisite fee and a copy of the work, or a sufficient portion thereof, as may be specified in the rules. Upon receipt of the application and verification of its contents, the Registrar shall, if satisfied that the work is eligible for copyright, enter the particulars in the Register of Copyrights and issue a certificate of registration. 

A request for respect filing application, indicating a desire to expedite the examination process, may be submitted alongside the standard application, provided that the applicant fulfills all criteria for such expedited consideration as prescribed by the Registrar. Registration is *prima facie* evidence of the facts stated therein and shall not be construed as an admission by the Registrar as to the validity of the copyright. Failure to register does not prejudice the right to copyright, but registration facilitates proof of ownership.

For the purposes of this Act, a registered proprietor shall notify any person who, to their knowledge, is applying for the registration of a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to their registered trade mark, and of which they have knowledge. Such notification shall be in writing and delivered to the applicant or their authorised agent within three months of the publication of the application in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to notify, subject to demonstrating reasonable cause, may be considered by the Trade Marks Registry when assessing bad faith objections to the application. Any person receiving a notification under this Act may, within one month of receipt, request further particulars regarding the basis of the objection. The Registrar may, if satisfied, extend this period.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, prior to acceptance of the application, cause a notice of the application to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, as prescribed under the rules made by the Controller. The Controller may, however, require the applicant to additionally notify any relevant trade association or industry body, if deemed necessary for ascertaining potential conflicts with existing marks or to facilitate opposition proceedings. Such notification shall be conducted in a manner specified by the Controller and shall include details of the mark, goods or services covered, and the applicant’s particulars. Failure to comply with the requirements to notify, where mandated, may render the application liable to be rejected, subject to a reasonable opportunity being granted to remedy the deficiency. Provided that, the Controller shall not impose a notification requirement where the mark is clearly devoid of any distinguishing character.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, upon becoming aware of a potential infringement of their registered trade mark, notify the infringing party in writing, detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and requiring cessation of the unlawful activity within thirty days from the date of such notice. Should the infringing party fail to comply with the notice, the registered proprietor may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining further infringement, and for an account of profits derived from the unlawful use. A proprietor desiring to oppose the registration of a mark shall notify the Trade Marks Registry within the prescribed time, failing which their right to do so shall be extinguished. Provided that, notification of a potential infringement shall not be construed as an admission of validity of the registered trade mark, nor shall it prejudice any other rights or remedies available to either party under this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Any false notification made with intent to cause harm may be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, upon becoming aware of a potential infringement of their registered trade mark, promptly notify the Registrar of Trade Marks in writing, detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and providing sufficient evidence to support the claim. The notification shall include the identity of the alleged infringer, the location of the infringing activity, and the specific goods or services in relation to which the infringement is alleged. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the notifying party to furnish further information or evidence within a specified timeframe. Failure to comply with such a requirement may result in the dismissal of the notification. Where a notification concerns counterfeit goods, the proprietor shall also notify the relevant law enforcement authorities, and provide a copy of the notification to the Registrar. Any person receiving a notification under this Act shall maintain confidentiality regarding the details contained therein, except as required by law or with the express consent of the notifying party.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark shall notify the Registrar of any change in the address of their registered office, within fourteen days of such change occurring, failing which a penalty as prescribed may be levied. Where a proprietor becomes aware that a third party is making unauthorized use of their registered trade mark, they may notify the alleged infringer in writing, detailing the nature of the infringement and demanding cessation of such use within thirty days. Subject to the provisions herein, a proprietor intending to assign their trade mark shall notify the Registrar and provide full details of the assignee, and the transfer shall not be effective until such notification and registration of the assignment is completed. Failure to notify the Registrar of any material fact affecting the validity of the trade mark may render the registration liable to revocation, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated.

Any person intending to assign a registered trade mark shall notify the Trade Marks Registry in writing of the intended assignment, and shall furnish such information as may be prescribed. Failure to notify the Registry prior to the completion of the assignment shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee, and subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Trade Marks Registry may, if satisfied that the non-notification was unintentional, waive the penalty, provided that the assignment is subsequently registered as provided herein. Where a notification is received, the Registry shall record the details of the assignment and publish notice thereof in the Trade Marks Journal. Any aggrieved party may, within sixty days of such publication, file a notice of opposition, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding opposition proceedings. A false notification made knowingly shall be punishable with imprisonment, or fine, or both.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark desiring to assign or otherwise transfer the ownership of the trade mark, or any right in relation thereto, shall notify the Trade Marks Registry in writing of such intention, specifying the particulars of the assignee or transferee, and the extent of the rights being transferred. Such notification shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the instrument of assignment or transfer, and a fee as prescribed in the First Schedule. The Registry, upon receipt of the notification and verification of the instrument, may record the transfer of ownership or rights in its records, subject to confirmation that the assignee or transferee fulfils all legal requirements for ownership under this Act. Failure to notify the Registry of any assignment or transfer shall not invalidate the transfer itself, provided that the assignee or transferee subsequently applies for registration of the transferred rights and satisfies the Registrar as to the validity of the transfer. The registered proprietor remains liable for any acts committed prior to such notification.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, aggrieved by any act which constitutes an infringement of their rights as provided herein, may serve a notice of intent to defend upon the alleged infringer, and simultaneously notify the Registrar of Trade Marks of such intent. Such notification shall include a detailed account of the alleged infringement, specifying the goods or services affected and the manner of infringement. Where a party receives a notice of intent to defend, they may, within thirty days of receipt, submit a counter-statement to both the registered proprietor and the Registrar, outlining grounds for disputing the claim of infringement. Failure to notify the Registrar within the prescribed timeframe may be considered an abandonment of the right to contest the infringement. The Registrar shall, upon receiving both the notice and any counter-statement, initiate a preliminary inquiry to determine if a prima facie case exists for further adjudication, subject to the provisions relating to rectification of the register.

Any person desiring basic registration of a trade mark shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and such application shall be accompanied by a statement of proposed use. The Registry, upon receipt of an application, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the Registry is satisfied that the application meets the requirements, it shall proceed to advertise the trade mark in the Trade Marks Journal. Following advertisement, any person may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition to the registration. The applicant shall be notified of any opposition filed and shall be afforded an opportunity to file a counter-statement. Should no opposition be received, or if any opposition is decided in favour of the applicant, the Registry shall register the trade mark, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. The Registry may, however, require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary before proceeding with registration, and shall notify the applicant of any such requirement.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark shall notify the Trade Marks Registry of any change in domicile or principal place of business within thirty days of such change occurring, failing which a penalty as prescribed may be levied. Where a trade mark is claimed to be a considered geographical indication, the applicant shall, along with the application for registration, submit a certificate of origin from the competent authority of the region concerned. The Registrar may, at any time, require further evidence to verify the authenticity of such claim. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing registration on grounds relating to geographical indication may file an appeal as provided herein. Failure to duly notify any assignment or transmission of rights in the trade mark shall render such assignment or transmission voidable at the option of the Trade Marks Registry, subject to a period of rectification not exceeding two years from the date of assignment.

Any person intending to assign or transmit a registered trade mark shall notify the Trade Marks Registry in writing of the intention to do so, within thirty days of the assignment or transmission. Such notification shall include full particulars of the assignee or transmittee, including their principal place of business and a certified copy of the instrument of assignment or transmission. Where a registered trade mark is subject to a permitted use license, the proprietor shall also notify the Registry of any material alteration to the terms of such license within the same timeframe. Failure to notify the Registry as provided herein shall render the assignment or transmission voidable at the option of the Registrar. Any person contravening this provision shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and the Registrar may, in addition, order the rectification of the Register. Repeated non-compliance may result in suspension of rights under this Act.

In this Act, “relation registered trade” signifies a legally recognized connection between a registered trade mark and goods or services not explicitly covered by the original registration, but falling within the scope of Class Nice Classification under which the trade mark is registered. Such relation shall be established where a substantial nexus exists, demonstrating a likelihood of confusion or association in the minds of consumers. A trade mark owner may, subject to due process as provided herein, seek to extend the protection of their registered trade mark to closely related goods or services. Provided that, the extension shall not infringe upon the legitimate interests of prior users of similar marks in relation to identical or similar goods or services, and any such claim shall be adjudicated upon considering all relevant factors including market conditions and consumer perception. The Registrar may, upon application, determine the existence of a relation registered trade.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act concerning its continued validity and renewal, and the proprietor thereof shall duly file the prescribed renewal application and pay the requisite fee within the stipulated period. Where a registered trade mark is associated with a series of goods or a class of goods, the proprietor may, subject to conditions as may be prescribed, apply for an amendment to the register to specify a relation registered trade, indicating a narrower scope of goods for which the mark is maintained. Any such amendment shall not prejudice the rights of prior users established before the date of such amendment. The Registrar may, upon reasonable cause being shown, and after notice to any affected party, direct the amendment of the register to reflect the relation registered trade. Failure to maintain the annual renewal fee, or to comply with the conditions relating to a relation registered trade, may render the registration liable to be removed from the register.

Any person who avails of a relation registered trade, whether by way of assignment, license, or other transfer of rights, shall be subject to the same obligations and liabilities as if the trade mark were registered in their name, as provided herein. However, a registered proprietor may, subject to the terms of any agreement with such person, initiate legal proceedings for infringement of the registered trade mark, notwithstanding the transfer of rights. Where a relation registered trade is used in a manner that causes confusion or deception, the original proprietor shall have recourse to remedies including injunction, damages, and an order for delivery up of infringing goods. A licensee shall, prior to commencing any action relating to the trade mark, notify the registered proprietor and provide a reasonable opportunity to participate in or assume control of the proceedings. The registered proprietor retains the right to seek an accounting of profits derived from the unauthorized use of the relation registered trade, even if a license was initially granted but subsequently breached.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to rectification proceedings before the Trade Marks Registry upon application made in the prescribed manner alleging that the trade mark is not distinctive, or has become deceptively similar to another trade mark used by another trader. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a trade mark, and claiming to be the owner of an earlier trade mark or continuous user of a descriptive term, may file a notice of opposition within the time specified under the rules made by the Central Government. Where a relation registered trade mark exists, and a complaint of passing off is made, the Registry shall consider evidence of concurrent use and the reputation of both marks, giving due weight to the first date of use as demonstrated by credible documentation. Provided that, the Registry may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct an inquiry to be conducted to determine the validity of the complaint and the extent of any damage suffered. The Registrar shall issue a reasoned order reflecting the findings of fact and the legal basis for the decision.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to rectification proceedings under this Act if it is proven to be devoid of any distinctive character at the time of its registration. Any application for rectification based on lack of distinctiveness shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within a period of five years from the date of registration of the trade mark, unless the applicant can demonstrate continuous use of the relation registered trade mark establishing acquired distinctiveness. Evidence of extensive advertising, sales figures, and market research demonstrating consumer recognition may be presented to substantiate claims of acquired distinctiveness. The Registry may, however, extend this period if satisfied with exceptional circumstances. A trade mark falsely representing association with another shall also be subject to rectification. Provided that, the Registrar may require an affidavit verifying the facts stated in the rectification application.

Any person who uses in the course of trade, a deceptive or confusingly similar mark in relation to registered trade marks, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such use, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Where the offence involves the sale of goods bearing such mark, all infringing goods found in possession of the offender shall be seized and may be destroyed as provided herein. The owner of the registered trade mark may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Court for an injunction restraining the offender from further use of the mark. Any application for injunction shall be heard expeditiously. A relation registered trade mark, if proven to have been applied to goods of a different class than that for which it was originally registered, shall not be considered a valid basis for such injunction, unless the owner demonstrates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. All penalties collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be executed in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. A license to use a registered trade mark may be granted, either generally or subject to limitations as to time, place or the manner of use, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive. Where a license is exclusive, the proprietor of the registered trade mark shall not use the trade mark himself, except to the extent permitted in the license. 

Any dispute arising from the terms of a license, or the scope of a licensed right in relation to a registered trade mark, shall be determined by the High Court. Assignment or licensing of a relation registered trade mark, without due registration, shall not affect the rights of the assignee or licensee against third parties. The proprietor may, at any time, revoke a license if the licensee fails to observe the terms and conditions of the license, provided that reasonable notice is given.

Any person who avails themselves of a relation registered trade, whether by way of assignment, license, or other form of transfer of rights, shall be subject to the terms and conditions governing such transfer, and shall exercise those rights in good faith and accordance with the provisions of this Act. Where a registered trade mark owner permits use of their mark by another, such permission, and any limitations thereon, may be documented in a written agreement specifying the scope of permitted use, duration, and territorial extent. Any dispute arising from a breach of such agreement shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court, and the aggrieved party may seek remedies including, but not limited to, injunctive relief and damages. Provided that, a registered owner may, under clauses sub section (2), revoke a license if the licensee fails to adhere to quality control standards established by the owner, subject to a reasonable opportunity to cure such deficiency. Failure to comply with these provisions may constitute an act of infringement as provided herein.

Any person who uses in the course of trade, a trade mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a relation registered trade mark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement under this Act. Provided that, where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, any promotion trade mark employed by the registered proprietor for advertising or promotional purposes, and which does not extend beyond the scope of legitimate self-promotion, shall not be construed as an infringement of another’s registered trade mark. However, such promotion shall not mislead the public or cause confusion as to the source or quality of goods or services. Any violation of this provision shall attract a penalty of imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine not exceeding three lakh rupees, or both. The Court may, in addition to damages, grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the offending mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a subject registration trade shall mean a trade mark applied for registration, or registered, in respect of goods or services falling within Class 31 of the Nice Classification, specifically agricultural, horticultural, and forestry products, as well as live animals, excluding those covered under veterinary services. A trade mark shall be considered subject to registration provided that it meets the criteria of distinctiveness and is not descriptive of the goods or services it represents. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence of inherent distinctiveness or acquired distinctiveness through use. Registration of a subject registration trade does not confer exclusive rights to the underlying agricultural practice, but solely to the identifying mark itself, and shall be governed by the principles of honest concurrent use.

Any person claiming ownership of a subject registration trade shall, prior to commencing any commercial exploitation thereof, furnish to the Registrar a detailed statement of the proposed use, including the class of goods or services to which it will be applied and the geographical area of intended operation. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the registration liable to revocation, subject to a hearing as provided herein. A registered proprietor may, notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, assign their rights in the subject registration trade, but such assignment shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Registrar, who may refuse consent if the proposed assignee is deemed unfit to hold such rights. Where a trade mark is registered in the name of a company and that company is dissolved, the rights therein shall vest in the liquidator, who may continue to exploit the trade mark for a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of dissolution, unless otherwise directed by a competent court. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the High Court.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorized agents. The instrument shall specify the trade mark assigned, the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and the geographical territory, if any, to which the assignment is limited. Subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, the assignee may apply to the Trade Marks Registry to record the assignment in the register. 

A license to use a registered trade mark shall be granted by the proprietor to another party, conferring a right to use the subject registration trade under specified terms and conditions. Such license may be exclusive, granting sole rights within a defined scope, or non-exclusive, permitting multiple licensees. Any material breach of the licensing agreement by the licensee shall entitle the proprietor to terminate the license, provided that reasonable notice is given. The registrar may, upon application, record details of the license.

Any person claiming ownership of a subject registration trade, and desiring to seek remedies under this Act, shall first demonstrate lawful use of the mark prior to the date of any alleged infringement, and shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the adjudicating authority regarding the geographical scope of such use. However, a mere declaration of intent to use shall not constitute lawful use for the purposes of establishing prior rights. Any application for registration that is refused may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and deposits the prescribed fee within sixty days of the refusal order. The Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions herein, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the adjudicating authority. A finding of bad faith on the part of the applicant shall be conclusive against them, notwithstanding any evidence of prior use, and the registration shall be deemed void *ab initio*. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board may seek recourse through a writ petition before the High Court.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be entitled to have the trade mark registered. An application for registration shall not be refused on the ground that the trade mark is not inherently capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, if, through use, the trade mark has acquired a distinctive character. Where a dispute arises regarding the registrability of a subject registration trade, the Trade Marks Registry may refer the matter to a Judicial Member for expert determination. The Judicial Member’s decision shall be binding on the Registry, provided that an appeal may lie to the High Court. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, permit the transfer of a registered trade mark. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may, within a period of ninety days, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall include a clear statement of the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. Where the assignment is of a part only of the goodwill of the trade mark, the assignee shall not be entitled to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services not included in the assigned goodwill. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of assignments and transmit a certified copy of every instrument of assignment to the assignee. 

A notice of assignment, conforming substantially to the form prescribed in the First Schedule, shall be filed with the Registry within the prescribed period. Failure to file such registration notice may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. Subject to the terms of any agreement between the assignor and assignee, the assignee shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if they were the original proprietor of the subject registration trade.

Any person claiming ownership of a subject registration trade, and alleging infringement by another, shall first submit a notice of intent to the Registrar, detailing the grounds of the claim and the nature of the alleged infringement. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the claim’s prima facie validity, direct the alleged infringer to file a response within thirty days. Should the response fail to adequately address the concerns raised, or if no response is received, the claimant may then initiate proceedings before the appellate authority. However, where the alleged infringement incorporates elements protected by copyright, the claimant must demonstrate that the trade mark registration predates the copyright claim, or that the copyright work is wholly derivative of the registered trade mark, and does not independently possess artistic merit. An appeal against the appellate authority’s decision shall lie with the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the appellate authority’s order. The Registrar retains the power to revoke a registration if fraudulent misrepresentation is established during any stage of these proceedings.

A plaintiff seeking relief under this Act may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from the unauthorized use of a trade mark, pending the final determination of the suit. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit stating the grounds for the injunction and demonstrating prima facie case, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience favouring the applicant. The court may, subject to such terms as it deems fit, grant the injunction if satisfied that the applicant is likely to succeed in the suit and the balance of convenience warrants such an order. Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing a parte injunction interlocutory may appeal to the appellate court as provided herein. The court, while considering the application, may also direct the applicant to furnish security for any damages that the defendant may sustain.

Any registered proprietor may, under this Act, apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for a temporary injunction, also known as a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from any acts constituting an infringement of, or passing off in relation to, their registered trade mark. Such application shall be accompanied by a verified statement detailing the grounds for the claim and the likely damage suffered, or to be suffered, should the infringing activity continue. The court may, subject to such terms as it deems fit, grant the injunction pending the final determination of the suit, provided that adequate security for damages is furnished by the applicant. Where the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case, balance of convenience favouring immediate relief, and a reasonable apprehension of irreparable harm, the court may issue the injunction even without notice to the defendant, though notice shall be served without undue delay thereafter. The court may also direct an accounting of profits made by the defendant through the unlawful use of the mark.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark, registered or unregistered, who is aggrieved by the use of a deceptively similar mark by another, may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction, also known as a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from such use pending the final determination of the dispute. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the ownership of the mark and the likelihood of confusion. The Court may, subject to such terms as it deems fit, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from using the mark, provided that the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case, the balance of convenience lies in their favour, and irreparable harm will result if the injunction is not granted. Where a plaintiff seeks a temporary injunction, the court may also direct the defendant to provide an undertaking as to account of profits, or to deposit funds sufficient to cover potential damages. Any person disobeying an order made under this Act shall be liable to imprisonment.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or likelihood of confusion, may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction, also known as a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from the use of the mark in question, pending the final determination of the suit. Such application shall be supported by affidavit verifying the grounds for the injunction and demonstrating prima facie case, balance of convenience in favour of the applicant, and irreparable harm likely to be suffered if the injunction is not granted. The Court may require the applicant to furnish security, as it deems fit, to cover potential damages to the defendant should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Where an ex parte injunction is granted, notice of the application and the order shall be served on the defendant forthwith. Any person aggrieved by an order of injunction may apply to the Court for its variation or discharge, subject to such terms as the Court may impose, including costs. The Court shall consider all relevant factors, including the public interest, when deciding whether to grant, vary, or discharge an injunction as provided herein.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or likelihood of confusion, may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction, also known as a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of the mark pending the final determination of the suit. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for the injunction and demonstrating prima facie case, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience favouring the applicant. The court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, direct the applicant to furnish security for potential damages to the defendant, should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted unless the court is satisfied that the applicant has made a diligent search to identify all potential defendants and has disclosed all material facts relevant to the claim. The court may vary or discharge the injunction at any stage if circumstances so warrant, and any non-compliance with these provisions shall be considered during the adjudication of the matter.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or well-known mark not registered in India but used here, may apply ex parte to a court of competent jurisdiction for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the mark. Such application shall be supported by affidavit verifying the grounds for the claim and demonstrating prima facie case, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience favouring the applicant. The court, upon being satisfied that a strong case exists and delay would cause irreversible damage, may grant a parte injunction interlocutory restraining the defendant for a period not exceeding such time as may be fixed by the court, but not exceeding thirty days. Failure to comply with this injunction shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Any person aggrieved by such injunction may apply to the court for vacation thereof, subject to notice to the applicant.

Any person desiring to assign or otherwise transfer the goodwill of a business, or a trade mark registered under this Act, shall, prior to such assignment or transfer, provide notice in writing to the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the particulars of the intended assignee and the scope of the transfer, including any limitations on the use of the trade mark. An application for registration of the assignment or transfer shall follow within thirty days of the notice, failing which the transfer shall be deemed voidable at the option of the Trade Marks Registry. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity or scope of such assignment, the court may grant a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the parties from acting in a manner inconsistent with the claimed rights, pending a full adjudication of the matter. Such injunction may be subject to conditions regarding security for damages and undertakings as to future conduct, as the court deems just. The assignee shall be liable for any infringement occurring after the date of the transfer, unless otherwise agreed.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or likelihood of confusion, may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction, also known as a parte injunction interlocutory, restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of said mark pending the final determination of the suit. Such application shall be accompanied by a verified statement detailing the grounds for the injunction and a prima facie case demonstrating substantial loss if the injunction is not granted. The Court may, subject to such terms as it deems fit regarding security for damages and undertaking to prosecute the suit diligently, grant the injunction ex parte, provided that reasonable notice of the application has not been served on the defendant, or that immediate harm will result if notice is given. Any order so granted shall not exceed a period of fifteen days unless extended by further order of the Court, and shall be subject to appeal to the Division Bench. Failure to diligently prosecute the suit may result in the discharge of the interlocutory injunction.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, and seeking urgent relief, may apply to the appropriate court for a parte injunction interlocutory order restraining the defendant from continuing the alleged infringement. Such application shall be accompanied by a clear and detailed affidavit demonstrating a prima facie case, irreparable harm, and balance of convenience favouring the applicant. The court, prior to granting such order, shall record its reasons in writing. Where the court is satisfied that the defendant is likely to continue the infringement despite the injunction, it may direct the defendant to provide a security deposit or undertake to pay a reasonable royalty, calculated on a pro-rata basis, for any goods sold or services rendered during the pendency of the suit. Failure to comply with the terms of the injunction shall constitute contempt of court, subject to penalties as provided herein. The court may modify or discharge the injunction at any stage, upon sufficient cause being shown.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark, or an exclusive licensee thereof, and alleging an infringement or likelihood of infringement, may apply ex parte to a court of competent jurisdiction for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from using the trade mark in question. Such application shall be supported by affidavit verifying the ownership of the trade mark and the grounds for seeking the injunction. The court, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists and that irreparable harm will be suffered if the injunction is not granted, may issue a parte injunction interlocutory order restraining the defendant pending disposal of the suit. However, such injunction may be subject to terms, including a requirement for the applicant to provide security for potential damages to the defendant, should the suit ultimately fail. The court shall not grant such an injunction unless it is satisfied that the balance of convenience lies in favour of the applicant. Any assignment of the trade mark shall be subject to the terms of any existing exclusive license.

An ex parte injunction may be granted by a court competent to hear cases under this Act, restraining the defendant from the unauthorized use of a registered trade mark, or a well-known mark, pending the outcome of a suit for infringement or passing off. Such an injunction shall be granted upon prima facie demonstration by the applicant of substantial loss or irreparable harm likely to result from the continuation of the offending acts. The applicant shall undertake to provide an affidavit verifying the truth of the allegations made in support of the application and shall also provide an undertaking as to damages, should the injunction ultimately be found to have been wrongly obtained. Where a trade mark is subject to a pending application for registration, an ex parte injunction may issue if the court is satisfied that the mark is likely to be registered and that the defendant’s acts constitute a clear infringement.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, or a person having a substantial interest in such trade mark, may apply ex parte to a court of competent jurisdiction for an injunction restraining the defendant from infringing the trade mark, or from passing off goods or services as those of the plaintiff. Such application shall be supported by an affidavit verifying the facts relied upon and demonstrating a prima facie case for the grant of an injunction. The court, if satisfied that a case for an ex parte injunction exists and that immediate action is necessary to prevent irreparable harm to the plaintiff’s goodwill or business, may issue an injunction pending a full hearing. However, such injunction shall not be granted unless the applicant undertakes to provide an undertaking to the court to indemnify the defendant against any loss or damage suffered by reason of the injunction, should the final decision be against the applicant. The court may also direct the applicant to provide security for such indemnity, as provided herein.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, or a person using a trade mark with his consent, who is aggrieved by an infringement of his trade mark, or by any colourable variation thereof sufficient to deceive or cause confusion, may institute a suit for the recovery of damages, an injunction, or other relief as is or may be available in law. Where an application is made to a court seeking an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from the manufacture, sale, or other disposition of goods bearing the plaintiff’s trade mark, the court may grant such injunction if it is satisfied that a prima facie case exists and the balance of convenience lies in favour of the applicant. However, such injunction shall not be granted unless the applicant undertakes to provide an account of profits, and to pay damages, if ultimately it is found that no infringement occurred. The court may also require the applicant to furnish security, as it deems fit, to cover potential losses suffered by the defendant.

Any registered proprietor may apply ex parte to a District Court of competent pecuniary jurisdiction for an injunction restraining the defendant from the manufacture, sale, offering for sale, distribution, or importation of goods bearing a trade mark deceptively similar to the registered trade mark, where such application is accompanied by a prima facie case demonstrating likelihood of confusion and irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted immediately. The Court, upon such application and subject to notice being served to the defendant, shall consider the balance of convenience and the potential harm to both parties. Provided that, the applicant shall undertake to provide an account of profits or damages, should the injunction ultimately be discharged against them. Where the defendant demonstrates a substantial defence on the merits, the Court may require the applicant to furnish security for potential costs before granting the ex parte injunction. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable by the Court as if it were a decree.

Any registered proprietor may apply ex parte to a court of competent jurisdiction for an injunction restraining the defendant from the manufacture, sale, or distribution of goods bearing a trademark deceptively similar to their registered trademark, where a prima facie case of infringement exists and the balance of convenience favours the applicant. Such application shall be accompanied by a verified statement detailing the grounds for the claim, including evidence of registration, use, and the likelihood of confusion. The court, prior to granting an ex parte injunction, shall record its reasons in writing, and may require the applicant to furnish an undertaking as to damages. The injunction granted shall remain in force until a final determination of the matter is reached, subject to modification or discharge upon sufficient cause being shown and compliance with the procedures as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an ex parte injunction may apply to the court for its vacation or modification.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or well-known mark not registered under this Act, may apply ex parte to a District Court for an immediate injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the mark. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement of facts supporting the claim of infringement and a verified copy of the registration certificate, if applicable. The Court, if satisfied prima facie of the validity of the mark and the likelihood of continuing infringement causing irreparable harm, may grant an ex parte injunction. Failure to comply with the terms of such injunction shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or both. Any person aggrieved by an ex parte injunction may apply to the Court for its modification or vacation upon providing adequate cause and security for damages. The Court shall consider such application expeditiously.

Any person claiming ownership of a registered trade mark, or a well-known mark recognized under this Act, and alleging an imminent threat of infringement or passing off by another, may apply to the High Court for an ex parte injunction restraining the alleged infringer from the manufacture, sale, offer for sale, or any other disposition of goods bearing the deceptively similar mark. Such application shall be accompanied by an undertaking as to damages, and a clear demonstration of the likelihood of irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted promptly. The Court, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists and the balance of convenience favours the applicant, may issue the injunction pending a full trial. Any assignment or licensing of rights in the mark, whether registered or unregistered, shall be disclosed to the Court during the proceedings, and the Court may consider such assignment or license when determining the scope of the injunction. Provided that, the Court may direct the applicant to provide security for potential damages suffered by the respondent should the injunction ultimately be discharged.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or well-known mark even if unregistered, may apply to a court of competent jurisdiction for an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, or importing goods or services bearing the infringing mark. Such application shall be supported by affidavit verifying the ownership of the mark and a prima facie case of infringement, and shall further demonstrate the likelihood of irreparable harm if the injunction is not granted immediately. The court, upon being satisfied of these conditions, may issue an ex parte injunction pending disposal of the suit, provided that the applicant undertakes to provide security, as determined by the court, to cover potential damages to the defendant should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Any order granting such an injunction shall be served forthwith upon the defendant, who may, subject to the rules of court, apply for a variation or discharge of the injunction upon reasonable notice. Appeals from any order relating to such injunctions shall lie to the appellate court as provided herein.

Any person making a lawful assignment of rights in a trade mark, or a license to use a trade mark, shall furnish the Controller with a certified copy of the instrument of assignment or license within thirty days from the date of its execution. Where an application for registration of assignment or license is made, and it appears to the Controller that the assignment or license is likely to be prejudicial to the interests of the assignee or licensee, the Controller may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, require the applicant to furnish further evidence. An ex parte injunction may be granted by a court competent to hear trade mark matters, restraining the assigned party from any further use of the mark, pending full adjudication of the validity of the assignment. Should the assigned mark relate to an article patented elsewhere, the court shall consider the patent holder’s rights subject to the provisions of this Act, and may direct an accounting of royalties due. Any such order shall be binding on all parties concerned.

Any person applying for an ex parte injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, or otherwise dealing in goods bearing a trademark similar to that registered in their name, shall demonstrate a prima facie case of ownership and likelihood of confusion.
