The court, however, may require the applicant to furnish an undertaking as to damages, should the injunction ultimately be discharged against them. Where the applicant’s trademark is registered in a convention country, and evidence of such registration is presented, the court shall give due consideration to the international obligations of India under relevant treaties. An order granting an ex parte injunction may be varied or discharged upon notice to the defendant, and any party aggrieved by such order may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein, subject to the conditions prescribed. The court retains discretion to modify the terms of the injunction pending the outcome of the appeal.

An ex parte injunction may be granted by a court competent to hear matters under this Act, restraining the defendant from the manufacture, sale, import, export, or other disposition of goods, including those embodying a semiconductor integrated circuit, that are alleged to infringe a registered trade mark or are deceptively similar thereto. Such injunction shall be issued pending the actual notice to the defendant and the opportunity for them to be heard, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates a prima facie case, the balance of convenience lies in their favour, and irreparable harm will result if the injunction is not granted. The court may require the plaintiff to provide security, as it deems fit, to cover potential damages to the defendant should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Any person aggrieved by an ex parte injunction may apply to the court for its variation or discharge.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark or a recognized geographical indication, alleging an imminent threat of infringement or passing off, may apply ex parte to a court of competent jurisdiction for an injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, or otherwise dealing with goods or services bearing the deceptively similar mark or indication. The court, upon being satisfied of a prima facie case and the likelihood of irreparable harm, shall have the power to grant an ex parte injunction, pending notice to the defendant. Provided that such injunction shall not be granted unless the plaintiff undertakes to provide an account of profits, and to pay damages, if ultimately found not to be entitled to the relief sought. A geographical indication plaintiff must also demonstrate a clear connection between the goods and the geographical region of origin, as established under this Act. The court may direct the defendant to furnish security, as it deems fit, for the due performance of the injunction.

For the purposes of this Act, a dramatic work shall include any piece of work of a dramatic character, whether or not in written form, including a scenario or a script. Such work encompasses works intended to be performed by one or more persons, and shall include a choreographic work in so far as it is fixed in a tangible or otherwise perceptible form. A cinematograph film shall not be considered a dramatic work, but any work forming part of a cinematograph film may, if it satisfies the criteria as provided herein, independently constitute a dramatic work. Where a work is adapted from a literary work, the rights in the dramatic work shall be subject to the rights subsisting in the original literary work, unless otherwise agreed. Any subsequent performance of a dramatic work in public requires prior authorization from the copyright holder.

A work consisting substantially of dialogue may constitute a dramatic work, notwithstanding the absence of any stage direction or any indication of setting or character. For the purposes of registration under this Act, a dramatic work shall be deemed to include a scenario or script of a film, whether or not it is intended to be adapted for performance on a stage. Any work of choreography, irrespective of whether it is recorded or not, shall also be considered a dramatic work, provided that it is fixed in a tangible medium of expression. An application for registration of a dramatic work shall clearly delineate the authorship and ownership of the work, and shall be accompanied by a complete script or, in the case of choreography, a detailed notation of the sequence of movements. Subject to the provisions herein, a dramatic work must be original to qualify for copyright protection. The registrar may require further evidence to ascertain the originality of the submitted work.

A dramatic work, whether originally expressed in writing or otherwise, shall be protected under this Act, and the author thereof shall possess the exclusive right to reproduce, adapt, perform, and communicate the work to the public. Any person who, without a license from the copyright owner or in contravention of any condition imposed by a duly authorized licensing body, performs or causes to be performed a dramatic work in public, or distributes copies of the work for the purpose of such performance, shall be liable to a suit for infringement. 

Provided that fair dealing with a dramatic work for the purposes of criticism, review, or reporting of current events, subject to the conditions of attribution and lack of prejudice to the commercial interests of the owner, shall not constitute an infringement as provided herein. The right to perform a dramatic work extends to all forms of public presentation, including theatrical performances, broadcasts, and digital streaming, and shall subsist for a period of sixty years from the date of the author’s death. Any aggrieved party may seek injunctive relief and damages for any loss suffered due to such infringement.

A dramatic work shall be construed to include a work of any kind, whether or not reduced to writing, which is intended to be performed before a public, including a scenario or a script for a film. Where a work is expressly created for the purpose of being performed by mechanical means, or by any other means not involving a human actor, it shall nevertheless be considered a dramatic work as provided herein. The author of a dramatic work is the person by whom the work is composed, and in the case of a collaborative work, the authorship shall be attributed to the persons jointly responsible for its creation, subject to any agreement to the contrary. Any person intending to perform a dramatic work in public shall be required to obtain the prior consent of the copyright owner, or their duly authorized agent, and such performance shall be subject to the payment of royalties as determined by the owner. A performance shall be deemed to be in public if it is accessible to a substantial number of persons outside of a private circle, and includes any transmission by broadcast or other electronic means.

A work consisting substantially of dialogue may constitute a dramatic work, notwithstanding the absence of any stage direction or action indicated therein, provided that such dialogue is intended to be performed before a public audience, whether live or recorded. Any arrangement or adaptation of a dramatic work shall be considered a derivative work subject to the provisions of this Act, and the author of the original dramatic work retains the exclusive right to authorize such arrangements. Where a dramatic work is performed in public, the performer shall obtain necessary licenses as provided herein, and the owner of the copyright in the dramatic work is entitled to receive royalties for each such performance. Any unauthorized performance of a dramatic work constitutes an infringement, and shall be subject to the remedies available under this Act, including injunction and damages. The right to perform a dramatic work may be assigned or bequeathed in accordance with the general principles of law relating to the assignment and transfer of property.

Any person who performs, reproduces, distributes, or communicates to the public a dramatic work, whether in whole or in part, without the lawful consent of the copyright owner, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. A dramatic work includes a screenplay, a stage play, a ballet, or any other work of a similar character intended to be performed before a public audience, and extends to cinematograph films insofar as they constitute a dramatic performance. Where a dramatic work is performed in public, the owner of the copyright shall have the right to receive royalties, the amount of which may be determined by mutual agreement or, failing such agreement, by the High Court. Any individual found to be facilitating the unauthorized performance of a dramatic work, including providing venues or equipment, shall be deemed an abettor to the infringement and subject to the same penalties. Penalties for infringement under this Act include imprisonment for a term not exceeding six years, or a fine, or both.

Any person desiring to license the right to perform, or to reproduce, a dramatic work, including cinematograph films where such film is considered a dramatic work under this Act, shall submit a written instrument of assignment or license to the Registrar of Copyrights, detailing the scope of permitted performances and reproductions. Such instrument shall clearly specify the geographical territory, duration, and any limitations on the exercise of the licensed rights. Where a dramatic work is jointly authored, all authors shall execute the instrument, or provide a duly authorized power of attorney for one author to act on their behalf. Assignment of copyright in a dramatic work shall vest ownership of all rights therein, subject to any existing contractual obligations. A licensee may, with the express written consent of the copyright holder, sub-license the rights granted, provided that such sub-license does not exceed the scope of the original license. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer.

A dramatic work, for the purposes of copyright protection under this Act, shall be construed to include a screenplay, a stage play, a ballet, or any other work of a similar character intended to be performed before a public audience, irrespective of the manner of such performance. However, a cinematograph film shall not be considered a dramatic work, but rather a separate work altogether, subject to the provisions relating to cinematograph films as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the classification of a work as a dramatic work, or its distinction from a cinematograph film, may be brought before the High Court having jurisdiction. The aggrieved party shall bear the onus of proving that the work in question meets the criteria for a dramatic work as defined herein, and that no existing copyright has been infringed. Appeals from any decision of the High Court shall lie with the Supreme Court.

A dramatic work, for the purposes of this Act, shall include a screenplay, a stage play, and any work of choreography intended for performance before a public audience, irrespective of whether such performance is accompanied by music or other artistic elements. Where a dramatic work is based upon or incorporates a breeder registered variety protected under the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, the copyright in the dramatic work shall not extend to the breeder’s rights in the said variety, and such rights shall remain subject to the provisions of that Act. However, the adaptation of a literary work into a dramatic work, as provided herein, shall not be construed as an infringement of copyright if the adaptation is undertaken for the purpose of educational or research purposes, provided that reasonable measures are taken to ensure that such performance does not generate commercial benefit for the adaptor. Any person claiming copyright in a dramatic work shall furnish a declaration to the Registrar of Copyrights detailing the origin and nature of the work, and any reliance upon protected plant varieties.

A company, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include any body corporate or other incorporated or unincorporated association of persons. Where a work is created by an employee of a company in the course of their employment, the company shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be the first owner of the copyright therein. However, a contract between the company and the employee may provide otherwise, specifying alternative ownership or royalty arrangements, provided that such contract does not contravene public policy or any other provision herein. Any rights conferred upon a company under this Act are transferable to another legal entity, subject to the terms of any existing agreements and notification requirements as may be prescribed. A company may also be assigned copyright.

A company desiring registration of a copyright in a work created by its employees, shall submit an application to the Registrar of Copyrights, detailing the nature of the work and the terms of employment governing its creation. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the company’s memorandum of association and articles of association, establishing its legal existence and authorized activities. Where the work is a cinematograph film, the company must also furnish details of all producers associated with the film’s creation. 

Provided that, if the work is jointly authored by employees and external individuals, the company shall demonstrate a clear contractual agreement assigning copyright ownership to itself, subject to equitable remuneration as provided herein. Any failure to fully disclose material information regarding the company’s structure or the authorship of the work may render the registration invalid. The Registrar may, at their discretion, request further clarification or documentation to ensure compliance with this Act.

Where a copyright work is created by an employee of a company in the course of their employment, the copyright therein shall, subject to a contract to the contrary, vest in that company. However, any rights accruing to the author under this Act, including the right to claim authorship, remain unaffected by such vesting. A company aggrieved by any infringement of copyright in a work vested in it, may institute a suit for remedies including injunction, damages, or account of profits, as provided herein. Provided that, if the infringement is proven to have occurred due to the negligence of a person acting on behalf of the company, the company shall be liable for such infringement, unless it demonstrates it took reasonable care to prevent the same. Any settlement reached between the company and the infringer shall be subject to the approval of a judicial authority to ensure fairness and compliance with this Act. The company may also assign its copyright to another entity, subject to the conditions outlined herein.

Any work in which the copyright subsists shall be deemed to be published when copies of the work are made available to the public, irrespective of the number of copies so made available. Where a work is published by a company, the officer of the company who authorised the publication shall be responsible for any infringement arising from such publication, subject to proof of direct knowledge or consent. A company intending to avail itself of the provisions relating to licensing for broadcasting or communication to the public shall submit a detailed statement of its operational structure and the designated officer responsible for copyright compliance. Should a dispute arise concerning the ownership of copyright in a work created by a company, the High Court having jurisdiction shall determine the rightful owner, considering the terms of employment and any agreements governing the creation of the work. Provided that, in cases where the work was commissioned, the commissioning company shall be presumed to be the first owner of the copyright unless otherwise agreed in writing.

A company intending to avail benefits under this Act relating to the licensing of copyrighted works shall maintain a register of all agreements entered into with authors or other copyright holders, detailing the nature of the licensed rights, the duration of the license, and the royalty rates agreed upon. Such register shall be open for inspection by any person having a legitimate interest, subject to reasonable notice and conditions as may be prescribed. Where a company undertakes the reproduction of a work in multiple formats, it shall, prior to such reproduction, ensure that appropriate permissions have been secured from the copyright owner or collective management organisation, as provided herein. Failure to maintain the aforementioned register or to secure necessary permissions may render the company liable to penalties, including statutory damages and injunctive relief. Any dispute concerning royalty payments shall be subject to the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. A company shall also be responsible for ensuring compliance by its agents and employees.

Any company found to be in violation of the provisions relating to technological protection measures, as provided herein, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such violation. Where an offence involving circumvention of such measures is committed with intent to facilitate copyright infringement, the penalty shall not be less than two lakh rupees. If a company continues the infringing activity after receiving a notice of violation from the investigating officer, an additional daily penalty of ten thousand rupees may be imposed for each day of continued infringement, subject to a maximum of one month. Any director, managing director, or other officer of the company who knowingly authorized or permitted the violation shall also be personally liable for the penalty, unless they prove they exercised due diligence to prevent the offence. Evidence of widespread or systematic infringement by the company shall be considered an aggravating factor in determining the penalty.

Any copyright subsisting in a work created by an employee of a company in the course of their employment shall, subject to a contract to the contrary, vest in the company. Where a work is commissioned by a company, but not created by an employee, the commissioning company shall be deemed the author, provided that the terms of commissioning, including ownership of copyright, are agreed upon in writing. A company desiring to assign its copyright may do so by executing an instrument in writing signed by a duly authorised officer. Any assignment of copyright by a company shall be subject to existing licenses granted by the company prior to such assignment, unless expressly superseded by the assignee. A company may grant licenses to use its copyrighted works, and such licenses shall be governed by the terms specified therein, and may include provisions for royalty payments or other consideration. The company shall maintain accurate records of all licenses granted and assignments made. Failure to do so may result in a presumption of improper licensing practices.

A company intending to claim copyright in a work created by an employee during the course of employment shall furnish proof of the terms of employment establishing employer-employee relationship, and demonstrate that the work falls within the scope of that employment, subject to the provisions herein. Where a dispute arises regarding ownership of copyright in such a work, and a claim is made by a former employee asserting independent creative contribution exceeding the bounds of assigned duties, the claimant shall submit evidence of such contribution to the High Court having jurisdiction. The Court may, after examining the evidence and hearing counsel, determine the extent of copyright vested in the company versus the individual, provided that the company can demonstrate a substantial investment in resources facilitating the work’s creation. Any appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court, and shall be heard within one year of the High Court’s judgment, unless exceptional circumstances are shown. Failure to adhere to these timelines may result in forfeiture of appeal rights.

A company desiring to commercially exploit copyrighted works through broadcasting shall obtain a license from the copyright owner, subject to the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon, or as determined by the High Court having jurisdiction. Any assignment of rights by a copyright owner to a company for broadcasting purposes shall be in writing and shall clearly delineate the scope of the assignment, including territorial limits and the duration of the license. A broadcasting organisation, being a company registered under the Companies Act, 2013, may, with the express consent of the copyright owner, simultaneously broadcast the same work on multiple platforms, provided that additional royalties are negotiated and paid. Where a company undertakes the broadcasting of sound recordings, it shall remit statutory royalties to the owner of the copyright in the sound recording as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the company liable to damages and injunctive relief. Any dispute regarding royalty rates or the interpretation of assignment agreements shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate High Court.

A convention application shall be an application for a patent filed under this Act by a person claiming priority from an application previously filed in a convention country. For the purposes of this definition, a “convention country” means any country or state which is a party to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, or to any treaty, convention, or reciprocal arrangement to which India is a party, and which provides similar privileges to applicants from India as are granted herein. The applicant shall, at the time of filing a convention application, identify the basic application from which priority is claimed, including its filing date and country of origin, subject to verification by the Controller. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application incomplete.

A person seeking protection for an invention under this Act, who has already filed an application in a convention country, may present a complete application along with a declaration stating that the application is a convention application. Such application shall be filed within twelve months from the date of the first application in the convention country, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the first application and, where applicable, a translation thereof into English or Hindi. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require the applicant to furnish additional documents or information to verify the details of the prior application. Failure to comply with the requirements relating to the convention application, or to furnish the necessary documents within the stipulated time, may render the application liable to be treated as a new application, losing the benefit of the priority date. The applicant shall also pay the prescribed fee for filing the convention application.

A person seeking a patent, who has already filed an application for the same invention in a convention country, may present a convention application to the Controller within twelve months from the date of the first filing, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such an application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the first application, duly translated if not in English, and a declaration verifying the particulars of the foreign application. The Controller may, however, require further statutory declarations or evidence as deemed necessary to ascertain the validity of the claim to priority. Failure to comply with these requirements within a period specified by the Controller shall render the convention application liable to be treated as a fresh application, losing the benefit of the priority date. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding a convention application may, within one month of the order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee.

A person seeking protection for an invention under this Act, who has already filed an application in a convention country, may present a complete application, together with a certified copy of the first application and a declaration verifying the same, as a convention application within the prescribed period from the date of the first application. The applicant shall, at the time of filing such convention application, indicate the country of first filing and the date of such filing. Where the convention application is not filed in English, a certified translation shall accompany the application, and the Controller may require an additional translation if the first translation is unsatisfactory. Priority may be claimed subject to the provisions herein, and the application shall be examined as if it were a new application filed on the date of the convention application. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application incomplete or subject to rejection, as determined by the Controller. The prescribed period for filing a convention application shall not exceed twelve months from the date of the first application.

A convention application filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a declaration stating that the application is the first application in respect of the invention made in a convention country, and that no application for a patent for the same invention has been filed in any other country outside of the convention country before the date of the first application. The applicant shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the first application, duly certified as a true copy by the competent authority of the convention country. Failure to submit such a certified copy may render the convention application incomplete, subject to a grace period granted at the discretion of the Controller. Where the applicant claims priority based on a provisional application filed in a convention country, evidence of such provisional application shall also be submitted. Any misrepresentation regarding the details of the first application shall be subject to the provisions concerning false statements made under this Act.

Any person making a convention application under this Act shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the first application, duly certified by the competent authority of the country of origin, and a translation thereof if not in English or Hindi. Failure to furnish such certified copy and translation, if required, shall render the convention application liable to be deemed withdrawn, and no right to priority shall accrue to the applicant. Provided that the Controller may, subject to payment of a surcharge as may be prescribed, allow a grace period of not more than three months for furnishing the said documents, if sufficient cause is shown. Any person providing a false certified copy or translation as herein provided shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller’s decision regarding the sufficiency of cause shall be final and not subject to appeal.

A person seeking to derive priority from an earlier application made in a convention country may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an application for a patent in India, termed a convention application, within twelve months from the date of the earlier application. Such an application shall contain a declaration stating the details of the first application, including the country of origin, the filing date, and the name and address of the inventor. The applicant shall, simultaneously with the convention application, furnish a certified copy of the first application or a duly authenticated translation thereof, as provided herein. Failure to submit such a copy within the prescribed period may render the application incomplete and subject to rejection. Any assignment of the convention application, or of the priority right derived therefrom, shall be governed by the general principles of assignment applicable to patent applications, and shall be evidenced in writing and filed with the appropriate authority. The applicant may, however, request a hearing should any dispute arise regarding the validity of the priority claim.

A person claiming a foreign priority in respect of an invention may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an application for a patent, termed a convention application, within twelve months from the date of the first application in a convention country. However, if the applicant fails to furnish, at the time of filing the convention application, a certified copy of the foreign application and a duly verified English translation thereof where the foreign application is not in English, the application shall be deemed to be a regular application made on that day, losing the benefit of the priority date. Any dispute regarding the authenticity or accuracy of the certified copy or translation, or the equivalence of the foreign application to that claimed, shall be subject to review by the Controller, who may require further evidence from the applicant or the opposing party. An appeal from any decision of the Controller on such matters shall lie to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit.

A convention application filed under this Act shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the priority claim and stating the date of the first application, along with a certified copy of the first application and, where applicable, its translation. The applicant shall, subject to the provisions herein, demonstrate a clear and unambiguous connection between the convention application and the initial filing in the country of origin. Where the subject matter of the invention relates to a distinct denomination variety of plant, the applicant must furnish evidence of the plant’s characteristics, including its genetic stability and reproducibility, as per the regulations established by the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority. Failure to provide such evidence may render the application incomplete. The Controller may, however, require additional information or documentation to satisfy themselves as to the validity of the priority claim or the distinctiveness of the variety. Any misrepresentation in the declaration shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

A convention application, if found to be lacking in priority date substantiation as provided herein, shall be deemed ineligible for expedited examination notwithstanding any representations made by the applicant. Any person submitting a convention application shall, within thirty days of filing, furnish a certified copy of the first application, translated if necessary, failing which the application shall be treated as withdrawn. Advertised acceptance relates to a patent application only after a request for advertisement has been duly filed and the prescribed fee paid; any acceptance prior to such advertisement shall be null and void. Should an applicant knowingly misrepresent the details of the first application in support of a convention claim, they shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller may, subject to justifiable cause, extend the aforementioned thirty-day period, but not beyond sixty days, and any extension shall be recorded. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the application subject to rejection under this Act.

A person filing a convention application under this Act, claiming priority from a prior application made in a convention country, shall submit a certified copy of the said prior application, duly translated if not in English, within the prescribed period. The Controller may, subject to payment of the requisite fee, extend this period by not more than three months upon demonstrating reasonable cause. Any assignment of a convention application, or of the patent resulting therefrom, shall be in writing and registered with the Patent Office as provided herein. Where a design register layout is incorporated into an invention claimed in a convention application, the applicant shall disclose the particulars of such layout in the complete specification. Failure to do so may render the patent vulnerable to revocation. A licensee of a patent originating from a convention application shall be bound by the terms of any assignment affecting the original application, unless otherwise agreed in writing. The Controller retains the authority to inspect records relating to such assignments and licenses.

A person claiming a foreign priority date in respect of a convention application shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the foreign application with a verified translation if not in an official language, as provided herein. Should the Controller raise an objection regarding the validity of the priority claim, or the authenticity of the supporting documentation, the applicant may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, request a hearing to present evidence substantiating the claim. In instances where the applicant fails to adequately address the Controller’s concerns, or where evidence of deliberate misrepresentation is established, the Controller may initiate security india action, requiring a deposit to cover potential damages. Any decision of the Controller regarding the acceptance or rejection of a convention application, or the imposition of security measures, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the time limits prescribed. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error.

A convention application shall be an application for a patent filed under this Act claiming priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, and shall comply with the requirements as to time limits and supporting documentation as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish a declaration stating the details of the prior application, including the country of origin, filing date, and application number. Where a proprietor layout design is claimed as part of the invention disclosed in a convention application, such layout design shall be clearly identified within the application documents and subject to the provisions relating to integrated circuits. Failure to adequately disclose the priority claim or relevant details of the earlier application may render the convention application ineligible for the benefits of priority.

Any act done in contravention of the provisions relating to revocation of a patent, as provided herein, shall constitute a commission offence, attracting penalties as specified in the Schedules to this Act. Where such a commission offence involves fraudulent intent, the penalty shall be enhanced by an amount not exceeding twice the value of the damages suffered by the patent holder, subject to a minimum fine of five thousand rupees. A person abetting the commission of such an offence, or attempting to commit such an offence, shall be deemed to have committed the commission offence and shall be liable to the same penalties. Provided that, if the offence is committed by a partnership firm, each partner shall be held jointly and severally liable for the penalties imposed. The burden of proving due diligence to prevent the commission offence shall lie with the accused.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a registered design as being his own, or sells, offers for sale, or distributes any article incorporating such falsely represented design, shall commit an offence under this Act. Where a design is registered in the name of a person other than the true creator, subject to the provisions herein, the true creator may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. The Controller, upon being satisfied that the registered proprietor is not the true creator, may direct that the register be amended accordingly. A commission offence shall be cognizable by any Magistrate and shall be triable by any competent court. Provided that no prosecution for a commission offence shall be instituted except with the prior written consent of the Controller, unless such offence is committed by a repeat offender as determined by the Controller. Any evidence admitted in a court relating to a design registration shall be considered prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein.

Any person who aids, abets, incites, or procures the commission of an offence under this Act shall be liable as a principal offender, notwithstanding that such person may not have directly committed the said offence. Where a commission offence shall have been committed by a partnership firm, each partner shall be jointly and severally liable for the penalty imposed, unless it is established that the offence was committed without their knowledge or consent and that they exercised all due diligence to prevent such commission. Any aggrieved person may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining any person from continuing the commission offence or from repeating it. The High Court may, after notice to the respondent, grant such injunction, if it is satisfied that the applicant has suffered or is likely to suffer irreparable harm due to the commission offence. Provided that no injunction shall be granted unless the applicant undertakes to pay such damages as the respondent may suffer due to the injunction.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, publishes or offers for sale any patented invention as if it were a genuine article, or knowingly sells or exposes for sale any article so resembling a patented invention as to be calculated to deceive purchasers, shall commit a commission offence and be punishable as provided herein. Where the patented invention is a process, the commission offence shall extend to the offering for sale, sale, or distribution of an article made by a process known to be substantially similar to the patented process. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Controller may, upon sufficient cause being shown, grant a license to a person who has committed a commission offence, provided that such person demonstrates a commitment to cease the infringing activity and compensate the patentee for any damages sustained. Any evidence of prior knowledge or deliberate concealment relating to the commission offence shall be admissible in proceedings.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a trade mark as being used on goods in which they do not have a proprietary right, shall commit an offence under this Act and be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the offence involves the sale of goods bearing such falsely represented trade mark, all such goods shall be deemed to be the proceeds of the offence and liable to confiscation by a Magistrate of first class. The commission offence shall also extend to any abetment of such falsification or sale. Provided that, if the person proves that they acted in good faith and had reasonable grounds to believe the representation was true, they may be subject to a lesser penalty as determined by the Court. Any appeal against a conviction under this provision shall lie before the High Court.

Any assignment of the right to a patent, or an interest therein, whether whole or partial, shall be made in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the assignment, including the territory and duration for which the assignment is effective. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding written assignment shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee, subject to principles of equity. Where a licensing agreement is entered into, the licensor may, as provided herein, stipulate reasonable royalties and conditions relating to quality control and usage. A commission offence shall arise where any person, not being an authorized agent, receives or offers to receive any consideration for negotiating or procuring the assignment or licensing of a patent. Any person found guilty of such a commission offence shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The patentee retains the right to revoke any assignment made without full and true disclosure of all relevant information.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, publishes or offers for sale any patented invention as if it were manufactured by him, or knowingly sells or exposes for sale any article so resembling a patented article as to be calculated to deceive purchasers, shall commit a commission offence and be punishable as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible information of such an offence, initiate an investigation and require the alleged offender to furnish evidence of lawful manufacture or import. Subject to verification, the Registrar shall forward the findings to the appropriate authority for prosecution. Provided that, if the patented invention is a process, the commission offence shall extend to the use of said process without due license or authority. Any evidence obtained during the investigation shall be admissible in court, subject to the rules of evidence. A false statement made to the Registrar in connection with any inquiry under this Act shall also constitute a commission offence.

Any person who undertakes, instigates, or assists in the commercial exploitation of a patent invention without due authorization from the patent holder, or knowingly facilitates an act that would constitute an infringement as provided herein, shall commit a commission offence and be subject to the penalties prescribed. However, a defendant alleging prior art sufficient to invalidate the patent invention may, pending determination of such invalidity by a competent authority, request a stay of proceedings relating to the alleged commission offence. Should the competent authority subsequently uphold the validity of the patent, the stay shall be lifted and the proceedings regarding the commission offence shall resume ab initio. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning the commission offence may appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods established under this Act, and such appeal shall be heard expeditiously. The burden of proving lawful authorization rests with the accused.

Opposition to a patent application shall be permissible as provided herein, and may be filed by any person alleging that the grant of a patent would be detrimental to the public interest or would infringe existing rights. Such opposition shall be filed within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the application under this Act, or, if an application for amendment is filed, within one month from the date of publication of the amendment. The applicant shall be entitled to file a response to the opposition within a further period of three months. A hearing may be conducted by the Controller, who shall consider the evidence and arguments presented by both parties, and shall issue a reasoned order either dismissing the opposition or requiring the amendment or rejection of the application. Revocation petitions, distinct from opposition, shall proceed according to separate provisions of this Act.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent, or, subject to the provisions contained in rule 85, within such extended period as may be allowed by the Controller. The opposition shall be based only on grounds specified under this Act, including lack of novelty, obviousness, or insufficient disclosure. A pre-grant opposition shall be accompanied by a statement setting out the grounds on which the opposition is based, and shall be supported by evidence where applicable. The applicant whose patent is opposed shall be entitled to file a counter-statement within one month of receiving the notice of opposition. Should the Controller deem the opposition to be frivolous, it may be dismissed with costs, and the patent may proceed to grant. A hearing may be conducted to determine the validity of the opposition, and the decision of the Controller on the opposition shall be final.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of the application for a patent. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a statement of the facts relied upon. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such notice, forward a copy thereof to the applicant, who shall be afforded an opportunity to file a counter-statement within one month. A hearing shall then be conducted by the Controller, at which both the opponent and the applicant may present evidence and arguments. 

Where an opposition is successful, the Controller may revoke the patent or amend it as justice may require. Should the opposition relate to a lack of inventive step, evidence of prior art shall be given significant weight. The applicant, subject to fulfilling all requirements under this Act, retains the right to appeal any decision of the Controller to the Appellate Board.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, at the Intellectual Property Office, within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of the application for a patent. The notice of opposition shall be in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds upon which the opposition is based. Grounds for opposition shall be limited to those specified in this Act, including but not limited to, lack of novelty, obviousness, and insufficient disclosure. Upon receipt of a notice of opposition, the Intellectual Property Office shall, within one month, notify the applicant. The applicant may, within three months of such notification, file a statement addressing the grounds of opposition. A hearing may be conducted by an officer duly appointed for the purpose, subject to the discretion of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Evidence may be submitted by both the opponent and the applicant, and cross-examination of witnesses may be permitted. The Controller shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, issue a reasoned order either upholding or dismissing the opposition.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a statement of the facts and evidence relied upon to support those grounds. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such notice, furnish a copy thereof to the applicant, who shall be afforded an opportunity to file a response within a period of three months. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed a waiver of the right to defend the application. Should the Controller, after considering the opposition and the applicant’s response, determine that a prima facie case exists, a hearing shall be conducted before an Opposition Board constituted for the purpose. The applicant shall be entitled to present evidence and arguments at such hearing, subject to the rules of natural justice. A decision of the Opposition Board shall be binding on the applicant and the objector, unless successfully appealed to the High Court.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of the application for a patent. Such opposition shall be based only on grounds specified under this Act, including lack of novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability. Failure to lodge an opposition within the prescribed time shall preclude consideration of the objection, unless the Controller is satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay. The applicant whose patent is opposed shall be entitled to file a statement and evidence in response. Should the Controller, after examining the opposition and response, determine that the grounds for opposition are well-founded, the patent application shall be refused. Any person found to be making frivolous or vexatious oppositions shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. All decisions of the Controller in matters of opposition shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any assignment of a patent application, or of a patent granted under this Act, shall be subject to a requirement of prior written consent from the Controller, unless such assignment is between persons controlled by the same ultimate beneficial owner. A prospective assignee may, prior to the completion of any such assignment, lodge a notice of opposition with the Controller, outlining reasons why the proposed assignment should not be approved, particularly if it contravenes public interest or negatively impacts the competitive landscape. Such opposition shall be adjudicated in accordance with procedures established for opposition to a granted patent, adapted as necessary. The Controller may, following examination of the opposition and representations from both the assignor and assignee, approve, reject, or modify the proposed assignment. Failure to obtain the requisite consent, or a successful opposition, shall render the assignment void ab initio, and any rights purportedly transferred thereunder shall be nullified, subject to provisions regarding bona fide dealings. Any licensing agreement affecting such assignment shall be similarly scrutinized.

Any person may file a pre-grant opposition against an application for a patent, subject to the provisions of this Act, if such person believes that the grant of the patent would be detrimental to the public interest or would unjustly impede the development of other technologies. Such opposition shall be filed in writing to the Controller, setting forth the grounds on which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The applicant shall be entitled to file a response to the opposition within a period of one month from the receipt of the opposition notice, failing which the Controller may proceed ex parte. Should the Controller deem the opposition to be frivolous or vexatious, it may be dismissed with costs. A decision of the Controller on an opposition may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit and accompanied by the necessary fee. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to any rights of appeal to the Supreme Court as provided by law.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent as provided herein, subject to the payment of a fee specified in the Schedule. Such opposition shall be based on grounds relating to inventiveness, obviousness, lack of novelty, or that the claimed pharmaceutical substance does not qualify for patentability under this Act. The applicant, upon receipt of the opposition, shall be afforded an opportunity to submit evidence in rebuttal, within a period not exceeding three months from the date of such notice. Failure to submit such rebuttal within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an abandonment of the application. Sustained opposition, if proven before the Controller, shall result in the rejection of the patent application and the forfeiture of any fees paid. Any person knowingly making false representations in an opposition proceeding shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

For the purposes of this Act, “associated trade marks” shall mean trade marks the use of which, in the opinion of the Registrar, is so closely connected as to be likely to cause confusion, or is likely to deceive or cause an unfair competition between those dealing with the goods or services of one owner and the goods or services of the other. An application for the registration of associated trade marks may be made by the proprietor of a registered trade mark, or by a person who is applying for the registration of a trade mark, and shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Where a trade mark is registered as an associated trade mark, the rights accruing under the registration shall be subject to the rights of the proprietor of the earlier trade mark.

For the purposes of registration as associated trade marks, an applicant seeking to register a mark as so associated with a registered trade mark shall submit a statement identifying the registered trade mark with which association is claimed, and demonstrating a clear and demonstrable connection between the two marks. Such connection may be established through common ownership, a licensing arrangement, or evidence of prior use indicating a deliberate intention to create an association in the minds of consumers. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require further evidence to substantiate the claimed association. Where the associated trade mark is identical to the registered trade mark, registration shall be permitted only if the goods or services covered by the associated trade mark fall within a different class as per the Nice Classification, or are otherwise sufficiently distinct to avoid consumer confusion. Failure to adequately demonstrate the requisite connection or distinctness may result in the refusal of the application for registration of associated trade marks as provided herein.

Any person who owns a registered trade mark and alleges an infringement involving associated trade marks may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from making further use of the offending mark. An application for such injunction shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the ownership of the trade mark and the likelihood of irreparable harm resulting from continued infringement. The Court, while considering such application, shall also assess whether the marks in question are indeed associated trade marks as determined under this Act, and whether the defendant’s use is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. Provided that, the plaintiff shall demonstrate a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and the likelihood of success in the ultimate adjudication of the dispute. The Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant the injunction pending the final determination of the suit, and may also direct the defendant to provide an account of profits. Any order made under this provision may be modified or vacated upon sufficient cause being shown.

For the purposes of determining similarity and likelihood of confusion under this Act, the Registrar shall, when examining applications for registration, consider whether trade marks are associated trade marks. A finding of association shall be made where one trade mark is identical with, or closely resembles, another trade mark, and both are used by the same person or by persons connected financially. However, association may also be established where one trade mark is a well-known trade mark and the other is not, subject to a demonstration of a clear link between the marks that would lead the public to believe in an association. 

Where a proprietor seeks to register associated trade marks, an application specifying the nature of the association shall be filed with the Registrar, and notice of such application shall be open to opposition as provided herein. The Registrar may, if satisfied that a genuine association exists, register the marks as associated, even if they would otherwise be considered conflicting. Failure to disclose a relevant association may be considered grounds for refusal or revocation.

Associated trade marks shall be registered in the prescribed manner, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. An application for the registration of associated trade marks may be made by the proprietor of a registered trade mark, demonstrating a clear connection between the marks and goods or services. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require evidence of bona fide use of both the principal and associated trade marks, and shall examine whether the association is likely to cause confusion among consumers. Where an application for associated trade marks is refused, the applicant may file a review petition within a period of one month from the date of the refusal order. The Registrar shall, when considering such petitions, adhere to principles of natural justice and may require additional evidence as deemed necessary. Registration of associated trade marks does not confer any right to use the marks independently of the principal trade mark.

Any person who uses, in the course of trade, any mark which is identical with, or deceptively similar to, an associated trade mark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. Where a complaint is made that a mark is being used in violation of the rights conferred by registration of an associated trade mark, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, direct that the complainant and the alleged infringer be joined as parties in the same proceeding. Any order made under this Act regarding non-use of a registered trade mark shall extend to all associated trade marks registered in the name of the same proprietor, unless otherwise specified in the order. Failure to comply with such an order shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The court may, at its discretion, also order the destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall, unless otherwise agreed, be deemed to include assignment of all associated trade marks owned by the same proprietor, provided that such associated trade marks are used in connection with goods or services identical with those for which the assigned trade mark is registered. Where an assignment is made of a trade mark which is part of a series of associated trade marks, the assignee may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar to have the assignment extended to the remaining trade marks in the series, demonstrating a clear intention to maintain the association. The proprietor of the assigned trade mark may, however, withhold consent to such extension if the continued association would be detrimental to their remaining business interests or if the assignee fails to demonstrate adequate control over the quality of goods or services bearing the associated marks. Any licensing agreement shall be construed to include all associated trade marks unless expressly excluded in the terms of the agreement.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark seeks to register a further trade mark belonging to him, or to which he is entitled, as an associated trade mark under this Act, he shall submit an application in the prescribed manner demonstrating a clear and demonstrable connection between the marks, and shall specify the nature of that connection. Any person aggrieved by the registration of such associated trade marks may, within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the registration, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, outlining the grounds upon which the registration is contested. Such opposition shall be subject to the provisions relating to opposition proceedings as provided herein, and the Registrar may, after considering the evidence and arguments presented by both parties, either allow the registration to proceed, or direct that the associated trade mark be severed from the register. An appeal from the decision of the Registrar shall lie to the High Court, subject to the conditions prescribed.

Associated trade marks shall be registered in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and an application for such registration may be made by the proprietor of one or more previously registered trade marks seeking to associate a new trade mark thereto. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, direct that the new trade mark be registered as an associated trade mark of the existing trade mark or trade marks. A patent filed designating the goods or services covered by the associated trade mark shall be submitted with the application, and the Registrar may require evidence of a genuine connection between the trade marks, demonstrating that consumers are likely to perceive a link between them. Provided that, where the associated trade marks are used on different goods or services, the Registrar shall consider the possibility of confusion or misrepresentation. Registration of associated trade marks does not confer any right to use the marks independently of each other, as provided herein.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to apply to the Trade Marks Registry for a finding as to whether trade marks are associated, and the Registry may, upon such application and after giving the proprietor of the trade marks concerned an opportunity to be heard, make an order directing that the trade marks shall be deemed to be associated. Where an order is made under this Act deeming trade marks to be associated, the Registry shall register them accordingly, and the rights and obligations of the proprietors of the associated trade marks shall be determined as if they were registered under a single ownership. Any person who, with intent to deceive, uses an associated trade mark in relation to goods or services in which the proprietor of the registered trade mark does not have a legitimate interest, shall commit an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine, and such commission offence shall be cognizable by any Magistrate. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, revoke an association order if it is proved that the association is detrimental to the public interest or the interests of the proprietors.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, pertaining to the refusal of registration or the rectification of a register, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under the relevant rules. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding condonation of delay as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, while considering such appeals, require the appellant to furnish evidence or undertake such investigations as it deems necessary. Where the Appellate Board confirms the order of the registrar, the aggrieved party may, provided that substantial questions of law are involved, seek recourse to the High Court. The registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs, and any person may inspect the register upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure by the registrar to properly maintain the register or to provide access as provided herein shall constitute grounds for disciplinary action.

The registrar shall maintain a register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs, and such register shall be open for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application to the registrar in the manner as may be prescribed, clearly stating the layout-design details for which inspection is sought. The registrar may, if satisfied that the applicant has a legitimate interest, permit inspection of the register or extracts therefrom. Where an application for inspection is refused, the registrar shall record the reasons for such refusal. 

A request for certification of a copy of any entry in the register, or any part thereof, may be made to the registrar, and the certified copy shall be accepted as prima facie evidence in any legal proceeding. The registrar shall, upon receipt of the prescribed fee, furnish a certified copy to the applicant within thirty days. Any error in the register, discovered by the registrar, shall be rectified promptly and a notice of such rectification published in the official gazette. The registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design is empowered to impose penalties for non-compliance with these provisions, as provided herein.

Any person desiring to obtain registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, including its topological arrangement and all layers constituting the integrated circuit. Subject to verification of the application and confirmation that the layout-design is novel and inventively conceived, the registrar may register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, if the registrar has reasonable grounds to believe the layout-design is not novel, or is substantially similar to an existing layout-design, registration shall be refused. All registered layout-designs shall be maintained in a public register accessible for inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration to a registered layout-design shall be notified to the registrar and may be subject to further scrutiny. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registration as provided herein.

Any person who falsifies or knowingly makes any false entry in any register maintained by the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. The registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require any person claiming to be the proprietor of a layout-design to furnish a declaration verifying the facts stated in the application for registration. Any application for registration found to contain a deliberate misrepresentation, or any material omission, shall be deemed invalid as provided herein. Furthermore, any person who, with intent to deceive, applies for registration of a layout-design knowing it to be not original shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. All fees and penalties collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. The registrar shall maintain a public record of all penalties imposed.

Any person being the proprietor of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to others for the use of such layout-design, either generally or subject to conditions, and such licenses may include the right to assign them to third parties. The registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall maintain a record of all registered assignments and licenses, and any transfer of ownership without proper registration shall be considered null and void. An assignment may be absolute, transferring all rights, or partial, retaining certain rights with the assignor, provided that such partial assignment does not unduly restrict the licensee’s reasonable use of the layout-design. Where a license is granted for a definite period, the registrar may, upon application by either party and subject to just terms, determine the reasonableness of any renewal terms proposed. Any dispute concerning the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, including the refusal of an application for registration or the rectification of a register, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the decision appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding condonation of delay as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, if it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it thinks appropriate, to cover the costs of the proceedings. The registrar shall furnish to the Appellate Board all documents and information relating to the case, and shall appear before the Board when required. Provided that, no appeal shall lie against an interlocutory order made by the registrar. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits, including the refusal of an application for registration or the revocation of a registered layout-design, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the decision sought to be appealed, subject to the provisions relating to condonation of delay as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, while considering such appeal, require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the fee originally payable for the registration of the layout-design. Any request for issuance of certified copies of documents relating to a layout-design, or for any form issuing under this Act, shall be addressed to the registrar in writing and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The registrar shall, within thirty days of receipt of such request and fee, furnish the certified copy or form to the applicant. Failure to do so shall be deemed a sufficient cause for appeal.

Every application patent india shall be examined by the Controller of Patents in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The Controller may, before examination, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information or documents as may be necessary to determine its patentability. Where an application relates to a new and useful invention not previously known to the public, and satisfies the criteria of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability as provided herein, the Controller shall proceed to grant a patent. However, an application may be refused if the invention is obvious, or if it falls within the scope of exclusions specified under this Act, including but not limited to inventions relating to atomic energy. Subject to payment of the prescribed fees and compliance with all procedural requirements, the Controller shall publish the application and grant a patent if no objection is sustained. Any person may file a representation against the grant of a patent, which shall be considered by the Controller as per established procedure.

Every application patent india shall be examined by the Controller of Patents in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. An applicant seeking a patent shall, subject to the provisions herein, furnish a declaration of inventive step, demonstrating how the invention differs from existing knowledge and is not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field. Where an application does not meet the requirements of novelty or inventive step, the Controller may issue an objection report detailing the grounds for refusal. The applicant may, within a period of one month from the receipt of such report, file a response addressing the objections raised, supported by relevant evidence and arguments. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed a withdrawal of the application. Provided that, the Controller may, at his discretion, extend the period for response, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Any amendment to the complete specification shall not extend the scope of the invention as originally disclosed.

Any person who publishes information relating to a patent application in India, concerning an invention which is the subject matter of such application, prior to the grant of the patent, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. However, such publication shall not be deemed a contravention of this provision if it is made with the express written consent of the applicant for the application patent india, or if it is necessary for a legitimate purpose and does not unduly prejudice the applicant. Where a person, subject to a duty of confidentiality arising from their involvement in the examination of an application, discloses any details of the invention without authorization, they shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with a fine, or with both. Any false representation made in connection with an application shall render the applicant ineligible for the grant of a patent, and may attract further penalties as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing an application patent india, or requiring the amendment of an application, or dismissing an appeal, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for a further period not exceeding thirty days if sufficient cause is shown. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of a petition for appeal, may require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the fee prescribed for the original application. 

Provided that, if the Appellate Board is of the opinion that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, it may dismiss the appeal with costs, and any sum deposited by the appellant shall be forfeited. Furthermore, a decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning errors of law apparent on the face of the record.

A services trade mark shall be registrable under this Act, notwithstanding that it is not used in relation to goods, where the applicant intends to use it, or authorize its use, in connection with the provision of services. For the purposes of this Act, ‘services’ include, but are not limited to, financial, banking, insurance, transport, educational, construction, and medical services. An application for the registration of a services trade mark shall be subject to the same conditions and requirements as an application for a trade mark for goods, provided that the specification of services must be clearly and accurately defined. The Registrar may, however, require further clarification if the specified services are vague or overly broad. Registration of a services trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the specified services.

A services trade mark, distinct from a goods mark, shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the services of one person from those of another. An application for registration of a services trade mark shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall include a clear indication of the services sought to be covered by the mark. The Trade Marks Registry may, prior to accepting an application, require the applicant to amend the specification of services to ensure clarity and avoid ambiguity. Where a mark is identical with or deceptively similar to an existing registered services trade mark, registration shall be refused, subject to the provisions relating to assignment, transmission, or licensing. However, concurrent use of similar marks for non-competing services may, at the discretion of the Registry, be permitted, provided that such use does not cause confusion amongst consumers. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registry may appeal to the High Court.

A services trade mark shall be registrable under this Act, notwithstanding that it does not fall within the definition of goods as conventionally understood, provided that the services are identifiable and capable of being distinguished. The registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to define the scope of the services sought to be registered with greater particularity. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration of a services trade mark may, within a period of two months from the date of such refusal, file an appeal with the appellate board. Where a registered services trade mark is not used for a continuous period of five years, it shall be liable to be removed from the register, unless the proprietor can demonstrate special circumstances justifying non-use. A proprietor of a services trade mark shall have the right to assign or transmit it, subject to any conditions imposed by the registrar and the rights of any existing licensees. Any assignment or transmission not duly recorded shall be void as against any subsequent assignee or licensee.

A services trade mark, distinct from marks used for goods, shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions herein concerning distinctiveness and descriptiveness. An applicant seeking registration of a services trade mark shall clearly designate the class of service according to the prescribed classification, and the application shall specify the geographical area in which the services are, or are proposed to be, rendered. The Registrar may, prior to accepting an application, require clarification regarding the nature of the services claimed, or evidence of genuine use of the mark in relation to those services. Where a mark is identical with or deceptively similar to an existing registered services trade mark, and the services offered are identical or closely related, registration shall be refused, unless the proprietor of the earlier mark has consented in writing. However, a mark shall not be deemed deceptively similar merely due to the inclusion of descriptive matter necessary to indicate the nature, quality, or kind of service. Any appeal against the Registrar’s decision concerning the registration of a services trade mark shall lie to the Appellate Board, as constituted under the relevant rules.

A services trade mark, distinct from marks applied to goods, shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the services of one person from those of others. An application for registration of a services trade mark shall be subject to a search for identical or deceptively similar existing marks, encompassing both goods and services classifications, to ascertain potential conflicts. Where a mark is proposed for services falling within the Nice Classification, compliance with the latest edition of said Classification, as adopted by the Registrar, is mandatory.
