Provided that, a mark descriptive of the services, or commonly used in the trade, may be registered if it has acquired distinctiveness through continuous use and substantial public recognition. The Registrar may, however, require evidence of such acquired distinctiveness, including proof of advertising expenditure and duration of use, to satisfy the requirements as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the application liable to refusal.

Any person claiming ownership of a services trade mark shall, prior to commencing provision of said services, apply for registration as provided herein, and failure to do so may attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a registered services trade mark is used by another person without the consent of the proprietor, a suit for infringement may be instituted in a District Court having jurisdiction. The Court, upon establishing infringement, shall grant an injunction restraining such use and may also award damages, assessed on the basis of lost profits or a reasonable royalty, to the aggrieved party. Any false application for a services trade mark, or any fraudulent misrepresentation in relation thereto, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, a registered proprietor failing to renew their services trade mark within the prescribed period shall be liable to a late fee, and the mark may be removed from the register if the delay exceeds six months.

Any assignment of a registered services trade mark shall be subject to an instrument in writing and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective. The assignee shall, upon registration of the assignment, become the proprietor of the trade mark for the services specified in the registration, and shall possess all the rights and remedies available to a proprietor under this Act. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be granted in respect of a services trade mark, and any such license shall be in writing and may be registered at the discretion of the Registry. Where an exclusive license is registered, the licensee shall, subject to the terms of the license, have the right to maintain an action for infringement as if they were the proprietor. Assignment or licensing of a services trade mark shall not be permitted if it is likely to be deceptive or cause confusion amongst the public, or if it contravenes any order made under this Act relating to the use of the mark. Any assignment not in compliance with these provisions shall be void.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a services trade mark and alleging infringement by another, shall initiate proceedings before the High Court having jurisdiction, subject to the provisions contained herein. An application for rectification of the register relating to a services trade mark, on grounds of non-use, may be filed after a continuous period of five years from the date of registration, unless the applicant demonstrates sufficient cause for the apparent lapse. However, a registered proprietor may, prior to any such rectification proceedings, file an affidavit demonstrating bona fide intent to continue offering the services associated with the trade mark. Where a dispute arises concerning the classification of services under the Nice Classification, the Court shall determine the appropriate class, considering the actual nature of the services rendered. Any appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

A services trade mark, distinct from marks applied to goods, shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the services of one person from those of another. An application for such a mark shall adhere to the prescribed form and be accompanied by a clear and concise description of the services sought to be identified. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require further clarification regarding the nature of the services. Where an applicant also possesses a design registered under the Designs Act, 2000, and intends to utilize said design as an integral component of the services offered under the trade mark, full particulars of the registered design, including its registration number, shall be furnished with the application. Provided that the use of the registered design does not create a likelihood of confusion with existing trade marks. The Registrar shall examine the application and, if satisfied that it meets the requirements as provided herein, shall proceed to advertise it in the Trade Marks Journal. Any objection to the registration of the services trade mark shall be filed within the prescribed period.

Any person who falsely applies a services trade mark to pharmaceutical products with intent to deceive, or causes any business to be carried on under a false trade mark so applied, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable for the punishment as provided herein, unless they can prove that the offence occurred without their knowledge and that they exercised due diligence to prevent such commission. Any pharmaceutical product bearing a counterfeit services trade mark shall be deemed forfeited to the Central Government and may be disposed of in any manner as the Government deems fit. A court may, in addition to any other punishment, order the destruction of such goods.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, or a person with a substantial likelihood of succeeding in a suit for rectification of the register, may, under this Act, apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from infringing the trade mark, or from passing off goods or services as those of the plaintiff. The Court, when granting an injunction subject to such terms as it deems fit, may require an undertaking as to damages, or order an account of profits, and may direct the disposal of goods and materials infringing the trade mark. Provided that no injunction shall be granted which would unduly restrain trade or be contrary to the public interest. Furthermore, the Court may, at its discretion, grant a temporary injunction pending the final determination of the suit, subject to the defendant providing security for damages that may be suffered by them. Any order for the delivery-up of infringing materials shall be executed promptly.

Any person aggrieved by a non-registered trade mark deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, or by a false application for registration, may seek an injunction subject to the provisions of this Act restraining the defendant from acting in violation of the rights of the proprietor of the registered trade mark. Provided that no injunction shall be granted unless the plaintiff demonstrates a prima facie case, irreparable harm, and the balance of convenience lies in their favour. Where an injunction is granted, the court may also order the defendant to account for profits made through the unlawful use of the mark, and may direct the destruction of all goods bearing such mark. Any person disobeying an injunction issued under this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The court may, at its discretion, require the applicant to furnish security for the due observance of the terms of the injunction.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a register of layout-designs, and such register shall be open for inspection subject to payment of such fees as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application to the registrar semiconductor in the manner as provided herein, specifying the layout-design or class of layout-designs to be inspected. The registrar semiconductor may, if satisfied that the applicant has a legitimate interest, permit inspection of the register, or any part thereof, upon such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit. A certified copy of any entry in the register shall be furnished by the registrar semiconductor upon request, and the fee for such copy shall be as prescribed. The registrar semiconductor shall be the final authority for determining the validity of any application for registration.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a register of layout-designs in such form and manner as may be prescribed, and such register shall be open for inspection by the public subject to payment of such fee as may be determined by regulations. Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the registrar semiconductor, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a detailed representation of the layout-design. The registrar semiconductor may, prior to registration, require the applicant to amend the representation to ensure clarity and compliance with the requirements as provided herein. Where the registrar semiconductor is satisfied that the layout-design is novel and intrinsically capable of being distinguished from any other layout-design, and that the application meets all procedural requirements, registration shall be granted. The registrar semiconductor shall issue a certificate of registration to the applicant, noting the date of filing and the registration number assigned to the layout-design. Any objection to the registration may be filed with the registrar semiconductor within a period of three months from the date of publication of the application.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the registrar semiconductor, pertaining to the refusal of registration or the rectification of a register of layout-designs, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under the relevant legislation, subject to the provisions contained therein. The Appellate Board shall have the power to confirm, vary, or set aside the order of the registrar semiconductor, and may direct fresh consideration of the application or matter in question. A person claiming ownership of a layout-design, and alleging infringement, shall be entitled to seek an injunction from a competent court restraining the defendant from the acts of infringement, as provided herein. Such injunction may be interim or permanent, and the court may also award damages to the plaintiff for the loss suffered due to the infringement. The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs, accessible for inspection by interested parties upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any false entry in the register made by the registrar semiconductor shall be rectified forthwith upon due notice and evidence.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a comprehensive register of layout-designs, ensuring accurate recording of all applications and subsequent registrations as provided herein. Any person desiring to register a layout-design shall submit an application to the registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee and necessary documentation demonstrating originality. The registrar may, subject to verification of the application and confirmation of compliance with the provisions of this Act, proceed with the registration process. 

Upon successful registration, the registrar semiconductor shall issue a certificate of registration to the applicant, establishing their proprietary rights over the layout-design. Any objection to the registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the registrar within the stipulated timeframe, and a hearing may be conducted to resolve the dispute. The registrar’s decision on such objections shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the appropriate appellate authority. All records pertaining to registered layout-designs, including amendments and transfers of ownership, shall be diligently maintained by the registrar for public inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a comprehensive register of layout-designs, ensuring accurate recording of all applications and subsequent registrations as provided herein. Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee and necessary technical documentation, including a detailed layout drawing and supporting data. The registrar may, subject to verification of the application’s completeness and compliance with the provisions of this Act, accept the application for examination. Upon successful examination and confirmation of novelty and originality, the registrar semiconductor shall register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration to the applicant. A layout-design may be subject to amendment, provided that such amendment does not materially alter the original layout and is duly approved by the registrar. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures for registration or maintenance may result in the removal of the layout-design from the register.

Any person who knowingly makes a false entry in the register maintained by the registrar semiconductor, or knowingly assists in making such a false entry, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. The registrar semiconductor, if satisfied that any entry in the register is false or misleading, may, after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard, cause such entry to be rectified or amended. Any application for rectification or amendment made to the registrar semiconductor shall be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed. Provided that, no rectification or amendment shall be made which would prejudice the rights of any person other than the applicant. Failure of the registrar semiconductor to act within ninety days of a valid application for rectification, subject to justifiable cause, shall constitute grounds for appeal to the High Court. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar semiconductor may, within sixty days, file an appeal.

Any assignment of a registered semiconductor layout-design shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a register of all assignments recorded under this Act, and any assignment not so recorded shall be void against subsequent assignees or purchasers for value without notice of the prior assignment. A licensee of a registered layout-design may, subject to the terms of the license, further assign or license its interest in the layout-design, provided that such sub-assignment or license does not contravene any restriction stipulated in the original license agreement. Where a layout-design is jointly held, no assignment may be effected without the consent of all registered proprietors, and the registrar semiconductor shall not register an assignment lacking such unanimous consent. The registered proprietor may, as provided herein, grant compulsory licenses in certain circumstances, and any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or the scope of a license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar semiconductor, including the refusal of an application for registration or the rectification of a register, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding condonation of delay as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, prior to the disposal of any appeal, require the appellant to deposit such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the fee originally payable for the registration of the layout-design in question, to secure payment of costs that may be awarded in favour of the respondent. Provided that, if the Appellate Board is satisfied that the appellant is reasonably justified in preferring the appeal, it may dispense with the requirement of pre-deposit. All decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available by way of writ petition to the High Court on grounds of error of law apparent on the face of the record.

The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a comprehensive register of all layout-designs, and any person aggrieved by an act of the registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, appeal to the Chairperson, who shall constitute a single-person bench for expeditious resolution of such disputes. Failure to accurately record a layout-design in the register, or any wilful omission thereof, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any false representation made to the registrar semiconductor, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The registrar may, with prior approval of the Central Government, prescribe fees for all applications, registrations, and inspections conducted as provided herein. Any officer of the registrar found to be in collusion with an infringer shall be summarily dismissed from service and subject to prosecution under relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code.

Any assignment of a registered semiconductor layout-design shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. The registrar semiconductor shall maintain a record of all registered assignments, and any change in ownership of a layout-design must be duly notified to the registrar for appropriate amendment of the register. A license to work a registered layout-design may be granted by the registered proprietor, and such license shall specify the scope, duration, and territorial limits of the permitted use. Should any person, knowing that a layout-design is registered, continue to exploit it without a valid license or assignment, they shall prevent commission offence and be liable to such penalties as are provided herein. The registrar may, upon application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, record any registered license in the register, providing public notice of the terms and conditions thereof. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate it, but such unregistered transfer may not be enforceable against a bona fide purchaser without notice.

Revocation of copyright shall be permissible under this Act where the copyright owner has demonstrably failed to exercise rights conferred by copyright, and such failure continues for a period of three years from the date of the original grant or subsequent transfer of ownership. Provided that, such failure is not attributable to any legally recognized impediment, including but not limited to force majeure or governmental restriction. Further, revocation proceedings may be initiated by any person aggrieved by the non-exercise of copyright, subject to the presentation of sufficient evidence establishing both the failure and the resultant prejudice. A finding of abandonment, constituting a form of revocation, requires clear and convincing proof of intent to relinquish rights. Any order of revocation shall be subject to appeal.

Any person claiming to be the owner of copyright in a work, and having duly registered such copyright under this Act, may apply to the Registrar of Copyrights for revocation of a registration granted to another, provided that such application is accompanied by evidence establishing a prior valid claim to the copyright in question. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such application and after affording reasonable opportunity for hearing to the registered owner, conduct an inquiry to ascertain the validity of the competing claims. Revocation of registration shall be ordered if the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the initial registration was obtained through misrepresentation or that the applicant is the rightful owner. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may also revoke a registration where the registered owner has failed to comply with statutory obligations relating to the remuneration payable to the author, and such failure continues for a period exceeding one year from the date of the last payment due.

Any person aggrieved by a continuing infringement of copyright, or by a threatened infringement thereof, may apply to the District Court having jurisdiction over the alleged infringer for a decree of injunction, and may also seek damages sustained by such infringement. However, where the copyright owner has, through demonstrable and willful neglect, failed to diligently pursue remedies available under this Act against widespread and ongoing infringement, the Court may, subject to sufficient evidence presented by the alleged infringer or any other interested party, order a temporary suspension of injunctive relief. Further, the Court shall have the power to revoke a copyright license granted to a licensee who has materially breached the terms and conditions of said license, provided that such breach substantially diminishes the value of the copyright. Such revocation shall be without prejudice to any accrued rights or liabilities of either party. The Court may also award costs in any proceeding relating to such revocation.

Any person aggrieved by a determination made under this Act relating to the ownership of copyright, or alleging infringement of their rights therein, may apply to the High Court for the revocation of any license granted in contravention of the provisions concerning compulsory licenses, or where the licensee has demonstrably failed to exploit the copyrighted work to a reasonable extent, subject to the payment of adequate compensation to the copyright holder. Provided that such application shall be made within a period of two years from the date of grant of the license, or from the date on which the aggrieved party became aware of the non-exploitation. The High Court, upon being satisfied that sufficient cause exists and after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, may, by order, direct the revocation of the license. Such revocation shall not prejudice any accrued rights or liabilities existing prior to the date of the order, and any subsequent licensing shall be conducted in accordance with the principles as provided herein.

Any copyright holder aggrieved by a substantial and persistent failure by a licensee to adhere to the material terms and conditions stipulated within a valid licensing agreement, may petition for revocation of said license, subject to the provisions herein. Such petition shall demonstrate a clear pattern of non-compliance, including but not limited to, consistent under-reporting of royalties, unauthorized sub-licensing, or deviation from agreed-upon usage limitations. Provided that, prior to initiating proceedings for revocation, the copyright holder shall furnish the licensee with a written notice detailing the breaches and affording a reasonable opportunity to remedy them. A failure to remedy within ninety days of such notice shall be considered sufficient grounds for pursuing revocation. The High Court, upon verifying the veracity of the claims and considering representations from both parties, may order the immediate revocation of the license, restoring full rights to the copyright holder. Any subsequent licensing arrangement shall not prejudice the rights accrued prior to the revocation.

Any person aggrieved by a demonstrable and persistent failure by a licensee to adhere to the terms and conditions stipulated within a valid licensing agreement, and where such failure materially prejudices the copyright owner’s legitimate economic interests, may petition the High Court for the revocation of said license. Provided that, prior to such petition, the copyright owner shall have issued a written notice of default to the licensee, affording a period of sixty days for rectification of the non-compliance. The Court, upon establishing a prima facie case of sustained breach, shall issue notice to the licensee and may, subject to the licensee’s satisfactory explanation or remediation, order immediate suspension of licensing rights. Should the Court determine that the breach is irreparable or indicative of willful disregard, it may proceed with the complete revocation of the license, and impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees on the licensee. Any amounts so collected shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any person to whom copyright has been assigned, whether wholly or partially, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, further assign such rights to any other person. However, an assignment of copyright in a work shall be revocable at the option of the assignor, provided that reasonable notice of such revocation is given to the assignee and that the assignee has materially failed to exploit the rights assigned. Material failure shall include, but not be limited to, a consistent inability to commercially benefit from the work within a period of two years from the date of assignment, absent demonstrable efforts to secure such benefit. Notwithstanding this, an assignee may petition for continued assignment if they can prove substantial investment in the work, even without immediate commercial returns, and demonstrate a clear plan for future exploitation. The assignor’s right of revocation shall not prejudice any existing licenses granted by the assignee prior to the notice of revocation, unless otherwise agreed.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the licensing authority pertaining to a compulsory license, may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Provided that the High Court, upon consideration of the appeal and subject to such terms and conditions as it may deem fit, may confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the licensing authority. Further, where a copyright owner demonstrates sustained and willful non-compliance with the terms of a compulsory license granted under this Act, a petition for revocation of said license may be filed with the High Court. The Court shall, following notice to the licensee and an opportunity to be heard, determine if sufficient cause exists for revocation. Any decision regarding revocation shall be final and binding, though subject to appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law. The High Court may also award costs in any such proceeding.

Any assignment of copyright, whether whole or partial, and whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be subject to a review mechanism as provided herein, particularly where the assignee demonstrably fails to commercially exploit the assigned rights within a period of three years from the date of assignment. The copyright owner, or their duly authorized agent, may petition for revocation of the assignment before the designated authority, demonstrating such failure. Provided that, such failure to exploit is not attributable to geographical restrictions reasonably imposed by the assignor relating to specific territories, or to force majeure events. The petition shall include evidence of reasonable attempts made by the assignee to license the copyright to third parties within the relevant attributable geographical area. The authority, upon satisfaction of these conditions and after affording the assignee a reasonable opportunity to be heard, may order the revocation of the assignment and restoration of the copyright to the original owner. Any such revocation shall not prejudice accrued rights.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights refusing an application for the revocation of a copyright license, may prefer an appeal to the Chairperson within sixty days from the date of the said order. The Chairperson, upon receipt of such appeal and after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the copyright holder, shall pass an order either confirming, modifying, or reversing the order of the Registrar. Provided that the Chairperson may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs. Further, any decision of the Chairperson regarding the revocation of a license shall be subject to judicial review before the High Court, provided an application is filed within ninety days of the Chairperson’s order. The copyright holder shall be entitled to present evidence rebutting the grounds for revocation as originally submitted.

An international application, as provided herein, shall be an application made under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, seeking to avail the benefits of Chapter II of this Act, and shall be treated as a complete specification for the purposes of determining priority, subject to the provisions contained in Rule 21. Where an international application designates India as an elected State or equivalent for the purposes of granting a patent, the applicant shall, within the prescribed period, file a demand for national phase in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a translation of the international application if it is not filed in an accepted language. Failure to so file shall result in the application being deemed withdrawn, unless justifiable cause is shown to the Controller. The Controller may, notwithstanding anything contained herein, require additional documentation if deemed necessary for proper examination.

An international application for a patent, as provided herein, shall be processed in accordance with the Patent Cooperation Treaty, to which India is a contracting state, and the regulations thereunder. Such an application shall be deemed to be a complete application only upon filing a priority claim, where applicable, and satisfying all requirements relating to translation if the application is not filed in an official language acceptable to the International Bureau. The applicant may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, request a preliminary examination of the international application to assess its potential patentability. Where the international application proceeds to the national phase before the designated or elected national office, including the Indian Patent Office, it shall be treated as a regular patent application under this Act. Any delay in furnishing the translation or priority claim may render the international application incomplete and liable to be refused, unless condoned by the Controller.

Any person desiring to seek a patent in India, having already filed an international application designating India, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a complete specification in the prescribed form with the Controller within thirty-six months from the date of the international application. The applicant may, however, request an extension of time, provided that such request is made before the expiry of the said thirty-six months and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to file the complete specification within the stipulated period, or extended period as the case may be, shall result in the abandonment of the international application as it pertains to India. 

Where a demand for evidence of inventorship is made by any person, the applicant shall furnish such evidence as the Controller may require, subject to a reasonable time frame being provided. Any dispute regarding the right to the patent, arising from the international application, shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

An international application for a patent, as provided herein, shall be processed in accordance with the provisions of the Patent Cooperation Treaty, to which India is a contracting state. The Controller of Patents shall, subject to the rules, designate a receiving office for the purpose of receiving such applications and shall maintain a register of international applications received. Where an international application designates India as an appointed designated or elected State, the applicant shall, within a period of thirty months from the priority date, file a demand for national phase before the Controller. Failure to so file shall result in the application being deemed withdrawn in respect of India. The Controller may, if satisfied that the requirements of this Act have been met, grant a patent based on the international application. Any amendment to the international application during the national phase shall be subject to the provisions relating to amendments of complete specifications under this Act, and shall not extend beyond the disclosure in the international application as filed. The Controller shall, upon request, transmit certified copies of relevant documents relating to the international application to the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization.

An international application for a patent, when filed with the designated International Receiving Office in accordance with the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be considered provisional for the purpose of establishing a priority date, provided that a complete specification, satisfying the requirements as provided herein, is filed with the Indian Patent Office within the prescribed period. The applicant shall furnish a declaration of priority, if claiming priority from a previous application, and such declaration must comply with the relevant regulations. Failure to submit the complete specification and any required translation within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the international application being deemed withdrawn. Any amendment to the specification following filing, but before acceptance, may be permitted subject to compliance with the provisions regarding novelty and inventive step. The Controller of Patents shall examine such applications according to the established procedures for national phase applications.

Any person desiring to seek a patent based on an international application shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a complete specification as prescribed, together with a statement of priority, if any, and the international application number with the Controller within thirty-six months from the date of the international application. Failure to furnish the statement of priority, where applicable, shall render the application incomplete and liable to be rejected. Any misrepresentation regarding the priority date in an international application, if discovered, may attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller may, however, allow a grace period of three months for rectifying any deficiency in the application, provided that a surcharge, not exceeding ten thousand rupees, is paid. All applications originating from an international application shall be subject to examination as provided herein, and any false claim made therein will be treated as an offence punishable with imprisonment.

Any person filing an international application under this Act, seeking protection for an invention in designated State parties to the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall furnish a declaration of inventorship as prescribed. Such declaration shall clearly identify all inventors and their respective contributions to the invention disclosed in the application. Where the applicant is not the inventor, a clear and complete assignment of the right, title, and interest in the invention, duly executed by the inventor or their legal representative, shall accompany the international application. Failure to provide a satisfactory declaration or assignment, where applicable, may render the application incomplete and subject to rejection. The Controller of Patents may, however, grant an opportunity to rectify any deficiency within a specified period. Any transfer of ownership of the international application during its pendency shall be recorded with the Controller, subject to verification of the transferor’s title and compliance with the prescribed fees. A licensee of the patent resulting from such an international application shall have no right to further assign their interest without the patentee’s consent.

An international application for a patent, filed at the designated International Bureau under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be treated as a complete application only upon submission of a duly certified translation into the English language, if the application was not originally filed in English, as provided herein. Should the applicant fail to furnish such translation within the prescribed period of sixteen months from the priority date, the application shall be deemed abandoned, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any dispute regarding the adequacy of the translation, or the claim of hardship preventing timely submission, may be raised before the Controller, whose decision shall be final unless overturned on appeal. The Appellate Board, in considering such appeals, shall have the power to extend the prescribed period, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated and no undue prejudice arises to other applicants or the public interest. A request for extension shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee.

Any person filing an international application under this Act shall furnish a declaration of inventorship, stating the full names and addresses of all inventors and their respective contributions to the invention, subject to the provisions contained herein. The registrar shall maintain a register of such declarations, and the title to any patent arising from such an international application shall be determined based on the information recorded therein, unless evidence to the contrary is presented and duly verified. A failure to accurately declare inventorship may render the patent vulnerable to revocation, and any aggrieved person may petition for rectification of the registrar register title. Provided that, the applicant may, within one year from the date of grant, submit an amended declaration, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and satisfaction of the Controller of Patents. Any dispute regarding inventorship shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction. The applicant shall be solely responsible for all costs associated with the international application process.

An international application for a patent, as provided herein, shall be processed in accordance with the procedure outlined in the Patent Cooperation Treaty, to which India is a contracting state. The Controller of Patents shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, examine such an application as if it were an application filed directly with this office, and shall determine its completeness. Where the international application does not meet the requirements of the Treaty or the regulations thereunder, the Controller may require the applicant to rectify the deficiencies within a period to be specified. Any indication of priority claimed in the international application shall be verified against the records of the originating office. Should the international application proceed to the national phase before this office, the applicant shall furnish a translation of the application, if not originally filed in an accepted language. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. The Controller may, at any stage, require evidence of the applicant’s right to make the application.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by a proposed registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to oppose the registration. Such opposition shall be initiated by filing a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, wherein the grounds upon which the opposition is based must be clearly stated. The notice opposition applicant shall simultaneously furnish with the notice, a statement of the case upon which the opposition is founded, and shall pay the prescribed fee. The Registry, upon receiving a valid notice, shall serve a copy upon the applicant for registration, allowing them a period of two months to deliver a counter-statement, failing which the opposition may proceed ex parte. Where a counter-statement is filed, the Registry may direct a hearing to determine the matter.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by reason of the potential registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions herein, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. Such notice shall be in writing and accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based, detailing the reasons why the mark should not be registered. The applicant filing the notice of opposition shall simultaneously deposit the prescribed fee with the Registry, failing which the notice shall be deemed invalid. Upon receipt of a valid notice of opposition, the Registry shall, without undue delay, serve a copy thereof upon the applicant for registration, affording them an opportunity to respond. A counter-statement, if any, shall be filed by the applicant within the time frame stipulated under this Act, and the Registry shall proceed with the adjudication of the matter, considering all evidence presented by both the notice opposition applicant and the original applicant.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by reason of the proposed registration of a trade mark shall have the right to file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, prior use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, lack of distinctiveness, or potential to deceive the public. The notice opposition applicant shall simultaneously deposit with the Registry a statement of the grounds and particulars of the opposition, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registry, upon receiving a valid notice, shall serve a copy upon the applicant for registration, affording them a period of two months to file a counter-statement. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe may result in the Registry proceeding ex parte, and the rights of the applicant may be adversely affected as provided herein. All evidence in support of the opposition or counter-statement shall be submitted in accordance with the rules prescribed by the Central Government.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. The notice opposition applicant shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, referencing relevant provisions of this Act or established principles of trade mark law. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, failing which it shall be deemed invalid and returned to the applicant. Upon receipt of a valid notice of opposition, the Registry shall, without undue delay, serve a copy thereof upon the applicant for the trade mark in question. The applicant shall then have a period of two months to file a counter-statement, addressing the grounds of opposition and providing evidence in support of their application. Should the applicant fail to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe, the Registry may proceed to decide the matter ex parte, based on the evidence presented by the notice opposition applicant. All pleadings and evidence submitted shall be subject to verification as provided herein.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The notice opposition applicant shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, referencing relevant provisions of this Act or established principles of trade mark law. Failure to adequately articulate such grounds may render the opposition untenable. A copy of the notice shall be served upon the applicant for registration, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe. Should the applicant fail to file a counter-statement, the Registrar may proceed ex parte, considering only the grounds raised in the notice of opposition. All submissions shall be accompanied by supporting evidence as required, and the applicant may request inspection of the evidence filed by the opposing party, subject to payment of a prescribed fee.

Any person intending to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and a prescribed fee. Failure to submit the prescribed fee within the stipulated timeframe shall render the notice of opposition invalid and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. The Registrar, upon receiving a valid notice opposition applicant, shall forthwith serve a copy thereof upon the applicant for the trade mark in question, requiring them to deliver a counter-statement within a period not less than one month. Should the applicant for the trade mark fail to file a counter-statement as provided herein, the Registrar may, after considering the notice of opposition and any evidence submitted, proceed to decide the matter ex parte, and such decision shall be final and binding. Any false or frivolous notice of opposition shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year or with fine, or with both.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding notice to the Trade Marks Registry and potential opposition. A proposed assignee, or applicant intending to assign, shall furnish the Registry with a clear statement of the intended transfer, including full particulars of the assignor and assignee, and the marks subject to assignment. Should a third party, possessing legitimate grounds for objection to the assignment—such as a prior right to the mark or a likelihood of confusion—desire to contest the transfer, they may file a notice of opposition with the Registry. The notice opposition applicant shall specify the basis of their objection and supporting evidence. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such notice, serve a copy upon both the assignor and the proposed assignee, allowing them a period of two months to submit a counter-statement. Failure to do so may result in the assignment being deemed void, as provided herein. All assignments are further subject to verification of title.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by a trademark application, and intending to oppose its registration, shall file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and a prescribed fee. The applicant, upon receipt of such notice, may, within a period of two months, file a counter-statement addressing the grounds raised by the notice opposition applicant. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe may result in the Registry proceeding ex parte. Should the Registrar deem the grounds for opposition to be prima facie valid, a hearing shall be scheduled, affording both parties an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. Evidence filed by either party shall be subject to cross-examination, and the Registrar, after considering all submissions, may either allow or dismiss the opposition, or direct amendment of the application, as provided herein. Any party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the High Court.

Any person desiring to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall, within the prescribed time and in the manner as provided herein, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, clearly stating the grounds on which the opposition is based and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registry, upon receiving such notice opposition applicant, shall promptly serve a copy thereof upon the applicant for the trade mark in question, affording them an opportunity to respond. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the concerns raised in the notice, or if the Registry deems the opposition well-founded, it may issue an order injunction sub, restraining the registration of the mark pending further adjudication. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registry may appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and the Court shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse such decision.

Any person claiming an interest and alleging that a trade mark sought to be registered is likely to deceive or cause confusion, or is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or is contrary to law, may file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond. Where the trade mark incorporates a geographical indication identifying goods originating from a specific region, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require evidence establishing the lawful user of such geographical indication by the opponent. The notice opposition applicant bears the burden of proving the grounds for opposition, and failure to do so may result in dismissal of the opposition.

Any person intending to oppose the registration of a trade mark shall file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. The notice opposition applicant shall clearly state the grounds for opposition, referencing relevant provisions of this Act and supporting evidence where applicable. Where a granted new patent exists for a technology directly related to the goods or services covered by the trade mark application, the Registry may require the applicant to demonstrate non-infringement or obtain a license. Failure to submit a complete and compliant notice of opposition within the stipulated timeframe shall render the opposition inadmissible. The Registry may, at its discretion, extend the time for filing a notice, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated and no undue prejudice arises to the applicant. All submissions shall be governed by the rules of procedure established under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing registration, or requiring the amendment or limitation of an application for registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. A request for reinstatement of an application for registration, where the Registrar has recorded a caveat against proceeding with it due to a prior claim, shall be considered by the Appellate Board as part of the aforementioned appeal process, provided that such request is filed concurrently with the initial appeal. The Appellate Board’s decision on the registration sub section, or any matter incidental thereto, shall be final and binding, subject to the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of India on a question of law. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall not be excused, unless sufficient cause is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board.

A trade mark application shall be deemed to be disclosed justified registration where the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, a genuine intention to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified, and provides evidence substantiating such intention, including but not limited to, business plans, marketing materials, or documented preparations for commercialization. Provided that, mere intention, without demonstrable preparatory steps, shall not constitute sufficient justification. The Registrar may, however, consider evidence of substantial investment made in anticipation of use, even if commercial launch is pending. Any representation made by the applicant regarding use, or intended use, shall be subject to verification, and any false or misleading statement may invalidate the application as provided herein. A finding of disclosed justified registration does not guarantee eventual registration, but establishes a foundational basis for proceeding with examination.

A trade mark application accompanied by a statement disclosing all known circumstances which could reasonably affect the registrability of the mark, and justifying the reasons for seeking registration despite such circumstances, shall be examined as provided herein. The Registrar, upon receiving such an application with disclosed justification, may require the applicant to furnish further evidence or clarification relating to the disclosed circumstances within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. Failure to comply with such requirement shall be deemed sufficient ground for refusal of the application. However, if the applicant satisfactorily addresses the concerns raised by the Registrar, and demonstrates that the mark is registrable subject to the disclosed limitations, the Registrar shall proceed with the examination of the application. A finding of disclosed justified registration shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks and shall be considered a valid basis for proceeding with the registration process, notwithstanding any potential objections that might otherwise arise. The Registrar retains the discretion to impose conditions on the registration reflecting the disclosed circumstances.

Any person who, not being the registered proprietor of a trade mark or an authorized user thereof, applies for registration of a trade mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a trade mark already registered under this Act, and discloses in their application facts which, had they been truthfully represented, would have justified the refusal of registration, shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that the Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, allow the applicant a period of three months to rectify the misrepresentation and demonstrate a bona fide intention to use the mark. Any continued misrepresentation after such period shall attract a doubling of the prescribed fine and may additionally result in a prohibition from applying for trade mark registration for a period of five years. All evidence presented in support of or rebuttal of a claim of disclosed justified registration shall be subject to verification by the Registrar.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, including a disclosed justified registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding written consent and recording of assignment with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, the assignee may apply to the Registry to become the registered proprietor, and such application shall be made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the instrument of assignment. The proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, grant licenses to other persons to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services. Any such license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be in writing and recorded with the Registry to be effective against third parties. Failure to record an assignment or license shall not invalidate the transaction but may affect its enforceability. A registered user, upon assignment of the registered trade mark, shall cease to be a registered user unless expressly agreed to by the new proprietor and recorded accordingly.

Any application for registration of a trade mark which discloses a justified reason for its adoption, notwithstanding any prior use by another, shall be subject to a rigorous examination as provided herein to determine the bona fides of the applicant and the extent of potential confusion. Where the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the disclosed justification outweighs the established rights of a prior user, registration may be permitted, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary to protect the interests of the prior user. However, any decision of the Registrar regarding such disclosed justified registration shall be appealable to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order, and the Board may, after hearing both parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision. A finding of bad faith on the part of the applicant shall be conclusive against registration, even if a technical justification is initially presented.

A trade mark shall be a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and may consist of words, numerals, graphic elements or any combination thereof. For the purposes of registration under this Act, a collective mark shall be considered a type of trade mark owned by the members of an association, and used to identify goods or services of those members. An applicant seeking trade mark registration shall demonstrate both inherent distinctiveness or acquired distinctiveness through use, subject to the provisions regarding well-known marks as determined by the Registrar. Registration confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, provided that such use does not contravene any other law for the time being in force.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of such trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. The application shall be in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the trade mark and a statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Where an application for trade mark registration includes a claim to colour as a feature of the trade mark, such claim shall be clearly indicated in the application. An applicant may, at the time of application, indicate the extent to which the trade mark is distinctive, and evidence supporting such claim may be submitted. Registration shall not be granted if the trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services or is likely to deceive the public, or is otherwise prohibited under this Act. Provided that, a trade mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registered, notwithstanding its initial descriptiveness.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of such trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained. The application shall be in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the trade mark and a statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Where an application for trade mark registration is filed, the Trade Marks Registry may, if it considers necessary, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information. An application shall not be accepted for examination unless the prescribed fee has been paid. 

Provided that, where a trade mark is identical with or deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, the Registry may, after giving the proprietor of the existing trade mark an opportunity to be heard, refuse the application. The Registry shall, upon examination, determine whether the trade mark is capable of being registered and whether it conflicts with any existing rights. A registered trade mark shall be deemed to be personal property and may be assigned or transmitted in the manner provided for in this Act.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration in the prescribed manner to the Trade Marks Registry. An application for trade mark registration shall include a clear representation of the mark, a list of goods or services for which registration is sought, and a statement of use. The Registry may, prior to acceptance of the application, require the applicant to amend the specification of goods or services to comply with the classification rules as provided herein. Where a mark is similar to an existing trade mark, the Registry shall, before registration, notify the proprietor of the earlier mark and afford them an opportunity to oppose the registration. Registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the certificate of registration, subject to any conditions or limitations imposed by this Act. Failure to renew the registration within the prescribed period shall result in the removal of the trade mark from the register.

Any person who falsely applies for the registration of a trade mark, or knowingly makes a false representation in an application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor without his consent or the consent of a duly authorised licensee, such use shall constitute an infringement of the trade mark, and the aggrieved party may institute legal proceedings for relief. Any goods bearing an infringing trade mark, or any material used in the manufacture of such goods, may be seized and destroyed as provided herein. A court, upon finding of infringement, may grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the trade mark and may also award damages to the registered proprietor, assessed on the basis of lost profits or actual damages sustained. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, rectify the register in cases of fraud or misrepresentation affecting trade mark registration.

Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark, or requiring the rectification or cancellation of an entry in the Register, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Trade Marks Registry, reverse it, or modify it, and shall record its reasons for doing so. A trade mark registration, once confirmed, shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and any unauthorized use constituting an infringement shall be actionable as provided herein. However, such rights shall be subject to the principles of fair use and the limitations imposed by this Act. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

Any person who falsifies entries in the Register of Trade Marks maintained by the India Registrar, or knowingly makes any false representation to the Registrar, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a trade mark registration is obtained through such falsification or false representation, the Registrar may, subject to such inquiry as may be deemed fit, revoke the registration and order the expungement of the trade mark from the Register. Any application for trade mark registration knowingly based on false information, or concealing material facts, shall be deemed invalid as provided herein. Furthermore, any person abetting or attempting to commit such offences shall be liable to the same penalties. The Registrar may, in addition to the above, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding twice the official fee payable for the relevant act.

A trade mark registration, once entered in the Register of Trade Marks and duly certified, shall be prima facie evidence of the absolute title of the proprietor to the trade mark, subject to any right arising from the use of a similar mark prior to the date of registration. Any certificate purporting to be a certified copy of an entry in the Register, or any extract therefrom, shall be received as evidence in any legal proceeding, and shall, until proved to the contrary, be presumed to be true. The Registrar may, at any time, require evidence to substantiate the continued use of the registered trade mark, and failure to provide such evidence may render the registration liable to be revoked. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, renewable for further periods of ten years each, as provided herein, upon payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with all applicable conditions.

For the purposes of this Act, an infringing copy shall be deemed to exist where a work is reproduced, distributed, or otherwise communicated to the public without the authorization of the copyright owner, or in a manner that violates the exclusive rights conferred by this Act. Such reproduction need not be identical to constitute an infringement; a substantial similarity, determined by qualitative and quantitative assessment, may be sufficient, subject to the principles of fair dealing as provided herein. A copy includes any derivative work based upon the original, and the making of multiple copies from a single infringing source shall be treated as separate infringements. Any person dealing in an infringing copy, including those facilitating its distribution, may be held liable as provided herein.

Any person who makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or distributes, or publicly exhibits any work, in respect of which copyright subsists, without the license of the copyright owner, or otherwise in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be deemed to have made an infringing copy. However, fair use of a copyrighted work for purposes such as private study, criticism, review, or news reporting shall not constitute an infringing copy, provided that such use is accompanied by sufficient acknowledgement of the work and the author. Registration of copyright under this Act shall create a rebuttable presumption as to the validity of the copyright and the ownership thereof. A person claiming infringement shall have the right to apply to the appropriate court for an injunction restraining the further making, sale, or distribution of the infringing copy, and for damages sustained by reason of the infringement. Any materials seized as infringing copy may be subject to destruction upon order of the court.

Any person who makes or procures the making of any infringing copy of a work, or causes any infringing copy to be distributed, whether for sale, hire, or otherwise, shall be liable to a civil remedy as provided herein. An infringing copy is defined as a reproduction or substantial adaptation of a protected work without the authorization of the copyright owner, or in contravention of any license granted under this Act. Where a person distributes an infringing copy knowing, or having reasonable grounds to believe, that such copy is infringing, such distribution shall constitute a separate act of infringement. 

The copyright owner, upon establishing infringement, may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, as well as damages for the loss suffered. Damages shall be assessed based on the actual loss sustained by the copyright owner, or, at the owner’s election, a reasonable royalty for the use of the work. Provided that, if the infringement is proven to be flagrant, the court may award enhanced damages. Any evidence of circumvention of technological protection measures shall be considered in determining the extent of damages.

Any person who makes or procures the making of any copy of a work in violation of the rights conferred by this Act shall be deemed to have made an infringing copy, and such act constitutes an infringement of copyright. Where a work is capable of being reproduced in multiple forms, each such reproduction, whether physical or digital, shall be considered a separate infringing copy for the purposes of determining remedies. A copy shall be deemed to include a record of the work in any medium, including but not limited to phonograms, video films, and computer databases. 

Provided that, fair dealing with a work for the purposes of private study, research, criticism, or review, as provided herein, shall not constitute an infringing copy, subject to the conditions that such dealing is accompanied by sufficient acknowledgement and does not unduly prejudice the legitimate interests of the copyright owner. The existence of an infringing copy shall be prima facie evidence of an infringement action, unless the defendant can demonstrate a lawful basis for its creation or possession.

Any person who makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or distributes, or publicly exhibits any work, in respect of which copyright subsists, or any infringing copy thereof, shall be deemed to have infringed copyright, subject to the provisions of this Act. However, no such act shall constitute an infringement where the work is a translation, adaptation, abridgement or otherwise altered, provided that such alteration does not materially affect the original work’s character or substance and due acknowledgement of the original author and copyright holder is made. A copy shall be considered infringing if it is made or imported without the authorization of the copyright owner, or if it is offered for sale or hire in a manner that violates the terms of any license granted by the copyright owner. Where a person proves lawful independent creation, it shall not be considered an infringing copy.

Any person who makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or distributes, or publicly exhibits any infringing copy of a work, shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein, and the work so made, sold, let for hire, distributed or publicly exhibited, together with all materials used in the making thereof, shall be deemed to be the property of the copyright owner. Where the infringing copy is in electronic form, the relevant digital rights management technology circumvented, or the rights management information removed or altered, the penalty shall be doubled. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the copyright owner may apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts. Any profits made from the sale of an infringing copy shall be recoverable by the copyright owner as damages, and the defendant shall bear the costs of the legal proceedings.

Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film shall be in writing and signed by the assignor or a duly authorised agent. Where the copyright in a work is assigned, the assignee shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if they were the original owner of the copyright, subject to the terms and conditions of the assignment. An infringing copy shall be deemed to be made when, without the license of the copyright owner or in contravention of the terms of a license, a work is reproduced, distributed, or made available to the public. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a license may be granted to a person to make an infringing copy for the purpose of educational or research use, provided that such use does not prejudice the legitimate interests of the copyright owner and is accompanied by reasonable remuneration. Any dispute regarding the determination of reasonable remuneration shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to royalty rates. The assignee shall furnish a copy of the assignment agreement to the copyright office within thirty days of its execution.

Any person who makes or procures the making of any copy of a work in which copyright subsists, without the license of the copyright owner, or otherwise in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be deemed to have made an infringing copy, and shall be liable to the remedies prescribed herein. However, such liability shall not extend to fair dealing with a copyrighted work for the purposes of private study, criticism, review, or research, provided that such dealing is not accompanied by any commercial exploitation. Where a claim of infringement is disputed, the alleged infringer may submit evidence demonstrating independent creation or lawful acquisition of the work in question, subject to verification by the court. Any appeal against a decision regarding an infringing copy shall be made to the High Court having jurisdiction, and such appeal must be filed within ninety days of the lower court’s judgment. The copyright owner retains the right to seek injunctions and damages as compensation for the unauthorized use.

Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film, whether made before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be subject to a requirement that the assignee secure the consent of the principal performer whose performance constituted an integral part of the film, and such consent shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the appropriate authority as prescribed. Where a copyright owner licenses the right to reproduce a work, and such reproduction constitutes an infringing copy, the copyright owner may, subject to the terms of the license, pursue remedies against the licensee. A legal practitioner acting on behalf of a copyright owner may, with leave of the court, serve notice on any person suspected of possessing or distributing an infringing copy, requiring them to disclose the source and extent of such possession or distribution. Provided that, any assignment or license failing to adhere to these provisions shall be deemed void *ab initio*, and the copyright owner shall remain entitled to all rights and remedies as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to judicial determination.

Any person who makes an infringing copy of a work protected under this Act shall be liable to a decree of injunction restraining the reproduction, distribution, or communication to the public of such copy. Where the infringing copy is made for commercial purposes, the owner of copyright may, in addition to the injunction, also claim damages, assessed on a reasonable royalty basis or, at the owner’s election, an account of profits derived from the sale of the infringing copy. However, a defendant may, subject to such terms and conditions as the court may deem fit, apply for a license to continue the use of the work, provided that reasonable notice of such application is given to the copyright owner. If a register disclosed details of the copyright owner are inaccurate, the copyright owner shall have a right to rectification of the register, and such rectification shall be deemed to have effect from the date of the original registration. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act may appeal to the High Court.

A person shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence notwithstanding any prior lawful act or omission, where such person knowingly facilitates or encourages an infringement of copyright, even if such person does not directly participate in the infringing act itself. Such facilitation or encouragement shall include, but not be limited to, providing the means for infringement, or receiving remuneration derived from infringing acts, subject to a demonstration of reasonable diligence to avoid such acts. However, a mere passive recipient of infringing material, unaware of its origin and without reasonable grounds to suspect infringement, shall not be held liable as provided herein. Any person convicted of a commission offence shall be punishable with imprisonment and a fine, as determined by the court.

Any person who, notwithstanding any contract or arrangement to the contrary, commissions the creation of a cinematograph film, sound recording, photograph, or any other work in which copyright subsists, shall be deemed to have infringed the exclusive right of the copyright owner, subject to the provisions of this Act relating to licensing and equitable remedies. However, such commission offence notwithstanding, a defendant may establish by evidence that they reasonably believed they had obtained valid authorization for the commissioned work, or that the copyright owner unreasonably withheld such authorization, thereby mitigating liability as provided herein. Any aggrieved copyright owner may pursue civil remedies, including injunctions and damages, and may also seek an order for delivery up of infringing copies. The quantum of damages shall be determined with regard to the actual loss suffered, or the reasonable royalty payable had the defendant secured a license. A court may, in exceptional cases, award enhanced damages to deter future infringement.

Any person who, notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act, engages in the commercial exploitation of a work without the requisite license or authorization, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence notwithstanding that such exploitation falls below a threshold of demonstrable financial gain. However, a determination of commission offence shall be subject to proof that the person reasonably knew, or ought reasonably to have known, that the work was protected by copyright and that their actions constituted an infringement as provided herein. Where the alleged infringement involves a digital work, evidence of technological measures circumvented, or attempts thereof, may be considered as corroborating evidence of such knowledge. The owner of copyright may, notwithstanding the initiation of legal proceedings, request a cease and desist notice be issued to the alleged infringer, and compliance with such notice shall not be construed as an admission of guilt.

Any person who, with knowledge of a copyright subsisting in a work, reproduces, distributes, or publicly exhibits such work in a manner that demonstrably prejudices the legitimate rights of the copyright owner, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act notwithstanding any claim of unawareness regarding the specific source of the infringing material. Where the offence involves commercial gain exceeding five lakh rupees, the penalty shall be imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and a fine not less than five times the value of the illicitly gained benefit. However, a court may, subject to the circumstances, impose a higher fine up to ten times the value of the benefit. Any equipment used in the commission of the offence shall be liable to confiscation as provided herein, and the burden of proving lawful origin shall rest upon the accused. Prosecution for a commission offence notwithstanding, a civil suit for damages remains permissible.
