Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film, whether made before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be subject to the condition that the assignee shall not exercise any right in respect of such copyright so as to prejudice the legitimate interests of the author or producer of the film, and any such exercise shall be deemed a commission offence notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. Where a copyright owner licenses a work for commercial exploitation, a clear and unambiguous accounting of royalties shall be furnished to the owner at intervals not exceeding six months, failing which the owner may seek redress as provided herein. Notwithstanding any prior agreement, the assignee or licensee shall, upon reasonable request, furnish evidence of actual sales or usage of the copyrighted work to verify royalty calculations. Any failure to do so shall constitute a breach of the assignment or license agreement and may result in termination of such agreement, subject to a thirty-day notice period.

A person shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act notwithstanding any prior contractual arrangement or purported license relating to the subject matter of the alleged infringement, provided that such arrangement or license does not constitute a valid defence as established by judicial precedent. Where a trade mark is a reference trade mark, meaning it indicates the character or quality of goods or services and is not used to distinguish goods or services of different undertakings, the application of the provisions relating to infringement shall be subject to such limitations as may be prescribed. Any determination of commission offence notwithstanding shall consider the totality of circumstances and the intent of the alleged infringer, subject to proof as per the Evidence Act, 1872. A bona fide intent to seek legal advice regarding potential infringement shall not, in and of itself, constitute a defence.

Any person who, with knowledge of a copyright subsisting in a work, engages in the commercial rental or lending of such work, or distributes copies thereof in a manner that demonstrably undermines the legitimate market for the work, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that the provisions of this clause shall not apply to educational institutions utilizing copyrighted works for non-commercial, instructional purposes, subject to the conditions that such use is limited to classroom settings and does not extend to systematic reproduction or distribution. A person shall not prevent commission offence by merely claiming ignorance of the copyright owner or the existence of the copyright. Where a collective management organization, duly registered, has authorized the use of a work, any unauthorized use, despite such authorization being reasonably accessible, constitutes a separate offence. Any individual found facilitating the infringement, including providing technological means to circumvent copyright protection, may also be held liable.

Any person who, with knowledge of a work protected under this Act, engages in the reproduction or distribution of such work without the requisite license or authorization, shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable as provided herein. However, a claim of innocent infringement may be considered, subject to the claimant demonstrating diligent effort to ascertain the rightful owner and obtain necessary permissions. Where a dispute arises regarding the commission of such an offence, any aggrieved party may submit a detailed representation to the appropriate authority, outlining the alleged infringement and supporting evidence. The authority shall, within ninety days, issue a reasoned order, and any party dissatisfied with said order may prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. The High Court’s decision shall be final, except in cases involving substantial questions of law, which may be subject to further review by the Supreme Court. It shall be the duty of the investigating officer to prevent commission offence by securing infringing materials.

Means register, when used in relation to a patent, shall denote the official record maintained by the Controller of Patents, wherein particulars of patents granted and applications for patents pending are systematically documented and accessible for public inspection as provided herein. The Controller may, subject to rules made under this Act, determine the form and method of maintaining such means register, including the electronic storage and retrieval of information. Any amendment to the means register, whether concerning the status of an application or a granted patent, shall be effected only upon due verification and confirmation of the relevant facts. A certified extract from the means register shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding concerning the patent in question.

The Controller shall maintain a register of designs, which register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public subject to payment of a fee as prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, and the Controller may, if satisfied, permit such inspection. The particulars entered in the register shall be deemed to be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein. Any alteration to the particulars of a registered design, including a change of ownership or address, shall be notified to the Controller and recorded in the register within thirty days of such alteration. A certified copy of any entry in the register, duly authenticated by the Controller, shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding. The means register shall be the definitive record of all registered designs under this Act, and no design not so registered shall be entitled to protection as provided herein. Failure to maintain an accurate register may result in penalties as determined by the Central Government.

The Controller shall maintain a register of patents, and such register shall be open for inspection by any person subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any application for the amendment of an entry in the register shall be made in writing to the Controller, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Controller, upon being satisfied that the amendment is justified and does not prejudice the rights of any other party, may allow the amendment and cause the register to be accordingly altered. Where an opposition is filed against the registration of a patent, the Controller shall, after considering the evidence submitted by both parties, make an order either allowing or rejecting the opposition, and shall record the order in the register. The accuracy of all entries in the register shall be the responsibility of the Controller, and any errors discovered therein shall be rectified without undue delay. A certified copy of any entry in the register shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding. The term “means register” for the purposes of this Act shall denote the official record maintained under the authority of the Controller, detailing particulars of all patents granted and applications pending.

Any assignment of the right, title, and interest in a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be in writing and shall be duly executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. The assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not operate as an assignment of any right to apply for or receive a patent in any other country. A licensee, with the express consent of the patentee, may further assign their interest in the licensed patent. The Controller shall maintain a register of all assignments recorded under this Act, and any person may inspect the register upon payment of the prescribed fee. The means register shall be conclusive evidence of the validity of any assignment recorded therein, subject to proof of fraud. Where an assignment is made without the written consent of the patentee, it shall be voidable at the option of the patentee, provided that such option is exercised within two years from the date of the assignment. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

The means register maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection by any person on payment of the fee prescribed for such inspection, subject to the conditions, if any, specified by the Controller. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a patent, and alleging that the patent was wrongly granted, may petition the Controller for revocation of the patent, provided that such petition is made within one year from the date of publication of the grant of the patent. The Controller, upon consideration of the petition and evidence submitted, may, if satisfied that the patent should not have been registered, order the cancellation justified registration, and cause the patent to be amended accordingly or revoked entirely. Any amendment or revocation made under this provision shall be recorded in the means register and shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court as provided herein. The Controller shall communicate any decision regarding registration or cancellation to the patentee and the petitioner, if any, in writing.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal of the registrar to make any entry in the means register, or by any alteration made by the registrar to an entry therein, may lodge an appeal with the Appellate Board established under this Act. The appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order of the registrar and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of such order. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the registrar’s decision was erroneous or contrary to the provisions of this Act, direct the registrar to make the requested entry or alteration, or to reconsider the matter. Provided that, the registrar shall decide upon any representation made regarding the accuracy of information contained within the means register, and such decision shall be final and binding unless overturned on appeal. Failure to comply with the directions of the Appellate Board shall render the registrar liable to such penalties as may be prescribed. Any rectification of the means register shall be noted with the date and reasons for such change.

The Controller shall maintain a register of patents, and such register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application in the prescribed form and pay the prescribed fee. The Controller may, if satisfied that the applicant has a legitimate interest, grant access to the register. Where an application for a patent is refused, the applicant may, within a period of one month from the date of the refusal, file an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. 

For the purposes of determining novelty, an invention originating in an invention convention country shall be treated as if it were part of the state of the art only if it was made available to the public before the date of filing of the complete specification in India. The means register shall be updated monthly with details of all applications received and patents granted. Any error in the register may be rectified by the Controller upon application and subject to verification of records.

The means register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be updated within thirty days of a determination made under this Act regarding the validity of a patent or an application for a patent. Any amendment to an entry in the means register relating to ownership or assignment of rights must be accompanied by a certified copy of the instrument effecting such change, and shall be subject to verification by the Controller. A filing application for restoration of a lapsed patent shall not be entertained unless the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that the delay in restoring the patent was due to sufficient cause. Provided that, such sufficient cause shall not include mere negligence or lack of diligence on the part of the applicant or their authorized agent. All entries in the means register are prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, unless and until duly rebutted. The Controller may, at any time, inspect the means register and verify its accuracy.

Any assignment of the right, title, and interest in a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be in writing and shall be duly executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. The assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not operate as an assignment of any right to apply for or receive a patent in any country other than India, unless expressly so provided in the instrument of assignment. Where the means register maintained by the authority registrar case indicates a prior assignment not duly recorded, a subsequent assignment shall be ineffective to the extent of the rights conferred by the prior assignment. The assignee may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Controller for the registration of the assignment. Failure to register an assignment shall not invalidate it, but such assignment shall not be enforceable against any person other than the parties to the assignment, unless so registered. Any dispute regarding the validity or effect of an assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

A registered user layout, for the purposes of this Act, signifies a layout-design, as defined herein, in which the applicant, at the time of filing, is the owner or has obtained the right to use, exercise, and enforce the rights in such layout-design. The applicant shall furnish a statement disclosing the extent of their ownership or right to use, and any encumbrances existing on the layout-design. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered user may assign their rights in the registered user layout to another person, provided that such assignment is in writing and duly registered with the Intellectual Property Office. Failure to accurately disclose ownership or existing encumbrances may render the registration of the registered user layout invalid, as determined by the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a layout-design as a registered user layout may file a petition for revocation.

A person desiring to be registered as a registered user of a registered layout-design shall submit an application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall include particulars of the applicant, including their legal name, principal place of business, and a statement of the extent of authorized use sought in relation to the registered layout-design. Upon receipt of a complete application and payment of the requisite fee, the Registrar shall, subject to verification of the applicant’s entitlement, register the applicant as a registered user. The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered users, which shall be open for inspection during office hours as provided herein. Any transfer of rights as a registered user, or any change in the extent of authorized use of a registered user layout, shall be recorded with the Registrar through a supplementary application and associated fee. Failure to do so may invalidate subsequent claims of authorized use.

A person registered as a registered user layout shall maintain a record of all licenses granted under the registered layout-design, specifying the duration, scope, and territorial extent of each license, and such record shall be open to inspection by the Registrar during office hours, subject to reasonable notice. Any registered user layout who fails to comply with the requirements of this provision shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees per day for the period of non-compliance, as determined by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. The Controller may, however, consider extenuating circumstances before imposing such penalty. 

Where a registered user layout intends to assign or otherwise transfer their rights in a registered layout-design, they shall notify the Controller in writing, providing details of the assignee or transferee. Such notification shall be subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. The Controller shall record the assignment or transfer in the Register of Registered User Layouts, and the assignee or transferee shall, upon such recordal, become the registered user layout.

A registered user, intending to commercially exploit a registered layout-design, shall furnish to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board a statement of intended commercial exploitation, detailing the manner and extent of such exploitation, within thirty days of commencing said exploitation. Failure to comply with this provision may render the registered user liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period by a further thirty days. Any person aggrieved by the actions of a registered user relating to a registered layout-design, and alleging improper commercial exploitation, may lodge a complaint with the Board. A registered user layout, if determined by the Board to have been exploited in a manner inconsistent with the statement furnished, shall be subject to revocation of user rights as provided herein. The Board shall consider any evidence of prior art before making a determination.

Any person who, without being a registered user layout, manufactures a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying a registered layout-design, or commercially exploits such a layout-design, or performs any act that, if the person were a registered user layout, would constitute an infringement under this Act, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than two years, but which may extend to five years, and with a fine not less than five lakh rupees, but which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, subject to the circumstances of the case, also order the seizure and destruction of all infringing articles and equipment used in the manufacture of such articles. A registered user layout may, however, assign their rights to another person, subject to notification to the appropriate authority as provided herein, and failure to do so shall attract a penalty of one lakh rupees. Any appeal against an order of penalty shall lie before the designated court within thirty days of the order.

Any registered user layout, upon formal assignment to a legal entity distinct from the original registrant, shall vest absolutely in the assignee, subject to the terms of any existing commercial agreement governing its exploitation. The assignee may, as provided herein, grant licenses, both exclusive and non-exclusive, to third parties for the manufacture or sale of semiconductor integrated circuits embodying the assigned registered user layout. Such licenses shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the appropriate authority to ensure enforceability against subsequent licensees. Where a registered user layout is jointly held by multiple registrants, any assignment requires the express written consent of all co-registrants, unless otherwise stipulated in a pre-existing agreement. Failure to obtain such consent may render the assignment voidable at the option of any dissenting co-registrant. A registered user may also bequeath their rights in a registered user layout through testamentary disposition, subject to applicable inheritance laws.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a registered user layout, or imposing conditions on such registration, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend the time for filing an appeal, but not beyond a further period of thirty days. Where the appeal concerns the validity of a registered user layout, the Board may direct the respondent to produce evidence supporting the claim of originality and independent creation, as provided herein. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to any remedies available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning errors apparent on the face of the record. Failure to exhaust this appellate remedy shall preclude any subsequent judicial review of the Registrar’s decision.

A registered user layout shall confer upon the user the right to use, reproduce, and distribute the layout-design, subject to the terms and conditions agreed upon with the proprietor, and as provided herein. Any registered user desiring to assign their rights in a registered user layout shall provide written notice to the proprietor, detailing the proposed assignee and the scope of the assignment, and obtain prior written consent, which may be granted or refused at the proprietor’s discretion. The proprietor’s refusal to consent shall not be deemed unreasonable if it demonstrably impacts the commercial exploitation of the layout-design. 

Registration mentioned clause pertaining to a registered user shall be valid for a period of five years from the date of registration, and may be renewed upon application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry, provided that all applicable fees are paid and the user continues to abide by the terms of use established by the proprietor. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registered user status.

Any person who, without being a registered user layout, manufactures a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying a registered layout-design, or commercially exploits such a circuit, shall be liable to a civil injunction as provided herein. Furthermore, such person shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five crore rupees for each such infringement, or a term of imprisonment not exceeding three years, or both. Where an infringement involves a layout-design also protected by a valid patent, the remedies under this Act shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, the remedies available under the Patents Act, 1970. A registered user layout may be transferred by assignment, operation of law, or by grant of license, subject to the terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Failure to maintain accurate records relating to registered user layouts shall attract a fine of up to one crore rupees.

A denomination variety shall be distinguished by a unique and readily identifiable name assigned to the plant variety for the purposes of registration under this Act, and such denomination must conform to the requirements as prescribed. The denomination shall be clearly distinguishable from all other denominations of varieties of the same kind, or of closely related kinds, whose existence is a matter of common knowledge to persons dealing with such varieties. Provided that a denomination which is likely to cause confusion with a variety already protected, or which is contrary to public order or morality, shall not be accepted. A variety essentially derived from a registered denomination variety may, subject to the provisions herein, retain a denomination incorporating the original variety’s name, with appropriate modification to indicate its derivation.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be clearly distinguishable by a unique and readily identifiable name assigned by the breeder or discoverer thereof. The proposed denomination shall not lead to confusion with varieties of the same kind or of closely related kinds, and shall not be deceptive or misleading as to the characteristics of the plant. An applicant seeking registration of a denomination variety may, subject to regulations, submit evidence of prior use of the proposed denomination in commerce, demonstrating a period of at least one year of consistent application. The Authority may, however, reject a denomination if it finds that the proposed name is commonly used by farmers in local parlance to describe a traditionally grown variety, thereby ensuring the protection of farmers’ rights as provided herein. All denominations shall be subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority to ensure compliance with these provisions.

A registered breeder of a new denomination variety shall have the right to save, sell, and exchange seeds of that variety, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Any farmer who is in possession of seeds of a protected denomination variety may save seeds for his own planting, provided that he does not sell or otherwise commercially exploit the saved seeds. Where a farmer undertakes essentially derived varieties from a protected denomination variety, he shall require the prior authorization of the breeder, and such authorization may be subject to reasonable royalty payments as determined by the Authority. The Authority may, upon application by any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a denomination variety, issue a cease and desist order and may also award damages for any loss suffered by the breeder as a result of the infringement. A breeder may also seek an injunction from a competent court to prevent further infringement of his rights as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the entitlement to benefit sharing arising from the utilization of farmers’ varieties or denomination varieties shall be settled through a mutually agreed mechanism.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be clearly distinguishable by a single, technically accurate designation, reflecting the plant’s characteristics and origin, and shall not mislead the public or create confusion with existing varieties. The applicant shall submit a statement of origin with the application, detailing the geographical location of development or first cultivation of the variety, and the rationale behind the chosen denomination. Provided that, where a variety is commonly known by a particular name in local usage, the Authority may, subject to verification of such usage through established agricultural records, permit the use of that name as the denomination. Any denomination found to be generic or descriptive of the plant’s characteristics shall be rejected, and the applicant shall be required to propose an alternative. The Authority reserves the right to request modification of a denomination if it deems it necessary to ensure clarity and prevent ambiguity in the register of plant varieties. A register of denominations maintained under this Act shall be open for public inspection.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall possess a clearly distinguishable denomination which enables its ready identification and shall not be likely to cause confusion with varieties of common knowledge or those already registered. The applicant seeking registration of a denomination variety shall submit a declaration affirming the distinctiveness of the proposed denomination and confirming that it is not a generic name commonly used to describe the plant variety in the relevant trade. Provided that, if a denomination is found to be substantially similar to a previously registered denomination, the Authority may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, require the submission of a new denomination. Any denomination incorporating misleading or deceptive elements shall be deemed unacceptable and registration shall be refused. The Authority may maintain a register of registered denomination varieties accessible to the public, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. A variety exhibiting essentially derived variety characteristics shall not disqualify a denomination if it otherwise meets the criteria as provided herein.

Any person developing or acquiring a new denomination variety shall ensure that such denomination is clearly distinguishable from all other registered varieties, and does not mislead or cause confusion regarding the source or characteristics of the plant. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to modify a denomination if it finds that the proposed denomination is similar to an existing one, or is likely to cause public deception. Provided that, if a denomination has been used for a considerable period in commerce, the Authority shall consider the established usage before directing a modification. Any false representation concerning a denomination variety, including the mislabeling of seeds or propagating material, shall be an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or both. The Registrar, upon sufficient evidence of such offence, may initiate proceedings as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a breeder’s right, submit a clear and unambiguous denomination for said variety, which shall conform to the requirements prescribed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The denomination must distinguish the variety from any other variety in common knowledge, and shall not mislead or be likely to mislead the public as to its characteristics. A transfer of breeder’s right, whether by assignment, testamentary succession, or operation of law, shall include the transfer of the registered denomination, subject to a notification requirement to the Authority. Should the registered owner desire to alter the denomination variety after registration, they may apply to the Authority, providing justification for the change and demonstrating that the new denomination also meets the criteria outlined herein. The Authority may, upon satisfactory review, approve the alteration and record it accordingly, and any subsequent propagation or sale must reflect the updated denomination. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the breeder’s right.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to accept a proposed denomination for a new plant variety, or by any alteration to a denomination as recorded, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days of the date of the order of refusal or alteration. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds on which it is based and a certified copy of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and any evidence submitted, shall determine whether the proposed denomination adequately distinguishes the variety from any existing, commonly known denomination variety, and whether it conforms to the principles of botanical nomenclature. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to compelling reasons, direct the applicant to submit an alternative denomination if the original is deemed misleading or confusingly similar to a registered variety. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person developing or commercially exploiting a denomination variety shall maintain a record of its lineage, including the origin of seed material and all subsequent breeding steps, subject to inspection by officers authorized under this Act. Where a denomination variety substantially replicates the expression of a copyrighted work, including but not limited to artistic depictions or literary descriptions of plant characteristics, the rights holder of such copyright may, notwithstanding the provisions relating to farmers’ rights, petition the Central Government for an inquiry into potential infringement. Failure to maintain accurate lineage records, or knowingly providing false information in relation to a denomination variety, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Repeated offences as determined by the Tribunal shall render the offender ineligible for registration of any new variety for a period of five years, and may further result in the revocation of existing registrations. Any variety found to be derived from illegally obtained germplasm shall be deemed ineligible for protection as provided herein.

A denomination variety shall be distinguished by a unique identifier assigned to it for the purposes of registration under this Act, and such denomination must be clearly reproducible, ensuring unambiguous identification of the plant variety in question. The application registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration, verify the distinctiveness of the proposed denomination against existing registered varieties and publicly available information to prevent confusion. Provided that, if a denomination is found to be similar to a previously registered variety, the applicant may be required to submit an alternative denomination or provide evidence demonstrating sufficient differentiation. Subject to the provisions herein, the registrar may reject an application if the proposed denomination is deemed misleading or likely to deceive the public regarding the characteristics of the variety.

A breeder who has developed a new denomination variety shall be entitled to registration, provided that such variety conforms to the criteria of distinctiveness, uniformity and stability as prescribed. Any person claiming rights in a denomination variety, and submitting an application for registration, may be required to furnish a certificate purporting to demonstrate the origin and development of said variety, and the Authority shall have the power to demand such documentation for verification purposes. The registered breeder shall have the exclusive right to commercially exploit the denomination variety, including the right to sell, distribute, and propagate the same, subject to the provisions of this Act. However, a farmer who has in good faith saved seeds of a protected denomination variety for personal cultivation shall not be restricted by these rights. Any infringement of the breeder’s rights shall be actionable, and the aggrieved party may seek appropriate remedies, including injunction and damages, as provided herein. The Authority may, upon sufficient cause, revoke the registration of a denomination variety if it is proven that the variety lacks the requisite characteristics or that the breeder has misrepresented material facts.

For the purposes of this Act, “transmission” in relation to goodwill shall mean the transfer of ownership, whether voluntary or involuntary, of a business, or a substantial part thereof, including but not limited to sale, assignment, lease, merger, or operation of law. Such transmission shall be deemed to include the transfer of the right to use a trade mark associated with the transmitted goodwill, provided that the transferor retains no material connection with the business after the transmission. Where a transmission occurs without a corresponding transfer of the trade mark registration, the transferee may, subject to the provisions herein, apply for registration of the trade mark in their name, demonstrating continued use and goodwill. Any assignment of a trade mark without concurrent transmission of goodwill shall be voidable at the option of the assignor.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing. The instrument shall identify the trade mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and include a statement of consideration, if any. An assignment of a trade mark, or an agreement to assign it, shall not be revocable except with the consent of the assignee or, in the case of a fraudulent assignment, as provided herein. 

Where the assignment involves the transmission of the trade mark to a person carrying on a business different from that of the assignor, the Registrar shall record the assignment upon application made in the prescribed form and subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to record such transmission may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. The assignee shall, within six months of the assignment, apply for registration of the assignment.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignment and, where the assignment is not recorded with the Trade Marks Registry, the assignee shall not be entitled to sue for infringement as provided herein. However, a transmission of rights arising from operation of law, such as through inheritance, succession, or amalgamation of companies, shall not require prior registration with the Registry, provided that the assignee or legal representative furnishes satisfactory evidence of the transmission to the Registry within six months of such occurrence. Failure to do so may result in a temporary suspension of rights to sue for infringement until such evidence is submitted and verified. Where a transmission occurs without due legal process, the registered proprietor may seek rectification of the Register to reflect the true owner, subject to the remedies available under this Act for misrepresentation and fraudulent practices. Any person aggrieved by a fraudulent transmission may apply to the High Court for relief.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorized agents. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, such assignment shall be deemed to be a transmission of the trade mark to the assignee, notwithstanding any defect in the title of the assignor. However, a transmission to a liquidator or receiver, or any person acting on behalf of a court, shall not be subject to the requirement of an instrument in writing. 

Provided that, where the assignment is made subject to a condition requiring the continued use of the trade mark by the assignor, the assignee may, subject to the provisions herein, apply to the Registrar for a direction as to the enforcement of such condition. The Registrar may, after giving the assignor an opportunity of being heard, impose such conditions as he deems fit regarding the continued use of the trade mark. Any failure to comply with such conditions may be considered a ground for revocation of the assignment.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the transmission of rights, and no assignment shall be valid unless it is in writing and certified by the Trade Marks Registry. The transmission of rights in a trade mark, whether by assignment, transmission by operation of law, or otherwise, shall not affect the validity of the registration, provided that the assignee or transmitted party furnishes the Registry with evidence of title within a period of six months from the date of transmission. Failure to provide such evidence may render the registration liable to revocation, subject to a hearing as provided herein. Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law due to the death or insolvency of the proprietor, the legal representative shall, within the same six-month period, notify the Registry and demonstrate sufficient interest. Any transfer without due compliance with these provisions shall be considered null and void.

Any unauthorized transmission of a registered trade mark, or a substantial reproduction thereof, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be deemed an infringement under this Act. Such transmission, whether by electronic means, telecommunication, or any other mode of conveyance, is strictly prohibited, subject to the provisions relating to fair use as determined by the Registrar. Any person found engaging in the transmission of counterfeit goods bearing a registered trade mark, or facilitating such transmission, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Furthermore, all infringing materials used in the transmission, including any apparatus employed, shall be subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. The burden of proving legitimate transmission rests with the accused. A second or subsequent offence shall attract enhanced penalties, including a minimum imprisonment term of one year.

Any registered trade mark shall be transmissible by way of assignment, mortgage or otherwise, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. An assignment shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly executed by or on behalf of both the assignor and the assignee, and notice of the assignment is sent to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. Where a trade mark is mortgaged, the mortgagee shall have the same rights and remedies as a mortgagee of other movable property, but no power to sell the trade mark without the leave of the court. A transmission by operation of law, including through inheritance or bankruptcy, shall vest in the successor-in-interest the same rights and obligations as the original proprietor, provided that the successor-in-interest duly notifies the Trade Marks Registry of such transmission. Any assignment or transmission not complying with these provisions shall be voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, and the Trade Marks Registry may refuse to record such assignment or transmission.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the transmission of rights, and no assignment shall be valid unless it is in writing and certified by the Registrar. Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, or by will, or by devolution, the proprietor of the trade mark immediately before such transmission shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to continue as the proprietor until such time as the transmission is duly recorded in the Register. An application for the recording of such transmission shall be made within six months of the date of transmission, failing which a penalty may be levied as provided herein. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of any such transmission, an appeal may be made to the High Court having jurisdiction, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the procedural requirements outlined in the Civil Procedure Code. The Registrar’s decision on the application for recording transmission shall be final, unless overturned on appeal.

Any transmission of a registered trade mark, whether by assignment, transfer, or operation of law, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of the new proprietor, and failure to comply with such provisions may render the transmission voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party. However, a transmission occurring as a consequence of a corporate restructuring, where a director of the original entity demonstrably authorized the transfer prior to the restructuring’s completion, shall be viewed differently. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of such a transmission, an application may be made to the High Court, and the Court shall consider evidence of authorization and the bona fides of all parties involved. Provided that, the Court may stay the transmission pending resolution of the dispute, and any continued use of the mark during the stay shall not be construed as an admission of valid title. Any appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie to the Supreme Court.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not be effective until an intimation of the assignment is furnished to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The intimation shall include details of both the assignor and the assignee, and a statement of the trade mark assigned, specifying the goods or services in respect of which the assignment applies. Where the assignment involves a basic application for registration still under examination, the rights and obligations pertaining to that application shall, subject to the approval of the Registrar, transfer to the assignee upon completion of the prescribed formalities. A request for recording the transmission of rights due to operation of law, such as by way of inheritance or succession, shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant legal documents establishing the transmission. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or transmission unenforceable as provided herein.

Any transmission of a registered trade mark, or a right in a registered trade mark, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by a written instrument duly executed by both parties, or by their duly authorised agents. Where a transmission occurs without such written instrument, the validity of the transmission may be challenged by any aggrieved person, and the onus of proving lawful transmission shall lie upon the transferee. A transmission shall not prejudice any existing rights of prior licensees, and such licensees shall continue to be entitled to the benefits of their licenses subject to the terms thereof. Any act constituting the use of a trade mark following an invalid transmission, and which is identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be deemed an infringement as provided herein, entitling the proprietor to seek remedies including injunction, damages, and delivery up of infringing goods. Provided that, a bona fide transmission for valuable consideration and without notice of any prior rights shall not, in itself, constitute infringement.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not be effective until an intimation of the assignment is furnished to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The Registry, upon receipt of such intimation, shall record the transmission of the right in the register and shall, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit, advertise the assignment in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to furnish such intimation shall render the transmission voidable at the option of the assignee. 

Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, including through inheritance, succession, or amalgamation, the legal representative or successor-in-interest shall, within six months of such transmission, apply to the Registry for the registration of the transmission. All applications for registration respect shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant legal documents establishing the transmission. The Registry may, if satisfied, register the transmission and issue a certificate of registration accordingly, failing which the rights associated with the mark may be prejudiced.

A pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to include any chemical substance, biological entity, or mixture thereof, intended for use in diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of any disease, disorder, or abnormal physical state or for improving the physical condition of humans or animals. Provided that a pharmaceutical substance must possess a demonstrable therapeutic effect and be capable of being isolated or chemically defined. Any substance claimed as a pharmaceutical substance shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be considered novel and involve an inventive step, being not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art. A ‘skilled person’ for the purposes of determining inventive step shall be a person possessing ordinary skill and common knowledge in the field of pharmaceutical chemistry or biotechnology.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel if it has not been previously made available to the public by any means, whether by written or oral description, by use, or in any other manner. The applicant seeking registration of a pharmaceutical substance shall furnish complete and detailed information regarding its chemical structure, composition, method of manufacture, and therapeutic efficacy, subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein. Any modification or derivative of a known pharmaceutical substance shall require demonstration of significant enhancement in known therapeutic properties or a demonstrable reduction in adverse effects to qualify for patentability. The Controller may, at their discretion, require comparative clinical trials to ascertain the claimed improvements. A pharmaceutical substance intended for use in a new method of treatment shall also satisfy the criteria of inventive step and industrial applicability. The term “industrial applicability” includes the capacity to be manufactured or produced by any means.

Any pharmaceutical substance, newly discovered and capable of industrial application, shall be patentable subject to the provisions of this Act, provided that such substance does not fall within the exclusions specified elsewhere herein. A patentee of a pharmaceutical substance shall have the exclusive right to import, manufacture, use, and sell the substance within the territory of India for a period of twenty years from the date of filing the application, subject to payment of renewal fees as prescribed. Any person infringing upon this exclusive right shall be liable to a suit for injunction and damages, the amount of which shall be determined by the Court having jurisdiction. However, the Central Government may, in circumstances of extreme urgency or public need, authorize another party to manufacture or use the patented pharmaceutical substance upon payment of reasonable compensation to the patentee, as determined by the Court. The rights conferred by this Act are personal to the patentee and are not transferable except as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity of a patent for a pharmaceutical substance may be adjudicated by the appropriate High Court.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include any novel chemical entity, salt, ester, isomer, polymorph, metabolite, prodrug, complex or combination thereof, exhibiting a demonstrable pharmacological effect. The Controller, subject to the provisions herein, may require the applicant to furnish detailed information regarding the method of manufacture and the pharmacological properties of such pharmaceutical substance, to ascertain its novelty and inventive step. Any application claiming a pharmaceutical substance shall also disclose, where applicable, data establishing its efficacy and safety, as per guidelines issued by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization. A claim for a pharmaceutical substance shall not be allowable if it lacks sufficient basis in experimental data, or if the claimed substance is obvious to a person skilled in the art, having regard to the prior art. Provided that, a combination of known pharmaceutical substances may be patentable if it demonstrates synergistic effects not previously known. The applicant shall bear the responsibility for the accuracy of all data submitted.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel subject to demonstration of inherent efficacy and a clear departure from prior art as established through diligent searching of both Indian and international patent literature. Any application claiming a pharmaceutical substance shall include comprehensive data regarding its chemical characterization, including structural elucidation and spectral analysis, and shall further detail the method of manufacture, ensuring reproducibility and scalability. Provided that, a substance previously known for a different therapeutic application may be patented if a new and non-obvious medical use is demonstrated, subject to rigorous clinical trial evidence. The applicant may also submit comparative data establishing improved bioavailability or reduced toxicity relative to existing treatments. Compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice guidelines is mandatory for all patented pharmaceutical substances intended for commercial production, as provided herein. Failure to adhere to these requirements may invalidate the patent.

Any person manufacturing, importing, selling, or distributing a pharmaceutical substance, not duly patented as provided herein, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. Where a pharmaceutical substance is demonstrated to be substantially derived from indigenous knowledge, including traditional Ayurvedic formulations, without due acknowledgement or benefit-sharing with the concerned communities, the penalty shall be doubled. The Controller of Patents, upon receiving credible evidence of such infringement, may issue a cease and desist order and initiate proceedings for recovery of damages. Any appeal against such order shall lie before the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order’s issuance, subject to deposit of a security equivalent to twenty-five percent of the claimed damages. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved.

Any assignment of the right to a patent for a pharmaceutical substance, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and shall specify the territory in which the assignment is to have effect. An assignee of such right or interest, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall possess the same rights and remedies as the original patentee in respect of the pharmaceutical substance, including the right to grant licenses to others for its manufacture, use, or sale. Where a pharmaceutical substance is jointly owned, the rights and obligations of the co-owners shall be determined by mutual agreement; provided that, in the absence of such agreement, no co-owner may grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other co-owners. Any license granted under this Act relating to a pharmaceutical substance may include provisions regarding quality control and access to regulatory data, as deemed necessary by the Controller. The Controller may, upon application, record any assignment or license relating to a pharmaceutical substance in the Register of Patents.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel subject to a rigorous assessment of prior art as determined by the Controller, and any challenge to such assessment may be brought before the Appellate Board. However, mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance, even if isolated, does not constitute inventive step unless significant modification or application is demonstrated. Where a pharmaceutical substance is claimed as an analogue of a known compound, substantial improvement in efficacy or reduced adverse effects shall be prerequisites for patentability, and the burden of proof rests with the applicant. Any dispute regarding the interpretation of ‘substantial improvement’ may be referred to a technical expert appointed by the Appellate Board, whose decision shall be final and binding, provided that such expert’s fee is borne by the disputing party. A claim for a pharmaceutical substance lacking demonstrable industrial application shall be deemed invalid.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel subject to a rigorous examination of prior art established through publicly available scientific literature and demonstrable technical effect. Any person claiming inventorship of such a substance must furnish complete and accurate details of its composition, method of manufacture, and intended medical use, as provided herein. Should a dispute arise regarding the true inventor, the Controller of Patents may, after due inquiry and consideration of evidence submitted by all parties, determine inventorship based on a preponderance of evidence. An appeal from any decision of the Controller regarding inventorship or novelty shall lie before the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit and accompanied by the requisite fee. Failure of any person to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the patent application or revocation of a granted patent.

A pharmaceutical substance shall be deemed to include any chemical entity, salt, ester, isomer, complex, or derivative thereof, exhibiting a demonstrable pharmacological effect and possessing a novel structural configuration not previously known or publicly available as provided herein. The determination of novelty shall be subject to a rigorous assessment of prior art, encompassing both published literature and publicly used substances. Where a pharmaceutical substance is claimed to originate from a specific geographical indication, proof of consistent characteristics attributable to that geographical origin, and a demonstrable link between the substance’s qualities and its place of production, may be required for the purposes of establishing authenticity and preventing misleading representation of goods geographical. Any substance failing to meet these criteria shall not be considered a pharmaceutical substance under this Act.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel subject to the provisions herein relating to prior art, and must demonstrate inherent efficacy as determined by established pharmacological testing protocols. Any claim to a pharmaceutical substance derived from or incorporating biological material originating from a breeder of plants or animals shall require full disclosure of the origin of said material and acknowledgement of the breeder’s contribution in the patent application. The Controller, upon reasonable grounds, may request supplementary information from the applicant regarding the biological origin and breeding process, and failure to provide such information within a period of ninety days may be considered grounds for rejection of the application. Provided that, where a pharmaceutical substance is substantially similar to a known substance, the inventive step must relate to a demonstrable improvement in therapeutic effect or a reduction in adverse side effects. Any dispute regarding the breeder’s contribution shall be subject to adjudication by a duly constituted expert committee as provided herein.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of grant of patent under this Act, shall be considered novel subject to a comprehensive search report establishing absence of prior public knowledge. Any proposed registered proprietor seeking patent for such a substance shall furnish detailed information regarding its efficacy, safety, and method of manufacture, conforming to standards prescribed by the Controller. Compliance with these standards is a necessary condition for processing the application. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, request additional data or clarification from the proposed registered proprietor if the initially submitted information is deemed insufficient. Failure to adequately address such requests within a stipulated timeframe may result in rejection of the application, as provided herein. The substance must also demonstrate a demonstrable therapeutic benefit over existing treatments to be eligible for patent protection.

An assignment denomination variety shall be considered distinct if it demonstrates the characteristics of a clearly distinguishable, uniform and stable variety, as evidenced by the results of relevant trials conducted in accordance with the guidelines established under this Act. A denomination, once assigned and registered, shall be the property of the breeder or his successor, subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licensing as provided herein. Any transfer of rights in an assignment denomination variety, including assignment, mortgage, or license, shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, a change in the breeder’s name or legal entity shall not constitute a transfer requiring separate registration, but notification to the Authority is mandatory. The Authority may refuse registration of a denomination if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing variety.

Any person applying for registration of a new plant variety shall, as a prerequisite to the examination of the application, propose a denomination for such variety which shall be distinct, and shall not cause confusion with any variety already registered or commonly known. The proposed denomination, conforming to the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, may be a breeder’s designation or a variety name, provided that it is not misleading or deceptive. An assignment denomination variety, once accepted by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, becomes the official designation for the registered plant variety and is recorded in the Plant Variety Register. Should the applicant fail to propose a suitable denomination, the Authority may assign one subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. The denomination shall remain associated with the variety throughout the period of protection granted under this Act, unless a valid request for amendment is approved. Any transfer of rights relating to the variety shall also include the assignment of the denomination.

Any registered breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, being an assignment denomination variety, shall have the right to sell, distribute, import, export, and produce seeds or other propagating material of such variety, subject to the provisions of this Act. A breeder may assign, by way of contract, the rights vested in him in respect of the variety, or any combination thereof, to any other person or entity, provided that such assignment is in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all assignments recorded under this Act, accessible for inspection during office hours. Where a farmer, by virtue of having substantially contributed to the development of an assignment denomination variety, is recognised as a breeder, the provisions relating to assignment shall apply mutatis mutandis, with the addition that any benefit sharing arrangement must be explicitly detailed within the assignment contract. Failure to register an assignment shall not invalidate the assignment itself, but may affect the enforceability of rights against third parties unaware of the transfer.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a certificate of registration, propose a suitable denomination for such variety which shall conform to the requirements prescribed under the regulations framed by the Authority. The proposed denomination, constituting an assignment denomination variety, must be distinct, readily distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same or closely related species, and not likely to cause confusion with existing denominations in the relevant sector. 

Provided that the Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, reject a proposed denomination if it considers it to be misleading, generic, or contrary to public order or morality. Where a breeder has assigned a denomination, such assignment shall be recorded in the Plant Variety Register and shall be binding on subsequent assignees of the breeder’s rights, unless otherwise agreed by the parties concerned and notified to the Authority. The Authority shall maintain a comprehensive index of all registered denominations to facilitate effective variety identification and prevent duplication.

Every applicant for registration of a new plant variety shall, prior to the commencement of the examination process, submit a declaration detailing the distinctness, uniformity and stability characteristics of the claimed variety, as provided herein. A proposed assignment denomination variety must be clearly and accurately represented in the application, and shall not cause confusion with any variety already registered or commonly known. The denomination shall be composed of letters and may include numerals, provided that it does not exceed thirty characters. Where a variety is derived from, or is essentially a descendant of, an existing registered variety, the applicant may request the retention of the parent variety’s denomination, subject to demonstrating substantial development and demonstrating a clear distinction in traits. The Authority reserves the right to reject a denomination deemed unsuitable or misleading, and may require the applicant to propose an alternative. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable denomination to that variety, ensuring it does not cause confusion with existing varieties, and shall submit the same with the application for registration as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to established procedures, reject a denomination if it is deemed generic, misleading, or protected by prior rights. A farmer or group of farmers who have developed an assignment denomination variety, and who seek registration, shall be entitled to retain the exclusive right to use that denomination in commerce. Any unauthorized use of a registered assignment denomination variety, or a denomination so similar as to cause deception, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the application liable to rejection and may attract further penalties under this Act.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, submit a clear and unambiguous assignment of the denomination proposed for that variety, demonstrating exclusive right to propagate and commercially exploit the said variety under this Act. The assignment shall specify the scope of rights transferred, including but not limited to, the geographical territory and duration of the assignment, and shall be executed in favour of the applicant or a legally permissible entity. Provided that, where the variety is jointly developed, the assignment may reflect proportionate ownership of the denomination and associated rights amongst the co-developers, subject to mutual agreement evidenced in writing. The Registrar may, however, refuse to accept an assignment if it deems the proposed denomination to be misleading or likely to cause confusion with existing registered varieties, or if the assignment does not adequately protect the interests of farmers and breeders as provided herein. Any transfer of an assignment denomination variety shall be registered with the Authority to ensure transparency and enforceability.

The aggrieved party, M/s. GreenLife Seeds, has filed an appeal before the Appellate Board contesting the Registrar’s refusal to recognize ‘Krishna Gold’ as a valid assignment denomination variety for its newly developed brinjal line. The Registrar, in its order dated 14th July, 2023, held that the proposed denomination lacked distinctiveness, being deceptively similar to a locally known traditional variety, ‘Kanaka’. GreenLife Seeds maintains that ‘Krishna Gold’ represents a significantly improved plant with enhanced yield and disease resistance, justifying its unique designation. The Registrar further noted that the applicant failed to adequately demonstrate the maintenance of a breeder’s book as required for a variety registered under this Act, and that the proposed denomination did not adhere to the principles of simplicity and ease of pronunciation. The Appellate Board, subject to verification of the breeder’s book and a comparative analysis of the characteristics of ‘Krishna Gold’ and ‘Kanaka’, may direct the Registrar to reconsider the application. Provided that, such reconsideration shall be limited to the issue of denomination distinctiveness.

Every applicant for registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a breeder’s certificate, propose a denomination which is clearly distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same or closely related species or genera, and which is not likely to cause confusion with varieties already known. The proposed denomination, constituting the assignment denomination variety, shall conform to the requirements specified in the regulations framed under this Act, and shall not include misleading or deceptive elements. Where the breeder has assigned the right to exploit the variety, or where the right has been transmitted by operation of law or by way of inheritance, the entitled assignment transmission of such rights shall be subject to the provisions relating to notification of change in ownership. The Authority may, however, require amendment of the denomination if it deems it necessary for clarity or to avoid conflict with existing denominations, provided that such amendment does not materially alter the identity of the variety.

Any person claiming to be the breeder of, or having a right to, a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, may apply for registration of such variety under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. Where a variety is registered, the breeder shall be entitled to sell, distribute, import, export, and produce the variety, provided that such activities do not contravene any other law for the time being in force. An assignment denomination variety, once registered, confers upon the registered breeder the exclusive right to commercialize the plant variety for a specified period. However, a farmer who has, in good faith, saved seeds of a protected variety for personal use shall not be restricted by the rights conferred herein. Should any person infringe upon the rights of the breeder, the aggrieved party, being the indication plaintiff, may seek redressal through civil proceedings, including an injunction and damages as determined by the competent court. The Authority may, upon sufficient cause, revoke the registration of a variety if it is proven that the variety does not meet the criteria for registration as provided herein.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a breeder’s right, assign a unique and readily distinguishable denomination to such variety, ensuring it is not likely to cause confusion with varieties already protected or commonly known. The assigned denomination, constituting the assignment denomination variety, must conform to the standards prescribed in the Common Regulations pertaining to the composition and presentation of variety designations. Provided that, if a variety is commonly known by a particular name in the relevant trade channels, the Authority may, subject to justifiable cause, permit the continued use of that name as the denomination, notwithstanding the requirement for uniqueness. Any transfer of the breeder’s right shall necessitate the corresponding transfer of the assignment denomination variety to the transferee, recorded with the Authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding denomination assignment may render the application for registration liable to rejection, or the breeder’s right subject to revocation. The Authority reserves the right to request modification of a denomination if deemed necessary for clarity or to avoid misleading the public.

Every applicant for registration of a new plant variety shall, prior to filing a complete application, ensure the proposed assignment denomination variety is clearly distinguishable from any commonly known denomination of any other variety of the same genus or species, or of a closely related species. The denomination must not mislead or deceive the public as to the characteristics of the variety. The Plant Variety Protection Authority shall, upon receiving an application, conduct a preliminary examination to verify compliance with these requirements and may require the applicant to amend the proposed denomination if it is found to be in violation. Provided that, if the applicant fails to amend the denomination to the satisfaction of the Authority within a period of ninety days from the date of such requirement, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. The Patent Office shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all assigned denominations, updated quarterly, to facilitate transparency and prevent future conflicts. Any dispute regarding denomination assignment shall be subject to the dispute resolution mechanism as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “person” shall include any natural person, artificial person, legal entity, or body, whether incorporated or not, capable of possessing rights and obligations and acting under the law. A “small entity” shall be deemed to be a person, and is defined as an individual inventor, or a start-up, or a micro, small or medium enterprise as defined under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. Where a person acts as an agent on behalf of another person, both the principal and the agent may be considered persons under this Act, subject to the terms of their agency. Any reference to a person shall, where the context so requires, extend to their legal representatives and successors in title.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial juridical person, firm, company, association, or body corporate, whether incorporated or not, and shall also extend to the Government and any agency thereof acting in a commercial capacity. Where an application for registration of a patent is made by a person not ordinarily resident in India, that person shall designate a local agent, being a person holding a certificate entitling them to practice before the Patent Office, to act on their behalf and receive notices. Any communication relating to the application shall be addressed to such agent, and service upon the agent shall be deemed service upon the applicant. A person claiming to be the assignee of a patent shall submit evidence of assignment as provided herein, and failure to do so may result in rejection of the claim. The term ‘small entity’ shall refer to a person meeting the criteria established by notification.

A person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, or by any act or omission of such Controller in the exercise of functions under this Act, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Any association of persons, duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and demonstrably representing the interests of inventors or patent holders, shall be deemed to have sufficient locus standi to bring such appeal. Provided that the grounds for appeal must relate directly to a refusal of a patent application, a revocation of a patent, or a determination concerning ownership of a patent. Where a person is deemed to be an ‘interested person’ as defined herein, and suffers demonstrable harm as a direct result of a patent grant or refusal, such person may seek redress through the established judicial process. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party, subject to limitations as may be prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial person, legal entity, or body, whether incorporated or unincorporated, recognized by law as having rights and obligations. Where an application is made jointly by multiple persons, each person shall be jointly and severally liable for all acts and omissions relating to the application, subject to any agreement to the contrary recorded with the Controller. A “small entity”, for the purposes of reduced fees as provided herein, shall mean a person, micro-enterprise, or non-profit organization meeting criteria established by notification. Any communication directed to multiple persons shall be deemed sufficient if addressed to one designated representative acting on behalf of all. Where a person is deemed incapable of acting, a legally appointed guardian or representative may exercise rights on their behalf, provided that proof of such appointment is furnished to the Controller. The Controller may require verification of the identity of any person claiming rights under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial person, legal entity, or body, whether incorporated or unincorporated. Where a person claims rights as an inventor, that person shall be deemed to have full capacity to exercise such rights, subject to the provisions relating to assignment and transmission as provided herein. Any application submitted under this Act on behalf of a minor or a person of unsound mind shall require the consent of a legally appointed guardian, and such guardian shall be responsible for all communications and undertakings made in connection with the application. A person who knowingly provides false information in any document filed under this Act may be subject to penalties, including revocation of any patent granted based on such information. Provided that, a nominee or legal representative acting on behalf of a deceased person shall be considered a person entitled to pursue proceedings under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial juridical person, firm, company, association, or body, whether incorporated or not, and shall extend to include an agent acting on behalf of any such entity. Any person found to be knowingly and falsely representing themselves as an inventor, with intent to deceive and obtain a patent, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any person who abets or conspires with another in such misrepresentation shall be subject to the same penalties as the principal offender. Where a patent is granted based on such false representation, the patent shall be void ab initio, and any profits derived therefrom shall be recoverable as damages. Subject to the provisions herein, the Controller may, after due inquiry, impose additional conditions on any person found to be repeatedly violating these provisions.

A person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the right to a patent, or any share therein, to any other person, whether natural or juridical, by a written instrument duly executed by both parties and attested by at least two witnesses. Any assignment not so executed and attested shall be void. Where a person, being the assignee of a patent, dies, the patent shall vest in his legal representatives, and they may assign the same in like manner as the original patentee could have done. A licensee, unless expressly authorized by the patentee, shall not further assign his interest in the license.
