The term “person” as used herein shall include any body corporate, association, or firm, and the Government shall be deemed to be a person for all purposes under this Act. Any agreement restricting the assignment of a patent to a person ordinarily resident in India shall be void, provided that such restriction is not otherwise lawful under any other enactment for the time being in force.

For the purposes of this Act, a “person” shall include any natural person, artificial juridical person, or a legal entity capable of holding rights and obligations, and shall extend to include a Hindu Undivided Family acting through its Karta. Any dispute regarding the determination of a “person” entitled to benefits as provided herein, or alleging misrepresentation as to the identity of a person claiming such benefits, may be raised before the Controller. The Controller’s decision on such a dispute shall be subject to appeal to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. Provided that, a claim of beneficial ownership by a person not directly named in a patent application requires demonstrable evidence of assignment or a legally valid chain of title. Furthermore, any person alleging infringement must establish their standing as a ‘person interested’ by demonstrating a direct commercial or research interest adversely affected by the alleged infringement. The Controller may, at their discretion, require corroborating evidence of such interest.

A person, for the purposes of this Act, shall include any legal entity, whether incorporated or not, and shall, where applicable, extend to assignees of right, licensees, and those deriving title under such assignees or licensees. Where a claim is made concerning a biotechnological application, the Controller may, subject to the provisions contained herein, require the applicant to demonstrate the standing of the person making the claim, particularly regarding ownership of the originating genetic material. Any application not complying with the requirements as prescribed, including those relating to the identification of the person and their domicile, may be deemed incomplete and shall be returned to the applicant with a statement of objections. The Controller shall, however, provide an opportunity for remedy, allowing the person a period of thirty days to rectify any deficiencies. A person aggrieved by any decision of the Controller may, as provided herein, file an appeal before the Appellate Board. Failure to respond within the prescribed timeframe will result in the application being rejected.

A person, for the purposes of determining entitlement to a patent as provided herein, shall be construed broadly to include any juridical entity capable of owning property and bearing legal obligations, notwithstanding any distinction between natural and artificial persons. Where a claim of prior art is asserted by a person alleging lack of novelty or inventive step, such person shall furnish detailed particulars of the alleged prior art, including date and place of public knowledge, to the Controller within ninety days of the filing of the complete specification. Should the Controller deem such particulars insufficient, a further period of sixty days may be granted, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. In cases involving technologies critical to necessary security india, the Central Government may, by notification, direct the Controller to expedite examination or maintain confidentiality of the application for a specified period, even if such action deviates from standard procedures. Any decision of the Controller may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates sufficient locus standi and irreparable harm.

A “means member appellate” shall refer to a person appointed by the Central Government from amongst persons possessing technical expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design or related fields, and shall serve as a member of the Layout-Design Appellate Board. The Layout-Design Appellate Board shall be constituted with a Chairperson and not less than two means member appellate, and may include additional members as the Central Government deems necessary for the efficient discharge of its functions as provided herein. Any vacancy amongst the means member appellate shall be filled by the Central Government in like manner, and the Board shall continue to function effectively notwithstanding any such vacancy, subject to a quorum of at least the Chairperson and one means member appellate being present. The terms and conditions of service of the means member appellate shall be such as prescribed by the Central Government.

Any person desiring to register a layout-design shall submit an application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in Schedule I. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, including its topological characteristics and the semiconductor integrated circuit in which it is incorporated. Where the applicant is not the creator of the layout-design, a statement of transfer of rights, duly executed by the creator, shall be furnished. The Registry, upon examination, may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information, and shall communicate any such requirement within thirty days of the application’s receipt. A request for reconsideration of a rejected application may be made to the Registry within sixty days. Any dispute regarding the validity of a registration, or the rights of a means member appellate, shall be subject to the provisions for appeal as provided herein, and the decision of the Appellate Authority shall be final and binding. Registration shall confer a right to prevent any unauthorized reproduction or commercial exploitation of the layout-design.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringing act has occurred or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The plaintiff shall, prior to the institution of such suit, provide the defendant with at least thirty days’ notice of the alleged infringement, detailing the nature of the claim and the specific layout-design asserted to be infringed. The Court, upon being satisfied of prima facie infringement and irreparable harm, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. A means member appellate, constituted for the purpose of hearing appeals from orders of the District Court relating to interim injunctions or damages, shall have the power to modify or vacate any such order. The aggrieved party may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, seek recovery of damages for the infringement, which shall be proportionate to the actual loss suffered or the profits unjustly gained by the defendant, whichever is higher.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with the decision of a Licensing Authority, may prefer an appeal to the means member appellate within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions contained herein. The appeal shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a certified copy of the order, all relevant documents relied upon, and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The means member appellate shall, upon receipt of such appeal, fix a date for hearing and issue notice to the Licensing Authority and any other party concerned, providing them with a reasonable opportunity to present their case. The means member appellate may, if deemed necessary, require the appellant to deposit a sum equivalent to the costs of the Licensing Authority, as a condition for proceeding with the appeal. Provided that, the means member appellate shall not entertain any appeal unless satisfied that substantial questions of law or fact are involved, and that the appeal is not frivolous or vexatious. All decisions of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as may be available under the Constitution.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar, or by a decision refusing to grant registration, may file an appeal to the means member appellate within sixty days from the date of such order or decision, subject to the payment of such fee as may be prescribed. The appeal shall be in such form and shall be accompanied by such documents, as may be determined by regulations. Provided that, the means member appellate may, for sufficient cause, extend the time for filing an appeal but not beyond an additional thirty days. All appeals shall be heard by a Bench constituted as provided herein, and the decision of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, except where a question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court. Any party to an appeal shall have the right to present evidence and arguments before the means member appellate. The Registrar shall transmit all relevant records to the means member appellate without delay.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a layout-design registered under this Act as their own, or uses such a layout-design without the authorization of the registered owner, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees. The court, as provided herein, may also order the seizure and destruction of all infringing articles and materials used in the manufacture thereof. A means member appellate, constituted for the expeditious hearing of disputes relating to infringement, shall have the power to impose such fines and direct such remedies. Any appeal against the decision of a means member appellate shall lie before the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. Failure to comply with an order of the court shall constitute a separate offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Any registered layout-design right, as provided herein, may be assigned, transferred, or licensed, wholly or partially, by the registered proprietor to any other person, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties and recorded with the appropriate authority. Where a license is granted, the licensor shall retain all rights not expressly granted to the licensee, and any subsequent assignment of the layout-design right shall be subject to the terms of such license. A means member appellate, constituted for the purpose of hearing appeals related to the validity of registrations or disputes concerning the exploitation of layout-designs, shall have the power to regulate its own procedure, consistent with the principles of natural justice. The registered proprietor may, by a written instrument, nominate a successor-in-title to whom the rights shall devolve upon the proprietor’s death or insolvency, and such nomination shall be effective upon intimation to the authority. Any agreement concerning the assignment or licensing of a layout-design right must be in writing and clearly define the scope of rights granted.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar, including the refusal of an application for registration or the revocation of a registered layout-design, may prefer an appeal to the means member appellate within a period of ninety days from the date of such order, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The appellate authority shall, upon receipt of a duly filed appeal and the associated records from the Registrar, constitute a bench for its adjudication. Provided that, the means member appellate may, for reasons to be recorded, extend the time for filing an appeal, but not exceeding a further period of thirty days. Any decision of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice. The Registrar shall transmit all relevant documentation to the appellate authority without delay upon notification of the appeal.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design, or rejecting an application for amendment of a registered layout-design, may prefer an appeal to the means member appellate within a period of ninety days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of such fee as may be prescribed. The appellate authority shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, and considering the evidence adduced before it, pass such order as it deems fit, confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal relates to a registered layout-design, any other person having a substantial interest and likely to be affected by the outcome of the appeal may be joined as a party, provided that such person demonstrates a legally relating registered right. Decisions of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, except where a question of law of general public importance arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, its essential features, and a representation thereof, which may be a schematic diagram or a photograph. A statement of ownership, clearly identifying the applicant as the proprietor, is also mandatory for successful registration. Should the application lack clarity or require amendment, the Registry may issue an examination report, allowing the applicant a period of thirty days to rectify the deficiencies. 

A means member appellate, constituted for the purpose of hearing and deciding on appeals arising from decisions of the Registry regarding the validity of registrations or refusals thereof. Any aggrieved party may, subject to the provisions herein, prefer an appeal to the means member appellate, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registry’s decision. The Registry shall, while processing applications, also consider any existing rights under the India Trade Mark Act, 1999, to prevent conflict and ensure clarity of ownership.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to the registration of a layout-design, or the refusal thereof, may appeal to the means member appellate within ninety days from the date of such order, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The means member appellate shall, upon receipt of an appeal, fix a date for hearing and shall give notice thereof to the Registrar and to the appellant. The Registrar, being a recording means person, shall furnish to the means member appellate all documents relating to the case within thirty days of receipt of the notice. The means member appellate may, if deemed necessary, require the attendance of witnesses or the production of further evidence. Any decision of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, subject to the provisions of writ jurisdiction by the High Court. Failure to prefer an appeal within the stipulated time shall not bar a party from seeking redressal through other legal remedies available.

Any aggrieved person may appeal to the means member appellate against any decision of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design or revoking a registration, subject to the provisions of this Act. The appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The means member appellate may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to furnish a bank guarantee or other security to ensure the payment of costs, if deemed necessary. A respondent may file a written response to the appeal within sixty days of receiving notice. 

Where a layout-design is registered jointly, any act of licence relating to the layout-design shall require the consent of all registered owners, unless otherwise agreed in writing. The means member appellate shall have the power to summon witnesses and documents, and to issue commissions for the examination of witnesses who are unable to attend before the appellate forum. Decisions of the means member appellate shall be final and binding, save for any right of judicial review as may be available under the Code of Civil Procedure.

An invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be understood as a novel solution to a technical problem, whether embodied in a product or a process. Such an invention must demonstrate a sufficient level of inventive step, meaning it is not an obvious variation of existing knowledge to a person ordinarily skilled in the relevant field. A mere discovery of a naturally occurring phenomenon, without human intervention to apply it to a new and useful purpose, shall not constitute an invention as provided herein. The potential for industrial application is a prerequisite; an invention lacking practical utility or incapable of being manufactured or used in any kind of industry shall not be patentable subject to the provisions contained herein. An invention may also be based upon an improvement in an existing invention.

An invention, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be deemed to include any new and useful art, process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, not previously known to the public. A claim for an invention must fully and clearly define the scope of the subject matter for which protection is sought, and shall be supported by a detailed description enabling a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. 

Provided that an invention shall not be patentable if it is merely a discovery of a naturally occurring substance, or an aggregation of known properties, unless a technical effect is demonstrated. Any combination of existing elements, to be considered an invention, must demonstrate synergy resulting in an effect not predictable from the individual components. The applicant shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out the invention.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act shall have the right to institute a suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred. The patentee, or assignee of the patent, may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from the acts constituting the infringement, and may also claim damages for any loss suffered due to such infringement. A court may, subject to the provisions contained herein, grant an order of account, requiring the defendant to pay the patentee a reasonable royalty for past use of the patented invention. 

Where a defendant proves invalidity of the patent, or revocation thereof, the court shall dismiss the suit. Any person making a frivolous or vexatious claim of infringement shall be liable to pay costs to the defendant. An invention, if proven to be novel and non-obvious, shall be eligible for patent protection as provided herein, and the rights conferred thereby are enforceable through the remedies outlined in this section.

An invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include any new and useful art, process, method or machine, apparatus, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, subject to the provisions contained herein. A claim of invention shall not be allowable if it merely results from a discovery of a naturally occurring substance, even if such substance is isolated. However, the purification of such substance, provided that it results in a demonstrable and significant enhancement of known properties, may be considered as potentially inventive. 

Any person alleging to be the true and first inventor shall submit a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect. The Controller of Patents may, at any stage of the application process, require the applicant to furnish further details or evidence to substantiate the novelty and inventive step claimed. Failure to comply with such a requirement may result in the rejection of the application, as provided herein.

An invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel only if it has not been anticipated by any prior publication, whether written or oral, anywhere in the world before the date of filing, or the date of priority, as provided herein. Should a prior publication exist, demonstrating identical features, the claimed invention shall not be deemed patentable, subject to the provisions relating to grace periods as may be prescribed. An invention incorporating traditional knowledge or agro-biological resources shall require demonstration of prior informed consent of the associated community and equitable benefit sharing, as applicable. The applicant shall furnish a clear and concise disclosure of the invention, enabling a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall further demonstrate sufficient enablement and best mode requirements. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements may render the patent application liable to be rejected. Any modification or improvement to a known process shall be considered an invention only if it results in a substantial and demonstrable enhancement of functionality.

Any person who publishes or causes to be published any information relating to an invention, whether patentable or not, with intent to prejudice the grant of a patent to another person, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a person, not being the inventor or the assignee of an invention, applies for a patent under this Act, knowing that such invention is not his own, such application shall be void and the applicant shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine, or with both. Provided that, if the applicant proves that he reasonably believed himself to be the inventor, the court may impose a lesser penalty. Any false representation concerning the inventive step of an invention, made to obtain a patent, constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, revoke a patent obtained through fraudulent means.

Any assignment of the right, title, and interest in any patent or an application for a patent shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the assignment, including any limitations on the exercise of the rights assigned. Where an invention, subject to a pending application, is assigned, the assignee may proceed with the application as if they were the original applicant, subject to fulfilling all requirements as provided herein. A license, whether sole or non-exclusive, granted to any person shall be construed as a contractual arrangement between the patentee and the licensee, and shall not affect the patentee’s right to grant further licenses. 

Any transfer of ownership of an invention, or right therein, without proper written assignment, shall be considered null and void. The patentee may, at their discretion, require the assignee or licensee to furnish security for the due performance of their obligations. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the patent, subject to a hearing as per the established procedures under this Act.

An invention, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be considered novel only if it does not form part of the state of the art prior to the date of the complete specification. Any allegation of prior art, submitted by a party opposing the grant of a patent, shall be accompanied by demonstrably authentic evidence establishing the date and source of such prior art, failing which the Controller may dismiss the opposition. Where a claimed invention is a modification or combination of existing processes, it shall be deemed to involve an inventive step only if such modification or combination results in a non-obvious improvement in functionality or efficiency. An appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding novelty or inventive step may be preferred to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Controller’s order and accompanied by a prescribed fee. The burden of proving lack of inventive step shall lie upon the party alleging it.

An invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be understood as a novel and useful product or process, exhibiting a demonstrable inventive step and capable of application in industry. Such an invention must not fall within the exclusions specified elsewhere in this Act, and shall be assessed based on its inherent qualities, irrespective of its potential commercial success. A valid registered proprietor of an invention, as determined through due process under this Act, shall have the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, importing, or distributing the invention without their authorization. However, this right shall be subject to the provisions relating to government use and compulsory licensing as provided herein, and may be revoked upon established grounds of invalidity. The determination of novelty shall be made with reference to prior art, both domestic and international.

An invention, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel only if it demonstrates a discernible advancement over existing publicly available knowledge, irrespective of whether such knowledge originates from India or elsewhere. A basic registration of the invention’s particulars, including the inventor’s name, address, and a detailed description of the inventive concept, is a prerequisite for proceeding with a full patent application. Provided that, the Controller of Patents may, subject to verification of the initial registration details, grant a provisional registration certificate valid for a period not exceeding six months. Any subsequent amendment to the registered invention shall require a supplementary registration filing and may be subject to examination as if it were a new invention. Failure to maintain the basic registration, including timely renewal of associated fees, may result in the lapse of priority rights as provided herein.

An invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include any new and useful art, process, method or machine, apparatus, substance, or other article, and any new arrangement or combination of existing elements, provided that such arrangement or combination is not merely a duplication of prior art. The Controller, upon examination of a patent application, may require the applicant to demonstrate sufficient inventive step, assessed against the state of the art immediately before the date of the complete specification. Where a patent has been granted for a term, the patentee may apply for renewal of the patent, subject to payment of the prescribed renewal fee and compliance with any conditions as may be stipulated. Failure to pay the renewal fee within the prescribed period shall render the patent liable to lapse, as provided herein, unless condonation is granted by the Controller. Any invention claimed must be clearly and concisely defined in the specification, and any amendment thereto shall not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure.

Any person who publishes or causes to be published any information relating to an invention, whether patentable or not, with intent to deceive the public or to induce the belief that such information constitutes a valid invention as provided herein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The scope of any claims submitted in support of an invention shall be strictly construed, and any claim extending beyond the matter originally described in the complete specification, or any claim which is unclear or indefinite, shall be deemed invalid and subject to revocation. Furthermore, any false representation concerning the novelty of an invention, or the inventive step involved therein, shall constitute an offence under this Act, attracting a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees. Any appeal against a decision regarding the validity of claims shall be made within sixty days of the order.

Justified registration of a trade mark shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean a registration obtained not merely through formal compliance with procedural requirements, but also upon demonstration of genuine use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, and further, a reasonable probability of continued use. A finding of justified registration may be rebutted by evidence establishing that the mark was applied for with intent to block legitimate trade or to unfairly hinder competition. However, a lapse in use, subject to a period not exceeding two years, shall not *per se* invalidate a justified registration, provided that the proprietor demonstrates sufficient cause for such lapse and a clear intention to resume use. The Registrar may, notwithstanding any other provision, require additional evidence to ascertain the veracity of a claim of justified registration.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be justifiably registered under this Act, provided that the application for registration satisfies all requirements as to distinctive character, user, and class of goods or services as detailed in the Schedule. An applicant seeking justified registration must demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, a genuine intention to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified. Where a mark is similar to an existing trade mark, but relates to entirely dissimilar goods or services, registration may be permitted subject to a reasoned finding that no likelihood of confusion exists between the marks, considering all relevant factors including the channels of trade and the consumer base. The Registrar may, however, require an undertaking as to limited co-existence, or a disclaimer of certain goods or services, to ensure clarity and prevent future disputes. Any registration obtained through misrepresentation shall be voidable.

A trade mark proprietor aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration, or requiring an amendment of the register, may, within a period of two months from the date of the communication of such decision, file an appeal with the High Court. Such appeal shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and the High Court shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal is filed, the High Court may, if satisfied that the decision of the Registrar was justified, impose costs on the appellant. However, a finding of justified registration, even if subsequently overturned, does not preclude a proprietor from seeking rectification based on grounds not previously considered. Any person opposing registration may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, request the Registrar to require the applicant to amend the application in a manner that addresses the grounds of opposition, provided that such amendment does not substantially alter the character of the trade mark.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be justifiably registered under this Act, notwithstanding any prior use of a similar mark by another party, provided that the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, a continuous and demonstrable intent to use the mark in relation to specific goods or services. Such intent shall be evidenced by documented preparations for commercialization, including but not limited to, substantial advertising campaigns, secured distribution channels, and significant investment in manufacturing or service provision. The Registrar may, however, require further evidence of such intent if the initial submission is deemed insufficient. 

Where a mark is registered based on a demonstrated intent to use, a statement of actual use must be filed within a period of three years from the date of registration, failing which the registration may be subject to revocation. A finding of justified registration shall not preclude a subsequent challenge based on grounds of deceptive similarity or lack of distinctiveness, as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding justified registration may appeal to the High Court.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be justifiably registered under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates prior, continuous and bona fide use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, and further satisfies the requirements regarding distinctiveness as laid down herein. Evidence of such use may include, but shall not be limited to, invoices, advertising materials, and statutory declarations detailing the extent and duration of commercial exploitation. Where the mark incorporates non-distinctive elements, justification for registration requires proof that the overall impression creates a unique identifier in the marketplace. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted evidence, require additional documentation to ascertain the veracity of claims concerning use. Failure to provide satisfactory proof of justified registration shall render the application liable to be refused, or registration revoked, as the case may be. Any misrepresentation regarding the extent of use will be considered grounds for invalidation.

Any person claiming justified registration of a trade mark, notwithstanding prior use by another, shall submit to the Registrar conclusive evidence of special circumstances demonstrating that non-registration would be detrimental to the interests of the public or the applicant. Failure to provide such evidence within ninety days of notice from the Registrar shall be deemed abandonment of the claim and the application shall be rejected. Where a mark is registered based on a finding of justified registration, the Registrar may, subject to a review petition filed within sixty days, impose reasonable conditions on its use, including limitations on the scope of goods or geographical area. Any contravention of such conditions shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees per instance, and repeated offences may lead to revocation of the registration as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all justified registrations and associated conditions.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right in relation thereto, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the mark, the goods or services in respect of which it is assigned, and the territorial extent of the assignment. A justified registration, being a registration obtained through demonstrable and lawful use, may be assigned with or without the goodwill of the business concerned, however, assignment without goodwill shall not prejudice the rights of the assignor to continue use of the mark in relation to goods or services not covered by the assignment. Where an assignment is made subject to a condition requiring ongoing royalty payments, such conditions shall be enforceable as per the terms stipulated in the instrument of assignment. The Registrar may, upon application, record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks, subject to verification of the instrument and satisfaction that it complies with the requirements as provided herein. Failure to record an assignment does not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against third parties.

A trade mark shall not be refused registration solely on the ground that it is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, provided that the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the mark has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, establishing a clear association in the minds of consumers with the applicant’s goods or services. Any party opposing a registration on this basis shall submit evidence of consumer surveys or sales figures to substantiate a claim of lack of distinctiveness. However, the Registrar may, subject to due process and opportunity for rebuttal, consider evidence of concurrent or prior use by others, even if not formally registered, in determining whether justified registration is appropriate. An appeal from the Registrar’s decision regarding justified registration shall lie before the High Court, with the burden of proof resting on the appellant to demonstrate an error in the Registrar’s assessment of acquired distinctiveness or relevant prior use.

A trade mark shall not be refused registration under this Act solely on the ground that it is descriptive of the goods or services in question, provided that the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Trade Mark Registrar, that through prolonged use, the mark has acquired distinctiveness in the relevant market. The Trade Mark Registrar, in assessing such acquired distinctiveness, shall consider evidence of actual use, advertising expenditure, sales figures, and consumer surveys, as may be deemed relevant. Any decision of the Trade Mark Registrar regarding justified registration may be appealed to the Appellate Board, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a mark is initially considered descriptive, the applicant bears the onus of proving secondary meaning sufficient to establish justified registration. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require a statutory declaration affirming the extent and duration of use, and the nature of evidence supporting the claim of distinctiveness. Failure to comply with such requirement may result in the application being deemed abandoned.

A trade mark proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a license or assign the right to use the trade mark, or a part thereof, to any person, whether corporate or individual, by a written instrument specifying the terms and conditions of such license or assignment, including duration, territory, and goods or services covered. Any assignment not fully complying with these requirements shall be voidable at the option of the assignee. Justified registration of an assignment, to be effective, requires filing with the Trade Marks Registry a memorandum of assignment, duly executed by both the assignor and the assignee, and payment of the prescribed fee. The Registry shall, upon satisfaction of these requirements, record the assignment in its records, thereby establishing a clear chain of title. A licensee shall not acquire any right in the trade mark beyond that expressly granted in the license agreement, and any use exceeding the scope of the license shall constitute an infringement. The proprietor remains responsible for the quality of goods or services associated with the mark, even when used by a licensee.

A farmer, for the purposes of this Act, shall mean any person engaged in the cultivation of land for the purpose of producing any agricultural crop, including seed saving as a traditional practice. Such a farmer may be a small or marginal farmer, as defined by the central government, or any other individual cultivating land, irrespective of the size of holding. Provided that a farmer shall be considered eligible for the rights conferred under this Act if they have demonstrably contributed to the development of a registered plant variety, either independently or through collaboration with breeders or other farmers. A registered plant variety, as defined herein, is subject to the provisions relating to essential characteristics and distinctiveness. Any person claiming to be a farmer shall be required to furnish evidence of their agricultural activity as may be prescribed.

A farmer seeking registration of a new, distinct and stable variety of plant shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, accompanied by the requisite fee and such evidence as may be required. The application shall clearly delineate the characteristics of the claimed variety, demonstrating its novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity, and shall include a declaration affirming that the variety has not been previously exploited commercially or by other means for a period exceeding four years. Any farmer who has bred or developed a new variety, or discovered and cultivated a new variety of any plant, shall be deemed an ‘essentially derived variety’ if it is demonstrably derived from a variety protected under this Act. Provided that, a farmer may retain the right to save, use, sow, replant and exchange farm-saved seeds of a protected variety, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. The Authority may, after examination, grant a certificate of registration to the applicant if satisfied that the variety meets the criteria as provided herein.

A farmer, whose seeds in any variety are registered under this Act, shall be deemed to have a right to save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange and sell such seeds, subject to the provisions contained herein and any notification issued by the Central Government regarding bio-safety or public health concerns. Provided that such farmer shall not be permitted to sell branded seeds of a protected variety, and any such sale shall constitute an infringement actionable as provided herein. Any farmer aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority relating to their rights, may appeal to the High Court, subject to the limitations prescribed by law. Where a farmer demonstrates sustained contribution to the development of a variety through traditional knowledge, they may be recognized as a co-breeder and entitled to a share in any commercial benefits arising from the exploitation of that variety, as determined by the Authority. The Authority shall maintain a register of farmers contributing to plant genetic resources for transparency and equitable benefit sharing.

A farmer shall be deemed to be a ‘breeder’ for the limited purpose of registration of extant varieties, subject to the fulfillment of requirements as may be prescribed, and shall be eligible to register a variety he or she has bred, evolved or developed. Provided that a farmer registering an extant variety under this Act shall not be required to provide proof of origin or essential characteristics other than a declaration affirming that he or she has, for a period of at least six years, been actively involved in the breeding or evolving of the said variety. Any farmer who is a breeder of a registered variety may sell, distribute, and exchange seeds of such variety, subject to the conditions specified in the certificate of registration. Where a farmer saves seeds from his harvest for replanting, such practice shall not be restricted as provided herein, and shall not constitute an infringement of any breeder’s rights. The Authority may, however, establish a system for monitoring seed saving practices to ensure the maintenance of genetic purity and diversity. A farmer aggrieved by any decision of the Authority may appeal to the Central Government.

A farmer shall be deemed to be engaged in the essential activity of crop improvement, provided that such activity results in a newly developed plant variety exhibiting distinct, uniform and stable characteristics. Any farmer saving, selling, sharing or distributing seeds of a protected variety, subject to the conditions prescribed herein, shall not be construed as an infringement of the breeder’s rights. However, a farmer may exercise such rights only for purposes of propagation and multiplication for personal use, and commercial marketing of such seeds requires prior authorization from the breeder or a license issued under this Act. Where a farmer is compelled to use seeds of a protected variety due to force majeure, no liability shall accrue to such farmer, provided that reasonable efforts were made to obtain alternative seed sources. The Registrar may, upon application, register a farmer as a seed producer, subject to verification of compliance with quality control standards.

Any farmer who, in good faith and without knowledge of an extant registered variety of like kind, propagates or multiplies any variety protected under this Act, for purposes of propagation and sale, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding two thousand rupees for each such propagation or multiplication. Provided that, if the farmer can demonstrate reasonable efforts to ascertain the existence of a registered variety prior to such propagation or multiplication, the penalty may be waived at the discretion of the Authority. Furthermore, a farmer knowingly selling seed of a protected variety without authorization, or falsely representing seed as a registered variety, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, and may be subject to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year. Any seed so sold, or represented, shall be deemed forfeited to the Central Government. The Authority may, however, consider extenuating circumstances relating to traditional farming practices when determining penalties applicable to a farmer.

A farmer undertaking the propagation of a registered variety shall be subject to the payment of a royalty, the amount of which shall be determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, taking into consideration the equitability of benefit sharing and the economic viability for both the breeder and the farmer. Provided that a farmer who is engaged in the preservation of a registered variety, and who undertakes propagation solely for personal consumption, shall be exempt from the payment of royalty as provided herein. Any farmer desiring to commercially exploit a protected variety through propagation, shall obtain a license from the breeder or the designated licensing authority, and such license shall specify the terms and conditions governing the propagation, sale, and distribution of the variety. The breeder may, at their discretion, assign the rights to receive royalty to a registered cooperative society of farmers, subject to intimation to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the farmer liable to penalties, including a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

A farmer aggrieved by the refusal of the Plant Variety Protection Authority to register a farmer’s variety, or by any decision concerning the benefit sharing arising from the commercial exploitation of such variety, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed in the Schedule. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both parties, pass an order confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any person claiming to be a farmer and asserting rights under this Act shall furnish proof of their bona fide agricultural activity to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board. Should the Appellate Board find that the appellant was not a genuine farmer at the time of the original grievance, the appeal shall be dismissed with costs. Further, any delay in filing an appeal beyond the stipulated ninety days may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown.

A farmer seeking registration of a new plant variety shall submit a complete application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, detailing the characteristics of the variety as per the established guidelines. The application shall include evidence of the farmer’s contribution to the development of said variety, and proof of its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. Any farmer claiming a right to a variety existing in common knowledge, or one traditionally used by farming communities, shall provide documented evidence of such usage spanning a period not less than twenty-four months prior to the date of the application. Provided that, a farmer who is not the original breeder but has substantially contributed to the development of a variety through repeated selection and improvement, may also submit an application subject to verification of their contribution. The Authority may, at its discretion, require additional information or samples from the farmer to facilitate a thorough assessment of the application. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

A farmer asserting a claim to a registered plant variety, alleging derivation from a locally adapted traditional variety, shall submit evidence of cultivation history extending back a minimum of twenty years, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of such evidence, or the claimed lineage of the variety, may be referred to a specially constituted Seed Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal shall consider, as relevant, any unique layout-design characteristics demonstrably incorporated into the farmer’s variety, distinguishing it from publicly available germplasm. Provided that, a mere resemblance in phenotypic traits shall not, in itself, constitute sufficient proof of derivation. An appeal from the decision of the Seed Tribunal shall lie before the High Court, and shall be heard expeditiously, not exceeding six months from the date of filing. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence, as determined by the Tribunal, shall result in dismissal of the farmer’s claim and may attract penalties as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be capable of being registered under this Act if it is distinctive and not descriptive of the goods or services to which it relates, and does not offend any established principles of morality or public order. The register of trade marks shall contain particulars of the trade mark, including a representation of the mark, the name and address of the applicant, and the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. An application to register trade marks shall be made in writing to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and shall be subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. Provided that, a mark already in use by another party may be subject to opposition proceedings as provided herein, to determine its registrability. Registration confers the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for the registration thereof, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Failure to register trade marks as provided herein shall not invalidate the right of the proprietor to enforce their rights at common law, but such unregistered marks shall not be entitled to the evidentiary benefits afforded to registered marks. Any fraudulent application to register a trade mark, or the filing of false evidence in support of such application, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, with prior approval of the Central Government, impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for any contravention of the provisions of this Act relating to the use of deceptive or falsely applied trade marks. All penalties imposed under this Act shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark for cosmetic preparations shall, in addition to the requirements as provided herein, furnish a certificate of compliance with the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, demonstrating that the formulation for which the trade mark is sought has undergone necessary testing and is approved for use. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted certificate, proceed with the examination of the application for use trade mark. However, the registration shall be provisional and contingent upon the continued validity of the certificate issued under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. Should the certificate lapse or be revoked, the registration of the trade mark shall be subject to review and potential cancellation. An applicant shall also disclose any adverse findings related to the cosmetic preparation, if any, during prior inspections conducted by the licensing authority. Failure to disclose such information may render the registration voidable.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (q) “package” includes any enclosure, wrapping, or container used for the containment, protection, transport, delivery or presentation of goods, whether such enclosure is of natural or artificial material, and whether it is a constituent part of the goods or separate therefrom. Provided that a label affixed to a package, bearing a trade mark, shall be deemed to be part of the package for the purposes of determining infringement under this Act. Furthermore, any device bearing a trade mark intended to be affixed to or displayed with goods, even if not physically part of a package, shall be construed as a package as provided herein, subject to the provisions relating to colour and get-up. A package shall not include any purely functional element devoid of any branding or trade mark application.

Provided that, where a package incorporates a design element distinct from the trade mark itself, such design may be subject to separate registration as an industrial design, subject to the provisions of the Designs Act, 2000. The applicant shall submit a faithful representation of the package as part of the application for trade mark registration, demonstrating its practical application and visual characteristics. A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to maintain a suit for infringement even if the offending package is not directly sold to the public, but is intended for distribution or use in a commercial undertaking.

context: A registered trade mark shall be a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and may consist of words, numerals, letters, devices, symbols, or a combination thereof. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and notice of such assignment shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry. A registered trade mark confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to renewal upon the expiration of the initial registration period of ten years, computed from the date of application, and thereafter every ten years, provided that the proprietor thereof applies for such renewal in the prescribed manner and pays the prescribed fee. Failure to renew a registered trade mark shall render it subject to removal from the Register, as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark has been in continuous use for a period of five years and is well known in India, it may be considered a well-known trade mark, enjoying enhanced protection against infringement, even if not renewed. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry and must be registered to be effective. The Register of Trade Marks shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars contained therein. A person aggrieved by a decision relating to a registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. Any person who, not being the registered proprietor or a permitted user, uses in the course of trade, a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be liable for infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the proprietor of a registered trade mark may maintain a suit for infringement, and may seek an injunction restraining the infringement, as well as damages for any loss suffered. Provided that, no suit for infringement shall be instituted in any court inferior to the District Court. The court, in exercising its jurisdiction, may order the accounts of the defendant to be examined and may award damages based on such accounts, or may grant an account of profits made by the defendant due to the infringement. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for ten years from the date of registration, and may be renewed indefinitely subject to payment of the prescribed fees.

A registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of that right. Where a trade mark has been registered for particular goods or the description thereof, the registration shall not confer any right to use the trade mark for goods which may, by reason of their nature, quality or intended use, be likely to cause confusion or deception. Any person who, not being the registered proprietor, uses in the course of trade a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement. Provided that, no suit for infringement shall lie against a person who uses the trade mark for the purpose of indicating the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, or geographical origin of the goods or services. The Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to such terms as he may deem fit, record a licensee of a registered trade mark in the Register of Trade Marks.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to continuous use for the purpose of maintaining its validity, and failure to demonstrate such use within a period of five years from the date of registration may render the registration liable to be revoked, as provided herein. However, a period of non-use shall not affect a registered trade mark if such non-use is attributable to circumstances beyond the control of the proprietor, including but not limited to acts of God, government regulation restricting trade, or economic hardship demonstrably impacting the proprietor’s ability to conduct business. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument duly executed by both parties and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. The Registry may, upon satisfaction of prescribed fees and verification of the instrument, record the assignment in its records, and such record shall be prima facie evidence of title. A licensee of a registered trade mark shall exercise rights only within the scope of the license granted, and any deviation therefrom may constitute an infringement.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a registered trade mark or a duly licensed user thereof, uses in the course of trade, or for the purpose of any business, any colourable variation of the registered trade mark, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such infringement, and the goods bearing such mark shall be deemed to be counterfeit goods as provided herein. Where the infringement involves goods of a dangerous or counterfeit nature, the penalty shall not be less than one lakh rupees. The Court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, also grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further use of the mark and order the destruction of all infringing goods and materials used in the manufacture thereof. Any appeal against an order of penalty shall lie before the High Court, and shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorised agents. The instrument shall identify the registered trade mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and state the consideration for the assignment, if any. Where the assignment is of a part of the goodwill of the trade mark owner, the assignee shall acquire only the rights assigned and shall not be entitled to any greater interest in the registered trade mark. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license to another person, provided that such assignment does not contravene any provisions contained within the original licensing agreement. The Registrar shall, upon application, record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks, and such record shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment. Failure to record the assignment does not invalidate it, but may affect the assignee’s ability to enforce their rights.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a registered trade mark and alleging an infringement thereof may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both, in the appropriate court. However, a defendant in such proceedings may, by counter-claim, seek rectification of the register on any of the grounds specified herein, including a claim that the registered trade mark is not a trade mark as defined under this Act, or that it is deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark. Where a claim of rectification is successful, the court may, in its discretion, award costs against the plaintiff, and may also direct that the proceedings for infringement be stayed pending final determination of the rectification claim. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted restraining the use of a registered trade mark unless the court is satisfied that the plaintiff has suffered irreparable harm and the balance of convenience lies in their favour. A registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding its continued validity, and the Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, register a transfer of the registered trade mark. Any assignment not duly recorded shall be invalid as against any subsequent assignee or any person acquiring interest in the registered trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence of title before registering a transfer, and shall refuse registration if the transfer would be contrary to law or public policy, or if the applicant fails to satisfy the conditions as provided herein.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a trade mark or a duly licensed user thereof, uses in the course of trade, or advertises for the purpose of trade, any deceptive variant of a registered trade mark, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorised agents. The Trade Mark Registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks, comprising both registered trade marks and applications for registration pending examination. Where the Registry is satisfied that the application meets the requirements, it shall proceed to advertise the application in the prescribed manner. An applicant registration, if accepted, shall confer a right in rem, but is subject to subsequent opposition proceedings as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any stage of the application registration registration process, require further information or clarification from the applicant. Failure to comply with such requests may result in the application being deemed abandoned.

Any applicant registration shall be subject to a diligent search conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain the existence of prior marks or applications which may conflict with the proposed mark. Should an objection arise based on such a search, the applicant shall be furnished with a statement of grounds for objection and afforded a period of thirty days to submit a response, demonstrating the distinctiveness of their mark or rebutting the asserted conflict. Where the response is deemed unsatisfactory, the Registry may, after considering any further submissions, direct the applicant to amend the application or, failing that, refuse registration. An aggrieved applicant may appeal such a refusal to the Appellate Board, providing evidence supporting their claim and demonstrating that the mark satisfies all requirements as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except where a substantial question of law is involved, allowing for further recourse to a higher judicial forum, subject to the limitations prescribed under this Act concerning india application processes.

An applicant registration shall be deemed to have effect from the date of entry in the Register, subject to the provisions contained herein. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon satisfaction of all statutory requirements and payment of the prescribed fees, register a trade mark in the name of the applicant. A certificate of registration shall be issued to the registered proprietor as conclusive evidence of their ownership of the mark, unless and until such registration is revoked or cancelled in accordance with the procedures outlined in this Act. Provided that, the registration of a trade mark shall not confer any right to exclusive use of the mark in relation to goods or services not specified in the application. Any assignment or transmission of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to notification to the Registry and entry in the Register.

Any person claiming to be the registered proprietor of a trade mark, and alleging an infringement thereof, may institute a suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding concurrent jurisdiction of courts. However, prior to the institution of such suit, a notice of intention to sue shall be served upon the alleged infringer, affording them a period of thirty days to remedy the infringement or submit representations. Should the alleged infringer dispute the validity of the registered trade mark, or assert a prior right to the use of a similar mark, the Court may, at its discretion, stay the proceedings pending determination of the validity of the registered proprietor trade. An appeal from any decree or order made by the District Court shall lie to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the decree or order.

A certification trade mark distinguishes goods or services from those of other undertakings based on specific qualities, and shall be registrable under this Act subject to the provisions herein. The proprietor of such a mark certifies that goods or services meet predetermined standards, and does not itself supply those goods or services. An application for registration of a certification trade mark shall include a statement of the criteria used in certifying those goods or services, and the manner of verifying compliance with such criteria. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the applicant is competent to perform the certification function, register the trade mark. Any alteration to the certified standards shall require prior approval of the Registrar, and public notice of such alteration shall be given as prescribed. Failure to adhere to the stated criteria may result in revocation of the registration, as provided herein.

A person seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, demonstrating that the applicant is authorized by the proprietor of the certification trade mark. The application shall include a statement of the particulars of the certification, being a description of the goods or services to which the certification relates, the standards or requirements in respect of those goods or services that are certified, and the manner of verifying that the goods or services meet those standards. The Registrar may, after examining the application and being satisfied that it conforms to the requirements of this Act, accept it and proceed with the advertisement of the trade mark in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, if the certification trade mark is used in relation to goods intended to be exported, the application shall also include evidence of use in the country of export. Any objection to the registration of a certification trade mark shall be dealt with as provided herein for opposition to the registration of an ordinary trade mark, subject to such modifications as the Registrar deems fit.

A certification trade mark, denoting goods or services meeting a defined standard, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to registration and renewal, provided that the proprietor of such mark shall demonstrate continued adherence to the standards certified at the time of each renewal application. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of certification to their goods or services, or by the revocation of certification previously granted, may submit a reasoned representation to the Registrar, who shall consider such representation and may, subject to such terms and conditions as deemed appropriate, direct a re-examination of the goods or services in question. Where a collective trade mark is also employed in conjunction with a certification trade mark, the rights of the collective mark holders shall not be prejudiced, but the certification mark shall take precedence in matters of quality assurance. Any false application of a certification trade mark, or any misrepresentation regarding certification status, shall be actionable under this Act, attracting remedies including injunction and damages.

A certification trade mark, distinct from a traditional trade mark denoting origin in a specific undertaking, shall be subject to a special regime as provided herein. An application for the registration of a certification trade mark shall include a statement detailing the nature of the certification, the standards to be certified, the manner of certification, and the persons or classes of persons authorized to use the mark upon certification. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require further evidence demonstrating the applicant’s capacity to effectively exercise control over the use of the certification trade mark and to ensure consistent standards. Any aggrieved person may, subject to prescribed procedure, apply to the Registrar for revocation of a certification trade mark where the standards certified are no longer maintained or where the applicant fails to exercise reasonable supervision over the use of the mark by certified users. The Registrar shall, in considering such applications, afford an opportunity of being heard to both the owner of the certification trade mark and any representative body of certified users. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the registration liable to be revoked.

A certification trade mark applied for under this Act shall be subject to examination to ensure compliance with the standards governing the goods or services certified, and the Registrar may require submission of evidence demonstrating adherence to such standards. The applicant shall, at the time of application, furnish a detailed statement outlining the nature of the certification, the standards applied, and the procedures for verifying conformity. Any alteration to these standards, or the procedures for verification, shall be promptly notified to the Registrar and may necessitate a re-examination of the certification trade mark. Where a certification trade mark is used in relation to goods failing to meet the certified standards, or where the certifying authority fails to independently verify compliance, the mark may be subject to revocation as provided herein. The owner of a certification trade mark shall maintain records demonstrating ongoing quality control and shall make such records available for inspection upon request. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the registration liable to be cancelled.

Any person falsely representing a certification trade mark as applied to goods or services shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The owner of a registered certification trade mark, or any designated agent, may initiate proceedings for infringement before a District Court having jurisdiction. Where a court finds a violation of certification trade mark rights, it may impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Furthermore, any goods bearing such false representation shall be deemed counterfeit and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Any person abetting the aforementioned offence shall be liable for the same penalties. The Registrar may, subject to due process, revoke a certification trade mark if the certifying body fails to maintain standards or exercises the right unfairly.

A certification trade mark, denoting goods or services conforming to specified standards, may be licensed by the proprietor to multiple traders subject to conditions ensuring continued adherence to those standards as determined by the certifying authority. Any such licensing agreement shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of its execution, failing which the agreement shall be deemed void. The proprietor of a certification trade mark shall maintain a register of licensees, accessible for inspection by any person upon reasonable request and payment of a prescribed fee. Assignment of the right to use a certification trade mark is permissible only with the prior approval of the Registrar, and shall be subject to a demonstration that the assignee possesses the capacity to maintain the requisite standards. Where a licensee materially breaches the terms of the licensing agreement or fails to meet the certified standards, the proprietor may, as provided herein, revoke the license after serving a notice of thirty days and an opportunity to be heard. The Registrar may, upon application, direct the proprietor to take specific actions to ensure compliance by licensees.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a certification trade mark, or by any direction made by the Registrar in respect of conditions governing the use of such mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. An appeal under this Act relating to a certification trade mark shall be adjudicated upon considering evidence pertaining to the standards and procedures established by the proprietor of the certification trade mark, and whether those standards are consistently applied. Where a dispute arises concerning the use of a certification trade mark and the adherence to prescribed standards, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, direct an inspection of the goods or services bearing the mark. Any decision of the Appellate Board may be challenged before the High Court on grounds of legal error apparent on the face of the record.

Any person employing a certification trade mark in a manner that falsely represents goods or services as certified by a legitimate certifying authority, or who forges such a mark, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of such unlawful use. The Registrar may, upon application and sufficient cause shown, grant an ex parte injunction restraining any person from making unauthorized use of a registered certification trade mark, provided that notice of such application has been served upon the alleged infringer and they have failed to appear or adequately respond. Any goods bearing a falsely applied certification trade mark shall be deemed counterfeit goods and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. A proprietor of a registered certification trade mark, aggrieved by any infringement, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or an account of profits. Repeated violations of these provisions shall attract enhanced penalties and potential imprisonment not exceeding two years.

The Registrar may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the form of petition for all applications and proceedings under this Act, including but not limited to applications for registration, rectification, revocation, and assignment of layout-design rights. Such form shall be designated as the ‘zm form petition’ and shall specify the particulars required to be furnished, the supporting documents to be annexed, and the fee payable, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any petition not conforming to the prescribed zm form petition, or lacking the required information or fee, may be rejected by the Registrar. The Registrar may, however, require rectification of any defect in the petition within a reasonable period, provided that such rectification does not materially alter the nature of the application or proceeding. All prescribed fees shall be non-refundable, except as otherwise provided.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a petition to the Controller of Patents, Designs and Trademarks in the prescribed form, hereinafter referred to as the zm form petition. The petition shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. Such petition shall contain a detailed description of the layout-design, including its topological arrangement and all essential characteristics. A clear and accurate representation of the layout-design, preferably in electronic format conforming to standards as may be notified, shall also be furnished. Where the applicant is not the creator of the layout-design, a duly executed assignment deed or a power of attorney authorizing the applicant to make the application shall be submitted. The Controller may, subject to verification of the submitted documents and satisfaction of the requirements as provided herein, proceed with the examination of the petition and grant a certificate of registration. Any deficiency in the petition may be communicated to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days for rectification.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right, and desiring to initiate proceedings for rectification, shall submit a zm form petition to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board having jurisdiction.
