Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design, or imposing conditions on registration, may, within ninety days of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The appeal shall be in such form and be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed, and shall set forth the grounds upon which the appellant relies. The Appellate Board may, after giving the respondent an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed from, or may remit the case to the Registrar with such directions as it may deem fit. Should the Appellate Board determine that the Registrar’s decision was substantially correct, it may impose costs on the appellant, subject to considerations of hardship. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may, within sixty days, apply to the High Court for review, provided that such application demonstrates reasonable cause. The procedure for such review shall be governed by the rules of the High Court.

Any person desiring to obtain registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by the appropriate fee as specified in the Schedule. The application shall contain a statement of ownership and a detailed description of the layout-design, and shall disclose how the specification does disclose the layout-design, including a top-level description of the functionality represented. Where the applicant is not the creator, a statement of assignment or transfer of rights from the creator shall be submitted. The Controller, upon receipt of the application, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification within a period of thirty days. The procedure for examination shall include a search for prior art and an assessment of the novelty and originality of the layout-design. Should the Controller deem the application to be in order, a certificate of registration shall be issued, subject to the applicant satisfying all requirements as provided herein. Any objection raised by the Controller shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, affording an opportunity for a hearing.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right shall, prior to the institution of any legal proceedings, serve a written notice on the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the infringement and demanding cessation of the unlawful activity. Failure to serve such notice, subject to exceptions provided herein for cases of wilful and deliberate infringement, shall render the claimant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a claimant seeks to establish a priority date for a layout-design, a complete and accurate record of creation, duly notarized, must accompany any application for registration, and any deliberate misrepresentation in such record shall attract a penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar regarding the procedure for registration or revocation shall be filed within sixty days of the date of the order, failing which the decision shall be final. Any person contravening the provisions of this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment.

Any person desiring to assign or license the rights in a registered layout-design shall submit an application to the appropriate Bench, in such form as may be prescribed. The application for assignment shall clearly identify the assignee and detail the scope of rights transferred, including territorial limitations, if any, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the instrument of assignment. Similarly, an application for license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall specify the terms and conditions of the license, including the royalty payable and the duration of the license. The Bench, upon receiving a complete application, may require further clarification or documentation from the applicant or the registered proprietor. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license, or the interpretation of its terms, shall be subject to the dispute resolution procedure as provided herein, and the Bench’s decision shall be final and binding, unless appealed to a higher court. Failure to comply with this procedure may render the assignment or license invalid.

A layout-design, to be registrable as provided herein, shall not be contrary to established principles of functionality or technical effect, and any claim to a layout-design must demonstrate a discernible inventive step beyond a mere aesthetic or trivial variation of a known arrangement. The determination of registrability shall hinge upon a substantive examination of the application, assessing whether the proposed layout-design satisfies the manner applications clause, meaning it represents a novel and non-obvious solution to a technical problem. Subject to the provisions relating to prior art, a layout-design incorporating only elements already publicly known, or representing a combination readily achievable by a person skilled in the art, shall be deemed lacking in inventive step. Furthermore, the Registrar may require evidence substantiating the technical advancement conferred by the layout-design, and shall consider the overall contribution to the field of semiconductor technology.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this Act, provided that the layout-design is capable of being distinguished from any other layout-design, and does not fall within the exceptions as provided herein. The applicant shall demonstrate a sufficient inventive step in the conception of the layout-design, and the application shall clearly delineate the manner of its application to a semiconductor integrated circuit for manufacture. Any layout-design which is merely a trivial variation of a known layout-design, or which is commonly known to those skilled in the art, shall not be registrable. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish further details regarding the novelty and the manner applications clause relating to the layout-design, including the specific technical problem solved by it. All applications must be accompanied by a detailed schematic diagram and a description of the layout-design’s functionality.

Any layout-design, to be registrable under this Act, shall demonstrate sufficient inventive step and be novel as determined in accordance with the provisions herein. An application for registration shall be deemed to lack novelty if the layout-design is identical to any other layout-design which, before the filing date of the application, has been made available to the public by publication, or in any other manner, anywhere in the world. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the applicant to furnish a detailed description of the layout-design and the manner of its creation. 

Furthermore, an application shall be refused registration if it concerns a layout-design which is merely a variation of a layout-design already registered, and does not demonstrate a discernible improvement in functional characteristics. The determination of whether a layout-design satisfies the manner applications clause, and thus possesses sufficient inventive step, shall be conducted with due regard to the state of the art in semiconductor technology at the time of filing. Any dispute regarding the novelty or inventive step of a layout-design shall be subject to the appellate procedures as provided herein.

Any layout-design, to be registrable under this Act, shall demonstrate sufficient inventive step and shall not be merely a trivial variation of a layout-design already known or publicly available. An application for registration shall be deemed to satisfy this requirement only if it demonstrates a discernible improvement in functional characteristics or a novel arrangement of components, and such improvement or arrangement is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating the claimed inventive step. Furthermore, the manner of application for registration shall include a detailed description of the layout-design’s functionality and the specific technical problem it solves. Provided that, a layout-design which is a mere aesthetic modification, lacking any technical effect, shall not be considered to satisfy the manner applications clause and will be rejected. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered layout-designs, accessible for public inspection as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the inventive step shall be subject to the appellate process outlined in this Act.

Any layout-design, to be registrable as provided herein, shall demonstrate a discernible manner of application to an article of electronic circuitry, and failure to so demonstrate shall render the application liable to rejection. Provided that, a layout-design incorporating only purely aesthetic features, or representing a trivial variation of a known layout-design, shall not satisfy the requisite manner applications clause, irrespective of novelty. Any person found to have falsely represented a layout-design as meeting this standard, with intent to deceive the Registrar, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. Furthermore, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct rectification of the register where a fraudulent representation has been established. All applications shall be accompanied by a declaration affirming compliance with these provisions, and any false declaration shall constitute an offence under this Act.

Any assignment of a registered layout-design right shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the assignor and the assignee, and such instrument shall clearly identify the layout-design right being assigned, including the registration number and the date of registration. A license to work a registered layout-design, whether sole or non-exclusive, shall be construed as a contractual arrangement governed by the terms specified in the licensing agreement, and such terms may include royalty rates, duration, and territorial scope. However, any license granted must not contravene the provisions of this Act, and any attempt to broaden the scope of the licensed right beyond the originally registered layout-design shall be deemed invalid. The Registrar may, upon application, record such assignments and licenses, and maintain a public register thereof. Any application for registration of assignment or license shall demonstrate a clear nexus between the assigned right and the manner applications clause as it relates to the commercial exploitation of the layout-design. Provided that, the assignee or licensee shall be bound by any existing obligations of the assignor or licensor, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

For the purposes of this Act, a visual recording shall mean any recording, however made, of a moving image, whether recorded on any medium capable of embodying a performance or the representation thereof, including but not limited to cinematograph film, magnetic tape, or digital storage. Such a visual recording is deemed to be a work, distinct from any sound track accompanying it, and shall be protected as a separate work under this Act. Where a visual recording incorporates a pre-existing literary or dramatic work, the copyright in the visual recording shall be subject to any existing copyright in such literary or dramatic work, unless otherwise agreed in writing between the copyright holders. Any alteration or adaptation of a visual recording, resulting in a derivative work, shall require the prior authorization of the owner of the copyright in the original visual recording, as provided herein.

Any visual recording, whether expressed by means of any medium, shall be deemed a work in which copyright subsists, subject to the provisions of this Act. A person undertaking the creation of a visual recording may apply for registration of copyright therein, by furnishing the requisite particulars and depositing a copy of the work with the designated Copyright Office. The application shall include a statement of authorship and ownership, and may be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. Registration shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, though it does not confer any additional rights beyond those already conferred by this Act. Where a visual recording incorporates a pre-existing literary or dramatic work, the copyright in the visual recording shall be independent of, and without prejudice to, the copyright in such pre-existing work, provided that necessary permissions have been obtained from the owner of the copyright in such work. Failure to register does not invalidate the copyright itself, but may affect the remedies available to the copyright holder.

Any person having an exclusive right of copyright in a work, being a visual recording, shall have the right to control the reproduction of that work in any material form, including the making of copies, or causing any copies to be made. Such right extends to the commercial rental or lending of the visual recording, subject to reasonable terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Where a visual recording incorporates a pre-existing sound recording, the owner of copyright in the sound recording shall be entitled to royalties as provided herein, calculated on a percentage basis of the price at which the visual recording is sold or commercially rented. 

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a fair dealing with a visual recording for the purpose of criticism or review, or for reporting current events, shall not constitute an infringement of copyright, provided that sufficient acknowledgement is made. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of the rights conferred under this Act may apply to the appropriate court for an injunction and damages.

A visual recording, whether expressed by means of any mechanical device or otherwise, shall be deemed to be a work in which copyright subsists, subject to the provisions of this Act. The author of a visual recording shall be the person by whom the recording is made, and in the case of a recording made on the direction of a person, that person shall be deemed to be the author. Where a visual recording is made as the result of a contract for work, the person who commissions the recording, subject to any agreement to the contrary, shall be the first owner of the copyright therein. 

Any person intending to make a copy of a visual recording for purposes other than private use shall obtain a license from the owner of the copyright, and such license may be subject to payment of a royalty as determined by mutual agreement. Failure to obtain such license, or contravention of the terms thereof, shall constitute an infringement of copyright as provided herein. The rights conferred by this Act in relation to visual recordings are subject to such limitations and exceptions as may be prescribed.

Any visual recording, whether expressed by means of any medium, shall be deemed to be a work in which copyright subsists, subject to the provisions of this Act. A person undertaking the creation of a visual recording, intending it for dissemination to the public, may register the same with the designated authority to establish a clear record of authorship and date of creation. However, such registration shall not be a prerequisite for claiming copyright. Where a visual recording incorporates pre-existing copyrighted material, the authorization of the right holder in such material shall be obtained prior to the creation of the derivative work, as provided herein. Failure to secure such authorization may constitute infringement. The owner of the copyright in a visual recording shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, and exhibit the work, subject to the limitations outlined in this Act regarding fair dealing and public interest. Any adaptation of a visual recording shall be considered a new work, and copyright therein shall vest in the author of the adaptation.

Any person who, without a license of the copyright owner or in contravention of any condition imposed by a duly authorized licensing body, makes for sale or hire, or sells or lets for hire, or distributes, or publicly exhibits any visual recording, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the offence involves a commercially released visual recording, the term of imprisonment may extend to six years and the fine shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Any equipment used in the making or distribution of such unlawful visual recording shall be liable to seizure and confiscation as provided herein. A court may, subject to the circumstances, order the destruction of any infringing copies of the visual recording. The copyright owner may pursue civil remedies in addition to criminal prosecution, including but not limited to, claims for damages and injunctive relief.

Any person possessing the exclusive right of copyright in a visual recording, being a cinematograph film as defined under this Act, may grant a license to another party for the purposes of exhibiting said visual recording in public, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon. Such license shall specify the territorial extent, duration, and scope of permitted exhibition, and may include provisions relating to royalty payments or other forms of consideration. Assignment of copyright in a visual recording requires a written instrument signed by the assignor or their duly authorised agent, and shall clearly delineate the rights being transferred, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and adaptation. Where a visual recording incorporates a musical work or sound recording, the copyright owner of such incorporated work retains all rights therein, notwithstanding any assignment of copyright in the visual recording itself, unless expressly transferred as part of the assignment. Any dispute arising from licensing or assignment of rights in a visual recording shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding civil remedies for copyright infringement.

Any visual recording, whether expressed by means of a cinematograph film or other process, shall be deemed a work under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding originality. A claim of authorship in a visual recording may be disputed on grounds of substantial derivation from a pre-existing work, and the burden of proving independent creation shall lie with the claimant. Where a dispute arises concerning the ownership of rights in a visual recording made for purposes of private use, the court may, considering the nature of the recording and the circumstances of its creation, determine equitable ownership. An appeal from any decision regarding such ownership shall lie before the High Court, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates irreparable harm. Furthermore, any alteration of a visual recording that prejudices the author’s reputation may constitute infringement, unless such alteration is demonstrably transformative and does not diminish the original work’s expressive qualities.

Any visual recording depicting the process for manufacturing a pharmaceutical substance, where such substance is protected by a valid patent under the Patents Act, 1970, shall be deemed a derivative work of the patented invention, subject to the provisions of this Act. However, a purely documentary visual recording of a publicly observable manufacturing process, lacking any creative or artistic contribution beyond faithful representation, may not automatically attract copyright. Should a claim of infringement arise concerning such a visual recording, the burden of proof shall lie on the claimant to demonstrate substantial similarity and originality extending beyond mere technical depiction. An appeal against the decision of the District Court regarding such claims shall lie before a designated bench of the High Court, provided that the appellant satisfies the Court of irreparable harm. The rights of the patent holder shall not be prejudiced by the existence of copyright in the visual recording, and remedies under both Acts are cumulative.

For the purposes of this Act, a visual recording shall mean any recording, whether on film, tape, or other medium, capable of reproducing still or moving images, and includes any sound track accompanying such reproduction. A visual recording is deemed to be a work in which copyright subsists, and the author of such a work is the person by whom the recording is made. Registration of a visual recording with the designated authority, as provided herein, constitutes *prima facie* evidence of ownership and the date of creation, subject to verification. However, failure to register shall not prejudice the right of the author to claim copyright. Any alteration or adaptation of a registered visual recording, resulting in a derivative work, requires the prior consent of the copyright holder.

Any person who publishes or communicates to the public, or causes to be published or communicated to the public, information relating to a means patent, knowing such information to be false or misleading, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Any application for a means patent which contains a false allegation as to the inventive step, or as to the novelty of the invention, shall be deemed to be void ab initio and the applicant shall forfeit any fees paid in relation to such application. Subject to the provisions herein, a person who proves prior art relevant to a granted means patent may, upon application to the Controller, request revocation of said patent, provided that such application is made within one year from the date of publication of the complete specification. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act relating to the maintenance of a means patent shall render it liable to lapse.

Any assignment of a patent, or an application for a patent, whether complete or incomplete, shall be in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. Where a patent is jointly held, the patent may be assigned only with the consent of all the patentees, unless otherwise agreed in a written agreement amongst them. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent, together with the right to make, use and sell the invention, may be assigned, mortgaged, or licensed, either wholly or partially, and for any term. Any license granted under this Act shall be construed as a personal right in favour of the licensee, and shall not create any interest in the patent itself. The assignee shall, within the prescribed period, notify the Controller of Patents of the assignment, and failure to do so may render the assignment unenforceable. A transfer of ownership of a means patent does not affect any existing licenses unless expressly stated in the assignment agreement.

A “means patent” shall signify a grant by the Controller of Patents, conferring on the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention in India, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Registrar, acting under the direction of the Controller, shall maintain a public register of all granted means patent and associated documentation, including specifications, claims, and any subsequent amendments. Any assignment or transfer of a means patent shall be subject to registration produced registrar, and no such transfer shall be valid without such registration as provided herein. A means patent, once granted, remains in force for a period of twenty years from the date of filing, unless revoked or surrendered in accordance with the procedures outlined under this Act.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, a “registered act” shall mean any transaction concerning a registered trade mark, including assignment, transmission, mortgage, license, or any other disposition thereof, which is duly recorded in the Trade Marks Registry. Such registration constitutes *prima facie* evidence of the rights of the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any instrument creating or transferring a registered act shall be in writing and shall identify the trade mark with reasonable particularity. A registered act, if not duly recorded, shall not be binding on any subsequent purchaser or assignee of the trade mark acting in good faith. The Registrar may require such further evidence as may be necessary to satisfy themselves as to the validity of any registered act, and shall maintain a public record of all such transactions.

Any act concerning a registered trade mark, including assignment, transmission, mortgage, or licensing, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and must be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be fully enforceable against third parties. A registered act, if not duly recorded, may be considered voidable at the discretion of the Registry. The Registry shall maintain a public index of all registered acts, accessible for inspection subject to prescribed fees. Any person intending to record a registered act shall submit the necessary documentation, including a certified copy of the instrument and a statement of consideration, if any. Provided that, failure to register a transmission of ownership within six months of the event may attract penalties as prescribed herein. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification to ensure the validity of the registered act and compliance with this Act.

Any person who performs a registered act in relation to a registered trade mark without the consent of the registered proprietor, and with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. A registered act includes, but is not limited to, the application of the trade mark to goods or their packaging, the advertisement of goods or services bearing the trade mark, and the import or export of such goods. Where a registered proprietor proves such infringement, they may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, as well as damages for loss suffered, or an account of profits made by the defendant. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the court may award costs to the prevailing party. A registered proprietor may, at their discretion, pursue both injunctive relief and monetary damages in a single action. Provided that, the court may, in exceptional circumstances, order the destruction of infringing goods.

Any act constituting an infringement of a registered trade mark shall be actionable by the registered proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. A registered act, being the lawful use of a trade mark by the registered proprietor, does not constitute infringement even if such use would otherwise resemble the mark of another. However, a registered proprietor may not assert rights against a party who demonstrates prior bona fide use of an identical or similar mark, provided that such use was continuous and uninterrupted before the date of registration of the mark in question. Where a party alleges non-use of a registered trade mark for a period exceeding five years, the Registrar may, upon application, initiate proceedings to revoke the registration, unless sufficient cause is shown to the satisfaction of the Registrar. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to verification by the Registrar and recorded in the register as provided herein, and failure to do so may invalidate subsequent claims of ownership. The remedies available for infringement shall include injunctions, damages, and account of profits.

Any act undertaken in relation to a registered trade mark shall be deemed a registered act, provided that such act is consistent with the conditions of registration as recorded in the Register of Trade Marks. A registered act, if performed by a person other than the registered proprietor, may be subject to scrutiny to ascertain whether it falls within the scope of a license granted by the proprietor or constitutes an infringement as provided herein. Where a registered proprietor knowingly permits a third party to perform a registered act without a valid license, the proprietor shall be estopped from claiming infringement based on that act. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to verification of title and compliance with the prescribed procedures, and until such verification is complete, the assignee may not exercise the rights of a registered proprietor. Failure to maintain the accuracy of details in the Register relating to a registered act may render the registration liable to revocation.

Any person who, not being a registered act authorized by or under this Act, performs any act which constitutes an infringement of a registered trade mark, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with fine, which may extend to two lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, in addition to the imprisonment and fine, order the seizure and destruction of all infringing goods and materials used in the manufacture of such goods. Where a registered proprietor proves that an offence under this Act has been committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the said offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against accordingly. Any appeal under this provision shall lie within thirty days of the order.

Any registered act concerning the licensing or assignment of a registered trade mark shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor or licensor. Where a registered trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, notice of the assignment shall be given to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignment unenforceable against subsequent purchasers or licensees. A license may be exclusive, granting the licensee sole right to use the trade mark for specified goods or services, or non-exclusive, permitting multiple licensees. Subject to any agreement to the contrary, the registered proprietor retains the right to use the trade mark alongside the licensee in cases of non-exclusive licensing. Any registered act creating a charge on a registered trade mark shall be duly registered with the appropriate authorities to ensure its validity and priority. The transfer of ownership, as provided herein, does not affect any existing rights or liabilities.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Officer refusing a registered act, or ordering the removal of a trade mark from the register, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Trade Marks Officer, or reverse it, or vary it in such manner as it thinks fit. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any appeal to the High Court on a question of law, provided that such appeal to the High Court must be filed within ninety days of the Appellate Board’s decision. Where a registered act is challenged on the grounds of prior use by another party, evidence of continuous use prior to the application for registration shall be admissible and given due weight. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall not constitute a valid ground for reopening the case.

A trade mark shall be considered a registered act upon its entry in the Register of Trade Marks and the issuance of a certificate of registration in accordance with the procedures as provided herein. The Registrar, upon satisfaction of all statutory requirements and payment of the prescribed fees, shall effect such registration. Any person claiming ownership of a trade mark may apply for registration under this Act, subject to due diligence and compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and non-deceptiveness. Where an applicant seeks protection in multiple jurisdictions, an international registration, designating India as a designated country, may be filed through the International Bureau, subject to the provisions of the Protocol relating to the Madrid Agreement. Such international registration shall be examined as if it were an application filed directly under this Act, and shall be subject to the same grounds for refusal or amendment. A registered act confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to seek legal remedies against any infringement thereof.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor, and subject to the conditions specified in the register, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. This right shall include the right to institute legal proceedings for infringement of such right and to restrain any unauthorised use of the geographical indication. The term ‘authorised user’ shall denote a producer who, at the time of application for registration, was carrying on a business of producing goods with the geographical indication and continues to do so, or who is granted a license by the registered proprietor to use the geographical indication. Any use of a geographical indication by an unauthorised user shall be deemed to be an infringement, provided that such use does not constitute a fair use as determined by the Controller.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor, or collective of producers, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. This right extends to preventing all acts of unauthorized use of such geographical indication by any person not authorised to do so, including acts of manufacture or trade. Any person dealing in goods with a falsely applied geographical indication, or a colourable variation thereof, shall be liable to prosecution and may be subject to injunction and damages, as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, grant licenses to other producers who meet the prescribed standards and quality requirements, to use the geographical indication. Such licensing shall be recorded and maintained as part of the register, and shall be revocable in cases of non-compliance with the stipulated conditions. The authorised user shall also be responsible for maintaining the quality and reputation of the geographical indication.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor, or collective of producers representing the geographical indication, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any person who, without authorisation, uses a geographical indication that is so registered, or any colourable variation thereof, in the course of trade, shall be liable to legal proceedings for infringement. The High Court, upon application by the registered proprietor, may grant an injunction restraining such unauthorised use and may also order the destruction or forfeiture of goods bearing such unauthorised geographical indication. 

Provided that, no injunction shall be granted if the use of the geographical indication is demonstrably fair use, or is necessary for the purpose of identifying the geographical origin of the goods. A collective of producers, duly authorised to represent the geographical indication, may also pursue civil remedies for loss of reputation or dilution of the distinctive character of the geographical indication, subject to establishing demonstrable harm.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor, or collective of producers recognised as such, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Such authorisation extends to the right to institute legal proceedings for infringement of such right, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person dealing in goods bearing a falsely applied geographical indication, or a colourable variation thereof, with intent to deceive the public, shall be liable to prosecution and may be subject to injunction and damages. The Controller of Geographical Indications may, upon sufficient cause being shown and after notice to the registered proprietor, authorise a licensee to use the geographical indication, particularly where the registered proprietor is unable to adequately meet demand. Any such authorisation shall be subject to terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit, ensuring the quality and reputation of the geographical indication are maintained. The register of geographical indications shall be open to inspection by any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall be subject to periodic review by the Board established for the purpose, to ensure continued adherence to the standards prescribed in the register of geographical indications. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, within six months of the close of each financial year, submit a declaration of production and sales figures to the Board, accompanied by evidence of quality control measures implemented. Failure to submit such a declaration may render the authorisation liable to revocation, provided that the registered proprietor is given an opportunity to be heard. Any modification to the specifications of the goods covered by the geographical indication shall require prior approval of the Board and a corresponding amendment to the register. The Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, authorise a qualified agency to inspect production facilities and verify compliance with the established standards.

Any person dealing in goods with a geographical indication authorised under this Act, and falsely representing such goods as originating from a geographical area in respect of which a registered geographical indication exists, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where the offence involves repeated contravention, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees. The Registrar, upon receiving credible evidence of such misrepresentation, may issue a cease and desist notice to the offending party, requiring immediate cessation of the unlawful activity. Failure to comply with such notice within thirty days shall constitute an aggravated offence, attracting enhanced penalties and potential criminal prosecution. Any goods found to be in violation of these provisions shall be liable to seizure and destruction, subject to the discretion of a designated officer. The burden of proof regarding the geographical origin of the goods shall lie with the defendant.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by the registered proprietor, provided that such arrangements are consistent with the maintenance and enhancement of the reputation of the geographical indication. The registered proprietor may, by instrument in writing, grant licenses to applicants demonstrating a substantial connection to the territory associated with the geographical indication and a commitment to quality control standards as prescribed. Any assignment of a geographical indication authorised herein shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry, and notice of such assignment shall be published in the Journal. Where a license or assignment is found to be detrimental to the established character or quality of goods bearing the geographical indication, the Registrar may, after due inquiry and opportunity of being heard granted to the parties concerned, revoke the license or declare the assignment invalid. A licensee shall be entitled to use the geographical indication only for goods originating from and produced within the defined geographical area, and any deviation shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license.

Any person alleging infringement of a geographical indication authorised under this Act may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Registrar for an interim injunction restraining the defendant from continuing the alleged infringement. The application shall be accompanied by a statement of facts and evidence supporting the claim, and the Registrar shall, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, issue an interim injunction pending disposal of the proceedings. However, no interim injunction shall be granted unless the applicant deposits with the Registrar such sum as the Registrar may deem fit, to cover potential damages to the defendant should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Any order granting or refusing an interim injunction shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within thirty days of the order’s communication, and the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises for the consideration of the High Court. The Registrar may, at any stage, direct a hearing to be conducted to determine the validity of the claim.

A geographical indication authorised under this Act shall be subject to periodic review by the Registrar, who may, with the approval of the Central Government, initiate such review at intervals not exceeding five years from the date of registration, or upon receipt of a substantiated complaint alleging misrepresentation or deterioration of quality. The Patent Office shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all authorised geographical indications, detailing the scope of the geographical area, the standards applicable to the goods, and the name of the registered proprietor or association of producers. Any modification to the specifications of a geographical indication, including expansion or contraction of the geographical area, shall require a formal application and subsequent approval as provided herein. Failure to comply with the prescribed standards or to maintain adequate quality control mechanisms may result in suspension or revocation of the authorisation, following due process and opportunity for hearing. Producers utilising a geographical indication shall conspicuously display the authorised symbol on all qualifying goods.

A registered layout is defined as a final or interim version of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout, irrespective of whether it is incorporated in a semiconductor chip. The layout shall be considered original if it demonstrates independent creative thought and is not derivative of any pre-existing layout or knowledge. A layout-design, to be eligible for registration under this Act, must be inherently capable of being distinctly identified and must not be identical with any other registered layout-design. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered layout confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and commercially utilize the layout. Any person dealing in semiconductor integrated circuits shall, prior to manufacture, ensure that the layout is not already subject to a valid registration.

A registered layout, upon fulfillment of the requirements as provided herein and successful registration with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry, shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout. The Registry shall maintain a comprehensive record of each registered layout, detailing the applicant, proprietor, and a precise depiction of the layout-design itself. Any transfer of ownership of a registered layout shall be subject to a written assignment, duly recorded with the Registry within the prescribed timeframe, failing which such transfer shall be deemed invalid. A person claiming to be the proprietor of a registered layout may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for infringement. The validity of a registered layout shall be for a period of ten years from the date of registration, or until the expiry of the commercial exploitation period, whichever is later, provided that renewal may be permissible under certain conditions.

A person who has registered a layout-design under this Act shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or import the layout-design, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any act infringing upon such exclusive right shall constitute an actionable wrong, for which the registered proprietor may pursue remedies before a competent court. Where a person, despite due diligence, unknowingly exploits a registered layout-design, the court may, at its discretion, grant relief subject to reasonable royalty payments determined by the court, considering the extent of the exploitation and the harm suffered by the proprietor. However, no such relief shall be granted if the exploitation occurred prior to the registration of the layout-design. The rights conferred by registration of a layout-design shall subsist for a period of ten years from the date of filing, or until the layout-design ceases to be commercially exploited, whichever is earlier. Any assignment or transfer of the registered layout-design shall be subject to the conditions prescribed and must be recorded with the Registry.

A registered layout shall vest in the proprietor and confer upon him the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout in India. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered layout shall obtain a license from the proprietor, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon. Where a person exploits a registered layout without a license, the proprietor may institute civil proceedings for infringement before a court competent to hear such matters, seeking injunction and damages. The quantum of damages shall be determined with reference to the actual loss suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement, or the reasonable royalty payable for the use of the layout, whichever is higher. 

A layout-design dossier, as filed for registration, shall be considered public document after the expiry of a period of three years from the date of registration, unless the proprietor opts for indefinite confidentiality. Any information contained within a confidential dossier, revealed without authorization, shall be actionable under the provisions relating to trade secrets. The Controller may, upon application, direct amendment of a registered layout, provided that such amendment does not materially affect the layout-design.

A registered layout shall vest in the proprietor and confer upon such proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered layout shall obtain a license from the proprietor, and the terms of such license shall be mutually agreed upon, failing which, recourse may be had to the appropriate authority for determination of fair and reasonable licensing fees. The proprietor of a registered layout may, at any time, assign or transmit the right, title, and interest in the registered layout to any other person, provided that such assignment or transmission is recorded with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. Failure to record such transfer shall not invalidate the assignment but may affect its enforceability against third parties. A registered layout shall subsist for a period of ten years from the date of filing, or until the layout ceases to be commercially exploited, whichever is earlier. Any act in contravention of these provisions shall be considered an infringement.

Any person dealing in or importing a semiconductor integrated circuit, or a product incorporating a registered layout, shall be liable for damages for any act constituting an infringement of a registered layout as provided herein. Where a registered layout is used in the manufacture of a semiconductor integrated circuit without the authorization of the proprietor, a civil court shall, upon proof of such unauthorized use, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from such manufacture and sale. Furthermore, the court may order delivery up or destruction of all infringing semiconductor integrated circuits, and all materials used in the process of manufacture. A proprietor of a registered layout may also seek compensatory damages, not exceeding Rupees one crore per layout, and may, at their discretion, pursue criminal remedies under the relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code, subject to the establishment of intent. Any false representation of a layout as registered shall be punishable with imprisonment.

Any person being the proprietor of a registered layout shall have the right to assign, or otherwise transfer, all or any of the rights vested in such registered layout to any other person, whether such transfer is by way of sale, gift, or otherwise, and such assignment or transfer shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties. Provided that, any assignment or transfer of a registered layout shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly registered with the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry as provided herein. The Registry shall, upon application and payment of the prescribed fee, register the assignment or transfer and issue a certificate of registration to the assignee or transferee. A commercial license relating to a registered layout may be granted by the proprietor, and such license shall define the scope of permitted use, including territorial limitations and the duration of the license. Any dispute arising from the interpretation or enforcement of such licensing agreements shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the competent court.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout shall, prior to the institution of proceedings before a competent court, furnish the alleged infringer with a notice of such infringement, detailing the specific registered layout and the nature of the alleged act of infringement. Provided that, such notice shall be served at least thirty days prior to the filing of the suit, and shall clearly indicate the claimant’s intention to seek legal remedy under this Act. The Registry, upon receipt of a complaint regarding improper service of notice, may conduct an inquiry and, if satisfied that proper service was not effected, shall direct the claimant to re-serve the notice. An appeal against any decision of the Registry regarding service of notice shall lie before the designated appellate authority within sixty days of the order. A registered layout, if proven to be originally generated, shall be presumed valid unless rebutted by evidence of prior art.

A registered layout shall vest in the proprietor and confer the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout-design, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person desiring to obtain a registered layout shall submit an application to the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and a detailed representation of the layout-design. The Registry, upon examination and satisfaction that the layout-design is novel and intrinsically capable of being distinguished from any other layout-design, shall register it and issue a certificate of registration. 

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the conditions as provided herein, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Registry concerning the refusal of registration or the revocation of a registered layout. The Appellate Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registry and its decision shall be final and binding. Failure to register a layout-design does not preclude a claim for damages based on independent grounds.

A registered layout shall be considered commercially exploited if it is reproduced, communicated, or exhibited to the public, including through the creation of any article incorporating the layout or any adaptation thereof. Any cinematograph film embodying a visual representation of an article containing a registered layout, whether directly or indirectly, shall be deemed to be a communication to the public for the purposes of determining commercial exploitation, provided that such embodiment is visible and identifiable within the film. The proprietor of a registered layout may, as provided herein, grant licenses to others for the commercial exploitation of the layout, subject to the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon. Failure to maintain accurate records of all licensing agreements relating to a registered layout shall render the proprietor liable to penalties. Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout must demonstrate a clear nexus between the alleged infringing act and the commercially exploited layout.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means register trade” shall denote the official record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry wherein particulars of trade marks are entered for the purpose of granting protection and establishing rights therein. An application for registration, if found to be in order and not conflicting with existing marks as determined under the examination process as provided herein, shall proceed to advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal. Following successful advertisement and subject to any opposition filed, the trade mark may be registered, and the applicant shall be recorded as the proprietor. The register shall be open for inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration in the particulars of a means register trade, such as a change of address of the proprietor, shall be duly recorded in the register upon submission of the required documentation and payment of the applicable fees. Failure to maintain accurate registration details may render the mark vulnerable to rectification proceedings.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a trade mark, or by any requirement imposed as a condition of registration, or by the alteration of a trade mark in the register, or by any decision of the Registrar relating to the validity of a means register trade, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the High Court for rectification of the register. Such application shall be made within such period as may be prescribed, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The High Court, upon consideration of the application and any evidence submitted, may allow the application, in whole or in part, or may dismiss it. Where an application for rectification is allowed, the High Court may direct the Registrar to make the necessary amendments to the register, or to remove the trade mark from the register altogether. A person who obtains registration of a trade mark fraudulently may have the registration revoked, and shall be liable to damages.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means register trade” shall denote the official record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry wherein particulars of trade marks are entered in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any application for registration, as provided herein, shall be subject to verification of the proposed trade mark against existing entries in the means register trade, and a search report reflecting such verification shall be a prerequisite for proceeding to examination. Where a trade mark is found to be deceptively similar to an existing registered trade mark, the applicant may be required to amend the application or submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness. The Registrar may, at their discretion, direct an applicant to provide a statement of use, detailing the manner in which the trade mark is being used in commerce, to substantiate a claim of bona fide adoption. Failure to comply with such direction may render the application liable to be abandoned. Any rectification of the means register trade shall be conducted in a manner consistent with the procedures outlined in this Act.

Any person desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and such application shall be accompanied by a statement of use affirming bona fide use of the means register trade within the territory of India. The application shall further disclose the class of goods or services to which the trade mark relates, and shall be subject to verification by the Registry to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. Where the Registry is satisfied that the application meets all requirements, it may proceed to examine the trade mark for distinctiveness and potential conflicts with existing registered marks. A notice of acceptance shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal, allowing for opposition by any aggrieved party, provided that such opposition is filed within the stipulated period as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

Any assignment of the right to use a means register trade shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, and shall specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. Where the assignment is made subject to conditions, those conditions shall be clearly stated in the instrument of assignment. The assignee of a means register trade may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Trade Marks Registry to have their name registered as the proprietor of the trade mark. 

An exclusive license granted in respect of a means register trade shall be equivalent to an assignment of the right to use the trade mark for the purposes of maintaining proceedings for infringement. However, a non-exclusive license does not confer such a right. Any transfer of a registered trade mark, whether by assignment, license, or otherwise, shall not affect the validity of the registration, provided that the transfer is duly recorded with the Registry. Failure to record such transfer may, however, impact the enforceability of rights against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to means register trade, or directing the rectification or removal of a trade mark from the register, may, within ninety days from the date of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, if it deems fit, require the appellant to furnish evidence in support of his appeal, and may also direct any other party to the appeal to produce any document or give any evidence. 

Provided that, where the order appealed against confirms the decision of the Registrar on an application for rectification of the register, the Appellate Board shall not entertain the appeal unless it is satisfied that substantial questions of law are involved. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties, subject to a writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

In determining the validity of a means register trade, the Controller shall, subject to the provisions contained herein, examine the application and accompanying evidence to ensure compliance with all prescribed requirements relating to distinctiveness and lawful use. Any false representation made in an application for registration, or any failure to disclose material facts, shall constitute a commission offence notwithstanding any other penalty provided for under this Act. The Controller may, if satisfied that a trade mark is not inherently capable of distinguishing goods or services, reject the application outright. Provided that, where a mark has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, the Controller may, at their discretion, allow registration. All decisions of the Controller regarding the means register trade shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, detailing the grounds for acceptance or rejection, and outlining any remedies available as provided herein. Any appeal against such decision shall be made within the stipulated timeframe.

Any assignment of the right to use a means register trade shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. The assignee of a registered trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry to register themselves as the new proprietor, and upon such application and subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, the Registry shall, if satisfied, register the assignee as the proprietor. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of any such assignment or the entitlement of the assignee, any aggrieved party may appeal to the board means appellate, which shall have the power to hear and determine the matter. A license to use a registered trade mark may be granted, either for the whole of India or for a specified area thereof, and such license shall be subject to such conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding registration of assignments or licenses shall render such transactions unenforceable.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall signify a trade mark entered in the Register of Trade Marks and subsisting in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and the date of registration shall be the date on which the particulars of the trade mark are entered in the Register. A trade mark so means registered confers upon the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a trade mark is means registered in the name of a person other than the actual user, such person shall be deemed to be the proprietor for all purposes under this Act, provided that such person demonstrates a bona fide intention to use the trade mark. Any assignment or transmission of a means registered trade mark shall be subject to the conditions specified herein.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall denote a trade mark entered in the Register and subsisting in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and a trade mark so means registered shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. A trade mark shall not be means registered if it is devoid of any distinctive character or is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, and the Registrar may, subject to the prescribed procedure, refuse registration on these grounds. Provided that, a trade mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may, notwithstanding the foregoing, be means registered. Any assignment or transmission of a means registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions relating to assignment and transmission under this Act, and the Register shall be accordingly updated. The continued registration of a trade mark is contingent upon the periodic payment of renewal fees as provided herein.

Any person who suffers loss or damage as a consequence of any fraudulent application for registration of a trade mark, or of the registration of a trade mark in violation of the provisions of this Act, shall be entitled to recover from the applicant or registered proprietor, as the case may be, such loss or damage, together with an appropriate accounting for profits. Where a trade mark is registered and the registration is subsequently expunged from the register, any rights acquired in good faith by any person under such registration, prior to the date of expungement, shall not be affected. However, such rights shall be subject to proof of legitimate use and reliance on the register as means registered. Any action for infringement based on a means registered trade mark shall be maintainable only if the plaintiff demonstrates genuine and continuous use of the mark prior to the date of the alleged infringement, and that such use was not merely token. The Court may, at its discretion, award exemplary damages in cases of flagrant or wilful infringement.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall be construed as entry in the Register of Trade Marks maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, and a mark so entered shall be deemed to confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. A trade mark shall not be considered means registered solely on the basis of an application for registration, but only upon the issuance of a certificate of registration as provided herein. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the registered proprietor may institute legal proceedings for infringement against any person using an identical or deceptively similar mark. However, such rights shall be subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the register. Where a trade mark is means registered in multiple classes, the exclusive right extends only to those classes. Any assignment or transmission of a means registered trade mark shall be subject to the recording of such transfer with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective against third parties.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall denote a trade mark entered in the Register and subsisting in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and a trade mark shall be considered means registered from the date of such entry. Any assignment or transmission of rights in a means registered trade mark shall be subject to notification to the Registrar, failing which such assignment or transmission may be deemed invalid as provided herein. Where a means registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services for which it was not originally registered, such use shall require prior application for amendment of the register, and compliance with all prescribed conditions. A proprietor of a means registered trade mark may, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, apply for renewal of the registration, and failure to do so within the stipulated period may result in the removal of the trade mark from the Register. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to a means registered trade mark may seek redressal through the established appellate mechanisms.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a trade mark, uses in the course of trade, or advertises for the purpose of trade, any colour as a trade mark, or any device or expression which is likely to cause confusion or deception, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that the court may, subject to the circumstances of the case, and in lieu of imprisonment, impose a monetary penalty not exceeding five times the value of the goods or services offered for sale under the falsely applied mark. Where a trade mark is means registered, the Registrar may, after giving the proprietor an opportunity to be heard, direct the removal of such mark from any goods or articles found to be in violation of this Act, and the costs of such removal shall be borne by the offender. Any goods so removed may be disposed of in a manner prescribed by the Registrar.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall denote full vesting of rights pertaining to a trade mark in the name of the registered proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, whether absolute or partial, shall be in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of both the assignor and the assignee, and a statement of such assignment, duly verified, shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is means registered in the name of a company, any transfer of ownership of the company shall not, of itself, operate as an assignment of the trade mark, but the new owner shall, within a period of six months, apply for a transfer of registration. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable as provided herein, and the Registry may, upon application, direct rectification of the register. A license to use a means registered trade mark shall be similarly documented and recorded to ensure clarity of rights and obligations.

In determining whether a mark is means registered, the Registrar shall consider evidence of continuous use as provided herein, but lack of such evidence shall not *ipso facto* disqualify a mark, subject to rebuttal by the opposing party. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing registration may file an appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order. The High Court, upon reviewing the appeal, may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision, and shall record its reasons in writing. A further appeal to the Supreme Court shall lie only on a substantial question of law. Where a mark is means registered despite a prior, similar mark existing, the proprietor of the prior mark may seek rectification of the register, demonstrating likelihood of confusion and potential damage to goodwill. The Registrar, in such cases, shall conduct a comparative assessment of the marks and the goods/services associated with them.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, a trade mark shall be considered means registered only upon full compliance with the procedures detailed herein and subsequent entry in the Register of Trade Marks. An application for registration, if successful, shall confer upon the applicant the status of registered proprietor, subject to the payment of all prescribed fees and adherence to ongoing renewal requirements. Notice of every registration shall be caused to be published in the Official Gazette as expeditiously as possible, and such publication shall constitute prima facie evidence of the registration. Any representation made during the application process, if found to be materially false, may invalidate the means registered status, even after publication in the Official Gazette. The Registrar may, however, allow rectification of the register in such instances, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated and appropriate amends are made. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the registration voidable at the discretion of the Registrar.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means registered” shall denote a trade mark entered in the Register and subsisting in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and the proprietor thereof shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as are herein provided. Any assignment of a trade mark means registered shall be subject to the Registrar’s approval, and shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, specifying the trade mark, the parties to the assignment, and the consideration, if any. Where an application for registration includes a reference to a provisional specification, the Registrar may require a complete specification to be filed within a period not exceeding six months from the date of the provisional specification, failing which the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. A license to use a trade mark means registered may be granted, and such license shall be in writing and subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon by the parties. Any dispute arising from such license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

The register of trade marks shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, contain all particulars of registered trade marks. A trade mark shall not be registered if it is identical with an earlier trade mark and relates to goods or services identical with those for which the earlier trade mark is registered; however, registration ought effected where the later mark is used by a person different from the proprietor of the earlier mark, and the use is permitted by the proprietor. Where a trade mark consists of a well-known mark, registration shall be refused unless the applicant proves legitimate use and demonstrates that the use of the mark will not cause confusion or dilution. Any application for registration failing to meet these criteria, as provided herein, shall be deemed invalid.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to any person to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and any such license may be granted in writing and shall specify the conditions, including duration, territorial extent, and the nature of the permitted use. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the same conditions as apply to a license, and the assignee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the trade mark as from the date of the assignment, provided that the transfer is duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with goodwill, the assignee shall be entitled to all the rights and remedies available to the assignor. However, registration ought effected only where the assignment does not contravene any existing contractual obligations or infringe upon the rights of any third party, and the Registrar may, upon sufficient cause shown, refuse to record an assignment if such contravention or infringement is established. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “legal representative” shall mean the person to whom the right in the patent or the application for a patent has been transmitted by operation of law, or by assignment, or by will or succession, and includes any person duly authorized by such person to act on their behalf. Where a patentee is a legal person, such as a company or corporation, the term shall extend to its duly appointed receiver, administrator, or liquidator, subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force. Any notice or communication required to be served on the patentee, as provided herein, may be validly served on their legal representative, provided that proof of representation is furnished. A legal representative acting under a power of attorney shall possess the authority necessary to conduct all proceedings related to the patent.

A person who, at the time of the death of the applicant or patentee, was their legal representative shall, subject to the provisions herein, have the right to make an application for the grant of a patent or to pursue an application previously made by the deceased applicant. Where a patent is granted to a legal representative, the patent shall be deemed to have been granted as of right to that representative, and the term of the patent shall be calculated from the date of the original application made by the deceased applicant. Should multiple legal representatives exist, they shall jointly exercise the rights conferred under this Act, unless a clear designation of a sole representative is filed with the Controller. Any assignment or transfer of interest in a patent by a legal representative shall be subject to the same conditions and requirements as apply to an assignment by the original patentee, and notice thereof shall be filed with the Controller as provided herein.

Where an applicant or patentee is deceased, or is otherwise incapable of conducting legal proceedings, any proceeding under this Act may be continued by their legal representative, subject to the provisions herein. For the purposes of this provision, the term ‘legal representative’ shall include a person appointed as executor or administrator of the estate of the deceased applicant or patentee, or any person authorised by a court of competent jurisdiction to act on their behalf. Should a patent application be filed jointly, the death or incapacity of one joint applicant shall not affect the rights of the surviving applicant or applicants to pursue the application, provided that such surviving applicant or applicants demonstrate to the Controller a clear intention to continue prosecution. Any assignment or transfer of rights relating to a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be valid and enforceable against the legal representative, insofar as those rights vest in the estate of the deceased or the assets of the incapacitated applicant or patentee.

Where an application for a patent, or any right arising therefrom, is pending or has been granted to a natural person who dies or is declared insolvent, the application or right may, subject to the provisions of this Act, be assigned to the legal representative of the deceased or insolvent. For the purposes of this provision, the term “legal representative” shall include a person who acquires the right to make an application for or pursue a patent by operation of law, or by will, or by assignment, or by any other legal means. Where the patentee is a firm, the legal representative shall be the surviving partner or partners, or, if there are no surviving partners, the person or persons to whom the business of the firm has been transferred. Any assignment made under this provision shall be deemed to have been made as of the date of death or declaration of insolvency, and shall be subject to the same conditions and liabilities as if the original applicant or patentee were still alive and competent to act. The Controller may, if satisfied that the legal representative is duly authorized, record the transfer of the application or patent in his registers.

Where an application for a patent, or any right or title in respect of an invention, is made by a deceased inventor, the application shall be capable of being pursued by the legal representative of the deceased inventor, subject to the conditions as provided herein. A legal representative, for the purposes of this Act, shall include an executor, administrator, or any person authorized to act on behalf of the estate of the deceased inventor. Should multiple legal representatives exist, they shall jointly act, or designate one amongst themselves to act as the sole representative for all proceedings under this Act. Any assignment or transfer of rights arising from the patent, made by the legal representative, shall be valid only if it is demonstrably in accordance with the applicable laws of succession and probate.
