The Controller shall require satisfactory evidence of representation before proceeding with any application or grant involving a deceased inventor, and may, at any stage, demand updated documentation confirming the legal representative’s authority. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the abandonment of the application.

Where any proceeding under this Act is pending before a competent authority and the applicant or patentee dies, the proceeding shall not abate but the legal representative of the deceased shall, subject to such directions as the competent authority may deem fit, have the right to prosecute or defend the same. If the legal representative fails to prosecute or defend the proceeding within a period of ninety days from the date of death of the applicant or patentee, the competent authority may, after giving reasonable opportunity of being heard, dismiss the proceeding. Any person claiming to be the legal representative shall submit an affidavit establishing their entitlement, and failure to do so may result in a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees. Provided that, the competent authority may, in exceptional circumstances, extend the aforementioned ninety-day period. Any false claim made regarding legal representation shall be punishable as contempt of this authority.

Where a patent application is filed by a person who subsequently dies or becomes incapacitated, or where a patent is held by a deceased person or a person under legal disability, all rights accruing to the applicant or patentee, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall vest in their legal representative. For the purposes of this Act, the term ‘legal representative’ includes a person who acquires the rights by operation of law, or by will, or by lawful succession, or by assignment, and shall be duly authenticated as such before the Controller. Any assignment of a patent or patent application by a legal representative shall be subject to the same requirements and limitations as apply to an assignment by the original applicant or patentee. Provided that, where multiple legal representatives exist, they shall jointly exercise rights unless otherwise agreed amongst themselves and documented with the Controller. The Controller may, if satisfied, accept a single legal representative nominated by the others. Any notice served on a legal representative shall be deemed to be valid service on the estate of the deceased or incapacitated person.

Where an applicant or patentee is deceased, or is otherwise incapable of conducting legal proceedings, any application or other document required to be filed under this Act may be filed by their legal representative, provided that such legal representative shall furnish evidence of their authority to act on behalf of the deceased or incapacitated applicant or patentee, accepted by the Controller. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of such representation, the Controller may require further evidence, including but not limited to, a grant of legal representation from a competent court. Any notice issued to the legal representative shall be deemed to be sufficient notice to the estate or interests represented, unless otherwise directed by a court of competent jurisdiction. Furthermore, any assignment of the patent by the legal representative shall be subject to the provisions regarding assignments as provided herein, and shall require the same level of scrutiny.

Where any proceeding for the rectification of a patent is pending before the Controller, and the patentee dies or is declared insolvent, the proceeding shall not abate but the legal representative of the deceased patentee or the assignee of the insolvent patentee, as the case may be, may, subject to such conditions as the Controller may deem fit, be substituted as a party to the proceeding. Should the legal representative fail to demonstrate sufficient interest in continuing the rectification proceeding within ninety days of being substituted, the Controller may, upon application by the opposing party and having considered a registry fee paid as prescribed, direct that the proceeding be dismissed. Any order made under this provision shall be final, save for a right of appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Controller’s order and accompanied by a certified copy of the said order. The Controller shall maintain a register of all substituted legal representatives.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “legal representative” shall mean the person to whom the right, title and interest in the patent has devolved by operation of law, or by will or by legal transfer, and shall include any person duly authorized by such person to act on their behalf. Where a patentee is deceased, the legal representative shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as the patentee. Any application or proceeding before a court having jurisdiction under this Act, may be conducted by the legal representative, provided that sufficient evidence of representation is furnished to the satisfaction of the court. The legal representative shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with all statutory obligations relating to the patent.

A person who, upon the death of the proprietor of a patent or a pending application for a patent, or upon the insolvency of the proprietor, or where the proprietor is a company, upon the winding up of the company, acquires the right to apply for the patent or to pursue the application, shall be deemed to be the legal representative of the proprietor for the purposes of this Act. Where a mark certification trade is registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, and the proprietor of such registered mark also holds a patent, the rights and obligations under this Act relating to the patent shall, subject to the provisions herein, extend to the legal representative of the proprietor of the mark. Any assignment or transfer of rights by the legal representative shall be governed by the rules relating to assignment as provided herein, and shall require prior notification to the Controller of Patents. Provided that, the legal representative shall furnish an affidavit establishing their status as such, along with the necessary documentation.

A claim to priority shall be permissible under this Act where an application claiming the benefit of an earlier application, whether in India or a convention country, is filed, provided that such earlier application satisfies the requirements as to form and substance. The priority date for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step shall, subject to the provisions herein, be the filing date of the earliest application upon which a claim to priority is based. However, no priority date claim shall be valid if the later application discloses matter extending beyond the content of the earlier application, unless such extension is supported by a subsequent application filed before the filing of the later application. A declaration establishing the connection between the applications shall accompany the later application.

A person claiming a right to a patent, having previously filed an application for the same invention in a convention country, shall, as provided herein, be entitled to a priority date relating back to the filing date in that convention country. Such a claim to the priority date shall be made within the prescribed period, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the first application, demonstrating sufficient disclosure to support the claim. Failure to submit the certified copy within the stipulated timeframe may result in loss of the claimed priority date, subject to justifiable cause being established to the satisfaction of the Controller. Where multiple applications claiming the same invention are filed in different convention countries, the priority date shall be determined based on the earliest filing date amongst them. However, this right is subject to the invention not having been made publicly known, through publication or otherwise, after the initial filing date and before the filing date under this Act. Any dispute regarding the validity of a priority date claim shall be adjudicated by the Controller, whose decision shall be final.

A claim in a complete specification shall be deemed to relate to matter disclosed in a provisional specification, subject to the provisions hereinafter contained. Where an application claiming priority under this Act is filed, the priority date for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step shall be the date of the earliest application filed in any convention country in respect of the same invention, provided that a certified copy of the priority document is furnished to the Controller within the prescribed period. However, if the applicant fails to furnish such copy within the prescribed period, the right to claim priority shall be deemed to have been relinquished. A subsequent application claiming the same invention, but not claiming priority, may proceed as if the earlier application had not been filed, unless the applicant demonstrates justifiable grounds for the delay in furnishing the priority document, and the Controller, having regard to the circumstances, may allow the claim to proceed. Any dispute regarding the validity of a priority date claim shall be adjudicated by the Controller as provided herein.

A claim to a priority date arising from an earlier application filed in a convention country shall be permissible, provided that the applicant furnishes a certified copy of the earlier application, accompanied by an English translation if the application is not in English, within the prescribed period as provided herein. Failure to submit such documentation within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the loss of the claimed priority date, unless sufficient cause is demonstrated to the Controller of Patents. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a subsequent application claiming the benefit of the earlier application must disclose all essential matter disclosed in the earlier application to support the claim. Where the earlier application relates to a different inventor or applicant, evidence of assignment or transfer of rights shall be submitted alongside the priority claim documentation. Any discrepancy in the details of the earlier application, including the applicant’s name or the invention’s subject matter, may render the priority date claim invalid.

Any assignment of an application for a patent, or of a patent, shall be made in writing and shall specify the claims assigned, and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. Where an inventor assigns their right to apply for a patent, or a patent itself, to a person or entity, the assignee shall be entitled to pursue the application or enjoy the patent subject to the terms of the assignment. A valid assignment, to be effective, must clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred, including any licensing provisions. 

In cases where multiple inventors contribute to an invention, and a priority date claim is established based on the first filing, subsequent assignments by any inventor shall not invalidate that established priority, provided that all inventors have duly assigned their rights. The assignee, however, may be subject to claims from co-inventors not party to the initial assignment, and appropriate remedies shall be available as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership without full disclosure of co-inventors may render the assignment voidable.

A claim to a priority date, as provided herein, shall be permissible where an applicant demonstrates prior art disclosure, subject to the conditions stipulated in this Act. However, such a claim may be contested by a third party alleging independent development of substantially similar subject matter, necessitating the submission of detailed laboratory notebooks and dated records as evidence. If the Controller, upon examination, finds the claimed priority date unsupported by convincing evidence of prior disclosure, the application shall proceed as if no priority date was ever claimed, and the effective filing date shall revert to the date of actual filing. An appeal from the Controller’s decision regarding the validity of the priority date claim may be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order, provided that the appellant furnishes a security deposit as prescribed. The Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of proven fraud.

A claim to a priority date under this Act shall be permissible where an applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that a complete specification was filed in a convention country within twelve months preceding the filing date in India. However, such a claim shall be subject to proof of the foreign application and its corresponding filing date, as evidenced by a certified copy duly submitted with the Indian application. Where the applicant alleges that the mark for which priority is claimed is a well known trade mark in India, the burden of proof regarding such recognition shall lie with the applicant, and the Controller may consider evidence of actual use and public reputation. An appeal from the Controller’s decision regarding the validity of a priority date claim, or the status of a mark as well known, may be made to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Controller’s order. Failure to substantiate the priority date claim may result in the application being treated as filed on the date of its actual filing in India.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be a variety which is clearly distinguishable by its phenotypical characteristics from any other variety whose existence is a matter of commonly known plant breeding practice. The applicant seeking registration of a distinct denomination variety shall submit to the Plant Variety Protection Authority evidence demonstrating the distinctness, uniformity, and stability of the claimed variety. Provided that, where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, as defined herein, the denomination assigned to the original variety shall not be permissible for the essentially derived variety, unless the breeder of the original variety has consented in writing to such use. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, refuse registration if the proposed denomination is likely to cause confusion with an existing variety.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel, stable, and uniformly reproducible, and shall be designated by a denomination which enables ready identification with the plant variety it represents. The applicant shall submit a clear and concise description of the proposed denomination, along with a declaration affirming its distinctness from any previously registered or commonly known variety, or any denomination likely to cause confusion. Provided that, if the denomination incorporates a generic name or a term descriptive of a characteristic of the variety, it shall be accompanied by a disclaimer clarifying its intended scope. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems necessary, require the applicant to modify a denomination if it is found to be misleading or deceptive. Any denomination assigned shall be subject to the provisions relating to change of denomination as provided herein, and the register of plant varieties shall reflect any such alteration. The variety’s essential characteristics, as demonstrated through field trials, shall support the claimed distinctness.

Any person who has, under this Act, had a distinct denomination variety registered in his name shall be entitled to market the seeds or propagating material of such variety, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, such right shall not extend to the commercial exploitation of the variety if it is demonstrated, to the satisfaction of the Competent Authority, that the variety is essentially derived from another variety which was commercially exploited prior to the registration of the distinct denomination variety. A farmer who has, in good faith, saved seeds of a protected variety for personal use, shall not be restricted in doing so, provided that he does not sell, distribute or otherwise commercially exploit such saved seeds. Where a registered variety is found to be not a distinct denomination variety, the registration may be revoked by the Authority, and any person aggrieved by such revocation shall have a right to appeal to the Appellate Board. The rights conferred by registration shall be subject to the public interest.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel, stable and uniformly reproducible, and shall be designated by an applicant in a manner consistent with the accepted principles of botanical nomenclature. The Plant Variety Protection Authority may, however, reject a denomination if it is likely to cause confusion with existing varieties, or if it is considered misleading or deceptive to the public. Should the proposed denomination not meet these criteria, the applicant shall be required to submit an alternative denomination within a period of thirty days from the date of notification of rejection. 

Provided that, where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, as established through prescribed testing procedures, the denomination of the initial variety shall not be assignable to the essentially derived variety. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding a denomination may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the designated appellate board. The register of plant varieties shall maintain a record of all approved denominations.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be clearly distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same crop or closely related species. The applicant seeking registration must submit a declaration affirming the distinctness of the proposed denomination, accompanied by a search report establishing that no other variety, whether registered or not, bears a confusingly similar denomination. Provided that, if a denomination has been in common use for a considerable period, the Authority may, subject to compelling justification and evidence of non-confusion, permit its registration. Any denomination incorporating misleading or deceptive elements, or one likely to cause public misconception regarding the characteristics of the variety, shall not be accepted. The Authority reserves the right to request modifications to a proposed denomination to ensure compliance with these provisions, and shall maintain a public register of all accepted denominations. A variety exhibiting essentially derived characteristics from a registered variety may, however, be assigned a denomination differing only to the extent necessary to distinguish it.

Any person claiming to have bred a distinct denomination variety shall submit a declaration affirming the breeder’s right to the said variety and demonstrating that the variety is substantially derived from a parent line bred or discovered by the claimant. Provided that, a variety which is not substantially similar to any other registered variety, or to any variety whose characteristics have been publicly known or reasonably available to the public before the date of application for registration, shall be considered a distinct denomination variety as provided herein. Any false declaration made under this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, revoke the registration of a variety found to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act relating to the maintenance of records pertaining to a distinct denomination variety shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, prior to the grant of a breeder’s certificate, submit a declaration of the distinct denomination variety proposed for its identification, ensuring such denomination is not likely to cause confusion with existing varieties registered under this Act or commonly known in the relevant agricultural community. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, approve the assignment of a denomination, provided that the proposed denomination conforms to the standards prescribed in the regulations. A breeder may, with the prior written consent of the owner of the denomination, assign the exclusive right to use the distinct denomination variety to another person for a specified period and territory, such assignment being recorded with the Authority. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to distinct denomination varieties shall render the application for registration liable to rejection, and any subsequent unauthorized use of an assigned denomination may attract penalties as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all assigned denominations.

The aggrieved party may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an appeal before the Appellate Board concerning the refusal of the Registrar to register a distinct denomination variety, provided that such appeal is presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and shall record the reasons for its decision. Where a dispute arises regarding the similarity of a proposed denomination to an existing one, the Board shall consider the likelihood of confusion amongst cultivators, and shall have the power to require evidence of actual use and market recognition of the earlier denomination. Furthermore, a variety exhibiting essentially derived characteristics from a registered variety shall not be considered a distinct denomination variety unless the breeder of the initial variety provides written consent. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel, stable and uniform, and clearly distinguishable by objective characteristics from any other variety whose existence is a matter of commonly known plant breeding practice. An applicant seeking registration of a distinct denomination variety shall submit a detailed description of the proposed denomination, demonstrating its distinctiveness and adherence to the principles of botanical naming conventions as prescribed by the Authority. Provided that, if a variety is also the subject of a patented invention, the applicant shall furnish evidence of the patent’s validity and scope, and demonstrate how the denomination does not conflict with any claims therein. The Authority may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, register the denomination if it satisfies the criteria outlined herein and is not likely to cause confusion with existing registered varieties. Any objection to a proposed denomination shall be considered in accordance with the established procedure for dispute resolution.

A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered novel, stable, and distinguishable from any other variety commonly known or commercially available in India, or in any relevant international system of plant variety protection. The applicant shall submit evidence demonstrating the distinct characteristics of the variety, including morphological, physiological, and, where applicable, molecular markers, as prescribed by the regulations. Provided that, where a denomination is likely to cause confusion with an existing variety, the Authority may require modification or rejection of the proposed denomination. All applications relating to varieties intended for cultivation within the territory of India shall demonstrate compliance with requirements pertaining to security india, including assessments of potential risks to agricultural biodiversity and food security. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all registered distinct denominations, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable fees. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding a denomination may file an appeal as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, prior to filing an application, ensure the proposed denomination adheres strictly to the principles of distinctness, uniformity, and stability as provided herein. A distinct denomination variety, for the purposes of this Act, must be clearly distinguishable from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge, or is evidenced by documented evidence presented to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Should a denomination be found to be deceptively similar to an existing variety, the application shall be rejected, and the applicant may be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any applicant intentionally misrepresenting a variety’s distinctness, particularly in relation to international standards such as those outlined in the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be subject to prosecution and a fine up to one lakh rupees, and the Authority may revoke any registration obtained through such misrepresentation. The Authority reserves the right to request additional evidence to verify the claimed distinctness.

An assignment denomination, for the purposes of registration of a new plant variety under this Act, shall be a name given by the breeder to the variety, and shall be distinctive, not likely to cause confusion with varieties known to exist, and conforming to the generally accepted principles of botanical nomenclature. Provided that, where a variety is commonly known by a particular name in any region, the Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, permit the use of that name as the assignment denomination. The assignment denomination may include an indication of the origin, breeding method, or other specific characteristics of the variety, but shall not contain misleading or deceptive elements. Any change to an assignment denomination following registration shall require prior approval of the Authority and notification in the Plant Varieties Journal, as provided herein.

Every applicant for registration of a new plant variety shall propose a suitable denomination, which shall be distinct and readily distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same or closely related species or genera, as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The proposed denomination, conforming to internationally accepted principles, may consist of letters, numerals, or a combination thereof, subject to the condition that it does not mislead or cause confusion. An assignment denomination, once accepted and associated with a registered variety, shall vest with the breeder or successor in title, and any subsequent change requires prior approval of the Authority and notification in the Plant Varieties Journal. Provided that, where a variety is commonly known by a particular name in trade, the Authority may, at its discretion, permit its continued use alongside the assigned denomination, ensuring clarity for farmers and preventing deceptive practices. The Authority reserves the right to reject a denomination deemed unsuitable or conflicting with existing registrations.

Any breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable denomination to that variety, which shall be maintained throughout the period of protection afforded under this Act. The assigned denomination must not cause confusion with varieties already registered or commonly known, and shall not be misleading as to the characteristics of the variety. A farmer, being the actual cultivator, may utilize a commonly known denomination for a variety traditionally grown by him, provided that such use does not infringe upon the rights of a registered breeder holding exclusive marketing rights. Should a dispute arise regarding the legitimacy of an assigned denomination, any aggrieved party may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for redress, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Authority shall, following due process and consideration of evidence, determine the validity of the denomination and issue appropriate orders, including the requirement for reassignment. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to assignment denomination shall render the application for registration liable to be rejected.

Every applicant for the registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a breeder’s certificate, propose a suitable denomination which shall be distinct, and shall not cause confusion with varieties already registered or commonly known. The proposed denomination, subject to the provisions herein, shall be considered an assignment denomination, and shall be recorded as part of the characteristics of the registered variety. Where a variety is commonly known by a particular name, the Authority may, at its discretion, require the applicant to adopt that name as the assignment denomination, notwithstanding any preference expressed by the applicant. Provided that, if the commonly known name is likely to cause confusion, the Authority may direct the applicant to propose an alternative denomination. Any person alleging that a proposed assignment denomination infringes upon their rights shall submit a notice of opposition to the Authority within a period of sixty days from the date of notification of the proposed denomination. The Authority shall, following due process and consideration of evidence, determine the validity of the objection and issue a reasoned order. A denomination once assigned and registered may not be altered except under exceptional circumstances and with the prior approval of the Authority.

Every breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, propose a suitable assignment denomination which is clearly distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same kind or of closely related kinds. The proposed denomination must comply with the requirements regarding brevity, ease of pronunciation, and absence of misleading characteristics, as may be prescribed. Provided that, if a variety is commonly known by a particular name in the relevant trade, the breeder may, subject to the approval of the Authority, retain that name as the assignment denomination. Any transfer of rights relating to a registered variety shall include assignment of the denomination, unless otherwise agreed between the parties and recorded with the Authority. The Authority may, where a denomination is deemed to be generic or misleading despite prior approval, require the rights holder to adopt a new assignment denomination within a specified timeframe. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable assignment denomination to said variety, conforming to the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The assignment denomination shall not cause confusion with any existing registered variety, nor shall it be deceptive or misleading to the public regarding the characteristics of the plant. Provided that, if a variety is commonly known by a particular name in local parlance, the Authority may, subject to verification of such usage and absence of conflict with existing registrations, permit its continued use as the assignment denomination. Any false representation concerning the assignment denomination, or any attempt to pass off a variety under a denomination already assigned to another, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all assigned denominations.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable denomination to the said variety, conforming to the requirements prescribed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The assigned denomination, constituting the ‘assignment denomination’, shall be clearly marked on all propagative material commercially sold, offered for sale, or otherwise distributed by the breeder or their authorized agents. Any transfer of rights, whether by way of assignment, license, or other means, in respect of a registered variety shall necessitate the formal notification of the change in ownership to the Authority, along with confirmation of continued adherence to the denomination requirements. Provided that, where a variety is commonly known by a designated common name, the breeder may, subject to the Authority’s approval, utilize such common name in conjunction with the assignment denomination for marketing purposes. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the registration liable to revocation, as provided herein.

Any person claiming rights over an extant plant variety, and seeking registration of the same under this Act, shall propose a suitable assignment denomination which is clearly distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same genus or species. The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration, may, if satisfied that the proposed assignment denomination is likely to cause confusion with an existing denomination, or is deceptive, require the applicant to submit an alternative denomination within a period of thirty days. Should the applicant fail to comply with such requirement, the application may be deemed incomplete and subject to rejection, provided that an appeal against such rejection lies before the Appellate Board. Furthermore, where a dispute arises concerning the assignment denomination of a variety already registered, any aggrieved party may petition the Appellate Board for rectification of the register, demonstrating that the existing denomination infringes upon their established rights or is otherwise contrary to the provisions of this Act regarding distinctness and clarity.

Every applicant for the registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of a breeder’s certificate, propose a suitable assignment denomination which shall be unique and readily distinguishable from denominations of other registered varieties of the same or closely related species. The proposed denomination shall not cause confusion with existing denominations, and shall conform to the requirements as prescribed in the regulations framed under this Act. Provided that, where a transmissible case of prior use of a similar denomination is established to the satisfaction of the Authority, the applicant may be required to modify the proposed denomination or provide evidence demonstrating non-confusion. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, approve or reject the proposed assignment denomination, and its decision shall be final and binding on the applicant. Any alteration to the denomination after registration shall require prior approval and may be subject to additional fees.

For the purposes of this Act, “industrial application” shall denote the use of a design in connection with articles manufactured by industrial processes, including any handcraft, but does not include methods or principles of construction or arrangement as well as any purely functional feature of an article necessary for its intended purpose. A design capable of industrial application must be new or original, and shall not be identical with any design which is, at the time of registration, known or has been previously published in India or elsewhere. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered design confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to apply that design to articles in the class of articles for which it is registered, and to manufacture, import, and sell articles bearing such design. Any act done without the consent of the proprietor shall constitute an infringement.

Any design, to be registrable under this Act, shall be novel and capable of being applied to an article by any industrial process, being any process or manner of manufacturing, separating, refining, colouring, embellishing, composing, or adapting any substance or article. The industrial application of a design shall not be limited to physical articles, but may extend to methods or systems, provided such methods or systems are associated with a tangible article capable of bearing the design. An applicant seeking registration must demonstrate, through a clear statement of intent and supporting documentation, the specific article or class of articles to which the design is intended for industrial application. Designs lacking demonstrable industrial application, or those solely conceived as artistic expressions without a connection to manufacture, shall not be eligible for registration as provided herein. The Controller may require evidence of practical application before granting registration.

Any person who, without lawful justification and with intent to deceive, applies a design that is substantially similar to a registered design to articles for industrial application, shall be liable to a civil action for recovery of damages. The owner of the registered design may, as provided herein, seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further such application, and may also claim an account of profits wrongly made by the defendant. Where a design is capable of being applied to multiple articles, the damages recoverable shall be assessed considering the scale of unauthorized industrial application. However, no action shall lie where the application relates solely to a feature dictated by technical necessity, or where the design is demonstrably common to the trade. A registered design proprietor may, subject to fulfilling the conditions prescribed, assign the right to apply the design industrially to another party, and such assignment shall be enforceable under this Act. Any contract relating to such assignment must be in writing and signed by both parties.

Any work which is capable of being used in any industry shall be deemed to possess industrial application for the purposes of this Act, and such capacity shall be determined with reference to the work’s potential for replication by a technically skilled person. Where a work, though novel, lacks demonstrable utility or a specific, identifiable industrial purpose, it shall not be considered to satisfy the requirement of industrial application as provided herein. The Controller, upon examination, may require the applicant to submit evidence substantiating the claimed industrial application, including but not limited to technical specifications, market analysis, or expert testimony. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence within a period of ninety days from the date of such request shall be construed as abandonment of the claim. However, aesthetic features alone, absent any functional utility, shall not constitute sufficient grounds for establishing industrial application, unless such features are integral to the work’s intended use and contribute to its marketability. Any dispute regarding the existence of industrial application shall be subject to review as per the established procedures.

Any work qualifying for copyright protection under this Act shall not be deemed to possess industrial application unless it demonstrably satisfies the criteria of sufficient novelty and inventive step, assessed with reference to existing knowledge in the relevant field. An application for registration claiming industrial application must be accompanied by detailed specifications outlining the process by which the copyrighted work is adapted or applied to an article or process. The applicant shall furnish evidence of commercial exploitation, or a reasonable and demonstrable prospect thereof, within a period of three years from the date of application, failing which the claim of industrial application may be revoked. Subject to the provisions herein, a design which constitutes the purely functional aspect of an article shall not be considered an infringement if independently created. Provided that, the aesthetic features of the work, distinct from its functional elements, remain protected under this Act.

Any person who, without lawful authority, commercially exploits a design—being an original aesthetic feature of an article—which is capable of industrial application shall be deemed to have infringed the exclusive right of the creator, as provided herein. The determination of industrial application shall not be limited to mass production, but shall extend to any instance where the design is utilized for commercial gain, irrespective of the quantity produced. However, a design which is dictated solely by technical functionality and lacks aesthetic originality shall not be considered protectable under this Act. Any article produced or imported in violation of this provision shall be liable to seizure, and the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Repeated offenses shall incur a doubling of the fine and a mandatory minimum imprisonment term of one year.

Any person possessing exclusive rights in a design, being a feature of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament, and intending to license the right to apply said design to articles, shall submit a notice of intention to the Registrar of Designs, detailing the scope of permitted industrial application. Such license shall be subject to the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon between the owner of the design and the licensee, and shall specify the duration, territory, and articles to which the design may be applied. Where a design is assigned, the assignee shall, within thirty days of such assignment, notify the Registrar and furnish evidence of title. Failure to do so may invalidate subsequent claims of infringement. The owner of a registered design may, as provided herein, grant licenses, and may revoke any license granted, subject to a reasonable notice period stipulated in the licensing agreement, or in the absence of such stipulation, a period of ninety days. Any dispute regarding the extent of permitted industrial application shall be resolved through arbitration.

Any work involving the industrial application of a design shall not be considered to infringe copyright as provided herein, provided that such application is demonstrably distinct from the original artistic work and does not constitute a substantial reproduction thereof. However, this exemption shall not extend to works where the industrial application is merely a slavish copy, lacking any significant modification or adaptation. Appeals regarding determinations of ‘significant modification’ may be made to the High Court, subject to the provisions relating to limitation periods under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Where a plaintiff alleges that an industrial application, though modified, unfairly exploits the aesthetic qualities of their copyrighted work, the burden of proof shall lie upon the defendant to demonstrate sufficient originality in the applied design. Any dispute concerning the scope of ‘industrial application’ itself shall be adjudicated based on prevailing technical standards and market practices.

Any process involving a novel and non-obvious application of a known substance, apparatus, or method, qualifying as an invention under this Act, shall be deemed to possess industrial application if it is capable of being manufactured or used in any industry. An applicant patent, submitted in accordance with the prescribed procedures, must clearly demonstrate such industrial application through detailed specification and, where applicable, working examples. The Controller of Patents shall assess the claimed industrial application based on evidence presented by the applicant and may require further clarification or supporting data. Should the Controller determine that the claimed invention lacks demonstrable industrial application, the application shall be rejected. However, an invention relating to traditional knowledge or folklore, even if possessing industrial application, shall be subject to the provisions regarding prior art and public domain as provided herein. The burden of proving industrial application rests with the applicant throughout the examination process. Failure to adequately demonstrate such application may result in the refusal of the patent.

Any article shall be considered capable of industrial application where it is capable of being made or used in any industry, and includes an article which may be made or used in more than one industry. However, the determination of industrial application shall not be solely based on the theoretical possibility of use, but rather on demonstrable potential for practical application within a recognized industrial setting. Where a promotion trade mark is affixed to an article demonstrating such industrial application, the owner of the copyright in the underlying work shall be entitled to remedies as provided herein, subject to establishing that the affixing of the trade mark does not fundamentally alter the character of the work. Provided that, if the article is solely intended for personal or domestic use and not for commercial distribution, such use shall not constitute industrial application for the purposes of this Act. Any dispute regarding the genuineness of industrial application shall be decided by the High Court.

Any work embodying industrial application, whether a design, process, or article, shall be deemed a copyrightable subject under this Act, provided that such application is novel and non-obvious, and not merely a trivial variation of existing works. Disputes regarding the novelty or non-obviousness of such industrial application may be submitted to a designated adjudicating authority for technical examination, the decision of which shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court. Furthermore, any digital work incorporating Right Management Information, intended to identify the author or owner of the copyright in relation to said industrial application, shall be protected from unauthorized removal or alteration. Any person who removes or alters such information with intent to deceive, or facilitate infringement, shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein, notwithstanding any claim of independent creation or fair use. The burden of proof regarding the authenticity of Right Management Information shall lie with the claimant.

The District Court having jurisdiction to entertain a suit concerning copyright shall be the District Court within whose local limits the defendant resides or voluntarily submits to the jurisdiction of such Court. Provided that, if the defendant does not reside within the limits of any District Court in India, the suit may be instituted in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the cause of action arises. Subject to the foregoing provisions, any suit for infringement of copyright involving a claim for damages exceeding twenty lakh rupees shall be instituted in the High Court exercising ordinary original civil jurisdiction. Furthermore, a plaintiff may elect to institute a suit in the High Court even if the claimed damages are less than twenty lakh rupees, provided that all defendants agree to such venue.

Any application for the registration of a copyright, or for the rectification of any entry in the Register of Copyrights, shall be presented to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the applicant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, if the applicant is not a legal person, the application may be presented to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the principal place of business of the applicant is situated. Where any dispute arises regarding the determination of the appropriate court having jurisdiction, the matter shall be referred to the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, whose decision shall be final and binding. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the High Court shall, upon being satisfied that the application is duly completed and accompanied by the prescribed fee, proceed to examine the same. Any objection to the registration shall be filed within sixty days of the publication of the application.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright, or any other right conferred under this Act, shall have recourse to a civil court for remedies, including injunction, damages, and rendition of accounts. The court having jurisdiction to entertain such suit shall be determined based on the place where the defendant resides, carries on business, or where the cause of action arises. However, where multiple defendants reside at different places, the plaintiff may elect to institute the suit in any court having jurisdiction over at least one of the defendants, provided that such election does not prejudice the rights of other parties. Subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force, a court may, at any stage of a proceeding, transfer a suit to another court of competent jurisdiction if it appears to be more convenient for the ends of justice. The grant of an injunction shall not be withheld merely on account of the difficulty of ascertaining the actual damages.

Any dispute concerning the validity or infringement of copyright, or any other right conferred under this Act, shall be cognizable by a court of competent jurisdiction, subject to the provisions contained herein. The determination of such competent jurisdiction shall, in the first instance, be governed by the pecuniary value of the claim asserted, and the territorial limits within which the cause of action arises. Where the alleged infringement occurs across multiple jurisdictions, the court first seized of the matter, and possessing jurisdiction over a substantial part of the claim, shall generally have exclusive jurisdiction to determine the dispute, provided that it demonstrates reasonable diligence in notifying other potentially relevant courts. However, a party may petition for a transfer of proceedings to a court deemed more appropriate, based on the location of evidence or witnesses, or the convenience of the parties, subject to the discretion of the court hearing the petition. The principles of res judicata shall apply to judgments rendered by any court having jurisdiction under this Act.

Any dispute concerning the infringement of copyright, or any right related to copyright, as provided herein, shall be subject to the provisions of this section regarding the determination of the court having jurisdiction. The court having jurisdiction over a matter shall be that situated in—(a) the place where the plaintiff transacts business and resides; or (b) the place where the cause of action arises; or (c) where the defendant resides or transacts business, provided that where the defendant resides outside the territory of India, the court at the place where the cause of action arises shall alone have jurisdiction. However, a single suit may be filed in respect of multiple infringements occurring in different places, subject to the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court. Where a copyright society is the plaintiff, the court having jurisdiction shall be that within the local limits of which the registered office of the society is situated.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright, or any other right conferred under this Act, may institute a suit in the court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, or where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, where the infringement is of a continuing nature, the court having jurisdiction shall be that where the defendant first engaged in the infringing act. The District Court shall have exclusive original jurisdiction to try such suits, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, relating to transfer of suits. Failure to comply with the jurisdictional requirements as provided herein shall render the proceedings voidable at the discretion of the court. Any person found to be intentionally circumventing these provisions, with the aim of delaying legitimate legal action, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any assignment or licensing of copyright in a cinematograph film, sound recording, or literary or dramatic work, intended for commercial exploitation within the territory of India, shall be registered with the designated Registrar of Copyrights to be effective against third parties. The Registrar, upon receiving a complete application for registration of such assignment or license, may, subject to verification of the authenticity of the instrument and the legal capacity of the assignor or licensor, grant a certificate of registration. Disputes concerning the validity or scope of any such assignment or license, or regarding the entitlement to royalties arising therefrom, shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the court having jurisdiction over the principal place of business of the assignee or licensee, or, in the absence of such place, the court having jurisdiction over the place where the cause of action arises. Provided that, where the assignment or license involves multiple assignees or licensees residing in different jurisdictions, the court having jurisdiction shall be determined by the High Court exercising original jurisdiction.

Any dispute concerning the validity of a copyright registration, or alleging infringement of rights as provided herein, shall be subject to the determination of a court having jurisdiction, which, unless otherwise expressly stipulated by any other enactment, shall be the District Court within whose local limits the defendant resides or voluntarily submits to the jurisdiction, or where the cause of action arises. However, if a plaintiff seeks interim relief, such as an injunction restraining further infringement, the court may, notwithstanding the foregoing, exercise jurisdiction based solely upon the location of the plaintiff’s principal place of business. Provided that, where the defendant is a non-resident Indian or a body incorporated outside India, the District Court in Delhi shall have exclusive jurisdiction, subject to the principles of private international law. Any aggrieved party may appeal from the decree of the District Court to the High Court, and thereafter to the Supreme Court, as per the provisions of the relevant appellate statutes.

Any dispute concerning the infringement of copyright, or regarding the validity or ownership of copyright, shall be cognizable by a court having jurisdiction as determined under this Act, provided that such court is duly empowered to adjudicate matters relating to intellectual property. Where a work is subject to a registered certification mark denoting adherence to specified quality or standards, any claim of misrepresentation regarding such certification, impacting the copyright holder’s rights, shall also fall within the purview of this jurisdiction. However, a plaintiff seeking relief must demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the court, a direct nexus between the alleged infringement and the certified quality represented by the mark. Subject to the provisions herein, the court shall have the power to grant injunctions, award damages, and issue other appropriate reliefs as deemed just and equitable. Compliance with procedural requirements regarding evidence of copyright and certification is mandatory for the maintainability of any suit.

Any assignment of copyright in a registered trade mark, or a license to exploit such copyright, shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the District Court within whose local limits the principal place of business of the assignee or licensee is situated, provided that where the assignee or licensee does not have a principal place of business within India, the District Court having jurisdiction shall be that within whose local limits the registered office of the copyright owner is located. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment, or the scope of a license, and it is alleged that a trade mark identical to the subject matter of the copyright is being used in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the assignment or license, the court shall consider evidence of such use as relevant to the determination of jurisdiction. All applications for the rectification of assignments or licenses shall be filed with the appropriate court having jurisdiction as determined herein. The copyright owner may, subject to such conditions as the court may deem fit, seek an injunction restraining any infringement arising from an improperly assigned or licensed copyright.

The District Court having jurisdiction over a matter concerning copyright shall be determined by the location of the defendant’s principal place of business or residence, subject to the proviso that where multiple defendants exist, the Court with jurisdiction over any one of them may proceed with the matter. However, a plaintiff may elect to institute a suit in a District Court within whose limits any relevant act constituting the infringement occurred. Where a registration of copyright is demonstrated to be invalid due to a lack of originality or other grounds as provided herein, the Court may, notwithstanding any prior finding of infringement, direct cancellation justified registration and dismiss the claim. Any appeal from such a decision shall lie to the High Court. The provisions of this Act shall apply mutatis mutandis to such cancellations.

Any application for registration of copyright, or any subsequent rectification thereof, shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the District Court within whose local limits the applicant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, if the applicant is not a legal person, the District Court having jurisdiction shall be that within the local limits where the work was first published, or, if unpublished, where the author was ordinarily resident at the time of creation. Where an objection is raised to the registration of a copyright, the matter may, at the request of either party, be referred to the Opposition Board for preliminary examination and report. The decision of the Court regarding jurisdiction shall be final and binding, and no appeal shall lie therefrom except as otherwise provided in this Act. All notices relating to proceedings before the Court shall be served in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Patents, in such form as may be prescribed. The application shall be accompanied by a detailed layout of the circuit, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to manufacture the semiconductor integrated circuit. A statement of ownership, clearly identifying the applicant as the proprietor of the layout-design, is also required. The register, maintained by the Controller, shall contain particulars of the layout-design, including the date of filing, the applicant’s name and address, and the status of the application. Subject to verification and confirmation of compliance with the provisions of this Act, the Controller shall register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, where the applicant is not the creator, a no-objection certificate from the creator shall be submitted alongside the application for registration. Any alteration to the registered layout-design shall be recorded in the register sub section, and a fee prescribed for such amendment shall be payable.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing to register a layout-design, or requiring an amendment of an application for registration, or revoking a registration, may, within ninety days of the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall, before disposing of any appeal, give an opportunity to the parties to be heard. Where an appeal is preferred against an order directing the rectification of the register, the Appellate Board may, if it considers appropriate, direct that the rectification be carried out, and the register shall be amended accordingly. 

A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the rights in the layout-design, or create an interest therein, by any means, including by way of mortgage or license. Any assignment or creation of interest shall be subject to the Controller maintaining a register sub section detailing such transfers, and notice of such assignment or creation of interest shall be filed with the Controller within thirty days of the transaction. Failure to comply with this requirement does not invalidate the transfer but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transaction.

Any person desiring to register a layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its originality. The application shall clearly identify the applicant and, where the layout-design was made under a contract of employment, shall include a statement confirming the applicant’s right to register the layout-design. A request for expedited examination may be submitted, subject to payment of an additional fee as specified in the Schedule. The Controller, upon receiving an application deemed complete, shall assign a filing date and enter the particulars in the register sub section, noting the date of application and applicant details. Provided that, if the Controller raises objections, the applicant shall have a period of thirty days to address them or the application shall be deemed abandoned. Failure to maintain the annual renewal fee, as provided herein, will result in the removal of the layout-design from the register.

Any person being the proprietor of a layout-design registered under this Act may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to others for the commercial exploitation of such layout-design, either generally or subject to conditions, and such license may be exclusive or non-exclusive, and shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the proprietor. An assignment of any right in a registered layout-design shall be effective only upon registration of the assignment with the appropriate office, and the register shall reflect the current proprietor following any such assignment. The application for registration of an assignment shall be made by the assignee or the assignor with the consent of the assignee. Where a layout-design is jointly held, no license or assignment shall be valid without the consent of all the joint proprietors, and the register sub section pertaining to the layout-design shall be updated to reflect the new ownership or licensed rights. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it, but it may not be enforceable against a third party without proof of notice.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing to register a layout-design, or rejecting an application for amendment of the register, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Controller a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Controller. Where an appeal is filed concerning a registered layout-design, the Controller shall, pending disposal of the appeal, furnish certified copies of the register sub section relating to that layout-design to the Appellate Board and to the appellant. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court. The High Court’s decision shall be final.

Any person possessing a registered layout-design shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in India. A license to use a registered layout-design may be granted by the registered owner to another party, and such license shall be in writing and specify the duration, scope, and territorial limits of the permitted use. Assignment of the exclusive right to a layout-design shall also be in writing and registered with the appropriate authority as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be void. 

The register sub section maintained by the Controller of Patents shall accurately reflect all current assignments and licensed uses of registered layout-designs. An applicant seeking to protect a layout-design incorporating a distinctive mark or sign may, concurrently with the application for registration, apply trade mark protection for such mark or sign, provided that the mark does not mislead regarding the origin of the layout-design itself. Any dispute concerning the validity of a license or assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an exploitation of a registered layout-design shall be liable to pay royalty to the proprietor, subject to the terms of any agreement entered into between the parties. Where a registered breeder variety, protected under the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, incorporates a semiconductor layout-design, the proprietor of the layout-design may, notwithstanding any other provision contained in that Act, seek remedies as provided herein for any unauthorized reproduction or commercial exploitation of the layout-design within the plant variety. The register sub section maintained by the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry shall be conclusive evidence of the particulars entered therein, unless and until duly amended in accordance with the procedures outlined in this Act. Any challenge to the validity of a registration, or to the particulars entered in the register, shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. The proprietor may assign or transmit the right to the layout-design by a writing signed by him or his duly authorized agent. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act shall render the offender liable to such penalties as may be prescribed.

The Registrar shall, upon examination of an application for registration and finding it meets the requirements as provided herein, cause the trade mark to be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal as a condition precedent to registration. Such advertisement shall specify the trade mark, the goods or services for which registration is sought, the applicant’s name and address, and a statement of any conditions subject to which the application is accepted. Any person may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition to the registration, detailing the grounds upon which the application is contested. The Registrar may, after considering any opposition and subject to such further evidence as may be required, either accept or refuse the application, or accept it subject to modifications or limitations. Gazette subject conditions shall be clearly stated in the certificate of registration if the mark is ultimately registered.

The Registrar, upon examination of an application for registration and being satisfied that the trade mark meets the requirements as provided herein, shall cause notice of the application to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, hereinafter referred to as the Gazette. Such publication shall be subject to conditions relating to the clarity of the mark’s representation and a declaration of use within the prescribed period. Any party desiring to oppose the registration shall file a notice of opposition in the prescribed manner within the stipulated timeframe from the date of publication in the Gazette. The Registrar may, at any stage, require the applicant to satisfy further conditions regarding distinctiveness or potential for confusion with existing marks. Failure to comply with these Gazette subject conditions may result in the application being deemed abandoned or registration being refused, notwithstanding any prior acceptance. A certified copy of the entry in the Register shall be conclusive evidence of ownership.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, upon satisfaction of the Registrar regarding the application, be published in the Trade Marks Journal, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Registrar may, prior to acceptance of the application, require the applicant to satisfy any outstanding objections or to amend the application to conform with the provisions of this Act. Should the application be accepted subject to conditions, the Registrar shall clearly specify those conditions in the Journal publication, including any limitations on the scope of goods or services covered by the mark. Any third party aggrieved by the publication, alleging a conflict with their existing rights, may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed period. Failure to comply with the gazette subject conditions, or to address any opposition filed, may result in the application being deemed abandoned, and the applicant shall have no recourse except as provided herein for review of the Registrar’s decision. The Registrar retains discretion to modify conditions if circumstances warrant, provided adequate notice is given to all affected parties.

The Registrar, upon examination of an application for registration and finding it meets the requirements as provided herein, shall cause notice of the application to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, hereinafter referred to as the Gazette. Such publication shall be subject to conditions relating to clarity of representation of the trade mark and the completeness of particulars regarding goods or services specified in the application. Any person may, within a period of four months from the date of such publication in the Gazette, file a notice of opposition to the registration of the trade mark, detailing the grounds for such opposition. The Registrar, having considered any opposition filed and any evidence submitted by the applicant or the opponent, may, if satisfied that the opposition is well-founded, reject the application. However, the Registrar may, subject to conditions deemed necessary to prevent confusion or deception, allow the application to proceed, even if an opposition has been filed, provided that the applicant demonstrates sufficient cause and remedies any deficiencies identified during examination. All decisions relating to the Gazette subject conditions shall be recorded in writing and be open to inspection.

The Registrar, upon accepting an application for registration of a trade mark, shall cause the particulars to be published in the Trade Marks Journal, hereinafter referred to as the Gazette. Publication in the Gazette is subject to conditions ensuring accurate representation of the mark and proper classification under the Nice Classification, as adopted herein. Any party opposing the registration must file a notice of opposition within the prescribed period, detailing the grounds for such opposition and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar may, at any time prior to registration, require the applicant to satisfy specific conditions regarding distinctiveness or potential for confusion with existing marks. Compliance with these Gazette subject conditions is mandatory for proceeding with the examination process. Failure to fulfill these conditions within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned, as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all fulfilled and unfulfilled conditions pertaining to each published application.

Any application for registration of a trade mark, subject to conditions specified in the Trade Marks Registry’s public gazette, shall be examined as provided herein, and failure to satisfy those gazette subject conditions within a period of thirty days from the date of notification of objection shall render the application liable to be deemed abandoned. Where an applicant seeks rectification of an entry in the register concerning a collective mark or a certification mark, evidence of consent from a majority of the members associated with said mark shall be furnished, failing which the application shall be dismissed with costs. Any person contravening the provisions relating to the use of such marks, or falsely representing association with a registered collective or certification mark, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, however, impose a lesser penalty in cases of minor infractions, subject to a reasoned order.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, subject to conditions relating to the use or licensing of the mark, shall be recorded in the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar, upon receipt of a request for such recordal, may require the assignee or applicant to demonstrate, to their satisfaction, that the conditions precedent to the assignment or registration have been duly fulfilled. Where an assignment is made subject to a condition requiring continued use of the mark by the assignor, the assignee shall furnish a statutory declaration confirming the assignor’s adherence to said condition within six months of the assignment date. Failure to provide such declaration may render the assignment voidable, as provided herein. The Registrar shall, prior to recording the assignment, publish a notice of the proposed recordal in the Trade Marks Journal, affording opportunity for opposition. Any objection to the recordal based on non-fulfillment of gazette subject conditions shall be adjudicated upon in accordance with the established procedures for opposing trade mark applications.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect. The description shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. A provisional specification, if filed, shall be deemed to be the complete and clear description for a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of filing, subject to the requirements for a complete specification being filed within that period. Where an application patent relates to a biotechnological application involving biological material, a deposit of such material in a recognized depositary institution shall be a prerequisite for processing the application, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application patent liable to be refused.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect. The description shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention. A provisional specification may be filed initially, subject to the requirement that a complete specification is filed within twelve months from the date of the provisional application, failing which the provisional application shall be deemed to be withdrawn. Where an application patent relates to a process, the specification shall clearly define the process and the manner in which it is performed. Any amendment to the complete specification shall not extend beyond the scope of the provisional specification, if any, and shall be subject to scrutiny as provided herein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents relating to the application patent, as deemed necessary for examination.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the invention for which protection is sought, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. The applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, amend the application patent at any time before the grant of the patent, provided that such amendment does not extend the scope of the invention beyond what was originally disclosed. Where a complete specification does not fully satisfy the requirements of this Act, the Controller may require the applicant to amend it within a period to be specified, and failure to do so may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to an application patent may, within the prescribed time, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller, and its decision shall be final and binding, subject to the right of appeal to the Supreme Court as provided by law.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. The description shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Where an application patent relates to a micro-organism, a deposit of the micro-organism with a designated depositary institution, as prescribed, shall be a necessary condition for the acceptance of the application. 

Provided that, where the micro-organism is not available for deposit, a full description of the characteristics of the micro-organism shall be furnished, subject to verification by the Controller. Any amendment to the application patent, after filing, shall not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure; however, the Controller may, upon reasonable cause shown, permit clarification of the description. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application patent liable to be refused, as provided herein.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. The description shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention.
