Provided that, where an application patent relates to a biotechnological invention, a deposit of the biological material shall be made with a depositary institution recognized by the Controller, and evidence of such deposit shall accompany the application. Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application patent claiming priority from a prior application filed in a convention country shall be examined within a period of eighteen months from the date of filing, or such extended period as may be prescribed. Any failure to comply with these requirements may render the application patent liable to be refused, as provided herein. The Controller may, however, require amendments to the application patent to ensure compliance.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a detailed specification, clearly and concisely describing the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. Any application patent found to be lacking such a specification, or containing a specification deemed insufficient by the Controller, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, allow a period of sixty days for rectification of the deficiency, subject to payment of a late submission fee as prescribed. Failure to rectify within this period shall result in the application being deemed abandoned. Furthermore, any person found to have knowingly submitted a false or misleading specification in an application patent, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. All fees levied under this Act shall be non-refundable, except as otherwise provided herein.

Every application patent shall vest in the applicant until lawfully assigned or transferred to another person or entity, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assignment of an application patent shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of such assignment, including the territory and duration for which the rights are assigned. Where an application patent is jointly held, no co-owner may grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a written agreement amongst them. 

The Controller shall maintain a register of assignments and transmissions of application patents, and any change in ownership must be recorded therein as provided herein. Failure to register an assignment within the prescribed period may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. A licensee of an application patent may, subject to the terms of the license, further assign their interest in the licensed rights, provided that such assignment does not exceed the scope of the original license.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the invention for which protection is sought, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Should an applicant claim priority from a previous application filed in another country, notice thereof, along with certified copies of the said application, shall be furnished within the prescribed period. Any failure to do so may render the application subject to rejection, unless satisfactory cause is demonstrated to the Controller of Patents. An applicant aggrieved by the rejection of their application patent may file an appeal before the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is made within the time limit as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case an appeal may be made to the High Court. Any dispute regarding the validity of a claimed priority date shall be adjudicated by the Appellate Board.

Every application patent shall be examined by the Controller in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and the Controller may require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information as may be necessary for the purpose of examination. Where a form filed patent is found to be incomplete or does not meet the requirements as prescribed, the Controller shall issue a statement of objections to the applicant, allowing a period of one month to remedy the deficiencies, subject to extension granted at the Controller’s discretion. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the objections within the stipulated timeframe, the application patent shall be deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to an application patent may, within the prescribed period, file an appeal to the Appellate Board, and the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, provided that such appeal does not contravene principles of natural justice. The Controller may, as provided herein, revoke a patent if it is proven that a prior claim exists.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a detailed disclosure of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and a clear and concise claim or claims defining the scope of the invention for which protection is sought. Should the Controller determine that an application patent lacks such sufficient disclosure, they may issue a notice requiring rectification within a period not exceeding six months. Failure to comply with said notice shall render the application patent liable to be refused. However, as provided herein, if exceptional circumstances exist and the invention addresses a matter of public importance, the Central Government may, after due notice to the patent holder, order a compulsory licensing of the patent, subject to reasonable remuneration being paid to the patentee. Any attempt to circumvent this provision, or to demand excessive remuneration, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall be subject to the condition that the assignee acquires the right to maintain and renew the trade mark. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise their rights, or permits the use of the trade mark by others without due control, a court may, upon application by any aggrieved person, order rectification of the register or grant other relief as it deems fit. Provided that, no such order shall be made unless the court is satisfied that the continued registration of the trade mark by the current manner registered proprietor would be detrimental to the interests of the public or likely to cause confusion. A registered proprietor may, as provided herein, seek an injunction against any infringement of their rights.

Any person claiming to be a registered proprietor who assigns or otherwise transfers the registered trade mark, or any right therein, without the prior written consent of any existing licensee, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise reasonable control over the use of a registered trade mark by a licensee, as provided herein, and such use results in damage to the reputation of the trade mark, the registered proprietor may be subject to an injunction restraining further use. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall not be relieved of liability for defects in the goods or services sold under the trade mark, even if such defects arise from the actions of the licensee. Any complaint regarding improper use by a licensee shall be adjudicated by the Registrar, and a finding of willful negligence on the part of the manner registered proprietor may result in revocation of the registration.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign the trade mark and the goodwill or part thereof in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. Any assignment shall be effected by a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the registered proprietor, and a copy thereof shall be furnished to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner prescribed. Where the assignment includes the transfer of goodwill, the assignee may, as provided herein, apply to the Registry to become the registered proprietor of the trade mark. 

A license, whether sole or otherwise, may be granted by the registered proprietor, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the license, including the duration, territory, and goods or services in relation to which the license is granted. The manner registered proprietor may revoke a license if the licensee fails to observe the terms and conditions of the license, subject to a reasonable notice period.

An order appellate under this Act shall be made to a designated authority established by the Central Government, possessing requisite technical expertise in the relevant field of patenting. Such authority shall be empowered to review any decision of a Controller of Patents, including refusals of applications, revocations of patents, and determinations regarding infringement. Subject to the provisions contained herein, any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the order appellate within a period of sixty days from the date of the order sought to be appealed. The appellate authority may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period by a further thirty days. Provided that, the appellate authority shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant has deposited the prescribed fee and furnished a certified copy of the order appealed against. Any decision of the order appellate shall be final and binding, except as otherwise provided for review to the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of a patent, or any decision concerning an opposition proceeding, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s order, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a statement of the grounds for the appeal. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend this period subject to sufficient cause being shown. The Controller shall transmit all relevant documents and records pertaining to the case to the Appellate Board without delay. An order appellate made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning errors of law apparent on the face of the record. The Board may, if deemed necessary, require expert evidence to be submitted.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of an appeal, and after giving the respondent an opportunity to be heard, either confirm, modify, reverse, or set aside the order of the Controller. An order appellate made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a right of appeal to the High Court on questions of law. Provided that, the High Court may, while hearing such appeal, direct the matter to be referred back to the Appellate Board for fresh consideration on specific issues. Any fees payable for filing an appeal shall be as prescribed.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such extension of time as the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, allow. The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of an appeal and after giving the Controller an opportunity to be heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. An order appellate of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of law. The Appellate Board may, while considering an appeal, require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems reasonable to cover the costs of the proceedings. Provided that, such deposit shall not exceed the original fee paid for the application under consideration. The Board shall dispose of every appeal within one hundred and eighty days of its filing.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to an application for a patent or the revocation thereof, may prefer an order appellate to the High Court. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to condonation of delay not exceeding an additional thirty days, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Court. The High Court, upon receipt of an appeal, may direct the Controller to furnish a certified copy of the relevant records within sixty days. The appellant shall deposit with the Court, at the time of filing the appeal, a sum equivalent to the fees originally paid for the grant or revocation of the patent in question, as a condition precedent to the Court’s consideration of the matter. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal inadmissible, unless otherwise directed by the Court. The High Court’s decision on the order appellate shall be final and binding.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, or any decision refusing an application for a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall, following a review of the record and consideration of submissions, issue an order appellate affirming, modifying, or reversing the Controller’s decision within ninety days of the filing of the appeal. Failure to issue such order within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed a contravention of this Act and attract a penalty of five thousand rupees per day of delay, payable to the aggrieved party. Any wilful misrepresentation of facts before the Appellate Board shall render the appellant liable to a fine not exceeding twenty thousand rupees, and may further disqualify them from filing future appeals. The decision of the Appellate Board constitutes a final order subject to judicial review only on grounds of jurisdictional error.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and subject to the provisions of this Act, may be assigned freely. Where an assignment is made under a contract containing a condition requiring the assignee to exploit the patent commercially, failure to satisfy such condition shall not invalidate the assignment, but may be grounds for an order appellate to restore the rights of the assignor. Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the assignment of a patent may, within ninety days of the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the designated authority. The authority shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the order, and such order appellate shall be final and binding. A register of assignments shall be maintained by the Controller of Patents.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to the provisions for condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of a duly filed appeal and payment of the prescribed fee, shall issue notice to the Controller and any other necessary parties. The Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to furnish evidence or documents to substantiate the grounds of appeal. Any decision of the Appellate Board constitutes an order appellate and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice. Provided that the Board may, with reasons recorded, stay the execution of the Controller’s order pending disposal of the appeal.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to the revocation of a patent or the amendment thereof, may prefer an order appellate to the High Court. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to such extensions as the High Court may allow for sufficient cause shown. The High Court, upon consideration of the appeal, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller, and may direct such further proceedings to be taken as it deems fit. Where an appeal is preferred alleging indication falsified concerning the efficacy or safety of a patented invention, the High Court shall, prior to substantive consideration, require the appellant to furnish evidence supporting such allegation. Failure to provide such evidence within a period stipulated by the Court may result in dismissal of the appeal. The High Court’s decision on such order appellate shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to the Supreme Court as provided by law.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents, relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to the conditions hereinafter stipulated. The memorandum of appeal shall clearly state the grounds upon which the order is contested and shall be filed within sixty days from the date of the Controller’s order. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of such appeal and after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, shall issue an order appellate affirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the Controller. Provided that, in cases where the appeal concerns a patent essential for security India relates to public health or national security, the Appellate Board shall expedite proceedings and render its decision within forty-five days. Failure to comply with the directions of the Appellate Board may result in the imposition of costs, as deemed appropriate.

Any person aggrieved by an order appellate made by the Controller of Patents, or any decision relating to an application for a patent, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the said order or decision. Should the Appellate Board find that the appeal was frivolous or vexatious, or that the indication plaintiff acted in bad faith, it may, in addition to dismissing the appeal, impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Failure to comply with any order of the Appellate Board, including orders relating to costs, shall be deemed a contempt of the Board and may attract a further penalty of imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or with fine, or with both. All penalties recovered under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

The patent office shall maintain a public register of all patents and patent applications, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding confidentiality during the examination process. Any person may inspect the register and obtain certified copies thereof upon payment of the prescribed fee. The patent office may, at its discretion and under rules established by the Central Government, grant access to patent applications prior to publication, specifically to those demonstrating a clear and legitimate research need. Provided that, such access shall be subject to a confidentiality undertaking by the requesting party. The patent office shall also be responsible for the archiving of revoked patents and related documentation for a period of not less than ten years.

The patent office shall maintain a public register of all patent applications filed under this Act, detailing the applicant’s name, address, and the title of the invention. Any person may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, inspect said register during office hours and obtain certified copies of any entry therein. The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete specification, conduct a formal examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Where the specification meets these requirements, the patent office shall assign a filing date and application number. An applicant may, within the prescribed period, file a request for expedited examination, contingent upon payment of an additional fee and demonstration of exceptional circumstances. The Controller may, however, refuse such a request if the invention appears to fall within excluded subject matter. All communications between the applicant and the patent office shall be recorded and maintained as part of the application file.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application and satisfaction of the prescribed fees, conduct an examination to ascertain the patentability of the claimed invention in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Should the examination reveal grounds for objection, the patent office shall communicate such objections to the applicant, affording a period of thirty days to address them, subject to extension granted at the discretion of the Controller. Any applicant aggrieved by a decision of the patent office relating to the rejection of an application, or the amendment thereof, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Appellate Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the patent office, and its decision shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court on grounds of error of law. Where a patent is revoked for non-payment of renewal fees, the patent office may, upon application and payment of arrears, restore the patent to effect, provided that such restoration does not prejudice the rights of any third party.

The patent office shall maintain a public register of all patent applications filed under this Act, ensuring accessibility subject to reasonable restrictions to protect confidential information as provided herein. Any person may inspect the register during office hours and obtain certified copies of any entry therein upon payment of the prescribed fee. The patent office may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, establish branch offices at such places as it deems necessary to facilitate the filing and processing of applications. All communications with the patent office regarding an application shall be in writing, and any documents submitted must be accompanied by a duly authenticated translation if not in an official language. Where an applicant fails to comply with a requirement of the patent office within the stipulated timeframe, the application shall be deemed abandoned, unless an extension of time is granted upon sufficient cause being shown. The Controller shall, prior to granting a patent, conduct a thorough examination to ascertain novelty and non-obviousness.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application in the prescribed form, conduct a formal examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application fail to meet such requirements, the patent office shall issue a statement of objections, affording the applicant a period of thirty days to remedy the deficiencies. Provided that, where the objection relates to a fundamental flaw in the application, such as a failure to disclose the nature of the invention in a clear and concise manner, the period for response may be extended by a further fifteen days subject to a reasoned request by the applicant. Any amendment made in response to an objection shall be supported by a declaration of inventorship. The patent office may, at its discretion, require experimental evidence to substantiate claims of utility, particularly in respect of biotechnological inventions, and shall maintain a complete record of all communications and actions taken in relation to the application.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application and fulfillment of the prescribed fees, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Any applicant found to have knowingly submitted false or misleading material representations during the application process shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, the patent office may, subject to a reasoned order, revoke any patent granted based upon such fraudulent submissions. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the patent office relating to penalties or revocations may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order. Provided that, the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except in cases of proven jurisdictional error. Failure to comply with the directions of the patent office, including requests for clarification or supporting documentation, shall constitute grounds for abandonment of the application.

The patent office shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses of patents, and any change in ownership or licensed use of a patented invention must be recorded therein. Any person becoming entitled to a patent by assignment or transmission shall apply to the patent office for entry of such assignment or transmission within the prescribed period, failing which the patent may be subject to revocation as provided herein. A license granted under a patent may be exclusive, non-exclusive, or sub-licensable, and the terms of such license, including royalty rates and duration, shall be clearly stated in the recorded instrument. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the patentee may assign or license the patent, or any interest therein, to any person or entity. The patent office may require such evidence as it deems necessary to verify the validity of any assignment or license before effecting its recordation. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the assignment or license unenforceable.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application and fulfillment of the prescribed fees, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the subject matter disclosed satisfies the requirements of this Act regarding novelty, non-obviousness, and industrial applicability. Should the patent office determine that the application does not meet these criteria, it shall issue a detailed examination report outlining the grounds for objection, and the applicant shall have a period of thirty days from the date of such report to file a response or seek a hearing. Any decision of the patent office rejecting an application may be appealed to the Appellate Board established under this Act, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the rejection order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the right of appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board may initiate such proceedings.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application for a patent, conduct a formal examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application lack necessary documentation, or fail to meet the prescribed format, the patent office shall issue a deficiency notice, allowing the applicant a period of thirty days to rectify the omissions. Any application claiming priority under the Paris Convention shall be subject to verification of the priority date with the originating designated office. Furthermore, the patent office may, at its discretion, request a search report regarding existing registry trade marks to assess potential conflicts with the claimed invention, particularly where the invention’s name or description closely resembles a registered mark. Failure to respond to a deficiency notice, or to adequately address concerns raised regarding prior art or trademark conflicts, shall be grounds for rejection of the application. All decisions of the patent office shall be communicated in writing, with a clear statement of reasons.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete assignment document relating to a patent, record the assignment in the Register of Patents within a period of ninety days from the date of such receipt, subject to verification of the authenticity of the instrument and confirmation of the assignor’s title. Any assignment not duly recorded shall be ineffective against any subsequent assignee or licensee unless the transferor is the trade marks proprietor and can demonstrate prior use establishing legitimate interest. Where an assignment is subject to a condition requiring further consideration to be paid, the patent office may, at the request of either party, hold a hearing to determine the reasonableness of such condition. Provided that, the patent office shall not intervene in disputes concerning the value of the consideration, but only its lawful execution. All fees associated with the recording of assignments as provided herein shall be payable as prescribed in the Schedule. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in a refusal to record the assignment.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application and fulfillment of the prescribed fees, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application satisfy these initial criteria, the patent office shall publish the application and initiate a search report detailing prior art relevant to the claimed invention. Any party may file a pre-grant opposition within a period of six months from the date of publication, outlining grounds for rejection under this Act. The gene fund shall be utilized to support research addressing ethical concerns arising from patenting of genetic material, and the patent office may, subject to the rules, direct a portion of opposition fees towards this fund. Decisions of the patent office regarding oppositions may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and deposits the requisite fee. Failure to comply with timelines established by the Appellate Board may result in dismissal of the appeal.

The patent office shall, upon receipt of a complete application and fulfillment of the requirements as provided herein, conduct an examination to ascertain the patentability of the claimed invention. Where an application is filed by an exclusive licensee, such licensee shall be deemed to possess the rights of the applicant for the purposes of examination and prosecution, subject to evidence of exclusive license duly recorded with the patent office. The patent office may, if satisfied that the applicant or exclusive licensee has failed to respond to an examination report within the prescribed period, deem the application to be abandoned. Provided that, the patent office shall issue a notice of abandonment before finalizing such deeming. Any restoration of an abandoned application shall be subject to the conditions specified in the rules.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be made to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner and shall contain such particulars as may be required. The registrar application must be accompanied by a statement of use, detailing the extent to which the trade mark has been used in relation to the goods or services specified. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar may, after examination of the application and the accompanying documents, accept the application or require such amendments as may be necessary to bring it into conformity with the requirements of this Act. Provided that, if the applicant fails to comply with any requirement or amendment within the stipulated period, the registrar application shall be deemed to have been abandoned. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, file an appeal.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for the registration of the trade mark under this Act. The registrar application shall contain a statement of particulars of the trade mark, including a representation thereof in the manner directed by the regulations. An applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, apply for registration of a trade mark for goods or services falling in more than one class. Where an application for registration is filed for services, the applicant shall indicate the description of the services in clear and unambiguous terms. The Registrar may, prior to accepting the application, require the applicant to amend the specification of goods or services to ensure clarity and compliance with the classification of goods and services as adopted under this Act. Provided that, no amendment shall be permitted which alters the essential character of the trade mark.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar concerning a registrar application, including but not limited to an order refusing registration or requiring amendment of the application, shall have the right to appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the High Court allowing an extension of time for sufficient cause. The appellant shall deposit with the High Court such sum as the Court deems reasonable to cover the costs of the proceedings, and this deposit may be adjusted towards the final costs awarded. A cross-appeal may be filed by the opposing party, limited to issues already raised before the Registrar. Provided that the High Court may, at its discretion, remit the matter back to the Registrar with specific directions for further consideration, particularly where evidence requires clarification or a point of law necessitates re-examination, and any such remittal shall not extend the overall statutory period for appeal.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark may apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner for the registration of the trade mark under this Act. The registrar application shall be accompanied by a statement of use, detailing the manner in which the trade mark is used, including specific goods or services to which it is applied. Should the application be incomplete or deficient in any respect, the Registrar may require the applicant to rectify the same within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. 

An application for registration shall not be refused solely on the ground that the trade mark is not distinctive, provided that the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and promotion. Where a mark is similar to an existing mark, the Registrar shall conduct a thorough examination to determine the likelihood of confusion, considering all relevant factors including the nature of the goods or services and the channels of trade. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, direct an applicant to amend the application to remove any misleading elements.

Any application for registration of a trade mark submitted to the Trade Marks Registry, constituting a registrar application, shall be accompanied by a statement of use, detailing the manner in which the mark is being used in relation to the goods or services specified. The statement shall be supported by evidence, which may include invoices, promotional materials, or statutory declarations, demonstrating bona fide use prior to the date of the application or, where use commenced after that date, a reasoned explanation for the delay. Failure to provide a satisfactory statement of use may render the registrar application liable to be considered withdrawn, subject to a period of thirty days for rectification of the deficiency. Where the application concerns a collective mark, evidence of membership and adherence to the rules governing the collective mark shall also be furnished. The Registrar may, at their discretion, request further clarification or evidence as deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the claim of use, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar relating to a registrar application, including but not limited to rejection of an application for registration or refusal to amend the register, shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented in writing within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. Failure to present the appeal within the stipulated time, or to pay the requisite fee, shall render the appeal inadmissible and the order of the Registrar shall become final. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish evidence of prima facie case before proceeding with the hearing. Any false representation made in the registrar application, or any deliberate omission of material facts, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both.

Any person desiring to become the registered proprietor of a trade mark shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, submitting a registrar application accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall include a clear representation of the mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and details of the applicant’s business. Subject to verification, the Registrar may, if satisfied that the application meets the requirements of this Act, accept it for examination. Where an application is accepted, notice shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal, inviting opposition to the registration. Any assignment of the right to the trade mark, or a license to use it, shall be subject to notification to the Registrar, and such notification shall be recorded in the Register. Provided that, failure to record such assignment or license shall not invalidate the right, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all assignments and licenses as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing a registrar application, or requiring an amendment of the application which is unacceptable to the applicant, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. The grounds for appeal shall be clearly stated and limited to matters of law or procedural irregularity. An opposing party served with notice of such appeal may file a counter-statement within one month, setting forth any facts or evidence supporting the Registrar’s decision. Should the Appellate Board determine that the Registrar’s decision was substantially correct, it may dismiss the appeal and require the appellant to pay costs. Any question relating to the registrability of a mark, arising during the appeal, shall be decided according to the principles established under this Act.

Every application for a registrar application shall be made in writing and shall be accompanied by a statement of use, detailing the manner in which the trade mark is applied to the goods or services concerned. An applicant desiring to apply trade mark shall ensure that the representation of the trade mark submitted is clear, legible, and accurately reflects the mark as used in commerce. The application shall further include a declaration verifying the truthfulness of all particulars furnished therein, and any omission or misrepresentation may render the application liable to be rejected. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional evidence or clarification regarding the use of the trade mark, or the goods or services in relation to which it is sought to be registered. Provided that failure to respond to such a requirement within a specified timeframe may result in the application being deemed withdrawn. All fees prescribed under this Act must accompany the application.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration of a trade mark, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding licensing and assignment, and no assignment shall be valid without being recorded in the Register. An applicant desiring to record an assignment, or a transfer of rights in respect of a trade mark, shall submit a registrar application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar, upon being satisfied that the assignment is genuine and in accordance with the provisions herein, shall record the assignment in the Register and issue a certificate of registration of the assignment. Notice rectification shall be permitted where the Registrar is satisfied that a recorded assignment is fraudulent or otherwise invalid, and such rectification shall be effected in accordance with the prescribed procedure. Provided that, the assignee may, subject to the conditions specified, apply for a new registration in their name. Any failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable.

A registrar application relating to a geographical indication shall be examined as provided herein, and the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application to conform to the requirements of this Act. Where the applicant claims to represent a collective of farmers producing the goods associated with the geographical indication, evidence of such representation, including resolutions passed by the concerned farmer associations, shall be submitted with the application. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, register the collective as the applicant. Provided that, if the application is found to be deficient or incomplete, the Registrar shall communicate the deficiencies to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days for rectification. Failure to rectify within the stipulated period may result in the application being deemed withdrawn.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark may apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner for the registration of the trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. The registrar application shall include a clear representation of the mark and a statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought. An applicant seeking registration based on an invention convention, where the mark originates from a treaty or reciprocal agreement, shall furnish evidence of such convention’s ratification by India and demonstrate compliance with its terms. The Registrar may, at any stage of the process, require further information or documentation to ascertain the validity of the claim. Provided that, failure to respond to such requests within a specified timeframe may render the application liable to be deemed abandoned, unless reasonable cause is shown. All applications shall be subject to examination as provided herein.

Where a company is proved to have committed an offence relating to the unauthorized reproduction of a copyrighted work, and it is demonstrated that such reproduction occurred with the knowledge or consent of a directing mind of the company, both the company and such individual shall be held liable for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. Should the alleged infringement concern a patented invention, and the company asserts the validity of a corresponding patent application pending before the Patent Office, proceedings regarding the alleged copyright offence shall be stayed pending a final determination by the Patent Office on the matter of patent validity. However, such stay shall not exceed a period of six months, and the aggrieved party may petition the High Court for expedited resolution if the Patent Office fails to render a decision within said timeframe. Any appeal arising from a decision concerning a company proved offence shall lie before the appellate authority designated under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods.

A trade mark shall be a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and may consist of words, numerals, graphic elements or any combination thereof. For the purposes of this Act, a collective trade mark is a trade mark distinguished by its capacity to identify goods or services originating from members of an association, and the association shall, subject to regulations, register the trade mark. A well-known trade mark, even if not registered, shall be entitled to protection as provided herein, and no adverse right shall accrue to any person by the prior use or non-use of such trade mark. Registration of a trade mark confers upon the owner the exclusive right to use the india trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.

A trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be registrable if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. An application for registration of a trade mark shall be filed in the prescribed manner with the Trade Marks Registry and shall include a representation of the trade mark and a clear indication of the goods or services to which it relates. Where a trade mark includes a reference to a geographical indication, registration shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, ensuring the authenticity and origin of the goods connected with that geographical indication. The Registrar may, after examination, accept or refuse the application, and shall notify the applicant of the decision. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, within the prescribed time, file an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. A registered india trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.

A trade mark used in relation to goods or services shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein and the payment of the prescribed fee. An application for registration of a trade mark shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain its distinctiveness and to ensure it does not conflict with any existing india trade mark or any prior rights. Where a mark is deemed similar to an earlier trade mark and relates to identical or similar goods or services, registration shall be refused, unless the proprietor of the earlier mark has consented to the registration. However, a registered proprietor may, subject to conditions specified by the Registrar, assign or transmit the registered trade mark. Any assignment or transmission not complying with these requirements shall be void. The Registrar may require evidence of use of the trade mark within a specified period, failing which the registration may be subject to revocation as provided herein.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark, and knowingly makes a false representation of material fact in the application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor without his consent or the consent of a duly authorized licensee, an action for trade mark infringement may be instituted against such person. Provided that, no such action shall lie if the use is by way of fair comment or criticism relating to the goods or services associated with the india trade mark. Any evidence admitted in proceedings under this Act shall be subject to the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as he may deem fit, direct an inquiry into any allegation of false representation or infringement. Failure to comply with any direction issued under this Act shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any registered trade mark shall be assignable in whole or in part, subject to the provisions of this Act and any regulations made thereunder, and the assignee shall have the same right to protect, sue for, and recover damages for any infringement of such trade mark as the assignor had immediately prior to the assignment. An assignment of a trade mark shall be in writing and signed by the assignor and assignee, or their duly authorised agents, and shall include a statement of goodwill relating to the trade mark being assigned. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the trade carried on under it, the assignment shall be taken to include the right to use the trade mark in connection with the same trade. However, assignment of a trade mark shall not be permissible if it results in a monopoly or undue restriction of competition, as determined by the Registrar. A licensee of a trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license to another party, provided that the assignment does not violate any conditions stipulated in the original licensing agreement concerning india trade mark usage.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar of Trade Marks refusing registration of a trade mark, or varying the terms of a registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision appealed against, reverse it, or modify it, and shall record the reasons for its decision. Where an appeal relates to a matter of rectification of the register, the Board may, if it considers it necessary, direct notice to be served on any person whose interests may be affected by the decision. A trade mark, even if registered, may be subject to revocation proceedings as provided herein, particularly where it has fallen into disuse or is deceptively similar to an existing india trade mark. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as permissible under the law.

Any government undertaking, being the proprietor of a registered trade mark used in the course of trade, shall have the right to maintain an action for infringement of such trade mark, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. Where a trade mark has been registered in the name of a government undertaking and subsequently that undertaking is dissolved or restructured, the rights in such trade mark shall vest in its successor entity, subject to notification to the Trade Marks Registry and fulfillment of such conditions as may be prescribed. A person claiming to be the lawful successor shall furnish proof of succession as provided herein. Any act of passing off, or the colourable imitation of a registered india trade mark belonging to a government undertaking, shall be actionable under this Act, and the aggrieved party may seek an injunction, damages, or an account of profits. Provided that, in cases involving essential services, the court may consider public interest while granting relief. The Registrar may, upon application, direct rectification of the register to reflect the change in proprietorship.

Any dispute relating to the registration or validity of a trade mark, or any infringement thereof, arising within the territories of India, shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the High Court having local jurisdiction over the place where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, in cases where the defendant has no place of business within India but actively targets the Indian market through commercial activity, the High Court in Delhi shall, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere, have jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate upon such disputes. 

Where a plaintiff seeks to enforce rights in a registered trade mark against a party located outside India, evidence of substantial connection between such party and India, including but not limited to, sales, advertising, or the maintenance of a website accessible within India, shall be presented to establish jurisdiction. The Registrar, as provided herein, may direct service of process on such foreign party through established diplomatic channels or in accordance with international treaties to which India is a party. Any order issued by a court regarding jurisdiction india trade shall be enforceable as if made by a court within its ordinary territorial limits.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a determination of jurisdictional competence by the Trade Marks Registry, and such determination shall be conclusive as to the Registry’s authority to proceed with examination of the application. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered by a person ordinarily resident outside India, proof of user within the territory of India, or a clear intention to adopt and use the mark in India, shall be a pre-condition for acceptance of the application, as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry may, however, waive the requirement of prior use or intention to use, if it is satisfied that the mark is well-known in India, and that registration would not be detrimental to Indian businesses or the public interest. All disputes regarding jurisdiction india trade shall be adjudicated by the appropriate High Court, and decisions of the Registry on jurisdictional matters are not subject to appeal, save as otherwise provided in this Act. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for all applicants.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark shall demonstrate exclusive adoption and use within India, and failure to do so may result in rejection of the application as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require evidence of such use extending back a period not less than five years prior to the date of application. Rights to a registered trade mark shall be transmissible, and any assignment or transmission not duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry shall be void against subsequent purchasers for valuable consideration without notice of such unrecorded transfer. Any false representation of ownership or licensing of a registered trade mark, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. All orders of the Registrar relating to jurisdiction india trade shall be final and subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark to which they are not rightfully entitled, or who knowingly makes a false representation in an application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor without a license or other lawful authority, such use shall constitute an infringement of that trade mark, and the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction restraining further infringement. Any goods bearing an infringing trade mark, or any material used in the manufacture of such goods, shall be deemed counterfeit goods and liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Furthermore, a court may, subject to the circumstances, order an account of profits made by the infringer, and award costs to the rightful owner of the relating trade mark. Any appeal against a decision of the court shall lie within ninety days.

A trade mark used in relation to goods or services shall be considered a relating trade mark if it is identical with or deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark, and the earlier trade mark is used in relation to goods or services which are identical or similar to those for which the later trade mark is used, creating a likelihood of confusion amongst the public, including association with the earlier trade mark. Where a person, not being the registered proprietor of a trade mark, applies a trade mark to goods or services with intent to deceive or cause confusion, or packages goods with a false trade mark, they shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Any magistrate empowered to try offences under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, may, upon credible information of a commission alleged offence, order a search and seizure of the offending goods and related materials. Provided that, such seizure shall be subject to the provisions of the said Code and any rules made therein. The Registrar may, following investigation, direct the destruction of seized goods if the offence is proven.

Any person who uses a relating trade mark in the course of trade, without the consent of the registered proprietor of that trade mark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person not being the registered proprietor, and such use constitutes an actionable wrong, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the unauthorized use and an account of profits. Matters relating registered trade marks, if falsely applied, shall be deemed a fraudulent practice and attract enhanced damages, not exceeding twice the actual damages suffered. Any goods bearing such falsely applied mark, or any material used in the fabrication thereof, may be ordered for destruction by the Court. A proprietor may, subject to such conditions as the Court deems fit, seek delivery up of infringing labels and packaging materials. Failure to comply with an order of the Court under this Act shall constitute contempt.

Registration of a trade mark shall confer upon the owner exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and subject to the provisions of this Act, the right to sue for infringement of that trade mark. An application for registration may be made by any person claiming to be the owner of the trade mark, and shall be in the prescribed form and be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The register of trade marks shall be open to inspection by the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, and a certified copy of any entry in the register shall be evidence of the facts stated therein. Provided that, registration shall not be refused solely on the ground that the trade mark is descriptive, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used or proposed to be used may apply for registration of the trade mark in the prescribed manner, subject to the provisions of this Act. An application for registration shall not be refused on the ground that the trade mark is not inherently capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, if, through use, the trade mark has acquired a distinctive character. The Registrar shall examine the application and, where the application meets the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder, shall accept it. Following acceptance, the trade mark shall be advertised in the manner prescribed, allowing for opposition as provided herein. Registration confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and subject to the provisions of this Act, to obtain relief in respect of infringement of such rights. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for ten years from the date of registration, renewable for further periods of ten years each.

A trade mark shall be subject to registration under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and meets the requirements as to inherent distinctiveness and descriptiveness as provided herein. An application for registration may be opposed on grounds including prior use by another party, or if the mark is deceptive or likely to cause confusion. Upon successful registration, the proprietor shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the registration certificate, subject to any conditions or limitations imposed. Any person who contravenes this right, or uses a deceptively similar mark, may be subject to injunction and damages. The Registrar may, however, allow the rectification of the register in cases of fraud or misrepresentation affecting the validity of the registration, and a registered proprietor failing to renew the registration shall forfeit all rights therein.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of the trade mark under this Act in the prescribed manner. The application for registration shall contain a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. Upon receipt of an application duly complying with the requirements as provided herein, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine it and, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit, accept it for proceeding to advertisement. 

Registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. However, such registration may be subject to limitations or conditions as may be specified in the register. Where a mark is deemed similar to an existing registered mark, the Registrar may require evidence of distinctiveness, and shall consider the likelihood of confusion among consumers. A certificate of registration shall be issued upon completion of all necessary procedures.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to goods or services may apply for registration of the trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisos contained herein. An application for registration shall be in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services to which it relates. The applicant shall furnish an address for service within India. Where the trade mark consists of a device, the representation shall be clear and accurately depict the device. Registration shall not be granted unless the trade mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and it does not fall within the absolute grounds for refusal as provided herein. A registered trade mark shall be evidence of ownership, and the rights conferred by registration are subject to the conditions and limitations specified in this Act. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of registration.

Any person claiming ownership of a trade mark not yet registered shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration in the prescribed manner and furnish such particulars as may be required. Failure to apply for registration, where such application is required as a condition precedent to the exercise of any right conferred by this Act, shall render the claimant ineligible to pursue remedies for infringement. Provided that, a registered trade mark shall be conclusive evidence of the absolute right to the use of the mark, subject to the right of prior users established to the satisfaction of the adjudicating authority. Any fraudulent application for registration, or the filing of false evidence in support thereof, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, in cases of demonstrable and willful misrepresentation, revoke any registration obtained through such means.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument of assignment shall clearly identify the trade mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and state the consideration, if any, for the assignment. An assignment shall not be valid against any third party unless it is so registered. 

Where the assignment is made subject to a condition, the assignee may, with the prior written consent of the Registrar, enforce the rights conferred by the registration of the trade mark, subject to such condition. The Registrar may, however, refuse such consent if it appears that the condition is contrary to public interest or unduly restricts the legitimate use of the trade mark by the assignee. Registration of the assignment constitutes conclusive evidence of its validity, provided that the assignee has acquired legitimate title to the mark.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of that trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. An application for registration shall not be refused solely on the ground that the trade mark is not inherently capable of distinguishing the goods or services to which it relates, provided that use of the mark has, through prolonged and extensive use, acquired a distinctive character. Where an application for registration is refused by the Trade Marks Registry, the applicant may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the refusal order. Should the Appellate Board uphold the refusal, the applicant may, subject to fulfilling conditions prescribed by the Board, seek rectification of the Register by demonstrating a substantial likelihood of confusion with a previously registered mark, or that the mark is descriptive of the goods or services. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a question of law arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Upon such examination, if the Registrar is satisfied that the trade mark is registrable and does not contravene any provisions contained herein, he shall proceed to advertise the said trade mark in the Trade Marks Journal. Objections to the registration of a trade mark may be filed within the prescribed period, and shall be adjudicated upon by the Registrar, or by a consist judicial member appointed for the purpose of hearing such objections. 

Where a trade mark is registered, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration, and the trade mark shall be entered in the Register of Trade Marks. Registration shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions of this Act. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, and may be renewed for further periods of ten years each upon payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of that trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein. An application for registration shall not be accepted if it is found, upon examination, to be identical with an existing registered trade mark, or deceptively similar such that it would cause confusion amongst consumers. However, a Registrar may, notwithstanding such similarity, permit the application if evidence is presented demonstrating continuous use of the mark for a period exceeding five years prior to the date of the application, and that such use has not resulted in any complaints of passing off or unfair competition. Any decision of the Registrar regarding acceptance or rejection of an application for registration may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to any recourse available through writ petition.

An application permitted amended shall not introduce any matter foreign to the original scope of the claim, and any amendment seeking to broaden such scope shall be disallowed, unless the applicant satisfies the Registrar that the amendment is necessary for rectifying an obvious mistake or for avoiding conflict with an earlier trade mark. Where an application has been advertised, any amendment shall be subject to opposition as provided herein, and the Registrar may, after considering any opposition filed, allow or disallow the amendment. Provided that an amendment altering the essential character of the trade mark shall be treated as a new application, requiring fresh examination and advertisement. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require an amended application to be re-advertised, even if no opposition is filed, should the amendment substantially affect the clarity of the register.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be permitted amended by the applicant prior to acceptance, subject to the provisions contained herein and the satisfaction of the Registrar. Any amendment seeking a substantial alteration to the trade mark represented in the application shall not be permitted, and shall be deemed a new application requiring a separate filing fee as provided in the Schedule. Where an application permitted amended relates to a correction of a clerical error or an obvious mistake, the Registrar may allow such amendment without requiring advertisement under this Act. However, if the amendment affects the essential characteristics of the trade mark or introduces new matter not previously disclosed, re-advertisement shall be necessary. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require an amended application to undergo a further examination to ensure compliance with all relevant provisions. Failure to comply with the requirements of this provision may result in the application being deemed abandoned.

Any person who has filed an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar to amend such application, provided that such amendment shall not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark as originally applied for. The Registrar may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, permit or refuse the amendment as deemed fit, and shall record the reasons for such decision. Where an application permitted amended relates to a matter of essential particular, notice of the amendment shall be advertised in the manner prescribed. Any aggrieved person may, within the prescribed time, file a notice of opposition to the amendment. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act regarding amendment shall render the application liable to be treated as abandoned. A request for amendment shall not be entertained if it introduces a new trade mark or seeks to revive an application previously deemed abandoned, unless exceptional circumstances exist and are duly justified to the satisfaction of the Registrar.

An application for registration, once duly filed and examined in accordance with the rules prescribed under this Act, may be permitted to be amended by the applicant subject to such conditions as the Controller deems fit, provided that such amendment shall not result in the trade mark differing substantially from that in the original application. Any amendment seeking to expand the scope of goods or services covered by the application shall require a further examination fee as specified in the Schedule. The Controller may, at their discretion, require evidence of use relating to the amended specification, should it be deemed necessary to ascertain the genuine intention to use the trade mark for those goods or services. Where an application permitted amended relates to a collective or certification mark, the amendment shall not alter the fundamental characteristics of the collective or certification mark as defined in the application. Any third party adversely affected by such amendment may file a notice of opposition within the prescribed time limit.

An application permitted amended shall not be subject to objection under this Act if the amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark. However, any amendment increasing the scope of goods or services covered by the trade mark requires a fresh search report and publication as if a new application were filed, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where the amendment relates to a disclaimer, the Registrar may require evidence of actual use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the original application. Provided that, if the amendment is solely for the purpose of correcting a clerical error, no such search report or publication shall be necessary. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, allow an application permitted amended even if it introduces a minor modification to the representation of the mark, provided that such modification does not alter the distinctive character of the trade mark. Any decision of the Registrar regarding an application permitted amended shall be communicated to the applicant in writing.

Any application permitted amended under this Act shall be subject to a scrutiny fee as prescribed in the First Schedule, and such amendment shall not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark as originally applied for. Provided that, if the amendment seeks to correct a clerical error or to clarify an ambiguity, no such fee shall be levied. However, an application permitted amended relating to a disclaimer or limitation, or a change in the goods or services specified, may attract an additional fee determined by the Registrar. Failure to pay any fee levied as provided herein within the stipulated period shall render the amendment invalid, and the application shall be deemed to have been abandoned. Any person fraudulently representing an amended application shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, restore an application erroneously considered abandoned.

An application for registration, once deemed formally complete, shall be subject to examination as provided herein, and any deficiency noted during said examination must be communicated to the applicant within a period of thirty days from the date of such examination. Should the applicant seek to remedy said deficiency through amendment of the application, such amended application must be filed within sixty days of the deficiency notice, failing which the application shall be deemed abandoned. However, an application permitted amended shall not introduce matter contrary to the original claim, nor shall it substantially alter the nature of the trade mark sought to be registered. Any objection raised by the Examiner to the amended application shall be communicated to the applicant, and a reasoned response may be submitted within thirty days. If the Examiner remains unsatisfied, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board, providing grounds for reconsideration of the amendment’s permissibility. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to rights of review as per general law.

Any application permitted amended under this Act shall be subject to a rigorous examination to ascertain whether the amendments fundamentally alter the nature of the trade mark as originally applied for, or introduce a clause invention not previously disclosed. Should the Controller determine that the amendment constitutes such a fundamental alteration, the application shall be deemed withdrawn, and the applicant shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any person knowingly submitting a falsely amended application, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, however, permit amendment if it does not prejudice the rights of prior applicants or affect the distinctiveness of the mark, provided that a fee of ten thousand rupees is paid. Failure to pay said fee shall render the amendment invalid.

An application permitted amended shall not be refused where the amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark as originally applied for, and the Registrar, having considered representations filed in opposition, deems the amended mark registrable. However, any amendment increasing the scope of goods or services beyond the original specification requires fresh advertisement as if a new application were filed, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. The National Gene Fund, established to promote research and development in genetic resources, may, in cases involving trade marks referencing biological material or traditional knowledge, submit expert opinion to the Registrar regarding potential conflicts with registered genetic resources. Any decision of the Registrar refusing an amendment, or imposing conditions on acceptance of an amended application, shall be appealable to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and has complied with all procedural requirements as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except on grounds of legal error.

Any person who applies a falsified trade mark to goods or services, or offers for sale, or sells, goods or services bearing a falsified trade mark, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, provided that such application is made without the consent of the registered proprietor of the trade mark. A trade mark is considered falsified where it is altered, removed, or has additions made to it, such that it no longer represents the original mark as registered. Where a person manufactures, possesses, or deals with materials used for the falsification of trade marks, with the knowledge that such materials will be used for the commission of an offence, they shall be liable as an abettor. Subject to the provisions herein, the falsification of a well-known trade mark shall be considered a more serious offence, attracting enhanced penalties as determined by the appropriate court. Any evidence of intent to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers shall be admissible in proceedings relating to falsifying trade marks.
