Provided that, if the asserted claim is subsequently determined to be novel and non-obvious, the penalty may be reduced or rescinded. Furthermore, any profits derived from acts induced by the false assertion shall be recoverable as damages, subject to a court order. Failure to comply with the terms of such an order shall constitute contempt of court.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing to grant a patent, or revoking a patent, or amending a patent in a manner prejudicial to the applicant or patentee, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Controller or reverse it or modify it. A key ground for challenging the Controller’s decision concerns the invention far claimed, specifically whether the scope of the claims extends beyond what is adequately supported by the description and drawings. Furthermore, if the Controller finds that a patented process was not duly and accurately described in the complete specification, the appeal may be dismissed. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

A trade mark shall mean a mark capable of being represented graphically including signs or combinations of signs, letters, numerals, figures, shape of goods or their packaging, colours, or combinations thereof, and shall include service marks and collective marks. For the purposes of this Act, a well-known trade mark means a mark which has become reputed among the relevant public by reason of the use thereof, and may, irrespective of the goods or services in relation to which it was originally used, be recognized as a distinctive mark. A descriptive trade mark, however, shall not be registrable unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the acquisition of secondary meaning. The register of trade marks maintained under this Act shall be the primary evidence of ownership.

A trade mark shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others. An application for registration shall be made in writing to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and shall include a representation of the trade mark and a clear indication of the goods or services to which it relates. Where a trade mark includes a reference to a geographical indication, registration shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, ensuring proper protection of the indication’s origin and quality. The Registrar may, before accepting an application, require evidence of bona fide use of the trade mark, or require the applicant to satisfy any other condition as may be deemed necessary. Provided that, a trade mark which is likely to deceive or cause confusion shall not be registered. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may, within the prescribed time, appeal to the Appellate Board.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. A registered trade mark shall be deemed to be personal property and the proprietor thereof shall have the right to assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of the same, subject to the limitations prescribed herein. Where a trade mark has been registered in the name of a deceased person, the rights therein shall devolve to his legal representatives. 

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a registered trade mark may be revoked upon application to the High Court, if it is proven that the trade mark has been abandoned for a continuous period of five years or more, or that the use of the trade mark is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public. Any aggrieved party may seek an injunction restraining the infringement of their registered trade marks, and may also claim damages for any loss suffered as a result of such infringement.

A trade mark shall be registrable under this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of other persons, and meets all conditions as to use and descriptiveness as provided herein. Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a search for prior identical or deceptively similar trade marks already registered or applied for, and the Registrar may require an amendment or reject the application if such prior marks exist. A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. However, such right shall not extend to prevent others from using the trade mark for honest use, or for the purpose of designating the kind, quality or place of origin of the goods or services, where such use is consistent with fair practice. Any assignment of a trade mark shall be subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry.

Any person who applies a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark of another person to goods or services with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with fine, which may extend to two lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, in lieu of imprisonment, impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any goods bearing such fraudulent marks, and any material used in the application of such marks, shall be deemed forfeited to the Central Government and may be disposed of as the court deems fit. A person aggrieved by such infringement may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit for recovery of damages or an injunction. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause shown, order removal of the infringing mark from the register of trade marks.

Any registered trade mark shall be transmissible by assignment, transmission or operation of law, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. An assignment of a trade mark shall be in writing and signed by the assignor, and shall specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark in connection with the business, subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the assignment. 

A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be granted in respect of a trade mark, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the license, including the duration, territory, and goods or services in respect of which the license is granted. Any assignment or license not complying with the requirements as provided herein shall be void. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all assignments and licenses of trade marks.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar of Trade Marks refusing to register a trade mark, or varying the terms of registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and may direct any necessary corrections to be made in the Register of Trade Marks. An appeal under this Act shall not operate as a stay of the Registrar’s order unless specifically directed by the Appellate Board. Furthermore, any claim of passing off, alleging that a registered trade mark deceives or causes confusion, shall be adjudicated upon considering the overall similarities in the marks and the goods or services offered, and the likelihood of association in the mind of the average consumer. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, remit the matter back to the Registrar for fresh consideration.

A trade mark used in relation to sound recordings shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding registrability of other trade marks. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark incorporating a sound recording, or a portion thereof, as a distinctive element, shall submit with the application a clear and accurate representation of the sound recording, along with a statement detailing its specific use in connection with the goods or services. The Registrar may, at any time, require evidence of legitimate ownership or licensing rights pertaining to the sound recording. Registration shall not confer any right to the underlying musical work or literary work embodied within the sound recording, and any claims relating thereto shall be subject to existing laws governing copyright. Where a trade mark is registered incorporating a sound recording, any subsequent alteration to the recording requiring material change to the mark shall necessitate a fresh application for registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a Bench shall consist of not fewer than two members, appointed by the Central Government, possessing expertise in semiconductor technology, law, or both. Such a Bench may be constituted for the expeditious hearing of applications, and for the purposes of determining the validity of any claim relating to a layout-design right, subject to the provisions contained herein. The Central Government may, by notification, specify the procedure for the constitution of a Bench and the manner in which its proceedings shall be conducted. A designated technical member shall always be present on any Bench hearing matters involving complex technical assessments, provided that the presiding member retains ultimate authority in matters of law. Any decision of a Bench shall be by majority vote.

A registered layout-design proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Controller for the creation of a Bench to facilitate expeditious resolution of disputes concerning alleged infringement within a specified geographical area. The application shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee as prescribed in the First Schedule and shall demonstrate a reasonable likelihood of ongoing or future infringement affecting a substantial commercial interest. The Controller may, after due consideration and notice to the alleged infringer, constitute a Bench comprising of technical and legal experts. Any decision of a Bench shall be subject to appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Provided that, the Controller may, at any time, dissolve a Bench if it is determined that the Bench is no longer necessary or is failing to effectively discharge its functions as provided herein. The composition of each Bench shall ensure representation from at least two qualified experts in semiconductor technology.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right, as provided herein, shall be entitled to commence proceedings for an injunction restraining the defendant from the further manufacture, sale, or distribution of articles embodying the infringed layout-design. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine such matters, and may, at any stage of the proceedings, appoint a technical expert to assist the Court in understanding the technical aspects of the case. A Bench, constituted of at least two Judges possessing appropriate technical expertise, shall be responsible for assessing the validity of the plaintiff’s claims and the extent of the infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the aggrieved party may also claim damages for the loss suffered due to the infringement, calculated on a reasonable royalty basis or actual losses, whichever is higher. The defendant may, however, demonstrate that the alleged infringement was not commercially significant and therefore warrants a reduced award of damages. Any order for damages shall be enforceable as a decree of a civil court.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Bench of the Appellate Board for such area or areas as may be specified therein, provided that the number of Benches shall not exceed two at any given time. Each Bench shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two other members, one of whom shall be a technical expert in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design or microelectronics. Any vacancy in a Bench, or the inability of a member to act, shall not invalidate any proceeding before that Bench, subject to the condition that the quorum is maintained as provided herein. The Chairperson of a Bench shall have the power to regulate the procedure of that Bench and to ensure the expeditious disposal of appeals. All decisions of a Bench shall be by majority vote, and in the event of a tie, the Chairperson shall have a casting vote. Any party aggrieved by an order of a Bench may apply for a review of that order to the same Bench within thirty days of the date of the order. The composition of a Bench, once constituted for a particular appeal, shall remain unchanged until the final disposal of that appeal, unless altered by the Central Government for sufficient cause.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right, as provided herein, shall first submit a statement of justification to the Controller, detailing the basis of the claim and identifying the alleged infringing activity. The Controller, upon receipt of such statement, may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, direct that a technical hearing be conducted. A Bench shall be constituted for the purpose of said hearing, comprising of at least two technical officers possessing expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits. The composition of the Bench may be altered by the Controller to ensure adequate representation of relevant technical fields. Evidence presented before the Bench shall be limited to that which directly supports the allegation of infringement or the defense thereto. Any party failing to comply with the directions of the Bench may be subject to penalties, including the dismissal of their claim or defense. The decision of the Bench, recorded in writing, shall be forwarded to the Controller for further action under this Act.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a layout-design registered under this Act as their own, or uses such a layout-design without the authorization of the proprietor, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees. Where the offence involves repeated contravention, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years. A Bench constituted to hear appeals relating to revocation of registration may, subject to due process, impose enhanced penalties where fraudulent intent is proven. Any evidence obtained through inspection of premises or seizure of materials, as provided herein, shall be admissible in proceedings under this Act. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may, in addition to criminal prosecution, seek civil remedies for infringement, including injunction and damages. Any appeal against the order of a Bench shall lie before the designated authority within sixty days of the order.

Any person being the proprietor of a layout-design, subject to the provisions of this Act, may assign to any other person the right, title and interest in the layout-design, either wholly or partially, and in respect of any specified territory. Such assignment shall be in writing and shall specify the territory in which the assignment is effective. Where an assignment is made for a definite period, the proprietor may, after the expiration of that period, assign the same to another person, subject to any existing obligations. 

A license to use a layout-design may be granted, either exclusively or non-exclusively, and any such license shall be in writing and shall define the scope of the license, including the territory and duration. A Bench may, upon application by either party, determine a reasonable royalty for the use of a layout-design where the parties have failed to agree upon such royalty. Any dispute relating to the validity or scope of an assignment or license shall be subject to the dispute resolution mechanism as provided herein.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with the order of a Licensing Authority refusing registration of a layout-design, may file an appeal to the Bench within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of such fees as may be prescribed. The Bench, constituted with at least two technical members, shall examine the appeal based on the submitted evidence and the grounds stated in the memorandum of appeal. Provided that the Bench may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to furnish further evidence or clarification. Where the Bench finds that the Licensing Authority’s decision was erroneous and contrary to the provisions of this Act, it shall set aside the order and direct the Licensing Authority to reconsider the application for registration. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Bench may, within ninety days, prefer a further appeal to the High Court, but only on a question of law. The composition of the Bench and its quorum shall be determined by regulations framed under this Act.

Any person seeking registration of a layout-design, incorporating a novel bench arrangement for enhanced processing speed, shall submit a detailed schematic diagram as provided herein. The applicant shall demonstrate, through documented testing, that the bench configuration demonstrably improves performance metrics over existing designs, and that such improvement is not attributable to software optimization alone. Where the layout-design is intended for use in pharmaceutical manufacturing equipment, specifically automated pill sorting or liquid handling systems, the applicant shall also furnish a validation report confirming compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice standards. Failure to provide complete and accurate documentation, or to demonstrate the claimed performance enhancement, may result in rejection of the application. A registered layout-design may be subject to revocation if it is proven to be substantially similar to a prior art bench configuration, even if applied in a different technical field, subject to a determination of inventive step. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs.

Any person who, without due authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design, constructs, imports, sells, or otherwise distributes an integrated circuit embodying a substantial reproduction of a registered bench, shall be guilty of an infringement as provided herein. A bench, in the context of determining infringement, shall be considered a discrete and identifiable portion of the registered layout-design, and its unauthorized replication shall constitute a violation of exclusive rights. Where a registered proprietor grants a licence patent relating to the exploitation of a layout-design, any breach of the terms and conditions of such licence shall be actionable, and the aggrieved party may seek specific performance or damages. Any evidence obtained through inspection authorized under this Act may be admissible in proceedings for infringement. Failure to comply with an order of the designated authority shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The proprietor may also seek an injunction restraining further infringement.

Any person possessing a registered layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the same, either wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to conditions, to any other person. Any assignment of a layout-design shall be in writing and shall specify the rights assigned, and a copy of such instrument shall be furnished to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. Where an assignment is made without specifying any rights, it shall be deemed to be an assignment of all rights subsisting in the layout-design. A Bench of the Registry may, upon application, record any such assignment or license. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of an assignment or the scope of a license, the aggrieved party may seek redressal as provided herein, and any decision rendered may be sought appealed to a higher authority. The assignor shall remain liable for any breach of conditions attached to the license by the assignee, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with the decision of a Licensing Authority regarding the grant or rejection of a license to practice the rights in a registered layout-design, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Bench. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Appellate Bench, constituted with technical members possessing requisite expertise in semiconductor technology, shall examine the record of the Licensing Authority and may, if deemed necessary, require further evidence or expert opinion. Where an appeal concerns a matter subject to the Aba Budapest Treaty, the Bench shall consider international best practices and treaty obligations when rendering its decision. The decision of the Appellate Bench shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, permitting an appeal to the High Court. Any party failing to comply with the orders of the Appellate Bench shall be liable to penalties as provided herein.

A Bench shall be constituted for the expeditious hearing of appeals and applications as provided herein, and shall consist of not less than two members appointed by the Central Government. The composition of a Bench may include individuals possessing technical expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, or legal professionals with demonstrable knowledge of intellectual property matters. Where a dispute involves a registered trade mark relevant to the identification of the layout-design, the Central Government may, subject to the rules, appoint a representative of the Trade Marks Registry to assist the Bench. Any decision of a Bench shall be by majority vote, and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as permissible under the Constitution. The Bench shall have the power to regulate its own procedure.

Commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design shall include any act, whether directly or indirectly, by or with the consent of the registered owner, or any licensee, that involves the reproduction, distribution, communication to the public, or adaptation of the layout-design. However, such commercial exploitation shall not extend to acts undertaken solely for private purposes and not for commercial gain. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the right to commercially exploit a layout-design vests exclusively with the registered owner. Any unauthorized commercial exploitation, including the manufacture, sale, or import of integrated circuits embodying the layout-design, constitutes an infringement. A person may obtain a license from the registered owner to undertake specific acts of commercial exploitation, subject to mutually agreed terms and conditions.

Any person deriving benefit from the commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design shall be deemed to have infringed the exclusive right of the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. The proprietor of any layout-design registered under this Act shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, import, or otherwise deal with the layout-design. However, such exclusive right shall not extend to acts done for private personal use or for the purposes of research, provided that such research does not prejudice the legitimate commercial interests of the proprietor. A layout-design, if not registered, may still be protectable under other applicable laws, but the remedies available under this Act are contingent upon valid registration. Any unauthorized commercial exploitation, including the manufacture or sale of integrated circuits embodying the layout-design without the proprietor’s consent, constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act. The registered proprietor may seek injunctions and damages for any proven infringement.

Any person who, without the prior written consent of the proprietor, performs any act of commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design, shall be liable to a civil action for infringement as provided herein. Such action may include an injunction restraining the defendant from further exploitation, and an award of damages not exceeding Rupees one crore, assessed with regard to the actual loss suffered by the proprietor, or the profits unjustly gained by the defendant, whichever is higher. Where the commercial exploitation involves a repeated or wilful infringement, the court may also award enhanced damages. 

A proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign, transfer, or license the rights in a layout-design, whether or not coupled with rights in the semiconductor integrated circuit embodying such layout-design. Any assignment or license shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial extent of the rights granted. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding written consent or proper assignment shall not invalidate the proprietor’s right to pursue remedies for unauthorized commercial exploitation.

Any person making, causing to be made, importing, selling, or otherwise distributing a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, which is identical to, or derived from, a registered layout-design, shall be deemed to have engaged in commercial exploitation of such registered layout-design, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, such acts shall not constitute infringement as provided herein if undertaken solely for private personal use and not for commercial gain. Where a person, having obtained a license from the proprietor of a registered layout-design, exceeds the scope of such license, or fails to comply with the terms and conditions thereof, such activity shall also be considered commercial exploitation. Any alleged act of commercial exploitation may be subject to an injunction obtained from a competent court. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may, in the event of commercial exploitation, pursue remedies including, but not limited to, damages and an account of profits. A finding of commercial exploitation shall be contingent upon establishing a clear nexus between the defendant’s actions and the registered layout-design.

Any person making commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design without the prior written consent of the proprietor shall be liable to such remedies as are provided under this Act. However, such commercial exploitation shall not be deemed to have occurred if it is incidental to the legitimate use of the integrated circuit in which the layout-design is incorporated, provided that such use does not unfairly prejudice the proprietor’s interests or diminish the commercial value of the layout-design. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions contained herein, grant licenses to others for the commercial exploitation of their layout-design, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial limits of such license. Any dispute regarding the terms of a license or alleged unauthorized commercial exploitation shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the designated authority, and the proprietor shall bear the onus of proving the unauthorized activity. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in injunctions and damages.

Any person who, without the authorization of the proprietor of a registered layout-design, engages in any act of commercial exploitation of the said layout-design shall be liable to a penalty not less than ten lakh rupees but which may extend to five crore rupees, assessed on a per-unit basis of the infringing articles or, in lieu thereof, an ad valorem royalty as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Where the commercial exploitation involves a repeated offence, the penalty shall not be less than twenty lakh rupees. The proprietor, subject to the provisions of this Act, may also seek an injunction restraining the unauthorized acts and may claim damages for any loss suffered due to such infringement. Any material or instrument used in the commission of the offence, and any infringing articles, shall be liable to seizure and destruction as directed by a competent authority. A false claim of registration or misrepresentation of rights under this Act shall attract a separate penalty of up to five lakh rupees.

Any registered layout-design right shall be transferable by assignment, testamentary disposition or operation of law, and the proprietor of such right may enter into agreements for licensing others to exercise the rights conferred by this Act. Any license granted under this Act shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the license, including the duration, geographical territory, and any limitations on the commercial exploitation of the layout-design. Subject to the terms of any such license, the assignee or licensee may exercise all the rights of the proprietor in respect of the assigned or licensed layout-design. Where a layout-design is commercially exploited without the consent of the proprietor, or in violation of the terms of a license, the proprietor may institute civil proceedings for injunction and damages. Provided that, any assignment or license shall be subject to the payment of the prescribed fee and registration with the appropriate authority as provided herein, failing which such transfer shall be deemed invalid. The proprietor shall retain the right to revoke a license upon reasonable cause and notice.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred, and may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement, as well as damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. However, a defendant may, in any such proceeding, file a counter-claim asserting the invalidity of the registration of the layout-design, or alleging that the acts complained of do not constitute commercial exploitation as defined herein. Should the Court find in favour of the defendant on such a counter-claim, the plaintiff’s claim for injunction and damages shall stand dismissed. An appeal from any decree or order of the District Court in such proceedings shall lie to the High Court, and further to the Supreme Court, subject to the usual terms and conditions. The burden of proving due diligence in preventing the infringement shall, in all cases, lie with the registered proprietor.

Any person who, without the authorization of the proprietor, engages in the commercial exploitation of a registered semiconductor layout-design shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each instance of such exploitation, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Where the commercial exploitation involves a denomination variety sub-type of layout-design, and is proven to be a deliberate and systematic act intended to deceive the public regarding the source or quality of the integrated circuit, the penalty shall not be less than two lakh rupees. The proprietor may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, seek an injunction restraining the unauthorized exploitation and claim damages for any loss suffered as a result. Any material used in the commission of the offence, including but not limited to manufacturing equipment and finished products, shall be subject to confiscation as provided herein. Appeals against orders imposing penalties may be preferred to the designated authority within sixty days of the order’s issuance.

Any registered layout-design, as provided herein, shall be subject to the exclusive right of the registered proprietor to commercially exploit the same, and such exploitation may include reproduction, distribution, import, or any act by which the layout-design is made available to the public. A legal practitioner, duly qualified to practice before any court, may, on behalf of the registered proprietor, initiate proceedings for infringement of such exclusive right. Registration of a layout-design does not preclude the right of a person to use the layout-design for the purpose of research or for educational purposes, provided that such use does not amount to commercial exploitation. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person intending to obtain a license for commercial exploitation must apply to the registered proprietor, and the terms of such license shall be mutually agreed upon.

A Judicial Member shall be a person who is, or has been, a Judge of a High Court, or a legal practitioner of ten years standing, and possesses such technical knowledge or experience as the Central Government may deem appropriate, and shall be appointed by the Central Government. The Central Government may, if it deems fit, appoint a Technical Member in addition to the Judicial Member, who shall be a person with demonstrated expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design or a related field. Where a Bench is constituted for the hearing of any matter under this Act, it shall consist of at least one Judicial Member and may also include a Technical Member, subject to the provisions herein. The decisions of any such Bench shall be by majority vote.

Any person desiring to be registered as a Judicial Member shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Central Government, accompanied by a non-refundable fee as may be determined. The application shall include proof of a Masters degree in Law from a recognized university, and a minimum of ten years of experience as a legal practitioner or judicial officer. A panel of experts, constituted by the Central Government, shall evaluate the qualifications and experience of each applicant, and recommend candidates for appointment. The Central Government may, subject to the recommendations of the panel, appoint a qualified individual as a Judicial Member. 

Provided that, the term of office for a Judicial Member shall not exceed five years, and reappointment is permissible only once, subject to satisfactory performance evaluation. The functions of a Judicial Member shall include the hearing of appeals and the adjudication of disputes arising under this Act, and shall exercise such powers as are conferred by or under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design right under this Act may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from the acts constituting the infringement, and such application shall be disposed of expeditiously. The Court, while granting such injunction, may require the applicant to furnish such security as it deems adequate. A Judicial Member, appointed by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, may be appointed to assist the Court in matters requiring technical expertise relating to semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the High Court shall have jurisdiction to try any suit or other proceedings arising under this Act. Any decree passed by the High Court in any such suit may include an order for delivery up or destruction of the infringing articles, and an account of profits. Provided that, no such order shall be made unless the defendant is given an opportunity to be heard. The aggrieved party may, as provided herein, seek damages for any loss suffered due to the infringement.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Tribunal to be known as the Semiconductor Layout-Design Tribunal. The Tribunal shall consist of a President and such number of other members as the Central Government may deem necessary. A qualified and experienced Judicial Member shall be appointed to the Tribunal, possessing a degree in law with not less than ten years of experience as a District Judge or equivalent. The qualifications of other members shall be determined by the Central Government, ensuring expertise in semiconductor technology or related fields. 

Any vacancy arising in the Tribunal, including that of the President or a Judicial Member, shall be filled by the Central Government in a timely manner. The Tribunal shall exercise jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to the registration, infringement, and revocation of layout-designs, as provided herein. All proceedings before the Tribunal shall be conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice and may be subject to such rules as the Central Government may prescribe. Decisions of the Tribunal shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Designs, or any decision relating to the registration of a layout-design, may appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. The Appellate Board shall consist of a President and such number of other members as the Central Government may deem necessary, including at least two Judicial Members possessing the qualifications prescribed. A Judicial Member shall be a person who is, or has been, a Judge of a High Court, or a District Judge with not less than seven years of experience. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Appellate Board shall have the power to regulate its own procedure. All appeals shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, and leave to appeal to the Supreme Court is granted.

Any person contravening the provisions relating to confidential information, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of such contravention. The adjudication of such penalties shall vest solely with a duly appointed Judicial Member, possessing qualifications equivalent to that of a District Judge, and functioning under the authority of the Central Government. Should a Judicial Member determine that the contravention was committed with intent to deceive or cause substantial loss, the penalty may be enhanced, not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Any appeal against the order of a Judicial Member shall lie before the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and must be filed within ninety days of the order’s issuance. Failure to comply with an order of the Judicial Member, including payment of penalties, shall constitute an additional punishable offence. The Central Government may, by notification, prescribe the procedure for filing appeals and the format thereof.

Any registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license, either wholly or partially, the right, title and interest in such layout-design to any other person. Any assignment or license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions governing such assignment or license, including the duration, scope, and territorial extent. Where an assignment is made without specifying any consideration, it shall be deemed to have been made for adequate consideration, and the burden of proving otherwise shall lie on the assignee. 

A Judicial Member appointed under this Act shall, prior to the execution of any assignment or license agreement involving a layout-design of national importance, ensure that the terms do not unduly restrict competition or innovation. The registered proprietor shall maintain a register of all assignments and licenses granted, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person upon reasonable notice and payment of a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license voidable at the option of the assignee or licensee.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with an order of the Registrar, may file an appeal before the designated Appellate Authority within a period of sixty days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of such fee as may be prescribed. The Appellate Authority shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both parties, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order of the Registrar. Where an appeal is filed against an order refusing registration, the Appellate Authority may, if satisfied that the layout-design is registrable, direct the Registrar to register it. A decision of the Appellate Authority shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court. The composition of the Appellate Authority shall include at least one Judicial Member possessing requisite legal expertise and experience in intellectual property matters, ensuring a fair and impartial adjudication of disputes arising under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Authority pertaining to the registration of a layout-design, or refusal thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Judicial Member within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, subject to deposit of such fees as may be prescribed. The appeal shall be in such form and shall be accompanied by such documents as are specified in the rules. The Judicial Member, upon receipt of an appeal and after giving the respondent an opportunity of being heard, shall pass an order affirming, modifying or reversing the order appealed against. Where the appeal relates to a dispute involving the application of plant breeding techniques, particularly concerning crop sciences indian varieties utilized in the fabrication process, the Judicial Member may consult with a technical expert possessing specialized knowledge in that field. Provided that, no appeal shall lie against an interlocutory order of the Licensing Authority. The decision of the Judicial Member shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

A Judicial Member shall be a person possessing such technical expertise and legal knowledge as the Central Government may deem fit, appointed from amongst persons with at least fifteen years of experience in relevant fields including semiconductor technology, microelectronics, or integrated circuits. The appointment of a Judicial Member shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Any petition relating to the validity of a layout-design, or seeking rectification thereof, including a zm form petition alleging improper derivation, shall be initially adjudicated upon by a Judicial Member, who may, after preliminary examination, refer the matter to a regular Bench if deemed necessary. The decision of the Judicial Member shall be subject to appeal as provided herein. A person so appointed shall hold office for a term of five years or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier.

A Judicial Member of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Board shall be a person of proven integrity and possessing a thorough understanding of integrated circuits technology and intellectual property law. The appointment of a Judicial Member shall be made by the Central Government from a panel of persons recommended by a Search-cum-Selection Committee constituted for the purpose. Any person aggrieved by the non-consideration of their candidature for appointment as a Judicial Member may, within thirty days of the communication of the appointment, register sufficient cause before the Board, detailing the grounds for their objection. The Board shall, following receipt of such registration, conduct an inquiry and submit its findings to the Central Government within ninety days. Should the Board determine that sufficient cause has been demonstrated and that the selection process was flawed, the Central Government may review the appointment and initiate a fresh selection process. A Judicial Member shall hold office for a term of five years or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, and may be eligible for reappointment.

A “Member” shall, for the purposes of this Act, denote a person who is registered as the proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, and includes their duly authorized agent or assignee, subject to the provisions contained herein. A ‘registered user’ is a natural or legal person who has lawfully accessed a layout-design for the limited purpose of manufacturing a semiconductor product, and such access does not confer membership as defined herein. Membership is contingent upon the filing of an application, accompanied by the prescribed fee, and subsequent verification of the layout-design’s originality. Provided that, a Member shall remain liable for any infringement arising from unauthorized use of the layout-design, even if such use occurs through a registered user. Any dispute regarding membership shall be adjudicated by the designated authority as provided herein.

A person shall be considered a member of the Semiconductor Layout-Design Registry if they have successfully submitted an application for registration, accompanied by the prescribed fee, and the Controller has determined that the application meets the requirements as provided herein. Membership is contingent upon the applicant fulfilling all obligations regarding disclosures of prior art and providing a clear and accurate depiction of the layout-design. Any alteration to the designated nominee or address of the member shall require immediate notification to the Registry, failing which the application may be deemed incomplete. A registered member may, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise rights relating to the exploitation and protection of their layout-design. The Controller retains the authority to suspend or revoke membership in cases of fraud, misrepresentation, or non-compliance with the regulations governing the Registry. The Registry shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all current members.

A person shall be deemed a Member if they have contributed to the creation of a registered layout-design, and their contribution is demonstrably significant, as determined by the Layout-Design Registry. Any Member, subject to the provisions herein, shall have the right to receive a fair share of any royalties or other consideration derived from the commercial exploitation of the layout-design, proportionate to their documented contribution. Provided that, a Member may, by written agreement with the proprietor, waive their right to such share. Where a dispute arises regarding the determination of a Member’s contribution or the appropriate share of royalties, any aggrieved Member may apply to the High Court for redress. The proprietor shall maintain accurate records of all Members and their respective contributions, and shall furnish such records to the Court upon request. Failure to do so may result in a penalty as prescribed under this Act. A Member’s rights are personal to them and are not transferable except by operation of law.

A person shall be considered a member of a consortium established for the purpose of collective enforcement of rights under this Act, provided that such person is engaged in the design, development, or manufacture of semiconductor integrated circuits. Any application for membership shall be submitted to the governing council of the consortium in the manner prescribed, and the governing council may, subject to verification of the applicant’s credentials and adherence to the consortium’s bylaws, admit such person as a member. A member shall be entitled to participate in the decision-making processes of the consortium, proportionate to their contribution as determined by the governing council. However, a member found to be in violation of the provisions of this Act, or the consortium’s bylaws, may have their membership suspended or revoked by a majority vote of the governing council following a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The consortium may, as provided herein, establish a dispute resolution mechanism for matters arising between members.

A person shall be considered a Member if they have submitted a complete application for registration of a layout-design, along with the prescribed fee, to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry and such application is pending consideration. Membership is contingent upon the applicant fulfilling all requirements as to the nature of the layout-design, specifically that it depicts a three-dimensional arrangement of electronic circuits. Provided that, a person previously declared ineligible for membership under this Act, or found to have submitted materially false information in any application, shall not be eligible for a period of three years from the date of such declaration or finding. The Registry may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, grant provisional membership pending full examination of the layout-design. Any Member may request a certified copy of their application details, and such request shall be processed within thirty days of receipt, as provided herein. Failure to maintain accurate contact information with the Registry may result in suspension of membership rights.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor or a duly licensed assignee, represents themselves to be a Member, or uses any business identifier or mark suggesting association with a registered Member, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a Member knowingly permits or facilitates any such misrepresentation, that Member shall be jointly and severally liable for the imposed penalty. Any act of falsely claiming membership, undertaken with intent to deceive and obtain undue benefit, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller, upon receiving credible information of such an offence, may initiate an investigation and, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct the relevant authority to commence prosecution. Evidence obtained through legitimate means shall be admissible in any proceedings under this Act, and the burden of proof regarding lawful use shall lie with the accused.

A person shall be considered a Member of a consortium for the joint development of a layout-design, provided that such membership is evidenced by a written agreement outlining the scope of contribution and proportionate ownership of resulting intellectual property rights. Any assignment of a Member’s rights in the jointly developed layout-design to a third party shall require the prior written consent of all other Members, subject to the terms of the consortium agreement which may provide for a right of first refusal. Where a Member fails to commercially exploit their assigned portion of the layout-design within a period of two years from the date of completion of development, the other Members may, acting unanimously, grant a license to a third party on reasonable terms, accounting for the defaulting Member’s original contribution as determined under the consortium agreement. A transfer of membership itself, without assignment of rights, shall be permissible, but notification must be provided to the registering authority as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design, or imposing conditions on registration, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such decision, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the Registrar’s order and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. A prospective *Member* of the Appellate Board shall possess such technical expertise as may be prescribed, and the Central Government shall maintain a panel of eligible individuals for appointment. Should a Member recuse themselves from hearing an appeal due to conflict of interest, the Appellate Board may, subject to the rules, appoint a substitute Member from the panel. Any order of the Appellate Board may be challenged before the High Court, and such challenge shall be filed within sixty days of the Appellate Board’s decision, unless a stay of execution has been granted as provided herein. The burden of proof in any appeal relating to the originality of a layout-design shall lie with the appellant.

A person shall be considered a Member of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry upon successful completion of the prescribed application process and payment of the requisite fees as provided herein. The Registry shall maintain a record of all registered Members, detailing their authorized representatives and subject registration trade details, including any changes thereto. Any alteration to the authorized representative or trade details must be promptly notified to the Registry in the manner specified. Membership may be suspended or revoked in cases of non-compliance with the provisions of this Act or upon a finding of fraudulent activity related to a registered layout-design. Subject to the rules established by the Registry, a Member may access and inspect registered layout-designs, provided that such access is for legitimate purposes and in accordance with the confidentiality obligations outlined herein. The Registry shall have the power to issue guidelines for the conduct of Members.

A person shall be considered a member of the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry upon successful completion of the prescribed application process and payment of the requisite filing application fees as detailed in Schedule I. Membership confers the right to file applications for the registration of layout-designs, and to receive official communications pertaining to such applications. Any change in the designated address for service of a member shall be notified to the Registry in writing within thirty days of such change, failing which, communications sent to the last known address shall be deemed to have been duly served. The Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant a temporary suspension of membership in cases of repeated non-compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein. A member may voluntarily relinquish membership by submitting a written request to the Registry, accompanied by proof of settlement of all outstanding fees. The Controller shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all current members. Any dispute regarding membership shall be adjudicated by the Controller, whose decision shall be final.

An india application shall be deemed to have been duly made only if it conforms to the requirements as to form and content prescribed under the rules made by the Central Government. Such application shall include a clear representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and a statement of use, or a statement of proposed use, as the case may be. Where an india application is found to be deficient in any material particular, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require the applicant to remedy the deficiency within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the application being deemed abandoned, provided that an opportunity for a hearing shall be granted to the applicant before any such decision is made.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be made in writing to the Controller of Trade Marks in the manner as prescribed, and shall be accompanied by a statement of proposed use indicating the goods or services to which the trade mark will be applied. An india application shall be deemed to be misstated if it does not accurately reflect the applicant’s intention to use the mark in relation to those goods or services. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the applicant to submit evidence of such proposed use within a period not exceeding twelve months from the date of the application. Provided that, failure to demonstrate a bona fide intention to use the trade mark may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein. The Controller shall maintain a register of all applications received and shall examine each application to determine its compliance with the provisions of this Act.

Every india application shall be accompanied by a statement of proposed use, detailing the specific goods or services in relation to which the trade mark is sought to be registered, and such statement shall be clear and unambiguous as to the nature of those goods or services. Where an india application concerns a collective mark or a certification mark, the rules governing such marks, as provided herein, shall apply mutatis mutandis. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to amend the india application to ensure clarity or to remove any superfluous matter. An india application found to be incomplete or deficient in any material particular may, at the discretion of the Registrar, be deemed abandoned after a period of thirty days from a notice requesting rectification. Provided that the applicant may, within the said period, submit a complete and rectified india application. All correspondence relating to an india application shall be addressed to the Registrar at the prescribed address.

Every india application shall be accompanied by a statement of use, detailing the extent to which the trade mark has been used in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, and such statement shall be verified by a duly authorized representative of the applicant. Where the application concerns a proposed use, a bona fide intention to use the trade mark must be demonstrated through submission of documented evidence of significant preparation for such use, including but not limited to, marketing plans and investment details. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require further evidence to substantiate claims of use or intention to use. An india application failing to meet these requirements may be deemed incomplete and shall be liable to be rejected. Provided that, the Registrar shall afford the applicant an opportunity to rectify any deficiencies within a period of thirty days from the date of such notice. Any false representation regarding use shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to confer a limited, non-exclusive license upon the Central Government for the purposes of official use, including but not limited to, publication in official gazettes and display on government websites, without any royalty or accounting. An india application shall be accompanied by a declaration affirming the applicant’s bona fide intention to use the trade mark and a statement detailing any prior rights claimed in relation to the mark. Assignment of an india application, prior to registration, requires the prior written consent of the Registrar, and such assignment shall be subject to a verification process to ensure the assignee meets the eligibility criteria as provided herein. Where an application is jointly made, each applicant shall be jointly and severally liable for all obligations arising under this Act. Failure to comply with the requirements regarding assignment or declaration may render the application liable to be refused. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional evidence to substantiate claims made within the application.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a prior search conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain the existence of any identical or deceptively similar marks already registered or applied for, as provided herein. Where such a mark is found, the Registry may issue an objection, and the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to rebut the said objection with evidence of distinctiveness or prior use. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the objection, the application shall be deemed abandoned. However, an aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision regarding the objection, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the decision. The Appellate Board shall consider the evidence presented and may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision, and its order shall be final and binding, unless subject to judicial review. An india application shall not be revived after abandonment without demonstrable cause and payment of a prescribed revival fee.

Any india application for registration of a trade mark, submitted to the Trade Marks Registry, shall be accompanied by a clear and concise statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought, and shall fully disclose all relevant prior art known to the applicant. Failure to disclose such prior art may render the trade mark vulnerable to revocation, and shall be deemed an act of misrepresentation under this Act. An application lacking sufficient disclosure, or containing false representations regarding the novelty or inventive step of the mark, shall be subject to immediate rejection. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the applicant to amend the application to rectify any deficiencies. Any person found to have knowingly submitted a fraudulent india application shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all such penalties imposed.

An india application for the registration of a trade mark shall be presented to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed, and shall contain a representation of the trade mark, particulars of the applicant including name, address, and nationality, a statement of the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought, and a clear indication of the class or classes of the Nice Classification to which those goods or services belong. The application shall further state the extent to which the trade mark is used or proposed to be used in relation to those goods or services. Where the applicant does not intend to use the trade mark, an application may still be accepted subject to the provisions for ‘application for registration’ as detailed herein, and shall be subject to a notice of opposition period.

Any person desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark in India shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry, adhering to the prescribed form and fee structure as provided herein. The india application shall clearly identify the applicant, including name, address, and nationality, and shall designate the trade mark sought to be registered, specifying the goods or services to which it relates. An applicant may claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a convention country, subject to fulfilling the stipulated conditions and timelines. Where the trade mark includes a claim of colour, this shall be explicitly stated in the application and supported by a representation. The application shall further include a statement regarding the use of the trade mark, or a bona fide intention to use it, and any relevant supporting documentation may be furnished to substantiate such claim. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from the applicant during the examination process.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing an india application, or requiring an amendment to an application, may file a written appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registry an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registry, reverse it, or modify it in such manner as it deems fit. Where an india application is refused solely on the ground of a prior, identical mark existing on the Register, the applicant may, within sixty days of the refusal, submit evidence of non-use of the prior mark for a continuous period of five years, potentially reviving the original application, provided that such evidence is deemed sufficient by the Appellate Board. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible, unless the Appellate Board, for sufficient cause, extends the period.

Every application for registration of a trade mark in India shall be made in writing to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed, and shall be accompanied by a statement of proposed use. An india application must clearly identify the applicant, including full name, address for service, and nationality, and shall detail the trade mark sought to be registered, with a clear representation thereof. Where the applicant claims priority from a prior application made in a convention country, such claim shall be filed with the application and be subject to the provisions relating to convention applications as provided herein. 

The application shall further classify the goods or services to which the trade mark relates, in accordance with the Nice Classification. Should the application be incomplete in any material particular, the Registrar may require the applicant to amend or complete it within a specified period, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned. All applications shall be subject to examination for compliance with the provisions of this Act.

Any application for registration of a trade mark in India shall be deemed a complete india application only upon fulfillment of conditions as provided herein. The applicant shall submit a statement of use demonstrating bona fide adoption and continuous use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified, and such use must extend to a substantial and recognizable portion of the relevant territory. Where the application concerns a mark not currently in use, a declaration of intent to use, accompanied by a detailed plan for commercial exploitation within a period of twelve months from the date of advertisement, shall be furnished. Failure to demonstrate actual use or commence use as declared may render the application liable to be abandoned. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar may require further evidence or clarification regarding the nature of use or intent to use, and the applicant shall comply within the stipulated timeframe. An application found deficient in any material particular shall be subject to objection and potential refusal.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of an india application, or by any condition imposed in the registration of a trade mark, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to prefer such appeal within the stipulated period shall render the order final and binding. Where the Appellate Board confirms the refusal, the applicant shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, notwithstanding any appeal pending before the Appellate Board, initiate proceedings for the removal of a trade mark from the register if it is proven that the mark was obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation. Any false statement made in an india application shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Any person being the proprietor of a trade mark, or a right to its use, may assign the goodwill of the trade mark, or the trade mark itself, subject to the provisions of this Act and any other enactment for the time being in force. An india application for the assignment of a registered trade mark shall be in writing and shall identify the trade mark, the parties to the assignment, and the consideration, if any, paid or agreed to be paid. The Registrar shall record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks upon being satisfied that the application is complete and accurate, and that the assignment does not conflict with any existing rights. Where an assignment is made without the transfer of goodwill, the Registrar may require evidence of the bona fides of the assignment and may, if satisfied, record the assignment subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary to protect the interests of the public. A licensee of a trade mark may, with the consent of the proprietor, apply for the registration of the trade mark in their name, provided that they demonstrate sufficient grounds for such transfer.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an application for rectification of the register where the Trade Marks Registry is satisfied that the trade mark was applied for not in good faith or that it is identical with or deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an india application for rectification, cause a notice to be served upon the proprietor of the trade mark in question, requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding two months. Failure to file such counter-statement may result in ex parte consideration of the application. If, after examining the evidence and submissions, the Registrar finds the application to be well-founded, they shall order rectification of the register accordingly. Any person dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar may, within ninety days, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be heard by a single judge designated for intellectual property matters.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be a request for an india application, and must conform strictly to the requirements as prescribed by the Central Government through notification in the Gazette. Any deficiency in such application shall be communicated to the applicant within one month from the date of receipt, and failure to remedy said deficiency within the stipulated period may render the application liable to be abandoned. Where an applicant seeks to transmit the india application to another person, a duly executed instrument of assignment or transfer, as the case may be, shall accompany the request for such transmission. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the instrument and satisfaction of all applicable conditions, record the transmission and recognize the transferee as the applicant. Provided that, no transmission shall be effected if it contravenes any provision of this Act or any other law for the time being in force. All records relating to the india application, including any transmission requests and associated documentation, shall be maintained in a secure digital repository.

An application for registration of a trade mark relating to goods or services shall be deemed a valid india application only if it conforms strictly to the requirements as prescribed under these rules. The applicant shall furnish a clear representation of the mark, specifying its essential characteristics and, where applicable, a transliteration or translation if the mark incorporates non-Latin characters. Any application claiming priority under a convention or agreement shall include a verified statement of such claim and the relevant priority details. Where the application concerns a services trade mark, a detailed description of the services offered shall accompany the application, classified according to the Nice Classification. Failure to provide complete and accurate information, or to satisfy the conditions relating to permissible use, may result in the application being deemed abandoned or refused, as provided herein. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification from the applicant to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act.

Any application for registration of a trade mark in India shall be deemed a complete india application only upon fulfillment of all requirements as provided herein, including the accurate classification of goods and services and payment of the prescribed fee. Where an application seeks registration of a mark intended to certify goods or services meeting certain standards, a registered certification trade mark shall be prominently displayed on all certified items, failing which the registration may be revoked. Any false representation concerning certification, or the use of a certification mark without authorization, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Registrar may, subject to a reasoned showing of irreparable harm, issue an injunction restraining the offender. Repeated violations of these provisions shall render the applicant ineligible for future registrations under this Act, and may constitute grounds for criminal prosecution. All records pertaining to such applications shall be maintained securely and be subject to inspection as per established procedures.

Any person desiring to transfer or assign an india application for a registered trade mark, or an application for registration thereof, shall submit a written instrument of assignment to the Trade Marks Registry, executed by both the assignor and the assignee. Such instrument shall clearly identify the trade mark, the class of goods or services covered, and the geographical territory to which the assignment relates. Where the assignment is partial, specifying the goods or services assigned is mandatory. An application for amendment of the register consequent upon an assignment may be made in Form Petition, duly completed and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the instrument and satisfaction of all legal requirements as provided herein, record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable and shall not relieve the parties of any liabilities accrued prior to the assignment. The Registrar retains the discretion to require further evidence or clarification regarding the validity of the assignment.

An india disclosed application shall mean an application for registration of a trade mark wherein the applicant voluntarily discloses, at the time of filing, details of prior use of the trade mark in India, irrespective of whether such use constitutes legitimate use under this Act. Such disclosure shall be recorded as part of the application and may be considered during the examination process. Provided that the disclosure must be accompanied by supporting evidence, including but not limited to invoices, advertising materials, or statutory declarations, to substantiate the claim of prior use. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, request further evidence to verify the veracity of the disclosed information. Failure to provide adequate evidence may render the disclosure ineffective for the purposes of examination.

An application for registration disclosing an india disclosed application shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed, and shall contain a clear representation of the trade mark as to its essential features. The applicant shall state the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought, categorized according to the Nice Classification, and shall indicate the class or classes accordingly. Where the application claims priority under the Paris Convention, a statement to that effect, along with particulars of the prior application, must be furnished within the stipulated period. The applicant may, subject to the provisions of this Act, claim colour as a feature of the trade mark, provided that a clear and unambiguous representation of the colour is included in the application. Any misrepresentation in the india disclosed application shall render the registration liable to revocation. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application to remove any ambiguity or inconsistency.

Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration of a trade mark following the examination of an india disclosed application, may file a written request for reconsideration within one month of the date of such refusal. Such request shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the initial decision is believed to be erroneous, and may be accompanied by any additional evidence or arguments supporting the applicant’s claim. The Registrar, upon receipt of such request, shall re-examine the application and issue a reasoned order either affirming the original refusal or directing the registration of the trade mark, subject to the payment of any outstanding fees. Where the Registrar directs registration, the mark shall be registered as of the date of the original application, provided that the applicant demonstrates no material change in the circumstances relevant to registrability. A party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s order on reconsideration may appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

Any application for registration of a trade mark, where the applicant discloses an india disclosed application, shall be subject to examination as provided herein. The disclosure must be a complete and accurate statement of all prior art known to the applicant relating to the mark, including any use of the mark or any similar mark by any other person, whether in India or elsewhere. Failure to disclose relevant prior art may render the registration vulnerable to revocation under this Act. The Registrar may, at any stage, require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the india disclosed application. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the application meets the requirements of this Act and that the disclosed information is complete and accurate, the application shall proceed to advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar shall, however, retain the power to reject the application if the disclosed information is found to be materially misleading or incomplete, even after advertisement. Any objection to the registration based on the india disclosed application shall be filed within the prescribed time limit.
