Any application for registration of a trade mark disclosing an india disclosed application shall be deemed to be a provisional specification, and the applicant shall, within a period of twelve months from the date of such application, file a complete specification in the prescribed form, failing which the application shall be treated as withdrawn as provided herein. The complete specification shall clearly and accurately define the goods or services to which the trade mark relates, and shall be accompanied by a representation of the trade mark. Where the application includes a claim to colour as a feature of the trade mark, such claim shall be clearly stated in the specification and shall be subject to examination for distinctiveness. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the complete specification meets all requirements under this Act, accept it and proceed with the examination of the trade mark. An applicant may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, extend the period for filing the complete specification, but such extension shall not exceed a further six months.

Any person who publishes details of an india disclosed application without the express written consent of the applicant shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that publication for the purposes of bona fide academic research, subject to full attribution and non-commercial use, shall not constitute an offence. Where a trade mark application is determined to be an india disclosed application, the Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of unauthorized disclosure resulting in demonstrable prejudice to the applicant, issue a cease and desist order to the offending party. Failure to comply with such an order shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any profits derived from the unauthorized use of information contained within the india disclosed application shall be recoverable by the applicant as damages, and the court may also grant an injunction restraining further dissemination. Any officer of a company found to be complicit in such unauthorized disclosure shall be personally liable.

Any person becoming entitled to an india disclosed application, whether by assignment, transmission, operation of law, or otherwise, shall, within the prescribed period, apply to the Trade Marks Registry to register the transfer of such application as if it were a new application, and shall include a certified copy of the instrument evidencing the transfer. Provided that failure to so apply shall not invalidate the original application but may be considered by the Registrar when examining the application for registration. An assignment of an india disclosed application shall not affect the right of the original applicant to proceed with the application unless the instrument of assignment expressly states otherwise. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, permit the rectification of the register to reflect the change in ownership of the india disclosed application. Any assignment not in writing shall be void. The assignee shall be deemed the proprietor for the purposes of this Act, subject to the fulfilment of all requirements as provided herein.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition to an india disclosed application within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the application in the Trade Marks Journal. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly state the grounds on which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, lack of distinctiveness or a likelihood of confusion with existing registered trade marks. The applicant whose application is opposed may, within one month of receiving the notice of opposition, file a counter-statement addressing the grounds raised. Should the Registrar, after examining the evidence and submissions of both parties, find that the opposition is frivolous or vexatious, costs may be awarded against the opponent. An appeal from the decision of the Registrar on any such opposition shall lie to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and deposits the prescribed fee.

Any person who publishes information relating to a trade mark application, constituting an india disclosed application, shall ensure complete and accurate disclosure of all material facts pertaining to the inventive step far claimed, and any omission or misrepresentation thereof shall be deemed a contravention of this Act. Where a Registrar, upon examination, determines that a published india disclosed application lacks sufficient disclosure regarding the scope of the invention far claimed, a notice of deficiency shall be issued to the applicant, affording a period of thirty days to rectify the deficiency. Failure to comply with such notice shall render the application liable to be abandoned. Any person aggrieved by a falsely disclosed india disclosed application may, subject to the provisions herein, lodge a complaint with the Registrar, and upon substantiated evidence of deliberate misrepresentation, the applicant shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, in addition, order the revocation of any registration obtained through such misrepresentation.

Any aggrieved party may file an appeal before the Appellate Board concerning the refusal of an india disclosed application, provided that such appeal is presented within ninety days of the refusal order issued by the Trade Marks Registry. The Appellate Board shall, subject to such rules as may be prescribed, consider evidence submitted by both the applicant and the opposing party, and may request further clarification or documentation as deemed necessary. Where the india disclosed application relates to the layout-design of an integrated circuit, the Board shall also consider any claims of prior art or lack of novelty specific to semiconductor technologies. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case an appeal may be made to the Supreme Court. The Registrar may, at any time, initiate a review of the Appellate Board’s decision if credible evidence of procedural irregularity is presented.

An exclusive licensee shall be a person to whom, for a specified period, the owner of copyright has granted, by a written instrument signed by such owner, the exclusive right to do, or authorize the doing of, any of the acts specified in section 13, subject to such conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties. The instrument granting the exclusive license shall clearly state that it is an exclusive license, and shall define the extent of the rights granted and the territory in which such rights shall be exercisable. Where an exclusive license is granted in respect of a work, the owner of the copyright shall not, except as otherwise provided in the instrument, exercise any of the rights in that work which are subject to the exclusive license, and any such exercise shall be deemed a violation of the license. A non-exclusive licensee does not possess such rights.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee in copyright shall register such exclusive license with the Registrar of Copyrights, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee and furnishing such particulars as may be required by the Registrar. The application for registration of an exclusive license shall be made in Form IX, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the license agreement establishing the scope and duration of the exclusivity. Registration of an exclusive license shall create a rebuttable presumption of its validity and the extent of rights conferred therein, unless otherwise proven. A copyright owner may, however, grant multiple non-exclusive licenses without affecting the rights of a registered exclusive licensee, provided that the terms of such non-exclusive licenses do not conflict with the registered exclusive license. Failure to register an exclusive license shall not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of its existence.

An exclusive licensee of a copyright in any work shall, subject to the terms of the license agreement, possess the right to sue for infringement of the copyright as if they were the owner of the copyright, and to recover all damages and costs as are recoverable by the copyright owner under this Act. However, such right shall be conditional upon the exclusive licensee providing notice to the copyright owner of any intended legal action, and affording the owner the opportunity to join as a party to the proceedings, at the licensee’s expense. Where the copyright owner declines to join such action, the exclusive licensee may proceed independently, but any recovery shall be subject to any pre-existing contractual obligations regarding profit-sharing or royalty payments. A non-exclusive licensee shall not have the right to sue for infringement, but may be entitled to claim damages from the copyright owner to the extent of any loss suffered due to the owner’s failure to enforce their rights. Any assignment of the license shall be subject to the prior written consent of the copyright owner, unless otherwise provided in the license agreement.

Any person who is an exclusive licensee of the copyright in a work shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be deemed to be the owner of the copyright in respect of the rights so exclusively licensed. An exclusive license shall be construed to include the right to assign or otherwise transfer the exclusive license, unless expressly provided to the contrary in the terms of the license. Where a copyright owner grants an exclusive license, they may, notwithstanding such grant, retain the right to collect royalties and other remuneration arising from the exercise of the licensed rights. However, such retention shall not prejudice the exclusive licensee’s right to enforce the copyright against infringement, provided that the copyright owner promptly notifies the exclusive licensee of any infringement of which they become aware. Any dispute regarding the scope of an exclusive license or the interpretation of its terms shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate High Court. The exclusive licensee shall be entitled to all remedies available to a copyright owner as provided herein.

Any person who is an exclusive licensee of a copyrighted work shall be deemed to be the owner of the copyright in respect of the rights so exclusively licensed, subject to the terms and conditions of the license agreement. However, such exclusive licensee shall exercise the rights conferred by this Act as if they were the owner, but only to the extent expressly granted in the license. Where the license agreement stipulates a term for the exclusivity, the rights of the exclusive licensee shall automatically revert to the copyright owner upon the expiration of said term, unless expressly renewed as provided herein. The copyright owner may, notwithstanding the existence of an exclusive license, pursue legal remedies for any infringement occurring prior to the grant of such license. Any assignment of the exclusive license by the licensee shall require the prior written consent of the copyright owner, and failure to obtain such consent shall render the assignment void.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee of a copyright in any work shall furnish to the Registrar of Copyrights a duly verified statement setting forth the terms and conditions of the license, including the duration and the territory in which the exclusive license is effective. Failure to furnish such statement within thirty days of claiming exclusivity shall render the license void *ab initio* and subject the claimant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where an exclusive licensee demonstrates to the satisfaction of a District Court that another person has infringed the copyright in the work, the Court may issue an injunction restraining such infringement and award damages not less than one lakh rupees. Any profits made by the infringer through the unauthorized use of the copyrighted work shall be recoverable by the exclusive licensee, and any appeal against an order of the District Court shall be subject to a penalty of ten thousand rupees if found to be frivolous or vexatious.

Any person being the owner of copyright, or having the right to license the copyright in a work, may, by instrument in writing, grant to another person an interest, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, in the copyright. Where an exclusive license is granted in respect of a work, the licensor shall not be entitled to grant further licenses of the same kind, and the exclusive licensee shall be deemed to be the owner of the copyright in respect of the licensed rights, subject to the terms and conditions of the license. An assignment of copyright shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and shall not take effect until a notice in writing has been filed with the appropriate authority. A license may be granted for a definite period, or in perpetuity, and may be subject to such terms and conditions as the parties may agree, including provisions for royalty payments and termination. Any dispute arising out of a licensing agreement shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the competent court.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee of a copyright in a work shall, prior to commencing any legal proceedings alleging infringement of such copyright, furnish to the copyright owner a notice in writing specifying the nature of the exclusivity claimed and the terms and conditions of the license agreement. Failure to provide such notice shall be a bar to maintaining said proceedings, subject to the discretion of the Court to allow such proceedings if sufficient cause is demonstrated. However, where the copyright owner disputes the validity of the exclusivity claim, or alleges a breach of the license agreement rendering the exclusivity ineffective, the burden of proof shall lie with the purported exclusive licensee to establish both the validity of the license and its continued subsistence. Any determination regarding the scope of the exclusive license shall be interpreted narrowly, considering the specific rights reserved by the copyright owner as evidenced in the written agreement. A finding of invalidity shall revert all rights to the copyright owner.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee of a copyright in a work shall submit to the Registrar an application, in the prescribed form, seeking registration of such exclusive license, accompanied by certified copies of the licensing agreement and a no-objection certificate from the copyright owner. The Registrar shall, subject to verification of the submitted documents and satisfaction that the applicant is indeed an exclusive licensee as per the terms of the agreement, register the license and maintain a registrar index registered detailing the scope and duration of the exclusivity. An appeal against the refusal of the Registrar to register an exclusive license may be preferred to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the refusal. However, registration of an exclusive license shall not be conclusive evidence of its validity, and any dispute regarding the interpretation or enforceability of the licensing agreement shall be subject to the ordinary course of civil proceedings.

An exclusive licensee shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to be the owner of the copyright in the copyright work licensed, subject to the terms and conditions of the license agreement and to the extent so authorized therein. Where a geographical indication registered under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, is incorporated into a copyrighted work, the exclusive licensee’s rights shall extend to preventing unauthorized use of said geographical indication in relation to that work, provided that such use would constitute infringement of the copyright. However, nothing herein shall prejudice the rights of the owner of the geographical indication under the said Act. Any assignment of the license shall be subject to prior written consent of the copyright owner.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee in copyright, and intending to avail remedies as provided herein for infringement, shall, prior to the institution of any suit or other legal proceeding, lodge a statement of his interest with the Registrar of Copyrights, setting forth the particulars of the license, including the duration and territory covered. The statement shall also identify the registered proprietor proposed as the party whose rights are being enforced by the exclusive licensee. Failure to lodge such a statement shall not, however, invalidate any existing license or preclude a claim for infringement, but may be considered by the court in determining the apportionment of damages or other relief. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of such statements, accessible for inspection subject to such fees as may be prescribed. A certificate of registration of the exclusive license, issued by the Registrar, shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the license.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall be the principal authority for the registration of geographical indications under this Act, and shall maintain a register of all such registered indications in a manner prescribed. The Registry may, subject to the approval of the Central Government, establish regional offices at such places as it deems necessary to facilitate the effective administration of this Act and to provide assistance to producers and applicants. Any person desiring to register a geographical indication shall apply to the Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee and a statement of case outlining the goods, the geographical area, and the standards applicable. The Registry shall examine the application to determine its conformity with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any objection raised by the Registry shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be afforded an opportunity to be heard.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a comprehensive register of all geographical indications registered under this Act, detailing the particulars of each indication, including its origin, characteristics, and the goods to which it applies. Any association of producers, or body of individuals representing the interests of producers, seeking registration of a geographical indication shall submit an application to the Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of case outlining the grounds for registration. The Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require further evidence or clarification from the applicant. Upon satisfactory examination and verification of the application, and confirmation that the geographical indication meets the criteria as provided herein, the Registry shall register the indication and issue a certificate of registration. The register shall be open for inspection by the public during office hours, and certified copies of entries may be obtained upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration to the registered particulars shall be notified to and recorded by the Geographical Indications Registry.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a register of all geographical indications registered under this Act, and such register shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the entry therein. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of the Registrar to register a geographical indication, or by any alteration made in the register, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board for rectification of the register. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, pass such order as it deems fit, confirming, modifying or setting aside the decision of the Registrar. Where a registered geographical indication is found to be falsely represented or used in a manner likely to deceive the public, the owner of the geographical indication may institute civil proceedings for injunction and damages. The court, upon being satisfied of such misrepresentation or use, shall grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the geographical indication and may also award damages to the owner.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a register of all geographical indications registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be made in writing to the Controller of the Geographical Indications Registry in the manner as prescribed. The Controller may, prior to registration, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence to satisfy themselves as to the authenticity and geographical origin of the goods. 

A register of authorized users shall also be maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry, detailing those permitted to use the registered geographical indication in relation to the specified goods. Any dispute regarding the inclusion or exclusion of an authorized user shall be subject to the dispute resolution mechanism as provided herein. The Controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the power to rectify the register, and any rectification shall be recorded in the register and notified to the applicant or registered proprietor.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a register of all geographical indications registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any member of the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any application for registration of a geographical indication shall be made in writing to the Geographical Indications Registry in the manner as prescribed, and shall include a clear representation of the goods to which the indication applies, alongside details of the region of origin. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, upon becoming aware of any infringement, notify the Geographical Indications Registry and provide evidence of such infringement within ninety days. The Registry may, subject to verification of the evidence, initiate appropriate action as provided herein. All records maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry shall be deemed public documents, unless otherwise restricted by order of a competent court. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties, including revocation of registration.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a comprehensive register of all registered geographical indications, accessible to the public subject to reasonable fees as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by an entry in, or omission from, the register may, within a period of ninety days from the date of such entry or omission, file a petition to the Registry for rectification. Failure to maintain accurate records within the Geographical Indications Registry, or deliberate falsification thereof by any officer of the Registry, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. Any application for registration knowingly containing a false representation shall be void, and the applicant shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Registry may, at its discretion, offer a one-time opportunity to rectify such misrepresentation subject to payment of additional fees.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer, or license the rights therein, wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to limitations, to any person or class of persons. Any assignment or transfer of rights shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the proprietor and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry, failing which such assignment or transfer shall be void. The Registrar of Geographical Indications may, upon application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, record the assignment or transfer in the Register of Geographical Indications. A license granted under this Act shall be binding upon the proprietor and the licensee, and may include provisions regarding quality control, duration, and territorial scope. Where a license is exclusive, the proprietor shall not grant further licenses for the same geographical indication in respect of the same goods. The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a public register of all recorded assignments, transfers, and licenses, accessible for inspection as provided herein.

The aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the decision of the Geographical Indications Registry regarding the refusal of registration or the modification of an existing geographical indication, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order of the Registry, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Appellate Board, upon receiving an appeal, may require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount of the registration fees originally paid. Any party opposing the appeal may file a counter-statement within thirty days of receiving notice from the Appellate Board. The Board shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, pass an order affirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the Geographical Indications Registry, and such order shall be final and binding, except as provided herein for writ petitions before the High Court.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall maintain a register of all geographical indications registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any member of the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any registered proprietor may, with the approval of the Registry and subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, grant licenses to other persons to use the registered geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Assignment of any right in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an application to the Registry and shall not be effective until recorded therein. The Registry may, upon sufficient cause being shown, refuse to record an assignment if it is deemed detrimental to the public interest or the interests of the producers associated with the geographical indication. A transfer by operation of law, including through inheritance or insolvency, shall also require notification to and recording by the Registry to maintain the validity of the registration.

The Geographical Indications Registry shall be the principal authority for the registration and protection of geographical indications under this Act, and shall maintain a register of all registered geographical indications in a manner prescribed. Any application for registration of a geographical indication filed in India shall be examined by the Registry to ascertain its conformity with the provisions of this Act and the associated rules. The Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. Provided that, if a filed application india does not meet the prescribed criteria, the Registry may, after providing a reasoned opportunity for hearing, reject the said application. The Registry shall also be responsible for maintaining records of all proceedings relating to applications and registrations.

An Integrated Circuit shall mean a three dimensional microelectronic structure, including all circuits and interconnections therein, which is intended to perform an electronic function, and which is wholly or partially fabricated in or on a semiconductor material or insulating material. For the purposes of this Act, a ‘layout-design’ is a plan of all or any layer of an Integrated Circuit, in which transistors, diodes, resistors, conductors, or other elements and interconnections are formed or intended to be formed, and includes such plan regardless of whether it is in the form of a mask, reticle, or other physical representation. Subject to the provisions herein, an Integrated Circuit shall not be considered identical if it differs in scale or minor modifications not substantially affecting its operation.

An integrated circuit, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be deemed to include any three-dimensional structure, or any combination of such structures, which are designed for the performance of electronic functions and which are capable of being mass-produced by semiconductor fabrication techniques. A layout-design, being a function of the integrated circuit, shall be registrable if it is original, and not previously disclosed to the public, anywhere in the world. The applicant for registration shall submit detailed drawings, or other graphical representations, demonstrating the layout-design and its relationship to the integrated circuit. Subject to verification by the appropriate authority, and payment of the prescribed fee, a certificate of registration shall be issued, conferring exclusive rights on the applicant for a period of ten years from the date of filing. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration may, within the prescribed time, submit a statement of grounds for reconsideration, as provided herein.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an integrated circuit, whether by manufacture, sale, import, or otherwise, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding rights in registered layout-designs. A registered proprietor of an integrated circuit layout-design shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, distribute, or commercially exploit the layout-design, subject to the terms of the registration and any limitations as provided herein. Where a person, without the consent of the registered proprietor, performs any of the acts prohibited under this Act, such proprietor may institute civil proceedings for actual damages, or statutory damages not exceeding rupees one crore, whichever is higher. 

Furthermore, a court may grant an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing such acts. Any person who assists another in the infringement of a layout-design shall be liable as if they were the primary infringer, provided that such assistance was knowingly rendered. The registered proprietor’s rights shall subsist for a period of ten years from the date of filing, or until the layout-design ceases to be commercially exploited, whichever is earlier.

An integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to be a final product originating from the expression of series of layers of semiconductor materials and insulating materials wherein, at least three layers of such materials are interconnected to form transistors, diodes, resistors or other functional elements, and includes a three-dimensional structure having such elements. Any layout-design, being an integrated circuit, shall be considered original if it is generated through independent intellectual effort, and is not derivative of any pre-existing layout-design or article. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the right to commercially exploit a registered layout-design shall vest in the proprietor. A person may apply for registration of a layout-design to the Intellectual Property Office, furnishing the requisite fee and particulars as prescribed. Provided that, the application shall be accompanied by a topographical representation of the layout-design, clearly indicating the layers constituting the integrated circuit. Any dispute regarding the validity of a registration or the infringement of a layout-design shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the designated court.

An integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered a finished product irrespective of whether it is incorporated into a module or system. Any person exploiting a layout-design, as provided herein, shall ensure strict adherence to the conditions of registration and maintain accurate records of all commercial transactions relating to the said layout-design. Subject to the provisions concerning national security, the licensing of a registered layout-design for defense purposes may be granted by the Central Government, notwithstanding any existing contractual obligations. A registered proprietor shall be entitled to equitable relief, including an injunction and damages, in respect of any infringement of their rights. Provided that, the quantum of damages shall be determined considering the actual loss suffered and reasonable royalty. Any person intending to commercially exploit a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design must first obtain the necessary authorization from the registered owner or a legally sanctioned licensing body. Failure to comply with these requirements shall attract penalties as prescribed.

Any person who, without the permission of the registered proprietor, manufactures, imports, sells, or distributes an Integrated Circuit, in whole or part, embodying a layout-design registered as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not less than ten lakh rupees but not exceeding five crore rupees, or imprisonment for a term not less than two years but not exceeding five years, or both. Where the violation relates to a layout-design registered for a semi-conductor chip intended for use in a national security application, the penalty shall not be less than twenty lakh rupees. Any material used in the manufacture of such infringing Integrated Circuit, and all articles incorporating the same, shall be deemed counterfeit goods and subject to seizure and destruction under the provisions of this Act. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may also seek an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement, and may recover damages for any loss suffered as a direct result of such infringement. Any appeal against an order of penalty shall lie before the designated court within thirty days of the order.

Any rights in a registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit layout-design shall vest with the proprietor, and such rights are subject to the provisions of this Act concerning licensing and assignment. A person may, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, obtain a license from the registered proprietor to commercially exploit the layout-design, provided that the terms of such license are mutually agreed upon in writing. Assignment of rights in an Integrated Circuit layout-design shall be valid only upon execution of a written instrument of assignment, clearly identifying the layout-design and specifying the scope of rights transferred. The assignee shall, within the time prescribed, notify the Controller of Designs of the assignment and furnish particulars thereof. Where a layout-design is created pursuant to a contract of service or apprenticeship, the rights therein shall, unless otherwise agreed, vest with the employer or master, as the case may be. However, the creator of the layout-design retains the right to claim authorship and to seek equitable remuneration as provided herein. Any transfer of rights without full and accurate disclosure of any existing encumbrances shall be voidable at the option of the transferee.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit layout-design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before the High Court, furnish to the alleged infringer a notice of such claim, detailing the specific layout-design infringed and the nature of the infringement, subject to the provisions contained herein. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of receipt of said notice, submit a counter-statement demonstrating that the layout-design is not original or that their actions do not constitute infringement as provided herein, the claimant may seek independent expert evaluation at their own expense. The High Court, upon consideration of such evaluation and any further evidence presented, shall determine whether a prima facie case of infringement exists. Provided that, if the expert evaluation confirms the validity of the alleged infringer’s counter-statement, the claimant’s suit shall be dismissed with costs. Any appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie before the Supreme Court, subject to the usual limitations. A registered Semiconductor Integrated Circuit, for the purposes of this determination, must demonstrate sufficient distinctiveness.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an Integrated Circuit, whether by manufacture, sale, import or otherwise, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act concerning layout-design rights. The layout-design of an Integrated Circuit shall be protectable as provided herein, irrespective of whether it is incorporated into articles and shall subsist until the expiry of ten years from the date of the first commercial exploitation. However, if an application for registration is filed, the layout-design right shall subsist for a period of ten years from the date of registration. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the layout-design right shall not confer any right to prevent any act protected under the Copyright Act, 1957, or any other law for the time being in force. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a layout-design right may institute a civil suit in a competent court, seeking injunction and damages. The court may, subject to the principles of equity, grant relief as it deems fit, including an account of profits.

An Integrated Circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be construed as a three-dimensional microelectronic structure, irrespective of its constituent materials, which is capable of performing an electronic function and which has been fabricated on a semiconductor substrate or insulating material. Any person desiring registration of a layout-design shall submit an application to the application registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating originality. The application registrar may, subject to verification of the application and the completeness of supporting materials, register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, if the application registrar has reasonable grounds to believe that the layout-design is not original or is substantially similar to an existing layout-design, they shall issue a notice of objection to the applicant. Any objection raised by the application registrar shall be addressed by the applicant within a period of thirty days from the date of the notice, failing which the application shall be deemed to be withdrawn. The register of layout-designs maintained by the application registrar shall be open for inspection during office hours, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

A new invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to be an invention not previously known to the public, anywhere in the world. Such novelty shall be assessed having regard to all matter which, as of the date of the claim, was made available to the public by any means, whether by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way. Provided that the discovery of a naturally occurring substance, even if isolated, shall not, by itself, constitute a new invention. An invention shall be considered industrially applicable if it can be made or used in any kind of industry, including agriculture. Subject to the provisions herein, a combination of existing elements is not a new invention unless it produces a synergistic effect resulting in a non-obvious improvement.

A claim for a patent shall be allowable only for a new invention, and no patent shall be granted for an invention that is obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field. For the purposes of determining novelty, any publication anywhere in the world prior to the date of filing the complete specification, whether written or oral, or by any other means, shall be considered prior art. An invention shall be deemed to involve an inventive step if it exhibits a significant improvement in functionality or efficiency over existing technologies, and is not merely a trivial variation thereof. Subject to the provisions herein, a process for manufacturing a new article shall be considered an invention, even if the article itself is not novel, provided that the process is demonstrably innovative and capable of industrial application. The applicant shall furnish detailed particulars demonstrating the technical advance achieved by the invention, and its distinction from prior art, as part of the complete specification.

Any person who demonstrates a new invention, being a product or process, and seeks protection under this Act shall submit a complete specification detailing the manner in which the invention may be worked. An applicant claiming priority for a new invention shall, subject to the provisions herein, be entitled to a patent if the invention is not publicly known and possesses an inventive step. However, a patent shall not be granted for an invention that is an obvious variation of existing knowledge, or one lacking practical utility. Should a patent be wrongfully granted for an invention not truly new, any aggrieved party may petition the Controller for revocation of said patent, and upon sufficient evidence of prior art demonstrating lack of novelty, the Controller may order the patent cancelled. The rights conferred by a patent shall extend to preventing others from making, using, selling, or importing the new invention without the patent holder’s consent, subject to licensing provisions as provided herein.

A new invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to possess novelty where it is not identically disclosed by any prior publication, whether written or oral, anywhere in the world before the date of the claim. However, the mere existence of prior art shall not *ipso facto* disqualify an invention from being considered new, provided that any differences between the claimed invention and said prior art are substantial and not merely trivial modifications. An invention shall not be considered a new invention if, having regard to the matter common knowledge in the relevant field, a person skilled in the art would find it obvious. 

Where an invention relates to a process, it shall be considered new subject to demonstration that the process itself, and not merely the product resulting from it, satisfies the criteria of novelty as provided herein. The Controller of Patents may, upon application, require the applicant to demonstrate the state of the art immediately before the filing date of the complete specification. Failure to adequately demonstrate such state of the art may be grounds for rejection of the patent application.

A new invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of novelty if it is not publicly known, whether by oral disclosure, use, or otherwise, before the date of filing the complete specification, or, where applicable, the priority date. However, any exhibition of the invention at a recognised international exhibition, as provided herein, within six months prior to the filing date, shall not be considered a prior art reference, subject to the applicant furnishing a certified copy of the exhibit report. Should the invention be derived from indigenous or traditional knowledge, documented evidence establishing its prior existence and public availability must be submitted. An invention shall not be considered novel if it is merely a variation of a known process or an obvious combination of existing art, and the burden of proving novelty rests with the applicant. Compliance with these provisions is essential for the grant of a patent.

Any person claiming to be the inventor of a new invention shall furnish to the Controller a complete and clear description of the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. An invention shall not be deemed new if it lacks novelty, and any publication of the invention, whether in India or elsewhere, prior to the date of filing the application, shall be considered detrimental to its novelty as provided herein. Should a person falsely represent another’s invention as their own, they shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any process for the manufacture of an invention, which is obvious to a person skilled in the art, shall not be patentable under this Act. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the inventor to submit evidence of the inventive step involved. Failure to comply with such requirement shall render the application void.

Any assignment of the right to a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be made in writing and shall specify the scope of the assignment, whether it is for the whole of India or for a specific territory. An assignment of a patentable invention, subject to the provisions of this Act, may be made for any term, but any assignment extending beyond the term of the patent shall be void. Where a new invention is jointly made, the right to apply for a patent shall be jointly determined by the inventors, unless an agreement to the contrary exists in writing. The assignee of a patent shall be bound by all the provisions of this Act as if they were the original patentee, and shall have the same rights and liabilities. Provided that, where the assignment is made without consideration, it shall be revocable by the assignor upon providing reasonable notice to the assignee and demonstrating that the assigned new invention has not been commercially exploited. Any licensing agreement shall be registered with the appropriate authority as provided herein.

A claim for a patent shall be allowable only for a new invention, and no patent shall be granted for an invention which is obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art, having regard to the existing knowledge. However, a combination of previously known elements, if it produces a synergistic effect resulting in a novel outcome, may be considered a new invention subject to satisfying the requirements as provided herein. Any objection raised by the Controller of Patents regarding the lack of novelty shall be communicated to the applicant, who may, within a period of one month from the date of such communication, submit evidence or arguments to demonstrate the inventive step. Should the Controller remain unconvinced, an appeal may be filed before the Appellate Board, and the burden of proof regarding the new invention shall lie with the appellant. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error.

A new invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include a semiconductor integrated circuit in which the topography has been independently created and is capable of being commercially exploited. However, any topography which is a mere copy of a layout publicly known or used prior to the filing of the application, or which is customary in the art, shall not be considered a new invention. An applicant claiming novelty based on a semiconductor integrated circuit topography shall submit detailed schematics demonstrating substantial differences from any prior art, and failure to do so may result in rejection of the application. Should an objection be raised regarding the inventive step, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act, providing further evidence of non-obviousness. The Board’s decision, subject to judicial review, shall be final and binding, unless a fundamental error of law is demonstrated. Any dispute concerning commercial exploitation shall be adjudicated by the High Court.

A new invention, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to possess novelty if it does not form part of the state of art prior to the date of the complete specification. The state of art shall encompass all matter which, at any place in the world, has been made available to the public by any means, whether by written or oral description, by use, or in any other way. Where an applicant seeks to claim a patent addition to an already patented invention, such addition shall be subject to the provisions relating to patentability, and must itself constitute a new invention, differing in a material respect from the main invention. An addition shall not be allowed if it is merely a variation of the main invention, lacking substantial inventive merit. The Controller may, however, consider an addition if it possesses a unique characteristic or application not previously disclosed. Any claim relating to a patent addition shall be examined independently, and a separate patent may be granted for the addition, dependent upon the parent patent.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, provided that the invention involving the modification or improvement arises from, or is substantially derived from, the invention for which the original patent was granted. An application for a patent of addition shall be made in Form 24, and shall contain a declaration stating that the invention for which the patent of addition is sought is a modification or improvement of the invention claimed in the original patent. The patent of addition shall be construed as if it were a single invention, and the terms of the original patent shall apply mutatis mutandis, subject to the provisions contained herein. No patent of addition shall be granted unless the applicant is the patentee, or an assignee of the patentee, of the original patent.

A patent of addition may be applied for under this Act by a patentee, being the person for the time being entered on the register as the proprietor of the main invention, if such patentee intends to protect an improvement or modification of that invention. The application for a patent of addition shall be filed in the prescribed manner and shall include a reference to the main patent. The controller, upon examination, shall determine if the improvement or modification is indeed connected to the main invention and merits protection as a patent of addition. Where a patent of addition is granted, it shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the main patent, and the expiry date shall be aligned with that of the original patent. A patent of addition shall not be granted unless the controller is satisfied that the requirements as to novelty and inventive step are met, subject to the scope of the main invention.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement of an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act. The applicant for a patent of addition shall be the patentee of the main invention, or a person legally deriving title from such patentee. An application for a patent of addition shall be filed in the prescribed manner and shall include a declaration stating that the invention for which the patent of addition is sought is a modification or improvement of the main invention. The patent of addition shall be granted for the unexpired term of the main patent. Where a patent of addition is granted, the main patent and the patent of addition shall be treated as a single patent for the purposes of renewal and assignment, and any infringement of the patent of addition shall also be deemed to be an infringement of the main patent. A licensee of the main patent shall not be entitled to exploit the invention claimed in the patent of addition without the consent of the patentee of the addition.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, or for which an application for a patent is pending, provided that the invention involving the modification or improvement is not separately patentable. An application for a patent of addition shall be filed in the prescribed manner and shall include a declaration stating that the invention is a modification or improvement of the invention claimed in the existing patent or pending application. The application shall be examined as if it were an application for a separate patent, subject to the condition that the patent of addition shall not be granted unless the main invention is also protected by a patent. The patent of addition shall be granted for the unexpired term of the main patent, and the patentee of the main patent shall also be the patentee of the patent of addition. Where a patent of addition is granted, the main patent and the patent of addition shall be treated as a single patent for the purposes of renewal fees and other administrative matters, as provided herein.

A patent of addition may be obtained for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act. An application for a patent of addition shall be made in Form 24, and shall include a declaration stating that the invention for which the patent of addition is sought is a modification or improvement of the invention patented, and that the subject matter of the patent of addition is not separately patentable. The application shall be examined as if it were an application for a separate patent, but the examination shall be limited to determining whether the claimed invention constitutes a sufficient modification or improvement of the patented invention. Where a patent of addition is granted, it shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the original patent, and the expiry date shall be the same as that of the original patent. A revocation of the original patent shall also extend to the patent of addition, unless the patentee of the addition proves to the satisfaction of the Controller that the addition is independently patentable.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement of an invention for which a patent has been granted, provided that such invention is not separately patentable, and subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person applying for a patent of addition shall file a declaration stating the basis of the claim to a patent of addition, referencing the main patent. Failure to provide such a declaration shall render the application liable to be refused. If a patent of addition is granted, it shall be subject to the same term of protection as the main patent, and any infringement of the patent of addition shall also constitute infringement of the main patent. Any false representation in the declaration regarding the inventive step or the connection to the main invention shall attract a penalty of imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. The Controller may, notwithstanding anything contained herein, require evidence of genuine connection between the inventions.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement of an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. An application for a patent of addition shall be made by the patentee or an assignee of the patent, or a person deriving title from such patentee or assignee, and shall be in the prescribed form. The application shall include a reference to the patent for which it seeks to be a patent of addition, and a declaration that the invention relating to the patent of addition is a modification or improvement of the invention claimed in the original patent. Where a patent of addition is granted, it shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the original patent, and the term of the patent of addition shall expire on the expiration of the term of the original patent. Any license granted under the original patent shall, unless otherwise agreed, extend to the patent of addition.

A patent of addition may be obtained for any invention which is a modification or improvement of an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning applications for patents. An application for a patent of addition shall be made in Form 24 and shall include a declaration stating that the invention for which the patent of addition is sought is a modification or improvement of the invention patented, and that the subject matter of the patent of addition is not separately patentable. Should the Controller object to the grant of a patent of addition, citing lack of inventive step or that the claimed invention is not a modification or improvement of the main invention, the applicant may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within the prescribed time. The Appellate Board, upon review, shall determine whether the requirements for a patent of addition have been met, and its decision shall be final and binding, unless a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court.

A patent of addition may be granted for any invention which is a modification or improvement of an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act. The so granted patent of addition shall be construed as if it were a single invention, and the date of the complete specification of the original patent shall be deemed to be the date of the complete specification of the patent of addition. Where a proprietor trade mark is registered for goods or services that are identical or nearly similar to those for which the main invention is utilized, the grant of a patent of addition shall not infringe upon the rights conferred by such trade mark, provided that the use of the patented invention does not create confusion or deception among consumers. Any proceedings relating to the validity of a patent of addition may be determined as if it were a patent for an independent invention.

A patent of addition may be obtained for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the conditions specified herein. An application for a patent of addition shall be made in Form 24, and shall be filed in the Patent Office with the prescribed fee, referencing the original patent by its number. The application shall contain a declaration stating how the invention is connected to the main invention and that the subject matter of the patent of addition is not separately patentable. Where an order adjudicating officer determines that the claimed invention does not meet the requirements for a patent of addition, the application shall be deemed to be an application for a separate patent, and processed accordingly. The patent of addition shall be granted for the unexpired term of the original patent, unless otherwise determined by the Controller. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for the successful prosecution of a patent of addition.

Permitted use of a registered trade mark shall extend to the use of the mark as specifically authorized by the proprietor, and subject to the conditions, if any, specified in the registered user agreement. Such agreement may delineate the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to, geographical territory, goods or services covered, and duration of the authorization. A registered user, while exercising permitted use, shall maintain standards of quality identical to those of the proprietor, failing which the proprietor may revoke the agreement. Any use exceeding the terms of the agreement, or use by an unregistered party, shall constitute an infringement as provided herein. The proprietor may, however, grant further or wider permissions, modifying the original scope of permitted use, through a supplemental agreement.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses, and may, subject to the conditions specified in the license and to the provisions of this Act, permit the use of the trade mark by another person. Any such permitted use shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and the Registry shall maintain a register of all permitted uses. A license or permission granted under this Act shall be personal to the licensee or permitted user, and shall not be transferable except with the prior written consent of the registered proprietor. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise control over the quality of goods or services offered under a permitted use, or fails to comply with the terms of the license, the Registry may, on application made by any aggrieved person, revoke the record of permitted use. The registered proprietor remains liable for any misrepresentation arising from such use.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses, and may stipulate conditions in the license regarding the quality of goods, including a condition that the goods shall be of a specified standard. Any permitted use of a trade mark by a registered user shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the license, and any breach of such terms or conditions shall be actionable by the registered proprietor as provided herein. Where a license contains a condition requiring the licensed goods to conform to a specified standard, and the registered proprietor refuses to accept goods meeting that standard without reasonable cause, such refusal shall constitute an infringement of the licensee’s rights. Notwithstanding the foregoing, a registered user shall not be permitted to assign or sub-license their rights under the license without the prior written consent of the trade mark proprietor, and any such unauthorized transfer shall be void. The proprietor may revoke a license for cause, following a notice period of not less than thirty days.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a license to another person, constituting such person a registered user in relation to the trade mark and specified goods. Any such license shall be in writing and may be subject to such conditions, including conditions as to the quality of goods, as the trade mark proprietor deems fit. The registrar shall, upon application made by the proprietor and the proposed registered user, record the license in the register of trade marks. A registered user shall have the right to use the trade mark as provided in the license and to obtain an injunction against any unauthorized use of the trade mark. However, such right shall not extend to uses which constitute infringement by the trade mark proprietor themselves. Any permitted use of a trade mark shall be consistent with the conditions of the license and the provisions of this Act, and the proprietor retains the right to revoke the license in cases of material breach. Failure to exercise control over the quality of goods bearing the trade mark by a registered user may constitute grounds for revocation of the license, as determined by the adjudicating officer.

Permitted use of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the conditions as provided herein, and any deviation therefrom may constitute grounds for revocation of such permission. A registered proprietor may, under this Act, grant licenses authorizing the use of their trade mark by another party, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial limits of such permitted use. Any permitted use extending beyond the terms of the license, or involving a material alteration of the registered trade mark, shall be deemed unauthorized. Furthermore, the quality of goods or services offered under permitted use must consistently meet the standards associated with the registered trade mark, failing which the proprietor may initiate action for passing off. The registered proprietor shall maintain a register of all permitted users and licenses granted, and shall furnish a copy thereof to the Registrar upon demand. Any transfer of a license for permitted use requires prior written consent of the trade mark owner.

Any person making permitted use of a registered trade mark, subject to the conditions of registration and as provided herein, shall not be deemed to be infringing the trade mark, notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act. However, such permitted use shall be strictly confined to the extent and in the manner as agreed upon in writing between the proprietor and the user, and any deviation therefrom, without prior written consent of the proprietor, constitutes a contravention of this Act. Where a dispute arises regarding the scope of permitted use, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for redress. Any person found to be in unauthorized use, despite a prior agreement outlining permitted use, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and the goods bearing the unauthorized use shall be deemed forfeited. The Court may, in addition to the penalty, grant an injunction restraining further unauthorized use.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a license to another person, authorizing that person to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services specified in the license, and such license may be assigned or otherwise transferred. Any permitted use of a registered trade mark by a licensee shall be deemed to be use associated with the registered proprietor, unless the license expressly stipulates otherwise and such stipulation is recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license contains a condition restricting the licensee’s field of use, the permitted use shall be limited to that field, and any use beyond it constitutes an infringement actionable by the proprietor. The proprietor may, by instrument in writing, revoke any license granted under this Act, provided that reasonable notice of such revocation is given to the licensee. Failure to comply with the terms of a license shall be a breach of contract, and remedies may be pursued accordingly. A license may also specify royalty payments or other consideration for the permitted use.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions herein, grant a license or assign the right to use the trade mark to another party, constituting a permitted use, provided that such license or assignment is in writing and specifies the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to the goods, services, geographical area, and duration. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of the scope of permitted use shall be subject to mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon mediator; however, if mediation fails, the aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Where a registered user exceeds the scope of permitted use, the registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining such unauthorized use and claim damages for any loss suffered. A bona fide user prior to registration, as established through evidence presented to the Registrar, shall not be affected by such permitted use.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the Common Regulations pertaining to licensing and assignment, have the right to assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of the trade mark and the goodwill thereof. However, any permitted use of a registered trade mark by a party other than the registered proprietor, or a registered user, shall be deemed a potential infringement unless expressly authorized by a written agreement conforming to the requirements of these regulations. Such agreements shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to, the geographical territory, the duration, and the specific goods or services in relation to which the use is authorized. Any extension of such permitted use beyond the terms stipulated in the agreement requires prior written consent of the trade mark proprietor and may be subject to revised royalty arrangements as determined by mutual agreement. Failure to adhere to these provisions may result in legal remedies as provided herein.

Any person utilizing a registered trade mark under a license, or otherwise obtaining a right to use the mark, shall be deemed a permitted user, subject to the terms and conditions of such license or right. However, such permitted use shall not extend to any manner inconsistent with the quality of goods or services associated with the trade mark, or likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. Where the permitted use involves a creation provided layout—specifically, a pre-existing arrangement of elements—any alteration to that layout without the express written consent of the trade mark proprietor shall constitute a material breach of the terms of permitted use. Any person contravening the provisions of this Act relating to permitted use, or engaging in unauthorized alteration of a creation provided layout, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such contravention, and the Registrar may, in addition, order the destruction of goods bearing the improperly used trade mark.

Any act undertaken concerning a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. A registered proprietor may, subject to the conditions prescribed, assign the registered trade mark, or any right therein, to another person, and such assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Failure to register such assignment within the stipulated timeframe may render the transfer invalid as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark is used by a licensee, the registered proprietor shall exercise reasonable control over the quality of goods or services provided under the license, to ensure consistency with the standards associated with the mark. Any act of use that deviates from such standards, or is undertaken without the express consent of the registered proprietor, may constitute grounds for revocation of the registration. A person claiming rights in a registered act registered must demonstrate continuous and genuine use of the mark.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor of a trade mark, uses in the course of trade, or advertises for the purpose of trade, any colour as a trade mark, or any device or expression which is likely to cause confusion or deception, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered act registered is performed in contravention of any condition entered in the register, the Registrar may, after giving the registered proprietor a reasonable opportunity to be heard, require the rectification of the register. Any application for rectification made under this Act shall be subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Provided that no rectification shall be made which would prejudice the rights of a prior user of a trade mark. Failure to comply with the requirements of the Registrar shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each continuing offence.

A trade mark shall be considered a determining trade mark for the purposes of establishing distinctiveness, where it is capable of distinguishing goods or services of one person from those of another, and is applied for by a proprietor connected in the course of trade with those goods or services. However, a mark consisting exclusively of a descriptive character, or one deceptively similar to a descriptive character, relating to the goods or services themselves, shall not be registrable as a determining trade mark, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. Provided that, such acquired distinctiveness must be demonstrated through evidence of continuous and widespread use over a period not less than five years prior to the date of application. Any mark that is contrary to decency or morality, or scandalous, shall not be considered a determining trade mark under this Act.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive within the meaning of this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and such capacity shall be assessed as at the date of application for registration. However, a mark consisting exclusively of a descriptive character relating to the goods or services, or one that has become customary in the trade, shall not be considered distinctive, unless sufficient use has resulted in public recognition as a trade mark. Where a mark contains matter customary to the trade, registration may be permitted if the mark, as a whole, possesses sufficient distinctiveness. Any person aggrieved by a decision refusing registration on grounds of lack of distinctiveness may, subject to the provisions herein, apply to the Appellate Board for a review of such decision. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence of actual use and public perception in determining whether a mark meets the criteria for registration as a determining trade mark, and may direct the Registrar to register the mark if satisfied.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive, for the purposes of registration under this Act, if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. However, a mark consisting exclusively of descriptive character, or one which is deceptively similar to a descriptive character relating to the character or quality of the goods or services, shall not be considered distinctive unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. Evidence of such acquired distinctiveness shall be admissible, and the Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require evidence of actual use extending over a period of not less than five years. Where a mark comprises both descriptive and non-descriptive elements, the overall impression created on the public shall be considered in determining whether it is a determining trade mark. A mark which is commonly used in the trade to designate the kind of goods or services shall not be registrable, unless it has attained a secondary meaning identifying it with the applicant.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive, as provided herein, if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and shall include shape, colour, or any combination thereof, where such shape or colour acquires distinctiveness through use. Any person claiming to be the owner of a determining trade mark, and alleging infringement by another, shall furnish to the adjudicating officer, within thirty days of notice served, a sworn statement detailing the extent and duration of such use establishing distinctiveness. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the claim inadmissible. Where a mark is not inherently distinctive, evidence of acquired distinctiveness through continuous and substantial use for a period of not less than five years shall be considered. Any false representation concerning the nature, manufacturing process, or characteristics of goods bearing a determining trade mark shall constitute an actionable offence, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine not exceeding two lakh rupees, or both.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under that trade mark, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services in respect of which the goodwill is assigned. However, an assignment of a trade mark without the goodwill shall not confer any right to use the trade mark, and the assignee’s rights shall be limited to receiving royalties as agreed upon in the instrument of assignment. A determining trade mark, being one which distinguishes goods or services of one person from those of others, may be subject to multiple assignments relating to different geographical territories, provided that such limitations are clearly stipulated in the assignment instrument. The Registrar may, upon application, record any such territorial limitations. Any licensing of a trade mark shall be governed by a written agreement outlining the scope, duration, and terms of the license.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive within the meaning of this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, including, but not limited to, marks that may not be inherently distinctive but have acquired distinctiveness through use. The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration, examine it to ascertain whether the trade mark applied for meets the criteria of being a determining trade mark as outlined herein, and shall record such determination. Where a mark consists of descriptive words or geographical names, evidence of acquired distinctiveness, demonstrating that the relevant public recognizes the mark as uniquely identifying the applicant’s goods or services, shall be admissible. Provided that the evidence presented must be substantial and demonstrate continuous use for a period not less than five years prior to the date of application. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require submission of affidavits or other documentary evidence to support claims of acquired distinctiveness. Any determination made by the Registrar regarding the distinctiveness of a trade mark shall be subject to appeal.

A trade mark shall be considered a recognition trade mark if, through extensive use, it has become widely known amongst the relevant public, even without formal registration under this Act. Such recognition need not be universal, but must extend to a significant portion of the class of persons likely to encounter the goods or services associated with the mark. Provided that, evidence of actual recognition, including but not limited to media coverage, sales figures, and consumer surveys, shall be admissible in determining the existence and scope of such recognition. A mark acquiring recognition shall be protected against use by others that is likely to cause confusion or dilution, subject to principles of fair use and honest trade practices as provided herein. The proprietor of a registered trade mark, even if not a recognition trade mark, may seek enhanced remedies in cases of infringement.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be a recognition trade mark if, through extensive use, it has acquired a distinctive character and is readily identifiable by the relevant class of persons as designating goods or services connected with the applicant.
