The Controller of Trade Marks may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence of such use, including but not limited to, documentation of sales figures, advertising expenditure, and market research data demonstrating consumer recognition. Provided that, the mark need not have acquired recognition in the entire territory of India, but substantial recognition within a significant portion thereof shall suffice. An application for registration of a recognition trade mark shall include a statement detailing the nature and extent of use relied upon to establish recognition, and failure to provide such a statement may render the application liable to be refused. The mark must also not be deceptive or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, as determined under this Act.

A trade mark, even if not formally registered, may be recognized as a recognition trade mark under this Act, provided that the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and has acquired substantial reputation in India through consistent and extensive use. The proprietor of a recognition trade mark shall have the right to seek an injunction against any person using a deceptively similar mark, irrespective of whether the defendant’s mark is registered or not. Such injunction may extend to preventing the import of goods bearing the infringing mark, subject to verification by the Customs authorities as per established procedure. Where a registered trade mark conflicts with a recognition trade mark, the registered proprietor shall not be entitled to remedies under this Act to the extent of the established reputation of the recognition trade mark. Any action brought under these provisions shall be subject to a limitation period of three years from the date the plaintiff knew, or ought to have known, of the infringement.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be a recognition trade mark if, through the proprietor’s use of the mark, the public has come to associate it with a specific geographical origin, even where such origin is not the actual place of manufacture or provision of services. The Registrar may, upon application supported by evidence demonstrating substantial and continuous use for a period not less than five years, register a mark as a recognition trade mark, subject to verification of the claimed association. Any person alleging that a trade mark is a recognition trade mark shall furnish proof of extensive advertising and promotional activities directed towards establishing the geographical link in the minds of the relevant public. Provided that, registration as a recognition trade mark does not confer exclusive rights to the geographical name itself, but solely to the use of the mark in connection with goods or services demonstrably linked to that geographical origin as established under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all recognition trade marks, open for public inspection. Any dispute regarding the validity of such registration shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be a recognition trade mark if it is capable of being recognised as distinctive by the relevant public, and has acquired such distinctiveness through the proprietor’s lawful use of the mark. The extent of recognition shall be determined with reference to the class of goods or services in relation to which the mark is used, and may extend to goods or services not falling within that class where a connection exists. However, recognition alone is insufficient; the mark must also be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. Where a mark has been used for a continuous period of not less than five years, a presumption of recognition may arise, subject to evidence to the contrary being presented. Any claim of recognition trade mark status shall be substantiated by evidence of actual use and public perception, as determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require submission of survey data or other relevant materials to assess the level of public recognition.

Any person who uses, in the course of trade, a deceptive or confusingly similar mark in relation to goods or services concerning a recognition trade mark, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such instance of use, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The proprietor of a recognition trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, or an account of profits against any person infringing their rights. Where a defendant proves that the use of the mark was reasonably necessary to identify the origin of the goods or services, or to make a fair comparison, the court may reduce the damages awarded. Any goods found to bear such infringing mark shall be deemed forfeited and may be destroyed as directed by the court. A false representation of a recognition trade mark shall be considered unfair trade practice.

A recognition trade mark, being a mark not fully registered but demonstrably known to the relevant public, shall be subject to the provisions regarding assignment and licensing as if fully registered, provided that the proprietor has filed an application for registration under this Act and such application is pending determination. Any assignment or license of a recognition trade mark shall be in writing and shall specify the geographical area of operation, the goods or services covered, and the duration of the assignment or license. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to reasonable cause being shown, record such assignments and licenses upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to record an assignment or license shall not invalidate it, but such unrecorded assignment or license may not be enforceable against a bona fide purchaser for value. A licensee of a recognition trade mark shall have no right to sub-license without the express written consent of the proprietor, and any such sub-license shall be void ab initio. The proprietor retains the right to revoke a license upon reasonable notice and subject to any terms stipulated in the licensing agreement.

A trade mark, even if not formally registered, may be recognized as a recognition trade mark under this Act, provided that the mark has acquired distinctiveness and goodwill through extensive use in India, sufficient to associate it in the public mind with the applicant. An application for recognition of a recognition trade mark shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating continuous use for a period not less than five years, and shall detail the nature, extent, and geographical scope of such use. Any party opposing the recognition of such a mark shall submit evidence of prior rights or likelihood of confusion, and the Registrar may, subject to due process, require the applicant to demonstrate a dominant presence in the relevant market. The Registrar’s decision regarding recognition may be appealed to the Appellate Board, and such appeal shall be heard within ninety days of the date of the order. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the application.

An order for erasure, also known as an erasure order injunction, may be granted by the court to a registered proprietor of a trademark, subject to the provisions of this Act and the principles of equity. Such an order shall direct a defendant to permanently remove or obliterate any unauthorized reproduction or depiction of the trademark from any article, packaging, or digital medium under their control. Provided that, the court may, at its discretion, limit the scope of the erasure order to specific channels of distribution or geographical areas. Where the defendant demonstrates substantial compliance with the terms of the injunction, the court may modify the order or grant a stay of execution. Any failure to comply with a valid erasure order injunction shall constitute contempt of court and be punishable accordingly, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by the continued online availability of counterfeit goods bearing a registered trade mark, or any material that falsely suggests an association with the trade mark owner, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction. Such application shall be accompanied by due diligence demonstrating reasonable efforts to notify the online platform or intermediary of the infringing content and its location. The Court, upon being satisfied of the genuineness of the trade mark and the prima facie case of infringement, may issue an order directing the online platform or intermediary to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing material. Provided that, the applicant shall furnish an undertaking as to damages, should the Court subsequently find no infringement occurred. The Court may also, as provided herein, direct the applicant to identify the specific URLs or locations of the infringing content to facilitate compliance with the erasure order injunction. Any failure to comply with such order shall be considered contempt of court.

Any person aggrieved by the use of a deceptive or falsely applied trade mark, or by any colourable variation thereof, likely to cause confusion or deception to the public, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction restraining the defendant from such use. The Court, upon being satisfied of the grounds for such application and subject to such terms as it deems fit, shall issue an injunction prohibiting the continued use of the offending mark. Provided that, before issuing such an injunction, the Court may require the applicant to furnish an undertaking as to damages, should the injunction ultimately be found to have been wrongly granted. Furthermore, the Court may, as part of the injunction, direct the defendant to actively erase all instances of the infringing mark from any goods, packaging, or promotional materials within a specified timeframe. Any failure to comply with an erasure order injunction shall be considered contempt of court and subject to appropriate penalties as provided herein. The Court retains discretion to award costs in favour of the prevailing party.

Any person aggrieved by the continued availability online of information infringing their registered trade mark, and who has duly notified the internet intermediary of such infringement as provided herein, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the trade mark registration and proof of prior notification to the intermediary. The Court, upon being satisfied that a prima facie case of infringement exists and that the balance of convenience favours the applicant, may issue an injunction directing the internet intermediary to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing information. Provided that, the intermediary shall not be liable for any failure to comply with such order if it demonstrates that it acted reasonably and without delay. The Court may also, subject to the rules, require the applicant to furnish security for any damages that may be suffered by any person as a result of the order. Any person aggrieved by an erasure order injunction may appeal to the appellate authority established under this Act.

Any registered proprietor aggrieved by the continued online availability of counterfeit goods or services bearing a deceptively similar trade mark, and which infringe their registered trade mark under this Act, may apply to the Court for an erasure order injunction. Such application shall be accompanied by sufficient evidence demonstrating the nature of the infringing material, its online location, and the applicant’s registered trade mark. The Court, upon being satisfied of the prima facie case and the potential for irreparable harm, may issue an ex-parte erasure order injunction directing internet intermediaries to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing content. Provided that, the intermediary shall not be liable for any failure to comply with the order if it demonstrates it acted reasonably and without delay. Any person aggrieved by such an order may apply to the Court for its modification or vacation, subject to notice to the applicant. Compliance with any such order shall be a condition precedent to continued operation of the online platform.

Any person aggrieved by the continued availability of counterfeit goods or the use of a deceptively similar mark online, and demonstrating prima facie a likelihood of confusion, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction. Such injunction shall direct the internet service provider, intermediary, or platform owner to expeditiously remove or disable access to the infringing content, subject to verification of the complaint by the respondent within forty-eight hours. Failure to comply with an erasure order injunction shall constitute contempt of court and attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of non-compliance. Provided that, the applicant shall furnish an undertaking to indemnify the respondent against any loss or damage suffered due to the implementation of the order. The court may, as provided herein, also issue a direction for the destruction of all infringing materials and impose costs on the defendant.

Any person who has lawfully assigned or licensed the right to use a registered trade mark, and who reasonably believes that such right is being infringed by an unauthorized party, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction, directing the alleged infringer to remove or obliterate any material containing the trade mark from any medium, including but not limited to digital platforms and physical goods. Such application shall be accompanied by proof of valid assignment or licensing agreement and a prima facie case of infringement. The Court, if satisfied, may issue an interim order pending a full hearing, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, including the provision of security. Where the infringement relates to goods in transit, the Court may also direct the customs authorities to detain such goods. A licensee, having obtained an erasure order, may further assign the right to enforce said order to another party, provided that the original assignor or licensor retains the ultimate right to control the enforcement proceedings.

Any aggrieved person, claiming ownership of a registered trade mark, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction against any person using a deceptively similar mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Court, upon being satisfied of the likelihood of confusion and irreparable harm, shall issue a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the offending mark pending a full hearing. An application for an erasure order, directing the removal or destruction of all materials bearing the infringing mark, may be granted concurrently with the injunction, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates a reasonable effort to identify and locate such materials. Any order issued under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of the Court. Appeals from any order granting or refusing an erasure order injunction shall lie to the Division Bench of the same High Court, and further appeals may be made to the Supreme Court as per established procedure.

Any person aggrieved by the continued availability of a registered trade mark that falsely represents their goods or services, and which causes demonstrable harm to their reputation or business interests, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction. Such an injunction shall immediately restrain the registered proprietor from further use of the mark and require its removal from all online platforms and promotional materials. Failure to comply with an erasure order injunction shall constitute contempt of court and be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or both. Where the registered proprietor demonstrates substantial grounds for legitimate alteration of the mark, an application for an alteration certificate registration may be considered by the Registrar, subject to due process and payment of the prescribed fee, but shall not suspend the operation of the erasure order injunction pending its determination. Any profits derived from continued use of the mark during the pendency of the injunction shall be recoverable as damages.

Any person aggrieved by the unauthorized reproduction, or use of a registered trade mark, or a deceptively similar mark, in relation to semiconductor integrated circuits, may apply to the High Court for an erasure order injunction restraining such acts. The application shall be accompanied by a verified statement detailing the grounds for the claim and evidence of prior registration of the trade mark. Provided that, the court may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the applicant to furnish security for costs. An appeal from any order granting or refusing such an injunction shall lie to the Division Bench of the same High Court. The court, while considering the application, shall have due regard to the potential damage to the applicant’s reputation and the extent of the unauthorized use. Furthermore, the court may order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark, as provided herein, and direct the respondent to cease all related activities.

Any person aggrieved by the continued availability of a registered trade mark which falsely suggests an endorsement by, or association with, a registered geographical indication, or which otherwise misleads the public as to the origin or quality of goods, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for an erasure order injunction. The application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating the likelihood of confusion and potential damage to the reputation of the geographical indication. The Registry, upon verification and subject to such conditions as it deems appropriate, may issue an order directing the removal of the trade mark from the register and prohibiting further use. Where the aggrieved party is a registered association of producers of the geographical indication, or the Farmers Rights Authority established under the Agricultural Produce Marketing Act, such application shall be given priority consideration. Any party against whom an erasure order injunction is issued may appeal to the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by the continued availability online of trade mark infringements, or material falsely representing association with a registered trade mark, may apply to the Court for an erasure order injunction. Such an injunction shall direct an intermediary, including but not limited to internet service providers and social media platforms, to prevent access to the infringing content. The Court may grant such injunction upon being satisfied that a prima facie case of infringement exists and that the continued availability of the content causes irreparable harm to the trade mark owner. Where the application relates to a clause invention relating to a novel process or product falsely advertised under the registered trade mark, the Court shall consider the potential for market disruption. Provided that the intermediary acts diligently in removing or disabling access to the content upon receiving actual notice of the infringement, it shall not be held liable for any subsequent re-publication. The Court may, subject to the principles of natural justice, issue an interim erasure order pending a full hearing.

The application registration shall be deemed complete only upon the Registrar receiving all requisite documents and fees as prescribed under the relevant rules. An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication must demonstrate a clear link between the goods and the geographical area of origin, substantiated by evidence acceptable to the Board. Such evidence may include historical records, traditional knowledge, or scientific data establishing the unique characteristics attributable to the place. Provided that, where a producers’ association exists, the application for registration may be filed collectively on behalf of its members. Subject to verification, the Registrar may, at their discretion, request additional information or clarification from the applicant to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. Any incomplete application shall be liable to rejection.

Any applicant seeking application registration shall furnish a detailed representation of the geographical area constituting the origin of the goods, demonstrating a clear and consistent link between the goods’ qualities, reputation, or other characteristics and that geographical origin. The Registrar, upon receiving such application, may require further evidence to substantiate the claimed geographical indication and its nexus with the goods. Provided that, if the application is found deficient, the Registrar shall communicate the deficiencies to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days for rectification. An authorised user, upon successful application registration, acquires the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in the registered class, subject to continued adherence to the specified standards and conditions. Any infringement of this right, as provided herein, shall be actionable under the remedies outlined in this Act, including injunctions, damages, and delivery up of infringing goods. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all authorised users, accessible for inspection during office hours.

An application for registration shall be presented to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by a statement of proposed use of the geographical indication, specifying the goods in relation to which the registration is sought. The applicant shall, as part of the application, furnish a detailed description of the characteristics of the goods, including the qualities, reputation, or other attributes that are attributable to their geographical origin. Where the applicant is not the sole producer, evidence of consent from other producers within the defined geographical area must be submitted, demonstrating a collective interest in maintaining the standards associated with the indication. 

The Registry may, subject to verification of the particulars furnished, require the applicant to provide further information or clarification. Any misrepresentation or false statement made within the application registration shall render the application liable to be rejected, and may further attract penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall, upon satisfaction of the requirements, proceed to examine the application.

Any application for registration of a geographical indication shall be presented in triplicate to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed, and shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the items for which the geographical indication is sought, along with a clear and concise description of the goods, their qualities, and the geographical area to which they relate. The applicant shall also furnish a statement of use, demonstrating current use of the geographical indication for those goods. Where the application concerns a multi-state geographical area, evidence of consensus or no-objection certificates from the relevant state governments shall be mandatory. Provided that, the Registrar may, subject to satisfactory justification, waive the requirement of triplicate submissions in exceptional circumstances. All fees associated with the application registration shall be remitted as per the prescribed schedule, and failure to do so may render the application incomplete. The Registrar shall, upon receipt, examine the application for compliance with the provisions of this Act.

Any person possessing a valid license for the use of a registered geographical indication, granted under this Act, may apply to the Registrar for assignment of such license to another eligible party, subject to the terms and conditions originally stipulated in the licensing agreement and any subsequent amendments thereto duly recorded with the Registry. The application for assignment shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a certified copy of the original license agreement, a no-objection certificate from the original licensor, and evidence demonstrating the assignee’s capacity to utilize the geographical indication in accordance with the established standards of production and quality. Application registration shall be completed within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of a complete application, failing which the Registrar shall provide a reasoned explanation for the delay. Provided that, the Registrar may reject the application if the proposed assignment is deemed detrimental to the reputation or quality of the geographical indication, or if the assignee fails to meet the eligibility criteria as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity of the assignment may be referred to the appropriate court.

Any applicant seeking application registration shall furnish a detailed representation of the geographical area constituting the origin of the goods, accompanied by a special trust or association of producers, demonstrably representing the majority interest within that area. Should the Registrar deem the application incomplete or lacking sufficient evidence of origin, a notice specifying the deficiencies shall be issued, allowing the applicant sixty days to rectify the same. Failure to comply within this period may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. However, a concurrent objection filed by a party claiming prior and continuous use of a similar mark, even if unregistered, may suspend the registration process pending resolution of the conflicting claims. The Appellate Board’s decision regarding such objections shall be final and binding, provided that the objection is demonstrably bona fide and not merely to delay legitimate application registration. Any appeal to the Board requires a prescribed fee and adherence to procedural rules as provided herein.

The application registration shall be subject to a review of the applicant’s demonstrable connection to the geographical area and the goods specified in the indication, as provided herein. Any collective or association of producers, or in the absence thereof, a primary producer—including a farmer cultivating the land yielding the goods—may submit an application for registration as an authorised user. The Registrar may, upon satisfactory verification of the application and payment of the prescribed fee, grant registration. A registered authorised user shall have the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in the specified region. Transfer of registration rights, or assignment thereof, requires prior written consent of the Registrar and adherence to established guidelines concerning continued quality control. Licensing agreements must be recorded with the Geographical Indications Registry, detailing the scope of permitted use and royalty arrangements, and shall be open to inspection by interested parties. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of registration.

The application registration shall be subject to a prior examination conducted by the Registrar to ascertain the veracity of claims regarding origin and adherence to established standards for the geographical indication as provided herein. Any objection raised by a party alleging prior and continuous use of a similar mark, or a conflicting geographical indication, shall be duly considered and a reasoned order issued within ninety days of the submission of such objection. Should the Registrar reject the application, an appeal may be preferred to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and deposits a security with the Board equivalent to the prescribed registration fee. Security India relates to the protection of national interests and the Board shall prioritize appeals concerning goods vital to national security or public health. Failure to comply with timelines established under this Act may constitute grounds for dismissal of the application or appeal.

The application registration shall be subject to a verification process conducted by the Registrar, ensuring adherence to the criteria as provided herein. An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication must demonstrate a clear connection between the goods, their origin, and the qualities or reputation attributable to that origin. The creation provided layout of the application form, as prescribed, shall include details of the geographical area, the characteristics of the goods, and evidence establishing a consistent link between the goods and their geographical origin. Provided that, the Registrar may require further evidence or clarification if the initial application is deemed insufficient, and may reject the application if the submitted information does not satisfy the requirements of this Act. Any registered geographical indication shall confer exclusive rights to the authorized users.

Registration shall apply to geographical indications of goods originating from a specific geographical area, where a quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin, and which has been determined as conforming to standards established under this Act. The Registrar, upon receiving an application and being satisfied that the goods meet the criteria as provided herein, may enter the particulars of the applicant in the Register of Geographical Indications. Such registration confers upon the applicant the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to those goods, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the code of practice established for the relevant geographical indication. Any alteration to the registered geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, and failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registration.

Any application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the Geographical Indications Registry as provided herein, and such examination shall be completed within a period of eighteen months from the date of the application, subject to the applicant fulfilling all requirements regarding documentation and fees. Registration shall apply to goods originating from a defined geographical area and possessing qualities or a reputation linked to that origin, and no registration shall be granted if the indication is likely to mislead the public or is contrary to public order or morality. The Registrar may, prior to accepting an application, require the applicant to provide a clear definition of the geographical area and a detailed specification of the goods. Provided that, where a prior right exists, the Registrar shall consider such right during the examination process and may require the applicant to obtain necessary consents. The register of geographical indications maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication, or by any act likely to cause such infringement, may institute civil proceedings in a court of competent jurisdiction as provided herein. Where a plaintiff successfully establishes infringement, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from the further unlawful use of the geographical indication, and may also award damages to compensate for any loss suffered by the plaintiff as a result of the infringement. Registration shall apply to the specific goods in respect of which it is granted and shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to those goods. However, honest local use of a geographical indication, prior to the filing of an application for registration, shall not be considered infringement, provided that such use does not mislead the public or cause confusion. The court may, in its discretion, also order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication. Any order for damages may consider the profits unlawfully made by the defendant.

Any application for the registration of a geographical indication shall be examined by the Registrar, and such examination shall be conducted as provided herein, with due regard to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the goods meet the criteria for registration, and that the application complies with all procedural requirements, the geographical indication shall be registered in the Register. Registration shall apply to the goods originating from a defined geographical area and possessing qualities or a reputation linked to that origin, and no registration shall be granted if it is likely to mislead the public or be contrary to public order or morality. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the applicant to furnish further evidence or clarification regarding the geographical area, the qualities of the goods, or the link to their origin. A register of geographical indications shall be maintained, open to inspection by interested parties upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration to the registered geographical indication shall require a separate application and be subject to the same scrutiny as the original registration.

Registration shall apply to all goods originating from a defined geographical area where a feature or quality of the product is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and possesses a reputation or character associated with that area. An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication must demonstrate a clear link between the goods, their origin, and the qualities or reputation claimed, substantiated by verifiable evidence as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to verification of such evidence, register the geographical indication in the Register, specifying the goods, the geographical area, and the standards applicable. Provided that, registration is contingent upon the applicant establishing a recognized association of producers or an entity capable of maintaining and enforcing the standards of the geographical indication. Failure to adhere to these standards post-registration may result in suspension or revocation of the registration, as determined by the Registrar following due process and consideration of representations. Any alteration to the defined geographical area shall require prior approval.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely represents goods as possessing a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of the falsely marked goods. Where an offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable for the penalties as provided herein. Registration shall apply to all goods falling within the scope of the registered geographical indication and any unauthorized use constitutes a violation.

Any person being a producer of goods registered under this Act, desiring to grant a license or assign the right to use the geographical indication associated with said goods, shall submit a notice of intention to the Registrar. Such notice shall clearly delineate the terms and conditions proposed for the license or assignment, including the territory, duration, and scope of permitted use. Registration shall apply to all licenses and assignments recorded with the Registrar, providing a public record of authorized users and preventing unauthorized exploitation of the geographical indication. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the applicant’s status as a registered producer and confirmation that the proposed terms do not unduly restrict legitimate competition, approve the license or assignment. Provided that, any assignment without prior notice and registration shall be considered a contravention of this Act and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all licensed and assigned rights, accessible for public inspection.

Any objection to the registration of a geographical indication shall be filed with the Geographical Indications Registry within a period of three months from the date of notification of the application for registration, provided that the Registrar may, for sufficient cause, extend this period not exceeding one month. Where an objection is filed, the applicant for registration shall be entitled to file a counter-statement within one month of the receipt of the objection. The Registrar, having considered the objection and the counter-statement, if any, shall conduct an examination and may require further evidence from either party. Registration shall apply only to those goods which meet the standards and quality requirements as specified in the register and as determined by the competent authority. Any dispute regarding the authenticity or origin of goods bearing a registered geographical indication may be referred to the Appellate Board established under this Act, whose decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review.

Registration shall apply to a geographical indication which, under the law of the country of origin, is protected as a geographical indication and is also a well-known mark registered trade in that country, provided that the applicant demonstrates a substantial connection between the goods and the geographical area of origin. Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication aggrieved by any infringement of such geographical indication, or by any act likely to cause confusion, shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for relief. Such relief may include an injunction restraining the infringement, damages, or an account of profits. Where a registered geographical indication is used by a person other than the registered proprietor without authorization, the court may, at the request of the registered proprietor, order the destruction or obliteration of all materials bearing the unauthorized geographical indication. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and authorized users thereof, facilitating transparency and preventing unfair competition.

Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision refusing an application for registration of a geographical indication, or rejecting a statement of proposed use as an authorised user, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and considering the evidence presented, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an application for registration is refused due to a lack of proper documentation establishing origin or quality, the Appellate Board may direct the applicant to submit additional evidence, provided that such evidence is submitted within a timeframe stipulated by the Board. A finding of the Appellate Board regarding the status of an application registrati authorised shall be final and binding, except where grounds of fraud are demonstrably proven before a court of competent jurisdiction.

Registration shall confer upon the applicant, subject to the provisions of this Act, the exclusive right to the use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application and verification of the particulars therein, register the applicant as the proprietor of the geographical indication. Provided that registration shall not prevent other producers in the geographical area from using the traditional methods and techniques associated with the goods, so long as such use does not mislead the public as to the source or origin of the goods. Any association of producers may, with the consent of the producers, apply for registration as a collective user, and the registration shall vest in the association. The registered proprietor may maintain an index of authorised users.

Registration of a geographical indication shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any association of producers, or a cooperative society, or any other legal entity representing the producers of the goods, may jointly apply for the registration of a geographical indication as provided herein. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration, conduct a thorough examination to ascertain the veracity of the claim and the goods’ origin. Provided that, registration shall not prevent other producers from using descriptive terms commonly used in trade, but such use shall not infringe upon the registered geographical indication’s distinctiveness. The Registrar may, after considering the examination report and any objections received, register the geographical indication, and a certificate of registration shall be issued. Any alteration to the registered geographical indication shall require a separate application and subsequent registration.

Registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered, and to seek legal recourse against any unauthorized use of that indication by any other person. Any person dealing in goods bearing a falsely applied geographical indication, or in goods which are a colourable imitation thereof, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty as may be prescribed. The registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil or criminal proceedings for infringement of their rights. Where a dispute arises concerning the authenticity or origin of goods bearing a registered geographical indication, the Court may, at the request of the registered proprietor, order an inspection of the premises where such goods are manufactured or processed. Provided that, the Court may also appoint a commissioner to examine and report on the matter, and the expenses of such commissioner shall be borne by the party requesting the inspection. The Registrar may maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and authorised users, accessible for inspection during office hours.

Registration shall be effected in the Register of Geographical Indications maintained by the Registrar, and such registration shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to the use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. Any association of producers, or any enterprise engaged in the production of goods identified with a geographical indication, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration. The application for registration shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a statement of case outlining the geographical area, qualities, and reputation of the goods, and evidence establishing such qualities and reputation. Provided that, where the applicant is an association, it shall demonstrate that it represents a substantial majority of the producers within the identified geographical area. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary, and shall examine the application to ensure compliance with the criteria as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application.

Registration shall be subject to the applicant demonstrating a clear and unequivocal link between the specified goods and the geographical area of origin, substantiated by evidence acceptable to the Registrar. Provided that, where the goods undergo processing, a substantial portion of such processing shall occur within the defined geographical area to maintain the inherent qualities and characteristics associated with the geographical indication. Any association, firm, or body of producers seeking registration as an authorized user must furnish proof of legitimate and continuous production of the goods within the specified region for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require inspection of production facilities to verify compliance with these requirements as provided herein. Failure to maintain the standards of quality and origin, or any misrepresentation thereof, may result in suspension or cancellation of registration.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely applies a geographical indication registered under this Act to goods not originating in the region to which such indication relates, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of the goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Registration shall not be granted if the geographical indication is likely to cause confusion with a previously registered trade mark or geographical indication, and the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require the applicant to obtain a no-objection certificate from the owner of such trade mark or geographical indication. Any appeal under this Act shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against.

Any person being a producer of goods possessing a registered geographical indication, desiring to grant a license to another for use of said indication, shall execute an instrument of license in writing, specifying the scope of the license, including the area of operation, the quality standards to be maintained, and the duration for which the license remains valid. Registration of such license with the Registrar, as provided herein, shall be compulsory and shall confer upon the licensee the right to use the geographical indication subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license and the provisions of this Act. Failure to register the license may render it unenforceable against third parties. Assignment of the license shall require prior written consent of the geographical indication’s owner, and the Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered licenses and assignments. Provided that, the owner of the geographical indication shall retain the right to revoke the license upon demonstrable breach of quality standards or terms of the agreement. Registration shall be deemed complete upon confirmation by the Registrar and payment of the prescribed fee.

Registration shall be subject to a rigorous examination conducted by the Geographical Indications Registry to ascertain the veracity of the claim concerning origin and the inherent qualities attributable to that geographical origin. Any objection to an application for registration, alleging lack of distinctiveness or misrepresentation, shall be filed with the Registry within a period of four months from the date of notification of the application in the Journal. The applicant, upon receipt of such objection, may file a counter-statement within two months, detailing evidence supporting the geographical indication’s unique characteristics. Should the Registrar deem the objection well-founded, registration shall be refused, and the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. However, a failure to respond to the objection within the stipulated timeframe shall be considered an abandonment of the application, and the Registry may proceed to close the file, subject to a final notice of thirty days.

Registration shall confer upon the applicant, subject to the provisions of this Act, the exclusive right to the use of the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered, and to seek legal recourse against any infringement of that right. Any person aggrieved by the use of a registered geographical indication not by an authorised user, may apply to the Trade Mark Registrar for an injunction restraining such use, and the Registrar may, after such inquiry as he deems fit, grant the injunction if satisfied that the use constitutes an infringement. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted unless the aggrieved party demonstrates a substantial connection to the geographical region and proves actual damage or likelihood of damage resulting from the unauthorized use. The Trade Mark Registrar, in considering any application for an injunction, may require the applicant to furnish security for costs, and shall issue its order within ninety days of the application. Any appeal against the decision of the Trade Mark Registrar shall lie before the High Court.

Registration shall be granted for a geographical indication of goods identifying those goods as originating from a specific geographical area and possessing qualities or a reputation attributable to that origin, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, registration ought effected only where the applicant demonstrates a demonstrable link between the goods’ characteristics and the geographical area, substantiated by evidence acceptable to the Registrar. Any objection to an application for registration, alleging lack of such link or prior public domain use of the indication for dissimilar goods, shall be adjudicated by the Appellate Board, whose decision shall be final and binding, save for errors apparent on the face of the record. A registered proprietor may, upon sufficient cause shown and with the Registrar’s approval, relinquish their registration, and the indication shall revert to the public domain. Disputes regarding concurrent registrations for similar goods shall be resolved through mediation, failing which, recourse lies with the Appellate Board.

The Appellate Geographical Indications Board, having considered the petition filed by the Darjeeling Planters’ Association against M/s. Himalayan Brew, hereby directs a temporary order injunction restraining the latter from manufacturing, selling, or otherwise dealing in tea products bearing the designation “Darjeeling” where such tea does not originate from the registered geographical indication area. This order is subject to the petitioner furnishing security, as determined by the Registrar, to cover potential damages should the injunction be ultimately discharged. M/s. Himalayan Brew, in its counter-affidavit, argued that its use of “Darjeeling” was merely descriptive of the flavour profile and not an attempt to mislead consumers; however, the Board finds this contention unsustainable given the established reputation and specific origin linked to the geographical indication. Any violation of this order shall be punishable as contempt of the Board, and further, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register as provided herein. The Board reserves the right to modify or dissolve this injunction pending a full hearing on the merits.

An alteration certificate registration shall be granted where the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design seeks to record any modification to the original layout-design, subject to the conditions as provided herein. The applicant shall submit a request accompanied by the prescribed fee and a clear depiction of the alterations made, demonstrating that such alterations do not fundamentally change the essential characteristics of the registered layout-design. Where the alteration involves a transfer of rights, evidence of such transfer, including a duly executed assignment deed, shall be furnished. The Registrar may, prior to granting the alteration certificate, require a statement verifying that the alterations do not infringe any existing intellectual property rights. The certificate, once issued, shall be evidence of the recorded alteration and shall be maintained as part of the original registration record.

Any person seeking to effect an alteration to a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit an application to the Controller of Designs in the manner as prescribed. The application for an alteration certificate registration shall clearly identify the layout-design to be altered and specify the nature of the alteration proposed, accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receipt of such application and verification of its completeness, the Controller may, if satisfied that the alteration does not fundamentally affect the original layout-design’s inherent characteristics, register the alteration and issue a certificate of registration for the altered layout-design. Provided that, if the alteration is substantial and creates a new layout-design, a fresh application for registration as per the provisions of this Act shall be required. The Controller shall maintain a register of all alterations and certificates issued, accessible for public inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any aggrieved party may, within a period of thirty days from the date of registration of the alteration, file a petition for review before the Controller.

Any person seeking an alteration certificate registration relating to a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a petition to the Controller, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a statement detailing the nature of the proposed alteration. The Controller may, subject to verification of the accuracy of the statement and satisfaction that the alteration does not fundamentally affect the original layout-design’s essential characteristics, grant the alteration certificate. Provided that, if the alteration involves a transfer of rights, evidence of valid assignment or licensing agreement, duly executed by all relevant parties, shall be furnished. The Controller shall maintain a register of all alterations and may, where the alteration significantly impacts the scope of protection, require a revised layout-design to be filed. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the application for alteration certificate registration liable to rejection, and the applicant may be required to submit a fresh application. Any aggrieved party may, within sixty days of the grant of an alteration certificate, file a petition for review.

Any person seeking to commercially exploit a layout-design that embodies an alteration of a registered layout-design shall, prior to such exploitation, apply to the Controller of Patents and Designs for an alteration certificate registration. The application shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the nature of the alteration, a comparison demonstrating how the altered layout-design differs from the original registered layout-design, and the prescribed fee. Should the Controller be satisfied that the alteration is substantial and does not invalidate the original registration, an alteration certificate shall be issued. Assignment of rights in an alteration certificate is permissible, subject to a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and filed with the Controller. A license to exploit a layout-design incorporating a registered alteration may be granted, and such license shall specify the scope of permitted exploitation and any applicable royalty terms. Failure to obtain the requisite alteration certificate prior to commercial exploitation renders such exploitation an infringement as provided herein. The registered proprietor of the original layout-design retains rights over the base design, even after an alteration certificate is granted.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing an alteration certificate registration, or requiring an amendment to an application for such registration, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the appellant has a prima facie case and that substantial grounds exist for an appeal, direct the Registrar to reconsider the application for alteration, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit. Where the Registrar, following such direction, continues to refuse registration, the Appellate Board shall, after hearing both parties, pass a final order confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the Registrar, and such order shall be binding. Any claim of prior art relating to the proposed alteration shall be considered during the appeal process, and the burden of proof regarding such prior art shall lie with the opposing party.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing an alteration certificate registration relating to a registered layout-design, or requiring an amendment to an application for such registration, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to errors apparent on the record and shall not extend to a re-evaluation of the merits of the original application. A proprietor registered layout, having demonstrated sufficient grounds for alteration, shall be entitled to a reasoned order from the Registrar, and any failure to provide such reasoning constitutes grounds for appeal. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend the time for filing an appeal if it is satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the rights of appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “Right Management Information” shall mean information conveyed in relation to a copyrighted work, including but not limited to the title of the work, the author, the copyright owner, the terms and conditions for making or distributing the work, and any identifying numbers or codes associated with the work. Such information may be embedded in the work itself, or accompany it in a manner reasonably likely to be perceived by the user. A copyright owner may designate an agent for the receipt of notices regarding infringement, and such agency details shall constitute Right Management Information. Any alteration, deletion, or falsification of Right Management Information, where done with the intent to deceive or facilitate infringement, shall be a violation as provided herein, subject to the remedies outlined elsewhere in this Act.

Any copyright owner intending to commercially exploit a work, whether literary, dramatic, musical or artistic, shall register the associated right management information with the designated National Registry. Such registration shall include details of the author, the first publication date, the nature of the rights licensed, and the duration of the license. The Registry may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, issue a digital certificate of registration, which shall serve as prima facie evidence of the copyright owner’s claim. Failure to register right management information shall not invalidate the copyright itself, but may limit the remedies available to the copyright owner in cases of infringement, particularly concerning digital works. A designated officer may, however, require such information as a condition of enforcing rights under this Act. The Registry shall maintain a publicly accessible database of registered right management information, ensuring compliance with privacy regulations.

Any person who creates a copyrighted work shall have the right to associate and communicate Right Management Information with such work, and such information shall include, but not be limited to, the identity of the author, the title of the work, and the terms and conditions governing its use. Any alteration, suppression, or removal of such Right Management Information by any person, without the express authorization of the rights holder, shall constitute a violation of this Act. A rights holder, upon discovering such unauthorized modification, may issue a notice to the infringing party demanding immediate restoration of the information or cessation of further distribution. Failure to comply with such notice within thirty days shall render the infringing party liable to pay damages, assessed at a sum not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of infringement, as determined by a civil court. Provided that, if the alteration was made inadvertently and the infringing party promptly rectifies the error, no damages shall be levied. The remedies provided herein are in addition to any other rights or remedies available to the rights holder under this Act or any other law for the time being in force.

Any copyright owner may affix or cause to be affixed to a copy of a work, or to a device through which a work is accessed, right management information, being data electronically associated with the copy or device, identifying the work, the author, the copyright owner, and terms and conditions for its use. Such information shall be sufficient to identify the work and shall not unduly restrict access to it. A collective management organisation, duly registered under this Act, may also affix such information on behalf of its members, subject to a written mandate from each member. Where right management information is removed or altered without full and accurate restoration, or where such information is intentionally concealed to facilitate infringement, the copyright owner may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining any further infringement. Any person who distributes or imports for distribution material containing right management information known to have been altered without authority shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed.

Any copyright owner intending to commercially exploit a work shall ensure the persistent association of Right Management Information with the digital copy of said work. Such information shall include, but not be limited to, the title of the work, the name of the author or authors, the name of the copyright owner, the year of first publication, and the International Standard Book Number where applicable. Any alteration, deletion, or suppression of this Right Management Information, whether intentional or resulting from negligent acts, shall constitute a violation of this Act, subject to penalties as provided herein. A service provider hosting such content shall, upon actual knowledge of such violation, promptly remove or disable access to the infringing material. However, such removal shall not prejudice the copyright owner’s right to pursue other remedies available under the law, including claims for damages and injunctive relief. The copyright owner bears the initial burden of proving the authenticity of the Right Management Information.

Any person who removes or alters any right management information, whether electronic or otherwise, accompanying a copyrighted work, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, provided that such information was lawfully affixed to the work by the copyright owner or with their authorization. The removal or alteration shall constitute a violation irrespective of intent, though the penalty imposed may vary based on demonstrable commercial prejudice to the copyright holder. Any distribution, importation, or communication to the public of a copyrighted work with such altered or removed right management information shall be treated as a separate and distinct offence. A court may, subject to the provisions herein, order the confiscation of devices used in the commission of such offences and impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Repeat offenders shall be liable to enhanced penalties.

Any copyright owner may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the right to communicate to the public any work, and any such assignment or license shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor or licensor. Where a copyright owner provides digital content incorporating Right Management Information, such information shall be sufficient to identify the work, the author, the copyright owner, and the terms and conditions governing its use. An assignment of copyright shall not operate to divest the assignor of the right to receive royalties or other consideration in respect of any use of the work after the assignment, unless expressly provided in the instrument of assignment. A licensee may, with the prior written consent of the copyright owner, sub-license its rights, provided that the terms of such sub-license are consistent with the original license. Failure to preserve intact Right Management Information, where reasonably practicable, shall be deemed a violation of the rights conferred under this Act, and may attract appropriate remedies.

Any person who publishes a work, or authorizes a publication of a work, shall conspicuously include right management information as prescribed, failing which such act shall be deemed a violation of the author’s exclusive rights as provided herein. Disputes regarding the accuracy or completeness of such right management information, including claims of deliberate misrepresentation, may be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. An aggrieved party, alleging insufficient or inaccurate right management information, shall first serve a notice of grievance to the publisher, allowing fourteen days for rectification prior to initiating legal proceedings. Should the publisher fail to rectify the information to the satisfaction of the aggrieved party, the latter may seek injunctive relief and damages. However, a publisher acting in good faith and demonstrating reasonable efforts to ascertain correct right management information shall not be liable for incidental damages. The burden of proof regarding good faith shall rest with the publisher, and appeals from the High Court shall lie with the Supreme Court.

Any person who removes or alters any right management information accompanying a copyrighted work, knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that such removal or alteration will induce, enable, facilitate or conceal infringement, shall be liable for damages as determined by the Court. However, this provision shall not apply to the lawful distribution of copies of the work, or to any act done solely for the purpose of providing access to the work, provided that such access does not circumvent any technological measures protecting the work. Where a validly licensed exclusive licensee demonstrates to the Court that the removal or alteration of right management information has materially prejudiced their ability to exercise rights granted under the license, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the offending party. Any appeal against an order of damages or injunction shall lie before the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The burden of proving lawful distribution or access rests with the accused.

In this Act, “Right Management Information” shall mean information conveyed in relation to a work, a performance, or a phonogram, including but not limited to the title of the work, the name of the author or performer, the owner of the rights in the work, the terms and conditions for making the work available, and any identifying numbers or codes associated with such rights. Such information may be embedded in a digital file or communicated through metadata. Where a work is subject to a registrar index registered under this Act, the information contained within that index shall be considered authoritative Right Management Information, unless proven otherwise. Any alteration, suppression, or misrepresentation of Right Management Information, undertaken with knowledge of its inaccuracy, shall be a violation as provided herein.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, serve a notice of intention to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing the grounds for the claim and specifying the trade mark in question. Such notice shall allow the alleged infringer a period of thirty days to demonstrate that their use does not constitute infringement, or to propose a settlement. Failure to serve such notice, or to adequately detail the grounds of the claim therein, may be considered by the adjudicating authority as a procedural irregularity impacting the merits of the case. However, this requirement shall not apply where the infringement is flagrant or malicious, and immediate injunctive relief is sought. Any decision regarding alleged infringement registered may be appealed to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and further to the Supreme Court upon points of law of general public importance. The burden of proving non-infringement shall rest with the defendant.

For the purposes of this Act, the expression “Patent Cooperation Treaty” shall denote the agreement concluded at Washington on the nineteenth day of June, nineteen seventy, as subsequently revised and amended, and any regulations issued thereunder, establishing a unified procedure for filing patent applications internationally. A national phase application, as provided herein, refers to the entry of an international application originating under the Patent Cooperation Treaty into the national phase before the Indian Patent Office. Subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, an applicant may elect to pursue protection for an invention through the aforementioned Treaty. The International Bureau’s functions, as defined within the Treaty, shall be recognized for procedural matters relating to international applications.

Any application for a patent claiming priority from a national filing under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall be processed in accordance with the procedure as prescribed under the relevant regulations. An applicant seeking national phase entry under the Treaty shall file a demand for national phase with the Controller within thirty months from the priority date, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a translation of the international search report and the international preliminary examination report, if any. The Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish any additional document or information deemed necessary for the processing of the application. Failure to comply with these requirements within a period of sixty days from the date of such requirement may be considered grounds for abandonment of the application, provided that an extension of time may be granted at the discretion of the Controller upon sufficient cause being shown. All communications regarding such applications shall be addressed to the Controller as provided herein.

Any applicant filing an international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall, upon request and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, be entitled to claim a priority date based on a corresponding Indian patent application filed within the preceding twelve months. Provided that such claim of priority shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the earlier Indian application as evidence of its filing date. Where a national phase application, designating India, is filed pursuant to a completed international search report and written opinion, the Controller of Patents may, subject to the provisions of this Act, expedite the examination process. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the International Searching Authority or the International Preliminary Examining Authority may, within ninety days of the communication of such decision, lodge an appeal with the High Court. The High Court shall have the jurisdiction to review such decisions and may, after considering the evidence, affirm, modify, or reverse the same, subject to the principles of natural justice and the provisions of the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the application vulnerable to rejection.

Any application for a patent, claiming priority from a previously filed international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be processed in accordance with the regulations prescribed herein, subject to the provisions of the Treaty itself. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the international application, along with a declaration verifying its authenticity and completeness, within a period not exceeding sixteen months from the date of filing the said international application. Where the international search report and written opinion are unfavorable, the applicant may, within the prescribed timeframe, submit arguments or amended claims to address the objections raised therein. The Controller of Patents, upon receiving such submissions, shall conduct a further examination to determine the patentability of the invention. Should the applicant fail to comply with the procedural requirements as stipulated in this Act or the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the application may be deemed abandoned, provided that an opportunity for rectification is granted subject to payment of the prescribed fees. Any dispute regarding interpretation of the Treaty shall be resolved in accordance with the administrative instructions issued by the International Bureau of WIPO.

Any application for a patent claiming priority from a national filing under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the priority document as prescribed, and shall comply with the requirements of the receiving Office as designated under the Treaty. An applicant intending to proceed with national phase applications following an international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall furnish a demand for national phase within the prescribed time limit, failing which the international application shall be deemed withdrawn in respect of this country. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Controller of Patents may, at his discretion, extend the time for furnishing the demand if sufficient cause is shown. All communications relating to the international application, including the international search report and written opinion, shall be submitted to the designated national office in the manner prescribed. Compliance with the requirements of the Patent Cooperation Treaty, as amended, is mandatory for all international applications seeking national protection herein.

Any Indian national or resident, intending to seek protection for an invention under this Act, shall, if desiring to file an international application, do so in accordance with the provisions of the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as stipulated within the Treaty, or as further clarified by notifications issued by the Controller of Patents, shall render the international application liable to be deemed withdrawn, and no rights shall accrue to the applicant. Any person found to have knowingly provided false information in relation to the priority date claimed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Controller may, subject to established guidelines, require supplementary information to verify the authenticity of any declaration submitted pursuant to the Treaty, and non-compliance with such a request will attract a penalty of ₹50,000.

Any assignment of a patent application filed under this Act, or of a patent granted under this Act, shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. An applicant intending to seek protection for an invention under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall file an international application in the prescribed manner, and such application shall be treated as equivalent to a corresponding national application filed on the international filing date. Where an international application designating India is filed, the applicant may, within the prescribed period, furnish a translation of the international application and any necessary supporting documents if the application is not filed in an official language of India. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, grant a license to another person to work the invention if the patentee fails to adequately exploit the patented invention within a period of three years from the date of grant. Any assignment not registered shall be invalid as against any subsequent assignee or any person deriving title under them.

Any applicant seeking a patent for an invention based on an international application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to proceed with national phase entry before the Controller of Patents. However, such entitlement shall be contingent upon the applicant demonstrating, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that the requirements of Chapter VI pertaining to amendments have been duly observed in relation to the international application as filed. Should the applicant fail to adequately address any objections raised by the Controller concerning said amendments, an appeal may be preferred to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition before the High Court on grounds of manifest error or jurisdictional excess. Furthermore, any claim of priority under the Patent Cooperation Treaty must be accompanied by a certified copy of the priority document, failing which the application shall be deemed abandoned.

Any applicant seeking a patent based on an international application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty shall, upon receiving notification of international preliminary examination, furnish to the Controller a verified statement as to the fulfillment of all requirements of this Act.
