Should any person, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the complete specification, lodge a notice of opposition with the opposition registration registrar alleging lack of novelty or inventive step, the Controller shall, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, determine the validity of the patent. A failure to comply with the requirements of this Act, or a successful opposition, may result in the rejection of the application or the revocation of a granted patent, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. The Controller may, provided that reasonable cause is shown, extend the time for filing the verified statement. Any fees associated with opposition proceedings shall be governed by the Schedule to this Act.

The Controller of Designs may, subject to the provisions of this Act, refuse to register a design if it is deemed to be contrary to public order or morality. A design application shall be considered to impact the security of India where its features, if implemented, could reasonably be utilized to the detriment of national defense, strategic interests, or public safety. Provided that, such determination regarding security india relates shall be made in consultation with such governmental authority as may be designated by the Central Government for this purpose. The Controller may require an applicant to submit evidence substantiating the non-prejudicial nature of the design, and failure to do so may result in refusal of registration. Any design found to compromise national security, even after registration, may be cancelled as provided herein.

Any design incorporating features fundamentally connected with, or essential for, the security of India shall not be registrable under this Act, and any application for such a design shall be deemed to be invalid. Provided that the Controller of Designs may, subject to the direction of the Central Government, register a design otherwise falling within the preceding prohibition if the Central Government certifies that the design’s registration is necessary for purposes demonstrably related to national security. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration on grounds of security india relates, or by the cancellation of a registered design on such grounds, may petition the High Court for redressal. The High Court shall, in such proceedings, consider any evidence presented by the Central Government relating to security concerns, and its decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Central Government may, as provided herein, direct the Controller to revoke a registration if subsequent information indicates a threat to national security.

Any design application disclosing articles primarily intended for use in military operations, or articles the disclosure of which would be prejudicial to the security of India, shall be subject to prior reference to the Department of Defence. The Controller of Designs may, and upon the request of the Department of Defence shall, suspend the processing of such application pending receipt of a report assessing the implications for national security. Provided that, if the Department of Defence fails to submit a report within a period of ninety days from the date of reference, the application shall proceed as if no reference had been made. 

The Controller shall, when considering a design, assess whether its features, if publicly known, could reasonably be exploited to the detriment of security india relates, including but not limited to, the compromise of defensive capabilities or the facilitation of hostile activities. Any design deemed to pose a risk shall be subject to restrictions on publication or may be refused registration, as provided herein. The decision of the Controller in such matters shall be final and binding.

Any design embodying a feature of an article intended for use in, or in connection with, the defence of India, or any article which, in the opinion of the Controller, is capable of being used in, or in connection with, such defence, shall not be registered unless a prior declaration of its security implications has been submitted to, and accepted by, the Central Government. The Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish such information as may be necessary to determine whether the design relates to the security of India. Provided that, if the Central Government determines that registration would be prejudicial to national security, the application shall be deemed to be withdrawn and no refund of fees shall be granted. Any person contravening the requirements concerning security india relates, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding all information pertaining to such declarations.

Any assignment of a registered design, or an application for registration, shall be subject to a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and assignee, and shall be registered with the Controller of Designs as provided herein. The Controller, upon registration of such assignment, shall record the transfer of ownership in the Register of Designs. Where a design is assigned for the purposes of security india relates, the assignee shall, prior to registration of the assignment, submit a statement to the Controller detailing the nature of such security interest and the extent to which the design’s exploitation is restricted. Failure to disclose such security interests may render the assignment voidable at the option of the original proprietor. A licensee of a design may, with the consent of the proprietor, further assign their interest in the design, subject to the same registration requirements. Any royalty arrangements arising from such assignments shall be clearly stipulated in the instrument of assignment.

Any design application incorporating features demonstrably essential to the security of India shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny as provided herein. The Controller of Designs may, upon reasonable grounds believing a design’s disclosure would be detrimental to national security, require the applicant to submit a detailed statement outlining the design’s potential applications and vulnerabilities. Claims asserting novelty and originality must, in such cases, be accompanied by a security assessment report from a designated governmental authority. Failure to provide such a report, or provision of a report deemed inadequate, may result in the application being held in abeyance pending further investigation. Provided that, the applicant shall be informed in writing of the reasons for such abeyance and afforded an opportunity to remedy the deficiency. The Controller shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding all information pertaining to designs impacting security india relates, and any unauthorized disclosure shall be punishable under relevant provisions of this Act.

The Controller of Designs may, if satisfied that the publication of a design is prejudicial to the security of India, refuse to register the design or require the applicant to modify the design to remove the prejudicial elements, subject to a reasoned order communicated to the applicant. Any application for registration involving designs with potential military or strategic applications shall be flagged for review by the designated security authority prior to acceptance. Provided that, the Controller may, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, grant a temporary registration for a limited period if immediate publication poses no demonstrable threat, but requires a full security assessment within that period. The applicant shall execute a non-disclosure agreement regarding all sensitive aspects of the design as a condition of registration, ensuring the confidentiality necessary to protect national interests and specify security india.

Any application for registration of a design, pertaining to articles ordinarily used for purposes of defence or security, shall be subject to prior approval from the Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence, before acceptance for examination as provided herein. The Controller of Designs may, if satisfied that the design concerns an article integral to national security, require the applicant to demonstrate a clear need for the design’s registration and to provide detailed specifications regarding its manufacture and intended use. Should the applicant fail to adequately address concerns regarding specify security india, the Controller shall refuse registration. Furthermore, the Central Government reserves the right to direct the Controller to revoke any such registration if, subsequent to grant, it is determined that the design poses a demonstrable threat to national security or is being utilized contrary to the interests of the State. Any transfer of ownership of such a registered design shall also require prior intimation to, and approval of, the aforementioned Department.

Any person who possesses confidential information relating to a design, and who, having obtained such information in the course of any proceedings under this Act, discloses it to any other person, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. However, such disclosure shall not be construed as an offence where it is made for the purpose of preventing serious injury to the public or to secure the safety of India. The Controller of Designs may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require any applicant for a design to furnish a security deposit to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act and to safeguard against frivolous or malicious applications. This security, if deemed necessary for the protection of national interests or to specify security india, may be increased at the discretion of the Controller. Any security so furnished shall be returned to the applicant upon satisfactory completion of the registration process or final determination of the application, less any costs or damages incurred by the Controller.

Any application for registration of a design, involving articles intended for use in or in connection with defence, shall be subject to prior approval from the Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence, and evidence of such approval shall be filed with the Controller of Designs as part of the application for registration. The Controller may, however, proceed with examination of the design pending receipt of such approval, provided that registration will be deferred until formal intimation of approval is received. Should the design incorporate elements deemed critical to national security, the applicant shall specify security india requirements in the application, detailing measures to prevent unauthorized reproduction or use. Failure to adequately address these requirements, or providing materially false information, may result in rejection of the application. The Controller, acting under this Act, may require the applicant to furnish additional information or undertake specific commitments regarding the design’s security implications, subject to verification by designated authorities.

Any person who, being in possession of information relating to a design registered or applied for under this Act, and having reasonable grounds to believe that such disclosure would be detrimental to the security of India, fails to report such information to the Controller, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine, or with both. The Controller, upon receiving credible intelligence concerning a design that may compromise national security, may, subject to the provisions herein, direct a temporary suspension of publication of the design application. Provided that such suspension shall not exceed sixty days, pending further investigation by a designated authority. Any wilful misrepresentation made to the Controller regarding the potential impact on specify security india shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. All evidence gathered during such investigations shall be admissible in any subsequent legal proceedings.

Any application for registration of a design, if it appears to the Controller that the design is capable of being used in connection with goods which may be prejudicial to the security of India, shall not be accepted for registration as provided herein. The Controller, prior to refusing such application, shall communicate with the applicant, requesting clarification regarding the intended use and potential implications for national security, and shall allow a period of thirty days for a response. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the concerns raised, or should the Controller, after due consideration of the response, remain convinced of the potential threat, registration shall be refused. Any aggrieved party may appeal such refusal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and the burden of demonstrating that the design does not compromise national security shall lie with the applicant. The Controller’s determination regarding matters of specify security india is final and binding unless overturned on appeal.

For the purposes of determining the novelty of an invention under this Act, any publication, whether written or oral, or any other means of making the invention available to the public, shall be considered as state of the art. However, the state of the art shall not include any information disclosed by the inventor relating to his invention, provided that such information was disclosed by him not more than six months prior to the filing of the complete specification. Any act reference provision relating to a prior art document shall be construed as a reference to the earliest document disclosing the essential features of the invention, irrespective of whether such document was published in India or elsewhere. Where a publication is available in a language other than an official language, a certified translation thereof may be furnished.

Any application for a patent, subsequent to its initial filing with the Patent Office, requiring reference to a prior art document not readily available within the Office’s established libraries, shall be subject to a supplemental fee as prescribed in Schedule I. The applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the referenced document, or a verifiable indication of its location, within ninety days of the examining officer’s request. Failure to comply with this provision may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to a final opportunity for rectification granted at the discretion of the Controller of Patents. Where the referenced document is a published work available through a national library, the applicant may submit a standardized citation, and the Patent Office shall undertake reasonable efforts to obtain the document. Any act reference provision contained within a claim shall be construed strictly, and ambiguity therein will be resolved against the applicant.

International registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the relevant rules, confer upon the applicant or registrant the same rights as if the trade mark had been registered in India directly under this Act. Provided that, where an international registration is refused, the applicant may, within a period of three months from the date of such refusal, file a statement setting out the grounds on which it is contended that the refusal was incorrect, and the Controller shall, after giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, reconsider the application. Any such reconsideration shall be conducted as if the application were a fresh application for registration. Furthermore, the effect of international registration shall be subject to any prior rights existing under this Act.

An international registration shall, upon fulfillment of requirements as provided herein and payment of the prescribed fee, be deemed registered in India from the date of the international registration, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where the international registration designates India, and the applicant is a national of a convention country or a member of the Organisation, the Registrar shall examine the international registration for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Provided that, if the Registrar finds any deficiency in the international registration, it shall issue a statement of grounds for refusal, and the applicant may, within the prescribed time, submit a response addressing such deficiencies. Any subsequent amendment to an international registration shall be recorded in the Register, provided it conforms to the requirements of this Act and does not materially affect the identity of the trade mark. The Registrar may, subject to conditions, require a certified copy of the international registration to be furnished.

An international registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer on the proprietor the same rights as if the trade mark had been registered in India directly under this Act. Where an application for registration is pending before the Trade Marks Registry at the time of the international registration, and the applicant satisfies the Registrar that the application relates to the same trade mark and goods or services as those covered by the international registration, the pending application shall be deemed to have been withdrawn as from the date of the international registration. Provided that, the applicant may, within a period of three months from the date of such deeming, elect to proceed with the pending application, in which case the international registration shall not confer any rights in respect of the goods or services covered by the pending application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may, within one month, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any time, require the proprietor of an international registration to furnish a certificate of renewal from the International Bureau.

An international registration shall, upon its entry into the Register, confer upon the applicant the same rights as if the trade mark had been registered under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained and the provisions of any relevant international convention to which India is a party. Where an international registration is refused, the applicant may, within a period of three months from the date of such refusal, file a statement setting forth the grounds on which the applicant disputes the refusal, and the Controller shall, after considering such statement and any evidence submitted, determine whether the refusal was justified. Provided that, if the Controller determines that the refusal was not justified, the international registration shall be proceeded with as if it had not been refused. Any person opposing an international registration shall follow the procedure as prescribed for opposing a national registration, with such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification, specify. The effect of an international registration extending to India shall cease if the basic application or registration upon which it is based is refused, withdrawn, or cancelled, unless a statement of entitlement is filed within six months of such event.

International registration shall confer, subject to the provisions of this Act, the same rights and remedies as if the trade mark had been registered in India directly under this Act, provided that such international registration is supported by a declaration of ownership and use filed with the International Bureau within the prescribed time. Any person intending to oppose an international registration shall file a notice of opposition within four months from the date of publication of such registration in the Trade Marks Journal. Where an international registration is refused, the applicant may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, request a review of the refusal. Failure to comply with the requirements relating to local representation, as provided herein, may render the international registration vulnerable to revocation. The Registrar may, at any time, require evidence of continued use of the trade mark in the country of origin to maintain the international registration.

International registration shall confer rights equivalent to those conferred by this Act in respect of the goods or services covered by such registration, subject to the provisions herein. Any person who, without due authorization, uses an internationally registered trade mark, or a mark deceptively similar thereto, in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, if the use is shown to be unintentional, the penalty may be reduced, but shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, upon application and sufficient cause shown, direct removal of the infringing material and recover the costs thereof from the offender. Any order imposing a penalty under this Act may be appealed to the High Court, and such appeal shall be heard expeditiously. Failure to comply with an order of the High Court shall constitute contempt of court.

Any international registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer on the owner the same rights as a registration effected under this Act in respect of the goods or services for which it is registered, and shall be subject to the same obligations. Where an international registration is assigned, the assignment shall be subject to the same requirements as an assignment of a national trade mark registration, including the necessity of a written instrument and intimation to the Trade Marks Registry. Provided that, the Registrar may, upon application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, record the assignment in the Register. An international registration may also be licensed, and any such license shall be in writing and may contain such terms and conditions as the parties deem fit, including provisions for quality control and royalty payments. Any dispute arising from such licensing shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the courts as provided herein. The holder of an international registration shall be entitled to maintain an action for infringement in any court competent to hear such cases.

An international registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the same effect as a registration in India from the date of its entry in the Register, provided that the applicant fulfils all requirements as to address for service and translation where necessary, and that no objection under rule 42 has been sustained. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision to accept or reject an international registration may, within one month of the order, file an appeal with the High Court, demonstrating substantial grounds for review. The High Court, upon consideration of such appeal, may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision, and shall provide reasoned orders. Where an international registration is challenged on the basis of prior use of a similar mark, the burden of proof shall lie with the challenging party to demonstrate continuous use prior to the international registration date. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in dismissal of the challenge.

International registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, confer the same rights as a registration effected directly in India in respect of the goods or services specified in the international registration, provided that the applicant fulfils all requirements for registration as if the application had been made directly under this Act. Where an applicant seeks international registration based on a priority claim derived from a national application, compliance with the Patent Cooperation Treaty, where applicable, shall be demonstrated to the Registrar through submission of a certified copy of the priority document. Any failure to maintain the international registration in the country of origin, or to comply with timelines prescribed by the designating office, may result in cancellation of the registration in India, subject to a notice period of sixty days. The Registrar may, however, extend this period if sufficient cause is shown.

Any transfer of an international registration, whether complete or partial, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignments and shall be recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. The registrar shall maintain an index of all registered international registrations, detailing any such transfer of ownership or licensing arrangements, and make such information available for public inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where an international registration is assigned, the assignee may, subject to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein, apply for a local trademark registration in respect of the assigned mark. A license granted under an international registration shall not affect the rights of the owner to further license or assign the mark, provided that the terms of each license or assignment are consistent with the overarching international registration. Failure to record any transfer or licensing agreement with the registrar may render such transaction unenforceable against third parties. The registrar index registered details shall be conclusive evidence of ownership for the purposes of any dispute.

International registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer the same rights and entitlements as if the trade mark had been registered directly under this Act, provided that the applicant demonstrates diligent pursuit of national registration where required by the designating country. Any objection to the international registration, arising from a prior right in India, must be filed with the Trade Marks Registry within a period of three months from the date of notification of the international registration. Should the Registry reject such objection, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Member Appellate Board, furnishing evidence supporting their claim of prior right and demonstrating that the international registration infringes upon said right. The Member Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition to a court of competent jurisdiction, and any delay in pursuing such appeal shall not be construed as abandonment of the prior right.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority within a period of ninety days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee and fulfillment of such conditions as may be specified in the rules. The appellate authority shall, upon receipt of such appeal and after giving the Controller an opportunity to be heard, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order appealed from, and shall record its reasons for doing so in writing. Provided that the appellate authority may, if it deems necessary, require further evidence to be submitted by either party. Any decision of the appellate authority shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the High Court. The Controller shall give effect to the order appellate authority within thirty days of its receipt.

Any person aggrieved by an order of a licensing authority, or by an order refusing to grant a compulsory license, may prefer an appeal to the order appellate authority within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The order appellate authority shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order of the licensing authority. Provided that, the order appellate authority may, if it considers it necessary, direct the licensing authority to rehear the matter and pass a fresh order in accordance with its directions. Any application for leave to appeal shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds on which it is based and a copy of the order appealed against. The decision of the order appellate authority shall be final and binding, except where a right of appeal to the High Court is otherwise provided for under this Act. Failure to avail of this remedy within the stipulated timeframe shall preclude any further recourse.

Any person aggrieved by an order of a licensing officer, or by any decision taken under the provisions relating to compulsory licenses, may prefer an appeal to the order appellate authority constituted under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fee as may be prescribed. The order appellate authority shall, upon receipt of a duly filed appeal and prescribed fee, provide notice to the licensing officer and any other relevant parties, affording them an opportunity to submit their representations. Provided that, the order appellate authority may, at its discretion and for reasons to be recorded, extend the time for filing an appeal or for submitting representations. All decisions of the order appellate authority shall be communicated in writing and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court. Failure to comply with an order of the order appellate authority shall attract penalties as prescribed.

Any assignment of a patent, or any interest therein, whether whole or partial, and whether vested or contingent, shall be in writing and registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. An application for registration of assignment shall be made by the assignor or the assignee, or their duly authorised agent, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Where the assignment is made subject to a condition requiring future consideration, the Controller may, before registration, require evidence of payment of such consideration or a legally enforceable agreement for its payment. Any dispute concerning the validity of an assignment or the terms thereof, may be brought before the order appellate authority established under this Act. The order appellate authority shall, following due process and consideration of evidence, issue a binding determination regarding the assignment. Provided that, the Controller shall not register an assignment if it appears to contravene any provision of this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it, but such assignment shall not be enforceable against any person other than the parties to the assignment.

Upon acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, the Registrar shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, record the particulars of the trade mark in the Register of Trade Marks and issue a certificate of registration in accordance with the prescribed rules. Where an application is accepted subject to conditions, those conditions shall be clearly stated in the certificate and shall be binding on the applicant and their successors in title. Any failure to satisfy these accepted conditions within a period of six months from the date of registration may render the registration liable to revocation, following a procedure established by the Registrar. 

The Registrar may, at any time prior to complete registration, require the applicant to furnish further evidence or clarification regarding the nature of the trade mark or the use thereof, particularly concerning its distinctiveness. Should the applicant fail to comply with such a requirement, the Registrar may, after providing reasonable opportunity for a hearing, withdraw the acceptance of the application. All decisions relating to application accepted conditions shall be subject to review as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar. Such notice shall be in writing, and shall clearly state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including any relevant prior rights or established common law usage. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a valid notice of opposition, serve a copy thereof upon the applicant for registration, requiring them to deliver a counter-statement within a period not exceeding two months. Failure to deliver such counter-statement may result in the Registrar proceeding ex parte. Evidence may be filed by both the opposing party and the applicant, and the Registrar shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, record a reasoned decision either allowing or dismissing the opposition. The Registrar’s decision regarding registrar opposition registration shall be final, subject to any rights of appeal as provided herein. A finding of prior rights shall be substantiated with documentary evidence.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Where an assignment includes the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, the assignee may apply to the Registrar to register the assignment and the transfer of goodwill. The Registrar shall, subject to verification of the instrument and satisfaction that the assignment is genuine, register the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks. 

An opposition to the registration of an assignment may be filed by any person alleging that the assignment is contrary to law or would be detrimental to their interests, and the Registrar shall, as provided herein, conduct an inquiry into the matter. The Registrar opposition registration shall be determined based on evidence submitted by both parties and in accordance with the principles of equity and fairness. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it, but it may affect the enforceability of the trade mark against third parties.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Registrar against the registration of a trade mark, provided that such notice is accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based and is submitted within the prescribed time limit from the date of advertisement of the application for registration. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such opposition, serve a copy thereof upon the applicant, allowing them a period of two months to submit a counter-statement addressing the grounds raised. Should the applicant fail to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe, the Registrar may, after considering the opposition notice and any supporting evidence, proceed to reject the application. However, any decision of the Registrar in respect of such registrar opposition registration may be appealed to the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee and fulfillment of other conditions as may be specified.

A notice applicant registration shall be deemed to have been duly served where, subject to the provisions of this Act, it is delivered to the applicant at their address for service as recorded in the Trade Marks Registry, or, in cases where no such address for service is recorded, at their last known address or principal place of business. Provided that, where the applicant has elected to receive notices electronically, service may be effected via electronic transmission to the designated email address. Any person intending to oppose an application for registration shall furnish a notice applicant registration to the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the grounds for such opposition and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the opposition invalid, as provided herein.

Any applicant for registration of a trade mark shall, upon satisfaction of the Registrar that the application meets the requirements as provided herein, receive a notice of acceptance. Such notice shall be recorded in the Trade Marks Register and shall be published in the Journal in a manner prescribed. A notice applicant registration, once published, shall be deemed to be a public declaration of the applicant’s intent to secure exclusive rights over the mark. However, this shall not prejudice any existing rights of prior users. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to submit further evidence of use or distinctiveness within a period not exceeding three months from the date of such request. Failure to comply with such request may result in the application being deemed abandoned, unless reasonable cause is shown. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all notices issued and actions taken in respect thereof.

Any person claiming prior rights in a trade mark, or who may be adversely affected by the registration of a trade mark, shall have the right to give notice to the Trade Marks Registry of an intention to oppose the registration of such trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such notice, constituting a notice applicant registration, shall be in writing, and shall clearly specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, lack of distinctiveness or a likelihood of confusion with existing marks. The Registry may, at its discretion, require further clarification or evidence in support of the grounds alleged in the notice. A failure to provide such clarification within a reasonable timeframe may result in the notice being deemed invalid. Provided that, a notice given without a reasonable basis, or with the intent to unduly delay a legitimate application, may be subject to penalties as provided herein, and the applicant may seek costs against the objector. The Registry shall maintain a public record of all notices received.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, as a condition precedent to the grant of registration, submit a statement of proposed use demonstrating bona fide intention to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. Where the Registrar has reason to believe that the applicant is not the proprietor of the mark, or that the mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion, notice applicant registration shall be issued requiring the applicant to furnish evidence of proprietorship and/or distinctiveness within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such notice. Failure to comply with the requirements of such notice may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to an opportunity for the applicant to rectify the deficiency. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, extend the period for furnishing evidence if sufficient cause is shown. Any evidence submitted shall be subject to verification and may be challenged by any interested party as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all notices issued and evidence received.

Any applicant for registration of a trade mark shall, upon receipt of an examination report indicating potential conflicts with existing marks, be issued a notice requiring a response within thirty days from the date of such notice. Failure to respond to this notice, or submission of a response deemed unsatisfactory by the Registrar, may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to a final opportunity for rectification. A notice applicant registration, if contested by a third party under this Act, shall necessitate the submission of evidence of prior use or distinctiveness, and the applicant shall bear the burden of proving such claims. Provided that, where the Registrar deems the evidence insufficient, the application may be refused, and an appeal may be filed with the appellate board as provided herein. Compliance with all prescribed procedures regarding the notice is mandatory for continued processing of the application.

Any applicant for registration of a trade mark shall, upon receipt of an examination report indicating grounds for refusal, be afforded a period of thirty days to file a response addressing the objections raised therein, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned as provided herein. Where an applicant seeks an extension of time to file such a response, a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the prescribed filing fee shall be levied. A notice applicant registration, demonstrating a legitimate interest and potential damage, may be filed with the Trade Marks Registry contesting the proposed registration, subject to payment of the stipulated fee and adherence to the prescribed format. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements for filing a notice shall render it invalid, and the Registry may impose a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees on the offending party. Any false representation in a notice applicant registration shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Any person desiring to assign or otherwise transfer the right, title, and interest in a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall comply with such requirements as may be prescribed. The Registry may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, record the assignment in its records, and upon such recording, the transfer of ownership shall be effective as against third parties. A notice applicant registration, detailing the proposed transfer, shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal for the purpose of inviting objections, provided that such notice shall clearly specify the goods or services in respect of which the transfer applies. Failure to provide adequate notice or to comply with the prescribed requirements may render the assignment unenforceable as provided herein, and the Registry reserves the right to refuse registration of the assignment. Any dispute regarding the validity of the assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act.

Any person claiming prior use of a mark, or asserting rights in a similar mark, may file a notice with the Trade Marks Registry contesting a notice applicant registration, provided that such notice is accompanied by a detailed statement of grounds and supporting evidence demonstrating the basis of the claim. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such notice, serve a copy upon the applicant and afford them a period of sixty days to submit a counter-statement. Failure to submit a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an abandonment of the application, subject to further review by the Registrar. Should the parties fail to reach a mutually agreeable resolution following exchange of statements, the matter shall proceed to a hearing before a designated officer, who may, after considering all evidence, uphold or dismiss the notice of opposition, and issue a reasoned order accordingly; any aggrieved party may appeal such order to the High Court having jurisdiction.

Any applicant for registration of a trade mark shall, upon satisfaction of the conditions as prescribed, submit a notice applicant registration detailing the proposed use of the mark and the class of goods or services it pertains to. This notice shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating genuine intent to use the mark in commerce. Where a registered user layout exists, detailing the scope of permitted use by a licensee, the applicant shall also furnish a copy of said layout, clearly indicating the territorial extent and limitations of the licensed use. Failure to provide a complete and accurate notice applicant registration may result in the rejection of the application or a delay in processing. The Registrar may, subject to verification, request additional information from the applicant to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. Any misrepresentation in the notice shall render the registration liable to revocation.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall furnish a clear and unambiguous notice of such application to the Trade Marks Registry, failing which the application shall be deemed defective and liable to be rejected as provided herein. Such notice applicant registration shall include a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and the applicant’s name and address for service. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered in association with a pre-existing, relating trade mark, the applicant shall disclose the nature of the connection, if any, and provide evidence of lawful use. Failure to accurately disclose such relating trade mark or to provide supporting evidence shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated non-compliance with these provisions may result in the Registrar refusing further applications from the offending party and initiating proceedings for fraud. The Registrar may, subject to due process, impose additional conditions as deemed necessary to ensure transparency and prevent undue advantage.

Any person desiring to obtain a license or assignment of a registered trade mark shall submit a written request to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement detailing the proposed terms of such license or assignment, including the territory, duration, and scope of permitted use. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such request and verification of the registry fee paid, issue a notice applicant registration to the registered proprietor, outlining the particulars of the proposed transaction. The registered proprietor shall, within sixty days of receiving said notice, either consent to the proposed license or assignment or file a statement of objection with the Registry. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed provisional consent, subject to further review if warranted. Any dispute arising from a license or assignment shall be subject to the dispute resolution mechanisms as provided herein, and the Registry retains the authority to amend or revoke any improperly executed instrument.

A registered design shall not be subject to cancellation under this Act if the Central Government determines that its continued registration is essential for the security of India. Any action taken under this provision, termed a “security India action,” shall be predicated upon a reasoned finding, recorded in writing, demonstrating a clear and imminent threat to national security arising from the widespread reproduction of the design. The Controller of Designs, upon receiving credible intelligence from a designated security agency, may initiate a review of the design’s potential impact. Provided that, such initiation shall be subject to a confirmatory assessment by a committee comprising technical experts and representatives from relevant ministries. Any person aggrieved by a security India action may, subject to the provisions of this Act, seek judicial review.

Any application for registration of a design, where the Controller has reasonable grounds to believe that the design is capable of being used in connection with goods which may affect the security of India, shall be subject to a security india action. The Controller may, prior to registration, require the applicant to furnish a statement detailing the intended use of the design and the goods to which it will be applied. Provided that, if the applicant fails to satisfy the Controller regarding the non-prejudicial nature of the design’s application, the Controller may refuse registration. Furthermore, the Controller may, as provided herein, direct an inquiry into the potential impact of the design on national security, and may consult with such governmental agencies as deemed necessary. Any design registered under this Act, subsequently found to pose a threat to the security of India, may be subject to revocation, and the proprietor shall be liable to such penalties as may be prescribed.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before any court, notify the registered proprietor of the design of the nature of the alleged infringement and the grounds upon which the allegation is based. The registered proprietor shall, within thirty days of receipt of such notification, furnish a statement of their defense, if any, to the alleging party. Should the registered proprietor fail to respond within the stipulated timeframe, or the alleging party deems the response unsatisfactory, they may then commence legal proceedings. 

However, where the infringement involves a design essential to national security, the Central Government may, acting *ex officio*, initiate a security india action, irrespective of any private complaint. Such action shall supersede any ongoing private proceedings and may include interim injunctions, seizure of infringing articles, and the imposition of penalties as provided herein. The Controller of Designs shall, upon receiving credible information regarding such security concerns, immediately notify the Central Government and cooperate fully with any investigation.

Any person possessing knowledge of a design registered under this Act, or of an application for registration, who reasonably believes that such design, if manufactured, would be prejudicial to the security of India, may forthwith report such belief to the Controller, detailing the grounds for such apprehension. The Controller, upon receipt of such report, shall initiate a confidential inquiry, and may require the applicant or registered proprietor to furnish such evidence as may be deemed necessary to satisfy the inquiry. Should the Controller, after due consideration, be satisfied that the design poses a genuine threat to the security of India, he may, subject to the provisions herein, direct the immediate suspension of registration or refuse registration of the design. Any action taken under this provision relating to security india action shall be without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act, and the Controller’s decision shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal may lie to the High Court on grounds of procedural impropriety. The Controller shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding all information received and actions taken pursuant to this provision.

Any application for registration of a design shall be subject to a rigorous examination to ascertain its novelty and originality, and compliance with all provisions of this Act. The Controller of Designs may, at any time during the examination process, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence to substantiate the claims made in the application. Where the Controller has reasonable grounds to believe that the publication of a design, even if registered, would be prejudicial to the security of India, the Controller shall not register the design. 

Furthermore, the Controller may initiate a security India action, requiring the applicant to demonstrate that the design does not compromise national security interests. Provided that, any such action shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of reasons and an opportunity for the applicant to respond. Failure to adequately address concerns raised during a security India action may result in the rejection of the application, even if the design otherwise meets all requirements for registration.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, applies for registration of a design not originally created by him, or knowingly imitates a design registered under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such design. Where a design is registered in contravention of the provisions relating to novelty, or where a design is registered which is not a design as defined herein, the Controller may, after giving the registered owner an opportunity to be heard, revoke the registration. Furthermore, if it appears to the Controller that a design was registered primarily for the purpose of obtaining a strategic advantage detrimental to the security of India, the Controller shall, notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act, immediately cancel the registration. Any person aggrieved by such cancellation may appeal to the High Court, subject to the conditions as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification, direct the Controller to undertake a security india action regarding any registered design.

Any person who, being the proprietor of a design, intends to license the right to make, sell, or import any article embodying such design, shall execute a written license agreement specifying the duration, territory, and scope of the license, and the royalty payable. Such agreement shall be registered with the Controller General of Designs within thirty days of its execution, failing which the license shall be voidable at the option of the licensee. Where a design is of critical importance to the security of India, the Central Government may, subject to payment of reasonable compensation, direct the proprietor to grant a license on such terms as it deems fit, even without the proprietor’s consent. Any assignment of the right in a design shall be subject to the same registration requirements as a license, and failure to register shall render the assignment unenforceable. The Controller may, as provided herein, refuse registration if the proposed assignment or license is demonstrably prejudicial to national security or public order, constituting a security india action. A registered user may petition the Controller for revocation of a license obtained through coercion or misrepresentation.

Any person alleging that a design registration infringes a national security interest may petition the Controller for a security india action, submitting evidence of such infringement and the potential harm to the sovereignty or integrity of India. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such petition, notify the registered proprietor and require them to submit a reasoned response within thirty days, subject to extension granted at the Controller’s discretion. Should the Controller find merit in the petition, they may, pending further inquiry, suspend the effect of the design registration. An appeal from the Controller’s decision regarding suspension lies with the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Controller’s order. The High Court, in considering such appeals, may appoint a technical expert to assess the validity of the security concerns raised and shall issue a reasoned order, binding on all parties, as provided herein. Failure to comply with a High Court order may result in penalties.

The Controller of Designs may, upon sufficient cause being shown and subject to the provisions of this Act, initiate a security India action where a design, or an article embodying a design, is reasonably suspected of being prejudicial to the security of India or likely to be used for purposes contrary to public order. Any person possessing goods incorporating such a design shall, upon receipt of a notice from the Controller, furnish a complete accounting of the quantity, origin, and destination of said goods within thirty days. Failure to comply with such notice shall be deemed an offence punishable as provided herein. The Controller, following such accounting, may direct the immediate seizure and disposal of the goods, or require modification of the design to remove the security risk. Provided that, any action taken under this provision shall be subject to review by the High Court having jurisdiction. The Controller shall maintain a confidential register of all security India actions undertaken and the associated findings.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, applies for registration of a design not original, or who procures the registration of such a design, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine not exceeding two lakh rupees, or with both. Where a design is registered which is demonstrably not novel, the Controller may, after notice to the registrant, revoke the registration, subject to an appeal to the High Court. Any action taken to secure India’s strategic interests, including but not limited to designs relating to agricultural implements or processes, may be initiated irrespective of prior registration, and the Controller shall cooperate fully with the Agriculture Commissioner in such matters. Failure to comply with a lawful direction issued under this Act relating to a security India action shall attract a penalty of fifty thousand rupees per day of non-compliance. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any person alleging a threat to the security of India arising from a registered design may petition the Controller of Designs, furnishing such evidence as may be required to substantiate the claim. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such petition, conduct a preliminary inquiry and, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, may initiate a security india action. Such action shall include, but not be limited to, temporary suspension of the design’s registration pending further investigation. A registered patent agent, acting on behalf of the petitioner or the design holder, may present arguments and evidence during the inquiry. Should the Controller determine that the design poses a genuine threat, it may recommend to the Central Government the permanent cancellation of the registration, subject to a right of appeal to the High Court. Any decision regarding cancellation shall be communicated to all parties concerned, and reasons for the decision must be recorded.

The Controller of Designs may, subject to the provisions of this Act, refuse to register a design if it is deemed contrary to public order or morality. A design disclosing features relating to articles used for, or in connection with, the security of India shall not be registered unless a certificate of approval from the competent authority designated by the Central Government has been obtained prior to application. Such certificate shall confirm that the design’s disclosure does not prejudice national security. The Controller shall, as provided herein, maintain strict confidentiality regarding any application or registration details pertaining to designs impacting security india explanation, and may require applicants to execute a non-disclosure agreement. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the design application or cancellation of registration, even if previously granted.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before any court, notify the alleged infringer of the particulars of the infringement and require them to cease the infringing act, subject to the provisions contained herein. Should the alleged infringer, upon receipt of such notice, fail to cease the infringing act within thirty days, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court having jurisdiction. The High Court, upon being satisfied of the prima facie case of infringement and considering the interests of security India explanation, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the design. 

Provided that, in cases where the design is integral to a product essential for national security, the Court shall, before issuing any injunction, consult with the Central Government to ascertain whether the injunction would be detrimental to the security of India. Any damages awarded shall reflect the actual loss suffered by the plaintiff, or a reasonable royalty, whichever is higher, and may include costs as determined by the Court.

The Controller of Designs may, subject to the provisions of this Act, refuse to register a design if such design is contrary to public order or morality. Where a design incorporates a feature that, in the opinion of the Controller, is essential to the defense of India, or is otherwise prejudicial to the security of India, registration shall be refused. An application for registration disclosing such a design shall be deemed confidential and shall not be published as provided herein. The Controller shall, prior to any such refusal, communicate with the Central Government and obtain its concurrence regarding the impact on security India explanation. Should the Central Government determine that the design, despite its potential impact, does not compromise national security, the Controller may proceed with examination. Any person aggrieved by a refusal based on security grounds may appeal to the High Court, subject to the established appellate procedures. The Controller shall maintain a secure register of all designs refused on grounds relating to the security of India.

The Controller shall, upon reasonable grounds believing that disclosure of a design’s particulars would be prejudicial to the security of India, refuse registration or impound any design application as provided herein. Any design incorporating features directly relating to defense installations, strategic materials, or technologies critical to national security shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny. An applicant seeking registration must submit a detailed declaration affirming the design’s non-detrimental impact on India’s security interests. The Controller may, prior to registration, request further clarification or evidence from the applicant regarding the design’s potential implications. Provided that, if the design is demonstrably for civilian applications and poses no discernible threat, registration may proceed. Failure to accurately disclose relevant security concerns shall render the registration voidable and may attract penalties. The Controller’s decision regarding security india explanation is final and not subject to appeal, except before the High Court.

The Controller of Designs may, if the disclosure of any design registration information is likely to be prejudicial to national security, refuse to permit inspection of the design register or copies of registered designs as provided herein. Any application for registration which, in the opinion of the Controller, relates to a design the publication of which would be detrimental to necessary security india, shall be treated as confidential. Provided that such confidentiality shall not extend beyond a period of ten years from the date of application, unless the Central Government, upon review, determines a continuing threat to national security warrants extended restriction. The Controller shall maintain a separate confidential register for such designs and may require applicants to execute a non-disclosure agreement as a condition of filing. Any breach of confidentiality shall be subject to penalties under this Act.

Any application for registration of a design, pertaining to articles intended for use in defense, military, or national security applications, shall be subject to prior clearance from the Department of Defence Production. The Controller of Designs may, prior to examination, require the applicant to demonstrate that the design does not compromise necessary security india, or to submit the application to the aforementioned Department for assessment. Should the Department raise objections regarding the design’s potential impact on national security, registration shall be deferred pending satisfactory resolution. Provided that, if the applicant fails to provide adequate justification or cooperate with the Department’s review within a period of ninety days, the application shall be deemed abandoned. The Controller shall maintain a confidential register of all such applications undergoing security assessment, and access to this register is restricted to authorized personnel only. Any disclosure violating these provisions is punishable as provided herein.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered design shall, prior to the institution of any legal proceedings, serve upon the alleged infringer a notice of such intention, specifying the nature of the infringement and the relief sought. The Controller may, subject to such terms as he may deem fit, grant a license to work a registered design where it is established that the design is capable of being worked by any industrial process, and the refusal to grant such license would be prejudicial to the public interest or impede the development of industries in India. 

However, where the design is essential for purposes of national defence, or is otherwise necessary for the security of India, the Central Government may, by order, direct the Controller to revoke the registration of such design, providing the registered owner with just compensation as determined by a designated tribunal. Any information pertaining to such revocation, or the grounds therefor relating to necessary security india, shall be treated as confidential and not disclosed except as authorized by law.

The Controller of Designs may, upon sufficient cause being shown and subject to the provisions hereinafter contained, require any applicant for a design or the proprietor of a registered design to furnish such security as may be deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the obligations under this Act. Any security so furnished shall be deposited with a designated nationalized bank and shall be subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller may specify, including but not limited to the form of security, the amount thereof, and the duration for which it shall remain in force. Where the security is deemed insufficient, the Controller may, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard, direct the applicant or proprietor to provide additional security. 

In cases where a design is reasonably suspected of being prejudicial to the necessary security india, the Controller may, pending investigation, temporarily suspend the registration of such design and require enhanced security commensurate with the potential risk. Failure to comply with the requirements regarding security, as provided herein, may result in the rejection of the application or the revocation of the registration, as the case may be.

Any design registration application relating to articles intended for use in defense, military applications, or strategic industries shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny as provided herein. The Controller of Designs may, upon reasonable suspicion that a design may compromise necessary security india, require the applicant to furnish detailed information regarding the design’s functionality, materials, and intended end-use. Failure to comply with such a request within thirty days shall be deemed sufficient grounds for rejection of the application. Furthermore, the Central Government reserves the right to direct the Controller to suspend processing of any application where disclosure of the design is considered detrimental to national security. Registered designs found to pose a risk to necessary security india may be subject to immediate revocation, and the proprietor shall be liable for any associated costs of remediation. Any transfer of ownership of such designs shall require prior approval from the designated authority.

Any person who, being in possession of confidential information relating to a design registered or applied for under this Act, and having reasonable grounds to believe that such information concerns necessary security india, shall disclose such information to any person not authorized to receive it, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Controller of Designs may, if satisfied that disclosure would be detrimental to national security, direct the withholding of such information from public inspection, subject to a review by a designated officer. Provided that, any such direction shall be recorded in writing with reasons stated therein. Any officer failing to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding confidential information, or abusing their authority in relation to design registration impacting necessary security india, shall be liable for disciplinary action, including removal from service. A false claim invoking national security to obstruct legitimate design examination shall attract a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.

Any assignment of a registered design relating to articles used in connection with necessary security india shall require prior written consent of the Controller of Designs, and such consent may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Controller deems fit to ensure continued national security interests. The Controller shall, within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of the application for consent, convey a decision in writing, stating the reasons for any refusal. Where the assignee is a foreign entity, additional scrutiny shall be undertaken to ascertain the ultimate beneficial ownership and potential for unauthorized transfer of technology. A licensee of a design subject to these provisions may, with the leave of the Controller, sub-license the design to another party, provided that such sub-license does not compromise the necessary security india. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the assignment or sub-license void *ab initio*, and may attract penalties as provided herein. The Controller may, at any time, revoke a license or assignment if it is determined that the design is being utilized in a manner detrimental to national interests.

Any application for registration of a design, relating to articles intended for use in, or capable of use for, defense purposes, shall be subject to prior clearance from the Department of Defence Production, Ministry of Defence, and evidence of such clearance shall be filed with the Controller of Designs. Should the Controller receive information suggesting a design application compromises necessary security india, they may, pending such clearance, suspend processing of the application and notify the applicant of the grounds for suspension. An applicant aggrieved by such suspension may, within thirty days, submit a detailed rejoinder addressing the concerns raised. If, following review of the rejoinder and the Department’s recommendation, the Controller determines the design does not jeopardize national security, processing shall resume. However, a final adverse determination by the Department of Defence Production is appealable to the High Court, with the Controller serving as a respondent in such proceedings. Failure to provide requested information or to reasonably address security concerns may result in the application being deemed withdrawn.

Any design registration incorporating elements demonstrably prejudicial to necessary security india shall be immediately suspended pending investigation by the Controller. The Controller may, as provided herein, demand production of all records relating to the design’s conception, development, and intended application. Failure to comply with such demand within thirty days shall incur a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Should a registered design be determined to compromise national security, the Controller shall revoke the registration, and all associated privileges are forfeited. Any person aggrieved by such revocation may submit a notice rectification shall be filed with the Controller, detailing grounds for appeal within sixty days of the revocation order; however, such appeal does not stay the revocation itself. Repeated violations of these provisions, or attempts to conceal relevant information, may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, alongside the aforementioned financial penalties.

Any application for registration of a design which discloses features intrinsically linked to articles essential for national security shall be subject to a rigorous examination as provided herein. The Controller of Designs, upon reasonable grounds believing a design threatens necessary security india, may require the applicant to demonstrate the design’s non-detrimental impact, or to modify it to remove such threats. Should the applicant fail to satisfy the Controller, or should the Controller remain unconvinced, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. Any aggrieved party, including the applicant, may appeal such a decision to the Opposition Board, furnishing evidence supporting their claim within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s communication. The Opposition Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to rights of appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is initiated within ninety days of the Board’s ruling. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the absolute forfeiture of any rights pertaining to the design.

The Controller of Designs may, if satisfied that the disclosure of any design registration information or application details would be prejudicial to the security of India, refuse to permit inspection or grant of copies of such information as provided herein. Any application for registration of a design which incorporates elements demonstrably impacting national security shall be subject to a mandatory review by a designated authority within the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion. Provided that, such review shall be completed within a period of sixty days from the date of application. The Controller shall, notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, act in accordance with the recommendations of said authority regarding designs affecting security india. Failure to comply with the requirements of this review may result in the rejection of the design application.

Any design, the publication of which would be prejudicial to the security of India, shall not be registrable under this Act, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein. An application for registration disclosing such a design may be refused, and the applicant shall be informed of the reasons for such refusal. However, the Controller of Designs may, subject to the direction of the Central Government, permit the registration of a design relating to an article primarily intended for the defense forces, provided that such design does not reveal critical technological information impacting national security. The Controller shall, prior to any such permission, conduct a thorough examination to ascertain the potential implications for security india and submit a detailed report to the Central Government. Any disclosure made during the registration process relating to such designs shall be treated as confidential and shall not be accessible to the public without explicit authorization. The Central Government may, at any time, revoke the registration of a design if it deems it necessary in the interests of security india.

Any person who possesses knowledge of a design registered under this Act, and reasonably believes that the design’s manufacture, import, or sale would be prejudicial to the security of India, shall immediately notify the Controller of Designs. The Controller, upon receipt of such notification and subject to verification of the grounds alleged, may, by order, direct the registered owner to cease all activities relating to the design. Provided that, such order shall remain in effect for a period not exceeding ninety days, unless extended by the Controller upon further evidence demonstrating continued threat to national security. 

Any person aggrieved by an order issued under this Act relating to security india, may appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of the relevant appellate jurisdiction rules. The registered owner shall be entitled to reasonable compensation for any loss suffered due to the temporary cessation of activities, as determined by the High Court, unless such loss is directly attributable to a proven threat to national security.

Any application for registration of a design, if it appears to the Controller that the design is capable of being used in connection with goods which may be employed for purposes prejudicial to the security of India, shall not be accepted for registration as provided herein. The Controller may, prior to refusal, require the applicant to furnish a statement detailing the intended use of the design and to demonstrate that such use will not compromise national security. Should the applicant fail to satisfy the Controller regarding the security implications, the application shall be deemed withdrawn. Furthermore, the Controller may, subject to the direction of the Central Government, direct the applicant to amend the design to remove elements considered detrimental to security india. Any design registered under this Act, if subsequently determined to pose a threat to the security of India, may be cancelled by the Controller following a review initiated either suo motu or upon receipt of a complaint from any person. The Controller shall, in conducting such reviews, adhere to principles of natural justice and provide the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard.

Any design registration application relating to articles intended for use in defense, military applications, or critical infrastructure shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny as provided herein. The Controller of Designs may, prior to registration, require the applicant to demonstrate that the design’s dissemination will not be detrimental to the security of India. Should the applicant fail to satisfy this requirement, registration shall be refused. Furthermore, the Central Government reserves the right to direct the Controller to revoke any registered design if, subsequent to registration, credible information emerges indicating a potential compromise to national security. Compliance with export control regulations and any applicable licensing requirements relating to dual-use goods is a prerequisite for maintaining a valid design registration. The Controller shall maintain strict confidentiality regarding all applications and registered designs pertaining to matters of security india, and any unauthorized disclosure will be subject to penalties under this Act.

Any person who, being in possession of confidential information relating to a design registered or applied for under this Act, discloses such information to any person not authorized to receive it, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that no disclosure shall be deemed an offence if made with the prior written consent of the Controller of Designs. The Controller may, subject to the requirements of security India, authorize disclosure to specified persons or entities for legitimate purposes, including national defense or public safety. Any attempt to circumvent this provision, including the transmission of confidential design information across international borders without authorization, constitutes a cognizable offence.
