Furthermore, any design produced utilizing illegally obtained confidential information shall be subject to immediate cancellation of registration as provided herein, and the proprietor shall forfeit all rights therein.

Any person alleging that a design registered under this Act infringes upon a prior art design, and that such infringement poses a demonstrable threat to the security of India, may petition the Controller for revocation of the registration. Such petition shall be accompanied by evidence establishing both the prior art and the nexus between the design and national security concerns. The Controller, upon receiving such petition, shall issue notice to the registered proprietor and invite their response within a period of thirty days. If, after considering the submissions of both parties, the Controller is satisfied that the design does indeed infringe and impacts security india, they may order its cancellation. Any aggrieved party may appeal such decision to the High Court within sixty days, subject to the deposit of such security as the High Court deems fit, to ensure the protection of legitimate design rights while safeguarding national interests. The High Court’s decision shall be final.

The omission register shall be maintained by the Controller of Patents in a manner consistent with the preservation of confidentiality and accessibility as provided herein. Any person alleging an omission of a relevant prior art reference from the register of patents may submit a detailed statement, supported by evidence, to the Controller for consideration. The Controller may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence and satisfaction that a genuine omission exists, direct the inclusion of such reference in the omission register. A separate index of omitted references, categorized by technical field, shall be maintained alongside the register. Provided that, the Controller may reject an application for inclusion if the submitted evidence is insufficient or the reference lacks relevance to patentability criteria under this Act. Any decision of the Controller regarding the omission register shall be subject to review.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where the annual renewal fee has not been paid, and where a notice requiring payment has been issued to the patentee, and remains unanswered for a period of six months from the date of such notice. Any person may inspect the omission register subject to payment of the prescribed fee and shall be provided with a certified copy of any entry therein upon further payment as determined by the Controller. An entry in the omission register shall not, however, be construed as automatic revocation of the patent, but merely as a record of non-compliance with renewal requirements as provided herein. The patentee may, within three months of the date of entry in the omission register, submit proof of payment or a valid justification for non-payment, failing which the Controller may proceed with revocation proceedings. The Controller shall remove an entry from the omission register upon receipt of satisfactory evidence of compliance.

Any person alleging a material omission from the omission register maintained under this Act may apply to the Controller for rectification of the register. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds on which the applicant relies, and shall be served upon the proprietor of the patent in question. The Controller shall, after giving the proprietor an opportunity to be heard, consider the application and may, if satisfied that the omission exists and is material, direct the Controller to make the necessary amendment to the omission register. A failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall render the application inadmissible. Provided that, where the omission relates to a fraudulent or wilful misrepresentation, the Controller may, in addition to directing amendment of the register, impose a monetary penalty on the party responsible for the omission, subject to a maximum amount as prescribed. Any order made by the Controller under this provision shall be final and binding, save for a right of appeal to the High Court.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register wherein particulars of patents deemed to have lapsed due to non-payment of renewal fees, or failure to comply with statutory requirements as provided herein, are recorded. Any person alleging an omission from the register, or an incorrect entry therein, may submit a petition to the Controller, supported by evidence establishing the grounds for such allegation. The Controller shall, subject to verification of the submitted evidence and a reasonable opportunity being given to the patent holder to respond, either confirm the omission or rectify the register accordingly. Provided that, if the patent holder fails to respond within a period of sixty days from the date of notice, the Controller may proceed *ex parte*. An appeal from the decision of the Controller regarding entries in the omission register shall lie to the High Court, and such appeal shall be presented within ninety days of the Controller’s order. The omission register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public during office hours, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where the prescribed fee for maintaining the patent in force has not been paid. Any person desiring to inspect the omission register shall submit an application to the Controller in the manner as prescribed and shall pay the fee specified in the Schedule. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, permit inspection of the omission register. An entry in the omission register shall be prima facie evidence of non-payment of the renewal fee, however, a patentee may, within one month of receiving notice of such entry, submit proof of payment to the Controller. Provided that, if satisfactory evidence is not furnished, the patent shall be deemed to have lapsed as provided herein. The Controller shall remove the entry from the omission register upon verification of satisfactory evidence. Any incorrect entry in the omission register may be rectified by the Controller following a procedure consistent with principles of natural justice.

Any person desiring to record an omission in the register of patents, relating to a prior publication or other relevant matter impacting novelty or inventive step, shall submit a detailed statement of the omission to the Controller of Patents, accompanied by supporting evidence demonstrating the date and source of the prior art. The Controller, upon receiving such statement, shall cause a thorough examination to be conducted and, if satisfied of the validity of the claim of omission, shall direct the entry to be made in the omission register. Failure to provide sufficient evidence, or a demonstration of mala fide intent in seeking to record an omission, shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any false entry made or knowingly maintained in the omission register, as provided herein, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, subject to reasonable notice, remove any entry from the register found to be erroneous or irrelevant.

Any assignment or licensing of rights in a patent, whether complete or partial, shall be recorded in the register maintained for that purpose, and no such assignment or license shall be effective against any person other than the assignor or licensor until such recordation is complete. The Controller shall maintain an omission register detailing all known instances where required recordation has not occurred within a period of six months from the date of assignment or licensing. A party alleging non-recordation may apply to the Controller for inspection of the omission register, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where a valid assignment or license remains unrecorded after notice from the Controller, the patentee or assignee may be subject to a penalty as provided herein. The Controller may, at their discretion, extend the period for recordation if sufficient cause is demonstrated, but such extension shall not exceed three months. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be adjudicated separately, and recordation in the omission register does not constitute an admission of validity.

Any person alleging a grievance arising from an omission in the omission register maintained under this Act may submit a petition to the Controller of Patents, setting forth the grounds for such allegation and accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such petition, cause an inquiry to be conducted, affording the complainant and any party likely to be affected by the proposed rectification of the omission register an opportunity to be heard. If, following such inquiry, the Controller is satisfied that an omission exists which materially affects the rights of the complainant, the Controller shall direct the rectification of the omission register accordingly. Any decision of the Controller regarding rectification of the omission register shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Controller’s order. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedure for challenging entries in the omission register shall not preclude a subsequent challenge based on newly discovered evidence, subject to the discretion of the Appellate Board.

Any person alleging a discrepancy in the omission register maintained under this Act may lodge a complaint with the Controller of Patents, setting forth the particulars of the alleged omission and the grounds upon which the complaint is based. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such complaint, cause an inquiry to be conducted and shall, if satisfied that an omission has occurred, direct the rectification of the register. However, such rectification shall not be effected without affording the party concerned an opportunity to be heard. Where a complaint relates to an invention for which a provisional specification has been filed but not a complete specification, the Controller may, subject to the payment of prescribed fees, direct that the invention be noted in the omission register as a pending application. Any order of the Controller regarding the omission register shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the complaint inadmissible.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where the prescribed fees for maintaining the patent in force have not been paid. Any person desiring to inspect the omission register shall submit an application to the Controller in the manner as prescribed. The application shall clearly identify the patent in question, referencing at a minimum the patent number and the name of the patentee as recorded on the register of patents. Where a patentee seeks to restore a patent following omission from the register, they shall submit a request for restoration within the period stipulated under this Act, accompanied by payment of the prescribed restoration fee and any outstanding renewal fees. The Controller may, subject to verification of the request and payment, reinstate the patent and record the restoration in the omission register, noting the date of restoration for purposes identifying goods manufactured under the patent after such reinstatement. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the patent being deemed revoked.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where the prescribed fee for maintaining the patent in force has not been paid, and such omission shall be recorded within thirty days of the expiry of the final date for payment of the renewal fee. Any person, being the patentee or an interested party, may apply to the Controller for restoration of a patent noted in the omission register, subject to the payment of a prescribed restoration fee and proof of diligent efforts to pursue the patent application. An application permitted amended to include a claim to priority under this Act, may be considered by the Controller, provided that such amendment does not introduce matter extending beyond the content of the original application as filed. The Controller shall, following examination of the application and verification of fee payment, either reinstate the patent or issue a reasoned order of refusal, which order shall be communicated to the applicant in writing. Any appeal against such order shall lie to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where a reasonable request for amendment to correct a material error or omission has been repeatedly denied by the patent holder, and such omission affects the clarity of the scope of the invention. Any person alleging an omission impacting their ability to commercially exploit a patented invention may apply to the Controller for inclusion of relevant details in the omission register, providing documented evidence of prior attempts to engage with the patentee. Should the Controller determine a justifiable omission exists, entry in the register shall be made within thirty days. A finding of omission may, subject to established criteria, trigger consideration for a compulsory licence, allowing for exploitation of the invention upon reasonable terms determined by the Controller, to address demonstrable public need not adequately met by the patentee. The patentee shall be notified of any entry and have a right to appeal.

For the purposes of this Act, trade mark identity shall exist where two marks are indistinguishable in appearance, pronunciation, or meaning, when applied to goods or services relevant to registration. A determination of trade mark identity requires a holistic assessment, considering the overall impression created on the average consumer, and shall not be limited to a dissection of individual elements. However, minor variations in presentation, such as colour or font, that do not materially affect the overall impression, shall not negate a finding of identity. Where a mark incorporates elements identical to an earlier trade mark, and those elements are significant and distinctive, a presumption of likelihood of confusion may arise, subject to evidence demonstrating a lack of such confusion among relevant consumers. The proprietor of an earlier trade mark may initiate proceedings as provided herein to prevent the use of a subsequently registered mark demonstrating such identity.

A trade mark shall not be registered if it is identical with, or deceptively similar to, an existing trade mark registered under this Act in respect of identical or similar goods or services, and such identity or similarity is likely to cause confusion amongst the public. For the purposes of determining such likelihood of confusion, consideration shall be given to the overall impression created by the marks, including their visual, aural, and conceptual characteristics. Where a mark consists of elements that are customary in the trade concerned, the distinctiveness of those elements shall not be taken into account when assessing trade mark identity. However, a mark may be registered even if it resembles an earlier mark, provided that the proprietor of the earlier mark has consented to such registration, or that a period of five years has elapsed since the registration of the earlier mark without any objection being raised. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence of genuine use of the trade mark to establish its distinctiveness.

Any person who avails themselves of a registered trade mark, or a trade mark deemed to be registered under this Act, shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor without their consent, such use shall constitute an infringement of the trade mark identity, and the registered proprietor may initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction restraining such use. However, a registered proprietor shall not be entitled to restrain the use of their trade mark where such use is by way of fair comment or criticism of the goods or services offered under that trade mark. Provided that, any claim for infringement shall be subject to proof of likelihood of confusion amongst consumers, and the court may consider all relevant factors including the degree of similarity between the marks and the nature of the goods or services. The registered proprietor may also seek delivery up of infringing goods.

A trade mark shall be deemed to possess trade mark identity where it is identical in its entirety with an earlier trade mark, irrespective of whether the earlier trade mark is registered or unregistered, and relating to identical or similar goods or services. However, mere visual or phonetic resemblance shall not, in and of itself, establish trade mark identity; a comprehensive assessment of the marks as a whole, considering their overall impressions, shall be undertaken. Where a mark incorporates elements of an earlier mark but presents substantial differences, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, determine that no trade mark identity exists. 

The determination of identity, and the potential for confusion arising therefrom, shall be assessed from the perspective of an average consumer, exercising reasonable care and diligence. A finding of trade mark identity may, provided that a likelihood of confusion exists, be sufficient grounds for the refusal of registration or the revocation of an existing registration, as determined by the appropriate authority. Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to trade mark identity may appeal to the High Court.

A registered trade mark shall be deemed to possess trade mark identity where it is identical in its entirety with an earlier trade mark, irrespective of any minor differences in presentation, and relating to identical or similar goods or services as those for which the earlier trade mark is registered. However, a finding of trade mark identity may be rebutted by evidence demonstrating material differences in the overall impressions created by the marks, including but not limited to differences in font, colour, or stylistic elements, provided that such differences are significant enough to dispel any likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Where a mark incorporates elements of an earlier trade mark but presents a distinct and readily discernible overall character, it shall not be considered to possess trade mark identity as provided herein. Any determination of identity shall be subject to a comprehensive assessment of all relevant factors, including the conceptual similarity and visual resemblance of the marks, and the nature of the goods or services concerned.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark, and knowingly provides a false representation of facts concerning the trade mark’s identity, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Where a registered trade mark is deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark used by another, and such use has continued for a period exceeding three years, a court may, subject to proof of likelihood of confusion and damage, order rectification of the register. Any alteration made to a registered trade mark affecting its essential characteristics, without due application to the Registrar, constitutes a violation punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. Provided that, a finding of trade mark identity requires a holistic assessment of visual, aural, and conceptual similarities. The Registrar may, upon complaint, initiate an inquiry into any alleged misrepresentation or fraudulent practice related to trade mark ownership and may impose penalties as provided herein.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the assignor and the assignee, and such assignment shall not be valid unless recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, the validity of the assignment shall be determined with reference to the extent of goodwill assigned, and the assignee shall be entitled to the use of the trade mark only to the extent of such goodwill. A license to use a trade mark may be granted, either wholly or partially, and may be exclusive or non-exclusive, subject to provisions contained in the instrument creating such license. The proprietor of a trade mark may, as provided herein, assign the trade mark or any right therein, including the right to use, sell, or import goods bearing the trade mark. Establishing trade mark identity is crucial in determining the scope of any assignment or license, and the Registry shall consider all relevant factors to ascertain whether the assigned or licensed mark maintains its distinctiveness and avoids confusion with existing marks. Any dispute regarding trade mark identity shall be adjudicated in accordance with the procedures outlined under this Act.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to examination as provided herein, and the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information to determine the distinctiveness and ascertain the trade mark identity. Where an objection is raised by the Registrar based on an existing trade mark, the applicant may file a counter-statement, demonstrating that the marks are sufficiently dissimilar and do not create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Should the Registrar remain unconvinced, an appeal may be filed with the Appellate Board, which shall consider evidence regarding the overall impression created by the marks, including visual, aural, and conceptual similarities. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error, and any party aggrieved by such decision may seek recourse through writ petition before the High Court, subject to the limitations of time prescribed under this Act.

A trade mark shall be deemed to possess distinctive character where, as a result of its use, the public is able to identify the goods or services associated with the mark as originating from a particular undertaking. Notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, where a trade mark incorporates or is identical to a registered breeder variety, as defined under the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, the proprietor of the breeder variety shall have the right to demonstrate non-use of the trade mark in relation to goods or services not covered by the scope of protection afforded to the variety. However, such demonstration shall not, in itself, constitute grounds for revocation of the trade mark, unless it is established that the continued registration of the trade mark creates a likelihood of confusion or deception as to the origin or quality of the goods or services, or diminishes the distinctive character of the trade mark identity. Any application for registration involving a breeder variety shall clearly indicate the registered status of said variety.

Any registered geographical indication shall be subject to forfeiture upon a finding of abandonment, demonstrated by non-use for a continuous period of five years, as established through evidence presented to the Registrar. A registered proprietor, or a duly authorized user, may apply to the Registrar for a declaration of non-abandonment, providing satisfactory proof of continued use. Where a conviction is directed against any person for an offence involving the fraudulent application of a registered geographical indication, or for the sale of goods bearing a falsely applied geographical indication, the adjudicating court may, as provided herein, order the forfeiture of the goods so marked and any equipment used in the commission of the offence. Such forfeiture shall vest absolutely in the Central Government. The court shall, prior to any order of forfeiture directed conviction, provide the convicted party an opportunity to be heard and present evidence contesting the allegations. Any proceeds derived from the sale of forfeited goods shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any registered geographical indication shall be subject to forfeiture upon a finding of abandonment, which occurs where the registered proprietor ceases to exercise the rights conferred by this Act for a continuous period of not less than five years, and fails to provide satisfactory justification for such cessation to the Registrar. Furthermore, a registered geographical indication may be forfeited following a conviction for offences relating to the misrepresentation of goods as possessing a protected geographical indication, or for the sale of counterfeit goods bearing such an indication. A forfeiture directed conviction shall automatically extinguish all rights pertaining to the geographical indication, vesting ownership with the Central Government. Provided that, any person aggrieved by such forfeiture may, within a period of sixty days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the High Court. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all forfeited geographical indications, detailing the grounds for forfeiture and the date of the order.

A variety registered act, signifying the formal recognition of a new plant variety, shall be deemed complete upon the issuance of a certificate of registration by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, subject to the fulfillment of all criteria as laid down in this Act and the rules made thereunder. The breeder, upon registration, acquires the right to commercialize the protected variety, encompassing activities such as production, sale, and distribution, for a specified period. However, such rights shall not prejudice the rights arising under the Seeds Act, 1966, or any other law for the time being in force. Provided that the registered variety must demonstrably possess distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, and that the applicant has provided a complete and accurate description thereof, as verified through a prescribed examination process. Any transfer of rights relating to a variety registered act requires prior notification to the Authority.

A variety registered act under this Act shall be valid for a period of fifteen years from the date of notification of the variety, and may be renewed for successive periods of fifteen years, subject to the payment of a renewal fee and verification of continued distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The renewal application shall be submitted at least six months prior to the expiry of the initial or any subsequent period of validity. Where a registered variety is found to have lost its distinctiveness, uniformity or stability, the Registrar may, after giving the breeder an opportunity to be heard, revoke the registration. However, a farmer who has in good faith saved, sold, shared or multiplied any variety registered under this Act, in the exercise of his right as provided herein, shall not be liable for any infringement of the breeder’s rights. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Central Government.

A variety registered act under this Act shall vest in the breeder, subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions as provided herein. The registered breeder may institute civil proceedings in a competent court of jurisdiction for any infringement of his rights, including seeking injunctions, damages, and an account of profits. Any person cultivating, selling, or distributing a protected variety without authorization shall be liable for such infringement. The court, upon establishing infringement, may also order the destruction or disposal of infringing material, and may grant a decree for specific performance. 

Provided that, a farmer who is in lawful possession of seeds of a registered variety shall be permitted to retain and reuse those seeds for personal cultivation, subject to conditions that do not prejudice the rights of the breeder. The breeder shall have the right to seek royalties from any commercial exploitation of the variety, and the appropriate royalty rate shall be determined by the Central Government.

A variety registered act under this Act shall be valid for a period of fifteen years from the date of notification of the variety, and may be renewed for successive terms of fifteen years each, subject to the payment of a renewal fee as may be prescribed. The renewal application shall be submitted at least six months prior to the expiry of the original registration period, and failure to do so may result in the lapse of the registered act. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the registered act may be revoked by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority if it is established that the variety does not meet the criteria for registration as provided herein, or if the breeder has failed to comply with the conditions attached to the registration. Any person aggrieved by the revocation of a variety registered act may file an appeal before the designated appellate authority within sixty days of the order of revocation. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all registered varieties, accessible for inspection during office hours. The register shall contain details of the breeder, the variety characteristics, and the scope of the registered act.

A variety registered act under this Act shall be valid for a period of fifteen years from the date of notification of the variety, subject to the payment of renewal fees as prescribed. The renewal fee shall be payable at intervals of six years beginning after the expiry of the initial fifteen-year period, and failure to pay such fee within the stipulated time may result in the lapse of the registration, provided that a grace period of three months shall be allowed for payment with a late fee. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a registered variety may apply to the Central Government for redressal. The Central Government may, after conducting an inquiry, issue an order restraining the infringer and awarding damages to the breeder, considering the actual loss suffered and any reasonable royalty due. A farmer, however, shall be permitted to save, use, sow, re-sow and multiply any variety registered under this Act for purposes of propagation on his own land, provided that such farmer does not sell, market or distribute such saved material.

Any person who, without due authorization from the registered breeder of a variety registered act, engages in the production, sale, marketing, distribution, import or export of the protected plant variety, or commercially exploits the harvested material obtained from such variety, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The Central Government may, subject to an investigation and confirmation of such unauthorized activity, impose a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for the first offence. Subsequent offences shall attract a penalty not less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Any material used or resulting from the offence, including harvested material and equipment used in the unauthorized production, may be seized and disposed of as directed by a competent authority. Provided that, a farmer who is in possession of saved seed of a registered variety for personal cultivation shall not be held liable under this provision, subject to the conditions as provided herein regarding seed exchange and benefit sharing.

A variety registered act under this Act shall vest in the applicant, subject to the provisions relating to research and experimentation and the rights of farmers as provided herein. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered variety shall obtain a license from the breeder, and the terms of such license, including royalty rates and duration, shall be mutually agreed upon by both parties. Where a license is not granted, or where the terms offered are considered unreasonable, any interested party may apply to the Central Government for compulsory licensing, demonstrating sufficient cause and a viable commercialization plan. Assignment of the rights conferred by a variety registered act is permissible, but all assignments shall be recorded with the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. The breeder may, notwithstanding any assignment, retain the right to receive royalties as stipulated in the original licensing agreement, unless otherwise agreed in writing. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding licensing and assignment shall render the offender liable to penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a variety, or by any decision taken regarding the validity of a variety registered act, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the aggrieved party and the Registrar a reasonable opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal relates to a variety registered act concerning a farmer’s right or a breeder’s right, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the variety possesses distinctiveness, substantiality and stability, direct the Registrar to register the variety, provided that such direction shall be subject to the payment of prescribed fees. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties, except where a question of law of general public importance arises, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court.

A variety registered act under this Act shall vest in the applicant, subject to the provisions relating to research and experimentation and the rights of farmers as provided herein. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered variety, including propagation, multiplication, distribution, sale, and import or export, shall obtain a license from the breeder or his duly authorized agent, upon terms mutually agreed upon, or failing such agreement, determined by the Central Government. The licensing agreement may include provisions for royalty payments, quality control, and duration of the license, and shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a licensee sub-licenses rights relating to a variety, such sub-license shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the original license and require prior written consent of the breeder. In cases involving section 36e ixd concerning the transfer of rights to a corporate entity, due diligence regarding the original breeder’s claim shall be mandatory before approval. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as prescribed.

Any person who, without lawful authority, harvests, sells, exports, or imports any material of a registered plant variety, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, and shall be liable to a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees. Where the offence involves a commercial plant variety, the penalty may be doubled, and the Authority may, in addition to the monetary penalty, order the destruction of all harvested material and any equipment used in the commission of the offence. A breeder whose registered variety is so infringed may, subject to providing proof of damages, initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction restraining further infringement. The registration act breeder shall maintain accurate records of all transactions involving the registered variety, and failure to do so may be considered an aggravating factor in any enforcement action. Any false representation regarding the origin of planting material is also punishable as an offence.

Any person convicted of applying for registration of a trade mark known to be identical with a registered trade mark, or deceptively similar thereto, and intending to deceive or cause confusion, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than one year but which may extend to three years, and with fine, which may extend to three lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, at its discretion, impose a lesser imprisonment term if the applicant demonstrates substantial grounds for believing, albeit incorrectly, that the mark was not identical or deceptively similar. Furthermore, any imprisonment term shall run consecutively with any other sentence imposed for related offenses under this Act, and the court may order the destruction of all infringing materials. Subject to appeal, the decision of the court regarding the imprisonment term shall be final.

Any person found guilty of applying for registration of a trade mark known to be identical with a registered trade mark, or one deceptively similar thereto, and with the intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be punishable as provided herein. Where such application is made with knowledge of the prior registration, the term of imprisonment shall not be less than one year, but may extend to a term of three years, and a fine of not less than one lakh rupees may also be imposed. However, if the applicant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing in the validity of their claim, despite the existing registration, the court may, subject to the circumstances, reduce the imprisonment term to a minimum of six months. Provided that, in cases where the offence involves the sale of counterfeit goods bearing the deceptively similar trade mark, the imprisonment term shall not exceed five years, and the fine may extend to five lakh rupees. Any fine levied under this Act shall be payable to the Central Government. The court may, at its discretion, order the destruction of all counterfeit goods seized.

Any person found to be in unlawful possession of counterfeit goods bearing a registered trademark, as determined by a competent authority under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed. Provided that, if the goods are of such nature as to pose a direct and immediate risk to the health or safety of the public, the term of imprisonment shall not be less than one year, but may extend to five years, in addition to a fine not less than one lakh rupees. Furthermore, where the counterfeit goods are found to be packaged or labelled in a manner designed to deceive consumers, the imprisonment term shall be enhanced by a period of six months. Subject to due process and opportunity for defence, any individual abetting such activity shall be treated as a principal offender and similarly penalized. The court may, at its discretion, order the destruction of the counterfeit goods.

Any person found guilty of forging or unlawfully dealing with a trade mark, or applying a counterfeit mark to goods or services, as provided herein, shall be subject to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or to a fine, or to both. The extent of the imprisonment term shall be determined by the adjudicating authority, considering the nature and extent of the deception caused, and the value of the goods or services affected. Where the offence involves marks registered associated with essential medicines or public safety, the minimum imprisonment term shall not be less than one year. Provided that, if the offender proves, to the satisfaction of the court, that they acted in good faith and exercised due diligence to avoid committing the offence, the court may reduce the imprisonment term or impose a lesser fine. All seized counterfeit goods and materials used in the commission of the offence shall be liable to destruction, subject to any orders passed by the court regarding samples for evidence. Any person aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court.

The appropriate registry fee paid for each class of goods or services, as specified in the First Schedule, shall accompany every application for registration of a trade mark under this Act. Any application not accompanied by the prescribed registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and shall not be processed further, subject to the provisions herein. Where an applicant seeks to amend an application after submission, an additional fee, equivalent to fifty percent of the original registry fee for the relevant class, may be levied. Should the applicant fail to pay said additional fee within thirty days of notice, the amendment request shall be rejected. The Central Government reserves the right to revise the amounts of the registry fee through official notification, and such revisions shall apply prospectively. A reduced registry fee shall be applicable for natural persons and small enterprises, as defined by the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to grant a renewal of registration of a trade mark, or requiring an amendment to the register, may, within one month from the date of such decision, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a prescribed registry fee paid to the Registrar, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government and may be varied from time to time. Failure to remit the requisite registry fee within the stipulated period shall render the appeal inadmissible, and the Appellate Board shall not entertain the same. Provided that, if sufficient cause is shown, the Appellate Board may, subject to such terms as it deems fit, extend the time for payment of the fee. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of the fee, transmit the appeal and all relevant documents to the Appellate Board without delay. Any further fees relating to the conduct of the appeal itself shall be as prescribed.

The applicant shall ensure that the appropriate registry fee, as determined by the published schedule, accompanies the application for registration of a trade mark, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected under this Act. Any deficiency in the registry fee paid shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be granted a period of thirty days from the date of such communication to rectify the deficiency, subject to payment of a late fee as prescribed. Provided that, if the deficiency is not rectified within the stipulated period, the application shall stand abandoned. Where an application is rejected due to non-payment of the requisite registry fee, a fresh application may be filed, and shall be subject to all applicable fees as if it were an original application. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, revise the schedule of fees, and such revision shall come into effect on a date specified in the notification. Any dispute regarding the amount of the registry fee shall be subject to review by the Registrar.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall remit the prescribed registry fee at the time of filing the application, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. Should the applicant fail to pay the registry fee within thirty days of notice of deficiency, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, strike the application from the register of pending applications. Any erroneous or insufficient payment of the registry fee may be rectified by the applicant within fifteen days of notice, upon payment of a penalty not exceeding twice the original deficiency. Furthermore, any deliberate misrepresentation regarding the amount of the registry fee paid shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both. The Central Government reserves the right to revise the schedule of fees periodically, and such revisions shall be notified in the Official Gazette.

Any person to whom a trade mark has been registered shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to assign the trade mark and the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark in connection with the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered. An assignment shall not be valid unless the assignment is in writing and authenticated by the assignor. The assignee shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry to register themselves as the new proprietor of the trade mark. Such application for registration of assignment shall be accompanied by a prescribed registry fee paid to the Registrar. Where the assignment involves a transfer of goodwill, proof of such transfer shall be furnished with the application. The Registrar may, subject to verification of documents and satisfaction of conditions as provided herein, register the assignee as the proprietor. Failure to pay the requisite registry fee shall render the application incomplete and liable to rejection.

Any person aggrieved by the assessment of a registry fee paid under this Act, or by any decision of the Registrar refusing a reduction or refund of such fee, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented in writing within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision sought to be appealed against, and shall state the grounds upon which it is based. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the registry fee was assessed incorrectly or that undue hardship would result from its full payment, direct a reduction or refund, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. Provided that no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant has paid the disputed registry fee, or offered sufficient security for its payment, to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law.

The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon determination of a dispute regarding the appropriate registry fee paid for an application for registration, conduct a review of the submitted evidence of payment and the classification of goods or services relevant to the trade mark. Provided that, such review shall be initiated only upon receipt of a formal objection from a party alleging insufficient or incorrect payment. If the Registry finds that the fee paid is demonstrably less than that prescribed for the relevant class, it may issue a deficiency notice to the applicant, allowing a period of sixty days for rectification. However, a trade proprietor registered prior to the amendment of Schedule IV in 2018 shall not be subject to retrospective application of increased fees, subject to proof of continuous use of the mark. Any decision of the Registry may be appealed to the High Court, as provided herein, within ninety days of the issuance of the order.

The appropriate registry fee paid for any application for registration of a trade mark, or for any subsequent amendment, renewal, or transfer thereof, shall be determined by the Trade Marks Registry through notification published in the Official Gazette. Any application not accompanied by the prescribed registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to the provisions of this Act, accept a late payment of the registry fee with an additional surcharge, not exceeding fifty percent of the original fee, if sufficient cause is demonstrated by the applicant. However, failure to pay the registry fee within the stipulated period, even with the surcharge, shall result in the abandonment of the application. All fees received shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

The appropriate filed registry fee for each class of trade mark, as specified in the First Schedule, shall accompany the application for registration, and no application shall be deemed to be properly filed without such accompanying fee. Where an application is filed electronically, a reduced filed registry fee, not exceeding fifty percent of the standard fee, may be prescribed. Subject to rules made by the Controller, a request for restoration of an application, where the prescribed time for filing has lapsed, shall also be accompanied by a late filing fee, in addition to the original filed registry fee for the relevant class. Any discrepancy in the amount of the filed registry fee, or failure to remit the same within the stipulated period, may render the application liable to be abandoned as provided herein.

The applicant shall remit the prescribed filed registry fee for each class of goods or services in respect of which a trademark is sought to be registered, and such fee shall accompany the application for registration as provided herein. Should the application be found deficient in any respect, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a period of thirty days from the date of such requirement. Failure to rectify the deficiency within the stipulated period may render the application liable to be abandoned. Any additional fee for rectification or amendment of the application, beyond the initial filed registry fee, shall be determined in accordance with the Schedule annexed to these rules. Provided that, if the applicant is a small enterprise, a reduced rate of the filed registry fee may be applicable, contingent upon submission of supporting documentation establishing their status.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall submit the prescribed filed registry fee at the time of filing the application, and failure to do so shall render the application incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify different rates of the filed registry fee for different classes of goods or services, and may also prescribe a reduced fee for small enterprises or start-ups, subject to such conditions as it deems fit. If the applicant fails to pay the full filed registry fee within the stipulated time, the Registrar may issue a notice requiring payment within a further period, and upon failure to comply, the application shall be deemed to have been abandoned. Any fee paid in excess of the prescribed amount shall not be refundable, except in cases where the excess payment is attributable to an error on the part of the Trade Marks Registry. A valid receipt for the filed registry fee shall be furnished as proof of payment.

The applicant shall, upon submission of a complete application for registration of a trade mark, remit the prescribed filed registry fee to the Trade Marks Registry. The amount of the filed registry fee shall be determined by the class of goods or services to which the trade mark relates, as detailed in the First Schedule appended to these rules. Provided that, in cases where the applicant qualifies as a small enterprise, as defined under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, a reduced filed registry fee, being fifty percent of the standard amount, shall be applicable. Any application not accompanied by the correctly calculated filed registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be returned to the applicant, subject to a processing fee as may be prescribed. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, extend the time for payment of the filed registry fee, but only upon receipt of a reasoned request and payment of a late fee. Failure to remit the required fee within the extended period shall result in the abandonment of the application.

All applications for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by the prescribed filed registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Payment of the filed registry fee constitutes a condition precedent to the processing of any such application, and any application not so accompanied may be deemed incomplete and subject to rejection under this Act. Should the applicant seek to amend the application after submission, an additional fee, commensurate with the nature of the amendment, may be levied. Provided that, if the applicant is a start-up as defined by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, a reduced rate for the filed registry fee shall apply, subject to the submission of supporting documentation establishing their status. Failure to maintain annual renewal fees shall result in the removal of the trade mark from the register, as provided herein.

Any application for the registration of a trade mark not accompanied by the prescribed filed registry fee shall be deemed to be incomplete and shall not be processed further, and the applicant shall be notified of the deficiency within thirty days from the date of filing. Should the applicant fail to remit the deficient filed registry fee within ninety days of such notification, the application shall be treated as abandoned and shall be removed from the register of pending applications. The Registrar may, subject to justifiable cause and upon payment of a late fee equivalent to twice the original filed registry fee, accept a delayed payment up to a maximum of one hundred and eighty days from the initial filing date. Any person knowingly providing false information regarding the payment of the filed registry fee, with intent to deceive, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the transfer of title and the recording thereof in the Register of Trade Marks. The transferor shall, within the prescribed period, furnish the Registry with a statement of the particulars of the assignment, including the consideration paid, if any, and a copy of the assignment instrument. Upon receipt of such statement and instrument, and verification of the filed registry fee, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, record the assignment in the Register. Failure to pay the prescribed registry fee shall render the assignment ineffective as against any subsequent assignee or licensee unless rectified within a period of one year from the date of assignment. A properly recorded assignment shall vest the rights in the trade mark in the assignee, and the assignee may thereafter exercise all rights as if originally the registered proprietor, provided that any pending proceedings relating to the trade mark shall not be affected by such assignment without the consent of all parties.

The applicant shall ensure that the prescribed registry fee accompanies the application for registration of a trade mark, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected under this Act. Any dispute regarding the correct amount of the filed registry fee shall be adjudicated by the Registrar, whose decision shall be final and binding, subject to an appeal to the High Court. However, if the applicant claims to have remitted the fee but provides insufficient proof, the Registrar may require additional evidence within thirty days from the date of such request. Should the appeal to the High Court concern a claim of excessive fee levied, the appellant shall deposit the disputed amount with the Court as a prerequisite for the hearing of the appeal, and the Court may, after considering the merits of the case, direct refund or further adjustment of the amount.

The appropriate filed registry fee for an application for registration of a trade mark shall be determined in accordance with the First Schedule, and shall be non-refundable, irrespective of the outcome of the application, save as otherwise provided herein. Any application not accompanied by the prescribed filed registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and may be rejected by the Trade Marks Registry. A registered breeder of animals, seeking to register a trade mark specifically identifying their breeding stock, may be eligible for a reduced filed registry fee, subject to submission of documentary evidence of registration with the National Livestock Mission and compliance with all other requirements as stipulated in this Act. Payment of the filed registry fee constitutes acknowledgement of the applicant’s obligation to comply with all provisions of this Act.

The applicant shall remit the prescribed filed registry fee contemporaneously with the submission of the trade mark application, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The application registrar shall, upon verification of the accompanying fee, issue an official receipt acknowledging the payment and indicating the application number assigned. Should the filed registry fee be insufficient or incorrectly calculated, the application registrar may notify the applicant of the deficiency and grant a period of thirty days to rectify the same, subject to the payment of a late fee as specified in the First Schedule. Any application not rectified within the stipulated timeframe shall be treated as abandoned. The Central Government reserves the right to amend the schedule of fees through notification in the Official Gazette. All fees received shall be accounted for and deposited into the Consolidated Fund of India, and the application registrar shall maintain detailed records of all financial transactions relating to filed registry fees.

Any application for the registration of a trade mark which is accompanied by a deficient filed registry fee shall be deemed to be incomplete and notice of the deficiency shall be immediately served upon the applicant, requiring rectification within thirty days from the date of such notice. Failure to rectify the deficiency within the stipulated period shall result in the application being treated as abandoned, and no appeal shall lie against such abandonment. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe a late filing surcharge not exceeding fifty percent of the original filed registry fee, subject to justifiable cause being demonstrated by the applicant. Repeated failure to comply with the fee structure as provided herein, even with application of the surcharge, may render the applicant ineligible to file further applications for a period of one year. Any person contravening these provisions shall be liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees.

The appropriate registry fee for each class of trade mark, as specified in the First Schedule, shall accompany every application for registration made under this Act. Any application not accompanied by the prescribed registry fee shall be deemed to be invalid and may be rejected by the Trade Marks Registry without further notice to the applicant. Where an applicant seeks to revive a trade mark removed from the register for non-payment of the renewal fee, a revival fee, in addition to the prescribed renewal fee and any applicable surcharge, shall be payable as provided herein. The amount of any surcharge shall be determined by the Central Government and shall be proportionate to the length of the delay in payment of the registry fee or renewal fee. Payment of the registry fee constitutes a condition precedent to the processing of any request or application.

The applicant for registration of a trade mark shall submit the prescribed registry fee alongside the application for registration, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The amount of the registry fee shall vary according to the class of goods or services for which the trade mark is sought to be registered, and a schedule of such fees shall be publicly available on the official website of the Trade Marks Office. Any application for amendment of the register, or for renewal of registration, shall also attract a separate registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined based on the nature of the amendment or the remaining period of registration. Provided that, in cases where the applicant is a small enterprise or a start-up, as defined by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, a reduced registry fee may be applicable subject to fulfilling the conditions stipulated in the relevant notification. All fees paid under this Act shall be non-refundable except in cases of demonstrable clerical error by the Trade Marks Office.

The applicant for registration of a trade mark shall submit the prescribed registry fee alongside the application for registration, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. Any objection raised by the Trade Marks Registry regarding the application, and communicated to the applicant, shall attract a separate fee for its consideration, which shall be payable within the stipulated timeframe. Should the applicant fail to remit the prescribed fee for addressing the objection, the application shall stand abandoned. A request for restoration of an abandoned application, subject to fulfilling all other requirements, may be considered by the Registry upon payment of a restoration fee, which shall be double the original registry fee. The Central Government reserves the right to revise the schedule of fees through notification in the Official Gazette, and such revised fees shall come into effect on a date specified in the notification. Any fee paid erroneously or in excess may, at the discretion of the Registry, be adjusted against future liabilities or refunded to the applicant.

The appropriate registry fee for each class of trade mark, as specified in the First Schedule, shall accompany every application for registration made under this Act. Any application not accompanied by the prescribed fee shall be deemed to be invalid and shall not be processed further, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding rectification of defects. Where an applicant seeks to amend an application after filing, a supplementary registry fee, equivalent to fifty percent of the original fee for that class, shall be payable. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, waive or reduce the registry fee in cases of demonstrable financial hardship, provided that a formal application for such waiver, supported by relevant documentation, is submitted. Any appeal against a decision regarding a registry fee, or the refusal of a waiver, shall be made to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of the order. Failure to remit the required fee within the stipulated timeframe may result in the abandonment of the application, as provided herein.

The applicant shall remit the prescribed registry fee for each class of goods or services in respect of which a trademark is sought to be registered, and such fee shall be non-refundable, save as otherwise provided herein. Any application not accompanied by the full and correct registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and may be rejected without further notice to the applicant. A reduced registry fee may be applicable for natural persons and small enterprises, subject to the submission of supporting documentation establishing their eligibility as determined by the Registrar. Where an application is amended to include additional classes of goods or services, a supplementary registry fee corresponding to those additional classes shall become due and payable within one month of the amendment request. Failure to remit such supplementary fee may result in the amendment being disallowed. The Registrar may, at their discretion, waive a portion of the registry fee in cases of demonstrable financial hardship, provided that a detailed justification is submitted with the application.

Every application for the registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by the prescribed registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Failure to remit the full registry fee at the time of application shall render the application incomplete and liable to rejection, subject to an opportunity being given to the applicant to rectify the deficiency within thirty days of a notice issued by the Registrar. Any applicant who knowingly provides a false declaration regarding the payment of the registry fee, or attempts to evade payment, shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees. The Registrar may, however, extend the time for payment in exceptional circumstances, provided that a late payment surcharge, calculated at ten percent of the original fee, is also submitted. All fees collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any person seeking to assign or transmit a registered trade mark, or any right in respect of such trade mark, shall submit a request to the Trade Marks Registry accompanied by the prescribed registry fee. The amount of such fee shall be determined by the class of goods or services covered by the trade mark and the specific rights being transferred, as detailed in the First Schedule. A reduced registry fee shall apply where the assignment is made to a related entity, provided that such related entity demonstrates a legitimate business interest in the trade mark. Failure to remit the appropriate registry fee, or to provide accurate particulars regarding the assignment, may result in the request being deemed incomplete and subject to rejection. The Registry may, at its discretion, extend the time for payment of the fee upon receipt of a satisfactory explanation for the delay, but a penalty fee may be levied. All fees paid under this Act shall be non-refundable, except in cases of demonstrable clerical error by the Registry.

The applicant, aggrieved by a determination of the Registrar concerning the appropriate registry fee for an expedited examination, may lodge an appeal with the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of a prescribed appeal fee. This fee shall be non-refundable, except in circumstances where the Appellate Board finds the initial determination of the Registrar to be wholly without merit and demonstrably arbitrary. Any objection to the quantum of the registry fee must be raised within thirty days of the notification of assessment, failing which, the assessment shall be deemed final and binding. A request for review of the registry fee, supported by detailed justification of claimed financial hardship, may be considered by the Registrar, provided that such review does not operate as a stay of proceedings. The Appellate Board’s decision regarding the appeal fee, or any related costs, shall be final and not subject to further appeal, except on grounds of demonstrated procedural irregularity.

The applicant for registration of a trade mark shall submit the prescribed registry fee alongside the application for registration, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected as provided herein. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, amend the schedule of fees. Any registered user of a trade mark, seeking to record their registered user trade with the Trade Marks Registry, shall also remit a separate registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined based on the class of goods or services covered by the principal trade mark. Provided that, a reduction in the applicable registry fee may be granted to applicants demonstrating status as a micro, small or medium enterprise, subject to verification of relevant documentation. All fees received shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. The Registrar may, at their discretion, extend the time for payment of any fee upon receipt of a valid request and payment of a late fee.

The appropriate registry fee for each class of trade mark, as specified in the First Schedule, shall accompany every application for registration made under this Act. Any application for registration originating from outside India, and filed as an application india, shall be subject to an additional fee equivalent to fifty percent of the prescribed registry fee for each class, to cover administrative costs associated with international processing. Should an applicant seek expedited processing of their application, a surcharge, not exceeding twice the standard registry fee for the relevant class, may be levied, subject to the discretion of the Registrar. Payment of the registry fee shall be accepted in Indian Rupees or in freely convertible foreign currency, as determined by the Central Government. Failure to remit the full and correct registry fee with the application shall render the said application incomplete and liable to be rejected, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the appropriate registry fee shall be adjudicated by the Registrar, whose decision shall be final.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to a prescribed registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined by the Trade Marks Office and publicly available. The assignee, or applicant intending assignment, may apply to the Trade Marks Office for a statement of the applicable fee schedule. Should the assignee be a patentee already registered under the Patents Act, 1970, a reduced registry fee, not exceeding fifty percent of the standard rate, may be considered, provided that the patent and trade mark are for related goods or services. Failure to remit the appropriate registry fee within thirty days of the assignment agreement shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the original proprietor. The Trade Marks Office reserves the right to revise these fees periodically, with notification published in the Official Gazette. Any dispute regarding the amount of the fee shall be subject to appeal as provided herein.

A geographical indication shall be understood as an indication that identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, serves to distinguish it from goods of similar nature which do not possess such qualities. The reputation of a registered geographical indication may, notwithstanding the continued use of the indication, be lost if the good no longer possesses the characteristics that formed the basis for its registration. Any association of producers seeking registration of a geographical indication shall be constituted as a registered association, or where no such association exists, the applicant shall demonstrate the support of producers in the specified region. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Registrar may, after examination, register the geographical indication.

Any person claiming to be interested in the registration of a geographical indication, and being the applicant, shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of proposed use of the geographical indication. The application shall clearly identify the goods to which the geographical indication relates, and shall delineate the geographical area within India constituting the region of origin. A register of all registered geographical indications shall be maintained by the Registry, open for inspection by the public subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Registration of a geographical indication shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. However, such right shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, and shall not prevent other producers within the defined geographical area from using descriptive terms customary in their trade. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of a registered geographical indication may be adjudicated as provided herein.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a registered geographical indication that is falsely represented as originating from a region to which it does not belong shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein, and the goods so represented shall be deemed counterfeit goods for the purposes of seizure and destruction. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to seek an injunction from a court of competent jurisdiction restraining such acts of misrepresentation, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to such unlawful use. A collective body representing producers of the registered geographical indication may, with the leave of the court, institute legal proceedings on behalf of its members. Subject to due process, the court may order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the false geographical indication, and may also impose a fine on the offender. Provided that, any action taken under this Act shall be without prejudice to any other remedies available under existing laws. The Registrar may maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications, accessible for inspection during office hours.

Any person claiming to be interested in the manufacture or business of goods to which a registered geographical indication applies may, subject to the payment of such fee as may be prescribed, apply to the Registrar for registration as a registered proprietor of such geographical indication. The application shall be in the prescribed form and shall include a statement of the particulars of the applicant, including name, address, and a description of the goods in relation to which the geographical indication is sought to be registered. Where a collective body, such as a producers’ organization, applies for registration of a registered geographical indication on behalf of its members, the application shall demonstrate adequate representation and authority to act on behalf of said members. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the application meets the requirements as provided herein, register the applicant as the registered proprietor, and a certificate of registration shall be issued. Any alteration in the registered proprietor’s name or address shall be notified to the Registrar in the manner prescribed.

A geographical indication registered under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor, or those authorized by them, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. This right extends to preventing all acts of unauthorized use of such registered geographical indication by any person not authorized, including acts of manufacture or trade. However, honest local use of a name or indication identical with the registered geographical indication, provided that such use has been continuous prior to the date of registration, shall not be considered an infringement as provided herein. Any person alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication may apply to the appropriate court for an injunction and damages. The court, upon being satisfied of the infringement and the extent of damage, may grant an injunction restraining the infringing acts and award damages not exceeding a sum to be determined by the court, subject to proof of actual loss or reasonable license fee. Failure to comply with the terms of any injunction issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court.

Any person causing false indication regarding goods bearing a registered geographical indication shall be liable to a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees, and the goods bearing such false indication shall be liable to seizure and destruction, as determined by a Magistrate of First Class or higher. Where a registered geographical indication has been falsely represented as originating from a region other than the true geographical area, the Court may, subject to the provisions herein, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from such misrepresentation and order delivery up and destruction of the offending goods. Any act of counterfeiting a registered geographical indication, or the packaging thereof, intending to deceive the public, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, with or without fine. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause shown, initiate suo motu inquiries into alleged violations of rights relating to a registered geographical indication.

Any person being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of the registration, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment, transfer or disposal of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an application in writing to the Registrar, specifying the terms and conditions of such assignment, transfer or disposal, and shall be registered in the Register. The Registrar may, prior to registration of such assignment, require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary to ascertain the validity of the transfer and protect the interests of producers associated with the registered geographical indication. Where a registered geographical indication is assigned, the assignee shall, subject to the terms of the assignment, possess all the rights and be subject to all the liabilities of the original proprietor. A licensee of a registered geographical indication may, with the consent of the proprietor, further license its use to others, provided that such sub-licensing arrangements do not contravene any conditions stipulated in the original license or as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or by any order made in respect of a registered geographical indication including an order for revocation, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of the decision or order appealed against, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, prior to disposal of the appeal, require the appellant to deposit with such Board such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount of the registration fee or the fee for renewal, as a condition for proceeding with the appeal. A registered geographical indication shall not be subject to transfer except with the prior permission of the Appellate Board, and any transfer without such permission shall be void. The Board’s decision on appeal shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ jurisdiction.

Any registered geographical indication shall, upon registration in the register maintained under this Act, confer upon the applicants, as defined herein, the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered.
