This right shall extend to preventing all acts of unauthorized use of such registered geographical indication by any person not authorized by the proprietor. However, honest local use of a geographical indication, or a name identical therewith, shall not be considered an infringement, provided that such use has been continuous prior to the date of application for registration. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register, and the Registrar shall, subject to due process, maintain an omission register detailing any such rectified entries. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding the use of a registered geographical indication may result in penalties as prescribed.

Any person being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, or a licensee authorized by such proprietor, may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, grant licenses to other persons for the use of the registered geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any assignment of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an investigation by the Registrar to ensure the assignee is demonstrably connected to the geographical area and possesses the requisite expertise to maintain the quality standards associated with the indication. The Registrar may, during such procedure investigation, require submission of evidence relating to the assignee’s production facilities, quality control mechanisms, and historical ties to the geographical area. Licenses granted under this Act shall be recorded with the Registrar, and any transfer of such license shall also be subject to similar notification and potential investigation. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment or licensing may render the registration of the geographical indication liable to revocation.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a geographical indication, or by any order made by the Registrar regarding the amendment, assignment, or transfer of a registered geographical indication, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such india application shall be filed within three months from the date of the order appealed against, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a certified copy of the order. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of an appeal concerning a registered geographical indication, may, if it deems necessary, require the appellant to furnish further evidence or clarification. Provided that, the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal unless it is satisfied that the appellant has a substantial and genuine interest in the geographical indication in question. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court. The Registrar shall give effect to the orders of the Appellate Board relating to a registered geographical indication without delay.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “director” in relation to a cinematograph film, shall mean the person who exercises overall creative control over the works incorporated therein, including but not limited to the artistic direction, visual composition, and narrative elements, and who is primarily responsible for the realization of the film as a unified artistic expression. A producer may, subject to a written agreement with the author of the copyright, be considered a director if they demonstrably exercise such control. Where a film results from a collaborative effort, the director shall be designated by the producer and such designation shall be conclusive, provided that the designated director possesses the requisite creative authority as herein defined. Any dispute regarding the exercise of creative control shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to ownership of copyright.

A person shall be considered a director of a cinematograph film for the purposes of registration under this Act, if such person exercises, whether alone or in conjunction with others, the principal authority over the creative aspects of the film’s production. Such authority shall encompass, but not be limited to, overall artistic control, including decisions relating to scripting, casting, cinematography, and final editing. Provided that a person claiming the status of director must demonstrate substantial creative contribution to the finished work, evidenced by documented involvement throughout key stages of production. Where a film is directed by a collective of individuals, all persons demonstrably exercising principal authority as described herein may be registered as joint directors. The Register of Copyrights may, subject to verification of submitted evidence, record the name and address of the director or directors as part of the film’s copyright entry. Any dispute regarding the designation of a director shall be resolved through evidence presented to the Register.

A director of a cinematograph film shall be deemed the author of the film, subject to any agreement to the contrary executed between the director and the producer, and shall possess the exclusive right to reproduce, communicate, and adapt the film as provided herein. However, where a work is commissioned, the commissioner shall, unless otherwise agreed, be entitled to the copyright in such work. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of the director’s copyright may, after providing reasonable notice of such infringement to the alleged infringer, apply to the District Court for an injunction restraining further infringement. The Court, upon being satisfied of the validity of the claim and the likelihood of continued infringement, may grant such injunction, and may also order the impounding and destruction of all infringing copies. A director may assign their copyright by instrument in writing, and such assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding transfer of copyright. Failure to comply with the terms of any assignment shall constitute a breach of contract, for which remedies may be sought in a court of competent jurisdiction.

A person appointed as a director of a copyright society shall, prior to assuming office, declare in a prescribed manner any direct or indirect interest which he may possess, whether as proprietor, shareholder, employee, or otherwise, in any undertaking that may be affected by the activities of the society. The Central Government may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, remove a director who has failed to make such a declaration or has provided a false declaration. Any vacancy arising from such removal shall be filled in accordance with the rules of the society, provided that the total number of directors does not fall below the minimum prescribed under this Act. 

A director shall exercise reasonable care and diligence in the performance of their duties and shall be jointly and severally liable with other directors for any loss or damage caused to the society through their negligence or misconduct. The director may request access to records and shall be entitled to reimbursement of reasonable expenses incurred in attending meetings and performing duties as provided herein.

A person shall be deemed to be a director of a work, for the purposes of determining entitlement to royalties and equitable remuneration as provided herein, if that person exercises, or is reasonably capable of exercising, control over the creative decisions relating to the work’s creation, including but not limited to, substantial direction of the literary, dramatic, musical or artistic elements. Provided that, a person merely providing funding or general oversight, without demonstrable influence on the creative process, shall not be considered a director. Where a work is created collaboratively, all persons meeting the criteria outlined herein shall be jointly designated as directors, and their respective shares of entitlement shall be determined by mutual agreement or, failing such agreement, by an independent assessment. Any dispute regarding the designation of a director, or the apportionment of entitlements amongst directors, may be subject to judicial review. A registered society, acting through its authorized representative, may also function as a director.

Any person who controls the creation of a cinematograph film, and is designated as the director thereof, shall be responsible for ensuring full compliance with all provisions of this Act relating to moral rights and economic rights in the underlying work adapted for the film. Should a director knowingly permit the inclusion of any material infringing copyright, or fail to secure necessary licenses as provided herein, they shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any director found to have deliberately misrepresented authorship or concealed relevant information regarding the origin of any incorporated work shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The liability of the director shall be independent of any liability attaching to the producer or any other party involved in the production or distribution of the film.

Any person who, by virtue of being a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, has exercised control over the creation of a cinematograph film, shall be deemed the first owner of the copyright in that film, subject to any agreement to the contrary executed prior to the commencement of the film’s production. However, such ownership shall not extend to any underlying literary or musical work incorporated within the film, the copyright in which shall remain vested in the author or authors thereof, unless expressly assigned as provided herein. A director may, by written instrument, assign all or any of their rights in the copyright of the cinematograph film to another person or entity, and such assignment shall be effective upon registration with the Registrar of Copyrights. Where a director is appointed by a producer solely for the purpose of directing the film, and receives consideration therefor, it shall be presumed that any copyright arising from the direction is owned by the producer, unless otherwise stipulated in a written contract. Any dispute regarding the ownership of copyright between a director and a producer shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to licensing and royalty payments.

A person appointed as director of a cinematograph film shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with all provisions of this Act relating to the exhibition thereof, and any failure to do so may attract penalties as provided herein. However, such responsibility shall not extend to acts committed independently by the cinema owner or operator, unless it is established that the director had knowledge of, and wilfully permitted, such acts. Any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the appropriate authority alleging a breach of duty by a director, and such authority shall conduct an inquiry, affording the director a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Should the inquiry confirm a violation, the authority may impose a fine, or, in cases of repeated or egregious offences, recommend suspension of the director’s authorization to oversee film exhibitions, subject to appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s decision shall be final.

Any person claiming to be a director of a copyright society, or intending to assign their rights in a cinematograph film, shall furnish to the licensing authority a statement in the prescribed form, detailing the nature and extent of their directorial or ownership interest. Such statement shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the entry register maintained by the society, verifying the director’s position and authority to act on behalf of the collective. Where a director’s mandate is subject to conditions, these shall be clearly articulated in the statement. Assignment of copyright, or a license to reproduce a work, may be deemed invalid if the assigning director lacked the necessary authorization, subject to a period of thirty days for rectification. The licensing authority shall maintain a public record of all such statements and associated entries, accessible for inspection as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions shall attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees.

Any person claiming to be the director of a work, and asserting authorship under this Act, shall furnish to the registering authority a declaration verifying the veracity of such claim, and detailing the extent of their creative contribution. Should a dispute arise concerning the true director of a cinematograph film, as alleged by multiple parties, the registering authority may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence of directorial control, including but not limited to, script approvals, final cut authority, and documented budgetary oversight. In the event of a contested claim and demonstrable misrepresentation, the registering authority shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the appropriate court, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register and potential imposition of penalties as deemed fit. Provided that, a bona fide director, acting under reasonable belief, shall not be penalized for unintentional errors in the initial declaration. Any appeal against the decision of the registering authority shall lie before the High Court.

A director, for the purposes of this Act, shall mean any person who is vested with the general management and superintendence of the affairs of an entity capable of owning copyright, whether incorporated or not. Such a director shall be accountable for ensuring compliance with all provisions relating to copyright ownership, licensing, and infringement occurring within the scope of their directorial responsibilities. Where a copyright work is subject to a patent application claiming inventive step relating to its creation or exploitation, the director shall maintain records demonstrating due diligence in assessing potential patent conflicts. Provided that a director may delegate specific tasks related to copyright management, but shall remain ultimately responsible for oversight. Any failure to exercise reasonable care in these matters may constitute grounds for action as provided herein.

The appellate board shall be comprised of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint. Members appointed to the appellate board shall be persons of eminence in the fields of law, science, technology, the arts, or commerce, and possess such experience as may be prescribed. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the appellate board may regulate its own procedure. Any decision of the appellate board shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal to the Supreme Court of India lies on a question of law. The appellate board shall have the powers of a civil court in respect of the summoning of witnesses and the production of documents, as are necessary for the proper adjudication of matters before it.

The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Works, detailing all particulars of copyright ownership and licensing as submitted by applicants. Any person claiming copyright in a work shall submit an application for registration to the Registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a true copy of the work itself. The application shall clearly state the author, publisher, and date of first publication. Should the Registrar require further clarification or evidence, the applicant shall furnish the same within thirty days. 

An appellate board shall be constituted to hear and determine any objection or appeal arising from a decision of the Registrar regarding the registration of copyright. The composition and procedure of the appellate board shall be as prescribed, and its decisions shall be final and binding, subject to writ jurisdiction. Failure to register a work shall not prejudice the right of copyright, but registration shall create a presumption of valid copyright and facilitate legal proceedings.

The appellate board shall, upon receipt of a petition alleging infringement of copyright, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the matter falls within its jurisdiction as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the licensing authority may, subject to the payment of such fee as may be prescribed, prefer an appeal to the appellate board within ninety days from the date of the said order. The appellate board may, if it deems necessary, require the petitioner to furnish evidence of irreparable harm likely to be caused if interim relief is not granted, and shall consider such evidence in its determination. Provided that the appellate board may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to explore the possibility of amicable settlement through mediation. All decisions of the appellate board shall be communicated in writing to the parties concerned, and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The appellate board shall, upon receipt of a petition alleging infringement of copyright and disputing the royalty rates fixed by the licensing authority, constitute a special bench comprised of at least three members possessing expertise in the relevant field of creative work. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the licensing authority regarding compulsory licenses, as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the appellate board within ninety days of the date of the impugned order. The appellate board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period by a further thirty days. All proceedings before the appellate board shall be conducted in accordance with regulations framed for the purpose, ensuring principles of natural justice are strictly observed. Evidence submitted shall be treated as confidential unless otherwise directed by the board. The appellate board shall endeavor to dispose of all appeals within one hundred and eighty days from the date of their institution, and its decisions shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of legal error.

The appellate board shall, upon receipt of a petition alleging infringement of copyright in a cinematograph film, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists, and shall, if satisfied, issue notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to submit a statement of account within thirty days. Provided that, such notice may also require the alleged infringer to disclose details of all copies distributed, and the revenue derived therefrom, subject to verification by an independent auditor appointed by the board. Any party failing to comply with the requirements of this notice shall be deemed to have admitted the allegations contained within the petition. The appellate board may, further, direct the impounding of infringing copies pending a full hearing, and shall ensure that such impounded copies are securely stored at a location designated by the board. All decisions of the appellate board shall be communicated in writing to all parties concerned.

The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging infringement of copyright as provided herein, conduct a preliminary inquiry to ascertain the veracity of the allegations and the potential gravity of the offense. If, following such inquiry, the Appellate Board is satisfied that a prima facie case exists, it shall issue a notice to the alleged infringer, requiring them to submit a written response within thirty days. Failure to respond to said notice, or submission of a response deemed unsatisfactory by the Appellate Board, shall constitute an admission of guilt and may result in the imposition of a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any person knowingly providing false information to the Appellate Board during the course of an investigation shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause, direct the seizing of infringing materials and their submission as evidence.

Any assignment of copyright, whether whole or partial, and whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be made by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor or duly authorised agent. Where the copyright is assigned in respect of a future work, the instrument shall identify the work with reasonable particularity and shall be subject to the condition that the work is actually created. The appellate board shall, upon application by any party claiming an interest in the copyright, adjudicate disputes arising from the validity or scope of any assignment, including the determination of fair consideration. Provided that, no assignment of copyright shall be effective until intimation of such assignment is given to the Registrar of Copyrights as prescribed. The Registrar may maintain a register of assignments and shall, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, make such register available for inspection. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the appellate board may, within sixty days, file an appeal to the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Officer, refusing or revoking a license to translate or reproduce a work, or imposing unreasonable conditions on such license, shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the appellate board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding condonation of delay as provided herein. The appellate board shall, upon receipt of an appeal and after giving the Licensing Officer an opportunity to be heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order. Provided that, the appellate board may, if it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the royalty that would have been payable had the license been granted unconditionally. Further, any party disputing the determination of royalty rates by the Licensing Officer may also approach the appellate board for redressal, demonstrating justifiable cause for disagreement with the assessed value.

The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a copyright register, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Where an application is found to be incomplete or deficient, the Appellate Board shall notify the applicant, specifying the deficiencies and granting a period of thirty days to remedy them. Any application not remedied within the stipulated period shall be deemed to be withdrawn, and no further consideration shall be given to it. However, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend this period if sufficient cause is demonstrated. Respect registered application, the Board shall ensure that all submissions relating to the rectification request are duly documented and maintained as part of the official record. The Appellate Board shall issue its reasoned order within one hundred and eighty days of the completion of the evidentiary proceedings. Failure to do so shall require a written explanation to the Registrar.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the District Court relating to copyright infringement, or the grant or refusal of a license under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the appellate board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order, subject to the appellate board being satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay. The appellate board may, if it deems necessary, require the appellant to furnish evidence of payment of court fees as prescribed by law. Provided that, the appellate board shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant demonstrates a substantial question of law involved in the case. All decisions of the appellate board shall be communicated in writing to the District Court and the parties concerned, and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The appellate board may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to appear before it in person.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights regarding the registration of a work, or the refusal or revocation thereof, shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of such appeal and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, conduct a hearing wherein both the appellant and the Registrar shall be afforded an opportunity to present their respective cases. Where the work in question originates from a 6referred convention country, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, consider any relevant documentation establishing the author’s claim to copyright in that country, provided such documentation is duly authenticated and translated as required. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a further appeal lies to the High Court as provided herein. All records pertaining to appeals before the Appellate Board shall be maintained in a secure and accessible manner.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act may present a court application to the High Court having jurisdiction over the alleged infringement. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the grounds for the allegation, including specific instances of the infringing act and identification of the defendant. The court may, subject to verification of the patent’s validity and the applicant’s standing, direct the defendant to furnish evidence relating to the alleged infringing activity. Provided that, the court may also require the applicant to furnish security for costs, to prevent frivolous or vexatious court applications. Any order made regarding security for costs shall be subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any person desiring to challenge the validity of a patent granted under this Act may lodge a court application with the High Court having territorial jurisdiction over the principal place of business of the patentee. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent and a statement of grounds on which the validity of the patent is contested, supported by relevant prior art and technical evidence. The applicant shall simultaneously serve a copy of the application and supporting documents upon the patentee, who may, within ninety days of such service, file a counter-statement. Provided that, the Court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the time for filing the counter-statement. All evidence presented shall be admissible as per the rules of civil procedure, and the Court may appoint an expert assessor to assist in the technical evaluation of the patent’s validity, if deemed necessary. The Court shall, after considering all evidence and submissions, issue a reasoned order either upholding or revoking the patent.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act may make a court application to a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringement occurred. The application shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the grounds for the allegation, including specific acts constituting the infringement and evidence reasonably believed to be in the possession of the applicant. The Court may, subject to verification of the grounds, issue a summons to the alleged infringer requiring them to appear and present their defense. A defendant, upon receipt of such summons, may file a counter-statement asserting the validity of their actions or challenging the patent’s legitimacy. Provided that, the Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to explore amicable resolution through mediation, but such mediation shall not be compulsory. The Court, upon hearing both sides and considering the evidence, shall determine whether infringement has occurred and may grant such relief as is just and equitable, including injunctions and damages. Any order made by the Court shall be enforceable as if it were a decree.

Any person desiring to challenge the validity of a patent granted under this Act may lodge a court application with the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent in question, alongside a detailed statement of grounds upon which the challenge is based, specifying with particularity the alleged deficiencies in the patent’s novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability. The applicant shall simultaneously serve a copy of the application and supporting documents upon the patentee, affording them a period of sixty days to file a counter-statement. The Court may, subject to due process and consideration of the evidence presented, direct the appointment of a technical expert to assess the validity of the patent. Provided that, the Court may, at its discretion, dismiss frivolous or vexatious applications and impose costs upon the applicant. Any evidence submitted shall be governed by the rules of evidence as applicable in civil proceedings, and the burden of proof rests with the applicant.

Any person desiring to challenge the validity of a patent granted under this Act shall submit a court application to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the patent in question, a detailed statement of grounds for challenging the validity, and a prescribed fee. Subject to verification by the Registrar of Patents, the High Court may, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, direct the patent holder to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days. Provided that the applicant shall demonstrate sufficient and substantial public interest in the matter, and shall not be a competitor engaged in identical technological pursuits. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render the court application inadmissible, and the High Court may impose costs on the applicant. Any evidence submitted as part of the court application shall be admissible as per the rules of civil procedure.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act may submit a court application to the High Court having jurisdiction over the alleged infringement. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed affidavit outlining the grounds for the allegation, including specific instances of unauthorized manufacture, use, sale, or import of the patented invention. The Court may, subject to verification of the affidavit and supporting evidence, issue a summons to the alleged infringer requiring a response within thirty days. Failure to respond to the summons, or failure to provide adequate evidence to rebut the claims of infringement, shall constitute contempt of court and may result in a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. The Court, as provided herein, reserves the right to award damages and injunctive relief to the patent holder upon establishing infringement. Any frivolous or vexatious court application shall be subject to costs, as determined by the Court.

Any person desiring to obtain a license under a patent, or to assign an interest in a patent, shall submit a formal court application to the appropriate High Court. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the grounds for seeking the license or assignment, including but not limited to, evidence of diligent efforts to secure terms from the patent holder. The Court may, subject to verification of the applicant’s standing and the validity of the patent, direct the patent holder to appear and show cause why the requested license or assignment should not be granted. Provided that, the Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant to furnish security for costs. Where an application for assignment is contested, the Court shall consider the commercial value of the patent and the potential public benefit accruing from the proposed transfer of ownership. The Court’s decision on any such court application shall be final and binding, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act may apply to the High Court having jurisdiction over the alleged infringement. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of the grounds for the claim, including specific particulars of the patented invention and the manner of its alleged infringement. The Court, upon receiving such an application, may direct the alleged infringer to furnish evidence relating to the validity of the patent and the nature of the alleged infringing activity. Provided that, if the applicant fails to demonstrate a prima facie case of infringement, the Court may dismiss the application with costs. An appeal from any order of the High Court regarding such a court application shall lie to the Supreme Court, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. The Court may, at its discretion, grant interim injunctions pending the final determination of the matter.

Any person claiming infringement of a patent, or alleging a threat of infringement, may present a court application to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, seeking such relief as is permissible under this Act. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the grounds for the claim, and shall be served upon the alleged infringer. Where the alleged infringement relates to a dramatic work performed publicly, the application shall specifically identify the performances constituting the infringement, including dates, venues, and the nature of the performance. The Court may, subject to verification of the patent’s validity, grant an injunction restraining further infringement, or award damages for past infringement, as deemed appropriate. Provided that, the Court may require the applicant to furnish security for costs.

A description trade mark shall be a mark consisting exclusively of descriptive words or indications which may serve in trade to designate the characteristics of goods or services. Such a mark may be registered as a trade mark, provided that use has resulted in distinctiveness. Where a description trade mark is sought to be registered, the applicant shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that through prolonged use, the relevant section of the public recognizes the mark as uniquely identifying the goods or services. A mark which is merely laudatory or which fails to acquire distinctiveness shall not be registrable as a description trade mark under this Act, even if extensive advertising has been undertaken. The Registrar may require evidence of actual and continuous use for a period not less than five years.

A trade mark consisting exclusively of signs capable of being represented graphically and indicating characteristics which may serve to distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings may be registered under this Act, provided that such signs do not fall within the exceptions specified herein. A description trade mark, being a mark comprising descriptive words or phrases relating to the goods or services sought to be identified, shall not be registered unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. Evidence of such acquired distinctiveness, including but not limited to, duration of use, extent of use, and advertising expenditure, shall be submitted with the application for registration. However, a mark which is merely laudatory or descriptive of the quality of the goods or services shall not be registrable, even with evidence of use, subject to the provisions relating to secondary meaning. An applicant seeking registration of a description trade mark shall demonstrate that the relevant public recognizes the mark as uniquely identifying the applicant’s goods or services.

A trade mark consisting exclusively of signs or designations which may serve to designate the characteristics of goods or services shall be registrable as a description trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. An application for the registration of a description trade mark shall be examined as to its distinctiveness, and the Registrar may require evidence that the sign or designation has acquired distinctiveness through use. Where a description trade mark includes matter customary in the trade, registration shall not be refused by reason only of the matter being customary, provided that such matter does not deprive the trade mark of its distinctive character. The Registrar may, however, require a disclaimer of any such customary matter. 

Any person opposing the registration of a description trade mark may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition, setting out the grounds on which the opposition is based. Such opposition shall be subject to the provisions relating to opposition proceedings as provided herein, and the onus of proving the grounds for opposition shall lie on the opponent.

Any person who uses a description trade mark, being a mark consisting exclusively of descriptive words or phrases directly denoting the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of the goods or services concerned, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, provided that such use does not acquire distinctiveness through prolonged and widespread use amongst the relevant public. Where a trade mark application seeks registration of a description trade mark, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require evidence of acquired distinctiveness before proceeding with examination. Failure to furnish satisfactory evidence of acquired distinctiveness within a period of six months from the date of such requirement shall render the application liable to be refused. Any person contravening the provisions herein relating to description trade marks shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, in cases of repeated infringement, order the destruction of all infringing goods.

A description trade mark, being a mark consisting of a description of the characteristics, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or the like of goods or services, shall be registrable under this Act subject to the provisions herein contained. Any assignment of a description trade mark shall be contingent upon the continued accurate representation of the described characteristics; a material alteration to those characteristics, post-assignment, may render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee, provided that such alteration substantially impacts consumer perception. Licensing of a description trade mark shall require a detailed schedule specifying the precise characteristics being licensed, and the licensor retains the right to audit the licensee’s adherence to said description. Where a description trade mark incorporates geographical origin as a defining characteristic, any change in the source of the goods or services necessitates prior written consent from the proprietor, failing which the license or assignment shall be deemed lapsed. The Registrar may, upon application, direct rectification of the register if a description trade mark is found to be falsely representing goods or services.

A trade mark comprising a description of the characteristics, quality, or quantity of the goods or services sought to be identified shall not be registrable unless such description is distinctive and not merely descriptive of the goods or services themselves. However, a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through long and continuous use may, subject to the provisions of this Act, be registered. An application for registration of a description trade mark shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a period of not less than five years of continuous use in commerce, and a clear showing that consumers primarily perceive the description as a brand identifier rather than a mere statement of fact. Any objection raised by the Registrar regarding lack of distinctiveness shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates a prima facie case of acquired distinctiveness based on evidence of extensive advertising and sales figures. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition.

For the purposes of this Act, a description trade mark shall consist of letters, numerals, or any combination thereof, capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include a reference to a characteristic of the goods or services themselves, provided that such description is not directly descriptive of the goods or services concerned. Where a trade mark incorporates a description, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence demonstrating that the mark has acquired distinctiveness through use. It is clarified that, in matters relating to novelty and inventive step, the principles governing treaty means patent applications shall apply analogously when assessing the distinctiveness of a descriptive trade mark, particularly concerning the established common knowledge in the relevant field. Any mark failing to meet these criteria shall not be registrable.

A trade mark consisting exclusively of a description of the characteristics of the goods or services, or exclusively of a description of one of the characteristics of the goods or services, shall not be registered, except where such description has acquired distinctiveness through use. However, a description trade mark may be registered if it has attained sufficient distinctiveness to identify and distinguish the source of the goods or services, and the applicant demonstrates a period of continuous use exceeding five years prior to the filing of the application. Where the mark incorporates a computer programme essential to the functioning of the goods or services, evidence of the programme’s unique features and its contribution to the overall distinctiveness shall be submitted. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a descriptive trade mark, and alleging lack of distinctiveness, may apply to the Registrar for revocation of the registration, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding evidence and procedure. The Registrar shall consider all relevant factors, including the extent of use and public recognition of the mark.

For the purposes of this Act, a reference trade mark shall mean a trade mark which is cited by an applicant for registration of a trade mark, or is relied upon by the applicant in support of their application, or is a trade mark in respect of which an opposition is filed under this Act. A trade mark shall not be considered a reference trade mark if it is shown to be devoid of distinctive character, or is descriptive, or has become customary in the relevant trade. However, a trade mark which is identical with, or nearly resembling, a reference trade mark, and is used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, may be subject to an action for infringement as provided herein, unless the applicant demonstrates legitimate use or non-use. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct that a trade mark be treated as a reference trade mark.

A trade mark application seeking registration shall not be refused registration under this Act solely on the ground that it is identical with or deceptively similar to a reference trade mark, provided that such reference trade mark has not been in continuous use for a period of at least five years prior to the date of the application for registration. Where a reference trade mark is registered in respect of goods or services which are not similar to those for which registration is sought, the application shall not be refused unless the applicant intends to use the trade mark in a manner likely to cause confusion or deceive the public. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require the applicant to submit evidence of bona fide use of the trade mark within a specified period. A trade mark consisting exclusively of a descriptive character, or one which is devoid of distinctive character, shall not be registered, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to oppose the use of a deceptively similar trade mark by another, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a trade mark is registered, and another mark is subsequently applied for, the applicant for the later mark shall be required to demonstrate that it does not conflict with any existing registered marks, including any established reference trade mark. A reference trade mark, for the purposes of this Act, is a mark lawfully used in India before the commencement of this Act, though not necessarily registered, which has acquired distinctiveness and reputation. The proprietor of a reference trade mark may, notwithstanding the absence of registration, seek injunctive relief against any unauthorized use likely to cause confusion. However, such relief shall be granted only upon proof of prior use and acquired goodwill, and may be subject to limitations as determined by the court, considering the equities involved and any acquiescence on the part of the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding a reference trade mark may appeal to the appropriate authority as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining a conflict between trade marks under this Act, a reference trade mark shall be a trade mark registered or unregistered, which is cited by an applicant for registration of a new trade mark, or is relied upon by a party opposing registration, as being identical or nearly resembling an earlier trade mark. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, direct the applicant or opposing party to submit evidence demonstrating the extent of use of the reference trade mark, including details of sales figures and geographical reach. Provided that, failure to comply with such a direction may be considered by the Registrar in assessing the likelihood of confusion. Where a reference trade mark is not actively being used, the applicant may present evidence to demonstrate non-use, and the Registrar shall consider such evidence in determining whether the reference trade mark retains sufficient distinctiveness to warrant protection. Any decision regarding the relevance of a reference trade mark shall be communicated in writing to all parties concerned, outlining the reasons for the decision.

A trade mark shall be considered a reference trade mark for the purposes of determining similarity under this Act, provided that such trade mark is registered and remains registered in the relevant class or classes in relation to goods or services which are identical or closely related to those for which the other trade mark is sought to be registered. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, consider evidence of actual use of the reference trade mark in determining the extent of its reputation and distinctiveness. Where a trade mark has been continuously used for a period of not less than five years prior to the date of the application for registration of the other trade mark, such use may be adduced as evidence of reputation, even if the mark is not registered. However, the use must be bona fide and in good faith, and not merely for the purpose of reserving rights. Any determination of similarity shall account for all relevant factors, including the visual, aural, and conceptual characteristics of the marks, and the perceptual connection between them.

Any person who uses, in the course of trade, a trade mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. Where a plaintiff seeks to restrain the defendant from using a trade mark which is not identical but is a variant of the plaintiff’s registered trade mark, the plaintiff shall also demonstrate that the defendant’s mark is likely to cause confusion, and that the defendant’s use constitutes an act of unfair competition. A court, when determining whether a mark is deceptively similar, may consider the overall impression created by the marks, and shall give due weight to any evidence of actual confusion. Furthermore, a party alleging infringement may, subject to the provisions of this Act, seek to establish that the defendant’s mark is a reference trade mark, and that the use thereof is likely to dilute the distinctiveness of the plaintiff’s mark. Any person found guilty of such infringement shall be punishable with imprisonment and a fine.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or a transmission of rights therein, shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be entered in the Register of Trade Marks. Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, notice of the assignment shall be sent to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and the Registry shall record the assignment in its records. A transfer of rights in a reference trade mark, being a trade mark cited by an applicant in support of their application, requires prior written consent of the proprietor of the reference trade mark, unless the transfer is to a successor in title of the original proprietor. Failure to obtain such consent may render the application subject to opposition. The proprietor of a reference trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to other parties for the use of the mark in relation to specified goods or services. Any such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of use.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be a reference trade mark for the purposes of determining the likelihood of confusion, and shall be considered irrespective of whether the marks are identical or similar, or whether the goods or services are identical or similar, if the earlier trade mark has a reputation in India. However, such reputation must be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Registrar, and evidence of extensive advertising, sales figures, and market research shall be admissible for this purpose. Any party alleging that a mark is a reference trade mark bears the onus of proving such reputation. An appeal from the Registrar’s decision regarding the establishment of a reference trade mark shall lie to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning appeals. The High Court may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision, and may direct further evidence to be taken. A finding that a trade mark is a reference trade mark does not automatically invalidate a later mark; it merely alters the assessment of likelihood of confusion.

A trade mark shall be considered a reference trade mark for the purposes of determining whether a mark is deceptively similar, notwithstanding any differences in the goods or services in relation to which the marks are registered or used. The Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, direct that a registered trade mark be recorded as a reference trade mark in the Register. Such direction shall apply certification trade marks, wherein the mark’s distinctiveness is assessed based on the certification itself and not the origin of goods or services. Provided that the applicant demonstrates prior extensive use and recognition of the mark amongst the relevant public. Any mark found to be deceptively similar to a recorded reference trade mark shall be subject to opposition as provided herein, and the owner of the reference trade mark may initiate proceedings for rectification or cancellation.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall have the right to oppose the use of a reference trade mark, where such reference is likely to cause confusion or deceptively affect the distinctive character of the registered trade mark. Any person claiming rights in a reference trade mark, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the High Court for a declaration as to the validity of such claim. Where a registered user registered under this Act, has been authorized to use the registered trade mark, the proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies against any infringement of the reference trade mark committed by such registered user, as if the proprietor were directly using the trade mark. Provided that, the registered user shall be liable to indemnify the proprietor for any damages or costs incurred in such proceedings, if the reference trade mark is found to be validly used. The Court may, in exercising its jurisdiction, consider the extent of similarity between the marks and the nature of the goods or services.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be examined by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain whether the mark applied for is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others. Where a mark applied for is identical with, or deceptively similar to, a registered trade mark, the applicant shall be required to furnish evidence demonstrating a legitimate right to use the mark, or to seek the consent of the proprietor of the reference trade mark. The Registry may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct the applicant to amend the application in a manner that avoids conflict with existing registered marks. 

An applicant seeking to register a mark incorporating a technical solution or invention may, in addition to the trade mark application, simultaneously register patents for the inventive aspect, provided that such patent application details are disclosed to the Registry during the trade mark examination process. Failure to disclose relevant patent applications may result in the rejection of the trade mark application, or revocation of registration if granted erroneously. The Registrar shall maintain a register of such linked applications.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a determination of whether the mark is deceptively similar to a reference trade mark, as defined under this Act, and whether such similarity is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers. A reference trade mark, for the purposes of this determination, includes a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, even if not formally registered. However, a mark incorporating a novel invention, protected by a valid patent, shall not be deemed deceptively similar solely on the basis of technical functionality, provided that the invention is clearly distinguishable in the overall presentation of the trade mark. The Registrar may, at any time, require evidence of genuine use of the trade mark to substantiate claims of distinctiveness. Failure to comply with a request for evidence within the stipulated timeframe may result in the rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may file a representation against the registration of a trade mark if they believe it infringes upon their established rights.

The trade mark proprietor shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. A registered trade mark proprietor may, where it appears to the Registrar that the trade mark is not being genuinely used, be subject to an application for revocation of registration. However, a proprietor may demonstrate continued use through submission of evidence of bona fide commercial activity. Any assignment of the trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark proprietor is a legal person, any notice required to be served upon them shall be deemed to have been duly served if sent to their registered office. The rights of a trade mark proprietor are not diminished by the mere fact that similar marks exist for unrelated goods or services.

The trade mark proprietor shall, upon registration of a trade mark under this Act, acquire the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. A registered trade mark shall be deemed to be personal property and the trade mark proprietor may assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of the trade mark, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Where a trade mark has been registered in the name of a deceased person, the legal representative of the deceased shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, become the trade mark proprietor. Any assignment or transfer of a registered trade mark shall be subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry, and until so registered, the transferor shall remain the trade mark proprietor for all purposes under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application, record the assignment or transfer in the Register.

The trade mark proprietor shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. Any person who, without the consent of the trade mark proprietor, uses a deceptively similar mark in relation to those goods or services, shall be liable for infringement. A proprietor may, as provided herein, initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, or an account of profits made by the infringer. Where goods bearing the infringing mark have been imported, the proprietor may apply to the Customs authorities for a notification to detain such goods. 

However, a registered trade mark shall not confer any right to prevent a person from using a descriptive term necessary to indicate the character or quality of the goods or services. Furthermore, a trade mark proprietor shall diligently use the mark, and failure to do so may render it vulnerable to revocation upon application by a third party, subject to the provisions of this Act.

The trade mark proprietor shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall be subject to an instrument in writing and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Where a trade mark proprietor fails to exercise their rights for a continuous period of five years, and there is no justifiable reason for such non-use, a petition for revocation may be presented to the Registrar. 

A registered proprietor may, at any time, apply to the Registrar for an order restraining any person from infringing their trade mark, and the Registrar shall, after such inquiry as may be deemed necessary, issue such order. The rights conferred by registration shall be subject to the rights of prior users, and no registration shall prejudice the rights of any person who, before the date of registration, was lawfully using the trade mark. Any dispute regarding the ownership of a trade mark shall be determined by the appropriate court.

The trade mark proprietor shall ensure diligent use of the registered trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and failure to do so may be considered grounds for revocation of the registration as provided herein. A registered trade mark proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark and the goodwill associated therewith, and any such assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark proprietor licenses the trade mark to another party, such license shall be subject to a quality control mechanism ensuring that the goods or services offered under the license maintain the standards associated with the trade mark. Any abandonment of the trade mark by the proprietor, demonstrated by a cessation of legitimate use and intent not to resume such use, shall render the registration liable to be removed. The trade mark proprietor bears the onus of proving continued use and diligent protection of the mark against infringement.

Any person who, without the consent of the trade mark proprietor, applies a trade mark to goods or their packaging, or offers for sale or distributes goods bearing an identical or deceptively similar mark, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that, if the application relates to goods lawfully rejected under quality control procedures established by the trade mark proprietor, such application shall not constitute an offence, subject to demonstrable proof of such rejection. Any person found guilty of such offence shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Furthermore, all goods infringing the trade mark, and all materials used in the manufacture of such goods, shall be liable to seizure and destruction, as determined by a competent authority. The trade mark proprietor may initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages sustained due to the infringement.

The trade mark proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to any person to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and any such license shall be in writing and may be subject to such conditions as the trade mark proprietor deems fit. Any assignment of the trade mark, or an agreement to assign it, shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry, and until so registered, the assignee shall not have any greater interest in the trade mark than that of a licensee. Where a trade mark proprietor licenses the use of their mark under a quality control agreement, such agreement shall specify the standards to be maintained by the licensee to ensure consistency with the quality associated with the registered trade mark. Failure to adhere to such standards may result in revocation of the license, as provided herein. The trade mark proprietor retains the right to monitor the quality of goods or services offered by the licensee and take appropriate action to protect the reputation of the trade mark.

The trade mark proprietor, aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. Any cross-objection to the appeal shall be filed within thirty days of the receipt of notice of the appeal, and failure to do so may render it inadmissible. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and any cross-objections, shall either confirm, modify, reverse or set aside the decision of the Registrar, and may direct further evidence to be taken or issues to be tried. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice, and such petition shall be filed within sixty days of the Appellate Board’s order. The Registrar, if satisfied that the trade mark proprietor has abandoned the mark, may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register.

The trade mark proprietor shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. Where a trade mark is used in relation to goods or services which have been certified by a certification trade mark proprietor, the rights of both proprietors shall be determined according to the terms of any agreement between them, failing which, the court shall determine priority based on the date of first use in commerce. Any person who, without the consent of the trade mark proprietor, uses a deceptive or confusingly similar mark shall be liable for damages or an injunction, as provided herein. A proprietor may assign or transmit the trade mark with or without goodwill, subject to any conditions imposed by the Registrar. The Registrar may, upon application, order rectification of the register where a trade mark is falsely registered or where the proprietor’s name or address is incorrect. Any aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court against any decision of the Registrar.

The trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to initiate proceedings for infringement of their registered trade mark before the High Court, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a plaintiff seeks interim relief, they shall demonstrate a prima facie case, the probability of irreparable harm, and the balance of convenience favouring the grant of such relief. A trade mark proprietor may also apply to the High Court for an order restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, or otherwise dealing in goods bearing the infringing mark. 

Notwithstanding the foregoing, where a trade mark is a well-known trade mark, as determined by the High Court, the scope of protection afforded extends beyond identical marks to include marks likely to cause confusion, or to be associated with the well-known trade mark. The Court may, in such cases, grant an injunction even where no direct competition exists, provided that the use of the defendant’s mark is likely to dilute the distinctive character or repute of the well-known trade mark. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the High Court may appeal to the Supreme Court.

The trade mark proprietor shall be entitled to commence legal proceedings for infringement of their registered trade mark, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any action initiated under this Act relating to goods providing services shall clearly specify the class or classes in which the trade mark is registered and demonstrate a direct nexus between the alleged infringement and those registered goods or services. Where a trade mark proprietor seeks an injunction, they shall satisfy the court that irreparable harm will be suffered if the injunction is not granted, and that the balance of convenience favours immediate relief. Provided that, the court may, at its discretion, require the trade mark proprietor to furnish security for potential damages if the injunction is subsequently found to have been wrongly issued. A proprietor failing to comply with the conditions of registration, including timely renewal of the trade mark, may forfeit certain rights as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be a trade mark proprietor who makes a false representation in an application or other document submitted to the India Registrar, or in any affidavit or evidence filed in support thereof, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a trade mark proprietor fails to comply with a requirement to furnish a statutory declaration regarding use of the mark, as provided herein, they shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for each class of goods or services in respect of which the declaration is required. The India Registrar, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, may extend the time for filing such declaration, provided that a reasonable cause is demonstrated. Any appeal against a penalty imposed under this Act shall lie before the High Court. Failure to respond to a notice issued by the India Registrar concerning rectification of the register may result in removal of the mark.

The trade mark proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to any person or persons to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and any such license shall be in writing and may be subject to such conditions as the trade mark proprietor deems fit. Any assignment of the registered trade mark, or an agreement to assign it, shall be subject to an application to the Registrar for the purpose of recording the assignment, and the Registrar shall, upon being satisfied that the assignment is genuine and consistent with the provisions of this Act, record the assignment in the Register. Where a license or assignment includes a registration mentioned clause, the terms of such clause shall be binding on both the trade mark proprietor and the licensee or assignee, and any dispute arising therefrom shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the trade mark proprietor.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark under this Act desiring to obtain protection in countries party to an international convention for the protection of industrial property, may apply for an international registration through the International Bureau, subject to the provisions of the said convention and the regulations thereunder. The application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement identifying the basic registration upon which the international registration is based. Where an applicant seeks to designate only certain countries within the international convention, the application shall clearly specify those designated countries. 

Provided that, the International Bureau may, upon notice to the applicant, require rectification of any deficiency in the application within a period not exceeding three months from the date of such notice. An international registration, once granted, shall be deemed to have the same effect as a registration under this Act, subject to the rights and obligations arising from the international convention and any limitations prescribed herein. The Registrar may, where necessary, issue guidelines for the conduct of international registration trade.

Any person contravening the provisions relating to international registration trade, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a trade mark is falsely represented in connection with an international registration, the Registrar may, after due inquiry, order the removal of such trade mark from the register and direct that all materials bearing such false representation be seized and destroyed. Any officer of the Trade Marks Registry acting under this Act, who wilfully and with intent to cause annoyance, makes an incorrect entry in the register of international registrations, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, no order for seizure and destruction shall be made without affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the owner of the goods. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a petition with the High Court contesting the validity of an international registration designating India, if such registration conflicts with a prior registered trade mark or a pending application for registration in India relating to identical or similar goods or services. The High Court shall, following notice to the proprietor of the international registration and any relevant parties, determine whether the grounds for contesting the registration are substantiated. Provided that, the international bureau’s refusal to grant protection in its country of origin shall be admissible evidence, but not conclusive. An appeal from any order of the High Court in respect of an international registration trade dispute may be made to the Supreme Court, subject to such conditions as the Supreme Court may prescribe. The burden of proving non-use, as provided herein, shall lie with the party alleging non-use.

The applicant for registration of a trade mark under this Act, seeking extension of protection to India based on an international registration, shall furnish the particulars international registration to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner prescribed. Such particulars shall include the international registration number, the designated Contracting Parties including India, the basic application details giving rise to the international registration, and a statement of entitlement to the international registration. Provided that, if the applicant is not the owner of the basic application, evidence of succession or assignment shall also be submitted. The Registry may, subject to verification of the submitted particulars, proceed with the examination of the application for registration in India. Failure to provide complete and accurate particulars international registration may render the application liable to be refused.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of particulars of international registrations designating India, adhering to the provisions of this Act and the relevant international agreements. Any person seeking to record such particulars international registration shall submit a statement verifying the accuracy of the details furnished, including the designated goods and services, and the priority date claimed. The statement shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a certified copy of the international registration. Provided that, if the International Bureau communicates any deficiency in the particulars, the applicant shall rectify the same within a period of three months from the date of such communication, failing which the application may be deemed to be abandoned. The Registrar may, subject to verification, record the particulars and assign a registration number. Any alteration to the particulars international registration must be notified to the Registry in writing and shall be subject to examination as provided herein.

The proprietor of an international registration designating India shall, within the prescribed period, file with the Trade Marks Registry particulars of the international registration, including a statement of extent to which the mark is used in India. Failure to file such particulars shall render the international registration vulnerable to revocation, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person alleging non-use may apply to the Registry for a finding of non-use, and the Registry shall, following due process and consideration of evidence submitted by both parties, determine whether sufficient use has been demonstrated. Provided that, the Registry may extend the time for filing particulars of use if satisfied with the reasons presented by the proprietor. A finding of non-use relating to particulars international registration shall not automatically invalidate the basic registration in the country of origin, but shall only affect the rights conferred by the international registration within India. The Registry’s decision on non-use shall be subject to appeal before the High Court.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of particulars international registration designating India, updating it with any relevant communication received from the International Bureau. Any person seeking to oppose an application based on such international registration shall submit a notice of opposition, accompanied by the prescribed fee, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the particulars in the Trade Marks Journal. The notice of opposition shall clearly state the grounds on which the opposition is based, referencing relevant provisions of this Act. 

Where the international registration relates to a collective mark or a certification mark, the Registry may, prior to proceeding with the opposition, request clarification from the International Bureau regarding the rules governing the use of such marks in the country of origin. Subject to the provisions herein, the procedure for opposition to a particulars international registration shall be the same as that for opposition to a national trade mark application, including the right to file counter-statements and evidence. All documents filed in relation to the opposition shall be open to inspection by any interested party, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person applying for the registration of a trade mark under this Act, who claims priority from an international registration, shall furnish particulars international registration with the application in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Failure to provide complete and accurate particulars international registration shall render the application liable to be refused, and the applicant may be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, however, require rectification of any deficient particulars within a period of thirty days from the date of such requirement. Any false statement made in the particulars international registration, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. A trade mark registered based on fraudulent particulars international registration may be subject to revocation as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all particulars international registration received.

Any person who is the proprietor of a registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark, or any right in respect of the trade mark, to another person. An assignment shall only be valid if it is in writing and certified by the Trade Marks Registry. Where an international registration is assigned, the assignee shall, within six months of the assignment, file with the Registry particulars of the international registration, including the International Registration Number, the designated countries, and the class of goods or services covered. Failure to file these particulars may render the assignment unenforceable in relation to India. The Registry may, at its discretion, require further evidence to verify the validity of the assignment and the continued entitlement of the assignee to the particulars international registration. Any licensing of rights stemming from an international registration shall be governed by the terms of the license and be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding assignments.

The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receiving notification of an international registration designating India, record the particulars international registration in the Register, subject to verification of compliance with requirements as provided herein. Any party opposing such registration shall file a notice of opposition within the prescribed period, detailing the grounds for contesting the claim of priority or inherent distinctiveness. Should the Registrar uphold the opposition, the particulars international registration shall not proceed to publication. However, an appeal against the Registrar’s decision may be preferred to the High Court, with the appellant bearing the onus of demonstrating substantial grounds for review.
