The High Court, in considering such appeals, shall have the power to direct the Trade Marks Registry to reconsider its findings or to affirm the initial decision, and its order shall be final and binding, unless otherwise provided by law. Failure to exercise due diligence in pursuing an appeal may result in the abandonment of the opposition.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of particulars of international registrations designating India, in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the relevant international agreements. An applicant who is a business entity incorporated in India, hereinafter referred to as a ‘business india applicant’, may file a statement of use, or a request for division of an international registration, relating to those particulars. Such statement or request shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the particulars international registration and satisfaction that the requirements of this Act have been met, record the statement or request. Provided that, where the international registration has been subject to provisional refusal in another jurisdiction, the Registrar may require additional evidence from the business india applicant before proceeding with the recordal. Any amendment to the particulars shall be processed as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a register disclosed shall mean a publicly available record maintained by the Trade Marks Registry containing particulars of registered trade marks, including the proprietor’s name and address, a representation of the mark, the classes of goods or services in respect of which it is registered, and the registration number. Any person may inspect the register disclosed during office hours subject to payment of the prescribed fee. However, access to information relating to a proprietor’s personal details, beyond that necessary to establish ownership, may be restricted. A certified copy of any entry in the register disclosed shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, unless proven otherwise. The Registrar shall maintain the accuracy and integrity of the register disclosed.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark, and desiring to obtain its registration, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form for registration of the trade mark, accompanied by a statement of proposed use. The application shall disclose the register in which the trade mark is sought to be registered, specifying the class of goods or services in relation to which the registration is desired. Where the applicant claims priority from an earlier application made in a convention country, such priority claim shall be stated in the application and supported by a certified copy of the earlier application, filed within the prescribed period. A clear representation of the trade mark shall be furnished as part of the application, and any disclaimer required under this Act shall also be included. The register disclosed shall be maintained electronically and open to public inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, and any person may obtain a certified copy of any entry therein.

Any person aggrieved by the non-disclosure of a material fact in a register disclosed during the examination of a trade mark application, or by a misrepresentation therein, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register. Such application shall be made within a period of one year from the date of registration of the trade mark, or from the date the applicant became aware of the non-disclosure or misrepresentation, whichever is later. The Registrar, upon receiving such application, shall cause an inquiry to be made and may require the applicant and the registered proprietor to furnish evidence in support of their respective claims. Provided that, if the Registrar is satisfied that the non-disclosure or misrepresentation is of such a nature as to substantially affect the validity of the registration, the Registrar may, after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard, order the rectification of the register accordingly and may also direct the removal of the trade mark from the register. Any order made under this provision shall be final and binding on all parties.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark and desiring to obtain its registration shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall include a clear representation of the trade mark as it is to be registered, and shall identify the goods or services for which registration is sought. Where the application seeks registration of a trade mark which is similar to an existing trade mark, the applicant shall disclose such similarity and provide a reasoned statement demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion. 

A register disclosed under this Act shall be open to inspection by any member of the public, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. The Registrar may, however, refuse access to confidential business information included within the register, provided that such refusal is justified and documented. Any objection to the registration of a trade mark shall be filed within the time period stipulated, and shall be accompanied by supporting evidence. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark shall ensure the register disclosed contains a clear representation of the mark as it is intended to be used, and shall further specify the goods or services to which it relates in accordance with the Nice Classification. Provided that, where a collective mark or certification mark is sought, the rules governing membership or the standards to be met for certification shall be prominently displayed within the register disclosed. An applicant may, subject to verification by the Registrar, claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a convention country. Failure to accurately represent the mark or to fully disclose the associated goods or services may result in the application being deemed incomplete or, as provided herein, subject to rectification after registration. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered trade marks, accessible for inspection during normal business hours. Any alteration to the register disclosed must be formally notified to the Registrar and recorded accordingly.

Any person who publishes or otherwise makes available to the public a register disclosed under this Act, save as expressly permitted by or under any provision herein, shall be deemed to have committed an offence. The disclosure of a register, including any amendments thereto, shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, and any unauthorized disclosure resulting in demonstrable prejudice to the rights of a trade mark proprietor shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, the Registrar may, in exceptional circumstances and upon sufficient cause shown, authorize the disclosure of a limited portion of the register, subject to strict confidentiality undertakings. Any officer of the Trade Marks Office found to have improperly disclosed a register shall be liable for disciplinary action, including removal from service, and may also be subject to prosecution under this Act. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to register disclosed shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall include a clear and unambiguous disclosure of the register disclosed particulars relating to the mark, including but not limited to the class of goods or services, the date of registration, and any limitations or conditions recorded against it. The instrument of assignment may provide for the transfer of the right to renew the trade mark, subject to the assignee fulfilling all obligations pertaining to renewal fees as provided herein. Where an assignment involves a partial transfer of interest, the instrument shall delineate with precision the scope of rights transferred and retained by the assignor. Failure to adequately disclose the register disclosed information may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. Any license granted under the trade mark shall be construed as an interest in property.

Where a dispute arises concerning the register disclosed relating to a trade mark, any person aggrieved by the entry or omission of any particular therein may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board. Such application shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order sought to be appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the said order. An application for registration, constituting a basic application as defined herein, shall not be deemed to be improperly admitted by reason only of a technical objection to the form of the application, provided that such objection does not prejudice the determination of the subject matter of the application. The Appellate Board may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, alter or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and may also direct any necessary corrections to be made in the register. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties.

Where a trade mark is registered and a register disclosed detailing the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered, any person claiming to be aggrieved by any entry in the register may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar to have the entry amended or removed. The proprietor trade mark, in opposing such application, shall furnish evidence supporting the validity of the register disclosed and demonstrating a genuine use of the mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Provided that, if the Registrar is satisfied that the entry is inaccurate or misleading, or that the trade mark is not distinctive, the Registrar may, after giving the proprietor an opportunity to be heard, direct the amendment or removal of the entry. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar under this provision may, within a period of ninety days, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Failure to respond to a notice issued by the Registrar regarding the accuracy of the register shall be deemed an abandonment of claim.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark shall submit a statement disclosing the use of the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which registration is sought, and such register disclosed shall be considered prima facie evidence of such use as of the date of application. The Registrar may, however, require further evidence to substantiate the claim of use, particularly where the nature of the goods or services necessitates verification. A qualified patent agent, authorized by the applicant, may submit the aforementioned statement and accompanying evidence on behalf of the applicant, provided that a power of attorney duly executed is filed with the Registrar. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar shall examine the register disclosed for compliance with the requirements of this Act and may raise objections if the statement is incomplete or inaccurate. Failure to adequately address such objections within the prescribed timeframe may result in the rejection of the application for registration. The Registrar’s decision regarding the sufficiency of the register disclosed shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the appropriate appellate authority.

A person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall contain a clear representation of the mark, details identifying the applicant, and a description of the goods or services to which the mark will be applied. Where the mark is proposed for collective or certification purposes, evidence of the relevant association or standards shall accompany the application. Subject to verification and absence of conflicting prior rights, the Registrar may, after examination, accept the application for advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, if the proposed mark is deceptively similar to an existing mark, the application may be subject to opposition as provided herein. Any application found deficient shall be returned to the applicant with a statement of objections.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall contain a clear representation of the mark, details of goods or services for which registration is sought, and a statement of use, or a bona fide intention to use, the mark in relation to those goods or services. Where the applicant seeks to register a mark which is similar to an existing mark, evidence demonstrating distinctiveness and lack of deceptive similarity shall be furnished. 

An applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, register a series of marks, provided that a common characteristic subsists amongst them. The Registrar may, at any stage, require further information or clarification from the applicant to ensure compliance with the requirements of this Act. Failure to comply with such requests may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks relating to pharmaceutical preparations shall, prior to acceptance of the application by the Trade Marks Registry, furnish a certificate of testing from a laboratory recognized by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, demonstrating bioequivalence to a previously registered formulation, subject to the provisions contained herein. Failure to submit such a certificate shall render the application liable to be rejected, and the applicant shall have no recourse to appeal unless the deficiency is remedied within ninety days from the date of notice. Where a certificate is found to be fraudulent or misleading, the Registrar may, notwithstanding prior registration, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register and impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. A registered proprietor aggrieved by a decision under this Act may apply to the High Court for review, provided that such application is made within sixty days of the decision. The rights conferred by registration of a proposed trade mark shall be subject to the rights of prior users established through continuous and lawful use.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall contain a clear representation of the mark, details of goods or services for which registration is sought, and the applicant’s description. Where the applicant seeks to register a mark which is not inherently distinctive, evidence of acquired distinctiveness through continuous use shall be furnished, subject to verification by the Registry. An affidavit attesting to the veracity of the information provided, and a statement of use, may be required as part of the examination process. 

Should a mark be similar to an existing registered trade mark, the Registry shall issue an examination report outlining the grounds for potential objection. The applicant shall then have an opportunity to furnish arguments or evidence to rebut the objections raised, or to seek amendment of the application. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned, as provided herein.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by a statement of use affirming bona fide intention to employ the mark. The application shall clearly delineate the goods or services to which the trade mark will be applied, and shall be classified according to the Nice Classification, as adopted under this Act. Should the applicant seek to register a mark identical or deceptively similar to an existing registered trade mark, a comparative statement demonstrating distinctiveness and non-infringement must be furnished. Provided that, where the proposed mark incorporates well-known marks, evidence of consent from the proprietor of such well-known marks shall be mandatory. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided herein. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require further evidence or clarification before proceeding with the examination of the register proposed.

Any person who falsely represents a trade mark as registered, or as being in the process of being registered, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a person applies to register a trade mark proposing use by another, and such proposed use is contingent upon conditions not fully disclosed at the time of application, the Registrar may, subject to such terms as deemed appropriate, refuse registration until satisfactory evidence of compliance with said conditions is furnished. Any assignment of the right to register proposed under this Act, without the prior written consent of the original applicant, shall be void ab initio and attract a penalty equivalent to twice the official fee applicable for registration. Failure to provide accurate particulars regarding the proposed registered user, or any misrepresentation thereof, shall render the application liable to be rejected, and the applicant may be barred from submitting a similar application for a period of one year.

Any person desiring to register proposed use of a trade mark, not currently being used in India, shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry demonstrating a bona fide intention to use the mark in relation to specified goods or services. The application shall detail the proposed manner of use, including the class of goods or services and a clear indication of the applicant’s plans for commercial exploitation within a period not exceeding eighteen months from the date of registration of the proposed use. Should the applicant fail to commence actual use within said period, the Registry may, subject to a review of extenuating circumstances, strike the proposed use from the register. Assignment of rights relating to a register proposed shall be permissible, provided that written consent of the original applicant is obtained and the assignment is duly recorded with the Registry. Any licensing arrangement concerning a register proposed shall be governed by the terms of a written agreement, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial limits of the license.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks, and believing themselves entitled to do so under this Act, shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry accompanied by a clear representation of the mark and a detailed specification of the goods or services to which it relates. Should an objection be raised by the Registry, or by any third party alleging prior use or similarity to an existing mark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to respond and present evidence supporting their claim. Failure to adequately address such objections may result in refusal of the application, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. An aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar, may initiate an appeal within ninety days of the order, providing grounds for review and any supporting documentation. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except in cases of proven fraud or manifest error.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks, particularly those incorporating elements subject to an international application patent filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall submit a statement of use within the period prescribed, failing which the application for registration shall be deemed abandoned as provided herein. However, an extension of time for such submission may be granted by the Registrar, subject to demonstrable cause and payment of a prescribed fee. An appeal against the Registrar’s decision to deny such extension shall lie before the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates a reasonable prospect of successfully establishing prior use or a bona fide intention to use the mark in commerce. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except on grounds of demonstrated procedural irregularity or manifest error of law, and any further challenge shall be limited to a writ petition before the High Court. A finding of bad faith in the initial application shall invalidate any subsequent registration.

A person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall contain a clear representation of the mark and a statement of the goods or services to which it relates. Where the applicant seeks to claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a 6referred convention country, such claim shall be made within six months from the date of the earlier application, and accompanied by a certified copy thereof, duly translated if necessary. Subject to verification by the Registry, the priority date of the earlier application shall be deemed to be the filing date of the current application. An incomplete application may be subject to objection and refusal as provided herein. The Registrar may require further information or documentation to facilitate examination.

Any person desiring to register proposed trade marks shall submit an application for registration to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The application shall contain a clear representation of the mark, details identifying the applicant, and a specification of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Subject to verification of the application’s completeness and compliance with the provisions of this Act, the Registry shall examine the mark for inherent distinctiveness and potential conflicts with existing registered trade marks. An application registration, once accepted, shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, allowing for opposition by interested parties. Provided that no opposition is sustained, or any sustained opposition is resolved, the Registry shall proceed to register the trade mark and issue a certificate of registration. The register shall be open for inspection by the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, and shall contain particulars of all registered trade marks. Any alteration to the registered trade mark shall require a separate application and be subject to the same scrutiny as the original registration.

Any company intending to register proposed trade marks relating to goods in Class 29, encompassing edible oils and processed foods, shall furnish a detailed declaration outlining the sourcing of primary agricultural produce. This declaration shall confirm that at least fifty percent of raw materials utilized in the manufacturing process are obtained from registered farmers or farmer producer organizations, subject to verification by the designated authority. An applicant may request expedited processing of a register proposed application, provided that a surcharge, as determined by the Central Government and notified in the Gazette, is duly remitted. Failure to provide complete and accurate information regarding sourcing, or any misrepresentation therein, shall render the register proposed application liable to rejection, and may attract penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional documentation to substantiate claims made within the application.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark if the application satisfies the requirements as provided herein and the mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. A trade mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing trade mark, or is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or is devoid of distinctive character. Provided that, a trade mark which has become distinctive through use may be registered notwithstanding its initial descriptiveness, subject to the Registrar being satisfied as to the extent and duration of such use. The Registrar may, before registration, require further evidence or clarification regarding the distinctiveness or use of the trade mark. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision may file a review petition within the prescribed time limit.

The Registrar shall register a collective mark, provided that the application demonstrates that the applicant is an association of individuals, companies, or firms, who collectively seek to use a particular mark to designate goods or services of their members. An application for registration of a collective mark shall include a statement of the conditions of membership in the association and the manner in which the mark will be used by members. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require the applicant to satisfy themselves as to the lawfulness of the association’s purposes and the authenticity of its membership. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar shall register the collective mark in the name of the association, and not in the names of individual members. Where the association fails to exercise reasonable control over the use of the registered collective mark by its members, the Registrar may, after giving the association an opportunity to be heard, revoke the registration.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark in the name of the applicant if, upon examination, the mark meets the requirements as provided herein and no valid grounds for refusal exist under this Act. However, the Registrar may, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee, require the applicant to amend the application in a manner that rectifies any deficiencies or clarifies the scope of the mark. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision to refuse registration, or by any condition imposed during registration, may file a written appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where a registered trade mark is used by a party without the consent of the proprietor, the proprietor may pursue remedies including injunction and damages, as are available under the general law relating to torts or under this Act.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark in respect of goods or services falling in Class 29, provided that the applicant satisfies the requirements as to distinctive character and is not prohibited by this Act or any other law for the time being in force. An application for registration shall be examined by the Registrar, and where the Registrar is satisfied that the trade mark is registrable, notice of the application shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal. Any person may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition to the registration of the trade mark. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Registrar shall, after considering any opposition filed and after making such inquiries as may be deemed necessary, either register the trade mark or reject the application. The Registrar may, at any time before registration, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information. Where a trade mark is registered, the Registrar shall enter the particulars of the trade mark in the Register of Trade Marks and issue a certificate of registration to the applicant.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark, subject to verification of the application and confirmation that it meets the requirements as provided herein. An application for registration shall be deemed complete only upon submission of a clear representation of the mark, a detailed specification of goods or services, and a declaration of ownership. The Registrar may, however, require further clarification or evidence to satisfy themselves as to the distinctiveness of the mark and the bona fide use thereof. Provided that, where the mark incorporates a foreign character or word, a transliteration and translation into the Devanagari script or Roman alphabet shall also be furnished. The Registrar shall maintain a register of trade marks, open for inspection during office hours, and shall issue a certificate of registration upon successful completion of the process. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, within the prescribed time, file an appeal.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark subject to verification of inherent distinctiveness and absence of deceptive similarity with existing registered marks, provided that an application for registration is accompanied by a clear representation of the mark and a detailed specification of goods or services it intends to cover. Any false representation made in an application, including misstatement of the date of first use, shall render the application liable to rejection and the applicant subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where the Registrar refuses to register a trade mark, an appeal may be preferred to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the refusal, subject to deposit of prescribed fees. Failure to comply with the directions of the Registrar or the Appellate Board as provided herein shall attract a daily penalty of one thousand rupees until compliance is effected, and repeated non-compliance may result in cancellation of any existing registrations held by the offending party.

The registrar shall register an assignment of trade mark ownership upon receipt of a duly executed instrument of assignment conforming to the requirements as provided herein, and shall record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks. Any assignment not so registered shall be void against any subsequent assignee or any judicial decision affecting title. Where the assignment is made subject to conditions, the registrar may require full particulars of such conditions to be furnished and recorded, ensuring they do not contravene the principles of this Act. A licensee of a trade mark may, with the consent of the registered proprietor, assign their license rights to a third party, but such assignment shall not prejudice the rights of the registered proprietor. The registrar may, at their discretion, require evidence of the registered proprietor’s consent before registering any assignment of a license. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark in respect of goods or services upon satisfaction that the application meets the requirements as provided herein, and that no prior conflicting mark exists on the register, or if such a mark exists, that sufficient grounds have been demonstrated to allow for co-existence or differentiation. However, any objection raised by a third party alleging likelihood of confusion shall be considered by the Registrar, and a reasoned order shall be issued detailing the basis for acceptance or rejection of said objection. An aggrieved party may appeal such order to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s communication, submitting a prescribed fee and detailed statement of grounds for appeal. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Registrar’s decision, no further appeal shall lie, except on a question of law. The Registrar may, subject to due process, amend the register to reflect any final order issued by the Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark if the application submitted therewith satisfies the requirements as provided herein and is accompanied by the requisite filing application fees as prescribed in the First Schedule. An application deemed incomplete due to insufficient fees or lacking necessary documentation shall be subject to a notice of deficiency issued to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days for rectification. Should the applicant fail to remedy the deficiencies within the stipulated timeframe, the application shall be deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, however, extend this period in exceptional circumstances, recorded in writing, subject to the payment of a late filing fee. Registration shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights in respect of the trade mark for the goods or services specified in the application, subject to any limitations imposed by this Act. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision regarding registration may file a review petition within sixty days of the decision, supported by relevant evidence and a prescribed fee.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, provided that the application for registration satisfies all material requirements as to form and substance. An application seeking registration of a mark incorporating a registered geographical indication shall additionally demonstrate a clear and verifiable connection between the goods and the geographical area of origin, as evidenced by official records or recognized trade practices. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require the applicant to furnish further evidence establishing such connection. Where a trade mark is registered, the Registrar shall maintain a register of such marks and shall make it available for public inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar may, within the prescribed time, file an appeal with the appellate authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in rejection of the application or revocation of the registration.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark subject to the provisions of this Act and upon satisfactory verification of a filing application demonstrating clear and lawful entitlement to ownership. Any person found to have knowingly submitted a false or misleading filing application, with intent to deceive the Registrar or secure registration improperly, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, the Registrar may, at their discretion, reject any application deemed to be frivolous or vexatious, and may impose costs upon the applicant. Should a registered trade mark be proven to have been obtained through fraudulent means, the Registrar shall revoke the registration forthwith and may, in addition to any other penalties provided herein, order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark. Failure to comply with any direction of the Registrar under this Act shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a false trade mark to goods or services shall be deemed to have committed an act of falsifying a trade. Such application includes the use of a mark deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, even if alterations, additions, or omissions are made to disguise the falsification. Where a registered proprietor demonstrates that falsification has occurred and that damage has resulted from such activity, the court may grant an injunction restraining further acts of falsification. A person falsely representing goods as certified or approved by a proprietor, or falsely indicating a connection between goods and the proprietor, also constitutes falsifying trade as provided herein. Compliance with labelling requirements regarding the origin of goods does not absolve a party from liability if the mark itself is falsified or deceptively similar. Any evidence of prior knowledge of the registered trade mark by the alleged falsifier shall be considered an aggravating factor.

Any suit alleging infringement of a registered trade mark shall be maintainable only in the High Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, where the defendant has a local representative within the jurisdiction of a District Court, such suit may also be instituted in that District Court. A plaintiff seeking relief for suit infringement registered shall, at the time of filing the plaint, furnish a certificate from the Trade Marks Registry confirming the registration of the trade mark and its current status. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Court may, at its discretion, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing mark, and award damages to the plaintiff for any loss suffered as a consequence of the infringement. Any order of the Court regarding damages shall consider the reputation and goodwill associated with the registered trade mark.

Any suit for infringement of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and may be instituted in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business. Provided that, where the defendant has a place of business in more than one district, the suit may be instituted in any one of those districts. A plaintiff seeking relief for suit infringement registered shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, serve a notice of intention to sue upon the defendant, detailing the grounds of the alleged infringement and seeking voluntary cessation of the infringing activity. Failure to serve such notice may be considered by the Court when determining the quantum of damages. The Court, as provided herein, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the trade mark, and may also order an account of profits derived from the infringement, or award damages as it deems fit. Any order for damages or account of profits shall be subject to the principles of proportionality and fairness.

Any suit alleging infringement of a registered trade mark shall be cognizable by a District Court, notwithstanding any other provision contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. A plaintiff seeking relief for suit infringement registered shall, prior to the institution of such suit, serve a notice of intention to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing the grounds of the claim and demanding cessation of the infringing activity. Such notice shall be served at least thirty days prior to the filing of the plaint, and proof of service shall be filed with the court. Provided that, if the plaintiff demonstrates to the court that immediate and irreparable harm will result from delay, the court may waive the requirement of prior notice. The court, upon being satisfied that a prima facie case of infringement exists, may grant an interim injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the mark pending final determination of the suit. Any person defending against a suit for infringement may, subject to such terms and conditions as the court may deem fit, apply for a counter-claim seeking rectification of the register or a declaration of non-infringement.

Any suit alleging infringement of a registered trade mark shall be maintainable only in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant ordinarily resides, carries on business, or where the cause of action arises, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where multiple defendants are impleaded, the suit may be filed in any District Court having jurisdiction over at least one of the defendants, provided that all defendants waive any objection based on territorial jurisdiction. A plaintiff seeking relief for suit infringement registered shall, prior to institution of proceedings, serve a notice of intention to sue upon the defendant, detailing the specific grounds of infringement and demanding cessation of the offending acts. Failure to comply with this notice requirement may render the suit inadmissible, unless the court, considering the circumstances, deems otherwise. The court may, at its discretion, grant interim injunctions pending final determination of the suit, subject to such terms and conditions as it may deem fit.

Any suit alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, or concerning rights therein, shall be subject to the jurisdictional provisions as provided herein, and no such suit shall be entertained by any court below the level of a District Court. Provided that, where a plaintiff demonstrates a credible case of imminent and irreparable harm resulting from continued use of the deceptively similar mark, the court may, notwithstanding the foregoing, grant an ex parte interim injunction pending a full hearing on the merits. Any person found to have knowingly and wilfully misrepresented the ownership of a registered trade mark, or to have abetted a suit infringement registered without reasonable grounds, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may further be subject to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. The court may, in addition to damages, award enhanced damages to the aggrieved party.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, signed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall include a statement of the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under that trade mark, the assignee shall, subject to the conditions specified in the instrument of assignment, have the same right to sue for infringement as the assignor. A suit for infringement of a registered trade mark may be brought by the assignee of the trade mark, provided that the assignment is recorded in the Trade Marks Registry. Should a registered trade mark be subject to a licensing agreement, the licensor may, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, institute a suit for infringement against any person who commits an act constituting an infringement of the trade mark. Any claim of suit infringement registered must be substantiated with evidence of valid assignment or licensing.

Any company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, engaged in the manufacture, import, or sale of goods or services, shall be deemed a proprietor for the purposes of a suit for infringement or for passing off referred to in section 13 4, irrespective of whether the trade mark is registered in the name of the company itself or a related entity. Where a company alleges acts likely to deceive or cause confusion, evidence of actual deception or likely confusion shall be admissible, and the court may consider the overall impression created by the defendant’s mark as compared to the plaintiff’s mark. 

Provided that, a company seeking relief under this Act shall demonstrate genuine use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application for registration or, in the case of unregistered marks, in relation to the goods or services for which the mark is being used. The court may, subject to the provisions herein, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement or passing off. Any discrepancy in the application fee accompanied shall be communicated to the applicant within thirty days of the application date, allowing for a period of sixty days to rectify the deficiency.

Any person aggrieved by any act of the registrar copyrights inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, or by any refusal or delay on the part of the registrar copyrights to perform any duty required by this Act, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the High Court for redress. The High Court, upon such application and after giving the registrar copyrights an opportunity of being heard, may make such orders as it deems fit for the purpose of securing the proper performance of the duties of the registrar copyrights. Where a claim of copyright infringement is made, and the registrar copyrights has failed to maintain a diligent and accurate record of copyright ownership, the claimant may, in addition to remedies available under this Act, seek exemplary damages. Provided that no order for damages shall be made unless the High Court is satisfied that the failure of the registrar copyrights materially contributed to the infringement. The registrar copyrights shall be subject to judicial review in all matters pertaining to copyright registration and recordal.

Any person intending to register a work under this Act shall submit an application to the registrar copyrights in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and a copy of the work to be registered. The registrar copyrights, upon examination of the application and the submitted work, may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification, which shall be provided within thirty days from the date of such request. Registration shall be subject to verification of the applicant’s title and the originality of the work. Provided that, the registrar copyrights may refuse registration if the work does not meet the criteria for copyright protection as provided herein, or if a prior valid copyright claim exists. Any objection to the registration shall be communicated to the applicant, allowing them an opportunity to be heard. The registrar copyrights shall maintain a register of all registered copyrights, open for inspection subject to reasonable restrictions.

Any person aggrieved by any act of the registrar copyrights inconsistent with the provisions of this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such act, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be in the form of a petition and shall state the grounds upon which it is based, and shall be duly verified. The High Court may, after giving the registrar copyrights an opportunity to be heard, confirm, modify or reverse the act complained of, and may also direct the registrar copyrights to pay such costs as it deems just. Failure to comply with the orders of the High Court under this provision shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. The registrar copyrights shall maintain a register of all appeals received and the outcomes thereof, subject to rules prescribed. Any false statement made in a petition under this provision shall be deemed a cognizable offence.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar copyrights, concerning the registration of a work, or the refusal to register a work, or any correction made or refused to be made in the register of copyrights, may, within thirty days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the office of the registrar copyrights is situated. Such appeal shall be in the form of a civil revision petition and shall be heard by a single judge of the High Court. The High Court, upon consideration of the appeal, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the registrar copyrights, and may direct such further action to be taken as it deems fit. Provided that no appeal shall lie against any decision made in respect of a work where the grounds for refusal were substantially similar to those previously adjudicated upon by the High Court in a separate but related matter. The registrar copyrights shall furnish all relevant records to the High Court within sixty days of the receipt of notice of the appeal.

Any person aggrieved by any act of the registrar copyrights inconsistent with the provisions of this Act may, within thirty days from the date of such act, prefer an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be in the form of a petition and shall set forth the grounds upon which it is based, and shall be duly verified. The High Court may, after giving the registrar copyrights an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the act complained of, or may remit the case back to the registrar copyrights for further consideration. Where an appeal relates to a matter also concerning a registered trade mark, the Trade Marks Registry may be directed by the High Court to provide relevant records or expertise to assist in the proceedings, subject to appropriate confidentiality undertakings. Failure to prefer an appeal within the stipulated time shall not preclude a civil suit for the same cause of action, provided that the court finds sufficient cause for the delay. Any order of the High Court under this provision shall be final and binding.

The registrar of copyrights shall maintain a comprehensive index of all registered works, detailing the author, publisher, and date of initial publication, and shall make such index available for inspection subject to reasonable fees as may be prescribed. Any person seeking registration of a copyright shall submit an application, accompanied by a copy of the work and the prescribed fee, to the registrar copyrights, who shall examine the application for compliance with the provisions of this Act. Where a work originates from a geographical location outside of India, but is first published within Indian territory, the application shall clearly state the country of origin and the basis for claiming copyright under this Act. Failure to accurately disclose attributable geographical origin may render the registration invalid, and subject the applicant to penalties as provided herein. The registrar copyrights may, upon reasonable cause, initiate an inquiry into the veracity of any information submitted during the registration process.

Any person desiring to assign or license the copyright in a work, or any part thereof, shall furnish to the registrar copyrights a detailed statement in the prescribed form, outlining the terms and conditions of such assignment or license, including the duration, territorial extent, and scope of rights transferred. The statement shall also identify the assignee or licensee and provide evidence of their legal standing. A certificate purporting to confirm the validity of the assignment or license, issued by a competent authority, may be submitted in lieu of detailed terms, provided that such certificate clearly delineates the rights conveyed. Subject to verification and satisfaction of the registrar copyrights regarding the completeness and accuracy of the information provided, a record of the assignment or license shall be maintained. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license unenforceable as provided herein. The registrar copyrights reserves the right to request additional information or clarification to ensure proper record-keeping and transparency.

Any person aggrieved by the decision of the registrar copyrights regarding the refusal of registration, or any order made in respect of an international registration opposed under this Act, may, within sixty days from the date of such decision or order, file an appeal to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the office of the registrar is situated. Such appeal shall be in the form of a memorandum of appeal, verified by affidavit, and shall set forth the grounds on which the decision or order is sought to be reversed or modified. The High Court may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, reverse, or modify the decision or order appealed from, or may remit the case to the registrar for fresh consideration, subject to such directions as the High Court may deem fit. Provided that no appeal shall lie from any order made with the consent of the parties. The registrar shall furnish a certified copy of all documents relating to the case to the High Court upon request.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be the definitive record of all patents granted and applications pending, and shall be updated not later than thirty days from the date of any relevant action. Every entry in the register shall include the patentee’s name and address, the filing date, priority date where applicable, and a concise summary of the invention. Subject to the provisions of confidentiality as provided herein, the entry register shall be open for public inspection during office hours. Any person may request a certified copy of an entry, upon payment of a fee as prescribed, and such copy shall be admissible as evidence in any proceeding. The Controller may, however, refuse access to information deemed commercially sensitive or relating to national security.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be the definitive record of all patent applications and granted patents, and shall be updated not later than thirty days from the occurrence of any relevant event. Any person intending to record a transfer of ownership, a license, or any other modification affecting the rights in a patent, shall submit the prescribed form and fee to the Controller, whereupon the particulars shall be entered in the entry register. Provided that, the Controller may require additional evidence to verify the validity of such transfer or license before making the entry. The Controller shall ensure the entry register is maintained in a secure digital format, with appropriate backup systems. Subject to the provisions of this Act, access to the entry register shall be available to any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee, and certified extracts therefrom shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding. Failure to maintain an accurate entry register may render the Controller liable for damages.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an entry register for all patent applications received, detailing the date of filing, applicant name, title of the invention, and priority claim details, if any. Every application, upon fulfilling the requirements as provided herein regarding form and content, shall be sequentially numbered and recorded in the entry register. Any alteration to the applicant’s name or address, or to the title of the invention, shall be duly noted in the entry register with the date of such amendment. 

The entry register shall be maintained in a secure and durable format, whether electronic or physical, and backups shall be created at regular intervals to prevent loss of data. Access to the entry register shall be restricted to authorized personnel of the Patent Office, subject to the Controller’s direction. Any person authorized to inspect the register shall execute a written undertaking of confidentiality. The Controller may, upon reasonable cause, direct a special audit of the entry register to ensure its accuracy and integrity.

The entry register shall be maintained in a digital format accessible through the online portal of the Patent Office, and shall contain particulars of every patent application filed under this Act, including the date of filing, applicant details, and a concise summary of the invention. All amendments to the application, including those relating to claims, shall be promptly recorded in the entry register. Any person intending to inspect the entry register shall first register on the portal and agree to abide by the terms of use, including a prohibition on automated data extraction without prior written permission. Provided that, access to confidential information, such as correspondence between the applicant and the Patent Office, may be restricted subject to a determination of legitimate interest. The Controller of Patents shall ensure the integrity and security of the entry register, and shall implement measures to prevent unauthorized alteration or deletion of data. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the responsible officer liable to disciplinary action as provided herein.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be deemed the official record of all patent applications and granted patents, and any omission or misstatement therein shall be subject to the penalties provided herein. Any person making a false entry, or knowingly omitting a material fact, in the entry register shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct rectification of any erroneous entry in the register. Provided that, no rectification shall be made without affording a reasonable opportunity for hearing to the parties concerned. Failure to maintain the integrity of the entry register, or to comply with a direction for rectification, shall constitute a cognizable offence under this Act. Any aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court against any order of the Controller relating to the entry register.

The patentee, or a person deriving title from the patentee, shall maintain a detailed entry register of all licenses granted under the patent, including both voluntary and compulsory licenses, and any assignments made of the patent or rights therein. This entry register shall be kept at the principal place of business of the patentee or assignee and shall be open for inspection by the Controller of Patents, upon reasonable notice, for the purposes of verifying royalty payments and compliance with the terms of the license or assignment. Any alteration to the terms of a license or assignment, or the termination thereof, shall be promptly recorded in the entry register. Failure to maintain an accurate and up-to-date entry register, or to permit inspection as provided herein, may be considered a material breach of the licensing agreement and subject to penalties under this Act. Provided that, confidential business information unrelated to the scope of the license or assignment need not be disclosed.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be deemed the authoritative record of all patent applications and granted patents, subject to the provisions herein concerning revocation and amendment. Any person alleging a discrepancy between the details recorded in the entry register and the actual circumstances pertaining to a patent’s ownership or validity may lodge a formal objection with the Controller, supported by documentary evidence. The Controller shall, following due process and affording opportunity for response to all affected parties, determine the veracity of the objection. Should the Controller uphold the objection, the entry register shall be amended accordingly, and notice of such amendment shall be published in the Official Gazette. An appeal against the Controller’s decision on matters relating to the entry register may be preferred to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Controller’s order. Failure to maintain an accurate entry register shall render the Controller liable for damages, subject to limitations as provided herein.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be a public document, subject to the provisions relating to confidential information as provided herein. Any person desiring to inspect the entry register shall apply to the Controller in the prescribed manner and upon payment of the applicable fee. The Controller may, if satisfied, permit inspection during office hours. Where an application for inspection is refused, the applicant may appeal to the Copyright Office for review of the decision, providing reasonable grounds for believing an error has occurred. All entries in the entry register shall be authenticated and maintained digitally, and the Controller shall ensure the integrity and security of this record. Provided that, the Controller may redact information deemed commercially sensitive prior to permitting inspection.

The entry register maintained by the Controller of Patents shall be the definitive record of all applications for patents and patents granted under this Act. Every application registration notice, detailing the particulars of a newly filed application, shall be entered chronologically in the said register within fourteen days of its issuance. The Controller may, subject to verification of prescribed fees, authorize amendments to entries in the register, noting the date and nature of such alterations. Any person intending to ascertain the status of a patent application or patent shall have access to the entry register during office hours. Provided that, access to confidential information, as determined by the Controller, may be restricted. The Controller shall ensure the integrity and security of the entry register, maintaining both physical and electronic backups as provided herein. Failure to accurately maintain the entry register shall constitute a breach of duty.

Any person desiring a licence of a patent, being a patent granted for a process for the manufacture of a substance intended for use in any industry, shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed manner, demonstrating sufficient grounds for the grant of such a licence. The application shall include a statement of the applicant’s intended use of the patented invention and the scope of the proposed manufacture. The patentee shall be notified of the application and afforded an opportunity to submit objections, subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein. A licence granted under this Act shall be non-exclusive, and royalty rates shall be determined by the Controller, considering the applicant’s manufacturing capacity and the patentee’s legitimate interests. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, refuse the application if the applicant fails to demonstrate a genuine intent to work the invention for the benefit of the public. Any dispute regarding the terms of the licence patent shall be subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any holder of a patent, desiring to ensure wider exploitation of their invention, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a licence under terms and conditions as mutually agreed upon with any other person. Such a licence patent shall convey the right to use, sell, and import the patented invention, but may be limited in scope, duration, or territory as specified within the instrument of licence. The patentee retains the right to revoke any licence granted, provided that reasonable notice is given to the licensee and adequate compensation is paid for unamortized costs and anticipated lost profits. Where a licensee breaches the terms of the licence, the patentee may seek an injunction restraining further exploitation and may claim damages for any loss suffered. Any dispute arising from a licence agreement shall be subject to arbitration as provided herein, and the arbitral award shall be final and binding on both parties, unless appealed to a court of competent jurisdiction. Failure to exercise rights under a licence patent within one year of the breach shall constitute a waiver of those rights.

A licence of a patent shall be granted by the patent holder to any person who demonstrates a legitimate need and offers terms and conditions not less favourable than those customarily granted for similar inventions, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any application for a licence patent shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the purpose for which the licence is sought, the scope of the intended use, and a proposed royalty structure. The patent holder may, within sixty days of receiving such application, reject the request with a reasoned statement; failing which, it shall be deemed that consent has been granted. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates that the patented invention relates to a field of public health or nutrition, the Controller may, after due inquiry, direct the patent holder to grant a licence on terms determined by the Controller. Any dispute arising from the interpretation or implementation of this provision shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court. Compliance with reporting requirements regarding the extent of licensed use is mandatory.

Any holder of a patent, desiring to grant a licence of the patent, shall submit a notice to the Controller, detailing the terms and conditions of the proposed licence, including royalty rates and duration. Failure to submit such notice prior to the execution of any licensing agreement shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a patentee grants a licence without adhering to the provisions as provided herein, the Controller may, upon application by any person aggrieved, revoke the licence and impose a further fine on the patentee, up to one hundred thousand rupees. A compulsory licence may be granted by the Controller if the patentee fails to reasonably address the needs of the public, or if the patent is not worked effectively. Any licensee found to be in breach of the terms of a valid licence shall be liable to immediate termination of the licence and may be subject to legal proceedings for damages. All disputes relating to licence patents shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction.

Any holder of a patent, desiring to secure the widest possible exploitation of the invention, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a licence under the patent to any person or persons. Such a licence patent shall be evidenced by a written instrument signed by the patentee, or duly authorised agent, and shall specify the scope of the licence, including the duration, the territory, and the fields of use. Where a licence is granted for a term, it shall be registered with the Controller within the prescribed time. The patentee may, in the instrument of licence, stipulate reasonable royalties or other consideration for the licence, and may also reserve the right to revoke the licence in the event of a breach of the conditions specified therein. Assignment of a licence patent is permissible, provided that the assignee obtains the prior written consent of the patentee, unless otherwise agreed in the original licensing instrument. Failure to obtain such consent shall render the assignment void.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board for revocation of a licence of a patent granted under this Act, alleging that the licensee has failed to adhere to the terms and conditions stipulated within the licence agreement, or that the licensed use unreasonably prejudices the patentee’s rights. The Appellate Board shall, following notice to both the patentee and the licensee, conduct an inquiry and may, if satisfied that a material breach has occurred, order modification of the licence terms, or, in cases of persistent and substantial non-compliance, direct its termination. However, a patentee seeking revocation must demonstrate irreparable harm resulting from the licensee’s actions and that remedies available under general contract law are insufficient. Any decision of the Appellate Board regarding a licence patent shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law.

A patentee aggrieved by a decision of the Controller refusing to grant a licence of their patent, or imposing unreasonable conditions upon a licence, may appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Any application for a licence patent shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the scope of the proposed use of the patented invention, and the terms and conditions sought for the licence. The Chairperson of the Appellate Board may, subject to such terms as they deem fit, direct the patentee to grant a licence, or to modify the conditions of a previously granted licence, if it appears that the applicant has demonstrated sufficient grounds for requiring the same. Failure to comply with any direction of the Chairperson regarding a licence patent shall be considered a contravention of this Act and may attract penalties as provided herein. A licensee shall have the right to seek redressal from the appropriate court should the patentee act in violation of the terms of the granted licence.

A geographical indication, as used in relation to goods, signifies an indication identifying those goods as originating from a specific geographical location where a particular quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, serves to distinguish the goods from those originating elsewhere. The reputation of a geographical indication may, notwithstanding the origin of the goods, be protected under this Act provided that a clear and demonstrable link exists between the goods and the geographical area. Any indication functioning as a collective mark identifying the producers of geographical indication goods shall also be considered a geographical indication, subject to registration as provided herein. The registrar may, where appropriate, require evidence of customary usage to establish the link between the indication and the geographical area.

Any applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication for goods shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, detailing the goods to which the indication applies and the geographical area from which the goods originate. The application shall include a statement of the qualities or reputation of the goods that are attributable to their geographical origin, and a standard of quality for the geographical indication goods, consistently maintained. Where the geographical indication also signifies a specific quality arising from a method of production unique to that region, a detailed description of such a process shall be furnished. The Registry may, subject to verification of the claims made, register the geographical indication if it satisfies the criteria as provided herein. Registration shall confer the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the registered goods, preventing unauthorized use by any other person. A register of geographical indications shall be maintained and open to public inspection.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication relating to geographical indication goods, may institute a civil suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, irrespective of the place of residence or domicile of the defendant. The suit shall be subject to a limitation period of three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication proves that an act of infringement has caused him damage, he shall be entitled to recover damages, or an account of profits, whichever is higher, together with costs. The Court may, at the request of the plaintiff, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. A false application of a geographical indication, or a false representation as to the source of geographical indication goods, shall be deemed a serious offence punishable with imprisonment and fine as provided herein. The registered proprietor may, with the leave of the Court, apply for the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication.

A geographical indication, when registered under this Act, shall confer upon the applicant and their successors in interest the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to those goods in respect of which it is registered. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, grant a license to use a registered geographical indication to an applicant who demonstrates a legitimate interest and a need to use the indication for purposes consistent with the protection of the reputation of the geographical indication goods. Any association of producers or artisans concerned with the production of geographical indication goods may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, exercise the rights conferred by this Act on behalf of the producers. A false application of a geographical indication, or a representation that goods are of a particular geographical origin when they are not, shall be actionable under this Act and may result in injunction and damages. The Central Government shall maintain a register of all registered geographical indications and shall make it available for public inspection.

Any producer seeking registration of a geographical indication for goods shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified goods and the geographical area of origin, substantiated by verifiable evidence as provided herein. The application shall include a detailed description of the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods that are essentially attributable to the geographical origin, and a defined geographical area where the link exists. Where a specification is claimed regarding a traditional method of production, the applicant shall furnish proof of consistent practice for a minimum period of fifteen years immediately preceding the date of application. A register of authorized users shall be maintained, and any person engaged in the production or processing of geographical indication goods within the defined area may apply for inclusion, subject to verification of adherence to the established standards. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the refusal of registration or revocation of existing rights, and any aggrieved party may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register.

Any person dealing in geographical indication goods, who falsely represents such goods as originating from a specific geographical area as protected under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, or both. Where the false representation relates to agricultural produce, the penalty shall not be less than two lakh rupees. Any evidence of intent to deceive, or repeated offenses relating to geographical indication goods, shall be considered an aggravating factor in determining the penalty. The Registrar, upon receiving a complaint and subject to verification, may initiate a summary inquiry and, if satisfied of the contravention, may impose a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. All penalties collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. Any order imposing a penalty may be appealed to the High Court.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer or license the rights therein, whether wholly or in part, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment, transfer or license shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry to be effective against third parties. The Registrar may, upon application, refuse to register an assignment, transfer or license if it is demonstrated that such action would be detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication goods or to the interests of the producers associated therewith. A licensee shall be entitled to use the geographical indication solely for the purposes and within the limits specified in the license agreement, and any use beyond those terms shall constitute an infringement as provided herein. Where a license contains a condition requiring the licensor to approve any sub-license, such approval may not be unreasonably withheld. The registered proprietor may, subject to a notice period of not less than sixty days, revoke a license upon the occurrence of any material breach of the license agreement.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a written complaint with the Geographical Indications Registry alleging improper use of a registered geographical indication in relation to geographical indication goods. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such complaint, serve notice to the alleged infringer and the complainant, directing both parties to submit evidence within a period not exceeding sixty days. Should the Registry, after examining the evidence, find sufficient grounds to believe that an infringement has occurred, it may order the alleged infringer to cease the unlawful use and to provide an account of profits derived therefrom. An appeal from any order of the Registry shall lie to the High Court having jurisdiction, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Registry’s order. The High Court may, at its discretion, grant interim relief pending the final disposal of the appeal, including an injunction restraining the continued infringement, and may also determine appropriate damages. Any determination of damages shall consider the reputation and market value of the geographical indication goods.

A geographical indication, signifying the origin of goods, shall be understood as an indication identifying a good originating from a specific geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, serves to distinguish it from goods of similar nature which do not originate in that area. Where a patent shall be obtained for an invention involving a process for the production of geographical indication goods, the rights conferred by such patent shall be exercised in a manner that does not prejudice the protection afforded to the geographical indication under this Act. Any alteration to the inherent characteristics of the geographical indication goods, resulting from the patented process, subject to quality control and prior approval, may be permissible provided that such alteration does not mislead the consumer as to the true origin or quality.

A geographical indication plaintiff, for the purposes of this Act, shall be a person, association of persons, organization or body of persons, registered as the proprietor of a geographical indication in respect of goods falling within the classes specified in the Fourth Schedule to this Act. Such a plaintiff shall possess the legal capacity to enforce rights in a court of competent jurisdiction and shall be subject to the provisions relating to assignment, transmission, and licensing as provided herein. Where a geographical indication is jointly owned, all registered owners shall be considered geographical indication plaintiffs, and any action taken by one shall bind all, unless otherwise agreed in writing. Any legal proceedings initiated by a geographical indication plaintiff shall be subject to the rules of civil procedure applicable in the relevant jurisdiction.

Any person claiming to be a geographical indication plaintiff, seeking registration of a geographical indication under this Act, shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of proposed use and a detailed description of the goods to which the geographical indication will be applied.
