The application shall clearly identify the region or locality in India with which the goods are associated, and demonstrate a consistent link between the goods’ qualities, reputation, or other characteristics, and that geographical origin. A register of geographical indications shall be maintained, open for inspection subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Where a collective body, such as a producers’ association, represents the interests of the producers, it may act as the geographical indication plaintiff, provided it possesses the legal capacity to do so and is duly authorized to represent the concerned producers. The Registry may, after examination, accept or reject the application, and shall notify the applicant of its decision.

A geographical indication plaintiff, being a registered proprietor of a geographical indication, shall have the right to institute civil proceedings for infringement of such geographical indication. Any person using a geographical indication that is identical or deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication in relation to goods for which it is registered, and such use is likely to cause confusion or misrepresentation, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. The court, upon finding infringement, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing geographical indication. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the court may also award damages to the geographical indication plaintiff for loss suffered as a consequence of the infringement. A proprietor may, alternatively to damages, seek an account of profits made by the defendant through the unlawful use. Provided that, where the defendant proves that the geographical indication was used in good faith and without knowledge of the registration, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Any order of injunction or damages shall be enforceable by the court as if it were a decree.

A geographical indication plaintiff, being a registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may institute a suit for infringement before a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Such a suit shall be subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as if it were a commercial suit, notwithstanding any other provision contained therein. The plaintiff shall, at the time of filing the suit, furnish a certificate of registration of the geographical indication relied upon as evidence. 

Any person, alleging to be likely to be injured by the infringement of a geographical indication, and not being a registered proprietor thereof, may apply to the Court for an injunction restraining the infringement. Provided that such application shall be accompanied by a statement of facts sufficient to show that the applicant is likely to be injured. The Court may, if it deems fit, require the applicant to furnish security for the due observance of such conditions as it may impose. A defendant in any suit under this Act may, in any pleading, set off any claim he may have against the plaintiff.

A geographical indication plaintiff, being a registered proprietor of a geographical indication, shall possess the exclusive right to use the said geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person dealing in goods bearing a falsely labelled geographical indication, or a colourable variation thereof, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be liable to legal proceedings. However, a producer who is not the registered proprietor may continue to use a traditional production method associated with the geographical indication, provided that such method does not mislead consumers into believing the goods originate from the registered geographical area. Where a collective body, such as a producers’ association, is recognized as the geographical indication plaintiff, it shall demonstrate ongoing quality control measures and adherence to a code of practice. Failure to maintain such standards may result in suspension of registration, as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may initiate proceedings for infringement before the competent court.

Any person claiming to be a geographical indication plaintiff, alleging unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication, may institute a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the unauthorized use occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The suit shall be subject to a limitation period of three years from the date of knowledge of such unauthorized use. Failure to commence proceedings within this period shall constitute an estoppel against the geographical indication plaintiff. Where a defendant is proven to have knowingly applied a false geographical indication to goods, or to have traded goods with a falsely applied geographical indication, the Court may, as provided herein, order the destruction or forfeiture of such goods. Any person assisting in the sale or distribution of goods bearing such false indications shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Court may also grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further unauthorized use.

A geographical indication plaintiff, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to others for the use of said geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Any such license shall be in writing and may be subject to conditions regarding the quality of goods, the area of production, and the duration of the license. Assignment of a geographical indication, or any right therein, shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Board, and shall be effected by an instrument in writing duly executed by the assignor and the assignee. The Board may, if it deems fit, refuse to consent to an assignment if it is of the opinion that such assignment would be detrimental to the reputation or quality of the geographical indication. A licensee shall not assign or further license their rights under the license without the prior written consent of both the geographical indication plaintiff and the Board. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the license or assignment voidable at the option of the plaintiff.

Any person claiming to be a geographical indication plaintiff, and alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The suit shall be subject to a limitation period of three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement. Provided that the Court, upon establishing prima facie evidence of irreparable harm to the geographical indication plaintiff, may grant an interim injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement pending the final determination of the suit. An appeal from any decree or order of the District Court in such a suit shall lie to the High Court, and further to the Supreme Court, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Court may, at its discretion, award costs to the successful party, considering the conduct of the parties and the complexity of the case.

A geographical indication plaintiff, being a body representing producers of goods originating from a defined geographical area, may initiate proceedings for infringement as provided herein. Any person alleging injury due to the unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication shall demonstrate a direct nexus between the unauthorized use and the alleged injury, substantiated by evidence admissible in a court of law. The Registrar, upon receiving a complaint of infringement concerning a registered geographical indication, shall notify the defendant and afford them an opportunity to submit a defense. Where a defendant admits to the use of a registered geographical indication but claims legitimate use or prior rights, the court may, subject to verification of such claims, grant a license on fair and reasonable terms. An injunction may be granted to restrain the defendant from further unauthorized use, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates irreparable harm. The court shall consider the extent of the unauthorized use and the potential damage to the reputation of the registered geographical indication when determining relief.

Any geographical indication plaintiff, being a registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement has occurred, or where the defendant resides, or carries on business. The plaint shall clearly demonstrate a prima facie case of misrepresentation likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public, and shall specify the relief sought, including injunction and damages. Filing application fees, as prescribed by rules made under this Act, must accompany the plaint, failing which the suit may be dismissed. Where a defendant is found to have knowingly and intentionally used a false geographical indication, the court may impose a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Repeated offences shall attract doubled penalties, and the court may also order the destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication. Any person assisting in the infringement shall be liable as a contributory infringer.

A registered layout-design shall mean a final three-dimensional arrangement of the elements, layers, and interconnections of an integrated circuit, which is capable of being manufactured and which is registered under this Act. The registration of a layout-design shall confer upon the applicant, being the registered proprietor, the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout-design. A commercial exploitation right, as provided herein, includes the right to sell, lease, or distribute an integrated circuit embodying the registered layout-design. Subject to the provisions relating to licensing, no person shall, without the permission of the registered proprietor, perform any of the acts constituting commercial exploitation. A layout-design must be original to qualify for registration, and shall not be identical to any existing layout-design.

A layout-design shall be considered registrable under this Act if it is an original creation, not previously known or used anywhere in India or, to the best of knowledge of the applicant, anywhere else in the world. The application for registration of a registered layout-design shall be made in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by the necessary fee, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where an application for registration discloses more than one layout-design, a separate fee shall be payable for each such layout-design. 

The Controller may, before registration, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information as may be necessary. A registered layout-design shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially use the layout-design. Provided that such right shall be subject to the provisions relating to licensing and compulsory licensing as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority.

Any person who, being the registered proprietor of a registered layout-design, discovers that any person has infringed such layout-design, may institute civil legal proceedings in the appropriate District Court, subject to the provisions of this Act. The registered proprietor shall, for the purposes of obtaining interim relief, have the same remedies as are available to a plaintiff in a suit for infringement of copyright. Where a defendant proves that the layout-design was not originally generated by the plaintiff or that the defendant had independently developed an identical layout-design, no relief shall be granted. 

A registered layout-design is commercially exploited when any article incorporating the layout-design is sold, hired, or otherwise distributed. The proprietor of a registered layout-design may also apply to the Court for an order restraining the defendant from the further manufacture, sale, or distribution of articles incorporating the infringing layout-design, and for an account of profits. Provided that, no such order shall be made unless sufficient proof of commercial prejudice is demonstrated.

Any person desiring to exercise rights in a registered layout-design shall furnish to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry a statement of licensing arrangements, if any, entered into by him, within thirty days of the registration of the layout-design, and any subsequent modification thereto shall be communicated to the Registry within the same timeframe. Failure to comply with this provision may render the registration liable to revocation, subject to a hearing conducted by the Controller of Designs. A registered layout-design shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially deal with the layout-design. However, such exclusive right shall not extend to acts done for private or non-commercial purposes. The term of protection for a registered layout-design is ten years from the date of registration, or ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation, whichever is earlier. Any dispute regarding the validity of a registered layout-design or the infringement thereof shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction. The Controller may, as provided herein, require additional evidence to substantiate claims of ownership or exploitation.

A registered layout-design shall be considered commercially exploited if it is sold, hired, or leased, or if any article embodying the layout-design is offered for sale or distribution. Any person making an application for registration of a registered layout-design shall furnish a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its originality. Subject to the provisions herein, the right to commercially exploit a registered layout-design vests exclusively with the registered proprietor. However, such exclusive right shall not extend to acts done privately and on a non-commercial scale. 

Where a layout-design incorporates a standard cell, the registration shall specify the extent of the layout-design that is protected, excluding the standard cell itself, provided that the standard cell does not contribute to the overall originality of the registered layout-design. Any assignment of a registered layout-design shall be in writing and registered with the appropriate authority as prescribed. Failure to comply with these requirements may invalidate the registration.

Any person who, without the consent of the registered proprietor of a registered layout-design, and knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that such act would constitute an infringement, manufactures, exercises, offers for sale, sells, hires, or distributes an integrated circuit embodying the registered layout-design, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees. Where the infringement involves commercial exploitation of the registered layout-design, the court may also order delivery up or destruction of all infringing articles and materials used in the manufacture of such articles. A person claiming to be the registered proprietor of a registered layout-design may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the infringer from the unlawful acts as provided herein.

Any registered layout-design shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by mutual agreement between the registered proprietor and a prospective licensee, and such agreements may provide for royalty payments, duration of license, and scope of commercial exploitation. Assignment of rights in a registered layout-design may be effected through a written instrument duly executed by the registered proprietor, and such assignment shall be subject to verification by the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. Where a registered layout-design is jointly held, no single proprietor may grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other co-proprietors, as provided herein. A licensee obtaining rights under this Act shall exercise such rights in a manner consistent with the terms of the license and shall not infringe upon any other intellectual property rights. The registered proprietor may, subject to the terms of any existing license, further license or assign the registered layout-design to other parties. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the license or assignment invalid.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Controller to register a layout-design, or by any order made by the Controller relating to the amendment or revocation of a registration of a registered layout-design, may, within ninety days from the date of such refusal or order, file an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be in the form of a memorandum of appeal, verified by affidavit, and shall state the grounds on which the appellant relies for setting aside or modifying the decision of the Controller. The High Court, upon consideration of the appeal and subject to such evidence as it may deem fit, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision appealed against, and may also direct the Controller to conduct a fresh hearing, if necessary. A commercial confidence agreement, if submitted as evidence, shall be admissible provided it was in force at the time of alleged infringement. The Controller’s decision regarding the validity of a registered layout-design remains enforceable pending the outcome of any appeal, unless the High Court directs otherwise.

A person who is the registered proprietor of a registered layout-design shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or import the layout-design in any manner, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any act undertaken without the express license of, or contrary to the directions of, the registered proprietor shall constitute an infringement of their exclusive right. Where a person, being the manner registered proprietor, reasonably believes that an infringement of their registered layout-design has occurred or is about to occur, they may apply to the High Court for a prohibitory injunction. The Court, upon being satisfied of the prima facie case, may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall not be entitled to relief where the alleged infringement relates to a layout-design that is demonstrably not novel or is otherwise ineligible for registration as provided herein. Any damages awarded shall be commensurate with the actual loss suffered, or the reasonable royalty due, whichever is higher.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design shall, prior to the institution of any suit, notify the alleged infringer of the particulars of the infringement. Such notification shall be served by registered post or through an advocate and shall specify the registered layout-design which is alleged to have been infringed, and the nature of the infringement. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a Layout-Design Office for the administration of this Act. All applications for registration, and any other documents required to be filed under this Act, shall be submitted to the Layout-Design Office. In the event of any dispute regarding the validity of a registered layout-design, or any matter arising under this Act, the Central Government may appoint a chairperson judicial member possessing requisite legal expertise to adjudicate upon such dispute. The decision of the chairperson judicial member shall be final and binding, subject to provisions for appeal to the High Court as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Layout-Design Office may seek redressal through the aforementioned process.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, represents a layout-design as being a registered layout-design when it is not, or knowingly sells, lets for hire, or distributes an integrated circuit embodying a layout-design in respect of which a registration application is pending, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees. Where a registered layout-design is falsely represented as being the subject of advertised acceptance, the penalty shall be enhanced by one-third. The court, as provided herein, may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of all integrated circuits and materials used in the commission of the offence. Any appeal against a conviction under this Act shall lie before the High Court.

A semiconductor integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, signifies a three dimensional microstructure, including all layers, of electronic and circuit elements and conductors, which is intended for the performance of electronic functions. Such a circuit shall be considered a finished form, irrespective of whether it is incorporated into a module or not. A layout-design, as detailed herein, is a plan of all layers of a semiconductor integrated circuit, including channel stops, diffusion types, junction locations, and all other structural features of the circuit. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a layout-design shall be considered original if it is generated through independent intellectual effort. Any design that is substantially similar to an existing layout-design may be deemed non-original, provided that such similarity is demonstrably proven.

A person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit an application to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, including a representation thereof, and shall identify the applicant as the creator. Any confidential information relating to the manufacturing process, if disclosed, shall be treated as privileged and subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein. 

A layout-design shall not be registered if it is identical to an earlier layout-design, or if it is substantially similar, and would cause confusion amongst those skilled in the art. Provided that, a layout-design incorporating only minor modifications of an existing layout-design may be registered subject to demonstrating significant technical advancement. The Registry may, prior to registration, require the applicant to submit additional information or clarification regarding the semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. Registration confers the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout-design.

Any person making an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to be the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein, and shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in India. Such exclusive right shall include the right to reproduce, import, sell, or otherwise distribute the semiconductor integrated circuit embodying the layout-design, or any article containing such circuit. Where a layout-design is exploited without the consent of the registered proprietor, an action for infringement may be instituted in any District Court having jurisdiction. The registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the infringing act, and may also claim damages for the loss suffered due to such infringement. A person who assists another in the infringement of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be liable for contributory infringement, and remedies available against the principal infringer shall also apply to such assisting person. Provided that, no action shall lie against a person who proves that the exploitation was done independently and without knowledge of the registered layout-design.

A semiconductor integrated circuit, for the purposes of this Act, shall be construed as a three-dimensional structure including all layers and elements therein, and shall be capable of performing an electronic function. Any person exploiting a layout-design without the authorization of the registered proprietor, as provided herein, shall be liable to legal proceedings. The applicant for registration of a layout-design may be either the creator of such layout-design or their assignee or the lawful representative. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the right to a layout-design shall subsist until the expiry of ten years from the date of filing, or, if the layout-design has been commercially exploited, ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation. Where a layout-design is incorporated in an article, the proprietor shall have the right to prevent any person from making, selling, or importing such article. Any dispute regarding the validity of a layout-design or the infringement thereof shall be adjudicated by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Evidence of commercial exploitation shall be prima facie proof of the date of first commercial exploitation.

Any person exploiting a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design commercially, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, ensure that such exploitation does not infringe any existing registered layout-design. A layout-design, to be eligible for registration, must be an original creation and shall not be essentially a copy of any existing layout-design or a trivial variation thereof. The applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may submit an application to the designated authority, accompanied by the prescribed fee and necessary documentation detailing the layout-design’s features. Provided that, where a layout-design incorporates a standard cell, the standard cell shall be disclosed in the application. Any layout-design found to be substantially similar to a prior art layout-design, as determined by a comparative assessment under this Act, may be subject to rejection or amendment. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registration or imposition of penalties, as provided herein.

Any person who, without the consent of the registered proprietor, manufactures, imports, sells, hires, or otherwise distributes a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying a layout-design registered as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not less than ten lakh rupees and not exceeding five crore rupees, or imprisonment for a term not less than six months and not exceeding three years, or both. Where the offence involves repeated infringement, the penalty shall not be less than twenty-five lakh rupees. A person claiming to be the rightful owner of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the appropriate court for an injunction restraining the infringer from the said acts. Any material used in the manufacture of such infringing semiconductor integrated circuit, or any packaging embodying the layout-design, shall be deemed to be contraband and subject to seizure. The court may, at its discretion, order the destruction of such seized material.

Any person possessing a right to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, whether arising from creation, assignment, or operation of law, may grant a license to another party for the commercial exploitation of said layout-design, subject to the terms and conditions mutually agreed upon in a written instrument. Such license shall define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to the territory, duration, and field of application. Assignment of all rights in a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be effected through a written instrument duly executed by the assignor and assignee, and such assignment shall be registrable as provided herein. Where a layout-design is created pursuant to a contract of service or apprenticeship, the rights therein shall vest in the employer or master, unless otherwise agreed in writing. A licensee may, with the express consent of the registered proprietor, further assign or license their interest in the layout-design, provided that such sub-licensing or assignment does not contravene any existing restrictions. The registered proprietor retains the right to seek equitable relief in cases of unauthorized use or exploitation of the semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall, prior to the institution of proceedings before a competent court, furnish to the alleged infringer a notice of such claim, detailing with reasonable specificity the nature of the infringement and the layout-design asserted to be infringed. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of receipt of such notice, submit a written request for further and more particular details relating to the alleged infringement, the claimant shall, within a further thirty days, provide such details, subject to maintaining the confidentiality of any trade secrets disclosed therein. 

However, a failure to provide such further details, or a provision of manifestly insufficient details, may be considered by the court as an indication of bad faith on the part of the claimant, potentially impacting costs awarded in any subsequent litigation. Appeals regarding the determination of ‘sufficient detail’ shall lie with the appellate authority as provided herein, and such appeals must be filed within sixty days of the lower court’s order.

Any person desiring to obtain a layout-design right in a semiconductor integrated circuit shall submit an application to the appropriate Office as provided herein. Such application shall include a detailed description of the semiconductor integrated circuit, including its constituent elements and interconnections, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. An applicant may, prior to filing a complete specification, submit a provisional specification, which shall be retained confidential for a period not exceeding six months, subject to the applicant fulfilling the requirements for a complete specification within said period. The right to a layout-design shall vest with the creator, unless an agreement to the contrary exists, and may be assigned, transferred, or licensed, wholly or partially, and for any term, to another person. Any license granted under this Act shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the license, including any limitations on use or territory. The registered proprietor shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses. Failure to do so may affect the enforceability of the layout-design right.

Any person alleging infringement of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall, prior to the institution of proceedings before the High Court, submit a detailed statement of the alleged infringement to the opposing party, including a clear depiction of the layout-design and the manner of its reproduction. Should the opposing party, within sixty days of receipt of such statement, demonstrate a prior art defense or a legitimate independent development, the claimant may, subject to the provisions herein, seek mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon technical expert. However, where the alleged infringement involves an indication used geographically to identify the source of the semiconductor integrated circuit, the claimant must also provide evidence establishing the origin and distinctiveness of said indication. Failure to comply with these pre-litigation requirements may be considered by the Court when determining costs, and shall not preclude a finding of infringement if sufficient evidence is otherwise presented. Any appeal arising from a decision regarding such pre-litigation matters shall lie with the Division Bench of the relevant High Court.

A semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, for the purposes of this Act, shall mean the original and distinctive three-dimensional configuration of the layers of elements and interconnections of an electronic circuit intended for fabrication on a semiconductor substrate. Such a layout-design may relate to any article of commerce, including but not limited to devices used in the processing or preservation of food products, or components thereof. A layout-design shall be considered distinct, subject to verification as provided herein, even if it incorporates elements commonly used in the art. The term includes all variations in shape, pattern, or dimension, and any combination thereof, provided that such variations are essential for the functioning of the semiconductor integrated circuit. Any layout-design substantially similar to a registered layout-design shall be deemed an infringement under this Act.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall submit a declaration affirming compliance with all provisions of this Act relating to the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources and traditional knowledge. The application for registration shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the plant variety, including its lineage, characteristics, and stability, as determined through trials conducted in accordance with the prescribed guidelines. Provided that, a breeder who has demonstrably complied with provisions concerning benefit sharing, as outlined in the National Biodiversity Act, 2002, may be granted a priority assessment of their application. The Authority shall, subject to verification of the breeder complied provisions and satisfactory completion of the designated trials, issue a certificate of registration, conferring exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, and import the protected variety. Any transfer of such rights shall be registered with the Authority to ensure transparency and traceability.

Any breeder who has, in the course of commercial exploitation of a protected variety, saved, sold, shared or otherwise disposed of seeds in a manner inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each such instance. However, a registered breeder shall not be held liable for incidental or accidental compliance failures, provided that such failures are promptly reported to the Plant Variety Protection Authority and do not demonstrate a systematic disregard for breeder complied provisions. Where a farmer, having lawfully saved seeds of a protected variety, sells or distributes such seeds in a manner not authorized by the breeder, the farmer shall be subject to a warning and a requirement to cease such activity; repeated non-compliance may result in a fine not exceeding one thousand rupees. The Authority may, subject to an inquiry, exempt a farmer from such penalty if it is demonstrated that the sale or distribution was necessitated by local custom or traditional practice and did not cause significant economic harm to the breeder. Any amounts collected as penalties under this Act shall be credited to the Plant Variety Protection Fund.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, alongside the application, furnish a declaration affirming compliance with all provisions relating to the protection of breeder’s rights as provided herein. Such declaration shall explicitly state whether the variety has been derived from any other variety, and if so, detail the parent variety or varieties and the manner of derivation. Where a variety is essentially derived from another, the breeder of the essentially derived variety shall require the prior authorization of the breeder of the initial variety, unless such derivation is clearly evident and does not require the expression of a new expression of characteristics. The Authority may, however, waive the requirement of prior authorization if it is established that the essentially derived variety represents a significant improvement over the initial variety. Any breeder failing to comply with these provisions shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and the Authority may reject the application for registration. The register of plant varieties shall maintain a record of all such breeder complied provisions and any associated waivers granted.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, full compliance with the provisions relating to essentially derived varieties as provided herein. Such compliance shall include the maintenance of detailed records documenting the lineage and characteristics of the parent line from which the new variety is derived, and the provision of such records upon request by the Authority or any aggrieved party. Provided that, a breeder may also demonstrate compliance through the submission of a statutory declaration affirming adherence to all breeder complied provisions and a commitment to ongoing monitoring for genetic drift. Failure to maintain adequate records or to truthfully declare compliance shall constitute grounds for rejection of the application or revocation of any granted protection, subject to a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The Authority may, at its discretion, require independent verification of the breeder’s claims.

Any breeder who, having obtained registration for a new plant variety, fails to comply with the provisions relating to seed production, quality assurance, and maintenance of the variety as stipulated in the registration certificate, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that the Authority may, considering the nature and extent of the non-compliance, reduce the penalty or issue a warning instead. Furthermore, repeated or willful non-compliance with breeder complied provisions, particularly concerning the availability of seeds to farmers, may result in suspension of the breeder’s registration for a period not exceeding three years. Any seed produced in violation of these provisions shall be deemed to be adulterated goods under the relevant standards act and subject to seizure. The Authority shall maintain a register of all penalties imposed and actions taken under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, any farmer or group of farmers, or any other person claiming rights over a registered plant variety, may file a complaint with the Plant Variety Protection Authority alleging non-compliance by the breeder with the provisions relating to breeder complied provisions as stipulated under this Act. Such complaint shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a prima facie case of such non-compliance, including but not limited to, records of seed acquisition, cultivation practices, and demonstrable genetic similarity to the registered variety. The Authority shall, upon receiving such complaint, issue notice to the breeder requiring a response within sixty days. Failure to respond, or a response deemed unsatisfactory after due inquiry, may result in the suspension of breeder rights, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any decision of the Authority regarding breeder complied provisions shall be subject to judicial review, and the burden of proof regarding compliance rests with the breeder.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, any registered breeder who fails to comply with the provisions relating to benefit sharing with farmers, or the maintenance of a seed stock of a protected variety as stipulated under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty as may be prescribed. However, such non-compliance shall not, *per se*, invalidate the breeder’s rights, provided that the Authority, upon receiving credible evidence of such failure, initiates an inquiry and affords the breeder a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Should the inquiry establish a prima facie case of non-compliance, the Authority may impose a financial penalty, and direct remedial action. Any determination of the Authority regarding breeder complied provisions may be appealed to the Appellate Board, subject to the conditions outlined herein. A claim of a new variety, even if demonstrably so, does not absolve the breeder from obligations under this Act. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

A geographical indication shall be applied to goods originating from a defined geographical area where a quality, reputation or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin, and which, in accordance with the provisions of this Act, is registered as a geographical indication. Any person who applies a geographical indication that is registered under this Act to goods not originating from the specified geographical area, or to goods whose quality, reputation or other characteristics are not substantially linked to that area, shall be deemed to have undertaken a misrepresentation. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct an applicant to modify a proposed geographical indication if it is likely to cause confusion with a previously registered geographical indication. Provided that, a registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, with the approval of the Registrar, assign the registration to another person, and such assignment shall be subject to the conditions specified in the register. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the geographical indication applied shall be subject to the remedies provided herein.

A geographical indication applied to goods shall be registered in the Register maintained under this Act, subject to the provisions herein and the rules made thereunder. An applicant seeking registration shall submit a statement of case, including a clear and unambiguous description of the goods, the geographical area to which the indication relates, and evidence establishing a link between the goods’ qualities or reputation and that geographical area. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the application meets the requirements, accept it for examination. Any false application of a registered geographical indication, or any act likely to deceive the public as to the origin of goods, shall constitute a commission offence attributable to the person so acting. The Registrar may, following due process and consideration of evidence, revoke a registration if it is proven that the geographical indication is no longer descriptive of the goods or that the conditions for registration are no longer met. A registered proprietor shall be entitled to initiate civil or criminal proceedings against any infringer.

There shall be established, for the purposes of this Act, an office to be known as the Copyright Office, functioning as the primary administrative arm for matters pertaining to copyright registration and enforcement. The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Copyrights, detailing particulars of works in which copyright subsists, and shall be responsible for the examination of applications for copyright. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar of Copyrights, who heads the Copyright Office, may require an applicant to furnish such documents or information as may be necessary to determine the validity of a claim. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office may, within a period of sixty days, submit a reasoned representation for reconsideration by the Registrar. The Central Government shall provide for the staffing and resources necessary for the effective functioning of the Copyright Office.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a Register of Copyrights, recording particulars of all published works in which copyright subsists, and all licenses granted in respect of such works, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any person claiming to be the owner of copyright, or deriving title under the owner, may apply to the Copyright Office for the registration of copyright in a work, and shall submit such particulars as may be prescribed. Upon receipt of an application and prescribed fee, the Copyright Office shall, after such examination as it deems necessary, register the copyright in the work, unless satisfied that the work is not eligible for registration as provided herein. The Registrar of Copyrights may require further information or evidence from the applicant, and shall communicate any objection to the application in writing. Registration in the Register shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, but shall not be conclusive proof of validity of copyright. The Copyright Office may, with reasonable cause, restore a copyright entry to the Register if it was cancelled due to administrative error.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Works, recording details of authorship, publication, and ownership as submitted by applicants and shall be open for inspection by any person subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration, or by any entry or omission in the Register, may, within sixty days of the date of such refusal or the knowledge of such entry or omission, submit a reasoned representation to the Registrar of Copyrights. The Registrar shall, following due consideration and affording an opportunity for hearing, pass an order either confirming the initial decision or rectifying the Register. Provided that, any rectification affecting the rights of another party shall require prior notice to such party and their consent, or a determination by a competent court. The Copyright Office may, with the approval of the Central Government, prescribe procedures for the electronic filing of applications and maintenance of the Register, ensuring data security and accessibility. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures may result in rejection of the application.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Copyrights, detailing all works in which copyright subsists, and shall be the authoritative record for establishing claims of ownership as provided herein. Any person claiming copyright in a work shall submit an application to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the work itself, or a reasonable reproduction thereof. The Registrar of Copyrights may, subject to verification of the application and satisfaction that the work meets the requirements for copyright protection under this Act, enter the particulars in the Register and issue a Certificate of Registration. 

The Copyright Office shall also be responsible for the receipt and processing of statements of assignment and licenses relating to copyright, ensuring public access to such information to the extent permissible and in accordance with established procedures. All records maintained by the Copyright Office shall be deemed public documents and admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding concerning copyright. The Registrar of Copyrights may require additional information or clarification from applicants to ensure the accuracy and completeness of the Register.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Works, recording details of authorship, publication, and ownership as submitted by applicants and deemed compliant with the requirements of this Act. All applications for copyright registration shall be made to the Copyright Office in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. The Registrar of Copyrights, acting on behalf of the Copyright Office, may require applicants to furnish further information or clarification to ensure the accuracy and completeness of the Register. Subject to verification and satisfaction of the conditions as provided herein, the Copyright Office shall issue a Certificate of Registration, which shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars entered therein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office regarding registration may, within sixty days, submit a statement of reasons for reconsideration to the Registrar.

The Copyright Office established under this Act shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Works, and any person making a false entry therein, or knowingly providing false information to the Copyright Office, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. Any application for registration, found to be frivolous or vexatious, may be rejected by the Registrar, and the applicant shall be liable to pay damages to the Copyright Office, assessed at a sum not exceeding twenty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require any applicant to furnish additional evidence to substantiate claims made in the application. Failure to comply with such requirement within thirty days shall render the application liable to be dismissed, and the applicant shall forfeit any fees paid. All records maintained by the Copyright Office shall be deemed public documents, but access thereto may be restricted in cases involving national security.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive register of assignments and licenses pertaining to copyright, and any proprietor of copyright intending to assign copyright, or grant a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall furnish particulars thereof to the Copyright Office in the manner as prescribed. Any assignment or license not so registered shall be ineffective against a purchaser or licensee for value without notice of the prior assignment or license. The Registrar of Copyrights may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, require the assignee or licensee to furnish evidence of title or interest. Where a copyright is assigned for a term, the Copyright Office shall record the duration of such assignment. A request for rectification of any entry in the register of assignments or licenses may be made to the Copyright Office, provided that such request is accompanied by a fee as specified in the Schedule. All records maintained by the Copyright Office shall be open to inspection by any interested person, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a Register of Copyrights, and any person aggrieved by a refusal of the Registrar to register a work, or by any correction made to the Register, may lodge an appeal to the High Court within which the applicant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Registrar’s order, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of said order and a statement of reasons for the appeal. The High Court, upon consideration of the appeal and any evidence submitted, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Provided that, the High Court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the period for filing an appeal. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may petition the Supreme Court for a final review, contingent upon satisfying the Court regarding a substantial question of law. The Registrar shall furnish a reasoned order for any refusal or correction.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a register of copyrights, and any person aggrieved by a refusal of the Registrar of Copyrights to register a work, or by any correction made to the register, may submit a reasoned statement of objection to the adjudicating officer appointed for this purpose. Such statement shall be filed within sixty days from the date of the Registrar’s communication regarding the refusal or correction. The adjudicating officer shall, after affording the aggrieved party and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, pass an order either confirming the decision of the Registrar or directing the rectification of the register. Any person dissatisfied with the order of the adjudicating officer may, within ninety days, prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Provided that no appeal shall lie from any order made with the consent of both parties, and the decision of the High Court shall be final, subject to any appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein.

The Copyright Office shall be the central administrative body for all matters pertaining to copyright registration and recordal as provided herein. It shall maintain a comprehensive Register of Copyrights, open for inspection subject to prescribed fees and conditions. Any person claiming ownership of copyright, or a trade mark proprietor seeking to record a copyright assignment relating to a brand identity, may apply to the Copyright Office for the registration of such rights. The Registrar of Copyrights, appointed by the Central Government, shall exercise all powers and perform all functions conferred by this Act relating to the Copyright Office. All notices and communications required to be served on the Copyright Office shall be addressed to the Registrar. The Office shall also facilitate the voluntary settlement of copyright disputes through mediation, where requested by the parties concerned.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive register of all published works in which copyright subsists, and any person claiming copyright in a work shall apply to the Copyright Office for entry in such register, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. An application for registration may be accompanied by a certified copy of any patent granted for an invention embodying a technical aspect of the work, where such patent is relevant to the copyright claim and demonstrates originality. The Registrar of Copyrights may, after examining the application and any accompanying documentation, and being satisfied that the work is eligible for copyright protection as provided herein, register the work and issue a certificate of registration. Should the Registrar refuse registration, an appeal may be made to the High Court, and the aggrieved party shall have thirty days from the date of the refusal to lodge such appeal. Any person aggrieved by an incorrect entry in the register may apply to the Copyright Office for rectification, and the Registrar shall, after due inquiry, make the necessary amendments.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive register of all published works in which copyright subsists, and all particulars of authors, publishers, and owners of copyright. Any person claiming copyright in a work shall submit an application to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the work, for entry in the register. The Registrar of Copyrights may, subject to verification of the claim and satisfaction of all procedural requirements as provided herein, grant a certificate of registration. 

Where a work is produced limits india, meaning it is manufactured solely for circulation within the territory of India, the applicant shall specify this limitation in the application form. The Copyright Office shall, upon receiving a request accompanied by a justification, consider applications for expedited registration of works of national importance. All records maintained by the Copyright Office shall be open to inspection by any member of the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with such conditions as may be determined by the Registrar. The Registrar may, with prior approval of the Central Government, prescribe forms and procedures for all matters relating to the functioning of the Copyright Office.

The Copyright Office shall maintain a comprehensive register of all published works in which copyright subsists, and all assignments and licenses relating thereto, as provided herein. Any person claiming copyright in a work shall submit a detailed application to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the work itself, or a representative portion thereof. Applications seeking registration based on priority claimed under the Madrid Protocol International shall include a certified statement of the original filing date and a verified copy of the international registration. The Copyright Office may, subject to verification of the claim and compliance with all procedural requirements, register the copyright and issue a certificate of registration. Failure to maintain accurate records of assignments and licenses with the Copyright Office shall not invalidate the copyright itself, but may affect the enforceability of rights against third parties unaware of such changes. All records maintained by the Copyright Office shall be open to inspection by any interested person, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

A “person interested” shall, for the purposes of opposition proceedings under this Act, include any person alleging to be injured by the grant of a patent. Such injury must be reasonably demonstrable and directly attributable to the potential commercial exploitation of the invention claimed in the patent application. A person engaged in active and legitimate competition with the applicant, and who can establish a substantial likelihood of competitive harm resulting from the patent, may also be considered a person interested. Provided that, a mere speculative interest or potential future competition shall not, of itself, qualify a party as a person interested. The Controller shall have the discretion to determine whether a party meets the criteria as provided herein, subject to principles of natural justice.

A person interested in making an application for revocation of a patent shall furnish to the Controller a notice of such intention, accompanied by a statement detailing the grounds upon which the revocation is sought and the evidence supporting such grounds. Such a person shall also deposit with the Controller a sum equivalent to the prescribed fee for an opposition, subject to refund as provided herein, if the Controller deems the grounds sufficient to warrant a formal examination. Any individual claiming to be a person interested must demonstrate a substantial connection to the subject matter of the patent or a legitimate commercial interest potentially affected by its continued validity. The Controller may, at any stage, require further evidence from any person interested to ascertain the veracity of their claims or the relevance of the submitted evidence. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the notice and the associated application. A registered patentee shall be notified of any such application for revocation and afforded an opportunity to respond.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent granted under this Act shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, or both, in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred. A person interested, for the purposes of seeking such remedies, shall include not only the patentee but also any licensee authorized by the patentee, or a successor in title to either, provided that such successor demonstrates a clear chain of title and a continuing commercial interest in the patented invention. The Court, subject to due process, may award costs to the prevailing party. Where a defendant proves invalidity of the patent, they shall be entitled to costs, and may also seek recovery of expenses incurred in defending the action. An order for damages may consider reasonable royalties or lost profits, as proven by the claimant, and shall not be excessive or punitive. Any appeal from a District Court’s decision shall lie to the High Court.

A person interested in opposing the grant of a patent under this Act shall, subject to the provisions herein, furnish to the Controller a notice of opposition, setting forth the grounds on which the patent is opposed, within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the application for a patent. The Controller may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period by a further period not exceeding three months. Any person alleging to be a person interested may, prior to the grant of a patent, file representations relating to the patent application, which representations shall be considered by the Controller as part of the examination process. For the purposes of determining whether a party is a person interested, due regard shall be given to evidence of commercial activity or demonstrable expertise in the relevant technological field. Provided that, a mere speculative interest shall not constitute sufficient grounds for being considered a person interested. The Controller shall, upon receipt of a notice of opposition, communicate a copy thereof to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to respond.

A person interested in opposing the grant of a patent under this Act shall submit a notice of opposition to the Controller within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of the application for a patent. Such notice shall contain a detailed statement of the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The Controller may, subject to such terms as he may deem fit, require the opponent to furnish further information or evidence in support of the grounds stated in the notice. Any evidence submitted shall be open for inspection by the applicant. A person interested, for the purposes of this provision, includes a legal entity demonstrably affected by the potential grant of the patent, and also encompasses any individual engaged in comparable technological development. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the opposition inadmissible. The Controller’s decision on admissibility shall be final.

Any person who, not being the patentee or a duly licensed assignee, exercises the exclusive rights conferred by a patent, as provided herein, shall be liable to a civil action for infringement. A person interested, meaning one having a demonstrable commercial stake or engaged in legitimate research directly impacted by the patented invention, may apply to the High Court for an order restraining such infringement and for recovery of damages sustained. The quantum of damages shall be determined based on actual losses or reasonable royalty, at the discretion of the Court. Any evidence obtained through unlawful means, specifically targeting the patentee’s confidential information, shall not be admissible. Failure to comply with an injunction issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine, or both. The patentee may also seek an account of profits derived from the infringing activity.

Any assignment of the right to a patent, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and shall specify the particulars of the invention, the patent, and the assignor and assignee. A license granted under this Act, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be construed as a transfer of an interest in the patent for the duration specified in the instrument, subject to the terms and conditions therein contained. A person interested, being a licensee or assignee, may apply to the Controller for a rectification of the register if any incorrect entry relating to their title or interest appears therein. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence establishing their legitimate interest and the nature of the discrepancy. The Controller, upon being satisfied that a prima facie case exists, shall give notice to the patentee and any other person affected thereby. Provided that, no assignment or license shall be valid as against any subsequent assignee or licensee without due registration as provided herein. Failure to register shall not invalidate the assignment or license but may affect its priority.

A person interested, for the purposes of opposition to a patent granted under this Act, shall demonstrate a sufficient proprietary interest, being either a holder of a valid patent relating to the same invention or a party demonstrably likely to be materially injured by the grant of the patent in question. However, mere commercial rivalry, absent evidence of specific and foreseeable damage to existing proprietary rights, shall not constitute sufficient interest to maintain an opposition. Any decision regarding the locus standi of a person interested may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Controller’s decision. The Appellate Board, in considering such appeals, shall have the power to require the applicant to furnish further evidence substantiating their claim of being a person interested and to determine whether the alleged injury is speculative or substantial. Failure to comply with the timelines as provided herein shall render the appeal inadmissible.

A person interested in opposing the grant of a patent under this Act shall be a person who possesses sufficient and legitimate interest in the subject matter of the invention, and may include a competitor engaged in similar technological fields or a licensee of a related patent. For the purposes of establishing such interest, ownership or registration of a relevant registered trade mark, indicating commercial activity related to goods or services embodying the invention, shall be considered as prima facie evidence of sufficient interest. However, mere speculative interest or a remote possibility of future competition shall not qualify a person as a person interested, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding public interest litigation. Any objection raised by a person not fulfilling the criteria of a person interested may be dismissed.

Any person interested, or alleging to be so, may, at any time after the filing of a complete specification, serve a notice on the Controller of Patents requesting him to furnish a report as to whether the claimed invention possesses novelty and involves an inventive step, having regard to the knowledge available in any relevant art. Such a request shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a clear demonstration of the requester’s legitimate interest in the subject matter of the invention. The Controller, upon receipt of such notice and verification of the fee, shall examine the specification and, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists for a new invention, prepare and furnish the report within a period of sixty days. Failure to demonstrate sufficient interest, or to pay the prescribed fee, shall render the request inadmissible and no report shall be furnished. The report so furnished shall be admissible as evidence in any subsequent opposition proceedings.

Any person interested, and alleging to be injured by any act of the patentee constituting an infringement of a patent granted under this Act, may institute a suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the act of infringement has occurred. The Registrar shall, upon receiving credible evidence of a threat of infringement, forward such evidence to the appropriate District Court, noting that this does not constitute an opinion on the merits of the claim. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the patentee may also pursue criminal remedies as provided under the relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code. Where a counter-claim is made alleging invalidity of the patent, the Court may, at its discretion, stay the proceedings until the validity of the patent has been determined in a separate proceeding. Provided that, the Court may direct the defendant to furnish security for damages pending such determination, if the plaintiff so requests. Any appeal from a decision of the District Court shall lie to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “prescribed manner” shall denote a procedure established by rules made under this Act, and includes any form, application, or documentation required to be submitted as a condition precedent to the exercise of a right or the grant of a benefit. Where a requirement is stated to be carried out in the prescribed manner, strict adherence to such rules is mandatory, and any deviation therefrom may render the act invalid, subject to the discretion of the Controller. A failure to comply with the prescribed manner shall not, however, be construed as an abandonment of the right itself, provided that reasonable opportunity for rectification is afforded. The Controller may, at their discretion, waive minor procedural irregularities if they do not materially affect the outcome.

Any person desiring to register a biological material as a new variety under this Act shall submit an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a detailed description of the characteristics of the said variety, demonstrating its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The application shall further include evidence of the origin and development of the variety, and a statement regarding the essential characteristics which are relevant for the purpose of assessment. Where the applicant claims a variety derived from another variety, full particulars of the parent variety shall be furnished, subject to the provisions relating to breeders’ rights as provided herein. The Plant Variety Protection Authority may, if satisfied that the application is complete and conforms to the requirements of this Act, proceed to examine the variety in the prescribed manner and grant a breeder’s certificate if the variety meets the criteria for registration. Any material submitted as part of the application shall be treated as confidential.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of a Controller of Patents, relating to the grant or refusal of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, subject to the provisions herein. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period. Where an appeal is preferred, the Controller shall furnish to the Appellate Board all documents relating to the case. 

The Appellate Board shall conduct the hearing in a prescribed manner, and may, at its discretion, require the attendance of witnesses or the production of further evidence. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of legal error. A failure to comply with the prescribed manner for filing an appeal shall render it inadmissible.

Any application for a patent, as provided herein, shall be deemed to be made in the prescribed manner only if it conforms strictly to the requirements of the First Schedule, and is accompanied by a complete specification as detailed therein. The Controller of Patents may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed necessary, allow an applicant to amend the specification if such amendment does not extend the scope of the invention beyond what is necessary to correct a manifest error or omission. A request for such amendment shall be submitted in writing and shall clearly identify the error or omission sought to be rectified. Where an invention relates to a process, the application shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the process, and any failure to do so may render the application not in the prescribed manner. The term “prescribed manner” includes the submission of all required documents in the format specified by the Controller and the payment of the applicable fees within the stipulated timeframe. Any deviation from these requirements shall be grounds for rejection of the application.

Any application for a patent, seeking extension of an existing patent, shall be submitted to the Controller in the prescribed manner, and shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the applicant’s belief in the truthfulness of all statements contained therein. The Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish further information or documentation deemed necessary for the proper examination of the application. Failure to comply with such requirement within a period of sixty days from the date of the communication shall be considered sufficient grounds for rejection of the application. Where an applicant claims priority from a convention country, evidence of the earlier application, duly certified, must be furnished in the prescribed manner. Any amendment to the application, after filing, shall be permissible provided that it does not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure and is made in the prescribed manner. A request for examination shall be filed within thirty-six months from the date of filing, failing which the application shall be deemed withdrawn.

Any person who, not being a licensee or authorized agent, undertakes any activity relating to a patented invention in a manner not prescribed herein, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement, and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where such infringement is demonstrated to have been undertaken with intent to deceive, or to gain an unfair commercial advantage, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees, and may additionally include imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. Any instrument or article made or used in contravention of this Act, and found in the possession of an infringer, shall be liable to seizure and forfeiture. The Controller, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, may order the destruction of any such forfeited article, or may direct its sale, with the proceeds accruing to the Government. “Prescribed manner” for the purposes of claiming exemption from penalties shall include full and truthful disclosure of all relevant facts to the Controller within thirty days of the alleged infringement.

Any assignment of the right, title, and interest in a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be made in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall specify the terms and conditions governing the assignment, including any royalty payable and the territory to which the assignment applies. Where an assignment is made otherwise than in the prescribed manner, it shall be voidable at the option of the assignor, subject to any existing contractual obligations. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be granted for a defined period or in perpetuity, and shall be construed as an assignment of limited rights as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity or scope of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court. The Controller shall maintain a register of assignments and licenses, and any alteration to the ownership of a patent must be recorded therein. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent vulnerable to revocation.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents refusing an application for a patent, or revoking a patent, or amending a patent in a manner prejudicial to the applicant or patentee, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the Appellate Board allowing an extension of time for sufficient cause. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and any evidence presented, may confirm, modify, reverse, or set aside the decision of the Controller. Where the appeal concerns a matter of ‘prescribed manner’ relating to the form or content of an application, the Appellate Board shall ensure strict adherence to the requirements as detailed in the First Schedule. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, if it deems fit, direct the Controller to re-examine the application in light of the Board’s observations, but only if the initial refusal did not involve a question of inventive step. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

Any application for a patent claiming a biotechnological invention shall be examined in the prescribed manner, with due regard to the potential for commercial exploitation within the territory of India and consistent with public interest. Where an application relates to a micro-organism, the deposit of said micro-organism with a recognised depositary institution shall be a condition precedent to the grant of a patent, and the details of such deposit shall form part of the complete specification. A transmissible case, containing all relevant documentation pertaining to the deposited micro-organism, shall be maintained by the depositary institution and made available to the Controller of Patents as provided herein. Failure to maintain such a case, or to provide access thereto upon request, may be grounds for rejection of the application. The Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish additional information or evidence regarding the deposited micro-organism to ensure compliance with the prescribed manner of examination. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the deposited material shall be adjudicated in accordance with established scientific principles.

Any application for a patent claiming a biotechnological invention shall be examined in the prescribed manner, and the Patent Office may require the applicant to furnish additional information or data relating to the biological material deposited with a recognized depositary institution, subject to the provisions of this Act. The applicant shall demonstrate that the deposited material is viable and capable of replication, and that access to such material will be provided to the Patent Office for the purposes of examination, in accordance with internationally accepted protocols. Provided that, failure to comply with the requirements regarding biological material, as detailed in the guidelines issued by the Patent Office, may result in the rejection of the application. Any challenge to the examination process shall be subject to review as provided herein, and the decision of the Patent Office shall be final, unless overturned by a competent court. The prescribed manner of claiming such inventions must also clearly delineate the scope of the claimed subject matter.

Any person failing to comply with the prescribed manner for submitting a request for examination of an application for a patent shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees.
