Where a Registrar determines that an applicant has knowingly misrepresented material facts in their application, the Registrar may, subject to a review process, revoke the benefit of the deemed date registration and assign a registration date reflecting the date of accurate disclosure. Any rectification petition concerning the register shall consider this principle of deemed date registration when determining priority of rights.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an agreement to assign it, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the licensing of trade marks, and such assignment shall not be valid unless recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where an assignment is made without a recorded transfer of right, title, and interest, the Registry may, upon application by a party claiming interest, deem a date of assignment for the purposes of establishing priority amongst competing assignees, provided that sufficient evidence of the equitable interest is furnished. The Registry shall, in determining such deemed date registration, consider the date of the initial agreement to assign, the nature of consideration, and any subsequent actions demonstrating intent to transfer. A licensee, with the consent of the registered proprietor, may further assign their licensed rights, subject to the terms of the original license agreement and the continued validity of the registered trade mark. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, where a trade mark, identical with or nearly resembling a registered trade mark, has been used continuously in India by a proprietor who is not the registered proprietor, and the use has been honest and bona fide, a court, upon proof of special circumstances, may deem a date prior to the date of application for registration of the originally registered trade mark as the date of first use for the purposes of establishing prior rights. Provided that, any such deeming of an earlier date shall be subject to the court being satisfied that the continued use was not with intent to deceive or cause confusion. An appeal from any order relating to the deemed date registration shall lie to the High Court, and such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final, subject to the possibility of review based on newly discovered evidence.

Any person claiming entitlement to the registration of a trade mark incorporating a distinctive name, and who has continuously used such name for a period not less than five years prior to the date of application, shall be deemed to have a date of registration equivalent to the earliest date of such continuous use, subject to the Registrar being satisfied as to the veracity of such claim through documented evidence. Failure to provide such evidence within a period of thirty days of a request issued under this Act shall result in the forfeiture of any claim to the deemed date registration. Any false representation made regarding the date of first use of a name, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Registrar may, in addition, order the rectification of the register.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration which has been accepted but not yet registered, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the assignment of goods will and goodwill. Where an application for registration is pending, and a party acquires the goodwill of the business concerned, such acquisition shall be deemed date registration equivalent to the date of transfer of the goodwill, for the purposes of establishing a connection between the applicant and the trade mark. Provided that, respect registered application for a mark already subject to a valid assignment agreement shall not be diminished by any subsequent transfer of goodwill not explicitly covered within the original agreement. The Registrar may, upon satisfactory evidence of such assignment and goodwill transfer, amend the register accordingly. Any license granted in respect of a pending application shall be construed as a license of future right, subject to successful registration. Failure to record an assignment within the prescribed period may render it unenforceable against a subsequent assignee without notice.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, where an application for registration of the mark ‘Shree Ganesh Textiles’ was filed on the fourteenth of January, two thousand and twenty-two, and the applicant subsequently established prior use dating back to the first of April, two thousand and eighteen, the Registrar shall, for the purposes of determining priority, deem the date of application to be the first of April, two thousand and eighteen. This determination is subject to the condition that the applicant provides satisfactory evidence of continuous use and demonstrable goodwill from said date. Further, the respondent, ‘Ganesh Fabrics Private Limited’, has alleged threatened infringement, claiming that the applicant’s mark is deceptively similar to their existing unregistered mark and that registration would cause irreparable harm. Any appeal against this deemed date registration shall be filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order, and shall be heard by the Appellate Board as provided herein, with consideration given to the evidence presented regarding the alleged threatened infringement.

Impliedly registration shall, for the purposes of determining the authenticity and origin of goods bearing a geographical indication, extend to the reasonable and consistent application of a sign or symbol denoting such indication, even absent explicit textual reference to formal registration under this Act. However, such implied registration is subject to the condition that the sign or symbol must be demonstrably linked to a defined geographical area and consistently associated with goods originating from that area, as evidenced by established usage and consumer perception. Provided that, the Registrar may, upon sufficient evidence of consumer deception or misrepresentation, require formal registration to clarify the status of the geographical indication. Any claim of rights arising from implied registration may be challenged before the Appellate Board.

Any person aggrieved by any act constituting an infringement of a registered geographical indication, or by any act likely to cause such infringement, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, or any other relief as is or may be available under any other law for the time being in force. Where a registered geographical indication is used by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a licensee authorized by the registered proprietor, it shall be deemed to be an infringement, unless such use is permitted under this Act. Impliedly registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered, and to seek legal recourse against any unauthorized use. The Court, while granting relief, may also order the destruction or obliteration of all materials bearing such unauthorized geographical indication, subject to due process and proportionate to the extent of the infringement. Any order for damages may include compensatory, nominal, and exemplary damages as deemed appropriate.

Any person causing a false indication of geographical origin, or the unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication in relation to goods, shall be liable to a penalty not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees, and the court may, at its discretion, also order the seizure of the falsely labelled goods. Where a collective body representing producers of a geographical indication fails to demonstrate diligent use of the indication in commerce, registration shall be subject to review and potential revocation, provided that such failure is established through evidence presented before the designated authority. Impliedly registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to sue for infringement, and any action brought under this Act must commence within three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement. Repeated offences under this Act shall attract a doubling of the penalty amount. The court may direct disposal of infringing goods to charitable organizations.

Any assignment of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an instrument in writing, duly executed by the proprietor of the geographical indication and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Registry as provided herein. The Registry may, upon sufficient cause being shown, refuse to register an assignment if it is demonstrated that the assignment would be detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication or to the interests of the producers associated therewith. Where a license is granted to use a registered geographical indication, the terms and conditions of such license, including duration, territory, and quality control measures, shall be clearly defined in a written agreement. Impliedly registration shall extend to the right to prevent third parties from using identical or similar signs in relation to goods of the same or similar kind, likely to cause confusion or misrepresentation. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate it, but such assignment or license shall not be enforceable against any person other than the parties thereto until so registered. The Registrar may require evidence of genuine use of the geographical indication by the assignee or licensee.

Any application for registration filed under this Act shall be subject to examination by the Registrar to ascertain its conformity with the provisions herein, and the Registrar may, prior to acceptance, require such amendments or evidence as may be deemed necessary to satisfy the requirements of this Act. Where a geographical indication is registered in favour of an association of producers, any member of that association shall, subject to the rules, be entitled to use the registered geographical indication in relation to goods of the class for which it is registered. However, impliedly registration shall not confer any right to use the geographical indication in relation to goods which do not meet the standards specified in the register or which are not produced within the defined geographical area. Any aggrieved person may, within a period of ninety days from the date of registration, file an appeal before the Appellate Board challenging the registration, provided that such appeal is accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed statement of grounds. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the writ jurisdiction of the appropriate High Court.

Any assignment of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Registrar, and such consent may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Registrar deems fit to secure the continued quality and reputation of the goods to which the geographical indication relates. Where a geographical indication is assigned, the Registrar shall record the assignment in the register, and the assignee shall, as provided herein, become entitled to the rights and subject to the obligations of the original registrant. Impliedly registration shall not confer any rights to an assignee unless such assignment is duly recorded. The transfer of ownership of goods bearing a registered geographical indication does not, of itself, constitute an assignment of the geographical indication itself. Any license granted in respect of a geographical indication shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the license, including the geographical area, the goods covered, and the duration of the license. Failure to comply with these provisions renders any such assignment or license voidable at the option of the Registrar.

Impliedly registration shall extend to circumstances where a geographical indication is represented in a manner that reasonably conveys the impression of registration, even absent explicit textual reference to the register maintained under this Act. Such implication may arise from the consistent application of symbols or designations commonly associated with registered geographical indications, or through promotional materials presenting the goods as possessing legally protected status. However, this shall not apply where the representation is demonstrably limited to a description of the geographical origin itself, without suggesting exclusive rights. Furthermore, any layout design register pertaining to packaging or presentation of goods bearing a geographical indication shall not, in and of itself, constitute implied registration of the geographical indication unless accompanied by indicia of registration as provided herein.

The Registrar, upon examination of an application for registration of a geographical indication, shall, where the application satisfies the requirements as provided herein, proceed to register the said geographical indication in the Register. Registration shall, unless sooner cancelled, be for a period of ten years from the date of application; and may be renewed for further periods of ten years each, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with such conditions as may be determined. Where a geographical indication incorporates a design element integral to its visual representation, such design shall be assessed for distinctiveness and conformity with the provisions relating to designs under the relevant legislation. Impliedly registration shall extend to the specific goods in respect of which the geographical indication is registered, and to goods substantially similar, save where such similarity is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration may, within a period of ninety days from the date of such refusal, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

A registered layout-design may be subject to cancellation justified registration where the registered proprietor fails to exercise rights as provided herein, or where such exercise is demonstrably inconsistent with the principles of natural justice or established trade practice within India rights. The Registrar may, upon receiving a petition alleging such failure or inconsistency and after affording reasonable opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned, direct the cancellation of the registration. Provided that, no cancellation shall be ordered unless the petition is accompanied by evidence establishing a prima facie case of abandonment or improper exercise of rights. Furthermore, a layout-design registration shall be deemed cancelled if the registered proprietor demonstrably relinquishes all rights therein through a duly recorded instrument. Any aggrieved party may appeal such decision to the High Court.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a petition alleging improper registration and accompanied by the requisite fee, conduct an inquiry to determine the validity of the claim for cancellation justified registration of a semiconductor layout-design. Such petition shall clearly demonstrate that the registered layout-design lacks originality or is substantially similar to a prior art layout-design, or that the applicant misrepresented material facts during the registration process. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require the petitioner to deposit a sum equivalent to a reasonable estimate of the costs incurred by the registered proprietor in defending the petition. This deposit, representing a form of gene fund, shall be utilized solely for the purpose of defraying legal expenses and expert witness fees. Any unused portion of said fund shall be returned to the petitioner upon conclusion of the proceedings, or to the registered proprietor if the petition is dismissed. The Registrar’s decision on cancellation shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any person who, without due authorization from the breeder or licensee of a registered variety, produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports, or exports the said variety, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, where the offence involves commercial exploitation of the registered variety, the fine shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Any essentially derived variety offered for sale without acknowledging the initial registered variety, or without the breeder’s consent, constitutes a violation as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, initiate an inquiry into any alleged contravention of these provisions and may impose penalties up to ten times the estimated value of the illegally produced or distributed material of the varieties registered. Any evidence obtained during such inquiry shall be admissible in any legal proceedings.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall be deemed to be a new and distinct variety, subject to the provisions contained herein, and shall be eligible for protection for a period not exceeding twenty years from the date of notification of grant of registration. The essentially derived variety, being a variety that is principally derived from the registered breeder variety, retains the characteristics of the latter, and is not substantially different, may be subject to the same rights and obligations as the registered breeder variety, provided that the breeder of such essentially derived variety obtains the necessary authorization from the breeder of the registered variety. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a registered breeder variety may apply to the competent authority for redressal, as provided herein. The scope of protection shall extend to the propagation, sale, and marketing of the registered variety.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and stock propagating material of the variety. However, such exclusive right shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and shall not extend to acts done privately and for non-commercial purposes. Any farmer who is in possession of seeds of a registered breeder variety may save, use, sow, re-sow, reproduce, exchange, and sell such seeds, provided that such farmer does not sell branded seeds of the registered variety. The Registrar may, upon application by any person, maintain a public register of all breeder varieties registered as provided herein, detailing the characteristics and propagation methods. A certificate of registration shall be prima facie evidence of a validly registered breeder variety. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding registration may file an appeal before the designated authority.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to commercially exploit the protected variety in any manner, including by production, sale, marketing, distribution, import, and export, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, the farmer shall have the right to save, use, sow, re-sow and multiply any farm-saved seed of a registered variety, provided that the farmer does not sell, market or distribute such saved seed in a manner that infringes the breeder’s rights. Any person who contravenes the exclusive rights of the breeder, or the farmer’s limited rights as detailed herein, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and may be subject to injunction restraining further infringement. The Authority may, upon application and subject to verification, grant compulsory licenses for the exploitation of a registered variety if it is determined to be necessary in the public interest. Any dispute relating to the infringement of rights, or the grant of compulsory licenses, shall be adjudicated by the designated Tribunal.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and stock propagable material of the variety in India. However, such exclusive right shall be subject to the provisions relating to research and breeding, and shall not extend to acts done solely for private and non-commercial purposes. Any farmer who is in possession of seeds of a registered breeder variety may save, use, sow, re-sow, multiply, and propagate such seeds for his own purposes, provided that he does not sell, market, or distribute such saved seeds or propagable material. The Authority may, upon application by any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied that an infringement has occurred, issue a cease and desist order. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Authority may appeal to the High Court. A registered breeder shall maintain a record of all transactions relating to the sale and distribution of the variety, as provided herein, and make such record available for inspection upon demand by an officer authorized by the Central Government.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall be subject to a period of validity as prescribed, and renewal thereof may be permitted subject to payment of the prescribed fee and demonstration of continued viability of the plant variety in question. Provided that, a registered breeder variety, if found to be essentially derived from another variety registered earlier, shall have its registration reviewed and may be subject to revocation as provided herein. Any farmer, seed producer, or other person utilizing the registered breeder variety shall be bound by the conditions of sale and usage stipulated by the breeder, unless otherwise exempted under provisions relating to farmers’ rights and seed saving. Compliance with post-registration monitoring requirements, including periodic seed quality assessments, is mandatory for maintaining the validity of the registration. Failure to comply may result in suspension or cancellation of the certificate, and the breeder shall be liable for any consequential damages. The Authority may, however, grant a temporary exemption in cases of unforeseen circumstances.

Any person cultivating a breeder variety registered under this Act with the intent to commercially exploit the genetic material without the breeder’s express permission, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, if the infringement relates to a variety of farmers’ saved seed, the penalty shall not exceed one lakh rupees, subject to proof of actual economic loss suffered by the breeder. Any evidence obtained through search and seizure operations conducted as provided herein, shall be admissible in any proceeding under this Act. The Authority may, after due inquiry, issue a cease and desist order to any person found violating the rights of a breeder, and may further direct the destruction of any harvested material embodying the illegally cultivated variety. Failure to comply with a cease and desist order shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. All penalties collected under this Act shall be credited to the Plant Variety Fund.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by mutual agreement between the breeder and any person seeking to propagate, multiply, or commercially exploit the said variety, provided that such agreement shall not unduly restrict research and development activities undertaken for the improvement of plant varieties. Any assignment of rights relating to a breeder variety shall be in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority, failing which such assignment shall be deemed invalid as against third parties. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, authorize the transfer of breeder variety rights to legal heirs upon the breeder’s demise, ensuring continued protection and benefit to those demonstrably engaged in the cultivation and preservation of the variety. Where a licensee defaults on royalty payments or violates the terms of the license, the breeder may seek redressal through established legal channels, including injunctive relief and damages, as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all registered assignments and licenses.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and commercially exploit the protected variety. The registrar shall maintain a register of all breeder varieties, detailing the essential characteristics, denomination, and the period of protection granted, which shall be for a period of fifteen years from the date of notification of the variety. Subject to the provisions herein, any farmer who is engaged in the propagation and multiplication of a registered variety, and who has saved seed and propagated it, may sell or market such seed, provided that the sale is not for the purpose of commercial exploitation. The registrar register shall be open for inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar may, within a period of ninety days, file an appeal before the designated authority as provided herein.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall be subject to a period of validity as determined at the time of registration, provided that such period may be extended in accordance with the provisions relating to renewal, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and demonstration of continued viability of the plant variety. The registrar copyrights pertaining to the essentially derived varieties, arising from the exploitation of the registered breeder variety, shall vest with the initial breeder, unless otherwise agreed in writing. Any person intending to commercially exploit a breeder variety registered herein must obtain authorization from the breeder or their designated agent, and failure to do so shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Where a dispute arises regarding the scope of authorization, the aggrieved party may seek redressal through established judicial processes, subject to the limitations as provided herein. The registrar shall maintain a public record of all registered breeder varieties and associated copyrights.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by mutual agreement between the breeder and any person seeking to propagate, sell, or otherwise commercially exploit the protected plant variety. The registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all licenses granted concerning registered breeder varieties, detailing the scope of permitted use, geographical territory, and duration of the license. Any assignment of rights in a registered breeder variety, or a license granted thereunder, shall be in writing and submitted to the registrar for recordation within thirty days of the transaction. Failure to record such assignment or license shall not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties unaware of the transfer. Provided that, the breeder retains the right to revoke a license in cases of material breach of its terms, subject to a thirty-day notice period and a reasonable opportunity for remedy. The registrar may, upon application, resolve disputes regarding the interpretation of license agreements.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright, prior to the institution of a suit, shall serve a notice of intention to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing the nature of the infringement and the remedial action sought, subject to the provisions contained herein. Such notice shall be served by registered post with acknowledgment due, or by any other means demonstrably establishing receipt. Where a defendant, upon receipt of such notice, submits a counter-claim asserting the validity of their actions or challenging the copyright itself, the claimant may, at their discretion, apply to the court for directions regarding the conduct of the proceedings. All applications for interim relief, including injunctions, shall be accompanied by a verified statement outlining the grounds for such relief and demonstrating a prima facie case. The principles of civil procedure 1908 shall govern the conduct of all suits relating to copyright infringement, including the rules pertaining to evidence, discovery, and the execution of decrees, provided that the court may, in its discretion, modify such rules as are necessary to ensure a just and expeditious resolution of the dispute. Failure to comply with these requirements may be considered by the court when determining costs.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Society pertaining to royalty rates or licensing terms, shall have recourse to an appeal before the District Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the impugned order, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy thereof. The District Court, in considering such appeal, may, at its discretion, direct the Copyright Society to produce records pertaining to the calculation of royalties and the rationale behind the contested licensing terms. The principles of civil procedure 1908 shall govern the conduct of such appeals, including rules relating to evidence and the issuance of summons. Provided that, the District Court may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, impose costs on the appellant. Any decision of the District Court shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the High Court on a substantial question of law.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright, prior to the institution of a suit, shall, as provided herein, serve a notice of intention to sue upon the alleged infringer, detailing the nature of the infringement and the remedies sought. Such notice shall be served not less than sixty days prior to the commencement of any judicial proceeding. Failure to comply with this requirement shall be subject to dismissal of the suit, unless the court, considering the specific circumstances, determines sufficient cause existed for non-compliance. Where a claim for damages is included, the notice shall also specify a reasonable estimate of the damages claimed. All disputes regarding the adequacy of the notice, or the sufficiency of cause for non-compliance, shall be determined in accordance with the principles of civil procedure 1908. Provided that, this provision shall not apply in cases where the infringement is of a flagrant nature and warrants immediate judicial intervention.

The Opposition Board shall be constituted for the purpose of hearing and deciding on oppositions filed against a granted patent, as provided herein. An opposition may be filed by any person alleging that the grant of the patent was not in accordance with the provisions of this Act. The Board shall consist of at least three members, possessing technical expertise relevant to the subject matter of the patent, and appointed by the Central Government. A designated officer may, subject to the directions of the Board, assist in the conduct of opposition proceedings. The Board shall, after considering the evidence and submissions presented by both the patentee and the opponent, issue a reasoned order either upholding or revoking the patent, or amending it as appropriate. Any decision of the Opposition Board shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to a High Court.

The applicant, upon receipt of an office action raising grounds for refusal, may file a response within a period not exceeding three months from the date of dispatch of such action, subject to extension granted by the Controller for reasons to be recorded. Should a third party lodge a pre-grant opposition as provided herein, the Controller shall transmit a copy of the opposition to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to furnish evidence and representations. The Controller shall, having considered the opposition and the applicant’s response, constitute an Opposition Board comprising of at least three persons possessing technical expertise relevant to the subject matter of the patent application. The Opposition Board shall conduct a hearing, allowing both the applicant and the opposing party to present their arguments and evidence, and shall submit a reasoned opinion to the Controller regarding the validity of the opposition. The Controller, after considering the opinion of the Opposition Board, shall pass a final order accepting or rejecting the opposition.

Any person may file a pre-grant opposition with the Controller against an application for a patent, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Upon receipt of such opposition, the Controller shall, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, constitute an Opposition Board consisting of three persons possessing such technical expertise as may be prescribed. The Opposition Board shall examine the representation made by the opponent and the applicant, and may require further evidence to be furnished. The Board shall, after such examination, submit a report to the Controller stating its findings and recommendations. The Controller shall, having regard to the report of the Opposition Board, pass an appropriate order either granting or rejecting the patent application. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may, within the prescribed period, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant has satisfied the Appellate Board that substantial questions of law are involved.

The Opposition Board shall consist of three or more persons, of whom at least one shall be a person possessing a degree in engineering or technology or possessing equivalent technical qualifications and having not less than five years of practical experience in the relevant field. Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, and shall be accompanied by a statement of the facts and evidence relied upon. The Controller shall, upon receipt of a notice of opposition, transmit a copy thereof to the applicant for the patent, who may, within three months from the date of such transmission, file a statement setting out his arguments against the opposition. The Opposition Board shall, after considering the notice of opposition, the applicant’s statement, and any other evidence presented, conduct a hearing and issue a reasoned order either upholding or dismissing the opposition. The decision of the Opposition Board shall be final and binding, subject to the provisions for appeal under this Act.

The Opposition Board shall, upon receipt of a notice of opposition under the provisions of this Act, constitute a hearing panel comprising at least three technically qualified individuals. Any party submitting a notice of opposition shall, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, be entitled to present evidence and arguments substantiating the grounds of opposition as detailed in the notice. The applicant, against whom the opposition is filed, may, within a period of thirty days from the service of the opposition notice, file a counter-statement addressing each ground raised. Provided that failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe may result in an ex parte decision by the Opposition Board. All evidence submitted shall be deemed confidential and accessible only to members of the Opposition Board and the parties involved, unless otherwise directed by the Board. The decision of the Opposition Board shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

Any person may file a pre-grant opposition with the Controller against the grant of a patent, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Upon receipt of such opposition, the Controller shall, if satisfied that grounds for opposition exist, refer the matter to the Opposition Board for adjudication. The Opposition Board shall, after hearing the applicant and the opponent, submit its findings to the Controller within a period of ninety days. Failure of the Opposition Board to submit findings within the stipulated period shall be deemed a violation, attracting a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any decision of the Opposition Board may be appealed to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Board’s decision. Knowingly providing false evidence to the Opposition Board shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Any assignment of a patent application, or of a patent granted under this Act, shall be subject to a recordal with the Controller of Patents, and such recordal shall be deemed to vest the legal title to the patent or patent application in the assignee. Where an opposition is filed before the Controller concerning the validity of a patent which is subsequently subject to an assignment, the Opposition Board constituted for the purpose of adjudicating said opposition shall, prior to commencing substantive examination, require confirmation from both the original patentee and the assignee regarding the validity of the assignment. Should the assignee be a foreign entity, evidence of compliance with applicable laws governing foreign investment in India shall also be furnished. Failure to satisfy the requirements of this provision may result in the opposition proceeding being stayed until such compliance is demonstrated, subject to the discretion of the Controller. Any licensing agreement pertaining to the patent shall be similarly recorded to ensure transparency and enforceability.

Any person may file a pre-grant opposition with the Controller against an application for a patent, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Such opposition shall be based only on grounds specified herein, including lack of novelty, inventive step, or industrial applicability. Upon receiving a pre-grant opposition, the Controller shall, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, transmit a copy of the opposition to the applicant and invite observations. If the Controller deems a prima facie case exists, the matter shall be referred to the Opposition Board for adjudication. The Opposition Board shall consist of three or more persons possessing technical expertise relevant to the subject matter of the patent application, and shall conduct a hearing, allowing both the applicant and the opponent to present evidence and arguments. The decision of the Opposition Board shall be binding on the Controller and may be appealed to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit.

Any person desiring to oppose the grant of a patent following basic registration under this Act shall file a notice of opposition with the Controller within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the acceptance of the patent application. Upon receipt of such notice, the Controller shall, within one month, transmit a copy thereof to the applicant. The applicant may, within three months of receiving the notice, file a statement setting out the grounds on which it relies for the grant of the patent. Failure to file such a statement within the prescribed time shall be deemed a relinquishment of the right to defend the application. All oppositions shall be adjudicated by the Opposition Board constituted for this purpose, and the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court. Any false or misleading representation made in a notice of opposition shall render the opponent liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any assignment of a patent application, or of a patent granted under this Act, relating to a pharmaceutical formulation incorporating a registered trade mark, shall be subject to the prior approval of the Opposition Board, unless the assignment is to a successor-in-title of the assignor, or to a company controlled by the assignor. The Opposition Board may, upon receipt of a petition for approval of such assignment, require the applicant to demonstrate that the assignment will not be detrimental to the public interest, or to the continued availability of the pharmaceutical formulation. Should the Opposition Board deem the assignment permissible, it shall issue a certificate of approval, which shall be registered with the Controller of Patents. Failure to obtain such approval prior to the assignment shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the Controller. The Opposition Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court as provided herein. Any licensing agreement related to such a patent shall similarly require notification to the Board.

Any person may file a notice of opposition to the grant of a patent, as provided herein, within a period of four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent. Such notice shall be in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including any prior art known to the opponent which may anticipate or suggest the invention. Where an opposition is filed, the Controller shall, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, transmit the notice of opposition and all accompanying documents to the Opposition Board. The Opposition Board shall, after hearing the applicant and the opponent, submit its decision to the Controller within a period of one year from the date of receipt of the notice. If the Opposition Board finds that the patent should not be granted, it shall so recommend to the Controller, and the Controller shall, subject to any further evidence or submissions, refuse the patent. Where a variety registered under the Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Authority is alleged to lack novelty, the Opposition Board shall give due consideration to the registration details. Any decision of the Opposition Board may be appealed to the High Court.

The Opposition Board shall be constituted for the purpose of hearing and deciding on any opposition filed against the grant of a patent, as provided herein. Any person may file a notice of opposition to the Controller of Patents within a period of four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent. Upon receipt of such notice, the Controller shall, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, appoint an Opposition Board consisting of at least three members possessing technical expertise relevant to the subject matter of the patent application. The Copyright Office may, upon request from the Opposition Board, provide assistance in determining the novelty of any subject matter relating to artistic works claimed within the patent application. Decisions of the Opposition Board shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, “means patent cooperation” shall refer to the procedural mechanisms established under international treaties and agreements, including but not limited to the Patent Cooperation Treaty, designed to streamline the process of filing patent applications simultaneously in multiple contracting states. Such cooperation may encompass the preparation of an international search report and a preliminary examination, subject to the applicant fulfilling all requirements as provided herein. A designated office, acting as a receiving office, shall facilitate this process, and any international publication resulting from means patent cooperation shall be considered a public disclosure. The controller may prescribe additional rules regarding the conduct of means patent cooperation to ensure compliance with international standards and the effective administration of this Act.

Any person engaging in acts contrary to established means patent cooperation, specifically the unauthorized disclosure of information pertaining to an international patent application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Such unauthorized disclosure, subject to proof of intent to cause harm to the applicant, may attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where the offence involves the systematic and repeated violation of confidentiality obligations, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees, and imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. Any officer or employee of the Indian Patent Office found complicit in such disclosure shall be subject to disciplinary action, including dismissal from service, in addition to any criminal penalties as provided herein. All recovered penalties shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India, and may be used for the promotion of patent awareness.

Any application for a patent claiming priority from a national filing date, and subsequently designating India as a country for which protection is sought through means patent cooperation under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, shall be subject to a preliminary examination as provided herein, to ascertain compliance with the requirements of this Act and the Treaty. Should the Controller of Patents determine that the international application does not meet the prescribed requirements, a notice of deficiency shall be issued to the applicant, affording them a period of sixty days to remedy the deficiencies. Any dispute arising from such a notice, including the adequacy of the remedy offered, may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that the applicant demonstrates substantial grounds for review. Failure to respond adequately within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the application being deemed withdrawn, subject to the right of the applicant to submit a new application. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except in cases of proven fraud or misrepresentation.

Means patent cooperation shall, for the purposes of this Act, refer to the collaborative procedures established under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, enabling a unified patent application process before designated national or regional patent offices. Such cooperation extends to the international search and preliminary examination of patent applications, facilitating efficient and streamlined processing. Relating registered designs, the Controller may, subject to the provisions herein, accept international design applications filed through the Hague System for the International Registration of Industrial Designs, treating them as equivalent to national filings. Provided that the applicant demonstrates compliance with all applicable requirements as stipulated by this Act and relevant international agreements, and that the design is not contrary to public order or morality.

Any person demonstrating substantial engagement in means patent cooperation, whether through filing international applications or participating in prescribed collaborative research initiatives, shall be designated a ‘cooperation participant’ subject to verification by the Controller of Patents. A registered user registered with the Patent Office, and subsequently designated as a cooperation participant, may nominate a representative to act on their behalf in all matters pertaining to the processing of their applications and the maintenance of granted patents. Should a cooperation participant engage in fraudulent misrepresentation concerning the scope of their collaborative efforts, they shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and their status as a cooperation participant may be revoked. Furthermore, any rights accrued under this Act relating to expedited processing or fee reductions, as applicable to cooperation participants, shall be immediately forfeited. The Controller may, provided that reasonable cause is shown, reinstate such rights subject to payment of applicable penalties and fulfillment of outstanding obligations.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish such measures as are necessary to facilitate means patent cooperation with other nations and international organizations, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Any such cooperation shall be conducted in a manner consistent with the sovereign interests of India and the protection of public health. Where a collaborative arrangement involves the sharing of patent applications or examination reports, the confidentiality of such information shall be maintained as provided herein. 

Conditions subject copyright relating to traditional knowledge, folklore, and artistic works, shall be determined by the Central Government in consultation with relevant stakeholders, ensuring equitable benefit sharing and preventing misappropriation. Any transfer of patent rights arising from such cooperation shall be subject to prior approval, and the terms thereof must not be manifestly detrimental to the national interest. The Controller of Patents shall oversee compliance with these provisions and may require periodic reports from cooperating entities.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (t) “register” means the Register of Trade Marks maintained in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and shall contain all particulars required herein. Any person aggrieved by an incorrect entry in the register may, subject to the prescribed fees, apply to the Controller for rectification of the register, providing sufficient evidence to support the claim. The Controller shall, following due process and consideration of submitted evidence, either allow or reject the application, and shall communicate the decision in writing to the applicant and any affected parties. Where a trade mark is removed from the register due to non-renewal of registration, a subsequent application for the same mark by the former proprietor shall be treated as a fresh application, subject to availability and no prior conflicting claim. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, grant an extended period for renewal if sufficient cause is demonstrated. Any false representation made in an application for rectification shall be punishable as contempt of this Act.

context: In this Act, “digital imprint” means any description which is made available to potential users and which reasonably conveys an association between a trade mark and a digital asset, including but not limited to non-fungible tokens, cryptographic keys, or metaverse locations. Such digital imprint shall be considered descriptive of goods or services if it directly describes a characteristic, quality, intended use, or geographical origin of those goods or services. A digital imprint may, however, acquire distinctiveness through extensive use, subject to the provisions relating to secondary meaning as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon application, determine whether a particular digital imprint is descriptive, considering all relevant evidence. Any claim of descriptiveness shall be substantiated by evidence of actual use in commerce.

context: Any person who publishes to the public, or causes to be published, a false representation likely to deceive the public, or to injure the character, reputation or goodwill of another, relating to the goods or services of another, shall be liable to action for damages, irrespective of whether any damage has been suffered by the other person. A representation shall be deemed false if it is not substantially true in all material respects. Where a defendant proves that the matter complained of was published in good faith, and for the purpose of fair comment on the goods or services in question, no action for damages shall lie. However, such defence shall not be available if the comment is made maliciously or is otherwise unlawful. Any description which is made available to potential users and constitutes such a false representation, shall be considered a violation as provided herein. The proprietor of the trade mark may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further publication of the false representation, subject to the principles of equity.

Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, the assignee may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for the registration of the assignment. Such application shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a copy of the assignment instrument. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the assignment is genuine and consistent with the provisions of this Act, register the assignment and shall enter the particulars thereof in the register.

Failure to register an assignment or license shall not invalidate the transaction but may affect the enforceability of the rights derived therefrom.

Furthermore, evidence presented regarding prior art, and particularly any prior use establishing common descriptive usage, shall be admissible and given due weight by the Appellate Board. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law.

A work shall not be considered a derivative work if it merely represents a trivial variation of the original, or if its creation does not involve a substantial degree of skill and judgment. context: In this Act, “cosmetic” means any article intended for application to the human skin for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance, and includes any device or apparatus intended for use therewith, but does not include a drug or a medicinal preparation as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. A cosmetic formulation, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be deemed to be adulterated if it contains any prohibited substance exceeding the permissible limits as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards. Any representation regarding the efficacy of a cosmetic, implying therapeutic benefit, shall be construed as a misleading claim and actionable as provided herein. The importer or manufacturer shall ensure compliance with labeling requirements, including a complete list of ingredients and potential allergens.

Any cosmetic preparation intended for retail sale shall be subject to registration with the Controller of Cosmetics, as provided herein, and no person shall sell, expose for sale, or distribute any such preparation without valid registration. An application for registration shall include a detailed formulation list, manufacturing process, and proof of compliance with the standards prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, including permissible limits for specified ingredients and contaminants. The Controller may, at their discretion, require submission of samples for analysis to ascertain conformity with these standards. Registration shall be granted only if the cosmetic preparation is deemed safe for intended use and does not contain any prohibited substances. Provided that, registration may be revoked if subsequent analysis reveals non-compliance or misrepresentation of ingredients. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all registered cosmetic preparations, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable fees. Any alteration to the registered formulation requires prior notification and approval.

Any person manufacturing, selling, distributing or importing cosmetics shall be subject to the provisions of the Cosmetics Act 1940, and any violation thereof may constitute grounds for refusal of trade mark registration or revocation of an existing registration, as provided herein. Where a trade mark is used in relation to goods falling within the ambit of the said Cosmetics Act, and such goods are found to be in contravention of the standards or regulations prescribed therein, the Registrar may, after due notice to the trade mark proprietor and opportunity to be heard, order suspension of the use of the trade mark for a period not exceeding two years. A proprietor aggrieved by such order may appeal to the High Court. Furthermore, any false or misleading representation concerning the composition, quality, or therapeutic effect of cosmetics bearing a registered trade mark shall be deemed to be misrepresentation under this Act, entitling an injured party to seek appropriate remedies including injunction and damages. Provided that, the remedies under this Act are in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other remedies available under any other law for the time being in force.

Any cosmetic preparation manufactured for sale, or offered for sale, or distributed, whether gratuitously or otherwise, shall be deemed to be goods subject to the provisions of this Act, notwithstanding any exemption that may be provided under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. Where a trade mark is used in relation to a cosmetic, and that cosmetic does not conform to the standards of quality or purity as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards, the registration of such trade mark may be revoked by the Controller, subject to a hearing as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller may prefer an appeal to the High Court within ninety days of the order. The Controller shall maintain a register of all registered trade marks relating to cosmetic preparations, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee. Provided that, information relating to the composition of a cosmetic, if claimed as a trade secret by the applicant, shall not be disclosed without prior consent. Any false label or misleading representation on a cosmetic package shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine.

Any cosmetic manufactured or imported for sale shall conform to the standards of quality and safety as prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, and any violation of these standards shall be deemed a contravention of this Act. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify additional requirements relating to the composition, manufacturing process, and packaging of cosmetics, subject to the provisions of the aforementioned Act. No person shall manufacture or sell any cosmetic which contains any prohibited substance or exceeds the permissible limits of any ingredient, as detailed in the schedules appended to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. Provided that, a manufacturer may apply to the Controller of Patents for an exemption from these requirements, demonstrating a compelling scientific basis for the use of such substance or exceeding such limits, and such exemption shall be granted only after thorough evaluation and subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary. Any cosmetic found to be non-compliant shall be liable to seizure and destruction, as provided herein.

Any person manufacturing, selling, importing or distributing cosmetic preparations, whether indigenous or foreign, shall ensure strict compliance with the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, and the rules made thereunder, particularly regarding permissible ingredients and labeling requirements. Failure to adhere to these standards, or the misbranding of any cosmetic preparation with false or misleading claims regarding its efficacy or composition, shall be deemed an offence under this Act. Any cosmetic found to contain prohibited substances, or not conforming to the prescribed standards, may be seized and destroyed by an officer duly authorized by the Controller of Trade Marks. A person convicted of an offence as provided herein shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, and the Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, order the cancellation of the registration of the trade mark associated with the offending cosmetic.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark used in relation to goods falling within the purview of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, which consent may be granted or refused at its sole discretion and shall be communicated to the applicant within ninety days from the date of receipt of a complete application. Where such consent is not granted, the assignment shall be deemed void ab initio. A licensee of a trade mark, where the licensed goods are regulated under the aforementioned Cosmetics Act, may, subject to the terms of the license agreement, petition the High Court for a declaration of its continued right to use the mark following an assignment of the trade mark by the proprietor. Any transfer of rights, whether by assignment or license, shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein, and failure to do so may render the transfer unenforceable against third parties. The proprietor shall remain liable for any defects in goods sold under the mark, even after assignment, unless expressly relieved of such liability in the assignment deed.

Any cosmetic preparation manufactured, sold, stocked or imported, and claiming to provide a therapeutic benefit, shall be deemed to be a drug for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any exemption provided under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940. However, such classification shall not apply where the therapeutic claim is purely incidental and does not form the primary reason for consumer purchase, as determined by the Registrar. Any aggrieved party may file a complaint with the Registrar alleging misclassification, and the Registrar shall, following due process and consideration of evidence including expert testimony, issue a reasoned order. An appeal against any order of the Registrar shall lie before the High Court having territorial jurisdiction, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order. The High Court’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to any rights of appeal to the Supreme Court as provided under law.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark deceptively similar to a registered trade mark used in relation to cosmetics falling within the purview of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement as provided herein. Where such infringement relates to goods falsely representing a standard of quality not reasonably attainable, or falsely representing a connection with another firm or establishment, the penalty shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Any goods found to be an infringing copy, and bearing such deceptive mark, shall be deemed forfeited to the Central Government and may be destroyed or otherwise disposed of as the Government thinks fit. The owner of the registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Court for an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement and for recovery of damages. Failure to comply with an order of the Court shall constitute contempt.

Any cosmetic preparation manufactured for sale, and claiming therapeutic properties, shall be deemed to fall within the purview of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940, notwithstanding any assertion of traditional knowledge or indigenous practice relating to its formulation. However, a cosmetic preparation utilising a Geographical Indication prescribed under the relevant rules, and demonstrably adhering to the traditional manufacturing processes associated with that indication, may be exempted from certain testing requirements as provided herein, subject to verification by the Controller of Trade Marks. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal before the Appellate Board against the Controller’s decision regarding such exemption, provided that the appeal is lodged within ninety days of the Controller’s order. Furthermore, any misrepresentation regarding the origin or ingredients of a cosmetic preparation, particularly concerning its claimed Geographical Indication, shall constitute grounds for revocation of the trade mark, and may also attract penalties under the relevant consumer protection legislation.

For the purposes of this Act, “cosmetic” shall mean any article intended for application to the human body for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance, including perfume, but excluding drugs as defined under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. A cosmetic product, subject to the provisions of this Act, may be registered as a trade mark if it meets the standards of quality and safety prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards. Registration shall not confer any right to exclusivity with respect to the cosmetic formulation itself, only to the identifying mark. Any misleading representation regarding the ingredients or effects of a cosmetic, as provided herein, shall be grounds for revocation of the trade mark. The Controller may, subject to due process, order removal of such misleading claims.

Any person desirous of registering a trade mark for cosmetics, or goods falling within the definition of ‘cosmetics’ as per the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a representation of the mark and a statement of the goods to which it relates. The application shall clearly indicate the composition of the cosmetic product, and shall be subject to verification by the Registry to ensure compliance with applicable standards. Where the mark incorporates a claim relating to a specific therapeutic or prophylactic effect, supporting documentation from a recognized testing laboratory shall be furnished. Registration may be refused if the proposed mark is deceptive or likely to cause confusion, or if the cosmetic product does not conform to the quality standards prescribed under the aforementioned Drugs and Cosmetics Act. A registered cosmetic trade mark shall be valid for ten years, renewable for further periods as provided herein.

Any person manufacturing, selling, importing or distributing cosmetics shall ensure that such cosmetics conform to the standards of quality and safety as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards, subject to the provisions of this Act. A registered proprietor of a trade mark used on cosmetics may, where such cosmetics do not conform to the prescribed standards, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register, seeking removal of the mark for deceptive practices. Any aggrieved person may, as provided herein, apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the manufacture, sale, import or distribution of non-conforming cosmetics bearing the mark. The Court may, in addition to injunctive relief, award damages to compensate for loss suffered due to the use of substandard cosmetics. Where a cosmetic is found to be dangerous to human health, the Central Government may, by notification, prohibit its manufacture, sale, import or distribution, and order its recall from the market. Any person contravening the provisions relating to dangerous cosmetics shall be punishable with imprisonment, or fine, or both. The standards for cosmetics shall be determined in consultation with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, to ensure public safety.

Any person manufacturing, selling, importing or distributing cosmetics shall ensure adherence to the standards of quality and safety as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards, in consultation with the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. A cosmetic product, for the purposes of this Act, includes any substance intended for rubbing, pouring, sprinkling or spraying on, into, or otherwise applying to the human skin or hair for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance. No cosmetic shall contain any substance prohibited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, or any other enactment for the time being in force relating to public health. 

The Trade Marks Officer, upon receiving a complaint regarding misbranded or spurious cosmetics, may direct the manufacturer or distributor to submit samples for analysis to a recognised laboratory. Provided that, such analysis shall be conducted within thirty days from the date of receipt of the samples. Failure to comply with this provision shall attract a penalty as provided herein, and may result in the suspension of the registration of the trade mark associated with the offending cosmetic.

All manufacturers and importers of cosmetics intended for sale within the territory of India shall ensure strict adherence to the prescribed standards for product safety and labeling, as provided herein. Any cosmetic formulation containing ingredients listed as restricted or prohibited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act shall require prior approval from the designated authority, failing which it will be deemed an infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, every package containing a cosmetic shall bear a clear and legible declaration of all ingredients in descending order of weight or volume. The label shall also prominently display the name and address of the manufacturer or importer, and a batch number for traceability. Provided that, natural or organic claims require substantiation through recognized certification processes. Any cosmetic found to be adulterated, misbranded, or posing a health hazard may be subject to seizure and penalties, and the responsible parties may be barred from future import or manufacture. Compliance with these regulations is mandatory for all entities engaged in the trade of cosmetics.

Any person desiring to manufacture, sell, distribute, or import cosmetics, being goods falling within the definition of ‘cosmetics’ as per the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall obtain a license from the Controller of Trade Marks, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Controller may, upon application, grant a license for the exclusive use of a registered trade mark in relation to specified cosmetics, provided that the applicant demonstrates a substantial and legitimate interest in maintaining the quality and safety of those goods. Assignment of any right, title, or interest in such a license shall be permitted only with the prior written consent of the Controller and the original licensor, and shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the original license. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding licensing and assignment may result in the revocation of the license and the imposition of penalties as provided herein. Any dispute arising from the transfer of such rights shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Trade Marks refusing registration of a trade mark for cosmetic preparations, or ordering its rectification, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months of the date of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark applied for is likely to deceive the public, or is descriptive of the character or quality of the cosmetics, or is contrary to decency or morality, confirm the Controller’s decision. However, should the Appellate Board find that the Controller erred in applying the provisions relating to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, it may direct the Controller to reconsider the application. Provided that, no appeal shall lie against an order dismissing an application for rectification on the ground of non-user, unless the appellant satisfies the Board that there was sufficient cause for non-use.

Any assignment of a registered trademark relating to cosmetics, or an application for registration of such a trademark, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and require prior written consent of the Trade Marks Registry. The Registrar shall decide, within a period of ninety days from the date of application, whether to grant or refuse such consent, considering the potential impact on public health and safety arising from the continued use of the trademark by the assignee. A license to use a trademark for cosmetics may be granted, subject to conditions ensuring quality control and adherence to the standards prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Any dispute regarding the validity or scope of such license, or the assignment itself, shall be adjudicated by the Trade Marks Registry, whose decision shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal may lie before the High Court. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of the trademark registration.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Trade Marks relating to the registration of a trade mark for cosmetics, and alleging that such cosmetics do not conform to the standards prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Provided that such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s decision, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the said decision and a statement of the grounds on which it is based. Notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark registration poses a demonstrable risk to public health, order immediate suspension of the mark pending a full hearing. Any party proceeding notwithstanding, the Board shall ensure a reasonable opportunity for all concerned to present evidence and arguments, and its decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review by the High Court. The burden of proof regarding conformity with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act shall lie with the applicant for registration.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark for edible oils, ghee, butter, or any other food article, shall, in addition to the requirements as provided herein, furnish a certificate of analysis from a laboratory duly recognized by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, confirming adherence to the prescribed standards for that particular food article and demonstrating the absence of food adulteration. The certificate shall not be older than six months from the date of application for registration. Failure to submit such a certificate shall render the application incomplete and liable to be rejected. The Registrar may, however, require further testing or analysis at the expense of the applicant, should any discrepancy be noted between the submitted certificate and the standards prescribed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Registration shall be subject to the ongoing compliance with these standards, and the Registrar reserves the right to initiate proceedings for rectification or revocation of the trade mark upon evidence of consistent non-compliance or proven instances of adulteration.

Any person manufacturing, storing, distributing, selling or exposing for sale any article of food for human consumption shall ensure that such article conforms to the standards prescribed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and the rules made thereunder. Where an article of food is found to be adulterated or substandard, the Food Safety Officer, acting upon complaint or independent verification, may initiate proceedings as provided herein. Any individual claiming ownership of a registered trade mark for such adulterated or substandard food shall be jointly and severally liable for the offence, subject to proving due diligence in preventing the adulteration. 

The Trade Marks Registry may, upon receiving a substantiated report of repeated instances of food adulteration linked to a specific trade mark, direct the owner to implement corrective measures within a specified timeframe. Failure to comply with such direction shall render the trade mark liable to revocation, notwithstanding any other provisions of this Act. Evidence of deliberate misbranding intended to conceal food adulteration will be considered an aggravating factor in determining penalties.

Any person desiring to obtain exclusive rights to use a registered trade mark in relation to processed foods, and intending to manufacture or distribute such foods, shall apply to the Controller for a license authorizing such use, subject to the provisions of this Act. The application shall be accompanied by a detailed formulation disclosure, specifying all ingredients and processing methods employed, and a certificate of compliance with the standards prescribed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The Controller may, if satisfied that the applicant possesses the technical capacity and financial resources to maintain consistent quality, grant a license for a specified period, renewable upon demonstration of continued adherence to said standards. Assignment of such license requires prior written consent of the Controller, and any transfer without such consent shall be void. Furthermore, the Controller may revoke the license if evidence of food adulteration, or a material misrepresentation in the original application, comes to light, as provided herein. A licensee shall maintain records open for inspection relating to quality control and manufacturing processes.

Any person engaging in the manufacture, distribution, sale, or import of goods bearing a registered trade mark, and such goods are found to be adulterated, shall be subject to the provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, notwithstanding any other provision contained within this Act. Where a complaint regarding food adulteration involving a registered trade mark is filed, the Appellate Board Chairperson may, subject to verification of prima facie evidence, direct immediate cessation of production and recall of the adulterated goods from the market. Compliance with the standards prescribed under the aforementioned Food Adulteration Act shall be a condition precedent to the continued validity of the trade mark registration, provided that the adulteration is proven through laboratory analysis conducted by a recognized authority. Any failure to comply with such directions or to rectify the adulteration within a period of thirty days shall render the trade mark liable to revocation. The burden of proof regarding the non-adulterated nature of the goods shall rest with the trade mark holder.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a comprehensive index classifying goods and services for the purposes of registration under this Act. This index classification of goods shall be aligned with the internationally recognised Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification, prescribe.
