An applicant seeking registration shall identify the relevant class or classes within the index classification goods corresponding to the goods or services for which registration is sought. Provided that, where a good or service does not fall neatly within an existing class, the Registry may, upon application and subject to a prescribed fee, assign it to a supplementary or newly created sub-class within the existing framework, ensuring clarity and precision in the register. The Registrar’s decision on such assignment shall be final.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a comprehensive index classifying goods and services for the purposes of registration under this Act, adhering to the Nice Classification as adapted by the Central Government. Any applicant seeking registration shall, at the time of application, indicate the relevant class or classes within the index that accurately describe the goods or services for which registration is sought. Should an applicant propose goods or services not readily ascertainable within the existing index classification, the Registry may, subject to due examination and a reasoned determination, assign a corresponding class or require further clarification from the applicant. The Registrar possesses the authority to amend or supplement the index classification goods as necessary to reflect evolving commercial practices and technological advancements. Any such amendment shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal and shall apply to applications filed thereafter, provided that existing registrations shall not be affected unless specifically directed by an appellate authority. The accurate assignment of goods and services to the correct index classification is a prerequisite for a valid and enforceable trade mark registration.

Any person who has duly filed an international registration designating India shall be entitled to the rights and benefits as provided herein, subject to the payment of the prescribed fees and compliance with all procedural requirements of this Act. An applicant seeking to rely upon an international registration in India may, at any time, furnish to the Registrar a statement of grounds on which the registration should be refused or amended, and the Registrar shall, following due examination, issue an order accordingly. Where a mark is identical with an earlier mark and the earlier mark is well known in India, the international registration shall not be registered unless the applicant demonstrates justifiable reasons for its use. Provided that, the Central Government may, by notification, prescribe a process for amicable settlement of disputes arising from the use of such marks, including mediation facilitated by designated experts. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act relating to international registration india may result in the cancellation of the registration or a refusal to renew it.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark subject to an international registration designating India shall, within the prescribed period, file a statement of use with the Trade Marks Registry, demonstrating bona fide use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the international registration. Failure to file such a statement shall render the international registration vulnerable to revocation, subject to a notice issued by the Registry and an opportunity for the applicant to be heard. An appeal from any decision of the Registrar refusing to accept a statement of use, or ordering revocation, shall lie to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the impugned order. Where a conflict arises between an international registration and a prior national trade mark application, the Registry shall conduct a comparative assessment, considering all relevant factors as provided herein, and issue a reasoned order. The International Bureau shall be duly informed of any final decision impacting the international registration india.

A trade mark shall be registerable under this Act if it is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. Register respect goods shall be determined in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe. A mark shall not be registerable if it is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or if its use would be likely to deceive the public as to the quality, nature or origin of those goods or services. Provided that a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registered notwithstanding its initial descriptiveness, subject to proof of such acquired distinctiveness. Any application for registration may be opposed on grounds specified herein.

A trade mark shall be registerable under this Act if it is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. An application for registration shall be made in the prescribed manner to the Trade Marks Registry, and shall include a clear representation of the mark and a statement of the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, require the applicant to limit the goods or services specified in the application. Where a trade mark is register respect goods falling within Class 31, relating to agricultural, horticultural and forestry products, the Registrar shall, prior to acceptance of the application, satisfy himself as to the origin of such goods and compliance with relevant agricultural standards as provided herein. A mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing trade mark. The Registrar may, after considering any objections, either accept or refuse the application.

A geographical indication shall be considered falsified when a product is presented in a manner that misleads the public, or is likely to mislead the public, as to its geographical origin. This includes, but is not limited to, the direct or indirect indication or suggestion that goods originate in a geographical area other than the true territory associated with the registered geographical indication. Furthermore, any unauthorized affixation, use, or display of a registered geographical indication on goods not originating from the specified region constitutes a falsification as provided herein. Where a collective or association is authorized to use a geographical indication, any use outside the parameters of that authorization shall also be deemed a geographical indication falsified, subject to established dispute resolution mechanisms. The term ‘falsification’ extends to material alteration of a genuine indication.

Any assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to verification by the Registrar, and no such assignment shall be valid unless recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications as provided herein. A licensee of a geographical indication may, with the prior written consent of the proprietor, sub-license the rights granted to them, subject to the terms and conditions specified in the original license agreement and any further stipulations imposed by the Registrar. Where a geographical indication is falsely represented as originating from a different geographical area, or where goods are offered for sale bearing a geographical indication that has been falsified, the proprietor of the registered geographical indication, or any authorized user, may apply to the court for an injunction restraining such acts. Any person dealing in goods with a geographical indication falsified, knowing or having reason to believe it to be so, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and the goods shall be deemed counterfeit for the purposes of seizure and disposal under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all assignments and licenses.

Any person aggrieved by the registration of a geographical indication, or alleging a geographical indication falsified, may file a complaint with the Registrar, setting forth the grounds upon which such registration should be cancelled or the falsification rectified. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such complaint, cause an inquiry to be made and may require the applicant or the registered proprietor, as the case may be, to produce evidence in support of their claim. Should the inquiry reveal prima facie evidence of a geographical indication falsified, the Registrar shall issue a notice to the registered proprietor, directing them to respond within a period not exceeding thirty days. Failure to respond, or submission of insufficient evidence, may result in the cancellation of the registration, subject to an appeal to the Appellate Board. Any decision of the Registrar may be appealed to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order, provided that a deposit of a prescribed fee is made. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

Any person desiring to obtain a license to use a registered geographical indication, or to assign any right in such geographical indication, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application for assignment shall clearly demonstrate that the proposed assignee is duly authorized to undertake the production or business associated with the geographical indication and possesses the necessary expertise. Where a complaint is made alleging a geographical indication falsified, and prima facie evidence supports the claim, the Registrar may, pending adjudication, grant a *parte injunction interlocutory* restraining the alleged infringer from continuing the unlawful use. Such injunction may be subject to conditions regarding security deposit or undertaking to compensate the complainant in case the final decision is unfavorable. Any transfer or assignment of rights without prior registration of the license or assignment with the Registrar shall be deemed null and void, and the continued use of the geographical indication by the unauthorized party will constitute further infringement as provided herein.

Any person desiring to obtain a license to use a registered geographical indication, or to assign rights therein, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application for assignment shall include details of the proposed assignee and evidence of consideration paid or to be paid. Where a geographical indication falsifies the true origin of goods, and is presented as originating from a region other than the one legally designated, the registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, initiate proceedings for injunction and damages. Any transfer of rights, including licensing or assignment, shall be registered with the Registrar to be effective against third parties. The Registrar may, after due inquiry, refuse to register a transfer if it is deemed detrimental to the reputation of the geographical indication or the interests of the producers associated with it. A licensee shall be bound by the terms and conditions of the license agreement and shall not exceed the scope of permitted use.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to a patent under this Act, the priority date shall, subject to the provisions herein, be the date on which the first application for a patent for the same invention was filed, either in India or in a convention country. Provided that, if an applicant has duly filed an application in a convention country and, within twelve months from that filing date, files an application for a patent in India, the Indian filing date shall be considered the priority date, notwithstanding any earlier publication or public knowledge of the invention. A subsequent application claiming the benefit of the earlier application shall clearly reference the original application number and country. Failure to do so may result in loss of priority. The applicant bears the burden of proving the earlier filing date.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall be accompanied by such drawings as are necessary for that purpose. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, such claim shall be made in the complete specification and shall specify the priority date and the country in which the earlier application was filed. The applicant shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the earlier application, duly authenticated by the competent authority of the convention country, as evidence of the priority date claimed. Failure to furnish such certified copy may render the claim of priority ineffective, subject to the Controller granting an extension of time for sufficient cause. Any publication occurring after the priority date, but before the filing date in India, may be considered novelty-destroying, unless it relates to knowledge already in the public domain.

A person claiming to be the inventor of an invention, or deriving title from such inventor, shall be entitled to apply for a patent as provided herein, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where two or more persons have independently made the same invention, the right to apply for a patent shall be determined by the priority date, being the date on which the invention was first disclosed to the public. However, a subsequent applicant may, notwithstanding an earlier priority date claimed by another, establish a right to the patent if they demonstrate diligent efforts to reduce the invention to practice and a reasonable belief that the earlier applicant has abandoned their pursuit. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding the priority date may, within one month of the order, appeal to the appellate authority. The appellate authority shall consider all evidence presented and may confirm, modify, or reverse the initial decision, ensuring equitable resolution of competing claims. A certificate of priority, obtained from a convention country, shall be admissible as evidence of the priority date.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall define the scope of the invention for which protection is claimed. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, such claim of priority shall be in writing and filed within the prescribed period from the date of the earliest such application constituting the basis for the claim. The priority date, when validly claimed, shall be the reference date for determining the novelty of the invention as disclosed in the complete specification. However, such a claim of priority shall not be valid if the earlier application was not a complete application as defined herein, or if the applicant fails to furnish, as required, certified copies of the earlier application within the stipulated timeframe. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the priority date shall be considered for the purposes of assessing the inventive step.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall define the scope of the invention for which protection is claimed. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, such claim of priority shall be in writing and filed within the prescribed period from the date of the earliest such application constituting the basis for the claim. The priority date, if validly claimed and accepted, shall be the reference date for determining the novelty of the invention as provided herein. Failure to comply with the requirements regarding the claim of priority, including the submission of relevant documents establishing the earlier application and its filing date, may result in the loss of the priority right. Subject to the provisions of this Act, an application claiming priority shall be examined as if it were filed on the priority date.

Any person claiming a patent shall establish a valid priority date, and failure to do so will render the application liable to be refused as provided herein. A claim to priority based on an earlier application filed in a convention country shall be substantiated by a certified copy of the earlier application, filed within the prescribed period, and any delay exceeding said period will incur a penalty not exceeding five times the applicable filing fee. Should a discrepancy arise regarding the scope of the earlier application forming the basis of the claimed priority date, the Controller may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, determine the true extent of the priority claim. Any false representation concerning the priority date, made with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with a fine, or with both. The Controller may, subject to justifiable cause, extend the period for filing the priority document, but such extension shall not exceed sixty days.

Any assignment of a patent application, whether prospective or actual, shall be in writing and shall specify the invention to which it relates, and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. Where an application for a patent has been filed, but a patent has not yet been granted, the assignee may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, proceed with the application as if they were the original applicant. However, any assignment of a patent application relating to an invention for which a convention application has been filed under this Act, shall be subject to the provisions of the Paris Convention, and the priority date established by that convention shall be maintained for the purposes of determining the novelty of the invention. Should a dispute arise regarding the validity of such assignment, the Controller of Patents may, after due inquiry, determine the rightful owner of the application, considering the earliest effective assignment date. Any subsequent assignment must be recorded with the Patent Office to be legally effective.

A claim to an invention shall not be allowed unless the applicant establishes a priority date, and such date shall be the filing date of the complete specification, subject to the provisions herein. Where an applicant claims priority from an application made in a convention country, proof of such earlier application, duly attested, shall be furnished within the prescribed period, failing which the priority date shall be the date of filing in India. However, any intervening publication, whether by the applicant or a third party, relating to the invention, may invalidate the claim to the asserted priority date, unless such publication was unavoidable and disclosed only information strictly necessary for the purpose of scientific advancement. An objection to the claimed priority date, raised by the Controller, may be appealed to the Appellate Board, and the Board’s decision shall be final, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law. The burden of proving the validity of the priority date rests with the applicant.

For the purposes of this Act, the priority date in respect of any invention shall be the date on which the first patent application for that invention was filed, whether in India or in a convention country, provided that such application contains a clear and complete description of the invention and its manner of performance. Where a person applies for a patent claiming a priority date based on a prior application, that claim shall be subject to verification by the Controller of Patents. Any representation made regarding the date of invention or the details of the earlier application, if found to be false in nature and intended to mislead, may be deemed a false trade description, attracting penalties as provided herein. The Controller may, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, reject the claim to a priority date if sufficient evidence is not furnished.

A complete application for a patent, as provided herein, shall establish a priority date, which date shall be the filing date of the application, unless otherwise determined under this Act. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, the priority date shall be the filing date of the earliest of those earlier applications, subject to the applicant satisfying the Controller of Patents with proof of such filing and a certified copy thereof. Should a dispute arise regarding the validity of a claimed priority date, the matter may be referred to the appropriate district court for adjudication, and the decision of such court shall be binding on all parties. An applicant failing to adequately substantiate a claimed priority date risks losing the benefit of that earlier filing date for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step. Any alteration to the specification after filing, without explicit consent, may also affect the established priority date.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall be accompanied by such drawings as are necessary for that purpose. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, the priority date for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step shall be the date of the earliest of those earlier applications, provided that a declaration claiming priority is filed within the prescribed period and satisfies the requirements as to form and content. An application for a patent may be supported by a certificate of registration issued by a competent authority in a convention country, verifying the filing date of the earlier application upon which priority is claimed. Such a registered certification shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, subject to proof to the contrary. Failure to adequately substantiate a claimed priority date may result in the application being treated as filed on the date of its actual filing before this office.

Any person claiming a right to a patent, based on an application filed in a convention country or a regional patent organization, shall, as provided herein, establish a valid priority date to benefit from the earlier filing date. Failure to submit a complete and verifiable priority claim, including a certified copy of the original application and a translation if necessary, with the registrar application within the stipulated timeframe, shall render the claim invalid and the application subject to the same examination criteria as a new application filed on the date of actual receipt by the Patent Office. Any false representation regarding the priority date, or deliberate omission of material facts relating to the original application, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Controller of Patents may, notwithstanding any other provision, reject any patent application where a fraudulent priority claim is established.

A patentee, as provided herein, shall have the exclusive right to exploit a patented invention, subject to the provisions of this Act relating to government use and licensing. These patent rights extend to making, using, selling, importing, and distributing the invention within the territory of India. A patent, however, does not confer the right to use, sell or import in respect of a process for producing a substance if the substance itself is already the subject matter of a valid patent. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a patent shall be subject to revocation on grounds of lack of novelty or inventive step, as determined by due process. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of these patent rights may seek redressal through civil proceedings. The term of these rights shall be twenty years from the date of filing the application.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of any new and useful invention relating to any process, machine, manufacture, or article of manufacture may apply to the Controller for a patent in the prescribed manner. A patent, once granted, shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights to exploit the invention, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to conditions as may be stipulated. These patent rights shall extend to preventing others from making, using, selling, importing, or stocking the patented invention without the patentee’s authorization. However, such rights may be subject to compulsory licensing as provided herein, particularly in cases of national emergency or public interest. Any assignment or transfer of these patent rights shall be registered with the Controller to be legally effective against third parties. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all patents and assignments.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of patent rights, or by any threatened infringement thereof, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding concurrent jurisdiction. The suit may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from the infringing act, and may also claim damages for any loss suffered by the plaintiff as a result of the infringement. Where a defendant proves that the patent is invalid, the Court may revoke the patent and order costs to be paid by the plaintiff. 

A licensee of a patented invention shall also have the right to bring a suit for infringement, provided that the terms of the license so permit and the licensor has not initiated proceedings. Any relief granted by the Court, including damages, shall be apportioned between the patentee and the licensee in a manner consistent with the terms of their agreement. The Court may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of any new and useful invention relating to any process, machine, manufacture, or article of manufacture may apply for a patent in the prescribed manner. A patent, once granted, shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights to exploit the invention, subject to reasonable licensing terms as may be determined by the Controller of Patents. These patent rights shall extend to preventing any other person from making, using, selling, importing, or stocking the patented invention without the patentee’s consent. 

However, such rights shall not extend to research and private non-commercial use, or to acts necessary for discovery and proof of the invention. Where a patentee fails to adequately work the patented invention within a period of three years from the date of grant, any interested person may petition for a compulsory license, subject to payment of reasonable royalties. The Controller shall consider such petitions and may grant licenses as provided herein, balancing the patentee’s rights with the public interest.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any person claiming patent rights in a biotechnological application involving biological material shall disclose the origin and source of said material in a manner consistent with prevailing international norms and the protection of traditional knowledge. A patent applicant shall, prior to grant, furnish a detailed description of the biological material, including its characteristics and any modifications made thereto, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements shall render the patent application liable to be rejected, and any patent granted based on incomplete or inaccurate disclosure may be revoked. Provided that, where the biological material is freely available to the public or has been lawfully acquired, such disclosure requirements shall be subject to reasonable limitations. The patentee shall also be responsible for demonstrating that the claimed invention possesses novelty and involves an inventive step, considering the prior art relating to the disclosed biological material.

Any person who, without lawful justification and with intent to deceive, represents a product as being patented, or applies any word or sign whatsoever calculated to lead persons into the belief that such product is the subject of patent rights, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a person, having knowledge of a valid patent, performs any act in contravention of the exclusive rights conferred thereby as provided herein, they shall be liable to pay damages to the patentee, assessed on a reasonable royalty basis and, in no case, less than five percent of the gross sales revenue derived from the infringing act. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, grant a license to a reasonably interested party where the patentee fails to adequately exploit the patented invention for the benefit of the public. Any appeal against the Controller’s decision shall lie with the High Court.

Any assignment of the patent rights arising under this Act shall be in writing and duly executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to nomination. A license, whether sole or otherwise, granted by the patentee or assignee of patent rights may be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of such license, including the duration, scope, and territory. Where a license is granted for a term exceeding five years, it shall be registered with the appropriate authority as provided herein, failing which such license shall be void. The patentee or assignee may, subject to the terms of any existing assignment or license, further assign or license the patent rights. Any dispute regarding the validity or scope of an assignment or license shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction. A transfer of patent rights shall not prejudice any existing rights or liabilities.

Any person alleging infringement of patent rights shall, prior to initiating proceedings before the High Court, furnish the alleged infringer with a notice of such claim, detailing the specific acts constituting the infringement and the patent claimed to be infringed. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of receiving such notice, submit a declaration of non-infringement supported by technical evidence, no suit may be instituted without first referring the matter to a technically qualified mediator appointed by the Controller of Patents. Provided that, if the mediator determines, within ninety days, that a prima facie case of infringement exists, the aggrieved party may then proceed with litigation. Any decision of the mediator shall not be binding, but may be presented as evidence in subsequent court proceedings. An appeal from the Controller’s appointment of a mediator, or the mediator’s refusal to act, shall lie with the High Court. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the infringement claim inadmissible, subject to the discretion of the Court.

Any person infringing any patent rights as provided herein shall be liable to a civil action for recovery of damages, which shall not be less than a reasonable royalty of the patented invention and may also include an injunction restraining the infringement. Where the Controller is satisfied, after due consideration of the representations of the patentee and interested parties, that a compulsory licence should be granted, it may so order, subject to the payment of adequate remuneration to the patentee, determined in accordance with the prescribed rules. Failure to comply with the terms of a compulsory licence, or any order of the Controller relating thereto, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Any evidence obtained through inspection authorized under this Act shall be admissible in any proceedings under this Act, notwithstanding any other law. The patentee may, at any time, withdraw an application for a compulsory licence, provided that adequate reasons are furnished.

Any assignment of the patent rights relating to a registered patent shall be subject to verification by the Controller of Patents, and no assignment shall be valid unless recorded in the registrar index registered and maintained under this Act. A licensee of a patent, with the consent of the patentee, may further assign their interest in the licensed patent rights, subject to the terms and conditions of the original license agreement. Where a patentee intends to grant a license, whether sole, exclusive, or non-exclusive, such license shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, scope, and terms of the license, including royalty payments. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the license unenforceable. The patentee shall, within thirty days of executing any assignment or license, furnish a copy thereof to the Controller for recordation in the registrar index registered. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions contained herein. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and no appeal shall be entertained by the High Court unless the appellant satisfies the Court that reasonable cause prevented the filing of the appeal within the said period. The High Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit with the Court such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the value of the claim in the appeal, as security for the payment of costs. Provided that, the Appellate Board’s decision regarding interim injunctions shall not be subject to appeal until the final adjudication of the matter.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller relating to an application for a patent, or the amendment or revocation thereof, or against any order made by the Controller under this Act concerning anticipation, obviousness, or inventive step. The appeal shall be presented in the prescribed form and verified in such manner as may be prescribed, and shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. No appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant has deposited with the Board such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of an appeal, may direct the Controller to furnish within such time as it thinks fit, a statement of the case and the documents relating thereto, and shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller.

Any aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller, save where such decision relates solely to a matter of administration or procedure and does not affect the substantive rights of the appellant. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. The grounds for appeal shall be clearly stated in the memorandum of appeal, and supporting evidence, if any, shall be submitted therewith. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the respondent to submit a reply within thirty days of receiving notice of the appeal. All appeals shall be heard in open court, and the Appellate Board shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller, or to remit the matter back for further consideration, as provided herein. A further appeal to the Supreme Court shall lie from any decision of the Appellate Board, subject to the provisions of any other law for the time being in force.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller relating to an application for a patent, or the amendment or revocation thereof, or against any order made by the Controller refusing to grant a patent or dismissing an application for the restoration of a patent. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to questions of law, and the Appellate Board shall not review findings of fact unless such findings are demonstrably based on no evidence or are manifestly erroneous. Provided that no appeal shall lie from a decision of the Controller relating to an interim order concerning the preservation of evidence or the conduct of proceedings. All appeals shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s decision, and a prescribed fee shall accompany the filing. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for the payment of costs. Any party to an appeal may, with leave of the Appellate Board, appear in person or be represented by a patent agent or legal practitioner.

Any aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order sought to be appealed against, and subject to the deposit of such fees as may be prescribed. No appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for questioning the correctness, legality, or propriety of the decision. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the production of further evidence or call for expert opinions to aid in its determination. Provided that, if the appeal concerns a matter of technical complexity, the Board shall constitute a special bench including a person with demonstrable expertise in the relevant field. All decisions of the Appellate Board shall be communicated to the parties in writing, and any request for reconsideration shall also be subject to the same time limitations as the initial appeal. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the appeal inadmissible.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, or any order made by it in the exercise of powers conferred by or under this Act, shall have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and no appeal shall be entertained by the Supreme Court unless the appellant has deposited with the Registrar of the Appellate Board a sum equivalent to the costs awarded by the Appellate Board, or, in the absence of such award, a sum of twenty thousand rupees. Failure to comply with this deposit requirement shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Supreme Court, however, may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period of ninety days. Any frivolous or vexatious appeal shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as a debt from the appellant.

Any assignment of a patent, or of any right in a patent, whether made before or after the grant of the patent, shall be in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee. Where a patent is assigned, the assignee shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, enjoy the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as the original patentee in respect of the patent. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register an assignment, or by any condition imposed in connection with the registration of an assignment, may appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of the order of the Controller refusing registration or imposing conditions. Provided that the Controller may, at the request of the parties, refer any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment to arbitration, and the decision of the arbitrator shall be final and binding. The assignee shall furnish the Controller with a copy of the instrument of assignment within thirty days of its execution.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with the refusal of an application for registration of a patent, or with any order of revocation made under this Act, shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board established for the purposes of this Act, provided that such appeal is presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to furnish security for the payment of costs which may be incurred by the respondent in defending the appeal. Further, any party disputing the validity of a patent granted under this Act may, instead of filing a civil suit, petition the Appellate Board for revocation, and the Board’s decision on such petition shall be final and binding, unless an appeal is preferred to the Supreme Court on a question of law. An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any decision of the Appellate Board on a substantial question of law.

Any aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller, provided that such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and subject to the deposit of such fees as may be prescribed. Where the Controller’s decision relates to a patent application originating from a Contracting State under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, the Appellate Board shall, prior to considering the merits of the appeal, satisfy itself that the applicant has complied with all relevant provisions concerning priority claims or equivalent rights as stipulated in the relevant international agreement. An appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for questioning the Controller’s findings and provides evidence of potential prejudice suffered as a direct result of the impugned decision. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require additional evidence or expert opinion before rendering its decision, and its order shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Geographical Indications Registry concerning the registration or refusal of registration of a geographical indication authorised under this Act, or by any order made in respect of such registration, shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the impugned decision or order, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the same. Failure to comply with this time limit shall render the appeal inadmissible, and no extension of time shall be granted except under extraordinary circumstances determined by the Appellate Board. Any false representation made in an appeal, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with a fine, or with both. The Appellate Board may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit a sum sufficient to cover the costs of the proceedings.

Any aggrieved person may appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller refusing to register a patent or revoking a patent, provided that such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order. The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of a memorandum of appeal and the prescribed fee, give notice to the Controller and the applicant or patentee, as the case may be, and shall afford them an opportunity of being heard. Should the Appellate Board determine that the Controller’s decision was erroneous, it may direct the Controller to register the patent or, conversely, to maintain the revocation. Any omission to record a rectification in the omission register, duly noted by the Controller, shall not, in and of itself, invalidate an otherwise valid appeal, but may be considered as a factor in determining the overall merits of the case. Further appeal from the decision of the Appellate Board shall lie to the Supreme Court.

In this Act, “mark relation goods” shall mean a demonstrable link between a trade mark and the goods or services for which it is registered or proposed to be registered, such that a consumer encountering the mark in relation to those goods or services would reasonably perceive a commercial connection. This relation may be established through evidence of actual use of the mark on the goods, extensive advertising linking the mark to the goods, or a consistent and prolonged association in the minds of consumers. Provided that, where the mark is used in relation to entirely dissimilar goods or services, the existence of such a relation shall be subject to a consideration of the likelihood of confusion or association. A mark’s relation to goods may also be inferred from the reputation of the mark itself, as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be registrable under this Act if it is distinctive, and not descriptive of the goods or services to which it relates, or likely to deceive the public. An application for registration shall specify the goods or services for which registration is sought, and shall be classified according to the Nice Classification, as adopted from time to time. Where a mark is sought to be registered in relation to goods or services falling within multiple classes, a separate application, with corresponding fees, shall be filed for each class. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, permit the amendment of an application to correct errors or to clarify the specification of goods. However, no amendment shall be permitted that alters the essential character of the mark or extends the scope of the goods or services beyond the originally disclosed mark relation goods. A mark identical with or resembling a registered trade mark, used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, shall be deemed to be an infringement, as provided herein.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to institute legal proceedings for infringement where another party uses a deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registered trade mark is used. However, such right to institute proceedings shall not be prejudiced by any prior use of the mark by the defendant, provided that such use was bona fide and continuous prior to the date of registration of the plaintiff’s trade mark. Where a mark relation goods is established, and the use by the defendant is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers, the court may grant an injunction restraining further use of the offending mark. Additionally, the court may award damages to the plaintiff, assessed in accordance with the loss suffered as a result of the infringement, or an account of profits made by the defendant. Any order for damages or account of profits may, subject to the discretion of the court, include an award of exemplary damages.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark relating to specified goods or a class of goods shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the proprietor, or duly authorised agent, and shall not confer any right to use the mark in relation to goods not included in the assignment. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, become the proprietor of the trade mark as regards the goods or services in respect of which the goodwill is assigned. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be granted in respect of a registered trade mark relating to goods, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, geographical territory, and the conditions governing its use. Any dispute arising from the terms of a license or assignment of a mark relation goods shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court, as provided herein, and may be determined by arbitration. The registrar shall maintain a register of all assignments and licenses.

A reference use mark shall mean a mark, not inherently distinctive, used in association with goods or services to indicate the source, quality, or characteristics of those goods or services, but which acquires distinctiveness through extensive and continuous use. Such acquisition of distinctiveness shall be demonstrable through evidence of actual use and public recognition, and may be established even if the mark is descriptive or deceptively similar to an existing mark, provided that such use does not cause confusion. A mark functioning solely as descriptive of the characteristics of the goods or services, without any acquired secondary meaning, shall not qualify as a reference use mark as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require evidence of such acquired distinctiveness before accepting an application for registration.

A person regularly engaged in trade may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for registration of a reference use mark, being a mark used by such person to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or other characteristics of goods or services. The application shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the nature of the reference use and the goods or services to which it relates. The Registry may, subject to verification of the submitted statement and satisfaction that the mark is genuinely descriptive and not deceptively similar to any existing registered trade mark, register the reference use mark. Registration of a reference use mark shall not confer exclusive rights to the mark itself, but only the right to use it in a manner consistent with its descriptive purpose, as provided herein. Any misuse or extension of such use beyond the stated characteristics shall be subject to legal action under this Act.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark, or a person using a trade mark with his consent, may, where another person is using a deceptively similar trade mark, seek remedies as provided herein, notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act. However, such remedies shall not be available against a person who uses the trade mark solely to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of the goods or services in question, or to describe the characteristics of the goods or services. 

Specifically, a defendant shall not be liable if the use of the mark constitutes fair use, including descriptive fair use, and is reasonably necessary to indicate the connection between the defendant and the goods or services offered. Where a mark is established as a reference use mark, the proprietor of the registered trade mark shall bear the burden of proving that the defendant’s use is likely to cause confusion or deceptively indicate a connection. Any injunction granted under this Act shall be subject to such terms and conditions as the Court may deem fit.

A trade mark shall be considered a reference use mark where it is legitimately used by a person other than the proprietor to indicate the kind, quality, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or characteristics of goods or services, or to indicate that such goods or services have been approved, endorsed or certified by the proprietor of the trade mark. Such use shall not be actionable as an infringement of trade mark, provided that the use is in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters. However, where the reference use mark directly imitates the trade mark of another, and is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, the proprietor may seek redressal as provided herein. Any person alleging reference use shall bear the burden of proving that their use falls within the parameters of legitimate reference and does not constitute passing off. The Registrar may, upon application, determine whether a particular use constitutes permissible reference, subject to such conditions as may be deemed appropriate to protect the interests of both parties. A finding of permissible reference shall not preclude a subsequent claim of dilution of brand reputation if such dilution is established.

A trade mark proprietor seeking registration of a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, or a mark pending registration, shall not be permitted to do so unless the applicant demonstrates legitimate use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application. However, where the mark applied for is used by the applicant only as a descriptive reference to a characteristic of the goods or services, or to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production or rendering of the services, it may be registered as a reference use mark. Such registration shall be subject to conditions imposed by the Registrar, including limitations on the scope of protection and requirements for prominent disclaimer of any claim to trade mark rights. Provided that, the use must be bona fide and not intended to deceive the public or to unfairly compete with existing trade mark holders, and the mark must not be descriptive of the goods or services themselves, but rather refer to a feature or aspect thereof.

Any person using a reference use mark, being a trade mark identifying the origin of goods or services with the consent of the proprietor of that trade mark, shall maintain accurate records of all such usage, including quantities, dates, and territories, subject to inspection by an officer duly authorized under this Act. Failure to maintain such records, or providing false information during inspection, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Where a reference use mark is employed in a manner likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers as to the source or quality of goods or services, the aggrieved proprietor may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining such use. Any person contravening the terms of an injunction issued as provided herein shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of contravention. The proprietor shall bear the burden of proving deceptive similarity.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark and the goodwill, if any, associated with the trade mark, in whole or in part, to any person or class of persons. Any assignment not in writing shall be void. Where a trade mark is assigned without any assignment of the goodwill, it shall be deemed to be a reference use mark, and the assignee shall only be entitled to use the mark in connection with the goods or services for which it was originally registered, and to the extent of the interest so assigned. The assignor retains the right to use the mark in relation to other goods or services not covered by the assignment, provided that such use does not cause confusion or deception amongst the public. An assignment of a reference use mark shall not affect the rights of any prior user of the trade mark. Any agreement relating to the assignment of a reference use mark shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein, failing which, the assignment shall be considered provisional.

A trade mark proprietor aggrieved by the use of a mark by another, alleging such use constitutes infringement, may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction restraining the latter from further use, pending adjudication of the matter. However, where the defendant demonstrates the mark is used solely to describe the characteristics of their goods or services, or to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production, such use shall not be deemed infringement, provided that such use is fair and honest, and does not cause confusion. Any claim of descriptive fair use shall be subject to proof of actual use and demonstrable benefit to the public. Furthermore, a mark functioning as a reference use mark, indicating merely that the goods or services are compatible with or suitable for use with those of the trade mark proprietor, is expressly excluded from the scope of infringement as provided herein, unless it is proven such reference use is likely to deceive. Appeals from decisions of the High Court shall lie with the Supreme Court.

Any person using a reference use mark, being a trade mark identifying the origin of goods or services with the consent of the proprietor of that trade mark, shall maintain accurate records of all such use, including quantities, dates, and territories, subject to inspection by the Registrar. Failure to maintain such records, or providing false information during inspection, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the unauthorized use of a trade mark, even where such use constitutes a legitimate reference, provided that such use is demonstrably likely to cause confusion or misrepresentation to the public. The High Court, in considering such applications, may also order the destruction of goods bearing the improperly used mark and award damages to the rightful proprietor, as provided herein. Repeated violations shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the goodwill of the trade mark with or without any part of the business in which it is used. Any assignment of a reference use mark shall be accompanied by a detailed statement outlining the scope of permitted use, including the specific goods or services for which the mark is assigned and any geographical limitations applicable to such use. Where an assignment involves a complex licensing arrangement, the Trade Marks Registry may, at the request of either party, appoint a chairperson judicial member to facilitate a fair and equitable determination of the terms. Such a member shall have the power to direct mediation or, failing that, to make recommendations regarding the assignment, which shall be binding unless successfully appealed. The assignee shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if they were the original proprietor, subject to the terms of the assignment and any conditions imposed by the Registry. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment voidable.

For the purposes of this Act, “services use mark” shall mean a mark used or proposed to be used in relation to services, and includes a mark used in advertising or promotion to identify services, but does not include a mark used solely to indicate the characteristics or quality of those services. A mark qualifying as a services use mark shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions relating to distinctiveness and descriptiveness as provided herein. Where a mark is used in relation to both goods and services, it shall be considered a mark used in relation to services if the primary commercial impression created is that of service provision. The Registrar may, however, require a clear indication of the specific services offered when examining such a mark.

Any person proposing to use a trade mark in relation to services, shall, prior to such use, conduct a search for identical or deceptively similar marks registered or applied for under this Act, and shall submit a report of such search to the Trade Marks Registry. Where a proposed services use mark is identical to an earlier trade mark registered for identical services, use shall be prohibited unless the proprietor of the earlier mark has consented in writing. However, a mark shall not be deemed deceptively similar merely due to phonetic resemblance, provided that visual and conceptual distinctiveness are demonstrably maintained. An application for registration of a services use mark may be refused if the applicant fails to demonstrate a genuine intention to provide the stated services. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to due process, require evidence of such intention. Any false representation regarding the scope of services offered in connection with a registered trade mark shall constitute an offence under this Act.

Any person using a trade mark in relation to services, where such use is likely to cause confusion, or is likely to deceive or cause unfair competition, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement as provided herein. A finding of infringement relating to services use mark shall be made irrespective of whether the mark is registered or unregistered, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates prior use and goodwill. Where a defendant claims legitimate use of a similar mark in connection with services, the Tribunal may, subject to sufficient evidence of honest concurrent use, grant a limited exemption. Any person found guilty of infringing a services use mark shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may also be subject to an order of injunction restraining further infringement. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. The Tribunal shall have the power to award costs to the prevailing party.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark used in relation to services shall be subject to a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and assignee, and shall be in the prescribed form. Where the assignment is made subject to conditions, those conditions shall be clearly stated in the instrument and shall be enforceable as provided herein. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, concerning a services use mark may be granted for a defined period, territory, or form of use, and such license shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective against third parties. The instrument creating the license shall specify the quality of goods or services to which the license applies, and any breach of such quality stipulations shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license. The registered proprietor of a trade mark used for services may, subject to the terms of any existing license, assign or transfer the mark, or any right therein, to any other person or entity. Any assignment or license failing to comply with these provisions shall be void.

Any person claiming use of a mark in relation to services, and alleging infringement by another, shall submit evidence of bona fide use as provided herein, demonstrating continuous application to those services for a period not less than five years prior to the date of the alleged infringement. However, the Registrar may, subject to compelling reasons and upon review of submitted affidavits, accept a shorter period of demonstrated use if the mark has acquired distinctiveness through extensive advertising or promotional activity. A dispute regarding the genuineness of such use, or the nature of the services offered under the mark, shall be adjudicated by the Appellate Board, with a right of appeal to the High Court. The determination of ‘services use mark’ shall consider the actual rendering of the service to the public, and not merely intent to provide such service. Any finding of deceptive similarity in the services offered, even with proven mark use, may invalidate a claim of infringement under this Act.

A business india applicant, for the purposes of registration of a trade mark as provided herein, shall be deemed to include any company incorporated in India, or any partnership firm registered under the Partnership Act, 1932, or any individual ordinarily resident in India. Where an application for registration is made by a business india applicant acting through a duly authorized agent, such agent shall file a power of attorney with the application. The applicant shall furnish a representation of the trade mark, clearly depicting the mark as it is intended to be used, and shall specify the class or classes of goods or services in relation to which registration is sought. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar may require further information or evidence from the applicant to satisfy themselves as to the validity of the application.

Any application for registration of a trade mark incorporating a representation of a geographical indication shall be subject to the provisions of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, and shall demonstrate a clear connection between the goods and the indicated geographical origin. An applicant claiming rights as a business india applicant shall furnish, along with the application, a certified copy of the resolution authorizing the filing of the application, and details of all directors and shareholders holding more than ten percent of the issued share capital. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the applicant is a bona fide user, proceed with examination of the application. Provided that, where the trade mark is proposed for use on goods not yet in the market, a statement of bona fide intent to use shall be submitted. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application liable to be refused as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a trade mark, or by any requirement subject to which the Registrar has required the registration to be effected, may appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is made within one month from the date of the order of the Registrar. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the order of the Registrar or set aside such order or modify it in such manner as it thinks fit. Where the Appellate Board sets aside the order of the Registrar, it may direct the Registrar to register the trade mark, subject to such conditions, if any, as it may deem appropriate. 

A business india applicant, demonstrating genuine user intent and commercial activity within the territory, shall be afforded expedited consideration of their application, subject to full compliance with all procedural requirements as provided herein. The Registrar may, however, require additional evidence of such genuine use and commercial activity if deemed necessary. Any false representation by a business india applicant shall be grounds for immediate rejection of the application and potential penalties.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, vested in business india applicant, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding consent and recording of assignment. A license, whether sole or otherwise, granted by business india applicant in respect of a registered trade mark shall be in writing and may be assigned or further licensed by or on behalf of the licensee, subject to the terms of the original license and the provisions herein. Where business india applicant proposes to assign the trade mark with or without goodwill, notice of such intention shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal, allowing for objections to be filed within a period of one month from the date of such publication. The Registrar may, subject to due diligence and satisfaction of all legal requirements, record the assignment or license upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license unenforceable as provided herein. Any dispute arising from such assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any application for registration of a trade mark incorporating the name “Business India” shall be subject to a prior search conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain existing rights and prevent potential conflicts with established entities operating under similar designations. Provided that, an applicant claiming legitimate use prior to the date of this Act’s amendment may submit evidence of continuous use for a period not less than five years, subject to verification by the Registrar. Should the Registrar determine a likelihood of confusion, the applicant shall be required to demonstrate distinctiveness beyond mere descriptive use, and may be directed to amend the application or provide a reasoned statement of differentiation. Any decision of the Registrar in this regard may be appealed to the Appellate Board, and further to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding timelines for filing appeals. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence of actual confusion, if any, in determining the merits of the appeal brought by Business India applicant.

A business India applicant, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to include any company incorporated within India, or any individual ordinarily resident in India, seeking to register a trade mark. An application for registration, as provided herein, shall be accompanied by a clear representation of the mark and a statement of the goods or services to which it relates. The register maintained under this Act shall contain particulars of all registered trade marks, including the applicant’s name and address, the date of application, and the class of goods or services. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Registrar may require further evidence to verify the applicant’s details or the legitimacy of the mark. Any false representation made in an application shall render it liable to be rejected, and may attract penalties as prescribed.

A mark registered in manner prescribed under this Act shall be deemed to be a property right vested in the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. The register of trade marks shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars entered therein, and no rectification proceedings shall invalidate a registration unless proven fraudulent or obtained through misrepresentation. Where a mark is registered in good faith and used continuously, it acquires enhanced protection against challenges based on prior use by another party, provided that such prior use was not widely known to the public at the time of registration. Any assignment or transmission of a registered mark shall be subject to the conditions specified in the register and shall be valid only upon proper recording. A mark registered manner includes details of goods, services, and proprietor details.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be registered in the manner prescribed by this Act, and the register of trade marks maintained by the Trade Marks Registry shall be the definitive record of such registration. Any application for registration must clearly demonstrate distinctive character and be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, subject to the provisions relating to well-known marks. Where a mark is registered in a series, each mark within the series shall be considered individually registered, provided that the collective series meets the requirements as to goods or services classification. The proprietor of a registered mark shall have the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement. A mark registered manner, if contested, may be subject to revocation proceedings based on grounds of non-use or misrepresentation, as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the prescribed procedure for assignment and recording.

A trade mark registered in a manner consistent with the provisions of this Act shall be maintained on the register subject to the payment of the prescribed renewal fee and the filing of the requisite affidavits of continued use, as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark has been in continuous use for a period of five years and the proprietor thereof makes application for its renewal, the Registrar shall, unless sufficient cause is shown to the contrary, renew the registration for a further period of ten years. However, a registered mark may be subject to revocation proceedings initiated by any aggrieved party alleging non-use, or use in a manner likely to cause confusion or deception. The Registrar, upon receiving such a petition and following due process of inquiry, shall determine whether the mark continues to meet the criteria for registration. Any alteration to the mark registered manner requires prior approval and may necessitate a fresh examination process, ensuring continued distinctiveness and compliance with the principles outlined in this Act.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark in a manner not in accordance with the provisions of this Act, or who makes a material misrepresentation in an application for registration, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a mark is registered in a manner that contravenes established principles of legitimate use and is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers, the Registrar may, subject to a reasoned order, direct rectification of the register. Provided that, such rectification shall not prejudice any rights accrued to a bona fide purchaser prior to the issuance of the order. Any individual found to be fraudulently claiming ownership of a mark registered manner, or engaging in the false representation of rights therein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar shall have the power to impose these penalties as provided herein.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and transmitted to the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument shall clearly identify the mark registered manner, including the registration number, class of goods or services, and the extent of the assignment, whether partial or complete. Where the assignment involves a series of trade marks, a schedule detailing each mark shall be annexed to the instrument. 

A license to use a registered trade mark may be granted, and such license shall be in writing and subject to such conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties, provided that any exclusive license shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective against third parties. The registered proprietor may, subject to the terms of any existing license, assign or transfer the trade mark, or any right therein, to any person or entity. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license invalid as provided herein.

Any person employing a mark registered manner, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Where a mark is deceptively similar to another, the court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from such use. Furthermore, any use of associated trade marks, even if not identical, which is likely to cause confusion or dilution of the registered mark, constitutes an infringement actionable as provided herein. The proprietor of a registered trade mark may, at any time, apply to the court for a decree of perpetual injunction against any such infringement. Failure to comply with an order of the court under this Act shall be punishable with fine and imprisonment, as determined by the court. Any goods found to bear an infringing mark may be seized and destroyed.

Any person claiming to be the registered proprietor of a trade mark, desiring to adduce evidence in support of an application for registration, or in opposition to any such application, or in any proceedings under this Act, shall furnish an affidavit verifying the facts stated therein. Failure to submit a duly verified affidavit, demonstrating a prima facie case for the claim made, shall render the application or opposition liable to be dismissed, and the claimant may be subject to a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Registrar may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, allow a period of thirty days for rectification of any deficiency in the affidavit. Any affidavit found to be deliberately false or misleading, intended to deceive the Tribunal or the Registrar, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The onus of proving the veracity of the affidavit registered proprietor rests solely with the declarant.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and assignee, and shall include a statement of the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. The instrument of assignment, when executed, shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry in the manner prescribed. Where the registered proprietor assigns the trade mark, they shall, within the prescribed period, file an affidavit verifying the particulars of the assignment, including the full name and address of the assignee, and the consideration paid for the assignment. Should the assignee seek to independently utilize the trade mark following assignment, they may apply for a separate registration in their name, subject to demonstrating legitimate use and providing evidence of the completed assignment. Failure to file the required affidavit registered proprietor may render the assignment unenforceable as against third parties. Any licensing agreement relating to the trade mark shall also be filed with the Registry.

Any person alleging a contravention of rights in a registered trade mark, and seeking rectification of the register, shall submit an affidavit registered proprietor demonstrating continuous and bona fide use of the mark, or reasonable grounds for non-use, subject to the provisions herein. Should the Registrar require further evidence of such use, or the veracity of the affidavit registered proprietor, a hearing shall be convened, and the claimant may be directed to produce additional documentation, including sales figures and marketing materials. An objection to the affidavit registered proprietor may be filed by any opposing party within thirty days of its service, detailing specific grounds for disputing its contents. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the dismissal of the rectification application, or a finding against the claimant, and an award of costs as deemed appropriate.
