Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, extend these timelines for sufficient cause shown.

Any person alleging a dispute regarding the proprietorship of a trade mark, or opposing an application for registration, shall submit an affidavit of the registered proprietor confirming the details of the mark and its continuous use as provided herein. Should the affidavit reveal inconsistencies or discrepancies concerning the claimed date of first use, the Registrar may require further evidence, including statutory declarations from licensees or evidence of advertising expenditure. Where a trade mark identical to an existing registered trade mark is sought to be registered for identical goods or services, the Registrar shall, after hearing both parties and considering the affidavit registered proprietor, refuse the application unless the applicant demonstrates a legitimate reason for the similarity. An appeal against the Registrar’s decision on such refusal may be filed with the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, within ninety days of the order. The court shall consider the original affidavit and any supplementary evidence presented.

A proposed registered proprietor shall, for the purposes of an application for registration of a trade mark under this Act, be deemed to include a person claiming to be the assignee of the future trade mark, subject to the provisions herein. Where an application is made claiming assignment of a future trade mark, the applicant, being the proposed registered proprietor, shall furnish to the Registrar a statement detailing the terms and conditions governing the intended assignment, including but not limited to, the effective date of transfer and any associated consideration. Provided that, such statement shall be subject to verification by the current registered proprietor, who may file an objection within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of notice from the Registrar. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person desiring to become the registered proprietor of a trade mark shall submit an application in the manner prescribed, demonstrating a bona fide intention to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services specified in the application. The application shall include a clear representation of the trade mark and a detailed description of the goods or services to which it relates. Where the applicant is not a natural person, proof of incorporation and the authority of the signatory shall be furnished. 

A proposed registered proprietor must, prior to acceptance of the application, satisfy the Registrar that the trade mark does not conflict with any existing registered trade mark or pending application, and that it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. Subject to verification, the Registrar may require evidence of prior use or a statement of use, and shall examine the application as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in refusal of registration.

A proposed registered proprietor, seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, shall furnish an address for service within the territory of India, which address shall be deemed to be the address to which all communications relating to the application and subsequent proceedings shall be sent. Should the proposed registered proprietor fail to maintain a valid address for service, the Registrar may, after reasonable notice, strike the application from the register. Furthermore, any registered proprietor intending to assign or transfer their rights in a trade mark, shall provide written notice to the Registrar, detailing the particulars of the assignee or transferee. Subject to the provisions herein, a transfer of ownership shall not invalidate any existing registrations, provided that the assignee or transferee demonstrates sufficient legal capacity to hold and utilize the trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence of title from the assignee or transferee to satisfy themselves as to the legitimacy of the transfer.

A proposed registered proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark shall submit an application to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed, demonstrating a bona fide intention to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified. The application shall include a clear representation of the trade mark and a detailed description of the goods or services. Where the application concerns a collective mark or a certification mark, evidence of the rules governing the use of the mark by members of the association or by those certified, respectively, shall be furnished. 

Any objection to the application, filed by a relevant party alleging a conflict with existing rights, shall be considered by the Registrar following the procedure outlined herein. The proposed registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a counter-statement addressing such objections. Failure to respond to a notice of opposition within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Registrar, having considered all evidence and submissions, may either accept or refuse the application.

Any application for registration of a trade mark, submitted by a proposed registered proprietor, shall be accompanied by a clear representation of the mark as it is to be registered, and a statement detailing the goods or services to which it relates, classified in accordance with the Nice Classification. The applicant, being the proposed registered proprietor, must demonstrate a genuine intention to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services. Should the application disclose a mark identical with or resembling an existing trade mark, the Registrar may, as provided herein, require evidence of distinctiveness and prior use to avoid confusion. A declaration verifying the truthfulness of all particulars furnished in the application, signed by the proposed registered proprietor or their duly authorized agent, is mandatory. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the application being deemed incomplete and subject to rejection. The Registrar reserves the right to request further information or clarification from the proposed registered proprietor during the examination process.

Any person claiming to be a proposed registered proprietor shall furnish to the Controller a declaration verifying the truth of the particulars entered in the application for registration, and any misrepresentation or omission of a material fact in such declaration shall render the application liable to be refused, and the applicant, and any person knowingly assisting in such misrepresentation, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that the Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as he deems fit, allow rectification of the declaration within a period of thirty days from the date of its submission. Furthermore, any false personation as a proposed registered proprietor, with intent to deceive, shall constitute an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding two lakh rupees. All fees associated with such declarations and rectifications shall be paid as prescribed.

Any assignment of the right to use a registered trade mark, or any agreement to grant a license to use such trade mark, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The registered proprietor may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, assign the right to use the trade mark to another person, or grant a license to use the trade mark. Where a proposed registered proprietor seeks to acquire such right, the transferor or licensor shall furnish a statement of all existing encumbrances, if any, relating to the trade mark. Any assignment or license not registered as provided herein shall be void against any subsequent assignee or licensee who registers their assignment or license. The Registrar may, upon application, record the assignment or license and issue a certificate of registration thereof, and such registration shall be conclusive evidence of the validity of the assignment or license. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the transaction unenforceable.

Where a dispute arises concerning the application for registration of a trade mark, and the Registrar has reason to believe that a party is falsely representing themselves as the proposed registered proprietor, notice shall be issued to all interested parties, including the applicant and any opposing party claiming prior rights. Any person alleging an interest may file a statement of grounds for objection, supported by evidence, within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such notice. The Registrar, having considered the evidence and submissions, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct that a hearing be conducted to determine the rightful proposed registered proprietor. Should the initial applicant be found to have misrepresented material facts, the application shall be deemed abandoned, and any associated fees shall not be refunded. An appeal from the Registrar’s decision on such matters may be made to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order.

Any person claiming to be a proposed registered proprietor shall, prior to the grant of registration, furnish a declaration verifying the absence of any existing legal impediment to the use of the trade mark as sought to be registered. Failure to submit such a declaration, or the submission of a materially false declaration, shall be deemed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the proposed registered proprietor to provide evidence substantiating the veracity of the declaration. Any trade mark obtained through fraudulent misrepresentation or suppression of material facts relating to the declaration shall be liable to revocation, and the Registrar shall have the power to order the destruction of all goods bearing such trade mark. A person aggrieved by the revocation may appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the order.

A proposed registered proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark, notwithstanding diligent searches conducted as provided herein, may encounter opposition based on pre-existing rights concerning a registered layout design of an article, where such layout design incorporates a visual representation substantially identical to the mark applied for. The Registrar, upon receiving such opposition, shall issue notice to the proposed registered proprietor, requiring them to demonstrate either non-infringement of the layout design right or a valid reason why the layout design right should not preclude registration. Failure to adequately respond within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of the opposition may be challenged by the proposed registered proprietor before the Appellate Board, demonstrating sufficient cause and providing relevant evidence of distinctiveness and lawful use.

A proposed registered proprietor, for the purposes of this Act, shall be a person who applies for the registration of a trade mark under this Act, and who satisfies the conditions as to user and description of goods or services as prescribed. Such a proposed registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions herein, claim priority based on an earlier application made in a convention country, provided that the claim is made within the prescribed period. Where a patent means patent, and a trade mark application includes a reference to a patented technology integral to the goods or services, the Registrar may require disclosure of the relevant patent details as part of the examination process. The Registrar shall, upon satisfaction of all requirements, proceed with the advertisement of the application.

Any person dissatisfied with an order issued by an Adjudicating Officer pursuant to an investigation conducted under this Act may, subject to the provisions herein, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Authority. The Appellate Authority shall be comprised of individuals possessing not less than five years of experience in the practice of law relating to intellectual property, or holding a postgraduate degree in law with a specialization in intellectual property rights. An application for an 112A order appellate review shall be filed within forty-five days of the date of the impugned order, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy thereof. The Appellate Authority may, if deemed necessary, require further evidence or submissions from the parties concerned, and shall issue its reasoned order within ninety days of the filing of the appeal. Provided that, the Appellate Authority’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a writ petition may be filed before a High Court.

Any person dissatisfied with an order issued under the provisions relating to rectification of the register, or an order concerning the assignment or transmission of a trademark, may apply to the Appellate Authority established under this Act for a review of said order. Such application shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed statement of the grounds on which the applicant seeks a reversal or modification of the initial determination. The Appellate Authority shall, following receipt of the application and any accompanying evidence, conduct a hearing where all parties concerned may present their arguments. An order of the Appellate Authority, constituting a 112A order appellate, shall be final and binding, save for recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of legal error. Provided that the Appellate Authority may, subject to justifiable cause, extend the time for filing an application or for submission of evidence. Failure to comply with the timelines as stipulated herein may result in the rejection of the application. The Appellate Authority shall endeavor to dispose of all appeals within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the date of receipt.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Inspector of Trade Marks under the provisions relating to rectification of the register, as provided herein, may apply to the Appellate Board for a statement of case, and such application shall be made within sixty days from the date of the order appealed against. The Appellate Board shall, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, examine the application and the records of the case and may, after giving the applicant and the opposing party an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Inspector. Where an application for a statement of case is made, the Appellate Board shall transmit a copy of the statement to the applicant and the opposing party. An order of the Appellate Board relating to a statement of case under this Act shall be final, except where a further appeal lies to the High Court. Any party desiring to challenge an 112A order appellate shall comply with the procedural requirements as prescribed by the rules. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the application is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs.

Any person dissatisfied with an order issued under the provisions relating to rectification of the register, or any decision concerning the removal of a trade mark, may apply to the Appellate Authority for a review of said order, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. The application for review, constituting an 112a order appellate, shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed statement of grounds for appeal, demonstrating substantial question of law or fact. The Appellate Authority may, if deemed necessary, require further evidence or clarification from the applicant or the opposing party. Provided that, no appeal shall be entertained unless filed within sixty days of the impugned order’s communication. The Appellate Authority shall, after considering all submissions and evidence, pass a reasoned order, which shall be final and binding, except as provided for recourse to the High Court under the writ jurisdiction. Compliance with these procedural requirements is mandatory for the valid consideration of any appeal.

Any person dissatisfied with an order issued by a designated officer pursuant to an investigation under this Act concerning the rectification of the register of trade marks, may, subject to the provisions herein, apply to the Appellate Board for a review of said order. The application shall be filed within sixty days of the date of communication of the order, and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board, constituted as provided for in the rules, shall consider the application and may, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the designated officer. Where the Appellate Board reverses the order, it shall record its reasons in writing. An order of the Appellate Board under this provision shall be final, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice, and any aggrieved party may pursue such remedy as is available under the law. A request for an 112a order appellate review does not operate as a stay of the original order unless specifically directed by the Appellate Board.

Any person aggrieved by the registration of a trade mark may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for rectification of the register, and such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such application, cause a notice to be served upon the proprietor of the trade mark, requiring him to state within a prescribed period whether he consents to the rectification sought. Should the proprietor consent, the Registry shall make the necessary alterations to the register and notify the applicant accordingly. If no consent is received, or if the proprietor disputes the grounds for rectification, the matter shall be referred to the High Court for determination. The High Court, acting as a rectification register court, shall consider the evidence presented and may, subject to the provisions of this Act, either confirm the registration, order its rectification, or dismiss the application. Evidence relating to prior use or inherent distinctiveness may be presented during such proceedings.

Any person aggrieved by any entry in the register of trade marks may apply to the court for rectification of that entry, subject to the provisions of this Act. The application for rectification shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall state the grounds on which the rectification is sought. The court, upon receiving such application, shall cause notice to be served on the proprietor of the trade mark and any other person likely to be affected by the rectification. Any opposing party may file a counter-statement, detailing the grounds on which they dispute the rectification. Evidence may be submitted by both parties, and the court shall consider such evidence in determining whether the entry in the register is inaccurate or misleading. Where the court determines that rectification is warranted, it shall order the appropriate amendment to the register, and such order shall be binding on all parties. A decision of the rectification register court is appealable to the High Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, recorded in the register of trade marks, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding rectification. A request for rectification of the register, concerning an assignment or transfer of rights, may be made to the rectification register court by any person aggrieved by such assignment or transfer, or by the Registrar, if satisfied that a valid objection exists. The court, upon receiving such a request, shall cause notice to be served upon the assignee, the assignor, and the Registrar, requiring them to appear and show cause. Provided that, where the assignment is made under a contract containing an arbitration clause, recourse to the rectification register court shall be subject to the prior exhaustion of arbitral remedies as provided in the contract. The court may, subject to due process and evidence presented, order the rectification of the register to reflect the valid transfer of ownership or interest in the trade mark. Any order of the court shall be final and binding on all parties.

Any person who proceeds with the registration of a trade mark knowing it to be falsely applied for, or with the intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a Registrar, having reasonable grounds to believe that an application for registration contains a false representation of the applicant’s right to use the trade mark, directs an inquiry, the applicant shall furnish all relevant documents within thirty days of such direction, failing which the application shall be deemed abandoned. Any evidence submitted as part of a proceed case registration, if found to be fabricated or materially misleading, shall constitute an offence punishable with a fine extending to fifty thousand rupees. The Trade Marks Officer may, subject to the provisions of this Act, initiate *suo motu* investigations into suspected fraudulent applications. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

A breeder variety registered under the Seeds Act, 2023, may proceed case registration as a plant variety, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning the registration of trade marks for agricultural products. An applicant seeking to register a trade mark comprising or relating to a breeder variety shall submit evidence of valid registration of the said variety with the Plant Variety and Farmers’ Rights Authority, as proof of distinctiveness and lawful origin. The Registrar may, at any stage of the registration process, require further evidence regarding the breeder’s rights or the scope of protection afforded to the variety. Provided that, a trade mark registration shall not confer any rights inconsistent with the provisions of the Seeds Act, 2023, or prejudice the breeder’s exclusive rights over the variety. Any dispute concerning the validity of the breeder variety registration shall be adjudicated by the appropriate authority under the Seeds Act, 2023, and not under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a register of such breeder variety registrations linked to corresponding trade mark applications.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or an application for registration of a trade mark, shall be subject to a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. The instrument shall clearly define the scope of the assignment, including the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is assigned, and any limitations or conditions attached to the transfer of ownership. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity or enforceability of such an assignment, any aggrieved party may seek redressal before the District Court having jurisdiction over the matter. The court may, at its discretion, require production of the original instrument of assignment and any supporting documentation to determine the rightful owner of the trade mark. A proceed case registration relating to an assignment shall be filed with the Registry within six months of the execution date of the instrument, failing which the assignment shall be deemed invalid unless condoned by the Registry.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication relating to goods geographical may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction, and an account of profits. The court, upon establishing such infringement and considering the nature of the infringement, shall award damages not less than such amount as it deems reasonable, having regard to the loss suffered by the registered proprietor. Where the infringement involves counterfeit goods geographical, the court may also order the confiscation and destruction of the infringing goods, and any materials used in the production or packaging of such goods. 

Provided that, no injunction shall be granted unless the court is satisfied that the continued use of the geographical indication by the defendant would cause irreparable harm to the registered proprietor. A registered proprietor may, as provided herein, also seek an order restraining the importer of goods bearing the false or deceptively similar geographical indication. The court may, in exceptional circumstances, award exemplary damages.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, shall examine it for conformity with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the application relates to goods geographical, the examination shall specifically ascertain whether the claimed geographical indication accurately represents the origin of the goods, and whether a demonstrable link exists between the qualities or reputation of the goods and their geographical origin. Any evidence submitted regarding traditional methods of production, or unique environmental factors contributing to the characteristics of the goods, shall be considered during this examination. 

Provided that, if the application seeks to register a geographical indication already registered for identical or similar goods, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate material differences justifying a separate registration. The Registrar may, at any stage, require further information or clarification from the applicant, and failure to provide such information within a specified timeframe may lead to rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications.

Any person who falsely represents goods as possessing a geographical indication, or who uses a false geographical indication in relation to goods, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where the offence involves goods intended for sale, such goods shall be liable to seizure and destruction, subject to the order of a designated court. The Registrar may, acting *suo motu* or upon a complaint received, initiate an investigation into any alleged misrepresentation concerning goods geographical indications. Any individual found to be aiding or abetting such an offence shall be deemed to be equally liable and subject to the same penalties as provided herein. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including potential revocation of any existing registrations held by the offender.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer, or license all or any of the rights vested in such geographical indication in relation to the goods geographical indication to any other person or entity, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment or transfer of rights shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the assignor and the assignee, and such instrument shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause being shown, refuse to register an assignment or transfer if it is demonstrated that the assignee lacks sufficient capacity or expertise to maintain the quality and reputation of the goods. Licensing agreements shall specify the scope of permitted use, the duration of the license, and the royalty payable, and any dispute arising from such agreements may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. A licensee shall not sub-license the rights without the prior written consent of the geographical indication proprietor.

Any person dealing in goods geographical in nature, who falsely represents such goods as originating from a different geographical area than their true origin, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Such misrepresentation shall extend to packaging, labeling, advertising, or any other form of commercial communication. Where a variety registered under this Act is falsely indicated as the source of goods, the penalty shall be a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two lakh rupees. Furthermore, any equipment used in the commission of the offence, including but not limited to packaging machinery and advertising materials, shall be liable to seizure. Repeated offences, as determined by the Registrar, may result in imprisonment not exceeding three years, in addition to the aforementioned fines. The burden of proof regarding the geographical origin of the goods shall lie with the accused, subject to verification by the designated officer.

A geographical indication comprised of a name, sign, or symbol indicating that a good originates from a specific geographical area, possessing qualities, reputation, or characteristics essentially attributable to its geographical origin, shall be registrable under this Act. Such a geographical indication shall be understood as a distinctive identifier, linking the good to its place of origin and conveying an assurance of quality or characteristics to consumers. Where a geographical indication also functions as a trademark, the rights arising from both shall be considered separately, subject to the provisions relating to conflict resolution as provided herein. The Registrar may, however, require evidence establishing a substantial connection between the specified goods and the geographical area claimed, and the reputation enjoyed by the goods in that area.

A geographical indication comprised of a name, sign, or symbol designating a specific location shall be eligible for registration under this Act, provided that such location is within the territory of India. An applicant seeking registration shall demonstrate a clear link between the goods and the geographical area asserting origin, establishing that qualities or reputation of the goods are substantially attributable to that geographical origin. The application shall include a detailed description of the goods, their characteristics, the production method, and the geographical area to which the geographical indication relates. Where a geographical indication also constitutes a trademark, the trademark owner shall provide evidence of prior use, subject to the provisions relating to conflict with existing rights. Registration shall confer upon the applicant the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. Any association of producers may, with the consent of the producers, apply for registration.

Any person who, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication comprised in respect of goods, discovers that any other person is using a deceptively similar geographical indication for identical or similar goods, may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the offending goods are sold or manufactured. The registered proprietor shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to an injunction restraining the unauthorized use of the geographical indication and to damages for loss suffered as a consequence of such use. Where the defendant proves that the use of the deceptively similar geographical indication is likely to cause confusion, or is descriptive of the goods, the Court may, instead of an injunction, order the rectification of the register or award an account of profits. Any order made under this Act shall be executable as if it were a decree of a civil court, and appeals shall lie as provided in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. A false representation of a geographical indication shall be actionable under the laws of tort.

A geographical indication comprised of a name or a sign identifying goods originating from a specific geographical area, which possesses qualities or a reputation attributable to that origin, shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. The applicant shall demonstrate a clear link between the goods’ characteristics, including quality, reputation, or other distinctive features, and the geographical area claimed as the source of origin. Where a geographical indication is also a trademark, the trademark owner may, subject to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein, seek registration of the geographical indication separately. The Register shall maintain a register of all registered geographical indications, detailing the goods to which the indication applies, the geographical area of origin, and any specific standards or requirements governing production. Any association of producers or artisans concerned with the goods may, with the prior consent of the producers, apply for registration of the geographical indication. The Register may, at any time, require further evidence to substantiate the claims made in the application, and shall examine the application in accordance with the prescribed procedure.

A geographical indication comprised within the meaning of this Act shall be eligible for registration, provided that the goods to which it relates are the product of a defined geographical area and possess qualities, reputation, or other characteristics attributable to that geographical origin, and which are distinguishable from goods not originating from that area. An applicant seeking registration shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified geographical area and the qualities or reputation of the goods. The geographical indication must be capable of identifying the goods as originating in that area, and its use shall not be likely to mislead the public as to the true origin of the goods. Where a geographical indication also constitutes a trademark, the trademark shall not be refused registration if it is registered for the same goods, subject to conditions ensuring due protection of the geographical indication. Registration shall confer exclusive rights to use the geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered.

Any person who falsely applies a geographical indication comprised of a registered geographical indication to goods not originating from the specified geographical area, or who, with intent to deceive, uses a false indication of origin, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where the offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable for the same. The Registrar, acting upon a complaint, may initiate an inquiry and, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, order the seizure of goods bearing the false geographical indication and their disposal in a manner deemed fit. Any appeal against such order shall lie before the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Any person being the applicant shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Geographical Indications Registry for the registration of a geographical indication comprised in respect of goods originating from a defined territory within India. The application shall be accompanied by a statement of proposed use of the geographical indication, detailing the manner in which the indication will be used in relation to the goods. Assignment of any right in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an instrument in writing, and the Registry shall maintain a register of such assignments. A licensee of a registered geographical indication may, subject to the terms of the license, exercise the rights conferred by the registration, but shall not assign such rights without the prior written consent of the registered proprietor. The registered proprietor may, as provided herein, grant licenses to other persons to use the geographical indication, and such licenses may be subject to conditions regarding quality control and monitoring. Failure to comply with the conditions of a license shall constitute grounds for revocation.

Any person claiming that a geographical indication comprised in a registered geographical indication has been infringed may, notwithstanding any other remedy available under law, apply to the Registrar for an interim injunction restraining the defendant from the infringing acts. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the registration certificate and a statement detailing the nature of the infringement, including particulars of the goods sold or manufactured by the defendant bearing the deceptively similar geographical indication. Provided that, the Registrar may, before granting such interim injunction, require the applicant to furnish security, as deemed fit, to compensate the defendant in case the injunction is subsequently found to have been wrongly granted. Any order passed by the Registrar under this provision shall be subject to appeal to the High Court, and such appeal shall be filed within a period of thirty days from the date of the order. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final and binding.

A geographical indication comprised within a class shall not be registered unless the applicant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Geographical Indications Registry a material connection between the goods and the geographical area alleged to be the origin of those goods. Any person seeking registration of a geographical indication shall submit with their application a detailed specification outlining the characteristics of the goods, the geographical area of origin, and the manner in which the geographical indication serves to designate the goods as originating from that area. The Patent Controller, acting as the Registrar under this Act, may require further evidence or clarification regarding the specification, and the applicant shall respond within a period of thirty days from the date of such request. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided herein. Registration shall be conditional upon ongoing quality control measures.

A dispute concerning a geographical indication comprised within the registered particulars of ‘Mysore Silk’ arose before the Registrar, wherein the applicant, a collective of silk producers, alleged improper use by a textile merchant based outside the traditionally recognized Mysore region. The Registrar, having considered evidence of origin and quality control, initially ruled in favour of the applicant, issuing a cease and desist order. This order was appealed by the merchant, who argued that their silk, though not woven within Mysore, utilized silk yarn sourced directly from registered Mysore silk farms and thus did not infringe. 

A legal practitioner person representing the applicant submitted that the essence of the geographical indication lay not merely in the raw material’s origin, but in the complete production process intrinsically linked to the Mysore territory. The Appellate Board, reviewing the case, upheld the Registrar’s decision, clarifying that a geographical indication’s protection extends to preventing misrepresentation of origin, even with genuine raw materials, subject to demonstrable proof of territorial connection.

A geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall identify goods originating from a specific geographical area, where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to that geographical origin. The term ‘geographical indication’ includes indications in the form of names, signs, or symbols, and may denote agricultural, natural, or manufactured goods. However, a geographical indication shall not be registered if it is likely to mislead the public or is contrary to public order or morality. Any association of producers, artisans, or persons engaged in the production of such goods may apply for the registration of a geographical indication, subject to the conditions as provided herein, and shall demonstrate a clear link between the goods and their geographical origin. The Registrar may, after examination, accept or reject the application.

Any person claiming a geographical indication prescribed for goods originating from a specific territory in India may apply for registration under this Act to the Geographical Indications Registry. The application shall be in the prescribed form and shall identify the goods, the territory, and the applicant, including details of the association, if any, representing the producers. A clear and concise description of the geographical indication, demonstrating how it designates the goods’ origin and links to qualities or reputation, shall accompany the application. Evidence establishing a nexus between the specified characteristics of the goods and their geographical origin must be submitted, subject to verification by the Registry. The application may also include a standard of quality for the goods, and a method for inspection to ensure continued adherence to that standard, as provided herein. Registration shall be granted only if the geographical indication is not contrary to public order or morality.

Any person who has suffered damage as a result of a false or misleading indication, or the use of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act in a manner which deceives or causes confusion, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the deceptive practice occurred. The suit shall be filed within a period of two years from the date on which the plaintiff knew, or ought to have known, of the damage. The court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from using the false or misleading indication, and may also award damages to the plaintiff, assessed in accordance with the actual loss suffered or, where such loss cannot be accurately determined, a reasonable sum. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, in addition to the remedies available under this Act, pursue remedies under the general law of passing off. Provided that, no suit shall be instituted without first providing written notice to the alleged infringer, outlining the grounds for the claim and requesting cessation of the infringing activity.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the application conforms to the requirements as provided herein and whether the claimed geographical indication is capable of distinguishing the goods as originating from a specific geographical area. Where the geographical indication is a prescribed one, the applicant shall submit a detailed registry of producers associated with that geographical indication, including their locations and production volumes, to facilitate verification of origin. Any person claiming rights in a geographical indication prescribed under this Act may file a notice of opposition within a period of two months from the date of notification of the application. The Registrar, subject to the provisions contained herein, may require the applicant to furnish additional evidence or clarification regarding the geographical area, quality, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods. Failure to comply with such a requirement may render the application liable to be rejected. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications.

Any goods bearing a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be deemed to originate from the territory associated with that indication, provided that such goods meet the standards established by the Board and are demonstrably linked to that geographical origin. A producer seeking registration of a geographical indication shall submit evidence of consistent quality and characteristics attributable to the specific geographical area. The specification of the geographical indication shall clearly define the territory, the goods, and the qualities or reputation linked to that territory. Any alteration of a registered geographical indication, affecting its essential characteristics, requires prior approval from the Board. Failure to adhere to the prescribed standards for production or processing within the designated geographical area may result in the revocation of registration, subject to a hearing as provided herein. The authorized user shall maintain records demonstrating compliance with these requirements.

Any person causing false application or representation of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, with intent to deceive the public or to cause injury to the business of a registered proprietor of such geographical indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where a contravention involves goods intended for export, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years, and the fine may extend to three lakh rupees. The court, subject to the provisions contained herein, may also order the seizure of all goods bearing such false geographical indication and their destruction. Any evidence obtained regarding the manufacture or trade of goods with a falsely applied geographical indication may be admissible in any proceeding under this Act, notwithstanding any other law. A registered proprietor aggrieved by any such act may initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages.

Any person being an applicant for the registration of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, desiring to assign or license the rights therein, shall furnish a notice in writing to the Geographical Indications Registry, specifying the terms and conditions of such assignment or license, including the duration, territorial scope, and the nature of the rights assigned or licensed. The Registry shall maintain a public register of all such assignments and licenses, accessible for inspection by interested parties subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any assignment or license not duly registered shall be void. Where a license is granted, the licensor shall retain the right to exercise control over the quality and characteristics of the goods bearing the geographical indication, ensuring adherence to the standards established for the prescribed geographical indication. Failure to exercise such control may constitute grounds for revocation of the license, as provided herein. The assignment or license shall not prejudice the rights of producers associated with the geographical indication.

Any person claiming that a geographical indication prescribed under this Act has been falsely applied to goods, or that the conditions of registration are no longer met, may lodge a complaint with the Registrar. Such complaint shall be in writing and shall clearly specify the grounds upon which the allegation of misrepresentation or non-compliance is based, and shall be supported by documentary evidence where available. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such complaint, serve notice to the registered proprietor of the geographical indication, affording them an opportunity to submit a defence within a period of sixty days. Should the Registrar, after considering the complaint and the defence, be satisfied that the allegation is well-founded, they may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register, or suspension of the registration, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any decision of the Registrar may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order.

Any indication functioning as a geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be subject to rigorous proof of origin, demonstrating a clear and direct correlation between the specified goods and the geographical area claimed. An indication plaintiff seeking registration must furnish evidence establishing that the qualities, reputation, or other characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to the geographical origin. Compliance with standards, whether traditional, technical, or quality control, relating to the production and processing of the goods within the defined geographical area is mandatory. Failure to demonstrate adherence to such standards shall render the application liable to rejection. The Registrar may, however, require further clarification or evidence as deemed necessary to ascertain the veracity of the claim. Provided that, the indication does not mislead the public as to the true origin of the goods, and that all relevant production stages occur within the designated geographical boundaries.

Any person who falsely applies a geographical indication prescribed under this Act to goods not originating in the territory associated with such indication, or who, with intent to deceive, uses a false geographical indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. The registrar, upon receiving credible information of such contravention, may initiate an investigation and, if satisfied, direct the cessation of the unlawful activity. Any aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board against any decision of the registrar concerning the imposition of penalties, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the decision. Failure to comply with an order of the appellate board shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved.

Any person being the applicant for registration of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, may, subject to the provisions herein, assign, transfer or license the rights to the said geographical indication, or any part thereof, to any other person or entity, whether incorporated or not. Any such assignment, transfer or license shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registry shall maintain a public register of all registered assignments, transfers and licenses, accessible for inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee. Where a geographical indication is subject to international registration protection under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, any assignment or license affecting the rights in that geographical indication shall also be notified to the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization, in accordance with the relevant regulations. Failure to register an assignment, transfer or license shall not invalidate the transaction, but may affect its enforceability against third parties. The registered proprietor shall remain responsible for ensuring the quality and standards of the goods bearing the geographical indication, even after assignment or licensing.

A geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be understood as an indication that identifies a good originating from a specific geographical area, where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, consequently, differentiates it from goods originating elsewhere. Any representation or allegation that a good possesses a geographical indication when it does not, or that a good not qualifying as a geographical indication is so indicated, constitutes falsifying trade. Such falsification shall be actionable under the relevant provisions of the Indian Penal Code, in addition to any remedies available under this Act. The Registrar may, subject to conditions, direct the removal of such false indications and impose penalties as deemed appropriate. A registered proprietor may initiate civil or criminal proceedings against infringers.

A statement of geographical indication, forming an integral part of an application for registration under this Act, shall clearly and accurately define the geographical area to which the goods relate, and shall delineate the boundaries of said area with sufficient precision to avoid ambiguity. The statement shall further detail how the specified geographical origin imparts unique qualities, reputation, or other characteristics to the goods, establishing a demonstrable link between the product and its place of origin. Provided that, where the geographical indication incorporates traditional knowledge or folklore associated with the goods, a comprehensive description of such knowledge, including its historical context and methods of transmission, shall also be included within the statement. Any applicant seeking registration of a statement geographical indication shall submit supporting evidence, including maps, historical records, and expert opinions, to substantiate the claims made therein, subject to verification by the Registrar.

Any person claiming to be adversely affected by an act constituting a violation of the rights conferred by the registration of a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for injunction, damages, or any other remedy as may be available under the laws in force. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the court for an order restraining any person from manufacturing or trading in goods bearing a false or deceptive indication of origin, or otherwise infringing the rights conferred by this Act. A clear and unambiguous statement geographical indication, demonstrating a link to the origin and qualities of the goods, shall be considered prima facie evidence of such rights. Where a collective or association of producers is authorized to represent the geographical indication, it may, on behalf of its members, pursue remedies for infringement. Any damages awarded shall account for lost profits and the costs of corrective action, including the removal of infringing labels. Provided that, no such action shall be taken without reasonable notice to the alleged infringer.

A statement of geographical indication, submitted to the Registrar, shall clearly delineate the goods for which protection is sought and shall be presented in a manner consistent with the provisions of this Act. The statement shall, without limitation, identify the territory, region, or locality in India to which the goods are linked, demonstrating a clear connection between the product’s characteristics and its geographical origin. Any applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication shall furnish a detailed description of the methods used to ascertain the quality of the goods, and shall specify how such quality is attributable to the identified geographical area. Provided that, where a statement geographical indication incorporates traditional knowledge, the applicant shall also submit evidence of its customary use and the community involved in its preservation. The Registrar may, subject to verification, accept a statement that relies on established reputation even if the goods do not originate entirely within the specified territory, provided a substantial portion of the production process occurs therein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application.

A statement geographical indication, when presented for registration under this Act, shall clearly and accurately define the goods to which it applies and the geographical territory with which those goods are associated. The applicant shall submit evidence demonstrating a substantive connection between the specified goods and the claimed geographical origin, including historical documentation or traditional practices. Any statement regarding the qualities, reputation, or characteristics of the goods attributed to their geographical origin must be supported by verifiable data and publicly available information. Provided that, where the geographical indication incorporates traditional knowledge, the applicant shall also furnish details of the community involved and their established practices relating to the goods. Failure to adequately substantiate the claimed link between the goods, the geographical area, and the asserted characteristics may result in the rejection of the application, subject to review as provided herein. The Registrar may require additional information or clarification to ensure compliance with these requirements.

Any person falsely representing a registered geographical indication, or a statement geographical indication even if unregistered but possessing a reputation, as applying to goods not originating from the designated geographical area, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Such misrepresentation shall include, but not be limited to, the direct application of the geographical indication to counterfeit goods, or the use of packaging or advertising materials that create a false association with the genuine goods. The Registrar may, upon receiving credible evidence of such an offence, initiate an investigation and, subject to due process, direct the relevant authorities to seize the offending goods. Any person convicted of an offence as provided herein shall be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties.

Any person being an applicant for registration of a geographical indication, desiring to license the right to use the registered geographical indication to another party, shall execute a written assignment agreement conforming to the provisions of this Act. Such agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of the license, including the territory, duration, and specific goods to which the licensed statement geographical indication applies. The licensor may, subject to the terms of the agreement, retain the right to sub-license or further assign the rights. Any assignment or license not in writing shall be void. 

Where the assignment involves a transfer of ownership of the geographical indication, the assignee shall, within a period of ninety days from the date of assignment, notify the Geographical Indications Registry of the change in ownership and provide a copy of the assignment agreement. Failure to do so may result in the revocation of the registration, provided that the original registrant is given an opportunity to be heard. The registered proprietor retains the right to monitor the quality of goods bearing the statement geographical indication, even after assignment.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a geographical indication, and alleging infringement of their rights as provided herein, may lodge a complaint with the Geographical Indications Registry. Such complaint shall be accompanied by a detailed statement geographical indication, specifying the goods to which the indication applies, the territory of origin, and the qualities or reputation linked to that origin. The Registry shall, subject to verification of the complaint and evidence presented, issue notice to the alleged infringer. An alleged infringer may file a counter-statement contesting the validity of the geographical indication or denying the act of infringement. Should the Registry find merit in the complaint, it may order provisional measures, including injunctions against the continued use of the infringing indication. Any party aggrieved by the order of the Registry may appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction, within a period of ninety days from the date of the order, seeking a review of the decision and appropriate relief.

Any person falsely representing a geographical indication as a statement geographical indication, or using any imitation thereof in relation to goods in respect of which a geographical indication is registered, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years and with fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where a person is convicted of an offence under this Act, the court may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, order the forfeiture of all instruments and things used in the commission of the offence. A convicted order forfeited shall vest in the Central Government. Any appeal against such forfeiture shall lie within thirty days of the order to the High Court. The Registrar may, with the approval of the Central Government, accept a petition for restoration of a forfeited geographical indication, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated.

A statement geographical indication, when assigned or licensed to another party, shall be accompanied by a detailed memorandum outlining the scope of rights transferred, including the specific goods covered and the geographical territory within which the rights are valid. Any assignment or license not conforming to these provisions shall be deemed void *ab initio*. The Registrar shall maintain a court rectification register detailing all registered assignments and licenses of statement geographical indications, accessible to public inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment or license, the aggrieved party may apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register, providing evidence of the irregularity. The Registrar, after due inquiry and affording opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, may order amendment of the register accordingly, and such order shall be final and binding. A licensee shall not sub-license the statement geographical indication without the express written consent of the assignor, subject to the terms of the original license agreement.

A statement of geographical indication, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall clearly and accurately define the geographical area with which the goods proposed to be registered are associated. Such a statement shall delineate the boundaries of said geographical area with sufficient precision to enable unambiguous identification. An application for registration must include a detailed description of the qualities or characteristics of the goods that are attributable to the geographical origin, and which distinguish them from goods originating elsewhere. Provided that, where a statement geographical indication incorporates traditional knowledge, evidence supporting such knowledge and its link to the goods shall be submitted as part of the application registration. The statement shall further specify how the geographical indication serves to designate the goods as originating from that territory.

Any association of producers desiring to register a geographical indication shall jointly apply to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, and such application shall identify the goods, the proposed geographical indication, the area of origin, and a description of the qualities or characteristics of the goods linked to their geographical origin. The Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require further information or evidence to substantiate the claim. Where a geographical indication is sought to be registered for agricultural goods, proof of adherence to established standards for quality control and environmental sustainability shall be submitted. It shall be the duty of the applicant to demonstrate that the geographical indication genuinely serves to designate the goods as originating from a specific territory and possesses qualities, reputation, or characteristics attributable to that place. The Registrar shall examine the application and, if satisfied, proceed with the advertisement of the application as provided herein, and shall apply geographical indication principles consistently.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication shall have the right to institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, and for an injunction restraining the infringement. Such proceedings shall be subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, as if the same were a commercial dispute. Where a registered geographical indication is used by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a licensee, without authorization, it shall constitute an act of unfair competition. The court, while granting relief, may also order the destruction or foreiture of goods bearing the unauthorized geographical indication, and may direct an accounting of profits made by the infringing party. It shall apply geographical indications to goods even if those goods have undergone processing, transformation, or modification, provided that the essential qualities, reputation, or characteristics of the goods are attributable to their geographical origin. The registered proprietor may, as provided herein, seek an ex parte interim injunction in cases of imminent harm.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a false or deceptively similar geographical indication shall be subject to an ex parte order issued by the Registrar, restraining such person from such dealing, and such order shall be enforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction. Provided that, prior to the issuance of any such order, the Registrar shall provide written notice to the alleged infringer, affording them an opportunity to present cause. Where a registered geographical indication is demonstrated to have been applied to goods not originating from the designated geographical area, a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees may be levied for each such instance. Furthermore, goods bearing such falsely applied geographical indications shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all orders issued and penalties imposed under this Act, and shall apply geographical indications consistently to ensure fair trade practices. Any appeal against an order of the Registrar shall lie before the High Court.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign, transfer, or license the rights vested in such geographical indication, or any part thereof, to any other person or entity. Any assignment or transfer of rights shall be in writing and registered with the Geographical Indications Registry, failing which such assignment or transfer shall be deemed invalid as provided herein. A license granted under this Act shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial extent of the permitted use of the geographical indication. The collective owners of a geographical indication shall, prior to any assignment or licensing, obtain the consent of a majority of the producers associated with that geographical indication. Where a geographical indication is assigned or licensed, the assignee or licensee shall be bound by the conditions and limitations originally attached to the registration, and shall also be subject to the same obligations regarding quality control and monitoring as the original proprietor. The continued application of quality standards shall apply geographical indications to maintain consumer trust and prevent dilution of reputation.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal of the Registrar to register a geographical indication, or by any direction of the Board requiring the rectification or cancellation of a registration, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of the order of the Registrar or the Board, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the said order and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board shall, before passing any order, give the applicant or the registered proprietor, as the case may be, an opportunity of being heard. Where a dispute arises concerning the geographical origin of goods claiming a geographical indication, the burden of proof shall lie upon the applicant to demonstrate that the goods genuinely originate from the specified territory and that the qualities or reputation associated with the goods are substantially attributable to that geographical origin. It shall apply geographical indications to products where such indications distinguish those goods as originating in a particular region and possessing qualities linked to that place. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the enforcement of such decision.

Any dispute concerning the registration or validity of a geographical indication, or alleging an infringement thereof, shall be subject to a jurisdiction try suit filed in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises. Provided that, where the defendant has a place of business in multiple districts, the plaintiff may elect to file the suit in any one of those districts. The Court, while adjudicating such a suit, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from using the geographical indication in question, and may also award damages to the plaintiff for any loss suffered as a consequence of the infringement. Furthermore, the Court may order the destruction or prohibition of sale of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Court shall have all powers necessary to ensure the effective enforcement of the rights conferred herein, including the power to grant ex parte interim injunctions. Any appeal from the decree of the District Court shall lie to the High Court.

Any dispute concerning the registration or validity of a geographical indication, or alleging an infringement thereof, shall be subject to a jurisdiction try suit filed in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises. Provided that, where the defendant has a place of business in more than one district, the suit may be filed in any one of those districts. The Court, while adjudicating such a suit, may appoint a commissioner to examine and report on any relevant matter, including the authenticity of the geographical indication and the extent of the alleged infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Court shall have the power to grant injunctions, damages, and other reliefs as it deems fit. Any appeal from the decree of the District Court shall lie to the High Court. The Court may also order the destruction or prohibition of sale of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication.

Any dispute concerning the registration or validity of a geographical indication, or alleging an infringement thereof, shall be subject to a jurisdiction try suit filed in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arises. Provided that, where the defendant is located outside the territory of India, the suit may be filed in the District Court of Delhi. The Court, upon finding a substantiated claim of infringement, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from unlawful use, and may order the destruction or forfeiture of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication. Non-compliance with any injunction issued under this Act shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or both. The Registrar may, subject to rules, impose a penalty up to one lakh rupees for contravention of any provision relating to false representation.

Any dispute concerning the registration or validity of a geographical indication, or any right arising therefrom, shall be subject to a jurisdiction try suit filed in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the defendant resides or carries on business, notwithstanding any other provision contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Provided that, where the defendant has multiple places of business, the plaintiff may elect to file the suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over any one of those places. An appeal from any decree or order of the District Court in such a suit shall lie to the High Court. Furthermore, any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the rectification of the Register of Geographical Indications may, within ninety days of the order, prefer an appeal to the High Court, subject to such conditions as the High Court may deem fit. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final.

The national gene fund is hereby established as a corpus to promote and facilitate the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to support the objectives of this Act. Contributions to the fund shall include proceeds from benefit sharing arising from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties and their essentially derived varieties, as well as any grants, donations, or other payments made for the purpose of plant genetic resource conservation. The fund may also receive amounts from the sale of propagating material of varieties protected under this Act, subject to rules prescribed by the Central Government. Utilization of the national gene fund shall prioritize initiatives for in-situ conservation, ex-situ conservation, and the development of new plant varieties, with due consideration given to the rights of farmers and breeders as provided herein.

The National Gene Fund shall be established and maintained by the Central Government as a trust to promote and facilitate the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to ensure equitable sharing of benefits arising from their use. All contributions received as benefit sharing from breeders of registered plant varieties, or from those commercially exploiting essentially derived varieties as provided herein, shall be credited to this Fund. The Fund may also accept grants, donations, and other contributions from national and international sources, subject to such terms and conditions as the Central Government deems appropriate. Funds accumulated within the National Gene Fund shall be utilized for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, and for the support of research and development activities relating to plant genetic resources, with priority given to indigenous and locally adapted varieties. A detailed accounting of all receipts and disbursements from the Fund shall be maintained and annually audited by a chartered accountant appointed by the Central Government.

The national gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders alike. Contributions to the fund may be made by the Central Government, State Governments, international organizations, and private entities, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Any revenue generated from the commercial utilization of varieties developed through research utilizing material from the national gene fund shall be shared with the originating farmers or communities, in a manner determined by the Authority, ensuring equitable benefit sharing. 

Provided that, a portion of such revenue shall be reinvested into the national gene fund to ensure its long-term sustainability and expansion of its resources. Farmers whose traditional knowledge contributed to the development of a registered variety, as evidenced by records maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, shall have a right to receive compensation, the amount of which shall be determined based on the commercial value of the variety and the extent of their contribution. Any dispute regarding benefit sharing or compensation may be referred to the Appellate Board for resolution.

The National Gene Fund shall be established as a corpus to promote and facilitate the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to support the objectives of this Act. Contributions to the Fund may be made by any person, institution, or organization, domestic or international, through donations, grants, or other forms of financial assistance, subject to such terms and conditions as the Central Government may, by notification, specify. The Fund shall be administered by a Management Committee constituted by the Central Government, comprising experts in plant breeding, genetics, agronomy, and relevant fields. 

The Management Committee shall be responsible for formulating policies regarding the allocation of resources from the Fund, prioritizing projects that enhance the capacity of farmers in conserving on-farm genetic resources and promoting the development of new plant varieties. Any income generated from the investment of the Fund shall be reinvested in activities aligned with the objectives of this Act, and the Management Committee shall submit an annual report detailing the financial status and programmatic achievements of the Fund to the Central Government. Provided that, any benefit sharing received from the commercial exploitation of varieties developed using genetic material sourced from the Fund shall be deposited back into the National Gene Fund.

The National Gene Fund shall be established as a corpus to promote and facilitate the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to support the objectives of this Act. Contributions to the Fund shall include, but not be limited to, a percentage of the sales value of seeds of varieties registered under this Act, determined periodically by the Central Government and adjusted for inflation. Provided that, any cultivator or community who has contributed traditional knowledge relating to plant genetic resources, and whose contribution is demonstrably linked to the development of a registered variety, may, subject to verification by the Competent Authority, receive a proportionate share of the benefit accruing from such variety. The Fund may also accept grants, donations, and other contributions from national and international sources, subject to conditions ensuring alignment with the principles of this Act.
