All funds received shall be accounted for and utilized for the purposes outlined herein, and an annual report detailing the Fund’s activities and financial status shall be submitted to Parliament.

The National Gene Fund established as provided herein shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders. Any person who misappropriates funds from the National Gene Fund, or utilizes said funds for purposes not authorized under this Act, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Furthermore, any organization receiving grants from the National Gene Fund shall maintain meticulous records of expenditure, subject to audit by a designated authority. Failure to comply with audit requirements, or the submission of false or misleading information, shall attract a penalty equivalent to twice the amount of the grant received. The Authority may, in exceptional circumstances, direct forfeiture of assets acquired through misuse of the National Gene Fund. All recovered funds shall be redeposited into the National Gene Fund.

The National Gene Fund established under this Act shall be administered by a Management Committee constituted by the Central Government, and all sums accruing to the Fund, including contributions from benefit sharing arrangements and any investment income derived therefrom, shall be accounted for in such manner as may be prescribed. Any breeder, upon commercialization of a variety registered under this Act, shall remit a percentage of gross sales, determined in accordance with the prescribed scale, to the National Gene Fund, subject to verification of sales figures by an independent auditor appointed by the Plant Variety Committee. The Management Committee may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, utilize the National Gene Fund for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, including the grant of research fellowships and the support of community seed banks. Provided that, a portion of the Fund may also be allocated to incentivize the development of new plant varieties specifically adapted to climate change resilience, as determined by the Committee. All assignments of rights to benefit sharing shall be recorded with the Plant Variety Committee.

The National Gene Fund established under this Act shall be administered by a Management Committee constituted by the Central Government, and all receipts accruing thereto, including contributions from benefit sharing as detailed herein, shall be accounted for in accordance with established governmental accounting procedures. Any cultivator or community of cultivators alleging improper accounting or diversion of funds may submit a petition to the Management Committee, which shall conduct an inquiry within ninety days of receipt, and provide a reasoned decision. Should the Management Committee fail to respond within the stipulated timeframe, or if the petitioner is dissatisfied with the decision, an appeal may be made to the Appellate Authority, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Management Committee’s decision or the expiry of the ninety-day inquiry period. The Appellate Authority’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to writ jurisdiction by the appropriate High Court, and any funds found to be mismanaged shall be restored to the National Gene Fund with applicable penalties levied against the responsible parties.

The National Gene Fund shall be maintained and administered by the Plant Variety Protection Authority and shall be applied for the promotion of plant research and development and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, as provided herein. Any literary work, including detailed documentation of traditional knowledge relating to plant genetic resources, submitted as evidence of a farmer’s contribution to the development of a registered variety, shall be duly acknowledged and preserved as part of the records associated with that variety. Contributions to the Fund may also be received from sources beyond benefit sharing, including grants, donations, and proceeds from the commercialization of technologies developed using resources from the Fund. The Authority may, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government, invest the Fund in secure and income-generating schemes to ensure its long-term sustainability and effective utilization for the purposes outlined under this Act. All transactions relating to the Fund shall be subject to audit.

The National Gene Fund established under this Act shall be administered by a Management Committee constituted by the Central Government, and all contributions thereto, including benefit sharing arising from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties and their essentially derived varieties, shall accrue to the Fund. Any person seeking to utilize genetic material conserved within the National Gene Fund for the development of a new variety, shall apply to the Management Committee and, upon approval and subject to the payment of a prescribed fee, may obtain a license for such use. The terms of such license shall specify royalty payments to be credited to the Fund, and conditions regarding the conservation and equitable sharing of benefits. Where a layout design is integral to the propagation of a variety utilizing material from the Fund, registration with the Layout Design Registrar shall be a prerequisite for license approval. Assignment of rights under any license granted from the National Gene Fund requires prior written consent of the Management Committee, ensuring continued benefit sharing as provided herein.

An issued breeder shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean any person who has bred, developed, or commercially exploited a new variety, and who is recognized as the breeder of such variety by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The breeder’s right shall extend to the right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and stock propagating material of the variety. However, such rights shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions as provided herein. A breeder may assign, bequeath, or license the breeder’s rights to another person, and any such transfer shall be recorded with the Authority. The Authority may maintain a registry of issued breeders and varieties protected under this Act, accessible to the public. Provided that the breeder’s right shall cease to exist upon the expiry of the period of protection.

A breeder who has developed a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, and who seeks registration as an issued breeder under this Act, shall submit an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee and a sample of the propagating material of the said variety. The application shall include a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, demonstrating its novelty, distinctness, uniformity and stability, and shall further specify the denomination proposed for the variety. Provided that, if the applicant is a legal entity, the application shall be signed by a duly authorized representative. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to furnish additional information or samples for the purpose of verification. Any person claiming to be a farmer and possessing seeds of a registered variety may, as provided herein, save and reuse the seeds for personal cultivation, subject to the conditions that such seeds are not sold, exchanged or otherwise commercially exploited.

An issued breeder, having registered a new plant variety as provided herein, shall possess the exclusive right to commercially exploit the said variety in India, subject to the limitations imposed by this Act and regulations framed thereunder. Notwithstanding such exclusivity, a farmer who has, in good faith, saved seeds of a protected variety for personal cultivation shall not be restricted from doing so, provided that sale, exchange or other commercialization of such saved seeds is prohibited without the express authorization of the issued breeder. Any person infringing the rights of an issued breeder may be subject to an injunction restraining further infringement, and the breeder shall be entitled to recover damages for any loss suffered as a direct result of such infringement. The Authority may, upon application and sufficient cause shown, grant compulsory licenses for the exploitation of a protected variety, particularly in cases of national emergency or extreme need, ensuring equitable remuneration to the issued breeder. A registered breeder shall maintain accurate records of seed production and distribution, and these records shall be open to inspection by officers authorized under this Act.

A breeder who has substantially contributed to the development of a new plant variety, and who qualifies as an issued breeder under this Act, shall be entitled to register said variety, subject to the provisions herein. The application for registration shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, demonstrating its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. The Authority may, if satisfied that the applicant meets the criteria, grant a breeder’s certificate. However, the rights conferred by such a certificate are subject to the farmer’s right to save, use, sow, re-sow, and multiply seeds of a protected variety for personal purposes. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right may apply to the Competent Authority for redressal, providing evidence of the infringement and the resulting damages. The Authority shall conduct an inquiry and may, if satisfied, issue an order for injunction and recovery of damages, as provided herein. A register of all registered plant varieties shall be maintained and open to public inspection.

Any issued breeder, intending to exercise rights under this Act in respect of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety, shall furnish a declaration affirming the origin of the biological material used in the development of said variety. Such declaration shall explicitly state whether the parental lines or initial variety used in the breeding process were obtained from farmers, local communities, or any other source, and detail any associated benefit-sharing arrangements. Provided that, if the variety is essentially derived from another variety, the issued breeder must demonstrate a clear and documented chain of descent and obtain necessary authorization from the breeder of the initial variety, subject to the provisions relating to research and breeding exemptions as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the breeder ineligible for the full extent of protection afforded under this Act, and may be grounds for revocation of any granted registration. The Registrar may, upon reasonable cause, request further clarification or evidence regarding the origin of the biological material.

Any issued breeder who, having obtained a certificate of registration for a new plant variety, fails to comply with the conditions relating to seed availability to farmers, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees for each such instance of non-compliance. Furthermore, if a registered variety is subsequently found to lack essential characteristics as detailed in the variety description, the Authority may, after due inquiry and affording the issued breeder an opportunity to be heard, suspend the certificate of registration for a period not exceeding one year. Repeated failures to maintain the purity and genetic identity of the variety, evidenced by official inspection, shall constitute grounds for permanent revocation of the certificate. Any farmer adversely affected by the actions of an issued breeder may lodge a complaint with the Authority, and the Authority shall conduct a prompt investigation. Knowingly making false statements in any application or report under this Act shall attract a fine of up to fifty thousand rupees.

Any issued breeder desiring to assign, license, or otherwise transfer the rights conferred by a certificate of registration for a new plant variety shall furnish a written instrument of assignment or license, as the case may be, to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, specifying the duration, scope, and territorial extent of such transfer. The instrument shall also clearly identify the transferee and detail any conditions attached to the assignment or license, including royalty rates or benefit-sharing arrangements. Where a license is granted for commercial exploitation, the issued breeder shall ensure that the licensee undertakes to maintain the genetic purity and distinctiveness of the variety, and to comply with all conditions stipulated in the certificate of registration. Failure to register such transfer within ninety days of its execution shall render the transfer void *ab initio* as provided herein. The Authority may, subject to reasonable cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. Any assignment or license shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions under this Act.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, any dispute regarding the validity of a certificate of registration granted to an issued breeder, or concerning the extent of rights conferred thereby, shall be subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the Tribunal established under this Act. However, a farmer exercising rights saved under this Act, and alleging infringement of those rights by the issued breeder, may first present their grievance to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, which shall endeavor to mediate a resolution within ninety days. Should mediation fail, or if the Authority determines a prima facie case exists for systemic abuse of farmer’s rights, the matter may be escalated directly to the Tribunal, bypassing usual procedural requirements, provided that the farmer demonstrates reasonable cause for such expedited review. Any decision of the Tribunal shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, warranting an appeal to the Supreme Court.

An issued breeder, having demonstrated a substantial contribution to the development of a new plant variety as recognized under this Act, shall possess the exclusive right to commercially exploit the variety, including propagation, sale, and marketing, for a period determined in accordance with the provisions herein. However, such rights shall be subject to the farmer’s right to save, use, sow, re-sow and sell farm-saved seed, provided that the farmer does not offer for sale, share with any other farmer, or distribute such seed in a manner that infringes upon the breeder’s rights. A registered proprietor may, in cases of infringement, seek an injunction restraining the infringing party, as well as claim damages for loss of profits or royalty due. The Authority may, upon application and subject to verification, grant licenses to third parties for the use of the protected variety in the public interest, ensuring reasonable compensation to the issued breeder. Any dispute regarding the extent of permissible farmer’s rights or the determination of damages shall be adjudicated by the designated Tribunal.

Any issued breeder who, having obtained a certificate of registration for a new plant variety, engages in the sale, distribution, or other commercial exploitation of propagating material derived from said variety without maintaining the characteristics specified in the essential derivation criteria, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any registered certification trade mark utilized in connection with such non-conforming propagating material shall be subject to immediate cancellation. Provided that, the Authority may, subject to compelling evidence of unintentional non-compliance and remediation efforts, reduce the penalty but not below one lakh rupees. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s rights, or misuse of a registered certification trade mark, may apply to the Authority for redress, and the Authority shall conduct an inquiry as provided herein, with powers equivalent to a Civil Court. Failure to comply with an order of the Authority shall constitute a further offence, punishable by imprisonment not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both.

Any issued breeder desiring to commercially exploit a registered variety, or a variety for which a register proposed application is pending, shall be entitled to license the propagation material thereof to any other person, subject to the terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the breeder and the licensee. The licensing agreement shall specify the scope of the license, including the permitted acts of propagation, sale, and distribution, and the duration for which the license shall remain in force. Provided that, where no such agreement is reached within a period of ninety days from the date of a written request by the proposed licensee, either party may apply to the Authority for determination of reasonable license terms. The Authority, upon such application, shall consider the interests of both the breeder and the licensee, as well as the public interest, and shall issue an order fixing the terms and conditions of the license. Any royalty payments due under a license granted as provided herein shall be determined in accordance with the provisions of this Act and shall be subject to periodic review.

For the purposes of this Act, an assignee shall be deemed to include the legal representative of a deceased assignee, and an assignee of the assignee, extending the scope of assignment through successive transfers of right. Where an assignment is made subject to a prior existing interest, the assignee’s rights shall be limited to the portion of the patent not affected by such prior interest, provided that full particulars of the prior interest are disclosed at the time of assignment. Any assignment not in writing shall be void, and no assignment shall be effective until recorded with the Controller as provided herein. The assignee, upon establishing clear title, acquires all rights of the original patentee, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding revocation and licensing.

Any patentee may assign the patent or any share therein to any other person, and every such assignment shall be in writing and shall specify the patent and the share, if any, assigned. An assignment made under this Act shall not be operative unless it is registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. The assignee, upon registration of the assignment, shall possess the same rights as the original patentee, subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the assignment deed. Where a patent is assigned jointly, all joint patentees shall be deemed assignees until the assignment is duly registered and reflects the respective shares assigned to each. The Controller may, if satisfied that the assignment is bona fide and in the public interest, require the assignee to furnish further evidence of title before completing the registration. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it, but it may affect the assignee’s ability to enforce the patent rights against third parties.

Any patentee may assign the patent and the right to make, use, and sell the invention as provided herein. An assignment shall be in writing and shall clearly identify the patent and the invention subject to assignment. The assignee, upon providing satisfactory evidence of title to the Controller, shall be entitled to all the rights and remedies available to the original patentee, subject to any existing licenses or security interests. Where an assignee assigns their interest further, the ultimate assignee shall likewise be recognized, provided that each successive assignment is properly documented and recorded with the Controller. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it but may affect its enforceability against third parties. A legal representative of a deceased assignee shall possess the same rights as an assignee, subject to the provisions of the relevant personal law governing succession. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or the identity of the proper assignee shall be adjudicated by the High Court.

Any patentee may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the patent and the rights subject matter thereof, either wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to conditions. An assignment shall not be operative unless it is in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor. The assignee of a patent shall, for the purposes of this Act, possess the same rights as the original patentee, subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the instrument of assignment. Where a patent is assigned, the assignee shall, within a period of ninety days from the date of assignment, notify the Controller of Patents in the prescribed manner, furnishing details of the assignment including the date of execution and the particulars of both the assignor and the assignee. Failure to comply with this notification requirement may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. An assignee may further assign their interest, and such subsequent assignee shall also be bound by the notification requirements as provided herein. The legal representative of a deceased assignee shall be deemed an assignee for the purposes of this Act.

Any patentee may assign the patent or any share therein subject to the conditions as provided herein. An assignment shall be in writing and shall clearly identify the patent and the share being assigned, and shall be duly executed by the assignor and the assignee. The assignee, upon obtaining an assignment, shall furnish notice thereof to the Patent Office within such time and in such form as may be prescribed. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. Where an assignee assigns a further interest, the rights and obligations pertaining to that subsequent assignment shall be governed by the same provisions. For the purposes of this Act, the term assignee includes a legal representative of a deceased assignee and any assignee of such legal representative. Any assignment made in contravention of these provisions shall be void.

Any person claiming to be an assignee of a patent, or a right to a patent, shall furnish to the Controller a declaration verifying the basis of their claim of assignment, and shall include therewith a certified copy of the instrument of assignment, if any. Failure to furnish such declaration and certified copy within a period of thirty days from the date of application for registration of assignment shall render the claim invalid, and subject the claimant to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. Where an assignment is made subject to a condition requiring further consideration, the assignee shall be deemed to have acquired a complete title only upon fulfillment of such condition, and any failure to fulfill said condition may be grounds for revocation of the assignment as provided herein. The Controller may, if satisfied that a fraudulent claim of assignment has been made, initiate proceedings for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, in addition to any penalties imposed under this Act. Any assignee failing to maintain accurate records of the chain of title shall be liable to inspection by a duly authorized officer.

Any patentee may assign the patent or any share therein to any other person, and every such assignment shall be in writing and shall specify the patent and the share, if any, being assigned. An assignment made under this Act shall not be operative unless it is registered with the Controller as provided herein. The assignee of a patent shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, enjoy the same rights as the original patentee in respect of the share assigned. Where a patent is assigned, the assignee may, with the consent of the assignor, make further assignments of any share of the patent. 

Provided that, the assignee shall furnish the Controller with a copy of the instrument of assignment within the prescribed time and manner. Failure to register an assignment may render it unenforceable against third parties. The legal representative of a deceased patentee or assignee shall, for the purposes of this Act, be deemed to be the assignee of the patent. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

Any person claiming to be an assignee of a patent shall furnish to the Controller a declaration verifying the basis of their claim to the patent, and shall include therewith evidence satisfactory to the Controller establishing the assignment and the chain of title, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a dispute arises regarding the validity of such assignment, any aggrieved party may file an appeal with the Appellate Board, providing detailed grounds for contesting the assignee’s claim. The Appellate Board shall, after due consideration of evidence and submissions, issue a reasoned order either confirming or rejecting the assignment. Provided that, if the assignee is a legal representative of a deceased inventor, a certificate of death and proof of legal representation shall be sufficient, unless challenged by a party demonstrating a superior claim. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of the patent, as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be an assignee of a patent shall furnish to the Controller a declaration verifying the basis of their claim to the patent, and demonstrating an unbroken chain of title originating from the original patentee. The declaration shall include details of all assignments, including dates of execution and consideration paid, and shall be accompanied by certified copies of all relevant assignment deeds. Where the assignee is a legal entity, the declaration shall be made by a duly authorized officer. 

An indication plaintiff, alleging infringement based on assignment, shall, as a condition precedent to maintaining an action, demonstrate to the court that they were the assignee at the time the cause of action accrued, and that all conditions precedent to the assignment, as provided herein, were duly satisfied. Failure to provide such evidence may result in dismissal of the suit, subject to the discretion of the court. Any assignment not complying with these provisions shall be deemed invalid for the purposes of this Act.

Any person claiming to be an assignee of a patent shall furnish to the registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout design, a declaration verifying the basis of such claim and detailing the chain of assignment, including dates of execution and consideration paid, subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Failure to provide a complete and accurate declaration shall render the assignment void ab initio, and the purported assignee shall have no right to exercise any of the privileges conferred by this Act. Any false statement in such declaration shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The registrar may, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, require additional evidence to satisfy themselves as to the validity of the assignment. An assignee failing to comply with a lawful request of the registrar shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any patentee may assign the patent or any share therein to any other person, and every such assignment shall be in writing and shall specify the patent and the share therein assigned, and shall be duly executed by the assignor and assignee or their respective legal representatives. The assignee of a patent shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, enjoy the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as the original patentee, as if the patent had been originally granted to the assignee. However, any assignment made in fraud of creditors or for an unlawful purpose shall be void. Where an assignment is made without full and true disclosure of all relevant facts, and such non-disclosure constitutes a commission offence under the Indian Penal Code, the assignment may be subject to revocation by the appropriate authority. Any person aggrieved by an assignment may apply to the Controller for appropriate relief. The Controller shall, after due inquiry, pass such orders as may be necessary to protect the interests of all parties concerned.

Any person claiming to be an assignee of a patent, or a right to a patent application, shall submit to the Controller a declaration verifying the basis of their claim and detailing the chain of assignment, commencing with the original patentee or applicant. Should the Controller, upon review of such declaration and supporting documentation, be unsatisfied with the veracity of the claim, or find evidence of fraudulent misrepresentation, they may, after affording the claimant an opportunity to be heard, reject the claim of assignment. An aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the Controller’s decision regarding assignment, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and within the time frame stipulated under this Act. The patent process, including the examination and grant of a patent, shall remain stayed pending resolution of any dispute concerning the rightful assignee. Provided that, the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except in cases of proven jurisdictional error.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “assignee” shall mean a person to whom a patent or an application for a patent has been validly assigned, whether such assignment is absolute or partial and includes the legal representative of a deceased assignee and an assignee of such assignee. Where an international application designating India has been filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the applicant, or where applicable, the applicant’s successor in title, shall be considered the assignee for the purposes of pursuing a national phase application as provided herein. Any assignment of a patent or application shall be in writing and shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The assignee shall possess all the rights of the original patentee, subject to the terms of the assignment and the provisions of this Act.

The patent controller shall exercise all powers and perform all functions as are conferred by this Act or any rules made thereunder, and shall be the final authority in matters relating to the grant or refusal of patents. The controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, delegate any of his powers to an officer subordinate to him, provided that such delegation does not extend to the power to grant or refuse a patent. Any decision of the patent controller may be appealed to the Appellate Board as provided herein. A register of patents shall be maintained by the controller and shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee. The controller shall also maintain a record of all applications for patents, and such record shall be deemed to be public document.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the patent controller regarding the rectification of a patent, or the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. The patent controller shall, prior to the disposal of any application for amendment of a patent, publish a notice of the application and afford opportunity to any person to present observations. Where the patent controller determines that a patent lacks novelty, or involves an obvious invention to a person skilled in the art, they shall issue a reasoned order rejecting the application. Provided that, the patent controller may, at any stage of proceedings, require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for proper adjudication. All decisions of the patent controller shall be communicated in writing to the applicant and any other interested parties, and shall include a statement of reasons. The patent controller’s records shall be open for inspection during office hours, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

The patent controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred by this Act, and may, for the purposes of ascertaining the true subject matter of any invention, require the applicant to furnish a declaration confirming the inventive step. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the patent controller may, within a period of sixty days from the date of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The patent controller may, if satisfied that the applicant has failed to comply with a requirement under this Act, direct that the application be deemed to be withdrawn. Where a patent controller reasonably suspects fraudulent intent in an application, they may initiate an inquiry and, upon confirmation, revoke any patent obtained through such means, and impose a monetary penalty on the applicant. Any fees paid in relation to a revoked patent shall not be refunded.

The patent controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, exercise such powers as are necessary to administer this Act and to ensure its effective implementation. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the patent controller may, within a period of sixty days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, in the manner prescribed. The patent controller may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, delegate any of his powers to an officer subordinate to him, provided that such delegation shall not absolve the patent controller of ultimate responsibility. 

Where a patent application is found to be lacking in clarity or completeness, the patent controller may require the applicant to amend the application within a specified period. Failure to comply with such requirement may result in the application being deemed abandoned, as provided herein. The patent controller shall maintain a register of patents and shall cause it to be open for inspection by the public, subject to payment of the prescribed fee.

The patent controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, exercise full authority in matters relating to the administration of this Act, including the examination of applications for patents and the granting or refusal of patents. Any person aggrieved by an order of the patent controller may, within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The patent controller may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant or any other person to furnish a declaration verifying the truthfulness of any statement made in connection with an application or other document. Failure to comply with such requirement shall be deemed a sufficient cause for rejecting the application or taking such other action as the patent controller may deem fit, subject to the principles of natural justice. All records maintained by the patent controller shall be open to inspection by any member of the public upon payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the patent controller relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of a patent, or concerning any opposition proceedings, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Failure to lodge such appeal within the prescribed period, which shall not exceed ninety days from the date of the order, shall render the order final and binding. The patent controller, upon receiving credible information of any fraudulent practice or misrepresentation made in obtaining a patent, may initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied, revoke the patent with immediate effect. Any person knowingly aiding or abetting such fraudulent practice shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. The patent controller’s discretion in imposing penalties shall be subject to principles of natural justice, and any decision may be challenged before the Appellate Board.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be in writing and registered with the Patent Office within the prescribed time. The patent controller may, upon sufficient cause shown, extend the time for registration of an assignment, provided that a penalty fee is duly paid as determined by regulations. Where a patent is jointly held, no assignment of a share therein shall be valid without the consent of all co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a written agreement filed with the patent controller. Licences granted under a patent may be assigned or mortgaged, subject to the terms of the original licence agreement and any restrictions imposed by the patent controller to ensure public interest. The patent controller shall maintain a register of all assignments and licences, which shall be open to public inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to register an assignment or licence shall not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the patent controller concerning an application for a patent, or the revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The patent controller, upon receipt of a notice of appeal, shall transmit to the Appellate Board all relevant documents and information pertaining to the case. Provided that the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend the period for filing an appeal. Any party to the proceedings before the patent controller shall be entitled to present evidence and arguments before the Appellate Board. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

The patent controller shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, exercise full authority in matters concerning the grant, revocation, and amendment of patents. Any person claiming rights in a literary work forming the subject matter of a patent application shall submit a certified copy of the registration, if any, under the relevant laws governing literary works, alongside the application. Provided that failure to furnish such registration shall not, in and of itself, invalidate the patent application, but may be considered by the patent controller during the examination process. The patent controller may, at any stage, require the applicant to provide further evidence regarding the originality and authorship of any incorporated literary work. All decisions of the patent controller shall be communicated in writing and shall state the reasons therefor, and any aggrieved party may seek review as provided herein. Compliance with these requirements is mandatory for all applications.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the patent controller relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit, or a layout-design thereof, as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of said order. Failure to lodge such appeal within the stipulated timeframe shall, unless sufficient cause is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Appellate Board, render the order final and binding. The patent controller, in exercising powers of examination or revocation, shall maintain a detailed record of all technical assessments undertaken, and any omission to do so will attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated non-compliance with record-keeping requirements may result in suspension of examination privileges. Any false representation made to the patent controller shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

A design shall be considered patented when a design application, complying with the requirements as provided herein, has been examined and a patent has been granted by the Controller of Designs. The right to a patented design shall confer upon the owner, subject to the provisions of this Act, the exclusive right to reproduce the design in any article, and to sell, offer for sale, or import any article embodying the design. A patented design, however, does not extend to articles which are merely functional or dictated solely by technical considerations. Where a design is substantially similar to a prior design, it may be deemed not novel and therefore ineligible for patenting, unless a significant distinguishing feature is demonstrated. Any person aggrieved by the grant of a patented design may, in accordance with established procedure, apply for its revocation.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall submit an application to the Controller of Patents in the prescribed manner, demonstrating a novel, non-obvious, and industrially applicable invention. An invention, to be patented, must not fall within the exclusions specified under this Act, including but not limited to mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance. A patent, once granted, confers upon the patentee the exclusive right to make, use, exercise, and sell the patented invention throughout India for a period of twenty years from the date of filing the application. Subject to the provisions herein, a patented article may be imported into India without the authorization of the patentee, provided that it is manufactured in a country that also provides patent protection equivalent to that afforded in India. The Controller may, after examination, refuse to grant a patent if the invention is not sufficiently disclosed or if it lacks the requisite inventive step. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may file an appeal as provided herein.

Any person who, without authorization from the patentee or a duly licensed assignee, makes, uses, sells, offers for sale, or imports a patented invention, shall be liable to a civil action for infringement as provided herein. The patentee, or assignee, may seek injunctive relief restraining the infringing party from continuing the unlawful acts, and may also claim damages for loss suffered as a consequence of the infringement. Such damages shall be ascertainable and may include a reasonable royalty for the use of the patented invention. 

Where a patented invention is embodied in an article, the importation of such article into India shall be deemed an infringement, subject to exceptions relating to bona fide personal use. A finding of infringement may also necessitate an order for delivery up or destruction of the infringing goods. Provided that, the court may, in its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party in any action brought under this Act. Any person alleging infringement must demonstrate a clear and convincing connection between the patented claim and the alleged infringing activity.

Any process resulting in a commercially viable product, and claiming novelty as provided herein, shall be subject to examination for patentability. An invention shall not be considered novel if it lacks a distinct step from existing knowledge, or if it is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Where a product is patented, the patentee shall have the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, or importing that product. However, such exclusivity shall be subject to licensing provisions under this Act, particularly in cases of national emergency or public interest. 

A patented invention may be revoked if it is proven, through due process, that it was not truly inventive, or that essential details were concealed during the application process. Any person alleging infringement of a patented invention may seek redressal through established judicial procedures. The Controller of Patents shall maintain a public register of all granted and pending patents, accessible for inspection as prescribed.

Any process resulting in commercial exploitation of a patented invention, without due authorization from the patent holder, shall be considered an infringement under this Act. A patented invention, even if incorporating a subsequently developed improvement not claimed in the original patent, remains subject to the original patent’s term, provided that such improvement does not independently qualify for patentability. Where a patented product is manufactured for the purposes of export, compliance with the provisions regarding licensing shall be demonstrated to the Controller of Patents prior to shipment. Any person alleging infringement may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the infringing party, subject to the posting of security as the Court deems fit. The patentee shall have the right to seek damages for any loss suffered due to the infringement, calculated according to reasonable royalty or actual loss, whichever is higher. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as prescribed herein.

Any person who manufactures, sells, offers for sale, or imports any product or process which is a patented invention, without the license or authority of the patentee, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such act of infringement, and the court may, at its discretion, also grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement. Provided that, if the infringement is shown to be unintentional, the penalty may be reduced, but shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Any evidence obtained through seizure of infringing goods, as provided herein, shall be admissible in court, subject to verification by an officer appointed by the Controller. The patentee may, in addition to the above penalties, claim damages for loss suffered due to the infringement, assessed based on reasonable royalty or actual losses incurred, whichever is higher. Any appeal against the order of the court shall be subject to the provisions of this Act.

Any assignment of a patented invention, or any interest therein, shall be in writing and shall specify the invention to which it relates. Such assignment shall not be operative until recorded with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. The Controller may require such evidence of title as he deems necessary before recording an assignment. Where a patented invention is jointly held, no co-owner may grant a license or assign his share without the consent of the other co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in writing. A license granted under this Act, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be assigned by the licensee with the prior written consent of the patentee, subject to the terms and conditions of the original license. Failure to comply with these provisions regarding assignment or licensing of a patented invention shall render such transfer voidable at the option of the patentee or his assignee. Any person deriving title to a patented invention through an unrecorded assignment does so subject to the rights of the original patentee.

Any person alleging infringement of a patented invention, or anticipating such infringement, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the alleged infringer from the continuation of the infringing act, provided that such application is accompanied by a detailed statement of the grounds upon which the claim of infringement is based. The Court, upon receiving such application and subject to verification of the validity of the patent, may grant an interim injunction pending a full hearing. However, a patent shall not be considered valid for the purposes of this Act if it is proven, through evidence admissible in a court of law, that the invention was obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art at the time of the patent application. Any decision of the High Court regarding such injunctions may be appealed to the Supreme Court, and the burden of proof regarding non-obviousness shall lie with the patentee.

Any assignment of a patented invention, or any interest therein, shall be in writing and duly executed by or on behalf of the assignor and assignee. Such assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall not operate to convey any right to exploit the invention in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the patent. Where a patented invention incorporates elements protected by copyright, the assignment of the patent does not automatically transfer copyright ownership; separate assignment of such copyright shall be necessary, and the terms governing the copyright may differ from those governing the patent. A licensee of a patented invention may, with the explicit consent of the patent holder, sub-license the invention, provided that such sub-license is recorded with the appropriate authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding assignment or licensing may render the transaction voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The patent holder retains the right to seek equitable relief against any unauthorized exploitation of the patented invention, even after assignment.

Any person alleging infringement of a patented invention, or asserting invalidity thereof, may lodge a complaint with the Appellate Board established under this Act, provided that such complaint is accompanied by a detailed statement of the grounds for the allegation and supporting evidence. The index names registered pertaining to the patented invention shall be deemed relevant evidence in determining the scope of the claim and establishing potential infringement. However, registration of index names does not, in and of itself, constitute proof of patent validity or ownership. The Appellate Board may, subject to due process and hearing of all parties, issue an interim injunction restraining the alleged infringer from further acts of infringement pending final determination of the matter. Any decision of the Appellate Board may be appealed to the Supreme Court, as provided herein, within ninety days of the order. Failure to comply with the orders of the Appellate Board shall attract penalties as prescribed.

A patent, once granted and remaining in force as provided herein, shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, or importing the patented invention. Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person who infringes upon a patented invention may be subject to civil remedies, including injunction and damages. The appellate board chairperson, appointed under the relevant rules, may, upon a reasoned application, direct interim measures to prevent further infringement pending the outcome of proceedings. However, such measures shall not be granted unless the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case of patent validity and infringement. Any license of right, or compulsory license, granted under this Act, shall be subject to reasonable terms and conditions determined by the appropriate authority.

Any person deriving title from an inventor of a patented invention, and who has not been duly authorized by the patentee, may apply to the Controller for a license under the patent, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall include a statement of the reasons why the applicant seeks the license, and the terms and conditions that the applicant proposes. The Controller, upon receiving such application, shall give notice to the patentee and may require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence as deemed necessary. Provided that, where the patented invention relates to a pharmaceutical product, the application shall demonstrate a prima facie case of reasonable requirement for public health. An application under this provision, referencing the application section 71, shall be considered independently of any other pending legal proceedings concerning the patent. The Controller’s decision regarding the grant of a license shall be final and binding, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Any person who exploits a patented invention without the authorization of the patent holder, or a licensee duly authorized under this Act, shall be liable to an action for infringement in a District Court having jurisdiction. Where an infringement involves a plant variety protected by a patent and subject to breeder complied provisions, the patent holder may, in addition to injunctive relief and damages, seek an accounting of profits derived from the sale of the unapproved variety. Provided that, the accounting shall exclude any costs legitimately incurred in independently developing the infringing variety, subject to proof satisfactory to the Court. A patent holder may elect to pursue either damages or an accounting of profits, but not both, as provided herein. The Court may, at its discretion, award enhanced damages in cases of willful infringement. Any order granting relief under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court.

An order adjudicating officer shall be a reasoned and speaking order, clearly stating the facts, the legal provisions relied upon, and the reasons for the decision reached, and shall be communicated to the parties concerned in the manner as may be prescribed. Where an application for rectification of a patent is heard by an adjudicating officer, the officer may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish a declaration verifying the grounds on which the application is based. Provided that failure to furnish such declaration shall not, in and of itself, be grounds for dismissal of the application, but the adjudicating officer may draw such inferences as are permissible under the law. Any party aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer may, within the prescribed time, seek a review of the order before the same officer.

Any person desiring registration of a plant variety shall submit an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in Schedule I. The Authority, upon receipt of such application, shall cause a formality examination to be conducted to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Should the application satisfy the formality requirements, the Authority shall publish a notice of the said application for a period of sixty days, inviting objections from any person alleging prior art or lack of distinctiveness. Following the expiry of the objection period, the Authority shall consider any objections received and may, if deemed necessary, direct a technical examination of the variety. An order adjudicating officer, appointed by the Authority, shall conduct said technical examination and submit a report detailing the variety’s novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. The Authority shall, subject to the findings of the order adjudicating officer and any other relevant considerations, grant or refuse registration.

Any person dissatisfied with an order adjudicating officer may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the High Court for the revision of such order. The application for revision shall be made within ninety days from the date on which the order was passed, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order sought to be revised, together with a statement of the grounds on which the application is based. The High Court may, if satisfied that the order is erroneous or unjust, set aside, modify or affirm the same. Provided that no revision shall be admitted unless the applicant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and has exhausted any available internal appeal mechanism. Where an application for revision is dismissed, the adjudicating officer’s original order shall remain in full force and effect, and no further recourse shall be available except as otherwise provided herein. The High Court, in exercising its powers under this provision, may also direct the payment of costs.

Any person against whom an order adjudicating officer is passed, determining liability for infringement of a patent, shall have the right to seek a review of such order, subject to the provisions contained herein. An application for review shall be made to the same adjudicating officer who issued the original order, and must be filed within thirty days of the date of communication of the said order. The application shall clearly state the grounds upon which review is sought, and shall be accompanied by any supporting evidence not previously considered. The adjudicating officer, upon receipt of such application, may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, direct a re-examination of the matter. Provided that, no new evidence shall be admitted unless the applicant demonstrates due diligence in obtaining such evidence prior to the initial determination. The decision of the adjudicating officer on the review application shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court as provided under this Act. Any delay beyond the stipulated period may, at the discretion of the adjudicating officer, be condoned upon demonstration of reasonable cause.

Any person against whom an order adjudicating officer is passed, pertaining to the revocation of a patent, shall have a right to seek a statement of reasons for such order within thirty days of the communication of the said order. The statement of reasons shall be furnished by the adjudicating officer within a further period of sixty days, subject to the condition that such furnishing does not prejudice ongoing investigations or reveal confidential information. Where the statement of reasons is deemed insufficient or unsatisfactory by the requesting party, an application for review may be made to the adjudicating officer, provided that such application is accompanied by supporting evidence demonstrating the inadequacy. Any review application shall be decided within ninety days of its receipt, and the decision of the adjudicating officer on review shall be final, unless an appeal is preferred as provided herein. Failure to comply with these timelines shall be considered procedural irregularity.

Any person failing to comply with an order adjudicating officer issued under this Act relating to the rectification of the register of patents, or the revocation of a patent, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where the non-compliance continues for more than thirty days after the date of the order, a further daily penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees may be imposed. The adjudicating officer, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, may direct the defaulting party to cease and desist from the infringing activity. Any appeal against an order imposing a penalty shall be made to the designated authority within sixty days of the order’s communication, provided that a reasonable cause for delay is demonstrated to the satisfaction of the appellate body. Failure to lodge an appeal within the stipulated timeframe shall render the order final and binding.

Any assignment of a patent application or a patent, whether complete or partial, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, and such instrument shall be registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. The Controller, upon registration of such assignment, shall record the title of the assignee in the Register of Patents and shall notify the parties concerned. Where an assignment is made subject to a condition requiring further consideration to be paid or other obligations to be performed, the Controller may, upon application, adjudicate upon disputes arising from such conditions. An order adjudicating officer, appointed by the Controller for this purpose, shall have the power to require evidence and examine witnesses, and their decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Controller. Failure to register an assignment does not invalidate it, but it may affect its enforceability against a subsequent assignee without notice of the earlier assignment. The Controller may, if satisfied that an assignment is fraudulent or otherwise unlawful, refuse registration.

Any person dissatisfied with an order adjudicating officer relating to the revocation of a patent, or the imposition of a penalty under this Act, may lodge an objection with the High Court, provided that such objection is filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the said order. The High Court shall, upon receipt of such objection, constitute a Special Bench to examine the merits of the case and may, after hearing the parties concerned and subject to such conditions as it deems fit, confirm, modify, or set aside the order of the adjudicating officer. Further, if the objection concerns a matter of substantial legal complexity, the High Court may refer it to a larger Bench for determination. Any decision of the High Court in such matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to appeal permissible under the general laws of the land.

Any assignment of right, title, and interest in a plant variety registered under this Act, or in a license to work the same, shall be subject to the prior approval of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and such approval may be granted subject to such terms and conditions as the Authority deems fit. An order adjudicating officer, appointed for the purposes of this Act, shall have the power to determine the reasonableness of any royalty or other consideration stipulated in any assignment or license agreement, and may direct modification thereof if found to be unduly restrictive or prejudicial to the interests of the breeder or the public. Where a plant variety is found to be essentially derived from a variety protected under this Act, the owner of the initial variety shall be entitled to a share in the proceeds from the sale of the essentially derived variety, unless otherwise agreed between the parties. Failure to obtain prior approval for an assignment, or to comply with an order of the adjudicating officer, shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the Plant Variety Protection Authority.

Any person dissatisfied with an order adjudicating officer may, within forty-five days of the order’s communication, lodge a reasoned representation with the Controller of Patents, setting forth the grounds for objection and supported by relevant evidence as provided herein. The Controller shall, subject to such terms as may be deemed fit, direct a re-examination of the matter, and may, if warranted, suspend the operation of the contested order pending completion of said re-examination. All inspections conducted pursuant to any order of the adjudicating officer shall be meticulously recorded in the inspection register, detailing the date, time, persons present, and scope of the inspection. Should the Controller uphold the original order, a further appeal may lie before a designated High Court, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review and deposits a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements shall render any objection or appeal inadmissible.

Any person intending to seek rectification of a mark international registration, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the adjudicating officer in the prescribed manner and with the prescribed fee. The adjudicating officer, upon receipt of such application and after providing an opportunity of being heard to the applicant and the proprietor of the mark, may, by order, either wholly or partially allow or reject the application. An order adjudicating officer refusing rectification may specify conditions subject to which the registration shall continue in force. Provided that, any party aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer may, within ninety days of the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final and binding, and no further appeal shall lie therefrom, except as otherwise provided herein. All applications and supporting documents shall be maintained as confidential records.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered, and to institute legal proceedings for infringement thereof. The term ‘well-known trade mark’ shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean a mark which has become recognised by the relevant public by reason of the proprietor’s use of the mark. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered trade mark shall be assignable and may be transmitted by operation of law, including by way of amalgamation, transfer of undertakings, or insolvency. However, such assignment or transmission shall be subject to any conditions or restrictions as may be recorded in the register of trade marks. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to trade marks registered may seek redressal as provided herein.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. The register of trade marks shall be open to inspection by the public, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee, and certified copies of entries therein may be obtained upon application. Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark, but not registered, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for registration, provided that such trade mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. Where a registered trade mark has been in continuous use for a period of five years, a certificate of enduring registration may be obtained, conferring additional evidentiary weight. Assignment of the trade marks registered under this Act shall be subject to conditions as may be prescribed. The Registrar may, where appropriate, require a disclaimer as to any part of the trade mark.

Any person who avails of remedies under this Act relating to trade marks registered shall be bound by such conditions as may be prescribed. A registered trade mark shall be subject to rectification proceedings, initiated either suo motu by the Trade Marks Registry or upon a petition filed by any aggrieved person, alleging reasons such as non-use or deceptive similarity with a prior mark. Where a registered trade mark is found to be deceptively similar to another trade mark, whether registered or unregistered, the proprietor of the earlier mark may seek an injunction restraining the use of the later mark. However, such injunction shall not be granted if the plaintiff has acquiesced in the use of the defendant’s mark for a period exceeding three years. Any assignment of trade marks registered under this Act shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Trade Marks Registry, unless it is a transfer as part of a business. The remedies provided herein shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other remedies available under any other law for the time being in force.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark registered under this Act may, subject to the provisions herein, apply to the Registrar for the rectification of the register in respect of the trade mark. Such application shall be in writing and shall set forth the grounds on which the rectification is sought, and shall be accompanied by evidence supporting the claim. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the application is well-founded, make an order for the rectification of the register accordingly. Where a trade mark is registered in contravention of any provision of this Act, or is identical with or deceptively similar to an earlier trade mark, the Registrar may, upon application, revoke the registration of the trade mark. Provided that no rectification shall be made affecting the title to a trade mark registered as trade marks registered in the name of different proprietors, unless the interests of all such proprietors are duly considered. The Registrar shall, prior to any order of rectification, provide notice to the registered proprietor and an opportunity to be heard.

Any person claiming to be the owner of trade marks registered under this Act, and intending to assign those trade marks, shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a statement of assignment in the prescribed form, duly verified, specifying the trade marks assigned and the consideration for the assignment. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the assignment shall be effective from the date of such statement being entered in the Register of Trade Marks. Where the assignment includes goodwill, it shall be accompanied by a certificate of the assignee’s entitlement to use the trade marks in connection with the goodwill assigned. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the assignment unenforceable as against subsequent purchasers for value without notice of the defect. A registered trade mark shall not be assigned to a person already possessing identical or deceptively similar trade marks for the same goods or services, unless a valid reason is demonstrated to the Registry.

Any person who applies for the registration of a trade mark under this Act, knowing it to be false, or who knowingly uses a trade mark registered by another, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services for which it was not registered, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, order the rectification of the register and require the removal of the offending mark from all goods and promotional materials. Any false representation concerning the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, or suitability for purpose of goods bearing registered trade marks shall constitute an unfair trade practice. Provided that, a bona fide industrial or commercial use of a descriptive term shall not be deemed a violation of rights in the trade marks registered. The Registrar shall have the power to impose monetary penalties not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such violation, as provided herein.

Any assignment of trade marks registered under this Act shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the assignor and the assignee and shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. A license, whether sole or otherwise, concerning trade marks registered herein may be granted by the registered proprietor, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and duration of the license, as well as the geographical area of operation. Where a registered trade mark is subject to a license, the licensee may, with the consent of the registered proprietor, assign or further license their interest in the licensed trade mark, subject to the original terms of the license and registration of such assignment with the Registry. Failure to register any assignment or license shall render it void against any subsequent assignee or licensee of the same trade marks. The registered proprietor retains the right to revoke a license upon reasonable cause and notice, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark, or requiring the rectification or cancellation of a registered trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Trade Marks Registry. Provided that, an appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant deposits with the Appellate Board such sum as the Board may determine, not exceeding five thousand rupees, to meet the costs of the proceedings. Where a dispute arises concerning the use of trade marks registered under this Act, and the parties fail to reach a mutually acceptable resolution through mediation, the Appellate Board may appoint an arbitrator to adjudicate the matter, and the decision of the arbitrator shall be final and binding.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall, subject to the provisions herein, confer upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. An application for registration claiming convention priority under Article 8 of the Paris Convention, commonly referred to as a 73 convention application, shall be filed within six months from the date of the earlier application, and shall be deemed to have been filed on the date of that earlier application, provided that all required documents and fees are submitted as prescribed. Where a mark is registered and subsequently assigned, or transmitted, the registrar shall record such transfer of ownership upon due application and payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to trade marks registered may, subject to the rules, file an appeal to the High Court. The registrar may, at any time, require evidence of continued use of a registered trade mark.

An assignable transmissible case arises where a registered trade mark is subject to a valid assignment or transmission of rights, and such transfer does not contravene any provisions contained within this Act. The proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee, assign or transmit the trade mark, either wholly or partially, and in respect of one or more goods or services included in the registration. Provided that, any assignment or transmission creating multiple exclusive rights in respect of identical goods or services shall be void unless specifically authorized by the Central Government. Any instrument of assignment shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein, failing which the assignment shall be deemed invalid as against any subsequent assignee. The validity of such assignment or transmission remains subject to the principles of law relating to passing off.

A registered trade mark shall be assignable and transmissible in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and such assignment or transmission may be effected inter vivos or by operation of law. Where a trade mark is assigned or transmitted with the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, the assignee or transmittee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark subject to any limitations specified in the instrument of assignment or transmission. However, any assignment or transmission of a trade mark which creates multiple exclusive rights in respect of the same trade mark shall be subject to the prior approval of the Registrar, and shall be voidable at the option of the Registrar if such approval is not obtained. An assignable transmissible case, where the mark is integral to a continuing business concern, requires full particulars of the transferor and transferee to be furnished to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of the transaction. Failure to do so may attract penalties as provided herein.

Any registered trade mark shall be assignable, and the right to the assignment shall vest in the assignee subject to the provisions of this Act and any other law for the time being in force. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark and to sue for any infringement thereof. However, assignment of a trade mark without any goodwill shall not confer any right to sue for infringement, except for the purpose of preventing further use of the mark by the assignor. 

An assignable transmissible case arising from such assignment, where the assignee seeks to enforce rights without goodwill, shall be subject to a determination of the extent of residual goodwill, if any, and the court may, at its discretion, grant relief limited to preventing the assignor’s continued use. The registrar may, upon application, record the transfer of ownership with appropriate documentation as provided herein.

Any trade mark registered under this Act shall be assignable or transmissible in accordance with the provisions herein, subject to the conditions specified and the procedures duly observed. An assignment or transmission of a registered trade mark shall be effected by executing a written instrument of assignment duly attested, and such instrument shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Where the assignment or transmission involves the transfer of goodwill, the assignee or transferee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the trade mark, and shall be entitled to all rights and remedies as if originally registered. 

However, in an assignable transmissible case where the assignment or transmission is proposed to be effected without any transfer of goodwill, the Registry may, upon application, require sufficient evidence demonstrating the continued association of the trade mark with the goods or services for which it is registered. The Registrar may, if satisfied, record the assignment or transmission, provided that such recording does not mislead the public as to the source or nature of the goods or services. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the assignment or transmission voidable at the option of the aggrieved party.

Any registered trade mark shall be assignable and may be transmitted in accordance with the provisions of this Act, subject to the conditions specified herein. An assignment or transmission of a trade mark shall be valid only upon registration of the transfer with the Trade Marks Registry and payment of the prescribed fee. Where a trade mark is assigned or transmitted as part of the goodwill of a business, notice of such assignment or transmission shall be given to the Registry within a period of six months from the date of assignment or transmission. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the assignment or transmission unenforceable. 

The validity of an assignable transmissible case is contingent upon the assignee demonstrating a legitimate interest and lawful use of the mark post-transfer. Any assignment or transmission undertaken fraudulently or with intent to deceive shall be deemed void ab initio, and the Registry may initiate proceedings for rectification. A transfer lacking clear documentation establishing full title shall be subject to scrutiny.
