Any right, title, and interest in a registered trade mark shall be assignable or transmissible, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. An assignment or transmission may occur with or without the goodwill of the business concerned, however, a transfer without goodwill shall not affect the proprietor’s right to pursue remedies for prior infringements. Where an assignable transmissible case arises involving a collective mark or a certification mark, the transferor shall provide written notice to the Trade Marks Registry, detailing the new proprietor and the scope of the transfer. The Registry may, upon satisfaction of due diligence, record the change of ownership. Any assignment or transmission not duly recorded shall be void against subsequent purchasers for value. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license, further license their interest to a third party, provided that such sub-licensing does not contravene any restrictions outlined in the original license agreement. The original proprietor retains the right to enforce the trade mark against any unauthorized use, even following assignment or sub-licensing.

Any registered trade mark shall be assignable or transmissible in manner provided by this Act, and the proprietor of such trade mark may, subject to the provisions herein, assign or transmit the same with or without the goodwill of the business concerned. However, an assignment or transmission creating multiple exclusive rights in respect of the same trade mark for identical goods or services shall be voidable at the option of the Registrar, unless the Registrar is satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist justifying such multiplicity. Any aggrieved party may, within ninety days of becoming aware of such assignment or transmission, file an appeal with the High Court challenging the validity thereof, demonstrating prejudice arising from the creation of competing exclusive rights. The High Court, upon review, may confirm, modify, or reject the assignment or transmission, and its decision shall be final and binding, provided that the court may direct restoration of the register as it deems fit to reflect the outcome of the appeal concerning the assignable transmissible case.

A registered trade mark shall be assignable and transmissible in a manner as provided herein, subject to the conditions specified in the register of trade marks and any other restrictions lawfully imposed. Any assignment or transmission of a trade mark, whether complete or partial, shall be evidenced in writing and submitted to the Trade Marks Registry for recordal, failing which such assignment or transmission shall be deemed invalid as against any subsequent assignee or transferee. Where an assignment or transmission creates multiple exclusive rights in relation to the same trade mark, the Registry may, upon application, require evidence of legitimate commercial justification. Any false representation regarding an assignable transmissible case, or any fraudulent practice employed to obtain registration of an assignment, shall constitute a commission offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine, as determined by a competent court. The proprietor of a registered trade mark remains liable for any acts committed prior to the effective date of the assignment or transmission.

Any rights vested in a registered trade mark, whether such rights are in respect of goods or services or both, shall be assignable or transmissible in a manner as provided herein, subject to the conditions set forth within this Act and any rules made thereunder. Where a trade mark is assigned or transmitted with the goodwill of the business concerned, no further evidence of the validity of the assignment or transmission shall be required beyond proof of the transfer of goodwill. However, in any case where the assignment or transmission is not accompanied by a transfer of goodwill, the assignee or transferee shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a clear and detailed statement of the circumstances surrounding such transfer, including the nature of the rights assigned or transmitted. 

The register said layout of the trade mark, as appearing on the register, shall be updated to reflect the new proprietor upon submission of the necessary documentation and payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to register said layout within the stipulated timeframe may result in a lapse of priority for the assignee or transferee. Any dispute regarding the assignable transmissible case shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court having jurisdiction.

Any trade mark which is duly registered under this Act shall be assignable or transmissible in accordance with the provisions contained herein, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and compliance with such conditions as may be stipulated by the Trade Marks Registry. An assignable transmissible case, however, requires demonstrable evidence of complete title transfer and a clear indication of continued use of the mark by the assignee or transferee. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of such assignment or transmission, or the proper ownership of the trade mark following transfer, any aggrieved party may seek redress before the Authority Appellate Board. The Board shall, following due process and consideration of submitted evidence, issue a binding order regarding the matter, provided that such order is consistent with the principles of this Act and does not contravene established legal precedent. Failure to comply with the orders of the Authority Appellate Board may result in penalties as prescribed.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark satisfies the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The registrar may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information or documents, subject to a reasonable timeframe specified by the registrar. Where the application is found to be deficient, the application registrar shall communicate the objections to the applicant in writing, detailing the grounds for such objection. Provided that, if the applicant fails to address the objections within the stipulated period, the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. The registrar shall maintain a register of all applications received and their current status.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the mark satisfies the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the application registrar has reasonable grounds to believe that the mark is not registrable, they shall issue a notice to the applicant specifying the grounds for objection and requiring a response within a period not exceeding thirty days. Should the applicant fail to respond within the stipulated timeframe, the application shall be deemed abandoned. The application registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require evidence of distinctiveness or proof of use, and may also initiate a search for prior conflicting marks. Provided that, the application registrar shall not reject an application without affording the applicant a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to amend their application, where permissible. Any decision of the application registrar may be subject to appeal to the appellate board.

The application registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Register as provided herein, and shall examine the application and the trade mark represented therein in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. If the application satisfies all legal requirements and no grounds for refusal exist, the application registrar may accept the application and proceed to advertise it in the prescribed manner. However, should the application registrar have reasonable grounds to believe that the trade mark is likely to cause confusion with an existing trade mark, or is otherwise not registrable, the application registrar shall issue a notice of refusal to the applicant, specifying the grounds for such refusal. Any aggrieved party may, subject to the prescribed time limits, file a statement of opposition to the registration of the trade mark, and the application registrar shall then initiate a hearing to determine the matter, ensuring due process and a fair opportunity to be heard for all parties involved.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Register as provided herein, with a view to ascertaining whether any trade mark identical with, or deceptively similar to, the mark applied for is already registered or pending. Where the application registrar has reason to believe that such a mark exists, they shall issue a notice to the applicant, detailing the grounds for potential objection and requiring a response within a period not exceeding thirty days. Should the applicant fail to respond within the stipulated timeframe, the application shall be deemed abandoned. 

The application registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to amend the application to clarify the distinctiveness of the mark or to remove any descriptive elements. Provided that any such amendment shall not substantially alter the character of the trade mark as originally applied for. All decisions of the application registrar shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, and an appeal may be preferred to the appellate board as prescribed.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Trade Marks Register as provided herein, and shall examine the application in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the application registrar determines that the application meets all statutory requirements and does not conflict with existing registered trade marks or pending applications, the registrar shall accept the application for publication. However, should the application registrar identify grounds for objection, a notice of objection detailing such grounds shall be issued to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to respond within a period not exceeding thirty days. Subject to the applicant’s satisfactory response or amendment of the application, the registrar may proceed with publication; otherwise, the application shall be deemed abandoned. The registrar may, at any stage, require further evidence or clarification from the applicant to ensure compliance with this Act.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a thorough examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark meets the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. If the application registrar determines that the mark is not registrable, they shall issue a reasoned notification of refusal to the applicant, specifying the grounds for such refusal and affording an opportunity for amendment or response within a period not exceeding thirty days. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe shall result in the application being deemed abandoned. Any person falsely representing themselves as the application registrar, or knowingly providing false information during the examination process, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. The application registrar may, subject to justifiable cause, extend examination timelines by no more than sixty days, notifying the applicant in writing.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete assignment deed relating to trade mark rights, conduct a verification of the assignor’s title and the assignee’s legal capacity to receive the assignment. Provided that, if the assignment is subject to a conditional transfer or encumbrance, the registrar shall require full particulars of such condition or encumbrance to be recorded in the register. Any assignment not duly recorded with the registrar shall be void against subsequent purchasers for value. The registrar may, at their discretion, require evidence of consideration paid for the assignment, subject to a reasonable determination of bona fide commercial practice. Where the assignment involves a series of trade marks, the registrar may consolidate the recordal process to facilitate efficient administration. Furthermore, the application registrar shall notify all parties of record regarding the pending assignment and afford them a period of thirty days to lodge any objection as provided herein.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark meets the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. If the registrar deems the application deficient, a notice of objection specifying the grounds for such objection shall be issued to the applicant, affording them a period of thirty days to file a response. Should the applicant fail to respond within the stipulated timeframe, or if the registrar remains unsatisfied with the response, the application may be refused. Any aggrieved party may file an appeal before the Appellate Board against the decision of the registrar, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and fulfillment of other procedural requirements. The Appellate Board shall consider the evidence presented by both parties and may confirm, modify, or reverse the registrar’s decision, and its order shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as permissible under the law.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Register as provided herein to ascertain whether any trade mark identical with, or deceptively similar to, the mark applied for is already registered or pending. Where the application registrar has reason to believe that a conflict exists between the applied-for mark and existing proprietors trade marks, notice of such conflict shall be issued to the applicant, requiring them to submit evidence addressing the potential for confusion. The application registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to amend the application to remove the grounds for objection. Provided that, if the applicant fails to satisfy the application registrar that the mark is distinguishable, the application may be refused. Any decision of the application registrar regarding the registrability of a trade mark shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, and an appeal may be lodged with the appellate board as prescribed.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a thorough examination as provided herein to ascertain its registrability in accordance with the criteria outlined within this Act. Where the application relates to a mark used in connection with layout-designs of integrated circuits, the registrar shall, subject to the provisions concerning semiconductor integrated circuits, also verify compliance with the relevant regulations pertaining to the protection of layout designs manufacturers and their intellectual property. Any deficiency in the application, or any conflict with existing registered trade marks, shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be afforded a period of thirty days to remedy the same. Failure to adequately address the registrar’s objections may result in the rejection of the application, and the applicant shall be notified accordingly. The registrar may, at their discretion, request further evidence or clarification from the applicant to facilitate a complete and accurate assessment.

The application registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark in India, conduct a thorough examination as provided herein to ascertain its registrability, and may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information within a period of thirty days from the date of such requirement. Should the application registrar determine that a mark is deceptively similar to an existing India trade mark, or is otherwise prohibited under this Act, they shall issue a reasoned refusal, detailing the grounds for objection. Any person aggrieved by such refusal may file a statement of grounds of appeal with the appellate board within sixty days. Failure to comply with the timelines stipulated herein, or providing false representations to the application registrar, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated non-compliance may result in disqualification from applying for trade mark registration for a period of five years.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete application for assignment of a registered trade mark, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain conformity with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Should the application appear to be in order, the registrar shall advertise the proposed assignment in the Trade Marks Journal, inviting any party to file a notice of opposition to the transfer within a period of four months from such advertisement. Any opposition filed shall be subject to the procedures outlined herein, including the provision of evidence and opportunity for hearing. The registrar may, subject to satisfactory evidence of title and due payment of the prescribed fees, register the assignment and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, where an application opposition registration is sustained, the registrar shall refuse to register the assignment and shall notify the applicant accordingly, with reasons for the refusal. The registrar’s decision on the validity of the assignment shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any person claiming a geographical indication for goods originating from a specific region in India may apply for registration thereof to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of case outlining the characteristics of the goods, the geographical area, and how the qualities, reputation or other characteristics of the goods are essentially attributable to that geographical origin. The application shall further include a standard of quality for the goods, verifiable and capable of ensuring consistent quality. Where a producers’ organization is established for the promotion and protection of the geographical indication, the application may be filed by such organization on behalf of the producers. Registration shall be subject to conditions regarding packaging, labeling, and permissible variations, as determined by the Registry and communicated to the applicant. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification as deemed necessary for proper examination of the application.

Any goods bearing a geographical indication shall be eligible for registration under this Act, provided that such indication identifies the goods as originating from a specific geographical area and possessing qualities or a reputation attributable to that origin. A geographical indication shall not be registered if it includes terms which are likely to mislead the public or are contrary to public order or morality. Applicants seeking registration of a geographical indication shall submit a statement detailing the characteristics of the goods, the geographical area of origin, and the methods of production traditionally followed in that area. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require further evidence to substantiate the claims made in the application. Registered proprietors of geographical indications shall be responsible for maintaining the quality and standards of the goods and for preventing unauthorized use of the indication. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the revocation of registration as provided herein.

Any person being the applicant for registration of a geographical indication, or claiming to be the owner thereof, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for the assignment of such registration to another person. The application for assignment shall be in such form as may be prescribed and shall be accompanied by a written instrument of assignment duly executed by the assignor and assignee. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of the application and instrument of assignment, examine the same and, if satisfied that the assignment is valid and in accordance with the provisions of this Act, shall register the assignment in the Register of Geographical Indications. A geographical indication, once assigned, shall vest in the assignee all rights and interests of the assignor in respect of that geographical indication, including the right to institute legal proceedings for infringement. However, assignment of a geographical indication shall not prejudice any rights existing prior to the date of assignment, and any continuing obligations under this Act shall remain binding on both the assignor and assignee. The Registrar may, if deemed necessary, require further evidence or clarification regarding the assignment before effecting the registration.

Registered varieties shall be subject to a period of protection as determined under this Act, contingent upon the continued payment of prescribed fees and adherence to conditions stipulated at the time of registration. Any person exploiting a registered variety without the authorization of the breeder, or in a manner inconsistent with the limitations imposed by the registration certificate, shall be deemed to have contravened the provisions herein. Farmers’ rights to save, use, sow, re-sow, exchange, and share seeds of registered varieties are expressly permitted, provided that commercialization of such saved seeds is subject to the breeder’s rights. The Authority may, however, direct cessation of such commercialization if it infringes upon the essentially derived variety provisions or the breeder’s exclusive right to produce, sell, and market. A register of all varieties registered act shall be maintained and open for public inspection, subject to reasonable restrictions. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as prescribed.

A patent shall be granted for an invention which is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application, subject to the provisions of this Act. A patent shall not be granted for an invention which, at the date of the application, was known to the public or had been described in any publication anywhere in the world, provided that such publication does not constitute prior art under the established principles of novelty assessment. Furthermore, a patent shall not be granted if the invention is prima facie obvious to a person skilled in the art, considering the existing knowledge in the relevant field. Any process for manufacture of a new article shall be considered capable of industrial application unless it is demonstrably frivolous or lacking practical utility.

A patent shall be granted for an invention relating to a pharmaceutical formulation, provided that the formulation demonstrates enhanced bioavailability as compared to existing formulations of the same active pharmaceutical ingredient, subject to verification by the Controller of Patents. The applicant shall furnish complete details of the manufacturing process, including quality control parameters, as part of the application. No patent shall be granted if the claimed formulation lacks inherent novelty or involves an obvious modification of a known pharmaceutical composition. Furthermore, a patent shall not be valid if it is established, through post-grant opposition proceedings, that the formulation fails to meet the prescribed standards of efficacy and safety as determined by the relevant regulatory authority. The patentee may, under this Act, seek an extension of the patent term based on reasonable delays caused by regulatory review processes.

A patent shall be revoked if it is proved to the satisfaction of the Controller that the patentee, or a person deriving title from him, has failed to fulfil any condition mentioned in this Act relating to the deposit of the biological material required for the purposes of section 41. Provided that such revocation shall not affect any rights accrued or liabilities incurred before the date of revocation. Any person aggrieved by the revocation of a patent, or by the decision of the Controller refusing to revoke a patent, may, within ninety days from the date of the order, appeal to the Appellate Board. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Appellate Board may, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, confirm, alter, vary or reverse the decision of the Controller. Where a patent is revoked, the Controller shall cause notice of the revocation to be published in the Official Gazette and the patent shall cease to have effect as of the date of such publication.

A patent shall be granted for an invention which is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where an invention relates to a pharmaceutical product, a patent may be granted if it demonstrates enhanced efficacy compared to existing formulations, provided that such enhancement is substantiated by complete and unambiguous clinical trial data filed with the application. No patent shall be granted for a method or apparatus relating to traditional Indian knowledge, unless it is demonstrably novel when considered in light of such knowledge, and the applicant provides evidence of origin and community acceptance. The Controller may, upon petition by any person, revoke a patent if it is proven that the invention was obvious to a person skilled in the art at the date of the patent application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller under this Act may prefer an appeal to the High Court. A patent shall cease to be in force if the renewal fees are not paid as prescribed.

A patent shall be granted for an invention which is a product or a process, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Provided that a patent shall not be granted for an invention which, at the date of the application, is known to the public in any place in India or anywhere in the world. Any application for a patent claiming a traditional knowledge or biodiversity resource shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the source and geographical origin of such knowledge or resource, and evidence of prior approval of the competent local authority. Furthermore, a patent shall be deemed to have been lawfully granted only if the applicant demonstrates sufficient inventive step and is not obvious to a person skilled in the art. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application or revocation of a granted patent, as provided herein.

No patent shall be granted for a pharmaceutical formulation unless the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Controller, substantial novelty arising from a demonstrable therapeutic benefit over existing treatments, as provided herein. Any person found to have falsely represented the therapeutic benefit of a patented formulation, with intent to deceive for commercial gain, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The Controller may, subject to due process, revoke any patent obtained through such misrepresentation. Furthermore, any profits accrued through the sale of falsely represented formulations shall be forfeited to the Central Government. A patent holder failing to adequately work the invention, despite reasonable opportunity and demand, may have their patent subject to compulsory licensing, as determined by a designated authority. Any appeal against the decision of the designated authority shall lie with the High Court.

Any patent shall vest in the inventor or, in the case of a jointly made invention, in the co-inventors, subject to any contractual agreement to the contrary executed prior to the filing of the complete specification. Where a patent is assigned or licensed, such assignment or license shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial limits of the assignment or license, and any conditions relating to quality or field of use. The patentee may grant licenses to others, and such licenses may be exclusive, non-exclusive, or limited in scope, as provided herein. Any assignment of a patent shall be subject to the provisions relating to mortgages, and the assignee shall be entitled to the benefits of such provisions. A patentee failing to diligently work the patented invention within a period of three years from the date of grant may be subject to compulsory licensing, provided that reasonable notice is given and adequate remuneration is paid. The rights conferred by a patent shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and any other applicable law.

A patent shall be granted for an invention involving a new and useful process for the extraction of rare earth elements from monazite sand, provided that the applicant demonstrates a substantial working of the process within the territory of India within three years from the date of grant, as evidenced by production figures submitted to the Controller. However, a patent shall not be granted if the claimed process is demonstrably lacking in inventive step, considering prior art relating to similar extraction techniques published before the priority date. Any person aggrieved by the Controller’s decision regarding inventive step may file an appeal before the Appellate Board established under this Act, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and within the time limit stipulated herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error, and may order rectification of the patent register accordingly.

A patent shall vest in the legal person who first lawfully acquires ownership of the invention, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding prior claims and public knowledge. Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be void as between the parties. Where a patent is jointly held, no co-owner may grant a license or assign their interest without the consent of all other co-owners, unless otherwise agreed in a written co-ownership agreement filed with the Controller. In cases involving complex technical subject matter, the Controller may, at any stage of the application or opposition proceedings, seek the advice of a judicial member technical possessing requisite expertise. The patentee shall maintain accurate records of all licenses granted and assignments made, and these shall be open to inspection upon reasonable notice. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the patent vulnerable to revocation.

A patent shall be granted for an invention which is new, involves an inventive step, and is capable of industrial application as provided herein. Any translation work, being a literary or dramatic work, submitted as part of a patent application, shall be accompanied by a declaration of its accuracy and completeness, certified by a translator duly qualified in the relevant language pair. Where a copy translation work is presented, the original language version shall be considered the primary document for the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require an applicant to furnish a certified copy of the original work if doubts arise regarding the fidelity of the translation. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent application liable to be refused. A patent shall vest in the applicant unless otherwise determined under this Act.

A patent shall be subject to the provisions contained herein and no application for a patent shall be accepted unless it satisfies the requirements as to novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability. Where a patent is granted for a product or process, the patentee shall have the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, or importing the patented product or process in India. However, such exclusive right shall not extend to uses by the Government of India for the purposes of research, experimentation, or for public service. Patents granted for pharmaceutical products shall be subject to provisions relating to compulsory licensing, as determined by the Controller of Patents, should circumstances so warrant and public health interests so require. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller may, subject to the prescribed procedure, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Controller may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant to furnish a declaration of inventorship.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be falsified if it is used or imitated in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion, as to the source of goods or services. The purpose falsifying used, in relation to a registered trade mark, includes any alteration of the mark, even if such alteration is minor, where the alteration is intended to create an impression that the altered mark is identical with, or closely resembles, the registered trade mark. However, any fair use of a descriptive term, or a term necessary to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, or other characteristics of the goods or services, shall not be considered falsification, provided that such use does not create a likelihood of confusion. Where a mark is falsified with intent to defraud, the penalties as provided herein shall be doubled.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, uses a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be liable for the tort of passing off, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where a person applies a trade mark to goods or their packaging in a manner that constitutes purpose falsifying used, intending that such goods shall be purchased as if they were the genuine goods of another, a civil remedy by way of injunction and damages shall be available to the owner of the registered trade mark. The court, in determining damages, may consider the profits wrongly made by the defendant, or the loss suffered by the plaintiff, as proven by evidence. Provided that, where the defendant proves they acted in good faith and had reasonable grounds to believe their use of the mark was lawful, the court may reduce the damages accordingly. A proprietor may seek an order for delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the falsified mark, as provided herein.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark identical with or resembling a registered trade mark to goods or services in relation to which it is not registered, shall be deemed to have engaged in the purpose falsifying used, and be subject to the penalties as provided herein. Where such application is made to goods intended for sale, or services offered for provision, the provisions relating to seizure of infringing goods and materials shall apply mutatis mutandis. The Registrar may, upon application by the owner of the registered trade mark and subject to such conditions as may be deemed appropriate, order the destruction of goods bearing the falsely applied mark. Any person abetting or assisting in such acts shall be liable as a principal offender. A court, upon conviction, may impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall be in the prescribed form. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under that trade mark, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services in respect of which the goodwill is assigned. However, assignment of a trade mark for the purpose of falsifying or deceptively imitating the mark, or for the purpose of gaining an unfair advantage, shall be void, and any rights acquired thereunder shall be extinguished. A license to use a trade mark may be granted, either generally or subject to limitations, and shall be in writing and signed by both parties. The proprietor of a trade mark may, as provided herein, assign or license the mark, or any right therein, subject to any conditions deemed necessary to protect the integrity of the mark and prevent its use for purpose falsifying used goods or services.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark identical with or resembling a registered trade mark to goods or services in respect of which it is not registered, shall be deemed to have engaged in the practice of purpose falsifying used, and such act shall constitute an infringement under this Act. However, such application shall not be considered an infringement if it is demonstrably for the purpose of fair use, being merely descriptive of the goods or services, or indicating the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, or geographical origin of the goods or services. Provided that, where a registered trade mark has been continuously non-used for a period exceeding five years, a party alleging infringement may, subject to providing sufficient evidence of prior legitimate use, seek rectification of the register and a stay of proceedings based on the alleged infringement until such rectification is determined. Any decision rendered under this provision shall be subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark identical with or resembling a registered trade mark to goods or services in relation to which it is not registered, shall be deemed to have engaged in the purpose of falsifying a used trade mark, and such act shall be actionable under this Act. Provided that, where the application of such mark is demonstrably incidental to the legitimate exercise of patent rights relating to a process or method of manufacture, the burden of proving intent to deceive shall lie with the complainant. However, this exemption shall not extend to instances where the goods or services themselves are directly misrepresented or are of inferior quality compared to those legitimately bearing the registered trade mark. Any appeal against a decision regarding such misrepresentation shall be heard by the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the timelines as provided herein. A finding of purpose falsifying used carries a mandatory minimum fine.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark to goods or services in the manner likely to be mistaken for those of another, shall be deemed to have engaged in the purpose of falsifying used goods, notwithstanding any prior use or lack of registration of said trade mark. Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, evidence of such registration shall be admissible, but not conclusive, in determining the intent to deceive. However, registration does not preclude a finding of purpose falsifying used if the application is demonstrably intended to mislead consumers regarding the source or quality of the goods or services. A claimant alleging such falsification may, subject to the provisions herein, seek an injunction restraining further application of the mark. Provided that, the court may consider the extent of actual confusion caused, if any, in determining appropriate relief. Any instrument used in the commission of this offence shall be liable to seizure.

For the purposes of this Act, and subject to the provisions herein, “international depositary authority” shall mean an institution duly designated under the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure. Any microorganism required to be deposited as part of a patent application, as provided herein, must be deposited with an international depositary authority. The applicant may, however, deposit the microorganism with a national depositary authority, provided that such authority furnishes an undertaking to the Controller of Patents to transmit a viable culture to an international depositary authority within a period of three months from the date of such national deposit. Viability of the deposited microorganism shall be demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Controller, and failure to do so may render the application incomplete.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent for an invention, being a microorganism or biological material, shall, in addition to the requirements as provided herein, deposit the said microorganism or biological material with a depositary institution recognized by the Controller and furnish a receipt of such deposit to the Patent Office within the prescribed period. The depositary institution shall, upon request, supply any person with a viable culture of the deposited microorganism or biological material, subject to the conditions specified by the depositary institution and in accordance with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding deposit and viability may render the application liable to be refused. Where a deposit is made under the Budapest Treaty, the applicant shall indicate the reference number assigned by the depositary institution in the patent application. The Controller may, however, waive the requirement of deposit in cases where the microorganism or biological material is readily available to the public.

Any person depositing a microorganism for the purposes of patenting under this Act shall, within three months from the date of such deposit, furnish to the Controller a statement indicating the source and date of deposit, as well as the depository institution. Should a deposit be made with an International Depositary Authority recognised under the Budapest Treaty, compliance with the requirements of that Treaty shall satisfy the obligations under this Act, provided that a copy of the deposit receipt is furnished to the Controller. Failure to furnish the requisite statement or proof of deposit in accordance with the provisions herein shall render the application liable to be treated as abandoned. Any dispute regarding the viability of a deposited microorganism, or the authenticity of the deposit, may be subject to review by the Controller, who shall consider evidence presented by both the applicant and any opposing party. The Controller’s decision on such matters shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court. A patent applicant shall bear all costs associated with the maintenance of the deposited microorganism.

Any person desiring to file a patent application for a micro-organism, or other biological material, shall deposit such micro-organism with a depositary institution recognized by the Controller under this Act and shall furnish a statement of such deposit to the Controller within the prescribed period. The depositary institution shall, upon request, furnish a copy of the deposited micro-organism to any person having a legitimate interest, subject to the conditions prescribed and payment of the fees as may be determined. Where a deposit relating to a patent application under the Budapest Treaty has been made with a depositary institution outside India, the applicant shall, within the time specified, file with the Controller a copy of the receipt of deposit issued by such institution. The Controller may, if satisfied that the depositary institution is not complying with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty, direct the applicant to effect a deposit with a depositary institution recognized under this Act. Failure to comply with the requirements relating to deposit, as provided herein, shall be deemed to be a ground for refusal of the patent. Any dispute regarding access to deposited material shall be adjudicated by the Controller, whose decision shall be final.

Any person seeking to deposit biological material for the purposes of patent applications under this Act shall comply with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure. Such deposit shall be made with any depositary authority recognized by the Controller and designated by the applicant, and notification of the deposit, including the date, accession number, and name of the depositary, shall be furnished to the Controller within sixteen days of the filing of the complete specification. Failure to furnish such notification, or to maintain a viable culture as evidenced by the depositary’s reports, may be considered grounds for objection to the patent application. Provided that, where the biological material is unavailable to the public prior to the filing date, and the applicant demonstrates reasonable efforts to obtain or produce said material, the Controller may grant a period of ninety days for compliance with this requirement, subject to satisfactory evidence of ongoing deposit procedures. Any dispute regarding the viability of the deposited material shall be adjudicated by the Controller, taking into account reports from the designated depositary.

Any person depositing a microorganism for the purposes of patenting an invention, and claiming priority under the Budapest Treaty, shall furnish to the Patent Office, within the period prescribed, a statement identifying the deposited microorganism with particularity and demonstrating its viability. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable to be refused, subject to a period of sixty days for rectification of the defect. Any false representation regarding the deposit or viability, made knowingly to obtain a patent, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller of Patents may, however, subject to conditions, extend the time for furnishing the statement if sufficient cause is shown. Any dispute regarding compliance with the Budapest Treaty, as provided herein, shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

Any person deriving benefit from a biological material deposited in a recognized international depositary authority pursuant to the Budapest Treaty, and seeking a patent in India relating to such material, shall furnish to the Controller a statement of deposit, certified by the depositary authority, demonstrating adherence to the viability requirements stipulated within the Treaty. Assignment of rights to such deposited biological material, or any patent derived therefrom, shall be governed by the provisions relating to assignment of patents under this Act, with the additional requirement that the assignee demonstrate a legally enforceable chain of title extending back to the original depositor. Subject to the provisions herein, a licensee of a patent claiming a deposited biological material may, with the explicit consent of the patentee and the depositary authority, access the material for the limited purpose of working the licensed invention. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the patent vulnerable to revocation, as provided herein, and shall constitute grounds for initiating proceedings before the appropriate court.

Any person claiming priority under the Budapest Treaty for the filing of a patent application shall, within the period prescribed, furnish a certified copy of the international deposit receipt issued by the competent International Depositary Authority, as provided herein. Should the Controller, upon examination, find the deposit receipt to be incomplete or lacking requisite details confirming the date of deposit, they may issue a notice requiring the applicant to rectify the deficiency within a period not exceeding three months. Failure to comply with such notice shall be deemed a waiver of the priority claim, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the deposit receipt or the interpretation of the Treaty itself, may be referred to the Appellate Board for adjudication, provided that such referral occurs no later than six months from the date of the Controller’s initial decision. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error established before a court of competent jurisdiction.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent for an invention, in respect of which an application has been filed under this Act, and who has deposited the described microorganism with an international depositary authority party to the Budapest Treaty, shall furnish to the Controller, along with the application or subsequently, a statement identifying the deposited microorganism and the date of deposit. The statement shall include the name and address of the depositary authority and the deposit number assigned by that authority. The Controller shall maintain a register of such deposits, being the relevant entry register, and shall make it accessible for inspection subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Failure to furnish the statement or to maintain the deposit in viable condition, as evidenced by the depositary authority, may be considered grounds for refusal of the patent, provided that the applicant is given an opportunity to remedy the deficiency. Any amendment to the deposit information shall be communicated to the Controller in writing.

A person found guilty of applying a false trade mark or trade description to goods, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, in cases where the goods are of a perishable nature, the court may, subject to the circumstances of the case, order the destruction of the goods instead of imposing a fine. Furthermore, any person who assists in the manufacture, sale, or distribution of goods bearing such false marks, knowing them to be counterfeit, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act and is liable to sentence imprisonment extending to two years. The court may also order forfeiture of any instrument or article used in the commission of the offence.

Any proprietor of a registered trade mark, aggrieved by an infringement thereof, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both, as provided herein. Where the infringement involves the counterfeiting of goods bearing the trade mark, and it is proven that the defendant acted with intent to deceive, or knew, or ought to have known, that the goods were counterfeit, the court may, in addition to damages and injunction, impose a sentence of imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. Provided that, no sentence of imprisonment shall be imposed unless the value of the illegally manufactured and sold goods exceeds five lakh rupees. The court may also order the destruction of all counterfeit goods and materials used in the manufacture thereof, subject to verification of legitimate goods. Any person assisting in such counterfeiting activities shall be deemed an abettor and shall be liable for sentence imprisonment equivalent to that of the principal offender.

Any person who counterfeits a registered trade mark, or knowingly sells, offers for sale, or distributes goods bearing such counterfeit mark, shall be liable for imprisonment. The extent of sentence imprisonment may extend to three years, or until a fine is paid, whichever is greater, and shall not be less than six months, subject to the discretion of the court. However, if the counterfeiting relates to goods likely to cause harm to the public, the sentence imprisonment may extend to five years. Where a company is found guilty of an offence under this Act, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable to the penalties herein provided, unless they prove that the offence occurred without their knowledge and that they exercised all due diligence to prevent such offence. A court may, as provided herein, order the destruction of counterfeit goods.

Any person who applies a trade mark to goods with the intent to deceive or cause confusion, as provided herein, shall be liable for an offence under this Act. Where such application is demonstrated to be for the purpose of gaining a fraudulent advantage, and the value of the goods bearing the falsely applied mark exceeds five lakh rupees, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, in cases where the offender is a first-time offender and the value of the goods does not exceed two lakh rupees, the court may, at its discretion, impose a sentence of imprisonment not exceeding one year, alongside a monetary penalty. Furthermore, any individual abetting the commission of such an offence, or conspiring to commit the same, shall be deemed to be equally responsible and subject to the same penalties, including sentence imprisonment. The court shall, prior to imposing any sentence, consider the nature of the goods, the extent of deception, and any mitigating circumstances presented by the accused.

Any person found to be in possession of counterfeit marks, as determined by a competent authority under this Act, and who cannot provide satisfactory evidence demonstrating legitimate acquisition or use of said marks, shall be deemed to have committed an offence. Provided that, if the possession is solely for the purpose of evidence in legal proceedings, or for the purpose of bona fide research, such possession shall not constitute an offence, subject to immediate notification to the relevant investigating officer. Where an offence is established involving marks applied to goods intended for sale, and the value of the seized counterfeit goods exceeds five lakh rupees, the offender may be subject to sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding seven years, alongside a fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees. However, a first-time offender, with a demonstrated lack of prior convictions and a proven intent to cease the unlawful activity, may be subject to a lesser penalty as determined by the adjudicating authority. All seized goods shall be subject to destruction as provided herein.

Any person who applies a false trade mark to goods with intent to deceive, or manufactures or sells goods to which a false trade mark has been applied, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, where the goods are of a perishable nature or are likely to deteriorate during the course of legal proceedings, the court may, instead of sentence imprisonment, order the destruction or disposal of such goods in a manner deemed fit. Furthermore, any person abetting the application of a false trade mark, or conspiring to commit such an offence, shall be deemed to have committed the offence as provided herein and be liable to the same penalties. The court may, subject to the circumstances of the case, also order the forfeiture of any instrument or equipment used in the commission of the offence. Any fine levied under this Act shall be payable to the Central Government.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by or on behalf of both the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, is granted to a person to use a registered trade mark, the licensor may, subject to any contract to the contrary, initiate infringement proceedings against any third party not bound by the license. However, any fraudulent or malicious use of a trade mark by a licensee, despite a clear stipulation against such use in the licensing agreement, shall constitute grounds for immediate revocation of the license and may, as provided herein, attract a sentence imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Failure to register an assignment within the prescribed period shall render the assignment void, and the original proprietor shall retain all rights to the trade mark. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, require further evidence of valid consideration for any assignment or license.

Any person found guilty of applying a false trade mark or trade description to goods with intent to deceive, as provided herein, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding three lakh rupees, or sentence imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with both. However, if the offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company itself, shall be deemed to be guilty. Appeals regarding the imposition of sentence imprisonment shall lie before the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and must be filed within ninety days of the lower court’s decision. The High Court may, after reviewing the evidence, confirm, modify, or set aside the sentence, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated for such review. Any appeal dismissed by the High Court shall be final.

Any person found guilty of counterfeiting a registered trade mark, or applying a false trade mark to goods with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, where the offence involves goods of a value not exceeding five thousand rupees, the term of imprisonment may extend to one year. The court, however, may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, also order the seizure and destruction of all counterfeit goods and materials used in the manufacture thereof. Furthermore, any person abetting or conspiring with another to commit such an offence shall be liable for punishment as if they were the principal offender. The Registrar of Trade Marks, upon receiving notice of a conviction under this Act, shall record the details of the offence and the punishment awarded. A subsequent offence involving a similar trade mark may attract enhanced penalties, including sentence imprisonment up to five years, and a fine double that prescribed for the initial offence.

Any person who broadcasts, whether through a broadcasting organisation or otherwise, a reproduction of a registered trademark in connection with goods or services for which the trademark is registered, and with the intent to deceive the public or cause confusion, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that, if the reproduction is demonstrably incidental to legitimate news reporting or fair comment, no offence shall be deemed to have occurred. However, a broadcasting organisation failing to promptly remove infringing material upon receiving a duly served notice from the trademark proprietor, and where such failure is proven to be willful, may be subject to a fine. Furthermore, any individual convicted of an offence under this provision shall be liable to sentence imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or to a fine, or to both. Subject to the provisions herein, the court may also order the seizure of all equipment used in the unlawful broadcasting.

Any person who applies a false trade mark to goods with intent to deceive, or manufactures, possesses, or sells goods bearing such a mark, shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, where the goods are of a perishable nature, the court may, in lieu of sentence imprisonment, order the destruction of the goods. Furthermore, if a registered trade mark owner proves to the satisfaction of the court that a registered trade mark has been applied to goods without their consent, and that such application constitutes a criminal act as provided herein, the court may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, order the revocation of the registration of that trade mark. The court shall consider the nature of the deception and the extent of the damage caused when determining the penalty. Any appeal against a decision regarding revocation shall be made within sixty days of the order.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, and shall be effected by an instrument in writing duly executed by both parties, or their duly authorised agents. Where a license is granted to use a trade mark, the licensor may, as provided herein, stipulate conditions regarding the quality of goods or services offered under the mark, and any breach of such conditions shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license. Should a fraudulent assignment or licensing agreement be proven, the assigning or licensing party may be subject to sentence imprisonment not exceeding three years, or a fine, or both. The adjudication of disputes concerning the validity of assignments and licenses, and the imposition of penalties, shall be overseen by a functions judicial member appointed under the relevant rules. Provided that, the aggrieved party may seek interim relief from a court of competent jurisdiction pending final determination of the matter. All assignments and licenses shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of execution.

Any person found to be in possession of counterfeit marks, fully aware of their illicit nature, and intending to sell or distribute such marks, shall be liable for imprisonment. The extent of sentence imprisonment may extend to a term not exceeding three years, or until a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees is paid, or both, as determined by the adjudicating authority. However, if the counterfeit marks are found to be deceptively similar to a registered trade mark under the register sub section pertaining to essential goods such as pharmaceuticals or food items, the term of imprisonment may extend to a maximum of five years. An appeal against the decision of the adjudicating authority shall lie before the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the order. The court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend this period by a further thirty days. Any evidence presented before the adjudicating authority shall be admissible in the appellate proceedings.

Goods imported into India shall be subject to examination as to their origin, and the Trade Marks Registry may, where it has reasonable grounds to believe that goods are not wholly or substantially produced within India, require the importer to furnish a certificate of origin issued by the competent authority in the country of origin. Provided that, if the goods are falsely represented as being produced in India, the Registry may, as provided herein, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register and may also direct the seizure of such goods. Limits India imported shall not apply to goods which have undergone substantial transformation within India, rendering the place of origin immaterial for the purposes of this Act. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding origin may appeal to the Appellate Board.

Goods legitimately manufactured and imported into India shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration, provided that such goods originate from a country that is a party to any reciprocal agreement with India concerning the protection of trademarks. An applicant seeking registration of a trademark for goods limits india imported must furnish evidence of lawful use of the mark in the country of origin, and demonstrate that the mark is distinctive in that jurisdiction. The Registrar may, however, require additional evidence to ascertain the genuineness of the imported goods and the legitimacy of the importer’s claim. Registration shall not be granted if the mark is identical or deceptively similar to an existing registered trademark for identical or similar goods, unless the proprietor of the existing mark provides a no-objection certificate. Any false representation regarding the origin of goods shall be considered grounds for refusal of registration and may attract penalties as provided herein.

Goods legitimately imported into India shall not be subject to seizure under this Act solely on the basis of alleged trademark infringement, provided that the importer demonstrates, through verifiable documentation, prior lawful use of the mark in the originating country. However, this protection shall not extend to goods knowingly manufactured with the intent to deceive, or goods that constitute a manifest imitation likely to cause confusion. Any party alleging infringement relating to limits india imported goods may initiate a complaint before the designated authority, furnishing evidence of both the trademark registration and the deceptive nature of the imported goods. Decisions of the authority shall be subject to appeal to the High Court, with a further right of appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law. The burden of proof regarding lawful use and intent to deceive shall lie with the respective parties asserting such claims, as provided herein.

A registration variety, for the purposes of this Act, shall denote a distinct, uniform and stable plant variety which is novel, being a variety developed from a wild relative or a traditional variety, or a substantially derived variety, or a transgenic variety, or a variety essentially derived from another variety, and which satisfies the criteria for registration as prescribed. The applicant seeking registration of a registration variety shall furnish a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, including its lineage, origin, and propagation methods, along with the results of any trials conducted to demonstrate its distinctness, uniformity and stability. Provided that, a variety which is not substantially similar to any other registered variety, and which possesses a clearly expressed phenotype, may also be considered for registration subject to verification by the Plant Variety Committee.

A variety shall be considered a registration variety only upon full compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein and issuance of a certificate of registration by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. An applicant seeking registration of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety shall submit a detailed description of the morphological, physiological, and biochemical characteristics of said variety, alongside evidence of its novelty. The Authority may, subject to verification of the submitted data and conduct of a growing trial, grant registration if satisfied that the claimed variety meets the criteria for protection. Provided that, a variety essentially derived from a registered variety, possessing the same characteristics as the parent variety except for differences resulting from specific acts of breeding, may also be eligible for registration upon demonstration of such derivation and consent of the breeder of the initial variety. The register of registration varieties shall be maintained and open for public inspection.

A variety proposed for registration shall be deemed to be a ‘registration variety’ if it satisfies the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, as determined through a prescribed process of examination conducted by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The applicant seeking registration of a registration variety shall submit a detailed description of the morphological, physiological and, where applicable, molecular characteristics of the said variety, alongside evidence demonstrating its stability over successive generations. Provided that, a farmers’ variety, being an extant variety traditionally developed by farmers, may be registered subject to a simplified procedure and reduced documentation requirements, as may be specified in the regulations framed under this Act. The Authority may, at its discretion, request additional information or samples from the applicant to facilitate a comprehensive assessment of the proposed registration variety. Any variety found to be essentially derived from another registered variety shall not be eligible for independent registration, unless the consent of the breeder of the initial variety is obtained.

A variety shall be considered a registration variety only upon fulfillment of the criteria as provided herein and subsequent entry into the Plant Varieties Register. To qualify, a variety must demonstrate distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, assessed through a prescribed field trial conducted in accordance with the guidelines established by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. Provided that, for farmers’ varieties, demonstrable distinctiveness based on locally adapted traits and traditional knowledge may be accepted in lieu of formal field trial data. Any applicant seeking registration of a registration variety shall submit a detailed description of the variety, including its lineage, characteristics, and propagation methods. Subject to verification of the submitted information and satisfactory completion of the field trial, the Registrar may grant a certificate of registration, conferring exclusive rights to the breeder or farmer, as applicable, for a specified period. The rights conferred shall be subject to the provisions relating to research and breeding, and the legitimate interests of farmers.

Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety, or their duly authorized agent, shall submit a complete application for registration variety to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, accompanied by the prescribed fee and such evidence as may be required to establish novelty, distinctness, uniformity, and stability. Provided that, a farmer who has bred or developed a new variety shall, subject to the provisions herein, be eligible to register said variety, demonstrating essentially derived varieties are not substantially similar. Failure to accurately disclose the parentage of a registration variety, or any material information relevant to its characteristics, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any false representation made in an application for registration variety shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority may, at its discretion, revoke the registration of any variety found to be in violation of these provisions.

A registration variety, to be considered for protection under this Act, shall demonstrate distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, as evidenced by a detailed description of the plant characteristics submitted with the application for registration. The applicant shall furnish proof of the origin and development of the variety, including the date of first commercialization or availability to the public. Where a mark international registration relating to the variety exists, a certified copy of the international registration and details of the designated countries shall accompany the application. Provided that, the applicant is a person who has effectively contributed to the creation of the variety, or has acquired the right from such a person. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application, subject to an opportunity for rectification as provided herein. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional evidence to verify the veracity of the claims made in the application.

Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, seeking protection as a registration variety under this Act, shall submit a complete application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, accompanied by the prescribed fee and relevant documentation establishing essential characteristics. Provided that, where the variety incorporates a traditionally used varietal name resembling a register trade mark already in use for similar agricultural goods, the applicant shall furnish a no-objection certificate from the trade mark holder or demonstrate non-infringement. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application incomplete and subject to rejection. Any false representation made in an application, or any wilful omission of material facts, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Authority may, subject to inquiry, revoke the registration of any variety found to be obtained through fraudulent means, and the breeder shall be liable for damages.

A “pharmaceutical formulation” shall mean a composition comprising an active pharmaceutical ingredient, together with excipients, carriers, or other non-active components, intended for use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of a disease in humans or animals, and presented in a form suitable for administration. The term “active pharmaceutical ingredient” refers to any substance, or combination of substances, intended to be used as a pharmacologically active agent in a pharmaceutical formulation. Subject to the provisions herein, a pharmaceutical formulation shall be considered distinct from a previously known formulation if it demonstrates a significant improvement in bioavailability, stability, or patient compliance. Any modification to an existing pharmaceutical formulation resulting in a novel polymorph or enantiomer shall also be deemed a pharmaceutical formulation for the purposes of this Act.

A pharmaceutical formulation claiming enhanced bioavailability of a known active pharmaceutical ingredient shall be registrable as a new invention, provided that such enhancement is not obvious to a person skilled in the art and is supported by comparative data demonstrating a statistically significant improvement over the prior art. An application for a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance shall disclose the method of manufacture to the extent necessary to enable a person skilled in the art to carry out the invention. The complete chemical characterization of the pharmaceutical substance, including polymorphs and stereoisomers, shall form part of the specification. Any clinical trial data demonstrating efficacy and safety, though not strictly required at the time of filing, may be submitted during prosecution to support claims of therapeutic utility. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent for a pharmaceutical invention shall be granted for a term of twenty years from the date of filing. Any subsequent modification to the formulation requiring further clinical trials shall be considered a separate invention.

Any pharmaceutical formulation claiming novelty and efficacy, and duly patented under this Act, shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive right to manufacture, use, and sell the said formulation within the territory of India. However, such exclusivity shall be subject to the provisions relating to compulsory licensing, as provided herein, particularly in cases of national emergency or extreme urgency. A person alleging infringement of a patent relating to a pharmaceutical substance may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the defendant from the acts constituting the infringement. The Court, upon being satisfied of the validity of the patent and the infringement, may grant an injunction and also award damages to the patentee, assessed on reasonable royalty or lost profits, whichever is higher. Any appeal from such decision shall lie to the Supreme Court, subject to the conditions stipulated for civil appeals. The patentee shall also have the right to seek recovery of costs associated with legal proceedings.

A pharmaceutical formulation, to be patentable under this Act, shall demonstrate enhanced efficacy as compared to prior art, substantiated by reproducible clinical trials conducted in accordance with internationally recognized standards and documented as provided herein. Any application claiming a new use of a known pharmaceutical substance shall include detailed preclinical and clinical data establishing the novelty and unexpected benefits of said use. The Controller may, subject to verification of data integrity, grant a patent for such a formulation or use. Where a pharmaceutical composition incorporates a naturally occurring substance, the inventive step shall relate to a purification process or novel combination resulting in a non-obvious therapeutic effect. A process for manufacturing a pharmaceutical intermediate, even if not the final drug substance, may be subject to patent protection provided it is novel and involves an inventive step. Any challenge to the patentability of a pharmaceutical invention shall be adjudicated by the appellate board following established procedures for technical evidence submission.

Any pharmaceutical formulation claiming novelty shall be subject to demonstration of enhanced efficacy as compared to existing, publicly known treatments for the same ailment, provided that such existing treatments are legitimately marketed within the territory of India. A manufacturer seeking patent protection for a pharmaceutical substance shall submit comprehensive data regarding clinical trials conducted in accordance with internationally recognized Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The data must demonstrate both therapeutic benefit and an acceptable safety profile. Subject to the provisions herein, a formulation incorporating a known pharmaceutical substance, but utilizing a novel delivery system demonstrably improving bioavailability, may be considered patentable. All applications relating to pharmaceutical compositions shall include a detailed description of the manufacturing process, ensuring reproducibility and quality control. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of any granted patent.

Any person manufacturing a pharmaceutical substance, whether alone or in combination with other active pharmaceutical ingredients, without a valid patent or license as provided herein, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five crore rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or both. Where the infringement relates to a pharmaceutical substance essential for public health, the penalty may be enhanced up to ten crore rupees. Any evidence obtained through search and seizure relating to the illicit manufacture of such substances shall be admissible in court, subject to the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code.
