A person claiming legitimate manufacture shall bear the burden of proving compliance with this Act, including demonstrating the novelty and non-obviousness of the pharmaceutical substance. Repeated offences shall attract cumulative penalties and potential revocation of manufacturing licenses. All seized materials shall be subject to disposal as directed by a designated court.

Any patentee of a pharmaceutical substance, being a process or a product, may grant licenses to other persons to work the patented invention, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon and recorded with the Controller. Where a license is granted in respect of a pharmaceutical substance essential to public health, the Controller may, upon application by any person, direct the patentee to grant a license to that person, if the patentee fails to do so within a reasonable time. Assignment of any right, title or interest in a patent for a pharmaceutical substance shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and all instruments of assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Controller. The assignee shall, for the unexpired term of the patent, possess the same rights as the assignor, provided that the assignee demonstrates sufficient manufacturing capacity for the pharmaceutical substance. Any royalty payments due under an assignment or license agreement shall be determined as per the terms agreed between the parties, but shall not be manifestly unreasonable.

Any pharmaceutical invention claiming a new form of a known substance shall require demonstrable efficacy, and such efficacy shall be substantiated by rigorous clinical trials conducted in accordance with internationally accepted standards, as provided herein. An application for a patent relating to such a pharmaceutical substance may be subject to pre-grant opposition based on lack of inventive step, particularly if the claimed form does not exhibit significantly improved therapeutic properties compared to the prior art. The Controller shall, upon receiving such opposition, issue a hearing notice to the applicant and the objector, allowing both parties to present evidence and arguments. Should the Controller determine that the claimed invention lacks sufficient inventive merit, the application shall be rejected; however, such rejection may be appealed to the Appellate Board. Furthermore, any challenge to the validity of a granted patent relating to a pharmaceutical shall be initiated through a revocation petition before the High Court, subject to the provisions concerning limitation periods as detailed under this Act.

Any registered proprietor of a pharmaceutical invention, being the valid registered proprietor as recorded in the Register of Patents, may grant licenses to others for the commercial exploitation of said invention, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties and consistent with the provisions of this Act. Any assignment of the patent relating to such pharmaceutical invention shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be deemed invalid as against any subsequent assignee or licensee acquiring interest in the patent in good faith. The Controller may, upon application, require the assignee to furnish evidence of valid consideration for the assignment. Where a license is granted for a pharmaceutical substance intended for export, the licensee shall ensure compliance with all applicable international treaties and conventions relating to intellectual property rights. A valid registered proprietor may revoke a license granted under this Act if the licensee fails to adhere to the agreed terms and conditions.

Any pharmaceutical formulation claiming equivalence to a patented composition, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be deemed to infringe the latter unless demonstrated to possess a demonstrable and significant alteration in bioavailability, impacting clinical efficacy. Where a party alleges non-infringement based on such alteration, the burden of proof shall lie with the defendant to establish said difference through rigorous clinical trials conforming to internationally recognized standards. An appeal from the Controller’s decision regarding equivalence, or lack thereof, may be made to the High Court, provided that such appeal is lodged within ninety days of the Controller’s order. Furthermore, treaty means patent provisions dictate that any formulation benefiting from a corresponding patent in a convention country shall be presumed equivalent absent compelling evidence to the contrary, and such presumption may be rebutted only with data satisfying the Controller. Any challenge to this presumption shall be subject to the appellate process as provided herein.

A pharmaceutical substance, for the purposes of this Act, shall be considered novel having regard to its efficacy, safety, and potential therapeutic effect, and must not fall within the exclusions specified herein. Where a claim relates to a pharmaceutical substance derived from or incorporating a breeder registered variety, proof of legitimate access to and use of said variety, consistent with the provisions of the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001, shall be a prerequisite for the grant of a patent. Provided that, the mere discovery of a known pharmaceutical substance in a breeder registered variety, without demonstrable inventive step, shall not be patentable. Any pharmaceutical composition claiming such a substance shall clearly delineate the novel aspects contributing to enhanced therapeutic benefit.

Any pharmaceutical substance claimed in an application for a patent shall be subject to rigorous examination as to its efficacy and safety, conducted by a duly constituted committee of experts appointed by the Controller. The article patented, if a novel dosage form or delivery system of a known pharmaceutical substance, must demonstrate a significant improvement over existing methods to warrant patentability, and such improvement shall be clearly articulated in the complete specification. A patent for a pharmaceutical shall not be granted unless the specification discloses a clear and demonstrable therapeutic benefit. Provided that, in cases where the pharmaceutical substance is a stereoisomer of a known substance, evidence of enhanced pharmacological properties is mandatory. The patentee may be required to submit clinical trial data as evidence of efficacy, subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable to be refused.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Board of Appeal to hear and dispose of appeals from the decisions of the Controller of Patents. Such Board shall consist of a President and such number of other members as the Central Government may deem necessary, possessing such qualifications as may be prescribed. The Central Government shall appoint the President and members of the Board, and shall have the power to remove them from office. All expenses incurred by the Board in the exercise of its functions, including salaries, allowances and travelling allowances payable to the President and other members, shall be charged to the Consolidated Fund of India. Provided that the Board may, with the approval of the Central Government, accept fees for any service rendered.

The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Registry of Plant Varieties, which shall be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. The central government shall appoint a Registrar of Plant Varieties who shall be the chief executive officer of the Registry. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the central government may, by regulations, provide for the procedures relating to the application for registration of new, distinct, uniform and stable varieties of plants. Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new variety may apply for registration, provided that the variety conforms to the criteria as laid down in the regulations. The central government shall maintain a database of all registered plant varieties and make it accessible to the public. The Registrar may, with the approval of the central government, prescribe fees for all applications, registrations, and other services provided by the Registry.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Intellectual Property Fund for the promotion of patent awareness and facilitation of patent filing by micro, small and medium enterprises. All contributions made to the Fund, including grants received from international agencies and any revenue generated from the Fund’s investments, shall be credited to the said Fund and utilized for the purposes as prescribed. Any unutilized amount remaining at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next financial year. The Central Government shall constitute a governing council to administer the Fund, comprising representatives from the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks, and relevant industry associations. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the governing council may formulate policies regarding the disbursement of funds and the criteria for eligibility of applicants. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the governing council may prefer an appeal to the Central Government, whose decision shall be final.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Committee of Experts to advise it on matters concerning the promotion of indigenous patent activity and the enhancement of technological capabilities within the nation. Such Committee shall consist of not more than fifteen members, appointed from amongst persons possessing expertise in science, technology, law, and commerce. The Committee shall submit its recommendations to the Central Government within six months of its constitution, unless otherwise directed. Any expenditure incurred by the Committee shall be borne by the Central Government, subject to budgetary allocations as approved by Parliament. Provided that, the Central Government may, if deemed necessary, dissolve the Committee prior to the expiry of the six-month period. All rules and procedures relating to the functioning of the Committee, including quorum and voting, shall be as prescribed by the Central Government. The decisions of the Committee shall be advisory in nature and not binding on the Controller of Patents.

The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Intellectual Property Fund for the purpose of promoting innovation and facilitating the commercialization of patented inventions. Contributions to the Fund shall be accepted from government sources, private entities, and international organizations, subject to such terms and conditions as the central government deems appropriate. Any expenditure incurred from the Fund shall be audited annually by a chartered accountant appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Provided that, the central government shall ensure that the Fund is utilized primarily for supporting research and development activities in areas of national importance, and for providing financial assistance to small and medium enterprises engaged in the exploitation of patented technologies. The central government may also formulate guidelines regarding the prioritization of applications for financial assistance, considering factors such as the potential for import substitution and employment generation, as provided herein. All records pertaining to the Fund shall be open to inspection by authorized officers.

Any person contravening the provisions relating to compulsory licensing, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a dedicated fund for the purposes of administering penalties collected under this Act and for promoting indigenous patent development. Should the Central Government deem that a patentee has failed to adequately work a patented invention within a period of three years from the date of grant, despite reasonable efforts by any licensee, it may direct the patentee to grant additional licenses on reasonable terms. Failure to comply with such direction shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees, continuing until compliance is achieved, and the Central Government’s decision in this regard shall be final. Any appeal against the imposition of penalties shall lie before the Appellate Board.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Fund for the Promotion of Patent Commercialization and Technology Transfer, to which contributions may be made by any person or entity, and the Fund shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government. Any patent holder desiring to assign or license a patent for public benefit, particularly in sectors of national importance as determined by the Central Government, shall submit an application to the committee outlining the terms proposed for such assignment or license. The committee, subject to ensuring fair and reasonable terms, may approve the assignment or license, and shall register the same with the patent office. Where the patent holder and the intended assignee or licensee fail to reach agreement, the committee may, with the approval of the Central Government, direct compulsory licensing under such terms as it deems fit, provided that adequate remuneration is paid to the patent holder. All revenues generated from licenses granted through the National Fund shall be credited to the Fund and utilized for further promotion of patent commercialization.

The central government may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to payment of the requisite fee, direct that a patent, even if validly granted under this Act, be revoked where the patented invention is determined to be essential for purposes of defense, or atomic energy, or public health emergencies declared by the appropriate authority. Any person aggrieved by such direction of the central government may, within sixty days of the order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board established under the administrative financial rules. Provided that, such appeal shall not operate as a stay of the revocation order unless specifically directed by the Appellate Board. The central government shall, prior to issuing any such direction, provide the patentee with a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to present evidence in rebuttal of the grounds for revocation, and any failure to do so shall render the direction voidable. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to the writ jurisdiction of the High Court.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that any patentable invention relating to national defense or atomic energy, even if it meets the criteria for patentability as provided herein, shall not be subject to licensing to any person other than entities authorized by the Central Government. Any infringing copy manufactured or imported in contravention of such direction shall be deemed to be an infringement of this Act, and the Central Government shall have the exclusive right to institute proceedings for such infringement. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Central Government may, in cases where an infringing copy is seized, dispose of the same by destruction or other means as it deems fit, and shall account for any proceeds derived therefrom. Provided that, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Central Government under this provision may, within sixty days, appeal to a designated High Court. The Central Government’s exercise of these powers shall be subject to judicial review.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that all patents relating to national emergency or varieties of plants shall vest in the Government undertaking designated for that purpose, subject to the payment of reasonable royalties as may be determined by the said Government undertaking. Any application for a patent in respect of such inventions or varieties, filed prior to such direction, shall, notwithstanding anything contained herein, be deemed to have been filed with the designated Government undertaking. The Central Government shall ensure that the designated undertaking possesses the requisite expertise and infrastructure for the effective exploitation of such patents. Provided that, any direction issued under this provision shall be subject to a review after a period of five years, and the Central Government may, based on such review, modify or revoke the direction. Compliance with the royalty determination process is mandatory for all parties involved.

A commission offence attributable to a person shall be deemed to have been committed if the act constituting the offence was directly authorised, ordered, or knowingly permitted by that person, whether as a principal officer, director, manager, secretary, or other similar position within a corporate body or other entity. Where the offence involves a failure to fulfil a duty as provided herein, such failure attributable to the negligence of any employee acting within the scope of their employment shall be considered a commission offence by the person responsible for the supervision of that employee. Subject to the provisions of this Act, proof of consent or knowledge shall lie on the party alleging it. Any benefit derived from the commission of an offence shall be recoverable as if it were a penalty.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, publishes or offers for sale any patented invention as if it were a genuine article manufactured under a valid patent, or knowingly sells or exposes for sale any such counterfeit article, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence attributable to a violation of the exclusive rights conferred by this Act. Where a commission offence is committed by a partnership firm, each partner shall be held jointly and severally liable, subject to proof of their active participation in, or knowledge of, the offence. The patent holder, or their duly authorized agent, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the offender from further acts of infringement and for recovery of damages sustained due to the deceptive practices. Provided that no such application shall be entertained unless the patent holder demonstrates a reasonable likelihood of continued commercial prejudice. Any evidence obtained through lawful means shall be admissible in proceedings relating to such offences, and the burden of proving due diligence in preventing the commission of the offence shall lie with the accused.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, publishes or offers for sale any patented invention as if it were a genuine article, or knowingly sells, offers for sale, or distributes any article so resembling a patented invention as to be calculated to cause confusion or deception, shall be deemed to have committed a commission offence attributable to a fraudulent intent. Where such an offence is committed by a partnership firm, each partner shall be held jointly and severally liable, subject to proof of their active participation in the deceptive practice. The Controller may, upon receiving credible information of such activity, initiate an inquiry and require the alleged offender to furnish evidence regarding the origin and authenticity of the goods in question. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall be considered an aggravation of the offence. Any evidence obtained during such inquiry shall be admissible in proceedings before any court. Provided that, no prosecution shall be initiated without prior approval of the Controller.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, publishes or offers for sale any patented invention as if it were his own, or knowing it to be falsely marked, shall be guilty of a commission offence attributable to fraudulent intent, and shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where such offence is committed by a corporation, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the corporation, as well as the corporation itself, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable to the same punishment, subject to proof of their knowledge or consent. The Controller may, in cases of minor infringement not amounting to a commission offence, issue a cease and desist notice, and repeated non-compliance with such notice shall attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Any assignment of a patent application or a patent, whether complete or partial, shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the assignment, including the geographical territory and field of use, if any, to which the assignment relates. Where an assignment is made in contravention of any condition stipulated in a license granted under this Act, it shall be deemed a commission offence attributable to the assignor, and the assignee may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, seek redressal from the appropriate court. A licensee, having obtained a license for a specific field of use, may not assign rights extending beyond that field without the prior written consent of the patentee. Failure to obtain such consent shall render any subsequent assignment voidable at the option of the patentee, and may constitute a further commission offence attributable to the licensee. Any person aggrieved by an unlawful assignment may apply to the court for an injunction restraining further exploitation of the patent.

Any commission offence attributable to a person acting on behalf of a patentee, or a licensee, or a person deriving title under them, shall also be deemed to be a commission offence by the patentee, licensee, or person deriving title, notwithstanding any contract to the contrary, unless such patentee, licensee, or person deriving title proves that the act constituting the offence was committed without their knowledge or consent and that they exercised all due diligence to prevent such commission offence. However, a finding of no due diligence shall not be made if the accused party demonstrates reasonable reliance on a qualified and independent legal counsel’s advice regarding the permissible scope of the patent claim in question. Any appeal against a determination of commission offence shall be made to the High Court, and such appeal must be filed within ninety days of the lower court’s decision, subject to potential extension granted by the High Court for sufficient cause.

A commission offence attributable to any person shall be deemed to have been committed if such person, with knowledge of the relevant facts, directly causes another to commit the offence, or abets the commission of the offence. Where a person engages in conduct that, though not directly constituting a commission offence, facilitates or encourages another to commit such an offence, and such facilitation or encouragement is known to the first person, liability shall vest accordingly. A design shall not be considered deceptively similar to an existing design if the differences between them are substantial and would be readily apparent to an informed user. Subject to the provisions herein, the burden of proving lack of knowledge or intent shall lie upon the accused. Any person convicted of a commission offence shall be liable to the penalties as prescribed.

Any commission offence attributable to a registered collective mark holder, whether a body corporate or otherwise, shall extend to all persons authorized by such holder to use the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, subject to proof of such authorization and the scope thereof. Where a collective mark is registered, any act in contravention of the conditions of registration, or any use of the mark in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion, shall constitute a commission offence. The mark owner may, prior to initiating proceedings, serve a notice requiring cessation of the infringing activity and outlining the terms of acceptable use. Provided that failure to serve such notice shall not invalidate any subsequent legal action, but may be considered by the adjudicating authority when determining appropriate remedies. Any person knowingly assisting in such an offence shall also be deemed to have committed an offence as provided herein.

Any commission offence attributable to a patented process for the production of a novel food substance, or a significant modification thereof, shall be subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein. Where such offence involves the deliberate misrepresentation of the food substance as originating from a lawfully patented process, or the knowing sale of food produced through an infringing process, the patent holder may, in addition to seeking injunctive relief and damages, apply to the appropriate court for an order directing the destruction of the infringing food product. Such destruction shall be at the expense of the offender. A person who aids, abets, or conspires with another in the commission of such an offence shall be liable as a principal offender, subject to the provisions of the Indian Penal Code. Provided that, a bona fide purchaser of the food substance, unaware of the infringement, shall not be held liable for the commission offence, but may be required to recall the product.

Any commission offence attributable to a person involved in the production or distribution of a cinematographic film, as understood under the provisions relating to producer relation cinematograph, shall be investigated by an officer duly authorized by the Controller of Patents. Such officer may, subject to the obtaining of a warrant issued by a Judicial Magistrate of First Class, enter any premises where reasonable suspicion exists of evidence pertaining to the offence being retained. The Controller shall maintain a register of all such investigations, detailing the nature of the alleged offence, the particulars of the accused, and the evidence collected. Where the offence involves the unauthorized use of a patented invention in the creation of the cinematographic work, the rights holder may submit a detailed report to the Controller, outlining the extent of the infringement. Failure to comply with the requirements as provided herein regarding the submission of such reports shall render the rights holder liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. Any evidence obtained during the investigation shall be admissible in any subsequent legal proceedings.

Any person who commits an offence relating to the use of an unregistered trade mark, or a falsely applied trade mark, or any other offence under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and the court may, in addition to such penalty, order the seizure and destruction of the goods bearing such mark. Where a commission alleged offence is established, the court may, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, direct the defendant to pay compensatory damages to the aggrieved party, assessed on the basis of actual loss suffered or likely to be suffered, or, in the absence of provable loss, a sum not exceeding the assessed value of the infringing goods. Provided that, such order for damages shall be subject to a period of limitation of two years from the date of the offence. The court may also issue an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing mark, and any disobedience of such injunction shall constitute a separate offence punishable under this Act.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a person is reasonably suspected of committing an offence relating to the use of a trade mark not owned by them, and such use constitutes a commission alleged offence, the registered proprietor may, prior to any formal complaint, demand a full accounting of profits derived from such unauthorized use. Provided that, such demand shall not prejudice the proprietor’s right to pursue statutory remedies as provided herein. A licensee of a trade mark may, with the express written consent of the registered proprietor, assign their license rights to a third party, subject to the terms and conditions of the original license agreement. Failure to register an assignment or license shall render it unenforceable against any subsequent purchaser or licensee of the trade mark. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be adjudicated by the High Court.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered trade mark alleging non-use, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain if the application meets the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application satisfy these requirements, the register court may direct the registered proprietor to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days. Evidence in support of continued use, or a justifiable reason for non-use, shall be submitted alongside the counter-statement. Failure to comply with this direction shall be deemed an admission of non-use, subject to further scrutiny by the register court. Any party aggrieved by an order of the register court may appeal to the High Court. The register court shall maintain a record of all rectification proceedings.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of the register under this Act, cause a notice to be served upon the proprietor of the trade mark, specifying the grounds of rectification and requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days. Provided that, where the application for rectification alleges bad faith on the part of the applicant for registration, the register court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the period for filing a counter-statement. Any evidence submitted by either party shall be admissible before the register court, and the court may, at its discretion, require further evidence or the examination of witnesses. The register court shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, deliver a reasoned order either upholding or dismissing the application for rectification, and such order shall be final and binding, unless appealed to a higher court as provided herein. All proceedings before the register court shall be conducted in accordance with rules prescribed by the Central Government.

The register court shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging a false designation of origin or a false representation of goods, conduct a preliminary inquiry to ascertain the veracity of the claims made therein and whether a prima facie case exists for the alleged infringement. Subject to the provisions herein, the register court may, if satisfied that a case for infringement exists, issue a notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to demonstrate non-infringement or to submit to an order for rectification. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the register court may appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the order. The register court shall maintain a record of all complaints, inquiries, and orders issued, and such record shall be open to inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee. Where a party fails to comply with an order of the register court, the court may impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered trade mark alleging non-use, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the application meets the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application be deemed procedurally deficient, the register court may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, dismiss the application with reasoned order. Where the application is found to be procedurally sound, notice shall be issued to the registered proprietor, requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding two months. Failure to file such counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an admission of the allegations contained in the application. Evidence in support of either the application or the counter-statement may be presented to the register court, subject to such rules of evidence as may be prescribed. The register court shall, after considering the evidence and submissions, render a decision, which shall be final and binding, unless appealed to a higher court. Any party aggrieved by the decision of the register court may, within sixty days, file an appeal before the appellate board.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of the register under this Act, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the application meets the procedural requirements as prescribed and is accompanied by the requisite fee. Should the application satisfy these initial criteria, the register court may direct the proprietor of the trade mark in question to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such direction. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an admission of the grounds for rectification, subject to further scrutiny by the register court. Any evidence submitted by either party shall be admissible, provided that it is relevant and obtained in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The register court shall, after considering all evidence and submissions, issue a reasoned order either allowing or dismissing the application for rectification, and such order shall be final and binding, unless appealed to a higher court as provided herein.

Any person who falsifies or materially alters any document required to be maintained by the register court shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The register court may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the rectification of any false or materially altered entry in the register. Any application for rectification made fraudulently or with intent to mislead the register court shall be deemed a cognizable offence under this Act. Provided that, no rectification shall be ordered unless the applicant has satisfied the register court that substantial grounds exist for believing the falsification was unintentional. Where a registered proprietor knowingly makes a false representation to the register court regarding use of the trade mark, they shall forfeit all rights to renew the registration, and a further penalty of ₹50,000 may be levied. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The register court shall, upon application made in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee, record the assignment in the register of trade marks. Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, the register court may, if it deems fit, require evidence of the assignment of any associated rights, including but not limited to, domain names and business registrations. An assignment shall not be operative against any person who acquires an interest in the trade mark before the assignment is registered, unless such person had actual notice of the assignment. Provided that, the register court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it may think fit, direct that an assignment take effect retrospectively, if it is satisfied that the assignee is a bona fide purchaser for value. Any dispute concerning the validity of an assignment shall be determined by the register court.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration, or requiring amendment of an application for registration, may, within a period of one month from the date of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The register court shall, upon receipt of a notice of appeal and prescribed fee, fix a date for hearing and shall issue directions for the production of relevant documents and evidence. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the time for filing an appeal. Any party desiring to adduce expert evidence relating to the distinctiveness of a mark or the likelihood of confusion shall notify the register court at least thirty days prior to the hearing. Failure to comply with this provision may result in such evidence being inadmissible. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The register court shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging infringement of a registered trade mark and accompanied by a duly sworn affidavit detailing the nature of the alleged infringement, issue a notice to the alleged infringer requiring them to demonstrate cause why an order of injunction should not be issued. Any goods suspected of infringing a registered trade mark and arriving into India may, subject to the provisions of the Customs Act 1962, be notified to the Principal Customs Officer for detention. Provided that the complainant shall deposit with the register court a sum equivalent to the estimated value of the infringing goods, as security for potential damages. The register court may, at its discretion, direct a preliminary inquiry to ascertain the prima facie case before issuing any injunction. All evidence submitted shall be subject to cross-examination, and the register court shall maintain a complete record of proceedings. Any party aggrieved by an order of the register court may appeal to the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered trade mark alleging non-use, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the application satisfies the requirements as prescribed manner. Should the application be deemed incomplete or lacking necessary documentation, the register court may, within thirty days of receipt, issue a notice to the applicant requesting rectification of the deficiencies. Failure to comply with such notice within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable to be dismissed. However, provided that the register court finds the application to be properly formatted and supported by sufficient evidence, it shall proceed to notify the proprietor of the trade mark, affording them a period of sixty days to submit a counter-statement. Any evidence submitted by either party shall be subject to verification and may be examined under oath, as provided herein, to ensure its veracity and relevance.

The register court shall maintain a comprehensive record of all applications for rectification of the register, and any failure to accurately update the entry register shall be deemed a contravention of this Act. Any person who knowingly provides false or misleading information in an application for rectification, or during proceedings before the register court, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, if the false information relates to a matter of opinion and not of fact, the penalty shall be a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees. The register court may, subject to the provisions herein, direct the removal of any improperly registered trade mark and impose costs upon the applicant who brought forth the false claim. All orders of the register court are final and binding, save for appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

The Registrar, when considering an application for registration of a trade mark, shall ensure strict compliance with the criteria for distinctiveness as provided herein. Any application failing to demonstrate inherent or acquired distinctiveness shall be subject to objection and may be refused. However, the Registrar may, subject to the rules framed under this Act, request evidence of acquired distinctiveness through actual use in commerce, provided that such use is substantial and extends to a reasonable geographical area. All requests for evidence shall be communicated in writing, specifying the deficiencies in the application and granting the applicant a period of sixty days to respond. The Registrar’s decisions regarding distinctiveness are subject to appeal, but such appeals shall not suspend the requirement for ongoing compliance with all relevant provisions of this Act. Any evidence submitted shall be considered in accordance with the established registrar subject rules and principles of natural justice.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign, transfer or license the rights in the geographical indication, or any interest therein, to any other person or entity. Any assignment, transfer or license shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry, failing which such assignment, transfer or license shall be void. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause being shown, refuse to register an assignment, transfer or license if it is demonstrated that the proposed assignee or licensee does not possess the requisite expertise or facilities to maintain the quality and reputation of the goods uses geographical indication. A licensee shall be entitled to use the geographical indication only for the purposes and within the geographical area specified in the license agreement, and shall be subject to quality control measures as prescribed by the registered proprietor. The registered proprietor may, as provided herein, revoke a license upon material breach of its terms.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an appeal before the Appellate Board against any decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or revoking the registration thereof, or modifying the register in respect of any geographical indication. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to errors apparent from the record, and shall not extend to a re-evaluation of evidence already considered by the Registrar. However, if the Appellate Board finds that the Registrar erred in determining that the claimed goods did not possess the requisite qualities, characteristics, or reputation associated with the specified geographical origin, it may direct the Registrar to reconsider the application. A determination that goods uses geographical indications improperly, or that the link between the goods and their geographical origin is weak or non-existent, constitutes valid grounds for refusal or revocation, and such decisions are final, save for the appeal process outlined herein. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the applicant to deposit costs associated with the appeal.

A geographical indication shall be considered a used geographical indication when it is applied in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and demonstrably indicates the origin of goods to the relevant public. Such use shall extend to the application of the geographical indication to the goods themselves, or to packaging wherein the goods are contained, presented, or transported for commercial purposes. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to conditions as may be prescribed, authorize another person to use the said geographical indication in relation to goods conforming to the standards specified. However, such authorization shall not diminish the original proprietor’s right to initiate legal proceedings for any infringement of the geographical indication as provided herein, and any such authorized use must be consistent with maintaining the reputation of the geographical indication.

A geographical indication, once registered under this Act, constitutes a ‘used geographical indication’ when it is applied to goods in a manner that indicates a connection between the goods and the geographical area denoting their origin. The application of a used geographical indication shall be visibly displayed on the goods or their packaging, and must be prominently placed so as to be easily noticeable by consumers. Any person dealing in goods bearing a used geographical indication shall maintain a register of such usage, detailing the quantity of goods, the period of use, and the geographical area of sale. Failure to maintain such a register may render the continued use of the geographical indication subject to review. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions herein, authorize other producers within the defined geographical area to use the used geographical indication through licensing agreements, ensuring consistent quality and origin. Any unauthorized use shall be considered an infringement.

Any person who, in the course of trade, causes any damage to the reputation of a registered geographical indication, or engages in unfair competition by reason of its use, shall be liable to legal proceedings for infringement as provided herein. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for relief. Where a used geographical indication is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public, or is likely to unfairly injure the character or reputation of the registered geographical indication, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the indication. The Court may also, at the request of the registered proprietor, order the removal of the used geographical indication from the goods, packaging, or any other materials in respect of which it is applied. Furthermore, the Court may direct the destruction or forfeiture of goods bearing such indication, or award damages to the registered proprietor for loss suffered. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the High Court.

A geographical indication, once registered under this Act, shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the said geographical indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. Any use of a registered geographical indication by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a person duly authorized by him, shall constitute an infringement of the exclusive right. However, an honest use of a descriptive term corresponding to a geographical indication, not constituting an act of unfair competition, shall not be deemed to be an infringement. 

Where a geographical indication has fallen into disuse in relation to the goods for which it was registered, the Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard, revoke the registration. A used geographical indication, even if not registered, may be protected under common law principles of passing off, subject to demonstrating sufficient goodwill and likelihood of deception. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and related particulars.

A geographical indication shall be considered a used geographical indication when it is demonstrably applied in trade, and the proprietor thereof maintains evidence of such use, including records of sales, marketing materials, and production volumes, subject to verification by the Registrar. Any individual or entity claiming rights in a used geographical indication shall submit a declaration detailing the nature and duration of such use, along with geographical boundaries where the goods bearing the indication are traded. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of continued use, or a reasonable explanation for temporary cessation, may result in the removal of the indication from the Register. The Registrar may, however, consider extenuating circumstances such as natural disasters or unforeseen market disruptions when assessing compliance with these provisions, provided that a remediation plan is submitted within ninety days of the event. A registered proprietor shall also ensure quality control measures are in place to maintain the reputation associated with the used geographical indication.

Any person who, in the course of trade, causes any damage to the reputation of a registered geographical indication, or engages in the false application of a used geographical indication, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such instance. Where a used geographical indication has been falsely applied to goods not originating from the region to which it refers, the Registrar may, upon application by the registered proprietor, order the removal of such indication from those goods and any associated packaging. Any goods bearing a falsely applied used geographical indication, or any material enabling such application, shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure. Furthermore, repeated violations, as determined by the Registrar, may result in imprisonment not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The registered proprietor may also seek injunctive relief to prevent further infringement, as provided herein.

Any person who, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, or authorized user thereof, desires to assign or license the right to use the said geographical indication, or any part thereof, shall execute an instrument of assignment or license in writing, specifying the goods in respect of which the assignment or license shall be effective. The instrument shall also define the geographical area in which the assigned or licensed right to use the used geographical indication shall be exercisable, and any conditions relating to the quality of the goods bearing the indication, ensuring maintenance of reputation. Subject to the provisions of this Act, such assignment or license may be subject to royalty or other consideration, and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registry may, upon application, record the assignment or license and a certified copy thereof shall be furnished to the parties concerned. Failure to register an assignment or license shall not invalidate it, but such assignment or license shall not be enforceable against any person other than the parties thereto.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a used geographical indication, or by any modification made by the Registrar in the register of geographical indications, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order of the Registrar. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and shall record the reasons for its decision. A geographical indication, once registered as used, shall not be subject to further challenge on the grounds of descriptiveness, unless it can be proven that the continued use has led to its genericization and loss of distinctiveness. However, a registered proprietor of a used geographical indication may initiate proceedings for infringement if another party applies the said indication to identical or similar goods not originating from the specified geographical area, subject to the provisions relating to prior use and honest practices. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available by way of writ petition to the High Court.

A geographical indication shall be considered a used geographical indication when it is applied in accordance with the provisions of this Act, in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered, and in a manner that distinguishes those goods from other goods of the same kind. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply the used geographical indication to goods not previously included in the register, provided that such goods originate from the specified geographical area and possess the qualities and characteristics associated with that area. Any application of a used geographical indication shall be consistent with established standards of fair trade practices and shall not be misleading to the public regarding the goods’ origin or quality, relating registered particulars to the actual characteristics of the goods.

A geographical indication, once registered and lawfully used in relation to goods originating from a defined geographical area, constitutes a used geographical indication and is subject to the provisions of this Act concerning its continued protection. Any natural or legal person demonstrating a legitimate and continuous use of a used geographical indication, as evidenced by documented sales and trade records extending at least five years prior to the date of application, may seek enhanced protection under this Act. An application claiming priority based on a 73 convention application shall be accompanied by certified copies demonstrating the original filing date and scope of protection sought in the country of origin. Failure to provide such documentation, or evidence of legitimate use, shall render the application incomplete and subject to rejection. The Registrar may, however, request additional evidence to ascertain the veracity of claims regarding the use of the geographical indication, and the applicant shall comply within a period of sixty days from the date of such request.

Any person registered as the proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of the right, title, and interest therein, subject to the provisions of this Act and any regulations made thereunder. Any assignment or transfer of a geographical indication shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry to be effective against third parties. The registered proprietor may, by a license in writing, permit other persons to use the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered, specifying the conditions of use, including the area of operation, quality control standards, and duration of the license. Where a geographical indication is assigned or licensed, the assignee or licensee shall be entitled to the same rights and remedies as the original proprietor, provided that such rights and remedies are not expressly limited by the terms of the assignment or license. A collective right holder, acting on behalf of producers of goods associated with a particular geographical area, may also grant licenses as provided herein, ensuring equitable benefit sharing amongst its members and maintaining the integrity of the plaintiff right geographical indication.

Any person claiming a right to a geographical indication, as provided herein, shall submit a detailed representation of the goods’ origins and characteristics to the Trade Marks Registrar, accompanied by a statement of proposed use. Should the Registrar determine the representation insufficient or lacking clarity, they may require further particulars within a period not exceeding thirty days. A refusal to comply with such a requirement shall be deemed a waiver of the claim. Where a dispute arises concerning the authenticity of the claimed geographical indication, any aggrieved party may file an appeal with the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be heard within ninety days of the filing date, and the Board’s decision shall be final, subject to a writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of natural justice. The burden of proof regarding the plaintiff right geographical indication rests with the claimant.

A geographical indication complained of, for the purposes of remedies under this Act, shall be deemed to be falsely applied if such indication does not correspond to the goods originating from the geographical area as defined in the register maintained by the Geographical Indications Registry. The proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute civil proceedings for infringement, subject to the provisions herein. Any person dealing in goods with a falsely applied geographical indication, or falsely representing such goods as originating from a specific geographical area, shall be liable to injunction and damages. However, a defendant may demonstrate that their use of the geographical indication was descriptive of the goods and not intended to deceive, and that reasonable steps were taken to verify the origin of the goods. Provided that, the court may, at its discretion, order the destruction of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication.

Any person claiming a geographical indication, as provided herein, shall apply for registration in the manner prescribed, furnishing a statement of case including an indication of the goods, their geographical origin, and details of the inspection undertaken to ascertain authenticity. The application shall also include a statement of the conditions governing the production and processing of the goods, demonstrating a consistent character, quality, or reputation attributable to that geographical origin. Where a geographical indication is sought to be registered for agricultural goods, proof of adherence to established standards or certifications relating to organic farming or sustainable practices may be submitted to support the claim. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed necessary, require further evidence or clarification regarding the geographical indication complained of, or conduct independent verification to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. A registered geographical indication shall be valid for ten years, renewable upon application and payment of the prescribed fee.

Any person aggrieved by the misrepresentation or improper use of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute a civil suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a court of competent jurisdiction. The proprietor of a geographical indication, or those authorized by them, may seek an order restraining the defendant from manufacturing or trading goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Damages awarded shall be commensurate with the injury suffered, and may include loss of profits, brand reputation, and costs associated with corrective advertising, subject to proof of actual loss. 

Provided that, where the defendant proves they were unaware and had no reasonable grounds to believe the use constituted an infringement of the geographical indication complained of, the court may award only nominal damages. A court may, as an alternative to damages, grant an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unlawful use, and order its delivery to the proprietor. Any order of injunction issued under this Act shall be enforceable by the court.

Any person aggrieved by any infringement of a registered geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred. The suit shall be instituted within a period of three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement, provided that the Court may extend this period for reasons to be recorded in writing, but not exceeding a further period of three months. Where a complaint of infringement of a geographical indication is made to the police, the officer in charge of the police station shall, if he considers it necessary, register a case and investigate the matter. 

Any false application for registration of a geographical indication, or any false representation as to the origin of goods bearing a geographical indication, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine as prescribed. A registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringement, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to the unlawful use of the geographical indication complained of.

Any person alleging an infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, prior to initiating proceedings before a court, furnish a written notice to the alleged infringer detailing the nature of the infringement and requiring cessation of the unlawful activity. Failure to provide such notice shall be subject to dismissal of the complaint, provided that the court may, at its discretion, condone the non-compliance upon demonstration of extenuating circumstances. A geographical indication complained of must be demonstrably linked to the origin of the goods, and evidence of such linkage, including traditional knowledge and production methods, shall be submitted as part of the complaint. The Registrar may, upon receiving a substantiated complaint, initiate an investigation and issue a cease and desist order pending adjudication. Any person found to be falsely representing goods as originating from a specific geographical area shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed under this Act, and the goods may be seized and destroyed. Compliance with labelling requirements, as detailed in the rules, is mandatory for all registered geographical indications.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely applies a geographical indication to goods, or sells, offers for sale, or distributes goods bearing such falsely applied geographical indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where a contravention involves goods of a value exceeding five lakh rupees, the court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of the offending goods. Any person aggrieved by the false application of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit for injunction and damages. The Registrar, upon receiving a complaint of a geographical indication complained of, may initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied, direct the relevant authorities to take necessary action.

Any assignment of a registered geographical indication shall be subject to an application in writing to the Geographical Indications Registry, and such Registry may, if satisfied that the assignment is in the public interest and does not prejudice the reputation of the geographical indication, register the assignment. A licensee of a registered geographical indication may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license to another party, provided that the assignor obtains prior written consent from the registered proprietor of the geographical indication complained of, and such consent shall not be unreasonably withheld. Where a geographical indication is assigned without registration as provided herein, the assignment shall be void, and the original proprietor shall continue to be the owner of the right. The registered proprietor may, by instrument in writing, revoke any assignment made under this Act, subject to a period of ninety days’ notice to the assignee and any affected licensees. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or revocation shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar refusing to register a geographical indication, or varying the terms of registration, or cancelling a registration, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within three months from the date of the decision of the Registrar, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the said decision and the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Where the appeal relates to a geographical indication complained of as being deceptively similar to a registered geographical indication, the Board shall consider evidence regarding the reputation and distinctiveness of the registered indication, as well as the likelihood of confusion among consumers. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the time for filing an appeal, but not beyond a further period of thirty days. Any person dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may apply to the High Court.

Any person alleging a false application of a geographical indication, or a misrepresentation concerning goods bearing a registered geographical indication, shall submit a complaint to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed. The complaint shall clearly delineate the geographical indication complained of, specifying the region of origin and the goods to which it applies, and shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the misrepresentation or false application. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication seeks to extend the scope of protection to a modification or improvement of the original good, a patent of addition may be pursued, subject to demonstrating a clear and direct nexus between the original geographical indication and the modified product. Failure to provide sufficient evidence or adhere to the prescribed format for complaints may result in rejection. The Registrar, upon receiving a valid complaint, shall initiate an inquiry and may require further information from the complainant or the alleged infringer, as provided herein. Any order issued following such inquiry shall be subject to appeal.

A geographical indication complained of shall be subject to opposition proceedings as provided herein, wherein any person may file a notice of opposition with the Registrar, alleging that the geographical indication is not descriptive of the goods in relation to their origin, or that its registration would be contrary to public policy or morality. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such notice, serve a copy upon the applicant for registration and shall, after affording both parties an opportunity of being heard, submit the case to the Opposition Board. The Opposition Board shall, after examining the evidence and representations, issue a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the opposition, and such order shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court. Any evidence submitted before the Opposition Board shall be treated as confidential.

The application for registration of a new plant variety shall be made to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed. Every applicant seeking registration shall submit a detailed description of the plant variety, including its lineage, characteristics, stability, and uniformity, alongside results of a variety trial conducted at institutions recognized by the india department agriculture. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to furnish additional information or samples for verification. A breeder who has substantially contributed to the creation of the variety, even if not the applicant, shall be duly acknowledged in the registration certificate. Provided that, where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, the applicant shall demonstrate significant characteristics distinguishing it from the initial variety, as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all registered plant varieties.

Any person cultivating a registered plant variety who harvests or propagates the said variety commercially without authorization from the breeder, or any designated agent, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement as provided herein, and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The india department agriculture, acting through its designated officers, may conduct inspections of agricultural holdings to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act, and any obstruction of such inspection shall attract a fine of up to twenty-five thousand rupees. Provided that, a farmer who is in possession of farm-saved seed of a registered variety, for purposes of propagation on his own land, shall be exempt from the penalties outlined herein, subject to adherence to the prescribed benefit-sharing mechanisms. Any appeal against a penalty imposed under this Act shall lie before the designated Appellate Authority within sixty days of the order. Failure to comply with a lawful order of the Appellate Authority shall be punishable by imprisonment, which may extend to one year.

Any person deriving economic benefit from the exploitation of a registered plant variety, including the production, sale, marketing, distribution, import, or export of such variety, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding benefit sharing and compulsory licensing. The India department agriculture, acting through its designated officers, may grant licenses to utilize a protected variety where a reasonable request for a voluntary license has been refused, and the variety is deemed essential for public interest or for the development of new varieties. 

Such licenses shall be non-exclusive and granted on terms determined by the Authority, considering the legitimate interests of both the breeder and the licensee, and shall be subject to adequate remuneration. Assignment of rights relating to a registered variety requires prior written consent of the breeder and notification to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the registration or imposition of penalties as provided herein, and the department may initiate proceedings for infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, “crop sciences indian” shall mean the body of knowledge, both traditional and modern, relating to the development, improvement, and sustainable utilization of plant varieties indigenous to India, encompassing agronomy, plant breeding, plant physiology, plant pathology, and related disciplines. This definition includes, but is not limited to, techniques of seed production, propagation, and conservation relevant to Indian agricultural conditions. A registered plant breeder or a farmer possessing demonstrably unique and stable germplasm, as evidenced by records maintained for a period of not less than three years, may contribute to the advancement of crop sciences indian. Any innovation arising from the application of traditional knowledge shall be subject to provisions regarding benefit sharing, as provided herein, ensuring equitable access and reward for knowledge holders.

Any person claiming to have essentially derived a variety, as defined under this Act, shall submit an application for registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed description of the characteristics of the derived variety, including its lineage and the parent variety from which it was derived. The applicant shall also furnish evidence demonstrating substantial similarity between the derived variety and the initial variety, acknowledging the breeder of the initial variety in the application. A farmer who has bred or developed a new variety of crop sciences indian, through a process of selection and propagation, may register the same subject to demonstrating novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity as per the established guidelines. Provided that, registration of farmers’ varieties shall be subject to a simplified process and lower fees, recognizing the traditional knowledge and practices involved in crop improvement. The Authority may, after examination, grant a certificate of registration if the application meets the criteria as provided herein.

Any breeder of a new variety of crop sciences indian, registered under this Act, shall have the right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, and export the said variety. However, such rights shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions as provided herein. A farmer who has, in good faith and without intending to commercially exploit the variety, saved seeds of a protected variety and used them for propagation, shall not be held liable for infringement. Where a breeder alleges infringement of their rights, they may apply to the Central Government for an order of injunction restraining the infringer. The Central Government, upon receiving such application and satisfying itself of the prima facie case, may issue an interim injunction pending final determination of the matter. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Central Government under this Act may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the order. The Authority established under this Act shall facilitate a fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the exploitation of plant varieties.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration of a new plant variety claiming crop sciences indian expertise, shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Should the application satisfy the initial requirements, the Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, initiate a substantive examination involving a detailed assessment of distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. A variety shall be deemed distinct if it exhibits clearly distinguishable characteristics from any other variety commonly known or commercially available, taking into account essential botanical characteristics. Provided that, the applicant may submit evidence of prior art to demonstrate the novelty of the claimed variety. The examination process may include field trials conducted at designated testing centers, and the applicant shall bear the costs associated with such trials, unless otherwise determined by the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding the rejection of an application may file an appeal to the Appellate Board, as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

All applications for registration of new plant varieties of crop sciences indian origin shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its lineage, characteristics, stability, and uniformity, as demonstrated through multi-location field trials conducted over a period of not less than three growing seasons. The applicant shall, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, submit evidence of the variety’s distinctiveness from any commonly known variety or existing registered variety. Provided that, in cases where the applicant claims a substantially derived variety, full details of the initial variety and the process of derivation shall be disclosed. Any farmer or group of farmers who have bred or developed a new variety, and who seek registration under this Act, may submit a farmer’s variety, subject to compliance with the prescribed procedural requirements and payment of applicable fees. The Authority may, at its discretion, require additional data or clarification from the applicant to ensure full compliance with the provisions herein.

Any person engaged in the commercial production, sale, marketing or distribution of crop sciences indian varieties, who, without due authorization from the breeder of such variety, sells, markets, distributes, imports, exports or otherwise disposes of seeds or propagating material of that variety, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than two years, but which may extend to five years, and with a fine not less than five lakh rupees, but which may extend to ten lakh rupees. Provided that the Authority may, subject to payment of adequate royalties as determined by it, permit the continued use of such variety by small and marginal farmers. Any act of knowingly inducing or assisting another person to infringe the rights conferred under this Act shall also be deemed an offence and attract the same penalties. The competent authority, upon receiving credible evidence of infringement, may issue a cease and desist order and seize all infringing material. Any appeal against such order shall lie with the High Court.

Any person deriving economic benefit from the exploitation of a registered plant variety, including through the commercial production or sale of seeds, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding benefit sharing and royalty payments. Licensing of rights to exploit a variety shall be governed by agreements negotiated between the breeder and the licensee, specifying the scope of the license, duration, and royalty rates, and such agreements shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Assignment of breeder’s rights may be effected through a written instrument duly executed by both parties, and notification of such assignment shall be submitted to the Authority within thirty days of the transfer. 

The Authority may, subject to conditions, grant licenses to facilitate the utilization of crop sciences indian for research and breeding purposes, provided that the breeder receives equitable remuneration. Failure to comply with royalty obligations or terms of the licensing agreement shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license, as provided herein, and may result in legal proceedings for recovery of due payments.

Any registered breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety of crop sciences indian, who alleges infringement of their breeder’s rights, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for redressal, submitting evidence of the initial variety and the allegedly infringing variety. The Authority shall, following notification to the alleged infringer and consideration of submitted evidence, conduct a comparative analysis of the characteristics of both varieties, focusing on substantial similarity. Should the Authority determine a prima facie case of infringement exists, it may issue an interim injunction restraining the alleged infringer from further propagation or commercialization of the variety in question. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Authority may file an appeal before the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Authority’s order. The High Court’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the provisions for further appeal as provided herein, and may include damages commensurate with the extent of the proven infringement.
