Any person deriving benefits from the exploitation of a registered variety of crop sciences indian, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to exercise rights in respect of the produce of that variety. A breeder, being the first to commercially exploit the variety, may assign, by way of license or outright transfer, the rights to another person, however, such assignment shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any petition particulars contained within an application for variety registration, including detailed descriptions of essential traits and purity levels, shall be considered confidential information and may not be disclosed without the explicit consent of the applicant or breeder. Licensing agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted exploitation, including geographical limitations and duration, and shall be subject to review by the Authority to ensure equitable benefit sharing with farmers and breeders alike. Failure to comply with the terms of a registered assignment or license may result in revocation of rights as provided herein.

The registered breeder of a new plant variety, desiring to commercially exploit the said variety, shall apply to the Agriculture Commissioner Government for a license under this Act, furnishing details of the proposed method of propagation and marketing. Such application shall be accompanied by a royalty payment schedule, subject to review by a committee constituted for the purpose. The Agriculture Commissioner Government may, after due consideration of the application and verification of the breeder’s claim, grant a license for a specified duration, not exceeding fifteen years from the date of grant. Any assignment of such license shall require prior written consent of the Agriculture Commissioner Government and notification to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, a farmer utilizing seeds of a protected variety for personal cultivation shall not require any license as provided herein, but shall be subject to the provisions regarding benefit sharing and seed conservation. The Agriculture Commissioner Government reserves the right to revoke the license in cases of non-compliance with the stipulated conditions or proven misrepresentation in the application.

The Agriculture Commissioner, appointed by the Central Government, shall exercise such powers as are necessary for the effective implementation of the provisions of this Act relating to the registration of new plant varieties and the protection of plant breeders’ rights. The Commissioner may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, delegate any of his powers to an officer subordinate to him, ensuring adequate oversight and accountability. A Plant Variety Committee shall be established to assist the Agriculture Commissioner in matters of variety registration, and shall consist of experts in plant breeding, agronomy, and related fields. The Commissioner shall maintain a National Register of Plant Varieties, open for inspection as provided herein, and shall be responsible for enforcing the provisions concerning farmers’ rights and benefit sharing. Any decision of the Agriculture Commissioner may be appealed to the Central Government.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting as the registrar under this Act, shall maintain a comprehensive register of all extant plant varieties notified for registration, detailing their characteristics, denomination, and breeder information as submitted by applicants. Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new, distinct, uniform, and stable variety may apply for registration to the Agriculture Commissioner in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and a detailed description of the variety. The Agriculture Commissioner may, subject to verification of the applicant’s claim and the variety’s compliance with the criteria outlined herein, grant a certificate of registration. Provided that, where a variety is essentially derived from an already registered variety, the applicant shall demonstrate substantial derivation and pay a royalty to the breeder of the initial variety, as determined by the Agriculture Commissioner. All registered varieties shall be subject to periodic examination to ensure continued conformity with the registered characteristics.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting on behalf of the Central Government and subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, shall investigate any complaint of infringement of a breeder’s right established under this Act, and may, if satisfied of the infringement, issue a cease and desist order to the infringer. Any person aggrieved by such order may, within sixty days of its issuance, file an appeal with the designated appellate authority, providing reasonable proof of hardship or exceptional circumstances. The Agriculture Commissioner shall maintain a register of all extant plant varieties, and shall, upon receipt of a valid request and payment of the prescribed fee, provide access to information contained therein to any interested party. Provided that, access to confidential information relating to breeding methods shall be restricted to protect the legitimate interests of the breeder. Farmers exercising their rights to save, use, sow, re-sow and exchange seeds of protected varieties shall not be subject to legal action, unless such acts demonstrably prejudice the breeder’s commercial exploitation of the variety.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting as the nodal officer for the implementation of this Act within each State, shall establish a State Level Seed Certification Standards Authority to ensure adherence to prescribed quality control measures for varietal purity and seed production. The Commissioner may, subject to the approval of the Central Government, delegate powers relating to inspection of seed farms and post-control testing to designated officers of the State Department of Agriculture. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the State Level Seed Certification Standards Authority regarding rejection of a seed lot may file an appeal to the Agriculture Commissioner within thirty days of the order. The Commissioner shall, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard, pass an order on such appeal, which shall be final and binding, provided that an appeal to the High Court lies in cases involving substantial questions of law. The Commissioner shall maintain a register of all registered plant varieties and shall publish such register annually. All fees collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of the State and utilized for the promotion of plant variety protection and farmers’ rights.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting on behalf of the Central Government, shall oversee the maintenance of a comprehensive database of plant varieties registered under this Act, ensuring its accuracy and accessibility to the public, subject to reasonable restrictions to protect breeder’s rights. Any person intending to commercially exploit a registered variety shall, prior to such exploitation, submit a declaration of intent to the Agriculture Commissioner, detailing the proposed method of propagation and the geographical area of operation. The Agriculture Commissioner may, following due process and verification of the declaration, issue a certificate of authorization, valid for a period not exceeding three years, and renewable upon satisfactory compliance with the conditions stipulated herein. Provided that, failure to submit a declaration or to adhere to the conditions of authorization shall render the exploitation unlawful and subject to penalties as prescribed. The Commissioner shall also conduct periodic inspections of seed production and distribution channels to ensure adherence to quality standards and prevent the proliferation of non-authorized seeds.

Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Agriculture Commissioner relating to the registration of a new plant variety, or the revocation thereof, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such decision, provided that such person deposits with the High Court a sum equivalent to five percent of the registration fee as a condition precedent to the admission of the appeal. Failure to comply with this provision shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Agriculture Commissioner, when conducting investigations into alleged infringements, shall have the power to enter any land or premises, examine any plant or relevant record, and seize any material believed to be evidence of an offence under this Act. Any officer of police may, upon reasonable suspicion, assist the Agriculture Commissioner in exercising these powers, and any obstruction thereof shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Commissioner’s decisions are final, subject only to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court as provided herein.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting as the designated authority for the purpose of licensing plant variety rights, may grant licenses to seed companies and other eligible entities, subject to the conditions prescribed herein and payment of the requisite royalty fees as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any assignment of rights relating to a registered plant variety shall be valid only upon registration of the assignment with the Agriculture Commissioner, and failure to do so will render the assignment null and void. A licensee, desiring to sub-license the rights granted to them, shall obtain prior written consent from both the rights holder and the Agriculture Commissioner, demonstrating a clear public benefit and adherence to the terms of the original license. The Agriculture Commissioner shall maintain a public register of all licenses and assignments, accessible for inspection during office hours, and may revoke a license in cases of demonstrable misuse or non-compliance with the provisions of this Act, following a due process of hearing. Provided that, the rights of farmers to save, use, sow, re-sow and exchange farm-saved seeds shall remain unaffected by any licensing arrangement.

Any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the Agriculture Commissioner against any decision of a Plant Variety Protection Officer refusing registration of a new plant variety or imposing conditions deemed unduly restrictive on the scope of the breeder’s rights, provided that such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The Agriculture Commissioner, upon receipt of such appeal and after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the Plant Variety Protection Officer, shall pass an order confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision. Further, any party dissatisfied with the order of the Agriculture Commissioner may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the High Court for review of said order; however, no such application shall be entertained unless accompanied by a deposit equivalent to the costs incurred by the Agriculture Commissioner in processing the initial appeal. The decision of the High Court shall be final and binding.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting on behalf of the Plant Varieties Protection Authority, shall investigate any complaint alleging an infringement of a breeder’s right established as provided herein, and may require the alleged infringer to furnish such information as deemed necessary for the purpose of such investigation. Any mark affixed to a variety, representing a registered breeder’s right, shall be prima facie evidence of such right, subject to proof of continued validity of the registration. Where the Agriculture Commissioner is satisfied that an infringement has occurred, they may issue a cease and desist order, directing the infringer to immediately halt the propagation, sale, or distribution of the protected variety. A person aggrieved by a decision of the Agriculture Commissioner may, within sixty days of the order, appeal to the High Court. Provided that, the Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, establish a fund to compensate breeders for losses incurred due to proven infringements, and such fund shall be managed in accordance with guidelines prescribed by the Authority.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting as the designated authority under this Act, shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index of all extant plant varieties registered herein, and shall update said index quarterly with details of any new registrations, amendments, or revocations. Any person intending to apply for the registration of a new plant variety shall first consult the registrar index to ascertain whether a substantially similar variety is already protected, and shall submit a report of such consultation with their application. The Agriculture Commissioner may, subject to the provisions contained herein, direct the registrar index to be made available for public inspection during office hours. Provided that, the Agriculture Commissioner reserves the right to redact information from the registrar index where disclosure would prejudice the legitimate interests of the breeder or be contrary to public order. All decisions of the Agriculture Commissioner regarding access to, or amendment of, the registrar index shall be final and binding, and may be challenged only through a writ petition before the appropriate High Court. Any false representation made regarding consultation of the registrar index shall render the applicant liable to prosecution.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting on behalf of the Central Government and subject to the provisions of this Act, shall maintain a register of all extant plant varieties notified under this Act, and shall update said register annually. Any person alleging a breeder’s right infringement may submit a detailed report to the Agriculture Commissioner, including evidence of substantial similarity and potential market disruption. Where the Agriculture Commissioner deems a prima facie case exists, they shall initiate an investigation and may require the alleged infringer to submit a response within thirty days. An exclusive licensee of a breeder, with documented proof of licensing agreement and breeder consent, may also lodge such a complaint on behalf of the breeder. Compliance with procedural requirements as stipulated by the Agriculture Commissioner is mandatory for all complaints, and failure to do so shall render the complaint inadmissible, provided that the Commissioner may, at their discretion, request clarification. All investigations shall be conducted in a transparent and impartial manner.

The Agriculture Commissioner, acting on behalf of the Central Government and in accordance with the provisions of this Act, may grant licenses for the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment of rights relating to a registered variety shall be registered with the Agriculture Commissioner within thirty days of such assignment, failing which the assignment shall be deemed invalid as against any third party acquiring an interest in good faith. The application for registration of assignment shall include details of the assignee, the assignor, and the scope of the assigned rights. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment, the Agriculture Commissioner may refer the matter to the Layout Design Registrar for an advisory opinion regarding the transfer of intellectual property rights, though such opinion shall not be binding. All licensing agreements shall be submitted to the Agriculture Commissioner for record and shall be open to inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the plant variety registration.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, that the variety is distinct, uniform, and stable, as provided herein. Compliance with the essential characteristics specified in the notification issued under this Act is mandatory for registration. Where a breeder has substantially derived a variety from a registered variety, and continues to propagate such derived variety without the authorization of the breeder of the registered variety, such propagation constitutes an infringement. However, a farmer who, in good faith and for purposes of propagation, saves and re-sows seeds of a protected variety, shall be exempt from such infringement, subject to the conditions that the seeds are not sold commercially. A breeder breeder complied with all procedural requirements outlined in the regulations, the Authority may grant a certificate of registration. The Authority shall maintain a register of all registered plant varieties.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a revolving fund for the purpose of promoting research and development in plant varieties, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders. Contributions to the gene fund shall include royalties and payments received from the commercial exploitation of protected plant varieties, as provided herein, and any grants or donations received from domestic or international sources. The Authority may, subject to the approval of the Central Government, invest the gene fund in such manner as to ensure its continued availability and growth. Utilization of the gene fund shall prioritize initiatives supporting conservation of plant genetic resources, training of farmers in seed production, and incentivizing the development of new and improved plant varieties, particularly those adapted to local agro-climatic conditions. Any surplus funds remaining at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next financial year.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a revolving fund for the purpose of promoting research and development in plant varieties, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders. Contributions to the gene fund shall include royalties received from the commercial exploitation of registered varieties, and any grants or donations received from domestic or international sources. The Authority may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, invest the gene fund in such manner as may be prescribed, ensuring the preservation of genetic diversity and the sustainable use of plant genetic resources. Funds allocated for farmer’s rights initiatives, as provided herein, shall be disbursed transparently and in accordance with guidelines established by a committee comprising representatives of farmers, breeders, and the Authority. Any surplus generated from the gene fund shall accrue to the fund itself and be utilized for the purposes outlined in this Act.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a revolving fund for the purpose of promoting the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to facilitate the equitable sharing of benefits arising from their commercial exploitation. Any person who, as provided herein, is found to have infringed the rights of a breeder or farmer in respect of a protected variety shall be liable to pay damages, the amount of which shall be determined by the Authority, and such amount shall be credited to the gene fund. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, utilize the gene fund to support research and development initiatives aimed at improving plant varieties and enhancing agricultural productivity. Provided that, not less than twenty percent of the annual accruals to the gene fund shall be allocated to the welfare of farmers and local communities involved in the conservation of plant genetic resources. Any unutilized portion of the gene fund at the end of a financial year shall not lapse but shall be carried forward to the next financial year.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall be applied for the promotion of plant research and development, and for the welfare of farmers and the conservation of plant genetic resources. Contributions to the gene fund may be made by any person, institution, or organization, and shall be received as donations or grants, subject to such conditions as the Authority deems appropriate. The Authority shall formulate guidelines for the administration of the gene fund, including procedures for the disbursement of funds and the maintenance of accounts. 

Any benefit sharing received from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, or essentially derived varieties, as provided herein, shall be credited to the gene fund. The Authority may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, invest the gene fund in such manner as may be prescribed, to ensure its growth and sustainability. A detailed annual report on the operation of the gene fund shall be submitted to Parliament.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall be applied solely for the promotion of plant breeding and the welfare of farmers, particularly small and marginal farmers. Contributions to the gene fund shall include royalties and benefit-sharing arrangements derived from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, as provided herein, and any grants or donations received from domestic or international sources. The Authority may, subject to the approval of the Central Government, invest the gene fund in such manner as to ensure its long-term sustainability and maximize returns. Provided that any investment shall be consistent with the objectives of this Act and shall not compromise the principles of equitable access and benefit-sharing. The Authority shall maintain detailed accounts of all receipts and disbursements from the gene fund, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government detailing its utilization. Any unutilized funds at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next financial year for continued application under this Act.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a revolving fund for the purpose of promoting research and development in plant varieties, and for ensuring equitable benefit sharing with farmers and local communities. Any person who utilizes genetic material sourced from registered plant varieties for commercial purposes, shall contribute a percentage of the resultant profit to the gene fund, as determined by the Authority. Failure to remit such contributions within the stipulated timeframe shall attract a penalty equivalent to twice the amount due, and may further result in suspension of registration privileges under this Act. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, utilize the gene fund to provide compensation to farmers for any loss suffered due to the use of their traditional knowledge or germplasm in the development of new varieties, provided that such loss is substantiated through evidence acceptable to the Authority. Any unutilized portion of the gene fund at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next year.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall be applied to the promotion of plant variety research and development, and the welfare of farmers and breeders, as provided herein. Any person intending to commercially exploit a registered variety, or an essentially derived variety thereof, shall contribute a percentage of net profits, as determined by the Authority, to the gene fund. Subject to rules made by the Central Government, the Authority may also accept voluntary contributions and grants to the gene fund from domestic and international sources. The Authority shall administer the gene fund through a committee comprising representatives of plant breeders, farmers, and relevant scientific institutions. This committee shall formulate guidelines for the disbursement of funds, prioritizing projects that enhance biodiversity, conserve indigenous plant genetic resources, and facilitate the development of climate-resilient varieties. Provided that, twenty percent of the gene fund shall be reserved for the support of on-farm conservation efforts undertaken by registered farmer communities. Any unutilized portion of the gene fund at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next year.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall be applied for the promotion of plant research and the welfare of farmers, particularly small and marginal farmers, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the allocation of resources from the gene fund, or the eligibility of a claimant to receive benefits therefrom, may be raised before the Authority, which shall conduct a hearing and issue a reasoned order. An appeal from any such order shall lie to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning limitation periods for appeals. Provided that, the Authority may, in cases of demonstrable urgency affecting livelihoods, authorize a temporary disbursement from the gene fund pending the resolution of any appeal. The Authority shall maintain detailed records of all contributions to, and disbursements from, the gene fund, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government. Any allegation of mismanagement or misappropriation of funds shall be investigated by a committee appointed by the Central Government.

The gene fund shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, with representation from plant breeders, farmers, and relevant scientific institutions, to ensure equitable distribution of benefits arising from the utilization of plant genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge. Any person alleging misappropriation of benefit sharing contributions to the gene fund, or improper disbursement thereof, may submit a grievance to the committee, supported by documentary evidence. Decisions of the committee shall be subject to appeal before the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the committee’s decision. Furthermore, where a dispute arises concerning the novelty or distinctiveness of a plant variety, and this impacts benefit sharing calculations, evidence of any registered layout design relating to a process for its creation may be admitted as corroborating evidence, subject to verification of its validity. The committee may, at its discretion, request an expert opinion on such matters.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, subject to the provisions herein. Any performer of traditional knowledge associated with registered plant varieties, demonstrably contributing to the development of said variety, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for equitable sharing in the benefits accruing from the gene fund. The Authority shall, following due process and verification of such contribution, determine the extent of benefit sharing. Contributions to the gene fund shall also include royalties received from the commercial exploitation of varieties incorporating indigenous knowledge, and any penalties levied for infringement of breeder’s rights as provided herein. The Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate guidelines for transparent and equitable distribution of funds, prioritizing initiatives that enhance farmer livelihoods and promote biodiversity.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a revolving fund for the purpose of promoting research and development in plant varieties, and for ensuring equitable sharing of benefits arising from the exploitation of such varieties and associated traditional knowledge. Contributions to the gene fund shall include royalties received from registered plant varieties, annual fees levied on breeders, and any grants or donations received from domestic or international sources. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, utilize the gene fund for incentivizing plant breeders, supporting conservation of plant genetic resources, and compensating farmers for their contributions to plant variety development. Registration ought effected in a transparent manner, and records of all financial transactions relating to the gene fund shall be maintained and audited annually. Provided that, any disbursement from the gene fund exceeding a prescribed limit shall require prior approval of the Central Government. The Authority shall submit an annual report detailing the utilization of the gene fund to the Parliament.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority as a dedicated repository for benefit sharing derived from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties and their essentially derived varieties. All contributions to the gene fund, including royalties and payments received under this Act, shall be deposited into such fund within sixty days of receipt, failing which a penalty, not exceeding twice the amount due, may be levied. Any farmer or community whose traditional knowledge contributed to the development of a registered variety may, subject to verification by the Authority, submit a claim for equitable benefit sharing from the gene fund. Disputes regarding the apportionment of funds or the validity of claims shall be referred to the civil court registrar for preliminary assessment of admissibility, prior to formal adjudication by a competent court. The Authority shall maintain a transparent accounting of all receipts and disbursements from the gene fund, accessible to public scrutiny as provided herein.

Any person dealing in goods, where the trade mark is applied to those goods, or where such goods are offered for sale or distributed, shall be liable for damages and an injunction restraining further dealing in such goods, subject to the provisions of this Act. A registered patent agent, acting on behalf of the trade mark proprietor, may initiate proceedings for recovery of damages and seek an ex parte order for seizure of infringing goods, provided that sufficient cause is demonstrated to the court. The determination of whether goods are ‘meaning act goods’ shall be based on a consideration of the overall impression created on the average consumer, and not merely a technical analysis of composition. Any defence claiming prior legitimate use shall be substantiated with verifiable evidence of continuous use preceding the date of registration of the trade mark. Remedies under this Act are cumulative and not mutually exclusive, and a court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall, in addition to the requirements as provided herein, furnish a statement as to the use of any descriptive matter appearing on the goods or their packaging, or in connection with the services, which is not itself a trade mark, but is intended to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, or geographical origin of the goods or services. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require the applicant to disclaim any such descriptive matter, to prevent trade description being falsely represented as a distinctive feature of the trade mark. Failure to comply with this requirement may result in the rejection of the application. Provided that, where the descriptive matter has acquired distinctiveness through extensive use, the Registrar may, at their discretion, allow its retention as part of the trade mark, contingent upon evidence demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness.

A trade mark shall not be registered unless the application specifies the goods or services for which registration is sought, and such specification shall be clear and unambiguous, adhering to the classification of goods and services as accepted internationally. The applicant may describe the goods or services in reasonable detail, provided that the description accurately reflects the nature of the offering and distinguishes it from existing marks. Where goods or services fall within multiple classes, a separate application, accompanied by the prescribed fee, shall be filed for each class. An application lacking a precise description of goods or services, or containing a description that is unduly broad or vague, may be subject to objection under this Act. Furthermore, the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the specification to ensure clarity and compliance with established practices regarding goods services description.

All applications for registration of a trade mark shall clearly and accurately describe the goods or services to which the trade mark relates, adhering to the accepted classification standards as prescribed by the competent authority. The description of goods and services shall not be excessively broad or vague, but shall be specific enough to define the scope of protection sought. An applicant may combine multiple classes of goods or services within a single application, provided that a separate fee is paid for each class. Where goods or services fall within multiple descriptions, the applicant shall nominate the primary description for the purposes of examination and registration. Failure to comply with these requirements regarding goods services description may result in the rejection of the application or limitation of the scope of the registered trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any amendment to the description shall be permissible, provided it does not substantially alter the character of the goods or services.

The register of trade marks shall be maintained in a manner accessible for public inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. A person desiring to effect a registration india shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by the necessary particulars and the prescribed fee. The application shall include a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and a statement of use, or an intention to use, the trade mark. Where a trade mark is identical with a registered trade mark, registration shall not be granted unless the applicant obtains the consent of the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, or demonstrates justifiable grounds for its use. Any rectification of the register may be undertaken as provided herein, following due process and opportunity for hearing.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration india in such manner as may be prescribed, to the Trade Marks Registry, specifying the goods or services to which the trade mark is to be applied. The application shall include a representation of the trade mark and a statement of the use of the trade mark. Where an application for registration is filed for a collective mark or a certification mark, the application shall include a statement of the rules governing the use of the mark. The Registrar may, prior to examining the application, require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a trade mark shall be registered if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another and satisfies all other requirements as provided herein. Registration shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the certificate of registration.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration india in such manner as may be prescribed. Upon acceptance of the application, the trade mark shall be registered in the Trade Marks Registry and the applicant shall be entitled to the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. However, such right shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and any other law for the time being in force. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for ten years from the date of registration, and may be renewed for further periods of ten years each, so long as the prescribed fees are paid and subject to any opposition proceedings as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark is infringed, the aggrieved party may institute a suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a competent court. The court may, at its discretion, grant an order of account of profits and may also direct the delivery up or destruction of the infringing goods.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of trade marks, distinctly identifying each mark and its proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration india in the prescribed manner, furnishing details of the mark, goods or services to which it relates, and the applicant’s particulars. The Registry may, prior to accepting an application, require clarification or amendment to ensure compliance with the requirements of this Act. Upon acceptance, the application shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, allowing for opposition by any aggrieved party. Should an opposition be filed, the Registry shall conduct an inquiry, affording both the applicant and the opponent a reasonable opportunity to be heard. A trade mark, once registered, confers upon the proprietor exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified, and shall be subject to renewal as provided herein, failing which it may be removed from the register. The Registry reserves the right to rectify the register for errors or omissions, or to remove a trade mark for non-use, in accordance with established procedure.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark capable of being represented graphically and distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings may apply for registration india in such manner as may be prescribed. An application for registration shall include a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and a statement of the claim to ownership. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to limit the goods or services specified in the application. Provided that, where a trade mark is similar to an existing trade mark, the Registry may require evidence of distinctiveness to avoid confusion in the market. All applications shall be examined for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and any application found deficient may be rejected or amended as necessary. Failure to respond to official objections within the prescribed time shall be deemed a withdrawal of the application.

Any person claiming registration india of a trade mark, and failing to diligently pursue such registration to conclusion within a period of five years from the date of initial application, shall be deemed to have abandoned the right to such registration, subject to the provisions contained herein. The Trade Marks Officer may, upon substantiated complaint and reasonable evidence of abandonment, initiate proceedings for the removal of the incomplete application from the register. Any false representation regarding the status of a pending registration india, made with intent to deceive, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any individual knowingly assisting in such misrepresentation, or providing false information as part of a registration application, shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both. All penalties levied under this Act shall be recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, or an application for registration india, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument of assignment shall clearly identify the trade mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and detail any limitations or conditions attached to the transfer of ownership. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license to a third party, provided that such assignment does not contravene any provisions contained within the original licensing agreement. Where a trade mark is assigned as part of the goodwill of a business, notice of such assignment shall be given to the Registry within thirty days of the transaction. Failure to register an assignment or license as provided herein may render the transfer invalid as against subsequent purchasers or licensees without notice.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration india of a trade mark, or requiring the limitation of a trade mark, or dismissing an application for revival of a trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as the Appellate Board may deem fit. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registrar, or reverse it, or vary it in such manner as it thinks fit. An application for registration of a trade mark shall not be refused solely on the ground that it is identical with a trade mark already registered in India for different goods or services, provided that such trade marks are not likely to cause confusion. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding on all parties, except where a substantial question of law arises for determination by the High Court.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark capable of distinguishing goods or services, and desiring to register it, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for registration india, indicating the class of goods or services to which the trade mark relates. An application for registration shall not be accepted unless it satisfies the conditions regarding inherent distinctiveness and is not descriptive of the goods or services concerned. Where an applicant seeks to simultaneously register a trade mark and a patent relating to a novel feature embodied within goods designated by the trade mark, the applicant may submit supporting documentation demonstrating the status of the corresponding application to register patents with the appropriate authority. The Registry may require evidence of prior use or other relevant information to determine registrability. Subject to compliance with all procedural requirements as provided herein, and upon satisfactory examination, the trade mark shall be registered and a certificate of registration issued. Failure to renew the registration within the prescribed period shall render it liable to be removed from the register.

Any person claiming ownership of a trade mark and seeking registration india shall submit an application to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as provided herein, accompanied by the prescribed fee. Failure to accurately represent the mark or to disclose prior rights known to the applicant shall render the registration vulnerable to revocation and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registry may, subject to due process, require additional evidence to verify the veracity of the claim. Any act of falsely representing a trade mark as registered, or using a registered trade mark without the consent of the proprietor, demonstrating a lack of registration respect, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. All decisions of the Registry regarding registration are final, save for appeal to the High Court as per established legal procedure.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration india, or requiring the amendment or limitation of an application for registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The design registry shall maintain a separate register of all appeals filed and their respective statuses, accessible to the public for inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee. An appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates a substantial question of law or fact requiring consideration. Furthermore, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to attempt mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed-upon mediator, provided that such mediation does not exceed thirty days. Failure to comply with the timelines prescribed herein may result in the dismissal of the appeal.

Any person found guilty of applying for registration of a trade mark known to be identical with a registered trade mark, or deceptively similar thereto, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein. Where such deceptive application results in actual damage to the owner of the registered trade mark, the court may, in addition to the penalty, order the imprisonment of the offender for a term not exceeding five years. However, such sentence imprisonment term may be waived if the applicant demonstrates immediate cessation of the infringing activity and provides a written undertaking of non-repetition. Furthermore, any individual abetting such an offence, or knowingly assisting in the fraudulent application, shall be subject to the same penalties. The court, subject to the provisions of this Act, may also grant an injunction restraining the offender from further use of the deceptive mark, and award damages commensurate with the harm suffered by the rightful owner.

Any person found guilty of applying for registration of a trade mark with intent to deceive or cause confusion, as provided herein, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act. Where a trade mark is falsely applied for, and the applicant knowingly misrepresents material facts in the application, the court may, after due consideration of the evidence presented, impose a sentence of imprisonment. Such sentence imprisonment term shall not be less than one year, but may extend to a period of three years, alongside a monetary penalty. The amount of said penalty shall be determined by the court, subject to a minimum of one lakh rupees and a maximum of five lakh rupees. Provided that, if the offence involves the counterfeiting of a registered trade mark and is demonstrated to be a repeat offence by the accused, the court may enhance the sentence imprisonment term up to five years and the monetary penalty to ten lakh rupees. All proceedings shall be conducted in accordance with the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where the assignee seeks to utilize the trade mark in a manner differing materially from the manner in which it was utilized by the assignor prior to the assignment, a notice of such intended alteration shall be filed with the Registry. Failure to comply with the registration requirements as provided herein shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignor or any lawful user of the mark. Should a fraudulent assignment be established, any person involved, including the purported assignee, may be subject to a sentence imprisonment term not exceeding five years, alongside a monetary penalty. The Registry may, at its discretion, require evidence of legitimate consideration for any assignment, and may refuse registration if such evidence is deemed insufficient. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment shall be adjudicated by the High Court having jurisdiction.

A patent, as provided herein, shall be granted for an invention that is new, useful, and not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art. The term “invention” includes a new and useful product, process, method or machine, and extends to alloys, compositions of matter, and any article produced by a new industrial process. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patent may be granted for a term of twenty years from the date of filing the application. Any anticipation of an invention, whether by prior publication, prior claiming, or prior use, shall be grounds for refusal of a patent application. Furthermore, patents act 1970 does not extend to inventions which are frivolous or which relate to mere discovery of a scientific principle. The controller of patents shall examine each application.

Any person applying for a patent under this Act shall furnish a statement and undertaking regarding prior art known to them, detailing all information which could reasonably affect the assessment of novelty and inventive step as required by this Act. The application shall be deemed incomplete if such statement and undertaking are absent or found to be materially deficient. A patent applicant may request a hearing if objections are raised concerning the sufficiency of disclosure, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where a patent is granted for a product or process involving a biological material, the patent specification shall disclose the origin and geographical source of said material. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent vulnerable to revocation proceedings, and any resulting damages shall be assessed according to the principles of equitable accounting as provided herein. The Controller of Patents shall maintain a publicly accessible register of all patents granted and applications pending, ensuring transparency in the patents act 1970 regime.

An alleged offence under this Act shall be determined through a process of due investigation initiated upon a complaint made in writing to the appropriate authority, or suo motu, where credible information suggests a contravention of the provisions herein. The commission of an offence may be established through demonstrable evidence of use of a deceptive or falsely applied trade mark, or through the possession of instruments primarily designed for the counterfeiting of registered trade marks, subject to the accused person demonstrating reasonable grounds for such possession unrelated to illicit activity. Where a corporate entity is implicated in an alleged offence, liability shall extend to every person who, at the time of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the corporation. Any finding of guilt shall be proportionate to the extent of damage caused to the rights holder.

Any person alleging an offence relating to the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, as provided herein, shall furnish to the Registrar a detailed statement of the grounds constituting the alleged offence, accompanied by certified copies of evidence supporting such claim. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, direct the alleged offender to appear before the Trade Marks Office for examination. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed an exacerbating factor in determining the severity of any subsequent penalty. Where the alleged offence involves the counterfeiting of goods, the complainant shall also submit samples of both the genuine article and the counterfeit goods for comparative analysis. The Registrar, upon reasonable suspicion of a cognizable offence, may initiate an investigation and, if warranted, refer the matter to the appropriate law enforcement agency. Any false allegation made with malicious intent shall attract penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person alleging an offence under this Act shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, provide to the Registrar a detailed statement of the grounds upon which the allegation is based, accompanied by supporting evidence reasonably believed to be true. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the complainant to deposit a sum sufficient to cover likely costs associated with investigation and potential damages, should the allegation prove unfounded. A complainant failing to provide adequate grounds or supporting evidence may have the complaint dismissed without prejudice. Where an offence is alleged to involve the counterfeiting of a registered trade mark, the proprietor shall furnish evidence of registration and demonstrate a prima facie case of deceptive similarity. Provided that, a finding of an alleged offence does not preclude a subsequent civil suit for damages or injunctive relief, as provided herein, and remedies available under this Act are cumulative and not mutually exclusive. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to an alleged offence may appeal to the High Court.

Any person alleging an offence under this Act shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, furnish to the relevant authority a detailed statement outlining the nature of the alleged offence, the evidence supporting such allegation, and the particulars of the alleged offender, subject to the provisions contained herein. The authority, upon receipt of such statement, may, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, initiate an investigation and may require the alleged offender to produce documents or appear before it for questioning. Should the investigation reveal sufficient evidence to support the allegation, the authority may, with the prior sanction of the Controller of Trade Marks, proceed with formal prosecution. However, no prosecution shall be initiated without affording the alleged offender a reasonable opportunity to be heard and present a defence. Any false allegation made with malicious intent shall itself constitute an offence punishable as provided herein, and the complainant may be subject to appropriate legal action. The burden of proving the alleged offence shall lie with the prosecution.

Any person committing an alleged offence under this Act shall be liable to investigation by a duly authorized officer of the Trade Marks Registry, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where such an officer has reasonable grounds to believe that an alleged offence has been committed, they may require the person reasonably suspected of committing the offence to produce documents or provide information relevant to the investigation. Failure to comply with such a requirement, without adequate cause, shall itself constitute an obstruction of justice and be punishable as an offence under this Act. Provided that, any information obtained during the investigation shall be treated as confidential and may only be disclosed for the purposes of prosecution or as directed by a competent court. The Trade Marks Registry may, with the prior approval of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, engage external experts to assist in the investigation of complex alleged offences.

Any person committing an alleged offence under this Act, involving the falsification of a registered trade mark or the fraudulent application thereof, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the alleged offence relates to goods of a significant value, exceeding five lakh rupees, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years. The court, however, may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, impose a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. A subsequent commission of an alleged offence within three years of a prior conviction shall be deemed an aggravated offence, attracting a minimum imprisonment of one year, irrespective of the value of goods involved. Any evidence obtained through lawful means, including digital records, shall be admissible in proceedings relating to such an offence, provided that the authenticity of said evidence is duly established. The Registrar may, with the approval of the Central Government, initiate investigations into suspected instances of such offences.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right arising under this Act, including a license to use the mark, shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties, and shall be evidenced in writing. Where an alleged offence relating to the use of a licensed trade mark arises, the licensor may, prior to any investigation or adjudication, require the licensee to demonstrate adequate quality control measures are in place to maintain the reputation of the mark. Failure to comply with such a requirement shall not, in itself, constitute an admission of guilt, but may be considered as evidence in determining the severity of any subsequent penalty. A transfer of ownership, whether by assignment or operation of law, does not prejudice any pending proceedings for an alleged offence committed prior to the transfer, and such proceedings may continue against the new owner subject to appropriate modification of orders. Any dispute concerning royalty payments or the scope of a license shall be resolved through arbitration as provided herein.

Any person alleging an offence under this Act relating to the use of an unregistered trade mark likely to cause confusion, shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, furnish to the Registrar a detailed statement of the grounds constituting the alleged offence, accompanied by evidence reasonably supporting such claim. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the prima facie case, direct the alleged offender to cease the impugned activity pending investigation. However, such direction shall not preclude the alleged offender from demonstrating legitimate use of the mark, or establishing a prior right to its use, as provided herein. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar concerning the alleged offence, or any direction issued, shall lie before the High Court, and must be lodged within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order. Failure to comply with these provisions may be considered an obstruction of justice.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, or an alleged offence relating to the use thereof, shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Registrar, unless the assignment or transfer is to a nominee already approved under the provisions of this Act. Where a licensing agreement concerning a registered trade mark is entered into, the licensor shall furnish the Registrar with a certified copy of such agreement within thirty days of its execution, failing which a penalty as prescribed may be levied. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of licensing terms, particularly concerning quality control or permitted fields of use, shall be referred to arbitration as provided herein. 

Furthermore, in cases involving an alleged offence committed during the course of an invention convention or exhibition, the onus of proving due diligence in preventing unauthorized use of the trade mark shall lie with the proprietor. The proprietor may, however, be absolved of liability if it is demonstrated that reasonable steps were taken to monitor and control the display and use of the trade mark at such event.

An alleged offence involving the use of a trade mark in a manner likely to cause confusion, or which constitutes an act of unfair competition, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. Where an application for registration includes an indication which is identical with, or closely resembling, a trade mark already registered in India for identical goods or services, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, require the applicant to furnish a statement demonstrating legitimate use of the mark. In cases involving international registrations originating from parties to the Budapest Treaty, the provisions relating to priority dates and permissible translations, as stipulated within that treaty, shall apply mutatis mutandis, provided that such registrations do not contravene any fundamental principles of Indian trade mark law. Any person aggrieved by a decision concerning an alleged offence may appeal to the High Court.

Any person alleging an offence relating to the use of a registered trade mark, or a mark deceptively similar thereto, shall submit a detailed statement of facts to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days of becoming aware of the alleged offence. The statement shall clearly identify the registered trade mark, the alleged infringing mark, and the nature of the unlawful activity. The Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the complainant to furnish further evidence or clarification. Where the Registry is satisfied that a prima facie case exists, it may initiate an inquiry and direct the alleged offender to submit a response. Failure to respond to such a direction, or to provide satisfactory evidence, may be considered an admission of the alleged offence and shall be recorded accordingly in the records of the Trade Marks Registry. Any order issued by the Registry shall be without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act.

Any person alleging an offence relating to the use of a registered trade mark, or a mark deceptively similar thereto, shall, prior to the institution of proceedings, provide a detailed statement of facts supporting the claim of infringement or misrepresentation to the Registrar. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the claimant to furnish evidence of prior searches conducted to ascertain the potential for conflict with existing registered marks, including those filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Should the alleged offence involve the importation of goods bearing the infringing mark, the claimant shall demonstrate reasonable efforts to notify the importer of the alleged infringement and afford them an opportunity to remedy the situation. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the dismissal of the claim, without prejudice to any other remedies available under this Act. A finding of an alleged offence does not automatically imply guilt, and all parties shall be entitled to a fair hearing.

An entry register document shall mean a certified copy of any entry made in the Trade Marks Register, and includes any document officially accepted as evidence of such entry for the purposes of establishing ownership or right to a trade mark as provided herein. Such an entry register document shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars contained therein, subject to proof of due process having been followed in making the relevant entry. Where a document is required to be filed with the Trade Marks Registry, a digitally signed copy conforming to the standards prescribed by the Central Government may be accepted as equivalent to an original physical document, provided that such digital copy is accompanied by a declaration of authenticity. Any alteration to an entry register document without authorization shall render it invalid.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall maintain a true and accurate entry register document detailing all licenses granted under the mark, including the duration, territory, and terms of each license. This entry register document shall be open for inspection by the Registrar during the course of any examination or proceeding under this Act. Failure to maintain such a document, or to present it when requested, may be considered prima facie evidence of an intent to deceive or cause confusion. A certified copy of any entry within the entry register document may be admitted as evidence in any legal proceeding concerning the trade mark. The Registrar may, subject to reasonable cause, direct amendment of the entry register document to reflect accurate licensing information. Provided that any material misrepresentation in the entry register document shall render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein. All amendments to the entry register document shall be dated and initialed by the registered proprietor.

Any person claiming ownership of a trade mark registered under this Act shall maintain a complete and accurate entry register document, detailing all assignments, transmissions, licenses, and any other dealings affecting the rights in the mark. Failure to maintain such a register, or to promptly record any changes therein, shall not, however, invalidate the registration itself, but may be considered as evidence in proceedings relating to the validity of any subsequent assignment or license. Where a registered trade mark is subject to a mortgage or charge, details of the mortgage or charge, including the identity of the mortgagee or charge holder, shall be recorded in the entry register document within thirty days of its creation. Any mortgagee or charge holder may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Registrar for inspection of the entry register document to verify the accuracy of the recorded details and to ascertain the extent of the secured interest. A certified copy of any entry in the register shall be admissible in evidence before any court.

Any person desiring to inspect the entry register document maintained under this Act shall submit an application in writing to the Registrar, specifying the particulars of the document sought and the purpose of such inspection. The Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, permit such inspection at such time and under such conditions as may be deemed fit. Provided that, access to any confidential information contained within the entry register document, including but not limited to details of licensing agreements or financial considerations, may be restricted at the discretion of the Registrar. Any certified copy of an entry register document, or any part thereof, shall be furnished by the Registrar upon request and upon payment of the fee as prescribed. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all applications for inspection and copies of documents furnished, and such record shall be open to inspection by any officer authorized under this Act. Any false representation made in an application for inspection shall render the applicant liable to prosecution as provided herein.

Any person desiring to inspect the entry register document maintained under this Act shall submit an application in writing to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form, accompanied by the applicable fee as specified in Schedule I. The Registry may, subject to verification of the applicant’s legitimate interest and purpose, permit access to the entry register document during office hours. Provided that access to confidential information, including details of licensing agreements or correspondence relating to ongoing disputes, may be restricted at the discretion of the Registrar. Any extract or copy of an entry register document certified as true by an officer of the Registry shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceedings. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures for inspection or copying, or any attempt to obtain unauthorized access to the entry register document, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with a fine, or with both. The Registrar may, however, refuse inspection if it would unduly disrupt the functioning of the Registry.

Any person making a false entry in the entry register document maintained under this Act shall be deemed to have committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where an offence involves the falsification of an entry relating to a registered trade mark, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, initiate an inquiry into the matter and, if satisfied of the falsity, direct rectification of the entry. Provided that no such rectification shall be effected without affording the concerned parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Any document submitted as evidence of ownership or transfer of rights, if found to be materially false, shall be inadmissible as proof and may attract a penalty equivalent to twice the official fee payable for registration. Failure to maintain the entry register document as required herein constitutes an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees.

Any assignment of right, title and interest in a registered trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be executed in writing and shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registrability and permitted assignments. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain an entry register document detailing all recorded assignments, transmissions, and other dealings affecting ownership of trade marks. Such entry register document shall be open for inspection by any person upon payment of a prescribed fee and subject to such conditions as the Registrar may deem fit. A certified copy of any entry in the entry register document shall be admissible in legal proceedings as prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein. Where a licensee obtains a right to use a trade mark, the terms of the license, if recorded with the Registry, shall be noted in the entry register document as a supplementary record of rights. Failure to record an assignment or license shall not invalidate the transaction but may affect the enforceability of rights against subsequent purchasers or licensees without notice.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to admit an entry in the register document, or directing the amendment of such entry, may, within a period of two months from the date of the order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and the relevant entry register document pertaining to the trade mark in question. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant a stay of the Registrar’s order pending the disposal of the appeal. Provided that no appeal shall lie against an order refusing to admit an entry where such refusal is based solely on a procedural irregularity curable by amendment of the application. Any party to the appeal may, within one month of receiving notice, file a counter-statement. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, allowing for further recourse as provided herein.

The entry register document, maintained under this Act, shall constitute prima facie evidence of the particulars therein contained, and shall be admissible in any legal proceeding as conclusive evidence of ownership and registration, subject to proof of authenticity as determined by the Registrar. Any alteration to such entry register document shall be effected only through formal amendment duly recorded and signed by an authorized officer. Where a trade mark application discloses a process or method protected under the Patents Act 1970, the entry register document shall also indicate the corresponding patent number, if any, for cross-referencing purposes. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional evidence to substantiate claims regarding ownership or validity, notwithstanding the contents of the entry register document. Failure to maintain an accurate entry register document may be considered during proceedings relating to rectification or revocation.

Any person desiring to inspect the entry register document maintained under this Act shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, permit access to such document, ensuring that no alteration or removal thereof is permitted. Where a registered trade mark has not been put to genuine use within a period of five years from the date of registration, any person may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence, demonstrating a prima facie case of non-use and offering reasonable terms. The Controller, upon being satisfied, may direct the registered proprietor to exercise their rights or grant a licence on terms determined by the Controller. Any request for inspection of the entry register document relating to a matter subject to a pending compulsory licence application shall be deferred until the matter is adjudicated. The Controller shall maintain a secure record of all inspections and applications.

Any person claiming ownership of a registered trade mark, and seeking to lodge a caveat against potential infringements, shall maintain a current entry register document detailing the scope of permitted use and any associated licensing agreements. This document shall be open to inspection by the Registrar upon reasonable request, and failure to produce such a register may be considered in assessing the good faith of the trade mark owner. Where the trade mark incorporates or is inextricably linked to a distinctive film sound, as a signature element identifying the goods or services, the entry register document must specifically delineate the parameters of that sound’s protected use. A proprietor may apply to the Registrar for an order directing an infringer to deliver up for destruction all materials bearing the unlawful mark, subject to demonstrating actual damage or a credible threat thereof. Provided that, the Registrar may, as an alternative to destruction, order a transfer of ownership of the infringing materials to the rightful owner. Any dispute concerning the validity of an entry in the register shall be subject to the remedies provided herein.

A variety shall be considered a registered breeder variety for the purposes of this Act if it satisfies the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, as determined through a prescribed testing procedure and registration process. The applicant for registration must be a person who has bred or discovered and developed the variety, subject to the provisions relating to essentially derived varieties. An essentially derived variety is one which is not substantially different from the parent variety, retaining the characteristics thereof, except for differences resulting from particular acts of breeding. Registration confers upon the breeder exclusive rights in respect of the commercial exploitation of the variety, including the right to produce, sell, and market the propagating material, subject to limitations as provided herein and the rights of farmers to save, use, sow, re-sow and sell farm-saved seeds. The period of validity for registration of a registered breeder variety shall be as prescribed.

A variety shall be considered a registered breeder variety only upon full compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein, including the submission of a complete application, payment of the prescribed fees, and satisfactory demonstration of distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability through field trials conducted in accordance with the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The applicant must demonstrate that the variety is novel, meaning it has not been made available to the public, by sale or other transfer, before the date of application. However, a reasonable period may be allowed for the purpose of making the variety available for experimentation. Any farmer who has bred or developed a new variety, and seeks registration, shall be entitled to claim the benefit of prior use, subject to the fulfillment of conditions relating to essential characteristics and demonstrable genetic lineage. The register of registered breeder varieties shall be maintained by the Authority and open for public inspection.

A registered breeder variety, upon establishment of validity under this Act, shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and stock propagating material of the variety. However, such rights shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions as provided herein. Any person who infringes these rights by engaging in the activities mentioned above without the breeder’s authorization may be subject to an injunction restraining such activity, and the breeder may also claim damages for any loss suffered due to the infringement. Provided that, a farmer who is in possession of saved seed of a registered breeder variety shall be permitted to re-sow such seed on his land, subject to the condition that he does not sell or otherwise commercially exploit the harvested material. The breeder may, at any time, apply to the competent authority for an order of rectification if it is established that the registered variety does not meet the criteria for registration, or that the registration was obtained through misrepresentation.

A registered breeder variety, for the purposes of this Act, shall be a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, the discovery or development of which required substantial effort. The application for registration of a variety shall be made in the prescribed manner to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall include a detailed description of the variety, including its characteristics and propagation methods. Where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, commonly known as a dependent variety, the applicant for registration of the dependent variety shall submit evidence demonstrating its derivation and dependence upon the initial variety. The Authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, register the dependent variety, provided that the breeder of the initial variety has been duly informed and has had an opportunity to submit objections. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a variety may file a complaint with the Authority within a period of ninety days from the date of registration, and the Authority shall conduct an inquiry in accordance with the procedures as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a register of all registered breeder varieties.

A registered breeder variety, for the purposes of this Act, shall be deemed to be a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, the discovery or development of which required substantial effort and shall be eligible for registration subject to the provisions herein. Any person claiming to be a breeder of a registered breeder variety must demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, that the variety has not been commercially exploited by anyone else for a period exceeding six years from the date of notification of the variety.
