Provided that, if the registered breeder variety is a hybrid or a variety which is not essentially derived, the period of commercial exploitation shall not exceed three years. The Authority may, however, extend this period in exceptional circumstances, subject to a reasoned order and consideration of the breeder’s investment. A farmer, who has bred a new variety using a registered breeder variety as a parent line, may be eligible for recognition as a plant breeder, subject to fulfilling the criteria for novelty and distinctiveness as prescribed.

Any person cultivating, processing, selling, exporting or importing a registered breeder variety without a valid license granted by the breeder, or in contravention of the terms and conditions of such license, shall be deemed to have committed an infringement under this Act and shall be liable to a penalty not less than five thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees for each instance of such infringement. Where an infringement involves the commercial exploitation of the harvested material of a registered breeder variety, the penalty shall not be less than ten thousand rupees but may extend to twenty thousand rupees per hectare. The competent authority, upon receiving credible evidence of infringement, may initiate an investigation and, subject to due process, issue a cease and desist order. Any farmer who is found to have unlawfully saved and reused seeds of a registered breeder variety for commercial purposes, in violation of any applicable restrictions, shall be subject to a fine as determined by the competent authority, provided that such farmer demonstrates no substantial commercial gain from the infringement.

Any registered breeder variety, upon grant of registration as provided herein, shall vest in the breeder the exclusive right to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and commercially exploit the variety. Notwithstanding this, the breeder may, by written instrument, assign or license any of these rights to any other person or entity, subject to the conditions specified in the instrument and the provisions of this Act. Any assignment or license of a registered breeder variety shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and no such assignment or license shall be effective against any third party until so registered. Where a license is granted, the breeder shall have the right to revoke the license upon reasonable cause and after providing due notice to the licensee, provided that such revocation does not affect any existing commercial transactions undertaken in good faith. The breeder shall also be entitled to receive royalties or other consideration as agreed upon in the licensing agreement, and disputes regarding such remuneration may be resolved through established arbitration mechanisms. A farmer, however, shall be exempt from these provisions when exercising the right to save, use, sow, exchange, and sell farm-saved seed of a registered breeder variety, subject to the limitations outlined elsewhere in this Act.

Any person claiming rights in a registered breeder variety, arising from an alleged infringement of rights as provided herein, shall submit a detailed statement of grounds for such claim to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority shall, within ninety days of receipt, direct the alleged infringer to file a counter-statement, failing which, ex parte proceedings may be initiated. A registered breeder variety, if proven to be essentially derived from another variety, shall not be considered an infringement, provided that the breeder of the original variety demonstrates substantial merit and novelty in the initial creation. Appeals against decisions of the Authority regarding infringement or essential derivation may be made to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. However, such appeals shall be subject to a limitation period of one hundred and twenty days from the date of the Authority’s order, and the appellant shall deposit a security equivalent to ten percent of the claimed damages. Any dispute concerning the scope of ‘essentially derived’ shall be adjudicated based on the characteristics of the plant variety as defined under this Act.

A registered breeder variety, upon successful completion of the distinctness, uniformity and stability tests as prescribed, shall be entered in the Registrar Index maintained for that purpose, noting the date of registration and the name and address of the breeder. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant a certificate of registration for a registered breeder variety to any person who has applied therefor and has demonstrated the requisite characteristics. Provided that, the application for registration shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a sample of the plant variety sufficient for conducting the necessary tests. Any amendment to the details of a registered breeder variety, including a transfer of rights, shall be recorded in the Registrar Index and a revised certificate issued, contingent upon verification of the amendment’s validity. The Registrar shall maintain the confidentiality of information relating to registered breeder varieties, except as required for the administration of this Act.

Any person asserting a right in a registered breeder variety, as provided herein, shall furnish to the Plant Variety Protection Authority a complete specification of the claim, detailing the characteristics which distinguish said variety from any commonly known variety, and demonstrating substantial novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. Failure to submit a claim complete specification within ninety days of notification by the Authority shall render the registration of the registered breeder variety void ab initio, and subject the claimant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any false representation in the claim complete specification, or any wilful omission of material facts relevant to the distinctiveness of the variety, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority may, notwithstanding any other provision, initiate suo motu inquiry into the veracity of any claim.

A registered breeder shall be a person who has bred, or is deemed to have bred, a new and distinct variety of any plant species, as specified in the First Schedule, and who has applied for registration of such variety under this Act. The application for registration shall be accompanied by such information and documentation as may be prescribed, including a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, and evidence of its novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. Provided that a farmer who has bred a new and distinct variety of a farmer’s variety, being a variety developed by farmers, may also be considered a registered breeder subject to fulfilling the criteria as laid down in this Act and the rules made thereunder, and upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any rights conferred upon a registered breeder shall be subject to the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and the public interest, as provided herein.

A person applying for registration as a registered breeder shall submit a declaration affirming the distinctiveness, uniformity and stability of the claimed plant variety, as per the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The application shall include the denomination proposed for the variety and a sample of the propagating material sufficient for evaluation. Where a breeder seeks to register a variety essentially derived from an existing registered variety, they shall furnish evidence demonstrating the derivation and the prior authorization of the initial registered breeder, subject to the provisions concerning farmers’ rights. The Authority may, after examination, require additional information or samples to verify the characteristics of the variety. Registration, once granted, confers exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, and import the protected variety, provided that the registered breeder diligently exploits the variety or takes appropriate measures to ensure its exploitation. Failure to do so may render the registration liable to revocation.

A registered breeder shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to save, sell, and multiply seeds of any variety registered under this Act. However, such rights shall not extend to varieties which are essentially derived varieties, except where the registered breeder has expressly consented to the exploitation of such essentially derived varieties, and terms are mutually agreed upon in writing. Any farmer who is engaged in the propagation, multiplication, or commercialization of seeds of a registered variety, without authorization from the registered breeder, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, provided that such farmer demonstrates a justifiable need to do so. The registered breeder may initiate proceedings before the competent authority for redressal of grievances relating to infringement of their rights, and the authority shall endeavor to provide a speedy and effective remedy. Where a registered breeder fails to exercise their rights diligently, the authority may, upon application by an interested party, revoke the registration of the variety.

A registered breeder, upon establishment of his claim as such under this Act, shall be entitled to register a new or extant plant variety, subject to the provisions herein concerning novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. The application for registration shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, including its lineage where known, and the location of a deposit of viable plant material. Where a farmer is also a registered breeder, the provisions relating to benefit sharing and reward, as detailed in Chapter VI, shall apply mutatis mutandis. Any person alleging infringement of a registered breeder’s rights may apply to the competent authority for redressal, providing evidence of the infringement and the extent of damage suffered. The competent authority may, after due inquiry, issue an injunction restraining the infringer and award damages commensurate with the loss sustained by the registered breeder, subject to verification of accounts and market value. A register of registered plant varieties shall be maintained and open for public inspection.

A registered breeder shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to register a new variety of any plant species, provided that such variety conforms to the criteria of distinctiveness, uniformity and stability as prescribed. The application for registration shall be accompanied by such information and documentation as may be required, including a detailed description of the plant variety and the results of relevant trials demonstrating its characteristics. A registered breeder may, with the prior approval of the Plant Varieties Protection Authority, assign, transfer or license the rights relating to a registered variety to any other person. However, any such transfer or license shall be subject to the conditions specified in the registration certificate and shall not prejudice the farmers’ rights as provided herein. Failure to comply with the prescribed conditions regarding the maintenance of the variety or the payment of renewal fees may result in the revocation of the registration, subject to a reasonable opportunity for the registered breeder to be heard.

Any registered breeder aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority denying or varying the terms of registration of a variety, or imposing a condition restricting the exercise of rights conferred by registration, may prefer an appeal to the High Court. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with the prescribed fee requirement shall render the appeal inadmissible. A registered breeder demonstrating wilful misstatement in the application for registration, or providing false information regarding the essentially derived variety, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, direct the removal of the variety from the register if such misstatement or false information materially affects the distinctness, uniformity, or stability of the variety. Any person abetting such an offence shall be deemed to be equally liable.

A registered breeder may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign, convey, license, or otherwise transfer the rights in a registered variety to any other person, whether corporate or individual, by a written instrument specifying the terms and conditions of such assignment, conveyance, license, or transfer. Any such instrument shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority within thirty days of its execution, failing which the transfer shall be deemed invalid as against any subsequent bona fide transferee. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all such registered transfers. A licensee of a registered breeder shall be entitled to use the protected variety for the purposes specified in the license, and no further rights shall accrue to such licensee unless expressly granted in the instrument. Provided that, a registered breeder may revoke a license if the licensee fails to comply with the terms and conditions stipulated therein, subject to a thirty-day notice period and a right to be heard. The Authority may, upon application, adjudicate disputes relating to the interpretation or enforcement of any such license.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register him as a registered breeder, or by any decision concerning the validity of a registration, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar a reasonable opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, modifying or reversing the decision of the Registrar. A registered breeder, demonstrating substantial contribution to the development of a new plant variety, may seek an amendment to the scope of protection, subject to proof of novelty and distinctiveness. However, any modification extending the scope shall not prejudice the rights of any person who relied on the original registration in good faith. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

A registered breeder, upon establishing novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity in a plant variety as per the criteria laid down under this Act, shall submit a complete application for registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The application shall include a detailed description of the variety, characteristics, and the denomination proposed for it. The Authority may, if satisfied that the variety meets the prescribed requirements, register the breeder as the owner of the plant variety, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any dispute regarding the veracity of the breeder’s claim, or the characteristics of the variety, shall be adjudicated by a Chairperson Judicial Member appointed to the Authority, who shall conduct a hearing and issue a reasoned order. Provided that, the registered breeder shall have the right to appeal any adverse decision of the Authority before the designated appellate forum, as provided herein. The registration shall be valid for a period specified in this Act, and may be renewed subject to continued compliance with all applicable conditions.

A registered breeder, upon successful application and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, shall be entitled to maintain a current index of varieties for which protection has been granted, to be known as the breeder’s index. The registrar shall maintain a central registrar index consolidating information derived from breeder’s indices, and this index shall be open for inspection by any person upon payment of a fee as determined by the Central Government. Any amendment to a breeder’s index shall be communicated to the registrar within thirty days of such amendment, failing which the registrar may initiate proceedings to rectify the central registrar index. Provided that, a registered breeder may, with the prior approval of the registrar, transfer rights pertaining to a registered variety to another person, and such transfer shall be recorded in both the breeder’s index and the central registrar index. The registrar may, as provided herein, require a statutory declaration confirming the authenticity of entries within either index. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to index maintenance may result in a penalty.

A registered breeder, upon establishing demonstrable infringement of a protected plant variety as provided herein, shall be entitled to seek relief before the competent authority. Any person who, without authorization from the registered breeder or a licensee, produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports, or exports a variety that is essentially derived from the registered variety, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per infringement. However, a farmer who, in good faith and for private and non-commercial purposes, retains and uses seeds of a protected variety shall exempt person from such penalties. The competent authority may, subject to verification of damages, order an injunction restraining further infringement and award damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the registered breeder, including any lost profits. Failure to comply with an order of the competent authority shall constitute a further offence punishable with imprisonment.

Any person desiring the rectification of any entry in the register of Patents shall submit a petition to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, setting forth the grounds upon which such rectification is sought and the particulars of the entry to be rectified. The petition shall be accompanied by such evidence as may be necessary to substantiate the claims made therein, and shall be served upon the patentee or their legal representative. The High Court, upon receiving such petition and after affording the patentee an opportunity to be heard, may, if satisfied that the grounds for rectification are well-founded, direct the rectification of the register. Where the rectification sought involves a question of title or ownership, the Court may require the petitioner to establish their locus standi. Provided that, the High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, order a stay of any proceedings relating to the patent in question pending the completion of the rectification process. The rectifying register shall be maintained as a public record, accessible for inspection during office hours.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, or desiring to have any entry amended or altered, may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register. Such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall state the grounds on which the applicant seeks rectification. The High Court, upon being satisfied that the applicant has established a prima facie case, shall issue notice to the patentee and any other person whose interest may be affected by the proposed rectification. Subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, the High Court may direct the Controller to amend the register accordingly. Provided that no rectification shall be made which would prejudice the rights of any person who has, in good faith, relied upon the register as it stood prior to such rectification. The Controller shall, following any order for rectification, update the register and notify all interested parties of the changes made, as provided herein. Any decision of the High Court regarding the rectifying register shall be final and binding.

The Controller of Trade Marks may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules to carry out the provisions of this Act, and all rules so made shall be subject to the prior approval of the Central Government. Such rules may provide for the procedure for filing applications for registration of trade marks, including the forms to be used and the fees payable. Rules carry provisions relating to the examination of trade mark applications, the hearing of oppositions, and the maintenance of the Register of Trade Marks. Provided that any rule made under this Act which imposes a fee shall be laid before each House of Parliament, and shall not take effect until approved by resolution of that House. The Controller may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, delegate any of the powers conferred by these rules to any officer subordinate to him.

The Registrar shall maintain a Register of Trade Marks in accordance with the provisions of this Act and may, with the approval of the Central Government, prescribe the manner of maintaining such Register. Rules carry provisions relating to the classification of goods and services for the purposes of registration, and such classification shall be in conformity with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may deem necessary. Any application for registration shall be examined as provided herein, and the Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. Provided that, where an application is refused, the applicant may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of such refusal. The Registrar may, by order, direct any person to produce documents or attend before him for the purpose of examining the application.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the right to obtain an injunction against any person dealing in goods or services bearing a mark deceptively similar to their registered trade mark, subject to proof of likelihood of confusion. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a trade mark, alleging it is likely to deceive or cause confusion, may apply to the High Court for rectification of the register, provided that such application is made within a period of one year from the date of registration. The Court, upon being satisfied of the grounds for rectification, may order amendment or cancellation of the registration. 

The Trade Marks Registry may, with the consent of the proprietor, record an assignment or transmission of a trade mark, and such record shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment. Rules carry provisions relating to the fees payable for all applications, registrations, and other proceedings under this Act, and the Registrar shall have the power to determine such fees, subject to the approval of the Central Government. Any false entry made in the register shall be subject to penalties as prescribed.

The Registrar shall maintain a public register of registered designs, and all applications for registration, and any amendments thereto, shall be recorded therein as provided herein. Rules carry provisions relating to the manner of maintaining such register, including the form and content of entries, and the procedures for inspection thereof by interested persons upon payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, prefer an appeal to the High Court within the time limit specified in the rules. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe the fees payable for all proceedings under this Act, and may differentiate such fees based on the nature and complexity of the application or matter involved. Provided that no fee shall be so high as to be prohibitive or unduly burdensome to applicants. All prescribed forms shall be readily available to the public, both in physical and electronic formats, and the Registrar shall ensure their consistent application.

The Registrar shall, with a view to ensuring diligent prosecution of applications for registration, establish a system of timelines for each stage of the examination process, and these timelines shall be publicly available on the official website. Any failure by the Registrar to adhere to these established timelines, without reasonable cause duly recorded, may be subject to review by the appellate authority as provided herein. Rules carry provisions relating to the acceptance of digital signatures for filing documents and conducting hearings, and such rules shall conform to the standards prescribed by the Certifying Authority. Provided that, any rule framed under this Act concerning fees shall be subject to prior notification and public consultation. The Registrar may, subject to these rules, require applicants to submit undertakings regarding the veracity of information furnished. Failure to comply with these undertakings shall render the application liable to be dismissed.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging the unlawful import of goods bearing a counterfeit mark identical to a registered trade mark, initiate an investigation without undue delay, and may require the complainant to furnish a security deposit equivalent to the estimated value of the goods in question, subject to a review of such amount if the complainant demonstrates financial hardship. Any person found guilty of importing goods bearing such counterfeit marks, as determined through investigation and evidence presented, shall be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may also be subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Rules carry provisions for the expedited hearing of cases involving counterfeit goods, and the destruction of seized infringing materials. Provided that, the Registrar may, at their discretion, order a sampling and testing of the goods to ascertain the veracity of the claim. Failure to comply with an order of the Registrar under this Act shall attract a further penalty of ten thousand rupees per day of non-compliance.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign the trade mark and the goodwill or part thereof in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. Any assignment not in writing shall be void. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall be entitled to use the trade mark in connection with the business as it was carried on by the assignor. However, the assignment of a trade mark shall not affect the right of the registrar to revoke the trade mark on any grounds subsisting at the date of the assignment. 

The Trade Marks Registry may, upon application by the assignee and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, register the assignee as the new proprietor of the trade mark. Rules carry provisions relating to the form of assignment, the evidence required for registration of the assignment, and the procedure for rectifying any errors in the register concerning assignments. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration and subject to verification of requisite documentation as provided herein, examine the application for compliance with all procedural requirements. Any objection raised by the Registrar regarding the application shall be communicated to the applicant, who may, within a period of thirty days from the date of such communication, file a statement of grounds and evidence in support of their application. Should the Registrar remain unsatisfied, a hearing shall be conducted, and the applicant afforded an opportunity to present their case. Decisions of the Registrar are subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the decision. Rules carry provisions for the conduct of hearings, including the admission of evidence and cross-examination of witnesses. The Appellate Board may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and its orders shall be final and binding, unless an appeal lies to the Supreme Court on a question of law.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete application for registration and finding the mark registrable, proceed to examine it as provided herein. Rules carry provisions relating to the examination process, including timelines for raising objections and the applicant’s response thereto. Any objection raised by the Registrar shall be clearly articulated and accompanied by supporting reasoning derived from established legal precedent and the principles of invention convention, ensuring fair and consistent application of the law. An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may file a review petition within sixty days of the order, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines or requirements shall be deemed a waiver of rights. The Registrar may, at their discretion, extend these timelines in exceptional circumstances, documented in writing. Any person claiming infringement of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to seek remedies under this Act, including injunctions, damages, and account of profits.

A person shall be considered a producer of a cinematograph film if they have assumed financial responsibility for the making of said film, and such responsibility is evidenced by a documented allocation of funds towards production costs, as provided herein. Registration of a cinematograph film with the Registrar of Copyrights shall require full disclosure of all producers involved, including details of their financial contribution and creative control exercised over the work. Where a cinematograph film is produced by multiple persons jointly, each shall be deemed a producer, and the registration shall reflect the proportionate share of financial responsibility undertaken by each. Any dispute regarding producer relation cinematograph shall be subject to verification of production accounts and creative input as determined by the Registrar. Failure to accurately declare producer details during registration may render the copyright invalid, subject to rectification procedures outlined in this Act. The Registrar may request additional evidence to substantiate claims of producer status.

Any person who, without the prior consent of the producer, engages in the unauthorized duplication, distribution, or public exhibition of a cinematographic film shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The term “producer” in relation to a cinematographic film shall include the principal director, and any person who finances or controls the production of said film, subject to a duly executed agreement establishing such control. Any cinematographic film imported into India which violates the provisions herein regarding producer relation cinematograph shall be liable to seizure by customs authorities. Upon conviction for an offence under this Act, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Repeat offenders shall be subject to enhanced penalties, including a doubling of the fine and a mandatory minimum imprisonment term of one year, as determined by the adjudicating authority.

A producer of a cinematograph film shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be deemed the first owner of the copyright in the cinematograph film, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary entered into prior to the commencement of the film’s production. However, any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film, or any license to reproduce, distribute, or otherwise exploit the film, shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the producer. Where a cinematograph film is produced by a person under a contract of service, the copyright shall vest in the employer unless otherwise agreed. Any transfer of rights relating to a producer relation cinematograph, including the right to make derivative works, shall require prior intimation to all parties holding significant creative control over the film’s constituent elements. Provided that, such intimation does not confer any right to object, but merely ensures transparency in the transaction. The producer may grant licenses for specific territories or durations, subject to reasonable royalty rates determined by mutual agreement.

A producer of a cinematograph film shall be deemed to be the first owner of the copyright therein, subject to any contract to the contrary expressly excluding such ownership. However, any person who makes any sound recording, whether in the form of discs, tapes or other devices, shall be deemed to be the producer in relation to that sound recording, and shall possess the rights as such. Appeals concerning the determination of ‘producer relation cinematograph’ and the validity of contracts impacting such ownership, shall initially be heard by the District Court having jurisdiction. Should the aggrieved party remain dissatisfied with the decision of the District Court, an appeal may be made to the High Court. It is clarified that a contract excluding ownership must be in writing and demonstrably entered into prior to the commencement of the cinematograph film’s production, failing which it shall be considered void as provided herein. Any claim of joint production shall require clear evidence of shared creative control and financial contribution.

For the purposes of this Act, “means invention” shall denote any new and useful art, process, method or machine, including any new arrangement or combination of existing arts, processes, methods or machines, and extending to alloys, compositions of matter, and products produced by such arts, processes, methods or machines. Provided that a mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance, even if previously unknown, shall not constitute an invention. Furthermore, an invention shall be considered commercially workable only if it is capable of being manufactured or used in any industry. Subject to the provisions herein, an invention relating to a traditional knowledge or agrochemical, or a biological diversity, shall not be patentable unless it demonstrates a significant technical advancement.

Any person who proves ownership of a means invention, and who has suffered damage as a consequence of an infringement of the patent rights granted under this Act, shall be entitled to seek remedies as provided herein. Such remedies shall include, but not be limited to, an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, and recovery of damages sustained by the patentee. Damages assessed may account for actual losses, reasonable royalties, and, in cases of willful infringement, enhanced damages up to three times the amount of actual losses. 

A licensee of a patented means invention, having a contractual right to exclude others, may pursue remedies for infringement subject to the terms of the licensing agreement. Where a means invention is subject to a compulsory license granted under this Act, the licensor shall be entitled to a share of any damages recovered by the licensee in an infringement action, proportionate to the royalty payable under the compulsory license. Any action for infringement shall be brought within three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement.

The determination of whether a subject matter constitutes a means invention, as provided herein, shall be predicated upon a rigorous assessment of novelty and non-obviousness. An application claiming a means invention must demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Controller, that the proposed invention is not previously known, either through written or oral disclosure, or by any other means, to the public before the date of the application. Furthermore, such invention shall not be obvious to a person skilled in the relevant art, considering the common general knowledge existing in that art. 

Where a means invention relates to a process, the process shall be capable of being observed, replicated, and applied industrially. A mere theoretical possibility, lacking demonstrable practical utility, shall not be considered a means invention under this Act. The Controller may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to furnish evidence substantiating the industrial applicability of the claimed invention, and failure to do so may result in the rejection of the application. Any adaptation or combination of existing technologies, lacking a discernible inventive step, shall not qualify as a means invention.

Means invention technology shall be construed as encompassing any novel process, apparatus, article of manufacture, composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, irrespective of its form or application, provided that such technology demonstrates a discernible technical effect. A means invention technology is deemed to be patentable subject to the provisions of this Act, and shall not include mere discovery of a naturally occurring substance, an abstract idea, or a mathematical method as such. However, the application of a mathematical method or abstract idea to bring about a tangible technical result may constitute means invention technology. Any combination of existing technologies, if resulting in a synergistic effect not predictable from the individual components, may also qualify as means invention technology, subject to satisfying the criteria of novelty and inventive step as provided herein.

Any person desiring registration of means invention technology shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by a detailed description of the technology, including its technical specifications and operational principles. The application shall also include a statement outlining the novelty and inventive step inherent in the proposed means invention technology, demonstrating a clear advancement over existing technologies. Supporting documentation, such as experimental data or simulations, may be furnished to substantiate claims of efficacy. 

An applicant may, subject to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein, claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a convention country. The Controller shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with procedural requirements and may require the applicant to amend the application if necessary. Registration shall be granted only upon satisfactory verification of the means invention technology’s patentability and payment of the prescribed fees.

Any person who has reasonably relied upon a published notification of grant of a patent, and thereby undertaken substantial work for the commercial exploitation of the means invention technology, shall be entitled to reasonable compensation from the patentee should the patent be subsequently revoked for lack of patentable subject matter or prior claiming of the invention. Such compensation shall include, but not be limited to, costs incurred in research and development, tooling, and marketing, subject to demonstrating a direct causal link between the published notification and the undertaken work. Where a patentee demonstrates that the revocation resulted from fraud or wilful misrepresentation by the compensated party, the patentee may seek recovery of the compensation paid. A court, as provided herein, may appoint an assessor with expertise in the relevant technology to determine the quantum of reasonable compensation, considering prevailing industry standards and the potential profits lost by both parties. The burden of proof regarding substantial work and reasonable reliance lies with the claimant.

The controller of patents shall, upon receipt of an application claiming a means invention technology, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the application satisfy such requirements, it shall be published in the Official Gazette, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. Any person may, within a period of three months from the date of publication, file a representation against the grant of a patent, alleging lack of novelty or inventive step in the claimed means invention technology. Such representation shall be supported by evidence and shall be considered by the controller, who may, if deemed necessary, require the applicant to amend the claims or submit further evidence. The controller’s decision on the representation shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the appellate board established under this Act. A patent for a means invention technology shall be granted only if it meets the criteria of novelty, non-obviousness, and industrial applicability, and is not prohibited under the provisions of this Act.

Any person desiring to secure a patent for a means invention technology shall submit a complete and clear specification detailing the nature of the invention, including any supporting drawings necessary for its full understanding. The specification shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention, and shall be drafted in a manner understandable to a person skilled in the relevant field. An applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, claim priority from a previous application filed in another country, provided that such application was filed within twelve months of the Indian filing date. All claims shall be clear, concise, and supported by the specification, and shall define the scope of protection sought. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the patent application or limitation of the granted patent’s claims. Any subsequent amendment to the specification shall not extend beyond the content originally disclosed.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a means invention technology as being original or legitimately patented, or knowingly sells, offers for sale, distributes, or imports any article bearing a false or misleading indication of patenting or originality, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, if the article in question is essential for public health or safety, the court may, subject to the circumstances, impose a higher fine. Any evidence obtained through lawful means demonstrating commercial gain derived from such deceptive practice shall be admissible as proof of intent. Furthermore, any person abetting or conspiring with the offender shall be liable for the same penalties as provided herein. The Controller of Patents may, upon sufficient cause, initiate an investigation into any such alleged offence and may seize relevant materials as evidence.

Any assignment of right, title, and interest in any means invention technology, whether patented or unpatented, shall be in writing and registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein. Such registration shall be effected upon submission of a prescribed form, accompanied by evidence of consideration paid or to be paid for the assignment, and a certified copy of the instrument of assignment. The assignee shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, possess all the rights of the assignor in respect of the assigned means invention technology. Where the assignment is made subject to a condition requiring further performance of an obligation by the assignor, the assignee may enforce such condition against the assignor. A licensee of a patented means invention technology may, with the consent of the patentee, assign their license to a third party, provided that such assignment does not contravene any terms specified in the original license agreement. Failure to register an assignment shall not invalidate it, but it may affect its enforceability against third parties.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent relating to means invention technology shall, prior to the institution of any suit, serve the alleged infringer with a written notice of such intention, detailing the specific claims infringed and providing reasonable evidence substantiating such infringement. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of service, submit a counter-notice disputing the validity of the patent or the claim of infringement, the matter shall be referred to a Technology Assessment Panel constituted under this Act. The Panel shall, subject to rules, conduct a preliminary examination and submit a report within ninety days. Dissatisfied parties may appeal the Panel’s report to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the Panel’s decision. The High Court’s decision on the validity of the patent shall be final, except for appeals to the Supreme Court on questions of law. Failure to comply with the notice provisions herein shall not, however, automatically invalidate a claim of infringement but may be considered by the court in determining damages.

Any person claiming ownership of means invention technology, whether through assignment, inheritance, or operation of law, shall furnish a detailed declaration to the Controller of Patents, outlining the provenance of title and the nature of the inventive contribution. Such declaration shall be accompanied by supporting documentation, including but not limited to, prior art searches and technical specifications demonstrating novelty. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the patent application subject to rejection, or invalidate any patent granted based on incomplete or inaccurate information. In the event of a dispute regarding ownership, a case proceeding may be initiated before the appropriate court, and the Controller shall suspend examination of the related application pending final determination. Provided that, the Controller may, subject to justifiable cause, extend the deadline for submission of the declaration by a period not exceeding sixty days. All submissions shall be deemed confidential as provided herein.

Any person employing means invention technology for commercial gain, without due acknowledgement of traditional knowledge associated with bio-diversity and agricultural practices, shall be deemed to have contravened this Act. The Farmers Rights Authority, constituted under this Act, may initiate inquiries into suspected violations, and shall have the power to demand production of books of account and other relevant documentation. Failure to comply with such demand shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any patented invention derived from indigenous varieties, and commercialized without benefit-sharing arrangements approved by the Authority, will be subject to revocation of the patent and a fine equivalent to three times the profits accrued. Repeated offenses, as determined by the Authority, may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, in addition to any financial penalties imposed as provided herein. All appeals relating to decisions of the Authority shall lie with the High Court.

Any person alleging infringement of a patent relating to means invention technology shall, prior to the institution of proceedings before any court, notify the alleged infringer in writing, detailing the specific patent claimed to be infringed and the nature of the infringement. Such notification shall include a reasoned statement demonstrating a prima facie case of infringement, supported by evidence as provided herein. Failure to provide adequate notification, or a notification deemed frivolous by the Controller, may result in a stay of proceedings. An appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding the adequacy of notification shall lie before the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patentee may seek interim injunctions from a court of competent jurisdiction, but such injunctions shall not be granted without due consideration of the potential harm to the alleged infringer. Any order granting or refusing an injunction may be appealed as per established judicial procedure.

The expression “means patent granted” shall denote a patent subsisting under this Act, whether originating from an application filed directly under this Act or through the international patent system as provided herein. A means patent granted shall be deemed to include any patent which, though applied for prior to the commencement of this Act, is granted thereafter. Where a provisional patent is converted into a complete specification and subsequently examined and granted, the means patent granted shall be reckoned from the date of such grant. Subject to the provisions contained herein, a means patent granted confers upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, and sell the invention across territories governed by this Act. Any assignment or transfer of a means patent granted shall be subject to the registration requirements as prescribed.

A means patent granted under this Act shall vest in the applicant upon fulfillment of all statutory requirements and subject to payment of the prescribed fees, and such vesting shall be recorded in the Register of Patents maintained by the Controller of Patents. The Register shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars entered therein, including the date of the means patent granted and the name and address of the patentee. Any alteration to the particulars of a means patent granted, such as a change in the patentee’s name or address, or a transfer of ownership, shall be subject to an application for amendment to the Register, accompanied by the requisite documentation and fee. A provisional specification, if filed, shall be deemed to be abandoned if a complete specification is not filed within the prescribed period, thereby forfeiting any right to a means patent. The Controller may, however, extend this period subject to justifiable cause.

A means patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention throughout the territory of India, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a patentee alleges infringement of a means patent granted, they may apply to the High Court for a decree of injunction and recovery of damages. The application shall clearly delineate the scope of the claimed invention and specify the acts constituting the alleged infringement. Any person opposing the grant of a means patent shall file a notice of opposition within a period of four months from the date of advertisement of the patent application. The Controller of Patents shall, after considering the representation of both parties, issue a reasoned order either accepting or rejecting the opposition. A licensee of a means patent may, subject to the terms of the license, enforce the patent against infringers, provided that the patentee has failed to do so within a reasonable time after being duly notified of the infringement.

A means patent granted under this Act shall be subject to a term of twenty years from the date of filing of the complete specification, unless otherwise provided herein. Notwithstanding this, a patent for a pharmaceutical substance may be extended by a period not exceeding five years, subject to demonstrating substantial clinical trials conducted in India and fulfilling conditions regarding public health needs as determined by the Controller. Any extension granted shall be recorded in the register and shall be published in the Official Gazette. Where a compulsory license is granted, the patentee shall be entitled to a reasonable royalty, the amount of which shall be determined by the Controller, considering the economic benefit accruing to the licensee. A patent application claiming a traditional knowledge or biological resource shall require prior informed consent of the associated community or authority, and equitable sharing of benefits derived from commercial exploitation, as prescribed. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the means patent.

Any person who infringes a means patent granted under this Act, or aids, abets, or procures such infringement, shall be liable to a civil suit for recovery of damages. The damages awarded shall not be less than a reasonable royalty for the use of the patented invention and may include lost profits, provided that such profits are reasonably ascertainable. Where infringement is proved to be willful, the court may increase the damages to not more than three times the amount found. Any order for damages may also include an injunction restraining the infringer from further infringing acts, subject to terms and conditions as the court deems fit. A person falsely representing a product as patented, or using the term “patent” without valid grant, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Any evidence obtained through unlawful means relating to a patent application shall not be admissible.

Any means patent granted under this Act, whether original or derived from an earlier patent, shall vest in the applicant or, where a patent is jointly made, in the joint applicants, subject to the provisions contained herein. An assignment of any such means patent, or any right therein, shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Controller of Patents as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be void. A licensee of a means patent may, subject to such terms as may be agreed upon with the patentee, assign their interest in the license to another person. Where a means patent is assigned, the assignee shall be entitled to all the rights and remedies available to the original patentee, provided that the assignee gives notice of the assignment to the Controller. Any agreement restricting the assignment of a means patent shall be voidable at the option of the assignor. The Controller may, upon application, rectify any error in the register of assignments.

A means patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention in India, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person desiring to avail of rights conferred by such a means patent shall be required to demonstrate a clear and direct nexus between the claimed invention and the manufacturing process employed. The Controller, upon sufficient cause being shown and after examination of relevant documentation, may grant a license to another party, provided that the patentee is adequately compensated as determined by the Controller. Registration common regulations pertaining to the maintenance of a public register of patents and associated administrative procedures shall be adhered to strictly. Failure to comply with these regulations may result in the lapse of the means patent. Any dispute regarding the validity of a means patent or the scope of the exclusive rights conferred thereby shall be subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court.

A means patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention throughout India, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any assertion of rights relating to trade marks devoid of inherent distinctiveness, or those acquired through deceptive practices, shall not be considered valid grounds for opposing the exercise of rights conferred by a means patent. The Controller may, upon sufficient cause shown and after due examination, revoke a means patent if it is proven that the invention lacks novelty or involves an obvious step to a person skilled in the art. Compliance with all procedural requirements as stipulated in the rules made under this Act is mandatory for maintaining the validity of a means patent, and failure to do so may result in its lapse. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the prescribed time limit.

Any person who infringes a means patent granted under this Act, by making, selling, offering for sale, or importing the patented invention without the license of the patentee, shall be liable to a suit for injunction and damages. The quantum of damages, subject to the provisions contained herein, shall be determined based on a reasonable royalty, or three times the actual losses suffered by the patentee due to the infringement, whichever is higher. Where the infringement is proved to be willful, the court may enhance the damages to five times the actual losses. All applications for injunction and damages shall be filed in the manner prescribed, and any delay beyond the prescribed period may be subject to dismissal. Failure to comply with an injunction order issued under this Act shall constitute contempt of court and attract further penalties as deemed fit.

A ‘means patent granted’ shall denote a patent validly issued under this Act, conferring upon the patentee the exclusive rights to make, use, exercise, sell or distribute the invention in India, subject to the provisions contained herein. The registrar shall consider all relevant evidence submitted by the applicant and any third party in determining the validity of such a means patent granted, including but not limited to prior art and the inventive step demonstrated. Provided that, a means patent granted may be revoked if it is proven to lack novelty or involve an obvious variation of existing knowledge. Any transfer of a means patent granted shall be subject to registration with the patent office as provided herein.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall file an application in India, in the prescribed form and manner, at the Patent Office. The application shall contain a complete specification describing the invention and shall be accompanied by such drawings, if necessary, as are required to explain the invention. Where an application is filed claiming priority from a convention application filed in a convention country, the applicant shall indicate the priority date and country in the application as provided herein. A request for examination of the filed application india shall be made within thirty-six months from the date of filing, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to make such a request may result in the application being deemed abandoned. The Controller may, however, extend the time for making the request upon sufficient cause being shown. All documents filed with the application shall be maintained as confidential until publication, except as otherwise provided under this Act.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall file an application in India, conforming to the requirements as prescribed under the rules made under this Act, and such application shall be examined by the Controller of Patents in accordance with the provisions herein. The application shall contain a complete specification, claims, and such other documents as may be required. Where an application is filed claiming priority from a convention country, the applicant shall furnish a certified copy of the priority document within the prescribed period, failing which the priority date shall not be considered. 

Subject to the provisions contained herein, an applicant may, before the expiration of thirty-six months from the date of the filed application india, file a divisional application relating to the same invention. The Controller may, if satisfied that the subject matter of the divisional application is disclosed in the complete specification of the first-mentioned application, allow the divisional application to proceed. All applications shall be subject to a request for examination and payment of the requisite fee.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall file an application in India, in a manner prescribed, demonstrating a novel and useful invention. The application shall include a complete specification, and claims defining the scope of the invention. Where a filed application india claims priority from a corresponding application filed in a convention country, evidence of such filing, duly authenticated, shall accompany the application and be submitted within the prescribed period. Subject to verification by the Controller, failure to provide such evidence may result in loss of priority. An applicant may, at any time before the grant of a patent, voluntarily amend the specification, provided that the amendment does not extend the scope of the invention beyond what was originally disclosed. All applications shall be subject to examination as provided herein, and compliance with the requirements of this Act is mandatory for continued processing. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for the purposes of examination.

Any person filing an application in India for a patent, and falsely representing themselves as the inventor, or knowingly making a false statement in relation to the entitlement to claim the invention, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Where a filed application india lacks sufficient basis in prior art as demonstrated through a search report conducted by an authorized international searching authority, the Controller of Patents may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, require the applicant to furnish a detailed statement of the inventive step. Failure to comply with such requirement within a period of ninety days from the date of the notice shall render the application liable to be deemed withdrawn as provided herein. Any appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding withdrawal shall be filed within sixty days to the Appellate Board, and non-compliance will result in forfeiture of all rights pertaining to the filed application india.

Any person being the applicant for a patent, or deriving title from such applicant, may assign the application, or the patent resulting from the application, to any other person, subject to the conditions, if any, specified in the assignment deed and as provided herein. An assignment of a filed application india shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Controller of Patents within such time as may be prescribed. The Controller shall maintain a register of assignments and shall record the particulars of every assignment registered. Where a patent or an application for a patent is assigned more than once, the last assignee registered shall be deemed to be the proprietor for the purposes of this Act. 

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, a license may be granted to another person to work a patented invention, and such license may be exclusive, subject to reasonable royalty or other consideration. Any assignment or license not registered as aforesaid shall be invalid as against any subsequent assignee or licensee who has registered their assignment or license.

The term of a patent granted under this Act shall, subject to the provisions herein contained, be twenty years from the date of filing of the complete specification, unless otherwise provided for in this Act. Where an application for a patent is filed for an invention relating to a pharmaceutical product, a term of patent may be extended by a period not exceeding five years, provided that such extension is justified by demonstrating significant clinical trials conducted after the filing date, and that such trials were necessary to obtain marketing approval from the appropriate regulatory authority. Any application for such extension shall be filed with the Controller of Patents within six months of the grant of marketing approval. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as laid down by the Controller shall render the application for extension invalid. Notwithstanding anything contained herein, the patentee shall pay the prescribed renewal fees annually to maintain the patent in force throughout its term; non-payment of such fees shall result in the patent lapsing.

The term of patent granted under this Act shall, subject to the provisions contained herein, be twenty years from the date of filing of the complete specification, unless otherwise provided. However, in the case of a patent for a pharmaceutical substance or a formulation thereof, or a pesticide, or a plant variety, the term may be extended by a period not exceeding five years, provided that an application for such extension is made at least six months prior to the expiry of the original term. Any extension granted shall be subject to the condition that the patentee demonstrates substantial improvements to the patented invention, and that such improvements are not obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field. Failure to comply with the requirements for extension shall render the patent invalid as of the date of its original expiry, and no claim for damages shall be admissible. The patentee shall maintain annual renewal fees as prescribed, failing which the patent shall cease to have effect.

The term of patent granted under this Act shall, save as otherwise provided herein, be twenty years from the date of filing of the complete specification, subject to the payment of prescribed renewal fees as determined by the Controller. Failure to pay any such renewal fee within three months of the due date shall attract a surcharge equivalent to fifty percent of the outstanding fee, and continued failure for a further period of three months shall result in the patent lapsing, unless a petition for restoration is filed with sufficient cause and accompanied by the outstanding fees and applicable penalties. Any person who falsely represents a patent as being in force, after its term has expired or it has lapsed due to non-payment, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine, or with both. The Controller may, however, extend the term of a patent relating to pharmaceutical products for a period not exceeding five years, contingent upon demonstrable public health need and subject to conditions prescribed by the Central Government.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, the amendment thereof, or the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeal shall be instituted by filing a notice of appeal with the Controller, accompanied by the prescribed fee, within a period of ninety days from the date of the Controller’s decision. Provided that the Appellate Board may, upon sufficient cause being shown, extend the appeal period by a further thirty days. An application for extension of time shall be accompanied by an affidavit explaining the reasons for the delay. No appeal shall be entertained unless the prescribed fee has been paid and the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for review.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, the rectification of a register, or the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, unless an application for a certified copy of the order has been made, in which case the appeal may be filed within ninety days from the date of receipt of the certified copy. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the appeal period by a further thirty days. All appeals shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a statement of the grounds on which the appellant relies, and failure to comply with these requirements may render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court on grounds of error of law.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, the rectification of a register, or the revocation of a patent, shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeal shall be instituted by filing a notice of appeal with the prescribed fee, within a period of sixty days from the date of the order or decision sought to be appealed against, unless an application for extension of time is duly made and allowed. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the appeal period by a further thirty days. Failure to comply with the stipulated appeal period shall render the appeal inadmissible, save where delay is proven to be attributable to circumstances beyond the appellant’s reasonable control and communicated to the Controller without undue delay. All supporting documentation relevant to the grounds of appeal must accompany the notice of appeal.

Any person dissatisfied with an order of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant, revocation, or amendment of a patent, or concerning any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be instituted by filing a notice of appeal with the prescribed fee within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, failing which the appeal shall be deemed to be barred and the order shall stand affirmed. Provided that the Appellate Board may, for sufficient cause to be recorded in writing, condone a delay of up to an additional thirty days in the filing of such notice. Any attempt to circumvent this appeal period through collusive acts or fraudulent misrepresentation shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may further disqualify them from pursuing any future patent applications. The Appellate Board’s decision on matters of appeal shall be final and binding, subject to rights of judicial review as provided by law.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, recorded in the Register of Patents, shall be subject to a right of appeal to the High Court, provided that such appeal is initiated within ninety days from the date of such recordation. Should the assignee seek to further assign their interest, a notice of intention to assign must be filed with the Controller of Patents, and any party claiming an adverse interest may lodge a caveat within thirty days of the publication of said notice. Failure to exercise the right of appeal or to lodge a caveat within the prescribed period shall be deemed a waiver of the right to contest the assignment. The Controller may, subject to justifiable cause, extend the appeal period by a maximum of thirty days, but no such extension shall be granted if it would unduly prejudice the interests of the assignee or any other party. All appeals shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the assignment record.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, revocation thereof, or any other matter determined under this Act, may lodge an appeal with the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, unless an application for certified copy of said order has been duly made, in which case the period shall run from the date of receipt of the certified copy. It is clarified that frivolous or vexatious appeals may be dismissed with costs, and the Appellate Board retains the discretion to extend the appeal period in cases of demonstrable and unavoidable delay, subject to sufficient cause being shown. Furthermore, a cross-objection to an appeal shall be filed within thirty days of the appellant’s appeal being lodged, and will be considered alongside the primary appeal. Failure to adhere to these timelines may render the appeal inadmissible.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, the rectification of a register, or the revocation of a patent, shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding condonation of delay. An appellant seeking an extension of this appeal period must demonstrate sufficient cause, and the Appellate Board may, if satisfied, extend the period not exceeding an additional thirty days. All applications for registration india relating to patents, and any associated records, shall be readily available for inspection by any party to an appeal, as directed by the Appellate Board. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, dismiss an appeal if the appellant fails to establish a prima facie case of grievance or if the appeal is deemed frivolous.

A basic application, for the purposes of claiming priority under this Act, shall mean the first application made in a convention country for a patent, or for a utility model, in respect of the same or substantially the same invention. Such an application must fulfill all requirements for a patent application as prescribed by the laws of that convention country. Provided that, where an application disclosing the invention was first made public prior to the filing of the basic application, the priority date shall be limited to the date of such public disclosure, subject to the provisions contained herein. An applicant claiming priority based on a basic application shall file a certified copy of said basic application with the Controller within the prescribed period. Failure to do so may result in loss of priority.

A complete application claiming priority from a basic application filed in a convention country shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the basic application, or an English translation thereof if the basic application is not in English. The applicant shall furnish a declaration stating that the complete application is a complete and accurate copy of the basic application, subject to any amendments permitted under this Act. Where the basic application is not available, the applicant may submit a sworn statement detailing the reasons for its unavailability and providing sufficient information to establish the filing date and contents of the basic application. Provided that, failure to submit the certified copy or translation within the prescribed period may render the claim of priority ineffective, unless satisfactory cause is shown to the Controller of Patents. Any subsequent amendment to the complete application shall not extend beyond the disclosure contained within the basic application, as provided herein.

Any person claiming priority from a basic application filed in a convention country shall, upon filing a complete specification as provided herein, declare the details of such basic application to the Controller, including the country of origin, the date of filing, and the application number. Failure to furnish such details may render the application subject to a period of grace, but shall not exceed six months from the date of filing in India. A request for restoration of priority may be permitted if the failure is proven to be due to unavoidable circumstances, and the applicant demonstrates diligent efforts to comply. The Controller may, subject to verification of the basic application details with the originating office, grant a priority claim. Provided that, if the basic application has been abandoned, withdrawn, or refused, the applicant shall forfeit any right to priority under this Act, and the application will be treated as a new filing as of its actual filing date. Any dispute regarding the validity of a claimed priority shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction.

A basic application, when duly filed with the Controller of Patents in accordance with the prescribed manner, shall establish a priority date for a corresponding Indian patent application, provided that such basic application originates from a convention country as defined under this Act. The applicant shall, at the time of filing the Indian application, furnish a certified copy or a duly authenticated translation of the basic application, together with a declaration verifying its authenticity and completeness. Where the basic application is not in English, a verified translation into English shall be mandatory and considered part of the complete specification. 

Subject to verification by the Controller, the priority date of the basic application shall be adopted for the Indian application, notwithstanding any intervening publication or public use of the invention, unless such publication or use was knowingly induced by the applicant. Failure to submit the required documentation relating to the basic application within the stipulated timeframe may result in loss of priority, as determined by the Controller under the established procedures.

A basic application, when filed in a convention country, shall confer a right to claim priority in India, provided that such right is explicitly asserted at the time of filing the complete specification as provided herein. The applicant shall submit a certified copy of the basic application, duly translated if necessary, within the prescribed period to demonstrate lawful origin and sufficient disclosure. Failure to furnish such documentation may result in the application being deemed incomplete and subject to rejection. Where the basic application is not in the name of the applicant, evidence of title or assignment demonstrating a clear chain of ownership shall be submitted. Any subsequent amendment to the basic application must be communicated to the Controller of Patents within one month of such amendment, failing which the priority claim may be invalidated. The Controller may, subject to due process, require additional evidence to verify the validity of the asserted priority.

Any person claiming a right to a patent based upon a basic application filed in a convention country shall, within twelve months from the date of such basic application, file a complete application as provided herein, failing which the right to apply for a patent based upon that basic application shall be forfeited. Provided that, the Controller may, subject to justifiable cause and upon payment of a prescribed fee, grant an extension of three months to this twelve-month period. Any application not accompanied by a certified copy of the basic application, or a duly attested translation thereof where the basic application is not in an official language, shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected. Failure to comply with these provisions shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and repeated non-compliance may result in a bar from filing further applications under this Act. The Controller’s decision regarding such penalties shall be final.
