Any person claiming to be the assignee or licensee of a basic application, whether such assignment or license is absolute or partial, and whether executed before or after the filing of such basic application, may apply to the Controller for the registration of such assignment or license as provided herein. The application for registration of assignment or license shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. Subject to verification, the Controller shall, if satisfied that the application is in order, register the assignment or license and shall enter the particulars thereof in the Register of Assignments and Licenses. Where an assignment is registered, the assignee shall be entitled to the patent and all rights therein as if he were the original applicant. Provided that, where a license is registered, the licensor shall remain the patentee, and the licensee shall exercise the rights granted under the license subject to the terms and conditions thereof. Any assignment or license not registered as per this Act shall be void against any subsequent assignee or licensee who obtains registration.

A basic application, when duly filed with the Controller as provided herein, shall establish a priority date for a subsequent complete application relating to the same invention, subject to the applicant demonstrating sufficient grounds for claiming such priority. However, any publication of the invention following the filing of the basic application, and prior to the filing of the complete application in India, may be considered detrimental to the claim of priority, unless such publication was necessitated by the display of the invention at a recognised international exhibition within six months of the filing of the basic application. Should a dispute arise regarding the validity of the claimed priority, the Controller may, following due notice to the applicant and any opposing party, require further evidence establishing the direct correspondence between the basic application and the complete application, and may reject the claim if sufficient evidence is not forthcoming. Any decision of the Controller in this regard shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board.

A basic application, for the purposes of claiming priority under this Act, shall be an application for a patent filed in a convention country, being a party to any treaty or convention to which India is also a party, relating to the same invention as claimed in the application filed in India. Provided that the Indian application is filed within twelve months from the date of the basic application. Subject to the provisions herein, an applicant may, as evidence of the filing of a basic application, submit a certified copy or a duly authenticated translation thereof. Furthermore, the applicant may, to substantiate the inventive step, register copyrights in detailed drawings or specifications relating to the invention, though such registration is not a prerequisite for the grant of a patent. Any application not meeting these criteria shall be considered a new application.

A basic application, when duly filed with the patent office, shall establish a priority date for the invention claimed therein, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any subsequent application claiming the benefit of such basic application must specifically reference said application and its filing date, as a condition for establishing entitlement to the priority date. The applicant may, at the time of filing a complete specification, submit a certified copy of the basic application to the Controller for verification. A registrar application, detailing the status of the basic application in its country of origin, may also be requested by the Controller to ensure compliance with international conventions. Failure to provide such registrar application within a reasonable timeframe, as determined by the Controller, shall not, however, *ipso facto* invalidate the claim to priority, but may be considered during the examination process. Provided that, the applicant bears the onus of demonstrating a clear and unbroken chain of derivation from the basic application.

Any person claiming priority from a basic application filed in a convention country shall, upon submitting the necessary documents as provided herein, be entitled to a priority date corresponding to the filing date of such basic application, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding novelty and inventive step. The Controller, upon verification of the claim and the supporting documentation, shall record the details of the basic application in the registrar index, noting the country of origin, filing date, and applicant details for purposes of subsequent examination and potential disputes. Should any question arise regarding the validity of the priority claim, the Controller may require additional evidence from the applicant to substantiate the connection between the current application and the asserted basic application. Failure to provide such evidence within a reasonable timeframe may result in the loss of the priority date, and the application shall be treated as filed on the date of its actual receipt. Any aggrieved party may seek redressal as provided under this Act.

A basic application, when duly filed with the Controller of Patents in accordance with the prescribed manner, shall establish a priority date for a corresponding patent application submitted under this Act, provided that such basic application originates from a convention country as defined herein. The applicant shall, at the time of filing the Indian application, furnish a certified copy of the basic application and a declaration verifying its authenticity. Any failure to submit these documents within the stipulated timeframe may render the claim of priority untenable, subject to the discretion of the Controller. 

Where rights pertaining to the invention are subject to India rights established through prior use or publication, the applicant must disclose such information as part of the application process. The Controller may, upon reasonable grounds, require the applicant to provide evidence substantiating the novelty and inventive step of the claimed invention, considering any prior art arising from these India rights. An application lacking sufficient disclosure or failing to address existing India rights may be subject to objection or refusal as provided herein.

Any person claiming a patent shall file a basic application detailing the invention with sufficient clarity and completeness as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it out. Failure to adequately disclose the invention in the basic application renders the subsequent patent application subject to rejection, and a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees may be levied. Where a denomination of variety claim is made concerning a plant or biological process, the applicant shall submit evidence of distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, and any misrepresentation in this regard shall attract a fine equivalent to twice the anticipated royalty. Any application lacking a properly documented basic application, or demonstrating fraudulent claims regarding denomination variety, shall be deemed void ab initio, and the applicant barred from future applications for a period of five years. The Controller may, subject to due process, order the destruction of any samples submitted in support of such a fraudulent claim.

In this Act, “service” means any action, task, or performance which is offered for consideration and which does not result in the transfer of title to any goods. A service may be provided by any means, including but not limited to electronic transmission, physical performance, or the rendering of assistance. Consideration shall be deemed to include any form of remuneration or valuable benefit. Where a service is provided in conjunction with goods, it shall be considered a service only to the extent that it is distinct from the supply of those goods and adds a discernible benefit beyond their inherent qualities. Any activity undertaken for charitable or pro bono purposes, without expectation of direct financial gain, shall not constitute a service as provided herein. The provision of advice, consultation, and expertise shall be included within the definition of service.

A service, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall include any activity, benefit or facility offered for consideration, whether by electronic means or otherwise, and encompassing both tangible and intangible provisions. An applicant seeking registration of a service mark shall clearly and accurately define the scope of services for which registration is sought, adhering to the classification of services prescribed in the Schedule. Provided that, where a service is ancillary to the sale of goods, the application shall specify the predominant character of the offering, being either a service or a good. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require further clarification or amendment to the specification of services to ensure distinctiveness and avoid ambiguity. Registration of a service mark confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the specified services, and to seek legal remedies against any unauthorized use thereof, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the classification of a service shall be determined by the Registrar.

A person providing a service under a distinctive name or mark, and claiming rights therein, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for registration of such service mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. Registration of a service mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the service for which it is registered. Any unauthorized use of a registered service mark by another person, in the course of trade, shall constitute an infringement of the proprietor’s rights, and remedies including injunction, damages, and an account of profits may be sought. However, such remedies shall not be available where the use is permitted by law, or is fair use, or is otherwise not infringing as provided herein. A registered service mark shall be transferable, and the Registry shall maintain a record of all assignments and transmissions of such rights. The proprietor of a registered service mark shall have a duty to use the mark diligently, and failure to do so may render the registration liable to revocation.

A service, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall include any activity, benefit or facility offered or rendered to another, whether by electronic means or otherwise, and encompassing but not limited to the provision of intangible goods. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark used in connection with a service shall clearly and accurately delineate the scope of said service in the application, adhering to the classification of services as prescribed by the Nice Classification, as adopted from time to time. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, require further clarification regarding the nature of the service if the initial description is found to be vague or ambiguous. Where a service is provided as an integral component of the sale of goods, the application shall specify both the goods and the service, and registration may be granted for either or both, as appropriate. Any dispute regarding the classification of a service shall be determined by the Registrar, whose decision shall be final and binding.

A service, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be understood to encompass activities, benefits, or satisfactions which are not resulting in the transfer of ownership of tangible property. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark used in connection with a service shall demonstrate genuine use of the mark in commerce, and shall furnish evidence satisfactory to the Registrar regarding the nature and extent of such use. Where a service is provided under a collective mark, the rules governing the use of such mark, including conditions relating to quality and standards, shall be submitted with the application. Any alteration to such rules, subject to the approval of the Registrar, may be recorded. Failure to comply with the stipulated conditions regarding the provision of the service, or to maintain the prescribed standards, may render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any time, require further evidence of continued use of the mark in relation to the service.

Any person providing a service under a name, sign, or symbol deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be deemed to have committed an act of infringement as provided herein. Where a service is offered which is identical or nearly identical with a registered trade mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services, and is likely to cause confusion among consumers, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the provision of such service. Any person contravening this provision shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per service offered, and may further be subject to an order for damages, assessed based on actual loss or loss of goodwill suffered by the registered proprietor. The Court may, in addition, order the destruction or obliteration of any materials used in connection with the infringing service. Failure to comply with an order of the Court shall constitute contempt.

Any assignment of the right to use a registered trade mark, as a mark for goods or a service, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall include a statement of consideration, if any. Where a license is granted to use a trade mark in connection with a service, the terms of such license, including the duration, geographical area, and conditions relating to quality control, shall be clearly defined in the licensing agreement. The proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, assign the trade mark, or any right therein, including the right to use the trade mark for particular services only. An assignment or license not complying with these provisions shall be void. Any transfer of ownership of goodwill of a business, including the right to use a trade mark as a service mark, shall be deemed an assignment of the trade mark itself, unless otherwise expressly agreed.

A service, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be understood to encompass activities, benefits, or facilities offered to the public, distinct from the sale of goods, and shall include the provision of intangible benefits. Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, file a complaint with the Registrar alleging misrepresentation in the description of a service associated with an application for registration. The Registrar, upon receiving such complaint and after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, may direct amendment of the description, or, if the misrepresentation is material and incurable, reject the application. An appeal from the Registrar’s decision on such complaint shall lie to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates substantial injury resulting from the alleged misrepresentation. The Appellate Board may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision, and its order shall be final and binding, subject to rights of appeal to the Supreme Court as per law.

Any person who, not being the proprietor of a registered trade mark for a service, or duly authorized to use such trade mark, applies the said trade mark to goods intended to be sold or distributed, or offers for sale or distributes goods bearing such trade mark, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. Where a person falsely applies goods with a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark for a service, and such application is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public, the proprietor of the registered trade mark may seek an injunction restraining such acts. The High Court shall have jurisdiction to grant such injunction, and may also award damages to the proprietor, assessed in accordance with the actual loss suffered or the profits wrongly earned by the infringer, whichever is greater. A proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, also seek an order for delivery up or destruction of the offending goods. Any relief granted under this Act shall be in addition to any other remedies available under law.

A service, for the purposes of this Act, shall be understood to encompass activities undertaken to satisfy a need, whether performed for or on behalf of another, and shall include the provision of intangible benefits. Any authorization granted for the use of a registered trade mark in relation to a service, constituting permitted use, shall be subject to a written agreement detailing the scope, duration, and geographical limitations of such use. The proprietor of the trade mark may, notwithstanding such permitted use, pursue remedies as provided herein against any unauthorized extension or deviation from the agreed terms. Failure to adhere to the conditions of permitted use, including but not limited to exceeding the stipulated territorial boundaries or altering the nature of the service, shall be deemed a violation of the rights of the trade mark proprietor. Any party claiming entitlement to continued permitted use shall maintain a comprehensive record of all agreements and modifications thereof. A clear demonstration of compliance with these provisions is essential for establishing a valid defense against claims of infringement.

Any assignment of the right to use a registered service, or a right in a geographical indication registered under this Act, shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. A license to use a service, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial limits of the license. The proprietor of a service may, subject to the terms of any existing license, grant further licenses to other persons. Any assignment or license of a service in relation to goods originating from a region designated by a geographical indication shall not prejudice the rights of the producers of those goods as defined under the relevant regulations. Failure to comply with the requirements for written documentation of assignment or licensing shall render such transactions unenforceable as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon application, record any assignment or license of a service, and such record shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the assignment or license.

In this Act, a trade description shall mean any description, statement, or indication, including names, marks, signs, figures, letters, words, or combinations thereof, applied to goods or their packaging, signifying the quality, quantity, area, manufacture, or origin of those goods. A trade description may also include any statement relating to the mode of performance of services. Any representation of a trade description, whether graphical or otherwise, shall be deemed to be included within the definition as provided herein. It shall not be necessary for a trade description to be directly applied to the goods if it is displayed prominently in connection with the offering for sale, sale, or distribution of such goods. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a false trade description shall be actionable.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark shall, as part of the application, furnish a clear and accurate trade description detailing the goods or services to which the mark relates, and specifying the class thereof according to the prescribed classification. The trade description shall not include any misleading indication as to the character, quality, or geographical origin of the goods or services. A trade description may, subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry, include a statement of colour, material, or other essential characteristics, provided that such statement is factual and does not create a false association with any other trade mark. Where the goods or services are manufactured or provided by a licensee, the application shall disclose the nature of the license and the conditions governing its use, and this shall form part of the registered trade description. Failure to accurately represent the trade description may render the application liable to be refused, or the registration subject to revocation as provided herein.

Any person applying a false trade description to goods with intent to deceive purchasers or to cause damage to the trade of another shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein. A trade description includes any statement, indication or allegation relating to the goods, including any statement as to the mode of manufacture, the origin, or the quality of those goods. Where a trade description is applied to a service, it shall include any statement or indication as to the nature of the service provided. Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit for injunction restraining the application of such false trade description. The Court, upon being satisfied of the falsity of the trade description and the intent to deceive, may grant an injunction and also award damages to the plaintiff. Provided that no injunction shall be granted if the defendant proves that they took all reasonable precautions to ascertain the truth of the trade description applied. The burden of proving reasonable precautions shall lie with the defendant.

Any person applying a trade description to goods offered for sale or distributed shall ensure such description is conspicuously displayed and accurately reflects the goods’ material characteristics, including but not limited to, quantity, size, composition, and geographical origin. A trade description shall not be deemed to be false or misleading merely because it indicates the goods are in conformity with an industrial standard. However, any claim of conformity must be substantiated by evidence acceptable to the adjudicating officer, as provided herein. Where a trade description incorporates endorsements or testimonials, the source and basis of such endorsements must be clearly stated. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require a person applying a trade description to submit samples or other evidence for verification of its accuracy. Failure to comply with these provisions shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment and a fine, and may further invalidate any associated trademark registration. Any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the Controller regarding a false or misleading trade description.

Any person applying a trade description to goods offered for sale or distributed shall ensure such description is conspicuously displayed and accurately reflects the goods’ material characteristics, including but not limited to composition, quantity, and geographical origin. A trade description shall not be misleading, either directly or by omission, and must conform to all standards prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards, as applicable to the specific goods. Where goods are packaged, the trade description shall be legibly marked on the packaging. Any alteration of a trade description after goods have left the control of the manufacturer or distributor requires demonstrable justification and shall not diminish the accuracy of the original description. Failure to comply with these provisions, as provided herein, constitutes an offence punishable by a fine and may additionally result in the seizure of the goods in question, subject to an order of a competent court. The controller may, following investigation, direct corrective action.

Any person applying a false trade description to goods with intent to deceive purchasers or to cause damage to the business of another shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The application of a trade description shall be deemed false where it indicates a connection with any other person, firm, or company, or is likely to mislead the public as to the source, sponsorship, or association of the goods. A trade description includes any statement, indication, or allegation relating to the goods, including any statement concerning the mode of manufacture, composition, or performance characteristics. Provided that, where the false application relates to essential safety characteristics, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees. Any evidence obtained by inspection under this Act shall be admissible in any proceedings. The adjudicating officer may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct the removal or destruction of goods bearing such false trade description.

Any assignment of the right to use a trade description, whether complete or partial, and whether existing or future, shall be in writing and shall specify clearly the scope of the assignment, including but not limited to the goods or services in respect of which the trade description may be used. A license to use a trade description may be granted, either exclusively or non-exclusively, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon by the parties, and such license shall be enforceable as if it were a contract. Where a trade description is assigned or licensed, the assignor or licensor shall have the right to seek an accounting of profits derived from the unauthorized use of the trade description beyond the scope of the assignment or license, provided that such right is expressly reserved in the instrument of assignment or license. Any transfer of ownership of goodwill shall be deemed to include transfer of the associated trade description, unless otherwise agreed. The assignee or licensee shall be bound by all conditions and limitations contained within the original registration of the trade description, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Trade Marks relating to the application of a trade description to goods, may, within a period of ninety days from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Such appeal shall be filed in the manner as prescribed, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, alongside a statement of grounds for the appeal. The High Court, upon consideration of the appeal, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Controller, and may direct the Controller to reconsider the matter. Where a trade description is found to be false or misleading, the High Court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, issue an injunction restraining the defendant from applying such trade description. Any party dissatisfied with the High Court’s decision may seek further recourse as permitted under the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, provided that such application is made within the stipulated timeframe.

Any person applying a trade description to goods with intent to deceive the public or to cause injury to the business reputation of another shall be liable to proceedings for recovery of damages, subject to the provisions of this Act. A trade description includes any statement, indication, or allegation relating to the goods, including their origin, quality, or fitness for a particular purpose. Where a trade description falsely suggests an association with a patented invention, the patent holder may, in addition to remedies available under this Act, pursue action under the Patents Act 1970, to prevent such misrepresentation and protect their exclusive rights. Any person aggrieved by a false trade description may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the continued application of said description. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted unless the applicant demonstrates a likelihood of irreparable harm and that the balance of convenience favours the grant of such relief. The Court may also order the destruction of goods bearing the offending trade description.

Any person applying a trade description to goods offered for sale or distributed, shall ensure such description is factually accurate and not likely to deceive the public or cause confusion with the goods of another. Where a trade description includes reference to a granted new patent, the patent number and the date of grant must be prominently displayed alongside the description, subject to the provisions of the Patents Act, 1970. Failure to accurately represent the scope of patent protection conferred by the granted new patent within the trade description, or any misrepresentation thereof, shall constitute an offence under this Act. A trade description shall not imply endorsement or affiliation with any entity without explicit and verifiable consent. Any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the appropriate authority, and upon investigation, remedies may include rectification of the trade description and imposition of penalties as provided herein. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for all manufacturers, importers, and distributors.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Officer refusing to register a trade description, or varying the terms of registration of a trade description, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be in such form and be accompanied by such documents as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board may, if it considers it necessary, require further evidence to be furnished by either party, and shall, after considering the evidence, pass such order as it deems fit, confirming, varying, or setting aside the order of the Trade Marks Officer. Where a mark is integral to the trade description, the Appellate Board shall consider whether the mark is descriptive or deceptively similar to an existing mark, and shall weigh evidence of distinctiveness and usage. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final, subject to a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of legal error.

The provisions of this Act shall extend to all registered trade marks and apply to provisions acts undertaken by licensees, subject to the conditions hereinafter stipulated. Any licensee utilizing a registered trade mark shall maintain standards of quality consistent with those established by the proprietor, and failure to do so may constitute grounds for revocation of the license as provided herein. A proprietor may, upon reasonable cause and with prior written notice of thirty days, conduct inspections of a licensee’s premises to ensure compliance with quality control measures. Provided that such inspections shall be limited in scope to the goods or services covered by the license agreement. Where a dispute arises regarding quality control, the parties may seek resolution through mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon arbitrator. Any assignment of a license without the proprietor’s written consent shall be deemed a material breach of the agreement and subject to legal remedies. All licensees shall conspicuously display the registered trade mark symbol alongside the goods or services offered.

The provisions act pertaining to rectification of the register shall be initiated upon a petition filed with the Trade Marks Registry alleging a material error or misstatement in any entry therein. Any person aggrieved by such an entry, or demonstrating a sufficient proprietary interest, may submit a basic application for rectification, detailing the grounds for their claim and providing supporting evidence. The Registry shall, following due examination and opportunity for response from all interested parties, issue an order either rectifying the register as prayed or dismissing the petition with reasoned findings. An appeal from any order of the Registry refusing rectification shall lie to the High Court, subject to the conditions prescribed herein, and must be filed within ninety days of the date of the Registry’s communication. The High Court’s decision shall be final, save for any recourse to a superior court on grounds of law.

A certification trade mark, distinct from a traditional trade mark denoting origin in a specific undertaking, shall serve to certify the qualities, characteristics, or other attributes of goods or services. Any person, including an institution or body of persons, may apply for registration of such a mark, subject to demonstrating lawful authority to verify and certify those attributes. The register of certification trade marks shall maintain a clear record of the standards being certified, and any alteration to those standards shall require notification to the Registrar and public advertisement. The owner of a registered certification trade mark shall ensure consistent application of the certification process and may, as provided herein, authorize competent inspectors to verify compliance. Any aggrieved party may seek redressal for misrepresentation of certification or unauthorized use of the mark, including injunction and damages. A false application for, or misuse of, a certification trade mark shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment and fine, and the goods bearing such false mark shall be liable to seizure. The Registrar may revoke the registration of a certification trade mark for failure to adhere to the prescribed standards or for abandonment of the certification process.

Any person claiming ownership of a certification trade mark shall, prior to its application, demonstrate to the Registrar a clear scheme for ensuring that goods or services meet defined standards, and that such scheme is independently verifiable. Failure to establish such a scheme, or any subsequent material deviation therefrom without prior notification to and acceptance by the Registrar, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Any false representation regarding certification, or the unauthorized use of a registered certification trade mark, shall be subject to a penalty of not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may further result in the revocation of the registration. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, direct periodic audits of certified entities to ensure continued compliance with the established standards, and any obstruction of such audit shall be deemed a cognizable offence. Any appeal arising from decisions concerning certification trade marks shall lie before the High Court.

A person desirous of registering a certification trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, demonstrating that the mark is used or proposed to be used in relation to goods or services in respect of which certification is granted. The application shall include a statement detailing the standards or qualities that the certified goods or services meet, and the manner in which those standards are verified. Where the certification mark relates to agricultural produce, evidence must be submitted establishing that the variety certified is not an essentially derived variety, unless the applicant possesses the necessary authorization from the breeder of the original variety. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the applicant meets the requirements as provided herein, register the certification trade mark and issue a certificate of registration. The register of certification trade marks shall be maintained separately from the register of ordinary trade marks, and shall contain such particulars as may be prescribed. Any alteration to the certified standards shall require prior notification to and approval of the Registry.

The Registrar shall consider an application for rectification of the register, subject to the provisions of this Act, and shall, prior to any such consideration, require the applicant to furnish a statement of the grounds on which the application is based. Where the application alleges that a registered trade mark is not distinctive, or has become deceptively similar to another trade mark, the Registrar shall consider evidence submitted by both the applicant and the proprietor of the trade mark in question. Provided that the Registrar may, at any stage, require further evidence or clarification from either party, and shall ensure that all submissions are relevant to the grounds of rectification as initially stated. The Registrar shall, following such consideration, issue a reasoned order either rectifying or refusing to rectify the register.

The Registrar shall consider an application for registration of a collective mark or a certification mark, ensuring strict adherence to the provisions of this Act regarding distinctiveness and lawful use. Any application lacking clarity regarding the membership or certification criteria shall be subject to objection and may require amendment before proceeding. The Registrar shall, prior to accepting an application, verify that the rules governing the use of the mark by members or licensees are clearly defined and accessible to the public. Provided that, if the application pertains to a mark used in relation to agricultural produce, the Registrar shall consider evidence of quality control mechanisms and adherence to established standards. Furthermore, the Registrar shall consider any relevant objections filed by interested parties and shall provide an opportunity for a hearing, subject to the timelines prescribed herein. The Registrar may require additional evidence or clarification to satisfy themselves as to the genuineness of the claim.

The Registrar shall consider any petition for rectification of the register relating to a registered trade mark, and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, make an order for rectification if satisfied that the facts alleged in the petition are established. Provided that, where the petition alleges that a trade mark was not lawfully registered, or that it has been obtained improperly, the Registrar shall not make an order for rectification unless the petitioner proves that they have suffered damage as a result of the wrongful registration. Further, the Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the petitioner to furnish evidence of prior use of a similar mark, to demonstrate a genuine connection between the petitioner and the subject matter of the rectification. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within a period of two months from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final.

The Registrar shall consider any request for the amendment of a registered trade mark, provided that such amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark. In determining whether an amendment is substantial, the Registrar shall have regard to the nature of the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered, and the degree of resemblance between the original and amended trade marks. Where the amendment involves a change in spelling, the Registrar may require evidence of usage demonstrating the adoption of the amended form prior to the date of the request. 

Furthermore, the Registrar shall consider any opposition filed against the proposed amendment, and shall afford the applicant an opportunity to be heard. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar may, if satisfied that the amendment does not contravene any legal requirements and does not mislead the public, allow the amendment to proceed. The decision of the Registrar on such matters shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the appropriate appellate authority as provided herein.

The Registrar shall consider an application for registration of a collective mark, provided that such application demonstrates a clear and unambiguous statement of the rules governing the use of the mark by members of the association claiming ownership. Any application submitted as provided herein must include a detailed description of the mechanisms for quality control, ensuring consistent standards are maintained across all goods or services bearing the collective mark. The Registrar shall further consider evidence of a functioning association, including its constitution, membership details, and a record of decisions relating to the use of the mark. Subject to verification of these details, and confirmation that the proposed use will not mislead the public or infringe existing rights, the Registrar may proceed with the advertisement of the application. Where the application lacks sufficient detail regarding quality control or association governance, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring rectification within a specified timeframe.

The Registrar shall consider any application for rectification of the register, submitted as provided herein, and may require the applicant to furnish such evidence as may be deemed necessary to substantiate the grounds for rectification. Should the Registrar, upon consideration, determine that the application is frivolous or vexatious, it shall be dismissed, and the applicant shall be liable to pay a penalty not exceeding twenty thousand rupees. Furthermore, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the proprietor of the trade mark in question, affording them a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Provided that, if the rectification sought involves a claim of non-use, the Registrar shall not entertain the application unless accompanied by a statutory declaration verifying the facts. Any person knowingly making a false statement in such a declaration shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

The Registrar shall consider any request for assignment of a registered trademark, provided that such request is submitted in writing and accompanied by the prescribed fee as detailed in Schedule I. Any transfer of ownership not duly recorded with the Registrar shall be void against any subsequent purchaser for value, or licensee of the trademark, without notice of the earlier transfer. Where an assignment involves a transfer of goodwill, the Registrar shall consider evidence of such transfer, including but not limited to, audited financial statements and affidavits from relevant parties. The Registrar may, subject to satisfactory verification of the assignee’s identity and legal standing, record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks. Furthermore, the Registrar shall consider any objection filed by a third party claiming an interest in the trademark, and shall provide an opportunity for all parties to present their case before making a final determination. Any assignment made in fraud of existing rights shall be null and void.

The Registrar shall consider any petition for rectification of the register alleging wrongful inclusion or exclusion of an entry, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee and fulfillment of all procedural requirements as provided herein. Provided that, if the petition is frivolous or vexatious, the Registrar may dismiss it with costs and direct the petitioner to refrain from further such applications. Any aggrieved party may, within one month from the date of the Registrar’s order, file an appeal before the Appellate Board, setting forth the grounds for challenging the decision. The Appellate Board shall, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to all parties concerned, consider the evidence presented and may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s order. Further, the Appellate Board may, if deemed necessary, remit the matter back to the Registrar for fresh consideration, specifying the particular aspects to be re-examined.

The Registrar shall consider an application for registration of a trade mark, assessing its distinctiveness and compliance with the provisions of this Act, and may require such evidence as may be deemed necessary to verify the particulars furnished therein. Where an application relates to an international registration trade mark designating India, the Registrar shall, subject to the provisions of the Protocol relating to the Madrid Agreement, examine the application as if it were a national application, and shall consider the basis of the right relied upon by the applicant in the designating country. Provided that the Registrar may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to be heard, refuse to register a mark if it is likely to cause confusion with an earlier trade mark, or is otherwise prohibited by this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered trade marks.

A firm applying for registration of a trade mark shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a statement of the particulars of the directors of the firm, and any change in the constitution of the firm or in the particulars of its directors shall be notified to the Registry within fourteen days of such change. For the purposes of this Act, and (b) “director”, in relation to a firm, includes any person who, exercising powers of general supervision and control, is accustomed to act as such; provided that a person merely holding a technical or administrative office shall not be deemed a director. The Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require additional evidence regarding the identity or authority of any director named in the statement. Failure to comply with the notification requirements as provided herein shall render the registration liable to revocation. Any false statement made regarding the particulars of a director shall be punishable as contempt of court.

context: Any importer of goods bearing an unregistered trade mark, or deceptively similar thereto, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and the Customs Act 1962, notify the Principal Deputy Controller of Patents and Trade Marks in writing of such importation within thirty days of landing the goods at any customs port. Such notification shall include a detailed description of the goods, the quantity imported, the declared value, and the name and address of the foreign manufacturer or exporter. The Principal Deputy Controller may, if satisfied that prima facie evidence exists of a potential infringement, direct the customs authorities to suspend clearance of the goods pending further investigation. Provided that, such suspension shall not exceed a period of fourteen days, unless extended by an order of a competent court. Any person aggrieved by a decision under this Act may file an appeal before the designated authority within sixty days of the order. Compliance with the provisions of the Customs Act 1962 regarding valuation and classification of goods remains mandatory.

Any owner of a registered trade mark for a pharmaceutical substance, or a class of such substances, may apply to the Principal Customs Officer in the manner prescribed, for a direction prohibiting the importation of goods bearing an infringing trade mark. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the registration certificate and a statement detailing the nature of the infringing goods and the grounds for seeking prohibition. The Principal Customs Officer, upon being satisfied of the prima facie validity of the trade mark and the likelihood of deception or confusion, may issue a notice to the importer requiring them to demonstrate non-infringement or to provide a security deposit. Subject to the provisions of the Customs Act 1962, the officer may, if satisfied, direct the Customs authorities to detain and, where appropriate, destroy any imported goods found to bear the infringing mark. Any person aggrieved by such a direction may appeal to the High Court.

A registered proprietor of a trade mark, or a licensee authorized by such proprietor, may apply to the Customs authorities to prevent the importation of goods infringing their trade mark, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Such application shall be accompanied by a copy of the trade mark registration certificate and a clear depiction of how the imported goods constitute an infringement as provided herein. The Customs authorities, upon reasonable suspicion and prior verification of the trade mark’s validity, may inspect, detain, and dispose of any imported goods suspected of bearing an infringing trade mark. Where goods are detained under the provisions relating to the customs act, the owner of the goods shall be notified and afforded an opportunity to present evidence disputing the infringement claim. Disposal may include destruction or other appropriate action, as determined by the Customs authorities in consultation with the trade mark owner.

Any owner of a registered trade mark, or a registered user thereof, may apply to the appropriate Customs authorities in writing to prevent the importation of goods infringing their trade mark rights, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the registration certificate and a clear representation of the trade mark. The Customs authorities, upon receipt of a valid application and satisfactory evidence of prima facie infringement, may issue a notice to the importer and detain the suspected goods. A period of twenty-one days shall be granted to the importer to submit evidence contesting the claim of infringement, or to provide a bond guaranteeing due resolution of the matter. Where goods are deemed infringing under this Act, they shall be liable to seizure and subsequent disposal in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962, or as directed by an order of a competent court.

Any importer of goods into India shall, prior to clearance by customs authorities, furnish a declaration as to the genuineness of the trade marks applied to such goods, where such trade marks are registered under this Act. Where a customs officer has reason to believe that imported goods infringe a registered trade mark, they may suspend clearance and require the importer to provide evidence of ownership or a valid license. Subject to such verification, the officer may allow clearance, or if satisfied of infringement, shall detain the goods and notify the right holder. The right holder may, within a prescribed period, initiate proceedings for infringement before a competent court. Where goods are legitimately imported but bear trade marks identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, and the right holder consents to their release upon fulfillment of certain conditions, such conditions shall be binding on the importer. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the customs officer under this Act may appeal to the appellate authority constituted for the purposes of the Customs Act, 1962.

Any officer of customs, duly authorized by the Central Government, may, if he has reason to believe that any goods imported into India infringe a registered trade mark, notify the Principal Registrar of Trade Marks of his intention to allow clearance of the goods subject to conditions, or to seize the goods. Upon receipt of such notification, the Principal Registrar shall, within such time as may be prescribed, convey his decision to the customs officer regarding the authenticity of the trade mark and whether the goods are, in his opinion, infringing. Where seized goods are subject to a claim of legitimate import, the importer may, within thirty days of seizure, apply to the Principal Registrar for a determination of the matter, providing evidence of lawful origin and ownership. The provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 shall apply mutatis mutandis to any proceedings relating to the seizure and disposal of goods under this Act, including provisions relating to warehousing and auction. Any decision of the Principal Registrar under these provisions shall be final and binding on all parties, subject to appeal to the High Court.

Any importer of goods bearing an unregistered trade mark, or any mark deceptively similar thereto, shall be subject to inspection by the customs authorities, provided that such inspection is conducted in accordance with the procedures established under this Act and the Customs Act, 1962. Where goods are suspected to infringe a registered trade mark, the customs authorities may detain such goods pending verification of the registration and the rights of the owner. The owner of the trade mark shall, within a period of ten days from the date of detention, submit a formal complaint and evidence of registration to the customs authorities. Failure to do so may result in release of the detained goods. Subject to the provisions herein, the customs authorities may, after due inquiry, initiate seizure proceedings as per the Customs Act, if satisfied that a prima facie case of infringement exists. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the customs authorities may appeal to the designated appellate authority.

Any importer who brings into India goods bearing a registered trademark, or colorable variation thereof, without the consent of the trademark proprietor, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. The Customs authorities, upon reasonable suspicion of such importation, may detain the goods and notify the trademark owner, providing an opportunity for inspection and verification of authenticity. Should the trademark owner confirm the infringement, the Customs authorities shall initiate confiscation proceedings as provided herein, and the goods shall be liable to seizure and disposal in accordance with the Customs Act, 1962. Any person assisting in the importation, packaging, or distribution of such counterfeit goods shall be jointly and severally liable for penalties, which may extend to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Appeals against any order of confiscation shall lie before the designated appellate authority within thirty days of the order.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, upon reasonable cause to believe that imported goods bearing an identical or deceptively similar mark are likely to cause confusion, lodge a complaint with the appropriate Customs authorities, detailing the nature of the infringement and providing sufficient evidence of registration and ownership. The Customs authorities, acting under this Act and in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962, may, subject to verification of the complaint and the authenticity of the trade mark registration, issue a notice of detention to the importer. Any assignment or licensing of rights in a registered trade mark shall be promptly notified to the Customs authorities to ensure continued enforcement at the border. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall undertake to bear all costs associated with the storage, examination, and, if necessary, destruction of the infringing goods, as determined by the Customs authorities. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the withdrawal of enforcement requests.

Any importer of goods bearing an unregistered trade mark, where a registered trade mark exists for identical or similar goods, shall be subject to detention by customs authorities, provided that the rights holder files a general notice of apprehension with the Principal Customs Officer. An appeal against the detention order may be filed by the importer within thirty days of such order before the designated appellate authority, furnishing security as may be prescribed. The appellate authority shall, after examining the evidence and hearing both parties, pass an order confirming, modifying, or revoking the detention order. Should the appellate authority find no reasonable grounds for detention, it may direct the release of the goods and award costs to the importer. Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the decision of the appellate authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. The burden of proof regarding the genuineness of the registered trade mark shall lie with the rights holder.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark, or a literary work forming part of packaging integral to goods subject to customs control, shall be subject to a prior notification to the Registrar, detailing the assignor, assignee, and the scope of rights transferred, including territorial limitations. The Customs authorities, acting under this Act and in conjunction with the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962, may detain goods suspected of infringing a registered trade mark where a valid assignment has not been recorded with the Registrar, or where the assignment is subject to a pending dispute adjudicated by a competent court. Provided that, the assignee may apply for release of the goods upon furnishing an indemnity bond guaranteeing due compensation to the original owner should the assignment be invalidated. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the assignment unenforceable against the Customs authorities, and the goods may be subject to seizure and disposal as provided herein. Any licensing arrangement must similarly reflect clear territorial boundaries and be registered to ensure effective enforcement at ports of entry.

A user party proceeding shall be instituted where a registered proprietor seeks relief concerning a trade mark and a registered user of that trade mark exists, utilizing the mark under a permitted use agreement as provided herein. Any individual or entity qualifying as a registered user, and not being the applicant in the originating action, may be joined as a party to such proceedings, subject to the discretion of the adjudicating authority. The purpose of including a user party is to ensure comprehensive representation of all interests affected by the outcome of the dispute. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall demonstrate reasonable efforts to notify the registered user of the pending action and afford them an opportunity to participate. Failure to do so may prejudice the proceedings.

Any person alleging a dispute regarding the use of a registered trade mark shall, prior to the commencement of any adversarial proceeding, furnish a statement of use as provided herein, detailing the goods or services in relation to which the mark is being utilized and the geographical scope of such use. Where a party asserts rights as a registered user, a user party proceeding shall be initiated to determine the validity of such claim and the extent of permitted use conferred by registration. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to reasonable notice, direct the applicant to join all known registered users as necessary parties to ensure a comprehensive adjudication of rights. Provided that, a registered user may elect to be represented by the proprietor of the trade mark in such a proceeding, with the proprietor bearing responsibility for adequate representation. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act regarding user party proceedings may result in the dismissal of the claim or the invalidation of asserted rights.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, as provided herein, may initiate a user party proceeding to determine the rights and obligations of a registered user of that trade mark. Such a proceeding shall be initiated before the appropriate court and notice of the same shall be served upon the registered proprietor, the alleged infringer, and the registered user. A registered user, upon being made a party to any proceeding concerning the trade mark, shall have the right to present evidence and be heard. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a registered user shall be liable for any acts of infringement committed by them in the course of their permitted use. However, provided that the registered user demonstrates reasonable efforts to ensure compliance with the terms of the permitted use, their liability may be limited to the extent of their own actions. The court may, at its discretion, order contribution to damages amongst the registered proprietor, the infringer, and the registered user, based on their respective degrees of fault and benefit derived from the infringement.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, as provided herein, may initiate a user party proceeding before the High Court, seeking a determination of the validity of any permitted use under which the alleged infringer claims right. Such a proceeding shall be initiated by filing an application accompanied by a statement of facts and supporting evidence demonstrating a reasonable apprehension of damage to the reputation of the trade mark due to the alleged infringer’s activities. The High Court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct that the registered proprietor and any user of the trade mark, whose permitted use is challenged, be joined as parties to the proceeding. Provided that, the court may, at its discretion, dispense with the joinder of a user party if it is satisfied that such joinder would unduly delay the proceedings or cause unnecessary expense. Any order made in a user party proceeding shall be binding on all parties, including any user not directly involved in the initial application, provided they have been given due notice and opportunity to be heard.

Any user party proceeding initiated under this Act relating to a registered trade mark shall require prior notice to be served upon all registered users of that trade mark, detailing the grounds for the proceeding and the relief sought. Such notice shall be served via registered post and electronic mail, with proof of delivery maintained by the initiating party. A registered user may, subject to the discretion of the adjudicating authority, participate fully in the proceeding, including presenting evidence and cross-examining witnesses. Provided that a registered user failing to respond to the notice within thirty days of service may be deemed to have waived their right to participate, unless sufficient cause is demonstrated. The adjudicating authority may, as provided herein, direct costs against a user party demonstrating frivolous or vexatious conduct during the proceeding. Any decision rendered shall be binding on all registered users, unless successfully challenged through established appellate mechanisms.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, as provided herein, may initiate a user party proceeding before the High Court, seeking a determination of the validity of any permitted use agreement. Should the Court ascertain that a registered user has materially contributed to the alleged infringement, such user shall be jointly and severally liable for damages, not exceeding the assessed profits unjustly gained by the infringer, or an amount up to Rupees five lakh, whichever is higher. Failure to join a necessary user party, identified through diligent search and disclosed to the Court, shall constitute an abuse of process and may result in dismissal of the infringement claim with costs. Any order made against a user party shall be enforceable as a decree of the Court, and any willful misrepresentation regarding the terms of a permitted use agreement will attract a penalty of Rupees one lakh.

Any assignment of a trade mark, whether complete or partial, shall be subject to the rights of a registered user of that trade mark, unless such user consents in writing to the assignment. A user party proceeding may be initiated by any registered user aggrieved by an assignment that impacts their permitted use of the trade mark, or by the assignee seeking to clarify the scope of permitted use post-assignment. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon application, direct the assignee and the user to participate in a conciliation process, facilitated by a designated officer. Provided that, if conciliation fails within sixty days, the Registry may direct the matter to be adjudicated as a dispute concerning rights in the trade mark. Any agreement reached during conciliation shall be binding on all parties, and may be recorded with the Registry as a supplemental agreement to the original assignment. A user’s rights, as established under this Act, shall continue unaffected by any subsequent assignment unless explicitly modified by mutual agreement.

Any party alleging infringement of a registered trade mark, as provided herein, may initiate a user party proceeding before the appropriate court to determine the extent of permissible use granted to a registered user. Such a proceeding shall be initiated by notice to the registered proprietor and the alleged infringing party, and shall be conducted in accordance with rules of civil procedure. A registered user, upon being joined as a party, may present evidence demonstrating the scope of their permitted use and any limitations thereof. The court, subject to verification of the user’s registration and the terms of the user agreement, may issue directions limiting the relief granted against the registered proprietor. Provided that, if the user’s actions independently constitute infringement beyond the permitted use, they shall be liable as a direct infringer. Any decision regarding the user party proceeding may be appealed to the appellate authority within sixty days of the order.

Any user party proceeding initiated under this Act relating to a registered trade mark shall require, as a condition precedent to its commencement, documented evidence of diligent efforts made to resolve the dispute through alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, including mediation, facilitated by a neutral third party acceptable to all concerned. Where a filing application pertaining to the trade mark in question is simultaneously pending before the Trade Marks Registry, the Registry may, at the request of any party, stay the user party proceeding until a decision is rendered on the pending application, provided that such stay shall not exceed a period of ninety days. However, the Registrar may extend this period subject to demonstrable cause. All submissions in a user party proceeding shall conform to the prescribed format and be accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in the First Schedule. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the proceeding inadmissible.

A user party proceeding shall be instituted where a registered proprietor seeks relief concerning a trade mark and a registered user of that trade mark exists, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may, and if so directed by the High Court, shall direct that such registered user be joined as a party to any opposition, rectification, or infringement proceeding. Should the registered proprietor fail to promptly join the registered user, the court may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct such joinder. In instances where the registered proprietor fails to diligently pursue a claim, the plaintiff forthwith may be required to demonstrate sufficient cause for not including the user party. Any order made under this Act regarding costs shall account for the participation of the user party.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark and the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark in relation to goods or services specified in the registration certificate. Any assignment not recorded in the Trade Marks Registry shall be void as against any subsequent assignee. Goods produced limits india shall, for the purposes of determining the origin of goods, be deemed to include any goods substantially manufactured or processed within India, even if some component parts are imported. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall be entitled to use the trade mark as if they were the original proprietor, provided that such use does not mislead the public as to the origin of the goods or services. An assignment may be subject to limitations agreed upon by the parties.

The applicant seeking registration of a trade mark for goods produced limits india shall, at the time of application, furnish a statement detailing the origin of such goods, specifying whether they are manufactured or produced within India or imported from outside India. Where goods are produced limits india, the applicant shall submit evidence establishing substantial local production, including details of manufacturing facilities, workforce employed, and value addition occurring within the territory of India. An applicant claiming use of a trade mark on goods produced limits india, but lacking demonstrable local production, may be required to provide a clear undertaking to establish such production within a specified timeframe, not exceeding two years, failing which the application may be subject to refusal. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted evidence, grant a conditional registration, contingent upon fulfillment of the production undertaking as provided herein. Any false declaration regarding the origin or production of goods shall render the registration liable to revocation.

Any person who manufactures goods or produces goods within the limits of India, and applies a trade mark to such goods, shall be entitled to institute legal proceedings for infringement of that trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. However, where goods are produced limits india and subsequently imported, the rights of the owner of the trade mark shall extend to those imported goods, provided that the owner demonstrates a material connection between the manufacture and the importation. A registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the manufacture, sale, or importation of goods bearing an identical or deceptively similar mark. Any person aggrieved by the application of a trade mark in a manner that constitutes unfair competition may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply to the Court for a declaration of their rights and for appropriate relief. The Court, while granting relief, may also order the destruction or forfeiture of infringing goods.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of registered trade marks and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, entertain and examine applications for the registration of trade marks. Any goods made or produced limits india and intended to be offered for sale, or sold, or distributed, shall bear a clear indication of the country of origin, as determined by the substantial transformation of materials or manufacturing processes occurring therein. Where goods are imported, the customs authorities may require a certificate of origin to verify compliance with this requirement. A proprietor of a registered trade mark may, subject to due process and payment of the prescribed fee, record a license with the Registry. Any dispute concerning the origin of goods, or the veracity of a certificate of origin, shall be subject to adjudication by the High Court having jurisdiction. Provided that, the High Court may appoint a special officer to assist in the examination of evidence relating to the place of production. The Registry may, at its discretion, refuse to register a trade mark if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing mark, or if the origin of the goods cannot be readily ascertained.

Any goods made or produced beyond the limits of India and offered for sale or sold, or kept for sale, in contravention of the provisions of this Act shall be deemed to be infringing goods, and subject to seizure as provided herein. Where any person deals in goods produced limits india, knowing or having reason to believe that such goods are counterfeit or falsely applied to, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, upon application and sufficient cause shown, direct the destruction of seized goods, subject to a hearing of the owner. Provided that, if the owner does not appear or fails to adequately demonstrate legitimate origin, the Registrar may order immediate destruction. Any officer authorized under this Act, acting in good faith, shall be indemnified against all legal proceedings arising from the seizure of goods. Failure to comply with an order of the Registrar shall attract a daily penalty.

Any person being the owner of a registered trade mark, or a trade mark pending application for registration, relating to goods produced limits india, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark, or any right therein, to any other person. An assignment shall be valid only if it is in writing and authenticated by the assignor. Where the assignment includes the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, notice of the assignment shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. The assignee may apply to the Registrar to register the assignment, and upon such application, the Registrar shall register the assignment subject to verification of title and payment of the prescribed fee. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may also be granted in respect of such trade marks, and all terms and conditions of the license shall be subject to the overriding provisions of this Act. Failure to comply with these provisions relating to assignment or licensing shall render the transaction voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, provided that such option is exercised within two years from the date of knowledge of the non-compliance.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark accompanied by a statement of proposed use in relation to goods produced limits india, examine such application as provided herein. If the Registrar has reason to believe that the goods, though proposed to be used in India, are substantially and wholly manufactured or produced outside of India, the applicant shall be required to submit documentary evidence establishing a substantial connection with India, including but not limited to, details of licensing arrangements or a local presence demonstrating genuine use. Any objection raised by the Registrar regarding the origin of the goods, and any appeal against such objection, shall be adjudicated upon in accordance with the established procedures for opposing trade mark applications. Provided that, if the applicant fails to satisfy the Registrar regarding the Indian connection, the application may be deemed abandoned, subject to a final opportunity for submission of evidence and a reasoned order. A decision of the Registrar may be appealed to the High Court.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be entitled to initiate proceedings against any person manufacturing, producing, or importing goods bearing a mark deceptively similar to their registered trade mark, subject to the provisions contained herein. Goods produced limits india shall be determined with reference to the place where the final assembly or significant processing conferring substantial commercial character occurs. Where goods are substantially transformed within India from imported components, they shall be considered produced within India for the purposes of this Act. The Parliament may, by resolution, designate specific goods or classes of goods as exempt from these provisions, provided that such exemption does not unduly prejudice the rights of trade mark owners or mislead the public. Any person claiming entitlement to produce goods outside of these limits must maintain verifiable records of origin and production processes, available for inspection as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements shall constitute an infringement of this Act.

Any goods made or produced beyond the limits of India and offered for sale or distributed within the territory of India shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, irrespective of whether such goods are accompanied by services integral to their function. However, a registered services trade mark, legitimately used in connection with such goods at the time of their importation, may be considered as mitigating circumstances during adjudication of infringement claims, provided that such use does not mislead the consumer regarding the origin of the goods. Any person dealing in goods produced limits india in contravention of this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per violation. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and may result in the seizure of the offending goods. The adjudicating officer, as provided herein, shall have the final authority in determining the extent of penalties and the appropriate course of action.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark relating to goods produced limits india shall be subject to a prior written consent of the Trade Marks Registry, unless the assignment is to a successor-in-interest of a business dealing with such goods. Such consent may be granted subject to conditions regarding quality control and continued use of the mark. Where a trade mark is assigned without such consent, the assignee may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registry for ratification of the assignment. The Registry shall, if satisfied that the assignment is not detrimental to the interests of the public or the owner of the trade mark, ratify the assignment. Any license granted to use a trade mark shall be recorded with the Registry, and the terms of such license, including any restrictions on mark use and geographical limitations, shall be clearly specified. Failure to record a license shall not invalidate it, but may affect its enforceability against third parties. A licensee may, with the consent of the registered proprietor, apply for registration of the trade mark in their own name, subject to the conditions prescribed herein.

Any person alleging that goods made or produced limits india infringe a registered trade mark, and seeking relief under this Act, shall first submit a statement of case to the Registrar, detailing the nature of the infringement and the particulars relating registration of the mark in question. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of such statement, notify the alleged infringer, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement within thirty days. Should the alleged infringer fail to respond, or their counter-statement be deemed unsatisfactory by the Registrar, an inquiry may be initiated. However, any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the initiation or conduct of such inquiry, or the determination of infringement, may appeal to the High Court, subject to such conditions as the Court may deem fit. Provided that the High Court’s decision shall be final, except in cases of substantial questions of law, which may be subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court.

Any goods made or produced beyond the limits of India and intended for sale or distribution within the territory of India shall be subject to registration under this Act, provided that such goods are not already subject to an existing registration or exemption as detailed in Schedule IV.
