The Consist Judicial Member shall be a person of eminence with at least ten years of experience as a Judge of a High Court, or a legal professional holding a law degree from a recognized university and possessing substantial knowledge of intellectual property law and practice. The Central Government shall appoint the Consist Judicial Member from a panel of names recommended by a Search-cum-Selection Committee constituted as provided herein. Any person appointed as a Consist Judicial Member shall hold office for a term of five years or until attaining the age of seventy years, whichever is earlier. A Consist Judicial Member may be removed from office for proven misbehavior, subject to an inquiry conducted in accordance with the principles of natural justice, and such removal may, in cases of egregious conduct, be punishable imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Layout-Design Office for the purposes of this Act, and shall appoint a Controller to head such Office. Any appeal under this Act concerning the validity of a registered layout-design shall be heard by a member appointed bench, constituted of at least three members, including a person possessing a degree in engineering or technology relating to semiconductor integrated circuits. Provided that, in cases involving complex technical issues, the bench may also include an assessor with specialized expertise in the relevant field, appointed by the Central Government for a specific case or a defined period. The decision of the member appointed bench shall be final and binding, subject to any appeal to the High Court as provided herein. All administrative matters relating to the functioning of such benches shall be determined by the Controller.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered layout-designs, and all applications for registration, along with supporting documentation, shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed manner. Any objection to an application shall be communicated to the applicant, who may, within a period of thirty days, submit a response. Where objections persist following the applicant’s response, the matter shall be referred to a member appointed bench for adjudication. Such a bench shall comprise at least one member possessing expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits and may include a legal expert as deemed necessary by the Registrar. Decisions of the member appointed bench shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to a designated authority as provided herein, and shall be recorded in the register of layout-designs. The Registrar may, with the approval of the Central Government, prescribe fees for all filings and related services under this Act.

The Registrar, upon receiving a petition alleging infringement of a registered layout-design, shall, subject to verification of the requisite fees and compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein, promptly notify the alleged infringer. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Layout-Design Office concerning validity or transfer of rights, may appeal to a member appointed bench of the Appellate Board. Such a bench shall invariably include at least one member possessing a legal background and one member with demonstrated expertise in semiconductor technology, ensuring a balanced assessment of technical and legal arguments. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, direct the parties to a dispute to engage in mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon mediator, provided that such mediation does not exceed a period of ninety days. Failure to comply with the directions of the Appellate Board, or to participate in good faith in any directed mediation, may be considered an obstruction of justice and shall be subject to penalties as prescribed. The decision of the member appointed bench shall be final and binding, subject to rights of appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Central Government shall, for the expeditious hearing and disposal of applications and rectifications under this Act, constitute a Layout-Design Office. The Layout-Design Office shall function as a member appointed bench, and shall be comprised of a President and not less than two Members possessing requisite technical expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, as determined by the Central Government. Provided that, in the absence of the President, the senior-most Member present shall preside over the bench. Any decision of the Layout-Design Office shall be by majority vote of the members constituting the bench, and in the event of a tie, the President, or the presiding member in their absence, shall have a casting vote. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Layout-Design Office may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, adopt such procedures as it deems necessary for the efficient conduct of its proceedings, including the acceptance of electronic filings and virtual hearings. All orders and decisions of the Layout-Design Office shall be recorded in writing and maintained as a permanent record.

The Central Government shall constitute a Layout-Design Office for the administration of this Act and for the registration of layout-designs. A member appointed bench of the Layout-Design Office shall hear appeals relating to the rejection of applications for registration, revocation of registrations, and disputes concerning the ownership of layout-designs, provided that such a bench comprises at least one member possessing expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits and one legal professional. Any party aggrieved by a decision of a single member may request the constitution of a member appointed bench for review, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. The Layout-Design Office may, as provided herein, delegate the initial examination of applications to qualified experts, but all final decisions regarding registration shall rest with a member appointed bench. Compliance with these provisions is essential for ensuring procedural fairness and the effective enforcement of rights under this Act.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Layout-Design Enforcement Bench for each of the four regions demarcated for the purposes of administering this Act, provided that the number of Benches shall not exceed four at any given time. Each member appointed to a Layout-Design Enforcement Bench shall hold office for a term of five years from the date of assumption of duty, or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. Any person found wilfully obstructing the lawful functioning of a member appointed bench, or knowingly providing false information to it during the course of an investigation, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Failure to comply with an order issued by a Layout-Design Enforcement Bench, subject to appeal as provided herein, shall attract a daily penalty of fifty thousand rupees for each continuing day of non-compliance. The Central Government reserves the right to remove any member for proven misconduct.

The registered proprietor of a layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the same, either wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to conditions, to any person or persons. Any assignment or license shall be in writing and shall specify the territory in relation to which it is to be effective, and the duration for which it is to subsist. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or scope of any such assignment or license, it shall be heard by a member appointed bench constituted for the purpose of resolving disputes relating to the transfer of rights. The composition of such a bench may include a legal expert and a person with specialized knowledge in semiconductor integrated circuits, provided that the bench shall always have an odd number of members to avoid deadlock. The decision of the member appointed bench shall be final and binding on all parties, subject to rights of appeal as provided herein. Any royalty or consideration payable under a license shall be determined by mutual agreement between the parties, or, in the absence of such agreement, by the bench.

Any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board against any order passed by the Registrar, concerning the refusal of registration, revocation of a layout-design right, or any other decision impacting rights as provided herein. Such appeal shall be heard by a member appointed bench, constituted specifically for the purpose of expeditiously resolving the dispute, and comprising at least one member possessing legal expertise and one member with significant technical knowledge in the field of semiconductor integrated circuits. The composition of the bench may be altered by the Appellate Board Chairperson, subject to ensuring a balanced representation of expertise. Should the member appointed bench be unable to reach a unanimous decision, the matter shall be referred to a larger bench, including the Chairperson, for a final determination. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the larger bench may seek clarification from the Board within thirty days of the order.

The Central Government shall constitute a Layout-Design Office and appoint a member appointed bench to hear and determine applications for registration and any disputes arising under this Act. Each bench shall comprise at least one member possessing a degree in engineering or technology, or equivalent qualifications, and one legal expert familiar with intellectual property law. Provided that, in cases involving complex technical subject matter, the bench may also include an additional technical member with specialized expertise relevant to the specific layout-design in question. Any layout-design claimed for registration must demonstrate an inventive step, meaning it must not be obviously derivable by a person skilled in the art. Failure to satisfy this requirement shall be grounds for rejection of the application. The decision of the member appointed bench shall be final and binding, subject to rights of appeal as provided herein. All proceedings before the bench shall be conducted in a transparent and timely manner.

Any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the Layout-Design Appellate Board concerning the revocation of a registered layout-design, or any decision relating to the assignment or transfer of rights therein, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Appellate Board shall be constituted by a member appointed bench of not less than three persons, including at least one legally qualified individual possessing a degree in law and experience in intellectual property matters, and one technical member with expertise in semiconductor integrated circuits. An invention means new, and any appeal concerning novelty shall be decided by a bench including a technical member who confirms that the layout-design, at the time of its first commercial exploitation, was not known or publicly available. Provided that, if the initial decision appealed against was made by a single member, the appellate bench may be comprised of only two members, with the legally qualified member presiding. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

The Central Government shall, for the expeditious hearing and disposal of applications for the registration of layout-designs and any disputes arising therefrom, constitute a Layout-Design Office, functioning through a member appointed bench. Such a bench shall invariably comprise at least one member possessing a degree in engineering or technology relating to semiconductor integrated circuits, and one legal expert familiar with intellectual property matters. Where an application includes a copy translation work, submitted to demonstrate prior art or novelty, the bench may request a certified translation from a translator approved by the Central Government, at the expense of the applicant. The decision of the bench shall be final and binding, subject to any appeal as provided herein, and all orders and directions issued by the bench shall be recorded in writing. Any member may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, recuse themselves from hearing a particular matter if a conflict of interest exists.

The Central Government shall, upon notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Layout-Design Office for the administration of this Act and for the registration of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs. All applications for registration, and any subsequent amendments thereto, shall be submitted to the Layout-Design Office in the prescribed manner. The Layout-Design Office shall maintain a public register of registered layout-designs, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Layout-Design Office regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Chairperson Judicial Member, whose decision shall be final and binding, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the impugned decision. The Chairperson Judicial Member may, at their discretion, require technical assistance from a qualified expert in determining the validity of any claim made in the appeal. All proceedings before the Chairperson Judicial Member shall be conducted in accordance with principles of natural justice.

The registered proprietor of a layout-design right may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign, transfer, or otherwise dispose of the layout-design right, or any right therein, to any person or entity, whether Indian or foreign, by way of a written instrument of assignment executed in accordance with the applicable law. Any assignment of a layout-design right shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the assignor and the assignee, including, but not limited to, royalty payments, territorial limitations, and field of use restrictions. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity or enforceability of such an assignment, the Chairperson judicial member of the designated authority shall have the exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter and issue appropriate orders. The authority may, at the request of either party, appoint an assessor with technical expertise to assist in the determination of complex issues relating to the layout-design. All assignments shall be registered with the appropriate office as provided herein to be effective against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar regarding the rectification of the register of layout-designs, or refusal to rectify such register, may prefer an appeal to the Chairperson Judicial Member within a period of sixty days from the date of the order appealed against. The Chairperson Judicial Member, upon receipt of such appeal and after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, shall either confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Registrar. Provided that the Chairperson Judicial Member may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit with the Registrar such sum as he deems fit, to cover the costs of notice to other interested parties. Further, any decision of the Chairperson Judicial Member shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice, and no further appeal shall lie under this Act. The Registrar shall transmit all records pertaining to the appeal to the Chairperson Judicial Member without delay.

The aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the decision of the Registrar regarding the validity of a semiconductor layout-design registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of the Registrar’s order. The Chairperson Judicial Member of the Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of such appeal and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, constitute a special bench for its expeditious hearing. Provided that, if the appeal concerns a matter of substantial legal complexity, the Chairperson may, at their discretion, include an additional technical member to the bench. Any decision of the Appellate Board may be challenged before the High Court, subject to the provisions contained within the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the High Court’s decision shall be final, save for any appeal to the Supreme Court on questions of law of general public importance as provided herein. The Registrar shall transmit all relevant records to the Appellate Board without delay.

Any person desiring cancellation of a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a petition to the Controller, accompanied by a fee as prescribed under the rules made herein. The petition shall clearly state the grounds upon which cancellation is sought, and shall be supported by documentary evidence demonstrating the basis for such claim. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a counter-statement to the petition within a period of thirty days from the receipt of the petition, outlining reasons for maintaining the registration. The Controller, after examining the petition, counter-statement, and supporting evidence, may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, direct a hearing. Provided that the Controller may, at any stage of the proceedings relating to cancellation registration layout, require additional evidence or clarification from either party as deemed necessary to ensure a just determination. Failure to comply with timelines prescribed herein may result in dismissal of the petition or ex parte decision.

Any person interested may petition the Controller for cancellation of registration of a layout-design, subject to the provisions of this Act, by filing a petition in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. The petition shall clearly state the grounds upon which cancellation is sought, and shall be supported by documentary evidence. Where the Controller is satisfied that sufficient cause exists, he shall issue notice to the registered proprietor, requiring him to furnish within a period of two months from the date of such notice, evidence in support of the validity of the registration. 

Failure by the registered proprietor to submit such evidence within the stipulated period shall be deemed sufficient ground for cancellation. The Controller, after considering the evidence presented by both parties, may, if satisfied that the registration ought to be cancelled, order the cancellation of the registration of the layout-design. An appeal from any order made by the Controller regarding cancellation registration layout shall lie to the High Court. The Controller may, as provided herein, direct rectification of the register.

Any person claiming an interest in a registered semiconductor layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Controller for the assignment of the registration of such layout-design to themselves, provided that such application is accompanied by a statement detailing the nature of their interest and the consideration offered for the assignment. The Controller shall, upon receipt of such application and after satisfying themselves as to the validity of the claim and the adequacy of the consideration, register the assignment in the Register of Layout-Designs. A registered proprietor may, with the prior written consent of the assignee, grant licenses to others for the use of the layout-design, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial limits of such license. Should a dispute arise regarding the validity of an assignment or the terms of a license, any aggrieved party may petition the Controller for resolution, and the Controller’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal as provided herein. An application for cancellation registration layout may be made if the assignee fails to exercise their rights within a period of two years from the date of assignment.

Any person aggrieved by the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design may petition the Controller for its cancellation, subject to the payment of a fee as prescribed. The petition shall clearly state the grounds upon which cancellation is sought, and shall be accompanied by supporting evidence demonstrating that the registered layout-design lacks originality or was publicly known or used prior to the filing date of the application for registration, as provided herein. Furthermore, a petition for cancellation may also be filed on the basis that the layout-design infringes upon existing intellectual property rights, including but not limited to, previously registered designs or patents. The Controller shall, after examining the petition and any evidence submitted, issue a notice to the registered owner, allowing them an opportunity to respond. Should the Controller uphold the petition, the registration of the layout-design shall be cancelled, and notice thereof shall be published in the official journal. An appeal against the Controller’s decision regarding cancellation registration layout shall lie before the High Court.

The Registrar shall maintain a National Register of Plant Varieties, and for the purposes of ensuring comprehensive documentation of plant genetic resources, all commercially viable plant varieties shall be subject to compulsory cataloguing. This cataloguing shall include, but not be limited to, details of the variety’s breeder, origin, characteristics, and extent of commercialization. Provided that, a variety may be exempted from immediate cataloguing if it is demonstrably undergoing a period of substantial development, as determined by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. The Authority may, subject to established guidelines, prescribe a phased implementation schedule for varieties compulsory cataloguing, prioritizing those with significant agricultural or horticultural importance. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding cataloguing may submit a representation to the Registrar.

The Plant Variety Protection Authority, upon receipt of an application for the registration of a farmer’s variety, shall cause a thorough examination of the claimed characteristics, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, and shall maintain a National Register of Farmers’ Varieties, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person aggrieved by the Authority’s decision to reject a farmer’s variety for inclusion in the National Register may, within ninety days of the communication of such rejection, file an appeal before the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. The Appellate Board shall, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard to both the appellant and the Authority, pass such orders as it deems fit, including directions for re-examination or acceptance of the variety. Provided that, if the rejection is based on a demonstrable lack of distinctiveness compared to a previously catalogued variety, the burden of proof shall lie upon the applicant to establish substantial differences. The Authority may, at its discretion, request assistance from recognised agricultural universities or research institutions in the process of cataloguing farmers varieties and assessing their characteristics.

A “variety” shall mean a group of plants of any species, or of any two or more species or varieties which, when multiplied, retain their identifying characteristics over several generations, and includes hybrid varieties, farmer’s varieties, locally adapted varieties, and transgenic varieties developed through biotechnological or genetic engineering processes, subject to the provisions of this Act and other relevant legislation. A “farmer’s variety” is defined as a variety which has been traditionally grown and evolved by farmers over generations, possessing distinct, uniform, and stable characteristics, and is notified by the Central Government as such. The Authority may, as provided herein, establish a register for the preservation of these varieties plants ensuring their continued availability and genetic diversity. Any person claiming rights over a variety shall be required to demonstrate its distinctiveness.

Any person claiming to have essentially derived a new plant variety from a registered variety, shall submit an application for registration as provided herein, demonstrating substantial similarity between the derived and initial varieties. The application shall include a detailed description of the traits of the derived variety, a comparative analysis highlighting the differences and similarities with the registered parent variety, and evidence of the process by which the derived variety was obtained. A breeder, seeking protection for a new plant variety, may also apply for registration, subject to fulfilling the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity. The Authority, upon examination, may require additional information or evidence to ascertain the veracity of the claim regarding varieties plants ensuring their protection. Provided that, a farmer who has bred or developed a new variety may also register it, following a simplified procedure and reduced fees, as stipulated by the Central Government. Registration shall confer exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute and import the variety.

Any person who, without due authorization from the breeder or as otherwise provided herein, produces, sells, markets, distributes, imports, or exports any protected plant variety, or commercially exploits the harvested material of such variety, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both. The Authority, upon receiving a complaint alleging infringement relating to registered varieties plants ensuring the integrity of the breeding process, may initiate an investigation and, if satisfied of the infringement, may issue a cease and desist order. Failure to comply with such an order shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved, and may further constitute grounds for criminal prosecution. Any profits derived from the unlawful exploitation of protected varieties shall be forfeited to the Central Fund established under this Act.

An entitled produce variety shall mean a variety of plant, whether commercially sold or not, which is derived from a registered variety, and which retains the essential characteristics of the registered variety, subject to such limitations as may be prescribed. Provided that a variety shall not be considered an entitled produce variety if it is essentially a mutant of the registered variety, unless the mutation confers a distinct, substantially improved, and stable trait. A farmer who has cultivated a registered variety, or an entitled produce variety thereof, shall be deemed to have a right to save seed of his harvest and reuse it, subject to the conditions as provided herein, and without prejudice to any other rights conferred under this Act. The scope of entitlement shall be determined based on the degree of derivation and the maintenance of essential characteristics.

Any farmer or group of farmers who have bred, developed, or systematically cultivated a new plant variety, or have contributed substantially to its development, may apply for registration of that variety as an entitled produce variety under this Act. The application shall be made to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. A variety shall be considered distinct if it demonstrates clearly distinguishable characteristics from any other variety commonly known or commercially available. Substantially derived varieties, being those predominantly derived from the registered variety, shall not be eligible for independent registration without the right holder’s consent, subject to provisions for equitable benefit sharing as determined by the Authority. The Authority may, after examination and verification of the applicant’s claim, grant a certificate of registration for the entitled produce variety, conferring exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, and distribute the variety. Registration shall be valid for a period of fifteen years from the date of grant, subject to renewal provisions as provided herein.

Any farmer who has, through his or her knowledge and efforts, developed a new or unique entitled produce variety, shall be deemed to be a breeder for the purposes of this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein. A farmer in possession of any variety of farmers’ variety shall have the right to save, use, sow, regrow, multiply, and commercialize such variety in the same manner as has been traditionally practiced. However, such rights shall not extend to the sale, export, or commercial marketing of any variety which is essentially derived from a registered variety protected under this Act, without the explicit authorization of the breeder of such registered variety. Where a breeder establishes that a farmer has infringed the rights pertaining to an essentially derived variety, the farmer shall be liable to pay damages, assessed in accordance with the principles of equitable compensation. Provided that, no action may be initiated against a farmer unless a complaint is filed within two years from the date of knowledge of the infringement.

A variety shall be considered an entitled produce variety if it satisfies the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity, as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority following an examination conducted in accordance with the prescribed procedures. The Authority may, subject to the payment of the applicable fee, initiate a verification process to ascertain the veracity of claims regarding the characteristics of a variety proposed as an entitled produce variety. A farmer who has bred or developed a new entitled produce variety, or has made a significant contribution to its development, shall be eligible to register the same, provided that such farmer demonstrates a clear lineage of propagation and cultivation. Any person alleging infringement of rights relating to an entitled produce variety shall furnish proof of origin and a detailed description of the variety, including its genetic properties. The Authority shall maintain a register of all entitled produce varieties, accessible to the public, and may revoke registration if it is established that the variety does not meet the stipulated requirements or if the breeder has failed to comply with the conditions prescribed herein.

A variety shall be considered an entitled produce variety if it demonstrably results from the exercise of an essentially derived variety or a substantially similar variety, and the breeder of the initial variety has not consented to the commercial exploitation of the entitled variety. Subject to the provisions herein, a farmer who has bred, developed, or cultivated a new entitled produce variety may register it with the Plant Variety Protection Authority, provided that such variety possesses distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. Registration shall confer exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, and import the entitled produce variety, subject to a requirement of declaring the parent variety from which it was derived. Any person intending to commercially exploit an entitled produce variety must obtain a license from the breeder of the initial variety, or demonstrate that the variety was independently developed without reliance on the protected characteristics of the initial variety. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person cultivating a commercially viable entitled produce variety, and claiming a right therein, shall maintain a record of all transactions relating to the said variety, including but not limited to seed production, sales, and distribution, for a period of not less than five years, subject to inspection by officers authorized under this Act. Failure to maintain such records, or provision of false or misleading information during inspection, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any farmer demonstrating independent development of an essentially derived variety, and subsequently commercializing it without acknowledging the initial breeder, shall be liable to a fine up to one hundred thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. The Authority may, however, consider extenuating circumstances such as traditional knowledge and customary practices in determining the appropriate penalty. Any appeal against a penalty imposed as provided herein shall lie before the designated Appellate Tribunal.

Any person claiming to be the breeder of, or having a right to an entitled produce variety, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner for the grant of a certificate of registration. The application shall include a declaration affirming the distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability of the variety, alongside relevant data demonstrating these characteristics. A breeder, upon obtaining a certificate, shall have the exclusive right to commercially exploit the protected variety, including its propagation, sale, and distribution, subject to the provisions of this Act. Assignment of rights relating to an entitled produce variety shall be permissible, and any such assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Authority to be effective against third parties. Licensing agreements may also be entered into, specifying the scope, duration, and royalty terms, and such agreements shall be subject to review by the Authority to ensure fair and equitable practices, particularly concerning farmers’ rights to save, use, sow, re-sow, and exchange farm-saved seeds of protected varieties. Provided that, the breeder shall not unduly restrict these farmers’ rights as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be a breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, or a farmer who has bred a new entitled produce variety, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for registration of such variety in accordance with the regulations prescribed. The Authority, upon examination of the application and evidence submitted, shall grant a breeder’s or farmer’s right, subject to verification of essential characteristics and novelty as provided herein. However, any denial of registration shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order, with the appellant bearing the onus of demonstrating substantial grounds for review. Furthermore, a registered variety holder may initiate proceedings against any alleged infringement of their rights, and the burden of proving non-infringement shall lie with the defendant. The Authority may, in cases of demonstrable hardship to a farmer practicing traditional methods, grant temporary exemptions from certain provisions relating to commercial exploitation of the entitled produce variety.

A variety shall be considered an entitled produce variety if it demonstrably possesses distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, as determined through trials conducted in accordance with such guidelines as may be prescribed. Any person claiming entitlement to a variety shall submit a complete application to the Registrar General Plant, including a detailed description of the plant’s characteristics and the results of such trials. Subject to verification of the submitted data and payment of the prescribed fees, the Registrar General Plant may grant a breeder’s certificate for the variety. Provided that, a variety which is essentially derived from another variety, where the essentially derived variety is itself protected under this Act, may only be registered with the explicit consent of the breeder of the initial variety. Compliance with post-registration obligations, including the payment of renewal fees and the maintenance of viable seed stock, shall be a continuing condition of the breeder’s certificate. Failure to comply may result in the revocation of the certificate, as provided herein.

Any person who commercially exploits an entitled produce variety, whether by sale, distribution, or any other mode of marketing, without a license from the breeder or a valid authorization as provided herein, shall be guilty of an infringement under this Act and shall be liable to a penalty not less than five thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees for each instance of such infringement. Where such infringement involves a process respect patent relating to the development of the variety, the penalty shall be doubled. The Authority may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the confiscation of all infringing material and the cessation of all related activities. Any profits accrued from the unlawful exploitation of the entitled produce variety shall be recoverable as damages, subject to a determination of actual loss suffered by the breeder. Repeated offenses shall attract enhanced penalties and potential imprisonment not exceeding one year.

A dispute concerning an entitled produce variety arising from the alleged misdeclaration of botanical source at the point of import shall be adjudicated as provided herein, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. Where a complainant alleges that imported agricultural produce, claimed to be of a registered variety, does not conform to the characteristics documented during registration, the Authority may, subject to the provisions of the Customs Act 1962 regarding seizure and examination of goods, direct a physical examination of a representative sample. Should the examination reveal substantial deviation from the registered characteristics, and the importer fails to demonstrate legitimate grounds for such variance, the Authority shall issue a cease and desist order. Any aggrieved party may appeal such order before the designated Appellate Tribunal within sixty days of the issuance, providing evidence supporting their claim of varietal authenticity or demonstrating justifiable cause for deviation. The Tribunal’s decision shall be final, subject to judicial review.

Any farmer or group of farmers, or any breeder, who has developed a new and distinct entitled produce variety of any crop, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for registration of such variety in accordance with the provisions of this Act. The application shall be in such form and shall be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed. A layout design consisting of a unique arrangement of characteristics demonstrably contributing to the distinctiveness of the variety may be submitted as supporting documentation. Registration shall be subject to a demonstration of the variety’s stability, uniformity, and distinctiveness, as determined through trials conducted or recognized by the Authority. Provided that, a variety which is essentially derived from an already registered variety shall not be eligible for independent registration unless substantial innovation is proven. The Authority may, after examination, grant the certificate of registration.

A government undertaking, for the purposes of this Act, shall mean any entity owned or controlled by the Central Government or a State Government, or any corporation established under any law for the time being in force, where such Government or Governments hold not less than fifty-one per cent of the share capital. Such an undertaking may, subject to the provisions contained herein, be granted a licence to work a patented invention without the consent of the patentee, if it is demonstrated that the invention is of particular importance for national defence, public health, or nutrition. Provided that, the government undertaking shall remit reasonable royalties to the patentee, as determined by the Controller of Patents. Any acquisition of a patent by a government undertaking shall be deemed to be for public purpose, notwithstanding any other provision contained within this Act.

Any invention arising from research undertaken by a government undertaking, whether wholly or jointly with any other person, shall vest in the Central Government. A government undertaking, for the purposes of this Act, is defined as a department of the Central or State Government, or a public sector company as defined in the Companies Act, 2013. Where such an invention is potentially patentable, the government undertaking shall, within a period of one year from the date of conception, submit a detailed disclosure to the designated authority. The authority may, subject to verification of the invention’s novelty and inventive step, proceed with filing a patent application in the name of the Central Government. Provided that, if the government undertaking fails to submit such disclosure within the stipulated timeframe, the right to file for patent protection shall revert to the inventor or inventors, as determined by the undertaking’s internal protocols. Any royalties or revenues derived from the exploitation of such patents shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any invention developed as a result of research undertaken by a government undertaking, or to which the government undertaking has acquired ownership, shall be deemed to be an invention for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any prior public knowledge or use thereof, provided that such invention is not disclosed to the public without prior intimation to the Controller. Where a government undertaking seeks a patent for such an invention, it may, subject to fulfilling all statutory requirements as provided herein, proceed directly to grant, bypassing certain procedural delays ordinarily applicable to patent applications. Should a dispute arise regarding the ownership of such an invention between the government undertaking and any other person claiming interest, the matter shall be referred to the High Court having jurisdiction. The government undertaking shall be liable to pay prescribed fees, though a reduced rate may be considered in cases of inventions demonstrably benefiting national security or public health. Any revenue generated from the exploitation of a patented invention owned by a government undertaking shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any invention arising from research and development undertaken by a government undertaking, whether wholly or jointly with any other person, shall be deemed to be an invention made for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any prior publication or communication to others, provided that such government undertaking demonstrates a clear and demonstrable public need for the invention. Where a government undertaking is established for a specific purpose under any law, the Controller, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, may direct that the patent application relating to such invention be expedited. Any royalty or other consideration accruing from the exploitation of such patented invention shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. A government undertaking may, with the approval of the Central Government, assign or license the patent to any other person or entity, subject to safeguards ensuring reasonable accessibility and affordability of the invention to the public. The provisions of this Act relating to revocation shall apply mutatis mutandis to patents held by a government undertaking.

Any government undertaking established for the purpose of research and development relating to pharmaceuticals, and engaged in the manufacture of patented inventions for public health needs, shall be deemed to have the requisite authority to utilize such inventions subject to the provisions of this Act. Provided that such government undertaking shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Controller, a clear and demonstrable national need for the pharmaceutical product in question. Furthermore, any such utilization shall be non-exclusive and royalty-bearing, with rates determined by the Central Government, and deposited into a designated fund for the promotion of indigenous research. A government undertaking seeking to utilize a patented invention must submit a detailed justification outlining the public health imperative and proposed manufacturing scale, and shall comply with all quality control standards as prescribed by the relevant regulatory authorities. Failure to adhere to these conditions may result in revocation of the authorization granted under this Act.

Any government undertaking engaged in the manufacture of a patented invention for purposes of public health or nutrition, and so authorized by the Central Government, shall be exempt from the requirement of obtaining a license from the patent holder, provided that such undertaking demonstrates a prima facie case of national emergency or compelling circumstances necessitating such manufacture. Failure to accurately report the quantity of the patented invention so manufactured to the Controller of Patents within thirty days of production shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any person alleging misrepresentation by a government undertaking regarding the purpose of manufacture, or the existence of compelling circumstances, may lodge a complaint with the Controller, who shall conduct an inquiry and, if satisfied of such misrepresentation, may revoke the exemption and impose a further penalty on the undertaking, up to ten lakh rupees. All penalties collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. A false claim made by an officer of a government undertaking shall be deemed an offence under the Indian Penal Code.

Any patentable invention arising from research and development undertaken by a government undertaking, whether wholly owned or partially owned by the Central Government, shall vest in that government undertaking. Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a government undertaking desiring to exploit such a patent shall, prior to commercialization, offer a non-exclusive licence to any person demonstrating a credible need and possessing the capacity to utilize the invention for public benefit. The terms of such licence shall be subject to negotiation, but shall not exceed a royalty rate equivalent to five percent of net sales. Where a government undertaking assigns its rights in a patent to a private entity, it shall obtain prior approval from the appropriate governmental authority, and such assignment shall be subject to a right of first refusal for other government undertakings. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the patent voidable at the instance of any interested party, and shall constitute a breach of trust warranting appropriate remedial action. A government undertaking may, however, retain exclusive rights where the invention pertains to national security.

Any invention arising from research undertaken by a government undertaking, and funded wholly from public revenues, shall be the exclusive property of that government undertaking, notwithstanding any novelty or inventive step demonstrated by said invention. However, a compulsory license may be granted by the Controller, subject to the payment of adequate remuneration, if a reasonable time, not exceeding five years from the date of patent application, has elapsed since the filing of the application and the invention is not being worked to address a national emergency or public health crisis. Any dispute regarding the determination of ‘adequate remuneration’ or the existence of a national emergency shall be appealable to the High Court, with the government undertaking retaining the right to present evidence of ongoing research and development costs. Provided that, the Controller’s decision regarding the grant of a compulsory license is final and not subject to appeal, except on grounds of procedural irregularity.

Any government undertaking established for the purpose of defense or atomic energy shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, be deemed to be a person for the purposes of making an application for a patent, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. However, any patent granted to such a government undertaking shall be subject to a special license for use by other entities, as determined by the Central Government, in cases of demonstrable public need or national emergency. Any dispute regarding the scope of such license, or the determination of public need, may be referred to a specially constituted tribunal for adjudication, and the decision of the tribunal shall be final and binding. The tribunal shall endeavour to resolve such disputes within a reasonable period, not exceeding one year from the date of reference, failing which the matter shall revert to the High Court having territorial jurisdiction. Provided that, the government undertaking may appeal the tribunal’s decision on grounds of procedural impropriety only.

A government undertaking, being a person as defined under this Act, may apply to the Controller for a registration of its undertaking as a designated entity for the purpose of utilizing patented inventions relating to essential medicines and technologies necessary for national defense or public health emergencies. Such application shall be accompanied by detailed documentation establishing the nature of the undertaking, its objectives, and the specific patented inventions for which utilization is sought. The Controller, upon satisfactory verification, shall register the undertaking and grant a non-exclusive, non-transferable licence to practice the patented inventions subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. Provided that, the Controller may, in exceptional circumstances and with due justification, grant an exclusive licence to a single government undertaking if it is demonstrated that such exclusivity is crucial for effective implementation of a nationally significant program. Any dispute regarding the scope or validity of such registration or licence shall be subject to the appellate process as provided herein.

A government undertaking, established for the purpose of agricultural research and development, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to an inventor’s certificate for a newly discovered and substantially different variety of plant, provided that such variety demonstrates a marked improvement in yield or disease resistance over existing publicly available varieties. The Controller of Patents shall, upon application by the government undertaking, undertake a detailed examination of the claimed variety, including a comparative analysis against established cultivars, and shall consider evidence of repeatability and stability of the characteristics. Where the claimed variety is determined to be an entitled produce variety, a certificate shall be granted conferring exclusive rights for propagation, sale, and distribution for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the date of grant. Any royalty accruing from the commercial exploitation of such a variety shall be credited to the consolidated fund of the government undertaking, to be utilized for further research and development activities as provided herein. The government undertaking shall maintain detailed records of all breeding programs and sales, subject to inspection by authorized officers.

The Registrar may, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to the provisions of this Act, order the cancellation of the registration of a trade mark. Such application for cancellation shall be based on grounds including, but not limited to, non-use of the trade mark for a continuous period of five years, or the trade mark having become deceptively similar to another trade mark registered for identical or similar goods or services. Provided that, prior to issuing an order for cancellation, the Registrar shall provide the registered proprietor with an opportunity to be heard and to submit evidence in rebuttal. Furthermore, a finding of honest concurrent use by another party, established to the satisfaction of the Registrar, may also constitute grounds for cancelling registration as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by the continued registration of a trade mark may apply to the Appellate Board for its cancellation, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and fulfillment of such conditions as may be stipulated in the regulations. Such application shall clearly demonstrate grounds for cancellation, including but not limited to, a trade mark that has become deceptively similar to another registered mark, or one that lacks distinctiveness due to prolonged and widespread use by others. The Appellate Board, upon receiving a valid application, shall issue notice to the registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to present cause why the registration should not be cancelled. Provided that, if the registered proprietor fails to respond within the stipulated timeframe, or fails to adequately rebut the grounds for cancellation, the Appellate Board may proceed *ex parte* and issue an order for cancellation. Any order of the Appellate Board regarding the cancelling registration shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court.

A registered certification trade mark shall distinguish goods or services from those in the same class as to source, quality or other characteristics, and shall not be used by any person other than the certified person or with their authorization. The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, grant licenses for the use of the mark to persons who meet the standards or requirements specified in the regulations filed under this Act. Any regulations governing the use of a registered certification trade mark shall be open to public inspection. Failure to adhere to the prescribed standards or to maintain proper oversight of licensees may constitute grounds for revocation of the registration, as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all certified users.

A registered certification trade mark shall be subject to regulations filed with the Trade Marks Registry, governing its application and use, and these regulations shall be publicly available for inspection. The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall ensure that the certification mark is applied only to goods or services meeting the prescribed standards, and any deviation from these standards may result in the revocation of the registration, as provided herein. Any person authorised by the proprietor to use the registered certification trade mark shall be bound by the terms of the regulations and subject to the proprietor’s oversight. The regulations may specify the testing procedures and the qualifications of the certifying authority, and shall include provisions for periodic re-certification of goods or services. Failure to adhere to the regulations shall constitute grounds for legal action under this Act, including but not limited to injunctions and damages. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause, direct amendments to the regulations to ensure compliance with prevailing standards.

The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall exercise control over the use of the mark in accordance with the regulations filed under this Act, and any failure to do so may be grounds for revocation of the registration. Any person being a manufacturer or merchant, who, being authorized to use a registered certification trade mark, contravenes the regulations governing its use, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Subject to the provisions herein, the owner of a registered certification trade mark may, in cases of unauthorized use, seek an injunction restraining such use and claim damages for loss suffered due to such infringement. A collective mark, being a special type of certification trade mark, shall be subject to the same rights and remedies as any other registered certification trade mark, provided that the regulations governing its use reflect the collective nature of the ownership. The Registrar may, upon application, direct an inquiry into any alleged contravention of these provisions and issue appropriate orders.

A registered certification trade mark shall be subject to regulations filed with the Trade Marks Registry, governing its application and use, and such regulations shall be publicly available for inspection. The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall establish and maintain a code of practice detailing the standards to which goods or services must conform to be certified. Any determination of conformity shall be conducted by a body demonstrably independent of the proprietor and approved by the Registry as a competent certifying authority. An application for such approval shall include evidence of the body’s technical competence and impartiality. The proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, revoke the approval of a certifying authority upon reasonable cause being shown and after affording the authority a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Failure to adhere to the filed regulations or to maintain a competent certifying authority may constitute grounds for revocation of the registered certification trade mark, as provided herein. Any aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the Registry regarding non-compliance with the established code of practice.

A registered certification trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act concerning collective marks, with such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification, prescribe. The proprietor of a registered certification trade mark shall ensure that all goods or services certified conform to the standards specified in the regulations filed with the Trade Marks Registry, and any deviation from these standards shall constitute grounds for revocation of the registration. Any person authorised to use a registered certification trade mark, following certification, shall conspicuously display the mark on the goods or their packaging, or in connection with the services provided. The regulations governing the use of the mark may provide for a system of periodic inspection of certified goods or services to verify continued compliance with the prescribed standards. Failure to permit such inspection, where reasonably requested, shall be deemed a breach of the regulations. Subject to the provisions herein, the proprietor may grant licenses for the use of the certification trade mark to those who meet the established criteria.

Any person falsely representing goods or services as certified by a registered certification trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered proprietor of a certification trade mark knowingly permits the use of the mark on goods or services not meeting the standards prescribed in the regulations filed under this Act, they shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Central Government may, by notification, establish a Certification Marks Committee to oversee compliance with these provisions and to investigate complaints regarding misuse or improper application of registered certification trade marks. Any appeal against the decisions of the Committee shall lie before the High Court. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may initiate *suo motu* inquiries into potential violations of these regulations, and may require the submission of evidence or attendance of witnesses as deemed necessary.

A registered certification trade mark shall be subject to licensing arrangements determined by the proprietor, provided that such arrangements are consistent with the standards and conditions for certification as originally submitted and approved under this Act. Any assignment of rights in a registered certification trade mark shall require prior notification to the Trade Marks Registry and shall be subject to a review to ensure the assignee is capable of maintaining the requisite standards of certification. The proprietor may, at their discretion, grant exclusive licenses for specific geographical areas or product categories, subject to periodic audits verifying adherence to established certification procedures. Failure to maintain these standards may result in revocation of the registration, as provided herein. Any dispute concerning the interpretation of licensing terms or the validity of an assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court. A licensee shall not sub-license without the express written consent of the proprietor, and any such unauthorized sub-licensing shall constitute grounds for termination of the license.

A dispute regarding the certification standards applied to ‘Organic Bharat’—a registered certification trade mark denoting organically grown agricultural produce—arose between the mark’s proprietor, the National Organic Farmers’ Association, and GreenGro Foods Limited. GreenGro Foods alleged that the Association was applying unduly restrictive standards, effectively creating a barrier to entry for genuine organic farmers who did not adhere to the Association’s specific, and arguably non-essential, cultivation practices. The Registrar, following an inquiry under this Act, determined that the Association had indeed deviated from the published regulations governing the use of the registered certification trade mark. An appeal was lodged by the Association with the Appellate Board, contending that the Registrar failed to adequately consider expert testimony regarding the preservation of traditional farming methods. The Board, however, upheld the Registrar’s decision, subject to a modification allowing a six-month period for the Association to revise its standards to align with the originally filed regulations, and further directed GreenGro Foods to submit samples for re-certification.

Any person falsely representing goods or services as certified by a registered certification trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, direct the removal of any material displaying such false representation, and the costs of such removal shall be borne by the offender. Any person who, with intent to deceive, applies a certification trade mark to goods or services not actually certified, or makes a false representation regarding certification, commits an offence under this Act. The Registrar, having regard to the nature of the offence and any prior convictions, may also order the forfeiture of goods bearing the falsely applied mark. Furthermore, any person infringing the rights associated with a registered certification trade mark, or any rights pertaining to registrar copyrights related to the certification scheme, shall be liable to damages as determined by a competent court.

A registered certification trade mark shall vest in the person or entity designated as the proprietor in the register, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where the proprietor is a juridical person and undergoes a lawful transmission, either by operation of law or by assignment, the Registrar shall, upon application made in the prescribed manner and subject to verification of the transmission, record the new proprietor in the register. Any aggrieved person may, within one month of such recordal, file an appeal with the appellate authority alleging that the transmission was not lawful or that the new proprietor does not meet the criteria for maintaining a registered certification trade mark as stipulated under this Act. The appellate authority shall, after providing an opportunity of being heard to both parties, issue a reasoned order either confirming the recordal or directing the Registrar to restore the previous proprietor, provided that such restoration does not prejudice any rights accrued to a bona fide purchaser. Failure to appeal within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed a waiver of objection.

A registered certification trade mark shall denote a mark capable of distinguishing goods or services which, in the course of trade, are certified by the proprietor of the trade mark in relation to origin, actual characteristics, or a particular quality of those goods or services, and shall be subject to the provisions of this Act. The proprietor of such a mark shall not, as a condition of certification, require the applicant to purchase any other goods or services from them. Where a certification trade mark relates to a process, the proprietor may, subject to rules, require evidence of patent validity for said process before granting certification. Any regulations governing the use of a registered certification trade mark shall be publicly available and consistently applied, and failure to adhere to these regulations may result in revocation as provided herein.

A certificate of registration, issued for a new plant variety as provided herein, shall be prima facie evidence of a validly protected right in respect of said variety, subject to subsequent proof of essential characteristics and distinctiveness. The certificate shall specify the designated name of the variety, the applicant’s details, the date of registration, and the period of validity, which period may be extended in accordance with the provisions relating to renewal. Where a variety is declared essentially derived from an existing registered variety, a separate certificate shall be issued denoting such derivation and identifying the initial variety from which it originates, and the holder of the certificate for the initial variety shall have rights over the essentially derived variety. Any transfer of the certificate registration shall be subject to notification to the Authority and recorded accordingly.

A person desirous of registering a new plant variety shall submit an application for certificate registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, accompanied by a prescribed fee and the requisite technical data concerning the characteristics of the variety, its origin, and its stability. The Authority shall, subject to verification of the submitted data and confirmation that the variety qualifies for registration as provided herein, grant a certificate of registration. Provided that, if the applicant claims derivation from an existing registered variety, evidence of such derivation and consent of the breeder of the initial variety shall be furnished. The certificate registration shall be valid for a period of nine years from the date of grant, subject to renewal for subsequent periods as prescribed. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of certificate registration may file an appeal before the designated appellate authority within ninety days of the order of refusal. The register of plant varieties maintained by the Authority shall be open for inspection during office hours.

A person applying for the certificate of registration of a new plant variety shall, upon satisfactory fulfillment of the requirements as provided herein, be entitled to receive said certificate from the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The certificate shall specify the designated name of the variety, the applicant as the breeder, the date of registration, and the period of validity, which shall be subject to renewal as prescribed. Any farmer who has bred, developed, or commercially exploited a registered variety, and who can demonstrate substantially derived varieties, may petition the Authority for equitable share in the benefits accruing from the exploitation of such variety. Provided that, such benefit sharing shall not prejudice the rights of the breeder or the validity of the certificate registration. The Authority may, following due process and consideration of evidence, direct the breeder to share benefits with the farmer, or provide reasonable compensation. Failure to comply with such direction shall render the breeder liable to penalties as stipulated, and may result in suspension or revocation of the certificate.

A certificate of registration, once granted for a new plant variety as provided herein, shall be valid for a period of nine years from the date of grant, subject to the payment of renewal fees as prescribed. The renewal fee shall be payable annually, commencing from the third year after the date of the initial certificate registration. Failure to pay the renewal fee within the stipulated period may render the certificate liable to lapse, but such lapse shall not affect the rights accrued prior to the date of lapse. 

Any person claiming to be a breeder or a farmer who has substantially contributed to the development of a registered variety may apply to the Authority for recognition of their contribution, and the Authority shall, following due inquiry, determine the extent of such contribution and record it in the register of plant varieties. Provided that, the Authority may, at its discretion, require evidence of breeding effort or traditional knowledge to substantiate any claim of contribution. The certificate registration shall be updated to reflect any such recognized contribution.

A certificate of registration, once granted for a new plant variety, shall be valid for a period of nine years from the date of notification, subject to the continued payment of annual fees as prescribed. The renewal of such certificate may be permitted for two successive terms of six years each, provided that the applicant demonstrates the continued distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability of the variety. Any farmer who has bred or developed a new variety, or essentially derived variety, shall be eligible to apply for registration, subject to compliance with the requirements regarding novelty, distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity. Where a variety is registered, the breeder shall have the exclusive right to commercially exploit the variety, except as otherwise provided herein. The Authority may, however, revoke the certificate registration if it is proven that the variety lacks the essential characteristics or that the information furnished during the application process was materially misleading. A register of all registered plant varieties shall be maintained and open for public inspection.

Any person claiming a right based on the registration of a new or distinct variety, as provided herein, shall apply for a certificate registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. Failure to submit a complete application, or to pay the prescribed fee, shall render the application liable to rejection, and the applicant may be subject to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees. Where a certificate registration is granted, the Authority shall maintain a public register detailing the variety’s characteristics and the breeder’s rights. Any falsification of information submitted in support of an application for certificate registration, or any attempt to obtain registration through fraudulent means, shall be a cognizable offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, revoke a certificate registration if it is proven that the variety lacks novelty or distinctiveness.

A certificate of registration, once granted for a new plant variety as provided herein, shall vest in the applicant or the breeder, subject to the provisions relating to benefit sharing and compulsory licensing. Any assignment of rights pertaining to such a certificate shall be effected through a written instrument, duly notarized and filed with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all such assignments, accessible for inspection during office hours. A licensee, upon obtaining a license for the commercial exploitation of the variety evidenced by the certificate registration, may sub-license its rights with the prior written consent of the breeder, and such sub-licenses shall also be recorded with the Authority. Failure to register an assignment or sub-license shall render the transaction unenforceable against third parties. Provided that, the breeder retains the right to revoke a license in cases of material breach of the licensing agreement, subject to a notice period of ninety days. The Authority may, upon application, rectify any errors in the register relating to assignments or licenses.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to grant a certificate of registration, or by any condition imposed in such certificate, may, within ninety days of the date of the order of refusal or imposition of condition, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be in such form and be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed, and shall state the grounds on which the appellant claims that the decision of the Registrar was erroneous or unjust. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and any evidence submitted by the parties, may confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, or may direct that a fresh consideration of the application for certificate registration be undertaken. Provided that, no appeal shall be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates substantial injury resulting from the Registrar’s decision, and that the variety in question possesses distinctiveness as provided herein. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to writ jurisdiction by the High Court.

A certificate of registration for a new plant variety shall be granted by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, subject to verification of substantial novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity as per the provisions of this Act. The Authority may, at its discretion, require the applicant to furnish additional evidence relating to the characteristics of the variety, or to conduct further trials to confirm said characteristics. Where the variety is a registered breeder variety, and the applicant is the breeder, the certificate shall vest absolutely with the breeder, granting exclusive rights to produce, sell, market, distribute, import, export, and otherwise commercially exploit the protected variety. Any assignment of rights arising from the certificate registration shall be recorded with the Authority and shall be subject to the terms and conditions specified herein, including provisions for royalty payments to the original breeder where applicable. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in revocation of the certificate, as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all assignments.

A design registered layout shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or commercially deal with the layout-design, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such exclusive right extends to any act involving the making, importing, selling, or distributing of an integrated circuit embodying the registered layout, or any circuit derived therefrom. A layout-design is considered ‘original’ as provided herein if it has been generated through independent intellectual effort and has not been previously published. The term of protection for a registered layout-design shall be ten years from the date of filing, or until the expiry of ten years from the date of the first commercial exploitation, whichever is earlier. Any person desiring to use a registered layout-design without the proprietor’s consent may apply to the appropriate authority for a compulsory license, subject to payment of adequate remuneration.

A person who is the proprietor of a design registered layout shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, or import an integrated circuit embodying such registered layout, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any act undertaken without the consent of the proprietor, constituting an infringement of these exclusive rights, shall be actionable under this Act. Where a person, knowing or having reasonable grounds to believe that a particular layout is a registered design layout, performs any of the prohibited acts, they may be subject to interim injunction from a competent authority. The registered proprietor may also seek damages for any loss suffered due to such infringement, assessed on a reasonable royalty basis or actual loss, whichever is higher. However, such rights shall not extend to acts done for private or non-commercial purposes, provided that such acts do not unreasonably prejudice the proprietor’s legitimate interests. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a layout-design may file a petition for revocation, demonstrating grounds such as lack of novelty or improper derivation.

A registered layout-design shall confer upon the applicant, subject to the provisions of this Act, the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and import the layout-design in any manner. The applicant, being the proprietor of a design registered layout, may assign, transfer, or license such rights to any other person, and any such assignment, transfer, or license shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon by the parties concerned and recorded with the Intellectual Property Office. Any commercial act undertaken without the express authorization of the registered proprietor, or a duly licensed assignee, shall constitute an infringement of the exclusive right. 

However, the exclusive right conferred herein shall not extend to acts undertaken solely for private personal use and not for commercial gain. Where a person, prior to the filing of an application for registration of a layout-design, has independently developed an identical layout-design, such prior development shall not be considered an infringement, provided that sufficient evidence of such prior development is presented to the appropriate authority.

Any person who, without the prior authorization of the registered proprietor of a design registered layout, manufactures, exercises, distributes, imports, exports, hires, sells or otherwise deals in a semiconductor integrated circuit embodying such registered layout shall be liable to a civil action for infringement as provided herein. The registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining the offender, along with damages for loss suffered due to the infringement, which shall not be less than five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any act of aiding, inducing, or procuring the infringement shall be deemed equivalent to direct infringement and attract the same penalties. A person claiming to be a legitimate manufacturer shall bear the burden of proving they did not infringe the registered layout, or that their actions fall within the scope of permissible fair use as defined under this Act. Any falsification of records relating to the creation or registration of a design registered layout shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine.
