Any assignment of a design registered layout shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, and shall specify the rights assigned, whether the assignment is total or partial, and whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to any person to use the design registered layout, and such licenses may be revoked by the proprietor in the manner as provided in the instrument of license. Where a license is granted for a definite period, it shall not be terminated except in accordance with the terms of the license, and any such termination shall be without prejudice to the rights of the licensee in respect of the unexpired portion of the term. The registered proprietor of a design registered layout, or a person deriving title from such proprietor, may assign the commercial exploitation rights to another person, and such assignment shall be subject to the payment of royalties as agreed upon between the parties, unless otherwise specified. Any transfer of ownership of a semiconductor facility incorporating a design registered layout does not, by itself, constitute an assignment of the layout design rights.

Any person alleging infringement of a design registered layout shall, prior to the institution of any suit, notify the alleged infringer of such intention, providing reasonable opportunity to respond and demonstrate that the layout-design in question does not constitute an infringement as provided herein. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of such notification, submit a counter-statement demonstrating a prior art reference establishing independent development of a substantially similar layout-design, the aggrieved party may, subject to verification by the Controller, elect to pursue mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon technical expert. However, if mediation fails or the alleged infringer fails to respond, the aggrieved party may then institute a suit for infringement. Any appeal against the Controller’s verification of prior art shall lie before the High Court having jurisdiction. A registered layout-design remains protected for a period of ten years from the date of registration, or until the expiry of ten years from the date of first commercial exploitation, whichever is earlier.

Any assignment of a design registered layout under this Act shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, and shall specify the layout-design so assigned, and the territory in which the assignment is to be effective. A licensee of a registered layout-design may, subject to the terms of the license, further assign or license its interest in the layout-design, provided that such sub-assignment or sub-license does not contravene any restriction stipulated in the original license agreement. Where a registered layout-design is associated with a trade mark registered in the same name and class of goods, the assignment of the layout-design shall not automatically transfer the rights in the trade mark, unless expressly stated in the assignment deed. The assignee of a design registered layout shall be entitled to the same rights and remedies as the original proprietor, subject to the terms and conditions of the assignment. Any assignment not complying with these provisions shall be voidable at the option of the assignor or the assignee.

A design registered layout shall be maintained by the Registrar in a register, forming part of the registrar index registered, and accessible for inspection subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. Any person desiring to inspect such a register shall submit an application to the Registrar in the manner as may be prescribed. The Registrar may, upon such application and payment of the fee, permit inspection of the register, or any part thereof, as the case may be. Where a layout-design is registered in the name of more than one person, the register shall state the nature of their respective interests. Any alteration in the ownership of a registered layout-design shall be recorded in the register upon submission of appropriate documentation and payment of the prescribed fee, as provided herein. The Registrar shall, upon such recording, issue a certificate of alteration of ownership. Failure to record such alteration shall not invalidate the registration, but may affect the enforceability of rights.

Any person who, without the prior authorization of the registered proprietor of a design registered layout, manufactures, exercises, offers for sale, sells, or distributes an integrated circuit embodying such layout shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. The registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages, an injunction restraining further acts of infringement, and an account of profits. Where an infringement occurs due to acts committed outside of India, recourse may be sought through the Madrid Protocol International system, subject to the provisions of that treaty and any corresponding national legislation. A registered layout proprietor may, at their discretion, pursue criminal remedies in addition to civil actions, including a complaint to the appropriate magistrate. Provided that, the court may, in determining damages, consider the value of the layout-design itself and the extent of the economic prejudice suffered by the proprietor due to the infringement. Any defense of prior art must be substantiated with clear and convincing evidence.

A design registered layout, being the final result of intellectual effort in the creation of semiconductor integrated circuits, shall be eligible for protection under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained. An applicant claiming to be a business india applicant, and seeking registration of a layout-design, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, demonstrating original conception of the layout. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, its functionality, and the manufacturing process employed. Any layout-design substantially similar to a prior layout-design, or lacking novelty, shall not be registered. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates that the prior layout-design is not commercially exploited within the territory of India, registration may be granted. The Controller may, after examination, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. A registered layout-design shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, sell, or import the layout-design, subject to the limitations as provided herein. Any person infringing upon such rights shall be liable to legal proceedings.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders, subject to the provisions herein. Contributions to the gene fund may include payments derived from the commercial exploitation of varieties registered under this Act, and any other sums received by the Central Government through benefit-sharing arrangements relating to plant genetic material. The fund shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, which may formulate guidelines for disbursement, prioritizing initiatives that support in-situ conservation, the development of new plant varieties, and the enhancement of farmers’ rights. Provided that, twenty percent of the gene fund shall be allocated annually to support local communities engaged in on-farm conservation of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of all contributions made to the gene fund established under this Act, detailing the source and valuation of each contribution. Any breeder, upon commercialization of a registered plant variety, shall contribute a percentage of profits, as determined by the Authority and subject to a minimum rate prescribed in the Schedule, to the gene fund. Provided that, contributions may be made in the form of seeds or propagating material of the registered variety, valued at prevailing market rates and accepted by the Authority. The Authority shall utilize the gene fund for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders, particularly those engaged in the development of new varieties. All disbursements from the gene fund shall be subject to audit and public reporting, ensuring transparency and accountability in its operation. The Authority may also accept voluntary contributions to the gene fund from any person or organization.

The Central Government shall establish a National Gene Fund to promote and facilitate the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and to support the benefit sharing arising from their use, as provided herein. Contributions to the Gene Fund may be made by any person, institution, or organization, and shall be received, held, and managed in accordance with such rules as the Central Government may prescribe. Any benefit derived from the commercial exploitation of varieties incorporating essentially derived varieties, or from the use of indigenous knowledge associated with plant genetic resources, shall be credited to the Gene Fund. 

Provided that a portion of the Gene Fund, not exceeding twenty-five percent, may be utilized for rewarding farmers and local communities for their contributions to plant genetic resource conservation and improvement, subject to a transparent and equitable mechanism established by the Authority. The Authority shall maintain a detailed record of all receipts and disbursements of the Gene Fund, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government. Farmers’ rights, including the right to save, use, sow, exchange, and sell farm-saved seed, shall not be prejudiced by the operation of this provision.

The Plant Variety Protection Authority shall administer a dedicated fund, known as the Gene Fund, for the purpose of incentivizing the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources for crop improvement. Contributions to the Gene Fund shall include a percentage of the sales value of seeds of protected varieties, as determined by the Authority in consultation with the Central Government, and any royalties received from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, subject to a minimum contribution rate established through regulations. The Authority may also accept grants, donations, and other contributions from national and international organizations dedicated to plant genetic resource conservation. 

Disbursements from the Gene Fund shall be utilized to support the maintenance of national, state, and local gene banks, to reward farmers and local communities for conserving on-farm genetic diversity, and to fund research and development activities aimed at enhancing crop resilience and productivity. Provided that, twenty percent of the annual disbursements shall be allocated specifically to benefit marginal and small farmers engaged in the conservation of traditional varieties. Any unutilized funds shall not lapse and shall be available for utilization in subsequent financial years.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders in accordance with the principles of equity and fairness. Contributions to the gene fund shall include, but not be limited to, a percentage of the sales revenue derived from commercially exploited varieties registered herein, adjusted annually based on a formula prescribed by the Central Government considering factors such as market value and production costs. Provided that, any entity utilizing germplasm sourced from the gene fund for research and development purposes shall contribute a portion of any resultant profits back into the fund, subject to a reasonable royalty determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, establish a transparent mechanism for disbursal of funds, prioritizing initiatives that enhance seed security and promote traditional knowledge associated with plant varieties. Any unutilized portion of the gene fund at the end of a financial year shall be carried forward to the next year.

Any person who commercially exploits a registered plant variety without lawful authorization, as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of exploitation, and the duration of such exploitation shall be considered as distinct instances. Where the exploitation involves the use of genetic material derived from a registered variety and contributed by farmers, a sum equivalent to twenty percent of the commercial sales value of the product incorporating such material shall be credited to the Gene Fund. The Central Government may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, utilize the Gene Fund for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for benefit sharing with local and farming communities. Failure to remit the aforementioned sum to the Gene Fund within sixty days of commercial sale shall attract a further penalty equivalent to the original amount due, and may result in suspension of the registration of the plant variety. Any appeal against these penalties shall lie with the designated Authority.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, and shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders. Any benefit derived from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties, including royalties and licensing fees, shall be deposited into the gene fund, subject to deduction of administrative costs as may be prescribed. A portion of the gene fund may be allocated to reward farmers for their contributions to the development of new plant varieties, as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority shall maintain a transparent accounting of all funds received and disbursed, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government. Assignment of rights to the gene fund, or a portion thereof, requires the prior written consent of the committee, and any such assignment shall be subject to the terms and conditions specified by the Central Government. Provided that, funds allocated for farmer welfare shall not be assignable.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be administered by a management committee constituted by the Central Government, and shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and breeders alike. Any dispute regarding the equitable distribution of benefits derived from the utilization of the gene fund, particularly concerning contributions from commercially exploited plant varieties, may be raised before the designated authority. Provided that, any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the decision of the designated authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding limitation periods for such appeals. The management committee shall maintain detailed records of all contributions to, and disbursements from, the gene fund, and such records shall be open to inspection by any person upon reasonable request and payment of prescribed fees. Furthermore, the committee may establish a system of rewards for farmers who contribute unique germplasm to the fund, fostering innovation and biodiversity.

The Gene Fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and breeders engaged in the development of new plant varieties. Contributions to the Gene Fund shall include royalties received from the sale of seeds of protected varieties, and any penalties imposed for violations of the provisions relating to farmers’ rights or breeders’ rights. Any trade marks registered relating to such protected varieties shall be noted with the Registrar of Trade Marks to indicate the benefit sharing arrangement linked to the Gene Fund. The Authority may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, disburse funds to support research and development initiatives, and to provide assistance to farmers in maintaining and improving their traditional plant varieties. Provided that, disbursement shall prioritize projects demonstrating clear linkages to biodiversity conservation and equitable benefit sharing. All transactions relating to the Gene Fund shall be subject to audit as provided herein.

In this Act, “published india” shall mean any work made available to the public by any means, including distribution of copies, communication to the public, or performance, where such making available occurs within the territory of India. A work shall be deemed to be published india irrespective of the nationality of the author or the place of first publication, provided that the act of publication itself takes place within India. Where a work is simultaneously published in India and elsewhere, it shall be considered published india. However, mere importation of a work into India shall not constitute publication within the meaning of this Act, unless accompanied by an express intent to offer the work to the public for sale or distribution. The determination of whether a work is published india shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding electronic publication and digital dissemination.

All works first published in India shall be deemed to be works published in India for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any place of simultaneous publication elsewhere. A work shall be considered published when copies or substantial extracts thereof are made available to the public, whether by sale, distribution, rental, public performance, or otherwise, and includes electronic transmission. Where a work is published simultaneously in India and in any country outside India, the date of first publication shall be determined by reference to the country where publication first occurs. However, for the purposes of establishing priority of publication, a work originally created in India and subsequently published abroad, shall retain its Indian origin. Subject to the provisions herein, registration of a work with the appropriate registry is not compulsory, but shall serve as *prima facie* evidence of the particulars entered therein. Any person claiming copyright in a published India work may apply for such registration as prescribed.

Any work first published in India shall be deemed to be a work published in India for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any subsequent publication elsewhere. However, where a work is simultaneously published in India and in any other country, the applicant for copyright shall, at the time of making the application, disclose the country or countries of such simultaneous publication. A work shall not be considered published unless copies have been made available to the public, whether by sale, distribution, public performance, or otherwise. Subject to the provisions herein, a person claiming to be the author of a work published india may apply to the Registrar of Copyrights for registration of copyright. The Registrar may, after satisfying themselves as to the particulars provided, register the work and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that registration is not conclusive evidence of validity of copyright. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may, within a period of sixty days, appeal to the High Court.

Any copyright subsisting in a work first published in India shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, vest in the author of the work until the expiry of the prescribed term. Where a work is published with the license of the copyright holder, the license shall be construed as a grant of rights to reproduce and distribute the work in India, unless expressly stated to the contrary. Assignment of copyright in a published India work requires a written instrument signed by the assignor or their duly authorised agent, specifying the rights assigned and the duration of the assignment. A copyright holder may, by a further instrument in writing, revoke any license granted, provided that such revocation does not affect any subsisting assignment. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to grant a license, or by the terms of a license, may apply to the High Court for appropriate relief, subject to the conditions as provided herein. The rights conferred by this Act are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed in the interests of the general public.

The registrar of copyrights shall maintain a Register of Copyrights in such form as may be prescribed, and such Register shall be open to inspection subject to the payment of such fee as may be determined by regulations. Any person aggrieved by any decision of the registrar of copyrights may, within thirty days of the date of such decision, file an appeal to the appellate authority constituted for the purpose. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights regarding the refusal of registration, amendment of entries in the Register of Copyrights, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the registrar copyrights appellate within sixty days from the date of the order. The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a Register of Copyrights in such form as may be prescribed, and all entries therein shall be open to inspection by any member of the public on payment of the prescribed fee. Where an appeal is dismissed, the Appellate Board may, subject to conditions it deems fit, direct reimbursement of costs incurred by the respondent. The Registrar copyrights appellate process is conducted with due regard to principles of natural justice and fairness.

The registrar of copyrights shall maintain a register of copyrights, and all applications for registration shall be made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the registrar may, within sixty days of the date of such decision, file an appeal to the registrar copyrights appellate, furnishing a statement of the grounds of appeal and a certified copy of the decision appealed against. The appellate authority shall, after examining the appeal and affording an opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, pass an order confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the registrar. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the appellate authority’s decision shall be final and binding, and no further appeal shall lie. Compliance with the prescribed procedures for filing appeals is mandatory, and appeals not conforming to these requirements may be rejected. The registrar shall promptly communicate all decisions to the applicant.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights relating to the registration of a work, or refusal thereof, or any other matter concerning copyright, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against and a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, pass an order confirming, modifying, or setting aside the order of the Registrar of Copyrights. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements as provided herein shall render the appeal unsustainable and subject to dismissal. Any willful misrepresentation before the registrar copyrights appellate or the Appellate Board shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, and may further result in the rejection of any pending application. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person desiring to assign the copyright in a work, or any part thereof, shall execute an instrument in writing specifying the work or part thereof assigned, and the extent of the assignment, and shall lodge the same with the registrar of copyrights for the purpose of recording. The registrar, upon receipt of such instrument and subject to verification of its authenticity, shall enter the particulars of the assignment in the Register of Copyrights. An assignment subsisting at the time of the author’s death shall be deemed to be a testamentary disposition, and shall be subject to the provisions of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, as if the copyright were movable property. 

Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment or the interpretation of its terms, any aggrieved party may apply to the registrar copyrights appellate for review of the decision of the registrar. The appellate authority shall, after affording a reasonable opportunity of being heard, issue a reasoned order which shall be final and binding, save for recourse to writ jurisdiction.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights concerning the registration of a work, or the rectification thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the said order, subject to deposit of prescribed fees and furnishing of an undertaking for security of costs. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar of Copyrights. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs. Further, any question relating to the validity of the copyright itself, as opposed to merely the registration, shall be determined by the appropriate District Court, notwithstanding any order passed by the registrar copyrights appellate. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, allowing for appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a Register of Copyrights, and all applications for registration, together with any accompanying documents, shall be subject to verification as provided herein. Any assignment of copyright in a work, or any license to utilize a copyrighted work relating to genetic resources and associated traditional ecological knowledge, shall be registered with the registrar of copyrights within sixty days of the effective date of such assignment or license. Where the copyright pertains to a work derived from or incorporating gene fund contributions, the assignee or licensee shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the registrar, evidence of equitable benefit sharing arrangements with the originating communities. For the purposes of determining inventive step, the specification shall disclose the invention in a manner which is clear and complete enough for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Such disclosure must extend to the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention at the time of filing. Provided that a failure to disclose the best mode shall not invalidate the patent if the disclosure is otherwise sufficient to satisfy the requirements of this Act. Where the specification relies upon a prior publication to fully disclose the invention, a copy of such publication shall be filed with the application, subject to the Controller’s discretion to waive this requirement. The specification does disclose a sufficient level of detail if it enables reproduction of the invention without undue experimentation.

A complete specification submitted under this Act shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention, and shall be framed in a clear and concise manner, enabling a person skilled in the art to work the invention. Provided that the specification may contain diagrams or illustrations as necessary for full and complete understanding thereof. Where a specification relates to a process, it shall clearly define the process and the apparatus, if any, necessary for carrying it out. Furthermore, any subsequent amendment to the specification shall not extend beyond the content originally disclosed therein; subject to a justifiable reason being recorded with the Controller, and provided that such amendment does not introduce matter extending beyond the scope of the original disclosure. It shall be the duty of the applicant to ensure the specification does disclose sufficient information to establish enablement and non-obviousness. Failure to meet these requirements may render the patent void.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of a Deputy Controller refusing to amend a specification, or requiring the applicant to amend the specification in a manner prejudicial to the applicant, may prefer an appeal to the Controller within one month from the date of the order of the Deputy Controller. The Controller shall, after giving the applicant and the Deputy Controller an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision of the Deputy Controller. It shall be a condition of any such appeal that the appellant deposits with the Controller, such fees as may be prescribed. Where the specification does disclose the invention in a manner which is not clear and complete for the purposes of this Act, the Controller may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to amend the specification, require the applicant to furnish such particular statements and drawings as may be necessary. Provided that no amendment shall be permitted which materially affects the subject matter of the invention. Failure to comply with a requirement under this provision shall be deemed a ground for refusal of the patent.

A complete specification submitted under this Act shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention, and shall be so clear and complete as to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry the invention into effect without undue experimentation. Where a specification relies upon a prior publication for any matter, a clear reference thereto shall be included, and a copy of such publication shall be furnished to the Controller, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Should the specification not disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for the purposes mentioned above, the Controller may, after giving the applicant an opportunity to amend the specification, refuse to grant a patent. Provided that, any amendment made shall not extend beyond the scope of the invention as originally disclosed; and further provided that, if the Controller is satisfied that the specification does disclose the invention, but is not clear or complete, he may require the applicant to furnish a declaration clarifying the matter. Failure to comply with such requirement may render the application liable to be refused.

A complete specification submitted under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall clearly and concisely define the scope of the invention for which protection is claimed. Where a specification relies upon a prior publication or prior art to define the invention, such publication or art shall be specifically identified and its contents fully explained as to how it contributes to the claimed invention. Provided that, if the specification does disclose the invention but lacks clarity regarding essential features, the Controller may require the applicant to amend the specification within a period not exceeding six months from the date of such requirement. Subject to the foregoing, failure to adequately disclose the invention, or to provide a clear and concise definition thereof, may be grounds for refusal of the patent. Any amendment made shall not extend beyond the content of the original disclosure.

Any person who knowingly publishes or exploits an invention disclosed in a patent application, prior to the grant of a patent therefor, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. However, such liability shall not arise if the publication is solely for the purpose of scientific research or for the defense of India, subject to the Controller being duly informed of such intent. It is specifically provided herein that the specification does disclose a clear and complete description of the invention, and any omission or misrepresentation in that regard shall be deemed a willful act. Where a patent is ultimately granted, the Controller may, notwithstanding the imposition of a penalty, direct the recovery of any profits derived from such exploitation, and such recovery shall be in addition to any damages awarded to the patent applicant. Any appeal against a penalty imposed under this Act shall lie before the High Court.

Any assignment of the patent or any right therein shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Controller as provided herein. Where a patent is assigned, the assignee shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, possess the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as the original patentee. A license, whether sole or non-sole, may be granted by the patentee or the assignee, and such license shall be in writing and registered with the Controller. The specification does disclose sufficient information to enable a person skilled in the art to work the invention, and any subsequent amendment to the specification which extends beyond the scope originally disclosed shall not be permitted. Provided that, an assignment or license may be subject to conditions regarding field of use, duration, or geographical territory, as mutually agreed upon by the parties. Failure to register an assignment or license shall not invalidate the same, but may affect its enforceability against third parties.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller refusing to amend a patent specification, or requiring the amendment to be made in a particular manner, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. It is hereby clarified that the specification does disclose the invention in a manner which is clear and complete enough for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and any amendment proposed must not extend beyond the scope of the original disclosure. Provided that, if the Controller finds that the proposed amendment introduces matter beyond the scope of the initial application, the appeal shall be dismissed. Furthermore, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish evidence of due diligence in pursuing the patent application.

For the purposes of this Act, a “well known trade mark”, in relation to any goods or services, shall mean a mark which has come to be regarded as distinctive by a substantial segment of the relevant public, irrespective of whether such public is limited to a specific geographical area or is national in scope. A mark shall be considered well known if, through the use made of it by its proprietor or by any other person, it has become capable of identifying the source of the goods or services to the average consumer. However, the recognition of a mark as well known shall not be limited to the goods or services for which it is registered, and may extend to related or similar goods or services, subject to the principles of likelihood of confusion and unfair competition as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any time, determine a mark to be well known.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to revocation on an application made to the Trade Marks Registry if, and only if, it has remained unused for a continuous period of five years, and there is no bona fide intention to use it in the future. However, non-use shall not be deemed to have occurred if circumstances beyond the control of the proprietor have prevented such use, provided that such circumstances are proven to the satisfaction of the Registry. Where a mark is registered in relation to specified goods or services, the determination of ‘use’ shall be assessed in relation to those goods or services only. 

Crucially, a finding of ‘use’ in relation to a mark requires a demonstrable connection between the mark and the goods or services offered, establishing a clear use mark relation in the minds of consumers. Any use by a licensee shall, for the purposes of this Act, be considered use by the proprietor. The Registry may require evidence of legitimate commercial activity to substantiate claims of use.

Any person who makes use of a mark which is identical with, or deceptively similar to, a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, shall be liable to an action for infringement under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. However, a use of a mark shall not be considered an infringement if such use is pursuant to a lawful determination by a court, or is demonstrably necessary for the purpose of fair comment or criticism. Where a registered trade mark owner demonstrates a clear ‘use mark relation’ between the defendant’s mark and their own, and proves likelihood of confusion amongst consumers, an injunction restraining further use may be granted. The court, in considering applications for injunctions, may also order an account of profits and award damages to the aggrieved party, taking into account the extent of the infringement and any mitigating factors presented by the defendant. Any order for damages shall be proportionate to the actual loss suffered.

Any use of a registered trade mark by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a duly authorized user, shall constitute an infringement of the exclusive right conferred by registration under this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein. The determination of whether a use creates a likelihood of confusion shall be made with reference to all relevant factors, including the similarity of the marks, the similarity of the goods or services for which they are used, and the overall impression created on the public. A crucial element in assessing infringement is the ‘use mark relation’, wherein the court shall consider the manner in which the allegedly infringing mark is presented and used in relation to the registered mark. Where a registered trade mark is a well-known mark, the scope of protection extends beyond identical goods or services, and any use that takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, its distinctive character shall be actionable.

Any person who uses a mark, where such use is likely to cause confusion, or is likely to deceive or cause injury to the reputation of another trade mark holder, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, the Court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, also order the destruction or obliteration of all materials bearing the infringing mark. Any order of destruction shall be executed at the expense of the defendant and under the supervision of an officer appointed by the Court.
