Any person who avails of goods or services bearing a registered trade mark deceptively similar to their own, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. A proprietor of a trade mark registered for specific goods or services may, subject to the provisions of this Act, restrain by injunction any person from using a deceptively similar mark in relation to those goods or services. Where a trade mark is used in relation to goods or services not covered by the registration, but which are closely related to the registered goods or services constituting the ‘goods services act’, the Court may grant relief, provided that such use is likely to cause confusion or deception. The Court may also order an account of profits and award damages to the aggrieved party. Any order of injunction shall extend to the stock, packaging, and all materials used in the infringement. A defendant may, however, demonstrate grounds for legitimate competitive behaviour as a defence.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark for goods or services, shall disclose in the application all facts relevant to the assessment of distinctiveness, including any prior use by any other person, and any adverse findings in any prior proceedings relating to similar marks. Failure to make such full and true disclosure shall be deemed a false representation and may result in the rejection of the application or the revocation of any registration obtained thereby. Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services not covered by the original registration, the proprietor shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each class of goods or services so extended. Provided that, the Central Government may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant a period of rectification to the trade mark proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a false representation or improper extension of goods services act may file a complaint with the Registrar.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark relating to specified goods or services shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall not be valid unless recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where the assignment is of the entire goodwill of the business, proof of transfer of such goodwill shall be sufficient evidence of the transfer of the trade mark registration, subject to verification by the Registry. A licensee of a trade mark, with the express consent of the proprietor, may assign their interest in the license to another party, provided that such assignment does not contravene any terms stipulated in the original licensing agreement. 

The proprietor of a trade mark may, as provided herein, grant licenses to use the mark in relation to goods or services not originally covered by the registration, but such extension of the goods services act requires a separate application and fee. Any assignment or licensing agreement shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, geographical limitations, and quality control measures to ensure consistency with the original trade mark standards. Failure to adhere to these provisions may render the assignment or license voidable.

For the purposes of this Act, “use” of a trade mark involves the application of the mark to goods or their packaging with the consent of the proprietor, or in relation to any business, the use of the mark in advertising or otherwise to promote the goods or services. Such use shall be deemed to occur at the place where the goods are applied to, or the business is carried on, and may extend to use on imported goods. A trade mark shall be considered to be in use in India if it is lawfully used in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and such use shall be continuous and genuine. However, mere display of the mark as stock in trade shall not constitute use as provided herein. Any mark use that is likely to cause confusion or deception is prohibited.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any use of an identical or deceptively similar mark by another person, in relation to identical or similar goods or services, where such use is likely to cause confusion, shall constitute an infringement of the registered trade mark, as provided herein. However, a registered proprietor may, subject to the conditions prescribed, grant licenses to other persons to use the mark. A mark used in accordance with the terms of a registered license shall not be considered an infringement. Furthermore, honest use of a descriptive term, necessary to indicate the character or quality of the goods or services, shall not be actionable, provided that such use does not create a likelihood of confusion with the registered trade mark. Continuous and genuine use of the mark is essential for maintaining its validity and enforceability under this Act.

Any person who makes use of a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for the purpose of any trade or business, shall be deemed to have engaged in mark use as provided herein. However, such mark use shall not be construed as an infringement of the rights of the proprietor if it is demonstrably necessary to indicate the intended purpose of the goods or services, or if it is descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction against any party committing an act of unlawful mark use. Where a defendant proves that the use was bona fide and for the purpose of fair comment or criticism, the court may reduce the damages awarded. Any order for damages may also include an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unlawful mark use. The court shall have the power to grant relief as it deems fit, considering all circumstances of the case.

Any person lawfully using a trade mark shall be entitled to obtain registration thereof under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained and the conditions specified in the Schedule. A registered trade mark shall be deemed to be personal property and the proprietor thereof shall have the right to sue for its infringement. Where a mark has been continuously used in India for a period of not less than five years prior to the date of application for registration, and is distinctive in nature, such use shall constitute sufficient ground for registration, notwithstanding any prior use by another person, provided that such prior use was not continuous or bona fide. 

However, use of a mark by a person other than the registered proprietor, which is necessary to indicate the character or quality of the goods or services, or to describe the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, or geographical origin of the goods or services, shall not be considered an infringement of the registered trade mark. Any determination of legitimate mark use shall be made by the Registrar, and appeals therefrom may be made to the High Court.

Any person lawfully using a registered trade mark shall be entitled to obtain an injunction against any person who is not a registered proprietor, preventing such person from using the mark in a manner likely to cause confusion. However, such entitlement shall be subject to the provisions relating to assignment, transmission and licensing of trade marks as provided herein. A registered proprietor may, notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force, institute legal proceedings for infringement of their trade mark. Where a mark has been used in a manner that constitutes a misrepresentation, the court may, at the request of the registered proprietor, order the defendant to destroy all goods bearing such mark. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted if the defendant proves legitimate use of the mark prior to the registration of the plaintiff’s trade mark, or that their use is merely descriptive of the goods or services offered. Any continued mark use after notice of infringement shall be considered aggravated infringement.

Any person who, not being the registered proprietor of a trade mark or a licensee thereof, uses the trade mark in the course of trade, shall be liable to a suit for infringement of that trade mark as provided herein. However, use of a trade mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark for purposes of comparative advertising, subject to the conditions prescribed by the Central Government, shall not be deemed to be an infringement under this Act. Any aggrieved party may apply to the Court for an injunction restraining such unauthorized mark use, and the Court may grant such injunction, along with damages not exceeding one crore rupees for each such instance of infringement. Furthermore, the Court may order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark and may require an account of profits made by the infringer. Failure to comply with a Court order shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to use the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and such licenses may be granted on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties, including provisions as to quality control and duration. An assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the same conditions and restrictions as apply to the assignment of goodwill of a business, and shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the mark, subject to any agreement to the contrary. Any agreement restricting mark use, whether by way of license or assignment, shall be construed as limiting the rights of the assignor or licensor only to the extent expressly stated therein, and shall not affect the rights of others. A transfer of ownership, even without formal assignment, resulting in continued mark use may be considered equitable assignment.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark and alleging a dispute regarding mark use, shall submit a statement of case to the Registrar, detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and the grounds upon which relief is sought. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, direct the parties to engage in mediation facilitated by a neutral third party, with a view to achieving an amicable settlement. Should mediation fail, or if either party declines to participate, the matter shall proceed to adjudication. An appeal from any decision of the Registrar, including a refusal to entertain a complaint or an order dismissing a case, lies to the High Court having jurisdiction. However, such appeal shall be limited to questions of law and shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Registrar’s order, provided that the High Court may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark, and desiring to register it, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, demonstrating bona fide use of the mark in relation to goods or services for which registration is sought. The application shall include a statement detailing the extent and duration of such mark use, and evidence satisfactory to the Registrar. Where the Registrar is satisfied that the mark meets the requirements as provided herein, and that no prior conflicting mark exists on the register, a certificate of registration may be issued. However, the Registrar’s decision regarding the acceptability of evidence of mark use, or the existence of a conflicting mark, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, and any authority registrar case relating to similar evidence shall be considered during adjudication. Registration confers exclusive right to the use of the mark, subject to the provisions of this Act.

A trade mark consists of a combination of signs capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, and may include words, numerals, letters, devices, shapes, colours, or a combination thereof, as represented in a manner to be capable of being registered in the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is not inherently distinctive, it may acquire distinctiveness through use, subject to proof of such use establishing a connection in the minds of the relevant public between the sign and the undertaking. A trade mark shall not consist exclusively of signs or indications which, in the course of trade, serve only to designate the characteristics of goods or services, including shape, size, or material, unless such signs have acquired distinctiveness.

A trade mark consists of a combination of words, devices, or arrangements thereof, sufficient to distinguish goods or services of one person from those of others, and may extend to colours, shapes, or numerals, or any combination thereof, provided that such combination is capable of being represented graphically and is capable of distinguishing the goods or services. Where a trade mark includes matter which is not capable of being represented graphically, the application for registration shall not be accepted unless the applicant demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Registrar that such matter can be represented in a manner that satisfies the requirements of this Act. A trade mark shall not be registered if it is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or if its use would be likely to deceive the public, or if it is contrary to law or morality. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered trade mark shall be the property of the proprietor and grant exclusive rights to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.

A trade mark consists of any sign, capable of being represented graphically, including words, numerals, and figurative elements, and shall be registrable if it is distinctive and not descriptive of the goods or services in relation to which registration is sought. However, a trade mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion with an earlier trade mark, and the proprietor of the earlier mark may apply for an injunction to restrain the use of the later mark. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered proprietor has the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of that right. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a trade mark, or by any other decision taken under this Act, may appeal to the High Court. Provided that, such appeal shall be filed within a period of ninety days from the date of the decision. A mark consisting of a well-known trade mark shall be protected even if it is not identical with the later mark.

A trade mark consists of any sign capable of being represented graphically, including words, numerals, letters, devices, shapes, colours, or combinations thereof, and any combination of such signs, used or proposed to be used to distinguish goods or services of one person from those of others, and may extend to sounds or the scent of a good, where such signs are capable of being represented in a manner that allows for precise identification. However, a trade mark shall not consist exclusively of a shape which results from the nature of the goods themselves or is essential for obtaining a technical result, or of a shape which gives substantial value to the goods. Subject to the provisions herein, a trade mark may be registered in part A or part B of the Register, and registration in either part shall confer rights as provided under this Act. Where a trade mark is not inherently distinctive, evidence of its use shall be admissible to establish distinctiveness, provided such use has resulted in recognition by the relevant public.

A trade mark consists of any sign, capable of being represented graphically, including words, numerals, and letters, and their arrangement, and shall be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. However, a trade mark shall not consist exclusively of a shape which results from the nature of the goods themselves or is essential for obtaining a technical result, and such shape shall not be capable of acquiring distinctiveness. Provided that, if such shape has become customary in the trade, it may not be registrable as a trade mark under this Act. Furthermore, a trade mark shall not consist of descriptive character, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. Any sign, including slogans or catchphrases, may constitute a trade mark subject to compliance with the provisions herein and registration as provided for in this Act. A collective trade mark may be registered in the name of an association, and shall be used only by members of that association.

A trade mark shall consist of a combination of marks, including names, symbols, or devices, used to uniquely identify and distinguish goods or services of one entity from those of others, and may extend to colours, shapes, or sounds where such elements are capable of constituting a trade mark under this Act. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument, duly executed by both the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry to be effective. A license granting rights to use a trade mark may be granted for a defined period, territory, or form of use, and such license shall be recorded with the Registry to provide constructive notice to third parties. Where a trade mark consists of a well-known mark, assignment or licensing shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny to prevent dilution or misrepresentation, provided that the interests of the public are duly safeguarded. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment or license invalid, and subject the parties to remedies as provided herein.

A trade mark consists of a combination of signs capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, and may include names, symbols, devices, or any combination thereof, represented in a manner sufficient to enable clear identification of the mark. Such signs shall be capable of being represented graphically, and shall be capable of distinguishing goods or services. Where a mark is not registered but is capable of functioning as a trade mark, and the use of a deceptively similar mark by another undertaking is likely to cause confusion, or to deceive or cause likelihood of deception, then such use shall constitute passing off. A trade mark shall not consist exclusively of descriptive character, or be contrary to law or morality. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, refuse to register a trade mark.

A trade mark shall consist of a combination of words, or devices, or both, and may include the shape of goods, their packaging or a combination of colours, provided that such combination is capable of being represented graphically and is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. Where a trade mark consists of a word or words, the relating trade mark shall not be deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, nor shall it be descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or commonly used in the trade to designate those goods or services. An application for registration shall be subject to a search for prior conflicting marks, and the Registrar may require an applicant to amend their application to avoid such conflict. The Registrar may, however, refuse registration if the mark is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public, or is scandalous or contrary to law or morality. A mark consisting solely of a geographical name shall not be registered unless it acquires distinctiveness through use.

A mark shall not be registered under this Act if it consists exclusively of marks or indications customary in the current language of the relevant trade, and accepting without further inquiry that such marks or indications fall into one of the categories specified in section 9. However, a mark comprising or containing such marks indications customary may be registrable if, through use, it has acquired distinctiveness, and such distinctiveness is demonstrable to the Registrar. Provided that, registration of a mark containing such customary indications shall not confer exclusive right to the use of such indications themselves. Any application for registration containing marks indications customary shall be subject to a detailed examination as to acquired distinctiveness, and the applicant shall bear the onus of proving secondary meaning. The Registrar may require evidence of continuous use for a period not less than five years to establish such secondary meaning.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to obtain such registration unless the trade mark is prohibited by this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Where a trade mark consists of or includes marks indications customary in the current language of the relevant trade, it shall not be refused registration by reason only of such lack of distinctiveness, provided that such marks or indications are used honestly and fairly by the applicant and are not descriptive of the goods or services sought to be registered. A registered proprietor may, as provided herein, assign the registered trade mark and the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark in relation to those goods or services. Any assignment not in writing shall be void. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, record the assignment in the Register of Trade Marks. A person aggrieved by a refusal to register a trade mark may, within the prescribed period, appeal to the Appellate Board.

A trade mark shall not be registered if it consists exclusively of marks or indications customary in the current language of the relevant trade, or becoming so, to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or rendering of services; provided that, registration may be permissible if such marks or indications have acquired distinctiveness through use, and such distinctiveness is demonstrable to the Registrar. Where a mark comprises descriptive matter, evidence of long and continuous use, coupled with substantial promotional expenditure, may be presented as grounds for registration, subject to the Registrar being satisfied that the public has come to recognize the mark as identifying the applicant’s goods or services. Any application for registration containing marks indications customary shall be subject to examination under this Act, and the Registrar may require evidence of actual use to determine registrability. The Registrar shall maintain a register of such marks and indications, and any party opposing a registration based on this ground shall bear the onus of proving the customary nature of the mark.

Any person who applies a trade mark to goods or their packaging, with the intent to deceive or cause confusion, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both, as provided herein. Where a mark consists of indications customary in the current language of the relevant trade, and used honestly to describe the goods or services, no infringement action shall lie unless such use renders the mark capable of distinguishing the goods or services. However, a registered proprietor may seek injunction against any use of marks indications customary that is demonstrated to be undertaken with intent to diminish the distinctiveness of their registered trade mark. Any evidence obtained in contravention of provisions relating to search and seizure shall not be admissible. The Registrar may, subject to due process, order removal of offending material and impose a levy equivalent to the assessed damages.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorised agents. Where a trade mark is assigned with or without goodwill, the Registrar shall, upon application made by the assignee, record the assignment in the Register. The instrument of assignment shall clearly specify the marks indications customary to the goods or services covered by the trade mark, and any limitations on the scope of the assignment. 

An assignment lacking such specificity may be deemed invalid, and the Registrar may require rectification. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may also be granted in writing and recorded as provided herein. The licensor retains the right to enforce the trade mark against infringement unless expressly waived in the licensing agreement. Any transfer of ownership or licensing shall not prejudice existing rights or pending proceedings.

The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration and subsequent examination, shall determine whether the mark contains marks indications customary to the trade concerned. Any objection raised by the Registrar regarding such customary marks shall be communicated to the applicant, affording them an opportunity to submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness acquired through use. Should the applicant fail to adequately demonstrate such acquired distinctiveness, the application may be refused. However, an aggrieved party may file an appeal before the Appellate Board, subject to prescribed fees and timelines, contesting the Registrar’s decision. The Appellate Board, after considering the evidence and arguments presented, may confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s order. Provided that, the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, permitting further appeal to the High Court as provided herein. Any evidence submitted during appeal must be demonstrably linked to the date of the original application.

Marks indications customary in the relevant trade shall not be registrable as trade marks under this Act, unless they have acquired distinctiveness through use. However, a mark otherwise registrable may be refused registration if it is likely to cause confusion amongst the public, considering the degree of resemblance to an earlier mark and the similarity of the goods or services concerned. An application for registration may be presented with a provisional specification, detailing the goods or services for which registration is sought, and the applicant may, within the prescribed period, limit the specification to certain goods or services. Where a mark consists of, or comprises, marks indications which are customary in the current trade, the Registrar may require evidence as to the distinctive character of the mark before accepting the application for examination. Provided that, the Registrar shall not require such evidence if the mark has been continuously used for a period of not less than five years. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Marks indications, for the purposes of this Act, shall encompass any sign, or any combination of signs, capable of being represented in a durable form and distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. A mark indication may consist of visual elements, including but not limited to letters, numerals, figurative devices, or a combination thereof; or of sounds, provided that such sounds are capable of being represented graphically. Subject to the provisions herein, marks indications shall not consist exclusively of signs descriptive of the goods or services in question, or customary in the relevant trade. However, a sign which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registrable even if initially descriptive. The Registrar may, in considering an application, require evidence of acquired distinctiveness.

Any mark indicating the source or origin of goods or services, and capable of being represented graphically, may be registered as a trade mark under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. A mark shall not be registered if it consists exclusively of marks or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or services concerned. However, such marks indications may be registered if they have acquired distinctiveness through use, and such distinctiveness is demonstrable to the Registrar. Registration of a mark shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. The Registrar may, upon application, require evidence of genuine use of the mark for the purpose of maintaining its registration, and failure to provide such evidence may result in the removal of the mark from the register.

The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the trade mark contains marks indications serving solely to designate characteristics of goods or services, the application may be subject to further scrutiny regarding inherent distinctiveness. Provided that, a mark indication designating trade characteristics shall not be refused registration if, through use, it has acquired distinctiveness in the relevant market, and the applicant furnishes evidence satisfactory to the Registrar demonstrating such acquired distinctiveness. Any evidence submitted shall be admissible subject to the rules of procedure established by the Central Government. 

The Registrar may, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, require the applicant to disclaim any mark indication which is descriptive or commonly used in the trade, unless such disclaimer is demonstrably waived by the Registrar. Failure to comply with a requirement for disclaimer may result in the rejection of the application, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board.

Marks indications serving to designate geographical origin shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, not be refused registration if such marks indications are customary in the relevant trade and understood by the public as indicating such characteristics. However, registration of a mark indication shall be subject to proof of continuous use for at least five years demonstrating a clear association with a specific geographical location. Where a mark indication relates to agricultural goods, the registering authority may, prior to registration, require evidence of adherence to established quality control standards for products originating from that region. Any application for registration of marks indications must include a detailed description of the geographical area and the specific qualities associated with goods originating therefrom, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application or subsequent revocation of registration.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark, or uses a mark indicating the characteristics of goods or services, shall be deemed to have warranted that such mark is not likely to deceive the public or cause confusion. Any false or misleading indication regarding the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, or fitness for a particular purpose of goods, affixed to or used in connection with goods, shall constitute an offence under this Act. A registered proprietor who knowingly uses marks indications likely to deceive shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, direct the removal of such misleading indications. Provided that, any aggrieved person may, through a civil suit, seek an injunction restraining the use of such deceptive marks and claim damages for any loss suffered. Failure to comply with an order of the court shall be punishable with imprisonment.

Any lawful assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the rectification of the register and the recording of such assignment. A license, whether sole or otherwise, may be granted in respect of a registered trade mark, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the license, including the duration, territory, and goods or services in respect of which the license is granted. Where marks indications are assigned or licensed as part of a business transfer, notice of such transfer shall be given to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. Failure to provide such notice may render the assignment or license unenforceable. The assignee or licensee shall be entitled to use the mark indications in accordance with the terms of the assignment or license, and shall be subject to the same rights and liabilities as the original proprietor, except as otherwise agreed. Any dispute arising out of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark incorporating marks indications, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. If the Registrar determines that the mark, while not directly prohibited, presents a likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark already registered or applied for, notice of such objection shall be served upon the applicant, affording them an opportunity to submit representations within a period not exceeding thirty days. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the objections, or if the Registrar remains unconvinced, the application may be refused. Any aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the procedural requirements as laid down. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

Marks indications serve to identify and distinguish goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings, and shall be registrable under this Act subject to the provisions herein contained. A mark indication may consist of any sign, or any combination of signs, capable of being represented graphically, including words, numerals, letters, devices, shapes, colours, or combinations thereof, provided that such signs possess the requisite distinctiveness. However, marks indications which exclusively designate characteristics relating to the nature, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of goods or services shall not be registrable, except where such marks have acquired distinctiveness through use. Where a mark indication is descriptive of the goods or services, evidence of long and continuous use establishing secondary meaning may be presented to demonstrate registrability.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application and to obtain relief in respect of infringement thereof. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor, or with his consent, in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, such use constitutes an infringement of the mark. However, a registered proprietor shall not be entitled to restrain the use of a mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to his registered trade mark, if such use is by way of fair use, and does not cause confusion. 

Marks indications serve to distinguish goods and services, and the use of such marks by any person, without lawful authority, shall be actionable as passing off. A proprietor may seek an injunction, damages, or an account of profits for any infringement of his registered trade mark, as provided herein, and the Court may also order the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods.

Marks indications serve to identify and distinguish goods or services, and as provided herein, shall be registrable subject to the provisions of this Act. An application for registration may be refused where the mark is descriptive of the goods or services, or lacks the requisite distinctiveness for registration, notwithstanding that it may be capable of acquiring distinctiveness through use. However, a mark which, though descriptive at the time of application, has acquired distinctiveness through extensive and continuous use in relation to the goods or services, may be registered, provided sufficient evidence of such acquired distinctiveness is furnished to the Registrar. The Registrar may, at any time, require the applicant to submit evidence substantiating claims of acquired distinctiveness. Furthermore, marks indications which are customary in the relevant trade shall not be registrable, unless such marks have become uniquely associated with the applicant’s goods or services. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the distinctiveness of a mark may appeal to the High Court in accordance with the procedure established by law.

Marks indications serve to identify and distinguish goods or services of different undertakings, and any use of a mark without due authorization as provided herein shall be deemed a violation of proprietary rights. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign, transfer or otherwise dispose of the goodwill or the trade mark associated with the goods or services. Any transfer of ownership shall be evidenced by a written instrument duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a mark is used in a manner likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers, the use shall be considered unlawful. Provided that, marks indications which are descriptive of the goods or services themselves, or customary in the relevant trade, may be permissible subject to established usage and absence of deceptive intent. The Registrar may, upon application, direct rectification of the register where a mark is found to be in conflict with these provisions.

Any person using in the course of trade, a deceptive mark or indication likely to cause confusion, or which is likely to deceive the public, or to indicate a connection between the current goods or services and some other person, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, where the use of such mark or indication is made in good faith and without intent to deceive, the penalty may be reduced at the discretion of the adjudicating officer. Marks indications serve not only to identify the source of goods or services, but also to guarantee a consistent level of quality, and any misrepresentation in this regard shall be considered a serious offence under this Act. Any goods found bearing such deceptive marks may be seized and destroyed, and the owner of the goods shall be liable for all costs associated with such seizure and destruction, as provided herein. Failure to comply with an order of seizure shall attract further penalties.

A trade mark shall be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another and may consist of any combination of names, symbols, devices, or colours, including three-dimensional shapes, as long as such combination is capable of being represented graphically. For the purposes identifying goods, a mark shall not be considered distinctive if it is devoid of any distinctive character, or if it is descriptive, or if it has become customary in the relevant trade. However, a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registrable, subject to proof of such acquired distinctiveness to the satisfaction of the Registrar. Where a mark incorporates matter which is customary to the trade, registration may be permitted if such matter does not exclude the distinctiveness of the mark as a whole.

A trade mark shall be registrable under this Act if it is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. An application for registration shall clearly indicate the goods or services for which the trade mark is intended, and such goods or services shall be classified in accordance with the prescribed classification of goods and services. Registration shall confer upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services for the purposes identifying goods, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where a trade mark consists of a combination of words, the application shall specify the prominent portion thereof, and registration shall be granted based on that prominent portion. Provided that a trade mark which is descriptive or devoid of distinctive character shall not be registered except upon proof of acquired distinctiveness through extensive use. The Registrar may require evidence of such use as deemed necessary.

Any person who, without the consent of the registered proprietor, uses a deceptive trade mark or a trade mark identical with a registered trade mark in relation to goods for the purposes identifying goods, shall be liable to a suit for infringement. However, such suit shall not be maintainable if the plaintiff fails to demonstrate actual damage or likelihood of damage resulting from the defendant’s actions, subject to a rebuttable presumption of damage in cases of intentional infringement. Where a registered trade mark is used by another person in a manner that is likely to cause confusion, or is likely to deceive or cause an association with the goods of the registered proprietor, an injunction may be granted restraining such use. The court, as provided herein, may also award damages, including exemplary damages, and order the destruction or disposal of infringing goods. A registered proprietor may, in addition to legal remedies, seek an order for delivery up of infringing labels and packaging materials.

A trade mark shall be distinctive, and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. Where a mark is not inherently distinctive, it may, subject to the provisions of this Act, acquire distinctiveness through use. Any person adopting a trade mark shall, prior to such adoption, effect a search for identical or similar marks existing on the Trade Marks Register, and shall satisfy themselves as to the availability of the mark for the purposes identifying goods intended to be sold under that mark. An application for registration shall not be refused solely on the ground that the mark is descriptive of the goods or services, provided that such description does not lack distinctive character and is not customary in the trade. The Registrar may, however, require evidence of acquired distinctiveness in such cases. Where a mark consists of a well-known mark, the Registrar shall, notwithstanding any other provision herein, refuse registration unless the applicant demonstrates a legitimate interest in the mark. Any aggrieved person may, as provided herein, apply to the High Court for rectification of the register.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be used for the purposes identifying goods if, and only if, it is applied to those goods, or to packaging in which those goods are contained, or to labels affixed to those goods or packaging, or is otherwise displayed in such a manner that the relevant public may reasonably perceive a connection between the mark and the goods. Where a collective mark is registered, use by any member of the association constituting the proprietor shall be considered use by the proprietor, provided that such use conforms to the rules governing the collective mark as filed with the Registrar. Any use for purposes identifying goods that does not meet the criteria as provided herein shall be deemed unauthorized. The Registrar may, subject to established procedures, require evidence of genuine use of the trade mark to maintain its registration, and failure to provide such evidence may result in the removal of the mark from the register.

Any person who applies a trade mark to goods intended for sale, or offers for sale, sells, or distributes goods bearing a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, shall be deemed to have infringed that trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where a trade mark is registered for specific goods, the application of that mark to dissimilar goods shall not constitute an infringement, provided that such application does not create a likelihood of confusion or association with the registered trade mark, or dilute its distinctive character. However, use for the purposes identifying goods as those of another shall not be a defence where such use is undertaken with intent to deceive. Any person found guilty of such infringement, as provided herein, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The court may also order the destruction of infringing goods and materials used in the commission of the offence.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, or their duly authorised agents. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall, subject to the conditions specified in the instrument of assignment, have the same right to use the trade mark as the assignor in relation to the goods or services for purposes identifying goods in connection with which the trade mark was formerly used by the assignor. However, assignment of a trade mark without assignment of the associated goodwill shall be permissible, provided that the assignee demonstrates a legitimate interest and proposes a use of the mark that does not cause confusion in the market. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all assignments and record the details of the instrument. Any assignment not duly recorded shall be ineffective as against any subsequent assignment. A licensee of a trade mark may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark, or varying the terms of registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal is preferred against a decision refusing registration, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, direct the Registrar to register the trade mark. However, such registration shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to the purposes identifying goods, and any conditions imposed by the Appellate Board. A failure to comply with the timelines prescribed herein shall not automatically invalidate the appeal, but the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, refuse to entertain the same, provided that sufficient cause is not demonstrated.

Any application for registration of a trade mark, intended for purposes identifying goods, shall be subject to a rigorous examination as to its distinctiveness and compliance with the provisions of this Act. The Controller of Trade Marks may, where the application concerns goods falling within a specialized technical field, require an assessment by a Technical Member possessing requisite expertise in that field. Such assessment shall be conducted within a period not exceeding ninety days from the date of referral, and the Technical Member’s report shall be binding on the Controller, provided that objections may be raised to the report in accordance with established procedure. A trade mark shall not be registered if it is descriptive of the goods themselves, or if its use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers. The Registrar may, however, consider evidence of acquired distinctiveness, subject to satisfactory proof of extensive use and public recognition. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark for purposes identifying goods, and knowingly makes a false representation in any application or document submitted as part of the registration process, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a trade mark is registered based on such false representation, the Registrar may, subject to a reasoned order, initiate proceedings to rectify the register and remove the improperly registered mark. Any individual who continues to use a trade mark after a final order for its removal, or who obstructs a legitimate inspection carried out as provided herein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with a fine, or with both. A party may proceed case registration only after satisfying all pre-application requirements. The Registrar shall have the power to impose additional conditions to ensure compliance with this Act.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark for the purposes identifying goods shall be subject to a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall be in the prescribed form. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, the assignee shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, acquire the right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services in respect of which the goodwill is assigned. However, an assignment may be limited in its manner issuing, restricting the assignee’s use to a defined geographical area or specific class of goods, provided that such limitation is clearly stated in the instrument of assignment. The registrar shall record the assignment upon satisfaction of the prescribed requirements and payment of the applicable fee. Failure to register the assignment does not invalidate it, but such unregistered assignment shall not be enforceable against any subsequent assignee who has duly registered their assignment.

A trade mark shall be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another and may consist of a distinctive sign, including names, symbols, or devices, capable of representation on the register. For the purposes identifying goods, a trade mark shall not be refused registration if it is customary in the relevant trade to designate the character of those goods in a manner which would otherwise infringe this Act. An application for registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions herein, be extended to other countries through the Madrid Protocol International system, affording a streamlined process for securing protection in multiple jurisdictions. Provided that, such extension shall be contingent upon the applicant fulfilling all requirements of the designated contracting parties.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark, as provided herein, shall furnish a declaration confirming that the applicant is a citizen of, or is domiciled in, or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India, or is a citizen of, or is domiciled in, or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in a Contracting State or a Contracting Organisation. Where an application is made by a person resident outside India, but claiming rights through association to a Contract ing State or a Contracting Organisation, such applicant shall submit evidence of such association, including documentation establishing the legal standing of the applicant within that jurisdiction. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require further verification of the applicant’s status and the nature of their connection to the relevant Contracting State or Organisation. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of such association shall render the application liable to be refused, and the applicant shall have no recourse under this Act. Any false declaration made under this provision shall be punishable as contempt of this Act.

context: For the purposes of this Act, a “real and effective industrial or commercial establishment” shall denote a place of business where a genuine and substantial economic activity is carried on, and which is not merely a post office box, a letterbox, or a mere transit point for goods or services. The existence of such an establishment shall be determined by consideration of all relevant factors, including but not limited to, the nature of the business activity, the level of investment, the number of employees, and the volume of sales. A nominee or agent acting on behalf of a principal who is not resident in India shall not, by that fact alone, be deemed to have a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment herein. However, subject to the provisions of this Act, a branch office or subsidiary of a foreign entity may constitute such an establishment if it demonstrates a demonstrable level of independent economic activity.

context: In this Act, the term “international registration basic” shall mean the application for registration of a trade mark filed in or under the law of the country of origin, which serves as the basis for an international registration under the Madrid Protocol. The country of origin, for the purposes of determining the international registration basic, shall be the country in which the applicant is domiciled or from which they are habitually present, or where their company has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment. Where a trade mark is jointly owned, the country of origin shall be determined by the domicile or habitual presence of the first applicant listed in the international registration basic. Any alteration to the international registration basic occurring after filing, but before the expiry of the opposition period, shall be communicated to the International Bureau as provided herein.

Any applicant seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, who has filed an application for registration in a Convention country, may, within six months from the date of the first application, claim priority from that application, subject to the provisions herein. Where an applicant seeks to designate India as part of an international registration, such registration shall be considered provisional until confirmation of the basic application is received from the country of origin. The effect of such an international registration basic shall be equivalent to a direct application filed under this Act, provided that all applicable fees are duly paid and the designated representative maintains a place of business in India. Failure to provide a certified copy of the basic application within the prescribed period may result in the lapse of the international registration with respect to India. Any objection to the international registration shall be subject to the provisions relating to opposition proceedings as provided herein.

A person who has lawfully registered a trade mark in a Contracting State may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for its international registration, designating India as one of the designated countries. Such an application shall be deemed to be an application for registration under this Act, provided that the applicant furnishes a certified copy of the basic registration and a declaration confirming the mark’s continued validity in the Contracting State. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the international registration basic meets the requirements of this Act, proceed with the examination of the application as if it were a domestic application. However, where the basic registration is subsequently cancelled or refused in the Contracting State, the Registrar may, upon notification, initiate proceedings for the revocation of the corresponding international registration in India. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the international registration basic may, subject to prescribed fees and timelines, prefer an appeal to the High Court.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, which is subject to an international registration basic, shall furnish details of the basic application or registration, including the country of origin and the filing date thereof, to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The Registry may, subject to verification of the international registration basic, proceed with the examination of the application for registration in India. Where the international registration basic is found to be deficient or incomplete, the applicant shall be given an opportunity to rectify the same within a period of thirty days from the date of such notice. 

Provided that, if the applicant fails to rectify the deficiencies within the stipulated period, the application may be deemed abandoned. The Registry shall maintain a register of all international registrations basic received and shall make such register available for inspection, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any dispute regarding the validity of the international registration basic shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to opposition proceedings.

A person seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, who has filed an international registration designating India, shall furnish a statement of use within the period prescribed, demonstrating genuine use of the mark in relation to the goods or services for which registration is sought. Failure to furnish such a statement, or to demonstrate such use, may render the international registration basic subject to revocation, as provided herein. The Registrar may, however, allow a grace period not exceeding three months for rectifying any deficiency in the statement of use, provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar that such deficiency was due to circumstances beyond their control. Where the international registration basic is dependent on a prior national or regional registration, evidence of the validity of that prior registration shall also be submitted concurrently with the statement of use. Any misrepresentation regarding the extent of use shall be deemed a material omission and may attract penalties under this Act.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark based on an international registration basic shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry, within six months of the notification of completion of the international registration, a statement of entitlement to protection in India, failing which the application for registration shall be deemed abandoned as provided herein. Where a challenge is made to such entitlement, the Registry may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require further evidence of ownership or right to use. Any false statement made in the statement of entitlement shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, notwithstanding any prior acceptance of the international registration basic, initiate *ex parte* proceedings against the applicant if satisfactory evidence is not furnished within the stipulated timeframe. Any appeal against the Registrar’s decision shall lie with the High Court, and non-compliance with the High Court’s order may result in a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees.

Any person who has filed an application for registration of a trade mark in a convention country may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration of that trade mark in India, claiming priority from the said application, provided that such application is made within six months from the date of the first application. Where an applicant seeks to rely upon an international registration basic, such registration shall be deemed to be the basic application for the purposes of claiming priority under this Act. The Registrar may, however, require satisfactory proof of the filing date and other details of the basic application. Assignment of the international registration basic shall be subject to the same conditions and requirements as apply to the assignment of a trade mark registered in India, and any such assignment shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the application liable to be refused.

For the purposes of this Act, the international registration basic shall mean the registration of a trade mark in the country of origin, which serves as the foundation for an international application seeking extension of protection to other countries party to any international convention or treaty to which India is a signatory. A notice applicant, being the applicant for such international registration, shall furnish details of the basic registration including the filing date, registration number, and a certified copy of the registration certificate as required under the relevant international arrangements. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the international registration basic shall be examined in accordance with the standards applicable to national trade mark applications, and any defects therein may be grounds for refusal of extension of protection. Provided that, where the basic registration has been cancelled or refused in the country of origin, the international application shall be deemed withdrawn.

A person who has lawfully registered a trade mark under this Act, and who has subsequently secured an international registration basic in a Convention country, shall be entitled to claim priority over any subsequent application for registration of an identical or deceptively similar mark in India, provided that such international registration basic was filed within six months of the initial Indian registration. However, this right shall not extend to marks for which an indication falsified has been established through due process of law, meaning a clear demonstration that the subsequent applicant acted in bad faith or knowingly misrepresented the origin or quality of goods or services. Any party alleging such falsification shall bear the burden of proof. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the international registration basic and satisfaction of all applicable requirements as provided herein, direct the expeditious examination of the subsequent application, and may refuse registration if the prior international registration establishes clear rights. Failure to exercise this right within a reasonable period may constitute a waiver.

A business basic application shall be an application for registration of a trade mark, submitted under this Act, wherein the applicant seeks protection for a mark used or proposed to be used in relation to goods or services falling within Class 35, specifically concerning business management, business administration, business planning, and related consultancy services. Such an application may proceed without a prior search report, provided that the applicant files a declaration affirming that to the best of their knowledge, no identical or deceptively similar mark exists on the Trade Marks Register. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to furnish additional evidence to substantiate the claim of genuine use or intention to use the mark in commerce. Any application failing to meet these requirements shall be deemed incomplete and liable for objection.

A person seeking registration of a trade mark, being a business basic application, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in the Schedule. The application shall indicate the class of goods or services to which the trade mark relates, and shall include a representation of the mark itself. An applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, claim priority from a prior application made in a Convention country, provided that such claim is made within six months from the date of the earlier application. Where the application is for a collective mark or a certification mark, evidence of the rules governing the use of the mark by members of the association or by the certifying body shall be furnished. The Registry may, if satisfied that the application meets the requirements of this Act, proceed to examine it. Any deficiency in the application shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall have a period of thirty days to rectify the same.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in relation to goods or services, and desiring to register it, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for a business basic application, demonstrating genuine use within the territory of India. The application shall include a clear representation of the trade mark and a statement of the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. Where an applicant seeks to claim priority under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, such claim shall be made within the prescribed period and accompanied by the necessary documentation. Should the Trade Marks Registry object to the application, the applicant may file a response within the stipulated timeframe, addressing the grounds of objection. Failure to respond may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to the provisions for restoration as provided herein. A registered trade mark confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register, and to seek remedies against any infringement thereof.

A business basic application for registration of a trade mark shall be presented in writing in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry in accordance with the rules made under this Act. The application shall contain a representation of the trade mark, the class of goods or services for which registration is sought, and the applicant’s description of goods or services. Where an applicant seeks to register a trade mark which is identical with a registered trade mark, or deceptively similar thereto, and the goods or services are identical or closely related, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, require the applicant to furnish a statement of use demonstrating genuine use of the mark in relation to those goods or services. Provided that failure to furnish such a statement within the time prescribed shall be deemed sufficient cause for refusal of the application. Any application not complying with the requirements as provided herein shall be considered defective and shall be subject to objection. The Registrar may, at his discretion, allow an opportunity to remedy such defects.

A business basic application for registration of a trade mark shall be presented in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, and shall comply with the requirements as to content and format as laid down in the First Schedule. The application shall indicate the class or classes of goods or services to which the trade mark relates, in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where an applicant seeks to claim priority under the Paris Convention, such claim shall be made within six months from the date of the earlier application, and supporting documentation evidencing the earlier application must accompany the business basic application. Any deficiency in the application, or failure to comply with the prescribed requirements, may be rectified by the applicant within a period of thirty days from the receipt of a notice from the Registry, provided that such rectification does not materially alter the nature of the application. Failure to rectify such deficiencies within the stipulated time shall render the business basic application liable to be refused.

Any person claiming entitlement to a business basic application shall submit a statement detailing the nature of the business and its projected commercial benefit, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable to be rejected. A false declaration within such a statement shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require additional evidence to substantiate the claims made in the business basic application. Any failure to comply with a requirement for supplemental evidence within sixty days of the notice shall render the application void. Where a business basic application is found to be frivolous or vexatious, the applicant shall be barred from submitting any further applications under this Act for a period of two years. All fees associated with the processing of a business basic application shall be non-refundable, even in the event of rejection, unless the rejection is attributable to the negligence of the Registrar.

Any person possessing a business basic application, being a simplified procedure for registration of trade marks primarily relating to micro, small and medium enterprises, may assign or license the same in whole or in part, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning assignment and licensing of registered trade marks. The assignee or licensee shall, within six months of such assignment or license, notify the Trade Marks Registry of the particulars of the transfer, failing which the rights of the assignee or licensee shall not be enforceable as against any person other than the assignor or licensor. Where a business basic application is assigned without the goodwill of the business concerned, the assignment shall be deemed to be an assignment of the trade mark only, and not of the right to use the trade mark in connection with the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. Any license granted under this provision shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of such license, including the duration, territory, and goods or services in relation to which the license is granted.

Any person claiming entitlement to a business basic application, in respect of goods or services not falling within any of the classes specified in the First Schedule, shall submit a statement to the Trade Marks Registry detailing the nature of the business and the scope of activities undertaken. The Registry may, subject to verification of submitted documentation and satisfaction that the business is genuine and conducted with reasonable diligence, register the application as a ‘basic business identifier’. However, such registration shall not confer any rights equivalent to a registered trade mark, and shall be subject to a reduced term of protection as provided herein. Any objection to the registration of a business basic application, alleging lack of genuine use or misrepresentation, may be filed within sixty days of public notice. Decisions of the Registry regarding such objections shall be appealable to the Appellate Board, and further to the High Court, in accordance with the established procedures under this Act. The Registrar may, at any time, initiate an inquiry into the continued viability of a registered business basic application.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark which constitutes a business basic application shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignment and transmission. Where the assignment is made as part of a larger transfer of a business, goodwill, or concern, notice of such assignment shall be furnished to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The assignee, upon satisfying the Registrar that the transfer represents a genuine transfer of business, may apply to have the trade mark registered in their name. However, an assignment intended to create a false or misleading impression regarding the source or character of goods or services, or to unfairly take advantage of the reputation of the registered trade mark, shall be deemed invalid as provided herein. Any assignment made in contravention of this provision, or where the purpose falsifying used is evident, may be subject to rectification of the register. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, require evidence of the bona fides of the assignment.

A business basic application for registration of a trade mark shall be presented in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, and shall contain a statement of the particulars relating to the applicant, including name, address, and description of the business. The application shall also state the trade mark the applicant seeks to register, and the class of goods or services for which registration is sought, in accordance with the Nice Classification. Where a mark has been used, but remains an unregistered trade mark, the applicant may, subject to demonstrating bona fide use prior to the application date, claim priority based on such use. However, such claim shall not prejudice any rights accruing to prior users of identical or similar marks. The Registry may require further information or evidence to satisfy itself as to the validity of the application and the distinctiveness of the mark, as provided herein. Any false representation in a business basic application shall render it liable to be refused.

Any person claiming a business basic application for a trade mark, being a natural person or a legal entity, shall submit a declaration affirming the genuine use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified, and demonstrating a demonstrable connection to India. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted evidence, grant a conditional registration for a period not exceeding two years. Should the applicant fail to demonstrate continued genuine use within this period, the registration shall lapse. However, a registered proprietor may apply for renewal, provided that sufficient evidence of use and a security india explanation detailing the measures taken to protect the mark from infringement and counterfeiting within the territory of India, are submitted alongside the renewal application. Any aggrieved party may, as provided herein, file a rectification petition challenging the validity of a registration obtained through a business basic application, based on grounds of non-use or misrepresentation. The Registrar shall adjudicate such petitions expeditiously, ensuring fairness and transparency in the proceedings.

In this Act, “registration common regulations” shall mean the standardized procedures and criteria established by the Trade Marks Registry for the processing of applications for registration, maintenance, and renewal of trade marks, and shall include provisions relating to the classification of goods and services, the examination of applications for distinctiveness and conflict with existing marks, and the determination of proprietorship. These regulations, as provided herein, are subject to periodic review and amendment by the Central Government to ensure alignment with international best practices and evolving commercial realities. Any dispute arising from the application of these regulations may be referred to the appropriate court having jurisdiction, provided that the applicant has exhausted all available administrative remedies. The Registrar may, at their discretion, deviate from these regulations in exceptional circumstances, recording the reasons for such deviation.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark under this Act shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, furnishing the requisite particulars and statement of use. The application for registration shall include a clear representation of the trade mark, specifying the goods or services for which registration is sought, and shall be subject to the provisions relating to inherent distinctiveness and deceptive similarity. Where multiple applicants seek registration of identical or similar trade marks for related goods or services, the Registry may, considering the date of application and bona fide use, determine priority in accordance with established principles of registration common regulations. A registered trade mark shall be maintained on the Register provided that the prescribed renewal fees are paid and the mark continues to be used in relation to the goods or services specified. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the removal of the trade mark from the Register, as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark, jointly with another, shall submit a declaration affirming a common intention to use the mark and to be jointly responsible for its lawful application. Such joint applicants shall, prior to registration, execute a written agreement detailing the proportionate ownership of the mark, the division of responsibilities regarding its use, and the mechanism for dispute resolution concerning its exploitation. The Registrar may, subject to satisfactory verification of this agreement, proceed with the registration process. Failure to furnish evidence of this agreement, or evidence demonstrating a lack of genuine common intention, may result in the rejection of the application as provided herein. Where a registered trade mark is subject to a dispute between joint owners, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for appropriate relief, and the Court shall consider the terms of the aforementioned agreement in its adjudication. Registration common regulations pertaining to co-ownership are essential for maintaining clarity and preventing future conflicts.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered under this Act, and intending to assign or otherwise transfer those rights, shall furnish a notice in writing to the Trade Marks Registry, specifying the particulars of the assignment or transfer, including the consideration paid and the nature of the rights transferred. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the assignment or transfer voidable at the option of the Registrar. Where multiple persons co-own a trade mark, registration common regulations shall apply to any alteration in the ownership structure, requiring unanimous consent for any transfer of interest. Any dispute arising from a non-compliant transfer or alteration may be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Registrar may, subject to due process, order rectification of the register to reflect the correct ownership.
