Any false declaration made in connection with such notice shall be punishable with imprisonment.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the goodwill of the trade mark together with the right to the use thereof, to any person or class of persons. An assignment shall be in writing and shall be executed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall specify the trade mark, the goods or services in respect of which it is assigned, and the geographical territory, if any, in which the assignment is to have effect. Where a trade mark is assigned without any assignment of the goodwill, the assignment shall be deemed to be a mere transfer of property in the trade mark, and the assignee shall not acquire any greater interest than that of a licensee. All assignments made under this Act shall be subject to registration with the Trade Marks Registry. Regulations governing such registration, including prescribed fees and forms, shall be determined by the Central Government and published in the Official Gazette. Failure to comply with these registration common regulations may render the assignment unenforceable.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a trade mark, or requiring the Registrar to limit the scope of the trade mark in question, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as the Appellate Board may deem fit. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an appeal is preferred concerning a matter of registration common regulations, the Appellate Board shall ensure strict adherence to the principles of reciprocity as established under international conventions to which India is a party. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to produce further evidence or documents relevant to the dispute, and failure to comply with such direction may be considered as an abandonment of the appeal. Any further appeal from the decision of the Appellate Board shall lie before the High Court.

Any person desiring to obtain registration of a trade mark for goods or services falling in Class 29, concerning agricultural, horticultural and forestry products, shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee and a clear representation of the mark as applied to such goods. The Registrar, upon examination, may require further information or evidence to ascertain the distinctiveness of the mark and its eligibility for registration common regulations. Where the mark incorporates a layout-design relating to integrated circuits, as provided herein, evidence of the validity of any rights in such layout-design shall also be furnished. An applicant may, subject to the provisions of this Act, claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a Convention country. The Registrar shall, after satisfying themselves as to the validity of the application and the absence of any conflicting marks, proceed to advertise the mark in the Trade Marks Journal. Objections to the registration may be filed within the prescribed period, and shall be adjudicated upon in accordance with the established procedure.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, “means contracting state” shall refer to a country which has ratified or acceded to this Act, or to any protocol extending its scope, and with respect to which this Act is in force. A means contracting state may, subject to the provisions herein, designate a competent authority to administer the registration of trade marks within its territory. The designation of such authority shall be notified to the International Bureau, and such authority shall be responsible for maintaining the register of trade marks as provided herein. Where a means contracting state is a member of a regional organization responsible for the registration of trade marks, that organization shall be considered the competent authority for the purposes of this Act. Any act performed by a competent authority of a means contracting state shall be deemed to be an act performed under this Act.

In this Act, a means contracting state shall be determined with reference to its adherence to the provisions of the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, and shall include any country which is a party to that Convention, or to any other international convention relating to trade marks to which India is also a party. A state may be designated as a means contracting state by notification in the Official Gazette, provided that such designation is reciprocal and consistent with India’s international obligations. Any application for registration originating from a non-means contracting state shall be subject to such additional requirements as may be prescribed, including proof of domestic registration or priority claim. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, refuse to accept an application if it is deemed not to comply with the requirements for a means contracting state. A designation as a means contracting state may be withdrawn if the state ceases to meet the criteria as provided herein.

Any person who suffers damage as a result of the fraudulent or deceptive use of a registered trade mark by a party operating from outside India, but within a means contracting state, shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining such use, as provided herein. The injunction may extend to an order for delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the fraudulent mark. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a court may, at the request of the aggrieved party, also award damages for loss suffered, or an account of profits made by the defendant. Where the defendant proves that they took reasonable care to avoid the infringement, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. A claim for damages shall not be entertained unless it is brought within three years from the date on which the plaintiff knew, or ought to have known, of the infringement. Any order for damages or account of profits shall be enforceable in the means contracting state, provided that reciprocal arrangements exist between India and that state.

For the purposes of this Act, a means contracting state shall be determined in accordance with the provisions hereinafter set forth, and shall include any country which has ratified or acceded to a treaty or agreement with India concerning the protection of trademarks and which extends reciprocal treatment to Indian nationals. Where a state is a member of an intergovernmental organization and the organization itself is a contracting state, the extent of that state’s obligations under this Act shall be subject to the specific provisions of the relevant treaty establishing the organization. Any dispute concerning the status of a state as a means contracting state, or the interpretation of reciprocal treatment, may be referred to the Central Government for determination. The Central Government’s decision shall be final and binding, provided that such determination is consistent with the principles of international law and comity. A state shall cease to be a means contracting state if it denounces any relevant treaty or fails to maintain the conditions necessary for reciprocal treatment, as determined by the Central Government.

A party seeking registration of a trade mark shall demonstrate sufficient connection with a means contracting state, and failure to do so may result in rejection of the application as provided herein. For the purposes of establishing such connection, evidence of a bona fide business operation, including but not limited to, import and export activities, shall be admissible. Any applicant claiming rights through assignment or transmission shall furnish proof of proper title and a clear chain of ownership extending to a person possessing a connection with a means contracting state. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, require additional evidence to ascertain the genuineness of the claimed connection. A registered trade mark shall be subject to renewal fees payable at intervals prescribed by the rules, and non-payment may lead to removal from the register. Provided that, a grace period of six months may be granted for payment of renewal fees with a surcharge. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may file an appeal within the stipulated timeframe.

Any person who falsely represents themselves as being authorized to act on behalf of a registered proprietor of a trade mark, or as being connected with such proprietor with the intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where an offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable for the penalty as provided herein. A means contracting state, for the purposes of determining jurisdiction over such offences, shall be deemed to include any territory for which the Central Government has international obligations relating to trade mark protection. Any evidence obtained through unlawful means relating to a trade mark shall not be admissible. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct an investigation into any suspected offence under this Act.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark to a person resident in a non-contracting state shall be subject to the prior approval of the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not contravene any provisions of this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Where the assignee is a nominee of a contracting state, the requirement for prior approval may be waived at the discretion of the Registrar, subject to satisfactory evidence of the nominee’s bona fide connection with that contracting state being furnished. A license to use a registered trade mark may be granted to a person resident in any state, but such license shall be subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. The rights and obligations of the licensor and licensee shall be governed by the terms of the license agreement, and any dispute arising therefrom shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the courts as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership to a person not ordinarily resident in a means contracting state requires a formal undertaking regarding continued use of the mark within India.

Any natural or juridical person alleging an infringement of a registered trade mark in a means contracting state shall, prior to initiating proceedings before the competent court of that state, notify the alleged infringer of the infringement and require them to cease the infringing activity within a period not less than sixty days. Should the alleged infringer dispute the validity of the registration, or the claim of infringement, they may, within thirty days of receiving the notification, submit a counter-statement to the complainant, detailing the grounds of their dispute. Failure to submit such a counter-statement shall be deemed an admission of the infringement, subject to judicial review. Where the complainant fails to commence proceedings within ninety days of the expiry of the sixty-day period, the right to pursue legal remedy shall lapse, unless extended by the court upon demonstration of sufficient cause. Any appeal arising from a decision of the competent court shall be filed within sixty days of the date of the order.

For the purposes of registration of a trade mark for pharmaceutical preparations, any person seeking registration who is a citizen of, or is domiciled in, or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in a means contracting state shall be eligible, subject to the provisions of this Act. An applicant intending to register a trade mark for a drug formulation shall submit a clear representation of the chemical composition and intended therapeutic use as part of the application. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, require additional evidence regarding the drug’s regulatory approval status in the means contracting state or its equivalent. Registration shall not be granted if the proposed trade mark is likely to cause confusion with an existing registered trade mark for a similar drug, or if the drug itself is prohibited by law in the means contracting state. Provided that, a trade mark previously refused registration may be re-submitted with appropriate amendments addressing the grounds for initial refusal.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a registered trade mark, aggrieved by any infringement of such trade mark by a party operating within a means contracting state, shall be entitled to institute a suit for recovery of damages. The suit may be filed in a District Court having jurisdiction over the location of the defendant’s business or, at the discretion of the plaintiff, in the High Court. The Marks Registry trade shall maintain a public register of all registered trade marks and shall, upon request and subject to payment of the prescribed fee, provide certified copies thereof to any interested party. A proprietor may, as provided herein, apply for rectification of the register where any entry is found to be inaccurate or misleading. Provided that, no rectification shall be permitted which prejudices the rights of an innocent purchaser of the trade mark. Remedies under this Act are cumulative and shall not prejudice any other rights or remedies available to the aggrieved party under any other law for the time being in force.

For the purposes of this Act, a “means contracting state” shall refer to any nation party to a reciprocal agreement with the Central Government concerning the recognition and protection of trademarks, and shall be determined by notification in the Official Gazette. The determination of such states shall be subject to review every three years, or as deemed necessary by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. Where a dispute arises regarding the status of a state as a means contracting state, the matter may be referred to a committee constituted by the Central Government, including representation from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and, where relevant, the Agriculture Commissioner Government, to advise on its continued eligibility. Any decision of the committee shall be final and binding, provided that appeal to the High Court may be permitted on grounds of procedural impropriety. The Central Government may, as provided herein, enter into agreements with means contracting states to facilitate the exchange of information relating to trademark applications and registrations.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘means contracting state’ shall be deemed to include any nation which has ratified or acceded to a multilateral treaty concerning the protection of trademarks to which India is also a party, provided that such nation affords substantially equivalent protection to Indian trademark owners. Any permitted use of a trademark by a person ordinarily resident outside a means contracting state, arising from rights legitimately acquired prior to the date of accession of that state to such a treaty, shall continue to be permissible subject to diligent use within a reasonable timeframe. However, such permitted use may be revoked if the owner of the trademark demonstrates that the continued use would be likely to cause confusion in the Indian market. Any transfer of rights relating to such permitted use shall be subject to the same conditions. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the cancellation of the registration of the trademark under this Act.

A transmissible case arises where rights to a trade mark are assigned or otherwise transferred, whether with or without the accompanying goodwill of the business. Such transmission shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignment, and the assignee or transferee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the trade mark for the purposes of this Act, provided that the transfer is duly recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, as in the case of succession or insolvency, the transmission shall be effective only upon application to the Registry and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any assignment or transmission made in contravention of these provisions shall be voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. The validity of a transmission may be challenged before the appropriate authority as provided herein.

A trade mark, registered under this Act, shall be transmissible upon the assignment, transfer, or devolution of the goodwill of the business concerned, subject to the provisions herein contained. Any transmission of a trade mark, whether absolute or partial, shall be evidenced by a written instrument duly executed by both parties, and filed with the Trade Marks Registry. The Registry may, upon satisfaction of the validity of the transmission and payment of the prescribed fee, register the new proprietor. A transmissible case, however, does not extend to instances where the transmission would result in a multiplicity of exclusive rights pertaining to the same mark, unless specifically permitted by an order of the High Court. Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, such as through inheritance or bankruptcy, notice of such transmission shall be filed with the Registry within six months of the event. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the transmission ineffective as against third parties.

A transmissible case arising under this Act shall be determined by the High Court having jurisdiction over the relevant geographical area, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a registered trade mark is assigned or otherwise transmitted, the proprietor of the trade mark, as recorded in the Register, shall, unless the High Court otherwise directs, continue to be the proprietor for the purposes of this Act, and shall remain liable for any infringement occurring prior to the date of assignment or transmission. However, any assignment or transmission of rights in a trade mark shall be subject to a clear and unambiguous instrument in writing, detailing the scope of rights transferred and any limitations thereof. Provided that, the assignee or transferee may, upon satisfying the Registrar as to the validity of the assignment and their bona fide intention to use the mark, apply to have their name registered as the new proprietor. The High Court may, in exceptional circumstances, direct immediate registration of the assignee or transferee, pending full adjudication of the transmissible case.

A trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be assignable and may be transmitted in connection with the transfer of the goodwill of the business carrying on the trade mark. Where a trade mark is assigned or transmitted without any goodwill, or in connection with only a part of the goodwill, the proprietor of the trade mark, or the assignee or transmittee, as the case may be, may apply to the Registrar to record the transfer subject to a limitation of the scope of the trade mark. The Registrar shall, upon such application and after giving the applicant and any affected person an opportunity to be heard, record the transfer subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, ensuring that the mark’s continued registration does not mislead the public as to the source or quality of goods or services. A ‘transmissible case’ arising from such partial transfer shall be adjudicated upon considering the nature of the goodwill transferred and the extent of continued use of the mark by both parties. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may appeal to the High Court.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be transmissible upon the assignment, transfer or devolution of the goodwill of the business concerned, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. Any assignment or transmission of a trade mark not accompanied by a corresponding transfer of goodwill shall be void, provided that where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, such as through inheritance or insolvency, the transmission shall be valid irrespective of goodwill transfer, subject to the assignee or legal representative applying to the Registrar within six months of the transmission for registration as the proprietor. 

Where a transmissible case involves a collective mark or certification mark, the Registrar may require evidence of consent from the members or certifying body, as applicable, before effecting the transfer of ownership. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the assignment or transmission unenforceable.

Any person claiming a right to a trade mark through assignment, transmission, or operation of law, constituting a transmissible case, shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a statement verifying the particulars of such acquisition within a period of six months from the date of such acquisition, failing which a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees shall be levied. The Registry may, subject to payment of additional fees, extend this period by a further three months if sufficient cause is demonstrated. Any false statement made in such verification shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Where a transmissible case involves a mark subject to a pending opposition proceeding, the Registry may suspend further proceedings until the validity of the acquisition is determined. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding registration of a transmitted trade mark shall render the mark vulnerable to rectification proceedings.

A trade mark, whether registered or unregistered, shall be subject to assignment and transmission as provided herein, and such assignment or transmission may occur with or without any associated goodwill of the business undertaking. Any assignment or transmission of a trade mark shall be evidenced in writing and shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry to ensure lawful transfer of ownership. Where a trade mark constitutes a transmissible case, meaning it is assigned with the goodwill of the business, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the mark in connection with the same goods or services as the assignor. However, assignment without goodwill does not automatically confer such rights, and the assignee’s use may be restricted to the scope explicitly outlined in the assignment agreement. The Registrar may, subject to due process and examination of relevant documentation, record the assignment or transmission in the Register of Trade Marks, thereby establishing a clear record of title. Failure to register the assignment may impact the enforceability of the trade mark against third parties.

A trade mark, registered under this Act, shall be transmissible upon the assignment or transmission of the goodwill of the business concerned, subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. However, any assignment or transmission not accompanied by a corresponding transfer of goodwill shall be deemed a wrongful act, and the aggrieved party may seek redressal through a suit for infringement. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of such a transmission, particularly regarding the extent of goodwill transferred, an application may be made to the High Court for determination of a transmissible case. The Court, upon examination of evidence including but not limited to accounting records and customer testimonials, shall issue a binding order establishing the rights of the parties. An appeal from any such order shall lie to the Supreme Court, provided that leave to appeal is obtained. Any person aggrieved by the High Court’s determination, and failing to secure leave, shall have no further recourse.

A trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be transmissible upon the assignment or transmission of the goodwill of the business concerned, and the proprietor of the trade mark, or upon the assignment or transmission of the right to use the trade mark. Where a transmissible case arises involving a mark registered for goods or services essential to public health or safety, the Central Government may, if it considers such assignment or transmission would be contrary to the public interest, issue an order prohibiting such transfer, subject to a reasoned opportunity for hearing to all parties concerned. Any aggrieved party may apply to the appropriate court for redressal of grievances arising from an unlawful transmission. Provided that, the court shall not entertain any application unless the applicant demonstrates a substantial and demonstrable loss resulting from the alleged unlawful transmission. The Central Government’s decision shall be final and binding, though appeal to a higher judicial authority remains open.

A trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act, shall be transmissible upon the assignment or transmission of the goodwill of the business concerned, and shall vest in the assignee or transmittee as it would have vested in the original proprietor. Where a trade mark is transmitted by operation of law, as in the case of death, insolvency or bankruptcy of the proprietor, the transmission shall not be deemed to have taken place until notification thereof is given to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The Registry may, upon receipt of such notification and subject to verification of title, register the assignee or transmittee as the new proprietor. An application for such registration shall be accompanied by the appropriate registry fee paid as stipulated in the First Schedule. Provided that, where the transmission occurs by reason only of a change in the legal entity of the proprietor, such as a corporate restructuring, the Registry may waive the requirement for a formal transfer deed, if satisfied that the identity of the trade mark’s ownership remains substantially unchanged. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registry regarding the registration of a transmissible case may appeal to the High Court.

Any trade mark which is a transmissible case, being subject to a condition requiring the continued use of the mark by the assignee or transferee for the purpose of maintaining the goodwill of the business carried on by the proprietor, shall be deemed to be assigned or transmitted with the goodwill of that business, unless it is expressly agreed otherwise in writing. Where a plaintiff seeks relief as an indication plaintiff, demonstrating prior continuous and extensive use of a mark in relation to specific goods or services, the court may, as provided herein, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the mark. Any person contravening the terms of such injunction shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and subsequent offences shall attract imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to due process, initiate proceedings for the revocation of a trade mark obtained through misrepresentation.

For the purposes of this Act, “register sufficient cause” shall mean a demonstrated and reasonable basis, substantiated by evidence admissible under the rules of evidence as applicable in civil proceedings, establishing a legitimate and justifiable reason for a request or action pertaining to a registered trade mark. Such cause may include, but is not limited to, proven instances of misrepresentation likely to cause confusion, or a material change in the circumstances surrounding the mark’s use. Provided that, the Trade Marks Registry may, subject to verification of the presented evidence, determine whether register sufficient cause has been established. A finding of register sufficient cause shall be a prerequisite for orders relating to rectification, revocation, or amendment of a trade mark registration as provided herein. Failure to demonstrate register sufficient cause shall result in the dismissal of the relevant application.

Any application for the registration of a trade mark shall be subject to a prior search conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain the existence of any identical or deceptively similar marks already registered or applied for, as provided herein. Where such a mark is found, the applicant shall be required to demonstrate sufficient cause as to why their mark should nonetheless proceed to registration, considering the goods or services specified and the likelihood of confusion amongst consumers. Failure to establish register sufficient cause may result in the rejection of the application. However, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require evidence of concurrent use or distinctiveness to further assess the application. An applicant may, provided that reasonable grounds exist, request a hearing to present their case regarding sufficient cause. The decision of the Registrar shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board.

Any party opposing an application for registration shall, within the prescribed time, file with the Trade Marks Registry a notice of opposition, detailing the grounds upon which the application is contested. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such notice, notify the applicant, affording them an opportunity to submit a counter-statement. Where the applicant fails to file a counter-statement within the stipulated period, the Registry may, after considering the notice of opposition, direct the application to be deemed abandoned. 

However, should the applicant submit a counter-statement, the Registry shall, subject to the provisions contained herein, determine whether sufficient cause exists to proceed with a hearing. Evidence presented by both parties shall be considered in ascertaining whether a *prima facie* case has been established, and whether the opposition raises a genuine dispute regarding registrability. The Registry may, at its discretion, require further evidence or affidavits to clarify any ambiguities, and shall record its reasoned findings regarding the existence of register sufficient cause before proceeding to a hearing.

Any person seeking to demonstrate register sufficient cause for the rectification of a registered trademark alleging misrepresentation in its application shall furnish detailed evidence of actual confusion amongst consumers, and such evidence shall be corroborated by market surveys conducted by a recognised agency and submitted with the application. Failure to provide such corroborating evidence may, at the discretion of the adjudicating authority, be deemed insufficient to establish a prima facie case. Where a rectification application is dismissed for lack of register sufficient cause, the applicant shall be liable to pay compensatory damages to the registered proprietor, not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, if the application is found to be frivolous or made in bad faith, the adjudicating authority may impose costs up to one hundred thousand rupees. Any appeal against an order imposing costs shall be heard expeditiously, subject to the payment of a prescribed fee. The Registrar may, where appropriate, initiate proceedings for professional misconduct against counsel presenting such frivolous applications.

Any party alleging infringement who fails to establish register sufficient cause for initiating proceedings under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate, require the complainant to furnish security for the due prosecution of the complaint. Where a registered proprietor grants a licence to another party, such licence shall be in writing and shall specify the conditions governing its use, including territorial limitations and quality control measures. Failure to adhere to the terms of a duly registered licence shall constitute grounds for revocation of the licence, and the licensee may be subject to injunction and damages. Any false representation regarding a licensed trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar shall have the power to impose these penalties following a summary inquiry.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right in relation thereto, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the registration of such assignment. A licensee, demonstrating register sufficient cause, may apply to the Registrar for the rectification of the register in respect of any matter affecting the title to the trade mark, including a claim that the mark falsely represents a geographical origin. Where a trade mark is assigned without a clear indication of the goods or services in respect of which it is assigned, the Registrar may require further particulars to be furnished within a specified period. Failure to comply with such requirement may render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee. Provided that, no assignment shall be valid as against any prior rights unless it is duly registered as provided herein. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed necessary, permit the sub-licensing of a registered trade mark, ensuring that such sub-licensing does not falsifies genuine geographical indications or mislead the public.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at their registered address, or at such other address as may be notified to the Trade Marks Registry in writing. This register shall record all licenses granted under the trade mark, including the terms and conditions of each license, the duration, the territory of effect, and the nature of the licensed rights. Any person may, subject to reasonable conditions as may be prescribed, inspect the inspection register during office hours. Provided that access to confidential commercial information contained within the register may be restricted. Failure to maintain a current and accurate inspection register, or to permit lawful inspection thereof, shall be deemed an infringement of the rights conferred by registration under this Act, and may attract penalties as provided herein.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at their registered address, or at such other address as may be notified to the Trade Marks Registry in writing. This register shall be open for inspection during usual business hours by any person interested in ascertaining the validity of the registration, subject to reasonable conditions as may be prescribed. Every inspection of the register shall be recorded in the register, detailing the date of inspection, the name and address of the inspector, and the specific entries inspected. Failure to maintain the inspection register as provided herein, or to permit lawful inspection thereof, may be considered as prima facie evidence of an intent to deceive or misrepresent. Any alteration to the register shall be initialed and dated by the proprietor, and any false entry or omission may render the registration liable to revocation under this Act. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon reasonable cause, require production of the inspection register for verification.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at their registered address, or at such other address as may be notified to the Trade Marks Registry. This register shall be open to inspection during usual business hours by any person interested in ascertaining the validity of the registration, subject to reasonable notice in writing to the proprietor. Any person making a request for inspection shall be entitled to a certified copy of any entry in the register, upon payment of the prescribed fee. Should the proprietor fail to maintain the inspection register or deny reasonable access thereto, any aggrieved person may apply to the High Court for an order compelling compliance. Such application shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the attempt to inspect and the refusal thereof. The Court, if satisfied, may issue an order directing the proprietor to maintain the register and permit inspection, and may impose costs as it deems fit. Failure to comply with a Court order under this Act shall constitute contempt of court.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain a register of all licenses granted under this Act, recording the terms and conditions of each license, including any limitations as to geographical area or goods or services. Such register, being the inspection register, shall be kept at the proprietor’s principal place of business and shall be open to inspection by any person interested in the trade mark, subject to reasonable conditions as may be determined by the proprietor. Any person desiring to inspect the inspection register shall apply to the proprietor in writing, specifying the purpose of the inspection and the trade mark in question. The proprietor may, if reasonably satisfied as to the bona fides of the applicant, permit inspection during usual business hours. Provided that, the proprietor may require a statutory declaration from the applicant confirming that the information obtained from the inspection register will not be used for any unlawful purpose or in a manner prejudicial to the rights of the trade mark proprietor. Failure to comply with the provisions of this section shall render the proprietor liable to a penalty as prescribed.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at its registered address, or at such other address as may be notified to the Trade Marks Registry in writing. Every inspection of the register by any person, including a licensing agent or assignee, shall be recorded chronologically in the inspection register, detailing the date of inspection, the name and address of the inspector, and the nature of the inspection undertaken. Any failure to maintain a current and accurate inspection register, or to permit access thereto upon reasonable request by an authorized officer under this Act, shall constitute an offence punishable by a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees. Provided that, where the proprietor is a legal person, proof of a designated officer’s responsibility for register maintenance shall be admissible as evidence of compliance. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to reasonable cause, conduct periodic audits to verify compliance with these provisions regarding the inspection register.

Every registered proprietor of a trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at their registered office, or principal place of business, in a manner as provided herein. Such register shall record all licenses issued by the proprietor, detailing the terms and conditions of each license, including duration, territory, and goods or services covered. Any failure to maintain a complete and accurate inspection register, or to permit inspection of the register by an authorized officer of the Trade Marks Office upon reasonable notice, shall be deemed an offence punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees. Provided that, a proprietor may, subject to the discretion of the Registrar, apply for exemption from maintaining the register if demonstrating substantial hardship. False entries or deliberate omissions within the inspection register constitute a cognizable offence, attracting a penalty of imprisonment not exceeding one year, or a fine not exceeding ten thousand rupees, or both. The Registrar may, following due process, direct rectification of any inaccurate entry.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right in it, including a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of such transfer. The proprietor of a trade mark, upon any such assignment or licensing, shall forthwith enter a memorandum of the particulars thereof in the inspection register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry. Such memorandum shall include the date of the assignment or license, the names and addresses of the assignor and assignee or licensor and licensee, and a clear description of the rights transferred or licensed, including any geographical limitations. 

The Registrar may, if satisfied that reasonable cause exists, permit inspection of the inspection register, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and adherence to conditions ensuring confidentiality. Failure to maintain an accurate inspection register, or providing false information therein, shall be deemed a material misrepresentation and may invalidate any subsequent assignment or licensing agreement, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the accuracy of entries may be referred to the Registrar for adjudication.

Any person registered as the proprietor of a trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at a specified address, open to inspection during usual business hours, subject to reasonable conditions as may be prescribed. Should a request for inspection be refused or access unduly hindered, any aggrieved person may lodge a complaint with the Registrar, supported by affidavit detailing the circumstances of such refusal. The Registrar, upon receiving such complaint and after affording an opportunity for explanation to the trade mark proprietor, may direct an inspection to proceed, and any costs incurred thereby shall be borne by the party found to have improperly obstructed the inspection. A proprietor failing to maintain a proper inspection register, or providing materially false information therein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. Any decision of the Registrar in this regard may be appealed to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order.

The proprietor of a trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at a specified location, being the principal place of business, and shall cause it to be open for inspection during usual business hours by any person interested in the examination of the register, subject to reasonable conditions as may be prescribed. Every inspection of the register shall be recorded in the inspection register, detailing the date of inspection, the name and address of the inspector, and the nature of the inspection. Where a trade mark application relates to a breeder variety registered under the Seeds Act, 1966, the inspection register shall also note the particulars of such registration, including the reference number and date of registration of the breeder variety. Failure to maintain the inspection register as provided herein, or to permit reasonable inspection thereof, shall be deemed a contravention of this Act and may attract penalties as prescribed. The Registrar may, upon application, direct an inspection of the register if satisfied that reasonable cause exists, and shall record such direction in the register.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain an inspection register at a specified location, open for inspection during usual business hours by any person intending to deal with the proprietor. Any failure to maintain such a register, or to permit lawful inspection thereof, shall be deemed a contravention of this Act and attract a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each such instance. Where an application for registration originates from an invention convention country, the Registrar may, subject to payment of a prescribed fee, waive certain procedural requirements relating to the inspection register, provided that such waiver does not prejudice the rights of any opposing party. Any false entry made in the inspection register with intent to deceive shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, upon reasonable cause, initiate an inquiry into the maintenance and accuracy of the inspection register.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain an inspection register wherein any person may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, inspect statutory registers, applications for registration, and other documents as provided herein. An entry in the inspection register shall record the date of inspection, the name and address of the inspector, and the particulars of the documents inspected. Access to the inspection register itself, and to certified copies of documents, may be granted to a registered patent agent acting on behalf of a client, upon presentation of a duly executed authorization. The Registrar may, however, refuse inspection of documents if such inspection would be prejudicial to ongoing investigations or compromise confidential information, and shall communicate the reasons for such refusal in writing. Any false entry made in the inspection register shall be an offence punishable under this Act.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark, or a person authorized by them, may maintain a computer inspection register to record all inspections of computer systems undertaken for the purpose of investigating potential infringements of the trade mark, subject to the provisions of this Act. Such register shall include the date and time of inspection, the location of the computer system inspected, the names of the individuals conducting the inspection, and a detailed description of the information accessed or copied during the inspection. Any information obtained during an inspection and recorded in the computer inspection register shall be treated as confidential and may only be disclosed as required by law or with the express consent of the trade mark proprietor. Failure to maintain an accurate computer inspection register, or the unauthorized disclosure of information contained therein, may be considered in proceedings relating to infringement or passing off, and may attract penalties as provided herein.

Any person having control over a computer containing evidence relating to a trade mark infringement or a falsification of an essentiality certificate, as provided herein, may apply to a Principal Judge for an inspection order. The application shall specify with particularity the computer and the evidence sought, and shall be supported by an affidavit. Upon receipt of such application, the Principal Judge may, if satisfied that there is prima facie evidence of wrongdoing, issue an order directing the applicant to furnish a computer inspection register. This register shall meticulously detail all actions taken during the inspection, including the date, time, personnel present, data accessed, and a precise description of any copies made. Any data copied shall be certified as a true and accurate reproduction of the information stored on the computer. Failure to maintain a complete and accurate computer inspection register may render the evidence obtained inadmissible under this Act. The register shall be open to inspection by any party to the proceedings.

Any person having lawful possession of a computer or computer system containing evidence relating to a trade mark infringement, or to an offence under this Act, may, with the prior authorization of a Judicial First Class Magistrate, secure such computer or system and preserve all information contained therein. The Magistrate shall, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, direct the officer in charge of the nearest police station to seize the computer or computer system and produce it before the Court. A detailed computer inspection register shall be maintained by the police officer, recording the date of seizure, details of the computer, a description of the information secured, and the names of witnesses present during the inspection. Any alteration or tampering with the seized computer or its contents, without prior Court approval, shall be deemed an obstruction of justice. The owner of the computer system may, provided that reasonable notice is given, inspect the computer inspection register and obtain copies of entries therein, subject to any restrictions imposed by the Court. Failure to maintain an accurate computer inspection register may result in disciplinary action against the responsible officer.

Any person having lawful authority to inspect a trade mark register maintained under this Act shall maintain a computer inspection register in a manner prescribed by regulations. The computer inspection register shall record the date of each inspection, the name and address of the inspecting person, the trade mark number or class inspected, and the specific purpose of the inspection, subject to the provisions contained herein. Access to the computer inspection register itself shall be governed by rules established by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, ensuring both transparency and the protection of commercially sensitive information. Any false entry or alteration made in the computer inspection register with intent to deceive shall be punishable with imprisonment, and a fine as may be determined by a competent court. The Controller may, upon reasonable cause, initiate an inquiry into the maintenance and accuracy of any computer inspection register, and require submission of relevant records for verification. Failure to comply with a lawful request for records shall constitute an offence under this Act.

Every authorised officer, when exercising powers of inspection of premises or equipment relating to suspected contraventions under this Act, shall maintain a computer inspection register detailing the date, time, and location of the inspection. The register shall also record the names and designations of all officers present during the inspection, and a comprehensive inventory of all digital devices and data storage media examined. Any data copied or extracted from such devices shall be meticulously documented in the computer inspection register, including hash values to ensure data integrity. Access to the computer inspection register shall be restricted to authorised personnel only, and any alteration or deletion of entries therein, subject to legitimate correction of clerical errors, is strictly prohibited. Provided that, in cases where inspection reveals evidence of a cognizable offence, a separate seizure memo, cross-referenced with the computer inspection register, shall be prepared forthwith. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the inspection invalid as provided herein.

Any person authorized under this Act to inspect a trade mark register, or any document relating thereto, shall maintain a computer inspection register detailing the date, time, and specific entries accessed. Failure to accurately complete and preserve the computer inspection register shall be deemed a contravention of this Act, attracting a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. The Registrar may, subject to reasonable cause being shown, authorize access to the computer inspection register for the purposes of audit or investigation. Any falsification of entries within the computer inspection register, with intent to conceal unauthorized access or modification of trade mark data, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, the Registrar may, in cases of minor discrepancies, issue a warning instead of imposing a monetary penalty. All records pertaining to the computer inspection register shall be retained for a minimum period of three years.

Any assignment of rights in a registered computer trade mark, or an application for registration, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignments and transmission. Where a licensee of a registered computer trade mark seeks to inspect the computer inspection register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry, such access may be granted upon payment of the prescribed fee and subject to such terms and conditions as the Registrar deems fit. The proprietor of the trade mark shall, within thirty days of any assignment or transfer of ownership, notify the Registry and furnish a certified copy of the instrument effecting such transfer. Failure to do so shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the assignee. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or the accuracy of entries in the computer inspection register shall be adjudicated by the Registrar, whose decision shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the High Court. A record of all licenses granted shall also be maintained by the proprietor and made available for inspection upon reasonable notice.

Any person alleging improper access to or alteration of data within a computer system used in the administration of trade mark applications, or concerning records maintained pursuant to this Act, may lodge a complaint with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks. Upon receipt of such complaint, the Controller shall, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, direct an inspection of the relevant computer system and its associated records. A detailed computer inspection register shall be maintained by the Controller, recording the date, time, scope, and personnel involved in each inspection, as well as a summary of findings. Any party aggrieved by an order directing inspection, or by the findings recorded in the computer inspection register, may file an appeal to the High Court within sixty days of the date of the order or the recording of findings. Such appeal shall be heard expeditiously, and the High Court may confirm, modify, or set aside the order or findings, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit.

Any authorised officer, upon reasonable suspicion of an offence under this Act relating to counterfeit goods or infringing material, may, subject to the provisions herein, inspect any premises where such goods are manufactured, stored, or sold. A detailed record of each such inspection shall be maintained in a computer inspection register, specifying the date, time, location, and names of all individuals present during the inspection. The register shall also include a comprehensive inventory of all items seized, with clear descriptions and estimated values. Any person aggrieved by actions taken during such inspection may initiate a prescribed proceeding appellate before the designated authority, provided that such appeal is filed within thirty days of the inspection date. Failure to maintain an accurate computer inspection register, or any falsification thereof, shall be deemed a separate offence punishable as provided herein. All seized materials shall be subject to verification by a magistrate.

Any person authorized under this Act to inspect a trade mark register, or any document relating thereto, shall maintain a computer inspection register detailing the date, time, and scope of each inspection undertaken, and shall make such register available for scrutiny by the Registrar upon demand. Failure to maintain an accurate computer inspection register, or providing false information therein, shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where the inspected trade mark application relates to a plant variety protected under breeder complied provisions, the inspecting party shall additionally declare any affiliation with a competing seed producer. Any unauthorized disclosure of confidential information obtained during inspection, particularly concerning breeder complied traits, may result in immediate suspension of inspection privileges and a further penalty of imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to due process, initiate investigations into any suspected breach of these provisions.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or a transmission of rights therein, including a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of such transfer. The proprietor of a registered trade mark, being the indication plaintiff in any dispute concerning the validity of the license, shall maintain a computer inspection register detailing all licenses granted, amendments thereto, and revocations thereof. This register shall be open for inspection by any person having a legitimate interest, subject to reasonable conditions as may be prescribed. Failure to maintain an accurate computer inspection register, or to permit lawful inspection thereof, may be considered prima facie evidence of an intent to deceive or misrepresent the scope of licensed rights. Any dispute regarding the interpretation of licensing terms, or the validity of an assignment, shall be adjudicated in accordance with the established principles of trade mark law, and the computer inspection register shall be admissible as evidence. A licensee may, with the consent of the proprietor, apply for registration of changes to the licensed mark.

Every proprietor of a registered trade mark, or a person claiming to be the proprietor, who has reason to believe that any computer or digital storage medium contains evidence bearing on acts constituting an infringement of their trade marks deemed to be well-known under this Act, may apply to a Principal District Court for an order directing the inspection of such computer or digital storage medium. Such application shall be accompanied by a statement setting forth the grounds on which the applicant believes the computer contains such evidence. The Court, if satisfied that there is sufficient cause, may issue an order directing the applicant to maintain a computer inspection register detailing all actions taken pursuant to the inspection, including the date, time, and scope of the inspection, as well as a list of all data accessed or copied. Any data obtained during the inspection shall be admissible as evidence, subject to the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and may be used in any subsequent proceedings relating to the alleged infringement.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark under this Act, intending to extend protection to goods or services beyond the territory of India, shall, at the time of making the application, indicate such intention in the prescribed manner. The applicant shall also furnish a statement detailing the countries or territories where protection is sought, and shall nominate a corresponding application or registration, if any, in those jurisdictions. Where an applicant seeks to rely upon an earlier application or registration in a convention country for the purpose of claiming priority, a certified copy of such application or registration shall be filed within the prescribed period. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, require the applicant to provide evidence of bona fide use of the trade mark in the nominated countries, or to demonstrate sufficient grounds for seeking international registration. Failure to comply with the requirements relating to informing international jurisdictions may render the application liable to be refused, as provided herein.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark who intends to extend the protection of their mark to goods or services not included in the original registration, shall apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner for an amendment of the register. Where an application for amendment seeks to include goods or services falling within the classes already registered, but not specifically enumerated, the Registrar may allow the amendment subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit. However, if the amendment seeks to extend protection to goods or services falling outside the originally registered classes, it shall be treated as a separate application for registration. 

A registered proprietor desiring to inform international organizations regarding a change in their registered trade mark, such as assignment of ownership or a limitation of the goods or services covered, shall notify the Registrar, who shall, in turn, fulfill the obligations for informing international authorities as provided herein. Failure to properly inform the relevant international bodies may result in loss of priority or protection in foreign jurisdictions. The Registrar may require evidence of due notification to international bodies before granting any further amendments or renewals.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search for prior conflicting marks as provided herein, and shall transmit a copy of such search report to the applicant. Where an applicant seeks to extend protection of a registered trade mark to goods or services not originally included in the application, a further search shall be undertaken with respect to those additional goods or services. Any party opposing the registration of a trade mark shall, within the prescribed time, file a notice of opposition detailing the grounds upon which the opposition is based. 

In cases involving international registrations designating India, the Registrar shall, subject to the provisions of the relevant international treaty, inform the International Bureau of any refusal of registration or any limitation imposed on the scope of protection. The Registrar may also, where appropriate, request further information from the applicant or the International Bureau to facilitate a determination on the matter. All communications relating to informing international bodies shall be documented and maintained as part of the official record.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark under this Act, who claims priority under the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a declaration stating the country of first filing and the date of such filing. Where an applicant fails to adequately inform the International Bureau regarding any change in representation or address relevant to the international registration proceeding, the Registrar may, after providing a notice of thirty days, deem the application abandoned, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Any aggrieved party may, within ninety days of such abandonment, file a petition for restoration, demonstrating sufficient cause and payment of prescribed fees. Provided that, if the failure to inform relates to a matter of substantial prejudice to another party, the Appellate Board may, in its discretion, dismiss the petition without requiring a full hearing on the merits. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all declarations received and actions taken regarding informing international bodies as provided herein.

Any person who is the registered proprietor of a trade mark and desires to license or assign the said trade mark in favour of a party located outside of India shall, prior to effecting such licensing or assignment, inform the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. Such intimation shall include details of the proposed licensee or assignee, including their country of domicile and principal place of business. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to verification of the particulars furnished, record the details of the foreign party against the relevant trade mark in the Register. Failure to comply with the provisions herein regarding informing international parties shall not invalidate the licensing or assignment agreement itself, but may render the proprietor liable to a penalty as prescribed under this Act. A register trade mark, properly licensed or assigned as provided herein, shall continue to enjoy the protections afforded under this Act, subject to the terms of the agreement and any applicable international conventions. The Trade Marks Registry reserves the right to request further documentation to ensure compliance.

The applicant, seeking registration of a trade mark incorporating a clause invention relating to a novel pharmaceutical compound, shall furnish detailed particulars of the inventive step to the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Any failure to disclose such particulars may render the application liable to be refused, subject to a reasoned order issued by the Registrar. An aggrieved party may file a petition with the Appellate Board challenging the Registrar’s decision regarding the inventive step, provided that such petition is filed within ninety days of the issuance of the order. The Appellate Board shall, upon receiving such petition, direct the applicant to submit further evidence informing international authorities of the claimed invention, if deemed necessary for establishing distinctiveness. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Registrar’s refusal, the applicant may appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act and any applicable rules framed thereunder. Any subsequent modification of the invention shall require a fresh application.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark desiring to avail of the provisions for informing international organizations regarding a relevant licensing arrangement, or a change in ownership, shall submit a prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the requisite fee as detailed in the Schedule. The Registry, upon verification of the submitted documentation, shall, within a period not exceeding thirty days, transmit the information to the designated international bodies, including the World Intellectual Property Organization. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of the trade mark relation underpinning the licensing agreement, or ownership transfer, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for appropriate relief. Provided that, no such application shall be entertained unless the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case of irreparable harm. Failure to accurately inform these organizations, or providing misleading information, may render the proprietor liable to penalties as provided herein, including potential revocation of the trade mark registration. The Trade Marks Registry retains the right to request additional documentation to ensure compliance.

Advertising an international registration shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean any communication by the proprietor of the registration, or with their consent, to the public, indicating that goods or services are offered for sale and are associated with the international registration. Such advertising may include, but is not limited to, displays at trade fairs, commercial advertisements in any medium, and business publications. A collective mark, as defined herein, shall be subject to the same provisions regarding advertising international registration as any other registered trade mark. Provided that, any advertising which falsely suggests association with a registered proprietor, or misrepresents the scope of protection conferred by the international registration, shall be deemed unlawful practice under this Act and subject to appropriate remedies. The registrar may, upon complaint, issue a cease and desist notice.

An application for advertising international registration shall be made in writing to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a statement identifying the basic application or registration relied upon for the international registration. The applicant shall, at the time of making such application, furnish a representation of the mark as it is registered in the country of origin, along with a declaration verifying the accuracy of the information provided. Where the advertising relates to goods or services not included in the basic registration, a separate application, accompanied by the requisite fee, shall be filed for each additional class. The Registry may, subject to verification of the international registration with the International Bureau, record the advertising in the Trade Marks Journal. Provided that, if the international registration is subsequently refused or cancelled, the advertising shall be removed from the Journal and no rights shall accrue to the applicant based on such advertising. Any false statement made in the application shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person who has lawfully applied for or obtained a trade mark registration in India may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for the international registration of such trade mark through the International Bureau, designating those countries which are parties to the protocol relating to the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. The application for advertising international registration shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a clear representation of the trade mark and a statement of the goods or services for which the trade mark is used or intended to be used. Where the application is found to be in order, the Trade Marks Registry shall, within a period not exceeding one month, transmit the application to the International Bureau. 

However, the Registrar may, prior to transmission, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information as may be necessary. Any opposition to the international registration, as provided herein, shall be filed within a period of three months from the date of advertisement of the international registration in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the application liable to be refused.

Any person applying for advertising international registration of a trade mark under this Act shall furnish a representation of the mark as it is to be advertised, along with a statement of the goods or services for which registration is sought, and a clear indication of the country of origin. The application shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Protocol Relating to the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks. Where the advertising international registration relates to goods or services falling within a class prohibited under the law prevailing in the designated country, the Registry may, after affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard, refuse the registration in respect of that country. Provided that, such refusal shall not affect the validity of the registration in other designated countries. The applicant may, within a prescribed period, appeal any decision of the Registry concerning the advertising international registration to the High Court. All fees associated with the processing of such applications shall be as prescribed by rules made by the Central Government.

Any person who, in the course of trade, advertises an international registration of a trade mark, knowing it to be false, or makes any false representation concerning an international registration, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where an advertising international registration relates to goods or services which are not specified in the registration, the aggrieved party may apply to the Registrar for an order restraining such advertising, and the Registrar, upon being satisfied of the falsity, may issue such order. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable by a Principal Civil Court. Provided that no such order shall be made unless the applicant demonstrates actual or potential damage resulting from the false advertising. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, direct the removal or alteration of the offending advertisement at the expense of the offender. Failure to comply with any order issued as provided herein shall constitute a further offence punishable with fine.

Any proprietor of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for the international registration of such trade mark through the International Bureau, provided that the application is based on a registration existing at the date of the application and the applicant is a national or domiciled in a country party to the Protocol relating to the Madrid Agreement. Where an advertising international registration is sought, the applicant shall furnish a statement identifying the goods or services for which advertising is desired in each designated country, and shall pay the prescribed fee for each such designation. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the application meets the requirements as provided herein, forward it to the International Bureau. Any assignment of the Indian registration shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks prior to any corresponding alteration in the details of the international registration, and the applicant shall provide evidence of such assignment to the International Bureau within the stipulated timeframe. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the cancellation of the advertising rights in the designated countries.

Any person claiming rights in a trade mark registered in a convention country may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar for the registration of an advertising international registration of that mark in India. The application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a certified copy of the basic application or registration and a statement identifying the goods or services for which the mark is registered in the country of origin. Should the Registrar object to the registration on grounds of conflict with prior Indian trade marks, the applicant may file a response within sixty days, demonstrating distinctiveness and lack of deceptive similarity. Any decision of the Registrar in this regard shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Registrar’s order. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, except where a substantial question of law is involved, allowing for further recourse to the High Court.

Any person being the proprietor of a trade mark registered under this Act, desiring to obtain an advertising international registration, shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by a statement identifying the basic registration upon which the international application relies. The application shall further detail any limitations to the scope of protection sought in designated countries, and shall be subject to the payment of the requisite fee as prescribed under the relevant rules. Where a registration mentioned clause is included in the basic registration, the applicant shall clearly indicate the extent to which such clause is to apply to the international registration. The Registry, upon verification of the application and confirmation of compliance with all procedural requirements, shall forward the application to the International Bureau within the stipulated timeframe. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the rejection of the application, provided that the applicant may, within one month of such rejection, submit a rectified application. Any assignment or licensing of the basic registration shall be promptly notified to the Registry.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a search of the Trade Marks Register as provided herein, and shall examine the application in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the application relates to a trade mark intended for goods or services to be sold or provided outside India, the applicant shall indicate the extent of such international trade. The manner informing international registration authorities regarding any refusal or limitation of protection shall be in accordance with the arrangements under the relevant international conventions and treaties to which India is a party. Any communication regarding such refusal or limitation shall include a statement of the grounds upon which it is based, and shall be transmitted within the prescribed time limits. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide additional information relating to the intended use of the trade mark abroad.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete application for registration of a trade mark and finding it to be in order, examine it as provided herein and shall, if satisfied that the trade mark is registrable, proceed to advertise it in the Trade Marks Journal. An applicant seeking to register a trade mark which is identical with or nearly resembling an earlier trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, demonstrate a legitimate interest in opposing such registration. The Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence relating to the manner informing international registrations, including details of any priority claims or subsequent designations. Any representation made to the Registrar shall be in writing and subject to verification. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the application being deemed abandoned, or registration being refused, as the case may be. The Registrar’s decision regarding registrability is subject to appeal.

Any person who desires to register a trade mark in respect of goods intended to be used in association with services, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner and furnish such particulars as may be required. Where an applicant seeks to claim priority under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, such claim shall be made within the prescribed period and accompanied by a certified copy of the earlier application. The Registry may, subject to verification of the claim, allow the priority date to be recorded. A registered proprietor aggrieved by any infringement of their trade mark, as provided herein, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both. The quantum of damages shall be determined based on actual loss or lost profits, and may include exemplary damages to deter future infringement. The manner informing international organizations regarding disputes shall be in accordance with established protocols and the provisions of the relevant treaties. Any appeal against the decision of the Registrar shall lie to the High Court.

The Registrar shall maintain a register of registered trade marks, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person interested in ascertaining whether a particular mark is registered, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Where an application for registration is refused, the applicant may, within a period of two months from the date of the refusal, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, modifying or setting aside the order of the Registrar.
