Any communication relating to international registrations designating India as a country, or seeking effect in India, shall be transmitted through the International Bureau in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Madrid Protocol. The manner informing international parties of decisions relating to their international registrations, including refusals and limitations, shall be as prescribed by the Central Government, and shall include a statement of the grounds for such decisions. The Central Government may, by notification, specify the procedure for filing and processing international applications.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain the distinctiveness of the mark and its eligibility for registration under this Act. Any communication regarding the outcome of such examination, including objections raised, shall be conveyed to the applicant in writing and shall specify the grounds for such objections with sufficient clarity. Where an applicant seeks to amend the application to overcome such objections, the amendment shall be subject to the registrar’s approval and must not substantially alter the character of the trade mark. 

The manner informing international organizations regarding registered trade marks, or the refusal of registration, shall be in accordance with the provisions of the relevant international treaties and conventions to which India is a party. Compliance with these treaties is mandatory, and the registrar may issue guidelines to ensure consistent application of these provisions. Failure to adhere to these guidelines may result in remedial action.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies for registration of a trade mark identical with or resembling a trade mark registered in a Convention country, and concerning goods or services identical with or similar to those for which the existing trade mark is registered, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that the applicant proves, on the balance of probabilities, that they acted in good faith and had no knowledge of the prior registration, no penalty shall be levied. The Trade Marks Officer may, following due process and subject to the provisions herein, direct the applicant to cease and desist from pursuing the application. Failure to comply with such direction shall attract a monetary penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The manner informing international organizations of such fraudulent applications, and the associated evidence, shall be determined by the Central Government through public notice. Any funds collected through penalties shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark desiring to assign the right, title, and interest therein, in whole or in part, including a license to use the trade mark, shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a statement of assignment in the prescribed form, accompanied by the prescribed fee. The statement shall clearly delineate the scope of the assignment, specifying the goods or services in respect of which the assignment applies and any geographical limitations, if applicable. Where the assignment involves a license, the terms and conditions of such license, including the duration, territory, and royalty payable, shall be explicitly stated. 

The Registry, upon receipt of a complete statement, shall record the assignment in its records and issue a certificate of registration of the assignment. Failure to comply with the requirements as provided herein may render the assignment unenforceable. The manner informing international organizations of such assignments, particularly concerning Madrid Protocol applications, shall be in accordance with the regulations prescribed by the International Bureau and communicated through the designated national office.

The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration alleging use of a trade mark in relation to goods or services, shall examine the application as provided herein and satisfy themselves as to the distinctiveness of the mark and the lawfulness of its proposed use. Where an objection is raised concerning the manner informing international obligations under the Madrid Protocol, the applicant may, within a period of thirty days from the receipt of the objection, file a statement addressing the grounds of the objection and providing evidence of compliance with relevant international treaties. Should the Registrar remain unsatisfied, an appeal may be preferred to the Appellate Board, which shall consider the matter de novo, giving due weight to the principles of reciprocity and the need for harmonisation of trade mark law internationally. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to the rights of appeal to the Supreme Court as per the provisions of the relevant legislation.

The Registrar shall, with a view to ensuring effective representation of Indian trade mark applications and registrations internationally, establish a publicly accessible register of authorized agents competent to conduct business before designated international organizations. A person seeking registration as a patent agent for the purposes of facilitating the manner informing international bodies regarding Indian trade marks shall submit an application to the Registrar, accompanied by proof of qualifications as prescribed. The register maintained under this Act shall include details of the agent’s practice area, contact information, and any disciplinary actions taken against them. Any communication regarding the status of an international application, or requests for information pertaining to a registered trade mark, may be directed through these registered agents, subject to the owner’s consent. The Registrar may, after due inquiry, remove an agent from the register for professional misconduct or non-compliance with regulations as provided herein.

The registrar shall, upon receiving an application claiming priority under the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain the validity of the priority claim and the manner informing international registration procedures as stipulated by the Convention. Any evidence of improper claiming, or failure to satisfy the time limits prescribed therein, shall be grounds for rejection of the application, subject to a right of appeal to the Appellate Board. Where the mark incorporates a distinctive film sound, the applicant shall submit a clear and unambiguous representation of the sound, alongside a transcript detailing its characteristics and duration. The registrar may require an expert opinion to verify the distinctiveness of such sound, and compliance with the provisions relating to non-conventional marks as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements within the stipulated timeframe may result in the application being deemed abandoned. All communications regarding priority claims shall be documented and maintained as part of the official record.

A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the goodwill of the trade mark together with the right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services in respect of which it is registered. Such assignment shall be subject to the conditions specified in the instrument of assignment and shall be in writing and signed by the assignor. Where an assignment includes the assignment of goodwill, it shall be deemed to include an assignment of the right to use the trade mark. However, no assignment of a trade mark shall be valid without the prior written consent of the Trade Marks Registry, and such consent may be granted subject to conditions. Furthermore, an assignment of a trade mark under section 36e ixd shall not affect the right of the assignor to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it was originally registered, provided that such use does not cause confusion.

A trade mark shall not be registered if, as provided herein, it consists exclusively of a depiction of the shape of goods which is incapable of distinguishing the goods from those of other undertakings, except where the shape has acquired distinctiveness through use. However, a mark may be registered if the shape has become distinctive in relation to the goods in question, and the applicant demonstrates genuine use establishing such distinctiveness to the satisfaction of the Registrar. Where a mark incorporates a shape, but also contains other elements, registration shall be considered subject to a determination that the overall impression is not solely dictated by the shape itself. Any claim of acquired distinctiveness under section 36e ixd shall be supported by evidence of continuous use for a period of not less than five years prior to the date of application for registration, and such evidence must demonstrate a substantial degree of recognition among the relevant class of persons. The Registrar may require statutory declarations or other corroborating evidence to verify such use.

Any person aggrieved by the non-removal of a deceptively similar trade mark from the register, despite a successful rectification proceeding establishing grounds under clause (d) of section 2, and specifically alleging harm arising from continued use constituting an act of passing off, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the registered proprietor from further use of the mark. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a prima facie case of passing off, including but not limited to, evidence of misrepresentation, goodwill, and damages suffered. The Court, if satisfied that the continued registration of the mark under section 36e ixd poses an imminent threat of irreparable harm to the applicant’s goodwill, may grant an interim injunction pending a full hearing. Provided that, the registered proprietor may, subject to conditions imposed by the Court, continue use of the mark for a limited period to allow for the orderly phasing out of stock legitimately bearing the mark, but shall not be entitled to any further registration or renewal. The Court shall also have the power to order an account of profits.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall, upon a finding of non-use as provided herein, be subject to an application for revocation of registration, notwithstanding any prior assertion of rights or commencement of use for a limited period. Any person alleging non-use may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, demonstrating a continuous period of three years during which the trade mark has not been put to genuine use in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such application, notify the registered proprietor, affording them a period of sixty days to submit evidence of continued use or to demonstrate sufficient reasons for non-use. 

Evidence of use shall include, but not be limited to, invoices, sales figures, and advertising materials. However, mere token use for the purpose of maintaining the registration shall not be considered genuine use. Where the registered proprietor fails to adequately respond or the evidence submitted is deemed insufficient, the Registry may proceed to revoke the registration, subject to section 36e ixd, which stipulates a mandatory review by a designated officer prior to final order. This review shall ensure procedural compliance and the proper application of the non-use provisions.

Any person claiming use of a mark registered under this Act, and seeking to demonstrate genuine use for the purposes of opposing an application for registration or for the revocation of a registration, shall furnish to the Trade Marks Registry a statutory declaration detailing the circumstances of such use. Such declaration shall specifically address the nature of goods or services in respect of which the mark is used, the geographical extent of such use within India, and the duration thereof, commencing from the date of registration. Where the mark is used through a licensee, full particulars of the license, including a certified copy of the license agreement, shall be submitted. Failure to comply with these requirements may be considered prima facie evidence of non-use. However, a finding of non-use under section 36e ixd shall not be automatic, and the Registry shall consider all evidence presented. Evidence of mere token use will not suffice to satisfy the requirements as provided herein.

Any person who applies for registration of a trade mark under this Act, falsely representing that such trade mark is associated with a geographical indication, shall be deemed to have committed an act of unfair trade practice and shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates a reasonable belief, substantiated by documented evidence, that the geographical indication was previously unregistered and available for use, the penalty may be reduced to a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any goods found to be bearing such falsely represented trade mark shall be subject to seizure and destruction, as determined by a Magistrate of First Class. Any officer authorized under this Act may initiate proceedings for such seizure. A repeat offense involving section 36e ixd shall incur a penalty doubling the initial amount and potential imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years. The aggrieved party may also seek damages in a civil court.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or a share therein, including an assignment by operation of law, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the prior rights of existing licensees. Where a trade mark is assigned with goodwill, the assignee shall, subject to the terms of any agreement with the assignor, be entitled to exercise all the rights which the assignor enjoyed immediately before the assignment, including the right to receive royalties and to enforce the trade mark against infringement. However, where the assignment does not include goodwill, the assignee’s rights shall be limited to the use of the trade mark in connection with the same goods or services as those for which it was previously used by the assignor. Any assignment falling under section 36e ixd, concerning the assignment of a trade mark as part of a larger business transfer, shall require a formal instrument of transfer registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Failure to register such transfer may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. The assignee may, with the consent of the assignor, grant further licenses.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark, aggrieved by any decision of the Registrar refusing to remove a mark from the register under the provisions relating to section 36e ixd concerning non-use, may file an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of the Registrar’s order, subject to deposit of a prescribed fee. Such appeal shall be heard by a single Judge, and the appellant shall demonstrate sufficient cause why the mark should not remain on the register due to demonstrable lack of bona fide use in relation to the goods or services specified in the registration. However, the High Court may, at its discretion, extend the time for filing the appeal if it is satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay. Any cross-appeal by the opposing party shall be entertained only if it relates directly to the grounds of the initial appeal and is filed within thirty days of the appellant’s filing. The High Court’s decision shall be final, save for any recourse to the Supreme Court as provided by law.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, aggrieved by any infringement of such trade mark by any person not being an authorised user, may institute a suit for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both, as provided herein. Where a registered proprietor demonstrates that a substantial portion of the trade mark has been applied to goods intended for sale, and that such application constitutes an infringement, the court may, at the request of the proprietor, order an account of profits. However, no such account shall be granted if the defendant proves that the use was by way of fair dealing or otherwise in accordance with this Act. A registered proprietor may, subject to the terms of any agreement with an authorised user, direct such user to take proceedings against an infringer. Failure by an authorised user to comply with such direction may be considered as grounds for revocation of the authorisation, and shall be subject to the provisions relating to section 36e ixd concerning non-use.

Any person aggrieved by the continued registration of a trade mark under this Act, and alleging that the trade mark has been abandoned, or has become deceptively similar to another trade mark, or is contrary to law or public policy, may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for a declaration of revocation. Such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall be accompanied by evidence supporting the grounds for revocation as provided herein. Where the Trade Marks Registry is satisfied that grounds for revocation exist under section 36e ixd, relating to non-use for a continuous period of five years and lack of bona fide intention to continue use, it may order the removal of the trade mark from the register. However, a registered proprietor may, within a period of sixty days from the receipt of notice of such application, file a counter-statement demonstrating continued use or a valid reason for non-use. Failure to do so shall be deemed an admission of the allegations and may result in the revocation of the trade mark.

The Copyrights Appellate Board shall be constituted for the hearing of appeals from the orders of the Copyright Office concerning the registration of copyrights and other related matters as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Office refusing registration, modifying a copyright entry, or imposing conditions on a copyright license, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the fees originally payable for the registration or license in question. Provided that the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant demonstrates prima facie grounds for believing a substantial question of law is involved. Decisions of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar of Copyrights regarding the registration of a work, or refusal thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions for condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The appeal shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the prescribed fee, and shall clearly state the grounds on which the order is challenged. The Copyrights Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, dismiss it with costs. All decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court. The Board shall have the power to regulate its own procedure and may, for the purposes of hearing an appeal, require any party to furnish such evidence or documents as it deems necessary.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Society, or by any decision of the Licensing Board established under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order or decision, and shall be filed in the manner prescribed. The Copyrights Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, reverse or vary the order or decision appealed from. The Board may, while considering an appeal relating to royalty rates, consult with experts possessing knowledge in the relevant field, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. Provided that no appeal shall lie from any order relating to the registration of copyright. All orders of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, and no further appeal shall lie to any court. The Board shall be empowered to impose costs as it thinks appropriate.

The Copyrights Appellate Board shall be comprised of a Chairperson and such other members as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint. A person shall be eligible for appointment as a member if they are a legal practitioner with at least ten years’ experience or possess a Master’s degree in law or commerce, alongside demonstrated knowledge of the creative industries. All appointments to the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be made for a term of five years, or until attaining the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. 

Any aggrieved party, dissatisfied with an order of the Registrar of Copyrights, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. Such appeal shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. The Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, admit an appeal even after the expiry of the ninety-day period. All proceedings before the Board shall be conducted in a manner consistent with principles of natural justice and shall be open to public inspection, provided that confidential information is appropriately protected.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Office relating to the registration of a work, or refusal thereof, or any other matter concerning copyright, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions regarding condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The Copyrights Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the appeal involves a substantial question of law, admit the appeal and direct the appellant to deposit a prescribed fee. All appeals shall be heard by a bench of the Copyrights Appellate Board consisting of at least two members, and decisions shall be rendered within one hundred and eighty days of the completion of pleadings, provided that extensions may be granted for reasons to be recorded in writing. The Board shall have the power to modify or reverse the order of the Copyright Office, or to direct fresh consideration of the matter. Any party failing to comply with the directions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be liable to penalties as prescribed.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Society, registered as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. The Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed from and shall pass such orders as it deems fit. Failure to file an appeal within the stipulated period shall not be excused, save upon demonstration of sufficient cause. Any wilful misrepresentation before the Copyrights Appellate Board, or the submission of falsified evidence, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may additionally render the appellant liable for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The decision of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to any remedies available under the writ jurisdiction of the High Court.

Any copyright owner aggrieved by an order of the Licensing Authority, or any other person claiming an interest in the subject matter of the copyright, may apply to the Copyrights Appellate Board for review of such order. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period. All assignments of copyright interest, whether whole or partial, shall be registered with the Licensing Authority, and a certified copy of such registration may be submitted to the Appellate Board as evidence of ownership. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to verification, accept other demonstrable evidence of valid assignment. The Appellate Board shall, after considering the application and any relevant submissions, issue its reasoned order within one hundred and eighty days, and such order shall be final and binding, save for recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law. Any transfer of copyright without prior intimation to the Licensing Authority shall render the assignment voidable at the option of the original copyright owner.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Licensing Board concerning royalty rates or terms of license, or by any decision relating to the compulsory licensing of works as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Copyrights Appellate Board shall, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard to the parties concerned, either confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Copyright Licensing Board. Decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse permissible under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning errors of law apparent on the face of the record. Further, any application for interim relief pending appeal shall be considered expeditiously by the Appellate Board, and may be granted if the applicant demonstrates a prima facie case and the balance of convenience favors such relief.

Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Copyright Office relating to the registration of copyright, or refusal to register, or the rectification of any entry in the Register of Copyrights, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. The appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order and a statement of the grounds on which it is sought to be reversed or modified. The Copyrights Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, reverse, vary or modify the order appealed from, or may remit the case back to the Copyright Office for fresh consideration, subject to such directions as it may deem fit. The Patent Office shall, upon request from the Copyrights Appellate Board, provide any technical assistance or expertise relating to the determination of originality or the existence of prior art, as may be relevant to the appeal. Decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a court of competent jurisdiction on grounds of legal error.

The Copyrights Appellate Board may, subject to the provisions of this Act, hear and decide appeals from the orders of the Registrar of Copyrights concerning the registration of copyrights, including those pertaining to works incorporating geographical indication goods. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or imposing conditions on registration, relating to such goods shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Board within ninety days from the date of the order. The Board shall, prior to the commencement of any hearing, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the registration fees that would have been payable had the appeal been dismissed. Provided that the Board may, in cases of demonstrable financial hardship, waive or reduce the amount of such deposit. All decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law is involved, in which case an appeal may lie to the Supreme Court. The Board shall adopt such procedures as it deems fit to ensure a fair and expeditious disposal of appeals, and shall maintain records of all proceedings.

Any assignment of copyright in a work, or any license to exploit a copyright work, shall be evidenced by a written instrument executed by or on behalf of the assignor or licensor, and shall specify, inter alia, the duration, territorial scope, and subject matter of the assignment or license. Where an assignment or license concerns a work incorporating a trade description, the accuracy of such trade description shall be a condition precedent to the validity of the transfer. Appeals arising from disputes regarding the validity or scope of such assignments or licenses, or concerning royalties due and payable, may be preferred to the Copyrights Appellate Board. The Board shall, subject to such rules as may be prescribed, conduct a hearing and issue an order enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court. Provided that, no appeal shall lie before the Board unless the aggrieved party has first exhausted remedies available under this Act, including mediation where appropriate, and has demonstrated a prima facie case of substantial loss. Any assignment failing to comply with these provisions shall be deemed void ab initio.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Officer concerning the registration of a copyright, or refusal thereof, may prefer an appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The Copyrights Appellate Board, upon receipt of an appeal, may, if it deems necessary, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the royalty or other remuneration that would have been payable had the copyright been validly registered. Where the appeal concerns a claim of authorship involving a subsequently issued breeder breeder variety of plant, the Board shall consider evidence of prior art and the distinctiveness of the new variety as provided herein. Decisions of the Copyrights Appellate Board shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises for reference to the Supreme Court. The Board may, in its discretion, impose costs on the unsuccessful party.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar of Copyrights relating to the registration of a work, or refusal thereof, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within which the Registrar’s office is situated, subject to the provisions of this Act. The memorandum of appeal shall clearly state the grounds on which the order is challenged and shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the High Court may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. All appeals under this Act shall be heard by a single judge of the High Court designated for handling intellectual property matters. The High Court, exercising its appellate jurisdiction, shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Decisions of the High Court on such copyrights appellate matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to the Supreme Court as per law. The High Court may also direct the Registrar to reconsider the application for registration, if deemed necessary.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Officer, whether relating to the registration of a work or the rectification thereof, or any decision concerning the grant or refusal of a license under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within which the Copyright Officer’s office is situated. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order and a statement of the grounds on which it is sought to be reversed or modified. The High Court, exercising its appellate jurisdiction, shall have the power to confirm, vary, or reverse the order of the Copyright Officer, and may also direct fresh consideration of the matter. 

Provided that, the High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, stay the execution of any order appealed against pending the disposal of the appeal. Further, all decisions of the High Court in these copyrights appellate matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to a superior court on grounds of law.

Any aggrieved person, dissatisfied with an order of the Copyright Office relating to the registration of copyright or the rectification thereof, shall have a right to appeal to the High Court whose territorial jurisdiction encompasses the location of the Copyright Office that issued the order. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding limitation periods. The appellant shall deposit with the High Court a sum equivalent to the fees originally paid for the registration or rectification process, as a condition precedent to the entertaining of the appeal. The High Court, exercising its appellate jurisdiction, may confirm, modify, reverse, or remand the order of the Copyright Office, and shall record its reasons in writing. Further, the High Court, in its capacity as the copyrights appellate authority, may, if deemed necessary, direct a fresh inquiry into any matter relevant to the appeal, ensuring due process and natural justice. Any decision of the High Court shall be final and binding.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Office relating to the registration of copyright or any matter incidental thereto, may prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for a further period not exceeding thirty days, if sufficient cause is shown. The High Court, upon consideration of such appeal, shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Copyright Office. Failure to comply with the procedural requirements for filing an appeal, as provided herein, shall render the appeal inadmissible. Knowingly making false statements in any appeal before the High Court, constituting a contempt of court, shall attract a penalty of imprisonment not exceeding two years, or a fine, or both. The decision of the High Court on such copyrights appellate matters shall be final and binding.

Any person desiring to assign or license any copyright, or any right therein, whether wholly or partially, shall execute an instrument in writing under his hand specifying the nature of the right assigned or licensed, and the duration and territorial extent of such assignment or license. Such instrument shall be registered with the Copyright Office within thirty days of its execution to be effective against third parties, though non-registration shall not invalidate the assignment or license between the parties thereto. The Copyright Office shall maintain a Register of Copyright Assignments and Licenses, open to inspection subject to such fees as may be prescribed. Appeals from decisions concerning the validity or scope of any assignment or license, or concerning the refusal of registration, shall lie to the designated copyrights appellate authority, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days of the decision appealed against. The appellate authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Copyright Office. Any assignment not complying with the provisions of this Act shall be voidable at the option of the assignor.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Office relating to the registration of a work, or refusal thereof, or any decision concerning the validity of a copyright claim, may prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction over the matter, subject to the provisions of this Act. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to points of law and demonstrable errors apparent on the record, and shall not extend to matters of fact unless fraud or manifest error is alleged and substantiated. An appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and a certified copy of the order and all relevant documents shall accompany the petition. The High Court, exercising its appellate jurisdiction, may confirm, modify, or reverse the order of the Copyright Office, and may direct such further action as it deems fit. Further appeals from the High Court’s decision on such copyrights appellate matters shall lie to the Supreme Court, subject to the usual terms and conditions. The High Court may require a deposit of costs as a condition for entertaining the appeal, particularly if the grounds appear frivolous or vexatious.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Copyright Office, including refusal of registration or revocation thereof, may prefer an appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such extension as the High Court may deem fit to grant upon sufficient cause being shown. The appellate court, upon receiving an appeal, may, if it considers necessary, require the appellant to deposit with it a sum equivalent to the fees originally payable for the registration or renewal of the copyright in question. 

Provided that, where the appeal relates to a matter involving a technological protection measure or rights management information, the appellate court may, at its discretion, consult with a technical expert from the Patent Office to ensure a proper understanding of the relevant technical aspects. The decision of the High Court on such copyrights appellate matters shall be final and binding, save for any recourse to the Supreme Court as provided under the Constitution.

Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with an order of the Principal Bench or a Regional Office concerning copyright registration, rectification of records, or infringement, may initiate appellate proceedings before the High Court having jurisdiction. Such appeal shall be preferred within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to condonation of delay for sufficient cause. The High Court, upon receiving an appeal, may, if it deems fit, direct the appellant to deposit with the Court a sum equivalent to the costs incurred by the opposing party. All applications for rectification of the court rectification register, whether pertaining to ownership or other material particulars, shall be subject to the same appellate process as original disputes. Provided that the High Court may, at its discretion, remit the matter back to the Principal Bench for fresh consideration, particularly where evidence suggests procedural irregularity or a need for further investigation as provided herein. The decision of the High Court on such copyrights appellate matters shall be final and binding.

Any article manufactured utilizing a patented process shall be deemed to infringe the patent rights conferred under this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding license of right. A process, to be registrable as an article patented process, must be novel, involve an inventive step, and be capable of industrial application, as determined by the Controller of Patents. Where a patented process is employed for the production of a substance, the article so produced, even if differing slightly in its composition, shall be considered an infringement unless it is demonstrated that such difference does not materially affect the efficacy of the patented process. The patent holder may, as provided herein, seek an injunction restraining the infringing manufacture or sale of the patented article. However, such injunction shall not apply to articles produced solely for research purposes. A clear and unambiguous description of the patented process is a prerequisite for registration.

Any person alleging infringement of an article patented under this Act shall, prior to the institution of any suit, provide the alleged infringer with a clear and detailed written notice specifying the patent and the manner of infringement. Such notice shall be accompanied by a marked copy of the patented article or, where the infringement relates to a process, a detailed description of the alleged infringing process, demonstrating how it falls within the scope of the claims of the patent. Where the infringement concerns an article patented process, the notice must further identify the article produced by that process and the quantity thereof alleged to be infringing. The Controller of Patents may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, direct an inquiry into the allegations contained within the notice, provided that a response is not received from the alleged infringer within thirty days of service. Any evidence obtained during such inquiry shall be admissible in subsequent legal proceedings. Failure to comply with the provisions herein shall not, however, constitute an absolute bar to the institution of a suit, but may be considered by the court in determining the appropriate relief.

Any person dealing with an article patented under this Act shall be deemed to have constructive notice of the patent, subject to the conditions stipulated herein. Where an article is manufactured by a patented process, and such article is not itself patented, any person dealing with the article shall not be liable for infringement of the patented process, provided that such person proves they exercised all reasonable diligence to ascertain whether the article was manufactured by a patented process. The patentee of the article patented process may, however, initiate proceedings to demonstrate that the diligence exercised was insufficient. A licensee of the patented article shall be bound by the terms and conditions of the license, and any breach thereof may be subject to remedies as provided herein. Failure to mark a patented article with the patent number shall not invalidate the patent, but may affect the remedies available to the patentee.

Any person dissatisfied with a determination made by an adjudicating officer relating to the revocation of a patent, shall have the right to submit a reasoned representation to the Controller of Patents within ninety days of the communication of such determination, provided that such representation clearly articulates the grounds for disagreement and proposes specific evidence for reconsideration. The Controller, upon receipt of said representation, may, if deemed necessary, constitute a special committee of technical experts to review the matter and submit a report within a further sixty days. Should the Controller uphold the original determination, the aggrieved party may then appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions concerning pre-deposit of costs as determined by the Controller. The adjudicating officer period for responding to requests for information from the Controller shall not exceed thirty days, failing which, the matter may proceed *ex parte*. Any delay attributable to the applicant will not be excused.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be in writing and registered with the Controller of Patents, failing which such assignment shall be void. Where an application for registration of assignment is made, the Controller may, after examining the documents and satisfying himself as to the validity of the assignment, register the same and shall issue a certificate of registration. An advertised acceptance of a patent application, even prior to full payment of fees, may be assigned subject to the conditions specified in the assignment deed and the continued validity of the patent. The adjudicating officer period for disputes concerning the validity or scope of such assignments, or concerning royalties due under the assignment, shall not exceed ninety days from the date of filing of the complaint, unless extended by the Controller for sufficient cause. Any assignment made fraudulently or with intent to deceive shall be null and void ab initio.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee, subject to such conditions as the Trade Marks Registry may deem fit to impose to protect confidential information. Any person possessing a proprietary interest in a trade mark recorded in the register may, upon application and satisfactory proof of such interest, obtain a certified copy of any entry therein. Where a trade mark is subject to a pending application for rectification, notice of such application shall be recorded in the register against the relevant trade mark, and no transfer or assignment of rights in such trade mark shall be registered without prior consideration of the rectification proceedings. The Trade Marks Registry may, at its discretion, refuse registration of a transfer or assignment if it is deemed contrary to public policy or to the interests of the registered proprietor. Any aggrieved party may appeal such refusal to the High Court, provided that the appeal is filed within ninety days of the order of the Registry.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register, distinct from any other official record, for the orderly recording of all applications for registration and all registered trade marks. Any person desiring to inspect the register maintained under this Act shall submit a written request to the Registrar, specifying the trade mark or class of trade marks to be inspected, and shall pay the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, permit access to the register during office hours. All entries in the register shall be deemed to be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein. Any alteration made to the register, whether by way of correction, amendment, or addition, shall be recorded with the date of such alteration and the initial of the officer responsible. Where an application for registration is refused, a note of such refusal, along with the grounds thereof, shall be entered in the register. The register shall be open to public inspection, provided that confidential information relating to the applicant or proprietor, as determined by the Registrar, shall be redacted.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open for inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee, subject to such conditions as the Controller may deem necessary to protect confidential information or prevent undue disturbance of the business of the Trade Marks Registry. Any application for inspection shall be made in writing and shall specify the trade mark or class of trade marks to be inspected. The Controller may, at their discretion, require a statutory declaration from the applicant as to the purpose for which the inspection is sought and may refuse access if the purpose is deemed improper. All entries in the register shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, and no alteration shall be made without the prior approval of the Controller. Any person aggrieved by a refusal to permit inspection or by any alteration to the register may, within thirty days, appeal to the High Court. The Controller shall ensure the register is regularly updated to reflect all current registrations and amendments.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee, subject to such conditions as the Controller may deem fit to impose to ensure the confidentiality of sensitive commercial information. Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents themselves as being authorized to inspect the register, or who knowingly makes a false entry into the register, or who fraudulently alters any entry therein, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Provided that, any amendment to the register necessitated by a judicial order shall be effected expeditiously and without imposition of additional fees beyond those prescribed. Failure by the Controller to comply with such order within sixty days shall constitute a cognizable offence, attracting a penalty of five thousand rupees per day of delay. All fees collected pursuant to inspection of the register shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to assign the trade mark and the goodwill of the business carried on under it to any person or entity. Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a recordation procedure established by the Trade Marks Registry, and no assignment shall be effective against any third party until such recordation is completed in the register maintained for that purpose. The register shall contain details of the assignment, including the date of transfer, the consideration paid, and the particulars of both the assignor and the assignee. An assignee may, with the permission of the Registry and subject to such terms as it may deem fit, apply to become the registered proprietor of the trade mark. Where a trade mark is assigned as part of a transfer of a business as a going concern, the Registry may, at its discretion, record the transfer without requiring formal assignment documentation, provided that sufficient evidence of the transfer is furnished.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of the prescribed fee, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding confidentiality of addresses and other sensitive information of the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by a refusal of access to the register, or by the imposition of unduly restrictive conditions on inspection, may submit a reasoned representation to the Controller of Trade Marks, who shall consider such representation within sixty days. Should the Controller uphold the refusal or conditions, the aggrieved party may appeal to the Appellate Board, providing a statement of grounds for appeal within ninety days of the Controller’s decision. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition to a High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of natural justice, provided that such petition is filed within ninety days of the Appellate Board’s order. Any alteration to entries in the register, following a successful appeal, shall be duly noted and publicly accessible.

The register maintained under this Act shall be open to inspection by any person upon payment of the prescribed fee, subject to such conditions as the Trade Marks Registry may deem fit to impose. Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, including a license, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and must be recorded in the register to be effective against third parties. An applicant seeking to assign a trade mark used in relation to trade description goods shall furnish a detailed statement of such goods and the manner of their description, as provided herein. The Registrar may, where an assignment is made without the consent of the registered proprietor, require evidence of justifiable cause. Failure to record an assignment within the stipulated period may render the transfer voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, and the register shall reflect the current ownership at all times. Any alteration to the registered proprietor’s name or address shall also be recorded.

The entry register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of the particulars entered therein and shall be admissible as evidence in any legal proceeding. Any person may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, inspect the entry register at the Trade Marks Registry during office hours. The Registrar may, if satisfied that the applicant has legitimate cause, permit inspection of the entry register even without payment of fee. Where a trade mark is subject to a pending application for rectification, a note indicating such pending proceeding shall be entered in the entry register against the relevant mark. Such entry shall serve as constructive notice to any person dealing with the mark. Any alteration made to the entry register shall be authenticated by the Registrar and recorded in a separate index maintained for that purpose.

Any person claiming ownership of a registered trade mark, and desiring to record a transfer of such trade mark, shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, and upon satisfaction of the Registry that the transfer is genuine and in accordance with this Act, an appropriate entry shall be made in the entry register maintained for that purpose. The entry register shall be conclusive evidence of the particulars recorded therein, subject to proof of fraud. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions herein, record a change of address with the Registry, and such change shall be noted in the entry register. Any incorrect entry made in the entry register may be rectified by the Registry upon application supported by evidence demonstrating the inaccuracy, provided that such application is made within a period of two years from the date of the initial entry. Failure to maintain an accurate entry register may be considered in proceedings relating to the validity of the trade mark.

Any person causing an incorrect entry to be made in the entry register maintained under this Act, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the incorrect entry relates to a registered trade mark and is made to facilitate the infringement thereof, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct rectification of the entry register upon confirmation of such fraudulent entry. Any application for rectification made without reasonable grounds, or with intent to harass, shall render the applicant liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees. Provided that, no rectification shall be ordered if it would unjustly prejudice the rights of a bona fide purchaser of the trade mark. All records pertaining to such fraudulent entries and rectification proceedings shall be maintained securely and shall be open to inspection as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an alteration made or proposed to be made in the entry register maintained under this Act, may, within one month from the date of such alteration or the receipt of notice of the proposed alteration, lodge an objection with the Registrar in the prescribed manner. Such objection shall be accompanied by a fee as specified in the Schedule. The Registrar shall, after giving the objector and the proprietor of the trade mark a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and considering any evidence submitted by either party, determine the validity of the objection. If the Registrar upholds the objection, the entry in the register shall be rectified accordingly. However, a decision of the Registrar refusing rectification of the entry register may be appealed to the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any appeal under this provision shall be filed within three months from the date of the Registrar’s order, and the High Court’s decision shall be final.

Any person aggrieved by an alteration made or requested to be made in the entry register maintained under this Act, may, within one month from the date of such alteration or request, lodge an objection with the Registrar. Such objection shall be in writing and shall clearly specify the grounds on which the alteration is disputed, and shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The Registrar, upon receipt of such objection, shall cause a notice to be issued to the proprietor of the trade mark, affording them an opportunity to be heard. The Registrar shall also maintain a registrar index of all such objections received, detailing the date of receipt, the nature of the dispute, and the status of resolution. Provided that, if the objection is found to be frivolous or vexatious, the Registrar may dismiss it and impose costs upon the objector, subject to an appeal to the High Court. Any decision of the Registrar in respect of such objection shall be final, unless appealed against within sixty days.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a geographical indication registered under this Act, or deceptively similar thereto, shall maintain a register of all transactions relating to the sale, distribution, and consignment of such goods, subject to the regulations prescribed by the Board. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication has reason to believe that any goods are being dealt with in a manner that indicates falsification of the genuine article, they may apply to the Board for an order directing inspection of the premises where such goods are manufactured, stored, or sold. The Board, upon such application and subject to verification of the grounds alleged, may issue an order for inspection. It shall be deemed an indication falsifies genuine if the goods inspected are found to be falsely labelled or packaged to suggest an origin different from that legitimately associated with the registered geographical indication, or if the quality or characteristics of the goods do not conform to the standards established for that indication. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Board may appeal to the High Court.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a geographical indication registered under this Act shall ensure strict adherence to the standards and specifications established for that indication, as recorded in the Register of Geographical Indications. Where a good is offered for sale, or otherwise made available to the public, with a geographical indication that falsely represents its origin, or falsely suggests a connection to a region or locality, it shall be deemed an indication falsifies genuine. However, a producer may, subject to prior approval from the Geographical Indications Registry, utilize descriptive terms alongside the registered geographical indication, provided that such terms do not diminish the distinctiveness of the indication or mislead consumers as to the true origin of the goods. Any misrepresentation regarding the qualities, characteristics, or method of production associated with the geographical indication is prohibited and shall be actionable as provided herein. Compliance with packaging and labeling requirements, as prescribed in the rules, is mandatory.

A geographical indication shall be considered to be falsified when goods are offered for sale, or otherwise presented to the public, in a manner which suggests a connection to a geographical indication, when no such connection exists. Any representation, direct or indirect, that goods originate from a region associated with a registered geographical indication, but do not, shall constitute an indication falsified as provided herein. Where a collective or qualifying mark is used in conjunction with a geographical indication, any misrepresentation regarding adherence to the standards or criteria for use of that mark shall also be deemed an indication falsified. The Registrar may, subject to such inquiry as may be deemed necessary, issue a notice to any person suspected of engaging in such practices, requiring them to demonstrate the veracity of their claims regarding the geographical origin of goods. Failure to adequately demonstrate such veracity may result in the initiation of enforcement proceedings under this Act.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a geographical indication that is falsely represented to goods not originating in the territory associated with such indication, shall be deemed to have engaged in an indication falsified, and such act constitutes a contravention of this Act. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication proves that another person has falsely applied the indication, or a deceptively similar indication, to goods, a decree of injunction may be granted restraining such person from so doing. The proprietor shall also be entitled to damages, assessed in accordance with the actual loss suffered or, where such loss cannot be ascertained, to an account of profits made by the defendant. Subject to the provisions herein, a court may, at the request of the registered proprietor, order the destruction or forfeiture of goods bearing the falsified indication. Any person aggrieved by the application of a falsified geographical indication may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, file a complaint with the appropriate court.

A geographical indication shall be considered to be falsified where any goods are offered for sale, or sold, or otherwise distributed, bearing an indication which falsely suggests a geographical origin. Any person dealing in goods with a falsified geographical indication shall be liable to such penalties as may be prescribed. However, no proceedings for an offence involving a falsified geographical indication shall be instituted except with the prior written consent of the Registrar. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, refuse such consent if the complaint appears to be frivolous or vexatious, or if the complainant has not suffered any substantial loss due to the alleged indication falsified. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication proves that any goods have been sold with a falsified indication, they may apply to the court for an injunction restraining the offender from dealing in such goods and for damages. The court, upon being satisfied, may grant such injunction and award such damages as it deems fit, and may also order the destruction or forfeiture of the goods bearing the falsified indication.

A geographical indication shall be considered to be falsified where goods are offered for sale, or otherwise traded in, bearing an indication which falsely suggests a geographical origin, even if the goods themselves originate from the region nominally indicated. Any representation, direct or indirect, that suggests a connection to a registered geographical indication, when no such connection exists, constitutes an indication falsified as provided herein. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a producer who is not an authorized user may not utilize a geographical indication, or a deceptively similar variation thereof, in the marketing of their goods. However, honest practices, including fair use and customary trade practices, shall not be construed as falsification. Provided that, any use intended to mislead the public regarding the true origin of goods will be deemed a contravention of this Act, and subject to penalties. The registrar may, upon application, order the removal or destruction of any goods bearing a falsified indication.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely represents goods as originating from a geographical indication registered under this Act shall be deemed to have committed an indication falsified offence. Such falsification includes, but is not limited to, the direct application of a registered geographical indication to goods not conforming to the standards established for that indication, or the alteration of a genuine geographical indication in a manner likely to mislead consumers regarding the goods’ origin. Where a collective body exists for a geographical indication, any misrepresentation concerning membership or authorization by that body shall also constitute an indication falsified offence. Upon conviction for an indication falsified offence, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, subject to the discretion of the adjudicating authority as provided herein. Repeated offences may incur enhanced penalties.

Any assignment of rights in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to a written instrument executed by the registered proprietor and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry. The instrument shall clearly identify the geographical indication, the territory to which the assignment relates, and the assignee’s particulars, including their address for service. Where a license is granted to use a geographical indication, the terms and conditions of such license, including duration, territorial scope, and quality control mechanisms, shall be documented in a written agreement and a copy furnished to the Registry. 

A transfer or license shall not be valid against any prior bona fide user of the geographical indication unless express provision is made for their continued use within the assignment or licensing agreement. Any indication falsified through unauthorized assignment or licensing, or through misrepresentation of the terms of a valid transfer, shall be actionable under this Act, attracting penalties as prescribed. The Registry may, upon application, rectify any inconsistencies arising from improper assignment or licensing records.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar regarding the falsification of a geographical indication, or alleging an indication falsified with respect to goods, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the decision or the occurrence of the alleged falsification. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the concerned parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, or direct further inquiry to be conducted. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, stay the implementation of the Registrar’s decision pending the disposal of the appeal. Furthermore, any authorized user demonstrating actual damage resulting from the indication falsified shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages, as provided herein, irrespective of any criminal proceedings initiated under this Act. The burden of proof regarding the falsification shall lie with the complainant.

Any person who offers for sale, sells, or otherwise distributes goods with a geographical indication that is an indication falsified, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed under this Act, notwithstanding any other remedies available under law. Where a falsified geographical indication poses a demonstrable threat to national security or critical infrastructure, the Central Government may, subject to judicial review, direct immediate seizure of the goods and any materials used in their production or distribution, initiating a security india action. The registered proprietor of the geographical indication, or any authorized user thereof, may institute civil proceedings for injunction, damages, and an account of profits against any person dealing in goods bearing the falsified indication. Any order of injunction granted shall extend to all intermediaries involved in the trade chain. Provided that, the court may, at its discretion, reduce the damages awarded if the defendant proves they acted in good faith and had reasonable grounds to believe their actions were lawful.

A geographical indication shall be deemed to be falsely applied if it is used on goods for which such indication is not, or is falsely represented as being, originated in the territory associated with the geographical indication. For the purposes of determining falsity, consideration shall be given to material, shape, appearance, and other characteristics of the goods, alongside the established customs of the territory. Where a good possesses qualities fundamentally derived from its place of origin, but does not fully meet the strict territorial requirements as defined herein, the Registrar may, subject to conditions, deem the use of the geographical indication permissible, provided that such use does not mislead the consumer as to the true origin. Any representation that falsely suggests an association with a registered geographical indication shall constitute a deemed falsify geographical indication under this Act.

Any person claiming to be the manufacturer of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall apply for registration in the prescribed manner to the Controller of Designs, furnishing all necessary particulars as detailed in Schedule I. The application shall include a statement of ownership and the right to make such an application, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. A layout-design, to be registrable under this Act, must be original and not have been previously published, except as permitted herein. 

Provided that a layout-design which has been commercially exploited anywhere in India or in a convention country, shall be eligible for registration subject to the applicant demonstrating sufficient grounds for the delay. The Controller may, after examination, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. Registration of layout designs manufacturers is crucial for establishing proprietary rights and enabling effective enforcement against infringement. The Controller shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs.

Any person alleging infringement of a layout-design registered under this Act shall, prior to the institution of any suit, serve a written notice on the alleged infringer, requiring them to cease and desist from the infringing act and to provide full and accurate details of production, sale, and import of articles embodying the layout-design in question. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of service of such notice, submit a statement of justification claiming that their actions do not constitute infringement, or that the layout-design is invalid, the aggrieved party may then proceed to file a suit before the competent court. The court, upon receiving evidence relating to the claim of invalidity by the defendant, may refer the matter to the Controller of Patents and Designs for expert opinion regarding the originality and distinctiveness of the layout designs manufacturers’ claim. A finding by the Controller that the layout-design lacks originality shall be binding on the court, subject to further appeal to the High Court.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable, as provided herein, if a skilled person, examining the prior art, would find differences between it and any existing registered layout-design, such that those differences would not lead to confusion amongst consumers. For the purposes of determining distinguishability, account shall be taken of the overall impression created by the layout-design, considering its arrangement of constituent parts and functional elements. However, minor variations which do not substantially affect the essential characteristics of the layout-design shall not be deemed sufficient for establishing a distinguishable registered layout-design. A layout-design incorporating a common or standard feature, subject to it being integrated in a novel manner, may still be considered distinguishable.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable from another registered layout-design if, and only if, a skilled person, exercising independent thought, would find a significant difference between the two when comparing their respective topological arrangements and features. The determination of such distinguishable characteristics shall be subject to a comparative analysis of the functional elements and their interconnections as depicted in the registered layout-designs. However, minor variations arising from routine manufacturing tolerances or purely cosmetic differences shall not be construed as rendering a layout-design distinguishable. An applicant seeking registration of a layout-design similar to an existing one may, as provided herein, submit evidence demonstrating substantial differences in functional characteristics, alongside a detailed comparative chart. The Controller shall, upon review, determine whether the proposed layout-design meets the criteria for a distinguishable registered layout, considering the overall impression created by the layout.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable from any other registered layout-design if a person ordinarily skilled in the art, upon comparison, would find sufficient differences to avoid confusion as to source or quality. However, mere variations in size or minor details shall not constitute a distinguishable layout-design, unless such variations result in a substantial alteration of the overall functionality or aesthetic impression. Any person who, subject to the provisions of this Act, demonstrates prior art anticipating a claimed layout-design feature may petition for revocation of the registration, provided that such prior art was publicly known or accessible before the date of application for registration. The registered owner may, as provided herein, seek an injunction against any unauthorized use of a distinguishable registered layout-design, and shall be entitled to recover damages for any loss suffered as a result of such infringement. A finding of distinguishable layout-design does not preclude a claim of infringement if the overall impression and substantial features are substantially similar.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable, as provided herein, if a reasonable person, exercising due diligence, would not confuse it with any previously registered layout-design, taking into account overall visual impression and functional differences. However, minor variations in the arrangement of repeating elements, or purely cosmetic alterations that do not affect the fundamental characteristics of the layout, shall not constitute a distinguishable registered layout. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a layout-design incorporating a standard cell, a mask common to a plurality of integrated circuits, or a layout which is a trivial modification of an existing layout, may still be registered if it demonstrates a novel combination of elements resulting in improved performance or reduced size. Any claim of distinctiveness shall be substantiated with detailed technical drawings and functional specifications, and may be subject to examination by the appropriate authority. A layout-design that is substantially similar to a prior art layout shall not be deemed distinguishable.

Any person who, without the permission of the registered proprietor of a distinguishable registered layout-design, manufactures, imports, sells, hires, or otherwise distributes an integrated circuit embodying such layout-design, or causes another to do so, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees for each such infringement, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Where the infringement involves a repeated offense, the penalty may extend to ten lakh rupees. A layout-design shall be considered distinguishable if, despite substantial similarity to a prior layout-design, a person skilled in the art would be able to differentiate it based on its unique features and functional elements. The court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement and order the seizure and destruction of infringing articles. Any evidence obtained as provided herein shall be admissible in proceedings.

Any registered layout-design, being a distinguishable registered layout, shall be subject to licensing by the registered proprietor to any person desiring to exploit it, upon such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties. Where a registered proprietor refuses to grant a license on reasonable terms, any person may apply to the appropriate authority for compulsory licensing, provided that such applicant demonstrates a genuine intention to commercially work the layout-design. Assignment of a registered layout-design shall be effective only upon registration of the transfer with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry, and notice of such assignment shall be given to the concerned parties. A licensee may assign their interest in the licensed layout-design, subject to the terms of the licensing agreement. The registered proprietor may revoke a license for non-compliance with the agreed terms, but shall provide reasonable notice and opportunity to remedy any breach, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding licensing or assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the designated court.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable from a prior layout-design only if the differences between them relate to features not essential to the functioning of the semiconductor device embodying the layout-design, and such differences are significant enough to impart a distinct visual impression to a person skilled in the art. However, mere cosmetic variations or modifications which do not materially affect the performance characteristics of the device shall not constitute a distinguishable registered layout. An applicant seeking registration of a layout-design similar to an existing one must demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the authority, that the proposed layout possesses novel features that overcome the limitations of the prior art, as provided herein. Any appeal against the refusal of registration on grounds of non-distinguishability shall lie before the designated appellate authority within ninety days of the refusal order, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and fulfillment of procedural requirements. The appellate authority may, after examining the evidence and arguments presented, confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the registering authority.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable if, despite substantial similarity to a prior registered layout-design, a person skilled in the art would find discernible differences affecting the functionality or performance of the semiconductor device incorporating it. Any assignment of rights in a distinguishable registered layout-design shall be evidenced in writing and filed with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. The assignee shall, upon such filing, become the holder of the rights as provided herein, subject to any existing, unexpired licenses granted by the original registrant. Where the registered layout-design bears a name or identifying mark, the assignment instrument shall clearly state the transfer of all rights to that name as well, unless otherwise expressly agreed. A license granted in respect of a layout-design shall be personal to the licensee and not transferable without the prior written consent of the registrant, provided that such consent may not be unreasonably withheld.
