Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the District Court.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable from a prior layout-design only if a person skilled in the art would find a discernible difference between the two, assessed visually and functionally, and not merely based on trivial variations. However, an assertion of distinctiveness may be rebutted by evidence demonstrating substantial replication of protected features, even if presented with minor aesthetic alterations. It is further clarified that where a specification does disclose elements essential to the functioning of the layout-design, such disclosure shall not, in and of itself, negate the claim of originality, provided that the disclosed elements are integral to achieving a demonstrable technical advantage. Any appeal regarding the determination of ‘distinguishable registered layout’ shall be adjudicated by the High Court having territorial jurisdiction, subject to the provisions of this Act, and the burden of proof lies with the appellant to demonstrate a clear basis for challenging the initial finding.

A registered layout-design shall be considered distinguishable from any other registered layout-design if a person skilled in the art, upon comparison, would find sufficient differences to avoid confusion as to source or quality, taking into account the overall visual impression created by the layout-design. The assessment of distinctiveness shall be made in relation to existing registered layout-designs and those publicly known before the filing date of the application for registration. An integrated circuit embodying a layout-design, even if comprising standard elements, may still support a finding of distinguishability if the arrangement of those elements presents a unique and non-obvious configuration. However, minor variations or trivial modifications of existing designs shall not be sufficient to establish a distinguishable registered layout-design as provided herein. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the applicant bears the onus of demonstrating such distinctiveness. A layout-design that is substantially similar to a prior art layout-design shall not be registered.

The registrar application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall be made in Form LD-1, duly completed and accompanied by the prescribed fee as specified in Schedule I. An applicant may submit the application electronically, subject to the regulations prescribed by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. The application shall contain a detailed description of the layout-design, including the number of layers comprising the layout and the function of each layer. Where the applicant seeks priority from an earlier application filed in a convention country, a certified copy of such application, along with a verified English translation if necessary, shall be furnished with the produced registrar application. Any misrepresentation in the application may render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein.

The applicant submitting a produced registrar application shall furnish a statement detailing the extent of commercial exploitation of the layout-design, if any, in India or elsewhere, and shall update such statement annually as provided herein. Any misrepresentation in such a statement regarding commercial exploitation may render the registration liable to revocation, subject to a hearing affording the applicant an opportunity to be heard. The Registrar, upon receiving a produced registrar application, shall examine the application and accompanying documentation to ensure compliance with the requirements of this Act. Where the application is found to be in order, the Registrar shall register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration. The certificate shall contain particulars of the layout-design, the applicant, and the date of registration. A request for expedited examination of a produced registrar application may be considered, contingent upon payment of the prescribed fee and demonstration of exceptional circumstances.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall present an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee, and containing all particulars as required under this Act. The application, upon being deemed complete, shall be recorded as a produced registrar application and assigned a unique reference number. Subject to verification of the layout-design’s originality and compliance with the provisions herein, the Registrar may, after conducting a thorough examination, register the layout-design. Should the Registrar raise objections regarding the application, the applicant shall be afforded a period of thirty days to address such objections, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned. A registered proprietor shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in India, and any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or commercial use thereof constitutes an infringement, giving rise to remedies as provided herein, including injunctions and damages. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the High Court.

The applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a complete application to the Registrar, including a detailed description of the layout-design and supporting documentation as prescribed. Every produced registrar application must be accompanied by the requisite fee, determined in accordance with the Schedule annexed to these rules, and any incomplete application shall be deemed non-compliant and subject to rejection. The Registrar may, however, require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification, which shall be provided within a period of thirty days from the date of such request, failing which the application may be considered abandoned. Where the application concerns a layout-design derived from a prior art layout-design, full particulars of such prior art, including its source and date of publication, must be disclosed. Subject to verification of the application and satisfaction of all procedural requirements as provided herein, the Registrar shall register the layout-design and issue a certificate of registration to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision regarding the application may, within sixty days, file an appeal with the designated appellate authority.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a complete application to the Registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee and all necessary documentation as provided herein. The produced registrar application shall clearly and accurately delineate the layout-design, including a detailed description of its functionalities and a representation demonstrating its three-dimensional configuration. Subject to verification, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish additional information or clarifications concerning the layout-design within a specified timeframe. Failure to comply with such a request may render the application incomplete and liable for rejection. An applicant may, with the Registrar’s permission, amend the application prior to its acceptance, provided that such amendment does not materially alter the scope of the claimed layout-design. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all validly produced registrar applications, accessible for inspection as per the regulations.

Any person applying for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall furnish with the registrar application a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its originality. Failure to accurately represent the layout-design, or to disclose any prior art relevant to its novelty, shall constitute a material misrepresentation and render the registration void ab initio. The registrar, upon reasonable grounds believing a false statement has been made in a produced registrar application, may initiate an inquiry and require the applicant to provide further evidence within thirty days. Should the applicant fail to comply, or if the inquiry confirms the misrepresentation, a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees may be levied. Repeated offences as provided herein shall attract a penalty up to one lakh rupees and potential suspension of future application privileges. Any aggrieved party may file a complaint regarding a fraudulent produced registrar application with the registrar, subject to verification of the complaint's veracity.

Any person desiring to obtain a license or to assign the rights in a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall submit a request to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed. The request for assignment shall include a complete transfer of all rights vested in the applicant, and shall be subject to verification of title by the Registrar, ensuring no encumbrances exist unless explicitly disclosed and agreed upon by all parties concerned. A produced registrar application relating to licensing shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, the duration of the license, and the royalty or consideration payable to the registered proprietor. The Registrar may require evidence of adequate consideration before registering the assignment or license. Where the registered proprietor is a legal person, the application must be executed by a duly authorized officer. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the application liable to rejection, as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all assignments and licenses.

Any person aggrieved by the order of the Registrar refusing to accept a produced registrar application, or requiring amendment thereto, may, within ninety days of the date of such order, file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such appeal shall be in the form and manner prescribed, and shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and any evidence submitted by the appellant or the Registrar, may confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Provided that, the Appellate Board shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant demonstrates substantial grounds for believing the Registrar’s decision was based on an erroneous interpretation of the criteria for evaluating layout-design originality as provided herein. Further, any party desiring to be heard before the Appellate Board shall submit a notice of intention to do so, along with a statement of their arguments, at least thirty days prior to the scheduled hearing.

The produced registrar application, complete with the requisite particulars as specified in the First Schedule, shall be filed with the Registrar, accompanied by the prescribed fee. Any deficiency in the application, or failure to furnish any required document, may be communicated by the Registrar to the applicant, who shall rectify the same within a period of thirty days from the date of such communication. Should the Registrar be satisfied that the application meets all requirements, a certificate of registration shall be issued. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the registration of a layout-design may prefer an appeal to the Member Appellate Board, subject to the provisions contained herein, within ninety days of the date of the Registrar’s order. The Member Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

The applicant for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall furnish with the prescribed application a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its originality. Any application not complying with the requirements as to form and content may be rejected by the Registrar. Where an application claims priority from a prior application made in a convention country, evidence of such prior application, duly certified, shall accompany the produced registrar application. It is clarified that the rights conferred by registration under this Act are subject to the provisions of the Copyright Act, 1957, and do not prejudice any rights subsisting in copyright. Provided that, where a layout-design incorporates a work protected by copyright, the proprietor of the copyright shall be duly acknowledged in the application. The Registrar may, if satisfied, record the application and proceed with examination. Failure to respond to any objection raised by the Registrar within the stipulated period may result in the application being deemed abandoned.

Any person who makes a false representation in a produced registrar application relating to a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. Where the registrar, upon examination of any such application, is satisfied that an alteration to a registered layout-design is necessary to correct a material error or to reflect a legitimate transfer of rights, an alteration certificate registration may be granted subject to the payment of a fee as prescribed. Failure to disclose all relevant information pertaining to prior art during the application process, or the deliberate misstatement of the date of first commercial exploitation, shall constitute an offence punishable as hereinbefore provided. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar concerning the validity of a produced registrar application shall be made to the High Court having jurisdiction.

A certificate of registration produced under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, and shall be admissible as evidence in all legal proceedings. The certificate registration produced, however, shall not be conclusive evidence of validity, and may be challenged on grounds permissible as provided herein, including but not limited to, prior art or lack of originality. Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design may rely upon the certificate registration as supporting evidence of ownership. Subject to verification by the appropriate authority, the date of creation as stated on the certificate registration shall be considered the relevant date for establishing priority. Provided that, failure to produce a certificate registration does not, *ipso facto*, invalidate a claim of rights under this Act.

The application for certificate registration produced shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed and shall contain a detailed description of the semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design for which protection is sought. Any layout-design registered under this Act shall be subject to a term of ten years from the date of filing the application, or until the expiry of ten years from the date of the first commercial exploitation, whichever is later. A request for expedited examination of an application may be granted, provided that the applicant pays an additional fee and demonstrates a compelling reason for such expedited processing. The Controller, upon satisfying themselves that the layout-design is novel and involves an inventive step, shall issue a certificate of registration. The certificate shall contain particulars of the layout-design, the applicant, and the date of registration, and shall be maintained as a public record. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of registration may file an appeal to the High Court.

The Controller, upon receipt of an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, shall examine the application and accompanying documentation to ascertain conformity with the requirements as provided herein. Where the Controller is satisfied that the application meets all prescribed criteria, a certificate of registration shall be issued to the applicant, confirming the legal protection afforded to the layout-design. The certificate registration produced shall serve as prima facie evidence of the validity of the layout-design and the proprietor’s exclusive right to exploit the same. 

However, the Controller may, prior to issuing such certificate, require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification deemed necessary for a complete assessment. Any request for supplementary details shall be communicated in writing, specifying a reasonable timeframe for response. Failure to comply with such a request within the stipulated period may result in the rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided under this Act. The Controller retains the authority to revoke a certificate if subsequent investigation reveals material misrepresentation in the original application.

Any person seeking certificate registration produced under this Act shall submit a detailed layout description, including all layers comprising the semiconductor integrated circuit, to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. The application shall be accompanied by a representation, in the form of a topologic diagram, clearly demonstrating the layout design’s configuration. A statement of ownership, affirming the applicant’s right to the layout-design, is mandatory, and must be duly notarized. Provided that, if the applicant is not the originator of the layout-design, a valid assignment agreement or license, demonstrating lawful authority, shall be furnished. The Registry may, subject to verification of the submitted materials and satisfaction of all procedural requirements as provided herein, grant a certificate of registration. Failure to accurately represent the layout-design or to disclose prior art may invalidate any certificate registration produced and render the applicant liable for penalties. All registered layouts shall be maintained in a publicly accessible database.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall be entitled to do so subject to the terms and conditions specified in the certificate of registration produced before the appropriate authority. Where the registered proprietor intends to assign the right, title, and interest in a layout-design, such assignment shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. A license to work a registered layout-design may be granted by the registered proprietor to any other person, and such license shall define the scope, duration, and territorial limits of the permitted exploitation. The registered proprietor may also grant exclusive licenses, subject to a requirement that the licensee diligently pursue commercialization of the layout-design. Failure to provide a duly registered assignment or license, as provided herein, shall render any commercial exploitation unlawful and subject to penalties under this Act. The certificate registration produced shall be prima facie evidence of valid ownership.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a certificate for a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, or by any order modifying or cancelling a registration, may file an appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The appellant shall deposit with the High Court a sum equivalent to the prescribed fee for registration of the layout-design, as a condition precedent to the entertaining of the appeal, which sum shall be refunded to the appellant if the appeal is allowed. Provided that, the High Court may, at its discretion, extend the time for filing an appeal if it is satisfied that sufficient cause existed for the delay. Any application for rectification of the register relating to a certificate registration produced shall be accompanied by a statement of the grounds on which the rectification is sought and any evidence in support thereof. The High Court’s decision shall be final and binding.

Any person intending to publish a translation work shall, prior to such publication, secure an assignment of copyright in the translation from the translator, unless expressly permitted otherwise by a written agreement between the publisher and the translator. Such assignment shall vest in the publisher all rights pertaining to the translation, including the right to reproduce, distribute, and adapt the work, subject to the provisions of this Act. Where the translator retains any rights in the translation, such retention shall be clearly delineated in the agreement, specifying the scope and duration of those retained rights. A publisher may, however, enter into a licensing agreement with the translator, granting specific rights for a defined period and royalty structure, provided that the terms are mutually agreed upon and documented in writing. Any dispute arising from the assignment or licensing of rights in a publish translation work shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the competent court. The owner of the original work’s copyright remains unaffected by the translation rights assignment.

A mark, for the purposes of this Act, shall mean a device, word, name, numeral, or the roman transliteration thereof, or a combination thereof, used or proposed to be used in relation to goods to indicate a connection in the course of trade between those goods and some person having the right either as proprietor or as a licensee to use the mark. Such a mark may be registered in a single class or multiple classes as prescribed under the rules made herein. A well-known mark, even if not registered, shall be afforded the highest level of protection, subject to the provisions relating to comparative advertising and unfair competition as provided herein. The mark must be distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others.

A mark, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be distinctive, and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. A mark consisting exclusively of descriptive character or characters which, in the language of the relevant trade, are commonly used to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, geographical origin or other characteristics of the goods or services, shall not be registered, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. However, a mark may be registered even if it is not inherently distinctive, provided that the applicant furnishes evidence of extensive and continuous use demonstrating acquired distinctiveness to the Registrar. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require the applicant to submit statutory declarations and supporting documentation to substantiate such claims of acquired distinctiveness. A mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion among the public, considering the overall similarities and the nature of the goods or services.

A registered mark shall vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any person who, not being the registered proprietor, uses in the course of trade, a mark identical with or deceptively similar to a registered mark, shall be liable for infringement as provided herein. However, a registered proprietor may, by a writing under his hand, grant licences to associate persons to use the mark, subject to such conditions as may be agreed upon. Where a mark has become deceptively similar to another mark and is likely to cause confusion, the Registrar may, upon application by the proprietor of the earlier mark, direct the rectification of the Register. The proprietor of a mark, aggrieved by any infringement, may institute civil proceedings for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both, against the infringer. Any remedy available under this Act shall be in addition to any other remedy available under any other law for the time being in force.

A mark, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be distinctive, and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. A mark consisting exclusively of a descriptive character or characters, or indicating the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of the goods or rendering of the services shall not be registered, unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use. Where a mark has not acquired distinctiveness, evidence of extensive and continuous use for a period of not less than five years shall be admissible to demonstrate such acquired distinctiveness. 

However, a mark shall not be deemed to be distinctive if it is customary in the trade to designate the goods or services with such mark, or if it is likely to cause confusion among the public. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to disclaim any part of the mark which is not distinctive. A mark that is deceptively similar to an existing mark shall not be registered, and any application for such a mark shall be refused.

A mark, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be distinctive, and not descriptive of the goods or services to which it relates, or commonly used in the trade to designate those goods or services. However, a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use, even if initially non-distinctive, may be registered subject to the Registrar being satisfied as to such acquired distinctiveness. Where a mark incorporates a geographical indication, registration shall be subject to compliance with the provisions of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, and the mark must not be likely to mislead the public as to the geographical origin of the goods or services. Any mark consisting exclusively of a shape resulting from the nature of the goods themselves or necessary to obtain a technical result shall not be registrable, provided that such shape is not capable of distinguishing the goods of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. An application for registration may be refused if the mark is scandalous or contrary to law.

Any person who applies a false trade mark to goods or packages, or sells, offers for sale, or distributes goods or packages bearing a false trade mark, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. A mark shall be deemed to be falsely applied if it is identical with or deceptively similar to a registered trade mark, and is applied without the consent of the proprietor. Provided that, where the application of the mark is made in good faith and without intent to deceive, the court may, subject to the payment of an adequate sum as damages to the proprietor, order the discharge of the accused. Any goods found to bear a false mark shall be deemed forfeited and may be destroyed as provided herein, and the costs of such destruction shall be borne by the offender. The Registrar may, upon application, direct the removal or obliteration of any such falsely applied mark.

Any registered mark, or a substantial part thereof, may be assigned or transmitted with or without goodwill, subject to the conditions, if any, recorded in the register relating to such mark. An assignment or transmission of a mark shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly executed by the assignor or transmitter, and the transferee or assignee. The Trade Marks Registry shall, upon receipt of an application for the registration of an assignment or transmission, examine the document and, if satisfied that it complies with the requirements of this Act, register the assignment or transmission. Where a mark is assigned with goodwill, the assignee shall be entitled to all the rights and remedies as if they were the original proprietor of the mark, but subject to any limitations or conditions specified in the assignment agreement. Any assignment not registered as provided herein shall be invalid as against any subsequent assignee. A licensee of a mark may, subject to the terms of the license, assign their interest in the license.

A mark, whether registered or unregistered, shall be deemed to be deceptively similar if, viewed as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, taking into account the overall impression created and the class of persons who are likely to purchase the goods or services in question. An application for rectification of the register, alleging that a registered mark is deceptively similar to a prior mark, may be filed with the Registrar, subject to the provisions of this Act. The Registrar, upon consideration of evidence submitted by both parties, shall issue an order either upholding the application or dismissing it, and such order shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. Provided that, if the Appellate Board finds that the Registrar’s order was based on a misinterpretation of evidence, it may direct a fresh hearing before a different Registrar. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board may, within ninety days, prefer an appeal to the High Court.

A mark, whether registered or unregistered, shall be deemed to be a trade mark within the meaning of this Act if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. The Registrar may, upon application and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, register a mark consisting of the shape of goods, their packaging, or a combination thereof, as a trade mark, provided that such shape does not result from the nature of the goods themselves or is essential to obtain a technical result. However, registration of a mark relating to package shall not confer exclusive rights to the shape of the goods contained therein. Any person aggrieved by the registration of a mark which incorporates a deceptive or misleading representation of the package may apply to the Registrar for rectification of the register. Such application shall be made within a period of one year from the date of registration, and shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the claim of deception. The Registrar, after due inquiry, may direct the amendment or cancellation of the registration as provided herein.

A mark, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be deemed to be distinctive if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, including the capacity to acquire distinctiveness through use. Any mark consisting exclusively of descriptive character relating to the goods or services, or capable of being directly identified by the trade name, shall not be registrable unless it has acquired distinctiveness prior to the date of application for registration. Where a mark incorporates a reference to place of origin of goods, registration may be refused if such reference is likely to deceive the public as to the actual origin. Subject to the provisions herein, a mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion among the public, considering the similarity of the mark and the similarity of the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar may, however, require evidence of actual use of the mark in relation to the specified goods or services before proceeding with registration.

Any person who falsely applies for the registration of a mark, knowing it to be already registered in the name of another, or who abets such application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a mark is subject to a prior respect filing application legitimately made and pending determination, any subsequent application for an identical or deceptively similar mark shall be deemed an act of unfair competition and attract a penalty equivalent to twice the official fee for registration. The Registrar may, as provided herein, direct the applicant to cease pursuing the application and may impose a further fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each day of continued pursuit after such direction. Any evidence obtained through fraudulent means relating to a mark shall not be admissible in proceedings under this Act. A false representation concerning the nature or geographical origin of a mark is also punishable as hereinbefore provided.

Any assignment of a registered mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument of assignment shall clearly identify the mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and state the consideration for the assignment, if any. Where an assignment is made without adequate consideration, the assignee may, as provided herein, be subject to claims from creditors of the assignor. Should the assignee fail to register the assignment within six months of its execution, the Registrar may, relating plaintiff forthwith, issue a notice requiring rectification of the register. A partial assignment of a mark, affecting only certain goods or services, is permissible, provided that it does not diminish the essential character of the mark as a whole. The assignor warrants to the assignee that they have full right and authority to assign the mark and that the mark is free from any encumbrances.

A mark, when applied for basic registration under this Act, shall be subject to examination as to its distinctiveness and shall not be registered if it is devoid of any distinctive character. However, an applicant may, prior to acceptance of the application, furnish evidence of acquired distinctiveness through actual use of the mark in commerce, demonstrating that a substantial and relevant section of the public recognizes the mark as identifying the applicant’s goods or services. Should the Registrar refuse registration based on lack of distinctiveness, the applicant may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the refusal. The Appellate Board, upon review, may uphold the Registrar’s decision, direct the Registrar to register the mark, or remit the matter for further consideration, provided that sufficient evidence of acquired distinctiveness is presented and the mark does not otherwise contravene the provisions of this Act. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review.

For the purposes of this Act, a “drug” shall mean any substance intended for use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of any disease or disorder in humans or animals, and shall include formulations, metabolites, and intermediates thereof. A substance may be considered a drug subject to its intended use, even if it also possesses characteristics of a cosmetic, foodstuff, or other article. Where a substance is presented as having therapeutic properties, it shall be deemed a drug as provided herein, notwithstanding any other classification. The Controller may, following expert consultation, determine whether a particular article falls within the definition of a drug under this Act, and such determination shall be final. Any mark associated with a counterfeit drug shall be subject to expedited removal proceedings.

Any person intending to register a trade mark for a drug, whether pharmaceutical or Ayurvedic, shall furnish with the application a certificate of standard quality issued by a laboratory recognized by the Controller General of Drugs, demonstrating adherence to the prevailing Indian Pharmacopoeia standards or equivalent internationally recognized standards. The certificate shall specifically detail the active pharmaceutical ingredient, excipients, and manufacturing process employed. Provided that, in the case of traditional Ayurvedic formulations, a certificate from an authorized research council under the Ministry of AYUSH, confirming the authenticity and composition of the drug, may be submitted in lieu of the aforementioned laboratory certificate. Registration shall be subject to verification of the submitted certificate and confirmation that the claimed drug does not contravene any provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, or any other applicable legislation concerning public health and safety, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application.

Any person manufacturing, selling, or distributing a drug bearing a registered trademark deceptively similar to another registered trademark, shall be liable to a suit for infringement as provided herein. However, no suit for infringement shall lie against a defendant who proves that the use of the trademark was necessary to describe the drug itself, or its character, quality, or intended purpose. A registered trademark owner may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from such acts, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to the infringement. Where a defendant proves that the drug was manufactured and sold under a license granted by the plaintiff, such license shall be deemed a complete defense, subject to the terms and conditions of the license. The court may, at its discretion, order the destruction or forfeiture of infringing labels and packaging materials. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the court may prefer an appeal to the appropriate appellate authority.

Any person manufacturing, selling, or distributing a drug, whether patented or generic, shall maintain a complete and accurate record of batch numbers, manufacturing dates, expiry dates, and distribution channels, as provided herein. Such records shall be open for inspection by an officer duly authorized by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, upon reasonable notice and subject to confidentiality undertakings. A trade mark applied to a drug formulation shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing registered trade mark for a similar pharmaceutical product, or if it falsely suggests a connection with another manufacturer. Where a drug is withdrawn from the market due to safety concerns, the trade mark owner shall promptly notify the Controller and provide details of the recall procedure. Any dispute regarding the authenticity or quality of a drug bearing a registered trade mark may be referred to the High Court having jurisdiction. Failure to comply with these provisions shall attract penalties including fines and suspension of trade mark rights.

Any person intending to register a trade mark for a drug, or a preparation containing a drug as a component, shall furnish with the application a certificate of registration issued by the licensing authority established under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, verifying compliance with all applicable standards and regulations pertaining to the manufacture and sale of such drug. Subject to the provisions herein, the Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional evidence of efficacy and safety, particularly where the drug is a novel formulation or intended for a sensitive patient population. Failure to provide a valid certificate or satisfactory evidence shall render the application liable to be rejected. A registered trade mark for a drug shall not confer any right to manufacture or sell a drug that does not conform to the prescribed standards, and any such act shall be a violation of this Act, irrespective of trade mark ownership. The mark’s use must also adhere to any packaging or labeling requirements mandated by the relevant pharmaceutical regulations.

Any person who manufactures for sale, sells, or otherwise distributes a spurious or adulterated drug, as defined in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. The manufacture, sale, or distribution of a drug bearing a counterfeit trade mark, or a mark deceptively similar thereto, shall constitute an infringement actionable as provided herein. Any packaging or labeling of a drug that falsely represents its efficacy, strength, or composition, with intent to deceive, is strictly prohibited. Where a complaint of such manufacture, sale, or distribution is made to a Magistrate, the Magistrate may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, order the seizure of the offending drugs and packaging. Any person convicted of an offence under this Act shall be liable to imprisonment not exceeding seven years, and to a fine not less than five lakh rupees. The court may, in addition to imprisonment and fine, order the forfeiture of any equipment used in the commission of the offence.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark used in relation to a drug, or a class of drugs, shall be subject to the prior written consent of the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, established under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Such consent may be granted or refused, and shall be accompanied by a reasoned order, within a period of ninety days from the date of application. Where the assignment involves a transfer of manufacturing rights, the transferee shall demonstrate to the satisfaction of the aforementioned Organisation, adequate facilities for maintaining the quality and efficacy of the drug as originally registered. 

A license granted for the use of a trade mark appurtenant to a drug shall not confer upon the licensee any right to sub-license or further assign such rights without the express permission of the trade mark proprietor. Provided that, any dispute regarding the scope of such license, or the quality control measures implemented by the licensee, may be referred to arbitration as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the assignment or license voidable at the option of the trade mark proprietor.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark for a drug, or varying the terms of registration of such trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within three months from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registrar, reverse it, or modify it, or may remit the case back to the Registrar with such directions as it may deem fit. Provided that no appeal shall lie from an order refusing registration where the refusal is based on the grounds that the trade mark is deceptive or likely to cause confusion, or is contrary to decency or morality, or comprises scandalous or offensive matter, unless the Appellate Board is satisfied that substantial questions of law are involved. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark deceptively similar to a registered trade mark used in relation to a drug, or packages or sells, offers for sale, or distributes any drug bearing such deceptively similar trade mark, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Where it is established that a trade mark has been falsely applied to a drug, or that the packaging of such drug has been falsified with intent to mislead, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, direct the removal or obliteration of the offending mark or packaging. Any person dealing in goods where a trade mark is used falsifying trade shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein, and such goods shall be deemed counterfeit. The provisions of this Act are in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other law for the time being in force relating to drugs and pharmaceuticals.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark to any drug, or to the packaging of any drug, knowing or having reason to believe that such application is likely to deceive the public, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The provisions of this Act shall apply to all descriptions of goods, including those intended for export, and any drug manufactured or imported in contravention of these provisions shall be deemed to be counterfeit goods. Provided that, where the drug is essential for life-saving treatment, the court may, subject to payment of adequate compensation to the rightful owner, order the continued manufacture or import of such drug for a limited period. Any evidence of adulteration or misbranding of a drug shall be admissible in proceedings under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing registration of a trade mark for a drug, or ordering its rectification, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the decision. However, such appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant demonstrates a substantial likelihood of confusion with a registered trade mark, or that the refusal was based on an erroneous interpretation of evidence relating to the drug’s efficacy or safety. The Farmers Rights Authority, where evidence presented concerns traditional knowledge relating to medicinal properties of a plant-derived drug, may be invited to submit an amicus curiae brief to the Appellate Board. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Registry’s decision, a further appeal may lie to the High Court, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Any claim of prior use as a defense against infringement relating to a drug shall be subject to rigorous proof of continuous use for a period of not less than five years immediately preceding the date of the application for registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a “drug” shall mean any substance intended for use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of any disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and shall include formulations, metabolites, and intermediates thereof, whether synthetic or naturally derived. Where a drug’s packaging incorporates a design registered layout, such layout shall be considered integral to the overall trade mark assessment, subject to proof of distinctiveness and non-functionality as provided herein. Any alteration to a registered design layout affecting the drug’s presentation may constitute misrepresentation under this Act. The Controller may, upon application, direct removal of the layout from the register if it is found to be deceptive or likely to cause confusion.

For the purposes of this Act, “food” shall mean any substance or article, whether processed, semi-processed, or raw, intended for human consumption, and shall include beverages, chewing gum, and any ingredient used in the preparation of such substances or articles. The term “food” encompasses agricultural produce, whether in its natural state or having undergone simple processing such as cleaning, grading, or sorting. Any article marketed or presented as a food substitute, or intended to be used as a component in the preparation of food, shall also be deemed to be “food” as provided herein. A “geographical indication” relating to food shall be considered a special category of trade mark, subject to the provisions regarding agricultural goods, and shall denote the origin of the food in a specific geographical area where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the food is essentially attributable to its geographical origin.

Any natural or juridical person seeking registration of a trade mark for food products, or any ingredient thereof, shall furnish with the application a detailed composition analysis certified by a laboratory accredited by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. The application shall further disclose the geographical origin of any key ingredient, particularly if claiming traditional or regional specificity, subject to verification by the competent authority as provided herein. A mark incorporating a claim of nutritional benefit shall be supported by documented scientific evidence demonstrating such benefit, and may be subject to scrutiny by a committee of experts appointed by the Registrar. Registration of a trade mark for food shall not confer any right to exclusively use a generic appellation or a term commonly used to describe the food itself, even if presented in a distinctive manner. Provided that, a trade mark combining a generic term with a fanciful element may be registrable if it acquires distinctiveness through continuous use. The Registrar may require an affidavit attesting to the bona fide use of the mark in commerce relating to food.

Any person who manufactures, packages, or sells food products bearing a trade mark not registered in accordance with this Act, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees for each such offence. However, such liability shall not apply where the person proves that they had reasonable grounds to believe a similar trade mark was legitimately in use by another entity prior to their commencement of business. A registered proprietor of a trade mark used on food shall have the right to seek an injunction restraining any unauthorized use of that mark, or any deceptively similar mark, likely to cause confusion amongst consumers. Provided that, the Court may, subject to the equities of the case, grant a license to the defendant to continue using the mark upon payment of reasonable royalty. Any appeal arising from a decision relating to such injunctions shall lie before the High Court, and must be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against. The burden of proof regarding the genuineness of the food product and its compliance with relevant standards rests with the manufacturer.

Any application for registration of a trade mark for goods falling within the class of prepared foods, or ingredients thereof, shall be subject to a rigorous examination as to its potential to mislead the public regarding the nature, quality, or origin of said food. The Registrar may, at any stage of the application process, require the applicant to furnish detailed compositional analysis and manufacturing processes, particularly where the mark suggests a specific geographical indication or traditional preparation method. Where a mark incorporates a claim of nutritional benefit, supporting scientific evidence, conforming to standards established by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, shall be submitted. 

Provided that, a mark descriptive of the food itself, or commonly used to describe the characteristics of such food, shall not be registrable unless it has acquired distinctiveness through continuous use. The Registrar shall also consider any existing standards relating to labelling and packaging of food, as provided herein, to ensure consumer protection and prevent unfair competition. Any dispute regarding the use of a mark in relation to food, and its conformity with these provisions, may be referred to the appropriate appellate authority.

Any application for registration of a trade mark for food products shall be subject to verification by the designated Food Safety Authority, confirming adherence to standards prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. A trade mark incorporating a geographical indication relating to food shall require a certificate of origin from the relevant authority empowered to verify such indications, provided that the application demonstrates a consistent and verifiable link between the food’s origin and its characteristics. Failure to furnish such certificates or satisfactory evidence of compliance with food safety regulations may result in the rejection of the application. Where a trade mark is used in relation to organic food, certification from a body accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Certification Bodies is mandatory. The Registrar may, at any time, require updated certification to ensure continued compliance with relevant standards as provided herein. Any misrepresentation regarding the nature or origin of the food, conveyed through the trade mark, shall be grounds for revocation.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a trade mark deceptively to any food article, or packages containing food, shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. The fraudulent or erroneous application of a trade mark to food, including but not limited to misrepresenting its origin, ingredients, or nutritional value, constitutes a violation. Where a mark is applied to food in a manner likely to mislead the public as to the true character or quality of said food, a civil remedy for damages may be pursued by any aggrieved party. Any evidence of adulteration of food, coupled with deceptive trade mark use, shall be considered an aggravating factor in determining penalties. A court, upon conviction, may impose a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may also order the seizure and destruction of the offending food articles. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, subject to the provisions herein.

Any person desiring to manufacture, sell, or otherwise distribute food products bearing a registered trade mark, shall obtain a license from the proprietor of the trade mark, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon. The licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the geographical territory, duration, and scope of permitted use, including specific food categories covered by the license. Assignment of rights relating to the manufacture or sale of such food shall be permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to abide by the terms of the original license agreement or obtains a fresh license from the trade mark proprietor. Where a license is granted for a limited period, renewal may be sought by the licensee, and the proprietor shall not unreasonably withhold consent, considering established market practices and the licensee’s demonstrated good faith. Failure to comply with the provisions of this Act regarding licensing and assignment shall render the offender liable to penalties as prescribed, and may result in the revocation of the license. Any dispute arising from these provisions shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person claiming trade mark registration for a mark used or proposed to be used in relation to food products shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, a clear and verifiable provenance of ingredients and adherence to standards prescribed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. An application may be rejected where the mark suggests a nutritional benefit not substantiated by scientific evidence, or where the descriptive elements falsely represent the origin or composition of the food. Appeals against such rejection shall lie before the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates reasonable grounds for believing the Registrar erred in assessing the evidence. Furthermore, a registered proprietor of a food trade mark shall be liable for misrepresentation if the quality of the food sold under that mark materially deviates from the standards declared at the time of registration, subject to a right of defence before the Board. Any dispute regarding the geographical indication of a food product shall be resolved in accordance with the provisions relating to geographical indications under this Act.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies a false trade mark or falsely represents goods, including any edible food product, as being of a particular quality or standard, shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Where an appeal against a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a registered trade mark involving such falsely represented food has been admitted, the period for compliance with any remedial order issued by the Registrar may, subject to the discretion of the appellate authority, be extended, provided that such extension shall not exceed ninety days from the date of the original order. Failure to comply with a final order, even after an appeal admitted expiry, shall render the offender liable to a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. Any food found to be in violation of this provision shall be liable to seizure and destruction.

Any person who avails of remedies under this Act in respect of goods providing services shall be bound by such conditions as may be prescribed. Where a registered trade mark is used by a person other than the registered proprietor, and such use constitutes an infringement of the trade mark, the registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute legal proceedings for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both. A court, when granting an injunction under this Act, may require the defendant to provide an account of profits made by the unlawful use of the trade mark. Provided that, no injunction shall be granted if the plaintiff has acquiesced in the use of the trade mark by the defendant, or if the defendant can prove that the use is necessary for the purpose of comparative advertising, subject to the conditions prescribed. Any order made by a court under this Act shall be enforceable by that court as if it were a decree. The registered proprietor may, at any time, assign the trade mark to any other person, subject to any conditions specified in the register.

Goods providing services shall, for the purposes of registration under this Act, be classified in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, deem necessary to adapt said classification to goods or services commonly available in India. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark for goods providing services shall clearly specify the class and description of those goods or services in the application, and any ambiguity or lack of clarity may result in objection by the Trade Marks Registry. Where goods fall within multiple classes, a separate application, accompanied by the prescribed fee, shall be filed for each class. The Registrar may, however, require an applicant to limit the specification of goods or services if it is considered unduly broad or lacking in specificity, provided that such requirement is communicated to the applicant in writing with reasons stated. Any dispute regarding the proper classification of goods providing services shall be subject to the appellate procedures as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing to register a trade mark, or varying the conditions of registration, or dismissing an application for revival of a trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registrar, or reverse it, or vary it, or remit the case back to the Registrar for fresh consideration, and shall record the reasons for its decision. Where an appeal relates to goods providing services falling within the Schedule to this Act, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion, direct that the registration be limited to a specific area or class of goods or services. Provided that no appeal shall lie against an order refusing registration where the Registrar has found a prior identical trade mark already registered for identical goods providing services.

For the purposes of this Act, goods shall be understood as movable property, and shall include all materials, substances, articles, and things, whether raw, processed, or manufactured. Services, however, shall denote the performance of any action, undertaking, or labour for the benefit of another, and may encompass intangible benefits conferred. A transmissible case arises where rights in a registered trade mark, relating to specific goods providing services, are legitimately assigned, transferred, or otherwise devolved to a successor in title, subject to the provisions herein. Any such transmission shall not prejudice the validity of the registration, provided that the transferor has duly extinguished their own rights and the transferee meets all requirements as stipulated under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application, record such transmission.

Any application for registration of a trade mark for goods or services relating to biological resources, or traditional knowledge associated with such resources, shall require a declaration as to the source and origin of said resources, and evidence of prior informed consent obtained from the concerned communities, where applicable, as provided herein. The Trade Marks Registry may, prior to registration, require the applicant to demonstrate compliance with the provisions of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. Furthermore, any royalties or benefits accruing from the commercial exploitation of such registered trade marks, pertaining to goods providing services derived from biological resources, shall be contributed to the National Gene Fund, in accordance with guidelines established by the Central Government. Failure to provide accurate information or comply with these requirements shall render the application liable to be refused, or the registration subject to revocation, under this Act. The Registry shall maintain a public register of all such declarations and contributions.

The Registrar may, upon receipt of an application and subject to the provisions of this Act, order the cancelling registration of a trade mark, if satisfied that the trade mark has been registered contrary to any law for the time being in force. An application for cancelling registration shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement of the grounds on which the cancellation is sought. Provided that, where the application alleges non-use, it shall demonstrate continuous non-use for a period of five years preceding the date of the application. The registered proprietor shall be entitled to file a counter-statement, and the Registrar, after considering the evidence, may, if satisfied of the grounds for cancelling registration, make an order accordingly. Any person aggrieved by such order may appeal to the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by the continued registration of a trade mark on grounds specified herein may apply to the Appellate Board for cancellation of such registration. Such application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by a statement of the grounds upon which the applicant seeks the cancellation, supported by evidence as may be required. The Appellate Board, upon receiving such application, shall cause a notice to be issued to the registered proprietor, requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated time shall be deemed an admission of the grounds alleged in the application. 

The Appellate Board, after considering the application, the counter-statement, and any evidence submitted by both parties, may, if satisfied that the grounds for cancellation exist, order the cancelling of the registration either in whole or in part, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. Provided that no order for cancelling registration shall be made unless the applicant has shown genuine use of a similar mark for a period of not less than five years prior to the filing of the application.

The Registrar may, after giving the registered proprietor an opportunity to be heard and subject to the provisions of this Act, order the cancelling of registration of a trade mark upon a finding of non-use for a continuous period of five years. Such finding shall be predicated upon evidence satisfactory to the Registrar, demonstrating both the period of non-use and diligent search efforts undertaken to ascertain current usage. Provided that, if the registered proprietor demonstrates legitimate reasons for non-use, such as government restrictions or unavoidable circumstances affecting trade, the Registrar may extend the period of non-use considered. An application for cancelling registration shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a statement detailing the grounds for the claim. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such application, notify the registered proprietor and afford them a period of three months to submit a counter-statement. Failure to submit a counter-statement within the stipulated period shall be deemed an admission of the allegations contained within the application.

Any person aggrieved by the continued registration of a trade mark, alleging that it is devoid of any distinctive character or has fallen into disuse, may petition the Appellate Board for cancellation of such registration. Such petition shall be accompanied by evidence substantiating the claim of non-use for a period not less than five years, and demonstrating that the mark has ceased to be capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. The registered proprietor shall be served with a notice of such petition and afforded an opportunity to present their case, including evidence of continued use or legitimate reasons for non-use, subject to the provisions relating to excusable circumstances. The Appellate Board, upon considering the evidence and submissions, may, if satisfied that the grounds for cancellation exist, order the cancellation of the registration, either in whole or in part, and may also direct the rectification of the Register accordingly. Any decision of the Appellate Board regarding cancelling registration shall be final and binding, unless appealed to the High Court.

Any person registered as the proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Trade Marks Registry to amend the register in respect of the trade mark. The application to amend register shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a statement of the alterations desired to be made and the grounds on which the application is based. Where the amendment sought relates to a matter of substance, the Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to satisfy it as to the correctness of the particulars on which the application is founded. Provided that no amendment shall be made which would substantially affect the identity of the trade mark. The Registrar may, after considering the application and any evidence submitted, allow or refuse the application, and shall notify the applicant of the decision.

Any person desiring to amend the register in respect of a registered trade mark shall submit a petition to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed. The petition shall clearly state the amendment sought, the grounds justifying such amendment, and shall be accompanied by a statement of use demonstrating bona fide adoption and continued use of the trade mark as amended. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence and satisfaction that the amendment does not adversely affect the rights of prior applicants or owners of existing marks, direct the amendment of the register. Provided that, where the amendment involves a change in the representation of the trade mark, a fresh search report shall be obtained and considered. Failure to demonstrate continued use, or evidence of intent to deceive, shall be grounds for rejection of the petition to amend register. The Registrar’s decision on the petition shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court as provided herein.

Any registered proprietor desiring to amend the register in respect of a trade mark, particularly concerning a transfer of rights or a change in ownership arising from a licensing agreement or assignment, shall submit a request to the Registrar in the manner as prescribed. Such request shall clearly delineate the nature of the amendment sought, including details of the assignee or licensee, the scope of rights transferred, and any limitations imposed upon the use of the mark. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the authenticity of the transfer and satisfaction that the amendment does not conflict with existing rights or cause confusion, allow the request and amend the register accordingly. Provided that, where the amendment involves a change in the proprietor’s name or address due to a corporate restructuring or merger, supporting documentation evidencing the legal basis for such change shall be furnished. Failure to provide complete and accurate information may result in the rejection of the request to amend register. The amended register shall be the conclusive evidence of ownership and rights.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Registrar to amend the register in respect of the trade mark. Such application shall be in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by a statement of the alterations desired to be made and the grounds on which the application is based. Where the application seeks to amend the register to reflect a change in the ownership of the trade mark due to a merger or acquisition involving a company, supporting documentation demonstrating the legal transfer of rights shall be furnished. The Registrar may, after examining the application and requiring such evidence as may be deemed necessary, allow the application, either in whole or in part, or may refuse the same. Should the Registrar allow the application to amend register, notice of the amendment shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any aggrieved person may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition to the proposed amendment, and the provisions relating to opposition proceedings shall apply.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, or an order of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, as provided herein, may prefer an appeal to the High Court. The appeal specified period for such preference shall be three months from the date on which the decision or order sought to be appealed against is communicated to the appellant. Provided that, the High Court may, for sufficient cause, extend this period by a further period not exceeding thirty days. Subject to the provisions contained herein, an appeal shall not be entertained if filed beyond the extended period, unless the High Court is satisfied that the delay was due to circumstances beyond the control of the appellant. All appeals shall be filed in accordance with the rules of the High Court.

A new variety shall be considered a variety substantially derived from another, registered variety if the propagation or harvesting of the new variety is wholly dependent on the registered variety, except for those traits that are naturally occurring or have been modified through generally observed and practiced methods of breeding. Provided that, a new variety exhibiting essentially the same characteristics as the registered variety, but differing only in one or more traits, may still qualify as a new variety if such differences are attributable to traits not substantially derived from the registered variety and do not affect its overall performance or utility. Subject to the provisions herein, determination of substantial derivation shall consider the overall similarity of characteristics, taking into account the specific characteristics for which the registered variety is protected. Any dispute regarding whether a variety is a new variety or substantially derived shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority.

A variety shall be considered a new variety for the purposes of registration under this Act, provided that it satisfies the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability as prescribed. Novelty shall be determined by reference to all publicly available knowledge relating to plant varieties, including documented evidence of cultivation or sale, at the date of filing of the application. A variety exhibiting substantial similarity to a known, commonly cultivated variety, or a variety derived from a parent line widely grown in the country, shall not be deemed novel. However, a variety may still qualify as new if it possesses a unique combination of traits not previously observed, subject to demonstration of its distinctiveness through comparative trials. The applicant shall furnish evidence of the origin and development of the variety, including the date of the first exploitation of the propagating material, to substantiate a claim of novelty. Any variety essentially derived from another variety, where the essentially derived variety is not itself a new variety, shall not be eligible for independent registration.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear distinction from any commonly known or publicly available variety, assessed through characteristics including morphology, physiology, and, where relevant, DNA profiling as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, a farmer who has bred or developed a new variety may apply for registration, subject to demonstrating that the variety possesses substantial characteristics differing from existing registered varieties and that it has been commercially exploited for a period of not less than three years. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a new variety shall have recourse to an appropriate tribunal, and may seek an injunction restraining further exploitation, as well as damages for loss suffered. The tribunal may, at its discretion, order the seizure and destruction of any propagating material of the infringing variety, and shall consider the legitimate interests of farmers in exercising their rights to save, use, sow, re-sow, and sell farm-saved seed, subject to the conditions prescribed herein.

A plant variety shall be considered a new variety for the purposes of registration under this Act if it satisfies the requirements of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, as determined by the Plant Variety Committee. Novelty shall be established by demonstrating that the variety has not been made available to the public, by sale or any other means, before the date of filing of the application for registration. However, a variety may be deemed novel even if it incorporates traits derived from commonly known or publicly available genetic material, provided that the combination of traits results in a plant that is substantially different from any known variety. Distinctiveness shall be assessed by comparison with other varieties whose characteristics are substantially similar. Uniformity requires that the variety consistently exhibits the specified characteristics across successive generations, and stability implies that those characteristics remain unchanged. Subject to the provisions herein, the Plant Variety Committee may require demonstration of these characteristics through field trials conducted in accordance with established protocols.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered distinct if it demonstrates the clearly distinguishable characteristics from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge. Such distinctness shall be established through a detailed description of the plant’s morphological, physiological, and, where applicable, molecular characteristics, conforming to the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. However, a variety which is essentially derived from another variety, as defined herein, shall not be considered a new variety unless the applicant demonstrates significant characteristics differentiating it from the initial variety. Provided that, the applicant fulfills the requirements regarding novelty, distinctness, uniformity, and stability, and submits evidence of the variety’s origin and breeder’s entitlement, registration may be granted subject to payment of the prescribed fees and compliance with all other provisions of this Act. Any false representation regarding the new variety’s characteristics shall render the registration voidable.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear distinction from any commonly known or publicly available variety, and such distinction shall be evidenced by objective characteristics as determined through prescribed trials. Provided that, a variety derived from an essentially derived variety, even if possessing novel traits, may be registered only subject to the rights of the breeder of the initial or essentially derived variety, and failure to secure such breeder’s consent shall constitute an infringement punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Any person falsely representing a non-distinct variety as a new variety, with intent to deceive, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The Registrar may, however, waive the penalty in cases of demonstrable hardship.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be deemed to possess novelty if it has not been exploited, sold or otherwise disposed of by any person anywhere in the world before the date of application for registration. Provided that, any act of exploitation, sale or disposal occurring not earlier than one year before the date of application shall not be considered for the purposes of determining novelty, subject to the provisions relating to farmer’s rights. Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new variety may apply for its registration, and shall submit a declaration affirming exclusive ownership of, or a valid license to, the genetic material constituting the variety. Assignment of rights to a new variety, whether whole or partial, shall be permissible and shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. A licensee of a new variety may, subject to the terms of the license, further assign their rights to a third party, with due notification to the breeder. The breeder retains the right to revoke a license in cases of material breach of the licensing agreement, as provided herein.

A dispute regarding the distinctiveness of a claimed new variety shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, provided that any person alleging a lack of novelty bears the burden of proving that the characteristics of the subject variety are not substantially different from those of any other variety commonly known or publicly available before the date of filing of the application. Should the Authority determine that the variety does not meet the criteria for a new variety, the applicant may appeal to the High Court, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and within a period of sixty days from the date of the Authority’s decision.
