The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case an appeal may be made to the Supreme Court. A variety essentially derived from another variety, while not itself a new variety, may be subject to royalty arrangements as provided herein, and the breeder of the initial variety shall have the right to equitable remuneration.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear distinction from any commonly known or publicly available variety, substantiated by documentary evidence acceptable to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new variety shall submit an application for registration, detailing the characteristics of the variety and the lineage tracing its development. The breeder of a registered breeder variety may, subject to the provisions herein, assign or license the rights to exploit the variety to any other person or entity, upon terms mutually agreed. Such assignment or license shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority to ensure enforceability against third parties. Provided that, any licensing agreement shall not unduly restrict access to the variety for research and breeding purposes, and shall include provisions for equitable benefit sharing with farmers and local communities contributing to the development of the variety. Failure to comply with the registration requirements for assignments or licenses may render such transactions void.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear and discernible advancement over existing, commonly known varieties, substantiated by documented evidence of its characteristics and performance. Any dispute regarding the novelty of a claimed new variety shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, following a process of comparative analysis with documented prior art, including but not limited to, publicly available germplasm data and expert testimony. Provided that, where the claimed new variety incorporates a unique layout-design of a substantially derived variety, the breeder of the substantially derived variety may file an objection, asserting infringement of their rights relating to the original layout-design. Such objection shall be considered alongside evidence of the new variety’s distinctiveness. An appeal from any decision of the Authority regarding novelty or layout-design shall lie before the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act. The burden of proof regarding novelty rests with the applicant.

Any person aggrieved by any act of the Controller inconsistent with the provisions of this Act may, subject to the provisions of this section, apply to the High Court for rectification of the register. The application shall be made in the prescribed form and shall state the grounds on which the applicant seeks rectification. The Controller shall, where an application for rectification is made, furnish to the applicant a statement of the grounds on which the Controller proposes to reject the application, and the applicant may, within one month from the receipt of such statement, file a reply thereto. Should the Controller, after considering the reply, still propose to reject the application, notice rectification shall be effected in accordance with the procedure prescribed by the rules. Provided that no rectification shall be made without affording the patentee an opportunity of being heard. The High Court may, if satisfied that the rectification is necessary, direct the Controller to make the necessary amendments in the register.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, or alleging title to a patent based on prior rights, may apply to the High Court for notice rectification of the register, subject to payment of a fee as prescribed in the Schedule. The applicant shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Court, a prima facie case for rectification and shall serve a copy of the application, along with supporting evidence, upon the patentee and the Controller of Patents. Failure to serve notice as provided herein shall render the application inadmissible. The High Court, upon hearing both parties and reviewing the evidence, may order the rectification of the register, including amendment of claims, or may dismiss the application with costs. Any false representation made in an application for notice rectification shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The decision of the High Court shall be final and binding, save for appeal to the Supreme Court as provided by law.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be in writing and shall clearly identify the patent and the interest assigned. The assignee shall, within a period of six months from the date of assignment, furnish to the Controller a copy of the instrument of assignment, duly authenticated by both the assignor and the assignee. Failure to comply with this requirement may render the assignment unenforceable as against subsequent assignees or licensees. Where a notice of assignment is received by the Controller, a rectification of the register of patents may be undertaken to reflect the change in ownership. 

However, notice rectification shall not be permitted if the assignment is demonstrated to be fraudulent or contrary to public order. Subject to verification of the instrument and satisfaction of all applicable fees, the Controller may record the assignment in the register. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment, or the accuracy of details provided therein, shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of Patents shall, subject to the provisions herein, apply to the High Court for notice rectification. Such application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant entry in the register and a statement of the grounds on which the rectification is sought. The High Court may, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, direct notice to be issued to the patentee and any other person likely to be affected by the rectification. Provided that, where the rectification sought relates to a matter of public interest, the High Court may dispense with the requirement of notice. Any party served with notice under this provision may file a written response within a period of sixty days, failing which, the High Court may proceed ex parte. The High Court’s decision on notice rectification shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court as provided under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification of such omission or incorrect statement. Such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall set forth the particulars of the omission or incorrect statement and the grounds upon which the applicant relies. The High Court, upon being satisfied that the omission or incorrect statement exists and that the applicant has a sufficient interest, may direct notice to be issued to the patentee or other interested parties, requiring them to show cause why the register should not be rectified. Where a party fails to respond to such notice within the time prescribed, the High Court may proceed to rectify the register *ex parte*, subject to such conditions as it deems fit.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, or alleging themselves to be the true and first inventor, may apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification of the register. Such application shall be in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, and shall clearly state the grounds for seeking rectification, supported by relevant evidence as provided herein. The Controller, upon receipt of such application, shall cause a notice to be served upon the patentee and any other interested parties, affording them an opportunity to file a counter-statement. Should the Controller deem the application well-founded and the evidence satisfactory, they may, after considering all submissions, order the necessary amendments to the register. However, any rectification affecting the validity of the patent shall be subject to a separate legal proceeding before a competent court, as determined under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, or by any entry wrongly remaining on the register, may apply to the High Court for rectification thereof, subject to the provisions of this Act. The applicant shall demonstrate a sufficient proprietary interest in the patent or application in question, and shall serve a notice of such application upon the patentee or applicant, as the case may be. Where direct notice rectification is sought, the applicant must prove that the party against whom rectification is sought had actual knowledge of the grounds for rectification at the time the patent was granted or the application was filed. The High Court may, if satisfied that the rectification is just and equitable, order the register to be rectified accordingly. Provided that, the High Court may require the applicant to furnish security for costs, if it appears that the application is frivolous or vexatious. Any order made under this Act shall be final and binding on all parties.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of Patents, and desiring rectification thereof, shall submit a petition to the High Court having jurisdiction. The petition shall clearly identify the specific entry requiring rectification and state the grounds upon which the petitioner relies for the proposed amendment. The High Court, upon receiving such petition, shall issue notice to the patentee and any other person whose interests may be affected by the rectification sought. A direct notice rectification procedure, as provided herein, shall be followed where the grounds for rectification are based solely on facts appearing on the face of the register or official documents. The High Court may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, direct the Controller of Patents to amend the register accordingly. Provided that, if the rectification involves a substantial change to the scope of the patent, a full hearing with evidence may be required. The Controller shall effect the rectification within thirty days of receiving the High Court’s direction. Any person served with notice under this provision shall file a response within the stipulated timeframe.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification of such omission or incorrect statement. Such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall clearly identify the specific entry or entries sought to be rectified, along with supporting evidence demonstrating the grounds for rectification. The High Court, upon being satisfied that sufficient cause exists, may issue notice to the patent holder and any other interested parties, requiring them to show cause why the rectification should not be effected. Provided that, where the rectification relates to a matter of public interest, the High Court may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, dispense with the requirement of notice to the patent holder. The High Court shall, after considering the submissions of all parties, pass an order directing the Controller of Patents to make the necessary amendments to the register, and such order shall be final and binding. Any amendment made pursuant to this process shall be recorded in the register and shall be deemed to have been made as of the date of the original entry.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification of such omission or incorrect statement, provided that such application shall be made within a period of twelve months from the date of the act giving rise to the grievance. The High Court, upon being satisfied that the omission or incorrect statement materially affects the rights of the applicant, shall issue a notice to the patentee and any other interested party, directing them to show cause why the register should not be rectified. Failure to respond to such notice within thirty days shall be deemed an admission of the grievance and the High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, order the rectification accordingly. Any person knowingly making a false statement in an application for rectification shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both.

Any assignment of a patent, or an interest therein, shall be evidenced by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and attested by at least two witnesses, and shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of assignments. Where a patentee, or a person deriving title under him, desires to rectify the register to reflect a valid assignment not currently recorded, they may apply to the appropriate High Court for direct notice rectification. Such application shall include a certified copy of the instrument of assignment and a statement of the grounds upon which rectification is sought. The High Court may, if satisfied that the assignment is valid and that sufficient notice has been given to all interested parties, order the register to be rectified accordingly. Should the assignment be contingent, the instrument must clearly specify the conditions precedent to its completion, and registration may be deferred until those conditions are met, subject to the discretion of the High Court. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the assignment unenforceable.

Any person aggrieved by any omission or incorrect statement in the register of patents, may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification of such omission or incorrect statement, provided that such application shall be made within a period of one year from the date of the act giving rise to the grievance. The applicant shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Court, a prima facie case establishing the error and potential prejudice suffered as a result thereof. The High Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct the Controller of Patents to issue notice to any person whose interests may be affected by the proposed rectification. Any party served with such notice may file a written statement within thirty days, contesting the application and presenting evidence in support of their position. The High Court’s decision on the rectification application shall be final and binding, and may include an order for costs. Appeals from such decisions shall lie to the Supreme Court, as provided herein.

Any person alleging that the particulars of a registered proprietor’s mark are deficient or misleading, or that a registered mark is otherwise not in accordance with the provisions of this Act, may apply to the High Court for direct notice rectification of the register. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a reasonable basis for the claim, and shall clearly specify the particulars sought to be amended or removed. Where the applicant demonstrates that the registered proprietor has demonstrably failed to use the proprietor use mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered for a continuous period of five years, the High Court may, subject to satisfactory proof of due diligence exercised by the proprietor, order rectification. Failure to comply with an order for rectification within ninety days shall render the registration liable to revocation, and the proprietor may be subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Any false claim made under this provision shall be punishable as contempt of court.

Any person claiming legal title to a patent, or an interest in a patent, arising from an assignment, transmission or operation of law, may apply to the Controller for direct notice rectification of the register where such title or interest is not reflected accurately. Such application for rectification shall be accompanied by evidence establishing the claimant’s right and a certified copy of the instrument, if any, effecting the transfer of interest. The Controller may, subject to verification of submitted documents and satisfaction of due process as provided herein, direct amendment of the register to reflect the correct ownership. A filing application relating to a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall also be considered as evidence of a legitimate interest for the purposes of rectification. Provided that, the Controller may require further evidence or conduct a hearing before issuing a rectification order, ensuring all parties with a demonstrable interest are afforded an opportunity to be heard. The Controller’s decision on rectification shall be final, unless appealed to the appropriate appellate authority.

Direct notice rectification of the register of patents shall be permissible where a person aggrieved asserts a right to challenge the validity of a patent, or a right to be registered as the patentee, based on grounds as provided herein. Any notice applicant seeking direct rectification must demonstrate sufficient interest and provide clear and unambiguous evidence substantiating the grounds for rectification. The High Court, upon receiving such notice, may direct the Controller to rectify the register accordingly, subject to a reasoned order and opportunity for the patentee to be heard. Provided that, the High Court may, at any stage of proceedings relating to direct notice rectification, require the notice applicant to satisfy such conditions as it deems necessary for the proper conduct of the case. Any rectification ordered shall be recorded in the register.

A person may apply to the Trade Marks Registry to register trade mark in respect of goods or services of a particular class, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. An application for registration shall include a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services to which it relates. The Registry may, after examination, accept or refuse the application, and shall notify the applicant of its decision. Where a trade mark is accepted, it shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, and any person may oppose the registration within the prescribed time. A registered trade mark shall be evidence of ownership, and the right to use the trade mark, subject to any limitations or conditions as may be specified in the register. The Registrar may, with reasonable cause, require evidence of genuine use of the trade mark.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark used or proposed to be used shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for the register trade mark, and upon such application and subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar shall, if satisfied that the trade mark is capable of being distinguished, and is not descriptive or deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, proceed to register it. Provided that, where a trade mark consists of a well-known mark, registration shall not be refused solely on the ground that it is descriptive. Failure to accurately declare prior rights or to disclose relevant information during the registration process shall render the registration voidable and subject the applicant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any person who falsely represents a trade mark as registered shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, at any time, require additional evidence to verify the veracity of claims made in support of a register trade mark.

A case proceeding concerning the rectification of the register shall be instituted either by way of opposition to an application for registration, or by way of a separate rectification proceeding initiated by any person aggrieved by the continued registration of a trade mark, or by the Registrar acting *suo motu* upon reasonable grounds. Such a proceeding may address grounds including, but not limited to, a trade mark being devoid of distinctive character, or its use being likely to deceive or cause confusion. Where a rectification proceeding results in a finding of non-use for a continuous period of five years, the registration may be revoked, subject to the provisions relating to revival of abandoned trade marks as provided herein. The High Court shall have jurisdiction to hear appeals arising from decisions made in any case proceeding.

Any person claiming ownership of a registered trade mark, or a right to its use, and desiring to institute a case proceeding relating to an alleged infringement or for rectification of the register, shall file a statement with the Trade Marks Registry specifying the grounds for such claim. The statement shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documents establishing prior use or assignment, as applicable, and a duly verified affidavit confirming the truth of the assertions made therein. Subject to payment of the prescribed fee, the Registry shall, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case exists, issue a notice to the opposing party requiring them to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding thirty days. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated time shall be deemed an admission of the claim, provided that the Registry may, for sufficient cause, extend this period. All case proceedings shall be conducted in accordance with the rules prescribed under this Act.

Any person alleging a dispute regarding the ownership or validity of a registered trade mark shall initiate a case proceeding before the High Court having jurisdiction, subject to the provisions contained herein. The plaintiff, in commencing such a case proceeding, shall demonstrate a prima facie case of ownership and likelihood of damage resulting from the alleged infringement. The defendant may, at any stage of the case proceeding, file a counter-claim asserting the invalidity of the plaintiff’s trade mark, provided that such counter-claim is directly related to the subject matter of the original claim. Where a case proceeding involves a claim of passing off, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from using the trade mark or any deceptively similar mark. Costs associated with a case proceeding may be awarded to the prevailing party, as determined by the court, and shall include reasonable legal fees. The court may, in exceptional circumstances, order specific delivery of goods bearing the registered trade mark.

Any aggrieved party may initiate a case proceeding before the High Court, subject to the provisions contained herein, alleging a dispute concerning the use of a registered trade mark or a well-known mark. The plaint initiating such a case proceeding shall clearly articulate the grounds for the claim, including but not limited to, instances of passing off, infringement, or unfair competition. The High Court may, at any stage of the case proceeding, direct the parties to explore mediation or conciliation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon mediator, provided that such mediation does not unduly delay the resolution of the dispute. Evidence submitted as part of the case proceeding shall be governed by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Where a party fails to comply with an order of the High Court during the case proceeding, the Court may impose costs or other sanctions as it deems appropriate. The decision in any case proceeding shall be final and binding, subject to any appeal permissible under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

Any case proceeding concerning the rectification of the register, or for a decision as to the validity of a registered trade mark, shall be instituted before the High Court, subject to the provisions contained herein. An application for such a case proceeding shall be filed in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, failing which it shall be deemed inadmissible. The applicant shall demonstrate a substantial question of law or fact requiring determination, and shall serve a copy of the application on the registered proprietor, allowing them a period of thirty days to file a counter-statement. Where a counter-statement is filed, the High Court may direct the appointment of a scientific advisor, possessing expertise in the relevant field, to assist in the determination of technical matters. Evidence presented in any case proceeding shall be governed by the rules of evidence as applicable in civil proceedings, and the High Court may, at its discretion, award costs to the prevailing party.

Any aggrieved party may initiate a case proceeding before the High Court alleging a contravention of the provisions of this Act relating to the use of deceptive or falsely applied trade marks, and the Court shall, upon being satisfied of the validity of such allegation, issue a summons to the defendant requiring appearance within thirty days. Failure to appear or adequately defend the allegation shall be deemed an admission of guilt, subject to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or both. The Court may, as provided herein, also order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark and restrain the defendant from further unlawful use. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a Civil Court, and appeals shall lie to the appellate authority designated by the Central Government.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a case proceeding relates to a dispute concerning the validity of an assignment, the Registry may, at the request of either party, direct that evidence be furnished relating to the beneficial ownership of the trade mark in question. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may be granted in respect of a registered trade mark, and such license shall be in writing and may contain such terms and conditions as are mutually agreed upon by the parties. Provided that any exclusive license shall be registered with the Registry. Failure to register an assignment or exclusive license shall not invalidate the transaction but may affect the rights of the parties as provided herein, particularly in any subsequent case proceeding concerning infringement. The assignee or licensee shall be entitled to all the rights and remedies available to the original proprietor, subject to the terms of the assignment or license.

Any party alleging a likelihood of confusion, or a misrepresentation likely to damage their goodwill, may initiate a case proceeding before the High Court, subject to the provisions contained herein regarding prior notice to the registered proprietor. The registered proprietor shall, within a period of thirty days from the service of notice, file a counter-statement setting forth the grounds on which the registration is valid and the allegations are denied. Failure to file such counter-statement may be considered by the Court as an admission of the allegations. Where a case proceeding concerns a claim of passing off based on unregistered rights, evidence of extensive use and reputation shall be admissible to establish the grounds for relief. The Court, in determining the matter, may order an inquiry and direct the parties to submit evidence, and shall issue a reasoned order detailing the basis for its decision, including any costs awarded. An appeal from any such order shall lie to the appellate court as prescribed under the relevant rules.

Any aggrieved party may initiate a case proceeding before the Trade Marks Registry, subject to the provisions contained herein, by filing a notice of opposition against a pending application for registration or against an existing registered trade mark. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such notice, notify the applicant or registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to submit a counter-statement. A member appointed bench, consisting of at least two officers of the Trade Marks Registry, shall be constituted to examine the evidence presented by both parties. The bench may, at its discretion, require further evidence or call for hearings. Decisions rendered following a case proceeding shall be communicated in writing, detailing the grounds for acceptance or rejection of the opposition, and may be subject to appeal as provided under this Act. The Registry shall maintain a complete record of all case proceedings and associated documentation.

Any case proceeding concerning the rectification of the register, or the removal of a trade mark, shall require the applicant to demonstrate a continuous and genuine use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where the applicant is not the registered proprietor, evidence of permission from the proprietor, or a legally demonstrable interest in the mark, shall be furnished as a prerequisite for initiating the proceeding. Security India, in instances involving claims of well-known marks, may be requested by the adjudicating authority to ensure the bona fides of the applicant and prevent frivolous litigation. The Registrar may, at any stage of the case proceeding, direct the applicant to provide further evidence or clarification, and failure to comply within the stipulated timeframe may result in dismissal of the application, provided that reasonable cause is not demonstrated. All submissions shall adhere to the prescribed format and be accompanied by the requisite fees.

Any case proceeding concerning the infringement of a registered trade mark involving goods originating from a registered breeder of animals shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, provided that the breeder demonstrates verifiable records of lineage extending back a minimum of three generations. Failure to produce such records shall constitute an impediment to the commencement or continuation of said case proceeding. Where a complaint is filed alleging unauthorized use of a trade mark in connection with animal breeding stock, the Tribunal may, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, order immediate seizure of the animals in question pending final determination of the matter. Any person found to have knowingly presented falsified breeder records shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with a fine, or with both. All costs associated with seizure and maintenance of animals during the case proceeding shall be borne by the defendant, unless otherwise determined by the Tribunal.

A registration mentioned clause, when included in an application for registration of a trade mark under this Act, shall be deemed to be a request to the Trade Marks Registry to record the particulars of such registration in the Register of Trade Marks. Such a clause may specify the country in which the trade mark is registered, the date of registration, and the registration number assigned by that country’s registry. Subject to verification of the submitted documentation, the Registry shall, upon satisfaction that the foreign registration is current and valid, record the particulars as requested. Provided that, if the foreign registration has lapsed or been cancelled, the Registry may refuse to record the particulars and shall notify the applicant accordingly. Failure to maintain the foreign registration shall invalidate any benefit derived from the registration mentioned clause.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register a trade mark, or by any condition imposed under this Act relating to the registration of a trade mark, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order refusing such registration or imposing such condition. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the Registrar and the applicant an opportunity of being heard, either confirm the decision of the Registrar or set aside such decision and direct the Registrar to register the trade mark, or to consider the application for registration afresh. Where a trade mark is registered with a registration mentioned clause limiting its use, any person who suffers damage by reason of any infringement of such a clause may institute a civil suit for recovery of damages. The court, in assessing damages, shall take into account the actual loss suffered by the plaintiff as a result of the infringement, and may also award exemplary damages. Provided that no such suit shall be instituted without prior notice to the registered proprietor.

Any application for registration mentioned in this Act shall be subject to a preliminary scrutiny conducted by the Trade Marks Registry to ascertain compliance with all procedural requirements as provided herein. The Registry may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information within a period of thirty days from the date of such requirement, failing which the application shall be deemed to be abandoned. Provided that, where the amendment sought relates to a substantial alteration of the trade mark, a fresh application may be necessary. Registration mentioned clause compliance is further contingent upon a search report indicating the absence of conflicting marks, and a clear demonstration of distinctive character. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registry regarding such scrutiny may file a review petition within sixty days. The Registry shall consider such petition and pass an order within ninety days thereafter.

Any person who falsely applies for the registration mentioned clause to a trade mark, or knowingly makes a false representation in an application, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a registered trade mark is used in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion, the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, direct that the mark be altered or that its registration be suspended for a period not exceeding one year. Any aggrieved person may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the wrongful use of a registered trade mark, and the Court may grant such injunction, with or without conditions, as it thinks fit. Provided that no injunction shall be granted if the plaintiff has delayed unreasonably in seeking relief, and such delay has caused prejudice to the defendant. All fines collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the goodwill of the trade mark together with the right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered. An assignment of a trade mark shall not be valid unless it is in writing and certified by the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, a notification of the assignment shall be filed with the Registry in the manner as prescribed. The registration mentioned clause relating to any assignment shall be subject to the conditions that the assignee undertakes to maintain the quality of goods or services associated with the trade mark. Failure to do so may render the assignment voidable at the option of the original proprietor or any aggrieved party, provided that reasonable opportunity for rectification has been afforded. Any license granted under this Act shall be recorded with the Registry to ensure transparency and enforceability.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board for rectification of the register where it appears that a trade mark ought not to have been registered, or has become subject to any impediment to its continued registration, and such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registrar may, prior to the hearing of any such application for rectification involving a question of law, direct the parties to submit written statements of their respective cases, and may, if deemed necessary, require the attendance of witnesses and the production of evidence. Should the Appellate Board determine that the registration mentioned clause was improperly granted, it may order the removal of the trade mark from the register, or direct an amendment thereof, provided that such amendment does not substantially affect the identity of the trade mark. Any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to appeal to the Supreme Court as provided in the relevant procedural laws.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Appellate Board for rectification of the register where it appears to such person that an entry in the register is likely to be misleading, or that a trade mark should not have been registered, or that a trade mark has fallen into disuse. The application for rectification shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall state the grounds on which the rectification is sought. The Registrar may, prior to the hearing of any such application, require the applicant to furnish further evidence or clarification. If the Appellate Board is satisfied that the grounds for rectification are well-founded, it may order the rectification of the register accordingly, and any such order shall be binding on all parties. A party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board relating to a registration mentioned clause may, within ninety days of the order, appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s decision shall be final.

An alleged offence relating to the manufacture, possession, sale, or distribution of counterfeit goods, as provided herein, shall be deemed to have occurred at the location where the goods were first introduced into commerce with intent to deceive. However, if it is proven that the offender acted solely as a distributor or vendor without knowledge of the counterfeit nature of the goods, the alleged offence reason shall be limited to the act of distribution or sale only. Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person who knowingly facilitates the movement of counterfeit goods, even without direct involvement in manufacture, may also be held liable. Any evidence of prior intent to commit such an offence shall be admissible in proceedings. The burden of proving lack of knowledge rests with the accused.

Any application for registration of a trade mark, alleging prior use, shall be accompanied by a statement detailing the specific grounds constituting such use, and the duration thereof, not exceeding a period of five years immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require further evidence to substantiate the alleged offence reason, including but not limited to affidavits of witnesses, copies of invoices, and records of sales. An applicant claiming user based on importation of goods shall furnish evidence of lawful import and continuous supply within the territory of India. Provided that, failure to adequately demonstrate the alleged offence reason, or to provide supporting documentation as requested, may result in the rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all such applications and associated evidence, accessible for public inspection as provided herein. Any false statement made in support of such an application shall be deemed an offence under this Act.

Any person who engages in the application of a deceptive trade mark, or a falsely applied trade description, with intent to defraud, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act, and shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed. However, a defendant alleging lack of knowledge of the deceptive nature of the mark or description may, subject to verification by the investigating officer, mitigate the penalty. The burden of proving reasonable care taken to ascertain the genuineness of the mark or description shall lie with the accused. 

Where the alleged offence reason stems from the sale of goods bearing such deceptive mark or description, the proprietor of the trade mark, or the person lawfully using the trade description, may initiate proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction restraining further sale. Provided that, such proceedings shall not preclude any criminal prosecution initiated by the appropriate authority. Any evidence of prior complaints regarding similar infringements by the accused shall be admissible as an aggravating factor.

Any person alleging an offence under this Act relating to the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, shall, prior to the initiation of proceedings, furnish to the Registrar a detailed statement outlining the basis of the alleged offence reason, including but not limited to, particulars of the mark, the goods or services in respect of which it is used, and the manner in which such use is claimed to constitute a violation. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require the complainant to provide evidence supporting the allegations contained within the statement. Where the alleged offence reason concerns a mark registered in a foreign jurisdiction, a certified copy of the foreign registration, duly translated into an official language, shall accompany the statement. Failure to comply with the provisions herein may render the complaint inadmissible, provided that the Registrar retains discretion to waive procedural deficiencies where substantial merit is demonstrably evident. Any evidence submitted shall be deemed confidential and subject to the provisions regarding non-disclosure as provided herein.

Any person alleging an offence relating to the use of an identical or deceptively similar mark, as provided herein, shall furnish to the adjudicating officer a detailed statement outlining the grounds for such allegation, including specific instances of use and the likely confusion arising therefrom. Such statement shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a prima facie case, including but not limited to, copies of the allegedly infringing mark, evidence of prior rights, and details of any consumer complaints received. Failure to provide sufficient evidence to substantiate the alleged offence reason may result in dismissal of the complaint. The adjudicating officer may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, direct the alleged infringer to cease use of the mark pending further investigation. Any wilful misrepresentation of facts in the statement shall constitute a separate offence punishable under this Act. A reasoned order detailing the basis for acceptance or rejection of the complaint shall be issued within sixty days.

Any person found to have committed an offence relating to the falsification of a registered trade mark, or the possession of counterfeit goods with intent to deceive, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding three lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both. The alleged offence reason, establishing culpability, must demonstrate a material connection between the accused and the infringing activity; mere possession absent intent to deceive shall not constitute an offence under this Act. However, if the offence is committed by a company, every person who, at the time of the commission of the offence, was in charge of, and responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and liable for punishment accordingly, subject to the ability to prove due diligence. Repeat offenders shall be subject to enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the rectification of the register and the recording of such assignment therein. A license, whether sole or otherwise, may be granted in respect of a registered trade mark, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the terms and conditions of the license, including the duration, territory, and goods or services in respect of which the license is granted. Where an alleged offence reason relates to a breach of the terms of a license, the aggrieved party, being either the proprietor or the licensee, may apply to the High Court for an injunction restraining the offending party from continuing such breach. The proprietor shall not be liable for any act committed by the licensee which constitutes an alleged offence reason, provided that the proprietor has exercised reasonable care to prevent such act. Any dispute arising out of a licensing agreement shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court as determined by the agreement itself, or failing such determination, the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the licensee carries on business.

Any assignment or licensing of rights in a registered trade mark relating to integrated circuits, or semiconductors embodying such circuits, shall be subject to a diligent prosecution requirement as provided herein. An alleged offence arising from the unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or commercial exploitation of a trade mark affixed to or embodied within a semiconductor, or an integrated circuit, shall be deemed aggravated if the assignor or licensor failed to exercise reasonable oversight to prevent such infringement. The Trade Marks Registry may, upon application, direct the assignee or licensee to demonstrate sufficient controls are in place to monitor and address instances of counterfeiting or unauthorized use. Provided that, the registry shall consider the nature of the licensing agreement and the extent of control retained by the original proprietor when assessing the alleged offence reason. Failure to comply with such direction may result in revocation of the assignment or license, subject to a hearing. Any royalty payments due in respect of infringing goods shall be withheld pending resolution of the matter.

Goods bearing a falsely applied Geographical Indication shall be deemed counterfeit goods for the purposes of this Act, and their possession, sale, or distribution constitutes an infringement actionable under the provisions herein. Any person dealing in goods with a false Geographical Indication, knowing or having reason to believe it is so applied, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed. The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may, through a duly authorized officer, initiate proceedings for the seizure of such counterfeit goods. Where a court finds a contravention of this Act relating to falsely indicated goods, it shall direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by which the offence was committed, including any materials used in the commission of the offence. Such forfeited goods may be disposed of in a manner deemed fit by the court, subject to any directions issued by the Central Government.

The suit may seek an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringement, and may also include a claim for damages, or an account of profits. Where a defendant is found to have engaged in a deliberate and wilful act of infringement, the Court may award enhanced damages, not exceeding three times the actual damages suffered. Furthermore, as provided herein, the Court may direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by means of which the infringement was committed, or to which the infringement relates. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the High Court, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The registered proprietor shall bear the burden of proving the infringement and the extent of loss or injury suffered.

The court, as provided herein, may also order the destruction or irreversible disposal of the falsely marked goods at the expense of the offender. Furthermore, any consignment of goods bearing such a false Geographical Indication discovered during import or export shall be liable to seizure. In cases where the offender is a habitual offender, or the scale of deception is substantial, the court shall direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by which the offence was committed, including packaging materials, labels, and any equipment used in the false application of the indication. Subject to due process and opportunity for hearing, the Registrar may initiate proceedings for the removal of the falsely registered Geographical Indication.

context: Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign, transfer or license the rights therein to any other person. Any assignment, transfer or license shall be in writing and registered with the Geographical Indications Registry, failing which such assignment, transfer or license shall be void. The Registrar may, on application made by the assignee, transferee or licensee, register the assignment, transfer or license, provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar as to the validity of the instrument of assignment, transfer or license. Where a registered proprietor fails to comply with the conditions of registration or makes a false representation in obtaining registration, the court may, after notice to the proprietor and subject to such terms as it deems fit, direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by way of material evidence of the infringement. Any person aggrieved by an order of the court relating to such forfeiture may appeal to the High Court.

context: Any registered proprietor who contravenes the provisions of this Act relating to the maintenance of the register of producers, or fails to furnish any statement or document required as provided herein, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a person, having the control or possession of any goods bearing a registered geographical indication, fails to produce records pertaining to the origin or authenticity of such goods when lawfully requested by an officer authorized under this Act, the court may, upon application by the Registrar, direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by which the offence has been committed. For the purposes of this Act, the term ‘recording means person’ shall include any employee, agent, or representative of the registered proprietor authorized to maintain such records. Provided that, such forfeiture shall not prejudice any lawful rights of any bona fide purchaser of such goods without knowledge of the contravention. Any penalty imposed under this Act may be recovered as arrears of land revenue.

context: A registered proprietor of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute civil proceedings for infringement of such geographical indication. Where a defendant in any such proceeding proves, to the satisfaction of the court, that the goods in question, though bearing the registered geographical indication, do not, in fact, originate from the geographical area in question, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from using such indication. However, the plaintiff forthwith ceased to be entitled to relief if it is established that the use of the geographical indication by the defendant was reasonably necessary to indicate the actual origin of the goods. Any order granting relief shall be executed in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Provided that no injunction shall be granted in any suit to which the provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 apply.

Upon a finding of infringement of a registered geographical indication, the aggrieved party may apply to the court for an injunction restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of said geographical indication. Should the defendant continue such unlawful use after the grant of an injunction, the court may order the impounding and destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication, subject to due process and opportunity for representation to the defendant. Where a plaintiff demonstrates irreparable harm and the inadequacy of monetary damages, a mandatory injunction may be issued directing the defendant to take specific actions to remedy the infringement. However, if the plaintiff forthwith ceased to suffer harm due to the defendant’s actions following the injunction, any further claim for damages shall be limited to those incurred prior to such cessation. Any person aggrieved by an order under this Act may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein, within a period of ninety days from the date of the order. The court may also award costs to the prevailing party.

Any person aggrieved by any infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to institute a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Upon the filing of a complaint alleging unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication, and pending adjudication of the matter, the plaintiff may apply to the Court for an interlocutory injunction restraining the defendant from further acts of infringement. Should the Court, after examination of evidence presented, determine that a prima facie case exists and that irreparable harm will result from continued infringement, it may grant such injunction. However, the plaintiff forthwith ceased any activity contributing to the alleged infringement upon receipt of notice from the Registrar, or upon being served with a copy of the defendant’s counterclaim asserting the validity of the geographical indication is in question. The Court shall consider the balance of convenience and the likelihood of success before issuing any such order, and may require the plaintiff to provide security for potential damages.

For the purposes of this Act, a party alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, upon reasonable grounds for believing that an unlawful act has occurred, be entitled to apply to the competent court for an order relating plaintiff forthwith to the seizure of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed affidavit outlining the nature of the alleged infringement and the location of the infringing goods. The court, subject to verification of the affidavit’s veracity, may issue a warrant authorizing officers of the police or other appropriate authority to enter any premises where infringing goods are reasonably believed to be located and to seize such goods. Provided that, any goods seized shall be subject to the provisions regarding disposal of counterfeit goods as provided herein, and the applicant shall bear the burden of proving legitimate grounds for the seizure.

Any person claiming to be interested in, and adversely affected by, the proposed registration of a geographical indication, may file a notice of opposition in the prescribed form with the Registrar within a period of three months from the date of notification of the application for registration. The Registrar shall, after receiving the notice of opposition, furnish a copy thereof to the applicant, requiring him to file a counter-statement within a period of two months. Should the applicant fail to file such counter-statement within the stipulated time, the Registrar shall, after considering the notice of opposition and any evidence submitted by the opponent, proceed to determine the matter. In cases where the opposition relates to a claim of prior use of a similar indication, the Registrar shall forthwith require evidence of such use, and may direct an inquiry to be conducted. The Registrar, having considered all evidence and submissions, shall, relating plaintiff forthwith, either register the geographical indication or reject the application, as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an act constituting a contravention of the provisions of this Act, or alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the contravention occurred or where the infringing goods are sold. The court, upon being satisfied that a prima facie case exists, shall, as provided herein, grant an ex parte interim injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, or otherwise dealing with the goods bearing the unauthorized geographical indication. Should the plaintiff demonstrate irreparable harm and a strong likelihood of success, the court may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the defendant to provide a full accounting of all goods bearing the infringing geographical indication. Furthermore, the court shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the determination of damages or an order for delivery up of infringing goods, consider the costs incurred by the plaintiff in establishing the validity of the geographical indication and in investigating the infringement. Any order for damages shall be calculated in accordance with the actual loss suffered or the profits unjustly gained by the defendant, whichever is higher.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon establishing a prima facie case of infringement, may apply to the High Court having jurisdiction for an interim injunction restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of said geographical indication. The Court, considering the potential harm to the reputation of the goods and the likelihood of consumer deception, shall, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant such injunction. Where a plaintiff demonstrates irreparable harm and a strong probability of success, the Court may, as provided herein, direct the defendant to forthwith account for all profits derived from the infringing use. However, such accounting shall not be ordered unless the defendant fails to demonstrate a legitimate independent source for those profits. Any order relating plaintiff forthwith shall include a clear specification of the prohibited acts and the geographical area to which the injunction applies. The Court may also direct the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication, ensuring due process and opportunity for representation to the defendant.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon establishing a prima facie case of infringement, may apply to the court for an ex parte order directing the alleged infringer to cease all activities contributing to such infringement, and such application shall be disposed of within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of the application by the court. Where the court is satisfied that the applicant has made out a strong case, it shall forthwith issue a notice to the alleged infringer, requiring them to appear before the court and show cause why an injunction should not be granted. Provided that, no such order shall be issued unless the applicant undertakes to provide security, the amount of which shall be determined by the court, to cover potential damages to the respondent should the injunction ultimately be discharged. The court, as provided herein, shall consider all evidence and representations, and may, relating plaintiff forthwith, direct immediate cessation of infringing activities pending a full adjudication of the matter, subject to compliance with the procedural safeguards outlined in this Act.

Any person aggrieved by the misrepresentation of a registered geographical indication, or the false application thereof, shall forthwith submit a complaint to the Registrar, detailing the nature of the infringement and the particulars of the offending goods. The Registrar, upon receiving such complaint and subject to verification of the allegations, may initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied of prima facie infringement, shall issue a notice to the alleged infringer. Failure to respond to such notice within thirty days shall result in an ex parte order restraining the sale, distribution, or export of the goods in question. Any person found to be in violation of an order issued as provided herein shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees per instance of infringement, and the goods shall be subject to seizure and destruction. The court, relating plaintiff forthwith to the harm suffered, may also award compensatory damages, assessed on the basis of lost profits or actual damages sustained.

Any person registered as the proprietor of a geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the right to assign, transfer or license the rights therein to any other person. Any assignment or transfer of the right shall be subject to such conditions as may be prescribed and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise their rights or adequately protect the geographical indication, and a request for rectification is made by an interested party demonstrating substantial and continuing harm, the Registry may, after notice to the proprietor, direct the proprietor to take necessary action. Should the proprietor remain unresponsive within a period of ninety days, the Registry shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the appropriate authority for the revocation of the registration, provided that such revocation shall not prejudice any accrued rights or valid licenses. Licenses granted under this Act shall be non-exclusive unless otherwise agreed upon in writing, and may be revoked for cause as determined by the Registry.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, aggrieved by any act constituting an infringement thereof, may institute a civil suit in a District Court not inferior to that of a Principal Civil Court, having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs, or where the defendant resides, or carries on business. Provided that, in cases where the infringement involves multiple defendants or complex issues of law, the Court may, at the request of the plaintiff and subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, transfer the suit to the High Court. Should the defendant demonstrate a reasonable belief of lawful use, the Court shall, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, consider such submission during adjudication. Furthermore, the Court shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the defendant’s asserted defenses, direct immediate discovery of all relevant documentation pertaining to the alleged infringement, including but not limited to production and sales records, and any evidence of prior art. Any appeal from the decree of the District Court shall lie to the High Court.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, upon reasonable cause being shown and subject to such terms as the court may deem fit, be relating plaintiff forthwith to the jurisdictional High Court possessing ordinary original civil jurisdiction. Provided that, where the alleged infringement also involves a registered trade mark for identical or similar goods, the plaintiff may, at their discretion, elect to pursue remedies under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, but shall not thereby be precluded from simultaneously seeking relief under this Act. The court, upon receiving a complaint, may direct the defendant to produce evidence of origin and manufacturing process, and may appoint a commissioner to inspect the premises of the defendant. Any order passed under this provision shall be subject to appeal to the appellate authority as constituted under the rules framed herein, within a period of thirty days from the date of the order. Failure to comply with such direction may be deemed an admission of guilt.

Any person aggrieved by an act constituting a contravention of the provisions of this Act, and claiming to be the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in a District Court not inferior to that of a Principal Civil Court, for the redressal of the grievance, and the court shall, upon being satisfied that such contravention has occurred, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from such contravention. The court shall, as expeditiously as possible, consider the application and, relating plaintiff forthwith to the alleged infringement, may direct provisional orders pending final determination. Justified registration of the geographical indication, evidenced by a valid certificate issued under this Act, shall be conclusive proof of the right to institute such suit. Provided that no suit for infringement shall be instituted after three years from the date of becoming aware of the infringement. The court may also award damages to the plaintiff, assessed on the basis of lost profits or actual damages suffered.

Upon a finding of infringement of a registered geographical indication, the Registrar may, and shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the appropriate court having jurisdiction over the matter, for the purpose of seeking such remedies as are available under this Act and other applicable laws. The court, upon receiving a complaint and verifying the prima facie case for infringement, may issue an ex parte order restraining the defendant from further use of the infringing geographical indication, pending adjudication. Provided that such ex parte order shall not remain in force for a period exceeding thirty days unless extended by the court upon sufficient cause being shown. Where the infringement defendant satisfies the court that the use of the geographical indication is not likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, the court may modify the order of restraint or grant such other relief as it deems fit. Any person aggrieved by an order of the court under this provision may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon reasonable grounds believing that any consignment of goods bearing an unauthorized geographical indication is being imported into India, shall forthwith notify the Customs authorities in writing, providing detailed particulars of the goods and the geographical indication in question. The Customs authorities, upon receipt of such notification and subject to verification of the registration certificate, may issue a notice of detention to the importer. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall furnish a bond, with such security india deems appropriate, to cover potential damages and costs arising from any wrongful detention. Failure to comply with the requirements of this Act regarding notification and security shall preclude the proprietor from seeking interim relief or damages related to the imported consignment. The Customs authorities shall, relating plaintiff forthwith to the registered proprietor, communicate any decision regarding the release or further action concerning the detained goods. Any appeal against the decision of the Customs authorities shall lie as provided herein.

A registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall, upon a finding of infringement under this Act, be entitled to relief, and the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of the geographical indication. Should the plaintiff demonstrate actual damage or loss resulting from the infringement, the court may also award damages, assessed in accordance with the principles of restitution and deterrence as provided herein. However, the plaintiff forthwith must present evidence of such damage, and the court may direct an account of profits made by the defendant through the infringing use, subject to the defendant demonstrating legitimate deductions. Provided that, where the infringement is proven to be unintentional, the court may, at its discretion, reduce the awarded damages. The court shall consider the defendant’s prompt cessation of the infringing activity as a mitigating factor.

Any person aggrieved by any infringement of a registered geographical indication, or by any false application of such indication, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the false application is made. The plaintiff forthwith, upon institution of the suit, shall furnish to the defendant a certified copy of the complaint and a specimen of the geographical indication registered in respect of the goods in question. Provided that, where the defendant resides outside the jurisdiction of the District Court, the suit may be instituted in the District Court having jurisdiction over the principal place of business of the defendant. The Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the plaintiff to produce evidence of the origin of the goods bearing the registered geographical indication and may, if satisfied that such evidence is insufficient, dismiss the suit. Any evidence admitted in one suit shall be admissible in any subsequent suit involving the same geographical indication.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to institute a civil suit in a District Court not inferior to that of a Principal Civil Court, having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs. The plaintiff forthwith, upon reasonable cause to believe that an infringement has occurred, may apply ex parte to a Magistrate for an order restraining the defendant from the further unlawful use of the geographical indication. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of the grounds for the claim and a verified copy of the registration certificate. The court, if satisfied of the prima facie case and the likelihood of irreparable harm, may grant an interim injunction. Provided that no such injunction shall be granted unless the plaintiff undertakes to provide security, as the court deems fit, to compensate the defendant for any loss that may be suffered by reason of such injunction being granted and subsequently found to be erroneous. Any person dealing with goods bearing an infringing geographical indication in good faith shall not be liable for damages.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon having reasonable grounds to believe that a contravention of this Act has occurred, shall forthwith institute a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the contravention occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The plaintiff forthwith demonstrating a prima facie case of passing off or misrepresentation, shall be entitled to an ex parte interim injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing, selling, or otherwise dealing in goods bearing the fraudulent or deceptive indication. Such injunction may be modified or vacated upon notice to the plaintiff and after hearing both sides. Provided that, the Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct the defendant to deposit a sum equivalent to the estimated value of the infringing goods as security. Any person aggrieved by an order under this provision may appeal to the High Court. The Court shall, as expeditiously as possible, determine the matter and render a decision consistent with the principles of natural justice.

Any person alleging the unlawful use of a registered geographical indication shall, forthwith, furnish to the Registrar a detailed statement of the nature of the alleged infringement, including specific instances of such use and evidence supporting the claim. The statement shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee as prescribed in Schedule III. Where the alleged infringement involves the sale or distribution of goods bearing a counterfeit geographical indication, the plaintiff forthwith shall submit samples of the counterfeit goods for examination by the designated laboratory. Subject to verification of the statement and payment of the prescribed fee, the Registrar may initiate an inquiry. Provided that, if the Registrar is satisfied that the statement is frivolous or vexatious, the Registrar may dismiss it and direct the plaintiff to pay costs. Any order for interim injunction issued by a court shall be communicated to the Registrar within fourteen days of its issuance, failing which the Registrar may suspend the enforcement of such order. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for the pursuit of remedies as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an act constituting a contravention of the provisions of this Act, or alleging an imminent contravention, may institute a suit in the District Court having jurisdiction, and the plaintiff forthwith, upon reasonable grounds, shall be entitled to an ex parte order restraining the defendant from continuing such contravention. Such order shall be granted within a period not exceeding ten days from the date of application, subject to the defendant being given notice and an opportunity to be heard. Failure to comply with an order granted under this Act shall constitute contempt of court and be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, no court shall grant any injunction unless it is satisfied that the geographical indication is duly registered and validly subsisting as provided herein. The court may, at its discretion, direct the destruction of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, upon reasonable grounds for believing such infringement has occurred, forthwith notify the Registrar and simultaneously serve a notice of such allegation upon the alleged infringer, detailing the nature of the infringement and the geographical indication in question. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of service, fail to submit a reasoned defense or cease the infringing activity, the plaintiff forthwith may apply to the court having jurisdiction. Provided that, the court may, subject to verification of the registration and prima facie evidence of infringement, grant an ex parte injunction restraining the continuation of such activity. Any person aggrieved by an order of the court under this provision may appeal to the appellate authority established under this Act, subject to the conditions prescribed and within the stipulated timeframe. The appellate authority shall consider any evidence submitted by either party and may modify or set aside the order of the lower court.

Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication has reasonable grounds to believe that an infringement of such registration has occurred, the plaintiff forthwith may institute civil proceedings in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Provided that, if the infringement involves a patented process utilized in the production of goods bearing the geographical indication, the plaintiff shall also submit evidence of said patent’s validity and scope to the court. Subject to the provisions herein, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringement, and may order the seizure and destruction of infringing goods. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the court may appeal to the High Court.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal of registration of a geographical indication, or by any modification or cancellation of a registration, may present a petition to the Appellate Board established under this Act. Such petition shall be presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order and the relevant documents. If the Appellate Board is satisfied that the refusal, modification or cancellation was improper, it may restore the application for registration or, as the case may be, reinstate the registration. Provided that, if the refusal was based on a prior existing right, the plaintiff forthwith must demonstrate clear and convincing evidence of continuous use and diligent protection of the geographical indication prior to the filing date of the opposing claim. In cases where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of renewal fees, the Appellate Board may, subject to applicable fees and conditions, consider a petition for restoration patent, provided it is filed within one year of the lapse.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon having reasonable grounds to believe that a contravention of this Act has occurred, shall forthwith initiate proceedings before a court competent to hear such matters, and may seek an ex parte order restraining the defendant from continuing the unlawful act. Provided that such application for an ex parte order shall be accompanied by a statement of facts supporting the claim of infringement, verified in the manner prescribed under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. The plaintiff forthwith, upon obtaining such order, shall serve a copy of the order upon the defendant, and shall, subject to the provisions of that Code, ensure due process is followed for a full hearing on the matter. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the ex parte order liable to be vacated, and the court may impose costs upon the applicant. Any person aggrieved by such an order may apply to the court for its modification or discharge.

Any person aggrieved by an act constituting a contravention of the provisions of this Act, and alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, may, and shall, if so directed by the Registrar, present a complaint to the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the unlawful act has occurred, and the plaintiff forthwith upon such presentation shall furnish security, the amount of which shall be determined by the Court. Where the infringement relates to a creation provided layout, such layout shall be submitted to the Court for examination as evidence of the original design. Failure to comply with the security requirement shall render the complaint inadmissible, and the Court may, subject to the provisions herein, impose a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Any order made under this Act shall be executable as if it were a decree of a civil court, and the defendant shall be liable for all costs incurred by the plaintiff in pursuing the action.

An indication plaintiff, being a person applying for registration of a geographical indication or already registered as the proprietor thereof, shall possess the legal standing to initiate proceedings for infringement under this Act.
