Such a plaintiff may also be a registered association representing producers of the goods to which the geographical indication relates, provided that the association’s constitution demonstrates sufficient control over the quality and standards of those goods and a demonstrable link to the territory of origin. Any individual or entity falsely representing a geographical indication, or trading goods not originating from the specified geographical area as if they do, shall be deemed to have infringed the rights of the indication plaintiff. Remedies available to the indication plaintiff shall include injunction, damages, and delivery-up of infringing goods, subject to the provisions herein.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, seeking registration of a geographical indication under this Act, shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a statement of proposed use. The application shall clearly identify the goods to which the geographical indication relates, and shall delineate the geographical area from which the goods originate, demonstrating a clear link between the goods’ qualities, reputation, or other characteristics and that geographical origin. A register of producers shall be maintained, subject to verification by the Registry, and shall be open for inspection. Where a collective or association of producers is the indication plaintiff, it shall demonstrate authority to act on behalf of all producers within the defined geographical area. The Registry may, at its discretion, require further evidence to substantiate the claims made in the application, including proof of traditional knowledge or established usage. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in rejection of the application.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, and alleging an infringement of a registered geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The indication plaintiff shall, prior to the institution of such suit, provide the defendant with at least two months’ notice of the intended action, specifying the nature of the infringement and the relief sought. A collective body representing producers of the geographical indication may, with the leave of the Court, act as the indication plaintiff on behalf of all concerned. Where an act constitutes an offence under this Act, the Court may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, impose a fine not exceeding rupees five lakh. Provided that the Court may, in exceptional circumstances and at its discretion, order the destruction of goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Any appeal from a decision of the District Court shall lie to the High Court.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, seeking registration of a geographical indication under this Act, shall submit an application to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall clearly identify the goods to which the geographical indication relates, and shall delineate the geographical area within India from which the goods originate, demonstrating a specific quality, reputation, or other characteristic attributable to that origin. A detailed statement of usage, including the period of continuous use of the geographical indication by the producers in the specified geographical area, shall also be furnished. 

Provided that, where the indication plaintiff is a collective body representing producers, evidence of authorization to act on behalf of said producers shall be submitted. The Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require further evidence or clarification regarding the application. Failure to comply with these requirements within the stipulated timeframe may result in the rejection of the application, as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, seeking registration of a geographical indication under this Act, shall submit a statement detailing the rules and conditions governing the use of that indication by producers within the specified geographical area. Such statement shall comprehensively outline how the qualities or reputation of the goods are attributable to the place of origin, and shall be supported by verifiable evidence of consistent production practices. A registered association of producers may, subject to the provisions herein, act as the indication plaintiff on behalf of all members. Where a collective group does not exist, individual producers may jointly apply, but shall designate a lead applicant responsible for all communications and compliance. Failure to adhere to the established rules, or misrepresentation regarding origin, shall render the registration liable to revocation, and may attract penalties as prescribed. The Registrar may, at any time, require updated documentation to ensure continued conformity with these requirements.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, alleging wrongful use of a registered geographical indication, may institute a suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the wrongful act occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The Court, upon satisfactory evidence of such wrongful use, shall grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the geographical indication. Damages awarded shall not be less than five thousand rupees per contravention, and may extend to three lakh rupees, subject to proof of actual loss or potential loss suffered by the indication plaintiff. A false designation of origin or presentation, even if not identical to the registered geographical indication, but likely to cause confusion, shall be deemed a contravention as provided herein. Any order of the Court may be executed directly by the Registrar, upon request by the indication plaintiff, and the costs thereof shall be borne by the defendant. Failure to comply with an injunction shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding two years, or a fine, or both.

Any indication plaintiff, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to others for the use of the geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Such licenses shall be in writing and may be subject to conditions regarding the quality of goods, the area of production, and the duration of the license. An assignment of any right in a geographical indication shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry as provided herein, and shall not be valid unless so registered. The indication plaintiff retains the right to revoke a license granted under this Act, provided that reasonable notice is given to the licensee and any material breach of the licensing conditions is established. Where a license or assignment is made without the prior written consent of all producers associated with the geographical indication, it shall be voidable at the option of such producers. Any dispute concerning the validity or scope of a license or assignment shall be adjudicated by the appropriate court.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, and alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, may institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs, or before the High Court designated by the Central Government for such purposes. The suit shall be filed within a period of three years from the date of knowledge of the infringement, subject to the court’s discretion for condonation of delay upon sufficient cause being shown. An indication plaintiff, to succeed, shall demonstrate a direct nexus between the impugned goods and the geographical indication, and prove that the use of such goods is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. Where a defendant proves legitimate prior use, or that the geographical indication has become generic through extensive public use, relief may be modified or denied, provided that such use does not unfairly compete with the registered indication plaintiff. Any order made by the District Court shall be subject to appeal before the High Court.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, seeking registration of a geographical indication under this Act, shall submit an application to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, demonstrating a prima facie connection between the goods and the geographical area of origin. The application shall include a statement detailing the characteristics of the goods linked to their geographical origin, and how these characteristics are attributable to that place. Registration of a geographical indication shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the indication in relation to the goods in respect of which it is registered. However, such registration shall not preclude the use of descriptive terms that are customary in the trade. Any unauthorized use of a registered geographical indication constituting infringement registered shall be actionable, subject to the provisions regarding limitations and exceptions as provided herein, and may result in injunctions, damages, or accounts of profits. The Registrar may, upon sufficient cause being shown, require further evidence to substantiate the claim of geographical origin.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, and alleging infringement of a registered geographical indication, shall have the right to institute a civil suit in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Application registration shall be prima facie evidence of the validity of the geographical indication and the plaintiff’s exclusive right to use it in relation to the goods specified in the register. The court may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant an injunction restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of the geographical indication. A plaintiff may also seek damages for loss suffered due to the infringement, or an account of profits made by the defendant. Provided that, where the defendant proves that the use was accidental or unintentional, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. The court may, at its discretion, order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff shall, prior to the institution of any legal proceeding under this Act, furnish to the Registrar a statement detailing the scope of the geographical indication, the goods to which it applies, and the region of origin. Such statement shall be accompanied by a certified copy of a resolution passed by the producers or their association authorizing the indication plaintiff to act on their behalf. Where a dispute arises regarding the authenticity of such authorization, the court having jurisdiction shall determine the validity of the resolution and the standing of the indication plaintiff. Failure to comply with the requirements of this provision may result in the dismissal of the legal proceeding, subject to the discretion of the court. Provided that the court may, at its discretion, allow rectification of the statement if the deficiency is remedied within a period of thirty days from the date of such observation.

Any indication plaintiff, being the registered proprietor of a geographical indication, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to other persons to use such geographical indication in relation to goods in respect of which it is registered. Such licenses shall be in writing and may be made absolute or subject to conditions, including conditions as to royalty, duration, territory, and quality of goods. Assignment of any right in a registered geographical indication shall be subject to a similar requirement of written instrument and registration with the Geographical Indications Registry. Any commission offence attributable to a licensee, arising from the use of the geographical indication, shall not be directly imputable to the indication plaintiff unless it is proven that the plaintiff had knowledge of, and consented to, such offence. The indication plaintiff retains the right to revoke a license in cases of breach of condition or non-compliance with the terms of the agreement, provided that reasonable notice is given to the licensee. Any dispute regarding licensing or assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

For the purposes of this Act, “essentially derived variety” means a plant variety that is principally derived from another variety, commonly known as the initial variety, in the propagation or exploitation of which the initial variety was used as a recurrent parent, or in the development of which the initial variety furnished a substantial portion of the genetic material, where such derivation maintains the phenotypic characteristics of the initial variety, except for differences necessary for the expression of a new trait or combination of traits. A “plant variety” shall be deemed to be distinct if it possesses one or more characteristics which are clearly distinguishable from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge. Crop sciences, encompassing the breeding, genetic modification, and agronomic practices relating to plants, are central to the determination of novelty and distinctness as provided herein. Any person claiming a right to a variety shall be subject to verification of these characteristics.

Any person claiming to have essentially derived a variety, as defined under this Act, shall submit an application for registration to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall include a detailed description of the characteristics of the derived variety, demonstrating its distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, and a clear indication of the initial variety from which it was derived. A declaration affirming that the applicant possesses legitimate access to the initial variety and has complied with the provisions relating to benefit sharing, where applicable, shall also be furnished. The Authority may, subject to verification of the claims and conformity with the established criteria for essentially derived varieties, register the variety and issue a certificate of registration. Provided that, registration shall not be granted if the derived variety lacks substantial novelty or if its production and propagation would be detrimental to the maintenance of the initial variety. The registrar may request additional information or samples as deemed necessary for a thorough evaluation of the crop sciences involved.

Any breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety of any crop sciences species, shall be eligible to register such variety under this Act, subject to the provisions herein. A farmer who has bred or developed a new variety on his own, may also apply for registration, provided that he can demonstrate the distinctiveness of the variety through verifiable means. Where a registered variety is found to be substantially derived from another registered variety, the breeder of the original variety shall have the right to seek royalty or an injunction against the continued propagation of the substantially derived variety. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court. The Authority shall maintain a register of all registered plant varieties and shall make it available for inspection by interested parties, subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Farmers’ rights to save, use, sow, exchange, and sell farm-saved seeds of registered varieties are expressly protected, notwithstanding any other provision of this Act.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration of a new plant variety in crop sciences, shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Should the application satisfy the initial requirements, the Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, initiate a substantive examination involving a detailed assessment of distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. A variety shall be deemed distinct if it exhibits characteristics which are clearly distinguishable from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge. The examination process shall include a growing trial conducted at designated testing centers, and the applicant may be required to provide samples of the plant variety for such trials. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates substantial equivalence to a variety already registered in a foreign country with reciprocal arrangements, the Registrar may, at their discretion, expedite the examination process. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may file an appeal with the Central Government within sixty days of the date of such decision, as provided herein.

Any person engaged in the development of a new or extant plant variety, and seeking registration under this Act, shall submit a complete and verifiable description of the characteristics of said variety, including its genealogy, stability, distinctiveness, uniformity, and the results of any relevant field trials conducted in accordance with established crop sciences protocols. Provided that, the applicant may, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, rely on data generated by recognized international testing authorities. All seed material submitted for evaluation shall be accompanied by a declaration of origin and a commitment to maintain breeder’s seed stock for a period not less than three generations following registration. Furthermore, any farmer cultivating a registered variety shall be responsible for ensuring that seed saved for propagation conforms substantially to the declared characteristics of the protected variety, and any deviation shall be reported to the Authority as provided herein. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registration or the imposition of penalties.

Any person who, without lawful authority, harvests, collects, or sells seeds of a registered plant variety, or commercially exploits such variety, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that, the establishment of commercial exploitation shall require proof of intent to profit from the unauthorized use of the protected plant variety, and the quantity of material involved must exceed de minimis levels as prescribed by regulations. Any farmer who, in good faith and without intent to deceive, saves, uses, sells, or exchanges seeds of a protected variety within their own holding, shall not be subject to penalty as provided herein. However, the sale of such seeds beyond the boundaries of their landholding, or for commercial purposes, requires prior authorization from the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any violation of these provisions shall attract a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to imprisonment for a term of up to three years, subject to the severity of the infringement and the demonstrated impact on crop sciences and the rights of the plant breeder.

Any person deriving a commercially viable crop variety through the application of protected plant variety information, as provided herein, shall be obligated to obtain a license from the registered breeder or the successor in title, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted propagation, sale, and distribution of the essentially derived variety, and shall include provisions for royalty payments calculated as a percentage of net profit derived from such commercial exploitation. Assignment of such licensing rights requires prior written consent of the original breeder, and notification to the Authority within thirty days of the effective date of assignment. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the commercial activity unlawful and subject to penalties as prescribed under this Act. Furthermore, any dispute regarding the terms of the license or the validity of the assignment shall be adjudicated by the designated appellate tribunal, considering the principles of equitable benefit sharing and the advancement of crop sciences.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Authority regarding the grant or refusal of a breeder’s right, or the revocation thereof, may file an appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such decision, provided that such appeal shall be accompanied by a deposit equivalent to the prescribed fee for the original application, as a condition precedent for its consideration. The High Court, upon review of the appeal and subject to such evidence as it may deem fit, shall either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Authority. Disputes concerning essentially derived varieties and the scope of permissible exploitation of a protected plant variety, particularly in relation to crop sciences, shall be adjudicated according to the principles of substantial derivation and the limitations outlined in this Act. Further, any claim of farmer’s right to save, use, sow, exchange, and sell farm-saved seed shall be considered in light of the legitimate interests of the breeder, balancing innovation with traditional agricultural practices.

Any breeder of a new or substantially derived plant variety of any crop sciences discipline, seeking registration under this Act, shall submit a complete and verifiable description of the characteristics of said variety, including its genealogy, purity, and stability, to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, a breeder may also apply for a restoration patent where a substantially similar variety, independently developed, is found to infringe upon the essentially derived variety, subject to demonstrating clear evidence of commercial prejudice. The Authority may, following a public hearing and examination of expert testimony, grant a restoration patent with a term commensurate to the remaining unexpired term of the original breeder’s rights. All applications shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a declaration affirming the veracity of the submitted information, and failure to comply with these provisions may result in rejection of the application or revocation of any granted protection. Any farmer demonstrating prior and continuous use of a protected variety for traditional agricultural practices shall be exempt from the provisions relating to commercial exploitation, as provided herein.

Compulsory licensing of a registered variety shall be permissible under this Act, provided that a reasonable royalty is paid to the breeder, and subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. Such a license may be granted by the Central Government in circumstances where a variety is essential for public health, nutrition, or addressing a national emergency. Consideration shall be given to the legitimate interests of the breeder, including the recovery of costs associated with research and development. The licensee shall demonstrate that efforts to negotiate a voluntary license with the breeder have been unsuccessful. Furthermore, a compulsory license may be issued where the breeder has failed to exploit the protected variety within a reasonable period, or where the variety is not readily available to the public at an affordable price, consistent with the objectives of this Act and the principles of equitable access.

Any person intending to exploit a registered plant variety without the authorization of the breeder, where such variety is essential for public health or national emergency, may apply to the Central Government for a compulsory license. The application shall contain a statement of the reasons for seeking the license, the scope of the intended exploitation, and the duration for which the license is sought, along with evidence establishing the essential nature of the variety for the stated purpose. The Central Government, upon being satisfied that the grounds for compulsory licensing exist, and subject to the payment of an equitable royalty as determined by it, may grant a license to exploit the variety. A farmer who has independently developed or retained a farm-saved seed of a registered variety, and who uses it for propagation, shall be exempt from the requirement of obtaining a license, provided that the act is not for commercial sale. The breeder shall have the right to seek judicial review of any decision regarding the grant of a compulsory license.

Any person, being a farmer, who has bred or developed a new or extant variety on his own land, shall be entitled to a benefit-sharing arrangement, subject to the provisions of this Act, with any person who commercially exploits such variety. Where a breeder of a variety fails to exploit the rights conferred by way of registration, or where the terms of a license are found to be unreasonable, the Central Government may, after giving the breeder a reasonable opportunity to be heard, impose conditions for compulsory licensing of the variety to any other person. Such compulsory licensing shall be granted for a period determined by the Central Government, and the licensee shall pay an equitable royalty to the breeder, as determined by the Authority. The Authority shall, while determining the royalty, consider the costs incurred by the breeder in developing the variety, and the benefits accruing to the licensee. A farmer whose variety is subject to compulsory licensing shall also be entitled to equitable benefit sharing, as may be prescribed.

A compulsory license for the commercial exploitation of a registered variety shall be granted by the Central Government if the reasonable needs of the public are not satisfied, and the registered breeder or his assignee fails to adequately exploit the variety. An application for such a license shall be made to the Central Government in the prescribed manner, demonstrating non-availability or inadequate supply of seeds or other propagating material. The licensee shall remit to the breeder or his assignee an equitable royalty, determined by the Central Government, taking into account the costs of development, production, and distribution. 

Assignment of the compulsory license may be permitted by the Central Government, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, ensuring continued access for the public. Furthermore, a compulsory license may be revoked if the licensee fails to comply with the conditions of the license or if the breeder remedies the unmet public need, as provided herein. The Central Government shall consider the interests of both the breeder and the public when making any determination regarding compulsory licensing or assignment.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the Central Government may, in the public interest, issue a license to undertake research and development on a registered variety to any person, subject to the payment of adequate remuneration to the breeder and fulfillment of conditions as may be prescribed. Any person aggrieved by the refusal of such compulsory licensing may prefer an appeal to the High Court within ninety days of the order, demonstrating substantial grounds for review and potential prejudice to national food security or farmer welfare. The breeder, similarly, shall have recourse to appeal should the remuneration determined be deemed insufficient, providing detailed cost accounting to substantiate claims. Provided that, prior to any appeal, a mandatory period of thirty days for amicable settlement through mediation, facilitated by an officer appointed by the Central Government, shall be observed. Failure to comply with this mediation requirement may render the appeal inadmissible.

Where the breeder of a registered variety has failed to make available seeds or other propagating material to the public, within a period of three years from the date of registration, or where the availability of such seeds or propagating material is insufficient to meet the requirements of the public, a compulsory licensing order may be made by the Central Government. Such order shall be subject to the payment of an equitable royalty, fixed by the Central Government, to the breeder. The application for such compulsory license shall be made in the prescribed manner and shall include a statement of the reasons why the applicant requires the license and evidence of public need. The licensee shall utilize the licensed variety only for the purpose for which the license was granted and in the prescribed manner, and any deviation from this shall render the license liable to revocation. Provided that, before making any such order, the Central Government shall give the breeder an opportunity to be heard. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may prefer an appeal to the High Court.

The sources gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority with the objective of promoting and facilitating the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources. Contributions to the fund may include payments derived from the commercial exploitation of varieties protected under this Act, and any other sums received by the Authority through prescribed mechanisms. The Authority shall utilize the sources gene fund for the reward and recognition of farmers, community conservators of plant genetic resources, and breeders who contribute to the development of new plant varieties, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government. Provided that, a portion of the fund may also be allocated towards strengthening the capacity of local gene banks and traditional knowledge systems relating to plant varieties. The Authority shall maintain detailed records of all transactions related to the sources gene fund and submit an annual report to the Central Government.

The registrar shall maintain a register of all registered plant varieties and shall record therein details of the sources gene fund established as provided herein. Any breeder seeking registration of a new variety, being a substantially derived variety or one dependent on a prior variety, shall disclose the origin of its genetic material and demonstrate contribution to the sources gene fund. The amount credited to the sources gene fund, derived from benefit sharing and annual fees, shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for rewarding farmers and breeders who contribute to the fund through the provision of traditional knowledge or unique germplasm. Provided that, the registrar may, subject to verification of claims, authorize direct disbursement from the sources gene fund to recognized gene banks or conservation programs. All transactions relating to the sources gene fund shall be subject to audit as prescribed. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding contribution to, or disbursement from, the sources gene fund may appeal to the designated authority.

The registered breeder of a new variety, or an essentially derived variety thereof, shall contribute to the sources gene fund a sum equivalent to a percentage of the sale price of the seed, as may be prescribed, and such contribution shall be remitted to the National Gene Fund established under this Act. Provided that the amount so contributed shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and breeders engaged in the development of new varieties. Any farmer who conserves and improves a landrace or traditional variety, and contributes to the sources gene fund through the provision of seed, may be eligible for recognition and reward, subject to verification by the Plant Varieties Protection Authority. The Authority shall maintain a transparent record of all contributions to, and disbursements from, the sources gene fund, and shall publish an annual report detailing the same. Any dispute regarding the calculation of contributions or the eligibility for rewards shall be adjudicated by the designated appellate authority as provided herein.

The National Gene Fund shall be established and maintained by the Central Government as a trust, dedicated to the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources for the benefit of farmers and the advancement of plant breeding. Contributions to the Fund shall include royalties received from the commercial exploitation of varieties registered under this Act, and any other sums received by way of grants, donations, or other contributions from domestic and international sources. The Fund may accept contributions in kind, subject to valuation by a committee constituted for the purpose. 

All amounts credited to the Fund shall be utilized for the promotion of research and development in plant breeding, the conservation of plant genetic resources, and the welfare of farmers, particularly small and marginal farmers. A portion of the Fund shall be specifically allocated to the maintenance and enhancement of the sources gene fund, ensuring the availability of diverse genetic material for future breeding programs. The Central Government shall cause annual audits of the Fund and publish reports thereof. Any unutilized funds shall not lapse and shall be available for the purposes of this Act.

The operator of a gene bank recognized under this Act shall maintain a transparent record of all accessions of plant genetic resources for research and breeding purposes, and shall submit an annual report detailing such accessions to the National Authority. Any commercial exploitation of genetic material sourced from the sources gene fund, whether through the development of new plant varieties or otherwise, shall require prior intimation to the National Authority and adherence to benefit-sharing provisions as prescribed. Provided that, access to genetic resources for non-commercial, educational, or research purposes, conducted by recognized public institutions, may be granted subject to a simplified notification procedure. The National Authority may establish a mechanism for equitable benefit sharing, considering the contribution of local and farming communities to the conservation and improvement of plant genetic resources. Failure to comply with these provisions shall attract penalties as outlined in this Act, including revocation of access rights and imposition of financial penalties.

The operator of any establishment engaged in the commercial exploitation of plant genetic resources, or the propagation of registered varieties, shall contribute a percentage of gross sales, as determined by the Authority, to the sources gene fund. Provided that such contribution shall be subject to a minimum threshold established by the Central Government, and adjusted periodically to reflect changes in market value. Any person who fails to remit the required contribution to the sources gene fund within the stipulated timeframe shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding twice the amount due, and may be subject to suspension of registration under this Act. The Authority may, in cases of repeated non-compliance, initiate proceedings for revocation of the registration of the variety or the propagation license. Furthermore, any false declaration regarding sales figures, intended to evade contribution to the sources gene fund, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment, or a fine, or both. The Authority shall administer the fund for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for benefit sharing with local and farming communities.

The registered breeder of a new variety, or an essentially derived variety thereof, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to equitable sharing of benefits arising from the commercial exploitation of the variety, including the contribution to the sources gene fund. Any person utilizing genetic material sourced from a landrace or traditional variety, in the development of a registered variety, shall, prior to commercialization, deposit a sum equivalent to five per cent of the gross sales of the seed, or propagating material, into the sources gene fund. The fund shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, and utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for benefit sharing with local and farming communities. Provided that, a registered breeder may, with the prior approval of the committee, assign their rights to benefit sharing to a third party, subject to conditions ensuring continued contribution to the fund. The committee may, further, establish a mechanism for transparent accounting and disbursement of funds to eligible stakeholders.

The aggrieved party may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file an appeal before the Plant Variety Tribunal concerning any decision relating to the equitable sharing of benefits arising from the exploitation of plant genetic resources or the determination of contributions to the sources gene fund. Any dispute regarding the ascertainment of the value of propagating material for the purpose of benefit sharing shall be adjudicated by the Tribunal, provided that the claimant demonstrates a direct causal link between the exploited plant genetic resource and the commercially exploited variety. The Tribunal shall, within ninety days of the filing of such appeal, issue a reasoned order, and any party dissatisfied with said order may prefer an appeal to the High Court. It is clarified that contributions to the sources gene fund shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, as determined by the Central Government. Failure to remit benefit sharing as stipulated herein constitutes a cognizable offence.

The sources gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit sharing arising from the commercial exploitation of varieties registered herein. Contributions to the fund may include payments derived from the sale of seeds or propagating material of protected varieties, and any royalties received from the exploitation of traits originating from locally adapted landraces. Provided that, any variety marketed under a reference trade mark, demonstrably linked to a traditional knowledge source, shall contribute a proportionate share of its commercial gains to the fund, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate guidelines for equitable distribution of funds to local communities and breeders engaged in conservation efforts.

The Gene Fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit sharing arising from the exploitation of such resources. Any person, including a breeder, utilizing sources gene fund material for the development of a new variety, shall, subject to the provisions herein, contribute a fair and equitable share of benefits to the Fund. The Plant Variety Protection Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, prescribe the modalities for determining such contribution, considering the commercial value of the variety and the extent of utilization of the sources gene fund. A complete and accurate record of all contributions received and disbursements made from the Fund shall be maintained and the Authority shall register said layout of financial transactions annually. Provided that, funds allocated for research and development shall prioritize indigenous and locally adapted varieties.

The sources gene fund established under this Act shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, comprising representatives from relevant ministries, agricultural universities, and farmer organizations. All contributions to the fund, derived from the commercial exploitation of registered plant varieties incorporating indigenous genetic resources, shall be deposited into this fund and accounted for in accordance with established financial procedures. Provided that, a portion of the fund may be allocated to incentivize the preservation of traditional knowledge associated with plant varieties, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Committee. 

Any sound recording documenting traditional farming practices relating to the collected genetic material, and submitted as evidence of prior art or traditional knowledge, shall be maintained as part of the fund’s archival records. The committee may, with the approval of the Central Government, utilize the fund to support research and development initiatives focused on crop improvement and biodiversity conservation, as provided herein, and shall submit an annual report detailing all financial transactions and project outcomes.

The sources gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and breeders engaged in the development of new plant varieties. Any benefit derived from the commercial exploitation of a registered variety, or an essentially derived variety thereof, shall contribute to this fund as prescribed. Provided that, contributions from breeders originating from a convention country, where reciprocal arrangements exist for the protection of plant varieties, may be subject to a reduced rate of contribution determined by the Central Government. The fund may also receive grants, donations, and other contributions from national and international sources, subject to acceptance by the designated authority. All disbursements from the fund shall be transparent and auditable, and prioritized towards initiatives that enhance the livelihoods of farmers and strengthen the national plant breeding program, as provided herein.

The sources gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders in accordance with the principles of equity and fairness. Any person intending to utilize resources from the fund for research or commercial purposes shall submit a detailed proposal to the Authority, outlining the intended use and benefit-sharing arrangements. Should any individual or organization lodge a valid opposition to the proposed utilization, alleging that it contravenes the objectives of the fund or harms the interests of farmers, the Authority shall conduct a thorough investigation and may, pending such investigation, suspend disbursement of funds related to that proposal. Failure to comply with the prescribed benefit-sharing arrangements, or knowingly providing false information in a proposal, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may result in revocation of access to the fund. The Authority may, subject to the provisions herein, direct the fund towards initiatives promoting traditional knowledge and farmer’s rights.

The gene fund sub shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority with the objective of promoting and facilitating the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and sharing benefits arising from their commercial exploitation. Contributions to the gene fund sub may include royalties received from the sale of seeds of protected varieties, and any other sums received by the Authority as provided herein. The Authority shall formulate guidelines for the transparent and equitable distribution of funds from the gene fund sub to support initiatives relating to the conservation of on-farm diversity, the development of new plant varieties, and the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any unutilized amounts in the gene fund sub shall not lapse and shall be available for the purposes of this Act.

The registrar shall maintain a register of all registered plant varieties, detailing the breeder, variety characteristics, and the extent of farmer’s rights associated therewith. Any person claiming a right in a registered variety, or seeking access to the gene fund sub, shall submit an application to the registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application shall clearly state the basis of the claim, including evidence of contribution to the development of the variety, or legitimate use of propagating material. Provided that, a farmer exercising rights to save, sell, share and replant seeds shall not be required to pay any fee for such activity, subject to the conditions as provided herein. The registrar may, after due inquiry and consideration of the evidence, grant or reject the application, and shall communicate the decision to the applicant in writing. Any aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the designated appellate authority within ninety days of the decision.

The gene fund sub, established as a dedicated mechanism for equitable benefit sharing, shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government, comprising representatives from relevant ministries, plant breeding institutions, and farmer organizations. Any breeder, upon commercialization of a registered plant variety or its essentially derived variety, shall contribute a prescribed percentage of revenue generated from the sale of seed or propagating material to the gene fund sub. Provided that, the contribution rate may be differentiated based on the category of variety and the scale of commercial operation, as determined by regulations. Farmers’ communities, who have contributed to the development of a variety through traditional knowledge or germplasm, may apply to the committee for a share of the gene fund sub, demonstrating their contribution through verifiable evidence. The committee shall, subject to verification of claims, disburse funds to support conservation of on-farm diversity, improvement of livelihoods, and further plant breeding initiatives benefiting farmers. Any dispute regarding the allocation of funds or the determination of farmer contributions shall be adjudicated by a designated tribunal as provided herein.

The gene fund sub-committee, constituted under this Act, shall oversee the equitable distribution of benefits arising from the exploitation of plant varieties registered herein, and shall operate subject to guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any person intending to utilize resources derived from registered varieties for commercial purposes shall contribute a percentage of resultant profits to the gene fund, the rate of which shall be determined by the Authority based on the nature of the utilization and the declared value of the variety. Provided that, farmers’ rights, as recognized under this Act, shall not be prejudiced by contributions to the gene fund. The sub-committee may, with the approval of the Authority, establish mechanisms for transparent accounting and disbursement of funds, prioritizing initiatives that support plant breeding, conservation of plant genetic resources, and the welfare of farmers and rural communities. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for all entities engaged in the commercialization of protected plant varieties.

The gene fund sub-committee, constituted under this Act for the equitable distribution of benefits arising from the exploitation of plant varieties, shall diligently assess contributions to the National Gene Fund and ensure transparent allocation to eligible stakeholders. Any breeder failing to remit benefit-sharing payments, as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding twice the outstanding amount. Provided that, repeated non-compliance, exceeding three instances within a five-year period, may result in the revocation of the breeder’s registration. The Authority may, subject to established procedures, initiate recovery proceedings for unpaid contributions, including attachment and sale of propagating material. Furthermore, any farmer demonstrating legitimate claim to benefit sharing, and subsequently denied, may appeal to the designated appellate tribunal, with timelines for resolution as provided herein. False claims submitted to the gene fund sub-committee shall attract a fine of up to five lakh rupees.

The gene fund sub, established as a dedicated repository under this Act, shall be utilized exclusively for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and plant breeders alike. Any rights to commercially exploited plant genetic material, originating from traditionally bred varieties registered herein, shall be subject to a mandatory contribution to the gene fund sub, the quantum of which shall be determined by the Authority based on the realized commercial value. Assignment of such rights, whether partial or complete, requires prior notification to, and approval from, the Authority, ensuring continued contributions to the fund. Provided that, a farmer exercising rights under this Act to save, use, sow, exchange and sell farm-saved seed shall be exempt from direct contribution, but may be eligible for benefit-sharing schemes funded by the gene fund sub. The Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate guidelines for the equitable distribution of funds to support research, development, and capacity building initiatives.

The aggrieved party may lodge a complaint with the Plant Variety Protection Authority where a breeder, despite having utilized germplasm sourced from the gene fund sub, fails to remit the prescribed benefit-sharing amount within ninety days of commercialization of the variety. The Authority shall, following a notice to the breeder and consideration of submitted evidence, determine the outstanding amount and issue a recovery order. Should the breeder dispute the Authority’s determination, an appeal may be filed before the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is accompanied by a deposit representing fifty percent of the contested amount. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except where a substantial question of law arises, in which case, recourse may be had to the High Court. Any amounts recovered under this provision shall be credited to the National Gene Fund and utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, as provided herein, and for the welfare of farmers and breeders engaged in plant variety development.

The gene fund sub, established under this Act, shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit-sharing arising from the exploitation of traditional knowledge associated with such resources. Any person seeking an application patent relating to a plant variety incorporating indigenous or traditionally developed genetic material shall, prior to grant of the patent, contribute a prescribed percentage of the anticipated royalties or profits to the gene fund sub. The Authority, after due assessment of the contribution and in consultation with relevant stakeholders, may determine the specific allocation of funds towards research, development, and the welfare of farmers and breeders. Provided that, contributions made to the gene fund sub shall be exempt from income tax and shall be managed transparently through an established accounting procedure. The Authority shall maintain a detailed record of all contributions received and expenditures made from the gene fund sub, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government detailing the same, as provided herein. Any unutilized funds shall be carried forward to the subsequent financial year for continued implementation of the objectives of this Act.

The gene fund sub, established as a revolving fund for promoting plant variety research and development, shall be administered by a committee constituted by the Central Government. Any person who utilizes genetic material sourced from a registered plant variety, and subsequently commercializes a product incorporating said material, shall contribute a percentage of the net profit to the gene fund sub, as determined by the committee. Failure to remit such contribution within the stipulated timeframe shall attract a penalty equivalent to twice the due amount, alongside an interest rate of twelve percent per annum calculated from the date of default. Furthermore, any entity found to be falsely claiming exemption from contributing to the gene fund sub, or misrepresenting the source of genetic material, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act, and may also face action relating to any trade mark registered under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, if such trade mark was obtained through fraudulent means connected to the misrepresentation. The committee may, subject to approval, direct forfeiture of assets in cases of persistent non-compliance.

The gene fund sub-account for the preservation of indigenous plant genetic resources shall be maintained by the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources, and contributions thereto may be made by any person, institution, or organization, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government. Any benefit derived from the commercial exploitation of varieties incorporating traits originating from registered geographical indications, particularly those associated with traditional knowledge, shall be preferentially allocated to this sub-account. The Bureau may, with the approval of the Central Government, license the use of genetic material held within the gene fund sub-account to registered plant breeders, provided that a royalty agreement is executed ensuring equitable benefit sharing with the communities from whom the genetic resource originated. Assignment of rights relating to such licensed material shall be subject to the prior consent of the originating community and the Bureau, as provided herein, and any transfer must be recorded with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the license voidable.

The gene fund sub-committee, constituted for the equitable distribution of benefits arising from the exploitation of plant varieties, shall, upon receipt of a complaint alleging improper allocation of funds, conduct a preliminary inquiry within thirty days. Should the inquiry reveal prima facie evidence of irregularity, the sub-committee may direct a formal inspection of the relevant records maintained by the implementing agency. All such inspections shall be documented in an inspection register, detailing the scope, findings, and any remedial actions proposed. Any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the sub-committee’s decision may file an appeal with the Plant Varieties Tribunal within sixty days of the order, providing a detailed statement of grounds for appeal. The Tribunal shall, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require the submission of the complete inspection register as part of the appellate proceedings, and its decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The Plant Variety Protection Authority shall maintain a register of all deposited genes forming the basis of a claimed trait in a new plant variety offered for registration under this Act. Any breeder seeking registration of a variety incorporating a compensation deposited gene shall submit, alongside the application for registration, a detailed provenance report outlining the source and conditions of deposit of said gene with a recognized international depositary authority. The Authority may, subject to verification of the provenance report and confirmation from the depositary, grant a registration certificate. 

Where the novelty of a plant variety relies not only on the genetic material but also on a unique layout-design of the plant itself, demonstrably contributing to its distinctiveness, the applicant shall furnish a comprehensive visual representation of said layout-design. Provided that, the layout-design does not contravene any existing intellectual property rights. The Authority shall, in determining the registrability of the variety, consider both the deposited gene and the layout-design as integral components of the claimed invention, and shall ensure equitable benefit sharing with the original source of the deposited gene as provided herein.

Any breeder securing a breeder’s right in a new plant variety incorporating a compensation deposited gene, shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to assignment of all rights pertaining to the commercial exploitation of said variety. Provided that, where a variety is derived from a parent variety protected under any other law, including a variety where an article patented relating to the genetic modification thereof is incorporated, the breeder of the new variety shall obtain a license from the owner of the parent variety, and the terms of such license shall be mutually agreed upon, failing which, recourse may be had to the Plant Variety Protection Tribunal. The breeder shall maintain a register of all licensees and submit an annual report thereof to the Registrar. Any transfer of rights relating to the compensation deposited gene, shall be subject to prior notification to the Gene Fund and a reasonable administrative fee as prescribed. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the breeder’s right.

A “compensation deposited gene” shall mean a gene or genetic material originating from a registered plant variety, for which adequate compensation, determined in accordance with the provisions of this Act, has been deposited with the National Gene Fund by a breeder or assignee of breeder’s rights, subsequent to the commercial exploitation of said variety. Such deposit constitutes evidence of compliance with benefit-sharing obligations as provided herein. Where a breeder publicly advertises acceptance of a standard royalty rate or benefit-sharing arrangement for the use of a compensation deposited gene, such advertised acceptance shall be binding on the breeder for a period of three years from the date of advertisement, unless withdrawn with prior notice to the Authority. Any dispute regarding the adequacy of compensation shall be subject to the grievance redressal mechanism established under this Act.

The claimant seeking to establish a right to utilise a protected plant variety shall submit a detailed application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, outlining the basis of such claim and demonstrating a clear nexus between the claimed utilisation and the permissible scope as provided herein. Any utilisation for research and breeding, or for purely private and non-commercial purposes, shall be exempt from the requirement of prior authorisation, subject to the condition that such activities do not infringe the breeder’s rights or result in the sale or other commercial exploitation of the variety. Where the claimed utilisation involves the production of essentially derived varieties, the claimant shall furnish evidence of substantial derivation and demonstrate that the essentially derived variety is not substantially different from the protected variety. The Authority may, following due process and consideration of all relevant evidence, grant or deny the application for utilisation, and shall communicate its decision to the claimant in writing. A register of all authorised utilisations shall be maintained by the Authority and be open to public inspection. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Authority regarding claims utilisation may prefer an appeal to the designated appellate tribunal.

Any person claiming utilisation of a registered variety, whether through commercial sale, distribution, or propagation, shall maintain a register of such utilisation, detailing the quantity and quality of material propagated and the geographical area of such propagation. Such register shall be open for inspection by an officer authorised under this Act, subject to reasonable notice. The claimant shall, within thirty days of the end of each financial year, submit a statement of accounts relating to the said utilisation to the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Failure to maintain accurate records or submit the required statement shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, a farmer exercising rights under this Act, utilising a protected variety for private and non-commercial propagation, is exempt from the provisions relating to registration of utilisation, but shall remain subject to the overall principles of equitable benefit sharing as provided herein. Any dispute regarding claims utilisation shall be adjudicated by the designated authority.

Any person utilizing a variety, as defined herein, for commercial purposes shall maintain a register of all such utilization, detailing the extent of propagation, sale, and distribution of the harvested material. Failure to maintain such a register, or the provision of materially false information therein, shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding five lakh rupees. Where the utilization involves essentially derived varieties, the claimant shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, a clear and unbroken chain of derivation and commercial connection with the initial variety. Any claim of utilization made without demonstrable evidence, or subject to conflicting claims, may be rejected, and the person making such claim shall be liable to pay damages, assessed by the Authority, to the breeder of the initial variety. Repeated non-compliance with the provisions regarding claims utilisation shall render the offender ineligible for any benefits conferred under this Act.

Any person claiming utilisation of a registered variety, whether through commercial sale, propagation, distribution or any other method, shall furnish a statement of account to the breeder or his successor, as provided herein, detailing the extent of such utilisation and the remuneration derived therefrom. The breeder may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the right to utilise the variety to any other person, and such assignment or license shall be in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a farmer is engaged in the utilisation of a variety for the purpose of research or for saving, selling, sharing or distributing seeds of such variety, such utilisation shall be exempt from the requirement of a statement of account, provided that such farmer is not engaged in commercial production. Any dispute regarding claims utilisation or the appropriate remuneration shall be adjudicated by the designated authority, and decisions shall be binding on all parties concerned, unless appealed to a higher court. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to statements of account may result in penalties as prescribed.

Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, or a farmer asserting a claim of essentially derived variety, shall submit a detailed statement of the grounds for such allegation or claim to the Tribunal. The Tribunal shall, upon receipt of such statement, issue notice to the respondent, requiring them to file a counter-statement within sixty days. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated period shall be deemed an admission of the allegation or claim, subject to further scrutiny by the Tribunal. Regarding claims utilisation, any commercially exploited material embodying the protected variety, or the essentially derived variety, must be fully disclosed to the Tribunal as evidence. An appeal from any decision of the Tribunal shall lie before the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Tribunal’s order, and is accompanied by a deposit representing fifty percent of the claimed damages or royalty, as determined by the Tribunal. The High Court may, at its discretion, modify the terms of utilisation.

Any person utilising a variety, whether by commercial production or otherwise, shall maintain detailed and accurate records of the provenance of the seed or propagating material, and the extent of utilisation, as provided herein. Failure to maintain such records, or provision of false or misleading information regarding claims utilisation, shall be punishable with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to one lakh rupees. Where a denomination variety sub-variety is utilised without the express permission of the breeder, or in a manner inconsistent with any conditions imposed on its utilisation, an additional penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees per hectare of cultivated land shall be levied. The Authority, upon receiving credible evidence of non-compliance, may initiate an investigation and, subject to due process, impose these penalties. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential suspension of registration privileges under this Act.

Claims utilisation, for the purposes of this Act, shall encompass the commercial exploitation of a protected plant variety, including propagation, distribution, sale, and any other act of deriving economic benefit therefrom. Any person interested, being a breeder, seed producer, or a farmer possessing essentially derived varieties, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for authorisation to utilise a protected variety subject to the payment of royalty as may be prescribed. Provided that, such utilisation shall not prejudice the rights of the breeder or the legitimate interests of other persons engaged in the development of plant varieties. The Authority may, after due consideration and subject to the provisions herein, grant or refuse such authorisation, and may impose conditions regarding the scope and duration of the utilisation. Any dispute regarding claims utilisation shall be subject to the grievance redressal mechanism as provided under this Act.

The aggrieved party, being a farmer or breeder, may apply to the Tribunal established under this Act seeking redressal of grievances arising from a contravention of rights conferred herein. Any person alleging a violation of a breeder’s right, or a farmer’s right under the provisions relating to essentially derived varieties, shall submit a detailed statement of the alleged infringement, accompanied by supporting evidence. The Tribunal shall, upon receiving such application, issue notice to the alleged infringer and facilitate a process of mediation, where appropriate, to arrive at an amicable settlement. 

Where mediation fails, the Tribunal shall proceed to adjudicate the matter, and may award damages, or grant an injunction restraining the infringer from further acts of infringement. A farmer exercising rights under the scheme for benefit sharing, as per the section 41 scheme, shall be entitled to legal representation before the Tribunal. The Tribunal’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the provisions for appeal as laid down in this Act, and any award made shall be executable as a decree of a civil court.

The competent authority, acting under this Act, shall establish a scheme for the implementation of the provisions relating to the collection and distribution of farmers’ rights, as detailed within the section 41 scheme. Any registered plant breeder seeking to avail benefits under this scheme shall submit a declaration of cultivated variety, accompanied by evidence of seed production and sales, to the designated authority within the prescribed timeframe. Provided that, farmers claiming rights to saved seeds shall maintain records of seed source and usage, subject to verification by the relevant Plant Variety and Farmers’ Rights Authority. The scheme may also provide for a dispute resolution mechanism, wherein complaints regarding non-payment of benefit-sharing or inaccurate reporting of seed sales shall be addressed through mediation or arbitration. All participating parties shall adhere to the guidelines established by the authority concerning transparency and accountability in financial transactions, and failure to comply may result in penalties as provided herein.

Any person cultivating a variety listed in the National Register of Plant Varieties, who suffers damage as a result of another person’s unauthorized production, sale, or distribution of such variety, may apply to the Tribunal established under this Act for redressal. The Tribunal, upon verification of the claim and subject to the provisions herein, shall determine the extent of damage suffered and may impose a civil penalty not exceeding twice the estimated loss. Furthermore, the Tribunal may, as part of the scheme for equitable compensation, direct the defendant to provide seeds of the protected variety to the aggrieved farmer, ensuring continued cultivation. Any appeal against the order of the Tribunal shall lie with the High Court. Failure to comply with an order of the Tribunal concerning the section 41 scheme shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with a fine, or with both. The burden of proof regarding unauthorized acts rests with the claimant.

The breeder of a new plant variety, desiring to avail of the benefits under the scheme established for commercial exploitation of the variety, shall submit a proposal to the Plant Variety Protection Authority outlining the terms of licensing proposed for third parties. Such proposals shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to, propagation, sale, and distribution of harvested material. The Authority may, subject to verification of the breeder’s rights and the novelty of the variety, approve the proposal, thereby initiating the section 41 scheme for that variety. Any person seeking a license to exploit the variety shall apply to the breeder, and the terms negotiated shall be consistent with the approved proposal. Where agreement cannot be reached, the Authority may, after due process and consideration of equitable principles, impose licensing terms. The breeder retains the right to assign their rights under any license granted, provided that the assignee adheres to the conditions stipulated herein and any subsequent modifications approved by the Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the license and associated benefits.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of a complete application for registration under the scheme established for the benefit of plant breeders and farmers, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. A farmer who is a traditional breeder, and who has demonstrably contributed to the development of a new or substantially improved variety, may, subject to the conditions prescribed, apply for registration of that variety under the section 41 scheme. Provided that the application includes a detailed description of the evolved variety, its characteristics, and evidence of its commercial cultivation. Any layout design commercially exploited in the production of the variety shall be disclosed as part of the application, and may be subject to verification. The Registrar may require additional information or evidence from the applicant, and failure to provide such information within the stipulated timeframe shall render the application liable to be rejected. Registration shall be granted only if the variety meets the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity as provided herein.

For the purposes of establishing claims relating to essentially derived varieties, a variety shall be deemed to be essentially derived from another variety where it is demonstrably the result of modification in the characteristics of the initial variety, retaining the characteristics that account for the initial variety’s identity, and meeting the requirements of distinctness and uniformity. Subject to the provisions herein, the breeder of the initial variety, or their successor, shall have the right to benefit from the exploitation of the essentially derived variety. However, a claim based on essentially derived variety status may be contested if the essentially derived variety is itself the subject of a breeder’s exemption as provided herein, or if the modification was achieved through a process that does not substantially alter the initial variety’s characteristics. Any dispute regarding claims purposes shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Tribunal.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall submit an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, demonstrating the distinctiveness, uniformity and stability of the said variety, as provided herein. The application shall clearly delineate the claims purposes for which the variety is being registered, specifying the intended commercial exploitation, including propagation, sale and marketing of propagating material. Subject to verification of the breeder’s entitlement, the Authority may, if satisfied that the variety fulfills the criteria outlined in this Act, grant a breeder’s certificate. However, registration shall not confer any right to collect or sell habitually saved seed of a variety, except as expressly permitted under the provisions relating to farmers’ rights and research exemptions. Any person alleging infringement of a registered variety may initiate proceedings before the designated tribunal, establishing a clear nexus between the registered claims purposes and the alleged infringement.

Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, as established under this Act, shall have the right to seek interim injunction from a District Court having jurisdiction, restraining the alleged infringer from the continued propagation, sale, or distribution of the protected plant variety. Claims purposes relating to essentially derived varieties shall be adjudicated considering the degree of phenotypic similarity and the manner in which the derived variety was developed, subject to proof of initial variety and clear demonstration of derivation. A farmer, who has been deprived of the benefit of his traditional knowledge relating to plant genetic resources, may approach the Plant Variety Protection Authority for redressal, provided that such knowledge was commercially exploited without his prior informed consent. The Authority may, after due inquiry, order the infringer to pay equitable compensation to the farmer, and may also impose a civil penalty not exceeding one crore rupees. Any appeal against the order of the Authority shall lie before the High Court.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for the protection of a plant variety, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and may require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information as may be necessary. Claims purposes, as delineated herein, shall be strictly construed to define the scope of protection sought and must clearly articulate the novel, distinct, uniform, and stable characteristics of the plant variety. Any claim extending beyond these established traits shall be deemed inadmissible. 

Provided that, where a claim relies upon essentially derived varieties, the applicant shall demonstrate a clear lineage and the maintenance of the breeder’s rights in the initial variety. The Registrar may, subject to a prescribed fee, conduct a search report to ascertain the existence of any prior art relevant to the claims. Failure to adequately address any objections raised by the Registrar within a stipulated timeframe may result in the rejection of the application, and the applicant shall have recourse to appeal as provided herein.

The breeder of a new plant variety, seeking registration under this Act, shall clearly define the claims purposes for which the variety is intended, specifying the traits and characteristics essential for achieving those purposes. Such claims shall be supported by detailed experimental data demonstrating the distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability of the variety, and must relate to the expression of those traits under normal growing conditions. A farmer, asserting a claim to essentially derived varieties, may submit evidence of consistent cultivation and demonstrable lineage tracing back to the registered variety, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, claims based on traditional knowledge relating to the variety shall be admissible, if substantiated with documented evidence of historical use and geographical indication. Any claims found to be false or misleading shall render the application liable for rejection, and may attract penalties as provided herein. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all valid claims.

Any person making a claim for essentially derived variety, as provided herein, shall furnish to the Plant Variety Protection Authority a detailed justification demonstrating substantial derivation from the initial variety, including evidence of phenotypic and genotypic characteristics. Failure to adequately substantiate such claims purposes with verifiable data, or providing materially false information, shall render the claim inadmissible and subject the claimant to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Authority may, notwithstanding the imposition of such penalty, initiate proceedings for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, if the false representation constitutes an offence therein. Any variety obtained in violation of this provision shall be deemed to infringe the breeder’s rights, and the Authority shall have the power to order its destruction, at the cost of the infringer. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential disqualification from future applications.

Any person being a breeder, or a successor of such breeder, desiring to obtain a breeder’s right in respect of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, shall make an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, clearly stating the claims purposes for which protection is sought, including but not limited to commercial exploitation, propagation, and the marketing of propagating material. The application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a detailed description of the variety, demonstrating its novelty and distinctiveness. Where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, as established through prescribed testing procedures, the applicant shall disclose the initial variety and the breeder thereof, and may be subject to a royalty arrangement determined by the Authority.
