Assignment of breeder’s rights shall be permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to the obligations stipulated under this Act, and any such assignment shall be registered with the Authority to be legally effective. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of the breeder’s right.

Any person asserting a claim to a variety registered under this Act shall submit such claim to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the manner as may be prescribed. The Authority shall, following receipt of a claim, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain its completeness and adherence to the procedural requirements as provided herein. Should the claim be deemed incomplete or non-compliant, the claimant shall be notified with a request for rectification within a period of sixty days from the date of such notice. Failure to rectify within the stipulated timeframe may result in the rejection of the claim, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. 

Disputes regarding the essentially derived variety status, or the scope of permissible acts relating to the protected variety, shall be adjudicated by the Appellate Board, whose decision shall be final and binding, unless a substantial question of law arises for reference to the High Court. Claims purposes, for the purposes of benefit sharing, require documented evidence of contribution to the development of the variety.

Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, or a farmer’s right, as established under this Act, shall submit a statement of claims purposes to the Plant Variety Protection Authority, detailing the nature of the alleged infringement and the relief sought. The statement shall include evidence reasonably sufficient to support the claim, including but not limited to, details of the protected variety, the infringing act, and the extent of damage suffered. Disputes arising from such claims, where the value of the claimed infringement does not exceed twenty lakh rupees, shall be adjudicated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority itself, following principles of natural justice. However, any aggrieved party may appeal the decision of the Authority to the District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Authority’s order. The District Court shall have the power to grant injunctions, award damages, and order specific performance, subject to the provisions of this Act and other applicable laws.

A claimant seeking registration of a new plant variety shall submit a declaration affirming the essentially distinct, uniform and stable characteristics of the variety, as determined through trials conducted in accordance with such guidelines as may be prescribed. The application for registration, accompanied by the requisite fee, shall detail the denomination proposed for the variety and provide evidence establishing the breeder’s entitlement to claim the variety. For registration claims purposes, a variety shall be deemed to be essentially distinct if it exhibits clear differences from any other variety commonly known or commercially available, taking into account the characteristics specified in the guidelines. Provided that, where a substantially similar variety already exists, the claimant must demonstrate a significant improvement conferring a notable benefit. The authority may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, grant a certificate of registration if satisfied that the criteria under this Act have been met, and the variety qualifies for protection. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding registration may file an appeal within sixty days.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration, shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the application satisfies the requirements as provided herein, including verification of the applicant’s locus standi to make registration claims purposes. Any deficiency in the application shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be granted a period of thirty days from the date of such communication to rectify the same. Failure to rectify the deficiency within the stipulated period may render the application liable to be rejected. Where the application appears complete in all respects, the Registrar shall initiate a substantive examination to determine the novelty, distinctiveness, stability and uniformity of the variety claimed. Evidence supporting these characteristics, including data from field trials conducted in accordance with guidelines issued under this Act, shall be considered. The Registrar may, at any stage of the examination, require the applicant to furnish additional information or evidence, or to undertake further trials, subject to reasonable timelines being specified. A claim shall be deemed withdrawn if the applicant fails to comply with such requirements.

Any person asserting a right to variety registration shall submit a detailed claim outlining the essentially derived variety, or the dependent variety, as the case may be, and shall provide demonstrable evidence of its distinctiveness, stability and uniformity, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable for rejection. Any false representation made in such registration claims purposes, including but not limited to the origin, characteristics, or breeding methods of the variety, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, the Registrar may, subject to a reasoned order, revoke any registration obtained through fraudulent means. Repeated offences under this Act, or attempts to circumvent the provisions relating to registration claims purposes, may result in disqualification from future applications for a period of five years. The burden of proof regarding the veracity of any claim shall lie with the applicant.

Any person claiming to be a breeder of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, or a farmer possessing a traditional variety, shall submit an application for registration purposes, accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed. The application shall include a detailed description of the characteristics of the variety, including its lineage, and evidence of its novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. A breeder may, subject to the provisions herein, assign or license any rights arising from a registered variety to any other person, and such assignment or license shall be in writing and registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a farmer possesses a traditional variety and seeks registration claims purposes, evidence of customary practices relating to its preservation and propagation shall be submitted. Provided that, the Authority may, if satisfied, grant a sui generis system for the protection of farmers’ rights and to safeguard their interests. Any transfer of rights relating to a farmer’s variety shall be governed by the customary laws of the relevant community.

Any person asserting a right to a variety under this Act, for registration claims purposes, shall submit a declaration affirming the distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability of said variety, accompanied by such evidence as may be prescribed. Should a claim be contested by another party alleging prior art or lack of genuine novelty, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, direct a comparative trial to ascertain the characteristics of the claimed variety and the allegedly prior art. Evidence presented in such trials shall be admissible as per the rules of evidence generally prevailing, but the Registrar retains discretion to weigh expert testimony regarding plant characteristics. An aggrieved party may appeal any decision of the Registrar to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order, provided that a deposit equivalent to twenty-five percent of the prescribed registration fee is made with the Board as a condition of entertaining the appeal. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal inadmissible.

Any person asserting a right to a plant variety through registration claims purposes shall submit evidence demonstrating distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, as assessed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. However, a claim based solely on a traditionally known variety, even if locally adapted, shall not be considered novel for the purposes of registration, unless compelling evidence of genetic modification or improvement is furnished. The Authority may, subject to verification of the applicant’s locus standi, request additional data pertaining to the plant’s origin and breeding history. 

Provided that, the claimed variety demonstrates industrial application, evidenced by demonstrable economic benefit or contribution to agricultural productivity, the Authority shall proceed with a detailed examination. Any decision of the Authority regarding the rejection of registration claims may be appealed before the designated appellate board within sixty days of the order, with a mandatory deposit of prescribed fees. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the claim ineligible.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for the protection of a plant variety as provided herein, shall cause a scientific examination of the variety to be undertaken to determine its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. Such examination shall be conducted in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government and shall include a growing trial, the duration of which may extend to a period not exceeding three years, subject to the nature of the plant variety. Where the plant variety is a hybrid or a substantially derived variety, the examination shall also assess the breeder’s right in relation to section 41 clause (d), concerning essentially derived varieties, and determine if the claimed variety possesses characteristics differing only in one or more traits. The cost of such examination shall be borne by the applicant.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for the registration of a new or distinct variety as provided herein, shall cause a scientific examination to be undertaken to verify the novelty, distinctness, uniformity and stability of said variety, and shall record the results thereof in the Variety Register. A breeder, seeking registration under this Act, shall submit a detailed description of the characteristics of the plant variety, including its lineage, and evidence demonstrating its distinctness from any commonly known variety or other registered variety. Where a variety is essentially derived from an already registered variety, the applicant shall demonstrate the maintenance of the characteristics of the initial variety, subject to reasonable differences arising from the act of derivation. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right, and seeking recourse under section 41 clause, shall furnish proof of legitimate interest and the extent of damage suffered, and the Registrar may, following investigation, issue a cease and desist order. The period for registration shall not exceed a period of two years from the date of application.

Any farmer who is adversely affected by the exercise of any right conferred by a breeder or any other person under this Act, may, subject to the provisions of this section, make an application to the Tribunal established under the relevant provisions of the Act. The application shall be made in such form and be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed, and shall state the grounds on which the claim is based. Where the Tribunal is satisfied that the rights of the farmer have been infringed, it may, as provided herein, grant relief including, but not limited to, equitable relief, damages, and an injunction restraining the breeder or other person from continuing the infringing act. 

Furthermore, a farmer demonstrating a reasonable likelihood of success on the merits, and facing imminent and irreparable harm, may apply ex parte for an interim injunction pending the final determination of the matter. The Tribunal, when considering an application under section 41 clause, shall prioritize the preservation of the farmer’s traditional knowledge and benefit-sharing arrangements.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for the registration of a new plant variety as provided herein, shall cause a scientific examination of the variety to be undertaken to verify its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. Such examination may be conducted by the Plant Variety Protection Authority itself or through a network of designated research institutions accredited for the purpose. Where the application relates to a farmer’s variety, and a claim for benefit sharing is included, the Registrar shall, in accordance with section 41 clause (a), forward a copy of the application and the results of the preliminary examination to the Biodiversity Authority for assessment of prior art and traditional knowledge. The Biodiversity Authority shall submit its report within a period of ninety days from the date of receipt of such application. Provided that, if the report is not received within the stipulated time, the Registrar may proceed with the examination of the application, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit. The applicant shall be informed of the outcome of the examination and afforded an opportunity to respond to any objections raised.

Any person who, in contravention of the provisions of this Act, sells, offers for sale, exports, imports or disposes of any variety of plant, which is protected under this Act, without the authorization of the breeder or his successor, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both. Provided that the Court may, subject to the circumstances of the case, including the extent of the unauthorized activity and any prior convictions, reduce the term of imprisonment or the amount of fine. Furthermore, any material used in the commission of the offence, including the harvested material of the protected variety, shall be liable to confiscation as provided herein. Where an offence involves a continuing violation of section 41 clause, a penalty may be levied for each day of the violation, not exceeding ten thousand rupees per day. The competent authority shall exercise due diligence in investigating such complaints.
